title: Alaska salmon: Smaller Bristol Bay sockeye mean lowest volume since 2014
content:
Across the US state of Alaska, harvesters are expected to catch some 190.1 million salmon this summer across all five species -- 269,000 Chinook, 46.6m sockeye, 124.2m pinks, 15.3m chum and 3.8m coho, the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) predicts. 

The total statewide harvest compares to a catch of 118m salmon last year -- 272,000 Chinook, 46.3m sockeye, 60.7m pinks, 8.6m chum and 2.4m coho. 

Pink salmon return to the state on distinct two-year cycles with odd-years more plentiful.

Two closely watched sockeye fisheries, Copper River, which has the distinction of being the first harvest of the summer, and the major Bristol Bay fishery, are expected to have decent seasons if ADF&G forecasts hold true. Copper River's sockeye harvest is expected to be 652,000 fish this season, compared to a lackluster 102,000 caught in 2020.

In Bristol Bay, biologists predict runs of 51.1m sockeye, which would allow for a potential total harvest of 37.4m fish. That compares to a 2020 harvest of 39.6m sockeye.

Auto updates: On
SEP 18:12 AM GMT
Smaller Bristol Bay sockeye mean lowest volume since 2014

Despite seeing sizable harvests of 40.3 million sockeye from Bristol Bay as of Aug. 28, a 1% rise from 2020 in terms of number of fish, much smaller than usual fish sizes will mean tight market conditions. 

That’s at least the conclusion of the McKinley Research Group, which produces a weekly summary of the season using data from the Alaska Department of Fish and Game.

READ MORE
AUG 3110:48 AM GMT
Scientists grapple to understand origins of chum crash

The mechanism that’s behind severely dismal chum salmon returns in western Alaska and along the US and Canadian Pacific coast isn’t yet clear. But researchers are on the case.

Alaska Public Media reported that the crash, which has closed commercial, recreational and subsistence fishing on Alaska’s Yukon River, among other areas, 

READ MORE
AUG 309:54 AM GMT
Low sockeye, pink inventories persist despite strong catches, Tradex says

Better than expected landings for Alaska sockeye and pinks have yet to overwhelm the market as demand remains strong, Canadian wholesaler Tradex Foods said.

Tradex said in its weekly “Three-minute market insight” video series that even though Alaskan sockeye harvests have topped 54 million fish, besting the pre-season forecast by some 8m, “the available sockeye that was on the market, has already sold, and very quickly”.

READ MORE
AUG 2711:23 AM GMT
OBI plant blows steam whistle as it reaches canned salmon milestone

Salmon processor OBI Seafoods blew the steam whistle at its Petersburg plant on Aug. 25, marking a production milestone of 200,000 cases of canned pink salmon.

The company, according to KTOO, last blew its steam whistle just two weeks ago when workers completed their 100,000th case of canned salmon. That production level has yet to break records for the plant but represents the result of strong pink returns to the region. 

READ MORE
AUG 251:24 PM GMT
Statewide pink harvests surpass 2019 levels

Year-to-date statewide pink harvests have now passed levels seen in 2019, the last odd-year cycle for the species, the latest data from the Alaska Department of Fish & Game (ADF&G) show.

According to a weekly summary of the salmon season compiled by the McKinley Research Group, ADF&G data show that 122.4 million pinks have been landed statewide. That compares to 109.8m pinks caught during the same period in 2019.

READ MORE
AUG 2412:39 PM GMT
Chum salmon lox recalled over listeria concerns

Seattle, Washington’s Loki Fish Company is recalling its four-ounce “Keta Salmon Lox” products overs concerns that they could be contaminated with Listeria Monocytogenes.

The US Food and Drug Administration said that the recalled product, made from chum salmon, is labeled “Wild Keta Lox” and does not carry a best by date.

READ MORE
AUG 2311:34 AM GMT
Major drug bust made in Bristol Bay fishing community

US federal and local law enforcement officials have announced the indictment of a man who reportedly attempted to ship some $220,000 worth of heroin and methamphetamine to the commercial salmon fishing hub of King Salmon, Alaska.

The US Department of Justice (DOJ) said in a press release that Naknek resident Kenneth Bruce Bishop, 61, was indicted after he reportedly arranged for an associate to fly from Anchorage to King Salmon with some 170 grams of meth and 50 grams of heroin. The drugs were detected by airport staff during a routine screening on July 28 and five days later, officials conducted a “controlled delivery” of the drugs using the post office in King Salmon, the DOJ said.

READ MORE
AUG 201:57 PM GMT
Peter Pan donates 14,600 meals in Dillingham

Peter Pan Seafoods has donated over 14,600 meals to food aid and cultural programs in the Bristol Bay community of Dillingham, the company said.

Some 500 pounds of the processor’s fish will support the Bristol Bay Food Bank, which offers community canning classes, Peter Pan said in a press release.

READ MORE
AUG 197:40 AM GMT
Chum catches beat 2020 but still below five-year average

Good news continues in many salmon fisheries across Alaska with elevated chum catches beating last year’s low returns.

READ MORE
AUG 181:11 PM GMT
Cook Inlet fishermen relocate to Bristol Bay to make a living

Several salmon fishermen in Alaska’s Cook Inlet, a region that his seen dwindling sockeye harvests, are leaving for areas with more bountiful returns such as Bristol Bay.

Alaska Public Media reported that one harvester, Taylor Evenson, made the move even though he remembers stories of Cook Inlet’s more prosperous days. 

READ MORE
AUG 1712:42 PM GMT
Bristol Bay’s sockeye bounty remains a mystery

With the Bristol Bay sockeye season largely over and more than 65 million fish returned, it’s clear that records were set this year.

What’s not yet clear is why, Alaska Public Media reported.

READ MORE
AUG 1611:53 AM GMT
Expert admits pre-season forecast for competing Russian harvest too conservative 

Salmon industry expert Vladimir Radchenko, executive director at the North Pacific Anadromous Fish Commission in Vancouver, British Columbia, says now that he was too conservative in his pre-season forecast for Russia’s landings of Pacific salmon in 2021, the Canadian seafood wholesaler Tradex reports in its latest 3-Minute Market Insight. 

Instead of the 450,000 metric tons he predicted earlier, Radchenko thinks now that Russia will land 500,000t during the current season due to strong pink salmon runs.

READ MORE
AUG 1311:17 AM GMT
Southeast pink harvests could surpass ADF&G forecast

Harvests of pink salmon in the Southeast region of the US state of Alaska are going so well that they may end up surpassing the pre-season forecast predicted by the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G).

According to KTOO, some 20 million pinks were caught in the region’s early season and fishing is far from over. 

READ MORE
AUG 1311:14 AM GMT
Southeast pink harvests could surpass ADF&G forecast

Harvests of pink salmon in the Southeast region of the US state of Alaska are going so well that they may end up surpassing the pre-season forecast predicted by the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G).

According to KTOO, some 20 million pinks were caught in the region’s early season and fishing is far from over. 

READ MORE
AUG 126:34 AM GMT
‘Wild Salmon Day’ celebrates fish’s importance

Residents of the 49th US state spent Aug. 10 celebrating Alaska Wild Salmon Day, an event designed to recognize the fish’s importance to their everyday lives and the economy.
According to KTOO, celebrations were in full swing on the Kenai Peninsula.
“You’d be very hard-pressed to throw a little river rock in this community and not hit somebody who’s deeply connected to salmon,” Branden Bornemann, executive director of the Kenai Watershed Forum, was quoted as saying.
Resident Hannah Etengoff spoke similarly. 
“To me, it really does feel spiritual,” she said. “Like, I’m connecting to the land and I’m connecting with the people who taught me how to fish and who taught me how to preserve fish. ‘Cause some of them have passed on now. And I feel like it’s just such an important way to keep them alive.”

AUG 1110:17 AM GMT
Pink catches reach 50% of pre-season forecast

Harvests of pink salmon across the US state of Alaska now number over 64.6 million fish, halfway to biologists’ 124m forecast.

A weekly summary of the salmon season produced by the McKinley Research Group using Alaska Department of Fish and Game data states that pink catches are up 10% statewide when compared to the 2019 season. Strong catches in the Arctic-Yukon-Kuskokwim region, where 261,000 pinks have been caught as of Aug. 7, and, especially, Southeast (19.7m) and Prince William Sound (35.1m) have led the increase. 

READ MORE
AUG 109:56 AM GMT
King catches stay below expectations in Southeast troll fishery

The first opener for summer king salmon catches in the Southeast Alaska troll fishery was underwhelming with only 69,000 kings being caught.

That compares to the allotment of 83,500 during the eight-day opener authorized by the Pacific Salmon Treaty that divides catches between the US and Canada, Alaska Public Media reported.

READ MORE
AUG 99:07 AM GMT
New airline plans international flights from Anchorage

A startup international airline based in Alaska’s largest city plans to soon launch flights to Asia that could offer the state’s seafood sellers another way to get their product to market.

According to the aviation news website Simple Flying, Rob McKinney of Corvus Airlines, which owns rural Alaska carrier Ravn Airlines, plans to launch flights from Anchorage to South Korea and Japan in the future. 

READ MORE
AUG 68:13 AM GMT
Invasive pike seen as threat to Southcentral salmon runs

A new study suggests that northern pike, a species that is native to northern Alaska but was later introduced to lakes and streams in the Southcentral region, is posing a risk to salmon runs there.

According to radio station KDLL, pike consume salmon fry that reduce runs in the Mat-Su Valley, Anchorage, and the Kenai Peninsula. The Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) has been looking into the problem.

READ MORE
AUG 511:07 AM GMT
Smaller sockeye mean higher costs, processing exec says

The prevalence of smaller than average sockeye in Alaska’s Bristol Bay means that processors will have to use more labor to handle an increasing number of fish.

Peter Pan Seafoods’ executive vice president of operations Jon Hickman told KDLG that because sockeye weigh much less on average — 4.5 pounds this year compared to 5.1 lbs in 2020 — they cost more to handle.

READ MORE
AUG 410:20 AM GMT
Alaska salmon harvest at 54% of 190m fish forecast

Alaska’s salmon harvest has surpassed the midpoint of its 2021 forecasted fish harvest and is already more than 10% past the year-to-date total for 2020, reports Dan Lesh, a consultant with the McKinley Research Group (formerly the McDowell Group), in Juneau.

As of Saturday (July 31), harvesters had landed about 54% of the 190 million fish they were predicted to catch throughout the season and were 5% above the five-year year-to-date average, Lesh said in his weekly email sent on behalf of the Alaska Seafood Marketing Institute.  

READ MORE
AUG 29:58 AM GMT
Russians having big season, too, and facing storage issues

Not to be outdone by reports of record sockeye catches in Bristol Bay, Alaska, the Russian salmon fishery experienced an explosive 100,000 metric tons harvested just over the past week, the Canadian wholesaler Tradex reports in its latest 3-Minute Market Insight. 

Russian officials are reportedly warning of possible shortages in cold storage capacity, as a result.   

READ MORE
JUL 3011:20 AM GMT
Multiple buyers for pinks turn Norton Sound season around 

A promising run of pink salmon has turned the summer around for fishermen in Norton Sound, with Icicle Seafoods emerging as a buyer.

A canceled chum season has been followed by a very strong pink run, reports KNOM Radio Misson.

READ MORE
JUL 294:41 AM GMT
Significant earthquake shakes Alaska coast

An 8.2-magnitude earthquake occurred some 258 miles from the salmon harvesting center of Dillingham, Alaska, late Wednesday night, June 28. The earthquake, the US Geological Survey said in a press release, had its center some 64.6 miles southeast of the community of Perryville in the Pacific Ocean south of the Alaska Peninsula. 

It had a depth of some 20.6 miles and generated a tsunami watch for the US state of Hawaii. This event was felt throughout the Alaska Peninsula and on the island of Kodiak, according to the University of Alaska – Fairbanks’ Alaska Earthquake Center.

READ MORE
JUL 2811:13 AM GMT
Pink harvests ‘especially strong’ but sizes are down

Pink salmon catches are rising across Alaska at least in terms of number of fish but average sizes appear to be down compared to prior years, data from the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) show.

The data, summarized weekly by the McKinley Research Group, show that 30,265 pinks have been caught to date, 24% of preseason productions. That represents the second week in a row 

READ MORE
JUL 2712:01 PM GMT
USDA to buy nearly 75,000 cases of canned salmon

US salmon suppliers have until Aug. 5 to send in their offers to the US Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) Agriculture Marketing Service, which is looking to buy 74,480 cases of canned salmon.

According to a bid solicitation from the USDA, the cases of canned sockeye are to be delivered to more than 40 cities across the US where they will be distributed for government food programs. In addition to school lunches, the government buys seafood for foreign and domestic food aid, among other programs.

READ MORE
JUL 269:48 AM GMT
Prince William Sound pink catches on the rise

Bristol Bay sockeye aren’t the only Alaska salmon in abundance this year. Pink salmon catches in the Prince William sound fishery have reached 16.6 million so far with wild and hatchery stocks both contributing, The Cordova Times reported.

Heather Scannell, a seine manager with the Alaska Department of Fish and Game said that the average size of pinks being harvested is 3.5 pounds. 

READ MORE
JUL 2310:27 AM GMT
Bristol Bay processors donate kings to villages where harvests were halted

Five salmon processors in Bristol Bay and freight companies have teamed up with the non-profit food bank supplier SeaShare to donate king salmon to rural Alaska villages that saw their subsistence harvests stopped due to poor returns.

According to The Cordova Times, the coordinated effort will see 25,000 pounds of kings split between two groups, the Yukon Delta Fisheries Development Association in Emmonak and the Tanana Chiefs Conference in Fairbanks. Due to very low king and chum returns, the Alaska Department of Fish and Game closed the Yukon River to all fishing earlier this year. 

READ MORE
JUL 229:58 AM GMT
Despite big sockeye landings, Tradex doesn’t see prices coming down

Sockeye salmon might be getting landed in Alaska at a pace to beat the band, but prices aren’t ticking down, reports British Columbia, Canada-based wholesaler Tradex.

As the season moves past week 28, traditionally the peak period, Alaska harvesters have already captured more than 40 million sockeye, Tradex said in its latest “3-Minute Market Insight”. That’s well ahead of the pace needed to match the 46.5m fish predicted in the preseason forecast.

READ MORE
JUL 2110:18 AM GMT
Sockeye surge means state will beat pre-season forecasts

Continued strong sockeye catches from the US state of Alaska’s Bristol Bay mean that 2021 harvests are likely to blow past 2021 pre-season expectations.

Some 45.96 million sockeye were caught statewide as of July 17, which compares to a year-over-year catch of 38.58m, according to data from the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G). The McKinley Research Group, which analyzes and summarizes the ADF&G data each week, said in its latest report that with 99% of the pre-season sockeye forecast of 46.5m caught, that number “should easily” be surpassed, at least in number of fish.

READ MORE
JUL 2011:58 AM GMT
Invasive green crabs seen as threat to Alaska salmon

Teams of volunteers and fisheries biologists are on the lookout for the spread of the European green crab, which was recently seen in British Columbia, Canada’s Haida Gwaii.

The invasive species, KTOO reported, is seen as a threat to juvenile salmon, Dungeness crab and other species in Southeast Alaska. None were seen on a recent volunteer monitoring effort in the Alaskan city of Petersburg.

READ MORE
JUL 1911:26 AM GMT
Rising runoff from Alaskan icefield to affect salmon spawning

An increase in snowmelt has led to rising runoff from glaciers in the Juneau Icefield in the US state of Alaska, which could affect where salmon spawn.

According to SitNews, the “peak runoff” from the icefield in Southeast Alaska is occurring earlier each year, researchers from the Alaska Climate Adaptation Science Center at the University of Alaska Fairbanks have found. 

READ MORE
JUL 1611:00 AM GMT
Wild salmon industry friend Murkowski has more cash than GOP rival

US senator Lisa Murkowski, an Alaskan Republican who has been an ardent supporter of the state’s wild salmon harvesting industry, ended the most recent quarter with a big cash advantage over her Republican rival Kelly Tshibaka, the Associated Press reports based on publicly available fundraising documents.

Murkowski has not yet announced whether she will be seeking re-election to a fourth six-year term in Nov. 2022, but she is likely to face an opponent in the primary who has been endorsed by former president Donald Trump.

READ MORE
JUL 158:56 AM GMT
Cook Inlet, Kenai runs slow as other areas remain strong

Sockeye salmon runs remain strong in the Alaska regions of Bristol Bay and the Alaska Peninsula but two fisheries, in particular, are lagging behind, according to the Alaska Journal of Commerce.

These are the Kenai River and Cook Inlet stocks, the publication said, citing data from the Alaska Department of Fish and Game.

READ MORE
JUL 1411:33 AM GMT
‘Very strong’ Bristol Bay run comes amid smaller fish size

The sockeye salmon run in Bristol Bay is continuing “very strong” as the pace of fishing is beginning to slow, according to a weekly summary of the season produced by the McKinley Research Group.

READ MORE
JUL 1312:24 PM GMT
NOAA to phase out Chinook production at Southeast hatchery

A hatchery in Alaska’s Southeast that’s been growing Chinook salmon for the benefit of commercial harvesters plans to phase out that aspect of its operations, radio station KTOO reported.

The research station at Little Point Walter operated by National Oceanic Atmospheric Administration Fisheries will shut down its Chinook efforts due to budgetary considerations but will continue its research focus on several salmon species.

READ MORE
JUL 1210:19 AM GMT
State, feds pledge better cooperation on Kuskokwim salmon management

Fishery management officials for the US federal government and the state of Alaska have pledged to work more closely together to avoid the regulatory confusion that’s been happening lately in the Kuskokwim salmon fishery.

According to Alaska Public Media, salmon fishermen recently complained to the state-run Kuskokwim River Salmon Management Working Group to express their dismay that while state officials had green-lit a June 28 opener for drift-netters, federal regulators said the opener was illegal. They claimed that the state didn’t have jurisdiction over the fishery. 

READ MORE
JUL 912:04 PM GMT
Alaska salmon safe from BC mines, group claims

Several mine projects in the northwest region of the Canadian province of British Columbia (BC) are safe for salmon in the US state of Alaska, a BC-based mining group claims.

Last month, US senators Lisa Murkowski and Dan Sullivan, as well as congressman Don Young, wrote to president Joe Biden’s secretary of state, Antony Blinken, asking him to continue to engage with the Canadian government over concerns that BC was not adequately requiring mines to set aside reclamation funds when projects are built. Of most concern, the lawmakers said, are BC mines that have the potential to impact transboundary waters, specifically the Stikine, Taku and Unuk rivers, shared with Alaska. 

READ MORE
JUL 810:40 AM GMT
9.6m sockeye caught last week but chum numbers still down

Alaska statewide sockeye catches continue to rise thanks to the strengthening run in Bristol Bay and continued large harvests in the Alaska Peninsula, data from the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) show.

A weekly summary of the agency’s data, written by the McKinley Research Group, takes note that 9.6 million sockeye were caught statewide in the week that ended Saturday, July 3. With 23.5m salmon, including Chinook, sockeye, pinks, chums and coho, landed as of that date, catches were at 96% of ADF&G’s pre-season projections. 

READ MORE
JUL 711:49 AM GMT
Beach erosion threatens Bristol Bay community’s set-net fishery

A beach-based set-net salmon fishery in the Bristol Bay community of Ekuk is rapidly losing its gravel, making it difficult for harvesters to access via truck.

According to radio station KTOO, the beach acts as natural infrastructure for the fishery and means that set-netters can use trucks, not a floating tender, to deliver their fish. This has typically been an advantage, although less so in recent years as more vessels have invested in chilling equipment.

READ MORE
JUL 61:42 PM GMT
State shutdown avoided, ADF&G ready for run’s peak

Staffers at the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) breathed sighs of relief last week with the evolution of an impasse between the state’s legislature and governor Mike Dunleavy. The dispute over a budget bill threatened to send some 17,000 government employees home in what would have been the state’s first-ever shutdown. 

That generated substantial uncertainty for the state’s seafood sector as even though commercial fishing is considered an essential industry, it was unclear which of ADF&G’s projects would have been allowed to continue and which would have had to close up shop.

READ MORE
JUL 511:42 AM GMT
One dead, two rescued after Bristol Bay vessel sank

Alaska State Troopers and Good Samaritan vessels responded to a report of a sinking fishing vessel in Bristol Bay on July 1 and were able to rescue two crew members.

However, the captain of F/V Pneuma, Lance Eric Norby, 45, of Arlington, Texas, was killed, Alaska Public Media reported. The sinking occurred in the south end of Nushagak Bay at around 5 a.m.

READ MORE
JUL 210:24 AM GMT
Nushagak District sees best sockeye harvest day ever

The harvest of 1,773,000 sockeye salmon on Wednesday (June 30) in the Nushagak District, one of the most productive in the US state of Alaska’s Bristol Bay, set a single-day record, reports Andy Wink, executive director of the Bristol Bay Regional Seafood Development Association.

Wink, who based his report on word received from an area biologist, said this year’s Bristol Bay sockeye harvest stands at 6.5m fish, 24% ahead of the previous five-year average through June 30.  The Bristol Bay sockeye harvest forecast for this year is 36m, he noted.

READ MORE
JUL 110:20 AM GMT
Study probes origins of Yukon River’s shrinking fish size

A recent study from researchers in the US and Canada found that climate change and increased competition in the ocean are the primary reasons that are producing smaller fish in the Yukon River, The Narwhal reported.

The study, conducted by researchers at the University of Alaska and Canada’s McGill University as well as several US agencies, found that Chinook salmon that call the Yukon home are on average 20% smaller than they were a few decades ago. Sockeye, chum and coho are getting smaller too in part because fish are maturing faster.

READ MORE
JUN 3010:31 AM GMT
Alaska lawmakers seek engagement with Canada over mines 

A trio of influential Republican lawmakers from Alaska is asking the administration of president Joe Biden to ensure that the US state’s salmon are protected from risks posed by Canadian mines.

On June 24, Senators Lisa Murkowski and Dan Sullivan, as well as Congressman Don Young, wrote to Biden’s secretary of state, Antony Blinken, asking him to continue to engage with the Canadian government over the issue. Of most concern, the lawmakers said, are mines in the province of British Columbia that have the potential to impact transboundary waters shared with Alaska. 

READ MORE
JUN 2912:18 PM GMT
Sockeye harvests to date are more than double 2020’s catches

As the sockeye salmon season picks up across Alaska sockeye salmon catches to date are more than double what they were last year at this time due to stronger showings from the Alaska Peninsula, Bristol Bay and Kodiak.

Data from the Alaska Department of Fish and Game show that statewide sockeye catches totaled 6.45 million as of June 26, which compares to 2.26m sockeye caught during the same period in 2020. The Alaska Peninsula has yielded 3.1m of this year’s catch so far, compared to 375,000 sockeye caught during the same period in 2020. And according to a weekly summary of the salmon season published by the McKinley Research Group, the numbers are set to rise further still. 

READ MORE
JUN 282:15 PM GMT
Sockeye catches pick up in Bristol Bay’s Naknek

Sockeye catches are rising in Bristol Bay, according to the latest data from the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G).

The agency said that escapement to the Naknek River, one of the nine river systems that serve Alaska’s most productive sockeye fishery, amounted to 18,000 sockeye on June 27. ADF&G has estimated total escapement for the river at 50,000 fish to date.

READ MORE
JUN 2510:22 AM GMT
Fish buyer diversifies with vegetables to supplement low returns

Several years of poor chum returns to the Yukon River have prompted Emmonak, Alaska-based Kwik’pak Fisheries to build greenhouses next to its processing plant, Alaska Public Media reported.

The company, which is the only salmon buyer in the lower Yukon employs 100 to 300 workers in season, the news organization said. But recent years of chum and coho returns encouraged the company to diversify. This year, the company will grow potatoes, carrots, lettuce, tomatoes, broccoli and peas in its greenhouses.

READ MORE
JUN 2410:37 AM GMT
Looming government shutdown threatens state’s fisheries

The Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) would have to join its fellow state agencies in shutting down on July 1 unless a budget impasse between the administration of governor Mike Dunleavy and the state legislature is resolved, KSTK reported.

The radio station said that if Alaska’s 15,000 public employees are sent home, it will also impede ADF&G from doing its job, which will delay the July 1 start of the troll fishery for Chinook salmon.

READ MORE
JUN 2310:39 AM GMT
Peninsula, Kodiak sockeye harvests mean statewide numbers are ticking up

The total number of salmon caught to date in the US state of Alaska so far this season is still lagging behind 2020 but this could change soon.

Rising harvests in the Alaska Peninsula and Kodiak regions have been big contributors to the 5.4 million salmon caught statewide as of June 19, an analysis of Alaska Department of Fish and Game data produced by the McKinley Research Group states.

READ MORE
JUN 229:39 AM GMT
Test fishery data show sockeye heading to Nushagak, Egegik

Data gathered from sockeye salmon test fishing near Port Moller in the US state of Alaska show that fish are returning to Bristol Bay’s Nushagak and Egegik river systems, according to the Alaska Department of Fish and Game. (ADF&G). 

The two river systems in the eastern part of the bay have been major contributors to sockeye returns in recent years. This year appears likely to be no different with 41%, 27.7% and 15.7% of the 175 samples taken from test fishing belonging to the Nushagak, Egegik and Wood River stocks, respectively, genetic analysis shows. 

READ MORE
JUN 209:48 PM GMT
In unusual move, Peter Pan lists early Bristol Bay price of $1.10/lb

Alaskan processor Peter Pan Seafood Co will pay $1.10 per pound as a base ex-vessel price for sockeye salmon from the US state’s Bristol Bay fishery, an announcement that it hopes will send a message to the fleet.

The public announcement, rare among large processors this early in the season, comes at a time of perceived overcapacity in the sector which has led to competition for fishing fleets’ loyalty. 

READ MORE
JUN 1810:51 AM GMT
Appeals court rules for Trout Unlimited in Pebble Mine decision lawsuit

A recent decision from the US Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals will allow the advance of a lawsuit challenging a 2019 decision by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to reverse water protections for the planned Pebble Mine near Bristol Bay, Alaska. 

The appeals court’s decision is good news for Trout Unlimited, which filed the lawsuit, and wants the EPA protections for the area authorized under the Clean Water Act to be put back in place.

READ MORE
JUN 1711:22 AM GMT
Coast Guard, Army to support Bristol Bay season with safety patrols

Inspection teams from the US Coast Guard (USCG) are being flown to Dillingham and King Salmon in Bristol Bay to carry out commercial fishing vessel exams and facility inspections ahead of the salmon season, Homeland Security Today reported.

Members of the USCG’s Marine Safety Task Force were flown to the region via a C-12J Huron aircraft piloted by the Alaska Army National Guard. Some task force members will be flown to smaller communities by members of the US Air Force Auxiliary’s Civil Air Patrol.

READ MORE
JUN 1611:50 AM GMT
McKinley: 1.2m salmon caught to date statewide

It’s still very, very early in the Alaska salmon season but 1.2 million salmon across all five species — Chinook, sockeye, pinks, chum and coho — have been caught statewide to date, which compares to a 2021 season projection of 190.1m salmon. 

Of the 1.2m, that includes 490,000 sockeye, 339,000 of which came from the Alaska Peninsula and the Aleutian Islands and 92,000 coming from Prince William Sound, primarily the Copper River District. The total catches also include 414,000 pinks from Area M, which is an 84% decline compared to the last odd-year harvest in 2019.

READ MORE
JUN 1510:48 AM GMT
E&E Foods will again buy salmon in Kuskokwim Bay

Seattle, Washington-based processor E&E Foods will for the second year in a row send a buyer up to Alaska’s Kuskokwim Bay north of Bristol Bay to buy salmon, radio station KYUK reported.

E&E will be purchasing Chinook, sockeye, chum and coho from harvesters there at prices that are to be determined, E&E Foods chief operating officer Ken Ng told the broadcaster.

READ MORE
JUN 1411:05 AM GMT
Biden reinstatement of forest’s ‘roadless rule’ could protect salmon

A change in US Forest Service policy implemented by the administration of president Joe Biden will restrict the construction of new roads in Alaska’s Tongass National Forest, which could help to protect rivers important to salmon spawning.

According to the news service Vox, the decision by the Biden administration to reinstate the “roadless rule” that was eliminated by his predecessor, Donald Trump, will protect 17,000 miles of freshwater habitat. New roads would have expanded logging within the forest.

READ MORE
JUN 1112:58 PM GMT
Tribes, harvesters, businesses call for Bristol Bay protections

Although the proposed Pebble Mine appears increasingly unlikely to be built, salmon harvesters, conservationists and others are seizing the moment to call on the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to permanently protect the area from development.

A coalition of groups calling themselves “Businesses for Bristol Bay” issued a press release on June 10 urging the administration of US president Joe Biden to direct the EPA to permanently block the mine’s development by using section 404 of the Clean Water Act. Those provisions were used previously to stall the mine under the administration of president Barack Obama but reversed when Donald Trump took office. 

READ MORE
JUN 101:30 PM GMT
Conservation easement for key road makes Pebble Mine even more unlikely

A $20 million deal that the Pedro Bay Corp., an Alaska Native corporation, struck with a non-profit group to protect land near Bristol Bay from development has made the prospect of the long-planned Pebble Mine even more unlikely.

According to the Washington Post, Pedro Bay recently sold conservation easements to the Conservation Fund for 44,000 acres that include a road the mine would need to transport its ore. The mine saw its permit application rejected by the US Army Corps of Engineers but is appealing the decision. Pedro Bay’s deal would make the mine’s development even harder.

READ MORE
JUN 912:31 PM GMT
Copper River fishing resumes after extended closure

Commercial fishing in Alaska’s Copper River District will resume Thursday, June 10 as salmon passage is picking up, the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) said.

The district’s sockeye and Chinook fishery had seen four out of the past seven openers, or fishing periods, canceled due to fears that that ADF&G’s inriver escapement goals wouldn’t be met. That is changing, the agency said.

READ MORE
JUN 89:34 AM GMT
Ocean’s Pacific salmon biomass hit 38-year low in 2020

The abundance of Pacific salmon in the ocean fell to levels last seen in 1982, according to data tracked by the North Pacific Anadromous Fish Commission (NPAFC).

The NPAFC finding, reported by the Canadian publication Business Vancouver, suggested that ocean conditions such as higher sea temperatures and lower zooplankton availability are behind the numbers.

READ MORE
JUN 79:42 AM GMT
Copper River still closed due to low returns

Biologists at the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) have closed the commercial sockeye and Chinook fishery scheduled to take place today, June 7. 

It’s the fourth opener in a row that they’ve canceled due to low fish passage. Commercial fishing in the district was last allowed on May 24. According to ADF&G, to-date harvests — 52,000 sockeye and 5,000 Chinook — for the fishery are the third-lowest for the fishery in the past 50 years. 

READ MORE
JUN 410:42 AM GMT
Icicle to buy, process pinks in Norton Sound

Icicle Seafoods will send a floating processing vessel to Alaska’s Norton Sound this season in order to process pink salmon, providing a buyer for the remote region’s fish, the Nome Nugget newspaper reported.

Icicle, which merged its processing plants last season with Ocean Beauty Seafoods to create OBI Seafoods, will also be sending four or five tender vessels to the region north of Bristol Bay to support the effort.

READ MORE
JUN 311:42 AM GMT
Copper River fishing remains closed

A sixth opener will not occur in the Copper River District today as planned due to continued low fish counts, the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) has said.

The department said June 2 that its inriver passage goal through June 1 is 148,048 salmon, but less than half of that goal, 63,585 fish have been caught on sonar. 

READ MORE
JUN 211:56 AM GMT
Copper River harvests at fourth-lowest levels in 50 years

Commercial fishing in Alaska’s Copper River District remains with harvests at their fourth-lowest levels in the past 50 years, the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) said.

The agency has canceled the last two out of the last five scheduled openers due to fish passage rates that were much lower than expected. Sonar counts through May 31 show the movement of only 54,154 salmon whereas more than twice than that, 132,531, by that date were needed to meet ADF&G’s inriver escapement goal. 

READ MORE
JUN 110:56 AM GMT
ADF&G opens salmon fishing in eastern Bristol Bay

It’s very early going still but the Alaska Department of Fish & Game (ADF&G) has officially opened up three districts in the eastern region of Bristol Bay to commercial sockeye salmon fishing.

ADF&G said in a May 31 press release that it was issuing emergency orders to open the Egegik, Ugashik and Naknek/Kvichak districts to commercial fishing on June 1. The orders apply to set and drift gillnet gear, except in the Kvichak section of the Naknek/Kvichak district, which is only open to gillnet gear.

READ MORE
MAY 319:50 AM GMT
ADF&G nixes fifth Copper River opener

The Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) canceled an opener for sockeye and Chinook salmon fishing that was planned for today, May 31, its second cancellation in a row.

ADF&G also canceled the opener that was scheduled to take place last Thursday, May 27, due to low fish passage. 

READ MORE
MAY 2810:51 AM GMT
US Army Corps: Pebble Mine appeal could take more than a year

The US Army Corps of Engineers said Thursday that it could take more than a year to weigh an appeal by the Pebble Limited Partnership (PLP) regarding its proposed building of a copper and gold mine in Alaska’s Bristol Bay region, the Associated Press reports.

The highly controversial project is believed by many to endanger the world’s largest sockeye salmon fishery. 
PLP was found to be “contrary to the public interest” and denied approval of a key permit by USACE’s Alaska District in November, AP recounted. The appeal, filed in January, is now under review by the corps’ Pacific Ocean Division, in Hawaii, and the administrative record in the case has only just been received from the Alaska District. 

READ MORE
MAY 279:14 AM GMT
ADF&G predicts lower Yukon River Chinook, chum returns

The Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) is anticipating lower returns of Chinook and chum salmon to the state’s Yukon River this year, which will reduce opportunities for commercial chum fishing.

According to KTOO, ADF&G predicts that the June Chinook returns will range between 102,000 and 189,000 fish, one of the weakest runs in recent years to a river shared by the US and Canada.

READ MORE
MAY 2610:51 AM GMT
ADF&G nixes fourth Copper River opener due to low returns

Biologists at the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) have nixed the fourth scheduled opener, or fishing period, of the season due to low fish passage.

Although commercial fishing has been closed, subsistence fishing will be allowed. 

READ MORE
MAY 252:36 PM GMT
After two openers, Copper River still underwhelms

Statistics provided after the conclusion of this season’s second opener in the Copper River District show that sockeye and Chinook salmon catches continue to underwhelm, according to the Alaska Department of Fish & Game (ADF&G). 

The department’s statistics show that 20,032 sockeye and 3,228 have caught to date. ADF&G said that 11,873 sockeye and 1,160 Chinook were caught in the second opener on May 20. A third opener was held  Monday, May 24, but catch data has not yet been reported.

READ MORE
MAY 2410:58 AM GMT
Peter Pan paying Copper River’s highest ex-vessel prices ever, it says

Peter Pan Seafoods, one of five buyers of salmon from the Copper River fishery, has said that it will pay what it says are the highest ex-vessel prices ever for sockeye and kings, $12.60 per pound and $19.60, respectively.

Peter Pan vice president of operations JonHickman announced the prices in a press release with the company saying it wants to set a “foundation for all fishermen, communities and the market”.

READ MORE
MAY 2110:01 AM GMT
Tribes, groups remain concerned about transboundary mining impacts

Several Alaska tribes and conservation groups did not have their concerns relieved about the impacts of transboundary gold mining on salmon runs after a recent inter-governmental meeting.

Four organizations said in a joint press release that the May 19 meeting of the Transboundary Bilateral Working Group (TBWG), which includes provincial British Columbian officials and representatives of the administration of Alaska governor Mike Dunleavy, showed a “lack of commitment to protect salmon rivers”.

READ MORE
MAY 2012:07 PM GMT
Second opener ongoing as ice blocks sonar use

Fishing has resumed in the Copper River District but there’s few sockeye to be had, according to the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G). 

The agency has allowed a second opener or fishing period, which began at 7 a.m., Alaska Standard Time, today. But icy conditions, which could also be affecting fish passage, have prevented ADF&G from deploying its sonar equipment on the south bank of the river. However, sonar readings from the north bank show that only 190 fish have passed through, far below the projection of 2,867 fish by this date. 

READ MORE
MAY 1912:30 PM GMT
Slow fishing but better than last year so far

The Copper River fishery opened ahead of last year’s weak season but catches thus far remain low, statistics from the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) reveal.

Some 8,000 sockeye were caught in the Monday, May 17 opener, the season’s first. That compares to 5,000 sockeye caught a year earlier and 119,000 caught in 2019, ADF&G said. The five-year average haul is 61,000 sockeye, statistics show.

READ MORE
MAY 181:24 PM GMT
Copper River opener is 2021’s first

The results aren’t yet in from the first 12-hour opener, or fishing period, that kicked off at 7 a.m. Alaska Standard Time May 17 in the Copper River District.

Some 540 independent boats are part of the king and sockeye fishery, according to the Copper River Prince William Sound Marketing Association.

READ MORE

title: Tuna 2018: Climate change to impact tropical tuna biomass in Pacific
content:
BANGKOK, Thailand -- Undercurrent News is reporting live from the Infofish Tuna 2018 conference and exhibition, held in Bangkok, Thailand, from May 28-30. 

The conference comes after a week of big news for the industry, as Chris Lischewski stood down as CEO of Bumble Bee Foods, after being indicted by the US government for his alleged involvement in a price fixing cartel. Lischewski maintains his innocence and told the company's staff, in an email seen by Undercurrent, he would fight "aggressively" to prove this. 

In the same week, Thai Union Group announced a settlement with Walmart in one of the civil lawsuits which have emanated from the Department of Justice probe of alleged price fixing in the sector. An analyst covering Thai Union said settling all the civil lawsuits alleging price fixing from tuna buyers could cost as much as $50 million. 

Auto updates: On
MAY 301:50 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Climate change to impact tropical tuna biomasses in Pacific

Scientific models predict a decrease in tropical tuna biomasses in the Pacific as well as a shift of the biomasses of tropical tuna towards the east, and towards the south for albacore, said Valerie Allain, senior fisheries scientist at the Pacific Community in New Caledonia, presenting her research on said the impact of climate change on tuna resources.

Climate change is going to have a strong impact at the national levels for coastal countries in the Pacific, Allain pointed out. The main driver of changes is the warming temperature, while ocean acidification is predicted to have a limited impact, according to Allain.

READ MORE
MAY 2911:04 PM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Maersk Line’s view on future seafood global shipping trends

Fish and seafood will remain amongst the cheapest proteins available, said Thue Barfod, global head of the fish and seafood cargo segment at Maersk Hong Kong, pointing out that the fish and seafood industry was “truly global” with cargo moving inter regional, from east to west, from south to north and between emerging and developed markets.

 The global trade of seafood moves throughout the year, extending seasonal loadings from the southern hemisphere.

READ MORE
MAY 2910:40 PM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
CO, tasteless smoke-treated tuna prices on rise

Tasteless smoke (TS) and carbon monoxide (CO) treated tuna products have risen in price in recent years (see graph below), said William Kowalski, president of the Hawaii International Seafood, analyzing new innovations, technology trends and market acceptance in the high value tuna category.

Tasteless smoke and carbon monoxide treatments lead the industry, in generating high value products in the high tuna category, Kowalski said.

READ MORE
MAY 2911:59 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Greenpeace: Ocean protection movement becoming mainstream

Ocean protection movement is rising, gaining momentum, said Oliver Knowles, senior adviser at Greenpeace. 

“There is a real sense of the moment in which ocean protection is shifting on top of the public agenda,” Knowles said, pointing that the level of public understanding around supply chain has grown substantially. 

READ MORE
MAY 299:11 AM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Thai Union’s McBain: Greenpeace ‘helped us go further in our commitments’ 

Thai Union Group’s “Sea Change” sustainability policy was launched well before the company inked an agreement with Greenpeace in July 2017. 

However, the agreement with the NGO, which targeted Thai Union globally for some time in a relentless campaign, has “helped us go further in our commitments”, said Darian McBain, the company’s director of sustainable development. 

READ MORE
MAY 298:33 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
OPAGAC claims its labor standards should be adopted for all EU tuna imports

The sustainability of tropical tuna fishing can only be achieved through decent working conditions for its fishermen, the Spanish organization of large tuna freezers (OPAGAC) said.

“This basic requirement encourages fair competition and fight against illegal fishing. The APR standard for responsible tuna fisheries should also be implemented by the European Union in its fish imports,” OPAGAC said in a press release sent to Undercurrent News.

READ MORE
MAY 298:16 AM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
FADs in top three highest-risk fishing methods for ghost gear

Fish aggregation devices (FADs) are third on the Ghost Gear Initiative’s (GGI) list of most risky gear types. 

Gillnets, traps and pots are the only two gear type groups the NGO considers to be riskier, according to Ingrid Giskes, chair of GGI, which was founded in 2015 and now counts the likes of Thai Union Group, Young’s Seafood, Tri Marine International, the World Wide Fund for Nature and UK retailer J. Sainsbury. 

READ MORE
MAY 295:39 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Walmart steps up focus on supply chain

US retailer Walmart, which is present in 28 countries, is increasing its focus on its supply chain, said Gavin Bailey, Walmart responsible sourcing, highlighting the increased demand for seafood sustainability worldwide.

Bailey pointed to some of the industry challenges, including a fragmented, layered and intermingled industry, forced labor, vulnerable workers, inter-dependency between environmental and social issues, regulation and enforcement and lack of data.

READ MORE
MAY 294:08 AM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
World purse seine group calls on RFMOs to control capacity, enforce closures 

The World Tuna Purse seine Organization (WTPO) issued a statement at the Tuna 2018 conference calling on regional fisheries management organizations (RFMOs) to get capacity under control. 

WTPO, which has over 200 purse seiner owners as members, said it is “concerned on the sustainable use of the tuna resource” and “would like to ensure the long term conservation and sustainable fishing of tuna stocks around the world”. 

READ MORE
MAY 293:55 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
DG Mare: EU mechanism to fight IUU shows positive outcomes, but all players must have a role to play

Cooperation with third countries on the EU established system of “cards”, has had tangible results, said Roberto Cesari, head of illegal, unreported, unregulated (IUU) fisheries policy at the EU directorate general for maritime affairs and fisheries (DG MARE) of the European Commission.

He pointed to 14 countries that are able to export maritime products to EU markets after positive cooperation with EU authorities.

READ MORE
MAY 293:07 AM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Tuna sales to North Africa, Middle East nosedive 

Tuna sales to North African and Middle Eastern countries plummeted in 2017. The two regions, big markets for tuna, were hit by high prices last year and also devalued currencies, as well as a tightening on credit in some countries, said Arnab Sengupta, of Phoenix Group. 

Sengupta displayed data showing Thai tuna sales to North Africa dived 42% year-on-year in 2017, to 60,832 metric tons. 

READ MORE
MAY 293:05 AM GMT
By Tom Seaman
Consultant: Thai Union’s ready-to-eat yellowfin slices would work well in Asia 

Thai Union Group’s ready-to-eat yellowfin tuna slices, which the company has launched into the US market, would be a hit in the Asian market, said Fatima Ferdouse, a seafood sector consultant. 

Ferdouse’s presentation focused on the Asian tuna market, which she said is very price sensitive. 

READ MORE
MAY 293:03 AM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Japan sees growth in farmed bluefin exports as domestic market contracts 

Japanese companies are bullish on boosting exports of fully farmed bluefin tuna, even as the country’s imports decrease and the domestic market reduces in size.

According to government information cited by Tomohiro Asakawa, a consultant focused on the seafood trade, the number of bluefin farms in Japan increased from 137 in 2011 to 175 in 2016. 

READ MORE
MAY 2811:13 PM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Latin America’s growing significance in global tuna industry

Tuna is a “big business” in Latin America, said Dario Chemerinski, senior project manager at Selecting Strategic Partners for Latin America and Asia brands, pointing out that Latin American countries consume about 15% of the world’s canned tuna. 

In 2016, the region imported 135,000 metric tons of tuna, he said, highlighting local processors produce 25% of global tuna output, led by Ecuador (see post earlier in the blog on Ecuadorean tuna production).

READ MORE
MAY 2810:59 PM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Increase in pouch, meal kit sales drive recovery in US market 

Although canned light tuna sales are down in the US, a strong increase in the sale of pouches and meal kits has driven overall market value up since the start of 2017. 

The market bottomed out in 2016, with sales of $1.81 billion. However, they recovered to $1.87bn in 2017 and are at $1.89bn for the 52 weeks to March 25, 2018, according to IRI Panel data presented by Dave Melbourne, vice president of marketing for Bumble Bee Foods. 

READ MORE
MAY 2810:25 PM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Thai tuna import, export quantities drop

The volume of Thailand’s tuna imports and exports dropped in 2017. 

However, the country — the world’s largest canned tuna producer — managed to increase its export value marginally, according to a presentation from Nat Onsri, an advisor to the Thai Tuna Industry Association. 

READ MORE
MAY 2810:24 PM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
EU canned tuna consumption up 3%

European canned tuna consumption rose to 745,592 metric tons in 2017, up 3% year-on-year, according to data from Eurostat. 

European canned production totaled 360,000t last year, accounting for almost half of the European consumption, said Juan Manuel Vieites Baptista De Sousa, president of Eurothon, an industry association.

READ MORE
MAY 2812:03 PM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Gap in figures, data quality slow WCPFC’s tuna management

The western and central Pacific is the only ocean where tuna stocks of all species, including bigeye, are currently not overfished nor subject to overfishing, said Feleti Teo, executive director at the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission (WCPFC). 

However, the gap in data and data quality slow WCPFC’s tuna management, he said.

READ MORE
MAY 2811:33 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Papua New Guinea’s rebate scheme to boost processing sector, but catchers not happy 

The rebate scheme introduced earlier this year by the Papua New Guinea’s (PNG) government, which encourages companies to land catches in the country, will improve the difficult situation of local canneries, Patrick Basa, PNG’s minister of fisheries and marine resources told Undercurrent News on the sidelines of the conference.

The rebate scheme was introduced to encourage local processing, Basa told Undercurrent, increasing employment. According to the agreement, companies fishing in PNG should land 10% of their catches in the country, but it isn’t really happening, Basa said. 

READ MORE
MAY 2811:06 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Ecuador aims to balance tuna sustainability with economic growth

The Ecuadorean government is working with the private sector to ensure the sustainability of its tuna fishery and its supply chain, said Ana Katuska Drouet Salcedo, the country’s minister of aquaculture and fisheries. 

Last year, the Ecuadorean fishing sector grew 2.6%, in line with Ecuador’s GDP growth.

READ MORE
MAY 286:12 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Korean fleet commits to ‘sustainable’ tuna fishing

The Korean tuna fleet is aiming for sustainable tuna fishing, said Sancho Kim, operation and sales manager at large Korean fishing firm Silla. 

The fleet has achieved some international certifications for some of its branded canned products, such as Marine Stewardship Council or Friend of the Sea. 

READ MORE
MAY 284:45 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Tuna industry efforts to comply with UN’s sustainable development goals

No tuna company has yet registered a plan with the United Nation (UN)’s ocean commitment page, in the work towards the UN Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) number 14, said Marcelo Hidalgo, consultant at Seafoodmatter.

The SDG number 14, which is part of the UN’s 2030 agenda, focuses on conservation of the oceans, seas and marine resources. 

READ MORE
MAY 284:04 AM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
IOTC exec teases new management measures 

“Hot of the press” after the group’s meeting last week in Bangkok, the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC) has a plan on new management measures. 

However, Christopher O’Brien, executive secretary of the IOTC, didn’t have many details available to present. 

READ MORE
MAY 283:54 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Spain, Seychelles-flagged tuna vessels slow catches in Indian Ocean to avoid meeting quota ‘too early’

Some tuna fishing companies active in the Indian Ocean are in the process of reducing their activity, in order to distribute their yellowfin quota until the end of the year, sources told Undercurrent News.

Some companies have already begun ceasing vessel activity and will do the same on more, including Spanish and Seychelles-flagged purse seiners. “And it won’t be the only closure,” one industry source told Undercurrent on the side of the conference.

READ MORE
MAY 283:29 AM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Further increase in tuna catches would be unhealthy, says FAO exec 

Audun Lem, of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), presented a chart displaying the dramatic increase in tuna catches globally. 

It would be “unhealthy if this continues”, he said. 

READ MORE
MAY 282:11 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
IATTC: Increase in capacity challenges sustainable development of ETP fishery 

Since 1961, fishing capacity in the Eastern tropical Pacific (ETP), or Eastern Pacific Ocean (EPO), has increased sharply, which poses an issue for management of tuna stocks in the region, said Guillermo Compean, director of the Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission (IATTC).

Meanwhile, the overall number of fishing sets in the region has decreased. However, the number of active fishing aggregating devices has sharply increased. 

READ MORE
MAY 281:29 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
ISSF’s five-year strategic plan to speed up efforts ‘towards a sustainable tuna industry’

The International Seafood Sustainability Foundation (ISSF) is putting its efforts across every key area at the regional fisheries management organization level, including harvest control, stock health, monitoring control and surveillance, said Susan Jackson, president of the ISSF.

Earlier this year, ISSF launched its 2018-2022 five-year strategic plan to improve the long-term sustainability of global tuna stocks.

READ MORE
MAY 281:01 AM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
FAO’s Lem: Policy makers ignore size of fish trade 

The global seafood trade is worth about the same amount as beef, pork and chicken combined, according to Audun Lem, of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. 

Global fish trade was worth $175.2 billion in 2017, up 2.5% year-on-year. According to Lem, this figure is set to increase in 2018, then again in 2019 and 2020. 

READ MORE
MAY 2812:54 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Bolton to source all tuna from MSC, ‘robust’ FIPs by 2024

Italian tuna giant Bolton Group plans to source 100% of its tuna products from raw material certified by the Marine Stewardship Council or from fishing companies taking part in a “robust” fishery improvement project by 2024, said Luciano Pirovano, sustainable development director at Bolton Food.

“As a market leader in the tuna industry it is our duty to become a point of reference in sustainability efforts,” said Pirovano, who is also chairman of the International Seafood Sustainability Foundation.

READ MORE
MAY 2812:11 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Thailand, Ecuador maintain leadership in world’s tuna exports

Thailand and Ecuador were the world’s two largest tuna exporters in 2017. 

In 2017, Thailand exported a total of 485,500 metric tons of tuna, while Ecuador exported a total of 218,100t, according to figures quoted by Patrick Basa, Papua New Guinea’s minister of fisheries and marine resources. 

READ MORE
MAY 2711:03 PM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Braving challenges: Towards a traceable, sustainable tuna industry

New technologies will play a pivotal role in documenting traceability in the tuna industry going forward, although the vast size of fishing zones and complexity of the supply chain remain a challenge, said Transform Aqorau, international fisheries law consultant from the Solomon Islands and chairman of the conference. 

Launching the event, Agorau pointed to the complexity of fisheries management, when total allowable catch is reached in one species but not in the others. 

READ MORE
MAY 2710:46 PM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
New president for FCF 

Fong Chun Formosa Fishery Company (FCF) has a new president, Max Chou. 

Chou took over the president role at the start of May, having previously been executive vice president for “about a year before that”, he told Undercurrent News. 

READ MORE
MAY 2710:35 PM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Greenpeace’s Taiwan human rights abuse allegations based on ‘old information’, says FCF president 

A Greenpeace report alleging labor abuses from Taiwan’s longline fleet, which the NGO then links to trading giant Fong Chun Formosa Fishery Company (FCF), relies on “old” information, the new FCF president said. 

In a statement, Max Chou,  now president of FCF, said Greenpeace report (see the document here) is misleading. 

READ MORE

title: Danfish 2015 blog: Another zero-season in Peru will see prices soar again, says TripleNine CEO
content:
Undercurrent News is reporting live from Danfish, Denmark's fishing equipment and technology show in Aalborg, which is expected to attract some 15,000 visitors this year.

Exhibitors from more than 25 countries are thought to be filling the space of the Aalborg Kongres & Kultur Center, which in 2015 is expanding over the 9,000 square meters it reached last year thanks to a mobile extension to the center.

This year sees Denmark's pelagics sector in a positive place, with prices for herring, mackerel, sand eel and sprat all fairly strong, the latter two buoyed by the demand for fishmeal.

Whitefish continues to be important to Danish fishers, with 2015 a particularly good year for plaice.

Auto updates: On
OCT 94:25 AM GMT
Havfisk’s Gadus Poseidon testing new noise measurement tech

Norwegian fishing firm Havfisk is currently testing a new technology by Scanmar, which produces sonar and other fishing equipment.

This latest is a new noise measurement device, designed to tell vessel owners how much noise their boat makes under water, how it effects fish, and what they can do about it.

READ MORE
OCT 93:49 AM GMT
New TripleNine CEO: Another zero-season in Peru will see prices soar again

If Peru announces another zero-quota season two for its anchovy fishing — as recent reports seem to indictae it will — fishmeal and oil prices are likely to follow the same pattern they did last year.

This was acording to the new CEO of Danish fishmeal producer TripleNine Group, Peter Jensen.

READ MORE
OCT 93:20 AM GMT
Canadian trawler modernizes with shrimp cooking gear

Exhibiting at Danfish, processing equipment manufacturer Intech International has a variety of on-board machines for coldwater shrimp fishing.

Two of those on show, a grader and a cooker, have been bought up by Canadian firm Frandan, which will put the machines on a new build vessel, currently under construction Intech managing director Leif Andersen told Undercurrent News. 

READ MORE
OCT 810:07 AM GMT
Scotland’s Lunar Fishing invests £45m in replacement vessels

Scottish pelagic fishing firm Lunar Fishing has two replacement vessels in the works, currently being constructed at Danish shipyard Karstensens.

The new builds – Pathway and Kings Cross – will replace existing vessels owned by Lunar under these names. The price indication given by the Danish yard is £22.4 million apiece.

READ MORE
OCT 810:03 AM GMT
Norwegian shipyard Stadyard now fishing with own vessel

Norwegian shipyard Stadyard has begun fishing with its own new build, which it completed in February this year, managing director Agnar Lyng told Undercurrent News.


The MS Torbas – a combined purse seiner and pelagic trawler, just under 70 meters in length – is capable of a rapid 20 knots for steaming, and can also travel very efficiently while fishing, said Lyng.

READ MORE
OCT 86:03 AM GMT
Turkish shipyard’s expansion to be completed next year

Cemre Shipyard is aiming to have completed its expansion — which will roughly double it in size — by the end of 2016.

“It’s been a huge investment,” commercial manager Sinan Kavala told Undercurrent News. “It might be finished by mid-2016, or the end of the year. It’s been such a big investment that we are staging it to coincide with our builds.”

READ MORE
OCT 85:43 AM GMT
Cemre close to delivering first of four new Samherji vessels

Turkish shipyard Cemre is soon to deliver the first of four new wetfish trawlers ordered by Icelandic fishing firm Samherji, commercial manager Sinan Kavala told Undercurrent News.

READ MORE
OCT 85:29 AM GMT
Baltic cod sector in decline as fishermen opt out

Many fishermen are opting to retire in the Baltic region, as the fishing becomes increasingly difficult, acording to Gunnar Asplund, owner of Swedish shipbroker Eos.

“The cod fishing for Sweden, Finland, Denmark, Estonia and that region is bad,” he told Undercurrent News. “For five years now, prices have been low. It’s not attractive — we see many vessels for sale and no buyers.”

READ MORE
OCT 74:00 PM GMT
African nations continue to come in for pelagic trawlers

West African countries are buying a number of refrigerated sea water (RSW), purse seine pelagic vessels, Ture Korsager, managing director of shipbroker Atlantic Shipping, told Undercurrent News.

This was a trend he noted at Iceland’s Icefish show in September 2014, and one that he feels has strengthened.

READ MORE
OCT 73:46 PM GMT
Shipbroker: Strong prices drive interest in shrimp-catching vessels

With coldwater shrimp prices as high as they are, shipbroker Atlantic Shipping has seen stronger interest in acquiring freezer trawlers suitable for catching shrimp as the primary species, rather than just as bycatch.

The company has seen this interest in Russia, Canada and Norway, said its managing director, Ture Korsager.

READ MORE
OCT 73:20 PM GMT
Tech firm contributing to Norwegian factory trawler

Danish processing equipment company Carsoe is producing a combination coldwater shrimp and pelagic, on-board factory for a new Norwegian trawler, a sales manager told Undercurrent News.

Though he declined to name which company the new build would be operated by, Jeppe Christensen did say it was currently under construction at a Turkish shipyard.

READ MORE
OCT 71:51 PM GMT
Danish shipyard pinpoints pelagics as the modernizing sector

Danish shipyard Karstensens Skibsvaerft identified the pelagic sector — all around the North Sea — as the one seeing the most activity in terms of vessel new builds.

“Anywhere there’s pelagic industry, right now we see interest in replacing older vessels with new,” Knud Degn Karstensen told Undercurrent News. “Denmark, Sweden, Scotland, Shetland, Ireland…”

READ MORE
OCT 78:59 AM GMT
Fuel adaptions a key investment for Danish fishermen

Danish bank Vestjysk Bank is seeing a shift in the mentality of fishermen from one of saving their money, to one of spending to modernize.

The owners of whitefish trawlers in particular have, in recent years, largely been putting money aside to invest later, Jorgen Eriksen told Undercurrent News. But lately there has been more investment — including that aided by loaning from his bank — in modernizing of older vessels.

READ MORE
OCT 76:44 AM GMT
Riga shipyard seeing Irish, Scottish interest in pelagic trawlers

Latvian firm Riga Shipyard has seen good interest in pelagic trawlers lately, according to its general manager for shipbuilding, Gennady Slyozkin.

The 102-year-old company carries out repairs and new builds for a range of industries, including fishing and wellboats for aquaculture.

READ MORE
OCT 76:27 AM GMT
Skagerak Pelagic targets 75,000t production by year end

It has been a strong year for Danish pelagic processors Skagerak Pelagic, which has already produced 60,000 metric tons of herring so far, Henning Jensen, purchasing manager for raw materials, told Undercurrent News.

The hope is for 10- 15,000t more by year-end, much of which (60- 70%) goes to high value markets in Holland and Germany.

READ MORE

title: Congress Acts to Stop Seafood Fraud, Following Oceana’s Nationwide Investigation
content:
Oceana, the largest international advocacy group working solely to protect the world’s oceans, applauds United States Representative Edward Markey (D-MA) today for introducing the Safety and Fraud Enforcement for Seafood (SAFE Seafood) Act to address the growing problem of seafood fraud, which can come in many different forms – from mislabeling fish and falsifying documents, to adding too much ice to packaging. If passed, this bill would help stop seafood fraud by requiring full traceability of all seafood sold in the U.S., from boat to plate.

This legislation follows the release of a new Oceana study, which found that one-third, or 33 percent, of the 1,215 fish samples it collected from 674 retail outlets in 21 states were mislabeled, according to U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) guidelines. Oceana campaign director Beth Lowell released the following statement of support for the SAFE Seafood Act:

 

“Seafood fraud is a national problem that requires federal attention. Rep. Markey should be applauded for his swift action to stop seafood fraud in the U.S.

Seafood fraud not only cheats consumers, but it also hurts honest fishermen and seafood businesses along the supply chain. Oceana is calling on Congress to pass the SAFE Seafood Act to ensure that the seafood sold in the U.S. is safe, legally caught and honestly labeled. 

Americans deserve to know more about the seafood they purchase, including the species name, where, when, and how it was caught, if it was farmed or previously frozen, and if any additives were used during processing.

By requiring fish to be tracked from boat to plate, the SAFE Seafood Act will protect our wallets, our health and our oceans.”

 

Rep. Markey was joined in the legislation by original co-sponsors Walter Jones (R-NC), John Tierney (D-MA), Bill Keating (D-MA), Lois Capps (D-CA) and Jo Bonner (R-AL).

Senator Mark Begich (D-AK) is expected to introduce a companion bill in the Senate in the coming days.

To access Oceana’s national seafood study, please visit www.oceana.org/fraudnationwide.

title: Oceana Investigation Finds Widespread Seafood Mislabeling in L.A.
content:
Oceana, the largest international advocacy group working solely to protect the world’s oceans, found widespread seafood mislabeling in the Los Angeles-area, according to a new report released today. DNA testing confirms that more than half (55 percent) of the seafood sampled by Oceana was mislabeled based on federal law.

“It is disheartening to know that consumers are not getting wait they pay for,” said Beth Lowell, campaign director at Oceana. “Seafood fraud is not only ripping off consumers, but it is putting their health at risk and undermining their efforts to eat sustainably.”

In May and December of 2011, Oceana staff and supporters collected 119 seafood samples from grocery stores, restaurants and sushi venues in Los Angeles and Orange counties. The targeted species included those that were found to be mislabeled in previous studies as well as those with regional significance such as wild salmon, Dover or other regional soles, red snapper, yellowtail and white tuna. 

Among the report’s other key findings include:

Fraud was detected in 11 out of 18 different types of fish purchased.
Every single fish sold with the word “snapper” in the label (34 out of 34) was mislabeled, according to federal guidelines.
Nearly nine out of every ten sushi samples was mislabeled.
Eight out of nine sushi samples labeled as “white tuna” were actually escolar, a species that carries a health warning for it purgative effects.

“Consumers are being asked to guess what they are eating,” said Dr. Kimberly Warner, senior scientist at Oceana. “The public should be provided with more information about the food they are purchasing. With such high levels of mislabeling, it is more important than ever for the government to increase inspections and require traceability of our seafood.”

Earlier this year, California State Senator Ted W. Lieu (D-Torrance) introduced legislation (SB 1486), sponsored by Oceana, that would require large restaurant chains to accurately label their seafood by species, country of origin and whether it is farmed or wild.

“The extent of seafood fraud found in California should be shocking to consumers, especially those that are paying extra for seafood they think is healthier and more sustainable,” said Geoff Shester, California program director at Oceana. “If enacted, this bill would provide a powerful first step to help turn the tide on seafood fraud.”

In late-October of 2011, Oceana also found mislabeling of nearly one in five fish fillets sampled in Boston-area supermarkets.

About Seafood Fraud

Oceana launched a new campaign in May of 2011 to stop seafood fraud, which can come in many different forms – from mislabeling fish and falsifying documents to adding too much ice to packaging.

In a recent report entitled Bait and Switch: How Seafood Fraud Hurts Our Oceans, Our Wallets and Our Health, Oceana found that while 84 percent of the seafood eaten in the United States is imported, only two percent is currently inspected and less than 0.001 percent specifically for fraud. In fact, recent studies have found that seafood may be mislabeled as often as 25 to 70 percent of the time for fish like red snapper, wild salmon and Atlantic cod, disguising species that are less desirable, cheaper or more readily available.

Despite growing concern about where our food comes from, consumers are frequently served the wrong fish – a completely different species than the one they paid for. With about 1,700 different species of seafood from all over the world now available in the U.S., it is unrealistic to expect consumers to be able to independently and accurately determine what fish is really being served.

Our seafood is following an increasingly complex path from fishing vessel to processor to distributor and ultimately our plates. Seafood safety is handled by a patchwork of laws with no federal agency definitively in charge of addressing seafood fraud. Little coordination or information sharing exists within the U.S. government and many of these laws are not being fully implemented.  

Oceana is calling on the federal government to make combating seafood fraud a priority, including implementing existing laws, increasing inspections, and improving coordination and information sharing among federal agencies. Oceana is also working to ensure that the seafood sold in the U.S. is safe, legal and honestly labeled, including requiring a traceability system where information such as when, where, and how a fish is caught follows it throughout the supply chain – from boat to plate – allowing consumers to make more informed decisions about the food they eat while keeping illegal fish out of the U.S. market.

For more information about seafood fraud and Oceana’s new campaign, please visit www.oceana.org/fraud.

title: Ethics and Accountability
content:
Code of Ethics

Around the world, Oceana is helping to protect and restore the oceans, in partnership with allies and communities. Oceana has set out in a Code of Ethics how we expect our staff to meet high standards of integrity, respect, and inclusivity in achieving our mission and safeguarding the contributions of our donors and supporters.

You can find relevant excerpts from our Code of Ethics here.

Internal Accountability, Whistleblower Policy, and Anti-Retaliation Policy

Oceana has taken several steps to ensure accountability with our standards of conduct.

A staff member who has experienced, observed, or learned about conduct they believe is contrary to Oceana’s polices or Code of Ethics must report it. Oceana has provided multiple ways to make such a report. Our Code of Conduct identifies specific staff to whom reports should be made. Alternatively, reports from staff members may be made through EthicsPoint, a third-party compliance company through which Oceana has arranged that reports may be made confidentially in writing or by telephone, in English or in local languages. To ensure that accountability extends to all staff including senior leadership, reports through EthicsPoint that implicate senior leaders are routed directly to Oceana’s Board of Directors.

When an employee reports a violation of this Code, Oceana will investigate and take action to correct violations. Employees are protected from retaliation for either reporting a violation or participating in an investigation. Any person found to have retaliated against an individual for reporting violations or participating in an investigation of allegations will be subject to appropriate disciplinary action.
