title: 20-Year Ocean Advocate and Award-Winning Actor Ted Danson to Testify before Congress about Chief Threats of Offshore Drilling
content:
Ted Danson, award-winning actor, longtime ocean advocate and Oceana board member, will testify before the House Committe on Natural Resources about the “Environmental and Commercial Perspectives on Offshore Drilling” Wednesday morning, February 11. In his testimony, Danson will describe the chief threats of offshore drilling, including the impacts of the approximately 120 million gallons of oil that are discharged into the world’s oceans each year.

Among the topics he will present to the Committee:

Threats posed by offshore drilling, including spills, leaks and other forms of pollution
Impacts of offshore drilling on marine wildlife, ocean ecosystems and our climate
Importance of switching from a dependence on fossil fuels to a focus on renewables such as offshore wind
Need to quickly reinstate the moratorium on offshore drilling
Urgency of stopping the expansion of oil and gas activities in the Arctic Ocean

For more than 20 years, Danson has worked to protect the oceans. Danson co-founded the American Oceans Campaign (AOC), which merged with other groups in 2001 to form Oceana, the largest international organization focused solely on protecting and restoring the world’s oceans.

WHO: Ted Danson, award-winning actor, longtime ocean advocate and Oceana board member

WHAT: Environmental and Commercial Perspectives on Offshore Drilling Hearing, House Natural Resources Committee, led by Chairman Nick J. Rahall (D-WV)

WHEN: Wednesday, February 11, 2009
9:45 a.m. press scrum in hallway outside hearing room
10 a.m. Danson’s testimony

WHERE: Longworth House Office Building
Room 1324

For more information about the hearing, please click here. To learn more about Oceana, please visit www.oceana.org.

title: Ted Danson Urges Congress to Reinstate the Offshore Drilling Moratorium
content:
Ted Danson, award-winning actor, longtime ocean advocate and Oceana board member, urged the U.S. House Committee on Natural Resources today to protect our oceans and climate from the threats of offshore drilling. In his testimony, Danson called on Congress to quickly reinstate the moratorium on offshore drilling, which was allowed to lapse in 2008.

“Oil and water simply don’t mix,” said Danson. “While not intentional, oil spills do happen and they harm everything from the smallest ocean organisms to the largest predators in the sea.”

Danson appealed to the Committee, led by Chairman Nick J. Rahall (D-WV), that the threats facing the Arctic Ocean will demand a separate and distinct planning process and that we should stop offshore oil and gas activities in the region until there is a comprehensive science-based conservation and energy plan.

Danson reported that approximately 120 million gallons of oil are discharged into the world’s oceans each year from platforms, marine transportation, vessel discharges and accidents. “Offshore drilling only looks good from an oil executive’s office,” added Danson.

Offshore oil drilling will have little if any impact on gas prices. Danson cited figures from the U.S. Energy Information Agency which show that even at peak production, increased drilling offshore would produce less than one percent of the current energy demand in the U.S. “This is merely pennies at the gas pump,” said Danson.

Danson also stressed the importance of a speedy transition from fossil fuels to renewable, clean and carbon-free energy, such as offshore wind and solar power. According to recent estimates, the offshore wind industry could generate nearly $950 billion in economic activity and more than 250,000 jobs over the next 20 years. [i]

“We need to work with the oceans, not against them,” said Dr. Michael Hirshfield, senior vice president for North America and chief scientist at Oceana. “The oceans can be a valuable resource in facing the global warming and energy crisis’.”

For more than 20 years, Danson has worked to protect the oceans. Danson co-founded the American Oceans Campaign (AOC), which merged in 2001 with Oceana, the largest international organization focused solely on protecting and restoring the world’s oceans.

Oceana, along with a diverse coalition of conservation organizations, recently called on President Obama and the 111th Congress to reinstate the offshore drilling moratorium and establish a rational policy for protecting our oceans and coasts from the impacts of offshore drilling for oil and gas.

[i] Rigas, Nicholas (2008). “An Offshore Wind Power Industrial Cluster for South Carolina.” [http://api.ning.com/files/785CrAzQ1nZRgkZIjhb7jRyCqZph3EbbS0fgTUcliTW73I8HriD9obiFsEIEwY3mBYUqotXCCovURI*IXGp4owHrQFn266r0/CharlestonSCOffshoreWindInstrustrialHubWhitePaper.pdf]. Accessed 2/3/09.

title: Congress Acts to Eliminate Mercury from Chlorine Plants
content:
Following the Obama Administration’s international statement about the need to control mercury, a bill that would phase-out the use of mercury in chlorine production, was reintroduced in the House of Representatives.  This mercury bill was originally authored by President Obama while serving as senator of Illinois.

The bill, H.R. 2065, would require the remaining four chlorine factories that use a mercury production process to stop doing so within two years of passage.  The use of mercury-based technology by these plants causes the release of the toxic chemical into air and water, as well as contamination of the chlorine plants’ products, especially chlorine’s co-product, caustic soda.

While 95 percent of chlorine produced in the United States uses a mercury-free process, four U.S. plants have continued to use an outdated mercury-dependent approach that releases the contaminant into the air and water surrounding the plant.

This contamination is entirely unnecessary because modern methods for chlorine production have been available for decades and are mercury-free. Lead bill sponsor Rep. Jan Schakowsky (D-IL) has garnered support from many of her colleagues for the bill.

“More than 100 facilities have already switched to mercury-free technology,” said Congresswoman Schakowsky. “Switching to cleaner membrane-cell technology improves chlorine plant operating efficiencies, creates higher profits and saves jobs. These benefits, along with reduced mercury pollution in the plant communities, are a win-win outcome for the companies and public health,” she added.

These four plants have failed to make investments in clean technology that would help them become more competitive in their industry.  Modernizing these plants with cleaner technology would help make them more efficient over the long-term and save local jobs.

“Failing to keep pace with their competitors puts jobs at risk at these four chlor-alkali plants,” said Jacqueline Savitz, senior pollution campaign director for Oceana. “But modernizing protects jobs, saves money and prevents mercury pollution,” she added.
For example, the Olin Corporation plant in Augusta, GA could save an estimated $17.6 million in energy costs alone over five years, according to Oceana’s calculations.

While coal-fired power plants remain the leading source of mercury pollution, these chlorine factories release more mercury than the average coal-fired plant, making them top emitters in their states. For example, the Olin Corporation facility in Tennessee has historically been the number one source of mercury pollution in the state, and the plant has impaired the river on which it’s located, according to local environmental officials.  The PPG Industries facility in West Virginia has failed to comply with mercury discharge limits in recent months, and the Olin facility in Augusta, Georgia has contaminated a canal on the Savannah River so badly that the state of Georgia has required the company to clean it up.

Mercury use in these plants also contributes to mercury contamination of caustic soda, a chlorine co-product which is frequently used to make high-fructose corn syrup and other food items. Recently, traces of mercury have been found in common food items, such as chocolate syrup and soft drinks. Using mercury-free technology would reduce the risk of further food contamination.

title: Oceana Praises President Obama for Protecting Oceans
content:
President Obama signaled today that protecting and conserving our oceans is a major goal for his Administration.

The President issued a Memorandum to federal agencies, paving a path for achieving comprehensive ocean conservation and management. 

Our oceans are currently managed by 140 laws, implemented by 20 federal agencies, without a unifying vision.  President Obama’s actions today will guide the process to improve coordination between federal, state and tribal governments to protect our oceans.

“Oceana applauds President Obama’s strong action to protect our oceans today.  With the oceans facing the triple threats of overfishing, pollution and climate change, they need attention at the highest levels of government.  We are committed to working with the Administration to ensure that the strongest possible ocean policy is developed,” said Andy Sharpless, CEO of Oceana. 

The Memorandum issued by President Obama calls for an interagency task force led by the Council on Environmental Quality to protect, maintain and restore marine ecosystems by creating a national ocean policy.  It also identifies the steps needed to implement that goal.  Additionally, the task force is charged with developing science-based, comprehensive ocean ecosystem planning to balance competing uses of our oceans.  President Obama also proclaimed June 2009 to be “National Oceans Month.”  He called on all Americans to learn more about the oceans and what can be done to save them.

Oceana thanks President Obama for taking this important step and looks forward to working with the President and the Administration as this process moves forward.

title: Peru passes important ocean protection law to protect the first five nautical miles at sea
content:
Peru has just achieved an important victory in the protection of the five nautical miles along its coasts. The approval of the law recognizing ancestral and artisanal fishing is a historic milestone that guarantees the protection of this zone, benefiting over 50,000 artisanal fishermen who provide 80% of the fish that feeds the Peruvian population.

It is worth noting that the first five nautical miles play a fundamental role in the life cycle of marine species inhabiting the Peruvian sea and are highly productive. These waters host the main upwelling systems in the ocean, providing vital nutrients for the reproduction and growth of the hydrobiological resources that sustain Peruvian fishing. Protecting this area is essential to preserve the abundance of our fishing resources and guarantee the employment of hundreds of thousands of Peruvians.

The law recognizes the first five nautical miles adjacent to the Peruvian coast as a protection zone and establishes the following measures:

Prohibits large-scale fishing within the 5-mile area, without exceptions (this prohibition existed only at the regulatory level and was subject to exceptions).
Prohibits mechanized purse-seiners of any size in the first 3 miles.
Orders the fishing authority to approve a list of the fishing gear that will be allowed in the area, which must exclude any gear harmful to the habitat.

The law also establishes a new classification for commercial fishing, which differentiates artisanal fishing (with a predominance of manual work), from small-scale fishing (with medium-sized boats that use mechanized fishing gear). This will make it possible to design differentiated management measures for both fleets, according to their fishing power and impact on the ecosystem.

Finally, the law also includes the express mandate for the fishing quotas to be established respecting biological reference points that ensure sustainability and that must be defined by the scientific authority. In addition, it orders to take measures to recover overexploited species.

This victory would not have been possible without the active participation of the artisanal fishermen themselves. They were the main spokespeople in this campaign and were even welcomed into the legislative chamber to witness the historic vote that ended in the unanimous approval of the law.

With this new law, Peru has taken a major step towards the protection of the five nautical miles, ensuring the food and employment of millions of people.

Oceana is the largest international advocacy organization dedicated solely to ocean conservation. Oceana is rebuilding abundant and biodiverse oceans by winning science-based policies in countries that control one-quarter of the world’s wild fish catch. With more than 275 victories that stop overfishing, habitat destruction, oil and plastic pollution, and the killing of threatened species like turtles, whales, and sharks, Oceana’s campaigns are delivering results. A restored ocean means that 1 billion people can enjoy a healthy seafood meal every day, forever. Together, we can save the oceans and help feed the world.

title: Oceana Calls on Gov. Jindal to Enforce TEDs on LA Shrimp Boats
content:
WASHINGTON- As the international sea turtle community gathers in New Orleans this week for the 34th Annual International Symposium on Sea Turtle Biology and Conservation, Oceana sent a letter today to Louisiana Gov. Bobby Jindal urging him to reverse a state law that leaves thousands of sea turtles unnecessarily vulnerable to drowning in shrimp trawls every year off the Louisiana coast.

Federal law requires most shrimp trawlers to use Turtle Excluder Devices (TEDs), which create an opening in trawl nets to allow trapped sea turtles to escape. Louisiana is the only state that refuses to enforce this federal law, which is designed to protect threatened and endangered species. Louisiana is a major player in the Southeast Shrimp Trawl Fishery and likely has a significant impact on sea turtle mortality.

Oceana’s letter also comes a week after the Louisiana Shrimp Task Force voted in favor of reversing the state law and allowing officials to enforce the use of TEDs, partly to help improve the conservation rating of Louisiana shrimp. Louisiana is currently the only state that is “red-listed” on the popular Monterey Bay Aquarium Seafood Guide.

In March, Oceana released the report “Wasted Catch: Unsolved Problems in U.S. Fisheries,” which identified nine of the worst bycatch fisheries in the U.S. The Southeast Shrimp Trawl Fishery, which includes fishermen operating off the coast of Louisiana, was named as one of the most wasteful, throwing out almost two-thirds of what they catch and killing more than 50,000 sea turtles every year.

Excerpt from the letter:

“As the largest international advocacy group working solely to protect the world’s oceans, Oceana firmly believes that maintaining healthy oceans pays dividends for future generations and is important to the livelihoods of fishermen and the communities in which they live. Our concern is that Louisiana’s law prohibiting the enforcement of regulations requiring Turtle Excluder Devices (TEDs) in shrimp trawls unnecessarily threatens sea turtles. This technology is required by federal regulations because it has been scientifically proven to reduce sea turtle deaths, does not reduce shrimp yield, and has even been shown to improve the quality of the catch.”

In the letter sent today, Oceana offers to meet with Louisiana officials to offer scientific expertise verifying that TEDs have been proven effective at reducing sea turtle mortality by 97 percent, as well as to alleviate any concerns or issues state officials may have, in order to improve the fishery.

To learn more about Oceana’s work protecting sea turtles, please click here.

 

-30-

 

Oceana is the largest international advocacy group working solely to protect the world’s oceans. Oceana wins policy victories for the oceans using science-based campaigns. Since 2001, we have protected over 1.2 million square miles of ocean and innumerable sea turtles, sharks, dolphins and other sea creatures. More than 600,000 supporters have already joined Oceana. Global in scope, Oceana has offices in North, South and Central America and Europe. To learn more, please visit www.oceana.org.

title: Groups File First Environmental Lawsuit Vs. New Trump Administration, Challenging Illegal Order to Undo Ocean Protections from Offshore Drilling
content:
Today, groups concerned about the threats from offshore drilling filed the first environmental legal challenge against the new Trump administration. One group is challenging an illegal order by President Trump to revoke former President Biden’s withdrawal of vulnerable areas of the ocean from future oil-and-gas leasing. Another set of groups is taking a related action asking a court to reinstate a federal court ruling that invalidated an attempt by the first Trump administration to undo Obama-era offshore protections. President Trump has attempted to open nearly the entire Arctic Ocean to drilling by reviving his first-term order.

President Biden protected areas off the Eastern Gulf, Atlantic, Pacific, and Alaska coasts by invoking his authority under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act. The law authorizes the president to withdraw offshore areas from oil and gas leasing, as eight administrations, including the first Trump administration, have routinely done. However, the law does not authorize the president to revoke the withdrawals of prior presidents, which a federal court confirmed when Trump attempted to undo Obama-era protections for the Arctic Ocean and portions of the Atlantic oceans during his first term.

In the new case, Earthjustice is representing Oceana, Center for Biological Diversity, the Surfrider Foundation, Greenpeace, Healthy Gulf, Northern Alaska Environmental Center, Alaska Wilderness League, and Turtle Island Restoration Network. Plaintiffs Sierra Club and the Natural Resources Defense Council are each representing themselves.

The plaintiffs in the related litigation to reinstate protections for the Arctic and parts of the Atlantic include League of Conservation Voters, Defenders of Wildlife, Natural Resources Defense Council, Sierra Club, Center for Biological Diversity, Northern Alaska Environmental Center, Greenpeace, and Alaska Wilderness League. These groups are represented by Earthjustice and Natural Resources Defense Council.

“President Trump’s executive order would roll back millions of acres of ocean protection, jeopardizing our coastal economies and the people who rely on healthy, thriving oceans,” said Oceana Campaign Director Joseph Gordon. “Leaders in both political parties, thousands of businesses, and millions of Americans support permanently protecting our coasts from offshore drilling. We are confident the court will continue to uphold the bipartisan tradition of presidents safeguarding these coastlines and protecting the people who live and work among them.” 

“We defeated Trump the first time he tried to roll back protections and sacrifice more of our waters to the oil industry. We’re bringing this abuse of the law to the courts again,” said Earthjustice managing attorney for oceans Steve Mashuda. “Trump is illegally trying to take away protections vital to coastal communities that rely on clean, healthy oceans for safe living conditions, thriving economies, and stable ecosystems.”

“Protecting the eastern Gulf has long been a bipartisan effort in Florida,” said Martha Collins, Executive Director of Healthy Gulf. President Trump used the same authority as President Biden to protect the eastern Gulf and Florida coastline from offshore oil and gas. President Biden simply made those protections permanent, something President Trump did not do. President Trump has now shown he could care less about protecting the eastern Gulf or Florida. Unfortunately we have to file suit to stand up against the rash and inconsistent policies of the Trump Administration to enforce what both FL Republicans and Democrats have fought for years on. Permanent protections from offshore oil and gas in Florida.”

“We shouldn’t have to file this suit again because President Trump already lost the last time he tried this,” said Gene Karpinski, President of League of Conservation Voters which led a coalition of groups’ successful challenge in the first Trump administration. “We are signaling to Congress, the President and the people of this country our commitment to defending already-protected coastal communities and waters from risky and dirty offshore drilling.”

“Trump’s putting our oceans, marine wildlife and coastal communities at risk of devastating oil spills and we need the courts to rein in his utter contempt for the law,” said Kristen Monsell, oceans legal director at the Center for Biological Diversity. “Offshore oil drilling is destructive from start to finish. Opening up more public waters to the oil industry for short-term gain and political points is a reprehensible and irresponsible way to manage our precious ocean ecosystems.”

“Offshore drilling is a dirty and damaging practice that is a direct threat to our thriving ocean recreation economy. Offshore drilling is also broadly unpopular and opposed by a majority of Americans who want to protect our nation’s coasts from oil and gas development. The Surfrider Foundation is pleased to join partners in challenging President Trump’s illegal order to revoke critical protections for U.S. waters,” said Dr. Chad Nelsen, CEO of the Surfrider Foundation.

“Living on the Gulf coast, I have seen first-hand the harmful impacts to people and places by the oil and gas industry,” said Joanie Steinhaus, Ocean Program Director for Turtle Island Restoration Network. “The western and central Gulf of Mexico has long been a sacrifice zone to place profit over people and our coast, and we will stand with our partners to ensure the protection of the fragile ocean ecosystem from the Trump administration.”

“We have seen the impact of offshore drilling on our vulnerable ocean waters, and what it does to the surrounding communities, marine life, and the health of the ecosystem,” said Sierra Club Senior Attorney Devorah Ancel. “When nearly 40 percent of Americans live in coastal counties that rely on a healthy ocean to thrive, removing critical protections shows how little care Trump has for these communities. Trump tried this illegal move to undo protections during his first administration, and he failed. We will keep working to ensure he won’t be any more successful this time around.”

“The Arctic Ocean has been protected from U.S. drilling for nearly a decade, and those protections have been affirmed by the federal courts,” said Sierra Weaver, senior attorney at Defenders of Wildlife. “Though these coastlines have been protected, the administration is showing no restraint in seeking to hand off some of our most fragile and pristine landscapes for the oil industry’s profit.”

“Trump’s executive order is an unlawful giveaway to the fossil fuel industry that puts marine ecosystems, coastal economies, and the climate at risk,” said Christy Goldfuss, Executive Director at NRDC. “The law is clear: once a president permanently withdraws ocean areas from oil and gas leasing, those protections cannot simply be undone. With the Trump administration aggressively dismantling environmental safeguards, the courts will be a crucial backstop. When Trump puts polluters over the law, we’ll see him in court.”

Earthjustice is representing Oceana, Center for Biological Diversity, the Surfrider Foundation, Greenpeace, Healthy Gulf, Northern Alaska Environmental Center, Alaska Wilderness League, and Turtle Island Restoration Network. Plaintiffs Sierra Club and the Natural Resources Defense Council are each representing themselves.

The plaintiffs in the related litigation to reinstate Arctic protections include League of Conservation Voters, Defenders of Wildlife, Natural Resources Defense Council, Northern Alaska Environmental Center, Greenpeace, and Alaska Wilderness League.

Background 

In January, former president Biden permanently protected the entire eastern U.S. Atlantic coast, or approximately 269 million acres of the Atlantic Outer Continental Shelf (OCS) from Canada to the southern tip of Florida; 65 million acres of the Eastern Gulf of Mexico; nearly 250 million acres of Federal waters off the coasts of Washington, Oregon, and California; and 44 million acres in the Northern Bering Sea Climate Resilience Area in Alaska. Earlier in his administration, Biden also protected 2.8 million acres of the Beaufort Sea and reinstated protections of 125 million acres in the Chukchi and Beaufort Seas as well as 3.8 million acres of canyon areas in the north and mid-Atlantic that Trump attempted to undo in his first administration.

Nearly 400 municipalities and over 2,300 elected officials across the Atlantic, Pacific, and Gulf coasts have formally opposed the expansion of offshore drilling in these areas. Hundreds of organizations and lawmakers supported the President taking this action. Nearly every Governor along the East and West coasts – Republican and Democrat alike – has expressed concerns about expanded oil and gas drilling off their coastlines.

Meanwhile, despite false claims that the Biden protections would disturb U.S. energy security, those withdrawals leave open most of the Gulf of Mexico for oil leasing, where nearly all of U.S. offshore drilling occurs. Moreover, the oil industry already has an excess under lease in the Gulf and the U.S. is currently producing more oil than any nation in history and is also the world’s largest producer of gas. Rather than opening whole new areas to drilling, both climate change and justice demand that we finally reduce the amount of leasing and drilling in the Gulf, where communities have too long borne the brunt of the harm caused by offshore drilling.

title: Boston 2024: Regal Springs asked to ‘nearshore’ Alaska processing; Canada lobster exports to China flip script
content:
BOSTON, Massachusetts, US -- The Undercurrent News team was live from Seafood Expo North America (SENA), held March 10-12.

Recap our blog below for all the news from SENA. 

 

Auto updates: On
MAR 1210:07 PM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Regal Springs sees demand for ‘near-shoring’ Alaska processing amid China issues

Tilapia producer Regal Springs has been contacted by buyers asking if it could use excess capacity in its plants in Latin America to process Alaskan seafood for the US market instead of sending it to China.

“This is not something we were looking to do; we’ve just been contacted by several parties now,” Vernon Bradley, Regal Springs’ head of marketing, told Undercurrent News.

READ MORE
MAR 125:37 PM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Seafood executives warn inflation is slowing consumer demand, particularly in the hospitality sector

As the US grapples with persistent inflation, seafood industry executives at the Seafood Expo North America mentioned about the impact on consumers’ spending habits, particularly in the restaurant and hotel sectors. 

The headline US inflation rate, as reflected in the  Consumer Price Index (CPI), has remained stubbornly above the 3% level. According to the February 2024 recent report, covering the 12-month period ending in January, the CPI stood at 3.1%. While this figure represents a slight decrease from December’s 3.4%, it remains higher than anticipated by many analysts.

READ MORE
MAR 125:28 PM GMT
By Kirsten Dobroth
Alaska pollock producers encouraged by strong interest at SENA

It’s been a good week for Alaskan pollock companies, according to Craig Morris, the chief executive officer of the Genuine Alaska Pollock Producers (GAPP).

Morris told Undercurrent News that this year’s trip to Boston has been the best one in years for the marketing group’s members. 

READ MORE
MAR 125:21 PM GMT
By Jason Huffman
Canadian lobster exports to China flipped script in 2023

China became Canada’s largest market for live lobsters for the first time ever in 2023, surpassing even the US, based on data Geoff Irvine, executive director of the Lobster Council of Canada, shared with Undercurrent News before the Boston seafood show. 

Canada sent China 24,480 metric tons of live lobster worth CAD 526.0 million ($390.0m) last year, 6% more volume and 14% more value than in 2022. The US, by comparison, imported 18,365t of live lobster from Canada worth CAD 460.8m.

READ MORE
MAR 125:19 PM GMT
By Masahiko Takeuchi
Japan’s Seafood Legacy plans expansion of sustainability consultancy throughout Asia

Seafood Legacy, a Tokyo, Japan-based social and environmental consultant, aims to increase awareness further on sustainability in seafood supply chains throughout Asia, Wakao Hanaoka, CEO and founder of the company, told Undercurrent News.

The consultant has held the Tokyo Sustainable Seafood Summit, the largest sustainable seafood event in Asia.

READ MORE
MAR 125:19 PM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Beaver Street aims for $100m in skin-pack sales

Beaver Street Fisheries is known as a US importer and distributor, but the Jacksonville, Florida-based company is building a sizeable skin-pack business.

The company is aiming to hit $100 million in skin-pack sales in the next few years, Mark Frisch, executive vice president of the family-owned business, told Undercurrent News at Seafood Expo North America (SENA).

READ MORE
MAR 125:14 PM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Norwegian H&G cod prices rocket past record $6,000/t for China deliveries after US Russian ban

Prices for Norwegian headed and gutted (H&G) Atlantic cod have rocketed to a record level for deliveries to processors in China, due to the US ban on Russian material and the reduced quotas in the Barents Sea.

Klaus Nielsen, CEO of A. Espersen, a large Denmark-based whitefish processing firm, confirmed to Undercurrent News the latest level for Norwegian 1-2.5kg H&G cod deliveries to Asia is over $6,000/t.

READ MORE
MAR 125:04 PM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Second generation of Brown family starts US smokehouse after award win for salmon salami

Jade Brown, the daughter of UK-born smoked salmon entrepreneur Jonathan, is starting her own business with her husband, Gantt Taylor, in Charleston, in the US state of South Carolina.

As Jade and Jonathan celebrated the best retail product win for their salmon salami at Seafood Expo North America, the younger Brown told Undercurrent News she and Taylor are starting a new smokehouse.

READ MORE
MAR 125:00 PM GMT
By Barb Dean-Simmons
Canadian oyster farmer sees potential for sales growth in North American market

A Canadian oyster farmer from the province of Prince Edward Island (PEI) is contemplating expansion to keep up with demand for its product.

Raspberry Point Oyster CEO Lucas Linkletter told Undercurrent News at the Boston seafood show that the PEI-based company is currently selling all the oysters it can produce.

READ MORE
MAR 124:48 PM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
American supermarket chain Publix  to feature SFP’s universal fish ID codes on crab packaging 

In a move towards enhancing transparency and sustainability in the seafood industry, American supermarket chain Publix announced at Seafood Expo North America that its swimming crab packaging will soon feature Sustainable Fisheries Partnership’s (SFP) universal fish identification codes.

This announcement comes after a collaborative effort between SFP, Thai Union Group, blockchain-based traceability solution Wholechain, and Publix on a pilot project focused on an artisanal blue swimming crab fishery in the Philippines, aimed at implementing these codes into practice, according to SFP.

READ MORE
MAR 122:59 PM GMT
By Kirsten Dobroth
New head of Bristol Bay salmon marketing group embracing opportunity in the year ahead 

The Bristol Bay Regional Seafood Development Association (BBRSDA) is focused on pushing quality and the Alaska story as it heads into the 2024 salmon season. 

“There’s a lot of opportunities in the domestic market,” said BBRSDA executive director Lilani Dunn. “Not only is [Bristol Bay sockeye] consumer preferred, but of course, there’s the executive order that went in to ban Russian product, so more than ever, I think that US seafood has an opportunity to get Americans to eat more of it.”

READ MORE
MAR 122:44 PM GMT
By Jason Huffman
‘Fall in Love with Seafood’ campaign credited for double-digit growth at H-E-B

A marketing campaign that made seafood seem more romantic worked.

The Seafood Nutrition Partnership announced in October 2023 at the Global Seafood Alliance’s Responsible Seafood Summit, in New Brunswick, Canada, that it would be rolling out a soft launch of its “Fall in Love with Seafood” test marketing campaign in a handful of US states. A much larger-scale test was to be tried in January 2024 in two retail chains in Texas and the Midwest, as reported by Undercurrent News.

READ MORE
MAR 122:00 PM GMT
By Jason Huffman
New CEO of land-based trout grower Riverence focused on operations, strengthening existing relationships

The Riverence Group, the largest grower of steelhead and rainbow trout in North America, is currently more focused on operational improvements than expansion, says Brandon Gottsacker, the Buhl, Idaho-based company’s new CEO.

“Our owners and team have a growth mindset so there are always 5–10-year plans being discussed,” he told Undercurrent News in a brief email exchange following his appearance this week at the Boston seafood show. “Today, we are focused on making improvements to our current operations by furthering our commitment to our customers by consistently producing the best tasting and highest quality trout and steelhead in the world.”

READ MORE
MAR 121:24 PM GMT
By Barb Dean-Simmons
Snow crab buyers, sellers approaching 2024 season with caution

The market for 5-8 oz snow crab leg clusters from Canada has not moved much beyond what it was last season, according to a seafood producer from the province of Nova Scotia (NS).

Undercurrent News caught up with Osborne Burke, president of the Nova Scotia Seafood Alliance, at the Boston seafood show on Tuesday (March 11).

READ MORE
MAR 1211:44 AM GMT
By Masahiko Takeuchi
Clearwater sees ‘steady’ demand for live lobster shipments to Japan amid record-high prices

Clearwater Seafoods, Canada’s largest shellfish harvester, is seeing a “steady demand” for shipments of live lobster to Japan, Hiroki Nakamoto, business development manager for the company told Undercurrent News.

As previously reported by Undercurrent, the wharf price in southern Nova Scotia has driven into a record high at CAD 17.00 ($12.52) per pound early this month, with a further hike to CAD 18.00/lb currently.

READ MORE
MAR 129:34 AM GMT
By Jason Huffman
New NFI Sushi Council builds steam in Boston

Michael McNicholas has the same reason as many of the now 13 members of the National Fisheries Institute Sushi Council (NSC) for helping to get the group off the ground this winter.

NSC’s first chairman and also the CEO and managing director of Culimer USA — a Ridgefield, New Jersey-based importer and wholesaler of sushi-grade seafood — believes it’s important to protect the reputation of the products. 

READ MORE
MAR 128:08 AM GMT
By Masahiko Takeuchi
Japan looks to buy more snow crab from Canada’s Gulf area this year

Japanese buyers are looking to purchase more snow crab from the Gulf of St. Lawrence, Canada, for the 2024 season, to replace Russia’s Far East products, a Tokyo-based source at Seafood Expo North America told Undercurrent News.

The move comes with Russian processors currently asking for a significant price hike for snow crab sections, blast-frozen at sea in its Far East. 

READ MORE
MAR 127:44 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Farmed shrimp producers navigate uncertainty amid potential US tariffs

In response to looming threats of anti-dumping and countervailing duties (CVD) on shrimp products destined for the US, producers in potentially affected countries are exploring alternative markets while bracing for potential setbacks.

On March 25, the US Department of Commerce (DOC) will announce preliminary CVD rates for shrimp from Ecuador, India, Indonesia, and Vietnam.

READ MORE
MAR 127:25 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Expected agreement with unions might resume Argentine provincial fishing in Chubut

Diego Alejandro Brandan, undersecretary of fisheries in the provincial government of Chubut in Argentina, has expressed optimism regarding the imminent resumption of provincial fishing activities. 

Brandan anticipates that a forthcoming agreement between unions and the fishing industry will pave the way for the resumption of fishing operations until the end of March or the beginning of April.

READ MORE
MAR 127:04 AM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Highland Farms’ Salmon salami, SK Foods shrimp sliders win best product awards

UK-based Highland Farms won the best retail product award for its Salmon Salami at the Seafood Excellence Awards during the Boston show.

Social Kitchens Professional/SK Foods Brands won the best foodservice product for its Premium Shrimp Sliders.

READ MORE
MAR 114:13 PM GMT
By Barb Dean-Simmons
Canadian companies expect small redfish from recently-opened fishery will be a hard-sell

Canadian companies already fishing and processing redfish from two commercial zones on the country’s east coast say the smaller redfish from the recently reopened fishery in the Gulf of St. Lawrence won’t be an easy sell.

The problem is that while the redfish in Unit 1 has grown in volume – the biomass is estimated at around four million tons – the fish are small, averaging 24cm or less, below the size the consumer market values.

READ MORE
MAR 112:17 PM GMT
By Barb Dean-Simmons
High Liner CEO open to more investments in aquaculture 

High Liner Foods recent $5 million spend for a 10% stake in Norwegian cod farmer Norcod is its first investment in a company directly involved in growing fish, but it may not be the last.

Company CEO Paul Jewer told Undercurrent News the company is “casting a wide net” as it considers future investments and acquisitions, including aquaculture.

READ MORE
MAR 112:17 PM GMT
By Masahiko Takeuchi
Tokai Denpun USA markets 4,000t of Japanese seafood annually, still seeing a growth


Tokai Denpun USA, a seafood importing and wholesaling arm of Tokai Denpun, one of the largest seafood traders in Japan, imports nearly 4,000 metric tons of Japanese seafood in the US market, an executive for the company told Undercurrent News.

After entering the US market around 30 years ago, the trading volume has seen a steady growth, he said. “In spite of an increase in quantity, in 2023, the sales revenue dropped year-on-year due to the price declines in major species.”

READ MORE
MAR 112:10 PM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Regal Springs partners with Channel Fish to process branded, breaded tilapia products

Regal Springs has partnered with Channel Fish Processing for as new range of breaded tilapia products for the US market under its brand.

The products will be hitting the market “in the next few months,” Vernon Bradley, Regal Springs’ head of marketing, told Undercurrent News.

READ MORE
MAR 111:40 PM GMT
By Masahiko Takeuchi
A chef cooking demonstration of Japanese seafood products attracted over 100 buyers, industry players

The Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO) ran an event focused on the “promotion of the appeal of Japanese seafood products in Boston,” in collaboration with the Consulate General of Japan in Boston.

At the event, Toru Oga, an executive chef and owner of Oga’s Japanese Cuisine, a local Japanese restaurant in Boston, provided cooking demonstrations and tastings using such Japanese seafood products as yellowtail, sea bream, and scallops.

READ MORE
MAR 111:12 PM GMT
By Kirsten Dobroth
Northline Seafoods freezer barge expected in Bristol Bay for 2024 salmon season

A new and one-of-a-kind processing vessel will be in the Bristol Bay region of the US state of Alaska this summer.

Northline Seafoods chief executive officer Ben Blakey told Undercurrent News that its 400-foot converted barge, called Hannah, is currently in drydock in Washington state, but will make its way up north in May, just ahead of the area’s 2024 sockeye salmon season.

READ MORE
MAR 1112:47 PM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Argentina’s in-shore wild red shrimp fishery enters full assessment for MSC certification, eyes boost in market access, prices

In a significant move for Argentina’s fishing industry, the nation’s in-shore fishery sector has announced the commencement of the full Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certification assessment process.

This development comes after a decade-long effort to meet the rigorous standards set by the MSC, marking a milestone eagerly awaited by stakeholders in the Argentine seafood industry.

READ MORE
MAR 1111:34 AM GMT
By Kirsten Dobroth
Demand for Alaskan crab continues to be bright spot 

Demand for Alaskan crab continues to be strong, according to Edmonds, Washington-based company Keyport, despite struggles for other sectors of the US state’s seafood industry.

Keyport reached a deal with Peter Pan Seafood Company company earlier this year to take over its Bering Sea Tanner, or bairdi, crab quota left stranded by the seafood processor’s decision to close for winter amidst turbulent market conditions.

READ MORE
MAR 118:24 AM GMT
By Jason Huffman
Bristol Seafood sees positive signs for scallop market in 2024

Scallop lovers have several reasons to be optimistic about the US domestic scallop season that begins in just a few weeks, based on the “Scallop Fact Book” published recently by Portland, Maine-based Bristol Seafood in advance of the Boston seafood show.

The 2023 season saw the fourth-consecutive reduction in US landings, coming in at 25 million pounds, down 21% from the prior year, and less than half of the recent peak (61m lbs harvested in 2019), noted Bristol CEO Peter Handy in the report. Though US scallop imports eclipsed the domestic harvest for the third year in a row at 51m lbs, the number was down from the 55m lbs imported the year before.

READ MORE
MAR 118:23 AM GMT
By Kirsten Dobroth
NOAA climate change panel draws attention to Alaskan black cod market crash

Black cod harvesters in Alaska could see management changes for the fishery in the near future aimed at boosting the market value of the fish.

The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), in coordination with the North Pacific Fishery Management Council (NPFMC) will consider easing rules that currently require individual fishing quota (IFQ) holders to keep all sablefish caught in Alaska’s black cod fishery, and instead, allow discards of smaller, less valuable fish.

READ MORE
MAR 118:23 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Chilean salmon producer Multi X launches new smoked products

Chilean salmon farming company Multi X has launched two new Latitude 45 branded products at the Boston seafood show. The new offerings, smoked salmon candy bites and smoked chipotle salmon, are poised to captivate consumers with their enticing flavors, according to the firm.

Latitude 45, known for its high-quality salmon products, aims to cater to consumers’ evolving tastes. Multi X said that the new products promise a ready-to-eat hot smoked experience, combining familiar sweet and spicy taste profiles to inspire culinary creativity among home cooks.

READ MORE
MAR 118:20 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
AquaChile launches Aqua Singular

Chilean salmon farming giant AquaChile launched a new product, Aqua Singular.

According to promotional material distributed by the company at the Boston seafood show, Aqua Singular is a D-trim fillet of premium quality raised in Patagonia. 

READ MORE
MAR 118:10 AM GMT
By Jason Huffman
Northern Wind hires Zurkan to lead new branded foodservice sales drive

New Bedford, Massachusetts-based scallop and lobster processor Northern Wind has hired Andrea Zurkan away from cross-town scallop competitor Eastern Fisheries to serve as its senior director of foodservice sales, a newly created position.

The new hires means a new tack for Northern Wind. Zurkan, a 20+-year veteran of the seafood industry, told Undercurrent News in an interview at the Boston seafood show that her new post involves leading a team of five sales professionals, a number she hopes to double, in a push to sell more branded products to major foodservice distributors.

READ MORE
MAR 117:41 AM GMT
By Masahiko Takeuchi
Japan’s scallop exporters to visit Mexico after SENA to finds processing for US market 

A mission of Japanese scallop exporters plans to visit processing facilities in Ensenada in the Mexican state of Baja California, for four days starting March 13.

The mission comes after the Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO) launched a pilot project to process Japanese scallops in Mexico to be re-exported to the US market. Ensenada is about 100 kilometers from the border with the US.

READ MORE
MAR 1010:10 PM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Chilean salmon farmer Camanchaca expands partnership with Spanish firm Frime

Compania Pesquera Camanchaca, a Chilean salmon farmer, is set to bolster its collaboration with Spanish tuna processor Frime. The partnership between the two firms, announced last year at the Boston seafood show, aims to broaden Frime’s tuna sales in North America through Camanchaca’s brand and established sales network.

Ricardo Garcia, Camanchaca’s CEO, told Undercurrent News that the firm plans to expand the initial partnership. 

READ MORE
MAR 109:25 PM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
CenSea’s Torch: Only thing changing after Captain Fresh deal is we’re getting better, stronger

The marriage of Captain Fresh’s technology-driven approach and US importer Central Seaway Company’s (CenSea) experience in the market will be a win-win, said Nate Torch and Jeff Stern, the latter’s co-presidents.

Addressing a room of customers and suppliers on March 10 in Boston’s Bistro du Midi, after the first day of Seafood Expo North America (SENA), Torch and Stern both expressed excitement over the future after the sale to India’s Captain Fresh.

READ MORE
MAR 108:39 PM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Global Shrimp Council announces board of directors

In a packed room at a hotel adjacent to the Boston Seafood Show, the Global Shrimp Council has announced its 2024 board of directors.

Comprising a diverse group of industry leaders from various shrimp-producing regions, the board aims to educate consumers about the nutritional benefits of incorporating shrimp into their diets.

READ MORE
MAR 106:33 PM GMT
By Barb Dean-Simmons
Newfoundland premier expects snow crab harvesters, processors to ‘get on with it,’ make deal

As the clock ticks closer to the start of the season in the world’s largest snow crab fishery, there’s no word on whether harvesters and processors in the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador (NL) are getting close to a deal to solidify a pricing formula.

The Association of Seafood Producers (ASP) and the Fish Food and Allied Workers (FFAW) are saying nothing; both sides agreed they would not say anything publicly while the talks continue.

READ MORE
MAR 104:56 PM GMT
By Masahiko Takeuchi
Japan’s surimi producer Kanetetsu Delica Foods plans to launch plant-based crab sticks for US market


Kanetetsu Delica Foods, the largest surimi producer in western Japan, has seen a growth in its export sales to North American market, Shingo Kurita, a manager in international sales division for the company told Undercurrent News.

Despite that Japan’s exports of surimi finished products or neri to the US declined 29% year-on-year in 2023, the export revenue for the Kobe-Hyogo based producer jumped by 1.3 times y-o-y.

READ MORE
MAR 103:47 PM GMT
By Barb Dean-Simmons
Ocean Choice president says plans still on the table for retail packaging plant in Nova Scotia 

Martin Sullivan assures Ocean Choice International (OCI) has not shelved its plans to set up a retail packaging facility in Dartmouth, in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia (NS).

Undercurrent News caught up with the OCI president at Seafood Expo North American on Sunday (May 10) in Boston.

READ MORE
MAR 103:28 PM GMT
By Kirsten Dobroth
USDA interest in Alaska seafood market continues to grow

Purchases made by the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) are a present opportunity for Alaska’s seafood industry, according to the Alaska Seafood Marketing Institute (ASMI), and represent part of its future, too. 

“USDA is becoming one of the largest buyers of Alaska seafood,” said ASMI executive director Jeremy Woodrow, noting $150 million in purchases of Alaskan seafood made already this year. “One of the great things about USDA in the last several months is they are coming to Alaska and wanting to learn more.”

READ MORE
MAR 102:45 PM GMT
By Kirsten Dobroth 
Circle Seafoods anticipates new floating freezer barge to be in Alaska this summer

Fishing vessels in Southeast Alaska could unload their fish at Circle Seafoods’ floating freezer barge as soon as this summer, according to the company’s co-founder Eren Shultz, as long as construction of the 400-foot long vessel continues to go according to plan.

Shultz told Undercurrent News that the Aberdeen, Washington-based company anticipates its floating freezer vessel will see 500,000 pounds of mostly pink salmon rounds per day when it’s up and running, with a daily capacity of 1.3 million pounds.

READ MORE
MAR 101:55 PM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Peruvian firms enter US market with Alaska wild salmon fillets

In a bid to diversify seafood imports and tap into new markets, some Peruvian firms have ventured into re-processing wild salmon from Alaska for the US market. 

Seafrost and Altamar, according to industry sources, initiated this endeavor last year, purchasing head and gutted (H&G) salmon to produce portions for the United States. 

READ MORE
MAR 101:37 PM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Regal Springs spend big on biosecurity, hatcheries after tough year in Latam

Indonesian tilapia production is going very well for Regal Springs, but the company does not “walk away” from the fact it had issues in Honduras, which could not be offset by its operation in Mexico.

As a result, the company’s owner Golden Springs Group, controlled by the billionaire Zuellig family, will invest “tens of millions” into the company’s farms again in 2024, having put a similar amount in last year, Vernon Bradley, the company’s marketing chief, told Undercurrent News.

READ MORE
MAR 101:14 PM GMT
By Barb Dean-Simmons
Canada’s fisheries minister seeks advice from Maine on how to manage elver fishery

Canada’s fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier says she is looking to the US state of Maine for examples of how to effectively manage an elver fishery.

Undercurrent News caught up with Lebouthillier at the Boston seafood show. On her trip to the US this week, she also visited with officials in Portland, Maine, to learn about their best practices for managing elver fishing.

READ MORE
MAR 1012:51 PM GMT
By Jason Huffman
David Caslow: Acme Florida plant two months from processing; expansion not limited to smoked fish

Acme Smoked Fish — the largest salmon smoker in the US — is 30-60 days from being ready to use its new plant in Pompano Beach, Florida, to handle processing, David Caslow, the co-owner and CEO, told Undercurrent News.

Undercurrent caught up with Caslow and Eduardo Carbajosa, who was recently promoted to CEO after nearly 17 years with the company, at their exhibit booth. 

READ MORE
MAR 1012:41 PM GMT
By By Masahiko Takeuchi
Alaskan pollock, cod suppliers see strong demand from Chinese processors due to US Russian ban


Alaskan pollock and Pacific cod processors are looking to expand the output of headed-and-gutted (H&G) products this year, driven by the stronger demand by Chinese processors, a source told Undercurrent News.

The increase in demand by Chinese processors comes after US president Joe Biden’s ban on Russian fish processed in third countries. “China processors need to keep their operation running anyway. So, instead of Russian H&G, they are eying to process Alaskan blocks and to ship the double-frozen fillets back to the US market,” the source said.

READ MORE
MAR 1012:38 PM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Alaskan Leader sees black cod, miso product as way to help beleaguered Alaskan fleet

Alaskan Leader Seafood is in talks with possible buyers for its new miso black cod product in both North America and Europe amid a tough time for the Alaskan fleet with low prices and demand in Japan.

The company’s Keith Singleton (left below) and Scott Sandvig (right below) said they have a packed Seafood Expo North America (SENA) show meeting with customers interested in the product, which is already in all the Costco Wholesale stores in Hawaii. 

READ MORE
MAR 1010:33 AM GMT
By Jason Huffman
Boston show exhibit hall grows again

The 42nd edition of the Boston seafood show has kicked off with a bigger floor and more exhibitors than last year, according to a press release published this morning by Diversified Communications.

This year’s three-day event, March 10-12, features 1,210 exhibitors, 6% more than the 1,141 at last year’s event, in a 249,665-square foot space, 5% larger than the 237,665 sq. ft. space used in 2023. Last year’s floor was 31% larger than in 2022.

READ MORE
MAR 107:39 AM GMT
By Masahiko Takeuchi
Japan has high hopes for US seafood exports with China market closed 

The US was the second-largest export market for Japanese seafood products in 2023, surpassing China, which imposed a ban last August after the release of treated wastewater from the defunct Fukushima nuclear power plant. 

In the US, the number of Japanese restaurants has increased approximately 1.8 times from 14,129 establishments in 2010 to 26,040 establishments in 2023, according to the Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO), a governmental arm that works to promote mutual trade and investment between Japan and the rest of the world.

READ MORE
MAR 107:16 AM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Boston Sword sees Gulf shrimp, more skin-pack as 2024 growth drivers

Boston Sword & Tuna (BST) sees Gulf shrimp from parent company Fortune International’s plant in Alabama as a growth driver in 2024, in addition to the added capacity for skin-pack production it created last year with a $12 million investment in its plant.

BST sees an opening to use more Gulf shrimp from its parent company, Fortune International’s plant in Alabama, for its customers in the US Northeast, said president Larry Dore while giving Undercurrent News a tour of the company’s plant expansion the day before the start of Seafood Expo North America in its home city of Boston, Massachusetts.

READ MORE
MAR 92:34 PM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Acme shifts long-time COO Viteri into biz dev, M&A-focused role

Acme Smoked Fish Corporation, the largest US salmon smoker, is moving Gabriel Viteri from chief operating officer (COO) to a new role focused on organic growth and also mergers and acquisitions (M&A).

Having promoted Eduardo Carbajosa to CEO, Acme has moved Viteri from COO to chief of new business ventures officer, “underscoring Acme’s commitment to long-term growth and to strengthening its leadership position in the industry,” the company said.

READ MORE
MAR 92:15 PM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Northern Wind hires Eastern Fisheries veteran Zurkan to lead foodservice sales

Private equity-backed US scallop and lobster supplier Northern Wind has hired Andrea Zurkan to lead its foodservice sales.

Zurkan joins Northern Wind after two ten-month spells with Eastern Fisheries, the largest US scallop seller, and Thai Union Group’s Chicken of the Sea Frozen Foods (COSFF). Prior to moving to COSFF in April 2022, Zurkan had spent 11 years with Eastern.

READ MORE
MAR 92:02 PM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Laitram snaps up shrimp processing equipment division of Icelandic rival

US-based Laitram Machinery has finalized the acquisition of the shrimp peeling business line from Martak, based in Iceland.

James Lapeyre, the president of family-owned Laitram, which invented the shrimp peeler, said the deal is a game-changer in a statement put out before Seafood Expo North America.

READ MORE

Contact the authors tom.seaman@undercurrentnews.com, matilde.mereghetti@undercurrentnews.com, jason.huffman@undercurrentnews.com, kirsten.dobroth@undercurrentnews.com, masahiko.takeuchi@undercurrentnews.com, barb.simmons@undercurrentnews.com

title: Barcelona 2022: Recap all UCN’s coverage from SEG
content:
BARCELONA, Spain -- Undercurrent News is reporting live from Seafood Expo Global (SEG) in Barcelona, Spain, finally returning after a two-year coronavirus-related hiatus.

SEG, the world's largest seafood trade fair, had about 1,560 exhibits registered – 77% of its 2019 record show – with just eight days to go before the event was scheduled to begin, on April 26.

Keep checking back for live updates as our team of journalists reports from the three-day event. 

Auto updates: On
MAY 23:57 AM GMT
By María Feijóo
Industrias Martec expects turnover to double in 2022 after acquiring AquaChile’s tilapia division 

After a 30% drop in 2020, Costa Rican producer Industrias Martec saw revenues grow by nearly 80% year-on-year to $50 million in 2021, the firm’s CEO Patrick Bornhausen told Undercurrent News. 

“After a year highly affected by the pandemic and the closure of foodservice, we almost doubled the company’s turnover during 2021. That is something we hope to repeat in 2022 thanks to the acquisition of Rainforest Tilapia,” he explained during an interview in Barcelona. 

READ MORE
APR 2910:51 AM GMT
By María Feijóo
Chile’s Camanchaca aims to raise EU sales to 10% through new office in Spain

The firm’s sales to Europe account for between 6% and 7% of the Chilean salmon farmer total sales, a percentage it aims to grow to 10% in the next two to three years through its new office in Vigo, in northern Spain. 

According to Tom Ruiz, the company’s sales and distribution director in Europe, Camanchaca’s 2021 efforts consisted mainly on enhancing the firm’s presence not only in Asia and the US but the EU also, with direct distribution to retail and foodservice chains.

READ MORE
APR 294:29 AM GMT
By María Feijóo
Russia’s invasion puts damper on Froxa plans to expand into Ukraine

Spanish frozen processor Froxa’s plans to expand sales into Ukraine this year have been disrupted by the ongoing violence caused by Russia’s invasion of the country in late February. 

According to the firm’s co-owner and Asia-Pacific director, Jose Javier Fernandez, this specific plan may not be resumed for several years.

READ MORE
APR 2811:18 AM GMT
By Louis Harkell
UK brown crab company considers European processing plant solution to Brexit challenges

One of the UK’s largest crab companies said it will build a processing plant in continental Europe in the next few years in order to more easily sell its products within the EU’s single market.

David Markham, managing director of The Blue Sea Food Company, told Undercurrent News the option “makes more sense” for the company, after difficulties faced exporting to key European markets since Brexit.

READ MORE
APR 2811:17 AM GMT
By Dan Gibson
Matorka growth plans rudely interrupted by volcanic eruption

The land-based farming industry has had its share of setbacks in the past year, but for the management at Iceland’s Matorka, volcanic eruptions were not high on the list of potential risks. After all, there had not been an eruption on the Reykjanes peninsular, near the capital Reykjavik, since the 12th century.

Still, to the company’s dismay, the nearby volcano of Fagradalsfjall erupted last year, just 12 kilometers from the company’s land-based Arctic charr farming site in Grindavik.

READ MORE
APR 2810:52 AM GMT
By Neil Ramsden
Icelandic capelin price for Japan down on 2021

Icelandic capelin being shipped to Japan this season is down in price from last year’s level of JPY 425 (around $3.90-$4 at that time) per kilogram CIF, sources told Undercurrent News.

Iceland’s 2022 production was significantly lower than expected due to “crazy” storms, but Japan still had stocks left from the prior year and the yen is currently suffering a serious crash; a combination which has meant Japanese import prices are down “at least two times” from 2021.

READ MORE
APR 2810:47 AM GMT
By Dan Gibson
Italian partner of Jangaard eyes ‘desalted’ factory expansion

Monti, an Italian processor of salted cod, is looking to grow its volumes substantially in the next few years, commercial director Paolo Monti told Undercurrent News.

The company is majority-owned by the Norwegian bacalao giant Jangaard Export, through which it receives its supply of salted cod.

READ MORE
APR 2810:31 AM GMT
By Dan Gibson
Price uncertainty looms for Norway’s salted cod this summer

Salted cod, or bacalao, has been one of Norway’s seafood products most affected by the pandemic, given its predominance in the foodservice markets of Portugal and Italy.

And while demand has recovered in 2022, there are now concerns that high raw material prices out of Norway are going to put off consumers later in the year, according to Odd Sperre, whitefish sales manager for Alesund-based Nils Sperre.

READ MORE
APR 2810:08 AM GMT
By Dan Gibson
Cod price hikes not yet carried through to consumers, says Insula

It’s been a strange year for cod processors in Norway; demand from Europe has never been higher, but issues with exchange rates, freight costs, and quota cuts are squeezing company margins like never before.

For Insula’s chief operations officer for whitefish, Morten Hyldborg Jensen, it’s proving a headache.

READ MORE
APR 2810:01 AM GMT
By Louis Harkell
Crayfish raw material prices higher but ‘not overheating’

The crayfish market has gone through ups and downs in recent years in the wake of strong Chinese demand and the pandemic. However, Spanish crayfish processor and exporter Alfocan reckons this year will be more in keeping with “normal” years past.

“[High prices] absolutely coincided with the craze in China in 2018. Then came a normal year in 2019, where prices went back to normal. Then COVID came and changed the whole story again,” Nicolas Roux, general manager at Alfocan, told Undercurrent News.

READ MORE
APR 289:49 AM GMT
By Dan Gibson
Cargill: Spiking fish oil prices reducing gap with algae alternatives

Recent spikes in the cost of fish oil have played into the hands of those manufacturers producing algal oil alternatives, according to Helene Ziv-Douki, head of aqua nutrition at global feed giant Cargill.

“Recently, with fish oil prices going through the roof, we’ve seen a lot of algae coming into the formula, because the spread of fish oil and fishmeal was getting less and less” she told Undercurrent News.

READ MORE
APR 289:12 AM GMT
By Louis Harkell
Irish mussel sector expected to consolidate 

Irish mussel farmer Kush Shellfish expects some more consolidation in Ireland’s industry after his company acquired a small cooperative farm with 400 metric tons of production capacity.

John Harington of Kush, which currently harvests around 1,000 metric tons of rope-grown in Kenmare Bay, off the southwest coast of Ireland, said consolidation is driven by a lack of immediate successors within families and an improvement in market conditions.

READ MORE
APR 288:12 AM GMT
By Tom Seaman
Iberconsa expands capacity at Argentina shrimp plant ahead of season

Spain’s Grupo Iberica de Congelados (Iberconsa) is increasing the capacity at its red shrimp plant in Argentina ahead of the upcoming fishing season.

Iberconsa, which is owned by US investor Platinum Equity, produced around 12,000 metric tons of land-frozen shrimp last season, with around 30% done in third-party plants.

READ MORE
APR 284:31 AM GMT
By Neil Ramsden
Ukraine’s canned pelagic purchases ‘three times’ higher than before Russia’s invasion

Denmark’s Sirena Group had already told Undercurrent News that some Ukrainian buyers had returned to the market for coldwater shrimp, and Latvian canner Karavela has seen very strong demand of late, it also told Undercurrent.

“Ukraine is a big buyer for us, and it will be this year still,” Karavela CEO Andris Bite said. “They did have a lot of stock; a friend of ours had lots of product in a warehouse, and it was destroyed by Russians.”

READ MORE
APR 282:39 AM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Klausen feels PBO pollock fillet prices have hit peak

Prices for pin-bone out (PBO) pollock are unlikely to increase much further, said Jens Peter Klausen, whose Nippon Suisan Kaisha-backed firm is a major player in the market.

According to the J.P. Klausen & Co. managing director, spot prices for PBO are up to around $4,600 per metric ton. However, a stabilization around $4,400-$4,500/t is more likely than an increase to $5,000/t, he said.

READ MORE
APR 282:21 AM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Brasmar sees competition for Norwegian cod hot up after Russia’s Ukraine invasion

Portugal-based processor Brasmar Group is seeing prices rise fast for Norwegian cod, as other buyers move away from Russia after the invasion of Ukraine.

Brasmar, which has always bought 90% of its cod from Norway and the rest mainly from Iceland, is seeing much more competition for raw material and rocketing prices, Sergio Couto Reis, the company’s CEO, told Undercurrent News at Seafood Expo Global.

READ MORE
APR 282:04 AM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Salmon prices are ‘unsustainable’, says world’s second largest farmer

The salmon farming sector may be raking in bumper profits, but the current prices are unsustainable for the sector as a whole, said the CEO of Cermaq Group, the world’s second-largest producer.

Cermaq, which has moved into the second spot in terms of 2021 production behind Mowi, is taking a long-term view in line with its Japanese owner, Mitsubishi Corporation.

READ MORE
APR 2712:45 PM GMT
By María Feijóo
Central American SMEs see show as ‘great opportunity to successfully enter’ EU market

This year, six small and medium-sized seafood companies (SMEs) from Panama, Honduras, and Costa Rica have been present at the Seafood Expo Global in Barcelona, intending to make their way into the EU market.

According to Carlos Virgilio Umanzor, general manager of the Honduran shrimp company Corporacion Acuicola de Centroamerica (CACESA), the firm has already negotiated five new contracts with some EU clients on the first day of the show.

READ MORE
APR 278:25 AM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Premium Brands on lookout for farmed salmon supply partner

Canadian food group Premium Brands Holdings is on the lookout for a supply partner on farmed salmon to work together on developing the North American market.

The company, which reported a turnover of close to CAD 5 billion in 2021, is looking to further develop its farmed salmon business, said George Paleologou, CEO of Premium, who is at the Seafood Expo Global show for the first time.

READ MORE
APR 278:04 AM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Milarex pushes through salmon price increases

With the rocketing prices dominating the news agenda at Seafood Expo Global, times are tough for the processing sector in Europe.

“Price increases for all markets, every day. That’s the agenda here and now,” Thomas Farstad, CEO of salmon processor Milarex, told Undercurrent News.

READ MORE
APR 276:59 AM GMT
By Neil Ramsden
Danish pelagics firm already seeing ‘balance’ in fishmeal production market after plant closure

Danish pelagics processor FF Skagen is already seeing more “balance” in the North Atlantic fishmeal production sector after closing one of its factories at the end of 2021, CEO Johannes Palsson told Undercurrent News.

The fishmeal and oil producer — owner of Scandic Pelagic — closed its factory in Hanstholm last winter. It cited intense competition for raw materials as the reason.

READ MORE
APR 276:51 AM GMT
By Neil Ramsden
MSC stats show commercial scale of Atlantic pelagics’ certification loss

Statistics presented by the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) during its “Seafood Futures Forum” show the commercial scale of North Atlantic pelagic species’ certification loss.

Volume sales globally of MSC-certified products were down 2% at 169,729 metric tons in 2021-2022 for canned goods, while volume sales in the UK and Ireland were down 13% at 153,552t, said MSC’s Nicolas Guichoux. Both of these figures were largely down to the loss of the certificate on North Atlantic mackerel and Atlanto-Scandian herring, he said.

READ MORE
APR 275:19 AM GMT
By María Feijóo
Ecuador shrimp industry must keep looking forward, says CNA

Despite the general concern in the shrimp sector regarding all current events worldwide, Jose Antonio Camposano, head of Ecuador’s national chamber of aquaculture, or CNA, believes it is time to continue to focus on the industry’s future.

“Once again, both exports and production have grown during the first quarter of the year, which in itself is a great reason to remain optimistic,” Camposano told Undercurrent News, in an interview at the Seafood Expo Global trade show in Barcelona, Spain.

READ MORE
APR 274:09 AM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Salmon prices set to range over 20% upward of ‘normal’ level

Farmed salmon prices could remain in a range of over 20% higher than what was previously considered “normal”, said Glenn Cooke, CEO of one of the world’s largest producers.

“There’s is what I would call a reset in salmon prices,” Cooke told Undercurrent News, in an interview at the Seafood Expo Global trade show in Barcelona, Spain.

READ MORE
APR 274:03 AM GMT
By Louis Harkell
Chinese tilapia prices hold firm after last year’s hike

Prices for farmed Chinese tilapia are holding firm and won’t decrease at least until after May, according to Nicholas Staub, marketing director at Shanghai-headquartered Ocean Treasure Seafood.

“It was predicted prices would decrease after the Qingming festival [in China], but prices increased,” said Staub, whose company generates some $70 million in annual turnover and sells mainly to Latin America.

READ MORE
APR 262:12 PM GMT
By Louis Harkell
Irish bemoan Brexit impact on raw material supply at Barcelona show

Almost 18 months since Brexit emotions are still raw for seafood companies in the island of Ireland dealing with the loss of fishing quota and new trade barriers with the UK.

John McGuiness, a manager at Killybegs Seafoods, a pelagic fishing and processing company, told Undercurrent News it had suffered a “big impact” from lower pelagic fishing quota, after Ireland lost a disproportionate share of the 25% reduction in EU fishing opportunities in UK waters.

READ MORE
APR 261:53 PM GMT
By Dan Gibson
Reduced proportion of large shrimp likely from India’s spring harvests

Despite seeing prices for large, lower-count shrimp approach records over the first couple of months of 2022, last year’s bad experiences are still likely to deter many of India’s shrimp farmers from growing out their crop to the largest sizes this season, Undercurrent News learned.

Pavan Kosaraju, CEO of digital trading platform Aqua Exchange, told Undercurrent that farmers in the primary farming state of Andhra Pradesh are wary after last year’s outbreak of COVID and disease problems during harvest seasons.

READ MORE
APR 261:18 PM GMT
By Neil Ramsden
Faroes’ Pelagos anticipates tough year of redistribution away from Russia

Faroese pelagic processor Pelagos anticipates a tricky year as it looks to shift away from its major markets of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus, CEO Johan Pall Joensen told Undercurrent News.

Its main production season runs from August to February, he explained, and so as Russia invaded Ukraine, Pelagos was essentially finished for the 2021-2022 season. However, later this year Joensen expects some difficulties.

READ MORE
APR 2610:30 AM GMT
By Neil Ramsden 
Ukrainian buyers in Barcelona for product to be delivered ‘now’

While the Russian invasion of Ukraine has had some severe impacts on the sales of coldwater shrimp there, Denmark-headquartered seafood firm Sirena Group has taken some optimism from the fact there are Ukrainian buyers at the Barcelona show.

“Ukraine takes some cooked, shell-on prawns from us,” Sirena chairman Peter Buhl told Undercurrent News. “They are here today, buying, for delivery now, pretty much, so that must be a good sign.”

READ MORE
APR 269:40 AM GMT
By Louis Harkell
Lockdowns, quarantines, flight costs keep Chinese firms away from Barcelona show

Nicholas Staub markets seafood produced and processed in China for Shanghai-headquartered Ocean Treasure Seafood. Normally based in Nantong, near Shanghai, the marketing director told Undercurrent News of the “big risk” traveling from China with a colleague to attend the Barcelona show.

One of just six companies from China registered to attend this year’s show, Staub expects to have to quarantine for up to a month-and-a-half on his return to China, and that’s if he manages to get a flight back.

READ MORE
APR 269:04 AM GMT
By Tom Seaman 
Those still dealing with Russia should be ‘embarrassed’, says Glenn Cooke

There’s no excuse for not finding alternatives to buying Russian seafood, or carrying on selling feed to its aquaculture sector, said one of the industry’s top entrepreneurs.

“There are producers still buying Russian products and I think it needs to stop,” Glenn Cooke told Undercurrent News in an interview at Seafood Expo Global in Barcelona, Spain.

READ MORE
APR 267:58 AM GMT
By Neil Ramsden
Loss of MSC on pelagics ‘doesn’t matter’ for some European buyers

The loss of the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certificate on mackerel, blue whiting, and Atlanto-Scandian herring “doesn’t matter” to some European buyers, one executive in charge of a pelagics company told Undercurrent News.

“I think they’ve just relaxed their policies, made adjustments, and largely carried on buying them,” he claimed, stating that even for markets like Germany — where MSC has traditionally been quite important — retail buyers will now take products either with or without the eco-label.

READ MORE
APR 265:53 AM GMT
By Neil Ramsden
Multi X still sees greatest market potential in US

Chilean salmon producer Multi X is looking to exploit what it sees as the greatest market potential globally, in the US, said general manager Christian Swett Pla.

The US and China are both “super interesting”, he said, but in China’s case, trying to increase the per-capita salmon consumption in line with the average of more established markets is a much longer-term endeavor — “we don’t see that happening soon”.

READ MORE
APR 263:20 AM GMT
By Neil Ramsden
Multi X not yet sure what to do about Russian sales

Speaking at the DNB/ Fish Pool seminar on April 25, Multi X general manager Christian Swett Pla said his firm had not yet decided what to do about the large volumes it had been shipping to Russia.

“It is a big market for us, when all of this began we had maybe 30 or so containers headed for Russia,” he said. “There are a few steps to the journey, with the final one being Rotterdam in the Netherlands to St Petersburg, at which point they can’t be recalled.”

READ MORE
APR 2510:59 AM GMT
By Dan Gibson
Don’t accept one week option contracts, DNB warns salmon sellers

In such strange market situations, many salmon companies are falling for traps in the contract market, warned DNB senior analyst Stale Johansen.

“Some of you are negotiating on salmon, and you should avoid the pitfall where the counterparty is asking you to hold the price for a week or so,” the risk management specialist explained. “That is a challenging situation due to the fact that you are giving away what is called an option contract in our market.”

READ MORE
APR 2510:40 AM GMT
By Dan Gibson
Salmon sector facing ‘very special market situation’ says Fish Pool

“What is happening?”

It’s the question that has been asked by countless salmon buyers over the past three months, as prices continue to break all-time records set in only the previous week.

READ MORE
APR 2510:36 AM GMT
By Neil Ramsden
DNB’s Aukner: Taxation, possible Chilean political issues among potential hard-to-predict ‘X-factors’

The looming figures of taxation and a political leader unfriendly to aquaculture are among the unpredictable “X-factors” that make getting a fix on future earnings and share prices for listed farming companies tricky, according to DNB Markets analyst Alexander Aukner.

“Taxation is actually one of the ‘maybes’ that scares me the most,” he said. “With prices so high there’s always a risk of politicians deciding to come in with new taxes.”

READ MORE
APR 259:41 AM GMT
Fearnley: Salmon earnings bonanza will make 2022 a record year for listed farmers

The week begins with the Fish Pool/ DNB seminar on farmed salmon. Earlier on April 25, Norwegian market analyst Fearnley Securities announced it had lifted its earnings estimates for all major salmon farmers in 2022 as a result of the record prices that have marked the first quarter of the year.

“2022 has shaped up better than we could have imagined at the start of the year, with prices breaching NOK 100 [per kilogram] for the first time ever,” writes analyst Nils Thommesen. “We see upside to Q2 expectations given a continued tight market, with a soft landing for H2 ensuring record-breaking earnings for listed players.”

READ MORE

Contact the authors neil.ramsden@undercurrentnews.com, tom.seaman@undercurrentnews.com, louis.harkell@undercurrentnews.com, Maria.Feijoo@undercurrentnews.com, dan.gibson@undercurrentnews.com
