title: Aquaculture America 2022: US aquaculture enjoys ‘strong’ USDA leadership support, exec says
content:
SAN DIEGO, CALIFORNIA US -- Undercurrent News is reporting live from the World Aquaculture Society's (WAS) Aquaculture 2022 triennial conference, Feb. 28-March 4.

Each year WAS organizes several regional aquaculture conferences around the world, including Aquaculture America, which was held last year in San Antonio, Texas. But every three years the group also combines its annual US conference with its triennial meeting.

The four-day event is a major gathering of hundreds of industry, academic and public sector experts covering all aspects of aquaculture from social license, economics, disease management, innovation in feed and genetics, and changes in regulation, among others. 

The meeting, which also includes a trade show of sector suppliers, will also cover in detail two promising methods that could eventually ramp up US seafood production-- offshore farming and recirculating aquaculture systems.

Auto updates: On
MAR 83:07 AM GMT
Exec: US aquaculture enjoys ‘strong’ USDA leadership support

Supporting aquaculture isn’t always the first thing to come to mind when people think about the work of the US Department of Agriculture (USDA).

However, Shefali Mehta the deputy undersecretary for the USDA’s Research, Education, and Economics (REE) Division, said that “aquaculture is agriculture”.

READ MORE
MAR 712:03 PM GMT
Neil Sims would like you to ‘stop throwing mud’

Neil Sims is well known in US fish farming circles as being a vocal advocate for offshore aquaculture, and, typically, he’s an optimistic one.

But, for now, Sims, the CEO of Hawaii-based Ocean Era, which is behind the Velella Epsilon demonstration project in the Gulf of Mexico, has a simple request: He’d like other aquaculture operators, including those who use land-based systems, to “stop throwing mud”.

READ MORE
MAR 73:19 AM GMT
US offshore aquaculture bill has four-decade history

If the generally optimistic tone used by the small community of US offshore aquaculture regulators and developers at Aquaculture 2022is any indication, progress on a series of bottlenecks is coming soon. 

However, as Sara Brenholt, the campaign manager of Stronger America Through Seafood (SATS), pointed out, legislative progress has been a long time coming and isn’t there yet. 

READ MORE
MAR 44:41 AM GMT
World Wildlife Fund throwing its ‘full weight’ behind aquaculture

Several non-governmental organizations and advocacy groups are actively working to stall or stop aquaculture projects in the US, particularly those offshore in federal waters. The World Wildlife Fund is definitely not one of those groups. 

Bailey Moritz, the seaweed and shellfish program officer at the globally known group’s US offices, said the organization is committed to advancing the global seaweed and shellfish farming industries.

READ MORE
MAR 43:42 AM GMT
Locals seen as key to ‘social license’ for aquaculture projects

Educating community members who will live close to where aquaculture developers want to site their projects is a vital part of obtaining the “social license” that those projects will need to be successful.

Kim Thompson, the manager of the “Seafood for the Future” program at the Long Beach, California-based Aquarium of the Pacific, defined social license as “the implied permission that society will give for resource extraction and development activities and this includes marine aquaculture”. 

READ MORE
MAR 35:22 PM GMT
NAA adapted farmed seafood messaging strategy as pandemic hit

In 2019 the US National Aquaculture Association’s (NAA) Linda O’Dierno along with a team of others started a project to figure out “how to get a more enabling atmosphere for aquacultured products in the US marketplace”. The team planned to do that by reaching chefs and restauranteurs via trade associations and culinary educators. In hindsight, the timing couldn’t have been much worse.

“In March of 2020, we were at the Javitz Center at the International Restaurant Show in New York doing a presentation. And that was right before everything closed down,” she said.

READ MORE
MAR 311:36 AM GMT
Data lags complicate picture of pandemic’s global seafood impacts

Some of the data is in on how recent years of the COVID-19 pandemic have affected the global farmed seafood sector and the picture is a bit surprising. 

Frank Asche, an economist and University of Florida professor, said that the pandemic and the government measures to contain it had “pretty dramatic” impacts both on consumer and company behavior. But a preliminary review of the global data available shows that the pandemic had a “relatively modest” impact on seafood supply chains with most shortages being relatively short-lived or limited to a few product groups.

READ MORE
MAR 31:16 AM GMT
US seaweed regulation still being developed

The practice of farming seaweed, seen as a promising new opportunity for aquaculturists, may be well established but the legal framework to govern the product is still being worked out.

Olivia Deans, an ocean and coastal law fellow at the National Sea Grant Law Center, said that while scientific definitions exist, legal definitions need to be created too.

READ MORE
MAR 312:25 AM GMT
Interest booming in Alaska seaweed farming

Judging by the standing-room-only crowd at the sessions at Aquaculture 2022, there’s a huge degree of interest in seaweed farming.

The sector, seen as a promising source of food, cosmetics, fertilizer and other inputs, is booming especially in the US state of Alaska, Melissa 

READ MORE
MAR 22:34 PM GMT
Ex-NOAA exec: Progress being made on Trump-era aquaculture order

A major aquaculture policy initiative drafted during the administration of former US president Donald Trump appears to be being upheld and not ignored under the administration of president Joe Biden.

At least that’s the view of Tim Gallaudet, the US former National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) deputy and a retired Navy rear admiral. In reviewing the May 7, 2020, order that he helped implement, he said that the current administration has largely stood by its provisions.

READ MORE
MAR 29:12 AM GMT
US farmers raising more catfish on fewer acres

The productivity of the US catfish farming sector is on the rise. Jimmy Avery, a professor and specialist in the subject at Mississippi State University, said that the total amount of US land dedicated to raising catfish was around 83,000 acres in 2013 but has dropped steadily since. It’s estimated to be around 58,000 acres in 2022.

“That’s about a 30% decrease over the ten-year average and then year-to-year variations of about -3%,” Avery said.

READ MORE
MAR 18:23 PM GMT
Belle: US aquaculture should focus on economic development

There’s been a growing push within US aquaculture for a sector-specific national economic development plan, and Sebastian Belle has put a lot of thought into how that might work in practice.

Belle, the executive director of the Maine Aquaculture Association, said that while US has substantial potential to develop land-based, freshwater and offshore aquaculture, it will take a plan to get there. In terms of economic development, he said, there are two ways to grow a sector: by focusing on existing players or by bringing in new players.

READ MORE
MAR 11:32 PM GMT
Professor: Regulatory ‘siloing’ is major issue for aquaculture

Capping a nearly 50-minute speech on the sustainability of the global aquaculture sector and how it’s evolved over the last two decades, Rosamond “Roz” Naylor ended with a call for better-coordinated regulation.

The Stanford University professor who was the keynote speaker for this year’s Aquaculture 2022 conference said that “regulatory siloing” poses an obstacle to the sector’s development.

READ MORE
MAR 110:21 AM GMT
Keynote speaker to discuss aquaculture’s sustainability

The oft-debated topic of the sustainability of commercial aquaculture will be front and center at this year’s Aquaculture 2022, the triennial meeting of the World Aquaculture Society (WAS).

Keynote speaker Rosamond “Roz” Naylor, the William Wrigley professor of earth system science at US-based Stanford University is slated to address the topic before an expected audience of several hundred industry professionals. 

READ MORE

Contact the author jason.smith@undercurrentnews.com

title: Untitled
content:
CAPE TOWN, South Africa -- Undercurrent News reported live from this year's IFFO conference for the global marine ingredients industry.

Held in Cape Town from Oct. 23-25, the event came at an interesting time for the industry, with fishmeal and fish oil prices at record highs due to the cancellation of the first anchovy season in Peru earlier this year.

Check below for all the blog posts.

Auto updates: On
OCT 274:56 AM GMT
Omega-3 markets continue to grow amid consumer awareness of health benefits

Omega-3 markets worldwide experienced a boost in 2022, driven by increasing consumer interest, according to Aldo Bernasconi, the vice president of data science at ABGOED.

Demand for Omega-3 has grown by 3.8% in 2022 globally, with experts predicting this upward trajectory will persist — yet Bernasconi noted that the industry will face a unique set of challenges as it expands.

READ MORE
OCT 274:03 AM GMT
China sees a drop in fishmeal production, jump in fish oil output thanks to Russian sardine

Maggie Xu, IFFO’s China director, pointed out that China’s economy is currently navigating choppy waters, with dampened capital flows contributing to the devaluation of the Chinese currency against the dollar last year. The recovery of domestic consumption has been slower than anticipated in the wake of the pandemic, impacting various sectors, including the marine ingredient industry, she explained in her presentation at the IFFO conference.

Marine ingredient consumption in China faces a dual challenge of oversupply and financial losses, particularly in the pig and aquaculture sectors. To adapt to sluggish farm gate prices and tight fishmeal supplies, inclusion rates of fishmeal in aqua and piglet diets have been reduced, according to Xu. This adjustment reflects the need for cost-effective solutions in the face of market challenges.

READ MORE
OCT 265:35 AM GMT
IFFO elects Pelagia CEO as new president

Following elections for the new IFFO management board (starting Jan. 1, 2024), IFFO has elected Pelagia CEO Egil Magne Haugstad as president.

Eduardo Goycoolea, who was one of the founders and first co-president of IFFO back in 2001 when it was created, has been named vice president.

READ MORE
OCT 253:02 PM GMT
Bachis: Fishmeal exports’ surge in India, Vietnam partially offset 2022 drop in Peruvian output

Enrico Bachis, IFFO’s market research director, highlighted the dramatic increase in fishmeal exports from India in 2022, catapulting the country to being the fourth-largest fishmeal exporter globally. 

Vietnam also demonstrated substantial growth in its fishmeal exports, according to Bachis. In contrast, in 2022, Peru experienced a decline in shipments, primarily due to the impact of La Nina. The graphs below show fishmeal and fish oil exports in 2021 and 2022.

READ MORE
OCT 252:20 PM GMT
Omega-3 requirements in fish: Critical vs desirable

The importance of omega-3 fatty acids, specifically eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), in the human diet is widely recognized for their numerous health benefits. Similarly, these fatty acids are crucial for the well-being of fish, especially those in aquaculture.

Douglas Tocher, a professor at the University of Shantou, highlighted the evolution of aquafeed and the emphasis on high-energy diets, particularly those rich in fat and lipids, to promote the growth of farmed fish while sparing protein.

READ MORE
OCT 252:08 PM GMT
Skretting: Filling data gaps for sustainable feeds

In a bid to advance sustainability within the feed industry, Skretting’s global sustainability manager, Jorge Diaz Salinas highlighted the critical need to address data gaps in lifecycle assessments (LCA). 

These assessments, carried out in accordance with Product Environmental Footprint Category Rules (PEFCR), are essential for measuring the environmental impact of feed production. Diaz emphasized that the availability of accurate data is not only essential for regulatory compliance but is increasingly being demanded by feed customers, retailers, and certification bodies.

READ MORE
OCT 253:26 AM GMT
Sparos CEO highlights ‘game-changing’ precision nutrition in aquaculture

Jorge Dias, CEO of Portuguese firm Sparos, espoused the value of new forms of precision nutrition to aquaculture, which he claims enhances performance, meets sustainability criteria, and offers precise nutrient supply. 

“This concept takes into account broader elements of production performance and sustainability criteria, but in particular focuses on the precise definition of nutrient and energy supply and the feed design specifications required to deliver that,” he said.

READ MORE
OCT 244:56 PM GMT
Mixed results in first three days of Peruvian anchovy exploratory fishing

The initial days of the Peruvian anchovy fishing have yielded mixed results, with some promising signs and challenges.

The season, a critical period for Peru’s fishing industry considering the cancellation of the first season earlier this year, is being closely monitored by the whole fishmeal industry due to concerns about the impact of warming waters on the anchovy population and global prices.

READ MORE
OCT 244:46 PM GMT
India’s sardine catches lag in ongoing season, fish oil price outlook uncertain

India’s fishing season, which runs between August and December, is in full swing, but local fishmeal producers said sardine catches have dipped compared to the previous year, which was a record year in terms of catches. 

The fishmeal prices in India range from approximately $1,800-$2,000 per metric ton. Fish oil commands a price tag of $3,500-$4,000/t, industry sources at the IFFO conference told Undercurrent News.

READ MORE
OCT 249:04 AM GMT
Southern Chile’s fishmeal producers thrive amid shortage from Peru

This year, fishmeal producers in southern Chile have capitalized on the shortage of products from Peru, reaping the benefits of high prices and good catches. 

Meanwhile, the situation in northern Chile has mirrored that of its Peruvian counterparts, posing challenges for the industry.

READ MORE
OCT 248:52 AM GMT
Pelagia CEO: Biotechnology to redefine omega-3 sector

Egil Magne Haugstad, CEO of Norwegian pelagics and fishmeal/ fish oil producer Pelagia, said some 25% of the oil extracted across the firm’s factories is channeled into the omega-3 industry, highlighting the significance of this essential fatty acid.

However, he suggested the industry should change how it considers the rest of the fatty acids in fish, often considered simply as “energy,” to recognize the value of each of these compounds. 

READ MORE
OCT 248:16 AM GMT
FAO official highlights rise in global undernourishment, stresses role of aquatic foods 

Manuel Barange, assistant director general and director of fisheries and aquaculture at the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, has presented recent statistics showing the recent rise in global undernourishment.

“After decades of improvement in the fight against undernourishment in the world, suddenly, over the last four or five years, it’s gone up,” said Barange. 

READ MORE
OCT 235:29 PM GMT
Uncertainty looms over Peru’s second anchovy season

Peru, the world’s largest producer of fishmeal and fish oil, is currently grappling with uncertainty surrounding its second anchovy season. 

The recent announcement of a quota of 1.682 million metric tons surprised many industry stakeholders. Expectations had been set between 800,000t and 1m metric tons, but the higher quota has left Peruvian industry sources between moderate optimism and suspicion.

READ MORE
OCT 238:24 AM GMT
MarinTrust, GDST collaborate to enhance supply chain traceability

Marine ingredients industry certification program MarinTrust is collaborating with The Global Dialogue on Seafood Traceability (GDST) to further improve traceability in the seafood supply chain, according to Francisco Alcon, the former’s CEO.

GDST’s data requirements provide a framework to enhance traceability, covering data collection, usage, transfer and management. MarinTrust is supporting the inclusion of marine ingredients within GDST, he said.

READ MORE
OCT 234:38 AM GMT
MarinTrust launches version three of its factory standard

Marine ingredients industry certification program MarinTrust has launched the latest version of its factory standard, version three. 

The program aims to enforce stringent standards within the marine ingredients industry — including both plant operations and vessels — promoting responsible practices. 

READ MORE
OCT 231:30 AM GMT
Peru establishes quota of 1.68m metric tons for second anchovy season

Peru’s production ministry (Produce) has officially greenlit the commencement of the second anchovy fishing season in the northern and central regions. 

The season will kick off on Oct. 26 at midnight, with a quota of 1.682 million metric tons, Produce said on Oct. 22. The announcement kicking off the full-scale anchovy season comes after a five-day exploratory anchovy season had started on Oct. 21.

READ MORE

title: Untitled
content:
VIGO, Spain -- The Undercurrent News team reported live from northern Spain, where the XI ANFACO World Tuna Conference ran Sept. 14-15.

Over 400 attendees from more than 30 countries gathered at the Afundacion headquarters for the event, organized by the Spanish canneries' association, ANFACO-CECOPESCA. It aimed to address the current challenges faced by the tuna industry, such as high raw material costs and a decline in demand in Spain over the past year.

It featured international speakers discussing the sustainable management of tuna stocks, innovation and technology, and the markets in different regions.

Auto updates: On
SEP 1511:19 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Thai Union France: The canned category must look beyond core usage to boost falling demand

Alexis Jacquand, Petit Navire’s general manager in France, shed light on the challenges and opportunities facing the canned tuna industry in the country amidst the economic downturn. France, being the fourth-largest European market for canned fish, has seen a significant impact due to shifting consumer behavior influenced by rising inflation.

Jacquand began by acknowledging the storm of economic challenges sweeping across Europe, leading consumers also in Spain and Italy to reduce their purchases of canned tuna due to inflationary pressures. While the French market has been on an upward trajectory, there has been a noticeable erosion in recent months, he noted.

SEP 156:09 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Frabelle: Decline in WCPO tuna catches impact Philippines’ exports

Significant declines in tuna catches in the Western and Central Pacific Ocean and consequent reduction in the number of active large-scale purse-seine vessels represent a challenge for the Filipino tuna industry, according to Francisco Tiu Laurel, president of the Filipino tuna company Frabelle Group.

Speaking at the Anfaco conference, Tiu pointed out that the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission (WCPFC) has observed a decline in tuna catches from 2018 to 2021 (see graph below). 

SEP 155:31 AM GMT
By María Feijóo
Global tuna fishing face ‘important challenges, misconceptions,’ says ICCAT’s president

Industrial and high-seas fishing, including tuna operations, have become targets of criticism from both activists and scientists who identify them as major contributors to the deterioration of global fishery resources.

“Calls for stricter regulations, and even outright bans, have gained momentum in recent years,” said Ernesto Penas, president of the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas, ICCAT.

SEP 155:28 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Tri Marine: Rising costs to drive consolidation in the Taiwanese tuna industry

Chris Hsu, Tri Marine’s general manager for Taiwan and Asia trading, issued a stark warning about the escalating costs within the industry. 

Hsu believes that this concerning trend will inevitably drive consolidation within Taiwan’s tuna fishing sector over the next five years. The rising expenses and the pursuit of economies of scale are pushing companies to consider mergers and partnerships, he noted during the Anfaco tuna conference.

SEP 154:50 AM GMT
By María Feijóo
Spanish authorities envision bright future for tuna sector, call for sustainability focus

Isabel Artime, Spain’s secretary general of fisheries, emphasized the significant potential of the tuna industry, citing its wide room for expansion in numerous countries due to its status as a highly valued consumer staple.

She also pointed out that the industry’s growth opportunities are “substantial,” and she underlined the importance of “staying attuned to customer preferences and needs,” which she considers pivotal in enhancing the product’s value.

SEP 152:04 AM GMT
By María Feijóo
Indian Ocean’s yellowfin tuna stock faces imminent threat of overfishing crisis

In stark contrast to the relative health of other oceans, the Indian Ocean is currently grappling with a looming overfishing crisis, particularly concerning its yellowfin tuna stock, explained Victor Restrepo, vice president for science at the International Seafood Sustainability Foundation (ISSF). 

Data reveals that the yellowfin tuna population in the Indian Ocean is in a perilous state, “with conditions expected to deteriorate further unless immediate action is taken to rectify the situation,” said Restrepo, who is also a member of the Marine Stewardship Council’s technical advisory board.

SEP 1411:52 AM GMT
By María Feijóo
Seafood consumption trends: what’s next?

The world’s seafood consumption landscape is bracing itself for significant changes over the next 12 to 18 months, said Miguel Barreiro, senior vice president of consumer intelligence company NielsenIQ.

These changes are set to be driven by “a blend of economic factors, evolving consumer preferences, and ongoing global instability due to inflation that continues to impact industries worldwide.”

SEP 1410:30 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Mexican firm Pesca Azteca set to resume tuna exports to Europe

Mexican fishing company Pesca Azteca is poised to resume its tuna exports to European markets soon, having achieved the necessary certification with the Mexican health authority COFEPRIS last July. 

The announcement was made by the company’s general manager, Evaristo Villa.

SEP 149:24 AM GMT
By María Feijóo 
Spain’s canned tuna seen as ‘relatively expensive,’ consumers seek for alternatives

The Spanish canned tuna sector, which has historically been resilient during economic downturns, is currently facing its own set of challenges, explained Miguel Barreiro, senior vice president of consumer intelligence company NielsenIQ.

“The perception of canned fish products being relatively expensive has prompted consumers to seek alternative, cost-effective options. Private label or store-brand products have seen a surge in popularity, representing 45% of total grocery spending in Spain,” he said.

SEP 148:29 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
EU’s proposed measures to prohibit products made with forced labor will impact the fishery sector

The EU’s proposal prohibiting products made with forced labor, which was published in September 2022, will have implications for the fisheries sector, according to Aldona Sek-Spirydowicz, a representative of the EU Commission’s DG GROW.

The proposed regulation, with its risk-based enforcement approach built on international standards, aims to eliminate products made with forced labor both within the EU and for products imported from non-EU countries. According to Sek-Spirydowicz, this move is not only a response to international law but also a significant step towards ethical and fair business practices.

SEP 146:09 AM GMT
By María Feijóo
Mintel: Fish substitutes surging ahead amidst stalled innovation in EU seafood sector

The European seafood industry has remained relatively stable in its offerings in the last few years, which could lead to market loss against plant-based seafood alternatives.

According to Isabel Evans, insight and innovation consultant at Mintel, over the past five years, the European seafood innovation landscape has seen “minimal changes,” with shredded tuna accounting for a significant 40% of all new product developments. 

SEP 143:50 AM GMT
By Matilde Mereghetti
Skipjack prices begin to ease, but industry hopes for further drops

After months of skyrocketing prices in the global tuna market, there appears to be some relief on the horizon. 

The cost of skipkack tuna, specifically in Bangkok, Thailand, has gradually declined from its staggering peak of $2,000 per metric ton. 

SEP 142:23 AM GMT
By María Feijóo
Satlink, Marine Instruments claim wins in Vigo Tuna Awards 

Spanish satellite communications provider Satlink and marine electronic equipment designer Marine Instruments won the top prizes at the second edition of the Tuna Awards. 

The biennial award, organized by ANFACO-CECOPESCA and Spain’s ministry of agriculture, fisheries and food, intends to highlight the tuna sector’s efforts in digitalization and sustainability and to reward innovative companies and initiatives, the organizer said.

title: Untitled
content:
Frozen shrimp inventories, primarily Ecuadorian product, in China's wholesale markets have declined following peak demand during the National Day Golden Week holiday (Oct. 1-8), according to industry sources.

Ecuadorian shrimp prices for shipping to China held steady during week 41 (Oct. 6-12) compared to the previous week, and import volumes are expected to recover in the coming months, according to Undercurrent News' latest weekly price assessment.

The cost-and-freight (CFR) price for the mainstream 30/40 semi-IQF size stood at $4.60-$4.80 per kilogram -- levels that many importers had been reluctant to accept in previous weeks. However, declining inventories are expected to compel restocking in the near term.

Here are brine IQF products in 12-kilogram bulk packaging.

Brine-IQF retail packs in 1.4-1.8kg packaging also largely leveled off, as shown below.

"Inventory has been drawn down a lot in recent weeks, and it's time to restock," a Shanghai-based importer told Undercurrent.

Global shrimp price tracker
Explore

"Ecuadorian offers have been firm for quite some time, with no signs of price cuts. It's worth noting that domestic wholesale spot prices haven't increased, despite faster product turnover. So you may see inventories tighten at some point in October or November," he added.

Another Beijing-based importer said buyers are taking a wait-and-see approach, looking for the right moment to place orders.

Speaking of inventories, he estimated that China currently holds around 6,000-8,000 containers, a level he considers to be a median.

"Only if Ecuadorian prices drop will China's inventories start to be drawn down more quickly," he said.

Brine-IQF in 1.4-1.8kg individual retail packaging is shown below.

Price movements for brine IQF bulk pack (12kg per box) shrimp are also shown below.

Export data shows that Ecuador's shrimp shipments to China fell 15% year-on-year to 48,484 metric tons in August, a marked reversal from earlier months when exports had rebounded. 

The pullback validates weeks of market chatter suggesting Chinese buyers were becoming increasingly reluctant to accept higher prices for Ecuadorian shrimp. Average unit values to China still rose 9% to $4.79/kg, but the volume decline offset much of the value gains.

Despite the setback in China, Ecuador's overall shrimp exports continued to expand in August, rising 3% to 107,430 tons as strong demand from Western markets compensated for China's weakness. The US, Ecuador's second-largest customer, increased purchases by 22%, while European buyers showed a remarkable appetite, with Spain up 44%, Italy surging 49% and France climbing 21%.

Looking at shrimp imports in China, Europe and the US below, you can see Ecuador's dominance in the former and growth in the latter two. 

Examining EU imports across the five main farmed and wild shrimp customs codes, Ecuador's level stands at 140,092t out of 371,419t through July, representing a 38% market share. In all of 2024, the EU imported 182,348t from Ecuador of a total of 621,861t, or 29%. 

Then, in the US, where Ecuador has a strong tariff advantage over Asian competitors in direct and indirect sales, the Latin country's market share is also rising. 

Through July, the US has imported 289.98 million pounds of shrimp from Ecuador, of a total of 1.07m, so a market share of 27%. In all of 2024, the level was 411.96m pounds of a 1.68m total, so a 24% share. 

Ecuador farm-gate prices up on larger sizes 

After a period of stability, farm-gate prices for larger shrimp in Ecuador rose once again in week 41.

Prices for 20/30-count shrimp edged up by $0.05/kg, while 30/40 count and 40/50-count sizes each increased by $0.10/kg in the latest week.

In contrast, smaller 70/80-count and 80/100-count vannamei have depreciated, losing around $0.10/kg in value as the market steadily diverges by size.

According to one source with a farmer, the country's ongoing protests and violence in many coastal states are having a knock-on effect on the supply and cost of input ingredients.

"Half of Ecuador is currently paralyzed, and the effects are already beginning to show in the animal feed industry," he said. "The continued removal of the diesel subsidy is causing losses in several sectors, with rising mortality rates and mounting production costs.

"As a result, prices are expected to climb further, and producers are facing tighter margins. While the unrest is largely concentrated in the Sierra region, the coast remains calm, for now."

Another Undercurrent contact, with an exporter, said that many local packing plants are also struggling to procure enough shrimp to process.

"Thus, they're raising prices in order to secure supply and meet demand," he said.

In China, vannamei shrimp prices have continued their ongoing surge in week 41, according to Undercurrent's latest sourcing data.

There has been a sharp CNY 4 ($0.56)/kg increase on 60-count prices from Guangxi in the latest week, while all other major shrimp-producing provinces have also risen by CNY 1-2/kg.

"Prices across the country continued to rise during the late holiday period, as the Mid-Autumn Festival (Oct. 6) overlaps with the Golden Week National holiday (Oct. 1-8)," a market source told Undercurrent.

Feed group Guangdong Haid has advised its farmers to harvest before the end of the national holiday, "as demand will quickly fall after then."

China's storm season is also playing a role, hitting the nation's shrimp production hubs.

"There are reports that large shrimp are now in short supply, as another typhoon hit Zhanjiang last weekend," he continued.

The first typhoon, Typhoon Ragasa, made landfall in Guangdong province on Sept. 24, destroying thousands of greenhouses in the Yangjiang area, a hub of the province's greenhouse farming operations.

This latest typhoon, Typhoon Matmo, has now made landfall to the southwest, still in Guangdong but closer to the border with Guangxi.

title: Week 41 farm-gate shrimp roundup: Indonesia prices down after FDA bombshell, Ecuador protests tighten supply
content:
Additional reporting by Lewis Hu, Tom Seaman, Maria Feijoo and Neil Ramsden.

Indonesian farm-gate vannamei shrimp prices are falling fast again in week 41 (Oct. 6-12) as the industry scrambles to meet new import certifications to the US, according to pricing data on Undercurrent News' price portal.

After shipments from one Indonesian exporter, Bahari Makmur Sejati (BMS), were stopped for detections of very low traces of the radioactive isotope Cesium-137, the rest of the country's shrimp traders were told by the US Food and Drug Administration that they must also meet new requirements relating to the isotope by Oct. 31.

With only limited price movement from other producing countries, Undercurrent's global index for 60-count vannamei continues to hold at $3.63 per kilogram in week 41, remaining marginally below year-ago levels.

Upgrade to Pro to view

There has been no shortage of drama from other shrimp-producing countries in the latest week.

Ongoing protests against the government of Ecuador's president, Daniel Noboa, have brought parts of the country to a standstill, with 10 provinces declared to be in a state of emergency. The unrest is having an impact on supplies of both feed ingredients and shrimp to packing plants.

In China, prices have continued to rise in the latest week as the country goes through a national holiday from Oct. 1-8, while typhoon season has wreaked havoc in some of the country's biggest greenhouse production hubs down south.

For other major origins, there was little to no change in farm-gate prices for week 41, but US tariff outlooks remain uncertain for India -- where exporters are holding out for a reversal of the eye-watering 50% duty -- and Vietnam, where the threat of heavy anti-dumping duties still hovers over some of the country's largest exporters.

It means the considerable price premium for 60-count shrimp from China, Vietnam and Thailand since the imposition of the new US tariff regime in early August remains in place. Shrimp from these origins are all trading at roughly 30% higher value compared to material from India, Indonesia and Ecuador, according to Undercurrent's price tracking data.

Indonesia in crisis after FDA announcement

Vannamei shrimp prices in Indonesia's East Java have responded to the FDA's latest announcement by falling abruptly, reversing the previous week's rise and returning to their rock-bottom level.

The benchmark 30-count size has slipped IDR 2,000 ($0.12)/kg, while the 40-count category also dropped by IDR 1,000/kg. Similar drops in value have been reported across all weights.

"[Prices] keep going down because packers are still in a wait-and-see mode, reducing purchases," Gerry Kamahara, whose company, Aqua Gallan Karyacipta, works with small-scale Indonesian farmers, told Undercurrent.

"Now, farmers try to sell large sizes because it’s where the money comes from. We avoid small sizes, as we need to sell larger shrimps to make money."

While a shortage of these smaller sizes played a role in last week's price recovery, Kamahara said the overall trend and outlook for Indonesia's farm-gate values is still downwards.

There remains confusion among packers over whether the Oct. 31 date introduced by the FDA is a ship-by or arrive-by date, with an arrive-by date seen as completely impossible for the sector to meet, Undercurrent reported previously.

The latest FDA directive is aimed at the island of Java and the Lampung Province on the island of Sumatra, which account for "99.9% of Indonesian shrimp exports to the US," a processing executive told Undercurrent.

"Doesn't it feel like a quasi-embargo already?"

Ecuador uptick on larger sizes

After a period of stability, prices for larger shrimp out of Ecuador rose once again in week 41.

Prices for 20/30-count shrimp edged up by $0.05/kg, while 30/40 count and 40/50-count sizes each increased by $0.10/kg in the latest week.

In contrast, smaller 70/80-count and 80/100-count vannamei have depreciated, losing around $0.10/kg in value as the market steadily diverges by size.

According to one source with a farmer, the country's ongoing protests and violence in many coastal states are having a knock-on effect on the supply and cost of input ingredients.

"Half of Ecuador is currently paralyzed, and the effects are already beginning to show in the animal feed industry," he said. "The continued removal of the diesel subsidy is causing losses in several sectors, with rising mortality rates and mounting production costs.

"As a result, prices are expected to climb further, and producers are facing tighter margins. While the unrest is largely concentrated in the Sierra region, the coast remains calm, for now."

Another Undercurrent contact, with an exporter, said that many local packing plants are also struggling to procure enough shrimp to process.

"Thus, they're raising prices in order to secure supply and meet demand," he said.

Indian prices flat amid harvests, outlook uncertain

Vannamei shrimp prices in India's main farming region of Andhra Pradesh were unchanged in week 41, having been steadily recovering since the 50% US tariff bombshell announced in August.

With disease issues rife and survival rates low, large 30-count shrimp continue to command a significant premium over all other sizes in the country.

"Prices remain steady for both black tiger and vannamei, both which 70% of the second crop has been harvested," Sheraz Anwar, director of exporter Abad Overseas told Undercurrent.

"Vannamei is in a new situation now with the tariffs, so we need to see how prices move with lower harvests through the end of the year until March next year."

His views echo those of exporters at the recent India International Seafood Show, where the message was that the full impact of the 50% tariff on farm-gate prices will not be felt until December.

Many Indian exporters are continuing to see out contracts made before the additional rate was announced, although US importers are telling them to slow down deliveries and keep the shrimp on their books for longer in the hope of a breakthrough in negotiations between India and the US that will see tariffs sharply reduced.

Prospects for black tiger, which is far less dependent on the US market, are much brighter, according to Anwar.

"We should see prices moving up in four weeks at least for black tiger as Chinese demand remains quite consistent, though export prices remain flat," he said.

China prices march upwards

Vannamei shrimp prices have continued their ongoing surge in week 41, according to Undercurrent's latest sourcing data.

There has been a sharp CNY 4 ($0.56)/kg increase on 60-count prices from Guangxi in the latest week, while all other major shrimp-producing provinces have also risen by CNY 1-2/kg.

"Prices across the country continued to rise during the late holiday period, as mid-auturn festival (Oct. 6) overlaps with the Golden Week National holiday(Oct 1-8)," a market source told Undercurrent.

Feed group Guangdong Haid has advised its farmers to harvest before the end of the national holiday, "as demand will quickly fall after then," the source added.

China's storm season is also playing a role, hitting the nation's shrimp production hubs.

"There are reports that large shrimp are now in short supply, as another typhoon hit Zhanjiang last weekend," he continued.

The first typhoon, Typhoon Ragasa, made landfall in Guangdong province on Sept. 24, destroying thousands of greenhouses in the Yangjiang area, a hub of the province's greenhouse farming operations.

This latest typhoon, Typhoon Matmo, has now made landfall to the southwest, still in Guangdong but closer to the border with Guangxi.

Vietnam prices for both largest, smallest shrimp edge up

Vannamei shrimp farm-gate prices in Vietnam remain relatively stable at prices well above the levels of Ecuador, India and Indonesia, with further increases expected at the extreme ends of the size spectrum.

"The trading pace of whiteleg shrimp to major processing factories remains relatively stable compared to last week," a market source told Undercurrent on Oct. 6. "However, overall shrimp production remains low, and the farming area for all shrimp sizes is expected to stay limited in the coming weeks."

"This week, farm-gate prices of whiteleg shrimp increased slightly for sizes 30-and 100-counts per kilogram, while prices for size 50-80 counts/kg remained stable," he concluded.

The latest pricing data available from Vietnamese data platform Tomota (below) only extends up to week 40 (Sept. 29-Oct. 5), but you can see how 30-count shrimp are now being bought at a huge 22% premium over sizes 40-count and below.

Processors have raised purchase prices for larger sizes in recent weeks to attract supply amid ongoing constraints in farming areas producing 30-count/kg shrimp and larger specifications.

For Vietnamese black tiger shrimp, there's a similar phenomenon, with the largest 20-count shrimp now trading at an annual high, and a price point roughly 30% higher than all other sizes below 30-count.

No change in Thailand

Finally, vannamei farm-gate prices in Thailand were once again unchanged in week 41, according to Undercurrent data.

The 60-, 70- and 80-count size categories have held steady w-o-w, maintaining the plateau first reached in early August, after the new US tariff regime had been confirmed.

title: Updated US forced labor report castigates but doesn’t downgrade Taiwan, Thailand
content:
Multiple seafood-producing countries, including Taiwan and Thailand, have maintained their previous rankings in the US State Department's 2025 Trafficking in Persons (TIP) Report.

The report, which provides a rating of the prevalence of forced labor and human trafficking in each of the world's nations, was released Monday (Sept. 29), three months late due to the fact that most of the staff responsible for preparing it were fired by the administration of US president Donald Trump, according to Reuters.

The report notes serious labor issues in the seafood industries of numerous countries that export to the US, including especially in Burma, China, Nicaragua, Papua New Guinea, Russia and Venezuela. All are identified as Tier 3 countries, the worst ranking in the report.

A Chinese fishing vessel known to belong to a company linked to using Uyghur forced labor. Photo courtesy of the Outlaw Ocean Project

However,  despite mounting calls from non-governmental organizations for a downgrade, led by US-based advocacy organization Global Labor Justice, Taiwan has maintained its Tier 1 status as a country of least concern.

"Insufficient inspection protocols and the siloing of authorities and responsibilities within different ministries continued to impede efforts to identify, investigate and prosecute forced labor of migrant workers, including those on fishing vessels in Taiwan's highly vulnerable distant-water fleet," the report said.

As many as 20,800 migrants are working onboard more than 2,000 Taiwanese distant-water vessels, and an additional 12,300 working on coastal vessels, and that many are victims of abuse, the report estimated.

FREE READ Labor activists criticize MSC for enabling abuses in fisheries

Migrant workers aboard Taiwanese fishing vessels "have experienced non- or under-payment of wages, long working hours, physical abuse, lack of food or medical care, denial of sleep, substandard safety equipment and poor living conditions while indebted to complex, multinational brokerage networks through the continued imposition of recruitment fees and deposits," the report found.

Additionally, they have been subject to "coercive tactics as threats of physical violence, beatings, withholding of food and water, retention of identity documents, wage deductions and non-contractual compulsory sharing of vessel operational costs to retain their labor."

In 2024, Taiwanese authorities increased their efforts to protect seafood industry workers, but the country's legal framework is inadequate and enforcement of existing laws is insufficient to address the labor issues widespread in Taiwan's fishing industry, according to the report.

"Vessel owners and operators take advantage of maritime jurisdictional complexities and ambiguities to perpetrate these crimes with relative impunity; they also frequently change their fishing vessels' names and nationalities of registry to evade detection by law enforcement," it said. 

Nevertheless, Taiwan's 16th straight Tier 1 ranking in the TIP report means the US government determined Taiwan made a sufficient effort to address human trafficking and met the minimum standards of the US Trafficking Victims Protection Act.

Thailand remains Tier 2

Thailand, which has also been the subject of a longstanding campaign on behalf of human rights groups to address labor issues in the nation's seafood industry, was once again placed in the Tier 2 list, which is composed of countries that have fully met human rights standards, but which the US government considers to have made a significant effort at improvement. 

However, the report warned of numerous labor-related problems in Thailand's seafood industry.

"Vessel owners, brokers, and senior vessel crew subject Thai, Burmese, Cambodian, Vietnamese and Indonesian men and boys to forced labor on Thai and foreign-owned fishing boats," it said.

"Some are paid little or irregularly, sometimes as infrequently as once a year, incur debts from brokers and employers, work as much as 18 to 20 hours per day for seven days a week, and are not provided adequate food, water or medical supplies. Some boat captains threaten, beat, and drug fishermen to work longer and sell fishermen drugs as a means to generate additional debt."

Burmese crew on a Thai fishing vessel. Photo courtesy of Shutterstock.

Workers often face wage deductions for confusing, unavoidable or nonexistent reasons and frequently have their identity documents taken from them and then have trouble leaving their vessels and returning home as a result. 

Recent reform efforts have improved the labor situation in Thailand's seafood industry, but a legislative effort driven by the sector to repeal those reforms -- including adding exceptions to minimum age requirements and removing enhanced penalties for child labor and forced labor violations in seafood processing -- is a threat to progress, the report asserted.

Additionally, Thai authorities do not conduct sufficient checks for labor violations or consistently have interpreters available for interviewing foreign crewmembers onboard fishing vessels, and the government "has never reported identifying trafficking victims as a result of labor inspections of fishing vessels," it found.

Underhanded behavior by Thai companies is ignored or exacerbated due to the corrosive influence of corruption, the report said.

"Smugglers, brokers, employers, and others exploit Thai and migrant workers in labor trafficking in commercial fishing and related industries, it said. "Credible reports indicate some corrupt officials protect … fishing vessel owners from law enforcement actions, inspections and prosecutions and collude with traffickers. Some government officials profit from bribes and direct involvement in extortion from and exploitation of migrants."

Other countries listed

Other seafood-producing and exporting nations achieving Tier 1 status in the 2025 report include Argentina, Australia, the Bahamas, Canada, Chile, France, Iceland, South Korea, the Philippines, Spain, the UK and the US. However, the Philippines and South Korea were cited as having some labor trafficking among migrant workers, especially in their fishing sectors.

Other Tier 2 countries included Bangladesh, Colombia, Ecuador, Ghana, India, Indonesia, Ireland, Italy, Japan, Mexico, New Zealand, Norway, Peru, Sri Lanka and Vietnam. However, Ghana, Indonesia, South Korea, Peru and Vietnam were each specifically called out for labor issues in their fishing and seafood processing industries.

Additionally, earlier this year, Ecuador's aquaculture and shrimp-processing sector was called to task by Monterey Bay Aquarium's Seafood Watch program for the prevalence of forced labor, human trafficking and hazardous child labor risks across the industry. In a report called

Tier 2 Watch List countries with a significant amount of seafood exports included Brazil, Fiji, the Solomon Islands and South Africa. 

A Ghanaian fisheries officer. Credit: FCWC Secretariat

'Sea Change' report

This year's TIP Report includes a special section titled "Sea Change: Combating Forced Labor in Fishing and Seafood Processing."

The section warns that the fishing, aquaculture, and seafood processing industries have "a darker side" related to the exploitation of migrant workers in forced labor through deception, wage withholding, debt-based coercion, and physical, psychological, sexual and other abuses "facilitated by some influential seafood companies, recruitment agencies, and complicit officials."

"The seafood caught and processed through these practices finds its way into markets all over the world," it said.

UN High Seas Treaty set to come into effect in early 2026

Forced labor is also used for environmental destruction, including ecologically damaging fishing practices and the killing of endangered species.

The report criticized the use of flags of convenience and the switching off of vessel-tracking systems by fishing vessels around the globe.

It called on global governments to "prioritize seafarer victim identification and protection in national anti-trafficking action plans and policies, including by training frontline officers and increasing random inspections of fishing vessels, seafood processing facilities, and recruitment agencies, and by referring findings to law enforcement."

"They can also pursue complementary accountability measures, such as import restrictions, sanctions and visa restrictions," it said. 

For their part, seafood companies "should ensure workers' rights to freedom of association, collective bargaining, effective grievance mechanisms and access to communication technology at sea," the report said.

The seafood industry "should also strengthen due diligence by mapping seafood supply chains with worker input, conducting risk assessments and implementing fair purchasing practices."

Otherwise, the report warned forced labor in fishing and seafood processing "will continue to distort competitiveness in the seafood sector against the backdrop of increasingly fragile marine ecosystems."

title: Ecuadorian woman who led search for missing fishing crew murdered in broad daylight
content:
Mariua Choez, a spokeswoman for the families of 21 fishermen who disappeared at sea aboard the "Patricia Lynn," was shot and killed on Sept. 25 in Manta, Ecuador, in what appears to be a targeted attack, reports Primicias.

Witnesses said gunmen arrived at Choez's food stall in a pickup truck and opened fire before fleeing. A burned vehicle, believed to have been used in the attack, was found nearby shortly after.

Choez had become a key voice in the search for the fishing vessel that disappeared on Dec. 21, 2024, after departing from Manta and sending a distress signal. No trace of the boat or the fishermen has been found.

Her murder has shocked the local community and devastated the families she represented, according to the newspaper. Authorities have not named any suspects, though the investigation remains ongoing.

The killing comes amid a broader surge in violence across Ecuador's coastal regions.

title: Canadian lobster industry unimpressed by latest DFO enforcement report
content:
While Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) appears to be making headway on cracking down on illegal lobster fishing on the country's east coast, the commercial harvester group that's been among the most vocal in its complaints is not yet ready to hand out gold stars.

DFO boasts that nearly 12,000 illegal lobsters have been returned to the ocean, 1,235 traps have been seized and 61 plants have been inspected in Atlantic Canada since June 1 as a result of beefed up enforcement efforts, as reported by Undercurrent News. 

"We're happy to see some enforcement, compared to the last number of years where we literally had none. But while the numbers that DFO quotes sound good, compared to how many traps are in St. Mary's Bay and the millions of pounds that are being removed, it's just a drop in the bucket," Colin Sproul, president of the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance (UFCA), told Undercurrent in a recent interview.

The real success will be measured by how many charges result in convictions, said Sproul, who has been the voice of commercial lobster harvesters in Nova Scotia and is particularly outspoken about illegal activity at Saulnierville Harbour, in St. Mary's Bay. It's 54 kilometers north of Yarmouth, one of the southernmost points in Nova Scotia.

DFO has not said how many formal charges have been laid as a result of the enforcement activity, saying only that investigations are ongoing. If charges are laid, convictions and penalties will have to be determined through a formal court process.

The Saulnierville Harbour location borders Lobster Fishing Area (LFA) 34, Canada's most prolific with 15,020 metric tons landed in 2024. It's next season begins on the last Monday of November and continues until May 31 of the following year.

Illegal activity has worsened in 2025, particularly at the wharf in Saulnierville, where about 25 boats were engaged in illegal lobster fishing in August, Sproul told Undercurrent at the time. 

The UFCA has been monitoring the activity using drones, as it did throughout the summer of 2024. The illegal harvesters are setting hundreds of traps every night and landing thousands of pounds of lobster, Sproul said. 

A DFO internal memo in 2024 estimated that anywhere from 10% to 30% of lobster landings in the region are unreported, according to a report by CBC News.

Some suggest the problem equates to a CAD 176 million to CAD 681m ($127.9m-$494.5m) annual loss for the industry. That figure was published in a social media post on the Gulf News Fishing Facebook page, citing information provided by a Chatbot via the site AIinvest, a US-based investment company that uses Artificial Intelligence to research and source financial news and stock trends.

A post in September on the Gulf Fishing News Facebook page cites information from a Chatbox via a US-based online financial research services organization

However, the Lobster Council of Canada (LCC) cautions that evaluating the dollar-value impact of illegal lobster fishing is very difficult.

"All we can do is estimate," LCC executive director Geoff Irvine told Undercurrent in an email. "For example, if a harvester sells part of their catch for cash, that money still gets into the economy. It is just not recorded and not taxed, and the landings may not be recorded."

He continued: "If a buyer buys for cash, then that lobster also moves through their plant, is sold and then is likely taxed as are all profits. Putting a dollar value on the impact is almost impossible."

It is not illegal in Canada for a licensed commercial harvester to sell his or her catch for cash, as long as the lobster has been caught legally, and is accounted for in logbook or dockside monitoring reports. What is illegal is fishing lobsters out of season and/or failing to report catches.

The problem continues

The issue is mired in the debate over First Nations' rights to a moderate livelihood fishery. Illegal lobster fishing extends beyond St. Mary's Bay to St. Peter's Bay in Nova Scotia's Cape Breton Island, and to other Maritime provinces. However, the spotlight is shining mainly on the harbor in Saulnierville, which is used heavily by members of the Sipknetakik First Nation.

Tensions in the area grew so severe in 2024 that some fisheries officers moved their families out of the area due to threats they were receiving, according to Sproul. In late 2024, Sproul warned about potential violence in southwest Nova Scotia if the fisheries minister did not act. 

Recent enforcement efforts by DFO don't seem to be creating a huge deterrent at that location, said Sproul, who went so far as to accuse some government bureaucrats of aiding the illegal activity.

Earlier this year, DFO installed a locked gate at the Saulnierville harbor, requiring a key pass to gain access. However, it seems the key passes have been given only to members of the First Nation, according to Sproul.

Licensed commercial lobster harvesters from the area, who would typically use that wharf during the fall and winter fishing season, are wondering whether they will also get access, Sproul said.

A DFO employee also removed a camera that the UFCA had set up on a pole at the harbor to monitor out-of-season activity there, said Sproul.

"So these are the types of actions that we see individual bureaucrats within the department performing to facilitate the legal activity," he said.

Drone footage posted on the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance Facebook page on Oct. 3, 2025, showed what appeared to be crates of lobster being loaded into a truck on the wharf in Saulnierville, Nova Scotia, during closed season. Screenshot from UFCA Facebook page

The fencing and access gate were installed to improve safety and security at the harbor for authorized users, and to ensure compliance with harbor rules of operations, DFO said in a statement to Undercurrent on Sept. 10.

"Users who have signed the Small Craft Harbours Berthage Agreement to use the Saulniverville harbour, or who have otherwise been permitted by DFO to conduct maintenance on the wharf, will be provided access," the federal agency added.

"Fishery officers have been present in Saulnierville as part of their ongoing patrol efforts," DFO said in response to the criticism. "Their activities include inspection of traps and catch, education of harvesters on licence conditions, and actions such as the seizure and release of lobster when necessary."

Meanwhile, negotiations between DFO and the Sipekne'katik around the First Nation's fishing rights continue.

"The department will continue to engage with Sipekne'katik to discuss the implementation of their right to fish in pursuit of a moderate livelihood during the commercial fishing season, as the department has done with other First Nation communities across Atlantic Canada and Quebec," DFO offered in another statement.

However, details about those negotiations, including dates, proposals and topics of discussion, remain confidential, the agency told Undercurrent.

Report called on increased dockside presence

A report by a Canadian parliamentary committee -- the standing committee on Fisheries and Oceans  -- in late 2024, made several recommendations to curb the lobster poaching problem, as well as other illegal fishing.

It called on DFO to increase its dockside monitoring efforts and increase the number of species subject to the surveillance, such as lobster and other high-value species with low abundance.

Currently, Newfoundland and Labrador is the only Atlantic Canadian province that has a dockside monitoring program to track lobster landings.

The report also suggested that DFO implement modern technology and computer systems for data collection, such as a digital and standardized catch register for all Canadian fishers, so that reporting requirements are more standardized across the country, as reported by Undercurrent.

The report was delivered to former fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier, for review. However, political changes in Canada through the fall and winter, including the resignation of Lebouthillier and the appointment of new fisheries minister Joanne Thompson, as well as a federal election in April, 2025, delayed a formal response by the minister.

Thompson has not yet officially endorsed any of the recommendations of the committee's report.

title: Southwest Atlantic squid fleet linked to human rights abuses
content:
Hundreds of industrial fishing vessels fishing for squid in the Southwest Atlantic are not only driving a keystone species towards collapse but also exposing workers to human rights abuses, according to a new investigation by the Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF).

Crew members from Indonesian and Philippine backgrounds reported violence, intimidation, wage deductions and grueling hours aboard primarily Chinese-owned vessels. Nearly two-thirds of these ships have been linked to deaths or assaults, alongside reports of shark finning and the killing of marine mammals, the NGO said.

In the EJF documentary, one worker reported he had to have several fingers partially amputated after 18-hour shifts in a Chinese vessel's freezer, and another said he would get beaten for small mistakes.

With minimal oversight, seafood tied to such abuses may be entering major markets in the EU, North America and the UK, according to EJF.

Image of a penguin on board a Chinese squid jigging vessel. Photo: EJF.

Argentine squid sustains dolphins, whales, seabirds and key fisheries such as hake and tuna, while providing millions in revenue for Argentina. Yet, fishing hours by Chinese vessels in "Mile 201" -- just beyond the national boundary -- increased 85% between 2019 and 2024, even as catches declined.

According to the NGO, the exploitation of this fishery, with little regulation in place, is almost completely uncontrolled, putting the entire ecosystem at risk.

In 2023, it provided 12.2% of the global squid catch, and fishing pressure in the unregulated high seas fishery is over four times greater than within the adjacent regulated Argentine waters, EJF claimed.

Photo: EJF.

"Without urgent action, we are heading for disaster," said Steve Trent, EJF CEO.

"Overfishing and climate breakdown are placing enormous pressure on this keystone species, while those responsible -- primarily from China -- commit shocking human rights abuses with impunity. A collapse could happen extremely rapidly, triggering cascading impacts on marine life. Governments must act now to bring regulation, transparency and accountability to this lawless fishery."

He stressed governments must work together to protect them, or risk a catastrophe that will reverberate far beyond these waters.

"First and foremost, they must endorse and implement the Global Charter for Fisheries Transparency, a set of low- or no-cost actions that any government can take to drive progress towards legal, ethical and sustainable fisheries," he said.

Alfonso Miranda, president of the Committee for the Sustainable Management of Giant Squid in the South Pacific (CALAMASUR), acknowledged that the report's findings should not only draw attention to what is happening in the South Atlantic but also in the Pacific.

"This concern should extend to those of us on the Pacific side, given that the fishing practices are exactly the same. In addition to the unfair treatment of crew members, we should also be concerned about the lack of scientific progress in defining catch limits that ensure the sustainability of what is caught on the high seas," he said.

He added that, in the South Pacific, although there is a regional fisheries management organization, very little progress has been made in adopting a stock assessment that would allow for recommending the level of exploitation for Asian industrial vessels operating on the high seas.

Pascual Aguilera, leader of the Chilean national coordinator of jumbo flying squid producers, reacted by drawing attention to the role that Latin American ports and shipyards play in providing logistical facilities that facilitate the operations of these vessels.

"These vessels need our countries to organize their operations. If they don't enter Peru, they enter Chile or Uruguay. They have no other options. Therefore, it is necessary for our governments to develop real coordinated actions to establish a common standard that does not make us complicit in abuses. Our fellow Indonesian and Filipino crew members need our Latin American solidarity," Aguilera said.

title: Canada continues crackdown on illegal lobster fishing
content:
Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) reports having seized 1,032 illegal lobster traps and released 4,463 lobsters since June 1 in St. Mary's Bay, in Lobster Fishing Area (LFA) 34, on the southwest shore of the province Nova Scotia.

LFA 34 is Canada's most prolific fishing area for lobster, responsible for 17,367 of Canada's roughly 95,000 metric tons landed throughout Canada during the 2023-24 season, based on figures shared with Undercurrent News by the Lobster Council of Canada (LCC).

The area has also been a hotspot for illegal lobster fishing, creating tensions between Indigenous harvesters who stand by their right to a moderate livelihood fishery for food, social and ceremonial (FSC) purposes, and commercial harvesters who say some First Nations are abusing those rights by landing substantial amounts of lobster and selling the catch for profit.

Tensions grew so bad that some DFO officers in southwest Nova Scotia refused to work in the summer of 2024, citing concerns for their safety, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

The Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance (UFCA), a group that represents licensed lobster harvesters in Nova Scotia, has long complained that DFO has not done enough to curb the poaching. While the UFCA welcomes DFOs latest reports on enforcement efforts, the real success will be measured by how many of those charges will result in convictions, UFCA president Colin Sproul told Undercurrent Wednesday (Sept. 3).

Boat seized, four arrested in latest enforcement effort

In the most recent incident, DFO officers boarded a fishing vessel at sea on Aug. 27 and charged four more individuals with violations of the federal Fisheries Act. The charges included fishing with unauthorized traps and fishing with sunken gear.

Fisheries officers seized 61 traps and nine crates of lobster, and seized and released 1,088 lobsters, DFO said. The fishing vessel connected to the arrests was also seized.

DFO officials also arrested four people a day earlier (on Aug. 26) for fisheries violations. Officers seized 58 lobster traps and nine crates, and seized and released 1,017 lobsters in that incident.

The 2025 commercial season for LFA 34 opens at the end of November 2024 and closed on May 31, 2025. But Indigenous harvesters are authorized by DFO to catch lobsters outside of the commercial season, in accordance with a 1990 Supreme Court of Canada ruling -- known as the Sparrow decision --  for a moderate livelihood fishery, for food, social and ceremonial (FSC) purposes.

Illegal lobster fishing problem grows worse in Canada

However, it is illegal to sell or trade catches meant for FSC purposes, and violators are subject to penalties under Canada's Fisheries Act, the DFO press release stated.

"Fishery officers are working to ensure this fishery can proceed without interference. Anyone caught selling, buying, or offering to buy or sell FSC-caught lobster may be arrested, have their catch and gear seized, and be charged," the DFO press release stated.

Meanwhile, DFO also continues to monitor lobster fishing activity beyond southwest Nova Scotia.

DFO officers carried out a two-day blitz in LFA 25, which spans from the southeast coast of New Brunswick to the western shores of Prince Edward Island.

"The goal was to remind harvesters of the importance of complying with regulations and the conditions of their licences, and to educate on and enforce marine mammal regulations," stated DFO in a Sept. 2 press release.

Officers inspected 180 vessels and 206 lobster traps, and issued 27 written warnings for offenses like failing to complete crew registries, electronic logbooks and harvester registrations, DFO reported. Eight tickets were issued for possession of berried females.

FREE READ Canadian fisheries officers add body armor, cameras following violent lobster season

Five lobster traps were seized, and one case is still under investigation, DFO said.

As many as 20 people in DFO's Maritime region were convicted of lobster fishing violations in the first six months of 2025, with fines ranging from CAD 1,000 ($737) to CAD 12,000, as previously reported by Undercurrent. 

"Fishery officers continue to have a strong presence on the water, as well as on and off the wharf to promote and enforce compliance with regulations and conditions of license, to support the sustainability and orderly management of the fisheries," DFO comments on its website.

"It is important to note that enforcement activity is not always visible, and it may not look the way people expect it to look," the agency added.

title: Daily recap: Live from GSF 2025; Kennemervis dissolves; Russia warns of ban on Chilean seafood
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Tuesday, Sept. 2:

GSF 2025: Trump gov't will pursue tariffs 'whatever it takes, wherever it takes us'; US shrimp consumption will soon be impacted

Undercurrent News is reporting live from the Global Shrimp Forum, held every September in Utrecht, the Netherlands. 

Kennemervis Groep no more: Mayonna to close after Werner Larsson sale

Mayonna, a Dutch retail-focused seafood processor, will shut down by mid-October 2025, drawing the curtain on more than two decades in business.

Russia warns of ban on Chilean seafood by end of September

Russia's agricultural watchdog, Rosselkhoznadzor, has indicated plans to suspend imports of Chilean fish, citing alleged labeling and paperwork violations.

New partnership targets large-scale use of insect protein for Ecuador shrimp feed

On the opening day of the GSF, BioMar Group, Innovafeed and French retailer Auchan have announced a significant industry commitment: the large-scale integration of insect protein into commercial shrimp feed in Ecuador.

Week 36 farm-gate shrimp roundup: Vietnam, Thai premium grows, India to go small with second crop

Global vannamei shrimp prices are generally holding flat in week 36 (Sept. 1-7) of 2025 as US tariff impacts dampen support in what is usually a lean period for the industry, according to Undercurrent's global shrimp farm-gate price round-up.

Cartels hijack Ecuador's shrimp heartland, threaten global supply chain

Ecuador's shrimp industry -- the world's largest producer of farmed shrimp -- is being battered by a deadly combination of gang violence, cartel infiltration, and adverse weather, Undercurrent has learned. 

Importers push to limit FDA alert for radioactive shrimp from Indonesia

Gunster, a major US law firm with 340 attorneys, is pushing the US Food and Drug Administration to edit its import alert that blocks all shrimp from Indonesia's Bahari Makmur Sejati.

China tilapia prices fall again in Guangdong, Guangxi

Tilapia farm-gate prices in some southern China provinces continued to fall in week 36 of 2025, as farmers sharply reduced stocking in response to prolonged market weakness.

title: Spanish seafood firm linked to illegal fishing operation in Gambia
content:
A year-long investigation has tied Chinese-controlled trawlers operating illegally in Gambian waters to Hansen Seafood, a processing plant owned by Spanish conglomerate Congelados Maravilla, reports the Gambia Journal.

At least 520 metric tons of fish processed at Hansen Seafood were exported to Spain in 2023, with catches linked to illegal fishing in zones reserved for artisanal fishermen. The fleet of trawlers responsible -- known locally as the Majilac fleet -- also used banned fine-mesh nets, satellite data and enforcement records show.

One such vessel struck and killed artisanal fishermen in March 2024, with no charges filed.

Congelados Maravilla, which acquired Hansen Seafood in 2022, said it ceased purchasing from the Majilac fleet last year but acknowledged previously exporting their catch under inherited contracts. The company denies owning the trawler fleet.

title: Conflicting rules force Norwegian salmon haulers to break law, industry says
content:
The Norwegian Logistics Association (NLF) has warned that the country's salmon haulers are being forced to break the law because of conflicting regulations from multiple agencies.

Norwegian investigation finds wounded salmon illegally shipped to Europe

To prevent ice-packed salmon from creating runoff of meltwater, fat and blood residues during transit, transporters must freeze fish at minus 10 to minus 20 degrees Celsius.

However, Norway's Food Safety Authority requires fresh fish to be transported at zero to four degrees, while the Public Roads Administration demands cargo to be secured to prevent runoff. Ferry companies refuse vessels leaking fish water due to safety hazards.

"No matter how we twist and turn it, we break the law," said Stein Inge Larsen, a transporter with over 30 years' experience, calling the situation a "cat-and-mouse game" between transporters and three regulatory agencies.

NLF proposes sealed boxes with absorbent material as a solution, costing an additional NOK 0.30 ($0.03) to NOK 1.00 per box. The industry has resisted the added expense.

"Transporters cannot be held responsible for problems they cannot control," said NLF CEO Knut Gravrak. The association intends to intensify dialogue with authorities to resolve the issue, he added.
