title: Catch the Current episode 43: Alaska on the brain
content:
Grab yourself some hot cocoa and get cozy. We're checking in with Alaska!

Undercurrent News editorial director Cliff White joins the podcast this week to share some M&A updates from the Alaska salmon and pollock space. Plus, reporter Jacob Resneck is back from Anchorage, where he attended the Alaska Seafood Marketing Institute's "All Hands on Deck" meeting. 

Listen to the latest episode below:

Thank you to our sponsor: Wisefish.

Subscribe now! Catch the Current is available on YouTube, Spotify, Amazon  Music, iHeartRadio, Pandora and other major podcast streaming platforms. Don't see Catch the Current on your favorite app? Reach out to podcasts@undercurrentnews.com.

Don't have time to listen? Find a full transcript of season 1, episode 43 of Catch the Current below:

Amanda Buckle (AB): You're listening to Catch the Current, the coolest seafood podcast out there, from the team at Undercurrent News, your trusted source for seafood prices, news and data. I'm Amanda Buckle.

Lorin Castiglione (LC): And I'm Lorin Castiglione. You're looking awfully tan this time of year.

AB: Thank you for noticing. I just got back from Turks & Caicos, where I ate my little seafoodie heart out.

LC: Good for you.

AB: My husband and I are celebrating our 10-year anniversary this year, so we planned a trip to take the kids to Jamaica, where we honeymooned ... And then, of course, Hurricane Melissa hit. We booked a Beaches property so we were able to pivot to Turks & Caicos, and we just had the best time.

It's an all-inclusive resort, so the kids were able to eat their pasta with butter, and Tom and I were able to order the crab cakes.

LC: Still keeping it real.

AB: Yeah, get the kids what they want. Exactly. But they had crab cakes, snapper. I had the spiciest clam linguine of my life.

"The spiciest clam linguine" from Beaches Turks & Caicos. Photo Credit: Amanda Buckle

But they even had a hibachi restaurant on the property. Have you ever taken your kids to hibachi?

LC: Oh, they loved it.

AB: Well, that's good. But did they eat?

LC: Maybe three or four bites of the mountain of food that they get. But a little bit, yeah.

AB: OK, good. My kids probably didn't even do that. I had to call for white rice. That's what was nice about it. I didn't feel bad about it. If I would have taken them to a restaurant here, at a hibachi restaurant at home, and they would have eaten nothing, I would have been like, "Are you guys serious?"

But since it was an all-inclusive resort, at the end of the night, I'm like, OK, whatever. We'll go next door and we'll get some pasta with butter to go.

Anywho, I'm tan, relaxed and ready to get back into the swing of things!

LC: Slow your roll there. Before we get started, a quick thank you to our sponsor, Wisefish. Wisefish has helped seafood businesses simplify the way they work for over 30 years. From aquaculture and wild catch to processing and sales, Wisefish brings everything together in one integrated platform. Just this week, they announced an agreement with First Water, an Icelandic land-based salmon farm, to implement Wisefish's new aquaculture solution -- bringing stronger transparency and control across production, cost tracking, and traceability from grow-out through processing and sales. Find out more at wisefish.com/catch-the-current.

"Mr. President, this is a photograph of the alien from the movie 'Alien.' This is what you could end up looking like if you eat some of the raw frozen shrimp being sent to the US by other countries. Now, let me tell you what I am talking about." -- US senator John Kennedy

AB: The radioactive shrimp saga continues this week. 

While there haven't been any more Cs-137-related recalls in nearly a month, and the first certified shipment of Indonesian shrimp officially hit the water, US lawmakers are still urging retailers to stop selling imported shrimp.

Republican senator John Kennedy of Louisiana -- the same fella who broke out that photograph of the alien from the 1979 horror movie "Alien" to claim that imported shrimp will turn you into a monster -- and fellow Republican lawmaker Bill Cassidy, they sent letters to Walmart, Kroger and Albertsons, urging them to prioritize shrimp from the Gulf, and requesting some information regaring the recent Cs-137 recalls.

LC: The lawmakers contend that there is a relationship between the US importing some $213 billion worth of agricultural products in 2024 and Americans spending over $550bn on imported food or foods containing imported ingredients and "serious increases" in food-safety incidents.

And, as Amanda mentioned, the topic that they are really riding on is the radiation contamination from Indonesian shrimp imports.

According to their letter, the FDA had issued eight safety alerts since August on imported shrimp from a single shrimp processor due to potential Cs-137 contamination. And they said that despite these safety concerns, the retailers in question continued to sell imported shrimp.

FREE READ US lawmaker calls for pause on all imported shrimp after radiation recalls

The letters request that the retailers provide any internal policies they have to evaluate the supply chain risk associated with imported shrimp and list any third-party certifications used to ensure that shrimp sold at their stores are free from contaminants.

AB: In happier retail-related news, as consumer preference continues to shift towards private label at retail, major US grocer Albertsons is expanding its Waterfront Bistro seafood brand with the launch of a new six-SKU fresh finfish program.

Do you buy a lot of private label? 

LC: I'd say mostly Kirkland. Kirkland brand, 100%.

AB: Agreed.

LC: Other things, I think it's on a product-by-product basis.

AB: Yeah, like I always had this thing with my mom growing up that she would buy us any brand cereal. I'm like, no, no, no. I need a certain brand cereal. The Cocoa Puffs are not the same as the Cocoa Bombs, you know?

But yeah, as a mom now shopping, I just picked up, I don't even know what, it was ShopRite's private label brand of peanut butter. So yeah, it really depends.

It was whatever was cheaper. But anyway, back to the subject at hand. I was just curious.

LC: Back to seafood.

Albertsons expanded its Waterfront Bistro line with new fresh finfish products. Photo Credit: Albertsons

AB: Yes, back to seafood. Albertsons first introduced its Waterfront Bistro brand in 2009 as a way to provide customers with a convenient, at-home version of a high-quality seafood bistro experience.

Just a few years after Albertsons "relaunched" the brand with a new, modernized logo and updated packaging, as well as an integrated marketing campaign called "Bring the Bistro Home," the line, which started with frozen finfish and shrimp, is now growing to vacuum-sealed fresh fillets of farmed Atlantic salmon, wild-caught sockeye salmon, tilapia and cod. All in an effort to make the Waterfront Bistro line a "one-stop shop" for seafood cravings.

LC: Another item to keep an eye out for at retail -- Popeye-brand seafood. Brazilian seafood processor Noronha Pescados intends to start processing salmon and other seafood products for retail in the US in early 2026, under a new partnership with a Miami-based firm.

The collaboration marks Noronha's first US-based processing venture and aims to strengthen its export business under the Popeye brand. Noronha will process, pack and distribute a wide range of internationally sourced seafood, including tuna, mahi, tilapia and shrimp, alongside its salmon line.

Brazilian firm Noronha to launch US seafood packing operation with Miami-based firm

Recall that the project initially focused on exporting branded seafood products from Brazil but was restructured this year following the US tariff announcement earlier in the year. 

AB: Guilherme Blanke, CEO of Noronha Pescados, told Undercurrent that the goal was to export branded products from Brazil, but with current tariffs, it made more sense to process in the US.

Under the agreement, the company will import raw materials, salmon from Chile, tuna from Ecuador, Vietnam and Indonesia, mahi from Peru, and tilapia from Vietnam or China, for processing and packaging in the US. The products will then be sold under the Popeye label to US retailers and foodservice clients. 

Blanke said that operations will be based in Miami, where the partner already manages seafood processing and cold-chain logistics. The company expects to finalize packaging and begin production at the Miami plant in January 2026, following the establishment of its US subsidiary, office and local team. Blanke said he could not disclose the name of the Miami-based plant until the production timeline for the new products had been fully agreed upon. 

As a seafood lover and collector of vintage Popeye memorabilia, I cannot wait to find these at my local grocery store. Read the full story on Undercurrentnews.com.

LC: You're excited about Popeye memorabilia. You know what I'm excited about? Undercurrent's new global salmon price tracker.

FREE READ UCN launches global salmon pricing tracker

Undercurrent News has launched its global salmon price tracker, providing a comprehensive view of the salmon supply chain, from farm and export levels to key wholesale markets in China, Europe and the US.

The tracker is the latest example of Undercurrent's expanding suite of species-specific data tools, following the success of our global shrimp price tracker. It brings together Undercurrent's proprietary weekly price assessments alongside verified wholesale data from major markets, allowing users to quickly compare prices across regions and species.

Through a single interactive dashboard, users can compare wholesale prices across China, France, Italy, Spain and the US. Plus, access Undercurrent's proprietary farmed and wild salmon quotations for US wholesale markets. And review export benchmarks for Norwegian salmon, Chilean salmon to Brazil and Scottish salmon delivered to UK factories. 

The great news is that the tracker is open to all users until Nov. 24, after which it will be available exclusively to UCN Pro subscribers. If you'd like to learn more about adding this tool to your subscription after Nov. 24, get in touch with us. We'll have a link in the show notes.

AB: Increasingly, farms are adopting digital tools to monitor production, track costs and ensure traceability. Wisefish provides exactly that, helping aquaculture businesses bring clarity to their operations. The platform gives transparency across cost tracking, allocation across batches, product segmentation from harvest to portioned products, and traceability from grow-out through processing, sales and delivery. Wisefish works with leading seafood companies worldwide, including First Water in Iceland and Tassal in Australia, supporting them with integrated systems that connect biological and financial data and help teams focus on smart, timely decisions that drive growth. Learn more at wisefish.com/catch-the-current.

LC: It's not a proper episode of Catch the Current without welcoming some friends. Hopping on the pod with us now is Undercurrent editorial director Cliff White, who recently checked in with some top Alaska-focused mergers and acquisitions experts.

Salmon being processed at a Silver Bay facility in Alaska. Photo courtesy of Silver Bay Seafoods.

Cliff White (CW): So, yes, I spoke with a number of finance, banking, advisory service experts and they gave me a rundown of how the M&A scene is looking for the Alaska salmon and Alaska pollock sectors and got some interesting tidbits from them.

So, for salmon, I was curious about how this year's season had impacted the near-term forecast for deals, and I had heard before speaking with these experts that maybe it wasn't the best year of runs in Alaska or overall statewide catches were down. But because the Bristol Bay sockeye season was once again so solid, it really meant that most of the companies that are still involved in the sector in a big way are actually doing pretty good, are feeling pretty good about how the season went.

They've got a good solid pack and they've sold it all and so things are looking good.

It was really interesting to hear about how consolidation has really changed the scene up there. Silver Bay Seafoods has become the big kahuna in Alaska. They've done a lot of buying and run a lot more processing operations. The push now is for quality. Before it was just a race to get all these huge runs processed.

There was a lot of fish left out for maybe too long. The quality pack wasn't that great. Now with this consolidation, there's a lot more a feeling of things are more settled.

Alaska salmon M&A update: Solid 2025 season sets up sector for success

Trident's still involved. Canfisco is still a big player in Alaska. But with things more settled after a couple of years of transition, all these companies -- and led by Silver Bay -- are really focusing on a push to improve fish quality, which they think will then improve the price they can get for their packs.

So along those lines, there's a feeling like there might be a few more smaller deals, but that things have mostly sorted themselves out.

One company mentioned as a potential acquisitor is Wild Alaska Company. They've talked about potentially stepping up.

Trident has stepped back, but they're still involved. We'll see if they sell more of their assets, but it seems like they've kind of finished up their right-sizing in Alaska of their footprint.

AB: Are you talking about Wild Alaskan Company, the company that does the direct-to-consumer seafood?

CW: I am, yes.

AB: Oh, wow.

CW: They were just founded in 2017, so they're a real new player on the scene, but they're looking to break more into retail and foodservice sales.

Images shared by Wild Alaskan Company CEO Arron Kallenberg on his LinkedIn page show new packaging.

So, potentially, they're maybe looking to get more vertically integrated. We'll see. Again, these are just people -- I wouldn't say speculating -- but using their best-informed outlook and knowledge of the market to think what might happen in terms of potential M&A.

So this is forward-looking, and there's no promises that any of these deals are going to happen, but I was really interested in looking to the future and what might happen in the next year to a couple, three years in Alaska in terms of M&A.

Obviously, you've had OBI disappear. They've been sold off, at least their Alaska assets, and now they're owned partially by Silver Bay.

Peter Pan is gone. Part of their assets were bought by Silver Bay.

And Canfisco has gotten bigger as well. It acquired E&E Foods and Big Creek Fisheries in the last five years. So again, Alaska's salmon scene is always fluid.

For the past, what, 70-80 years, there's just been a constant change in who the players are in that scene. And this is just the latest evolution in that. And the next step is these floating processors, Northline Seafoods and Circle Seafoods, who have both built these barges that are going up and doing primary processing at the source to try and -- again -- that focus on quality, trying to keep the fish at the highest quality possible before it gets to consumers.

So those are kind of the big players right now. And in terms of outlook, like I said, everyone's taking a breath, taking stock, evaluating where they stand, and then kind of strategizing how they want to move forward. And it seems like that's kind of where the situation is this year.

AB: So that's all talking about the salmon side of things. Cliff, is pollock seeing something similar?

Alaska pollock M&A update: Jones Act seen as long-term threat as aging fleet, costs stall deals

CW: Pollock is a different kettle of fish. So, while salmon fishermen are largely decentralized, they're these independent captains that then contract with these companies to provide them fish, pollock is dominated by big catcher-processors.

So these huge vessels that are out there catching enormous amounts of fish, they're led by American Seafoods, but you've got Global Seas, and you've got a handful of other companies that operate these vessels, often coming out of Seattle to fish for two seasons, the A and B season.

And a huge issue facing this fishery and these companies is American legislation called the Jones Act. For anyone who's not familiar, it requires essentially that any ship that fishes or carries US-caught seafood needs to be built in the US and operated by US crews -- primarily. This rule has been really frustrating and has impeded the deals in this sector because, essentially, you're stuck with the fleet you've got.

It's nearly impossible to build a modern state-of-the-art catcher-processor for Alaska pollock in the US because the costs just automatically make it non-competitive with foreign fleets like the subsidized fleet that's being built in Russia. So you now see an aging of the fleet and you also see potential delta between what the owners of these companies think that their company is worth and what potential or prospective buyers think that they're worth, because they're essentially stuck with these aging boats.

That's the big catch right now facing the Alaska pollock M&A scene.

There's other factors. A lot of this pollock gets sold abroad and the US dollar has been having some fluctuating movements based on tariffs and other US economic policy. So that's causing some complications in the deal-making process.

You got higher labor and cold storage costs, minimum wage increases in Alaska and Washington. You've got a lot of these headwinds that are impeding deals.

The big deal that everyone has been waiting for to happen forever is the sale of American Seafoods. They put themselves up for sale several years ago and they paused their sale process in 2024. From what I hear, there have been several offers. They haven't taken any.

Fishing vessels, including the Northern Eagle, which is owned by American Seafoods Group, docked at the Port of Dutch Harbor; August, 2023 (Kirsten Dobroth)

There seems to be that disconnect that I talked about between what the owners of the company think their company's worth and what people are willing to pay for it. And again, from what I hear, it's based around these vessel assets and what the valuation is perceived or actual on these boats, which have a lifespan. And for some of them, they're going to need, eventually, sooner or later, to be replaced.

And the question is, how are you going to do that?

AB: Joining us now on the pod is reporter Jacob Resneck, who has hopefully finished defrosting after spending a few days in Anchorage, Alaska, at the annual Alaska Seafood Marketing Institute's "All Hands On Deck" meeting.

Jacob, is this an event that you've attended in the past?

Jacob Resneck (JR): Yes, and I just want to go on record saying that it was dark, cold, and snowy as it is November in Anchorage, but I will never complain about visiting Alaska. It's a place that just always blows me away.

ASMI All Hands on Deck 2025: Alaska Wildlife Troopers confirm investigation into Kodiak trawl industry group

I was there last year and it's a marketing meeting, so there's a lot of cheerleading that has to happen. But I will say that compared to last year, when all the talk was, "we're going to turn things around. Really, we mean it this time." This year, there was a lot less of that really forced optimism and there were actually some good figures to report. So that was edifying to see that at this year's All Hands on Deck compared to last year.

AB: I was going to say, I think we could both agree that the industry overall has been hit with many different challenges, but it was nice to see in your live blog that there was a lot of optimism in the room.

JR: Yeah, and not just optimism. I mean, the numbers have improved. This year's salmon fishery really performed. I mean, a lot of it, especially Bristol Bay's sockeye, the fish showed up and they were a lot bigger than last year. They had record small sockeye last year and that was a very worrying trend. We had like a $541 million salmon fishery in 2025 in Alaska.

It's all wild salmon. That's like ex-vessel, that's stock value. So you look at the multipliers of wholesale and other markets.

But it was nearly, I think it was 195 million salmon, kind of all species. I don't like to throw too many numbers in a podcast, but the headline was it reversed the four-year decline. Things were on the upswing for this year.

AB: And yeah, not wanting to talk about a lot of numbers on a podcast. I don't blame you there. But another headline that stood out to me was Alaska's 2025 seafood value projected to reverse multi-year decline.

JR: Right, nearly 195m fish ... $541 million was the ex-vessel value. So those are the numbers for just this year.

The marketing numbers and the more figures that you can trust, they go back to 2024. And ASMI this year, they commissioned this independent study where they were looking at Alaska wild salmon compared to the other salmon on the market. And you gotta remember, wild-caught salmon is dwarfed by aquaculture.

A fishing tender receives a brailer bag loaded with wild sockeye salmon in Bristol Bay, Alaska, US. (Photo courtesy of ASMI)

But they're really having to push what makes their product different. Not necessarily better, but different. Because I know some people do prefer Atlantic salmon to the wild sockeye, but there's a lot of diehards there.

And that wild price premium, according to their research, wild-caught Alaska sockeye's got a 34% price premium over Atlantic salmon. So they can't beat it in volumes, but they can try to market it and get it as more of a niche product, I would say. So that was the tact that ASMI continues to take.

And when they have the kind of volumes they had coming out of Bristol Bay this summer, that creates a lot of value for that US fishery.

AB: And the meeting also came at an interesting time because a record-long government shutdown is where we're in the middle of right now.

We're recording this episode on Wednesday, Nov. 12. So today the House is actually expected to vote on ending a shutdown. But what was the general feeling at the meeting? Because there's a lot of fisheries that depend on the government to fish, correct?

US gov’t shutdown threatens to disrupt 2026 groundfish harvests

JR: Right. I mean, I think the feeling in the room with the government shutdown, the political impasses, I think it's exhaustion and just frustration.

I mean, we're talking a lot about salmon. Those are near-shore, state-managed fisheries. But there's a lot that the federal government does. And then the big volume fisheries, of course, in Alaska is the groundfish and the crab.

And that's federally managed. The National Marine Fisheries Service has been shut down for going on over 40 days. There's been some real concerns that they're not gonna be able to do stock assessments based on the most latest and greatest surveys, trawl surveys that they did this summer.

They're gonna have to rely a lot on their data from last year. And that's not the end of the world. But when you're trying to have a science-based fishery and you're having to use old data, that's really concerning.

And the other problem is the division that transfers permits. They were down to a very skeleton crew. Some people were working unpaid. I talked to harvesters who were waiting for quota transfers that they'd filed these requests before the shutdown. And the quotas haven't shown up in time. So they won't even be able to fish on these IFQ quotas this year. They're going to have to wait until next year.

So there've been some serious disruptions to Pacific halibut. There's been real questions about managing the ground fisheries, like with pollock and other whitefish. And I think that the crab fishery, it's been like burning the candle at both ends.

I wanna use some kind of mixed metaphor, but the federal government was having to -- the federal scientists, I should say, some of them working unpaid just to get these quotas announced in time for the crab fleet to go fishing. So it's the kind of thing, I think we can say they probably survived this shutdown, but it's really put a lot of stress on the system.

AB: Because we all need a little bit, just a little bit more stress.

So, as someone who records a podcast and hosts a podcast, I have to say is that I'm always looking for a little bit of drama to spice things up. So I was happy to see that your live blogging also included news on a criminal probe. Tell me all about that.

Alaska Wildlife Troopers confirm trawl bycatch at center of criminal probe

JR: Well, I'll tell you as much as we know -- which the information's incomplete so far -- but there were search warrants served on a Kodiak, Alaska-based trawl industry group that reps not only the trawl fleet, but also the processors in the Gulf of Alaska, pollock and other groundfish. And there has been an issue that was actually brought to the North Pacific Fishing Management Council last month, that the longstanding practice of taking bycatch from the trawl fleet -- and that can be Pacific halibut, it can be crab, it can be salmon. I think it's mostly salmon and halibut. They can take it and grind it up into fishmeal. There's a cooperatively owned fish meal plant in Kodiak.

And the processors, they do profit a little bit off of this bycatch. And this is a very, very politically fraught issue because the other gear groups who make their livelihoods on the salmon and the halibut and the crab, they don't want any profiting done at all off of bycatch because it's not supposed to be... There should be no economic incentive to profit off something that you're not trying to catch.

And no one's accusing the trawlers of trying to catch the bycatch, but it does happen. So there was this longstanding issue, longstanding practice of some fishmeal being made from bycatch. I should also pause it and say, this was only bycatch that they couldn't donate to the food share programs. It was unfit for human consumption.

So the argument is like, look, we caught this stuff. There's nothing else we can do. Either dump it or use it for something good, right? And like pet food or whatever.

AB: Yeah, let's not just throw it out.

JR: But the regulators were taking a harder look at this over the summer, and they told the trawl fleet that they can't deliver to the fishmeal plant. So they did, from what we heard at testimony -- Oct. 2, I think it was -- is they had stopped this summer delivering to the fishmeal plant, and they were just dumping it overboard and having to take special trips.

And they complain, this is a waste of resources. This is a great waste of fuel. This is a waste of time. Sometimes we have to go out in rough seas and do this, like let's figure something out.

So there was discussion at the council about should we change the regulations and open up this whole can of worms. Anyway, flash forward to last week, maybe 10 days ago, the offices of the trawl industry group that oversees a lot of this stuff got raided.

And they took the electronics and the computers and stuff like that. And the statements we've got from the state authorities said that they're looking at, in legal language, a potential fraud of profiting off prohibited species: bycatch.

What we don't know is, is there like this wider, grander, I'll say conspiracy that there are actually some processes are selling bycatch commercially? If so, that would be a huge scandal in Alaska fisheries.

Or is it just this fishmeal issue that was actually already spoken about in open meetings last month? That's the big question.

The trawl industry groups I've talked to, they're saying it's just this fishmeal process, and they don't understand why law enforcement would go in with this kind of heavy-handed tactics and seize computers when they were already talking about it openly and trying to figure it out.

We won't really know until the full investigative documents are unsealed, if charges are actually pressed, you know, we have charging documents, and see what the scope of this investigation.

But I can't overstate how big of a deal this is for everyone who is a fisheries observer in Alaska. Whether you're in the trawl industry or you're another peer group who is watching, you know what's going on in the Gulf of Alaska.

AB: That's it for today's episode. A final word from our sponsor, Wisefish. From egg to plate, Wisefish supports seafood businesses in aquaculture, fisheries, processing, and sales with one integrated platform. Trusted by companies worldwide, including Iceland Seafood International, Tassal, and Nils Sperre, and now the newly announced land-based fish farming company First Water. Wisefish helps control costs, improve margins, and make smarter financial decisions. Learn more at wisefish.com/catch-the-current.

title: Untitled
content:
Harvesters in British Columbia's roughly CAD 400 million ($295m) commercial wild fisheries say they've been working harder for less for years, but the federal government might finally be ready to listen.

After decades of warnings about corporate and investor control of fishing licenses and quotas, Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) confirmed with Undercurrent News last week that it's examining the potential for Atlantic-style "owner-operator" rules on the West Coast.

Approximately 100 pages of analysis and briefing materials gathered in relation to the matter sheds new light on income trends for Canadian fishers. The documents were obtained by Undercurrent, including an October 2025 presentation to federal policymakers in Ottawa by Rick Williams, a Nova Scotia-based policy researcher affiliated with the Fisheries for Communities Network.  

Williams' analysis highlights how BC's share of fishing income has lagged behind regions where licenses are reserved for working fishers.

Average fishing income on Canada's West Coast rose only 32%, compared with 137% in Atlantic Canada, between 2010 and 2019, Williams reported, citing the most recently available region-level data from Statistics Canada.

Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans is reviewing Atlantic-style 'owner-operator' rules for the West Coast, a move that could redefine who controls access to the region's fisheries. Photo: Liza Mayer

Had BC harvesters captured the same income share of landed value as Atlantic fishers, their average 2019 fishing income would have been about CAD 6,000 higher, he said. The data suggest that a greater proportion of BC's landed value is allocated to license and quota holders, processors, and investors, rather than to working crews.

Williams attributes this gap to the absence of fleet-separation and owner-operator safeguards in BC licensing policy.

"These are structural, not biological, differences," Williams wrote in one of the 2023 policy briefs he shared with Undercurrent through Ecotrust, a Vancouver-based nonprofit. "The same public resource produces very different economic outcomes depending on who is allowed to control the licences."

Modernizing Pacific fisheries policy

DFO's review falls under the West Coast Commercial Fisheries Modernization initiative, launched in 2021 to assess licensing and management frameworks in Pacific fisheries.

The federal agency has conducted more than 70 consultation sessions in the past year and plans to launch two new surveys -- of processors and harvesters -- to expand on its 2022 beneficial-ownership survey. These studies will provide a clearer picture of who participates in BC fisheries and how, helping define "fishery-specific options" for future policy, Benjamin Stanford, DFO regional director of communications-Pacific region told Undercurrent.

For many on the West Coast, this marks the latest chapter in a debate that has been rumbling for nearly a decade.

In 2017, the federal government enshrined owner-operator and fleet-separation rules into law for Atlantic Canada to protect independent harvesters from processor and investor control.

Two years later, a House of Commons committee investigating corporate concentration in BC's quota fisheries released a landmark report, "West Coast Fisheries: Sharing Risks and Benefits," calling for a similar framework for the Pacific. That report concluded that only 7% of license-holders controlled half of all quota value, while working harvesters retained as little as 10-25% of their landings' worth.

Williams and the Fisheries for Communities Network -- a coalition of harvesters, coastal community groups and policy researchers advocating for greater local control over fisheries access -- have urged Ottawa to adapt Atlantic-style protections for smaller, independent fleets in BC.

Their analyses estimate that corporate or processor interests now control 80-90% of access in some quota fisheries such as halibut and sablefish.

Political momentum builds for reform

Support for reform has widened since last year, when British Columbia premier David Eby, a member of the New Democratic Party, wrote to then-prime minister Justin Trudeau, a Liberal, backing a "made-in-BC owner-operator" approach and citing concerns raised in provincial money-laundering investigations about opaque ownership structures in the industry.

Eby's letter, dated May 2, 2024, said the province was prepared to work with Ottawa on a licensing regime that would prioritize reconciliation, community viability and transparency.

BC premier David Eby (pictured) wrote to then prime minister Justin Trudeau in May 2024 supporting, a 'made-in-BC' owner-operator approach to ensure more fishing income stays in coastal communities.
Photo: Government of BC

In May 2025, Sonia Strobel, CEO of Vancouver-based Skipper Otto, launched a letter-writing campaign urging the new federal minister of fisheries and oceans to introduce an owner-operator system for BC.

Strobel, who has advocated for similar reforms since 2018, argued that the province's current structure enables corporate and investor control, leaving independent fishers "financially locked out" and vulnerable to exploitative leasing arrangements. Strobel did not respond to Undercurrent's request for an interview.

Split views within BC fisheries

But not everyone supports the idea of applying Atlantic-style policies on Canada's Pacific Coast. 

Most West Coast fisheries are smaller and more diverse, often with more licenses than available fish, Christina Burridge, executive director of the BC Seafood Alliance, told the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Oceans during a hearing held at the end of October. She described the situation as chronic over-capacity.

"Individual catch quotas and other measures have significantly improved conservation outcomes, and conservation should not be compromised or traded for social ends," Burridge said. "This does not mean ignoring unintended consequences of those measures."

"The Atlantic and Pacific are completely different systems," Burridge continued. "We don't have the high-volume, high-value fisheries that support thousands of independent harvesters."

The BC Seafood Alliance, representing 90% of BC's wild fisheries value, opposes Atlantic-style owner-operator rules, saying the province's fisheries need region-specific policies. Photo: BC Seafood Alliance's Instagram page

During the same hearing -- part of the committee's ongoing review of the Fisheries Act -- Burridge said BC's licensing issue should not be dealt with through the Act or its regulations. She warned that some groups might use the review to push for Atlantic-style licensing policies, but stressed that such changes belong in policy, not legislation.

She instead endorsed other solutions, including a provincial loans board to help working fishers purchase licenses and a comprehensive license-and-quota registry to clarify who controls access.

The BC Seafood Alliance is comprised of 30 member organizations, representing approximately 90% of the landed value of the province's wild fisheries, which lends significant weight to its position in policy discussions.

Labor and community advocates counter that the current system has concentrated wealth at the top while squeezing those who do the fishing.

Emily Orr, business agent for the United Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union – Unifor, a BC-based union affiliated with Unifor and sister to Newfoundland's Fish, Food and Allied Workers' Union, told the same parliamentary hearing that the Fisheries Act still lacks clear protection for independent harvesters.

'The economic and social benefits of the fishery should flow to the people doing the work,' Emily Orr, rep for United Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union told lawmakers in October. Photo: Screengrab from the Canadian parliament video

She called for targeted tools, such as a loans board and transition programs, to help working fishers regain control, but stopped short of endorsing a full Atlantic-style regime.

"The economic and social benefits of the fishery should flow to the people doing the work," Orr said, adding that any policy must reflect BC's diverse fisheries rather than impose a "one-size-fits-all" solution.

Beyond the policy debate, the data portray an industry showing signs of decline: Between 2010 and 2019, total employment income across BC fisheries rose just 3%, compared with 81% in the Atlantic provinces, according to the same Statistics Canada dataset. Around 40% of BC harvesters are now over 55, and there are fewer young entrants replacing them.

A 2025 report from the BC Fisheries for Communities Network -- compiled by policy researcher Williams and presented to federal officials in October -- warned that if current trends continue, independent participation could fall by half within a decade.

What's next

DFO has not set a timeline for concluding its review under the West Coast Commercial Fisheries Modernization initiative, launched in 2021 to examine policy, licensing and management frameworks on the Pacific coast. Upcoming surveys of processors and harvesters will inform the next round of consultations with First Nations and licence holders, Stanford told Undercurrent.

Any potential policy changes would likely be phased in on a fishery-specific basis, said Stanford, but the department has not addressed whether compensation or buy-outs for current quota owners are under consideration.

In his closing brief to federal policymakers, Williams argued that Ottawa already has the tools it needs to rebalance benefits toward working harvesters.

"The federal government already has the authority to do this. It's a matter of political will," he wrote.

title: Vibrio mortalities cost Norcod $4m in Q3, dent 2026 harvests
content:
Norwegian cod farmer Norcod experienced "significant mortalities" at one site in the third quarter of 2025, linked to a strain of Vibrio not covered by the existing vaccine.

Norcod raises $16m via investment from Portuguese retailer

The incident dented its Q3 earnings and is expected to mean a reduction in 2026 volumes, including a "harvesting pause" for Q1 2026, it said.

"During the quarter, Norcod experienced significant mortalities at the Jamnungen site due to Vibrio infection. Investigations confirmed that the incident involved a bacterial strain not covered by the existing vaccine."

"In close consultation with veterinarians at the Norwegian Food Safety Authority, it was decided to treat the affected fish with medicine feed to treat the infection and secure fish welfare."

The mortalities came despite continuous monitoring and prompt and effective treatment, it said.

"Norcod’s vaccination program uses autogenous vaccines, enabling adaptation to emerging bacterial strains. The identified Vibrio strain will therefore be included in future vaccine formulations to prevent recurrence."

Norcod does not give a guide harvest for 2026, but says it is on track for its long-term goal of 25,000 metric tons. Two new sites, Snyen and Selsoy, are currently being prepared for stocking in 2026.

"During 2026, we plan to stock fish at four sites -- two in the spring and two in the autumn. This expansion will result in an increase of approximately 50% in total stocking volume compared with the current year."

In Q3, revenues were up 17.6% year-on-year at NOK 37 million ($3.7m), with earnings before interest and tax at NOK -64.7m -- an improvement from NOK -73.2m.

That was despite harvest volumes being less than half what they were in Q3 2024, at 515t whole fish equivalent.

"At the start of Q3, Norcod temporarily paused harvesting to allow the fish to grow and reach an average weight aligned with market demand. This period was also used to upgrade the Krakoy processing plant, including the installation of a new gutting machine."

Production cost at sea was NOK 58 per kilogram, versus NOK 56 in Q3 2024, due to the low harvest volume and extraordinary mortality. The mortality event itself cost some NOK 43m.

"The cod market is continuing its strong outlook and demand with y-o-y sales prices up 31%," Norcod noted.

"We have aligned our future production plan at new and existing locations to have an ideal balance between spring and fall releases, which will ensure a stable 12-month production and harvest in the future. This results in a temporary lower level of biomass at sea but lays the foundation for profitable growth."

Alongside the Q3 announcement, Norcod revealed a private placement raising gross proceeds of NOK 157m directed towards Jeronimo Martins Agro-Alimentar, a wholly owned subsidiary of Portuguese food retailer Jeronimo Martins SGPS.

It said the new equity will support Norcod's expansion plans and bring the company closer to achieving large-scale production of low-intensity farmed cod.

title: Untitled
content:
Venezuela's largest shrimp producer has refused to identify a Turkish investment group that acquired a stake in the company three months ago, raising questions about the source of capital flowing into the government-seized operation.

Grupo Lamar exported some $200 million worth of product to Europe annually, accounting for roughly 80% of Venezuela's shrimp production, before it was seized by the Venezuelan government in November of last year after the founding Rincon family was accused of plotting to overthrow president Nicolas Maduro's regime, as Undercurrent News reported.

The company received an investment from a Turkish investor around August, according to sales manager Frank Sanoja. 

When pressed for details at the China Fisheries and Seafood Expo in Qingdao, China, Sanoja declined to name the investors or disclose the amount.

Jose Gregorio Briceno, Venezuela's vice minister of fisheries and aquaculture processing and distribution, at the China Fisheries and Seafood Expo 2025 in Qingdao, China. Credit: Louis Harkell / Undercurrent News

"They are putting a lot of money in the Lamar group," Sanoja told Undercurrent News in an interview at the Qingdao show, China’s largest international fisheries trade event, where Venezuelan seafood companies exhibited at a joint stand. He said the identity of the investor is "confidential."

Grupo Lamar, which employed over 9,000 workers and managed 13,000 hectares of shrimp farms, had been planning to double production to 100,000 metric tons by the end of 2025 before the takeover.

Undercurrent's requests for clarification from Venezuela's Instituto Socialista de la Pesca y Acuicultura, the country's aquaculture industry body, also went unanswered. Sanoja did not reply to emailed follow-up questions.

A source in Turkey named members of the Mildon family, which owns Miller Holding, as a potential partner. The source said the family members linked to the Lamar investment might not be the branch involved in Miller. The Turkish conglomerate, which has operations in Africa, did not respond to requests for comment. 

Venezuelan industry minister Alex Saab (left) duirng a visit to Grupo Lamar's facilities in August. Source: Lamar's Instagram profile

The timing of the Turkish investment suggests a connection to Venezuelan industry minister Alex Saab, a controversial figure who has been instrumental in facilitating foreign investment while navigating US sanctions. In August, Saab was part of high-profile visit to Lamar facilities, alongside Zulia state governor Luis Caldera and fisheries minister Juan Carlos Loyo, according to Lamar's social media.

It was around this time that the Turkish investment was made, based on Sanoja's timeline. Also in August, Venezuela's agriculture ministry announced Turkish enterprises would partner in reactivating state-owned sugarcane processing plants, but again, it did not identify the investors by name. Saab was also involved in that transaction.

Saab is linked to multiple companies in Turkey set up on his behalf, according to a Nordic Monitor investigation.

Fire damages Venezuela’s largest shrimp plant following gov’t takeover

Sanoja said the Turkish investors have experience in aquaculture and other sectors and represent "a huge" conglomerate. The funds will expand Lamar's entire value chain, from hatcheries to processing facilities, with production expected to reach 70,000t annually by 2026 -- a more modest target than the company's pre-seizure goal.

Under Lamar's new management, the company plans to export 85% of production to Europe -- primarily Spain, the Netherlands, France and Portugal -- with 10% to Asia and 4% to the US, said Sanoja.

"We will mostly sell to Europe because European demand is constant throughout the year with the best prices," Sanoja explained. "At certain times, Asia does not have the best prices," citing competition from Ecuador, India, Vietnam and Iran.

However, Lamar's European business has floundered since the departure of its founding family. Through August of this year, the EU imported 15,000t of shrimp from Venezuela worth $95m, down significantly from the 42,000t worth $219m in full-year 2023, according to data available on Undercurrent’s trade portal.

Sanoja claimed Lamar's shrimp farming operations were halted for a period as the company needed to undertake overdue maintenance. It brought in experts with over 25 years of shrimp-farming experience to clean 15,000 hectares of production ponds, he said. A shrimp processing plant also caught fire in April, further delaying production.

"The previous owners didn't do the correct maintenance," Sanoja claimed. "So ponds were dirty. The shrimp didn’t grow a lot. They had some problems with quality."

Rebuilding bridges to Europe?

At full capacity, Lamar's Atlantico processing plant can handle 250t of raw material daily, producing cooked, head-on shell-on, headless and peeled-and-deveined shrimp.

Prior to the government's takeover, Lamar exported large quantities of shrimp to Europe via its then majority-owned distribution arm, Pescafacil, a cooker based in Burgos, Spain -- but that arrangement has ended.

In May, Undercurrent reported the Rincon family had sold its stake in Pescafacil to an Ecuadorian farmer and processor, Grupo Diosmar. 

"We have better options," Sanoja told Undercurrent at CFSE, though he declined to name new European clients.

But Lamar has scarce alternative markets outside Europe. Venezuela's sales to China -- though increasing -- remain modest. In the first nine months of this year, China imported 6,300t of shrimp from Venezuela, well short of replacing the company's lost exports to Europe.

Jose Gregorio Briceno, Venezuela's vice minister of fisheries and aquaculture processing and distribution, said at the trade show that Venezuela's seafood industry is ripe for development. Foreign investment is growing despite US sanctions, he claimed, with Turkish, Chinese and European capital flowing into the sector.

"There is good participation of foreign investment," Briceno told Undercurrent. Investors have "full security in legal issues" with government guarantees. "They only have to navigate the sanctions imposed on us by the US financial system," he said.

Turkey, China and Russia are "really important" to Venezuela's seafood development, Briceno said. A 2023 sanitary protocol with China opened that market to all Venezuelan marine species, he said.

title: Alaska Wildlife Troopers confirm trawl bycatch at center of criminal probe
content:
The raid of an Alaska groundfish industry group's offices conducted by wildlife-related law enforcement officials in the US state last week has been confirmed as being in relation to allegations of bycatch being sold by processors.

Alaska Wildlife Troopers executed a search warrant on the Kodiak office of the Alaska Groundfish Data Bank (AGDB), a long-established trawl industry group representing harvesters and processors in the Gulf of Alaska, on Tuesday (Nov. 4), Austin McDaniel, a spokesperson for the agency, told Undercurrent News over the weekend.

The officers seized office equipment and then, when executive director Julie Bonney returned to the office after a trip, they also seized her laptop and cellphone, as Undercurrent earlier reported.

Alaska trawl group targeted in apparent criminal probe

McDaniel said state authorities are leading a criminal investigation "involving allegations that large volumes of commercial bycatch, classified as Prohibited Species Catch (PSC), including species such as halibut, and salmon species, were unlawfully entered into commerce by multiple seafood processors."

That suggests -- though it does not completely verify -- that the focus of the investigation is the legality of the longstanding practice of bycatch landed by trawlers being ground into fishmeal for sale by a cooperatively owned processing plant in Kodiak.

Bonney declined to comment on the Alaska Wildlife Troopers statement.

The National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) informed the North Pacific Fishery Management Council last month that it had become aware  that bycatch was being sold as fishmeal, despite regulations prohibiting it from being "sold, purchased, bartered, or traded." NMFS said a rule change would be needed to permit this practice.

Bonney told the council's virtual meeting on Oct. 2 that, after NMFS had reinterpreted the rules, the trawl fleet was forced to make special trips to dump overboard bycatch unfit for human consumption and ineligible to be donated to foodbank programs.

"There are safety and logistic considerations for vessel crews to store and discard PSC at sea, especially in poor weather," Bonney said. 

She said dumping would not help to reduce the rate of bycatch caught by the trawl fleet that targets Alaska pollock and other groundfish species, a politically fraught issue as it includes crab, halibut and salmon.

NPFMC may still consider Gulf of Alaska trawl closures to conserve Tanner crab despite advisory panel punt

News of the searches alarmed many in the groundfish industry, with the AGDB writing in a message to its members that the Kodiak-based organization "does not have anything to hide" and was disappointed in the heavy-handed tactics.

One longtime industry veteran rushed to Bonney's defense, saying she had a strong reputation for integrity, and pointed out that the executive director had spoken openly about the issue at last month's NPFMC meeting.

"Julie went to the council to [try and] fix it," said the industry figure, who asked to remain anonymous. "People like this that spend time and money [on a raid on their offices], they give law enforcement a bad name, frankly."

Alaska state authorities, in their statement to Undercurrent, pointed out that it is unlawful for bycatch to be sold in any form.

"Both Alaska state law and federal fisheries regulations strictly prohibit the sale or commercial use of PSC to protect sensitive species, ensure sustainable management of Alaska's fisheries, and preserve fairness within the commercial fishing industry," McDaniel wrote in a statement.

No arrests have been made, nor have any charges been filed, and the contents of the search warrants will remain confidential unless they are filed as part of charging documents in court, McDaniel added.

title: Alaska trawl group targeted in apparent criminal probe
content:
Law enforcement agents in Alaska raided the downtown office of a long-established trawl industry group in Kodiak on Tuesday (Nov. 4), seizing electronics as well as devices belonging to its executive director, Undercurrent News has learned.

Alaska Groundfish Data Bank, an organization that represents the commercial trawl fleet and shoreside processors in the Gulf of Alaska, notified its membership earlier this week that Alaska State Troopers had served a search warrant at its downtown office while its executive director was off-island for a medical appointment.

Julie Bonney has worked for the Alaska Groundfish Data Bank since 1991 and has led the Kodiak, Alaska-based trawl industry group since 2001. (Photo courtesy of LinkedIn)

Upon the return of executive director Julie Bonney, authorities intercepted her and served a second warrant, seizing her personal electronics, including her computer and cell phone.

"We are in communication with legal teams and handling this situation as best we can," wrote Chelsae Radell, AGDB's assistant director. "Julie has spent 40 years being a transparent, honest advocate for all of you, the seafood industry as a whole and Alaska’s coastal communities, sacrificing a lot personally in the process."

She added that the industry group "does not have anything to hide, so it's extremely unfortunate that authorities have chosen to take this route."

The story was broken Friday (Nov. 7) by Deckboss, a blog maintained by a long-time former Anchorage Daily News reporter.

Alaska State Troopers did not immediately respond to messages on Friday. 

Bonney declined to comment.

It wasn't immediately clear the scope of the criminal probe.

"We cannot comment on an ongoing investigation," a law enforcement source within the National Marine Fisheries Service told Undercurrent.

title: Norwegian firm Nordlaks targeted in brand fraud
content:
Norwegian seafood company Nordlaks said it has uncovered a case of brand fraud connected to an upcoming documentary series on Norwegian aquaculture, airing on NRK in early November.

Before the release of the second episode on Nov. 4, NRK provided Nordlaks with images showing allegedly falsified product labels, WhatsApp messages, and photos of fish.

The company confirmed that the labels were fake and that it could not verify whether the fish shown came from Nordlaks. A Norwegian export company, which has never been a Nordlaks customer, is accused of falsifying Nordlaks labels and misusing its brand to export lower-quality "production fish" as premium products, violating Norwegian export laws, NRK reported.

Current Norwegian regulations prohibit the export of production fish unless the product has been corrected to meet legal standards, Nordlaks pointed out.

"We strongly condemn the misuse of our brand in this way. Our business is built on producing high-quality food, and for someone to falsify documents and exploit our name is something we view as extremely serious," said Heidi Torkildson Ryste, Nordlaks' head of marketing and communications.

Nordlaks has reported the matter to the police and is working with legal counsel as the investigation continues.

title: Spanish firms await Cape Verde decision on former Atunlo plant concession
content:
Seafood group Frescomar, which is part of Spanish firm Ubago, is still awaiting a decision from the Cape Verdean government on the future management of the Mindelo cold-storage platform and tuna processing facility, sources told Undercurrent News.

Pernas progresses with Atunlo asset takeover but clashes over Portuguese JV sale

The plant was previously operated by the now-liquidated Atunes y Lomos (Atunlo), which had established operations in Cape Verde to handle tuna loins for export. When Atunlo declared bankruptcy, its operations there ceased, and the platform was left inactive, disrupting local supply chains and putting many workers out of jobs, sources told Undercurrent News.

When Atunlo had a concession at the Mindelo plant, it worked closely with Ubago, said one source. Atunlo managed the platform for raw loins, while Ubago processed the cooked and frozen loins for export to Europe. During that time, Ubago had 1,700 direct employees and around 5,000 indirect jobs.

After Atunlo halted operations, Ubago was forced to suspend its tuna loin production line. Ubago has since resumed limited activity through a new collaboration with Jealsa Foods, one of Spain's largest canneries. Still, full recovery depends on regaining access to the cold storage platform formerly managed by Atunlo, according to sources.

"The government must decide whether to grant the concession to a consortium or launch a new public tender," the source explained. "Meanwhile, the platform remains idle, and former workers are being supported [financially] by the local government," he said. 

Cape Verde's ministry of maritime economy has yet to confirm when a final decision will be made.

"Everything remains on hold while we wait for the launch of the international tender," one of the sources said. The Cape Verde authorities are reportedly working on the process, and the tender will be announced soon, one of the sources confirmed to Undercurrent on Nov. 11. 

Ubago, which produces canned fish for major supermarket chains in Spain, including Mercadona, is reportedly ready to expand production in Cape Verde if granted full control over the former Atunlo plant.

The business already sells its own brands in Cape Verde, the US, and Europe, according to sources. But without the platform functioning, Ubago's Frescomar can't increase storage capacity or stabilize supply, according to sources. The country relies heavily on tuna imports and has limited cold storage capacity.

The firm is reportedly ready to invest and create more jobs, according to sources. "But everything depends on this decision," one of the sources stressed. 

Last August, Jealsa told Undercurrent that Ubago is leading plans, and declined to add any additional details, stressing that at this stage, it is only "a project." Ubago also told Undercurrent it was premature to explain any details at that stage.

"At this time, the project is not fully defined," it said.

Meanwhile, in Cape Verde, another seafood processor -- Gustinh -- is expanding, aiming to further increase international sales thanks to a new processing plant.

Simone Duarte, CEO of Gustinh.

Gustinh is a family-owned company now managed by its fourth generation, with more than 70 years of operation, according to its CEO Simone Duarte.

In 2023, the firm launched a new processing plant with a capacity of 2 metric tons per day, which is currently processing approximately 30t per month.

Its product range includes fillets, fresh and frozen whole fish, and fish burgers, including but not solely tuna, Duarte said. The company operates with a single vessel and employs 40 workers.

Agostinho also produces artisanal "gourmet" canned tuna products made from fresh skipjack, offered in a variety of sauces and flavors, according to Duarte.

title: Crab harvesters urge Canada to increase fines for illegal fishing
content:
Penalties for illegal snow crab landings in Canada's Gulf of St. Lawrence are too low to discourage offenders, complains the Acadian Crab Fishermen's Association (ACFA), an industry group representing mid-shore snow crab harvesters in the province of New Brunswick.

"The fines are really low compared to what people earn from illegal landings," said ACFA's general manager Marcel Hebert in a recent interview with Radio Canada, noting a case from August 2024, when a fisherman was fined just CAD 2,500 ($1,783).

"If you arrive with an illegal shipment of 10,000 pounds at CAD 5.00 a pound, that's CAD 50,000, and you get caught for CAD 2,500 -- it's ridiculous," Radio Canada quotes Hebert as saying.

The gulf snow crab fishery is Canada's second-largest, with a quota of 18,334.49 metric tons in 2025, a 28% decrease from its 2024 quota, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

Illegal fishing undermines the sustainability of the resource, the ACFA said, pointing out that natural mortality rates in the southern gulf are now around 35-45%, compared with 20-25% in healthy populations. 

The group is calling for enhanced surveillance at fishing ports. It proposes limiting the number of designated landing ports, installing cameras on docks, and using drones to detect illegal fishing or landings.

ACFA continues to collaborate with DFO to report suspicious activities, said Hebert, noting that in 2024, DFO officers detected some illegal landings thanks to cooperation with its members.

title: Cooke prepares higher Avramar bid amid delay in delivery of restructuring plan
content:
Canadian seafood powerhouse Cooke is reportedly upping its offer for Avramar, Greece's largest aquaculture producer, hoping to yank it out of the grasp of Abu Dhabi-based investor Aqua Bridge Group.

Cooke is reportedly preparing a third enhanced offer, expected to exceed €120 million ($139m) and potentially accompanied by a memorandum of understanding with Avramar's creditor banks and majority shareholder Amerra Capital Partners.

This would bring Cooke's proposal closer to Aqua Bridge's estimated €150m package, which includes immediate and near-term payments plus a seven-year repayment plan with interest, as Undercurrent News previously reported. Aqua Bridge's bid also relies on a 70% across-the-board haircut on bank debt, as defined in the September 2025 term sheet.

Cooke's advantage lies in its promise of rapid payment -- by the end of 2025 -- versus Aqua Bridge's phased approach. At least one major lender is reportedly leaning toward the Canadian offer due to its broader exposure, according to Kathimerini.

Cooke's new offer will be accompanied by a business plan for the future of Avramar Greece, Kathimerini reported. Sources close to Cooke told Kathimerini the company's interest in Avramar is linked to a strategy to strengthen its presence in the European Union, especially as the US has targeted Canada with tariffs.

Avramar group CEO Eugenio Meschini, who was appointed by Amerra in 2024 to stabilize the troubled business, has backed Cooke's bid, as reported by Undercurrent. Meschini was removed from Avramar’s board of directors earlier this year by the creditor banks, who also informed him that his contract will not be renewed when it expires.

Cooke declined to comment. "We do not offer public comment on rumored or speculated business dealings such as acquisitions," it said. Aqua Bridge and Avramar did not reply to a request for comment in time for this article. 

Restructuring plan delayed

Any deal is contingent upon the delivery of Avramar's long-awaited restructuring plan.

Initially due at the end of October, the reorganization file, built around Aqua Bridge's winning bid in Avramar's 2024 international tender, is now expected to reach the Athens Court of First Instance on Nov. 24-28, Naftemporiki reported.

The delay was blamed on the complexity of finalizing legal documentation of the deal handing over control to Aqua Bridge, but could be partially due to the expectation of a higher offer from Cooke, according to Kathimerini.

Avramar chairman Leonidas Kolioulis is personally overseeing the preparation of the restructuring file, Capital reported.

If the schedule is overturned again, Avramar's financial data will need to be refreshed up to September 2025 to reflect third-quarter reporting, adding another delay of at least 10-15 days for submitting the file to the court, according to Capital. 

Shifting financial situation

As of Dec. 31, 2024, Avramar's total liabilities exceeded €580m, of which €546.6m were short-term, according to Capital.

However, with Avramar's earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) projected at €50m this year, the stakes for involvement in the sale process are rising. Avramar's recent improved financial performance, supported by strong fish prices and suspended loan repayments, has strengthened its negotiating position, Undercurrent reported.

Seabass and seabream prices, which typically decline after the summer peak consumption period, remained stable in recent weeks, due to good demand and relatively slow supply. Bass prices in particular are trading at a strong premium to their bream equivalents and at a higher level compared to previous years, as shown in the graphs below. 

Upgrade to Pro to view
Saudis exit

Earlier this month, a Saudi Arabian-based company engaged in developing investment prospects in fishing and aquaculture, Saudi Fisheries, announced that its memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Aqua Bridge had expired without a mutual agreement being reached, Argaam reported.

The nonbinding MoU, signed in January, was intended to create a framework for cooperation in aquaculture, outline potential areas of collaboration and explore potential partnership opportunities.

Saudi Fisheries stated that neither party now has any mutual obligations following the termination of the agreement.

Saudi Fisheries also did not reply to a request for comment as to how that might impact Aqua Bridge's involvement with Avramar.

title: Canada report blames stability failures, safety gaps for deadly sinking of Quebec trawler
content:
An unsafe load causing vessel instability, and poor emergency preparedness were key factors in the 2023 sinking of the Quebec trawler Silver Condor, a tragedy that claimed the lives of three of the six people onboard, concludes a report by the Transportation Safety Board of Canada (TSB).

The 60-foot-long stern Silver Condor had been returning to its home port of Blanc-Sablon following a redfish trip under an experimental fishing license when disaster struck. The vessel began taking on water in the early hours of Sept. 25, 2023, near La Tabatière, Quebec.

Shortly after midnight, as winds increased to 30 knots and waves built, crew members were awakened by the sound of water splashing below deck. The vessel was listing heavily to port and flooding through the galley window, the report details.

The mate issued a Mayday call over VHF radio, but there were no other vessels in the area to receive the distress signal.

The six people on board -- five crew members and one fisheries observer -- mustered in the wheelhouse as water surged through the accommodation space, the report details, recounting the crew's desperate attempts to abandon ship.

Only five of the available eight immersion suits could be retrieved in time, and several crew members were unable to fully don them. One wore only a life jacket.

The crew was also unable to access the vessel's seven-person life raft, which was stowed behind the vessel's wheelhouse on the port side, with fishing gear overhead, and positioned so that its access hatch extended slightly over the edge of the upper deck.

To safely enter the life raft, the crew would have had to lift it from its cradle and reposition it.

This photo from the Transportation Safety Board of Canada report on the sinking of the Silver Condor shows how the life raft was positioned. Photo from TSB report issued Nov. 4, 2025

The life raft failed to release from its cradle as the vessel sank by the stern, leaving the crew no choice but to jump into the frigid waters of the North Atlantic Ocean.

Around 2:30 a.m., the vessel's Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacon transmitted a signal, and the Canadian Coast Guard launched an emergency response.

Three survivors were located in the water about four hours later by a Coast Guard search and rescue (SAR) Cormorant helicopter crew. The SAR crew recovered three bodies.

Dean Lavallee, 53, Yves Dones, 65 and Damon Ethbridge, 36, all from Blanc-Sablon, Quebec, died in the sinking, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

According to the TSB report, the trawler's load configuration during its return voyage likely exceeded its safe stability margins.

The weight of the catch on the fatal trip may have exceeded the vessel's weight limitation of 22.68 metric tons, as defined in its stability booklet, noted the TSB.

"Silver Condor crew members estimated that, at the time of the occurrence, they had caught and stored up to 36t of redfish, with approximately 0.8t of incidental catch stored in a commercial fish tote on deck," the report explained.

That factor, combined with deteriorating weather, would have caused the vessel to lose buoyancy and stability rapidly, the TSB concluded.

The agency also flagged long-standing concerns about stability awareness and emergency training in Canada's small-vessel fishing fleet. Between 2013 and 2023, the TSB investigated 18 cases in which compromised stability contributed to fishing vessel losses, resulting in over 30 fatalities.

"These issues continue to recur," the report noted, emphasizing the need for "realistic safety drills" and crew training that simulate flooding and evacuation under adverse conditions.

 While no new formal recommendations were issued, the Board urged the industry and regulators to prioritize vessel stability assessments and ensure that crews are equipped and trained to respond effectively to emergencies.

The full TSB report is available here.

title: Chile’s highest court upholds sanctions against krill fishing firm for illegal discards
content:
Chile's Supreme Court of Justice, it's highest court, has confirmed a ruling that rejected an appeal of sanctions for fishing firm Pesca Chile and the captains of the vessel Cabo de Hornos, according to the country's fishing authority, the Servicio Nacional de Pesca y Acuicultura (Sernapesca).

Pesca Chile is a Chilean Antarctic krill fishing company formerly owned by Spain's Grupo Pescanova. It was earlier sanctioned by Sernapesca's regional office in Aysen for unauthorized discarding of hydrobiological resources, a decision that was upheld by the court of appeals in Coyhaique. The violations involved the illegal disposal of southern hake and Patagonian grenadier during fishing operations.

The company was ordered to pay a fine of approximately CLP 155 million ($164,000) and the two captains were each fined about $7,000. 

Sernapesca said it detected the infraction through video footage from the vessel's onboard monitoring system, which revealed systematic and unjustified discarding in violation of Chile's General Law on Fisheries and Aquaculture.

Regional director Daniela Leiva praised the ruling.

"This Supreme Court ruling not only validates the technical and legal work of the service, but also reaffirms our commitment to protecting fishery resources and strictly complying with current regulations," she said. "This ruling sets an important precedent in fisheries oversight and compliance, reaffirming Sernapesca's role as guarantor of the responsible management of the country's aquatic resources."

title: MSC rejects claims its label on Indian ocean tuna is ‘misleading’
content:
The Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) has stressed that certified canned tuna with its eco-label is sourced exclusively from "healthy, non-overfished stocks," following the publication of a German report that claimed the certification cannot rule out bycatch of endangered species and greenwashing.

A new report by the consumer rights organization Foodwatch, in collaboration with NGO BLOOM, claims that MSC-certified tuna fisheries in the western Indian Ocean contribute to overfishing and widespread greenwashing.

"Evaluations show that at the time of the study, certified fleets [in the Indian Ocean] caught up to 47% of overfished species in some cases. This is not sustainable, but consumer deception," Foodwatch said.

It pointed to high levels of bycatch, the unintended capture of non-target species, such as turtles, sharks and some marine mammals, as well as yellowfin and bigeye tuna by MSC-certified fleets, including the Spanish and French vessels operating in the Indian Ocean.

"These are species that have long been considered overfished in the region," it said.

Official MSC reports document that one certified Spanish fleet caught 173 metric tons of endangered silky sharks (approximately 1,730 individuals) and 77t of protected whale sharks during monitored fishing trips, according to the report. Another fleet recorded catches of 4,486 silky sharks, 70 oceanic whitetip sharks, two whale sharks, three manta rays, and several sea turtles, the NGO said. The actual numbers, according to Foodwatch, are likely higher due to limited monitoring.

Much of the tuna from FAO-51, the Western Indian Ocean's major fishing area, is caught using purse seine nets and fish aggregating devices (FADs), floating objects that attract not only tuna but also juvenile fish and protected marine species, according to the report. In 2022, more than half of the 666,000t of skipjack caught came from such methods. Oceanic shark and ray populations have declined by about 71% since the 1970s, partly due to fishing with FADs, claimed Foodwatch.

Photo: Ja! tuna cans sold online.

A can of "Ja!" private-label skipjack tuna sold by German retailer Rewe was traced back to a vessel active in the Indian Ocean, whose catches between 2018 and 2022 included 47% overfished yellowfin and bigeye tuna.

Foodwatch argues that retailers must stop selling tuna from FAO-51 unless it can be proven to come from FAD-free or longline fisheries, which produce far less bycatch.

"Supermarkets cannot hide behind certification labels," said Annemarie Botzki, campaigner and researcher at foodwatch. "They must use their market power to end destructive fishing practices."

Foodwatch is demanding that the MSC stop certifying fisheries using FADs and mixed catches, calling such practices incompatible with the label's sustainability promise. The organization also urges the EU Commission to ban drifting FADs in the western Indian Ocean, warning that continued inaction threatens marine biodiversity and accelerates the depletion of tuna stocks.

MSC's response

MSC responded by stating that "Foodwatch has regrettably based its allegations related to MSC-certified canned tuna products on incorrect assumptions and a misunderstanding of the MSC certification program."

"The MSC program is the strictest and most recognized worldwide certification program for sustainable fisheries. It meets all the requirements of the international umbrella organization for environmental and social standard setters, ISEAL, as well as those of the UN Food and Agriculture Organization for transparent and credible certification programs. We welcome and support calls for transparency and credibility in sustainability claims on food products."

The organization also emphasized that its certification is highly targeted, referring to clearly defined fishing units that consist of a specific target species, fishing gear, and vessels.

"Fish products sourced from fishing units or fishing activities that do not meet the MSC fisheries standard criteria cannot be labelled or marketed as MSC-certified. This is rigorously applied across the entire MSC certification system."

A fishing company with a valid MSC certificate for catching one species may also catch other species for which they are not MSC-certified and which currently may not meet the strict criteria of the MSC fisheries standard, the organization confirmed.

"Those other species cannot be labelled as MSC-certified. Consumers can trust that MSC-labelled products only contain fish from sustainable, MSC-certified fisheries.  Positive change in global fisheries is complex and takes time. The MSC approach -- to certify specific components of a fishery -- is consistent with common practice in many highly credible and well-recognized certification programs, such as organic farming," it said.

Even if initially limited to one single target species in a fishery, each MSC-certified product is an important step in the right direction and creates incentives to improve standards across other parts of the same fishery, according to MSC.

"By working with fisheries and brands to drive improvement, MSC is making a significant contribution towards global efforts to build a sustainable fishing sector that ensures the long-term health of our oceans," it said.

Progress in the Indian Ocean

Meanwhile, two new Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC) rules came into force on Oct. 21, 2025, and will be applied in 2026. Those include resolution 25-03, which sets catch limits for skipjack tuna to prevent overfishing and ensure sustainable stock levels and resolution 25-04, which sets catch limits for bigeye tuna, requiring countries to manage their fishing fleets within agreed-upon quotas. 

The 2026-2028 TAC has been set at 92,670t for bigeye and at 615,632t for skipjack. 

The skipjack resolution does not bind India, Korea, and Somalia, and the bigeye tuna does not bind India and Somalia.

In December 2024, the IOTC's stock assessment indicated an 89% probability that the yellowfin tuna biomass in the Indian Ocean is no longer subject to overfishing. The IOTC Scientific Committee recommended a total allowable yellowfin catch for 2026 of between 416,000t and 430,000t, reflecting the yellowfin stock's recovery.

title: Canadian fisherman fined CAD 76,000 for illegal halibut catch
content:
A fisherman from the Canadian province of Nova Scotia has been fined more than CAD 76,000 ($54,035) for fishing halibut in a closed area and lying about where he was fishing, reports CBC.

Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) said the department authorized Grant William Cameron to conduct a test fishery on Sept. 7 and 8, 2022, in a defined area to determine the presence of species not fished there commercially, like Atlantic cod.

Instead, Cameron fished for Atlantic halibut 120 kilometers away from the test area, in a place that was closed to groundfish fishing.

When an at-sea observer asked for his vessel's coordinates, Cameron provided the location where he was supposed to be, rather than where he was actually fishing, said DFO.

A Nova Scotia provincial court judge fined Cameron CAD 40,000 for fishing during a closed time and for failing to provide the correct coordinates to the observer. An additional fine of CAD 36,561 was also ordered, the equivalent of the gross profits from the sale of the 1,900 kilograms of Atlantic halibut that Cameron had fished.

Cameron is also banned from fishing groundfish in two designated fishing areas for one year and is required to use a vessel monitoring system on his boat during that time.
