content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Tuesday, Nov. 18:

Week 47 farm-gate shrimp roundup: Indian prices lift on tight supply, Ecuador slip

Vannamei shrimp farm-gate prices in India rose across all size grades in week 47 (Nov. 17-23), ending a five-week stretch of stability as the farming season continues to slow and limited supply pushed values higher.

Heightened scrutiny for US crab fishery after whale entangled in Pacific Northwest

A beached juvenile humpback whale in the US state of Oregon had to be euthanized on Monday (Nov. 17) after becoming entangled in lines and buoys that included commercial crab gear.

Norway's whitefish processors sweat on soaring prices for next year's haddock lifeline

With Barents Sea cod stocks in sharp decline, the one piece of good news for northern Europe's whitefish buyers at the recent Groundfish Forum was the clear rebound expected from haddock next year.

Canadian province establishes unit to stop illegal lobster sales


Canada's biggest lobster fishing province is setting up a dedicated enforcement unit to combat illegal purchasing and processing of lobster and other seafood, Nova Scotia's fisheries minister Kent Smith announced at a press conference on Monday.

Masoval boosts biomass but struggles with Q3 profitability amid weak salmon prices

Norwegian salmon producer Masoval reported a narrower third-quarter loss, as higher biomass and improving biological performance helped soften the impact of lower salmon prices (see Q3 levels below) and reduced harvest volumes.

Rising prices hit frozen, shelf-stable retail sales in October

The trend of rising US seafood prices continued in October, and some grocery shoppers appear to be responding by tightening their purse strings.

Norway is expected to deepen its focus on Asian markets for salmon exports in 2026 amid its tariff disadvantage in the US and growing demand in China, according to analysts and executives.

title: Canadian province establishes unit to stop illegal lobster sales
content:
Canada's biggest lobster fishing province is setting up a dedicated enforcement unit to combat illegal purchasing and processing of lobster and other seafood, Nova Scotia's fisheries minister Kent Smith announced at a press conference on Monday (Nov. 17).

Four officers from the province's Department of Natural Resources will be tasked with focusing on ports and seafood facilities where there is known illegal activity, he said.

Nova Scotia is also establishing a new audit program and developing more severe summary offense tickets with penalties that match the seriousness of the activity, Smith explained in a press release. That could lead to suspension or termination of a fish buyer and/or processor license, he said.

The officers will be empowered to issue fines, suspend licenses, and impose formal charges, Smith explained.

EU import rules for 2026 rattle Canadian lobster industry

The news was welcomed by the industry.

Basically, it's more eyes on the paper trails and on the wharves, Kris Vascotto, executive director of the Nova Scotia Seafood Alliance (NSSA), told Undercurrent News on Tuesday (Nov. 18).

That trade group, which represents the majority of processors in Nova Scotia, also expects to see much more intense activity within plants, with officers visiting operations regularly to ensure license conditions are being followed.

"We have been asking for this for a while," Vascotto added, noting the extensive media coverage of illegal lobster fishing and processing over several years.

"The only way to get past some of these issues is by making sure we have a strong compliance body in place, that's why we're quite supportive of this," he said.

'A small step in the right direction'

But will four officers be enough?

"We're not going to know until they actually start doing their work, but at least it's a small step in the right direction," offered Vascotto.

"While most harvesters and buyers play by the rules, it has become clear in recent years that much more needs to be done to effectively deter and root out illegal or unreported transactions from our industry," added Nat Richard, executive director of the New Brunswick-based Lobster Processors Association, who was also quoted in the government's press release.

"This requires urgent and collaborative actions by both levels of government. Nova Scotia continues to show the way forward with the deployment of this new compliance team," he said.

The province has not said when the new enforcement unit will become active.

However, the biggest lobster season in Atlantic Canada begins in just a couple of weeks, as harvesters from Lobster Fishing Areas (LFAs) 33 and 34 usually plan on setting their first pots of the season on the last Monday in November.

In 2023, LFA 33 landed 7,477 metric tons while LFA 34 landed 15,105t, adding up to 22,582, roughly 21.2% of Canada's total landings of 106,896t last year, based on data shared with Undercurrent by the Lobster Council of Canada (LCC).

The black market deals in cash

It's estimated that about 30% of the lobsters caught every year in the Atlantic region go unreported, representing approximately CAD 400 million ($285m) in under-the-table sales, Smith noted in his press release.

That's skewing the economics for the industry, said Vascotto, noting the black market deals in cash.

Canadian, US lobster lose more of Chinese market to Pacific competitors

"When they do go into these cash sales-type of scenarios, they buy a discount as well. So what you end up with is someone who is trying to compete for a market price when they've had to pay much more for raw materials," he said.

Those who have purchased lobsters legally, paying the going market price, are at a competitive disadvantage against those who have paid less, with cash, Vascotto said.

If the new team of dedicated enforcement officers is successful at tracking down those cash sales, it should help create a level playing field for all lobster processors, said Vascotto.

While the province oversees regulation and enforcement of processing regulations, oversight of fishing activity lies with Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO)..

Since June 2025, DFO enforcement officers have seized nearly 12,000 illegal lobsters from around Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick, and returned them to the ocean, as previously reported by Undercurrent News. 

However, commercial lobster harvesters in the region, particularly on the southwest coast of Nova Scotia, where the issue is complicated by a debate over aboriginal fishing rights, have been frustrated by what they see as a lack of action against illegal lobster fishing.

"We're happy to see some enforcement, compared to the last number of years where we literally had none. But while the numbers that DFO quotes sound good, compared to how many traps are in St. Mary's Bay and the millions of pounds that are being removed, it's just a drop in the bucket," Colin Sproul, president of the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance (UFCA), told Undercurrent in September.

title: Vietnam approves plan to implement amended WTO fisheries subsidy rules
content:
Vietnam has approved a plan to implement the amended World Trade Organization (WTO) agreement on fisheries subsidies, marking a significant step toward meeting its global commitments and enhancing sustainable fisheries management, Vietnam Plus reported.

The decision, signed by deputy prime minister Bui Thanh Son on Nov. 16, outlines how the country will enforce rules adopted at the WTO's 12th ministerial conference in 2022, which ban subsidies that fuel overfishing or support illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) activities.

The plan calls for updated reporting on fisheries management, assessments of fish stocks, IUU violations and subsidy programs.

It also assigns ministries to revise existing regulations, develop new guidance, and build a digital system to track subsidy information.

Vietnam will form a task force, seek technical assistance, and expand outreach to authorities, fishermen and businesses. Activities will run from late 2025 through 2027, supported by state funds and additional external resources.

title: Editor’s choice: Canadian, US lobster lose more of Chinese market; Arctic Fisheries sells majority stake to PE
content:
EMEA editor Neil Ramsden brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week.

Last week's most-read story was on the fact that China imported 13% more lobster over the first nine months of 2025, and paid 22% more for it, than it did during the same period in 2024 -- but neither Canadian nor US exporters are seeing any of that extra business. In fact, they are on pace to lose more ground this year thanks in large part to their respective countries' trade conflicts.

Also in North America, the raid of an Alaska groundfish industry group's offices conducted by wildlife-related law enforcement officials in the US state was confirmed as being in relation to allegations of bycatch being sold by processors. Alaska Wildlife Troopers executed a search warrant on the Kodiak office of the Alaska Groundfish Data Bank, a long-established trawl industry group representing harvesters and processors in the Gulf of Alaska.

Then, a US importer and distributor has sold a majority stake in the company to a private equity investor based in Austin, Texas, the latter's first deal in seafood, Undercurrent News has learned. Buffalo, New York-based Arctic Fisheries, which traces its history back to 1921, has sold a controlling stake to SNH Capital Partners, based in Austin, Texas.  

And a century-old US law is threatening the future of the Alaska pollock sector. The Jones Act -- formally Section 27 of the Merchant Marine Act of 1920 -- was ostensibly created to protect the US domestic shipbuilding industry but, combined with higher US labor and steel costs, it has left Alaska pollock fishing companies unwilling or unable to undertake new-builds and with no choice but to continue operating 30- or 40-year-old ships, industry sources told Undercurrent.

A Newfoundland and Labrador provincial court has dismissed charges of improper snow crab handling and processing against Quinlan Brothers, one of Canada's biggest snow crab processors, the company announced.

While an acquisitive US seafood group owned by a well-known industry figure is seen as the frontrunner to buy Cox's Wholesale Seafood, a Gulf of Mexico and Atlantic shrimp supplier based in Tampa, Florida, sources told Undercurrent.

And during an exclusive interview at its Tokyo headquarters, Maruha Nichiro told Undercurrent it is looking at moving further downstream in pollock processing in the US, as the company invests in its recently acquired Van der Lee Seafish operation in Europe to cut blocks.

title: Charges dismissed in Newfoundland rotten crab case
content:
A Newfoundland and Labrador provincial court has dismissed charges of improper snow crab handling and processing against Quinlan Brothers, one of Canada's biggest snow crab processors, the company announced in a statement issued Thursday (Nov. 13).

The dismissal came Thursday (Nov. 13) after provincial government attorneys decided they would call no evidence in the case, which had been set to be heard in the Provincial Court of Newfoundland in Harbour Grace in early December.

"The crown's review determined there was no reasonable prospect of conviction on any of the charges. This decision reflects what our company and its employees have maintained from the outset: the allegations were unfounded, unsupported by evidence, and should never have proceeded," Quinlan Brothers' president Robin Quinlan said in a press release.

The company, which operates a 22,700 square-foot factory in Bay de Verde, 170 kilometers west of St. John's, was charged in July 2024 with violations of Sect. 13 (1) of the Fish Inspection Act, which prohibits the processing or marketing of seafood "intended for human consumption if the fish or marine plants are tainted, decomposed or unwholesome," as reported by Undercurrent News.

Quinlan Brothers was ordered to throw out about 50,000 pounds of boxed crab worth about CAD 250,000 ($175,641). Government inspectors had deemed the crab to be criticaly dead or weak before it was processed. The company was staring at a possible maximum penalty of CAD 20,000. 

Quinlan had vowed from the start that the charges were without merit and pleaded not guilty during a court appearance in February 2025.

The charges also sparked heated debate between members of the Association of Seafood Producers (ASP), the trade group representing most of the province's snow crab processors, and Gerry Byrne, the province's fisheries minister at the time.

Quinlan and ASP, at a press conference on Aug. 1, 2025, expressed frustration with the inspection protocols used by provincial fisheries inspectors to decide that the crab should not be processed, as reported by Undercurrent.

However, Byrne noted that a 2024 report on snow crab quality was proof that the inspection protocol was working and regulators should "stay the course," as reported by Undercurrent.

It is important to note that today's outcome unfolds under a new provincial government, which played no role in the decisions or public commentary that led to this matter, Quilan added in his press release.

The province is now under a Progressive Conservative government, following an election in October.

"We appreciate that the current government was not responsible for these actions, and we look forward to constructive engagement as we move forward," said Quinlan.

"As next steps, Quinlan will be seeking a meeting with the [province's] minister of fisheries to discuss the broader implications for enforcement practices and to determine a path toward resolving the financial losses incurred because of the improper and illegal destruction of product in 2024," the company said.

title: Chilean court rejects Joyvio’s effort to block former Australis owner appeal
content:
Chile's Santiago Court of Appeals has unanimously rejected a new petition filed by Chinese conglomerate Joyvio Group in the ongoing legal dispute over Australis Seafoods, Undercurrent News has learned.

The decision confirmed the admissibility of a "nullity appeal" submitted by the defense of Australis' former owner, Isidoro Quiroga, and Asesorias e Inversiones Benjamin (AIB), representing him. The term describes an effort to reverse the decision of a tribunal.

Australis dispute escalates as former owners’ family group seeks to void arbitration outcome

In August 2025, a tribunal at the Arbitration and Mediation Center of the Santiago Chamber of Commerce ordered Quiroga and related parties to pay roughly $300 million in connection with the sale of Australis Seafoods.

Following the ruling, the Quiroga family filed a nullity appeal seeking to annul part of the award.

In late October, Joyvio responded with a motion for reconsideration, arguing that the nullity appeal lacked legal grounds and was an attempt to reopen matters already settled by the arbitral tribunal, Undercurrent also learned.

But, on Tuesday (Nov. 11), the Court of Appeals rejected Joyvio’s petition, clearing the way for the nullity appeal to proceed for full judicial review.

The appellate judges determined that Joyvio's arguments "failed to disprove the reasoning considered in the impugned resolution," and therefore, "there is no merit to the petition for reconsideration," their ruling stated.

The Quiroga family's nullity appeal argues that the award "seriously and manifestly violates fundamental principles and rules of Chilean law," alleging that the arbitral tribunal ordered a partial restitution of the sale price of Australis Seafoods, a measure that was never requested by the parties nor discussed during the proceedings.

$300m Australis award blasted by former owner’s attorney as ‘incoherent’; appeal coming

This aspect of the award has the "manifest purpose of leaving without effect a valid and enforceable contract between the parties," the defense attorneys argued, referring to the 2019 purchase of Australis Seafoods by Joyvio Group from entities controlled by Quiroga for approximately $880 million.

Joyvio, a subsidiary of the Chinese conglomerate Legend Holdings, has accused the sellers of allegedly concealing overproduction of salmon at Australis prior to the sale, a claim that led to a high-profile arbitration process in Santiago.

The arbitral tribunal's award was partially favorable to Joyvio, ordering restitution of part of the purchase price. However, the Quiroga family's legal team argued that this outcome exceeds the tribunal's authority and contravenes basic procedural and contractual principles under Chilean law.

Joyvio did not respond to a request for comment from Undercurrent by the time of publication.

Court's reasoning and next steps

The Court of Appeals' latest decision effectively clears the way for the nullity appeal to be heard on its merits, marking a crucial procedural victory for the Quiroga family.

The resolution stipulates that the case should be given preferential scheduling for oral arguments and final decision, acknowledging the legal significance and potential economic implications of the dispute.

China’s Joyvio accused of using threats, false testimony in high-stakes Chilean legal battle

The resolution also notes that, while Food Investment, Joyvio Group and Joyvio Zhencheng Technology submitted the required responses to the court's Oct. 14 order, Isidoro Acosta Sanchez, another party in the case, did not present his filings within the deadline, and his submissions will therefore be disregarded.

The decision was formally recorded and notified on Tuesday, and may now move forward to the argument stage before the same appellate chamber.

Additionally, in an official statement following the ruling to which Undercurrent has had access, AIB expressed satisfaction with the Court's decision:

"The Court of Appeals of Santiago has unanimously rejected the petition filed by Joyvio, confirming the admissibility of the nullity appeal presented by the Quiroga family," the statement said.

"This confirms that the appeal will now proceed to be heard, seeking to correct an arbitral award that seriously infringes fundamental principles of Chilean law and alters the scope of a valid and binding contract," it concluded.

title: Med meeting yields modest gains on vessel transparecy amid broader compliance delays
content:
The annual meeting of the General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean (GFCM), which took place in Malaga, southern Spain, between Nov. 3 and 9, concluded with limited progress, according to NGO group the Med Sea Alliance.

Countries agreed on new vessel transparency rules but delayed key compliance measures aimed at combating illegal fishing, it said.

Mediterranean nations have approved a requirement for International Maritime Organization numbers on all vessels exceeding 20 meters, enhancing traceability and aiding in the combat of illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing.

However, conservation groups said the rule falls short of best practices, which recommend applying it to vessels over 12m.

"The GFCM's decision is a step in the right direction but falls short of delivering true transparency," said Helena Alvarez, senior marine scientist at Oceana, also noting that "rejecting the EU's proposal to include smaller vessels leaves loopholes open."

In a setback for enforcement, the GFCM has postponed the full implementation of its 2023 compliance mechanism until 2028, thereby delaying key reporting and enforcement measures.

Some progress was made in regional monitoring tools such as the vessel monitoring system and the monitoring, control and surveillance portal, but discussions on remote electronic monitoring technology did not advance.

The GFCM also added one vessel, the "Sonia," to its IUU vessel list, a move welcomed by environmental groups.

title: Judge in Dungy crab price-fixing suit orders US telecoms to fork over phone records
content:
A federal judge has ordered a big telecom carrier to turn over phone records for more than 100 individuals requested as part of an effort to disprove price fixing in the US West Coast Dungeness crab fishery. 

The ruling, made Monday (Nov. 10) by magistrate Alex Tse, was sought by Pacific Seafood Group, which has gone on the offensive in advance of its trial in the US District Court for the District of Northern California. The subpoena seeks to compel Ozzie Gregoria, a self-described whistleblower, to hand over text messages and other records as it builds its defense against "cartel and price-fixing claims," as Undercurrent News reported.

US Dungy crab buyer’s motion to quash subpoena denied in price-fixing lawsuit

The Clackamas, Oregon-based seafood giant, which has rejected accusations of any price-fixing or unlawful conduct, declined comment this week.

Gregorio is the owner of Eureka, California-based buyer Triple G Seafood. Pacific Seafood has complained that, since May 5, he has been noncooperative with defendants and even threatened to "sic his dogs on, and then to shoot" representatives attempting to serve him a subpoena. 

"Gregorio's information forms the basis for at least 87 paragraphs of the complaint's allegations," Matthew Segal, an attorney for Pacific Seafoods, wrote the court, adding that these allegations have been the basis for the judge to allow the lawsuit to proceed after dismissing the previous legal action last year, as Undercurrent reported.

Meanwhile, the plaintiffs' attorney has successfully convinced the magistrate to order US telecom giant Verizon to turn over a decade's worth of phone records of an unspecified list that the judge wrote exceeds 100 individuals involved in the Dungeness crab market. Verizon had resisted complying with the subpoenas unless directly ordered by the magistrate.

"The subpoenas do not request the contents of text messages or transcripts of phone calls, but rather records about texts and calls, such as time and date, duration, and origin and destination numbers," the San Francisco, California-based judge wrote.

Exceptions were made for individuals who have filed motions to quash the subpoenas, a process that's still unresolved in many cases.

Pacific Seafood is seeking records of its own, having filed subpoenas against roughly 60 commercial crabbers. Court filings suggest text messages between crabbers could show that the communications between buyers, which are at the heart of the price-fixing allegations, are routine to verify the prices of their competitors cited by fishermen. 

Plaintiff attorney Stuart Gross, in a sworn declaration, states that the evidence uncovered so far disproves that theory. He also wrote that only four of the 58 served with subpoenas were directly involved in the allegations made in the lawsuit.

Pacific Seafood's attorneys might be retaliating against critics, Gross has suggested. 

"Several of the putative class members to whom subpoenas were issued are known to have spoken out against the conduct of Pacific Seafood and other defendants," Gross wrote.

Whale concerns delay California Dungeness crab season until 2026

But the two sides have worked out an understanding with Pacific Seafood agreeing not to enforce the subpoenas while the judge considers a motion to quash. 

The two plaintiffs are California harvester Brand Little and Robin Burns, the widow of a deceased fisherman, on behalf of as many as 1,400 harvesters, against Pacific Seafood Group for allegedly using its clout to dictate dock prices over the past decade.

It makes sweeping allegations against wholesale buyers and processors in one of the West Coast's most lucrative commercial fisheries, spanning the US states of Washington, Oregon and California.

title: Family of fisherman killed by US in attack off Venezuela coast plans lawsuit
content:
The family of a fisherman killed by the US military in a recent vessel strike in international waters off the coast of Venezuela is seeking damages for his death, according to the New York Times.

Alejandro Carranza, a Colombian fisherman, is one of more than 80 people who have been killed in the ongoing attacks conducted by the US military in response to the US president Donald Trump administration's efforts to stop the entry of drugs into the country.

More than 20 attacks have occurred since September, igniting a feud not only between governments, but the families of men who say they were wrongly killed.

Carranza was on a vessel that was struck by the US military on Sept. 15. Trump said the vessel had "confirmed narcoterrorists from Venezuela." However, Carranza's family maintains that he had nothing to do with drugs and occasionally took jobs piloting boats for others, which they believe raises the possibility that he may have been involved in something illicit without his knowledge. 

"If the people on the boat were suspected of drug trafficking, they should have been arrested, not killed," Dan Kovalik, the American human and labor rights lawyer Carranza's family hired to sue the US for damages, told the New York Times.

"This case is important from two points of view. First, the family deserves compensation for the loss," he said. "Second, we want this case to help stop these killings from taking place again. This is murder, and it is destroying rule of law."

The White House's response to Kovalik reiterated that the people killed in the attack were narcoterrorists. 

Colombian president Gustavo Petro previously spoke out about the missile strike that killed Carranza, as reported by Undercurrent News. Petro also said that the fisherman had no connection to drug trafficking when the vessel he was on, which was adrift in Colombian sovereign waters and transmitting a distress signal due to engine failure, was attacked.

"US government officials committed murder and violated our sovereignty in territorial waters," Petro wrote in an X post.

Trump responded by calling Petro an "illegal drug leader" and threatening to cut off aid to the country.

Meanwhile, the most recent attack conducted by the US military occurred on Saturday (Nov. 15), as confirmed by a post on X shared by US secretary of war Pete Hegseth. Per the post, three "male narco-terrorists" were killed in a lethal kinetic strike on a vessel that intelligence confirmed was carrying illicit narcotics.

title: Two killed, 12 missing as Chinese vessels capsize off South Korea coast
content:
Two separate incidents in the waters off South Korea’s west coast have resulted in multiple fatalities and missing crew members aboard Chinese‑flagged fishing vessels operating in the Yellow Sea.

According to Chinese state media Xinhua, the first incident occurred early Sunday (Nov. 9) morning, about 6:50 a.m., when a 98‑metric-ton Chinese‑registered fishing vessel capsized in international waters about 80 kilometers off Gageo Island.

The vessel had 11 crew onboard. Six were rescued by a passing Chinese fishing boat, and subsequently, two more were found by the Korean coastguard in cardiac arrest and pronounced dead. Three remain unaccounted for.

Just roughly one day later, at 8:53 a.m. local time on Monday (Nov. 10), a second Chinese fishing vessel of 99t capsized off Eocheong Island near Gunsan, around 150km southwest of the island.

Of the 11 crew aboard, two were rescued by a nearby commercial vessel; nine remained missing as the Korean coastguard deployed more patrol vessels, aircraft and helicopters in a multi‑asset search.

The two incidents have resulted in at least two confirmed deaths, though the exact numbers may still shift as more official data becomes available.

title: US scallop processor, staffing agency sued over alleged wage theft, kickback scheme
content:
Marder Trawling, a US scallop processor based in New Bedford, Massachusetts, is being sued by several employees who allege that their wages were extorted and stolen.

The 42-page complaint, filed Friday (Oct. 24) in the US District Court for the District of Massachusetts, also names the processor's staffing partner, Workforce Unlimited. It aims to recover wages that the plaintiffs -- employees Maximiliano Diaz Perez, Lorenzo Suar Panjoj, Maria Lucrecia Tzampop Gomez, Yohangly Mishell Garcia Mendez and Maily Adriana Velasquez Morales -- claim they were forced to pay weekly as a "condition of employment" between the period of Jan. 1, 2021 and May 27, 2025.

The suit additionally names former Marder plant manager Francisco Ixcotoyac Dionicio and Workforce Unlimited principal Andrew Wilke as defendants.

The employees at Marder's New Bedford seafood plant -- which processes scallops, lobster, Pacific cod, shrimp and crab -- allege they were required to pay Ixcotoyac Dionicio roughly $100 per week in cash to keep their positions.

Further, the lawsuit claims that employees contracted to work through Workforce who lived in the US state of Rhode Island were required to take transportation from vans owned by Ixcotoyac Dionicio and pay $60 per week (or $12 per day).

Size 15-25 Atlantic scallops being seared in a pan. Photograph by Jason Huffman.

The plaintiffs said these deductions were coerced and the company's actions targeted vulnerable low-wage workers. The suit claims that Marder knew and benefited from the agreement between Ixcotoyac Dionicio and Workforce because "it was able to reduce its labor cost."

The complaint accuses the companies of violating the Fair Labor Standards Act, the Massachusetts Wage Act, the Massachusetts Minimum Wage Law, and the Temporary Workers Right to Know Law. It seeks back pay, triple damages under state law, and attorneys' fees, as well as injunctive relief to stop the alleged practices.

Undercurrent News contacted both Marder CEO Todd Michalik and Workforce parent company AREVO Group CEO Michael Brannock for comment. Marder responded with a statement.

The company said it has not yet been served with court documents but "the allegations concern conduct that, if true, would represent a serious breach of Marder's values and policies." Ixcotoyac Dionicio has been arrested, and Marder will cooperate with law enforcement regarding any alleged workplace financial crimes, it said.

A separate investigation by Undercurrent found court documents that show Ixcotoyac Dionicio was arrested in June and charged with nine counts, including rape, assault, lewd behavior and intimidation. The rape counts were later dropped by prosecutors, however, evidentiary procedures have begun in advance of a trial.

Ixcotoyac Dionicio has not been employed by or present at Marder Trawling since May 27, 2025, the statement read. "Upon learning in June that this person had been arrested on serious criminal charges, the company immediately initiated an internal investigation, acted expeditiously, and has been cooperating fully with the appropriate authorities," it continued.

"Upon learning of the criminal accusations against this former employee and completing our internal investigation, Marder Trawling took immediate steps to strengthen workplace safeguards. As part of our ongoing commitment to transparency and employee welfare, the company has engaged an independent, highly respected firm to conduct additional workplace training."

Marder said it also undertook compliance reviews and provided counseling services for employees, reaffirming its "dedication to maintaining a professional, supportive, and lawful work environment for all team members."

The company's statement concluded: "Marder Trawling has deep roots in the New Bedford community, built on the principles of respect, accountability and safety. We categorically reject any form of exploitation, retaliation, or misconduct in our workplace. The company maintains strict policies against unauthorized wage deductions or improper treatment of employees and will continue to enforce those policies vigorously. Marder Trawling will respond to the lawsuit through the legal process, but our focus remains where it has always been -- on the safety, dignity and well-being of our people."

title: US seafood wholesaler’s former CFO gets 36 months for embezzling millions
content:
Antonietta Nguyen, the former chief financial officer of ABS Seafood, a San Francisco, California-based seafood wholesaler and importer, has been sentenced to 36 months in prison for her role in "orchestrating multiple fraud schemes" against her employer, the US Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California confirmed Monday (Nov. 17).

She must also serve three years of supervised release and repay more than $121,000 in unpaid taxes.

Nguyen was convicted by a jury in June of 12 felony counts, including wire fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, money laundering and tax evasion, as reported by Undercurrent News. Recall how she was accused of using company funds not only to buy luxury items from brands like Louis Vuitton, Hermes Las Vegas and Chanel, but also to pay state property taxes and even cover vacations and a relative's college tuition

Though she was initially charged in May 2023 of five counts of wire fraud in connection to the embezzlement of $2.7 million, ultimately the jury determined -- after a two-week trial -- that her fraud schemes actually cost ABS Seafood more than $9m over six-and-a-half years.  

Nguyen is expected to begin serving her sentence Feb. 6, 2026. A restitution hearing is scheduled for Jan. 16, 2026.

title: Quinlan Brothers president seeks compensation, provincial policy changes after rotten crab case dismissed
content:
The president of Quinlan Brothers, one of the largest snow crab processing plants in the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador (NL), feels vindicated, and now Robin Quinlan is seeking compensation for his company and policy changes from the NL government.

"We'd like to get the value of that crab returned to the company," Quinlan told members of the media at a press conference Friday morning (Nov. 14) in NL's capital city of St. John's, a day after a provincial court judge in Harbour Grace dismissed charges of improper snow crab handling and processing that had been levelled against the company in 2024, as reported by Undercurrent News.

The case was dismissed after lawyers for the province informed the court that they would not be presenting any evidence in the case, as there was no reasonable prospect of conviction on any of the charges, the company noted in a press release on Thursday (Nov. 13).

However, before the court process even began, inspectors with the provincial fisheries department ordered the company to dump approximately CAD 500,000 ($356,492) worth of snow crab that had been processed at Quinlan's Bay De Verde plant in July 2024, as reported by Undercurrent at the time.

Quinlan, along with the Association of Seafood Producers, the trade association representing the majority of snow crab processors in the province, protested the decision, stating that the province's inspection protocols utilized outdated technology, unlike the technology employed by a government-sanctioned dockside grading company that checks for critically weak or dead crab.

"We're confident that we could have, and still could, prove that all of that crab was not just safe, but was of the highest quality. But we have a situation where a genuinely innocent party had to go through this. So clearly the system is flawed and changes are necessary," Quinlan said Friday.

This is not just about the value of the snow crab that was seized and dumped, said Quinlan, but about the seafood inspection policies of the province's fisheries department.

Those policies need to change, he said, suggesting that the industry and the province should collaborate to reflect on what happened in this case and to improve policies and protocols.

"We've learned a lot through this process. I think the government has learned a lot. So let's take what we've learned, come around the table and do what's right to set guidelines that protect food safety, and make sure it's done properly so that everybody is playing by the same rulebook," said Quinlan.

As for the matter of compensation for the lost snow crab, there are a couple of legal routes, said Quinlan Brothers' vice president and lawyer John Mate. One option is to file a formal lawsuit against the province in the Supreme Court of Newfoundland and Labrador. The other option is an alternative dispute resolution process, which would allow the parties to settle through mediation, with both sides agreeing to a final settlement. Alternatively, a binding arbitration process could be employed, whereby an arbitrator hears the arguments from both sides and delivers a decision binding on both parties.

"Quinlan Brothers would be open to any and all options. We're not going to be unreasonable here in this situation. The first thing we'd like to do is just have a discussion," said Quinlan.

title: Alaska fishermen accused of falsifying IFQ records as part of illegal halibut harvest
content:
US authorities have charged five commercial fishermen in Southeast Alaska with conspiring to illegally harvest at least 10,700 pounds of Pacific halibut.

In a statement released Monday (Aug. 4), the US Attorney's Office for the District of Alaska said a federal grand jury has delivered an indictment against Jonathan Pavlik, Vincent Jacobson, Kyle Dierick, Michael Babic and Thomas Ross that charges the "experienced commercial fishermen" with conspiring to illegally harvest halibut near Yakutat on multiple occasions between 2019 and 2023.

Alaska vessel owner sentenced in crab export conspiracy, fined $1.18m over unrelated pollution

The men intentionally falsely reported that the halibut caught was creditable to their respective Individual Fishing Quota (IFQ) permit balances, according to the statement.

The federal prosecutors allege that, between Aug. 31, 2023, and Oct. 11, 2023, Pavlik sold and intentionally made false statements regarding more than 9,600 lbs of halibut that was caught on the F/V Bad Intentions but illegally transferred to the F/V New Era before landing for sale.

Pavlik is charged under the Lacey Act with four counts of conspiracy, five counts of  unlawful sale and five counts of false labeling. Jacobson, Dierick, Babic and Ross are each charged with one count of conspiracy.

The defendants are scheduled to make their initial court appearances over the next two weeks before US magistrate judge Matthew Scoble of the US District Court for the District of Alaska. If convicted, they face up to five years in prison for each count and up to a $250,000 fine.

title: US Coast Guard failed IUU interdiction goals, Homeland Security report finds
content:
The US Coast Guard (USCG) might be cracking down on illegal fishing in federal waters this year, but a new report issued by the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) found that the maritime agency "missed opportunities" and failed to meet its interdiction goals for fiscal years 2023 and 2024.

USCG is just one of the federal agencies that fights illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing, and according to the report, is uniquely positioned to combat IUU as it is the only agency with the infrastructure and law enforcement authority throughout the US Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). 

For fiscal years 2023 and 2024, the USCG set its interdiction goal at 40%. However, in an 18-page report, published by the DHS Office of Inspector General on June 6, found that the USCG only interdicted 21% of foreign fishing vessels detected illegally inside US waters.

DHS said it reviewed Living Marine Resources (LMR) summary reports, which are submitted monthly by all USCG area commanders. Based on the reports, DHS said the agency interdicted 55 of 265 detections in FY '23, and 61 of 281 detections in FY '24. 

The USCG failed to meet its goals two years in a row because it "did not prioritize the IUU fishing mission, when compared with its other statutory missions," according to the report. Meanwhile, it also noted that the Coast Guard attributed its missed goals to "competing priorities and insufficient resources."

Focus on the Gulf of Mexico

While the USCG is broken up into nine districts across the US, the DHS report puts a specific emphasis on District 8. Headquartered in New Orleans, Louisiana, the District 8 Coast Guard is responsible for 26 states, including the Gulf of Mexico coastline from Florida to Mexico.

A map showing the different Coast Guard districts. Photo Credit: USCG

Per the report, 98% of the IUU interdictions in FY '23 and FY '24 occurred in the Gulf of Mexico, which was recently renamed the "Gulf of America" under the US president Donald Trump administration.

The DHS Office of the Inspector General recommends that USCG conduct an analysis to "determine how best to use available resources in District 8 to increase its IUU fishing interdiction rate."

In response to the report and recommendation, USCG said it's already taking action against IUU fishing in District 8 this year. The agency said it has worked "within the interagency working group to establish a mechanism for criminally prosecuting small Mexican fishing vessels illegally fishing in US waters, which will commence before the end of April 2025."

You'll recall that last month, four fishermen from Mexico were indicted by a grand jury in Brownsville, Texas, for unlawfully transporting fish harvested from the Gulf of Mexico, as reported by Undercurrent News. The US Attorney's office said that it is the first illegal fishing case in the Southern District of Texas in which prison time is possible. The fishermen entered guilty pleas just the other week.

Just last week the USCG seized approximately 1,500 pounds of red snapper and detained 13 Mexican nationals for IUU fishing in the Gulf of Mexico. Another seven men were detained in a separate event last month, as reported by Undercurrent.

title: Baldvinsson steps down as Samherji CEO
content:
Thorsteinn Mar Baldvinsson, CEO of Icelandic seafood business Samherji, is to step down in June 2025.

He has served as CEO for 42 years, since the company was founded in 1983. The board of directors has appointed Baldvin Thorsteinsson -- one of Samherji's largest shareholders and chair since 2023 -- as the next CEO.

Thorsteinsson is Baldvinsson's son, and the majority shareholder and supervisory board chair at Alda Seafood, to which Samherji sold its foreign operations in 2022. Alda confirmed to Undercurrent that Thorsteinsson will continue in his role as supervisory board chair.

"The seafood industry has been my life's work, and it has been a true privilege to build this company alongside you over the past four decades," said Baldvinsson.

"I decided a long time ago that I would step down as CEO on my own terms before I got old and grumpy. After more than four decades in this demanding role, it is natural to feel like stepping down, and the timing is right. When my cousins ​​and I started the business, the office was in the kitchen at home, but today, Samherji employs over 800 people on the group level. I am immensely proud of this team."

Baldvinsson will not retire entirely, but will continue to serve on the boards of Samherji fiskeldi (Samherji Fish Farming) and Sildarvinnslan in Neskaupstadur, where he has been chair since 2003.

Baldvinsson had previously stepped aside temporarily as Samherji CEO when an investigation into the so-called 'Fishrot' scandal was launched in 2019, returning to the position in March 2020.

The scandal saw disclosures by whistleblower and former Samherji employee Johannes Stefansson, alleging that Samherji had paid millions of dollars through tax havens such as Cyprus and the Marshall Islands to bribe high-level officials in Namibia in exchange for trawling rights.

It resulted in the resignation and subsequent arrest of several Namibian officials, including fisheries minister Bernhard Esau and justice minister Sacky Shanghala. Both former ministers have been indicted with corruption, fraud and money laundering by the Namibian authorities.

Samherji hired Wikborg Rein, a Norwegian law firm, to investigate the events. While Baldvinsson's company acknowledged some "mistakes" in a 2021 statement, it denied any involvement in criminal activity, attributing it to Stefansson, who ran operations there. The investigation, while acknowledging the issues, did not find direct evidence of bribery by Samherji.

title: US Coast Guard detains 4 Mexican nationals suspected of illegally harvesting red snapper
content:
The US Coast Guard's (USCG) crackdown on illegal fishing in the Gulf of Mexico continued on Tuesday (May 13) with the detention of four Mexican fishermen.

The four Mexican nationals were spotted allegedly engaged in illegal fishing in US federal waters off the coast of Texas. USCG crews conducted an inspection and found approximately 450 pounds of red snapper on board, along with fishing gear and equipment. The fishermen were taken into custody and were later transferred to US Customs and Border Protection for processing. 

Following previous seizures and arrests in March, four other fishermen from Mexico were indicted on May 15 by a grand jury in Brownsville, Texas, for unlawfully transporting fish harvested from the Gulf of Mexico.

Miguel Angel Ramirez-Vidal, 32, Jesus David Luna-Marquez, 20, Jesus Roberto Morales-Amador, 27, and Jose Daniel Santiago-Mendoza, 22, were detained on April 17, 2025, after attempting to transport and export approximately 315 kilograms of red snapper illegally harvested from US waters, according to a press release from the office of the US attorney for the southern district of Texas.

The men have an arraignment hearing on May 22. If convicted, each could face up to five years in federal prison and fines of up to $250,000, as reported by Undercurrent News.

title: Untitled
content:
An estimated 90,000 people conducted a 48-hour protest in the northern Peruvian fishing towns of Paita, Sechura and Catacaos demanding the government increase the quota for jumbo flying squid.

From Sept. 30-Oct. 1, artisanal fishermen and their supporters blocked roads and disrupted retail, transport and logistics services throughout northern Peru, Infobae reported.

The jumbo flying squid (Dosidicus gigas) fishery is the most important source of income for Peru's small-scale fleet, involving over 4,400 vessels and generating direct employment for more than 14,000 fishers. It also has a broader economic impact on around 70,000 people, with annual exports exceeding $600 million, making it a critical resource for the national economy.

The protests were triggered by a decision from Produce, the country's ministry of production, to set a total allowable catch of 40,000 metric tons for the season, which runs through Oct. 18, and to reduce the maximum catch per trip for vessels of all sizes, as Undercurrent News previously reported.

A subsequent flying squid fishing season will begin on Nov. 17 and extend through Dec. 31. The authorized quota for that period is 42,432t.

Even though Produce previously authorized an increase in the maximum total allowable catch to 559,804t, the protestors complain stricter limits on vessel operations, including mandatory use of jigging lines, catch limits based on vessel size and enhanced traceability via satellite monitoring threaten their livelihoods and favor the large-scale commercial fleet, as well as the hundreds of distant-water jiggers from China and Taiwan fishing extensively beyond Peru's 200-mile exclusive economic zone.

The country's largest commercial fishing trade group, the National Society of Industries (SNI), criticized the protests.

"Violence cannot be a mechanism of pressure nor an acceptable form of protest," SNI said in a press release.

The group called on the Peruvian government to break up the protests to ensure public safety and allow regional businesses to resume operations, and said if order was not restored, it might shut down operations in the region permanently.

It called for "technical and transparent dialogue" between the government and both the large-scale and artisanal fishing sectors "to address concerns without compromising public safety or institutional order."

After a sharp downturn in 2024, Peru's flying squid exports recovered in the first half of 2025, driven by soaring demand from Asia, Undercurrent reported.

title: Uruguay ends 80-day fishing strike after violent union standoff
content:
Uruguay’s fishing sector is beginning to restart after an 80-day strike that halted operations, cost the industry an estimated $50 million, and exposed deep divisions within the fishermen’s union, SUNTMA, reports MercoPress.

The strike began over union demands to add an extra crew member on coastal vessels, a measure rejected by companies due to higher costs.

As tensions escalated, union assemblies turned violent, with armed workers issuing threats.

Under growing pressure from employers, who warned ships would stay docked until January, SUNTMA leadership agreed to end the strike and resume dialogue.

title: Illegal lobster fishing problem grows worse in Canada
content:
The Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance (UFCA), a group that represents licensed lobster harvesters in the province of Nova Scotia, is happy to see Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) get tough recently on those suspected of violating lobster fishing rules.

However, Joanne Thompson, one of Newfoundland and Labrador's representatives in the Canadian Parliament and the fisheries minister since March, must do much more to crack down on illegal fishing, said UFCA president Colin Sproul.

"The current minister certainly isn't responsible for what happened in the past. But the onus is on her now to take action," he told Undercurrent News in a recent interview. "We are asking minister Thompson to take immediate and appropriate action at Saulnierville, with nothing less than swift measures by DFO and [Royal Canadian Mounted Police] officers to seize vessels and arrest people at the wharf who are clearly breaking the law in front of everyone."

DFO enforcement officers seized 1,909 lobsters on July 31, during an inspection at Lobster Rock Wharf in Yarmouth County, on Nova Scotia's southern shore, the federal agency said in a statement on its website. Six people were arrested and will be charged with violations of Canada's Fisheries Act, DFO added, though no details were provided on the specific charges.

"Fishery officers are working to remove the untagged lobster traps and seized vessels from the water," DFO also noted in the statement.

Southwest Nova Scotia. Image from Google Maps.

The federal agency has kept busy this summer.

As many as 20 people in DFO's Maritime region were convicted of lobster fishing violations in the first six months of 2025, according to information on the DFO website. Fines handed out for the offenses ranged from CAD 1,000 ($737) to CAD 12,000. 

FREE READ Canadian fisheries officers add body armor, cameras following violent lobster season

However, the convictions don't seem to be a huge deterrent, said Sproul. He noted illegal activity at the wharf in Saulnierville, St. Mary's, 54 kilometers north of Yarmouth, one of the southernmost points in Nova Scotia. The location borders Lobster Fishing Area (LFA) 34, Canada's most prolific LFA, which holds it season between the last Monday of November and May 31.

LFA 34 was responsible for 14,270  metric tons of the 95,253t of lobster landed throughout Canada in 2023, based on figures shared with Undercurrent by the Lobster Council of Canada (LCC). In 2023-24, landings in LFA 34 were 17,367t, based on the latest LCC data.

Saulnierville was known to be a center for out-of-season lobster fishing in 2024, and the situation is just as bad in 2025, Sproul told Undercurrent.

"There's a lot more activity now in the early part of the poaching season than we've ever seen before," said Sproul, who estimated that about 25 boats from Saulnierville harbour are engaged in illegal lobster fishing.

None have faced any charges or penalties from DFO, he said.

“We know that they're setting hundreds more traps every night, landing thousands of pounds of lobster," Sproul said, adding that the UFCA continues to monitor the activity at the harbor using drones, as it did last year. 

"DFO should be sending enforcement officers to that harbor to make arrests and seize boats," he said.

Colin Sproul, president of the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance. Photo from UFCA Facebook page

Sproul and others had a chance to raise the illegal lobster fishing issue with Thompson, when she visited Nova Scotia in mid-July, The UCFA is willing to give the new minister some time to resolve the issues, but they also expect action, he said.

First Nation rights issue unresolved

One of the issues at the center of the problem is the unresolved question of the treaty rights of First Nations members, and the definition of a 'moderate livelihood' fishery, the right of aboriginals to fish for personal use or ceremonial purposes.

Some Indigenous harvesters assert they do not need DFO approval to pursue their treaty right to fish for a moderate livelihood. The Supreme Court of Canada has ruled in previous cases that First Nations have a right to a moderate livelihood fishery, but federal and provincial governments also have the authority to make the rules for those fisheries.

The Canadian government and the Sipekne'katik First Nation, based in Meteghan, Nova Scotia, have been embroiled in a legal battle for nearly a year over what constitutes a moderate livelihood fishery.

The Sipekne'katik First Nation, filed a lawsuit against DFO and Canada's attorney general after officers seized lobster traps belonging to a band member in St. Mary's Bay in 2023, claiming DFO had violated the moderate-livelihood fishing rights of its members.

The Supreme Court of Nova Scotia, the highest court in the province, on December 2024, gave the two sides until June 16, 2025 to reach a settlement through mediation before ruling on the matter itself. 

Although a lawyer for the Sipekne'katik, in April, indicated the two sides were close to a deal, there has been no word since on a final agreement.

The Sipekne'katik cancelled the lawsuit in June, 2025.

Canadian First Nation cancels lobster lawsuit against federal fisheries dept

An official for DFO told Undercurrent the agency remains committed to implementing Indigenous fishing rights and working with First Nations to collaboratively manage fisheries to ensure sustainability for all harvesters.

"The department will continue to engage with Sipekne’katik to discuss the implementation of their right to fish in pursuit of a moderate livelihood during the commercial fishing season, as the department has done with other First Nation communities across Atlantic Canada and Quebec," Debbie Buott-Matheson, DFO's manager of strategic communications, offered in an email statement to Undercurrent.

DFO will continue to be guided by three key principles: the conservation and sustainability of fish stocks, further implementation of Indigenous fishing rights, and transparent and stable management of the fisheries," Buott-Matheson said.

However, details on the progress of negotiations, including dates, proposals and topics of discussion, are confidential and cannot be shared, Buott-Matheson added.

Meanwhile, the UFCA continues the legal actions it launched last year.

The group filed a notice of action in the Nova Scotia Supreme Court in August 2024 against both the Sipekne'katik First Nation and Canada's attorney general, as reported by Undercurrent. It is asking the court to declare illegal the self-regulated lobster fishery in St Mary's Bay, launched by the Sipekne'katik in 2020, and demand that DFO impose regulations under the federal Fisheries Act.

The UFCA argues that the unregulated fishery has significantly depleted lobster stocks in the bay, forced commercial fishermen out of the area, and led to the closure of a local processing plant.

The group has also launched a civil action against some lobster buyers in the province, claiming that Independent Fisheries Limited and its president, Xiaoming Mao, of Sable River, Shelburne County, have bought lobsters caught illegally in St. Mary's Bay. The lawsuit, which is seeking damages of CAD 10m, also names Jason Lamrock and Tyler Nickerson of Fisher Direct and Wesley Nickerson of Seawell Holdings as parties to the illegal activity.

The court process is still in early stages, with statements of defense to be filed and court dates to be set, said Sproul.

title: Canadian fisheries officers add body armor, cameras following violent lobster season
content:
Enforcement officers with Canada’s Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) have added body armor and cameras to their uniforms this year, reports Global News.

The new equipment follows the recommendation of a report last year by Canada’s labor department that concluded heavily-armed criminals pose a threat to DFO’s enforcement officers in the Maritime provinces. That report called on the department to take immediate steps to reduce the danger, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

Organized crime infiltrated Canada’s Maritime lobster industry in recent years, with reports of violence involving guns. 

In the summer of 2024, some enforcement officers with DFO in the province of Nova Scotia refused to work, citing concerns over safe working conditions. Enforcement officers had warned DFO that year that someone would be killed if officers did not have better protection, reported the Globe and Mail at the time. 

That November, just prior to the start of the season in Canada’s biggest lobster fishing area, LFAs 33 and 34, the owner of Lobster Hub in Meteghan, reported that his house had been shot at, as reported by Undercurrent.

Similarly, the elver fishery in the Maritimes has also been infiltrated by organized crime.

The lucrative fishery has also seen tensions between licensed commercial harvesters and First Nations members who are permitted a moderate livelihood fishery. The First Nations fishery, which allows aboriginal groups to take lobsters for personal use and ceremonial purposes, has been a cause of tension for years, and the cause of clashes and lawsuits between the two groups.

A Canadian parliamentary committee report last September urged DFO to take action to deter illegal poaching of lobster and elvers.

title: CNN: Forced labor persists in Taiwan’s distant-water fleet
content:
Taiwan’s distant-water fishing industry continues to be plagued by forced labor and abuse, with many migrant workers facing violence and exploitation aboard tuna vessels, reports CNN.

Despite reforms meant to improve conditions, fishermen from Southeast Asia described brutal treatment, including wage theft, excessive overtime, and confiscation of their identity documents. Some were trapped at sea for years without pay.

Taiwan introduced the 2017 Act for Distant Water Fisheries to increase oversight, but critics say enforcement remains weak and regulators often prioritize industry interests over labor rights.

The US Department of Labor has blacklisted Taiwanese tuna and other seafood products produced under forced labor conditions.

Activists urge stronger inspections and reforms to protect thousands of workers who power the island’s billion-dollar tuna export industry.

title: US fishing boat captain sentenced for meth-related assault on deckhands in Gulf of Mexico
content:
A federal judge in Tallahassee, Florida, has sentenced a commercial fishing captain to seven years in prison after he pleaded guilty to assaulting his deckhands. 

Terry Carrington, 38, of Carrabelle, Florida, was on a multi-day commercial fishing trip for red snapper in the Gulf of Mexico in April 2024 when he, "without provocation," assaulted his deckhand, according to a news release from the US Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Florida.

Carrington struck the first victim, "breaking his jaw" and "rendering him unconscious," according to the statement. 

The boat captain then proceeded to retrieve a rifle, which he used in an attempt to shoot the second victim. Multiple shots were fired before one of the victims was able to wrestle the rifle from Carrington. The captain was then subdued by the victims, who returned to land and alerted law enforcement of the assault.

An investigation into the incident later revealed that drug use played a role in the incident as Carrington had taken an illegal stimulant, which led to the violence, according to the Miami Herald.

"What the evidence actually shows is that (Carrington) used methamphetamine, became delusional, and assaulted Victim 2 and tried to kill Victim 1," who "had fished with (him) prior to the April 22, 2024, fishing trip," a court filing states.

content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Thursday, June 12:

Aquaculture Canada 2025: Cooke mum on Grieg acquisition possibilities

Undercurrent News reported from the Aquaculture Canada conference, hosted by the Aquaculture Association of Canada, from June 8 to 11.

Seoul Food 2025: South Korean eel sector faces major threat; New president kicks off fisheries reform

Undercurrent has also been reporting from Seoul Food & Hotel 2025, South Korea's largest international trade show for the food, beverage, and hospitality industries.

Coldwater shrimp sellers hope easing supply picture can bring price increases

The European cooked and peeled coldwater shrimp market remains quite stable as several important fisheries get underway in 2025, while the shell-on shrimp trading picture is far more dynamic, sources told Undercurrent.

Ecuador cracks down on organized crime to protect shrimp sector amid rising extortion

Amid a surge in extortion and violence threatening its shrimp industry, Ecuador has launched a sweeping crackdown on organized crime, reinforcing security on land and water routes vital to one of its most important export sectors.

Stolt Sea Farm targets 24,000t production by 2035 amid construction boom

Spain's Stolt Sea Farm, the land-based aquaculture division of global shipping and logistics provider Stolt-Nielsen, is undergoing a rapid expansion as it pursues its ambitious goal to reach 24,000 metric tons of annual turbot and sole production by 2035.

Chinese production is big question mark in global shrimp market outlook

The world is getting hungrier for shrimp. But the big question facing producers is how much of that hunger is growing in China and whether domestic production will satiate Chinese appetites.

UCN launches price assessments for world's largest seafood trade: Ecuador-China shrimp

Undercurrent has expanded its price assessment portfolio with comprehensive weekly pricing for Ecuadorian vannamei shrimp exported to China, taking the total number of datasets on our prices portal to just under 3,700. 

New UCN weekly skipjack tuna price assessments show Bangkok, Manta steady after early June drop

Skipjack prices for delivery in Bangkok, Thailand, and Manta, Ecuador, have remained roughly stable in week 24 (June 9-15) of 2025, following a decline in late May and early June compared to early May levels.

title: Ecuador cracks down on organized crime to protect shrimp sector amid rising extortion
content:
Amid a surge in extortion and violence threatening its shrimp industry, Ecuador has launched a sweeping crackdown on organized crime, reinforcing security on land and water routes vital to one of its most important export sectors.

The effort is being led by Ecuador's National Chamber of Aquaculture, or the CNA, in coordination with government-run emergency response and public safety organization ECU 911, the police, and the ministry of defense, in a campaign that combines military force, surveillance technology, and legal reforms.

FREE READ UCN launches price assessments for world’s largest seafood trade: Ecuador-China shrimp

The initiative aims to protect the shrimp sector, which sustains over 300,000 direct and indirect jobs and contributes significantly to the country's gross domestic product.

"Behind every pound of shrimp exported is a family, a community, and a nation working toward honest progress," said the CNA in a statement. "This is more than about protecting a product, it is about defending a way of life."

In recent months, criminal groups have escalated attacks on shrimp farms, transport vehicles, and river routes, demanding illegal payments and threatening workers. The CNA sounded the alarm earlier this year, prompting swift action from national security forces and emergency response agencies.

From January to April 2025, authorities executed 2,347 operations in rural and aquatic zones, arresting 1,522 individuals linked to crimes including armed robbery, drug trafficking, extortion, and illegal weapons possession.

Many of these crimes were directed at shrimp farms, transport vehicles, and fishing communities, particularly in high-risk areas such as the Gulf of Guayaquil and the Jambeli Archipelago, said the CNA.

In response to rising threats along Ecuador's river routes, the Navy increased patrols in the most vulnerable areas. In March alone, 231 river patrols were conducted, 339 vessels inspected, and several citations issued.

The Ministry of Defense also confirmed that operations have targeted at least 25 criminal organizations, including the Choneros, Tiguerones, Lobos, and Latin Kings, which had expanded their operations into maritime and rural zones.

Ecuador posts record shrimp exports in April, forecasts slower yearly growth

"We've built an interoperable network that allows real-time coordination between producers and emergency response teams," the CNA also stated. "This is a model of public-private cooperation that strengthens our response capacity."

One of the new strategy's most notable elements is the deployment of a "digital shield" that connects shrimp companies with the national video surveillance system operated by ECU 911.

GPS trackers, communication radios, and mobile apps are being integrated across the industry to monitor activity in real time and respond swiftly to threats. This technology-based approach is enabled by an executive decree, which allows public and private systems to operate together in a unified security network.

Authorities have also mapped several high-risk zones along Ecuador's fluvial and terrestrial infrastructure.

"Danger hotspots include the inner channels of the Gulf of Guayaquil, areas around Puerto Bolivar and Isla Costa Rica, the estuary of the Chone River, and land routes such as Playas–Guayaquil, Naranjal–Puerto Inca–Balao, and Chone–Portoviejo, where frequent robberies and extortion checkpoints have been reported," according to the CNA.

"We are not just reacting; we are building a proactive defense system rooted in technology and trust," it added.

To complement operational measures, the CNA has launched a campaign to encourage timely and anonymous reporting of criminal activity.

Citizens and workers are urged to use secure channels, including ECU 911 for emergencies, the 1800-DELITO hotline for confidential reporting, the police's web platform, and the Attorney General's Office for formal legal complaints.

US shrimp imports see massive 38% volume, 47% value surge ahead of tariff judgment day

Yet fear remains a significant barrier.

"More than 70% of the alerts we receive come from anonymous sources," the CNA also stated. "The fear of retaliation is real, and that's why we must do more to protect those who report crimes. Institutional trust must be rebuilt."

Despite this, the shrimp industry remains determined.

The CNA continues to advocate for stronger protections, better coordination with government forces, and greater trust between communities and authorities. The goal, it says, is not only to protect a valuable economic sector but also to uphold the lives and livelihoods of the families behind it.

"Ecuador must not only be known for the quality of its shrimp, but for the strength of its security model," the CNA said.

"We are showing that when the public and private sectors work together, we can resist the threats, we can protect our people, and we can move forward," it concluded.

title: US orders squid caught by Chinese-flagged vessel detained under withhold release order alleging worker abuse
content:
US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) issued a withhold release order (WRO) against Chinese-flagged squid-fishing vessel Zhen Fa 7 on Wednesday (May 28), meaning all seafood harvested by the vessel that is then exported to the US will be confiscated.

Per the WRO, Zhen Fa 7's operations show indications of forced labor, including worker abuse, isolation, retention of identity documents, subpar living conditions, debt bondage and physical and sexual violence.

Examples of some of these abuses were previously documented in an October 2023 investigative series from the Outlaw Ocean Project. The Zhen Fa 7 is one of hundreds of fishing ships that supply the state-run China National Fisheries Corporation (CNFC), the largest distant-water fishing company in the world, the Washington DC-based nonprofit journalism organization reported.

“Combatting forced labor is central to CBP’s mission to protect the economic security of the United States,” CBP acting commissioner Pete Flores said in a statement. “The president recently charged us to restore American seafood competitiveness by combatting unfair trade practices, and issuing this order is one way we are contributing to that goal."

US president Donald Trump issued an executive order to "restore American seafood competitiveness" on April 17, as reported by Undercurrent News.

"Unfair trade practices have put our seafood markets at a competitive disadvantage," the executive order reads. "Nearly 90% of seafood on our shelves is now imported, and the seafood trade deficit stands at over $20 billion. The erosion of American seafood competitiveness at the hands of unfair foreign trade practices must end."

The WRO issued to Zhen Fa 7 is the sixth issued to a fishing vessel by the CBP since 2020.

title: Tensions between fisheries officers, bosses boiled over threats of violence in Canadian lobster, eel fisheries, gov’t documents reveal
content:
Someone could be killed if Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) doesn't offer their officers better protection due to the lawlessness in the province of Nova Scotia's lobster and elver fisheries.

That's what DFO officers warned the federal agency in 2024, reveals some 837 pages of government documents obtained via the country's Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act (ATIPPA), reports the Globe and Mail, a Canadian news service.

As many as 35 of the 125 fishery officers in DFO's Maritimes region, most of them from the south shore of Nova Scotia, where illegal lobster fishing has been rampant, refused to work last July until they received adequate personal protective equipment, including bulletproof vests, to protect them from danger, according to the article.

The officers experienced increasingly dangerous conditions including, but not limited to, the risk of physical violence, verbal harassment, personal threats, organized crime and poaching and a rise in the use of long guns that puts them at risk in the course of their regular duties, an official of the union that represents fisheries officers told Undercurrent News in September 2024.

It got to the point where some fisheries officers moved their families out of the area because of the threats they were receiving, said lobster harvester Colin Sproul, who is president of the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance, a group that represents lobster harvesters in Nova Scotia, in an Undercurrent in an interview last October.

According to the government documents, the officers said they had "intel on threats to the lives of fishery officers," which "the department has, that they're sitting on," and disciplinary actions had been brought against officers who "brought concerns up."

It wasn't until the officers filed complaints against DFO through Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) that things began to change, the Globe and Mail reports.

The ESDC investigation found that protocols provided by DFO had not been reviewed for three years, and "that the protective equipment and tactical protocols currently provided to address this hazard are inadequate," the article said.

The ESDC ordered DFO to take immediate action to protect its officers, and most of the officers who had been refusing to work since July 2024 were back at work by October.

title: Lobster issues dominate Canadian election in Atlantic province
content:
Fishing industry issues are a central issue in the federal election campaign in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia (NS), particularly along the province's southern shore, where the lobster industry is the main industry in many coastal communities, reports the CBC.

Canadians will go to the ballot box on April 28 to elect a new federal government. The election was spurred by the resignation of former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau in March, followed by the election of former governor of the Bank of Canada, Mark Carney, as Liberal leader and prime minister. Soon after winning the Liberal leadership on March 14, Carney called a federal election.

Two NS political ridings (districts), South Shore-St. Margarets and Acadie-Annapolis, represent some of the country's most lucrative lobster fishing areas.

The lobster industry in the region has been in turmoil for nearly a decade, with reports of illegal fishing frustrating licensed harvesters, as reported by Undercurrent News. The federal government has struggled to adopt regulations to satisfy both the commercial license holders and First Nations communities that say they have a treaty right to fish for a moderate livelihood fishery, including fishing outside the DFO-regulated seasons.

In 2024, Nova Scotia's highest court granted more time for Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans and the Sipekne'katik First Nation, a Mi'kmaq community in southwest NS, to find an agreement through mediation, Undercurrent reported.

At around the same time, the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance, representing commercially licensed harvesters in southwest NS, launched its own lawsuit against the Sipekne'katik nation's lobster fishery. That case is still pending.

Rick Perkins, a member of the Conservative Party of Canada (CPC), is aiming to hold on to his South Shore-St. Margaret seat. In 2021, Perkins defeated Liberal and former DFO minister Bernadette Jordan.

He's promising that a CPC government in Ottawa would enforce the commercial lobster fishing seasons.

Former lobster fisherman Chris d'Entremont, who was elected to Canada's House of Commons in 2021, also hopes to keep the Acadie-Annapolis seat for the CPC.

He's up against three other candidates, including Liberal Ronnie LeBlanc, who served in the Nova Scotia legislature from 2021 to 2021 and was a lobster fisherman for three decades before that."
