title: Tuna groups call on IOTC to strengthen social, environmental responsibilities
content:
Campaign group the Global Tuna Alliance (GTA) is calling on the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC) to adopt sweeping reforms that address not just environmental concerns but the human cost of tuna fishing in the region.

Meanwhile, the International Pole & Line Foundation (IPNLF) and The Pew Charitable Trusts called on the IOTC to adopt stronger, science-based measures to protect tuna stocks and improve fisheries management. 

This comes ahead of the IOTC annual meeting, which will take place on April 13-17 in La Reunion, an island in the Indian Ocean that is an overseas department and region of France.

GTA, representing a network of international retailers and supply chain companies, has launched a new campaign urging IOTC members to take action to improve labor conditions aboard tuna vessels. 

Investigation reveals North Korean forced labor on Chinese fishing vessels

Its appeal comes amid growing evidence of human rights abuses at sea, including reports of forced labor, violence, and unsafe working environments.

"Fishers are the backbone of this industry, and for our partners, decent working conditions at sea are not negotiable," said Daniel Suddaby, executive director of the GTA.

He called on IOTC delegates to develop labor standards based on the International Labor Organization's Work in Fishing Convention (ILO C188) and the commission's socio-economics working party to take up the issue.

Various retailers, including French supermarket giant Carrefour, are backing the initiative. The company has pledged to implement 100% observer coverage on industrial tuna fishing vessels that supply its own-brand canned tuna.

IPNLF, Pew call for more decisive action
China challenges Indian Ocean tuna quotas as yellowfin stocks rated ‘green’

The IPNLF, which champions one-by-one tuna fisheries, is urging IOTC members to take decisive steps to ensure long-term sustainability for both tuna stocks and the coastal communities that rely on them.

For skipjack tuna, IPNLF warned that recent abnormally high recruitment rates -- likely driven by environmental conditions -- have now declined. The organization urged the commission to adopt precautionary catch limits and enforce compliance. It pointed to 2022 data showing that skipjack catches exceeded agreed limits by 33%, highlighting the urgent need for greater accountability.

Regarding yellowfin tuna, IPNLF stressed that the ongoing issues surrounding the standardization of catch-per-unit-effort data in the 2024 stock assessment must be resolved to restore transparency. While this process is underway, the group called for a precautionary catch limit and insisted that any new limits must be equitable and free from formal objections to ensure compliance.

IPNLF also said it opposes proposals that would allow the creation of new support vessel categories that are likely to sidestep current limitations. It called for improved reporting through expanded mandatory data submission, coastal state notifications, and more apparent observer program timelines.

It backed the GTA's call for new crew labor protections, advocating for binding labor standards similar to those adopted by the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission in 2023.

Pew echoed the call for science-based, precautionary action, highlighting that while IOTC has taken steps towards sustainable fisheries -- including the adoption of management procedures for swordfish, skipjack and bigeye tuna -- more must be done to implement these policies effectively.

Yellowfin tuna are among several commercially important Indian Ocean species that stand to benefit from a shift to precautionary, science-based management. Photo: Ellen Cuylaerts Ocean Image Bank.

Harvest strategies offer a long-term framework for setting catch levels based on scientific benchmarks rather than annual political negotiations. Pew emphasized that implementation guidance is critical to ensuring these tools work as intended.

The organization also underscored the opportunity to revive work on a management procedure for yellowfin tuna, especially in light of an improved stock outlook. Pew argued that had such a framework been in place, catch limits might already reflect this positive development.

To boost compliance and monitoring, Pew called for wider use of electronic monitoring (EM) and observer coverage following IOTC's 2023 move to adopt EM standards. It further recommended enhancing vessel tracking through satellite-based systems and catch documentation to ensure traceability from ocean to market.

The International Seafood Sustainability Foundation (ISSF) also emphasized the need for science-based fisheries management.

In a recent article, ISSF's scientists outlined urgent priorities for IOTC member states, including enforcing catch limits for yellowfin, bigeye, and skipjack tuna in line with scientific advice.

It also requested expanding observer coverage, adopting EM systems, and reforming vessel monitoring and port state controls to curb IUU fishing. It said that strengthening protections for bycatch species like sharks and sea turtles should be a priority at the upcoming IOTC meeting.

title: Bumble Bee Foods sued by fishermen alleging forced labor
content:
Bumble Bee Foods has been sued by a group of fishermen alleging they experienced human trafficking and forced labor onboard vessels that caught tuna the company eventually sold in the United States.

The suit, filed on behalf of four Indonesian fishermen on Wednesday (March 12) in the US District Court for the Southern District of California, alleges the San Diego, California-based tuna giant violated the US Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act. The law allows victims to sue companies that "knew or should have known that they were benefitting from participation in a venture engaged in forced labor, debt bondage or other abuses," the complaint explains.

Greenpeace USA, which has an attorney acting as co-counsel for the plaintiffs, has carried out a multi-year campaign against Bumble Bee and FCF Inc., Bumble Bee's parent company, linking their vessels to labor abuses and illegal fishing, as Undercurrent News previously reported.

"[These fishermen] expose a broken system where thousands of other workers in the industrial fishing sector are trapped in conditions of human trafficking and forced labor in one of the most isolated workplaces on the planet. Today, I am optimistic that through this case they will get the justice they deserve and that corporations will know their power is not unmatched," Sari Heidenreich, senior human rights advisor for Greenpeace USA, said in a prepared statement.

Value of MSC check questioned in lawsuits against Bumble Bee, Walmart

The lawsuit alleges the four fishermen "were subjected to physical abuse and violence, deprived of adequate food, and denied medical care (and put back to work) even when seriously injured."

It states: "The men were ensnared by debt bondage, which meant they would owe money if they quit their jobs. The fees, deductions, and penalties left them with little to no wages for their months of hard labor. Because the supply chain was structured so that the vessels stayed at sea – supply ships restocked the fishing vessel and collected the catch on the high seas, a practice called transshipment – the men were isolated, at the mercy of the captain and cut off from sources of potential assistance. The men repeatedly asked to go home, even banding together in work stoppages, but were not permitted to leave their vessels."

The lawsuit alleges the tuna harvested by forced labor was imported by Bumble Bee, the US' second-largest tuna canner, and sold to grocery stores nationwide.

Besides financial compensation, the suit demands FCF, Bumble Bee and its venture partners stop using manning agencies that charge recruitment fees, promise to ensure fishermen are paid at least monthly, halt all at-sea tuna transshipments, and ensure no fishing trip lasts more than three months while providing fishermen 10 rest hours per 24-hour period and 10 days of paid shore leave between journeys.

The suit also requests all fishing vessels in Bumble Bee's supply chain be equipped with appropriate medical equipment and supplies and training be provided to use them, as well as functional wi-fi access for the entire crew and provisions for medical evacuations when necessary.

Additionally, the suit demands 100% human or electronic observer coverage on all of Bumble Bee's tuna-supply vessels "to ensure vital data on catch composition, bycatch, interactions with protected species, and overall fishing practices are reported by independent and impartial parties."

Greenpeace finds labor issues, ‘alarming’ shark catches in North Pacific fishing

Bumble Bee spokesperson Liz Conant said in an email to Undercurrent on Wednesday that "Bumble Bee just became aware of the filing and will not be commenting on pending litigation."

In 2022, the company opposed an effort by the US' National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration to revise existing anti-IUU rules to harmonize legal enforcement provisions relating to forced labor currently found in other legislation. 

"Globally, the industry-wide employment challenges are complex and must be addressed through collaboration and a shared commitment to action and improvement with NGOs and governments worldwide," Bumble Bee spokesperson Dan Barber told Undercurrent at the time.

Greenpeace's Heidenrich acknowledged there are barriers in filing such a case given the dearth of previous suits that have been adjudicated on the legal premise the plaintiffs are arguing. She nevertheless said her organization believes the case is worth pursuing.

"It is good that this pathway to justice exists in the US legal system and that these workers are able to seek justice that way," she said. "And yet, the barriers to filing such cases are extremely high, as evidenced by the decades of reporting on forced labor in US supply chains and the comparatively small number of TVPRA cases that have been brought."

She continued: "Survivors of human rights abuses should not have to wait years for justice or wade through complex legal systems for a chance to get the remedy they deserve. Seafood companies at all stages of the supply chain need to act now to address these repeated and pervasive issues. The extended isolation that put these individuals, and countless others, in extremely vulnerable positions, must end."

title: Status quo TAC, beefed-up regulations for Canada’s 2025 elver fishery
content:
Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) confirmed on Monday (March 3) that a commercial elver fishery will go ahead in Atlantic Canada in 2025 with beefed-up regulations, but there will be no increase in the total allowable catch (TAC).

The elver fishery occurs in Southwest New Brunswick, the Upper Bay of Fundy, Southwest Nova Scotia, along the Eastern Shore of Nova Scotia, and in portions of Cape Breton Island.  The TAC for the 2025 season has been set at 9,960 kilograms, the same as in the 2022 and 2023 seasons, DFO said in a press release.

The elver fishery usually opens in March, but an opening date has not yet been set for 2025. DFO officials are consulting with license holders to finalize an opening date in the coming weeks, the department said.

New regulations, which came into force March 1, will guide the fishery in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick this season. The updated rules were developed in response to criminal activity that has plagued the fishery for years.

"Under the new regulations, elver fishing and possession license holders are required to submit reports to DFO to manage the movement of elvers in the export supply chain. Individuals or businesses need a possession license to possess elvers once they have been deposited at a holding facility, and an export license to arrange for elvers to be exported from Canada," DFO said in its statement.

In 2024, DFO minister Diane Lebouthillier shut down the commercial fishery for that year, saying that without significant changes, the risks to the conservation of the species couldn't satisfactorily be addressed, and an orderly fishery could not be maintained.

FREE READ DFO confirms 37 people charged with elver poaching in 2024

There's a high demand for elvers in Asia, mainly China, where they are grown out in aquaculture facilities to feed the sushi market. That's pushed the price per kilo into the stratosphere.

During the 2023 season, one kilogram of baby eels fetched fishers record prices of CAD 5,000 ($3,694), the equivalent of CAD 2,272 per pound. The fishery has generated CAD 19m for the NS economy and CAD 49m annually for NB over the past few years.

However, the lucrative fishery has also drawn criminals to the river, and illegal activity has escalated to involve guns and threats of violence, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

Canada’s elver license holders bash DFO math, seek higher TAC

Through 2024, the DFO held consultations to explore several options for countering illegal activity in the fishery, including a proposal to redistribute the quota to more people. However, that proposal was quashed earlier this year after strong opposition from longstanding elver harvesters, as reported by Undercurrent. 

Instead, DFO announced in January that it would divide the quota that had previously been shared among nine companies, giving half to First Nations.

"The distribution of the TAC among First Nations is based on population size. We continue to consult with First Nations in preparation for this season," DFO said in its latest press release.

This season, license holders must also use an Elver Management and Tracking (EMT) app to provide elver data to authorities.

"The EMT application collects data on elver fishing activity, catch, the transfer of elvers between authorized holding facility locations, and the shipment of elvers from an authorized holding facility to a place of export," DFO explained.

Reporting data collected through the application will enable fishery officers to differentiate between legal versus illegal elver shipments and to help prevent unlawfully harvested elver from entering the legal supply chain, DFO added.

title: Investigation reveals North Korean forced labor on Chinese fishing vessels
content:
Chinese tuna fishing vessels operating in the Indian Ocean employed North Korean workers under conditions of forced labor between 2019 and 2024, potentially violating UN sanctions, according to evidence in a new investigation.

The Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF) identified North Korean workers across 12 Chinese tuna longliners through interviews with Indonesian and Filipino crew members. Some North Korean workers were reportedly trapped at sea for up to 10 years without being allowed to return to land. 

Sysco, Trident among big firms asked for updates on forced labor sourcing investigations

"Six Koreans were not allowed to go home even after they completed their four-year contract. They were just moved from one ship to another," one Indonesian crew member told investigators.

Four of the implicated vessels are authorized to export seafood to the EU and UK markets. The investigation traced potential supply chains through trans-shipment operations, finding that after collecting catch from the fishing vessels, refrigerated cargo ships visited ports in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan.

You can view the full report here.

No escape

Investigators found vessel captains actively concealed the North Korean workers' presence, particularly during port visits in Mauritius. According to crew testimony, North Korean workers were transferred to other vessels before port calls. In one instance, eight North Korean workers were allegedly hidden in a lower compartment of a vessel during a port inspection.

"The North Koreans weren't allowed to be seen in Mauritius. Whenever we docked, the North Koreans would be transferred," reported one crew member.

Workers onboard a Chinese tuna vessel. Credit: EJF

Widespread illegal fishing practices reportedly took place alongside the labor violations. Five vessels were accused of shark finning and capturing protected species, including dolphins. One incident involved the deliberate capture of a dolphin whose teeth were extracted to make jewelry.

FREE READ Chinese squid fishing vessel disembarks 15 critically ill crew in under three years

Working conditions aboard the vessels were consistently reported as abusive. Crew members described physical violence, excessive working hours, document retention, and deceptive wage practices. In one case, a North Korean worker suffered a head injury when a fishing line snapped but allegedly received inadequate medical treatment. 

"Every time we saw them, they looked very stressed... even six months [at sea] are too long [for me], I would be stressed. I could not imagine it being for years," one Indonesian crew member said of the North Korean workers.

Steve Trent, CEO of EJF, called the findings "a damning indictment of the failure to regulate our oceans," noting that while illegal fishing and human rights abuses are widespread in China's distant-water fleet, "the use of North Korean forced labor for such long periods is a particularly severe example of the egregious misconduct uncovered."

Credit: EJF

"This constitutes forced labor of a magnitude that surpasses much of that witnessed in a global fishing industry already replete with abuse," he said.

The organization called for mandatory vessel tracking and stricter regulation of at-sea transfer of catch between vessels. Port states should also be better equipped to identify and intervene in forced labor cases.

EJF said its report was the first documented case of North Korean labor on distant-water fishing vessels, though China is estimated to host 100,000 North Korean workers in other industries, including seafood processing.

The use of North Korean labor outside the country is prohibited under UN Security Council sanctions aimed at restricting funding for North Korea's nuclear weapons program. The EU and US also ban imports of goods produced using North Korean labor.

title: Canadian transportation company charged in relation to elver seizure
content:
Charges have been filed against a transportation company in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia in relation to the seizure last year of roughly CAD 250,000 ($174,820) worth of juvenile eels that were allegedly caught illegally, the CBC reports. 

Igloo Transport Ltd., in Halifax, was arraigned last month in a provincial court in Dartmouth on the charge that it possessed, sold or purchased elvers in contravention of the Fisheries Act or its regulations. The juvenile eels were to be delivered to Toronto for export.

Two people were also charged in the case, according to the news service.

Igloo declined to comment, according to CBC.

Last spring's season was canceled by Canadian fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier following several years of chaos and violence in the highly lucrative fishery, a move that effectively made any elver fishing along Nova Scotia and New Brunswick rivers illegal, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

The charges also come as Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans faces heavy criticism for what some complain is poor enforcement and is introducing new regulations it hopes will help better plug the sale and export of illegally caught elvers.

Commercial elver license holders in Atlantic Canada have also bashed the math used by DFO to allocate quotas for 2025, and are seeking a higher overall total allowable catch for the coming season, as Undercurrent reported.

title: Canada’s elver license holders bash DFO math, seek higher TAC
content:
Commercial elver license holders in Atlantic Canada have bashed the math used by Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) to allocated quotas for 2025, and are seeking a higher overall total allowable catch (TAC) for the coming season.

"DFO's reallocation of elver quota was intended to result in a 50/50 allocation of the [TAC] between First Nations and commercial fishers. However, the recently announced allocations reflect a far larger uncompensated reduction in quota, up to 73.6%, for most commercial license holders," said Genna Carey, president of the Canadian Committee for a Sustainable Eel Fishery (CCSEF), reacting on Wednesday (Jan. 29) to information in a letter from the DFO to the industry two days earlier.

In its letter on Monday (Jan.27) to license holders in the provinces of New Brunswick (NB) and Nova Scotia (NS), the DFO said half the commercial quota for 2025 will be given to new entrant First Nations that not have access to the fishery prior to 2022, as reported by Undercurrent News. 

The annual elver quota since 2006 has been 9,860 kilograms, divided among nine commercial license holders.

Winners and losers as Canada shuffles baby eel quota

However, the share of the quota to First Nations will be higher than 50%, said the CCSEF. 

The redistribution means 63.5% is now allocated to First Nations because the DFO did not count the commercial communal quota held by Waycobah First Nation, Carey explained.

Waycobah, a First Nations company, and Shelburne Elver, a cooperative, are getting more because Ottawa wants to increase the participation of Indigenous and "co-operative-like" operations, the DFO said when it announced the quotas for the nine commercial license holders.

"This approach is both illogical and directly contradicts DFO's position during the 2022 and 2023 seasons when all other commercial license holders were required to surrender 14% of their quota to First Nations while Waycobah was exempt. This discrepancy must be addressed and corrected before the season begins," said Carey.

The group also offered a solution.

Why not use the CAD 260 million ($181m) earmarked by DFO but rejected by First Nations to allow Indigenous people to buy out commercial license holders who are willing to sell? 

In December 2024, DFO minister Diane Lebouthillier offered the funding to First Nations chiefs in Atlantic Canada to help them purchase fishing licenses, boats and gear.

The offer was rejected by the Assembly of Nova Scotia Mi'kmaw chiefs, who said they feared the offer could threaten their Treaty Rights, as reported by Undercurrent.

Canadian elver industry says DFO plan is a ‘smash and grab’

Since that money is obviously available, it could be used to compensate longstanding elver license holders for loss of quota, suggested the CCSEF.

"Based on DFO's own frequently cited valuation, less than one-third of the unwanted 'Marshall Money' could be used to fairly compensate license holders for the 4,980 kg of quota being appropriated and allocated to First Nations to support their moderate livelihood rights. This approach aligns with the precedent set in other fisheries, where the Crown fulfills its obligations to Indigenous fishers," offered Carey.

Many concerns about the 2025 elver season

In addition to concerns over the loss of quota, the CCSEF has other worries about the overall TAC and enforcement for the 2025 season.

Scientific data suggests that the overall TAC for the elver fishery could be substantially increased without any adverse effects on conservation, Carey said, noting that 204 adult eel licenses have been retired since 2000, but there has been no increase in the elver TAC since then.

An increased quota could be more equitably shared between the First Nations and commercial fishers, the CCSEF offered.

"DFO's own elver experts have indicated that several new river systems could be used to expand the fishery, and the quota on some currently utilized systems could be safely expanded. This adjustment should be implemented before the 2025 season," Carey said.

DFO minister Diane Lebouthillier canceled the Atlantic Canada commercial elver fishery in 2024, saying she had considered all options and concluded that, without significant changes, the risks to the conservation of the species couldn't satisfactorily be addressed. Nor could an orderly management of the fishery be restored, she determined, as reported by Undercurrent.

The elver fishery on Canada's east coast has been plagued by illegal fishing for many years.

Nova Scotia fisheries minister challenges Canada over handling of elver fishery

Commercial license holders told a Canadian Parliamentary committee in 2023 that illegal fishing had exploded on rivers in NB and NS, driven by the value of the tiny baby eels, which have been selling for prices ranging from CAD 3,000/kg to CAD 4,685 and higher in recent years, as reported by Undercurrent.

The eels are sold mainly to China, where they are used as broodstock in aquaculture facilities where the tiny, translucent fish are grown to adult size for the sushi market.

"With a lack of regulations around the transferability of First Nation commercial communal quota, we are concerned that this moderate livelihood quota may be leased to non-Indigenous fishers, while individual First Nation members fish elvers unlicensed in the pursuit of a moderate livelihood. This could result in exactly the same chaotic scenes that lead the minister to close the fishery after only 18 days in 2023 and not open it at all in 2024," said Carey.

On the issue of enforcement, the department has enacted new regulations on the possession and export of elvers and developed an electronic monitoring and traceability system, the DFO stated in its Jan. 27 letter to the industry.

There's still no official word on whether there will be a commercial elver fishery in Atlantic Canada in 2025. That decision will be made by Lebouthilier in the coming weeks, a spokesperson for DFO told Undercurrent on Jan. 30.

In the past, the elver season has opened in March.

title: Canada postpones discussion on elver pilot project
content:
Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) has indefinitely postponed information sessions on its proposed pilot project to transfer elver quotas from longtime license holders, reports the CBC.

The DFO plan to redistribute up to 50% of the current annual elver quota to allow 150 new licenses and increased access for First Nations, with no compensation to long-standing license holders for the expropriation, was vehemently criticized by the industry in the provinces of Nova Scotia (NS) and New Brunswick (NB).

The Canadian Committee for a Sustainable Elver Fishery, led by commercial license holder Stanley King, called it a "smash and grab," as previously reported by Undercurrent News. 

In an email on Tuesday (Jan. 14), the DFO told elver license holders that an information session planned for next week is postponed indefinitely and the agency will contact fishers "as soon as a decision is received" on the future of the fishery, reported the CBC.

When asked if the postponement signals that the pilot project is being abandoned, a DFO official said the agency is still considering "input."

Recall that fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier canceled the 2023 elver season in the Atlantic provinces over concerns of illegal fishing and the conservation of the species.

Canada to crack down on elver fishery following reports of organized crime, guns, violence

While the quota for elvers — also known as glass eels — is small, at just 9,860 kilograms in total in NS and NB, the value is high. In recent years, elvers have fetched prices of CAD 3,000 ($42,225) per kilogram to CAD 5,000/kg. The elvers are highly valued in Asian markets, where they are grown out in aquaculture facilities to supply eels to the sushi market.

The season in Atlantic Canada usually begins in March.

title: Untitled
content:
Harvesters in Canada's largest lobster fishery continue to be challenged by weather and low catches as the season enters its second month, keeping prices at the dock higher than usual.

Lobster fishing areas (LFAs) 33 and 34, off the southeastern and southwestern shores of the province of Nova Scotia, are among Canada's most prolific. Combined they accounted for an estimated 21,405 (22%) of the country's 95,253 metric tons of landings in 2023, according to figures shared with Undercurrent News by the Lobster Council of Canada.

However, since the two LFAs kicked off their seasons in late November, bad weather has plagued the fishing fleets. 

While there is no official tally of daily or weekly landings during the season, there are reports that catches are down by about 20% in LFA  34 compared to a year ago, Heather Mulock, executive director of the Coldwater Lobster Association (CLA), one of the trade groups that represents harvesters in the area, told Undercurrent News this week.

Harvesters in St. Mary's Bay in LFA 34 are having a "horrible season overall,
 she said. And it's not just because of the weather.

Canadian court grants more time for mediation over lobster fishing rights

"When you have out-of-season and, in some cases, illegal fishing continually going on month after month every summer, for several years, it's impacting them," said Mulock, referencing the ongoing issue of illegal fishing in the area.

The Nova Scotia lobster industry has flagged the St. Mary's Bay area as an active one for illegal fishing.

The Unified  Fisheries Conservation Alliance (UFCA), a non-profit alliance of fishing groups in Nova Scotia, said in September that more than a couple dozen commercial-sized lobster boats were fishing for lobster out of harbors from Saulinerville to Yarmouth, with landings of up to 25,000 pounds of lobster some nights, during the closed season, as reported by Undercurrent.

UFCA launched a lawsuit that month against a lobster processing company and several individuals, alleging they had bought lobsters illegally caught in St. Mary's Bay.

Lobster fishing areas in Atlantic Canada. Map courtesy of Lobster Council of Canada.

While that case plays out in court, licensed harvesters in the area have had to fish further and further from shore each year to find the shellfish, said Mulock.

"Unfortunately, we will likely see some of those licenses for sale because they can't make a go of it in that bay anymore," she predicted.

"It's going to be interesting to see what happens here in the spring, as our season continues. I'm hoping the landings will pick up a little bit more, and we have some holidays coming up that we'd like to capitalize on, like Valentine's Day and Mother's Day. But, overall, it's been a slow start to the season," said Mulock.

Lower-quality catches

Shore prices continue to hold at around CAD 12.00 ($8.34) per pound, with some dealers paying up to CAD 12.50/lb, some sources tell Undercurrent.

It's stayed at CAD 11.50 to CAD 12.00 for weeks now, roughly where prices were to start the season, said Mulock. Recall that shore prices opened the 2023 season at roughly CAD 10.50/lb seen a year ago, which was a significant gain over the CAD 7.50/lb price paid at the beginning of the 2022 season.

"To the regular consumer, that price might seem high, but the point I often make is that, with operational costs, for some guys, they're barely making ends meet, especially if they're fishing further offshore," Mulock said.

Canadian lobster dock prices stay high as harvesters battle bad weather, trap-invading Jonah crabs

"It (shore price) is not horrible, it's not great, but it's just right in that spot where we can make a go of it, but a little bit more would be great," Mulock offered.

However, dealers are facing challenges because of the high dock price, especially since the quality of the catch has not been up to scratch, according to Stewart Lamont, president of Tangier Lobster, a Nova Scotia-based lobster exporter. A significant portion of some catches have been undesirable for the live market, he told Undercurrent.

"I think it's about 20% to 30% undesirable in the catch, a combination of soft, medium-shelled, and single-claw lobster. And the loss on that for shore dealers is CAD 2.00 to CAD 3.00/lb," he said.

FREE READ US wholesale: Lobster meat prices continue to rally amid supply constraints; tails full steady in week 2

What that means is that the other 70% of the catch has to be premium A grade, if you're paying CAD 12.50 at the docks, because of the loss on the B-grade lobster, he explained. B-grade lobster is either processed for meat and tails or sold to clients who buy single claw lobsters at a deep discount, at CAD 1.00 to CAD 3.00/lb less than cost.

Another dealer, who asked not to be named, said he's seeing around 10% to 15% of B-grade lobster in the landings so far. The landings have been slow because of weather, he said, and it will take a few more weeks to determine whether the quality will improve.

It's not surprising to see lower-grade lobsters at this time of year, because they are in post molt, said Lamont.

"What is shocking is that the quality is this challenged, and … that we are paying the prices we are for a substandard lobster," said Lamont, adding that this season, so far, "has been an unfortunate to an unmitigated disaster" for the majority of lobster buyers.

"From a dealer standpoint, it's been a massive challenge. The quality is substandard, the international market is weak, and we have paid premium prices for a process-grade lobster. As an industry, we have made every mistake in the book to now," said Lamont.

Meanwhile, the bad weather continues to hinder the fishing fleets. This week the boats won't be able to get back on the water until Saturday (Jan. 11), a source told Undercurrent. 

Wholesale prices inch up

Wholesale prices for live North American lobster have inched up since the opening of the LFA 33 and 34 seasons. A 1.25-pound hard shell lobster, better known as a "quarter," was going for an average range of $11.50-$11.75/lb this week after selling for $11.25-$11.50/lb during the first week of December.

Meanwhile, live lobster export prices have dropped over the past month. One exporter was charging $12.59/lb for quarters sent to Shanghai, China, this week, down 2% from the $12.88/lb price charged during the first week of December, for example. Similarly, the exporter was charging $12.26/lb for quarters sent to Paris, France, this week, down 4% from the $12.75/lb charged during the first week of December.

Upgrade to Pro to view

Meanwhile, wholesale prices for frozen North American lobster tails have not changed since week 49 of 2024 (Dec. 2-8), based on the latest update of UCN's wholesale price database. The common size of 4-5 ounces remained $24.00/lb during week 2 of 2025 (Jan. 6-12). 

"The market appears firm at listed levels. Buying patterns remain steady, and inventory is on the light side. As a result, prices are supported," wrote Gary Morrison, head of growth and strategy for UCN's price reporting agency. 

Frozen lobster meat prices, however, are up slightly, according to the UCN database. Tail claw knuckle meat, for example, was selling for an average $42.00/lb during week 2 of 2025, up from $41.00/lb during week 49.

"There is limited replacement in the market and concerns over future inventory," Morrison said.

title: Editor’s choice: UCN’s most-read stories of 2024
content:
EMEA editor Neil Ramsden brings you a roundup of some of the biggest stories of 2024 based on our most-read statistics.

In April, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration declared new disaster designations for three commercial salmon fisheries in the US states of Alaska and Washington, following poor or restricted fishing and significant declines in the value of harvests during the years 2021 and 2022. Set-netters on the east side of Alaska's Cook Inlet have seen the value of the commercial sockeye fishery shrink due to restrictions implemented to protect dwindling late runs of Chinook, or king salmon, that have significantly curtailed harvests or closed the fishery altogether.

In September, the US National Marine Fisheries Service closed the pollock trawl fishery in the central Gulf of Alaska after two fishing vessels caught an "unprecedented" amount of Chinook (or king) salmon as bycatch. The closure left just over 50,000 metric tons in the water, uncaught. 

US giant Trident Seafoods decided it would not reopen its St. Paul, Alaska, processing plant for the winter snow crab season in October, leading to scrambling among Bering Sea communities as harvesters and processors had to reallocate snow crab quota shares on a tight deadline. After two successive closures due to collapsing crab stocks, US fisheries regulators announced they would reopen the snow crab fishery to a limited harvest. However, Trident's decision meant there was no processor in the northern region where dedicated quota shares are based. 

US seafood chain Red Lobster -- at the time owned by Thai Union Group -- filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection with hundreds of millions of dollars in outstanding debt in May. Fortress Investment Group acquired the world's largest seafood restaurant group in September and named Damola Adamolekun as CEO. 

Back in Alaska, Northline Seafoods and Circle Seafoods made waves in the US state this summer. The two Washington state-based companies anticipated fishermen would be able to unload their catch at their floating freezer barges during the salmon season in a first for the state's salmon fisheries, which have traditionally depended on shoreside plants for processing. 

Tensions built in Canada's largest lobster fishery this year, with Colin Sproul, president of the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance, warning something terrible could happen should fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier not act. "There's going to be an explosion of violence in southwest Nova Scotia," he told Undercurrent News. Nova Scotia fisheries minister Kent Smith said the fishery had a problem not just with First Nation groups harvesting during closed seasons but also with organized crime.

Only days ago, on Dec. 19, shipping giant Maersk confirmed it would halt its trans-Pacific freight service from Alaska's largest US seafood ports by volume in February 2025, taking US seafood producers by surprise. The last shipment scheduled is for Feb. 11, 2025 -- in the middle of the pollock "A" season, which opens Jan. 20, 2025, and typically runs into April.

In October, Undercurrent's readers were interested to hear that Israeli researchers had successfully bred the world's first gene-edited giant freshwater prawn using CRISPR technology, a tool that allows scientists to precisely modify specific genes to enhance traits like growth and disease resistance. The development could change shrimp farming significantly by helping prawns grow faster and resist diseases, making the industry more efficient and sustainable.

And in February, they were dismayed to read that Trident, High Liner Foods and Sysco Corp. had all suspended business with a large processing firm in China, Dalian Haiqing Food Co., over a bombshell report by the Outlaw Ocean Project over the use of North Korean labor. Having created a storm in the seafood sector in 2023 with revelations of Uyghur labor in Chinese processing plants, Outlaw Ocean director Ian Urbina turned his team's focus to North Korean workers.

title: Nova Scotia opposes DFO’s proposal on eel quota for Atlantic Canada
content:
The government of the Canadian province of Nova Scotia says the federal Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) should reconsider its proposal to redistribute the quota baby eels in Atlantic Canada, reports the Canadian Press. 

It's not a good idea for DFO to redistribute licenses to people already working for commercial companies that harvest the elvers, Nova Scotia's premier, Tim Houston, said in a year-end interview.

The DFO proposal, explained in a letter to commercial elver companies on Dec. 5, is to redistribute 50% of the annual quota to First Nations in the region to increase their participation in the fishery, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

The three-year pilot project would allow 150 new commercial licenses to enter the fishery. But that would mean an 80% to 90% reduction in the quota for companies that have held licenses for years, a move that commercial license holders have called a "smash and grab."

Recall that last year, a Canadian parliamentary committee studying the problem of illegal fishing heard tales of violence, death threats and even organized crime involvement in the elver fishery on a handful of rivers in Atlantic Canada as the value for the catch skyrocketed in recent years to as much as CAD 5,000 ($3476) per kilogram. 

Baby eels are in demand in Asia, where they are grown in aquaculture facilities for the sushi market.

Recall that in October, a report by a Canadian parliamentary committee tasked with examining the issue of illegal fishing in Canada said DFO should take action to increase enforcement to deter illegal fishing, as reported by Undercurrent.

However, the Nova Scotia government said adding up to 150 new participants in the eel fishery would make it harder to monitor illegal activities.

The reallocation of the quota would make it nearly impossible for banks and funding institutions like the Nova Scotia Fisheries and Aquaculture Board to provide financial support to the businesses, the province said.

"I urge you to reconsider this proposal and instead focus on policies that respect the contributions of existing license holders," said the province's fisheries minister, Kent Smith, in a letter to DFO minister Diane Lebouthillier.

title: DFO confirms 37 people charged with elver poaching in 2024
content:
More than three dozen people -- 37 to be exact -- have been charged with offenses related to illegal elver fishing in Canada's Maritime provinces in 2024, reports the CBC. 

However, the number of charges is far less than the number of arrests Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) made in 2024. Officers arrested 169 people this year and seized 396.3 kilograms of elvers, the department noted on its website.

Among the cases trickling into court include charges against five people from the US state of Maine, who were arrested by fisheries officers in April near Meteghan River, in the province of Nova Scotia.

Recall that Canada's fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier shut down the commercial elver fishery in the Maritime provinces this year, saying the decision would help enforcement officers address the issue of illegal fishing, as reported by Undercurrent News. 

Though the combined elver quota for Nova Scotia and New Brunswick is small, around 9,860 kilograms annually since 2006, the value of the catch has been sky-high in recent years, ranging from CAD 3,000 ($2,225)/kg to CAD 5,000/kg in the past decade.

The high prices for elvers have brought poachers to the rivers in both provinces. This has led to dangerous confrontations and evidence of organized crime.

Charges related to the elver fishery require approval by the Public Prosecution Service of Canada, a process that has led to months of delays between an arrest and the laying of a charge, reported the CBC.

"Fishery officers are working with the Public Prosecution Service of Canada to complete their ongoing investigations related to enforcement actions taken in 2024 related to unauthorized elver harvesting, which may result in additional charges," the DFO said in a statement to the CBC.

title: Canadian elver industry says DFO plan is a ‘smash and grab’
content:
A proposal being contemplated by Canada's fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier to redistribute the elver quota in Atlantic Canada amounts to nothing more than a "smash and grab," says commercial elver harvester Stanley King, who heads a group representing long-standing elver harvesting companies in the region.

"It's straight-up expropriation, right out of a communist playbook," King told Undercurrent News this week.

The DFO proposal, explained in a letter to commercial elver companies on Dec. 5, is to redistribute 50% of the annual quota to First Nations in the region to increase their participation in the fishery.

A three-year pilot project would also allow 150 new commercial licenses to enter the fishery; 120 of them, with a quota of 22 kg each, would be issued to people already involved in elver fishing as employees of existing commercial license holders.

But that would mean an 80% to 90% reduction in the quota for companies like King's Atlantic Elver Fishery, which has been involved in the fishery for years.

"It's anti-business. I just don't know how any business could survive the threat of having its quotas taken away and given to its employees," said King, who speaks for the Canadian Committee for a Sustainable Elver Fishery,

"Businesses will be lucky to survive," he said.

Stanley King, acting president of the Canadian Committee for a Sustainable Elver Fishery, addresses the House of Commons Standing Committee on Fisheries and Oceans on Dec. 7. Photo screenshot from video

Currently, nine businesses in the Maritimes hold commercial licenses to harvest juvenile American eels. Those companies employ about 200 people to fish the rivers to collect valuable elvers. The elvers are primarily sold to China, where they are grown in aquaculture facilities to supply the sushi market.

Though the combined elver quota for Nova Scotia and New Brunswick is small, around 9,860 kilograms annually since 2006, the value of the catch has been sky-high in recent years, ranging from CAD 3,000 ($2,225)/kg to CAD 5,000/kg in the past decade.

For the past couple of years, the fishery was estimated to be worth about CAD 19 million ($14.9m) annually in NS.

But those high prices for elvers have brought poachers to the rivers in both provinces. Along with that has come dangerous confrontations and evidence of organized crime, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

There was no DFO-authorized elver fishery in the Atlantic provinces in 2024. Lebouthillier shut down the fishery on the premise that this move would enable DFO enforcement officers to better detect illegal eel fishing on Atlantic Canadian rivers.

Report increases pressure on Canadian fisheries department to tackle illegal fishing of lobster, elvers

In a meeting with the elver industry on Wednesday (Dec. 11), DFO officials said enforcement officers had arrested 169 illegal eel fishers in 2024 and seized 29 vehicles and 396.3 kg of elvers. However, department officials would not say how many of those arrests had led to charges or convictions.

The elver fishery usually begins in March. Minister Lebouthillier has stated publicly that if a plan for the 2025 fishery can't be finalized by then, the commercial fishery will remain closed next year.

As commercial elver businesses face the threat of major cuts to their quota through expropriation, a better solution would be for the federal government to buy back the elver licenses from established businesses, suggested King.

"The government is just being a bully because they … could sort of wash this expropriation clean, lessen the animosity in the industry, and just pay for the quotas that these communities and our businesses have dependent on for decades," offered King.

"But instead of taking the right path, the reasonable path, it seems DFO would rather just smash and grab it from us because they know we're a small industry and we can't fight back. But that's just not a Canadian thing to do," he said.

title: Canada seeks private charter to patrol for illegal lobster traps
content:
Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) is planning to hire a private contractor to help DFO officers patrol the Bay of Fundy between the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, reports the CBC.

In a request for proposals published on its website last week, the DFO said it is seeking a vessel and crew to take its enforcement officers on patrols to search for and seize illegal lobster fishing gear.

The contract would run from Jan. 1 to March 31, 2025, but could be extended to the spring of 2026, the DFO said. This would allow patrols to happen outside of commercial fishing seasons when industrial-scale lobster fishing should not be happening.

This is not the first time DFO has chartered private vessels to aid patrols, said a DFO spokesperson.

But this contract would provide an increase in surveillance and enforcement, said the DFO. The Bay of Fundy is an area of Atlantic Canada where illegal lobster fishing has been a major problem, as previously reported by Undercurrent News. 

In its request for proposals, the DFO said it hopes to be out on the water three days a week for 12-hour patrols.

The deadline for submission of bids for this DFO contract is Dec. 19.

title: Canadian lobster buyer’s home shot at as Nova Scotia season begins
content:
A lobster buyer in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia said he believes he was sent a threatening message on Saturday night (Nov. 23), just days before the start of the season in lobster fishing areas (LFAs) 33 and 34, reports SaltWire.

Geoffrey Jobert, the owner of Lobster Hub, in Meteghan, on Nova Scotia's south shore, said that he discovered a series of holes passing through his garage door, kitchen, dining room and living room and eventually found a bullet lodged in a hardwood rocking chair. He believes the shots were fired Saturday night, but because it had been stormy that night, the family did not hear them.

On the road outside his house, he found a spent shell casing.

The incident comes as lobster fishermen in the region are being encouraged to boycott buyers allegedly profiting from the out-of-season lobster fishery in St. Mary's Bay during the summer.

About 1,800 fishing boats headed to sea on Tuesday morning for the first day of the season in LFAs 33 and 34, two of the largest lobster fishing areas in Atlantic Canada. 

Recall that the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance (UFCA), a group that represents commercially licensed lobster harvesters in Atlantic Canada, filed a civil lawsuit on Nov. 4, alleging that Independent Fisheries Limited and its president, Xiaoming Mao, of Sable River, Shelburne County, bought lobsters caught illegally, as reported by Undercurrent News.

The lawsuit also named Jason Lamrock and Tyler Nickerson of Fisher Direct and Wesley Nickerson of Seawell Holdings as parties to the illegal activity.

While there's no proof that any of those companies were linked to the Nov. 23 incident at his home, Jobert said he believes someone was trying to intimidate him.

Canadian fisheries officers seize CAD 100k worth of lobster in Nova Scotia

Last season, when a local fisherman stopped selling to BMC Seafoods, a company that lists Xiaoming Mao as one of its directors, and started selling to Lobster Hub, Jobert said he was threatened with being "targeted" by a local crime family.

"We were sent videos of my home at night. I tried to not pay attention to it," Jobert is quoted by SaltWire.

The fisherman who started selling to Lobster Hub also received threats, said Jobert.

The lobster fishery in Atlantic Canada has been marked by tension over the past few years, driven by the issue of out-of-season fishing.

Over this past summer, frustrations have been mounting among commercial license holders as the UFCA began collecting evidence of illegal fishing in St. Mary's Bay, as reported by Undercurrent.

Recall that in September, the UFCA warned that if Canada's fisheries minister did not act to curb illegal lobster fishing, the level of illegal activity and threats of violence would increase, as reported by Undercurrent.

Since July 1, there have been arsons involving five buildings and four vehicles, including an RCMP cruiser burned in Meteghan. Some of that violence was tied to an organized crime group that profits from the sale of illegal lobsters, the RCMP told SaltWire in September.

Meanwhile, Lobster Hub won't be intimidated from buying from licensed fishermen who want to sell their catch, said Jobert.

"I'm not going to stop buying. That's just giving in to this crime bullshit," Jobert is quoted by SaltWire.

title: Canadian elver fishers lose another court challenge
content:
A Canadian court has ruled that Canada's fisheries minister had broad discretion and used it reasonably in deciding to transfer a portion of the elver quota in the Maritime provinces to First Nations without compensating commercial elver license holders, reports the CBC. 

The case stemmed from a 2022 decision by Joyce Murray, former minister of Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO), to transfer 14% of the elver quota from eight commercial license holders to Indigenous groups in the region.

Three commercial license holders challenged that decision in the Supreme Court in 2023, but that court ruled that the process used by Murray in 2022 was fair and reasonable and within ministerial discretion to manage the fishery.

The three license holders involved in that lawsuit took the matter further, filing an application to the Federal Court of Appeal.

Following a hearing in Halifax, Nova Scotia, last week, three justices with the federal appeals upheld the lower court decision, ruling that the federal fisheries minister had "broad discretion" in the matter.

None of the license holders involved in the original court challenge questioned that First Nations should have more access to the elver fishery, but they were upset that the DFO had abandoned the "willing buyer, willing seller" approach that would have compensated elver license holders if they voluntarily gave up the quota.

The elver fishery in the Canadian Maritimes has been fraught with tension and controversy in recent years, with allegations of organized crime being involved in this very lucrative fishery as glass eels have been worth up to CAD 5,000 ($3,567) per kilogram in Asian markets, as reported by Undercurrent News. 

Earlier this year, current DFO minister Diane Lebouthiller shut down the elver fishery in Atlantic Canada, saying that without significant changes, the risk to the conservation of the species could not be addressed.

The commercial harvesters involved in the recent court challenge said the industry had hoped the appeals judges would have addressed the "absolute power" of the fisheries minister to make decisions that have a severe financial impact on license holders.

"I think I really would like to emphasize that this is frightening for anybody investing a nickel in the fishery," Brian Giroux of Shelburne Elver,  one of the companies involved in the court challenge, was quoted by CBC.

The elver fishers have 60 days to file an appeal with the Supreme Court of Canada, if they so choose.

title: Canadian harvesters seek CAD 10m in illegal lobster lawsuit
content:
A Canadian commercial fish harvesters group says private investigators have gathered so much evidence about the illegal sale of lobsters on Nova Scotia's southwest coast that they have a good chance of winning a civil case and damages of CAD 10 million ($7.7m).

The Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance (UFCA), a non-profit group that represents lobster fishing throughout the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, filed a notice of action in the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia on Monday (Nov. 4) against Independent Fisheries Limited and its president, Xiaoming Mao, of Sable River, Shelburne County. It alleges that the company has bought lobsters caught illegally in St. Mary's Bay, on Nova Scotia's southwest coast.

The lawsuit also names Jason Lamrock and Tyler Nickerson of Fisher Direct and Wesley Nickerson of Seawell Holdings as parties to the illegal activity.

"UFCA alleges all of the defendants are engaged in a conspiracy to violate the Fisheries Act and cause damage to the regulated, commercial fishery," the group's lawyer, Richard Norman of the law firm Cox and Palmer, said in a press release.

The action by the UFCA should also serve as a warning to anyone dealing in illegal lobsters, said UFCA president Colin Sproul.

Colin Sproul, president of the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance. Photo from UFCA Facebook page

"I have a message for anybody in Atlantic Canada who would choose to be involved in the illegal purchase and sale of these lobsters. We know who you are, we have evidence against you. We're continuing to collect it, and you're next," Spoul told Undercurrent News. 

This not only applies to the illegal activity in St. Mary's Bay, which has been widely reported, but also to out-of-season season lobster fishing in St. Peter's Bay, Cape Breton Island, Nova Scotia, he added.

While much attention has been focused on the illegal lobster fishery in lobster fishing areas (LFAs) 33 and 34, which account for nearly a third of Canada's world-leading 100,000 metric tons in annual production of North American lobster (Homarus americanus), Sproul said a similar problem exists around Cape Breton, the island portion of Nova Scotia.

"The truth is that indigenous groups in Cape Breton are destroying St. Peter's Bay lobster as we speak, with impunity," Sproul said.

UCN used drones last summer to gather video footage at the Saulnierville wharf on Nova Scotia's St. Mary's Bay to show the public and the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) the level of illegal activity, as reported by Undercurrent.

About 24 to 30 commercial-sized lobster boats were fishing out of harbors in southwestern Nova Scotia, from Saulnierville to Yarmouth, landing up to 25,000 pounds of lobster some nights, Sproul said at the time, adding that most of the activity was centered around the Saulnierville wharf, and involved fishing boats owned by the Spikne'katik First Nation.

Drone footage posted on the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance Facebook page on Oct. 3 shows what appears to be crates of lobster being loaded into a truck on the wharf in Saulnierville, Nova Scotia. Screenshot from UFCA Facebook page

The UFCA has continued to pass on information to federal and provincial officials, but commercial harvesters are outraged and exasperated that DFO hasn't done much to shut down the illegal fishery or penalize those involved, Sproul told Undercurrent on Wednesday.

"We've provided mountains of tips and evidence to the (Canadian) government over the last couple of years, imploring them to act, telling them where exactly to act, and yet they refuse to. They let the perpetrators take the pots, take the lobster, take it to market," he said.

Recall that the DFO and the Sipekne'katik First Nation entered into a mediation process earlier this year to settle the question of what constitutes a moderate livelihood lobster fishery. Canada's Attorney General gave the two sides until Dec. 14 to negotiate a "nation-to-nation" resolution, as reported by Undercurrent. If they don't reach an agreement by that date, the matter will return to the Supreme Court of Canada for a trial process.

Canadian First Nations receive blessing to continue in-season lobster fishing

Meanwhile, the UFCA lawsuit in the Nova Scotia Supreme Court system will likely take weeks or months to get to the trial stage.

Independent Fisheries declined to comment about the allegations in the UFCA lawsuit when contacted by Undercurrent. 

The company has 15 days to file a statement of defense with the Supreme Court. Following that, the court will set a date for a hearing.

However, UFCA hopes that, while this case may take weeks or months to proceed through the court system, it will immediately deter other lobster businesses from illegal activity.

"If you are illegally selling lobster or illegally buying lobster – know that you are being watched every day and every hour. We are gathering evidence against you at this very moment. We aren't going to hesitate to seek compensation for your illegal actions and the harm you are causing fishing communities across this province," Sproul said.

title: Taiwanese tuna giant accused of failing to address environmental, human rights abuses
content:
Fong Chun Formosa (FCF), one of the world's largest tuna suppliers, is failing to act on severe environmental and human rights violations within its supply chain, a new investigation by NGO Shark Guardian has alleged.

The Taiwanese tuna giant, which supplies major global supermarket chains and owns US-based Bumble Bee Foods, has been accused of making empty promises regarding sustainability and human rights reforms.

Shark Guardian's report, called "Empty Promises, Empty Oceans," alleges significant discrepancies between FCF's public pledges and the actual practices of its suppliers.

While FCF claims that 100% of its tuna supply is traced and verified, Shark Guardian found repeated instances of environmental destruction and labor abuses within its operations. These include the mistreatment of fisheries workers and the continued endangerment of shark species.

This week, we launched a year long investigation into Taiwanese tuna giant Fong Chun Formosa, otherwise known as FCF. We found shocking environmental and human rights breaches in its supply chain. A thread. 🧵https://t.co/lQHCD4wXjC pic.twitter.com/dVY7RySeCr

— Shark Guardian (@Shark_Guardian) October 25, 2024

"The FCF supply chain has been tainted by illegal fishing and ongoing breaches of human, labor and environmental standards. Despite its public promises, FCF’s supply chain lacks rigorous examination, its audits are not transparent, and reported violations have little repercussion. Rather than delivering on existing sustainability targets, FCF continuously sets new ones, creating a pattern of delays and obfuscation," the report states.

According to the report, despite its stated commitment to transparency, FCF's complex supply chain, which spans America, Asia Pacific, and the Atlantic and Indian Oceans, remains opaque.

"FCF is such a huge supplier of tuna that its policies impact fishing and fisheries everywhere and while they say the right thing, our report reveals a serious disparity between the tuna giant’s published ambitions and its actions."

Independent organizations struggle to verify the fleet of over 500 vessels associated with the company, many of which have been linked to severe labor abuses, including forced labor, physical and sexual violence, and withholding of identity documents, according to the investigation. A 2019 case even involved the death of a fisherman who was beaten aboard one of FCF's associated vessels.

Brendon Sing, founder of Shark Guardian, criticized both FCF and the regulatory bodies meant to monitor the fishing industry. He called out "a deeply worrying lack of action" and accused the company of using sustainability claims as a public relations cover.

"Our report exposes not only serious environmental and labor abuses but a cynical lack of transparency by FCF and a deeply worrying lack of action by the organizations created to monitor bad practices by fisheries," he said.

The investigation also highlights FCF's involvement in Fisheries Improvement Projects (FIPs), multi-stakeholder initiatives designed to address environmental and social issues in the fishing industry. However, five FIPs connected to FCF have been found to pose an increased risk of forced labor and human trafficking. These FIPs have consistently delayed taking action, applying for extensions rather than implementing necessary reforms, Shark Guardian said.

Alex Hofford, Shark Guardian's marine wildlife campaigner, noted the global impact of FCF's policies. "FCF is such a huge supplier of tuna that its policies impact fishing and fisheries everywhere, and while they say the right thing, our report reveals a serious disparity between the tuna giant’s published ambitions and its actions," he told Undercurrent News.

Shark Guardian is calling on FCF to ensure its suppliers and fleet uphold sustainability promises and comply with global human rights, labor, and environmental protection standards, he added.

FCF did not reply to a request for comment from Undercurrent.

Source: Shark Guardian's report Empty Promises, Empty Oceans: Fong Chun Formosa Fishery Company’s Sustainability Commitments.

title: Canadian First Nations receive blessing to continue in-season lobster fishing
content:
For the fourth year in a row, four aboriginal groups on Canada's east coast have permission from the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) to pursue a moderate livelihood fishery for lobsters during commercial seasons in lobster fishing areas (LFAs) 33, 34 and 35 off the coast of the province Nova Scotia.

Fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier announced in a press release last week the continuation of "interim authorizations" for four Kespukwi Mi'kmaw First Nations: Wasoqopa'qa'q (Acadia), Annapolis Valley, Bear River and Glooscap. The authorizations allow them to fish for and sell lobsters during the DFO-sanctioned commercial seasons.

DFO first announced a Kespukwitk Moderate Livelihood Understanding in 2021. At the time, fish harvester associations in southwest Nova Scotia supported the verbal agreement between DFO and the First Nations.

Then, in November 2023, DFO announced it would allow the Kespukwi groups to use 50% more traps in LFAs 33 and 34, moving from 3,500 to 5,250, as reported by Undercurrent News.

At the time, DFO clarified that the changes wouldn't increase the overall size of the fishery since the traps allocated to the First Nations are from the number removed or retired from commercial fishing and "banked."

Former DFO official says Canada must clarify Indigenous fishing rights

However, the DFO decision was not welcomed by commercial lobster fishing associations in the three LFAs, including the Bay of Fundy Inshore Fishermen's Association, the Coldwater Lobster Association, Brazil Rock 33/34 Lobster Association and the Scotia Fundy Inshore Fishemen's Association. They rescinded their support for the Kespukwitk Moderate Livelihood Understanding, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

"Terms of the agreement supported by the fishing industry have been abandoned. DFO has failed to uphold the understanding and deceived fishing communities in a flagrant breach of faith with harvester organizations," the groups stated in a joint press release issued in November 2023.

Colin Sproul, a commercial harvester from the Nova Scotia community of Litchfield, who speaks for the groups, could not be reached for comment for this story.

Meanwhile, the verbal agreement between DFO and the Kespukwitk nations continues for 2024.

"Consistent with last year, the overall number of traps currently being authorized is 6,300, which will be fished in a distributed manner across LFAs 33, 34 and 35, with a limit of 1,000 traps in LFA 35," last week's DFO press release explained.

"The department continues to work with the Kespukwitk Collective Fisheries Committee on the fishing plan that is supported by this authorization. Should this result in any additional access being provided, it will be done in a way that does not increase overall fishing effort or the limit of 1,000 traps in LFA 35," the department added.

High dock prices expected as fall lobster fishery kicks off in Canada’s Bay of Fundy

The season for LFA 35 began Oct. 14, while LFAs 33 and 34 are scheduled to open on Nov. 25 -- the last Monday of November.

LFA 35, which is scheduled to close its fall season on Dec. 31, accounted for landings of 2,176 metric tons in 2023, based on preliminary counts provided by the Lobster Council of Canada. That also included landings made there between Feb. 28 and July 31, during its earlier spring/summer season.

LFAs 33 and 34, with a season that runs from the last Monday of November until the end of the following May, regularly accounts for the most lobster landings in Atlantic Canada. The combined landings from both areas totaled 21,405t in 2023, according to the LCC.

Moderate livelihood fishery debate drags on

The moderate livelihood fishery has been a long-standing point of contention, dating back to the 1999 Supreme Court of Canada ruling, also known as the Marshall Decision. It affirmed First Nations' treaty rights to fish, hunt and gather in pursuit of a moderate livelihood under the terms of the Peace and Friendship Treaties of 1760 and 1761.

Since Marshall, the Canadian government has spent nearly CAD 1.0 billion ($731 million) buying commercial lobster licenses and transferring them to First Nations. However, while the Marshall decision affirmed treaty rights, the court did not lay out the rules around a moderate livelihood fishery, leaving it to the DFO and First Nations to work that out.

Tensions have been high between commercially licensed lobster fishermen in Nova Scotia and First Nations members on evidence that some First Nations have been fishing outside of the DFO-sanctioned seasons.

Canadian province seeks federal help to kick organized crime out of largest lobster fishery

Through August and September 2024, the Unified Fisheries Conservation Association (UFCA), which represents several fishing groups in southwest Nova Scotia, has been documenting illegal activity at the Saulnierville wharf, in LFA 34 near the territory of the Spikne'katik First Nation. That First Nation does not have an agreement with DFO like the one between the fisheries depatment and the Kespukwitk.

Although the fishery is permitted during the official season, Spikne'katik officials have previously rejected DFO's allowable limit of 45,000 pounds.

As previously reported by Undercurrent, drone footage collected by the UFCA in September showed lobster crates in the water and being loaded onto container trucks at the Saulnierville wharf in St. Mary's Bay.

"They're fishing on an industrial scale. We've seen upwards of 25,000 pounds of lobsters being landed some nights," UFCA president Sproul told Undercurrent in September.

Report increases pressure on Canadian fisheries department to tackle illegal fishing of lobster, elvers

Earlier this year, the Sipekne'katik First Nation and the Attorney General of Canada were heading to federal court to settle the question. A pre-trial hearing was set for June 21, 2024 to prepare for a 2025 trial. However, a day before the pre-trial hearing, the two sides asked the judge to postpone the pre-trial so the two sides could begin a mediation process, as reported by Undercurrent.

The judge gave both sides until mid-December to settle the matter through mediation. There has been no word since then on whether the Canadian government and the Sipekne'katik nation are close to or have reached a deal, leaving the potential of another courtroom showdown looming for the future.

title: Canada proposes pilot project for Maritimes elver fishery
content:
Licensed elver fishermen in Atlantic Canada have been told the Canadian government will take up to 75% of their quotas in 2025 without compensation for redistribution, SaltWire News reports. 

The commercial fishermen who harvest juvenile American eels from rivers in the Maritime provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick received a letter from Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) on Tuesday (Oct. 15) detailing a proposed pilot project that would begin with the spring elver run in 2025 and possibly continue until 2027.

"Quota redistribution for pilot participants is proposed without fishing pressure on the stock, and redistribution would not be accompanied by financial assistance or compensation to existing license holders," reads the DFO letter, which was obtained by SaltWire.

Recall that Canadian fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier shut down the commercial elver fishery in 2024 because of rampant illegal fishing, as reported by Undercurrent News.

Though the combined elver quota for Nova Scotia and New Brunswick is small, around 9,860 kilograms annually since 2006, the value of the catch has been sky-high in recent years, ranging from CAD 3,000 ($2,225)/kg to CAD 5,000/kg in the past decade.

However, the high prices for elvers have brought poachers to the rivers in both provinces. Along with that has come dangerous confrontations and evidence of organized crime, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

Commercial license holders were told this spring that 50% of the 9,960 kg commercial quota would go to First Nations. If DFO goes ahead with its latest proposal, another 20 to 25% of the elver quota will be distributed among 150 new entrants.

The DFO proposal does not sit well with the licensed operators.

"This is a misguided attempt to level the playing field," Stanley King, spokesperson for the group Canadian Committee for a Sustainable Elver Fishery, was quoted by SaltWire.

"Businesses will be lucky to survive," King said.

Currently, nine businesses in the Maritimes hold commercial licenses to harvest juvenile American eels. Those companies employ about 200 people to fish the rivers to collect the valuable elvers. They are primarily sold to China, where they are grown in aquaculture facilities to supply the sushi market.

title: Canadian report says fisheries enforcement officers need better protective equipment
content:
An investigation by Canada's labor department has concluded that heavily armed criminals pose a threat to enforcement officers with the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) in the Maritimes, and the department must take immediate steps to reduce the danger, reports the CBC.

In a report on Friday (Oct. 4) to the DFO, a senior investigator with the federal Labor Department's compliance unit concluded that the protective equipment and tactical protocols used by DFO enforcement officers are inadequate. As a result, officers could "reasonably expect" a serious threat to their lives and health as they carry out their duties.

"Therefore, you are hereby directed to take measures to correct the condition that constitutes the danger immediately," the document stated, as reported by CBC.

As previously reported by Undercurrent News, some enforcement officers with DFO  in the province of Nova Scotia filed refusal to work notices in August, citing concerns over safe working conditions.

Sources told Undercurrent on Sept. 9 that about 15% of the enforcement officers assigned to enforce the rules in southwestern Nova Scotia, in Lobster Fishing Areas (LFAs) 33 and 34,  which account for one-third of Canada's annual 100,000 metric tons of lobster landings, are not showing up for work.

The DFO-sanctioned lobster season doesn't begin in the area until mid-November, but legally licensed lobster harvesters have complained for some time that illegal fishing is out of control. The department has taken action to address the directive from the labor investigation, said an official.

On the same day the DFO received the labor report, it issued a statement warning unlicensed lobster harvesters that they could be charged if they assault or endanger fisheries enforcement officers.

"Violence or harassment towards fishery officers will not be tolerated and will be reported to the appropriate police force, which could result in charges under the Criminal Code," the department stated.

title: Canada says it will not tolerate violence against fisheries officers
content:
Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) is warning unlicensed lobster harvesters that they could be charged if they assault or endanger fisheries enforcement officers, reports SaltWire News.

"Violence or harassment towards fishery officers will not be tolerated and will be reported to the appropriate police force, which could result in charges under the Criminal Code," reads a statement issued by the DFO on Friday (Oct. 4).

The department pointed to two recent incidents, one on Sept. 19, when DFO officers boarded a boat fishing out of Saulnierville in the province of Nova Scotia.

"Fisheries officers were subjected to an attempted assault while conducting routine at-sea enforcement activities," the DFO alleged.

Court records show that one person has been charged with assault with a weapon causing bodily harm, assaulting a peace officer and obstruction. They are scheduled to appear in provincial court in Digby on Nov. 18.

The vessel and its unauthorized lobster traps were seized and towed back to Meteghan. That night, the vessel was stolen from the wharf and steamed back to Saulnierville, where fisheries officers seized it again the following morning.

A second incident occurred on Sept. 25. DFO is investigating a potential charge of obstruction of a fishery officer, the department said in a statement.

As previously reported by Undercurrent News, tensions are high in the St. Mary's Bay area of Nova Scotia, home to the largest lobster fishery in Canada.

Lobster fishing areas (LFAs) 33 and 34 account for nearly a third of Canada's world-leading 100,000 metric tons in annual production of North American lobster (Homarus americanus).
