title: Report increases pressure on Canadian fisheries department to tackle illegal fishing of lobster, elvers
content:
Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) should take action to increase enforcement of the Fisheries Act to deter the illegal poaching of species like lobster, elvers, tuna and salmon, to protect these aquatic populations and the people who legally harvest them.

That's one of the recommendations in a sweeping report released Friday (Oct. 4) by a Canadian parliamentary committee tasked with examining the issue of illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing in Canada.

During its study, which began in 2022 and heard testimony from multiple witnesses, including officials within the DFO as well as industry groups across the nation, the Fisheries and Oceans Standing Committee identified gaps that need to be addressed by the DFO in order for the department to have a fully informed response to IUU fishing.

"The frustrations that were expressed over a lack of enforcement resonated with the committee," the committee stated.

"More needs to be done to determine how much IUU fishing is taking place, intelligence-gathering and sharing needs to be improved, and enforcement actions in relation to IUU fishing need to be strengthened, including in relation to the role of organized crime," the report concluded.

Canadian lobster leader warns of ‘explosion of violence’ in major fishery if minister doesn’t act soon

In recent months the DFO and fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier have been under constant pressure to clamp down on out-of-season lobster fishing in the southwest area of the province of Nova Scotia and on the New Brunswick side of the Bay of Fundy, as reported by Undercurrent News.

Recall that legally licensed commercial elver fishers in the Maritimes were told in March 2024 that there would be no DFO-sanctioned fishery this year. With no commercial fishery at all, fishery officers would be more able to address illegal fishing, reasoned minister Lebouthillier.

Nova Scotia fisheries minister challenges Canada over handling of elver fishery

The parliamentary committee report calls on DFO to increase its dockside monitoring efforts and increase the number of species subject to dockside monitoring, such as lobster and other high-value species with low abundance.

The report recommended that the DFO implement modern technology and computer systems for data collection, such as a digital and standardized catch register for all Canadian fishers, so that reporting requirements are more standardized across the country.

The report also urged cooperation between the federal government and the provinces.

"The Government of Canada (should) collaborate with provinces on establishing more effective deterrents to illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing by increasing the certainty of apprehension through better enforcement and supporting provincial efforts to aggressively pursue charges, timely prosecution of accused fishers and sanctions upon convictions that reflect the severity of the fishing offense and related actions that harm the public's sense of security and confidence in the rule of law," the committee stated as recommendation number 20.

The report also noted that policy and legislative gaps regarding the implementation of Aboriginal and treaty rights to fish have contributed to tension and uncertainty in some communities.

To reduce the likelihood of conflict and division, the report recommended that the federal government undertake public outreach and education campaigns in specific regions to promote public understanding of First Nations inherent and treaty fishing rights;
reduce misinformation, and promote the shared goals and values of responsibility and accountability in ensuring the sustainability of fisheries.

The report recommended that the DFO also release all agreements made with First Nations regarding the management of fisheries and access to fisheries.

"Many of the issues that were raised are longstanding. The committee urges all relevant federal departments to work together expeditiously to support the harvesters and communities that play such an important role in feeding Canadians and who contribute to the Canadian economy," the committee stated in its report.

The 32 recommendations in the parliamentary committee report cover a range of issues related to IUU fishing. The full report is available here. Canada's fisheries minister will now review it and decide whether or not to adopt any of the recommendations.

title: Nova Scotia minister frustrated after face-to-face with Canada’s fisheries chief Lebouthillier
content:
The fisheries minister for the Canadian province of Nova Scotia said he was "incredibly frustrated and incredibly disappointed" after a face-to-face meeting with Canada's fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier on Thursday (Oct. 3) to discuss the issue of illegal lobster fishing in the province.

"What I heard from the minister today is that she doesn't intend to do anything differently than what her department is doing right now," said Smith in a Facebook post late Thursday afternoon.

Recall that Smith wrote to Lebouthillier on Aug. 30, expressing concern about illegal and out-of-season lobster fishing in southwest Nova Scotia, in lobster fishing areas (LFAs) 33 and 34, which together account for nearly a third of the 100,000 metric tons of lobster landed annually by Canada.

As reported by Undercurrent News, the minister for the Canadian Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) responded in writing to Smith a month later, on Sept. 25, saying, some of the responsibility for action also lies with the province.

"Any serious effort to end the criminally intertwined in Nova Scotia's fisheries must include regulation -- or outright elimination -- of cash sales," Lebouthilier wrote.

Diane Lebouthillier, Canada's fisheries minister, during question period on Sept. 16, 2024, as the Canadian Parliament resumed sitting after summer recess. Screenshot photo from the Canadian Parliamentary Channel

It appears the minister held fast to that point again in Thursday's meeting with Smith.

Following Undercurrent's request to the DFO for more details about the meeting between Smith and Lebouthillier, department officials pointed to a readout -- essentially the department's synopsis of the meeting -- which was posted on the DFO website later that day.

Canada’s fisheries minister under fire in Parliament over cod, lobster decisions

The two ministers also discussed how unreported cash sales in our fisheries need to be eliminated because it has contributed to an environment where criminal activity is taking place, the readout notes.

"Though the regulation of cash sales is a provincial matter, minister Lebouthillier reiterated that the federal government stands ready to support the government of Nova Scotia in any efforts to end cash sales, noting our longtime collaborative efforts on many fisheries issues," the readout stated, repeating almost verbatim the points Lebouthillier had made in the Sept. 25 letter to Smith.

"While this step falls squarely within the province's area of responsibility, the federal government stands ready to support you if you decide to undertake this critical step to ending the easy access criminals have to wealth within Canada's fisheries," the readout continued.

"Minister Lebouthillier concluded the meeting by making it clear that fishery officers will continue to conduct enforcement activities on land and on the water to deter and prevent the unauthorized harvest and sale of lobster without a commercial license," the department stated.

Smith: Do the same at home as you're doing in the Pacific

Soon after the meeting with Lebouthillier, Smith posted a short video on Facebook, expressing his frustration and disappointment.

"While I was encouraged that the minister was willing to meet, I remain in disbelief with the lack of meaningful actions brought to the table by the federal government and astounded that DFO continues to point to illegal cash sales as the issue at hand," Smith said later in a prepared statement.

The Nova Scotia minister said he asked Lebouthillier to prioritize enforcement of illegal fishing in the province, and to ensure DFO conservation and protection officers were properly resourced and supported.

"Once again, I asked ... that her department co-ordinate activities with other relevant federal agencies to ensure there are no enforcement gaps," Smith said.

"They recently announced they are working to detect and deter illegal fishing internationally, in the Pacific Ocean," Smith noted, referencing the announcement by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans on Oct. 1 that it had assigned Canadian Coast Guard Ship Sir Wilfred Laurier and 20 officers for a two-month mission in the North Pacific, as reported by Undercurrent.

The Canadian Coast Guard Ship Wilfred Laurier is currently participating in Operation North Pacific, a two-month-long Canadian-led mission to combat illegal fishing on the high seas. Photo screenshot from DFO promotional video

"We need them to do the same here at home to put an end to ongoing illegal fishing in Nova Scotia, which is the root cause of serious crimes that are terrorizing parts of our province," said Smith.

Lobster harvesters in southwest Nova Scotia are not the only ones expressing concern about the level of illegal activity and lack of enforcement.

Members of the Fundy North Fishermen's Association, which represents more than 150 lobster license holders in LFA 36, in the Bay of Fundy, staged a demonstration at St. Andrews, in the province of New Brunswick, on Sept. 14, to raise awareness about the illegal lobster fishing in that area. The group also called for Lebouthillier's resignation, as reported by Undercurrent.

In recent days, DFO officers in southwest Nova Scotia appear to have made some progress in cracking down on illegal lobster fishing.

On Wednesday (Oct. 2) officers raided a lobster pound in the southwest area of the province, and seized 13,000 pounds of lobsters valued at CAD 100,000 ($73,880), Undercurrent reported.

Illegal fishing continues

However, on the same day the two ministers met, members of the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance (UFCA) posted more footage on its Facebook page of what appears to be lobster crates being taken from the water and loaded onto a truck at a wharf in Saulnierville on the south coast of Nova Scotia.

Local licensed harvesters have said this wharf is a prime landing spot for illegal lobster fishers, and DFO should be focusing its efforts there in particular.

Drone footage posted on the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance Facebook page on Oct. 3 shows what appears to be crates of lobster being loaded into a truck on the wharf in Saulnierville, Nova Scotia. Screenshot from UFCA Facebook page

More than two-dozen boats have been fishing for lobster out of harbours in south west Nova Scotia, from Saulnierville to Yarmouth, UFCA president Colin Sproul recently told Undercurrent. 

"They're fishing on an industrial scale. We've seen upwards of 25,000 pounds of lobsters being landed some nights," Sproul said.

Sproul could not be reached for comment before deadline on Friday.

Meanwhile, the Maritime regional office of DFO issued a statement of its own on Friday morning (Oct. 4), saying the department is troubled by the ongoing pattern of violent and threatening behaviour towards fishery officers.

Canada’s DFO details efforts to curb lobster poaching, while minister challenges province to act

"For example, on Sept. 19 in St. Marys Bay, Nova Scotia, fishery officers were subjected to an attempted assault while conducting routine at-sea enforcement activities," the Maritimes office stated in a press release.

Despite the attempted assault, fishery officers made arrests and seized a vessel and unauthorized lobster traps for offences under the Fisheries Act, including obstruction of a fishery officer, DFO officials said.

"On Sept. 25 in St. Marys Bay, fishery officers attempted to board and inspect a vessel when the operator of the vessel made maneuvers to evade the boarding, resulting in the two vessels making contact," the Maritimes office said.

DFO is conducting an investigation into a potential charge for obstruction of a fishery officer as a result of this action, while the alleged assault was referred to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for investigation. 

"Violence or harassment towards fishery officers will not be tolerated and will be reported to the appropriate police force, which could result in charges under the Criminal Code," the department stated.

The Nova Scotia fisheries minsiter said he continues to hear directly from harvesters and harvester organizations that there is not enough enforcement on the water.

"This responsibility falls squarely on the federal minister, and her unwillingness to prioritize actions to prevent illegal fishing is unmistakably the source of the problem," said Smith, adding he's heard  from fishers who have been threatened, had their property damaged, and who live in fear of repercussions for speaking out.

"The potential for this issue to escalate is real. Our communities need clear, decisive action, and we need it now," Smith said.

title: Canadian fisheries officers seize CAD 100k worth of lobster in Nova Scotia
content:
Enforcement officers with Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) seized 13,000 pounds of lobster worth CAD 100,000 ($73,880) on Wednesday (Oct. 2) after executing a search warrant in Shelburne County, in the province of Nova Scotia.

An individual was arrested for an offense under the Fisheries Act, including maintaining a lobster pound without the required license, the DFO said in a press release. The officers also seized documents and electronic records, and the matter is under investigation for potential charges, the DFO added.

The DFO did not identify the lobster pound's location or the owner's name.

Shelburne County includes the communities of Shelburne and Barrington Passage and Clark's Harbour on Cape Sable Island, on the province's southeast coast.

"Fishery officers are also conducting other enforcement activities to deter and prevent the unauthorized sale of lobster harvested without a commercial license, working closely with provincial partners in this effort," the DFO stated.

Canadian fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier has been under constant pressure for months to clamp down on illegal lobster fishing in the Maritimes.

Lobster harvesters not impressed by Canada’s enforcement efforts

In recent weeks, licensed lobster harvesters who fish in lobster fishing areas (LFAs) 33, 34, 35 and 36 in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have been particularly outspoken.

Recall that the DFO reported that in the first nine months of 2024, up to Sept. 23, officers had seized three vessels and 876 lobster traps in the southwestern area of Nova Scotia for lobster fishing offenses, as reported by Undercurrent News. 

Much of the focus on the illegal lobster fishing problem has been centered around Nova Scotia's Digby County.

The southwest area of Nova Scotia is on the doorstep of lobster fishing areas (LFAs) 33 and 34, which account for nearly a third of Canada's world-leading 100,000 metric tons of annual production of North American lobster.

The commercial fishery there doesn't open until mid-November.

First Nations in the area are permitted a moderate livelihood fishery, with a small quota for community and ceremonial purposes.

However, as previously reported by Undercurrent, the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance (UFCA) has complained that members of the Spikne'katik First Nation from the community of Meteghan in Digby County have been fishing on an industrial scale.

"We've seen upwards of 25,000 pounds of lobster being landed some nights," said UFCA president Colin Sproul.

title: Canada’s DFO details efforts to curb lobster poaching, while minister challenges province to act
content:
Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) reports it has seized three vessels and 876 lobster traps up to Sept. 23 this year in the southwestern area of the province of Nova Scotia for offenses related to lobster fishing.

"One individual has been charged, but no one has been convicted to date for unauthorized lobster fishing offenses that have taken place this year," the department told Undercurrent News on Wednesday (Sept. 25) in response to a request for information.

"A number of investigations are in progress, and fishery officers are working with the Public Prosecution Service of Canada towards laying charges," a DFO official said in an email, adding the courts determine the scheduling of court proceedings and "it is not uncommon for processes to take over a year."

Licensed commercial lobster harvesters in Canada's Maritime provinces have expressed frustration over what they see as a lack of enforcement by DFO to crack down on poachers who are setting traps in lobster fishing areas (LFAs) 33-36, along Nova Scotia's southwest coast and in the Bay of Fundy, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

Canadian lobster harvesters say little resolved in meeting with high-ranking DFO officials

Recall that on Sept. 18, DFO seized a vessel and 18 lobster traps from St. Mary's Bay, in LFA 34, where illegal fishing is purported to be rampant. But licensed lobster harvesters, represented by the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance (UFCA), which represents nearly a dozen groups in the Maritimes, contend that DFO is not doing enough.

"The entirety of the illegal lobster traps that have been removed from St. Mary's Bay this year is like 210, which is pathetic," Colin Sproul, president of the UFCA, told Undercurrent on Monday (Sept. 23).

On Tuesday morning (Sept. 24), Sproul and other industry representatives walked out of a lobster advisory meeting with DFO Maritimes when the department refused to agree to a motion that the focus of the discussion should be on illegal lobster fishing and the lack of enforcement by DFO.

This image, captured by the United Fisheries Conservation Association on Sept. 9, using a drone, shows lobster crates in the water at the wharf in Saulnierville, in southwestern Nova Scotia. The commercial lobster fishery in that area is currently closed. Photo still from video on UFCA Facebook page

Sproul and five other lobster industry leaders met later that day with senior DFO officials, who happened to be in the province for other meetings. But the harvesters said nothing was resolved.

"We are ready to return to the table to provide advice to DFO on the management of the lobster fishery, but the discussion must start with a plan to end the black market out-of-season fishing, which is an enormous threat facing our industry," the harvester groups said in a joint press release on Sept. 24.

The following day (Sept. 25), Chris D'Entremont, a Conservative member of Canada's House of Commons for the Nova Scotia federal riding of West Nova, shared on his Facebook page a letter he had written on Sept. 20 to Canada's fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier, urging her to take action.

"It has been more than a year since I urged you to take urgent action against illegal poaching. This only fuels acts of violence which give rise to criminal activity," D'Entremont wrote.

"Having personally reported far too many events to you, you also know that these criminal acts continue unabated, posing a significant threat to both the sustainability of our seafood industry and the safety of our communities.

"This is irresponsible, unacceptable, and we have had enough," D'Entremount declared, as he requested a meeting with Lebouthiillier as soon as possible to have a discussion to "develop a robust solution."

Lebouthillier responds with a challenge to Nova Scotia government

On the same day, D'Entremont wrote Lebouthillier, the minister herself, penned a letter to Kent Smith, the minister responsible for fisheries in Nova Scotia.

Recall that Kent Smith wrote Lebouthillier on Aug. 22, asking the minister to beef up enforcement and help take criminals off the water, as reported by Undercurrent.

"The inability of DFO to prevent even a portion of the illegal and out-of-season harvesting of lobster in this year over the past years has enabled and emboldened the growth of organized crime that is terrorizing the community," Smith wrote at the time.

Canadian province seeks federal help to kick organized crime out of largest lobster fishery

In a letter to Smith dated Sept. 20, Lebouthillier offered no specifics about DFO's current enforcement efforts or actions to be taken, saying simply that DFO "uses its authorities under the Fisheries Act to require accurate reporting from harvesters and those purchasing their landings for commercial purposes."

However, the federal minister suggested some of the responsibility for action also lies with the province.

"Any serious effort to end the criminally intertwined in Nova Scotia's fisheries must include regulation -- or outright elimination -- of cash sales," Lebouthilier wrote.

"While this step falls squarely within the province's area of responsibility," she stated, "the federal government stands ready to support you if you decide to undertake this critical step to ending the easy access criminals have to wealth within Canada's fisheries."

Nova Scotia has already enhanced its efforts, Smith said, noting the province has increased inspections at lobster pounds around the province.

The province has also doubled the number of Royal Canadian Mounted Police officers at the detachment in Clare, Nova Scotia, in the St. Mary's Bay area,  boosting the staff from seven to 14 and making the detachment operational around the clock every day of the week.

Smith has been seeking a meeting with the minister since August.

Lebouthillier's letter suggested department officials are willing to talk.

"My team remains available to you should you wish to discuss how we can move forward together on this important file, including difficult discussions about cash sales in our fisheries," Lebouthillier wrote.

Canada’s fisheries minister under fire in Parliament over cod, lobster decisions

Meanwhile, DFO fisheries officers will continue to conduct enforcement activities to deter and prevent the unauthorized sale of lobster harvested without a commercial license, the minister said, without offering specifics.

Department officials would not confirm for Undercurrent whether DFO had increased the number of fisheries enforcement officers in Nova Scotia since the beginning of 2024.

"To maintain operational integrity like any law enforcement organization, Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) does not disclose the number of active fishery officers nor what specific enforcement activities they are undertaking," the department said.

Earlier this summer, some DFO enforcement officers in Nova Scotia refused to work out of concern for personal safety, saying they and their families had been threatened and harassed.

The department offered that while some officers in the Maritimes region continue to refuse to work, the majority are working in the field.

title: Canadian lobster harvesters say little resolved in meeting with high-ranking DFO officials
content:
A hastily organized meeting between senior officials of Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) and commercial lobster harvesters from the Maritime provinces on Tuesday (Sept. 24) did not succeed in allaying concerns among fishermen about illegal fishing and insufficient enforcement in the region, reports the CBC. 

The meeting was pulled together just a few hours after representatives for about 3,000 lobster harvesters walked out of a DFO Maritimes region lobster advisory committee meeting in Dartmouth, in the province of Nova Scotia. The walk-out was in response to DFO officials rejecting a motion to change the agenda for the advisory meeting to deal only with enforcement and illegal fishing.

The motion was proposed by Colin Sproul, president of the Unified Fisheries Conservation Association (UFCA), which represents several lobster fishing groups, including those who fish in lobster fishing areas (LFA) 33 and 34. These account for nearly a third of Canada's world-leading 1,000 metric tons in annual production of North American lobster (Homarus americanus).

As previously reported by Undercurrent News, the DFO has been facing increasing pressure from the UFCA and the provincial government to crack down on out-of-season lobster fishing in St. Mary's Bay.

However, the problem is not confined to southwest Nova Scotia, lobster fishermen told media after walking out of the originally planned advisory committee meeting.

Lobster is also being fished out of season around Cape Breton Island, said Michael Barron of the Cape Breton Fish Harvester's Association.

"This is not just a southwest Nova Scotia concern, it's an industry-wide Atlantic Canada concern that the department appears to be putting politics ahead of conservation. We've had enough," Barron was quoted by the SaltWire network. 

"It's the number one industry in Atlantic Canada and we feel abandoned," Dan Fleck, executive director of the Brazil Rock 33/34 Lobster Association, told reporters after walking out of the morning session, as reported by CBC.

By mid-afternoon Fleck and four other industry reps were sitting around a table in a hotel lobby for a meeting with DFO's associate deputy minister Adam Burns, Maritimes region director general Doug Wentzell and director general of conservation and protection Anik Michelle Chartrand.

Burns and Chartrand, who normally work out of the nation's capital in Ottawa, were available for the Dartmouth meeting because they were in Halifax for other meetings. The Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization, which manages and regulates fishing activity on the high seas just outside Canada's 200-mile limit, is holding its annual meeting in Halifax Sept 24-27.

The meeting between the lobster harvester groups and DFO senior officials lasted 35 minutes.

Little was resolved, according to Fleck.

title: Lobster harvesters not impressed by Canada’s enforcement efforts
content:
Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) seized a vessel and just over a dozen traps last week in the nation's largest lobster fishery as part of an effort to crack down on illegal harvesting, but the head of a local fishermen's group says it's not nearly enough.

"They're just attempting to create the appearance of enforcement by taking these nominal actions," Colin Sproul, president of the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance (UFCA), told Undercurrent News on Monday morning (Sept. 23).

An official from DFO verified late Monday night that officers had seized 18 untagged lobster traps and a 40-ft-long fishing boat.

"The entirety of the illegal lobster traps that have been removed from St. Mary's Bay this year is like 210, which is pathetic," said Sproul, adding, "Anybody could go and get three times that many in one day."

An official at DFO confirmed for Undercurrent News over the weekend the enforcement actions that took place on Wednesday (Sept. 18) in St. Mary's Bay, Nova Scotia, in Lobster Fishing Area (LFA) 34). Charges have been laid under the Fisheries Act, a DFO official said, but the department did not specify how many people were charged or whether court dates have been set.

The action is maybe the most seen from the federal government in response to the ongoing claims of illegal lobster harvesting in Atlantic Canada, a saga that Undercurrent has been following closely.  

DFO said some of its fishery officers were assaulted while conducting the arrests on Wednesday, and the matter has been turned over to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for investigation.

Late on Monday the DFO confirmed for Undercurrent that formal charges have not yet been laid.

"The matter is currently under investigation for potential charges for offences under the Fisheries Act and regulations. Generally, appearance and plea dates are set after charges are laid," said the official.

Still, Sproul maintains that the DFO effort is all smoke and mirrors. His group represents licensed lobster harvesters in LFA 34, one of Canada's most lucrative lobster fishing areas, which accounted for about 15,335 metric tons of landings in 2022.  

"I stand by my previous statements that the minister's office is attempting to create the appearance of enforcement while not actually doing any real enforcement," he told Undercurrent on Monday.

Colin Sproul, president of the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance. Photo from UFCA Facebook page

"They (DFO) still refuse to remove the thousands of illegal lobster traps that are set within the bay or take the only reasonable enforcement action that everybody in the region wants and expects them to take, which is to conduct enforcement patrols at Saulnierville harbor and monitor the tens of thousands of pounds of lobster coming into that harbor each night and seize them on the wharf," he said.

The Saulnierville wharf is used by the Spikne'katik First Nation. While the First Nation has a right to a moderate livelihood fishery, to take lobsters and other fish for ceremonial and community use, they are fishing on an industrial scale, said Sproul.

Recall that the UFCA has been using drones to monitor activity at Saulnierville, which appears to be a key location used by lobster poachers, as reported by Undercurrent.

While LFA 34 is closed to commercial lobster fishing -- the DFO-sanctioned season doesn't open until late November -- the drone footage is reported to show up to 25,000 lbs of lobster being landed at that wharf some nights, Sproul said in a previous interview with Undercurrent.

The out-of-season fishery is harming lobsters that are in post-molt stage, juvenile lobsters and egg-bearing females, he added. The post-molt lobsters are thrown back overboard, but because their shells have not hardened, they're "like jelly," said Sproul.

"All those are lost," Sproul added.

The UFCA continues to monitor activity at Saulnierville, said Sproul, and will continue to do so.

This image, captured by the United Fisheries Conservation Association on Sept. 9, using a drone, shows lobster crates in the water at the wharf in Saulnierville, in southwestern Nova Scotia. Photo still from video on UFCA Facebook page

The UFCA and its members have no intention of backing down on their efforts to pressure the Canadian government to crack down on illegal activity, he addedl.

If the DFO and fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier want to prove they are intent on stopping illegal lobster fishing, they should do at least one thing, Sproul offered.

"Just show up at Saulnierville wharf with a fleet of fishery officer trucks and seize all the vessels and seize all the catch that's coming to shore and arrest everybody that's engaged in criminal activity. Until we see those actions, anything short of that is just politics," he said.

More action in New Brunswick, too

On the New Brunswick side of the Bay of Fundy, which encompasses LFA 36, the Fundy North Fishermen's Association (FNFA) also noticed more DFO activity last Wednesday.

Amanda Johnson, executive director of the FNFA, noted in a press release on Friday (Sept. 20) that on Wednesday afternoon, DFO was patrolling the Passamaquoddy Bay area by sea and air, using three patrol vessels and a Coast Guard helicopter.

"There were no arrests made. By Friday there was just one DFO vessel left," said Johnson, adding the association learned that enforcement officers were brought in from other areas of Canada to increase patrols for a couple of days.

"We are committed to ensuring that illegal fishing is brought under control, and will monitor the situation closely to hold DFO accountable," said Johnson.

FREE READ Province still waiting for reply from Canada’s fisheries minister regarding illegal lobster fishing

Recall that members of the FNFA held a demonstration on Sept. 14 at the harbor in Saint Andrews, a tourist town on the south coast of the province of New Brunswick, as reported by Undercurrent.

The FNFA said it will continue to push for continuous and effective enforcement. The group represents more than 150 lobster license holders in LFA 36, which accounted for 2,415t of lobster landed in 2022.

Licensed harvesters in LFA 36, are seeing plenty of evidence of illegal fishing in recent weeks, said Johnson, including lobster gear being marked by seagull and duck decoys to mark the position of illegal traps. During its Sept 14 demonstration, the group called on minister Lebouthillier to resign.

title: Canada’s First Nations hopeful on 25th anniversary of Marshall decision
content:
On the 25th anniversary of a landmark Canadian Supreme Court ruling that declared First Nations have a right to fish, hunt and gather for a moderate livelihood, some say there's still a long way to go, reports the CBC.

Known as the Marshall decision, the Supreme Court ruled on Sept. 17, 1999, that Donald Marshall, a Mi'kmaw man from Membertou, in the province of Nova Scotia, who was charged in 1993 with selling eels without a license, was justified in doing so under the Peace and Friendship Treaties signed in 1760 and 1761.

The ruling affected about three dozen Mi'kmaq and Wolastoqiyik First Nations in the Maritimes and the Gaspé region of Quebec.

However, the Supreme Court did not clearly define "moderate livelihood" and that's one of the factors that has contributed to the long-running tensions between First Nations and commercial license holders.

As previously reported by Undercurrent News, commercial lobster harvesters in Nova Scotia have warned that there will be violence on the water again this year if Canada's fisheries minister Diane Lebouthiller doesn't take action soon to curb illegal fishing. 

Kerry Prosper, an elder-in-residence at St. Francis Xavier University, in Nova Scotia, was chief of Paqtnkek Mi'kmaw Nation when Marshall was arrested. Marshall had been fishing in Pomquet Harbour near Paqtnkek with permission from the band when he was detained. 

Twenty-five years after the Marshall ruling, Prosper said he's hopeful for a cooperative management system for treaty fisheries and non-native commercial fisheries.

"We need to begin looking at how we can actually share the resource without harming each other," the CBC quoted Prosper.

Canada's fisheries minister also issued a statement on the 25th anniversary of the court ruling.

"As we highlight the landmark Marshall decision, we re-affirm our commitment to working with First Nations communities to further implement their right to fish in pursuit of a moderate livelihood," Lebouthillier said in a statement on the Department of Fisheries and Oceans website.

"While much has been accomplished by First Nations since 1999, the Government of Canada will continue to work in partnership with Indigenous communities to ensure that the rights conveyed through the Marshall decisions are met, without increasing overall fishing effort," she wrote. "Together, we must find ways to reach common ground, where all harvesters can share their perspectives, where Indigenous voices and ideas are shared, heard, and respected."

title: Canadian lobster harvesters demand minister’s resignation over handling of illegal fishing crisis
content:
Pressure is mounting on the Canadian government and fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier amid growing tension over illegal lobster fishing in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.

The latest salvo has been fired by the Fundy North Fishermen's Association (FNFA), a New Brunswick-based group that represents more than 150 lobster license holders in Lobster Fishing Area (LFA) 36, in the Bay of Fundy. They have asked Lebouthillier to resign.

"Fundy North is the first to put in writing that we are asking for her resignation. She's failed fishermen and coastal communities and is failing to protect the resource," Amanda Johnson, executive director of the FNFA, told Undercurrent News on Friday (Sept. 13).

Diane Lebouthillier, Canada's minister of Fisheries and Oceans. Photo from Diane Lebouthillier Twitter/X page

"We can no longer tolerate the disregard for our industry and the lack of action to stop illegal fishing activities in our waters," said the FNFA in a press release issued days earlier.

"The claims made this week by DFO [Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans] that enforcement continues in southwest Nova Scotia and southwest New Brunswick are misleading and do not state that each LFA has sufficient patrol with the ability to haul illegal gear and make arrests. A picture is being painted that the department has this under control when they do not," said the FNFA in its release, referring to the statement issued by the DFO on Sept. 9.

The DFO statement had assured: "For absolute clarity, fisheries enforcement activity in the Maritimes region is active – to suggest otherwise is false."

Duck, seagull decoys used as buoys

To raise awareness of the issue of illegal lobster fishing and to continue pressure on Canada to take action, members of the FNFA sailed into St. Andrews, on New Brunswick's southern shore, on Saturday (Sept. 14) for a peaceful demonstration in the tourist town

"We wanted to spread awareness to the general public of the issues that are going on, the issues we're having with mismanagement," explained Johnson, adding about 50 lobster boats participated in the protest.

Members of the Fundy North Fishermens' Association staged a peaceful protest in St. Andrews, New Brunswick, on Saturday (Sept. 14). The main focus of the event was to educate the public on the issues around illegal lobster fishing. Photo by Fundy North Fishermen's Association

The issues highlighted by the FNFA repeat the concerns recently expressed by the lobster industry and the provincial government in Nova Scotia. Recall that politicians from Nova Scotia called out Lebouthiller recently for lack of enforcement, as reported by Undercurrent. 

Just last week, the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance, an organization representing several fishing industry groups in Nova Scotia, warned that violence would escalate if the DFO did not act soon to increase enforcement, as also reported by Undercurrent.

LFA 36 is a relatively small lobster fishery, accounting for 2,415 of Canada's nearly 96,500 metric tons of lobster landed in 2022. Its first DFO-sanctioned season runs from the end of March until the end of June before it opens again in mid-November and runs until mid-January.

The other area where illegal lobster harvesting is prolific, LFA 34, in southwest Nova Scotia, by contrast, accounted for about 15,332t in landings in 2022.  

Licensed harvesters in LFA 36, are seeing plenty of evidence of illegal fishing in recent weeks, said Johnson. 

"Just this week, I was sent photos of (lobster) gear that is being marked with seagull decoys and duck decoys that are used for hunting. From a distance it just looks like birds on the water. But if you were to go up close, you can see that these are decoys that are marking traps or trawls that are illegal," she said.

Lobster fishing areas in Atlantic Canada. Graphic by Fisher King Seafoods.

Members of the FNFA are frustrated because there's not much they can do about the situation other than keep reporting it to DFO, said Johnson.

"But right now, we have no enforcement," she said, referencing the fact that some DFO offices in the Maritimes have refused to work, citing safety issues, including threats against themselves and their families, as reported by Undercurrent. 

However, local DFO detachments were severely understaffed even before that development, said Johnson.

Canada’s black market for lobster creates data gaps for fisheries managers

"We've always had illegal fishing issues here," said Johnson, noting that on the New Brunswick side of the Bay of Fundy, the issue is complicated by the fact that LFAs 34 and 38 are close to the international line that separates the Canada and US fishing territories.

The FNFA says US lobster fishermen are dodging over that line to catch lobster in Canadian waters.

The DFO needs to implement an enforcement plan and restore order in the region by a specified deadline, "or risk local fishermen taking matters into their own hands to patrol the waters," the FNFA stated in its press release.

While Saturday's protest raised awareness of the issues, the FNFA will continue to advocate, said Johnson.

"Our work is far from over. Fundy North will continue to press the government for concrete action on enforcing regulations and addressing illegal fishing," she said.

"We plan to engage in more direct advocacy, including trying to meet with officials, further public outreach, and maintaining pressure on the fisheries minister. We’re committed to ensuring that these issues remain front and center until real solutions are implemented," said Johnson.

On Sept. 9, Undercurrent requested information from the DFO regarding the level of staffing at detachments in the Maritimes region, including the number of arrests made, charges laid and convictions handed out for illegal lobster fishing to date in 2024.

"It is taking some time to compile the information you have requested. A response early next week is likely," a DFO official said in an email received on Sept. 10.

Earlier, on Sept. 5, Undercurrent requested an interview with minister Lebouthillier, or DFO deputy minister Annette Gibbons, on the issue. However, neither the minister nor her deputy have yet agreed to make themselves available.

title: Editor’s choice: Canadian lobster leader warns of violence in major fishery; Northwest Alaska’s dismal chum salmon harvest
content:
Editorial and managing director Tom Seaman brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week  

Tensions are building again in Canada's largest lobster fishery and -- unless fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier acts soon -- something terrible is going to happen, warns Colin Sproul, president of the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance, a non-profit alliance of fishing groups in Nova Scotia.

"There's going to be an explosion of violence in Southwest Nova Scotia," Sproul told Undercurrent News in an interview last week.

The ticking timebomb is in lobster fishery areas 33 and 34, which account for nearly a third of Canada's world-leading 100,000 metric tons in annual production of North American lobster (Homarus americanus).

Big bucks are at stake. Note that Canada's lobster industry is estimated to be worth CAD 2.0 billion ($1.5bn). Read more about what's going on by clicking here. 

Then, in Northwest Alaska, this year's salmon chum harvest on Kotzebue Sound was the lowest since the US state began record-keeping in 1962.

"It's pretty much a disaster," Mike Scott, managing partner of Arctic Circle Wild Seafood, one of two processors buying fish in Kotzebue, told Undercurrent on Sept. 11. "We can't have a repeat of this ... we're not a big company so when you lose money, it comes right out of your pocket. There's nobody backstopping you."

The Alaska Department of Fish and Game wrote in its Sept. 11 summary that a total of 41,793 pounds of chum salmon was sold at an average price of $0.60/lb.

That translated into a measly $25,091 catch for the two-dozen permit holders, the lowest since 2002 when the agency said market conditions constrained that year's harvest. For comparison purposes, consider that the Kotzebue District's chum season has averaged $728,025 annually between 1962-2023 with some years exceeding $2 million.

title: Daily recap: Canada lobster dispute may turn ugly; Report exposes Indonesian forced labor
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Friday, Sept. 13:

Canadian lobster leader warns of ‘explosion of violence’ in major fishery if minister doesn’t act soon

Tensions are building again between commercial fishers and First Nation harvesters in Canada's largest lobster fishery and -- unless fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier acts soon -- something terrible is going to happen, warns Colin Sproul, president of the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance (UFCA), a non-profit alliance of fishing groups in Nova Scotia.

New report exposes forced labor in Indonesia’s shrimp industry

A new report from three Indonesian NGOs -- Akatiga Center for Social Analysis, Institute for Policy Research and Advocacy (ELSAM), and Migunani Research Institute -- has uncovered significant labor exploitation in Indonesia’s shrimp sector, which it attributes to unsustainable prices paid by major retailers in the US, UK and EU.

Rabobank projects global soybean price crash as feed sector heads for record surplus

A record soybean surplus is expected in the next 12 months, likely to produce a sharp reduction in aquafeed prices, according to Rabobank's agri-commodity research managing director Carlos Mera.

European investor snaps up Indian Ocean-based French seafood group

Reunimer-Pecherie du Sud, a major integrated producer and exporter of Indian Ocean seafood to France with an annual turnover of €70 million, has been acquired by a European private equity for an undisclosed sum.

Harris Teeter, Publix to join in expansion of US seafood marketing campaign

Two major US retail grocery chains -- Harris Teeter Supermarkets and Publix Super Markets -- have agreed to join in on the US-wide "Fall in Love with Seafood" marketing campaign started by the Seafood Nutrition Partnership (SNP), SNP announced Sept. 12.

UK supplier suffers loss in ‘challenging’ market for fish ‘n chips

UK fish and chip shop supplier T. Quality reported a loss of £829,143 ($1.09m) for the year ended Dec. 31, 2023, compared to a profit of £2.24m in 2022, according to the company's annual financial report.

title: Canadian lobster leader warns of ‘explosion of violence’ in major fishery if minister doesn’t act soon
content:
Tensions are building again in Canada's largest lobster fishery and -- unless fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier acts soon -- something terrible is going to happen, warns Colin Sproul, president of the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance (UFCA), a non-profit alliance of fishing groups in Nova Scotia.

"There's going to be an explosion of violence in Southwest Nova Scotia," Sproul told Undercurrent News in an interview this week.

The ticking timebomb is in lobster fishery areas (LFAs) 33 and 34, which account for nearly a third of Canada's world-leading 100,000 metric tons in annual production of North American lobster (Homarus americanus).

Big bucks are at stake. Note that Canada's lobster industry is estimated to be worth CAD 2.0 billion ($1.5bn).

For at least the past four years, the Spikne'katick First Nation has attempted to harvest lobster in LFA 34 -- the larger of the two sections -- in advance of the commercial season, which doesn't start until the last Monday of November, weather permitting. The licensed commercial harvesters there have taken offense, leading to multiple acts of protest, violence and -- in one extreme instance -- the complete destruction of a lobster pound. 

In October 2020, commercial fishermen raided and vandalized two lobster pounds in West Pubnico, on Nova Scotia's St. Mary's Bay. One of the lobster pounds was burned down, in what the Royal Canadian Mounted Police termed a "suspicious" incident, as reported by the CBC at the time. It led to the arrest of more than two dozen individuals.

Lobster fishing areas in Atlantic Canada. Graphic by Fisher King Seafoods.

The First Nation harvesters are at it again, said Sproul.

Currently, there are about 24 to 30 commercial-sized lobster boats fishing out of harbors in southwestern Nova Scotia, from Saulnierville to Yarmouth, he said, adding most of the activity is centered around the Saulnierville wharf. UFCA reports to have video footage showing lobster crates being unloading from fishing boats by the Spikne'katik.

"They're fishing on an industrial scale. We've seen upwards of 25,000 pounds of lobsters being landed some nights," Sproul said.

"We're counting the crates and assuming that each one has 100 pounds of lobster," he said, adding each standard-sized lobster crate can hold up to 130 pounds.

"We've been taking videos pretty much every night, and we see the same thing every night … large lobster trucks hauling away tens of thousands of pounds of lobster," he said.

This image, captured by the United Fisheries Conservation Association on Sept. 9, using a drone, shows lobster crates in the water at the wharf in Saulnierville, in southwestern Nova Scotia. Photo still from video on UFCA Facebook page

Spikne'katik not subject to earlier agreement

First Nations point to a 1999 Supreme Court of Canada ruling that determined that 34 of their groups on the Atlantic coast have a right to fish on Canadian waters and hunt on Canadian lands whenever they want in order to earn a "moderate livelihood."

The treaty right, the high court determined, was subject to federal regulation to ensure conservation.

Since then, the Canadian government and several First Nations have signed agreements related to lobster fishing. In December 2023, for instance, Lebouthillier announced that, for the third consecutive year, an interim authorization had been issued to Wasoqopa'q (Acadia), Annapolis Valley, Bear River and Glooscap First Nations, which would see them able to fish and sell their catch during the commercial fishing seasons in Lobster Fishing Areas (LFAs) 33, 34 and 35. This year those First Nations were allowed 6,300 lobster traps, an increase from 5,250, to accommodate more moderate livelihood harvesters.

The DFO-sanctioned seasons in LFAs 33 and 34 end in May. In LFA 35, seasons run from mid-October to Dec. 31, and March 1 to July 31.

However, the Spikne'katik First Nation does not have such an agreement with DFO.

In 2020, the group developed its own plan for LFA 34, issuing a limited number of licenses and tags and carrying on a lobster fishery outside of the regulated commercial season. It rejected DFO regulations that set a limit of 45,000 pounds for the moderate livelihood fishery.

Former DFO official says Canada must clarify Indigenous fishing rights

The action prompted the violent confrontations noted above.

Earlier this year, the Canadian government and the Spikne'katik, who were about to do battle in the Supreme Court, decided instead to try mediation first to settle the matter, as reported by Undercurrent. The UFCA saw that as more stalling, however, and launched its own lawsuit to ask the court to resolve the issue.

How are illegal lobsters getting to market?

The battle between commercial harvesters and the Spikne'katik is just one of the dicey situations confronting DFO in the Nova Scotia lobster fisheries.  

Recall that sources told Undercurrent earlier this year that container loads of lobsters from Atlantic Canada are being sold on the black market. That illegal activity means a loss of data for DFO science to properly assess the health of lobster stocks, and the under-the-radar business activity also cheats the nation out of tax revenue, the industry noted.

Lobster buyers in Atlantic Canada are flouting the rules, Sproul said, adding that a grey zone between the United States and Canada is also enabling black market activity.

That grey zone is a 110-square-mile area of disputed territory between the United States and Canada around Machias Seal Island, southwest of Grand Manan Island in the Bay of Fundy. Both the US and Canada claim sovereignty over the area, which encompasses a portion of LFA 38.

Southwest Nova Scotia. Image from Google Maps.

A summer fishery is authorized within the western portion of LFA 38 outside of the regular LFA 38 season, the DFO explains in an online document here. 

The portion of LFA 38 fished during the summer is referred to as Area 38B (the Disputed Zone). The area is claimed as territorial waters by both Canada and the United States. All fish harvesters holding an LFA 38 license are eligible to apply for an Area 38B license.

That situation provides an opportunity for criminals to ship out illegal lobsters, Sproul said.

"People are transshipping lobsters by sea from St. Mary'sBay in Nova Scotia through Grand Manan and selling them as grey zone lobsters," Sproul offered.

15% of enforcement officers refuse to work

To compound the issue this year, DFO enforcement officers in Southwest Nova Scotia have been refusing to work, citing concerns over safe working conditions, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

Sources told Undercurrent on Sept. 9 that about 15% of the enforcement officers assigned to DFO detachments in the region are not showing up.

These fishery officers face increasingly dangerous conditions including, but not limited to, the risk of physical violence, verbal harassment, personal threats, organized crime and poaching and a rise in the use of long guns that puts them at risk in the course of their regular duties, said an official of the union that represents them.

It's gotten to the point where some fisheries officers moved their families out of the area this summer because of the threats they were receiving, said Sproul.

Colin Sproul, president of the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance. Photo from UFCA Facebook page

"Fishery officers have been documenting the hazard and making recommendations for years, to no avail," said Shimen Fayad, national president of the Union of Health and Environment Workers (UHEW), in an email.

Canada's minister of labor is currently investigating the officer's concerns, Fayad said.

Among the things the union is seeking for the officers is better body armor, to protect them from high-powered firearms, Fayad confirmed, adding the current body protection worn by officers does not protect them from weapons like long guns.

The union did not issue a deadline ultimatum for response to the officers' requests, Fayad explained, but said the UHEW is "monitoring the process."

Meanwhile, the DFO assures it is policing the lobster fishery.

On Monday (Sept. 9), the federal agency issued a statement in response to what it termed "speculation about the state of enforcement" in DFO's Maritimes region.

"For absolute clarity, fisheries enforcement activity in the Maritimes Region is active – to suggest otherwise is false," the department said, referring specifically to its operations in southwestern and eastern Nova Scotia, and southwestern New Brunswick, in light of ongoing job action by enforcement officers.

"Fishery officers have been taking enforcement measures ranging from compliance awareness to making arrests and seizing unauthorized catch, equipment and vessels," stated the release from DFO headquarters in Ottawa.

Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans has been using social media to update the public about its enforcement actions in Southwest Nova Scotia. Photo from DFO-Maritimes Twitter/X

"In Southwest Nova Scotia, fishery officers have seized vessels and traps and have returned lobsters to the ocean. In addition, fishery officers have arrested individuals, who have since been released and are currently under investigation for potential charges for offenses under the Fisheries Act and regulations," the department said.

"Fishery officers take a variety of enforcement approaches. So enforcement activity is not always visible, and it may not look the way people want or expect it to look," the department added.

The DFO also stated that fishery officers patrol the Canada-US boundary year-round.

"Since the beginning of August this year, fishery officers in Southwest New Brunswick have seized American lobster traps that were placed over the boundary line in Canadian waters for offenses under the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act," the department said.

However, the UFCA is not assured by DFO's promises.

Although the DFO sent a patrol vessel, the Canadian Coast Guard's Corporal Teather, to the area on Thursday (Sept. 10), Sproul suggests that the ship is not the right tool for the job.

The Canadian Coast Guard Ship Corporal Teather. Photo from the Department of Fisheries and Oceans website

That Class C ship is a midshore patrol vessel, designed to board large ships, and has no ability to haul and remove lobster gear or conduct any type of inshore patrols, offered Sproul.

"It's like sending a Lamborghini to a car accident instead of an ambulance," he said.

"If the minister really cared about ending the illegal fishery, she would order the local DFO officers to go to the wharf and seize all the vessels or the catches," he said, adding the UFCA video clearly shows lobster crates floating in the harbor at Saulnierville, evidence that lobsters are being fished during a closed season.

Industry says province needs to step up, too 

While the UFCA places the bulk of blame on DFO for inaction on illegal lobster fishing, Sproul said the Nova Scotia government must take some responsibility too.

"The federal government has authority over harvesting and things that take place in all waters, but once the lobsters hit the wharf, the province has the authority over fish buyers in Nova Scotia," Sproul pointed out.

Part of the problem is that the previous provincial Liberal government "completely gutted" the enforcement division at Nova Scotia's Department of Environment -- which oversees inspection of fish processing and other food manufacturing operations -- to the point where there are just two officers and a supervisor for the entire province, Sproul said.

"That's part of the reason why it's out of control," Sproul said, adding that while the province decided last year to jack up maximum fines under Nova Scotia's Fisheries and Coastal Resources Act to deter commercial lobster buyers and processors from purchasing illegal lobsters, there's no evidence that anyone has ever been convicted or fined.

The maximum fine on conviction under that law increased from CAD 100,000 to CAD 1.0m.

However, a report by CBC in 2023 noted that the province had no records from recent years to indicate that the provincial courts had ever convicted a commercial buyer or levied a fine.

Canadian province seeks federal help to kick organized crime out of largest lobster fishery

The provincial government has also been taking heat on the issue in the legislature.

During the legislative question period on Sept. 6, opposition leader Zach Churchill pushed premier Tim Houston to commit to increasing enforcement staff and efforts to monitor lobster buying and processing, and to reinstate a zero-tolerance policy for convicted offenders.

This government has backed off on the zero-tolerance policy for those who are caught. There have been no charges under this government for those folks who are caught purchasing illegal lobsters," said Churchill.

"I'm with him (Houston) for blaming DFO for part of it. My question to the premier is, will he accept his responsibility and help deal with this catastrophe?"

"We have stepped up on the law enforcement, and doubled the law enforcement resources in the area," Houston responded.

FREE READ Canadian lobster harvesters file suit to stop First Nation fishery

Recall that the Nova Scoita's justice minister Barbara Adams, in a letter to DFO minister Lebouthillier on Sept. 5, said the province was providing funding to beef up policing in the municipal district of Clare, in Digby County, home of the Sipekne'katik First  Nation, as reported by Undercurrent.

The number of RCMP officers at the Clare location has been increased from seven to 14, and the detachment is now operational 24 hours a day, seven days a week, Adams noted in her letter.

Meanwhile, the province continues to throw the ball back to the federal government.

"We really need the federal government to get on board on this one," Houston said.

title: Papua New Guinea plans JV with Filipino firm as first step in tuna sector overhaul
content:
The Papua New Guinea (PNG) government aims to bolster its fisheries sector with the approval of a plan to develop a "Pacific marine industrial zone (PMIZ)" in the Madang province.

However, according to some tuna industry insiders, the new strategy will be challenged by several structural issues affecting the country.

The plan -- announced by the country's minister for international trade and investment, Richard Maru, earlier this week in a press briefing -- is designed to transform PNG from a mere "rent collector" in the fisheries industry to a self-sufficient "fishing state," PNG Business News reported.

In the first phase of the plan, the government will establish a fishing joint venture (JV) with the Filipino fishing company and processor RD Corporation, which supplies canned tuna to the US and EU markets, Maru said.

Cash flow issues have affected RD since 2022, forcing the firm to suspend its fishing operations in PNG and limiting the company's ability to buy raw materials to keep its cannery in PNG in operation, as previously reported by Undercurrent News. However, the firm has sold some of its fishing vessels in the region and managed to continue its processing and sale operations, according to industry sources.

RD still has at least eight vessels in the region, which, according to sources, it plans to restart operating, possibly later this year.

This JV plan aims to create a PNG-based fishing company, developing local expertise and ownership in the industry. Details of the proposed deal between the Filipino firm and the government have not yet been disclosed.

Maru said PNG needs its own fishing vessels and knowledgeable fishermen, stating, "We have to learn to crawl before we can walk." This strategic partnership will leverage RD's existing facilities, industry knowledge, and global market experience while the state injects equity and immerses nationals into the business," he said.

Photo: RD Fishing tuna vessel. Global Seafood Alliance, 2021.

Maru also highlighted the excessive costs and lack of expertise that make direct government entry into the fisheries sector impractical. Establishing necessary infrastructure such as wharves, processing facilities, cold storage, and vessels could cost upwards of $500 million. Instead, the JV with RD presents a viable path to build local capacity and eventually achieve full domestic control over the fisheries industry, he said.

However, political instability poses a challenge to the initiative, according to Undercurrent industry sources. In recent months, PNG has experienced an escalation of violence, including widespread looting and rioting triggered by unpaid civil servant salaries in January 2024. Additionally, the country lacks sufficient infrastructure and processors need to import all the needed raw materials.

According to Undercurrent sources, inconsistent government policies in PNG have caused a struggle for processors based there.

The PNG government has provided preferential vessel day scheme (VDS) rates to PNG-flagged and locally-based foreign-flagged vessels to support the tuna processing sector. Despite initial governmental support, abrupt fee hikes for the vessel day scheme in the territorial waters led to operational constraints. 

However, it was recently forced to reduce a previous increase in the daily fee as some of the fishing companies with vessels registered in PNG had started to move to other neighboring countries. 

According to Maru, PNG's current lack of expertise leads to significant economic losses. 

"We are earning a net revenue of only PGK 300 million ($79m) a year when we could be earning PGK 5 billion," he said. He stressed the need to stop the outflow of 80% of the catch for overseas processing. This JV aims to change that dynamic, ensuring more fish is landed and processed in PNG, generating jobs and increasing revenue.

If the first phase succeeds in establishing a stable fishing operation, the second phase will involve building a cannery and other related businesses within the 250-hectare PMIZ. This phase will take advantage of special economic zone benefits, aiming to attract further investment.

PNG's exclusive economic zone spans 2.4m square kilometers and accounts for approximately 18% of the world's tuna catch. However, most of this catch is currently processed abroad. The government's plan aims to reclaim these benefits, contributing to a projected revenue between $4bn and $5bn.

Maru praised the Marape-Rosso government for its policy shift, describing it as the biggest game-changer in PNG's fishing industry since independence.

The government has tasked a state negotiating team, led by chairman Dairi Vele, to finalize the JV agreement with RD within the next four weeks for cabinet approval.

RD did not reply to a request for comment in time for this publication.

title: Albacora repatriates Spanish workers attacked in Ecuador
content:
Some Spanish workers, mostly from Galicia, employed by the fishing firm Albacora, have been repatriated after their bus was ambushed and shot last week near Guayaquil, Ecuador.

Albacora told Undercurrent News a bus carrying personnel in charge of a vessel repair in Ecuador had been the target of an attack by an unidentified group of people.

"This attack has been repelled by the security personnel accompanying the transport, and fortunately, no personal injuries have been caused," it said.

Albacora confirmed to Undercurrent it has coordinated the return to Spain of those people who expressed their willingness to return, and all of them arrived safely at their homes over the weekend.

Publico reported last week that six assailants on three motorcycles fired at least 17 shots at the bus carrying 30 Spanish workers, who managed to escape the ambush. The incident happened around 2:00am local time on the road connecting Posorja with the shipyard. The workers have since taken refuge in a hotel in Posorja. 

This incident is part of a broader pattern of escalating organized crime and violence in Ecuador, which has led to increased military presence on the streets and protests by local transportation workers.

title: Latin American fishing alliance condemns Mexican exec’s murder
content:
The Latin American Alliance for Sustainable Fisheries and Food Security, also known as ALPESCAS, has expressed "deep concern" over the increasing violence associated with criminal groups following the murder of a top fishing industry executive.

Minerva Perez Castro, the president of Baja California's delegation to the Mexican National Chamber of Fishing and Aquaculture Industries, was brutally murdered in Ensenada earlier this week. Perez was a staunch opponent of the infiltration of criminal syndicates in Mexican fisheries.

According to Alpescas, the act of violence can be related to cartels or mafias that operate with illegal fishing.

The group's president, Osciel Velasquez, condemned the murder and highlighted the gravity of the situation.

"We are determined to combat illegal fishing, which is the third most lucrative illicit activity in the world after drug and arms trafficking. It is a dangerous crime that causes significant harm to the population, ecosystem, and public health," he said in a statement sent to Undercurrent News.

Illegal fishing is a major global issue, with an estimated 26 million tons of fish and other marine resources being captured illegally each year, Alpescas said. 

In response to the murder, Alpescas has called on Latin American governments and authorities to intensify their efforts to combat illegal fishing and the criminal networks behind it. Velasquez emphasized the need for a thorough investigation and justice for Perez, urging regional cooperation to protect responsible and sustainable fishing practices.

Alpescas signed an agreement in June 2023, known as the Panama Agreement, with member countries including Panama, Mexico, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Ecuador, Peru, Chile, Argentina, and Brazil. This agreement aims to eradicate illegal fishing and strengthen the monitoring and control of foreign fleets operating in adjacent waters.

The agreement encourages national governments to enhance their legislation and improve their enforcement efforts to prevent illegal fishing activities and to adhere to the principles of responsible fishing promoted by the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization.

Alpescas said that Perez played a crucial role in advocating for better nutrition and health through sustainable fishing practices, with her recent public denunciation of the increase in illegal fishing in Baja California underscoring her commitment to the cause.

title: Luke’s Lobster exec explains reservations over pursuing MSC restoration
content:
LONDON, UK -- There can be grim unintended side-effects of regulations and certifications in fisheries that should be protected against, warned Ben Conniff.

"A lot of these regulations and certifications and systems and tech solutions are expensive, and they're onerous, and they're really hard to manage for fishermen and for small and medium enterprises," said the co-founder and chief information officer at  Luke's Lobster, in the US town of Portland, Maine.

Conniff, whose business manages both a lobster shack restaurant chain while also serving as a lobster processor and supplier, was speaking Wednesday (May 22) on a panel during the second and final day of the Blue Food Innovation Summit in London, UK, an event that boasts more than 350 ocean-industry leaders as attendees.

Still fresh on the seafood exec's mind, clearly, was the US North American lobster fishery's loss of its Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certification in November 2022 as a result of a federal judge's decision months earlier in response to a lawsuit filed by conservation groups, as reported by Undercurrent News.

The ruling tentatively forced the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to go back to the drawing board on its rules regarding the protection of whales and other creatures endangered by lobster fishing.

Ben Conniff, co-founder of Luke's Lobster (far right), speaking at an event in Portland, Maine. Photograph by Jason Huffman.

Luke's declared at the time of the MSC certification suspension that it was "due to a legal technicality." It explained: "Not all sustainable fisheries are MSC certified, certification requires resources many fisheries lack, but certification is required by some large seafood buyers, so it affects lobstermen's ability to sell their catch."

The lobster industry has been cleared to seek restoration of its MSC certification since December 2022, when Congress included provisions in a massive, nearly $1.7 trillion omnibus fiscal year spending bill that required NOAA to wait at least six more years, until Dec. 31, 2028, before implementing and enforcing new lobster fishing restrictions.

Instead, however, the group that managed the sector's MSC certification inexplicably withdrew from the program in February 2023 and has yet to express an interest in trying to regain its status. 

'A layer of bureaucracy'

Conniff said Wednesday that Luke's had a "pretty good sense of how we could regain MSC for Maine lobster."

Hypothetically, he said, "let's say I have an investor who's interested in me. Using the six-figure sums it would cost to go get that certification, and then I do all that work and I think, okay, I'm going to create [an MSC] client group of one -- me."

"Nobody else cared enough about sustainability to go get this certification. I did all the work, I deserve it," he said, metaphorically playing the fictional part of someone going for certification alone. "So then the retailers out there, they hear there's MSC-certified Maine lobster again, so they start demanding that, because 'we want that sweet blue [eco-label] check,' but the only place they can get it is me," he said.

"So then I suck up all those sales accounts, and my competitors start to go out of business. I absorb their buyers, which used to be competitive, and now they're not. So then my investor needs their exit, they're ready to go, but I'm still managing these ongoing costs of certification, the tech and the traceability. And so my margins aren't there, but I've consolidated the supply. So what do I do? I go to the fishermen, I beat down the price. I get my margins down to where I need them."

A Luke's Lobster restaurant in Portland, Maine.

The enterprise value of the business hits targets, and the investor gets its exit with "a beautiful story of sustainability," but what they've actually done is add a layer of bureaucracy to fishermen that were already operating sustainably, he said.

"We've put money in the pockets of a bunch of people thousands of miles away from the fishermen, and then we've impoverished the very fishermen that we rely on for our food."

Impoverished communities can suffer from all manner of socioeconomic ills, like opioid addiction, alcohol addiction, and domestic violence, he noted, "all starting from getting an eco-certification -- a good thing by any standard, right?"

US lobster fishery withdraws from MSC, ends talk of quick certification recovery

He continued: "But the point is that if we're not thinking about the third- and fourth-order sociocultural impacts of decisions that we make to implement programs that are only executable by the most well-resourced companies, then we're really at risk of dismantling a delicate ecosystem of harvesters, small and medium and large supply chain businesses that are necessary for the health of our overall fisheries."

Lobster harvesters understand global economics

Conniff painted lobster harvesters as a difficult but smart group.

"People think that lobstermen are resistant to change because they're backward and stubborn people. And sometimes they are!" Conniff said. "But the reality is they're resistant to change in large part because they understand how global economics work. When they see this slew of regulations and technology and solutions coming their way, they see the opportunity for corporate consolidation of their fishery."

Luke’s Lobster co-founder: Industry won’t abandon MSC certification efforts

Maine's lobster fishery is one of the few left where "every lobsterman is their own entrepreneur with their own boat," he said, adding:

"There's a bevy of diverse companies of different sizes that have to compete for their catch at the dock, and that keeps money in the local communities, in the lobstermen, in their families' pockets. It makes for a strong fishery."

"But as we see more and more tech solutions, expensive certifications, bureaucracy required, that could mean that some of the biggest companies edge out all of the small ones because they're the only ones left with market access when we've created the demand for all this new stuff."

MSC: Small-scale harvesters can be protected

Erin Priddle, North Europe regional director of the MSC and speaking on the same panel as Conliff, agreed it was vital to protect stakeholders. She pointed to the UK's Poole Harbour clam and cockle fishery, certified in 2018, as an example of a community that accessed funding for bringing the fishery up to standard from the MSC itself.

"This is the time we really need to be smart about how to use sustainable finance, this capital out there, to be able to support small-scale holders and other efforts to really drive economies of scale in the sector," she said. "You can guard against smallholders being weeded out of the system, and regulation has a really strong role to play here as well."

A member of the crew of the Jaylin Lucas hands off a bin of just-caught North American lobsters. Photograph by Jason Huffman.

Priddle said she'd worked in government policy for about 10 years before joining the MSC and that, through smart policymaking, "you can make sure that you have social policies in place, economic policies in place that actually guard against consolidation."

The MSC can work with a fishery on establishing client groups in a "pre-competitive space" to operate at economies of scale and not have smallholders bear all of those costs on their own, she added.

title: The New Yorker chronicles Atlantic Canada’s First Nation lobster fights
content:
The fight between commercial lobster harvesters in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia and the Mi'kmaq First Nation groups that started their own lobster fishery in defiance of the federal government is chronicled in an article published in The New Yorker on Tuesday (May 21).

"Nova Scotia's Billion-Dollar Lobster Wars: How Indigenous fishermen are defending their rights—and corporate profits—in the most lucrative fishery in North America" tends to paint a more sympathetic portrait of the First Nation groups, describing the violent attacks they sustained in late 2020, including the burning of a Sipekne'katik lobster wharf in Saint Mary's Bay.

"By some metrics, the Sipekne'katik's radicalism had been a political success," wrote  Abe Streep, a journalist and book author based in the US state of New Mexico. "The band's loudest critics—the white fishermen—had their reputation badly damaged by the incidents of arson and violence, and, amid international outrage, the [Canadian Department of Fisheries and Oceans] had reached new agreements with other First Nations about their treaty fisheries. Yet the Sipekne'katik refused to negotiate with the DFO, or to allow outside oversight of its treaty fishery, arguing that doing so would compromise their sovereignty."

The article also recalls the acquisition of shellfish giant Clearwater Seafoods in January 2021 by Premium Brands in a deal that included a major 50% stake being taken by a coalition of Mi'kmaw nations, including the Sipekne'katik. The coalition had secured about $350m in financing in order to participate.

"It is expected that it will take many years—perhaps decades—for the Mi'kmaw coalition to pay off its debt from the Clearwater deal," Streep wrote. "But the power that it brought was immediate. (Earlier this year, the coalition refinanced its loan, substantially lowering its interest payments.)"
