title: Canada seizes major shipment of illegal elvers worth CAD 500k
content:
An illegal shipment of baby eels worth about CAD 500,000 ($367,037) was seized at Toronto (Ontario) International Airport on May 15 by enforcement officers from Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) and Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA). The approximately 109 kilograms of elvers were destined to be shipped overseas.

"The magnitude of this elver seizure is an important development," said DFO minister Diane Lebouthillier in a press release issued on Friday (May 17).

No arrests were made related to the seizure. DFO officials said an investigation is ongoing for violations of Canada's Fisheries Act.

Department of Fisheries and Oceans officers seized 109 kilograms of illegal elvers at Toronto Pearson Airport on May 15. Photo credit: DFO

The airport seizure is the latest in DFO's crackdown on illegal elver fishing in Nova Scotia. DFO officials said they have made 149 arrests since March 6 this year, seized 23 vehicles, and confiscated about 207kg of elvers.

"Once again, our message is crystal clear: Do not travel to Nova Scotia to illegally fish or export elvers this year; enforcement officers will be waiting for you," said Lebouthillier.

Recall that in March, Lebouthillier decided to shut down the commercial elver fishery altogether, saying it was not possible to have a safe and sustainable fishery in light of the reports that the fishery had been overrun by poachers, organized crime and violence, 

That decision angered legitimate commercial harvesters, who will collectively lose nearly CAD 45m in revenue this season. They had offered DFO suggestions to curb poaching, even offering to foot the cost themselves for a digital traceability system to give border agents a means to verify legal shipments of baby eels and avoid a complete shutdown.

However, Lebouthillier said she considered all options and concluded that, without significant changes, the risks to the conservation of the species couldn't satisfactorily be addressed.

title: Canada reports making progress on curbing elver poaching
content:
Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) says arrests and seizures are "having a significant deterrence" on unauthorized elver fishing in the Maritime provinces this spring, reports CBC News. 

"This is due to the sheer number of officers we have on patrol. The number of arrests we've made and the vehicles we've seized," Tim Kerr, the top enforcement officer for DFO in the Maritimes, told an advisory committee meeting on Thursday (May 2).

So far this year, DFO officers have made 132 arrests while seizing 157 kilograms of elvers, 21 vehicles and hundreds of fyke nets, Kerr said. 

Among the arrested were five people from Maine, who were detained on April 20 in Nova Scotia, reported New Centre Maine. In that case, DFO officers reportedly seized about 7.5 pounds of baby eels, a vehicle, three dip nets and one fyke net. The department did not identify the individuals nor say if they will face charges.

Fishery officers from the Pacific, Ontario, Quebec, Newfoundland and Labrador and the Gulf region have been brought in to disrupt the illegal fishery.

In March, fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier decided to shut down the commercial elver fishery, saying that without significant changes, the orderly management of the fishery could not be restored, as reported by Undercurrent News.

The decision was controversial. With baby eels fetching up to CAD 5,000.00 per kilo ($3,659.00), it's the most valuable fishery, per kilogram, in the world. However, the legal, commercial fishery has been inundated with poachers on rivers in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.

The elver fishery in the Maritimes was worth CAD 47 million ($35m) in 2022, with DFO-approved licenses held by eight commercial harvesters and some Mi'kmaw and Wolastoqey communities.

The baby eels are sold to Asian aquaculture operations, where they are raised to adulthood for food.

Last year, a Canadian senate committee studying the issue of illegal and unregulated fishing, heard reports of organized crime involvement and growing violence in the elver fishery, Undercurrent reported. 

DFO said it intends to launch public consultations as soon as next month to explore regulations to curb poaching.

title: Needed Chile salmon M&A being held up by overvalued assets, DNB says
content:
There is probably pent-up demand for further consolidation in Chile's multi-billion-dollar salmon industry, said Norway's DNB, the industry's largest lender.

The bank, which has an office in Santiago, doesn't expect any deals to go through in the short-term because valuations in both M&A talks and for other types of financial transactions are too high, said Esteban Szasz, the company's Chile-based senior vice president.

"Today the gap is too wide. People believe Chilean companies are valued too high, therefore the bid ask price is too narrow," Szasz said at the recent Aquasur trade show, in Puerto Montt, Chile. "When these elements change, we should start seeing that consolidation occurring in the sector." 
 
Despite a period of prolonged high prices, Chile's industry has not shown to be as profitable as Norway, the only farming nation that sells more salmon than the South American country. DNB showed a slide that puts the superior financial performance of Norwegian farming operations into stark contrast.

Even Mowi, the world's largest salmon farming company, makes much more money in Norway than it does at its Chilean operations.  

Camanchaca’s profit takes dive in Q4 amid declining salmon prices, rising costs

 
Chilean producers are less profitable because they achieve lower prices in the US and are in part affected by the need to treat farming operations with antibiotics, because of the presence of salmonid rickettsial syndrome (SRS) in Chile's Pacific fjords. Valuations are also affected by regulatory factors, and heightened political risk, DNB said.

The disagreement over the worth of Chilean companies has also affected their ability to operate in Nordic equity and bond markets, Szasz said.   
 
Chilean salmon prices fell 7% last year, chiefly due to the biological challenges of climate change and rising sea lice levels. Norwegian salmon prices increased during 2023. But DNB predicts the delta between Chile and Norway prices will narrow in the key US markets, mainly because of supply shortages.  

Chilean supply will dip 5% in 2024, and by a further 1% in 2025, while Norway will experience growth, DNB said. Chile's salmon industry could return to positive growth in 2026.

Political risk

The political climate is still a key factor when it comes to any type of M&A negotiation involving Chilean salmon companies, DNB's Szasz said. The left-leaning government of Gabriel Boric was elected in 2019 after abrupt social violence. Boric, whose father was a mayor in a key salmon-producing region, targeted the industry during his presidential campaign.  

The salmon industry challenged a decision last year by the government to phase farming out of protected areas. The ruling could have wiped out 60% of production and 70,000 jobs, an industry association said.

A key turning point in the debate occurred when thousands of salmon farm workers protested in cities across southern Chile. The salmon industry is the main employer in the three farming regions of Chile, including Aysen, Los Lagos and Magallanes.   

Chile set for ‘good prices’ underpinned by strong US market, says DNB

Boric's government, which has combated low economic growth and high inflation during most of his term in power, communicated that it intended to review regulatory policy and tax considerations, well before Norway's government introduced a new resource tax in 2023. However, the government's immediate focus appears to be changing Chile's fishing laws.

The government is also trying to push through an overall pension and tax reform before the next presidential election in 2026.  

The proposed and modified fishing law, which currently provides the rules for aquaculture, would put more pressure on salmon farmers to publish data on their use of antibiotics, anti-parasite medication as well as mortality and production numbers. Companies experiencing fish escapes would receive higher fines and must implement tighter measures to prevent them. 

In addition, Chile's salmon industry has been coming under increasing pressure from environmental groups to phase them out of the Magallanes region, on the southernmost tip of Chile. The region is a sparsely populated area with lots of national parks.

M&A activity  

The last major M&A movement in Chile's salmon sector came in 2018 and 2019 when Agrosuper's unit Los Fiordos acquired local rival Aquachile for $850m, making it the largest salmon group in Chile. The new group also absorbed two smaller players – Salmones Magallanes and Friosur – for almost half a billion dollars.  

Chinese company Joyvio, controlled by Legend Holdings, purchased Australis Seafoods for $921m, also in 2019. The deal ended in controversy and is being disputed in an international tribunal because Joyvio said they overpaid Australis Isidoro Quiroga.

The Chinese said Quiroga concealed information about environmental infringements, which forces salmon farmers to curb output or pay penalties. The complexity of Chile's farming regulations, which were introduced in a patchwork of reforms in the 2010s, also complicates any further major M&A transactions.  

Blumar sees revenue, profit dip in Q4 amidst aquaculture struggles

There is a natural cadence to the Chilean sector, and indeed the industry at large. Many farming companies are still in the hands of the foundational owners, many of which started their businesses in the 1970s and 1980s. Most of these companies are in a transition phase where ownership is transferred to second-generation owners.

Several founders, including Gonzalo Vial of Agrosuper and Victor Puchi, who started AquaChile, have passed away recently.  

The other megatrend in salmon has been the interest of other protein groups in purchasing seafood companies.

Japan's Mitsubishi, which holds a broad range of assets in its food commodities portfolio bought Cermaq, one of the world's largest salmon farming companies, in 2014. Brazil's JBS, the world's largest meatpacking company, bought Australian salmon farmer Huon in 2021.

JBS has reportedly scoured Chile's salmon industry for potential acquisitions. The company will likely want assurances regarding the future of the industry before getting more involved.

title: Strike-threatening Newfoundland crab harvesters misinformed on pricing formula, processing group leader asserts
content:
Misinformation is the problem that's leading snow crab harvesters in the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador (NL) to talk about another fishing strike, says the head of the local processors' group.

Harvesters are threatening to tie up again in the world's largest snow crab fishery over a decision by the NL Standing Price-Setting Panel to choose the price-setting formula proposed by the Association of Seafood Producers (ASP), as reported Wednesday (April 3) by Undercurrent News. This just two days before the season is set to begin on Saturday (April 6).

The formula maintains a CAD 2.60 ($1.97) per pound "floor" price, which harvesters say is unfairly low. However, it's wrong to assume that's the fixed price for 2024, Jeff Loder, ASP's executive director, told Undercurrent in an interview.

"There's an incredible amount of misinformation being spread on social media by the Fish Food and Allied Workers (FFAW) union and its members about what the panel actually decided," Loder said. 

In previous years, under the legislated final-offer selection process, the ASP and FFAW would each suggest a price, and the panel would choose one of the proposals to govern the rest of the season. However, under the new formula, the dock price would adjust weekly in tandem with the US wholesale price for frozen 5-8 ounce crab clusters.

The CAD 2.60/lb floor price is based on the current Urner Barry (UB) data that currently shows CAD 7.37 to CAD 7.71/lb for 5-8 ounce frozen clusters.

All it would take to increase the dock price to CAD 3.00/lb is for the UB wholesale price for frozen 5-8 clusters to get to CAD 8.11/lb, an increase of CAD 0.40-0.74/lb, Loder explained.

Meanwhile, the ASP commits that the floor price for harvesters will never go lower than CAD 2.60/lb this season, even if the UB market drops below its current value.

"So the processors are taking the risk on that one," said Loder.

This chart in the Association of Seafood Producers' proposal to the NL price-setting panel shows how much crab harvesters would gain each time Urner Barry increased its average wholesale prices for frozen 5-8 ounce snow crab clusters.

The ASP is optimistic that wholesale prices will rise this year, triggering a subsequent increase in dock prices, Loder said.

"Remember, Urner Barry is reflecting on crab from last year. When crab starts this year, we will likely see an increase immediately," he said.

Panel found flaws in FFAW price-setting proposal

In its final decision on Monday, the province's price-setting panel said it could not accept the FFAW's price-setting formula proposal, which suggested a modified version of the formula from the 2023 Blackwood report.

The FFAW suggested holdbacks, involving partial payments for crab landings if dock prices exceeded CAD 3.00/lb, with a final reconciliation on harvesters' crab sales at the end of the season. That approach would be beneficial, the FFAW told the panel, because it adjusts with the market while providing an initial margin for both harvesters and companies to operate.

The FFAW proposed a sliding scale formula for setting dock prices for snow crab. Screenshot from FFAW document

However, the FFAW's formula would also have created a problem, said the panel, noting that at a UB 5-8 oz price of CAD 7.71, the minimum dock price would be CAD 3.00/lb, but the initial payment to the harvester using the FFAW formula would be CAD 3.05/lb.

"This would result in an overpayment to the harvester at UB prices between CAD 7.71/lb and CAD 7.82/lb, meaning that, at the end of the season ... the harvester would have to pay back the overpayment to the producer or start the next season owing the processor money," the panel said.

"That (ASP) proposal also showed that the harvesters will always obtain at least 53.90% of the share of the market price and remain constant at 56.9% once the UB market price reaches CAD 8.02/lb," the panel noted.

The panel emphasized that its decision on a pricing formula would remain in effect for the 2024 season only, meaning the fight over the approach could start up again before the next season.

Harvesters got a few wins

While the price-setting panel agreed with the ASP's approach to the price-setting formula, it sided with the harvesters union on other points, Loder pointed out.

The panel also weighed in on other conditions related to the purchase of snow crabs at the dock, including tolerances for small crabs, quality issues and trip limits. The panel agreed with the FFAW that harvesters won't be penalized for landings in which 20% of the crabs have a carapace less than four inches wide.

"They will still be paid the premium price, even if 20% of the crab is in that smaller range," explained Loder, adding the ASP had asked for 5% tolerance.

Déjà vu for 2024 Newfoundland crab season as harvesters threaten another holdout

"There were some wins for the union, certainly some positions where we argued for a different outcome. But it is a balance, and I think the panel struck the right balance," Loder said.

With the crab season opening date set for April 6, Loder added the processors are hopeful there will be no further delays.

"We're going to do everything we can to move forward with the season, so we don't face the same type of impacts we faced last year," he said, referencing the 39-week holdout by harvesters in 2023. 

This season, the NL quota for snow crab is the highest it's ever been at 57,568t.

As for the prospect of more demonstrations by fish harvesters opposing the new price-setting formula, Loder said, "I will repeat the same position I repeated all last year. It is 2024 (and) intimidation, threats and violence should not be tolerated in our society."

Critical hour approaches

The question now is whether the ASP explanation will assuage harvesters.

Late Wednesday night the FFAW advised its members via Facebook that union president Greg Pretty had been in contact with the provincial government and "we are working toward a solution."

Up to noon NL daylight time on Thursday the union had not provided any further updates.

Crab harvester and protest leader John Efford, meanwhile, was holding firm on the threat of a strike.

Pricing formula chosen for Newfoundland snow crab fishery

"We have all decided that no fish will be processed until we have a proper, fair deal, that will not see us going broke," he posted on his own Facebook page Wednesday night.

"We will show by letting an opening date pass and ALL of our boats stay at the wharf," Efford stated, while throwing a hint about more protests to come, saying, "I hear the weather in St. John's on Monday is going to be nice, especially just after sunrise at 7 a.m."

title: Newfoundland crab harvesters warned against acting like ‘angry mob’ as protest rolls into day two
content:
Snow crab harvesters in the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador (NL) continued their protests for a second day at the province's House of Assembly Thursday morning (March 21), but the lead organizer, John Efford, has advised them to remain peaceful.

"We are going to have a peaceful protest. We are not going to give anybody any reason to call us an angry mob. We're not going to give anybody a reason to call us ignorant," Efford said, speaking through a megaphone to address the protestors who began arriving again at 6 a.m. NL daylight time.

"We're going to show self-control. That's more important than losing your mind, losing your patience," Efford said.

"Do not, do not get caught up in cat-calling. Do not get caught up in incitement. If anybody says anything to you today, say, 'Have a nice day.'"

Photos from Newfoundland and Labrador radio station VOCM shared on Twitter/X show the scene at the Confederation Building,in St. John's, on Thursday morning, March 21.

A court injunction has been issued to prevent anyone from blocking access to the building, or interfering with public servants trying to enter the building. To ensure the protestors abide by the rules of the injunction, the Royal Newfoundland Constabulary (RNC) police are at the Confederation Building in full riot gear, reported CBC News. 

As reported earlier by Undercurrent News about 1,000 fish harvesters showed up at the government building on Wednesday (March 20) to pressure the government to change the system that, they say, eliminates competition for their catches and reduces dock prices. 

This just weeks before the new season is expected to begin in the world's largest snow crab fishery with a dock price yet to be set.

The protestors, led by Efford, want the government to allow outside buyers to do business with local harvesters. They also want the province to eliminate the rule that imposes a cap on the amount of crab that can be processed by any one factory in the province.

The Fish Food and Allied Workers (FFAW) harvesters union also supports the protestors' demands, as previously reported by  Undercurrent.

The protestors blocked all points of entry to the building on Wednesday (March 20), the day the provincial government planned to introduce the budget for 2023-24.

Some civil servants were able to gain access to the building, but not without a lot of pushing, shoving and heated exchanges. Angry protestors yelled and cursed and, in at least one case, told an aide to premier Andrew Furey to "Go the f*** home."

Newfoundland government postpones budget discussions due to ‘unsafe’ conditions caused by crab protest

By 11:00 a.m. Newfoundland daylight time on Wednesday, the provincial government decided to delay the budget, saying, "Presently, the conditions are unsafe for employees and visitors to the complex, and there is a threat of violence."

The budget is now expected to be delivered Thursday. 

Meanwhile, to show support for the St. John's protestors, harvesters on the province's west coast are also planning a demonstration on Thursday at government offices in Corner Brook.

title: Newfoundland government postpones budget discussions due to ‘unsafe’ conditions caused by crab protest
content:
A protest by snow crab harvesters at the Newfoundland and Labrador (NL) House of Assembly on Monday (March 20) has forced the Canadian province to postpone its plans to deliver and vote on an annual budget.

The province's Department of Finance said, in a press release issued at 11 a.m. Newfoundland daylight time, that the delivery of the fiscal 2024 budget is delayed "due to an unsafe environment in which fish harvesters are preventing public service employees from entering the Confederation Building complex. 

"Presently, the conditions are unsafe for employees and visitors to the complex, and there is a threat of violence," the department statement continued.

The province has asked the Supreme Court for an injunction -- a cease and desist order -- against the demonstrators, reports CBC News. Other media are reporting that the injunction was granted and the protestors have begun dispersing. 

As previously reported by Undercurrent News, fish harvesters began gathering at the province's House of Assembly at 6:00 a.m. as part of a demonstration in which they are calling for the provincial government to allow more processing licenses and the sale of snow crab to buyers from outside of NL as a response to low dock prices. 

Newfoundland crab harvesters block access to legislature on budget day

Video from the scene showed altercations between the harvesters and officers of the Royal Newfoundland Constabulary, the provincial police force, as well as confrontations between harvesters and public employees who attempted to get into the building.

The postponement of the budget is unprecedented in the history of the province.

title: Santa Priscila now Ecuador’s largest employer with 16,000 staff
content:
Santa Priscila, Ecuador's largest shrimp exporter by volume, has also now become its single largest employer. 

The firm's recent move to employ an additional 1,100 'young individuals' in response to the Ecuadorian government's 'Organic Law of Economic Efficiency and Job Creation' was documented when the Ecuadorian president Daniel Noboa Azin visited one of the company's factories in Duran, Guayas on March 13, reported El Universo. The shrimp processing giant employes now over 16,000 people.

During the visit, Noboa said that 63,890 young individuals between the ages of 18 and 29 have entered the job market in the country since a new job creation law was approved last December.

Con el objetivo de verificar los beneficios de la Ley Orgánica de Eficiencia Económica y Generación de Empleo, en empresas del país, el presidente @DanielNoboaOK visitó la planta camaronera Santa Priscila donde han generado 1.100 empleos para jóvenes, luego de la aplicación de la… pic.twitter.com/0qoEy1eIbJ

— Presidencia Ecuador 🇪🇨 (@Presidencia_Ec) March 13, 2024

Cristina Salem, Santa Priscila's chief financial officer, said the law, introduced on Dec. 20, 2023, has had a positive impact on youth employment during a deeply troubling time for the country.

En #ElNuevoEcuador los jóvenes son parte fundamental del desarrollo del país. 🇪🇨👏

✅️ Más de 60 mil empleos generados con la Ley de Eficiencia Económica y Generación de Empleo. pic.twitter.com/UQ4ebdMHuD

— Presidencia Ecuador 🇪🇨 (@Presidencia_Ec) March 13, 2024

Ecuador's president said earlier this year his country is "at war" after drug gangs took more than 130 prison guards and other staff hostage and briefly captured a TV station during a live broadcast. Noboa had then declared the existence of an internal armed conflict and ordered the national army to restore order in the streets of the country.

In January alone, Ecuador saw at least 391 violent deaths. Last year was the most violent in the country’s modern history, registering 7,872 murders, equivalent to 43.2 deaths per 100,000 inhabitants, according to Aljazeera. 

In the past, the country's Chamber of Aquaculture (CNA) stressed that insecurity had become a matter of deep concern for the shrimp farming sector. According to figures collected by the CNA's security directorate, from January to late November 2023, a total of 76 criminal incidents have been recorded, resulting in 58 injured individuals and four fatalities. 

Although security remains an industry concern, according to Ecuadorian industry sources at the Seafood Expo North America 2024, the security situation has significantly improved over the last two months thanks to the national army.

title: Canada’s fisheries minister shuts down Atlantic elver fishery
content:
Canada's fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier will not allow a commercial elver fishery in Atlantic Canada this year.

The Quebec-based member of Parliament announced the position many feared she would take in a press release issued late Monday (March 11). She said she considered all options and concluded that, without significant changes, the risks to the conservation of the species couldn't satisfactorily be addressed. Nor could an orderly management of the fishery be restored, she determined.

"That is why I have made the difficult decision to not issue elver licenses and not open the Maritimes Region elver fishery in 2024," Lebouthillier said. "This will assist our fishery officers in addressing unauthorized harvesting."

Stanley King, acting president of the Canadian Committee for a Sustainable Elver Fishery, was quick to respond on Monday. He said Lebouthillier's decision to shut down the fishery "highlights the failings of her department, who have not taken this issue seriously over the last four years."

King, in a written statement to Undercurrent News, said the closure will only hurt law-abiding license holders, and cost 1,100 families their jobs, many of whom are Indigenous. He also doubts the closure will accomplish anything.

Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) "has had two previous closures to deal with rampant unlicensed fishing and they have turned a blind eye on each occasion. We doubt this time will be any different," King said.

"It is clear to all stakeholders, including license holders, the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick ... that canceling the 2024 season is heavy-handed and unnecessary," he said.

'A financial hardship'

The debate over whether or not to allow an elver fishery has been contentious. Just two weeks ago, Kent Smith, the fisheries minister for the province of Nova Scotia (NS), where the elver fishery is reported to be worth about CAD 19 million ($14.9m) for legally licensed harvesters, said that a shutdown would harm the wrong people. 

Canada needs to put some elver rules in writing, harvesters tell Senate panel

"The only foreseeable outcome from this proposed closure is financial hardship inflicted upon our law-abiding license-holders," Smith wrote in a Feb. 15 letter to Lebouthillier.

Though the combined elver quota for Nova Scotia and New Brunswick is small, around 9,860 kilograms annually since 2006, the value of the catch has been sky-high in recent years, ranging from CAD 3,000 ($2,225)/kg to CAD 5,000/kg in the past decade.

The high prices for elvers has brought poachers to the rivers in both provinces. Along with that has come dangerous confrontations and evidence of organized crime, as previously reported by Undercurrent News. 

At the Boston Seafood show on Sunday (March 10), Lebouthillier told Undercurrent she had met with regulatory officials in Maine to learn more about how they manage their elver fishery. 

"Maine has a lot of experience, and for me, it will be important to continue to work together,” she said. “But the first objective is also to protect the species . . . to ensure that future generations can have access to the fishery.

“There is important work that . . . will continue over the next year to tighten the rules on elvers," she said.

Arrests made

Lebouthillier's department has also faced criticism about its efforts to enforce elver fishing rules.

A Canadian parliamentary committee exploring the issue of illegal and unregulated fishing heard testimony in December 2023 that, even though legal elver fishers made numerous reports of poaching to DFO officers and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP), very little action was taken.

DFO officials, however, told the committee that, in 2023, officers made 100 arrests.

On the same day that Lebouthillier announced she would not allow a commercial elver fishery, her department also issued a press release saying it had recently made arrests on rivers across Southwest Nova Scotia.

On March 6 and 7, 2024, in separate incidents across Southwest Nova Scotia, fishery officers arrested and later released a total of five individuals who are under investigation for infractions of the Fisheries Act and Maritimes Provinces Fishery Regulations for the unauthorized harvest of elver, the department said.

Canada’s fish minister riles eel industry with talk of shutdown to handle poaching crisis

Fishery officers also seized two vehicles, some elver fishing equipment and approximately 1.14kg of elvers, which were released live back into their river of origin.

"Fishery officers are patrolling rivers, facilities and export points to deter and disrupt unauthorized elver harvest, sale and export from the region," DFO said in a press release. "Fishery officers also continue to work with other law enforcement agencies to combat the illegal harvest, sale and export of elver as well as threats to public safety and criminal activity," the release stated.

But King remains unimpressed.

"It is unfortunate that the minister did not consult, meet with, or hear the alternative solutions of license holders or First Nations before deciding to close the fishery," King said. "Obviously, she has blindly taken the advice of Maritimes Region DFO, who have a history of mismanaging the elver fishery."

title: Nova Scotia fisheries minister challenges Canada over handling of elver fishery
content:
Kent Smith, the fisheries minister for Nova Scotia, has expressed what he describes as "extreme disappointment" in Canada's management of his province's elver fishery in a letter to federal fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier, reports SaltWire Networks. 

Earlier this year Lebouthillier raised the ire of commercial elver fishers after she said she may not allow a commercial elver fishery in Nova Scotia this year.

As previously reported by Undercurrent News, Lebouthiller wrote to commercial fishers on Feb. 13 saying that because of the harassment, threats and violence "between fishers and toward fishery officers" during the 2023 season, as well as the complaints of trespassing, property damage, weapons offenses and organized crime activity, "it is my view that it is not possible to have a safe and sustainable elver fishery in 2024, and therefore the fishery should not be opened."

Canada to crack down on elver fishery following reports of organized crime, guns, violence

In his letter to Lebouthillier, sent Feb. 15, provincial minister Kent said that decision will harm the wrong people.

"The only foreseeable outcome from this proposed closure is financial hardship inflicted upon our law-abiding license-holders," he wrote.

While the commercial elver fishery is one of the smallest in volume, the recent annual quota is 9,860 kilograms -- it is the most valuable by weight. In 2023 one kilogram of baby eels fetched record prices of CAD 5,000 ($3,694), the equivalent of CAD 2,272 per pound.

Over the past few years, the elver fisheries have generated CAD 19m and CAD 49m annually for the provincial economies of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. However, the high-value catch has led to criminal activity on NS and NB rivers.

In his letter, Smith lamented the lack of action by Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) to curtail elver poaching.

 "… Despite repeated calls from my department for increased enforcement and prosecutions to curtail the poaching activities, there are no tangible results that indicate your department is protecting the resource and harvesters," he wrote.

Despite receiving more than 1,400 reports of illegal harvesting of juvenile American eels last year on East Coast rivers, DFO only laid 60 Fisheries Act charges, SaltWire said it found. The Public Prosecution Service of Canada won't confirm whether it has prosecuted to completion any Fisheries Act charges related to illegal elver fishery within the past three years.

Smith also asked the minister to ensure that DFO gives special attention to protecting the East River in Chester, Nova Scotia, where poachers and vandalism have repeatedly disrupted a long-term study into elver and American eel abundance.

title: First Nations offer Canada’s fish minister options to maintain elver fishery
content:
Some First Nations leaders in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia have offered national fisheries minister Diane Lebouthilllier an alternative to shutting down the elver fishery, reports CBC News.

The Assembly of Nova Scotia Mi'kmaq Chiefs proposed that eight Mi'kmaw communities in the province would share a 3,600-kilogram total allowable catch (TAC), which this year would be 36% of the annual 9,960 kg quota for the Maritimes.

That would amount to a 14% increase from the 2023 quotas allocated to the six First Nations communities in New Brunswick and four Mi'kmaw communities in Nova Scotia.

Gerald Toney, fisheries co-lead for the Assembly of Nova Scotia Mi'kmaq Chiefs, said communities still need to discuss future plans and whether harvesters will continue to fish even with a ban in place.  

The elver fishery in Atlantic Canada has become an outlaw fishery in recent years with widespread poaching and reports of organized crime, as recently reported by Undercurrent News. The illegal harvesters are chasing gold, as the value of baby eels -- in demand in Asia to grow out in aquaculture operations to serve the sushi market -- has soared to as much as CAD 5,000 ($3,703)/kg.

Earlier this month Lebouthillier indicated she was contemplating shutting down the eel fishery entirely in 2024. As reported by Undercurrent the minister wrote licensed harvesters on Feb. 13, saying, "It is my view that it is not possible to have a safe and sustainable elver fishery in 2024, and the fishery should not be opened."

The minister said she would consult with licensed harvesters and the First Nations communities before making a final decision.

The Assembly of First Nations gave Lebouthillier and the DFO until March 8 to respond to its proposal.

title: Newfoundland crab processors must open books if they want compensation for holdout, harvesters say
content:
If snow crab processors in the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador (NL) want to be compensated for any losses caused by an inshore harvester holdout in 2023, they'd better be ready to produce some financial records, says the harvesters' union.

The Fish Food and Allied Workers (FFAW) issued a statement on Wednesday (Feb. 21), a day after the Association of Seafood Producers (ASP) went public with the arbitrator's ruling that determined the union was responsible for the tie-up and liable for damages, as reported by Undercurrent News.

In a 50-page ruling, arbitrator David Orsborn, a retired NL supreme court judge, determined the union had declared a cessation of business, contrary to the Fishing Industry Collective Bargaining Act (FICBA) and the Master Collective Agreement (MCA), the legislation that governs collective bargaining between harvesters and processors in NL.

While it's not illegal for a harvester to decide not to fish or a processor to choose not to process fish, it is unlawful for processors or fishers -- acting as a group --  to engage in a cessation of business to reach an agreement by economic force or pressure, Orsborn said.

The ASP has not said how much it is seeking in damages. That will be determined in the second part of the grievance process, which is expected to start within weeks.

The FFAW, however, in its press release, indicated the processors are seeking significant compensation.

"ASP has sought millions of dollars in damages in the grievance it filed," said union president Greg Pretty.

FFAW president Greg Pretty. Photo courtesy of FFAW.

"If they truly expect us to believe that they suffered losses when they were able to get crab for so cheap, they must produce the paperwork to prove it," he continued. "We look forward to getting all of the financial records from all the crab processors in the province, which ASP will need to provide."

Pretty maintains, as well, that the tie-on in 2023 was the only recourse for fish harvesters.

"Unfortunately, fish harvesters felt they had to act but outdated legislation makes it illegal for harvesters to strike, as well as illegal for the Union to 'authorize or declare a cessation of business dealings."

The snow crab fishery is the most valuable fishery for NL. In 2022, during a year of record high prices, the landed value was nearly CAD 1 billion ($739.6m)

However, the American market for crab tanked in 2023, as reported by Undercurrent.

Newfoundland harvesters on hook for damages from 2023 snow crab holdout

And that led to dock prices throughout Atlantic Canada as low as CAD 2.20 last year. The landed value for 2023 was CAD 70.6m, reports the Canadian Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) in its latest statistics.

Pretty continues to lay blame at the feet of the ASP.

"Instead of helping to resolve the catastrophically low price in spring of 2023, ASP sat back and watched the fishery fall -- only later deciding to take legal action six months after the issue was resolved and fishery complete," he said.

As for the arbitrator's ruling, Pretty offered this interpretation:

"Luckily, the arbitrator recognized that outdated legislation makes it impossible for the FFAW to do its job of representing fish harvesters during a tie-up. The arbitrator acknowledges that if the price is so low, no harvester has to fish.

"However, the arbitrator decided that FFAW has to wait for the tie-up to happen before we are allowed to start talking about it. Because the union relayed publicly what we were hearing from our members before they made the ultimate decision to delay the fishery -- we were therefore liable of 'declaring' people would not fish. In the future, to comply with legislation, the arbitrator states the union would have to wait until the problem actually occurs and boats stay tied up before we were to start talking about it."

Newfoundland crab harvester co-op in business but processor deal falls apart

Pretty also blames the current legislation that rules collective bargaining for the fishing industry, calling it "a backward system that doesn't allow the union to work on finding solutions to problems until they've already started."

The FFAW confirmed it will not seek a judicial review of Orsborn's decision.

Meanwhile, Orsborn made one observation in his ruling that both sides might agree on.

"The history of the fishing industry in [NL] could not be described as that of a tranquil sea, the gentle sounds of the waves accompanied by harmonious chords from the blended voices of the participants," he observed.

"Regrettably and unfortunately for the province and its residents, that history shows a long-standing animosity -- including episodes of violence -- not only between but among the representatives of the diverse interests."

title: Canada’s fish minister riles eel industry with talk of shutdown to handle poaching crisis
content:
Commercial elver fishers in Atlantic Canada say they proposed a solid idea to the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) for combatting the industry's ongoing poaching crisis and protecting their multi-million-dollar legal fishery, but DFO rejected the plan.

Instead Diane Lebouthillier, Canada's fisheries minister, is talking about the prospect of shelving the season.

Because of the harassment, threats and violence "between fishers and toward fishery officers" during the 2023 season, as well as the complaints of trespassing, property damage, weapons offenses and organized crime activity, "it is my view that it is not possible to have a safe and sustainable elver fishery in 2024, and therefore the fishery should not be opened," Lebouthillier said in a letter delivered to harvesters on Tuesday (Feb. 13).

Member of Parliament Diane Lebouthillier when she was named minister of fisheries, oceans and the coast guard by prime minister Justin Trudeau. Image tweeted by Lebouthillier's office.

The new regulations and a traceability system were needed to reduce illegal elver fishing but "despite the department's best efforts, these changes will not be in place to support a 2024 fishery," she said.

The letter is sparking outrage in the elver industry, Stanley King, a commercial eel fisher and spokesperson for the Canadian Committee for Sustainable Eel Fishing, told Undercurrent News Wednesday (Feb. 14). 

DFO has had plenty of time to work on solutions for the fishery, noting the poaching problem began long before last season, he contends. The industry has been "begging and pleading" for a traceability system for the past 10 years, he said.

Commercial license holders even offered to foot the bill themselves to adopt a digital traceability system that would give the department and border agents a means to verify shipments of live baby eels.

Small quota but astronomical value

While the elver fishery quota is minimal compared to other commercial fisheries, with just 9,860 kilograms allotted for commercial fishing in Nova Scotia (NS) and New Brunswick (NB), this tiny silver fish is the most valuable by weight.

There's a high demand for elvers in Asia, mainly China, where they are grown out in aquaculture facilities to feed the sushi market. That's pushed the price per kilo into the stratosphere.

During the 2023 season, one kilogram of baby eels fetched fishers record prices of CAD 5,000 ($3,694), the equivalent of CAD 2,272 per pound. They've generated CAD 19m and CAD 49m annually for the economies of NS and NB over the past few years.

Those high prices for a fishery that's as simple as setting up a small fyke net in a river have driven a crime spree, however, with poachers flocking to Atlantic Canadian rivers to cash in on fast money.

Last year, a Canadian parliamentary committee exploring the issue of illegal, underreported and unreported (IUU) fishing heard tales of briefcases full of money, violence, death threats and even organized crime in Canada's elver fishery on a handful of rivers in NS and NB as reported by Undercurrent. 

Canadian province asks for federal help to stop illegal elver fishing

Legal license holders have been asking for more enforcement, higher penalties for illegal fishing, and more oversight by DFO and the Canadian Border Services Agency (CBSA) to track eel shipments.

DFO announced on Dec. 8, 2023, that it would aim to have new rules in place by this March, saying the department was considering things like a new system to trace elver exports. However, as the weeks went by, King said it became apparent to commercial fishers that DFO was not moving on a traceability system.

So, the fishers decided to seek a solution themselves, finding companies able to provide traceability software.

"We went out and found the vendors, the companies that could actually make the software, and they said they could do it for this (2024) season," said King.

One of the companies they contacted was BlueFin Data, which provides the traceability system for the elver fishery in the US state of Maine.

That state had a similar problem with elver poaching, King noted, but it "closed the door on illegal elver fishing by imposing high fines and tracking what was going through the export chain."

America’s lone eel farmer seeks to displace shady imports

However, when the harvesters suggested the Bluefin system to DFO last fall, officials said there would be a problem with using the US vendor because the company doesn't store its data in Canada, King recounted.

The harvesters also approached Veritech, a Canadian company that's developed an electronic logbook (e-log) system that's already being used by some commercial fish harvesters in Canada in preparation for 2024, when DFO is expected to make that system mandatory to replace paper logbooks, as recently reported by  Undercurrent. 

Testing of Canada’s Fisheries app in progress as DFO eyes e-logs

King said Veritech told his group it could adapt its software and have a traceability system for the eel fishery before the season starts in March.

"They said time was running out, but 'we could still do it if you guys jump on this now,'" King said.

He said either of those systems would cost about CAD 50,000 to implement, and the commercial fishers were willing to pay the entire cost. But DFO did not bite.

With the government unwilling to consider those options, King said the elver industry could not go further.

"So the government would rather shutter a $45 million industry than spend $50,000 for traceability," he said, summing up the situation.

Shutdown would make illegal fishing easier to spot

News of the potential shutdown of the 2024 elver fishery led to some testy exchanges in a parliamentary committee hearing on Wednesday. 

Word of Lebouthillier's letter to harvesters came just hours before the emergency meeting of the fisheries and oceans panel to hear from department officials on plans to prevent violence on the rivers this season.

The committee exploring IUU fishing in Canada adopted a motion the previous day to call the minister, or her deputy and other high-ranking officials, to testify specifically about the elver fishery.

Despite widespread poaching in Canada, no evidence found of illegal baby eel exports

With the commercial fishery just weeks away -- the season usually runs from April to June -- the committee wanted to find out whether DFO had made any progress on its Dec. 8 commitment to adopt new regulations for 2024.

Lebouthillier did not show up, but deputy minister Annette Gibbons did, flanked by assistant deputy minister Adam Burns, regional director general for the Maritimes Doug Wentzell, and acting director general for conservation and protection Brent Napier.

Rick Perkins, a Conservative member of Parliament from Nova Scotia, who introduced the motion for the emergency meeting, asked Gibbons to explain how shutting down the legal fishery would curb poaching.

Canadian eel harvesters challenge federal re-distribution of quota

Gibbons responded that it's difficult for enforcement officers to determine who is abiding by the rules and who is breaking them on the 200 rivers in NS and NB

"At present, where there is an authorized harvest, there is a mixing of the authorized harvest and the unauthorized harvesting.. which makes it very difficult to know what is the authorized portion and what is not," Gibbons said. "That makes it very easy for those acting illegally to carry on their activity."

"That's just bunk," Perkins shot back. "Every licensed harvester is assigned to a specific river, with a specific DFO license number on their net. Everybody else is a poacher. It's easy to identify poachers."

A history of shutdowns

If Debouthillier shuts down the elver fishery this season, she won't be the first to do so. The fishery has been closed in mid-season twice in the last four years, most recently in 2023, by former minister Joyce Murray, because of rampant illegal fishing.

Perkins contends those decisions accomplished nothing.

"In 2020 you (DFO) said this (closing the fishery) would help, and poaching doubled," he told DFO officials at the committee hearing.

He said that poaching increased again in 2021 and "quadrupled last year" even though the minister shut down the legal fishery midway through the season.

Gibbons, though, held to the logic that a complete shutdown would "provide clarity," adding that "any harvest will be illegal. Anything that our officers see would be subject to enforcement."

That logic did not win over Perkins.

"This department and six ministers in eight years have mismanaged this fishery," he said, adding the elver industry "told you how to fix this, and the department has done nothing since then."

Legal fishers say they're being sabotaged

If DFO wants a game plan to follow for the management of the elver fishery, it should consider how the US state of Maine beefed up its elver fishing regulations, King said. While some poachers have been charged and fined in Canada, the fines are insignificant compared to the penalties in that state.

"If you get caught once, it's a US 25,000 fine. If you get caught a second time, you go to jail," he said.

In Canada, the fines are about CAD 500, if charges even lead to convictions, he said.

Elvers at center of dispute between Nova Scotia First Nation, DFO

Maine also requires elver exporters to notify the state's Marine Patrol 48 hours before preparing to ship eels. It allows the officer to witness the weighing and packing of the eels and to mark the package with a seal that must remain unbroken until the shipment reaches its destination.

The state also uses a monitoring system that records the weight and value of every sale to ensure no one exceeds quota.

In Canada, we need a traceability system, and we need real penalties for illegal elver fishing, said King.

"But the government just doesn't listen," he said. "Seems they would rather let the criminals have our jobs and our tax dollars and our natural resources."

King figures elver poachers made away with CAD 100m of baby eels for the black market last year.

Meanwhile, he said, Lebothillier has "sabotaged" legal fishers with her letter indicating she won't be issuing commercial licenses for 2024.

While the department's official line is that the minister will consult with the elver industry and First Nations participants over the next 10 days, the Feb. 12 letter to individual elver fishers suggests to many that Lebouthillier has her mind made up.

Stanley King, acting president of the Canadian Committee for a Sustainable Elver Fishery, addresses the House of Commons Standing Committee on Fisheries and Oceans on Dec. 7. Photo screenshot from video

King said the 10-day consultation period publicly announced by DFO the same day as the minister's letter holds no meaning.

"She (Lebouthillier) has explicitly stated her intention to shut down the fishery, and I believe, as a bureaucratic step, they have to say they will 'consult,'" he said.

"She's just saying, tell me what you think in the next 10 days. And then she's going to go ahead and do what she wants anyway. So I don't think it's real, genuine consultation," said King.

Based on the minister's letter and the committee testimony this week, King draws his own conclusion.

"They're just gonna let the poachers have at it this year and keep the legal fishermen on the sideline."

Black eye for Canada

The impact of a fishery closure won't be felt just in the local economy, with the loss of up to CAD 45m, King added.

Ultimately, he said, DFO's inability to bring the hammer down on elver poaching is damaging Canada's reputation as a global leader in the fight against illegal fishing.

Just last year DFO inked a deal with a Canadian company to provide satellite tracking of fishing activity around the Indo-Pacific region, as reported by  Undercurrent.

Over 3,000 illegal shark fins discovered in Canada-US surveillance operation in North Pacific

"They've given tens of millions of dollars to curb IUU far away in the Pacific, but that does not help the 1100 people they just put out of work here," said King.

For the 2024 season, King said, Canada's fisheries minister had a choice to make.

"The choice was to support a regulated, safe, elver fishery by providing adequate enforcement or to let a transnational organized crime ring steal the jobs of Canadians, the tax dollars of Canadians and our natural resources.

"It's embarrassing to say she seems to be going with the second option."

title: Israeli company produces world’s first 3D-printed eel
content:
Steakholder Foods, based in Rehovot, Israel, has launched the world's first plant-based, 3D-printed eel, it said.

US startup making progress on cultivated halibut

The company, which is a pioneer in 3D meat and fish printing technology and cultivated cell innovation, said it was able to "accurately replicate the complex texture of eel through precision layering and a unique combination of materials" using its proprietary 3D-printing technology.

Steakholder said the eel is made from plant-based materials, but it expects to include cultivated eel cells in the future.

In a press release, the company said it is exploring collaborations to commercialize its printed eel by offering proprietary 3D printers and ink capable of generating revenues in the short term.

Arik Kaufman, CEO of Steakholder, said, "The launch of our printed eel marks a pivotal moment in the seafood industry, showcasing the vast potential of our DropJet technology -- Steakholder Foods' solution for fish and seafood printing."

He said the technology is designed to enable partners to generate products on a potential industrial scale of hundreds of tons monthly, not only at lower costs compared to wild eel but also with the flexibility to create a variety of printed products using the same production line.

"Such versatility could significantly boost profitability for food companies and lead the way to a shift towards more efficient and sustainable practices in the industry."

The global eel market, valued at $4.3 billion in 2022 with a compound annual growth rate estimated at 2.19%, primarily relies on wild eel.

Canada to crack down on elver fishery following reports of organized crime, guns, violence

"This industry faces several critical challenges, including overexploitation and the risk of extinction, particularly in Japan, which accounts for a major portion of global eel consumption," said Steakholder.

The company added the challenge of breeding eel in farms, as well as issues like poaching and black-market trading, further exacerbate the situation and highlight the need for sustainable alternatives.

Steakholder is an international deep-tech food company at the forefront of the 3D printing meat and cultured meat revolution. Incorporated in 2019, it is listed on the Nasdaq Capital Market under the ticker STKH.

title: Lobster bait prompts questions in Canadian Parliament about mackerel catches
content:
A box of lobster bait labeled "product of Canada" has prompted two lawmakers to question whether harvesters are undermining the rules of the nation's mackerel moratorium.

However, the owner of the company that processed the fish says he has a perfectly good explanation.

Canada to crack down on elver fishery following reports of organized crime, guns, violence

Conservative members of Parliament Clifford Small, who represents the Coast of Bays-Central-Notre Dame riding in Newfoundland and Labrador (NL), and Rick Persons, who represents the South-Shore riding in Nova Scotia, told Undercurrent News on Wednesday (Dec. 20) that they remain concerned about the discovery they reported during a Nov. 30 hearing of the Fisheries and Oceans Standing Committee.

The Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) has maintained a moratorium on fishing mackerel in all of the Atlantic Canada provinces and Quebec since 2022.

Clifford Small during a question period in the Canadian House of Commons. Image is still from video.

"It's been brought to our attention that mackerel is being packed and sold as a product of Canada mackerel, a product of Quebec," Small said during the hearing. "The mackerel fishery is currently under moratorium, which is this year's mackerel."

Small told Undercurrent he posed the question because Perkins discovered boxes of mackerel labeled "product of Canada, 2023" being loaded aboard fishing boats on the first day of the lobster fishery season this fall on Nova Scotia's South Shore.

Rick Perkins is a Conservative member of the House of Commons, Canada, representing the Nova Scotia riding of South Shore-St. Margarets. Image is from video.

"What surprised me when I was out on dumping day for the traps was that some lobster fishers had bought mackerel bait from a company in Quebec," Perkins told Undercurrent Wednesday (Dec. 20)

"It was curious to me because they were selling it as commercial bait … so somebody is catching it," he said.

Quebec company offers explanation

There's no big secret here, though, according to Irving Roberts, owner of I&S Seafood, the Quebec company that boxed up the mackerel for bait. His company, located near Saint Paul's River, processes several species, including several pelagic and groundfish species, but mostly snow crab and lobster.

I&S Seafoods of Quebec, employs about 100 people in its processing plant near St. Paul's River, on the Gulf of St. Lawerence coast. Photo from company website

He explained to Undercurrent on Wednesday that the mackerel that ended up as bait was bycatch from this year's herring fishery, which is worked by seiners on the Lower North Shore of Quebec. They fish inshore, within a 50-mile area from the Labrador border to St. Augustine, Quebec, and are allowed a 10% bycatch of mackerel, he said.

"I think I did around 4 million pounds of herring this year, and about 6-7% of that was mackerel picked up with the herring from the seiners," Roberts told Undercurrent.

FFAW, harvesters report ‘good signs’ of mackerel in Newfoundland waters

DFO confirmed for Undercurrent that while harvesters are prohibited from fishing for mackerel when engaged in a fishing trip for herring "they may retain a quantity of incidentally caught mackerel that does not exceed a percentage of the weight of the herring caught."

The percentage varies by gear type and area, the federal agency said.

DFO also noted: "The Fisheries Act prohibits persons from purchasing, selling or possessing any fish that has been caught in contravention of the Act or the regulations (question of sourcing). That said, there are no provisions prohibiting the packing of mackerel in Canada."

DFO needs to beef up its enforcement to ensure there's nothing illegal at play with mackerel or any other fishery, Perkins said.

"With all the other issues we've been having in my province, whether it's elvers or the poaching of lobster that's being taken out of season, DFO needs to enforce the law," he said.

Small added that DFO also needs to reconsider its policy around bycatch.

"I don't agree with anything being dumped or wasted. Canada needs an anti-dumping policy, like they have in the EU," he said. "If it comes over the rail of a boat, then it needs to come ashore to be accounted for and something done with it."

The DFO declined to comment on whether it is investigating the mackerel matter raised by Small in the committee hearing.

"To protect the integrity of any potential or ongoing investigation, Fisheries and Oceans Canada cannot comment further or provide any information on any accrued evidence," DFO said in an email to Undercurrent.

Bays full of mackerel

The bigger issue here is whether the mackerel fishery should continue to be closed, Roberts told Undercurrent.

"We've had an abundance of mackerel here for the last two or three years. And the herring fishers … sometimes when they're catching herring, they end up with too much mackerel, and they have to let it all go," he said. "We've had the bays full of mackerel this year."

The mackerel that came in as bycatch from the herring fishery, he said, was around 4-6 grams, what he calls "a nice-sized mackerel," large enough to get a good-sized filet.

Many in Atlantic Canada's seafood industry share Roberts' opinion. In a recent press release, the Fish Food and Allied Workers (FFAW), the union that represents NL's inshore harvesters, said a sampling program its members are participating in is seeing large schools of mackerel and a good mix of large and small mackerel to indicate a healthy stock.

Mackerel on ice. Credit: Mikaela Toczek, Marine Conservation Society

"It's clear the stock is much healthier than what DFO says, but unfortunately, DFO Science has not prioritized evaluating the extent of mackerel biomass throughout the region," said FFAW secretary-treasurer Jason Spingle.

Roberts said harvesters on the lower north shore of Quebec are seeing similar things.

"We've had it here, miles and miles of mackerel breaching on the water."

That's impacted some herring fishers in that area, he said.

"There were guys here who had to stay ashore (from herring fishery) because there was too much mackerel."

title: Former DFO official says Canada must clarify Indigenous fishing rights
content:
A former senior official at Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) says clarity on Indigenous fishing rights in the Maritimes is needed from the federal agency and the courts or "anarchy will reign" reports CBC News.

"The frustrations can be mitigated by clearly communicating the rules, having an orderly and regulated fishery, and then providing an adequate monitoring and compliance presence to effectively implement the rules," Morley Knight, now a fisheries consultant in Newfoundland and Labrador, told the parliamentary standing committee on Fisheries and Oceans in Ottawa on Monday (Dec. 11).

"While that sounds simple, it is not. And while patience is required, action is also required before the situation explodes or stocks are harmed," he added. 

The committee is examining illegal, unregulated and unreported (IUU) fishing.

For a part of his 16-year career with DFO, Knight was in charge of DFO's conservation and protection branch in Atlantic Canada.

Indigenous fishing of baby eels — also called elvers — and lobster without DFO authorization has surfaced repeatedly during the committee's hearings.

Some Indigenous fishers assert they do not need DFO approval to pursue their treaty right to fish for a moderate livelihood. The Supreme Court of Canada has ruled in previous cases that First Nations have a right to a moderate livelihood fishery, but federal and provincial governments also have the authority to make the rules for those fisheries.

Knight told MPs the rights of Indigenous fishing must be clarified once and for all by the courts.

Without that, he said, "anarchy will reign and there can be no effective compliance program, and the risk is greater than what the courts may decide."

The committee also heard this week that illegal fishing and organized crime were undermining the elver fishery in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, as reported by Undercurrent News.

Threats and intimidation tactics by poachers, who sell the elvers in cash deals to buyers to supply a black market in China, are driving legal fishers off the rivers, elver fisher Stanley King told the committee.

Baby American eels, also called glass eels, are in high demand in China. Photo from Canadian Committee for a Sustainable Elver Fishery

King and Nova Scotia MP Rick Perkins also told the committee DFO enforcement in that fishery was nil to non-existent.

"Elver fisheries license holders have made countless reports of poaching and have provided DFO with vehicle descriptions and license plate numbers, the names of reported buyers, the addresses of reported holding facilities, and even flight details for upcoming export shipments of black market fish," said King.

DFO took no action on these tips, Perkins added, even though, in one particular case, one poacher advertised on Facebook when and where he would be illegally buying elvers.

A day after that testimony, DFO announced it was considering ways of improving the tracking of elver fishing and export.

The department is holding public consultations to gauge opinion on proposals that include measures like conditions for export licenses that would require exporters to notify the DFO when a container of elvers will be packaged for export, allowing a DFO official to "verify the contents of each container destined for export, weigh the elvers and seal the container."

The department hopes to have new rules in place before the start of the 2024 elver fishery.

In his testimony, Knight said DFO needs a clear plan that sets out clear expectations of what is permitted and what is not permitted in Aboriginal rights to the lobster and elver fisheries.

"DFO needs to execute the plan and arrest those who don't comply. It's as simple as that," Knight told the committee.

He also urged dockside monitoring for the lobster industry, more resources for the conservation and protection branch and certification of catches to prove seafood was legally caught and recorded.

title: Daily recap: Trident plans to sell four Alaska plants, cut staff; Norway to see dip in farmed salmon output for 2023
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Tuesday, Dec. 12:

Trident plans to sell four Alaska shoreside plants, cut staff in 'comprehensive restructuring'

Trident Seafoods announced Tuesday that it's begun a "comprehensive restructuring initiative" that involves seeking potential buyers for four of its Alaska shoreside plants among other moves. The news coming from the vertically integrated, Seattle, Washington-based giant may be unsettling as it suggests financial woes at one of the US seafood industry's oldest and largest players. Trident has been operating continuously in Alaska for more than 50 years and maintains a significant presence in the Alaskan whitefish and salmon arena while also operating processing plants globally. 

2023 to end with 'modest decline' in Norwegian farmed salmon production

Norwegian seafood consultancy and data company Kontali Analyse has projected that 2023 will conclude with a modest 1% decline in Norway's farmed salmon production, despite earlier optimistic signs in the industry.

Tuna commission halves FAD closure period in Western Pacific

A move to reduce the "veda," or fishing closure, in the Western and Central Pacific Ocean is expected to increase skipjack tuna catches in the region, according to the Parties to the Nauru Agreement. The Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission has agreed to reduce fish aggregating device closure periods for purse seine vessels.

Russian Far East fishery business Sokra declared bankrupt

Russian fishery and seafood company Sokra has been declared insolvent by a local court, while fishery agency Rosrybolovstvo has moved ahead with lawsuits to freeze and cancel its fishing quotas.

Canada to crack down on elver fishery following reports of organized crime, guns, violence

Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans is developing new regulations to crack down on illegal elver fishing following explosive testimony heard last week by a parliamentary panel. The Fisheries and Oceans Standing Committee heard tales of briefcases full of money, violence, death threats and even organized crime in Canada's elver fishery on a handful of rivers in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick in a hearing held Dec. 7.
