title: Canada to crack down on elver fishery following reports of organized crime, guns, violence
content:
Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) is developing new regulations to crack down on illegal elver fishing following explosive testimony heard last week by a parliamentary panel.

The Fisheries and Oceans Standing Committee (FOPO) heard tales of briefcases full of money, violence, death threats and even organized crime in Canada's elver fishery on a handful of rivers in the provinces of Nova Scotia (NS) and New Brunswick (NB) in a hearing held Thursday (Dec. 7).

"This once peaceful fishery has recently seen kidnapping, robbery, assault, gun violence and an overall disruption of the peace," Stanley King, a commercial elver fisher appearing on behalf of the Canadian Committee for a Sustainable Eel Fishery, a group of commercial fishing licence holders for juvenile American eels (Anguilla rostrata), told the panel.  

Stanley King, acting president of the Canadian Committee for a Sustainable Elver Fishery, addresses the House of Commons Standing Committee on Fisheries and Oceans on Dec. 7. Image is still from video.

He and others are asking for stepped-up enforcement by DFO, and they might not have to wait too long. The federal agency on Friday (Dec. 8) issued a press release announcing that it had begun a public consultation on the issue and aimed to have new rules in place by March 2024 for the fishing and export of elvers.

Under the proposed regulations a license would be required for anyone to possess and/or export elvers.

Small quota, big money

The 30-year-old baby eel fishery in Atlantic Canada is small in size but big business.

The total allowable catch for the fishery has been 9.96 tons since 2006. The season usually runs from the beginning of April until the end of May or early June.

There are close to 100 licensed elver rivers in the region, although licensed commercial harvesters typically fish only about a third of them. Fishing happens at night, noted King, whose family has harvested elvers for 25 years. 

The live eels are air freighted to China, where they are grown out in aquaculture facilities to adult size, mainly for the sushi market. China currently buys 100% of the elvers fished out of East Coast rivers, mainly from the provinces of New Brunswick (NB) and Nova Scotia (NS).

With the average price of elvers have ranged from CAD 2,000/kg ($1,474) to CAD 5,000/kg over the past 12 years, the landed value of the fishery in NS and NB has ranged from CAD 19 million to CAD 49m annually.

The value of elvers has been rising since 2011, when the average price increased dramatically to almost CAD 2,000 per kilogram, doubling to just over CAD 4,000/kg in 2012. Since then prices have fluctuated from CAD 3,000/kg to CAD 4,685 and higher.

During the 2023 season, one kilogram of baby eels -- also known as glass eels because of their silvery, almost transparent appearance -- fetched record prices of CAD 5,000.

China opens world’s largest indoor RAS eel farm

They weren't always that valuable. From 2002 to 2010, the average price of elvers ranged from CAD 112.00 to CAD 787.00/kg, with an average of CAD 393/kg for the period, according to data from DFO.

Poaching 'exploded' in 2023

As the value of the elvers increased, so too did illegal harvesting, King told the committee.

Before 2020, he said, a typical fishing night would see two people fishing each river, one on each side using dip nets to capture the elvers. However, in 2020, during the worst year of the COVID pandemic, King said he noticed 10 or more people showing up on the rivers he fishes in Nova Scotia. 

It grew from there, he said, particularly in 2021 when there was less enforcement.

"It exploded in 2023 when licensed fishers were outnumbered 10 to one by poachers," he said, noting estimates by DFO that about 45% of the overall quota was stolen by unlicensed harvesters.

"There would be 50 people unlicensed on each side of the river, with one licensed fisher on each side. So, you can see the logistics. It's just unbelievable," said King.

A Department of Fisheries and Oceans map shows the number of licensed elver rivers in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Image is screenshot.

Poaching became so rampant in 2022, and again in 2023, that then Canadian fisheries minister Joyce Murray closed the season on April 15, just a couple weeks after it had begun.

That meant lost revenue for those who hold legitimate commercial licenses, costing them their livelihoods, while the poachers -- disregarding any rules -- continued to fish, said King.

The thought of quick cash is drawing all sorts to the rivers, he told the committee. They're coming from the province of New Brunswick, the city of Toronto, Ontario, and the US state of Maine, he said.

"We've talked to people from [British Columbia] that have told us: We heard we could make some quick money down here (and) there's no enforcement. So we came to do that," said King.

Bags of cash and guns

The poachers have no trouble finding buyers, King said.

China has "an insatiable appetite" for live baby eels to supply aquaculture facilities that will grow the elvers to market-sized adults within one year. That means they need a steady supply of elvers to maintain the cycle, he explained to the panel.

"They will buy as much as they can, and they don't really care how they do it," he said.

"Chinese buyers readily buy black and gray market elvers from anyone, and [are] paying cash, which has opened the door for global organized crime," he continued, noting how buyers show up with "bags of cash for black market transactions."

The cash deals are undermining the legitimate fishery and the local economy, he said.

Canadian province asks for federal help to stop illegal elver fishing

"They're stealing tax dollars, they're stealing jobs (and) our fishery is getting shut down."

Threats and intimidation tactics by poachers are also driving legitimate harvesters off the river, King added. 

He noted how licensed commercial operators, like himself, employ people to collect eels on the rivers. Many of those employees are women, trying to earn legitimate income to support their families.

"We've had employees quit over this," he said. "One of them that fished for us for 15 years, who has two small children under the age of 5, said she will not return to work this year because it's too dangerous."

Member of Parliament describes death threats

Nova Scotia Conservative House member Rick Perkins, who represents the federal riding of South Shore-St. Margaret's, one of the hotspots for elver fishing, said during the hearing that he's witnessed evidence of the illegal fishery.

"Every night I was home during the legal elver fishery, and I was going out every Friday and Saturday night, at midnight, looking at the rivers to see what was going on," he said. "And . . . many of them which were not even licensed (elver fishing) rivers, had poachers on every river."

He said he was the target of intimidation.

"I had death threats, as did my wife, during this time," he said.

Rick Perkins, Conservative MP for the Nova Scotia federal riding of South Shore-St. Margaret's. Image is still from video.

"There was a lot of criminal activity from the US, Quebec all over, but there was also a lot of indigenous illegal fishing. I talked to and saw them firsthand," Perkins said.

The lawmaker said his local office staff "called the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) detachments on the south shore of Nova Scotia almost every day, asking if DFO had been contacting them for assistance. And every day they said, 'No'."

Meanwhile, King said he saw DFO officers come out in the daytime to check on the rivers. However, he pointed out, "This is a fishery that happens at night, so those (daytime) patrols were completely useless."

"The response from both DFO and the RCMP to this organized crime ring has been almost non-existent," said King.

"Elver fisheries license holders have made countless reports of poaching and have provided DFO with vehicle descriptions and license plate numbers, the names of reported buyers, the addresses of reported holding facilities, and even flight details for upcoming export shipments of black market fish," he said.

DFO took no action on these tips, Perkins claims, even though in one particular case, one poacher advertised on Facebook when and where he would be illegally buying elvers.

"We forwarded this information to RCMP officers but, again, no action was taken. ... We call the RCMP. We give tips. We call DFO. Nobody will do anything. And it's costing Canadians jobs and tax dollars," said King, adding: "It's gonna cost us this industry if they don't get their act together soon."

Canadian elver fisher seeks court order to stop alleged poaching by First Nations

As previously reported by CBC News, an official of the Canadian Border Services Agency (CBSA)  told the parliamentary committee earlier in November that the agency found no evidence of illegal shipments of elvers this year. 

"We have effected a variety of different examinations to ensure compliance and have not found anything that was illicit or destined abroad that had been harvested illegally or was the result of unreported fishing," said Daniel Anson, director general of intelligence and investigations for border services. 

He added that the agency works with other government departments to ensure that fish and seafood importations and exports comply with established policies.

"These activities primarily include verifying that any required licenses, permits, certificates or other documentation required to import and export the goods to and from Canada are provided," Anson said.

Meanwhile, CBC  reported in April that a shipment of about 25 kilos of live baby eels worth about CAD 112,000  were seized by DFO at the Halifax (Nova Scotia) Stanfield Airport.

Canada pursues illegal lobster, eel, crab fishing charges against 54 Mi’kmaw members

At the Parliamentary committee hearing on Nov. 21,  Doug Wentzell, regional director general for DFO's Maritimes region, said the DFO has engaged other law enforcement, including the RCMP, on several different incidents involving the elver fishery.

"Officers made over 100 arrests last year alone," he said.

Wentzell said the elver fishery "presents a number of unique challenges given how lucrative it is and how the elvers are shipped out of the country. ... We are doing a management review of the elver fishery right now to figure out if there are additional tools we need to manage, given how unique this fishery is," he told the committee.

'We need real penalties'

King had a few suggestions for combatting the illegal fishing and trade of elvers.

"We need enforcement . . . and we need increased fines," he said.

Noting a recent poacher was fined just $500 for illegally fishing elvers, King said that penalty is no deterrent.

"You have to consider that they can go out and make CAD 10,000, CAD 15,000 or CAD 20,000 in a single night, sometimes more.

"We need real penalties," he said.

DFO, the RCMP, and CBSA also have to do a better job of working together to track the illegal shipment of elvers, he said.

"I don't blame so much the CBSA," he said, "because they should be informed by the DFO and the RCMP on what to look for, what time of year to look for it, so they can do their job more effectively."

He said the DFO acknowledges that at least 4.5 metric tons of elvers were fished illegally in 2023.

Poachers continue to fish eels in Nova Scotia despite shutdown

"The real number," King and others suspect, "is probably closer to 25t.

"And they all went through airports and flew out of this country to China," he said.

DFO acknowledged the gaps in tracking illegal elver fishing and export in its Friday announcement.

"There is no federal oversight or monitoring of the elver supply chain from harvest to export," the federal agency said.

To close the gaps, DFO said conditions for export licenses could include, among other things, a requirement to notify DFO when a container of elvers will be packaged for export, allowing a DFO official to "verify the contents of each container destined for export, weigh the elvers and seal the container."

The public consultation process on the proposed regulations is open for comment until Dec. 20.

title: AquaChile notes first shipment of fresh coho to Israel as milestone
content:
Chile's largest salmon producer, AquaChile, has completed its first shipment of fresh coho salmon fillets to Israel.

Israel's recent conflict with Hamas has dragged on now for more than two months, making headlines internationally for both the bloody violence and protests that have occurred over Israel's handling of the matter. But AquaChile makes no mention of the controversy in it latest news.

The firm described its delivery to Israel as a "significant milestone in its commercial history." It further explained that Israel ranks among the countries with the highest per capita consumption of salmon globally, making it a key market for AquaChile.

"Despite the challenging times and uncertainties in the aviation industry, the company has achieved this goal through its entire team's dedication and hard work. Salmon has become an integral part of the Israeli culinary culture, finding its place on consumers' daily menus in restaurants and supermarkets," AquaChile said.

Alejandro Cuevas, AquaChile's sales manager, expressed his satisfaction. "In this context, it is crucial for AquaChile to establish a presence in this demanding market, which places high expectations on both our fresh and frozen product offerings," he said.

Cuevas further emphasized that the move represents a significant step forward in AquaChile's international expansion strategy and underscores the company's commitment to providing products of the highest quality, irrespective of the global challenges faced.

AquaChile has sharply increased its production of coho salmon in recent years. The group has been making substantial commercial efforts to boost its consumption in other markets beyond Japan, including China and the US.

title: Sealing industry advocates say EU ban should be discussed at Canada-EU Summit
content:
Members of Canada's sealing industry and advocates for a seal hunt say a Canada-European Union summit in St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador this week (Nov. 23 and 24) would have been a great opportunity to talk about the 14-year-old EU ban on seal products, CBC Radio-Canada reports.

EU officials arrived in St. John's on Thursday for bilateral meetings on Friday involving Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, and European Council President Charles Michel.

The war in Gaza was expected to be a main point of discussion between the leaders, reported Global News. Climate change, energy and trade were also on the agenda.

The Global News report noted that European officials said Trudeau chose Newfoundland and Labrador (NL) as the location for the latest bi-annual summit. In that province, seals number in the millions, and the sealing industry used to be an important part of coastal community economies.

The EU banned the import of seal products in 2009 on ethical grounds.

Radio Canada reported that when they asked if the seal issue would be on the agenda at the summit, they were directed to the office of federal fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier. Her spokesperson did not answer the question.

Gil Theriault, head of an association that represents Quebec's seal hunters, told Radio Canada that planning two days of Canada-EU meetings in NL without raising the issue of the seal hunt ban "sends a message of complete disregard for the people in coastal communities."

The Canadian Sealers Association used social media channels to push Canada to raise the seal issue at a meeting with the EU this week.

Groups like the Canadian Sealers Association (CSA), representing seal hunters and processors, contend the European ban is the result of campaigns staged by animal-rights groups, who depicted the hunt as an inhumane slaughter.

"Those laws are based on propaganda," said Jim Winter, founder of the CSA.

Meanwhile, the population of seals off Canada's East Coast has grown.

The 2022 report of the Atlantic Seal Science Task Team, commissioned by Fisheries and Oceans Canada to examine the impact of seal herds on fisheries, noted the population of harp seals alone in 2019 was approximately 7.6 million.

A graph in a 2022 report shows the increase of the harp seal population off Canada's east coast. Source: Fisheries and Oceans Canada

There is concern that many animals, whose diet includes fish and shellfish, are impacting the recovery of cod, mackerel and herring stocks around Atlantic Canada.

That debate has fired up frequently in the past few years, especially as mariners have been sharing information on social media.

In 2021, a video of five miles of seals in Trinity Bay, on Newfoundland's northeast coast, went viral in a report by SaltWire Networks.

Jason Branton, who captured the video, said he and his crew encountered the seals about 60 miles out from Baccalieu Island in Trinity Bay and the seals "were on prime fishing grounds."

Prior to the EU ban, about 6,000 people were involved in the hunt in NL, landing just over 200,000 seals, according to Dion Dakins, who processes seal oil and markets seal pelts through his company, Carino.

He told media this week that since the EU ban, the number of hunters had dropped to 2,000, and they captured only 40,000 animals.

"With a ban on a species that is clearly having an enormous impact on fisheries sustainability, perhaps there's common ground to sit down at the table and find a better way forward," Dakins told Radio Canada.

Study: Grey seals severely depleting yellowtail flounder in Gulf of Saint Lawrence

Meanwhile, two federal government committees — a House of Commons committee and a Senate committee on Fisheries and Oceans — have been exploring the seal issue, posing questions on topics like the impact of seals on other marine stocks and the impact of animal rights campaigns on the industry.

At a Senate committee hearing on Nov. 9, Paul Irngaut, vice president of Nunavut Tunngavik, said seal populations around Nunavut, in Canada's North, have been "robust."

"For Nunavut Inuit, seal harvesting merges food security, food sovereignty, cultural continuity, health and community well-being, the Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit language and self-sufficiency," he said.

When asked about the impact of international regulations on the ability of Inuit communities to continue to engage in sealing activities, Irngaut replied, "Trade bans on seals have been in place for a long time. These were emotionally driven efforts by animal rights groups and by non-governmental organizations, or NGOs.

"The bans had a huge impact on families who rely on income from seals. In the 1970s and early 1980s, it caused devastation to a lot of Inuit communities that rely heavily on the by-products of seals," he said.

Irngaut added that when the EU first started talking about bans on seal products, they said there would be exemptions for Inuit.

He added, however, that the exemptions didn't work for the Inuit because "the ban is already in place, and there is no market."

Still, he said, the people of Nunavut have not stopped hunting seals.

They still harvest seals for meat and personal use, and they sell seal products where they can find markets "in like-minded countries."

"That's not going to stop," he said.

Irngaut, wearing a sealskin vest, noted, "The by-product -- which is what I’m wearing today -- is one that we have been using for centuries."

The final report of that Senate committee is expected within the next couple of months.

Sealing advocate Danita Burke, on the eve of the Canada-EU summit, wrote a commentary for The Conversation saying a discussion on the EU seal product ban needs to be reopened.

Burke, who holds a PhD in international politics and founded the Women in the Arctic and Antarctic initiative at the University of Southern Denmark, has written extensively on the sealing industry.

She calls the seal ban a "cultural violence against working-class sealers," saying it needs to be addressed.

title: One in four fishing vessels accused of forced labor ‘owned by European companies’
content:
Some 22.5% of industrial and semi-industrial fishing vessels accused of forced labor between 2010 and 2023 were owned by European companies, topped by Spain, Russia and UK firms, according to a new report by the Financial Transparency Coalition (FTC) -- a group of 11 NGOs from across the world. 

The report -- entitled "Dark links: uncovering those behind forced labour on fishing fleets." -- is the most extensive analysis of forced labor abuses in commercial fishing vessels to date, FTC claimed. It also found that companies from just five countries -- China, Taiwan, Thailand, South Korea and Spain -- own almost two-thirds of accused vessels for which legal ownership data is available, it said.

In total, 128,000 fishers, mostly from the global South, were trapped in forced labor aboard fishing vessels in 2021, often on the high seas, although the true figure could be much greater, according to the United Nations International Labour Organisation (ILO).  They suffered abuses ranging from physical violence and debt bondage to abusive working conditions.

"Forced labor aboard commercial fishing vessels is a human rights crisis, affecting more than 100,000 fishers every year, leading to horrific abuses and even deaths among fishers who mainly come from global South regions like south-east Asia and Africa," said Matti Kohonen, executive director of the FTC. "Yet those owning these vessels mostly hide behind complex, cross-jurisdictional corporate structures ranging from shell companies to opaque joint ventures."

The report warns that beneficial ownership information is rarely, if ever, requested by most countries when registering vessels or requesting fishing licenses, meaning that those ultimately responsible for the abuses are not detected and punished. 

"Forced abuse in commercial fishing vessels is widespread and is often linked to other violations such as illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing, which generates more than $11.4 billion a year in illicit financial flows from Africa alone every year, vessel identity fraud and tax abuses," said Alfonso Daniels, the lead author of the report. "Yet financial secrecy still surrounds the fishing sector, with little political will to improve financial transparency that is required to target those responsible for these crimes."

Other report key findings include:

More than 40% of industrial and semi-industrial fishing vessels accused of forced labor operated in Asia, followed by Africa (21%), Europe (14%) and Latin America and the Caribbean, or LAC (11%).
A quarter were flagged to China, and one-fifth carried flags of convenience with lax controls, financial secrecy and low or non-existent taxes.
The top 10 companies own one in nine vessels accused of forced labor. Of these, seven are from China -- some partly owned by the Chinese government -- two are from South Korea, and one from Russia.
Indonesia emerges as the global hotspot for forced labor cases, with nearly one-fourth of detected vessels operating in its waters. 45% of accused vessels operated in just five countries: Indonesia, Ireland, Uruguay, Somalia and Thailand.

The FTC has, therefore, called for an improvement in publicly available vessel information: "Before awarding a fishing license or authorization, flag and coastal states should require information on the managers, operators and beneficial owners of the vessel. In addition, unified and publicly available lists of vessels accused of forced labor and IUU fishing should be created," it said.

It wants to see the creation of publicly accessible beneficial ownership registries. Unless there is publicly available beneficial ownership information, states will only end up sanctioning or fining the vessel’s captain, crew or the vessel itself, without being able to pursue the legal and beneficial owners who are profiting from these natural resource crimes and forced labor, it argued.

Forced labor and IUU fishing should be identified as predicate offenses for money laundering purposes, it continued. "Fisheries-related crimes should also be considered 'predicate offenses' for money laundering, i.e., an illegal activity that generates proceeds of crime that are then laundered, and therefore treated as illicit financial flows."

Key international conventions should be ratified, it said, to prevent forced labor and IUU fishing. This includes the ILO Work in Fishing Convention of 2007 -- whose objective is to ensure that fishers have decent work conditions on board fishing vessels and has only been ratified by 21 countries -- and the Cape Town Agreement of 2012. 

And extractive industry reporting should be expanded to include fisheries, it said. "Fisheries should be included as an extractive industry in key initiatives including the Extractives Industry Transparency Initiative and other global and regional initiatives concerning regulation and transparency of extractive industries."

FTC said in its report that none of the companies linked to its investigation had responded to requests for comment. 

Quarter of vessels accused of forced labor flagged to China

Of the 475 identified commercial vessels suspected or reported to be involved in forced labor, FTC found flag information for 268 of them, representing 56% of the total.

In total, 26% of detected vessels for which flag data was available were flagged to China (71 vessels), followed by Taiwan (42), Thailand (16), Panama (16) and Ireland (13).

These five countries alone accounted for 58% of all the vessels accused of forced labor, it said. In terms of regions, 54% of detected forced labor vessels were flagged to Asian countries, whilst 14.5% were flagged to LAC countries led by Panama (16 vessels) and Belize (eight).

Another 10% were flagged to Africa, led by Cameroon (four), Guinea (three) and Namibia (three). In addition, 15.7% flew European flags, led by Ireland with 13 vessels, Russia with seven vessels, and Spain with five vessels, while 3.4% were flagged to Oceania.

FTC also said its report reveals that the 10 companies most involved with vessels linked to forced labor own 11.4% of the vessels, or one in nine, reported to have been involved, totaling 54 vessels.

This represents a quarter of vessels for which legal ownership information is available, which is 228 vessels.

"We gathered legal ownership and beneficial ownership information for vessels at the time of the reported labor and human rights offenses using mainly the S&P Lloyd’s Global IHS Markit and Moody’s Orbis databases."

"Of the top 10 companies, seven are from China, two from South Korea and another from Russia. This reflects the fact that China’s distant water fleet (DWF) is by far the largest in the world, with at least 3,000 vessels and believed to represent 36% of the world’s DWF capacity."

Its activity is concentrated in Africa, Latin America and Asia where national authorities have limited monitoring and control capacity, the NGO coalition noted.

"Local populations in West Africa in particular, but also across many regions in the global South tend to depend on fishing for their protein intake and livelihoods. We contacted all these companies for comment and to understand whether they have implemented any measures to ensure protection of their labor force in the future, but have not received any replies."

title: Daily recap: Bass, bream players squeezed tight by price drop; Canada salmon sector hopes for ‘real reset’
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Thursday, July 27: 

Bass, bream price drop comes as industry's largest player seeks solution to €400m debt

The Mediterranean seabass and seabream industry is facing a challenging situation with lower prices and high costs, with the issues most acute for its highly leveraged largest player, Avramar Seafood, sources told Undercurrent News.

Canadian net-pen aquaculture industry hopes naming of new fisheries minister allows for 'real reset'

Canadian salmon growers are hoping that the naming of Diane Lebouthillier on Wednesday as the new minister of fisheries, oceans and the coast guard represents an opportunity for a fresh beginning, especially when it comes to the sunsetting of net-pens on the coast of British Columbia. 

Russian seafood ban sees Norway's US crab sales rocket

When the US government imposed a ban on seafood imports from Russia last year for its ongoing invasion and occupation of Ukraine, little did Norway realize that this would prove to be beneficial for them.

Harvesters divided over Alaska sockeye mediation push

Alaska sockeye harvesters are having mixed reactions over a trade group's attempt to gather enough support to bring in state mediators to bring transparency to next year's base pricing.

In response to a concerning increase in violence and extortions, Ecuador's president Guillermo Lasso has declared a state of emergency in the Duran canton of the Guayas province, as well as in the Manabi and Los Rios provinces.

title: CNA: Ecuador’s state of emergency does not apply to logistics chain, exporters
content:
In response to a concerning increase in violence and extortions, Ecuador's president Guillermo Lasso has declared a state of emergency in the Duran canton of the Guayas province, as well as in the Manabi and Los Rios provinces.

One of the key measures is the suspension of the right of freedom of movement between 10 pm and 5 am in these areas, with the exception of individuals involved in the logistics chain, including those in the export sector, Ecuador's national chamber of aquaculture, the CNA, announced.

Ecuador exporter corporation calls for state of emergency to combat rising crime rates

"To ensure compliance with this exception, workers in the designated sectors must always carry their credentials. This requirement aims to guarantee the smooth continuation of productive and export operations, even during rotating shifts," said the chamber. 

The state of emergency declaration comes as a response to the alarming surge in violent crimes in the abovementioned provinces.

"Homicides, assassinations, contract killings, and extortion have been on the rise, posing a significant threat to the safety and security of the local population," the CNA pointed out. 

President Lasso's administration is taking decisive actions to address this serious situation and restore peace and order in the affected areas. By implementing the state of emergency, the government aims to provide law enforcement agencies with the necessary tools and resources to combat criminal activities effectively, it said. 

The suspension of the right to freedom of movement during specified hours is crucial in curbing criminal activities. By restricting movement during nighttime hours, authorities hope to deter criminals and create a safer environment for residents.

"As the state of emergency takes effect, the government will closely monitor the situation and assess the impact of these measures," it concluded.

However, according to Jose Antonio Camposano, head of the CNA, this measure is "insufficient," as it should add other regions too. 

"The current situation is unsustainable. We need immediate action from the government to protect the industries and their workers," he said through his Twitter account. "Santo Domingo, Guayas, Santa Elena, and El Oro provinces in Ecuador are also 'red zones,' due to the alarming rise in violence posing a significant threat to the safety and security of their residents."

As Undercurrent News previously reported, the shrimp, fishing, banana, cocoa and plantain sectors, represented by the Ecuadorian exporter corporation CORDEX, had sent a letter to president Lasso requesting the declaration of a state of emergency to regain control in the provinces of Santo Domingo, Santa Elena, Manabi, Los Rios, Guayas and El Oro, identified as "dangerous."

The corporation also emphasized the importance of acting immediately to reduce the number of fatalities and injuries, which have already reached around 500 victims this year, as well as economic damage, which has already exceeded $4 million.

"In addition, the private sector invests over $200m annually in security systems, such as video surveillance cameras, monitoring equipment, satellite tracking, satellite locks, scanners, radios, hiring guards on rotating shifts and armed mobile custody, among others, in order to combat insecurity. However, the situation is out of control," CORDEX stated.

title: Newfoundland processors say harvesters jumped gun with talk of new snow crab offer
content:
Processors say harvesters in the world's largest snow crab fishery are exaggerating how close the two sides are to ending their month-long deadlock.

Jeff Loder, executive director of the Association of Seafood Processors (ASP), the trade association that represents processors in the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador (NL), told Undercurrent News on Thursday (May 11) that the Fish, Food and Allied Workers (FFAW-Unifor), the union that represents inshore harvesters, jumped the gun when they published a press release spelling out the details of a prospective new deal that could put boats on the water.  

The two parties met twice in the previous 48 hours and a tentative deal was discussed via e-mail, but it was not formally tabled for consideration, he stressed. 

"I want to make it clear to everyone that ASP has not offered anything. There is no offer on the table. We will examine any offer … but it's time to start fishing," Loder told Undercurrent. 

A statement from ASP issued after our interview further clarified: "ASP did not send the FFAW the proposal that is currently being internally discussed by the FFAW relating to the raw material price for snow crab for the 2023 season. As stated previously, our association will continue to follow and abide by the Standing Fish Price Setting Panel decision."

The FFAW-Unifor did not immediately return requests for comment.

On May 9, snow crab harvesters rejected a new offer from ASP that included a price of CAD 2.20 per pound ($1.64/lb) for the 2023 season -- the same as the rate set earlier by the panel -- with the ability to reconsider prices if the market improves. It also included trip limits and an overage fund, as Undercurrent has previously reported.

Further muddying the waters is ASP's allegations of continued harassment within the union of harvesters who wish to break ranks. On the morning of May 11, several boats in different parts of the province took on bait and were blocked from heading out to fish, Loder said. 

Processors suggest intimidation used to keep snow crab harvesters from breaking rank

He said he is penning a letter to the province to ask for enforcement aid, as such behavior would violate the province's Fish Industry Collective Bargaining Act. 

"It's time to address these issues. We are losing value every single day that the crab fishery does not start," he said. 

The NL snow crab fishery is the world's largest, with 54,717 metric tons budgeted for the 2023 season. Harvesters have been refusing to fish since the season opened on April 10 in protest of the CAD 2.20/lb minimum price set by the panel. The harvesters had originally asked for CAD 3.10/lb.

The union has previously called on its membership to refrain from any harassment of harvesters who wish to break ranks and fish.

"The most important thing here is to remain united in our objective of standing up for a fair share. We cannot allow ourselves to fight against each other, we cannot resort to threats of violence or intimidation, and we cannot let it erode the leadership structure of our organization," said FFAW-Unifor president Greg Pretty in a statement earlier in May.

As for trip limits, Loder said processors would be forced to organize themselves if there is no agreement reached to prevent a surge. 

"What I would like to make very clear is in the absence of an agreement on trip limits, producers will organize ourselves and implement a trip limit schedule that's fair to all producers of all sizes in a fair way," he said. "We will have an orderly fishery and a fair fishery."

title: Union rejects latest snow crab price offer in Newfoundland
content:
The price dispute between snow crab harvesters and processors in the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador (NL) is now a "crisis of epic proportions," said the leadership of the union representing the former. 

NL snow crab harvesters rejected a new offer from the Association of Seafood Producers (ASP), leaving the fishery in deadlock, the Fish, Food and Allied Workers (FFAW-Unifor) union said in a statement this week. 

The new offer included a minimum price of CAD 2.20 per pound ($1.64/lb) for the 2023 season, with the ability to reconsider prices if the market improves. It also included trip limits and an overage fund.

About 800 harvesters, processing plant workers and others rallied in front of Newfoundland and Labrador government buildings to ask provincial government officials for help in resolving a snow crab pricing dispute on April 17, 2023. Photograph courtesy of FFAW-Unifor.

"Leadership throughout the province have been clear today: the crab is staying in the water until harvesters get a higher share of the price," said FFAW-Unifor president Greg Pretty. "FFAW-Unifor will formally reject ASP's proposal, and the bargaining committee is preparing to meet for further discussions."

The union said an overage fund "of any kind" is a major sticking point. More clarification is also needed on trip limits. 

FFAW-Unifor is also demanding a guarantee that processing companies will not bring in outside crab while harvesters are "on any sort of limits or scheduling." Outside companies reportedly offer up to CAD 2.90/lb, so NL harvesters "will continue to explore outside sales options," the union said. 

Harvesters accused of intimidation in ranks

Union members have been accused of intimidating harvesters threatening to break the picket line, as Undercurrent News previously reported. 

The NL snow crab fishery is the world's largest, with 54,717 metric tons budgeted for the 2023 season. Harvesters have been refusing to fish since the season opener on April 10 in protest of the CAD 2.20/lb minimum price set by the province's Standing Fish Price-Setting Panel. The harvesters had originally asked for CAD 3.10/lb. 

"The most important thing here is to remain united in our objective of standing up for a fair share. We cannot allow ourselves to fight against each other, we cannot resort to threats of violence or intimidation, and we cannot let it erode the leadership structure of our organization," Pretty said in the union update.

Snow crab traps on a pier in St. John's, Newfoundland & Labrador, Canada. Photograph by Jason Huffman.

At the same time, leaving the snow crab fishery moribund is hurting FFAW members and the economy of the province at large, he said. 

"Nearly 10,000 people in our province rely on the snow crab fishery as their primary or sole source of income. Their ability to pay their mortgage and bills, put food on the table, put their children in sports or activities, let alone save for education or retirement funds, is dependent on the success or failure of the Newfoundland and Labrador snow crab fishery," he said.

The union will continue to appeal to the federal government for benefit extensions, Pretty added. 

"The bottom line is this crisis isn't ending here today. We need immediate action from our provincial government on a snow crab marketing board, and to mandate a pricing formula. Provincial intervention is desperately needed to work on long-term solutions to protect this industry," Pretty says.

Low prices erode margins 

On the other side of the dispute, ASP has argued that higher dock rates would push processors' margins into the red. 

"Any decision regarding the use of ASP's reconsideration for snow crab will be based on sound reasoning, regarding where the market is moving and how that intersects with plant operations and business realities of the sector," said executive director Jeff Loder in a May 2 statement. "As of May 1, 2022, Newfoundland and Labrador had 31,609,768 pounds of snow crab landed. As of today, we have zero. The Gulf and the Maritimes have landed 45.9% and 21.5%, respectively at a CAD 2.25 price."

The price dispute also risks the brand integrity of NL snow crab, Loder said.

"The longer the fishery is delayed, the greater impact it has on the premium product NL seafood is known for. As the season progresses, the risk increases of exposure to softshell crab, briny tasting meat, and eventually new hardshell," he said. "We do not want NL product to be associated with inferior product versus the Maritimes and Gulf."

Wholesale pricing still suffering 

The NL price dispute isn't happening in a vacuum. Wholesale prices have been trending down, as Undercurrent previously reported. 

Snow crab on display at the 2023 Boston seafood show. Photograph by Jason Huffman

Concurrent with Loder's May 2 statement, Urner Barry posted an average price range of $4.65-$4.85 for frozen clusters from NL, just slightly up from the $4.65-$4.80/lb price range posted on April 27.

That's the lowest rate published by UB since snow crab wholesale prices began dropping back in late 2021, when 5-8s from NL were reported to be averaging $16.80/lb. The only NL snow crab currently being sold is holdover from the 2022 catch - now more than a year old.

title: Canadian province asks for federal help to stop illegal elver fishing
content:
The fisheries minister for the Canadian province of New Brunswick is asking for federal help to police illegal baby eel fishing in the Maritimes, reports North Shore News.

"Please intervene in this matter and impress upon your department the importance and urgency of acting within hours, not days to address this matter," wrote New Brunswick fisheries minister on May 5 to federal minister of agriculture, aquaculture and fisheries Margaret Johnson.

Poachers continue to fish eels in Nova Scotia despite shutdown

The fishery for baby eels - also known as elvers - was closed for 45 days beginning April 15 by the federal government to protect the stock and curb threatened violence tied to alleged illegal fishing. 

Some commercial harvesters have complained that illegal fishing enforcement has been lax since the closure. Elvers can be worth up to CAD 4,000 ($2,985) per kilogram. 

Closing the fishery without appropriate enforcement support "risks the imminent devastation of this resource, increases tension and materially increases the risk of violence in fishing communities," wrote Johnson.

title: Processors suggest intimidation used to keep snow crab harvesters from breaking rank
content:
Snow crab harvesters in Newfoundland and Labrador (NL) are being kept from breaking rank and bringing their landings to local processors by other harvesters using fear and intimidation tactics, hinted the head of the Canadian province's seafood processor association on Tuesday (May 2). 

"We have been informed that there are harvesters who want to begin fishing, however, they have not begun for reasons that should cause Newfoundlanders and Labradorians great concern," said Jeff Loder, executive director of the Association of Seafood Producers (ASP), during a media briefing in St. John's, according to a transcript of his comments shared by ASP.

"Producers will always respect the decision of harvesters to not fish, a right enshrined in legislation, based on their individual business situation," he said. "Which is why when we hear those individual decisions are being impacted by fear, intimidation, and harassment, we feel an obligation to address the issue. These types of behaviors are not acceptable in 2023, we do not tolerate it in our schools, our workplaces, and it should not occur in the fishery."

Snow crab traps sit on a dock in Newfoundland and Labrador. Photograph by Jason Huffman.

Fish Food and Allied Workers (FFAW), the union that represents NL's harvesters, didn't deny that some of their members might be intimidating others when contacted for a response by Undercurrent News, but it suggested the group was not part of any such effort. 

"The union doesn't support or endorse any threats of violence or intimidation," FFAW replied. 

In an earlier statement, the union had accused Loder of making such comments to "further drive a wedge between fishing fleets in order to get a crab fishery started at bottom of the barrel prices." 

'The minimum price of CAD 2.20 will remain'

It's now been 23 days since Canada's Department of Fisheries and Ocean opened the world's largest snow crab fishery for harvesting after giving fishers a total allowable catch (TAC) of 54,717 metric tons, an 8.4% increase over the 2022 season. NL harvesters have vowed to not take to the water, however, until they can be paid more than the CAD 2.20 ($1.61) per pound minimum dock rate that the NL Standing Fish Price Setting Panel set in early April, picking the ASP's proposed price rather than the CAD 3.10/lb ($2.27/lb) suggested by FFAW.

FFAW has argued that harvesters can't operate in the black at the panel's rate. The group represents 10,000 inshore fish harvesters as well as more than 3,000 onshore processing workers, roughly 7,500 of which rely on the snow crab fishery.

"The [FFAW] negotiating committee was clear that [CAD] 2.20 was not a viable price to fish at," FFAW president Greg Pretty said in a statement. "It wasn't a viable price two weeks ago, on Friday, or today, and it won't be viable tomorrow or next week."

However, ASP has argued that its processors also can't operate profitably at a higher dock rate, and Loder declared Tuesday that they would not be budging on the minimum price.

"The minimum price of CAD 2.20 will remain until such a time it is changed by the price-setting panel," he said, adding: "I would like to reiterate that every day that goes by is another day of lost opportunity to compounding the competitive position of harvesters, plant workers and producers to extract value from the crab fishery."

Each side is granted one opportunity to apply for a price adjustment from the panel during the season, however, Loder vowed to "not seek a reconsideration on the price of snow crab for at least 21 days, effective Friday, April 28." He said the promise was made, in writing, "to demonstrate our sincerity to the FFAW and its members." 

About 800 harvesters, processing plant workers and others rallied in front of Newfoundland and Labrador government buildings to ask provincial government officials to help resolve a snow crab pricing dispute on April 17, 2023. Photograph courtesy of FFAW.

FFAW matched fire late on Tuesday, reporting that its inshore council and crab chairs held a call to review the ASP presentation and said harvesters were "determined to hold strong for their fair share of the market price."

The union added: "The overwhelming majority of regions and fleets remain firm that the price of [CAD] 2.20/lb remains unviable for their enterprises and a fishery will not proceed."

Also, Pretty was not moved by ASP's three-week commitment. 

"A disingenuous offer to fish for three weeks at [CAD] 2.20 would only serve to help a very select few in the industry, while the vast majority of harvesters would be left in the lurch. The companies are manipulating a broken system and it's unacceptable," he said.

Wholesale prices still low

As harvesters and processors continue to wage war over the landing price for snow crab in NL, harvesters in other parts of Atlantic Canada are making landings. Fishers in the Southern Gulf of Saint Lawrence and the Maritimes areas have landed 45.9% and 21.5% of their allotted quotas respectively at a price of $2.25/lb, he reported.

As reported earlier, DFO gave harvesters in the gulf a combined TAC of 35,216t, an 8.3% increase in quota over 2022. 

For comparison purposes, NL snow crab harvesters had landed 31.6m lbs (14,338t) by May 1, 2022, Loder said on Tuesday.

But one of the main reasons processors' backs are against the wall is that wholesale prices for snow crab continue to sink. Urner Barry on Tuesday (May 2), posted an average price range of $4.65-$4.85 for frozen clusters from NL, just a hair better than the $4.65-$4.80/lb price range posted on Thursday (April 27).

Thursday's rate was the lowest rate published by UB since snow crab wholesale prices began dropping back in late 2021 when 5-8s from NL were reported to be averaging $16.80/lb. Thursday's average range was 3-5% less than the previous low $4.80-$5.05/lb range that UB had maintained for roughly a week.   

Of course, the only NL snow crab being sold is holdover frozen 2022 inventory, some of which is now at least a year old.

Thawed out frozen snow crab clusters from Canada for sale in a Maryland grocery store in early April 2023. Photograph by Jason Huffman.

Recall that it was snow crab consultant John Sackton's report on March 17 to the price-setting panel that as much as 10,000t of snow crab remained unsold in Canada from last year that helped influence the lower rate. He said the "un-exported carry-over volume in Canada was twice the average of the past three years."

A wholesaler interviewed by Undercurrent on Tuesday said that much of that 2022 inventory has now been burned through, however. The source, who normally contends that UB's snow crab prices are conservative and sometimes inflated, said this time that its average rates seemed low compared to what he was seeing.

UB's average price range for 5-8 oz. frozen clusters from the gulf was $4.85-5.10/lb on Tuesday, the same as a week earlier. 

"Gulf quotations with new season pricing for 2023 remain unchanged and are steady at
listed levels," UB said in its analysis, adding: "Newfoundland quotations, which is 2022 production, adjusted lower on 10-ups while the balance of the market held unchanged. A few still lower offers are noted on 2022 production out of Newfoundland. Fishing in Newfoundland has not started yet for 2023. The undertone throughout the snow crab complex continues to be somewhat unsettled."

Processors now buying shrimp and lobster 

Loder provided more of an update on the ongoing fight between harvesters and processors in an interview with Undercurrent on Tuesday.

He said processors are now receiving some coldwater shrimp landings from NL harvesters at the rates earlier chosen by the price-setting panel: CAD 1.00/lb (landed at the plant) to CAD 1.05/lb (trucked to the north) or CAD 1.08/lb (trucked from elsewhere on the province).

Undercurrent reported earlier how processors had agreed to end their holdout and buy lobsters from NL harvesters at the rates established by the price-setting panel, which are based on UB prices. All but one of NL's roughly 20 processors handling lobster had refused to buy when the province's lobster fishing areas (LFAs 1-14c) began opening on April 17, according to FFAW, which had accused the processors of collusion. 

That leaves snow crab as the one remaining species for which the two sides are apart.

Loder noted in his presentation to the media that there are 22 snow crab processing facilities in NL that each employ between 150 and 650 seasonal workers from over 400 communities.

Lobster traps stacked up in Petty Harbor, Newfoundland and Labrador. Photograph by Jason Huffman.

"The economic impact of the delay in the snow crab fishery is significant," he said. "Not only does it affect plant workers, but also graders, equipment, packaging, and delivery companies, as well as local convenience stores, grocers, and restaurants. The fishery is a catalyst for economic growth in which rural communities rely on. It's the foundation of our culture and plays a significant role in tourism and often is what attracts people to our province, a place like no other."

He added: "It's time to get the fishery started. There are too many livelihoods that depend on it." 

Because the NL snow crab fishery season ends on June 30, Undercurrent asked Loder if there was a point where it no longer made sense to fish. 

"A fishery that starts in the middle of June is not going to work," he answered. "There will not be enough time to catch the crab. So, it's not a question of what ASP thinks or anybody else thinks. It's a pure factor, the reality of our fishery. You can't catch 25m lbs a week, or whatever, because that introduces all kinds of other issues."

Newfoundland and Labrador. Map from Victor Maschek / Shutterstock.

Loder also stressed again that ASP is against opening up a new season in the fall to compensate for the loss of landings during the summer. He said the quality of snow crabs in NL won't be as good during the later part of the year, as the crab shells are softer and their meat brinier.

When asked if he saw any hope of the two sides reaching a resolution, Loder answered: "It has to get resolved, given the economic impact for Newfoundland, but the answer is not through producers paying more. It's time to start fishing. There are many economic implications outside of the realities for harvesters or producers. There are rural communities, and all the businesses in those communities are being impacted. And every day that goes by is potentially lost value because the season is only so long and as the year goes along, there are more and more quality issues."

title: Insecurity, heavy rains still Ecuador shrimp sector’s main concerns with prices on rise
content:
BARCELONA, Spain -- The Ecuadorian shrimp sector is very concerned about the prevailing insecurity in some regions of the country and extreme rains hitting the country since March, also expected to continue in the coming days.

During Seafood Expo Global (SEG), several shrimp processors spoke to Undercurrent News on their views on the sector, with these issues becoming a center of conversation amongst them as production, transportation and security costs have grown "exponentially." 

"Insecurity, let there be no doubt, is affecting us, not only as a sector but as a country too, very deeply," an executive from Winrep, a Guayaquil-based seafood firm primarily involved in the export of frozen shrimp, told Undercurrent. "We now have to add this to our list of increasing costs, which is already quite long."

Another executive from Langosmar, an organic no-feed shrimp producer based in the Gulf of Guayaquil, also claimed this situation is "spiraling out of control" and that the government should take more effective measures to tackle it.

Moreover, due to this critical situation, many small and medium shrimp farmers are seeing their businesses "come to grief," with many forced to shut down. 

"We don't know if we and our businesses will still exist tomorrow. Seeing how fellow farmers are forced to close down and look for different jobs is deplorable," a small shrimp producer, who spoke on condition of anonymity, explained to Undercurrent. 

"Some do it because they can't go into debt anymore and decide to sell their farms to neighboring facilities or bigger shrimp farmers. Others, however, don't want to end up dead in a ditch somewhere or endanger their families," he pointed out. 

A second small shrimp farmer also told Undercurrent that many businesses, not only those related to the shrimp farmer sector, have started to close down on Guayaquil and its surroundings due to what they have called 'la vacuna' [the vaccine, in English], a new method for theft and extortion. 

"Thieves extort money from businesses, threatening their owners and staff or killing them and their families. It is crazy," he said. "Last week, the military forces started patrolling the streets and the shopping centers. There is news every day of murders and kidnappings. For its part, the government seems to be more focused on existing rather than governing."

Compared to the same period last year, thefts in farms have increased by 35%, with shrimp and balanced feed theft rising to 35% and 25%, respectively, and the number of injuries doubling, according to Jose Antonio Camposano, head of Ecuador's national chamber of aquaculture.

"We have never lived in such defenselessness, with the government doing nothing. There are no efficient plans to deal with the high levels of violence sweeping the country now. There are people continuously assaulting others on their way to work or home," Camposano said. 

"The government must guarantee a peaceful environment to do our job. If the State provides no security, there is nothing we can do. Ecuador is currently being taken over by organized crime," he added. 

Heavy rains also affect ex-farm prices

Additionally, heavy rainfall and landslides caused by Cyclone Yaku also affected crops, triggering further issues for the industry and grow-out shrimp ponds and pushing Ecuadorian vannamei shrimp prices further up.

"This is another significant issue, more serious even than that of insecurity in the country, although the latter is very worrying," a spokesperson from shrimp exporting firm Total Seafood also told Undercurrent during the SEG trade show. "All this amounted to a significant increase in our costs, with subsequent reduction in our profit margin," she said. 

According to the chart below, available on the Undercurrent price portal, average prices for HOSO Ecuadorian shrimp stood at $4.60 per kilogram for 20/30 count shrimp; $4.35/kg for 30/40; $4/kg for 40/50; $3.50/kg for 50/60; $3.10/kg for 60/70; and $2.70/kg for 70/80; $2.10/kg for 80/100; $1.80/kg for 100/120; and $1.60/kg for 120/140 counts in week 17 (April 24-30). 

Yet, this means an increase in the range of $0.05/kg and $0.30/kg across most large and medium sizes compared to the week before. 

"Irregular harvests, delays, collapsed buildings and roads cut off by flooding and landslides are a significant problem. In the first place, there is little to no product in some farms, but even if there were some, it has become tough, nearly impossible, to transport shrimp to processing plants "n schedule," the second shrimp farmer concluded.

title: Newfoundland harvesters ask processors not to buy snow crab from outside province
content:
The Fish Food and Allied Workers (FFAW), the union that represents Newfoundland and Labrador's inshore harvesters, is asking for a commitment from local processors to refrain from buying snow crab produced outside of the Canadian province.

The two sides are reportedly more than a dollar apart amid their negotiations over the minimum dock price to be paid at the start of the season in the country's largest snow crab fishery. And sources have suggested that harvesters are prepared to not fish for weeks if the price picked by the Standing Fish Price Setting Panel is too low.

"We're hearing concerns from our members in both harvesting and processing about what could happen if companies start bringing snow crab in from other provinces before the details in our own fishery are sorted," said FFAW president Greg Pretty in a statement. "In the interest of good faith bargaining, of not making a mockery out of the negotiations process, and of preventing additional conflicts within our communities, we're asking companies to refrain from bringing in any outside crab until it's clear our own fishery can be fully executed in an orderly manner."

Greg Pretty. Picture courtesy of Fish Food and Allied Workers.

On March 30, Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans announced a total allowable catch of 54,717 metric tons for the NL snow crab fishery for the 2023 season, a 4,247t or 8.4% increase over the 2022 season. DFO also announced a start date of April 10 in some zones.

The quota increase is expected to further impact the already-low prices paid at wholesale, having "serious economic impacts on inshore enterprise owners and crew members," Pretty said. "Prices that are undoubtedly impacted as a result of adverse markets, skyrocketing inflation and the resulting consequences on luxury seafood markets."

FFAW and ASP seemed to be interested in working out their differences when they called a joint press conference on Feb. 16 to announce they would begin negotiating an agreement before the panel process. But on March 28, both groups declared that their efforts had failed and they were withdrawing from the talks, as reported by Undercurrent.

FFAW then submitted a final offer of CAD 3.53 ($2.62) per pound to the panel on Thursday (March 30), while the Association of Seafood Producers (ASP), the trade association that represents processors, submitted a final offer of CAD 2.15 ($1.60)/lb.

A decision is expected from the panel as soon as Wednesday (April 5). 

"Fishing industry workers have serious concerns they could be in physical danger going to work if companies start bringing crab in from other provinces without ensuring a smooth and peaceful fishery in our own province," Pretty said. "Non-union sanctioned threats of violence have already been a concern this year, and this cannot be tolerated or endorsed in any manner. Bringing crab into the province will throw fuel onto an already volatile situation."

Pretty continued: "We're in a very precarious situation right now with many small business owners in jeopardy of going bankrupt, not to mention the thousands of crew member families they support through the snow crab fishery," Pretty said Tuesday. "Folks are in an extremely tough situation, and we need a commitment from companies to do everything in their power to prevent additional civil discord."

title: Editor’s choice: India shrimp exporters go all in on value-added; Pescanova sale heats up
content:
Neil Ramsden, EMEA editor of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

Our most-read exclusive last week was the news from the India International Seafood Show in Kolkata -- attended by Dan Gibson -- that for all that India's vannamei trade with the US dropped off last year, there was one sparkling success story apparent at the show: the output of value-added seafood products from India is booming.

Second was the news that ABANCA Corporacion Bancaria has held meetings with US-based Red Chamber and Canada's Cooke to propose a flexible financing structure that allows them to plan a complete takeover of Grupo Nueva Pescanova. 

On March 24, Undercurrent then reported that US-based Platinum Equity, the majority owner of Spain's Grupo Iberica Congelados (Iberconsa), was being tipped as a third bidder for Nueva Pescanova.

An earthquake shook southern Ecuador and northern Peru on March 18, causing more than $10 million in estimated damages to the shrimp sector.

Readers also enjoyed recapping Undercurrent's coverage of the Boston seafood show, at which there was quite a flurry of merger and acquisition activity; no less than six major deals were announced during, just before or after the three-day event.

Fish Food and Allied Workers, the union that represents inshore harvesters in the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador, let it be known last week that it stands behind an effort by fishermen in the zone known as 3L to restore their allocation of snow crab quota; but it also warned against harvesters threatening union officials.

Meawhile, groundfish harvester Blue Harvester Fisheries is closing its wetfish processing operation in New Bedford, Massachusetts, at least temporarily, to focus instead on updating its fleet.

In further news from the Boston show, Undercurrent reported lobster tail prices were still rising as a supply shortage continues. "We're talking about putting them under lock and key," joked John Norton, founder and CEO of Portland, Maine-based processor Cozy Harbor Seafood, of his firm's frozen tail display.

It's no secret that the past few years have seen a resurgence in black tiger shrimp farming in India, and it was clear to see at last month's 2023 India International Seafood Show that interest in the species has grown exponentially since the previous show in 2020.

Skipjack tuna prices for delivery in March to Bangkok, Thailand, have sharply increased over the last two weeks, jumping above their equivalents in Manta, Ecuador.

And Iceland is seeing the first steps taken towards an offshore salmon farming industry, with the news that a financial consultancy has invested in Norway's Aqualoop with plans to bring the technology to the island nation.

title: Newfoundland union supports snow crab quota protest but admonishes harvesters for threats of violence
content:
Fish Food and Allied Workers (FFAW), the union that represents inshore harvesters in the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador (NL), let it be known on Wednesday (March 22) that it stands behind an effort by fishermen in the zone known as 3L to restore their allocation of snow crab quota.

But it also warned against harvesters threatening union officials.

"Since this protest began on Monday [March 20], there have been threats of violent intimidation, personal harm, and property damage made against volunteer, elected members of the FFAW’s inshore council," said newly elected FFAW president Greg Pretty and secretary-treasurer Jason Spingle in a statement. "These actions cannot be tolerated by any fish harvester in our province. 

As reported by Undercurrent News, about 100 3L harvesters descended Monday on a Sheraton hotel in St. John's where officials are meeting to set prices for the new season, which typically starts in early April. Their fishing zone, which ranges from Conception Bay to St. Mary's Bay as far as Bonavista Bay, has had its total allowable catch reduced recently as a result of the way Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) has applied its new precautionary approach, maintaining separate inshore and offshore quotas.

Snow crab traps on a pier in St. John's, Newfoundland & Labrador, Canada. Photograph by Jason Huffman.

The change means inshore harvesters are fishing crab at the upper limit of their biomass, while offshore harvesters are only taking about 25% of their biomass, according to Bay Bulls fisherman Jason Sullivan, one of the leaders of the protest.

DFO reportedly defended its approach in a statement to CBC, saying it was developed through peer-reviewed science and provides a level of stability and predictability for setting quotas.

The 3L harvesters also have spoken critically of FFAW for not previously getting involved in the dispute, and there may be some bad blood between the groups. Sullivan ran for the FFAW presidency in January but was disqualified due to his prior participation in a rival group, as reported by Undercurrent. A formal grievance challenging the election process is pending in advance of a lawsuit.

The union's leaders have risen to address the challenge. 

"The FFAW’s Snow Crab Negotiating Committee is expressing their full support and solidarity with the 3L inshore fleet," Pretty and Spingle said in FFAW's statement.

The two men said they have raised the issue with Canadian labor minister Seamus O’Regan and senior DFO managers, as well as emphasized the need for support from the provincial government, but are still awaiting a response.

"The federal officials have requested time to assess the situation, but our union has made sure they understand the urgency of this issue," Pretty and Spingle said. 

"With shared challenges, we can work together and find solutions to the problems facing our industry," they continued in their appeal to the disgruntled harvesters. "Such misdirected actions only serve to disrupt the industry as a whole, sustaining negative stereotypes and public misgivings about professional fish harvesters and the inshore fishery in our province." 

A larger fight is expected soon between snow crab harvesters and processors over dock prices. Both groups were reported to be dollars apart in advance of the negotiations that started earlier this week with the NL fish price-setting panel required to pick one of the two proposals soon. Sources have warned that harvesters could refuse to fish and processors could refuse to buy if the price selected is not conducive to their side. 

Neither side has yet to reveal its price proposal or negotiating stance.

Processors asked Canadian fisheries minister Joyce Murray, during the Boston seafood show, to not increase quota in any of the snow crab fisheries, as Undercurrent earlier reported.

title: Seychelles, Somalia object to IOTC dFAD ban resolution
content:
Seychelles and Somalia are the two latest members of the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC) to object to, and opt out of, its new measures on fishing with drifting fish aggregating devices (dFADs).

On March 17, Seychelles submitted its official objection to the 72-day dFAD ban, which was recently approved at a special session of the IOTC.

Europeche again claims ‘bias’ behind IOTC’s dFAD ban

The fishing nation has "grave concerns" about how rapidly the resolution was adopted, including measures that will have "dire consequences on the social welfare and economic stability of our country", it said.

It claimed the resolution has no scientific basis or recommendation.

"Furthermore, the resolution was adopted without taking into account the cooperative and collaborative approach of the [IOTC] as provided for in the agreement and other international law," it wrote.

According to Seychelles, the resolution would disproportionately harm and burden its economy, which heavily relies on tuna exports.

The country also said it was "clear" that the intent of the proponents of this resolution was not to "engage in a cooperative spirit of discussion" but to "destabilize and sabotage the purse seine fishing industry, which Seychelles is part of and is heavily dependent upon".

It called on the IOTC to "collaboratively work towards achieving this important function of the commission [supporting the interests of developing coastal states], which has been given minimal importance" at the next meeting.

Last week, on March 13, Somalia objected to the resolution without explaining its rationale.

Kenya, Oman and Comoros have submitted official objections to the 72-day ban on dFADs that was recently approved at a special session of the IOTC. Therefore, they won't be bound by the measure either.

If objections to an adopted measure are made by more than one-third of the commission's members, the other members will also not be bound by that measure.

Seychelles' objection was the fifth to be submitted. 

The European fishing industry and Mauritius have criticized the ban but have not yet officially objected.

Meanwhile, on March 6, French NGO Bloom said it had sued the French state over alleged infringement procedures involving the operations of its industrial tuna fleet in the Indian Ocean.

"While the world is praising the laborious completion of the UN treaty on the high seas, a concrete and urgent EU-Africa example shows that all the treaties in the world will not put an end to the violence of the unsustainable and inequitable exploitation of the resources of the South by industrialized countries," it said in a press release sent to Undercurrent News.

"Today, Bloom has no choice but to sue the French state in two separate proceedings, one before the French Council of State, the other before the Administrative Court, for its destructive and irresponsible attitude in the Indian Ocean. Conflict of interest, illegal derogations, lack of fleet control, withholding of environmental data, etc. France holds an impressive record of complicity in tropical tuna fisheries, which are operated by 23 French industrial vessels in African waters and especially in the Indian Ocean," it said.

title: At least 25 fishermen killed by extremists in northeast Nigeria
content:
Islamic extremist rebels of Boko Haram have killed at least 25 fishermen during an attack in northeastern Nigeria's Borno state, reports The Washington Post.

Insurgents attacked the fishermen in the remote Mukdolo village of Borno, where the years-long extremist violence is concentrated, said local police chief Abdu Umar.

The village is close to the Sambisa forest, a Boko Haram stronghold, which has been fought over by Islamic State West Africa Province, also active in the area. 

"There is no human being in that place because it has been abandoned, but the villagers from Dikwa go there to fish. Unfortunately, Boko Haram surrounded the place this time and killed 25 of them. Nine escaped," Umar said.

Locals, however, reported more than 30 killed in the attack.

"The Boko Haram people said they now own the river, and no villager would be allowed to fish there except their members," Abba Modu with the local security outfit in Borno added.

title: Aquaculture advocate says death threats, cyber harassment, won’t muzzle him
content:
NEW ORLEANS, Lousiana, US -- An independent licensed and accredited veterinarian working in aquaculture has faced intimidating behavior on Twitter due to his advocacy for the industry, but he is resolute in defending the sector and spreading the word about its benefits.

Dr. Hugh Mitchell, a fish veterinarian with 34 years of experience in wild and farmed fish medicine in the US and Canada, joined Twitter four years ago to connect with like-minded people and share his knowledge about aquaculture, science, fish diseases, and ocean conservation. Despite his relatively modest Twitter following of 700, Mitchell's enthusiastic advocacy for aquaculture has led to him being targeted by anti-aquaculture activists, who have subjected him to intimidating behavior, he said.

Credit: Drew Mitchell, BFA

Mitchell told Undercurrent News on the sidelines of the recent Aquaculture America 2023 conference that he believes that the anti-aquaculture movement is ideologically based and not scientifically based. He said that some researchers within the movement practice "normative science", which is information developed with a preference for a particular policy or outcome. 

Mitchell asserts that aquaculture is a way to conserve ocean resources rather than being a threat to them, as well as help our massive seafood deficit and ensure seafood security. Anti-aquaculture activists often use fear to garner support, playing up the risks and dangers associated with aquaculture to ridiculousness, he said.

He believes that scientists are responsible for interacting with the public and explaining complex scientific concepts in a way that's understandable to the lay public. He admits that this is tough for most scientists, and some have institutional restrictions against doing so. As a veterinarian, however, he said it is his role to distill complex scientific concepts to his clients. For example, he uses Twitter to share pro-aquaculture information and combat misinformation about fish-food production, which activists often malign as "factory farming".

However, Mitchell has faced backlash for his advocacy work, including death threats and cyber harassment, he said. In addition, some anti-aquaculture activists have used a technique called "Gish gallop" to spew falsehoods and misrepresentations about aquaculture, making it difficult for anyone to engage in productive conversation, he said.

Despite the harassment, Mitchell remains steadfast in defending aquaculture. He said it is a viable solution to conserving ocean resources. Death threats and cyber harassment would not silence him, he said.

"There are threats of physical violence against me. Someone on Twitter has invited me to a fistfight. I think threats like these are helping us because it's showing how unreasonable and ideologically stuck these people are," Mitchell said.

"I am not afraid for myself because I've sold my practice. I can retire now if I want to. I have no obligatory financial ties to aquaculture that I'm accountable to, but it's been my life's work, and I know my clients are the ones who are affected," he said. 

Mitchell acknowledges the challenges associated with aquaculture but believes that the industry can overcome these challenges through responsible practices and informed decision-making.

"This is how society works. You work together to overcome challenges. Watchdogs are extremely important – but everyone must act in good faith," he said. 

He challenges anti-aquaculture activists to consider whether their opposition to aquaculture is purely ideological or based on a realistic assessment of the potential risks and benefits.

"I help my clients grow food efficiently and keep the animals humane and healthy using methods and, if necessary, medicines that are human-food safe and environmentally approved. That's what I do as a food animal veterinarian," he said.

He steadfastly believes that aquaculture will play a big role in humanity's future.

"As with the shift from hunting to farming for meat, we must adopt new methods. The agricultural revolution transformed society, granting us the luxury of free time to indulge in artistic pursuits, invent spaceships, and even journey to the moon. Aquaculture presents us with a similar opportunity. We must learn to cultivate the seas," he said.

title: Masked protesters destroy trout farm in southern Peru
content:
Masked protestors attacked and destroyed all the facilities of a trout farm belonging to Piscifactorías de Los Andes in the southern Peruvian city of Puno.

The fishing and aquaculture committee of Peru's industry association National Society of Industries (SNI) condemned the "terroristic attack". It said the company, which exports trout to the US, has existed for 44 years and is a pioneer in aquaculture in Peru.

The president of the SNI's fishing and aquaculture committee, Alfonso Miranda Eyzaguirre, urged the government to guarantee the sector's security and stability.

He said that such attacks "scare away investments in this area", despite the recent approval of the aquaculture promotion law.

Miranda warned that what happened was a serious threat to the entire productive sector of Peru.

Over the last two months, Peru has seen a historic wave of protests and escalation of violence. Unrest erupted after president Pedro Castillo was removed from power and vice president, Dina Boluarte, took power.

Demonstrations nationwide have called for her resignation, but Boluarte has responded with hostile rhetoric and a heavy-handed crackdown. So far, at least 60 people have been killed in the upheaval, according to media reports.
