title: War between First Nation, other lobster harvesters still simmers in Canada
content:
The dispute between First Nation lobster harvesters and federal conservation officers in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia has cost the former 7,000 lobster traps in two years, including 2,000 this year, a sign that the battle is far from over, The Canadian Press reports. 

The Indigenous harvesters, who sparked the controversy by fishing out of season in a vain attempt to assert a treaty right, see little progress occurring despite efforts by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) Canada, said Hubert Nicholas, fisheries director with the Membertou First Nation in Cape Breton.

"Gear is still being cut by non-natives, and DFO is still seizing traps," Nicholas said. "The non-natives allowed us to fish for a few days (in 2020) … But every time somebody put a trap in the water, they were cut … We heard about someone pointing a gun at somebody here just a couple of months ago."

As Undercurrent News has reported, the incident that reportedly sparked the controversy in Lobster Fishing Area 34 occurred in September 2020. That's when the Sipekne'katik First Nation announced the Canadian Supreme Court-affirmed opening of an off-season lobster fishery using a lobster pound in Middle West Pubnico. Some non-indigenous commercial harvesters said the fishery was illegal. 

Less than a month later, on Oct. 13, 2020, a large crowd of commercial harvesters allegedly descended on a pound on St. Mary's Bay to harass a harvester. Three days later, the pound was further burned to the ground, leading four Canadian cabinet ministers to condemn the attack.

The Department of Fisheries and Oceans has stepped up patrols in the region to ensure safety and compliance with the rules, said Tim Kerr, DFO's director of conservation and protection in the Maritimes.

title: Threat of robberies, murders, cartels costs Ecuador shrimp sector as much as $500m annually
content:
GUAYAQUIL, Ecuador -- When major aquafeed maker Skretting was hit by a spate of robberies at Piedra de Punta in Ecuador, general manager Carlos Miranda knew he had to act. The armed robbers regularly forcibly emptied its shrimp feed barge loaded with over 100 metric tons of feed, and the country's navy seemed helpless.

"Our barges were getting hit at Piedra de Punta almost every week," Miranda, whose company is the largest aquafeed company in Latin America, generating $1 billion in annual shrimp feed sales in the region, told Undercurrent News.

The company hired three boats with armed guards, which now escort Skretting's barges as they travel from farm to farm, for $70,000 a month. This comes on top of $40,000 a month for security at its aquafeed factories, he said.

"The robberies have fallen dramatically," he said.

The perimeter fence of a shrimp farm near Guayaquil, Ecuador. Credit: Louis Harkell / Undercurrent News.

The hidden drama is one of the less talked about aspects of Ecuador's shrimp sector, an industry forecast to generate $7bn in exports in 2022, some 40% above 2021's levels. Behind the scenes, it is wrestling with one of the worst security crises in its history.

"All the security issues in our country have become worse in the last few years, and it's probably going to get worse still," Fernando Luis, general manager of Totem, Ecuador's largest provider of remote security monitoring services, told Undercurrent. "It's an issue not only for the shrimp industry; it's an issue in every industry in Ecuador."

According to Luis' estimates, between 7-15% of production from Ecuador's shrimp industry is lost to theft annually. The extraordinary sum -- which includes shrimp and shrimp feed -- amounts to "over $500 million in losses" each year, he said.

A shrimp farm near Guayaquil, Ecuador. Credit: Louis Harkell / Shutterstock

"There's a clandestine market operating in parallel with the official one. Whole communities rely on stolen shrimp and feed they sell on the black market. Sometimes it's just 100 or 400 pounds of shrimp; other times, it's the entire pond. If you buy shrimp from a local seafood market in Guayaquil, chances are it's stolen," he said. Rumor has it one exporter sources stolen shrimp, he adds.

"It's impossible to trace, so how could you know for sure if it's stolen shrimp or not?" he said.

A shrimp farm near Guayaquil, Ecuador. Credit: Louis Harkell / Shutterstock

Others cite much lower figures. Ecuador's Camara Nacional de Aquacultura (CNA), estimates losses from theft of $80m a year. However, Jose Camposano, head of CNA, told Undercurrent that robberies occur weekly and the situation is "very challenging".

Behind the deteriorating security issue are Mexican drug cartels, a depressingly familiar problem in Latin America, as well as increased poverty since the pandemic. According to local media, cartels back local gangs vying for territory, funneling cocaine through Guayaquil's container port and laundering the profits through Ecuador's economy, which uses the US dollar.

Last year, 2,400 murders were recorded nationally, the majority in Guayaquil, according to official statistics, almost double the previous year. The resulting rise in crime, flood of guns, and robberies targeting shrimp companies, many of which are headquartered in Guayaquil and whose farms line the nearby Guayas River estuary, have unsettled the business community.

A security guard patrols a shrimp farm near Guayaquil on a motorcycle. Credit: Louis Harkell / Undercurrent News

"The incursion of heavily armed groups in Ecuador has affected the industry for decades," Camposano told Undercurrent.

"But the situation is getting worse due to inadequate laws used by criminals to be left free after they're caught," he said. 

"Additionally, violence rates are increasing in Ecuador due to the lack of resources for police, navy and other public agents," he said.

"In the last 14 years, Ecuador has been penetrated by the most important Mexican cartels," added Miranda. "And why would the Mexican cartels want to come to Ecuador? Very simple. Because Ecuador is a huge container export country. We export hundreds of thousands of containers worldwide," he said.

Smaller farm, bigger challenge

Luis said smaller farms with inadequate security face the biggest dangers, although larger farms and feed companies are also targeted.

Small, unelectrified farms are hit at night where pond security is lax. Several months ago, on Puna Island, south of Guayaquil, armed robbers took 20 farm workers hostage. The workers were forced to harvest an entire pond of shrimp, which the gang then spirited away in a truck, said Luis.

"They [robbers] use speed boats, canoes, trucks, they use everything," he said. "And when they steal the shrimp, they sell it in probably two hours and get paid in cash. It's really easy to get away with."

Marco, a guard at Omarsa's shrimp farm near Guayaquil. Credit: Louis Harkell / Undercurrent News

Bigger farms with better security, like Omarsa Group's huge 1,000-hectare farm outside Guayaquil, which Undercurrent visited, are less at risk. Marco, a 30-year-old security guard at the farm, told Undercurrent that Omarsa's farm has had no incursions for five years, bar a foiled robbery attempt about two years ago, according to his knowledge.

Some 30 armed security guards patrol Omarsa's farm on shifts, 24 hours a day, with approximately one guard for every ten farm workers. At the farm's perimeter, guards ride motorcycles and communicate with walkie-talkies.

A 20-meter tower with an infrared camera scans the farm, offering 360-degree vision.

Marco is still wary of canoes passing by the farm along tributaries of the Guayas River, which are lined by dense mangrove forests. "Sometimes they look suspicious. But you don't look too closely -- it's dangerous," he said. Marco understands it to be more dangerous in areas further north. 

Camposano said the shrimp industry is shouldering the cost of security, spending around $80m a year.

A security tower at a shrimp farm near Guayaquil, Ecuador. Credit: Louis Harkell / Undercurrent News

"[The government] has done very little. Police do not have the necessary resources to do their job. It is the same with the navy. The CNA has strongly requested for more resources -- more personnel, vehicles and weaponry -- but the response from the government has been disappointing."

Skretting's Miranda agrees Ecuador's shrimp industry has to deal with the situation largely itself. "What the shrimp industry has done in the last five to 10 years, especially the "technified" farmers, the big farmers that have implemented technology, is they have invested huge amounts of money in security," he said.

"But the small-sized or medium-sized farmer, those that don't have enough guards, the night vision cameras, the electric fences, and cannot afford a security company to take care of the farms, they get robbed brutally," said the Skretting LatAm boss.

Miranda said Skretting also still suffers occasional robberies. "I'm spending more than $100,000 a month that I shouldn't have to spend. That's almost $1.3m a year to be able to provide security for the product that I'm sending to the shrimp farms," he said. "We still get hit maybe three or four times a year."

Security tech upgrade

This summer, after a spate of murders and car bombs, the Ecuadorian government announced a fourth state of emergency in Guayaquil. At the recent AquaExpo held in the city, conference venues were guarded by armed security and police.

On Nov. 1, just over a week after AquaExpo, Guayaquil was placed under another state of emergency and a 9pm curfew, along with regions Guayas and Esmereldas. A contact in the city confirmed to Undercurrent he was unable to leave his home after 9 p.m. 

Luis said he is unsure how things will develop but that new security technology is helping businesses secure their property and employees.

A barge docks at a jetty at a shrimp farm near Guayaquil, Ecuador. Credit: Louis Harkell / Undercurrent News

Since last year, Totem uses computer vision software that automatically categorizes movement picked up by video cameras, developed in collaboration with UK software company Intelex Vision. The software means fewer staff are required to watch monitors and identify threats.

His firm charges $1,500 per month, per camera. Each camera covers 300-450 hectares of a shrimp farm, as long as no mangrove trees are in the way. "The cost is less than a security guard, and it can cover much more area; we can see 1.2 kilometers in a straight line," he said. The company remotely monitors 70,000ha of shrimp farms in Ecuador in total -- almost a third of the country's farming area -- 24 hours a day, 365 days a year.

Shrimp tech firms flock to Guayaquil, keen on a slice of the Ecuador pie

The company also monitors shrimp farms in Honduras, Nicaragua, Peru and Panama -- countries with their own security challenges -- as well as Ecuadorian firms involved in bananas, mining and construction. 

Miranda said it was important not to be daunted. Last month, the company opened a $6m shrimp research and development center in Guayaquil.

"We've been dealing with organized crime for 40 years. The cartels have added drama to business, but every major player in the feed business is here in Ecuador today, and they have invested a lot of money. I do think it's still attractive [to invest in Ecuador]," he said.

Delphine Debennerot, export sales executive at Omarsa, who moved from her native France to Ecuador, told Undercurrent that it is important to put things in perspective.

"Guayaquil is a city of 2m people. Most people are getting on with their lives," she said. She continues to visit restaurants and bars in Guayaquil with friends in areas deemed safe, while on weekends, they visit each others' homes to spend time by the pool and have barbeques. 

For middle-class Ecuadorians, who live in gated communities, the violence in poorer neighborhoods can seem a world away, said Luis.

"The shrimp company owners don't live on the farms. They live in areas away from where the danger is," he said.

title: Spain’s Froxa sees new growth opportunities in LatAm, Africa, as Chinese demand stays low
content:
VIGO, Spain -- Spanish frozen processor Froxa is actively seeking new destination markets as well as new origins for its seafood products and new species to work with, the firm's co-owner and Asia-Pacific director, Jose Javier Fernandez, told Undercurrent News.

The firm, which has seen sales increase to pre-pandemic levels and expects to end 2022 with double-digit growth, has seen demand surge in Latin America and Africa this year.

"In all this uncertainty, we cannot stand still. We must continue looking for new ways to grow our business," he explained. "Spain is our main market, but we have seen many opportunities lately in Latin America, which has aroused great interest. We are already present in Mexico, Colombia, Chile, the Dominican Republic and Peru, and we aim to grow further towards selling in other countries there."

Spain’s Froxa expects 2022 turnover to hit €42m, further consolidation in markets

According to him, the Conxemar 2022 fair has meant a big opportunity to make new contacts "of great importance" for the company's future development plans in that part of the world.

Froxa has also found demand for seafood increasing in Africa, opening a new door for the firm to explore this market. "Africa will become a vital market for seafood in the future, and we want to get a head start there."

Via Ceuta and Melilla -- Spain's enclaves sitting on the northern shores of Morocco's Mediterranean coast and Europe's only landmasses in continental Africa -- the company's products are already present in north Africa, he shared.

"This market demands completely different products than the others, mainly seeking whole or gutted fish for smoking," Fernandez also explained to Undercurrent. "However, there are some African countries like South Africa or Namibia now demanding more high-quality, value-added seafood products. There has certainly been a growth in those who can be classified as 'middle class' in Africa over the last few decades, which is also driving change in consumption patterns there."

The firm also had plans to expand sales into Ukraine this year, but those were disrupted by the ongoing violence caused by Russia’s invasion of the country in late February. According to Fernandez, this specific plan may not be resumed for several years.

“We were already in negotiations with two different firms in the country to sell our products there, but everything has come to a halt. We have no idea when we will be able to carry out our plans in this market,” he previously told Undercurrent. However, he declined to comment on which firms those were.

Demand from China continues to be low after experiencing a slight recovery during the second half of the year.

"We are still seeing many customers that have decided not to buy due to an overall cost overrun at the purchasing process. Many importers prefer not to make any new purchases until the situation there has returned to normalcy," he pointed out. "Also, there are still many sanitary controls which together with the yuan hitting record lows against the US dollar makes it very difficult to export there without suffering clear economic losses."s

Spanish seafood companies announce new product launches, investments at Conxemar

He also mentioned that other Asian countries such as Vietnam, Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines have increased their purchasing power and are currently looking to import more goods. "We are discussing with potential clients there to carry out new projects in those countries."

All this, together with the firm hitting many monthly sales records this year and solid demand through foodservice -- which accounts for around 85% of its sales -- have made 2022 a good year for Froxa.

“We have seen strong demand this year even during periods when we usually see declines,” he said. "We expect to see growth in our revenue this year as well, although we are hesitant to give a specific figure given everything that is happening globally."

Back in May, however, Fernandez told Undercurrent that the company expected to reach over €42 million ($41.7m, now) in revenue this year.

"There is much more uncertainty in the market now than there was back then, which makes it more difficult to speak about new plans or financial stuff. We have chosen to remain cautious," he concluded.

title: Bumble Bee against NOAA plan to add forced labor definition to anti-IUU rules
content:
The global fight to end illegal, unreported or unregulated (IUU) fishing and the problem of the use of forced labor at sea are two often-connected issues but aren't quite the same. However, in the US at least, regulatory efforts to fight both problems could soon converge.

The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) is proposing to tweak existing anti-IUU rules to "harmonize" legal enforcement provisions relating to forced labor currently found in other legislation. The NOAA proposal also aims to: amend procedures under the Moratorium Protection Act that spell out how foreign importing nations are identified and certified as having anti-IUU legislation similar to that in the US; make "high seas" fishing permits renewable annually instead of every five years; and, increase the amount of information that foreign fishing boats landing their catches in US ports have to disclose. 

Some of the proposed changes are receiving opposition from the seafood sector, including from Bumble Bee Foods, the US' second-largest tuna canner, which has repeatedly faced scrutiny related to labor practices on the vessels that catch its fish.

"Our view is that the problems of forced labor and IUU fishing are different and require different solutions and approaches. To eliminate forced labor throughout the supply chain, measures must be taken by governments that apply to all its vessels regardless of where they fish," Bumble Bee wrote in a comment letter opposing the NOAA proposal.

While opposing anything that purports to fight forced labor isn't a good look, especially for a company that has been repeatedly publicly criticized by the advocacy group Greenpeace for its buying practices, the situation is much more nuanced. It comes down to contrasting approaches in how the administrations of two former US presidents sought to combat IUU and forced labor.

A new definition

During his tenure, former US president Barack Obama signed into law two bills that addressed IUU fishing: the IUU Fishing Enforcement Act of 2015 and the Ensuring Access to Pacific Fisheries Act of 2016. NOAA's proposed rule would amend the 2015 act and another law, the High Seas Driftnet Fishing Moratorium Protection Act, to explicitly include anti-forced labor provisions. Specifically, the new IUU definition would include seafood caught using vessels where "all work or service which is exacted from any person under the menace of any penalty for its nonperformance and for which the worker does not offer [themself] voluntarily", the rule states. That also includes the use of child labor.

Another law, passed in 2019 under the administration of former president Donald Trump, the Maritime Security and Fisheries Enforcement (SAFE) Act and preferred by Bumble Bee, relied on an earlier definition of IUU fishing.

"The SAFE Act did not require forced labor to be included in the definition of IUU fishing because we believe while the issues of IUU and forced labor are associated, they are not the same. Had Congress desired to include forced labor into the definition of IUU fishing, it would have stated so in the legislation," Bumble Bee wrote.

The company's two-page comment letter questioned the effectiveness of the NOAA proposal.

"Using the identification and certification process under the Moratorium Act to eliminate forced labor is clumsy, time-consuming, and limited to the high seas," the company wrote. "Moreover, it does not require industry participation and ignores the lessons we have learned from our efforts to end forced labor."

Bumble Bee, owned by Taiwan's FCF Co, has been repeatedly accused by Greenpeace of purchasing tuna from vessels that had enslaved migrants to catch its fish. Bumble Bee, which is carrying out a $40 million, five-year sustainability plan to safeguard fish stocks, ocean health and labor rights, wrote to NOAA, promoting alternatives to its proposed rule.

"Instead, we believe initiatives such as NOAA's CALM-CS, which is solely focused on forced labor throughout the entire global seafood supply chain, hold more promise in ending forced labor," its statement added. "Industry must be part of the solution, which is why the public-private partnerships envisioned by the CALM-CS focused exclusively on forced labor is [Bumbe Bee's] preferred alternative."

When contacted by Undercurrent News, a Bumble Bee spokesperson, Dan Barber, reiterated the points made in the letter, again making the pitch for CALM-CS.

"Globally, the industry-wide employment challenges are complex and must be addressed through collaboration and a shared commitment to action and improvement with NGOs and governments worldwide," Barber said in an email.

Shrimpers' support

Others, however, would be glad to see NOAA's changes. The Southern Shrimp Alliance, a US organization of Gulf of Mexico shrimp harvesters and processors, embraced the proposal.

"A regulatory approach that holds that the use of enslaved fishermen aboard a boat operating in international waters constitutes IUU fishing but ceases being IUU fishing once that vessel crosses into territorial waters lacks any reasonable or logical basis," SSA's letter states.

Gwen Lee Hassan also questioned Bumble Bee's approach. She is a Chicago-based attorney who, while not familiar with the proposed NOAA change, works extensively with human rights violations at her work as a self-employed chief compliance and risk officer and as part of a podcast she hosts, "Hidden Traffic with Gwen Hassan".

"It's like they're saying: 'If it can't be perfect, then we're not doing it'. It's like they're making the perfect the enemy of the good," she told Undercurrent. 

Greenpeace's concerns

Bumble Bee's letter comes after Greenpeace East Asia (GEA) made fresh allegations against the company in a report, titled "Fake My Catch -- the unreliable traceability in our tuna cans". The report alleged that more than 10%, or 13 of 119 Taiwanese-flagged vessels that had supplied Bumble Bee had violated Taiwanese fishery regulations and were on Taiwan's IUU list, as Undercurrent has written.

Bumble Bee responded by saying that the GEA report "contained several inaccuracies" but did not specify what they were. It conceded that Bumble Bee also believes "that more progress can be made in ensuring responsible labor practices are followed on tuna vessels."

GEA and Bumble Bee have tangled before. The crew of a Taiwanese fishing vessel that had supplied the company was indicted earlier this year by Taiwanese officials for allegedly enslaving more than 20 migrant workers in a criminal case first brought to light by Greenpeace in 2019.

A Greenpeace spokesman told Undercurrent that the international attention, and Taiwanese criminal investigation, were spurred by his organization's December 2019 report, "Seabound: The Journey to Modern Slavery on the High Seas" and a 2021 follow-up report, "Forced Labour at Sea: The Case of Indonesian Migrant Fishers." 

The 52-page 2019 document compiles the results of interviews with 34 Indonesian migrant fishers on 13 fishing vessels. The fishers said they were the victims of deception in recruiting practices and physical and sexual abuse while being kept at sea for six months straight without pay. 

Liz Conant, a spokesperson for Bumble Bee, declined to comment on the indictment at the time of the publication of a previous article. However, two days later, she sent Undercurrent an email in which she said that Bumble Bee was "not sourcing [tuna] from the vessel at the time of the report, nor have we sourced from them since."

Not entirely against the rule change

When contacted by Undercurrent, a NOAA spokeswoman called the rule's proposed changes "largely procedural in nature" but needed as forced labor and IUU fishing often occur "in conjunction".

"These practices may include charging workers recruitment fees, confiscating and withholding workers' passports or identity documents, threats or physical violence, and using fraudulent recruitment tactics such as contract switching," NOAA said.

Despite its opposition to the forced labor addition, Bumble Bee applauded NOAA's plan to expand the US definition of IUU fishing to include IUU activities that occur within a foreign country's exclusive economic zone and not just the high seas.

Bumble Bee "supports this new element as clearly fishing in a foreign nation’s waters without the permission of that nation is illegal and must be stopped. This change is directly targeted at reducing unauthorized foreign fishing which is a major contributor to global IUU fishing," the company said in its letter.

Bumble Bee is about two years and $14m into a five-year plan to spend $40m globally on improving fish stock sustainability, ocean health and labor rights, with some successes: 71% of the seafood volumes that Bumble Bee sources is now classed as sustainable by Global Sustainable Seafood Institute-compliant program, or is moving that way by 2025, as Undercurrent has written. 

That includes the bulk of the tuna canner's albacore stocks, processed by FCF but harvested by independent longliners. Last year, 250 FCF-affiliated Taiwanese albacore longliners entered the MSC assessment process, according to a report offered by the company. 

Bumble Bee not the rule's only critics

Other comments on NOAA's proposed rule change were generally supportive, but also criticized aspects of it.

The Center for Biological Diversity supported NOAA's attempt to curb human trafficking, but said that provisions of the change would contradict the Moratorium Protection Act, a federal law that, according to NOAA, requires NOAA "to produce a biennial Report to Congress that lists nations the United States has identified for IUU fishing, bycatch of protected species, or shark catches on the high seas or nations that do not have regulatory measures comparable to the United States." 

Valinor, a Louisiana-registered company, said that the proposed change lacked many specifics and was thus unenforceable.

"There is no mechanism identified in the proposal that asserts a base comparison of what would be expected 'non-forced labor' rates to make a determination of forced labor. There also is no mechanism provided in the proposal to effectively conduct an analysis whether small or large to make the determination that forced labor was used, nor did the study the NMFS [NOAA National Marine Fisheries Service] referenced include comparisons over a time period where it focused on US Fisheries to get a baseline of 'acceptable labor.' "

Earthjustice, a nonprofit NGO dedicated to litigating environmental issues, called the change "an important tool for combatting IUU fishing and increasing conservation of sharks and protected living marine resources." 

Christopher Lish, a San Raphael, California, resident said that the rule change attacking human trafficking was overdue and "does not go far enough.

"As a seafood consumer, I want to be assured that my seafood is safe, legally caught, responsibly sourced, and honestly labeled, without illegal activities and the use of forced labor," Lish wrote. "NOAA’s current IUU definition limits the agency’s ability to identify other nations for IUU fishing and subsequent trade restrictions. As unsustainable fishing practices make fish scarcer and vessels need to travel further, operators may try to maintain their profit margins through reducing their labor costs via forced labor."

Public comments on the proposed rule change can be found here. NOAA will consider the comments as part of issuing a final ruling. If issued, the rule change would have "a period of delayed effectiveness. The delay allows the public to take the necessary measures to come into compliance with the new regulation," a NOAA spokesperson, said.

title: Pescanova faces new demonstrations against octopus farming plans ahead of launch
content:
Grupo Nueva Pescanova's plans to open the first commercial octopus farm in 2023 has raised many doubts among conservationists and researchers, with Pacma, Spain's party for the animals, leading the latest demonstration against.

On Aug. 12, Pacma called for a new demonstration to "kill the project" that Nueva Pescanova intends to build in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, in the Canary Islands, reports eldiario.es. 

Moreover, the Spanish party had already presented new allegations to the Canary Islands regional government, also signed by a hundred ecological groups and environmental experts that are fully against its construction.

Pescanova back to M&A with deal for Argentina’s Pesquera Veraz

In a statement sent at that time, the signatory entities defended that the proposal, which develops one of the most sought-after patents in the aquaculture sector in recent decades, has "many loose ends", which could cause a serious impact on local ecosystems.

"The information provided by the company in order to obtain all necessary permits in relation to the farm's environmental impact seems incomplete," it stated.

Also, it questioned whether the farm is necessary or can really contribute to the objectives the firm indicated in the project report, such as reducing the fishing effort on these species in the wild.

"On the contrary, a review of the project immediately reveals the serious environmental problems that can arise from these farms, such as the spread of unknown pathogens and diseases that cultivated octopus could contribute to spreading to the wild marine ecosystem," it added. 

Pacma also claimed that feeding the octopuses would require "a carnivorous diet that is based on unsustainable fishing practices, creating greater pressure on already scarce marine resources", for which it understands that the project seems incompatible with both the guidelines for a more sustainable EU aquaculture and the European Green Deal.

Nueva Pescanova did not respond to a request for comment from Undercurrent News. 

On July 22, People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PEFA) -- an American animal rights nonprofit organization based in Norfolk, Virginia -- also published a statement under the headline 'Help stop the world's first octopus farm' to show its displeasure towards the initiative.

"While Nueva Pescanova has not publicly released a plan for how the octopuses will be kept, it is assumed that they will be forced into cramped living conditions, likely leading to cannibalism and other violence among the animals," PEFA claimed.

"The firm also shared that the octopus survival rates are “estimated to rise to 50%,” meaning that more than half of the octopuses that the company is currently breeding in its preliminary tests die prematurely," it said. 

Additionally, many other mainstream media outlets such as the BBC, Le Monde or The Independent, among many others, have echoed all these concerns regarding Nueva Pescanova's plan, which aims to produce some 3,000 metric tons of octopus annually in a 52,000-square-meter facility.

Seguimos luchando contra la apertura de la primera granja de pulpos del mundo en Las Palmas. Esta tarde, si estás en la ciudad, no faltes al acto de repulsa que convocamos a las 18h en el paseo de Las Canteras.

Es una aberración y no podemos permitirlo.https://t.co/Iflyt8Scym

— PACMA (@PartidoPACMA) August 12, 2022

title: Indonesia’s new rules aim to better protect migrant workers aboard foreign vessels
content:
Indonesia has issued much-anticipated new rules to protect migrant workers aboard foreign commercial fishing vessels, reports the news service Mongabay. 

The government says the regulation, which was ratified on June 8 by the administration of president Joko Widodo, will streamline the recruitment and placement process of Indonesian migrant deckhands, while better protecting their labor rights. 

The move follows a lawsuit filed May 31 by three former migrant deckhands that accused the government of failing to enshrine protections that could have prevented a long history of abusive and even deadly treatment of migrant deckhands. They've described conditions in which they experienced overwork, withholding of wages, debt bondage, and physical and sexual violence.

A key change includes having the Ministry of Manpower as the official authority to produce the permit for recruitment agencies to assign candidate migrant workers.
The new regulation also includes new standards based on a global convention on work in fishing by the United Nations’ International Labor Organization, known as ILO C-188.

The government decree is being handled as a derivative of the country’s 2017 law on migrant worker protection and is applicable to foreign commercial and fishing vessels, including distant-water boats.

It was expected to be passed in March but was held up due to the need for signatures.

title: UK fisheries alliance decries recent report on welfare abuses for migrant workers
content:
The Fishermen's Welfare Alliance (FWA) -- formed of four UK national representative organizations for fishermen -- has condemned the reports of abuse and exploitation published a week before by the UK's University Of Nottingham Rights Lab.

"It is a reality that migrant workers are a vital and likely permanent feature of parts of the UK fishing sector, much as they are in other industries and professions. We value the contributions these workers make to our industry and in turn, we want them to feel valued," said Elspeth Macdonald, CEO of the Scottish Fishermen's Federation, on behalf of the FWA in a second statement issued on this topic.

"The FWA, therefore, unreservedly condemns the reports of abuse and exploitation that were published last week. Such behavior is deplorable and utterly indefensible," she added.

However, she claimed it is wrong to assume that the issues raised in the report are endemic across the UK fishing fleet.

"They are not, and indeed the University of Nottingham report made clear that its findings were based on a small sample that was not chosen at random, so its findings cannot be generalized," she explained. "It is clear that these reports, while they represent a tiny and atypical minority, undermine the credibility of this ambition."

Macdonald added that the immigration system needs to work better and calls on the government to work collaboratively on addressing existing issues and identify and implement collective solutions.

"Finally, given the severity of the issues contained in these reports, we fully expect that the information has been shared with the police and other relevant authorities to take the appropriate action. We neither want nor will tolerate individuals who behave in the manner alleged in our industry," she concluded.

The Seafarers' Charity, which distributed the report's findings previously, did not respond when Undercurrent News asked if the police had been notified.

Research claimed:

35% of fishing crew in the study reported suffering regular physical violence
However, 65% stated they would never report a grievance out of fear of being blocklisted from future employment opportunities
19% of those included in the research would qualify as probable cases of forced labor when applying the International Labour Organization's guidelines in the Forced Labour Convention
100% of the non-EEA crew within the research study experienced immigration-related vulnerabilities caused by using a "transit visa", which places them at increased risk of labor exploitation. Transit visas are designed for seafarers traveling to reach their departing ship and are unsuitable for workers based within the UK as lacking many basic labor protections in respect of pay and working hours

The research report, "Letting Exploitation off the Hook? Evidencing Labour Abuses in UK Fishing", is available in full here.

title: Report finds welfare abuses for migrant workers in UK fisheries
content:
New research published by the UK's University Of Nottingham Rights Lab claims to have found evidence of poor treatment and lack of decent working conditions for some migrant workers on UK fishing vessels.

The research report "Letting Exploitation off the Hook? Evidencing Labour Abuses in UK Fishing" sought out views of the fishing crew and heard directly from them about what it is really like to work within the UK fishing industry, according to The Seafarers' Charity, which said it "stood ready to support migrant workers".

The report is available in full here.

Increasing difficulties in recruiting UK fishing crew means that many workers are recruited from countries outside the European Economic Area (EEA), such as the Philippines and Ghana, and "can experience very different working conditions and practices to their UK colleagues".  

Research claimed:

35% of fishing crew in the study reported suffering regular physical violence
However, 65% stated they would never report a grievance out of fear of being blocklisted from future employment opportunities
19% of those included in the research would qualify as probable cases of forced labor when applying the International Labour Organization's guidelines in the Forced Labour Convention
100% of the non-EEA crew within the research study experienced immigration-related vulnerabilities caused by using a "transit visa", which places them at increased risk of labor exploitation. Transit visas are designed for seafarers traveling to reach their departing ship and are unsuitable for workers based within the UK as lacking many basic labor protections in respect of pay and working hours

  
The Seafarers' Charity's CEO, Catherine Spencer, said the NGO had been "shocked and saddened at the working conditions and treatment of migrant fishing crew revealed in this new research".

"I am sure that many people, including owners of fishing businesses and other stakeholders, will share our concerns about the treatment of migrant workers in the UK fishing industry. We stand ready, as a grant funder, to play our role in supporting improvements in the working conditions and treatment of migrant workers in the UK fishing industry, and we call on others involved in UK fishing to act swiftly to stamp out the abhorrent treatment of migrant workers and prevent the risk of such poor practices ever becoming accepted in UK fishing."

Julie Carlton, head of seafarer safety and health at the Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA), said the organization would continue to support those working across the fishing sector, "making sure they are treated fairly and taking action when we know they are not".

"The MCA continues to work with vessel owners on the UK flag to make sure they meet the required international standards of ILO188 and, cooperate closely with other government agencies who enforce other aspects of living and working conditions for seafarers."

However, the  Fishermen's Welfare Alliance (FWA) -- formed of four UK national representative organizations for fishermen -- said that "at first reading [the report] contains much that fishing industry representatives do not recognize, and is not representative of the situation across the UK as the report itself states".

The study accepted that it did not use a random sample of fishers, wherein every fisher working on a UK-flagged vessel had an equal chance of being systematically selected to participate in the study to represent the entire population of fishers in the UK -- "the primary limitation of this approach".

"As a result, these findings are not generalizable across the industry," it noted. "However, though the industry conducts multiple surveys regularly, including Seafish's fleet survey, these approaches often exclude fishing crew from sharing their experiences as they focus on vessel owners. Thus, while the sample limited this study, it still presents one of the first attempts to assess working conditions independently across the UK through fishers' first-hand account of their experiences."

Elspeth Macdonald, chief executive of the Scottish Fishermen's Federation, speaking on behalf of the FWA, said:

"As industry representatives, we deplore and condemn the bad practice and crew members being badly or unfairly treated, regardless of their nationality or immigration status. Many of non-UK crews employed in the UK industry have been returning to work on the same vessels for many years and have contracts that take ILO188 and UK employment law into account. There is much that the industry is doing to continually improve working conditions, including agreeing recently to work with a major UK retailer to help prepare non-UK crews for working in the UK fishing industry. We will continue to drive forward to ensure that all our workers are respected and well cared for."

Transit visas exploited?

One claim to have arisen from this study -- and another briefing issued this week by the International Transport Workers' Federation (ITF) -- was that transit visa loopholes are being used to exploit migrant fishers on UK fishing vessels.

UK inquiry ‘struck by gov’t failure to grasp labor issues’

"We welcome the ITF's conclusion that the transit worker visa is not fit for purpose and does not meet the UK’s modern fishing industry requirements," said Macdonald. "Those parts of the industry that employ non-UK fishermen through the transit visa system have been lobbying the government for many years for improvements, and were successful in having fishermen recognized as skilled workers in the new immigration system, but other barriers mean this route cannot be used in the way that industry had hoped. We would welcome the opportunity to look at this in more detail with the government."

UK industry body Seafish said that while the welfare issues raised in the University of Nottingham report were not reflective of every fishing vessel in the UK, "the findings are concerning and highlight there is still work to do".

Then, "the ITF briefing paper makes sensible recommendations on how to improve the visa system and we know that these are issues the fishing industry has been proposing and working towards for many years," it went on.

"We disagree with the suggestion that the UK fishing industry has made use of the transit visa system to enable the exploitation of non-UK workers. The transit visa system was established to allow merchant seamen to travel to the UK for the purpose of boarding ships at UK ports. Until recently, it provided the only visa option for fishing businesses to bring in crew from overseas to work on commercial UK vessels fishing outside territorial waters. The UK fishing industry have been working hard to find a better system."

title: First Nation lobster fishery starts season without Canadian OK
content:
The first lobsters caught under the treaty fishery on Canada's Prince Edward Island came ashore on Lennox Island Monday (May 9) without incident -- but with some simmering tension, CBC News reports.

The Lennox Island First Nation (LINF) fishery is not authorized by the Canadian Department of Fisheries and Oceans after negotiations failed. So DFO calls this an "unauthorized" fishery, which means it could be subject to enforcement, including trap seizures or fines.

The LINF group says none of the 240 traps set have been seized or disturbed by fisheries officers. The group plans to set 1,000 in what they say represents the "moderate livelihood" to which they are entitled.

But with no understanding with DFO in place, it is raising tensions in the fishing community.

The crews on three licensed commercial boats said fishing without a license has the potential to damage lobster stocks, and if DFO does not take action, some commercial fishermen might choose to do so. This has already happened, disastrously, in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia (NS).

As Undercurrent News has reported, 25 people were accused of ransacking a Canadian lobster pound in October 2020 as part of their dispute involving an Indigenous self-regulated fishery on NS. 

The incident reportedly began amid tensions that had been brewing in Lobster Fishing Area 34 since September 2020, when the Sipekne'katik First Nation announced the Canadian Supreme Court-affirmed opening of an off-season lobster fishery using a lobster pound in Middle West Pubnico in NS. 

Some non-indigenous commercial harvesters who worked in the area said the Sipekne'katik fishery was illegal. Less than a month later, on Oct. 13, 2020, a large crowd of commercial harvesters allegedly descended on a pound, on St. Mary's Bay, to harass a harvester who was unloading his catch. Lobsters were reportedly strewn out on the pavement.

Then, three days later, the pound was further burned to the ground, leading four Canadian cabinet ministers to condemn the attack, as reported by Undercurrent. One man was reportedly hospitalized with life-threatening injuries and the lobsters still kept at the pound were all destroyed.

title: Spain’s Froxa expects 2022 turnover to hit €42m, further consolidation in markets
content:
BARCELONA, Spain -- After a promising 2021 marked by recovery from the pandemic, Spanish frozen processor Froxa expects to continue to grow year-on-year in 2022 and reach over €42 million ($44.1m) in revenue, the firm's co-owner and Asia-Pacific director, Jose Javier Fernandez, told Undercurrent News. 

"We have seen steady growth during 2021, after a 30% drop in the firm's 2020 turnover, and we expect this growth will continue further this year," he said during Seafood Expo Global. "While other companies have not been able to cover the market demand, we luckily have always had enough stock to supply our clients."

Additionally, the firm has already experienced a 45% y-o-y growth in the value of its sales during the first quarter of the year, which, according to Fernandez, has been led by the increase in the prices of all raw materials and the rising costs of logistics and energy.

Barcelona 2022: Recap all UCN’s coverage from SEG

"We expect volume billing to be higher than last year and closer to pre-pandemic levels seen in 2019, as we see strong demand for our products," he added. Froxa's sales amounted to around €43.8m in 2019, up 15% from $38m in 2018. 

"Moreover, the company expects to consolidate further in the markets where it is already present and drive on with our intentions to expand to new ones," he told Undercurrent. 

Froxa has plans to expand into Latin America, where it already has a presence in the Caribbean Islands, mainly in the Dominican Republic; Mexico; Asia, and Africa.

“We aim to grow further in Mexico and expand to Peru and Colombia in both foodservice and retail, as well as looking for new markets in Asia and Africa, where there is enough room and opportunity for our offer,” he also said.

Also, Froxa had plans to expand sales into Ukraine this year, but those have been disrupted by the ongoing violence caused by Russia’s invasion of the country in late February. According to Fernandez, this specific plan may not be resumed for several years.

“We were already in negotiations with two different firms in the country to sell our products there, but everything has come to a halt. We have no idea when we will be able to carry out our plans in this market,” he added.

However, he declined to comment on which firms those were.

Spain’s Froxa sees sales surge close to pre-pandemic levels

"Sales to China have come to a halt, with the country battling its biggest COVID wave yet and people enduring new lockdowns there," Fernandez also told Undercurrent. "Much uncertainty remains in this market."

However, he also mentioned that other Asian countries such as Vietnam, Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines have increased their purchasing power and are currently looking to import more goods. "We are discussing with potential clients there to carry out new projects in those countries."

In terms of launching new products, Froxa has plans it would like to fulfill in the next few years, but Fernandez thinks it still is not the best moment to carry on with them. 

"We always have new products in mind that we would like to develop, but maybe it is not the right time to launch them because of the uncertainty surrounding the industry," he concluded. "Consequently, launch prices could be extremely high, which is not ideal given the current global scenario."

title: EJF lays bare Chinese distant water fleet’s overfishing, abuses
content:
Around half of China's distant water fleet catch is from African waters, caught by vessel crew engaging in human rights abuses, often with no regard for endangered and protected marine life, alleges a damning new report by the NGO Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF). 

EJF's CEO Steve Trent said the findings highlighted in the report -- the most comprehensive of China's distant water fishing fleet to date -- underline the "overarching failure of the Chinese government to effectively control and regulate its distant-water fleet". 

Senate-passed version of China trade bill includes toned down SIMP language

According to EJF, some 78.5% of the Chinese government-approved fishery projects in other countries' waters are in Africa.

This has resulted in a huge increase in Chinese catch from African waters, with an estimated 2.35 million metric tons of seafood caught every year from West Africa alone. 

"The Chinese fleet has become a substantial presence in many developing countries and regions that have limited capacity for monitoring fishing vessels yet are heavily dependent on fishing for local food security and livelihoods," the report shows.
 
"Africa stands out, accounting for 78.5% of the Chinese government-approved fishery projects in other countries' waters. Many fish populations in Africa are heavily exploited, to the point of possible collapse, which would spell disaster for impoverished coastal communities."

The report shows that as much as half the annual catch of China's entire distant water fleet is from West African waters, worth $5 billion a year. In Ghana, at least 90% of the nation's industrial trawl fleet is suspected to be owned by Chinese corporations, who use local 'front' companies to register as Ghanaian and circumvent the law.

Where the fish caught by the fleet ends up is also shrouded by opacity, making it difficult or impossible to trace supply chains. 

Testimony from over 100 crew aboard 88 vessels also shows 95% reported witnessing some form of illegal fishing, EJF said.

China accused of violating neighbors’ EEZ in South China Sea

"Over a third of the interviewees reported that protected species such as turtles and seals were caught and killed on their vessels," said EJF. Almost all the crew interviewed by EJF said that sharks were illegally finned on their vessels, and the shark is thrown overboard to die. 

These destructive practices are enabled by gross human rights abuses of migrant crew, on vessels subsidized by the Chinese government to the tune of around $1.8 billion a year, according to EJF. 

Workers spoke of physical and verbal abuse, grueling hours, inadequate food and water, and forced labor at the hands of Chinese captains and senior crew.
 
"The testimony and footage EJF received revealed Indonesian crew being beaten with metal pipes and threatened with knives by senior Chinese crew. Overall, 58% of the crew EJF interviewed said they had witnessed or experienced physical violence and 85% reported abusive working and living conditions."

One Indonesian crewman described being restrained and hit and being beaten across "every part of my body", he said. In addition, almost all the crew (97%) interviewed said they had experienced some form of debt bondage or had documents such as passports confiscated.

Trent said the findings require nations importing fish caught by Chinese vessels to demand "full transparency along the whole supply chain". 

"These findings highlight the overarching failure of the Chinese government to effectively control and regulate its distant-water fleet, but also reveal a wider international problem: the shocking lack of transparency across the sector.

"As well as China controlling its fleet, any nation importing fish caught by Chinese vessels should be demanding full transparency along the whole supply chain. That is the only way we can be sure that we, as consumers, don't end up eating slave-caught fish and driving the destruction of our ocean."

title: Russian fisheries in danger of losing MSC label over auditor group’s decision
content:
The Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) will not act immediately to remove its blue sustainability labels from Russia's many certified fisheries, including those for cod, pollock, salmon and crab, in response to the country's invasion of Ukraine, based on a statement made Thursday (March 10) by MSC chief executive Rupert Howes.

But it may not have to.

Assurance Services International (ASI), the body that oversees the firms that assure that fisheries are meeting MSC's sustainability standards, has advised that it has temporarily suspended conformity assessment bodies (CAB) from doing work in Russia following a review of integrity risks.

"The review confirmed operational and reputational risk associated with ASI’s assessment of CABs and oversight of schemes in Russia, both for itself and its business partners," ASI said in a statement on its website dated March 8. "Further, we cannot exclude risks to the safety of the people involved, if onsite assessments were to be conducted.

"While respecting our contractual obligations with CABs and scheme owners, ASI will limit its activities in Russia where possible," the group continued. "As a consequence, we will suspend the geographical scope of 'Russia' for all the programs that we oversee, which implies that CABs will not be able to conduct any new certification activities in this country. Further, ASI will not accept any new oversight work in Russia."

MSC later clarified to Undercurrent News that the ASI's actions would not impact current certification holders, including those that are going through reassessment. Sources earlier had suggested that ASI's stance would impact the ability of firms to conduct MSC audits, something that happens at least once per year.

"ASI will fulfil existing contractual obligations, meaning that current certificate holders will not be affected, including those going through reassessment," another source clarified. "But we believe that the sweeping sanctions being imposed on Russia will increasingly impact on future certification activities, due to the logistical difficulties now facing certification bodies."    

ASI reports to oversee more than 85 CABs operating in over 150 countries.

A quick search for "Russia" on the MSC site identifies eight certified fisheries but there are many others. They include, just for starters: the Fishery Shipowners Association (FSA) East Kamchatka and North Kuril Islands walleye pollock fishery; a red king crab fishery in the Barents Sea; a snow crab fishery in the Barents Sea; a sockeye salmon fishery in the Ozernaya River; European perch in the Bratsk Reservoir; Greenland halibut in the Barents Sea; salmon in VA-Delta Kamchatka; and a pink and chum salmon fishery in Narody Severa Bolsheretsk.

One of Russia's most valuable fisheries is the massive Atlantic cod, haddock and saithe fishery in the Barents Sea, where an MSC certification is due to expire on March 19 after five years. In 2020, the fishery accounted for 90,067 metric tons of cod, 24,848t of haddock and 1,466t of saithe. It comprises 16 Russian vessels, operating in Norwegian, Russian and international waters, using demersal or bottom otter trawls, according to MSC.

Also of note, FSA walleye pollock fisheries in East Sakhalin and an FSA pollock fishery in the western part of the Bering Sea as well as a Norebo mid-water trawl pollock fishery in the Sea of Okhotsk are identified as being in the middle of assessments now.

FSA is a group controlled by the Russian Fishery Company, which is able to sell under the main certificate the Pollock Catchers Association.

'Profoundly shocked and deeply concerned'

The MSC has come under fire recently for not immediately pulling its certifications from Russia following the invasion of Ukraine, which started on Feb. 24. A spokesperson was quoted by another publication roughly a week ago as saying the organization with the label best recognized across the world for assuring the sustainability of fisheries was studying the situation and not yet ready to take such a position. 

"The silence from the MSC has been deafening," one commercial seafood industry source told Undercurrent this week. "Governments and businesses the world over have acted with moral clarity in the wake of Russia’s atrocities in Ukraine. They have moved quickly to isolate the Russian economy and inflict economic pain on Russia’s corrupt leadership and war machine. Meanwhile, the MSC has been MIA. Does the MSC really think it’s viable to continue vouching to global seafood consumers that Russian seafood is the most ethical purchasing choice they can make?"

Rupert Howes, chief executive at MSC. Image is still from video produced by Deutche Bank.

In a statement provided to Undercurrent on Thursday (March 10), MSC's Howes indicated his group would not be immediately removing its labels from the Russian fisheries, suggesting that its mission remains tightly focused on the sustainability of fisheries.

"We are profoundly shocked and deeply concerned by the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the ongoing and worsening plight and suffering of the Ukraine people caught up in this senseless war," he said. "Since the invasion began, the [MSC], along with our partners in the seafood supply chain, have been grappling with what these tragic events mean for our work on sustainable fishing in Russia and how best we can respond.

"The MSC's mission is to end overfishing and this is a global endeavor, reliant on international co-operation - involving fishers, businesses, NGOs and governments.  Conflict threatens this progress, with the future of our oceans and sustainable seafood supplies at stake," he said. "The nature of our third-party certification program ensures that MSC cannot influence the outcome of the independent scientific assessment of fisheries nor intervene to withdraw or suspend fishery certificates."

However, Howes left a clue as to how the Russian fisheries could lose their blue labels without MSC immediately intervening.

Credit: Gidrostroy

"Irrespective of this, it appears likely that the impact of economic sanctions imposed on the Russian economy, and the likelihood of further and more extensive sanctions being implemented, could lead to the loss of MSC certification of Russian fisheries as independent certification bodies are prevented from engaging in required auditing, assurance and surveillance activities," he said, adding:

"As the hostilities continue, a growing number of retailers and supply chain companies have also announced that they will reduce or no longer source seafood from Russia."

Howes said MSC is offering its "ongoing support to any fishers and supply chain partners with queries about the latest situation", and he added: "Our thoughts are with the innocent civilians in the middle of this conflict; we join others around the world in calling for a complete end to the violence in Ukraine."

ASI said it is in close contact with scheme owners who have active certificate holders in Russia to "advise on risk, assure credible and robust maintenance and/or transitioning of certificates and see if assurance and certification activities shall be further reduced." It said it will "continue monitoring the situation and evaluate in-depth the business relationships, competence and impartiality of the CABs that are currently active in Russia".

title: Daily recap, March 8: McDonald’s shutters Russia outlets; UK retailers pull Russian fish from shelves
content:
Here's a recap of the daily seafood news from Tuesday, March 8:

McDonald's is shuttering its Russia locations with impacts on Espersen plant likely

A Russian processing facility that Denmark's A. Espersen uses to service McDonald's is likely to be impacted by the announcement that the fast-food chain will temporarily shutter its 850 Russian locations. McDonald's will cease all operations in Russia with CEO Chris Kempczinski stating that the conflict has "caused unspeakable suffering to innocent people" and "we join the world in condemning aggression and violence and praying for peace".

UK retailers pull Russian fish from shelves

UK retailers Asda and Wm Morrison Supermarkets are removing some Russian fish products from sale, the companies told Undercurrent News. Asda and Morrisons, the UK's third and fourth-largest food retailers, are the first to explicitly mention removing fish items. 

Major Russian importer: Only domestic seafood will be on sale soon 

The dive in Russia's currency and the impact of the sanctions on the country's economy means imported seafood could soon be priced out of the market. Russia's ruble has collapsed to a record low following the impact of sanctions imposed on the country's banks in the wake of the invasion of Ukraine. As a result, Russian importers of pelagics, salmon, shrimp and whitefish such as Defa Group are in a very tough situation.

Coldwater shrimp sector sees little impact from European conflict, still expects price increase

Though still early, the coldwater shrimp sector has not yet seen any great impact from Russia's invasion of Ukraine, sources told Undercurrent. Both nations are importers of coldwater shrimp -- chiefly frozen, shell-on -- and while Russia has a fishing fleet, it largely supplies the domestic market.

China's Evergreen acquires country's 'biggest shrimp importer', plans IPO

China's Evergreen Group has acquired the largest shrimp importer in the country, it said, aiming to take the company public within three-to-five years. Evergreen announced on March 4 that it has acquired a 51% stake in Quanlian Aquatic Products Collection (Guangdong) Co., a seafood importer and trading company based in Zhangjiang, Guangdong province.

title: McDonald’s is shuttering its Russia locations with impacts on Espersen plant likely
content:
A Russian processing facility that Denmark's A. Espersen uses to service McDonald's is likely to be impacted by the recent announcement that the fast-food chain will temporarily shutter its 850 Russian locations.

Espersen faces massive pollock price inflation for Russian McDonald’s plant

According to the BBC, McDonald's will cease all operations in Russia with CEO Chris Kempczinski stating that the conflict has "caused unspeakable suffering to innocent people" and "we join the world in condemning aggression and violence and praying for peace".

Espersen, which processes Russian pollock for the chain's fish sandwiches, employs around 100 people at its plant, in Veliky Novgorod, between Moscow and St. Petersburg. Undercurrent News quoted the Danish fish company's CEO, Klaus Nielsen, as saying that the company planned to continue operating its Russia plant even as it faced dramatic cost inflation for pollock raw material.

On March 9, Nielsen told Undercurrent that McDonald’s decision "will have an impact on our Russian business".

"We have a board meeting later today [March 9] and will we send out an official statement later in the week. Our main priority is to talk to our employees and other stakeholders first," he said.

Although Espersen uses Russian pollock fillets in the plant, these are traded in dollars. The Russian ruble has devalued more than 30% against the US dollar due to the sanctions placed on Vladimir Putin's government after the invasion of Ukraine. At the same time, pollock prices are close to record levels anyway due to strong demand and quota cuts in Russia and the US.

Nielsen, who was not immediately able to be reached for comment, said earlier this week that the company was prepared to comply if it was told to stop operating in Russia.

"If the [Danish] government or EU or somebody else tells us to stop operating in Russia, then obviously we do so instantly. We would probably have to leave the keys at the doorstep and say, 'thank you', for now," the CEO said.

However, a source close to the fish company told Undercurrent that it has not been decided if the Espersen plant will close. It remains possible that the plant could be used to produce fish for McDonalds in other European companies as Espersen's other plants are operating at capacity, the source said.

title: UK ‘women in fisheries’ network launches
content:
The UK Women in Fisheries network has officially launched, seeking to make "connections across the board, and get the whole sector communicating more", it announced.

"All women working in the sector are welcome to join, wherever they may be. Women work as female fishermen, in fisheries associations, they are fleet managers, policymakers and charity workers. They are active at all levels within the commercial operations of retail, wholesale and export of fish and fish products," it said.

"They are leading fisheries training centers, they are entrepreneurs in the fishing industry and often play crucial roles as partners of fishers, taking responsibility for administration in addition to having their own income and running the household. If you are involved in fish in any way, the network is for you."

Research carried out into the role that women play in fisheries and UK fisheries, (Gustavsson, 2020) found that women are crucial to the fishing industry, community and to fishing families, and "provide a backbone to the industry", but also found that:

"Women experience issues around pay, abuse and violence, as well as prejudiced and traditional beliefs. There is a lack of adaptation to women's bodies in the industry and few opportunities for women to start fishing," it said.

As a result of this body of research, a policy brief was written that recommended the
establishment of an organization to represent women in fisheries.

title: More criminal charges likely in 2020 attack on Canadian lobster pound
content:
Twenty-five people already accused of ransacking a Canadian lobster pound in October 2020 will face more charges for their alleged roles in a dispute involving an Indigenous self-regulated fishery, the Welland Tribune reports.

Prosecutor Robert Kennedy, however, said the government is willing to discuss "resolutions" for "at least some" of the accused, which would avoid further court proceedings.

As Undercurrent News has reported, the incident reportedly began amid tensions that had been brewing in Lobster Fishing Area 34 since September 2020, when the Sipekne'katik First Nation announced the Canadian Supreme Court-affirmed opening of an off-season lobster fishery using a lobster pound in Middle West Pubnico in the province of Nova Scotia. Some non-indigenous commercial harvesters who worked in the area said the Sipekne'katik fishery was illegal. 

Less than a month later, on Oct. 13, 2020, a large crowd of commercial harvesters allegedly descended on a pound, on St. Mary's Bay, to harass a harvester who was unloading his catch. Lobsters were reportedly strewn out on the pavement.

Then, three days later, the pound was further burned to the ground, leading four Canadian cabinet ministers to condemn the attack, as reported by Undercurrent. One man was reportedly hospitalized with life-threatening injuries and the lobsters still kept at the pound were all destroyed.

In January 2021, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police announced that 23 people were facing a charge of breaking and entering, with eight also charged with mischief, for their roles in the Oct. 13, 2020, incident, as Undercurrent reported. Kennedy said a total of 25 people face charges and that in November 2021, the special prosecutions office recommended adding the charges of forcible entry and unlawful assembly against all of the accused. 

He said that during a Dec. 17 hearing in Yarmouth provincial court, the proceedings involving all 25 were set over to Jan. 21, as talks between prosecutors and defense lawyers continue.

The ransacking was among the cases cited in a complaint by the Sipekne'katik First Nation to the United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination. The First Nation alleged "acts of racist violence against Mi'kmaq".

As Undercurrent reported, Canadian federal leaders condemned the violence, which prompted a show of solidarity in the Nova Scotia capital of Halifax, bringing hundreds of people to Grand Parade Square to support Mi'kmaq fishers.

At the time, Bernadette Jordan, then minister of fisheries and oceans, indigenous services minister Marc Miller, Crown-indigenous relations minister Carolyn Bennett and public safety minister Bill Blair made statements reinforcing the Supreme Court-afforded right to the Mi'kmaq of a "moderate livelihood". 

"No act of violence will prevent Canada from upholding that right nor the Mi'kmaq people from exercising that right," Miller said, calling the attacks by non-Indigenous harvesters "disgusting".

Charges of arson were laid against Nova Scotia residents Brendon Douglas James Porter of East Pubnico and Sean Roy Messenger of Shelburne County in relation to the Oct. 16 arson.

Kennedy said that resolutions weren't being discussed at this point for arson cases.

title: Foreign fleets lurk at edge of Argentinian EEZ months before squid season
content:
Over 100 giant distant-water fishing vessels are approaching Argentina's exclusive economic zone (EEZ) intent on catching squid and other commercial species, said marine conservation specialist Milko Schvartzman through his Twitter account.

"Also, thanks to infrared imagery, I could identify a total of 55 squid jiggers already roaming the area two months before the kick-off of Argentina's squid fishing season," he explained. "Vessels that scot-free prey for resources in the South Atlantic are back again."

With a breakdown by nationality and type, these vessels are mainly Chinese (around 60%), South Korean (15%), Taiwanese (14%) and Spanish (11%) squid jiggers, longliners and bottom trawlers, Schwartzman added.

Also, the foreign vessels are led by officers from these countries but crewed by nationals of Indonesia, the Philippines and Africa, mainly.

"Crew members are poorly paid and, in many cases, their possessions are seized before boarding in violation of international labor standards," he said, adding that crew members can "end up dying on board from preventable causes, such as toothache or malnutrition"

Additionally, according to Juan Redini, president of the Argentinian squid industry association CAPA, the Chinese fishing fleet received fuel subsidies from their government, paid meager wages and offloaded catch to refrigerated cargo vessels on the high seas.

"We cannot compete with that," he claimed.

"This is a problem that has been dramatically on the rise for many years now since the success of Argentina's fishing companies depends heavily on what those vessels do out there," Redini told Undercurrent News. 

In total, CAPA includes around 70 squid jiggers, "one-sixth only of the number of vessels that are waiting for the resource to migrate outside our EEZ," he added. "At least we know we will count this year with three patrol vessels instead of two in charge of monitoring all fishing activities starting at our 200-mile limit."

The Chinese embassy in Argentina, CAPPMA -- the Chinese seafood producers association -- and the International Media Center for China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not respond to Undercurrent requests for comment on the claims made against the Chinese fleet. 

However, back in July, and amidst discussions between the Chinese and Ecuadorian governments, China reiterated its willingness to respect international agreements, the sovereignty of Ecuador and maintain "strict control" over its vessels to ensure that they do not engage in illegal activities.

However, in 2020, the Argentine coast guard captured three vessels fishing illegally. Yet, there are concerns that the temporary suspension and fines of $150,000 for any foreign vessel found fishing in the EEZ will not be sufficient deterrence for the new fleet.

Moreover, interactions between the country's coast guard and suspected illegal fishing vessels have escalated to violence, with some deeming the conflict "a literal war", Undercurrent previously reported.

According to the conservation group Oceana, Argentina maintains one of the world's largest squid fisheries, generating an average of $597 million for South America's economy and, in particularly favorable years, can generate as much as $2.4 billion.

title: Nova Scotia First Nation chief happy to have clean slate with new fisheries minister
content:
Mike Sack, chief of the Sipekne'katik First Nation, the group at the center of the dispute over a "moderate livelihood" off-season lobster fishery in Nova Scotia, is happy to have a clean slate with Canada's newly appointed fisheries minister, the Canadian news service Global Affairs reports.

As reported by Undercurrent News, multiple seafood aquaculture, harvester and processing groups have written to welcome Joyce Murray, a member of Parliament (MP) from British Columbia, in her new role as the minister of fisheries and oceans for the Justin Trudeau administration. 

She replaces former Nova Scotia-based MP Bernadette Jordan, who recently lost in her September re-election effort. Jordan had come under fire for her handling of the lobster fishery dispute along the south shore of her home province between commercial and Indigenous fishermen.

Sack reportedly told Global News this week that he is encouraged that the new minister is not from the area.

"It should be more of an unbiased opinion, in my mind," he reportedly said.

As earlier reported, the Sipekne'katik set off a firestorm in September 2020 when the band launched a self-regulated fishery in Lobster Fishing Area 34, Canada's most prolific by far, months ahead of the federally regulated season. The move led to protests and violence by other commercial harvesters in the area, which was followed by Jordan, in March, promising to enforce the seasonal limitations and Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans even arresting Sack himself.

The First Nation group has argued that a 1999 Supreme Court of Canada decision affirming its members' treaty right to fish allows them to harvest lobster year-round to earn a "moderate livelihood."

Sack said he has been "waiting patiently" for Trudeau to name a new minister and that he plans to reach out to Murray soon.

title: First Nation, Canadian harvesters like new deal
content:
Annapolis Valley First Nation members who harvest Canada's Bay of Fundy say that they like the interim agreement that their tribal government has negotiated, Salt Wire reports.

Nation members Steve Grant, a fishing captain, and his crew members, Alisha Hazelton and Keith Malle, hope the neighboring Acadia and Glooscap First Nations will accept the agreement -- ultimately as a step toward the end of the violence that has torn at relations between non-aboriginal fishing communities and First Nations seeking to implement their moderate livelihood rights.

As Undercurrent News has reported, two First Nations have reached an agreement earlier this month to commercially harvest no more than 3,500 lobster traps in Lobster Fishing Areas 33, 34 and 35 (which encompasses the waters of the Bay of Fundy and southwestern Nova Scotia).  Each member Bear River and Annapolis Valley Mi'kmaw harvester is entitled to fish 70 tagged traps, with a maximum of 210 traps being fished per boat. 

Commercial fishermen have lauded the agreement.

As Undercurrent has reported, Canada has been enforcing regulations that prohibit lobster harvesting out of season since Bernadette Jordan, Canada's former fisheries minister, declared that intention in March. The enforcement came in response to reports that First Nation groups would begin fishing months early in Lobster Fishing Area 34 where the season typically is scheduled to begin in late November. 

The decision was a major development in an ongoing spat with the commercial lobster industry that started when the Sipekne'katik band, in September 2020, launched its own self-regulated "moderate livelihood" lobster fishery in St. Mary's Bay in southwest Nova Scotia, as reported by Undercurrent.
