title: US Customs hits Fiji-flagged tuna longliner with WRO over forced labor concerns
content:
US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) is keeping up its hard press against the alleged use of forced labor by foreign seafood harvesters, issuing a withhold release order on Wednesday against the Fijian-flagged and owned tuna longliner Hangton No. 112.

The order stops the import into the US of any fish that might've been landed by the vessel, which is owned by the Hangton Pacific Company Ltd., based in Fiji's capital city of Suva.

The Hangton No. 112. Image from a ship database maintained by the Western & Central Pacific Fisheries Commission.

CBP said it received information that "reasonably indicates the use of forced labor in the vessel's fishing operations", identifying at least three of the International Labor Organization’s 11 indicators during its investigation: withholding of wages; debt bondage; and retention of identity documents.

"Foreign fishing vessels like the Hangton No. 112 continue to lure vulnerable migrant workers into forced labor situations so that they can sell seafood below market value, which threatens the livelihoods of American fishermen," said Troy Miller, CBP's acting commissioner, in a statement. "CBP will continue to stand up against these vessels’ abusive labor practices by preventing the introduction of their unethically-harvested seafood into the US market."

Based on a profile found in a directory for companies involved in seafood trade, Hangton Pacific has been in operation for more than 10 years and manages a fleet of longline vessels while also purchasing from other vessels that make landings in Fiji. Its target species are reported to be big-eye and yellowfin tuna. It specializes in both fresh and frozen products with its major markets being Japan and the US, while selling a small amount of volume to Taiwan, Vietnam, Sri Lanka and Thailand.

A ship profile maintained by the Western & Central Pacific Fisheries Commission describes the Hangton No. 112 as been a 34-meter (111 feet) longliner with seven freezers, maintaining a crew of 13.

The CPB isn't the first to accuse Hangton No. 112 of abusive labor practices. The boat was also cited in a Dec. 2019 investigative report, titled Seabound, by Greenpeace Southeast Asia and the Indonesian Migrant Worker Union. The operator denied the allegations at the time.

While it's not clear that CPB opened up its investigation against Hangton Pacific in response to the Greenpeace report, general manager Jitendra Mohan responded in an email to a request for comment by Undercurrent on the WRO by criticizing Greenpeace Indonesia, calling the group "very unprofessional" for vilifying the company.  

Mohan said the advocacy group has "not responded nor rectified" its earlier report, "which had caused a lot of inconvenience to us". He said Hangton Pacific has also written its local government's ministry, which performs an audit each time a boat comes into port. 

"The Indonesian embassy in Fiji is easily accessible to crew and have intervened if enquired. Some recruits who are first-timers have terminated their contracts after first fishing trip and their repatriation have been arranged," Mohan said.

He said he hopes "the US Customs agency contacts us for verification. We have been exporting to USA for two decades and our boats are MSC [Marine Stewardship Council] certified." 

Hangdon Pacific is a "fully Fijian-owned company without any foreign shareholders", he stressed.

CPB On the warpath

The CPB, an agency within the Department of Homeland Security, has continued its crackdown on forced labor in recent times even thru the change of presidential administrations. Undercurrent News reported in May how CBP had issued a WRO against Dalian Ocean Fishing Co., a giant Chinese-based fishing company, over forced labor concerns.

CBP said it identified all 11 of the ILO indicators of forced labor during that investigation, including physical violence, withholding of wages and abusive working and living conditions. It was the first WRO against an entire fishing fleet, though the Chinese government responded by accusing the administration of president Joe Biden of grandstanding and acting based on a fabrication.

Based on an email sent by CBP to reporters, the US imported $1.8 million worth of seafood harvested by Dalian in 2019 and $320,808 worth of seafood in 2020. In 2021, thru April 30, the US imported $763,115 worth of seafood caught by Dalian.

Earlier, in January 2021, CBP issued WROs against the Taiwanese tuna vessel Lien Yi Hsing No. 12.  It issued WROs against the Taiwanese tuna vessels Da Wang in August 2020 and the Yu Long No. 2 in May 2020. 

The ILO estimates that 25m workers suffer under conditions of forced labor worldwide, CPB noted, adding that the distant water fishing industry is at high risk of forced labor as foreign companies often coerce vulnerable migrant workers to perform hazardous labor for little or no pay aboard fishing vessels that may spend months at sea without making port calls.

Helping to push CBP, too, is a report issued in June 2020 by the Government Accountability Office (GAO). The GAO, often referred to as Congress’ "watchdog agency", spent more than a year responding to a request by US representative Raul Grijalva, an Arizona Democrat and the chairman of the House Natural Resources Committee, in September 2018, to investigate how CPB, a division of the Department of Homeland Security, was enforcing section 307 of the Tariff Act of 1930.

There’s little doubt US consumers have, more than once, purchased seafood in which forced labor was used, the GAO suggested. The US spends more than $22.5 billion per year on imported seafood annually, based on data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

Trade attorney Jessica Rifkin.

Jessica Rifkin, a trade expert and senior attorney with the Glen Burnie, Maryland-based firm of Benjamin L. England & Associates, recently warned of intensifying efforts at CPB during a webinar sponsored by Undercurrent. She pointed to both the GAO report and also a report from NOAA that could be helping to fuel the fire. 

In a report delivered in December called "Human Trafficking in the Seafood Supply Chain", NOAA  identified Fiji as one of about 30 countries where individuals were most at risk of falling prey to human trafficking, including forced labor in the seafood industry. The country was responsible, in 2018, for sending the US 12,417 metric tons of seafood worth $78.3m, NOAA noted.

"Recruitment agencies, vessel owners, and other crew subject migrant fishers from Southeast Asian countries, especially Indonesia, to forced labor on Fiji-flagged vessels or foreign-flagged fishing vessels transiting Fijian ports and waters," the NOAA report said.

"Victims of forced labor experience threats of violence, passport confiscation, debt-based coercion, excessive working hours, and abusive living and working conditions. Fijians have also been reported as crew members subjected to forced labor aboard foreign vessels, including PRC, Korean, and Taiwan-flagged vessels. The government continues to lack guidelines for victim identification and did not train labor, customs, or immigration officials on trafficking. The government has not adequately investigated labor violations for indicators of human trafficking or provided adequate support to victims. There are some reports that suggest officials are complicit in impeding anti-trafficking efforts. The Fiji police has a human trafficking unit, but it has been shown to lack adequate resources to effectively conduct investigations."

title: How the US salmon supply chain has a highway bandit problem
content:
Additional reporting by Oriana Aguillon

Every day, an army of refrigerated trucks make the 1,033-kilometer (641 mile) trip to Santiago, Chile's main international airport for an eight-hour overnight flight to cold storage units in Miami. The valuable cargo, to the tune of 8,000 metric tons a week, is Atlantic salmon grown in the fjords of Patagonia, for consumption across the US. 

That cargo has increasingly become the target of 21st-century highway banditry. Most of the attacks have occurred in Araucania, an area in southern Chile through which the trucks pass. It's also an area to which an indigenous group has traditionally fought with authorities over land claims and better opportunities for the Mapuche indigenous group. 

Chile's main salmon farmers from AquaChile to Mowi have always contended with salmon theft to some degree, both at the farm level and supplies otherwise finding their way into an informal domestic market for fish. But the attacks have escalated during the pandemic and have gotten to the point where most salmon farmers are avoiding nighttime trips through troublespots. 

"The trucks are avoiding some of the most conflictive areas at certain times of night," one industry source told Undercurrent News, in response to a recent spate of attacks.  

Part of the problem is down to Chile's unique geography. Chile is one of the world's most oddly shaped countries, being 2,630 miles long and on average only 110 miles wide, hugging the western Pacific coastline.  

The salmon trucks can only use the Pan American highway which runs up the spine of the country. Large tracts of the highway are desolate and poorly lit. Trucks that make an almost 4,000-kilometer overland trip to Brazil use the same highway. The road is also used to carry salmon smolt, often grown alongside rivers flowing from the Andes Mountains, down to the Patagonia region. 

The biggest attack on the industry of late was by an armed group that attacked five trucks traveling in convoy and carrying smolt from the Araucania region. The vehicles were set on fire in an indiscriminate attack, injuring the lorry drivers and destroying the smolt. 

Salmon farming giant Cermaq, which is owned by Mitsubishi Corp., has been subject to an arson attack at a hatchery site it operates in the Araucania region. The attack occurred amid growing unrest in the region in May last year, at the start of the pandemic. 

Farming industry group SalmonChile condemned the attacks and has appealed to authorities to set up a working group with regional leaders to diffuse the situation. The Chilean government has been struggling to contain discontent in what is the poorest region of the country. Attacks have grown on forestry assets, effectively the region's only source of income. Local groups with alleged ties to the indigenous movement have chased out local landowners through arson attacks and police exchanged gunfire with one group in July. 

"We have been suffering from this problem for the last 20 years, it has been increasing more and more, this year we have suffered several attacks on houses, trucks, and workers in the agricultural sector", Gustavo Valenzuela, president of a local chamber of commerce, told a television channel. 

Valuable haul for bandits

Amid the violence, robbery has become commonplace. The single theft of a truck, as occurred last year, provides a haul worth CLP 150 million (about $200,000) to bandits.  

Chile's salmon industry became profitable in 2016 after a prolonged loss-making period because of disease and spells of low prices. Robberies of trucks started in about 2016, and also as Chile's growing middle-class developed a taste for Atlantic salmon. Chile's GDP per capita crossed the $10,000 threshold about a decade ago and now stands at $18,511, largely attributable to the country's endowment of wealthy minerals such as copper and lithium. 

The industry clawed back a victory against banditry last month when the Chilean police pounced on an illegal group that was selling smoked salmon made from fish that had died from disease in its sea phase growth and was being sent to make fishmeal. Dubbed "Operacion Atlantico", 130 detectives from southern Chile raided 26 homes in June to track down the gang, impounding more than a dozen vehicles, financial assets worth half a million dollars, and firearms. 

Region linked in pandemic

Authorities and the industry hope that recent tensions will quell as Chile's economy returns to normal after the pandemic ends. The South American country has one of the highest vaccination rates in the world. Largely relying on Chinese vaccines, the country has vaccinated 62.2% of its population with at least two doses, more than Israel, according to Bloomberg.  

Chilean economic activity soared 14% in April, the highest level on record, according to the central bank. But even with strong economic growth and a new social payment system that the government enacted during the pandemic, Chile is still on the verge of civil unrest following widespread protests in late 2019. 

The country is in the middle of rewriting a new constitution in response to the violence, and recently elected a Mapuche leader to preside over this change. Chile also holds presidential elections in November, and both leading candidates are from non-traditional political parties. The situation in Araucania is likely to be closely tied to these events, industry leaders say. 

"There is uncertainty in Araucania with respect to what is about to happen, but it's not just about the salmon industry, it concerns everything that is going on here in Chile," an industry executive told Undercurrent. "The new constitution and the political situation is complex. With the situation with the trucks in particular, I don't think it's a focused threat. It's more about the terrorism that you see in the region and it's generalized."

title: Untitled
content:
The looming victory of a hard-leftist presidential candidate in Peru and the surprising emergence of a communist party member for the Chilean elections this year have unsettled the outlook for two key segments of the global seafood industry. 

Pedro Castillo, who still awaits the final count of votes to be declared winner of the Peruvian elections, has already announced his intentions to raise taxes on the key mining sector. Daniel Jadue, a Santiago mayor, represents Chile's Communist Party and has emerged as a frontrunner to stand against right-wing candidates Gabriel Boruc and Joaquin Lavin.  

"The industry is literally wetting themselves right now," one Peruvian fishing industry source told Undercurrent News, in anticipation that Castillo will emerge as winner of the elections after the vote-counting conflict ends. 

Pedro Castillo. Photograph by Braian Reyna Guerrero on Flickr.

Adverse political pressure on both the Chilean and Peruvian seafood sectors will have knock-on consequences for global markets. Peru, along with Chile, produces about two-thirds of all fishmeal and fish oil sold on international markets, underpinning key aquaculture industries. Chile is the world's second-largest salmon farmer after Norway and is the No. 1 supplier to Brazil and the US. 

Jadue has taken aim principally at foreign mining companies in Chile, which is the world's largest copper producer, but suggested that all foreign companies operating in Chile will have to "pay more" in an interview with Bloomberg.  

Polls show the strongest support for a far-left candidate in Chile in decades, with Jadue leading polls over Lavin, a popular center-right candidate who narrowly missed out on becoming president in 2000.

Beyond individual candidates, 46% of polled Chileans said they were undecided on who to vote for, providing an uncertain picture for Chile's near-term political future. Among many uncertainties, an independently voted group of representatives of society will have a key role in writing a new constitution for Chile, which could mean deep reform to business legislation. The process to rewrite the constitution arose from the 2019 protests.

Jadue's rise in popularity comes amid social tensions that boiled over in 2019 when riots made Chile a geopolitical hotspot alongside Hong Kong. The salmon industry saw some skirmishes in the regional capital Puerto Montt and protestors burned down a security gate outside a salmon processing plant.

Other salmon companies, including Norwegian giant Cermaq, have suffered from acts of violence in the Araucania region, which has long been a hotspot for conflict with local Mapuche indigenous groups.

Former Chilean President Michelle Bachelet, who is now the UN high commissioner for human rights, said in an event organized by the Economist, on June 24. that democracy, in the eyes of many citizens of the region and others, has "failed to deliver".  Many people don't believe they have fared better with liberal economic policy, something that could fan populism and more violence, she said.

Daniel Jadue. Photograph by Leonardo Rubilar on Flickr.

Peru no stranger to political instability 

Chile has long been seen as the most stable country in Latin America. That is not the case in Peru, which had three presidents in one week during November 2020 as a result of a political crisis linked to corruption.

As part of his government program, Castillo said he would raise taxes to mining companies, although reform could affect other natural resource companies, including fishing. 

"Castillo really has his sights set on the mining industry," a fishing industry source told Undercurrent. "There's a hope that the [fishing] sector might pass under the radar." 

Leaders of the Peruvian anchovy industry have long claimed that politics have adversely affected the sector. Several have questioned the political independence of Imarpe, the country's maritime institute that calculates the average size of the biomass in the Pacific Ocean each year using acoustic surveys.  

Peruvian anchovies. Credit: Imarpe

Some companies, including leading producers Tecnologica de Alimentos, Pesquera Diamante and Pesquera Exalmar, are in the spotlight as part of an anti-corruption scandal involving former Imarpe officials, who were accused of inflating the key anchovy biomass figures in 2019.

An emergency decree issued in the midst of the controversy made Imarpe lose its autonomy to designate a president by restructuring its institutional management. The decree took away Imarpe's freedom of choosing its own board of officials and president, requiring prior approval by the government to designate. The previous set-up guaranteed independence from private and public pressure, according to the scientists, which included fishing expert Ray Hilborn.

With Peru's presidential campaign all but decided, Castillo will arguably be able to directly influence decision-making within Imarpe. Further south, Chile's salmon industry will be keeping its eye on both this year's presidential elections and the outcome of constitutional change.

title: Hooded men burn trucks transporting salmon in southern Chile
content:
A Chilean transport company, Jorquera Transport, has condemned arson attacks that affected some of its trucks carrying farmed salmon on July 12 in southern Chile, Today.in reported.

Five trucks were attacked by a "group of armed hooded strangers" in the Pidima sector, Ercilla commune, La Araucania region, and also left three workers injured. Four of the five trucks attacked were transporting salmon, according to the transport firm's general manager, Rodrigo Gandara. The executive described the "violent attacks" as an act of cowardice, indicating that the unknown men fled after burning the trucks.

Five trucks and a destroyed van were left burning on the Ruta 5 Sur highway, while those injured were transferred to assistance centers in the region, Radio Bio Bio added.

Although it is unknown what salmon companies owned the cargos that were being transported by those trucks, sources in the industry were said to be concerned by the attacks and condemned the violence.

Earlier this year, Norwegian farmer Cermaq Group suffered an arson attack at one of its hatcheries in central Chile. The Jan. 28 fire took place at a hatchery in the municipality of Vilcun in the Araucania region, an area that has recently been the site of protests and unrest. Police are looking into the matter, the company said.

Last year, a weeklong strike involving hundreds of Chilean truck drivers caused significant disruption to the country's farmed salmon supply chain. The strike followed a high-profile shooting in the city of Araucania where a nine-year-old girl was injured.

title: Foreign vessels ‘pillaging’ Argentine waters for squid, other fish, Oceana reports
content:
Hundreds of foreign commercial fishing vessels, primarily from China, are "pillaging" the waters off Argentina for shortfin squid (Illex argentinus) and a few other species, the conservation group Oceana says it found in a recent study.

In a 10-page report released Wednesday, Oceana said it analyzed the activity of fishing vessels along the border of Argentina's national waters for about 40 months -- between Jan. 1, 2018 and April 25, 2021 -- using Automatic Identification System (AIS) data provided by Global Fishing Watch (GFW), an independent nonprofit founded by the group in partnership with Google and SkyTruth. AIS devices transmit such information as vessel names, flag states and locations. 

Oceana said it documented more than 800 foreign vessels logging more than 900,000 combined hours of fishing, but China was the most active. As much as 69% of the fishing was done by more than 400 Chinese vessels.

Korean, Spanish, and Taiwanese vessels conducted 26% of the fishing activity, with nearly 200 vessels fishing for approximately 251,000 hours.

By comparison, 45 of Argentina's vessels conducted 9,269 hours of visible fishing in the area during the same period — less than 1% of the total amount.

The shortfin squid. Image courtesy of Oceana.

 

There were more than 6,000 gap events, instances where AIS transmissions were not broadcast for more than 24 hours, which can indicate that vessels have potentially disabled their public tracking devices, Oceana said. These vessels were invisible for more than 600,000 total hours, hiding fishing vessel locations and masking potentially illegal behavior, such as crossing into Argentina's national waters to fish.

The Chinese fleet was responsible for 66% of such gap incidents, Oceana said it found.

Note that, in April 2020, approximately 100 squid jiggers (i.e., vessels with bright lights and hooks designed to catch squid), mostly Chinese-flagged, were allegedly caught fishing illegally in Argentina's national waters, each with their public tracking devices apparently turned off.

Interactions between the Argentine Coast Guard and suspected illegal fishing vessels have escalated to violence, with some deeming the conflict "a literal war", Oceana said.

Spanish vessels also are identified by the report as likely bad actors. Nearly 90% of the Spanish vessels that fished along Argentina's national waters appeared to turn off their public tracking devices at least once, and Spanish vessels spent nearly twice as much time with AIS devices off as they did visibly fishing, according to the conservation group.

Other findings of note:

More than two-thirds of the vessels and over half of all the fishing (575,294 hours) can be attributed to squid jiggers, which were the most used fishing gear type. Trawlers accounted for much of the remaining fishing (255,455 hours).
More than half (56%) of the vessels that appeared to have AIS gaps engaged in at-sea transshipment events. During transshipment, fishing vessels can transfer their catch to refrigerated cargo vessels. Transshipping at sea can be a weak link in the seafood supply chain, potentially allowing illegally caught fish to be mixed with legal catch, Oceana warned. 
Of the vessels with AIS gaps, 31% visited the Port of Montevideo, Uruguay at the end of their trip. This port has allegedly been favored by vessels engaging in illegal activity.

"Fishing at this scale, under the radar, and without regard for laws and sustainability can have detrimental impacts on entire ecosystems, as well as the people and economies that depend on them," said Marla Valentine, Oceana's illegal fishing and transparency campaign manager, in a statement.

"This is just one example of how unregulated distant water fishing fleets can take advantage of a lack of transparency and enforcement at sea. It has become increasingly clear that Chinese commercial fishing interests are far-reaching and have no boundaries; the world cannot afford to ignore the massive impacts of fleets like this on our oceans. The constant use of AIS devices on all fishing vessels is essential for transparency at sea and traceability in the seafood supply chain."

Argentina counts on its commercial fishing industry to make a $2.7 billion economic impact each year, constituting 3.4% of its gross domestic product, Oceana reported. Though the South American nation maintains more than 330 types of finfish and 120 deep-sea species along its coastline, it counts on just four species — shortfin squid, hake, red shrimp, and grenadier —for 75% of its total catch.

Argentina maintains one of the world's largest squid fisheries, generating an average of $597 million for South America's economy and, in particularly favorable years, can generate as much as $2.4bn, according to the conservation group.

Chief among Oceana's recommendations in its report is that governments and regional fishery management organizations require the constant use of tamper-resistant AIS devices on all fishing vessels. The group additionally advocates for the public sharing of vessel monitoring system data and that countries maintain a public list of all foreign and domestic vessels licensed and/or authorized to fish in its exclusive economic zone.

Oceana also suggests countries require transshipping be handled only at ports where authorities can closely monitor.

title: China denies forced labor charges against Dalian, calls US import ban grandstanding
content:
The Chinese government has responded to the decision from the administration of US president Joe Biden to ban imports of seafood from China's Dalian Ocean Fishing Co. over allegations of forced labor, saying the action is grandstanding and based on a fabrication.

Undercurrent News reported late Friday how US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), an agency within the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), had issued a withhold release order (WRO) against the giant fishing company based on information that "reasonably indicates the use of forced labor" in its harvesting operations.

The order, which is reported to be the first WRO against an entire fishing fleet, instructs CBP personnel at all US ports to begin immediately detaining all tuna, swordfish and other seafood harvested by Dalian that might be otherwise imported in the US. 

However, Wang Wenbin, a spokesperson for the Chinese Foreign Ministry, on Monday, called the ban groundless and grandstanding, "given that the firm in question has never sold anything to the US", reports The Global Times, a newspaper produced by China's communist party. 

Wang Wenbin. Photograph from China s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

CBP's claims of "forced labor" in the Chinese fishing company's operations are completely inconsistent with the facts and are pure fabrication, Wang said during a press conference, according to the Chinese newspaper. To his knowledge, he added, Dalion has complied with laws and rules, and it has a strict and comprehensive management mechanism, earning a good reputation in the industry.

"The fact is that there is no product to be detained and the so-called 'forced labor' claim is groundless," he said.

Dalian is a large long-line tuna fishing company based in Dalian, Northeast China's Liaoning Province. As reported by Undercurrent, it operates a fleet of 33 ultra-low temperature vessels.

The technical standards and modernization levels of tuna fishing boats are relatively high, and the operation process is basically automated, so there is no need for labor-intensive practices, Wang said.

"China firmly opposes political manipulation, and calls on the US to respect basic facts and revoke erroneous decisions," he said, "China will take all necessary measures to safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises."

Wang's statements run contrary to an email sent by CBP to reporters late on Friday that said the US imported $1.8 million worth of seafood harvested by Dalian in 2019 and $320,808 worth of seafood in 2020. In 2021, thru April 30, the US imported $763,115 worth of seafood caught by Dalian.

CBP said it identified all 11 of the International Labor Organization’s indicators of forced labor during its investigation, including physical violence, withholding of wages and abusive working and living conditions.

In May 2020, the Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF) and Advocates for Public Interest Law (APIL) called for an investigation into Dalian's fleet operating in the western Pacific Ocean after details emerged of human rights abuses to the Indonesian crew members working onboard, as reported by Undercurrent.

According to the EJF, four crew members working on the fleet were understood to have died due to the working conditions and a lack of medical care over the previous six months. Survivors from the vessels reported that the victims all suffered from swelling, chest pain and breathing difficulties for weeks, but vessel captains reportedly refused to go to port to access appropriate medical care, EJF said.

Alejandro Mayorkas, secretary of the Department of Homeland Security.

Later, in October, reports surfaced of at least two more deaths aboard Dalian vessels.

DHS "will continue to aggressively investigate the use of forced labor by distant-water fishing vessels and by a wide range of other industries," Homeland Security secretary Alejandro Mayorkas said on a call with reporters Friday. "Producers and US importers alike should understand that there will be consequences for entities that attempt to exploit workers to sell goods in the United States."

In January, the US began barring entry of all cotton products and tomatoes from Xinjiang. The US, European Union and UK have placed sanctions on Chinese officials and goods over alleged human-rights abuses against Uyghurs in Xinjiang. 

The action against Dalian came at the end of a busy week for the subject of forced seafood labor in Washington, DC.

The US Trade Representative announced Wednesday that it has submitted a proposal to the World Trade Organization aimed at including force labor provisions as part of an agreement being finalized with regard to limiting fishery subsidies, as reported by Undercurrent.

On Thursday, a forced seafood labor amendment was approved by the US Senate for addition in a larger bill related to making the US more competitive with China in relation to technology and trade, as reported by Undercurrent. The bill now sits idle, waiting for Congress to return from its recess and finish debate on the matter.

title: US Customs stops Chinese tuna, swordfish imports over forced labor findings
content:
US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) on Friday announced that it has issued a withhold release order (WRO) against China's Dalian Ocean Fishing Co. Ltd. based on information that "reasonably indicates the use of forced labor" in its harvesting operations. 

The order, which is reported to be the first WRO against an entire fishing fleet, instructs CBP personnel at all US ports to begin immediately detaining all tuna, swordfish and other seafood harvested by Dalian that might be otherwise imported in the US. 

CBP said it identified all 11 of the International Labor Organization’s indicators of forced labor during its investigation, including physical violence, withholding of wages and abusive working and living conditions.

Alejandro Mayorkas, secretary of the Department of Homeland Security.

"Companies that exploit their workers have no place doing business in the United States," said Alejandro Mayorkas, secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, the agency within which CBP is situated, in a statement.

"Products made from forced labor not only exploit workers, but hurt American businesses and expose consumers to unethical purchases," he said. "This [WRO] will ensure we continue to protect the human rights of those working in the distant water fishing industry, while also upholding safeguarding our national and economic security."

Dalian, which reports on its website to operate as many as 33 ultra-low temperature longline fishing vessels, is one of China's largest seafood harvesting companies. But it has a recent history with accusations of forced labor and abusive practices. 

In May 2020, the Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF) and Advocates for Public Interest Law (APIL) called for an investigation into Dalian's fleet operating in the western Pacific Ocean after details emerged of human rights abuses to the Indonesian crew members working onboard, as reported by Undercurrent News.

According to the EJF, four crew members working on the fleet were understood to have died due to the working conditions and a lack of medical care over the previous six months. Survivors from the vessels reported that the victims all suffered from swelling, chest pain and breathing difficulties for weeks, but vessel captains reportedly refused to go to port to access appropriate medical care, EJF said.

No autopsies were conducted in any of the cases, with the first three buried at sea despite contracts requiring vessel owners to repatriate their bodies.

According to the EJF, workers were made to toil for 18 hours a day, sometimes for two days continuously without rest -- the vessels themselves remained at sea for over a year without calling into port.

Furthermore, despite contracts stipulating payment of a monthly salary of $300, many of the crew were paid as little as $42 a month, with some even scarcely earning $300 for the whole year's work. The first three month's wages were also withheld, a practice indicative of forced labor.

Longline tuna fishing vessels registered by Dalian Ocean Fishing Company to fish in the Western and Central Pacific. Source: WCPFC

On top of this, crewmembers report that the fleet engaged in shark finning while at sea, catching more than 20 animals per day. While China does not forbid the practice, it remains illegal in the western central Pacific ocean.

Later, in October, reports surfaced of at least two more deaths aboard Dalian vessels.

In an email sent subsequently to reporters, CBP noted that Dalian is a major supplier to a seafood distributor, though the US is not its largest market. The US imported $1.8 million worth of seafood harvested by Dalian in 2019 and just $320,808 worth of seafood in 2020. In 2021, thru April 30, the US imported $763,115 worth of seafood caught by Dalian.

The action against Dalian comes at the end of a busy week for the subject of forced seafood labor in Washington, D.C.

The USTR announced Wednesday that it has submitted a proposal to the World Trade Organization aimed at including force labor provisions as part of an agreement being finalized with regard to limiting fishery subsidies, as reported by Undercurrent. On Thursday, a forced seafood labor amendment was approved by the US Senate for addition in a larger bill related to making the US more competitive with China in relation to technology and trade, as reported by Undercurrent.

title: Easter morning fire at Newfoundland union HQ was arson, says president
content:
A fire that damaged the Fish, Food & Allied Workers Union (FFAW) headquarters, in St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador, on Easter morning was a deliberate act of arson, FFAW president Keith Sullivan said.

The Royal Newfoundland Constabulary (RNC) has labeled the event, which happened shortly before 4:30 a.m. on Sunday (April 4), as suspicious and said it is under investigation, the CBC reports. They're asking anyone with relevant closed-circuit or dashcam video to step forward.

But Sullivan, whose group represents inshore harvesters and processing company workers in the province, has no doubt about the malicious intent of the act.

"We're very concerned. We are taking it very seriously," he is quoted by the CBC as saying. "It was intent to do damage there, and it was an intentional act of active violence."

No FFAW staff were present at the time of the fire, but given the proximity to a nearby residential area, Sullivan said he is relieved that nobody was injured.

"We have 50 people who have the office as a second home, and spend all kinds of hours there," he said.

Sullivan said the FFAW is working with police to get as much information as they can about the fire, and to find out who is responsible.

"Though this incident has displaced us from our workplace, we continue to show up to fight for our membership," FFAW said in a statement released Tuesday. "We cannot understate the gravity of this attack against our Union office this weekend and that this was also an act of violence against over 13,000 FFAW-Unifor members.

"The important services that we provide for our membership will not be stopped, and will continue this week without interruption."

title: Cermaq hatchery in Chile struck by arson
content:
A salmon hatchery in central Chile operated by Norwegian farmer Cermaq was struck by arson on Thursday, Jan. 28, an attack being condemned by industry groups.

The reasons for the fire at Piscicultura Collin, a unit owned by Cermaq subsidiary Yadran, were not given, according to Chile's La Tercera newspaper.

But Chile's Salmon Council, a group of farmers including Cermaq, condemned the attack in a statement.

"We regret these events that greatly affect the development of a productive activity, along with putting the safety of the workers who carry out their work and the surrounding communities at risk," the council said. "We are sure that violence will never be the way to resolve differences and we call on the institutional channels to resolve them."

title: 23 charged for attacking Canadian lobster pound holding First Nation’s catch
content:
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) this week announced that it has charged as many as 23 individuals in relation to the October ransacking and burning of a lobster pound off the coast of the province of Nova Scotia, the Chronicle Herald, a Canadian newspaper, reports.

Tensions have been brewing in Lobster Fishing Area 34 since Sept. 17, when the Sipekne'katik First Nation announced the opening of an off-season lobster fishery. Less than a month later, on Oct. 13, a large crowd of commercial harvesters allegedly descended on a pound, in Middle West Pubnico, on St. Mary's Bay, to harass a harvester who was unloading his catch. Lobsters were reportedly strewn out on the pavement.

Then, days later, the pound was further burned to the ground, leading four Canadian cabinet ministers to condemn the attack, as reported by Undercurrent News. One man was reportedly hospitalized with life-threatening injuries and the lobsters still kept at the pound were all destroyed.

No charges have been filed yet in relation to the burning of the pound, according to the newspaper. However, the RCMP said Tuesday that it has charged the following with breaking and entering: Devin Edward Belong, Leslie Edward Belong, Roderick Bruce Conrad, James Alfred D’Entremont, Marcel Renald D’Entremont, Kevin Paul D’eon, Kevin Mark Donaldson, Christopher Howard Goreham, Curtis Leigh Conrad Goreham, Josh Andrew Larkin, Shawn Joseph Muise, Travis Nickerson, Sterling Scott Penney, Troy Warren Irvin Penney and Jered Owen Scott.

It also has charged the following with mischief and breaking and entering: Tyler Leslie Belong, Samuel Spencer Corning, Blair Daniel Dentremont, Charles Richard Hines, Sean Roy Messenger, Michael Pearle Nickerson, Gordon Malcolm Stoddard and Merle Kevin Swaine.

"The Nova Scotia RCMP will continue to take steps to ensure that those who unlawfully interfere with or threaten the safety of any person or property be held accountable in accordance with the laws of Canada," reads a statement from RCMP sergeant Andrew Joyce.

title: COVID-19 recap, Nov. 24: Alaska processors’ woes; Cooke UK’s dip; Premier’s pain
content:
The novel coronavirus COVID-19 continues to upend the global seafood trade, reducing foodservice demand and complicating supply chains. If you have any stories on how your company is dealing with the crisis, please email us, editorial@undercurrentnews.com. Here's a recap of pandemic-related seafood news from Tuesday, Nov. 24:

The mechanism by which processors in the US state of Alaska determine how much to pay sockeye salmon fishermen is a "black box", and especially so this year amid the COVID-19 pandemic that sent base prices tumbling. Andy Wink of the Bristol Bay Regional Seafood Development Association, which represents the bay's drift-net fleet, and other panelists spent a 90-minute meeting last week sharing data and anecdotes to help explain why base ex-vessel prices paid to fishermen are down so sharply this year.

US processor and distributor Fortune International has completed a deal for another such firm, based in Windsor, Wisconsin: Neesvig’s. The company also operates Empire Fish, a Wauwatosa, WI-based retail store, and a state-of-the-art "fulfillment operation" in DeForest, WI.

In Chile, Salmones Camanchaca has doubled the capacity of its plant in the city of Tome after a $5 million investment to add a production line, and plans to produce 5,500 metric tons of value-added product monthly. The COVID-19 pandemic has provoked substantial demand for value-added products such as portions.

Meanwhile, there were only small changes in the prices for Chilean farmed salmon destined for the US and Brazil in week 46; US prices were marginally down, but Brazilian were up a little more.

In the Pacific, where tuna fishing observer coverage has been suspended due to the pandemic, UK NGO Human Rights at Sea has urged the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission to implement new measures on fisheries observers' safety and compliance with human rights after a spate of violence.

And Cooke Aquaculture UK said it saw an initial slump in its main salmon markets as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic, but said most of these turned out to be quite robust and that trading remained steady, if lower than usual.

Lastly, South African firm Premier Fishing and Brands saw an unfortunate combination of factors coalesce to hurt its financial performance in the financial year ended Aug. 31, 2020.

The company rated its year "reasonable" given "all the local and global challenges that the industry faced during the 2020 financial year".

title: Canadian lobster dock prices plummeted weeks before ‘Dumping Day’
content:
Canadian lobster harvesters weren’t just sharing a bad dream.

The shore prices on live hardshells in lobster fishing areas (LFAs) 35-38 really did drop as much as CAD 3.50-4.00 ($2.68-$3.06) per pound, from roughly CAD 11.00/lb to CAD 7.00/lb -7.50/lb, over a recent, nearly three-week period, reports Stewart Lamont, managing director of the Tangier Lobster Company, a large exporter in the province of Nova Scotia.

Another drop of at least $0.50 to $1 is likely on the way, predicts one Boston, Massachusetts-based dealer interviewed recently by Undercurrent News. 

That's because on Monday, Nov. 30 -- the traditional last Monday in November -- Canada is set to allow harvesting to begin in LFAs 33 and 34, the country's most prolific lobster fishing zones off the southwest coast of Nova Scotia, responsible for nearly 30% of the almost 100,000 metric tons of Homarus americanus caught annually by the country. 

It's the event hailed as "Dumping Day", named for the massive number of traps dropped into the cold Atlantic Ocean, and generally considered the true beginning of Canada's next lobster year. Though normally met with celebration, the 2020-21 lobster year in Canada is to be accompanied by even more angst than usual due to the unknown market that awaits and its corresponding prices. 

A map of Canada's lobster fishing areas as produced by the Cape Breton Fish Harvesters Association.

Of course, there’s no guarantee the two big LFAs will open on time. The season is delayed almost every year, and last year was pushed by one day before harvesters were then kept off the water further by bad weather, including gale-force winds. Canada’s lobster fishing industry considers wind speeds above 25 knots (29 miles per hour) to be unsafe.

The winds along the southwest shore were at 25 to 30 knots on Saturday before diminishing to 10 to 15 knots Sunday evening, a little more than a week out, based on the federal government's monitoring service.

Export market 'not superb, but it's not horrible'

Lamont believes he knows what caused lobster prices to rise and then fall so sharply recently. 

For starters, the US season, which is all year long but really picks up at the end of July, didn't get off to a strong beginning, and Canada was largely at the end of its supply of live lobsters when, on Oct. 14, LFA 35 -- an area known casually as the Bay of Fundy -- started its season. But that region is worked by just 99 harvesters, Lamont said.

LFAs 36, 37 and 38 -- known as the Grand Manan area -- started their season on Nov. 10 but only has about 200 harvesters.

Consider that, during Canada's 2018-19 lobster year – the most recent year for which data is available -- all four early-start LFAs produced a combined 10,352t of lobster. By comparison, LFAs 33 and 34 have more than 1,800 harvesters and produced 28,928t, almost three times more.

Stewart Lamont, managing director of Tangier Lobster, in Nova Scotia. Photograph by Jason Huffman.

The perceived lack of supply drove prices up. However, those prices then dropped when China, which is Canada's second-largest buyer of lobster behind the US, began sourcing more from the US, even though it had to pay hefty tariffs to do so. Also, both US and European demand dropped due to the coronavirus pandemic rising again and hurting the restaurant business.

"The reason the market has really come down that nobody spells out is that our Chinese clients have more availability from America at dramatically lower prices," he said. "As catches have increased, our product has been more available in the last three weeks than it was in the previous three weeks. … All [China] had to do was slow down on the buy and we would adjust our price downward, desperate for that market."

A quick review of Canadian lobster export data, as shared with the United States recently by the Lobster Council of Canada, shows how reliant the Canadian lobster industry has become on China as a buyer. 

The Canadian lobster industry still relies most heavily on the US as an export destination. The US spent $1.2 billion on Canadian lobster in 2019, though that also includes lobster that was caught in the US, processed in Canada, and sent back to the US to sell to consumers. 

China is a distant second on the list of export destinations for Canadian lobster, having spent $387.2m in 2019, though that's 144% more than the $158.5m it spent in 2018, the year the US-China trade war started. In the first eight months of 2020, China bought $286.7m worth of Canadian lobster.

Overall, Canada exported $1.0bn worth of lobster in the first eight months of 2020, which gives it a lot of ground to catch up with the final 2019 total of $2.0bn.

The export market at the moment, Lamont said, is "lackluster".

"It's not superb, but it's not horrible," he told Undercurrent. "There is less demand than normal everywhere in the world, except mainland China, in my view, and in mainland China, there's normal demand. It just has to be at a pricing that China wants."

The pandemic and the US trade war with China are just two of the unique factors at play in the Canadian lobster scene. The industry also has been dealing with the heated controversy surrounding the Sipekne’katik First Nation starting an out-of-season lobster fishery in LFA 34 in September, an action that has sparked protests and violence, including the burning of a lobster pound in Nova Scotia.

Last week the Sipekne’katik reported having caught 45t of lobster since its launch, according to Global News. The First Nation group has yet to set an end date for its own season but has said that it plans to sit out LFA 34's regular commercial season, which ends May 31.

'It sends a signal'

Meanwhile, after their big descent, lobster dock prices have been holding relatively steady in Canada for roughly the past two weeks, Lamont said.

Likewise, Undercurrent's Boston dealer source said wholesale prices in the US have changed little since Nov. 12, when Urner Barry published a range of $8.40/lb-$9.00/lb on 1.25 lb hardshell lobsters and $6.50-$7.00/lb for 1.25 lb new shell lobsters. 

But could the prices being paid now in LFAs 35-38 serve to keep the rates in LFAs 33 and 34 from sinking further?

"It certainly sends a signal," Lamont said. "Every commercial fisherman in 33 and 34 looks to see what is being paid in other LFAs, and they will have every expectation that they will get CAD 7 plus or even higher because, of course, their lobsters are better and it’s closer to Christmas."

But LFAs 33 and 34 are much larger and have much more influence, he added. And though their seasons continue for six months, it’s been estimated that as much as 30% of the lobsters harvested in the two big LFAs are typically caught in the first four days.

"It's not unexpected for prices to drop as more harvesters go on the water," Lamont said.

Few Canadian dealers are, right now, holding lobsters in storage, Lamont said. That could change at the end of the month after LFAs 33 and 34 get going, especially if prices drop.

A fisherman throws a lobster trap into coastal waters of the northwest Atlantic. Credit: 154039004/Shutterstock.com

Another big influence on lobster prices could be the prices being paid dockside in the US. A source at one wharf on Maine’s mid-coast told Undercurrent Thursday that harvesters were getting a little less than $5/lb for new shell lobster.   

Most Maine lobsters, at this time of year, are new shells, while Canadian lobsters are predominantly – anywhere from 60% to 90% -- hard shell, Lamont estimated. Hardshell lobsters are a "significantly better lobster biologically", he said. 

"Better lobster means a harder shell, a higher blood protein and more meat yield, a better dining experience," he said, adding:

"What we don't know is whether [Mother Nature will] continue this trend on Dec. 1 with the Southwest Nova Scotia season, which is the biggest season of the year. If she does, it's very helpful. If she doesn't, we're extracting 10%, 15% ... we've extracted up to 40% of the catch before ... to make sure that our client's got legitimate premium, hardshell lobster for which they will pay a premium."

The ‘joy deficit’

So, what could turn prices higher at the dock and with wholesalers?

The world’s "joy deficit", answered Lamont, referring to the lackluster lives many consumers have led since the pandemic began, sheltering in their homes and unable to enjoy public outings or socialize fully if at all.

Though restaurants may still be closed or face occupancy restrictions, Lamont hopes Americans will want to compensate by holding big celebrations at home and serve lobster during the upcoming holidays, including especially New Year’s Eve, which traditionally has been one of the US’ biggest occasions for consuming the crustacean.

Credit: Oscar C. Williams/Shutterstock.com

He pointed to several supermarket promotions held earlier in the year, including as early as May and June, where lobsters were sold for $5.99/lb, and also noted supermarkets’ previous practices of offering customers cooked products three or four days before Christmas or New Year’s.

"Ironically, I expect more lobsters to be sold in America from Canada in the month of December this year," he told Undercurrent. "I just expect them to be sold dramatically more on the retail-distribution side, as opposed to the wholesale-distribution side to restaurants, hotels, food service. All that kind of business will be dramatically, dramatically down, while the supermarket promotions will be double or triple normal, I assume."

The Nova Scotia exporter believes the best time to sell lobsters will come in January in advance of the next Chinese New Year (Feb. 12, 2021).

"January, leading into Chinese New Year, will be our time in China, as it always has been," he said, concluding with a message of hope for Canadian exporters.

title: Canadian First Nation announces plans to join others in commercial fishing
content:
Charles Sampson, chief of the Walpole Island First Nation, has informed the Canadian province of Ontario of his group's plans to establish a commercial fishing industry and is first eyeing Lake St. Clair as well as "the surrounding waters of our traditional territory", the Chatham Daily News reports.

Lake St. Clair is a 430 square-mile body of water shared with the US, resting between two of the Great Lakes, Huron and Erie. It's in close proximity to the major US city of Detroit, Michigan, and it's known for its population of walleye, yellow perch and sturgeon among other fish. It's also known for its history of concerns related to the presence of mercury. 

However, Sampson said Walpole Island officials are considering a collaboration with other First Nations in the area to look at fishing also in Lake Huron and Lake Erie.

"We believe it’s our inherent right to utilize the lakes and waters that surround us because our ancestors used those lakes, not only for routes of transportation but they also used it to sustain their livelihoods in their families in the past," Sampson said.

Sampson's announcement follows the controversial decision by the Sipekne'katik First Nation group to launch a first-of-its-kind, rights-based lobster fishery in the middle of the country's most prolific lobster fishing area (34), off the coast of Nova Scotia, during the offseason. The action has sparked anger, protests and violence, leading to the destruction of a lobster pound in Nova Scotia.

The Sipekne'katik have pointed to a Supreme Court of Canada decision on Sept. 17, 1999, affirming a treaty right for Indigenous peoples to hunt, fish and gather in pursuit of a "moderate livelihood" arising out of the Peace and Friendship Treaties of 1760 and 1761.

Sampson's remarks were made unexpectedly during a press conference in Wallaceburg, Ontario, Friday, that was focused on the province providing CAD 7.3 million ($5.6m) in funding for a local hospital.

"This economic activity will begin in the very near future and will create opportunities for our people," Sampson said about his First Nation's fishing plans. "We want to advance with our own licensing program to license our own commercial fisherman."

The Walpole Island chief reportedly acknowledged the ongoing controversy in Nova Scotia and described that situation as being on "a common action or front".

Walpole Island is known as the resting place of Tecumseh, a prominent 19th-century leader of the Native American tribe known as the Shawnee.

title: Canadian provincial seafood group declares opposition to out-of-season lobster fishery
content:
The Nova Scotia Seafood Alliance (NSSA), a provincial group that represents more than 100 seafood harvesters, processors and wholesalers, has declared its opposition to First Nation groups harvesting in Canadian lobster fishing areas (LFA) out of season, CBC reports.

NSSA president Osborne Burke is quoted as telling the news service that his group supports treaty rights to make catches as part of a "moderate livelihood" fishery but believes all harvesters should work within the regulated season and be policed by federal authorities. 

"Very clearly we're of the position that fishing should take place within the regulated seasons that have been established over the years," Burke told CBC.

The news organization said it's the first time a Canadian seafood industry group has staked a position on the controversy that picked up steam in September when the Sipekne'katik launched a first-of-its-kind, rights-based lobster fishery in the middle of the country's most prolific LFA, 34, during the offseason. The action sparked anger, protests and violence, leading to the destruction of a lobster pound in Nova Scotia.

Burke said the industry does not accept assertions from academics and the Mi'kmaq that moderate livelihood fisheries are too small to pose a conservation risk to stocks.
Commercial seasons are closed to protect molting and hungry lobsters, which are easier to catch in large numbers, he said.

"There's a reason why those seasons were established by science, by DFO [Department of Oceans and Fisheries], and by harvesters to protect a stock when they're vulnerable," he is quoted as saying. "I guess we'll have to agree to disagree on that."

Burke added, however, that his trade group does "not approve or condone threatening behavior of violence, destruction of property, vigilantism or racism of any type", adding that such behavior is not "reflective in Nova Scotia harvesters".

The comments came on the same day the federal fisheries minister raised conservation concerns in St. Peters Bay, Cape Breton, on the northeastern-most end of Nova Scotia, where a moderate livelihood fishery was launched last month by the Potlotek band. Bernadette Jordan, Canada's fisheries minister, has expressed concerns that harvesting activities have increased significantly in the area.

"What was originally intended to be fished in the number of gear and the number of vessels quickly exceeded what was originally discussed with harvesters, and that led to even further frustrations within the fishery," Burke said.

Earlier in the week, the Sipekne'katik threatened to sue the province over a law that prevents the purchase of lobster harvested by moderate livelihood licenses issued and regulated by individual bands, CBC reported.

title: EJF: Ghanaian workers report abuse aboard Chinese-owned fishing vessels
content:
An investigation by the Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF) claims to have uncovered illegal fishing practices carried out by Chinese trawl vessels operating in Ghana and abuses to local workers.

Foreign ownership of trawlers is illegal in Ghana but Chinese companies are using front companies to control the industry, EJF said. Around 90% of industrial trawlers in Ghana are ultimately owned by Chinese companies in this way, it claimed.

Chinese nationals occupy the more senior positions onboard the vessels, with Ghanaian crew in lower roles. Reports of violence, abuse, and illegal fishing are common, the EJF said in a new report and documentary.

Ghanaian workers told the NGO about human rights abuses aboard Chinese-owned trawl vessels, from beatings to a lack of drinkable water or basic medicines and punishing working hours. This abuse of the crew goes hand-in-hand with threats, the bribery of fisheries observers, and large-scale illegal fishing, it said.

According to EJF, the testimonies of Ghanaian workers "are a deeply troubling indication of the treatment of local crew onboard Chinese-operated trawlers, which are ubiquitous along the West African coast".
 
All ten Ghanaian crew interviewed by EJF had personally experienced or witnessed physical abuse at the hands of Chinese captains and officers. One man said: "Violence occurs all the time. […] those who are not fast, the captain will take anything he will get and hit you with it. Whether a stone or anything they will get. Especially the captain."

On another vessel, a Chinese national allegedly used a basket to hit a Ghanaian crew member in the head. When he retaliated, the Chinese officer is alleged to have threatened him with a knife. This treatment is combined with grueling working hours, said the men, stating that sometimes they are not allowed to sleep at all in 24 hours.
 
Living conditions on board are also appalling, the men testified. They are not allowed to sleep in the cabins, where the Chinese crew sleep, but must stay on deck under makeshift tarpaulins. The water they are given to drink is often filthy and sometimes makes them unwell. One man said: "The tank we drink from is very dirty and rusty, but we still drink from that same tank…sometimes after drinking the water, we suffer from stomach pains, vomit, and diarrhea".

In addition to the appalling conditions reported on board, none of the crew members interviewed had entered into written contracts, and some stated that they either were not told their wages at all or were given a fixed sum regardless of how long the trip took. Companies also make deductions from wages that are not agreed to in advance, said the interviewees.  

Illegal fishing

Abuse of the crew was matched by aggression towards fisheries observers, in a bid to silence them and prevent reporting of widespread illegal fishing. The three observers interviewed by EJF reported incidents such as a captain threatening to hit an observer with a metal bar when he was found trying to preserve evidence of illegal fishing. In another case, a captain threatened an observer with a knife when he tried to prevent juvenile fish from being dumped at sea. All the crew and observers EJF interviewed stated that the vessels they worked on engaged in illegal fishing practices.

Elizabeth Naa Afoley Quaye, Ghana's minister of fisheries

Chinese trawlers also target small fish closer to the coast, which would otherwise be targeted by local fishermen on small canoes. They then sell it back to local communities for profit, a practice -- known as "saiko" -- that is pushing Ghanaian fisheries to the brink of collapse, the EJF claimed.

The Ghanaian ministry of fisheries and aquaculture development did not reply to a request for comment on EJF's documentary sent by Undercurrent News.

Last year, the Ghanaian minister of fisheries, Elizabeth Naa Afoley Quaye, said it was Ghana's priority to ensure the illegal practice of saiko ended, Safety4Sea reported.

title: Canadian gov’t appoints facilitator to handle Nova Scotia lobster fishery dispute
content:
The Canadian federal government has appointed a facilitator to settle the escalating dispute between a First Nation group and commercial harvesters over an off-season lobster fishery in Nova Scotia, reports CBC.

Liberal politician Allister Surette has been appointed to resolve the dispute, sparked by the creation of an off-season fishery by the Sipekne'katik First Nation in Canada's most prolific lobster fishing zone.

However, Sipekne'katik chief Mike Sack is reportedly in talks with the federal government regarding the group's management plan, and is less concerned about discussions with local fishermen.

Sack has also raised concerns about Surette's capacity to be a neutral third-party in the matter.

The decision by the First Nation group to set up its own off-season fishery last month has led to an escalating conflict with angry commercial harvesters. A Sipekne'katik lobster pound was later burnt down, killing all lobsters inside, and leaving one man with life-threatening injuries.

Although the First Nation group's right to harvest lobster in pursuit of a "moderate livelihood" was affirmed by Canada's Supreme Court in 1999, opponents argue that fishing outside of the regulated season poses a threat to the fishery, which forms a central part of the economy in southwestern Nova Scotia.

title: Canadian cabinet ministers condemn fire, violence at lobster pound
content:
Four Canadian cabinet ministers, including Bernadette Jordan, the minister of fisheries and oceans, on Monday condemned a destructive fire at a Nova Scotia pound, used to hold lobsters caught by a First Nations group, and other acts of violence.

Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) responded to the fire in Middle West Pubnico, in the southwestern part of the province, a little after midnight on Saturday, according to multiple news accounts. One man was found to be injured and was hospitalized with life-threatening injuries. The lobsters kept at the pound were all destroyed.

The facility was one of two raided and vandalized by commercial fishermen as part of a protest of the launch of a "moderate livelihood" lobster fishery by the Sipekne'katik First Nation last month, according to multiple news accounts. 

The flames were so intense that they woke a nearby resident, who then filmed the fire from the steps of her home, CTV News reported.
 
“I could hear it before I saw it and I already knew what it was, pretty much, when I heard it. So I looked out the window and it was orange,” Pierrette D’Entremont reportedly told the news service. 

Later on Saturday morning, Perry Bellegarde, the Assembly of First Nations' national chief, called on the federal government to send police or the military for protection.

The RCMP have made two arrests in relation to the incidents, with one man charged with assault against a local Indigenous chief and another man charged with arson for allegedly burning a vehicle.

Bernadette Jordan, Canada's minister of fisheries and oceans

As reported earlier by Undercurrent News, the Sipekne'katik First Nation fishery is operating in lobster fishing area 34, Canada's most prolific, ahead of the federal season start date, which is the last Monday in November, famously known as "dumping day". The group said it plans to take less than 5% of the lobster in the area.

The new fishery's launch, on Sept. 17, came 21 years to the day after a Canadian Supreme Court ruling that affirmed a treaty right to hunt, fish and gather in pursuit of a "moderate livelihood", a term that was not problematically not defined. 

The 1999 decision affected 34 Mi'kmaq and Maliseet First Nations in the provinces of New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and also the Gaspé region of Quebec, CBC recounted. It involved Donald Marshall Jr., a Mi'kmaw man who had six years earlier caught and sold 210 kilograms of eel with an illegal net and without license outside of a Department of Oceans and Fisheries season.

The escalating violence prompted a show of solidarity in the Nova Scotia capital of Halifax on Sunday, bringing hundreds of people to Grand Parade Square to support Mi’kmaq fishers.

In a first official response from the federal government to the acts of violence, Jordan, indigenous services minister Marc Miller, crown-indigenous relations minister Carolyn Bennett and public safety minister Bill Blair held a press conference on Monday to reinforce the Supreme Court-afforded right to the Mi’kmaq of a “moderate livelihood,” the Canadian Press reported.

“No act of violence will prevent Canada from upholding that right nor the Mi’kmaq people from exercising that right,” Miller said, calling the recent attacks by non-Indigenous fishers “disgusting”.

Blair said more RCMP officers from around the eastern part of the country would be deployed to Nova Scotia to aid in peacekeeping efforts.

Additionally, prime minister Justin Trudeau said he was appalled by the acts of violence and vowed that the perpetrators would be held accountable.

“We have been working with the Mi’kmaq to implement their Treaty right – and we will continue to do so. This is the way forward,” Trudeau said.

Conservative Leader Erin O’Toole criticized Trudeau’s response as hiding behind empty words.

"His government’s dismal handling of this situation and his lack of leadership are undoing decades of relationship building since the Marshall decisions and putting lives and livelihood at risk,” O'Toole said in a statement. ​

The four Liberal Party ministers also sent a letter to Anthony Rota, speaker of the House of Commons, requesting an emergency debate so that members of Parliament could voice their concerns. The session began late Monday and, after four hours, was to resume Tuesday morning.

Speaking at the debate Monday evening, New Democratic Party leader Jagmeet Singh called on the Liberal government to develop a plan to ensure the safety and livelihood of the Mi’kmaq people, according to Global News.

“We need timelines, we need a clear plan, a clear plan of action to protect the Mi’kmaq people,” he said. “We need to see a clear plan to protect them on land when their fishery operations are on that and in water.”

Singh reportedly said there is “no question” that the Mi’kmaq fishing operation poses no threat to lobster conservation.

“Any suggestion that this is about conservation is wrong [and] is clearly an example of systemic racism,” he said.

title: First Nation starts off-season lobster fishery in Canada’s most prolific catch area
content:
The Sipekne'katik, a Canadian First Nation group, has launched a first-of-its-kind, rights-based lobster fishery in the middle of the country's most prolific lobster fishing area (LFA 34) during the offseason, and it's sparking anger, protests and violence, CBC reports. 

The Sipekne'katik's fishery, opened Sept. 17 in the province of Nova Scotia's St. Marys Bay, about 250 kilometers west of the city Halifax, is granting licenses to band members who meet management plan requirements, according to the news service. Each Sipekne'katik license authorizes 50 traps per fisher, which are to be monitored. Licenses and lobster trap tags were granted to seven harvesters on the first day.

The group said it plans to take less than 5% of the lobster in the area.

But non-indigenous commercial harvesters who work in the area say the Sipekne'katik fishery is illegal. They want the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) to enforce regulations that prohibit a commercial lobster fishery from operating when the season is closed. During the off-season — which runs from late May until late November — non-indigenous fishermen give the crustaceans time to molt and reproduce.

The dispute boiled over last weekend when about 350 lobster traps were removed by non-indigenous fishermen in St. Marys Bay, an action the Sipekne'katik say amounts to theft and vandalism.

The new fishery's launch came 21 years to the day after a Canadian Supreme Court ruling that affirmed a treaty right to hunt, fish and gather in pursuit of a "moderate livelihood", a term that was not problematically not defined, according to the CBC. 

The 1999 decision affected 34 Mi'kmaq and Maliseet First Nations in the provinces of New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and also the Gaspé region of Quebec, CBC recounted. It involved Donald Marshall Jr., a Mi'kmaw man who had six years earlier caught and sold 210 kilograms of eel with an illegal net and without license outside of a DFO season.

The court ruled that Marshall was justified because he was pursuing a "moderate livelihood" under the Peace and Friendship Treaties signed in the 1700s. 

The Canadian government of prime minister Justin Trudeau government has reached "moderate livelihood" agreements with three bands — one in Quebec and two in New Brunswick -- in the past year, according to the news service. And Bernadette Jordan, the country's fisheries minister, said earlier this month that another agreement is close in New Brunswick.

But there are no deals near for Nova Scotia.

A meeting held Monday between Jordan, Sipekne'katik chief Mike Sack, indigenous relations minister Carolyn Bennett and other chiefs produced a statement affirming that the  Mi'kmaq have a constitutionally protected treaty right to fish in pursuit of a moderate livelihood. It also said DFO, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and coast guard would deploy officers to help prevent any dangerous situations.
