title: Editor’s recap: Chile truck strike; Sykes CEO on M&A, Brexit; Red Lobster re-fi
content:
Tom Seaman, editorial director of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

As if the market impact for Chilean salmon farmers wasn't enough, truck drivers in the South American country started a strike on Aug. 27, cutting off the industry from all main markets.

The strike, which revolves around violence in the south of the country, means there will be no trucks to take salmon fillets on the 1,000 kilometer trip from processing plants to the international airport in Santiago, where the fish is loaded onto aircraft bound for US hubs like Miami or Los Angeles, Matt Craze reported. 

A drivers' protest is the latest blow to afflict the salmon industry since the outbreak of COVID-19. The sector has suffered lockdown in several farming areas, a sharp drop in prices resulting from the lengthy shutdown of hotels, restaurants and bars, and workers getting sick from coronavirus.

Sykes CEO talks Brexit, shrimp peeling issues 

Meanwhile, the fallout of the coronavirus crisis in the UK has Sykes Seafood looking at opportunistic foodservice acquisitions in its home country, Alan Dale, the company's CEO, told me. 

Sykes is in talks to acquire two London-centric foodservice distributors, Dale said. However, the uncertainty around what shape Brexit will take means Sykes' plant investment focus is in continental Europe, not the UK.

It's fair to say Dale does not have much faith in the UK government's ability to handle Brexit, which will come after the economic devastation from the coronavirus-driven lockdowns.  

"I think it's just going to be a mess. If you're looking at organizational skills needed for massive projects, let's have a quick look at how COVID has been handled," he said. "I don't have much faith in the government when COVID has been mishandled. Thirty-seven people under 40 with no previous health problems have died, the median age of death is 79.5 and they have totally trashed the economy. Absolutely trashed it."

As a result, Sykes is currently investing around €5 million in expanding the Klaas Puul Beheer plant in Edam, the Netherlands, which the UK company closed a deal for at the end of March. When the project is finished in November, the plant's capacity will have increased by some 15,000 metric tons to 25,000t, Dale said. The increase will take Sykes to 45,000-50,000t of production across all its plants. 

The pandemic is also causing significant issues for the North Sea shrimp sector, which is reliant on labor-intensive peeling houses in Morocco, Dale said. 

"Having so many peelers in production facilities has been very, very hard with COVID. And Tangier, where our main factories are, is being locked down. Buying the product has not been hard, but the associated cost of peeling has been very, very high, and hard to do. What's been difficult has been getting volume. There have been limits on how many peelers can be in production halls, and how many hours can be worked," he said. 

Thai Union not ruling out role in Red Lobster re-fi 

In the US, the pandemic has hit foodservice hard. Between April-June, US restaurant chain Red Lobster Seafood Co lost around $90m. 

It's "too early" to say if Thai Union Group will be required to provide financial support to Red Lobster, said Joerg Ayrle, group chief financial officer of the seafood group, on the firm's recent Q2 earnings call.

April-June was the "worst quarter ever" for Red Lobster, he said. Thai Union has a 25% stake in Red Lobster, with Golden Gate Capital, a private equity, owning the rest. 

It's "too early to say yes or no" as to whether financial support from Thai Union will be needed, said Ayrle. "There are no commitments out there at this moment, and the discussions are far too early to say there is or is no financial report required."

There's plenty of time for a deal to be done with lenders, he said.

"We have another nine-to-12 months to refinance the business. I think it's far too early to discuss how this will happen. Red Lobster has started discussing with several banks. They have started to reach out to the current term loan lenders, what their view is", as well as engaged Guggenheim and Solomon, said Ayrle.

Pollock fillet, surimi output down 

In Alaskan waters, the production of pollock fillets and surimi is being hampered by slow catching in US B season, as well as smaller-sized fish, sources told me. 

As of Aug. 8, US vessels have caught 928,361t of the 1.39m-metric-ton quota in the Bering Sea and the Aleutian Islands. The 2020 catch level is 67% of the quota, compared to the 74% caught to Aug. 10, 2019. In addition to the slow catching, the COVID-19 outbreak on the American Dynasty factory trawler, owned by American Seafoods Group, has also had an impact on overall production, sources said.

Up to Aug. 8, US vessels and plants have produced 41,000t of surimi, down 23% year-on-year. For pin-bone out (PBO) fillets and blocks, production is 20,100t, down 43% y-o-y. Deepskin pollock production is down 34% y-o-y, to 15,000t.

"Demand is good, so it [the lower PBO production] is not lack of orders. It is all related to fishing and fish size. Yields are much lower this season. The number of small fish is way up; you can see that in the fishmeal numbers," an experienced pollock sector source, who spoke under an agreement of anonymity, said. 

Fishmeal production is at 14,600t, down 28% y-o-y. Block production will be hard this season," he said.

Chinese province is latest to ban sale of Ecuador shrimp

Authorities in the Chinese province of Shanxi -- just to the west of Beijing -- have issued a notice banning the purchase and sale of vannamei shrimp imported from Ecuador. 

The Shanxi Provincial Market Supervision Administration issued the order on Aug. 21, temporarily suspending the purchase, sale and use of the shrimp from that date.

It states all food production and catering services in the province will suspend the purchase of Ecuadorian shrimp, and that shrimp from that country will be immediately removed from shelves.

Authorities were ordered to trace the origin of all inventories to ensure they were not from Ecuador.

This comes hot on the heels of a decision by authorities in the Chinese city of Jinan, the capital of Shandong province, to ban the sale of Ecuadorian shrimp imported before Aug. 17.

EU confirms current number of Dutch pulse trawl vessels in breach of new laws

The European Commission has responded to a complaint from the environmental NGO Bloom, acknowledging that the current number of Dutch pulse trawl vessels is in breach of the EU regulations on the practice imposed last year. 

As part of the new regulations, the Dutch are permitted to operate pulse trawl gear aboard 5% of their fleet, or 15 vessels, for research purposes until July 1, 2021, when a full and total ban on pulse trawling will be enforced by the EU.

However, 22 trawlers are still operating with pulse gear according to the environmental NGO Bloom, which it claimed puts the Dutch fleet in breach of EU law in a referral to the EU ombudsman on June 5 this year.

The European Commission has responded by confirming the validity of Bloom's complaints and acknowledging the Dutch had infringed on the new law.

India veteran urges farmers to focus on VAP as shrimp market could reach ‘all-time low’

An Indian shrimp veteran has urged farmers in India and Ecuador to focus on value-added products and to diversify their export markets, anticipating that the shrimp market could reach an "all-time low" if the coronavirus crisis extends into next year, Matilde Mereghetti reported. 

Talking during an online event organized by the Ecuadorian Camara Nacional de Acuacultura, which is taking place on Aug. 26 and 27, Manoj Sharma -- owner and director of Mayank Aquaculture, a shrimp farming company in Gujarat, India -- pointed out that raw shrimp prices have dipped below $4 per kilogram, while for value-added they range from $8-$10/kg.

US grocer files for Chapter 11, threatening Ideal Fish, Sushi Mara, Congressional

KB US Holdings, parent of the combined five-state, 35-location Northeast US grocery chains Kings Food Markets and Balducci’s Food Lover’s Market, has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection while owing money to several notable seafood distributors among others, Jason Huffman reported. 

But at least some relief may be on the way, as the Parsippany, New Jersey-based company is the subject of a $75m stalking-horse bid from New York investment firm TLI Bedrock, court documents reveal. 

The situation is one to watch for Ideal Fish, a Waterbury, Connecticut-based recirculating aquaculture system producer of branzino, a.k.a. European sea bass. Almost since the moment that the company launched, in mid-2018, Kings and Balducci’s have been among its biggest champions in retail.

Ideal Fish sells its fish to Porky Products, a Newark, New Jersey-based distributor, which then sells to the two related grocery chains, explained James MacKnight, Ideal’s director of sales and marketing, on Wednesday. Porky is KB’s largest unsecured creditor, owed $2.8m, according to the petition filed in the US Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of New York on Aug. 23.

Pandemic kills BBNC-American Seafoods deal talks

The Bristol Bay Native Corporation (BBNC) has broken off deal talks with Bregal Partners over the possible acquisition of American Seafoods, with sources citing the ongoing coronavirus pandemic as the primary cause.

BBNC's plans to put together a group to acquire American are on hold, sources said. Anchorage, Alaska-based McKinley Capital Management, a private equity involved in Rodger May's planned acquisition of Peter Pan Seafoods, was also supposed to be included in the deal plans.

"With the COVID situation, they have decided not to press on for now," one sector executive, who asked not to be named, told me.

American had COVID-19 outbreaks on three of its trawlers during the Pacific hake season in June. Then, in July, American Triumph -- one of the vessels impacted during the hake season -- had another COVID-19 outbreak while catching pollock.

title: Chile’s salmon farmers prioritize contracts, pray for quick end to truck strike
content:
As previously reported by Undercurrent News, a truckers strike started in Chile on Aug. 27 and has severed the salmon industry from its markets, as shipments can’t reach Santiago's international airport.

Producers will have prioritized shipments to their contractual customers this week, leaving the spot market for trim-D salmon fillets to be underserved if the labor action lingers, industry sources said. 

"I think the majority of producers prioritized complying with contracts at the start of the week," one senior industry source told Undercurrent. "We all think that the strike should be resolved soon, in which case it would scarcely impact the market."

Truckers cut off highways in protest at violence in Chile’s Araucania region, where members of an indigenous group are accused of carrying out random attacks on isolated highways. The truckers union announced its intention to block highways at the start of the week, to push for stiffer prison sentences for perpetrators.

The salmon industry based in southern Chile sends product on a daily basis on the 1,000 kilometer trip to Santiago, where fillets are loaded onto overnight flights to Miami, the seafood processing hub of the US. 

The uncertainty may have helped the industry to curb free-falling salmon prices in the US. Spot prices in Miami have been trending upwards this week, the industry source told Undercurrent. Prices for trim-D fillet FOB Miami declined by $0.02 last week to reach $3.50 a pound, DataSalmon said Aug. 24. That's the lowest price since 2015, and well below the breakeven cost for the industry.

Upgrade to Pro to view

A second industry source confirmed that shipments were made to clients, given the truckers announced their plans four days before taking action, allowing for contingency plans. Chile’s transport and telecommunications ministry said the Pan-American highway that dissects the South American country was partially blocked on Aug. 27. 

The truckers union has said only passenger vehicles, first responders, and trucks carrying medical supplies are allowed to travel through blockades. Chile’s interior minister, Juan Francisco Galli, said on Aug. 27 that it will hold talks with the union, but without threats or acts of extortion. 

The salmon industry relies on both the truckers and the blocked routes for the movement of key aquaculture inputs such as feed and pharmaceuticals. 

The industry has already been contending with quarantine measures to control the outbreak of COVID-19 in Chile. The city of Puerto Montt, considered the hub of the salmon industry, has been in lockdown for more than a week and the temporary measure has now been extended until Sept. 2. Though salmon industry workers are allowed to transit in the city, several industry executives said operations were partially affected as a result of lockdown.

title: Chile’s salmon industry faces fresh angst as truckers plan to sever supply routes
content:
Chilean truck drivers plan to start an indefinite stoppage as of Aug. 27, cutting off the salmon industry from all main markets.

The strike, which revolves around violence in the south of the country, means there will be no trucks to take salmon fillets on the 1,000 kilometer trip from processing plants to the international airport in Santiago, where the fish is loaded onto aircraft bound for US hubs like Miami or Los Angeles. 

A drivers' protest would be the latest blow to afflict the salmon industry since the outbreak of COVID-19. The sector has suffered lockdown in several farming areas, a sharp drop in prices resulting from the lengthy shutdown of hotels, restaurants and bars, and workers getting sick from coronavirus.

Chile salmon prices go on falling, Scottish rebound, Norwegian dip
 

The truck drivers' threat to halt activities results from a violent ambush of a truck carrying cement in the Araucania region, which is in the center-south of Chile. Ambushers are said to have injured the nine-year-old daughter of a truck driver during an attack on a road linking two cities in the region, before setting fire to the vehicle. The Araucania region has seen a recent uprising by groups representing the interest of the Mapuches, an indigenous group. 

"The situation in the Araucania region is at the very limit and the government needs to enforce rule of law," Alejo Apraiz, a truck drivers' union leader, said in a televised broadcast.  

The stoppage will be punishing for the salmon sector, which relies totally on trucks to deliver salmon processed in the far south of Chile to Santiago. Trucks also take major supplies of frozen salmon overland to the Brazilian market, crossing Argentina. 

The truck drivers’ action will go on indefinitely until an agreement is reached by the government to resolve the violence in Araucania, it said. The union called for a series of measures to guarantee safety in Chile which, according to them, is succumbing to terrorists and narco-terrorists. One of the measures include draft law changes in congress to stiffen criminal penalties for attacking trucks.  

A lengthy dispute will be painful for Chile’s salmon farmers. Salmones Camanchaca recently announced losses for the second quarter of the year, impacted by very low prices of coho salmon and heightened costs including freight charges that surged amid COVID-19. Several other salmon companies will publish second-quarter reports in the coming days and weeks. Prices for Atlantic salmon are their lowest since 2015. 

The farming companies in the past have had to declare force majeure on shipments to major US retail customers. An example of that occurred in 2016 when fishermen on the island of Chiloe, where two-thirds of Chile’s processing plant capacity is located, severed routes to the mainland. 

The industrial action will also hurt the industry in other ways, from supplying raw materials to feed plants in Los Lagos to the movement of other key inputs such as smolt from freshwater sites and sea-pen equipment to fjord areas.

title: EJF claims abuse, illegal fishing in Taiwan’s fleet
content:
Surveys conducted by the Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF) led the NGO to claim that violent abuse of migrant workers and flagrant illegal fishing are systemic problems across Taiwan’s distant water fishing fleet.

It surveyed crew from 62 vessels, with 24% reporting physical abuse and 92% claiming to have had their wages withheld. Sharks were finned and bodies discarded on half of the vessels, crewmembers said.

Between August 2018 and November 2019, EJF interviewed 71 former Indonesian fishers who had worked on 62 Taiwanese vessels. Workers from nearly a quarter (24%) of the vessels reported violent physical abuse, mostly being kicked and beaten by the captain or senior crew. One man, Supri from Indonesia, claims he was locked in a freezer by the captain while he was still wet from the shower.
 
On the same trip, Supri said he was electrocuted with a stun gun by a fellow crew member under orders from the captain. The tool is used to kill fish, and the shocks left Supri weak and in pain.   
 
"The individual stories are damning, but the systemic nature of the issues informs a series of reforms that NGOs say are urgently required, including the introduction of cameras on vessels," said EJF. "Despite recent encouraging statements from Taiwan’s government promising to adopt key international standards, vessels currently operate with limited oversight. Over three-quarters of overseas ports used by Taiwan’s fishing fleet have no Taiwanese inspectors."
 
92% of the crew interviewed claimed to have had their wages withheld, creating conditions that can lead to debt bondage. 82% worked excessive overtime, with many fishers reporting that they had to work up to 20 hours per day with very little time to rest.

The abuse of the crew was matched by the flagrant disregard for ocean wildlife and the law. Protected species of dolphins were harpooned as they rode ships’ bow waves, hauled aboard, and used as bait to catch sharks. These practices were reported by workers from eight of the vessels. The crew from half of the vessels reported illegally finning sharks and discarding the bodies, and on seven of the boats, the crew reported catching and killing false killer whales.

EJF’s findings follow a report released by Greenpeace East Asia in March 2020 that documented "suspected forced labor and environmental destruction" on Taiwanese vessels. 
 
The 2020 Trafficking in Persons report released by the US State Department last month also raised serious concerns, saying "migrant fishermen have reported senior crew [to] employ such coercive tactics as threats of physical violence, beatings, withholding of food and water, retention of identity documents, wage deductions, and non-contractual compulsory sharing of vessel operational costs to retain their labor".

The report also found that "insufficient staffing and inspection protocols continued to impede efforts to combat forced labor on Taiwan-flagged and -owned fishing vessels in the highly vulnerable distant water fleet". Though these findings did not result in Taiwan being downgraded in the report’s rating system, they point to the urgent need for reform, said EJF.

title: MSC to fund £100k for observer safety research; action follows death
content:
The Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) on Thursday announced that it was allocating £100,000 ($126,941) to help fund projects and initiatives aimed at improving the safety and welfare of fishery observers.

The action follows the death, in March, of Eritara Aati Kaierua on board the Win Far 636, a tuna purse seiner, in the Western Central Pacific Ocean. As reported, the 40-year-old father of four was found lying on the floor of his locked cabin with a head wound and bruising to his neck.

The incident, which is still being investigated by police, followed persistent reports of the dangers, including violence and intimidation, that observers are facing globally. It's something that MSC said it condemns. Greenpeace, the Association of Professional Observers, and the publication of a recent report by the organization Human Rights at Sea have all recently drawn attention to the issue. 

MSC said its contribution would be deployed through its Ocean Stewardship Fund in the next round, which opens for applications in September 2020. The money will also support initiatives focused on the use of electronic monitoring and other technologies designed to help observers and deliver assurance of fishing operations.

MSC clarified that it does not require fisheries to work with observers as a part of its certification requirements. Still, it added that, in practice, many fisheries rely on observers to collect the crucial evidence needed for sustainable fisheries management, especially in remote parts of the world.

"Observers play a vital role ensuring the monitoring, compliance, and surveillance of commercial fishing activities," MSC said in a statement. "Mandated by fishery management organizations, their work focuses on collecting data to enable effective regulation of marine activity. However, according to the Association of Professional Observers, the isolated and sometimes contentious nature of their jobs can lead to attempts at bribery, intimidation and violence."

"Governments, law enforcement agencies and regulatory authorities must do more to ensure observer safety," said Rupert Howes, MSC's CEO. "But we recognize – as part of the wider sustainable seafood community - that MSC also has a part to play. We want to do so in a way which is practical, by helping those who are already working in this field, pilot and test promising initiatives. By working collaboratively with others, we believe we can help protect the human rights of observers and support them to carry out their vital work safeguarding our oceans."

title: US crab chain sues county officials for not protecting business from protests
content:
A chain of five crab restaurants in the US state of Maryland is suing officials for $400,000 for allegedly failing to protect its business from protests and other activities that were a response to racist social media posts by the owners' son.

Vince's Crab House names Baltimore County executive John Olszewski, the area's top government official, and Melissa Hyatt, chief of the Baltimore County Police Department, in the lawsuit filed in a state court.

As reported earlier by Undercurrent News, the business owned by Vince and Brenda Meyer has confronted protesters in front of at least two of its locations, in the towns of Middle River and Fallston, since early June.

Screenshots of Vincent Meyer II's social media accounts that circulated online included one on Facebook where he took a jab at Black Lives Matter, writing: "There is one place I bet the protesters/rioters won't light on fire or break into or even block the road to ... the social services buildings." The message was followed by four laughing emoji.

More than 100 protesters were reported to have descended on the restaurant locations between June 6 and at least until about July 1. The Baltimore County Police Department began dispatching one to three patrol cars daily, but "failed to make any arrests, write any police reports or issue citations for illegal activity," the restaurant owners say in their 23-page civil complaint, filed in the state's Circuit Court for Baltimore County.

Brenda Meyer said she was told by police officers on several occasions that they were ordered to "stand down".

Protesters have trespassed onto the business property, opened the doors of the business to yell at customers, employees and family and followed customers to their vehicles to call them racists, the complaint said. They've followed the owners home and even attempted a physical attack on the owners' daughter, it said.

The owners said they've received telephone calls in the middle of the night and received death threats, forcing them to spend $40,000 to hire private security guards.  The owner's Social Security number was reportedly posted online.

"This litigation is not about plaintiff's agreement or disagreement with the inspiration for the protesters, or the viewpoints expressed by the people occupying that area," the complaint states. "Instead, it is about the Baltimore County's active, knowing endorsement and support of a destructive occupation of a small Middle River business to the detriment of the well-being of those who own, patronize, and work in the small business." 

Linda Brown, the Laurel, Maryland-based attorney representing the restaurant chain, did not return earlier calls from Undercurrent for comment. However, as reported earlier, the owner's son tried apologizing for his posts, commenting that 75% of his parents' customer base is black.

"I have a ton of remorse," Vincent Meyer II said in a video. "I haven't been able to express it. Obviously my apology video wasn't apologetic enough. ... I was kind of blindsided. I wasn't prepared. Some of the stuff was so old I had forgotten I had even said these things."

The protesters, meanwhile, have presented a different story. They told a local station that the business owners came outside, taunted them and aimed sprinklers at them, creating an environment that caused customers to threaten protesters with violence, even spitting. One June 21, police arrested one man for threatening protesters at the Middle River business with a bat, the Baltimore Sun reported.

"Until we see a 'For Lease' sign on the building, our mission is to keep pressing on, our mission is to change this world into a world where racism is not tolerated," said Kellie Vaughn, a woman who reported to be the leader of the "Shut Down VCH Protest".

title: Labor rights group cites fishing cases in request for US to drop Thailand trafficking grade
content:
The US State Department should demote Thailand in its upcoming trafficking report based on its record of abuses in the fishing sector especially, the Seafood Working Group (SWG) recommends.

The coalition of about 60 human rights, labor and environmental organizations, put together by the International Labor Rights Forum, issued a 32-page report on Tuesday that it says makes the case for the US State Department moving the Southeast Asian nation from its current standing of Tier 2 to the Tier 2 Watch List in its 2020 Trafficking in Persons (TIP) Report, expected in June.  

The SWG report details as many as 23 cases of labor abuse from organizations who work directly with migrant workers in a range of labor sectors throughout Thailand, known especially for its exports of shrimp and tuna among other seafood species. That includes an incident in 2018 where seven children from Myanmar between the ages of 14 and 17 were recruited by a labor broker and told they would be working at a poultry slaughterhouse but instead were brought to a fishing boat in the Pattani province.

“After experiencing horrible working conditions and witnessing physical violence of other workers, one 17-year-old child jumped off of the boat into the sea,” recounts the report.

Credit: Bumbim Pensinee/Shutterstock.com

After the child was rescued by another fishing boat, he was taken to a juvenile detention center and interviewed by a human trafficking team. The employer, after discovering the one worker missing, transferred all of the other children on to a boat and returned them to Myanmar. The case was difficult to prosecute, as the witnesses refused to travel back to Thailand to testify and the boat owner ultimately was acquitted.

In another case, reported in May 2019, a more than 50-year-old Thai fisherman jumped out of a second-floor window of a karaoke bar in the Songkhla province and hurt his knee. The fisherman had been unable to escape his debt to a boat owner, who was going to sell him to another fishing boat.

What it means to move down in grade

Tier 2 countries are determined to not fully meet the minimum requirements of the U.S. Trafficking Victims Protection Act (TVPA), a law passed in 2000, but are found to be “making significant efforts to bring themselves into compliance with those standards,” the State Department explains in its June 2019 report.

Also on the Tier 2 list, which includes about 100 countries, are Germany, Greece, India, Indonesia, Ireland and Italy.

The 40 countries on the Tier 2 Watch List, however, are seen as having a high number trafficking victims and a failure to provide evidence of efforts to combat the problem. They also include the likes of Vietnam and Nicaragua. 

Should Thailand fall even further to a Tier 3 rating, the US government could determine to no longer provide the country with nonhumanitarian, nontrade-related foreign assistance or withhold funding for government official or employee participation in educational and cultural exchange programs.

About 20 countries are on the Tier 3 list, including China, Cuba, Iran, Russia and Venezuela.

'The Thai government must do more...'

The Thai seafood industry began facing the threat of trade sanctions from Western nations after media exposure in 2014 of poor working conditions and slave labor. In response, Thailand's government began instituting reform measures, most effectively by strengthening its legal, policy and regulatory framework. But the measures have apparently failed to substantially cut the use of forced labor.

SWG's report highlights abuses in other sectors, too, including the apparel industry where nearly 45,000 migrant worker are registered under a precarious legal status that denies them labor protection, are rarely paid minimum wage, and are intimidated by employers when they try to negotiate for better working conditions, the group advised.

The report also describes examples of apparent favoritism for employers by enforcement authorities and inadequate support, including state-run shelters that were intended for trafficking victims being used to hold migrants.

It says the Thai government has failed to make sufficient progress in several key areas, particularly in the identification and prosecution of forced labor and in undertaking effective labor inspections. The government has not effectively addressed some of the root causes that make migrant workers vulnerable to human trafficking: widespread debt and document retention practices and obstacles to workers changing employers, the report advises.

“The information we obtained indicates that migrant workers remain highly vulnerable to human trafficking. The Thai government must do more to adequately protect victims and prosecute offenders,” said Esmeralda López, ILRF’s legal and policy director.

Thailand’s ranking has steadily increased in the TIP report since 2015, when the government initiated significant reforms following exposés of illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing practices and labor abuse on vessels, SWG noted.

In January 2019, the Thai government became the first in Asia to ratify International Labor Organization Convention 188 on Work in Fishing. However, labor abuse and exploitation of migrant fishers is ongoing and widespread, the group said.

UN report finds working conditions improving

The SWG report came on the same day that the United Nation's International Labor Organization (ILO) issued a report, based on surveys conducted in 2019, that suggests working conditions are otherwise getting better in Thailand's seafood sector, which employs more than 350,000, according to the Associated Press.

The monthly pay has improved for workers, however. Those working in fishing in 2019 were paid an average THB 12,730 ($404), up 28% over 2017, and those in the seafood industry were paid THB 10,640, up 15%, the ILO found.

However, the ILO report also noted that its survey found 14% of those engaged in fishing and 7% of those in seafood processing were subject to some form of forced labor,The ILO report also noted the use of migrants workers from neighboring Myanmar and Cambodia being widespread, especially on fishing boats.

title: AquaChile plants attacked as protests continue to disrupt Chile salmon shipments
content:
With additional reporting by Tom Seaman and Matt Craze in Qingdao, China

Arsonists and looters attacked Chilean salmon farmer Empresas AquaChile's plants in the Los Lagos region earlier this week, as demonstrations in the country continue to disrupt Chilean salmon exports, industry sources told Undercurrent News.

AquaChile, which is owned by Chile's largest salmon producer, Agrosuper, managed to avoid the destruction of its plant in Calbuco, after an intentional fire was set at the facilities in the evening of Oct. 29, a company spokesperson told Undercurrent. At the same time, a group of people tried to loot the firm's Calbuco plant, also in the Los Lagos region, and set fire to it, but security guards at the plant were able to extinguish the fire and prevent people from entering.

"We actually had an incident yesterday [on Oct. 29] at the Calbuco plant. The intentional fire they set was in the gatehouse, and could be controlled in time so it did not affect the facilities of the plant," an AquaChile's spokesperson confirmed to Undercurrent on Oct. 30.

"Last night in the Los Lagos region we had a couple of unfortunate incidents that we managed to control. On the one hand, a group of people tried to loot our Calbuco plant and set fire to the goal, but the timely action of those present allowed to extinguish the fire and prevent outsiders from entering. On the other hand, in Quellon, a group tried to enter the plant, but the support of security and our own collaborators managed to dissuade them," the spokesperson explained. 

"The last days have been complex for the whole country," AquaChile's spokesperson also said, adding it decided to close its Quellon plant, having agreed with its workers to stop "when there is violence". "We hope that public security will soon be restored in Quellon," the company added.

Fellow salmon producer Salmones Austral has also suspended processing activity completely at its plant in Quellon last Tuesday for a week while keeping its Puerto Montt plant open with reduced activity, a source with the company told Undercurrent.

Protests' disruption continues

Meanwhile, most plants in Chile are operating at a rate of only one shift a day, to avoid workers entering and leaving processing plants at night-time, at least five industry sources told Undercurrent.

Chile’s salmon farmers are navigating the protests to get deliveries to their customers despite prolonged protests in the South American country. 

The protests are affecting all three major stages of production, from harvest to the processing plant and distribution, a major producer in the Aysen region of Chile told Undercurrent. The company is currently only operating one eight-hour shift a day, compared to three shifts usually, but without any hindrance in distribution, the person said. A prolonged conflict would create problems at the farm level.

“The problem is that you have the fish in the water and they keep eating,” the executive at the Aysen producer also noted. “Once they get over a certain weight they start to lose value and companies will start to lose money.”

The protests in Chile are hitting the country’s salmon logistics and mean supply is short for China, said Eduardo Goycoolea, the chairman of sales joint venture New World Currents.

The protestors against the government have cut off logistics from the island of Chiloe, where a big chunk of Chile’s salmon comes from. So, a route of trucking to Santiago for flying to China, the US and other markets is out of action. 

Similarly to May 2016 during a fishermen’s protest, processors located on the island of Chiloe have struggled to ship salmon to the mainland for the 1,000 kilometer trip to Santiago airport, as protestors erect roadblocks on the sole main road that connects the town of Quellon with the ferry crossing of Pargua. The island is home to about two-thirds of Chile’s salmon processing capacity, plus feed plant Salmofood.

One major company consulted by Undercurrent said it is managing to send about 30% to 40% of its scheduled shipments to the mainland amid the chaos. The situation changes from one day to the next, the person said.

A fourth company, which processes its salmon on the mainland, has not experienced any setbacks with its distribution side of the business.

Most of the processors on Chiloe have also experienced disrupted shifts as workers join flash protests that have been seen around the country to push for better living standards and higher public sector spending.

Huge demonstrations ongoing in Chile, sparked by a now-suspended metro fare hike in Santiago, the country's capital, have widened to the rest of the country since Oct. 18, with roadblocks and flight suspensions disrupting salmon shipments.

Chile has pulled out of hosting two major international summits, including a UN climate change conference, due to anti-government protests. President Sebastian Pinera said the decision had caused him "pain" but his government needed "to prioritize re-establishing public order", BBC reported.

title: Arson suspected in destruction of Nova Scotia First Nation’s fishing vessel
content:
The Cape Breton Regional Police Service, in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia, is investigating the burning of a fishing vessel belonging to the Membertou First Nation following recent tensions over fishing rights.

The Membertou II, which was discovered engulfed in flames early on Saturday morning at the Dobson Yacht Club, in Westmount, NS, in Sydney Harbor, sustained significant damage, reports CTV, an Atlantic Canada TV network. The vessel is captained by John Paul, the son of Membertou chief Terry Paul.

It wouldn't be the first time the Membertou have suffered from acts of vandalism in recent times. According to a statement from the First Nation, 100 lobster traps were cut in September, leading to a loss of CAD 10,000 ($7,558) to the community.

title: Irish fishing chief warns of no-deal Brexit ‘flashpoints’ at sea
content:
The chief executive of the Killybegs Fishermen’s Organisation in Ireland has warned that failure to achieve an orderly Brexit will precipitate “chaos and conflict at sea” with port blockades across Europe being a very real prospect. 

Sean O’Donoghue also stated that should Irish and other EU fleets be denied access to UK waters after midnight on Oct. 31 next, "there will be flashpoints all across Europe in the Irish Sea, North West of Donegal, off the South East Coast of Ireland, the English Channel and in the North Sea in scenes potentially reminiscent of the cod wars of the 1940s, ‘50s and ‘70s".

Flow of UK trucks into France could drop to 40-60% on day one of no-deal Brexit

French fishermen will not stand on ceremony, and port blockades which would deny access to all fish, fishery products as well as other products irrespective of origin and the resultant disorder, chaos, and most likely violence, will not be pretty, he said. "We got a taste of what can happen at sea last year with a scallop dispute between UK and France in the Channel."

The situation would be uncontrollable, with almost 3,000 kilometers of a "water border" to be policed and potentially devastating consequences for fleets which would have to be tied up, he added. "The reaction of the French will be the acid test, they won’t respond favorably to being denied access to UK waters but neither will the Irish and the other EU fleets which have traditionally fished in UK waters."

Ultimately, it would be the death knell for many coastal fishing communities with the demise of the Irish seafood sector to the tune of between 30% and 50% and projected job losses of between 30% and 40% in the Irish fishing industry, said O’Donoghue.

He stressed that it wasn’t too late to avoid a ‘no-deal’ Brexit and emphasized the importance of maintaining the link between fisheries negotiations and the Future Trade Agreement as well as sound science-based fisheries management. "Even in a no-deal, we have to avoid this mayhem at sea and ashore. The EU offer to apply the status quo in the short-term, provided it was reciprocated by the UK, would go a long way to avoiding this immediate chaos."

Irish fishermen are on the verge of being unable to access the waters which provide on average more than 30% of their catch -- and this average masks the reliance they have on UK waters for mackerel (60%) and nephrops (40%) which are the two main money “spenders” for the industry.

title: UK expert warns violence at sea could be reality of no-deal Brexit
content:
Fears are growing that a no-deal Brexit could lead to serious disorder in the UK's waters and possible loss of life – which could then trigger a wider escalation of tensions, reports the Independent.

Following a no-deal Brexit there could be “a real risk” of violence breaking out between British and EU fishermen, many of whom depend on access to UK fishing grounds for their economic survival, believes one UK fisheries expert.

“A toxic mix of historical grievances, real and perceived unfair treatment, and, in some cases, a lack of clarity about legal rights is bound to result in fishing disputes,” said professor Richard Barnes of the University of Hull.

“Together with inflammatory newspaper headlines, broken political promises, and broken livelihoods, we will have all the ingredients for violent confrontations at sea,” he said. “This is likely to be part of the reality of a no-deal Brexit."

He stated the UK lacks the practical capacity to fully enforce fishing law in all its waters -- something the government has just accidentally all but confirmed.

title: ‘Comprehensive’ soy assurance body adopted by ASC for final 2019 feed standard release
content:
The Aquaculture Stewardship Council (ASC) has announced that it recognizes the Round Table on Responsible Soy Association (RTRS) as the most comprehensive standard for soy feed in the upcoming final release of its official feed standard in Q1 2019.

The ASC's official standard for feed was publicly announced in August 2014 and has since gone through two public consultations in 2015 and 2017. In all previous editions, the RTRS standard has been acknowledged as the most comprehensive certification available for soy suppliers, and this will not change in the feed standard's definitive version -- due to be published in Q1 2019.

“We are pleased to see the ASC join a number of other organizations that recognize and promote the value of the RTRS standard," said RTRS executive director Marcelo Visconti in a press statement.

The organization sold over 70,000 credits of certified soy in 2017 to a multitude of ASC members across the US, South America, Asia and Africa, a quantity that Visconti said "demonstrates the strong commitment of the industry to sustainable chains". 

RTRS has increased the volume of credits sold year-on-year, with 2017 representing an 8% rise relative to 2016. Visconti is optimistic this trend will continue.

"I am convinced that this process will increase in scale soon," he said.

Most recently, RTRS brought together 50 leaders who were interested in incorporating certified soy into their own value chains at a workshop with Chilean feed supplier Salmofood in November.

From 2006 to the present

The RTRS was founded in Switzerland in 2006, following the rules set out in the Basel Convention. The organization has nearly 200 members, which in turn cover three constituencies.

According to RTRS vice-president Belinda Howell: "There's the growers, industry trade and finance, and the civil society, which is effective for environmental and social NGOs. It’s a carefully structured, multi-stakeholder organization to balance the views and inputs of all of those different constituencies". 

Soy supply has become an increasingly important bottleneck in the salmon aquaculture supply chain. Argentina's soybean meal and lecithin, and Brazil's soybean protein concentrate are both crucial ingredients in salmon feed, with few economically viable alternatives available to European salmon farmers.

The RTRS standard exists to provide assurances for feed producers and retailers that their soy has been produced responsibly -- an issue becoming more and more prevalent as consumers come to demand much greater product traceability, says Howell.

"If they [feed companies] have RTRS-certified soy in their feed supply chain, then they are assured for instance that it avoids deforestation, and a whole range of other good practices around the use of pesticides, fertilizers and the like," Howell told Undercurrent News.

"Similarly, we have standards on social issues, ensuring good worker conditions and economic development for local communities around these soy farms."

According to an RTRS presentation, the organization certified over 4 million metric tons of soy produced in 2017, primarily in Brazil and Argentina, but also with certified producers in the US, India and Mozambique among others.

On the other hand, the majority of aquaculture producers purchasing RTRS soy are based in Europe, with 47% of the total RTRS soy being acquired by the Netherlands, and a further 18% by feed producers in Scandinavia.

"Generally, aquaculture producers and retailers will specify in their buying policies RTRS-certified soy for their feed," said Howell. "This means the retailers can then specify RTRS-certified soy as an example of how they take action against deforestation in their supply chains, for instance."

Accroding to Howell, RTRS has a third-party certification system, Global Accreditation Services, which accredits its certification bodies. To obtain RTRS certification, soy suppliers must therefore turn to one of the accredited auditors, who will then conduct a thorough assessment of a sample of its farms to determine if it meets the criteria set out by RTRS.

The auditing process can take several days, depending on a company's previous affiliations with RTRS.

"How long that whole certification process takes from start to end depends on the level of preparedness of the company itself. Long-term members of RTRS who have been working on the standards for some time will be in a better position than someone who is starting from scratch, as it takes some preparation time for companies to be ready for certification," Howell told Undercurrent.

The Brazilian report

A scathing report was released in October which identified instances of violence, deforestation and slave-like employment taking place at three Brazilian soy companies: Caramaru, Selecta and Imcopa. The trio supplied soy to some of the largest aquafeed firms in Norway, including Marine Harvest, Skretting and BioMar Group.

Howell confirmed that of the companies named in the report, which had been a joint project by The Future in Our Hands and the Rainforest Fund, only Selecta had been certified by the RTRS for 60,000t of its production. She noted that BioMar and Skretting (via its partnership with Nutreco) were also RTRS members.

However, Howell clarified that the RTRS standard had not been called into question by the ongoing investigation, and that the code of conduct breaches under scrutiny had taken place in other parts of Selecta's business.

"There have not been any major investigations of RTRS certification itself," she told Undercurrent. "RTRS would typically investigate where its certification is being questioned by a complaint or accusation against it; but I don't believe that's the case here."

"It is advisable for those soy producers and the aquafeed companies to become members so they can start to get closer to those requirements of the standards as well, and learn how certification will help them to prevent these kinds of accusations," she added.

Contact the author dan.gibson@undercurrentnews.com

title: Key Norway aquafeed soy suppliers accused in report scandal
content:
Three Brazilian soy companies that ultimately act as suppliers to some of Norway’s largest fish-farming companies are alleged to have an association with violence, deforestation and slave-like employment, Dagbladet reports.

The report, set to be published by The Future in Our Hands and the Rainforest Fund at the end of October/ early November, details the business practices of Caramaru, Selecta and Imcopa. The trio supply soya, which is eventually used in feed at some of the largest aquafeed firms in Norway, including Marine Harvest, Skretting and BioMar.

Ola Helga Hjetland, communications manager at Marine Harvest – which is the fourth largest seafood company in the world, according to Undercurrent News’ 2018 report – said the firm would need to review their existing supply contract in light of the allegations.

"We are very serious about the accusations presented in the report from the Rainforest Foundation and the Future in our Hands. If this is correct, there is a clear breach of both our ‘code of conduct for suppliers’, which all suppliers must follow, and our ‘feed policy’” said Hjetland, according to Dagbladet. “We will now review our documentation and address this with our suppliers as soon as possible.”

Directors at Cargill, Skretting, Europharma, and BioMar also contacted Dagbladet indicating that should the accusations prove true, they too will consider there to have been a breach of the company’s supplier code of conduct. Skretting added that it has contacted an independent auditor in Brazil to check the findings of the report and the production practices of their suppliers.

Jan Sverre Rostad, vice-president of BioMar, also added that Norway's fish-farmers have become increasingly dependent on the Brazilian market since Brazil's non-genetically modified soy is the Scandinavian country's only permitted alternative for use in fish feed.

title: ‘Lobster War’ documentary to debut at Boston film festival
content:
Lobster War, a new documentary by award-winning Boston (Massachusetts) Globe reporter David Abel and filmmaker Andy Laub, blame climate change, increased lobster populations and a centuries-old land dispute for helping to breed discontent between lobster harvesters in the US state of Maine and those in Canada, the Boston edition of Metro reports.

The film, which is set to premiere Sunday on the closing night of the GlobeDocs Film Festival, in Boston, focuses on the 277 square miles of disputed waters – dubbed the "gray zone" – off the coast of Machias Seal Island. The dispute over which country owns a thin strip of land in the area dates back to the Revolutionary War, but incidents of sabotage and threats of violence have increased recently.

title: Human Rights Watch: labor abuses persist in Thai fishing fleets
content:
The Thai government has failed to address widespread labor rights abuses in Thailand’s fishing fleets, Human Rights Watch (HRW) said Tuesday in a letter to senior EU officials.

HRW urged the EU to renew efforts for "serious reforms" of Thai policies and practices to "effectively curtail forced labor and other abusive treatment of migrant fishing workers", stating that Thai government pledges to improve labor rights have resulted in "little improvement". 

The letter comes as the European Parliament sends a "positive signal" about the EU upgrading Thailand’s status in regard to illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing from the current ‘yellow card’ given to the country by the EU in 2015, reports the Nation. 

During a consultation between the European Commission’s directorate-general for employment and the Thai Ministry of Labour on May 16-17, 2018, in Brussels, Thai government officials pledged to improve labor conditions in its fishing industry. It followed by pledging in June to ratify International Labour Organization (ILO) protocols. 

However, HRW said migrant workers still enter into fishing work in debt bondage, and are prevented from changing employers, not paid on time, and paid below the minimum wage, citing its own 2018 report, “Hidden Chains: Rights Abuses and Forced Labor in Thailand’s Fishing Industry.”

"Captains compelled predominantly Burmese and Cambodian fishing workers to work overtime hours well beyond those set out in law. Boat owners and captains violated legal requirements to pay wages at least monthly, frequently paying fishing workers once every six months – or in some cases once a year at subminimum wages. And a reform requiring monthly wage payments by electronic bank transfer has been thwarted by unscrupulous captains who keep the fishing workers’ ATM cards and bank books."

"Threats, intimidation, and physical violence by captains, officers, and fleet owners against fishing workers were still reported," it said.

HRW added labor inspections at Port-in, Port-out (PIPO) checkpoints remained "perfunctory", while labor inspections at sea often failed to follow basic procedures. Obstacles remained to establishing unions.

The Thai government should, therefore, "immediately take all necessary steps to ensure that [ILO's Forced Labour Convention (No. 29)] is implemented effectively", adding it should also ratify ILO Conventions on Freedom of Association (No. 87) and the Right to Organize and Collective Bargaining (No. 98).

“The Thai government’s reforms in the fishing industry still fall far short of resolving serious labor rights abuses,” said Brad Adams, Asia director at HRW. “The EU should further press Thailand to protect the rights, health, and safety of migrant fishing workers. European consumers should be confident that their seafood from Thailand does not involve trafficked or forced labor.”

title: Greenpeace claims evidence links Taiwan fleet, FCF to human rights abuses
content:
New evidence links human rights abuses to Taiwan’s international fishing fleet, including major seafood trader Fong Chun Formosa Fishery Company (FCF), according to NGO Greenpeace.

"This has serious implications for its global supply chains, and exposes the ongoing failure of the Taiwan government’s approach to address human trafficking and labor abuse."

Conducted over the course of more than a year, investigations show that Taiwan’s fishery supply chain is still tainted by human rights abuses, despite the law change in early 2017 to protect migrant fishers on Taiwanese vessels, said Yi Chiao Lee, global investigation lead for the report at Greenpeace East Asia.

"This means there is high probability that tainted seafood is making its way into sushi shops and dinner plates in Asia, Europe and the Americas.”

In the Greenpeace East Asia report, "Misery at Sea", investigators from Taiwan and New Zealand found five members of the convicted human trafficking ring, Giant Ocean, living openly in Taiwan, it claimed. "Despite being considered fugitives, at least some of the individual members continue to be involved in the recruitment of migrant workers - predominantly from South East Asia - for Taiwanese fishing vessels, with the full knowledge and negligence of Taiwanese authorities."

Taiwanese labor rights group Yilan Migrant Fishermen Union provided evidence to Greenpeace on the death of a young Indonesian fisherman, who it claimed was beaten and abused. Yet Taiwanese authorities failed to properly investigate his death, and there was no prosecution. Taiwan’s Fisheries Agency claims he simply died from sickness.

In another investigation, prison-based interviews shine a new light on the 2016 murder of the captain of the Vanuatuflagged Taiwanese-owned vessel, Tunago No. 61.

"Speaking with the six convicted crew members, Greenpeace investigators learnt that in the days and months leading up to the Captain’s murder, the crew were frequently forced to work 20 hours a day and seven days a week, faced repeated physical violence and verbal abuse, sleep deprivation, a lack of adequate sustenance, discrimination, and were scared for their lives."

Misery at Sea analyses Taiwan’s low-cost business model and chronic flaws in legal and regulatory framework, which helps create an environment where cases of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, human rights violations and labor abuse are all too common, said Greenpeace.

In 2015, Taiwan was given an EU "yellow card" warning for its insufficient cooperation in combating illegal fishing, which defy international standards. In September 2018, EU officials will review Taiwan’s status and decide whether to lift the warning.

The report also looks into the role of FCF, which is one of the world’s big three traders, and has strong links to markets in Japan, Americas and Europe. FCF was implicated in two of the three cases, Greenpeace claimed.

"The Taiwan government must guarantee in-depth investigations of such cases,” said Yi Chiao Lee. “It must put in place legislation that protects workers and human rights and ensure full implementation; and companies like FCF must urgently review their business models and put in place the means to ensure that human rights abuses and poor environmental standards endemic to parts of this industry are effectively eliminated.”

title: Labor conditions improving in Thai fishing industry, survey finds
content:
Things are getting better for workers in the Thai commercial fishing industry, but some problems persists, finds a study funded by the European Union.

Some 434 workers in Thailand's commercial fishing industry from across 11 provinces, including mostly migrant laborers, were surveyed between March and April 2017 for the International Labor Organization’s three-year Ship to Shore Rights Project. The results show fewer reports of physical violence and few workers (less than 1%) under the age of 18. Also, workers reported higher average monthly wages (before deductions) and almost half (43%) with written contracts, up from four years ago.

However, several disparities remain. More than a third (34%) of workers are still being paid less than the minimum wage and nearly a quarter (24%) saw their pay withheld by vessel owners, some for 12 or more months, the survey showed. Also, 34% did not have access to identity documents.

title: EJF film reveals labor rights violations on Taiwanese vessels
content:
A new investigative film from the Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF) claims to have uncovered evidence of beatings at gunpoint, bonded labor, dangerous working conditions and squalid living conditions on Taiwanese fishing vessels.

The film shows that although some new rules have been introduced in Taipei, out at sea human rights abuses continue.

EJF interviewed dozens of migrant fishermen who have worked aboard Taiwanese-owned fishing vessels operating both in national waters and across the world. You can see the film at the end of this article.

ILO convention on vessel labor enters into force

The fishermen -- the majority of who are from Indonesia and the Philippines -- reported violence, abuse and threats, squalid conditions and heavy financial deductions for food, travel, medical checks and accommodation. They reported working long hours, in unsafe and inhumane conditions for little or no money.

"The film highlights the shocking levels of human rights abuses, and the need to take urgent action to protect people working in the Taiwanese fishing industry," said EJF. "The film highlights the need to ratify and implement the International Labour Organisation convention designed to protect the rights of workers in the fishing industry. All countries need to ensure that legislation is in place that secures prosecutions against people involved in human trafficking."

EJF called on all governments and the private sector to introduce the readily available measures to ensure transparency from "net to plate" that will enable fisheries managers and enforcement officials to ensure fish is caught legally, sustainably and ethically.

Taiwan is a major supplier of seafood, shipping annual exports worth around $2 billion to Europe, the US, Japan, and other major economies.

Many vessels in the Taiwanese distant water fleet do not return to port for months or even years at a time, simply transferring their catch to other boats out at sea.

These long fishing periods allow vessels to exploit marine resources to the maximum, while the extreme isolation on the high seas means that crew are vulnerable to abuse, with no government measures in place to inspect their conditions. Prosecutions for human trafficking in the industry are almost non-existent, said EJF.

Taiwan has been repeatedly criticized over its failure to protect human rights in the fishing industry in the last five Trafficking in Persons reports from the US Department of State. The EU is also set for a fact-finding mission to Taiwan in March, to see what progress has been made in combating illegal fishing practices.

Exploitation and Lawlessness: The Dark Side of Taiwan's Fishing Fleet from Environmental Justice Foundation on Vimeo.

title: Mexico’s anti-IUU fight an uphill battle
content:
Mexico has taken extraordinary measures in recent years to protect marine life threatened by illegal fishing in its waters, but fishermen and drug cartels that profit off illegal fishing have pushed back, reports World Politics Review.

Organized crime is a growing concern in the fisheries industry as criminal syndicates are involved in the illegal harvesting of totoaba, shark, red snapper, and other marine life, such as sea cucumbers, according to Johan Bergenas, senior director for public policy at Vulcan, and David Soud, head of research and analysis at I.R. Consilium.

Unrest in the artisanal fishing community has also resulted in attacks on government inspectors working to combat totoaba fishing and protect the vaquita population. NGO vessels and personnel have also faced violence, including the shooting down of a Sea Shepherd drone in December.

"The Mexican Navy faces a challenge common to many countries: militaries do not have the bandwidth to take on the plethora of emerging security challenges, as they are stretched thin confronting more traditional defense and security threats, such as countering narcotics trafficking."

title: Consumer goods group tightens loop on forced labor in SE Asia seafood sector
content:
The fight to eradicate forced labor from seafood supply chains in Southeast Asia is just getting started, said the Consumer Goods Forum (CGF), which represents a who’s who of multinational retailers.

The group, which sells €3.5 trillion ($4.1trn) of goods annually, has targeted the issue of forced labor as its number one target and Southeast Asia’s seafood industry is under the spotlight, Didier Bergeret, director of social sustainability at the CGF, said at a sustainability seminar recently held in Puerto Varas, Chile.

Thailand is perhaps unfairly singled out because of its government’s willingness to cooperate with forced labor eradication programs, Bergeret said. This may have given other countries in the region a false sense of security because they are out of the limelight, he said. 

Many Asian countries employ migrant laborers to work on fishing vessels in the Indian Ocean and utilize different forms of coercion including violence and retention of pay. Many of these are small-scale seafood processors that sell their output to global markets, Bergeret said. Companies that form part of the CGF -- from Unilever to Walmart -- have agreed to ensure that their supply chains are free of forced labor, he said.

The elimination of “forced labor is really around the corner", Bergeret said. “There is no way that goods can be exported if there any allegations of forced labor.”

CGF also has environment goals including the elimination of net deforestation by 2020 by targeting the pulp and paper industries, ranching, and soybean cultivation.  

Eliminating forced labor is a difficult task because there are more subtle forms of coercion  such as working hours or passport retention, Bergeret said. He warned that even countries like Chile that have clearly defined labor laws need to be alert for acts of coercion with a large influx of immigrants arriving from Caribbean and other South American countries.

Fishing in Southeast Asia, along with palm oil farming, is a priority because it employs many immigrant laborers and also contributes to environmental degradation. Eliminating forced labor is challenging because fishing attracts vast amounts of migrant labor and occurs mostly offshore, Bergeret said.

Thai Union Group, a major global supplier of tuna, shrimp and other seafood, has been very public in supporting a campaign to ensure fair labor practice in its operations and among its supply chains.

title: Investigator who led Greenpeace probe of tuna sector hails deal with Thai Union
content:
New Zealander Tim McKinnel, a former policeman who led Greenpeace’s probe of the tuna sector in the lead up to an agreement with Thai Union Group, said an agreement with the world’s largest canner is “one of the most substantial” in the environmental group’s history.

Greenpeace and Thai Union announced a deal on Tuesday whereby the processor will halve the tuna it sources from vessels using fish aggregation devices, as well as other sweeping supply chain changes.

Thai Union has been a target for Greenpeace, due to a belief it could help lift the game of the global fishing industry, McKinnel told the New Zealand Herald.

If it implemented measures agreed it could claim to be a leader on the twin issues of the treatment of fishermen and of the fishery, he said.

In the interview, McKinnel describers some of the situations he has witnessed in the global tuna sector.

"I interviewed one guy who worked on a tuna longliner where his captain would shoot his crew with a slug gun from the bridge to get their attention. They were working in the tropics but they took to wearing raincoats to protect themselves,” he told the Herald.

"I don't know how you would define that other than criminal violence but these guys would come into port and couldn't leave the boat because they were owed too much money,” he said.

title: China-US trade relations hit bump with 2017 TIP report
content:
The US State Department did not mention fishing or seafood labor issues as a driver when it put China on its human trafficking report's blacklist on Tuesday, but the seafood industry still could see backlash over the decision.

China's downgrade to Tier 3--the lowest level on the Trafficking in Persons (TIP) report--created a bump in the road for US-China trade relations, with reverberations that have the potential to escalate. Sources, however, told Undercurrent News the impact on seafood trade flows won't likely be as severe as the department's 2014 decision to rank Thailand Tier 3, as the current situation is largely different.

At the release of the report on Tuesday morning, China’s government issued harsh words to the US government over the downgrade.

"China firmly opposes the US’ irresponsible remarks on other countries' fight against human trafficking, based on its domestic laws,” Lu Kang, spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said in a statement widely circulated on Tuesday.

The Tier 3 rating can trigger sanctions limiting access to US and international aid. There is a 90-day process put into place for deciding on such restrictions, which are ultimately set at the discretion of the White House, Susan Coppedge, ambassador-at-large for the Office to Monitor and Combat Trafficking in Persons, said during a press briefing Tuesday afternoon. US presidents have often waived such actions in the past.

However, President Donald Trump has been known to break with tradition when it comes to wielding his power as president, with his number of executive orders issued so far as of June 20 putting him on track to issue more of them than any other president since Dwight Eisenhower over half a century ago. He also he faces some pressure to do so here and has been a vocal critic of Chinese trade practices.

Congressman Chris Smith, a Republican who represents New Jersey, said in a statement on Tuesday he hopes to get sanctions imposed on China as a result of the downgrade.

“Hopefully, the new tier ranking coupled with robust diplomacy—including the imposition of sanctions authorized under Tier 3—will lead to systemic reforms that will save women and children’s lives and ensure that Chinese exports are not made with slave labor,” said Smith.

Smith is a senior member of the House foreign relations committee who sponsored the bill for the Victims of Trafficking and Violence Protection Act of 2000, which ultimately established annual TIP report.

Smith's press secretary, Jeff Beck, told Undercurrent there is a wider movement among members of congress to achieve such sanctions, but confirmations of this claim were not attainable as of press time.

Whether Trump will be sympathetic to any call for sanctions remains to be seen, but cracking down on human trafficking is clearly of importance to Ivanka Trump, his daughter and senior White House advisor. She has enough sway with the president that she was reportedly influential in his decision to launch military action against Bashar al Assad in Syria.

During the release of the report on Tuesday morning, Ivanka indicated work is already underway to “determine steps we can take to better execute a strategy to finally end human trafficking,” citing conversation with NGOs, victims, members of congress and others.

Secretary of state Rex Tillerson, the first to speak at length during the unveiling, used the opportunity to shine a light on China’s downgrade, which he said came “because it has not taken serious steps to end its own complicity in trafficking – including forced laborers from North Korea that are located in China.”

Whether or not Tillerson would support sanctions remains to be seen, but he does support calls for a closer look at doing business in China.

“American consumers and businesses must also recognize they may have an unwitting connection to human trafficking. Supply chains creating many products that Americans enjoy may be utilizing forced labor. The State Department does engage with businesses to alert them to these situations so that they can take actions on their own to ensure that they are not in any way complicit.”

The Guardian called the downgrade of China a “surprise” stating it marked “the first major, public rebuke of Beijing’s human rights record by the Trump administration.”

During the press briefing Tuesday, reporters probed ambassador Coppedge for the reason the downgrade happened this year, after three years of China being on the Tier 2 watch list and having received a waiver last year. China would have been eligible for a waiver this year if the country had submitted a national action plan, Coppedge said.

When asked whether China submitted an action plan, Coppedge said, “I don’t recall,” and the briefing concluded.

Seafood not a major driver in downgrade, yet still under pressure

No mention of fishing or seafood industry forced labor was made in the China section of the TIP report, indicating that while overall references to forced labor may indeed include these industries, they were not a major driver in the downgrade decision.

Throughout its explanation of China’s status, the TIP report repeatedly references sex trafficking and forced labor in government facilities as the major reasons for China’s status.

Nonetheless, the downgrade itself — regardless of whether sanctions are imposed — still has implications for seafood companies, considering it calls into question the general nature of the nation’s supply chains.

“I suspect the downgrade will send a message that food companies importing goods from a country ranked at Tier 3 need to look into whether the downgrade is connected at all to the products they sell,” Katrina Nakamura, seafood social responsibility consultant and founder of the Labor Safe Screen, told Undercurrent. “If it is, for example if forced labor in seafood or fishing work are cited, then risk-based due diligence is called for.”

It remains to be seen whether any force labor in the fishing or seafood processing industries is unearthed. If it is, then Nakamura has more advice for suppliers.

“For suppliers operating in Tier 3 countries, where forced labor risk in seafood has been identified by competent authorities, the key is to build a list of the vessels, farms, and processing facilities behind the product, at minimum,” Nakamura said. “That’s the way to safeguard the product, to have the information on where it came from at the ready. Opening a channel to frontline migrants' rights organizations is the most protective thing a company can do.”

Amid the downgrade news, however, some question whether it will have any impact.

"I don't think it will make a lot of difference. Some have already turned away from China in the US market, they do not want to see ‘made in China’ on the box,” an industry source with processing operations in China, wishing to remain unnamed, told Undercurrent. “Many want to find alternatives, but they can’t.”

Price remains the important driver in purchasing decisions, the source added.

“So, people might make public statements about not wanting to buy from China, but then they end up buying, as the price is the lowest,” the source said.

China’s Tier 3 downgrade is unlikely to have the same impact as that of Thailand’s in 2014, which was, in fact, largely driven by shortcomings in the Thai government’s effort to crack down on forced labor in the fishing industry. Thailand's downgrade sparked industry response across the international supply chain. For instance, it caused Thai Union Group to publicly address human trafficking in the seafood industry, an effort the company remained committed to last year even after Thailand's upgrade to Tier 2 watch list--a ranking it kept on this year's report.

title: Armed gangs rob Chilean salmon trucks causing major losses
content:
Gangs have committed several armed robberies of trucks transporting salmon on Chilean roads in the past week making off with inventories worth $1 million or more, sources told Undercurrent News.

The robberies that took place in the last week were more frequent and violent than usual, sources told Undercurrent.

Most of the robberies -- sources said at least three and as many as five or more were committed -- took place on the road connecting Pitrufquen in the region of La Araucanía and Cabrero in the Bío Bío region.

The gangs have acted with unusual violence, intercepting trucks and intimidating the drivers, forcing them to hand over the keys to the vehicles, Radio Bio Bio reported on Sunday.

Each truck carried at least 20 metric tons of salmon, destined for international markets. 

"The trucks could have carried whole salmon or products with aggregated value, i.e. fillets without skin, so each truck's value could have been much higher than CLP120m ($177,109), up to almost the double of that figure," one source said.

A source told Undercurrent that the number of robberies normally intensifies during the holidays because thieves know that it was easier to resell the product in the local market as demand grows.

Typically, Chile sells a small percentage of its production to the local market. Meanwhile, salmon prices in Europe and Asia are on the rise.

title: Greenpeace claims Thai fleet moving to Indian ocean to avoid regulation
content:
Thailand’s overseas fishing fleets are intentionally shifting to isolated waters to avoid fishing regulations, Greenpeace Southeast Asia has claimed in a new report, named 'Turn the Tide'.

The findings of the report -- issued following a 12-month investigation, and following a human rights exposé by the Associated Press -- and demonstrate a clear case for banning transshipment at sea, the NGO said.

“The Thai government has tried to clamp down on human rights violations in the fishing industry but these Thai fleets remain as ruthless as ever,” said Greenpeace Southeast Asia oceans campaigner, Anchalee Pipattanawattanakul.

“Our investigation shows that rather than changing the way they fish to meet the regulations, they are just shifting to isolated and less regulated fishing grounds outside the region.” 

Between 2014 and 2016, Greenpeace tracked Thailand’s rogue overseas fishing vessels and found that, after fishing restrictions were imposed by the governments of Indonesia and Papua New Guinea in August 2015, as many as 76 Thai flagged vessels shifted their operations to the environmentally-fragile Saya de Malha Bank in the Indian Ocean -- more than 7,000km away from Samut Sakhon, Thailand’s seafood epicentre, it said.

Maintaining fishing fleets in the distant Saya de Malha Bank requires routine journeys by reefer vessels of over 7,000 kilometers, "making transshipment at sea central to the Thai business model".

This model allows the fishing vessels to remain at sea and out of the reach of authorities, where they can operate outside the law. The reefers deliver supplies and sometimes trafficked workers, and pick up fish, with some shipments reportedly including up to 50% sharks, according to Greenpeace.

The report also found that the negligent use of trafficked, abused and underpaid local and foreign workers can lead to horrific outcomes, including the outbreak of beriberi disease. An official investigation into six beriberi fatalities concluded that the men had died of heart failure caused by poor nutrition, overwork, and long periods at sea without returning to port, situations that Greenpeace says were enabled by transshipment at sea. 

Among 15 survivors of human trafficking interviewed by Greenpeace, almost half experienced physical violence on vessels. One of the main reasons for beatings was illness, especially when there was insufficient food on-board and exhausted crew members would try to sneak off to rest.

“The powerful Thai Overseas Fishing Association, which controls much of the billion dollar fishing industry, have eroded trust in their willingness to operate modern, sustainable and ethical businesses. Greenpeace and human rights NGOs are asking them to change the way they operate to meet regulations for the sustainability and viability of the fishing and seafood sectors,” added Pipattanawattanakul.

Greenpeace’s supply chain investigations demonstrate the unacceptably high risk of tainted surimi entering numerous seafood and non-seafood supply chains throughout 2016, including products destined for export which end up being raw ingredients for sushi and pet food products sold around the world, it wrote.

"As long as transshipment at sea continues, it will be nearly impossible for any seafood company to guarantee that the fish they are selling is both sustainable and ethically caught,” said Greenpeace New Zealand sustainable tuna project leader Oliver Knowles.

“The case for banning transshipments at sea grows stronger by the day. The evidence in our report puts more pressure on the Thai and international fishing industry to phase out this deeply problematic practice that allows so many issues to flourish.” 

Greenpeace is calling for greater control, including prioritizing  efforts to eliminate risky practices like transshipment at sea, to be exerted over Thailand’s distant water fishing fleets. Greenpeace recommends stricter monitoring and enforcement measures from the Thai government to ensure that only sustainably and ethically-produced Thai seafood reaches the shelves, freezers, sushi bars, and cat bowls around the world.
