title: EU extends grace period before Thai trade ban decision
content:
The EU has given the world's third-largest seafood exporter Thailand another six months to end illegal fishing, said Thai deputy prime minister Prawit Wongsuwon, over a year after Brussels threatened Bangkok with a trade ban.

Thailand's fishing industry employs more than 300,000 people, many of them migrant workers from neighboring countries who are often subject to ill-treatment, reports Reuters.

The industry's reputation has been tarnished by instances of human trafficking to meet manpower demand, forced labor and violence.

The European Union gave Thailand a "yellow card" in April 2015 for failing to prevent illegal and unregulated fishing catch entering the supply chain and ending up in seafood exports to Europe. The warning required Thailand to clean up in six months or face a trade ban.

In May, a three-month grace period had been rumored.

"Good news," Prawit told reporters on Monday. "We won't get the red card... They have delayed this because we have always cooperated."

The EU in Thailand declined to comment to Reuters, citing the confidential nature of meetings between its officials and Thai authorities.

A Thai team went to Brussels to discuss progress last week. Since receiving the warning from the EU, Thailand has a instigated new license and monitoring systems for fishing vessels, the director general of the Thai Fisheries Department, Adisorn Promthep, told Reuters last week in Brussels.

Bangkok has also tightened regulations and imposed limitations on the catch, Adisorn said.

The EU yellow card had been a "wakeup call" to deal with an obsolete fisheries law, he added.

Authorities were also making more regular checks on vessels and demanded employers give workers written contracts, he said. That was to prevent labor abuses and human traffickers selling people on to boats, Adisorn said.

title: US state department: Labor abuses in Thai seafood continue
content:
Labor abuses continue on Thai fishing vessels and processing plants, despite progress made by the country's government on policies to prevent people trafficking, according to a report from the US Department of State.

Last year, the US kept Thailand on tier 3 of its annual TIP report. In April 2015, a few months before the release of the TIP report in July, the government reaffirmed its “zero tolerance” policy for human trafficking and re-emphasized combatting trafficking in persons (TIP) as a national priority.

"Nonetheless, the lack of clarity in law and practice on what constitutes forced labor or debt bondage undermined the government’s efforts to identify labor trafficking victims and prosecute forced labor," said the US state department, in a report on human rights practises.

The government reported investigating 280 trafficking cases, prosecuting 155 traffickers, and obtaining convictions against 151 traffickers during 2014. Of the 280 trafficking cases, 58 investigations -- 20% -- involved suspected cases of forced labor. Twenty traffickers received prison sentences of more than seven years, and the majority of convicted offenders received prison sentences of at least two years.

There were reports some convicted forced labor offenders fled the country after judges granted bail under the appeal process.

Reports of abusive work environments, including forced labor, continued in many sectors, including Thai-flagged seagoing trawlers and labor-intensive industries such as food and seafood processing facilities, as well as in the informal sector and in domestic work, particularly in those sectors where foreign migrant labor was common, according to the state department.

Up to 90% of workers in the seafood processing industry were migrant workers.

An Associated Press investigative series into slavery in the country’s seafood industry allegedly led to the release of more than 2,000 trapped fishery workers during the year.

The reports also led to a dozen arrests, millions of dollars’ worth of seizures, closure of some shrimp-peeling sheds, and proposals for new national laws.

Human trafficking and slave labor allegations against the Thai industry are escalating
Read more
In 2014, the last year for which information was available, the Ministry of Social Development and Human Security reported assisting 303 victims at government shelters, of whom 236 were foreign nationals and 195 were victims of forced labor.

Civil society observers criticized government handling of vulnerable migrant workers and undocumented migrants who may have been victims of human trafficking.

Language barriers, lack of legal status, lack of education, lack of an understanding of local law, and ineffective complaint mechanisms for non-Thai speakers increased vulnerability to exploitation for the large numbers of migrants from Burma, Cambodia, and Laos concentrated in those sectors.

A 2013 International Labor Organization (ILO) report highlighted abusive labor conditions in the fishing sector, including approximately 17% of persons “working against their will and unable to leave for a variety of reasons including financial penalty/withholding wages, threat of violence or to inform authorities.”

Migrant workers often assumed debts to informal labor brokers or local moneylenders, some of whom charged interest rates as high as 20%; these practices led migrant workers, in some cases, into conditions of debt bondage.

Some workers on fishing vessels were reportedly unable to return to shore, and their employers forced them to continue working in harsh conditions with low pay and very limited protection and benefits. In some cases employers, subcontractors, or brokers (both formal and informal) charged excessive fees to workers to acquire documentation, such as passports from origin countries, or transportation, exacerbating vulnerability to debt bondage.

There were reports of employers who confiscated registration and travel documents of migrant workers, which restricted their internal movement and contributed to their vulnerability to forced labor with little recourse under the law. The law limited noncitizens in their choice of occupation. To avoid deportation illegal migrants often paid additional fees or bribes to police and immigration officers.

Progress made 

The government established a new prime minister-led national committee to combat human trafficking, forced labor, child labor, illegal migration, and illegal fishing to address problems in a more integrated manner.

The government updated many laws to enhance its regulatory powers in sectors with significant labor concerns and increase punishment for violations related to human trafficking.

For example, the labor protection ministerial regulation on sea fishing vessels issued in December 2014 requires a minimum of 10 hours of rest per 24 hours, written contracts, and regular salary payments for workdays and holidays.

Additional legal reforms included marine department regulation on boat registration, a fisheries act, amendments to the anti-TIP act, and new criminal code to criminalize child pornography. Penalties for conviction under the amended anti-TIP laws range from four years to life imprisonment and a fine of THB 80,000 to THB 400,000 baht ($2,220 to $11,090).

The amended anti-TIP law also provides protection to whistle blowers and gives authoritative power to halt operations temporarily or suspend licenses of businesses and vehicles involved in human trafficking.

title: Greenpeace: Chicken of the Sea should focus on cleaning up supply chain
content:
In response to a Chicken of the Sea lifestyle and wellness initiative to increase seafood consumption, Greenpeace Oceans campaign director John Hocevar published a blog post advising the tuna company to focus less on marketing and more on cleaning up its supply chains.

In his post titled 'Slave-caught seafood isn't healthy", Hocevar highlighted the recent legal battle involving Chicken of the Sea's parent company, Thai Union Group, and reports of human trafficking, violence and slavery in the company's supply chain.

Human trafficking and slave labor allegations against the Thai industry are escalating
Read more
"Here is some free advice for Chicken of the Sea, Thai Union and the supermarkets and seafood businesses that sell their products. Rather than spending your money trying to tell Americans what to eat, maybe you should focus your resources on cleaning up your supply chains. No one wants to buy seafood tainted with human rights abuses," he said.

Hocevar also accused the company of pushing Americans to eat more tuna for "corporate self-interest", rather than a genuine concern for public health.

"Americans have been eating less canned tuna each year, though, so it is no wonder Chicken of the Sea is trying the health angle to convince people to buy more cans of its watery grey mush," Hocevar said.

title: EJF names Thai firm responsible for murder, slave labor
content:
Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF) has said new investigations, both on land and at sea, prove that violence, slavery, human trafficking and illegal pirate fishing persist in the Thai seafood industry.

An EJF investigation has apparently uncovered a sophisticated system of slavery and severe human rights abuses aboard “pirate” fishing fishing vessels operating from the Thai fishing port of Kantang. The new report, 'Thailand’s Seafood Slaves', lays out detailed evidence of the abuses and names those responsible, the NGO said.

EJF names one of the most powerful individuals in Kantang -- the owner of the Boonlarp Fishing company, Sompon Jirotmontree, who controls a fleet of 62 fishing vessels and is president of the Kantang Fishing Association -- as having run his operations using forced and slave labor, claiming many workers were murdered by his security guard.

Intelligence has been corroborated by in-depth interviews with victims of slavery escaped from key fishing operators, the NGO said.

It claims to have documented the route and processes used to enslave trafficked workers from Myanmar on to fishing boats, gained detailed eye-witness testimony to the violence and murders at sea on fishing vessels and on land, and reported corruption and involvement of local police in the on-going human rights abuses and illegal fishing operations.

In 2013, EJF’s investigative report Sold to the Sea uncovered cases of human trafficking, labour abuse and the routine use of violence and murder in the Thai seafood industry.

By returning to Kantang, EJF challenges claims that slavery and violent abuse alongside illegal fishing in Thailand’s export-oriented seafood sector have been effectively addressed, it said.

Despite the Royal Thai Government introducing a raft of new controls throughout this year, 'Thailand’s Seafood Slaves' demonstrates how some government flagship initiatives are failing to identify and assist victims of exploitation and abuse.

EJF concludes that both public and private sector safeguards designed to prevent and combat trafficking, forced and slave labor remain inadequate, and calls on the international community to maintain strong pressure on Thailand until it can demonstrate an end to the human rights abuses and illegal and destructive fishing.

“What we observed with Boonlarp in Kantang is symptomatic of the problems we are seeing across Thailand," said Steve Trent, executive director of EJF.

"The Thai fishing industry continues to use trafficked, bonded, forced and slave labour to crew vessels which are often fishing illegally to maximise profits and minimise costs. Despite the recent arrests that have been reported by local media, violence, slavery and illegal fishing remain a systemic problem in Thailand’s vast fishing fleet."

"These companies are using trafficking, debt bondage, torture and even murder to produce a raw material which is entering a diverse and large number supply chains: from shrimp and pet food to poultry and fertiliser, some of which is destined for consumers in the EU and US."

"Though some progress has been made to control illegal ‘pirate’ fishing in the region, the government is still failing to deliver on its promises to clean up one of the most exploitative and unsustainable industries on the planet. In a high-level meeting in Bangkok in September 2015, EJF gave the authorities evidence of violent abuse and murder, providing recommendations on how to eliminate the widespread use of human trafficking, stressing the need to deliver a coherent national programme of forensic, intelligence-led enforcement that targets the Thai nationals coordinating these abuses and benefitting most from them."

"We have also highlighted the need for the courts to support effective enforcement, ensuring due process of law and application of serious deterrent penalties to those found guilty."

"At the same time, industry actors and market countries need to apply a zero tolerance approach to these violent abuses, making the steps they have taken to ensure their supply chains are free of slavery public. Consumers in Europe and the U.S. do not want to use products made by slaves or through the destruction of invaluable natural resources”.

EJF’s new report comes as Thailand faces increasing global pressure to address human trafficking and the use of bonded, forced and slave labor and combat highly destructive illegal fishing in its seafood sector.

In the 2015 U.S. State Department Trafficking in Persons (TIP) report, Thailand was listed on Tier 3 for the second year running, retaining lowest possible ranking alongside countries such as North Korea and Iran. In October, the European Parliament adopted a resolution on Thailand, highlighting concerns about the trafficking of workers and encouraging the Thai government to step up its efforts to put an end to slavery.

The European Commission, having warned Thailand in April this year for its failure to address illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing (issuing a so-called “yellow card”), sent a delegation to Bangkok on Oct. 21 to examine progress on the issue.

An update on this decision is due in the near term and could see a ban on Thai wild-caught seafood exports to the European Union.

Pressure is also growing as several global companies face class action lawsuits from consumers in the US over allegations that their products are tainted by slavery taking place aboard Thai fishing vessels.

EJF’s 'Thailand’s Seafood Slaves' report and film are available at its website.

title: Tuna treaty could help with anti-trafficking push, industry says
content:
A longstanding treaty between the United States and Pacific island nations could help in the global fight against human trafficking in the seafood sector, US tuna fleet leaders told Undercurrent News.

The 1987 South Pacific Tuna Treaty, which provides US purse seine vessels access to the Western and Central Pacific Ocean fisheries, has been extended through interim agreements since 2013, but a longer-term renewal hasn't been agreed to.

At a meeting this week in Brisbane, Australia, the United States and Pacific island nations party to the treaty agreed to an extension through 2016, said Doug Hines, executive director of South Pacific Tuna Corp., which represents 14 purse seine vessels fishing under the treaty. Company owners attended the Australia meeting.

In addition to fishing rights, the treaty also provides a mechanism to address the issue of human trafficking and forced labor that is plaguing the global seafood industry, tuna industry officials say.

“We believe that human trafficking related to fisheries is a problem that can best be resolved by government policies and actions,” Brian Hallman, executive director of the American Tunaboat Association, told Undercurrent.

“This treaty … not only sets forth the terms of fishing access for the US fleet to the waters of the Pacific island countries, but is a vehicle for cooperation on all manner of fisheries matters,” Hallman said.

The trafficking issue is “another reason to continue the US Treaty ensuring our engagement in the region", Hines told Undercurrent.

The treaty not only allows for participation in conservation measures, but it also allows the United States to provide resources within the islands to assist in the anti-trafficking fight, Hines said.

Both Hines and Hallman emphasized that there is no link between the US-flagged purse seine tuna fleet and the human trafficking issue.

But many of the Pacific island signatories to the tuna treaty were not ranked highly in the State Department’s Trafficking in Persons report released last week. And Asian-flagged vessels were listed as part of the problem in their waters.

The Marshal Islands was downgraded to Tier 3 from its spot on the Tier 2 watch list list year. US officials assign the Tier 3 ranking to nations who's governments they say don’t fully comply with minimum standards in the Trafficking Victims Protection Act and aren’t making significant efforts to do so.

In the Marshall Islands, foreign business owners recruit girls from the island nation to engage in prostitution with crew members of foreign fishing and transshipping vessels that dock in Majuro, the State Department report said.

Foreign women living in the nation as long-term residents have been forced into prostitution in establishments patronized by crew members of Chinese and other foreign fishing boats, the report said.

In Papua New Guinea, which was upgraded to the State Department's Tier 2 watch list from Tier 3 status last year, Malaysian and Chinese logging companies and foreign businesspeople arrange for women from Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, China and the Philippines to voluntarily enter Papua New Guinea on fraudulently issued visas.

They are then turned over to traffickers and forced into prostitution and domestic servitude in fisheries, logging and mining camps and entertainment sites.

In territorial waters and ports of the Solomon Islands, which is on the report's Tier 2 watch list, the State Department said fishing crew members from Indonesia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Sri Lanka, North Korea, and Fiji have reported severe living conditions, violence, limited food supply and nonpayment of wages.

According to the State Department, migrants from Southeast Asia have said they have worked in conditions indicative of human trafficking on Asian fishing vessels in the territorial waters of Micronesia, which was ranked Tier 2 in the report. The Tier 2 level indicates nations don't fully comply with the minimum standards but are making significant efforts to do so.

Another Tier 2 country, Fiji, is a a transit area for trafficking, the State Department said. Workers from Cambodia, the Philippines, Burma, Indonesia, North Korea, China and Singapore — who are deceptively recruited in their home countries and transit through Fiji or board fishing vessels from Fiji ports and waters — live in poor conditions, accrue debt larger than promised wages, and work for little or no compensation on Chinese and Taiwanese fishing vessels in Pacific waters, the TIP report said.

In Tier 2 Kiribati, Asian men in visiting ship crews exploit children and some women in prostitution, the report said.

In the waters of Palau, also Tier 2, foreign workers on fishing boats experience conditions indicative of human trafficking, the State Department said.

“This is an ongoing challenge in many areas of the sector, however, not with US-flagged vessels,” Hines said.

In addition to individuals and companies having long standing human rights policies against human trafficking and abuse, the US fleet is also under the oversight and management of the US Coast Guard, Hines said.

US inspectors have complete access to crew members, and vessels have independent observers who report to the Pacific Islands Forum Fisheries Agency, he said.

That information is also shared with the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration  and “any violations that are noted in the report are aggressively prosecuted", Hines said.

“US operators and its regulatory agencies view these infractions as serious with zero tolerance,” he said.

title: Greenpeace issues open letter to seafood sector
content:
After the ninth issue of its Carting Away the Oceans report, Greenpeace has issued an open letter to the seafood sector calling for more work to me done.

The letter, from David Pinsky, who authors Greenpeace USA’s annual seafood sustainability report for the nation’s largest supermarkets, calls for holding major companies accountable and shifting seafood practices that have global impacts on our oceans.

You can read the letter in full below:

Last week, Greenpeace released its ninth edition of Carting Away the Oceans, an annual report ranking U.S. supermarkets on seafood sustainability. While most companies (20 out of 25 profiled) received passing scores, there is significant work the U.S. retail sector must do to address destructive fishing, overfishing, and growing concerns about human rights abuses and violence in the global seafood industry.

Front-runners Whole Foods, Wegmans, Hy-Vee, and Safeway lead the pack, with publicly available sustainable seafood policies, increased labeling and information for customers, and efforts to offer ocean safe tuna, protect sensitive marine habitat like the Bering Sea canyons and call on Congress to help stop Illegal, Unreported and Unregulated (IUU) fishing.

Laggards like Walmart, Kroger, Albertsons, and Publix continue to stall on important sustainability and social responsibility efforts. Rather than change their supply chains, strengthen policies, and publicly advocate for the protection of both the ocean and seafood industry workers, these retailers are offering excuses and empty promises to their customers.

Publix is a noteworthy example. Coming in at an underwhelming 23rd this year, Publix is the only one of the ten largest U.S. grocery retailers to fail our report. Publix ties Kroger in selling the most Red List species of any profiled retailer (18), and when Greenpeace called into question its poor performance, Publix attempted to placate the public’s concerns by saying there’s simply too much it’s doing to share for inclusion in the Carting Away the Oceansreport. 

Perhaps Publix could take a few notes from industry leaders to get an accurate perspective of what “too much” work entails. From the scant information it shares publicly, Publix is failing on multiple fronts.

Unfortunately, industry front groups like the National Fisheries Institute continue to answer for the biggest tuna brands in the country and greedy supermarket chains that prefer to exploit the oceans and human beings in the quest for short term profits. Rather than focus on science-based solutions, too many companies in the seafood industry prefer to spread misinformation from front groups tied to notorious PR firms like CounterPoint Strategies. Luckily, U.S. supermarkets and the public are wary of such bombastic rhetoric, and are clear that the state of our oceans and seafood industry workers are in peril.

Let’s have a direct conversation about what can and must be done, not industry talking points delivered by front groups. I invite companies like Kroger and Publix to sit down with Greenpeace and have an honest conversation about the state of our oceans and discuss solutions to the rampant human rights abuses occurring worldwide in the industry. We can disagree about tactics, though the fundamental truth is that unless things change, we’ll be lucky if there are many fish left to catch in a few decades. There are options to more sustainably harvest seafood, and continuing to ignore the cost to our environment and human beings is not a sustainable business model.

If not for the sake of our oceans and the people who depend on them to survive, think of your shareholders and your customers. What will they say when more progressive retailers are continuing to move ahead in sales and brand image? How will future generations view your actions? What legacy are you ready to leave when you retire?

While I speak specifically to retailers that are dragging along, like bottom contact gear that rips up the seafloor day after day, this is an open call to the global seafood industry to transform its operations. Listen to the conservation, labor, and human rights communities, stop hiding behind industry trade groups, and think about the future, if not for the ethical reasons, for the sustainability of your company.

We’re watching and waiting. And we’ll be back next year to evaluate your progress, or lack thereof, for the continued benefit of our oceans and the people worldwide that rely on them.

title: Short-lived Sernapesca strike further dents Chile’s reputation as seafood supplier
content:
The strike by Chile’s National Fisheries and Aquaculture Service (Sernapesca) that began last week ended quickly before causing much market impact to the seafood industry.

But, although it was a far cry from the customs strike that left some Chilean salmon importers without fish from May 20-28, the Sernapesca strike put another dent in the South American nation’s reputation as a seafood supplier.

The strike at the regulatory body, which issues health certificates required for salmon imports into the European Union and Canada, began at the start of Friday and lasted until noon that day.

Sernapesca had said the work stoppage, in protest of recent attacks on staff, could have lasted until Tuesday morning.

Sernapesca called off the strike early after representatives reached a temporary agreement on increased safety for field workers, a Sernapesca spokesperson told Undercurrent News.

The spokesperson said a quick response by the government helped the strike end early.

While the government did address Sernapesca’s concerns, the situation is still developing as the regulatory body is waiting on the finalization of a taskforce involving the government and Sernapesca.

In terms of market effect, the Sernapesca strike was “not very damaging due to the shortness," said Matias Cruz, imports and exports manager for UK-based Chilean swordfsh importer Ocean Waves. "Monday service was service as usual," he said.

He had been expecting the strike to cost the company a week’s worth of sales, or about 15 metric tons of finished product.

But the work stoppage is "still very damaging in terms of country’s image especially after [the] previous strike,” Cruz said.

The labor unrest is irksome, a source at a US importer and distributor told Undercurrent.

Especially with the customs strike, Chile’s reputation as a supplier has been “tarnished", he said.

Although the company still does a lot of business with Chile, it has been diversifying its sources of supply into Norway, Scotland in the UK and British Colombia in Canada.

“We have moved some of our business elsewhere,” the source said.

The Sernapesca strike came after a reported attack on four auditors in the Maule region marked the latest in a string of violence against the authority.

The regulatory body has seized more than 80t of illegal hake in the region.

In addition to labor-related woes for the Chilean salmon industry, Costco Wholesale is switching some of its fresh farmed salmon purchases from Chile to Norway.

title: Sernapesca strike to disrupt Chilean seafood exports to Europe; US seen less affected
content:
A strike of Chile’s National Fisheries and Aquaculture Service will dampen sales next week for at least one European swordfish importer, while another source says the situation likely won’t affect the US salmon market very much.

Known as Sernapesca, the regulatory body — which issues health certificates required for salmon imports into the European Union and Canada — said it would start a strike Friday that could last until Tuesday morning, in protest of recent attacks on its staff, Aqua.cl reported in Spanish.

Matias Cruz, imports and exports manager for UK-based Chilean swordfish importer Ocean Waves, told Undercurrent News he expects the strike to cost the company a week’s worth of sales, or about 15 tons of finished product.

The strike will affect certificates for fresh, wild-caught exports from Chile, Cruz said, speculating that the strike could extend for another week.

Although some salmon customers in the United States require the health certificates, the US government does not, a source at a US importer told Undercurrent.

He does not anticipate his company losing sales to the strike, which he said would affect European and Canadian markets more because their governments require the health certificates for imports from Chile.

If the strike is prolonged and companies can't sell fresh fish to markets that need health certificates, then the strike could could end up pushing prices down into the United States, this source said.

But a strike lasting only three or four days isn’t likely to pressure US prices, he said.

The Sernapesca strike — which comes after a reported attack on four auditors in the Maule region marked the latest in a string of violence adjacent Sernapesca — is the latest source of instability in the Chilean seafood industry. The regulatory body has seized more than 80 tons of illegal hake in the region.

This week, Mundo Maritimo reported the Chilean port employees union was planning a strike starting Thursday.

Some Chilean salmon importers were left without fish from May 20-28 amid a customs strike.

In addition to labor-related woes for the Chilean salmon industry, Costco Wholesale is switching some of its fresh farmed salmon purchases from Chile to Norway.

title: Thailand yellow carded by EU
content:
BRUSSELS, Belgium --The European Commission has Tuesday put Thailand on formal notice for not taking sufficient measures in the international fight against illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing (IUU).

As a result of a thorough analysis and a series of discussions with Thai authorities since 2011, the commission has denounced the country's shortcomings in its fisheries monitoring, control and sanctioning systems and concludes that Thailand is not doing enough, it said.

“Our EU rigorous policy on a harmful practice such as illegal fishing, together with our genuine capacity to act, is paying off. I urge Thailand to join the European Union in the fight for sustainable fisheries. Failure to take strong action against illegal fishing will carry consequences," said European Commissioner for environment, maritime affairs and fisheries, Karmenu Vella.

This comes after the US Department of State downgraded Thailand to Tier 3 in its Trafficking in Persons (TIP) report.

The TIP report stated that the Thai government had demonstrated insufficient efforts to address trafficking, particularly as a result of its systematic failure to “investigate, prosecute, and convict ship owners and captains for extracting forced labor from migrant workers, or officials who may be complicit in these crimes".

The decision from the European Commission starts a formal procedure of dialogue with the Thai authorities to make them take the necessary corrective measures. They will be given six months to implement a corrective tailor-made action plan.

Should the situation not improve, the EU could resort to banning fisheries imports from Thailand. Such measures were taken in the past with Belize, Guinea, Cambodia and Sri Lanka. Imports from Belize were banned last year but due to the reforming efforts of the authorities they are now allowed.

The commission has acknowledged that two fishing nations, Korea and the Philippines, have carried out appropriate reforms of their legal systems and are now equipped to tackle illegal fishing. It therefore stops the "identification" procedure that had started with a yellow card to Korea in November 2013 and the Philippines in June 2014.

Since they were issued with warnings, both Korea and the Philippines embarked on a series of reforms to upgrade their fisheries governance. Their legal systems are now aligned to international law.

“Thai authorities exert very little control over their fishing vessels, with many activities illegally damaging fish stocks and the marine environment, and this is linked to some of the most exploitative and inhuman working conditions documented anywhere," said Steve Trent, executive director of the Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF), in a statement sent to Undercurrent News in reaction to the yellow card.

"These conditions include the use of slaves and extreme violence. It is time for the Thai government to take swift action to control the Thai fleet and end this environmental and human crisis," said Trent.

According to EJF, a 2014 study estimates that up to 39% of wild-caught seafood entering the US market from Thailand has been caught illegally.

Thailand’s legal and regulatory framework governing fisheries and fishing practices was mostly established in 1947. “It is outdated and does not reflect the current status of either industry practices or marine resources,” states EJF.

A new Thai Fisheries Act, due to come into force in July 2015, aims to redress current regulatory deficiencies and impose harsher penalties for violations of fisheries regulations.

In January 2015, Thailand’s Ministry of Agriculture and Cooperatives announced a six point plan to combat IUU fishing.

“Robust and effective implementation of these measures will be essential to avoid a future red card from the EU,” said EJF.

Yellow, red cards at odds with fisheries improvement?

During Monday's European Tuna Conference, there where some good questions about the the EU Directorate-General for Maritime Affairs and Fisheries’ policy in yellow and red cards for non-cooperating fisheries.

Director Stefaan Depypere’s response was to advise: “if a country you source from were to receive a yellow card, perhaps it’s time to think about sourcing from elsewhere”.This seems to run counter to the idea of stakeholder involvement in fisheries, which it is generally said should see buyers support the countries they source from, and encourage and aid them in improving their sustainability criteria.This was something UK retailer Tesco spoke out on at the GOAL conference in 2014, when it explained why it stayed engaged with Thailand following allegations of slave labor being used in the supply chain for farmed shrimp. These allegations prompted French and US retailers to drop Charoen Pokphand Foods as a supplier.

Depypere’s comment came in response to a question from New England Seafood CSR representative Melissa Pritchard, who asked if DG Mare has considered consulting industry before yellow or red-carding countries deemed to be non-cooperative in the first against IUU fishing.

The director said that this had not yet been considered, and seemed somewhat unfeasible given the length of time it would take to consult. New England only found about the red carding in the press, said Pritchard.

Speaking after the conference, one source told Undercurrent another concern with the red cards was the point at which it enters into force. If a valuable container of tuna is on the water having been ordered, and the red card is announced, is that container lost to the buyer? These are still unknowns in the system, and a concern for firms doing business with ‘improving fisheries’, he said.

It’s fair to say New England, as well as several other UK and French importers of fresh tuna, were unimpressed that Sri Lanka was banned from selling to the EU in January 2015 despite a number of them being involved in fisheries improvement partnerships there.

Regarding timelines of the yellow and red cards imposed by the EU, Depypere said once a country receives a red card it may be expected to take six months to revert back to a state at which it can trade with the EU again.

This differs from source’s views of how long the Sri Lanka ban could last – feelings have been that a ban lasting less than year would not act as enough of a deterrent to other nations in the future.

He emphasized that the cards were not designed as a punitive measure, but a last resort and a cooperative process. "Many coutries are happy to receive the red card," he suggested. "For the fisheries minister there, it means public attention on an area he's been trying to get funding for for years."

The EU has agreements with the US and Japan to try and ensure that all major seafood markets are on the same page when it comes to denying access to the most non-cooperative countries.

"The cards have been a successful policy so far, and we will pursue it rigorously in the future, he said.

title: Camanchaca plant attacked amid fishermen demonstration
content:
Pesquera Camanchaca has released a public statement condemning acts of violence and vandalism after the attack of its plant in Coronel, Chile, on Tuesday.

The company's subsidiary Camanchaca Pesca Sur was attacked when artisanal fishermen in the Bio Bio region demonstrated to request the government's review of the Fisheries Act.

Camanchaca said the attack was carried out by "criminals and organized vandalism", that destroyed other firms' assets and various public transport services.

"About 40 protesters, carrying weapons and blunt objects, violently entered the plant, causing major damage in this place, including the sales area that was recently opened to serve the community of Coronel," Camanchaca said.

Police forces partially repelled the attack and managed to vacate the premises, it said.

The company is currently assessing the impact on its assets after the attack.

Despite the damages, Camanchaca has launched a contingency plan to continue operations as quickly as possible, it said.

title: Pressure still on Thailand to clean up tuna sector
content:
Critics in the US remain unimpressed with the progress made so far by the Thai government in ending the exploitation of foreign workers in the seafood sector, reports Bloomberg.

The pressure is building on the tuna industry in particular to clean up questionable labor practices. Four out of five workers in the canneries are foreign, part of an economic web of some 4 million migrants employed in Thailand’s factories, fishing fleets, and brothels, the news site said.

Last June, just after the coup, the annual US report on human trafficking downgraded Thailand to Tier 3, the worst level, for nations that don’t meet the minimum standards to protect workers as laid out in the Victims of Trafficking and Violence Protection Act of 2000.

Many migrants in Thailand are undocumented. The US Department of State said in its report that they are often “forced, coerced, or defrauded into labor or exploited in the sex trade.” Both Thai Union Frozen Products, the country's largest player, and Chotiwat Manufacturing, say they adhere to strict labor codes.

Before Chotiwat held elections for a worker council last year, it ran workshops for 5,500 employees on the basics of democracy. Now 17 worker representatives meet monthly with company managers, COO Rick Heroux told Bloomberg.

There’s been some progress in registering migrant workers, said Abby McGill, campaigns director for the International Labor Rights Forum, a Washington-based non-profit.

But the Thais haven’t addressed the crushing debt loads that workers take on to pay the agents who land them jobs. Until these practices change, she says, “Thailand should remain on Tier 3.”

title: Bubba Gump Shrimp to open in Egypt, Kuwait ‘as soon as possible’
content:
Bubba Gump Shrimp Co. franchisee Mubarak Al-Hassawi Restaurant Development Group's launch of the Forrest Gump-based restaurant's first Europe location in London's renowned Trocadero Centre last fall came in the midst of an over-six-year delay in launching into the Middle East.

Madame Fazir, who reached the agreement with Landry’s to open Bubba Gump restaurants in the UK and Middle East on behalf of Al-Hassawi, did not respond to repeated requests for comment from the PR agency for Bubba Gump London, posed by Undercurrent News for two weeks, on its new site plans.

A Bubba Gump London spokesperson, Shelley Sofier, told Undercurrent the company plans to open new locations in Egypt and Kuwait “as soon as possible”. It also plans to open up four more UK locations -- in addition to its most recent Trocadero location -- over the next four years.

“The Mubarak Al-Hassawi Group will be be looking for locations in major cities – they need big units, which can generate a big footfall, and there aren’t that many of those around,” Sofier said.

The group seems to be stepping back into the public eye with its London launch, giving some hope that it will perhaps re-ignite plans it announced in February of 2008, when it inked its deal with Bubba Gump Shrimp Co. Restaurants to become the company's exclusive franchisee in the Middle East.

At the time, the publicly-announced a plan to open its first location in Dubai in the fourth quarter of that year, but according to Bubba Gump Shrimp’s website, no such locations have opened yet. It lists a total of 11 foreign locations in regions as far away from Landry’s Houston headquarters as Tokyo, but none are in the Middle East.

Kuwait location a mystery

Plans for Kuwait stalled after a location was advertised to the public, it seems. An April 2013 post on the Kuwait-based online gossip portal TwoForyEightAM  features a photo of a Bubba Gump Shrimp banner at “Symphony Mall” with the words “coming soon” underneath and commentary from one of the website’s users celebrating the supposed coming of the restaurant.

The reasons Al-Hassawi has stalled remains unclear, barring the obvious hurdles of civilian violence and near-civil-war in Egypt. Undercurrent was also unable to reach Landry's for comment on the plans.

From a business standpoint, the restaurant concept has had strong success making inroads into cultures that are vastly different from the American-rooted Tom Hanks film the restaurant chain perpetually commemorates.

Bubba Gump Shrimp lists 11 foreign locations far away from owner Landry’s headquarters in Houston, Texas, on its website, among them Bali Indonesia; Makati City, Philippines; Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia; and three locations in Japan. It also lists 32 locations in the United States.

Sales dollars brought in by the 1994 movie Forrest Gump show strong international interest, as 51.3% of the movie’s total lifetime gross sales of $677.9 million came from overseas, according to Box Office Mojo. 

Location, location, location

Al-Hassawi's stalled plans could be in part due to its efforts to secure the right location.  Its most recent location opening in Trocadero, in the location formerly occupied by Planet Hollywood, is “massively important” to the company, Al-Hassawi said in a question and answer sheet on the opening.

“It’s an iconic location, and with the average footfall levels in this street being so massive, we’re excited at being able to secure this site,” the group said, adding later that the Trocadero has one of the highest footfall areas in the entire United Kingdom.

“Location is so important in London, as it is outside London too, so every Bubba Gump restaurant has to be in a fabulous high priority location – if we open 10 Bubba Gumps here, they will be in ten great locations,” the company said

The company plans to maintain the same large portions at its restaurants regardless of the location. Menu offerings may be a different story. In the 2008 announcement, the company said it planned to offer items to satisfy regional cuisine at its Middle East locations.

Which suppliers will benefit?

While shrimp is the species that Forrest Gump and his friend Bubba muse about during their days of fighting in Vietnam in the movie, the restaurant modeled after their discussions ventures into a much more vast array of seafood offerings, with London-area Galaxy Foods set to handle the sourcing.

Suppliers of salmon from Norway and haddock from the North Sea, both of which are brought in fresh to its London location, stand to gain with the restaurant’s new openings, as do those of popular whitefish. The company brings in frozen mahi mahi fron New Zealand, Ecuador and Chile; and hoki from the Pacific Ocean.

Al-Hassawi sees its shrimp offerings as particularly important to the London launch since it fills a niche for shrimp not offered in the fish and chips-focused seafood restaurant arena, but it sees a general “gap in the market for a strong chain of restaurants specializing in seafood".

title: International condemnation hits Thailand over plan to use prisoners in fishing industry
content:
Forty-five human rights organizations sent a letter to Thai Prime Minister Prayut Chan-o-cha on Wednesday asking him to end a pilot project to recruit prisoners from Thailand's correctional facilities to fill a labor shortage in the fishing industry.

Among the global list of signatories were US-based FishWise and Greenpeace Southeast Asia, Cambodia's Chab Dai Coalition to Indonesia-based Kontra.

Multiple reports have documented gross labor violations on Thai fishing boats, including forced labor, physical violence, illegally low wages and human trafficking, the ILRF said.

“Thailand cannot run from the trafficking problem in its fishing fleet,” ILRF executive director Judy Gearhart said. “And sending prisoners to sea will not address the systematic, pervasive labor problems in Thailand’s fishing industry. It is time for the Thai government to recognize that its treatment of migrant workers lies at the heart of the problem and take real, meaningful steps to ensure all workers within its borders work in dignified, just conditions.”

The groups cited rights abuses as a primary reason that explains labor shortages on fishing boats, and said the prison program would do nothing to end those abuses. They also expressed concern that the plan would merely augment the migrant workers from Burma and Cambodia who currently comprise the majority of the workforce on Thai fishing vessels with Thai prisoners who are equally vulnerable to abuses. Migrant fishers are almost entirely undocumented and without legal status, making them afraid to report to Thai authorities about rights violations they suffer on fishing boats.

The signatories also predicted the prison labor plan could have negative economic and political consequences for Thailand.

Western retailers and buyers are already increasingly wary that Thai seafood is produced in supply chains dependent on forced labor and other labor rights abuses and warn that this scrutiny would intensify if buyers have to deal with new concerns regarding conscripted prison labor in their supply chains.

“The retailers we have worked with in Australia are very responsive to the threat of forced labor in their supply chains,” Mark Zirnsak, director of the Justice & International Mission at the Uniting Church in Australia Synod of Victoria and Tasmania, said. “We are working with them, and with Thai suppliers, to increase transparency and ensure just working conditions on Thai fishing vessels. We are deeply concerned that the prison labor program could make it more difficult for the industry partners we work with to verify workers in their supply chains are working without threat of coercion.”

The letter also noted that the plan could be considered evidence by the US State Department that the Thai government is unable, or unwilling, to address the risk of human trafficking in its fishing fleets.

Thailand was downgraded to the lowest rank, Tier 3, in the United States’ 2014 Trafficking in Persons Report, and the fishing industry cited as a major area of concern.

“Thailand has repeatedly said that it’s committed to end forced labor and human trafficking, but this pilot project heads in precisely the opposite direction and will make things worse,” said Phil Robertson, deputy Asia director of Human Rights Watch. “This prisoners on fishing boats project should be immediately scrapped.”

title: American Seafoods accepting applications for Alaska community grant program
content:
The Community Advisory Board (CAB) of American Seafoods Group, one of the nation’s largest seafood harvesters and processors, announced on Monday it is now accepting applications for its Alaska community grant program.

The deadline to submit applications is Nov. 17, 2014.

Since its inception in 1997, the American Seafoods CAB has granted over $1.20m to organizations and programs in Alaska. The CAB meets three times a year to distribute awards. In the summer of 2014, the annual total of distributions was increased to $90,000 per year.

“Our goal is to provide assistance and financial support to organizations that are making a real difference in the communities where we operate,” said Inge Andreassen, president of American Seafoods. “The people and organizations we provide assistance to are an important part of our business, and we look forward to continuing the American Seafoods CAB grant program for many years to come.”

A total of $43,000 will be allocated by the American Seafoods CAB to community projects addressing issues such as hunger, housing, safety, education, research, natural resources and cultural activities.

The majority of grant awards range from $500 to $3,000 per organization. Grant recipients will be selected at the American Seafoods CAB meeting on December 4th.

At the American Seafoods CAB’s meeting in February 2014, $31,000 was awarded to a variety of Alaskan organizations. Out of the 33 organizations earning grants at that meeting, some examples include:

Bristol Bay Regional Food Bank ($3,900), Unalaskans Against Family Violence ($3,000), City of St. Paul Volunteer Fire Department ($2,500), Kodiak Public Library Association ($2,500), Bean’s Café ($1,400), Cordova Friends of the Imagination Library ($1,200), and Copper River Watershed Project ($1,000). The CAB also awarded $15,500 in scholarships at its meeting in May 2014.

The American Seafoods CAB evaluates each proposal based on the following criteria: the need in the community, project benefits, the number of people who will benefit from the program, and the ability to garner additional funding.

title: UK economy no yet ready for interest rate rise, says BoE governor
content:
International News

French economic growth will grow 0.7% this year against Francois Hollande’s forecast of 1% which is where the government has based its economic and financial plans. With unemployment set to rise to 10.2% just short of the 14 year high of 10.3%.

USD declined after reports showed durable goods orders fell to -1.0% in May from 0.8 April and US GDP fell to -2.9% in Q1 from 2.6% previous showing the sharpest pullback for the US economy since the recession started 5 years ago.

EURUSD made gains throughout the day moving from the low of 1.3598 to reach the high of 1.3651 after the release of US GDP, this morning the pair have opened at 1.3641.

The dollar was set for the tightest quarterly trading range in almost two years against the yen as stimulus from central banks in the world’s biggest economies pushes volatility to record lows.

The yen rose against most of its major peers after violence in Iraq reduced risk appetite within the markets. GBPJPY fell from 173.11 to 172.62.

SEK weakened amid speculation Riksbank will intervene to help Sweden’s economy emerge from the falling consumer prices that Nobel laureate Paul Krugman identified as a potential deflationary spiral. With the ECB already easing monetary policy Riksbank may need to lower interest rates to succeed. GBPSEK traded as high as 11.4514.

UK News

Yesterday saw the pound start on the back foot against, amid investor speculation that its rally to the highest level in more than five years was excessive.

GBPUSD started the session at 1.6948 before recovering slightly after the release of US GDP to end the session near the high of 1.7004. This morning the pair has opened at 1.6975.

GBPEUR fell away from recent 18 month highs to hit the low of 1.2446 from the earlier high of 1.2480. The pair has opened today at 1.2450.

The Confederation of British Industry’s gauge of UK retail sales dropped to 4 in June from 16 in May which is considerably lower than the 24 that analysts had predicted.

Carney will testify today at the BOE’s semi-annual financial stability report, this is amid speculation measures may be taken to cool the UK property market. This follows his comments on Tuesday that he was surprised by the lack of wage growth in the economy, damping speculation of an imminent increase in interest rates.

title: Thai abuses ‘some of the worst seen’ by EJF exec
content:
Campaign group Environmental Justice Foundation has welcomed the US Department of State’s decision to downgrade Thailand to Tier 3 in this year’s Trafficking in Persons (TIP) report.

“Today’s decision by the United States Department of State to downgrade Thailand is the right course of action given the damning evidence that has continued to emerge throughout 2013 and 2014,” said EJF executive director Steve Trent.

“It sends a clear message to the Thai government that speeches and public promises must be followed by robust action to tackle the appalling human rights abuses which continue have been documented. We hope the downgrade will spur the Thai government to take swift, practical and meaningful steps to end slavery, forced and bonded labor in the seafood sector and other industries.”

This year’s downgrade should also raise further alarm for companies sourcing products from Thailand, who must also shoulder some of the blame for failing to insist on action despite years of warning, he added.

“The question now is whether these companies can, and will, insist that their Thai suppliers work with them to root out and eradicate these abuses. This will be a real test for the significance and sincerity of industry commitments to eradicate slavery from seafood supply chains and a clear measure of whether product supply or human rights is considered more important in their boardrooms.”

“The abuses EJF has uncovered in Thailand are some of the worst I have seen in 25 years of environmental and human rights campaigning, and I remain deeply concerned about the situation facing trafficked migrant workers in Thailand,” said Trent.

“The international community must now ensure urgent action is taken to resolve the abuses, preserve human rights and protect the environment. EJF will continue to monitor these vitally important issues, working collaboratively with all stakeholders.”

Tier 3 of the system is reserved for countries judged as not having made sufficient progress in tackling human trafficking or making significant efforts to do so.

Following four consecutive years on the Tier 2 Watchlist, according to the rules, Thailand had to be either upgraded to Tier 2 or downgraded to Tier 3, the country could not spend a fifth year on the Tier 2 Watchlist.

The decision to downgrade Thailand in the 2014 Trafficking in Persons (TIP) report follows a series of reports by EJF, other civil society groups and the media this year apparently documenting the systemic use of modern-day slavery in Thailand’s seafood industry, including child and forced labour, forced detention, extreme violence and murder.

The downgrade means Thailand could potentially face sanctions, which might include the withdrawal of US non-humanitarian and non-trade-related assistance. It should also raise serious concerns for companies sourcing products from Thailand, particularly those who have made public commitments to eradicate slavery from their supply chains, said EJF.

Despite the threat of a downgrade, Thailand has consistently failed to act on the recommendations made in the US Department of State’s 2013 Trafficking in Persons (TIP) report, as well as falling short of its own commitments to tackle human trafficking made in documents such as the 2013 National Action Plan to Prevent and Suppress Human Trafficking (NAP), the campaign group said.

content:
International News

EURUSD traded within a fairly tight trading range yesterday, hitting a high of 1.3579 against a low of 1.3530. With no High tier data being released from the currency bloc yesterday, the pair were fairly resilient. Currently this morning the pair are holding strength around the 1.3572, look for resistance around the 1.36 level before this pair can move any higher.

The Australian Dollar under performed in overnight trade, slipping against its major counterparts. This was triggered by the release of minutes from June’s RBA policy meeting, where the central bank sounded rather dovish. GBPAUD currently sits around 1.8164 having opened at 1.8076 this morning.

US CPI figures will have the spotlight later today, where we have seen gradual improvement to consensus forecasts since the start of the year. Any positive outcome could well see a bounce in the US Dollar. EURUSD is sat at around the 1.3557 level this morning.

The JPY rose versus most of its major peers as violence in Iraq spurred concerns oil supplies will be disrupted and bolstered the appeal of haven assets. Japan’s currency touched the strongest level in four months against the euro after Iraq’s military attacked insurgents who had captured territory north of Baghdad. The zloty fell for a third day against the euro, weakening 0.5%to 4.1406, after recordings of a conversation between the central bank’s governor and a minister cast doubts about Marek Belka’s future and triggered a government crisis. GBPPLN is currently trading at 5.1705

INR strengthened against the pound this morning on the back of poor UK inflationary data mentioned above, the pair have moved this morning from the highs of 102.60 to already trade to the lows of 101.86. UK News

The British pound remains fairly bullish for the time being and all eyes will look to the release of the policy meeting minutes due out tomorrow morning. GBPEUR rose to a high of €1.2563 yesterday, the highest rate since October 2012. The market opened this morning at 1.2503, briefly dropping to 1.2489.

Released this morning at 930am was UK CPI measuring Inflation, showing growth of 1.5% in May after expectations of a 1.7% increase. This shows the slowest rate of inflation month on month in 4 years. GBPEUR dropped below the 1.25 level and now sits circa 1.2489.

The next BoE related event is the release of the June MPC minutes tomorrow when markets will assess how much further the MPC has moved towards considering a rate hike. The vote remained 9-0 to an increase hike at last month’s meeting and with Mark Carney speaking last Thursday in a rather bullish tone expect to see the voting pattern change this time around.

title: Report implicates CP Foods, US retailers in Thai slave labor sourcing
content:
Slaves forced to work for no pay for years at a time under threat of extreme violence are being used in Asia in the production of seafood sold by major US, British and other European retailers, the Guardian has reported.

A six-month investigation has established that large numbers of men bought and sold like animals and held against their will on fishing boats off Thailand are integral to the production of shrimp sold in leading supermarkets around the world, including the top four global retailers: Walmart, Carrefour, Costco and Tesco.

The investigation also found that the world's largest shrimp farmer, Thailand-based Charoen Pokphand Foods (CP Foods), buys fishmeal which it uses to make shrimp feed from some suppliers that own, operate or buy from fishing boats manned with slaves.

Men who have managed to escape from boats supplying CP Foods and other companies like it told the Guardian of horrific conditions, including 20-hour shifts, regular beatings, torture and execution-style killings. Some were at sea for years; some were regularly offered methamphetamines to keep them going. Some had seen fellow slaves murdered in front of them.

Fifteen migrant workers from Burma and Cambodia also told how they had been enslaved. They said they had paid brokers to help them find work in Thailand in factories or on building sites. But they had been sold instead to boat captains, sometimes for as little as £250.

title: Aquamar blog: EMS in Mexico could hit hard again in a month’s time
content:
The city of Veracruz in Mexico is hosting Aquamar International 2014 from Wednesday May 14 to Friday May 16.

The event aims to create a meeting point for industry players linked to Mexican aquaculture and fisheries.

The future of shrimp farming is a major topic up for discussion, with special emphasis on the largest producing regions of Sinaloa, Nayarit and Sonora, which were hit last year by the early mortality syndrome (EMS), losing about 70% of their annual shrimp production, estimated at around 100,000 metric tons.

The potential of tilapia farming for export to the US and for domestic sale are also set to be hot topics, as is domestic consumption in a country with a growing middle class and population of 120 million.

Keep clicking back for news as our reporter Alicia Villegas updates the blog from the show.

***

May 16, 2.20pm: Giant squid catches in Mexico up by 30% as local market strengthen consumption

Giant squid landings in Mexico are up by around 30% so far this year when compared with the same time a year ago, after a flat 2013 with catches at 60,000 metric tons, Juan Pedro Vela, facilitator at the National Committee of Giant Squid, told Undercurrent News.

Even when catches have improved in 2014, they are far from the 120,000t registered in peak years such as 1987 or 1996. Since then, volumes have fluctuated, but showing a downward trend.

As a consequence of lower volumes, exports have decreased in recent years, as giant squid players prefer to sell to the local market since it pays better.

Click here for full story.

***

May 16,  11.22am: US market demands organic trout from Mexico

Trucha Mexiquense, a trout producers' cooperative involving 92 farms based in the state of Mexico, is in talks with distributors to export to the US.

The cooperative has already trucked 150 kilos to the US, but almost its whole production -- 200 metric tons of trout per year -- goes to the domestic market, veterinary Jorge Martinez, from Trucha Mexiquense, told Undercurrent News.


"Some distributors from the US have asked us about exporting our trout to their country, as some states such as Texas or California have demand for fresh, organic trout that we produce," Martinez said.

The US market is paying more for organic trout -- MXN 90 per kilo, against MXN 65/kg the Mexican market pays.

"In Mexico, housewives prefer to buy tilapia over trout, as it is much cheaper, this is why we are looking at exports," Martinez said.

The cooperative is planning to increase production by 20% on the back of an investment of MXN 20 million -- of which the Mexican government contributes to 70% of financing.

The state of Mexico -- one of Mexico's 32 states -- is the largest trout producer of Mexico, contributing about 60% of national production with 6,000t.

***
May 16, 9.03am: EMS in Mexico could hit hard again in a month's time

Mexican shrimp farmers' need to find solutions against early mortality syndrome (EMS) is more imperative now than ever as temperatures will be much higher in a month's time, Miguel A. Castro, president of the State Committee of Shrimp Production in the state of Sonora told Undercurrent News.

Higher temperatures increase the risk of outbreaks that will hit harvests hard again.

After losing more than MXN 1 billion ($77 million) as a consequence of the EMS disease last year, Sonora's shrimp farmers are looking at new farming techniques, said Castro.

According to Castro, the key is monitoring, which would eventually allow to improve volumes.

"In Guatemala, for example, they are producing higher volumes with fewer hectares, obviously they are not hit by EMS as us, but with better control we could produce more in Sonora," Castro said.

As a consequence of EMS, Sonora is far from achieving the 84,000 metric tons of shrimp which it produced in 2010, despite having 127 farms and a potential of 300,000ha for farming operations, Castro said.

Last year, Sonora's shrimp output was less than half when compared to usual production; however, international prices and the aid from Mexican authorities were enough "so farmers could survive".

***

May 16, 8.07am: EMS could come from larvae

Shrimp farmers in the Mexican state of Sinaloa suspect early mortality syndrome (EMS) can come from larvae, Marben L. Miranda, director of fishing and aquaculture development of Sinaloa, told Undercurrent News.

Larvae from laboratories have poor genetic diversity, resulting in systemic problems such as less success in adapting to the environment or more vulnerability to diseases, Miranda said.

"Labs have told us they will improve larvae genetics, but I think the EMS problem is linked to this," Miranda said.

A shrimp farmer of Sinaloa, who preferred to not be quoted by name, echoed Miranda's opinion.

"The problem is in the larvae, the most difficult phase is when shrimp is at 2 to 5 grams in size, then is when they die," he said.

The producer, who has a farm of 100 hectares, has seen 50-60% of his production ravaged at this year’s first harvest, started in April.

"Prices are helping, but obviously we are worried, I haven't seen much improvement from last year in this harvest," he said.

***

May 15, 3.55pm: Mexico needs expertise to combat EMS, technology to exploit new species

The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) is already providing expertise to shed light on early mortality syndrome (EMS), which is hitting shrimp aquaculture in the Mexican states of Sinaloa, Nayarit and Sonora.

"We have experts from China and Italy working to shed light on this problem," Eduardo Garcia, assistant of programs for Mexico at FAO, told Undercurrent News.

The organization is also advising Mexican authorities on fishing and aquaculture regulations, to maximize the efficiency of laws and public funds, Garcia said.

According to Garcia, the economic and environmental sustainability of seafood production in Mexico depends on technical training and better coordination of fishing and aquaculture local producers.

Echoing Garcia's view, Maximiliano Lopez, from Algas and Bioderivados Marinos SA, said fishermen and farmers need greater training and  better technology to exploit new species.

"There are many species under exploited due to lack of technology; innovation is needed, but also applied research to improve production," Lopez said during a conference about optimization of fishing and aquaculture resources.

"Technology is important, but the first step is to provide technical training to improve aquaculture production," said Vicente Camporredondo, in charge of farmers' training at Mexico’s National Commission of Aquaculture and Fisheries (Conapesca).

"With basic techniques farmers can improve production and even decrease costs with no economic investment and then, they can invest in technology," said Camporredondo.

***

May 15, 2.49pm: Tilapia fresh fillets to US hit record volumes in 2013, keep prices high

Tilapia imports of fresh fillets were at record levels in 2013 with a total of 59 million of pounds, up by 7.27% year-on-year, Angel Rubio, chief market analyst at Urner Barry said during the conferences at the Aquamar expo.

Despite high demand, average prices remained flat to stronger last year at $4.15 per pound, due to pre-arranged sales to same clients at similar prices.

Prices are now at $4.25 per pound, an upward trend linked to the shift from tilapia production to shrimp in Ecuador.

Click here for full story.

***

May 15, 11.34am: Mexico's tilapia farming growth driven by local demand

Tilapia is one of the species with largest potential in Mexico, Miguel A. Flores, manager of business management and corporate social responsibility at Regal Springs Mexico, said during a conference about tilapia farming at the Aquamar International expo.

The potential is linked to the country's geographic situation, its tropical climate and the abundance of waters to harvest, but also to high tilapia demand in Mexico.

"Mexico produces around 70,000t metric tons of tilapia annually, and it consumes 130,000t, so the potential is there," Flores said.

The rest of production Mexico consumes -- 60,000t -- is imported from China.

Real Springs' division in Mexico has been established in Chiapas since 2006, but it took two years to start tilapia production with 800t.

Since then, the company's operations have strengthened the aquaculture sector in Chiapas, with tilapia volumes that contribute to 31% of production in Mexico.

In the following years, Chiapas is expected to produce 50% of national tilapia, pushed by the Real Springs' plans to increase production to 70,000 by 2016.

***
May 15, 9.01am: Regal Springs could invest up to $50m in Mexico

Regal Springs Tilapia will make an investment that could reach up to $50 million over the next three years to up production in Mexico to 70,000 metric tons.

The investment is part of the company’s growth strategy to hit $400 million in turnover by 2016.

After processing about 11,500t tilapia in its plant in Chiapas last year, Regal Springs –headquartered in Miramar — aims to up production to 20,000t by end of 2014.

The aim is to fully exploit its licenses’ allowance to farm up to 70,000t by 2016, Miguel A. Flores, from Regal Springs Mexico, told Undercurrent News.

To reach this goal, the company could make an investment of up to $50m to improve equipment and expand production capacity of its hatchery and processing plant.

***
May 14, 4.22pm: Mexico's octopus fishery to issue a certificate of origin

Mexican octopus producers plan to issue a certificate of origin to boost exports to the EU, where bid volumes can be commercialized.

Producers also plan to undergo a quality assessment to obtain certificates to sell on a large scale in Europe, Carlos Mauricio Beytia, fishing subsecretary of Campeche at the Ministry of Fisheries and Aquaculture (Sepesca), told Undercurrent News.

The Mexican states of Campeche and Yucatan contribute 94% of national octopus production, which has remained at 25,000 metric tons in the last three years.

Annual octopus production in Mexico is valued at MXN 557 million ($43m).

***
May 14, 3.45pm: Mexican market with great potential, but consumption still low

Mexican authorities are working to boost seafood consumption in the domestic market, where demand remains low at only nine kilos per capita, Rosa E. Acosta, from the fishing association CONACOOP, told Undercurrent News.

Despite having 11,122 kilometers of coastline and being the fourth largest fish producer in the Americas, seafood consumption in Mexico is quite low in comparison to other countries, Acosta said, mainly due to the locals' lack of knowledge about how to cook and store fish.

"It is not a problem of prices, as there are many cheap species, the problem is people in Mexico don't know how to store fish to keep it fresh longer, and how to cook it in different ways," Acosta said.

Another important challenge is to improve logistics so the distribution process is more efficient.

"The government is already working to overcome this challenges," Acosta said.

***
May 14, 1.42pm: Sardine producers shift to squid as catches drop 200,000t

Mexican producers of sardine, the most important species in the country in terms of catches, saw landings at 600,000 metric tons last year, an important figure but still lower than previous years, Norma Lucio from Natural Resources Management organization (Marea) told Undercurrent News.

Sardine catches totaled about 800,000t two years ago, but in 2013 landings decreased by 200,000t, due to changes in climate and ecosystems as a consequence of currents from California.

The drop in catches has hit Baja California and Baja California Sur Mexican states particularly and, as a consequence, sardine producers are shifting to loligo squid this year.

"Prices of loligo squid are much higher than sardine at $4,200 per ton and, due to a convenient availability of the resource right now, industrial sardine producers in Baja California and Baja California Sur have decided to shift sardine to loligo squid," Lucio said.

"The problem of squid is nobody knows when and where it will be available," she added.

Around 70% of Mexican sardine production is exported to China mainly for processing, with prices of $2,200 per ton.

Due to higher production costs in China, however, important Mexican producers such as Bajamarin have started a process of certification to export to Europe, as the Eastern part of the continent is seen now with high potential for processing.

***
May 14, 12.11pm: Mexico’s wild shrimp volumes up 5% so far this year, after flat 2013

Mexico’s wild shrimp harvest is up by a modest 5% so far this year, the president of the country’s National Chamber of Fisheries and Aquaculture, Fernando Medrano, told Undercurrent News.

Wild shrimp catches in Mexico were flat in both 2013 and 2012, at around 60,000 metric tons, said Medrano.

The president of Wild Shrimp Production in Campeche -- an association of producers --Cesar M. Ceballos said the increase of catches in the state might be linked to fewer boats fishing in the north part of Mexico, as a consequence of insecurity and violence in the area.

Click here for the full story.

***
May 14, 11.00am: Small hopes for farmers as first harvest shows y-o-y increase

Volumes reported by Mexico’s shrimp farmers after the end of the year’s first harvests in April suggest that production is slightly up from the same time last year, a government official told Undercurrent News.

But farmers are remaining cautious, as outbreaks of early mortality syndrome (EMS) ravaged production at some farms in two states in April this year.

EMS devastated Mexican production last year, with volumes plummeting to 55,000 metric tons from 120,000t in 2012.

This has forced farmers to decrease production densities using better systems of monitoring, said Juan Antonio Perez, production chain director at Mexico’s Secretariat of Agriculture, Livestock, Rural Development, Fisheries and Food (Sagarpa).

Since April this year, shrimp farmers in the northwestern states of Sinaloa, Sonora and Nayarit — Mexico’s main production regions — have already harvested around 80% of their total farming area, which is around 60,000ha.

A recovery is likely three years' away, said Perez.

The president of the National Chamber of Fisheries and Aquaculture, Fernando Medrano,said there have been already outbreaks in this year’s first harvest circle, ravaging production of some farms at Sinaloa and Nayarit.

“This year will be difficult, although we tend to be optimistic,” said Medrano.

Click here for the full story.

***
May 14, 10.55am: Shrimp exports drop as local market prices double

Shrimp prices in Mexico have doubled as a result of lower volumes and higher demand from emerging middle classes, said Juan Antonio Perez, production chain director at Mexico’s Secretariat of Agriculture, Livestock, Rural Development, Fisheries and Food (Sagarpa).

In comparison, export prices to the US have risen by around 50%, to $22 per kilo, when compared to the last year, he said.

As a result, producers are selling more of their harvest to the domestic market.

“Shrimp producers prefer to sell to the local market than exporting, as prices have gone up much more in Mexico than in the US, where only the largest sizes are exported,” Perez said.

In 2013, exports to the US accounted for 20% of domestic production -- down from 30% in previous year, he said.

title: Mexico’s wild shrimp volumes up 5% so far this year, after flat 2013
content:
Mexico's wild shrimp harvest is up by a modest 5% so far this year, the president of the country's National Chamber of Fisheries and Aquaculture, Fernando Medrano, told Undercurrent News.

Wild shrimp catches in Mexico were flat in both 2013 and 2012, at around 60,000 metric tons, said Medrano, speaking during the Aquamar International Expo in Veracruz.

Although this year's increase is not to to the levels of the 84,000t peak reached in 2011, it has sparked optimism among some catchers.

In the Mexican state of Campeche, for example, landings have increased by 5% so far this year. The first fishing season runs from August to end of May.

The president of Wild Shrimp Production in Campeche -- an association of producers --Cesar M. Ceballos said the increase of catches in the state might be linked to fewer boats fishing in the north part of Mexico, as a consequence of insecurity and violence in the area.

In the north, shrimp vessels operate only during particular months: August, September and part of October and November, while in the South -- where Campeche is located -- boats operate all year round.

"In Campeche we produce now more wild shrimp with less effort," Ceballos said.

Last year, wild shrimp catches in Campeche totaled around 3,000t, with an average sales price of $7,80 per pound.

Production was sold mainly to the domestic market, due to a combination of factors: high demand from emerging classes and tourism, less supply from aquaculture and lower logistic costs involving sales in the local market.

"Now is a good moment for the local market, producers in Campeche do not want to risk profits by selling to the US, as exports increase logistic, insurance and production costs," said Ceballos.

title: Untitled
content:
The government of president Michelle Bachelet apologized in the name of the Chilean state to the indigenous Mapuche tribe “for taking their lands”, and said it has a pending debt in terms of public policies that will allow the La Araucania region, where 600,000 of the Indians live, to emerge from poverty.

In Araucania, indigenous militants have torched vehicles, highway toll booths and lumber shipments as part of a struggle to reclaim lands the Mapuches lost during a 19th century “pacification” campaign. Those lands are now largely occupied by lumber, and agricultural and aquaculture interests.

The statement was made by the new governor of the zone, Francisco Huenchumilla, one of the regional officials named by newly re-elected president Bachelet.

“The state's payment of this debt is pending and for more than 130 years it has implemented public policies that have not managed to bring this region out of poverty and from among the last areas of national development,” the governor said.

Huenchumilla, himself a Mapuche, said that to move forward along this road he will meet with all the organizations of the productive sectors that “have been affected by the violence,” given that in this new scenario “all must be heard.”

The governor also called on prosecutors of the region to collaborate in creating a climate of respect and tolerance in the area, saying, “We must calm the spirits.”
