title: MEPs call for Thailand to address forced labor
content:
The Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF) has welcomed a European parliament vote recommending that Thailand be required to address human trafficking and forced labor in its fishing industry, as part of trade negotiations between it and the EU.

The resolution, proposed by the president of the European parliament fisheries committee (PECH) Gabriel Mato MEP, highlighted that “the ILO and various NGOs have recently uncovered serious shortcomings with regard to social and labor conditions and respect for human rights in the Thai fishing industry”.

The resolution calls for Thailand to “respect, promote and implement internationally recognized labor standards…including those on forced labor and child labor”.

It also calls for Thailand to be required to cooperate in fighting illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing, citing the involvement of Thai-owned fishing vessels in IUU fishing in West Africa.

It passed with 503 in favor, 69 against and with 32 abstentions.

“This decisive resolution by the European Parliament clearly demonstrates that any trade agreement with Thailand must be conditional on the Thai Government resolving the issues of human trafficking and human rights abuses in its fishing sector,” said Steve Trent, executive director of EJF.

“Crucially, we need to see the Thai Government working towards a sustainable and ethical fishing industry and taking firm and decisive action against business owners and corrupt officials exploiting modern day slaves. Members of the European Parliament have sent a clear message that European consumers do not want seafood associated with slavery on their plates.”

EJF presented its findings on human rights abuses in the Thai fishing industry to Members of the European Parliament in July 2013 in an event also attended by high-ranking officials from the Thai Mission to the EU.

In the Slavery at Sea report launched last week, EJF revealed further evidence of human trafficking and the routine use of violence in the Thai fishing industry, along with the failure of the Thai Government to identify and prosecute criminals, corrupt officials and unscrupulous business operators.

title: Trafficking, slavery still critical issue in Thai fishing industry, says EJF
content:
Trafficking of slave labor remains prevalent across Thailand's fishing industry, and the Thai government is failing to address the issue, said a new report by the Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF).

The report comes as Thailand is facing a possible downgrade on the US' human trafficking watch list in April.

"Investigations in 2014 document the continued prevalence of trafficking in the Thai fishing industry, with operators now taking greater precaution to avoid detection, including transhipping trafficked workers at sea," said the NGO in a new report released on Tuesday.

In 2013, to address a series of criticisms made by observers, Thailand's ministry of social development and human security (MSDHS) released a national action plan to prevent and suppress human trafficking (NAP), said EJF.

However, said the NGO, "the document itself is broad in scope and undermined by vague objectives. EJF investigations have revealed evidence that the Thai government is falling far short of critical commitments made in the action plan."

The issue of labor conditions is a critical one for Thailand and its exporters. Last year Thai Union Frozen Products, struggling to cope with a 'perfect storm' of ravaging shrimp diseases, volatile tuna prices and wildly fluctuating exchange rates, nevertheless identified Thailand's labor issues as the company's greatest challenge ahead.

Corruption is a major obstacle to fighting trafficking of workers in Thai fisheries, says EJF

In particular, exporters are concerned that the US might downgrade Thailand’s ranking on the human trafficking watch list in April.

A downgrading by the US could pose a big problem, said Thai Union's president and CEO Thiraphong Chansiri.

Thailand has spent four consecutive years on the Tier 2 Watchlist of the US department of state’s trafficking in persons report. It faces a mandatory downgrade to Tier 3 in 2014 if the major issues are not adequately addressed, said EJF.

The country is the world's third largest seafood exporter, with seafood exports valued at $7.3 billion in 2011. The European Union imported more than $1.15bn worth of seafood from Thailand in 2012, while exports to the US exceeded $1.6bn in 2013.

However, said EJF, "the Thai fishing industry remains heavily reliant on trafficked and forced labour. It is clear that rising overheads, exacerbated by the need to spend more time at sea for smaller catches due to over-fishing and chronic mismanagement of the fishery will continue to encourage these abuses."

"As boat operators have looked to cut costs, working conditions and wages have suffered, causing many workers to turn away from the industry and forcing some employers to rely on criminal trafficking networks to meet the labor shortfall," it said.

The NGO identified corruption as a key obstacle to fighting human trafficking in Thailand, citing evidence of police collusion and of local officials protecting and assisting "unscrupulous brokers and business owners" engaged in trafficking and abuse of migrant workers.

In its report Sold to the Sea last year, the NGO documented the case of 14 men rescued from a port in Kantang, after having been trafficked from Myanmar to Thailand and forced into fisheries. After nearly a year in government shelter and little progress on their case, however, the victims "told EJF in 2014 that they are frustrated and now more focused on returning home than pursuing their case", it said.

The case reveals "serious structural failings in how Thai authorities deal with human trafficking victims and cases more generally", said EJF.

"Without determined action at the highest levels of government to identify and successfully prosecute criminals, corrupt officials and unscrupulous business operators, alongside the introduction and enforcement of comprehensive measures to regulate Thailand’s fishing fleets and recruitment practices, violence, exploitation and slavery will remain an ongoing feature of Thailand’s seafood industry," said the NGO.

Its report can be read here in full.

title: Senegal’s seizure of Russian trawler could impact trade with Russia
content:
Russia's veterinary authority Rosselkhoznadzor has said it will take the situation surrounding the Russian trawler Oleg Naydenov into account when making its decision on inspecting Senegalese fish processing companies, reports Interfax.

"When deciding on inspections, we will take into account the entire range of circumstances. We are interested in expanding the Russian fish market, but we are also interested in full cooperation that excludes violence towards trawlers and fishermen," the watchdog's official representative Alexei Alexeyenko told Interfax.

Before the new year, Senegal and Uganda had contacted Rosselkhoznadzor requesting to inspect fish enterprises of the two countries in order to organize fish imports into the Russian market. Inspection terms have not yet been determined, and Russian specialists still need to reach an agreement with the customs union.

Alexeyenko said that Rosselkhoznadzor is hoping that the situation will reach a civilized level and the issue will be resolved in a diplomatic manner. "There are specific agreements operating in the waters that must not be broken," he said.

"In my opinion, coincidences like these do not occur - simultaneously arresting our trawler and requests to begin importing fish," said head of Russia's federal fisheries agency (Rosrybolovstvo) Andrei Krainy.

title: Chile’s artisanal fisheries denounce slashed quotas, threaten to demonstrate
content:
Chile's artisanal fisheries, which represent 55% of the quota share in Chile, expressed their dismay over the near 450,000 metric tons cut in total allowable catches (TACs) for the country’s main stocks – anchovy, sardine, hoki and hake -- for 2014.

The sector fears slashed quotas will have drastic social and economic effects, hitting the artisanal fishermen working in Chile. These are estimated to number 91,437, according to data from Sernapesca, the national fisheries institute, collected in 2012.

One association that represents artisanal fishermen -- Chilean National Confederation of Artisanal Fishermen (Conapach) -- recently told Undercurrent News that the cuts would mean $10 million in losses and the destruction of 20,000 direct jobs for the country’s artisanal fisheries.

"The unilateral announcement of lower quotas ratifies the announced death of artisanal fisheries, as this will cause a wave of unprecedented unemployment, the worst in our history,” said Miguel Avalos, director of Conapach in the Chilean fishing region III.

Although the fisheries directorate Subpesca said the new fisheries law establishes compensation measures for fishermen, ships’ crews and processing plants workers in the case of the stocks getting exhausted, these actions will be only effective once management committees are set throughout this year.

Conapach argues the law is being poorly implemented, since quotas cannot be reduced to half without doing a full audit of fisheries, as is required by law, and without establishing a recovery program yet.

“We believe the best way to proceed is through the management committees to decide together the mitigation measures and deadlines for the recovery of resources," Zoila Bustamante, president of Conapach, said in a statement.

According to the artisanal associations, the scientific committees have overreacted in their desire to protect fisheries. The associations argue the committees do not know the reality of artisanal fisheries, and are not familiar with the management of different fisheries.

Lobbying for a repeal of the law

Another Chilean fisheries association, Condepp, has reportedly threatened to demonstrate if it does not reach an agreement with the government to change the country's new fishing law at a meeting scheduled for Jan. 9 with Felix de Vicente, Chilean's minister of economy.

Condepp says it already held a meeting with the new elected president of Chile, Michelle Bachelet, and claims the president pledged to review the law, particularly issues related with quota property.

"We are going to fight, and there will be violence between police and us, the government is stomping on us," Jorge Bustos, one of Condepp told 24horas.cl.

Taking power away from the 'seven families'

Condepp claims the sea must be for artisanal fishermen and not for the "seven families", referring to Chile's fishing dynasties: the Angelinis (Corpesca and Orizon), the Lecaros (Pesquera Coloso), the Yaconi-Santa Cruz and Sarquis families, both owning Blumar, the Stengel family (Pesquera Biobio), the Fernandez (Camanchaca) and the Izquierdo family (Alimentos and San Antonio).

But Conapach has distanced itself from Condepp.

The advent of Chile’s fishing law, which entered into force on Jan. 1, 2013, actually saw artisanal fisheries given 55% of the total fishing quotas, up from 52%, an increase valued by Subpesca at the time at $30m.

This seems to contradict Condepp's claim that the Chilean sea is controlled by the industrial sector.

“[Condepp's] criticisms on the fishing law hide their personal interests, pushing authorities and confusing the public opinion,” said Conapach.

In fact, even the artisanal fleet itself is hugely concentrated in the hands of a few -- according to Subpesca, 10% of the artisanal fleet is responsible for catching 90% of the artisanal quota.

That would mean that 1,354 artisanal boats control half of Chile’s national fishing quotas.

It is these vessels that will feel the strongest impact from the new law, Subpesca told Undercurrent in January 2013. According to the directorate, those boats are in turn controlled by what could be described as almost semi-industrial family-owned companies.

A member of Conapach told Undercurrent Condepp is in fact following the interests of the industrial fleet, as since last year they wanted fisheries to be able to bid for quota transfers without any restrictions.

In the past, Chile's new fishing law quotas were permanent, but as of the new law, quota licenses only last for 20 years, with the possibility of being renovated in case fisheries do not commit infringements. Once licenses expire, quotas are open for bids.

The law also establishes if fisheries are not overexploited, after five years, up to 15% of the industrial quota could be offered to be sold.

title: NGO: Close western markets to Thai shrimp
content:
The Environmental Justice Foundation has called for western markets to boycott Thai shrimp until Thailand corrects the labor abuses that a new report by EJF says are rife in its processing sector.

“This is a blunt tool, and not wanted, but if the Thai government, international community and retailers do not work together to end the abuses soon, it will be necessary,” Steve Trent, executive director of EJF, told Undercurrent News.

“Shutting the market is not asking for the impossible. If this was a food hygiene issue, market access be closed off immediately. The EU has a duty to protect its citizens – it also has a right to protect Thailand's migrant laborers.”

EJF says the processing industry in the Asian nation, which is the world's largest exporter of warmwater vannamei, does not just have a problem with human rights abuses, but is built on it.

Research for its latest report was carried out in October 2012 and March 2013, but the NGO can categorically say abuses are still happening, said Trent.

“This is the economic model of the industry - 90% of the workforce is migrant, and a large proportion is unregistered, and trafficked. Some will be there because they wanted to be, many are not,” he said.

Despite invitations from the Thai processing industry to visit and inspect plants, EJF suspects this is purely to calm critics such as the US justice department. When audits are genuinely held, corruption means they are either not really unannounced, or officials turn a blind eye.

“Everyone in Thailand knows what's going on. They know about the levels of wages, that there's unprotected laborers. It's simply to protect market access,” said Trent.

“The Thai industry's not going to change until it's denied access to profitable markets. It needs to open up to closer scrutiny, genuinely unannounced audits, and not just checks of the glossier side. There are around 2,000 [shrimp processing] sheds in operation in Thailand, and around 400 of them registered with the TFFA [Thai Frozen Foods Association].”

'The Hidden Cost: Human Rights Abuses in Thailand’s Shrimp Industry' follows EJF’s 'Sold to the Sea' report, published in May this year, which revealed evidence of human trafficking, labor abuse and the routine use of violence, including murder, in the Thai fishing industry.

The new report says it exposes the reliance of Thailand’s shrimp industry on migrant workers, many of whom are trafficked and face arduous journeys, and even armed robbery, before enduring abusive conditions in shrimp processing factories.

It examines how global demand for cheap shrimp is fueling exploitation in the Thai shrimp sector. Inadequate regulation by Thai authorities, unscrupulous brokers, corrupt officials and a lack of supply chain transparency have allowed uncontrolled pre-processing facilities to operate beyond scrutiny, at a hidden cost to those working in the industry, said EJF.

The NGO recorded four testimonies from migrants trafficked by brokers from Myanmar to Thailand to work in the shrimp industry, which it said included reports of gruelling journeys on foot, cramped conditions in vehicles, armed robbery, rape and the detention of property including mobile phones.

It also interviewed five former workers at a pre-processing factory owned by a Captain in the Royal Thai Police.

They had all been trafficked into debt bondage and had their identification documents confiscated, their movements restricted and were forced to work up to 16 hour shifts. One of the interviewees was just ten years old at the time and recalled eight or nine children working in the factory, peeling shrimp and extracting excrement until 8pm every day.

Fuel for the fire

This report comes just one day after the International Labor Rights Forum urged governments to consider the implications of a different report into human rights abuses in Thailand.

In June, Walmart supplier Narong Seafoods was accused of various human rights infringements, though a Global Aquaculture Alliance audit reportedly found nothing to suggest it should not go on with its GAA certification.

These reports have fueled anger on the part of some seafood businesses in the EU which, with a possible free trade agreement covering seafood on the horizon, insist any nations importing into Europe should have to match the same labor conditions, wages, and standards that they do inside the EU.

title: ILO study finds standards shortfalls in Thai fishing industry
content:
A new report co-authored by the International Labour Organization (ILO) and the Asian Research Centre on Migration at Chulalongkorn University has found shortfalls in Thailand’s fishing industry in relation to national and international labor standards.

The report is based on 596 interviews, making it the largest survey to date of working conditions in the Thai fishing sector, and found around 17% of those surveyed said they were working against their will and unable to leave because of the threat of penalties.

These workers fell into two groups; those who could not leave because of a financial penalty (12%), and those who cited other reasons including the threat of violence or denunciation to the authorities (4.9%).

Conditions were found to be worse for those who had been at sea for more than one month; nearly 25% were subjected to deceptive or coercive labor practices.

While most of the fishers surveyed entered the fishing sector voluntarily, 5.4% stated that they were deceived or coerced into work in fishing. The problem was especially pronounced among long-haul fishers, with nearly one in six of the long-haul fishers surveyed stating that they did not willingly decide to work on a fishing vessel.

Of these 32 respondents, 17 workers stated that they were “deceived or forced to work by the agents from the country of origin”, nine workers said it was agents from Thailand and six their family or relatives.

The survey also found 33 children under the age of 18 working on fishing vessels, of whom seven were under 15.

The report concludes that many of the problems faced by fishers are compounded by a lack of employment contracts; 94% of those surveyed did not have a written contract. As such, working hours and the terms of payment, including the method for calculating pay (usually incorporating a share of the sale of the catch), frequency of pay and deductions, are not clearly defined.

Other contributing factors include the irregular status of migrant fishers, limited monitoring by the labor inspectorate or other bodies, and the lack of any representative workers’ group.

“The ILO report substantiates our conviction that human rights abuses are widespread in the fishing industry, both in Thailand and elsewhere,” said Steve Trent, executive director of Environmental Justice Foundation, which itself published a report into human rights abuses in the Thai fishing industry.

“The uncomfortable truth is that fish caught on such vessels has been tracked through international supply chains to the European and US seafood markets. Fish caught by these modern-day slaves is reaching our own plates,” he said.

title: Euro boosted by increased manufacturing activity
content:
International news

The euro trimmed losses against the dollar, as better than forecast euro zone data buoyed the single currency, but the dollar remained supported after July’s Federal Reserve minutes indicated that the bank is on track to start tapering this year. EURUSD pulled back from 1.3298, the lowest since August 15, to hit 1.3341 during U.S. morning trade, still down 0.11% for the day.

French Flash Manufacturing PMI for August was today reported as unchanged at 49.7, falling short of analysts’ estimates for expansion to 50.4. However, the survey for the services sector contracted from 48.6 to 47.7 and suffice to say disappointed expectations for 49.3.

German Flash Manufacturing PMI for August beat expectations for 51.1 and improved to 52.0 after July’s 50.7, revised up from 50.3. Germany’s Flash PMI Services was also well above the median economists’ forecast for 51.7 actually progressing to 52.4. Still, the positive surprise was offset by the significant downward revision of July’s data, from 52.5 to 51.3.

The number of Americans filing new claims for jobless benefits held near a six-year low last week and U.S. manufacturing activity hit a five-month high this month, suggesting the economy is starting to find firmer footing. Initial claims for state unemployment benefits climbed 13,000 to 336,000.

A gauge of the U.S. economy's health rose in July, pointing to stronger growth in the second half of the year. The Conference Board says its index of leading indicators increased 0.6 percent last month to a reading of 96.0. The increase followed no change in June and 0.2 percent increase in May.

Core retail sales in Canada fell unexpectedly in June, while total retail sales figures also declined. In a report, Statistics Canada said core retail sales, which exclude automobile sales, fell by a seasonally adjusted 0.8% in June, confounding expectations for a 0.1% increase. GBPCAD is currently trading at 1.6489 the highest level since March 2010.

And Stock markets in the United Arab Emirates and Qatar rose to new multi-year highs despite a sell-off in emerging markets around the world, as retail investors in the Gulf bought selected stocks. Egypt's bourse rose on the back of a reduction in street violence.

UK news

The Pound fell to session lows against the euro on Thursday with GBPEUR dropping to a low of 1.1664 as markets opened across the Atlantic. The single currency was boosted after data showed that manufacturing activity in the euro zone expanded at the fastest pace in 26 months in August.

GBPUSD hit 1.5576 during European morning trade, the lowest since August 15; the pair subsequently consolidated at 1.5583, shedding 0.4%. The dollar strengthened after the minutes of the Fed’s July meeting showed that officials were comfortable with plans to start unwinding the bank’s $85bn per month bond buying program.

Bank of England commitee member Martin Weale says theBoE may need to resort to further “quantitative easing” if the economy stalls again. In an interview with The Daily Telegraph he said that he could “envisage circumstances in which it would be sensible to undertake further asset purchases” on top of the Bank’s recently announced policy of forward guidance.

Britain's biggest banks face a compensation bill for up to £1.5bn to pay for six years of mis-sold credit card and identity theft insurance. The City regulator is expected to confirm the details of a nationwide redress scheme for as many as 4m Britons sold useless cover between 2005 and 2011.

This morning has seen positive Q2 GDP figures for the UK. The revised figure for the second estimate has shown a 0.1% increase to 0.7%. Sterling has moved up slightly across the board and is trading at €1.1702 and $1.5623.

title: EJF: Thai labor abuse report not focused on isolated incident
content:
The Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF) is not using an isolated incident to apply to the entire Thai seafood industry, said Steve Trent, EJF executive director.

On May 29, EJF published its investigation into human rights abuses in the Thai fishing industry, and has called for immediate action after finding evidence of human trafficking, torture and murder.

In response to the report, John Sackton, publisher of Seafoodnews.com, said work on the issue is being done and the report highlights a worst case example.

Trent disagrees. His response is published in full, below:

"Whilst the report focused on one specific case involving 14 trafficked men who were forced into labor on fishing vessels, our work alongside partner organizations in the region sadly showed that the harrowing stories from these men are not unique to this one incident.

"As highlighted by Mr. Sackton, there are multiple initiatives aimed at addressing human trafficking in Thailand’s fishing industry. We support the work being done by the International Labour Organisation (ILO), other UN agencies, and crucially by migrant workers themselves.

"However, meaningful progress on addressing human trafficking will only be made when the Thai Government demonstrates the political willingness to do so.

"Mr Sackton highlights that: “In the first week of May, Labor Minister Padermchai Sasomsap met with a representative from the ILO to assure him that the Thai government has been placing its emphasis on enhancing the quality of life of workers and eradicating human trafficking.”

"Statements of this kind may be encouraging, but they are entirely meaningless without actual action by the Government agencies tasked with addressing human trafficking and protecting migrant workers.

"This action must include severe penalties for those boat owners and seafood companies that ‘buy’ trafficked workers, and the officials that too often facilitate (and even benefit from) human trafficking.

"In researching Sold to the Sea, EJF observed a human trafficking investigation from close quarters and spent significant amounts of time with victims.

"We documented how the police used trafficked men as forced labor, worked in concert with their murderous broker, and allowed the boat owner access to the victims in order that he could attempt to bribe them not to give evidence against him.

"So far, neither the boat owner nor the corrupt officials involved have been properly investigated.

"Whilst we welcome the fact that Thailand’s Department for Special Investigation (DSI) is now reviewing the evidence following the release of the report, this case reflects very badly on the Government’s progress at dealing human trafficking in the fisheries sector.

"Equally damning is the finding in the US State Department’s 2012 Trafficking in Person’s (TIP) Report that the Thai Navy failed to identify any suspected trafficking cases during over 1,000 inspections at sea in 2011.

"So far, there is no evidence that this trend of weak enforcement has been reversed. Meanwhile, an estimated 200,000 migrant workers (some of whom are minors) ply the Gulf of Thailand and Andaman Seas without protection, often subject to forced and bonded labor, violence and even murder.

"All too often these people are forgotten at the high-level meetings or press conferences where commendable commitments are made.

"In documenting this case, and releasing Sold to the Sea, we wanted to ensure that the victims of this brutal trade are heard, and that the gap between the recent statements of the Thai Government and the reality of the situation on Thailand’s fishing boats and in its ports is exposed.

"And whilst the case highlighted may be characterized as “the worst of the worst”, it remains highly relevant to the international seafood supply chain.

"We have been able to document the link between the fisheries products caught by the boats involved in this case and the European and US seafood supply chain.

"We are now working constructively with a number of stakeholders to address this issue and ensure importers of Thai seafood are not inadvertently fuelling human trafficking.

"The British Retail Consortium has supported the report, and encouraged the Thai Government to follow the report's recommendations as a matter of urgency, to combat trafficking and ensure that there are robust systems in place to monitor working conditions in the fishing industry.

"Our ambition, and that of many of the seafood companies and retailers we are talking to, is that no human trafficking should exist in the international seafood supply chain.

"To achieve this is going to require a paradigm shift, not sluggish and superficial change. EJF aims to work with the ILO and the other concerned agencies, governments and businesses to eradicate this modern day slavery."

title: Calls for Thai action against human rights abuses
content:
The Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF) has published its investigation into human rights abuses in the Thai fishing industry, and has called for immediate action after finding evidence of human trafficking, torture and murder.

EJF said the report gathered first-hand evidence, verified by independent third party sources, to draw a number of frightening conclusions, including the fact that 59% of people surveyed had witnessed the murder of a crewmember aboard a vessel.

"Not only was it a surprise just how bad the situation in Thailand was, it was also a surprise just how extensive it seems, and how this is a crime that is not operating under cover of darkness," Steve Trent, executive director of EJF, told Undercurrent News.

"My belief is there is a wide knowledge of what is going on within the industry in Thailand, within the enforcement agencies charged with protecting these people, and within society at large," he said.

He was also shocked by the overwhelming use of casual, yet severe, violence, in the industry which represents the world's third-largest by export value.

"This is astonishing, and the fact is you can be sure some of these products made using forced and slave labor are coming to our tables."

The companies employing trafficked people to work on their vessels range from small operations, up to some big Thai fishing firms, Trent said. EJF is unable to name them yet as the case is ongoing, but Trent said a more comprehensive and global investigation is planned for the very near future.

Thai companies are at the very least turning a blind eye, and have the responsibility, and culpability, to make changes, he added.

"But the other dynamic is the agencies and authorities of the government, the police and so on, are not doing their jobs," Trent said.

"We need to see a turnaround in terms of political leadership in Thailand to address this, and give it priority. It's a scandal they're not looking at it. I think there's an awful lot of people turning a blind eye because it makes good business."

Damning evidence

The core of the NGO's report was evidence taken from six men rescued from a port in Kantang by local police.

All had been trafficked into working on fishing vessels for up to 20 hours a day with little to no pay, and all had been at sea for over five months, according to the report.

Two of the interviewees reported seeing a crewmember tortured and executed for trying to leave, as well as five other murders. Another former boat worker interviewed on a separate occasion said he witnessed multiple deaths, with the bodies being dropped into the sea.

According to EJF there is evidence of Thai authorities willfully ignoring the cases, and even taking advantage of human trafficking. One boat worker reported being forced to work on a rubber plantation owned by a senior Thai police officer while in port.

“The court process is ongoing,” said EJF. “The likelihood of the process taking a year or more, the men’s inability to work, a lack of legal representation, and an apparently compromised judicial system are all adding to questions over the prospect of a successful conviction.”

The Thai fishing industry is experiencing a labor shortage, with long hours, low pay, physically difficult work and long periods at sea meaning unemployed migrants to Thailand are being funneled onto vessels.

As a result of its failure to address human trafficking, Thailand has been on the Tier 2 watchlist of the US state department’s Trafficking in Persons (TIP) report for three years, narrowly avoiding a mandatory downgrade to Tier 3 in 2012, following the submission of a written plan to address the issues by the Thai government.

"Thailand should urgently build the capacity of the police, navy, immigration officials, prosecutors and labor inspectors to deal effectively with trafficking cases and ensure those responsible for human trafficking are held to account"

Many fear for the seafood industry, as such a downgrade would have a significant impact on Thailand’s export-driven economy, with the US representing the country’s second largest export market.

EJF has pointed to corruption and failings among those Thai officials responsible for the safe and fair employment of individuals as a reason the practice is allowed to continue. Evidence suggests police willingness to allow traffickers and brokers to bribe or threaten witnesses under their protection, while the workers themselves have said many of their boats have been guilty of fishing illegally, and fleeing patrol vessels.

As a result of its investigation, EJF has called for Thailand to take a number of measures, including the implementation of the 2000 UN Human Trafficking Protocol, and Thailand’s own 2008 Anti-Human Trafficking Act.

“Thailand should urgently build the capacity of the police, navy, immigration officials, prosecutors and labor inspectors to deal effectively with trafficking cases and ensure those responsible for human trafficking are held to account,” said EJF.

Women sorting fish. Photo: EJF

“In particular, Thailand must ensure that those that employ trafficked workers, and public officials that facilitate human trafficking, are investigated and prosecuted.”

The NGO also recommended Thailand work with Myanmar to address their porous border, through which many of the 200,000 migrants working on Thai vessels move.

The next step for EJF is to produce an overview of different geographic regions, in an effort to highlight the overarching practices of slave and forced labor, said Steve Trent.

"Our interest is identifying the strategic pressure points that we can leverage to stop this. It's not about flag-waving, but about giving economic, real-world solutions delivered by governments and inter-governmental agencies to stop it, to drag the supply chain out of the shadows."

title: Bangkok Post: Thai shrimp business needs to face up to child labor problems
content:
An editorial in The Bangkok Post has slammed the Thai shrimp industry for not ‘shaping up’ when it comes to child exploitation in the labor market.

The newspaper criticized the industry’s reaction to a PBS documentary shown in the US that investigated the working conditions of migrant workers, especially children, in the Samut Sakhon province.

PBS, in a broadcast made in September, accused the Thai shrimp industry of abusive working practices including corruption, trafficking and violence.

“As if on cue, the authorities and major shrimp exporters in Samut Sakhon immediately came out to deny the PBS report. This is unwise. Instead of going on the defensive, Samut Sakhon, as the centre of the shrimp industry, must come up with effective measures to regulate the shrimp industry to keep the loyalty of its US market, which is the industry's biggest customer,” the editorial said.

The Post has called on the shrimp industry to improve working conditions in the national interest, or run the risk of US consumers boycotting Thai products because of the negative publicity.

title: Norwegian investigation finds wounded salmon illegally shipped to Europe
content:
An investigation by Norwegian media outlet NRK has uncovered routine illegal shipments of wounded or below-standard salmon, so-called "production fish" or "prodfisk," at a factory in Europe.

The journalists agreed to conduct their investigation with a guarantee of anonymity for the salmon sellers and buyer, so no businesses have been accused of wrongdoing.

Masoval finds subsidiary has been selling salmon ‘unsuitable for human consumption’

Norwegian law states that farmed salmon carrying wounds, deformities, ulcers etc cannot be exported as whole, fresh fish. It must be processed in-country and can later be sold as, for instance, salmon burgers.

"We can't send this to customers. We can't send this to anyone," said one of the employees at the factory visited by NRK. "Before, maybe one in a thousand fish had ulcers. Now we find ulcers in almost every delivery, even if it is supposed to be 'superior' quality."

Krister Hoaas of trade organization Sjomat Norge told NRK it is the "serious players who are hit hardest by those who do not follow laws and regulations."

"We think it is good if illegalities are uncovered and followed up by the authorities, and we want unscrupulous individual actors to be uncovered and not allowed to operate at the expense of the vast majority in the industry."

The Norwegian Seafood Council and Sjomatbedriftene echoed this, as did Mowi in a comment on LinkedIn, in which it insisted it does not sell production fish.

Early in 2024, salmon farmer Masoval informed the stock exchange that an investigation into its majority-owned processing and sales company had revealed some customers were supplied with fish that were unsuitable for human consumption.

The Norwegian Food Safety Authority, Mattilsynet, intensified its efforts to combat the export of prodfisk as a result.

Last year, Norway's levels of production fish escalated dramatically, to the extent that the EU Commission said it would open talks with Norway after finding the regulations on processing in-country should be considered a "barrier to trade."

Better biological conditions and successful vaccine rollouts have seen the volumes of prodfisk come down in 2025, but clearly some exporters are still acting illegally.

title: Penalized British Columbia trout farmer misses court’s cleanup deadline
content:
A trout-farming company that admitted operating illegally in the Canadian province of British Columbia and was ordered to pay a CAD 350,000 ($250,205) fine in August 2024 is facing renewed pressure from environmental lawyers to remove its aquaculture structures.

West Coast Fishculture, based in Powell River, remains in breach of a sentencing order that required all out-of-tenure structures to be removed by Aug. 31, 2025, according to new correspondence sent last week to Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) by lawyers at Ecojustice. The group is acting on behalf of the Vancouver-based advocacy group Watershed Watch Salmon Society. 

Photos taken last week also show fish-farming infrastructure still standing at the Lois Lake site, located on BC's southern coast near the town of Powell River.

Photo taken by Watershed Watch Salmon Society on Oct. 21 shows remaining fish-farming infrastructure on Lois Lake, near Powell River, BC still in place despite a court-ordered removal

The documents, obtained by Undercurrent News, include an agreed statement of facts filed in the Powell River Provincial Court showing that West Coast Fishculture pleaded guilty last year to operating outside its federal aquaculture license.

The company is owned by AgriMarine, a BC-based aquaculture technology firm that is a subsidiary of the Toronto-based investment company Dundee Corporation.

AgriMarine was among the first companies in BC to dip its toes into recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS), developing early versions of land-based and semi-closed containment technologies, as Undercurrent reported. It operated trout and salmon farms in BC and Liaoning Province, China, and also launched a subsidiary, AgriMarine Technologies, in 2014 to market its aquaculture and water-treatment designs.

The company has not been publicly active in recent years.

Lawyers asked DFO to act under Section 38(7.1) of the Fisheries Act, which empowers the federal agency to take corrective measures to protect fish and their habitat, including removing offending structures at the operator's expense. They said the derelict gear poses risks of pollution, wildlife entanglement and navigation hazards.

Court records indicate federal inspectors first identified issues at the site in 2021, following public complaints about fish escapes. Their investigation found the company's active pens sitting 300 to 500 meters beyond its authorized tenure and continuing to receive fish transfers despite regulatory warnings. The agreed statement of facts notes that all fish sold during that period were "illegally harvested."

The facility has been inactive since late 2023.

Undercurrent has requested comment from Dundee Corporation and to DFO but has yet to receive a reply.

title: Pacific Seafood hit with class-action lawsuit over yearlong data breach
content:
US processor Pacific Seafood Group is facing a proposed class-action lawsuit over an allegation it failed to safeguard sensitive employee and customer data during a cyberattack that went undetected for more than a year.

The complaint, filed Tuesday (Oct. 28) in the US District Court for the District of Oregon by former employee and customer Alex Lester, accuses the Clackamas, Oregon-based company of negligence, breach of implied contract and fiduciary duty, unjust enrichment and invasion of privacy following a 2024 data breach that exposed personal and medical information belonging to more than 40,000 individuals.

According to the filing, hackers gained access to Pacific Seafood's systems between June 24 and 25, 2024, but the breach went undiscovered until Sept. 29, 2025 -- a delay of more than 462 days. The company began notifying affected individuals on or about Oct. 14, 2025, according to the suit.

Pacific Seafood taps beverage CFO to helm finance division

The stolen information allegedly included names, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, driver's licenses, passports, financial account details and medical and health insurance data.

The suit claims the breach and subsequent response were the result of "multiple failings" by the company, including deficient protection and monitoring of its digital networks.

Lester, a resident of Maupin, Oregon, claims he has suffered harm from the breach in the form of increased spam communications, anxiety and lost time spent monitoring his accounts. He is seeking damages and injunctive relief on behalf of all individuals whose information was compromised.

The lawsuit argues that Pacific Seafood's offer of complimentary credit monitoring services was "woefully inadequate" given the heightened risk of identity theft faced by victims. The plaintiffs also allege that the company violated federal data protection standards under the Federal Trade Commission Act by not maintaining appropriate safeguards for personally identifiable and health information.

A spokesperson for Pacific Seafood, which operates more than 40 facilities across North America and Europe, said the company believes the data breach only affected employees and former employees, not customers.

"Protecting the privacy and security of information is a top priority for Pacific Seafood. Upon detecting unauthorized access to our network, we immediately contained the incident and launched an investigation with assistance from leading cybersecurity professionals. The investigation determined that an unauthorized party accessed our network between June 24, 2024, and June 25, 2024," the spokesperson said. 

"We have notified all impacted individuals to the best of our ability and have established a dedicated, toll-free response line to assist anyone seeking additional information," the spokesperson added.

In a statement posted on its website, Pacific Seafood -- which is owned by parent entity Dulcich, Inc. -- encouraged those affected by the data breach to place a fraud alert and security freeze on their credit files. 

"We have no evidence of any identity theft or financial fraud related to this incident. However, out of an abundance of caution, Dulcich encourages impacted individuals to take actions to help protect their personal information," it said.

title: Major fire severely damages farmed salmon cold storage in southern Chile
content:
A major fire has severely damaged a cold storage facility in Puerto Montt, southern Chile, which reportedly held frozen seafood products, including farmed Atlantic and coho salmon, multiple sources told Undercurrent News.

The facility, called "Frigorifico Sake," is said to have stored thousands of metric tons of the two species, which may have been affected, though the extent of the damage has yet to be confirmed.

"The facility handles a significant volume of product from several major producers, including farmed Atlantic and coho salmon," a senior sales executive at a leading Chilean company told Undercurrent, adding that it was still too early to assess the full scale of the losses.

Frigorifico Sake has offered a frozen storage capacity of approximately 7,800 pallet positions since 2022, making it one of the leading automated cold storage facilities in Chile's Los Lagos region, according to its website.

The blaze broke out around 7 a.m. Monday (Oct. 20) at the Frigorifico Sake facility, located along Route 5 Sur in the Loteo San Ignacio industrial area near Puerto Varas, said Septima Compania de Bomberos Valparaiso, the local fire brigade. 

Firefighters worked for more than 12 hours before bringing the fire under control. Three firefighters were injured during the operation, the brigade added.

The brigade's statement noted that dense smoke and high temperatures made it difficult to access the upper sections of the multi-story warehouse, and multiple firefighting units from surrounding districts were called in to contain the flames.

Authorities have not yet disclosed the cause of the fire, though early indications suggest a possible electrical fault in one of the refrigeration systems, reports local news outlet Radio Bio Bio.

Environmental monitors have been deployed to assess potential contamination from ammonia and other refrigerants used in the plant.

The Los Lagos regional government has launched a technical investigation and is coordinating with the National Fisheries and Aquaculture Service to evaluate whether the incident could affect seafood supply chains or export operations in the Puerto Montt–Puerto Varas area, reports local news outlet EHA Noticias.

title: US fisheries officers crack down on illegal stone crab harvesting at start of season
content:
The US Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) has wasted no time stepping in to stop the illegal harvesting of stone crabs in Florida.

The commercial season started Oct. 15, but FWC already has hit a captain and his crew for multiple commercial resource violations related to 65 pounds of illegally landed crab, reports local outlet Pasco News Online.

Officers launched their investigation into illegal harvesting in late September when a continuous line of blue crab traps was found near Gulf Harbors, according to the news service. Suspecting that the traps were being used for the illegal harvesting of stone crab, officers continued to conduct surveillance until the season opened Oct. 15. At that time, officers said they observed a commercial vessel pulling the traps and illegally harvesting stone crab. 

The stone crab claws were seized and sold to the highest bidder in the industry, according to Pasco News.

Florida's stone crab season runs until May 1.

title: Calls grow for ban on new salmon farms in Scotland following Mowi fish escape
content:
The Scottish government has launched an investigation into the mass escape of around 75,000 farmed salmon from Mowi's Gorsten site in Loch Linnhe, following damage caused by Storm Amy earlier this month.

FREE READ Mowi loses 75,000 salmon in Scotland during storms

The incident has intensified calls to halt the expansion of salmon farming in Scotland, amid warnings that such escapes pose a serious threat to wild salmon populations and the wider marine environment.

Ariane Burgess, member of Scottish parliament for the Green Party, said the escape highlights the urgent need for stronger regulation and enforcement.

"This is a clear example of why we need to pause licensing any new salmon farms or expanding existing ones," she said. "Thousands of farmed fish escaping is not only polluting our seas but directly increasing the risk of extinction to wild species."

A recent parliamentary report warned that Scotland's marine ecosystem faces "irrecoverable damage" from further expansion of the industry, with one in five salmon farms currently failing to meet statutory environmental standards.

Although Scotland does not yet impose automatic fines for mass escapes, the government confirmed the Fish Health Inspectorate is investigating the incident and that financial penalties are being considered for introduction in 2026–2027.

Mowi, the world's largest producer of farmed salmon, confirmed the escape and said the average weight of the lost fish was 860 grams, reports The National. The company expressed regret over the incident but defended its handling of the event.

"We regret the loss and continue to strive for zero escapes," a Mowi spokesperson said. "Storm Amy caused widespread damage throughout the region, despite containment measures being in place."

Mowi denied that the escape poses a significant risk to wild populations, referencing a 2021 incident at Carradale in which post-event genetic testing found almost no interbreeding between escaped and wild salmon.

However, critics argue that voluntary targets and post-hoc assessments are not enough to prevent environmental harm. Burgess called for "real, consequential penalties for breaches" and tighter controls to protect Scotland's coastal ecosystems.

No new fish farms are currently being licensed in Scotland, pending further assessment of the industry's environmental impact.

title: Canadian fisheries officers seize more lobsters in Nova Scotia
content:
Enforcement officers with Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) have made another major seizure of lobster in the province of Nova Scotia.

During an inspection on Thursday (Oct. 16) of a commercial fish plant in Delaps Cove, located 52 kilometers north of the town of Digby, on the Bay of Fundy, DFO officers seized 112 crates of lobster, the department said on its website.

The crates contained about 11,200 pounds of lobster with an estimated value of CAD 112,000 ($78,347), Debbie Buott-Matheson, DFO's manager of strategic communications for the Maritimes Region, said in an e-mail to Undercurrent News on Monday (Oct. 20).

One person was charged for the illegal purchase of lobster that had been harvested for food, social and ceremonial (FSC) purposes, and will have a first appearance in provincial court on March 2, 2026, DFO noted in its release.

Delaps Cove, Nova Scotia, is located north of Digby, on the Bay of Fundy. Screenshot from Google Maps

While First Nations in Atlantic Canada are permitted to harvest lobsters for FSC purposes, it is illegal under Canada's Fishery General Regulations to barter, buy or sell those lobsters.

The 8,078 lobsters seized during the Oct. 16 inspection have been released, live, to the ocean, DFO added.

The name of the company was not identified by DFO.

"The investigation into this matter is still underway, so we cannot offer any more details at this time," said Buott-Matheson.

These lobsters were seized Oct. 16 from a company in southwestern Nova Scotia. Photo from Department of Fisheries and Oceans Canada Facebook page

The latest charges come just two weeks after DFO seized 13,000 lbs of lobster following the search of a facility in Shelburne County, Nova Scotia, on Oct. 1.

The value of the seized lobster was more than CAD 100,000 ($71,190). A spokesperson for DFO confirmed at the time that it was the most lobsters seized at one time in DFO's Maritimes region this year, reported CBC.

In that case, one person is being investigated for potential charges under the Fisheries Act in connection with maintaining a lobster pound without the required license. DFO did not identify the name of the person or company under investigation.

Fishery officers in southwestern Nova Scotia have completed 61 plant inspections, inspected 4,207 lobster traps, seized 1,478 lobster traps and six fishing vessels, and released 19,453 lobsters back to the ocean since June 1, DFO also noted in a release on Oct. 16.

The seizures relate to violations of license conditions, including fishing a during closed season.

Illegal lobster fishing has been a longstanding issue in Atlantic Canada, particujarly in the province of Nova Scotia.

One of the issues at the center of the problem is the unresolved question of the treaty rights of First Nations members, and the definition of a 'moderate livelihood' fishery, the right of aboriginals to fish for personal use or ceremonial purposes, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

Commercially licensed lobster harvesters say while they are encouraged by this year's efforts by DFO that have resulted in seizure of illegal lobsters, the real measure of success depends on the outcome of the court process, as reported by Undercurrent.

title: Colombia shuts down Van Camp’s tuna vessels over labor violations
content:
The Colombian labor ministry has temporarily closed three vessels belonging to Seatech International, the producer of Van Camp's tuna, following a surprise inspection at its Cartagena facilities, various local media reported, including El Espectador.

The inspection was triggered by complaints from 196 Colombian and Ecuadorian sailors who reported poor working conditions. Authorities found that many employees lacked formal contracts, social security and occupational risk protection, which, according to labor minister Antonio Sanguino, constitute clear violations of labor law.

During the visit, inspectors also encountered attempts to obstruct their work. Some employees had reportedly disappeared during the inspection and were later found to have been confined in company warehouses to prevent them from speaking with officials.

Union leader Alicia Cardiles from Sinaltrainal alleged further abuses, including illegal wage deductions, denial of medical leave and even possible human trafficking linked to the hiring of Ecuadorian workers.

As an immediate measure, the ministry sealed three of the four vessels inspected for 10 days, pending correction of the identified irregularities. The government's investigation continues to determine the full extent of Seatech's labor violations.

title: DycodeX founder denies participation in eFishery fraud
content:
Andri Yadi, founder of Indonesia-based DycodeX, said he never had any role in the financial operations or investment decisions of troubled Indonesian aquatech startup eFishery.

Yadi and eFishery founder and CEO Gibran Huzaifah were detained by Indonesian police on July 31, as national authorities investigate allegations the company engaged in embezzlement. 

Hufaizah has admitted he kept two sets of accounting books in an effort to inflate his company's profile to attract investors. At its zenith, the firm had a valuation of $1.4 billion and around 2,000 staff, but it is now worth a fraction of that and is accused of losing more than $300 million of investors' money.

In his first public statement since his arrest, Yadi said in a press release issued through his legal representative his responsibilities at eFishery were limited to technology and product development and that he did not have authority to make financial decisions.

"My focus [was] entirely on the development of technology products, especially the Internet of Things and artificial intelligence," Yadi said.

The unusual financial mechanisms used by eFishery to acquire DycodeX have been the subject of scrutiny from the consulting firm now running the company, as Undercurrent News has reported.

US business consulting firm FTI Consulting, which was appointed as active manager of eFishery in January following revelations the company misrepresented financial figures for years, is looking at the DycodeX acquisition as part of its larger investigation into potential fraud committed by company executives, as brought to light by an internal whistleblower complaint.

The complex transaction was completed through an "acqui-hire" scheme, under which eFishery paid IDR 15 billion ($920,000) to four subsidiaries, which then hired all of DycodeX's employees.

Yadi claims he did not receive any additional payments outside of the official IDR 15 billion purchase price.

"There was no flow of funds outside the contract, no cashback and no additional profits earned," he said.

Andri Yadi. Photo courtesy of GSMI.

In fact, according to Yadi, DycodeX "actually suffered real losses."

"All of DycodeX's obligations to employees (layoffs, severance pay, salaries), vendors, and taxes must be completed first as a prerequisite. DycodeX, which originally existed as a startup, finally stopped operating, all assets and technology built over the years were handed over. Andri's professional reputation as an IoT practitioner was also affected by unbalanced news," he said.

The investigation is being handled by the Criminal Investigation Branch of the Indonesian National Police. The investigation is ongoing and no court verdict yet has been issued, Yadi said.

"My statement is not to defend myself in court, but solely as a correction of facts so that the public gets balanced information," he said.

title: Thai parliament approves controversial amendments to fisheries law
content:
Thailand's parliament has approved a controversial amendment to the country's Fisheries Act over the protests of local and international environmental groups, Bangkok Post reports.

The 71 amendments to the country's 2015 Fisheries Act, approved on Sept. 17, represent a significant rollback of protections put in place after Thailand attracted global attention for lax regulation of its seafood industry, including shortcomings in its environmental and labor protections.

The National Fisheries Association of Thailand, representing the large-scale commercial sector, supported the changes, which include a reduction of penalties for a variety of fisheries-related offenses.

It also removes restrictions on offshore fishing, restructures provincial fisheries committees and limits fishing licenses to Thai nationals. And it allows seafood processing plants under investigation for labor abuses to keep operating and permits the use of seine nets with mesh sizes smaller than 2.5 centimeters beyond 12 nautical miles from shore.

Thailand Fisheries Department director-general Bancha Sukkaew defended the revisions in a Sept. 29 press conference, saying they will improve the prospects for Thailand's small-scale fishing sector.

"The new law will preserve marine resources as a sustainable food source while improving fisherfolk's incomes," he said.

However, the Federation of Thai Fisherfolk Association has criticized the changes to the law, saying that allowing fine-mesh fishing will decimate marine stocks, especially juvenile fish.

"This law only benefits about 175 commercial trawlers, while small-scale fisherfolk who depend on mature fish will suffer the most," Piya Tetyan, the group's chairman, said.

A group of 57 local and international environmental non-governmental organizations, including Greenpeace and the Environmental Justice Foundation, signed a letter sent to the Thai government in January 2025 opposing the regulatory rollback, saying it would undermine Thailand's international commitments to sustainable fishing.

Now that the amendments have been passed and will go into effect, Tetyan said his group plans to launch a campaign to raise public awareness of the ecological risks they present.

title: Malta former fisheries director denies charges in alleged tuna export racket
content:
Malta's former fisheries department director, Andreina Fenech Farrugia, has denied charges of money laundering, trading in influence, disclosing official secrets, and bribery linked to an illegal tuna export investigation, reports Malta Today.

She appeared in court on Sept. 29 alongside Giovanni Ellul, director of Malta Fish Farming, who also denied charges including falsification of documents and participation in organized crime.

The case involves allegations that large quantities of tuna were illegally exported from Malta to Spain via Marseille, using the same documents as legally exported fish shipped by air.

Spanish and Maltese police uncovered an operation moving undeclared tuna to a warehouse in Valencia, on Spain's eastern coast.

Court evidence included intercepted messages showing attempts to influence politicians and manipulate quotas. Financial analysis revealed suspicious money transfers involving Fenech Farrugia.

Both accused pleaded not guilty. The court ruled there is a case to answer and adjourned the hearing until November.

title: Untitled
content:
Demers Good Group, the US distributor of frozen seafood meal brand Scott & Jon's, has joined retailers Trader Joe's and Walmart this week in issuing a recall for ready-to-eat meals containing pre-cooked pasta that may be contaminated with Listeria monocytogenes.

Nate's Fine Foods, a pasta supplier based in Roseville, California, shared a statement on Monday (Sept. 29) that it was voluntarily recalling select products after being notified of a potential connection to a multistate outbreak of Listeria. The company linked to a recall notice published by the US Department of Agriculture's (USDA) Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) on Sept. 25 for Marketside brand linguine with beef meatballs & marinara sauce sold at Walmart stores, and a private label Cajun-style blackened chicken breast fettuccine alfredo sold by Trader Joe's.

The recall expanded over the course of the week, with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) adding select Scott & Jon's shrimp scampi with linguine products, distributed to wholesale distributors and operators between Sept. 15 and Sept. 25, to the list of potentially impacted products.

Demers Food Group noted in the recall notice that no other Scott & Jon's products are involved and that no illnesses have been reported to date in connection with the Demers Food Group recall.

Recall related to months-long FDA investigation

The FDA has been investigating a deadly Listeria outbreak since June, when 17 cases of illness were reported in 13 states. Of those documented, 16 were hospitalized, with three deaths attributed to the strain. The FDA investigation also noted that there was one pregnancy-associated illness in a mother that resulted in a fetal loss.

At the time, the FDA linked the strain to FreshRealm's pre-made chicken alfredo product sold at Kroger and Walmart under the Marketside and Home Chef brands.

There wasn't another government update on the Listeria outbreak until Sept. 26, when the USDA FSIS, which primarily handles recalls for meat and poultry, issued the alerts for Trader Joe's and Walmart.

As of the latest FDA Listeria outbreak, published Thursday (Oct. 2), a total of 20 people have been infected with the outbreak strain of Listeria linked to pre-cooked meals. Of those 20 with the documented illness, 19 have been hospitalized and four deaths have been reported.

title: Untitled
content:
Greenland's largest pension fund, SISA, has acquired a 5% stake in Polar Seafood, becoming the Atlantic fishing and processing firm's first ever external investor, it announced.

Effective Oct. 1, 2025, SISA will acquire 5% of the shares in Polar Seafood Greenland, with plans in place to acquire an additional 5% of the group over a number of years.

This will make over 44,000 Greenlandic pension savers co-owners of Greenland's largest privately owned company, said SISA. The deal marks a shift in ownership, which has so far been divided between two families, and "strengthens the foundation for both economic and social sustainability."

"For us at SISA, the investment is not just about returns -- it is about securing Greenlandic jobs, strengthening the country's most important industry and creating co-ownership for our members," said Jess Berthelsen, chair of the board of SISA.

"Polar Seafood Greenland is a cornerstone of Greenlandic fisheries, and we are proud to be able to contribute to the company's continued development."

Soren Petersen, CEO of SISA, added that the investment was made based on a thorough investigation of Polar Seafood Greenland, after which SISA concluded that the expected return on the investment is in reasonable proportion to the risk.

"Investments in SISA are made with respect for the fact that we manage the members' money," he noted.

The pension fund said Greenlandic fisheries -- "constantly developing and changing" -- are crucial for society. This partnership would help to secure jobs and procurement opportunities in Greenland, it said. 

"It is with great pleasure that we welcome SISA on board as a co-owner," said Polar Seafood Greenland director Bent Salling. "We take the new fisheries act seriously, and we contribute to more people getting a share in our common resources through the partnership with SISA. We look forward to continuing our development with a partner who shares our values ​​and vision for a strong and value-creating Greenlandic fishery."

New fisheries regulation was passed in 2024 -- a move which Polar had warned a government consultation could prompt the business to pursue legal challenges for the expropriation of quota without compensation.

The government said the changes would mean more freedom for fishermen to increase the value of their catch and modernize their tools, though it accepted not everybody would be happy.

Polar's director, Miki Brons, added that the pension fund's buy-in meant the "future begins now -- together with SISA and with our dedicated employees, we continue to build on our strong heritage."

SISA -- which has DKK 6.5 billion ($1.02bn) under management -- noted Polar Seafood Greenland was founded in 1984 and has since grown to a billion-dollar turnover company.

Today it consists of, among other things, eight ocean-going factory trawlers, four coastal shrimp vessels, three coastal crab vessels, six procurement/production facilities and some 600 employees in Greenland.

Last year, the company delivered a profit of DKK 119m before tax.

title: FAO group finds 5 small pelagic stocks in West Africa overexploited
content:
Five small pelagic stocks in West Africa are overexploited, and four are fully exploited, according to the latest findings of the  Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations' Fisheries Committee for the Eastern Central Atlantic (CECAF).

Climate change is exacerbating these pressures, as evidenced by fishing campaigns since 2023, which have reported abnormally high temperatures and the absence of sardines south of Cap Blanc.

Speaking at the Global Roundtable on Marine Ingredients (GRT) workshop, which was held in Nouakchott, Mauritania, in July, Cheikh Baye Braham -- chair of CECAF-North -- stressed the urgency of coordinated action.

"Faced with these challenges, scientific and regional management of migratory stocks is essential. The implementation of management plans, investment in data monitoring and the promotion of the ecosystem approach to fisheries appear to be priorities. Finally, the sustainable development of fishmeal and fish oil industries must be reconciled with West African food security," he said.

The July 2025 workshop brought together 60 representatives from governments, local communities, civil society, and the industry. Discussions centred on data systems, regulatory alignment, fishery improvement projects, and promoting direct human consumption.

The final report calls for stronger regional governance, better infrastructure, and investment in value-added processing to reduce dependence on raw material exports.

"The West African sub-region faces declining fish stocks due to overfishing and climate change, alongside economic competition and shifting consumer preferences. Without strengthened regional institutional cooperation, we will face enormous difficulties," said Arni Mathiesen, independent chair of the GRT.

Participants highlighted small pelagics as vital for both nutrition and livelihoods, underscoring their role in sustaining food security and the blue economy.

Meanwhile, a recent investigation in the Netherlands was the latest to warn that West African pelagics are being taken to feed farmed fish for European consumers, undermining food security in the region.

It tracked Senegalese fish, produced with small pelagics caught locally, to seabass, trout and salmon sold in Albert Heijn, the largest supermarket chain in the country, it said.

title: Frozen shrimp worth £100,000 stolen from UK’s Sykes
content:
A trailer carrying frozen shrimp valued at £100,000 ($134,500) has been stolen from UK seafood company Sykes Seafood in what is being described as a targeted and well-planned theft, reports BBC. 

Sykes said the fully loaded trailer was taken from its secure processing facility at the Sefton Lane Industrial Estate in Maghull, Merseyside, in the early morning hours. 

The company is offering a £25,000 reward for information that leads directly to the identification and conviction of the perpetrators, as well as the safe recovery of the stolen goods.

"We are appealing to anyone with information to come forward and assist the police in their investigation," Neil Townend, managing director of Sykes Seafood, said.

"Our priority is to recover the stolen stock and ensure those responsible are brought to justice."

title: US domestic shrimp groups back ‘manifest transparency’ bills to beef up import screening
content:
Two US domestic shrimp industry groups are backing companion bills that would require more detailed shipping manifest data for goods imported into the US.

The Manifest Modernization Act of 2025, SB 1259, reintroduced for the second straight Congress by US senator Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana Republican, in April, would extend the data requirements beyond ocean vessels to aircraft, truck and rail shipments, which account for around 50% of US imports.

The legislation has two co-sponsors, including Democratic US senators Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada.

It also has a companion bill (HR 2653), which was introduced in the lower chamber in April by US representative David Schweikert, a Texas Republican, and has five cosponsors, including three Democrats (Lloyd Doggett of Texas, Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois and Judy Chu of California), as well as two other Republicans (John Moolenaar of Michigan and Beth Van Duyne of Texas). 

New US Senate bill would apply escalating tariff rates on Indian shrimp

Both bills would amend the Tariff Act of 1930 to require the name and address of the shipper, general character of the cargo, number of packages and gross weight, name of vessel or carrier, port of exit, port of destination and country of destination to be reported to US Customs and Border Protection for every shipment sent to or through the US via air, land or sea.

They would improve customs enforcement and supply chain oversight, which could help aid US authorities in spotting illicit seafood shipments and preventing seafood not fit for human consumption from reaching US consumers, its champions argue.

"We need transparency on every shipment crossing our borders, not just half," Cassidy said when he introduced his bill in the 118th Congress in 2023. "The law is falling short of a goal Congress set decades ago. This fix is overdue and urgent."

The Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA) and American Shrimp Processors Association (ASPA) said the amendment would help them monitor trade patterns that impact the domestic seafood industry, which they represent. Currently, there is no practical way to monitor goods initially shipped to Canada or Mexico before entering the US, the organizations said.

"This greatly limits supply chain transparency and the ability to detect merchandise that may be evading our trade laws or is otherwise noncompliant with laws designed to protect American consumers from unhealthy imports," they said in written comments submitted in March to the House Ways and Means Committee.

The bills require all cargo shipments to be filed with the harmonized tariff codes under which they are classified.

"For the shrimp industry, this additional information will make it much easier to ascertain whether wild-caught shrimp from countries not certified by the US Department of State under the Section 609 program is being shipped to the United States in violation of law," SSA said.

Air cargo being loaded. Photo courtesy of Air Transport Services Group.

SSA and ASPA have backed the legislation as part of their advocacy for a broader suite of regulatory changes designed to level the playing field for domestic producers. 

They have also called for more FDA testing of imported shrimp, strengthening the US Seafood Import Monitoring Program and more stringent enforcement of the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act.

Additionally, they have called for Congress to give US Customs and Border Patrol more authority in their investigations so they can continue in circumstances when importers change names mid-probe.

The groups also support the Leveling the Playing Field 2.0 Act, introduced in the Senate in February by Indiana Republican Todd Young and Minnesota Democrat Tina Smith as SB 691, and by Alabama Republican Terri Sewell and Texas Republican Beth Van Duyne in the House as HR 1548. Those bills would strengthen US antidumping and countervailing duty enforcement to counteract unfair or evasive trade practices undertaken by foreign exporters, their champions argue.
