title: Untitled
content:
Chile's Fiscalia Nacional Economica (FNE), the national economic prosecutor's office, has filed a lawsuit accusing seven seafood processing companies and eight of their executives of participating in an organized scheme to fix the dock prices paid to artisanal king crab fishermen in the Magallanes region.

Elaboradora de Alimentos Porvenir, International Seafood, Pesquera Cabo Froward, Productos Marinos Puerto Williams, Proyecta Corp, Sociedad Pesquera Bahia Chilota, and Bakkavor are all named as defendants in a complaint filed with the Tribunal de Defensa de la Libre Competencia (TDLC), which translates to the Tribunal to Defend Free Competition.

The prosecutors are asking the TDLC to impose significant financial penalties on the accused, amounting to a combined 62,406 annual tax units -- the equivalent of about CLP 51.9 billion ($54 million) for the companies, and an additional 511 in tax units, approximately CLP 424m, for the executives found responsible. 

Together, the companies named in the charging documents control the vast majority of the market, acquiring between 81% and 88% of all live Chilean king crab (Lithodes santolla) caught by artisanal fishermen in the region between 2017 and 2021, the prosecutors said.

FNE alleges that, between 2012 and 2021, the named companies and executives coordinated to set purchase prices at the beginning of each fishing season and to delay or contain any increases throughout the harvesting period, which runs from July to November each year.

The product was later processed and exported almost entirely abroad, with China, the US and Mexico as the main destinations.

According to the FNE's filing, the companies coordinated their actions through a network of in-person meetings, phone calls, emails, and WhatsApp messages, exchanging sensitive and strategic information about purchase prices.

These communications occurred not only at the start of the season, when companies agreed on an initial price to pay fishermen, but also during the harvest period, when they sought to slow or contain subsequent price increases jointly.

The FNE argued that this repeated exchange of information "effectively replaced competition with coordination, enabling the firms to act collectively and suppress prices that would otherwise have been set higher in a competitive market."

It continued: "The companies confirmed among themselves what their competitors were paying or planned to pay, neutralizing independent decision-making and the uncertainty that should exist in a competitive environment."

Chile’s seafood exports lean on Western markets amid Chinese slowdown

The result was significant harm to artisanal fishermen, who received less for their catch for years than they would have in a fair and open marketplace, the federal agency said.

The investigation that led to the complaint began in July 2020, after the FNE received a tip-off from a whistleblower who alleged the existence of a long-standing cartel among companies in the region.

Acting on the information, the FNE launched a formal investigation and used the full range of tools available under Chile's antitrust laws, including telephone interceptions, search and seizure operations, and document reviews. These actions, carried out with judicial authorization, targeted company offices in Porvenir and other locations across the Magallanes region.

In February 2021, the FNE granted leniency to Bakkavor and three of its executives after they admitted their participation in the cartel and provided valuable evidence that helped the agency piece together the scheme. Their cooperation, the FNE said, was instrumental in revealing the details of how the companies coordinated prices and monitored each other's actions.

The investigation uncovered extensive evidence of collusion, including internal emails, chat records, call logs, and witness statements. Many of these documents show company executives discussing the prices paid by competitors, sharing information received from fishermen, and agreeing on strategies to resist price increases.

In several cases, the FNE found records of executives explicitly acknowledging that they were trying to "hold the line" on prices and avoid competing against one another.

Executives questioned by the FNE also confirmed under oath that they had been in contact with their competitors. Some attempted to downplay the behavior as "informal" or "customary" information exchanges. Still, the agency concluded that these interactions went "well beyond permissible contact" and amounted to a deliberate, sustained effort to suppress competition.

BioMar, Skretting, Salmofood face up to $78.5m in combined fines related to Chile’s long-running salmon feed price collusion case

The FNE emphasized that under Chilean competition law, any agreement or concerted practice that restricts or limits competition -- including the exchange of strategic pricing information among rivals -- is strictly prohibited.

"With this action, we reaffirm our commitment to pursue cartels wherever they occur and to sanction collusion in regional markets with the full rigor of the law," national economic prosecutor Jorge Grunberg said.

He added that while nearly all the king crab caught in Magallanes is exported to foreign markets, the cartel's effects were deeply felt within Chile, particularly by artisanal fishermen whose livelihoods depend on fair prices for their catch.

The FNE also highlighted that this case is part of a broader effort to strengthen oversight in regional markets, which have historically received less scrutiny than national or metropolitan ones.

"Although this is a product that largely leaves the country, the harm caused here was local, and it affected Chilean workers and families," Grunberg concluded.

title: EU Commission examines Mowi’s full takeover of Nova Sea
content:
The European Commission (EC) has launched an investigation into Mowi's proposed acquisition of Nova Sea.

The merger, which would see Mowi take full control of Nova Sea, is now under scrutiny for its potential effects on competition in the European and global seafood markets.

Mowi’s harvests surpass 500,000t in 2024, but top 10 salmon farmers’ output down

The EC is carefully reviewing the transaction to assess whether it could significantly reduce competition, particularly within the European Economic Area, it said.

With both companies active in the same market segment -- salmon farming and processing in Norway -- the merger has raised concerns about the potential for reduced market choices and price hikes for consumers and businesses alike.

While the EC has yet to make a final decision, its preliminary investigation will analyze whether the deal could lead to anti-competitive outcomes in the seafood sector.

As part of the review process, it has invited interested third parties to submit their observations on the proposed merger. Stakeholders, including businesses, competitors, and consumers, have 10 days from the Sept. 22 publishing date to provide their input on the deal's potential effects.

title: Five crew members lost after Spanish fishing vessel sinks off Mauritania
content:
Spanish fishing company Baipesca Fish has confirmed the sinking of its vessel Tafra 3 in Mauritanian waters, a tragic accident that has claimed the lives of five crew members.

In a LinkedIn post, the company expressed its "deep sorrow" over the incident, calling the loss "irreparable" and emphasizing the strong bonds that united the crew professionally and personally. "This irreparable loss saddens our entire company and all of us who share life at sea," the firm said.

"More than colleagues, they were an essential part of our family. Their dedication and commitment will remain forever in our memory and in the history of our work," the firm added.

Baipesca Fish also took the opportunity to recognize the courage and dedication of mariners worldwide, acknowledging the sacrifices made daily in sustaining the fishing industry.

"We also extend our appreciation to all seafarers who, with courage and dedication, face the immensity of the ocean every day. Their effort and sacrifice make this noble activity possible, to which we offer our eternal gratitude."

Details surrounding the circumstances of the sinking have not yet been made public, and authorities in Mauritania are reportedly assisting with the investigation.

The Tafra 3 was one of three vessels operated by the Galician-based company, which has a strong presence in the Mauritanian fishing grounds. It specializes in frozen fish and seafood, including squid and wild seabream.

Javier Gestido, captain of the Tafra 3, survived after being thrown into the sea when his ship sank rapidly following a collision with the factory vessel Right Whale, Faro de Vigo reported. The accident happened off Mauritania, where Gestido and 20 other crew members were rescued, though five Mauritanian sailors remain missing.

Gestido, deeply shaken and saddened by the tragedy, has avoided looking at photos or videos of the sinking. He was the last person inside the ship as it went down in just five minutes, managing to help others with life jackets and lifeboats before being forced into the water himself.

The Right Whale, a 104-meter vessel with Gambian flag and foreign ownership, struck the smaller Tafra 3 on its starboard side, dragging it and tearing a fatal hole.

After days in the Mauritanian port of Nouadhibou, where he expressed gratitude for the support received, Gestido traveled through Nouakchott and the Canary Islands before heading back to Vigo, Spain. He remains very affected by the loss of the missing sailors but thankful to those who assisted, including locals, Spanish authorities, and his shipping company.

title: Canada seizes nearly 12,000 lobsters in 3.5 months as part of crackdown on illegal fishing
content:
Close to 12,000 illegal lobsters have been returned to the ocean in Atlantic Canada since June 1 as a result of enforcement efforts by Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO).

DFO officers in the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, over the past 3.5 months, have completed 61 inspections of lobster processing plants and holding pounds, seized 1,235 lobster traps and 19 crates of the valuable crustaceans, and released 11,853 live lobsters back to the ocean, the federal agency noted in its latest enforcement update, issued last week.

The latest major seizure was on Wednesday (Sept. 10), in the eastern part of New Brunswick. During a targeted surveillance operation, officers seized 2,175 live lobsters and a refrigerated truck, DFO reported.

"The seizure was carried out without incident, and the live lobsters were safely returned to their original fishing grounds. An investigation of this matter is still ongoing," the agency said.

Meanwhile, multiple at-sea arrests and seizures were carried out in Nova Scotia in early September. DFO officers once again focused on St. Mary's Bay in Lobster Fishing Area (LFA) 34 in southwest Nova Scotia, which has become a hotspot of illegal lobster fishing, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

LFA 34 is Canada's most prolific fishing area for lobster, responsible for 17,367 of Canada's roughly 95,000 metric tons landed throughout Canada during the 2023-24 season, based on figures shared with Undercurrent by the Lobster Council of Canada (LCC).

DFO enforcement officers seized 433 lobsters and 31 traps on Sept. 7. Officers also arrested two people for violating Canada's Fisheries Act by fishing traps that they were not authorized to fish.

Canada continues crackdown on illegal lobster fishing

Earlier that week, officers on patrol in Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, in LFA 33, boarded a vessel at sea and arrested three people for violating the Fisheries Act, including fishing with untagged lobster traps. Fishery officers seized the vessel and 15 lobster traps and released 376 lobsters.

LFA is also among the biggest of the LFAs in Atlantic Canada. In 2024, 6,557t of lobster were landed by commercial harvesters in this zone, according to LCC data.

In addition to those arrests, fishery officers seized and released 688 lobsters and 64 lobster traps as part of enforcement operations Sept. 4 to 7 in Southwest Nova Scotia. Traps were seized for a variety of violations, including expired or unassigned tags.

The investigations continue, said DFO.

All of these cases have yet to be tried in court.

title: US state cracks down on illegal catfish harvests, sales
content:
The US state of Kentucky's Department of Fish and Wildlife (DFW) reports having uncovered widespread cases of illegal commercial catfish harvests and sales following a seven-month investigation that involved executing 10 search warrants. 

Under "Operation River Raid," Kentucky game wardens executed warrants across the state, from Paducah to Ashland, DFW said in a statement on its website. Because the investigation is active and ongoing, the names of those facing charges, as well as the evidence seized, will be released at a later date.

"We will not allow the illegal exploitation of resources inhabiting Kentucky's rivers and lakes to go unanswered," said Jeremy McQueary, DFW's director of law enforcement, is quoted as saying. "This operation demonstrates our commitment to protecting both the resource and the public who depend on it."

Commercial catfish harvesting on the Ohio River is heavily regulated to avoid overfishing. The department's press release comes a year after nine individuals in the state were charged with illegal commercial catfish harvesting. Wildlife officials said in a Facebook post at the time that the accused faced 180 charges related to their involvement in illegal operations.

title: Editor’s choice: Mowi Canada hatchery greenlit amid die-off; Royal Greenland’s exec changes
content:
EMEA editor Neil Ramsden brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week.

Last week, Undercurrent News' team of journalists was on the road again, this time reporting from Vigo, northern Spain, for the XII ANFACO World Tuna Conference. You can catch all the updates from the event here.

Our most-read stories of the week both concerned salmon-farming giant Mowi's operations in Canada. Firstly, last week found fish processing plants in Newfoundland and Labrador (NL) running double shifts to manage an influx of salmon following a significant die-off at a Mowi site on Aug. 30. An initial investigation attributed the Aug. 30 die-off of around 400,000 salmon to high water temperatures and low oxygen.

Then, Mowi Canada East won cabinet-level approval for its CAD 51 million ($37.4m) expansion of the Indian Head Hatchery, in Stephenville, NL, nearly six years after first filing its proposal. With the order in hand, Mowi must move quickly to satisfy regulators. The company faces a multi-front challenge: preparing detailed monitoring and protection plans, winning approvals from multiple provincial and federal agencies, and demonstrating annual compliance in public reports.

Also in Canada, Greenlandic seafood giant Royal Greenland announced it has parted ways with Simon Jarding, who served as managing director of the company's operations in NL for the past eight years. The business's head office also last week appointed Toke Binzer as its new CEO, effective Dec. 1, 2025, replacing Preben Sunke, who has served as interim CEO for the company since February 2025. 

At the recent Global Shrimp Forum, Undercurrent spoke to several Indonesian executives and heard that over 600 farming businesses have had their market access drastically reduced after the US red-listed the Bahari Makmur Sejati (BMS) plant in Medan, which is close to 2,000 kilometers from the BMS Banten site from which the containers with radioactive traces emanated.

As Undercurrent adjusted its price assessments on frozen Russian and Norwegian headed and gutted (H&G) cod and haddock up again to new record levels in week 37 (Sept. 8-14), yet another trade quirk in the US emerged, which seems likely to move prices on the latter species. The narrow gap on Russian and Norwegian H&G haddock compared to cod is driven by the fact that fish from the former can still go to China and other processing hubs, then be sent to the US as fillets and other products. However, this loophole on H&G haddock looks set to end on Jan. 1, 2026.

Three long-time figures in the North American lobster industry -- Curt Brown, Pete Daley and Betsy Lowe -- have joined forces to launch their own enterprise and acquire a historic processing facility in the US state of Maine.

And a trade deal struck in July between the US and European Union that sets EU tariffs for US seafood to zero is in jeopardy following critical comments made by the chair of the European Parliament's trade committee. Bernd Lange, a member of the Social Democratic Party and representative of Germany, said he and several of his parliamentary colleagues have "doubts" about aspects of the EU's trade deal and said it was likely there would be amendments added to it during the legislative process.

title: Untitled
content:
Fish processing plants in Newfoundland and Labrador are running double shifts to manage an influx of salmon following a significant die-off at a Mowi site on Aug. 30.

An initial investigation attributed the Aug. 30 die-off of around 400,000 salmon to high water temperatures and low-oxygen. The mortality events affected three sites: Broad Cove, Harvey Hill East and Harvey Hill South, as Undercurrent News reported. That suggests about 1.3m mid-cycle fish remain in the system given the officially declared total of 1.7m fish in those sites.

Recall that earlier figures published by the Norwegian salmon farmer suggested a much larger die-off of roughly 1.5m or more fish, but the company subsequently amended its reports to clarify that the number was smaller, as reported by Undercurrent.

Mowi Canada East declined to confirm the surviving tonnage or whether all fish at the affected sites have been harvested, when contacted by Undercurrent.

Local processors, including those in Hermitage-Sandyville and Harbour Breton, have ramped up operations to keep pace.

Steve Crewe, the mayor of Hermitage-Sandyville, a town of just 450 people on Newfoundland's southern coast, described the processing activity as being "as busy as usual," with the local plant now operating two shifts.

"Our plant is working, and they're doing their own fish as well as others," he told Undercurrent News on Thursday (Sept. 11).

"Everybody's still working. There's only one farm site [affected] right now," Crewe added. "Once the site is cleaned out, they'll move the employees through other sites."

The community's dependence on aquaculture remains strong. "Without the aquaculture industry, Hermitage-Sandyville would barely exist," Crewe added.

He also pointed to broader demographic challenges. With population decline and a wave of retirements, foreign workers have become essential to maintaining the local labor force.

"We've had foreign workers in our town for a couple of years now, because there's not enough locally. Everybody who wants to work is working," he said.

title: US red-listing of Indonesia’s BMS strands shrimp farmers almost 2,000km from contamination site
content:
Over 600 Indonesian shrimp farming businesses have had their market access drastically reduced after the US red-listed the Bahari Makmur Sejati (BMS) plant in Medan, which is close to 2,000 kilometers from the BMS Banten site from which the containers with radioactive traces emanated, Indonesian executives told Undercurrent News.

The US red-listing means a temporary market ban for all three BMS plants, in Banten, Medan, and Makassar, even though the impacted containers came only from the site in Banten.

FREE READ Catch the Current bonus: Shrimply the best of the Global Shrimp Forum

The plant in Banten, where a nearby metal recycling facility seemingly contaminated containers of shrimp sent to the US, is some 1,700km from Medan and Makassar and, in fact, on different islands, said Liris Maduningtyas, the CEO and co-founder of Jala Tech, an Indonesian shrimp aquatech company, who is also on the board of industry association the Shrimp Club Indonesia (SCI).

BMS Banten is in the far west of Java, whereas Medan is 1,700km northwest on Sumatra. Then, Makassar is some 1,700km across the Java Sea in the south of Sulawesi.

US lawyers are working on behalf of importers to get the BMS Medan and Makassar plants unblocked, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

For farmers in the Banten and Makassar areas, there are other options, but not so in Aceh and North Sumatra, which supply the BMS Medan plant, Maduningtyas told Undercurrent on the sidelines of the Global Shrimp Forum (GSF), held from Sept. 2-4 in Utrecht, the Netherlands.

"In Banten, farmers can sell to Jakarta, but not farmers from Aceh and Medan. In Makassar, farmers can also sell to other factories," said Maduningtyas, who is acting as a spokesperson for SCI.  

Week 37 farm-gate shrimp roundup: Indonesia prices slump on US BMS ban, Ecuador, India rise

BMS Medan buys around 20,000-25,000 metric tons of raw material annually, sending over 80% of its finished products to the US market, said Maduningtyas.

"We can only really sell to BMS," said Gerry Kamahara, whose company Aqua Gallan Karyacipta works with small-scale shrimp farmers in Aceh and North Sumatra.

"So, BMS Medan has been impacted, even though we have nothing to do with all that happens in Banten; it is 2,000 miles away," Kamahara told Undercurrent during GSF.

"The exporting port is different. The container yard is different. The raw material is different. There is no product transfer between Medan and Banten. But they close us down too," he said.

In Medan, BMS absorbs around 85% of the volume, with the rest going to small plants, said Kamahara.

Fallout from BMS red listing in US, Trump tariffs will hit Indonesia shrimp exports in H2

Ayu Bumi Sejati, the next largest processing option in the area, only buys around 2,000-4,000t, said Maduningtyas.  

"Some other areas have other plants: BMI, First Marine, Sekar Group, Mega Marine, Tamron, etc. So, farmers can sell at a discounted price. In Aceh, Medan and Padang, farmers don't know where to sell it, even at a discounted price," Kamahara told Undercurrent.

This situation has crashed prices in Aceh and North Sumatra, said Kamahara.

Farm-gate prices in Aceh are some 25-30% lower than the levels seen in central, east and west Java, which are also trending down, he said.

So, a 30-count shrimp in Aceh is currently selling for IDR 59,000/kg, including delivery of IDR 3,000-IDR 4,000/kg to the plant, Kamahara said.

That's compared to IDR 72,000/kg for the same size in East Java, as a pure farm-gate price not including delivery, he said. "So, the like-for-like is IDR 54,000-IDR 59,000/kg, compared to IDR 72,000/kg, so a 30-33% difference on this size."

BMS has "extensive coverage" buying across the country and sends around 80% of its products to the US market, so the situation also impacts prices in other regions, said Kamahara. "They [BMS] buy from suppliers who take shrimp from Sumatra, Java, Sulawesi, Lombok and Sumbawa. But BMS absorbs products from the whole of Indonesia, from east to west."

She said that around 630 intensive and traditional farm owners in the Aceh and North Sumatra area are being impacted, covering as much as 18,000 hectares of farming area.

This means around 3,500 direct and 6,000 indirect jobs are impacted.

Indonesian metal facility likely source of radioactive shrimp contamination

With the support of Jala, the company Maduningtyas runs, farmers in Aceh and North Sumatra are looking to deliver products to Jakarta.

"Working with Jala, we try to deliver our product directly to Jakarta for processing. But it is seven days away, some 2,300km. Think of the fuel costs for the farmers. But that's the only option we have, now," he said.

'Radioactive’ narrative in US can damage whole sector

The shrimp sector must work to dispel the untrue "radioactive shrimp" narrative being pushed in the US from the top level of government, which can have an impact on all suppliers, Maduningtyas also told Undercurrent.

Indonesian exec: Incorrect US ‘radioactive shrimp’ narrative is danger to whole sector

Evidence has emerged that the low-level radioactive traces of Cesium-137 found in four containers of frozen shrimp in US ports from BMS came from a nearly metal recycling plant, according to the government investigation. The metal facility is close to one of BMS's three plants, in Serang, in the province of Banten, on the island of Java.

"Shrimp cannot be radioactive. We want to make sure that people know it is [the radioactive traces found in the containers] not coming from shrimp farms, it is not coming from the water, it is not coming from the factory," said Maduningtyas. 

The issue may be impacting BMS and Indonesia more broadly, but the reputational damage could hit the whole sector unless the narrative is countered, Maduningtyas said. 

"This is an isolated incident in one batch from one factory. People have to know that, because the whole narrative is very damaging. And it can really damage the whole shrimp business," not just Indonesia, she said. "Indonesia does not have a nuclear power industry, so this is something alien to us."

title: Untitled
content:
The shrimp sector must work to dispel the untrue "radioactive shrimp" narrative being pushed in the US from the top level of government, which can have an impact on all suppliers, said a leading Indonesian industry figure.

Evidence has emerged that the low-level radioactive traces of Cesium-137 (Cs-137 found in four containers of frozen shrimp in US ports from Indonesia's Bahari Makmur Sejati (BMS) came from a nearby metal recycling plant, according to the government investigation. The metal facility is close to one of BMS's three plants, in Serang, in the province of Banten, on the island of Java.

Week 37 farm-gate shrimp roundup: Indonesia prices slump on US BMS ban, Ecuador, India rise

BMS's other two plants, which are close to 2,000 kilometers in either direction of Banten and on other islands, are also blocked in the US, a situation lawyers are seeking to amend.

"Shrimp cannot be radioactive. We want to make sure that people know it is [the radioactive traces found in the containers] not coming from shrimp farms, it is not coming from the water, it is not coming from the factory," Liris Maduningtyas, the CEO and co-founder of Jala Tech, an Indonesian shrimp aquatech company, told Undercurrent News.

Maduningtyas, who is also on the board of the Shrimp Club Indonesia (SCI), an industry association, was interviewed on the sidelines of the 2025 Global Shrimp Forum (GSF) in Utrecht, the Netherlands. She qualified that she was speaking on behalf of BMS and SCI and not Jala Tech.

The issue may be impacting BMS and Indonesia more broadly, but the reputational damage could hit the whole sector unless the narrative is countered, she said.

"This is an isolated incident in one batch from one factory. People have to know that, because the whole narrative is very damaging. And it can really damage the whole shrimp business," not just Indonesia, she said. "Indonesia does not have a nuclear power industry, so this is something alien to us."

FREE READ Catch the Current bonus: Shrimply the best of the Global Shrimp Forum

The Indonesian nuclear regulatory agency, known as Bapeten, found radioactivity at several scrap-metal collection sites approximately 100 meters from the factory. The site was then sealed off, according to an Aug. 26 report from news service Mongabay. 

Bapeten also emphasized that the shrimp farms that supplied BMS in Lampung and Pandeglang had no contamination. This suggests that the source of contamination likely came from external airborne dust or environmental exposure, not from the shrimp or the farms, a spokesperson said. Operations at the BMS plant have been halted as a result. 

The International Atomic Energy Agency also said the contamination may have originated from improperly disposed radioactive scrap, potentially from recycled medical or industrial devices at a nearby facility, the Associated Press reported on Sept. 5.

Over 300 shipping containers were recalled before reaching consumers. Retailers such as Walmart, Kroger, and others pulled multiple shrimp brands -- including Great Value, Arctic Shores, Sand Bar, Best Yet, First Street, and Great American.

The way the incident is being used in the US can be seen from comments made by US senator John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, at a congressional hearing on water contamination Thursday (Sept. 4).

Fallout from BMS red listing in US, Trump tariffs will hit Indonesia shrimp exports in H2

"Mr. president, this is a photograph of the alien from the movie 'Alien,'" he said while pointing to the image of a fictitious monster in a 1979 horror movie on a poster mounted behind him. "This is what you could end up looking like if you eat some of the raw frozen shrimp being sent to the US by other countries."

This claim is a stretch, given the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) confirmed Cs-137 in a sample of frozen breaded shrimp from BMS measured approximately 68 Bq/kg -- well below the action level of 1,200 Bq/kg.

"Eating 1kg of shrimp at this level is the same as eating four bananas," said Maduningtyas, of the naturally occurring radiation in the fruit.

Bananas are naturally radioactive due to their potassium-40 (K-40) content, which is a natural process. Bananas naturally absorb K-40 from the soil, whereas Cs-137 is a man-made byproduct of nuclear fission.

"The level is very low, but I understand that the FDA wants the root cause. But this is not from the shrimp," she said. 

"We have the early result of the investigations," said Maduningtyas during GSF.

"What is clear is that this did not come from any shrimp farm area. All of the farms have been tested, and there is no contamination whatsoever. Also, they tested the water at the farms. They also didn't find any radioactive material inside the factory," she said.

However, they found low-level radiation in several locations on the plant's site and then in the metal facility, she said. "There was low-level contamination on the chimney and the rain gutter piping on the outside of the building."

FREE READ GSF 2025 day three recap: BMS red listing, tariffs to hit Indonesia shrimp; Ecuador now Japan’s fourth largest supplier

As to how this happened, the Indonesian government is still investigating, she said.

"Smoke goes into the sky from the smelter, which is very hot. Then a container is very cold. So, maybe it's something to do with the pressure from hot to cold, made it come down, and then the traces are found in the containers," said Maduningtyas. "Of course, the containers are opened to load the shrimp."

The "how" is what the Indonesian authorities are working on, she said. "We have five ministries working on it, the parliament and the president. There's the ministry of energy, industry, environment, and trade."

Then, they are working with Indonesia's nuclear department, she said. "Indonesia does not have a nuclear power industry. But we do have a department of nuclear to detect contamination because Indonesia is an energy country, a big oil and gas producer."

The focus is on finding the precise source of the Cs-137, before submitting to the FDA, she said.

"That's something that we don't know clearly yet. What is the source? Because it could be from anywhere. The process is taking time as the government needs to know where the traces come from. It can come from medical equipment, sensors, all sorts of things. It could be from anywhere."

title: Catch the Current bonus: Shrimply the best of the Global Shrimp Forum
content:
More than 500 people from almost 50 countries gathered in Utrecht, the Netherlands, for the Global Shrimp Forum, last week, a three-day jam-packed event covering everything from market outlets to commodity trends. 

Couldn't attend this year? You seriously missed out. 

Fortunately, we sent a team of reporters who are ready to report back on all the major takeaways.

To break it all down for this special Global Shrimp Forum bonus episode, Catch the Current hosts Amanda Buckle and Lorin Castiglione recently welcomed to the pod: Tom Seaman, the co-founder and editor-in-chief of Undercurrent News; Louis Harkell, global head of price reporting and data journalism; Dan Gibson, EMEA deputy editor; and Gary Morrison, principal price reporter.  

Thank you to our sponsor: Wisefish.

Listen now on YouTube!

Subscribe now! Catch the Current is available on YouTube, Spotify, Amazon Music, iHeartRadio, Pandora, and other major podcast streaming platforms. Don't see Catch the Current on your favorite app? Reach out to podcasts@undercurrentnews.com.

Don't have time to listen? Find a full transcript of the Global Shrimp Forum bonus episode of Catch the Current below:

Amanda Buckle (AB): You're listening to Catch the Current, the coolest seafood podcast out there, from the team at Undercurrent News, your trusted source for seafood prices, news, and data. I'm Amanda Buckle.

LC: And I'm Lorin Castiglione.

As promised, we've got a special episode today all about the Global Shrimp Forum, which took place in Utrecht, the Netherlands, from Sept. 2-4.

Before we dive in, a quick shoutout to our sponsor Wisefish. With over 30 years in the seafood industry, they’re powering aquaculture, fisheries, processors and seafood sales with one integrated platform that makes managing complex operations simpler. Check them out at wisefish.com/catch-the-current.

FREE READ Track global shrimp prices from farm-gate to wholesale with new UCN tool

AB: We've got a party joining us on the pod to talk about the big takeaways from the Global Shrimp Forum. Calling in from London is Tom Seaman, the co-founder and editor-in-chief of Undercurrent News, Louis Harkell, our global head of price reporting and data journalism, and EMEA deputy editor Dan Gibson.

And then joining us from beautiful New Jersey is Gary Morrison, our principal price reporter.

LC: Okay, guys, let's get down to the nitty-gritty because this event came at a time when global shrimp trade flows are reshuffling due to US tariffs. Plus, in the US, a major import alert banning shrimp from a major Indonesian producer. So let's start there.

Tom, was BMS's import alert for Cesium-137 contamination brought up at all during the forum?

Tom Seaman (TS): It was. It was quite a big discussion point because there's a lot of concern in the sector, which maybe Gary can also talk more about later, that it could cause kind of wider reputational damage to shrimp as a product with this kind of "radioactive shrimp" tag being widely used. And it was interesting to speak to some Indonesian industry figures about this.

Aris Utama from BMI, which is another big processor, spoke on a panel about how there's not really clear where this actually came from. It's kind of an anomaly.

Indonesia isn't a nuclear power in any way. So there's no real way that people were thinking this contamination could have happened, given that Indonesia has no nuclear power at all.

Indonesian metal facility likely source of radioactive shrimp contamination

And then I spoke with Liris [Maduningtyas], the CEO of JALA, which is an Indonesian aquatech company supplying farmers with technology. And it's obviously a very critical issue for them because their customers, the farmers that supply BMS, which is one of, if not the largest, Indonesian shrimp exporters to the US. They are obviously being heavily impacted by this. And it was very interesting to chat to her.

She kind of gave a message, which has then been reported by the AP and other news outlets that the findings of Indonesian investigations into this show that it wasn't from the shrimp farms. This very low level contamination. It wasn't from the shrimp farms, wasn't from the BMS plant, and it wasn't from the water they'll be using in the shrimp farming. It seems the contamination has come from a nearby metal smelting disposal facility, which is in the same kind of industrial area as this one BMS plant, which is in Banten, which is in West Java, so kind of not too far from Jakarta.

And that seems to be what now is being highlighted as where this has come from. So it's kind of traces that somehow got into the containers before they shipped. It was only four containers, I think, that went to four separate US ports from this one plant.

But then obviously the knock-on effect of that is there's two other BMS plants in different parts of Indonesia. One is in a place, Medan, which is kind of another island, it's on North Sumatra, kind of the northern bit of the Sumatra Island. So this is 2,000 miles from where this kind of contamination took place.

And this plant is also basically unable to export to the US, so there's kind of no intertrade between it and the other plant that's impacted because it's so far away.

Liris was explaining to me it's pretty terrible for the farmers in that area because they don't have any other processing plants to sell to. They have this BMS plant, and then there is one very much smaller plant.

BMS is processing maybe 20,000-25,000 [metric] tons in that plant. The other plant does about 4,000. So the farmers in that area are suffering huge decreases in price and demand because they just don't have any other markets for their product.

Importers push to limit FDA alert for radioactive shrimp from Indonesia

And this plant has kind of really got nothing to do with this. It's just owned by the same company, but it's sort of 2,000 miles from the one that's had this incident. So it's something I think where, Amanda, you've reported on, that there's lawyers working on behalf of the Indonesian exporters to get these two other plants that the BMS owned potentially reopened, even if the one where the contamination originated from remains closed.

A very interesting issue.

AB: Yeah. And they're close. I mean, they are having conversations now with the FDA. They're waiting to hear back if their request to have those other facilities be allowed to be taken off that import alert. So we should have an answer within the next week or so.

But unfortunately, it's still not -- I don't think -- enough. Just last week, US senator John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, spread fear surrounding the import of radioactive shrimp from Indonesia on the floor of the Senate, saying that you can grow an ear and you could look like an alien. So...

TS: There is a fear. That's what Liris from JALA was saying. This could potentially impact all countries of origin. There was a couple of Ecuadorian processors I spoke with kind of saying, oh, this could be positive for us because it'll be associated with Asian shrimp. But I don't really think that the US consumer would necessarily be making a distinction between Ecuadorian or Asian shrimp.

US lawmaker compares radioactive shrimp to threat of sci-fi/horror film creature

I think that you never quite know with these things. Sometimes these things just kind of fizzle out and go away with the crazy news cycle that we have now. And sometimes they kind of stick and do impact demand. And I guess it's very hard to know where this one will go.

But what is kind of emerging is that, you know, there is this isn't an issue about the shrimp. I mean, it really could have been like anything in those containers that then reach the US. It's kind of more about proximity between this shrimp factory and then this kind of metal smelting facilities.

Gary Morrison (GM): What I've talked to people about, especially at the Global Shrimp Forum, there's definitely headline risk. You know, US consumers hear radioactive shrimp and it's broad throughout the industry.

I don't think they're going to identify just Indonesian-sourced shrimp. I think there is going to be some sort of risk for all shrimp if this continues to stay top of mind and in the news. Because I don't know if the US consumer differentiates where their shrimp come from in terms of imported farm-raised product.

I moderated the plenary closing session, which looked at the outlook over the short- to medium-term next three to six months on, you know, all these different factors that are influencing higher cost structures throughout the value chain, as well as trade flow changes because of them.

And, you know, we had some real, real expertise on the panel. I was honored to host it and moderate it and be a part of a panel with some of the people in the industry that we had: Angel Rubio, Gabriel Luna, Watanabe Yutaka and Jacob George. We talked about what's going on mostly from a US perspective, but how these trade flows are going to change globally.

Photo Credit: Global Shrimp Forum

So on the panel, I think the big takeaways, and Tom talked about a little bit with Indonesia and India, and Ecuador thinking that they have an advantage and not only because of some of the alerts, but because of the tariff advantage and competitiveness that they have over some of the Asian sourced countries. But, you know, I think the big takeaways are Ecuador, they were moving into value-add prior to tariffs.

They wanted to meet the needs of the US consumer a little bit better, but the tariffs are accelerating it. But number two, there is going to be a challenge. They are at capacity right now, so they can't fulfill any more demand, or very minimal in excess of what they're doing now.

So the other main takeaway is that India and other Asian sourced countries are going to be key partners still because each one of those countries have their own unique strengths and capabilities, and it's going to be hard for other countries to make that capital investment in the short term.

Maybe structurally, long-term, things start to change. But right now, it's not only Ecuador. US importers do have to source from their Asian partners.

And, you know, right now, businesses really want certainty. They think things can change on a dime with this administration. So I think, you know, they want to make sure they can plan and uncertainty is certainly a risk for them.

LC: So Gary was up on stage. We talked about Amanda being up on stage last week. Dan, my sources are telling me that you were just in the audience eating shrimp. Is that right?

Dan Gibson (DG): Well, yeah, it has played problems listening back to my dictaphone from that meeting. I can largely hear myself chewing for most of it. I occasionally hear Amanda over the top, but that's about the extent of it really.

From what I can glean from it, I mean, the main takeaway from the Global Shrimp Council session was that they are in the coming weeks going to be launching their first campaign outside of the US in both France and Spain.

And it's personally quite interesting they're going for both because, the whole reason they avoided Europe to begin with is because whereas the US is such a nice big market, we all speak the same language.

Europe is such a split-up, divided market where everybody would need a different tailored marketing campaign for their different cultural tastes. Like what they eat in Spain is very different to what they eat in France, what's very different to what they eat here in the UK. And so it's interesting they've targeted both.

And I think that then ties in very nicely to probably my biggest takeaway from the whole show, which is that Europe right now is the boom market for shrimp and nobody saw it coming.

This morning we published the headline that the EU is expected to increase its imports to 400,000t this year. And last year it was 320,000t.

I mean, the EU is an incredibly mature market. It hasn't really changed for about a decade.

You either like shrimp and you buy it or you don't, so you don't. And good luck finding a European who doesn't know what a prawn is or how to cook it.

So, yeah, it's just stunning. There's been this sudden increase year on year, and that's expected to continue for the rest of the year, even as the US is dropping off and as China is turning more to its own domestic production.

FREE READ Ecuador’s July shrimp exports reveal increased emphasis on value addition

And it sounds like the big driver basically has been that it's better than expected winter consumption. And as soon as Trump announces his tariffs in April and the price of shrimp drops globally, everybody around Europe went, all right, let's get in while prices are low.

And it seems like every country has had the same idea. Basically, just had this sudden huge increase. And for the most part, I'd say the two big beneficiaries have been Ecuador and India, obviously the two biggest producers. So if you need more shrimp, they're the ones you speed dial.

And I'd say on the Ecuadorian side of things, Venezuela, their biggest producer, Grupo Lamar, got taken over by the Venezuelan government. And that has absolutely slashed volumes out of there.

Their loss has been Ecuador's gain. Very similar products, so they just swoop right in. Their volumes to Europe so far this year are up 39%. That's mad.

And then on the flip side, India, they're up about 25% this year. And for them, I mean, given that there's now this huge tariff to the US, this is potentially huge for them as an outlet. If they're struggling to get any fresh demand from America, try Europe, basically. That's the big thing there for them.

So I suppose it should also be mentioned, the elephant in the room where India is concerned is that there is a list, a new antibiotic list. And I believe this has been well published before, but basically the EU, in its infinite wisdom, has drawn up a list of countries who are allowed to export organic materials to the EU. And India is not included as of yet.

EU shrimp buyers could shift from India in early 2026 if antibiotic list issue not rectified

And this list will take effect next September. And their government basically needs to prove that they are doing or taking sufficient steps and due diligence to enforce these rules that no antibiotics are used in the production of farmed shrimp, among other things.

And what was interesting at the show was to see the huge cultural difference between how Indians operate and how Europeans operate, or at least how the EU operates.

And I mean, it would be funny if there weren't so many livelihoods at stake. But basically, India has a very much, "Oh, it's a year away. We'll deal with it. It'll be fine. You know, who's to worry about it?"

And then Willem van der Pijl, the show host, he knows how long European bureaucracy takes. I think they wrote an entire book in which, you know, they just have to get permit from French bureaucracy.

And that's enough to create an entire story about it. He's saying, this would take, if you don't make it on the list, it will take at least nine months to get you on it in the future. So deal with it now. Give yourself more time than you could possibly think you would ever need to deal with, because this is Europe you're dealing with. This is the EU. Allow basically half a lifetime to get stuff done.

AB: So, Louis, last but not least, we heard from everybody else there. I know you ate your fill of shrimp, but what were your big takeaways from the Global Shrimp Forum?

Louis Harkell (LH): I think my big takeaway was the fact that it appears that most of the main big producers just seem to be able to keep exporting increasing volumes of shrimp. Ecuador, India, Vietnam and Indonesia are all reporting higher export volumes. And I suppose that's a surprise.

You expect maybe one or two among them, but all four of the biggest producers in the world, yeh, they're all exporting more shrimp. And so if you're an industry, I mean, I presume that's great news, right? I mean, people around the world are eating more shrimp and farmers are getting more people farming and more people earning money through the supply chain. So, yeh, that was the key takeaway, I think.

I think the big hitter is, as always, Ecuador. And the exports have really gone gangbusters at the start of this year, growing by 17%. And I think when a country is exporting over a million tons of shrimp every year already, that's an enormous increase.

It's about 200,000 tons over a calendar year. So, when you think that Thailand is producing around 200,000 tons or exporting around that much, you know, that's a huge increase in volume on the global market, right? And we've already mentioned, India, Vietnam and Indonesia are already also exporting higher volumes. So, I think that was kind of the key takeaway for me.

Ecuador really just powering ahead. And I think the interesting thing was, you know, what the explanation for that was. And that came from Sandro Coglitore of Omarsa.

Photo Credit: Global Shrimp Forum

And he kind of put it down to, because last year, Ecuador's export growth was pretty flat, like they didn't grow. And everyone was like, OK, well, Ecuador has reached the ceiling. China's not really buying much more and that's their main market. But actually, it turned out that they were just having a kind of a breather after all this consolidation of these shrimp farms around the country.

And Sandro said, now that we're rolling out this new technology to these smaller farms, the yields are increasing. And that's why, in 2025, we've seen this big increase. And he expects that to continue into next year.

That is possibly going to be alarming for other producers around the world. To think that Ecuador could be producing yet more shrimp, not just in the second half of this year, but then going into 2026. And also, prices haven't collapsed yet. And so obviously, if there's a big collapse in prices, that's going to be putting a hold on things.

But at the moment, prices are still, you know, relatively OK. I mean, I don't think producers are seeing dollar signs when they're harvesting and selling their shrimp to processors and exporters. But it seems like prices are holding OK for Ecuador to keep producing these huge volumes.

So I think that's going to be one to keep an eye on. Like Ecuador, can it maintain this growth? And yeah, you can see more on our blog.

title: Untitled
content:
Still at the center of the radioactive shrimp saga, Indonesia has again emerged in the spotlight after a small, three-year US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) probe found it the top source of short-weighted frozen seafood shipments.

Short-weighting happens when exporters count the protective ice glaze as part of the declared net weight, inflating prices while delivering less seafood. Glazing itself is a normal step to keep products from freezer burn, but the ice must not be included in the labeled weight.

FDA applies a threshold of about 1% below the declared weight across a shipment lot before taking action, and -- in this case -- the shortfalls ranged from 2.3% to nearly 10%.

On Tuesday (Sept. 2), FDA released the findings of a three-year assignment (2022–2024) conducted exclusively to assess short-weighting in frozen seafood. Inspectors sampled 28 shipments -- mostly frozen shrimp -- from four countries at US ports of entry and other import locations, testing 48 packages from each shipment lot. Ten shipments, or 36%, failed to meet labeling requirements because their net weight included too much ice glaze.

Sixteen of the shipments checked were from Indonesia, nine from Ecuador, two from China and one from Vietnam. Eight -- half of the shipments from Indonesia -- were found to be non-compliant. Another two found out of compliance were squid from Vietnam and China.

"All 10 violative samples resulted in refusal of entry for that shipment into the US," the agency said in its announcement.

FDA's sampling of frozen seafood shipments for shortweighting, 2022–24.

While the FDA summary of findings did not name the five companies, the agency noted that those firms were placed on Import Alert 99-47, which lists specific exporters subject to detention without physical examination at the border.

As of Wednesday (Sept. 3), the Red List under Import Alert 99-47 includes companies cited for short-weighting violations: two from Indonesia for shrimp -- PT Bumi Pangan Utama (added May 16, 2025) and PT First Marine Seafoods (added Aug. 1, 2025). The alert also names Vietnamese company Thanh Hao Seafood Co. (added Apr. 2, 2024) and Chinese company Yantai Ruihe Foods (added Jun. 5, 2023), both for squid.

Because FDA updates its import alerts on a rolling basis, not all current listings necessarily relate to the 2022–24 sampling assignment.

FDA cautioned that the exercise was limited in scope and not designed for country-to-country comparisons, but the results highlight how susceptible frozen seafood remains to economically motivated adulteration. FDA said it will continue targeted sampling of shrimp, squid and other fishery products to deter fraud and protect consumers. It warned that it may pursue criminal investigations where appropriate as part of its broader mission to combat food fraud and safeguard consumers.

The findings come as Indonesia continues to grapple with fallout from a separate food safety crisis. On Aug. 14, FDA issued Import Alert 99-51 against Bahari Makmur Sejati (BMS), Indonesia's largest supplier of EZ peel shrimp, after detecting cesium-137 contamination in its products, as Undercurrent reported. The alert triggered recalls by Walmart, Southwind Foods, Beaver Street Fisheries and AquaStar, collectively pulling tens of thousands of packages from US retail shelves.

BMS's US importers are now lobbying FDA to narrow the scope of the ban to a single facility identified in traceability documents, arguing that other shipments should be cleared for entry.

Trade data from Undercurrent’s trade portal shows how shrimp imports from Indonesia, Ecuador, Vietnam and China compared between 2019 and 2024. Ecuador is the US' second-largest shrimp supplier, behind India, but Indonesia is third largest.

title: Three brothers accused of killing co-worker on US commercial fishing vessel
content:
Three brothers have been accused of stabbing to death a co-worker while onboard a commercial fishing vessel in the US state of Louisiana.

Siblings Josiah Cottrell, 28, Timothy Cottrell, 25, and David Cottrell, 22, all of Broussard, Louisiana, were arrested on Aug. 28 and charged with second-degree murder, according to the New Orleans Times-Picayune.

The male victim, who has not yet been identified by police, was stabbed multiple times at around 10:30 p.m. while onboard the vessel traveling through the Red Pass waterway west of Venice, in Plaquemines Parish, Louisiana.

The man and the Cottrells all worked as deckhands on the vessel, which was not identified by the Plaquemines Parish Sheriff's Office. An investigation into what caused the incident is still underway.

title: Latest shrimp mislabeling probe finds restaurants flouting Alabama disclosure law
content:
A new study reports to show significant shrimp mislabeling in Mobile, Alabama, a US city with a deep shrimping heritage.

SeaD Consulting, a Houston, Texas-based firm specializing in rapid genetic testing of seafood, said it checked shrimp dishes being served in 44 randomly selected restaurants in the Mobile area and found 10 of them serving imported shrimp despite marketing it as "gulf" or "local."

All 10 broke Alabama's seafood labeling law by marketing imported shrimp as local, SeaD said. "The majority described their shrimp as gulf, local, or domestic either verbally or on menus," the firm said, while one implied gulf or wild-caught sourcing through branding or marketing.

The law, which took effect in October 2024, requires restaurants to disclose whether seafood is imported or domestic and whether it is wild-caught or farmed.

The Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA), representing shrimp fishermen and processors in eight warmwater states, funds SeaD's multi-state investigations and publishes the results on its website.

The investigation in Mobile is the latest in a string of exposes conducted by SeaD. Earlier work reportedly uncovered shrimp mislabeling in New Orleans, Louisiana, the Mississippi Gulf Coast, and New York City, with fraud rates ranging from 13% to as high as 96%, as Undercurrent News reported.

The SSA said the results highlight the need for stronger state and federal labeling laws to prevent seafood substitution and protect both consumers and domestic shrimpers.

title: US’ NMFS warns about unredacted dead marine mammal photos inviting harassment of trawlers
content:
The National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) is pushing back against releasing unredacted images of dead whales, sea lions and other marine mammals entangled in fishing gear as demanded in a lawsuit filed by activists seeking greater transparency of bycatch by the Alaska trawl fleet.

US Department of Justice attorneys argued in the US District Court in Alaska on behalf of NMFS this month that online activists already use open-source intelligence to call out individual vessels. A full release of images could lead to "public identification of their vessels and crew, reveal fishing methods and practices, and enable harassment" of crews, they warned.

Oceana sues US gov’t over data on trawl bycatch of marine mammals

"The plain language of the Magnuson-Stevens Act's confidentiality provision prohibits the public release of photographs taken by (onboard) observers," assistant attorney general E. Bryan Wilson wrote in an Aug. 25 filing asking for US district court judge Sharon Gleason to dismiss the case.

Gleason recently green-lit two Alaska Native tribes to intervene on behalf of Oceana, which alleges NMFS improperly obscured or withheld more than 1,200 images of marine mammal entanglements in trawl nets in federal waters off Alaska, as Undercurrent News earlier reported. 

DOJ attorneys have filed 34 exhibits that include screenshots of social media posts identifying or seeking to identify specific trawl vessels in the Bering Sea and Gulf of Alaska.

DOJ attorneys argued there were only 18 vessels permitted to harvest flatfish in the Bering Sea in 2022, and images that were not heavily pixelated to conceal the type of gear used would make it easy to identify them.

Open-source marine Automatic Identification System (AIS) tracking logs vessel movements and shows real-time locations, and can be cross-referenced with unredacted images.

DOJ also submitted samples from social media and the Reddit online forum, with an individual posting an image of two dead orcas on the deck of a trawler in an attempt to identify the specific vessel using sophisticated techniques, such as identifying digital metadata in the image files.

A post on the popular online forum website Reddit from four years ago purports to show dead orca whales aboard a commercial trawl vessel. Commenters discussed ways of stripping the metadata from the image file to identify the vessel. (Photo from US DOJ court filing)

"These Reddit forums were not dedicated toward such activities, but groups on Facebook such as 'STOP Alaskan Trawler Bycatch' also show motivation and awareness of tools for similar investigations, as well as threats of violent action against trawlers and their crew," Wilson wrote.

The moderator of the Facebook group responded that activists in the online forum want to raise public awareness and not harass men and women doing their jobs.

"I agree that the faces of crew members should never be exposed, but the public has a right to know which companies are running vessels that kill whales and other protected species," David Bayes, a Homer, Alaska-based charter captain and frequent contributor, told Undercurrent. 

"A blurry outline of a whale tells consumers nothing," Bayes added. "If the government is going to promote trawl fisheries as eco-friendly, then it should not also be protecting wealthy corporations from public scrutiny."

A post on a popular Facebook group criticizing the trawl fleet in Alaska waters identifies the real-time location of a 264-foot catcher/processor harvesting groundfish in salmon-rich Bristol Bay, Alaska. (Image from US DOJ court filing)

The Dec. 19, 2024 lawsuit's legal arguments against fuller disclosure are part of a larger fight being waged online largely by outspoken critics of the trawl industry. On Wednesday, (Aug. 27), the Seattle, Washington-based United Catcher Boats (UCB) released a statement decrying the vitriol directed at its members over the bycatch of chinook salmon.

North Pacific council bucks critics, preserves status quo for Alaska trawlers

"Attacks against the US Bering Sea pollock trawl fleet fishing off Alaska — and against science itself — have run rampant on social media," the Seattle, Washington-based industry advocacy group that represents more than 60 catcher vessels targeting pollock, whiting and Pacific cod in Alaska and the West Coast, wrote on social media.

"One of our last posts on king salmon declines was a clear example: the comments were full of blame, personal attacks, and rhetoric that does nothing to help Alaska's king salmon," UCB wrote in an unsigned post.

Attorneys for the conservation group Oceana, which has asked the court to rule that NMFS had unlawfully withheld unredacted images from marine mammal takes, have until Sept. 22 to file their response.

To date, no industry group has intervened in the lawsuit.

title: Untitled
content:
Icelandic salmon farmer Kaldvik, majority-owned by Masoval and the largest Icelandic salmon producer by volume, has reduced its harvest guidance for 2025 after a tough second quarter.

Icelandic salmon farmer’s CEO steps down, interim chief appointed

The company, which had been targeting a sharp 44% year-on-year hike to 21,500 metric tons of production this year, has now lowered its annual ambitions to just 18,000t after the first half's conclusion. 

The main cause, it said, was the challenging 2023 smolt generation, which it described as "suboptimal," and the "last generation not benefiting from new winter wound vaccine and investments in our land facilities."

Furthermore, unusually low sea temperatures in Q4 of last year and the first quarter of this year reduced growth, while periods of reduced appetite were observed in Q2 owing to poor underwater visibility from algae blooms.

The last of the 2023 smolt generation is due to be harvested out over the remainder of this year, while the following year "is showing clear signs of improved performance compared to previous generations," Kaldvik said.

Altogether, the company produced 1,235t of salmon in the latest quarter, and 7,618t since the start of the year. Towards the end of production at the firm's Vattarnes site, in Iceland's Eastfjords region, winter wounds resulted in a lower share of superior-grade fish -- Kaldvik's total superior-grade harvest for the quarter amounted to just 40%.

A further 2,300t is guided in Q3, with a much busier 8,100t harvest on the cards in the final quarter of the year. Even if its short of the original guidance, this would still represent a 20% increase in y-o-y harvest volumes at the firm.

On a financial basis, the 1,235t harvest translated to quarterly revenue of €7.9 million, but an operational loss before interest and tax (EBIT) of €4.3m (below). The sharp drop in price level was both a function of the challenging market and the low superior-grade share, the group said.

Still, the bulk of H1 harvests were conducted profitably in the first quarter, and so operational EBIT across the group remains a positive €5.5m year to date.

Credit: Kaldvik's Q2 2025 report

Outgoings and investigations

The last few months have been highly eventful for Kaldvik, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

For starters, CEO Roy-Tore Rikardsen stepped down with immediate effect earlier this month, to be replaced by Vider Aspehaug on an interim basis. Aspehaug, who joined Kaldvik in 2022, has overseen fish health and quality management at the company for the last three years.

Minority shareholders representing over 10% of Kaldvik's capital also submitted a resquest to Iceland's district court in June to begin an investigation into the $18.8 million agreement reached between Kaldvik, Heimsto and Osval relating to the former's deal for property company Mossi, fish box producer Djupskel and 33% of fish processor Bulandstindur, completed in March this year.

Board member Adalsteinn Ingolfsson had resigned in January in protest, claiming the assets had been overvalued and majority shareholder Heimsto was "profiting abnormally at the expense of other shareholders."

The legal matter should be resolved this fall, Kaldvik said.

title: Figures linked to Ricardo Fuentes among 7 convicted in Spain tuna scandal
content:
Seven businessmen have been convicted in Spain for participating in a network that sold illegally caught bluefin tuna, some of it in a state of decay and linked to cases of food poisoning.

Two of the men have ties to the Ricardo Fuentes Group, one of the world's largest exporters of bluefin tuna, reports La Vanguardia. 

The case, heard by Spain's National Court, stems from "Operation Tarantelo," a 2018 investigation that uncovered tuna shipments from Malta, Italy and other countries entering the Spanish market without proper documentation or sanitary checks.

Prosecutors said the network operated between 2017 and 2018, using a secret warehouse where tuna was handled in "appalling" conditions and outside official oversight. The lack of hygiene and falsified paperwork erased any traceability, creating what prosecutors called "an evident danger to public health."

Tests revealed histamine levels far above safe limits, and several cases of consumer illness were linked to the contaminated fish. While much of Ricardo Fuentes' business was legal, prosecutors said part of its supply chain relied on irregular practices, with spoiled tuna repackaged and sold to supermarkets and other buyers.

The seven defendants accepted sentences of one year and nine months in prison and fines ranging from €24,000 to €143,200. Prosecutors also asked for charges against an eighth suspect to be dropped.

In a short statement sent to Undercurrent News, the Ricardo Fuentes Group said the court's final ruling dismissed allegations that it described as "having nothing to do with reality" and confirmed that the company itself had been excluded from the case months earlier.

The group insisted that its products "have offered and continue to offer all the guarantees for consumers" and that "none of our tuna has ever generated any food safety problems."

It also said the plea deal was intended to end a process that could have dragged on for years, despite what it called the "great personal cost" of the agreement.

title: Untitled
content:
The US Food and Drug Administration's blocking of radioactive shrimp from Indonesia has made it on the radar of US secretary of health and human services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a polarizing celebrity policymaker in the administration of Donald Trump.

And he's looking to make sure the president is aware of the issue, too.

Trump's cabinet meeting on Tuesday (Aug. 26) is being hailed as a "marathon," lasting more than three hours and covering a wide range of topics, from saving whales to seeking the death penalty for murders committed in DC, and Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce's engagement. But seafood also had its moment.

"The South Asian nations are now dumping shrimp on our country. Their shrimp is heavily contaminated," Kennedy said. "We just stopped a shipment that was contaminated with cesium-157 [sic] [Cs-137], which is radioactive. They are farming these shrimp and they use bactericides and antibiotics and all kinds of chemicals."

Kennedy was referring in particular to FDA's ban of the shrimp sold by Bahari Makmur Sejati (BMS) and related recall announcements, including those made by Walmart.

Robert F. Kennedy Jr. (far left) brought up the latest news regarding chemically contaminated shrimp during a cabinet meeting at the White House on Tuesday (Aug. 26). Screenshot: White House/ YouTube

FDA is part of the Department of Health and Human Services, overseen by Kennedy. 

FDA import alert 99-51, dated Aug. 14, was a first-of-its-kind notice. No other countries have ever been flagged for radioactive chemicals in an import alert. And Indonesia's BMS, the largest supplier of easy-peel shrimp to the US, was the only company listed for Cs-137 contamination. 

The imported shrimp are "so contaminated, the European nations won't take them," Kennedy continued.

"So they're dumping them all here, and they're putting out of business [sic]," he said. "We have the most sustainable, highly regulated fishery in the world. What our fishermen do is a good thing. And all of the trawlers in the gulf and Alaska are being shut down because we're getting shrimp dumped here. So we have now increased FDA inspections of shrimp to make sure that Americans are not eating, buying and eating contaminated shrimp and putting our shrimpers out of business."

Shrimp was just one of many topics covered by Kennedy, who also spoke about how ending offshore wind will help commercial fishermen. 

An intensifying situation

There's a lot to unpack in Kennedy's comments as it combines quite a few issues facing the domestic shrimp fishery. It's important to note that while BMS has been "red-listed" due to Cs-137 contamination, it has not been found to be involved in dumping.

But there's no denying that FDA inspections of domestic shrimp imports have recently intensified -- especially for Indonesia.

The federal agency issued 58 entry line refusals for Indonesian shrimp between Jan. 1 and Aug. 12, 2025, according to data compiled by the Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA), which represents the US domestic shrimp sector and sees shrimp imports as the enemy. That's compared to a total of 27 entry line refusals for Indonesian shrimp in 2024 and 44 in 2023.

The problems that the FDA identified in Indonesian shrimp extend beyond radioactive isotopes, as reported by Undercurrent News. Shipments were refused due to issues including undeclared sulfites, contamination with salmonella and veterinary drug residues.

Indonesia is the US's third-largest shrimp source nation. India holds the top spot, followed by Ecuador at number two. Vietnam and Thailand round out the top five source countries, as the chart below illustrates.

title: Red Chamber says Argentine contract in force amid legal rumbles
content:
US fishing firm Red Chamber has issued a statement addressing claims over its contractual relationship with the Argentine province of Chubut, asserting that the agreement remains legally valid and fully enforceable.

Its Argentine subsidiary, RCA, is allegedly competing with Spain's Profand Fishing Holding for control of the valuable assets of the Argentine fishing business Alpesca.

US-based Red Chamber alleges espionage as it vies for control of Argentine firm’s assets

RCA has filed a criminal complaint before the Comodoro Py federal courthouse, alleging a case of corporate espionage linked to the expropriation process of Alpesca. It is leasing Alpesca's assets from the provincial government, but seems to be facing a battle to keep that arrangement. 

Amid the beginnings of a court investigation, Gustavo Gonzalez -- representative of the chamber of Chubut province's "yellow fleet" -- claimed on Facebook that "Red Chamber has done a lot of harm to the sector and doesn't respect agreements." He also claimed that Red Chamber's contract with the province of Chubut has already expired.

In a statement sent to Undercurrent News, Red Chamber rejected what it described as "unfounded public statements and unsubstantiated press reports."

"According to our legal counsel, the contract governing our relationship with the province of Chubut remains in full force and effect," the statement said.

"Red Chamber Argentina continues to operate in good faith under the existing contract and expects nothing less from the Province of Chubut," the company further said, emphasizing its ongoing commitment to its operations, its investment, and the thousands of jobs sustained over the past decade.

"Our priority remains the integrity of our operations, the protection of our investment as
well as the future well-being of our people, whom we have employed for the past 10 years," it said.

A separate source familiar with the matter, who asked to remain anonymous, also told Undercurrent that Red Chamber has an existing contract.

"That contract is in place and survives its term until the assets of Alpesca are expropriated. The [Argentine] government has taken over 10 years and has not finalized the process of expropriation; therefore, the current contract continues to be in place legally," he noted.

Sources and some articles in the Argentine media alleged that Profand has been working with the provincial fishery secretary and other local groups to interfere with Red Chambers' "existing and valid contract."

Profand declined to comment to Undercurrent.

Red Chamber also confirmed that it has filed a criminal complaint in Federal Court No. 7, located in Comodoro Py, Buenos Aires, as reported by Undercurrent on Aug. 26. The complaint targets a group of unidentified individuals accused of unlawfully entering the company's plant in Chubut.

The company stated that the case is now in the hands of the judiciary and expressed confidence that the investigation "will shine a bright light upon those responsible for the wrongdoing perpetrated upon Red Chamber Argentina and its group of companies" while ensuring "a just outcome."

Alpesca's assets include a processing plant, employing 400 people, along with seven national fishing permits and five provincial fishing permits, according to sources.

title: Untitled
content:
US fishing firm Red Chamber's Argentine subsidiary (RCA) and Spain's Profand Fishing Holding are allegedly vying for control of the valuable assets of Argentine fishing business Alpesca, a dispute now spilling into the Latin American country’s federal courts.

RCA has filed a criminal complaint before the Comodoro Py federal courthouse, alleging a case of corporate espionage linked to the expropriation process of Alpesca, sources told Undercurrent News. The federal court officially started an investigation on Aug. 22.

Individuals who entered its facilities in May claiming to represent Argentina's Tribunal de Tasacion (national appraisal court) were, in fact, posing under false identities, reported Parte de Pesca.

RCA suspects the operation was enabled by Chubut government officials, particularly provincial fisheries secretary Andres Arbeletche, to benefit third parties.

The firm's legal representative argued before federal prosecutor Zulma Manllauix that the inspection was a maneuver intended to harm RCA and facilitate a transfer of exploitation rights of Alpesca's assets to another company.

In the complaint, seen by Undercurrent, RCA alleges the men identified themselves as technical advisors but carried suspicious documents and spoke with a notably Spanish accent.

This raised concerns that they were linked to the Spanish fishing group Profand, according to Parte de Pesca.

In 2014, Alpesca went into bankruptcy, declaring its public utility assets subject to expropriation, according to sources. The provincial government of Chubut retained the assets and leased them to the Argentine subsidiary of the American company Red Chamber.

Alpesca's assets include a processing plant, employing 400 people, along with seven national fishing permits and five provincial fishing permits, according to sources. "That is why it is so highly sought after," one source observed.

The current Chubut administration plans to terminate that contract, and one of the interested parties is the Spanish company Profand, sources told Undercurrent.

Parte de Pesca reported that RCA also presented a letter from the Chubut Food Industry Workers' Union (STIA), which expressed workers' concern over rumors that the plant's operation might be handed over to another firm. 

STIA general secretary Luis Nunez told Alpesca's employees in an assembly that Arbeletche had informed him the government is negotiating a new contract with Profand, rather than renewing RCA's lease, reported Parte de Pesca.

Gustavo Gonzalez, representative of the chamber of Chubut province's "yellow fleet" (CAFACh) -- primarily focused on shrimp and hake and fishing out of Puerto Rawson -- recently claimed on Facebook that "Red Chamber has done a lot of harm to the sector and doesn't respect agreements." He also claimed that Red Chamber's contract with the province of Chubut has already expired.

Gustavo Gonzalez. Photo: CAFACh on Facebook.

"They have special licenses, freezer permits, and a super-low lease... and yet they still don't comply with anything," Gonzalez said. Regarding the future of the former Alpesca plant, Gonzalez noted that there are already companies interested in taking over the plant, with significant investment plans that could generate employment and foster productive development in the province of Chubut.

He added that the provincial government should ensure that the operation of the former Alpesca plant is carried out under conditions that respect both workers and commitments to suppliers and the local community, claiming repeated breaches by Red Chamber.

While the companies' administration has issued no official confirmation and there is no clarity on ongoing negotiations between the Chubut government and RCA or other interested parties, rumours that Profand is the chosen successor for Alpesca's assets are fueling industry speculation.

Profand declined to comment to Undercurrent, while Red Chamber did not reply to requests for comment ahead of publication.

title: Wildlife deaths at Tassal salmon farm sparks calls for industry overhaul
content:
The deaths of a protected fur seal and 15 cormorants at Tassal's West of Wedge salmon farm on Tasmania's Tasman Peninsula in Australia have sparked renewed calls for a full review of the salmon industry and its environmental oversight, reports ABC News.

According to documents released under right to information, the seal died on June 13 after being hit with two sedative darts during an attempted removal.

It "was not noted to resurface after this… it was found to be dead at the bottom of the pen." A necropsy was inconclusive but noted "significant lung damage."

Just days later, 15 cormorants were also found dead at the same site. 10 drowned in the pen, while five were entangled in a splash fence.

The documents state that it is assumed the birds "drowned due to lack of access to [an] escape ramp." The netted walkway had prevented them from escaping after feeding.

Independent MP Peter George said the review promised by the state government must "look into all elements of this industry."

"If it doesn't cover all those areas, that will not be a proper investigation… I would reject it," he said.

"We're not confident that the government will look at these regulatory issues. That is why the Greens are working very, very hard to make sure that it is a tight review," Greens leader Rosalie Woodruff added. 

Tassal said it had made "upgrades to marine infrastructure" and is "continuing to invest in new innovations and equipment to keep wildlife and our people safe," but did not answer questions about bird nets or specific actions taken since the incidents.
