title: US wholesalers Southwind, Beaver Street join Walmart in recalling BMS shrimp over radiation concerns
content:
Southwind Foods and Beaver Street Fisheries (BSF), two large US seafood importers and wholesalers, announced this week that they are also recalling shrimp products from Indonesian exporter Bahari Makmur Sejati (BMS) over concerns about radiation contamination.

The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) stopped imports of BMS raw frozen shrimp last week after finding the radioactive isotope Cesium-137 (Cs-137). The federal agency also notified consumers that Walmart, the US' largest retail superstore with nearly 4,600 locations, had ordered a recall of products sold under its Great Value brand, as reported by Undercurrent News.

The story has gained national attention after first being reported by Undercurrent, with most major daily newspapers and national news services focused on the Walmart recall. 

FREE READ Catch the Current episode 31: Did anyone have ‘radioactive shrimp’ on their 2025 Bingo card?

Carson, California-based Southwind, which trades as Great American Seafood Imports, lists 13 different products on a website-posted recall notice, including under the brands Sand Bar, Arctic Shores, Best Yet, Great American and First Street.

The shrimp products in question were distributed to retailers in the states of Alabama, Arizona, California, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Utah, Virginia and Washington between July 17 and Aug. 8, 2025, the company said.

Southwind is one of the US' largest seafood wholesalers and growing. CEO Sam Galletti told Undercurrent in January 2024 that his company was aiming to get past $600 million in turnover and 120 million pounds of product volume by the end of the year.

The company opened a new 40,000 square foot state-of-the-art skin-pack processing and distribution facility in Salt Lake City, Utah, in September 2024, creating 35 new jobs and investing $30 million in the local economy, as also reported by Undercurrent.

"We are acting in accordance to FDA guidance and our commitment to always delivering the highest level of integrity and consumer assurance for the products and brands we sell," Galletti told Undercurrent via email. "We feel that these actions actually build consumer confidence."

"We did not pack this product in any of our US-owned and operated facilities," he continued. "In this case we are part of a complex supply chain. We have a responsibility that requires transparency to consumers. We take this very seriously."

BSF is Walmart supplier

BSF, which is based in Jacksonville, Florida, lists just one product in its recall notice: Great Value brand frozen raw shrimp EZ-peel & deveined tail-on 21-25 per lb.

The product was distributed to Walmart stores in the states of Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Missouri, Mississippi, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Texas and West Virginia between July 28 and Aug. 7, 2025, the company said. 

The Great Value brand is solely distributed by Walmart. While the retail giant owns and markets the private label products, the products themselves are manufactured and packaged by different companies. Beaver Street appears to be at least one of the suppliers of Walmart's Great Value brand frozen shrimp in the 21-25 per lb size in the states mentioned above.

BSF, which does around $800m in revenue and is targeting $1.5b from acquisitions and organic expansion, also markets the Sea Best brand of seafood products in the US. Those products are not impacted by the recall. 

Undercurrent reached out to BSF executive vice president and co-owner Mark Frisch for comment but he could not be reached at presstime.

Scary references

The FDA notice, published Thursday (Aug. 21), states that there have been no illnesses reported to date and that an active investigation into the Cs-137 contamination is underway. 

"Traces of Cs-137 are widespread and can be present in the environment at background levels, and at higher levels in water or foods grown, raised, or produced in areas with environmental contamination," the update explains.

"The primary health effect of concern following longer-term, repeated low-dose exposure (e.g., through consumption of contaminated food or water over time) is an elevated risk of cancer, resulting from damage to DNA within living cells of the body."

While the FDA's import alert gave the example of Cs-137 contamination occurring from accidents such as "Chernobyl in 1986 and Fukushima in 2011," it does not explain how the Indonesian company's shrimp would come to be contaminated in such a way.

FDA intensified focus on Indonesia months before issuing radioactive shrimp alert

However, the industry maintains that the issue did not originate with the shrimp, but rather "stems from external factors beyond the industry's control," as Andi Tamsil, general chairman of the Shrimp Club Indonesia, told news site Tempo.

Notices released by the US government state that containers at four different ports were stopped for the detection of levels of Cs-137. At least one sample collected from breaded shrimp tested positive for Cs-137, as reported by Undercurrent.

Contact the author amanda.buckle@undercurrentnews.com

title: Catch the Current episode 31: Did anyone have ‘radioactive shrimp’ on their 2025 Bingo card?
content:
Seafood made its way into the mainstream US news this week -- and not for a great reason.

An import alert from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) that banned shrimp products from major Indonesian exporter Bahari Makmur Sejati (BMS) for potential radiation contamination exploded as the FDA urged retail giant Walmart to recall its Great Value Brand shrimp.

What is Cesium-137 (Cs-137)? How did the shrimp get contaminated? Catch the Current hosts Amanda Buckle and Lorin Castiglione are joined by Undercurrent News editorial director Cliff White and UCN price analyst Gary Morrison as we answer questions and share some insights on how this radioactive shrimp fiasco will impact the market.

And, of course, it wouldn't be an episode without our weekly update on tariffs and the US trade war.

Plus, Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA) editor Neil Ramsden calls in from Trondheim, Norway, where he's reporting live from Aqua Nor 2025. Also, Lorin and Amanda talk about Cracker Barrel's new seafood menu item. 

Thank you to our sponsor: Wisefish.

Listen now on YouTube!

Subscribe now! Catch the Current is available on YouTube, Spotify, Amazon Music, iHeartRadio, Pandora, and other major podcast streaming platforms. Don't see Catch the Current on your favorite app? Reach out to podcasts@undercurrentnews.com.

Don't have time to listen? Find a full transcript of season 1, episode 31 of Catch the Current below:

Amanda Buckle (AB): You’re listening to Catch the Current, the coolest seafood podcast out there, from the team at Undercurrent News, your trusted source for seafood prices, news and data. I’m Amanda Buckle.

Lorin Castiglione (LC): And I’m Lorin Castiglione.

AB: Before we dive in, a quick shoutout to our sponsor Wisefish. With over 30 years in the seafood industry, they’re powering aquaculture, fisheries, processors and seafood sales with one integrated platform that makes managing complex operations simpler. Check them out at wisefish.com/catch-the-current.

Lorin, I don't know if you know this about me but I'm a pretty big Bingo player. I take my 91-year-old grandma out with me and we have a great time. 

But I got to tell you, what happened this week was not on my 2025 Bingo card.

LC: It has got to be the radioactive shrimp.

AB: The radioactive shrimp.

Major Indonesian exporter BMS banned from US over radioactive shrimp

It took me some time to wrap my head around the original import alert that the US Food and Drug Administration, the FDA, released because it was a first-of-its-kind alert. We've been in the seafood industry, Lorin, for eight years now, and I've never seen anything like this.

LC: We keep getting one-upped, but this will be pretty tough to beat.

A lot is still unfolding, but we're breaking down everything we know so far -- including this import alert, 99-51.

AB: Yes, so 99-51 was published on Aug. 14, and is described as "detention without physical examination of human food products that appear to have been prepared, packed or held under insanitary conditions resulting in chemical contamination."

I talked to sources who explained that this alert, 99-51, was created specifically for the issue encountered with major Indonesian seafood processor Bahari Makmur Sejati, also known as BMS. The problem is listed as Cesium-137, or Cs-137. And the example that the FDA gives in its alert for Cs-137 is that elevated amounts can be present at locations where contamination settled from accidents such as Chernobyl in 1986 and Fukushima in 2011.

Those are two events that you do not want to see in an import alert.

LC: Have you watched the "Chernobyl" show?

AB: That was a great show.

LC: I couldn't even finish it because it scared me.

AB: It was super scary.

LC: I'm having some PTSD here.

But we're talking about Indonesian shrimp -- grown in ponds in Indonesia and nowhere near nuclear events that occurred, like Chernobyl and Fukushima.

So, how is this shrimp getting contaminated?

Well, let's start with talking a little bit more about Cs-137. It's a radioisotope created via nuclear reactions. But while it generally occurs in nuclear power plants, the FDA also notes that it is "commonly used in medical and other industrial applications."

Exposure to Cs-137 can be harmful to the body, even in low doses spread out over a period of time. High doses can lead to acute radiation syndrome. The FDA says that the primary concern, though, is cancer 

The import alert goes on to state that the FDA considers the totality of the circumstances, on a case-by-case basis, to determine whether a food appears to have been prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby it has become contaminated with a chemical contaminant that may have rendered it injurious to health. 

And the FDA ultimately decided to add BMS to its red list, meaning all of its products are subject to detention without physical examination.

Walmart caught up in FDA alert over BMS shrimp due to radiation concerns

AB: One source I talked to early this week said that they anticipate this ban of products from BMS to be a big hit for retail, as its the largest supplier of easy-peel shrimp to the US.

Before I could even report that, news broke that the FDA was urging Walmart -- a huge player in the grocery game with nearly 4,600 locations -- to recall three different lots of products that include frozen raw shrimp from BMS and sold under its "Great Value" brand. So yes, big hit for retail indeed. 

LC: Joining us now on the pod to talk more about the potential impact on the market is Undercurrent News editorial director Cliff White and UCN price analyst Gary Morrison.

Gary, this first question is for you. Tell us a little bit about Indonesia in general as a player in the US shrimp market. 

Gary Morrison (GM): Well, Lorin, they're a pretty important player. Indonesia is the third largest source country of shrimp imports into the United States. They sent nearly 300 million pounds, valued at $1.1 billion, to the US in 2024.

Over the last 10 years, they've averaged roughly 19% market share of US shrimp imports. So I know I said they were the number three source country. They were number two for a long time, up until about 2021 when Ecuador overtook them, so a pretty important trade partner with the US.

From the Indonesian producer perspective, the US market is the most important. It is the largest market for Indonesian exports for shrimp. But the key issue with this new development for the Indonesian shrimp industry, as a whole, is it's very consolidated with the top four companies in that country, with BMS right there at the top, accounting for around 60% of the trade with the United States. So you're taking out a pretty big player, the number one player with a 60% market share.

And it's not only the company, right, but the specific products and forms that are coming here.

It's increasingly black tiger shrimp. And for vannamei, it's forms like easy peel, which we mentioned earlier in the pod, BMS being the top provider of this type of shrimp to the US. And cooked that dominates the trade. And these types of shrimp have been already tough to replace.

Imported Indonesian shrimp in a Safeway grocery store in Silver Spring, Maryland, in March 2025. Photograph by Jason Huffman.

So this is going to make it even more difficult. In response to the news this week, US wholesale prices reacted with significant gains in these types of shrimp. And these factors point to a continued firm market.

So it's going to be a challenging time, especially for retailers that look for easy peel shrimp as one of their top products.

LC: I was just going to say, it sounds like there's going to be a big shakeup in the shrimp markets because of this.

GM: Yeah, obviously there's a lot of things going on. It's going to impact what companies can do business right now in the US, and can some of these other companies in Indonesia fill that void when they're already trading with the US in great quantities?

So the other three out of the other four top countries are already significant players here. Do they have enough product with their other trade to make up that shortfall?

AB: And another thing I feel like you have to factor into all this, too, is the tariffs. Cliff, you're our tariff guy, updating the blog almost every day for us. Indonesia was on the lower end of the tariff side from Trump's hits, correct?

Cliff White (CW): It's about in the middle. I think it's 19%. Gary can correct me on that. But yeah, I would say it's it's about average, slightly higher than Ecuador at 15% and slightly lower than some of the other Asian countries at 20%.

So not nothing but not egregious. Well, some exporters may say it's all egregious, but yeah, it's right in the middle.

Ecuador captures 40% of EU shrimp market volume as H1 imports surge

AB: If Indonesia is now losing this market, directing people potentially towards these other markets that even have lower tariffs, they could potentially be losing.

GM: I mean, it's going to be tough, right, Amanda? I mean, the tariffs are one thing, but it's really the product form.

So Ecuador, which has that really big advantage over Indonesia, typically does not produce easy peel or cooked, and they don't produce black tiger. So they're going to have to go to some other Asian source countries, which may be right around that tariff rate.

CW: There's so much stuff shifting around across the world of seafood. Shrimp is really interesting to follow from a journalistic perspective. There are so many countries that produce it and they're all now at different or slightly different tariff rates.

They also have -- you're talking about anti-dumping duties, countervailing duties. Each of these countries has different product specializations. You've got wild shrimp, also an interesting alternative for buyers.

You've got black tiger shrimp versus vannamei. I'm jealous that Gary gets to follow so closely because it's so interesting once you get into the world of seafood to follow what's going to be happening over the next six months to two years to see how trade flows change because of these tariffs. I agree with you.

AB: It's extremely interesting. And then when you add radioactive into the mix.

FDA intensified focus on Indonesia months before issuing radioactive shrimp alert

CW: Amanda, you're positively glowing right now.

AB: I want to get down to it ...How did this shrimp get contaminated? Because that's the real question here. And I can tell you with certainty that an investigation is underway. An advisory that was released a few days ago after the import alert states that the FDA is actively investigating reports of CS-137 contamination in frozen shrimp products processed by BMS, as well as shipping containers.

And this isn't like a one container, one location type of thing. Gary, you're always looking at where all these ports are.... this is impacting four ports. Shipping containers at four US ports -- Los Angeles, Houston, Savannah and Miami. 

GM: So, I mean, the producers that I talk to, obviously they're awaiting this investigation pretty closely because they're saying that the containers where they started weren't washed correctly.

That's their story. And obviously they're holding out for a positive investigation on their end because they just have no idea how this radioactive substance was found because it wasn't anywhere near where they source, where they farm and produce, or they process the shrimp.

AB: Again, I want to reiterate that the investigation is active. What we do know right now is that the FDA did collect multiple samples. And one of the interesting things to know is that they confirmed the presence of CS-137 in one sample of breaded shrimp.

But again, it was just one sample. They didn't detect it in the other products tested. But the FDA said they cannot rule out contamination because of that. So it could, like Gary said, it could be a container issue.

What the government agency did confirm is that all containers and products testing positive or alerting for Cs-137 have been denied entry into the country. Of course, that didn't stop the FDA from urging Walmart to issue a recall. The FDA says that it learned that Walmart received implicated raw frozen shrimp, imported after the date of first detection of Cs-137 by CBP, but from shipments that did not alert for Cs-137. That's why the FDA recommended Walmart recall the shrimp.

And just to reiterate, it's not all shrimp at Walmart. Just certain lots in certain states. So check the show notes for those details.

------

--------

LC: Amanda, where do we go from radioactive shrimp? 

AB: Tariffs! If there is anything that could beat radioactive shrimp, it's Trump and his tariffs.

So Cliff, there was some tariff breaking news right before we went on to record this. So what is the latest there?

CW: The US and European Union put out a joint statement on Thursday morning, and high up in the statement is a mention of seafood. Seafood, according to this agreement, which is not formalized, but is in the process of being formalized, will have to go through a vote of the European Parliament. But if that happens, under the dictates of this agreement, all US seafood will go to the EU tariff-free starting Sept. 1.

Trade deal surprise: EU to eliminate tariffs on US seafood, including processed lobster

I don't think this agreement will be finalized by that time, but will be retroactive to Sept. 1. So US exporters suddenly have a much better angle to get their products into the EU, as there were many types of US seafood that previously faced tariffs going to Europe.

GM: Yeah, I think that Cliff is right. I think the access becomes better, right? And I think pollock and lobster are the two largest exports to the European Union as a whole.

So at least from the lobster market, I can talk. Canada has been shipping live to the EU under recent agreements. But the people that I talked to indicate that we may see more live lobster coming to the US now for processing, which would allow frozen tails and meat to head over to Europe untariffed.

So, still a developing story, but certainly better access with no tariffs is a positive sign and welcomed by those in the industry.

AB: Thanks, Cliff. Thanks, Gary. More on the latest tariff news in the show notes.

Cliff, before you go, last week we had Gary on, and he sorely disappointed us with his tale of how he incorporated seafood -- or rather failed -- to incorporate seafood into his family vacation to Croatia.

Cliff, please tell us you've come back from Scotland with tales of juicy langostinos and salmon.

CW: Yeah, I didn't need to eat any US seafood in Scotland. I ate all the local stuff there. Scotland is, I think, an underrated seafood mecca. I feasted there.

So I had, obviously, farmed salmon. Local farmed salmon. It's cool, they mention the locality where the salmon is farmed on a lot of menus there, which you don't see in the US. Kind of neat. Had some delicious oysters, mussels, crab. The local crab there's really good.

But my super all-time new favorite seafood is langoustino. Langoustino. Langoustines? Langoustines.

They're like little mini lobsters. They're also called Norway lobsters. They kind of look like mutated crawfish. They're so delicious. Oh, my gosh. I don't know if we could get some here in the US. I think that's probably blasphemy living in Maine to think about that.

But yeah, I would totally buy those things whenever I could. They're so delicious.

AB: I'm pretty sure Lorin and I had langoustinos on a Red Lobster pizza once.

LC: Yes, we did.

AB: That's one of the reasons why I love the Boston seafood show. Scotland usually has this really nice setup booth. Actually, maybe it was Barcelona. A couple of years ago I feasted and I was able to eat some of the langoustines. And man, they were delicious.

CW: I have seen those at trade shows for a decade, but never somehow managed to eat any of them. So needless to say, there was much anticipation ordering these things.

And I thought they were pretty good value, actually. I mean, especially compared to like European lobster, like Scottish lobsters, like 40 euros at least. So we got six of them for like 30 euros.

And they're a lot of work. I won't deny ... there was a lot of anticipation as we were cracking into these things, but it was so worth it. Really good.

AB: I think I know why you never had a chance to try these at those trade shows. It's because if you probably look at Lorin and I's output compared to Cliff's story output. How come Cliff submitted 50 stories? And Amanda and Lorin over here, snapping pictures of every piece of food we eat.

LC: We have a social aspect...

GM: You guys are just taking pictures and matching outfits. Oh, that's fine.

AB: Hey!

LC: How dare you.

Yes, Gary, we do love a matching outfit.

CW: The seafood from Scotland assignment fills very quickly on the spreadsheet. There's a lot of competition to get into that seafood from Scotland booth. So maybe I'll have to be on it earlier next year.

AB: All right. This week, we have one more special guest joining us under current EMEA editor Neil Ramsden. But before Neil joins us, Lorin, Gary, any final market thoughts?

LC: So I'll give an update on scallops. I haven't done that in a while.

Scallops are trending smaller as we move into fall. Most of the fleet is focused on closed areas one and two.

Closed area one is shutting down mid-November. We see that every year. Not uncommon.

Area one is coming out of spawn. Some of the landings are still showing that milky condition, but that's been waning.

As waters get colder, the scallops shrink, which means that there'll be more 10-20s, 20-30 meats in the market.

Large scallops are still hard to come by and continue to command firm premiums. In New Bedford, landings rebounded in week 33 to just over 330,000 lbs worth nearly $6m.

Dock prices eased slightly. And we're also seeing the price gap between 10-20s and 20-30s narrow as buyers lean more heavily on mid-range meats.

In the wholesale market, despite the docks' softer raw values, wholesale prices are holding firm, especially in week 34, which we're in.

Scarcity in large counts and steady food service demand continue to underpin the market.

Normally, importers lean heavily on Japanese scallops when US supply tightens, but it doesn't look like that's able to happen this year. Japanese product is already expensive due to weaker harvests, high domestic processing costs and unfavorable exchange rates. And then you add on that 15% US tariff, and it effectively prices out many US buyers.

So importers are delaying contracts, leaving the US with fewer alternatives to fill that gap.

US wholesale: Scallop market tilts smaller as dock prices ease, tariffs complicate trade

Census data from the Undercurrent News trade portal shows US scallop imports have been declining month over month since February. So looking ahead, the fishery is still expected to exceed early projections for the 2025-2026 season.

There was a surprise boom out of Nantucket Lightship West back in May that gave the season a little bit of a lift. But that seems like a one-off event unless we see some major storm like we're, you know, kind of in the middle of right now, uncover hidden beds. But no one's expecting another surge like we saw back in May.

Framework 39 originally set the harvest cap at 19.75m lbs.

But once you back out observer and research set asides, that leaves it closer to 18m for the limited access fleet. So overall, more smaller scallops, fewer larger scallops. Japanese imports are kind of off the table at this point, and a domestic fishery that's on pace to beat expectations, but it still feels tight and unpredictable heading into the autumn season.

AB: Lorin's analysis can be found in our show notes.

Gary, any final market thoughts?

GM: You know, nothing on the market. It just seems that each week the seafood industry is dealing with something outside of what they can control. So it's really good to have a team like Undercurrent behind you to keep up to date on what's going on so companies can stay informed and agile.

AB: Joining us now is Undercurrent EMEA editor Neil Ramsden, who's calling us from Trondheim, Norway, for aquaculture technology event Aqua Nor 2025. This event runs from Aug. 19 to 21, so we're catching you after a very long day, Neil.

But for those who aren't familiar with Aqua Nor, tell us a little bit about this event.

Neil Ramsden (NR): Yeah, so it's Norway and I'm tempted to say the world's biggest trade fair and conference for all things aquaculture technology, basically. And it's feeling pretty international this year.

I've been speaking to a delegation from New Zealand. There's Canadians, Chileans. I've not done this event for a few years now, and it was a lot more international this time than it was last time.

AB: Oh, well, it's really interesting. I love when you get to cover an event for multiple years in a row and you can see how it evolves. You can't ignore all the global things happening right now.

One of your latest posts is about how the US tariffs are impacting New Zealand businesses. Were tariffs top of mind at the event? What was the big topic that everyone was talking about this year?

FREE READ Aqua Nor 2025 day three recap: Genetics giant poised for salmon gene editing approval; Stingray plans second plant

NR: The thing that's affecting more or less everybody at Aqua Nor, I think, it's pretty Norway- centric, really.

The Norwegian government has brought in new salmon farming regulations. And I'm sure I'm just scratching the surface of what is going on. But under the new regulations, I think salmon farmers are basically gearing up to really increase the precision and monitoring of what they do.

I'm sure it hasn't felt especially to them like oversight has been relaxed in recent years, but it's going to require the farmers to pay even more attention to really full data collection and then using that data to prove full compliance to the new regulations.

I spoke to one M&A expert today who suggested that that's going to mean more capital expenditure upfront at the start of each salmon farming cycle on just technology to monitor. But then if it's done right, that should mean lower operating expenditure throughout the cycle and at the end of it. But because of that, we've seen a few businesses at the event focused on really the digital side of aquaculture.

So monitoring what happens in the pens and kind of real-time feeding that information back. I think that's that's looking like the direction that things are going to move even more towards is more data, probably more AI to parse that data.

The Norwegian government is also looking to bring mortalities down to under 5%, which means that understanding fish health and then tools and initiatives to look at fish health and help them stay healthy are probably going to get more attention and funding than ever.

AB: Wow. So this seems like it was event full of all good things. There's no concerns about where this funding is coming from? Or if businesses can keep up?

NR: Well, obviously, the Norwegian salmon farmers have received new taxes just in recent years. But the fact that they would maybe dispute with me is they still maintain pretty healthy profits every quarter at this point. So of all of the global aquaculture sectors, they're the ones that can really afford to kind of look into this sort of innovation and moving into the digital space.

In a decade, perhaps, this could be filtering down to shrimp aquaculture and that sort of thing. The guys that maybe don't have so much money to throw at it at the moment. 

AB: Be sure to check out Neil's live blogging from the event, Aqua Nor 2025, right at the top of our website.

Thanks, Neil, for joining us and safe travels home.

NR: Thank you very much.

AB: Before we go, I've got one more story to talk about that made national headlines this week, and that's Cracker Barrel.

The Lebanon, Tennessee-headquartered restaurant chain, which has over 650 locations across the US, has been struggling in recent years and this week unveiled a new logo to go along with its new fall menu.

FREE READ Cracker Barrel brings catfish back for breakfast

The logo's getting mixed results from fans. Lorin, have you seen it?

LC: I have not.

AB: So Lorin hasn't seen it.

LC: I'm Googling right now.

AB: So I'll explain it because you should look it up. They got rid of the barrel.

LC: The guy in the chair next to the barrel. They just modernized it a little bit. Yeah.

AB: People are upset about it. Honestly, I don't really care.

Have you ever been to a Cracker Barrel?

LC: I have not.

AB: Oh, my gosh. Well, I have been and there is one in New Jersey. And I feel like...

LC: There is? 

AB: Yes. But I feel like you can't go to it. I feel like it can only be a thing you go to in the southern states. I've only gone to it whenever I've been driving south.

So I went to it a couple of times on my way to Tennessee. I've stopped at different ones and they're fun. They're great. They have little games inside for the kids to play.

I've ate there with my parents back in the day. But why it matters to us is that Cracker Barrel has quite a few seafood offerings on its lunch and dinner menu, from shrimp to cod, catfish and rainbow trout. But with the return of "Uncle Herschel's Favorite" to its fall breakfast menu, it's getting seafood back at breakfast, which is really cool.

Seafood traditionally hasn't stood as an American breakfast staple, although smoked salmon and crab and eggs. Shrimp and grits. Oysters and grits.

Cracker Barrel's fried catfish fillets are now available as a morning breakfast meat side. Photo Credit: Cracker Barrel

But catfish at breakfast, not really your normal choice. Except for supposedly in the south.

And that's kind of what inspired Cracker Barrel to bring it back. It's in line with what Cracker Barrel chief marketing officer Sarah Moore said that the restaurant "aims to deliver the country nostalgia experience while leaning into seasonal flavors." So they want the country nostalgia experience, but all the while updating a logo.

LC: Right, but taking it out of the logo.

AB: But again, we're all for adding ... there's already seafood on breakfast menus, but it's cool to add catfish. I'd be interested in it. We'll do a road trip. Like I said, it's not like a real Cracker Barrel experience if you're not eating in the south, but I'll take you to one in New Jersey, Lorin.

LC: All right. That's awesome. You're very good at these last-minute stories where I'm like, where is she going with this? And then you tie it all into seafood.

AB: Just hop on the train. You'll always enjoy the ride. I promise.

LC: I'm always pleasantly surprised. So that does it for us this week. For links to stories and more information, visit the show notes

title: Untitled
content:
Chaohu Daxin Foodstuffs, a Chinese processor of crawfish and other seafood as well as several agricultural goods, has been issued a warning letter by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for adulterated ready-to-eat cooked crawfish products.

The warning letter, dated Feb. 3, 2025, was published by the FDA on Tuesday (Aug. 19). Per the notice, the FDA inspected Chaohu Daxin Foodstuffs' facility in Zhegao Town, Chaohu, in the province of Anhui, in July 2024 and found "serious violations of the seafood Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) regulation."

The company responded to the FDA with descriptions of its corrective actions; however, the US agency determined its response was inadequate.

Looking at specific violations, the FDA noted that the monitoring process for ensuring appropriate temperature was inadequate, as it did not include "continuous monitoring of cooking temperature, belt speed after any adjustments, and measurement of crawfish after every raw material lot change." Further, the conveyor belt speed recorded during the cooking process was "not consistent with the speed and time values listed in the HACCP plan."

FDA advised the company: "Your firm should validate your cook process to ensure the cook time and temperature are adequate to control pathogens such as Listeria monocytogenes."

Chaohu Daxin Foodstuffs must address the deviations noted by the FDA or risk being placed on detention without physical examination.

title: Clearwater vessel accused of harvesting scallops in closed Canadian zone
content:
Officers with Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) on Wednesday (Aug. 12) boarded a scallop fishing vessel owned by Clearwater Seafoods, Canada's largest shellfish company, after it was detected harvesting in a closed zone, DFO said in a statement published Friday (Aug. 15) on its Facebook page.

They arrested one individual and seized about 22,000 kilograms (49,795 pounds) of scallop meat valued at about CAD 1 million ($724,000), according to the post.

The 43-meter vessel, known as the Atlantic Protector, was spotted inside Scallop Fishing Area 29D, off the southwest coast of Nova Scotia, by officers in DFO's Barrington, Nova Scotia, barracks using a vessel monitoring system, according to the statement. The area is known for producing premium-quality scallops, CBC News reported.

DFO said its team visually confirmed the activity, offloaded shucked scallops in Shelburne, and returned the live, unshucked scallops to the ocean. DFO said the investigation is ongoing. 

Clearwater's website boasts that the Atlantic Protector can shuck and dry-freeze scallops within an hour of being caught.

Clearwater said in a statement to CBC that it's committed to sustainable and legal fishing. The company said the vessel's captain was accused of being "just over the boundary for a short time" and that it was conducting its own investigation.

title: Untitled
content:
Ecuador may have received one of the lowest tariff rates delivered by president Donald Trump to the US' largest shrimp source nations but its exporters are still bracing for steep financial losses, advises Ecuador's National Chamber of Aquaculture (CNA).

Starting Thursday (Aug. 7), Ecuadorian shrimp have been saddled with a 15% tariff, an amount that's higher than the 10% generalized rate most countries have been carrying since early April and much more than the duty-free status maintained for years by Ecuador.

Still, that's better than the new 19% tariff slapped on Indonesian shrimp per a trade deal, the 20% tariff confronting Vietnamese shrimp via another trade deal, or the punitive 25% rate applied to Indian shrimp, an amount that is expected to double on Aug. 27.

Indian shrimp already among seafood’s biggest casualties of Trump trade war

For this reason, Ecuador is considered one of the winners in the US tariff scenario compared to its competitors. 

India, Ecuador, Indonesia and Vietnam, in that order, are the US' four largest suppliers of shrimp. In 2024, Ecuador shipped 412 million pounds of shrimp worth $1.28 billion to the US, according to CNA.

The graph below, from Undercurrent News' trade portal, illustrates the increase in Ecuadorian frozen shrimp exports to the US between 2019 and April 2025.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view

The US is still importing a lot of Ecuadorian shrimp.

CNA pointed out that in the first half of 2025 alone, exports to the US reached 296m lbs, valued at $867m. The Ecuadorian industry has already paid $45m in tariffs this year, according to the industry association. 

"With the tariff increase announced by the Trump administration, $20m will be paid monthly in reciprocal tariffs this second half of the year, i.e., an additional $120m through December," said Jose Antonio Camposano, the CNA's executive president. "If the measure is maintained, the total cost to the shrimp sector in 2025 will reach $170m."

CNA pointed out that the impact of the new tariffs is compounded by an existing 3.78% countervailing duty imposed on Ecuadorian shrimp following a US investigation into alleged subsidies. Together, these charges bring the total tariff burden to 18.78% for Ecuadorian shrimp entering the US market, CNA pointed out.

Ecuadorian industry executives warned that the added costs threaten Ecuador's competitive position in the global shrimp trade and jeopardize more than 300,000 jobs linked to the sector.

The CNA urged the Ecuadorian government to prioritize negotiations for a trade agreement that restores favorable access to the US market.

title: Labor rights groups call for Wi-Fi to protect migrant fishers in Taiwan
content:
A coalition of labor rights groups, led by US-based advocacy organization Global Labor Justice, is renewing its push for mandatory Wi-Fi on Taiwan's distant-water fishing vessels.

The campaign comes amid mounting evidence of forced labor and abuse affecting migrant fishers, a stark contrast to industry claims that such incidents are isolated.

A recent CNN investigation uncovered harrowing accounts of exploitative practices onboard Taiwanese vessels, where fishers, mostly recruited from Indonesia, face long periods of isolation, debt bondage, and retaliation for reporting grievances.

Global Labor Justice, which champions workers' rights internationally, argues that constant connectivity is essential.

"Wi-Fi is not a luxury -- it's a bridge between rights on paper and rights in practice," said Valery Algaza, the group's deputy director. Without reliable access to the internet, fishers remain unable to contact their unions, verify wages, or alert authorities when abuses occur, she added.

Critics say that both the Fisheries Agency and industry associations have downplayed the severity of the allegations, ignoring systematic issues that have led to recurring deaths and injuries at sea.

Advocates now insist that the Taiwanese government enforce its own guidelines on Wi-Fi access and adopt comprehensive labor reforms.

"It's time to stop denying the problem and start protecting those who power the industry," added labor activist Lennon Wang.

title: Untitled
content:
Indonesian police have detained the co-founder of Indonesian aquaculture technology startup eFishery, reports Bloomberg.

At least $300 million of investors' money has been lost by the firm, whose former CEO, Gibran Huzaifah, faked a second set of accounts, bringing in several of the world's most high-profile venture players.

Former CEO of eFishery details 6-year accounts fakery

Huzaifah and two other former eFishery executives were detained on July 31, and remain in custody, the director of special economic crimes at the National Police's Criminal Investigation Agency confirmed to Bloomberg.

The three have been "officially named as suspects," according to the police, though it was unclear if any have been officially charged with wrongdoing.

Huzaifah's detention comes months after he gave the news site a detailed account of how he inflated revenue at a startup once valued north of $1 billion. The company, which deployed feeders to fish and shrimp farmers in Indonesia, incurred several hundred million dollars in losses between 2018 and 2024.

It began unraveling after a board investigation revealed the startup may have inflated its revenue and profit over several years.

Apart from Huzaifah, police detained and named two other suspects in the probe, Angga Hadrian Raditya and Andri Yadi. Both are former vice presidents and have been interviewed by internal investigators.

title: Big bird of prey at center of Chesapeake Bay menhaden controversy
content:
A regional regulatory panel could kill the big Atlantic menhaden fishery in the US Chesapeake Bay if it moves ahead with the measures aimed at protecting osprey recommended by conservation groups, Omega Protein, a division of Canadian seafood giant Cooke, is warning. 

The Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission's (ASFMC) Atlantic Menhaden Management Board (AMMB) will discuss the plight of the osprey on Thursday (Aug. 7), the last day of its three-day summer meeting in Arlington, Virginia. On the table are management proposals that include re-evaluating the current 51,000 metric ton cap on the reduction fishery to better protect the fish-eating bird known for its five-to-six foot wingspan. 

The proposals are courtesy of the Atlantic Menhaden Work Group (AMWG), which was established in 2024 by the ASMFC to evaluate potential actions for precautionary management in Chesapeake Bay. It has met nine times from September 2024 to April 2025 before presenting its recommendations to ASMFC in May.

Menhaden. Credit: NOAA photo library

AMWG also has recommended more monitoring of fishing activity in Chesapeake Bay with mandatory real-time reporting systems on all reduction vessels and catch reporting for both bait and reduction fisheries. 

Options for seasonal or area closures of the menhaden fishery should also be considered, the AMWG suggested.

Such measures are needed to save the osprey from starvation after it came back from its endangered species status in the 1970s, when pesticides like DDT almost wiped it out, a coalition of conservation groups and recreational harvesters has argued.

Other factors

But the restrictions being recommended could devastate the 150-year-old fishery counted on by several big companies and their employees, warns Peter Himchak, a senior scientific advisor for Omega Protein. His letter is included in the 500 pages of documents prepared for ASMFC's three-day meeting, half of which are related to the menhaden issue.

Omega Protein is a Reedville, Virginia-based processing company and a division of the Canadian seafood giant Cooke. It makes fishmeal and oil from menhaden, which it sources from Ocean Harvesters, a fishing company that operates in both the Chesapeake Bay and the Gulf of Mexico.

"While there is a tendency to look for easy answers, the likelihood is that there are a multitude of potential causes, as Geological Survey (USGS) osprey scientists recently pointed out," wrote Himchak, a former state fisheries biologist and long-time ASMFC advisor.

Ocean Harvesters catching menhaden in the Chesapeake Bay. Photo: Omega Protein

Factors like the documented population increase of bald eagles, which prey on osprey, as well as climate changes that might impact the timing of the osprey migrations, and the abundance of other forage species they rely on, must also be considered, noted Himchak.

"Rather than attempt to investigate the issue, the [precautionary management] group charged forward with draconian management recommendations without determining if there is or is not an adequate supply of menhaden to support predatory demand in the Bay," Himchak wrote.

"Neither Ocean Harvesters nor Omega Protein can survive without the current low level of access to the menhaden resource in the bay. There simply are not enough 'fishable days' -- that is, days where the weather and sea conditions allow vessels to operate -- in a year to safely conduct a profitable fishery solely in the ocean," Himchak stated.

The Atlantic menhaden fishery, known as a reduction fishery for fish oil production and also a bait fishery for the crab and lobster industries, has maintained average annual landings of 51,000 metric tons for the past five years, according to ASMFC. 

US Atlantic menhaden fishery heads to crucial showdown over osprey concerns

Current operations represent the lowest sustained harvest levels since the 1950s, and further limits would threaten jobs and profitability, Himchak wrote.

"The commission must be guided by science. Precipitous actions, taken in the name of precaution, are not always harmless," wrote Himchak.

He's proposed the ASMFC's technical committee consider four areas of investigation: whether osprey declines align with fishing activity in time and space; whether predators like striped bass or bald eagles are outcompeting ospreys; the impact of the rebounding bald eagle population on osprey, and whether factors like climate change and hypoxia might impair osprey foraging.

Information war heats up

The conservation groups and their allies are undaunted.

"The Chesapeake Bay is in crisis. This has been ongoing as menhaden stores have been grossly depleted after years of misregulation of the largest estuary on the continent," the Richmond (Virginia) Audubon Society wrote in a bluntly worded Aug. 1 letter to the ASMFC.

Although the osprey population has increased in recent years, conservation groups like the Audubon Society, the Chesapeake Bay Foundation (CBF) and the Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership, are concerned that menhaden harvests are falling and young osprey are starving to death in large numbers due to their more limited supply of the fish, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

"Ospreys have now reached an unsustainable level of breeding. There are no menhaden available to feed them or their offspring. Chicks are dead in the nests up and down the Chesapeake Bay," wrote Julie V. Kacmarcik, conservation chair for the Richmond Audubon Society.

"The trend is clear. Osprey will disappear from the bay if purse seine nets are not removed from the bay," Karmarcik wrote.

Osprey. Photograph by Andy Moffett.

Meanwhile, the CBF pointed to a survey by Bryan Watts of the College of William and Mary's Center for Conservation Biology, which documented a 90% decline of nesting osprey on Virginia's Delmarva Peninsula.

"Compared to historic accounts and benchmark surveys conducted during the 1970s and 1980s, the 2025 survey reveals a nearly complete collapse of the population," the CBC noted in a June 28 press release, adding the Watts survey concluded that "the most likely cause of the decline is prey."

Virginia is the only state along the Atlantic coast that still allows industrial menhaden reduction fishing in its state waters, with well over 100 million pounds of menhaden harvested annually by Ocean Harvests, the CBF also noted in its press release. 

However, the Menhaden Fisheries Coalition (MFC), a collective of commercial fishermen, related businesses and supporting industries along the Atlantic and gulf coasts of the US, took issue with that press release, saying it was riddled with misinformation.

For one thing, the MFC pointed out, the US Geological Survey (USGS), in a 2025 letter to Congress, said "adult Osprey capture a variety of fish species, and several studies have shown that Osprey diet composition differs in various regions of the Chesapeake."

"They identified both menhaden and striped bass, a species that has been overfished by recreational anglers for years, as possible primary prey types, and also cited Atlantic croaker, gizzard shad, and catfish as important osprey prey species," the MFC noted in its press release.

Getting Trump involved

The conservation groups opposed to the commercial harvest of menhaden have argued that Ocean Harvesters is owned by Cooke, a foreign company, which Cooke and Ocean Harvesters have vehemently denied, as reported by Undercurrent.

They've even gone so far as to launch a national campaign, urging US president Donald Trump to issue an executive order restricting foreign-controlled fleets from harvesting forage fish like menhaden, herring and mackerel, as reported by The Daily Signal, a conservative-oriented news service.

The campaign, titled "Make America Fish Again," calls on Trump to end reduction fishing of bait fish in US waters and set science-based catch targets to protect predator species. It was introduced this week at a virtual news conference with participants from Virginia, Maryland, Louisiana and other coastal states, according to the news service.

Opposition to the menhaden fishery already has had some luck in getting Trump's attention. In July they succeeded in getting the president to share a roughly 4.5-minute video on his Truth Social platform, building concerns that the US president might target the Canadian seafood giant, as reported by Undercurrent.

ASFMC's Aug. 7 meeting won't settle the matter. There will also be a public consultation process through September to allow further comment. Then, in October, the AMMB will vote on whether to accept or amend the proposed measures for the 2025-26 season.

title: Untitled
content:
A US commercial fisherman sentenced earlier this year for masterminding a failed bid to export crab out of Alaska in search of higher dock prices has now been ordered to pay more than $1.18 million in civil penalties for unrelated pollution violations.

Kodiak vessel owner Corey Potter was sentenced to federal prison in May and banned from fishing for two years for directing his son and another man to attempt to illegally export a harvest of golden crab despite knowing the risk of disease infecting the catch in 2024, as Undercurrent News reported.

Alaska crabber pleads guilty to illegally transporting catch

The US Coast Guard announced on Aug. 1 that an environmental enforcement case was filed on October 24, 2024, by the US Department of Justice on its behalf against Potter and his companies after authorities discovered unregistered oily bilge waste was routinely discharged from the engine room of the fishing tender Knot EZ in the Gulf of Alaska and Bering Sea.

That discovery was made when the Coast Guard responded to the vessel sinking in Kodiak Harbor in July 2022. Its subsequent investigation identified a pattern of illegal oil discharges and related violations throughout the summer fishing season. The Coast Guard said the vessel had been taken out of service and removed from the ocean.

Potter's three vessels are contracted with seafood buyers to supply the Bristol Bay fishing fleet and ferry seafood caught by smaller vessels to shoreside processing facilities. 

Potter had not responded to the charges detailed in court filings. That triggered the default judgment by US District Court judge Sharon Gleason in Alaska, who on July 30 ordered a fine of $1,182,265 to be levied.

"This enforcement action reinforces the importance of safety and pollution prevention measures within this fleet of fishing vessels," Captain Christopher Culpepper, Commander of the Coast Guard's Sector Western Alaska and US Arctic, said in a statement. "Commercial fishing vessel owners and operators must take care to operate safely and prevent oil discharges into our nation's waters."

A federal public defender assigned to represent Potter had asked for leniency, the Alaska Beacon reported. Potter, 64, "has been reduced to relying upon family for assistance and has no viable means to support himself," the online outlet reported.

title: China’s Joyvio awarded $298m in Chilean salmon farmer Australis acquisition dispute
content:
Chinese seafood giant Joyvio Food has won a $297.6 million international arbitration award against the former shareholders of Chilean salmon producer Australis Seafood, according to a regulatory filing released by the company.

The Santiago Arbitration and Mediation Center found that the former owners of Australis Seafood violated an equity acquisition agreement by failing to make "complete and accurate representations" about the company's status and "not disclosing key information related to environmental regulations." 

China’s Joyvio accused of using threats, false testimony in high-stakes Chilean legal battle

The Aug. 1 ruling orders the respondents to pay $217.2m in principal damages plus $80.4m in interest accrued since July 2019, with additional interest continuing to accumulate until full payment is made.

Having acquired Australis for $920m back in summer 2019, the compensation amounts to roughly one-third of what Joyvio paid for Australis. 

"Food Investment will quickly initiate recognition and enforcement procedures in multiple countries," Joyvio Food said in its filing. "We will spare no effort to advance the recognition and enforcement procedures in other countries, striving to obtain the final arbitration enforcement results in the shortest possible time."

The tribunal rejected the claimant's request to terminate the acquisition agreement and return the acquisition target, instead supporting the continuation of the agreement with compensation.

The award marks a major breakthrough for Joyvio, which launched proceedings against Australis’ former shareholders -- principally former majority shareholder Isidoro Quiroga -- back in April 2023. Over the following months and years, Joyvio would file lawsuits in the US and UK, where Quiroga and family members held assets.

Joyvio claimed it was deceived into buying Australis at an inflated price. The Beijing-based company had intended to grow annual production to over 100,000 metric tons, but these plans were scuppered by Chilean environmental rules

Joyvio accused Quiroga of withholding information regarding overproduction at Australis during the acquisition's due diligence phase. However, Quiroga insisted Joyvio was forced to knowingly "overproduce" after buying Australis due to its debt burden. 

TIMELINE: Joyvio-Quiroga Legal Battle

April 2023: Australis files criminal charges against former Australis Seafoods owner and director Isidoro Quiroga Moreno and four other former executives for "mismanagement" and other claims.

June 2023: Food Investment SpA files fraud charges against Quiroga and seven other former controlling shareholders, directors, and executives. Due to close factual connections, prosecutors combine both cases.

June 2023: Australis, Food Investment, and other Joyvio subsidiaries file civil lawsuit against Quiroga and other former executives in UK High Court of England and Wales.

July 2023: Australis and Food file for judicial assistance in Florida court to collect evidence related to the Chilean criminal cases given Quiroga's residency in the US state.

October 2023: Australis files supplementary charges, adding "illegal transactions" and "money laundering" to the mismanagement allegations.

June 2024: Food Investment files additional charges for "disclosure of false information to securities markets."

December 2024: UK High Court agrees to temporarily suspend proceedings, accepting Quiroga's forum non conveniens argument that Chile is the appropriate jurisdiction.

December 2024: UK High Court orders Joyvio to pay £1.2m (over $1.5m) to Quiroga and his family for legal expenses, marking Joyvio's "fourth defeat" according to Quiroga's representatives.

January 2025: Santiago criminal court approves prosecutor's investigation findings that implicate three defendants -- former shareholders, directors, and executives --in mismanagement and fraud crimes.

February 2025: Santiago court holds procedural rights hearing for defendants and orders prosecutors to regularly update case files and provide proper notification of witness summons.

February 2025: Florida court orders third parties to provide banking documents related to a "highly confidential agreement" between Quiroga and former Australis CEO that allegedly involved a $2.5m illegal payment.

title: Trump signs executive order to finalize 50% tariff on Brazil
content:
US president Donald Trump signed an executive order (EO) on Wednesday (July 30) ramping up the tariff on Brazilian goods to 50%, a rate that threatens to hit a few major seafood import items.

Trump cites "recent policies, practices, and actions by the government of Brazil that constitute an unusual and extraordinary threat to the national security, foreign policy, and economy of the United States" as the rationale for the increase.

"President Trump has successfully used tariffs in the past to advance America's interests and address other urgent national security threats and is doing so again today," the White House said in a press release accompanying the order.

Brazil is the US' 19th most valuable source of seafood, accounting for 39,188 metric tons worth $231.9 million in 2024, 27% more volume and 29% more value than in 2023. In particular, the new tariffs most threaten US imports of tilapia (10,119t worth $51.1m in 2024), red snapper (4,742t worth $42.1m in 2024) and rock lobster (827t worth $34.1m in 2024).

Trump first announced he would raise Brazil's tariff rate from 10% to 50% on July 9, citing the ongoing prosecution of the country's former president, Jair Bolsonaro, as one reason for the move, as Undercurrent News reported.

In his EO, Trump reiterated that justification and also claimed the Brazilian government has operated to the detriment of US social media companies operating in Brazil, requiring them to moderate posts. Trump said when they have refused, they have been threatened with prosecution and one had its assets frozen.

"President Trump is defending American companies from extortion, protecting American persons from political persecution, safeguarding American free speech from censorship, and saving the American economy from being subject to the arbitrary edicts of a tyrannical foreign judge," the EO said.

US domestic seafood producers look to piggyback on Trump Section 301 investigation of Brazil

The EO ostensibly references orders from Brazil's Supreme Court to block several social media accounts belonging to Bolsonaro's supporters as part of an ongoing investigation into the spread of disinformation in the country, the BBC has reported.

The EO cites Trump's authority under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), claiming it allows him to impose tariffs in response to a national emergency caused by a foreign power. The authority has been challenged by seven separate federal lawsuits, as Undercurrent has reported. If any of the lawsuits succeed, tariffs imposed by Trump under the IEEPA could be rendered invalid.

Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva said on July 24 that his government has been unsuccessful in trying to negotiate a lower tariff rate.

"We had already 10 meetings with the United States. On May 16, we sent them a letter asking for clarification on the proposals we had made. They didn't respond. They responded through a website," Lula said, referencing Trump's July 9 Truth Social post in which he initially declared the 50% tariff.

Brazilian World Trade Organization ambassador Philip Fox-Drummond Gough warned, on July 23, that WTO member states are witnessing "an extremely dangerous shift toward the use of tariffs as a tool to interfere in the domestic affairs of third countries," the Associated Press reported.

"Arbitrary tariffs, chaotically announced and implemented, are disrupting global value chains and risk throwing the world economy into a spiral of high prices and stagnation," Gough said.

title: Norwegian authorities probe new ISA case as outbreak numbers rise
content:
Norwegian authorities are investigating a suspected case of infectious salmon anemia (ISA) at a fish farm in northern Norway, adding to growing concerns as outbreaks rise across the country.

The Norwegian Food Safety Authority (Mattilsynet) reported on Monday (July 28) that seafood producer Holmoy Havbruk's site at Innerbrokloysa in Sortland municipality, Nordland county, showed positive PCR test results for the virus on July 25.

Nordlaks to cull 1.9m salmon after ISA outbreak

Authorities have imposed movement restrictions on the facility while awaiting confirmation from the Veterinary Institute. If confirmed, the site may face mandatory culling.

The facility already lies within a monitoring zone established for a previous ISA outbreak at the nearby Holand site.

This follows Nordlaks' culling of 1.9 million salmon (averaging 850 grams) at its Dragnes facility in June after samples tested positive on June 5.

Norway has recorded 14 confirmed ISA cases in 2025, with two additional farms under investigation. Most outbreaks are concentrated in Nordland and Troms regions, according to equity analyst Mindaugas Cekanavicius at Norne Securities, with this year's trajectory matching 2021 levels, when 36 cases were recorded.

title: EU court ruling pressures UK retailers over tuna FADs, say NGOs
content:
A European court ruling has intensified pressure on UK supermarkets to eliminate tuna caught using drifting fish aggregating devices (FADs) from their supply chains.

The General Court of the European Court of Justice ruled that the European Commission must review its decision to block measures protecting Indian Ocean tuna stocks from drifting FADs, following a challenge by NGOs Blue Marine Foundation and Bloom Association.

Princes exec: Customers not accepting FAD-caught tuna, even with MSC approval

The Commission must now reconsider measures including a proposed 72-day ban on drifting FADs in the Indian Ocean.

The judgment comes as conservation groups renew calls for UK retailers to stop selling tuna caught using the fishing method, which critics say contributes to overfishing and captures juvenile fish before they can breed.

Blue Marine's investigation found that while many UK supermarkets have banned drifting FAD-caught tuna in their own-label ranges, most continue to sell brand-name products sourced using the same methods. Major brands, including John West and Princes, source from fleets using drifting FADs in the Indian Ocean.

"UK supermarkets have been well aware of the harm caused by drifting FADs for years, evidenced by the fact that many have made public commitments to ban them in their own-label tuna. Yet, despite these promises, they continue to sell brand-name tuna caught using the same destructive methods," said Jess Rattle, head of investigations at Blue Marine Foundation

Research estimates that 1.41 million drifting FADs were deployed between 2007 and 2021. The EU-owned purse seine fleet alone catches 30% of the Indian Ocean's tuna using these devices.

Marks & Spencer emerged as the only major UK retailer ensuring all its canned tuna is sourced without drifting FADs across both own-label and third-party products.

title: Iceland sanctions processing equipment firm over alleged links to Russia
content:
Icelandic processing equipment supplier Velfag has been subjected to economic sanctions by the government over alleged links to Russian ownership.

Iceland's foreign minister, Thorgerdur Katrín Gunnarsdottir, confirmed the sanction process -- the first case of Icelanders facing a potential freezing of funds, she said.

News site RUV said that Velfag used to be owned by Russia's Norebo Holding, and that its new owner is still connected to Norebo's owners, the Orlov family.

Velfag itself said the business is 18% owned by its founders and 82% by Titania Trading Limited (TTL), "based in Hong Kong, which is fully owned by a Swiss investor."

"Norebo acquired a majority share in Velfag in 2022, prior to the conflicts and trade sanctions, but sold all its shares in the company in 2023 to TTL. Norebo has no current connection to the ownership, control, or operations of Velfag."

RUV said Norebo's Vitaly Orlov appeared to have transferred ownership of many of his companies to his son Nikita. The ownership was then transferred to a company in Hong Kong.

"In July, the company was registered to a banker and financial advisor from Liechtenstein living in Switzerland, Ivan Nicolai Kaufmann. He has previously worked with the Orlovs. The change of ownership was announced after the European Union announced in May that Norebo would be subject to trade sanctions," the news site wrote.

The Icelandic firm continues to cooperate with Icelandic authorities, it said. 

"The sanctions taken against the company have had a significant impact, despite the company having provided full transparency. The company will continue to fully cooperate with the authorities to resolve the matter and restore its reputation and strongly opposes being included in a case based on assumption or insufficient investigation."

CEO Trausti Arnason said the 30-year-old business has no current operations in Russia, and is based in Olafsfjordur and Kopavogur, with a development team in Akureyri, and a total of 33 employees.

Gunnarsdottir said Iceland's financial institutions make decisions on economic sanctions in consultation with the Central Bank and the Tax Authority. However, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs receives requests for exemptions, such as to ensure salary payments and maintain certain agreements. These are under review.

Earlier this year, the European Commission leveled sanctions on Norebo, the largest fishing firm in Russia, and Murman SeaFood, also a major player in cod and haddock. Both companies refute the allegations of espionage contained in the May 20 sanctions, the day they went into effect for payments to the Russians.

Norway has also followed suit in sanctioning the firms.

title: Untitled
content:
African fishers have been subjected to poor working conditions and withheld payments on European tuna fishing vessels, according to a new report by UK charity Blue Marine Foundation (BMF).

The report, "The hidden cost of tuna," claims to reveal how Senegalese and Ivorian crew members working on board European-owned tuna fishing boats operating in the Indian Ocean face discrimination, poor working conditions and delayed or withheld payments.

The investigation also contrasts the profitability of many of the European fishing companies with their seeming reluctance to pay crew members the minimum wage set by the International Labour Organization (ILO) as their base salary, said BMF.

Italian tuna giant Bolton focuses on human rights as it renews NGO partnerships

The publication of the report coincides with renewed negotiations between representatives of West African crew members and the European companies that employ them to work on board distant-water tuna purse seine vessels that catch the tuna sold in most UK supermarkets.

These negotiations are focused on updating an agreement between European fishing companies and unions representing Senegalese and Ivorian crew members that was signed in September 2023, and which was only meant to last for six months while negotiations continued, the NGO explained.

The agreement put in place a temporary minimum basic salary of "franc FCA" (the currency used across African countries) 250,000 per month -- approximately $414 -- far below the ILO minimum base wage for 2023 of $658 per month.

The report amplifies the first-hand accounts of discriminatory treatment faced by many West African crew members, both on board and on shore, it added. These issues were experienced to varying degrees on different vessels and ranged from insufficient medical care to unexplained dismissals, and from unfair employment terms to excessive working hours.  

"Our time spent working in Senegal and Cote d'Ivoire has revealed a troubling pattern of racism and discrimination experienced by many crew members working on board the European fishing vessels that supply the tuna that lines our shelves," said Jess Rattle, BMF head of investigation and co-author of the report.

"Some of these crew members gave decades of their lives to a fishing company before being let go without explanation, with others continuing to work gruelling hours at sea while still not being able to adequately provide for their families back home. We call on the fishing companies concerned to revise and improve the way in which their crew members are treated and have listed eight ways in which they can do so in our new report." 

The report also highlights how crew members' payslips were often written in multiple languages, were overly complex and contained opaque calculations and unexplained deductions, making it difficult to understand whether they were paid what they were owed, BMF said.

These experiences are contrasted by the report's financial analysis, which underscored the significant profits generated by several of the European tuna fishing companies.

The investigation found that the combined turnover of the companies analysed was more than €420 million ($493.3m) in 2023. In addition, several of them paid dividends to their shareholders in the past five years, and these totaled nearly €60m.

The report calls for significant improvements in working and living conditions that align with internationally recognised labour standards, including:

Guaranteeing the ILO minimum monthly wage as a base salary, as well as fair catch compensation
Timely, regular salary payments with free, accessible means to send money home
Compliance with ILO standards on working hours, rest periods, and overtime pay
Transparent and accurate social security, health, and retirement contributions
The provision of sufficient, nutritious food and potable water that respects cultural and religious needs
Appropriate medical equipment and supplies on board and timely access to medical treatment on shore
Reasonable and equitable access to communication facilities such as Wi-Fi
The eradication of racism, abuse, and discrimination on board. 
Report 'startling' given laws, voluntary schemes in place

The 'Tuna Group' of Europaen fishing industry association Europeche told  Undercurrent News it was "truly startled by the tone and content" of the report, "which levels serious accusations against the EU tropical tuna purse seine fleet, despite its consistently high social and labour standards."

Europeche calls for elimination of duty-free tuna loin import quotas

Director Anne-France Mattlet said the surprise was greater given that European vessels apply not only strict regulatory frameworks but also go beyond compliance through voluntary initiatives.

"The ILO Work in Fishing Convention (C188) was transposed into EU law through Directive 2017/159. This was achieved thanks to the initiative and strong support of European social partners (Europeche and the European Transport Workers' Federation). France and Spain have also ratified the Convention and therefore mandate regular inspections on their flagged vessels."

Sustainable Fisheries Partnership Agreements (SFPAs) also include a social chapter, recently modified and updated, she said. "This new version was notably inserted in the new protocol with Cote d'Ivoire."

"Our vessels follow rigorous third-party certifications such as the AENOR "Atun de Pesca Responsable" label, regularly audited, or the French AFNOR rule (NF V45-076), both of which include high and comprehensive labour and social criteria."

The social and labor conditions of crew members are of the utmost importance to Europeche and its members as a "core value and responsibility of the EU fleet, of which we are proud," she continued.

"In case of any documented and verified abuse, we would be the first to condemn it, without hesitation. Not only would such behaviour violate EU and member state regulations, but it would also breach the strict code of conduct adopted by Europeche and its members."

"That said, we wonder about the methodology and approach used by BMF," Mattlet concluded. "The report lacks transparency about the seafarers interviewing process, as well as on their declarations on the market and supposed 'wealth' and economic situation of the fishing companies.

"The BMF is a UK-based conservation charity dedicated 'to protect and restore life in the ocean,' not a body specialized in labor or social auditing or economic evaluation."

title: US fisherman sentenced for lying to federal agents, false trip statements
content:
A South Carolina federal judge has sentenced a US commercial fisherman to a year and a day in prison after he was found guilty of lying to National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) agents about his snowy grouper and tilefish catch, reports The Sun News.

Don Michael Rynn, 61, of Augustine, Florida, was convicted of making false statements following a three-day trial this past March. The case involved a March 21, 2023, incident in which a commercial fishing vessel owned by Rynn ignored federally imposed quotas, bringing in approximately 560 pounds of snowy grouper, which is almost three times the limit, and 450 pounds of tilefish, one-and-a-half times what's allowed.

Rynn was sentenced Tuesday (July 22), a month after judge Richard Gergel for the US District of South Carolina rebuffed a defense challenge to the jury verdict, according to the news service. The fisherman's public defender attorney had asked Gergel to grant his client probation, but the federal prosecutors were opposed.

The prosecutors argued that probation would send a message "that this was in fact a crime of no seriousness and would undermine respect for the country's environmental laws, laws regarded by many as second-tier crimes that are more nuisance than necessary." 

The said: "To begin to effect change, Rynn must go to prison."

Recall that Rynn attempted to hide the catch by attributing some of it to another vessel, which had not caught any fish, as previously reported by Undercurrent News. When a tip led to a subsequent investigation of Rynn's suspected commercial fish overage, the commercial fisherman attempted to dispose of the fish in order to evade law enforcement. He then proceeded to lie to NOAA agents about the catch, telling them the "snowy grouper and tilefish had been contaminated by a fuel spill while at sea, and that he had disposed of them in a dumpster."

The fisherman also lied when he implied that a report from the US Coast Guard addressing an unlawful discharge into a local creek was inaccurate and should have been attributed to his vessel, which the attorney's office said "would have bolstered his fuel spill story."

Gergel also ordered Rynn to pay a $7,500 fine.

title: NGO files lawsuit against Samherji, UK subsidiaries over Fishrot scandal
content:
A Scottish NGO has filed a major lawsuit in London's Commercial Court against Samherji and seven other affiliates for the group's alleged role in Namibia's 'Fishrot' corruption scandal.

Icelandic investigation on Fishrot scandal concludes, prosecutor decision looms

The NGO, Restitution Litigation (RL), filed its suit on June 3, and the commercial contracts and arrangements claim is currently active. RL has enlisted London-based law firm Pallas Partners in the case.

The lawsuit relates to Samherji's business dealings in Namibia from 2012-2019, during which it allegedly paid millions of dollars in bribes to key Namibian officials in return for access to fishing quotas. Details of Samherji's activities were leaked by whistleblower and former Samherji employee Johannes Stefansson in November 2019 on WikiLeaks, under the so-called 'Fishrot Files.'

The list of nine defendants includes Icelandic fishing giant Samherji, its holding firm, and former CEO Thorsteinn Mar Baldvinsson. It similarly features Scottish subsidiary Onward Fishing Company, and Onward Investment, the umbrella entity which handles the Samherji group's UK assets.

UK Fisheries, the Hull-based distant water fishing fleet which Samherji operated in a 50/50 joint venture with Parlevliet & Van der Plas until December 2022, is also listed as a defendant.

Samherji has officially sold its ownership stakes in all its overseas businesses to Alda Seafood, owned by Baldvinsson's son, Baldvin Thorsteinsson. But the two firms remain closely connected, with Thorsteinsson now CEO of Samherji and supervisory board chair at Alda.

Samherji's two former division chiefs in Namibia -- Adalsteinn Helgason and Egill Helgi Arnason -- are also among the defendants in the case. The final defendant is Ingvar Gudmundr Juliusson, former CFO of Samherji's Cyprus operations, which were allegedly used to shift profits overseas to avoid Namibian tax and to conceal bribes to Namibian officials under the guise of fees.

As reported by Undercurrent last month, Arnason has since resurfaced as the CEO and a shareholder of the Omani fishing firm Rawanq Al Salam International. Baldvinsson himself stepped down from the helm of Samherji after 42 years in charge in May this year.

The defendant's legal representation is not yet listed.

Back in Iceland, the five-year investigation into Samherji's activities in Namibia concluded at the start of June, with nine individuals listed as defendants -- including Baldvinsson, Juliusson, Helgason, and Arnason once again, according to Heimildin.

The district prosecutor will now decide whether to press charges.

Meanwhile, artist "ODEE" saw his appeal against a UK High Court judgment that found him liable for passing off, copyright infringement, and malicious falsehood against Samherji dismissed.

The court held that while artistic and political expression is important, it does not extend to intentional impersonation, deceit, and use of intellectual property to mislead.

title: Untitled
content:
Approximately 800 salmon escaped from a Cermaq fish farm in Rypefjord near Hammerfest in northern Norway on the night of July 18, prompting concerns about potential impacts on wild salmon populations in nearby rivers, NRK and iFinnmark reported.

The escape occurred when a pipe transporting fish to land came loose, allowing the salmon to swim freely into the sea. Cermaq's regional director, Gunnar Bragi Gudmunsson, called the incident "shocking" and said an investigation is underway.

"The salmon escape in Hammerfest could harm the wild salmon in both the Repparfjord River and the Alta River," said Torfinn Evensen, from Norwegian Salmon Rivers, urging stricter safeguards in aquaculture. 

Environmental authorities have been notified, and Norway's Directorate of Fisheries will determine potential repercussions for Cermaq. In 2024 alone, over 90,000 farmed salmon escaped in Norway, according to the Institute of Marine Research figures. The aquaculture industry estimated that only 10% were recaptured.
