title: Daily recap: Norebo says Norway sanctions may hit Barents quotas; Canada’s spring lobster fishery ends
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Friday, July 18:

Russia's Norebo: Norway sanctions could have 'direct impact' on joint setting of Barents Sea cod, haddock quotas

Norway's decision to follow the European Commission and sanction two major Russian fishing companies could impact the collaboration between the countries on jointly managing the Barents Sea quotas for cod, haddock and other fish, a senior executive with Norebo Holding told Undercurrent News.

That's a wrap for Canada's spring lobster fishery with landings down 10-15%, dock prices up 25-45%

Overall landings in Canada's 2025 spring lobster fishing season, which will wrap up Friday (July 18), were off by 10-15% compared to the 2024 season. But on the bright side -- for harvesters at least -- dock prices jumped 25-45% from the beginning of the latest spring season until the end.

Grieg's Rogaland salmon holdings undervalued by stock market, BC assets' worthless,' say analysts

Having agreed to divest its less valuable farming divisions, Grieg Seafood's share price is expected to increase rapidly to reflect the true value of its Rogaland, Norway salmon farming assets, according to market analysts.

US domestic seafood producers look to piggyback on Trump Section 301 investigation of Brazil

Champions of US domestic producers of shrimp, west coast groundfish and crawfish are jumping on president Donald Trump's recent return to using his Section 301 tariff authority against Brazil by asking him to do the same against their import competitors.

Frosta H1 earnings up 14% as branded sales hike offsets private label drop

German frozen food manufacturer Frosta saw a double-digit hike in earnings during the first half of 2025, driven by excellent sales of the company's branded products.

Norway salmon spot prices fall to lowest point since 2022; Chile rebounds; Scots dip too

Spot prices for Norwegian farmed salmon have fallen once again in week 29 of 2025 (July 14-20), this time to their lowest level of the summer so far, while those for Chilean salmon to the US have rebounded during a national public holiday, industry sources told Undercurrent.

Mitsubishi aims for 190% seafood profit jump after Cermaq's Grieg deal

Japanese conglomerate Mitsubishi Corp. is aiming to increase its net profit from seafood operations by 190% by the fiscal year ending March 2028, compared to fiscal 2024 levels, following the acquisition of Grieg Seafood's farming assets by its wholly owned subsidiary Cermaq Group, a spokesperson told Undercurrent.

title: US domestic seafood producers look to piggyback on Trump Section 301 investigation of Brazil
content:
Champions of US domestic producers of shrimp, west coast groundfish and crawfish are jumping on president Donald Trump's recent return to using his Section 301 tariff authority against Brazil by asking him to do the same against their import competitors.

The US Trade Representative (USTR) announced its Section 301 investigation against Brazil in a Federal Register notice published on Tuesday (July 15) just one week after Trump declared he would be using his authority under the  International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) to slap a 50% tariff on goods imported from Brazil starting on Aug. 1. 

"At president Trump's direction, I am launching a Section 301 investigation into Brazil's attacks on American social media companies as well as other unfair trading practices that harm American companies, workers, farmers, and technology innovators," USTR ambassador Jamieson L. Greer declared in a statement.

Seafood is not specifically mentioned in either the notice nor the statement, but that doesn't necessarily mean that it won't be impacted if Greer decides that the investigation warrants a "responsive action."

Brazil is the US' 19th most valuable source of seafood, accounting for 39,188 metric tons worth $231.9 million in 2024, 27% more volume and 29% more value than in 2023, as reported by Undercurrent News. Most threatened would be US imports of tilapia (10,119t worth $51.1m in 2024), red snapper (4,742t worth $42.1m in 2024) and rock lobster (827t worth $34.1m in 2024).

Recall that Section 301 was the same power Trump used to begin a trade war with China in mid-2018 that escalated to tariffs of 25%, survived the former president Joe Biden administration, and has now cost US seafood importers more than $1.6 billion in extra fees for Chinese seafood.

Unlike IEEPA, Section 301 tariffs require a public review process and are limited in the duration of time they can be implemented, but can be renewed by USTR following another comment period.

The USTR said its investigation of Brazil "will seek to determine whether acts, policies and practices of the Government of Brazil related to digital trade and electronic payment services; unfair, preferential tariffs; anti-corruption interference; intellectual property protection; ethanol market access; and illegal deforestation are unreasonable or discriminatory and burden or restrict US commerce."

Separate Section 301 investigation requested

On Monday (July 14), the day before USTR could announce its Section 301 investigation of Brazil, other US domestic seafood groups were asking Greer to investigate the use of banned veterinary drugs by aquaculture operations in China, India, Indonesia and Vietnam.

The letter -- from the Oregon Trawl Commission, Southern Shrimp Alliance and four Louisiana-based crawfish companies -- refers to president Trump's April Executive Order 14276, "Restoring American Seafood Competitiveness," which declares that foreign seafood imports produced with unfair trade practices "present an existential threat to numerous US seafood industries."

Credit: Phensri Ngamsommitr / Shutterstock

While the US "should be the world's most dominant seafood leader," the reality is that around 90% of US seafood is imported, the letter states. The issue lies in the fact that these foreign competitors don't have the same regulations as the US, which could harm domestic producers, it maintains.

"The use of veterinary drugs in foreign aquaculture is reported to be concentrated in the four Asian countries that account for nearly one-third of the value of total US seafood imports," the letter continues, referring to China, India, Indonesia and Vietnam.

The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) reported refusing 671 entry lines of seafood for reasons related to veterinary drug residues between 2019 and April 2025, the letter recounts. Of these 671 entry lines, 519 (77.3%) originated from the four targeted countries -- China (204), India (177), Indonesia (5), and Vietnam (133).

The letter concludes: "In order to protect American consumers from unsafe imports and level the unfair playing field that has benefited Chinese, Indian, Indonesian and Vietnamese farm-raised seafood producers, strong and immediate action is needed. As such, we respectfully urge the USTR to initiate a Section 301 investigation, with a particular focus on the use of veterinary drugs in farm-raised seafood production from China, India, Indonesia, and Vietnam."

title: Russia’s Norebo: Norway sanctions could have ‘direct impact’ on joint setting of Barents Sea cod, haddock quotas
content:
Norway's decision to follow the European Commission (EC) and sanction two major Russian fishing companies could impact the collaboration between the countries on jointly managing the Barents Sea quotas for cod, haddock and other fish, a senior executive with Norebo Holding told Undercurrent News.

On July 7, Norway sanctioned Norebo, Russia's largest fishing company, and Murman Seafood, also a significant player, for alleged espionage after the EC's move on May 20. Norebo and Murman Seafood lose access to Norwegian ports and waters, which they previously utilized for fishing and offloading as part of the close cooperation between the two countries. 

H&G cod, pollock prices keep rising even as Chinese buyers, end markets push back

The move from Norway comes after scientists announced a recommendation to cut the Barents Sea cod quota by 21% in 2026 to 269,440 metric tons, with prices at record levels. On haddock, the recommendation is for an 18% increase to 153,293t. In October, the Joint Norwegian-Russian Fisheries Commission (JNRFC) meets every year to set the quota based on this scientific advice, a cooperation that has continued after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

"It is our concern that the sanctions will have a direct impact" on this collaboration on management, said Sergey Sennikov, deputy director and chief sustainability officer for Norebo, which has a fleet of more than 40 vessels and plants in the Moscow, Murmansk and Kaliningrad regions.

"It’s up to the government of Russia to decide if the fishery agreements are violated by Norway, and in this case, it may have a direct impact. So, it is our concern," Sennikov told Undercurrent.

Joint fisheries management between Norway and Russia goes back to 1975, while the access to each other's EEZ was established in 1976. That year, Norway and the USSR signed a foundation agreement on bilateral fisheries management, which created the JNRFC. In 2010, Russia and Norway solidified this cooperation, signing a treaty in Murmansk concerning "Maritime Delimitation and Cooperation in the Barents Sea and the Arctic Ocean."

Espersen stops buying from Norebo, Murman as Russian sanctions further pressure cod prices

The move from Norway "could be in violation" of the treaty of 2010 and the agreement on fishery cooperation of 1976, said Norebo's Sennikov, "as well as wider food safety and long-term fish stock sustainability."

Norwegian executives are also on high alert over the situation.

"My main concerns are whether this [the sanctions] will affect the work of the Joint Norwegian-Russian Fisheries Commission in monitoring and managing our common fish stocks, and whether Russian vessels might be forced to catch more small fish in the Russian zone," one high-level Norwegian source, who asked not to be quoted by name, told Undercurrent.

Sennikov reiterated, in more detail, Norebo's defence that the basis for the EC's sanctions of alleged espionage and sabotage by Norebo vessels in the Netherlands and Norway is without merit.

"The irony is that the EU seems to have based its designation substantively on alleged wrongdoing from Norway. When asked, Norway confirms it has no claims of wrongdoing, but then Norway copy-pastes the EU decision," he told Undercurrent.

Russia calls Norwegian sanctions on Norebo, Murman ‘absurd’

"First of all, the waters of Norway and the EU and their ports are highly regulated, and subject to control, monitoring and inspections by the respective authorities. The coastguards, police, veterinary, and armed forces continuously monitor and inspect vessels," he said. "This is an industrial standard that has been ongoing for decades. If any thread or risk were present, special forces would have arrested vessels and done additional inspections. This never happened."

None of the authorities in the EU, Norway or any other country have, so far, put forward any official claim for the grounds mentioned by the EC, he said.

"This is especially grave as espionage and sabotage are severe crimes in EU and Norway. To the best of our knowledge, the EU seems to have imposed sanctions on Norebo relying heavily on Norwegian media — which has distorted and mischaracterized events and regulations," said Sennikov.

He said Norwegian officials had been given the opening to clarify if there are any active claims against Russian vessels for espionage, during the last meeting of the permanent committee JNRFC. "The Norwegian delegation confirmed there were no claims," said Sennikov.

Norway also sanctions Russia’s Norebo, Murman

In addition, he cited a comment from the Norwegian Coast Guard that, "We in the Coast Guard have never accused Russian fishing vessels of doing anything illegal."

The other key episode in the EC sanctions, then the Norwegian ones, is the cessation by the Dutch authorities to issue exemptions to Russian-flagged vessels in May 2024.

On May 16, a vessel belonging to Arctic Shipping, part of Norebo, had its entry to the Dutch port of Eemshaven canceled, despite having all the necessary paperwork, according to Russia's Association of Shipowners of the Fishing Fleet (ASRF). It tried to land instead to Velsen in the Netherlands or in Germany, but also to no avail.

The ASRF has blamed the release of an investigation by Dutch journalism platform Pointer, which claimed to outline Russian efforts to use fishing vessels for espionage.

There was "gross media distortion" of this incident, said Sennikov, as the move did not only apply to Norebo.

"In May 2024, the Dutch Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management decided to stop issuing exemptions on the basis of increasing geopolitical tensions, upcoming tightening restrictions envisaged by the EU, as well as it not being necessary for Russian ships to transport food into the EU, as alternative transportation routes existed," he said.

"This was not a targeted ban against a specific vessel or company, but a global decision to stop issuing exemptions. Meanwhile, most media sources singled out Norebo or its vessels making distorted narratives there was a targeted ban. This is not a true depiction of facts," said Sennikov.

EC response on Norebo, Murman sanctions unclear on key question of 2x China fillet payments

Sennikov also highlighted that food is not normally used by the EU in sanctions.

However, the sanctions on Norebo and Murman Seafood do not technically stop fish from the companies coming into the EU, but they stop European companies paying them.

"Another very suspicious point is that food is generally exempt from sanctions. However, the designation classified the issue not as a food matter, but an alleged espionage matter. For this reason, the decision was able to bypass the regular approval process in the EU, whereby various associations and bodies in member states participate in the decision," he said.

"Whether this was mostly 'political' in order to comply with the geopolitical agenda, or an instance of 'commercial lobbying' to inflate prices and drive up profits for local competitors, the case appears to have been carefully engineered to bypass the normal process," he told Undercurrent.

title: Untitled
content:
Sea Horse brand easy peel shrimp is being recalled by Soline Trading Ltd., a Saint Laurent, Quebec, Canada-based food distributor. The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) published a notice on Saturday (July 12) alerting consumers that the seafood product has undeclared sulphites.

The country of origin of the recalled shrimp was not identified in the recall. 

Sulphites naturally occur in certain foods, and shrimp is one of them, according to studies. Sulphites are also often added to food as a preservative or additive to prevent spoilage. However, sulphites can cause allergic-like symptoms in some individuals. 

"The affected product is being recalled from the marketplace because it contains sulphites which are not declared on the label," the notice explains.

CFIA said the recall was triggered by test results. There have been no reported reactions associated with the consumption of the product, but the agency said its investigation could lead to the recall of other products.

title: Tribes join lawsuit over withheld documents of marine mammal bycatch in Alaska groundfish fleet
content:
A US judge has given the green light for Alaska Native tribes to intervene in an environmental lawsuit alleging the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) had improperly obscured or withheld documentation of marine mammal entanglements in trawl nets in the North Pacific.

NOAA assesses 30 years of orca whale entanglements, deaths in Alaska

As Undercurrent News reported, NMFS released heavily redacted documents in response to freedom of information requests filed from 2021 to 2023 seeking records, photos and videos of marine animals -- including whales, walrus, seals and sea lions -- killed or critically injured after being caught in non-pollock trawl nets as bycatch in the Bering Sea and Gulf of Alaska.

Oceana sued last year, asking judge Sharon Gleason of the US District Court in Alaska to compel the federal agency to provide more complete information beyond the images it complained had been rendered unrecognizable through a pixelation technique and text blacked out.

NMFS releases six photos of dead marine mammals in response to an April 2021 Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request that distorted everything except the animal. Oceana complained in its lawsuit that the redactions removed key information necessary for viewers to understand the relationship between the animal becoming entangled, injured, and/or killed and the fishing operations. (Source: Oceana court filing, July 7, 2025)

In court documents, US government lawyers argued that the redactions were necessary to uphold the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)'s enforced confidentiality requirements for the groundfish fleet as required by the Magnuson-Stevens Act.

"NOAA determined that redactions were necessary to avoid direct or indirect disclosure of confidential observer information or identifying features of fishing vessels," wrote US attorney Michael J. Heyman in a June 12 filing asking for the case to be dismissed.

Oceana argued that the trawl fleet targeting groundfish is responsible for more than half of the nearly marine mammals killed or seriously injured by human activity between 2016 and 2020. 

It also highlighted that at least nine orcas were killed in 2023 by non-pelagic catcher/processors caught as bycatch in fishing gear, leading to a NMFS investigation and political outcry against the Amendment 80 fleet, as Undercurrent reported. 

"Trawler crews have reported increases in orcas present near their boats, suggesting that orca bycatch in these fisheries may continue," wrote Andrea A. Treece, a staff attorney for Earthjustice in San Francisco, California, which is litigating on behalf of the plaintiffs.

Environmental group threatens legal action over Bering Sea orca bycatch

Three Indigenous tribes in Southeast Alaska had asked the judge to allow them to intervene on behalf of the conservationists, arguing that they had a "deep and longstanding connection to the marine ecosystems of the North Pacific Ocean and a unique cultural and legal interest in the protection of marine mammals."

Judge Gleason granted the request the following day, allowing the Organized Village of Kake, Hoonah Indian Association and Organized Village of Kasaan to file briefs on behalf of the plaintiffs. 

The tribes' attorney celebrated that as the case moves closer to trial.

"It is vitally important that the court hear the perspective of Tribal Nations on the sacred significance of orcas, the broader impacts of industrial trawling, and the need for transparency from the federal government on fisheries bycatch data," staff attorney Oliver Stiefel at the Crag Law Center, an environmental legal aid nonprofit in Portland, Oregon told Undercurrent via email.

Representatives of the Seattle, Washington-based Groundfish Forum, which is not party to the lawsuit but represents the Amendment 80 fleet, declined to comment.

Deadlines for another round of filings are set to conclude briefing on the case by mid-August.

title: BioMar, Skretting, Salmofood face up to $78.5m in combined fines related to Chile’s long-running salmon feed price collusion case
content:
Chile's national economic prosecutor's office (Fiscalia Nacional Económica, or the FNE) is seeking record-breaking fines against three of the world's largest salmon feed producers for allegedly operating a secret price-fixing cartel that spanned over a decade.

The FNE, on July 1, in a case that could set a major precedent in Chile, asked the country's competition tribunal (Tribunal de Defensa de la Libre Competencia, or TDLC) to impose on BioMar, Skretting and Salmofood the maximum penalties allowed under legislation in force at the time of the alleged violations.

Chile seeks up to $70m combined price-fixing fine from feed giants after Cargill blows whistle

Each company faces fines of up to 30,000 annual tax units, totaling more than CLP 75.5 billion, or approximately $78.5 million combined.

The FNE said its investigation found the companies colluded between 2003 and 2015, coordinating the prices of salmon feed through both informal and structured mechanisms.

Initially, they allegedly exchanged pricing lists and aligned feed value increases. However, as the cartel evolved, coordination shifted to the cost of raw materials, allowing them to influence how prices were presented and charged to salmon producers, FNE said.

"This was not incidental or occasional behavior: it was a deliberate, long-standing cartel that undermined competition in one of Chile's most strategic industries," said Eduardo Aguilera, deputy head of the FNE's litigation division, during public hearings before the TDLC.

The collusion dates back to around 2000, when the companies began exchanging market-sensitive information under the pretext of responding to Exapesca, a supplier group for fish oil, one of the primary ingredients in salmon feed.

Undercurrent News first reported on this investigation in 2019, when the FNE confirmed it had opened a probe into suspected collusion in Chile's salmon feed industry. Moreover, Cargill confirmed the sector probe to Undercurrent in 2016, amidst reports that Cargill, Skretting, BioMar, and Salmo had all had their offices raided.  

"We are aware of an ongoing investigation, and we are collaborating with authorities on the matter," Einar Wathne, then CEO of Cargill Aqua Nutrition, told Undercurrent at the time.

Now, the case has advanced significantly, as the FNE has filed a formal legal complaint before the country's competition tribunal, revealing for the first time the inner workings of the alleged cartel, the executives involved, and the detailed evidence underpinning its claims.

Evidence presented included internal emails, executive communications, and testimonies collected during raids on the companies' offices. Much of the case was built on the cooperation of competitor EWOS Group, a part of Cargill since 2015, which applied for leniency and provided key evidence that helped uncover the alleged collusion.

The agency requested an exemption for EWOS because it acted as a whistleblower in the case.

According to the FNE, top-level executives -- including general managers, commercial directors and procurement heads -- were directly involved in the alleged scheme throughout its operation.

Cargill confirms Chile feed sector under investigation by competition authority

This included exchanging confidential cost data and coordinating projected prices for key ingredients such as fishmeal, fish oil, vegetable oil, soy, gluten and feather meal.

With Chile ranked as the world's second-largest producer of farmed salmon, any artificial pricing in feed inputs can have broad consequences, affecting local producers, international buyers and consumers.

In a particularly telling internal email, a Biomar executive allegedly remarked that even though actual costs were lower, they were coordinating to "apply the maximum increase," effectively manipulating the system under the cost-plus pricing model.

According to official documents reviewed by Undercurrent, another executive admitted they would inflate their input costs reported to clients to maintain or increase profit margins, all while pretending to comply with contractual pricing frameworks.

The FNE emphasized the systemic nature of the conduct and its prolonged impact. Aguilera noted that the coordination among the companies "was sophisticated and carefully concealed, with participants using encrypted communications and confidential meetings to evade detection."

Executives even allegedly used coded language internally, referring to each company by color or nicknames such as "the Ugalde family" and "the club of Toby," and gave instructions to delete emails or avoid written communication entirely.

One particularly illustrative spreadsheet seized during a raid at Skretting in 2009, titled "COMPETENCIA 2009," detailed the costs of raw materials from competitors and contained pricing manipulation strategies. The spreadsheet showed that even when raw material costs dropped, companies allegedly aligned to raise prices.

The TDLC's ruling is expected in the coming months. In addition to the fines, the companies could face civil lawsuits from affected salmon producers, potentially leading to further financial and reputational consequences.

The FNE has stated that this case reflects its broader commitment to enforcing competition law and protecting the integrity of Chile's markets.

"When companies conspire to fix prices, they don't just break the law, they break the trust that sustains a fair economy," Aguilera said. "We intend to hold them accountable."

If the tribunal rules in favor of the FNE, the penalties would mark one of the largest sanctions ever imposed in a Chilean antitrust case.

title: Trump slaps Brazil with 50% tariff, threatens US imports of tilapia, snapper, rock lobster
content:
US president Donald Trump on Wednesday (July 9) announced that he will be slapping a 50% tariff on goods imported from Brazil starting on Aug. 1, partly in retaliation for the ongoing prosecution of the country's former president, Jair Bolsonaro.

Brazil is the US' 19th most valuable source of seafood, accounting for 39,188 metric tons worth $231.9 million in 2024, 27% more volume and 29% more value than in 2023. In particular, the new tariffs most threaten US imports of tilapia (10,119t worth $51.1m in 2024), red snapper (4,742t worth $42.1m in 2024) and rock lobster (827t worth $34.1m in 2024).

US imports of Brazilian goods have been getting charged with the generalized 10% tariff rate per Trump's April 2 "Liberation Day" decree and were set to continue receiving the same rate after Aug. 1 when tariffs switch to nation-specific amounts. However, in a letter to Brazil's current president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, shared on his Truth Social network, the president complained about Bolsonaro's treatment and also what he said was a "very unfair trade relationship" between the two countries.

"I knew and dealt with former President Jair Bolsonaro, and respected him greatly, as did most other Leaders of Countries," the letter from Trump begins. "The way that Brazil has treated former President Bolsonaro, a Highly Respected Leader throughout the World during his Term, including by the United States, is an international disgrace. This Trial should not be taking place. It is a Witch Hunt that should end IMMEDIATELY!" 

Trump also claimed that Brazil's trade policies have caused "unsustainable Trade Deficits against the United States," which threaten the US economy and national security.

Trump's letter threatens further additional matching tariffs should Brazil seek to retaliate.

The US has a goods trade surplus with Brazil, which totaled $7.4 billion in 2024, according to the Office of the US Trade Representative, according to CNBC.

The US is also launching an investigation into potential unfair trade practices by Brazil, Trump said.

title: Untitled
content:
The South Carolina Shrimpers Association (SCSA), a trade group that represents the US state's wild-caught shrimp industry, has expanded a federal lawsuit to accuse as many as 40 restaurants of promoting imported shrimp as domestically harvested and sourced.

The suit was filed on June 13 in the US District Court for the District of South Carolina against "John Doe Restaurants 1-40," an apparent placeholder, alleging "false and misleading representations." A subsequent filing made on July 2 identified 25 restaurants by name.  

SCSA is seeking a jury trial with damages in an amount to be determined. However, it should be noted that South Carolina is not currently one of the US states with a seafood labeling law in place.

Case stirred on by genetic testing firm 

At the heart of the lawsuit is SEAD Consulting, a rapid genetic testing firm based in Houston, Texas, that for months has been making southern restaurants sweat their shrimp-sourcing practices.

While the company is not named explicitly in the seven-page complaint reviewed by Undercurrent News, the court filing references a "seafood technology consulting company" that conducted a study on shrimp at Charleston, South Carolina, restaurants in May 2025.

FREE READ US city launches campaign to promote restaurants serving wild-caught, domestically-sourced seafood

This past May, the Southern Shrimp Alliance commissioned SEAD to conduct genetic testing on shrimp dishes served at 44 Charleston-area restaurants. The research company shared its results last month, which it says found that only four out of 44 restaurants are serving genuine wild-caught shrimp.

SEAD said the 40 remaining restaurants are "misleading" consumers, with 25 establishments "found to be outright fraudulent."

David Williams, the fisheries scientist who founded SEAD, and Erin Williams, the company's chief operations officer, previously told Undercurrent that they only highlight and name the restaurants that are confirmed to be serving authentic US wild-caught shrimp. 

An example of a restaurant dish that SEAD Consulting says uses authentic wild-caught shrimp. Photo Credit: SEAD Consulting

Restaurants respond

Page's Okra Grill, a family-owned restaurant in business since 2006, was one of the restaurants named in the amended complaint. A message shared on the restaurant's Facebook page on July 2 stated that they are "floored" to be in a lawsuit about defrauding guests on the origin of shrimp being served.

"We agree that restaurants should not advertise using all local shrimp on their menus which is why we don't do that and so we are angry to be lumped in that category. We do not claim on any of our menus that our shrimp is all local or East Coast," the statement reads.

Page's Okra Grill, which has two restaurants and a food truck in the state, says its business serves about 3,000 pounds of shrimp a week and uses both "East Coast wild-caught shrimp and responsibly farmed imported shrimp" due to sourcing issues.

"We tried using 100% local (East Coast) shrimp several years ago and it was just a disaster from a supply standpoint and a severe hardship on labor to cut and devein shrimp often dropped on our doorstep hours before service," the restaurant further explained, adding:

"Make no mistake, we appreciate people that support local businesses but don't think worse of folks that also eat at restaurants with out of state, or out of city ownership. People have to do what is best for their families on a daily basis so why would we call out anyone for making that decision? It's not realistic to expect everyone to choose local for every single meal or every single cup of coffee. We prefer to just focus on us and providing great Southern hospitality and serving up great quality Lowcountry recipes at fair pricing so people can afford a great dining experience when they walk through our doors."

Page's Okra Grill said that it sources both wild-caught and farmed shrimp for its menu items. Photo Credit: Page's Okra Grill

Meanwhile, Hyman's Seafood, with a history dating back more than 100 years, and which boasts to have served a long list of celebrities, from Martha Stewart to the members of Limp Bizkit, said in a statement to ABC News 4 that the claims against them all stem from "miscommunication" with their social media manager.

"At Hyman's Seafood, we take great pride in supporting the Lowcountry community, including the hardworking local shrimpers and seafood producers who are an essential part of the Charleston identity. We have always made an effort to incorporate locally sourced products into our operations and highlight those ingredients when appropriate," the statement read.

"Recently, our restaurant was mentioned in connection with an investigation into misleading advertising related to local shrimp," the statement continued. "We want to provide some important clarity on the situation. We have learned that, on more than one occasion, our social media posts implied that we were serving fresh shrimp, when in fact we were serving imported shrimp at those times. This was due to miscommunication with our social media manager and was in no way intended to mislead the public or to show disrespect to our local shrimping community."

The restaurant said that it takes "responsibility for not reviewing the posts prior to publication" and has not only addressed the issue internally, but it has "clarified expectations moving forward, and put steps in place to ensure accuracy across all communication channels."

The restaurant concluded: "We are committed to earning and maintaining the trust of our guests and community," the statement concludes. "We regret that this error occurred, and we thank those who brought it to our attention."

Gedney Howe III, a lawyer representing SCSA, told ABC 4 that the restaurant "chose the path of integrity," adding:

"We hope this collaboration sets an example, not just for restaurants and fishermen, but for everyone who cares about honesty, sustainability, and the legacy of the Lowcountry." 

The following restaurants were named in a July 3 summons included in the case file: Avocet Hospitality Group dba Pier 101; Bottle Cap Management Group dba Sunset Waterfront Dining; Carrigg's Seafood; CCH-Market dba Charleston Crab House; CCH-Market dba Oyster House and O-Bar; Charleston Hospitality dba Wreckfish Bar & Grill; Cod Tail of Charleston dba Cod Tail Seafood & Chicken; Crab Du Jour of Charleston; Crave Hospitality Group dba The Mill Street Tavern; Ghost Kitchen dba Taters Sea & Soul; Happy Crab Cajun Seafood; Homegrown Hospitality dba Pearlz Oyster Bar; Hushpuppies Seafood Company; Hymans Seafood Company; O'Charley's dba Dockside Charlie's; Page's Incredible Kitchen dba Page's Okra Grill; Poseidon's Playground; Redwing dba Red's Icehouse; Retail Mount Pleasant Seafood Co. dba Mount Pleasant Seafood; Restaurante La Costa; Rivers 1018 dba Family Seafood Market; Southern Roots BBQ; Saltwater Cowboys; and Tavern & Table; Water's Edge. 

The summons also lists "John Doe restaurants 1-15," leaving room for more establishments to be identified later.

title: Daily recap: Espersen confirms closure of UK plant; New CEO at Acme Smoked Fish
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Tuesday, July 8:

Espersen confirms closure of UK plant, aims to stop processing mid-November

Denmark's A. Espersen has confirmed it will close its Grimsby, UK, plant and plans to finish processing in November.

Acme Smoked Fish CEO Carbajosa to retire; Snyder named as replacement

Acme Smoked Fish CEO Eduardo Carbajosa will be replaced by Rob Snyder, the company's chief people and sustainability officer, by the end of the year, the company announced.

German retail giants switch portion of pollock supply from Russian, US single-frozen to Chinese 2x

Three German retail giants have opened to sourcing more double-frozen pollock from China for coated products in the second half of 2025, having previously been focused on single-frozen from Russia and the US, sources told Undercurrent News.

Week 28 farm-gate shrimp roundup: Regional stability masks tariff uncertainty ahead

Global vannamei shrimp farm-gate prices remained largely stable in week 28, with US president Donald Trump's sweeping tariff announcements on Monday yet to materialize in farm-gate pricing.

'Good faith' talks should see tariffs reduced but removal unlikely, NFI counsel warns shrimp industry

"Reciprocal" tariffs in some form are likely here to stay, asserted Robert DeHaan, executive vice president and general counsel for the US' National Fisheries Institute, speaking to a worldwide collection of shrimp producers during a sobering session on US trade at the recent 2025 Shrimp Summit in Bali, Indonesia. 

Vietnamese pangasius farm-gate, fingerling prices see fresh falls

Vietnamese pangasius farm-gate prices have fallen to their lowest levels of 2025 by some distance, according to the latest updates from a Ho Chi Minh City-based consultancy commissioned by Undercurrent to gather and analyze data.

Australis Seafoods reports fuel leak at Chilean salmon farm, investigation underway

A hydrocarbon spill at a salmon farming center operated by Australis Seafoods in Glacier Sound prompted a swift emergency response by the Chilean Navy on Sunday.

Religious observance keeps boats tied up in Alaska even after salmon season kicks off

There were just a few hours left before commercial fishing in the Nushagak District closed on Monday, but dozens of vessels stacked in the city's boat harbor hadn't moved in two days.

title: Untitled
content:
The tuna fishing vessel Beti Aurrera capsized onto its starboard side while in dry dock at a shipyard in Madagascar, industry sources told Undercurrent News.

The incident occurred during a maintenance stop, Puente de Mando reported.

Built in 2002, the vessel measures 84.5 meters in length and 13.85 meters in beam. It is registered under the flag of Seychelles and is based in Port Victoria.

Photos circulating in maritime media show the ship lying on its side, though no injuries or environmental impacts have been reported at this time.

Sources indicate that the vessel belongs to the Spanish fishing company Albacora, a major operator in the global tuna industry. The vessel, previously known as Playa de Aritzatxu, was the purse seiner that Pesqueria Vasco-Montanesa, also known as Pevasa, recently sold to Albacora.

This transaction was part of a strategic shift for both companies, with Pevasa reducing its fleet in the Atlantic Ocean and Albacora expanding its operations.

The cause of the incident remains under investigation. Undercurrent's sources were unaware of what caused the incident, just the result.

"We are currently evaluating the causes and consequences of this unfortunate incident that occurred during repairs. Fortunately, no injuries were reported," Albacora told Undercurrent.

title: Australis Seafoods reports fuel leak at Chilean salmon farm, investigation underway
content:
A hydrocarbon spill at a salmon farming center operated by Australis Seafoods in Glacier Sound prompted a swift emergency response by the Chilean Navy on Sunday (July 6).

The incident occurred in a remote area between Kawesqar National Park and the Gran Campo Nevado. According to the Navy, the Chilean salmon company issued the initial alert, enabling the Natales Port Captaincy to deploy containment efforts quickly.

Authorities classified the spill as medium-scale and have launched an investigation to determine its causes and circumstances.

Australis breaks ground on Vietnamese processing facility

Australis Seafoods reported that the spill occurred on Friday (July 5) during a scheduled maintenance operation at Tank 33 of the Pan de Azucar farming center, reports local TV channel ITV Patagonia. 

A hydrocarbon leak was detected during cleaning procedures involving a pump, prompting immediate action from the onboard crew.

Six crew members activated the company's officially approved contingency plan, suspending operations and notifying the Navy, the National Fisheries and Aquaculture Service, Sernapesca, and the Environmental Superintendency.

As part of the containment protocol, floating barriers and absorbent pads were deployed around the affected pontoon and surrounding waters.

The incident comes just weeks after a major legal defeat for Australis Seafoods, whose proposed expansion project at another farming site in Barros Arana Peninsula, in the Magallanes Region, was annulled by Chile's Third Environmental Court in Valdivia.

Undercurrent News has learned that the court revoked the environmental qualification resolution that had authorized Australis to increase its biomass production from 5,140 to 7,500 metric tons.

China’s Joyvio accused of using threats, false testimony in high-stakes Chilean legal battle

The ruling resulted from a legal challenge led by the Kawesqar Indigenous community Grupos Familiares Nómades del Mar, along with the ATAP and Residente Rio Primero indigenous communities.

These groups, supported by civil society organizations -- including NGOs FIMA, AIDA, and Greenpeace -- argued that the project "posed serious risks to marine biodiversity, traditional ways of life, and the integrity of the Patagonian fjords."

The court agreed, citing deficiencies in Australis' environmental impact assessment, particularly regarding the effects on marine fauna, landscapes, tourism, vessel traffic, and nutrient dispersion from aquaculture waste.

The tribunal found that these factors were either "inadequately studied or overlooked entirely" in the company's application.

The plaintiffs emphasized that the accumulation of biomass, including uneaten feed, fish waste, and antibiotic use, threatened to cause ecological collapse in the area.

They also criticized the project's lack of consultation with Indigenous communities and claimed that Australis had unlawfully increased production before obtaining full environmental approval.

Australis did not respond to a request for comment in time for this publication.

title: Untitled
content:
The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) is urging vessel operators to install smoke and fire detectors in engine rooms and other high-risk spaces following a fire that destroyed the commercial fishing vessel Tarka II off the Washington state coast in September 2024.

The Tarka II, a 66-foot-long, king crab fishing boat, sank after a fire broke out in its engine room about four miles southwest of Tatoosh Island on Sept. 2, recounted NTSB in its recently released investigative report. The fire spread quickly, forcing the two crewmembers aboard to abandon ship.

They were rescued by the US Coast Guard (USCG). But the vessel, which carried roughly 1,000 gallons of diesel fuel, could not be recovered and was declared a total loss, valued at $460,000.

NTSB, in its 10-page Marine Investigation Report 25-24, said investigators found the engine room was not equipped with a smoke or fire detector. Also, though the vessel had a closed-circuit TV system linking the engine room to the wheelhouse, the camera was inactive at the time.

The fire was only discovered when the captain noticed smoke coming from the exhaust stacks.

The Tarka II before it sank. Image from NTSB report.

Detectors in the galley and outside the engine room did not activate until the engine room door was opened, by which point the blaze had grown too big to control. Detectors in uncrewed machinery spaces are essential to early fire detection, allowing more time for effective response or evacuation, NTSB stressed in its report.

"Vessel operators can improve fire safety by installing detectors in all areas susceptible to fire, such as the engine room and galley, and spaces that contain machinery, hot exhaust tubing and fuel sources," the report stated.

Additionally, the detectors should be capable of notifying crewmembers throughout the vessel of fire or smoke and should be routinely checked to ensure they are in good working order, the report advised.

The probable cause of the fire aboard the Tarka II was an unknown source within the engine room, the report concluded. The NTSB also noted that the boat had completed a USCG dockside exam in May 2023, and the only deficiency noted then was expired emergency flares, which the captain subsequently replaced.

title: US ICE officers detain workers, customers at Texas seafood market
content:
About a dozen people, including seven employees at Groomer's Seafood, a retail market in San Antonio, Texas, were detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers during an early morning raid on Wednesday (July 2), reports KSAT News.

ICE later confirmed that the detainees included nationals from Honduras, Mexico and Venezuela who were suspected of being in the US unlawfully, according to the television station.

ICE and the Department of Homeland Security Investigations requested assistance from the San Antonio Police Department (SAPD), according to a city memo obtained by KSAT. Two SAPD officers and a sergeant were assigned to provide perimeter security under Texas Senate Bill 4 (SB4), which mandates local cooperation with federal immigration, KSAT also reported. 

This was the first such request in months, and it met the SB4 requirements, an ICE spokesperson said.

Groomer Seafoods has not publicly commented on the detentions, the TV station reported.

Meanwhile, there are expectations that ICE will exponentially increase its efforts to track down, arrest and deport illegal immigrants after US president Donald Trump signs his "One Big, Beautiful Bill" on Thursday (July 4). The mega tax legislation, which contains over 1,000 pages outlining the government's plans for spending and cuts, budgets $170 billion for Trump's border and immigration goals, making it the largest law enforcement agency in the US, reports National Public Radio (NPR).

Earlier in the week, White House border czar Tom Homan told reporters that Congress needed to pass the bill to allow the federal government to buy more detention beds.

"The more beds that we have, the more bad guys we arrest," Homan is quoted as saying by NPR.

title: Fresh listeria recall for Polar Salmon in Denmark amid regulatory scrutiny
content:
Danish seafood processor Polar Salmon Hjerting Laks, owned by Greenland's Polar Group, has recalled sliced smoked halibut products sold across major retail chains after detecting listeria contamination, marking the company's latest incident involving listeria, reports Fodevare Watch.

The recall affects halibut sold under the Premieur brand at Netto stores with a best-before date of July 18, 2025, and products sold under the Salling Princip brand at Fotex and Bilka stores with a July 22, 2025 expiry date. All affected products carry lot number 27749254.

Polar linked to four deaths from salmon listeria in Denmark

The company urged consumers to discard the products or return them to stores.

The recall comes just months after Danish authorities filed a police report against the company in January for failing to properly notify authorities or initiate recalls during previous listeria contaminations that occurred between 2023 and 2024.

The company, owned by Greenlandic firm Polar Seafood, has been linked to a listeria outbreak that killed four people in Denmark between 2018 and 2024, according to health authorities. The Statens Serum Institut reported that 27 people were infected with invasive listeria during that period, with extensive DNA analysis tracing the outbreak to the company's products.

Authorities discovered that the company had detected listeria in salmon through analyses conducted in 2023 and 2024 but failed to inform regulators or recall the contaminated products, leading to the police report filed earlier this year.

The incidents have sparked internal upheaval, with co-owner Christoph Kjaergaard earlier removed from his position.

Polar CEO Henrik Leth has previously pledged a thorough investigation into the company's food safety practices.

title: Icelandic investigation on Fishrot scandal concludes, prosecutor decision looms
content:
The Icelandic district attorney has concluded a five-year investigation into alleged corruption at seafood firm Samherji, Heimildin reported.

Nine individuals, including former CEO Thorsteinn Mar Baldvinsson and other current and former Samherji employees, are facing charges with the district attorney's office.

The prosecutor is now deciding whether to press charges, Icelandic publication Ruv reported. Ruv also wrote that it's not possible to say when the prosecutor's decision will be made.

The case, first exposed in 2019 by Kveikur, Stundin, Wikileaks, and Al Jazeera, involves allegations that Icelandic fishing company Samherji paid bribes to Namibian officials to secure lucrative fishing rights. Profits were allegedly funneled through a global network to evade taxes.

Baldvinsson resigned as CEO on June 26 this year, passing leadership to his son Baldvin Thorsteinsson, as reported by Undercurrent News. He and co-owner Kristjan Vilhelmsson have transferred their shares to their children.

The case also prompted the resignations of Namibia's justice and fisheries ministers.

Whistleblower Johannes Stefansson, a former Samherji executive, played a key role in the investigation, which included over a thousand messages exchanged with Baldvinsson. District prosecutor Olafur Thor Hauksson highlighted the case scope and complexity.

title: Untitled
content:
UK wildlife activists who researched conditions at Scottish salmon farms were covertly surveilled by private spies linked to ex-British army elite Damian Ozenbrook, the Guardian has reported following an investigation.

Scottish court upholds order preventing anti-aquaculture campaigner accessing Mowi sites

Corin Smith and Don Staniford filmed the conditions at some Scottish sea farms in 2018. Their footage was posted online and broadcast by the BBC that same year. It showed fish crawling with sea lice, with some having chunks of their flesh torn away, and others having twisted spines.

After that, operatives from Ozenbrook’s firm, Blue Square Global, photographed and tracked the two activists, sometimes with family, the newspaper said.

According to the Guardian, a leaked intelligence report from that time proposed using false identities and investigating Smith’s finances. 

The Scottish Salmon Company -- now owned by Bakkafrost, but at that time majority-owned by Northern Link, a private equity backed by Edinburgh-based, Ukrainian-born banker Yuri Lopatinsky -- allegedly commissioned this report. 

In September 2024, Bakkafrost Scotland sought an interim interdict to prevent Staniford from making unauthorized visits to its fish farm sites, claiming he had made intrusions as recently as Aug. 23, 2024. That came after a similar legal action by Mowi Scotland, which successfully obtained an interdict barring Staniford from kayaking near its pens.

title: South Korean seafood processor hit with warning letter from US FDA
content:
Yongdae Hwangtae Union Corp, a seafood processor from South Korea, has been issued a warning letter by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for adulterated desalted pollock.

The warning letter, dated Jan. 16, 2025, was published by the FDA on Tuesday (June 24). Per the notice, the FDA inspected Yongdae Hwangtae Union's facility in June 2024 and found "serious violations of the seafood Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) regulation."

The company responded to the FDA with "promises to make corrections" to a number of issues, including environmental monitoring, calibrations of equipment used during manufacturing and employee training.

However, the FDA said Yongdae Hwangtae Union's response was "not adequate."

"Accordingly, your refrigerated and frozen desalted pollack in modified atmosphere packaging products are adulterated, in that they have been prepared, packed, or held under conditions whereby they may have been rendered injurious to health," the FDA stated in the warning letter.

The FDA said the company operates an outdoor location in Bung-Myeon, Gangwon-do, South Korea, where pollock is exposed to the natural environment, which could contaminate the ready-to-eat item with filth pathogens from animals and insects.

Yongdae Hwangtae Union Corp must address the deviations noted by the FDA or risk being placed on detention without physical examination.

title: Untitled
content:
Environmental organizations are celebrating a historic ruling in Chile that convicted former executives of salmon farming giant Nova Austral for significant environmental crimes.

The ruling marks a milestone in holding the aquaculture industry accountable for marine ecosystem damage, they said.

Chilean court finds former Nova Austral execs guilty of water pollution, falsifying data

Leading NGOs Greenpeace Chile, the Environmental Prosecutor's Office (FIMA, in its Spanish acronym), and the Interamerican Association for Environmental Defense (AIDA, in its Spainish acronym) praised the decision made by the Oral Criminal Court of Punta Arenas on June 11 as "a landmark moment" in environmental justice, reports El America.

As Undercurrent News previously reported, the ruling found four former executives guilty of repeated water contamination and falsification of data submitted to regulatory authorities in Chile's southern Magallanes region.

"This is a historic verdict that breaks new ground in the fight against environmental impunity," said Greenpeace attorney Roxana Nunez. "For the first time, salmon industry leaders face criminal prosecution -- not just administrative penalties -- for harming Chile's fragile marine ecosystems."

The court convicted former regional manager Drago Covacich and former general manager Nicos Nicolaides as perpetrators of repeated water contamination. Former executives Isaac Olivet-Besson and Rigoberto Garrido were convicted as accomplices.

In addition, Covacich was found guilty of submitting false information to Chile's national fisheries and aquaculture service, Sernapesca, by altering environmental and health reports.

While the executives were acquitted of subsidy fraud, the environmental groups are urging prosecutors to appeal that part of the ruling.

"The investigation shows the company had a systematic and organized approach to committing crimes and illegitimately benefited from around CLP 60 billion ($63.9m) in subsidies under the Navarino Law [a law granting tax and customs benefits to companies in Chile's southernmost regions], funded by taxpayers," said Sofía Barrera, litigation coordinator at FIMA.

Nova Austral falsified salmon mortality figures, concealed seabed damage, and exceeded authorized production limits. These actions reportedly generated over CLP 3.7bn in illicit profits while causing irreversible harm to marine ecosystems.

"The conviction was based on rigorous legal standards. In our view, this was a deliberate corporate decision to violate the law and damage the environment," the organizations stated jointly.

All three are now calling for exemplary and proportionate sentences, which are expected to be announced in the coming days. They argue strong penalties are necessary to deter other companies from profiting through environmental degradation.

Chilean environmental authority reveals new lawsuits against Nova Austral

"These crimes have invisible but very real victims: the ecosystems, marine biodiversity, and the natural heritage of all Chileans," said Cristina Lux, spokesperson for AIDA.

The evidence presented included witness testimony, expert analyses, documents, and physical proof compiled by the Public Prosecutor's Office and the State Defense Council.

While the court found the proof sufficient for pollution and falsification charges, it deferred judgment on any mitigating or aggravating circumstances ahead of the sentencing hearing, which is set for July 5.

A source close to the company emphasized that, following the events for which former Nova Austral executives are currently on trial, the company completely overhauled its executive team and reinforced its internal controls and corporate governance practices.

They also noted that, after a court-approved reorganization process, Nova Austral underwent a change of control in September 2024.

"As a result, the company now operates under entirely new management, with a different shareholder structure and a board of directors that is 100% distinct from the one in place at the time of the alleged events," the source told Undercurrent.

Contact the author Maria.Feijoo@undercurrentnews.com

title: Daily recap: EU to revise antibiotic ban list; Ecuador farm-gate shrimp prices on rise
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Tuesday, June 24:

2025 Shrimp Summit: EU will revise antibiotic residue country ban list before enforcement next year

Undercurrent News is reporting live from the 2025 Shrimp Summit, held at the Grand Hyatt Bali hotel in Nusa Dua, Indonesia.

Week 26 farm-gate shrimp roundup: Ecuador prices on rise as China, Vietnam levels keep falling

Farm-gate shrimp prices have increased in Ecuador, while levels in China continued to decline for all provinces aside from Fujian, with Vietnam also down, according to Undercurrent's week 26 (June 23-29) market assessment.

Frozen warmwater lobster tail prices top coldwater ahead of expected US import surge

US wholesale prices for frozen warmwater lobster tails from Brazil and the Caribbean are standing firm ahead of an expected surge in imports and have, in a rare occasion, risen above those being paid for frozen coldwater tails.

Russia revises expected Far East salmon catches up by 50,000t

After a fast start and yet better fishing to come, Russia has revised its forecast for salmon landings in the Far East upwards by some 50,000 metric tons.

Shrimp now far from 'endless' at Red Lobster

US restaurant chain Red Lobster, which emerged from bankruptcy in September 2024, is working to rein in costs associated with its shrimp offerings.

Former Samherji exec linked to Namibia 'Fishrot' case leads Omani tuna deal with Dutch giant P&P

An Icelandic executive, who is under investigation in Iceland for his alleged role in Namibia's "Fishrot" scandal -- but denies any wrongdoing -- is now running a company in Oman that recently acquired three tuna vessels from a French fishing firm controlled by Dutch fishing giant Parlevliet and van der Plas.

Red Lobster's Crabfest evolution from Dungy to seafood boils

Red Lobster has been using 90s boy band singer Joey Fatone to promote its $19.99 value shrimp deal for the past couple of months. But it's time to say "Bye, Bye, Bye" to the NSYNC alum, because it's out with the seafood chain's three-course "Shrimp Sensation" deal and in with its fan-favorite "Crabfest" promotion. 

Spanish fishing firm buys new vessel for West African operations

The Spanish fishing company Grupeixe has acquired a vessel previously operated by seafood processor Pesquera Loira, itself based in Marin, northern Spain, industry sources told Undercurrent.

title: Untitled
content:
An Icelandic executive, who is under investigation in Iceland for his alleged role in Namibia's "Fishrot" scandal -- but denies any wrongdoing -- is now running a company in Oman that recently acquired three tuna vessels from a French fishing firm controlled by Dutch fishing giant Parlevliet and van der Plas (P&P).

Egill Helgi Arnason is the CEO and a shareholder of the Omani fishing firm Rawanq Al Salam International. 

The Omani firm, which already operated three large pelagic vessels, bought three tuna purse-seine vessels earlier this year from the French tuna company Compagnie Francaise du Thon Oceanique (CFTO).

The vessels, which were part of CFTO's Indian Ocean fleet, have been reflagged to Oman to continue their operations in the Indian Ocean, as Diek Parlevliet -- CEO of CFTO's parent company, P&P -- confirmed to Undercurrent News after the deal was concluded earlier this year.

The three tuna vessels are now operating "successfully" in the Indian Ocean, industry sources told Undercurrent.

"The Omani tuna operations are going very well," one informed industry source said in May, referring to Rawanq Al Salam International's tuna vessels. Tuna catches in the Indian Ocean have slowed in June, after excellent catches last month, as reported by Undercurrent.

Just over two months ago, the firm conducted its first tuna landing in Seychelles, according to a LinkedIn post by the firm's acting general manager and pelagic and tuna fleet manager, Muath Al Nadabi. 

The acquisition of the three CFTO vessels allowed Rawanq to double its fleet size, diversify its geographical and product spread, and enter new end markets.

Arnason in Namibia

The up-and-coming Omani industrial fishing company is relatively unknown to the broader fishing sector. Established in February 2021, the firm is co-owned by its founder, Arnason, and Omani institutional investors.

Arnason was formerly a director at Icelandic fishing giant Samherji, which faced intense scrutiny over its alleged payment of bribes to Namibian officials in return for horse mackerel fishing quotas while operating in the country from 2012 to 2019. 

The executive, who has denied any wrongdoing in Namibia, has over 20 years of experience in the fishing industry, previously managing fishing operations primarily in the territorial waters of Mauritania and Morocco. 

He served as a director on the board of Esja Investments and was also the managing director of ArcticNam. ArcticNam was owned by Walvis Bay-based Esja, which acted as one of Samherji's key subsidiaries in Namibia during its time operating in the country.

Namibian court rejects asset restraint order on ex-Samherji execs, Fishrot rumbles on

After whistleblower and former Samherji executive Johannes Stefansson reported the firm's alleged corruption in November 2019, Arnason, along with other senior Samherji executives, left Namibia, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

Arnason and two colleagues were initially sought for extradition from Iceland to stand trial in Namibia, but Iceland refused to comply as there is no extradition agreement between the two nations.

A trial in Namibia involving nine domestic government officials and businessmen implicated in the case is understood to be ongoing in the African country. Six of them, including former fisheries minister Bernhard Esau and former justice minister Sacky Shanghala, have been in custody since early 2020. The trial in Namibia, which currently involves 10 Namibian defendants facing charges, has been postponed until August this year.

Arnason and the other Samherji executives are not included in Namibian proceedings, as previously reported by Undercurrent, although the case is still under investigation by Iceland's prosecutor general.

The district attorney's office in Iceland recently said it hopes that the investigation into the Samherji case will be completed this summer, Icelandic publication Heimildin reported. The case will then be reviewed by the prosecution department, and a decision will be made as to whether charges will be issued, according to the news site.

Meanwhile, Samherji, Iceland's largest fishing company, which stood accused of bribing Namibians to secure lucrative horse mackerel fishing quotas over seven years, has closed its operations in Namibia and continues to operate in other fishing grounds, having increased its sales in 2023.

Samherji's CEO, Thorsteinn Mar Baldvinsson, who is stepping down this month, led the company throughout its period of operations in Namibia. He had previously stepped down after the leaks were made public, but later returned to his position. He consistently denied any personal involvement in the Fishrot scandal, asserting that the company's former Namibia operations director, Johannes Stefansson, acted independently. 

Arnason in Oman

Arnason has played a key role in the recent acquisition of the CFTO vessels Drennec, Glenan, and Trevignon and in the company's recent expansion in the pelagic industry, according to industry sources.

Following the acquisition, Rawanq started operating a fleet of six vessels, including three pelagic trawlers licensed to fish in Omani and Mauritanian waters and three tuna seiners authorized to operate in the Indian Ocean.

When Undercurrent asked about his involvement in the Fishrot case, Arnason denied any wrongdoing. Asked about the ongoing trial, he declined to comment on the grounds that he was not part of the proceedings.

In 2023, a group of fishing crew members filed a lawsuit over the non-payment of court-ordered dismissal compensation, alleging their former employer, ArcticNam, failed to comply with the ruling, according to Africanlii.

Arnason said he was confident the crew matter case would "be resolved amicably between the remaining parties."

"I was subpoenaed in this crew matter case, but the crew members have since withdrawn and dropped all claims against me," he noted.

He also said that he believes the "ongoing investigation in Iceland will confirm his innocence of any wrongdoing."

Team and other vessels

According to LinkedIn, Rawanq Al Salam's financial manager is an Icelandic individual, while fleet manager Al Nadabi joined the firm in September 2021.

One of the fleet's captains joined Rawanq Al Salam in September 2022, having previously worked as a captain in Icelandic and Russian fishing firms and Katla Seafood, another subsidiary of Samherji. 

Beyond the three tuna vessels recently acquired, the Omani firm operates three large pelagic vessels under the country's flag: Al Rahma, Al Baraka, and Al Nasr, with a range of 77 meters to 120 meters.

Al Rahma (in the photos below as it is now and how it was before being renamed), a factory ship built in 1988 and 120m long, was previously one of Samherji's vessels in Namibia, then going by the name Geysir.

The vessel left the Namibian port of Walvis Bay under the "cover of darkness" in February 2020, as the Namibian Sun reported at the time. The vessel is still fishing in West Africa, and it was tracked in Mauritania in late March 2025 and mid-April 2025, according to Vessel Finder.

The firm's other vessels, Al Baraka and Al Nasr, were recently tracked near Omani waters.

Al Rahma, a 120m long fishing trawler, today. Photo: LinkedIn.

Al Rahma (Galleon / Geysir / Jose Marti). IMO: 8607141. Equipment delivered: 2013. Buyer: Sjólaskip, Iceland. Year built: 1988. Type: Fishing Trawler. Source: Naust Marine.

title: Canadian fisheries officers charge multiple individuals for illegal fishing at Nova Scotia fish ladder
content:
Several individuals have been arrested and charged for illegally fishing gaspereau within a protected zone near a fish ladder in Grand River Falls, Nova Scotia, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) said.

In one incident on May 26, officers arrested two people for harvesting gaspereau directly inside the fish ladder, seizing 350 pounds of fish, a truck, and a 20-foot trailer. The individuals have been charged with fishing within 23 meters of a fishway and possession of fish caught in contravention of the Fisheries Act, the department said in a Facebook post on Tuesday (June 17).

Just days later, fishery officers arrested three more individuals in connection with another illegal fishing event at the bottom of the same fish ladder, located in Richmond County. In that case, officers seized 836 kgs of gaspereau and additional gear, DFO said in a LinkedIn post on Thursday (June 19). An investigation remains underway.

"Fish ladders" are structures designed to help migrating fish bypass barriers such as dams or waterfalls, allowing them to complete critical parts of their life cycle. Fishing in or near such structures is prohibited under federal law, as it can block migration routes and undermine conservation efforts.

"These laws are in place to support healthy stocks and sustainable fishing," DFO said, reminding the public that fishing is not permitted within 23 meters downstream of a fish ladder.

title: Report reveals what caused $250,000 Alaska fish tender to sink
content:
Unsecured watertight doors contributed to the sinking of an Alaska fish tender transiting Chiniak Bay this past November, the US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has determined. 

Based on a 10-page report delivered May 29, 2025, the Cape Douglas, a 110-foot, 80-year-old industrial vessel owned by North Bay Corporation, was operating as a fish tender to dispose of fish byproduct. The vessel was near Kodiak, Alaska, when it began taking on water at around 12:55 local time on Nov. 6, 2024.

Attempts to control the flooding were unsuccessful, and the vessel sank with an estimated 400-600 gallons of diesel fuel on board, according to the report. It was declared a total loss with a value of $250,000, according to NTSB.

The captain and a crew member, who were forced to abandon the vessel into a towed skiff, however, were rescued by a Good Samaritan. 

Cape Douglas docked in 2022. (Source: Alaska Marine Surveyors, Inc.)

The NTSB investigation noted that concerns about the condition of the vessel had been raised by the City of Kodiak harbormaster about seven months before the Cape Douglas sank.

"The vessel's age (80 years old), visual signs of rust and deterioration, and documented hull wastage suggest a general degradation of the vessel and onboard systems, such as the deck washdown system," the report continued. 

NTSB determined that the probable cause of the sinking was "flooding of a below-deck passageway or the pump room from an undetermined failure in the vessel's deck washdown system." 

Because the Cape Douglas was not salvaged, NTSB said it can't further assess the vessel or its systems. However, the federal agency was able to note that it was equipped with watertight doors in the engine room and companionway spaces. Those doors remained open. Had they been secured, the flooding may have been contained.

"Maintaining watertight integrity of a vessel is a fundamental principle of safe operations on water," the report said. "Within the hull, watertight bulkheads and watertight doors are designed to prevent progressive flooding by containing any incoming water to the compromised space."

title: Russian firm Murman looks to navigate EU sanctions with direct China sales
content:
Russia's Murman SeaFood is "consulting" with other companies with experience in direct sales to China for processing after the EU's bombshell sanctions, which it claims are based on misunderstandings. 

Murman was sanctioned along with the larger Norebo Holding by the European Commission (EC) in May, preventing European companies from making direct payments to them.

The sanctions -- which Murman said are totally unfounded -- mean the company is looking to sell direct to China and other countries rather than via EU traders, CEO Vladimir Khizhnyakov told Undercurrent News.

Wide price spread on Russian H&G cod, haddock amid ongoing market confusion on Norebo, Murman sanctions

"Murman has no experience working with Chinese buyers directly. Previously, we sold all our products to European traders. They sent some of it to China," he said.

Obviously, the EU traders can no longer buy headed and gutted (H&G) cod and haddock directly from Murman or Norebo, which has caused prices to rise. However, EU buyers feel they can continue to buy fillets from China, produced using H&G from Norebo and Murman. So, direct sales channels need to be established. The EC has not responded to requests for clarification on this process from Undercurrent. 

"However, our other companies have such experience [on direct sales to China and others], and we will consult with them," Khizhnyakov told Undercurrent.

Khizhnyakov declined to comment on how this might happen.

"I cannot tell you what the payment route from China will be, because I do not know. But even if I knew it, I would hardly have informed it for publication," he said. "The main thing here is that there are potential buyers and sellers for goods. And it is already working."

Russian, Norwegian H&G cod prices up $300/t with Norebo, Murman EU stock in limbo

Even prior to the sanctions, Murman and other Russian companies were struggling to get payments. "The fact is, all our companies have long been in very difficult conditions in terms of transferring money for sold products to Russia, even though they are not under sanctions, as we were before. We cannot receive service for our ships in ports, because we cannot make payments through the European banking system."

Basis for sanctions disputed

Norebo and Murman refute the EC allegations that they "are part of a Russia-state sponsored surveillance campaign that has conducted espionage missions and sabotage on critical infrastructure, including undersea cables."

According to Murman's Khizhnyakov, the incidents are "misunderstandings… which were investigated bу the Norwegian police. As а result of these investigations, no illegal activities on our part and no violation of fishing regulations were found."

For Murman, the sanctions are justified by claims Melkart-5, a vessel owned and operated by the company, "has repeatedly shown untypical behaviour inconsistent with its regular economic practices and fishing activities, including its presence in close vicinity to an ongoing NATO military exercise, and regular presence close to Norwegian critical infrastructure and military sites," reads the EC document.

Russian group claims Norebo vessel denied entry to Dutch port over ‘espionage’ fears

The EC alleged Melkart-5 also "showed highly unusual navigation practices in the immediate vicinity of a subsea cable in the Norwegian North Sea, crossing the cable multiple times, immediately before the cable was severely damaged. In addition, the crew of Melkart-5 violated Norwegian on-shoring regulations while being caught setting off to investigate a Norwegian bridge critical for military logistic purposes in a clandestine manner."

In January 2022, one of two underwater fibre-optic cables connecting Spitsbergen to mainland Norway was cut in the Greenland Sea west of Spitsbergen. A month later, a preliminary investigation concluded that human activity was the cause of the break, the Barents Observer reported.

Four Russian vessels, including Melkart-5, were operating in the area where the cables pass, according to automatic identification system data for Jan. 5-9 published in a detailed report by the Norwegian Broadcasting Corporation, NRK. Melkart-5 passed over the cables 20 times in the days before and after the break was discovered, it was reported.

"It was stated that our vessels demonstrated unusual navigation practices in the Norwegian North Sea. We officially declare that our company's vessels have never been engaged in commercial activities in the Norwegian North Sea and, in general, have never been there," said Khizhnyakov.

According to the Barents Observer, the crew of the Murman vessel was questioned by Norwegian police while calling at Batsfjord. Police later closed the case without bringing any further charges against the Melkart-5 or any other Russian fishing vessels in the area at the time, it was reported.

On July 17, 2022, crew members of Murman's Melkart‑5 reportedly violated Norwegian regulations by using a small boat to cross the harbour area of Kirkenes and approach Strommen Bridge -- a restricted military zone, the Russian language site of the Barents Observer reported. The Finnmark police fined the fishermen for disembarking in a closed area without permission.

"Accusations against us of actions in the case of the bridge in general, аrе absurd, аnd not subject to any criticism," Murman's Khizhnyakov told Undercurrent.

"The incidents in question, which presumably served as the basis for the accusations, took рlасе in the Greenland Sea, nеаr the Spitsbergen archipelago, and directly in the Norwegian port of Kirkenes, which has nothing to do with the jurisdiction of the European Union. Our vessels wеrе engaged in normal typical fishing activities and wеrе serviced in the port of Kirkenes," said Khizhnyakov.

Murman has been working with European companies since 1997, he said.

"During this time, we have developed close business relations with them, and, as it seems to us, the Murman SeaFood company has а good reputation in the Еurореап market.

"Our activities are aimed at producing food products from fish, and nothing more. In our work, we are always open to all control and supervisory state bodies of the countries where we operate," he said.

"In our opinion, this decision was made either erroneously or deliberately, but in no way corresponds to the essence of the case," said Khizhnyakov. "This decision causes us nothing but surprise and disappointment. We believe that all our European partners share the same opinion."

title: Bornstein Seafoods issues recall in US, Canada for nearly 45,000 lbs of RTE shrimp meat
content:
Bellingham, Washington-based Bornstein Seafoods issued a recall announcement Tuesday (June 10) for 44,550 pounds of its cooked and peeled, ready-to-eat coldwater shrimp meat following the detection of Listeria monocytogenes during routine sampling.

Though distribution of the product has ceased, the shrimp meat was already sent directly to distributors and retailers in the US states of California, Oregon and Washington, as well as British Columbia, Canada, according to the company. Its possible the products were further distributed to retailers nationwide, it advised.

No illnesses have been reported to date and Bornstein said it is continuing its "root cause investigation" into what caused the contamination.
