title: Untitled
content:
A lawyer representing the US domestic farmed salmon industry -- whose sole member is Canadian seafood firm Cooke, which operates farms in the US state of Maine -- is raising concerns of potentially illegal dumping of Norwegian salmon in the US market.

 A spike in Norwegian salmon exports to the US this year raises concerns about "companies that are unloading fish at less than their cost of production," said John Herrmann II, the Washington DC-based chair of law firm Kelley Drye's international trade practice, told Undercurrent News in an interview Monday (June 9).

"Volumes are up significantly … and prices are down," Herrmann said. "Obviously, that's something that catches our attention."

John Herrmann II. Photo courtesy of Kelley Drye.

Herrmann said if he gathered enough evidence to show dumping was occurring, he would consider filing a request with the US Department of Commerce to commence an investigation on "whether a remedy is appropriate."

Herman previously served as senior advisor to the US assistant secretary of commerce for import under former president George W. Bush. He now represents the US salmon industry, which is dominated by Blacks Harbour, New Brunswick based Cooke Inc. 

"We're simply looking at this very closely and evaluating our options," he told Undercurrent.

In 2025, UCN trade data shows US imports of salmon from Norway were up 26% year-over-year through April across the three main harmonized tariff codes that include Atlantic salmon.

UCN salmon market analyst Lorin Castiglione said the sharp increase is due to a milder-than-usual winter in Norway, which led to improved biomass growth early in the year, especially for fish that had remained in the water due to prior sea lice treatments.

"Warmer sea temperatures, reaching 12-13°C in northern Norway, helped accelerate growth during a period when production is usually constrained. That, paired with emergency harvesting triggered by an algal bloom in key farming zones, pushed more fish into the market, particularly in sizes suited for US buyers," Castiglione noted.

In May, Undercurrent reported Norway's US salmon exports hit a record high volume of 7,019t, up 32% y-o-y. Thus far in 2025, Norway has exported 36,000t of salmon to the US worth NOK 5.4 billion ($535.4 million) -- up 40% in value and 56% in volume.

Monthly Norwegian salmon exports to the US reveal a surge in 2025 volumes. Chart courtesy of NSC.

While Cooke may be the largest farmer of salmon in the US, that's a small amount of fish. Cooke supplies much more of its salmon from its farms in Canada, which competes with imports from Norway.

As reported by Undercurrent earlier, while Norway saw its share of the US Atlantic salmon import market grow to 20% in the first quarter of 2025 from 13% in the first quarter of 2024, Canada saw its share drop to 14% from 20%.

As US exports rise, prices collapse

In the May export update produced by the government-run Norwegian Seafood Council (NSC), CEO Christian Chramer said there had been a shift toward the US, with the US taking 11% of all exported Norwegian salmon, up from 8% y-o-y. 

US puts preliminary shrimp anti-dumping rates of 58% on CP Foods

Norwegian salmon is currently subject to a 10% US tariff thanks to president Donald Trump's so-called Liberation Day, but that rate is set to increase to 15% on July 9. So a surge of salmon shipped to the US could possibly be the result of exporters rushing to get frozen salmon into the US before the deadline.

However, the majority of Norwegian salmon imported by the US is fresh or chilled, somewhat nullifying the ability of exporters to frontload their shipments to avoid the higher tariff rate.

Chramer said the US shift was a result of a unique situation in the market.

"Good access to large whole salmon, changing competitive conditions and increased demand have led to a shift in the flow of goods from Europe to overseas markets," he said.

At the same time, salmon prices have plummeted.

In May, the average price for Norwegian salmon was NOK 75.78 per kilogram, a 35% fall from the same month last year (NOK 116.68/kg, which was the third-highest average price recorded for a month). The NOK 40.88/kg decline y-o-y is the largest drop ever recorded, NSC noted.

"Record-high export volumes for the month of May, as a result of better production conditions, have led to a record-breaking weakening of the salmon price this year compared with last year," NSC seafood analyst Paul T. Aandahl said in the update.

UCN pricing data confirms the trend, with prices averaging NOK 78.55 in week 23 (June 2-8), up from NOK 62.84 in week 21.

While prices have softened due to increased availability, the trend aligns with broader biological and seasonal cycles common to salmon farming in Norway, Castiglione said. 

"Demand typically dips during the summer months, and pricing tends to follow suit to help stimulate movement," she said. "These factors should also be considered when raising concerns about potential illegal dumping into the US market."

Chilean fillets and Canadian whole salmon are still cheaper than Norwegian equivalents, UCN data shows.

'Monitoring this situation very carefully'

Herrmann said he's seen reports Norwegian producers are selling at barely break-even or even at a loss.

"All this has us on alert and monitoring this situation very carefully," he said.

The US Commerce Department considers dumping to be occurring if a product is sold in its home market or a third country at a lower price than it is in the US, while also taking into account the cost of production.

"In instances where you've got reporting indicating that Norwegian producers are selling in the home market at less than their cost of production, that's something that catches our attention," he said.

Norwegian gov’t postpones new salmon farming regulations until 2026 at earliest

A Commerce Department decision takes around 13 months to conduct once a petition is filed. But the federal agency can issue a preliminary dumping determination in as little as three months, and if it does so, duties on the items in question must be collected when they enter the US. 

It falls upon the petitioner -- in this case, the US salmon industry -- to prove the case.

Herrmann said he might also request an investigation into possible subsidization of the salmon industry by the Norwegian government, which would be done in a similar manner to a dumping inquiry, and which could result in the Commerce Department imposing a countervailing duty order.

Once Commerce has made its decisions, the bipartisan International Trade Commission (ITC) is responsible for evaluating them and determining whether US domestic industries are being harmed. If it agrees, a final order is issued and antidumping and countervailing duties are formally implemented.

"The point would be to ensure that Norwegian salmon coming into the United States is fairly priced, and that imports that are found to be injurious are not harming the domestic production of salmon here in the United States," Herrmann said.

Currently, there are two hurdles standing in the way of a speedy dumping or subsidization ruling. First, the ITC lacks three of its required six commissioners, and Herrmann guessed it could take 12 to 18 months for Trump to nominate candidates to fill the vacancies and to have them confirmed by the US Senate. In the meantime, the commission is functioning at reduced capacity.

Secondly, Herrmann will need to work to develop a better case that the Norwegian industry is subsidized. 

"It's something that we will need to update if a decision is made to go forward," he said. "Typically, what the Commerce Department looks at is loans at less-than-market interest rates, grants to the industry, the provision of inputs at less-than-market prices and export subsidies to encourage the production of products that are exported. And frankly, it's been a while since we've looked at those type of programs in Norway. So we need to update our research if the decision is made to go forward and come up with a petition."

History as warning

US antidumping or countervailing duties may be a long way off from becoming reality, but the Norwegian salmon industry learned how painful they could be in 1991, when the US imposed antidumping duties on Norwegian exporters ranging from 5% to 24%, depending on the company.

The duties were removed in 1996 after the Norwegian government agreed to require the industry to set minimum prices and to limit exported volumes, but Norwegian salmon industry's presence in the US market did not recover until 2012, when the antidumping order was fully revoked.

Norwegian Seafood Federation international department director Trond Davidsen

The NSC did not respond to a request for comment. Norwegian Seafood Federation international department director Trond Davidsen said his industry trade group is "not aware of any dumping accusations in the US market."

"We see absolutely no reason why such accusations should occur," Davidsen said. 

Norway's largest salmon producers -- Mowi, SalMar, Leroy, Cermaq and Grieg -- did not respond to requests for comment either.

Asked whether the salmon industries in other countries might face similar scrutiny, Herrmann said his focus remained on Norway for now.

Herrmann said the fact that the US industry is actually being represented by a Canadian company -- Cooke's Canadian and Chilean production dwarves its US output -- is irrelevant.

"If there's unfair trade that is occurring, that's going to be of concern to the industry producing salmon in the United States," he said.

Herrmann said he had no immediate plans to file a petition with the Commerce Department, but that "it's an evolving story."

"We're obviously going to keep a close eye on what's coming into the United States in the weeks and months to come, and we'll see where this goes," he said.

title: Smoked king salmon product recalled in Washington state over Listeria concerns
content:
Smoked wild white king salmon sold by a US butcher shop called Sunrise Meats Inc. of Port Angeles, Washington, is being recalled due to possible contamination with Listeria monocytogenes. The notice was published by the Washington State Department of Agriculture (WSDA) on Saturday (June 7).

WSDA reported that it discovered the Listeria contamination during routine sampling of Sunrise Meats. While the company has not received reports of illnesses associated with the recall, Sunrise Meats is said to be continuing to work with WSDA on its investigation into the source of the problem.

Screenshot: WSDA/ Facebook

The smoked wild white king salmon products impacted by the recall have a sell by/use by date of 7/21/2025. Products should be returned to the place of purchase for a refund.

title: California wildlife officers seize over 150 lbs of ‘black market’ salmon roe
content:
The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) is working to crack down on illegal caviar trafficking during fisheries closures, announcing recently that it seized more than 150 pounds of packaged salmon roe. The amount suggests about 75 salmon were illegally taken.

Officers with the CDFW's special operations unit and Delta Bay enhanced enforcement program were monitoring for illegal fishing activity along Sacramento Bay when a Dungeness crab trafficking investigation led to the discovery that the suspect was also involved in salmon poaching, according to the state agency.

"Evidence revealed a conspiracy to illegally harvest and process salmon roe for black market distribution," CDFW said in a press release.

Meanwhile, another investigation into sturgeon poaching led to two individuals being arrested and formally charged with taking an endangered or threatened species. Citations were issued to other individuals who were observed tying off illegally possessed sturgeon in an effort to evade wildlife officers.

This is not the US state's first problem with black market caviar rings. Eight people associated with a San Francisco, California, scheme were arrested in 2022 on suspicion of poaching white sturgeon from Sacramento Valley waterways. CDFW said in a press release at the time that multiple people were suspected of processing the sturgeon roe into caviar to sell in the illegal wildlife market.

title: Untitled
content:
NEWPORT, Oregon, USA -- The North Pacific Fishery Management Council (NPFMC) is asking the US groundfish fleet to develop rolling closure areas ahead of next year's A pollock season to conserve salmon and crab from bycatch caught in pelagic gear. 

The US pollock industry will report back at the NPMFC's December meeting held on the eve of 2026's A season to develop a plan for dynamic closures based on winter pot surveys and tagging data to conserve Bristol Bay red king crab harvests in the Bering Sea.

Alaska pollock industry reports successful A season, but chinook bycatch spiked

The 11-0 vote happened on Sunday (June 8), the seventh day of the nine-day meeting in Newport, Oregon, a fishing community that is the homeport of many groundfish trawlers fishing off the West Coast and Alaska.

It falls far short of demands by many crab and salmon harvesters -- and conservationists -- to crack down on pelagic gear from contacting the seafloor, which the industry admits is out of compliance with the decades-old definition for the midwater nets.  

US regulatory body rebuffs trawl critics

The NPFMC's advisory panel rejected calls by critics within its own ranks to reclassify pelagic gear to prohibit bottom contact on the seafloor, as Undercurrent News reported.

Instead, the NPFMC also moved to reclassify pelagic gear used for the midwater trawl nets for the first time in decades to make allowance for "salmon excluders" designed to reduce chinook and chum bycatch in the Bering Sea and Gulf of Alaska.

"Pelagic trawl gear has evolved since 1993, and the outdated regulations constrain innovation, including improvements for efficiency and bycatch avoidance," said NPFMC member Jon Kurland, the top Alaska official at the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS).

US efforts advance to curtail chum salmon bycatch in Alaska pollock fishery

That was in line with what the US pollock industry had been seeking.

"These updates are not only long overdue, they are also essential to ensuring the gear definition accurately reflects current fleet operations," said Andrea Keikkala, executive director of United Catcher Boats, one of the major pollock industry groups present at the meeting.

Tensions had been high between crab harvesters and trawlers over the impacts of pelagic gear on the seafloor, with Alaska harvesters complaining the meeting was being held more than a thousand miles away on the eve of the busiest time of year for salmon harvesters, as Undercurrent reported.

Crab harvesters like Kevin Abena of Kodiak, who fishes for Tanner crab in the Gulf of Alaska, complained that the NPFMC had sidestepped clarifying standards for pelagic gear for years.

"We need to know where you guys actually stand on this thing," Abena said during public comment.

Others, like Kodiak trawler Don Ashley, claimed that prohibiting bottom contact wouldn't be workable in practice.

"Nets do odd things when they're under the water," Ashley told the council. "They do things that we don't predict. And it can, it can go wrong very quickly."

New pelagic trawl definition protects status quo

The new definition will allow the status quo to continue by removing references to banned metallic components, flotation aids and other innovations that are used in salmon excluders to reduce bycatch that are also required in the fishery.

That answered the pollock industry's concern that the fleet should not be penalized for upgrading its gear to reduce bycatch.

"Any revision to this highly technical definition should not introduce new compliance challenges," said Glenn Merrill, a representative of Glacier Fish Company, which operates groundfish trawlers in the Bering Sea.

Gulf of Alaska groundfish closures advance to reduce Tanner crab bycatch

Most NPFMC members supported the direction to incrementally gather more information before imposing any radical reforms on the largest US fishery by volume. 

Crabbing interests on the NPFMC acknowledged that its pace won't satisfy critics demanding more concrete action.

"We've heard from many stakeholders that they want to see this definition state whether or not the expectation is that the gear will have bottom contact," said NPFMC member Jamie Goen, executive director of Alaska Bering Sea Crabbers.

She added:  "I agree that we need to be more clear on that expectation."

That will come from the industry-led "Gear Innovation Initiative" that studies the efficacy and challenges of the pelagic gear with a report deadline set for the NPFMC's April 2026 meeting. 

The only opposition came from NPFMC member Anne Vanderhoeven, a trawl industry executive whose reappointment by the administration of US president Joe Biden was a source of controversy, as Undercurrent reported.

"Industry has typically been able to step up and meet these kinds of requests," Vanderhoeven said. "But I think we have so many demands on them at this point in an incredibly challenging time, we're asking them to move mountains without enough information, time or resources to do so, and I think that kind of sets them up for failure in the public eye."

Tribes decry revolving door with industry

The apparent symbiosis between US regional fishery councils and the seafood sector they are charged with regulating has been a simmering source of controversy, especially among Indigenous tribal groups and conservationists who complain that industry has an outsized voice, as Undercurrent reported.

Alaska tribes call for cap on chum bycatch for Bering Sea pollock trawlers

That charge was voiced by Indigenous activists during public comment.

"It's no secret that many council members are directly employed by or financially tied to the industry sectors that stand to benefit from their decisions," said Craig Chythlook, fisheries policy director for Native Peoples Action, a campaign group based in Anchorage, Alaska.

"How can we expect fair and science-based policy and the same companies that profit from pollock trawling are the ones drafting motion, shaping the science and setting the rules," Chythlook added.

It's true that almost all of the NPFMC's council and panel appointees are employed in the seafood industry. But ultimately, the two motions that passed came from government officials, rather than industry professionals. The initiative to redefine pelagic gear to bring it in line with modern practices was introduced by Kurland, a senior NMFS administrator. 

The motion to set a timeline for industry-led working groups to craft closure areas to conserve Bristol Bay red king crab and revisit pelagic gear performance came from Rachel Baker, a deputy commissioner for the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G).

Even so, in making her motion, ADF&G's Baker made it clear that the regulatory body would be taking its cues from industry.

"These are voluntary measures that the council is requesting the pollock industry to take on," she said.

title: Canadian retailers get failing grade on seafood traceability in new report
content:
Half of the seafood sold by major Canadian retailers is excluded from their own sustainability and ethical sourcing policies, according to findings published in the recent "Seafood Progress" report from environmental advocacy group SeaChoice.

The report is the first of its kind to review what measures Canadian retailers are taking to keep products tied to human rights abuses off store shelves, as well as which stores, products and brand types their seafood policies actually apply to, SeaChoice said in a press release.

The report gave failing grades on human rights and environmental due diligence to all but one grocery retailer assessed.

METRO, a food retailer with locations in Ontario and Quebec, was noted to have "an adequate response."

Pattison Food Group, western Canada's largest grocery retailer, which is based in the province of British Columbia (BC) and owns chains such as Save-On-Foods and Buy-Low Foods, received the lowest overall score for ongoing failures to improve traceability, according to the SeaChoice report.

Others, like Ontario-based Loblaws, and Atlantic Canada-based Sobeys, were heavily criticized for sidestepping accountability and transparency obligations in the face of mounting global evidence of abuse.

"The investigations are piling up. Retailers can't afford to keep turning a blind eye," said Dana Cleaveley, a SeaChoice supply chain analyst.

"None of the companies assessed are meaningfully incorporating worker perspectives into sourcing decisions, and that's a critical failure when it comes to effective due diligence," Cleaveley stated in a press release.

The silence from retailers, despite such exposés, highlights a dangerous pattern of "conscious avoidance," said SeaChoice.

The report also criticizes the overreliance on voluntary eco-certifications and social audits, which have repeatedly failed to detect human rights abuses. With North American regulatory frameworks still lagging, retailers need to adopt due diligence approaches and advocate for stronger enforcement, the advocacy group said.

"Retailers are leaving themselves exposed -- legally and reputationally -- by continuing to sell products linked to forced labour and illegal fishing," Cleaveley said. "The only way forward is for retailers to take responsibility and build robust, traceable supply chains that protect both people and the planet."

The report also spotlights inconsistencies in policy coverage. For instance, Loblaw's seafood sustainability commitments apply to its Real Canadian Superstore banner but not to T&T Supermarket, a major seafood seller under its umbrella. Similar policy gaps were found in seafood-containing products like pet food and health supplements.

With tariffs and trade pressures increasing demand for local seafood, SeaChoice suggests retailers have an opportunity to refocus sourcing efforts closer to home, where traceability is often more feasible.

"Canadian retailers can lead by example by prioritizing domestic, responsibly harvested seafood," said Cleaveley.

SeaChoice is a collaboration of three environmental organizations, including the David Suzuki Foundation and the Living Oceans Society, based in the province of British Columbia, and the Nova Scotia-based Ecology Action Centre.

The report's release coincided with the launch of season two of the Outlaw Ocean Project's podcast, which continues to expose egregious labour and environmental crimes in the global seafood sector.

title: Untitled
content:
As the world's largest snow crab fishery steams along, with 27,728 metric tons, or 44.4%, of the 62,463t quota remaining to be caught in the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador (NL), more bad blood is brewing between the harvesters' union and crab processors.

Historically, the two sides have had a testy relationship, mistrusting each other over crab prices and disagreeing on fishing polices while maintaining a tit-for-tat series of allegations on a myriad of industry topics.

The latest episode in the longstanding saga came Friday (May 30) when Dwan Street, president of the Fish Food and Allied Workers (FFAW), the union that represents crab harvesters and some plant workers, called a NL radio talk show alleging that some processors were up to some shenanigans to try to limit out-of-province crab-buying competition. 

Dwan Street. Photo from her Facebook page.

Some members of the Association of Seafood Producers (ASP), the trade group representing most NL crab processors, have been shipping unprocessed crab to processor friends in the Maritimes to squelch competition, she alleged.

That amounts to collusion, Street told Undercurrent News in an interview this week, specifically naming Ocean Choice International (OCI) and Quinlan Brothers as being guilty of supplying crab to processors in Nova Scotia in return for a promise that they won't compete against NL processors.

"It's clear what's going on here. They're stifling competition, they're stifling prices, and they're putting plant workers' livelihoods at risk," Street told Undercurrent.

That's nonsense, contend Blaine and Martin Sullivan, the two brothers who lead OCI.

"Our company is fully committed to Newfoundland and Labrador's processing sector and the communities that depend on it. Any suggestion otherwise is simply false," they said in an email statement to Undercurrent.

They said OCI has consistently imported crab from harvesters in the Maritimes to support production at its facilities in NL.

Sweeping changes announced for world’s largest snow crab fishery

"Over the last five years, we have brought in millions of pounds, providing dozens of extra weeks of employment and supporting longer operating seasons at our crab processing plants in the province," the Sullivans stated.

OCI acknowledged that it did ship a "small amount" of crab to a longstanding partner in Nova Scotia during peak production time this season to accommodate landings from harvesters and manage plant capacity.

"Overflow product was shipped out during peak landings to ensure that all harvested crab could be handled in a timely and responsible manner," the Sullivans said.

And there's nothing illegal about that.

Officials at Quinlan Brothers could not be reached for comment.

Provincial action sought

Under NL regulations adopted last year to allow the shipment of unprocessed crab from the province, buyers from other provinces can access NL crab, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

Rough Water Traps, a one-man operation based in Placentia, NL, has been arranging crab shipments to Nova Scotia, thanks to the province's new "outside buyer" rules implemented in 2024 by former fisheries minister Gerry Byrne. 

That company has been buying crab from NL harvesters since last season and shipping it to a processor in Nova Scotia, basically acting as a buying agent for that company, owner Matt O'Leary told Undercurrent in a recent interview.

Before last year's rule change, all crab landed in NL had to be processed (cooked and frozen) in the province.

However, Street suggests something more nefarious is at play.

Crab harvesters in the Maritime provinces were paid as much as CAD 8.00 ($5.86) per pound for their catches earlier this spring. In contrast, NL harvesters settled for a dock price of CAD 4.97/lb, with a formula that could see them paid extra at the end of the season, if average wholesale prices increase through the season, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

The FFAW contends NL processors don't want processors from other provinces to tempt NL harvesters with higher prices.

"What is happening here is members of the ASP, namely Quinlan Brothers and OCI, maybe others, but these are the two that I had the first-hand evidence on, are going to the Maritimes (processors) and saying: 'If you agree to not come down here and pay harvesters, then we'll make sure that there's crab pumping through your plants and your operations are going smoothly,'" Street said on the VOCM Open Line program. Street's comment come at the 02:05:31 mark of the May 30 episode.

Street did not share more details about that "first-hand" information or where it came from during her radio call-in.

But she did offer some extra details to Undercurrent.

"We've had harvesters come forward to say, I watched my crabs that I sold to Quinlan Brothers go on a truck. The plant is closed, and the truck is headed straight to the mainland. And it was 100,000 lbs, that one shipment, of high-quality RSW (recirculating seawater system) premium crab," said Street.

Meanwhile, unionized crab plant workers, as well as some people at non-union plants, have contacted the FFAW to say they are worried about getting enough hours of work this crab season to qualify for post-season employment insurance benefits, said Street.

Pace of crab landings in Newfoundland expected to increase with better weather, regulation change

"Quinlan Brothers is not unionized, but their workers have still been reaching out to us with their concerns. And at the Independent Fish Harvesters in Brigus, not our members, but we're hearing from those workers as well, that production is significantly slower than last year. They're being sent home early and have weekends off, which is completely unprecedented," said Street.

"We're calling on the provincial government to dig into this, to start holding these crooks accountable, to hold their feet to the fire, ask them what exactly is going on," Street told the moderator of the Open Line program.

The union also plans to seek answers from Nova Scotia, said Street, indicating letters will be sent to the premier of Nova Scotia on the matter.

Crab trade is two-way street between NL, NS

In Nova Scotia, there's bemusement over the allegations.

"I watched the noise about this argument about collusion, and I really don't see it," offered Kris Vascotto, executive director of the Nova Scotia Seafood Alliance, the trade group representing most of the province's seafood processors.

"I would argue that Nova Scotia processors are helping keep prices up in NL. They are providing demand for a product," Vascotto told Undercurrent in an interview this week.

Even if Nova Scotia processors were coming directly to NL to purchase crab, the cost factors are such that there's very little likelihood of higher dock prices for NL harvesters, added Vascotto.

"I can give you a great example. I have one processor in Nova Scotia who was procuring crab from NL. He sent a truck and driver over to Newfoundland to pick up the product, and the driver was stuck in Newfoundland for well over a week because of weather and ferry delays. So the cost of bringing crab over was a lot higher than anticipated," Vascotto told Undercurrent.

"So that gives you an idea of the economic forces that are in play in terms of softening the prices for NL crab," he said.

Besides, said Vascotto, crab shipments go both ways. 

Crab from the Gulf of St. Lawrence fishery, which typically starts earlier than the NL fishery, is also trucked into NL for processing, helping power up some plants and get people back to work ahead of the NL crab season, noted Vascotto.

"In the spring there's a real need for Newfoundland to access Nova Scotia product. Without it, your operations get compressed into a couple of months and financial viability goes way down," he said.

"Any rational person can look at this from a business sense and say: it works both ways and it's an incredibly expensive proposition to get product out of there (NL), so this is not collusion. It's just about people trying to operate plants," said Vascotto.

Processor, province react

Meanwhile, the NL Department of Fisheries, Forestry and Agriculture (DFFA) said it is reviewing the FFAW's concerns. The agency also reiterated the rules applicable to shipping unprocessed crab from NL.

Licence holders are exempt from minimum processing requirements, but for each shipment going out of province, they must provide the department with at least 12 hours' written notice prior to the shipment. 

"The written notice to the department shall include all bill of landing and shipping documents," the department noted.

"Issues related to price collusion or price fixing could potentially be addressed under the federal Competition Act," the department told Undercurrent in an email statement on behalf of fisheries minister Lisa Dempster.

On Thursday (June 5) the FFAW succeeded in getting a meeting with NL premier John Hogan to offer a suggestion.

“FFAW-Unifor has proposed provincially monitored sales reporting as a condition of licence. This would ensure fish harvesters don’t bear the brunt of bad-faith market manipulations and would also eliminate the need to ship product out of the province," the FFAW said in a Facebook post that day.

The FFAW met with Newfoundland and Labrador premier John Hogan on Thursday (June 5) and posted an update from that meeting on their Facebook page. Photo screenshot from FFAW Facebook page

As for plant workers' worries over hours of work, OCI said its facilities have been operating near full capacity this season, with any processing delays due primarily to weather.

"Workers are receiving hours comparable to previous years, and there are no concerns regarding employees not getting sufficient work," said the Sullivans.

The company also pointed out that FFAW and crab harvesters in NL have long advocated for access to outside buyers and a more open, free-enterprise system.

"So it is surprising and disappointing to now face criticism for pursuing the very measures they've supported for years," said the Sullivans, adding, "We intend to hold the president of the FFAW accountable for her actions and statements on this matter."

Ocean Choice International's Chief Executive Officer Martin Sullivan (left) and Chief Operating Officer Blaine Sullivan, at Seafood Expo North America 2025. Photo by Barb Dean-Simmons

This is not the first time harvesters have alleged collusion among fish processors.

In 2019, the Federation of Independent Seafood Harvesters-NL (FISH-NL), a group headed by Ryan Cleary, asked Canada's Competition Bureau to investigate collusion when a shrimp harvester in the province, who had been selling to one processor, was rejected when he tried to make a deal with another processor to buy his catch.

"Officials with the Competition Bureau say the people they interviewed wouldn't give up names, and they couldn't get the information they needed to carry out an investigation," Cleary said in a media interview at the time.

title: Norwegian gov’t postpones new salmon farming regulations until 2026 at earliest
content:
The Norwegian parliament, the Storting, has agreed to postpone sweeping aquaculture reform proposals until next year at the earliest.

Norwegian government proposes big changes in aquaculture permitting

The six largest parties in the Storting adopted a broad compromise on June 5 which sees the new regulatory framework proposed by the current centre-left Labour government put on hold while investigations are conducted into the potential impact of the different models on the table.

The idea is that a new proposed system will return to parliament, backed by broader political support to give the salmon sector greater predictability between governments.

In the meantime, the existing maximum allowed biomass and 'traffic light' system will remain in place.

However, a new 'technology-neutral' license framework will still be introduced from this autumn to incentivize farmers with zero lice emissions at sites in western Norway, in production areas three and four near Bergen.

Both zones are currently rated red by the traffic light scheme and farmers will therefore be forced to reduce biomass, but under the new scheme, farms that have invested in technology to eliminate all sea lice emissions from their sites will be spared.

Then, 2026 may see the new environmental incentive scheme expanded beyond western Norway, depending on the outcome of next year's traffic light evaluations.

Sjomat Norge happy to see proposal postponed

Back in April, the government proposed in its Havbruksmelding white paper a system that would see production growth tied to company sea lice figures, alongside a tax on excessive salmon mortalities. This would also see a transition from traditional farming licenses to quotas on the total sea lice released from farms.

However, critics in the industry said the white paper was light on detail about how these lice quotas would be calculated. According to bank analysts at DNB, if measures were taken to immediately pursue the mortality thresholds and lice targets within the proposal, it would slash national salmon production by roughly 500,000 metric tons overnight.

Current form of Norway’s salmon white paper would cut production by 500,000t, says DNB

The decision to postpone the move to new regulations was welcomed by Norwegian seafood representative body Sjomat Norge.

"The Storting has concluded that the industry needs new regulations, but that we need more knowledge about the different models on the table," said Sjomat Norge CEO Geir Ystmark.

"It is important that the industry is not thrown into a dramatic restructuring, as was proposed in the Havbruksmelding, without the consequences having ben studied. The Storting understood that."

Economists had also raised queries over the impact that phasing out licenses would have on the industry's financial structure, given that existing biomass licenses from the cornerstone of most farmers' debt collateral.

The Storting has also requested that the existing Directorate of Fisheries be expanded into a new 'Deparment of Fisheries and Aquaculture'. 

"Aquaculture is one of the few industries that does not have its own specialist directorate," said Ystmark. "The administration is very fragmented; this leads to long case processing times. Therefore, it is necessary that such a directorate be given sufficient powers to cut through."

A final version of the white paper will go to a parliamentary vote on June 12.

title: Untitled
content:
Shareholders representing about 30% of Icelandic salmon farmer Kaldvik have requested an extraordinary general meeting to investigate a controversial acquisition completed in March, the company said on Wednesday (June 4).

The shareholders are seeking a probe into Kaldvik's NOK 190 million ($18.8m) purchase of Icelandic fish box producer Djupskel, property company Mossi, and a 33% stake in fish processor Bulandstindur from related parties Heimsto and Osnes. 

Kaldvik completes $18m deal for Iceland processing assets

The transaction, completed on March 25, has drawn criticism since it was announced. Board member Adalsteinn Ingolfsson resigned in January in protest over the planned deal, claiming the assets were overvalued and that majority shareholder Heimsto was "profiting abnormally at the expense of other shareholders."

The Oslo-listed company operates under Norwegian company law. If 10% or more of share capital represented at the meeting votes in favor, shareholders can force an investigation to be opened. The outcome of any such probe would be difficult to predict, Kaldvik said.

The controversy centers on allegations that the deal constituted a conflict of interest, with Heimsto being Kaldvik's largest shareholder through its 55.29% stake via real estate firm Austur Holding. Two board members who voted for the transaction are Heimsto's CEO and CFO, according to Ingolfsson's resignation statement.

The former board member had criticized the use of newly issued shares priced at NOK 27.6 each to fund much of the purchase, arguing this was below analyst valuations of NOK 35-41 per share. 

Board member resigns from Icelandic salmon farmer over price of planned M&A

The shareholder revolt comes as Kaldvik moves ahead with other capital market activities. On Thursday, the company announced it had completed a substantial NOK 532m private placement, issuing 38m new shares at NOK 14 each to fund biomass build-up and debt repayment.

Heimsto's Austur Holding was allocated about 27m shares in the placement, maintaining its controlling position.

Kaldvik also said it may conduct a subsequent offering of up to 4.3m shares for eligible shareholders who were excluded from the private placement, subject to board approval at an extraordinary meeting expected around June 19.

The company has not yet announced a date for the shareholder-requested investigation meeting.

DNB Carnegie, Arion Banki and Nordea served as bookrunners for the private placement, while law firm Thommessen advised Kaldvik.

title: Chile’s Blumar reports turnaround in profitability during Q1, driven by salmon sales
content:
A sharp recovery in its aquaculture segment benefited Chilean seafood company Blumar's financial performance in the first quarter of 2025.

The group's revenue surged 50% year-on-year to $209.3 million during the quarter, while earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) rose 55% to $35.6m, as shown in the table below.

Blumar's quarterly revenue, EBITDA and profit. Source: Blumar's Q1 results.

The company's net profit was $28m, reversing a $1.8m loss in Q1 2024.

Aquaculture segment drives growth

Blumar's aquaculture division was the key contributor to the improved results, benefiting from a 186% increase in harvested volumes, especially in Chile's Magallanes region. The company reported a harvest of 20,000 metric tons WFE (whole fish equivalent) in Q1 2025, up from 7,000t in the same period last year. 

Atlantic salmon prices remained stable, averaging $7.23 per kilogram WFE, slightly above the $7.16/kg recorded in Q1 2024.

Operational efficiency also improved significantly. Lower feed costs and higher volumes contributed to a reduction in ex-cage cultivation costs, helping boost EBIT margins. The salmon division is expected to see a sharp improvement in EBITDA during 2025, as shown in the graph below.
The Aysen and Magallanes regions delivered positive EBIT results, with the Magallanes region standing out due to strong sanitary and production performance, Blumar said.

Salmon spot prices rose by 10% following the announcement of US reciprocal tariffs, then dropped 10%, returning to early April levels. The firm also noted that Chile and Canada lost market share in the US, while Norway's share increased.

Blumar's sales, broken down by products. Salmon sales rose by 164% y-o-y during Q1 2025.

Blumar also reported it is in the final phase of recovering insurance related to the fire at its EntreVientos plant in the Magallanes region, which had previously impacted operations.

Subsidiary St. Andrews, which specializes in mussel production and commercialization, experienced a strong recovery in sales prices, helping restore business margins, as shown in the table below.

St. Andrews's results. Source: Blumar's Q1 results.

While the aquaculture segment drove the bulk of Blumar's Q1 2025 growth, the firm's fishing division delivered steady operational performance, supported by improved efficiency and favorable catch conditions.

Blumar's jack mackerel season started off well, with catch volumes in line with those of Q1 2024, the firm said.

There was a significant 51% drop in purchases from artisanal fisheries in northern Chile, due to lower fish availability. In contrast, the south saw a strong recovery in artisanal raw material supply, up 62% compared to Q1 2024, thanks to an earlier start of the artisanal fishing season, according to Blumar.

Prices for fishmeal and fish oil were adjusted downward due to increased supply from Peru.

Fishmeal prices. Source: Blumar's Q1 results.

Fish oil prices. Source: Blumar's Q1 results.

Chilean fishmeal prices were especially impacted, falling 19%, while fish oil prices have yet to see significant contract closures, according to Blumar. The regional fisheries organization quota for jack mackerel has been increased by 25% for 2025, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

Meanwhile, Blumar said the new legislation modifying the allocation system is in its final processing stages and is expected to take effect in 2026.

The firm noted that the Chilean congress approved changes to quota allocations for 17 out of 18 fisheries. It pointed out that the jack mackerel industrial quota would be reduced from 90% to 70%, while for sardine and anchovy, the industrial quota would be reduced from 22% to 10%.

For hake, the industrial quota will be decreased from 60% to 48%. This must still be ratified by both legislative chambers, Blumar noted, adding that companies affected by these changes (current allocations were valid until 2032) are considering legal action, claiming the quota shift is an unlawful expropriation of property without compensation.

Moreover, a proposal to auction off quota increases for jack mackerel was rejected. As a result, a joint committee will explore alternatives to cover the resulting fiscal shortfall, since artisanal quotas are not taxed. One option under consideration is introducing a license fee on international jack mackerel quotas purchased by the industry from other countries. 

The firm also said that the Bruma boat accident is under investigation, with responsibility still being determined.

title: FDA places 5-year import ban on large Mississippi seafood wholesaler
content:
Quality Poultry and Seafood (QPS), the Biloxi, Mississippi-based seafood wholesaler that pleaded guilty last year to conspiring to mislabel seafood and commit wire fraud by marketing frozen imported fish as more expensive locally caught species, is now also blocked from making imports.

The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) announced Thursday (May 29) in the Federal Register that it's "debarring QPS for a period of five years from importing articles of food or offering such articles for importation into the United States."

The order stems from the company's 2024 conviction of conspiring to commit misbranding and wire fraud.

An FDA investigation, in 2018, found that QPS, which supplied seafood and poultry to restaurants, casinos and retail markets, was fraudulently purchasing frozen seafood from foreign countries and selling it as local premium species. QPS continued to sell mislabeled seafood "even after the September 2018 search of QPS facilities," the federal agency said.

Photo Credit: Quality Poultry & Seafood Facebook

As part of its guilty plea, the company ultimately ended up forfeiting $1 million and paying a $150,000 fine, as reported by Undercurrent News.

QPS failed to issue a timely response to FDA's notice of import debarrment, sent in February, thereby waving its opportunity for a hearing,  the FDA said in its Federal Register notice.

The case against QPS also involved the company's sales manager, Todd Rosetti, and business manager, James Gunkel, who pleaded guilty to misbranding seafood. Mary Mahoney's Old French House, a fine-dining restaurant in Billoxi, Mississippi, was also sentenced in a federal court on charges related to its participation in the conspiracy to misbrand imported seafood.

The restaurant was given five years probation and issued a $1.5m penalty, which included the forfeiture of $1,350,000 and a criminal fine of $149,000. In addition to that, Mary Mahoney's was ordered to maintain records in which it describes species, sources and the cost of the seafood it acquired, as reported by Undercurrent.

title: FDA issues warning letters to four foreign seafood processors
content:
Seafood processors from Venezuela, South Korea, Nicaragua and France have all received warning letters from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the federal agency recently revealed.

The FDA made the letters available just this past month, but issued them in 2024. One letter, sent Nov. 1, 2024, to Venezuela's Yeshua Bendito, highlights a handful of violations from a foreign remote regulatory assessment conducted by the FDA in June 2024. 

"During our assessment, we found that you had serious violations of the Seafood Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) regulation," the US agency noted in its letter. 

The primary complaint is that the company's cooked, ready-to-eat, refrigerated- and frozen-crab is adulterated, in that it has "been prepared, packed, or held under conditions whereby they may have been rendered injurious to health." 

The FDA flagged another foreign processor of ready-to-eat seafood products in a separate letter, dated Nov. 6, 2024. This letter, also published in May 2025, was sent to South Korea's Eden F&C Co. The US agency said an April 2024 inspection found "serious" HACCP violations of its ready-to-eat seafood-containing corn dog products. 

The final two warning letters published by the FDA last month were both sent in December 2024.

One letter was sent to Nicaragua-based Rey de los Camarones S.A. on Dec. 23, 2024, stemming from an August 2024 inspection. Per the notice, the company's dried and salted sea cucumber products were determined to be adulterated.

Another letter was sent to France's Reunipeche SAS on Dec. 26, 2024, based off a July 2024 inspection. According to the warning letter, the company's whole fresh fish was found to be "adulterated, in that they have been prepared, packed, or held under conditions whereby they may have been rendered injurious to health."

The FDA is threatening to place all of Reunipeche's products on a "detention without physical examination" (DWPE) list if the company does not respond in 15 days, or if the response is found to be "inadequate."

title: Untitled
content:
Tariffs on, tariffs off... Tariffs on? We've got whiplash this week.

The Undercurrent News team is continuing to follow the day-to-day chaos that is US president Donald Trump's trade war with the entire world. But we're not letting tariffs dominate the complete conversation on Catch the Current this week. 

Undercurrent's Dan Gibson joins Catch the Current hosts Amanda Buckle and Lorin Castiglione, fresh off his flight from Iceland where he was covering the Icelandic Aquaculture and Oceans Forum (IAOF). Dan shares some insight on Iceland's aquaculture industry and how the country can compete in the farmed salmon space. 

Also featured this week is American Seafoods' chief sustainability officer Tim Fitzgerald and At-Sea Processors Association vice president Caitlin Yeager, who called in from Seattle, Washington, on Wednesday (May 28) to talk about the pollock industry's Net Recycling Day and its importance.

Plus, Lorin provides market updates for scallops and salmon, and UCN analyst Gary Morrison drops in to share the latest on snow crab. Listen to the latest episode below on YouTube.

Subscribe now! Catch the Current is available on YouTube, Spotify, Amazon Music, iHeartRadio, Pandora, and other major podcast streaming platforms. Don't see Catch the Current on your favorite app? Reach out to podcasts@undercurrentnews.com.

Don't have time to listen? Find a full transcript of season 1, episode 19 of Catch the Current below:

Amanda Buckle (AB): You're listening to Catch the Current, the coolest seafood podcast out there, from the team at Undercurrent News, your trusted source for seafood prices, news and data. I'm Amanda Buckle.

Lorin Castiglione (LC): And I’m Lorin Castiglione. Well, the plan wasn't to talk about US president Donald Trump and his tariffs in this week's episode... but surprise, surprise, here we are.

On Wednesday evening, the US Court of International Trade -- in response to two separate cases filed by businesses and US states impacted by the tariffs -- declared that the president lacked the authority to impose tariffs under the 1977 International Emergency Economic Powers Act or IEEPA. 

AB: So, what does that mean?

LC: Tell me, please. And quickly!

US president Donald Trump announcing retaliatory tariffs on April 2, 2025. Photo Credit: The White House/ Facebook

AB: Well, my understanding is that the courts order halts the 10% Liberation Day tariffs that Trump put in place last month. And it also halts the order on the 30% tariff placed on China and 25% tariffs of Canada and Mexico. As Undercurrent has been reporting, some of these tariff have been postponed or already reduced by subsequent declarations from the president.

So, all that information is up to date on our website. I'm not even going to try to give that to you in podcast form here. 

LC: What this ruling from the court doesnt impact are the tariffs that were set under Section 232 or Section 301 of the Trade Expansion Act, which includes some tariffs on Chinese seafood.

The court gave the White House up to 10 days to unwind the tariffs impacted by its decision. But a White House spokesperson told the New York Times that it plans to file an appeal.

The spokesperson said: "It is not for unelected judges to decide how to properly address a national emergency," adding that Mr. Trump would use "every lever of executive power to address this crisis."

Trump’s tariffs switched back on by federal appeals court

AB:  Spoiler alert! Things have already changed since we recorded this podcast. The US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit has paused a ruling that nullified most tariffs imposed earlier this year by US president Donald Trump. This all happened on Thursday, May 29, in the afternoon. The court granted the Trump administration's request to temporarily pause a ruling issued May 28 by the US Court of International Trade. So stick to UndercurrentNews.com for all the latest information because I cannot update this podcast again before we publish it. 

Now we're excited to welcome UCN's Dan Gibson, fresh off a flight from Iceland's capital, where he was reporting live from the third annual Icelandic Aquaculture and Oceans Forum.

The two-day event, which is hosted by Arion Bank, was created to represent the growing aquaculture sector in Iceland -- including sea-based and land-based farms. 

So Dan, you had some pretty interesting headlines in the blog this week. One of them was that Canadian processor High Liner sees a big future for Icelandic seafood in the US. What else can you tell us from the event?

Dan Gibson (DG): Surprisingly, first of all, there were some really, really big names there. This is the third year they've been running it. And aquaculture is not a huge industry in Iceland, but it is growing and you can see how seriously they took it by some of the people who were there.

IAOF 2025: ‘Party over’ for US salmon sales within a year; Atlantic Sapphire concerns less of a threat to investor interest

There was the CEO of Skretting, Bastiaan van Tilburg. There was of course the CEO, as you mentioned there, of High Liner, Paul Jewer. High Liner has made no secret that they are looking to gain access to raw material in Europe and especially in Norway, they've made investments in NorCod, a cod farmer, and Andfjord Salmon, the land-based flow-through salmon farmer up there. So to see him in Iceland, he again makes no secret that they want to make more investments to gain stakes in these resources.

And when you think about it, it makes a lot of sense because Iceland right now only produces 50,000 tons of salmon a year. So for perspective, Norway harvests 1.5 million metric tons a year. So Iceland is just a drop in the ocean, but they have big, big plans for land-based salmon farming, especially in the south of the country.

And in total, they've got five huge projects -- they're talking over €3 billion of capital expenditures will be required to build them. And then when they're finished, the idea is you're looking at about 170,000t of production. And the thing, of course, is that Iceland does not have particularly big processing facilities for salmon.

Land-farmed Icelandic salmon from First Water. Credit: First Water's website

It's quite a new species for a new sector. So you can imagine that Paul Jewer and High Liner are very interested in helping to take some of that burden off their hands, especially if these plans come to fruition. And they're going to be seeing so much raw material coming online. I was actually taken on a tour of First Water, one of the largest of these upcoming projects.

They've already, I think, been funded with around about €250 million. And their plan is to grow and to build a farm that would produce 50,000t in this one plot of land on the south of the country. So you're basically talking all of Iceland's national current production of salmon, repeated again, just from one site. And you could see that the building work was going on.

AB: So they were in the middle of construction?

DG: Yeah. So they're at this point where they are just piecing it together, really. They've got the first phase. It's one they've been working through, and they've got a design that means that you can add batches of tanks online at a time rather than, say, for instance, something like Atlantic Sapphire down in Florida, that sort of built one big, huge unit and now has to follow that with another big, huge unit that's going to take several years.

And each of these Icelandic operations, they're talking about adding 4,000-5,000t of capacity each year. From there, it will be a question of how fast they can utilize that capacity, as well as the question of will it be profitable.

That's the other thing. Because I should make clear here, unlike Atlantic Sapphire, these land-based operations, they're not recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS). They are hybrid flow-through. So whereas with a RAS system, you're talking 100% the water goes in staying in the flow and very little of it is ever replaced, with a hybrid flow-through system, only about 30% to 70% of it is recycled. The rest is sort of new water being pumped up from underground. And they've demonstrated that it works as a form for growing salmon.

There's a company -- Salmon Evolution in Norway -- they produced close to 5,000t last year. So they demonstrated that it does work and you can successfully grow salmon with very low mortalities.

The problem, of course, is that it is capital-intensive. As I mentioned, huge sums of money are needed to build these facilities. And so for them, a high salmon price is not so much something they'd like as it is a necessity in order to make the whole project economically viable and to get a good return on investment for the people who have invested in it.

Of course, one of the big topics of conversation this year, salmon prices have surprisingly tanked about half of where they were at the same time last year. And so there were investors asking and sort of finding out -- what's the prospect for the future? Because the salmon industry has thrived basically on having this gap between supply and demand where they have a constant shortage of supply versus demand. But this year demand just isn't there. So obviously they're very hopeful it comes back.

The other question is from Iceland's point of view. They're right next door to the biggest growing salmon market in the world in the US. And when you consider the volumes that the US currently takes in -- they're taking in 200,000t of salmon annually from Chile. So you can see 175,000t, if this comes to fruition, coming out of Iceland, where's that going to go? It's very obvious that Canada and the US are the clear number-one destinations since demand doesn't really change in Europe and China and the Far East, and the Norwegians have that locked up.

So it does seem like that. They are going to be very dependent on there being the demand they need from North America. And so to have to come back to the start there, to have High Liner present and taking an interest is a really promising sign for them.

AB: And Dan's full blog ... I was reading through it. Dan, I can't even believe it was two days. It's like a novel's worth of content you were able to wrap up from there. It's truly amazing. So people should definitely check out that blog if you have not done so already.

So with farm salmon covered, also joining us on the pod today to talk about wild salmon is UCN's Jacob Resneck.

So Jacob, what's going on with Alaska's wild fisheries right now? Because your latest article just came out and Copper River is temporarily not fishing right now. Is that correct?

Jacob Resneck (JR): They're just taking a little break.

Alaska fishery conservation measures temporarily halt Copper River salmon harvest

So we're really early. I mean, really early in what would be the Alaska salmon harvest, because Copper River heralds the official opening of the wild salmon season. It opened May 22.

They have limited fishing opportunities. They usually fish twice a week for these $12 openings. And there's been a really excellent forecast of nearly 2m sockeye salmon projected for 2025. Now to put that in context, we had about 1.37m harvested commercially last year, which exceeded the forecast by the state managers. So there's a lot of optimism right now.

They've run two openers so far. The fish have not been showing up yet. The numbers were a little lackluster for sockeye, down from what they had this time last year. But the concern was the chinook, the king salmon, which there's a lot of scrutiny on for conservation.

So what they do, and what they've done -- they announced just the other day -- is they're going to shut down the anticipated fishery.

They were supposed to be fishing, or expected to be fishing, on Thursday, May 29. And they're taking a break. And they're going to reassess over the weekend to see how much escapement has come through. And there's hope that they'll resume fishing next week.

**Editor's note on Thursday (May 29) evening it was announced that the fishery would reopen for 12 hours on Saturday (May 31).

AB: Now is this something that happens every year?

JR: This is something that can happen anytime you have dynamic fishing management like what is done by the Alaska Department of Fish and Game. They measure the escapement, which is the fish that are not captured by the fleet, that get up to freshwater to spawn for future seasons.

They have to make sure they get that escapement, because if they don't, they won't have runs in the future. So the biologists, they manage every couple of days. They open and close the fishery to make sure they get that escapement. And so this is something that definitely can happen.

It's not doom and gloom. Sometimes the run shows up late. But the reason there's a lot of scrutiny on this is because it's a very hyper-marketed niche product, Copper River salmon. It's a delicacy known the world over.

Alaska Airlines hits ‘pause’ on Copper River salmon red carpet at Seattle airport

It's also the first sockeye and wild king salmon from Alaska that hits the market because it's the first fishery. So it fetches a high price there too. So there's hoping that the run will pick up. But yeah, they're just taking a little breather right now.

AB: And of course, that's not the only drama that's going on up in Alaska right now. And as someone with an entertainment journalism background, I live for the drama. So I have been just living for your coverage of Northline's Hannah. Can you just give a brief recap there?

JR: Yeah, so we'll switch over to Bristol Bay, which is the largest wild sockeye fishery in the world. And that doesn't get going until the end of June and really usually peaks around the July 4 holiday.

As our listeners know, there's been a lot of consolidation in the processing side with Silver Bay Seafoods taking a stake in OBI Seafoods. So we're down to four major players buying fish on Bristol Bay, this huge fishery. And so there's a lot of concern because Northline Seafoods, one of the four, they have this flagship freezer barge that they built in 2023 and last year was its first season, which they run up to the Nushagak district. It anchors off in Clark Point and it takes in fish. And a lot of the work that was done to make this vessel into this floating seafood platform, a lot of the vendors have still haven't been paid. We covered that earlier in the year. Well, the plot thickened when one of the lienholders, a welding contractor, filed in federal court under maritime law asking for US authorities to seize the vessel over non-payment.

And the judge went as far as signing a warrant, allowing the vessel to be seized over this. It didn't quite happen in the eleventh hour. It looks like Northline Seafoods was able to secure a bond as alternative collateral.

AB: It was a real nail-biter there.

JR: Yeah, because if the vessel was seized or there had been an injunction precluding them from leaving port in Bellingham, Washington and not being in Alaska in time, this could have taken out one of the four major players and really just shaken up the whole salmon buying scene up in Bristol Bay.

I have been tracking the vessel. It departed last weekend and it is now in Chatham Strait in southeast Alaska. Looks like it's a little east of Baranof Island, just south of Sitka.

AB: Sticking with the US West Coast for a moment, I had the opportunity to talk with American Seafoods' chief sustainability officer Tim Fitzgerald, and At-Sea Processors Association Vice President Caitlin Yeager, while they were at Pier 91 in Seattle, Washington for Net Recycling Day, an event that united the Alaska pollock industry, including the At Sea Processors Association's five member companies, American Seafoods, Arctic Storm Management Group, Coastal Villages Region Fund, Glacier Fish Company and Trident Seafoods. Take a listen.

Volunteers at the 2025 Net Recycling Day in Seattle, Washington. Photo Credit: Alaska Pollock Fishery Alliance

I know American Seafoods has been doing this for years now, but what brought about this collaborative effort across all the At Sea Processors Association members this year?

Tim Fitzgerald (TF): We were in the early stages of planning for this year's event, and Sarah Nayani from Arctic Storm had heard about the event previously and was interested in learning more and wanted to see how Arctic could get involved. And then once that happened, it all kind of snowballed and we reached out to the other three member companies and everyone was super excited to partner and really make this an industry-wide thing as opposed to just one of the single companies.

And we've gotten great participation from all the companies. And literally as we speak, they're out hacking up nets across about an acre of Terminal 91 at the Port of Seattle.

American Seafoods gathers Seattle’s pollock industry for Net Recycling Day

Caitlin Yeager (CY): As Tim mentioned, American's been running this event for a couple of years and APA has been really focused on gear development and innovation and research lately.

So when the time arose for this to come up again, all of the members expressed interest and largely because it presents an opportunity where you have a lot of other mission critical staff have the chance to work with the gear, work with the fishermen and increase their knowledge base about how each part functions and what it serves. So I think not only is it the recycling aspect that we look forward to, but it builds solidarity amongst the companies and our vendors. One of the reasons I enjoy working in the fishing industry is the vibrant maritime community. And I think this is a great chance to get everyone together and learn a little more about what we do.

AB: Safety first, then teamwork. It's one of my favorite phrases.

So you guys got your safety first. So volunteers, they're cutting, they're sorting, they're preparing for retired fishing nets for recycling. I know these are big vessels, so these got to be some big nets. I know you said across like an acre?

Volunteers at Net Recycling Day in Seattle, Washington. Photo Credit: Alaska Pollock Fishery Alliance

TF: We're actually we're doing a competition. Everyone guessed how many pounds or tons of plastic we would recycle throughout the course of the day. And we'll hopefully have a tally at the end of the day. But we're hoping for between 75,000-100,000 pounds of plastics that get recycled as a result of this event.

AB: And what have you guys done in the past?

TF: The first year that American did this, we only did one net with 20 volunteers and it was about 20,000 lbs. We went from one net to two nets, to now four nets. And on average, it depends on which type of net we're recycling. But they're about 20,000 lbs of plastic each.

And then we'll also be recycling the chain and the cable as scrap metal. That'll even be on top of the plastic tally.

AB: How long do fishing nets usually last?

CY: Different components of the gear have different lifetimes. For instance, a cod end experiences a lot more wear and tear than a net or a bridle or a mid-body section. One area that we're particularly concerned with, for instance, is what they call an extended, like a packing tube section, because that area is where our salmon excluders lie. So, for instance, if that's not flowing properly or becomes stretched out with time, the salmon excluders lose their efficacy.

So another benefit of going through and Marie Kondo -- get rid of the old and make way for the new -- is that it gives us the ability to employ the newer technology and some of the improved methods that we're constantly searching to find.

TF: As Caitlin said, the material technology and the construction technology of the nets definitely changes over time. And the old nets don't perform the same way that the newer nets do.

And I would say on average, we're probably we're probably retiring one or two nets per vessel per year.

CY: We touched briefly on salmon excluders. I mean, there are a number of tradeoffs to consider with gear improvement.

It's not just about efficiency. It's also reduction in bycatch and making sure that we're operating in a responsible way. Sort of as Tim had mentioned, recycling the gear is a complex process and accumulation of marine debris in communities is something we're very concerned about.

So I like that we're expanding the pool of people who understand what to do with this and how to dispose of it. Hopefully those lessons can be parlayed into not just the pollock fishery, but other sectors as well. And then back towards the gear innovation, we're testing new technology like live feed cameras and using those in novel ways.

We're looking at different types of sensors to model how the gear flies through the water to better inform not only how we fish, but to work into the scientific process and going about it in a really standardized and a systematic way. That way, not only are we better informing the fishery and our Alaska fisheries management, but those tools can be used in other fisheries globally, since this is an increasing concern that we're facing.

Retired pollock nets to be recycled. Photo Credit: Alaska Pollock Fishery Alliance

LC: I think we need to get out there for next year's event.

But moving along, let's talk markets. So the news this week in scallops is a surge in domestic landings out of the Nantucket Lightship West area, where harvesters are reporting catch rates up to 4000 lbs per day, which is triple the pace seen this time last year, with reports of over 100 boats active in the area.

Landings at New Bedford's BASE auction hit a season high of over 500,000 lbs last week, fueling renewed optimism that the 2025 season could exceed the projected 18 million lbs total, which would be very, very welcomed.

This unexpected supply bump is putting real pressure on prices. Wholesale values for larger sizes like U10 and U12s dropped by 15-18% in just one week, and auction prices are now at their lowest point of the season. Still, quality has improved from earlier concerns linked to early spawning, particularly in Georges Bank, which is helping maintain steady market flow.

As landings continue and pricing adjusts, the industry will be watching closely to see whether strong supply is matched by summer demand or if we're heading into a prolonged period of downward pricing pressure.

Fresh salmon fillet on ice. Credit: Ostancov Vladislav/Shutterstock.com

The Chilean salmon market continues to trend lower this week, with fresh fillet average values dropping by $0.15-$0.20 per pound across core sizes. This reflects a broader seasonal softening as supply normalizes following earlier disruptions tied to Chile's national holiday last week and brief labor-related delays.

What is notable is a growing shift in strategy among some producers. They're choosing to freeze product rather than harvest into a soft fresh market. This move is aimed at easing the downward pressure on fresh pricing, which continues to face headwinds from some cautious consumers, high retail prices and slower post-Mother's Day demand.

On the frozen side, however, fillets are now becoming more available after earlier tightness. Portions, particularly 6-8 ounce sizes, remain tight and steady, with some suppliers booked out until late Q3. So looking ahead here, market players expect continued pressure as supply builds seasonally in Q3, while demand shows little signs of picking up.

It's shaping up to be a challenging summer across the salmon markets.

AB: As promised last week, joining us to talk about the crab market is UCN's price analyst Gary Morrison.

Frozen Canadian snow crab legs share a display with lobster tails in a Maryland grocery store. Photograph by Jason Huffman.

Gary Morrison (GM): I'm sad to report that I didn't go to any parties with snow crab on the menu. Maybe next year, as we talked about.

But in the US wholesale market, you know, prices have stabilized here this week. What we're seeing is Norway and the Gulf of St. Lawrence, they pretty much ended their season. So they're working through the inventory that they have.

It's really the Newfoundland and Labrador region, which is roughly about 50% landed. That is really supplying the market. Now, when we're talking about Canada's largest snow crab, it's mostly 5-8 and 8-10 ounce clusters. So that's providing some opportunity for people to price shop for those sizes.

But the larger sizes, they have a positive bias because they're really limited this year. So they're waiting to see if they can get some of those larger ones.

Overall, demand still remains really good at these prices and where people can shift origins, they are where there's limited inventory on gulf crab and Norwegian product. There's also a little full steadiness to the market and a little bit less willingness by sellers to the discount product.

AB: OK, now, before we go, Lorin, let me quickly set the stage for you for our final story. Yet another new Catch the Current podcast segment. I am calling "WTF: What the Fish."

LC: Love it.

AB: So, Lorin, pretend you and I are in beautiful, sunny Florida.

LC: Okay, okay.

AB: We've hired a commercial fishing boat captain to take us out on the water so we can try our hand at catching red snapper.

LC: Love it. I'm assuming we've already taken out our Dramamine.

AB: Of course, we can't even be on a docked boat without it. But the fish are biting. We're having a great day...Oh, hey, look, there's dolphins!

LC: Oh, I love dolphins.

AB: And then, bam, our fishing boat captain takes out a 12-gauge shotgun and starts firing at the dolphins that surface near a vessel. Children scream.

FREE READ US commercial fisherman sentenced for poisoning, shooting dolphins in Gulf of Mexico

LC: I'm screaming. Wait. And also, we've got kids on board, Amanda, WTF.

AB: Yes, exactly. The perfect story to kick off our "WTF: What the Fish" segment, where we highlight a news story that was so whack that we need to talk about it.

Zachary Barfield, a commercial fisherman and licensed charter fishing captain in Panama City, Florida, has been sentenced to prison for killing dolphins. According to a press release from the US Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Florida, Barfield poisoned and shot bottlenose dolphins on multiple occasions in the Gulf of Mexico between 2022 and 2023.

LC: So WTF. I like that you also keep these stories hidden from me so that I can have an actual reaction here. But this is an aptly named segment.

AB: Yeah. So this guy, he put this pesticide into bait fish. And so NOAA estimates that he poisoned up to 70 dolphins, likely resulting in multiple dolphin deaths. But they don't know. And then their investigation also found that he shot at least five dolphins with a 12-gauge shotgun, with one confirmed death. And he reportedly used this gun to shoot dolphins near his vessel, including shooting a dolphin in front of two elementary school-age children.What a traumatizing experience. So this is the worst part, though. You'll never guess his sentence.

LC: It gets worse.

AB: He was only sentenced to 30 days in prison and fined $51,000 for violating the Marine Mammal Protection Act and the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, Rodenticide Act.

This has happened -- well, some of it happened -- while he was on a charter fishing boat, but he's also a commercial fisherman.

LC: You would think he would capitalize on, hey, come fishing with us and come see the dolphins.

AB: But no. They'll eat your red snapper right off the line. Yeah. So anyway. Wow. "WTF: What the fish," right?

LC: Yeah. Way to end the podcast, Amanda. We can always count on you.

AB: Thanks for listening, guys. We'll see you back here next week.

LC: Bye bye.
