title: US seafood importers downplay impact of court decision nullifying Trump tariffs
content:
Most of the tariffs implemented by US president Donald Trump on global trading partners were declared unlawful by a Wednesday (May 28) ruling from the US Court of International Trade, but US seafood importers are not rushing into any assumptions Trump's tariffs are gone for good.

The Trump administration is appealing the ruling to the US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, which could issue an injunction unfreezing the tariffs. If that court doesn't rule in Trump's favor, he can then appeal to the US Supreme Court.

Trump can also use other, previously approved mechanisms for imposing tariffs, such as Section 122 of US trade law, Section 301 investigations and Section 338 of the Trade Act of 1930, according to a research note from Goldman Sachs.

US Court of International Trade declares Trump lacks authority to impose tariffs

"This ruling represents a setback for the administration's tariff plans and increases uncertainty but might not change the final outcome for most major US trading partners," Goldman Sachs economists said in their note, as reported by CNBC. "For now, we expect the Trump administration will find other ways to impose tariffs."

For across-the-board tariffs affecting all goods from a certain country, Trump could use Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, which does not require a formal investigation and which could be used to implement tariffs for up to 150 days before requiring congressional review.

Trump could also initiate Section 301 investigations, as he did on Chinese goods during his first term. However, it's a more time-consuming process, with the US Commerce Department and other federal agencies required to formally investigate whether tariffs are justified as a result of economic damage done to domestic US industries.

Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 allows for targeted action against goods deemed vital to national security, and has already been used by Trump to tariff steel, aluminum and car imports.

Trump could also choose to impose levies of up to 50% on imports from countries deemed to be discriminating against the US under Section 338, but Goldman Sachs noted it has not been used before and could therefore also face a legal challenge.

Some legal scholars are skeptical Trump would be successful in pursuing other routes to enact broad tariffs. Ilya Somin, a George Mason University law professor, told Politico other statutes don't offer the expansive authority Trump claimed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), which was struck down by the US Court of International Trade yesterday.

"I don't think they could impose anything this sweeping under another statute," Somin said. "The reason why they wanted to use IEEPA in the first place is because they thought that it could grant them this vast, sweeping authority they couldn't get otherwise."

In the short term, the Trump administration has other work to do. It has 10 days to withdraw the tariffs impacted by the ruling, which include the 10% "Liberation Day" tariffs, as well as the 30% tariff placed on China and 25% tariffs on Canada and Mexico. The court's ruling also means that the government may have to pay back duties it has already collected. 

"Anybody that has had to pay tariffs so far will be able to get them refunded," Somin said.

It also faces a tougher negotiating position with countries with which it has been seeking trade deals, a list that includes Japan, Vietnam, India and the EU. In arguments made to the US Court of International Trade in the tariffs case, US deputy assistant attorney general Brett Shumate said an unfavorable ruling would "kneecap" the president's efforts to strike new trade deals before Trump's chosen deadline of July 9.

"An injunction would be extremely disruptive while the president is in the middle of foreign negotiations with other countries about trade deficits and about the fentanyl crisis," Shumate said.

Other countries' negotiators "may be tempted to hold off making further concessions to the U.S. until there is more legal clarity," said Wendy Cutler, a former US trade official who is now vice president at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

Seafood importers react

US seafood importers were still digesting the impact of the court's decision on Thursday (May 29), and weren't yet ready to make any business decisions on the market-shaking news.

"It's far too early to have any idea what kind of functional effect this ruling may have. At a start, it's certainly going to be challenged in every possible way through immediate appeal," Matthew Fass, the president of Newport News, Virginia-based seafood importer Maritime Products International, told Undercurrent News. "There is much more that needs to unfold in the days ahead to have any sense of an upcoming roadmap on trade -- certainly any sense of a longer term, but even the roadmap for the short and medium term."

Maritime Products International president Matthew Fass. Photo courtesy of MPI.

Fass said he was not jumping to take advantage of the sudden absence of tariffs on items he imports, such as Chinese scallops, Vietnamese pangasius or Argentine red shrimp.

"We have all also seen enough with this administration to understand that just about anything could be imposed with no warning or 'shipping grace periods' -- especially in a circumstance like this -- such that it would seem a little premature to make significant decisions at this moment and assume no tariff by the time anything could possibly arrive," he said.

The court ruling is the latest example of fast-changing market conditions being created by the Trump administration, said Justin Conrad, the president of Greensboro, North Carolina-headquartered importer Bay Hill Seafood, which primarily imports whitefish such as pangasius and tilapia from Asia.

"We're not going to try to rush in and buy anything, because I'm not sure the risk is worth the reward," he said. "Everybody thinks that they're going to appeal the decision and continue to collect the tariffs in the interim. So for us, I won't say it's business as usual, because there's nothing usual about this, but it's business as it's been for the last several months, which is you watch your inventory, you watch pricing, and you don't get overextended."

Justin Conrad. Photo courtesy of Justin Conrad/LinkedIn.

One immediate point of relief that could be created by the court ruling is the suspension of the requirement tariffs be paid within 10 days of product arriving in the US, Conrad said.

"It's a major cash flow hit for companies like ours, because there's no way you're turning your inventory that fast," he said. "Even if the tariff is 10%, that's a lot. We're the seafood business -- we're not making 10% on anything, so that substantial carrying cost is hurtful."

Bay Hill's operational strategy has become more conservative since Trump assumed office in January, Conrad said.

"You have to be incredibly careful. Business conditions change almost contract by contract. We're not the biggest importer in the world, but we're not a smaller company, either. And for us, it becomes incredibly difficult to do any business at all," he said.

Conrad said it's hard not to feel frozen by the constantly changing market conditions.

"The only thing we know is that we don't know anything. And it's true things have been uncertain since the very beginning of the Trump administration," he said. "It's crippling."

Contact the author Cliff.White@undercurrentnews.com

title: US commercial fisherman sentenced for poisoning, shooting dolphins in Gulf of Mexico
content:
Zachary Brandon Barfield, a commercial fisherman and licensed charter fishing captain in Panama City, Florida, has been sentenced to prison for killing dolphins.

On Wednesday (May 21), Barfield was sentenced to 30 days imprisonment and fined $51,000 after violating the Marine Mammal Protection Act and the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide and Rodenticide Act. 

Barfield, 31, poisoned and shot bottlenose dolphins on multiple occasions in the Gulf of Mexico between 2022 and 2023, according to a press release from the US Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Florida.

An investigation into Barfield's actions on the water began in 2023 after a special agent with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) received a tip that a fisherman was killing bottlenose dolphins.

A NOAA Fisheries investigation found that Barfield placed methomyl, a highly toxic pesticide, inside baitfish to poison dolphins, which he blamed for eating red snapper from the lines of his charter fishing clients. NOAA estimated Barfield poisoned up to 70 dolphins, likely resulting in multiple dolphin deaths.

NOAA's investigation also found that Barifield shot at least five dolphins with a 12-gauge shotgun, with one confirmed death. Barfield reportedly used a 12-gauge shotgun to shoot dolphins near his vessel, including shooting a dolphin in front of two elementary school-aged children. 

"Barfield was a longtime charter and commercial fishing captain. He knew the regulations protecting dolphins, yet he killed them anyway -- once in front of children. This sentence demonstrates our commitment to enforcing the rule of law. It should deter others from engaging in such conduct," said acting assistant attorney general Adam Gustafson of the US Justice Department's Environment and Natural Resources Division. 

Barfield was facing up to one year in prison for each count of dolphin killing and another 30 days on the pesticide charge. In February, he agreed to a deal through which he pleaded guilty to two counts of killing a marine animal and prohibited use of a registered pesticide, as reported by local ABC news affiliate WDHN. 

In addition to his 30-day prison sentence and $51,000 fine, Barfield will also have a one-year term of supervised release.

title: US grocery sushi supplier announces salmonella-related recall linked to cucumbers
content:
JFE Franchising, the Houston, Texas-based parent company of Snowfox, a full-service sushi kiosk company with over 1,400 locations across 38 US states, has issued a recall related to a salmonella outbreak linked to cucumbers.

The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) initiated a recall last week for cucumbers sold by Bedner Growers, a produce wholesaler based in Delray Beach, Florida, due to salmonella contamination.

The recall has since been expanded, and companies that used the recalled cucumbers in ready-to-eat and other prepared products have issued their own warnings.

JFE Franchising's recalled items, which include the affected cucumbers, include Snowfox's Arizona Roll and Dynamite Roll, which feature tuna; California Roll, which uses imitation crab; and Dragon Roll, which contains salmon. The full list of recalled items can be found here.

The recalled sushi items from Snowfox were distributed to more than 140 Weis Market stores in the US states of Delaware, Maryland, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Virginia and West Virginia. Snowfox also recalled affected sushi products distributed to more than 70 Kroger stores in Arkansas, Kentucky, Mississippi and Tennessee.

The recall announcement was published by the FDA on Friday (May 23), but the company said it initiated its recall on May 20.

While there have no illnesses or consumer complaints reported in connection with Snowfox's products, the FDA reports there have been 26 total illnesses related to the wider salmonella outbreak, including nine hospitalizations.

title: France seizes UK vessel over alleged illegal activity in English Channel
content:
French authorities have impounded a UK fishing vessel accused of operating illegally in French waters, further straining cross-Channel relations just days after a controversial UK-EU agreement on fishing rights, reports the BBC. 

The French Navy stopped the vessel late Thursday night (May 22) during patrols in the English Channel. According to the French Coastguard, the crew was allegedly fishing without a valid licence.

‘Sold out’ or stability? EU, UK both say fisheries deal brings latter to sector

The vessel was diverted to the port of Boulogne, where it remains under detention while French officials consider prosecution.

The UK government confirmed it is providing consular assistance to a UK citizen involved and is in contact with French authorities. "As the vessel remains subject to an ongoing investigation by French fisheries authorities, we are unable to comment further at this time,” a UK government spokesperson said.

The seizure follows the announcement of prime minister Keir Starmer’s new deal with the EU, which allows EU fishing vessels access to UK waters for another 12 years in exchange for eased trade terms.

UK fishing groups and opposition parties have criticized the deal, arguing it gives too much away to Brussels.

title: Investigation finds UK retailers selling bass, bream linked to chronic overfishing in Senegal
content:
A new investigation from NGO DeSmog and newspaper The Guardian has discovered several major UK supermarkets are selling Turkish seabass and seabream produced using fishmeal from heavily overfished waters in Senegal.

FREE READ ClientEarth, Oceana sue Spanish authorities for inaction on African IUU

The report found Waitrose and Partners, The Co-Operative, Lidl, Aldi and Asda are all selling bass from Turkish farms fuelled by fishmeal and fish oil produced from the small 'feed fish' found in waters off Western Africa, and particularly Senegal.

DeSmog discovered that Kilic Deniz and its subsidiary Agromey, which provide roughly 25% of all the UK's Turkish bass and bream imports, have sourced more than 5,400 metric tons of fishmeal and oil from Senegalese waters since the start of 2021, shedding light on what had previously been an opaque supply chain.

For its part, Kilic denied to Undercurrent News that it had imported any fishmeal from Senegal in the past two years. The firm also said any feed ingredient shipments from Senegal, which it claims arrived over two years ago, accounted for less than 1% of its total fish feed usage.

Kilic added that Senegalese fishmeal had been used exclusively for fish sold in the domestic market, and not for export markets. Since 2023, it said, it has secured new fishmeal supply agreements from the Black Sea region and Peru.

The farmer did not respond to comment on why it had stopped sourcing fishmeal and fish oil from the West African country.

Altogether, Turkey supplies 85% of the UK's total farmed bass market, and imports grew by 7% last year. New England Seafood International and Ocean Fish are among the biggest wholesale buyers of bass and bream from Kilic and Agromey, importing 473t in the last four years -- equivalent to 5 million fillets (see below):

Credit: Brigitte Wear and Hazel Healy, DeSmog

Senegal's hunger crisis

Senegal's local fish markets are heavily dependent on pelagic fish for business and food security, but unsustainable overfishing driven by fish feed demand has created soaring unemployment among market workers -- chiefly women -- and environmental pollution at fishmeal factories along the coast.

FREE READ EU halts fisheries agreement with Senegal as IUU escalates

This overfishing is well-documented, and Senegal received a yellow card from the EU for taking insufficient action to prevent overfishing last year.

Kilic holds Aquaculture Stewardship Council (ASC) certification, which requires farmers to source their feed ingredients from "well-managed fisheries," yet it has still sourced from Senegalese waters in every one of the last four years, DeSmog alleges.

The NGO has calculated that the volume of fish taken from Senegalese waters and processed into Kilic's feed could have "met the recommended dietary needs" of 2m people over the last four years.

The fishmeal factory Omega Fishing opened in Senegal in 2011, and has since largely priced market traders out, causing the supply of small fish like sardinella, a staple of the Senegalese diet, to decline sharply.

According to DeSmog, 500 grams of 'keccax' -- a mix of dried and smoked sardinella -- now costs £1.00-£2.00, where it had only been £0.13 before Omega Fishing opened.

In 2023, Senegal's fishmeal exports climbed to an eight-year high, while persistently high food costs have pushed hundreds of thousands of people into crisis levels of hunger.

Data from UN Comtrade. Credit: DeSmog

Senegal's fish stocks have fallen to record lows in recent years, with annual landings dropping from fluctuations between 100,000t and 250,000t during the 2010s to roughly 10,000t annually since 2020.

A report out earlier in May from the Environmental Justice Foundation cited research that shows 57% of fish populations across Senegal are witnessing a similar state of collapse.

"If we continue like this, the sea will become a liquid desert," said Diaba Diop, head of a Senegalese national network of women fish workers. "When people don't have enough to eat, we can't use it to feed animals."

Who bears responsibility in UK?

Chris Packham, a well-known naturalist, author and television presenter in the UK, was quick to hold supermarkets to account for failing to label fish accurately so that buyers may make ethical purchasing decisions.

Consortium questions satellite firm Iridum for tuna overfishing complicity

"This is robbing consumers of their right, in a climate and biodiversity crisis, to use the most powerful forms of protest, which is economic protest," he said. "Until [supermarkets] accept their corporate responsibility to allow us to make ethical choices in those aisles, they're in dereliction of duty."

The other key question raised by the investigation is the scrutiny that must once again be placed on food assurance schemes, which Dale Vince, campaigner and founder of the Green Britain Foundation, said allowed food producers to "claim exactly what you are not, deny exactly what you are."

"In light of this expose, UK supermarkets should immediately take all Kilic products off their shelves and take a good, hard look at all farmed fish products they sell -- a simple accreditation or assurance is not enough, and the British public should stop buying it."

Eva Douzinas, from Aktaia, a coalition of Greek communities calling for stronger protections from fish farming, also noted the direct environmental impact of Mediterranean aquaculture itself was falling under the radar.

"Seabass and seabream farms are accelerating the degradation of Poseidon seagrass meadows, which serve as vital nurseries for wild fish, support marine biodiversity, protect coastlines, and sequester carbon," she said. "The industry is expanding with little oversight."

title: Five Dutch firms, 10 countries own most of global fishing fleet, new reports claim
content:
Two recent investigations claim to have shed light on the ownership structure of the world's large-scale fishing fleet, highlighting the concentration of control in the hands of a small number of countries and companies.

According to the findings, 10 countries are responsible for the legal ownership of more than half of the global industrial fishing fleet, while five Dutch companies hold a significant share of Europe's fishing capacity and have expanded their presence internationally.

A study commissioned by Oceana and conducted by the EqualSea Lab at the University of Santiago de Compostela, in Spain, "Beyond the Flag: Who really owns the world's large-scale fishing (LSF) fleet?", mapped nearly 7,000 vessels classified as LSF.

The research found that 62% of LSF vessels lacked publicly available legal ownership data, and 16% were flagged in a country other than the one in which the owning company was incorporated.

"Without knowing who owns these vessels, enforcing rules is nearly impossible," said Daniel Skerritt, senior manager of science and strategy at Oceana. "This isn't just a data gap. It's a political choice that undermines accountability."

The report also reveals that these fishing vessels are responsible for around 60% of marine fish landings and receive more than 80% of government subsidies.

Yet many operate under so-called "flags of convenience," countries like Panama, Belize, and Honduras that permit foreign ownership with minimal transparency or regulatory oversight.

Spanish firms alone account for nearly a quarter of all mismatched vessels, while Chinese companies dominate in vessel count, often operating through single-country, vertically integrated structures.

In contrast, Spanish conglomerates spread ownership across complex networks of subsidiaries in Latin America and Africa, reaping profits while sidestepping local regulations.

"This is about more than enforcement," said Maisie Pigeon, director of the Coalition for Fisheries Transparency. "It's about who controls public marine resources and who gets left behind."

Africa and Oceania are particularly affected. Nearly 30% of LSF vessels flagged in Africa are owned by foreign firms, mainly from Europe. In Oceania, the figure is 26%, with many vessels owned by Asian companies. Meanwhile, Europe and Asia largely keep control in-house: less than 3% of their fleets are owned outside their regions.

A hidden empire at sea

Separately, an investigation by French NGO BLOOM, "The 'Big Five': The grip of five Dutch corporate giants on the global ocean," analyzed five Dutch fishing firms: Parlevliet & Van der Plas, Cornelis Vrolijk, Van der Zwan, Alda Seafood, and the De Boer family group.

The research examined company records and vessel registries to document their ownership of around 230 vessels and a network of over 400 subsidiaries worldwide.

The BLOOM report notes that these companies operate across several continents and are active throughout the entire seafood supply chain, from fishing to processing and distribution. 

"Fishing vessels, storage sheds, processing plants, distribution chains and even crew recruitment agencies -- the Big Five control every stage of the fishing industry. This enables them to buy fish from their own subsidiaries at artificially low prices to reduce the wages paid to crews, who are often paid by the share, and to transfer profits to tax havens," the report claims.

It also says that the five companies not only dominate fish quotas, sidelining small-scale fishermen, but also wield significant influence over European fisheries policy and are active members of 15 different lobbying groups.

"Thanks to a network of opaque subsidiaries, a fleet of technologically over-equipped vessels, and an aggressive takeover strategy, these multinationals reign over global fishing," said Laetitia Bisiaux, head of the industrial fishing campaign at BLOOM. 

"Behind a facade of competition, these companies cooperate closely: they join forces to crush the other players in the sector," she added.

'Big Five' companies and their subsidaries, mapped based on their 2023 annual reports and completed with data from Company.info, Orbis, North Data and Companies House, among others. As a result, company ownership may be outdated. Credit: BLOOM

Finally, both reports call for sweeping reforms, including mandatory disclosure of vessel ownership at registration, public ownership registries linked to international databases, stricter flag state responsibilities, tighter quota allocation rules, and limits on lobbying influence and corporate consolidation in fisheries.

"This isn't just about sustainability," said Oceana's Skerritt. "It's about equity, governance, and democracy. Who controls our ocean resources, and who benefits, should not be a mystery."

title: Popular US east coast oyster bar, shellfish farm damaged by fire
content:
Matunuck Oyster Bar, a popular restaurant and aquaculture farm in the US state of Rhode Island, has been damaged in a fire that broke out early Tuesday (May 20) morning.

Union Fire District Steve Pinch told local TV news station WRPI 12 that firefighters arrived at the South Kingston restaurant at 3:44 a.m. to find heavy smoke and flames coming from the two-story building. While wind proved to be a challenge, Pinch said the fire was contained by 6 a.m.

"Our firefighters did a tremendous job, in extreme heat and wind conditions in a difficult building," Pinch said in a statement. "It was a pretty stubborn fire. Everyone did a remarkable job to stop the fire as quickly as they did. We had a lot of things working against us, but they did a great job overcoming those obstacles. Thankfully, we had no injuries, which is always nice."

Pinch added that the building sustained "significant damage."

"It's still standing, but between the water, fire and smoke damage, the structural problems are significant," said Pinch.

An investigation into the cause of the fire is underway.

Matunuck Oyster Bar, described by Pinch as a "cornerstone of the community," has been in business since 2009. However, prior to opening the restaurant doors, owner Perry Raso, in 2002, founded Matunuck Oyster Farm, a seven-acre wading-depth commercial aquaculture farm on Potter Pond in South Kingston's East Matunuck area.

The Matunuck Oyster Bar in South Kingstown, Rhode Island. Photo Credit: Matunuck Oyster Bar

Raso's operations grew as the oyster farm began to sell oysters across the country. In 2009 he opened the Matunuck Oyster Bar in a former rundown restaurant with a commercial dock located on the pond.

In addition to serving fresh oysters, the business also began offering tours of its oyster farms, where visitors can see and learn about the different species of shellfish available at the restaurant. As the restaurant expanded, Raso even developed Matunuck Vegetable Farm, a nine-acre certified organic farm with a focus on salad greens.

The fire comes just a few months after Matunuck Oyster Bar was highlighted as one of 44 restaurants on the USA TODAY Restaurants of the Year 2025 list. It boasts a following of more than 35,800 on Instagram. WRPI 12 reports that the operation attracts thousands of customers over the summer.

title: Canadian First Nation accuses fisheries department of aggressive enforcement after lobster traps seized
content:
Mi'kmaq lobster harvesters from Lennox Island First Nation, located in the Canadian province of Prince Edward Island (PEI) have accused Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) with "aggressive enforcement" after lobster traps were seized from band members in Malpeque and Alberton, PEI, on Sunday (May 18), reports the CBC. 

The Mi'kmaq contend they have a right to fish for a moderate livelihood outside of the commercial lobster fishery regulated by DFO, thanks to a 1999 decision by Canada's highest court. Lennox Island has been managing a moderate livelihood fishery since 2022.

"Our treaty-protected fishery follows a community-developed plan that aligns with conservation priorities and voluntarily mirrors DFO regulations," CBC quoted Lennox Island First Nation chief Darlene Bernard.

"DFO's actions are a blatant violation of our rights, and we will not tolerate this kind of intimidation," the chief told CBC.

The chief is demanding that DFO return the seized traps.

Lennox Island is located on Malapeque Bay on the northwestern shore of Prince Edward Island. The 540-hectare island is home to the Lennox Island First Nation, the largest Mi'kmaq band on PEI. Screenshot photo from Google Maps

DFO said it authorized Lennox Island community members to use up to 1,000 lobster traps in Lobster Fishing Area 24 during the 2025 spring commercial season under a one-year authorization. The season opened on April 25 and runs until June 25.

"Authorized community members in Lennox Island are required to meet licence conditions, including the use of DFO tags. The situation at Malpeque and Alberton in Prince Edward Island is under DFO's Conservation and Protection investigation," reads a DFO statement provided to the CBC.

"This is about more than traps or lobster -- this is about our right to self-determination, economic justice, and the survival of our way of life," Bernard was quoted by CBC. "We are not backing down. Our fishers are out there with the full support of our nation and our ancestors behind them."

Members of the Lennox Island First Nation indicated to the CBC they would be setting more traps on Tuesday (May 20).

title: Newfoundland’s crab-fishing union VP accuses Canada fisheries office of violating privacy
content:
The vice president of the Fish Food and Allied Workers (FFAW) union, which represents the majority of fish harvesters in the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador, has accused Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) of overreach and violation of privacy, reports the CBC. 

Jason Sullivan, a crab harvester, said he's being investigated over allegations that, sometime between April 10 and April 30, 2025, he authorized another person and a fishing vessel to retrieve crab gear that had been set by his boat, the Atlantic Outlaw.

That is a violation of Section 43.4 (1) of Canada's Fisheries Act, although the allegations have yet to be proven in court.

As part of the investigation, Sullivan said his cell phone was confiscated, and he's worried about his personal information, and sensitive union information, on the device.

"It is just a total violation of privacy; my personal phone has nothing to do with fishing activities," Sullivan stated in a post on the Newfoundland Fishermen's Forum, a Facebook page he administers.

DFO officers searched his boat and took navigation aids, which Sullivan said he doesn't have a problem with, but he draws the line at his cellphone, CBC reported. The cellphone isn't a tool he uses for fishing, Sullivan said, adding that he isn't sure why it was taken or when it might be returned.

Sullivan alleges he was threatened with being handcuffed if he refused to hand over his phone.

Jason Sullivan went public on the Newfoundland Fishermen's Forum Facebook page to express his concerns about DFO officers confiscating his cell phone after charging him with a violation of the Fisheries Act. Screenshot photo from Newfoundland Fishermen's Forum Facebook page

"If they can just come up with these wild accusations, get a warrant. You wouldn't know but we're smuggling cocaine or something," Sullivan was quoted by the CBC.

DFO declined to provide information because the investigation was ongoing, CBC reported.

Meanwhile, Sullivan said the FFAW leadership supports him and will take action.

"If we have to sue DFO, if we have to sue the fisheries officers that are involved in this and that are pushing this kind of behaviour, we're gonna have to do it," CBC quoted Sullivan as saying.

title: Nova Scotia town defends pre-vetted shellfish sites selection process amid ‘secret deals’ allegations
content:
Facing an Ombudsman probe and angry residents, the town of Argyle in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia is defending its shellfish site selection process after Freedom of Information documents revealed alleged backroom deals between officials and oyster farmers to secure prime aquaculture locations near homes.

"These allegations of conflict are without merit and intended to discredit the council and staff that assisted the province of Nova Scotia's Aquaculture Development Area (ADA) program in good faith," said warden Nicole Albright,  the elected head of the Municipality of Argyle, in an email response to Undercurrent News on Monday (May 19).

"We insisted on an independent investigation of the matter to avoid any further claims of malfeasance," Albright added, emphasizing the municipality's commitment to transparency.

Albright's response comes after the Association for Responsible Aquaculture (ARA) obtained documents that the group said suggested that municipal staff secretly collaborated with oyster farmers to influence the selection of ADA sites. 

The ADA, a program designed to pre-approve shellfish aquaculture sites, has been in development for four years. The initiative fast-tracks the permitting process, allowing operators to set up at sites already deemed suitable. In April 2024, the program announced the availability of the first six out of 53 pre-vetted sites suitable for shellfish aquaculture. However, controversy soon followed.

In the latest allegations, ARA said municipal officials worked behind the scenes with industry insiders to secure prime aquaculture locations, some near residential areas. It also alleged that officials did not sufficiently consult the public, as Undercurrent reported. ARA made its allegations known last week in a press release.

These allegation inflamed residents who claim they were excluded from key decisions, ARA said in the press release. Despite repeated calls for transparency, the municipality has yet to address these concerns, it added.

While the municipality of Argyle maintains that the province of Nova Scotia led and managed the ADA process, residents and the ARA have raised questions about municipal officials' role in the selection process.

In response, Albright said: "It is puzzling how municipal staff or council can be engaged in bid-rigging, when the entire bidding process was led, managed and determined by the province." 

Albright also responded to claims that the municipality imposed excessive fees for Freedom of Information requests and used provincial legislation to block certain disclosures. "The investigation into these allegations will address these concerns," she said.

Earlier in 2024, the municipality admitted to communication shortcomings in the ADA process, acknowledging that although public notification protocols were followed, it failed to adequately engage the community, as Undercurrent reported. Albright noted that the municipality has since proposed appointing a dedicated communications staff member to improve transparency.

title: Untitled
content:
Argyle, a town in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia, is facing a formal investigation following allegations that municipal officials secretly collaborated with oyster farmers to influence the selection of sites to be included in a program designed to ease the permitting process for shellfish aquaculture.

Documents obtained through freedom of information requests made by the Association for Responsible Aquaculture (ARA) suggest the town's staff worked behind the scenes with industry insiders to secure them prime shellfish farming locations, many located near residential areas, while failing to adequately involve the public in the decision-making process, ARA has implied.

In 2024, the municipality of Argyle launched a pilot project to approve 53 shellfish aquaculture sites, but residents criticized the process, claiming they were not included in the process for making key decisions. The group said the controversial selection of sites has led to accusations of favoritism, secrecy and conflicts of interest.

"It's clear now that the farmers cheated," ARA member Chris Thibedeau said in a press release issued last week. "The email evidence shows individuals inside the municipality helped them. These are no longer perceived conflicts -- they are real, and they must be investigated."

Despite its calls for transparency, the town has not addressed its concerns, the group claimed. As a result, the Nova Scotia ombudsman has launched an investigation into the municipality's failure to conduct proper public consultations, while an independent third-party investigator has also been hired.

The investigation will focus on Argyle's role in the alleged conflicts of interest and bid-rigging related to the aquaculture site selection process.

Among further escalating tensions, residents allege that the town has stifled public oversight by imposing excessive fees for freedom of information requests and labeling certain information disclosures as "trivial" under recent provincial legislation.

"Seeing local councillors refuse to represent and listen to their constituents is extremely alarming," said Lorelei Murphy, a Liberal candidate for Argyle in the 2024 Nova Scotia provincial election. "It's council's obligation to hold an open and unbiased review of their decisions and act accordingly."

With the integrity of the approval process under scrutiny, residents are calling for a halt to further aquaculture approvals until an independent review is completed. The group said rebuilding public trust will require a fair and transparent process moving forward.

The controversy follows the municipality's admission in June 2024 that its communication regarding the approval of ADA sites was insufficient. The town council insisted it followed the required notification protocols, but acknowledged failing to engage the public adequately. It has since proposed appointing a staff member dedicated to communicating with the public regarding the issue, as Undercurrent News reported.

Undercurrent contacted the municipality of Argyle for its response to the announced investigations, but has yet to receive a response.

title: Mowi loses RSPCA approval in Scotland over animal cruelty allegations
content:
Norwegian salmon farmer Mowi has seen its RSPCA Assured certification suspended following allegations of animal cruelty at its facility on Scotland's Isle of Skye, the Times reported.

FREE READ UK millionaire pledges to invest in more covert salmon farming probes

The move follows the release of undercover footage by environmental campaign group Green Britain Foundation, showing fish being suffocated, beaten repeatedly, and one reportedly crushed under a worker's heel at its Loch Harport site.

NGO the RSPCA described the video as "extremely upsetting," and its certification standard has launched an investigation. UK supermarkets J. Sainsbury and Waitrose and Partners are reviewing contracts with Mowi, with Sainsbury's suspending supply from that site pending the outcome, the newspaper reported.

The footage, filmed over a month, allegedly shows violations of animal welfare guidelines, including exceeding the 15-second out-of-water limit and improper use of a percussive stun device.

Mowi said it had "reviewed" the video and that husbandry staff at the farm were removing a small number of poorly performing fish from a large pen.

"We do understand why the footage showing these fish being dispatched may be concerning to some people, but percussive stun to dispatch fish is the most effective and humane method in these circumstances," a company statement said.

Refresher courses would be given to staff, it added, to ensure the requirements of the RSPCA welfare scheme were upheld at all times.

In the fall of 2024, sites belonging to Scottish Sea Farms, Mowi, and Bakkafrost were temporarily suspended from the RSPCA's welfare certification scheme after a video emerged of live fish suffocating out of water.

content:
Oysters from South Korea are once again being recalled in the US due to norovirus contamination.

The notice was issued May 5 by Vernon, California-based Pacific American Fish Company (PAFCO) regarding certain raw frozen oyster half shells imported from South Korea and processed by JBR following testing and illness reports.

The oysters impacted by the recall can be recognized by lot # B250106 and the harvest date of 01/06/2025. The recall is part of an ongoing investigation, according to PAFCO. The company said it's collaborating with the California Department of Public Health (CDPH)

Oysters from South Korea were under investigation by CDPH just a few months ago, as reported by Undercurrent News. In March, Los Angeles, California-based seafood wholesaler Sea Win recalled 650 cases of frozen half-shell oysters imported from South Korea, after the state's public health department received notifications of multiple illnesses related to their consumption. The recall was expanded a few weeks later, but no updates have been issued since March 26.

title: Listeria outbreak in US linked to ready-to-eat tuna sandwiches, other items
content:
A US food supplier of ready-to-eat (RTE) sandwiches and snack items, including tuna sandwiches, is recalling several products after a suspected Listeria monocytogenes outbreak resulted in at least 10 people being hospitalized in the states of California and Nevada.

The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) shared on Saturday (May 10) that it is collaborating with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on an investigation of illnesses linked to RTE foods or products produced by San Fernando, California-based Fresh & Ready Foods.

Fresh & Ready Foods is voluntarily recalling some ready-to-eat sandwiches and snack items sold in Arizona, California, Nevada and Washington. Photo Credit: Fresh & Ready Foods

Per the notice, the FDA and CDC began investigating a cluster of listeria infections in 2024, but did not have enough evidence to "identify a source for the outbreak." The investigation into the multistate listeria outbreak reopened this past April when a routine surveillance inspection by FDA at Fresh & Ready Foods resulted in the collection of listeria samples.

According to the FDA, whole genome sequencing allowed them to confirm that the strain of listeria found at Fresh & Ready Foods matched the strain causing illnesses.

More than 80 products are included in the recall, including five tuna-based products: Fresh & Ready Foods tuna salad multigrain sandwich, Fresh & Ready Foods Mike's tuna mac pasta, Fresh & Ready Foods tuna salad on wheat sandwich, Fresh Take Crave Away Mike;'s tuna mac pasta, and Fresh Take Crave Away tuna salad on wheat sandwich. A full list of items impacted by the recall can be found here.

Recalled products can be identified by the "Use By" dates from 4/22/2025 to 05/19/2025. The items were sold in the US states of Arizona, California, Nevada and Washington at a variety of retailers and foodservice locations, such as hospitals, hotels and airports.

As noted above, there have been 10 reported illnesses -- all of which resulted in hospitalizations.

title: China’s Joyvio accused of using threats, false testimony in high-stakes Chilean legal battle
content:
What began as a record-breaking foreign investment in Chile's salmon industry has spiraled into a legal and diplomatic crisis involving accusations of false testimony, witness tampering and obstruction of justice.

Chinese conglomerate Joyvio Food, which in 2019 acquired Australis Seafoods in an $880 million deal, once again is finding its top executives at the center of a criminal complaint filed in a Chilean court.

The Fourth Guarantee Court of Santiago, on Monday (May 5), declared admissable testimony received from Chilean businessman Isidoro Quiroga in which he accused key figures at Joyvio, including chairman Shaopeng Chen and CEO Yonggun Huang, and Australis general manager Andres Lyon of orchestrating a campaign of judicial manipulation.

Quirogo, who sold Australis to Joyvio, had provided his comments nearly a week earlier, on April 30.

Joyvio Food offloads loss-making Chilean salmon farmer Australis to avoid de-listing

According to the legal filing, the Joyvio executives launched a broad legal offensive against Quiroga and his inner circle, accusing them of fraud, embezzlement, money laundering, and providing false market information.

But the new complaint, to which Undercurrent News has been provided full access, alleges that those charges were baseless from the start, and worse, that Joyvio knowingly built its case on fabricated claims.

This opens a new legal chapter in what Quiroga's legal team described as a "studied strategy of judicial, communicational, diplomatic and personal extortion" orchestrated by Joyvio.

"They knew the allegations were false"

At the heart of the complaint is the accusation that Joyvio launched a criminal investigation based on information they knew to be untrue. The Chilean filing states:

"The defendants filed criminal charges […] fully aware that the accusations they contained were completely false."

Specifically, Joyvio has claimed it was misled during the sale and that Australis's former owners concealed historical overproduction of salmon. But Quiroga's team points to internal documents and testimony showing that information was, in fact, disclosed well before the deal closed.

"The information on historical and projected harvests for each of Australis's farming sites, as well as the respective environmental production caps, was provided to Joyvio, its representatives, and technical advisors completely, timely, and repeatedly," the complaint also reads.

Internal emails cast doubt on Joyvio’s ignorance about Australis overproduction

Among the key pieces of evidence is a 2024 sworn statement by Jose Gago, Joyvio's technical advisor during the sale, who confirmed he and others received detailed projections "site by site, through 2030," during due diligence.

The complaint also states that Andres Lyon, one of the accused, met with Gago and reviewed this same information before any criminal charges were filed.

It also escalates beyond misrepresentation, accusing Joyvio executives of "actively obstructing justice through threats and manipulation."

The Chilean plaintiffs claim Joyvio and its senior executives "offered bribes to witnesses to secure false statements, threatened others to discourage testimony, and altered and hid evidence that disproved their accusations."

The filing alleges: "They even went so far as to cut up a document that contained information unfavorable to them."

Chilean court imposes travel ban on former Australis execs, sets 180-day investigation

Further, the plaintiffs say that some of the statements submitted to Chilean prosecutors were entirely fabricated, made by individuals "induced" by the defendants. "Some of the defendants, and other individuals acting under their direction, gave false testimony before the Public Prosecutor's Office," it says.

The complaint frames these acts not as isolated incidents but as part of a broader scheme:

"The acts of obstruction […] are part of a carefully designed and executed plan by Joyvio to unduly pressure Isidoro Quiroga, his family, and his collaborators."

That plan, it adds, includes aggressive media campaigns, defamatory statements, and multiple failed legal actions in foreign jurisdictions, "all meant to publicly discredit and legally corner the former owners of Australis."

From flagship deal to diplomatic dilemma

What once showcased Chinese investment in Chile has now become a case study in cross-border corporate conflict. Observers of international business law are also closely watching the case, as it raises questions about due diligence, disclosure standards, and the use of criminal courts in private commercial disputes.

Quiroga's lawyers describe Joyvio's actions as "an attempt to rewrite the facts of a deal they now regret."

"The criminal accusations made by Joyvio are based on a central claim that historical overproduction was concealed, a demonstrably false claim and one the defendants knew was false at the time."

Joyvio, for its part, has previously claimed that it was misled in the acquisition and that it is simply seeking accountability. The company has not yet responded publicly to the complaint.

This latest legal twist follows a string of international court rulings that have rejected Joyvio's claims. Most recently, on March 13, 2025, Delaware's Chancery Court dismissed a third lawsuit filed by Joyvio against Quiroga, marking the fifth consecutive loss for Joyvio across multiple jurisdictions.

The court found the case lacked both procedural merit and substantive connection to Delaware, echoing earlier dismissals in Florida, England, and Delaware Superior Court.

title: Canada hits steel giant with 200 Fisheries Act violations over pollution allegations
content:
Environment and Climate Change Canada announced this week that it has filed criminal charges against the world's second-largest steel producer for allegedly allowing its ore mining operations in the province of Quebec to pollute fish-bearing streams. 

ArcelorMittal Canada, Inc., a subsidiary of the Luxembourg-based mining giant, stands accused of 200 violations of the Fisheries Act in formal charges filed April 30, Environment and Climate Change Canada announced on May 1.

"These investigations were conducted into alleged deposits of deleterious substances into several fish-bearing waterways made by the Mont-Wright mining complex and the Fire Lake mine in the Fermont region of Quebec," the federal ministry said. "The incidents reportedly occurred between May 2014 and June 2022."

Study points to threats to Alaskan salmon habitat from future mining projects

Environment Canada said the alleged pollution was discovered following several investigations launched by the ministry's enforcement officers. 

The alleged violations occurred in tributaries of the Moisie River, which is a provincially planned aquatic reserve. The ministry said it's also one of the largest Atlantic salmon rivers in North America.

ArcelorMittal will be required to answer the charges in court and is innocent until proven guilty, the Canadian government noted. Therefore, the federal agency said it would not comment further. 

ArcelorMittal did not immediately return a message seeking comment.

title: Trump administration petitioned to investigate Ecuador shrimp industry for mangrove destruction, child labor
content:
The Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA), a group that represents the harvesters and processors of wild-caught shrimp in the southeastern US, has petitioned the US Commerce Department to investigate the Ecuador shrimp industry for alleged illegal deforestation of mangroves, forced labor and its receipt of funds from the World Bank.

Importers of Ecuadorian frozen shrimp could be forced to pay more in countervailing duties (CVDs) should the more-than 1,600 page-filing and letter written on behalf of SSA by the lawfirm of Picard Kentz & Rowe, in Washington, D.C., prove successful. The filing and letter, sent Thursday (May 1), are addressed to commerce secretary Howard Lutnick.

The latest action by SSA goes beyond the earlier investigations by the Commerce Department in relation to anti-competitive behavior by the shrimp sectors in Ecuador, India, Vietnam and Indonesia. Those were in response to the October 2023 request made by the American Shrimp Processors Association (ASPA), another group that represents US domestic harvesters and processors.

ASPA's request resulted in importers of shrimp produced by Ecuador's Industrial Pesquera Santa Priscilla being forced to pay a subsidy rate of 3.57%, while importers of shrimp from Sociedad Nacional de Galapagos (Songa) are forced to pay 4.41% and importers of all other Ecuadorian shrimp must pay 3.78%.

ITC rules US shrimp industry suffered as a result of imports, cements AD, CVD rates

The International Trade Commission cemented the new CVD rates in November, finding the US domestic shrimp sector did suffer as a result of the actions taken by the Ecuador, India, Vietnam and Indonesia shrimp industries, as reported by Undercurrent News. 

Commerce, on March 6, formally initiated "expedited reviews" of the earlier CVD orders as requested by six Ecuadorian shrimp exporters in an attempt to remove the duties, according to an SSA press release. However, Commerce's requirements already have resulted in two of the companies withdrawing their requests while complaining that they anticipated "the department would adopt more streamlined procedures," SSA said.

Ecuador is the US' second-largest source of shrimp, sending it 187,040 metric tons worth $1.3 billion in 2024, behind only India, which sent the US 294,333t worth $2.2bn last year, as earlier reported by Undercurrent.

Now, in the US shrimp producers' latest move against importers, SSA has "formally asked Commerce to look into government benefits provided to the Ecuadorian shrimp industry that were not evaluated in the original investigation," the trade group explains.

In particular, SSA charges that Ecuador's shrimp industry has wrecked the environment, costing it 16.4% of its mangroves between 1985 and 2022, in violation of its national law that forbids such deforestation. Additionally, Ecuador has failed to enforce its anti-child labor laws, SSA charges, and its government has successfully obtained $700 million in funding from the World Bank to help its shrimp sector but has failed to manage it legally.  

"For too long, our trade laws have treated companies engaged in unfair trade with kid gloves," said John Williams, SSA's executive director, in the statement. "An America First Trade Policy requires that our unfair trade laws create a level playing field. Although it is not what the Ecuadorian shrimp exporters intended, the US shrimp industry hopes that Commerce will accept their invitation to conduct an even more in-depth investigation of their unfair trade."

title: Scottish salmon industry chief faces ethics probe over lobbying
content:
The head of industry association Salmon Scotland is under formal investigation by the Scottish parliamentary ethics watchdog over allegations of improper lobbying practices and intimidation of an elected official, according to recent reports.

Tavish Scott, CEO of Salmon Scotland and a former Scottish Liberal Democrat party leader, is being investigated by Holyrood's Ethical Standards Commissioner following claims he "verbally attacked" a member of the Scottish Parliament (MSP) and failed to properly register lobbying activities as required by Scottish law. 

FREE READ UK millionaire pledges to invest in more covert salmon farming probes

The investigation centers on a 2023 meeting between Scott and Conservative MSP Edward Mountain. During this encounter, Scott allegedly threatened Mountain after the parliamentarian raised concerns about salmon mortality rates and food safety. Scott reportedly told Mountain that the salmon industry board was "very unhappy" with him and "willing to take action" unless Mountain retracted statements made in parliament.

The incident came to light when Mountain publicly disclosed the alleged threats during a parliamentary committee meeting in October 2024. According to reports, the meeting in question was not recorded in Scotland's mandatory lobbying register.

Dale Vince -- a British renewable energy entrepreneur, founder of the Green Britain Foundation, and anti-aquaculture activist, who filed the complaint -- characterized the situation as revealing "an industry that believes it can bully its critics into silence."

A spokesperson for Salmon Scotland told Undercurrent News: "Salmon Scotland fully complies with the lobbying register." Scott, who maintains parliamentary access through credentials granted to former elected officials, has denied any wrongdoing.

title: Fortune accuses $500m Norwegian salmon giant’s new US entity of unlawfully going direct to Boston Sword customers
content:
Fortune International has filed suit against the US division of Norwegian salmon giant Vikenco and its president Chris Marchese, alleging they conspired to steal confidential business information and trade secrets while Marchese was working as director of salmon and key accounts at Fortune subsidiary Boston Sword and Tuna (BST).

Fortune, a large Bensenville, Illinois-headquartered seafood distributor majority owned by Investcorp since 2020, alleges it caught Marchese "red-handed" violating confidentiality, non-solicitation and non-competition agreements by sending incriminating emails to senior executives at Vikenco, which is 51% owned by farmer and processor SalMar and generates around NOK 5 billion (close to $500 million) in revenue annually.

Mowi wins skin-pack supply relationship with Trader Joe’s at expense of US processors

Marchese joined Vikenco as CEO of its North American subsidiary in December 2024 following a 13-year tenure at BST, which Fortune acquired in May 2023.

"While Marchese was employed by BST, he was simultaneously working with senior executives of Vikenco's Norwegian parent, Vikenco AS, to establish a U.S. entity (i.e., Vikenco) that would compete directly with [BST]. Moreover, Vikenco was entirely complicit in this process," the lawsuit stated. "The forbidden competition is all the more egregious because, to accomplish it, Defendants expressly relied upon [BST's] confidential and proprietary information, which Marchese brazenly e-mailed to Vikenco senior personnel using his BST e-mail account for a period of approximately six months prior to his resignation from BST."

Marchese and Vikenco "used the stolen information to set up a competing business and to engage in direct competition" with BST and to solicit its clients, "in direct violation of Marchese's common law and contractual obligations," Fortune alleges in its lawsuit.

The suit, filed Tuesday (April 29) in US District Court for the District of Massachusetts, alleges Marchese violated several agreements he signed with BST, including an employee restrictive covenants agreement and a transaction bonus agreement, under which he received $200,000 but was prohibited from disclosing confidential information to anyone outside the firm.

Marchese was recruited by Vikenco CEO and general manager Per Olav Mevold and vice president and chief operating officer Jonny Smage to build up the company's US operation, which was created in November 2024 with the goal of bringing the Norwegian salmon processor "deeper into the US market," as Undercurrent News reported.

$500m Norway salmon processor sets up US operation with former Boston Sword exec

Vikenco was a longtime supplier of Boston, Massachusetts-based BST, but proprietary information forwarded by Marchese to Mevold and Smage allegedly allowed it to quickly scale up its US business, partially at the expense of BST and Fortune, which claims to have proof it lost several customers as a result. 

"[Marchese's actions] allowed Vikenco to enter the market more expediently and at a fraction of the cost," Fortune alleges.

Earlier in the year, Undercurrent reported that BST had lost a chunk of skin-pack business with retailer Trader Joe's, although this is not mentioned in the lawsuit. 

In its suit, Fortune said it received three emails a BST customer inadvertently sent to Marchese's old BST account, seeking to place purchase orders with Vikenco. Upon investigation, Fortune says it discovered a trove of documentation that Marchese was actively working to steer business to Vikenco and undermine BST's relationships with its customers.

In June 2024, Marchese sent a customer list of BST's salmon buyers to Vikenco that included purchase volumes and sales by region, and the next month, Marchese forwarded another email detailing the farmed salmon program of one of BST's largest customers, including contact information and its request for a new type of cut of salmon requiring special processing, Fortune alleges. A subsequent email forwarded by Marchese to Vikenco included details of the negotiations between BST and the customer about the new salmon cut, Fortune says.

The emails Marchese sent to Vikenco "represented a veritable who's who of BST's most significant clients and customers," representing more than $150m in 2024 sales, and provided a blueprint for Vikenco to undercut BST and steal its business, Fortune alleges.

The emails found by Fortune were sent through BST's email systems, but the lawsuit speculates that additional incriminating materials could be found by a search of Marchese's private email account and texting history. 

Boston Sword can take skin-pack program ‘national’ with Fortune backing

Fortune is seeking a restraining order to block Vikenco from using BST's trade secrets, a return of any misappropriated information, monetary damages including punitive compensation and attorneys' fees.

The lawsuit argues that without swift judicial intervention, the damage to BST and Fortune's competitive position "will become irreparable."

Fortune president and CEO Sean O'Scanlainn declined to comment on the suit.

Marchese's joined BST 13 years ago and it was his first job in the seafood industry, Fortune alleges. He rose through the ranks to become chief operating officer in 2019 and was promoted to director of salmon and key accounts in November 2024, overseeing the purchase, sale, packaging, processing, and distribution of more than 300,000 pounds of salmon per week. 

Marchese was highly paid -- in 2024, he earned more than $330,000, and in 2023, he earned nearly $550,000. As part of BST's senior leadership team, he received a $200,000 bonus when BST was bought by Fortune.

According to the suit, Marchese submitted his resignation to BST president Larry Dore on Dec. 6, 2024, at which time he told Dore Vikenco did not plan to compete with BST, "but rather that it was designed to be a U.S.-based presence for Vikenco AS to support its existing customers, and that Marchese's role with Vikenco would be beneficial to BST as it would enhance Vikenco AS's service to BST."

"Marchese expressly represented that he and Vikenco would not be pursuing BST's customers or competing with BST," the suit alleges.

Marchese formally departed from BST on Dec. 20, 2024, and joined Vikenco in January 2025, receiving a 15% ownership stake in Vikenco North America following his move, the suit alleges.

Boston Sword deal will take Fortune past $1bn turnover

On Jan. 21, 2025, Vikenco registered as a foreign corporation in the US, with a principal place of business in Tewsksbury, Massachusetts, at the same address as the home of Marchese's father, according to the lawsuit.

In an email, Mevold confirmed Vikenco had been informed of the suit.

"Vikenco North America, Inc.'s view is that there are no grounds for the claims and has engaged an attorney to assist in the case. As the case is pending before the court, Vikenco North America, Inc. has informed that it does not wish to comment any further on the matter at this time," Mevold told Undercurrent in an email.

Marchese has not responded to a request for comment.

In addition to aiding Vikenco, Marchese allegedly hindered BST's own business before his departure.

"The purpose of this appears to have been twofold: first, to lock BST into supply contracts with Vikenco AS that were favorable to Vikenco AS, and thus would be beneficial to Marchese's new employer Vikenco, and, second, to undermine BST's relationships with other customers and vendors, such that those third parties would be likely to do business with Vikenco as opposed to BST," Fortune alleges.

Marchese allegedly provided BST customers with above-market prices "so that he could later step in and offer a lower price from Vikenco." He also withheld information about business opportunities that he received in his last months at BST, and provided competitor Great Eastern Seafood with proprietary pricing information for a BST customer. 

"A competitor having access to this information would be able to use the knowledge and insights that BST built over many years to get a jump-start on determining how to operate its business without putting in the hard work that BST did and undermine BST's competitive advantage in the marketplace," Fortune says in its suit.

title: Cocaine seized on Ecuadorian tuna vessel near Galapagos
content:
On April 26, Ecuadorian authorities intercepted the tuna vessel Monte-Cristi near the Galapagos Islands, Ecuador, uncovering 71 bundles of suspected cocaine and arresting 22 individuals, El Diario reported.

The vessel had departed from Manta on April 24 with a registered crew of 21, but a hidden Mexican national was found during inspection.

The operation, led by the Ecuadorian navy and coast guard, was part of routine patrols targeting illegal fishing and maritime crimes.

The suspects were taken to San Cristobal naval base and handed to prosecutors.

The boat was seized for further investigation.

Officials suspect links to international drug trafficking networks, as Manta is a known departure point for narco-shipments. The cargo’s estimated street value may exceed $30 million.

title: Five US fishermen caught falsifying records for nearly 60,000 lbs of Louisiana crab
content:
Officers with the US state of Louisiana's Department of Wildlife and Fisheries (LDWF) issued citations to five commercial fishermen in Cameron Parish earlier this month after an investigation found that the individuals falsified records for nearly 60,000 pounds of crab.

Law enforcement agents with LDWF began investigating commercial fishermen Selema Frank (53), Wendy Hill (43), Edward Naquin (61), Angela LaBove (50) and Francis Theriot (60) after hearing reports about falsified trip tickets. According to the agents, a commercial dock in Grand Chenier, Louisiana, was working with the five fishermen to "falsify the trip ticket information by putting them in other people's names than the actual person harvesting the crabs."

Through the investigation, LDWF agents discovered 125 falsified trip tickets that contained 175 falsified daily transactions and 59,834 pounds of illegally documented crab.

On April 16, LDWF agents cited Frank for injuring public records, filing false public records, criminal conspiracy and failing to maintain records. Hill was cited for criminal conspiracy. Naquin was cited for failing to complete trip tickets and criminal conspiracy. LaBove was cited for injuring public records, criminal conspiracy and filing false public records. Theriot was charged with failing to complete trip tickets, criminal conspiracy and injuring public records. 

Failure to maintain records brings a fine up to $500 and up to 90 days in jail, while injuring public records and filing false records carries a fine up to $5,000 and five years in jail. LDWF noted that criminal conspiracy "brings fines and imprisonment in the same manner as the offense contemplated by the conspirators."

The latest citations come a few weeks after LDWF agents issued citations to four other fishermen who were engaged in illegal crab harvesting in Terrebonne Parish. Those fishermen were found to be in possession of immature female crabs, as reported by Undercurrent News.

title: Namibian court rejects asset restraint order on ex-Samherji execs, Fishrot rumbles on
content:
As the "biggest corruption trial in Namibia's history" continues into its sixth year, a high court judge has refused to issue an asset restraint order against three Icelandic executives representing six companies involved in the Fishrot case -- regarding the alleged corrupt sale of Namibian fishing quotas.

The decision was taken on the grounds that she does not believe the trio will ever be charged in the country in connection to the case, according to a report from The Namibian.

Namibia’s Fishrot scandal: Recap every development from 2020

The Fishrot scandal, begun by 2019 leaks from whistleblower and former Samherji employee Johannes Stefansson, implicated the Icelandic fishing giant in the alleged bribery of Namibian officials to secure horse mackerel fishing quotas worth over $650 million, according to Namibia's Financial Intelligence Centre.

In March 2025, Namibian high court judge Orben Sibeya ruled that Namibia's prosecutor general, Martha Imalwa, had failed to demonstrate that Icelandic citizens and former managers of Samherji's Namibian operations Adalsteinn Helgason, Egill Helgi Arnason, and Ingvar Juliusson would be extradited so they may be prosecuted in Namibia.

Imalwa was pursuing a restraint order against assets belonging to the three men, who each helped to run Samherji's six former subsidiaries in Namibia: Esja Holding, Mermaria Seafood, Saga Seafood, Heinaste Investments Namibia, Saga Investments and Esja Investments.

It's the latest ruling around the three men, who were originally charged by the Namibian state in February 2021 on 14 counts of money laundering and tax evasion, among other misdemeanors.

The three were due to stand trial at Windhoek High Court in April of that year but did not make an appearance, leading the judge dealing with the case to remove their names from the indictment.

While the Namibian state said it had initiated extradition proceedings for the three men, Iceland intervened, with the public prosecutor's office saying in definite terms that Iceland does not permit the extradition of its citizens to other countries.

Namibia's state prosecutor then asked Interpol for assistance in 2022 to track down Helgason, Arnason, and Juliusson. At the time, the three requested permission to testify from outside and not have to travel to Namibia for proceedings, as reported by Icelandic publication RUV.

'Fishrot Six' still awaiting trial

The trial in Namibia, which currently involves 10 Namibian defendants facing charges, has been significantly delayed so far.

This has now been postponed until August this year due to issues with legal representation, according to The Namibian.

Former Namibian fisheries minister claims to have been ‘used’ in Fishrot scandal

The accused include former Namibian justice and fisheries ministers Sacky Shanghala and Bernhard Esau, who have been in custody awaiting trial for over five years. 

Others include former Fishcor chairperson James Hatuikulipi, his nephew Tamson Hatuikulipi, former Namgomar Pesca owner Ricardo Gustavo and businessmen Pius Mwatelulo, who together with the two ministers comprised the original so-called 'Fishrot Six' arrested in November 2019.

Four others have also since been charged in relation to the case: former Fishcor CEO Mike Nghipunya, Otneel Shuudifonya, Phillipus Mwapopi, and Nigel van Wyk.

The 10 accused men are being prosecuted on 42 charges; they have all pleaded not guilty. The Icelandic executives mentioned earlier are not included in the trial as they are not being prosecuted in Namibia.

Fishrot's 10 defendants. Photo: The Namibian.

In June 2021, US authorities imposed sanctions on the two former Namibian cabinet ministers for their involvement "in corrupt acts that undermined the rule of law and the Namibian public's faith in their government's democratic institutions and public processes."

However, according to a separate report from Namibia's Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) released in November last year to mark the five-year anniversary of the initial leak, no sanctions have yet been imposed on the Icelandic suspects. 

The first of two reports from the IPPR was published in March 2024, highlighting the ongoing impact of Fishrot on fishing communities in Namibia.

The report also showcases the profound effects the case has had on Namibian fishing communities, documenting the struggles of former fishermen on the three vessels Samherji used to operate in Namibia -- the Heinaste, the Saga, and the Geysir -- who have subsequently faced economic hardship.

The IPPR found that almost 90% of those previously employed by Samherji have not been able to find subsequent employment in the sector, with 80% now dependent on family and friends for assistance. Moreover, 86% claim to have fallen into poverty and debt since Samherji left Namibia and lost personal property as a result of being unable to find follow-up jobs.

Many were from the countryside, who had come to Walvis Bay to work in the fishing sector but suddenly found themselves unable to pay rent, evicted from their houses, and forced to return to the country, with much bleaker employment prospects.

Icelandic investigation ongoing

Meanwhile, in Iceland, a district prosecutor handling the case has named nine suspects, according to the IPPR, but to date, no Icelandic citizen has been charged with any crime.

Iceland's district prosecutor's office confirmed to Undercurrent News at the start of 2025 that the investigation on the case is still ongoing in Iceland and being handled by the prosecutor general, without specifying further details.

Samherji itself has so far avoided any serious consequences from its seven years of operation and alleged bribery in Namibia, UNCAC Coalition reported.

The company did not reply to a request for comment in time for this article.

Last year, the case was briefly back in the public sphere after Icelandic artist Odee created a spoof website mimicking Samherji's to draw attention back to their alleged involvement in the scandal.

In November, the UK's high court subsequently ruled in favor of Samherji, deeming Odee's work had used the company's registered trademark and intellectual property in violation of its corporate rights.

Fishermen's unresolved pay remains an issue

In 2023, 23 former employees of ArticNam, a joint venture between Icelandic and Namibian companies and a key entity in the Fishrot dispute, claimed they had been unfairly dismissed at the end of 2018 and claimed NAD 1.8m ($99,000) plus interest as compensation each, the African L11 reported.

Settlement awarded for Namibian fishermen cast aside in Heinaste dispute

The fishermen have issued summons against three defendants for payment, asking for compensation: Esja Investments, a Samherji subsidiary; Arnason, who at the time was a director on the board of Esja and also the managing director of ArticNam; and ArticNam, which was owned by Esja. 

According to the summons, Esja and Arnason had allegedly transferred large sums of ArcticNam money out of Namibia illegally, leaving the company without the funds needed to pay the 23 employees their salaries and ArcticNam without the money to pay its creditors.

When the awards for unfair dismissal were first made, ArcticNam officials in Namibia said that officials in Iceland were responsible for any discrepancies and that they had been trying to get their counterparts to take responsibility without success.

The attorney acting for the 23, Norman Tjombe, said since ArticNam had no assets, it was necessary to act against the managing company, Esja, and Arnason.

Tjombe said he believed Esja still had remaining capital in Namibia, which it hadn't been able to get out of the country and which it was trying to hide. Some of this figure, however, has already been frozen by the state prosecutor.

For example, the Heinaste, a fishing vessel originally linked to Samherji, was first seized in the wake of the Fishrot expose and then sold on to Namibia's Tunacor Fisheries.

However, since the original report in 2023 on the fishermen's pay dispute with ArticNam's former executives, there has been no further news, so there is a chance that the dispute has been settled or is being negotiated among the parties without being reported.

Namibia's justice ministry did not respond to Undercurrent with an update on the case from the government's perspective when contacted for comment.

title: Third dock collapses in US scallop capital, raising maintenance concerns
content:
Concern is growing about the maintenance of the docks in the US scallop capital of New Bedford, Massachusetts, after a hunk of pier fell into the New Bedford Harbor on Wednesday (April 23), The New Bedford Light reports. 

The collapse, which is the third in less than two years, caused no injuries but dropped a metal storage shed into the water. 

The asphalt-surface dock and the shed dropped into about 20 feet of water outside the processing plant of Sea Watch International, on Antonio Costa Avenue, Gordon Carr, executive director of the New Bedford Port Authority, reportedly told the news service.

Sea Watch, a clam and quahog producer, used the pier to unload catch, Carr said. The property is owned by the city and is part of a parcel, just over an acre, that's been under a 99-year lease to Sea Watch since 1981 at the rate of $3,960 a year.

The effort to maintain the Sea Watch property has been complicated by a "disagreement about who is responsible" for repairs, Carr said, adding: "We're continuing those discussions."

The collapsed pier, which had been supported by concrete pilings, stood between two sections of the dock that fell into the water in separate incidents in October 2023 and April 2024. The stretch of three properties runs about 400 to 450 feet, Carr said. 

The properties in the two previous incidents are owned by a real estate company owned by executives at Eastern Fisheries, a major scallop producer based in New Bedford. 

Carr said the focus was now on infrastructure improvements, which is similar to a statement he made after a section of pier collapsed in April 2024 in an area where Eastern Fisheries docks scallop boats, the news service reported. There were no injuries on that occasion either.

However, four people were thrown into the water when a dock collapsed in October 2023, and two were treated at a hospital for injuries that were not life-threatening.

Carr said there was a "small sheen" on the water Wednesday, but it was not clear what, if anything, was in the shed and if anything spilled into the water.

Tobia Brewer, a lieutenant in the US Coast Guard Marine Safety Unit, in New Bedford, said a boom appeared to be working to contain the sheen and noted that an investigation into the incident has begun. 

New Bedford is the US' most valuable commercial fishing port, responsible for $443.2 million worth of landings in 2022, most of them Atlantic scallops. However, the 2024-25 scallop season, which ended March 31, 2025, was a rough one for harvesters and garnered only $213.8m at the New Bedford docks, as reported by Undercurrent News.
