title: Venezuela’s Lamar vows swift recovery after fire at key shrimp processing plant
content:
Venezuela’s Grupo Lamar has pledged a rapid recovery following a fire that damaged one of its primary processing plants over the weekend.

Fire damages Venezuela’s largest shrimp plant following gov’t takeover

The blaze occurred on Sunday, April 20, at the Antartica plant, located in the San Francisco municipality, in the state of Zulia, Venezuela. It was the largest facility in the country's once-dominant Grupo Lamar conglomerate.

While the company confirmed there were no injuries, the incident caused significant material losses, including "damage to machinery, infrastructure, and inventory destined for both domestic consumption and export markets."

In an official statement, Grupo Lamar’s administrative board described the fire as an “unusual incident" and confirmed that Venezuelan security agencies "are conducting a full investigation into the cause."

The firm also noted that the plant had recently undergone a comprehensive round of preventative maintenance, part of a broader investment strategy over the past three weeks.

“All losses were strictly material,” the statement read, listing destroyed equipment and production goods among the affected assets. The company emphasized that operations across its wider network -- including shrimp farms, laboratories, and other processing facilities -- remain fully functional.

The business also reassured employees and clients that it would maintain both its production schedule and workforce. “We guarantee the continuity of production and employment, as well as the recovery of the damaged infrastructure,” the company said.

CEO of Venezuelan shrimp giant flees country after coup plot accusation

The cause of the fire remains under investigation. Authorities have yet to release further details.

As Undercurrent News reported, the fire broke out around 9:30 a.m. and was brought under control roughly two hours later, according to local sources who witnessed the incident. Firefighters battled intense flames, which produced a towering column of black smoke visible for miles. 

The Antartica plant was one of six processing facilities that once made up the core of Grupo Lamar, a seafood empire that dominated 80% of Venezuela's shrimp production before being seized by the government of Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro on Nov. 28, 2024.

The government takeover left operations across the group's facilities paralyzed, including at the factory in question. Before the fire, it had reportedly been operating at minimal capacity, if at all.

Once a major exporter, Grupo Lamar fell into difficulty last year, when the Venezuelan government launched a crackdown on its founder, Jose Enrique Rincon, and his sons, accusing them of terrorism and links to drug trafficking -- claims widely viewed as politically motivated.

The company was producing 50,000 metric tons of shrimp annually and was heavily focused on the European market prior to the seizure.

title: Untitled
content:
A massive fire has dealt significant damage to Venezuela's largest shrimp processing plant on Sunday (April 20), Undercurrent News has learned.

The "Antartica" plant, located in the San Francisco municipality, in the state of Zulia, Venezuela, was the largest facility in the country's once-dominant Grupo Lamar conglomerate.

Though it's not clear yet how damaged the Antartica plant is, its destruction would further dim the prospects of reviving Venezuela's shrimp industry, which once supported over 11,000 jobs and played a vital role in bolstering the nation's non-oil exports.

The fire broke out around 9:30 a.m. and was brought under control roughly two hours later, according to local sources who witnessed the incident.

Firefighters battled intense flames, which produced a towering column of black smoke visible for miles. While no casualties have been reported, the fire caused extensive damage to the plant.

CEO of Venezuelan shrimp giant flees country after coup plot accusation

The Antartica plant was one of six processing facilities that once made up the core of Grupo Lamar, a seafood empire that dominated 80% of Venezuela's shrimp production before being seized by the government of Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro on Nov. 28, 2024. The government takeover left operations across the group's facilities paralyzed, including at the Antartica plant.

Dozens of officers from the Bolivarian National Police, the Zulia State Police Corps, and the San Francisco Police cordoned off the area, halting traffic and keeping bystanders at bay as emergency teams worked to extinguish the blaze. Authorities say the cause of the fire is still under investigation.

State security forces have launched an investigation into the "unusual circumstances" surrounding the plant fire, VTV reported.

According to a source familiar with the company, Antartica was the largest in the group and primarily focused on value-added products.

Once a major exporter, Grupo Lamar fell into difficulty last year, when the Venezuelan government launched a crackdown on its founder, Jose Enrique Rincon, and his sons, accusing them of terrorism and links to drug trafficking -- claims widely viewed as politically motivated.

The company was producing 50,000 metric tons of shrimp annually and was heavily focused on the European market prior to the seizure.

"The regime did everything possible to scare them, force the Rincón family to leave the country and seize the facilities, claiming they were abandoning the country and conspiring to overthrow the government," the source told Undercurrent. "Everyone knows it's false, but these regimes can't stand someone succeeding and accumulating power."

Before the fire, the Antartica plant had reportedly been operating at minimal capacity, if at all.

Venezuelan gov’t cancels export licenses for Lamar shrimp on water to overseas ports

"Production is almost down to zero right now," the source added, noting that most of the country's shrimp farms "are no longer functional."

"There's no food, no logistics, the processing plants are closed … that's the regime," they added.

After the government takeover, the first shipments were handed over to Chinese intermediaries, but sources say the venture quickly faltered.

"Now they don't know how to collect. Production is dwindling to a minimum. And I don't think that in the midst of this political storm, the Chinese or Russians … want to operate the plants," one source also stated.

"Look at Venezuela's export numbers now: close to zero," the source also told Undercurrent.

title: Untitled
content:
William Porter McHenry, a commercial fishing boat captain in the US state of California, has been fined close to $17,000 for polluting local waters near the port of Ventura, according to a news release from the Ventura County District Attorney's Office.

McHenry is the owner of the Sea Pearl, a 67-foot commercial fishing vessel. 

On December 6, 2024, California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) officers observed the Sea Pearl dumping stick water, a harmful substance created during the squid-fishing process, while on its way to the state water boundary line. Officers then observed the Sea Pearl turn around before crossing the state water boundary line. Legal disposal requires that the stick water, which contains high levels of ammonia, be released at least three nautical miles offshore.

Prior to heading to the state water boundary line, the Sea Pearl had offloaded 206,298 pounds of market squid in the Ventura Harbor. After offloading the squid, the vessel then received back the stick water from onshore tanks operated by Silver Bay Seafoods. When a CDFW warden boarded the Sea Pearl, an inspection found that three of the four fish holds were "completely empty, with only s small amount of stick water remaining in the fourth hold."

McHenry has been ordered to pay $8,444.69 9 for environmental restoration. The district attorney's office said funds will go to the Ventura County Fish and Wildlife Fund and the California Department of Fish and Wildlife. In addition, McHenry has been ordered to pay an additional $6,555.31 in penalties and investigation costs to the district attorney's office, and $1,889.39 for unfair business practices.

"This case highlights the importance of protecting our coastal waters," senior deputy district attorney Karen Wold said in a news release. "Illegally dumping harmful waste threatens our marine ecosystem and the livelihoods of those who depend on it."

title: Bluefin tuna corruption probe into Malta’s ex-fisheries chief ends
content:
A years-long corruption inquiry into Malta's former fisheries director, Andreina Fenech Farrugia, has concluded, Times of Malta reported.

The investigation, led by Spanish authorities, focused on an illegal bluefin tuna trafficking ring involving Spain, Malta and Italy.

Fenech was suspended in 2019 after intercepted phone calls suggested she may have solicited payments from Spanish tuna trader Jose Fuentes Garcia in exchange for facilitating illicit tuna exports. She denies any wrongdoing.

The alleged racket involved misreporting tuna harvests from Malta-based farms, forging documentation, and smuggling unregistered bluefin tuna -- often in unsanitary conditions -- into the European market. Additives were reportedly used to make spoiled or frozen tuna appear fresh, causing multiple food poisoning cases in Spain.

Malta was reportedly a key player in the fraudulent bluefin supply chain, with illegal stock routed through a warehouse in the Spanish city of Valencia.

The inquiry's findings have been forwarded to Malta's attorney general and police, though no formal charges have been announced. Fenech's lawyer maintains her innocence and said she has not been contacted by authorities.

title: Untitled
content:
The demise of the Indonesian aquaculture tech 'unicorn' eFishery has undeniably dented investor appetite for projects in the sector, but speakers on a panel at the Blue Food Innovation Summit in London, the UK, agreed it was not as dire for the sector as perhaps first feared.

eFishery -- which is backed by investors including SoftBank Group and Temasek Holdings and is nearly 20% owned by investor Aqua-Spark -- is under investigation for numerous financial irregularities. In January, a probe estimated that management had inflated revenue by almost $600 million in the nine months through September 2024. That would mean more than 75% of its reported figures were fake.

Blue Food Summit: ‘A lot of retailers don’t know where their seafood comes from’

Undercurrent News previously reported the resignation of veteran aquaculture executive Cameron Maclean from eFishery, which he tendered last November. 

Maclean resigned before its co-founders, Gibran Huzaifah and Chrisna Aditya, were suspended from their CEO/CFO and chief product officer posts, in December. Huzaifah and Aditya were abruptly removed amid an investigation into alleged financial fraud at the company.

Claire Pribula, managing director and co-founder of the Yield Lab Asia-Pacific, said the emergence of the eFishery news had "changed some of the dynamics of venture capital and innovation in regards to the types of rounds that are being raised; they've halved, and in some in some cases quartered, valuations have come down."

However, eFishery's rapid rise brought an upside for other aquatech firms that hasn't been utterly damaged since, she said.

"It was such a great thing for the industry, the momentum that came from it was felt in other deals. Everybody was fighting to get into aquaculture tech."

"I'm thinking of [Indonesian aquatech business] Jala and Liris [Maduningtyas, who presented shortly before the investor panel] -- they got a little tailwind from eFishery. Her round was about the same time; she was originally raising a $5m round for series A, which turned to $10m this year. then it went up to $12m. I can't say how much, but she's still got reserves in the bank," said Pribula. The Yield Lab is one of Jala's investors.

"I think what we can be proud to say is there is now -- because of us [investors], that are focusing on the industry and other reasons -- a lot of innovation in aquaculture. We have no end of deal flow that we're looking at."

She also noted that some of the fundraising that had been expected in the sector "swung into venture debt, which is very useful as these companies start to grow up and their capital expenditures increase."

Maria Velkova, chief portfolio officer at Aqua-Spark, was understandably asked for her take on the eFishery situation, as far as she could give it as an investor in the firm.

"I think we forget that this kind of thing is happening in every other industry," she said of the unicorn's failure. "I don't ever want to say this is normal because I don't think it is. But at the same time, I think we are much more resilient than just thinking that one company that failed is going to have a massive impact. I can imagine how this can be used by skeptics to say 'I told you so,' but I completely disagree. I think we have a lot of amazing examples that can rectify this and show that there is much more there."

"It's very, very unfortunate, and it's very emotional as well, because I think we were all looking forward to a success."

US tariffs put aquaculture investors globally on edge

She, too, emphasized there were plenty more aquaculture innovation firms around of interest. Both she and Pribula noted that investment in other sectors is not immune from expensive mistakes.

"We should really stop making it bigger than it is. I don't think oil and gas investments stopped after [the scandal at] Enron. Look at the financial sector -- if you talk to someone coming from there, they wouldn't even raise an eyebrow," said the Aqua-Spark executive, while Pribula said tech industry start-ups have a "75% failure rate."

"Listening to all these discussions around companies that have been building their businesses and working on their ideas for 10-plus years, it's just confirmed what we at Aqua-Spark believe: that if you want to change the world, you can't do it overnight, and you can't do it with a traditional structure where you make an investment and you're already looking to exit in five years.

"It's difficult, it takes time, because, again, our thesis revolves around changing the industry. Really shifting it towards different practices and elevating it, supporting founders and teams, being there and giving them confidence that they have an investor that is going to support them."

Rabobank 'unfazed' but a pause for reflection

Jeroen van der Staay, executive director of Rabobank’s Rabo Ventures, said he didn't think the eFishery debacle had rocked many boats.

"Obviously, unfortunately, what happened with the company, first and foremost, was bad for all people directly involved; employees, shareholders, and so on. But [investors should] have a fundamental understanding of what this industry is trying to do, the impact it has, and also the potential that it holds. I'm relatively unfazed about what happened, personally."

Credit: Aqua-Spark CEO Mike Velings on LinkedIn

"It may be that other people think the industry is a bit less far ahead than they thought it was. But underlying, slowly we should be growing -- at a different pace perhaps, but it's moving forward."

Nadir Ait-Laoussine, vice president for platforms and programs at US investor SeaAhead, said it "definitely created a pause for reflection," but he also stressed this wasn't a situation unique to the food production sector.

"It happens in finance, in tech, in energy, and all of those sectors continue to thrive. I do think the fundamentals of the food economy are intact. We're in an innovation climate with competency. We should not mix up this one case with many more opportunities that we're having in this sector."

And Alan Liu, vice president of Denmark's Novo Holdings, said controversies in other sectors showed it was about the lessons that could be learned and carried into the future.

"I think this space, in general, requires more patience in the funding and the approach. It is a tough task for a good reason, because doing things in the ocean, doing things with the ocean, is not easy."

Contact the author neil.ramsden@undercurrentnews.com

title: Former CEO of eFishery details 6-year accounts fakery
content:
The former eFishery CEO Gibran Huzaifah has gone into detail on how he faked the Indonesian aquaculture technology start-up's accounts over six years in an in-depth interview with Bloomberg.

At least $300 million of investors' money has been lost, with the news site noting, "It's unclear exactly how much all individual funds may have lost, and it's possible some sold shares at a higher valuation."

Six years after Huzaifah, running out of cash, began a second set of accounts -- a real one for his team and a second, inflated book for investors -- eFishery was one of Asia's brightest startups with a valuation of $1.4 billion and around 2,000 staff.

It was backed by several of the world's most high-profile venture players, from Japan's SoftBank Group Corp., Singapore's Temasek Holdings and Sequoia India and Southeast Asia (now Peak XV) to Abu Dhabi's 42XFund and Chamath Palihapitiya's Social Capital.

By the time it collapsed, the scheme had become a multinational web of fake shell companies and padded accounts. The company claimed revenues of $752m in the first nine months of 2024, while the true number was just $157m, according to an internal investigation.

Huzaifah told Bloomberg he wanted to state publicly that he didn't steal money and to make clear that the bulk of his employees weren't aware of what was happening.

"I just want to say, my deepest apology for everyone impacted, especially the farmers because they're the reason why I do this."

He claimed that in 2018 -- trying to secure investors to join Aqua-Spark in a series A fundraise -- he was told by other Indonesian start-up founders through vague and coded tips to essentially to fudge the numbers.

"They said that they massage the numbers, that they have some 'growth hacking' initiatives that they do and usually they do it prior to the fundraising," he said. "I knew it was wrong. But when everyone is doing it and they're still doing okay and never got caught, you question if it's really wrong."

As a result, the series A raised $4m in total, including a third tranche from Aqua-Spark, which took its investment to a total of $1.5m at that time.

title: US scallop vessel that ran aground now leaking fuel off Massachusetts
content:
A US commercial fishing vessel homeported in New Bedford, Massachusetts, ran aground on Friday (April 11), according to a US Coast Goard report.

Watchstanders at Coast Guard Sector Boston received a broken radio transmission from the Eileen Rita, a 90-foot scallop vessel, at 7:46 a.m. on Friday. Members of the Coast Guard were aided by the Boston Police and Fire in rescuing the vessel's captain and two crew members off the coast of Green Island. 

Upon further inspection, the Coast Guard said that personnel "observed the vessel begin to list and discharge diesel fuel and oil. The vessel reportedly carries a maximum of 4,000 gallons of diesel fuel, in addition to 50 gallons of lubricating oil. The Coast Guard said the discharge rate is "unknown."

Commercial scallop vessel Eileen Rita. Photo Credit: USCG

"The Coast Guard is working closely with the responsible party to mitigate fuel discharge," lieutenant commander Alfred Betts, public affairs officer for Sector Boston, said in a statement. 

"Simultaneously, methods to safely remove the vessel from the island are being evaluated. The contracted oil recovery organization is deploying absorbent boom to mitigate the spread of spilled fuel. Contracted divers are assessing the vessel to plan a path forward."

Fabienne Alexis, spokesperson for the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection (MassDEP), told local news outlet WCVB that fuel appears to be leaking from a crack in the vessel's hull.

Commercial scallop vessel Eileen Rita. Photo Credit: USCG

The spokesperson added that MassDEP is "actively working at the scene with the US Coast Guard and the Massachusetts Environmental Police to ensure all appropriate containment and cleanup measures are swiftly implemented."

Meanwhile, an investigation into why and how the Eileen Rita ran aground is also underway. Early reports alleged captain was asleep, and it was low tide, according to WCVB.

title: ASMI board member faces felonies over Kodiak salmon permit swapping scheme
content:
Police in the US state of Alaska have accused a prominent Kodiak fisherman who sits on the Alaska Seafood Marketing Institute (ASMI) of profiting from an illegal scheme by transferring salmon fishing permits in violation of state laws limiting ownership.

Duncan Fields, a 69-year-old harvester on the state marketing board and former member of the North Pacific Fishery Management Council, faces felony charges of perjury, fraud and other charges along with three members of his family.

Alaska Wildlife Troopers wrote that the Fields family had a coordinated scheme that involved committing perjury and manipulating permits that made the family fishing business more than $1 million by transferring permits to crew members and then back to the family and then covering it up.

"Over 21 crewmembers were interviewed, revealing a coordinated scheme involving false statements under penalty of perjury and permit manipulation to defraud the state and fish buyers," Alaska State Troopers wrote in a dispatch posted on Wednesday (April 8).

The Alaska Beacon reports that in response to the criminal charges, state lawmakers had hit pause on a pending bill that would allow setnet fishermen to pool their fish as a cooperative before landing them on a tender.

Fields told KMXT public radio in Kodiak in a text message that his family and crew had been gifting permits to each other for 30 years in what he described "is a common practice in the industry." He added that he thinks his family has "been singled out to try to set an example," and that the charges are not supported by the facts.

Even so, Alaska representative Louise Stutes of Kodiak has paused work on House Bill 117 after the investigation and charges were made public.

"It wasn't Duncan that brought this issue to us," Stutes told the Alaska Beacon. "But he's right in the middle of it, and so I just feel like it's better to stand down on that bill for now."

State prosecutors argue in their initial charging document that the gifted setnet permits violate a state law that prohibits them from being "pledged, mortgaged, leased, or encumbered in any way, transferred with any retained right of repossession or foreclosure, or on any condition of requiring a subsequent transfer."

However, Fields claimed in a separate interview with a local newspaper that he's done nothing wrong and added the language in the 24-page court filing is meant to prejudice public opinion before he can defend himself in court.

"Somebody has an axe to grind, and somebody’s out to get people in our family, and it just comes clear through the documents," Fields told the Kodiak Daily Mirror.

Alaska State Troopers told lawmakers their investigation was prompted by a referral by the Commercial Fisheries Entry Commission (CFEC), which regulates fishing permits.

"You really have to give CFEC some kudos for catching it," Stutes told the Alaska Beacon. "It tells me the system does work."

title: Vessel collision suspected in disappearance of Chilean fishing crew
content:
A suspected maritime collision off the coast of Coronel, Chile, has left seven artisanal fishermen missing, prompting a criminal investigation, La Tercera reported.

The vessel Bruma, which departed from Constitucion on March 30, was later found partially submerged, with no sign of the crew or its emergency raft. Among the missing are Jose Luis Medel Sepúlveda and his son, both seasoned fishermen.

The incident occurred in a high-traffic maritime zone, and Chilean authorities now suspect that Bruma was struck by an industrial fishing vessel.

Comienzan a aparecer más restos de la embarcación Bruma en la cuadra de búsqueda cercano a la Isla Santa María. No hay rastros aún de la balsa salvavidas. Sigue la esperanza de encontrar a los 7 pescadores de Constitución con vida @Cooperativa pic.twitter.com/awEpGgIrlw

— Cristofer Espinoza (@CEspinozaQ) April 1, 2025

 

Focus has turned to the Cobra, owned by Chilean seafood company Blumar. The vessel showed hull and propeller damage consistent with a collision. Several crew members of Cobra have been named as suspects, and one has gone missing.

The case has sparked national attention and raised concerns over industrial fishing safety practices and oversight in Chile's maritime economy. 

Blumar said it would strengthen logistical support in its search for missing fishermen, Aqua reported.

"We understand the pain and difficult times of the families of the missing crew members," said Blumar CEO Gerardo Balbontin.

title: Seafood burgers recalled in Connecticut after allergic reaction
content:
Caraluzzi's Markets, a family-owned and operated group of grocery markets in the US state of Connecticut, has issued a recall for its Italian Style Seafood Burgers after a consumer report of an allergic reaction.

Caraluzzi's Markets sold its Italian Style Seafood Burger, made with cod, salmon, shrimp, and scallops, at all four of its stores, located in Bethel, Wilton, Newton and Danbury, Connecticut. The product, which comes in an 8-oz clear packaging with a blue overwrap label, has an expiration date of 1/16/2026 on it.

Per the notice posted by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the recall was initiated following a consumer complaint. Upon further investigation, the FDA found that product containing egg was "distributed in packaging that did not reveal the presence of egg."

The FDA said that the mislabeled product has been removed from shelves. Consumers who purchased the product are urged to return them to Caraluzzi's Markets for a refund.

title: Huon fish health manager departs for Scottish Sea Farms
content:
Scottish Sea Farms has appointed Helen Conlon as fish health and welfare manager for its mainland south operations.

Conlon joins the Scottish salmon producer after spending nearly two years at Tasmania-based Huon Aquaculture, where she served as fish health technical officer during one of the company's most challenging periods. 

"After spending time working in the Tasmanian salmon industry with the great team at Huon Aquaculture, I'm excited to be back in Scotland," Conlon said in a statement on Linkedin.

The appointment comes as Huon Aquaculture continues to address fallout from Tasmania's worst-ever mass mortality event, with over 5,500 metric tons of salmon deaths reported industry-wide earlier this year due to a bacterial outbreak involving Piscirickettsia salmonis.

This week, Huon announced that it has begun antibiotic treatments for Piscirickettsia at two pens in its Storm Bay site. The announcement indicates that the disease spread from the initial outbreak at pens in the D'Entrecasteaux Channel.

The Tasmanian producer, owned by Brazilian meat processor JBS, recently lost its RSPCA Australia certification following drone footage that showed workers placing live salmon in bins with dead fish during the mortality event. The footage, captured by environmental group the Bob Brown Foundation, led to investigations by both the RSPCA and Tasmania's Department of Natural Resources and Environment.

Conlon previously was quality and accreditation manager at Loch Duart Salmon and held management positions at cleanerfish habitat and lice skirt provider Nordic Cover.

title: Ecuador’s symbolic tariff move may portend global trend
content:
Ecuador's elimination of 30% tariffs on imported shrimp will not have a significant impact on US exports to the South American powerhouse vannamei producer.

But the move just might help Ecuador avoid punishing reciprocal tariffs slated to be announced on Wednesday, April 2.

Ecuador's foreign trade committee said the measure, implemented on March 29, came in response to US president Donald Trump's "Fair and Reciprocal Plan," under which US trading partners are being evaluated and will be graded based on a calculation of the trade barriers they have in place against US goods. 

In a 397-page report delivered Monday (March 31) by the US Trade Representative, each foreign trading partner to the US has been evaluated in five categories: tariffs the nation imposes on US products, unfair taxes imposed, cost to US businesses and consumers from another country's policies, exchange rates and any other practices the trade representative's office determines is unfair.

A poor grade could result in punitive tariffs -- a fate Ecuador is likely seeking to avoid.

"It was a joint decision between CNA and the Ecuadorian government to demonstrate our willingness to keep trading with the US," Jose Antonio Camposano, executive president of Ecuador's National Chamber of Aquaculture (CNA), told Undercurrent News via email. "The United States has become one of Ecuador's most important markets for shrimp exports, with shipments to the US growing steadily."

In 2024, the US shipped 58 metric tons of shrimp valued at $388,000 to Ecuador, a pittance compared to the 186,862t of shrimp Ecuador sent to the US, which had a value of $1.33 billion. 

Overall, Ecuador had a $992.6 million trade surplus with the US in 2024, a year during which Ecuador shipped $4.6bn worth of products to the US, or 21% of Ecuador's total exports. 

Camposano stressed the importance of continued bilateral trade between the two countries.

"The broader trade relationship further underscores Ecuador's strategic importance to the US market," he said.

Camposano noted that in 2023, bilateral trade reached $15.2bn, with US agricultural exports to Ecuador achieving record levels. 

"American exports of wheat and soybean meal are essential to Ecuador's food supply chain and agricultural industry. US wheat supplies most of Ecuador's consumption, as domestic production covers only 2% of demand, while soybean meal is critical to Ecuador's poultry and aquaculture sectors, including shrimp farming," Camposano said.

Ecuador's game plan is not unique. In February, India cut tariffs on a range of items, including motorcycles and luxury cars. It also agreed to ramp up purchases of US energy after Trump threatened the country with tariffs, as Undercurrent previously reported.

India is the top exporter of shrimp to the US, while Ecuador has climbed into second position in recent years.

Economic headwinds dent Ecuador shrimp exports, $1.5bn revenue hole looms large

In an interview with Undercurrent at the 2025 Seafood Expo North America in Boston, Massachusetts, in March, Camposano called Trump's tariff threats "a negotiation strategy."

"He wrote an entire book about it. It's very transactional. He puts his eye on you because he wants to get something back from you," he said. "In our case, trade between Ecuador and the US, my belief is that it has been very good two-way trade. We sell shrimp to the US -- it's our second-biggest market. At the same time, Ecuador is the fifth largest soybean importer in the world; even though we are so small, but we have a very big protein industry with shrimp and other terrestrial proteins, and around 60% of the soybean that we buy comes from the US. 

So the US imports shrimp from Ecuador that's pretty much fed with US soy. In my mind, that's a very balanced trade relationship."

Camposano criticized the US domestic shrimp sector for pushing to block imports.

"That's not the right thing to do. The US relies heavily on imported seafood, and for shrimp, close to 97% of the shrimp that's consumed is imported. We've gone through the US [warmwater shrimp countervailing and antidumping] investigations, and we won, which demonstrated there is no unfair competition. So this shouldn't be a problem. But something that I've learned in the last 15 years … is that you can never be too sure of anything. We've seen it with China. We saw it with the EU last year with some technical, sanitary policies that Spain imposed, which they had to take back … it's an ever-changing market, and that is why we keep our current production allocated in different markets. It's not easy, but it's the best way to deal with the situation."

title: Untitled
content:
A 61-year-old commercial fisherman from the US state of Florida has been found guilty of making false statements on trip reports and lying to federal agents.

The US Attorney's Office for the District of South Carolina confirmed last month that a federal jury convicted Don Rynn of Augustine, Florida, following a three-day trial.

"Those who attempt to circumvent federal fishing regulations and deceive law enforcement will be held accountable," acting US attorney Brook B. Andrews for the district of South Carolina said in a statement. "Our marine resources are vital, and we will not tolerate those who prioritize personal gain over sustainable practices and the rule of law."

An investigation found that Rynn, who managed several commercial fishing areas in the McClellanville area of South Carolina, ignored federally imposed quotas. One incident that occurred in March 2023 resulted in one of the vessels managed by Rynn bringing in "almost three times the limit of snowy grouper on board, and one and a half times the allowable number of grey tilefish."

Rynn had ordered the deckhands to move some of the fish from one vessel to a separate vessel that had not caught any. Additional fish were then transported to another dealer. In the mandatory trip report, Rynn only recorded the catch up to the limit, hiding that one vessel overfished and transferred it to another.

The South Carolina Department of Natural Resources ultimately received a tip about suspected overfishing, which led to an investigation of Rynn and the vessels he managed. Rynn then proceeded to lie to National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration law enforcement agents, telling them that "the snowy grouper and tilefish had been contaminated by a fuel spill while at sea, and that he had disposed of them in a dumpster."

Following a three-day trial presided over by US district judge Richard M. Gergel, Rynn was found guilty of making false statements and lying to federal agents. Gergel is set to sentence the commercial fisherman after receiving and reviewing a sentencing report prepared by the US Probation Office. 

Rynn faces a maximum penalty of five years in federal prison, as well as a fine of up to $250,000, restitution and three years of supervision following imprisonment.

title: Rapid genetic testing firm has US restaurants sweating shrimp-sourcing practices
content:
SeaD Consulting has been making a name for itself over the past few months by using its rapid genetic testing to shame the US restaurant industry for promoting domestic wild-caught shrimp while instead using imported farmed shrimp.

The Houston, Texas-based company uses a technology, developed and patented in collaboration with Florida State University, called The RIGHTTest. This genetic testing is available in a portable kit and can inexpensively ascertain a seafood item's true species in two hours (compared to several days), to bring truth in labeling to restaurants and retailers in coastal states, David Williams, the fisheries scientist who founded SeaD, and Erin Williams, the company's chief operations officer, told Undercurrent News on the sidelines of Seafood Expo North America, in Boston, Massachusetts, last week.

Catch the Current episode 10: Spring dreams of snow crab and baseball; Guest SeaD Consulting

The company is doing its work in a part of the country where people care more than usual about where their shrimp comes from, too.

There are 490,000 restaurants in the US Gulf of Mexico and South Atlantic Coast regions, 73,000 of which sell seafood, SeaD has estimated. The average amount of shrimp consumed per restaurant is 100 pounds per week, for a weekly total of 2,993,000 lbs and an annual total of 155,636,000 lbs.

Backed by domestic shrimp sector

SeaD has accepted funding from the Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA), an industry group that represents domestic shrimp fishermen and processors around the Gulf of Mexico and Southeastern US, Erin Williams confirmed to Undercurrent, though she did not say how much. 

SSA, which has been waging a war against foreign shrimp importers for years, has contracted SeaD to go to different shrimp-producing states to get a snapshot of what is being served versus what is being advertised. SeaD, as a third party, then promotes its findings in press releases sent to local and national media. 

David Williams described his company's approach as interfacing academia with media and also industry, saying: "If nobody hears you, nothing happens."

SeaD made its big splash ahead of the Super Bowl, in February, releasing a new round of genetic test results from 24 randomly selected restaurants in the game's host city of New Orleans, famous for its reliance on locally caught seafood. It reported catching three restaurants serving foreign, farm-raised shrimp under the guise of "gulf" or "authentic" shrimp, as reported by Undercurrent at the time.

But Erin Williams told Undercurrent that their company has found businesses in Louisiana to be less likely to commit seafood fraud than those in other shrimp-producing states.

"We believe a significant portion of that is due to not only the culture there, but also the regulation on the legislative side," she explained.

As of Jan. 1, 2025, Louisiana requires restaurants to disclose the origin of all the seafood listed on their menus. A first offense results in a fine of up to $15,000, as reported by Undercurrent.

An example of a shrimp dish that SeaD Consulting tested in Tampa-St. Pete. Photo Credit: SeaD Consulting

But while Louisiana may be on the lower end, SeaD Consulting has found fraud rates up to 96% in cities across the southeastern US.

SeaD's rapid genetic test documented its "highest rate" of fraud in Tampa-St. Petersburg, Florida, the company executives said. Out of the 44 restaurants tested in that market, just two were determined to be serving domestic wild-caught shrimp, they said.

Attracting attention

So far SeaD has tested in Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Florida and Georgia, but the company is looking to test further into Alabama, North Carolina and South Carolina.

However, don't expect to find a SeaD "tour schedule" online. 

"We don't say where we're going next for a reason," Erin Williams told Undercurrent. Surprise is the only way SeaD is able to get a true authentic gauge of what the marketplace looks like, she said.

"What I can say is we work very closely with industry -- so packers, distributors, producers," she said. "After we go into the marketplace we get a call from them saying, 'Our phone won't stop ringing. People are calling repeatedly, people in some cases we've never heard of now looking to sell the authentic product.'"

A look at shrimp for testing during a survey in Georgia. Photo Credit: SeaD Consulting

While SeaD is looking to expose seafood fraud occurring in the US, the company isn't turning this testing into a witch hunt.

Instead of naming the restaurants that are advertising locally caught shrimp but are actually serving imported farmed shrimp, SeaD is highlighting the restaurants that it has determined are serving authentic, wild-caught gulf shrimp, the two executives said.

Of course, with that said, earlier this month the company was involved in the testing of shrimp dishes at US seafood chain Bubba Gump Shrimp Co. in New York City, which was featured in Inside Edition's recent investigation into seafood mislabeling.

The long-running news show tested other restaurants in New York City, as well as in Louisiana. Inside Edition named the restaurants that claimed to be selling gulf shrimp, but were instead serving imported farmed shrimp.

The video featuring SeaD Consulting has garnered more than 2.1 million views since it was released on March 11.

[More from SeaD Consulting's David and Erin Williams' SENA interview can be heard on this week's episode of Catch the Current. Subscribe now to be one of the first ones to hear it. title: Untitled
content:
A US state of Utah court has approved the transfer of assets belonging to NaturalShrimp Inc. to two entities tied to financier John Fife, a man the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has accused of securities violations related to unregistered penny stock dealings.

The decision, made at the conclusion of a March 21 hearing in Utah's Third Judicial District Court, effectively grants ownership of the aquaculture company's assets to NaturalShrimp Farms, Iowa Shrimp Holdings and Texas Shrimp Holdings. The three entities were established by Streeterville Capital and Bucktown Capital, the company's primary lenders and plaintiffs in the land-based farmer's receivership case.

Streeterville is wholly owned and controlled by Fife, while Bucktown is also tied to him through his network of investment firms.

Receiver for US RAS producer NaturalShrimp seeks approval to sell $16.8m in assets

NaturalShrimp is headquartered in Dallas, Texas, and has production facilities near San Antonio, Texas. The assets transferred in the sale include its production sites in Texas and Iowa as well as related equipment and intellectual property, all valued at around $16.8 million. The judge indicated that a mandatory seven-day waiting period would apply before the transfer becomes final.

The ruling effectively ends the shrimp farmer's independent operations and leaves shareholders with significant losses.

On Wednesday (March 26), a shareholder who attended the hearing virtually told Undercurrent News that the judge ruled in favor of the proposed sale after no higher bids were submitted by the March 3 objection deadline. The court had received written objections from him and several other shareholders before the hearing, but he said they were not allowed to speak during the proceedings.

Sued by SEC

Streeterville Capital and Bucktown Capital had extended over $33m in secured debt to NaturalShrimp, which defaulted on the notes in August 2024, according to filings from the court-appointed receiver, Ampleo Turnaround & Restructuring LLC. The two entities moved to place NaturalShrimp into receivership in September 2024.

Fife describes himself on his website as a principal investor specializing in private investment in public equity (PIPE), referencing a financing deal where private investors buy shares of publicly traded companies, usually at a discount. It allows companies to raise capital quickly and gives investors a chance to buy into a growing business at a potentially lower price. Fife's website claims he is managing more than $150m in assets.

Fife was the subject of an SEC lawsuit filed in September 2020. In that case, which is still pending in the Northern District of Illinois, the SEC alleged Fife and five of his companies – including Chicago Venture Partners, Iliad Research and Trading, St. George Investments, Tonaquint and Typenex – operated as unregistered dealers.

From 2015 to 2020, these firms allegedly acquired and sold more than 21 billion shares of penny stocks from about 135 issuers, earning over $61m in profits. By not registering as dealers, Fife and his companies avoided regulatory oversight, financial reporting requirements and inspections, the SEC alleges.

Some NaturalShrimp shareholders allege Fife employed a similar strategy with the shrimp-farming firm. 

NaturalShrimp's agreements with Fife-linked companies involved convertible notes allowing the lender to acquire discounted shares upon default, they said in interviews and court filings. The resulting dilution, they argued, depressed the stock price and contributed to the company's collapse.

NaturalShrimp’s share price has plunged 99.14% over the past year, closing at $0.0001 on Wednesday (Mar. 26). Source: Yahoo Finance

"Toxic financing" is a practice where funds are provided to small businesses that are typically short on cash in exchange for convertible debt. If the borrowers fail to repay, the lender can convert that debt into shares at a reduced price, sell those shares on the market for a profit, and then continue this cycle. Critics argue that this approach can drag down the company's share price and threaten the company's stability.

Undercurrent has engaged with shareholders in two Facebook groups and a Reddit community discussing NaturalShrimp, where users have voiced concerns about the company's future and their financial losses.

One shareholder, who began investing in 2018, said he believed in producing shrimp indoors near major markets. He alleged the firm stopped communicating with shareholders in August 2023 and expressed frustration that the court proceeding did not offer them an opportunity to speak.

Ahead of the hearing, several shareholders petitioned the court to block the sale, order an independent valuation, require full transparency through any investigation and investigate potential breaches of fiduciary duty by the company's board, according to posts in the forums and documents seen by Undercurrent.

One shareholder, in a letter to the court, proposed to allow existing shareholders to retain equity in any successor entity through a rollover mechanism.

However, without legal representation, shareholders have limited recourse. One investor told Undercurrent that he had consulted lawyers but found the cost of pursuing a lawsuit prohibitive, with estimates starting at $100,000 to assess the case. Others said they plan to continue pressing the SEC to take action to protect their investments.

A history of financial struggles

NaturalShrimp's assets, as outlined in a Feb. 11, 2025 court filing, include its shrimp production facilities, intellectual property and real estate holdings, as Undercurrent reported.

The company's Webster City, Iowa, facility is its largest single asset, valued at $7.0m, while additional properties in two other Iowa towns – Blairsburg and Radcliffe – and one in Texas bring the company's total real estate valuation to almost $9.9m.

NaturalShrimp reported just $36,618 in total sales in the second quarter of 2024 ending June 30, 2024, a sharp drop from the $205,872 it posted in the same period a year earlier. At the same time, its quarterly operating expenses surpassed $2.06m, resulting in a net loss of $2.8m in Q2 2024.

The shrimp-farming venture continued issuing shares to raise capital in the quarter, but the proceeds were insufficient to stabilize its financial position.

The receiver's Feb. 11 court filing noted that its Webster City facility was operating at only one-third capacity, producing 400–500 lbs of shrimp per week, with most of its product ending up in Chicago, Illinois, and a few smaller markets. No production was occurring at its Blairsburg or Radcliffe facilities.

The company's intellectual property, including a proprietary recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) technology, are valued at $5.7m. Other assets, such as vehicles, equipment and personal property, round out the company's total valuation of approximately $16.9m.

Despite ongoing financial troubles, Streeterville provided a $500,000 line of credit to help sustain operations at NaturalShimp while legal proceedings unfolded, according to a September 2024 press release. However, Streeterville declined to extend further loans, leaving NaturalShrimp unable to bridge its financial shortfall.

In total, Streeterville has invested nearly $22m in the aquaculture company, primarily through secured promissory notes issued in December 2021 and August 2022.

US RAS shrimp farmer NaturalShrimp quietly entered receivership in September 2024. Photo: NaturalShrimp

According to the last available financial statement filed with the SEC for Q2 2024, the business had just $4,978 in cash at the end of the quarter, down from $115,525 three months earlier. Total assets at the end of that quarter stood at $248,968, while total liabilities reached $39.7m.

Undercurrent reached out to NaturalShrimp CEO Gerald Easterling by phone and text message, and to Chris Tyson, executive vice president at MZ North America — an investor relations firm that has previously represented the aquaculture business in communications with shareholders and the media — but did not receive a response by press time. A voicemail was also left for Wayne Graffis, the consultant with Ampleo, which is overseeing the receivership.

Mark Rose, counsel for the receiver, didn't respond to Undercurrent's request for comment from him or Fife on the outcome of the hearing and plans for the company moving forward.

title: Vietnam shrimp export prices to US, China jump in February
content:
Vietnam's vannamei shrimp exports were down month-on-month but up year-on-year in February 2025, while the average export price across all products lifted, driven by strong increases in the US and China, according to a Ho Chi Minh City-based consultancy compiling trade data for Undercurrent News.

You can find the breakdown of individual countries' imports below the subheading.

"[Vannemei] shrimp exports in March are expected to have recovered gradually, constrained by a limited number of new orders," it added in its latest report. "Processing plants continue to struggle with price negotiations, facing stiff competition from India and Ecuador."

February saw Vietnam's exports of vannamei shrimp dip 7% m-o-m to 17,608 metric tons, though that was up 16% y-o-y.

"The decline was mainly driven by lower exports to China and Hong Kong (-30%), the EU (-17%), and the UK (-19%). However, other markets showed modest growth, including the US (6%), Japan (9%), and South Korea (2%).

The average export price across all vannamei products sold to all markets continued its upward trend, this time rising a more substantial 5% m-o-m to $9.01 per kilogram.

February 2025 vannamei data

"Most major processing plants resumed normal raw material procurement from the beginning of February after the Lunar New Year holiday, with overall demand similar to January," said the consultancy.

"However, transactions for small-sized shrimp, 100-count [per kg], tended to decrease due to limited purchases by Chinese traders. Factories increased purchase prices for 20-40 counts to maintain stable procurement in the context of limited supply, while prices for 50-100 counts decreased compared to January."

As a result, farm-gate prices in February saw 20-40 counts lift by between 1% and 3%, while smaller sizes saw prices ease by up to 5% m-o-m.

Upgrade to Pro to view

As can be seen in the chart above, which shows farm-gate prices as recorded by data service Tomota, the reverse trend has been true in March, with larger sizes coming down in price and smaller sizes coming up a little.

A March update from the Vietnam Association of Seafood Exporters and Producers stated that shrimp exports in January 2025 showed signs of a good recovery y-o-y, with 71,301t sold worth $631.2 million -- up 20% in volume and 32% in value.

It said sales there have been aided by the clarity of announcements on the anti-dumping and countervailing duty investigations targeting Ecuador, India, Indonesia and Vietnam.

Undercurrent's new US wholesale pricing platform states that for week 12 (March 17-23), "changes in the imported, farm-raised white and black tiger shrimp market were limited in scope as counterparties are meeting and discussing the industry's state at Seafood Expo North America. However, there is some cautious optimism during these conversations. Given its current value, shrimp is positioned well against other seafood species and proteins as a whole."

Meanwhile, February also saw a drop in black tiger shrimp exports from Vietnam, down 21% m-o-m but up 7% y-o-y to 1,475t. 

"Exports to China and Hong Kong, the EU, and Korea experienced a considerable decline of 51%, 54%, and 15%, respectively. Meanwhile, other markets saw an increase in import volume, including Japan (11%), the US (29%), and the UK (87%). The export price increased, driven primarily by price hikes in the top four markets: China, Japan, the US, and the EU."

The average export price for all specifications of black tiger products to all markets rose 14% to $12.77/kg, it said.

"Raw black tiger shrimp transactions remained sluggish in February, mirroring the prior month," said the consultancy.

"This was driven by limited export contracts for processing plants and constrained off-season supply as slow farming activities since late 2024 resulted in low availability of large-sized shrimp in early 2025. To sustain production and export, factories raised prices for 20-50 counts and 80-counts, subsequently pushing up farm-gate prices by 1% or 2%

February 2025 black tiger data

Prices leap in US, China

US imports of Vietnamese vannamei have eased since October and begun 2025 low in relation to 2024 levels (though y-o-y, January and February combined have seen only marginally lower imports).

However, Vietnamese customs data shows prices have lifted in February, by 5.8% to $10.90/kg. That's the highest since March 2023. February volumes were 2,837t, up slightly m-o-m and y-o-y.

Chinese import prices, too, reflected a strong lift in the second month of 2025; 9.1% to $7.20/kg. Again, that's the highest level since March 2023.

Volumes fell to 1,637t, the lowest single month since February 2023.

In Japan, February export prices rose 5.6% to $9.50/kg, while import volumes edged up m-o-m to 3,062t -- up by around 1,000t y-o-y.

And Korea also saw the price lift -- 5.3% to $8.00/kg, even as January-February export volumes strengthened y-o-y.

The only market not to look positive for Vietnam in February was the EU. Here, volumes dipped to 2,500t -- the lowest since February 2023 -- and prices eased 1.3% to $7.60/kg. 

That remains healthier than for much of 2024 but is the second decline in as many months.

Almost all black tiger prices up

China was the single largest market for Vietnamese black tiger shrimp in February, though exports there dwindled -- as they also did in February 2024. 

While they fell to 353t, export prices climbed 14.1% to $10.50/kg m-o-m, the highest in just about a year.

In Japan, import volumes remained at a relative low compared to 2024, though they crept up m-o-m and y-o-y to 326t. 

Prices were up 16.7% to $14.70/kg, the highest since summer 2023.

It was a similar story in the US -- volumes were up a little from January but well below most months in 2024 at 162t. 

But prices jumped 11.3% to $17.80/kg, the highest in a little under a year. 

The EU finally saw a small upturn in export prices, of 3% to $10.20/kg. It's the first rise since October. 

Volumes more than halved y-o-y at 103t, though the same happened in 2024, and may be something to do with when the Vietnamese New Year holiday fell. 

Finally, Korea's imports of black tiger dipped for the third consecutive month to 87t -- still up y-o-y, though.

The average prices eased 2.6% to $11.40/kg, but that remains fairly stable in relation to the past two years.

title: Profand’s largest squid-jigging vessel undergoes repairs following collision
content:
The Espadarte, the largest squid-jigging vessel of Grupo Profand, has survived a collision with a South Korean vessel and is undergoing repairs at the Coserana shipyard, Mar Y Pesca Noticias Patagonicas reported.

The collision, with the Oryong 756, happened while both vessels were fishing in national waters off Rawson’s coast.

Despite the impact, all crew members were unharmed, according to the news service. The vessel was carrying 430 metric tons of squid at the time of the incident, but all were successfully unloaded upon arrival at Puerto Deseado, Argentina. Although Espadarte sustained external damage above the waterline, its structural integrity remained intact, allowing it to reach the port under its own power. 

The Argentine coast guard has launched an investigation, following orders from the federal court of Rawson. The captain and crew provided confidential statements, while the Oryong 756 crew testified separately in Mar del Plata, where their ship is docked.

title: Polar linked to four deaths from salmon listeria in Denmark
content:
Four people have died in Denmark in recent years after consuming listeria-contaminated salmon from food company Polar Salmon Hjerting Laks, according to local authorities, Nyheder24 reported.

The Statens Serum Institut reported that 27 people had been infected with invasive listeria between 2018 and 2024, with fatalities occurring within 30 days of diagnosis.

Extensive DNA analysis traced the outbreak to the company’s products, with two listeria strains identified between 2023 and 2024. Polar Salmon Hjerting Laks is ultimately owned by Greenlandic firm Polar Seafood.

This is not the company's first scandal. In January 2025, the company sold listeria-contaminated salmon without informing the authorities or recalling the products, and a case in February concerned a lack of notification when recalling hot-smoked pulled salmon.

Before the company was taken over by Polar, it was also connected to a listeria outbreak that killed three.

Polar CEO Henrik Leth has pledged a thorough investigation.

The company now faces potential fines, legal action, and stricter regulatory oversight. The scandal has also triggered internal turmoil, with co-owner Christoph Kjaergaard removed from his position. Polar Seafood Denmark plans to take over his shares, but the case could yet impact the ownership structure.

title: Untitled
content:
A fire has destroyed five newly constructed buildings at salmon farming company Alsaker Fjordbruk's coastal facility in Tysnes, an island municipality in Vestland county, western Norway, reports NRK.

The complex, known as Alsaker Brygge, was nearing completion and intended to serve as the company's new administrative headquarters.

Alsaker Fjordbruk, which harvested 40,000 metric tons of salmon in 2020 with revenues of NOK 1.91 billion ($181.6m), has been expanding its operations in the region.

The company recently applied for permits to produce up to 100,000t of salmon at a land-based facility elsewhere in Tysnes municipality, signaling its strategic diversification beyond traditional net-pen farming.

Two additional buildings suffered significant water damage, though authorities reported no injuries. "We will now have to use the old office building on the site," said Kristian Rasberg, Alsaker Fjordbruk's communications officer.

Police in Norway's Western Police District have launched an investigation, with the cause of the fire currently unknown.

title: Seafood chowder pouches recalled due to potential contamination with clostridium botulinum
content:
SeaBear Company, based in Anacortes, Washington, is recalling two of its seafood chowders due to potential contamination with clostridium botulinum, a bacteria that the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) says grows in low-oxygen conditions.

The two chowders being recalled are SeaBear Smokehouse's Salmon Chowder and Alehouse Clam Chowder, shelf-stable products that are sold in 12-ounce pouches. Per the announcement published by the FDA on Saturday (March 15), the products were distributed in physical retail stores in the US states of Alaska, California, Colorado, Oregon, and Washington and also through direct home delivery via SeaBear’s website.

SeaBear issued the recall after a customer alerted them to an issue with a pouch seal. Further investigation into the issue revealed a mechanical issue with equipment, which caused the seals of some pouches to not fully bond and leak.

Clostridium botulinum can be fatal and cause "general weakness, dizziness, double-vision and trouble with speaking or swallowing," the FDA warns.

SeaBear's Smoked Salmon Chowder is being recalled. Photo Credit: SeaBear

SeaBear is urging customers who purchased the product not to consume it and to contact its customer service team for a refund.

title: Untitled
content:
Additional reporting by Louis Harkell.

China's frozen shrimp market is again embroiled in a public scandal after multiple processing plants in China's Zhanjiang city were found to have breached regulations on phosphates to artificially increase product weight.

According to the investigation by state broadcaster CCTV, shrimp sampled in processing plants in Zhanjiang contained phosphate levels up to six times the legal limit -- with one company using treatment periods exceeding 10 hours.

The story, aired on March 15 during CCTV's annual Consumer Rights Day programming, named four processors: Zhanjiang Baohui Aquatic Products, Zhanjiang Liangji Frozen Food, Zhanjiang Zhongqing Ocean Aquatic Products, and Zhanjiang Shangfangzhou Food. 

China steps up inspections on Ecuadorian shrimp after metabisulfite rejections

The investigation comes a year after a Chinese social media influencer sparked online consternation after he claimed imported shrimp, particularly from Ecuador, breached metabisulfite regulations. Ecuador's shrimp industry denied the claims.

Chinese regulations limit phosphoric acid and phosphates in headless peeled shrimp to 0.5% (5 grams per kilogram), but the investigation found one company using concentrations of 3%.

"Roughly speaking, 100 kilograms of headless shrimp turned into 124kg after soaking, gaining an extra 24kg," a factory worker told investigators.

The shrimp -- produced with locally farmed raw material -- were then quickly moved to freezing lines, where they were coated with a thick layer of ice, further increasing their weight. "That extra weight is the company's profit," CCTV reported.

Sanitary pads & diapers made from defective material. Frozen shrimp injected with water. Disposable underwear treated with toxic chemicals😳 No wonder CCTV's annual Consumer Day "315 Gala" has been dominating trending topic lists on Chinese social media this weekend, from Weibo… pic.twitter.com/Cr9plKn7pk

— Manya Koetse (@manyapan) March 16, 2025

Packaging from at least one company failed to disclose phosphate use, listing "only shrimp and water" as ingredients. "Nobody pays attention to this label," said a sales representative from the company involved.

The shrimp samples were sent to a testing agency, with results showing that the phosphate levels exceeded legal limits by 51.4% to 145%. The broadcaster warned that "long-term excessive intake of phosphates can pose health risks, including digestive issues, calcium-phosphate imbalance, calcium deficiency, and even cardiovascular diseases."

Guolian distances itself from scandal

Zhanjiang Guolian Aquatic Products, Zhanjiang's largest shrimp processor, issued a statement on March 16 through a securities filing clarifying it has no connection to the four companies named in the investigation.

The company emphasized its "raw peeled and deveined shrimp" products contain no water-retaining agents and that its promotional claims are accurate. Guolian products continue to be available on major e-commerce platforms.

On March 17, Guolian announced a strategic cooperation agreement with e-commerce giant JD.com.

"Guolian has been cooperating with JD.com for over 10 years," said Li Chunyan, Guolian's executive director. "We believe that through our joint efforts and in-depth cooperation, we will be able to drive the development and upgrading of the aquaculture industry."

Chinese authorities have not yet announced regulatory actions against the implicated companies.

title: Report on sinking of Canadian fishing vessel says boat was well equipped for emergency
content:
Canada's Transportation Safety Board (TSB) has determined that the crew of a fishing boat that sank off the coast of the province of Newfoundland and Labrador on July 17, 2024, were highly skilled in distress communication and were even carrying devices not required by regulation, like satellite communication devices and cell phones, reports the CBC. 

The TSB, the lead agency for marine accident investigations in Canada, noted in its final report on Wednesday (March 12) on the sinking of the fishing vessel Elite Navigator that the captain and six crew members were well prepared for an emergency.

The crew of the Elite Navigator spent nearly three days adrift, in foggy weather miles from shore, in Notre Dame Bay, after their 56-foot longliner caught fire and sank.

The seven men were eventually spotted by a Canadian Coast Guard aircraft late Friday night, July 19, in their liferaft. The men, dubbed the Lucky Seven by media and community,  returned to a hero's welcome on Saturday, July 20, in their hometown of Valleyfield, in Bonavista Bay, about 100 km north of the town of Gander, as reported by Undercurrent News.

The rescue made headlines across Canada and North America.

While there's usually evidence of weak safety cultures in marine accidents, the Elite Navigator was an exception, the TSB noted in its report.

"The master and crew members were in the practice of talking through emergency scenarios and responses," the report stated.

The fire that caused the vessel to sink likely also damaged the emergency position-indicating radio beacon, preventing the device from sending a signal to allow searchers to pinpoint where the vessel went down, the report noted.

It is impossible to know what caused the fire on board the Elite Navigator, as the fishing vessel was never recovered, the TSB report concluded.

title: US bill to halt financial support of foreign shrimp farms returns with bipartisan support
content:
A group of US lawmakers from states bordering the Gulf of Mexico have brought back a bipartisan bill intended to block the funding of foreign shrimp farming, processing or export to the US. 

The Save Our Shrimpers Act of 2025, which doesn't yet have a bill number, was introduced Tuesday (March 11) by representative Troy Nehls, a Texas Republican, according to a statement from his office. 

The legislation would prohibit federal funds from being made available to international financial institutions (IFIs) to finance any activity relating to shrimp farming or processing, or the export of shrimp from any foreign country to the United States.

Additionally, it would trigger an investigation within the US Government Accountability Office and require annual reports to Congress examining to what extent US executive directors at IFIs comply with USC 262(h), a law that prevents them from funding the production of any commodities that might compete with US products. Nehls maintains there have been too few instances where the US Treasury Department has enforced the provision. 

ITC rules US shrimp industry suffered as a result of imports, cements AD, CVD rates

Nehls said 13 other Republicans support the bill, including: Texas' Vincente Gonzalez, Randy Weber, Brian Babin and Michael Cloud; as well as Alabama's Barry Moore; Florida's Byron Donalds, Gus Bilirakis and Anna Paulina Luna; Louisiana's Clay Higgins and Julia Letlow; Mississippi's Mike Ezell; North Carolina's Greg Murphy; and South Carolina's Nancy Mace. Also in support is Louisiana Democrat Troy Carter.  

American shrimpers, including some in Nehls' 22nd district, are struggling to stay afloat as a result of the flood of cheap imported shrimp, he said Tuesday, adding: "Worse, American tax dollars are being used to finance foreign shrimp farms, which are driving our own shrimpers out of business." 

The new legislation is also supported by the Louisiana Shrimp Association and the Texas Shrimp Association, according to the statement from Nehls' office. 

Nehls introduced a similar bill (HR 7932) in April 2024 during the 118th Congress, gathering support from 21 Republicans and two Democrats. However, it never found its way out of the House Committee on Financial Services.

SSA report says India, Ecuador benefited most

Both of Nehls' bills follow a 39-page report delivered in August 2023 by the Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA), a group that represents harvesters and processors of US wild-caught shrimp in the gulf and along the southeastern coast of the US. 

SSA, which supports the legislation, said it found that billions of dollars have been used to finance shrimp aquaculture development abroad, with such efforts increasing in the past decade, resulting in the flooding of the global market with excess shrimp supply, driving wholesale prices down, and severely harming US shrimpers. 

IFI financing of shrimp aquaculture has been concentrated in India and Ecuador, which combined account for 70% of all US shrimp imports, the group said. Since 2000, private Ecuadorian shrimp producers and exporters have received at least $195 million in development funding for shrimp aquaculture for eight projects, SSA said. IFI funding has also benefited the shrimp aquaculture sectors in India, Indonesia, Vietnam and other nations.

A glut of imported shrimp forced down the per-pound value of US imports by 15% from 2022 to 2024, from an average $4.28/lb to $3.62/lb, SSA reported. In tandem with that trend, the total value of US shrimp harvesters' landings plummeted from $522m in 2021 to $268m in 2023, and remained near this level in 2024.

In an op-ed column to promote his earlier bill, Nehls repeated the SSA's claim that taxpayer dollars have been used for decades to "bankroll foreign shrimp operations across the globe, which in part has contributed to the devastation of our own shrimp industry."

In reviewing the Treasury Department's reported voting positions since 2004, US directors have voted to support projects 25,041 times (88.7%), abstained from voting on 2,325 projects (8.2%), and voted no on just 880 projects (3.1%), according to Nehls.

Others have come to bat on behalf of the cause.

US representative James Comer, the Kentucky Republican who chairs the House Committee on Oversight and Accountability, joined Nehls and Higgins in sending a letter to the GAO in November 2024 that formally requested an investigation of Treasury's efforts. US senator Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana Republican, last week sent a letter to US treasury secretary Scott Bessent asking him to take all necessary actions to prevent any future funding of shrimp aquaculture development.

The shrimp war has been escalating

US harvesters and processors of wild-caught shrimp have been steadily escalating their attacks on foreign shrimp.

US bill would require foreign shrimp producers satisfy equivalency standard

The American Shrimp Processors Association (ASPA) succeeded last year in getting the US Department of Commerce to investigate India, Ecuador, Indonesia and Vietnam over complaints of unfair practices. In November 2024, the US International Trade Commission concluded the battle with a final determination that the US shrimp industry had suffered harm from the actions, cementing earlier-set antidumping and countervailing duty rates, as reported by Undercurrent. 

Bills advocating for other measures protecting the domestic shrimp industry or combating foreign imports have been introduced in both state legislatures and in the US Congress.

In February, US senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Mississippi Republican, introduced The Safer Shrimp Imports Act (S.667), legislation that would require foreign shrimp facilities to satisfy inspection standards that are equivalent to those required of US shrimp producers if they want to keep exporting to the US, as reported by Undercurrent News.

title: Large cocaine shipment seized in Italy hidden among tuna cans
content:
Italian authorities at the Port of Genoa have seized 240 kilograms of pure cocaine hidden inside canned tuna containers. The drugs, worth an estimated €40 million to €50m on the black market, arrived from Guayaquil, Ecuador, aboard a cargo ship, Rai News reported.

The discovery was made by the anti-fraud unit of the Genoa 1 customs office and the provincial command of the Guardia di Finanza. Five duffel bags containing 200 bricks of cocaine were found during the inspection of the suspect containers.

This drug bust resulted from advanced risk analysis using data from both administrations' databases. The cocaine was intended to supply drug markets across Italy.

The investigation continues as authorities work to dismantle the criminal network behind the shipment.

title: Masoval grants Nordic Halibut option to purchase processing, sales division
content:
Aquaculture business Nordic Halibut has entered into an agreement with Masoval to use processing and sales firm Pure Norwegian Seafood (PNS)'s facilities in Averoy, on Norway's mid-western coast.

The deal aligns with Nordic Halibut's plans to boost production capacity, with the company targeting annual production of 10,350 metric tons of halibut by 2031.

The agreement also includes an option for the firm to purchase 100% of PNS' shares from its main shareholder, Norwegian salmon farmer Masoval.

The acquisition, subject to additional agreements with minority shareholders in PNS, will further solidify Nordic Halibut's control over the entire value chain of halibut production, the company said.

The purchase price for the shares has not been disclosed.

"We are excited to partner with PNS and are looking forward to integrating their skilled personnel into our operations," said Edvard Henden, CEO of Nordic Halibut.

"This collaboration not only strengthens our production capabilities but also underscores our commitment to securing and creating jobs locally. The integration of their processing facility is a key part of our plans to scale up production and improve operational efficiency," he said.

As Undercurrent News previously reported, Masoval is establishing its own fully controlled sales division after PNS was found to have supplied fish unsuitable for human consumption in 2024.

Masoval acquired a 65% stake in PNS in June 2021 after partnering with it since 2018. Adding the Averoy-based firm made the group fully vertically integrated for the first time.

An investigation early last year found that PNS had allowed "certain customers to buy frozen salmon that, according to Norwegian regulations, is not suitable for human consumption."

"Sold fish includes fish that either should have been discarded/ensiled, or production-graded fish that should be elaborated in secondary processing before export. The investigation estimates that this turnover of fish not suitable for human consumption constituted just under 1% of the total volume of fish and approximately 0.5% of PNS's revenue over the last three years."

title: Untitled
content:
An Alaska fisherman has been sentenced to six months in a US prison for falsifying records and ordering a crew member to open fire on a whale while longlining for sablefish, US prosecutors announced Monday (March 10).

As Undercurrent News reported, Dugan Paul Daniels, skipper of the Pacific Bounty, pleaded guilty to federal fishing crimes following a multi-year investigation.

The US Department of Justice cited court documents showing that, in late 2020, the veteran longliner submitted false records to make it appear that he lawfully caught sablefish in federal waters on two separate occasions. An investigation, however, showed that he'd caught the fish – also known as black cod – in state-managed waters.

Prosecutors said the contraband catch had an estimated market value of $127,528.

Alaska fisherman pleads guilty to ordering shooting of whale

Daniels also violated the Endangered Species Act when he ordered his crew to open fire on a protected sperm whale he complained was stealing the black cod out of his fishing gear.

That happened in March 2020, when the Pacific Bounty was longlining for sablefish southwest of Yakobi Island in the Gulf of Alaska. Daniels had a crewman shoot the whale multiple times and tried to ram the whale with his 50-foot vessel.  

"Though he had been a fisherman for over 20 years, Mr. Daniels showed a blatant disregard for endangered animals, the laws that protect them and the regulation of commercial fishing," US Attorney Michael J. Heyman of the District of Alaska wrote in a statement.

Evidence in court records was from seized text messages from a GPS communication device. In some messages, Daniels wrote he wished he "had a cannon to blow" the whale out of the water and that he hoped "to be reeling in a dead sperm whale." 

NOAA agents wrote that they do not know if the whale survived. No sperm whale carcass was reported in Southeast Alaska in 2020. 

Daniels pleaded guilty on June 6, 2024, to one count of violation of the Lacey Act for false labeling and one count of Endangered Species Act violation for an illegal take. In addition to the prison time, he was fined $25,000 and sentenced to three years on supervised release, with a one-year ban on commercial fishing, plus 80 hours of community service as special release conditions. 

It's unclear when Daniels will begin serving his sentence. Federal and state prison databases didn't list anyone under his name who is currently incarcerated.

title: Fishing vessel makes grisly discovery off Massachusetts coast
content:
A commercial fishing vessel in waters off the US state of Massachusetts made a grisly discovery upon pulling up its nets this week: a body entangled in its catch.

Celebrity gossip site TMZ broke the news about the incident, which reportedly happened about 40 miles offshore from Boston. The owners of the vessel requested that it not be identified. 

"We're told the crew wasn't pulling up much in the way of fish that morning ... and, they were surprised when this particular net was so heavy -- with tons of fish covering the body," reports TMZ.

It wasn't until the crew started picking through the fish that they made the discovery and contacted the US Coast Guard.

The Suffolk District Attorney's office told the television station NBC 10 Boston that the death is not being considered suspicious and prosecutors have said there will be no further investigation. Graphic images obtained by TMZ show the body bound. However, an autopsy found it belonged to a woman in her 60s who had cancerous tumors.

The body was embalmed, "apparently in line with how someone would be buried at sea," NBC 10 Boston reported.
