title: Untitled
content:
An oil tanker collision in the North Sea near the UK coast on March 10 had raised concerns about disruptions to shipping routes into the seafood processing hub of Grimsby, but fears look to have been allayed.

Simon Dwyer, CEO of the Grimsby Fish Merchants Association (FMA), informed the region's seafood sector on March 10 that the "catastrophic vessel collision" close to the Humber Estuary had appeared to have caused shipping movements to be suspended.

The FMA would monitor the situation concerning vessels due, carrying fresh fish from Iceland and the Faroe Islands, he'd said.

However, on the morning of March 11, he told Undercurrent News that shipping operations had resumed, and no significant short- or long-term delays were anticipated. 

The BBC reported that the incident involved the oil tanker MV Stena Immaculate and the cargo vessel MV Solong. The collision resulted in fires on both vessels and a jet fuel spill into the sea.

Rescue operations ensured that 36 of the 37 crew members were safely brought ashore, with one individual hospitalized. However, a search for the missing crewmember was called off late on March 10.

Experts said the incident might have a "devastating" impact on marine life, as investigations began into its cause, the Guardian reported.

title: Argentine authorities recover some stolen goods following Iberconsa’s warehouse robbery
content:
Authorities in Puerto Deseado, Argentina, have recovered several stolen tools following a robbery at Pesquera Santa Cruz, part of the Iberconsa Group, Mar y Pesca Noticias Patagonicas reported.

The theft occurred on Feb. 16, when unknown individuals broke into a warehouse on Oneto Street by forcing a gate and breaking a window. The stolen items included drills, grinders, a portable welder, batteries and hand tools. It is an episode of minor theft amounting to about $1,000, a source with the firm told Undercurrent.

After an investigation by the DDI Puerto Deseado, multiple home raids were conducted yesterday across six locations. While no stolen goods were found at the first three addresses, successful recoveries were made at two homes on Almirante Brown Street. 

Three men, aged 29, 35 and 37, were identified and placed at the courts' disposal. The operation involved various police divisions and was overseen by senior security officials.

Investigations are ongoing to determine if the suspects are linked to other crimes or if more individuals were involved in the Pesquera Santa Cruz robbery.

title: RSPCA suspends Australian firm’s certification over salmon mortality handling
content:
Animal welfare charity the RSPCA has temporarily suspended its certification of Australian salmon producer Huon Aquaculture following the release of drone footage showing live fish being dumped in tubs alongside dead ones, ABC reported.

Australian salmon sector deaths of 5,500t amount to worst-ever incident

The incident occurred at a Huon site near the D'Entrecasteaux Channel, south of Hobart, in Tasmania, Australia, amid an ongoing mass mortality event caused by a bacterial outbreak.

Huon, owned by Brazilian multinational JBS, was the only Tasmanian salmon company with RSPCA certification, which allowed its products to carry "RSPCA approved farming" labels, signifying adherence to animal welfare standards. The certification will be suspended for 14 days while the RSPCA investigates, describing the handling of live fish seen in the video as "inhumane" and "completely unacceptable."

FREE READ Australian salmon farmers face ‘unprecedented’ mortalities

The salmon industry in southeast Tasmania is grappling with elevated fish deaths linked to the bacterium Piscirickettsia salmonis, with more than 5,500 metric tons of dead fish reportedly disposed of, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

Environmental groups have criticized Huon's practices, and Tasmania's Department of Natural Resources and Environment has launched its own inquiry into the incident.

Huon stated it would undertake its own investigation. General manager of stakeholder and government relations, Hannah Gray, also said the company immediately informed the RSPCA and would "participate fully in the investigation."

"Since the start of this unprecedented disease outbreak, Huon has been transparent with regulators and the community and will continue to engage proactively," she said.

Meanwhile, Salmon Tasmania, the industry's peak body, apologized for the "unprecedented" mortality event and promised to review operations to prevent similar occurrences in the future, ABC also reported.

title: Untitled
content:
The Tasmanian salmon industry is reeling after more than 5,500 metric tons of dead fish were disposed of at waste facilities in February, marking the largest fish mortality event in its history, reports ABC News.

Australia's Environment Protection Authority (EPA) has launched an investigation into the cause, which is said to be linked to warmer water temperatures and an endemic bacterium.

The fish, primarily from pens owned by Huon Aquaculture and Tassal in the D'Entrecasteaux Channel, between Bruny Island and the southeast of the mainland of Tasmania, Australia, represent around 6% of the industry's annual production.

Stocks are facing a new strain of rickettsia-like organism or RLO, a bacteria that has long existed in the local farming environment, according to Tori Percival, fish production manager at salmon farmer Huon Aquaculture, in a video created by Huon in collaboration with Salmon Tasmania, also shared by Tassal.

EPA director of finfish compliance Darryl Cook told ABC Radio National on March 3 that salmon companies were not previously required to provide fish death data to the EPA, but that would change this month.

The crisis is ongoing, with more dead fish expected, and comes amid political debates over salmon farming in Tasmania.

Australia's prime minister, Anthony Albanese, faces pressure to balance industry interests with environmental concerns, particularly regarding operations in Macquarie Harbor, home to the endangered Maugean skate. Industry leaders and conservationists are urging the government to provide clear legislative direction to ensure ecological preservation and economic stability.

In October 2024, it emerged that over 1,000t of salmon died in Macquarie Harbour feedlots between September 2022 and March 2023, according to figures from Tasmania's Department of Natural Resources and Environment.

Last year, scientists advising the Australian government recommended a dramatic scaling back or complete removal of the salmon industry from Tasmania's Macquarie Harbour to prevent the extinction of the Maugean skate.

But late in the year, Tasmania's parliament passed a motion calling for Australian federal authorities to end an environmental review of salmon farming in the harbor amid an industry campaign highlighting concerns about regional jobs.

title: eFishery’s DycodeX acquisition under auditor scrutiny
content:
Troubled Indonesian aquatech start-up eFishery's March 2024 acquisition of DycodeX is being scrutinized by the consulting firm now running the company.

Washington DC-based independent business consulting firm FTI Consulting, which was appointed as active manager of eFishery in January following revelations the company misrepresented financial figures for years, is looking at the DycodeX acquisition as part of its larger investigation into potential fraud committed by company executives, as brought to light by a whistleblower complaint.

The FTI probe previously uncovered evidence eFishery drastically inflated its auto-feeder sales and found as many as 16 company executives were in some manner involved in allegedly inflating sales and fudging accounting practices.

Investors in Indonesia’s eFishery face heavy losses as firm struggles with financial collapse

FTI's private draft independent report, obtained by Undercurrent News, also raised questions about eFishery's acquisition of  PT Dycodex Teknologi Nusantara (DycodeX). The complex transaction was completed through an "acqui-hire" scheme, under which eFishery paid IDR 15 billion ($920,000) to four subsidiaries, which then hired all of DycodeX's employees.

DycodeX, which describes itself as an "artificial intelligence and Internet of Things enabler," was acquired to enhance eFishery's aquatech offerings with cutting-edge technology, Undercurrent reported at the time.

In a press release announcing the acquisition, eFishery confirmed it was planning to launch 10 new products, including IoT and generative AI products, as well as other aquaculture intelligence solution, by 2026. eFishery CEO Gibran Huzaifah said in the statement he was creating an IoT and cultivation intelligence product division to be headed by DycodeX CEO Andri Yadi, and that the hirings of the DycodeX staffers would speed up the firm's product development cycle by three to four times.

DycodeX CEO Andri Yadi. Photo courtesy of DycodeX.

"Andri Yadi and his team can strengthen and accelerate the implementation of AI and IoT in the eFishery ecosystem," he said." The steps we are taking align with eFishery's mission to address challenges related to food and respond to the needs of sustainable growth while increasing eFishery's contribution to the aquaculture industry in Indonesia through the provision of affordable technology."

Officially completed in March 2024, the acquisition was in the making for over two years, according to the release. FTI said an unsigned draft conditional sale and purchase agreement between MTN and DycodeX exists dating to October 2022, but it appears the agreement was not consummated.

That relatively long timeline was partially related to issues over financial reporting. According to FTI's report, Huzaifah said DycodeX had never been audited, and a direct acquisition and consolidation of DycodeX as a subsidiary of eFishery would mean an audit would have had to be performed on DycodeX for the three financial years prior to 2024.

Ostensibly looking to avoid that, Huzaifah instead structured the deal as an "acqui-hiring" arrangement, whereby eFishery subsidiary PT Multidaya Teknologi Nusantara (MTN) entered into service agreements with four limited partnership entities -- CV Deeptech Solusi Indonesia, CV Teknologi Terkini Mandiri, CV Solusi Teknologi Harmoni and CV Integrasi Teknologi Terdepan -- which then issued signed agreements that resulted in the acquisition of DycodeX and the hiring of its employees. 

In its report, FTI clarifies it is still seeking information about the transactions, including details about how money was transferred to the four CVs and agreements "signed in respect of [the] DycodeX acqusition, including the agreements between DycodeX and Andri Yadi."

After aiming for 10,000t in US shrimp sales for 2024, eFishery exported one container

FTI found eFishery's agreements with its four CVs, outlining the services to be provided by the DycodeX employees, were all signed Dec. 29, 2023 -- three months before the acquisition was officially announced. That same day, MTN issued termination agreements to DycodeX affiliates Susando Tedharto Hokandar, Jaka Susanta and Triyanto.

FTI said it is investigating subsequent bank transfer statements from the four CVs to "an unidentified payee" of a total of IDR 5bn ($304,000), each dated Jan. 12, 2024. 

FTI said it discovered personal guarantee letters signed on Dec. 13, 2023 between Huzaifah and the four DycodeX employees -- Annisa Faza, Muhammad Alpi Gandamanah, Ramadhan Azka and Rezki Fitrazaki  -- showing the four CVS were all controlled by Huzaifah and not eFishery.

FTI said it is in the process of obtaining any and all agreements signed between DycodeX and CEO Andri Yadi and the four CVs, and all bank statements available from the four CVs.

An FTI spokesperson declined Undercurrent's request for additional comment on the DycodeX transaction or the current state of its internal probe.

title: Untitled
content:
Hong Kong-based CK Hutchinson, accused by US president Donald Trump of being a tool of the Chinese Communist Party, has sold Panamanian ports on either side of the Panama Canal to US investment firm BlackRock.

The purchase, announced Tuesday (March 4), will see CK Hutchinson sell its 80% interest in 43 ports in 23 countries and its 90% stake in Panama's Balboa and Cristobal ports to Blackrock's Global Infrastructure Partners and Swiss firm Terminal Investment for $22.8 billion, according to a joint press release. The acquisition will require regulatory approval and due diligence confirmation.

The deal is important to the seafood industry as the Panama Canal is a significant trade route, especially from Central and South America to the US West Coast, explained Gary Morrison, head of growth and strategy for UCN's price reporting agency.

"Maintaining consistent supply chains is imperative for the industry, as any interruptions can cause increased costs as well as uncertain planning," he said. 

Soon after taking office on Jan. 20, Trump demanded the Panama Canal be returned to US control and insinuated CK Hutchinson, owned by the family of Li Ka-shing of Hong Kong, had ties to China's ruling party and might use the ports for military purposes, including tracking US ship movements, as Undercurrent News reported.

The Li family began shopping CK Hutchinson two weeks ago in response to the perceived political pressure and received four bids for the assets, according to The New York Times.

FREE READ IMO proposes pricing mechanism for global vessel emissions

CK Hutchison co-managing director Frank Sixt said the transaction was the result of "a rapid, discrete but competitive process in which numerous bids and expressions of interest were received."

"I would like to stress that the transaction is purely commercial in nature and wholly unrelated to recent political news reports concerning the Panama ports," he said in the release.

Fink briefed Trump, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent, US secretary of state Marco Rubio and other senior American officials on the deal and received their approval before announcing it, The New York Times reported.

CK Hutchison has run the Balboa and Cristobal ports under a concession granted by the Panamanian government in 1997 and extended four years ago through 2047. Trump has expressed frustration the US paid to build the canal and relinquished it in 1999 without receiving just compensation. He also has complained about allegations of higher fees charged to US vessels.

Panamanian president Jose Raul Mulino previously asserted CK Hutchinson's ownership of the ports did not represent a military threat or breach the canal's neutrality.

US secretary of state Marco Rubio (right) visited the Panama Canal on Feb. 2. Photo courtesy of Office of the US Secretary of State

The sale relieves pressure on both Mulino and CK Hutchinson, as the Panamanian government had initiated an audit of the company's contract and faced a decision as to whether to cancel it, Bloomberg reported. 

"Hutchison could see the writing on the wall, that strategically it was best for them as well for Panama to pursue its interests elsewhere," said Evan Ellis, a Latin America research professor with the US Army War College.

Mulino's office and the Trump administration did not immediately provide any public comment on the deal. 

However, on Feb. 24, the Office of the US Trade Representative released its "Report on China's Targeting of the Maritime, Logistics, and Shipbuilding Sectors for Dominance" following a 10-month investigation under Section 301 of the US Trade Act.

The report found China's government has crafted and pursued an overt strategy of using its shipping sector to assert greater control over the global economy, partially channeled through its Belt and Road Initiative. The country's Marine Economy 13th Five-Year-Plan called for Chinese entities to "strengthen cooperation among international ports, support large-scale port and shipping companies to implement international development strategies, and according to market demand, participate in overseas port management, waterway maintenance, and maritime rescue through acquisitions, equity participation, leasing, etc."

China holds majority ownership in 13 foreign ports, "the majority of which have the potential for [Chinese] naval use and also are located in the Global South," according to the paper.

The USTR also found Chinese firms own stakes in one or more terminals at 96 overseas ports, 36 of which are among the world's top 100 ports by container throughput. Chinese state-owned banks provided lines of credit to state-owned shipbuilding and shipping enterprises to help them attain global dominance, the agency said.

China's network of ports and terminals "creates risks for competitors and dependent host nations" -- though the risks were primarily commercial, according to the paper. It cited an independent report that found "where Chinese firms operate ports, they appear to modify the host countries' trade toward China and away from former trade partners."

Tradex warns freight rates from China rising fast

China's recent Belt and Road Initiative investments in overseas ports have been a central part of China's shipping strategy, encouraging companies to "expand international routes with overseas investment ports as nodes."

"For nearly three decades, China has targeted the maritime, logistics, and shipbuilding sectors for dominance and has employed increasingly aggressive and specific targets in pursuing dominance of the maritime, logistics, and shipbuilding sectors," the report said. "China has largely achieved its dominance goals, severely disadvantaging US companies, workers, and the US economy generally through lessened competition and commercial opportunities and through the creation of economic security risks from dependencies and vulnerabilities."

The report's conclusion was that USTR has found sufficient evidence to support retaliatory action by the US government. It suggested charging up to $1.5 million for Chinese-built vessels or $500,000 for companies that have Chinese vessels as part of their fleets to enter US ports.

The USTR will hold a hearing on March 24 to discuss the report's proposals, according to Reuters.

title: Nicaragua seafood processor hit with warning letter by US FDA
content:
Mariscos Procesados (CAMPRESA), a seafood processor from Nicaragua, has been issued a warning letter by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for adulterated mahi-mahi fillets. 

The warning letter, dated Nov. 5, 2024, was published by the FDA on Tuesday (March 4). Per the notice, the FDA inspected the Mariscos Procesados facility in August 2024 and found "serious violations of the seafood Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) regulation."

While the company issued the FDA a revised HACCP plan, the US agency said the plan was inadequate.

"Accordingly, your frozen mahi-mahi fillets in vacuum-packaging products, are adulterated, in that they have been prepared, packed, or held under conditions whereby they may have been rendered injurious to health," the FDA noted in the warning letter.

Specifically, the FDA flagged CAMPRESA for failure to control histamines during transit to its facility, and also failure to control the hazard of C. botulinum toxin formation during finishing of frozen mahi-mahi fillets in vacuum-packaging product storage.

title: Untitled
content:
Ocean Trout Canada, a steelhead farmer based in Bedford, Nova Scotia, and its subsidiary, Nova Fish Farms, located in St Albans, Newfoundland, are facing numerous workplace safety charges following the death of an employee at their Newfoundland operation in July 2023.

The Occupational Health and Safety Division of Newfoundland and Labrador announced the charges last week after concluding its investigation, which it said uncovered a pattern of violations of workplace safety regulations. Both the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) and the provincial Occupational Health and Safety Division had conducted investigations into the circumstances surrounding the fatality.

As Undercurrent News reported, the RCMP received notification of an incident at the St Albans facility before 2:00 pm on July 6, 2023, and soon after found the employee unresponsive. Attempts to resuscitate the employee were unsuccessful. 

The charges against Ocean Trout Canada and Nova Fish Farms allege several serious breaches of Canadian labor law, including a failure to ensure a safe workplace and provide necessary safety equipment and neglect in training employees on workplace hazards. The company has also been charged with failing to ensure adherence to proper safety procedures, a lack of enforcement regarding the use of personal flotation devices in potentially dangerous situations and a failure to maintain a clear and hazard-free working environment on a vessel. Furthermore, a supervisor at Nova Fish Farms faces charges for failing to ensure the health, safety and welfare of all workers under their supervision.

Court appearances for both the companies and the supervisor were scheduled for this week at the Provincial Court in Grand Falls-Windsor in Newfoundland.

The fatality marked a particularly challenging period for Nova Fish Farms, which experienced several setbacks in 2023. One day prior to the employee's death, the company reported the loss of approximately 17,000 steelhead trout during a transfer from its hatchery in Prince Edward Island to its marine site at Muddy Hole in Newfoundland, as Undercurrent reported.

Ocean Trout Canada has yet to release any statement concerning the workplace safety charges. Undercurrent has contacted the company for comment but has not yet received a response.

title: Washington state man charged with posing as captain to steal $8m fishing vessel
content:
In what could potentially be the most bizarre story of the week, a man was arrested after allegedly attempting to steal an 80-foot-long commercial fishing vessel worth $8 million.

The US state of Washington's Department of Fish and Wildlife (WDFW) Police took to its Facebook page on Wednesday (Feb. 26) to share the details, and the story has now been picked up by multiple local news stations. 

The subject boarded the vessel, Jamie Marie, and woke the crew, advising them that "they needed to get underway," WDFW reported. He then allegedly proceeded to start the vessel and navigate it onto the Grays Harbor bar.

"The newer crew did not know the captain, but didn't argue, thinking he was an alternate operator, or someone sent by the real captain," the WDFW said, attempting to explain the crew's compliant response. 

However, the state agency said the crew "finally figured out something was wrong" when the imposter started talking about "meeting the Chinese mothership." At that point, a call to the real captain of the Jamie Marie revealed someone had stolen the vessel with the crew onboard, according to WDFW.

The agency said the imposter skipper "eventually brought the vessel back to port," where he was taken into custody by Westport Police Department. He was also found to be in possession of $4,000 cash and "a large quantity of individually weighed and packaged marijuana," it said.

Further investigation found that the individual, who has not yet been publicly identified, also boarded another large vessel that morning, WDFW said. He attempted to "rally the crew for a trip to sea" but was unsuccessful and they "ran him off," according to the agency.

The thief has been charged with Theft 1, Possession of Stolen Property 1, vehicle prowl 1, and VUCSA manufacture/delivery," WDFW said.

title: Albacora investigates sexist harassment of observer aboard vessel
content:
Spanish fishing firm Albacora is investigating allegations of severe sexist harassment reported by a female observer aboard its tuna vessel the Albacora Quince.

The observer, Celia (a pseudonym), is employed by the Madrid-based company Investigacion, Planificacion y Desarrollo (IPD), and alleged that she faced sexist harassment from several officers while contracted to monitor the Albacora Quince.

The incidents reportedly took place between Dec. 11, 2024, and Jan. 3, 2025, during her time on the vessel.

According to Celia's complaint, she was subjected to derogatory remarks such as, "A woman has no place on a boat, you only cause trouble," and offensive comments about her physical appearance, Faro de Vigo and El Correo reported. She claims that despite having another scheduled voyage, she was forced to disembark in Abidjan, Cote d'Ivoire, which left her without income due to her fixed-discontinuous contract.

Celia has also accused Spain's Council Superior of Scientific Research (CSIC) of failing to support her, alleging that the organization did not provide her with adequate protection or psychological support after she reported the harassment. Repeated requests for psychological assistance were ignored until she arranged private therapy at her own expense, she said.

While IPD asserted that Celia's disembarkation was due to the end of the campaign and a mechanical issue with the vessel, the Albacora Quince reportedly returned to fishing on Jan. 8 without further technical problems. A male observer has since replaced her.

In a statement, Albacora said it was conducting a thorough investigation into the claims.

It said the reported events do not align with the company's experience in the fishing industry, where the presence of female observers aboard their vessels has been common practice.

The business reaffirmed its stance against any form of harassment or discrimination in the workplace, and said it has collaborated immediately with all parties to investigate.

title: Seafarms records H1 loss but sees route back to life for vast shrimp project
content:
Australia's Seafarms Group has reported a financial loss for the first half of financial year 2025 (the six months ended Dec. 31, 2024), reflecting its ongoing investments in its vast shrimp farming effort, Project Sea Dragon (PSD).

Towards the end of the 2024 financial year, the Federal Court of Australia ruled that liquidators would be appointed for PSD after the black tiger shrimp project in the Northern Territory saw a final appeal to halt the liquidation dismissed.

Australia’s Seafarms warns of possible flood damage to shrimp farms

The project was once proposed at a construction cost of AUD 1.5 billion ($984 million), with a target production of 150,000 metric tons of black tiger shrimp.

However, the farming group has always disputed that the project was insolvent at any time prior to the appointment of administrators on Feb. 13, 2023. The federal court has found in its favor on this and against Justice Derrington's original verdict, which ruled that the project had been insolvent since 2020.

Now, the court-appointed liquidators of PSD are seeking court approval to appoint themselves as administrators, with a hearing scheduled for March 4, 2025. They have also decided, following their own investigations, to remove PSD from liquidation and to place it back into voluntary administration -- a "positive development" that Seafarms fully supports, the company said. See the subheading below for more on this.

Thus, Seafarms continues to invest in getting PSD off the ground.

"Seafarms Group continues to invest in the development of PSD, both with the increased sales of exports to develop markets in readiness for PSD production and the investment of time, funds and energy into the project team, licenses, approvals and a number of key potential investors that continue to seek involvement in the project subject to a resolution of the liquidation matter," it said in its results.

Its first-half loss of AUD 6.7m "reflects the continued investment in PSD," it said.

In order to keep up its investments, it has sold two farm sites in a deal that became unconditional on Aug. 20, 2024, with completion scheduled for April 30, 2025. Sale proceeds of AUD 7.6m were received last year, and the remaining AUD 5.9m is expected on April 30.

Meanwhile, it continues to produce shrimp at its Queensland operations. Some 480t of shrimp were produced in the first half of FY 2025, down from 697t in the prior H1, "consistent with a planned reduction in anticipation of poor market conditions that proved correct."

Of those, 75t of raw tiger shrimp were exported, bringing total exports from the "calendar year [CY] 2024 tiger crop" to 131t --  "a significant increase from the 76t exported in CY2023. This growth reflects ongoing investment in developing the export market for PSD."

It also produced 299t of "banana prawns," down from 697t in the previous corresponding period, a decline attributed to a decision to produce no frozen raw banana shrimp due to the high volume of cheap wild product in the market, and a "planned reduction in fresh production in response to a forecast decrease in consumer demand for premium products due to cost-of-living concerns."

Half-year sales revenue came to AUD 11.3m and included AUD 1.2m from the sale of post-larvae to other producers, "highlighting the success of our breeding and domestication program."

Life in the dragon yet

Seafarms explained in its results that there is now a viable route via which PSD could be reinstated as a live company and its subsidiary.

As mentioned, the court-appointed liquidators have decided to remove PSD from liquidation and to place it back into voluntary administration, with a view to PSD making a new proposal for a "deed of company arrangement," or DOCA.

"The liquidators have applied to the Supreme Court to become PSD’s administrators in order to effect the presentation of the [Seafarms] DOCA to creditors. If the liquidators are successful in that application and the DOCA is subsequently effectuated, then at the end of that process, [PSD] will return to the control of newly appointed directors and as a wholly owned subsidiary of the company."

It is, unsurprisingly, "fully supportive of this positive step" and continues to develop the potential PSD export markets while "continuing to engage with prospective investors."

Minutes from a February annual general meeting recorded that Seafarms saw "strong current interest from third-party international specialist seafood brokers that are ready to run a process to secure investment in the...project."

However, "third-party brokers are reluctant to progress the investment while PSD remains in liquidation."

Meanwhile, Seafarms is also engaged in a legal wrangle to reclaim funds provided to PSD's former administrators. 

When Robert Hutson and David Johnstone were appointed as PSD's liquidators by the court on Nov. 1, 2024, they replaced the project's former administrators. At that date, the former administrators held the sum of AUD 3.8m, provided to them by Seafarms, comprising the "balance of loan money to continue the operations during administration and the deed fund to settle the [previous] DOCA."

Seafarms sought the return of those funds under the terms of the DOCA. "The liquidators have also sought to claim those funds despite the clear words of the DOCA to the contrary. The liquidator claims that those funds are an asset of PSD. [Seafarms] has made an application to the Supreme Court to recover those funds which is set down for hearing on March 5, 2025."

title: China’s Joyvio faces second delisting warning amid ongoing legal battle over Chilean salmon business
content:
Chinese seafood giant Joyvio Food faces another delisting warning from the Shenzhen Stock Exchange but received a rare legal victory in challenges involving its Chilean salmon operations, according to company filings.

Last week, the seafood group announced it expects to report a negative net asset value for fiscal 2024, with projected losses between CNY 390 million and CNY 780m ($53.8m-$108m). Under Shenzhen exchange rules, this would trigger a "delisting risk warning" when the company releases its annual report. 

Chinese seafood leaders project heavy losses amid sector headwinds

The delisting warning adds pressure on Joyvio as it pursues its multi-jurisdiction legal battle against Australis Seafoods' former owner Isidoro Quiroga. The company acquired the Chilean salmon producer for $921m in 2019, which remains China's largest overseas acquisition in the seafood sector.

Joyvio claims Quiroga and other former executives deliberately hid overproduction at the company to inflate its value for a sale.

In the latest development, on Feb. 19, a Florida court ruled that third parties must provide banking documents related to a "highly confidential agreement" signed by Quiroga and former Australis CEO Ricardo Misraji during the company's acquisition, which reportedly involved a $2.5m payment claimed by Joyvio to be an "illegal transaction."

Joyvio said the Florida court's proceedings are "highly related to the Chilean criminal case." The Chilean lawsuit -- which is proceeding through Chile's criminal justice system -- has yet to be heard in court.

It follows a Chilean court ruling that imposed national travel restrictions on Quiroga and former executive Santiago Garreton, requiring them to check in quarterly with authorities. Ex-executive Santiago Garreton, who resides in Spain, must report to the Chilean consulate. 

The restrictions last for a 180-day period of further investigations into the case. Any request to leave the country will require a $10m bond.

The Florida court ruling represents a rare legal victory for Joyvio, which has suffered setbacks in other jurisdictions. In December, the UK High Court of England and Wales ordered Joyvio to pay £1.2m ($1.5m) to cover Quiroga's legal expenses after suspending the case in favor of Chilean jurisdiction. 

Chilean court imposes travel ban on former Australis execs, sets 180-day investigation

The charges focus on overproduction from 2018 to 2022, which allegedly exceeded legal limits by more than 98,000 metric tons. The financial impact, including potential regulatory fines and compliance costs, is estimated at over $140m.

The limits placed on Australis' future growth serve as a persistent headache for Joyvio, which previously stated ambitions to produce 100,000t of salmon a year.

As of Feb. 26, Chilean environmental regulators had rejected Australis' compliance plans for 12 of its 35 farming centers, according to Joyvio filings. The company has filed administrative appeals for 11 of these rejections.

At the Obstruccion farming center alone, regulators require Australis to reduce salmon production by 2,821t across three production cycles, while the Humos 2 center must cut 2,449t.

TIMELINE: Joyvio-Quiroga Legal Battle

April 2023: Australis files criminal charges against former Australis Seafoods owner and director Isidoro Quiroga Moreno and four other former executives for "mismanagement" and other claims.

June 2023: Food Investment SpA files fraud charges against Quiroga and seven other former controlling shareholders, directors, and executives. Due to close factual connections, prosecutors combine both cases.

June 2023: Australis, Food Investment, and other Joyvio subsidiaries file civil lawsuit against Quiroga and other former executives in UK High Court of England and Wales.

July 2023: Australis and Food file for judicial assistance in Florida court to collect evidence related to the Chilean criminal cases given Quiroga's residency in the US state.

October 2023: Australis files supplementary charges, adding "illegal transactions" and "money laundering" to the mismanagement allegations.

June 2024: Food Investment files additional charges for "disclosure of false information to securities markets."

December 2024: UK High Court agrees to temporarily suspend proceedings, accepting Quiroga's forum non conveniens argument that Chile is the appropriate jurisdiction.

December 2024: UK High Court orders Joyvio to pay £1.2m (over $1.5m) to Quiroga and his family for legal expenses, marking Joyvio's "fourth defeat" according to Quiroga's representatives.

January 2025: Santiago criminal court approves prosecutor's investigation findings that implicate three defendants -- former shareholders, directors, and executives --in mismanagement and fraud crimes.

February 2025: Santiago court holds procedural rights hearing for defendants and orders prosecutors to regularly update case files and provide proper notification of witness summons.

February 2025: Florida court orders third parties to provide banking documents related to a "highly confidential agreement" between Quiroga and former Australis CEO that allegedly involved a $2.5m illegal payment.

title: Investors in Indonesia’s eFishery face heavy losses as firm struggles with financial collapse
content:
Indonesian aquatech unicorn eFishery is facing significant financial challenges, and recent investigations have revealed a situation much worse than previously anticipated, reports Bloomberg News. 

According to several documents reviewed by Bloomberg, investors -- including SoftBank Group and Temasek Holdings, among others -- may recover less than 10 cents for every dollar they invested in the company.

The startup, which deploys AI-driven fish and shrimp feeders to farmers in Indonesia, has been operating at a loss since 2018, with hundreds of millions of dollars in accumulated deficits. The company has also been found to have misrepresented its financial figures over the years, leading to a loss of investor confidence.

As Undercurrent News previously reported, an audit, conducted by an undisclosed global firm and involved in interviewing "dozens" of eFishery employees, reportedly identified a scheme of alleged dual financial reporting, shell companies and false transactions designed to make eFishery more attractive to investors, according to DealStreetAsia.

Aquaculture veteran Maclean resigns from eFishery prior to financial fraud probe  

Ex-CEO Gibran Huzaifah allegedly first created a false set of accounting books in order to inflate revenue by 20-25% to meet the $4 million target set in its first Series A funding round.

A presentation from FTI Consulting Singapore, which was hired to review eFishery's operations and assist in its management, concluded that the company is "not commercially viable in its current form."

Once considered a rising star in Indonesia's startup scene, eFishery was valued at $1.4 billion in 2023 after raising $200m from Abu Dhabi's 42XFund and other investors. Overall, global investors poured around $315m into the company over five rounds of funding.

However, in late 2024, allegations of inflated sales and misconduct emerged, leading to the dismissal of eFishery's co-founders, Huzaifah and Chrisna Aditya.

A preliminary, ongoing probe into the business estimates that management inflated revenue by almost $600m in the nine months through September last year. That would mean more than 75% of the reported figures were fake.

As of mid-February 2025, the company had $50m in cash left, and the consultants recommended winding down much of the business.

For investors, the recovery appears bleak.

FTI Consulting running eFishery with shareholders set to vote on sale, wind-down

Under a "conservative scenario," they may receive just 8.3 cents on the dollar. In the more optimistic case, they could recover 9.5 cents on the dollar. For example, Abu Dhabi's G42, which invested $100m in 2023, may see just $8.3m returned on its investment.

According to DealStreetAsia, that investment was followed by Japan's SoftBank Group at $25m, Singapore's Temasek Holdings at $23.9m, and Northstar Group at $20.3m.

eFishery's financial difficulties are compounded by poor debt collection practices. The company facilitated loans for farmers to purchase fish feed but faced high default rates, leaving it on the hook for unpaid debts.

Investigations also revealed that eFishery had far fewer deployed feeders than it had claimed. Instead of the 400,000 it had reported, only around 6,300 feeders are active, and many of the systems were not functioning as promised.

Additionally, an independent report investigating potentially fraudulent practices at Indonesian aquatech startup eFishery lists the names of company executives believed likely to have had information about financial and operational problems.

title: Untitled
content:
UK supermarket chain Tesco has filed an antitrust lawsuit against six of the largest Norwegian salmon-farming firms, alleging they conspired to fix prices of fresh salmon Tesco bought from them.

Filed on Tuesday (Feb. 18) at the competition division of the High Court in London, Tesco's suit names Cermaq Group, Leroy Seafood Group, Scottish Sea Farms, Bremnes Seashore, Grieg Seafood, Grieg Seafood UK, SalMar and Sjór as defendants.

The Norwegian firms were initially targeted by a European Union investigation initiated in 2019. In January 2024, the EU released a preliminary view finding they had breached EU antitrust rules by colluding to distort competition in the market for spot sales of Norwegian farmed Atlantic salmon in the EU. 

Tesco Stores' suit also names Booker, Booker Direct, Budgens Stores, Booker Retail Partners (GB) and Makro Self Service Wholesalers as claimants.

Asda Stores, Aldi Stores, Iceland Foods, Wm Morrison Supermarkets, Marks and Spencer (M&S), Ocado Retail and The Cooperative Group filed their own lawsuit in March 2024 against the aforementioned Norwegian salmon farmers, plus SSF Hjaltland UK and SSF Shetland. The group of retailers claimed estimated losses at over £675 million ($860m).

However, Tesco, Lidl and J. Sainsbury were not part of that claim. A Tesco spokesperson did not immediately respond to Undercurrent News' request for comment on the suit.

A separate lawsuit filed at the specialist UK Competition Appeal Tribunal on behalf of UK consumers by Waterside Class in June 2024 seeks as much as £382 million ($484.7m) from the Norwegian salmon farmers for allegedly fixing the prices of fresh farmed Atlantic Salmon sold at UK retailers between October 2015 and May 2019.

The Norwegian salmon firms have previously denied wrongdoing in statements issued to Undercurrent, and have asked the UK Competition Appeal Tribunal to throw out the claims against them.

In September 2022, they agreed to an $85 million settlement with direct purchaser plaintiffs alleging price-fixing that occurred in the US, including Euclid Fish Company, Euro USA, Schneider's Fish and Sea Food Corporation, Beacon Fisheries, Cape Florida Seafood, The Fishing Line and Hesh's Seafood. In October 2022, a separate settlement netted US indirect purchasers of Norwegian farmed salmon $33m.

In October 2023, the same Norwegian salmon-farming firms paid CAD $5.2m to settle price-fixing claims in Canada.

title: Singapore aquaculture CEO charged in $336,000 bribery case
content:
The former CEO of a vertical fish farm in Singapore faces corruption charges for allegedly accepting a SGD 450,000 ($336,000) bribe from an engineering firm director in 2018, reports Channel News Asia.

Prosecutors say Apollo Aquaculture Group CEO Ng Woei Kiat used the funds for a condominium down payment and failed to declare related-party seafood trading transactions. 

Indonesia’s eFishery suspends co-founders over financial investigation

Apollo Aquaculture, backed by state investor Temasek, was a pioneer in vertical fish farming in Singapore, having launched the country's first multi-story aquaculture facility in Lim Chu Kang district in 2015. The company operated an eight-story fish farm capable of producing nearly 3,000 metric tons of fish annually including grouper, coral trout, shrimp, and sturgeon, Ng told CEO Magazine back in 2021.

Originally founded in 1969 as an ornamental fish exporter, the company later expanded into food fish production using recirculating aquaculture systems. However, Apollo Aquaculture entered judicial management in May 2022.

If convicted, Ng could face up to 10 years' imprisonment. The next hearing is scheduled for March 13.

title: Untitled
content:
Two men have been detained by the US Coast Guard (USCG) following a commercial fishing vessel boarding near Port Isabel, Texas, on Friday (Feb. 14).

USCG agents from the South Padre Island station boarded the Los Nietos, an 82-foot-long fishing vessel, and identified a crewmember as a "Mexican alien illegally present in the US," per a press release. Upon further investigation, it was discovered that the captain of the Los Nietos had an outstanding felony warrant for weapons charges.

"The Coast Guard remains steadfast in its commitment to ensuring the security of our nation," said Nina Mcdonald, enforcement division chief with the USCG in Sector Corpus Christi. 

"The at-sea apprehension of an alien illegally present in the US and a vessel's captain with an active arrest warrant underscores the critical role we play in both immigration enforcement and national security," McDonald added.

The USCG was assisted by the US Border Patrol, which is processing the undocumented crewmember. Members of the South Padre Island Police Department also assisted in the case. The vessel's captain was booked into the South Padre Island Jail.

It's been a busy start to the year for the USCG in Texas. Earlier this month the agency reported detaining 11 Mexican fishermen in the Gulf of Mexico and seized 1,595 pounds of allegedly illegally caught red snapper, as reported by Undercurrent News.

In January, the USCG detained another three Mexican fishermen for illegally fishing in federal waters off the coast of Texas. As much as 200 lbs of red snapper was seized during that USCG investigation.

title: Receiver for US RAS producer NaturalShrimp seeks approval to sell $16.8m in assets
content:
NaturalShrimp, a recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) producer of shrimp based in Dallas, Texas, has fallen into receivership and its creditors are pushing for liquidation, according to court filings and the company's SEC disclosures.

A federal court-appointed receiver has requested a judge in Utah to approve the sale of the company's assets, valued at about $16.8 million based on the court filing nearly a week ago. If approved, the sale would include NaturalShrimp's farming facilities, intellectual property and other holdings.

The motion was filed by Utah-based turnaround specialist Ampleo Turnaround and Restructuring in the Third Judicial District Court for Salt Lake County. It seeks authorization to sell NaturalShrimp's assets, either to its primary creditors — Streeterville Capital and Bucktown Capital — which have acted together as secured creditors in this case, or to any higher bidder.

NaturalShrimp, publicly traded over the counter in the US under the symbol SHMP, was placed under receivership in September 2024 after Streeterville Capital and Bucktown Capital jointly petitioned the Third Judicial District Court for Salt Lake County, Utah, citing unpaid debts and the company's inability to meet its financial obligations. The company, founded in 2001, saw its shares valued at just $0.0003 on Friday (Feb. 14), according to MarketWatch.

NaturalShrimp’s assets, as outlined in the Feb. 11, 2025, court filing, include its shrimp production facilities, intellectual property, and real estate holdings. The Webster City facility in Iowa is the largest single asset, valued at $7m, while additional properties in two other Iowa towns – Blairsburg and Radcliffe – and one in Texas bring the total real estate value to $9.87m.

The company’s intellectual property, including its proprietary RAS technology, is valued at $5.7m. Other assets, such as vehicles, equipment, and personal property, round out the total valuation of approximately $16.87m.

Despite the company's financial troubles, Streeterville provided a $500,000 line of credit to help sustain its operations while the legal proceedings unfolded, according to a September 2024 press release. However, it ultimately could not extend further loans, leaving NaturalShrimp unable to bridge its financial shortfall. In total, Streeterville has invested nearly $22m in NaturalShrimp, primarily through secured promissory notes issued in December 2021 and August 2022.

According to NaturalShrimp's last available financial statement, filed with the SEC for the second quarter ending June 30, 2024, the company had just $4,978 in cash at the end of the quarter, down from $115,525 three months earlier.

Total assets at the end of that quarter stood at $248,968, while total liabilities reached $39.7m.

Credit: NaturalShrimp

The company reported just $36,618 in total sales for its second quarter, a sharp drop from $205,872 in the same period a year earlier, while its quarterly operating expenses surpassed $2.06m, resulting in a quarterly net loss of $2.8m.

NaturalShrimp continued issuing shares to raise capital in the quarter, but the proceeds were insufficient to stabilize its financial position.

Not enough shrimp production

The receiver's Feb. 11 court filing noted that NaturalShrimp's Webster City facility was operating at only one-third capacity, producing 400-500 lbs of shrimp per week, with most sales going to Chicago, Illinois, and a few smaller markets. No production was occurring at its Blairsburg or Radcliffe facilities. 

"The receivership entities have one customer that buys shrimp at the Webster City facility and then transports them to nearby retail markets. Current income from the sale of shrimp does not cover operating and overhead expenses, and, in receiver’s opinion, the receivership entities cannot survive as a going concern without additional capital or debt,” the receiver said.

In May 2024, NaturalShrimp announced plans to expand its market reach, citing increased production at its Webster City, Iowa, facility and efforts to secure new commercial outlets for its "sushi-grade shrimp," as Undercurrent News reported. The company had expressed optimism about sales growth in the Upper Midwest, including Minnesota, Wisconsin and Michigan. However, its financial struggles have since deepened, culminating in its receivership and the proposed asset sale.

Another past report detailed how financial missteps and operational challenges contributed to its downfall. The company previously sought to merge with the special purpose acquisition company (SPAC) Yotta Acquisition Corp, but the deal fell through in 2023. It also faced operational setbacks, including a devastating fire at its La Coste, Texas, facility in 2022 and significant legal costs, including a $29.4m settlement in a shareholder lawsuit.

Receiver gets first dibs; shareholders cry foul

Frustration is mounting among NaturalShrimp's retail investors regarding the asset sale. Many worry they will see no returns, as the company’s assets are less than what it owes. This means secured creditors – Streeterville Capital and Bucktown Capital – will likely take a loss, and since they have priority, there will be nothing left for retail shareholders once secured debts are settled.

A Facebook group with more than 4,300 members has become a hub for the frustrated shareholders voicing their concerns. Posts on the forum show that these investors learned through a letter from the court-appointed receiver that secured creditors will get first dibs from the sale proceeds, should the court approve the sale.

Peter Maxfield, founder of the Facebook forum "Natural Shrimp Shareholders Group," launched the chat group in February 2019 as a space for investors to discuss the company's progress.

From the NaturalShrimp Shareholders Facebook page.

Reflecting on the receivership, Maxfield told Undercurrent over the weekend: "I think we all thought it was going to be successful. What they were telling us when they told us, and what we saw or at least [were] led to believe we saw, it all seemed to be legit and like they were on the right track."

He said some investors noticed signs of hardship at NaturalShrimp, but "not to the point of shutting the doors and turning off the tanks."

Another member of the chat group, "Bobby," who has declined to provide his full name, told Undercurrent in a Facebook chat that several shareholders have contacted the SEC, though the agency has not confirmed or denied an investigation. He criticized NaturalShrimp's management for consistently promoting optimistic projections through interviews and investor updates, which he said misrepresented the company's true financial struggles.

US RAS shrimp farmer NaturalShrimp quietly entered receivership in September 2024, and its $26.75 million in assets may soon be sold pending court approval. Photo: NaturalShrimp

"They even talked many times about uplisting to a major exchange, but clearly that was never even close," the investor said.

He said the company's shrimp production figures never aligned with its lofty projections. Instead of generating meaningful revenue from sales, NaturalShrimp primarily survived by issuing and selling large volumes of stock, diluting the value of its stock to its existing shareholders, he said.

"It became clear that shrimp sales were never going to be anywhere close to sustaining the company," he said.

Stock price fell 98.5%

NaturalShrimp's stock price dropped 98.5% over the last year, falling from $0.02 in February 2024.

Many investors in the Facebook forum have mentioned buying shares at prices between $0.03 and $0.90, with most spending around $0.20 to $0.50 on average. Some of these investors lost tens of thousands of dollars and expressed frustration at what they said was false hope given by the company's management.

Source: Google Finance

Some have accused Streeterville Capital of "scamming" them out of their stake in the company and have called for complaints to be filed with the SEC. Others have voiced frustration over what they see as a lack of accountability in the process.

Undercurrent has contacted the legal representatives handling the receivership and the management of NaturalShrimp for comment but has yet to receive a response.

title: Untitled
content:
The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has determined that hydraulic system failure for a piece of on-deck fishing equipment likely led to the August 2024 fire aboard the vessel Three Girls in the Gulf of Maine.

Recall that the Three Girls, an 81-foot groundfish trawler registered in the Port of Maine, caught fire off the coast of New Hampshire on the evening of Aug. 11. The vessel was approximately 105 nautical miles east of the city of Portsmouth when it issued a mayday call about the fire, alerting the US Coast Guard that the crew would be abandoning ship.

All six people aboard the vessel, including a National Marine Fisheries Services observer, were able to safely abandon and were rescued by the US Coast Guard without injury. 

The fishing vessel Three Girls post-fire.
Photo Credit: National Transportation Safety Board

NTSB has since conducted an investigation and determined that the fire on board the vessel likely originated in the "port, forward corner of the engine room between the hydraulic return oil filter housing and the winch engine." Further, investigators said they discovered that "hydraulic hoses from the hydraulic return oil filter box were detached from their aluminum filter housing covers, which had been melted away by the fire, indicating the hoses, their fittings, or another component of the box had failed."

"The cause of the fire was likely the ignition of pressurized hydraulic oil spraying on components of the running winch engine exhaust system," according to the report.

The fire resulted in an estimated $1.3 million worth of damage to the vessel. A full copy of the report can be found here.

title: Corruption, safety risks exposed in Argentine fishing sector after near-fatal capsizing
content:
A near-fatal capsizing of the artisanal fishing vessel BP Carlillo on Feb. 7 has raised alarms about safety and corruption in Argentina's fishing industry, reports Pescare. 

The vessel overturned 17 nautical miles south of Rawson Port, in Chubut Province, southern Argentina, with its crew of five rescued safely by nearby fishing boats. Initial investigations suggest that improper loading may have contributed to the incident.

The vessel had been targeting shrimp in the area and had set sail early that morning. The crew was treated for minor injuries and hypothermia at the local hospital.

This incident has drawn attention to the ongoing issue of overloading in the artisanal fishing fleet, a practice that many believe is tolerated or even encouraged through bribes to bypass regulations.

Julio Cesar Dominguez, the vessel’s owner, publicly accused the industry of widespread corruption, claiming that vessels "regularly exceed legal weight limits, sometimes paying up to $30,000 to do so."

In response, Argentina's secretary of fisheries Andres Arbeletche has promised an investigation into the capsizing and claims of illegal practices.

title: Untitled
content:
An independent report investigating potentially fraudulent practices at Indonesian aquatech startup eFishery lists the names of company executives believed likely to have had information about financial and operational problems.

The probe, conducted by FTI Consulting, was launched on Dec. 15, 2024, after a whistleblower complaint was received by eFishery's board of directors. According to the FTI audit, eFishery allegedly inflated revenue by almost $600 million from 2018 to 2024.

Based on company records, interviews with 23 eFishery employees, data collected from personal computers, laptops, mobile devices, email accounts and WhatsApp and Slack messages, FTI identified 16 executives it claims were in some manner involved in allegedly inflating sales and fudging accounting practices.

FTI divided its list into two categories of implication, labeled "Category 1" and "Category 2." Those in Category 1 were either actively involved in the falsification of financials or supporting documents, executing bank transfers, managing bank accounts or deleting data, according to FTI. Category 2 employees either had knowledge of the company separate internal and external accounting books or helped to inflate the company's financial figures without informing the board of directors of any malfeasance, FTI explained.

Ten employees are listed in Category 1. They include: former CEO and co-founder Gibran Huzaifah; corporate finance and investor relations vice president Angga Hadrian Raditya, shrimp business senior vice president Kristin Dax Veriga, corporate planning head Wirabhama Kirana, corporate planning specialist Kheren Yutinsia Hersan, corporate planning associates Kariza Sharfina, Felicia Kusmali and Kanisa Krisnata Adiputri, cash operation senior manager Martin Ramdhany, and revenue assurance lead Bagus Martantio.

The six employees identified in Category 2 are: chief product officer and co-founder Chrisna Aditya Wardani, senior vice president of fish business Junandar Indra Togam Panggabean, chief human resource officer Caecilia Pudji Widyarti, Financial Controller Head Tubagus Tommy Apriadi, accounting and senior tax manager Aris Gustiana, and treasury head Hamdinal Rahman.

Additionally, FTI named four eFishery employees it said were potentially implicated in wrongdoing: treasury and cashflow lead Elsa De Balqis, cash management associate Asep Sutrisna, asset management manager Selvi Sopiantika, and commercial and general accounting manager Heru Setiono.

FTI Consulting running eFishery with shareholders set to vote on sale, wind-down

FTI cautioned its list is preliminary.

"Please note that this list is still subject to changes, and further interviews being conducted," its audit said. "There may be additional employees who are potentially implicated in the fraud who will need to be interviewed to understand their level of involvement and any instructions received."

Reached by Undercurrent, one of those implicated, Kristin Veriga, a former Regal Springs and Grobest executive who landed at eFishery in 2022 after a stint at the failed startup JET Seafood, called the naming of implicated employees "disparagement."

"I have limited knowledge of the situation but it is clear from the many inaccuracies and omissions that this is an interim/WIP report and I cannot and will not comment on a live, ongoing investigation," Veriga said. "Having said that, I strongly deny any allegations of participation in or concealment of any alleged misconduct. Given that this remains an ongoing investigation that has yet to reach a final conclusion my focus remains on providing shareholders, stakeholders and the investigators all the necessary support to help reach a swift and accurate final conclusion."

Veriga said he had pushed FTI to publicly disseminate a statement or document revising its conclusion, but it had not done so as of Thursday (Feb. 13).

FTI did not respond to Undercurrent's request to comment on Veriga's status or answer other questions regarding its investigation.

Kristin Veriga

Thus far, the only two employees who have lost their jobs as a result of the scandal have been co-founders Hufaizah and Aditya, both exiting in December 2024.

FTI is continuing its investigation, with the objective of investigating "allegations relating to the manipulation of the financial statements that involved inflating revenue as much as four times, fictitious expenses, capital expenditures … as well as misappropriation of funds."

In addition to its audit, FTI has been appointed as an active manager of eFishery as of January 2025 and is preparing to ask shareholders in the coming weeks to vote on whether to sell, restructure or wind down the company, as Undercurrent previously reported.

Indonesian police have received complaints against Huzaifah and Aditya, DealStreetAsia reported on Feb. 7.

Separate complaints were filed in February, March, April and May 2024. Some are currently under investigation, while others remain in the preliminary inquiry stage, Trunoyudo Wisnu Andiko, the public information bureau head at the Indonesian National Policeʼs Public Relations Division, told the publication.

The complaints have been forwarded to regional and national police units in Indonesia, as well as Indonesia's Financial Services Authority, and those agencies are now conducting a joint review, according to Andiko.

eFishery laid off an additional 100 employees in the past week, following the previous dismissal of around 300 employees in January, DealStreetAsia further reported.

title: ProPublica: Alaska investment fund missed red flags before investing $29m in Peter Pan deal
content:
An investor group tasked with investing millions of dollars from the US state of Alaska's sovereign wealth fund missed red flags and failed to look into the background of US seafood entrepreneur Rodger May before partnering with him to acquire Peter Pan Seafoods in 2021, reports ProPublica.

The investigative report – co-published with the Anchorage Daily News and Northern Journal – recounts how staff at the Alaska Permanent Fund were nervous about entrusting McKinley Capital – an Anchorage based firm controlled by the son of a now-deceased Alaska billionaire investor – with $100 million in funds for in-state private equity investment.

"We couldn’t, politically, not choose McKinley," an unnamed former employee told the reporters, an assertion derided as "poppycock" by the Permanent Fund's then-chair Craig Richards.

Rodger May’s former partners cry foul over his play for Peter Pan assets

Even so, the investigation found that May, a seafood businessman with a wide-ranging resume that includes producing B movies, had earlier made headlines over a failed venture in Golden Harvest – an Alaska fish processing plant in Adak in the Aleutian Islands – where scores of unpaid fishermen and evidence of financial fraud had triggered an FBI investigation.

May's involvement with Golden Harvest was noted in investment prospectus but not that the venture had folded just months before. May had been one of the firm's four board members. 

A forensic audit commissioned by some of the company’s investors found evidence of  fraud, including "improprieties" in financial submissions to a bank, according to a copy of the document obtained by ProPublica. 

May reportedly told ProPublica that he was aware of the FBI investigation but was never interviewed by agents. He denied he was the target of any criminal probe, saying "we were one of the largest losers in this debacle." 

No due dillgence done

A source reportedly told ProPublica the formal vetting process did not turn up the allegations of financial fraud at Golden Harvest. Nor of at least two instances -- in 2000 and 2006 -- when he'd run afoul of authorities for marketing tainted fish, the latter instance in which he pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor.

Jason Scharfman, a due diligence expert, said that McKinley or its partner should have uncovered lawsuits over Golden Harvest's breakup and conducted "boots on the ground" research on May’s past businesses.

"It’s not clear that McKinley and its business partners were asking questions that would surface such concerns," said Scharfman, after a reporter read him an excerpt of the "quality of earnings" report on May’s business.

As for the Permanent Fund, Allen Waldrop, the fund official who oversees private equity investments, reportedly told ProPublica the staff doesn’t interfere with the individual investment decisions of their private money managers.

But the staff had at least one opportunity to raise objections: The Permanent Fund’s agreement with McKinley contained a "concentration limit" that restricts how much money could go into a particular deal. The investment team asked the Permanent Fund to waive the cap for Peter Pan, to which staffers agreed.

Two weeks after the report on May’s businesses was delivered, the new business partners closed the deal on Dec. 31, 2021, as Undercurrent News reported. 

Peter Pan Seafoods shutters abruptly in 2024

Alaska residents were about to wager a small piece of the Permanent Fund -- $29 million -- from the fund that pays out its annual dividend checks to every man, woman and child resident of the state. 

The venture didn't work out. The seafood processor began shuttering plants last year before being forced into receivership by its lead creditor San Francisco bank Wells Fargo, as Undercurrent reported.

Silver Bay joins May-led group on future of former Peter Pan King Cove plant, inks deal for Dillingham, Port Moller ops

But in an auction held last year, May was able to leverage the $40 million he'd invested of his money to regain control of vast swathes of the century-old seafood company that shut down four years after he'd taken the reins, Undercurrent reported.

Silver Bay Seafoods has since purchased several of Peter Pan's core assets. But the plant in King Cove remains under May's control.

The sale of Peter Pan's modern processor in Port Moller, Alaska to Silver Bay is also the subject of separate litigation as well as a joint venture for a Seattle area canning plant with OBI Seafoods, as Undercurrent reported.

title: Untitled
content:
Norway's largest cod farmer, Norcod, has announced its intent to pursue an additional private placement on Oslo's Euronext Growth market as it aims to expand towards an eventual goal of 25,000 metric tons of production annually.

Farmed cod on path to 70,000t but no replacement to wild catch shortfall

The firm said it is contemplating another equity raise of a minimum NOK 150 million ($13.3m), with some of its largest shareholders already indicating their support to cover the minimum amount.

Norcod has engaged DNB Markets as financial advisor for the placement, which it expects to take place in Q1.

The farmer has also secured an additional debt commitment from DNB of up to NOK 150m, encouraged by current record prices for fresh cod exports and the expectation that Barents Sea cod quotas will remain historically low for the foreseeable future.

In its Q4 report, the farmer revealed that these strong price trends have caused it to revise its growth strategy towards one "that aligns with the current favorable market dynamics."

Combined, both the placement and the debt commitment would give Norcod an additional NOK 300m of funds with which to speed its growth towards that 25,000t target.

As part of the revised strategy, Norcod is also increasing its harvesting at its Krakoy processing plant in Q1 to manage maturation. This means the fish harvested from its Frosvika site will likely be smaller than originally budgeted.

"These changes will negatively affect cash flow from operations for the 2025 financial year, compared to the Q3 2024 report where Norcod indicated that positive cash flow from operations in 2025 was within reach."

Altogether, the firm posted NOK 124m in revenue for Q4, up 47% on the previous year, while harvests more than doubled y-o-y to 2,390 metric tons.

Of this, 1,850t were exported, accounting for 60% of total farmed cod exports from Norway in Q4. At the year's end, its biomass at sea came to 6,746t, though this is down by 13% from the 7,817t it had stocked at the end of 2023.

Norcod's share of Norway's total farmed cod market at the end of 2024. Credit: Norcod

For now, Norcod remains loss-making as it steadily ramps up production. In the latest quarter, the farmer still recorded an operating loss of NOK 35m, though this is a 66% reduction from the loss of NOK 104m in the same quarter of the previous year.

Production costs were also reduced y-o-y, from NOK 48.3/kg to NOK 46/kg.

Its site at Jamnungen, in Froya municipality near Trondheim, has also been granted an increase in its maximum allowable biomass from 3,600t to 5,200t, while five pens at a new location in Bjornvika have also been stocked, it said.

Regarding the November escape of up to 22,979 cod from its farm in Labukta, Nordland county, Norcod said the exact cause remains under investigation.

Norcod's financial results for Q4 2024. Credit: Norcod

title: Labor issues persist in India’s shrimp-processing sector, according to new report
content:
Labor issues in India's shrimp-processing sector, first reported in March 2024 by the Corporate Accountability Lab, the Associated Press and the Outlaw Ocean Project, are still a huge problem, according to CNN.

The reports found rampant labor law and rights violations across India's shrimp-processing sector, including forced labor, child labor, low pay and unsanitary working conditions, though the Indian shrimp industry disputed the findings.

Despite the investigations and the subsequent listing of Indian shrimp on the US Department of Labor's 2024 List of Goods Produced with Forced Labor in September 2024, serious problems persist, CNN reported.

Late surge of US shrimp imports in 2024 not enough to make up for earlier deficit

CNN interviewed 13 women working in shrimp-peeling sheds in India's Andhra Pradesh state. Of those, eight said they worked 12-hour shifts, with a break of two to three hours, seven days or nights a week -- about 70 hours a week on average, without overtime or days off.

Their monthly pay is around 11,000 Indian rupees ($130), which is less than the minimum monthly wage dictated by Indian law, which also calls for a maximum of 60 work hours per week, with overtime paid after 48 hours, and a minimum of one day off every 10 days. 

India's Marine Products Export Development Authority (MPEDA), the country's seafood industry trade group, told CNN that 192 of the 496 shrimp-peeling establishments inspected by Andhra Pradesh's Labour Department had received charge sheets for labor law violations in 2024. 

"[We] take all allegations regarding labor issues with the utmost seriousness," MPEDA said in a statement. "[We] welcome collaborative engagement and open dialogue … to ensure that all voices are heard, concerns are addressed, and our shared commitment to protecting labor rights and promoting fair labor practices is reinforced." 

Most of the labor issues center around female migrant laborers brought to peeling sheds by recruiters, many of them working for third-party contractors, according to CNN. Using third-party contractors allows companies to hire laborers who don't have formal documentation or labor cards and are therefore not eligible for social security benefits, according to the International Labour Organization.

The ILO said women make up 70-80% of India's shrimp-processing workforce, of which 50% are migrant laborers who mostly live in bunkhouses at the factories with limited freedom of movement.

Indian shrimp giant acquires North American lobster supplier from industry veteran

The women interviewed by CNN reported being overworked and underpaid, and that their movement was restricted. Several reported being unable to access adequate health care.

Additionally, despite Indian law forbidding the employment of children under the age of 14, CNN reported that one of the workers it interviewed was 13 years old and that numerous other minors worked alongside her peeling shrimp. One of the workers interviewed reported more than 50 minors were employed by her company, who were hidden by management when they were notified a government inspection was imminent. 

"There are huge bungalows where they would keep them… And there will be others who would be guarding the place," she said. 

India's Ministry of Commerce and Industry reported national seafood production increased to 17.5 million tons in the 2022-2023 financial year, up from 16.2m tons in the previous year. Of the total, Andhra Pradesh contributed over 5m tons, mostly of farmed shrimp. Final volume totals for 2023-2024 have not yet been released, but the ministry said they reached an all-time high and were worth $7.38 billion, though UCN's Trade Portal shows shrimp exports declined significantly in 2024 (see chart below).

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view

The country has set its sights on continued shrimp industry growth as part of a $12 billion seafood export target for 2026. The US and China are India's top two customers, accounting for more than 50% of total exports. Secondary markets include Japan, Vietnam, Thailand, Canada, Spain, Belgium, the United Arab Emirates and Italy. 

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
Labor issues persist in India’s shrimp-processing sector, according to new report - Undercurrent News

However, that growth is bringing more pronounced problems to the sector's labor situation, according to J.N.V. Gopalan, a leader with the Centre of Indian Trade Unions. Gopalan told CNN that as more laborers are needed for the growing shrimp industry, "working conditions and health care is deteriorating further," and that workers suffer from a lack of basic human rights.

In response, MPEDA said it had hosted a series of meetings along with India's Department of Commerce "to address the concerns raised about labor abuse in the sector by the USA-based organizations."

Together, MPEDA and the Commerce Department formed "Tripartite Committees" comprised of government agencies, company and labor union leaders "to safeguard and ensure the implementation of labor welfare measures in the value chain," and formed a Joint Task Force to identify unregistered pre-processing units. Several Indian shrimp companies also joined the Seafood Task Force, which is dedicated to addressing labor issues in Asian seafood supply chains.

"Processing units, if engaging migrant workers, are required to obtain the license necessary from the labor department," MPEDA said.

title: Untitled
content:
A fishing vessel with four crew members capsized and sank off the coast of Nova Scotia, Canada, on Thursday (Feb. 6) night, resulting in the deaths of two of its crew members.

According to the Facebook forum Nova Scotia Buzz, Fortune Pride, an 18-meter (60-foot) fishing vessel built in 1988, was returning to port with a catch of silver hake when it encountered trouble near Sambro, a coastal community southwest of Halifax, the province's capital.

On Friday, the Facebook forum, with over 100,000 followers, shared updates on the incident, citing authorities and those familiar with the situation. Per the reports, an incident triggered an emergency response after Fortune Pride's distress beacon late Thursday. The Joint Rescue Coordination Centre (JRCC) in Halifax, Nova Scotia, sent Canadian Coast Guard boats and Royal Canadian Air Force planes to the last place the fishing vessel was seen. The search and rescue teams reportedly faced tough weather, with big waves and strong winds, to get to the location.

The vessel's owner, Jose Teixeira, told City News-Halifax that he had communicated with the crew at approximately 8:30 pm on Feb. 6, and at that time, there was no indication of distress. Shortly after, at around 10 pm, the Joint Rescue Coordination Centre received an emergency beacon signal from the vessel, indicating it was in trouble approximately 18 km southeast of Sambro.

JRCC spokesperson Lt-Cmdr Len Hickey told the publication that rescuers found three crew members Thursday night—two conscious and one unconscious. The fourth crew member was located in a life raft Friday morning and was unresponsive when rescued.

On Sunday, local publication Coast Reporter said that the two who died were identified as the captain, John Allen Baker, and deckhand Phil MacInnis.

Possible causes under investigation

Authorities, including the Transportation Safety Board of Canada, are investigating the circumstances that led to the capsizing.

Initial reports suggest that adverse weather conditions may have played a role, while the vessel's heavy haul of fish — estimated between 18,000 and 23,000 kilograms — could have affected its stability, reported the Canadian Press and Coast Reporter.

Fortune Pride, registered in Canada, was built by Glovertown Shipyard in Newfoundland and Labrador. It had a gross tonnage of 102 and was one of three vessels owned by Teixeira.

The vessel was previously mentioned in a July 2024 Undercurrent News report regarding the bankruptcy and asset sale of Chester Basin Seafoods Group (CBSG), a Bridgewater, Nova Scotia-based seafood company. Fortune Pride was one of three vessels included in CBSG's assets acquired by 4519497 Nova Scotia Ltd (451), a company owned by Teixeira, as part of a court-approved purchase. The vessel was also referenced in a legal dispute among CBSG shareholders, with allegations of negligence in its maintenance and operation.

On Friday premier of Nova Scotia Tim Houston, expressed condolences to the victims' families and support for the survivors.

"Today, Nova Scotians have another unfortunate reminder of the dangers of working on the sea as the fishing vessel Fortune Pride capsized in the waters near Sambro last night," Houston said.

"I want to express my sincere condolences to the families and friends of the souls we lost -- you are in my thoughts and prayers, as are the two fishers who survived this heartbreaking tragedy."
