title: US food culture is unique challenge for domestic shrimp
content:
Harvesters and processors of domestically-caught and raised shrimp in the US can't follow the same script as Europe when it comes to marketing, suggests aquaculture consultant Philip Buike.

The long-standing US preference for headless, shell-less shrimp – often frozen or breaded – has been cultivated over decades by convenience-driven consumer habits, making it one of the most challenging markets for domestic producers to navigate, he told Undercurrent News in a recent interview.

This dynamic starkly contrasts countries like Spain, where food culture prioritizes quality, local production and the time spent preparing meals.

Spain-based and British-born Buike, whose 40-year career spans global shrimp farming projects in South America, Europe and Southeast Asia, explained that these entrenched preferences have shaped a market dominated by imports.

Philip Buike in the hatchery of Norwegian King Prawns, which produces 100 metric tons of shrimp annually in Southern Norway. As a technical adviser, Buike highlights the shrimp's focus on quality and storytelling for discerning northern European clients—a market advantage US producers often lack

The US imports approximately 800,000 metric tons of shrimp annually, while domestic aquaculture production remains negligible.

"For every shrimp consumed in the US, five are imported," he said.

"Since I've been involved in the industry for 40 years now, the US has dictated the prices and presentation because of the size of that market. The market doesn't differentiate in terms of quality, origin, ecological awareness, or any of those supposedly benefits for a domestic product," said Buike.

"This overwhelming reliance on imports not only sets the price and product standards but also marginalizes the benefits of domestic shrimp, such as its sustainability and freshness."

The challenges for American shrimp farmers go beyond consumer habits. Buike pointed out that high production costs in the US – spanning feed, labor, energy and land – make it nearly impossible to compete with producers in countries like Ecuador and Vietnam, where natural advantages and lower costs drive profitability.

For example, fishmeal, a key ingredient in shrimp feed, has reached record prices due to a poor fishing season in Peru, further driving up costs for US producers.

"Most shrimp farms outside the US can produce at costs far below what's possible domestically," Buike said.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view

Efforts to establish a viable shrimp farming industry in the US have often centered on small-scale, high-end operations catering to niche markets, such as premium restaurants. While some have found limited success, these businesses lack the scale needed to sustain an industry.

Buike explained that a true domestic shrimp sector requires not just farms but the development of feed plants, processing facilities and distribution networks — an infrastructure that niche players alone can support.

Changing the story around shrimp

Buike argued that changing the narrative around shrimp in the US is critical, starting with consumer education and a long-term marketing strategy. Americans need to be made aware of the benefits of domestic shrimp, including its lower carbon footprint and higher quality.

However, Buike acknowledged that shifting deeply entrenched consumer preferences would take time – likely generations.

He pointed to Spain as an example of how food culture shapes seafood markets. In Spain, where shrimp is consumed widely, consumers prioritize quality, freshness and local sourcing. Spaniards also spend more of their income on food and dedicate more time to meal preparation.

In contrast, Buike observed that American households generally favor convenience, which has driven the market toward low-cost, pre-prepared products.

Buike said policy changes could provide some relief, but these measures come with risks.

Shrimp options at Costco include farmed shrimp from Ecuador and wild shrimp from Argentina, reflecting global market dominance. Photo: Liza Mayer

Tariffs on imported shrimp or stricter hygiene regulations could help level the playing field for domestic producers, but they might also drive consumer prices up, potentially reducing demand.

"There's a balance to be struck," Buike noted, adding that policies alone won't solve the industry's systemic issues.

Global experience

Buike's career underscores his authority on the subject.

From his early days as a research scientist in Ecuador, where he identified the cause of the viral shrimp pathogen Taura Syndrome during his time at the Center for Marine Investigation (CENAIM) in Ecuador, to designing Europe's first commercial shrimp hatchery in Austria, he has spent decades navigating the complexities of shrimp farming. His perspective reflects a deep understanding of the interplay between technology, economics and consumer behavior.

"The US shrimp market is uniquely difficult," Buike said. "Unlike other countries, it has been shaped by decades of imports and a preference for low-cost convenience. Building a true domestic industry means changing that narrative, and that's not something that happens overnight."

While niche players may continue to find limited success, he stressed that the future of US shrimp farming depends on scaling up production, investing in infrastructure and reshaping consumer perceptions. Without these changes, the market will likely remain a formidable challenge for domestic producers.

title: Untitled
content:
Four consecutive months of year-on-year volume improvements to end 2024 by the US shrimp import sector weren't enough to overcome previous months of underwhelming results. US shrimp imports finished the year behind.

The US imported 762,804 metric tons of shrimp worth almost $6.1 billion in 2024, 3% less volume and 6% less value than the 788,209t worth more than $6.4bn imported in 2023. That's what the final month of US import data just published by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) shows. 

Given the turbulence experienced in the industry last year, however, US shrimp importers are probably breathing a sigh of relief that the year-end numbers weren't worse.

To hear Gary Morrison, head of growth and strategy for UCN's price reporting agency, tell it, the year was one that began with one story and ended with another.

"The industry entered the year in an oversupply situation, further pressured by uncertainty regarding antidumping and countervailing duties," he said. "In addition, consumer sentiment was negative, and they perceived seafood and shrimp as luxury items. As lower prices were filtered to the consumer and a definite ruling on the AD/CVD [anti-dumping and countervailing duties], imports started to bounce back."

Morrison is referring to the US Commerce Department investigations of India, Ecuador, Indonesia and Vietnam -- the four largest shrimp-producing nations -- that kicked off in early 2024 over complaints of unfair practices by the US domestic shrimp industry, as reported by Undercurrent News.

The US International Trade Commission, in November 2024, concluded the battle with a final determination that the US shrimp industry had suffered harm from the actions, cementing the AD/CVD rates set earlier.

The final rates were not as dramatic as originally proposed, and the decision allowed US shrimp importers to have cost certainty, facilitating the signing of contracts. But during the months preceding the rulings, US shrimp imports saw some big jumps and declines.

The following month-by-month accounting of overall US shrimp imports tells the up and down story: 

January 2024 -- 59,629t worh $462.4m (14% less volume, 21% less value year-on-year)
February 2024 -- 59,668t worth $456.5m (12% more volume, 6% less value y-o-y)
March 2024 -- 63,495t worth $481.8m (8% more volume, 1% less value y-o-y)
April 2024 -- 50,901t worth $397.6m (10% less volume, 14% less value y-o-y)
May 2024 -- 63,973t worth $486.7m (3% more volume, 7% less value y-o-y)
June 2024 -- 53,358t worth $418.2m (14% less volume, 18% less value y-o-y)
July 2024 -- 61,213t worth $481.8m (12% less volume, 16% less value y-o-y)
August 2024 -- 66,299t worth $535.2m (10% less volume, 11% less value y-o-y)
September 2024 – 71,196t worth $601.1m (1% more volume, 4% more value y-o-y)
October 2024 – 74,699t worth $607.8m (2% less volume, less than 1% more value y-o-y)
November 2024 -- 71,782t worth $602.9m (1% more volume, 6% more value y-o-y)

In December 2024, the US imported 66,650t worth $563.8m (2% more volume, 9% more value y-o-y).

Also on the bright side for shrimp importers, overall average prices have climbed back a bit. After hitting a high point of $4.73 per pound in April 2022, the overall average price fell to $3.57/lb in March 2024 and then rose to $4.01/lb in December, as illustrated by the UCN trade portal chart below.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
Late surge of US shrimp imports in 2024 not enough to make up for earlier deficit - Undercurrent News
India ends year on positive note

The US' largest import source, India, accounting for 39% of the market, finished 2024 a little behind its performance in 2023. The US imported 294,333t worth $2.2bn, 1% less volume and 4% less value than the year before.

India saw a bit of a surge in December, sending the US 23,714t worth $193.7m, 4% more volume and 11% more value y-o-y. The average overall price to finish the year was $3.90 per pound, 10% more than the $3.56/lb seen a year ago.

Late surge of US shrimp imports in 2024 not enough to make up for earlier deficit - Undercurrent News
Ecuador suffers disappointing finish

Ecuador, the US' second-largest source of shrimp, had an even worse conclusion to the year. It sent the US 187,000t of shrimp worth $1.3bn worth in 2024, 9% less volume and 8% less value. 

The average price paid in December was $3.52/lb, up from the $3.10/lb seen a year earlier.

Late surge of US shrimp imports in 2024 not enough to make up for earlier deficit - Undercurrent News
Indonesia even worse off

Indonesia, the US' third-largest shrimp source, sent it 134,803t worth $1.0bn in 2024, 8% less volume and 12% less value than in 2023. Average prices on Indonesian shrimp also have risen, hitting $3.83/lb in December 2024, up from the $3.47/lb seen a year earlier.

Late surge of US shrimp imports in 2024 not enough to make up for earlier deficit - Undercurrent News
All smiles for Vietnamese shrimp

The US shrimp source that had the best outcome in 2024 was Vietnam. It sent the US 69,295t worth $691.6m, which represented a 13% improvement in volume and a 6% increase of value. The average price in December was $4.95/lb, up from the $4.55/lb seen a year eariler.

Late surge of US shrimp imports in 2024 not enough to make up for earlier deficit - Undercurrent News
A few changes in the wholesale market

In his latest projection of US wholesale prices for shrimp, week 6 of 2025 (Feb.3-9), Morrison said pricing has been flat for white shrimp of Latin American origin.

"After two weeks of change focused on this category, prices remained steady this trading period," he said. "The recent discounts in headless shell-on and head-on shell-on have stabilized and market in general balance. Interest in peeled product still has the market called fully steady to firm. "

However, he noted "some adjustments" in the white shrimp of Asian origin category. 

"The most broad-based changes are reflected in easy peels," he said. "Discounts are noted to better align buying activity with supply. There is a single change higher in the 8-12 count peeled and deveined, tail-on product."

title: Norway’s salmon producers want UK price-inflation case thrown out
content:
Norwegian salmon producers have urged the UK's Competition Appeal Tribunal to throw out claims by several retailers for £675 million ($843.9m) in damages, arguing it does not have jurisdiction to hear the case, reports Global Competition Review.

Daniel Jowell KC, counsel to Mowi, attacked the claims during a hearing at the tribunal on Feb. 4.

UK retailers sue Norwegian salmon farmers after EC price fixing statement

The lawsuits, filed last March by Asda, Iceland, Marks and Spencer, Ocado, Wm Morrison Supermarkets, Aldi and The Co-operative, are based on an ongoing European Commission probe. But EU infringement decisions are not something that the UK tribunal can give "any weight to" following the UK's exit from the bloc, nor is it obliged to hear any of the evidence and issue a ruling on such claims, Jowell said. 

The claimants brought this damages action no doubt anticipating that the alleged cartel would have been established by an EU infringement decision by now, he said. No sanctions have yet been issued -- and a parallel investigation by the US Department of Justice was discontinued without any finding of an infringement, Jowell added.

That came after a US federal judge formally approved an $85m settlement between some of Norway's salmon farmers and a slew of plaintiffs who said that they were harmed by alleged price-fixing that took place in the industry.

It is possible the commission won't issue any infringement decision at all. Even if it does -- and Mowi will "vigorously contest any finding of a cartel" -- that would not bind the tribunal nor the addressees as far as the UK is concerned, said Jowell.

The supermarkets claim that the alleged cartel inflated spot prices for Norwegian-farmed Atlantic salmon, causing them to suffer losses through overcharges on purchases made in the UK. The Nasdaq Salmon Index influenced global farmed Atlantic salmon prices, meaning the cartel affected not only spot and contract prices but also direct and indirect sales of those products, the supermarkets allege.

Jowell said the allegations relating to the Nasdaq index go "far beyond" the European Commission's press release summarising its statement of objections, which is limited to the Norwegian spot market.

If the claimants can't establish that the collusion was on the Nasdaq index, then the whole claim fails, which means it is a "foundational issue" to the case, he said.

title: US gov’t scientists chafe at Trump admin’s offer of severance, threats against disloyalty
content:
Shakeups in US government agencies are affecting the work of federal scientists tasked with conducting stock assessments for West Coast fisheries, Undercurrent News has learned.

There was a sigh of relief when the incoming US Commerce Secretary promised not to disrupt the work of the federal agency that regulates commercial fisheries, as Undercurrent has reported. 

But a flurry of unsigned memos authored by the administration of US president Donald Trump has threatened to tear up existing contracts related to telework, stamp out diversity policies, offer early resignations guaranteeing full pay until the end of September, while instituting an unspecified "performance culture" for those that remain.

Trump’s commerce secretary pick, Howard Lutnick, vows not to dismantle NOAA

Even then, the memos -- dated between Jan. 22-31 -- promise impending cuts to federal agencies like the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) which regulates US fisheries beyond the 3-nautical mile line.

"While a few agencies and even branches of the military are likely to see increases in the size of their workforce," a Jan. 28 memo reads, "the majority of federal agencies are likely to be downsized through restructurings, realignments, and reductions in force."

A screenshot of an email that US federal employees received.

A deadline to accept the proffered severance deal is Wednesday (Feb. 5) and it's unclear if any federal employees have accepted to leave in exchange for approximately eight months' salary as severance.

A NOAA Fisheries official said it's too early to tell what the effects the policies and proposed buyouts will have on its workforce.

"The process is still to be determined," agency spokesperson Katherine Silverstein told Undercurrent via email. "NOAA remains dedicated to its mission, providing timely information, research, and resources that serve the American public and ensure our nation's environmental and economic resilience."

'Stick it out as an act of defiance'

But one veteran scientist said there's not much talk around the water coolers of anyone planning to go.

"I think most people are more likely to sort of stick it out as an act of defiance," the Seattle-based scientist said.

They asked not to be identified for fear of reprisals.

A memo promising to update its "standards of conduct" appears to make implicit threats to agency federal employees perceived to be disloyal to the Trump administration's political agenda.

Trudeau says Trump has paused Canada tariff threat

"Employees who engage in unlawful behavior or other misconduct will be prioritized for appropriate investigation and discipline, including termination," the Jan. 28 memo entitled "Fork in the Road" reads, which links to a general webpage for all federal employees.

One federal employee said the agency workers are proud of their record as apolitical technocrats and chafe at suggestions otherwise. 

"I think a lot of people are insulted and offended by all the language in it, and view it as an attempt to bully people out of the service," a veteran employee said.

Public sector union pushing back

The International Federation of Professional and Technical Engineers (IFPTE), which represents many of the federal fisheries scientists, has advised its membership not to agree to anything as the union researches its rights.

In a statement, it called the administration's offer "reckless" and urged its members not to agree to anything.

A screenshot of an email that US federal employees received.

"Most people -- that I've talked to -- think of it as kind of government spam," one federal scientist active within the union told Undercurrent. "They don't really pay attention to it." 

The public sector union has about 85 members, according to labor filings, and represents scientific staff within the Alaska Fisheries Science Center and Northwest Fisheries Science Center both headquartered in the Puget Sound area but with employees throughout the region.

The right to mostly work remotely -- the contract calls for two days on-site per pay period -- is enshrined in collective bargaining agreements and cannot be overridden by presidential directive, one of the memo admits.

"People have gotten used to it -- it makes their lives a lot better," one scientist who said he works mostly in the office anyway. "It helps us both attract and retain high-quality personnel."

The work of the two science centers gathers and analyzes the data that's integral to managing science-based fisheries by the regional fishery management councils. 

These winter months are the season that major stock assessments are getting underway.

"It's like a big push to do all these really important assessments for the fishing industry," the scientist said. "People just want to be able to do their jobs."

title: Indonesia’s eFishery drastically inflated auto-feeder sales, internal audit reveals
content:
Indonesian aquatech startup eFishery drastically overstated the number of auto-feeders it sold and rented to Asian shrimp and tilapia farmers, according to an internal probe.

The probe, conducted by Washington D.C., USA-based independent business consulting firm FTI Consulting, was launched on December 15, 2024, after a whistleblower complaint was received by eFishery's board of directors. The probe is investigating potential fraud and financial mismanagement alleged to have been committed by eFishery senior executives, including its co-founders, Gibran Huzaifah and Chrisna Aditya, who were suspended from their CEO and CFO posts in December and who subsequently resigned.

FTI Consulting's initial report, obtained by Undercurrent News, found eFishery's leaders may have inflated revenue by $600 million in 2024 alone on claimed earnings of $752m versus actual revenue of $157m. It presented investors with a $16m profit for the first nine months of 2024, but the investigation found the firm actually generated a $35.4m loss.

Much of the inflated revenue came from false sales of auto-feeders, considered eFishery's marquee product. A decade ago, while attending the Bandung Institute of Technology, Huzaifah developed an auto-feeder that allowed for more efficient feeding of both fish and shrimp, offering both sales and leases of the technology to local farms.

Farmers could operate the technology from their smartphones, and the feeders were able to analyze fish or shrimp behavior to estimate hunger levels and dispense food, saving farmers money and speeding up their harvest cycles.

At the height of the company's success, eFishery claimed it was serving more than 70,000 fish and shrimp farmers across Indonesia and that it had sold or leased 400,000 auto-feeders. However, according to the FTI report, the actual number of feeders deployed was approximately 24,000.

"Gibran explained that eFishery was incurring losses with a depleting cash position. As the actual cash position was being presented to the Board, Gibran instructed that CAPEX spendings on feeders be inflated as a way to justify the declining cash position of the Company," the report found.

According to the report, eFishery had a total CAPEX on feeders of $2.8 million, with a net book value of feeders classified as fixed assets and inventory of $2.1 million. FTI noted eFishery had installed 12,585 feeders and had 8,015 feeders in inventory as of Nov. 30, comprising of as follows. But it reviewed the serial numbers of the deployed feeders and found only 15,010 unique numbers.

"FTI is in the process of understanding the reason for the overlapping serial numbers in the listing provided," it said in its report. "We understand that the auditors requested for an inventory count of the feeders in the warehouse, but did not request physical sighting of the rented feeders that were installed at the farms."

More broadly, FTI identified a scheme of alleged dual financial reporting, shell companies and false transactions designed to make eFishery more attractive to investors while covering losses. Based partially on its inflated financial results, eFishery secured $200m in a series D funding in July 2023, achieving a $1.4bn valuation in the process.

Sustainable aquaculture investment fund Aqua-Spark owns nearly 20% of eFishery on a $16.9m initial investment, which soared up to a value of $284m prior to the uncovering of the alleged fraud. According to DealStreetAsia, 42X Fund has invested $100 million in eFishery, followed by Japan's SoftBank Group at $25m, Singapore's Temasek Holdings at $23.9m, and Northstar Group has invested $20.3m.

FTI disclosed a member of eFishery's board of directors received a whistleblower complaint on Nov. 19, 2024 alleging significant bad collections – mostly non-recoverable – and longstanding, ongoing fraudulent behavior, with "a concerted effort to double down on the cover up." The whistleblower alleged Huzaifah was "struggling due to the growing mountain of disinformation he has been providing to shareholders and the Board."

Since it began its investigation, FTI has interviewed dozens of eFishery employees, performed significant data collection including contracts, bank statements, internal communications and reports from the company's accounting software. In a summary of its high-level takeaways from its initial review, FTI confirmed eFishery had maintained two sets of books and dual reporting dating back to 2018.

FTI is continuing its investigation, with the objectives of investigating "allegations relating to the manipulation of the financial statements that involved inflating revenue as much as four times, fictitious expenses, capital expenditures … as well as misappropriation of funds."

title: Trump’s tariffs take effect Tuesday, lean on emergency powers to avoid delay
content:
There will be no time for the seafood industry to prepare. Neither will there be a chance to provide public comment in advance. 

The new 25% tariffs on Canadian and Mexican products as well as an additional 10% tariff on China included in three executive orders signed by US president Donald Trump on Saturday (Feb. 1) take effect three days later -- on Tuesday (Feb. 4) at 12:01 a.m. -- threatening the seafood industry with up to $1.5 billion in new annual costs.

Trump has used the authority given him by the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), according to the language contained in the first executive order to be made public by the White House over the weekend. The law, passed in 1977, has never before been used to enact tariffs, according to trade attorney Jessica Rifkin, a principal and head of the customs and trade practice at Olsson Frank Weeda.

Previously, it's been used instead to address acts of terrorism, like after the 9-11 attacks, and impose sanctions, she said. 

IEEPA, unlike the Section 301 authority Trump previously used to place tariffs on China, allows the actions to go into immediate effect with a simple stroke of the president's pen and requires no public vetting, Rifkin explained. 

All Trump needed to do was declare a "national emergency arising from 'an unusual and extraordinary threat' to the national security, foreign policy or economy of the US," she said.

Trump signs seafood industry-punishing order to place 25% tariffs on Canada, Mexico; 10% on China

Trump paints a grim picture in his latest executive order, titled "Imposing duties to address the flow of illicit drugs across our northern border." It describes how Canada "has played a central role" in allowing a flood of illicit drugs, including fentanyl, to enter the US. "There is also a growing presence of Mexican cartels operating fentanyl and nitazene synthesis labs in Canada," it says.

"[T]he amount of fentanyl that crossed the northern border last year could kill 9.5 million Americans," the order asserts. 

The new EO joins Proclamation 10886, "Declaring a National Emergency at the Southern Border," which was issued on Jan. 20, addressing a "national emergency with respect to the grave threat to the United States posed by the influx of illegal aliens and illicit drugs."

Product on the water is safe

The EO will affect all goods that are placed on vessels after Tuesday at 12:01 a.m. EST, it makes clear in section 2 of the document, meaning seafood already on vessels should be safe from the tariffs.

The 25% ad valorem rate of duty "shall apply with respect to goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern time on February 4, 2025, except that goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, after such time that were loaded onto a vessel at the port of loading or in transit on the final mode of transport prior to entry into the United States before 12:01 a.m. Eastern time on February 1, 2025, shall not be subject to such additional duty, only if the importer certifies to CBP as specified in the Federal Register notice," the document states.

The EO leaves open the door for bigger tariffs, should Canada, Mexico or China retaliate.

"Should Canada retaliate against the United States in response to this action through import duties on United States exports to Canada or similar measures, the President may increase or expand in scope the duties imposed under this order to ensure the efficacy of this action," the document says under sect. 2, subsection (d).

The tariffs include an important carve-out for Canadian energy products, charging them only 10%. 

Congress could overrule order

Rifkin had correctly predicted Trump was planning to use IEEPA before the publication of the latest EO confirmed it. The "building blocks" were in place, she said.

"While he didn’t actually go through with it, Trump did threaten to use IEEPA to impose 5% tariffs on Mexico in 2019 and went as far as issuing a statement to that effect in May of 2019; however, Trump abandoned that attempt after Mexico pledged to do more to fight the flow of migrants and drugs across its border," she noted.

"Unlike Section 301, which requires an agency investigation and notice to the public and opportunity for public comment, all of which takes months, neither an agency investigation nor congressional action or approval is required for the president to regulate imports, including imposing tariffs, under IEEPA," Rifkin wrote Undercurrent in an email.  

"Instead, all that’s required is: (1) The president must declare a national emergency under the National Emergencies Act; (2) The president must issue a proclamation or executive order saying he’s imposing tariffs to address the national emergency under IEEPA’s authority (this can either be in the declaration of national emergency itself or in a subsequent executive order or proclamation); and (3) After he takes the tariff action, the president must report what he’s done to Congress.  All of this can be accomplished far more quickly than Section 301 actions (within days)."

Trump alluded to the fentanyl crisis again in his comments on Friday (Jan. 31), before signing the document, while also taking shots at former president Joe Biden's administration, claiming it allowed too many illegal immigrants into the US and Canada and ballooned the US trade deficit.

"As you know we have about a $200bn deficit with Canada -- getting close to $200bn. They've treated us very unfairly," he said. "And I said, 'Why should we be subsidizing Canada?"

When asked whether he was seeking a concession from Canada, he answered: "No, we're not looking for a concession."   

The US Congress has the power, under the National Emergencies Act, to terminate a national emergency by passing a joint resolution of disapproval, however, it has never successfully done so to-date, and it’s questionable whether the votes would be there to do so now, she said.

However, at least one Republican lawmaker -- US senator Susan Collins of Maine -- has made known her opposition to the tariffs in a post on her Facebook page, noting in particular how her home state's residents rely on Canada for 95% of their heating oil.

She said she is working with the Trump administration to "help its officials better understand the potential ramifications of certain tariffs on Maine and to find out more about their implementation, scope, duration, and other important information, including any exemptions they may make for northern border states, certain industries, agricultural producers, and others who rely on trade with Canada."

Expect sparks to fly in Congress on Thursday (Feb. 6) when the US Senate Finance Committee holds its nomination hearing for Jamieson Greer, Trump's choice to head the office of the US Trade Representative.

Rifkin expects the order to be challenged in court. However, former US president Richard Nixon used the Trading with the Enemy Act (IEEPA’s predecessor statute) to impose tariffs in 1971, and his action was upheld by the former US Court of Customs and Patent Appeals, which is now the US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, she noted.

"While we can’t game this out with certainty, it may be hard to find a judge that would be willing to issue a preliminary injunction preventing tariffs from going into effect," she said. "The more likely scenario would be that the tariffs would go forward while the court challenge proceeded."

The seafood industry, meanwhile, is also working to inform the administration about the damage that will be caused.

"Yes, we’ve been in touch with our members and are working to educate the administration about the impact of this effort," Gavin Gibbons, chief strategy officer at the National Fisheries Institute, told Undercurrent on Friday.

"The administration is rightly grappling with some severe national security challenges," he said. "But deploying – and sustaining – tariffs on seafood to address those unrelated problems will create difficulties for the world’s most traded protein and will exacerbate food inflation here in the US, an enduring problem the president was elected to solve. Taxing seafood will not directly impact the issues targeted by this action but will hurt American families, which cannot be the administration’s preferred outcome."

Lobster, snow crab hardest hit

The seafood industry, including US importers and Canadian and Mexican producers, have been dreading the potential of tariffs since Trump first threatened them in November, as reported by Undercurrent. He promised to deliver them on his first day in office on Jan. 20, but then said later an announcement would come Feb. 1.

As also reported earlier by Undercurrent, the seafood items that look to be the hardest hit by the coming tariffs are Canadian lobster, snow crab and Atlantic salmon, as well as Mexican shrimp and Chinese tilapia. 

The US imported 40,522t of lobster worth $1.2bn from Canada in 2023. A 25% tariff would've cost importers $293.2m. The US imported 53,536t of snow crab worth $688.8m from Canada during the same year, which would've been tariffed $172.2m. The 63,869t of Atlantic salmon worth $589.6m that was imported by the US from Canada in 2023 would've come with tariffs totaling $147.4m.

Trump's tariffs take effect Tuesday, lean on emergency powers to avoid delay - Undercurrent News
Trump's tariffs take effect Tuesday, lean on emergency powers to avoid delay - Undercurrent News

The US imported 15,641t of shrimp worth $196.3m from Mexico in 2023, which would've come with $49.1m worth of tariffs.

Lastly, the US imported 113,279t of tilapia from China worth $318.9m in 2023. That tilapia was already tariffed at a rate of 25%, costing importers $77.5m. But with another 10% added, the tariff price tag would've increased by roughly $32.0m.

title: Peru former congressman accused of selling out tuna fishing rules
content:
Former Peruvian congressman Darwin Espinoza is facing serious corruption charges after being accused of receiving a PEN 1 million (around $267,500) bribe to influence the country's tuna fishing regulations, reports Infobae. 

The bribe, reportedly paid by multiple businessmen in the fishing industry -- whose names have yet to be revealed -- was intended to secure changes that would benefit their companies, including the controversial allowance of tuna quotas being transferred to foreign vessels.
 
According to investigations, Espinoza, a former spokesperson for the Accion Popular party, is linked to a network of lawmakers known as "Los Ninos," who allegedly used their political influence to push for key appointments and regulatory changes.

Espinoza reportedly facilitated the appointment of his brother-in-law, Javier Perez, to a high-ranking position at the country's ministry of production (Produce) in exchange for the bribe.

Investigations show that Espinoza communicated with various officials, including his brother-in-law, to orchestrate government appointments and push for the regulatory changes.

In one key exchange, Espinoza celebrated the appointment of Jorge Prado as minister of production in November 2021, just days before his brother-in-law was appointed director of tuna fishing in the ministry.

The bribery scheme was allegedly orchestrated by businesswoman Sada Goray, who connected Espinoza to a key intermediary, Jorge Ricardo Torres Cubas, working for fishing tycoon Fernando Pazos Huaymares.

However, Pazos denied any involvement in the bribery.

The money was reportedly handed over in several installments, including a PEN 200,000 payment in December 2021, linked to further government appointments.

Espinoza's actions reportedly led to changes in the tuna fishing law, which were finalized in June 2022. Following the decree's publication, Espinoza allegedly received an additional $50,000 as a reward for his role in the deal.

title: US fishing vessels collide south of Block Island, Rhode Island
content:
Four US fishermen had to be rescued Thursday (Jan. 23) after a scallop vessel collided with a trawler south of Block Island, Rhode Island, the US Coast Guard reported. 

Coast Guard Sector Long Island Sound reported a distress call around 8:30 pm regarding two vessels colliding 10 miles south of Block Island. The 87-foot scalloper Vanquish, with six crew aboard, reported no damage. But the other vessel, the 55-foot trawler Mattie and Maren II, reported flooding in its engine room.

All four of its crew members donned survival suits in anticipation of abandoning ship.

US Coast Guard suspends search for missing Maine fishermen

The Coast Guard dispatched a helicopter from Coast Guard Air Station Cape Cod. Personnel also arrived about 45 minutes later on a motor lifeboat and boarded the sinking vessel with a P-6 dewatering pump. However, deteriorating weather conditions caused them to abandon the effort.

All four crew members were transferred to the Coast Guard's 47-foot motor lifeboat and taken to the Coast Guard's station in Montauk, New York with no reported injuries. 

"The quick thinking and preparedness of the crew, including donning survival suits and readying emergency equipment, played a crucial role in their safe rescue despite challenging conditions," Coast Guard Lt. Jonathan Roth, a Sector Long Island Sound command duty officer said in a statement.

Sector Long Island Sound has issued a safety marine information broadcast for the Mattie and Maren II as it was still adrift in the Atlantic Ocean as of the last update on Jan. 24.

The cause of the collision is currently under investigation and the undamaged Vanquish returned to its homeport in New Bedford, Massachusetts, the Coast Guard added.

title: US immigration agents raid New Jersey seafood plant, arrest 3
content:
The US seafood industry has tasted its first engagement with president Donald Trump’s crackdown on illegal immigration.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), a division within the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), conducted a raid on Ocean Seafood Depot’s processing and distribution plant, in Newark, New Jersey, on Thursday (Jan. 23), based on multiple media reports. 

A press conference organized by Newark mayor Ras Baraka on Friday (Jan. 24), which included 10 different speakers, filled in many of the details.

ICE agents arrested three Ocean Seafood Depot workers in the raid, which began with officers entering the facility through the company’s retail fish market. Despite not showing a warrant, the ICE agents then proceeded into the nonpublic warehouse and arrested three undocumented immigrants and a US citizen working at the facility, according to multiple accounts.

Four other employees were issued court appearance slips, according to Fox 5 New York.

Founded in 1998, Ocean Seafood Depot provides live, fresh, and frozen seafood to restaurants in New York City and New Jersey. 

"I feel like we have to be a country of law, but we have to go after bad people, not working people," Ocean Seafood Depot co-owner Luis Janota said, according to ABC 7 New York. "These are family people. These are people who show up to work every day."

Trump, who was sworn in a little more than a week ago, on Jan. 20, has promised to reduce the US’ problem with illegal immigration and mass deportations. Similarly, Tom Homan, his appointed border czar, has vowed to undertake raids of workplaces and other gathering places for undocumented immigrants across the country, especially targeting so-called “sanctuary cities” – U.S. cities with local governments that have chosen to limit their cooperation with federal immigration enforcement authorities.

“You’re going to see the numbers steadily increase, the number of arrests nationwide, as we open up the aperture. Right now, it’s concentrating on public safety threats [and] national security threats. That’s a smaller population," he reportedly told ABC News. "So we’re going to do this on a priority [basis], that’s president Trump’s promise. But as that aperture opens, there’ll be more arrests nationwide.”

ICE raids have subsequently taken place in cities including Chicago, Illinois, Boston, Massachusetts, and New York City, resulting in more than 500 arrests, according to the agency.

However, an ICE officer reportedly told FOX 5 NY the Ocean Seafood Depot action was a routine operation and not part of Trump's mass deportation plan. The raid was conducted in response to ICE receiving a tip that undocumented immigrants were working at the company’s facility.

"ICE may encounter U.S. citizens while conducting fieldwork and may request identification to establish an individual’s identity, as was the case during a targeted enforcement operation at a worksite today in Newark, New Jersey. This is an active investigation and, per ICE policy, we cannot discuss ongoing investigations,” the official said.

In a joint statement, US senators Cory Booker and Andy Kim, both New Jersey Democrats, said they had forwarded questions about the Ocean Seafood raid to DHS.

“Actions like this one sow fear in all of our communities – and our broken immigration system requires solutions, not fear tactics,” they said in a post on X.

X post made by US senators Corey Booker and Andy Kim on Jan. 23, 2023.

title: FDA targets two foreign seafood processors, one US importer for HACCP violations
content:
The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has hit three seafood companies with warning letters, including two foreign seafood processors and one seafood importer based out of Buffalo, New York.

While the FDA published the three warning letters on Tuesday (Jan. 21), the letters were actually issued to the companies late last year for seafood Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) violations. Per the FDA, HACCP plans are required to provide a systematic approach to identifying, evaluating and controlling food safety hazards.

One warning letter, sent to Vietnam's Duong Ha Processing Trading Seafood Company on Nov. 26, 2024, says the FDA found serious violations of the company's HACCP plan during an inspection of the processing facility in July. Per the document, the company's frozen, raw, vacuum-packaged, scombrotoxin-forming fish are adulterated "in that they have been prepared, packed, or held under conditions whereby they may have been rendered injurious to health."

COFISA - Conservas de Peixe da Figueira, based in Portugal, also had its processing facility inspected by the FDA in July. In a letter dated Dec. 18, 2024, the FDA declared that the company's canned tuna and canned sardines are adulterated due to being prepared or packed in unsanitary conditions.

Lastly, Nyumbani Hakuna Matata, a seafood importer based in Buffalo, received a letter about non-compliance with HACCP regulations in September 2023, according to the FDA. At the time, the agency said it found dried Nile perch, dried Lake Tanganyika dagaa (sprat) and dried Migebuka (perch) were prepared, packed or held in unsanitary conditions. In a follow-up inspection on Nov. 13, 2024, the FDA inspectors documented that the company did not make the appropriate changes to address the violations.

Each company has been given 15 days to address the violations. Warning letters that go unaddressed can result in fines, product recalls and potential legal action.

title: Investigation underway after fatality at Mowi’s Atlantic Canada operations
content:
The death of an employee at a Canadian salmon hatchery owned by Norwegian salmon producer Mowi has been confirmed by the company.

"We are utterly devastated by the death of a friend and colleague. Employees are being offered grief support as we assist authorities with their investigation. Our thoughts at this time are with family and friends," Mowi said in a brief statement shared with Undercurrent News on Thursday (Jan. 23).

An internal email sent to employees earlier by managing director Gideon Pringle and obtained by Undercurrent identified the team member as Paul Drake, who worked at the hatchery in Stephenville, Newfoundland and Labrador (NL).

"The events surrounding Paul's passing are being investigated by the relevant authorities, so at this time, I cannot provide you with any further details," Pringle wrote in the email. He added that Mowi is supporting Drake's family and colleagues in coping with the loss and is fully cooperating with the investigation.

While details of the incident remain unconfirmed, a source told Undercurrent that the fatality was said to have involved oxygen distribution being left on while welding, though the source acknowledged this remains hearsay. The source added that workplace fatalities and injuries are typically reported, and Mowi is expected to issue a formal release once the cause is determined.

Pringle described the news as "very disturbing" for employees and encouraged those affected to seek support.

The Stephenville facility, also known as the Indian Head Hatchery, has been a key part of Mowi's operations in NL since 2011. The approval of six new salmon aquaculture sites for Mowi in NL has led at least one group to urge the Canadian provincial government to include the licenses in the ongoing environmental review of the hatchery's expansion, Undercurrent earlier reported.

WorkplaceNL, the provincial workplace safety agency, has not yet responded to Undercurrent's inquiries about the incident.

Further updates will be provided as more information becomes available.

title: Icelandic police again drop Arctic Fish salmon escape investigation
content:
The Westfjords police commissioner in Iceland has, for the second time, dropped an investigation into the August 2023 escape of farmed salmon from Arctic Fish's sea pens in Patreksfjordur, Mbl reported.

Authorities concluded the case was unlikely to lead to a conviction, citing insufficient evidence under Article 145 of the Criminal Procedure Act.

The incident involved approximately 3,500 salmon escaping through two holes in a sea pen housing over 72,500 fish. Despite extensive recovery efforts, including deploying divers from Norway, escaped farmed salmon were found in rivers nationwide.

Arctic Fish CEO Stein Ove Tveiten had been under investigation for potential negligence in ensuring adequate equipment at the fish farm. The Icelandic Food and Veterinary Authority, known as MAST, also pushed for an official inquiry into possible violations of the aquaculture act.

In December, police ended the investigation, despite the state prosecutor previously ordering its continuation in April 2024 following complaints from MAST and others. This marks the second time the case has been closed without charges.

Arctic Fish is an Icelandic salmon farming company that is majority-owned by Norwegian salmon farmer Mowi.

title: Probe finds eFishery may have inflated revenue by $600m in 2024 alone
content:
The initial probe into alleged financial impropriety at Indonesian aquatech startup eFishery has found the firm may have inflated its revenue and profit over several years, reports Bloomberg.

Interim eFishery CEO exits amid reports co-founder was cooking books from 2018

A preliminary, ongoing probe into the business -- which is backed by investors including SoftBank Group and Temasek Holdings, among others -- estimates that management inflated revenue by almost $600 million in the nine months through September last year. That would mean more than 75% of the reported figures were fake, the report said.

Investors were initially enticed by its profitability at a time when layoffs, CEO resignations and plummeting valuations in the Indonesian tech sector dominated headlines, Bloomberg noted. It presented a $16m profit for the first nine months of 2024 to investors, but the investigation commissioned by the board alleges the firm actually generated a $35.4m loss.

Revenue for the period was estimated at $157m, rather than the $752m investors were told, according to the report. Management also inflated revenue and profit numbers for several previous years, the report said.

Undercurrent News previously reported the resignation of veteran aquaculture executive Cameron Maclean from eFishery, which he tendered last November. 

Maclean resigned before its co-founders, Gibran Huzaifah and Chrisna Aditya, were suspended from their CEO/CFO and chief product officer posts, in December. Huzaifah and Aditya were abruptly removed amid an investigation into alleged financial fraud at the company.

title: Ecuador’s Luna forecasts minimal growth for shrimp exports, sees ‘technical tie’ ahead
content:
The latest data on shrimp exports reveals a flat outlook for the industry between 2023 and 2024, with growth expected to be minimal -- at best, a modest 1%, according to Gabriel Luna, Ecuadorian shrimp farmer and owner of GLuna Shrimp.

According to the most recent figures, the shrimp sector is poised to experience what Luna called a "technical tie" in terms of overall export volume.

"We can confidently say that the year-to-year performance will be essentially flat. There is little to no real growth to speak of, which is a bit of a technical tie when you consider the large volumes involved," he said on one of the latest The Shrimp Cast episodes. 

"Between 2023 and 2024, we're either going to hit a 0% growth or a 1% growth, which is really low when we're talking about millions of pounds of shrimp processed and shipped abroad. This is a technical tie," he added.

The shrimp industry has faced several challenges in recent months, with fluctuations in monthly export volumes between August and October. Exports dropped from 230 million pounds -- or around 104,300 metric tons -- in August to 190m (86,200t) pounds by October.

However, November surprised many with a sharp increase to 260m pounds (around 118,000t), a result attributed to delays in shipments that carried over from October. These shipments helped compensate for the lower export numbers in previous months, but Luna cautioned that this peak is unlikely to represent a sustained growth trend.

"We had a peak in November, yes, but it wasn't because the industry suddenly took off. It was because shipments were delayed from October," explained Luna. "It's important to remember that these peaks are temporary, and we need to look at the bigger picture. If we average out the numbers, we'll see the overall export volume stays consistent with last year."

This way, the 2024 outlook is closely mirroring 2023. "When we look at the monthly average for both years, we see that the export volume for 2024 is averaging about 224m pounds per month, compared to 223m pounds per month in 2023. That's practically no change. We're in a holding pattern right now."

Despite the flat growth, Luna noted that the shrimp export market remains a significant contributor to the economy, even if it's not experiencing the kind of robust expansion seen in other sectors.

"This is not a bad year. It's just not a year of big leaps forward. We're talking about huge volumes of shrimp, so even flat growth means we're still moving a lot of product," he said. "But the reality is, unless there's some kind of major disruption or breakthrough, we're not expecting anything dramatic."

For now, the outlook for the shrimp export market remains stable but unremarkable. While growth potential remains, it's clear that the industry will be navigating a year of technical stability rather than a major expansion.

Ecuadorian shrimp struggled in 2024 amid sanitary disputes, tariffs, global competition

"As much as we'd like to see a big jump in exports, the numbers we're seeing suggest that 2024 will finish pretty much where 2023 did," Luna concluded. "In this industry, steady is often the best you can hope for."

As Undercurrent News previously reported, the Ecuadorian shrimp sector struggled through a turbulent 2024. 

The shrimp sector's prospects somehow worsened in the final quarter of the year, with a combination of regulatory setbacks and market contraction signaling a bleak close to the year.

Despite being one of the world's leading shrimp exporters, Ecuador has struggled to maintain the strong growth it has seen in recent years. Weak demand in major markets, coupled with fluctuating global prices, has put pressure on the industry. 

One of the major setbacks came early in the year when China, Ecuador's largest shrimp market, temporarily blocked imports from nine Ecuadorian companies due to alleged violations of sanitary standards.

The shrimp industry also faced significant challenges in the US, Ecuador's second-largest export market. Following a 2023 investigation into potential "dumping" practices, the US imposed additional tariffs on Ecuadorian shrimp, citing that it was being sold at unfairly low prices and allegedly subsidized by the Ecuadorian government.

In December 2024, Ecuadorian shrimp faced yet another blow when Brazil, a smaller but important market, suspended imports of farmed shrimp from Ecuador.

The Brazilian authorities cited "preliminary findings" of sanitary irregularities, though the suspension was not based on definitive conclusions.

Following all this, the outlook for 2025 also remains uncertain.

Felipe Ribadeneira, executive president of the Ecuadorian Federation of Exporters (Fedexpor), expressed cautious optimism. He pointed to the growing demand in the US and the EU, as well as Ecuador's resilience in adapting to changing market conditions in an interview with Forbes.

However, he stressed the importance of staying vigilant in managing internal challenges, such as the impact of climate change, power outages, and the potential fallout from the shifting political landscape in key export markets.

Staying in the US, and abundance-based restrictions on halibut bycatch for the non-pollock trawl fleet are the law of the land. title: Chilean court imposes travel ban on former Australis execs, sets 180-day investigation
content:
Fraud allegations against Former Australis Seafoods owner Isidoro Quiroga, along with ex-executives Martin Guilof and Santiago Garreton, have been formalized on Jan. 15, in the case surrounding the company's 2019 sale to China's Joyvio Group for $921 million.

Chile's public prosecutor's office accused the defendants of fraud and mismanagement in connection with the transaction. The prosecutor also alleged that the executives orchestrated a plan of "sustained overproduction" at Australis's facilities, exceeding legal limits and violating environmental regulations.

This information, the prosecutor claimed, was concealed from the Chinese buyer to artificially inflate the company's price, resulting in an estimated financial loss of around $620m to Joyvio.

Prosecutor Constanza Encina argued that the defendants intentionally misrepresented the company's production capacity and profitability, disregarding environmental consequences in their pursuit of a higher sale price.

"This was done with full knowledge of the potential harm to both Joyvio and the company," Encina said.

Chilean prosecutor formalizes allegations against former Australis owner, execs

In defense, Quiroga's lawyer, Alex van Weezel, is hitting back, rejecting the allegations of fraud, stating that the production data was fully disclosed to Joyvio's representatives long before the sale.

"The information was available a year prior to the purchase agreement and consistently shared until the deal was signed," van Weezel said. He also contested the mismanagement claims, suggesting that the environmental standards at the time were different from those currently in place.

The court established a 180-day period for further investigation and imposed national travel restrictions on Quiroga and Garreton, requiring them to check in quarterly with authorities. Any request to leave the country will require a $10m bond.

For his part, Guilof, who resides in Spain, must report to the Chilean consulate.

The charges focus on overproduction from 2018 to 2022, which allegedly exceeded legal limits by more than 98,000 metric tons. The financial impact, including potential regulatory fines and compliance costs, is estimated at over $140m.

Quiroga's defense team has criticized the investigation for technical flaws, pointing to expert reports that dismiss the financial damages claimed by the prosecution, Undercurrent News has learned.

"The formalization is based on supposed facts that the prosecutor herself knows are false," van Weezel said in a statement. He took particular issue with the prosecution's fraud claims, asserting that the production data was fully disclosed to Joyvio's representatives.

"The prosecutor claimed that fraud occurred because the production situation was hidden from Joyvio. However, the prosecutor herself confirmed that Joyvio's negotiator, representative, and technical advisor had detailed knowledge of all production data. You cannot hide information from someone who already knows it," he explained.

Van Weezel also contested the charge of mismanagement, arguing that the production plan in question was provided to Joyvio before the sale, evaluated, and ultimately approved by the Chinese conglomerate.

UK court orders China’s Joyvio to pay over $1.5m to former Australis owner

"The alleged crime of mismanagement is based on a production plan that was given to Joyvio before the sale, and was processed, evaluated, approved, and implemented by the Chinese group," Van Weezel said.

He further emphasized that the due diligence process was focused on validating the feasibility of the plan, a process that included a detailed review of production capacities and legal conditions. "This feasibility was confirmed by Joyvio and all its expert advisors after reviewing all the production and legal information."

Furthermore, Van Weezel dismissed the prosecutor's claims of financial harm, pointing out that several expert reports had completely undermined the damages presented by the prosecution.

"The alleged damages cited by the prosecutor, based solely on reports from FK Economics submitted by the plaintiffs, were completely dismissed by expert reports from Oscar Landerretche, Andres Gemez-Lobo, Ronaldo Bruna, Fernando Coloma, Jorge Quiroz, and Patricio Arrau," he stated.

"In fact, as shown in the case file, the report by Landerretche, Gomez-Lobo, and Bruna concluded that the report the prosecutor relied on to formalize the investigation 'contains very basic technical and conceptual errors, which invalidate it as a technical document for informing the lawsuit," he concluded.

content:
The interim CEO of Indonesian aquatech unicorn eFishery has reportedly stepped down as allegations surface his predecessor and the company's founder, Gibran Huzaifah, was cooking the company's books for as long as six years. 

Interim CEO Adhy Wibisono, appointed to replace Huzaifah last December while fraud and financial misdealing allegations were investigated, has reportedly left the company in the same week as a sensational report from DealStreetAsia published on Thursday (Jan. 16). 

After aiming for 10,000t in US shrimp sales for 2024, eFishery exported one container

Although nothing has been communicated internally, several well-placed sources told Undercurrent they understand Wibisono has left. 

Preliminary findings from the investigation into alleged financial fraud at eFishery, according to DealStreetAsia, suggest that the company may have been inflating its revenue and profits from its first Series A round in 2018. 

Wibisono, who is listed online as group CFO of NWP Property, a Jakarta, Indonesia-based real estate company, was brought in with Albertus Sasmitra, an executive with eFishery investor Northstar Group, as an interim CFO. 

In a separate article, DealStreetAsia published a damning comment from Patrick Walujo, co-founder and managing partner of Northstar, on eFishery. 

Aquaculture veteran Maclean resigns from eFishery prior to financial fraud probe  

"I think the damage that they have done to Indonesia, to the startup community, and to our credibility is massive. So we'll get to the bottom of it, and I think we'll take this very seriously," said Walujo, who is an early investor in eFishery through Northstar. 

Undercurrent was unable to reach Wibisono for comment. Earlier on Friday (Jan. 17), Undercurrent also reported the resignation of veteran aquaculture executive Cameron Maclean from eFishery, which he tendered last November, a month before news broke of the suspension of Huzaifah and Aditya.

The current audit, conducted by an undisclosed global firm and involved in interviewing "dozens" of eFishery employees, has reportedly identified a scheme of alleged dual financial reporting, shell companies and false transactions designed to make eFishery more attractive to investors, according to DealStreetAsia.

Ex-CEO Huzaifah allegedly first created a false set of accounting books in order to inflate revenue by 20-25% to meet the $4 million target set in its first Series A funding round.

The firm was originally backed by Dutch investor Aqua-Spark and Indonesian venture capital Ideosource, who had joined from the seed round in 2015.

At the time of writing, Aqua-Spark remains eFishery's largest single shareholder, with a 19.83% stake valued at $284m from a $16.9m investment, according to DealStreetAsia. The investor did not respond to a request for comment from Undercurrent in time for publication.

As previously reported by Undercurrent, eFishery secured $200m in its Series D funding back in 2023, with $100m coming from United Arab Emirates-based 42XFund, the China-focused investor backed by AI and cloud computing technology firm G42. At the time, eFishery was valued at $1.33 billion.

According to DealStreetAsia, 42X Fund has invested the most of any investor in eFishery, followed by Japan's SoftBank Group ($25m), and Singapore's Temasek Holdings ($23.9m) and Northstar Group ($20.3m), the next largest investors in absolute terms.

title: Aquaculture veteran Maclean resigns from eFishery prior to financial fraud probe
content:
A well-known aquaculture sector executive has resigned from the Indonesian aquaculture tech firm eFishery, which is in the middle of a financial fraud investigation.

Cameron Maclean, brought in from Regal Springs Group, resigned in November last year, "almost a month before the current issues at eFishery broke," he told Undercurrent News.

After aiming for 10,000t in US shrimp sales for 2024, eFishery exported one container

Maclean resigned before its co-founders, Gibran Huzaifah and Chrisna Aditya, were suspended from their CEO/CFO and chief product officer posts, in December 2024. Huzaifah and Aditya were abruptly removed amid an investigation into alleged financial fraud at the company.

In 2023, eFishery raised $200 million in a series D at a valuation of $1.3 billion, making it aquatech's first unicorn.

"I am currently working through my 90-day notice period as stipulated in my contract," said Maclean.

Maclean declined to comment further to Undercurrent. Executives with eFishery did not respond to requests for comment. 

Huzaifah and Aditya founded the company at university, around the concept of supplying auto-feeders and other services to Indonesian tilapia farmers, then collecting data to help improve performance.

The company also planned to export tilapia to the US. The status of this project is not yet clear, but sources previously told Undercurrent containers were on the water.

On Jan. 10, Undercurrent revealed that eFishery had exported one container of shrimp to the US, having said it aimed for 10,000 metric tons in 2024.

title: Italian prosecutors uncover €4m fish farm fund fraud
content:
EU prosecutors have charged nine individuals and five companies with fraud over attempts to obtain €4 million ($4.1m) in EU aquaculture funding.

The European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) in Rome alleges the accused submitted falsified documentation and fake insurance policies to secure funding for fish tanks and a fishing vessel through the European Maritime and Fisheries Fund.

Four cooperative societies received €1.4m in advance payments after claiming construction had begun on new fish tanks, investigators said. Subsequent inspections revealed no work had been undertaken, according to the EPPO.

Prosecutors blocked an additional €2.6m payment request during their investigation, which was supported by Italy's Guardia di Finanza and local port authorities.

Four of the five companies involved faced anti-mafia preventive measures, with one being barred during the initial application process and three others following the launch of the investigation, the EPPO said.

The suspects face charges of aggravated fraud for obtaining public funds, embezzlement, and money laundering.

title: Ecuadorian police seize 1.2t of cocaine in tuna shipment bound for Spain
content:
Ecuadorian police seized more than 1.2 metric tons of cocaine hidden in a shipment of canned tuna bound for Spain at Guayaquil's Estero port terminal on Dec. 23, reports Diario de Pontevedra.

Police discovered 23 jute bundles containing 1,257 cocaine packages concealed among legitimate tuna cargo destined for the port of Vigo. The operation was part of ongoing surveillance of the Ecuador-Galicia drug trafficking corridor.

The seizure, valued at approximately €30 million ($33m) in Spanish street markets, comes after authorities intercepted a record 7.5t cocaine shipment along the same route in 2022.

Law enforcement officials said the drugs were linked to at least two criminal organizations, highlighting Ecuador's role as a major transit point for international drug trafficking. An investigation is underway to identify the perpetrators.

title: Ecuadorian shrimp struggled in 2024 amid sanitary disputes, tariffs, global competition
content:
Ecuador's shrimp industry struggled through a turbulent 2024. Despite its strong market position, it is poised to end with little to no year-on-year growth, Undercurrent News has learned.

According to the latest trade data available, Ecuador exported some 999,239t of shrimp worth $4.9 billion between January and October, continuing to hold its position as the country's leading non-oil export. However, it was down by 7% in volume and 1% in value y-o-y.

The shrimp sector's prospects somehow worsened in the final quarter of the year, with a combination of regulatory setbacks and market contraction signaling a bleak close to 2024.

As Undercurrent previously reported, Ecuador's average monthly export volume in 2024 is 220m lbs, slightly lower than the 223m lbs average from 2023.

"If we can hold steady in exports during the final two months, we might end up with a technical tie to 2023, which would be a significant achievement given the current market conditions," said Gabriel Luna, Ecuadorian shrimp farmer and owner of GLuna Shrimp. 

However, other industry sources are forecasting "a disappointing close to the year," with final numbers for 2024 expected to be in the red.

Despite being one of the world's leading shrimp exporters, Ecuador has struggled to maintain the strong growth it has seen in recent years. Weak demand in major markets, coupled with fluctuating global prices, has put pressure on the industry. 

One of the major setbacks came early in the year when China, Ecuador's largest shrimp market, temporarily blocked imports from nine Ecuadorian companies due to alleged violations of sanitary standards.

The Chinese authorities detected levels of sodium metabisulfite above the allowed threshold in shrimp shipments between February and March. Although the suspension was lifted in June, the effects have been lasting.

By October, Ecuador's shrimp exports to China had not only failed to fully recover but had also dropped by 19% in volume and 10% in value to 535,781t worth $2.4bn. The economic slowdown in China, coupled with reduced domestic demand and stiff competition from other Asian producers, led to a dramatic contraction of the market for Ecuadorian shrimp.

Jose Antonio Camposano, president of Ecuador's National Chamber of Aquaculture, also known as the CNA, noted that while there was a slight recovery in the second half of 2024, "it was largely driven by demand for the upcoming Chinese New Year."

However, this short-term boost has done little to offset the significant losses Ecuador has experienced in this key market. 

The shrimp industry also faced significant challenges in the US, Ecuador's second-largest export market. Following a 2023 investigation into potential "dumping" practices, the US imposed additional tariffs on Ecuadorian shrimp, citing that it was being sold at unfairly low prices and allegedly subsidized by the Ecuadorian government.

Although the US International Trade Commission's preliminary findings in April 2024 led to reduced tariff rates for some Ecuadorian companies, the final decision in October reaffirmed the tariffs on subsidies, keeping the burden on Ecuadorian exporters.

According to CNA's figures, Ecuador's shrimp exports to the US saw a 25% drop in volume and a 19% decrease in revenue to 178,583t worth $1.08bn between January and October 2024. Despite this, the US still accounts for almost a fifth of Ecuador's shrimp exports.

Ecuador trade group seeks retaliation against Brazil over shrimp import ban

In December 2024, Ecuadorian shrimp faced yet another blow when Brazil, a smaller but important market, suspended imports of farmed shrimp from Ecuador.

The Brazilian authorities cited "preliminary findings" of sanitary irregularities, though the suspension was not based on definitive conclusions.

This move came despite ongoing dialogue between Ecuador's ministry of production and Brazilian authorities, and a visit from Brazilian technical experts in November that had praised Ecuador's sanitary protocols.

The CNA asserted that the decision, which went into effect on Dec. 9, is "unjustified" and "politically motivated," citing "nonexistent health risks" as the rationale provided by Brazilian authorities. Camposano condemned Brazil's decision, labeling it as "politically driven" and "orchestrated" to favor Brazilian shrimp producers.

He emphasized that Ecuador complied with Brazil's demands to export only cooked, peeled, and deveined shrimp, which international standards deem safe. Camposano noted that Brazilian inspectors found no discrepancies in Ecuador's shrimp production processes during their visit. In an interview with Forbes, Camposano added that Brazil has "always sought to block shipments" and that "Brazil is the most protectionist country on the continent."

According to Ecuadorian sources, Brazil imported $7.2m worth of Ecuadorian shrimp in 2024, a 21.8% increase from the previous year, Undercurrent also reported. The ban jeopardizes Ecuador's share of Brazil's growing shrimp market, where imports have emerged alongside domestic production. 

A shrinking global market

Beyond these specific trade issues, the global shrimp market has been facing broader challenges.

The demand for Ecuadorian shrimp in China, historically the largest importer, has been severely hampered by the country's economic slowdown and its internal shift towards alternative suppliers like Vietnam.

Meanwhile, the growth of other shrimp-producing countries, such as India and Honduras, has further intensified competition. In light of these difficulties, Camposano projected that Ecuador's shrimp production and export volumes would contract by 4% by the end of 2024, with a corresponding decline in export revenues of around 8%.

Ecuador shrimp sector hopes for recovery with price gains, strong year-end forecast

Following all this, the outlook for 2025 remains uncertain.

While the sector continues to face significant obstacles, including the volatile geopolitical landscape and trade tensions, particularly between the US and China, there are some signs of potential recovery.

The EU, which has been a consistent market for Ecuadorian products, including shrimp, has shown growth. The EU's demand for Ecuadorian shrimp increased significantly in 2024, accounting for 20% of total shrimp exports as of October.

Felipe Ribadeneira, executive president of the Ecuadorian Federation of Exporters (Fedexpor), expressed cautious optimism. He pointed to the growing demand in the US and the EU, as well as Ecuador's resilience in adapting to changing market conditions in an interview with Forbes.

However, he stressed the importance of staying vigilant in managing internal challenges, such as the impact of climate change, power outages, and the potential fallout from the shifting political landscape in key export markets.

The future of Ecuadorian shrimp exports will depend not only on overcoming the current trade barriers but also on the ability to diversify markets and respond to shifting global demand patterns.

Now, all eyes are on the coming months, with hopes for a rebound that hinges on strategic adjustments and a favorable global market recovery.

title: Oyster norovirus-related recall continues to expand in US, Canada
content:
The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has expanded on an earlier recall announcement after the Washington State Department of Health (WSDH) and the Interstate Shellfish Sanitation Conference (ISSC) confirmed a norovirus outbreak in oysters and manila clams earlier this month, as reported by Undercurrent News.

The latest advisory from the FDA was posted on Friday (Dec. 27) and is directed towards restaurants and food retailers in the US state of California that may have purchased Taylor Shellfish Canada brands. The full list of products can be found here, but brands include Fanny Bay, Sunseeker and Cloudy Bay oysters that were harvested from the Canadian province of British Columbia (BC).

A recall for certain Taylor Shellfish Canada oysters was also issued by the Canadian government. That notice simply states that the products may have possible norovirus contamination, which can cause serious gastrointestinal illness. 

That was not the only recall to be issued last week. ISSC issued a notice on Friday that the WSDH was in the process of conducting a recall of shellstock related to a norovirus outbreak.

Per the notice, the shellstock oysters were harvested by Ruco's Shellfish of Shelton, Washington, between Dec. 2 and Dec. 17. The oysters being recalled were from a portion of the state's Hammersley Inlet growing area. They were distributed within Washington state and Oregon, according to WSDH.

The start of an outbreak

As further details come to light, it appears as if a food-related gathering hosted by the Los Angeles Times on Dec. 3 was the first to be hit by the norovirus outbreak. More than 80 people fell ill after eating raw oysters at the 101 Best Restaurants event, prompting the Los Angeles Department of Health to launch an investigation.

Hillary Manning, spokesperson for the Los Angeles Times, said the oysters were supplied by Fanny Bay Oysters and sourced by Santa Monica Seafood, which was also a sponsor of the event. The oysters were provided to one of the restaurants featured in the 101 Best Restaurants list, as previously reported by Undercurrent. 

Those oysters have since been recalled.

title: Norcod escape saw up to 23,000 cod flee net breach
content:
On Nov. 28, Norwegian cod farming firm Norcod reported a significant fish escape from its Labukta fish farm in Nesna, Nordland.

The discovery followed a notification from the country's directorate of fisheries, which had received a report from a local fisherman who found cod in the wild that may have originated from Norcod's facility.

Norcod promptly notified the directorate, activating its emergency response procedures in coordination with the authorities. Since the breach was discovered, recapture efforts have been underway. As of today, approximately 4,530 fish have been recaptured by emergency fishermen, though Norcod estimates that the total number of escaped fish could be as high as 22,979.

Upon receiving the alert, divers already en route for a routine inspection of the farm's nets found an opening in one of the farm's cages. The breach was located 13 meters underwater between two panels of a newly installed net. The seam of the net was immediately sealed to prevent further escape.

The farmed cod, which are more localized than other species such as salmon, may be more easily recaptured, and Norcod remains hopeful that a significant portion of the escaped fish can be recovered. The current recapture rate stands at 16.5%, with fishing operations continuing.

"We are doing everything possible to retrieve the fish," said Chris Guldberg, chief operating officer and spokesperson for Norcod. "While the recapture rate is promising, we are not stopping until we have recovered as many fish as possible."

To confirm the origin of the escaped fish, samples of the recaptured cod will be analyzed. In addition, a thorough net inspection will occur in January 2025, with representatives from the directorate and net supplier ScaleAQ. The aim is to determine the exact cause of the breach.

"This is a serious incident," Guldberg added. "Until we have conducted a full investigation into the net in January, we are refraining from speculating on the cause. Norcod has a zero-tolerance policy regarding escapes, and we are committed to learning from this incident to prevent future occurrences."
