title: Anti-aquaculture campaign files complaint over Scottish industry lobbying
content:
An anti-aquaculture campaign group has lodged a formal complaint with Scotland's Ethical Standards Commissioner, urging an investigation into claimed potential breaches of lobbying regulations by industry body Salmon Scotland.

The complaint has been lodged by Green Britain Foundation (GBF), founded by millionaire Dale Vince, who has also vowed to invest "substantial resources" into launching more covert investigations to expose environmental breaches in the salmon farming industry.

GBF said the complaint outlines nine incidents between October 2022 and November 2023 where Salmon Scotland allegedly failed to properly record lobbying activities in the official register. 

These incidents include unregistered meetings with members of Scottish parliament (MSPs), government officials, and regulatory bodies, as well as a reported confrontation between Salmon Scotland CEO Tavish Scott and an MSP.

"The public has a right to know which vested interests are whispering in our politicians' ears," said Vince in a press release issued by his energy company, Ecotricity.

"If Salmon Scotland's been playing fast and loose with lobbying laws, what else are they hiding? This reeks of an industry that thinks it's above the rules -- whether that's environmental regulations or democratic transparency. It's time to drag their murky dealings into the light."

Yahoo News noted that as a former MSP himself,  Scott is entitled to hold a parliamentary access pass, and that there is no evidence Scott has broken rules using the pass. He has denied the allegations.

He said: "Dale Vince has a vegan food business and campaigns to ban all types of animal farming so that he can make even more money, making him a hypocrite of the worst kind. We will not be intimated by rich millionaires who choose to waste public resources on vexatious complaints and want 12,000 people who depend on fish farming to lose their jobs."

A Salmon Scotland spokesperson added: "None of these meetings involved registered lobbying and several meetings did not even involve any individual where lobbying register rules would apply. Salmon Scotland complies with the lobbying register, and there are at present 166 returns publicly available."

title: Christmas Eve blaze damages lobster boat in US port
content:
A lobster boat docked at Merrill's Wharf in the US fishing hub of New Bedford, Massachusetts, caught fire early Tuesday (Dec. 24), Christmas Eve.

The New Bedford Fire Department responded to a report of a fishing vessel fire at Merrill's Wharf Tuesday at 8:38 am, according to a Facebook post from the fire department. Crew that arrived first said smoke could be seen coming from inside the pilot house of a 30-foot-long lobster boat.

Engine 1 deployed a 1 3/4 hose line to extinguish the fire. A marine vessel also aided the fire department in containing the oil spill in the area of the vessel. 

The New Bedford Fire Department said that its Fire Investigation Unit is investigating the cause of the fire.

New Bedford, Massachusetts, is the US port with the highest value of seafood landed, according to the latest Fisheries of the United States report from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Per the report, in 2023 New Bedford landed 76.9 million pounds (34881 metric tons) of seafood -- the primary being scallops and lobster -- valued at $363.3m.

title: Mowi reports salmon escape at northern Norway site, full scale unclear
content:
Mowi has reported a fish escape incident at its Kviteberg site in Troms county, which occurred over the weekend of Dec. 21-22.

The escape was discovered during a routine delousing operation, Mowi said.

The company has set up recovery nets around the site and, as of Dec. 23, has managed to recapture 13 fish with an average weight of just under 2 kg. The full extent of the escape is still unclear, and further efforts are ongoing to recover any remaining escaped fish.

Norway's directorate of fisheries has confirmed that it will follow up the incident with an inspection in accordance with standard procedures. The inspection will focus on assessing the company's response and ensuring that all necessary measures are in place to mitigate any potential environmental impact.

As investigations continue, the cause of the escape and the scope of the incident are expected to be clarified in more detail.

title: EU police forces break contaminated shellfish smuggling ring
content:
Law enforcement authorities from France, Portugal and Spain have arrested 62 people in a sting operation looking to prevent the illegal fishing and trade of contaminated mollusks in Iberian waters, according to the EU law enforcement agency Europol.

European glass eel smuggling crackdown sends prices in China soaring

The organization seized 30 metric tons of mollusks and 6t of glass eels, which it valued at €10 million altogether.

The catch was primarily Japanese clams, which are a big draw for locals and tourists during the Christmas period. The gangs under scrutiny falsified the documentation to present the clams as suitable for human consumption, Europol said, despite contaminated mollusks posing a threat of serious diseases such as hepatitis.

One kilo of these clams can sell for up to €25, Europol noted. The gangs exploited fishers of Asian origins by paying them just €1/kg for their illegal catches made in Portuguese waters, which were then sent over the border to Spain.

The vast gap in prices paid and received means that Europol was able to link environmental crime and human trafficking to labor exploitation for the first time in EU legal history.

The same investigation also uncovered a criminal network involved in the illegal poaching, gathering and smuggling of glass eels across France, Portugal and Spain, according to Europol.

Six of the gang members arrested by the authority were also considered 'high value targets', it said.

title: Editor’s choice: Maersk to cancel Alaska service; Canadian snow crab processors, union agree final prices
content:
Deputy EMEA editor Dan Gibson brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week.  

Last week's top story was the bombshell news that Danish shipping and logistics giant Maersk intends to halt its trans-Pacific freight service from Alaska's largest seafood ports by volume in February 2025, slap-bang in the middle of the pollock 'A' season.

Public officials and fish processing executives in the affected ports of Dutch Harbor and Kodiak said the move "came out of the blue," and leaves companies such as Nissui's UniSea, Maruha Nichiro's Westward Seafoods and Trident Seafoods' Akutan plant scrambling to find new carriers.

On the Atlantic shores of North America, snow crab harvesters in the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador finally reached a settlement with regional processors to set prices for 2024 at CAD 3.75 ($2.60)/lb, which should mean a bonus for some harvesters right before Christmas.

In another piece of shellfish news from Canada's Eastern seaboard, the country's Department of Fisheries and Oceans slashed next year's scallop quota by 39%. On the back of similarly severe cuts to quotas in the US and Japan, it means 2025's global scallop supply is going to be exceptionally thin on the ground.

Next, the Venezuelan government takeover of Lamar Group is sending ripples through the European shrimp sector, with importers and processors from France and the Netherlands particularly impacted, as Venezuelan product accounts for a large percentage of their total supply. Lamar's owners, the Rincon family -- who were accused of plotting a coup by the Maduro regime -- have meanwhile fled to Spain, while a government official has been placed in charge of the company.

There were also a couple of major US M&A stories to round out the week. In the first, announced Dec. 18, Trident confirmed it had completed the sale of three Alaskan processing plants in Kodiak to Oregon-based Pacific Seafood Group as part of its restructuring plans.

Then, the following day, California's Tsar Nicoulai Caviar was confirmed to have completed the acquisition of Sterling Caviar, one of the US' first and largest sturgeon farmers. Sterling had been suffering from financial struggles and entered receivership in April this year, with debts exceeding $23 million at the time.

title: Clean Seas reduces yellowtail harvest guidance again as scale of year-class losses becomes apparent
content:
Australian yellowtail farmer Clean Seas Seafood has advised a further reduction to its forecast sales volumes from the 2024 year class, in its latest business update.

Clean Seas suffers heightened mortalities in 2024 year class

The company had originally advised back in November that it had been experiencing higher-than-expected mortalities within the class, and reduced its harvest guidance for next year from 3,000 metric tons to 2,550-2,650t.

An investigation was launched into the cause of the mortalities and to better assess their impact on next year's production; the final verdict has been to further reduce next year's guidance to just 2,200-2,300t.

Moreover, sales volumes are expected to decline further for 2026 to just 2,050-2,200t, according to Clean Seas, before improving back to the usual rate of 3,000t for 2027, it estimates.

Altogether, Clean Seas says it is reducing its guidance from the current year class by approximately 600t from the November update. Harvests are expected to begin in April 2025, with the shortfall to be made up through delayed harvesting of the earlier year class and expedited harvests of the next one.

"Consequently, the financial impact of reduced sales will primarily be felt in H2 FY 2025 and H1 of FY 2026," Clean Seas said.

A year of problems

Clean Seas originally observed a decline in the performance of the current year class back in March, although no reduction in harvest expectations was considered necessary at the time.

Then, in July, issues over the transition and consolidation of farming activities from the firm's various farms into a single site led to missed feed days and health treatments, resulting in lower-than-expected fish growth rates this year.

Splitting and grading of the year class then took place roughly six months later than had originally been planned as a result of "operational challenges", and when cages were counted it was clear that many fish had been eaten by predators.

This, in turn, led to the November guidance reduction to 2,550-2,650t.

"Suboptimal feeding and bathing practices, coupled with inadequate predator management, contributed to the count losses identified in October 2024," the company wrote.

"These deficiencies created a sub-population of less resilient fish within the Year Class 24 cohort, rendering them more vulnerable to background stressors, including parasites, disease, and environmental factors, resulting in the elevated mortalities currently being experienced."

However, after further review, Clean Seas said it had observed elevated mortalities among the remaining fish in the cohort, which on its own is often the case as sea temperatures rise in the run up to summer.

After analyzing the health of the impaired year class, Clean Seas found that 98% of the mortalities exhibited a 'condition factor' below 1.30. Moreover, 77% of the remaining fish have a health status above this level, and as such the company estimates that 25% of the remaining year class are unlikely to survive through to harvest.

This, in turn, means the firm sees an estimated harvest potential in the range of 250,000 to 300,000 fish.

Clean Seas noted that it has commissioned two senior consultants and a new general manager of operations to improve performance.

title: Chilean prosecutor formalizes allegations against former Australis owner, execs
content:
Chile’s public prosecutor’s office has recently informed the involved parties that it intends to formalize allegations brought by China’s Joyvio Group against Australis Seafoods’ former owner, Isidoro Quiroga, and other executives.

The allegations relate to the sale of the company six years ago, in 2019. The formalization process, which is a crucial step in Chile’s legal system, is expected to move the case forward.

UK court orders China’s Joyvio to pay over $1.5m to former Australis owner

Joyvio has also accused Quiroga, former president Martin Guiloff, and ex-CFO Santiago Garreton of fraud and mismanagement in connection with the sale of Australis to the Chinese company. The prosecutors’ decision to advance the case marks an important development in what has already been a prolonged legal dispute.

"The formalization of charges against Quiroga, Guiloff, and Garreton confirms the position of Joyvio and Australis since the beginning of these criminal proceedings," stated a representative of Joyvio’s legal team, which includes attorneys Jorge Bofill, Alberto Eguiguren, and Gabriel Zaliasnik.

"Multiple pieces of evidence have been meticulously gathered during the investigation, leading the Public Prosecutor’s Office to make this decision. We are confident that the biggest fraud in Chile's history will not go unpunished. This is a clear signal to foreign investors that our judicial system is functioning," it added. 

Joyvio’s legal team also contends that Quiroga and the Australis board hid critical information regarding serious overproduction problems in the company’s salmon farming operations.

The transaction at the heart of the case, Joyvio acquiring Australis for $921m, has since become a source of controversy.

During the 2019 due diligence process, Joyvio claims it was never informed of the full extent of these environmental issues, which reportedly involved massive overproduction of salmon at Australis’ farms.

Joyvio files lawsuit against Australis’ Quiroga, top execs for ‘massive fraud’ in buyout deal

The plaintiffs argue that these overproduction problems were a crucial factor in the company’s environmental violations and regulatory fines, amounting to more than $70m, and were concealed in order to inflate the sale price.

As a result, Joyvio is accusing Quiroga of defrauding them, alleging that the true extent of the operational and environmental problems was only revealed after the deal was completed.

In addition to annulling the sale, Joyvio is seeking compensation for damages, demanding that Quiroga return the $921m paid for Australis and an additional $300m for damages and other costs related to the alleged fraud.

The company’s legal representatives have argued that these costs represent the ongoing financial and reputational harm caused by the alleged concealment of key facts during the transaction.

Request for case dismissal

Quiroga’s legal team, however, has vehemently denied any wrongdoing since the very beginning, arguing that the allegations from Joyvio are based on a selective and misleading reading of the facts.

Quiroga’s legal team, however, has vehemently denied any wrongdoing, asserting that the allegations from Joyvio are based on a selective and misleading interpretation of the facts.

Juan Domingo Acosta, Qurioga’s attorney, pointed to the substantial evidence in the case, which he argued disproves the allegations. He noted that the prosecutor’s file contains “hundreds of communications, dozens of testimonies, and reports” that undermine the claims made by Joyvio.

Acosta also addressed the accusation of mismanagement, asserting that no conduct had been “manifestly contrary” to the interests of Australis or its shareholders. He highlighted two expert reports that confirm neither Australis nor its shareholders suffered any financial harm from the sale.

UK court orders China’s Joyvio to pay over $1.5m to former Australis owner

The defense emphasizes that, at the time of the transaction (2018-2019), the overproduction of salmon was not understood as an infraction. This understanding only shifted in 2021, when Chile's regulatory authority, the Superintendency of the Environment (SMA), changed its enforcement criteria.

Acosta also pointed out that foreign courts have already rejected Joyvio’s claims.

He cited a recent ruling from the High Court of England and Wales, which on December 3 ordered Joyvio to pay £1.2 million (over US$1.5 million) in legal costs to Quiroga and others in relation to the London trial. “None of the foreign tribunals where Joyvio has pursued its claims have ruled in their favor,” Acosta concluded.

In light of these arguments, Quiroga’s legal team has requested the “definitive and total dismissal” of the case, questioning the prosecutor’s actions as “difficult to understand.” They have expressed concern that the case is politically motivated and driven by the media, with Joyvio allegedly seeking to force a settlement through public pressure.

Key testimony could undermine fraud charges 

The evidence in the prosecutor’s file refutes the accusations made by Joyvio, Acosto maintains.

"The prosecutor’s file contains hundreds of communications, dozens of testimonies, and reports that completely discredit the allegations in the complaints," he said. "For example, the representative and chief technical advisor for Joyvio during the purchase process was called to testify by the Prosecutor's Office. In his testimony, he dismissed any concealment or deception and confirmed that all parties involved in the deal understood the environmental regulations in the same way."

Chinese-owned salmon farmer Australis files first lawsuit against former owner, top execs

This way, Jose Gago, the salmon industry executive who led the due diligence for China’s Joyvio in the 2019 purchase of Australis, could undermine fraud charges against Isidoro Quiroga, reports local newspaper El Mostrador.

In his testimony, Gago confirmed he had full access to all requested information during the due diligence process.

"I was given everything I requested," Gago said, detailing how he obtained data on Australis' concessions, historical performance, and future planting and harvest plans.

He emphasized that Joyvio had the same access to all this information, which was sufficient to evaluate the company’s production capacity.

Despite Joyvio’s claims, Gago explained that no red flags were raised about the company's overproduction.Regulatory changes related to overproduction occurred after the deal closed, he said.

"The overproduction issue came up much later, and no sanctions were imposed during the sale process," Gago stated.

Gago’s testimony also included key details on inspections made on 45 of Australis' 95 concessions. He stressed that the information was shared with Joyvio's executives and that there were no significant delays in obtaining data.

"There was a common interest in ensuring that any missing information was quickly provided," he concluded.

Ex-regulator claims shift in overproduction enforcement

Finally, a report by Cristobal de la Maza, former head of Chile's superintendency of the environment, or the SMA, revealed a shift in regulatory criteria regarding overproduction after the sale of Australis to Joyvio, reports local newspaper El Mercurio in its printed edition.

De la Maza, who led the SMA between 2019 and 2022, states that from 2020, the SMA changed its approach, focusing on total production (tonnage) rather than just overstocking farms. This shift, he argued, made it difficult for companies like Australis to anticipate such scrutiny, as the regulator had previously been less strict.

The new criteria were formalized by 2021, after the sale of Australis, with the SMA now considering production volume as part of its environmental oversight.

Joyvio’s legal team disputes this claim, arguing that the change in enforcement was not significant and was thoroughly investigated. They maintain that the evidence shows the regulations were not altered.

title: Daily recap: Vietnam shrimp extend price gains; Avramar sale should finalize in Q1
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Tuesday, Dec. 17.

Week 51 farm-gate shrimp roundup: Vietnam extends gains as Asian prices diverge

Vietnamese farm-gate shrimp prices continued their upward trajectory in week 50 (Dec. 9-15), bucking a broader trend of flat or softening in other major producing regions, according to price data from Undercurrent News.

Avramar sale should finalize in Q1, ties with Spanish ops to be maintained

The United Arab Emirates-based firm Aqua Bridge Group is in advanced negotiations to acquire seabass and seabream farmer Avramar's Greek assets, with a deal expected to be finalized early next year, sources familiar with the process told Undercurrent on Dec. 17.

Indonesia's eFishery suspends CEO, exec over financial investigation

Indonesian unicorn startup eFishery has temporarily suspended CEO Gibran Huzaifah and chief product officer Chrisna Aditya, both co-founders of the company, reports the Jakarta Globe.

Canada cuts offshore scallop quota 39%, contributes further to coming world shortage

The world's future scallop supply keeps shrinking, and the latest news coming out of Atlantic Canada only contributes to the bleak outlook.

Skipjack tuna prices show signs of decline in Bangkok

Bangkok, Thailand -- a major hub for tuna processing -- has not seen skipjack prices for delivery in December increase month-on-month as previously expected, and various industry sources reported a slightly bearish trend for the current month.

After vetoing state funding, Alaska governor now wants $10m for seafood marketing

With the stroke of his veto pen, the governor of the US state of Alaska has had an apparent change of heart after blocking $10 million in funding for the Alaska State Marketing Institute.

Ecuador shrimp sector hopes for recovery with price gains, strong year-end forecast

Ecuador's shrimp farming industry is grappling with several hurdles as it heads toward the close of 2024, Gabriel Luna, Ecuadorian shrimp farmer and owner of GLunaShrimp, said on the latest The Shrimp Cast episode. 

Canadian aquaculture group accuses US of fueling activism against Newfoundland marine sanctuary

US-funded environmental activists are undermining Newfoundland and Labrador's fishing and aquaculture industries through their support for the proposed South Coast Fjords marine sanctuary, the Newfoundland Aquaculture Industry Association claimed in a statement on Monday (Dec. 16).

title: Canada cuts offshore scallop quota 39%, contributes further to coming world shortage
content:
The world's future scallop supply keeps shrinking and the latest news coming out of Atlantic Canada only contributes to the bleak outlook.

Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) has cut the overall quota for the offshore scallop fleet to 3,195 metric tons in 2025, a 39% reduction from the 5,205t quota allowed in 2024, sources tell Undercurrent News.

Though a formal memorandum has yet to be received, a list of the eight harvest regions shows Georges Bank A suffering the biggest blow, seeing its quota reduced from 4,000t to 2,100t (-1,900t). Georges Bank B also has suffered a cut, from 750t to 400t (-350t).

Canada's offshore scallop fishing areas. Image courtesy of Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans.

Canada's new offshore scallop season kicks off on Jan. 1.

The offshore fleet accounts for the largest percentage of Canada's Atlantic scallop (Placopecten magellanicus) landings.

The country exported 7,752t of scallops worth $194.4 million in 2023, a 3% increase in volume and a 10% jump in value over the 7,510t worth $177.3m exported in 2022, as revealed in the UCN trade portal chart below.

Over the first 10 months of 2024, Canada has exported 6,539t of scallops worth $166.6m.

Canada's biggest recent year for offshore quota was in 2020 when harvesters were given access to 6,540t. But the country exported only 6,276t worth $126.5m that year.

US, Japan also to deliver less

The news follows an earlier report from Undercurrent that the New England Fishery Management Council voted 15-1 on Dec. 5 to recommend new harvesting rules that would cause a further 25.6% reduction in projected landings during the US' 2025-2026 season, which starts April 1, 2025.

Framework 39, which is expected to be approved by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, would allow one 12,000-pound trip each into two limited areas as well as 24 days at sea (DAS) in open-bottom areas.

NEFMC staff has projected landings of 19.75 million lbs (8,958t), generating roughly $348.25m in dock value. However, once the observer and research set-aside landings are taken out, the projection drops to 18.0m lbs (8,165t) primarily for the limited access fleet. That's far less than the 24.2m lbs earlier projected for the limited access fleet during the 2024-25 season, though -- based on the latest report that just 13.6m lbs have been landed -- that number seems out of reach. 

To make matters worse, concerns are mounting over a sharp decline in Pacific scallop (Patinopecten yessoensis) harvests in Hokkaido, Japan, anticipated over the next two to five years due to a significant drop in spat or larvae collection this year, as reported Monday (Dec. 16) by Undercurrent.

Japan is the world's second-largest producer of scallops, behind only China, according to the latest United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization data. It harvests between 400,000 and 500,000t annually, while relying on two primary methods of farming: the "seabed fishery" and "hanging aquaculture." Both depend on larvae collection.

Japanese scallops from Bristol Seafood at a Wegmans supermarket in Columbia, Maryland. Photograph by Jason Huffman.

Japan grew 43.93 billion juvenile scallops from larvae in 2022, according to an official from the country's Fisheries Agency (Suisan-cho), a division of the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries of Japan. Hokkaido, the second-largest island of Japan and the largest and northernmost prefecture, contributed 79% of the total.

"This year, widespread reductions in larvae numbers have been confirmed, with cooperatives from multiple regions reporting shortages," an official from Hokkaido's fisheries department told Undercurrent. The Fisheries Agency corroborated these concerns, calling it an unprecedented prefecture-wide decline.

Industry sources speculate that last summer's unusually high sea temperatures weakened parent scallops, resulting in fewer larvae during spawning. However, the exact cause remains unclear, prompting research institutions, including the Hokkaido Research Organization, to accelerate their investigations, said the officials.

The US counted on Canada for 4,006t (17%) of its 23,092t of scallop imports in 2023, while relying on Japan for 7,403t (32%) and China for 4,824t (21%), another chart from UCN's trade portal shows

Clearwater hit hardest

The news of Canada's quota reduction is particularly bad for five Canadian companies that divvy it up, including Clearwater Seafoods, in Bedford, Nova Scotia. Clearwater, a division of British Columbia-based Premium Brands, owns 43.8% of the offshore scallop quota. 

It's also bad news for three other Nova Scotia companies that, in February, increased their offshore scallop quotas by buying out and divvying up the 16.77% owned by Newfoundland and Labrador-based Ocean Choice International (OCI): Mersey Seafoods, in Liverpool; Comeau's Sea Foods, in Saulnierville; and LaHave Seafoods, in LaHave. As reported by Undercurrent, OCI sold its quota following the sinking of its scallop fishing trawler.

In March 2021 the 143-foot Atlantic Destiny went down about 115 miles south of Nova Scotia after a catastrophic engine failure caused an explosion and fire, requiring a dramatic rescue of some 31 crew members amidst high sea swells. 

It's not known how much quota Mersey, Comeau and LaHave now hold. A fifth company, Adams & Knickle, in Lunenburg, Nova Scotia, holds 9.77% of the quota.

Because a "permanent" scallop quota previously sold for over CAD 100-per pound, the value of OCI's share was estimated to be worth about CAD 200m.

title: Indonesia’s eFishery suspends co-founders over financial investigation
content:
Indonesian unicorn startup eFishery has temporarily suspended CEO Gibran Huzaifah and chief product officer Chrisna Aditya, both co-founders of the company, reports the Jakarta Globe.

The decision comes as part of an ongoing investigation into alleged financial misconduct. The company said investors and shareholders have been informed of the investigation, which centers around reports of financial performance and revenue discrepancies linked to the two executives. Huzaifah and Aditya each held about 9% of the company's shares, the Globe wrote.

eFishery tech used by 60 farms in India in inaugural year

eFishery's institutional investors include UAE's 42XFund, Switzerland's responsAbility, Singapore's Temasek, Japan's SoftBank, Malaysia's Kumpulan Wang Persaraan, Northstar Ventures, and 500 Global.

The business secured $200 million in series D funding in July, bringing its valuation to over $1 billion, making it a unicorn.

Adhy Wibisono has been named interim CEO, while Albertus Sasmitra will serve as interim CFO.

The company told Undercurrent News: "eFishery is now operating under the leadership of Adhy Wibisono as an interim CEO and Albertus Sasmitra as an interim CFO. This decision, reached in unison with our shareholders, showcases our commitment to improving the company's governance."

The firm has confirmed the investigation but has not given specifics. Earlier reports from Deal Street Asia indicated that some investors had raised concerns about the accuracy of financial reports provided by the two executives. Both suspended executives are currently under internal investigation for potential manipulation of performance and revenue reports, wrote the Globe.

title: Hokkaido spat shortage threatens Japan’s scallop future, global supply chain
content:
Concerns are mounting over a sharp decline in scallop harvests in Hokkaido, Japan, anticipated over the next two to five years due to a significant drop in spat or larvae collection this year.

Japan is one of the world's second-largest producer of scallops, behind only China, according to the latest United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization data. It harvests between 400,000 and 500,000 metric tons annually.

But Japanese scallop production relies on two primary methods: the "seabed fishery" and "hanging aquaculture," both of which depend on larvae collection, making it a critical step.

Japan grew 43.93 billion juvenile scallops from larvae in 2022, according to an official from the country's Fisheries Agency (Suisan-cho), a division of the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries of Japan. Hokkaido, the second-largest island of Japan and the largest and northernmost prefecture, contributed 79% of the total.

But the state of larvae collection in Japan is not positive, officials told Undercurrent News. "While localized declines have occurred before, this is the first time the downturn has affected the entire prefecture," they said.

In the Okhotsk Sea and Nemuro regions, seabed harvesting involves releasing juvenile scallops into shallow waters, where they grow on the seabed for two to four years. Peak harvest seasons vary, with Okhotsk flourishing from summer to autumn and Nemuro from winter to early spring.

Credit: Hokkaido Federation of Fisheries Cooperative Associations.

Meanwhile, in Funka Bay, the hanging aquaculture method begins in June with growing juvenile scallops in underwater baskets. In their second year, the scallops are transferred to ropes to grow to market size before being harvested between winter and spring.

Japan’s Hokkaido Okhotsk scallop harvest declines 4% to 303,000t for 2024

Larvae are typically collected from April to June using specialized collectors. Over a year, the larvae develop into juvenile scallops, which are then distributed to fishery cooperatives or raised to maturity locally.

"This year, widespread reductions in larvae numbers have been confirmed, with cooperatives from multiple regions reporting shortages," an official from Hokkaido's fisheries department told Undercurrent. The Fisheries Agency corroborated these concerns, calling it an unprecedented prefecture-wide decline.

Industry sources speculate that last summer's unusually high sea temperatures weakened parent scallops, resulting in fewer larvae during spawning. However, the exact cause remains unclear, prompting research institutions, including the Hokkaido Research Organization, to accelerate their investigations, said the officials.

In the Okhotsk Sea, Yubetsu Fishery Cooperative described the situation as "extremely severe." The Oshamambe Fisheries Cooperative in the waters of Funka Bay was only able to secure half of the minimum required annual amount of 150 million larvae this year. Typically, they collect 300m, considering thinning and other needs.

Japan’s Aomori aims to double Mutsu Bay scallop exports by 2034

Some Hokkaido cooperatives report up to 60% cuts in larvae collection. Poor harvests elsewhere also mean they face challenges purchasing juvenile scallops from other regions.

Meanwhile, some fisheries cooperatives are trying to avoid culling juvenile and young scallops to sustain scallop populations. "If the shellfish grow well, harvest volumes could stay at normal levels," a source in Hokkaido told Undercurrent.

Calls for enhanced research 

In response to the crisis, the Hokkaido Scallop Promotion Association (HSPA) and the Hokkaido Fisheries Federation submitted a formal request to the prefectural government on Dec. 5, as the Japanese news service Suisak Keizai reported.

The industry bodies called for improved research infrastructure, advanced larvae collection technologies and better information-sharing practices.

"This year, The production of juvenile scallops, essential for scallop growth, is at significant risk across the prefecture," HSPA chairman Takakuma Yasufumi said.

"By following the successful example of Mutsu Bay [in Aomori Prefecture], we plan to leave a certain number of parent scallops next year and improve the design of larvae collectors," added Yuichi Takano, the vice chairman representing the Funka Bay district.

Reduced US scallop harvest plan for 2025-26 season advances

Toshihiko Abe, the vice chairman selected from the Okhotsk region, emphasized the need for a unified approach, stating, "Research stations across Hokkaido hold valuable information about the causes of poor larvae collection, but there is insufficient coordination."

Hirofumi Yamada, a vice chairman representing the Rumoi district -- which supplies 60% of Hokkaido's scallop larvae -- expressed alarm, saying, "Next year, we can only ship less than 50% of the larvae needed by our supply destinations. If this trend [a shortage in spat collection] happens again next year, it will pose a serious problem."

Shoguns and emperors

Japan's scallop harvesting industry has a rich history that dates back to the Edo period (1603–1868) when the shogunate designated scallops as a key export product and imposed strict fishing limits.

However, with the lifting of restrictions during the imperial Meiji era (1868–1912), overfishing led to a sharp decline in natural scallop populations, pushing the industry to collapse.

A turning point came in 1971 when Japan successfully undertook large-scale releases of scallop larvae for the first time. This marked the beginning of managed fisheries, a practice that has sustained the industry ever since.

Hokkaido leads the nation in scallop production by a significant margin. According to the Hokkaido Federation of Fisheries Cooperative Associations, in 2023, the region's scallop landings amounted to 336,000t of wild-caught scallops and 70,000t of farmed scallops. This accounts for 65% and 14% of Japan's total domestic production, respectively.

Outside of Hokkaido, Aomori Prefecture's Mutsu Bay is renowned for harvesting baby scallops, semi-mature scallops aged 8 to 10 months. However, Mutsu Bay has faced challenges, including poor seed collection in 2022 and 2023 and massive scallop mortality in 2023 due to abnormally high water temperatures.

'Indispensable in the US market'

Following China's complete ban on imports of Japanese seafood in August 2023, Japan has accelerated efforts to diversify scallop export destinations. By October 2024, Japan's scallop exports had recovered nearly 90% of their pre-ban levels.

Re-opening of closed US scallop area didn’t bring expected price relief

The main export markets for Japanese scallop products now include the US and Taiwan for frozen meats, while shell-on scallops are primarily shipped to Thailand, Vietnam and Indonesia.

Japanese scallops have gained a strong foothold in the US, the world's largest scallop market in recent years.

In Southeast Asian countries, scallops are deshelled and re-exported to the US as products of Japanese origin, allowing them to maintain their premium branding in US markets.

"With reduced Atlantic scallop production, Japanese scallops are becoming indispensable in the US market," a Tokyo-based scallop distributor told Undercurrent. "If the reduction in production from Hokkaido becomes a reality, it will likely affect not only the domestic market but also international market conditions."

title: US wild-catch shrimp group opposes Biden’s trade commission nominee
content:
The Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA), a group that represents domestic, wild-catch harvesters and processors of shrimp in the US Gulf of Mexico and southeastern coast, has expressed its opposition to one of president Joe Biden's nominees for the International Trade Commission.

Halie Craig has been too critical of president-elect Donald Trump's trade policies, which have included the heavy use of tariffs on imported products, SSA argues in a lengthy opinion piece published Wednesday (Dec. 11).  

ITC, which has been heavily involved in settling disputes related to shrimp imports lately, has two of its six commissioner spots open, and terms for three of the four remaining commissioners have expired, SSA notes in its article. The only other commissioner, Jason Kearns, will see his term expire next week. 

Biden, who needs to fill out the panel before the end of his administration, nominated on Nov. 21, Craig, who currently works as the policy director for technology on the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation, a post she has held for two years.

ITC rules US shrimp industry suffered as a result of imports, cements AD, CVD rates

Previously, Craig worked for eight months as a senior advisor to US senator Pat Toomey, a Pennsylvania Republican, and a little more than a year as a staff member on the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs.

But SSA believes she is a bad fit for the post.

"Because Ms. Craig's public views have unfairly and absurdly ridiculed president-elect Trump's actions with respect to international trade, the Southern Shrimp Alliance strongly opposes this nomination," SSA said in its letter.

The group points to multiple articles written by Craig in which she criticized the former and future president's positions on steel tariffs and his section 301 action against China, which has cost the US seafood industry more than a billion dollars.

SSA has benefited from the ITC, which recently found that the US shrimp industry was materially injured by the unfair trade practices of the Ecuador, India, Indonesia and Vietnam shrimp industries, ordering antidumping and countervailing duties be paid.

All four remaining ITC commissioners at the time voted in favor of an affirmative determination, SSA noted. The action marked the eighth time that the ITC and its predecessor, the US Tariff Commission, have investigated the state of the American shrimp industry since 1961, SSA noted. 

"Over the last 65 years, the political appointees of commissioners to the ITC have played a significant role in the operations of the US commercial shrimp fishery," SSA said. "Relief from fair trade has not been granted lightly to the domestic shrimp industry and, despite the eight investigations, trade remedies on shrimp imports have only been imposed on two occasions."

John Williams, SSA's executive director, continued: "The US International Trade Commission has played a central role in the shrimp industry's ability to combat unfair trade. Our nation's recent election demonstrates that there is strong opposition to the free-trade ideologies that have destroyed communities throughout our country.

"With president-elect Trump set to take office in a matter of weeks, there is simply no justification for installing someone to serve in a federal agency responsible for administering US trade laws who has repeatedly claimed that president Trump's trade policies harm Americans."

title: Untitled
content:
A sales manager at Quality Poultry and Seafood (QPS), a major seafood wholesaler in Mississippi, was sentenced to prison for his involvement in an extensive seafood fraud scheme. Another manager and QPS were also sentenced, the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Mississippi announced on Wednesday (Dec. 11).

The case, heard in the US District Court for the Southern District of Mississippi, revealed that QPS mislabeled cheaper imported fish as premium local species, misleading customers and restaurateurs alike.

QPS was sentenced to five years of probation, $1 million in forfeitures and a $500,000 criminal fine, according to the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Mississippi.

QPS must also maintain detailed records for five years, documenting the species, sources and costs of the seafood it acquires. These records must be made available to federal, state and local government authorities, as well as customers who inquire about the seafood they purchase. Additionally, QPS is required to answer truthfully any questions about the seafood's species, origin, and cost, according to the court announcement.

Sales manager Todd A. Rosetti received a harsher sentence than the other manager involved. Rosetti was ordered to serve eight months in prison, followed by 180 days of home detention, one year of supervised release, and 100 hours of community service. Meanwhile, QPS business manager James W. Gunkel was sentenced to two years of probation, 12 months of home detention, and 50 hours of community service.

The defendants were convicted of conspiring to misbrand seafood and commit wire fraud by marketing inexpensive imported fish as more costly premium local varieties. Prosecutors emphasized that this scheme negatively affected local fishermen and deceived consumers.

Quality Poultry and Seafood facility. Photo: Company's Facebook page

QPS admitted this past summer to participating in a scheme that involved substituting fish served at local fine-dining restaurant Mary Mahoney's and other establishments. Prosecutors noted that this fraudulent activity continued from 2002 until November 2019. QPS also mislabeled seafood at its retail shop and cafe during this time, passing off imported fish as fresh local varieties.

In August 2024, QPS acknowledged its involvement in the scheme that falsely exchanged local fish with cheaper imports during the same timeframe. The company suggested and sold foreign fish to restaurants as if they were the local species advertised on menus.

Court documents indicated that after Food and Drug Administration (FDA) agents inspected QPS for selling mislabeled fish, the company continued offering frozen fish from Africa, South America and India as substitutes for local varieties for over a year.

Kerry Mannion, acting special agent in charge at the FDA Office of Criminal Investigations, stated, "US consumers expect their seafood to be correctly identified. When sellers purposefully substitute one fish species for another, they deceive consumers and create potential food safety hazards."

Mary Mahoney's case

Mary Mahoney's, a Mississippi corporation operating as Mary Mahoney's Old French House restaurant in Biloxi, faced its own legal consequences. A client of QPS, Mary Mahoney's and Anthony Charles Cvitanovich, its co-owner and manager, pleaded guilty in May 2024 to conspiracy to misbrand seafood and wire fraud during 2018 and 2019.

Mary Mahoney's, a restaurant in Biloxi, Mississippi. Image from restaurant website.

During sentencing in November, the restaurant reached a plea deal with the government. It was sentenced to five years of probation and ordered to pay a total penalty of $1.49 million, including $149,000 as a criminal fine and $1.35m in forfeiture for some of the proceeds it had obtained from its fraudulent seafood sales to its customers. The court required Mary Mahoney's to keep records of the species, sources, and costs of its seafood for at least five years and to provide them to relevant government agencies upon request.

Mahoney's co-owner/manager, Anthony Charles Cvitanovich, 55, was sentenced to three years of probation and four months of home detention. He was also ordered to pay a $10,000 fine.

A civil case against the restaurant, initiated by Todd McCain of Alabama, is still pending. He represents customers allegedly misled into overpaying for frozen fish they believed was fresh from the Gulf of Mexico. Mary Mahoney's and QPS have filed motions to dismiss McCain's claims, arguing that his assertions of financial injury are speculative and that proving he consumed misrepresented fish is virtually impossible without forensic testing.

title: Genetic testing detects shrimp mislabeling in US Gulf Coast restaurants
content:
Seafood fraud made headlines in the US states on the Gulf of Mexico coast this fall when testing conducted at multiple "local" seafood festivals caught vendors using imported shrimp and claiming it to be wild-caught.

Now, SeaD Consulting, a Houston, Texas-based firm, says its new genetic testing reveals that seafood fraud is also on the rise in many Mississippi restaurants.

Using its RIGHTTest technology, SeaD said it sampled 44 restaurants in Biloxi, Gulf Shores and other surrounding Mississippi Gulf Coast areas that market "fresh local seafood." It found 17 were selling imported shrimp while marketing it as locally caught white shrimp.

Of the 44 restaurants tested, 24 featured a menu that listed "Royal Red Shrimp" or Pleoticus robustus, a species found in the Gulf of Mexico, the firm reported. SeaD said 92% of the restaurants -- 22 out of 24 -- admitted they were instead serving imported Argentinian red shrimp, Pleoticus muelleri, which the firm described as an "inferior," lower-cost species. 

"The investigation revealed that fraudulent shrimp dishes were often priced as high as $24.95 per plate, meaning consumers are paying top dollar for inauthentic products," SeaD said in a news release.

"On average, diners spent $16.72 per fraudulent dish, with additional costs for gratuities, transportation, and parking further inflating the total," the firm reported.

SeaD said it has conducted a handful of other tests this fall with mixed results. Its RIGHTTest technology found that every vendor at this past October's Lousiana Shrimp Festival & Shrimp Aid 2024 event maintained a "100% local seafood promise."

The same couldn't be said for the 51st Annual National Shrimp Festival in Gulf Shore, Alabama, also in October. SeaD said its testing found that, out of five shrimp dishes sampled, only one contained wild-caught shrimp from the Gulf of Mexico, while the others all used imported farm-raised shrimp.

title: Bumble Bee tuna linked by Greenpeace to forced labor aboard Indonesian vessels
content:
Bumble Bee Foods' canned tuna has been linked to allegations of forced labor aboard commercial fishing vessels in Indonesia, according to a new report from environmental activist group Greenpeace.

Greenpeace Southeast Asia released its latest report investigating "unresolved human and environmental exploitation at sea" on Monday (Dec. 9), just ahead of Human Rights Day, observed annually around the world on Tuesday (Dec. 10). 

The 67-page report, reviewed by Undercurrent News, investigates complaints about forced labor and illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing from 10 Indonesian fishermen that were filed with the Indonesian Migrant Workers Union (SBMI) between 2019 and 2024. Those complaints were linked to 12 Taiwanese-flagged vessels.

Greenpeace said it found that four of those cases can be linked to US tuna brand Bumble Bee, which is owned by Taiwan-based parent company FCF Co.

"The vessels -- Chaan Ying, Guan Wang, Shin Lian Fa No. 168 and Sheng Ching Fa No. 96 -- supplied Bumble Bee across multiple trips and often a number of years, indicating a continued relationship with these vessels," the report states.

Greenpeace said it found -- via fisher complaints and follow-up interviews -- that crew members on board the vessels experienced "various forms of forced labor." Top forced labor indicators included "deception, retention of identity, abuse and vulnerability and debt bondage," the group said.

NOAA to propose seafood import monitoring expansion again, acknowledge forced labor

Crew members had wages withheld and one fisher was even denied compensatory medical insurance following an eye injury, Greenpeace alleged. When fishermen requested to go home, they were denied, according to the group. One crew member reportedly claimed to be held hostage after requesting his identity documents from the recruitment agency that landed him the job on a vessel.

Greenpeace said it sent a letter to Bumble Bee Foods regarding the accusations on Nov. 27, 2024, and again on Thursday (Dec. 5). The organization said it had not received a reply as of Friday (Dec. 6).

Undercurrent reached out to PR agency Fleishman Hillard, which represents Bumble Bee, for comment on Monday, but didn't receive a reply before publication.

'Trace My Catch'

Also mentioned in the report is Bumble Bee's "Trace My Catch" tool, an initiative the company launched in 2015 to allow consumers to track the origin of their fish "from catch to can" via a code found on products.

A demo using an albacore tuna product code on the website shows that the consumer can learn more about albacore tuna and even the fishing method used to catch it. The tool also provides vessel information, including the nation of record, when the trip began and ended, and information on where the fish was caught, processed and canned.

Greenpeace said it used the Bumble Bee tracking tool to confirm that at least four vessels named in the report have supplied tuna to Bumble Bee and are also connected to alleged forced migrant workers from Indonesia.

Greenpeace East Asia said it launched its own "Fake My Catch" report in 2022, tracing "fish from vessels to US supermarket shelves, uncovering links between vessels that supplied Bumble Bee tuna and human rights violations and IUU fishing."

A call for action

"As Bumble Bee neither publishes a vessel list nor any public information on their grievance policy, what our research uncovered is likely the tip of the iceberg," Arifsyah Nasution, global lead for the Beyond Seafood campaign and senior oceans campaigner for Greenpeace Southeast Asia, said in a press release issued Monday.

"Therefore, Greenpeace will continue doing investigations to uncover the murky side of the seafood supply chain and advocate for a more fair, just, and sustainable global seafood industry for the sake of fishers, consumers, and our ocean's future," said Nasution.

Greenpeace urges ratification of ocean treaty to fix ‘broken fisheries system’

Greenpeace is calling on Bumble Bee and other tuna brands to "own up to their responsibility and the role they play in this industry."

Charli Fritzner, Beyond Seafood project team lead for Greenpeace USA, added: "They need to actively engage with upstream suppliers to ensure there are real grievance mechanisms in place as well as work with them to install wifi aboard vessels."

SBMI is also using the report as an opportunity to call on the Indonesian government to do a better job in protecting its migrant fishers, according to GreenPeace.

title: Kroger sushi recalled after linked to salmonella cucumber outbreak
content:
Sushi sold at some US Kroger grocery store locations is being voluntarily recalled after being linked to an outbreak investigation of salmonella in cucumbers. 

GBC Food Services, doing business as Yummi Sushi, announced this week via the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) that it is launching a voluntary recall of multiple sushi products that contain cucumbers.

The Farmers Branch, Texas-based company, is a major sushi supplier to Kroger, which in 2023 claimed to have generated between $400 million and $600m from more than 40m pieces sold annually, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

Yummi Sushi Spicy Salmon Roll. Photo Credit: Kroger

The products included in the recall notice were packaged in clear plastic grab-n-go containers at Kroger stores.

The FDA said in late November that it was collaborating with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), as well as state and local partners to investigate a multistate outbreak of salmonella typhimurium infections linked to American/slicer cucumbers that were grown by Agrotato, SA de CV in Sonora, Mexico.

As of the time of this publication, the CDC had reported 68 salmonella cases linked to cucumbers, including 18 hospitalizations, within 19 states.

title: Untitled
content:
Climate change is having strong negative impacts on Scotland's salmon aquaculture sector, and as businesses invest and work hard to adapt, help from the government would be very welcome, said Mowi's chief operating officer for Scotland, Ireland and the Faroes, Ben Hadfield.

On Dec. 4, a Scottish parliament Affairs Committee heard evidence first from Sean Black of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals and Sarah Evans of the Marine Conservation Society, then representatives of the aquaculture industry itself, discussing sustainable growth.

Climate change was an important talking point, especially with the industry pointing to this as the reason for its less-than-satisfactory mortality numbers in recent years.

"Climate change is a huge risk; we're already in a climate crisis and seeing the impacts, in particular mortalities," said Evans. "Feed is another area we'll see impacts, particularly with the El Nino effects in the fisheries used to provide fishmeal and oil, which have already seen shocks in recent years."

"There are some challenges we're facing now and others we're not yet sure of, and the industry will need to adapt rapidly and will need help to do that," she said.

Facing questions a short while later, industry representatives agreed. Hadfield was asked about a Guardian article from October that said, "More than a million dead fish, the biggest mass die-off of farmed salmon in Scotland in a decade," had been recorded at two adjacent Mowi Scotland sites in Loch Seaforth on the Outer Hebrides.

Scottish salmon farming moratorium debate heats up as MSPs weigh future

"The mortality was just over 50% of the fish that were put in, and it was due to string jellyfish -- usually found at great depths in the ocean, but the last couple of years it's come to the surface, been pushed into the lochs, and caused gill damage that kills fish."

He said Mowi had done its absolute best to protect its fish, but has suffered still.

"In terms of what we'll do in the future, we're using AI technology to identify jellyfish species; we're using remote sensing to look over wider areas and see the coming; we're using bubble curtains and aeration, and we're seeking to relocate some sites to less vulnerable areas."

"But what we shouldn't do is stop producing a very sustainable, high-value protein in Scotland. We need to continue production and find ways to improve the level of survival, which we think is not high enough. Every working day, our teams focus on improving fish welfare and survival."

Asked about how to grow Scotland's market share, he noted that first, Scotland would have to grow its output, and the simplest way to do that was improve survival rates and grow the fish a kilogram bigger.

"But if the Scottish and UK governments really want to help and support, they should evaluate the headwinds the industry has been subject to over the last four or five years and try to ease those while still maintaining the highest standards of environmental management -- which is what we have in Scotland, much higher than the rest of the world."

"We need to back ourselves, set about producing more, keeping more of the wealth creation in Scotland, and governments need to seriously think 'how do we help this industry to succeed,' because it's been too much over the last decade now."

Specifically, he said, Scotland competes on the world market with high quality and price achievement, packaged with Scottish provenance.

"The headwinds we've seen have been an increase in regulation, partly in response to fairly niche activism -- I don't say we shouldn't listen to them, we should, but we shouldn't react by showing the regulatory teeth every time, and that is what's been happening, and it's reducing Scotland's competitiveness."

He and others during the event cited the statistic that Scottish salmon production was 10% of the global market around five or six years ago, which has slipped to 6%.

"The biggest risk to Scottish salmon's position within 'brand Scotland' is slow growth," said Anne Anderson, head of sustainability and development at Scottish Sea Farms.

"We as an industry need to work better with regulators and government, there's aspects on both sides for improving that relationship." The former chief officer of "compliance and beyond" at the Scottish Environment Protection Agency (SEPA), she said it was essential that both sides fully understood Hadfield's points around headwinds.

"But it's not that complicated to overcome, it's about investing the time to understand. Issues in the sea mean we have to move -- physically move the farm and move our heads around the issues. We need to do it right now, and it needs to occur among regulators and parliamentarians."

Scottish aquaculture businesses "cannot move a farm quickly," she said, "and I want to move a lot of our farms to different locations, and to consolidate, and we have a plan to do that... But for the sector's longevity, you need the ability to move fast."

"I think salmon pen infrastructure is a real critical one, like roads or rail networks -- what would it look like to think of it that way? Would we have faster movement?"

Illegal burials explained

Also in October, the media reported that thousands of rotting salmon carcasses had been illegally dumped on a beach in North Uist, Scotland, prompting SEPA to investigate.

It had been uncovered by an investigation funded by environmental activist Dale Vance, who has since vowed to continue putting money into such work.

FREE READ UK millionaire pledges to invest in more covert salmon farming probes

Hadfield -- whose firm uses the mortality disposal company in question, Whiteshore Cockles -- said the facility was a licensed one and, while it "doesn't look pretty," it's a sustainable way to dispose of dead salmon, sequestering the carbon into beaches.

After a great deal of time and over £6 million invested in circular economy work on mortalities -- extracting fish oil and turning and creating a pellet that can be burned as a fuel or used as fertilizer -- Whiteshore has finally gotten licensing.

When this system broke down earlier this year, it decided to bury some mortalities in the previous landfill -- but the license had expired in March 2024, and it buried some fish in May. This was filmed by activists in May and then "sat on" before they released it "two days before the parliamentary inquiry," said Hadfield.

Whiteshore's facility is now fully up and running and producing biofuel in a far better way of handling morts, he added.

Scottish Sea Farms' Anderson added she was angry at the "unacceptable lapses" at a farm on the Isle of Mull after drones operated by NGO Animal Equality captured footage of live fish spending up to two minutes out of the water as farmhands carried them in nets earlier this year.

It was not an incident that reflected normal behavior on the firm's farms, but as a result, it has "taken steps to refresh, renew and reinforce and confirm fully the RSPCA code in respect to the handling of moribund fish," ensuring farmers have the equipment to hand to euthanize sick animals quickly.

title: Search suspended for five Alaska fishermen after vessel capsizes
content:
After scouring an area of the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Alaska that was about 108 square miles over a nearly 24-hour period, the US Coast Guard (USCG) announced Monday (Dec. 2) evening that it suspended its search for the five crew members on board the Wind Walker.

The commercial fishing vessel had sent a distress call early on Sunday (Dec 1). 

"We stand in sorrow and solidarity with the friends and family of the people we were not able to find over the past 24 hours," chief warrant officer James Koon, a search and rescue mission coordinator at Coast Guard Sector Southeast Alaska, said in a press release.

Neither the press release nor any of the press accounts from local media say what the 50-foot vessel was after when it departed Auke Bay on Saturday (Nov. 30). Within hours of being on the water, the crew reportedly faced conditions consisting of heavy snows, 45-60 mph winds and six-foot seas.

One crew member had contacted the USCG early on Sunday to alert it that the Wind Walker, then off Point Couverden, southwest of Juneau, was overturning, as reported earlier by Undercurrent News.

After further attempts to contact the vessel were unsuccessful, the USCG launched a rescue team and issued an urgent marine information broadcast. An Alaska Marine Highway System (AMHS) ferry, AMHS Hubbard, overheard the broadcast and offered to assist. The ferry vessel was the first to arrive on the scene and began a grid search in what a state transportation department spokesperson described to Anchorage Daily News as "almost zero visibility" conditions.

Seven cold-water immersion suits and two strobe lights were found during the search, according to the USCG.

"I am deeply grateful for the swiftness of our crews and other search assets who came together to amplify our efforts and completely saturate our search areas," said Koon. "Our collective hearts are with the friends and families who are experiencing the effects from this loss."  

A dangerous profession

It was nearly five years ago that the Alaska USCG was out in difficult weather conditions searching for missing fishermen after the Scandies Rose, a 130-foot-long commercial fishing vessel, capsized with seven crew members on board, as reported by Undercurrent.

The vessel was south of Sutwik Island, Alaska, on Dec. 31, 2019, when it sank in conditions that the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) later found were "more extreme than forecasted."

The Scandies Rose. Photo Credit: National Transportation Safety Board

While two crew members survived, five others were never found. NTSB chairman Robert Sumwalt declared in 2021, following an investigation into the incident, that commercial fishing was the most deadly occupation in America in 2019.

"Commercial fishing had a fatality rate of 145 fatalities per 100,000 full-time employees. Compare that to the average of all workers, which is 3.5 fatalities per 100,000," said Sumwalt.

And up until the recent disaster, it looked like things had improved in the industry. The USCG reported the first fatality-free fiscal year in the Alaskan fishing industry in 2022, the first since 2015.

To compare, the Alaska Department of Fish and Game said that between 1980 and 1988, an average of 31 fishermen died in Alaska each year.

Scott Wilwert, commercial fishing vessel safety coordinator for the USCG 17th District, credited the reduction in fatalities then to the fishing industry. Many vessel owners and operators have become mindful of the importance of properly maintaining their vessel's life-saving equipment and training crew on proper emergency procedures, he said.

Wilwert also gave credit to the efforts of USCG vessel examiners and maritime organizations, who he said "play a vital role in preparing fishermen to survive an incident at sea."

title: WCPFC adopts first ever crew labor standards, fails to regulate transshipments
content:
The Pacific Islands Forum Fisheries Agency (FFA) has welcomed the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission (WCPFC) 's adoption of new crew labor standards.

The decision was made during the WCPFC's annual meeting in Fiji, Suva, from Nov. 28 to Dec. 3. It established binding rules to improve working conditions for fishing crew members in the region.

The new conservation and management measure addresses fair wages, safe working environments, and protection against exploitation. The measure ensures alignment with international best practices and addresses critical areas such as fair remuneration and access to medical care, safe and decent working conditions and protections against forced labor, abuse and exploitation, according to the FFA.

It claimed this marks the first time a regional fisheries management organization (RFMO) has adopted such comprehensive labor protections, aligning with global best practices.

New Zealand and Indonesia co-chaired the initiative, which was developed with significant input from FFA members. A three-year implementation period will follow.

Electronic monitoring, transshipment

Ahead of the meeting, the International Seafood Sustainability Foundation (ISSF) had called for electronic monitoring to be implemented for all gear types operating in the Western and Central Pacific Ocean.

At present, while purse seine vessels must have 100% coverage, longline vessels require only 5%. Unlike other tuna RFMOs, WCPFC has yet to adopt electronic monitoring standards despite years of discussions, ISSF stressed. 

NGO the Pew Charitable Trusts said the WCPFC's annual meeting had achieved some important progress on electronic monitoring. However, it pointed out that it had gone another year without updating how it manages transshipment or the transfer of catch from a fishing vessel to a carrier vessel.

"After a decade of work, the Commission adopted interim electronic monitoring standards, which will ultimately help improve oversight of the region's valuable fisheries. By allowing managers to augment human observers with onboard cameras and other technology, electronic monitoring can increase data collection and help ensure that fishers are following WCPFC rules."

"WCPFC now joins other tuna RFMOs in the eastern Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian Oceans, which also recently adopted electronic monitoring standards, ensuring that better data on fishing activities will soon be collected oceanside," said Dave Gershman, a senior officer for Pew's international fisheries project.

However, the region's rules remain out of alignment with United Nations recommendations and lag behind the standards adopted by the other four tuna RFMOs having yet again failed to agree to improve the management and monitoring of transshipment, he said.

"While the adoption of electronic monitoring standards is something to celebrate, WCPFC members must continue to find ways to reduce risks to sustainability, starting in 2025 with a serious recommitment to updating how it manages transshipment."

The WCPFC annual meeting took place less than a month after The Death at Sea justice campaign released a video that revealed key evidence from CCTV footage related to the death of fisheries observer Eritara Aati Kaierua in 2020 in international waters near Kiribati.

The footage (see below) shows his body being moved nearly 24 hours after his last appearance, raising critical questions about the ongoing investigation, according to the Death at Sea justice campaign.

Meanwhile, Operation Kurukuru, a collaborative effort to fight illegal fishing, concluded at the end of October, covering 21.3 million square kilometers in the Western and Central Pacific.

Led by the FFA and its members, alongside the Pacific Quadrilateral Defence Coordination Group, the operation aimed to enhance maritime security and ensure sustainable fisheries.

The operation spanned the waters of 15 participating members and adjacent high seas, with contributions from nations including Australia, Fiji, Kiribati, Papua New Guinea, and the US.

title: Japan’s Yokohama City halts bluefin tuna sales over unverified origins
content:
The Yokohama City government in Japan announced on Thursday (Nov. 28) that it had ordered a halt to selling 12 bluefin tuna purchased by an intermediate wholesaler at Central Wholesale Market due to concerns about their origin.

The tuna, purportedly sourced from Oma in Aomori Prefecture, could not be verified after unsuccessful attempts to contact the businesses involved in its distribution.

The issue arose when the intermediate wholesaler acquired 12 bluefin tuna on Oct. 28 and Nov. 5, which the supplier claimed originated from Oma or Aomori. However, when the wholesaler requested certification documents, such as those from landing ports or local authorities, the supplier could not provide them.

Taiwan’s largest tuna group launches FIP, targets MSC

Japan’s Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry, and Fisheries clarified on Nov. 5 that while the Fisheries Act does not immediately permit sales restrictions in such cases, further verification of the catch reports was deemed necessary.

Yokohama’s Economic Bureau investigation revealed that the tuna’s reported origin and harvesting details could not be substantiated under Japan’s fishing regulations.

The tuna had been labeled as originating from “Oma Port in Aomori Prefecture” based on the supplier’s invoice. Although this labeling complied with Japan’s Food Labeling Act, as there was no definitive evidence of falsification at the time of sale, the lack of supporting documentation raised red flags.

The Economic Bureau instructed the wholesaler to suspend tuna sales acquired on Nov. 5. It also formally notified all seafood intermediaries at the market, emphasizing the importance of handling only goods with proper certification.

The city plans to report its findings to the ministry and the Fisheries Agency for further action.

title: UK millionaire pledges to invest in more covert salmon farming probes
content:
A UK multimillionaire businessman has vowed to invest "substantial resources" into launching more covert investigations to expose environmental breaches in the salmon farming industry, reports The Times.

Scottish salmon farming moratorium debate heats up as MSPs weigh future

A police investigation was launched in October after The Times published footage which appeared to show rotting and diseased fish being dumped illegally. The undercover investigation was funded by Dale Vince, a green energy firm owner, who issued the warning to Holyrood's rural affairs and islands committee.

Vince, said his Green Britain Foundation (GBF), an environmental charity and campaign group, would bankroll further surveillance operations.

"I can assure you and the general public that GBF will be dedicating substantial resources to investigating and publicizing the lack of effective oversight and regulation of this industry," he wrote to the all-party group of Scottish parliament members.

Vince said his preference would be for the "immediate closure of all salmon farming operations in Scotland."

title: CEO of Venezuelan shrimp giant flees country after coup plot accusation
content:
Jose Enrique Rincon, owner and CEO of Venezuela's largest shrimp production firm Lamar Group, has been accused by the government of orchestrating a coup against president Nicolas Maduro, reports Que Pasa. 

The allegations, made by Diosdado Cabello, minister for interior, justice and peace of Venezuela, on Nov. 23, claim that Rincon, along with his sons Juan Diego and Jose Enrique Jr., were central figures in a plot aimed at destabilizing the government.

Venezuela’s Lamar Group bets big on Europe amid 100,000t production goal

According to the authorities, Rincon was not only involved in these but also led a powerful judicial mafia in the Zulia region of northwestern Venezuela.

The Venezuelan government has a history of seizing private businesses under controversial circumstances.

Lamar Group, based in Maracaibo, in Zulia, is a dominant player in Venezuela's shrimp industry, producing an estimated 80% of the nation's total shrimp output, Undercurrent News previously reported. 

With its vast network of shrimp farms, hatcheries, and processing plants, the firm has become an economic powerhouse for Venezuela, employing over 10,000 people and holding 13,000 hectares of shrimp farms.

The company's reach extends far beyond Venezuela's borders, with Lamar exporting 80% of its product to Europe. Its expansion plans have also been aggressive, as it planned to double production to 100,000 metric tons in 2025 -- with consumers in Europe the cornerstone of its expansion strategy.

"We don't want to compete with Ecuador," explained commercial director Juan Gomez-Behr during the recent China Fisheries and Seafood Expo in Qingdao, referring to Latin America's largest shrimp producer. Instead of pursuing the high-volume, head-on, shell-on shrimp market that Ecuador dominates, Lamar was focusing on what it does best: producing the larger, darker, cooked shrimp that European companies particularly value.

Venezuelan shrimp farmer Lamar eyes US expansion with new value-added plant

In addition, the firm also shared with Undercurrent its intentions to expand in the US and China.

At its stand during Seafood Expo Global in Barcelona in Aprl, Jose Enrique Jr. discussed the company's plans to increase sales in China and the US market, aiming to establish a new value-added plant next year in the latter country.

However, the recent political scandal has raised questions about the company's future.

As authorities ramp up their investigation into the Rincon family's alleged involvement in the coup plot, reports have surfaced that the family members have fled the country, likely to avoid arrest. According to Cabello, Rincon and his sons left Venezuela shortly after learning of the investigation, though their whereabouts are currently unknown.

CEO of Venezuelan shrimp giant flees country after coup plot accusation - Undercurrent News
A bit of context

Under Rincon's leadership, the company has grown exponentially since its early days in the 1990s, particularly after 2018, when government support helped propel Lamar's shrimp production from 10,000t annually to 60,000t in 2023.

The rise of Lamar Group was closely intertwined with Venezuela's political landscape. In 2016, the company received significant public support, with the government of then-governor Francisco Arias Cardenas and the ministry of fisheries, Angel Belisario Martinez, inaugurating a $3.5 million shrimp feed factory.

The factory's opening was heralded as a key example of collaboration between the private sector and the Bolivarian government's economic model. Martinez praised the project as a symbol of Venezuela's commitment to its "new productive economic model" and a step towards economic diversification.

However, despite the early government backing, relations between Rincon and the Maduro government have since become more complex.

In recent years, president Maduro has publicly accused Rincon of using his wealth and business influence to fuel a broader conspiracy against the state. In a TV program, Maduro referred to Rincón as the "leader of the Zulia economic mafia," claiming that his fortune was built upon corrupt ties to the government.

The allegations became more serious when Cabello linked Rincon and his sons to the opposition, suggesting he had orchestrated a conspiracy to destabilize the government, with connections to Colombian paramilitary groups and narcotrafficking organizations.

Disruption could create shake-up in EU

The implications of this scandal extend far beyond Venezuela's borders. Lamar Group is a major player in the global shrimp market, and its sudden disruption could have deeper consequences.

Industry experts have noted that the Rincon family's departure is likely to cause significant turmoil within the company, which reportedly holds $50 million worth of shrimp in its ponds and an additional $15m in cold storage, according to The Fish Site.

This loss of production could lead to supply chain disruptions, particularly for Lamar's European customers, and benefit other shrimp-exporting countries, notably Ecuador, whose producers may step in to fill the void.
