title: Seafood processors in Venezuela, Japan, Thailand slapped with FDA warnings
content:
A Venezuelan crabmeat processor and three other foreign seafood processors have been issued warning letters by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

The letters, published by the FDA on Tuesday (Nov. 26), were sent to the companies between May and October 2024. All identify violations in relation to Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) standards and insanitary conditions.

Most recently, in mid-October, Grupo VPAS C.A., in Venezuela, and Marahachi Muramatsu, in Japan, were notified of negative findings.

In its letter to Grupo VPAS, the FDA stated that it found multiple deviations from the HACCP requirements, including some serious violations, during an assessment of its seafood processing facility in Venezuela's state of Miranda in January 2024. The findings were in relation, in particular, to fresh-frozen IQF medregal fillets.

Grupo VPAS responded to FDA's findings via email in February, but sent the documents in Spanish and didn't respond to requests for translated copies, the federal agency said.

"Therefore, we used Google Hub Translate, a trustworthy tool, to translate the documents you submitted in your Feb. 16, 2024 response," the FDA said in its warning letter. "Our evaluation is based on our review of this translation."

FDA warned that the company's fish could be refused admission in the US if it don't respond and take the appropriate action.

The FDA also sent a letter to a Japanese seafood processor, Maruhachi Muramatsu Inc., Danchi Factory, on Oct. 17. The FDA had inspected the company's facility in Japan's Shizuoka prefecture in April and found that its reduced oxygen packaged (ROP) soup Noko Dashi Katsuo (skipjack tuna extract soup base) is adulterated in that it has been held in insanitary conditions.

Maruhachi Muramatsu also has been ordered to address HACCP violations or risk being placed on detention without physical examination (DWPE).

A third warning letter from the FDA, dated Aug. 30, was sent to Thailand's Kyokuyo Global Seafoods. It addressed HACCP violations discovered while inspecting the company's processing facility in January, including the finding that raw and cooked mackerel and frozen red shrimp were found to have been adulterated. 

Kyokuyo Global also has been warned about its products being placed on DWPE if the company didn't respond.

The final FDA letter that was published Tuesday by the FDA was sent on March 6 in response to an inspection at Procesadora Vikingo CA's facility in Zulia, Venezuela. The processor's ready-to-eat crabmeat was deemed to be adulterated. Addtionally, the company failed to list the food safety hazard of undeclared allergens, as blue crabs are considered a "major food allergen," the FDA advised.

These are not the only warning letters the FDA published in November. This month the federal agency also published warning letters for a Venezuelan processor and a Chinese processor, as reported by Undercurrent News.

title: Trump vowed to end offshore wind, but will cabinet pick make good on promise?
content:
Donald Trump has promised to end offshore wind in the US on day one of his next presidency -- a commitment that many in the commercial fishing industry applaud -- but will his cabinet pick carry out the task? 

Trump announced Doug Burgum, the Republican governor of North Dakota since 2016, was his pick to run the Department of Interior (DOI) on Nov. 14, putting him in charge of the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM), the division within DOI that has the power to propel or stall offshore wind development. 

Assuming he is confirmed by the US Senate, the 68-year-old politician is also expected to lead a newly created National Energy Council that will seek to establish US "energy dominance" around the world.

Like past interior secretaries under Trump, Burgum has previously described himself as having an "all-of-the-above" position when it comes to energy. As of 2023, North Dakota was getting 55% of its electricity from coal-fired power plants and 36% from wind energy, the sixth-highest share of wind power for any state, according to the US Energy Information Administration. 

Burgum was still a relatively new governor in 2017 when North Dakota was in the midst of a major surge in wind energy development, with production doubling between 2015 and 2023, E&E News reported.

Image from Shutterstock.

Also, despite Trump's earlier pledge to do away with windfarms, at least one Washington, D.C.-based group that represents the offshore wind, oil and gas industries trusts Burgum to champion the energy source. 

"Governor Doug Burgum has a proven track record in North Dakota and has been a strong advocate for energy policies that prioritize domestic production and streamline regulations," Erik Milito, president of the National Ocean Industries Association (NOIA), said in a statement voicing his support for Trump's pick.

"His deep understanding of American energy resources and public lands positions him to tackle critical issues such as enhancing energy affordability, alleviating inflation, creating high-paying jobs, and strengthening the US in the global energy marketplace," Milito said. "We are excited about his leadership..."

FREE READ US harvesters hold floating protest against New England offshore wind project

Another US trade group more focused on offshore wind, the American Clean Power Association, has yet to make a statement about the pick.

The rest of Burgum's background doesn't provide much of a hint about his offshore wind positions either. He served as a software executive for Great Plains Software, which Microsoft bought for $1.1 billion 2001. He briefly ran for president in the 2024 Republican primary but suspended his campaign in Dec. 2023 and instead endorsed Trump, who later considered him as a candidate for vice president.

Unlike several of Trump's other cabinet picks, Burgum seems to hardly ignite controversy. The Union of Concerned Scientists, an NGO that promotes efforts to fight climate change, however, has expressed concern about his ties to fossil fuels. It noted several red flags in a recent article, describing how he once helped organize an "infamous dinner at Mar-a-Lago where Trump solicited $1 billion in campaign donations from oil and gas executives."

'They kill the birds, they kill the whales'

The 45th and soon-to-be 47th president of the US has made a lot of dramatic promises to be accomplished the day after he is sworn in on Jan. 20, 2025, including beginning mass deportations of illegal immigrants, pardoning Jan. 6, 2021 rioters, firing a large number of federal employees and -- recently -- unleashing a whole new slew of tariffs.

It seems unlikely that all can be accomplished so quickly.

But at a campaign rally in Wildwood, New Jersey, on May 11, he said something that the commercial fishing industry hopes was a firm commitment.

"We are going to make sure that that ends on day one," Trump said about offshore wind. "I'm going to write it out in an executive order. It's going to end on day one."

He continued: "They destroy everything. They're horrible, the most expensive energy there is. They ruin the environment, they kill the birds, they kill the whales."

Trump's statements about offshore wind were starkly different than those made by outgoing president Joe Biden. Way back in 2021, Biden established a target to employ tens of thousands of workers to create windfarms that will generate 30 gigawatts (30,000 megawatts) of offshore wind by 2030, a commitment known as "30-by-30."

The departments of Interior, Energy, and Commerce said at the time that meeting the goal will not only trigger more than $12 billion per year in capital investment in projects on both US coasts, but also generate enough power to meet the demand of more than 10 million American homes for a year. The energy will also avoid 78m metric tons of CO2 emissions, they said.

While the current administration touts the pros of offshore wind, the areas where these projects are taking place are surrounded by some extremely lucrative fishing grounds, including those for lobster and scallops.

Offshore wind fight could be headed to US’ highest court with earlier lobster ruling playing part

The commercial fishing industry has expressed frustration about being left out of the conversations regarding offshore wind, and for the lack of research on how the location of these massive turbines will impact the fisheries.

Environmentalists have also expressed concerns about the overall impact of offshore wind on marine life, with a lot of uncertainties surrounding how the turbines might further threaten endangered North Atlantic right whales.

Not as easy as an executive order

Ending offshore wind isn't as easy as writing out an executive order, Tina Zappile, director of the Hughes Center for Public Policy at Stockton University, in New Jersey, countered in a recent article for the Associated Press.

In fact, it's unlikely Trump's presidency will even do much to slow progress for the industry in the US, even after day one, she believes.

"Offshore wind might appear to be on the chopping block -- Trump's explicitly said this was something he'd fix on the first day -- but when the economics of offshore wind are in alignment with his overall strategies of returning manufacturing to America and becoming energy-independent, his administration is likely to back away slowly from this claim," she said. "Offshore wind may be temporarily hampered, but its long-term prospects in the US are unlikely to be hurt."

Trump’s return to White House threatens more seafood tariffs, end of Russia ban

The Register, a global news service based in London, also expressed skepticism back in May, when Trump first made his anti-offshore wind declaration.

"[E]ven for wind farms that are completely under the jurisdiction of the federal government, such an executive order would probably result in a court case," it reported.

But others believe Burgum could do damage to the initiative.

TGC 4C Offshore, a UK-based offshore wind information service, has suggested that "Burgum's emphasis on carbon management and land-based projects may deprioritize federal support for offshore wind development, slowing its momentum or shifting funds to other renewable and transitional technologies like carbon storage."

The firm further advised, however: "While Burgum's policies could temper federal enthusiasm for offshore wind, state governments and private stakeholders may continue to drive these projects independently. The long-term impact will likely depend on legislative dynamics and broader political pressures in a new administration."

Prior interior secretaries encouraged offshore wind

The White House provided a politically-driven update on offshore wind efforts in September, boasting that while the Biden administration has approved its 10th offshore wind project so far, accounting for a combined 15gw of power, enough to supply 5.25m homes, the "previous administration approved none."

While that may be the case, it would not be accurate to say that Trump was altogether opposed to offshore wind during his first term. At least one of his first interior secretaries, Ryan Zinke (2017-2018), in fact, was supportive.

In April 2018, when two areas off Massachusetts -- approximately 390,000 acres -- became available for commercial offshore wind energy, Zinke said that the Trump administration supports "an all-of-the-above energy policy and using every tool available to achieve American energy dominance," the Associated Press reported at the time.

Then, in October 2018, Zinke boasted in a press release that the Trump administration had delivered "historic progress" on offshore wind. That progress included  also the environmental review of a proposed wind project off the Rhode Island coast and the "next steps to a first-ever wind auction in federal waters off of California."

Photo Credit: Vineyard Wind

"I'm very bullish on offshore wind, and harnessing this renewable resource is a big part of the Trump administration's 'Made in America' energy strategy," Zinke said, adding:

"We are always looking at new ways to increase American innovation and productivity to provide abundant and affordable energy for our homes and manufacturers. I think this is a win for America. Working together with states, fishermen and the energy industry, we are making offshore wind a reality, and these three historic announcements are proof."

In December 2018, following the bidding for offshore Massachusetts leases, the DOI announced the winners in a press release with a headline that read: "BIDDING BONANZA! Trump administration smashes record for offshore wind auction with $405 million winning bids." 

Zinke added: "To anyone who doubted that our ambitious vision for energy dominance would not include renewables, today we put that rumor to rest. With bold leadership, faster, streamlined environmental reviews, and a lot of hard work with our states and fishermen, we've given the wind industry the confidence to think and bid big."

Also important to note, however, is that Zinke issued his resignation letter around the same time, ending his short tenure with a total of 18 federal investigations into his behavior, as reported by Citizens for Ethics. He remains active in Congress, having been elected to the House of Representatives for Montana in 2023. 

Trump's next interior secretary, David Bernhardt (2019-2021), met with fishermen in July 2020 to discuss their concerns regarding offshore wind. He used the opportunity to reassure them that, while the Trump administration was supportive of offshore wind, it also was taking the commercial fishing industry into account.

Leading up to Trump's exit from the White House in January 2021, the interior solicitor, Daniel Jorjani, issued an opinion in December 2020 stating that any offshore wind development that the DOI permits must have minimal conflict on the fishing industry and other activities that take place in the water. 

Photo Credit: Vineyard Wind

That move did slow the offshore wind process a bit in that the opinion made offshore wind company Vineyard Wind withdraw its construction and operation plans for federal waters off of Martha's Vineyard. However, the company resubmitted the plans once Biden entered office and, by May 2021, Biden-appointed interior secretary Deb Haaland announced the approval of the construction and operation of the Vineyard Wind Project, the first large-scale offshore wind project in the US.

Operations at Vineyard Wind were suspended this summer when a blade broke, littering the ocean with fiberglass debris. While some construction on the project has resumed, operations and power production were still halted as of an Oct. 23, 2024 update from the company.

title: Clean Seas suffers heightened mortalities in 2024 year class
content:
Listed Australian yellowtail kingfish farmer Clean Seas Seafood has withdrawn its 2025 outlook guidance for the time being as it gets to grips with a mortality event impacting one year class of fish.

The reason for the "higher-than-expected mortalities within the year class 2024 cohort" remains under investigation, as is the ongoing treatment for the remaining fish, and work is underway to assess the impact on the business for the current and subsequent periods, it said.

Clean Seas completes farming consolidation, sees feed costs ease

"Whilst it is not uncommon to see an increase in mortality rates in the warmer summer months, the losses currently being experienced, combined with a preliminary assessment of the condition of a sub-population of the remaining live fish, indicates that mortality rates will be in excess of the levels which formed the basis of previous guidance."

As a result, Clean Seas has withdrawn its previous guidance as to the 2025 financial year's sales volumes and operating earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization.

They had stood at 2,550-2,650 metric tons and a "modest loss," already revised once this month on the back of the "ongoing impact of operational challenges reported in July 2024."

While the performance of the 2024 year class is disappointing, Clean Seas is seeing an "encouraging performance to date in the year class 2025 cohort," it said.

"As previously reported, Clean Seas has made significant changes to its organizational and operational structure, and the benefits of these changes continue to be seen on the farms and in the performance of the year class 2025 cohort."

A new automated feed barge, the Eyre Spirit, has been deployed on its farm and is performing as expected. "This crucial piece of infrastructure will bring lasting benefits with respect to operating costs and capability, feed conversion rates, and diet and feeding practice development," it said.

title: Fatal Nova Scotia fishing vessel sinking was result of ‘severe’ weather
content:
A fatal vessel sinking that occurred off the shores of the Canadian province Nova Scotia in March 2022 was a result of "severe" weather conditions, according to a new 55-page report from the Transportation Safety Board of Canada (TSB).

The Mucktown Girl, a 42-foot vessel designed for lobster fishing but adapted to fish halibut using longline, was more than 160 kilometers southeast of Canso, Nova Scotia, with its crew of five when it ran into engine trouble on March 11, 2022, Undercurrent News reported at the time. The incident led to the death of one member of the fishing crew and the injury of two Canadian Coast Guard (CCG) members.

A subsequent investigation by TSB found that escalating weather conditions ultimately caused the tow arrangement to fail, and a breakdown in communication as a result of environmental conditions led to the death of one of Mucktown Girl's crew.

The CCG vessel, the Jean Goodwill, responded to a request for help from Mucktown Girl and began to tow the boat back on March 12. However, a failure with the towing arrangement during increasingly difficult weather conditions -- and concerns about causing further damage while re-attaching the tow line -- left Mucktown Girl adrift.

The Jean Goodwill was ordered to stand by until conditions improved and the tow could be re-established, according to the report. But hours later, the Mucktown Girl began taking on water. That's when fatal mistakes were made as the Mucktown Girl was hit with winds of 45 to 50 knots with 8 to 10 m seas, heavy rain and dense fog, according to the report.

Rough seas. Credit: Oskar Porkka/Shutterstock.com

The investigation determined that the weather and high seas forced the Mucktown Girl crew to stay on board the disabled vessel and for the Jean Goodwill to keep a safe distance. But that also meant that it took about 40 minutes for the CCG to return to the vessel and attempt to get into a position to rescue crew members.

The situation only worsened when, "without advising the Jean Goodwill, and in very rough seas," the crew of the Mucktown Girl abandoned the vessel to enter a life raft.

"With the vessel rolling heavily and the deck awash with debris, two members of the Jean Goodwill crew were severely injured during the urgent preparations for the rescue," TSB's findings concluded. 

Multiple crew members jumped from the life raft without waiting for instructions from the Coast Guard, according to the report. One of those crew members, while wearing an immersion suit, was hit by a wave and ended up in the water. The crew member was found via a helicopter hours later and brought to Cape Breton Regional Hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

Actions for the future

In addition to TSB's investigation confirming the causes and contributing factors to the fatal at-sea incident, the report also highlighted "conditions, unsafe acts or safety deficiencies," which were not a factor in the Mucktown Girl's sinking but could be a risk in a future incident.

TSB reiterated that contingency planning and emergency drills using realistic scenarios could help vessel crews if they face a similar situation in the future. The Canadian agency also noted that there is "no mandatory post-occurrence drug and alcohol testing of crews involved in maritime occurrences." 

In the case of Mucktow Girl, TSB said that the use of drugs and alcohol was reported on the vessel before and during the voyage. However, current Canadian laws do not require drug and alcohol testing following a marine accident or incident. Because of this, investigators said they have a limited ability to determine if drugs and alcohol were a factor.

title: Investigation claims ASC-certified, unsustainable Chilean salmon sold in Europe
content:
The Aquaculture Stewardship Council (ASC) faces scrutiny over its certification of Chilean salmon farms operating in protected areas following an investigation by the Dutch news outlet Follow the Money.

Nova Austral gets new board, owner as restructuring takes effect

Follow the Money found ASC-certified farms are operating in Chilean nature reserves and national parks, including facilities run by Nova Austral in the Alberto de Agostini National Park.

Nova Austral, which operates 19 farms in the park -- six of which are ASC-certified -- has previously faced sanctions for overproduction and environmental violations. Follow the Money traced its ASC-certified salmon to major European retailers, including Albert Heijn and Delhaize.

ASC head of standards Michiel Fransen told Follow the Money the organization plans to evaluate its protected areas certification policies next year.

title: Vietnam seafood processor issued FDA warning letter after histamine poisoning incident
content:
Golden Shrimp Seafood Joint Stock Company, a Vietnam-based seafood processor, has been issued a warning letter by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) following a complaint involving a consumer getting histamine poisoning from one of the company's saku, cubed and ground yellowfin tuna products.

The FDA's Center for Food Safety and Applied Nutrition posted the warning letter on its compliance page on Tuesday (Nov. 19) after sending the document to Golden Shrimp company director Phuc T. Vo in May. 

Golden Shrimp had its seafood processing facility in Thuan Yen Village inspected by the FDA on Dec. 11 and 12, 2023. During the inspection, the agency reportedly found "serious violations of the seafood Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) regulation."

The company sent multiple responses to the FDA in the weeks that followed, which included corrective actions, product testing, and updated raw ingredient sampling procedures for histamine. However, the FDA said the company's response was "not adequate."

Among the significant violations at Golden Shrimp was that the firm's HACCP plan for its "Frozen Yellowfin Tuna CO/TS treated, Cut into Loin, Saku, Cube, Steak, Strip, Crazy, Portions" did not list adequate critical limits, FDA said. 

While the company did take multiple samples to test for scombrotoxin (histamine) formation, the FDA said it recommended sampling a different portion of the fish loin in order to "provide the best information about the histamine content of the fish."

Golden Shrimp provided the FDA with corrective actions for its sampling procedures, but the agency said that it failed to update its HACCP plan. 

"Therefore, regarding your updated sampling practices, we cannot evaluate the adequacy of your corrective actions," FDA said.

If Golden Shrimp fails to respond, or the FDA finds the company's response inadequate, the agency said it could take further action to refuse the product's admission into the US. The company is already placed on the FDA's Import Alerts "Red List," which means that its imports are subject to "detention without physical exam" or "DWPE."

title: US mislabeling scheme saga continues with seafood restaurant’s sentencing
content:
Mary Mahoney's Old French House in the US city of Biloxi, Mississippi, and its co-owner and manager, Anthony Charles Cvitanovich, have been sentenced in a federal court on charges related to their participation in a conspiracy to misbrand imported seafood as local, premium fish.

The fine-dining restaurant has been a staple in the historic Biloxi building since 1964, and is even referenced in some John Grisham novels. However, this past year, the restaurant made undesired headlines after it was discovered that one of its co-owners and managers was involved in a long-standing conspiracy to fraudulently sell imported frozen fish as fresh, domestic-caught seafood.

In May 2024, Mary Mahoney's Old French House and Cvitanovich pled guilty in the US District Court for the Southern District of Mississippi to conspiracy to misbrand seafood and wire fraud, as reported by Undercurrent News. The court, on Monday (Nov. 18), accepted the sentencing terms of the plea agreement, federal prosecutors said in a press release. 

The company was given five years of probation and issued a $1.5m penalty, which includes the forfeiture of $1,350,000 and a criminal fine of $149,000. 

In addition, Mary Mahoney's must also maintain records -- for no less than five years -- in which it describes species, sources and the cost of the seafood it acquires for sale to its customers. Those records will be available to any federal, state or local governmental authority that regulates or monitors service and distribution of food for human consumption, or any agency that regulates harvesting, storage, labeling or sale of seafood, according to the Justice Department.

Cvitanovich has been sentenced to three years of probation and four months of home detention. He must pay a $10,000 fine.

The crackdown continues

The Mary Mahoney saga doesn't end here though. More sentencing in the conspiracy to misbrand seafood are expected when Biloxi seafood wholesaler Quality Poultry and Seafood (QPS) and two of its managers return to court on Dec. 11.

QPS is the largest wholesaler on the Mississippi Gulf Coast. This summer the company admitted to participating in the scheme to substitute fish with Mary Mahoney's and some other local restaurants. Prosecutors said that the scheme ran from 2002 through November 2019, with QPS also mislabeling seafood at its own retail shop and cafe.

Large Mississippi wholesaler to forfeit $1m for mislabeling frozen, imported fish

Between Dec. 2013 and Nov. 2019, Mary Mahoney's Old French House reportedly sold about 58,750 lbs of frozen and imported fish from Africa, India and South America, falsely claiming it was fresh, domestic caught.

The fish  was described on Mahoney's menu as premium higher-priced local species, such as snapper and grouper from the Gulf of Mexico, when it was actually Lake Victoria perch from Africa, triple tail from Suriname, unicorn filefish from India and others, as reported by Undercurrent.

Further, QPS is accused of continuing to mislabel seafood even after knowing it was under federal investigation.

"When imported substitutes are marketed as local domestic seafood, it depresses the value of authentic Gulf Coast seafood, which means that honest local fishermen and wholesalers have a harder time making a profit," Todd Gee, the US attorney for Southern Mississippi, said in August when QPS had to forfeit $1m.

"These convictions should serve as a warning: Restaurants and wholesalers will face criminal prosecution if they are not honest with customers about what they are actually buying."

title: Ex-bankrupt with past seafood theft conviction buys back UK plant in pre-pack deal
content:
A new UK seafood company that has inked a pre-pack administration deal for a processing plant is connected to a man with a history of fraud and theft in the industry, Undercurrent News has learned. 

Ramus (Grimsby) was named late last month as the buyer of Grimsby-based D&A Seafood Solutions, which entered administration following unsuccessful attempts to restructure, according to a statement from administrator Quantuma Advisory.

Quantuma handled the sale of D&A -- which was founded in 2015 to supply chilled, pre-pack seafood to UK retail and wholesale -- to Ramus (Grimsby) via a so-called "pre-pack" administration. A pre-pack is where the sale of a business is agreed prior to the administrator being formally appointed, to a connected or unconnected buyer.

Barclays, Nordic whitefish suppliers out of pocket from £4m Cook & Lucas bankruptcy

What Quantuma does not state in the press release, however, is the links between Ramus (Grimsby) and D&A, which was owned by Alistair Ramus, who was prohibited from being a company director until 2022 due to a past personal bankruptcy and was sentenced to three years in prison in 2009 for theft and false accounting.

Ramus -- whose criminal conviction stems from his defrauding of M&J Seafoods in 2007-2008, after which he ran a similar scam on Ocean Trawlers -- did not respond to a request for comment from Undercurrent News. 

Quantuma also did not respond to Undercurrent when asked for more details on the sale of D&A, which has been producing seafood under the Mawgan Bay and Ramus Seafood brands.

The Ramus Seafood range. Credit: Ramus Seafood's Facebook page

The pre-pack deal happened just over two years after Ramus was formally named a director of D&A on Sept. 15, 2022, the day after his 12-year bankruptcy restriction order (BRO) was lifted.

A BRO can last for between two and 15 years, depending on the severity of the conduct of the individual. BROs are put in place "if you are bankrupt and the official receiver thinks you have been dishonest or are to blame for your debts," the UK government's website states.

The company also used the Mawgan Bay brand. Credit: Mawgan Bay Facebook page

The BRO was placed on Ramus on Sept. 14, 2010, after he'd declared personal bankruptcy in June 2009. The bankruptcy declaration came the month before the UK's High Court of Justice ruled in favor of Ocean Trawlers, now named Norebo Holdings, in its civil action against Ramus, an accomplice, and a company named Ocean Hawk.

Ramus was sentenced to three years and three months in prison on March 9, 2009, for theft and false accounting while managing the Park Royal branch of M&J in northwest London. Between August 2007 and February 2008, Ramus sold M&J's fish for his own benefit, netting around £400,000 ($507,000), London's Metropolitan Police said at the time.

In April 2008, while under investigation for the M&J theft, Ramus got a job with what was then Ocean Trawlers UK, public court documents from the time state.

Cook & Lucas smokehouse closes with Barclays-appointed administrator chasing assets

Prior to his dismissal by Ocean Trawlers in November 2008, he defrauded the company of $7 million, according to the court documents in the civil case brought at the time.

Like the M&J scam but on a larger scale, Ocean Trawlers claimed Ramus used Ocean Hawk to sell its fish and then kept the cash, it was stated in legal documents. 

D&A pre-pack deal

After serving his time for the M&J theft, Ramus got going in the seafood sector again, seemingly undeterred by the BRO for the Ocean Trawlers scam. On Nov. 25, 2010, his wife Donna was named a director of The Fine Seafood Company, which was the first entity the Ramus' used to operate in the sector.

They then moved to use D&A in 2015, then a company named MBR Group was registered in 2019. Donna became a director first, with Alistair being formally named on Sept. 15, 2022, after the BRO expired and just over two years before the D&A pre-pack deal. The pre-pack sale of D&A was closed on Oct. 31 to Ramus (Grimsby), which was registered on May 30, 2024, meaning 32 staff transferred across to the new business.

Despite the buyer's name, neither Alistair nor Donna Ramus are currently directors of Ramus (Grimsby). George Constantinescu is shown as the only director and controlling shareholder of Ramus (Grimsby), having been terminated from the same role at D&A on March 8. 

However, "it is also understood" that Alistair Ramus "is likely to become a director of Ramus (Grimsby)," states an administration report from Quantuma filed to Companies House on Nov. 12.

In addition, a company named Ramus (Trading) was incorporated on Oct. 28, 2024, with Alistair Ramus as the director. Ramus (Trading) has the same address in London as the one used to register Ramus (Grimsby), although the latter has since been shifted to one from Grimsby.

UK processor owned by Ferrari-loving ex-bankrupt abruptly closes plant

The D&A deal, which was done for £65,000, with £5,000 paid upfront and the rest due over the next eight months, was also secured with personal guarantees from Constantinescu and Ramus, the Quantuma report states.

Then, the BRCGS -- formerly British Retail Consortium -- certification site has Alistair Ramus listed as a point of contact for Ramus (Grimsby). 

The pre-pack sale comes after D&A's financial position deteriorated significantly, with company records showing net liabilities had increased to £474,700 ($611,665) by December 2022, more than doubling from £230,853 the previous year. Trade creditors had also risen sharply to £952,718 from £424,837.

D&A went under with creditors of £1.46m, however, with the largest at £450,000 being MBR, of which Alistair and Donna Ramus are directors.

Next is HM Revenue & Customs, the UK's tax, payments and customs authority, which is owed £401,862.

The next largest creditor is SP Hull (2021), a salmon supplier which is owed £357,628.77.

Path to pre-pack

According to the Quantuma administration report, D&A was registered in 2015 in Wembley, northwest London, to supply pre-packaged fish and seafood. In mid-2017, the company moved to Grimsby, having outgrown its Wembley premises, the report states.

At the end of the year, the "business hit extreme hardship" when one of its major customers went into liquidation, leaving it with an uninsured debt of £90,000. "The business re-financed in 2018 and again in 2019, which gave it the leverage to move forward," Quantuma states.

In May 2019, D&A was merged with Ramus Seafoods -- the business founded by Alistair's late father, Chris -- which owned fishmongers in Harrogate and Ilkley in Yorkshire.

Cook & Lucas director’s son sets up in Kirwin factory processing for chippy chain Papa’s

Ramus Seafoods was then owned by a private equity firm, and the ownership structure moved to MBR, of which Donna Ramus was appointed a director in March 2019. Alistair Ramus was then appointed a director of D&A, MBR, and Ramus Seafoods in September 2022 after his BRO had run its course.

Ramus Seafoods "was debt laden and the deal was under financed, and the group struggled to cope with the creditors that it had," according to Quantuma.

In early 2020, as the COVID-19 pandemic hit, Ramus Seafoods' outlets closed and did not reopen, ultimately relaunching as a "premium seafood supplier to the retailers," states Quantuma.

At this point, Alistair Ramus was still restricted from being a director under his BRO from 2010. However, he was named in the press as the owner of Ramus Seafoods while under the BRO.

According to a Yorkshire Post article on the 2021 suicide of Chris Ramus, the shops in Harrogate and Ilkley closed "under the ownership of his son Alistair."

The Harrogate Advertiser also described him as the owner of the business in a Jan. 29, 2020, article about the closing of its operation in the Yorkshire town and switching to sell in via Fodder Farmshop & Cafe, also based in Harrogate. Fodder did not respond to a request for comment from Undercurrent on whether this continues, but there is no mention of Ramus Seafoods on its website. 

Ramus also made the news twice in 2022. Firstly, in May, it emerged he had been spared a driving ban, "having failed to give information to Yorkshire police about the identity of a driver of 62-reg Mercedes believed to have committed an offence," the Hampshire Chronicle reported.

"He had pleaded guilty under the single justice procedure at Humber Magistrates Court. Magistrates heard that regarding a ban there were mitigating circumstances: effect on reduction in staff, effect on mother, and financial implications on family," the report states.

FREE READ UK smokehouse owner loses £37,000 in London salmon scam

In 2022, the Ramus family made the news again when Elizabeth Ramus, Chris' widow, "lost a court battle against her daughter for control of the family's inheritance after a judge ruled she was rich enough to look after herself," as Today's Wills and Probate reported.  

Claire Holt, daughter of Chris and Elizabeth, "appeared to be concerned that Mrs. Ramus was seeking a capital sum for the use of the couple's son, Alistair, who had a difficult relationship with the family and a criminal conviction for fraud for which he served a custodial sentence," according to a blog post from law firm JMW on the case.

"Holt claimed whilst her father was alive her brother persuaded their mother to leave their father because he no longer financially supported him. She also alleged her brother had attacked their father and threatened to kill him," the Today's Wills and Probate report states.

Judge Mark West ruled that Alistair Ramus played no active part in the proceedings, but it was inferred that Elizabeth Ramus wanted the fund so she could pass the inheritance on to her son, according to Today's Wills and Probate. 

HSBC pulls financing

In addition to the legal issues, the Ramus' were struggling with D&A in 2022. In July of that year, D&A ran into issues when lender HSBC withdrew its financial support on a risk basis, which required Ramus "to go to a new invoice finance provider which was significantly more expensive," the report states.

Then came the Russian invasion of Ukraine, and the global food inflation that followed, which saw D&A hit with "significant price increases on raw material, packaging, utilities and waste and could not react with price increases quicker than the cost rise."

Despite having some success with mitigation measures, the business by this stage could not cope with the payments to its legacy creditors. It tried a so-called company voluntary arrangement (CVA), a UK insolvency process that allows a business to restructure its debts and continue trading while paying creditors over a set period. However, it was unable to maintain the payments under the CVA.

Quantuma were first approached by the company in July 2023 in relation to the preceding CVA and was then instructed on Sept. 4 in relation to the administration and pre-pack deal.

title: ITC rules US shrimp industry suffered as a result of imports, cements AD, CVD rates
content:
The anti-dumping (AD) and countervailing duty (CVD) rates that the US handed importers of shrimp from India, Ecuador, Indonesia and Vietnam are now set in stone, and probably in place for at least another 18 months.

The US International Trade Commission (ITC) voted unanimously, 4-0, on Tuesday (Nov. 19) in a finding that the US domestic shrimp industry has been materially injured by both the imports of frozen warmwater shrimp from Indonesia at less than fair value and also by the subsidies paid to shrimp producers in Ecuador, India and Vietnam.

As a result, the AD and CVD-related rates set by the Department of Commerce on Oct. 22, as reported by Undercurrent News, will not be extinguished as might've been hoped by those big shrimp-producing countries. Neither will duties be repaid.

Frozen head-on vannamei shrimp at a plant in Ecuador. Credit: Louis Harkell / Undercurrent News

Also, the rates are likely to continue until at least 2027, as an administrative review won't be started until the end of 2025 or beginning of 2026, and the procedure will likely take at least 18 months, one source explained to Undercurrent.

Such an outcome was never assured, sources tell Undercurrent. In September 2013, the Department of Commerce found that foreign shrimp producers in China, Ecuador, India, Malaysia and Vietnam had received countervailable subsidies of between 1.15% and 54.5% but the ITC determined that the domestic industry was not injured by imports and no trade relief was imposed. 

It was a different outcome this time. 

"In these investigations, the domestic industry's share of US apparent consumption continues to be substantially less than the share supplied by either subject or nonsubject imports, ranging from 5.5% to 6.8% on an annual basis over [the period of investigation]," the Ad Hoc Shrimp Trade Action Committee, a group representing domestic producers, wrote in its arguments sent to ITC Thursday (Nov. 14).

"However, subject imports now constitute a substantial majority of the US market, with subject imports from Ecuador and India alone accounting for between 57.9% and 64.1% of annual US apparent consumption over [the period of investigation]."

The chart below from UCN's trade portal shows how the US imported 788,087 metric tons of shrimp worth $6.7 billion in 2023, 90% of which came from the four countries involved in the recent action. 

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
Devi stuck with 5.87% subsidy rate

As a result of Tuesday's decisions, importers of shrimp produced by India's Devi Sea Foods Limited can look forward to paying a subsidy rate of 5.87% for the next couple of years, while importers of shrimp from Sandhya Aqua Exports will pay 5.63% and importers of all other Indian shrimp pay 5.77%.

Importers of shrimp produced by Ecuador's Industrial Pesquera Santa Priscilla will be forced to pay a subsidy rate of 3.57%, while importers of shrimp from Sociedad Nacional de Galapagos (Songa) will be forced to pay 4.41% and importers of all other Ecuadorian shrimp will pay 3.78%.

It could've been worse for the Ecuadorians. Songa, the US' second-largest source of shrimp from Ecuador, was earlier handed a 0.0% dumping rate by Commerce -- a big difference from the 10.58% in the preliminary determination. Santa Priscila kept its 0.48% de minimis dumping rate.

However, importers of shrimp produced in Indonesia, other than Bahari Makmur Sejati (BMS), will be forced to pay an AD rate of 3.9%. BMS won an exemption from the AD duties.  

Vietnam's Soc Trang Seafood Joint Stock Company was earlier handed a 2.84% subsidy rate, but fellow Vietnamese producer Thong Thuan Company Limited was issued a 221.82% subsidy rate. The Department of Commerce noted that Thong Thuan's rate was "based on adverse inferences." This rate is up from the 196.41% issued in the preliminary rates.

US wholesale update: Shrimp prices take bullish stance after final AD/CVD determinations

Thong Tuan is considered an outlier. Sources previously told Undercurrent that the high rate was likely punishment for the company not fully cooperating with investigators. All other Vietnamese exporters and producers were issued a final CVD rate of 2.84%.

Domestic producers grateful

The ITC's affirmative determination is in response to petitions for trade relief filed in October 2023 by the American Shrimp Processors Association (ASPA), a group that reports to represent about 85% of the US domestic frozen warmwater shrimp production, as reported by Undercurrent.

"Domestic landings fell by a sharp 28.6% from the first half of 2022 to the first half of 2023," ASP had testified at the time. "Dockside prices also crashed. From June of 2022 to June of 2023, ex-vessel prices for a 26/30 size Gulf [of Mexico] shrimp fell by a staggering 44.7%."

Trey Pearson, ASPA's president, issued a statement late on Tuesday, saying his group is "thrilled with the outcome" of the ITC decision. He said more than 800 shrimp boats expressed their support for his group's petitions, and "dozens of processors and an unprecedented number of shrimp harvesters took the time to fill out questionnaires for the Commission's injury investigation."

He added: "Today’s vote validates what we have known all along – that dumped and subsidized imports are the reason our industry has been thrown into crisis."  

The Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA), a group that represents domestic harvesters and processors in the Southeastern US, also celebrated the decision with a statement released Tuesday. ITC based its determination on evidence provided by 20 US processors of shrimp and 388 shrimp harvesters, SSA noted. 

"The Southern Shrimp Alliance welcomes the US International Trade Commission's acknowledgement of the pain that our industry has experienced over the last couple of years due to a flood of unfairly-traded shrimp imports," said John Williams, SSA's executive director.

title: Peltola defeat, Golden win among 11 US election results that matter to seafood
content:
Mary Peltola appears out as Alaska's lone member of the US House of Representatives, but one of her fellow Democrats in the lower chamber, Jared Golden of Maine, has won re-election.

The two lawmakers' 2024 election efforts were among at least 11 of consequence to the US seafood industry that Undercurrent News followed closely but whose results were delayed due in part to their states' use of ranked-choice voting (RCV).

Peltola, who has served in the House for just two years, was trailing Republican challenger Nick Begich by a 149,192 (46.3%) to 156,415 (48.5%) vote count -- a 7,223-vote difference -- with 98.8% of the first round votes counted, Alaska's News Source reported Tuesday morning (Nov. 19).

Peltola gained some ground when some 4,000 absentee ballot votes were counted on Monday (Nov. 18), but she doesn't seem to have much of a chance.

Credit: Peter Hermes Furian/Shutterstock

Peltola was hoping to be saved by Alaska's RCV system, which counts second-choice selections when no candidate achieves at least 50% of the overall vote. The other candidates in the race had 16,677 votes. The final results are expected to be reported on Nov. 20. 

Begich declared himself the winner on Saturday (Nov. 16). "Alaskans have spoken," he said in a social media post. "It will be the honor of a lifetime to have the opportunity to serve as your voice in Congress."

Decision Desk HQ, a respected election results website, projected Begich the winner on Saturday morning, too.

Peltola's expected loss would appear to give Republicans at least 220 of the House's 435 seats, more than the 218 needed to hold a majority, meaning the GOP now looks to hold the trifecta of the White House, Senate and House starting in 2025.

Peltola polarizing in seafood industry

Alaska is the US' most important seafood state, responsible for 2.2 million metric tons of landings worth $2.1 billion in 2022, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). It has eight of the US' 20-biggest landings ports, according to NOAA.

But Alaska is limited to just one critical US House seat.

Recall that Peltola took the at-large seat previously held for 49 years by Republican Don Young, a champion of the commercial fishing industry, when he died in early 2022 at the age of 88. She won an emergency election against Begich and former Alaska governor Sarah Palin, also a Republican, in August 2022 and then defeated them again in a regular election in November 2022 to hold the seat. 

She has been a polarizing figure in the seafood industry. She was the co-sponsor of multiple Magnuson-Stevens Act (MSA) reauthorization bills introduced by US representative Jared Huffman, a California Democrat and the ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee's oceans panel. The seafood industry generally opposed the legislation.

Don Young during one of his many campaign promotional events. Photograph from Wikimedia.

In May 2024, Peltola introduced HR 8507, a bill that would mandate every regional fishery management council that permits the use of bottom trawl gear to define what is meant by "substantial" versus "very limited" bottom contact. It would require the designation of "bottom trawl zones," limiting the areas where gear that scraped the seafloor is allowed.

A coalition of no less than 53 seafood-related groups signed their names to a seven-page letter sent to Peltola in June, asking her to repeal her bill, as reported by Undercurrent.  

However, Peltola, who declared herself the "pro-fish" candidate in the latest election, has done some good things for the US domestic seafood industry, too. She personally lobbied for and helped secure some $300m of federal fishery disaster relief for Alaska sea crab harvesters in the massive fiscal 2023 US omnibus spending.

US seafood industry PACs spend nearly $245k on election, leave $1.3m in tank

She also was among the lawmakers to promote legislation aimed at blocking the US import of Russian seafood and also part of a group that fought to block the US import of Indian shrimp. During her brief time in the House, she helped create a bipartisan "fish caucus" to advance fisheries legislation.

The Pacific Seafood Processors Association Political Action Committee (PAC) contributed $2,000 to Peltola's campaign, which outraised the Begich campaign by $11.4 million to $2.0m. Undercurrent was not able to find a single donation by a seafood PAC to Begich.

Nick Begich. Image from 2024 campaign.

During a fish-related debate held in Kodiak, Alaska, in late October, Begich and Peltola both advocated measures to reduce bycatch, the Alaska Beacon reported. They also both said they supported legislation that would accelerate relief payments during disastrously low fish harvests and emphasized that the farm bill under consideration in Congress should provide more equitable treatment for Alaska seafood. 

Begich and Peltola differed on the use of foreign workers in Alaska's fishing industry. Seafood processors frequently bring in seasonal labor under the H-1B visa program, and Peltola said she supports continuing the practice. Begich opposes it.

"There's a 4% unemployment rate in Alaska. I want to make sure that we're prioritizing Alaskans who want to work first, before we start prioritizing people from outside of our nation to come in and take those jobs," he reportedly said during the event.

A change that threatens Murkowski

Interestingly, a ballot initiative aimed at repealing the RCV system that Peltola hoped would help her win re-election is also on the verge of passage, but it's coming down to the wire.

As of Tuesday morning, the "yes" on Ballot Measure 2 had 157,124 votes (50%) to the "no" votes, which tallied 156,932 (50%) -- a 192 vote difference with 98.8% counted. The margin is also well within the 0.5% threshold that would trigger a state-funded recount.

An official result was not expected to be announced until Nov. 20 with certification happening on Nov. 30.

As reported earlier by Undercurrent, one lawmaker who is considered a champion of the seafood industry has battled hard to keep RCV alive in Alaska. Republican senator Lisa Murkowski, who has served in the upper chamber for 22 years and is not up for re-election for another four years, has relied on RCV to insulate her from attacks from Trump in the past.

Murkowski was one of the few Republicans in the Senate to vote for Trump's impeachment in 2021, and he responded by backing her challenger in 2022.

Fisheries booster Murkowski urges Alaskans to keep ranked choice voting

RCV allows voters to rank their preferences and if a person does not win more than 50% in the first round, their second choice is redistributed. That allowed Murkowski to defeat far-right, Trump-backed Republican Kelly Tshibaka in 2022 after 300,000 votes for Democrat Pat Chesbro were redistributed in the second round, allowing Murkowski to cruise to victory with 53% of the vote.

Another Alaska initiative of consequence to the seafood industry is Ballot Measure 1, which would raise the state's minimum wage from $11.73 per hour to $15.00/hour by 2027, require medical leave for companies with 15 or more employees and prohibit employers from holding mandatory meetings on political and religious affairs unrelated to the workplace.

The measure has been declared victorious, having secured 179,200 "yes" votes (57.8%) against 130,885 "no" votes (42.2%) with 98.8% of the vote counted.

The Pacific Seafood Processors Association (PSPA) had declared its opposition to the matter, as reported by Undercurrent, saying the requirement to pay sick leave to employees would add at least $16.5m to the annual labor costs of shoreside processors. PSPA didn't oppose raising the state's minimum wage, saying its members in Alaska already pay more than the state's current minimum rate.

Where lobsters matter as much as votes

But it's not only about Alaska. Maine is another state of massive consequence to the US seafood industry as it is responsible, by far, for the largest number of North American lobster landings: 42,517t worth $464.4m last year.

Golden, as earlier reported by Undercurrent, had fought for the support of Maine's North American lobster industry in his race against Trump-backed Republican Austin Theriault to win Maine's 2nd district seat, one of only two seats held by the state in the US House.

The 2nd district, which skews Republican, includes much of the state's shoreline and is dominated by both the lobster and logging industries. 

Golden was declared victorious on Friday (Nov. 15) with 197,151 total votes compared to Theriault's 194,445, a difference that grew from 2,159 to 2,706 after the ranked choice votes were counted, according to Maine Public Media. Prior to counting the second choice votes, Golden had 48.65% of the vote to Theriault's 48.11%.

Jared Golden. Image from Golden's campaign Facebook page.

Recall that Theriault, a 30-year-old Republican state representative and former NASCAR driver, held a roundtable meeting with a few of Maine's roughly 5,000 licensed lobster harvesters in August. Then, in late September, he began running a 30-second advertisement on television and social media that suggested he was concerned about the Maine fishermen because "Washington politicians" are allowing Canadian lobster harvesters to fish illegally in US waters, as reported by Undercurrent.    

The ad didn't cite data but appears to refer to a long-running territorial dispute between US and Canadian harvesters in a part of the Gulf of Maine known as the "gray zone," a 277 square mile area of sea that both claim. Theriault promised to "put people over politics" and "hold Canada accountable."

Image is still from Austin Theriault advertisement promising action against Canadians catching lobsters in US fishery.

Not to be outdone by Theriault, Golden won praise from the Maine Lobstering Union (MLU), also known as Lobster 207, which operates as a co-operative.

In a press release published by the Maine AFL-CIO (American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations), a chapter of the US' largest collection of unions, the group applauded Golden's efforts in helping Lobster 207 secure a Small Business Administration (SBA) loan following a significant coastal storm in January that damaged multiple wharves in the state. 

Theriault's campaign has requested a recount. The election results must be certified and sent to the governor by Maine's Nov. 25 deadline, though state law grants an exception for recounts, the Associated Press reports. The recount is expected to begin around Thanksgiving and continue into December, Maine secretary of state Shenna Bellows said.

Seven other races of consequence to seafood

There were a few other races that mattered to the seafood industry, too. 

Mississippi Republican Roger Wicker will return to his seat in the US Senate after trouncing his Democratic challenger, Ty Pinkins, by a 730,555 (63.2%) to 422,555 (36.5%) count. Wicker, a senator since 2007, is best known in the seafood industry for his continued sponsorship of legislation that would ease regulations for offshore aquaculture, dating back to 2018. 

Stronger America Through Seafood, a coalition of pro-aquaculture companies, have been using the lame duck months of the current congressional session to better position offshore aquaculture for more success in the new session, as recently reported by Undercurrent.

Another US senator of consequence to the US seafood industry who won her reelection effort easily was Washington state Democrat Maria Cantwell. She scored 2,233,259 votes (59.4%) to Republican challenger Raul Garcia's 1,529,070 (40.6%) with 94% of the votes counted. Cantwell, who is returning for her fifth term since 2001, received donations totaling $10,000 from five different seafood PACs.  

Washington senator Maria Cantwell. Photograph from the Center for American Progress.

Cantwell, in 2020, stood alongside Wicker in pushing for legislation to streamline disaster relief for US fisheries. In 2022, she was among 11 lawmakers to push the US Department of Agriculture to favor west coast states in seafood-related purchases. 

US House members Rob Wittman, a Virginia Republican, and Cliff Bentz, an Oregon Republican, maintained their seats to the relief of many in the seafood industry.

Wittman has championed US domestic producers on a slew of issues, from H2B visa problems to expanding the ban on Russian products to include seafood processed in China and also further investigation of blue crab imports from Venezuela. 

Bentz, the chairman of the House's Natural Resource Committee's fisheries subcommittee, received $8,000 in contributions from the Dulcich Inc. Pacific Seafood Group Employee PAC, a group that takes donations only from employees of the Clackamas, Oregon-based seafood giant.

The biggest recipient of donations from the seafood PACs this time around was Democratic representative Suzan DelBene, who used the $11,600 given her by four seafood PACs to help her win her re-election bid for her seat in Washington state's first district. She smoked Republican challenger Jeb Brewer, 226,872 (63.2%) to 132,331 (36.8%) with 91% of the votes counted.

Jeff Van Drew.

Jeff Reichle, the chairman and owner of Lund's Fisheries, a seafood harvester and processor based in Cape May, New Jersey, and Wayne Reichle, the company's president and Jeff's son, must have been relieved to see Republican representative Jeff Van Drew won his re-election bid in New Jersey's second district. The Reichles donated $23,335 to Van Drew's campaign.

Van Drew, who has held his seat since 2019 and is known as a staunch opponent to offshore wind farms, beat Democratic challenger Joe Salerno by a 214,182 (58.3%) to 150,660 (41.0%) vote.  

Another House member whose re-election was of consequence was Huffman, the California Democrat who serves as ranking member of the Natural Resources Committee's fisheries panel. Huffman has been the architect of multiple MSA bills that've attempted to interject more climate change-related changes into fishery regulations.

Huffman won his contest in California's second district by a blow out 249,429 (81.0%) to 94,893 (27.6%) vote over Republican challenger Chris Coulombe with 81% of the votes counted.

title: Masoval sets up own sales division, will acquire part of controversial subsidiary
content:
Norwegian salmon farmer Masoval is establishing its own fully controlled sales division after its majority-owned subsidiary, Pure Norwegian Seafood (PNS), was found to have supplied fish unsuitable for human consumption earlier this year.

"As part of this effort, Masoval has entered into an agreement with PNS for the acquisition of their sales department, with takeover during Q4 2024. This agreement covers sales, logistics, and the systems related to sales operations. The intent is to retain a skilled and knowledgeable sales department with control over the entire value
chain," it said.

Masoval announces internal reshuffle to separate taxed farm assets

"Masoval Sales" should be operational by 2025, the firm said.

Masoval acquired a 65% stake in PNS in June 2021 after partnering with it since 2018. Adding the Averoy-based firm made the group fully vertically integrated for the first time.

An investigation early this year found that PNS had allowed "certain customers to buy frozen salmon that, according to Norwegian regulations, is not suitable for human consumption."

"Sold fish includes fish that either should have been discarded/ensiled, or production-graded fish that should be elaborated in secondary processing before export. The investigation estimates that this turnover of fish not suitable for human consumption constituted just under 1% of the total volume of fish and approximately 0.5% of PNS's revenue over the last three years."

In February, Masoval sold its harvesting arm in Vartdal, named Western Seaproducts, to cod farmer ODE. However, it remains in the primary harvesting business, having bought a former Mowi harvesting facility in Ulvan in Trondelag country, west of Trondheim, in January. It intended to use the facility to increase its own harvesting capacity, it said at the time.

2025 harvest estimates exceed expectations

Late in October, Masoval warned that a tough biological picture for the third quarter had pushed it to a loss of NOK 62 million ($5.6m) and had prompted it to reduce its 2024 harvest guidance once again, this time to 24,700-25,700 metric tons, gutted weight.

"Further reduction in the volume guidance after the ISA [infectious salmon anemia]-incidence is due to extraordinary high lice pressure resulting in loss of feeding days and higher mortality," it said.

It has guided for a full-year harvest for 2025 of an estimated 29,000-31,000t, including an estimated 15-20% of that on commercial co-location agreements. 60-65% of the annual volume is expected to be harvested in Norway's Region Mid, it said.

Theodor Rosenberg, analyst with Fearnley Securities, said that was above his expected 28,500t, "providing support for the share [price] today."

"Given solid growth in pipeline and proven ability to deliver top-bracket margins, Masoval screens attractively."

Helge Kvalvik, Masoval's CEO, said: "Q3 was a challenging quarter."

"Higher sea temperatures than seasonal normal in our region resulted in high sea lice pressure, which hampered growth and elevated our delousing costs. Moreover, we experienced ISA on two sites in the quarter. Harvesting salmon with low weight resulted in high cost and low prices."

In the Sales & Processing segment, the firm also reported a negative operational result, primarily driven by start-up costs at the harvesting facility TL52 at Hitra.

TL52 became operational on Sept. 3, 2024, ramped up quickly, and is today at the expected harvesting capacity for one shift, the company said. "There are still certain optimizations to be made during Q4. Masoval will initiate testing of the filleting line to gain experience ahead of the winter period."

The new facility has a capacity of 150-200t gutted weight per shift, and a value-added product capacity of 35t per shift. 

Although Q3 was a challenging one, Kvalvik highlighted the continuing positive trend in Region West, with improved biological performance yielding lower costs, higher superior shares, and increased harvest weights. "Overall, the quarter provided valuable insights that further strengthened our approach."

title: NOAA to propose seafood import monitoring expansion again, acknowledge forced labor
content:
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) on Thursday (Nov. 14) gave a preview of what it intends to do in next stab at expanding its Seafood Import Monitoring Program (SIMP).

The federal agency aims to add more high-risk species to the program and, for the first time, formally address forced labor issues in the global seafood supply chain.

The announcement follows the withdrawal, in November 2023, of a SIMP expansion proposal that was heavily criticized and comes amid rising congressional pressure to strengthen labor protection in relation to seafood imports, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

NOAA, in its just-released four-page action plan, said it intends to increase the number of high-risk species covered under SIMP, which currently covers only 13 species groups, and close loopholes allowing illegally sourced and mislabeled seafood into the US market.

The plan introduces a two-tier system to prioritize traceability based on species risk level to help authorities identify and intercept illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) products more effectively. It includes a new pre-entry screening process to prevent non-compliant seafood imports from entering the US.

Max Valentine, director of Oceana's Illegal Fishing and Transparency Campaign, noted in an interview with Undercurrent on Thursday that the exact requirements won't be clear until NOAA releases its proposed rule. However, NOAA will likely require seafood companies to provide more detailed data on transshipment activities and the duration of fishing trips, she suggested.

Transshipment happens when fishing vessels meet with refrigerated cargo ships at sea to transfer their catch without coming into port. It can obscure illicit activities by mixing legal and illegal catches, Valentine stressed. Requiring this information could help flag potential forced labor, as longer fishing trips often limit crew members' access to resources and support, she said.

Requirements, timeline still unclear

It's not yet clear how fast NOAA might make new requirements mandatory. The agency said it is "prioritizing the implementation of these changes, with plans to issue a proposed rule, with an opportunity for public comment." The agency is targeting 2025 for broader updates.

"The potential for the seafood import monitoring program to be applied to all species is a huge step forward," Valentine said. "Right now, with so little seafood covered, there are many loopholes for illegally caught fish to enter our supply chain."

While NOAA has not specified which additional species it will include, Oceana suggested prioritizing several high-risk species, such as squid and eels. The organization is also concerned about expanding SIMP coverage to all snapper varieties— not just red snapper, as currently covered — and to both farmed and wild salmon, where there is potential for mislabeling farmed salmon as wild.

Valentine said she was also encouraged by NOAA's plan to develop advanced data analytics to identify better high-risk seafood shipments, which would benefit importers and border authorities. She hailed the inclusion of data elements related to forced labor as a significant milestone.

"This is the first time we've seen NOAA acknowledge that forced labor is a serious issue in the seafood supply chain," Valentine told Undercurrent. She added that years of increased public awareness and engagement on forced labor issues have helped drive this progress.

To tackle labor abuses, NOAA will work with US Customs and Border Protection and the Labor Dept. Photo: USCBP

To tackle labor abuses, NOAA said it will work with US Customs and Border Protection and the Department of Labor, collecting targeted data to identify forced labor risks within seafood supply chains.

As Undercurrent reported earlier, a US House of Representatives panel questioned NOAA and other federal agencies in a recent hearing about the effectiveness of SIMP in identifying parties involved in illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing and seafood fraud.  

Lawmakers highlighted how IUU fishing undercuts domestic production, costing the US seafood industry millions and contributing to global losses of up to $23 billion annually. Congressional representatives emphasized the economic harm posed by illegal imports, which drive down prices for US-caught seafood and compromise the integrity of global supply chains.

They were in part fueled by the Outlaw Ocean Project's investigation, published in The New Yorker in October 2023. Led by Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Ian Urbina, the report exposed abuses in China's distant-water fishing fleet, detailing cases of crew members held captive, beaten and malnourished. 

NOAA's original proposal, published in December 2022, sought to expand SIMP from 13 species groups to 1,670, adding various tuna and snapper species and squid, eels, octopus and others, as Undercurrent reported.  Industry representatives opposed the proposal, arguing that it added regulatory burdens without meaningfully addressing IUU fishing or seafood fraud.

In November 2023, NOAA Fisheries launched a comprehensive review of SIMP to improve its impact and effectiveness. It involved consulting with over 7,000 stakeholders, including Customs brokers, seafood business owners, foreign governments, university researchers, NGOs, other US agencies and the public.

The agency said Thursday that the broad stakeholder input has informed its current action plan, and it believes it's better positioned to address previous concerns while improving monitoring capabilities.

"The NOAA Fisheries action plan serves as a roadmap to bolster and enhance SIMP. We are fully committed to strengthening confidence in the process, driving greater transparency, and maximizing its overall effectiveness," said Janet Coit, NOAA fisheries assistant administrator, in a statement.

Differing views

The US seafood industry remains cautious about expanding SIMP, questioning its data’s value and effectiveness. In November 2023, the National Fisheries Institute (NFI) argued that an expanded program would increase regulatory burdens without effectively addressing IUU fishing.

NFI CEO Lisa Picard criticized the proposal as a misuse of resources, calling the existing program flawed. NFI chief strategy officer Gavin Gibbons also expressed relief over NOAA’s initial decision to withdraw the proposal, as Undercurrent reported.

The National Aquaculture Association, whose members include domestic producers competing with imports, told Undercurrent that it "welcomes and strongly supports efforts to ensure seafood imported to the United States is harvested, handled, processed, and packaged to the same environmental, human health and labor standards required of the US wild-harvester."

While seafood groups criticized the original proposal for going too far, conservation groups, including Oceana, said it didn't go far enough. The proposal covered less than half of imported seafood and lacked a clear rationale for selecting certain species over others, they complained, as Undercurrent reported.

Sally Yozell, senior fellow and director of the environmental security program at the Stimson Center, called the proposal "the bare minimum," stating that it offered limited transparency and didn't fully address forced labor concerns.

Valentine voiced concerns about potential gaps in the new plan, such as the proposed de minimis exemption for smaller seafood shipments, stating that more clarity is needed on these points. She believes the timeline is achievable but noted that political support will be essential to meet the 2025 target.

"It's completely doable to issue a proposed rule and finalize it in 2025, as long as we don't encounter political hurdles," she said.

title: US lawmakers demand probe into whether taxpayer dollars are funding Ecuador’s shrimp boom
content:
Three US lawmakers are calling for a deep look into whether American taxpayer dollars support shrimp farms in Ecuador, making life harder for US shrimpers.

Republican representatives James Comer, Troy Nehls and Clay Higgins, all on the House Committee on Oversight and Accountability, have asked the Government Accountability Office (GAO) to review whether the US Treasury Department has been following laws requiring it to oppose funding for international projects that might harm American industries.

The law (US Code Title 22, Section 262h) instructs Treasury representatives to vote against projects funded by institutions like the World Bank or International Monetary Fund (IMF) if they threaten US businesses or cause "substantial injury" to American industries. Since the US contributes significant funds to these institutions, taxpayer dollars indirectly support projects these institutions support.

The lawmakers' call for an investigation came in a letter to the GAO on Nov. 12. This follows years of frustration among US shrimpers over low-priced shrimp imports from Ecuador, which they say undercut their market. This frustration was also echoed in a 2023 letter by Nehls and others urging commerce secretary Gina Raimondo to protect Gulf Coast shrimpers from price drops driven by Ecuadorian imports.

Ecuador shipped 277.175 million pounds of shrimp to the US in 2020. By 2023, that figure had jumped to 453.469 million lbs.

Ecuador's shrimp exports continue to shift towards the US, helping shrimp producers in that country diversify its customer base for a variety of reasons, as covered by Undercurrent News. 

The Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA), a trade association that represents domestic US shrimp harvesters and processors, and other industry groups say that international funding from organizations that the US helps fund has made Ecuador a tough competitor for American producers.

"These taxpayer dollars are supposed to protect US jobs, not eliminate them," said SSA executive director John Williams. "We appreciate the efforts of chairman Comer, Rep Nehls and Rep Higgins to address this oversight and protect our industry."

At the center of this is the Save Our Shrimpers Act, HR7932, a bipartisan bill introduced by Nehls in 2024 that would bar US taxpayer funds from backing foreign shrimp farming and processing projects. The act also demands annual reports to Congress to check if the Treasury is really sticking up for American industries. The bill is awaiting further action from the House Committee on Financial Services.

title: EJF claims systemic illegal driftnet fishing in Moroccan waters
content:
Morocco's illegal driftnet fishing fleet has more than doubled to 846 vessels in the past two decades, threatening Mediterranean fish stocks and potentially disrupting European seafood supply chains, according to a new report.

The investigation by the Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF) found widespread violation of national and international fishing laws in the Alboran Sea, a key source of swordfish for European markets. 

FREE READ NGOs call for new measures to safeguard Atlantic swordfish, tuna at ICCAT meet

"With the use of illegal nets more than doubling, from 370 vessels in 2004 to 846 in 2024, this threatens the rich marine biodiversity of the Alboran Sea," said Steve Trent, CEO and founder of EJF.

Morocco ranks as the EU's fourth-largest fish products supplier by value. The investigation revealed that nearly all Moroccan swordfish catches are exported, with Spain receiving 79% of exports before re-distributing much of the catch to other EU markets, particularly Italy.

The report highlighted a shift from industrial vessels toward smaller wooden boats operating without oversight. Field visits to five Moroccan ports in August and September 2024 confirmed the active use of driftnets, which have been banned in Morocco since 2010 and are restricted under various international agreements.

Market impact

The findings could affect European seafood supply chains, as Italy represents 84% of Spanish swordfish exports by value, the report said.

Previous attempts to eliminate driftnet fishing, including EU-funded buyback programs that provided €1.25 million ($1.33m) annually until 2019, have largely failed. 

Spain’s WOFCO ups turnover 16% even before Conarpesa, Fandicosta deals

Local fishing communities cited economic hardship and insufficient support for transitioning to alternative fishing methods as key factors behind continued driftnet use.

"Nowadays, working at sea doesn't provide enough to live on," one Moroccan fisher told investigators. "The catch is so scarce that you can't even cover your expenses for fuel, bait, fishing gear, and everything else."

The EJF called for stricter import controls by EU member states and increased support for fishing communities to transition to sustainable practices.

"The EU and its member states, particularly Spain and Italy, need to take the responsibility of closely inspecting the imports," said Jesus Urios Culianez, ocean campaigner for EJF.

Driftnets, which can stretch for kilometers, pose significant risks to protected species, including whales, sea turtles, and sharks. When abandoned, they can continue to trap marine life for years while contributing to plastic pollution.
