title: Another case of oyster MSX suspected in Atlantic Canada
content:
Officials in the Canadian province of New Brunswick say a case of the oyster disease multinucleate sphere, better known by the moniker MSX, may have been discovered at Spence Cove, on the province's eastern shore.

The discovery was made through the provincial government's surveillance program, and oyster samples are now being analyzed by the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA), which is the regulatory lead for animal disease issues, the provincial government explained in a press release issued Friday (Nov. 8).

MSX is caused by a protozoan, Haplosporidium nelsoni, and can result in high levels of mortality in oyster populations.

While MSX does not pose any risk to human health, and oysters are still safe to consume, the disease can kill oysters.

Recall that a discovery of MSX around the province of Prince Edward Island (PEI) in July shut down the wild oyster fishery in Bedeque Bay, near the town of Summerside on that province's south coast, as reported by Undercurrent News. 

Spence Cove is almost directly across from Bedeque Bay, on the Northumerbland Strait, the body of water that separates PEI its New Brunswick and Nova Scotia neighbours.

Spence Cove, New Brunswick, is located in the Northumberland Strait, across from Prince Edward Island. Photo screenshot from Google maps

MSX prevents oysters from thriving, resulting in smaller oysters, and comes with a devastating 90-95% mortality rate. Oysters that are over two years old are particularly susceptible, the CFIA notes on its website.

The oyster industry in Atlantic Canada has been jittery since the disease was first discovered in July, in Bedeque Bay, near Summerside in Prince Edward Island.

The US imported 3,939 metric tons of oysters from Canada, worth $41.4m in 2021 and 6,028t worth $64.0m in 2022, a record year. Then, in 2023, the US took 5,430t worth $60.0m, a slight decrease but still way head of most other years.

New Brunswick is the second largest exporter of oysters to the US from Atlantic Canada, behind PEI, and in third place, behind British Columbia and PEI, in the national oyster export picture.

Rising US oyster demand has Canadians pondering expansion

“Our department will continue to work collaboratively with the Canadian Food Inspection Agency throughout this investigation,” said Pat Finnigan, New Brunswick's minister of Agriculture, Aquaculture and Fisheries.

“The department is committed to keeping industry stakeholders informed and ensuring that they have access to timely updates and essential information. We recognize the uncertainty surrounding the full economic impact of this situation and we are prepared to work with affected producers as more information becomes available," Finnigan said in a press release.

Sources in the industry say that MSX has not been detected on any farms, and information from Statistics Canada shows that the volume of oyster exports to date from PEI is holding steady, as reported by Undercurrent.

However, oyster farmers in both PEI and the neighboring province of Nova Scotia, who would normally source the majority of their oyster seed from the wild, will have to source disease-resistant seed from hatcheries for future crops, which will require science and time, said Luke Linkletter, owner of Raspberry Point Oysters of PEI, one of the largest oyster farmers in Atlantic Canada.

Now, some of the same protocols adopted in PEI are coming to New Brunswick.

The chief veterinary officer in New Brunswick's aquaculture department, under the authority of the Aquaculture Act, has ordered a quarantine in the area, prohibiting the movement of oysters from the Spence Cove area.

title: Canadian lobster crewman’s death prompts new guidelines
content:
New safety guidelines are in place in the lobster fishery in the Canadian province of Prince Edward Island (PEI) after a crew member was fatally injured by a boom in June 2024, reports the CBC. 

After a months-long investigation into the incident, officials responsible for PEI's occupational health and safety regulations determined several factors on the lobster boat created a dangerous working environment that violated the province's Occupational Health and Safety Act.

Workers were allowed to move around underneath the boom while it was hoisting a suspended load, and the joystick used to operate the device did not have safety measures to prevent it from activating if accidentally hit.

The hoist on the boat had not been certified by an engineer after it was installed.

The crowded working area, as well as the rocking of the boat, also added to the hazardous environment, officials said.

The boat was fishing out of North Lake, off the northeastern end of PEI, at the time of the incident.

Since June, health and safety officials from the province have been visiting fishing wharves around the province to remind crews of the dangers of operating hoists, the CBC reports.

title: Untitled
content:
The US Federal Trade Commission has been asked to investigate claims that the Best Aquaculture Practices (BAP) program is involved in misleading practices related to its certification of Indian shrimp. 

The petition was filed Friday (Nov. 1) by the Corporate Accountability Lab (CAL), a Chicago, Illinois-based not-for-profit focused on human rights abuses, and the Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA), a group that represents the harvesters and processors of wild-caught shrimp in the southeastern US, Undercurrent News has learned.

BAP, a program managed by the Portsmouth, New Hampshire-based Global Seafood Alliance (GSA), had certified as many as 3,959 facilities in 43 countries as of the end of 2023, including processing plants, farms, hatcheries and feed mills.

However, when it comes to the suggestion that Indian shrimp is "responsibly sourced and ethically produced," the certification represents "false or deceptive advertising- or marketing-related activities," CAL and SSA argue in a statement released Friday.  

CAL said its three-year study indicates that many BAP-certified shrimp facilities in India are associated with labor abuses, including forced labor, unsanitary living conditions, restricted movement, wage underpayment and groundwater contamination in villages near the plants. Despite BAP's claims of adhering to rigorous standards, CAL said it found no significant differences in working and environmental conditions between BAP-certified and uncertified facilities.

Additionally, CAL said it identified harmful groundwater contamination near certified farms, contradicting BAP's environmental standards.

"GSA, BAP and retailers promote BAP certification as a tool consumers can use to ensure the seafood meets strict environmental and labor standards," said Charity Ryerson, CAL's executive director, in the statement. "In practice, BAP certification is little more than a marketing tool. It misleads consumers into thinking all is well, while workers at BAP-certified facilities report severe exploitation and dangerous working conditions, and communities suffer from pollution that has destroyed fisheries and contaminated drinking water."

The SSA highlighted that BAP-certified farms accounted for a significant portion of antibiotic-related import refusals by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), with 87% of such refusals in 2024 linked to BAP-certified shippers. Despite testing only 0.1% of imports for banned antibiotics, the FDA refused 71 entry lines of adulterated shrimp between January and September 2024, of which 62 were attributed to BAP-certified shippers.

In September, shrimp from India was added to the US Department of Labor's 2024 forced labor list following evidence from multiple investigations, as Undercurrent News reported.

The CAL and SSA complaint points out that, while BAP certification aligns with consumer demand for ethical production, recent studies show that products with environmental, social and governance (ESG) claims, including BAP, have experienced an average growth in sales of 8% over five years. A 2024 survey revealed consumers are willing to pay nearly 10% more for sustainably produced products.

Indian shrimp accounted for 296,392 metric tons (38%) of the 788,087t of shrimp imported by the US in 2023, based on the latest data on UCN's trade portal. Over the first eight months of 2024, it accounted for 183,811t of the 478,649t imported -- still 38%.

"BAP's industry-led certification scheme has clearly failed to fix the many safety, ethical and environmental problems plaguing the Indian shrimp sector," said John Williams, SSA's executive director, in the statement. "Rather than improving conditions, the certification often masks exploitative practices, misleading US consumers into believing they're purchasing ethical and sustainable products. We urge the Commission to address as soon as possible this marketing-related practice that hides egregious human rights violations."

Undercurrent's request for comment from BAP was not returned as of the time of publication.

title: Class action law firm pursues US sushi giant’s parent company for data breach
content:
A US law firm reports that it has filed notice of a data breach at True World Holdings, the parent company behind the largest distributor of fresh fish to sushi restaurants in North America, with the Attorney General for the US state of Maine. 

True World, based in Rockleigh, New Jersey-based, which owns True World Foods, discovered the cybersecurity attack on Aug. 23, according to Oklahoma City, Oklahoma-based Federman and Sherwood. The law firm is seeking individuals who might participate in litigation against the company.

"True World immediately launched an investigation into the incident. An ongoing review of information gathered during the investigation determined that certain individuals' personal and sensitive information was exposed and/or acquired by an unauthorized third party," noted Federman and Sherwood.

The type of information potentially exposed includes full name, social security number and other sensitive personal information, said the law firm, which contacted Maine authorities on Oct. 18. 

Under Maine law, a company, regardless of its location, must report a data breach if personal information for just a single Maine resident may have been compromised, the law firm advises.

Undercurrent News reached out to True World for a comment but didn't receive a response prior to publication.

Federman and Sherwood says it has led several class-action lawsuits involving data breaches involving business, academic and government institutions. To date, in 2024, the firm has also filed data breach-related class action suits against Kootenai Outpatient Surgery, Integris Health and New Enchantment Group.

title: Winners of Gulf of Maine wind leases urged to engage with fishing industry
content:
The Responsible Offshore Development Alliance (RODA), a coalition of US commercial fish harvesters, is urging the winners of the offshore wind lease sale in the Gulf of Maine to engage with the fishing industry and "listen to the impacted communities" before moving forward.

The Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM), a US agency within the Department of the Interior, conducted its first offshore wind lease sale in the Gulf of Maine on Tuesday (Oct. 29), awarding four lease areas to two companies.

"The conservation community has echoed our programmatic analysis request and questions about the cumulative ecological impacts of large-scale ocean habitat conversation," RODA said in a statement before the auction began. "Unfortunately, BOEM has decided to proceed with the auction without conducting this critical step."

RODA is a membership-based coalition of fishing industry associations and companies looking to collaborate with regulatory agencies and scientists on new offshore development. The group has been vocal leading up to the auction, repeatedly calling for a programmatic environmental analysis for the Gulf of Maine before any offshore wind decisions and investments. 

For the fishing industry, the issues with offshore wind mainly revolve around the "unknown," RODA said. One argument is that there is a lack of research to see how the impact of burying cables, or the vibrations that are generated through construction, maintenance and operation, impact fisheries.

Another issue is that offshore wind project locations have displaced some fishermen from their traditional areas. Maine governor Janet Mills took this up in 2021, signing legislation to prohibit offshore wind projects in state waters of the Gulf of Maine, where up to 75% of the state's commercial harvesting occurs. As a trade off, she also signed a bill advancing the nation's first research area for floating offshore wind in the Gulf of Maine's federal waters.

A big step towards Biden'S offshore wind goal

Offshore wind has stayed out of the Gulf of Maine's state waters, but now big movements are happening in federal waters as part of the government's goal of deploying 30 gigawatts of offshore wind in the US by 2030 and 15 gigawatts of floating offshore wind energy by 2035.

The US president Joe Biden, vice president Kamala Harris administration announced last month that it would be holding an offshore wind energy lease sale for eight areas on the outer shelf off Massachusetts, New Hampshire and Maine. Four of those areas were successfully auctioned off on Tuesday, with the winning bids totaling more than $21.9 million.

"Since the start of the Biden-Harris administration, we've been committed to achieving our ambitious clean energy goals," interior secretary Deb Haaland said in a press release following the auction.

BOEM is part of the Department of the Interior (DOI).

"With 10 approved offshore wind projects capable of powering over 5 million homes, we are well on our way to a clean energy future," Haaland said.

The administration approved the 10th offshore wind project -- US Wind's project offshore Maryland -- just last month. Since the start of the administration in 2021, the DOI has introduced more than 1.3m new acres for development, according to a White House fact sheet.

And the winners are...

As noted above, two winners emerged from the Gulf of Maine auction: Avangrid Renewables and Invenergy NE Offshore Wind. Together the winning bids for the four lease areas totaled more than $21.9m.

Avangrid Renewables was awarded Lease OCS-564, which consists of 98,565 acres. The company, which is headquartered in Portland, Oregon, but a subsidiary of Scottish Power Finance US, paid $4,928,250 for the area. 

'Gulf of Maine Final Sale Notice (FSN)' OCS-A 0564'
Screenshot from BOEM's Offshore Renewable Activities map

Avangrid also won OCS-568, which encompasses 124,897 acres. The winning bid was $6,244,850. Both lease areas are approximately 29.5 nautical miles from Massachusetts.

The company said in a statement that the two lease areas are located in "relatively shallow waters within the limits of existing floating wind technology."

Avangrid did not address the fishing industry in its press release, but it did note that the areas "largely deconflicted from other ocean users following a rigorous federal public engagement process."

Also important to note is that Avangrid is a 50% owner of the Vineyard Wind 1 Project, which is located offshore of Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket, Massachusetts. The Vineyard Wind 1 project is currently under investigation by the US Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement following a July 2024 incident in which a turbine blade fail resulted in fiberglass debris littering the seabed and washing ashore.

"Gulf of Maine Final Sale Notice (FSN)' OCS-A 0568'
Screenshot from BOEM's Offshore Renewable Activities map

Invenergy NE Offshore Wind was awarded two leases as well, including OCS-562, which consists of 97,854 acres, approximately 46.2 nautical miles from Maine. The winning bid was $4,892,700.

"Gulf of Maine Final Sale Notice (FSN)' OCS-A 0562'
Screenshot from BOEM's Offshore Renewable Activities map

Invenergy also was granted OCS-567, which consists of 117,780 acres, approximately 21.6 nautical miles from Massachusetts. The winning bid was $5,889,000.

"Gulf of Maine Final Sale Notice (FSN)' OCS-A 0567'
Screenshot from BOEM's Offshore Renewable Activities map

A call for engagement

Fishing is a vital part of the Gulf of Maine's economy. Maine commercial fishers earned more than $611m at the dock in 2023, according to the Maine Department of Marine Resources.
 
But the Gulf of Maine is also home to some of the highest sustained wind speeds in the world, which as governor Mills' office previously pointed out, gives the state a unique opportunity to create good-paying jobs and help Maine residents with clean heating solutions.

Together, the four leased areas have the potential to power more than 2.3 million homes with clean energy, BOEM said. But while it is certainly a play in the fight against climate change, the fishing industry wants to ensure that they're not forgotten along the way.

"We encourage future leaseholders to engage with the fishing industry, listen to impacted communities and consider regional level impacts in all steps of their development process," RODA said in a statement ahead of the auction.

"These corporations must be willing to take a flexible approach to mitigation based on the financial commitments they are willing to invest in a paper lease. The lease siting did not avoid impacts, so a willingness to spend millions of dollars on leases must entail an equal commitment to minimize and mitigate the environmental and socioeconomic impacts to small business owners." 

The Maine Lobstermen's Association (MLA) expressed a deeper disappointment in the latest auction, which it says is "another dangerous step toward the industrialization of one of the world’s most productive marine ecosystems."

"The MLA remains steadfast that no area of the Gulf of Maine should be industrialized with offshore wind," the membership-based association, made up of leaders of Maine's lobster industry, said in a statement.

"With 20,000 individuals employed aboard Maine’s fishing vessels or directly in the seafood supply chain, the productive and fragile waters of the Gulf of Maine should not be used as testing ground for new offshore wind technology or to site large industrial wind farms.”

title: FCF stresses sustainability commitment in response to supply chain abuse allegations
content:
Taiwan's Fong Chun Formosa (FCF), one of the world's largest tuna suppliers, has reiterated its dedication to advancing sustainable and socially responsible practices within its operations.

Taiwanese tuna giant accused of failing to address environmental, human rights abuses

This follows a report from NGO Shark Guardian, which alleged FCF is failing to act on severe environmental and human rights violations within its supply chain. Shark Guardian's report, called "Empty Promises, Empty Oceans," alleged significant discrepancies between FCF's public pledges and the actual practices of its suppliers.

The company expressed a willingness to engage with stakeholders on matters of environmental impact and labor practices, but it pushed back against the claims made by Shark Guardian, labeling them as "outdated" and, in many cases, not supported by "reliable evidence."

FCF clarified that many of the issues raised had already been addressed through coordination with regulatory bodies, vessel operators, and relevant authorities. According to FCF, these efforts included imposing sanctions and enforcing corrective actions where necessary.

"In many cases, FCF has already worked with regulators, vessel owners and
operators to resolve past concerns through both sanctions and corrective actions," it pointed out.

In an official statement, FCF acknowledged its responsibility in addressing critical environmental and social issues affecting the seafood sector. The company emphasized its efforts toward positive progress through internal initiatives and collaborative partnerships.

"As one of the global seafood leaders, FCF recognizes our responsibility to continue to close the gap on some of the biggest sustainability and social challenges impacting our business, industry, and world. We are making great progress through a strategic combination of internal initiatives as well as external projects and partnerships," it said.

FCF underscored its commitment to enforcing strict policies against IUU fishing and forced labor, reiterating that any vessel implicated in credible allegations faces immediate suspension pending a thorough investigation.

"FCF maintains a strict policy against IUU fishing and forced labor practices and swiftly suspends business with any vessel facing credible allegations until thorough investigations are concluded," the firm stated. "If necessary, corrective actions are not taken, we remove the vessels from our supply chain."

title: Untitled
content:
Norway lobster (Nephrops norvegicus) -- aka Dublin Bay prawn, langoustine shrimp, or scampi -- is headed to the deep fryer in the US this holiday season. The fast food chain Long John Silver's revealed this week that its fan-favorite Norway Lobster Bites are back for a limited time.

A Lobster Bites Tail Pack, served in lobster-tail-shaped packaging, is being offered to consumers at a price of $4.99.

"We know the return of our fan-favorite Lobster Bites will make waves, and we're excited to offer multiple ways to enjoy them this season," said Christopher Caudill, Long John Silver's senior vice president of marketing and innovation, in a press release promoting the offering.

"Our Lobster Bites provide the perfect blend of sweet flavor with crispy texture, delivering great value on wild-caught Norway lobster at fast food prices."

Norway lobster is a pretty unusual item to see on a quick-service restaurant menu as it's not a product that many people in the US are familiar with. Just 371 metric tons valued at $5.6 million were imported into the US in 2023, based on data available on the UCN Trade Portal. Norway was the biggest source, accountable for 220t worth $1.9m.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view

In the US, the term "lobster" is generally thought of as either Homarus americanus, the North American species, or Homarus gammarus, the European species. Norway lobster looks like a small lobster but it has texture similar to that of shrimp. 

Credit: irabel8/Shutterstock.com

Long John Silver's, which has close to 500 locations in 35 US states, specializes in serving batter-dipped whitefish, shrimp and chicken. Its core seafood item is wild-caught Alaska pollock, but the restaurant chain also offers meals featuring cod and salmon -- both items promoted as being wild-caught in the US. Long John Silver's shrimp is farmed but sourced solely from farms that are Best Aquaculture Practices (BAP) certified.

The Norway lobster product is certainly a departure from the chain's norm, but it has become a fan favorite over the years -- especially after Long John Silver's briefly stopped selling it for a few years after a 2009 investigation by the Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) Division of Advertising Practices.

While Long John Silver's product and marketing material clearly labels the limited-time menu item as "Norway Lobster Bites," prior to 2009 they were simply labeled "Lobster Bites." Marketing materials at the time did identify the product as being made from langostino lobster, "rather than the American species more commonly associated with the term lobster." However, the fast food chain was running television commercials "depicting American lobster in a manner that suggested Long John Silver's 'real lobster' bites were made from the American species," the FTC said.

The FTC did not recommend any "enforcement action" at the time because Long John Silver's made assurances about revising the marketing materials. With that said, it wasn't until 2014 that the chain brought back its lobster bites, repackaged as "Norway Lobster Bites."

title: Canada completes mission to deter illegal fishing in Pacific
content:
Operation officers and crew of the Canadian Coast Guard Ship (CCGS) Sir Wilfred Laurier are back in port in the city of Victoria, in the province of British Columbia, after completing a two-month mission to deter illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing in the North Pacific.

Pacific North Guard (OP.NPG) involved 20 officers from the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) and was supported by funding from the Pacific Salmon Strategy Initiative, which aims to enhance conservation, protection, and enforcement efforts in high-risk areas for Canada's Pacific salmon stocks, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

During the Op.NPG mission officers and support personnel patrolled approximately 20,000 kilometers and conducted inspections of 15 fishing vessels, the DFO said in a press release on Monday (Oct. 29).

"Fishery officers found illegally harvested shark fins, evidence of fishing during a closed season and unreported catch, and documented instances of marine pollution," the department said.

In addition, DFO found several vessels with their monitoring systems switched off, commonly referred to as "dark vessels."

The boardings also presented Canadian officers with their first opportunity to enforce the newly adopted ban on Pacific salmon retention, which has been enforced in the North Pacific fishing fleets since this July, the department added.

Besides at-sea monitoring and enforcement patrols, the operation also involved conducting daily aerial surveillance out of Hokkaido, Japan, flying 50,419 nautical miles in 34 patrols and visually inspecting 407 vessels.

Four fisheries officers from Japan participated in air patrols for three weeks, and one Korean Coast Guard representative also joined two patrols. This year marked the first time Canada conducted joint air patrols with officers from Japan and Korea, said the DFO.

"Officers reported incidents of shark finning, the targeted harvest of dolphins, pollution incidents, and vessel marking violations," stated the DFO press release.

Canada is now working with the appropriate flag states to support further investigations and sanctions on offending vessels, the department added.

title: Untitled
content:
A group of 11 bipartisan Maryland and Virginia lawmakers from both chambers of the US Congress have asked president Joe Biden to direct the International Trade Commission to investigate the import of Venezuelan blue crab.

"Domestic seafood producers in Maryland and Virginia have experienced significant strain due to the influx of imported Venezuelan crabmeat, some of which is mislabeled and contaminated," the lawmakers said in a letter sent Wednesday (Oct. 23), a copy of which has been secured by Undercurrent News.

The letter points to an outbreak of Vibrio parahaemolyticus in 2018 that resulted in multiple hospitalizations and was blamed on Venezuelan crabmeat mislabeled as originating from Maryland.

Before closing its investigation, the US Food and Drug Administration said it found as many as 26 laboratory-confirmed cases of vibrio linked to fresh Venezuelan crab meat consumed in seven states and the District of Columbia, as reported by Undercurrent. The first documented cases of vibrio, in early July 2018, led several crab importers to announce tough new measures to improve the safety of their product, including the extensive use of high-pressure processing. 

But more than the threat of food pathogens, the lawmakers said last week that the overall competition of imported crabmeat is hurting harvesters and processors of domestically caught crab. As the chart from UCN's trade portal below illustrates, the US crab import business has grown to a roughly 30,000 metric ton, $800 million per year industry.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
Maryland, Virginia lawmakers ask Biden to investigate Venezuelan blue crab - Undercurrent News

"The supply of imported crabmeat has increased, threatening the future livelihood of domestic industry and creating the conditions for a 62% decrease in domestic supply," the lawmakers wrote. "This has harmed crab fishing industries throughout the Chesapeake Bay, which produces 50% of the United States' total blue crab harvest, a proportion that is now diminishing year over year." 

The letter notes that there are now fewer than 20 Maryland crab picking and seafood processing companies, down from 53 in 1995.

The letter also asks Biden to "use the full array of informal actions [available] to address this issue, including through negotiations, utilization of World Trade Organization committee, bilateral dialogues and other activities." 

The letter is signed by US senators Chris Van Hollen (Maryland), Ben Cardin (Maryland), Tim Kaine (Virginia) and Mark Warner (Virginia), all Democrats. It's also signed by Maryland Democratic representatives Dutch Ruppersberger, John Sarbanes, David Trone, Glenn Ivey and Kweisi Mfume as well as Maryland Republican representative Andy Harris and Virginia Republican representative Robert Wittman.

Exponential growth

Venezuela, in particular, has seen its blue crab exports to the US grow exponentially in recent years.

It sent the US 3,668t worth almost $83.0m in 2022, its biggest year ever. In 2023, the numbers fell to 3,281t worth $58.8m.

Unlike blue swimming crab (Portunus pelagicus), found in Indonesia and other Southeast Asian countries -- the most common kind of crab imported by the US -- Venezuelan blue crab is the species Callectinectus sapidus, the same as the blue crab caught in the Chesapeake Bay. As a result, it is often used as a substitute in the making of crabcakes and other food items.

Most recently, in August, Venezuela sent the US 347,663 pounds worth $11.04/lb. This despite a 90-day conservation period that started on Aug. 15.

Maryland, Virginia lawmakers ask Biden to investigate Venezuelan blue crab - Undercurrent News

Urner Barry, on Thursday (Oct. 24), reported an average wholesale price range of $23.25-$23.75/lb for Venezuelan blue crabmeat, down 11% from the range of $26.00-$26.75/lb being reported on Aug. 15, the first day of the moratorium.

title: Untitled
content:
The Department of Commerce (DOC), on Tuesday (Oct. 22), announced its final determinations regarding the anti-dumping (AD) and countervailing duty (CVD) investigations of frozen warmwater shrimp from India, Ecuador, Indonesia and Vietnam. 

The clear winner appears to be Ecuador, as reported by Undercurrent News, with a combined duty of 3.78%, a reduction from the initial determinations of 13.47%.

Now that the risk associated with the uncertainty is gone, an issue that previously impacted imports by the US, the Latin American country is back to having a competitive advantage. And increased demand is likely. 

How we got here

Shrimp imports into the United States grew 28% from 2019 to 2021 to just shy of one billion pounds annually. Demand from both retail and foodservice grew as both segments fought for market share as the country reopened at a time when consumer interest in shrimp expanded. But the market needed to rebalance, as this put the industry in a classic oversupply situation. 

Imports declined 12% from 2021 to 2023 as a result. The trend has continued this year, with shrimp imports through August down just over 5% compared to the same period last year.

Ecuador was the only major trade partner to see an increase in shrimp exports in the two years to 2023 -- to the tune of 12%.  

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view

As a result of the oversupply situation, importers paired inventory at lower prices for nearly two straight years into the early part of 2024. The supply and demand picture appeared more balanced at this time. 

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
US wholesale update: Shrimp prices take bullish stance after final AD/CVD determinations - Undercurrent News
Price action now

That's not to say there are no other challenges even with the release of the determinations. Seafood, unlike most other food commodities, is reliant on a well-functioning supply chain as the majority of seafood consumed in the United States is imported. Any breakdown can have major implications. 

The factors that suggest higher prices seem to be forming a bullishness tone in the US wholesale market. Supply gaps that have been noted throughout the year, leading to more cautious buying patterns because of AD/CVD seem gone and interest is higher to fill needs, container rates are still elevated, cost of capital is high, and cold storage costs are up. 

The targeted changes in wholesale prices this week were on the 21-25 and 31-35 counts headless, shell-on, Latin origin product averaged $4.15/lb. and $3.75/lb., respectively. The 40-50 and 50-60 count head-on shell-on prices averaged $2.95/lb. and $2.80/lb.  

While the reduction in rates for Ecuador could lead to lower prices at the source, the other factors seem to be weighing sentiment to the positive for future pricing.  

Gary Morrison, Undercurrent News' new head of growth and strategy, brings nearly 20 years of expertise in driving transparency within agriculture and seafood commodity markets. A strategic professional with deep knowledge of supply chains and price dynamics, Morrison is dedicated to delivering actionable insights and market clarity to our subscribers.

title: Fish cakes recalled in Canada due to undeclared allergen
content:
The Canadian government issued a recall for Jinju brand Fish Cakes on Thursday (Oct. 24). The surimi product, which was distributed in the provinces of Alberta, British Columbia and Manitoba, is being recalled because of undeclared egg.

Jinju brand Fish Cakes were recalled by the Canadian Food Inspection Agency on Oct. 24, 2024. Photo courtesy of CFIA.

Seoul Trading Corp. is the recalling firm in this case, which includes packages of the company's Jinju's Fish Cake 500g (UPC 8 801077 529805) and 1kg  (UPC 8 801077 510308).

The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) confirmed that the recall was triggered by test results that showed egg was in the product, but not declared on the packaging.

There have been "no reported reactions associated with the consumption of these products," CFIA said. However, the federal agency is asking retailers and food service providers not to serve, use, sell or distribute the product.

CFIA said it is conducting a food safety investigation that "may lead to the recall of other products." The agency is also verifying that the industry is removing the recalled products from the marketplace.

title: Ecuador shrimp industry sees final US antidumping, CVD decisions as vindication
content:
Ecuadorian companies are still reviewing the US Department of Commerce's (DOC) final antidumping (AD) and counter-vailing duty (CVD) determinations for frozen vannamei shrimp, but the group that represents the industry sees the actions as proof that it is playing fairly.

"We are still evaluating the results of the final CVD determination; however, it is very evident today that Ecuador does not engage in any form of unfair competition," Jose Antonio Camposano, president of Ecuador's National Chamber of Aquaculture (CNA), told Undercurrent News on the sideline of the Aqua Expo conference, in Guayaquil, Ecuador, this week.

"We maintained this stance at the beginning of these accusations, and we uphold it now," he asserted.

Some of Ecuador's largest shrimp exporters secured major victories in the battle against the AD and CVD investigation with DOC's final determinations, as reported Tuesday (Oct. 22) by Undercurrent News. 

Ecuador shrimp big winner in final US AD determination; India biggest loser on CVDs

Sociedad Nacional de Galapagos (Songa), Ecuador's second-largest shrimp exporter to the US, saw its preliminary antidumping rate of 10.58% slashed to 0.0%, effectively freeing importers of its products from the tariffs. However, it's final subsidy (CVD) rate was 4.41%.

Industrial Pesquera Santa Priscila, the nation's largest shrimp producer, maintained its earlier favorable de minimis dumping rate of 0.48%. It received a final subsidy rate of 3.57%.

Santa Priscila, which has heavily invested over the last few years in increasing its processing capacity to be able to deliver a wide range of value-added products, has ranked in recent months as the US top shrimp importer.

Another major player, Omarsa, also emerged free from the antidumping duties. However, all other Ecuador producers were given a final subsidy rate of 3.78%.

content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Tuesday, Oct. 22:

IFFO 2024: Soybean surplus sinks meal prices; Veramaris sees algal oil make gains

Undercurrent News is reporting live from the Marine Ingredients Organisation's annual conference, which was held in Lisbon, Portugal, from Oct. 21 to 23.

GSA summit 2024: Tilapia output to crack 7m tons next year; Salmon likely to be in short supply again in H1

Undercurrent is reporting live from St. Andrews for the 2024 Responsible Seafood Summit.

Russian pollock TAC not set above scientific advice, industry asserts

Russia's Pollock Catchers Association has issued a statement in response to what it called "false information" in seafood trade media regarding pollock quotas for 2025, after other publications wrote that the catch had been set 7% higher than scientific advice.

NOAA reports slight 1% growth of endangered North Atlantic right whale population

There were about 372 North Atlantic right whales left in the world in 2023, a slight 1% increase over the 367 estimated to exist in 2022, based on the latest report from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Ecuador shrimp big winner in final US AD determination; India biggest loser on CVDs

Ecuador has won the US Department of Commerce's final determination in its antidumping duty investigations of frozen warmwater shrimp. However, Indian exporters weren't as lucky in relation to countervailing duties (CVDs). 

Russian pollock CEO: Whitefish exports to EU could drop to zero if new vessels don't get licenses

Saveliy Karpukhin, the CEO of Russian Fishery Company (RFC), used his presentation at the 2024 Groundfish Forum last week to deliver a warning to the European Union processing sector.

CNA: Power cuts threaten to cripple Ecuador's shrimp production growth

The biggest challenges for Ecuador's shrimp production sector lie not only in international market trends but also in Ecuador's domestic situation, particularly the ongoing energy crisis, according to Jose Antonio Camposano, executive president of Ecuador's National Chamber of Aquaculture.

Peter Pan's Port Moller plant transfer to Rodger May challenged in appeals court

A California investor who lost nearly all of the $10 million he'd lent to the bankrupt Peter Pan Seafood Company is asking a higher court to review the transfer of one of its remote Alaska salmon processing plants to former co-owner Rodger May.

High Liner hopes to launch Norwegian farmed cod before year-end as wild volumes drop, prices rocket

Canada's High Liner Foods hopes to launch the sale of Norwegian farmed cod before the end of 2025, sourcing from a company it invested in earlier this year, CEO Paul Jewer told Undercurrent during the 2024 Groundfish Forum in Copenhagen, Denmark.

title: Ecuador shrimp big winner in final US AD determination; India biggest loser on CVDs
content:
Ecuador has won the US Department of Commerce's final determination in its antidumping duty (AD) investigations of frozen warmwater shrimp. However, Indian exporters weren't as lucky in relation to countervailing duties (CVDs). 

Commerce released its final determinations on both its AD and CVD investigations Tuesday (Oct. 22), a few weeks later than the previously predicted Oct. 4 release date. There were a few variations from the preliminary determinations released earlier this year, as reported by Undercurrent News.  

Sociedad Nacional de Galapagos, more commonly referred to as Songa, the US' second-largest source of shrimp from Ecuador, was handed a 0.0% dumping rate -- a big difference from the 10.58% in the preliminary determination. Industrial Pesquera Santa Priscila (Tropical Packing Ecuador Tropack), Ecuador's largest supplier to the US, kept its 0.48% de minimis dumping rate.

Indonesia was the only other country that Commerce included in its AD investigation for frozen warmwater shrimp. PT Bahari Makmur Sejati was handed a 0.0% dumping rate, while PT First Marine Seafoods (PT Khom Foods) was given a 3.90% rate. All others in Indonesia also have a 3.90% dumping rate.

Meanwhile, Indian exporters, who were left out of Commerce's AD investigations but included in its CVD investigations, were issued CVD subsidy rates ranging from 3.57% to 4.41%.

As for the final determinations in the CVD cases, Commerce investigated Ecuador, India, Indonesia, and the Socialist Republic of Vietnam. In regards to the final subsidy rates, India is the biggest loser.

India's Devi Sea Foods Limited, including Devi Sea Foods Inc. and other related companies, was handed a 5.87% final subsidy rate. Fellow Indian exporters and producers Sandhya Aqua Exports Pvt. Ltd., including Neeli Sea Foods and other related companies, were handed a 5.63% CVD rate. All other Indian exporters have a 5.77% subsidy rate.

Ecuador's Songa was determined to receive a 3.57% CVD subsidy rate, and Santa Priscila 4.41%. All other Ecuadorian shrimp producers were handed a 3.78% subsidy rate.

Indonesia only had two exporters and producers named in the CVD investigation. PT Bahari Makmur Sejati was handed a 0.20% (de minimis), and PT First Marine Seafoods (PT Khom Foods) was issued a 0.71% (de minimis).

Vietnam's Soc Trang Seafood Joint Stock Company was handed a 2.84% subsidy rate, but fellow Vietnamese producer Thong Thuan Company Limited was issued a 221.82% subsidy rate. The Department of Commerce noted that the rate was "based on adverse inferences." This rate is up from the 196.41% issued in the preliminary rates.

Thong Tuan is considered an outlier. Sources previously told Undercurrent that the high deposit requirement is likely punishment for the company not fully cooperating with investigators. All other Vietnamese exporters and producers were issued a final CVD rate of 2.84%.

The reduction and now certainty of rates will likely shift risk back to importers, said Gary Morrison, Undercurrent News market reporter and head of growth and strategy. Instead of delivery duty paid (DDP) purchasing, it has been reported that companies are likely to revert to free on board (FOB) pricing. The drop in rates will likely increase demand, further pressuring prices higher.

Morrison also noted that inventory is an issue, with supply gaps in the US worsened by delays. In addition, Ecuador is pulling shrimp from ponds early because of the power cuts, so smaller shrimp is more prevalent in this harvest.

It will take a few days to digest the impact and get sentiment from US importers as many are in Scotland at the Global Seafood Alliance's Responsible Seafood Summit, taking place in St. Andrew from Oct. 21 - 24.

While this was Commerce's final determination for the AD and CVD investigations of frozen warmwater shrimp, the International Trade Commission (ITC) will make its final determination on Dec. 5, 2024. If there is a final affirmative determination from ITC, then the issuance of orders will take place Dec. 12, 2024.

title: Alabama seafood dealer pleads guilty to buying, selling illegally harvested red drum, sea trout
content:
Richard Michael Collier Jr., the owner of P.J. Seafood, a seafood dealer in the US state of Alabama, has pleaded guilty in an Alabama federal court to conspiring to buy and sell more than $350,000 worth of illegally harvested red drum and sea trout, court documents confirm.

Collier, also known as "Lil' Ricky," pleaded guilty on Oct. 2 in the US District Court Court for the Southern District of Alabama to one count of conspiracy to violate the Lacey Act and six counts of violating the Lacey Act, confirms his 36-page plea agreement, a copy of which was secured by Undercurrent News.

He potentially faces up to five years imprisonment, a fine of as much as $250,000 and three years of supervised probation, the maximum sentences available.

According to a Facebook page for the business, P.J. Seafood, in Coden, Alabama, specializes in oysters, shrimp and "fresh fish straight off the boat." However, agents with US Fish and Wildlife and the Alabama Marine Police conducting surveillance found that -- in addition to oysters, shrimp and "fresh fish" -- Lil' Ricky was also buying and selling illegally harvested game fish between 2019 and 2022.

Red drum. Photo: Wikipedia

Collier planned to sell the game fish in interstate commerce or to interstate distributors of fish, according to the plea agreement. 

Collier was caught by US Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) and Mississippi Department of Marine Resources (MDMR) officers when the two departments began an investigation into trip ticket falsification in the state. While harvesting red drum and spotted seatrout to sell commercially is illegal in Alabama, harvesting is allowed in Mississippi with restrictions.

Trip tickets are a requirement for Mississippi commercial fishermen who are harvesting red drum and spotted seatrout for commercial sale. They provide information on the person who caught the fish, where it was caught, how many pounds it was, and the location of where it was sold. When harvested with the completed trip ticket, these fish can be sold in interstate commerce. 

In its joint investigation, USFWS and MDMR officers found Collier falsifying information on the trip tickets and knowingly purchasing illegally harvested fish. Further surveillance showed Collier had purchased red drum and spotted seatrout from hidden compartments.

Per the plea agreement, the seafood business owner must also make full restitution "in an amount determined by the court." He also agreed to surrender his Alabama gill netting license and agreed that he "will not operate a business involving the sale of seafood, the exception being that he may operate a business involving the sale of oysters."

title: Smoked salmon recalled in Canada due to listeria
content:
Vasco & Co.'s Filet Royal Smoked Atlantic Salmon is being recalled by the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) due to potential Listeria monocytogenes contamination. 

CFIA issued the recall notice on Oct. 11, noting that the product was distributed in the Canadian province of Quebec. The affected product in question is the 170g size, lot no. 399417. CFIA is warning those with that specific smoked salmon product not to "consume, use, sell, serve or distribute recalled products."

Listeria monocytogenes is a pathogenic bacteria that can be transmitted when food is harvested, processed, prepared, packed, or even transported or stored, in a contaminated environment. The bacteria most often causes food poisoning, with symptoms including vomiting, diarrhea, fever and muscle aches, amongst other symptoms. 

CFIA said the recall has been triggered by inspection test results and that no illnesses associated with the product have been reported so far. The government agency is conducting a food safety investigation and noted that it may lead to the recall of additional products. CFIA said the department is also verifying that the industry is removing recalled products from the marketplace.

title: US importer recalls Korean seaweed due to undeclared allergen
content:
A US importer, wholesaler and distributor of Asian food products is recalling its Korean seasoned seaweed product due to an undeclared allergen. 

The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) shared the announcement published by Santa Fe Springs, California-based Wismettac Asian Foods on Friday (Oct. 11), confirming that 3.52 oz packages of the company's Shirakiku brand Korean Seasoned Seaweed "contains the undeclared allergen of sesame on an outer package." The FDA noted that a further investigation found that the issue was caused by the "unintentional use of incorrect packaging materials for the product."

"People who have an allergy or severe sensitivity to sesame run the risk of serious or life-threatening allergic reaction if they consume these products," the FDA noted.

Wismettac Asian Foods distributed its product to retail stores and restaurants in Arizona, California, New Mexico, Nevada, New York, Texas and Washington. While no related illnesses have been reported, the FDA has urged consumers to return the product to the place of purchase for a full refund.

title: Canadian cod expert skeptical of fishery department’s science model switch
content:
A well-known Canadian cod scientist told a parliamentary committee on Wednesday (Oct. 9) that the decision by Canada's fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier to end the moratorium on a commercial cod stock on the east coast does not provide for precautionary management and sustainable fisheries, and opposes the spirit of the Fisheries Act.

Dr. George Rose testified before the Fisheries and Oceans/Pecheries Oceans (FOPO) Standing Committee as the committee continues its examination of the impact of the reopening of a commercial cod fishery in zones 2J 3KL -- known historically as the "northern" cod stock of Atlantic cod -- in the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador (NL).

The FOPO began its study of this issue on Monday (Oct. 7) with testimony from high-ranking Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) officials, as previously reported by Undercurrent News. 

Recall that, in June, Canada's fisheries minister announced she was ending the 32-year-long moratorium on the northern cod stock. The fishery will move from a stewardship fishery with a limit of 12,999 metric tons annually to a commercial fishery with a total allowable catch (TAC) of 18,000t for 2024, as reported by Undercurrent.

Canada’s fisheries minister ignored staff cod advice, court documents reveal

That decision came nine months after DFO officials announced a new limit reference point (LRP) to determine the health of the stock. Instead of using data dating back to 1983, when the overall biomass was at its lowest point, fisheries scientists said they recalculated using fishing data dating back to the 1950s when the spawning biomass (SSB) was estimated at 2.0m tons, as reported by Undercurrent. 

With that new data, the stock was assessed as being in the cautious zone under DFO's precautionary framework for fisheries management.

The latest stock assessment for northern cod, released in March, suggested the SSB was around 300,000t to 400,000t. DFO scientist Paul Regular told reporters at a technical briefing in March that it's been holding steady at that level since 2016, as reported by Undercurrent. That is a considerable increase from the results of assessments from the early to mid-2000s when the SSB was just 10,000t, said Regular.

However, Rose was critical of the DFO's decision to declare cod in the cautious zone using a new LRP.

"It's very important to emphasize that despite being moved into the cautious zone, the stock itself did not grow into the cautious zone," he told the committee. "They (DFO) simply lowered the bar to jump over the line into the cautious zone."

Canadian cod scientist Dr. George Rose testified before the Fisheries and Oceans Standing Committee on Oct. 9, 2024. Screenshot from Parliamentary webcast

"It's also important to emphasize that the lowering of the LRP was substantial. Historically, it was considered the stock needed at least a million tons of spawning biomass to remain productive," Rose noted.

"And as recently as 2023, the LRP was considered by DFO and by other scientific analysis, including some done by myself and my colleagues, to exceed 800,000 tons."

However, he said the new LRP used by DFO for the 2024 decision reduces it to just above 300,000t.

"So this rewrites science history," stated Rose. He said there is little evidence to support the idea that the new LRP is justified.

"So while I applaud DFO science for their investigations and research, I will remain skeptical about this new lowered and unverified LRP until there's evidence that the stock can be as productive … with such a low spawning biomass."

The current stock assessment indicates that the stock is in a very weak position for growth, Rose added. Even with no fishing and projections that suggest further decline, it seems clear that the assumed management objective has not been met with stock growth, he said.

Canadian politicians question DFO officials in study of Northern cod decision

"Up until this year and this recent decision, DFO has done an admirable job of keeping those removals low enough so as not to result in stock decline even when environmental conditions were poor," he told the committee.

The decision to increase the quota by nearly 50% and to add two new entrants in the offshore increases the likelihood of stock decline, even to the extent of another collapse, said Rose.

Under questioning by the committee, Rose said he wouldn't go as far as to say the new LRP model is incorrect, but it was applied too quickly.

"I am skeptical about such a rapid rewriting of scientific history on this stock. We're supposed to accept this? Well, science doesn't work that way. Science remains skeptical until there is convincing evidence," Rose said.

Harvesters union laments quick end to summer cod fishing season in Newfoundland

Other witnesses before the committee on Oct. 11 were Gerry Byrne, fisheries minister for the province of NL; Dwan Street, president-elect of the Fish Food and Allied Workers (FFAW) union, which represents about 10,000 inshore harvesters; and FFAW senior fisheries scientist Dr. Erin Caruthers.

The meeting can be viewed on Canada's Parliamentary website here.  

Meanwhile, the 15,000t quota allocated for inshore fishing fleets in 2024 has nearly been taken. Harvesters in zones 3KL were advised by DFO on Oct. 10 that 180t remains, and the fishery would reopen on Friday morning (Oct. 11) to allow them to finish taking the quota. 

Offshore Canadian fleets have not yet started fishing for the 1,000t allocated for them inside Canada's 200-mile limit. Historically, the offshore fleets pursued the fishery in the winter.

title: Faulty hatch, open doors led to tragic sinking of Argos Georgia, investigation finds
content:
A preliminary report from the UK's Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) has revealed that the fishing vessel Argos Georgia's sinking off the Falkland Islands on July 22 was due to the failure of a starboard side door, Faro de Vigo reported.

The accident occurred 190 miles from Port Stanley, Falkland Islands, during a severe storm with 10-meter waves and winds over 50 knots. The door, designed to close upwards like a shutter, gradually opened, allowing water to flood the ship uncontrollably.

"The ongoing investigation has found that the shell door in the starboard side of Argos Georgia descended slowly into the fully open position. This allowed significant quantities of water to enter the vessel," the UK government said in its report.

The crew could not stop the flooding as internal doors were left open, facilitating water spread to various compartments. Despite the crew's desperate attempts, the vessel's flooding intensified, ultimately leading to its sinking. The disaster claimed the lives of 13 crew members, including four Spaniards, while 14 others survived.

The ship's emergency distress signal was recorded at 14:11 local time, and the main engine stopped around 14:45. By 16:00, some crew members began evacuating the vessel in lifeboats. However, the official abandonment order wasn't given until 16:23.

The report stressed the urgent need to evaluate side doors on ships and the importance of keeping internal doors closed during potential flooding. Survivors, corroborated by the second officer and three Indonesian crew members, have attributed the tragedy to the starboard door failure.

"All owners, operators and skippers of fishing vessels fitted with side shell doors are recommended to urgently ensure that a suitable and sufficient assessment of the risk of water entering the vessel through the side shell door has been undertaken and documented," the UK government said.

title: Untitled
content:
US shrimp importers continued to struggle with year-on-year declines in August 2024, but the latest trade data released by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) also reveals that it was the best month of the year so far.

The US imported 66,299 metric tons of shrimp worth $535.2 million in August 2024, 10% less volume and 11% less value than the 73,617t worth $599.6m imported in August 2023. As previously reported by Undercurrent News, August marks the third straight month of a y-o-y decline in volume following a brief upturn in May.

The good news is that August continues the upward trend in both volume and value, which was seen in July.

January 2024 -- 59,629t worth $462.4m
February 2024 -- 59,668t worth $456.5m
March 2024 -- 63,495t worth $481.8m
April 2024 -- 50,901t worth $397.6m
May 2024 -- 63,973t worth $486.7m
June 2024 -- 53,358t worth $418.2m
July 2024 -- 61,213t worth $481.8m
August 2024 -- 66,299 worth $535.2m

The average overall price has also followed that trend. In August, the average overall price was $3.82 per pound compared to $3.71/lb in July 2024 and $3.69/lb in June 2024. The chart created below using the UCN Trade Portal shows monthly US imports of shrimp. Also note that shrimp prices vary by country source and size. 

Prices for imported shrimp have been falling -- at time sharply -- since April 2022. As reported by Undercurrent, the overall average in April, before the fall, was $4.73/lb.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
US shrimp imports see best month of 2024 despite year-on-year declines - Undercurrent News

Looking at the first eight months of the year, the US has imported a total of 478,537t of shrimp valued at $3.7 billion. As the chart below shows, the US is currently on course to import 5% less volume and 11% less value than it did in 2023.

The chart below from the UCN Trade Portal shows the five largest source countries for US imports of shrimp in terms of value.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
US shrimp imports see best month of 2024 despite year-on-year declines - Undercurrent News

Of the top five source countries, three were hit with preliminary countervailing duties (CVD) earlier this year. The US began an investigation into shrimp imports after the American Shrimp Processors Association (ASPA) filed a countervailing duty petition against Ecuador, India, Indonesia and Vietnam in October 2023. An antidumping duty petition on imports of frozen warmwater shrimp from Ecuador and Indonesia was also filed at the time.

As reported by Undercurrent, preliminary rates were set in April, with India, Ecuador and Vietnam required to pay CVD duties ranging from less than 2% to as much as 196%. Indonesia was issued a negative determination, meaning no deposit would be required.

Duties, and the evolving regulations in the US market, has certainly kept the industry on edge.

India sees y-o-y drop in volume, value

India is the leading shrimp source to the US, sending 26,302t worth $203.1m in August. While July 2024 didn't see much change in terms of volume (0%) or value (-4%), the same can't be said for August, which saw a -14% change in both volume and value.

In the first eight months of the year, the country sent 183,436t, a 2% drop in volume from last year. Value-wise, India saw a 9% change in y-o-y. So far this year, shrimp imports from India are valued at $1.4b compared to $1.5b last year.

The average price paid for Indian shrimp in August was $3.66/lb, which is actually up $0.01 from the $3.65/lb paid in August 2023.

US shrimp imports see best month of 2024 despite year-on-year declines - Undercurrent News

Willem van der Pijl, the founder of the Global Shrimp Forum (GSF), told event attendees in Utrecht, the Netherlands, last month that Indian vannamei production is likely to stay in line with last year. Currently, the industry is facing issues related to disease outbreaks and flooding. However, one trading executive, who wished to remain anonymous, told Undercurrent this week that demand from the US is "increasing daily." 

Ecuador continues decline

Ecuador remained the number two trade partner to the US, sending 15,462t worth $107.2m in August. Volume decreased 17% compared to the same period last year, while value decreased 14%.

In the first eight months of the year, Ecuador sent 127,308t to the US, a 6% drop from last year. The value was also down compared to last year -- $860.4m in 2024 compared to $921.9m in 2023.

The average price paid per pound for Ecuador shrimp in August was $3.25/lb, up from $3.24/lb in July 2024. At this time last year the average price for shrimp from Ecuador was $3.12/lb.

US shrimp imports see best month of 2024 despite year-on-year declines - Undercurrent News

Ecuador's shrimp industry is currently facing disruptions in the form of ongoing electricity cuts. The energy crisis is impacting production as electricity is needed for critical functions, like freezing products for quality and food safety standards, and pumping water at farms to maintain oxygen levels. Sources told Undercurrent that the situation could hinder holiday preparations.

Indonesia and Vietnam see some wins

Indonesia ranks third as a source country for US shrimp imports. August saw the country export 10,945t of shrimp with a value of $84.3m; a 7% drop in volume and 14% drop in value y-o-y. 

From June through August, the US imported 83,481t from Indonesia, down from the 97,512t imported during the same period in 2023. Import value also decreased y-o-y. So far this year Indonesian shrimp imports are valued at  $629.0b versus $794.5b in 2023.

The average price per pound is on the rise, up from $3.63/lb this July to $3.72 in August. However, the average price per pound is down from $3.89/lb in August 2023.

Meanwhile, the fourth source country for shrimp, Vietnam, sent 7,747t in August 2024. Of the consistent top four source countries for shrimp imports into the US, Vietnam is the only one to see a positive percent change in the latest batch of data. Volume increased 14% y-oy, while value increased by 11%. August 2024 shrimp imports from Vietnam were valued at $80.3m versus $72.4 in August 2023.

When looking at the first eight months of the year, the volume of shrimp imports from Vietnam is up 6% to 39,065t. However, value for January through August is down. So far this year shrimp imports from Vietnam are valued at $384m versus $395m the year before.

Price per pound for Vietnam saw a sharp increase from $4.59/lb in July 2024 to $4.95/lb in August 2024. The price per pound is also slightly up y-o-y, as the average was $4.93/lb in August 2023.

US shrimp imports see best month of 2024 despite year-on-year declines - Undercurrent News

More charts and information can be found on the UCN Trade and UCN Prices Portal.

title: Royal Greenland to resume selling Canada site post-investigation into fire
content:
Royal Greenland plans to resume talks over selling the site of its fire-damaged Canadian factory, Fruits de mer 'Est du Quebec, once the investigation into what happened there is complete, CEO Susanne Arfelt Rajamand told Undercurrent News.

The firm announced it was to close its coldwater shrimp, lobster and snow crab processing factory in Matane in March 2024, just days before a fire caused widespread damage to the facility.

"That was a terrible experience, but the most important thing was that nobody was hurt," said Arfelt Rajamand.

"The investigation is still going on into what caused the fire. We are, of course, supporting the authorities in that. As for the future of the site, the current plan [closing] remains the policy. It will depend on the outcome of the investigation and the market conditions at that time, but we stay true to that conversation that happened before the fire broke out."

Royal Greenland had been in the process of arranging the sale of the site when the fire occurred, but then "everything came to a standstill, and we just had to focus on supporting the authorities," she said.

Back in April, Kristina Michaud -- the Bloc Quebecois member of parliament for Avignon-La Mitis-Matane-Matapedia -- had said the community hoped another seafood processing company might be interested in buying and operating the facility.

title: Editor’s choice: Conxemar recap; More twists in Peter Pan auction; CapVest lines up US smoker deal; Japan M&A
content:
Editorial and managing director Tom Seaman brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week  

Undercurrent News was reporting live last week from the Conxemar trade show in Vigo, Spain.

During the show, Undercurrent reporters interviewed major companies such as Grupo Iberica de Congelados, Grupo Pereira and Grupo Nueva Pescanova, to name a few. Outside the blog, you can also read stand-alone stories from Conxemar about a new Ecuador shrimp plant, shrimp prices in this country, and a salmon factory in Latvia. 

The week ended with another twist in the Peter Pan Seafood Company saga, as an investor challenged former co-owner Rodger May's takeover in a receivership auction sale in court on Friday, Oct. 4. 

A day after the judge signed off on the assets sale to May, attorneys for California investor John Ketcham filed an appeal Friday in King County Superior Court in Seattle seeking to prevent May from taking possession of a salmon processing facility in Port Moller, Alaska.

Ketcham had loaned Peter Pan $10 million last year in return for a lien on one of the company's Alaska salmon processing plants. 

May is paying about $25.3m cash with about $12m credit for secured loans he'd advanced his own company since acquiring it with the help of two private equity funds in 2021. Those same investors have since supported a rival bid from Silver Bay Seafoods, alleging that May had misled them when the company began running into financial trouble.

There was also a flurry of other scoops on acquisitions. On Friday, Undercurrent revealed that a UK-based private equity company, CapVest Partners, is in talks to acquire Honey Smoked Fish Company in the US. 

Earlier in the week, two Japanese deals broke. On Oct. 2, Japanese seafood giant Nissui Corp. announced a deal for a plant in Saint-Hernin, France, from Guyader Traiteur Frais to expand its tapas product lineup, a rapidly growing category within the EU market. 

The acquisition, finalized on Jun. 28 through Miti, a France-based subsidiary of Nissui's European processing division, Cite Marine, is part of Nissui's strategy to broaden its tapas offerings to include seafood such as octopus, squid, and sardines.

On Sept.30, last Monday, Japanese seafood trading company Hanwa Co. acquired an 80% stake in Marugo Fukuyama Suisan Co., a seafood processor based in Hokkaido, Japan's northernmost island. 

The acquisition is expected to strengthen Hanwa's processing capabilities and boost sales to markets in North America and Southeast Asia, further expanding its global seafood operations, the Tokyo-based conglomerate said in a statement.

In Canada, enforcement officers with the country's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) seized 13,000 pounds of lobster worth CAD 100,000 ($73,880) on Oct. 2 after executing a search warrant in Shelburne County, in the province of Nova Scotia.

An individual was arrested for an offense under the Fisheries Act, including maintaining a lobster pound without the required license, the DFO said in a press release. The officers also seized documents and electronic records, and the matter is under investigation for potential charges, the DFO added.

The DFO did not identify the lobster pound's location or the owner's name.

One story, a short-lived East Coast US port strike, looked set to blow up but fizzled out. "This strike is going to really wreak havoc," one US East Coast wholesaler told Undercurrent on Oct. 1. 

However, the strike ended on Oct. 4 after dock workers struck a deal with port operators.

title: Shrimp industry grapples with rising tide of regulations, duties
content:
UTRECHT, The Netherlands -- Evolving regulations in major markets like the US and EU are placing new burdens on the global shrimp supply chain -- but some shrimp industry experts argue the changes offer new business opportunities

Concerns over rising costs and complexity from new US traceability rules and anti-dumping investigations dominated discussions at the Global Shrimp Forum in Utrecht, the Netherlands, last month. But others voiced support for enhanced traceability in supply chains.

"We don't see that as an unbearable cost or overburden. It's actually fundamental to our business model," said Kristin Veriga, senior vice president of Indonesian aquatech startup eFishery.

Guus Pastoor, chairman of APICE, at Global Shrimp Forum in Utrecht, the Netherlands. Source: GSF

Much of the recent focus has been on recent US anti-dumping probes into shrimp imports. Since October of last year, the US Commerce Department has investigated alleged subsidies on shrimp imports from Ecuador, India, Indonesia and Vietnam. Preliminary rates -- set in April -- range from 1.69%-10.58%.

Robert DeHaan, executive vice president of the National Fisheries Institute, the largest US seafood trade association, said the cases could have a long-term impact on shrimp given their scope and complexity.

Robert DeHaan of NOAA. Source: NOAA website.

"These are actually six cases. It's four dumping cases and two subsidy cases," DeHaan explained. India and Vietnam already have a dumping margin on their products and are excluded from the dumping cases.

DeHaan noted that the current rates, while preliminary, require immediate action: "Once the preliminary rate has been established, you must start withholding that rate... Until the numbers change."

The cases were initiated by US processors of domestic Gulf of Mexico shrimp who are "quite upset with the competition from imported products." However, DeHaan said that even if dumping is proven, petitioners must still demonstrate injury to domestic producers.

He cited a previous case involving Vietnamese pangasius where the US International Trade Commission ruled petitioners had not proven injury, despite findings of dumping.

"These cases are often litigated for years after the numbers are set, and the results are determined," DeHaan said. "During that period, you're living with those [preliminary duties], but it's the fact that if the Commission or the Department of Commerce does something wrong procedurally, they could get reversed."

The broad scope of the investigations -- which cover most shrimp products except for specific categories like breaded, fresh, and canned shrimp -- can complicate the process. Up to 15 various governmental bodies are involved in seafood import regulation.

"Our system is highly confusing in my opinion. It involves a kind of ping pong between the International Trade Commission, which is an independent agency, and the Department of Commerce," which is overseen by US Congress, DeHaan said.

Exporters' better prepare' for US traceability rules

DeHaan said stricter regulations governing traceability outlined in the Food Safety Modernization Act (FSMA) rule 204 -- set to take effect in 2027 -- could also prove challenging for shrimp companies. 

NFI exec warns new 2026 seafood traceability plan has flown ‘below radar’

While not directly about food safety, the rule aims to enhance the ability to trace products during foodborne illness outbreaks. "The rule is about recalls that are triggered by outbreaks," DeHaan explained. "You have no obligation until someone gets sick, and then it triggers the obligation."

Despite the 2027 compliance date, DeHaan advised companies to start preparing much sooner. "You have to have the paper documented for your supply chain and your critical tracking events starting on January 2026," he warned.

The rule introduces the concepts of Critical Tracking Events (CTEs) and Key Data Elements (KDEs), requiring companies to marry these up throughout the supply chain. DeHaan said the complexity this introduces, especially for companies further down the supply chain handling multiple food products, could create "interesting conversations" between suppliers and buyers.

"The further you go down the supply chain the more difficult it gets," he remarked.

For those with an eye for detail, specific exemptions can be found for certain products, if companies can determine when a product falls under the rule's scope or not. "Remember that all of these things happen down the supply chain, but then if subsequently you cook it or salt it, you're out," DeHaan said.

EU 'regulatory superpower'

Turning to Europe, Guus Pastoor, chairman of AIPCE, the EU Fish Processors and Traders Association, described the EU as a "regulatory superpower" intent on more stringent traceability and sustainability requirements.

"Our politicians and policymakers are not really sleeping," said Pastoor. "They are quite busy and they are making more and more regulations." 

eFishery tech used by 60 farms in India in inaugural year

Pastoor said the EU's social and environmental standards could be regarded as de facto trade barriers. "If you look at all those regulations, and you add them all up, it's quite a lot. And then if you then add the social element then it's going to be even more complicated," he said.

Imports that violate EU rules face an uphill battle to enter the bloc under standard procedures. Since 2017, EU border authorities have tested every second container of Indian shrimp for antibiotic residues, after laboratories found traces of chemicals on products from the country, adding to costs.

"The Commission is still saying that they need extra guarantees from India. That they're waiting for certain papers and certain guarantees, and that they're not able to change their regime," said Pastoor.

This lack of progress, according to Pastoor, demonstrates how legislative changes can be slow to materialize. "We're one year later [from GSF 2023] and you can see that things haven't changed at all. That shows how legislation can fill a lot of time before you get any change," he said.

Overall, Pastoor said that complaints about dumping could be moot with "so many complicated EU rules" on traceability and health issues. "I don't think we'll need anti-dumping at a certain point to see that products are not allowed to enter into the market anymore because of other reasons."

Other industry members sanguine

Despite regulatory pressures, industry leaders were confident in their ability to meet traceability demands. 

In an audience poll, most respondents rated their level of concern about the anti-dumping and countervailing duties around six out of 10. In another audience poll, respondents rated their preparedness for new traceability rules at a similar six out of 10 on average.

Aris Utama, a director at Indonesian shrimp company BMI, said he had no complaints about the rules. "We've been doing it for a very long time," he said. "We export to European countries also that require this much earlier on and we learned that requirement very early already."

Choudary Karuturi, managing director of APex Frozen Food, underlined the importance of traceability beyond regulatory compliance: "Beyond just a regulatory compliance, you need it for yourself... We cannot live without traceability anymore at this point in time."

Meanwhile, Heath England, president of Trace Register, a traceability service provider, framed the issue as one of digitization rather than traceability itself. "We have a digitization problem," England asserted.

"For years I have literally stood in Southeast Asia, in hatcheries with people handwriting records down. They can tell you exactly where that fingerling or that embryo came from... but it's written in a language I don't understand on a piece of paper in a filing cabinet in a country 2,000 miles away from where a food outbreak or a food safety outbreak problem just happened."

England argued that proper implementation of traceability systems could provide return on investment for companies. "If implemented correctly, you're actually making money by being fully traced," he said. "It's a good thing for you, no matter where you are in the supply chain."

However, DeHaan warned of the cumulative impact of proliferating regulations.

"The critical point for us is the cumulative impact of that set of regulations in raising prices for your customers and consumers in the US to get your products," DeHaan said, noting that US consumers are "very concerned about price" amid broader inflation.
