title: Experimental gear helps Bering Sea trawlers avoid whale deaths
content:
US trawlers in the Bering Sea targeting flatfish have deployed an experimental type of gear this summer to avoid entanglements with killer whales, the Anchorage Daily News reports. The vessels employ underwater web fences to keep killer whales from getting entangled in their nets, which get pulled along the ocean bottom. 

One killer whale was caught during a trial run of the gear held from May through September. This was an improvement over the previous year, when nine whales were caught in nets.

Industry figures express cautious optimism

"We're hopeful that we have come up with a good solution here," Chris Woodley, executive director of the Groundfish Forum, told the newspaper. His trade association represents five companies with a fleet of 19 bottom trawlers in the US state of Alaska. 

"But these whales are really intelligent," he added. "They're adaptive. And what works one season may not work the next."

The web fence stretches across a wide swath of the net mouth, acting as a barrier to whales while not blocking fish passage into the net. 

The newspaper report said the killer whale caught in June was in a deep area of the Bering Sea where five bottom trawl vessels pursued a mix of flatfish, such as Greenland turbot and black cod. The information was disclosed this week by industry officials, who were scheduled to testify about their avoidance efforts at a Thursday meeting of the North Pacific Fishery Management Council in Anchorage.

NOAA assesses 30 years of orca whale entanglements, deaths in Alaska

According to Marjorie Mooney-Seus, US federal agency spokesperson, the vessel immediately withdrew from that fishery upon finding the whale. A federal observer took tissue samples of the dead marine mammal for analysis.

Criticism has been leveled at the fleet since last year's take of nine killer whales by bottom trawlers. Trawlers have long drawn criticism for a wide range of bycatch, including halibut and crab, which are prohibited species for these vessels and must be discarded. 

Surge in orca deaths prompts review

A National Marine Fisheries Service investigation found that one of the killer whales caught last year was seriously injured but alive when released; six died after they became entangled with nets, and two were believed to be already dead when they entered the nets.

Last year's surge in killer whale deaths and injuries prompted an expanded research effort -- funded by the fishing industry and the US government -- to develop better gear to keep them out of the nets. 

Earlier this year, nearly a dozen researchers and vessel captains went to Memorial University in St. John's, Newfoundland, to test the fence design in a large flume tank that can pulse with a current to simulate underwater conditions and has a large glass window for observation.

"You can see what the net shape looks like when you're setting the gear, and when you're hauling it back and when it's actually on the bottom during the fishing process," Sarah Webster, the science project director for the Alaska Seafood Cooperative, an industry group that seeks to improve management of the bottom fish harvests told the newspaper. 

The web fence is placed ahead of the net's foot ropes with webbing made of "echoreflective" material to help the whales detect it through their sonar soundings. 

It is also a physical barrier to keep marine mammals out. The design still allows fish passage as they can move over or under the fence and into the net or enter the trawl through the holes in the webbing.

The experimental web fence was developed for gear used by four of the trawlers during the deep-water flatfish harvest. They operated throughout the entire season without bringing a whale on board. Researchers said that a fifth vessel caught the whale and used a different net design, so the fence likely did not work as designed. 

"We think what likely happened was that the fence just didn't deploy or was not in the right position or taking the right shape when the take occurred," Webster said.

US law protects marine mammals

Killer whales -- also known as orcas -- are afforded special status under the Marine Mammal Protection Act, which requires vessel owners or operators to report injuries or deaths.

In addition to the nine orcas taken in 2023 by the bottom trawl fleet, one was also taken aboard a vessel targeting pollock. Another whale died after it became entangled in longline gear put in the water by a vessel contracted by NOAA Fisheries to do a survey.

Longliners, who string baited hooks along the ocean bottom to fish for black cod and halibut, have a long history of encounters with marine mammals that stretch back decades. The whales have learned to strip their catch off the hooks, prompting some to switch to pots so that their catch is not preyed upon.

Larger freezer longliners have also struggled when they switch from targeting Pacific cod to Greenland turbot favored by orcas. That prompted their industry group to seek a change through the federal fishery council to allow their vessels to use pots rather than hooks when they target the Greenland turbot prized by killer whales.

Chad See, executive director of the Freezer Longline Coalition, said that the rule approving his fleet's gear switch to pots for Greenland turbot is expected to be finalized this year.

"That's our goal," See told the newspaper. "To harvest these fish with much less whale predation."

title: North Atlantic right whale death attributed to Maine lobster gear in first for fishery
content:
The lobster industry in the US state of Maine has officially had its first North Atlantic right whale (NARW) death attributed to the fishery. A necropsy on NARW #5120 has been completed, confirming that the juvenile endangered whale found with rope identified as belonging to the Maine lobster industry died as a result of chronic entanglement.

An Unusual Mortality Event (UME) was declared for NARWs in 2017 after 35 whales were reported as dead or injured. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has been documenting the counts of mortality, serious injury and morbidity (sublethal injury or illness) cases, and so far have reported 16 cases this year -- including #5120, a female right whale who was found dead near Joseph Sylvia State Beach on Martha's Vineyard, Massachusetts, on Jan.  28, 2024.

The Maine Lobstermen's Association (MLA) released the following statement:

"The MLA is deeply saddened by the death of the juvenile right whale that NMFS attributed to the Maine fishery in February. No Maine lobsterman would ever want to intentionally harm a right whale. The MLA has not yet been allowed to view the gear removed from the whale because the NOAA Office of Law Enforcement investigation remains open."

Whale #5120 was the only known calf of #3720 (aka Squilla) and had been born during the 2021 calving season. In August 2022, an aerial team with the Canadian Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) observed #5120 with multiple wraps of line around her tail and flukes. DFO officials also reported seeing two small buoys at the flukes, as well as an estimated 100 feet of line trailing behind her. The whale's entanglement was deemed serious due to its age. It was noted at the time that the rope around her tail stock would likely tighten as she grew.

Attempts were made to help disentangle the whale but were ultimately unsuccessful. Aerial observers with the Northeast Fisheries Science Center last spotted #5120 in June 2023, approximately 60 miles northeast of Shippagan, New Brunswick. It was noted at the time that while she was feeding with other whales, "her overall conditions had declined and the wounds from the wraps of rope at the peduncle appeared to be more severe."

Photos taken by the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, one of the agencies that responded to the stranded whale incident in January, show how deeply embedded the gear became in the whale's tail over time.

A close up of the tailstock anchored with a black towing strap used to pull the whale out of the surf for further documentation. Above the strap, law enforcement officials made rope cuts to remove a portion of the entangling rope for further analysis. However, the rope is still present, deeply embedded in the wounds on the tailstock that officials could not remove. Necropsy teams will continue to collect gear as it becomes accessible. Credit: Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution/Michael Moore NOAA Permit # 24359

NOAA later revealed that an analysis of the gear recovered showed that it was consistent with the rope used in Maine state water trap/pot buoy lines. 

Since a UME was declared in 2017, NOAA has documented a total of 10 mortalities due to entanglement, 33 serious injuries due to entanglement, and 53 sublethal injuries or illnesses due to entanglement. Out of all of those entanglements, the death of whale #5120 is the only one attributed to lobster gear belonging to a Maine fishery.

Another section of rope that was entangled around North Atlantic right whale #5120; this one has a full 1-foot purple zip tie. Credit: NOAA Fisheries

"The fact is we know that entanglement in Maine gear is extremely rare. This is the first reported entanglement of a right whale in Maine lobster gear in 20 years and the first death attributed to the fishery," said the MLA. "Maine lobstermen have made significant changes to how they fish over the last 25 years to avoid entanglement."

Despite efforts to protect whales from entanglements and vessel strikes, lobstermen have been hit with a series of new rules and regulations, from tracking devices to ropeless gear. With that said, the Maine lobster industry did score a major victory last June in a federal appeals court. The US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit ruled that the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) "distorted the science driving the regulation, relying improperly on assumptions and worst-case scenarios when determining the risk posed by industry to right whales."

Undercurrent News asked MLA acting COO Patrice McCarron if she thought the cause of death would impact future regulations, to which McCarron replied, "It's really too soon to know."

"However, when drafting the most recent whale regulations implemented in 2022, NMFS assumed that the Maine lobster fishery was responsible for 3 to 6 right whale deaths each year," explained McCarron. "MLA's legal victory will no longer allow NMFS to use that sort of unreasonable assumption."

The lobster fishery is important for the state of Maine, not only from a cultural standpoint but also because of its contributions to the state's economy. In 2023, Maine lobstermen landed 93.7 million pounds of lobster, valued at $464.4m.

title: Scottish authorities investigate ‘illegal’ salmon disposal
content:
Thousands of rotting salmon carcasses have been illegally dumped on a beach in North Uist, Scotland, transforming the picturesque site into a "toxic wasteland," the Scottish Sun reported.

As revealed by footage from Ecotricity, Whiteshore Cockles, a waste disposal company, continued dumping fish remains even after the practice was banned in January 2024.

Concerns have risen about cross-contamination. The Scottish Environment Protection Agency (SEPA) has launched an investigation after being assured by the company that carcasses were sent to mainland facilities for disposal.

Environmental activist Dale Vance condemned the illegal burials, highlighting health risks and demanding accountability. Whiteshore Cockles is used by Mowi Scotland to dispose of its salmon.

title: Close ties between US fisheries regulators, Alaska pollock sector under fire in news investigation
content:
A critical piece entitled "Deadly Harvest" by investigative news outlet The Lever accuses US regulators of being too cozy with the nearly $2 billion Alaska pollock fishery and turning a blind eye to the destructive impact on marine life and other commercial fisheries.

Critics say the North Pacific Fishery Management Council (NPFMC), which regulates federal fisheries in Alaska, is allowing the trawl fleet to take an outsized bite out of other species through bycatch. That's despite smaller-scale fishermen targeting salmon and halibut, state lawmakers, and tribal governments who complain the system is designed to protect the industry's status quo.

The piece from The Lever points to the revolving door between the NPFMC and the industry, singling out figures such as Stephanie Madsen, who chaired the council from 2003 to 2007 while simultaneously serving as the vice president of the Pacific Seafood Processors Association.

Alaska judge hears tribal lawsuit over Bering Sea pollock fleet’s salmon bycatch

Another example cited was Chris Oliver, who served on the council for 16 years before joining major pollock company American Seafoods as an adviser on government affairs. Oliver is back on the council, joining five other members who represent trawl interests. 

The piece also notes that earlier this year, president Joe Biden's administration reappointed Anne Vanderhoeven, the current director of government affairs for Arctic Storm Management Group, a large trawl company, to the council. That was despite Washington state governor Jay Inslee recommending a tribal advocate, which would've tipped the balance of the council away from the trawl industry's favor, Undercurrent News reported at the time.

"The average fisherman who goes into a council meeting, they don't even know who's working for who," The Lever quoted an unnamed "former council member" who it said asked not to be named for fear of blowback. "There's a game within a game."

Neither the NPFMC nor some of its sitting members responded to repeated requests for comment, The Lever reported.

Conservation-minded pick for US North Pacific panel nixed in favor of trawl industry reappointment

US representative Mary Peltola, the first indigenous Alaska Native elected to the US Congress, told The Lever she's disturbed by apparent conflicts of interest in federal fisheries management. 

"I am concerned about the perception -- and actuality -- of industry people being in these policymaking decisions," she is quoted in the article. "The council process works very well if you have the personal connections or have the money, but it does not reflect the diversity of the people who depend on all of these Bering Sea resources."

The Lever piece also said the US government is subsidizing the US pollock industry by purchasing more than $66m worth of fish through the US Department of Agriculture. It pointed to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Saltonstall-Kennedy Program grant of $300k to the Genuine Alaska Pollock Producers to promote its products.

The piece said people inside the fishing sector were intimidated from openly criticizing the US pollock industry -- responsible for catching about 40% of US seafood by volume -- for fear of losing jobs or losing access to lucrative markets.

The Alaska Pollock Fishery Alliance, which represents the region's pollock companies, said these fears are "unfounded," The Lever reported.

The entire 4,200-odd word feature article was also republished in The Nation magazine.

title: Spanish bluefin giant posts significant loss after years of big profits
content:
Spanish bluefin tuna business Grupo Ricardo Fuentes e Hijos has reported significant financial losses for the year 2023.

This marks a sharp decline from the company's profitable run in previous years.

According to its latest results, the company, which recorded a profit of €55 million ($60.8m) in 2022, reported a loss of €23.9m in 2023, as shown below.

Additionally, the group's earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization dropped from €76.6m in 2022 to a loss of €30.3m in 2023, and its operating result plummeted from €68m in 2022 to negative €36.4m last year, as shown.

Photo: A screenshot of Ricardo Fuentes' 2023 results.

The graph above also indicates that the firm's 2023 revenue dropped 31% year-on-year to €261.8m.

The company attributed this downturn to several factors, including a sharp decrease in tuna sale prices.

According to the company, the rise in quotas set by the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas -- shown in the graph below -- and increased production from 2022 led the market to adjust prices downward. This price drop was more drastic than anticipated, severely impacting revenues, Ricardo Fuentes said in its report.

ICCAT's tuna quotas. Photo: Ricardo Fuentes' results.

However, the firm expressed optimism for 2024, predicting a recovery in tuna prices despite the quotas remaining high, as has been the "cyclical trend" in previous years.

The graphs below compare fresh and frozen bluefin tuna prices in Japan and France in dollars over the last year and the past five years.

VIEW GRAPH
Bluefin tuna, domestic, fresh, monthly, Toyosu
© 2025 Undercurrent News
To view the full datas
GO PREMIUM
Upgrade to Pro to view

Grupo Ricardo Fuentes expects to return to profitability as prices stabilize and adjustments are made to purchase costs. Furthermore, the company expects to benefit from operating its latest-generation freezer vessel.

"The results of the last fiscal year are in line with market cycles. We continue to have the confidence of our customers around the world, betting on innovation and strengthening our investment to offer the best bluefin tuna. A clear example of the latter is that we have doubled our fleet of deep-freezer vessels, from two to four in just two years," the firm said in a statement sent to Undercurrent News.

Grupo Ricardo Fuentes is a family-run business with six siblings at the helm. The third generation of the Fuentes family is currently integrating into management.

"Today Grupo Ricardo Fuentes is the largest exporting organization of bluefin tuna and annually harvests an average of 15,000t of this tuna for the market, between the Mediterranean and the Atlantic." It also operates nurseries in Cartagena and San Pedro del Pinatar (in the Spanish region of Murcia), Tunisia, and Malta. It sells to 12 Japanese companies, three Korean and two Chinese, it wrote in its results.

The firm's customers include Japanese giants Mitsui & Co. and Maruha Nichiro Corp.

The company conducts bluefin tuna farming, combining its fishing operations with acquisitions from third parties. Its fishing fleet, which includes three purse seiners, operates primarily in the Mediterranean, where the tuna are transferred to one of the group's four ranching farms. The company said it was conducting research programs on these farms to improve the raising of the fish in captivity.

Over the years, Grupo Ricardo Fuentes has undertaken various projects in aquaculture, including a long-standing partnership with Spain's Institute of Oceanography to develop technology for large-scale bluefin tuna farming. These efforts have resulted in successful advancements, such as closing the bluefin tuna lifecycle in captivity, and in 2014, the company became the first to sell Atlantic bluefin tuna born in captivity commercially, according to the firm.

Photo: Ricardo Fuentes on Facebook.

The company is also currently studying the presence of skipjack tuna, a subtropical species, in the waters off the Murcia region. Rising Mediterranean temperatures, driven by climate change, have caused shifts in the geographic distribution of certain fish species.

The firm told Undercurrent that this project has now been completed, with "the observation of these subtropical specimens" and training for fishermen to spot them. 

Earlier this year, after nearly six years of investigation, Spain's National Court directed eight individuals and 12 companies, including Ricardo Fuentes, to trial over allegations of illegal tuna fishing and money laundering. The charges stem from the company's alleged involvement in selling illegally caught bluefin tuna commercially and laundering significant profits from this illicit activity.

The group employs more than 900 people, according to Murcia Plaza.

title: Major seafood restaurants issued letter by US Federal Trade Commission about ‘misleading’ customers
content:
US Foreign Trade Commission (FTC) commissioner Alvaro M. Bedoya is not messing around when it comes to restaurants misleading people into thinking their seafood is "wild, fresh-caught or local" if it's actually "farmed, frozen and shipped in from afar."

Bedoya revealed in a post to the Twitter/X social media platform that he sent a letter Tuesday (Oct. 1) to all 10 of the country's highest-grossing seafood restaurants to "relay" recent guidelines about "not giving consumers the wrong impression -- specifically, if they are serving wild-caught, American seafood when they are actually serving foreign, farm-raised imports."

The media post blacks out who was sent the letter, but Bedoya reportedly told Reuters that some of the restaurant chains he messaged include Red Lobster, Long John Silver's and Legal Sea Foods. 

"This is a new reminder to companies that it is all of the ways you're communicating to a consumer, the net impression of that communication needs to be accurate," said Bedoya.

The letter to leading seafood restaurants comes a few weeks after the FTC published a blog post about what the agency calls "net impression," or misleading customers into thinking that the product they are eating is wild, fresh caught, or local, when in reality it's actually farmed, frozen and imported. 

The FTC blog sets the scene. 

"Imagine a waterfront restaurant with beachy décor," it read. "Fishing nets hang from the ceiling and pictures of shrimp and fishing boats cover the wall. You sit down at a table draped in red, white, and blue, and your server, dressed in a shirt that says, 'We catch 'em, you eat 'em!' hands you a menu. It says, 'Eat local! Try our seasonal fresh catch of the day!' You order that seasonal fresh catch and enjoy the sunset. While you're waiting for your food, you check out the restaurant's Instagram account and scroll through post after post of fishermen hooking glimmering fish and scooping nets full of shrimp out of the sea. 

"Given this scene, would you be surprised to find out that the seasonal fresh catch was actually farmed seafood, frozen overseas and shipped in?"

The FTC said that while the restaurant "never said it outright," it gave their customers the "net impression" that they would be eating fresh and local fish.

"Not only is it illegal to mislead customers about where the seafood is from, it's also not fair to other restaurants that tell the truth and play by the rules," the blog continued.

In his follow-up letter to leading seafood restaurants, Bedoya made note that what they are receiving is not a warning letter, a notice of penalty offence letter, or a notice of law enforcement investigation of a business. 

"Identical letters are being sent to all 10 of the highest grossing seafood restaurants in the country," he wrote. "That said, I will not hesitate to request a law enforcement investigation if I am presented with credible evidence of a law violation."

Contact the author amanda.buckle@undercurrentnews.com

title: Pacific Seafood expands on defense against charges it shorted US shrimpers millions
content:
The Pacific Seafood Group last week issued a second, expanded statement in relation to the lawsuit brought against it by a former employee that alleges the Clackamas, Oregon-based processing giant underpaid shrimpers in the US Gulf of Mexico and cheated them out of millions.

As earlier reported by Undercurrent News, Justin Ottman, a former finance director, filed a 16-page complaint on Sept. 23 against Dulcich Inc., Pacific Seafood's parent company, in Oregon's Multinomah County Circuit Court, seeking almost $2.3 million for alleged wrongful termination, violating the Oregon Family Leave Act and whistleblower retaliation.

The lawsuit recounts how Ottman, who had worked for Pacific dating back to September 2018, was dispatched to Galveston, Texas, "for the purpose of examining one of the brands owned and operated by Pacific Seafood, Galveston Shrimp Company [GSC]." 

Pacific Seafood shorted US shrimpers out of millions, lawsuit alleges

While investigating potential concerns about self-dealing at GSC, a business purchased by Pacific roughly 10 years earlier, Ottman said he discovered evidence of a "much larger and more serious problem," an alleged "long-running scheme to intentionally misrepresent the weight and grade of catches brought in by shrimp boats, resulting in lower pay to the small businesses that operated them, and fraudulent profits for Pacific Seafood." 

Pacific, which maintained two separate accounting systems for each catch, used the scheme to illegally profit between $10m and $20m, Ottman alleged. He said he was later denied benefits and had his position eliminated by the company on Dec. 1, 2023, after bringing the matter to its attention in the form of a 170-page report.

'Mr. Ottman is no whistleblower'

But that's Ottman's account of what happened. Pacific asserted in its second response sent to Undercurrent late last week that its former finance director's claims are false and that he played a smaller role in the initial investigation of GSC than he suggested.

"Mr. Ottman is no whistleblower," asserted a spokesperson for Pacific. "He was part of a team sent to Galveston, Texas, at the direction of Pacific Seafood's legal department to investigate concerns we had related to our business partner at [GSC]. The team provided their findings to legal, as requested. Mr. Ottman had a very limited role in that investigation and his recollection is both factually inaccurate and an inappropriate breach of the company's attorney-client privilege."

The Pacific spokesperson continued, saying "it is absolutely false that Mr. Ottman's separation from the company had anything to do with his limited involvement in the Galveston investigation. Mr. Ottman was very upset when his position was eliminated, and he appears to be taking his frustrations out in court." 

The statement concludes: "We are confident that the facts will show Pacific Seafood has done nothing wrong."

Pacific also provided Undercurrent with contact information for a Texas shrimp harvester who has a good relationship with the company. Craig Wallis, the owner of W&W Dock, told Undercurrent he maintains a fleet of nine shrimp harvesting vessels, including seven owned and two others managed. 

He said he's been working with Pacific via GSC for the past two years and has no complaints. He said the company has been competitive in its pricing, and his vessels keep a careful eye on the weights and quality of their catch, so he doesn't believe he's been underpaid.

"Pacific has a quality plant that's fairly new, and we need every packer we can get," he said. 

Pacific: Excess inventory forced write-downs

As reported earlier by Undercurrent, the alleged self-dealing Ottman said he was investigating at Galveston Shrimp was almost certainly a case involving Nello Cassarino, the former CEO of GSC. Cassarino sued Pacific for millions in a state court in October 2023 for allegedly breaching his contract at the business, which was owned by his family until it was sold to Pacific in 2011.

Pacific counter-sued Cassarino in a federal court in February 2024 but had the case transferred to the same Multnomah County state court a month later. The lawsuit charges him with breach of fiduciary duty, breach of contract, fraud and unjust enrichment among other allegations. The company is asking for $3.2m in damages. 

In its 50-page complaint, Pacific described a long list of alleged schemes by which Cassarino steered business while acting as a manager for the company to line his own pockets.

It alleges that Cassarino formed a new limited liability company, for example, to acquire a 13,000-square foot distribution and cold storage facility previously owned by Bay Area Seafood, and then began his own business under the name "Aquarius Cold Storage." He then redirected GSC product to Aquarius, charging GSC cold storage and transport fees.

"GSC paid at least $596,000 in fees to Aquarius Cold Storage, in addition to costs for labor, worker's compensation insurance, fuel, and other supplies used by Aquarius Cold Storage, all of which Cassarino benefitted from personally," the complaint alleges. 

Shrimp boats on the Dickinson Bayou in Galveston, Texas. Photograph by Gallimaufry on Shutterstock.

Beginning in 2020, Cassarino also allegedly led GSC to purchase significant quantities of brown shrimp from the Brownsville (Texas) Shrimp Dock, which he owns and manages, rather than directly from the vessels. Between 2020 and 2023, GSC has paid the dock $425,000 for "unnecessary 'boat offloading fees,' the payment of which benefitted Cassarino personally," according to the complaint.

Between 2021 and 2023, GSC paid $4.8m for purchases of more than 1.2m lbs of shrimp, including a $0.50 to $1.00/lb surchange, according to the complaint, causing the company to overpay between $614,428 and $1.2m for shrimp.

The complaint also alleges that Cassarino allowed GSC's shrimp inventory to grow to an excessive 1.5m lbs valued at more than $8.4m as of July 2023, ultimately leading to a significant write-down and losses. 

Cassarino, who voluntarily resigned from his post at Pacific in August 2023, couldn't be reached for comment at press time.

Pacific also sued two former GSC employees in a Texas federal court in December 2023 to stop them from allegedly stealing proprietary client information, as reported by Undercurrent. The men, who were allegedly working for Cassarino at an unregistered Texas seafood company, were accused of causing Pacific to lose six of its 25 shrimp-buying customers, resulting in a reduction in business at GSC of 60%.

title: US shrimp boat intercepted without valid permit near Florida
content:
A US Coast Guard (USCG) vessel intercepted a commercial fishing boat carrying 45,000 pounds of shrimp in the southernmost tip of the US state of Florida, only to discover the boat's fishing permit had expired.

The USCG said in a press release that the intervention occurred near the Marquesas Keys, about 32 miles west of Key West.

Upon discovering the sizable quantity of pink shrimp aboard the boat and the lack of a valid fishing permit, the USCG instructed the crew to terminate their fishing expedition and return to a port in Alabama.

The vessel is returning to its homeport in Alabama, where National Marine Fisheries Service officers will meet with the captain for further questioning.  

Details regarding the vessel's name remain undisclosed at this time due to the ongoing nature of the investigation.

The US fisheries sector contributes more than $240 billion to the economy annually, with around 20% of species being overfished, the USCG said, citing data from NOAA Fisheries.

In 2022, 14.5 million lbs of pink shrimp were caught, worth $37m.

title: Untitled
content:
The Peruvian government, through the production ministry (Produce), has denied claims that the current scarcity of jumbo (giant) squid in its waters is due to illegal fishing by Chinese vessels. Instead, the ministry attributed the crisis to climate conditions, specifically the impact of the El Nino phenomenon.

Artisanal fishermen have raised concerns about foreign boats, particularly Chinese fleets, illegally fishing in Peruvian waters by deactivating their satellite tracking systems. These fishermen argue that this alleged illegal activity is depleting squid stocks.

The situation has led to soaring prices in local markets for squid, a critical protein source for many Peruvians. This exacerbates food insecurity in a country where millions already face difficulties accessing affordable food.

The graphs below show that giant squid prices in China have progressively risen this year and are at historically high levels. 

VIEW GRAPH
Large jumbo flying squid, wing, China ports
© 2025 Undercurrent News
To view the full datas
GO PREMIUM
Upgrade to Pro to view

One executive with a processing firm told Undercurrent News the situation is so critical that it has become news on national TV in Peru. "Very little squid is arriving, and it is extremely expensive. No one can process it because there's so little and so costly. It's priced between $5-6 per kilogram, which is why it only goes to local markets for Peruvian consumption. Yesterday, the price was $6.40/kg," said Dario Alvites, general manager of Peruvian firm Perupez. 

According to Alvites, the Peruvian marine institute IMARPE has not conducted research cruises for four years. "So we don't know how recruitment, size composition, or sexual maturity are progressing. We're in the dark," he noted. He also said that the Chinese fleet typically catches small fish, which might not have been reproduced yet. At the same time, climate factors might have concentrated squid's food into a particular area, impacting the fishing.

However, a spokesperson for Produce stated that their investigations found no evidence of foreign vessels fishing within the 200-mile maritime limit. He emphasized that the reduction in squid catches is linked to environmental factors. According to the ministry, the scarcity should ease by December as the ocean conditions stabilize. In the meantime, they advised fishermen to diversify their catch and focus on other species, like mahi-mahi (Perico), whose season begins in October.

The map illustrates the presence of fishing vessels active near Peruvian waters.

Despite the government's explanation, the Peruvian industry association National Society of Industries' fishing and aquaculture committee expressed skepticism. 

In a press release sent to Undercurrent, they criticized the government for not enforcing existing regulations, such as requiring foreign vessels to use satellite tracking systems. 

Alfonso Miranda, president of the SNI fishing and aquaculture committee, said that while some authorities say that foreign squid fishing vessels that enter national ports do not practice illegal fishing, dozens of artisanal fishermen claim to have seen them fishing in the Peruvian sea.

"Given both versions, I believe the Peruvian artisanal fishermen who are at sea every day," said Miranda, who recalled that artisanal fishing is experiencing the "worst crisis in the last 30 years" and that "if control measures are not taken, unemployment and paralysis of fishing for human consumption will be dramatic before the end of the year."

Furthermore, the SNI committee pointed out that the El Nino phenomenon had not severely impacted other marine species, such as anchovy, mackerel, or bonito tuna, raising doubts about its role in the squid shortage. 

While the government remains firm in its stance, acknowledging the frustrations of the artisanal fishing sector, the committee and fishermen continue to demand stricter enforcement against illegal fishing and the resumption of marine research expeditions to monitor squid populations. They also argued that the lack of research over the past four years has hindered accurate forecasting of the species' availability.

Alvites pointed out that Peruvian processing plants that work exclusively with jumbo squid are in "serious trouble."

"Since mid-last year, raw materials have been expensive, and international prices are low, leaving them without profits. This year has been even worse, with no improvement, and some have not processed anything at all. I don't know exactly how the companies are doing, but I estimate several are facing serious problems. Those of us who produce other products are also struggling. It's been a bad year, but we are holding on. For example, we have started processing scallops, etc," he said.

Meanwhile, Peruvian congressman Miguel Ciccia Vasquez said he would propose interpellation and possible censure of the production and defense ministers for their "abandonment and lack of interest in Peruvian natural resources and national sovereignty."

title: USITC’s ‘The Year in Trade 2023’ report highlights efforts to end IUU fishing
content:
The US International Trade Commission has released its annual "The Year in Trade" report, a more than 200-page document that reviews the global trade environment in 2023, from antidumping and countervailing duty investigations and reviews, to developments with selected trade partners.

The document covers a wide range of industries, but in terms of fisheries, a big focus in 2023 was on ending illegal, unregulated and unreported (IUU) fishing.

In 2023, 55 of the 164 current World Trade Organization (WTO) members, including the US, formally accepted the Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies, the USITC recalls. The agreement was adopted in June 2022 to prohibit illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing.

Upon signing the agreement, the WTO ministers committed to "eliminate the most harmful fisheries subsidies that are fueling depletion of fish stocks and depriving fishing communities of their livelihoods."

The agreement is the first by the WTO with a primarily environmental objective, USITC noted. And, as of the end of 2023, a second round of negotiations on fisheries subsidies was still ongoing. 

The continued fight against IUU fishing was also highlighted in a section of the report on new developments in the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), which has been in place since July 2020. The USMCA includes commitments to promote trade in goods that are "produced in compliance with the USMCA's Labor chapter," which includes not importing goods produced with forced labor.

The USMCA also contains provisions that address IUU fishing and fisheries subsidies. In 2023, a big focus was on efforts to protect the vaquita porpoise, an endangered marine animal that has become a victim of bycatch in the illegal fishing and trafficking of totoaba fish. 

Mexico and the US went back and forth multiple times in 2023 in an effort to come up with a compliance action plan that worked for both parties. The last action plan from Mexico came in July 2023 and proposed implementing gillnet bans, investigating organized crime groups that are involved in illegal fishing and trafficking of totoaba, and more.

IUU fishing prevention efforts were also noted in the US-Chile Free Trade Agreement and the US-Panama trade promotion agreement.

title: Unreported bluefin tuna fishing leads to indictment of 74-year-old man in Japan
content:
Over 10 metric tonnes of unreported bluefin tuna fishing have led to the indictment of Yuichi Sasaki, a 74-year-old drift net fishing vessel captain from Kesennuma City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan, the Asahi Shimbun reports.

Sasaki was suspected of violating the Fisheries Act by illegally landing regulated bluefin tuna without properly reporting the catches. An investigation revealed that Sasaki, the owner of fishing vessel Kazumaru No.18, allegedly caught 893 bluefin tuna—equivalent to 10.1t—over 22 fishing trips between August 2023 and May 2024 in waters between Hokkaido and Miyagi Prefecture.

Instead of reporting the catches to Japan's Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry, and Fisheries, Sasaki reportedly landed the tuna at a small port in Karakuwa Town, Kesennuma, where his vessel was docked, and sold the tuna illicitly to dealers.

Another 92t of unreported bluefin tuna catch found in Japan

Sasaki's vessel had a legal quota of 3.2t for bluefin tuna this year, which should have been landed at Kesennuma Port and officially recorded through the local fishing cooperative.

Sasaki has admitted to the charges. The Coast Guard began an investigation after receiving an anonymous tip, which led to a June search of Sasaki's vessel and residence. The Kesennuma Coast Guard Office sent Sasaki to the Sendai District Public Prosecutor's Office on Sept. 18. 

This is Japan's second case of illegal bluefin tuna fishing, following a similar crackdown last year in Aomori Prefecture.

title: Norway’s salmon giants set for EU price-fixing hearing
content:
Six of Norway's largest salmon producers are set to contest charges of price-fixing with the European Commission at a closed-door hearing in Brussels, Belgium, next week, reports Reuters.

The hearing will see Mowi, Mitsubishi Corporation's Cermaq Group, Grieg Seafood, Leroy Seafood Group, SalMar and Bremnes Seashore, defend allegations that they exchanged commercially sensitive information, including sales prices and production volumes, between 2011 and 2019.

The hearing will take place in front of senior antitrust officials at the European Commission, national watchdogs, and potentially third parties, according to Reuters. It regards the sale of Norwegian farmed Atlantic salmon to the EU on the spot market only, and not sales on long-term contracts.

Should the firms be found guilty, their fine will be up to 10% of their global turnover -- although it is rare for any price-fixing charge to be this extreme, a top competition lawyer in Norway told Undercurrent News earlier this year.

It has been eight months since the European Commission announced its preliminary view that the firms had breached price-fixing laws, sending shockwaves through the sector.

In separate cases, the six firms have previously agreed to pay $85 million in 2022 to resolve antitrust claims from salmon purchasers.

Back in February, after the news of the EU's preliminary verdict was first announced, seven UK retailers filed another suit pursuing losses of $860m, while a separate suit on behalf of UK consumers is seeking up to $484m. 

The US department of justice also closed its own investigation into Mowi, SalMar, Leroy and Grieg in 2023, after sending subpoenas to the four firms back in 2019.

title: Scottish salmon farms suspended from RSPCA scheme after fish suffocate
content:
Sites belonging to Scottish Sea Farms (SSF), Mowi, and Bakkafrost have been temporarily suspended from the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (RSPCA) welfare certification scheme after a video emerged of live fish suffocating out of water.

Aftermath of Norway’s torrid winter hits SalMar’s Q2, Scottish rebound continues

SSF, speaking to The Times, admitted to "unacceptable lapses" at its farm after drones operated by NGO Animal Equality captured footage of live fish at a site on the Isle of Mull spending up to two minutes out of the water as farmhands carried them in nets.

RSPCA guidelines insist that live fish can spend a maximum of 15 seconds out of the water unless anesthetized.

The drone recordings were captured throughout April, July and August 2024 on Loch Alsh; Fiunary, Sound of Mull; and Ardcastle, Loch Fyne -- sites operated by Mowi, SSF, and Bakkafrost, respectively.

Loch Alsh is a known supplier to Sainsbury's. Two of the farms are RSPCA Assured; the other is Aquaculture Stewardship Council accredited, noted Animal Equality.

SSF supplies salmon to Marks & Spencer (M&S), which ensures that all of its salmon is sourced from RSPCA Assured fish farms. The company is M&S' main supplier of farmed salmon, although the retailer stopped sourcing from the Mull site earlier this year following an oil spillage from a sunken landing craft.

In response, SSF's head of fish health and welfare said it has taken immediate remedial action at the Mull site, giving refresher training and guidance on how best to humanely cull sick fish.

An RSPCA Assured spokesperson said: "We have launched an immediate investigation into these allegations and suspended membership of the three farms from the RSPCA Assured scheme, pending further investigation. This means they cannot currently market or sell any products under the RSPCA Assured label."

"As our enquiries are ongoing, we are unable to comment further at this time. Animal welfare is our absolute priority and we always take any complaints of poor welfare extremely seriously. We would urge anyone with any concerns about the welfare of animals on an RSPCA Assured certified farm to contact us straight away, without delay, so that we can immediately investigate and address any welfare issues as a priority."

title: US adds Indian shrimp to forced labor list
content:
The US Department of Labor (DOL) has added shrimp from India to its 2024 List of Goods Produced with Forced Labor following a petition submitted earlier this year by the Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA), a group that represents US domestic shrimp harvesters and processors.

The decision was supported by evidence from investigations by labor rights organization Corporate Accountability Lab, the Associated Press and the investigative journalism initiative, The Outlaw Ocean Project, according to SSA.

The list, also known as the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act (TVPRA) list, additionally includes shrimp from Bangladesh, Burma and Cambodia. Despite being added to the TVPRA List, shrimp from India is still allowed into the US. However, the new designation may lead to more regulatory attention and reputational risks for US companies failing to address forced labor concerns in their supply chains.

That'll be no easy task for importers.

India is the US' largest source of shrimp, sending it 157,134 metric tons worth $1.2 billion over the first seven months of 2024, accounting for 38% of the market, as reported by Undercurrent News. Bangladesh was the US' 17th largest source of shrimp during the period, sending it 452t worth $5.9m. 

Nathan Rickard, a partner at Picard Kentz & Rowe LLP and representative of the SSA, told Undercurrent on Thursday (Sept. 5) that the falling prices of imported shrimp in the US are not due to technological advances but to increasing labor exploitation.

"There is no technological innovation associated with farmed shrimp production that is bringing prices down; rather, workers at all levels of the supply chain are receiving less and being squeezed harder," Rickard said.

DOL also announced on Thursday that it has called for input on whether shrimp from India should be added to the list of products produced with child labor. If approved, this would impact federal procurement policies under Executive Order 13126, which prevents government agencies from buying goods made with child labor.

Thailand removed from child labor list

In a related development, DOL removed shrimp from Thailand from the list of products made with forced or indentured child labor. The decision comes after reports showed significant improvements in the Thai shrimp industry's labor conditions, though adult forced labor remains a concern, the federal agency said.

However, the production of fishmeal and fish oil — essential for feeding farmed shrimp in Thailand — remains flagged for labor exploitation.

Labor abuses taint the entire shrimp supply chain, from farming to shrimp feed production, Rickard said. "There is simply nothing within the industry safeguarding how shrimp feed is produced," he noted.

He also expressed concern that US importers abandoned Thailand as it improved labor practices and instead shifted sourcing to India, where labor violations are prevalent.

"American importers pursue shrimp from countries that afford them the highest margin," he said. "This practice encourages horrible abuse of people involved in the foreign production of shrimp and discourages sincere efforts to improve working conditions."

SSA will advocate for full traceability of shrimp back to its source and stricter import policies, Rickard said.

US shrimpers demand tougher restrictions on Peru, Guatemala

"Absent actual efforts from importers to address these problems, the domestic industry will work to prohibit the importation of any shrimp associated with human rights abuses."

In an unrelated action, SSA and the Port Arthur Area Shrimpers' Association, a group that represents harvesters in Southeast Texas, have joined forces to call for stricter enforcement of sect. 609 of P.L. 101-162 against the countries Peru and Guatemala, as reported by Undercurrent.

The law requires shrimp imports to meet the same standards for protecting marine mammals that US companies must comply with, including the Marine Mammal Protection Act. In particular, the trade associations suggest these foreign sources of shrimp aren't doing enough to avoid sea turtle bycatch.

title: NGO raises concerns over MSC ecolabeling, forced labor in tuna fishing
content:
Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) 's fisheries standard only requires companies to submit self-declarations that fishers are not at risk of debt bondage or forced labor without conducting further investigations or verifying the information, and that's a problem, says Global Labor Justice.

Responding to a Nature report titled "Is Tuna Ecolabeling Causing Fishers More Harm Than Good?", the NGO complained in a statement sent to Undercurrent News that this allows companies to avoid scrutiny and fails to address forced labor and other forms of labor abuse.

More robust measures, such as enforceable brand agreements and collective bargaining agreements with independent and democratic unions representing fishers, are needed to tackle these issues better, the group argues.

Nature's report exposed flaws in MSC's self-reporting procedures for labor issues, Global Labor Justice maintains. The report revealed that there are currently vessels in MSC-certified fisheries where fishers have reported incidents of forced labor. While these vessels remain in the program, the NGO said that MSC tuna products currently on supermarket shelves have likely been produced under forced labor conditions.

The MSC has stated that it is "already sending a strong signal by withdrawing certification if fisheries are convicted of forced or child labor abuses" and published a Sustainable Tuna Handbook where it expressed "concerns about the scale of forced labor and human rights issues in tuna supply chains" and that "the best way for tuna buyers to significantly reduce exposure to the above risks [of forced labor] is to choose MSC certified tuna."

Howes says MSC will amend requirements this summer after forced labor criticisms

"The MSC's blue label appears on seafood products in supermarkets worldwide, creating the false impression that it is a seal of approval for the labor practices used to catch or harvest the seafood," said Valery Alzaga, Global Labor Justice's deputy director. "When consumers purchase MSC-labeled tuna, they reasonably expect that the product is free from human and labor rights abuses, but in fact, there are MSC-certified fisheries where the fishers are subjected to forced labor and unacceptable working conditions. The MSC only requires companies to submit self-declarations, allowing some of the largest seafood brands to ignore forced labor in their supply chains and avoid being accountable to fishers and their unions." 

Alzaga continued, "Clearly, seafood brands cannot rely on MSC certification to claim their seafood is responsibly sourced. The best way to stop forced labor is not through certification schemes but by empowering fishers to improve their jobs and hold their employers accountable through collective bargaining agreements and enforceable brand agreements, as we have seen used effectively in other sectors."

In a statement replying to Nature's article, MSC said it recognizes "forced and child labor is a complex and distressing issue affecting the seafood industry".

"However, the focus of MSC's work is to address the immense challenge of overfishing and the environmental difficulties that this poses for the ocean. Contrary to the article's assertion, the MSC ecolabel does not offer an assurance on forced or child labor. The article's claim that we do is based on isolated use of the word taken out of context, ignoring the multiple times that we have emphasised the ecological focus of our program and the absence of a social claim from our ecolabel. Independent research shows that this environmental focus of our ecolabel is well understood by consumers," MSC said.

"Whilst addressing overfishing is our main purpose, we do support global efforts to tackle forced and child labor in seafood supply chains. We require any vessel implicated in a conviction for forced or child labor to withdraw from certification for two years. To our knowledge, there has been no conviction involving any of the vessels cited in the report. We recognize this is a complex area. The purpose of the public self-reporting templates cited in the report, although not intended to provide assurance, is to shine a light on industry practices. This transparency is intended to empower stakeholders to make decisions about how they interact with fisheries. The issue of forced and child labor can only be addressed by partners and stakeholders from across the sector working together to find lasting solutions," it further said.

title: US House panel peppers Biden administration with questions about IUU fishing
content:
Leading members of the US House of Representatives' Natural Resources Committee on Wednesday morning (Sept. 4) peppered the president Joe Biden administration with a long list of questions about illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing raised by a series of recent investigative articles.

"IUU fishing threatens domestic seafood production and economic prosperity for Americans," said the eight letters sent by the lawmakers. "Cheaper illegal seafood imports cost the US commercial seafood industry millions of dollars annually by driving down the cost of American-caught and processed seafood. Globally, $10 billion to $23bn are lost annually due to the impacts of IUU fishing on global markets."

They quote a report from the US International Trade Commission that says 11% of the $2.4bn worth of all US seafood imports are derived from IUU fishing.

All of the letters are signed by Democratic representatives Raul Grijalva (Arizona), the committee's ranking member, Jared Huffman (California), Melanie Stansbury (New Mexico), and Republican Garret Graves (Louisiana).

Letters to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ) are also signed by committee chairman Bruce Westerman, an Arkansas Republican.

Joint US Congress, White House panel schedule hearing to discuss report on use of forced labor in Chinese seafood

Rick Spinrad, the under secretary of commerce for oceans and atmosphere, has been given until Sept. 18 to provide all letters, emails, communications and other documents to answer a series of five questions, including details about any steps NOAA has taken to investigate recent reports by the Outlaw Ocean Project (OOP) or Associated Press.

Congress has been paying much more attention to US seafood imports since early October 2023 when OOP, a journalism outfit started by Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Ian Urbina, had a series of articles published by The New Yorker. The series provided haunting details about crew members being held captive, beaten and suffering from malnutrition aboard vessels in China's distant-water fishing fleet.

It also provided a thorough accounting of the Chinese program used to enlist and transport a large number of Uyghurs from Xinjiang, in the land-locked, northwestern part of China, over 1,000 miles to seafood processing plants in Shangdong, on the eastern coast.

Many subsequent articles have followed, including a report published in July that was critical of the way the Philippines protects its migrant workers in the fisheries sector. 

Indian shrimp supplier accused of labor abuse, antibiotic fraud in new report

The congressional query also seeks to know how NOAA is assessing its processes under the Seafood Import Monitoring Program (SIMP) and whether SIMP has identified any parties guilty of IUU fishing or fraud. 

The request to CEQ seeks information about the organization's engagement with other relevant federal agencies to use existing authorities to address reports of IUU fishing and forced labor in the seafood industry. 

Other federal agencies, too, are the subject of the congressional investigation, including the Department of Labor. The lawmakers have asked labor secretary Julie Su, among a list of 12 questions, how her agency is "working to ensure that national human trafficking task forces recognize the fishing industry as a source of trafficking and exploitation."   

The lawmakers have asked Troy Miller, the senior official performing the duties of the commissioner for US Customs and Border Protection, what steps his agency is taking to enforce import bans intended to block seafood caught through IUU fishing. They've asked about the frequency of inspecting incoming seafood shipments and what steps the agency is taking to increase the number of inspections related to IUU fishing forced labor.

In particular, the lawmakers want to know about CBP's efforts to enforce Sect. 307 of the Tariff Act of 1930 and, more specifically, about the work of CBP's Commercial Targeting and Analysis Center, seafood import inspections, the Automated Commercial Environment system, withhold release orders, and the Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force. 

Other agencies included in the investigation are the US Department of Agriculture (USDA), Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the State Department and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC).

From the USDA and FDA, the lawmakers seek to know more about efforts to secure the safety of imported seafood. The letter commends State's recent addition of seafood as a high-priority sector for enforcement under the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act, but it also asks about efforts to strengthen domestic and international governance to combat IUU fishing and forced labor. 

The lawmakers ask FTC about its efforts to ensure the fair marketing of seafood within the seafood industry.

title: Farmed salmon spill at Icelandic land-based facility
content:
The Icelandic Food Agency has received a report from salmon farmer Kaldvik regarding an accident involving the spillage of farmed salmon at the company's land-based facility in Kopaskeri while fry were being transferred from its Randinn farm to a well boat.

The investigation revealed that equipment used for transporting the juvenile salmon broke apart on the deck of the well boat, leading to the release of up to 300 fry into the sea. The leak was promptly stopped, and Kaldvík's staff implemented their contingency plan, deploying nets to contain the escaped fish. However, after 13 hours of monitoring, no salmon were captured in the nets.

The Icelandic Food Agency continues to monitor the situation, ensuring all protocols are followed to prevent further incidents, it said.

content:

The restaurant was located on the Damariscotta River, in a quaint part of downtown. It included indoor and outdoor seating with live music outside, featuring many local artists.

title: Blumar saw 22% sales drop in Q2 of 2024
content:
Chilean salmon farmer and seafood processor Blumar saw sales of $160.54 million in the second quarter of 2024, 22% less than the $206.8m generated in Q2 2023, the company said in its latest financial report for the three-month period ended June 30. Net income was $7.37m, down 63% from the $19.87m seen a year ago.

The outcome no doubt was the result of Blumar's many challenges experienced during the first half. 

Chile's superintendence of the environment, or the SMA, announced in May that it had initiated a sanctioning process against Blumar due to alleged significant overproduction at its CES Cordova 1 site, as reported by Undercurrent News. The facility is located within the Kawesqar national reserve in the Magallanes and Chilean Antarctic region. Overproduction allegedly occurred during the 2019-2021 production cycle, leading to potentially severe penalties for the firm. 

Blumar is authorized to produce a maximum of 5,875.2 metric tons of salmon in the facility through 24 cages spread over an area of 10.01 hectares. However, in 2023, Chile's national fisheries and aquaculture service, Sernapesca, lodged complaints against Blumar for exceeding these limits. Subsequent investigations by the SMA allegedly showed that the firm harvested around 6,337t of salmon from the site and experienced 202.6t of mortalities for a combined total "production" of 6,540t. 

Blumar announced, in July, the opening of a new facility in Chile's southernmost region some five months after a fire destroyed a plant in Punta Arenas which the company shared with Multi X, as reported by Undercurrent. The structure is located in a leased facility managed and operated only by Blumar, not Multi X. Blumar invested just over $1 million in the setup, which has a maximum monthly processing capacity of 3,960 metric tons, reported Diario Acuicola. 

Blumar saw net income of $5.54m on sales of $300.55m throughout H1 2024 compared to net income of $34.04m on sales of $389.21m during H1 2023.

title: Large Mississippi wholesaler to forfeit $1m for mislabeling frozen, imported fish
content:
A seafood wholesaler in the US state of Mississippi and two of its managers have pleaded guilty to conspiring to mislabel seafood and commit wire fraud by marketing frozen imported fish as more expensive locally caught species, federal prosecutors report.

Quality Poultry and Seafood Inc. (QPS), the largest seafood wholesaler on the Mississippi Gulf Coast, agreed on Tuesday (Aug. 27)  to forfeit $1 million and also pay a $150,000 fine, according to a statement from the US District Attorney for the District of Southern Mississippi.

Additionally, Todd Rosetti, the company's sales manager, and James Gunkel, the business manager, have pleaded guilty to misbranding seafood. 

The latest developments relate to an earlier settlement involving Mary Mahoney's Old French House, a well-respected, 62-year-old fine-dining restaurant in Biloxi, Mississippi, and Anthony Cvitanovich, its co-owner and manager. The restaurant agreed in May to pay nearly $1.4m to settle charges that it misidentified frozen, imported seafood on its menu as fresh, domestic-caught fish, as reported by Undercurrent News. Cvitanovich pled guilty to conspiracy to misbrand seafood and wire fraud.

Between December 2013 and November 2019, the restaurant, Cvitanovich and its previously unidentified co-conspirators fraudulently sold as fresh, domestic caught about 58,750 pounds (over 29 metric tons) of frozen and imported fish from Africa, India and South America. 

Mary Mahoney's, a restaurant in Biloxi, Mississippi. Image from restaurant website.

Cvitanovich admitted that, between 2018 and 2019 alone, he was involved in mislabeling approximately 17,190 pounds of fish sold at the restaurant. The fish was described on Mary Mahoney's menu as premium higher-priced local species, such as snapper and grouper from the Gulf of Mexico, when the fish was actually Lake Victoria perch from Africa, triple tail from Suriname, unicorn filefish from India and others.

Genetic testing of fish by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) confirmed the fraudulent scheme, the prosecutors said at the time.

Prosecutors said Tuesday that QPS admitted participating in a scheme to substitute fish from 2002 through November 2019, working with Mary Mahoney's and multiple other restaurants in the area. QPS also mislabeled imports that it sold to customers at its own retail shop and cafe.

The indictment alleges that even after agents from the FDA executed a criminal search warrant at QPS to investigate its sale of mislabeled fish, QPS continued for over a year to sell frozen, imported fish as substitutes for local premium species.

Sentencing for Mary Mahoney's and Cvitanovich, who faces a maximum penalty of three years of prison and a $10,000 fine, is set for Nov. 18, according to court records. Sentencing for QPS, Rosetti and Gunkel is set for Dec. 11.

US restaurant agrees to pay nearly $1.4m for selling frozen, imported fish as fresh, domestic

"QPS and company officials went to great lengths in conspiring with others to perpetuate fraud for more than a decade, even after they knew they were under federal investigation," said assistant attorney general Todd Kim of the Justice Department's Environment and Natural Resources Division in a statement. "Mislabeling seafood harms local wholesalers and fishermen who compete to sell locally sourced, premium fish in a market unfairly flooded with less expensive fish, frozen and imported from overseas."

US attorney Todd Gee for the Southern District of Mississippi added: "When imported substitutes are marketed as local domestic seafood, it depresses the value of authentic Gulf Coast seafood, which means that honest local fishermen and wholesalers have a harder time making a profit. This kind of mislabeling fraud hurts the overall local seafood market and rips off restaurant customers who were paying extra to eat a premium local product. These convictions should serve as a warning: Restaurants and wholesalers will face criminal prosecution if they are not honest with customers about what they are actually buying."

title: Greenpeace finds labor issues, ‘alarming’ shark catches in North Pacific fishing
content:
A Greenpeace investigation, conducted alongside their Beyond Seafood Campaign, claims to have revealed labor abuses aboard fishing vessels operating in the North Pacific's Emperor Seamounts. It also found high levels of shark fishing.

The investigation found that crew members, particularly vulnerable migrant fishers from Indonesia, often endure months or years at sea under substandard conditions, isolated from their families and without the ability to report abuse. These labor violations fall far below international standards set by the International Labour Organization and United Nations guiding business and human rights principles, it said.

The industrial fishing industry in this region, driven by the $40 billion global tuna market, is linked to labor rights abuses and illegal, unregulated, and unreported fishing, which, according to Greenpeace, contribute to the depletion of tuna stocks and the bycatch of marine life.

Additionally, Greenpeace's "High Cost of Cheap Tuna" report highlighted that while some US retailers have made progress in sourcing tuna sustainably, many still fail to address these critical human rights and environmental issues.

High levels of shark fishing

The investigation also revealed high levels of shark fishing across the North Pacific's Emperor Seamounts. This underwater mountain chain, extending north from Hawaii, plays a crucial role in the cultural and food security of Indigenous Hawaiians and other Pacific communities, said Greenpeace.

According to the NGO, longline fishing vessels in the region utilize cables that can stretch up to 100 kilometers and deploy thousands of hooks, leading to significant bycatch, including a "startling number" of sharks, whose populations are already declining, it claimed.

During 25 hours of documentation, Greenpeace investigators recorded 84 sharks being pulled from the waters, an average of three sharks per hour. The majority of these sharks were either already dead or were swiftly killed onboard, with no apparent regard for their age or conservation status.

Additionally, the haul revealed approximately 4,000 empty hooks, "underscoring the destructive potential of longline fishing in depleting marine species in this sensitive area," it said.

Greenpeace wants the region to be designated a marine protected area under the recently adopted Global Ocean Treaty.

title: US harvesters hold floating protest against New England offshore wind project
content:
Roughly two dozen fishing boats, both large and small, participated in a floating protest of the Vineyard Wind offshore windfarm project, off the coast of the US state of Massachusetts, on Sunday (Aug. 26), reports WCAI, a local national public radio station. 

They said the fiberglass debris strewn in the water in July from a broken wind turbine blade has only made them more concerned about living with turbines. Three offshore wind blades of the type used at Vineyard Wind have suffered failures since May, the most recent on Thursday in the United Kingdom.

“We're really concerned about wind farms in the ocean-based environment, and we’re not happy with what's going on with the current one,” Nantucket charter fishing captain Carl Bois is quoted as saying.

Simultaneously, a small group of Nantucket residents reportedly protested on the island at Cisco Beach, according to the radio station.

Blade manufacturer GE Vernova is investigating what it calls “an isolated blade event that occurred during commissioning,” according to an emailed statement from the company. Commissioning is a process of inspection and testing that follows installation.

“GE Vernova’s Wind Fleet Performance Management team has initiated investigation protocols into the event in coordination with our customer,” the company statement said.

In May, when the first Haliade-X turbine sustained damage — also at Dogger Bank — GE Vernova attributed it to an installation error.

In response to the incidents, the conservation group Oceana said responsible development of offshore wind remains a necessity to further the transition away from fossil fuels. The organization said it supports creating a conservation buffer south of Martha’s Vineyard and Nantucket to separate wind development from whale habitat.

title: Sea Harvest sees improved numbers in H1 despite tough start to year
content:
South Africa's Sea Harvest Group still managed to post year-on-year improvements to revenue and profits during the first half of 2024 despite facing a multitude of challenges.

Those headwinds included higher interest rates, low catch rates and reduced sales volumes for hake as well as reduced demand in key abalone markets and -- worst of all -- the tragic loss of a fishing vessel and its crew. 

The company, headquartered in Cape Town, reported Tuesday (Aug. 27) that it saw revenue of ZAR 3.3 billion ($185m) during the six months ended June 30, a 3% y-o-y increase from the ZAR 3.2 billion it saw during the same period in 2023. It reported earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) of ZAR373 million, a 6% y-o-y increase from the ZAR 352m it saw during the first six months of 2023.

In the first half of 2024, the group completed its acquisition of Terrasan subsidiaries, helping the company diversify into pelagics (anchovy and pilchard) fishing and abalone aquaculture. The deal, which was finalized in May, gives Sea Harvest 100% ownership of Terrasan subsidies Sea Harvest Pelagic and a 63% stake in Aqunion.

Sea Harvest completes ‘transformative’ abalone, pelagics deal to close on $400m turnover

As earlier reported by Undercurrent News, the Terrasan acquisition gives Sea Harvest 60 fishing vessels in South Africa and Australia, seven fish-processing facilities, close to 10,000 metric tons of cold storage, almost 7,000 employees, four abalone aquaculture farms, two abalone ranching operations and two abalone processing facilities.

"The abalone business doubles in size, creating a world-class and competitive aquaculture business of scale," the company noted in its mid-year report.

"This transaction is of strategic beneﬁt to Sea Harvest as it has increased the group's hard currency earnings, created a stronger merged business, increased black ownership in the fishing and abalone industries, and broadened
Sea Harvest's shareholder base," said Sea Harvest chairman Fred Robertson in a press release.

Loss of fishing crew mourned 

The first half of 2024 also saw the company experience one of its toughest moments:  the sinking of its trawler, MFV Lepanto, and the loss of 11 crewmembers in May, as reported by Undercurrent.

"The first six months of this year have been some of the toughest months in the history of the group with the tragic sinking of the MFV Lepanto. The board, management and staff extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the 11 crewmen lost at sea," said Sea Harvest Group CEO Felix Ratheb.

Sea Harvest trawler sinks off South African coast, 11 crew lost

"We continue providing support to the affected families, whilst continuing to cooperate with the investigation into the incident by the South African Maritime Safety Authority," he added.

Other challenges for the company during the first half of 2024 included 5% lower catch volumes from the company's South African fishing operations, though that was partially offset by higher prices.

The company also reported good growth of its abalone stock but a tough market with reduced demand and increased competition in that sector, impacting prices.

"Overall, the group's earnings continue to be weighed down by persistently higher interest rates," the company said.

"As we continue into the second half of 2024, we look forward to the ﬁsh volumes still available to be caught by the group, supported by ﬁrm local and international hake markets, and the improvement of our H2 weighted operations in Australia," Ratheb said. "With the addition of Sea Harvest Pelagics and Aqunion and the potential decrease in interest rates, the group looks forward to an ease in operating conditions for the rest of the year."

title: Masoval Q2 profits, costs impress despite ISA outbreak
content:
Norwegian salmon producer Masoval experienced a significant profit increase in the second quarter, driven by reduced costs and elevated prices.

However, a recent outbreak of infectious salmon anemia, or ISA, on two of its farms in the Norway Mid farming region put a dampener on the quarter, forcing Masoval into a downward revision of its annual harvest forecast.

The firm's Q2 operational earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) rose 41% year-on-year to NOK 297.7 million ($28.2m), as shown in the table below. The company attributed this achievement to operational solid performance in its farming segment, lower farming costs, and anticipation of the new TL52 harvesting plant.

Photo: Masoval's Q2 results.

The firm also reported revenues reaching NOK 934m during the quarter, a 16% increase from NOK 804m in the same period last year. The company said that the increase was due to a combination of higher prices (NOK 100.5 pr kg vs NOK 92.4 pr kg) and higher sales volume.

CEO Helge Kvalvik highlighted the volatility in salmon prices throughout the quarter, describing it as a "rollercoaster."

"Salmon prices were a real rollercoaster this quarter with large volatility. Our harvesting profile was somewhat tilted towards the end of the quarter when prices were low. All in all, we nonetheless realize prices that were NOK 8 higher than the same quarter last year," he noted.

The farming segment delivered strong margins, with the group's realized cost per kilogram of gutted weight equivalent dropping to NOK 51, down from NOK 63 in the previous year.

However, the detection of ISA at the site Fjolvaeret and pancreas disease at the site Langoya resulted in somewhat accelerated harvesting at end of the production cycle and some extra cost due to sanitary harvesting and wellboat requirements, Masoval said.

Looking ahead, Kvalvik expressed excitement about the upcoming launch of the TL52 harvesting plant in September, which is expected to "improve the value chain" by enhancing integration between sales and processing.

As previously reported by Undercurrent, Masoval has revised its annual harvest guidance down to 26,500-27,500 metric tons for 2024, although this is still higher than the 24,500t it harvested in 2023.

"Lower volume guidance is a consequence to the accelerated harvest at the two sites, Espnestaren and Maoydraga, following the detection of ISA and the government-mandated timeline to empty the sites," the firm said.

"This figure [full year harvest estimate] includes an estimated 5-10% of the total volume harvested on the Froya Laks co-location agreement. Around 70-75% of the annual harvest volume is expected to be harvested in region Mid.

Nils Thommesen from Fearnley Securities said Masoval's EBIT was close to the consensus estimate. The farming segment outperformed expectations, with Region Mid achieving an EBIT per kilogram of NOK 51, higher than the forecast NOK 41, due to strong cost management, he noted.

Region West also surpassed estimates with an EBIT per kilogram of NOK 45, driven by favorable pricing.

Thommesen said that Masoval's sales and processing segment reported an EBIT loss of NOK 8m, impacted by low price achievements, legal costs, and a fish recall.

"For Q3 2024, management guides higher cost levels from a low level (in line with Fearnley Securities' estimate) and has raised 2024 capex guidance by NOK 20m to 340m due to growth and maintenance. Masoval harvested 6,700t in the quarter, and the deviation to the trading update corresponds to Froya Laks volumes," he wrote.

Subsidiary sanction wouldn't impact finances, says Masoval

After irregularities in Masoval subsidiary Pure Norwegian Seafood (PNS)'s frozen salmon sales were identified earlier this year, an investigation by Mattilsynet and Okokrim has also been initiated. Masoval owns 65% of PNS.

While it's uncertain if sanctions will result, similar cases have led to significant fines and forfeiture of profits, though these are unlikely to impact Masoval's overall finances, according to the firm.

Masoval said it had terminated its long-term agreement with PNS but agreed to a temporary contract for the rest of 2024. The farmer also said it is establishing its own fully integrated sales department and has signed a letter of intent to acquire PNS's sales operations, ensuring control over the entire value chain.
