title: Newfoundland’s repeat fisheries minister puts old issue at top of to-do list
content:
The newly minted fisheries minister in the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador (NL) takes less than a second to reply when asked what is the highest priority on his to-do list.

"Joint management with Ottawa," Gerry Byrne told Undercurrent News in a recent one-on-one interview.

It's not the first time a provincial fisheries minister has touted the idea of sharing decision-making authority with the Canadian federal government over commercial fishing in provincial waters. The thought of a regime that would see Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) collaborating with the province to manage crab, cod, capelin and other species fished around the NL coast has been on the minds of a long succession of provincial fisheries ministers and governments.

A report commissioned by the Liberal government in 2003 noted that the province had proposed joint management of the fisheries as far back as the late 1970s.

The quest is still just a dream. However, something significant happened recently that raises optimism, said Byrne. At a meeting in mid-July with other premiers from across Canada, NL premier Andrew Furey achieved unanimous consensus on the issue.

Newfoundland premier Andrew Furey (far right, front) with other Canadian premiers at a meeting in July. Screenshot from Andrew Furey Facebook page

"The 13 governments of our country, of our federation, all 13 governments said, and said loudly and clearly, they believe that Newfoundland and Labrador deserves joint management with Ottawa of our adjacent fisheries," said Byrne about the vote.

That's a "game changer," he added.

"The unity of our country demands that Ottawa accept the voices of the premiers, of the 13 governments of our country, and now act on joint management," he said.

So what happens next?

"We will start to structure what we see joint management as," said Byrne, adding that the idea has always been focused on something similar to the 1987 Atlantic Accord agreement, which granted the province some decision-making powers and financial benefits from the development of oil reserves off its coast.

"But let me be straightforward and clear-minded about this. Joint management won't occur in a day, week, or a month. It's a complicated process," he said.

"We've got work to do to prove that we deserve joint management. We know we deserve it from the point of view of what brought to this nation," said Byrne, referencing the fact that NL's decision to join Canada in 1949 provided the nation with a geographic advantage when the country later established its 200-mile marine boundary in 1977 under the Law of the Sea Convention.

The green line on this map denotes Canada's 200-mile marine boundary on its east coast. Screenshot from Fisheries and Oceans map.

Thanks to the island of Newfoundland's location in the North Atlantic, Canada gained jurisdiction over most of the continental shelf off its east coast, a rich area for cod and other groundfish.

Ottawa must now accept the will of the federation of Canadian premiers and work towards joint management, said Byrne.

"The people have spoken. Now we need to get them [the federal government] to pronounce fully, clearly, and positively on this issue and without any ambiguity right now. That's what I'm working toward. That's a major significant component of my efforts," he said.

No stranger to controversy

Just two weeks after taking on the role of NL's fisheries minister, Gerry Bryne became embroiled in a controversy.

Snow crab processors in the province have challenged the province's protocol and processes for seafood inspection after Quinlan Brothers was charged with violations of the province's Fish Inspection Act, as previously reported by Undercurrent. 

Byrne didn't hesitate to step into the fray, offering media interviews almost immediately after a press conference by Quinlan Brothers president Robin Quinlan, and the Association of Seafood Producers, as reported by Undercurrent. 

While he was willing to discuss the issue with the industry, Byrne warned that if the province tweaked the regulations too much, there could be repercussions.

Newfoundland fisheries minister open to discuss crab inspections with industry but warns of potential fallout

"If we go down this road, we may be subject to criticism. The marketplace may not necessarily react positively to this. As a result, the price that is acquired by our wholesalers and the price that our processors can give to our harvesters may be impacted," said Byrne.

In his last stint as provincial fisheries minister, 2018-2020 — making him the longest-serving minister in recent years — Byrne similarly took a hard line when Mowi subsidiary Northern Harvest Sea Farms had a substantial salmon die-off at its aquaculture operation on the province's south coast in 2019.

More than 2.6 million salmon had to be disposed of. The company blamed high water temperatures and failed to report the extent of the mortalities.

With pressure mounting from the province's political opposition, some accusing the provincial government of attempting to "cover up" the incident, Byrne suspended the salmon farmer's NL licenses and ordered an investigation and cleanup, as reported by Undercurrent.

Changes were also made to the province's aquaculture act to force companies to publicly disclose reports of any such incidents in the future. 

Same old issues second time around

Returning to the portfolio, Byrne is encountering some familiar issues, such as the debate over dock prices for snow crab. It's an annual battle between crab harvesters and seafood producers in the province, particularly this season and last, with protests and tie-ups delaying the start of the fishery, as reported by Undercurrent.

Newfoundland harvesters have long argued that they have no competition for their landings because the province does not allow companies outside the province to buy crab and other catches.

Byrne is also familiar with the issue of outside buyers. In February 2019, he initially said the province had no intention of changing its policy. He later allowed a two-week pilot project to test the interest of outside buyers. Nothing came of it, Byrne later declared in a CBC interview.

When companies calculated the cost of workers' compensation, shipping and other factors, "it wasn't economical for them," Byrne was quoted as saying at the time.

Now, it seems he appears willing to revisit the issue.

"What is unique about 2024, is that there has been an expectation, by fish harvesters, by industry for more free enterprise," he said, in reference to a March protests led by fish harvester John Efford and later joined by fish harvester union executives over the issue.

Crab harvesters from around Newfoundland and Labrador began arriving at the province's legislature at 6 a.m. on March 20, 2024, to continue their protests for changes to the province's processing rules and regulations. Photo from Facebook page of Melissa Loveman Chippett.

"That is unusual. Unions do not necessarily always embrace free enterprise. So, shame on me not to respond favorably to that."

However, he added that there's some work ahead to be done.

"We still have to determine what is in the cards for moving from a regulated fishery to a free enterprise fishery. It will be interesting to see how we engage with the fish price collective bargaining act [and] the fish price setting act, and whether or not that's an instrument that meets the 21st-century standard of free enterprise," he said.

Some guidance on those issues will likely come from a report commissioned by his predecessor, Elvis Loveless, to examine the fish processing system in the province. The report is expected to be finished before the end of this year.

Ultimately, any changes to the province's rules and regulations on processing or price setting will be determined by the will of the people, said Byrne.

Byrne: 'I'll be friendly, but I won't be your friend'

While he's not making hard and fast promises on potential policy and regulatory changes, Byrne does assure that he won't choose favorites in the industry.

"I'll be friendly, but I will never be your friend," he said.

"I'll keep an objective distance and look at things with eyes that see the full picture, that are not clouded by biases of personality or relationships," Byrne further explained.

The title of fisheries minister in this particular province is not for the faint of heart, given that the industry seems to be continually at war.

Byrne, though, doesn't seem daunted.

"I wanted this … cabinet position. I love it. I love the industry. I love the communities. I love everything about this portfolio," he said.

So, how does he plan to cope with slings and arrows that are bound to come his way?

"I'm gonna give you a little insight into Gerry Byrne. For what it's worth, I've lasted 28 years in public life and part of how I've been able to accomplish that is I respect people," he said.

Newfoundland names new-old fisheries minister

"I am not afraid to tell them what they don't want to hear, what they'd rather not hear. And they often respect me because I'm truthful to them," said Byrne.

Not everyone likes that, he admitted.

"If you were to do a poll, you would probably get a high number of people saying Gerry Byrne is full of shit -- and you can quote me on that, use that language. But you'd also probably also hear them say this guy don't back down when he feels he's right. And he's always gonna tell you what he really, really thinks," he said.

Sometimes people would rather be lied to, be told what they want to hear, he said.

"But I tell people what they need to know, as uncomfortable as that is," said Byrne.

"And I really don't care who does or who doesn't like me," he continued. "What I do care about is whether those who I respect, respect me in return, because that's how I measure myself."

title: Dozens of foreign workers allegedly trafficked by Scottish fishing firm
content:
Dozens of foreign workers may have been trafficked into the UK to work for TN Trawlers, a small, family-owned fishing company based in Annan, Scotland, reports BBC. 

According to data from the Home Office, 35 men -- hailing from the Philippines, Ghana, India, and Sri Lanka -- who worked for TN Trawlers and its sister companies were recognized as victims of modern slavery after being referred to the Home Office between 2012 and 2020.

The TN Group, owned by the Nicholson family, has denied any wrongdoing. The company asserts that it treats its workers well and pays them fairly.

The company has been the subject of two long-running criminal investigations. However, no cases of human trafficking or modern slavery have been brought to trial. Some of the affected men reportedly waited years to provide evidence.

A 2012 police briefing also highlighted ongoing concerns about TN Trawlers. The briefing noted that six Filipino fishermen had swum ashore from TN boats, reporting mistreatment and exploitation. This incident prompted the launch of Operation Alto by police in Dumfries and Galloway, an investigation focused on human trafficking and labor abuse at TN Trawlers.

The investigation into TN Trawlers has also led to 18 former employees being referred to the Home Office’s National Referral Mechanism. This system is designed to identify and support victims of human trafficking. 

In 2007, TN Trawlers was prosecuted for illegal fishing operations, resulting in a substantial financial penalty. Tom Nicholson and the company were ordered to pay £473,000 ($613,254) under proceeds of crime laws for their unlawful catches, which were worth hundreds of thousands of pounds.

Additionally, between 2009 and 2011, TN Trawlers faced further penalties, including nearly £150,000 in fines and costs, after the UK Maritime and Coastguard Agency discovered numerous defects and safety breaches on their vessels.

title: Chinese authorities uncover fake shrimp scheme, importer arrested
content:
Chinese authorities uncovered a fraud scheme involving imported Ecuadorian shrimp, discovering that 16 shipping containers purportedly containing shrimp were instead filled with ice, according to officials.

The scheme was uncovered in July when a buyer at a Shanghai wholesale market retrieved three containers of shrimp stored for months in a cold storage facility. Upon opening the containers, the buyer found just a few hundred kilograms of shrimp, with the majority of the containers packed with ice. 

Indian shrimp supplier accused of labor abuse, antibiotic fraud in new report

After reporting the issue to police, authorities inspected all Ecuadorian shrimp containers stored in the same facility. In total, they discovered 16 containers filled entirely with ice, with an estimated market value in China of CNY 1 million ($139,000) each.

Authorities identified the primary suspect as the head of a Shanghai-based shrimp importing company. Investigators believe the importer was attempting to capitalize on sluggish 2023 imported shrimp prices by passing off ice as shrimp.

Jin Huang, CEO of DXD Supply Chain, another Shanghai-based frozen seafood importer, posted on WeChat claiming the person detained is Jia Xueying, an importer with over 10 years experience in the sector. Jia could not be reached by Undercurrent News.

Jia's company first loaded containers with ice at a facility in Baiyangdian, Hebei province, which were then trucked to the Shanghai cold storage warehouse, Jin claimed. Jia reportedly insisted containers not be opened for inspection during delivery.

Jia has been detained amid an ongoing investigation into the 16 containers connected to the importing company, according to Jin.

Jin said no buyers appear to have suffered financial losses, as the scheme was uncovered before transactions occurred.

title: Sanctions no obstacle for Russian senator’s business in Norway, investigation claims
content:
Despite international sanctions, Russian senator Igor Zubarev has continued his profitable business activities in Europe through a complex network of nominee ownerships and strategic legal transfers, an investigation published by the Barents Observer -- produced in collaboration with Chronicles.Media -- has claimed.

Zubarev -- a senator from Karelia who ranked second in the 2022 list of the richest fishery industrialists in Russia's northwest, behind only Vitaly Orlov and his firm Norebo Holding -- fell under sanctions following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. To circumvent these restrictions, he transferred his business assets, including major firms like Fishing Company Virma and Fishing Company Variant, to trusted nominees and management firms, the investigation has found.

Norwegian firms have paid nearly $2 million to companies linked to Zubarev, who has continued to supply fish to Europe through Norwegian ports, it said.

Although Norway has imposed restrictions on Russian vessels, Zubarev's ships have been spotted in several Norwegian and Danish ports, raising concerns about potential sanctions violations.

Norwegian companies involved in these transactions claim to have conducted due diligence and found no direct ownership ties to Zubarev, the investigation said. However, nominee structures and closed-end funds have allegedly been used to obscure the true ownership of these businesses, allowing Zubarev to bypass sanctions and continue trading with Europe.

title: Norwegian study finds delousing can change salmon fillet coloring
content:
Nofima, the Norwegian research institute, has released a study examining the status and challenges of pigmentation in salmon fillets among Norwegian fish farmers.

According to Nofima scientists, the mapping also provides insights into some solutions that can be pursued further.

The research, led by senior scientist Trine Ytrestoyl and her team, sheds light on factors affecting fillet color, particularly the negative impact of repeated mechanical delousing, a previously undocumented connection.

The study reveals that repeated mechanical delousing significantly diminishes fillet pigmentation, likely due to stress-induced increases in antioxidant consumption, such as astaxanthin, and reduced feed intake. This reduced feed intake may lead to lower slaughter weights, exacerbating the color issue. The findings suggest that fish slaughtered at lower weights to avoid further delousing treatments show even poorer pigmentation.

The investigation, funded by the Norwegian Seafood Research Fund, is based on industry questionnaires from 2023, fillet color data from commercial productions between 2012 and 2023, and data from Nofima's research. According to Ytrestoyl, the strong correlation between the survey responses and the data analysis supports the study's validity, using a realistic picture of the current situation.

The study highlights the variability in how fish farmers experience pigmentation issues. While some report pigmentation problems in only 2% of their fish, others face challenges in 20-40% of their production. There is also variation in the acceptable minimum color standard, with targets ranging from 24 to 27 on the SalmoFan scale and between 5 and 7 milligrams of astaxanthin per kilogram of fillet.

Historical data indicate that the intensity of salmon fillet color in Norway decreased between 2012 and 2021, with a slight recovery after that. However, the variation in fillet color has increased, echoing the survey results that some farmers struggle more with pigmentation than others.

Most fish farmers have addressed pigmentation issues, including increasing astaxanthin levels in feed and incorporating more omega-3 fatty acids and vitamins. Although these measures have had positive effects, they are costly, prompting further investigation into the underlying causes of pigmentation challenges.

The study also points to seasonal variations and rapid growth as factors affecting pigmentation. The researchers were surprised by the significant difference in color at slaughter between suppliers of hatchery fish, suggesting that the hatchery phase may have a substantial impact on final pigmentation. This aspect will be explored further in future research.

title: US shrimp imports finish first half down by 3% after rough month of June
content:
If the glut of shrimp in the US is really behind the low prices being paid at wholesale, the first half of 2024 may have helped a little. But the month of June definitely didn't make importers smile.

The US imported 351,025 metric tons of shrimp worth $2.7 billion during the first six months of the year, 3% less volume and 10% less value than the 361,693t worth $3.0bn imported during the first half of 2023, according to the latest update of seafood import data available from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

Imported shrimp prices have been in almost complete freefall in the US since April 2022 when the average across sizes and country sources was $4.73 per pound. The overall average price was $3.69/lb in June 2024, down 4% from the overall average price of $3.86/lb seen in June 2023, as the chart from Undercurrent's trade portal below illustrates. 

Donelson Berger, the shrimp category manager for Boston, Massachusetts-based processor Stavis Seafoods, told Undercurrent last month that he believed an earlier year-on-year decline in shrimp import volumes seen in April 2024 was the result of the recent actions taken by the US Department of Commerce (DOC) in response to a request to level the playing field by the US domestic wild harvest shrimp industry.

In an email exchange with Undercurrent, Berger pointed to the total shrimp imports seen over the most recent five months by the US as evidence of how April represented such an unusual dip and not indicative of the overall trend. 

January 2024 -- 59,629t worth $462.4m
February 2024 -- 59,668t worth $456.5m
March 2024 -- 63,495t worth $481.8m
April 2024 -- 50,901t worth $397.6m
May 2024 -- 63,973t worth $486.7m

Berger said he believed the US would finish 2024 with more shrimp than in 2023 as bigger import numbers come over the rest of the year. He noted the common pattern of the US seeing 40% of its annual shrimp imports during the first half of the year and 60% in the second half. He said he also expected retail sales to be steady.  

May saw a 3% jump in volume, and it seemed like the trends were returning to normal. However, the June numbers look similar to those seen in April. The US imported 53,358t of shrimp worth $418.2m that month, 14% less volume and 18% less value than the 61,969t worth $511.2m that were imported in June 2023. 

The UCN trade portal chart below shows how import volumes and prices have varied for each of the five largest source countries from month to month.

India 1% ahead of 2023 pace

The US' largest source of shrimp, India, accounted for 37% of the import market in the first six months of 2024 and its volume was 1% ahead of its pace in 2023, though value was down 8%. It sent the US 130,404t of shrimp worth $960.4m over the first half of the year. 

The average price paid in June 2024 for Indian shrimp in the US was $3.58/lb, 2% more than the average $3.52/lb paid in May and 3% more than the average $3.46/lb paid in April 2024, an indication that prices might be climbing back. It was 3% less than the average $3.70/lb paid in June 2023, as shown in the UCN trade portal chart below.

Ecuador close to par

Ecuador, the second-largest source of shrimp for the US, accounted for 28% of the market in the first half of 2024, sending it 98,933t worth almost $664.0m. That's nearly on par with the volume and value seen by Ecuador in the first six months of 2023.

This in spite of Ecuador's April performance, when it sent the US just 9,881t of shrimp worth $67.5m, the worst month for Ecuadorian shrimp exports to the US since February 2021. It was less than half (45%) the volume and 54% of the value seen in March 2024. 

The low numbers were related to preliminary countervailing duty (CVD) rates announced on March 26 by DOC. The DOC told everyone involved in or affected by the CVD investigation surrounding Ecuadorian shrimp that importers of shrimp from Industrial Pesquera Santa Priscilla, Ecuador's largest producer, would have to pay a preliminary rate of 13.41%, as reported by Undercurrent. The amount would have to be provided in upfront cash deposits, DOC declared.

A shrimp processor near Guayaquil, Ecuador. Credit: Louis Harkell / Undercurrent News.

Importers of shrimp from Sociedad Nacional de Galapagos, known as Songa, were informed that they would have to pay a preliminary 1.69% rate and importers of all other Ecuadorian shrimp would have to pay 7.55% in upfront deposits.

On April 19, DOC informed all parties that it made a mistake in its calculations and it was reducing Santa Priscila's preliminary CVD rate to 2.89% while maintaining Songa at 1.69%. It declared that the Songa rate was de minimus and therefore not required upfront. Importers of all other Ecuador shrimp are now required to pay an upfront fee of 2.89%. 

Still, June was not a great month either. The US imported just 13,610t of shrimp from Ecuador worth $92.5m, 20% less volume and 23% less value y-o-y.

The average price paid for Ecuadorian shrimp in June 2024 was $3.19/lb, 4% better than the $3.07/lb paid in May but 4% worse than the $3.31/lb paid in June 2023, based on the UCN trade portal chart below. 

Indonesia still sliding

Indonesia, the US' third-largest source of shrimp, accounted for 17% of volume in the first half of 2024. It sent the US 62,232t worth $466.3m over the six-month period, 16% less volume and 23% less value than the first half of 2023.

June was another down month for Indonesia. It sent the US 9,192t of shrimp worth $69.5m, down 9% in volume and 14% in value y-o-y. 

It was the 22nd consecutive month in which Indonesia saw a y-o-y decline in shrimp exports to the US, dating back to August 2022.

The average price paid for Indonesian shrimp in the US in June was $3.58/lb, down a penny from the $3.59/lb paid a month earlier and 5% from the $3.75/lb paid in June 2023.

Vietnam sent US 10% more volume

Vietnam was again the US' fourth-largest source of shrimp during the first half of 2024, sending it 25,528t (7% of the market) worth $247.5m. That was 10% more volume and 1% less value than the first six months of 2023.

June by itself was not as positive, as Vietnam sent the US 5,132t of shrimp worth $49.9m, 8% less volume and 17% less value than in June 2023.

This is despite Vietnamese farmed vannamei shrimp exports being up overall month-on-month again in June 2024, with volumes reaching a two-year high, according to a Ho Chi Minh City-based consultancy compiling trade data for Undercurrent.

In fact, Q1 saw a marked improvement in export volumes of vannamei from Vietnam with a total export of 30,452 metric tons, up 8% month-on-month and 19% year-on-year.

The average price paid in the US for Vietnamese shrimp in June 2024 was $4.58/lb, 5% more than the $4.35/lb paid in May and 8% less than the $4.96/lb average seen in June 2023, based on the UCN trade portal chart above.

title: UK foodservice giant Brakes launches frozen branded range
content:
UK foodservice firm Brake Bros has launched a range of frozen fish and seafood under the "Portico Seafood" brand.

Sysco Corp.-owned Brakes plans to grow the range to 150 products over the next 18 months. All the products are freshly frozen to provide maximum convenience and year-round availability, it added.

"Sourced from specially selected fisheries, Portico Seafood combines quality, value and consistency to provide customers with the best of the catch, allowing them to capitalize on the growing demand for alternative center-of-plate options."

The initial range has a choice of frozen fish such as monkfish, Cornish sole and seabass, as well popular everyday menu items including scampi, Marine Stewardship Council (MSC)-certified breaded cod, salmon fillets "supreme," and shrimp.

The brand offers two distinct tiers -- "classic" and "premium" -- helping customers to more easily identify the products that best meet the quality and value that they need, Brakes said.

"Portico Seafood Classic offers high quality products that are equal to or better than other national or leading brands, while Portico Seafood Premium delivers exacting specifications, premium performance, and exceptional value."

Paul Nieduszynski, CEO at Sysco GB, said the firm was confident that the wide range would "contain all the key ingredients to make fish a tasty part of any menu."

Brakes and Sysco stressed their commitment to "protecting the fishing industry and fish stocks and ensuring our people and suppliers consider the environment at every part of the procurement and supply chain process."

Sysco is one of 13 heavyweight seafood buyers asked by a coalition of 18 US non-governmental organizations to tell them more about the steps they are taking to investigate concerns regarding sourcing from Chinese companies that rely upon forced labor.

Portico Seafood products fall under Sysco’s Food Safety & Quality Assurance criteria, many of which are MSC-certified, it said.

title: Search for Argos Georgia’s missing mariners unsuccessful so far
content:
In an ongoing recovery effort for missing crew members of the fishing vessel Argos Georgia, a search conducted by MV Pharos SG and another vessel yielded no new results, Mercopress reported. The Falkland Islands government reported that neither missing persons nor debris were found.

FREE READ Nine crew members confirmed dead from sinking of Argos Georgia

Thirteen crew members departed the Falkland Islands on July 27 via a military flight provided by Spain. One crew member remains in Stanley, awaiting return to their home country. The bodies of the nine deceased crew members are under the care of the coroner and will be flown to the UK for autopsies before being released to their families.

Vessels traversing the search area are advised to remain vigilant and report any findings to the Falklands Maritime Authority. The search and recovery operation has been distressing, and the Falkland Islands government expressed gratitude to all involved.

The UK's marine accident investigation branch has launched an inquiry into the incident, which resulted in nine deaths, four missing crew members, and fourteen survivors. Spain's standing investigation committee will also investigate the technical causes.

title: Another 92t of unreported bluefin tuna catch found in Japan
content:
An additional 92 metric tons of unreported bluefin tuna catch was found in Japan's most famous fishing region, exposing the country's lack of proper fishery resource management.

The Aomori Prefecture announced on Monday (July 29) that the unreported catch for fiscal years 2019 and 2020 amounted to 92.6t. This is the outcome of an additional investigation after the local government found 92t of under-reported tuna catch for fiscal 2021 last year.

The bluefin tuna of Aomori origin is highly branded nationwide, including tuna landed in Oma Town. The Oma tuna sold at Tokyo Toyosu Market on the first business day this year fetched JPY 114 million ($736,000) per fish, the fourth highest price since record-keeping began in 1999.

WCPCF lifts bluefin quota 50% for large-sized fish

The breakdown of the unreported catches was 3.5t -- 2.2t of large-sized fish weighing over 30 kilograms and 1.3t of small-sized fish tuna below 30kg -- in 2019, and 89.1t -- 82.7t of large fish and 6.4t of small fish -- in 2020.

Fishermen affiliated with the fisheries cooperatives in Oma, Okudo (Oma Town), and Ohata Town (Mutsu City) violated Article 17 of the Act on Conservation and Management of Living Marine Resources in 2019 and 2020. The detailed breakdown of violations by each fisheries cooperative is not disclosed.

The unreported catches accounted for 1% of the allocated quota in 2019 and 10% in 2020. The fish were sold directly to local wholesalers, but the company names were not disclosed.

An officer at the prefectural government told Undercurrent News that there is no legal basis for taking administrative sanctions under the act for the unreported catches in 2019 and 2020.

However, for the unreported catches in 2021, the prefecture is proceeding with administrative sanctions by Article 30 of the Fisheries Law, which was amended in December 2020.

The officer added that the prefecture will write the investigation results to the country's Fisheries Agency on July 30.

FREE READ Spanish court moves to trial for Ricardo Fuentes, other firms over illegal fishing allegations

After receiving the report from the prefecture, the agency will recalculate the catch results for 2019 and 2020. "If [the revised numbers] exceed [the quota], the agency will work on deducting the excess amounts from the current or the following year's allocated quota," an agency officer told Undercurrent.

Regarding administrative procedures, the agency will then formulate measures to address the excess catches and consult with the council for national fisheries policy.

Meanwhile, the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission's Northern Committee agreed on July 16 that the annual catch quota for Pacific bluefin tuna would increase by 50% for large-sized fish in the western Pacific Ocean and 10% for small-sized fish starting in 2025, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

"The prefecture is committed to preventing such violations from occurring again by working closely with the national government and ensuring strict guidance for fishermen and other stakeholders," Soichiro Miyasita, governor for Aomori Prefecture, commented in the statement.

title: Device data ‘a gamechanger’ for Indian shrimp improver projects
content:
CHENNAI, India -- The explosion of data collection devices among Indian shrimp ponds since the pandemic represents "a gamechanger" for the infamously opaque sector, offering routes to certification that have never existed before, according to George Chamberlain, president of the Center for Responsible Seafood (TCRS) and former president of the Global Seafood Alliance (GSA).

Collaborating with farm data providers such as India's AquaExchange and Vietnam's Otanics Technology -- owner of the Tomota brand -- TCRS hopes to create a viable improver program for the country's many smallholder farmers.

"Even though smallholder farmers dominate production in Asia, they are beyond the reach of certification; they're too small," said Chamberlain. "They may only have three or four ponds, it's family run, and you can imagine the relative cost of bringing in international monitors to check their operations -- it's impractical."

According to Chamberlain, the average farm size in India is roughly two hectares, of which only about 1% are certified.

"But about 25% of the volume is certified because only the big farms can make it to certification. So how do we reach the other 75% of volume and 99% of farms?"

The smallholder farming panel at the 2024 Shrimp Summit Credit: Dan Gibson/Undercurrent News

Previous efforts have centered on using a 'cluster' model, effectively sampling from groups of 20-30 farms to create a theoretical medium-sized farm representing an entire area on which buyers can base their purchasing decisions.

Chamberlain explained that even within the same region, farmers would operate based on very diverse individual preferences, buying feed from different mills, sourcing post larvae from different hatcheries, and selling to different processors.

"It's really not a cooperative, so these clusters tend to fall apart; they just don't last. In some cases, they do, but there isn't a business reason for them to stay together."

However, the explosion of data collection tools on many of these small farms -- developed by companies such as AquaExchange, though Chamberlain took pains to make clear they would only be the first such data partner in the program -- means that inputs and outputs from small family-run operations can now be digitally tracked.

This data, which tracks feed inputs, monitors biomass levels and judges the value of any growing crop, is already being used by AquaExchange to provide farmers with access to financial credit at lower rates of interest.

"With this emergence of affordable digital technology, now there’s a wealth of information," he said. "The irony is there's going to be more information from the small farms than we have from the medium and large farms; it's turning the whole equation on its head."

This data can also serve traceability purposes, Chamberlain believes.

"Because the inputs are known in these systems because they are purchased through the app, not only do we know the farm, but we know the source of the post-larvae, the source of feed for the farm, and where the post-harvest went: all the key elements of traceability," he told listeners.

Other sustainability metrics, such as survival rate, growth rates, pond productivity, energy and feed efficiency, and effluent load, are also tracked by the app.

Soft data

Complimenting the farm data, the improver program proposed by Chamberlain would also use a validated third party to gather what he described as "soft data."

"There's a number of other criteria we think are going to be important to supplement the information that the devices collect," he explained. "But if we can have a database where the device data can be complemented by soft data... now we have something that's very valuable to the market."

These soft data criteria will cover:

Legal issues: whether the farmer has proper ownership of their land
Social issues: whether they are paying proper wages to their staff
Environmental issues: whether mangroves have been destroyed or the habit altered by the farm
Food safety issues: whether the farmers have used antibiotics and stored harvested shrimp with suitable quantities of ice
Animal welfare issues: whether the shrimp have been adequately protected from disease and stocked at the proper densities

There is still a question of what would be the necessary statistical sample size for routine soft data collection, Chamberlain added.

"For each 100-hectare region, should we just check 10 hectares?" he asked. "We can decide on what should be the proper sampling frequency to bring all these farms into the improver program in a very affordable way."

Devi, Aqua Star, Publix involved in pilot

Chamberlain confirmed that the first step of this data-driven improver program will be a pilot scheme, to be funded by environmental non-profit The Nature Conservancy in collaboration with AquaExchange, Otanics and third-party verifier Seafood Solutions.

Shrimp from farms involved in the program will be purchased by Devi Seafoods, imported into the US by Washington State-based wholesaler and distributor Aqua Star, then sold to Southeastern US retail chain Publix.

"Then once the pilot has run for a while and shaken out some of the bugs, we hope we can expand this and make it available to many more retailers," said Chamberlain.

While this remains just an improver program for now, Chamberlain is hopeful that the project will attract the attention of larger certification bodies like the GSA's Best Aquaculture Practices scheme or the Aquaculture Stewardship Council.

"Imagine if certification bodies could access these data sets and maybe add to it additional data to achieve their level of certification," he concluded. "It could even go on to tell the story of aquaculture, another level -- this database can serve many purposes."

The need to drive improvements within the Indian shrimp sector -- whether destined for export or not -- were thrown sharply into the spotlight earlier this year by an Associated Press investigation that uncovered labor and environmental violations across India's shrimp industry.

This, in turn, has also prompted questions of the effectiveness of social audits, while the Marine Stewardship Council is also looking to add social elements to its own certification criteria.

Elsewhere, TCRS is not alone in pushing for a verification program for Asia's extremely fragmented shrimp industry. Last year, Undercurrent News reported on the efforts by Seafood Watch, the veteran seafood sustainability program established by the US' Monterey Bay Aquarium, to independently verify the practices of Vietnam's thousands of small-scale black tiger shrimp producers.

title: Editor’s choice: Wild salmon supply in focus; Canadian live lobster prices climb
content:
Editorial director Tom Seaman brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week  

Two stories on salmon supply and one on lobster prices got a lot of reads last week. 

According to figures recently released by the North Pacific Anadromous Fish Commission, the North Pacific wild salmon catch amounted to 727.6 million fish in 2023, breaking the record of 660.1m set in 2021.

The 2023 harvest totaled 1.1m metric tons by weight, marking the third highest on record. The record catch was fueled by historic pink salmon harvests in Russia's Far East and the US state of Alaska.

Then, harvests of sockeye salmon have started to slow in Alaska, where nearly 36.8m fish across all species have been caught by fishermen so far this season. 

That's the latest from McKinley Research Group's harvest report for statistical week 28, which encompasses data through July 13, and the latest landings reports from the Alaska Department of Fish and Game. 

On lobster prices, levels of live Canadian exports have climbed dramatically in just the past five weeks and are promising to go even higher, thanks in part to the end of the spring season. 

New data gathered from a prominent lobster exporter in Atlantic Canada and made available on the Undercurrent News pricing portal shows 560-670 gram (1.23-1.48 pound) live hard shells, known as "quarters," being offered to Shanghai, China, for $10.46/lb, and to Paris, France, for $10.59/lb, during week 29 of 2024 (July 13-19).

Those prices, which include freight on board, are up 25% and 26%, respectively, from the $8.34/lb and $8.38/lb prices seen during week 24 (June 8-14). 

You can find all of last week's top stories below:

Record pink catch led to largest North Pacific salmon haul
Alaska's Bristol Bay sockeye salmon harvest passes peak
Canadian live lobster prices climb as spring season closes out
Alaska salmon task force releases sweeping new research plan
Ocean Wise revokes sustainability badge for Southeast Alaska salmon fisheries
'Project 2025' seeks 'breakup' of NOAA, reverse of conservation, climate change initiatives
Week 29 Indian shrimp prices rise as US demand meets short supply; Ecuador continues in doldrums
Norway cod customers could pull MSC label from packs 'regardless of outcome'
Sysco, Trident among big firms asked for updates on forced labor sourcing investigations
Newfoundland harvester union seeks to challenge cod decision in Canada's highest court

title: Worry grows in Atlantic Canada oyster industry over MSX outbreak
content:
Oyster farmers around Atlantic Canada are growing more anxious following the discovery of a parasitic disease on the southern shore of Prince Edward Island (PEI).

The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) confirmed on Saturday (July 13) that multinuclear sphere X (MSX), a disease caused by the microbial parasite Haplosporidium nelson (H. nelson), has been found in wild oyster samples collected in Bedque Bay, PEI, near the town of Summerside. 

"This is the first occurrence of MSX in the region," a CFIA official told Undercurrent News on July 17. He said the agency is continuing to test in the area.

MSX is not known to be dangerous to humans, and oysters infected by the disease can be eaten without ramifications. However, the disease threatens to wreak havoc on an Atlantic Canadian shellfish industry estimated to be worth over CAD 40 million ($29.14m) annually.

The MSX virus was recently discovered in wild oysters in Bedeque Bay, on the southwestern side of Prince Edward Island. Screenshot from Google Maps.

MSX prevents oysters from thriving, resulting in smaller oysters, and comes with a devastating 90-95% mortality rate. Oysters that are over two years old are particularly susceptible, the CFIA notes on its website.

It's too early to assess the full impact MSX could have on the PEI oyster industry, which harvested CAD 24m ($17.5m) worth of oysters in 2023, with total production of 6,350 metric tons, Peter Warris, executive director of the PEI Aquaculture Alliance, told Undercurrent.

One positive is that there are no oyster farms in the area where MSX was discovered and, to date, there have been no reports of MSX on aquaculture sites in the province, most of which are located on the province's north shore, Warris noted.

Another blessing is that the disease does not affect mussels. PEI is a massive producer of mussels, producing 80% of all mussels in Canada, with an annual value of around CAD 30m, according to the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO). 

Using wooden tongs with a rake at the end, an oyster fisherman harvests oysters in Prince Edward Island, Canada. Photo from Prince Edward Island Seafood website

However, Bedeque Bay, a prime area for wild oysters, is now off-limits to shellfish harvesting. The impact on harvesters and the processors they supply is immediate.

Burleigh Brothers Seafood, in the town of East Bideford, is one of the largest oyster dealers in PEI. The company has been in business for 90 years.

About 30% of the oysters they buy come from Bedeque Bay, company manager Thomas Burleigh told the CBC.

"So for us, that's about two million oysters per year that have just been knocked off the market, basically… It could mean millions of dollars in lost revenue," he is quoted as saying.

Meanwhile, across the Cumberland Straight from PEI, oyster growers in the province of Nova Scotia have been closely following updates on the MSX situation.

Nova Scotia growers have sourced seed and spat from PEI in the past. But, due to the recent detection of MSX, some have removed PEI locations from their intake and transfer permits to prevent the possible spread of the virus, said Jeff Bishop, executive director of the Aquaculture Association of Nova Scotia.

Rising US oyster demand has Canadians pondering expansion

In the longer term there could be a larger trickle-down impact, Bishop said.

"If PEI is out of the question in the future as a source of spat or seeds for our members, then how do we make changes here to look for that within our own borders?" Bishop asked in a recent interview with Undercurrent.

Atlantic Canada has seen MSX before

This is not the first time MSX has been detected in Atlantic Canada. In the autumn of 2002, an outbreak occurred in the Bras d'Or Lakes area, a salty body of water on Cape Breton Island, in the province of Nova Scotia. The last case of MSX in Nova Scotia was confirmed in 2016.

Harvesters and processors in the Cape Breton area were "decimated" by MSX, Bishop recalled in his interview with Undercurrent. Before the arrival of MSX, about 80% of the oysters grown in Nova Scotia came from the region.

An oyster farm in Nova Scotia. Photo from Aquaculture Association of Nova Scotia Facebook page.

Fortunately, the virus did not spread beyond the Bras D'or Lakes, said Bishop. And there is work underway to rebuild the oyster industry there.

In 2022, the government of Nova Scotia, in collaboration with the federal government, invested CAD 2.0m to redevelop the oyster industry in the Bras d'Or Lakes by developing a land-based oyster hatchery to prepare breeding stock and healthy spat to oyster growers.

Rising US oyster demand has Canadians pondering expansion

Also, despite the MSX problem in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia still has a healthy oyster farming industry, with operations scattered from the Cumberland Straight on the province's north shore to the French shore in the south.

The Nova Scotia industry hopes for a similar story in PEI.

Researchers at the University of Cape Breton have been studying MSX since the 2002 outbreak. But what's frustrating and contributing to the worry is that science has not been able to determine with certainty how the pathogen gets started, said Bishop.

Mysterious disease threatens US East Coast oyster farms

"There are some aspects of it that are well understood, like the fact that the [disease] is not a threat to human health," said Bishop.

But there's still a lot to learn.

Anecdotal evidence indicates that H. nelsoni was introduced into the marine environment in Bras d'Or Lakes in ballast water, according to a 2014 DFO document on the subject.

The DFO also offers tips for control of the spread of the disease, including reducing oyster grow-out time in high salinity, warmer waters, citing a 1988 science report that suggests "infections can be cured in two weeks by exposing oysters to mean salinities of 10 parts per trillion or less and temperatures above 10 degrees Celsius."

Part of the investigation being done by the CFIA in PEI is tracking any movement of oysters from Bedeque Bay to processors and whether the virus might have spread to other areas as a result. The industry is awaiting those answers.

Until then, all oyster farmers can do is to take precautions to help prevent the spread of MSX, said Warris. 

Even if MSX is in PEI to stay, that doesn't necessarily mean complete devastation for the industry, he added.

FREE READ US initiative seeks to breed tastier, climate-resilient oysters, strengthen northeast shellfish sector

The disease has also been detected previously along the US east coast and in British Columbia, on Canada's western shores, the CFIA noted.

A 2013 report commissioned by the PEI Aquaculture Alliance noted the MSX parasite had moved steadily along the Eastern Seaboard of North America since it first appeared in Delaware and Chesapeake Bays in the 1950s.

In the US, the industry has adapted to the presence of MSX in a variety of ways, the report noted.

"In the Chesapeake region, oysters slowly developed resistance against MSX (over 50 years) due to the constant influx of oyster spat from areas free from MSX disease pressure. And in Maine, a disease outbreak in 2010 was contained within one river system by a variety of measures, primarily centered on restrictions of movement into and out of the designated containment zone," the report stated.

For the PEI industry, there's some hope in those examples.

"If you look at Virginia and Maine, they have very successful oyster industries in the presence of MSX. They've adapted to it with broodstock program, selective breeding and so on," added Warris.

title: Alaska’s Sullivan seeks to add IUU amendment to national defense spending bill
content:
US senator Dan Sullivan, an Alaska Republican, is aiming to beef up the federal government's ability to battle the import of fish harvested illegally with an amendment to the Department of Defense's spending bill for fiscal year 2025. 

Sullivan has gained seven bi-partisan co-sponsors since he introduced the Fighting Foreign Illegal Seafood Harvest (FISH) Act (S. 1227) way back in April 2023, but the legislation has remained stalled in the Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation.

Sullivan has described his bill as an "all-hands-on-deck" effort to crack down on illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing. If enacted, it would lead to the creation of a "black list" of vessels that have engaged in such actions either on the high seas or in the economic exclusive zone (EEZ) of another country.

Examples of IUU behavior that would land a vessel on the list include forced labor, exceeding established catch limits, or providing services to another vessel already on the list, among other offenses.

American Seafoods CEO joins US senators’ call for Russia to be removed from MSC, hit with more sanctions

Black-listed vessels would be subsequently "denie[d] benefits, such as port privileges, certain travel through, delivery or receipt of supplies or services, or transshipment in waters within the jurisdiction of the United States," according to the legislation.

"Our fishery's extraordinary abundance is the result of responsible stewards who've followed the rules and sustainably managed this incredible resource," Sullivan said of his bill. "But not all vessels and countries abide by these rules, ravaging fish stocks without regard for other users or future generations—particularly the worst offender, China."

Among his initial co-sponsors were Democratic senators Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Brian Schatz of Hawaii as well as Republican senators Lisa Murkowski, also of Alaska, and Roger Wicker of Mississippi. Senators Jeff Merkley and Chris Coons, Democrats from Oregon and Connecticut, respectively, and senator Lindsey Graham, a South Carolina Republican, have since signed on as co-sponsors, too.

Sullivan reintroduced the FISH Act last week (July 9) through an amendment for the next fiscal year's defense spending bill, which was introduced the day before, on July 8.

This is at least the second time around for the bill, which was introduced as S.1227 in August 2022 but died along with the 117th Congress. Whitehouse was the first bill's only co-sponsor.

Sullivan has criticized Chinese labor practices, in particular, when it comes to the seafood industry, and blamed both China and Russia for the crash in ex-vessel and wholesale prices that rocked the US state of Alaska's seafood industry last year.

Sysco, Trident among big firms asked for updates on forced labor sourcing investigations

Sullivan, along with Murkowski and US representative Mary Peltola, an Alaska Democrat, were some of the main proponents of the expanded ban on Russian seafood products entering the US, which was signed into law in December of last year by US president Joe Biden.

Sullivan has also pushed for the leaders from G7 countries to enact their own bans on imports of Russian seafood, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

title: New report claims Philippines fails its migrant fisheries workers
content:
A new piece by investigative journalists at the Outlaw Ocean Project (OOP) has warned the Philippines does not do enough to protect the huge numbers of its citizens that head out around the world to work in the fisheries sector.

You can find the full report at the Filipino news site PhilStar.

Sysco, Trident among big firms asked for updates on forced labor sourcing investigations

In the last decade, the Philippines has annually sent abroad some two million workers, approximately 400,000 of whom are employed in work at sea each year. Filipinos are often in high demand internationally because many speak English and tend to be better educated than workers from other Southeast Asian countries, the report noted.

"The Philippine government insists that it does not promote the export of workers, merely helping to manage the process, but experts who study the country reject this claim. Filipinos working overseas have sent more than $160 billion in wages back to the Philippines to be pumped into the national economy in the last five years, fueling the country’s GDP growth."

That return, according to a study for the Migration Policy Institute by Georgetown University’s Global Human Development Program fellow Maruja Asis, has led the Philippine government into complacency, relying on this steady inflow of capital and avoiding needed reforms that would encourage growth in the domestic job market, it said.

In 2022, workers sent back $36.1bn to the Philippines, accounting for nearly 10% of the country’s entire economic output for the year. Sea-based labor alone generated more than $6.5bn remitted to the Philippines that same year.

The Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) -- established in 2022 via a merger of several pre-existing government agencies -- was created to act as the regulator of this secondary economy. "Yet its oversight has come up short, even when there are signs of abuse," said OOP.

"The Philippines’ manning agencies -- the private companies that connect workers to foreign companies looking for sea-based labor -- are governed by law dictating that they are to make sure the companies they place Filipinos with are compliant with labor laws and human rights standards, and it is the legal responsibility of the DMW to enforce these requirements.

"However, reporting by The New York Times has shown that the manning agency system is full of cracks. These gaps have gone overlooked by the DMW, landing migrant workers in physically and economically exploitative situations."

title: Some 5,000 fish thought to have escaped from Samherji land-based farm
content:
A land-based salmon farming facility in Oxarfjordur, Iceland, operated by Samherji's aquaculture business, has suffered an escape of over 5,000 juvenile fish, according to the country's food and veterinary authority, known as Mast for short.

Samherji reported an accident in May, when it found salmon fry in the facility's "settling pond." It is believed the incident took place when the water level in the fry tank rose, allowing fish to be sucked through the overflow outlet.

The fish were 70-80 grams, and Samherji could not guarantee that no fish had reached the sea. It found 868 fry outside their correct tank, but were not sure exactly how many had escaped.

Mast has investigated the incident and Samherji's response, it said. It added that it had not had confirmation of all the missing fish being located. 

"During the investigation of the case, it was found that the operator could not account for 5,196 fish, and [Mast] concludes that this is the number of fry that may have... washed out into the sea."

"It is clear that the fish farm was not equipped with farming equipment that was sufficiently fish-proof. At the time, the fish farm was not equipped with enough fine-woven nets to catch the fry that escaped from the station," it said, adding that it would continue to monitor.

title: Daily recap: Acme snaps up New York smokehouse; Global shipbuilding faces major setbacks
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Monday, July 15:

Acme snaps up fellow family-owned New York smokehouse

Acme Smoked Fish Corporation, one of the largest salmon smokers in the US, has acquired a fellow family-run Brooklyn, New York-based smoker.

Global shipbuilding faces major setbacks amid post-COVID cost surge

In the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, the global shipbuilding industry is experiencing significant disruptions, marked by a widespread freeze in new constructions, according to fishing industry sources.

'Project 2025' seeks 'breakup' of NOAA, reverse of conservation, climate change initiatives

Based on what's contained in "Project 2025," don't be surprised to see a major push to diminish the powers of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the US agency charged with regulating commercial fishing and reversing president Joe Biden's climate-change-related initiatives should Republican Donald Trump win the 2024 presidential election. 

Norwegian salmon export giant aims for aggressive growth after 2023 sales pass approach $370m

Norwegian salmon exporter Sekkingstad is aiming to win market share in 2024 amid a "zero growth scenario," new CEO Andreas Mikalsen told Undercurrent News.

Ocean Wise revokes sustainability badge for Southeast Alaska salmon fisheries

Ocean Wise, a conservation group based in Vancouver, Canada, has withdrawn its sustainability recommendation for salmon harvested in Southeast Alaska, meaning it can no longer carry the organization's sustainability label.

Sysco, Trident among big firms asked for updates on forced labor sourcing investigations

Sysco Corp., Trident Seafoods and High Liner Foods are among 13 heavyweight buyers of seafood that've been asked by a coalition of 18 non-governmental organizations to tell them more about the steps they are taking to investigate concerns regarding sourcing from Chinese companies that rely upon forced labor.

Outstanding surge in anchovy fishing pushes Peru landings to new heights

In April 2024, Peru's fishery landings amounted to 870,800t worth PEN 510.2 million ($135.7m), up 494.2% in volume and 158.4% in value compared to the same month last year, as shown by data published by the country's ministry of production, known as Produce.

Boom in Argentina's illex squid sales eases hake, red shrimp export slump

Argentina saw its seafood exports rise in May with a 26.9% increase in volume and a 9.7% increase in value compared to the same period a year before.

title: Sysco, Trident among big firms asked for updates on forced labor sourcing investigations
content:
Sysco Corp., Trident Seafoods and High Liner Foods are among 13 heavyweight buyers of seafood that've been asked by a coalition of 18 non-governmental organizations to tell them more about the steps they are taking to investigate concerns regarding sourcing from Chinese companies that rely upon forced labor.

The effort relates to reports by the Outlaw Ocean Project (OOP) and Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Ian Urbina first published by The New Yorker in October 2023.

The series provided haunting details about crew members being held captive, beaten and suffering from malnutrition aboard vessels in China's distant water fishing fleet, as well as a thorough accounting of the Chinese program used to enlist and transport a large number of Uyghurs over 1,000 miles from Xinjiang, in the land-locked, northwestern part of China, to seafood processing plants in Shangdong, on the east coast.

Subsequent reports detailed the abuse of North Korean laborers.

The reports have led to congressional hearings and multiple pleadings with the president Joe Biden administration to step up the pressure on seafood imports from China that involved forced labor, as reported by Undercurrent News.

In the latest action, a long list of NGOs, including Freedom United, the Transitional Justice Working Group and the Committee for Human Rights in North Korea, have launched a coordinated campaign that involves sending letters to more than a dozen companies to ask them about their practices. 

Trident’s Bundrant commits to investigate China’s use of North Korean labor

One letter sent to US food distribution giant Sysco, a copy of which was shared with Undercurrent, reminds the company of the commitment it made to investigate its sourcing practices. It asks Sysco to provide its preliminary findings or outcomes and examples of steps it has taken to cease relying on suppliers or sub-suppliers participating in forced labor programs.

"We believe that maintaining a supply chain free from forced labor is not only a legal and ethical imperative, but also crucial for the sustainability of the seafood industry," stated the letter, which gave the company three weeks to respond.   

Sysco, Trident and High Liner all reported suspending business with a large processing firm in China, Dalian Haiqing Food Co., in January 2024 over the OOP series, as reported earlier by Undercurrent. 

According to trade records, Trident was buying from Haiqing as recently as December. The company was "the consignee for shipments of seafood, including pollock," from the Chinese company between October 2017 and December 2023.

Other companies targeted by the NGOs include, according to sources: Ahold Delhaize, Lidl, Albertsons, Metro, Aldi South Group, Carrefour, Cite Marine, Nichirei Seafoods, Nomad Foods and Young's Seafood.

title: Spanish court moves to trial for Ricardo Fuentes, other firms over illegal fishing allegations
content:
After nearly six years of investigation, Spain's National Court has directed eight individuals and 12 companies, including Ricardo Fuentes Group, to trial over allegations of illegal tuna fishing and money laundering, Infobae and other local media reported.

The charges stem from the company's alleged involvement in the commercial sale of illegally caught bluefin tuna and laundering the significant profits gained from this illicit activity, La Verdad reported.

The investigating judge, Maria Tardon, has formally accused the two brothers leading the Cartagena-based firm, Jose and Juan Pedro Fuentes Garcia, of selling tuna under unsafe conditions and laundering substantial financial gains. These accusations are part of a larger case involving several companies and individuals linked to the illicit trade of bluefin tuna.

Among the accused are also senior figures from Grupo Pescnortmar -- Carlos Fernandez Fernandez, Javier Amoros, and Khalid Mouslim -- and a civil guard officer stationed in the town of Torre Pacheco who allegedly provided the network with inside information about ongoing investigations.

Spanish authorities to widen Maltese tuna investigation

The allegations include multiple severe charges: document falsification, public health violations, environmental crimes, consumer rights violations, disclosure of secrets, participation in a criminal organization, and money laundering. Tardon has given prosecutors and plaintiffs 10 days to either request a formal trial or drop the charges.

The court documents revealed that the illegally caught tuna was reportedly injected with additives to enhance its appearance, despite being in poor condition and posing serious public health risks. The investigation also uncovered that the facilities used by the accused operated without proper health inspections, maintaining deplorable sanitary conditions.

Moreover, the constant mixing of legally and illegally sourced tuna in the market created significant traceability issues, making it difficult to determine the origin, condition, and safety of the fish. Some samples analyzed showed dangerously high levels of histamine, leading to cases of food poisoning.

This trial is the result of Operation Tarantelo, initiated in 2018, which saw cooperation between the Civil Guard, Spanish authorities, and Europol. The operation led to 79 arrests and the seizure of over 80,000 kilograms of illegally sourced tuna.

title: Canadian fisheries minister orders external investigation of eel poaching arrests
content:
Canadian fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier has announced an external review into an incident involving two Mi'kmaw fishermen in Nova Scotia, who alleged racism after being detained by federal officers for allegedly poaching elvers, or baby eel.

CBC reported Monday (July 8) that the incident occurred in March 2024, when Blaise Sylliboy of the Eskasoni First Nation and Kevin Hartling of the Membertou First Nation were apprehended by fisheries officers for allegedly fishing after the season had closed.

The men were reportedly stripped of their footwear and phones and left at a rural gas station at around 1 a.m., and they had to walk for several hours before finding assistance. The article doesn't indicate whether either man was criminally charged.

Lebouthillier confirmed the external review would be conducted independently, with no involvement from Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) or the government involved in the investigative team's day-to-day operations.

"The allegations brought forward regarding the treatment of the two individuals are simply unacceptable," said Lebouthillier in a statement.

The review will examine the March 26 incident, departmental policies, enforcement practices and procedures to address potential systemic biases or racism. Following the investigation, a detailed report with findings and recommendations will be made public, the news release said.

"This external review must, and will, involve Indigenous leadership," the minister said. "Further engagement with Mi'kmaw communities will be critical before selecting the external review panel."

Prime minister Justin Trudeau, who visited Dartmouth, in Nova Scotia, days after the incident, described the reports as "very troubling" and supported a full investigation, the CBC reported.

Eskasoni chief Leroy Denny and other Mi'kmaw leaders have had multiple meetings with the federal fisheries minister to address what they describe as systemic racism within the DFO. Initially, the DFO proposed an internal review, but Mi'kmaw chiefs pushed for an external investigation with Mi'kmaw representation.

The Assembly of Nova Scotia Mi'kmaw Chiefs released a statement highlighting ongoing issues faced by Indigenous harvesters and called for better treatment by Canada, CBC reported.

The elver fishery is highly lucrative due to high demand in Asia and the collapse of eel fishing in Europe, pushing market values up to CAD 5,000/kg ($3,600). The surge led to the DFO canceling the fishery season for the second year, a decision criticized by both commercial and Mi'kmaw fishermen.

title: Head of Mexican fishing association assassinated after denouncing illegal fishing
content:
Minerva Perez Castro, the president of Baja California's delegation to the Mexican national chamber of fishing and aquaculture industries, also known as CANAINPESCA, was murdered in Ensenada on July 8, according to industry sources.

Perez had been a vocal critic of the infiltration of criminal syndicates into Mexican fisheries, industry sources told Undercurrent News.

Perez had highlighted this issue in an interview just hours before her death, criticizing the market penetration of illegally caught fish, which bypass production costs faced by legitimate businesses.

"Illegal fishing reaches the same market as the legal product but without all the production costs associated with a legally constituted company," she stated (see video interview in Spanish in the link below). She also reported extortion and attempted illegal charges in a protection racket and called on authorities for greater presence to curb illegal fishing, sources said.

Her vehicle was found in front of the facilities of the seafood firm Atenea en el Mar -- of which she was the director -- with multiple gunshot wounds, and she subsequently lost control, crashing into a trailer, Infobae reported.

Minerva Pérez Castro, presidenta de la Canainpesca en Baja California, fue asesinada la tarde de este lunes en #Ensenada; horas antes había denunciado la pesca ilegal en la región

LEE: https://t.co/DdwPiVTkbB pic.twitter.com/S9ZCw8eW8L

— La Jornada Baja California (@LaJornadaBC) July 9, 2024

The Center for Sustainable Development and Fisheries (CeDePesca) expressed in a statement its immense sorrow for the "murder of our partner and friend Minerva Perez Castro."

She "was a great businesswoman, an exceptional leader, and a dear friend. We strongly condemn what happened and join the various expressions of repudiation and indignation that have arisen in response to this lamentable episode," CeDePesca also stated.

CeDePesca called on Mexican authorities at all levels to conduct a thorough investigation and to not allow the crime to go unpunished.

"We also urge all entities and organizations we work with, both within and outside of Mexico, to speak out in similar terms," it said.

 

 
 
 
 
 
View this post on Instagram
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 

A post shared by CeDePesca (@cedepesca)

Baja California's governor, Marina del Pilar, immediately condemned the murder on social media channels.

Perez, who had been named president of CANAINPESCA on June 15, was the first woman to lead the position in Baja California. 

Perez had already been the victim of an attack a year ago.

title: US shrimp imports climbing again, though prices remain low
content:
US shrimp imports began climbing again in May, even in spite of both countervailing and antidumping duties being levied against some of the biggest source nations.

That's what the latest seafood trade data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) shows.

The US imported 63,973 metric tons of shrimp worth $486.7 million in May 2024, 3% more volume albeit 7% less value when compared to May 2023. This after the US imported 50,901t of shrimp worth $397.6m in April 2024, 10% less volume and 14% less value than in April 2023. 

The year-on-year drop in value in May 2024 can be blamed in large part on the average price paid, which was $3.59 per pound, 3% less than the average $3.70/lb paid in April 2024 and 8% less than the average $3.92/lb paid in May 2023. 

The continued drop in average prices keeps the industry asking the same question: Have we hit bottom yet?

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
US shrimp imports climbing again, though prices remain low - Undercurrent News

Here's the data broken up for the top five source nations.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
US shrimp imports climbing again, though prices remain low - Undercurrent News

Despite the higher volume in May, the US has yet to catch up with the pace of imports kept last year. Over the first five months of 2024, 297,666t of shrimp worth $2.3 billion were imported, 1% less volume and 8% less value than the first five months of 2023. 

'Sucky demand'

Donelson Berger, the shrimp category manager for Boston, Massachusetts-based processor Stavis Seafoods, believes the US' April shrimp import numbers were a result of the recent actions taken by the US Department of Commerce in response to a request to level the playing field by the US domestic wild harvest shrimp industry, as reported by Undercurrent News.

In an email exchange with Undercurrent on Monday (July 8), Berger pointed to the total shrimp imports seen over the most recent five months by the US as evidence of how April represented such an unusual dip and not indicative of the overall trend. 

January 2024 -- 59,629t worth $462.4m
February 2024 -- 59,668t worth $456.5m
March 2024 -- 63,495t worth $481.8m
April 2024 -- 50,901t worth $397.6m
May 2024 -- 63,973t worth $486.7m

Berger believes the US will finish 2024 with more shrimp than in 2023 as bigger import numbers come over the rest of the year. He noted the common pattern of the US seeing 40% of its annual shrimp imports during the first half of the year and 60% in the second half. He said he also expects retail sales to be steady.  

Berger also doesn't see shrimp prices getting much lower and maybe even rising sometime during the final three months of the year.

Donelson Berger

"We hit bottom in 2023," he said. "I don’t expect prices to go below that level,  but certainly down to those levels. ... We are sold through the high-priced inventories from 2021 and 2022, but imports are still ahead of demand, which is keeping prices low and flat. Seafood is a luxury food and people don’t indulge in it when they feel pinched. Thus sucky demand."

Ecuador gets back on track

The improved volume numbers in May have much to do with the turnaround by Ecuador, which sent the US 19,130t of shrimp worth $125.2m during the month, 15% more volume and 10% more value than in May 2023.

Compare that to April when Ecuador sent the US just 9,881t of shrimp worth $67.5m, less than half (45%) the volume and 54% of the value seen in March 2024, as reported by Undercurrent. It was the worst month for Ecuadorian shrimp exports to the US since February 2021. 

US stands pat on antidumping rates for Ecuador shrimp

The low numbers were related to preliminary CVD rates announced on March 26 by DOC. DOC told everyone involved in or affected by the CVD investigation surrounding Ecuadorian shrimp that importers of shrimp from Industrial Pesquera Santa Priscilla, Ecuador's largest producer, would have to pay a preliminary rate of 13.41%, as reported by Undercurrent. The amount would have to be provided in upfront cash deposits, DOC declared.

Importers of shrimp from Sociedad Nacional de Galapagos, known as Songa, were informed that they would have to pay a preliminary 1.69% rate and importers of all other Ecuadorian shrimp would have to pay 7.55% in upfront deposits.

Then, on April 19, DOC informed all parties that it made a mistake in its calculations and it was reducing Santa Priscila's preliminary CVD rate to 2.89% while maintaining Songa at 1.69%. It declared that the Songa rate was de minimus and therefore not required upfront. Importers of all other Ecuador shrimp are now required to pay an upfront fee of 2.89%. 

Also, on May 23, DOC announced its preliminary antidumping duties, giving Santa Priscila a low 1.54% rate while slamming Songa and all other Ecuadoran producers with a 10.58% rate, as Undercurrent reported. DOC officials declared on June 26 that they wouldn't be adjusting the AD rates for Ecuador either, as reported by Undercurrent.

Combined, importers of Santa Priscilla shrimp are looking at a 2.89% rate going forward, while importers of shrimp from Songa must pay a combined 10.58% rate and importers of all other Ecuadorian shrimp must pay a combined rate of 13.47%. 

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
US shrimp imports climbing again, though prices remain low - Undercurrent News

The average price paid in the US for Ecuador shrimp in May 2024 was $3.07/lb, 4% less than the $3.20/lb paid in April 2024 and 5% below the average $3.22/lb paid in May 2023, based on the data shared by the UCN Trade Portal (See above).

Despite its struggles, Ecuador, during the first five months of 2025, sent the US 85,324t of shrimp worth $571.5m, 4% more volume and value than in May 2024.

Ecuador continues to be the US' second-largest source of shrimp, behind only India. It accounted for 29% of the US shrimp import market during the first five months of 2024.

India 4% ahead of pace

India also ratcheted up its exports slightly in May 2024, sending the US 22,271t worth $164.0m, 2% more volume though with 8% less value than in May 2023. India remains ahead of its 2023 pace, sending the US 110,581t of shrimp worth $812.0m during the first five months of 2024, 4% more volume and 6% less value than the first five months of last year. 

India has accounted for a leading 37% of the US shrimp import market so far this year.

The average price paid in May 2024 for Indian shrimp in the US was $3.52/lb, 2% more than the average $3.46/lb paid in April 2024 and 9% less than the average $3.86/lb paid in May 2023, as shown in the UCN trade portal chart below.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
US shrimp imports climbing again, though prices remain low - Undercurrent News

Recall that DOC hit Indian producers Devi Sea Foods Limited and Sandhya Aqua Exports with preliminary CVD rates of 4.72% and 3.89%, respectively while charging 4.36% for importers of shrimp from other Indian shrimp producers.

Indonesia continues descent

Indonesia, the US' third largest source of shrimp (18% of the market), continued to spiral down in its exports in May. It sent the US 11,735t of shrimp worth $88.9m, 15% less volume and 20% less value y-o-y.

It was the 21st consecutive month in which Indonesia saw a y-o-y decline on shrimp exports to the US, dating back to August 2022.

Over the first five months of 2024, Indonesia sent the US 53,041t worth $396.8m, 17% less volume and 24% less value than during the first five months of 2023.

The average price paid for Indonesian shrimp in the US in May 2024 was $3.59/lb, just a hair above the $3.58/lb rate seen in April 2024 and 5% less than the $3.77/lb seen in May 2024.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
US shrimp imports climbing again, though prices remain low - Undercurrent News

It doesn't help that Indonesia's largest producer, First Marine Seafoods, and all other shrimp producers were hit with 6.3% preliminary CVD rates by DOC. 

Vietnam makes progress in US market

Vietnam, the US' fourth-largest shrimp source nation, gained some more ground in May, sending the US 5,128t worth $47.4m, 8% more volume and 8% less value than in May 2023, based on NOAA data. This after Vietnam sent the US 4,071t of shrimp worth $39.7m in April 2024, 11% more volume and less than 1% more value than in April 2023. 

During the first five months of 2024, Vietnam sent the US 20,396t of shrimp worth $197.6m, 16% more volume and 4% more value than the same period in 2023. 

The average price paid for Vietnamese shrimp in May 2024 was $4.35/lb, 5% less than the $4.59/lb average seen in April 2024 and 14% less than the $5.05/lb average seen in May 2023.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view

Farm-gate prices for Vietnamese farmed shrimp eased throughout June but looked as if they may have hit the bottom at the beginning of July, as reported by Undercurrent.

In May, vannamei trading continued to show signs of picking up, with Vietnamese export volumes up 16% month-on-month and 3% year-on-year at 28,305 metric tons, according to a Ho Chi Minh City-based consultancy commissioned by Undercurrent to analyze market trends, export data, and prices. In May, the average vannamei farm-gate price eased 1% or 2% for the smaller sizes, while the larger shrimp (30-50 counts per kilogram) fell 4%.
