title: Spanish cannery, now retailer-owned, leases rival’s plant after food fraud, bankruptcy case
content:
Spanish cannery Congelados y Pescados Plaza Chica, which entered bankruptcy proceedings earlier this year after it was implicated in a food fraud case, has ceased operations and rented out one of its two facilities, according to industry sources.

Sources in southern Europe told Undercurrent News that Plaza Chica has rented its plant in Alfaro, Spain, to Galician cannery Industrias Cerdeimar, which has taken over the business. Cerdeimar, one of the oldest canneries in Galicia, founded in 1884, is now trying to win back Plaza Chica's private-label tuna contracts in Italy, sources said.

Ceirdeimar itself has been taken over by Spanish hypermarket chain Family Cash, led by Jose Canet.

The retailer, which -- according to its website -- has 40 stores in Spain, acquired Ceirdeimar earlier this year from fish processor Blady Gros, the holding company behind fish processor Blady Tuna Market, sources said. Valencia-based Blady went bankrupt late last year, just months after buying Ceirdeimar, sources also said. 

According to Oncadero, Plaza Chica's bankruptcy this year left 46 workers without jobs at one of the firm's two factories. According to El dia de la Rioja, 60 Plaza Chica workers resumed their jobs at the Alfaro plant in March 2024.

Despite efforts to maintain operations and employment, the dismissed workers' hopes were dashed when a prospective deal with a Malaga-based firm fell through, Oncadero reported last month. This development, along with the expiration of an ERTE (temporary layoff) arrangement and a rental contract with the local municipality, led to the plant's closure, Oncadero wrote. 

Plaza Chica, Family Cash, and Ceirdemar did not reply to a request for comment from Undercurrent in time for this publication.

One source in Italy said that in previous years, Plaza Chica had gained several contracts with Italian retailers through a very aggressive pricing strategy.

He added that it had later been discovered that it was able to offer cheaper prices using low-quality oil labeled as olive oil at a time when olive oil prices were increasing to a record high. 

"Plaza Chica was very aggressive with olive oil products in glass jars. The company could offer prices 20% lower than other competitors, but then it was discovered that it used pomace oil -- an olive oil waste [product] -- instead of olive oil in the jars. Despite the closure of Plaza Chica, competition in the Italian [canned tuna] market has remained high, given that there are both national and international players," he said.

Sources said that this new business venture is trying to regain Plaza Chica's business in Italy, "using the corpse of Plaza Chica and the same workers in Navarra, including the former owner."

Alimarket reported in March that Plaza Chica had been forced to close and file for bankruptcy due to a legal case opened against it for food fraud. It added that the firm had rented out one of its two plants to Cerdeimar.

Voz de Galicia reported in March that Cerdeimar has taken over the management of Plaza Chica's cannery.

Voz de Galicia and Gamaconsumer also reported that in April 2023, the Valencia-based Blady Gros had acquired Cerdeimar, allowing its factory to resume full operations.

Blady Gros, which started its operations in 2022, also owned Blady Tuna Market in Valencia, specializing in packaging tuna in special sealed bags and claiming to be the leader in this format in Spain, according to Voz de Galicia.

In December 2023, Alimarket reported that Blady Tuna had filed for bankruptcy just a few months after acquiring Cerdeimar. Despite Blady Tuna's financial troubles, Cerdeimar continued its industrial operations. 

Blady Tuna experienced rapid growth in recent years, earning revenue of €60 million ($65m) in its most recently reported 18 months of operation. It sold its pouch-packaged tuna mainly to the hospitality sector and export, according to Alimarket.

Arrests after food fraud case

Plaza Chica's closure came after revelations earlier this year that it had been involved in re-labeling and selling low-quality tuna, resulting in significant product seizures and arrests, as Undercurrent previously reported.

The Spanish Guardia Civil's Operation Matsu, in collaboration with Italian carabinieri and Europol authorities, uncovered an international food fraud originating in La Rioja Baja, northern Spain.

Investigations revealed clandestine operations where returned cans were re-labeled and redistributed, including products destined for the Italian market with incorrect labeling. 

Following the investigation, four individuals were arrested, 120,000 cans of tuna and 45,000 liters of oil were seized, and 21 bank accounts were frozen, La Rioja reported. The investigation began in late August 2023 following a tip-off and culminated on Dec. 13 with raids on two factories and a residence to prevent the distribution of fraudulent products, many destined for Italy.

In the raids, authorities found a clandestine operation where returned cans were re-labeled with new expiration dates. Some cans contained water, causing rust marks, and many were labeled only in Italian, which is not permitted for products sold in Spain. Lab tests revealed that 33 out of 40 analyzed cans contained lower-quality oil than advertised, and one had substandard tuna.

According to La Rioja, Plaza Chica expanded its operations in 2020 and employed over 100 people. Despite the ongoing investigation, the company maintained on its website that it uses the best raw materials and adheres to strict food safety standards.

title: Gigante Salmon faces fine for delayed reporting of increased facility costs
content:
Gigante Salmon is under scrutiny from the Oslo Stock Exchange following an investigation into the company's disclosure practices relating to an updated cost estimate for its Rodoy facility.

The situation stems from Gigante's stock exchange announcement on March 19, which detailed an updated cost estimate for completing the Rodoy facility.

Norway’s Gigante revises investment requirements up by $33m, fires CEO

As Undercurrent News previously reported, the land-based aquaculture facility in Rodoy, Nordland, will now cost the firm an additional NOK 350 million ($32.9m), taking the total investment amount for the construction work until completion of the production site to an estimated NOK 995m.

"The cost increase forecast is mainly due to longer construction time, including costs for rigging and operation," it said.

"The cost increase will require new capital to the company. This work has been initiated. The plan is that the cost increase will be covered through a combination of equity and debt financing."

The Oslo Stock Exchange has now issued an advance notice of a decision, indicating that a violation fine may be imposed on the company for failing to ensure the timely publication of information about the cost overrun.

The final decision on whether a fine will be levied, and its size, will be determined after the company provides input on the advance notice. Gigante has been given until Aug. 12 to submit any comments or objections to the advance notice.

title: South Korean news site says forced labor-linked imports from China at 4,000t
content:
More than 4,000 metric tons of seafood products imported by South Korea from China were made using North Korean labor, reports the Chosun Daily, which has been following up findings from the Outlaw Ocean Project (OOP).

The seafood was processed by North Korean workers under forced labor conditions in China and then sold to South Korea, violating United Nations (UN) sanctions and potentially supporting North Korea's nuclear development via salaries, according to the article. The UN Security Council's sanctions against North Korea prohibit third-country companies from employing North Korean workers for this reason.

OOP, an independent journalism group, reported in October 2023, as part of a two-part series appearing in The New Yorker, how a Chinese program was used to enlist and transport a large number of Uyghurs over 1,000 miles from Xinjiang, in the land-locked, northwestern part of China, to seafood processing plants in Shangdong, on the east coast. The investigation found also a heavy reliance on North Korean laborers.

Report: South Korean supermarkets sold seafood produced by North Korean labor in China

Data from US financial sanctions and supply chain analysis firm Sayari, analyzed by the Washington DC-based nonprofit OOP and Chosun, found that five Chinese seafood processing companies exported approximately 4,360t of seafood processed by North Koreans to 36 South Korean companies across 158 shipments between 2021 and 2023.

These shipments were worth around KRW 30 billion to 40bn ($21.6 million-$28.8m). They were shipped from Dalian and Dandong in China to Incheon and Busan in South Korea and then distributed nationwide, ending up in large supermarkets and local seafood markets.

The US government has indicated possible sanctions against the Chinese companies involved and may call on allies, including South Korea, to participate.

title: NGOs launch new ‘Death at Sea’ justice campaign
content:
Human Rights at Sea International (HRSI), supported by the Blue Marine Foundation (BMF) and the Sustainable Fisheries and Communities Trust (SFACT), has launched a new "Death at Sea" justice campaign.

The group said the initiative aims to raise awareness about the safety and well-being of fisheries observers at sea and call for global policy reform at domestic and international levels. Alongside the film's release, it will also advocate for justice for Eritara Aati Kaierua, a Kiribati fisheries observer who died in March 2020.

The award-winning film "Death at Sea," directed by Sara Pipernos, documents Kaierua's death and the experiences of his family and other Pacific fisheries observers. The movie premiered on Jan. 30, 2024, in London and has been shown at various global venues, earning a Royal Television Society award.

Alongside his family's testimony, other Pacific fisheries observers recount the abuses
they have witnessed and experienced at sea.

The campaign will feature an interactive multi-lingual website detailing policy goals, the investigation into Kaierua's death, and behind-the-scenes content from the film. The campaign's priorities include supporting Kiribati authorities in securing worker compensation for Kaierua's family and advocating for enhanced protections for fisheries observers worldwide.

David Hammond, HRSI's executive director, emphasized the campaign's goal of setting a global precedent for justice and improved practices for fisheries observers. Jess Rattle, BMF's head of investigations, highlighted the vital role of fisheries observers in marine resource management and the need for their protection against threats and abuses. John Burton, chair of SFACT, expressed commitment to supporting the justice campaign and improving welfare security for observers' families.

The campaign will engage with international bodies, such as the International Labor Organization and the International Maritime Organization, to push for global policy reforms.

title: Canadian cattle firm fined CAD 545k for salmon habitat destruction
content:
Altherr & Schellenber Cattle, a cattle company in the Canadian province of British Columbia (BC), has been fined a total of CAD 545,000 ($397,733) for destroying salmon habitat along the Chilcotin and Kleena Kleene rivers, reports CBC. 

The fine was issued following a six-year investigation by Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO). Altherr & Schellenberg Cattle pled guilty to violating Canada's Fisheries Act.

From 2017 to 2020, the company -- which operated on two privately owned ranch lands near the rivers -- altered the landscape to expand its farming area by removing river habitat, filling in water channels, diverting streams and blocking fish passages without approval, according to the article. 

Joe Alphonse, chief of the Tsilhqot'in First Nation, an Indigenous people who live between the Fraser River and the Coast Mountains in west-central BC, highlighted the significant damage to salmon habitats, particularly impacting chinook salmon, which are vital to the local ecosystem and the Tsilhqot'in people.

Bayliff Enterprises, a contractor hired to clear land along the Kleena Kleene River, also pleaded guilty and was fined CAD 90,000 for violating the Fisheries Act as well as BC's Forest and Range Practices Act.

title: New details emerge from Regal Springs’ deadly ammonia escape in Indonesia
content:
New details have emerged regarding the tragic ammonia escape at Regal Springs' facility in Indonesia earlier this month, which resulted in the death of an engineer and left two other workers injured, a source within the company told Undercurrent News. 

The June 9 incident at the Aquafarm Nusantara facility, in Lubuk Naga, occurred during a routine maintenance inspection of ammonia equipment by a dedicated engineer with over 10 years of service in the company. Jaimi Muhammad, a 36-year-old worker from Pasar Baru Village, Teluk Mengkudu District, was killed and Suardi, 35, from Ara Payung Village, Pantai Cermin District, was sent to intensive care at a local hospital, as earlier reported by Undercurrent.

The third worker was not identified.

"Tragically, we lost a highly experienced and dedicated person," the source, who requested anonymity, told Undercurrent. "Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with his family, and naturally, we are providing them with comprehensive support during this difficult time. Two other employees sustained injuries, but we are pleased to report that both are recovering well."

The source disputed earlier claims of a major explosion, explaining that the incident "was confined to a maintenance error involving a pressured valve."

"Given the fact that we lost a human life, the police, along with other local authorities, are involved in surveillance of the scene, but I can assure you there was no major explosion as reported," the source said.

"As for the root cause of the incident, experts can only identify possible incorrect handling of equipment, difficult to pinpoint in its own right, in the routine maintenance of a pressured valve," the source added. 

Safety protocols at the facility, which also includes a fish hatchery, played a crucial role in minimizing the impact, the source told Undercurrent.

Ammonia leak at Regal Springs’ Indonesia tilapia operation causes deadly explosion

"Fortunately, the incident happened on a Sunday when staffing was minimal, and our rigorous safety protocols ensured a swift evacuation of the few present. The area was promptly cordoned off for investigations by our experts and external authorities," the source said.

The processing plant was closed temporarily as a precautionary measure but has since resumed full operations. The source also emphasized that the company's supply chain would not be interrupted due to the incident.

"Our precautionary measures and buffer stocks have ensured that our customers will not be affected by this brief closure," the source noted.

An investigation into the exact cause of the ammonia escape is ongoing, with the company's chief engineer and external experts closely examining the maintenance procedures.

"Getting to the root cause of the incident has not been easy. Experts can only identify an incorrect procedure, difficult to pinpoint in its own right, in the routine maintenance of a pressured valve," the source said.

"Regal Springs continues to prioritize the health and well-being of its employees and their families, committing to long-term support for those affected by the incident," the source added. "Our primary concern is the health and well-being of our employees and their families. We immediately extended assistance to the bereaved family and the two injured employees, and we will continue to support them long-term."

Indonesian frozen seafood exporter latest firm to face China COVID ban

Despite the tragedy, Regal Springs is determined to enhance safety measures and ensure such an incident does not recur, the source said, adding: "Of course, it goes without saying that there are standard operating procedures in place to follow, and we will continue to strengthen understanding here. It is desperately sad that we lose a life in the process." 

Regal Springs, established in Indonesia in 1988, operates in Lake Toba in North Sumatra. The company employs over 4,000 people and is a significant tilapia producer, with 95% of its products exported to Europe, the US and other markets.

title: New bill would empower US food safety agency to destroy rejected seafood, prevent ‘port shopping’
content:
A bipartisan-supported bill introduced on Thursday (June 27) would grant the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) the authority to discard imported seafood that fails health inspections at the border.

Introduced by US representative Clay Higgins, a Louisiana Republican, and co-sponsored by Troy Carter, a Louisiana Democrat, The Destruction of Hazardous Imports Act (HR 8861),  seeks to build on the FDA's existing powers to dispose of hazardous imported medicines and medical devices to protect public health.

The lawmakers said in a press release that they are concerned about the routine violation of US health and safety standards by some foreign seafood suppliers. These suppliers contaminate their products with harmful chemicals, posing significant health risks.

"The United States must prioritize the health and safety of the American people," said Higgins. "Currently, billions of pounds of un-inspected foreign seafood continue to enter the country, causing major health concerns. God only knows what's in the shipments that enter through our ports. This legislation provides the FDA with the authority to destroy illegal seafood imports and ensure they do not reach American markets."

They also said that suppliers have been known to circumvent initial inspection failures by attempting entry through different ports.

"By granting the FDA the necessary authority to destroy food products that fail to meet our stringent health and safety standards, we are closing a dangerous loophole that has allowed contaminated seafood to enter our markets. This bill protects consumers from potential health risks and upholds the integrity of our food supply chain while supporting Louisiana fishermen and seafood processors," said Carter.

The new bill follows last year's HR 1057, or the Imported Seafood Safety Standards Act, which was also introduced by Higgins. It would hold foreign countries and exporters to the same standards that US seafood producers and processors abide by.  

The latest initiative has received support from local legislators, the National Aquaculture Association and the Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA), which represents US wild-caught shrimp harvesters and processors.

When shrimp imports are refused entry into the US, the current system allows importers to destroy or export the shrimp within 90 days of refusal, SSA noted. However, the alliance, which conducted its investigations, said containers of shrimp that were once refused entry into the US due to safety concerns were re-exported — only to be shipped back to the US.

Despite efforts by the FDA and the US Customs and Border Protection to combat this practice, known as "port shopping," the risk of contaminated seafood reaching American consumers remains, SSA warned.

"The US shrimp industry has long advocated for reform of US law to prohibit hazardous seafood from being re-introduced into international trade. The Destruction of Hazardous Imports Act substantially improves existing law by providing the FDA with the authority needed to protect public health," said the alliance.

title: Grieg dealt with bout of low oxygen, harmful plankton at BC salmon farm
content:
Grieg Seafood has acknowledged dealing with a naturally occurring low dissolved-oxygen event and harmful plankton that impacted its salmons' health and welfare at one of its farms last month on the Canadian west coast.

However, despite reports by an observer of suspected dead fish removal, the Norwegian company has yet to disclose any mortality figures.

In a press release issued last week, Grieg Seafood did not mention the number of fish impacted by the May incident at its farm in Nootka Sound, a remote inlet on Vancouver Island, in British Columbia. But a report in the Times Colonist, a local news service, on Monday (June 24) detailed observations of the vessel Knight Dragon appearing to pump something out of the farm, while another hose discharged water into the open ocean.

The BC vessel Knight Dragon is owned by Campbell River-based contractor, Brown's Bay Packing Company.

Scientist Stan Proboszcz, a staunch opponent of open net-pen salmon farming, told the publication that he suspected the vessel was removing dead fish from the bottom of the farm's nets and discharging the water. He later contacted Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) to report the incident.

Emails seen by Glacier Media, publisher of the Times Colonist, revealed that Brenda McCorquodale, DFO's senior director of aquaculture management, confirmed an investigation into the die-off allegations but declined to comment further.

Grieg operates 22 farms and a hatchery in BC, which employ 180 people and yield 23,400 metric tons of salmon annually for North American and Asian markets.

Grieg puts BC investments on ice following Canada decision to shutter salmon net-pens

Last week, its Norwegian parent announced that it's suspending all of its investments in BC in response to the Canadian federal government's announcement that it will be banning open net pens in the province by no later than June 30, 2029, as Undercurrent News reported.

The salmon farming giant said, in a statement made public on the Norwegian stock exchange, that it will "await [Canada's] draft transition plan to assess further actions," which is expected by the end of July 2024.

Undercurrent reached out to Grieg Seafood BC for comment about the low dissolved oxygen in May but has yet to hear back.

title: Ammonia leak at Regal Springs’ Indonesia tilapia operation causes deadly explosion
content:
An explosion at a Regal Springs tilapia operation in Indonesia has resulted in a tragic incident, leaving one worker dead and another severely injured.

The explosion on June 9 at the Aquafarm Nusantara facility, in the Pantai Cermin District, is suspected to have been caused by an ammonia gas leak from one of the company's rooms.

Jaimi Muhammad, a 36-year-old worker from Pasar Baru Village, Teluk Mengkudu District, was killed and Suardi, 35, from Ara Payung Village, Pantai Cermin District, remains in intensive care at a local hospital.

The incident has prompted an intensive follow-up investigation by North Sumatra police, reports Waspada.co.id. 

Authorities are reported to be working diligently to determine the exact cause of the leak and ensure the facility's future safety. As a result, the facility has been closed since the investigations began, Undercurrent News has learned.

Before re-examining the crime scene, the investigative team sought clarification from the company's representatives regarding the incident. Following the meeting, the investigation team proceeded to re-examine the site of the explosion.

Due to the lingering strong smell of ammonia gas, which posed significant inhalation risks, the team has collected air samples for further analysis.

"We are taking necessary precautions to ensure safety while gathering crucial evidence," authorities said. "We have to wait for the results of the investigation from the North Sumatra Police Labfor Team."

Regal Springs did not respond to Undercurrent's request for comment in time for this publication.

PT Aquafarm Nusantara, established in Indonesia in 1988 by Regal Springs, operates in several locations, including reservoirs in Java and Lake Toba in North Sumatra. The company expanded to Lake Toba in 1998 and now manages five main sites in three districts: Simalungun, Samosir and Toba Samosir regencies.

The company operates a fish hatchery, processing plant and feed mills in the Serdang Bedagai regency, where the incident occurred. Employing over 4,000 people, PT Aquafarm Nusantara processes tilapia to produce frozen fillets, with 95% of the product exported to Europe, the US and other countries in North America and Asia.

The five sites on Lake Toba, Indonesia's largest lake and the largest volcanic crater lake in the world, operate with over 600 cages and serve as a critical hub for the company's operations, including a logistics hub at Ajibata.

title: Iceland’s SVN backs out of deal for 50% of Ice Fresh
content:
After announcing a deal for half the shares in sales company Ice Fresh Seafood in the fall of 2023, Iceland's Sildarvinnslan (SVN) has now said it has pulled out of the deal.

Samherji -- which owns 100% of Ice Fresh and 30% of SVN -- was in full agreement to reverse the deal, SVN said in a note to NASDAQ Iceland.

Iceland’s SVN concludes deal for 50% stake in Ice Fresh

The deal had valued Ice Fresh at €42.9 million ($45.6m at that time), equivalent to 1.76 times the book value of equity on Dec. 31, 2022.

"In the opinion of the board of SVN, the Competition Authority has gone too far in examining the case and data requests in no way in accordance with the framework of the transactions, especially in light of the fact that it is only a matter of selling products on foreign markets," SVN said. "So it looks like the data collection is starting to revolve around something else and more than the business in question."

SVN did say it had handed over everything requested and that it had wanted to finalize the deal, but that a decision to end the process had been made "not least because of the extensive projects surrounding the activities of Visir in Grindavik [acquired in 2022], but last week another volcanic eruption began in the vicinity of the town."

Attention may return to bolstering its sales and marketing once more urgent projects in the whitefish business have been completed, it said.

"This is also the opinion of the management of SVN that Icelandic fishing companies need to strengthen their position in order to maintain the competitiveness of the Icelandic fishing industry in the international business environment, where Iceland's share is tiny."

"This difference has been increasing recently as foreign fishing companies, which are in competition with the Icelandic companies in foreign markets for the sale of marine products, are constantly expanding and expanding their activities. The same applies to individual buyers," it claimed.

Samherji has a fraught relationship with Icelandic authorities, not least since the "Fishrot" scandal, which in 2019 saw WikiLeaks publish over 30,000 documents obtained from a former Samherji employee that, according to the organization, showed the Iceland-based fishing giant paid "millions of dollars" to Namibian officials and politicians for fishing access.

Before that, in 2016, then-Samherji chief financial officer Sigursteinn Ingvarsson retired, citing burnout and stress after he and other management were falsely accused of wrongdoing by the Central Bank. In September 2015, management at Samherji were cleared of all wrongdoing in an investigation brought against them by the Central Bank, after a special prosecutor dismissed the case.

title: US Coast Guard blames high captain, commercial pressures for fatal Dungy crab boat sinking
content:
The US Coast Guard (USCG) has -- after more than five years -- concluded its formal investigation into the capsizing of the Mary B II, a 42-foot Dungeness crab fishing vessel, off the Oregon coast, killing all three crew members.

In a 156-page report, completed in December 2023 but made public only this week, the federal agency has chiefly blamed Stephen Biernacki, the then 50-year-old captain who it said was impaired by a combination of methamphetamines, alcohol and fatigue at the time of the Jan. 8, 2019 disaster in Yaquina Bay.

Biernacki was killed along with his fellow harvesters, James Lacey and Joshua Porter. 

Other factors included Biernacki's lack of experience with the bay's treacherous winter conditions and "the commercial pressures created by the harvesting of Dungeness crab in the Pacific Northwest," the USCG said. 

The vessel was trying to cross a notoriously treacherous sandbar while facing down 15-foot breakers at the time of the incident, according to the report. It capsized in spite of being escorted by two Coast Guard vessels, which "methodically illuminated" the waterway with rocket-propelled flares. 

"During the inbound transit, seas were building and breaking at heights up to 14-16 feet," the report recounts. "At 10:04 p.m., the Mary B II slowed to approximately 2-4 knots and began to move off the center of the channel towards the dangerous seaward end of the North Jetty. Approximately two minutes later, the [USCG] escorts observed a series of larger waves interact with the Mary B II near the North Jetty and, as a result, the Mary B II capsized and sank.

"Search and Rescue efforts were immediately initiated, including the dispatch of a [USCG] helicopter and local fire department assets. All three of the crew perished in the sinking and the vessel was a total loss."

The USCG report also describes a five-day hearing that was held in Newport, Oregon, in May 2019. As many as 29 witnesses were called.

Investigators heard how Biernacki was observed "talking excessively quickly, cursing and demonstrating an overall aggressive behavior" when he picked up bait at a store between 4 a.m. and 6 a.m. on Jan. 8, 2019. 

One of the employees asked him why he was going out when every other vessel was headed back to port due to forecasted inclement weather for that day and evening. Later in the day the National Weather Service issued a gale warning. 

Biernacki reportedly responded that he was "going to show these guys how it was done."

A toxicology report later found Biernacki had methamphetamine, amphetamine and alcohol in his system at the time of his death. 

Bills to pay

The moments before and after the ocean delivered its final, fatal blows to the Mary B II are laid out in grim detail.

"At approximately 10:07 p.m., the Mary B II experienced a series of waves," according to the report. "The first set of waves impacted the Mary B II and went under the vessel. The Mary B II was observed by the [USCG] boats on scene to turn about 90 degrees and settled beam to (perpendicular to) the incoming waves. The second wave that impacted the vessel caused the Mary B II to turn its bow to (facing) the waves.

"The largest wave of the series impacted the Mary B II, striking the vessel’s bow. Based on witness observations, the wave size was estimated to be 18 feet. That caused the vessel to pitch-pole and capsize into the waters north of the Yaquina Bay North Jetty tip.

"Crewmembers Lacey and Porter were ejected from the vessel and entered the water. The water temperature was 50.2 degrees Fahrenheit and air temperature was 47.7 degrees Fahrenheit."

The dead bodies of all three men, who were wearing personal flotation devices, were found within 12 hours of the sinking. Biernacki's body was found trapped in the vessel's wheelhouse by debris. None of the crew were wearing immersion suits, which would have prevented them from being shocked by the cold water temperatures. The suits were found in the wreckage and floating in the surrounding water.

One of the saddest details included in the investigative report is a text message exchange between Porter and his wife. The crew member expressed both his frustration with the decisions being made by his captain, saying he was "not to [sic] bright," and his concerns about the weather. His wife, whose name is blacked out, rushed to a position where she could watch the vessel arrive.

Roughly 40 minutes before the vessel capsized, Porter told his wife not too worry because the USCG was "going to be right there." At 10:15 p.m. his wife told him that she would meet him at the dock, but there was no response.

While Lacey had experience working with Biernacki, Porter was hired on a temporary basis, as he had a longer-term job slated to begin later in the month. He told his wife at 3 a.m. on the morning that the Mary B II was set to head out that he didn't want to go because he was uneasy about the weather and the captain's experience level but had to because they had bills to pay.

"We were a month behind on everything, and he had to go," the wife testified. "He said, 'I have to go.'" 

Stricter rules for small vessels

The USCG additionally, in its report, recommended stricter regulations, including that a national advisory committee on fishing vessel safety consider rules to mandate licensing and drug and alcohol testing for captains of all fishing boats. The tests and licensing are now required only for captains of large commercial fishing boats.

However, an advisory committee, which reports to the secretary of Homeland Security, ultimately rejected all the recommendations for additional oversight, citing the potential cost for the industry, reports Radio Pacific.

title: Logistics firm takes on global shipping giant over spoiled seafood container
content:
French seafood inspection and consulting firm OFCO Group has accused global shipping companies CMA CGM and Bollore Logistics of various dishonest practices, including concealing the potential health risks to consumers from an improperly stored seafood shipment in Vietnam.

In a case that has lasted just over a year without being resolved, Jean-Charles Diener, OFCO's director, has tried to get CMA CGM -- which bought Bollore in February 2024 for €4.85 billion -- to take responsibility and refund OFCO and the shipment owner for an alleged error in temperature maintenance he claimed was the freight firm's fault, he told Undercurrent News.

Further, he does not believe this incident -- which occurred in April 2023 -- is an isolated event, claiming that he has several other customers who have received shipments they believe were not stored at the correct temperatures while with CMA CGM but who were confident enough to sell the shipments on to the market rather than get into arguments with the shipping giant.

These customers were not willing to speak to Undercurrent about this, as they face far worse trouble for admitting to selling seafood that carries these potential health risks.

It should be noted that none of Undercurrent's sources could confirm any issues with shipments in or out of Vietnam. Diener has decided to go public with his claims alone, confident that he has all the email correspondence with the shipping firms to prove them.

"In the intricate network of international seafood commerce, trust and dependability are of utmost importance," he told Undercurrent in a prepared statement. "Both buyers and sellers rely on the honesty of shipping lines and forwarders to ensure their products reach their destinations in prime condition. However, a recent incident involving two industry giants, CMA CGM and Bollore, raises alarming questions about business ethics and public health safety."

CMA CGM makes the safety of customers’ refrigerated cargo a priority, it told Undercurrent in a response to the allegations, speaking on behalf of both it and Bollore.

CMA CGM in this instance was the shipping line and the owner of the container; the original client hired Bollore as the freight forwarder, who in turn hired the services of CMA CGM. Since early 2024, though, they have been two divisions of the same company.

"We closely monitor temperatures and atmospheric conditions to protect perishable foodstuffs and immediately and systematically inform customers of any anomaly. The group categorically denies false allegations claiming said refrigerated container’s power was deliberately shut down at our request, and that any temperature anomaly was concealed from the customer. We noticed a temperature issue and immediately informed our customer, as per our usual process."

"We are taking this situation very seriously and are conducting thorough investigations in close collaboration with partners involved. This matter being currently pending before French courts, we cannot make further comments and we reserve our rights to disclose the full background of the case before the court."

The incident

On April 22, 2023, a Vietnam-based seafood business delivered a seafood container to CMA CGM in Ho Chi Minh City. OFCO has the documents to show it was in perfect condition and that CMA CGM accepted it without reserve, Diener said. OFCO is acting on behalf of the beneficiary, who retains ownership of the raw materials sent to Vietnam for reprocessing, and is committed to maintaining confidentiality regarding the identities of both the Vietnamese processor and the goods' owner.

Two days later, CMA CGM shipped the container to another Vietnamese port, Vung Tau, where issues were found and OFCO stepped in to prevent the container's export.

"For a month, CMA CGM and Bollore categorically refused to provide the container's temperature data logger, which is essential in such situations to understand what transpired during those two days," Diener told Undercurrent. They then insisted the only data they could send was a "small, illegible graph," he claimed.

When it eventually received the proper data logger, OFCO found that during the 15-hour trip barge trip from Ho Chi Minh to Vung Tau, "the electricity was switched off most of the time."

"We observe a clear pattern in the way the electricity is switched on and off, which seems to prove that the system is automated. During the trip, electricity is only switched on for exactly 14 minutes every exactly two hours," said Diener. 

Part of the data log sent by Bollore to OFCO on May 23, 2023, showing the log while the container was being transported by barge under the responsibility of CMA CGM. Credit: OFCO

"During this month [before the temperature data logger was made available], CMA CGM and Bollore repeatedly attempted to shift the blame for the temperature discrepancy onto the producer, pressuring them into shipping the goods despite the potential health risks, which they actively tried to conceal from the producer and other parties involved," OFCO alleges.

Part of this pressure came via the sheer number of emails sent by Bollore to the seafood producer -- 17 in the first four days after an issue was detected alone, OFCO said.

"They minimized the potential risk created on the goods, downplaying the severity of the situation. The exchange of emails reveals a pattern of manipulation, threats, evidence concealment," Diener alleged. 

He also claimed CMA CGM tried to apply financial pressures first to allow the container to ship and then later to charge OFCO heightened fees to release the container.

OFCO also claims CMA CGM had the data logger a month before sharing it and spent that time trying to pressure the seafood producer and other parties involved into shipping the goods "despite what they already knew for sure would have put consumer safety at risk."

The logger itself shows that CMA CGM extracted the data for the first time on April 25, 2023, at around 10.00 am Vietnamese time, Diener explained.

OFCO worked to arrange the unloading of the container with all involved parties -- including the shipping firms -- present. All agreed that the entire shipment had suffered from temperature variation and that the further away from the center of the container, the more significant it became. OFCO claims this proves that the goods suffered from temperature variation inside the container and after the loading.

One year after the initial survey of the container, CMA CGM and Bollore have yet to issue any refunds to OFCO. Negotiations persist, with attempts to undervalue the compensation owed to the owner of the goods, valued at over $500,000, claimed Diener.

"Although Bollore advised destroying the goods shortly after the survey, they failed to facilitate this process. Currently, they are also reneging on their initial commitment to cover the storage fees in Vietnam, despite having been obligated to do so from the start," he added.

The shippers imposed a "cancellation fee" and upfront payment for electricity, demurrage fees, and other port-related charges, though they offered to waive these costs if the producer signed off on exporting the goods, OFCO said. 

When the producer instead pulled its container out of the port, CMA CGM asked for payment first, and -- OFCO claims -- double the correct amount, only lowering that when this was pointed out.

title: ‘Deadlist Catch’ star Nick Mavar Jr. dies at 59
content:
A longtime star of the US reality television show Deadliest Catch has died.

The Anchorage Daily News reports that Nick Mavar Jr., a deckhand on the fishing vessel Northwestern, died unexpectedly after suffering a medical emergency at the Naknek Boatyard in Alaska's Bristol Bay region on Thursday (June 13) at the age of 59.

Mavar appeared on nearly 100 episodes over 17 seasons of the reality show, which depicts life aboard several fishing vessels participating in Alaska's Bering Sea crab fisheries. He also operated his own commercial salmon fishing vessel in Bristol Bay.

An investigation into Mavar's death is ongoing.

Tributes, however have poured out for him since his death on social media, including from Sig Hansen -- Mavar's longtime captain on Northwestern.

"I have known [N]ick [M]avar for my entire fishing career, he has worked on our family boat for 25 plus years. He was more than a crew member, he was a very good friend and a right hand man," Hansen wrote in a Facebook post Saturday, noting that word of his passing had spread quickly amongst the fishing community.

"This is no surprise because of how well-known and respected he was by the fishing fleet," he said.

title: Untitled
content:
The shrimp season in Argentinian waters began on May 25 with promising initial catches of large sizes, primarily composed of the sought-after L1 size, making up approximately 60% of early hauls, according to industry sources.

However, as more vessels arrived in the fishing zones, the abundance of large shrimp diminished, prompting the fleet to disperse southward in search of better yields.

In the southern waters, the shrimp have been predominantly sized L2, with significantly fewer L1 and sparse L3 sizes. As a result, there have been calls to explore new areas, both further south and north. While these new areas have shown good volume results, the shrimp size remains smaller than desired. 

Consequently, the price of L1 shrimp is expected to remain stable at around $7.60 per kilogram free on board, while L2 and L3 sizes are priced at $6.00/kg and $5.90/kg, respectively, according to sources. The graphs below show the strength of L1 prices compared to L2 and L3, as well as the bearish impact of weakening Ecuadorian farmed shrimp prices on Argentinian wild L3 shrimp prices in recent years.

VIEW GRAPH

"The season started well, with good sizes, better than last season. The prices are good because in Europe, there was not much stock, particularly of the L1 (largest) size. This coincided with the fact that at the beginning, we fished a lot of L1 north of the 41st parallel," an executive with a large fishing firm told Undercurrent News.

The demand for L1 shrimp remains robust, but there is a noticeable lull in the market for other sizes. According to sources, this hesitancy might be partly due to the market waiting to see the outcome of the season's catches and subsequent sales before the peak summer period begins.

Meanwhile, the market for shrimp tails (head-off, shell-on) has seen a recent uptick in activity. After weeks of sluggish movement, transactions are now closing successfully both for blocks intended for reprocessing and retail products, sources said. Prices for C1 tails are hovering around $8.00/kg free on board, but there is still uncertainty regarding the price for C2 tails due to limited market interest.

According to sources, there is also some positive movement in the value-added products sector, particularly for peeled and deveined shrimp. Although prices have dipped slightly due to decreased demand, there appears to be a slow but steady reactivation in this segment.

Looking ahead, while Europe is expected to maintain its consumption levels, sources said uncertainty about demand from China could lead to falling prices. Nevertheless, for now, the shrimp supply remains at acceptable levels.

According to the first source, the future might not be as bright.

"There will be a significant volume of catches, and although Europe will consume its own, I am not so sure that China will do the same, which is why prices will fall. We'll see how far! But the important thing is that Argentina shrimp is currently in acceptable quantities," he said.

US market

Federico Angeleri, commercial director of one of Argentina's largest shrimp fishing and processing companies, Pesquera Veraz, told Undercurrent that, in the US, Argentine wild shrimp prices have risen significantly over the past two years due to various factors like inflation, wage increases, and supply chain costs.

Argentine wild shrimp fishery. Photo: Pesquera Veraz.

"There is so much pressure on the wild shrimp category because of some of the market conditions over the past 12-18 months with farmed shrimp. We are aware of these conditions, so we are looking for ways to support partner programs throughout the US to help promote sales by what we think is still great overall pricing for both the size and value of the product. For us, it is tough because we deal with a wild species and in a country where there really are inflationary pressures on all inputs to production."

Despite the challenges, Angeleri noted some positive trends. "Supermarkets in the US have begun to see better sales in recent weeks, raising our expectations during the peak season as inventory replenishment will be needed."

China forced labor controversy

Last week, the US Department of Homeland Security's Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force announced that Chinese seafood processor Shandong Meijia Group Co. has been added to its "entity list" under the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act.

Two of the subsidiary members of Shandong Meijia -- Rizhao Meijia Aquatic Foodstuff Co. and Rizhao Meijia Keyuan Food Co. -- are active exporters of Argentinian red shrimp to the US and Canada.

The Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA), a trade association representing harvesters and processors of US wild-caught shrimp, requested Shandong's addition to the list in October 2023. SSA said it reviewed bills of lading and ship manifest data to determine that as much as 12 million pounds of Argentinian red shrimp was processed in China and shipped to the US in 2023.

That amount would be nearly a third (32%) of the 31.5m lbs of Argentinian red shrimp imported by the US last year.

Responding to this news, Spain's Worldwide Fishing Company (WOFCO) immediately sought to reassure its clients that its operations remain compliant with international labor standards and that its products are unaffected by the forced labor-related import bans recently imposed by the US.

WOFCO stressed in a statement shared with Undercurrent on June 13 that this latest action does not impact all Chinese plants handling Argentinian red shrimp.

Angeleri said he had noticed increased caution among retailers when selecting products from that origin, likely to avoid such controversy. 

Regarding production transparency, Angeleri claimed to see a "regulatory gap."

"US legislation requires importers to indicate the product's origin, but shrimp seems a little different compared to how headed and gutted fish is handled, for example. It seems for most further processing related to shrimp, it is not technically required to be as transparent with labeling regarding where the shrimp may have been processed after harvest. So, while Argentine shrimp is labeled 'Product of Argentina,' consumers can't know exactly where it comes from," he said.

"This difference is significant for products like [Pesquera Veraz's], which are entirely processed in Argentina, unlike those processed abroad," he added.

Angeleri pointed out he was confident that some Chinese plants comply with all regulations and social standards just as well as any European factory. "Unfortunately, the recent investigations highlight that not all do."

Pesquera Veraz recently sold its Mar del Plata processing plant and the fishing vessel "Centauro 2000" to a local company. "This sale helps us realign our financial commitments and focus on our core business in Patagonia, not only processing shrimp but also expanding our hake operations," Angeleri explained.

The company is also constructing a new vessel to operate in Rawson, aiming to capture approximately 2,000 metric tons of shrimp annually. "This vessel will be a crucial asset, enhancing our capacity to meet market demands," Angeleri said.

title: Calculation error let pair of Danish fishing giants exceed quota limits
content:
An investigation by Danish media site TV2 and Danwatch has found that a pair of fishing giants had been catching well in excess of their correct quota for several years due to a calculation error by the country's fishing ministry.

Danish magnate earns $365m selling pelagic interests at home, abroad

Last year, this excess catch granted to Astrid Fiskeri and Rederiet Isafold, the first and sixth-largest firms by allocated quota, was worth a reported DKK 15 million ($2.1m), said the news site.

During this same period, which stretches back to 2017, other smaller fishers were required to dispose of quotas that they were actually entitled to.

To compound matters, the ministry knew about the mistake for over a year and a half before it was finally rectified. The ministry became aware of the calculation error in September 2021, but current minister Jacob Jensen was only informed in January 2023, with the Danish parliament, the Folketing, finally told five months later, TV2 reports.

Jensen has publicly apologized that it took so long to address the issue.

The Danish Pelagic Producer's Organisation, representing the two firms, claims the quota ceilings continued the same quotas the companies had held for years, so were never questioned.

title: Australia expects China to lift lobster export ban soon after Premier’s visit
content:
Australia's trade minister Don Farrel anticipates the imminent lifting of China's ban on live lobster imports from Australia, coinciding with Chinese Premier Li Qiang's visit to the country, reports AP News. 

China imposed the ban, along with other trade barriers on Australian products like beef, barley, coal, wood, and wine, in 2020 after Australia called for investigations in China into the COVID-19 pandemic. The ban cost exporters around AUD 20 billion ($13bn) annually.

Farrell stated that Li's visit, the first by a Chinese premier to Australia in seven years, would likely see the removal of the final trade barrier on lobsters.

"I think there's both the willingness on our part and the part of the Chinese government to remove all of the impediments in our relationship," Farrell said. "I'd be very confident that the visit will result in a very successful outcome for lobster producers."

title: Not all Chinese plants processing Argentinian shrimp on US ban list, large supplier WOFCO stresses
content:
Spain's Worldwide Fishing Company (WOFCO) has sought to reassure its clients this week that their operations remain compliant with international labor standards and their products are unaffected by the forced labor-related import bans recently expanded upon by the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

"We firmly believe in guaranteeing the social, economic and environmental sustainability of our activity," the company asserted in a statement shared with Undercurrent News on Thursday (June 13).

WOFCO was responding to the announcement made Tuesday (June 11) by DHS' Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force (FLETF) that it had added Shandong Meijia Group Co. Ltd. (also known as Rizhao Meijia Group), another big Chinese seafood processor, to the "entity list" maintained under the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA), as reported by Undercurrent News. 

Two of the subsidiary members of Shandong Meijia — Rizhao Meijia Aquatic Foodstuff Co. and Rizhao Meijia Keyuan Food Co. — are active exporters of Argentinian red shrimp to the US and Canada.

US expands ban on Chinese seafood over forced labor concerns, includes Argentinian red shrimp

The Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA), a trade association representing harvesters and processors of US wild-caught shrimp, had brought the request to DHS for Shandong's addition to the list in October 2023. SSA said it reviewed bills of lading and ship manifest data to determine as much as 12 million lbs of Argentinian red shrimp was processed in China and shipped to the US in 2023.

That amount would be nearly a third (32%) of the 31.5m lbs of Argentinian red shrimp imported by the US last year. 

DHS' actions follow a report by the independent journalism outfit, The Outlaw Ocean Project, published in The New Yorker in 2023, that found Chinese seafood plants using workers from the Muslim Uyghur minority who were allegedly forcibly displaced from their home province, Xinjiang, to produce value-added products which were then sold to significant customers in Europe and North America.

Independent investigations

But it is important to note that not all Chinese plants handling Argentinian red shrimp are impacted by this latest action, WOFCO stressed in a statement shared with Undercurrent on Thursday (June 13).

WOFCO is a major supplier of Argentinian red shrimp and uses Chinese plants to process some of its product, which is heavily exported to the US. The company also processes Argentinian red shrimp in Argentina and Peru, and soon will be processing in Paraguay, where it is building a plant, as reported by Undercurrent.

In Oct. 2022, WOFCO acquired 45% of Continental Armadores de Pesca, also known as Conarpesa, a major Argentinian shrimp fishing firm. According to the firms, the purchase of the minority stake in the company was the fruit of a longtime partnership, as WOFCO was one of the main buyers of Conarpesa's shrimp for years. 

Some of Wofco's shrimp products. Photo: Undercurrent News.

Conarpesa operates a fleet of over 20 outrigger, coastal and deep-sea fishing vessels and has four processing plants in Patagonia.

WOFCO asserted that none of its processing plants in China employ Uyghur workers. It emphasized its strong stance against forced labor and other human rights violations, saying that it maintains standards for itself and its suppliers.

"At WOFCO, as in any responsible company, we are clearly positioned against any type of forced labor or any other violation of fundamental human rights, so we apply and respect all the international regulations applicable in this matter, likewise we get involved to that our suppliers/partners share and comply with these same principles," the company said in its statement.

The company also underscored the importance of independent investigations to shed light on forced labor issues within global seafood supply chains, advocating for transparency and ethical practices. WOFCO said it utilizes social certifications, like SMETA (Sedex Members Ethical Trade Audit), to ensure human rights are upheld among its suppliers. 

"At WOFCO we are always open to collaborating honestly and transparently with other actors in global product supply chains of the sea, to jointly eradicate any type of violation and contribute to discourage bad practices that put both the sector as a whole and our company and our clients," the company concluded in its statement.

title: US imports of Ecuador shrimp cut in half by CVD rate scare
content:
The initial announcement by the US Department of Commerce (DOC) regarding preliminary countervailing duty (CVD) rates put a big hurt on US imports of Ecuadorian shrimp, the latest update of seafood trade data by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) shows.

The US imported just 9,881 metric tons of frozen warmwater shrimp from Ecuador in April 2024, less than half (45%) the 21,754t imported the month before. It was the worst month for Ecuadorian shrimp exports to the US since February 2021, illustrates a chart created by UCN's trade portal.

Recall that DOC told everyone involved in or affected by the CVD investigation surrounding Ecuadorian shrimp, on March 26, that importers of shrimp from Industrial Pesquera Santa Priscilla, Ecuador's largest producer, would have to pay a preliminary rate of 13.41%, as reported by Undercurrent News. The amount would have to be provided in upfront cash deposits, DOC declared.

Importers of shrimp from Sociedad Nacional de Galapagos, known as Songa, were informed that they would have to pay a preliminary 1.69% rate and importers of all other Ecuadorian shrimp would have to pay 7.55% in upfront deposits.

On April 19, DOC informed all parties that it made a mistake in its calculations and was reducing Santa Priscila's preliminary CVD rate to 2.89% while maintaining Songa at 1.69%. It declared that the Songa rate was de minimus and therefore not required upfront.

Importers of all other Ecuador shrimp are now required to pay an upfront fee of 2.89%. 

Regardless of the subsequent CVD rate peel back, significant damage was done, NOAA's data shows. 

Of course, the cutback looks more extreme because the March 2024 volume represented a big spike in US imports of Ecuadorian shrimp, likely in anticipation of the coming CVD rate increase, as reported by Undercurrent. The volume of Ecuador shrimp imported by the US in April 2024 represented a 20% decrease from the 12,307t imported in April 2023.

The total value of Ecuador shrimp imported by the US in April 2024 was $67.5 million, 32% less than the $98.7m value of shrimp imported in April 2023 and 54% less than the $148.1m value of shrimp imported in March 2024.  

The average price paid in the US for Ecuador shrimp in April 2024 was $3.24 per pound, not quite 1% less than the average $3.22/lb paid in April 2023 and a penny more than the average $3.19/lb paid in March 2024.

Next two months to tell more of the story

But don't cry too much for Ecuador. The nation's frozen shrimp exports reached a record high in April 2024, as reported earlier by Undercurrent, defying expectations after three consecutive months of year-on-year declines between January and March, according to the latest data from the country's national chamber of aquaculture, or CNA.

The country exported 111,684t of frozen shrimp worth $539 million in April, representing a 19% increase in volume and a 4% rise in value compared to the same month last year.

China remained Ecuador's top shrimp trade partner for the month, purchasing over 62,000t of shrimp valued at $278m. However, this represented a 10% decline in value and a 16% drop in average unit price compared to April 2023, despite a 6% increase in volume.

The US, Ecuador's second-largest market, was sent a 28% increase in volume and a 19% boost in value year-on-year, with 18,391t of frozen shrimp exported at a value of $107m. 

Credit: Larisa Blinova / Shutterstock

Why might Ecuador shrimp export numbers not match US import numbers? The most likely answer is that it takes four to six weeks to transport shrimp from Ecuador to the US, meaning bigger numbers could be showing up in the US in May, in conjunction with the reduction in CVD rates.

Also, on May 23, DOC announced its preliminary antidumping duties, giving Santa Priscila a low 1.54% rate while slamming Songa and all other Ecuadoran producers with a 10.58% rate, as Undercurrent reported.

Combined, importers of Santa Priscilla shrimp are looking at a 2.89% rate going forward, while importers of shrimp from Songa must pay a combined 10.58% rate and importers of all other Ecuadorian shrimp must pay a combined rate of 13.47%. 

As a result, NOAA's June shrimp import data could be equally telling. 

Shrimp prices up 4% from March overall

The massive decline of US imports of Ecuador shrimp in April 2024 was a big factor in the US' overall combined drop in shrimp import volumes during the month. The US imported a combined 50,901t worth $397.6m, 10% less volume and 14% less value than the 56,267t worth $461.4m imported in April 2024, according to NOAA.

It was 20% less volume and 17% less value than the combined 63,491t worth $481.8m imported one month before, in March 2024.

The average overall price of US imported shrimp was $3.70/lb in April, 4% less than the average $3.85/lb seen in April 2023 but 4% more than the average $3.57/lb seen in March 2024, as illustrated in the UCN trade portal chart below.

Through the first four months of 2024, the US is behind its 2023 pace. It imported 233,633t worth $1.8 billion of shrimp, 2% less volume and 8% less value than the 237,323t worth $2.0bn in the first four months of last year.

India 5% ahead of 2023 pace

India, the US' leading source of shrimp, sent it 21,168t worth $152.6m in April 2024, 1% less volume and 9% less value than in April 2023. However, India remains ahead of its 2023 pace, at least as far as volume goes, sending the US 88,310t worth $648.0m during the first four months of 2024, 5% more volume and 5% less value than the same period in 2023.

The average price paid in April 2024 for Indian shrimp in the US was $3.46/lb, 7% less than the $3.72/lb seen in April 2023 but 1% more than the $3.41/lb paid in March 2024, as shown in the UCN trade portal chart below.

Recall that DOC hit Indian producers Devi Sea Foods Limited and Sandhya Aqua Exports with preliminary CVD rates of 4.72% and 3.89%, respectively while charging 4.36% for importers of shrimp from other Indian shrimp producers.

Indonesia didn't help itself

Ecuador's weak April pushed Indonesia into the position of the US' second-largest source of shrimp during the month, but it did little to help itself. Indonesia sent the US 10,390t of shrimp worth $78.5m in April 2024, 23% less volume and 15% less value.

Indonesia is now pretty far off its 2023 pace, having sent the US 41,306t of shrimp worth $307.9m during the first four months of the year, 18% less volume and 25% less value than the first four months of 2023.

The average price paid for Indonesian shrimp in the US in April 2024 was $3.58/lb, 5% less than the $3.77/lb rate seen in April 2023 and 1% more than the $3.54/lb seen in March 2024.

Indonesia's First Marine Seafoods and all other shrimp producers were hit with 6.3% preliminary CVD rates by DOC. Bahari Makmur Sejati was given only a de minimus 0.39% CVD rate. 

Vietnam 19% ahead of 2023 volume pace

Vietnam, the US' fourth-largest shrimp source nation, gained some ground in April, sending the US 4,071t of shrimp worth $39.7m during the month, 11% more volume and less than 1% more value than in April 2023. 

During the first four months of 2024, Vietnam sent the US 15,268t worth $150.2m, 19% more volume and 9% more value than the same period in 2023. 

The average price paid for Vietnamese shrimp in April 2024 was $4.59/lb, 8% less than the $5.01/lb average seen in April 2023 and 4% less than the $4.80/lb average seen in March 2024.

title: Indonesian activist cleared in hate speech case over illegal shrimp farms criticism
content:
An Indonesian court has overturned the sentence of environmental activist Daniel Frits Maurits Tangkilisan, convicted on hate speech charges for highlighting the damage caused by illegal shrimp farms in Karimunjawa National Park, reports The Good Men Project. 

The Semarang High Court's ruling on May 21 quashed the April 4 sentence by the Jepara District Court, which found Frits' Facebook posts constituted hate speech and caused public unrest.

The judges noted Frits was defending the right to a healthy environment protected by Indonesia's Constitution.

Frits was one of four activists charged under the 2008 law on online speech. The other three activists, Hasanuddin, Datang Abdul Rohim, and Sumarto Rofi'un -- who were reported to local police in November 2023 for posting a video opposing the illegal shrimp farms -- are still under investigation for a 2019 video opposing illegal shrimp farms.

These farms have proliferated in Karimunjawa -- a protected marine area spanning 1,100 square kilometers known for its coral reefs and diverse marine life -- despite regulations banning them.

Recent revisions to the 2008 law aim to tighten defamation requirements, but advocates call for further review to protect freedom of expression. From 2019 to 2022, Amnesty International documented 328 incidents of assaults on human rights advocates in Indonesia, including environmental activists.

title: Daily recap: Trident, Silver Bay announce False Pass plant deal; AquaBounty names new CEO
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Friday, June 7:

Trident, Silver Bay announce deal for False Pass plant

US seafood giants Trident Seafoods and Silver Bay Seafoods have reached a deal on the former's plant in False Pass, Alaska.

AquaBounty names Melbourne as CEO, replaces Wulf

AquaBounty Technologies' Sylvia Wulf announced that the land-based grower of the first genetically engineered salmon has named David F. Melbourne, Jr., as its new CEO, replacing her, though she will remain as the non-executive chair of the board of directors.

Strong Peruvian anchovy catches stabilize fishmeal prices in China

Strong catches of Peruvian anchovy have stabilized market prices of fishmeal in China, as shipments of the marine ingredient begin to flow in large volumes to the country.

US regulator: Cooke menhaden supplier 'in compliance' with foreign ownership law

Although Cooke might be dealing with a civil lawsuit that accuses it of violating foreign ownership rules in the US' massive menhaden fisheries, the US Maritime Administration -- the chief regulator charged with enforcing such rules -- told Undercurrent News that it found no evidence of wrongdoing in a 2020 investigation.

Blue economy financing grows but still falls short, experts say

Funding for the "blue economy" is growing quickly but still falls short of what is needed to transition to more sustainable models, according to experts at a recent conference in London, UK.

Norwegian, Chilean, Scots salmon prices all fall as summer slump continues

Spot prices for farmed Norwegian salmon are expected to drop by a further NOK 10/kg in week 24 (June 10-16), with Scottish and Chilean prices also following steep downward trajectories.

title: US regulator: Cooke menhaden supplier ‘in compliance’ with foreign ownership law
content:
Cooke might be dealing with a civil lawsuit that accuses it of violating foreign ownership rules in the US' massive menhaden fisheries, but the US Maritime Administration (MARAD) -- the chief regulator charged with enforcing such rules -- tells Undercurrent News that it found no evidence of wrongdoing in a 2020 investigation. 

"MARAD reviewed documentation which would demonstrate whether a non-citizen was exerting impermissible control over Alpha Vessel Co.," Thomas Johnson, an agency spokesperson, wrote in an email. "MARAD's review of the documentation found it to be satisfactory and in compliance with fishery endorsement requirements." 

A lawsuit filed in the US District of New York for the Southern District by plaintiffs W. Benson Chiles and Chris Manthey in June 2021, but not unsealed until April 23, 2024, alleges that Cooke, its menhaden-processing subsidiary Omega Protein and several affiliates are operating in violation of the American Fisheries Act (AFA), as reported by Undercurrent. The 1998 law mandates that non-US citizens can not have "effective control" over vessels that fish in US waters.

However, that wasn't the first move made by the two litigants against Cooke.

A menhaden catching vessel. Photograph courtesy of Omega Protein.

Johnson said Chiles and Murphy filed a complaint with the agency on Dec. 9, 2020, alleging that Alpha Vessel Co., a company also known as Ocean Harvesters, was flouting provisions in AFA that prohibit non-US citizens from exercising "impermissible control" over US fishing vessels.

If a corporation wants its vessels to be endorsed to fish in US waters, the AFA requires it to file annual affidavits that ask for the citizenship details of its shareholders and to guarantee that control of the US corporation doesn't actually rest in the hands of foreigners. 

It was amidst MARAD's investigation of their complaint that Chiles and Manthey filed their 2021 suit against Alpha Vessel Co., Seth Dunlop, Glenn Cooke, his eponymous seafood company, and several others. The civil lawsuit was filed on behalf of the US government as a "whistleblower" action under the False Claims Act, alleging that the defendants' "figurehead fraud" cost the US government "hundreds of millions of dollars".

In April, the US government declined to join Chiles' and Manthey's litigation as an intervenor, although the Department of Justice (DOJ) said it reserved the chance to do so at a later date, court filings indicate.

The family connection

The case brought against Cooke dates back to 2017 when the Canadian company spent $500 million to acquire then publicly-traded Omega Protein, in Reedville, Virginia.

Omega owned and operated a fleet of 38 vessels. However, as part of a corporate reorganization, the vessels were moved under the umbrella of Ocean Fleet Services, the parent of Alpha Vessel Co., which does business under the name Ocean Harvesters.

Alpha Vessel is 80%-owned by Seth Dunlop, Glenn Cooke's nephew. He is described in the whistleblower lawsuit as a US citizen and Canadian resident as well as Ocean Fleet's chief executive officer, chairman and director.

US gov’t sticks to sidelines in ‘figurehead fraud’ lawsuit against Cooke, Omega Protein

In addition to his relation to the CEO, the suit alleges that Dunlop is a longtime employee of the Cooke group and has been a vice president for at least four Cooke subsidiaries. Ocean Fleet's corporate secretary is Seth Dunlop's father, Gregory, Glenn Cooke's brother-in-law, according to the complaint. 

Alpha Vessel co-issued $30m worth of notes alongside Cooke subsidiary Cooke Omega Investments at the time of the reorganization, some $28.75m of which -- along with a $1m investment from Dunlop -- were used to purchase the vessels, according to the lawsuit.

Plaintiffs Chiles and Manthey, are described respectively in the claim as a "professional investigator and researcher" and a participant in the "fisheries management industry." 

Chiles' LinkedIn account describes him as a "strategic consultant for conservation organizations" who has worked with advocacy groups such as Earthjustice and the Environmental Defense Fund in the past. Manthey's profile describes a career with over three decades of experience in investigations and research.

'We don't see how it's relevant'

When contacted by Undercurrent, plaintiff attorney Brendon DeMay said that neither MARAD's finding nor the DOJ's decision to not join the lawsuit are likely to harm the litigation's chances of success. 

"We don't see how it's relevant," he said. 

DeMay asserted that MARAD's investigations failed to see through "misrepresentations" made by AlphaVesselCo/Ocean Harvesters about the relationship between Dunlop and Cooke. Additionally, the DOJ has the authority to run its own investigation, he added. 

He said that he believes that the DOJ chose not to join his litigation so far simply because, while the government has seen many successful False Claims Act cases in the defense and medical sectors, suits against this type of "figurehead fraud," involving the alleged skirting of foreign ownership restrictions, are "novel".  

However, the lawyer added that he believes several companies in the seafood sector are using US citizens as nominee vessel owners even though foreign interests have effective control. That contravenes the AFA rules, DeMay said.

Atlantic menhaden

Cooke spokesman Joel Richardson declined to comment for this story, though the company and Ocean Harvesters, through its spokesperson, Ben Landry, have called the plaintiffs' claims "meritless."

"Ocean Harvesters continues to strongly defend itself against the inaccurate allegations of wrongdoing and maintains that the recently filed lawsuit is meritless. We look forward to setting the record straight in court," Landry said in a statement to Undercurrent.

title: Cleanup started at Royal Greenland’s fire-damaged Canadian plant
content:
Two months after fire caused major damage at Royal Greenland's Canadian factory, Fruits de mer 'Est du Quebec, cleanup of the site has started, reports Radio Canada, CBC's news service in the Canadian province of Quebec.

As earlier reported by Undercurrent News, the factory in Mantane, a small town 350 kilometers northeast of Quebec City, was destroyed by fire on March 29. The fire came just two weeks after the company announced it was shutting down the factory, citing recent cuts to the northern shrimp quota in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, a labor shortage and low market prices for seafood among the reasons for the decision.

The cause of the fire is still not known. The investigation was turned over to the major crimes unit of the Quebec provincial police.

Meanwhile, the community is hopeful that another seafood company might be interested in purchasing the property, which is located directly on the wharf at the Matane port.

The factory in Matane, Quebec, has been owned by Royal Greenland since 2005. Photo from Les Fruits de Mer de l'Est du Quebec-Royal Greenland Facebook page

Last year Royal Greenland won approval from the Quebec government to buy lobsters from Quebec harvesters. Until then the company, which had invested CAD 4 million ($2.9m) to add a new lobster processing line to the Matane factory, was only permitted to buy lobsters from the Maritime provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island.

With that approval, Royal Greenland said it could increase its lobster production from 600,000 pounds to over a million lbs annually.

The plant in Mantane, which was created in 1967, used to process shrimp. With the decline of shrimp stocks in the region, however, the factory shifted to processing snow crab, adding the lobster processing line in 2022. Royal Greenland bought the facility in 2005.

title: Filipino crew abandoned in US finally secure unpaid wages
content:
Nearly a dozen Filipino crew members, employed by McAdam's Fish, a supplier of sushi-grade Albacore tuna, have found themselves in a wage dispute and unable to step on US soil due to visa restrictions, reports The Associated Press. 

One of the Filipino fishermen affected, Reyner Dagalae, spent three months confined to a tuna ship in Westport, Washington. Yet his pay arrived sporadically -- $200 one month, nothing the next. 

By Christmas, pay stubs shared by Dagalea and his employer, a supplier of sushi-grade Albacore tuna, revealed he and five other crew members were paid less than half of their promised wages, amounting to $8 per day.

Despite the fishermen's arduous efforts, the fleet of four US-flagged vessels they worked on became the first in 15 years to be listed as abandoned by the United Nations.

According to the AP, McAdam's Fish acknowledged the payment delays, attributing them to Pescadores International, a recruitment agency from the Philippines, which the company claimed was slow to disburse the wages it paid in advance.

Pescadores' owner, Ricardo De Joya, provided no explanation for the delays but asserted that past earnings had far exceeded the minimum wage.

The situation drew the attention of US Homeland Security Investigations, the principal investigative arm of the US Department of Homeland Security, and union advocates from the International Transport Workers' Federation.

Following their intervention, Pescadores paid each of the complaining fishermen approximately $4,000, covering much of their owed wages. Federal authorities also granted the fishermen temporary immigration status, enabling them to move to a rental house in Seattle, the northernmost major city in the US.

title: Untitled
content:
A "very slow" and stable market for Vietnamese pangasius is seen as a step up from a tough 2023 and start to 2024 by Undercurrent News sources.

"The market is very slow, and China is pushing the price down, but only very slowly," Jean-Charles Diener, director of Vietnamese shipment inspection and consulting firm OFCO Group, told Undercurrent. 

Vietnamese pangasius fingerling price slide indicates lack of farmer interest

"It's not like a few months ago, before [the Vietnamese holiday] Tet [Feb. 10], when prices were going down; now we are used to this situation, people accept it, it is slow but stable."

The market has gone from being overstocked to having a good balance, he said.

"Before, we had overstock, and the market collapsed. Now the market is very slow -- demand and supply are not very strong, so it matches. Farmers reduced their pond stocking, but demand is low, so there's no shortage for the market."

"Of course, if China starts to buy like crazy, we'll have a lack of product, but I don't see that coming. The market being slow is not a negative, I think -- now the farmers are not so scared, and the factories are not so scared. But there is no strong demand coming in any market."

A "clear market price" is making it more comfortable for buyers to make purchases compared with a few months ago, he said, adding that price was roughly $2.10 per kilogram for 100% net weight "regular fillet" shipped out of Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam.

"It's cheap -- buyers feel the price can't go down too much because there's not enough supply for the price to collapse. But they also don't think that the price will increase crazy, so it's quite stable."

Thuy Trang Le, sales manager with trading firm Siam Canadian's Vietnam office, confirmed the market had been "quiet and stable" for a while, putting prices at $2.70/kg for 100% net weight fillets meeting EU requirements for import.

That's been the price level for some time, according to sources, with EU demand having never really recovered from the price spike during the COVID-19 pandemic.
