She said raw material prices had been stable since week 14 at around VND 28,500-VND 29,000/kg due to the quiet market, though "the price of the smallest sizes, four-ounce [fillets], are higher than other sizes as farmers don't want to sell, they want to stock the fish to earn better prices."

That's not quite shown in the farm-gate prices provided to Undercurrent by a Ho Chi Minh-based consultancy, as shown below, though it does show the smaller sizes being on a par with larger fish until quite recently.

"At the time being, hot weather, drought and saltwater intrusion due to El Nino are serious, farmers are worried the fish will die, and they don’t want to start a crop," Trang added. "This weather will cause a shortage of raw material in August and September, which is the main time for year-end shipments and usually pushes prices higher."

As mentioned above, Diener was only worried about a real shortage of raw material if demand suddenly picks up -- a sentiment that was echoed by Undercurrent's consultant and Nguyen Ngo Vi Tam, CEO of Vietnam's largest pangasius exporter Vinh Hoan Corporation.

"Early this year, raw material prices went up, and then the market turned out to be slow and steady," noted Tam. "The raw material price in the market was then adjusted but did not plummet. It has been steady, slightly up and down just a bit in the last four-to-six weeks and at a quite healthy and normal level for farmers."

This has been down to a steady raw material supply, not too high, and some improvement in export markets, especially the US and China, she said.

"Raw material supply has not been too much and has been quite under control in terms of both volume and price; we anticipate that it could cause a more serious shortage if the fillet markets get stronger and stronger over the months," she said, adding that Vinh Hoan does expect to see a continued recovery from key export markets over the next three months.

The consultant source accepted that raw material supply could run a little short come September, but also felt that was a fairly normal occurrence for the time of year.

"In February, March, the fingerling price usually runs higher, so farmers quite often hold off stocking for the first quarter of the year," he said. "A couple of months later, that tends to go back to normal again, and maybe you get an oversupply again because they started stocking again when the fingerling price came down."

This source, like Trang, noted the worse weather conditions than usual; "it's been odd for a few months, and only in the last few days has it started raining," he said on May 23. 

"That's pushed the season back a little bit, it's been incredibly hot, so there's a shortage of water. Combine that with the [farm-gate] prices, and nobody's really been stocking. That's where the talk of a shortage comes from, I think, but it's not too unusual."

Demand still on the upturn?

He and Vinh Hoan's Tam both said they expect to see the export markets continue to pick up as 2024 progresses, given a nudge by the lack of Russian fish now making its way to the US and European markets (or at higher duties) and the resulting high prices for cod and haddock.

As reported by Undercurrent, Vietnamese customs data showed another decent month in April in terms of small signs of demand recovery, with export volumes of 77,325 metric tons up 21% month-on-month and 37% year-on-year.

Prices to China are down at their lowest in roughly three years, but for the US market, they have been climbing gently since December 2023.

The initial data for May 2024 suggests that demand continued to improve a little, he added; "it's not massively increased, but it's certainly not declining."

Vietnam's Association of Seafood Exporters and Producers, or VASEP, has welcomed the news that the US is beginning to talk about recognizing Vietnam as a market economy. It believes this could be a great advantage for Vietnamese businesses, especially in administrative reviews of anti-dumping taxes on shrimp and pangasius and anti-subsidy investigations. In addition, other barriers and regulations may also be reviewed in a more relaxed and favorable manner.

While Vietnam's pangasius sales to the EU were down 7% y-o-y at some $70 million in the first five months of 2024, VASEP believes Vietnamese firms can capitalize on the EU-Vietnam Free Trade Agreement to take advantage of the continued economic difficulties there.

Pangasius data for April 2024

VASEP forecasts that pangasius exports can climb 10% in Q3 with fuel and logistics costs cooling, though that may have been before freight rates shot back up late in May.

On May 26, the Financial Times reported that the cost of international shipping has soared as businesses prepare to ship goods for the festive season far earlier than usual, "in a sign of the far-reaching effects of disruption from attacks in the Red Sea."

The average cost of shipping a 40-foot container between the Far East and northern Europe at short notice, the figure that is most sensitive to market prices, hit $4,343 late in May, roughly three times higher than the same time in 2023, it said.

Melissa Woodhouse, vice president of US importer Western Edge Seafood, told Undercurrent that "although shipping has become more prompt recently, the steady rise in vessel costs is likely to drive prices even higher from Q3 2024 through early Q1 2025."

She said the US had seen the supply of raw materials for 3-5oz and 5-7oz fillets become constrained, leading to a "7-8% increase in prices over the past month."

"It seems raw material supply for smaller sizes should rebound by Q4," she added.

title: Inuit shrimp harvesters in Canada cry foul over quota shares
content:
A group of fishermen from Nunatsiavut, an Inuit regional government in the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador, is threatening to take legal action if they don't get access to the communal shrimp quota this season, reports Newfoundland's daily newspaper, The Telegram.

Nunatsiavut has a quota allocation in shrimp fishing areas 4 and 5 by virtue of the 2007 Labrador Inuit Land Claims Agreement. Two other land claims agreements — the 1993 Nunavut agreement and the 2005 Nunavik Inuit agreement — also designate a share of the overall shrimp quota to Inuit harvesters in Labrador and Quebec.

In 2023, the total allowable catch (TAC) in SFA 4 was 12,944 metric tons, and the TAC in SFA 5 was 14,200t. Nunatsiavut's share is 10% of the TAC in SFA 4 and 9.9% in SFA 5, with the quota shared among inshore harvesters and offshore fleets.

However, seven inshore harvesters say a Nunatsiavut government policy adopted in 2021 is driving them out of the fishery. The tiered system favors harvesters who own their own fishing vessel, putting them at the top of the priority list for a share of the quota assigned to Nunatsiavut, while those who lease boats are at the bottom.

One harvester who is out of luck is Darryl Flowers, who has had access to a share of the communal grant for the past eight years. Last year, he and his crew had 300,000 pounds to catch. This year, he said, he could end up with nothing because he leases a fishing boat.

Meanwhile, the harvesters say the Nunatsivut government allocated 43% of its quota to an Inuit designate to be caught by an offshore factory-freezer trawler.

The seven harvesters also say they have Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) documentation from 2003 that dictates that the shrimp quota is to be assigned specifically to inshore fishermen. They also raise conflict of interest questions because the offshore quota was reportedly given to a former Nunatsiavut government minister who was once in charge of the fisheries portfolio and who is related to the current minister responsible for lands and natural resources.

The inshore harvesters said Monday (June 3) that they have hired a lawyer and sent a written request asking for their shrimp allocations to be reinstated. 

DFO reportedly told The Telegram that the share of the quota under communal licenses is within the purview of the license holder, and the Nunatsiavut government has the authority to decide who it wants to designate to fish its northern shrimp allocations.

"DFO will not be conducting investigations into how these allocations are being distributed by the license holder," the department stated.

title: Russian group claims Norebo vessel denied entry to Dutch port over ‘espionage’ fears
content:
A Russian fishery sector body has declared the country faces new restrictions on supplying fish to Europe after a Norebo Holding vessel was turned away from landing at two ports in the Netherlands, reports RBC.

On May 16, a vessel belonging to Arctic Shipping, part of Norebo, had its entry to the Dutch port of Eemshaven canceled, despite having all the necessary paperwork, according to Russia's Association of Shipowners of the Fishing Fleet (ASRF).

It tried to land instead to Velsen in the Netherlands or in Germany, but also to no avail.

The ASRF has blamed the release of an investigation by Dutch journalism platform Pointer, which claimed to outline Russian efforts to use fishing vessels for espionage.

On May 14, shortly after the publication of the investigation, Dutch defense minister Kajsa Ollongren made it clear to the country's House of Representatives that Russian fishing vessels were no longer welcome in Eemshaven because they might be involved in espionage activities, RBC wrote.

"The restrictions affected the entry of vessels flying the Russian flag; there are no restrictions on the supply of fish products," Norebo emphasized, adding that its fish products "remain in demand in the EU countries and beyond."

title: Viciunai under investigation for exporting sanctioned goods to Russia
content:
Lithuanian law enforcement authorities are investigating the potential export of sanctioned goods to Russia by a company owned by the Viciunai Group, reports LRT. 

Four individuals have been identified as suspects in the case.

"The investigation is ongoing, and all necessary pre-trial investigative actions are being performed," said the prosecutor general's office, without disclosing whether the suspects include shareholders or senior executives of the group. 

The probe was initiated on April 11 following allegations that Plunges Kooperatine Prekyba, a subsidiary of the firm, had exported sanctioned goods to Russia.

According to LRT, Plunges Kooperatine Prekyba has shipped dual-use goods to Russia at least 11 times since the onset of the war in Ukraine. These shipments reportedly included high-priority battlefield items crucial for arms production, such as bearings used in the manufacture of Russian tanks.

The recipient of these shipments was Viciunai-Rus, the group's factory in Sovetsk, Russia, which was sold in April. The business has admitted to shipping them but said it had no idea they could be used in a war effort.

title: Editor’s choice: Fallout as Red Lobster files for bankruptcy; Live from Thailand, London
content:
EMEA editor Neil Ramsden brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week  

Our most-read story last week was our live blog from the Infofish World Tuna Trade Conference & Exhibition, held in Bangkok, Thailand. Two reporters covered the three-day event in-depth, and you can catch up with the blog here.

We were also live for two days in London, UK for the Blue Food Innovation Summit; you can recap that blog here.

Second was our deep dive into the bankruptcy filing by US restaurant giant Red Lobster, which revealed that Performance Food Group, one of the US' largest foodservice distribution companies, is the unsecured creditor with the most to lose from the process. The Orlando, Florida-based chain, mostly owned by Thai Union Group, filed on May 20 for Chapter 11 protection and laid much of the blame for its spiral on Thai Union and former CEO Paul Kenny.

Also last week, US importers of frozen warmwater shrimp from Sociedad Nacional de Galapagos (Songa) found out they will be required to pay a preliminary dumping rate of 10.58%, an amount that will be required as an upfront cash deposit. Industrial Pesquera Santa Priscila, the US' largest source of shrimp from Ecuador, was described as the big winner by US buyers.

title: Blumar faces heavy sanctions for salmon overproduction in protected Chilean waters
content:
Chile's superintendence of the environment, or the SMA, has initiated a sanctioning process against salmon farmer Blumar due to alleged significant overproduction at its CES Cordova 1 site.

This facility is located within the Kawesqar national reserve in the Magallanes and Chilean Antarctic region. Overproduction allegedly occurred during the 2019-2021 production cycle, leading to potentially severe penalties for the firm. 

Blumar is authorized to produce a maximum of 5,875.2 metric tons of salmon in the facility through 24 cages spread over an area of 10.01 hectares.

However, in 2023, Chile's national fisheries and aquaculture service, Sernapesca, lodged complaints against Blumar for exceeding these limits. Subsequent investigations by the SMA allegedly showed that the firm harvested around 6,337t of salmon from the site and experienced 202.6t of mortalities for a combined total "production" of 6,540t. 

Chile’s supreme court upholds Sernapesca appeals, fines two salmon firms in full

That figure surpasses the authorized limit by 665t, marking an 11% overproduction, according to the SMA. The superintendence has categorized this as a "severe infringement," as the exceeded production took place without any environmental permission and within a state-protected wilderness area.

"Such violations are considered severe and could result in the revocation of the environmental qualification resolution, closure of the facility, or fines reaching up to 5,000 annual tax units (UTA)," it said in a statement. 

In Chilean pesos, that fine could go up to CLP 3.9bn ($4.37m). 

Marie Claude Plumer, superintendent of the environment, in a statement underscored the significance of regulatory compliance in protected areas.

"The oversight of the aquaculture sector has been substantially strengthened in recent years through various actions and strategies. This enhanced scrutiny has led to a better understanding of the industry's activities and greater certainty in verifying compliance with environmental obligations," Plumer said.

Blumar sees revenue, profit dip in Q4 amidst aquaculture struggles

"The case of CES Cordova 1 is particularly critical due to its location in a protected area, which holds key conditions for ecological balance. Compliance with environmental regulations and authorized limits is imperative for all operators to maintain the integrity of these ecosystems," she added.

In response to the SMA's findings, Blumar has been given 10 business days, starting on May 24, to submit a compliance program and 15 business days to present its defenses.

Blumar did not respond to a request for comment from Undercurrent News in time for this publication.

title: MarinTrust updates standard for ‘world that has changed’
content:
It's been seven years since MarinTrust made major changes to its certification program for marine ingredients. In that time "the world has moved on a lot," according to Libby Woodhatch, executive chair of the London, UK-based organization.

Its updated standard -- called simply 'Version 3' -- is the organization's attempt to keep pace, as well as "future-proof" the standard for whatever lies ahead.

"The reception has been very good," Woodhatch told Undercurrent News during a conference for IFFO members in Miami, Florida, last month. "And the reason why is that we've involved the industry all the way along."

IFFO Miami: Initial Peruvian landings, yields offer fish oil price relief

MarinTrust is the world's most widely used standard for marine ingredients, the vast majority of which go into aquafeed used to produce farmed fish, like shrimp and salmon. Last year, some 50% of the world's fishmeal and fish oil production, the two biggest products produced by the sector, were certified as meeting the standard, which means "responsibly sourced," according to MarinTrust.

"We've grown pretty fast since we started in 2010. But we are still a pretty small organization -- small but nimble," Woodhatch said. Today the organization employs nine full-time staff, all based in London.

Woodhatch explained that the new criteria in Version 3 address evolving expectations around issues like social responsibility and traceability, particularly as new technologies come to the fore.

"When MarinTrust first reviewed the standard with its multi-stakeholder Governance Committee in 2020, a key decision was whether Version 3 would represent a simple revision or more of a step-change," explained Woodhatch, who presented the updated standard to IFFO members in Miami. "The consensus among the committee, which includes representation from fishmeal producers, feed companies, retailers, processors and environmental NGOs, was that significant changes were needed to keep pace with evolving expectations in the four years since Version 2 was released in 2017," she said.

Libby Woodhatch, executive chair at MarinTrust.

Although MarinTrust had social criteria within Version 2, the world had "changed a lot" in terms of expectations and understanding of workers' rights and protections.

"Traceability has always been a pillar of our standard too, but again, it's moved on a lot when you've got things like the Global Dialogue for Seafood Traceability. It's not just about traceability; it's traceability of what? Making sure we identify what the data is that's needed up that whole value chain so that everybody's collecting relevant data, not obsolete data that you can verify because it's easy."

Raw material sourcing

One major change in Version 3 relates to the MarinTrust program's requirements around raw material sourcing. While Version 2 required an in-depth fishery assessment for each individual fishery supplying whole fish, the updated standard shifts to a risk-based approach for byproduct raw material. 

Global fishmeal output down 27% before Peru’s good anchovy fishing

"A prerequisite in Version 2 was a fisheries assessment," Woodhatch explained. "When you're looking at byproducts, and you might have 20, 30, 40 species -- particularly if you're in northern Europe -- and you won't always know in a year what they're going to be, it made accessibility complicated. You could argue that, well, those byproducts have come from fish that's been landed legally for direct human consumption, so if it's been landed legally, why are we putting another layer on top? So we've gone down a risk-based approach for that using ratings from IUU [illegal, unreported and unregulated] Fishing Index and other publicly available sources. It simplifies the process and makes it much more accessible."

To ensure Version 3 reflected the needs of industry while still driving progress in sustainability, MarinTrust carried out an extensive multi-phase development process over several years. This included public consultation on the Terms of Reference, input from stakeholder committees, and field-testing of the draft standard in Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America.

"All of that process has been done the whole way through with our stakeholder committees," said Woodhatch. "We've trialed it, field-tested, it's about making sure it's workable for the industry, but we've got that extra layer of scrutiny through the NGOs, through the other parts of the value chain that sit on our committees. They might say the bar needs to nudge a little bit higher or we need to be clear about our intent."

Libby Woodhatch presenting at the IFFO members conference in Miami, April 16, 2024.

Thanks to this more inclusive approach, she said program participants have been well-prepared for the transition, with pushback limited. Most concerns have come from European producers already subject to robust regulations, who questioned the need for additional oversight.

"Of course, you know you can't be everything to all people," Woodhatch acknowledged. "In Europe, there's a lot of legislation and producers might feel that well, it's legislated anyway. But the reality is, just because there's a law, it doesn't mean you're necessarily regularly checked. So if there is a law, then it just means in the audit process, it's going to be very easy for you to prove those things."

The other 50%

Currently, as mentioned, MarinTrust certifies about half the global production of marine ingredients, which largely comes from a few major regions like Peru, Chile and the North Atlantic. To expand that scope, the organization is focusing heavily on its Improver Program, which provides a pathway for fisheries in developing regions to work toward certification.

"That other 50% is going to be some of the slower burn," said Woodhatch. "It will be things like the Improver Program, and that does take time because you're dealing with countries where they might not have robust fisheries management systems. So it's about giving them that platform. We could be talking 10 years plus. But if you want to make change, then it is going to take time." 

Peru fishing

Asia represents a key area of potential growth, but one where the diversity of species used in marine ingredients poses a challenge for traditional assessment models. To address this issue, MarinTrust is developing its multispecies criteria.

"Asia is a classic example," Woodhatch said. "We have two Improver Program projects, one in the Gulf of Thailand and one in Vietnam, and it's the complexity of the fisheries. When you're dealing with fisheries of 300 species, it doesn't fit the existing model. That's why we're developing these multispecies criteria. It takes time, but once that's developed, there will be more scope to increase the volumes coming from Asia." 

New version of the MarinTrust factory standard enters into force

Ultimately, Woodhatch said she would love to see MarinTrust volumes reach 75% of global production in the next five to 10 years, up from around 50% currently. But she stressed this figure includes both certified production and volumes coming from the Improver Program. And she acknowledged that some fisheries may be hampered by factors outside the industry's direct control.

"There's always going to be things out of our control; a classic example is blue whiting," she said, referring to the North Atlantic species where international quota-sharing disagreements have created sustainability challenges. "Big volumes, but if you're relying on governments that can't agree on something they've not been able to agree for years, it makes it really difficult. There are always going to be anomalies."

Despite these challenges, Woodhatch remains optimistic about the future of MarinTrust and the marine ingredients industry's future sustainability despite the constant vigilance required by emerging trends.

Howes says MSC will amend requirements this summer after forced labor criticisms

"We need to make sure we keep horizon scanning and understand what's coming next," she said. "What we don't want is things imposed upon us. It's much better if we are proactive and say, 'Yes, we acknowledge there are areas where you need greater assurance,' for example, on human rights, and make sure that we remain fit for purpose. The marine ingredient sector needs to make sure it takes the lead and looks ahead at what's coming in terms of understanding its value chain."

Not a silver bullet

One area where Woodhatch acknowledged required greater improvement is in labor issues, as highlighted by recent investigations into Chinese seafood processing plants and distant water fishing fleets by The Outlaw Ocean Project and others. But she cautioned that third-party certification programs like MarinTrust should be viewed as just one tool for driving change and not a silver bullet. 

Aquaculture Stewardship Council to cease operations in China

"It's really difficult because sometimes people expect a certification or a standard to solve everything, and when you look at the reason why, unless we address global poverty, then you are going to get people going into these situations because they're desperate," she said. "So we need to be realistic. Certification is not going to be able to tell the Chinese government to ban the use of Uyghur labor in seafood processing plants. But what it hopefully does is it makes companies scrutinize who they're getting their fish from." 

Woodhatch pointed to the decision by the Aquaculture Stewardship Council to stop auditing Chain of Custody certificates in China as evidence of the limitations of voluntary certification in the face of systemic challenges.

"An audit is a snapshot in time," she said. "It may prevent some things, but unless you get the government legislation, like the US seafood import monitoring program or the EU's red card, yellow card schemes, you will always have bad actors. I think from a reputational perspective, it's about making sure we have systems in place to try and identify issues."

At the same time, Woodhatch said she believes growing government oversight, like the US' Seafood Import Monitoring Program, as well as increasing use of technologies like electronic catch documentation and traceability systems, will make it easier to drive labor and environmental improvements over time.

"I think what we'll see is legislation blocking potential areas of risk and we've seen it already with things like the EU's IUU carding system," she said. "As traceability systems become more commonplace in the supply chains for direct human consumption, I think some of the information we're asking for on the marine ingredients side will become much easier to get as well."

title: Daily recap: Santa Priscila the winner of US shrimp probes; Bangkok skipjack prices edge up
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Friday, May 24:

Ecuador's Santa Priscila is big winner of US shrimp investigations

Now that the smoke has cleared around all of the preliminary duties from the Department of Commerce's combined frozen warmwater shrimp countervailing and antidumping investigations, it's apparent that one company is the big winner, US shrimp importers told Undercurrent News.

Bangkok skipjack prices edge up on slight demand recovery, lower catches in Western Pacific

Skipjack tuna prices for delivery in Bangkok, Thailand, are seeing a gradual lift after hitting the bottom at $1,300 per metric ton earlier this year, industry sources told Undercurrent at the Infofish World Tuna Trade Conference & Exhibition.

Luke's Lobster exec explains reservations over pursuing MSC restoration

There can be grim unintended side-effects of regulations and certifications in fisheries that should be protected against, warned Ben Conniff. "People think that lobstermen are resistant to change because they're backward and stubborn people. And sometimes they are! But the reality is they're resistant to change in large part because they understand how global economics work. When they see this slew of regulations and technology and solutions coming their way, they see the opportunity for corporate consolidation of their fishery," said the co-founder and chief information officer at Luke's Lobster, in the US town of Portland, Maine.

Big Chinese, US sales make for another strong month for Vietnam pangasius exports

Vietnam's exports of pangasius were up quite strongly again in April 2024 after March's lift, with China and the US really driving sales, according to a consultancy commissioned by Undercurrent to gather and analyze customs data.

Norway salmon spot prices tumble, Chile flat again, Scottish ease slightly

Spot prices for farmed Norwegian salmon look to be dropping quite steeply for delivery in week 22 of 2024 (commencing May 27), while Chilean remain flat once again and Scottish ease a little, sources told Undercurrent.

title: Ecuador’s Santa Priscila is big winner of US shrimp investigations
content:
Now that the smoke has cleared around all of the preliminary duties from the Department of Commerce's combined frozen warmwater shrimp countervailing (CVD) and antidumping investigations, it's apparent that one company is the big winner, US shrimp importers told Undercurrent News on Thursday (May 23).

That's Industrial Pesquera Santa Priscila, the US' largest source of shrimp from Ecuador.

The Department of Commerce handed importers of shrimp produced by Santa Priscila a low 1.54% preliminary antidumping rate on Thursday (May 23), while slamming importers of shrimp from Sociedad Nacional de Galapagos (Songa), the US' second-largest source from Ecuador, and all other Ecuadoran shrimp producers with a 10.58% rate.

Ecuador's shrimp is among the cheapest imported by the US, costing an average $3.19 per pound in March, confirms a review of Undercurrent's trade portal.

So, given the low preliminary CVD rate of 2.89% earlier applied, that means importers of shrimp from Santa Priscila could likely charge an average $3.28/lb and be $0.25/lb cheaper than rival Songa and $0.34/lb cheaper than all other Ecuadoran producers. 

Santa Priscila wasn't in such a great position back on March 26 when Commerce announced that it was going to hit the company with a preliminary CVD rate of 13.41%, as reported by Undercurrent. However, just a few weeks later, on April 19, the US agency called officials involved in the case to concede that it made a mistake in calculating the Ecuadoran company's rate and dropped it precipitously, as also reported by Undercurrent. 

A final determination on CVD rates is expected on Aug. 5, 2024. A final determination on dumping rates is scheduled for Oct. 4, 2024.

Commerce has yet to publish its preliminary dumping duties in the Federal Register, which will trigger them to go into effect. That could happen in the next few days.

Jose Antonio Camposano, head of Ecuador's national chamber of aquaculture (CNA), declined to provide comment on Thursday, noting how DOC has yet to explain how it arrived at its calculations. He told Undercurrent that it was "too early to determine the impact of the issue."

Another Ecuador shrimp industry executive, who requested anonymity, said the impact of the dumping rates will now depend on how Santa Priscila responds, and if they take advantage of their position to keep their prices lower.  

The market will feel pressured to follow and reduce their own margins if Santa Priscila keeps its prices lower, but "the market will not absorb the duty," he said.

Ecuador's cost advantage over India negated

The other shrimp company that got a big boost on Thursday was Bahari Makmur Segati (BMS), the US' largest source in Indonesia. Importers of shrimp from BMS won't have to pay any tariffs as a result of either investigation, though importers of shrimp from Indonesian competitor First Marine Seafoods and all other Indonesian shrimp producers will be required to pay a dumping rate of 6.3%.

Given the average $3.54/lb paid for Indonesian shrimp in March, that works out to a nearly $0.22/lb advantage for BMS over other producers in the country.

US importers of Ecuador shrimp hit with dumping duties above 10%; Indonesia over 6%

As for the overall US shrimp import market, none of the importers Undercurrent interviewed said they see a major shift among the major source countries as a result of the two sets of duties.

Ecuador, the US' second-largest source of shrimp, responsible for a market share of 26% in 2023, has been one of the US' cheapest sources. But India, the US' largest source of shrimp, with a market share of 38% in 2023, also got hit with duties as did Indonesia, the US' third-largest source of shrimp with a market share of 19%, and Vietnam, the US' fourth-largest source of shrimp with a market share of 8%.

Combined, the four countries accounted for 91% of all the imported shrimp consumed in the US in 2023. And none of the four will likely lose their dominant positions, agreed Jeff Stern, co-president of Central Seaway Company (CenSea), in Northbrook, Illinois, and Donelson Berger, the shrimp category manager for Boston, Massachusetts-based processor Stavis Seafoods.

"I don't see a significant change in supply," Stern said. "India was hoping that Indonesia and or Ecuador would get high rates, and that didn't happen. Vietnam didn't gain anything. Had high rates been implemented, higher cost producers like Thailand would have had an opportunity to get back in the market in a bigger way. It's kind of a wash for everybody except for Santa Priscila, in Ecuador.”

The new tariffs will negate Ecuador's cost advantage, and bring them more even with India, Berger said, but it's not enough of a shift to make a major difference.

Likewise, several of the importers interviewed by Undercurrent don't see domestic harvesters gaining a significant enough advantage to change their circumstances.

The dumping and CVD cases were initiated following petitions filed by the American Shrimp Processors Association (ASPA), a group that represents US harvesters and processors behind roughly 85% of the US' domestic frozen warmwater shrimp production. They claimed the low prices charged for imported farmed shrimp were enabled by programs organized by the exporters' nations and have caused prices for domestic shrimp to also crash.

'Slogging in the mud'

Berger noted how shrimp imports "seemed to pop" with year-on-year gains in February and March of 2024, as reported by Undercurrent. He believes it was likely a result of importers trying to grab product before the CVD or dumping duties were declared.

"We all bought a little extra as a hedge, and then the [CVD] rates came out and we looked pretty damn smart. And then four weeks later, oops, they yanked it back out," Berger recounted, describing how Santa Priscila's CVD rates initially were high and then reduced.

"We had a good 10% runup and then the party ended and it came scooting right back, and we're now sitting kind of slogging in the mud," Berger commented. 

The current year is on pace to be the third-highest in US shrimp import history, behind 2021 (896,696t worth $8.0bn) and 2022 (841,505t worth $7.8bn), he noted. In 2023, the US imported 788,209t worth $6.4bn.

It's possible that import numbers might now flatten out a bit as a result of the tariffs being known and companies having significant inventory holdings, Berger said. Given the "predatory rates structure" being used in public cold storage, it's more difficult to hold on to shrimp, he said, adding:

"It'll cost you $0.06/lb and, in a flat market, $0.06/lb after a couple of months is your margin in many respects."

Shrimp on a cutting board. Photograph by Bigc Studio on Shutterstock.

In general, there's still more shrimp in inventory than there is demand, he said. 

"We're still in a market where we are trying to shove 100 pounds of supply into an 80-pound bucket of demand," Berger said.

But he doesn't think the volumes are going to drop off. It's normal for the pace of shrimp imports to increase in the second half of the year, he said. It's typical for the second half of a year to account for 60% of all US shrimp imports.

"I have no reason to think you're not going to see good big supplies coming in because you've got the packers that are shipping to themselves as well as various companies that are buying for their own needs," he said. "So I think you're going to be looking at an oversupplied market for the duration. And I do think that the run up early this year was the wish and hopes of the duty push in the market, and it just failed."

title: Big Chinese, US sales make for another strong month for Vietnam pangasius exports
content:
Vietnam's exports of pangasius were up quite strongly again in April 2024 after March's lift, with China and the US really driving sales, according to a consultancy commissioned by Undercurrent News to gather and analyze customs data.

For April, export volumes of pangasius products were up 21% month-on-month and up 37% year-on-year at 77,325 metric tons.

"Except for the EU (-2%), other markets saw an increase in import volume, including Brazil (+58%), Mexico (+40%), China and Hong Kong (+33%), the US (+32%), the UK (+4%) and ASEAN (+4%)," the consultancy told Undercurrent.

"The sharp increase in exports compared to the same period last year was mostly contributed by the remarkable rise in exports to the US (+84%). Nevertheless, according to Agromonitor, with recent trends, the US market tends to reduce import volumes after two-three months of strong increases."

"Therefore, since US imports peaked in March and April, the export volume to his market is projected to decline in the following two months. Similarly, the EU market is also expected to slow down in May and June after a sharp rise in March and April."

The average export price still shows no real signs of improving, though. After a 3% lift in March, April saw the average price across all products -- from the heaviest glaze to the top-of-the-range, Aquaculture Stewardship Council-certified fillets, and what limited value-added products are shipped -- slip 1% to $2.17 per kilogram. 

"The export price of pangasius is projected to recover in 2024 in line with an increase in demand from the US and EU," the consultancy had said earlier this year.

China prices hit new low

China and Hong Kong's imports of Vietnamese pangasius were back at healthy levels relative to the last few years in April, up m-o-m at 24,327t. 

It remains the largest market, but export prices to this market have been sliding since November; from a longer-term view, since the fall of 2022. In April 2024 they followed March's uptick with a 6.4% decline to $1.89/kg.

The US also continues to look brighter after a tough 2023, with volumes and average prices up each month.

April saw volumes reach 13,415t -- the highest in two years -- while prices also rose 2.4% to $2.90/kg.

The Vietnam Association of Seafood Processors and Exporters (VASEP) noted the US market is considering recognizing Vietnam as a market economy, with the US Department of Commerce hearing testimony on May 8 on the topic. Conclusions are expected in July.

VASEP believes this could be a great advantage for Vietnamese businesses, especially in administrative reviews of anti-dumping taxes on shrimp and pangasius and anti-subsidy investigations. In addition, other barriers and regulations may also be reviewed in a more relaxed and favorable manner.

Exports to the EU were stable in April at 6,695t, while prices lifted 4.3% to $2.55/kg -- their highest since September 2023.

Vietnamese news site VOV used customs data on sales values to state that pangasius sales to the EU were, as of mid-April, down 13% at $47 million y-o-y. As can be seen from Undercurrent's data, that's down to export prices being significantly lower y-o-y:

VASEP said pangasius exports to the EU reached almost $9m in April alone, down 14% y-o-y. Some companies may be trying to increase their shares of value-added products, but frozen fillets made up 95% of sales to the EU in the first quarter of 2024.

The Netherlands' imports have declined 10% y-o-y in Q1, while Germany's were down 30% in January, 50% in February, and 9% in March.

After a good increase in import volumes in March, ASEAN markets were stable in April at 8,354t. The average price eased 2.1% to $1.88/kg. 

Mexico's imports rose again in April to 2,047t, up y-o-y and m-o-m. After a drop in prices the prior month, April saw them rise 7.4% to $2.30/kg.

Export prices to the UK had been steady at more than $3.00/kg over the winter, but March saw a dive, and that was followed in April by a decline of 4.4% to $2.62/kg. 

Volumes were flat at 1,291t, also stable y-o-y.

The Brazilian market has long made grim reading for Vietnamese exporters, but April brought a second consecutive price rise of 0.7% to $2.73/kg, and a lift in volumes to 2,736t. 

That's almost double April 2023's volumes.  

Vietnam's Association of Seafood Processors and Exporters noted in April that pangasius exports to Canada reached $2.3 million in the first half of March alone, up 7% y-o-y.

As of March 15, it had imported over $8m worth in 2024, up 43% y-o-y. 

In January, that equated to over 900t worth $2m -- down 10% in value but up 28% in volume.

title: US importers of Ecuador shrimp hit with dumping duties above 10%; Indonesia over 6%
content:
US importers of frozen warmwater shrimp from Sociedad Nacional de Galapagos (Songa), one of Ecuador's biggest shrimp producers, will be required to pay a preliminary dumping rate of 10.58%, an amount that will be required as an upfront cash deposit.

Those sourcing from Industrial Pesquera Santa Priscila, Ecuador's largest, will be hit with a "de minimis" 1.54% rate and not be forced to provide deposits. But all other Ecuadorian shrimp will also come with a 10.58% dumping rate and a 10.18% upfront cash deposit.

Those were the preliminary determinations made known by the US Department of Commerce (DOC) Thursday (May 23) to those involved in the anti-dumping investigation being conducted by the International Trade Commission. A public notice in the Federal Register is not expected for several more days. 

DOC has also informed officials that importers of shrimp from major Indonesia producer Bahari Makmur Sejati (BMS) will not be required to pay an anti-dumping duty, though importers of shrimp from First Marine Seafoods/Khom Foods and all other Indonesian shrimp will be hit with a preliminary duty of 6.3%. 

Final determinations are expected by Oct. 4, 2024.

As the quarterly chart below shows from the Undercurrent News data platform, Ecuador and Indonesia are the number two and three US shrimp suppliers behind India. 

The rates are on top of the preliminary countervailing duties required by DOC in relation to shrimp imported from Ecuador, India, Indonesia and Vietnam.

Following a correction downward from 13.41% in April, importers of shrimp from Santa Priscila have been required to pay a preliminary CVD rate of 2.89%. All other Ecuador shrimp has come with a rate of 2.89%, a reduction from 7.55%.

However, shrimp from Songa was determined to receive a 1.69% preliminary CVD rate and no cash deposit requirement.

Omarsa CEO: US shrimp duties make marketing push ‘more necessary than ever’

DOC had earlier issued a negative preliminary CVD-related determination for Indonesia's BMS (0.39%) and First Marine (0.71%).

As part of the CVD case, importers of shrimp from India were required to deposit 4.72% of the amount paid for products supplied by Devi Sea Foods, 3.89% from Sandhya Aqua Exports, and 4.36% from all other Indian suppliers. For shrimp from Vietnam, the deposit requirement is 2.84% for Stapimex, 196.41% for Thong Thuan, and 2.84% for all other Vietnamese suppliers.

Both the anti-dumping and CVD cases were initiated following petitions filed by the American Shrimp Processors Association, a group that represents US harvesters and processors behind roughly 85% of the US domestic frozen warmwater shrimp production. They claim the low prices charged for imported farmed shrimp were enabled by programs organized by the exporters' nations and have caused prices for domestic shrimp to also crash.

Though they are being investigated for CVD-related transgressions, neither India nor Vietnam are involved in the anti-dumping cases.

title: Maldives’ MIFCO to boost capacity 650% with three new canneries
content:
BANGKOK, Thailand -- The Maldives Industrial Fisheries Company (MIFCO) recently agreed on a plan to build three new canneries across the country, an executive with the company told Undercurrent News.

Each new cannery will have a production capacity of 100 metric tons per day and be equipped with cold storage facilities, fishmeal production, and fish oil production units, said Hafzath Ahmed, MIFCO's general manager of marketing.

The facilities should be built by the end of 2025, significantly boosting MIFCO's processing capacity from the current 40t per day to 300t per day. 

The Maldives currently has a total tuna canning capacity of approximately 80t to 100t per day, with MIFCO contributing around 50% of this volume and Horizon the remaining 50%. According to sources, Ensis is currently not operational after it stopped purchasing raw materials last year.

Earlier this week, during the Infofish tuna conference in Bangkok, Thailand, Ahmed Shiyam, Maldives' minister for fisheries and agriculture, said the country aims to increase its domestic tuna processing. 

According to Shiyam, the country catches around 100,000t of skipjack, 60% of which is exported as raw material to be processed elsewhere in the world, with only 40% being processed locally. The Maldives' new government, which was elected in September 2023, aims to change this in the coming years, ensuring that the majority of the catch is processed domestically and thereby increasing the economic benefits for the local fishing industry, the minister said.

"We want to ensure that all this is no longer a raw material provider but adds value to our product locally. Our priority is to develop value-added products and infrastructure that will increase our exports to new markets and create new employment opportunities for our people," he said.

MIFCO's new canneries are expected to focus primarily on producing canned tuna and tuna pouches, catering to "high-demand" markets in Europe, especially the UK, where there is a strong consumer preference for sustainably sourced seafood, Ahmed said. The Maldives' pole-and-line fishing method, known for its environmental sustainability and minimal bycatch, is a significant selling point in these markets, he said.

According to MIFCO, the canneries will be built with prefabricated warehouses and machinery from Chinese suppliers, Ahmed told Undercurrent.

He also said an issue with payment delays to fishermen due to increased tuna purchase prices and market price fluctuations last year had been resolved in March, and payment to fishermen has resumed as normal. The new administration addressed these issues earlier this year, stabilizing payments and re-aligning purchase prices with market conditions, said Ahmed.

With this substantial increase in capacity and the added capabilities of the new canneries, Mifco is poised to lead the Maldivian tuna industry into a new era of growth and sustainability, ensuring better returns for fishermen and greater economic benefits for the nation, according to Ahmed.

Meanwhile, MIFCO's CEO and managing director, Ahmed Shamah Rasheed, was dismissed from his position this week. According to Hafzath Ahmed, he has been moved to a different position within the fisheries ministry, and a new CEO will be appointed. Management positions at the business are politically appointed. 

Shamah was suspended after the country's Privatization and Corporatization Board conducted investigations into complaints it received regarding corporate governance issues, Edition Maldives reported in March.

The suspension was lifted in late April.

Sustainability of sector on political agenda

Talking about sustainability, the Maldives' minister noted that the global fisheries industry has faced challenges due to the impact of climate change, including changes in fish migration and fish stock.

This affects the sustainability of the tuna stocks and threatens the socioeconomic situations of those who depend on them.

"The urgency of addressing climate change cannot be overstated, and it is our moral obligation to senior generations. As we strive to create a more sustainable and inclusive fisheries industry, we must ensure that the particularly vulnerable communities are not left out," Shiyam said.

He also pointed out that the fishing sector is deeply tied to the country's livelihood and cultural identity. He noted his ministry's mandate had been expanded to cover the ocean and all its resources, not just fisheries. 

Fisheries is the only primary industry in the Maldives and the second-biggest contributor to the country's economy, said Shiyam. 

The Maldivian government has been in continuous discussions with the EU to reduce the duty of fish products exported from Maldives into the region, and the government has said they are confident that these discussions are going forward well, Edition Maldives previously reported. Currently, a 22% duty is taken from fish products exported from Maldives.

title: Thai Union rebuffs Shark Guardian claims of greenwashing, labor abuses
content:
A report by a UK charity for shark and marine conservation, Shark Guardian, has accused Thai Union Group (TUG) of alleged greenwashing, labor rights violations within its supply chain, shark finning, and overfishing.

The investigation, "The Art of Greenwashing: Thai Union's Sustainability Smokescreen," carries allegations that TUG, the world's largest tuna processor, has not fully implemented measures to address sustainability and labor rights issues.

A TUG spokesperson, however, reaffirmed the company's commitment to these fields, citing various initiatives and progress made in 2023 alone.

"TUG is committed to the sustainability of the oceans, to protecting their biodiversity, and to providing a safe, decent, and equitable workplace to the women and men that work on the vessels and farms we source from," they said. 

Shark Guardian claimed a "pattern where, rather than meeting existing sustainability or workers' rights targets, Thai Union simply publishes new goals" and that there were "critical disparities between the company's commitments and promises and evidence of a lack of progress in addressing either ocean sustainability or labor abuses."

In response, TUG's spokesperson said the business has been "actively driving continuous improvement of labor and ethical conditions in the fishing sector since we launched our vessel code of conduct and vessel improvement program (VIP) in 2017. The Fisher Work and Welfare program provides clear guidance on working conditions on board the vessels TUG sources from and encourages better practices at sea."

"Our SeaChange 2030 sustainability plan entails the broadest-reaching commitments in our industry," they continued. "Committing the entire 2022 net profit of $200 million must invariably come with measurable and tangible progress, which we will show for all our 11 commitments," they added.

TUG said that it was the first tuna processor to make a 100% commitment to source only from tuna vessels with "on-the-water" monitoring; that 79% of the tuna volume it sourced was actively working towards improvements in welfare and working conditions through its VIP; and that it continued to deploy resources to the ports from which it sources, as just some examples of concrete progress it had made in 2023.

However, Shark Guardian remains unconvinced. "Talk is cheap and meaningless without action," remarked Brendon Sing, co-founder of the UK charity.

"The disparity between TUG's promises and its actions has major implications for the health of our ocean. Customers are being hoodwinked by empty promises while shark populations collapse, especially in the Indian Ocean where TUG stamps its destructive ecological footprint," he added.

TUG supplies over a third of the canned tuna sold in the UK, including under the John West brand and for major retailers like Tesco, Aldi, and Wm Morrison Supermarkets.

You can read Shark Guardian's full report here.

title: IOTC members reject tuna fishing closure proposals at annual meeting
content:
BANGKOK, Thailand -- The latest annual session of the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC), held in Bangkok, Thailand, concluded on May 17, leaving a trail of mixed sentiments among stakeholders. While some hailed progress in modernized management for certain species, others expressed deep concerns over the approved measures.

A proposed three-month ban on FAD fishing was not approved during the meeting last week, held before the World Tuna Trade Conference & Exhibition, also in Bangkok from May 20-22. Similarly, a proposal for a month-long fishing ban for all gear was rejected despite ongoing overfishing (see slide above). 

Following the meeting, European fishing industry bodies voiced strong opposition to the measures approved for managing fish aggregation devices (FADs), warning of severe consequences for the EU fleet.

Infofish Tuna 2024: New canneries for Maldives, Oman; Ecuadorian canneries, software provider test ‘transformative potential’ of AI in tuna processing

According to Orthongel, the French industry association of frozen and deep-frozen tuna producers, the approved revision for drifting FADs, which was approved last minute, mandates a further gradual reduction in the number of operational beacons per vessel and assistance vessels (between 2025 and 2028). In addition, it mandates the introduction of a FAD register and a transition to fully biodegradable drifting FADs. 

However, less stringent provisions have been made for contracting parties with fewer than two purse seiners (South Korea and Tanzania) and for small island states (Seychelles, Mauritius), particularly a smaller reduction in the number of operational beacons per vessel.

Orthongel, in a statement, lamented the rejection or weakening of proposed measures aimed at enhancing monitoring, control, and surveillance and combating illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing. The organization particularly highlighted the rejection of proposals to set up a boarding and inspection system on the high seas and the reduction of ambitions in scientific observation coverage.

According to Orthongel, this session was marked by a "poisonous climate created by the repeated attacks this week by certain NGOs, aimed at portraying the European fleet as disrespectful of the rules."

"This strategy serves the cause of those who are currently increasing their fishing effort and catches and who are contravening all transparency and data transmission measures out of sight, taking advantage of the fact that the spotlight is on the thirty or so European purse seiners (increasing the number of transshipment vessels, rejecting the ban on discards, rejecting the ban on shark finning...)," said Orthongel.

The French association stressed that its fleet is perfectly monitored (by VMS, ERS and 100% scientific observation coverage), complies with all applicable rules (quota, FAD monitoring, social responsibility) and is one of the most innovative fleets in terms of adopting best fishing practices. This has earned it Marine Stewardship Council certification in Indian and Atlantic Oceans.

European fishing association Europeche echoed similar sentiments, expressing regret over the rejection or weakening of measures to improve transparency and data for scientific analysis.

The European fleet welcomed the adoption of a management measure for skipjack and a clear calendar towards FADs' full biodegradability. According to Europeche, the EU purse seiners have requested this for several years now, and it is coherent with their sustainable fishery and MSC label approach.

Despite this, Europeche said that IOTC members focused once again on measures directed towards FAD management without scientific backing, which will have severe consequences on the EU fleet. At the same time, other gears will not be affected by these decisions. According to Europeche, this will unlevel the playing field, notably through the unequal access to supply vessels and the erratic decrease of the number of FADs with multiple exemptions.

"Focusing on FADs, the IOTC Commission diverts the attention from the real problem in IOTC: the yellowfin tuna recovery plan is still not implemented by several CPCs, and no additional management measures are required from other gears that represent nearly 70% of the catches," Europeche said.

NGO Blue Marine Foundation said it was disappointed to see the adoption of a "weak and unambitious" resolution on drifting FADs that "allows for little transparency and, worst of all, fails to implement the necessary closure period for these harmful devices used by EU purse seiners to catch overfished juvenile tuna in their millions".

"We are deeply disappointed in the outcome of the 28th session of the IOTC, which failed, once again, to deal with the most pressing issues facing the region’s shark and tuna populations. Despite the best efforts of the delegation from Pakistan, who worked tirelessly to find a solution to the yellowfin tuna overfishing crisis, the IOTC missed yet another opportunity to adopt a responsible and equitable recovery plan for the stock, which will now enter its 10th year of overfishing," said Jess Rattle, head of investigations at the Blue Marine Foundation. "The EU continues to be the largest obstacle to the effective management of drifting fish aggregating devices (FADs) in the Indian Ocean, despite clear science that shows that, short of closing the entire Indian Ocean tuna fishery for two or three months, the most impactful measure would be a three-month, ocean-wide closure of the FAD-associated purse seine fishery," Rattle also said.

However, amidst the discord, there were acknowledgments of progress. NGO Pew Charitable Trusts highlighted the adoption of the world's first management procedure for swordfish and efforts to fight IUU fishing. 

Glen Holmes, a senior officer at Pew, lauded the IOTC's actions but expressed concern over the ongoing struggle to rebuild the yellowfin tuna stock despite its depleted status and continued overfishing.

"The Indian Ocean Tuna Commission adopted the world's first management procedure for swordfish, demonstrating that this modern fisheries management approach can be used to improve the health and resilience of other highly migratory species beyond tunas. Skipjack tuna fishing limits have been exceeded annually since 2016, and the stock will now also have a full management procedure in place that will help prevent overfishing in the future," said Holmes.

He also highlighted that the IOTC took an important step in the fight against IUU fishing by now requiring that all those who benefit from or support such activities be investigated and held to account. 

"Yellowfin tuna, however, remains a serious hurdle. Despite its overfished status and continued overfishing, the Commission was yet again unable to agree to a path to rebuild the stock," Holmes also pointed out.

The World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) also criticized the IOTC for failing to adopt the "critical measures needed to safeguard Indian Ocean yellowfin tuna."

"Despite scientific advice, IOTC's Contracting Parties and Cooperating Non-Contracting Parties (CPCs) decided against the needed catch reductions, deferring the decision to the next annual session in 2025, when new stock assessment data will be available," it said in a statement.

"It is deeply disappointing that IOTC has failed to curb overfishing. The Scientific Committee has reported that yellowfin tuna's spawning stock biomass has halved over the last 15 years. This alarming decline highlights the commission's inability to develop effective solutions, pushing required reduction targets ever higher, indicating that yesterday's lower limit is today's upper limit." 

Yet, the WWF said there had been some progress in some areas, including the approval of the comprehensive management strategy for drifting fish aggregating devices, or dFADs.

"The IOTC successfully adopted 10 proposals and two recommendations covering a range of important areas. However, it did not reach an agreement on several critical issues, including area closures, a 31-day closure for all fishing gear, and a conservation and management measure to protect sharks, which recommended fins to remain naturally attached to all sharks, and a ban on the use of wire tracers and shark lines," WWF said. 

During the Infofish conference, Paul de Bruyn, the IOTC's executive secretary, pointed out that yellowfin and bigeye tuna stocks in the Indian Ocean are currently overfished. He also noted that between 2018 and 2022, four of the 29 IOTC members -- Indonesia, Iran, the EU and India -- caught over 50% of the tuna in the IOTC area, as show in the slide below.

title: Peru fishermen call for tougher action as Chinese vessel gets ‘token fine’ for IUU fishing
content:
Peru's ministry of production, Produce, has come under heavy criticism for imposing a mere PEN 250 ($67.19) fine on Chinese vessel Tian Xiang, caught illegally fishing within its exclusive economic zone.

According to Edwin Houghton, vice president of Peru's national society of artisanal fisheries, or SONAPESCAL, the fine could be reduced to an even more paltry PEN 100 with early payment benefits. 

"Peruvian fishermen face hefty fines, criminal charges and confiscation of the vessels and equipment, while large foreign industrial vessels receive minimal sanctions," he claimed. 

According to SONAPESCAL, since Sergio Gonzalez took office as minister of production on April 2, 2024, 26 recorded arrivals of Chinese vessels at Peruvian ports have occurred without compulsory satellite monitoring.

The situation is exacerbated by reports from artisanal fishers of frequent encounters with Chinese squid vessels near the 200-mile maritime boundary and close to major ports such as Chimbote, Callao, and Pisco, it claimed.

There are allegations that these vessels enter Peruvian naval shipyards for repairs, enabling them to continue operations in Peruvian waters.

In a recent incident, the Tian Xiang was detected fishing within Peruvian waters on Sept. 19, 2023. Despite this clear evidence, SONAPESCAL said, the vessel was allowed to leave without a thorough investigation or confiscation of its illegal catch.

Adding to the controversy, Produce allowed the entry of another Chinese vessel, the Hua Ying 78, into Paracas Bay in Pisco on April 15. The vessel had previously turned off its satellite equipment for extended periods, raising suspicions of illegal fishing activities.

"Despite these infractions, the ministry permitted its entry without significant repercussions," Houghton added.

In light of these issues, he proposed a total ban on the entry of vessels that refuse to use the required satellite devices, arguing that "token fines" foster "an environment of impunity and threaten the sustainability of marine resources."

title: US Coast Guard responds to sunken crab boat at Seattle pier
content:
A crabbing vessel sunk at a pier in the US city of Seattle, Washington, pier on Tuesday (May 14), prompted a response from the US Coast Guard (USCG), the state's environmental department and other emergency agencies.

According to a USCG press release, watchstanders received a call Tuesday morning that the 91-foot crabber North American had sunk at a pier on the south side of the Lake Washington Ship Canal, just east of the Ballard Bridge. 

The fishing vessel North American sunk at a Seattle on May 14. Photo USCG

No one was injured and no other vessels were damaged, however USCG personnel and the Washington Department of Ecology were monitoring any fuel leakage. The vessel's maximum capacity of diesel is 32,500 gallons.

A containment boom was deployed Tuesday, and divers were plugging any other vents or holes in the ship to prevent the discharge of any additional liquids, according to the press release. 

The USCG said the cause of the sinking is under investigation.

title: US gov’t sticks to sidelines in ‘figurehead fraud’ lawsuit against Cooke, Omega Protein
content:
The US government is thus far remaining on the sidelines of a lawsuit levied in a Manhattan, New York, federal court by two "whistleblowers" who allege that Canadian seafood giant Cooke committed "figurehead fraud" when it acquired US menhaden processor Omega Protein in 2017.

However, this could change at a later date should "good cause" for the government to intervene arise, Damian Williams, the US attorney for the Southern District of New York, wrote in a March 8 filing to New York City-based federal judge Jesse Furman.

In the lawsuit, which was filed in June 2021 but not unsealed until April 23, 2024, plaintiffs W. Benson Chiles and Chris Murphy allege that Cooke, Omega Protein and several affiliates violated the American Fisheries Act (AFA). The law mandates that non-US citizens can not have "effective control" over vessels that fish in US waters.

A menhaden catching vessel. Photograph courtesy of Omega Protein.

The menhaden-harvesting vessels operated by Reedville, Virginia-based Omega Protein in the US' Chesapeake Bay were previously wholly owned by the company when it was publicly traded on the New York Stock Exchange. This changed in 2017, however, when the vessels were transferred to Alpha Vessel Co. Holdings Inc, a Delaware-registered corporation also known as Ocean Fleet Services, according to the lawsuit.

The newly created company co-issued $30 million worth of notes alongside Cooke subsidiary Cooke Omega Investments. Some $28.75m of those funds along with a $1m investment from Seth Dunlop went to purchase the vessels.

Dunlop is described in the suit as a US citizen, Canadian resident, Ocean Fleet's chief executive officer, chairman, director and "nominal owner" of 80% of the company's stock. He is also nephew to Cooke CEO Glenn Cooke, a longtime employee of the Cooke group, and has been a vice president for at least four Cooke subsidiaries, the suit alleges. Ocean Fleet's corporate secretary is Seth Dunlop's father, Gregory, Glenn Cooke's brother-in-law, according to the complaint. 

Also, according to the lawsuit, Ocean Fleet acquired Omega Protein's vessels when it purchased subsidiary Alpha Vessel Co, LLC, which does business under the name Ocean Harvesters.

The litigation alleges that this arrangement violates the AFA.

"From the beginning, each of these closely connected persons, as well as Omega, shared an understanding that Cooke and Omega would control the Omega vessels and the Delaware shell [Ocean Fleet]. And from the acquisition up and through this day, Cooke and Omega have in fact controlled them," the suit alleges.

Additionally, the suit charges that the defendants "submitted, caused the submission, and or conspired to submit false and fraudulent fishery applications" to the US Department of Transportation's Maritime Administration, known as MARAD, and the US Coast Guard. 

Cooke and Omega declined to comment on the lawsuit's claims in detail but have denied wrongdoing.

In a separate statement sent to Undercurrent News, Ocean Harvesters said it believes "the recently filed lawsuit is without merit."

The company pledged to "vigorously defend against all allegations of wrongdoing," adding that "Ocean Harvesters is committed to compliance with all applicable laws and to continuing to conduct responsible, sustainable fishing operations along the Atlantic coast and in the Gulf of Mexico." 

US government's role

Although the US government won't participate in the lawsuit for now, the plaintiffs will still need to obtain written consent from the "court and the attorney general" if they want to drop the lawsuit and explain their reasons for doing so, Williams wrote.

Similarly, the federal prosecutor asked the judge to require the plaintiffs to obtain the government's permission should they seek to "settle, or otherwise discontinue" the case.

Plaintiffs Chiles and Manthey, are described respectively in the claim as a "professional investigator and researcher" and a participant in the "fisheries management industry." 

Chiles' LinkedIn account describes him as a "strategic consultant for conservation organizations" who has worked with advocacy groups such as Earthjustice and the Environmental Defense Fund in the past.

Manthey's profile describes a career with over three decades of experience in investigations and research.

One of Ocean Harvesters' many purse seiners heads to sea to catch menhaden. A still from an Omega Protein video.

The two men filed the suit "on behalf of the United States of America" under the False Claims Act, a law that allows private individuals to sue those who they believe defrauded the federal government. Plaintiffs in such litigation, known as qui tam lawsuits, are referred to as relators or whistleblowers can potentially obtain a portion of the funds recovered from any exposed fraud.

In this case, the total damages could be extensive. The lawsuit suggests that "falsely certifying" compliance with the AFA's citizenship rules "likely exceeds several hundred million dollars and could exceed $2 billion".

Judge Furman scheduled the case for an initial pretrial conference for Aug. 13 at 9 a.m

title: Howes says MSC will amend requirements this summer after forced labor criticisms
content:
Rupert Howes, CEO of the non-profit organization the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC), recently addressed the challenges and ongoing developments surrounding the organization's approach to social auditable criteria.

Eleven Chinese plants linked to forced labor were MSC-certified

During a Q&A session at the Seafood Futures Forum in Barcelona last month, he acknowledged the absence of explicit social auditable criteria within MSC's current framework, highlighting the organization's historical focus on ecological sustainability over social factors. MSC's eligibility criteria do hinge on auditors ensuring the absence of successful prosecutions for labor violations among fisheries and supply chain entities, however, Howes recognized the need for more robust social auditing practices.

In 2022, MSC updated its pre-entry requirements to the program relating to forced and child labor. According to the MSC's standards, certified supply chain businesses that process and pack certified seafood must undergo a third-party labor audit or submit a self-assessment report to the MSC, allowing the organization to commission its own independent audit. In some circumstances, processors are required to provide an audit from a credible third-party labor scheme, according to the MSC.

Howes detailed MSC's efforts to incorporate self-declarations and third-party social audits within their supply chain requirements. These steps were intended to solicit information about policies and practices to prevent child labor and enforce fair labor standards, he said. Despite these initiatives, Howes conceded that the effectiveness and reliability of such audits have come into question within the broader social responsibility discourse.

Marine Stewardship Council to rework new standard

Reflecting on the complexity of the MSC's version three certification standards, Howes acknowledged the challenges posed by the evolution of the organization's criteria over 25 years.

He outlined the MSC's phased approach to addressing these issues, with immediate amendments planned for July 2024 to enhance clarity and coherence within the latest version of the standard.

"We have some issues with the launch of version three [of the certification]. We have a project to look at how we can get some amendments out there to ensure clarity of intent requirements within a feasible application of the standard. So there is a lot going on," he explained.

When pressed about the criticisms of social audits, Howes admitted their limitations but stressed the importance of working collaboratively with stakeholders to navigate the complexities of human rights and labor standards within the context of MSC's mission.

Howes stressed that, on the social audit, there was no "silver bullet."

"Social audits, to some degree, have been discredited, but they have a place in other areas. I think the human rights movement isn't 100% sure what the solutions are, but our board direction is to work with others, make sure we're aware of what's going on, and I suspect we will review what we're doing and make changes," he said. 

"The MSC standards are focused on fisheries' environmental performance and sustainability and seafood supply chain assurance. However, we share the widespread concerns regarding social issues in the seafood industry and are working with other organizations to find practical solutions. We continuously improve our program, including incorporating third-party labor auditing schemes and introducing transparency measures," the MSC states on its website.

An MSC spokesperson added that the organization is "exploring a revised approach to forced and child labor"—one that is "practical, supports global efforts and is in line with MSC’s environmental remit". 

Other views

On the side of the MSC event, the sustainability manager of a large processor commented to Undercurrent News that MSC had been speaking about the potential introduction of social criteria into its standard "for a long time" without "doing much about it" so far. He added those changes would be welcomed.

Seafood companies are under increasing pressure to ensure their sourcing practices protect not just the oceans but also workers' rights throughout the industry. In recent weeks, the EU has approved a ban on products made with forced labor, and an Associated Press investigation uncovered labor and environmental violations across India's shrimp industry.

Last year, research by the Financial Transparency Coalition, a Washington, DC-based nonprofit that tracks illicit money flows, concluded that hazardous, forced work conditions, sometimes akin to slavery, have been detected on nearly 500 industrial fishing vessels around the world, The Independent reported.

In 2023, the Outlaw Ocean Project's investigation into Chinese seafood processing plants in Shandong province using forced Uyghur labor transferred from Xinjiang found the plants carried the MSC chain-of-custody certificate, causing concern across the sector.

Considering this context, the Conservation Alliance for Seafood Solutions recently launched guidance for seafood companies that it said provides a comprehensive framework to help them address environmental sustainability and human rights and labor issues throughout their supply chains. 

Asked about potential solutions, Ryan Bigelow, the director of projects for the Conservation Alliance, emphasized that achieving social and environmental responsibility in the seafood industry was not a straightforward task. 

"There is no panacea for social or environmental responsibility in seafood. No one company has 'finished' its sustainability journey."

"Still, the very act of due diligence to examine supply chains can reap multiple rewards. Through thorough analysis and a commitment to transparency, companies uncover areas of concern, put pressure on outdated systems and forge new pathways for improvement. Whether by engaging with suppliers to enforce good labor practices, investing in sustainable sourcing or seeking ethical alternatives, they can future-proof their business while driving reforms that resonate throughout global supply chains," Bigelow said. 

Similarly, Alexandra Golub, the sustainability manager for Acme Smoked Fish, highlighted the crucial need for accountability within the seafood industry concerning social and environmental commitments.

Golub told Undercurrent that the guidance provided by the Conservation Alliance was pivotal in providing a roadmap for businesses to enhance accountability and meet the expectations of consumers, regulators, and stakeholders throughout the supply chain.
