title: Lobster Boys open to re-employ infamous Illinois embezzler if granted home confinement
content:
Lobster Boys, a lobster wholesaler with operations in both the US and Canada, employed one of the US' most infamous embezzlers before the company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in December 2023, and it's prepared to do so again, court documents reveal.   

Sultan Issa worked for Lobsterboys, in Chicago, Illinois, for nearly two years, from June 2019 until March 2021, before he voluntarily reported to the Federal Correctional Institute (FCI) in Milan, Michigan, to begin a sentence of 200 months -- more than 16 years -- for misappropriating over $70 million from more than a dozen victims and financial institutions. 

Justin Maderia, who co-owns Lobster Boys with his brother Travis Maderia, revealed their employment of Issa in a letter sent to judge Andrea Wood in the US District Court for the Northern District of Illinois. He was one of several individuals, including also several family members, to express their support for Issa's request for an early release from FCI to home confinement due to the convicted felon's poor health.

Wood has yet to respond to the request, which has been repeated several times since August 2023, though court filings on behalf of Issa paint a desperate situation in which he is wheelchair-bound, confined to his quarters, struggling with a heart condition and has had to have life-saving procedures performed multiple times.

Sultan Issa cooks a lobster with Travis Maderia at his home in Hinsdale, Illinois. Photograph provided by source.

"We understand that Sultan's medical conditions have worsened from his long post covid infection amongst other health ailments, and we are adamant and able to provide him with the proper health insurance and annual compensation to recover from his symptoms of long covid, [Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome], hypertension and his auto-inflammatory diseases that have become worse since he contracted COVID-19 in April 2023," Justin Maderia wrote. "We would also be able to provide some working capital to provide a proper living arrangement at his mother's house ..."  

The Lobster Boys co-owner said he is even prepared to offer Issa another full-time management job.

"We are in full support to employ him while he serves the remainder of his incarceration on home confinement under the strictest terms given," he wrote. "We would gladly welcome Sultan back into our business and plan to employ him in a management role, similar to the position he held prior to his incarceration, if he is permitted to do so. The employment would be full-time."

Lobster Boys to sell Canadian plant as part of bankruptcy plan

The letter continues: "We would do what is required to accommodate any concerns that the Bureau of Prisons might have in permitting Sultan to continue his incarceration from home."

Justin Maderia's letter was filed with the Chicago federal court on Dec. 12, 2023, the same date that Lobster Boys filed for bankruptcy protection in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York, as earlier reported by Undercurrent News. The company was in arrears on more than $4.5m in loans. 

As part of a reorganization plan, Lobster Boys has agreed to sell a property and plant in Dipper Harbour, New Brunswick, for CAD 2.2m ($1.6m) to an "industry-related buyer who wants to close on the sale quickly following confirmation of the plan," according to a court filing made on April 26. It plans to continue operating with the use of its remaining properties in Shags Harbour, Nova Scotia, and Huntington, New York. 

Issa bought real estate, planes, yachts, guns

Issa was 46 years old and living in Hinsdale, Illinois, when he pled guilty, in January 2020, to having engineered multiple fraudulent schemes over the course of roughly 11 years, from 2007 until 2017, during which he illegally enriched himself using money plundered from more than a dozen investors, according to charging documents and the accounts of multiple newspapers, including the Chicago Tribune.

He was hardly low-key about his actions, using the ill-gotten funds to buy 25 homes, from Montana to Mexico, including three apartments in Chicago's Trump Tower, a Lamborghini dealership, two private planes, four motor yachts, 60 guns, jewelry and other luxuries, according to the charging documents and newspaper accounts. 

For the purchase of the Trump properties, Issa reportedly created a shell company he called "Combover LLC," an apparent jab at the former president's hair.

Issa used his position as a chief financial officer and certified public accountant for the family office of retired Chicago banking tycoon Roger Weston to transfer tens of millions of dollars in funds and other financial assets into accounts he controlled, the charging documents recounted. He forged signatures and provided false information on loan documents.

Other victims included three ex-Chicago Blackhawks hockey players, a trustee of the Art Institute of Chicago, and a widow who trusted him to invest $500,000 from her dead husband's estate.

Some of the money Issa stole was from a trust account set up to pay the medical expenses of a family member suffering from an incapacitating illness, one article reported. 

Trump Tower in Chicago, Illinois. Photograph by Gareth123458.

Issa, who accepted his conviction as part of a plea agreement with federal prosecutors, also was ordered by the judge to pay more than $72m in restitution to his victims. In rendering her sentence, Wood noted her dismay at how Issa named two of his children after members of the Weston family in an attempt to "ingratiate himself" to the family.

"It is one of the things that really stood out to me here as an aggravating factor, just the degree to which this appears to have been a very personal scheme, at least with respect to the Westons," the judge said.

Issa later appealed his sentence, claiming the victim impact statements that were taken were inadmissible, but his appeal was rejected in December 2021.

Issa was also sued civilly by Weston in the Cook County, Illinois, Circuit Court in 2018 for $100m in damages. Another lawsuit filed against Issa by Weston reportedly charges that he forged his name on bank documents as collateral to obtain a $5m loan using antique Chinese ceramics and other artwork owned by Weston as collateral. The lawsuits remain pending.

'He showed up every day, worked his tail off...'

In an affidavit filed in late December, Travis Madeira described how Lobster Boys purchased lobster in bulk from fishermen in Canada to sell mainly in Canada and the US, storing the crustaceans in temperature-controlled locations in Shag Harbour, Nova Scotia, and Dipper Harbour, New Brunswick.

Historically, the company has sold its lobsters to customers in the Southern District of New York, including in Manhattan, Bronx, Westchester, Rockland, Putnam, Orange, Dutchess and Sullivan counties, generating about $660,000 per year, he said. 

The company's facility in Huntington also has a large storage area for holding lobsters, he said.

Previously, Lobster Boys maintained an additional holding/distribution location in Chicago, Illinois, but that proved to be unprofitable and was closed on or around Jan. 1, 2023, Travis Maderia said in his affidavit. It was the Chicago facility, which incurred a considerable expense due to improvements, that played a large part in the bankruptcy filing, he said.

Issa maintained the alias of "Anthony (Tony) Isaacson" while working at Lobster Boys during a period that overlapped with the investigation and his prosecution in relation to his criminal activities, one source told Undercurrent. The source, who requested anonymity, said he and a handful of other employees resigned from Lobster Boys when they discovered Issa's true identity and the crimes he was accused of committing.

The source said he also left the company because he disapproved of some of the Lobster Boys' business practices.   

He said Issa played a major role in helping to run Lobster Boys while he was there and was integral in helping the company and its related businesses successfully obtain at least six US government-backed loans from the US Small Business Administration's Paycheck Protection Program worth a combined $394,712 in 2020 and 2021.

Based on SBA records maintained by ProPublica and reviewed by Undercurrent, three of the loans worth more than $240,000 have been forgiven. The statuses of loans worth more than $78,000 and nearly $75,000 have not been disclosed.

Justin and Travis Maderia, co-owners of the Lobster Boys, a lobster buyer based in New York with operations also in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, Canada. Image is still from video shared by company on Facebook.

However, if Issa had anything to do with the company's financial struggles, there's no evidence of that in the bankruptcy court filings or in Justin Maderia's letter to the judge.

"Prior to his incarceration Sultan kept his promise, he worked extremely hard and added tremendous value to our business," Justin Maderia wrote. "He showed up every day, worked his tail off, and did all of his work efficiently and well. He helped our business grow significantly."

Justin Maderia said his company gave Issa "a fresh start, and he made the most of it prior to being taken to prison."

Undercurrent has been unsuccessful in efforts to reach the Maderia brothers for comment.

title: ‘Huge reputational damage’ to UK shellfish caused by sewage discharges
content:
The head of the UK's largest shellfish industry group told Undercurrent News the country's repeated sewage dumps into coastal waters are causing "colossal damage" to consumer confidence in eating mussels, oysters and other bivalves.

England and Wales suffer some of the worst quality coastal waters in Europe. When compared with the EU's 27 member countries for coastal water quality, England ranks behind Albania in fifth, based on latest available data. Recently Oxford and Cambridge universities were advised to cancel their annual boat race on the River Thames due to high E. coli levels.

According to an investigation carried out by the UK political party Liberal Democrats, matters worsened last year. Water companies released untreated sewage into designated shellfish harvest areas for 192,000 hours in England, a 20% increase over 2022's 159,000 hours.

Thousands of shellfish acres shut down in Massachusetts over sewage worries

The problem has been blamed on monopolistic water companies and weak regulatory bodies, which has led to chronic underinvestment in the UK's aging sanitation infrastructure, much of which dates back to the Victorian era.

David Jarrad, CEO of the Shellfish Association of Great Britain (SAGB), told Undercurrent the association regularly receives comments on social media from people saying they "wouldn't touch UK shellfish" due to the pollution. This is even though the biggest mussel farms are out to sea and so far from sewage outflows. 

"Last year, we ran a short promotional program on Facebook, and we had a huge number of comments about how they wouldn't touch UK shellfish due to the pollution in the waters," Jarrad said. "Huge reputational damage is being done by water pollution, not just to the bivalve shellfish sector, like mussels, oysters, and clams, but to the wider seafood industry," he said.

The pollution adds additional costs to the £22 million ($27.6m) British shellfish industry, which farms 12,200 metric tons of mussels and 3,000t of oysters annually. When sewage is discharged, farms may be forced to temporarily close or harvest prematurely. Cleaning shellfish also takes time and labor.

Purple zone - designated area for native oyster faming; red dots - Pacific oyster cultivation; green squares - mussel cultivation; star - cockle cultivation. Source: SAGB

X marks where sewage outflows have occurred in the past 48 hours, status on May 6, 2024. Outflows occur mainly after rain. Source: Surfers Against Sewage

The above two maps highlight the problem: sewage outflows are located at regular intervals along the coast of England and Wales, where mussels, oysters, cockles and other shellfish are harvested.

Largely as a result of the discharges, only 9% of England's coastal waters are rated "class A," the highest water quality designation, compared to 30% in Ireland and 35-40% in Spain and Italy, according to Jarrad. After Brexit, the EU stopped accepting B-class shellfish from the UK and now only imports higher-quality A-class products.

John Holmyard, managing director at Offshore Shellfish, told Undercurrent that none of some 750m mussels produced by his company over more than 10 years have been reported as causing illness. 

However, he said he has been forced to temporarily close a mussel farm due to pollution. 

Last November and December, a farm site stretching between three and six miles offshore tested positive for E.coli. This forced the company to halt harvesting twice for two weeks during the busiest time of the year. 

Holmyard said the test coincided with an extended discharge near Exmouth. "The Environment Agency has told us that [water company] South West Water was not responsible. But I think other people take a different view on that," he said.

As a result of the positive test, the farm will need to close for those same two months this year when it is temporarily downgraded from class-A to class-B waters; currently, the company can only export class-A mussels.

"That is hugely disruptive for us as a business," said Holmyard. "During that period we are paying staff and crew. It also means our customers will buy from elsewhere. And will they come back?"

Worst offenders in the south

According to the Liberal Democrats' investigation, the worst polluter is South West Water, which is responsible for the water supply and waste water treatment services throughout Devon and Cornwall, and in small areas of Dorset and Somerset. It doubled the hours of sewage dumped into shellfish water from 50,000 in 2022 to 98,000 last year. Its total sewage spills also rose to 12,900. 

EU shellfish ban leaves UK mussel firm tending potentially unsellable crop

Southern Water -- which is responsible for water works in the southeast, and owned by Australian global financial services group Macquarie Group -- also doubled the hours of sewage discharged to 73,000 hours in 2023.

Fishing hubs Chichester Harbour, Exe and Morecambe Bay were also affected -- they suffered a total of some 15,000 hours of sewage discharged over some 700 spills between them. Overall, since 2020, there have been 108,360 sewage spills into shellfish-designated waters, the investigation found.

Jarrad said the UK government's goal to improve 50% of waters over the next 25 years is "not exactly aspirational," warning that at current pollution levels, "we won't have any industry left." "There's not the urgency we need. Downgraded water quality from sewage dumps can put you out of business," he said.

'Polluter pays' principle

To address the issue, Jarrad said the shellfish industry is calling for the "polluter pays principle" to be enforced on water companies and other sources of pollution like agricultural runoff. This would require polluters to pay cleanup costs and compensate shellfish businesses for lost revenue from harvesting bans and extra product purification expenses.

"Pollution costs our industry as we have to purify the shellfish prior to sale to ensure we sell a clean and healthy product, which is a must to stay in business," Jarrad said. "This is a tangible cost on the shellfish producer to rectify the pollution caused by another party."

Holmyard added that it was important to differentiate types of shellfish farming and consumption. Mussels tend to be eaten cooked and can be farmed offshore, while oysters are typically grown near estuaries and consumed raw. 

"We grow our mussels offshore where the effects of dilution reduce risks from pollution contamination. But currently, one brush is used to tarnish the entire industry," he said. 

A spokesperson for industry body Water UK said: "Water companies understand and sympathize with the issues these businesses and coastal communities are facing, which is why we are proposing to spend £11 billion to reduce spills as quickly as possible, halving spills into shellfish water by 2030."

An environment department (Defra) spokesperson said: "We're already taking action to clean up shellfish sites by driving the water industry to deliver the largest infrastructure program in history -- £60bn over 25 years -- to cut spills by hundreds of thousands each year."

title: New research points to gray whale increase on US West Coast
content:
Researchers with the US' National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) say that, after years of sharp declines, the number of gray whales on the US West Coast have increased 33% just in the past year.

The uptick is significant enough that NOAA researchers have suspended their investigation into what was causing a die-off of the animals between the years 2018 to 2023, the Oregon Capital Chronicle reports. 

There are now an estimated 19,260 gray whales along the West Coast, according to the newspaper, up from the 14,530 whales counted during the same period between 2022 and 2023. That figure was the lowest number of the whales recorded in the region since the early 1970s.

NOAA launched an investigation into the population decline after hundreds of strandings between Mexico and Alaska in 2019, according to the Chronicle. Other deaths were linked to observed malnutrition, along with entanglements with fishing gear and vessel collisions.

While researchers say it seems like the species is entering recovery, they also cautioned that it's still too early to say the whales are in the clear.

title: Canada’s integrity commissioner probes DFO over salmon farming science interference allegations
content:
Harriet Solloway, Canada's public sector integrity commissioner, is launching an investigation into allegations that officials at the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) tried to silence scientists involved in research related to the impact of open-net fish farms on Pacific salmon, the Globe and Mail reports. 

The investigation is in response to concerns raised by Tony Allard, chair of Wild Salmon Forever (WSF), a conservation group based in the province of British Columbia (BC). WSF has been lobbying to move fish farms out of the Pacific Ocean.

In an April 23 letter obtained by the news service, Solloway said she is looking into whether officials may have seriously breached the ethics policy "by attempting to silence scientists through reprimands, to dissuade them from communicating with the media and the public about their research."

The commissioner indicated that she is also reviewing whether DFO officials attempted to obstruct or influence the testimony of scientists who provided evidence to the House of Commons standing committee on fisheries and oceans.

Allard said WSF welcomes the investigation.

"We hope the commissioner's investigation will prompt government to the important work of restoring public trust in DFO science," Allard offered in a prepared statement.

title: US FDA hits Choice Canning with three shrimp import refusals
content:
Add import refusals by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to the list of troubles plaguing the Choice Canning Company, a big Indian shrimp packer and trader.

The FDA, over the weekend, identified Choice Canning Company Unit II, a division of Choice Trading Corp., as one of at least three Indian companies and one Chinese business for which it has stopped 15 shrimp import lines chiefly over adulteration-related concerns.

Under-fire Indian shrimp firm Choice to open new factory

Choice had three entry lines refused for shrimp contaminated with veterinary drug residues by the federal agency's West Coast office on April 4, show FDA online records.

Following the publication of this article, a Choice Canning spokesperson told Undercurrent News that Choice was not actually the company involved in the packing of the shrimp, explaining that another company had taken over its old plant and assumed its identity and registration number. Choice's explanation of the incident can be found here. 

Other Indian companies to have their shrimp refused entry include Kader Exports, Unit 5, and B-One Business House. Kader had one entry line refused by the FDA's West Coast office for containing nitrofurans, veterinary drug residues and filth on April 12. B-One had one entry line refused on April 2 by the FDA northeast office for containing nitrofurans and veterinary drug residues.

Shandong Tongxing Foodstuffs Co., a Chinese company, had 10 entry lines of breaded shrimp refused for being contaminated with veterinary drug residues and unsafe additives by the FDA's West Coast office on April 12, 2024.

US shrimpers file request with CBP to ban Indian imports made with ‘forced labor’

Choice already is facing scrutiny following allegations of falsifying documents, knowingly shipping antibiotic-positive shrimp to the US, and mistreating workers, made by the Outlaw Ocean Project (OOP), the same investigative journalism outfit behind earlier findings of forced labor in China, as reported by Undercurrent News.

OOP published a report in March in which it shared evidence provided by Joshua Farinella, a former general manager at Choice Canning's Amalapuram factory in Andhra Pradesh, who joined in October 2023. The company has denied the allegations, though lawmakers in both chambers of the US Congress have demanded investigations and tariffs, as also reported by Undercurrent.

Indian shrimp supplier accused of labor abuse, antibiotic fraud in new report

The company, in its response to the OOP investigation, made a claim that it can no longer argue; that no Choice Canning shrimp shipment has ever been rejected by the FDA for testing antibiotic-positive.

The firm runs two screening processes for antibiotics. Shrimp that has tested positive on an initial screening has tested negative on second "more vigorous" screenings, the company said.

US domestic industry on the attack

The Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA), a trade association that represents the harvesters and processors of wild-caught US shrimp, is drawing attention to the latest action taken against Choice. SSA, in a press release issued Monday, noted how the FDA stopped a total of 89 seafood entry lines in April.

"All four exporters currently operate under Best Aquaculture Practices certifications," SSA said.

SSA said it received data from the FDA in response to a Freedom of Information Act that indicates that, through the end of fiscal year 2023, the agency sampled had just 21 shipments of shrimp from Choice Canning since fiscal year 2002.

US wild-catch sector pushes to add Indian shrimp to child, forced labor product lists

"Thus, over a span of more than two decades, the FDA had, on average, subjected less than one shipment from the company to the United States each year to testing for banned antibiotics," it observed. "In sum, the example of Choice Canning once again highlights the difficulty faced by the FDA in preventing antibiotic-contaminated imported seafood from reaching US consumers at the extremely low levels of testing currently conducted by the agency."

The SSA, in March, submitted a petition to the Department of Labor's Office of Child Labor, Forced Labor and Human Trafficking to have Indian shrimp added to two lists that identify products produced with the use of child or forced labor, as reported by Undercurrent.

title: FDA warns US importer, processor about HACCP violations
content:
Euro USA, an importer and distributor of specialty food and fresh seafood, has been issued a warning letter by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for serious violations at its seafood processing facility in Cleveland, Ohio.

The violations were discovered during an inspection conducted from July 10 to July 25, 2023, and were detailed in a letter dated Nov. 22, 2023. The FDA publicized the letter only months later, on April 16, as is the protocol, reported Foodsafetynews.com.

The FDA said it found significant deviations from seafood Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) regulations and good manufacturing practices, as well as hazard analysis and risk-based preventive controls for human food regulation (CGMP & PC rule). These violations render the fish and fishery products adulterated, potentially posing risks to public health, FDA said in its warning letter.

Critical violations identified in the warning letter include inadequate HACCP plans and critical limits, failure to implement monitoring procedures as specified in the HACCP plans and deficiencies in corrective actions following deviations from critical limits. The FDA also cited Euro USA for failing to monitor sanitation conditions and practices with sufficient frequency to ensure compliance with current good manufacturing practice requirements.

Among the seafood identified in the warning letter were shucked and raw scallops in cans and pasteurized crabmeat as well as scombroid fish.

In response to the FDA's findings, Euro USA said it was reviewing its HACCP plans and would make necessary revisions. However, the FDA deemed this response inadequate, as corrective actions had yet to be implemented and no timeframe was provided to complete revisions, the publication reported.

title: Japan’s salmon supply likely to drop below 400,000t for first time in years
content:
The following story is from Suisan Keizai, Japan's leading newspaper specializing in seafood and fisheries, in partnership with Undercurrent News.

The total supply of salmon and trout to Japan will likely reach some 385,000 metric tons for the 2023/24 season (from May to April) -- below the 400,000t level for the first time in recent years.

This is largely due to an unexpected significant reduction in harvests of Hokkaido chum salmon and a continuous decrease in imports, while the carryover inventory from the previous season was about 10,000t higher.

Meanwhile, domestic consumption is estimated to be around 301,290t, just barely surpassing the 300,000t mark. This estimate could fluctuate depending on whether exports turn out to be higher than expected or if the inventory at the end of April surpasses expectations. For example, if the inventory remained at 80,000t, consumption could drop to 290,000t.

Skills: Chilean salmon prices for US, Brazil soften further

In short, the supply and demand situation for the 2023/24 season continues in the vein of recent years, with both shrinking. Considering the persistently unfavorable exchange rate environment and high international prices, the upcoming 2024/25 season is expected to face similarly challenging headwinds.

The relentless decrease in supply is largely due to the Hokkaido autumn chum salmon, which once accounted for 30% of the total supply but now only makes up 15%. Expectations raised by the previous year's recovery were quickly dashed, leading to a reassessment of supply, bringing back high prices.

There are growing concerns about the decline in salmon returns to the Tohoku and Sanriku regions, which have compensated for unforeseen shortages in Hokkaido in recent years. The lack of returns has even made collecting fish eggs for release impossible.

Moreover, pink salmon -- primarily from set-net fishing in the Sea of Okhotsk -- have also become scarce, necessitating urgent investigation into the causes beyond just abnormal rises in sea temperatures.

Imports, ranging from fresh salmon for sashimi to frozen fillets and processed products like smoked salmon, continue to decrease. It's estimated that the quantity imported during the "salmon year" from May to April will be around 214,500t, about 6% less than the previous salmon year.

Downward trend continues

In the calendar year from January to December, imports totaled 212,900t for 2023, fresh, frozen, and processed products combined. This was 12% less than the previous year's 240,000t. Specifically, imports of farmed salmon from Chile dropped sharply from 95,000t, with an additional reduction in shipments of frozen fillets and air-freighted fresh fish.

The decline in air-freighted salmon is attributed to the persistent high prices and the chronic rise in transportation costs since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and the depreciation of the Japanese yen.

Both Norway and Chile, major producers of Atlantic salmon, have experienced stagnant production, tightening the supply-demand balance internationally and affecting prices of Chilean salmon, sockeye salmon, and trout in Japan.

Notably, Chile’s farmed coho salmon was once predominantly destined for Japan but has increasingly diverted to other markets in recent years. Chilean farmers shipped over 40% of production to other markets for the 2022/23 season, and it's estimated that up to half could be shipped outside Japan for the current season.

Coho salmon for other markets

However, Chile’s supply of coho salmon to Japan is expected to be around 85,000t for the May to April period, unchanged from a year ago. This is because Chilean farmers prioritize large-sized fish production with a focus beyond Japan, thus ensuring that the supply to Japan doesn't diminish significantly.

Chilean shipments of farmed trim-C coho to Japan decline 30%

Nevertheless, if the shortage of Atlantic salmon persists, relatively cheaper Chilean fillets may flood markets in North America and Brazil as substitutes, posing continued uncertainty. The production of farmed coho salmon in Chile for the 2024/25 season is expected to be similar to the previous season, with some farmers shrinking or withdrawing from farming coho salmon operations while others aim for expansion.

As a significantly cheaper market compared to other countries, Japan may not be prioritized in the future.

Meanwhile, sockeye salmon supply was ample for the 2023/24 season, as Japan procured the depressed-priced Alaskan fish, which was carried over from the previous season. For the upcoming season from May, Japan will likely secure over 10,000t from Russia as usual, depending on fishing conditions.

In North America, the outlook for sockeye harvesting in Bristol Bay, a major supplying region in Alaska, sees a reduction to 2.5 million fish for the 2024 season from last summer's 4.05m fish (about 100,000t). This quantity might not even satisfy local demands.

The US has depleted its inventories of frozen sockeye salmon. With the current currency exchange rate, Japan might not be able to purchase fish for the 2024 season, with a possibility of a sharp decline to 2,000t or 3,000t.

Skills: Chilean salmon prices for US, Brazil soften further

The only stable supply comes from domestic farmed salmon in Miyagi, Iwate, Sakaiminato and other regions, with a small share in the overall salmon supply. It doesn't have a significant impact due to a large proportion being sold fresh. Rather, concerns arise about the effect of seawater temperature, with a trend of earlier shipments observed annually. Reductions in production are anticipated in Miyagi this year.

It's necessary to pay attention to whether land-based farming and the expanding sea-based aquaculture across the country will eventually take up a portion of the supply without being swayed by climate and exchange rates, Suisan Keizai added.

title: Untitled
content:
BARCELONA, Spain -- The recent decision from the US to abstain from imposing preliminary countervailing duty rates on shrimp imports from Indonesia has been met with relief within the industry, Jala Tech CEO Liris Maduningtya told Undercurrent News. 

"This decision signifies a promising turn of events for all those involved in the import-export dynamics between Indonesia and the US," she said. "Moreover, this development is expected to have a positive impact on US-Indonesia market dynamics moving forward."

If imposed, the duties could have led to import tariffs as high as 37.36% for Indonesian shrimp, the industry feared.

"The US market constitutes a substantial portion of Indonesia's total shrimp exports -- around 70% -- so this was very worrying, with producers experiencing declining prices and some even halting production due to increased uncertainty," she also explained.

As earlier reported by Undercurrent, the Department of Commerce (DOC) has been investigating the US' four largest shrimp source nations for allegations of illegal subsidies made by its domestic harvesters. In advance of a final determination expected by Aug. 5, DOC, on April 1, began requiring importers of shrimp from Ecuador, Vietnam and India to pay preliminary CVD rates ranging from 1.69% to 196.41%.   

However, DOC issued a negative preliminary determination for the Indonesian companies, Bahari Makmur Sejati, known as BMS (0.39%) and First Marine (0.71%), however. No deposit will be required.

US Commerce Department makes public, explains correction made to Santa Priscila, Ecuador CVD rates

A separate investigation is being conducted against Ecuador and Indonesia over alleged dumping violations, however, preliminary rates related to those aren't expected to be known until May.

Still, DOC's early actions are providing some relief to the Indonesian shrimp industry.

"Now that the preliminary decision is positive and is out there, we expect prices to get better for Indonesian shrimp," Maduningtya said.

According to the data available on Undercurrent's prices portal as part of a partnership with Jala, Indonesian shrimp prices are experiencing a rebound across most sizes, reflecting a recovery in the market in week 16 (April 15-21) of 2024. 

Thus, average prices across Indonesia increased to over IDR 80,000/kg and IDR 75,100/kg for 30- and 40-count shrimp.

Prices for 50, 60 and 70 counts also rose to IDR 67,200/kg, IDR 63,600/kg and IDR 59,500/kg, as did the price for 100 counts to IDR/kg.

Following a different trend, the price for 80-count shrimp stayed mostly flat at IDR 56,300/kg, while the price for 90 counts saw a slight drop to IDR 53,000/kg.

In dollars (see the second chart below), prices were $4.94/kg and $4.64/kg for 30- and 40-counts; $4.15/kg and $3.93/kg for 50 and 60-counts; $3.67/kg and $3.48/kg for 70 and 80-counts; and $3.27/kg and $3.21/kg for 90 and 100-counts.

Upgrade to Pro to view

Taking a closer look at 60-count, farm-gate shrimp prices from other origins, Indonesian shrimp prices remain among the highest globally. In week 16, shrimp prices in Indonesia stood at almost $4/kg, ranking them as the third highest globally after Chinese and Vietnamese shrimp.

The price for 60-count vannamei shrimp from Thailand, which ranked fourth, fell to $3.53/kg, while the price for same-sized shrimp in India's Andhra Pradesh mainly stayed flat at around $3.20/kg.

Comparatively, Ecuadorian shrimp prices remain the lowest in the world at $3.05/kg and $2.70/kg for 50/60 and 60/70 counts.

Indonesia to expand market reach

One critical aspect for Indonesia is establishing "a more substantial brand presence" in global markets, Maduningtya also told Undercurrent during the Seafood Expo Global show held here, April 23-25. 

She emphasized the importance of establishing a more substantial brand presence in global markets and called for more governmental aid and new initiatives to enhance Indonesia's international reputation in seafood production.

"I am very disappointed with Indonesia's lack of branding," she said. "It is key, and we need more governmental aid and new initiatives to help us improve our international reputation in seafood production. We are missing out on numerous chances to achieve something truly remarkable."

Maduningtyas also outlined Jala's strategic vision for 2024, emphasizing continued investment in Indonesia's shrimp industry through digitalization, financing, and market expansion. 

"We in Jala will continue to focus on enhancing traceability and sustainability through technology, enabling consumers to trace origins and farming practices directly from product packaging," she said. 

Indonesia shrimp. Credit; Jala Tech

When discussing potential expansion into new species or international markets, Maduningtyas reiterated Jala's commitment to consolidating its position within the shrimp sector in Indonesia.

She emphasized the vast potential for growth and development within the country's shrimp market, indicating that Jala's primary focus "remains on maximizing opportunities domestically."

"We need a shift in focus from reliance on export markets to the development of domestic consumption and be more aware of the risks associated with depending solely on global markets," she also told Undercurrent. 

Data from Statistics Indonesia indicates that the Indonesian shrimp market faces hurdles in achieving this target. Despite the nation's vast coastal resources and rich aquaculture heritage, shrimp consumption per capita remains relatively low, with an average of 430 grams per capita.

"The overreliance on exports, coupled with the sluggish uptake of shrimp within the domestic market, presents challenges to the viability of vannamei shrimp farming. Fluctuations in the global market further exacerbate these difficulties, highlighting the urgent need for diversified strategies," Maduningtya pointed out.

"Efforts to address these challenges are underway, focusing on boosting domestic consumption, improving production techniques, and enhancing market access both locally and internationally. However, we need more governmental aid in achieving these goals and overcoming the obstacles facing Indonesia's shrimp industry," she concluded.

title: US Commerce Department makes public, explains correction made to Santa Priscila, Ecuador CVD rates
content:
The US Department of Commerce (DOC) on Thursday (April 25) made official and explained its big correction to the preliminary countervailing duty (CVD) rates being charged importers of frozen warmwater shrimp sold by Industrial Pesquera Santa Priscila, Ecuador's largest shrimp exporter, and other Ecuadorian shrimp producers.

"Based on comments filed by interested parties in this investigation, Commerce is amending the preliminary affirmative [CVD] determination on shrimp from Ecuador to correct significant ministerial errors," DOC's International Trade Administration (ITA) declared in its latest Federal Register notice.

As a result of the changes, Santa Priscila's preliminary CVD rate drops from 13.41% to 2.89%, ITA confirmed. That also has resulted in a reduction in the CVD rate charged importers of other Ecuador shrimp producers from 7.55% to 2.89%.

Also, ITA has confirmed that because the preliminary CVD rate charged Ecuador's Sociedad Nacional de Galapagos (Songa) is at 1.69%, below the 2% threshold, it now qualifies as "de minimus" and, therefore, its shrimp exports are not subject to an early cash deposit requirement. 

US makes big reduction to preliminary CVD rates charged for Ecuador shrimp

As first reported by Undercurrent News nearly a week ago, DOC called parties involved with the alleged illegal subsidy case on Friday afternoon (April 19) to inform them that they discovered an error made in calculating the illegal subsidies allegedly paid to Santa Priscila by the Ecuadorian government, according to sources.

Ecuador is one of four countries, along with India, Vietnam and Indonesia, under investigation by DOC for illegal subsidies. Final determinations are expected by Aug. 5, the same as the due date for final determinations in relation to anti-dumping duty cases also brought against both Ecuador and Indonesia. 

The cases were initiated following petitions filed by the American Shrimp Processors Association (ASPA), a group that represents US harvesters and processors behind roughly 85% of the US' domestic frozen warmwater shrimp production. They claim the low prices charged for imported farmed shrimp were enabled by programs organized by the exporters' nations and have caused prices for domestic shrimp to also crash.

Despite much speculation that the Ecuador rates were in error, DOC, on April 1, posted notices in the Federal Register that maintained the earlier preliminary rates, putting them into effect on that date, as reported by Undercurrent.

In addition to the actions taken against shrimp from Ecuador, importers of shrimp from India were required to deposit 4.72% of the amount paid for products supplied by Devi Sea Foods, 3.89% from Sandhya Aqua Exports, and 4.36% from all other Indian suppliers. For shrimp from Vietnam, the deposit requirement is 2.84% for Stapimex, 196.41% for Thong Thuan, and 2.84% for all other Vietnamese suppliers.

DOC issued a negative preliminary determination for the Indonesian companies, Bahari Makmur Sejati, known as BMS (0.39%) and First Marine (0.71%), however. No deposit was required.

The changes to Ecuador's rate are retroactively in effect as of April 1, ITA clarified in the Federal Register posting. The rates imposed on India, Vietnam and Indonesia have not been amended. 

'Timely-filed ministerial error allegations'

Jose Antonio Camposano, executive president of the Camara Nacional de Acuacultura (CNA), the trade association that represents Ecuador's shrimp producers, explained to Undercurrent earlier this week how DOC got Santa Priscila's CVD rate wrong. Instead of looking at the company's tax level to assess a CVD rate, the DOC mistakenly looked at its income, he said.

"They looked at the wrong line [in Santa Priscila's figures]," Camposano said. "We knew right away it was a mistake. It is important to note that the size of a company does not influence the outcome of countervailing duty determinations."

US corrects ‘administrative error’ which put bumper duty on Ecuador’s Santa Priscila

In its Federal Register posting, DOC more thoroughly explained the error.

"Specifically, when calculating a countervailable subsidy rate attributable to Santa Priscila under the Tax Incentives for Priority Sectors under the 2010 Organic Production Code (Priority Sectors) program, we inadvertently used the wrong tax deduction amount with which to calculate the benefit attributable to Santa Priscila under the Priority Sectors Program," DOC said.

"Further, we inadvertently calculated a countervailable subsidy rate attributable to Santa Priscila under both the Priority Sectors program and the Investment Contract program that should have only been calculated pursuant to one program, i.e., the Priority Sectors Program."

DOC said it was influenced by letters received from the Ecuador shrimp industry.

"From March 28 through April 2, 2024, we received timely-filed ministerial error allegations from Industrial Pesquera Santa Priscila S.A. (Santa Priscila), Sociedad Nacional de Galápagos C.A. (SONGA), the petitioner, and the government of Ecuador (GOE). Santa Priscila, SONGA, and the GOE alleged in their ministerial error allegations that Commerce made significant ministerial errors in the preliminary determination with respect to Santa Priscila and SONGA's subsidy rates."

title: Report: South Korean supermarkets sold seafood produced by North Korean labor in China
content:
Seafood produced by North Korean workers in China was sold in major South Korean supermarkets, violating United Nations sanctions, reports Chosunilbo. 

Over 420 metric tons of seafood items -- including clams, squid, Alaska pollock and sea cucumbers -- were confirmed to have been processed by North Korean laborers at three Chinese seafood companies and exported to South Korea from 2020-2022. The products arrived at Busan Port from Dalian Port in China before distribution across the country.

The revelations -- which are based on an investigation by Outlaw Ocean Project in February -- found seafood processed by North Korean forced labor was sold at major South Korean supermarkets and online retailers. Products exported by Dandong Taihua, a Chinese processor, received positive ratings on a major supermarket's website. 

The plants in the report were predominantly located in Donggang, Liaoning province, close to the China-North Korea border.

While South Korea lacks laws specifically barring imports produced by North Korean forced labor, the US has sanctioned several Chinese companies for employing North Koreans.

title: Arnarlax’s ISK 120m fine for fish farming violations confirmed
content:
On April 11, a ruling by Iceland's ministry of agriculture, food and consumer affairs confirmed a decision by the Food Agency to impose an administrative fine of ISK 120 million ($849,077) against salmon farmer Arnarlax. 

This penalty was upheld due to the firm's failure to report the removal of farmed fish from a pen in Arnarfjiordur, a large fjord in the Westfjords region of Iceland, in June 2022, resulting in the unaccounted removal of 81,564 salmon.

The investigation revealed discrepancies following the slaughter of fish in October 2022. Despite initially recording 33,097 discarded fish, only 18,315 salmon were identified post-slaughter, highlighting a substantial loss of fish from the hatchery, where 132,976 salmon had been introduced between October 2020 and July 2021.

Arnarlax had reported a hole in one at-sea net pen in August 2021, and the company's response was deemed compliant with requirements for such incidents. However, investigations following the October 2022 slaughter revealed significant deviations in feeding since June 2021, preceding the reported incident by two months.

"This discrepancy should have raised suspicions within the company about potential issues affecting the fish population," said the Food Agency. 

The investigation determined that these violations posed "a serious threat to wild commercial stocks and the environment, contravening the Act on Fish Farming's objectives of promoting responsible fish farming and protecting wild commercial stocks."

title: US makes big reduction to preliminary CVD rates charged for Ecuador shrimp
content:
The US Department of Commerce (DOC) is making significant reductions to the preliminary countervailing duty (CVD) rates it earlier announced for frozen warmwater shrimp imported from Ecuador, Undercurrent News has been informed by multiple sources.

DOC officials called parties involved with the case on Friday afternoon (April 19) to inform them that they discovered an error made in calculating the illegal subsidies allegedly paid to Industrial Pesquera Santa Priscila, Ecuador's largest shrimp exporter, by its government, according to sources.

As a result, the Commerce officials said, they are reducing the preliminary CVD rates for which importers must make cash deposits to 2.89% from 13.41%.

The US agency is maintaining the preliminary 1.69% rate it charged for shrimp bought from Ecuador's Sociedad Nacional de Galapagos, known as Songa. However, the officials have now clarified that because Songa's rate is below 2%, it now qualifies as "de minimus" and, therefore, is not subject to a cash deposit requirement. 

Also, as a result of the change, shrimp purchased from other Ecuadorian companies will now come with a preliminary CVD rate of 2.89% instead of the earlier-ordered 7.55%.

Undercurrent was the first to report on March 26 that DOC had called parties involved in the investigation of illegal subsidies paid to companies in four of the US' biggest import source nations to inform them that importers of shrimp from three of them would be forced to pay preliminary CVD rates (Ecuador, India and Vietnam) pending a final investigation. 

Ecuador shrimp sector body hopes 13.41% US preliminary duty for Santa Priscila is ‘error’

Indonesian companies received a negative disposition, meaning no preliminary CVD rates are required for shrimp from that country.

Final CVD determinations are expected to be issued by no later than Aug. 5, 2024, the same date as final determinations in relation to anti-dumping duty cases also brought against both Ecuador and Indonesia. 

Many involved in the US shrimp import sector were hopeful that DOC might declare the preliminary CVD rate for Santa Priscila to be in error and reduce it. Others maintained that the high rate was not a mistake, pointing to Santa Priscila's very high quantity of directly owned farms.

DOC, on April 2, posted notices in the Federal Register that maintained the earlier preliminary rates, putting them into effect on that date, as reported by Undercurrent. 

DOC has yet to publish a new Federal Register notice to confirm the reduction of preliminary CVD rates. 

Three of four largest US shrimp source nations hit with preliminary countervailing duties

The CVD and AD rates are the result of a petition filed against the four countries' shrimp exporters by the American Shrimp Processors Association (ASPA), a group that represents US harvesters and processors behind roughly 85% of the US' domestic frozen warmwater shrimp production.

ASPA argued that the low prices charged for imported farmed shrimp were enabled by programs organized by the exporters' nations and have caused prices for domestic shrimp to also crash.

title: Peruvian fishermen question irregular entry of Chinese vessel into national waters
content:
On the night of April 18, around a hundred artisanal fishermen from the port of Chimbote in the Ancash region of Peru were forced to halt their fishing activities. This occurred due to the unexpected appearance of a large Chinese fishing vessel, as reported by the Peruvian national artisanal fisheries trade body, also known as Sonapescal. 

Despite being thousands of kilometers from its home waters, the vessel "sailed nonchalantly as if under a protected status," prompting serious scrutiny and concern, according to a Sonapescal's statement sent to Undercurrent News. 

The Peruvian fishermen who witnessed their work disrupted quickly documented the incident with photographs and shared them on social media. The unusual encounter swiftly went viral, drawing widespread public attention in Peru.

Photo: Sonapescal.

The vessel in question was identified as the Chinese ship JIN HAI 728, boasting a 500 cubic meter cargo hold and a length of 45 meters, owned by the Zhoushan Jin Hai Ocean Fishery company. This vessel is licensed for squid fishing in international waters under the South Pacific Regional Fisheries Management Organization (SPRFMO). Peru is also a member of the SPRFMO.

Sonapescal mentioned in its statement a recent investigation carried out by American journalist Ian Urbina, a Pulitzer Prize winner, which covered the JIN HAI 728 in the Outlaw Ocean Project.

Urbina's investigations previously included a 2019 video capturing the vessel's crew placing a dying Indonesian crew member in a coffin instead of providing medical assistance, Sonapescal pointed out.

Henry Juarez, president of the Peruvian association of artisanal fishermen and shipowners of Caleta de Parachique in Sechura, recalled past incidents where Chinese vessels deactivated their satellite systems to fish in Peruvian waters illegally.

Juarez explained that those incidents gained global attention, leading the government to issue Supreme Decree No. 016-2020-PRODUCE, requiring foreign vessels fishing for squid in international waters to install Peruvian government-monitored satellite tracking if they wish to utilize Peruvian maintenance services.

This regulation significantly reduced the number of Chinese vessels entering Peruvian ports annually. However, since the visit of the Chinese ambassador to former fisheries and aquaculture vice minister Desilu Leon, now secretary-general of Peru's production ministry, Chinese vessels have resumed entering without satellite monitoring, said Juarez.

Peru's general directorate of supervision, inspection, and sanction confirmed through a memorandum that the JIN HAI 728 (see photo above) has been docked in Chimbote since April 4, entering Peru without using the required satellite device mandated by law, according to Sonapescal. The vessel declared its presence in Peru was solely for crew change purposes.

Global Fishing Watch, a public access portal, also reported that the vessel ceased transmitting its coordinates, making its whereabouts untraceable until reported by local fishermen, according to Sonapescal.

"A crew change does not take over two weeks, nor should such operations occur within a shipyard's dry dock. There appears to be a willful facilitation of irregular vessel entries," Juarez said.

Reports from 2023 by the satellite technology organization Artis0nal indicate similar unauthorized entries of twelve Chinese vessels.

Sonapescal urged the newly appointed production minister to take decisive action on this matter.

"If Gonzalez wishes to make a difference, he must demand these vessels comply with the satellite monitoring requirements," Juarez said.

title: Viciunai finally sells Russian factory
content:
Lithuanian surimi giant Viciunai Group has finally sold its factory in Sovetsk, Kaliningrad, bringing its two-year sales process to an end, it confirmed to Undercurrent News.

Report: Viciunai finds buyer for Russian operations

Viciunai has said it has been trying to sell the plant since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022.

While not officially confirmed by the company, reports in Russian media said that Russia's Ocean Group Management Company -- acting on behalf of Unifrost -- had been looking to finalize a deal for the Sovetsk plant earlier this month.

The unnamed "Eastern" buyer has also acquired the right to use the 'VICI' trademark in CIS country's territories. To avoid confusion, Viciunai said it would "gradually transform" the VICI trademark as it expanded the group's brand portfolio. 

"Starting the process, we did not know it would be so complicated," Viciunai said, in a statement.

"Buyers changed, opinions of permitting institutions shifted, and media pressure varied. Simply leaving the factory to operate alone and leaving was not possible due to threats from power structures to the employees and unfulfilled obligations to credit institutions and partners."

"Starting the sale, we did not know what principles the Russian government would apply in its financial war without rules. Therefore, everything took time, but now we want to inform you, colleagues, that we have sold a factory operating in the Kaliningrad region of Russia, logistics and trading companies, and completely withdrawn from Russia and other countries belonging to the Commonwealth of Independent States markets."

The group goes on to describe the deal as "the most difficult deal in the life of Viciunai."

"And the first feeling at its completion is not joy but relief," Viciunai added. "It is obvious that we were playing not our own game, according to foreign rules or without them at all, so we can only state that we succeeded and thank the advisors and the team of company specialists, who had enough professionalism and determination to move consistently in the same direction. Thank you all for your support and for being with us during the hardest times."

Sale comes amid sanction furore

News of the deal's completion comes a week after a Lithuanian media investigation found Viciunai had transported goods sanctioned as high-priority battlefield goods to its Russian factory on 10 separate occasions.

Lithuanian retailers may drop Viciunai after reports firm violated Russian sanctions

Viciunai did not deny the claims but argued that the goods were intended for food processing equipment and were not sold outside the group, adding that had not appreciated they were sanctioned.

A subsequent investigation by Lithuania's customs department is now underway, aiming to determine whether Viciunai knowingly breached trade sanctions.

Maxima Group, one of the largest retail chains in the Baltics, has said will consider terminating its contract with Viciunai if the customs investigation finds proof of wrongdoing, while other retailers such as Rimi and Lidl have said they are already moving to other non-Viciunai surimi suppliers.

The Sovetsk plant has also been highly profitable for the firm; LRT reported earlier this year that Viciunai-Rus's turnover exceeded €183m ($198.3m) in 2023, and profits reached €12.8m.

Furthermore, for its continued involvement in Russia since the war began, Ukraine added Viciunai to its list of 'International Sponsors of War' earlier this year.

title: Human rights group urges Indian gov’t, shrimp sector to probe supply chains
content:
After the Seafood Exporters Association of India (SEAI) questioned the March reports into alleged labor abuses in the Indian shrimp sector, first the Associated Press (AP) and now the Corporate Accountability Lab (CAL) have responded.

"The [SEAI] recently tried to dismiss out of hand the findings of separate reports that found labor abuses in the Indian shrimp industry. CAL, author of one of those reports, is an independent, not-for-profit human rights organization with extensive experience carrying out in-depth investigations into labor abuses in supply chains. CAL does not accept funding from private companies or industry associations, and our investigative findings are entirely independent of any industry actor. We conducted our study of Indian shrimp carefully, and we stand by that study."

Indian trade body says recent ‘forced labor’ report was ‘shot through with flaws’

It urged the Indian government and relevant industry actors to conduct immediate supply chain investigations and to rectify any abuses in accordance with domestic and international norms.

"Companies should not wait for reporters and non-profit organizations to expose their shortcomings. They should take proactive measures to ensure their supply chains are ethical and that the impacted workers are treated decently and fairly."

CAL's report alleged unsafe and forced labor conditions in the Indian shrimp processing sector. SEAI has disagreed with the findings on a number of points, but its chief claim is that CAL and AP have conflated "rogue operators" whose product never makes it to the export market with established firms that sell to the US and EU.

SEAI has suggested the lack of specific details in the reporting about where and when incidents occurred and to whom undermine its credibility.

US shrimpers file request with CBP to ban Indian imports made with ‘forced labor’

"While investigating abuses in the Indian shrimp sector, we found that workers, who are primarily from vulnerable populations, were often too scared of retaliation to speak openly about their work," said CAL.

"CAL's Indian investigators -- many of whom are experienced journalists -- invested extensive time and energy building trust with workers during many field visits to Andhra Pradesh. Including identifiable information about workers who chose to speak with us in our report would be a violation of that trust. CAL's responsibility to these workers is to ensure their identities remain anonymous so that they do not face repercussions. The need to make the information about abuses in the Indian shrimp sector public, as a first step toward improving conditions in the sector, must be balanced against the need to protect our sources."

CAL said its goal in publishing this report was to bring to light systemic issues in the Indian shrimp sector so that they can be addressed appropriately by Indian producers, US buyers, and their respective governments.

"We hope that Indian and US companies engaged in producing and buying Indian shrimp take a hard look at widespread, abusive practices and make changes to ensure that workers are adequately compensated, able to work under safe conditions, and treated as a matter of course in a respectful and dignified manner. The report urges US companies to maintain relationships with Indian shrimp suppliers and cooperatively implement changes to end widespread, abusive practices."

title: UK’s largest scampi firm buys first vessel, names skipper fleet manager
content:
The UK's largest producer of scampi (breaded nephrops tails) has acquired its first vessel -- the Northern Ireland-based Golden Ray -- with a view to growing its fleet in the future, it told Undercurrent News.

Skipper Darren McClements, who has been fishing for over 37 years, will join Whitby's Northern Irish firm Kilkeel Seafoods as fleet operations director. As suggested by the title, Whitby's "long-term investment strategy" is to own more vessels, it confirmed.

The Golden Ray

McClements was a "Fisherman of the year" winner at the 2023 Fishing News Awards, nominated for "undertaking leading work for the industry," which included collaborating with Whitby and SafetyNet Technologies on "ground-breaking gear trials," it said.

"The announcement is further evidence of Whitby Seafoods' commitment to improving welfare and innovation on fishing boats. This is part of a long-term investment strategy for the business and the first boat the company will own outright."

The Golden Ray has partnered with Whitby to undertake many fishing gear trials, including work on a number of gear selectivity devices, catch handling innovation and more efficient propulsion.

New technologies being tested on the boat could give clear sight of the fishing grounds so the Golden Ray can head directly to the best fishing areas to reduce fuel usage and the impact on the sea bed, said the scampi business.

"This important purchase means we can showcase best practice in gearing and technology and the highest welfare standards," said Whitby managing director Daniel Whittle.

"This investment shows Whitby Seafoods’ tangible commitment to provide real on-the-water solutions to further improve the welfare of fishers and the sustainability of scampi, the dish we are famous for."

Whitby recently announced it had coordinated a cross-industry agreement to move to an "In Transition to MSC" [Marine Stewardship Council] fishery improvement scheme to gain accreditation for scampi caught in the waters around the British Isles.

The first in-person meeting of the project will take place in Edinburgh, Scotland, on April 30.

The UK's nephrops fishery has come under scrutiny lately. A fishery improvement project (FIP) was established in 2018, spearheaded by FIP organizer Project UK, which itself counts the MSC as its secretariat.

Scottish NGO Open Seas recently claimed that major UK retailers, including The Co-operative Group, Waitrose & Partners, Marks & Spencer, and Whitby Seafoods itself, had missed a reporting deadline for assessing human rights abuses in their scampi supply chains.

Whitby said the move to join the "In Transition" scheme was a "pioneering agreement between the scampi fishermen of England, Scotland and Northern Ireland," and that it was a "vital step in our mission to ensure sustainability lies at the heart of the UK’s scampi fishery."

Late in 2023, Whitby abandoned merger plans after a regulator warned it could lead to a price hike for customers.

The company confirmed to Undercurrent it would no longer proceed with its proposed acquisition of Kilhorne Bay Seafoods after the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) referred the deal for a "phase-two investigation," citing price and quality concerns.

title: Lithuanian retailers may drop Viciunai after reports firm violated Russian sanctions
content:
Major Lithuanian retail chains, including Maxima Group, have said they will drop surimi giant Viciunai Group's products from their shelves if proof emerges that the company violated sanctions to sell goods to Russia, reports LRT.

Report: Viciunai finds buyer for Russian operations

The original LRT investigation alleges that Viciunai transported goods sanctioned as high-priority battlefield goods to Russia on 10 occasions, such as bearings used in tank production, specifically to a factory located in Sovetsk, within the Kaliningrad region.

Viciunai acknowledges that it transported the goods, but claims it did not know they were sanctioned. This export route was stopped as soon as the company learned of the sanction's existence, and an internal investigation launched, it said.

Viciunai's Russian plant is supplied with European goods via Lithuania, and more than €5 million worth of such goods have been transported to the factory since the war began.

Following the announcement, Lithuania's customs department said it would start its own investigation into the matter and whether the firm had breached sanctions, reports Delfi.

Multiple Lithuanian members of parliament have also written to the prosecutor general's office requesting a pre-trial investigation into the business of Plunges kooperatine prekyba, the part of Viciunai responsible for the transport of sanctioned battlefield goods.

Now, retail chains have weighed in on possible reaction if the customs department finds proof the sanctions were breached.

Maxima released a statement saying it would "consider" terminating its contract with Viciunai if the department found proof of wrongdoing. Rimi has already said it will launch private-label crab sticks made using surimi from non-Viciunai suppliers in the summer, and Lidl said the number of private-branded products produced for them by Viciunai is steadily decreasing.

For its part, Viciunai said the sanctioned products moved to its Kaliningrad factory were not intended for battlefield use but for the maintenance of food processing equipment and not sold outside the group.

Viciunai finds buyer for Russian plant

Viciunai has found itself under considerable scrutiny since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, as the company is perceived to have dragged its heels over the end of its Russian operations.

Viciunai’s Russian arm made €12.8m in 2023 as search for buyer continues

The firm said it had finally found a buyer for its plant in Kaliningrad in April, reportedly Russia's Ocean Group Management Company, acting on behalf of Unifrost.

Viciunai has consent from Russian authorities to sell a plant with a capacity of more than 120,000 metric tons of finished product per year, it reports.

The plant has been highly profitable for the firm; LRT reported earlier this year that Viciunai-Rus's turnover exceeded €183m ($198.3m) in 2023, and profits reached €12.8m.

According to data provided by the "STOP Trade in Russia" initiative, known for scrutinizing economic activities in Russia, Viciunai-Rus could have contributed €23.2m to the Russian budget in 2023.

For its continued involvement in Russia, Ukraine also added Viciunai to its list of 'International Sponsors of War' earlier this year.

title: Indian trade body says recent ‘forced labor’ report was ‘shot through with flaws’
content:
The Seafood Exporters Association of India (SEAI) has questioned the integrity of, and motives behind, March reports into alleged labor abuses in the Indian shrimp farming and processing sector.

"It has been clear from the start that an Associated Press [AP] article disparaging the Indian shrimp export industry was shot through with factual flaws and instigated by agenda-driven actors and irresponsible reporting methods that ignored ethical guardrails," claimed Jim McCarthy, SEAI spokesman.

Indian export body says shrimp labor abuse report gives ‘wilfully distorted view’

"As part of our ongoing effort to set the record straight, SEAI sent a detailed request for correction to supervising editors and the AP masthead. Despite a written assurance from editors that the matter would be examined, we have heard nothing from AP in more than two weeks. It appears they have nothing to say for themselves."

Therefore, SEAI has released the letter, which it suggests should make stakeholders wary of the AP's future work.

The AP has now responded and shared its letter to SEAI with Undercurrent News. The news organization is content that none of its reporting was unethical or agenda-driven in any way.

AP did acknowledge that the initial report into working conditions, by Corporate Accountability Lab (CAL), had mentioned seeing shrimp from a peeling shed -- the use of which is generally regarded as unethical for their often poor working conditions -- loaded onto a "NEKKANTI" branded truck, seemingly pulling supplier Nekkanti Sea Foods into the line of fire.

The allegations raised by the CAL's report, "Hidden Harvest: Human Rights and Environmental Abuses in India’s Shrimp Industry," and subsequent article led Sysco Corporation, the largest foodservice distributor in the US, to suspend purchases from Nekkanti, pending further investigation.

That was even before Nekkanti told the AP that it only uses its own factories, and leases out its trucks.

SEAI described this as the AP journalist "publicly accus[ing] one of our members of workplace abuses that in fact occurred at an entirely different company, one that plays no part in the export market."

AP replied: "Responding to your assertion that reporter Martha Mendoza accused one of your members of workplace abuses, this seems to allude to the passage: 'AP journalists observed dozens of women working in unsanitary and dangerous conditions...' The story goes on to say (and to show with photos and video) that 'The shrimp at this facility were later loaded in large plastic crates into a truck with the brand “NEKKANTI” painted in large letters.'"

"The story says managers at the shed said Nekkanti and other major brands often outsource peeling. AP then published Nekkanti’s response to this, including that it only uses its own state-of-the-art processing plants and that it leases out its trucks. We believe by publishing this response, we gave Nekkanti ample opportunity to clarify its involvement," said AP's vice president for standards and editor at large, John Daniszewski.

Alleged conflict of interest

SEAI suggested that what it called errors in reporting have a thread in common: that AP journalist Mendoza is "deceptively conflating well-regulated companies that operate state-of-the-art facilities and export to the US market with rogue actors that do not export to the US market."

US shrimpers file request with CBP to ban Indian imports made with ‘forced labor’

That framing, which "maligns all Indian shrimp operations with no distinctions made, is also the same rhetoric used by the activist foundations that are directly funding AP's reporting on this topic. AP claims its editorial judgment is unaffected by the high seven-figure donations it has received for years from those groups. But in light of the details above, we must ask if you still stand by that declaration?"

Daniszewski assured SEAI that the AP's reporters and editors "are not permitted to be in contact with grant funders, nor do the funders have any rights to influence the journalism that the AP reports, and this is recognized in our grant agreements. The AP is solely responsible for the stories that it transmits."

The American Shrimp Processors Association (ASPA) has just filed a request with the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to ban imports of shrimp from India allegedly made with "forced labor," as required under section 307 of the Tariff Act of 1930.

It has also filed an allegation with the US government, arguing that the government of India's failure to enforce its most basic labor laws provides a subsidy to Indian shrimp producers, according to a press release.

AP story put together in 'troubling way'

SEAI's letter, signed by president Pawan Kumar, states the organization has taken issue with a "series of factual inaccuracies and errors in reporter Martha Mendoza’s recent article on our industry," as well as raising concerns about the "troubling way that story was put together."

"Ms. Mendoza never contacted our group at any time, and so we have been obliged to ourselves retrace the various situations and settings that are described in her piece.  We discovered many disturbing discrepancies."

Sysco stops buying from Indian shrimp supplier after reports allege environmental, labor issues in sector

The AP's Daniszewski replied: "[SEAI] was not approached for comment because we were unaware of your organization’s existence. However, each company mentioned in the story was approached for comment in keeping with AP standards. None of them referred us to your association for comment."

The SEAI also took issue with AP reporting that "another member company 'destroyed critical ecosystems' in mangrove areas, yet the photography AP used for that anecdote is not a mangrove region at all and is in fact a regulated location that has authorization from the Indian government's environmental authorities. Ms. Mendoza wrote that one of our members released wastewater into local fields, but AP's photography shows that she was in fact at a location nearly 50 miles away from the company’s actual operations."

Previously, SEAI has claimed that the company in question in this instance, Wellcome Fisheries, was not contacted for comment -- a claim it did not repeat in this more recent letter to AP.

AP replied that it simply did not report that Wellcome had dug shrimp ponds in mangrove areas; "rather, the report describes a Wellcome truck being loaded with shrimp pulled from a pond."

SEAI suggests the initial CAL report is "almost entirely unsubstantiated in connection with any specific company," lacking "the basic detail such as who, what, where, and when the incidents are supposed to have occurred."

"We can find no evidence in Ms. Mendoza’s reporting that AP made any effort whatsoever to verify any of the details, situations, individuals, or companies to which the CAL report alludes."

AP noted that its journalists had traveled to Andhra Pradesh to document the working conditions reported by CAL. "AP journalists obtained access to shrimp hatcheries, growing ponds, peeling sheds and warehouses, and interviewed workers, supervisors and union organizers."

Further arguments around Nekkanti

SEAI claimed that AP journalists "confronted a wide range of its customers with accusations that a Nekkanti facility lacked 'adequate safety and hygiene protections' and showed them lurid photos of worker injuries she blamed on Nekkanti," before contacting the company itself.

Indian shrimp supplier accused of labor abuse, antibiotic fraud in new report

"She stated all this to those customers as plain fact. But her claims were entirely false. The operation to which she was referring was not part of Nekkanti’s business at all."

The AP replied that it had contacted customers of Nekkanti, Wellcome, and other companies understood to be in the supply chain network about the issues raised in the CAL report, and "showed them photographs taken by AP photographers that were authentic and not lurid."

"This was to get their responses prior to publication in keeping with journalistic best practice."

SEAI also says Mendoza claimed to the Nekkanti customers she spoke with that workers were "under guard and are not allowed to leave more than once a month."

It said Nekkanti can demonstrate worker entry/exit logs and several platforms for complaints to be made by workers, and that it told Mendoza this when it was eventually contacted for comment. Informing customers of these labor concerns "as fact" has damaged Nekkanti, it said.

AP did not address this specific claim directly.

Wellcome hard done by?

SEAI also makes several claims over CAL and AP's reporting on Wellcome's operations.

It said claims that Wellcome uses antibiotics is entirely false -- it uses "probiotic systems to cultivate beneficial microbes that help maintain shrimp health and water quality."

"All of that company’s harvested shrimp are subject to two- or three-stage antibiotic testing to ensure no antibiotics are used. Those test reports for each batch of processed shrimp are readily available for verification, though apparently Ms. Mendoza made no such effort."

It claimed photos and video editing conflated Wellcome's legitimate operations with "rogue" operations based miles away.

AP addressed this only briefly, stating: "Thanks to your letter, we did realize we had made a factual mistake about the location of a truck labeled: Wellcome KingWhite. Rather than being next to Jonnalagaruvu village, the truck was about 40 miles away. A correction will be forthcoming."

CAL did not respond to Undercurrent's request for comment in time for publication.
