title: US shrimpers file request with CBP to ban Indian imports made with ‘forced labor’
content:
The American Shrimp Processors Association (ASPA) has filed a request with the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to ban imports of shrimp from India allegedly made with "forced labor," as required under section 307 of the Tariff Act of 1930.

Section 307 of the Tariff Act of 1930 prohibits importing any product that was mined, produced, or manufactured wholly or in part by forced labor, including forced or indentured child labor. CBP enforces the prohibition, but how ASPA would prove which Indian shrimp is allegedly produced from forced labor is not stated. 

ASPA, which made the filing to the CBP on Monday, April 15, has also filed an allegation with the US government arguing that the government of India's failure to enforce its most basic labor laws provides a subsidy to Indian shrimp producers, according to a press release.

US picks up pace on shrimp imports in advance of new tariffs

The US shrimp group asked the US Department of Commerce (DOC) to include the subsidy in the ongoing countervailing duty (CVD) investigation that was launched in response to ASPA's petitions on shrimp imports filed in October of last year.

As a result of the ASPA's petition, new preliminary CVDs were announced on March 26 and went into effect from April 1, when the DOC published them in the Federal Register.

The new duties will see a CVD of 4.72% applied to Devi Sea Foods; 3.89% applied to Sandhya Aqua Exports, Neeli Sea Foods, Vijay Aqua Processors, and Neeli Aqua Farms; and 4.36% applied to all other exporters.

The tariffs will be refunded if investigators determine that the countries are not guilty of providing illegal subsidies or if subsidized imports are not injuring the US shrimp industry, but a final determination is not expected until the fall or winter of 2024, meaning importers will likely have to front the cost for most of the rest of the year. 

ASPA's latest pushes to the CBP and DOC over India come after allegations of forced labor in a March 20 report from the Corporate Accountability Lab (CAL) and a subsequent story in the Associated Press detailing labor rights and environmental abuses in the Indian shrimp sector.

The Seafood Exporters Association of India subsequently said the CAL report and AP story leave "readers with a wilfully distorted view of Indian shrimp exporters."

Indian shrimp trade group to fight US duties, but traders relieved

Separately, an article from The Outlaw Ocean Project focused on a whistleblower at Choice Canning Company, another large Indian processor, which also denies any wrongdoing. 

"The brutal working conditions documented in India's shrimp industry are appalling," said Trey Pearson, president of ASPA. "These producers exploit the most vulnerable workers imaginable, and then export their artificially low-priced product to the United States, harming our own domestic shrimp harvesters and processors. ASPA will do everything we can to fight back against these abhorrent practices and defend American shrimp producers."

India accounts for 40% of US shrimp imports, and shrimp imports from India reached 650 million pounds valued at $2.3 billion in 2023.

In addition to the preliminary CVD rates for India, importers of shrimp from Ecuador will be required to deposit 13.41% for products from Industrial Pesquera Santa Priscila, 1.69% from Sociedad Nacional de Galapagos, known as SONGA, and 7.55% from all other Ecuadorian suppliers.

US sticks to preliminary 13.41% CVD rate for Santa Priscila shrimp in public posting

For shrimp from Vietnam, the deposit requirement will be 2.84% for Stapimex, 196.41% for Thong Thuan, and 2.84% for all other Vietnamese suppliers. Sources told Undercurrent that Thong Thuan's high rate is likely punishment for the company not cooperating fully with investigators.

DOC's Federal Register posting confirms that it has issued a negative preliminary determination for the Indonesian companies Bahari Makmur Sejati, known as BMS (0.39%) and First Marine (0.71%); however, no deposit will be required.

Furthermore, Indonesia and Ecuador also face preliminary anti-dumping rates, as part of a separate petition filed by the ASPA.

Preliminary anti-dumping rates for Ecuador and Indonesia are expected on May 22. The US shrimp industry has asked for anti-dumping duties as high as 118%, which will be added on top of the CVD rates.

title: CEO of Maldives tuna firm suspended over corruption allegations
content:
Government authorities in the Maldives have suspended the CEO of a state-owned tuna company over multiple claims of corruption.

Ahmed Shamah Rasheed
Mifco's CEO. Photo: Mifco.

The country's Privatization and Corporatization Board (PCB) recently prolonged the suspension of Ahmed Shamah Rasheed, managing director and CEO of the Maldives Industrial Fisheries Company (MIFCO); initially set to conclude at the end of March, his suspension has been extended until April 12, according to an announcement made by PCB on March 31.

During his suspension, Shamah continues to receive his salary and allowances. The decision to extend the suspension comes following a series of corruption allegations brought against Shamah, prompting an investigation by PCB.

PCB received complaints through its whistleblower portal, citing multiple infractions allegedly committed by Shamah.

Maldives president assures fishermen skipjack price will not fall below $1,300/t

These allegations range from misuse of company resources for election campaign purposes to questionable expenditures on trips and allegations of nepotism in hiring practices. He has strongly denied all allegations.

PCB vice president Mohamed Firaz said the extension of Shamah's suspension is intended to ensure an unbiased investigation, free from potential interference.

Maldives’ MIFCO embarks on major tuna storage, processing expansion

However, critics, including some parliamentarians, have questioned the transparency and procedural correctness of PCB's actions. They argue that the severity of the allegations does not warrant Shamah's suspension without more explicit evidence, reports local media MV Plus. Others disagree.

MIFCO's CEOs are politically appointed, and the company has recently experienced a fast turnover of top executives.

MIFCO's ice plants

Meanwhile, three Maldives ice plants have been restored to operation, easing the challenges faced by fishermen in obtaining ice, PSM News reported. The country's fisheries and ocean resources ministry, working with MIFCO, is leading the effort to reactivate these essential facilities.

To further support the fishing industry, the ministry is constructing ice plants in nine regions to improve fish quality and ensure fair prices for fishermen, PSM News also reported.

Minister Mohamed Muthalib revealed that ice plants will be operational within six months in Dhidhdhoo, Rasdhoo, Maamendhoo, Meedhoo, Rathafandhoo, Naifaru, Veyvah, Fiyoaree, and Maavah. The government has Saudi financial backing for five projects, four of which stalled in 2023.

The ministry also plans to equip 200 fishing vessels with refrigerated seawater systems and facilitate bank loans for fishermen.

According to MIFCO's website, the firm is currently still upgrading two existing cold storage and brine freezing facilities; one in Felivaru, which includes a 4,000-metric-ton cold storage, 200t capacity for brine freezing, and a 100t new factory; and one in Kooddoo, which also includes a 4,000t cold storage and a 120t brine freezing facility as well as a 1,250t container yard. Additionally, the firm is upgrading the existing harbor in both locations. 

The Maldivian firm is also working on the development of four additional collection sites for tuna.

title: Untitled
content:
Vietnamese shrimp firms such as Sao Ta Foods (known as Fimex Vn) have prepared comprehensive documentation and engaged with industry associations and trade defense agencies for guidance in the face of the US' new anti-subsidy investigation, CafeF reported.

Indian shrimp trade group to fight US duties, but traders relieved

The US Department of Commerce (DOC) recently announced preliminary countervailing duties (CVDs) on shrimp from India, Ecuador, Indonesia and Vietnam.

DOC has set the preliminary anti-subsidy tax rate for Vietnamese enterprises at 2.84% for a single mandatory defendant enterprise and for all remaining enterprises. Additionally, it set a duty of 196.41% for a single defendant business that did not participate in the case.

Vietnam also faces a risk of raw material shortages as many farmers have been put off stocking their ponds by a prolonged period of weak demand and prices. 

According to data from the Vietnam Association of Seafood Exporters and Producers (VASEP), despite those recent challenges, Vietnam's shrimp exports rose by 24% in value during the first three months of 2024, surpassing $620 million. Export turnover to the US market is estimated to have increased by 26%, while the Chinese market is estimated to have lifted by more than 140%, VASEP said.

Ho Quoc Luc, chairman of Fimex, said his firm had documents for the DOC. The CVDs may yet be altered or refunded if shrimp imports are found not to have harmed the US market.

Fimex will apply to the DOC to be a mandatory defendant in the anti-subsidy case to create safety for the company and receive a US government inspection team to inspect its Tin An factory, he added.

In July 2023, Fimex opened a new farming site in Vinh Thuan, expanding its farming area by 203 hectares and bringing the total to 525ha, supplying some 16,000 metric tons of raw shrimp per year.

title: Editor’s choice: Another frenetic week in Canadian snow crab, Alaska salmon M&A
content:
Managing and editorial director Tom Seaman brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week  

Another turbulent week in the build-up to the snow crab fishery in the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador (NL) and mergers and acquisitions (M&A) in processing in the US state of Alaska dominated the news agenda last week.

The NL snow crab fishery, the world's largest with a total allowable catch of 54,727 metric tons, is set to open on April 6, following a five-day delay. 

Strike-threatening Newfoundland crab harvesters misinformed on pricing formula, processing group leader asserts

However, many fish harvesters are unhappy with the new price-setting formula approved last week by the province's price-setting panel and have threatened to hold out. Protests could happen early this week, sources told Undercurrent News. 

Based on current Urner Barry data on wholesale market prices, the formula suggests a dock price of CAD 2.60/lb to start the season.

Under the formula, dock prices will be adjusted weekly as the wholesale market changes. The Association of Seafood Producers (ASP) said the prices will likely increase as this season progresses.

Misinformation is the problem that's leading NL snow crab harvesters to talk about another fishing strike, Jeff Loder, ASP's executive director, told Undercurrent in an interview.

On Friday, April 5, Undercurrent also reported that snow crab landed in NL could soon be on the way to other Canadian provinces for processing.

Click the links for the last week's top stories

Newfoundland approves more crab processing licenses, outside buyers in deal with harvester union
Pricing formula chosen for Newfoundland snow crab fishery
Alaska seafood processing workforce shrinking, state study shows
Trident finalizes sale of Petersburg processing plant to E.C. Phillips & Son
Leonardo DiCaprio joins call to shut down salmon farms on Canada's West Coast
With no word from Peter Pan, Alaska salmon harvesters flock to other buyers
China claims to have rejected 43 Ecuador shrimp shipments in first two months of 2024
US pollock fillet sellers get domestic premium while cheap Chinese, Russian volumes keep EU market down, for now
Silver Bay set for full Peter Pan takeover after inking deal to buy its Valdez plant, operate two more
Major customer exodus at Chinese tuna giant after Dolphin Safe label loss, EJF report

After NL's fisheries minister Elvis Loveless agreed to allow companies from other provinces to buy crab from NL harvesters, the province's Department of Fisheries, Forestries and Agriculture (DFFA) said it had received eight buyer license applications.

The applications are being reviewed to determine whether they meet eligibility requirements, a DFFA spokesperson told Undercurrent on April 4. 

"Once that process is complete, approvals will be considered by the minister," the spokesperson said in an email.

Earlier in the week, Undercurrent reported that snow crab harvesters in NL would benefit from more buyers this season thanks to a deal between the harvesters' union, the Fish Food and Allied Workers (FFAW), and the provincial government.

Loveless confirmed in a letter sent to FFAW late last Monday that he was granting additional processing licenses to handle up to five million pounds of crab and allowing harvesters to sell to processors from outside the province.

Alaska salmon M&A 

In Alaskan M&A, a significant story broke at the end of the week, with Silver Bay Seafoods confirming it's set to acquire all of its struggling rival, Peter Pan Seafood, after the 2024 salmon season, having inked a deal to acquire one of its plants and operate two more. 

The companies announced the plant deals in a joint press release Thursday evening (April 4). The release noted that the deals were part of a larger, still-in-the-works restructuring plan for Silver Bay to acquire Peter Pan's processing facilities and support sites after the upcoming season.

Silver Bay, based in Seattle, Washington, will acquire Peter Pan's processing plant in Valdez and operate the Peter Pan facilities in Port Moller and Dillingham, in the Bristol Bay region, for the upcoming salmon season.

In addition to the plants covered in the first stage of the planned deal, Peter Pan's largest factory is in King Cove, which the company opted not to open earlier this year. As of Thursday, there was still no confirmation from either company whether the King Cove plant would reopen for the summer salmon season.

Peter Pan also has Alaska support facilities in Dillingham, Naknek, and Sand Point and a warehouse in Seattle, Washington. 

Earlier in the week, Undercurrent reported that many fishing vessels and tenders in Alaska were moving away from Peter Pan. 

One such enterprise is the company owned by Tim Heuker and his family, which operates seven tender vessels in the state's Bristol Bay and Area M regions. They've delivered to Peter Pan processing plants for more than 30 years.

The Heukers have signed on with other companies – Canadian Fishing Company subsidiaries North Pacific Seafoods and Leader Creek Fisheries, Trident Seafoods, and Silver Bay, instead – for the upcoming season, as the uncertainty mounts, Tim Heuker told Undercurrent before the Silver Bay deal broke.  

Then, in another piece of Alaskan seafood M&A, the sale of Trident's plant in Petersburg, Alaska, officially went through. 

E.C. Phillips & Son, a year-round seafood processor based in Ketchikan, Alaska, closed its deal to acquire the plant from the Seattle, Washington-based company on April 1, according to a statement published by Trident on April 3. 

Undercurrent reported in March that Phillips had agreed to acquire a bunkhouse, galley and two housing units in addition to the plant. The Petersburg plant is one of four Trident announced in December it would sell as part of a restructuring plan.

Since then, Trident and Silver Bay also announced that the latter would acquire the company's processing facility in Ketchikan, in a joint statement last month. The deal is yet to close. 

Also, looking at Alaska, after reaching a 10-year peak in 2015, the number of seafood processing jobs in the state has steadily fallen – in large part due to the pandemic, and tough market conditions that have led to low prices, plant closures and selloffs.  

That's according to new data from Alaska's Department of Labor and Workforce Development (DLWD) in its April newsletter, which was published April 1.

DLWD points to 21,300 processing jobs held back in 2015. It was during the summer when plants in Alaska reach peak production levels for salmon season. By 2019, that number had fallen by 1,000 workers. Then, during the pandemic, the number of people employed in seafood processing plants during the summer fell to 16,000. 

Tuna majors stop buying from Chinese giant 

In a developing story in the tuna sector, major buyers, including FCF and Bolton Group, confirmed to Undercurrent they will cease purchases from China's Zhejiang Ocean Family (ZOF) after the company was suspended from the Earth Island Institute's Dolphin Safe tuna program and faced allegations of illegal fishing and labor abuses.

ZOF, one of China's largest tuna companies and which reportedly lands 15% of all Chinese-caught tuna, failed to take required measures to prevent its nets from killing dozens of dolphins and whales in the Western and Central Pacific, according to an investigation by the International Marine Mammal Project (IMMP).

A parallel investigation by the UK-based NGO Environmental Justice Foundation also found ZOF engaged in disturbing fishing practices and labor abuses, including the netting of dolphins, whales and even penguins, also in the Western and Central Pacific. The report describes systematic illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing over a five-year period.

ZOF's Dolphin Safe status was revoked on March 8, IMMP told Undercurrent.

Shrimp, pollock updates 

In China, the country's General Administration of Customs (GACC) claimed on March 27 that a total of 43 shipments of Ecuadorian shrimp had been rejected in January and February, mainly due to excessive sulfite levels.

This marks China's first official response to the sulfite controversy surrounding Ecuadorian shrimp. In March, Ecuadorian executives told Undercurrent they hoped to have exports to China back on track soon after some plants were blocked and containers rejected for higher than permitted levels of sodium metabisulfite, a preservative commonly used in the food industry to prevent oxidation.

Among the 43 rejected containers from Ecuador, 34 were dismissed due to excessive use of the food additive. At the same time, the remaining rejections were attributed to documentary discrepancies, excessive "volatile basic nitrogen," or animal diseases.

Looking at pollock, US fillet sellers are getting a premium on domestic sales of up to $250/t compared to exports to the EU, where cheaper Chinese and Russian fillets are impacting the market in the short term, sources told Undercurrent. 

The year has got underway with pollock fillet prices continuing to fall amid uncertainty in both the European and US markets, due to political measures. Vladimir Putin's ongoing war in Ukraine has caused the US to totally ban any products using Russian raw materials.

The EU has removed Russia from the 0% duty autonomous tariff quota program, meaning both single-frozen Russian fillets and double-frozen using Russian raw material are at 13.7%. Donald Tusk, prime minister of Poland, is calling for the EU to follow the US and totally ban Russian food products, including food, however.

Tusk stated in a joint press conference on March 4 with Ingrida Simonyte, his Lithuanian counterpart, who also supports a complete EU ban, Bloomberg reported. 

DiCaprio joins call for BC salmon shutdown 

Also, Hollywood actor Leonardo DiCaprio joined the call to shut down salmon pens in the waters of British Columbia, Canada, criticizing the Canadian government in an Instagram post for considering extending the licenses for open-net pen salmon farms for up to six years.

In his post, the Oscar-winning actor said extending the salmon farming licenses "would break their promise to phase out open-net pen salmon farms, which contain non-native Atlantic Salmon, from coastal BC waters by 2025."

He also urged his fans to join Wild First Canada, a Vancouver, BC-based group that promotes the preservation of wild-caught Pacific salmon, in the fight to stop license extensions.

title: Major customer exodus at Chinese tuna giant after Dolphin Safe label loss, EJF report
content:
Major tuna buyers including FCF and Bolton Group have confirmed to Undercurrent News they will cease purchases from China's Zhejiang Ocean Family (ZOF) after the company was suspended from the Earth Island Institute's Dolphin Safe tuna program and faced allegations of illegal fishing and labor abuses.

ZOF, one of China's largest tuna companies and which reportedly lands 15% of all Chinese-caught tuna, failed to take required measures to prevent its nets from killing dozens of dolphins and whales in the Western and Central Pacific, according to an investigation by the International Marine Mammal Project (IMMP).

Report: Tuna caught by Chinese vessels that netted penguins, whales linked to Bumble Bee

A parallel investigation by UK-based NGO Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF) also found ZOF engaged in disturbing fishing practices and labor abuses, including the netting of dolphins, whales and even penguins, also in the Western and Central Pacific. The report describes systematic illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing over a five-year period.

ZOF's Dolphin Safe status was revoked on March 8, IMMP told Undercurrent.

Taiwan's FCF, one of the world's largest buyers of tuna, confirmed to Undercurrent it halted all purchases from ZOF following the label loss and the EJF report. Luciano Pirovano, director of sustainability, told Undercurrent Tri Marine owner Bolton Group also "immediately ceased purchases."

Bumble Bee Foods, which is owned by FCF, told Undercurrent it ceased purchases from ZOF in 2018. StarKist Co. -- which is owned by Dongwon Enterprises -- told Undercurrent it does not buy tuna from ZOF's fleet nor from ZOF subsidiaries. A Thai Union Group spokesperson also told Undercurrent it "does not purchase any tuna from ZOF."

Zhejiang Ocean Family's tuna plant near Zhoushan, east China, a joint venture with Japan's Mitsubishi Corporation. The tuna here was not caught by purse seiners involved in dolphin deaths, but long-liner vessels. Credit: Louis Harkell / Undercurrent News

The dolphin deaths caused by ZOF's practices accounted for 12.7% of all observed cetacean mortalities in 2019 in the Western and Central Pacific tuna fishery, the last year of unimpeded observer programs before the COVID-19 pandemic. This was even though ZOF's fleet of four purse seine vessels represented just 1.3% of the region's roughly 300 tuna boats, IMMP said. ZOF vessels averaged 10.75 cetacean deaths each, far higher than any other company.

ZOF did not respond to multiple Undercurrent requests for comment. 

"ZOF has clearly failed to take required measures to avoid the injury and death to dolphins," David Phillips, director of IMMP and co-founder of Earth Island, told Undercurrent. The number of cetacean deaths their boats caused in 2019 was "staggeringly disproportionate," he said.

Chinese tuna fishing firm sees IPO plans fizzle

The loss of its status will have "a big impact on ZOF's business," Phillips went on to claim, with more than half of its catch previously sold to Dolphin Safe companies worldwide. Prior to its suspension, ZOF exported tuna from Dolphin Safe-eligible catch to buyers in the US, Mexico, Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands, Thailand, Fiji, Kiribati and other countries, he said.

As a private company, ZOF does not release its production figures, but it claimed in a 2021 stock exchange listing application its revenues were CNY 3.3 billion in 2020, or $456 million at current exchange rates.

Following the moves, Bolton's Pirovano said his company had requested an internal investigation by ZOF. Meanwhile, FCF said its pause in buying would last until it saw "satisfactory corrective and remediation evidence."

"FCF enforces a strict policy against the acceptance of any seafood products originating from IUU fishing or forced labor," said the spokesperson. "Consistent with our policy, we will suspend all dealings with vessels implicated in public allegations supported by substantial evidence until these investigations are concluded."

Legal imperative for dolphin safe

The exodus of major customers for ZOF underlines the importance of Dolphin Safe tuna to the tuna industry, which has had a history of entanglements with dolphins, particularly in the Eastern Tropical Pacific.

Under US law and Earth Island's standard, tuna labeled "Dolphin Safe" must be caught without nets being intentionally deployed on dolphins to be imported into the country. Tuna caught with accidental by-catch of dolphins killed or seriously injured must also be processed separately on board. 

ZOF's super-frozen tuna storage facility near Zhoushan, east China.

Today, more than 800 tuna companies globally participate in the Dolphin Safe program, according to IMMP.

Phillips explained the Dolphin Safe label was originally aimed at addressing the hundreds of thousands of dolphin deaths then occurring each year in the Eastern Pacific tuna fishery, where boats routinely chased and encircled mixed schools of tuna and dolphins with large purse seine nets. After US and global tuna companies were pressured into avoiding tuna caught by setting nets on dolphins, observed mortalities in the region declined by more than 95%, he said. 

By contrast, the Western and Central Pacific fishery -- where ZOF's fleet mainly operates -- has not historically been associated with high levels of dolphin bycatch, as tuna and marine mammals in the region do not swim together in large mixed schools. Most fishing is conducted around fish aggregating devices (FADs) that attract tuna but not dolphins. Still, dolphins and whales can occasionally become entangled in nets, especially when sets are made in low-light conditions.

"In the Eastern Tropical Pacific, it's almost all yellowfin tuna and the vast majority are caught by chasing and netting dolphins," Phillips said. "In the Western and Central Pacific, it's almost all skipjack tuna caught on FADs, so there's less of a direct association with dolphins, but it still happens."

While most tuna companies operating in the Western and Central Pacific have strong records of avoiding marine mammal bycatch, with many going entire fishing seasons with zero cetacean mortality across their fleets, an IMMP analysis found a handful of bad actors are responsible for the majority of dolphin deaths.

Three Chinese-owned firms with 10 vessels accounted for nearly 14% of all observed dolphin mortalities in 2019, even though they represented just 3% of the region's purse seiners. However, ZOF stood out as by far the worst offender, Phillips said.

WCPFC report revelations

For its investigation, IMMP analyzed observer data from the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission (WCPFC), the international body that manages the region's tuna fishery. While WCPFC observers documented the deaths of 338 dolphins and whales in purse seine nets in 2019, their reports are typically anonymized, making it difficult to trace which vessels are responsible.

However, by cross-referencing WCPFC data with dolphin mortality figures self-reported by member countries and with supply chain records obtained from Dolphin Safe companies, IMMP was able to zero in on the outsized role played by ZOF and other Chinese-owned vessels, Phillips said. Two other Chinese firms with six vessels accounted for another 1.2% of dolphin deaths.

Tuna commission halves FAD closure period in Western Pacific

IMMP said WCPFC's figures are hard to verify as the 100% observer coverage doesn't include seiners operating within their own territorial waters, nor does it disclose bycatch data for individual vessels or countries. Based on IMMP's own analysis of the limited observer data available, IMMP estimates that around 1,000 dolphins likely die each year as a result of tuna fishing in the region. 

"If 338 cetacean mortalities were just what was reported, you can imagine the real number is significantly higher when including unobserved mortality on seiners not covered by WCPFC observers," Phillips said. "There could be 1,000 or more dolphins and whales dying annually from the fishery as a whole."

IMMP was also able to assess some of the key drivers of increased cetacean bycatch. Its analysis found that 58% of dolphin mortalities occurred in fishing sets made before sunrise when the presence of marine mammals is difficult to detect prior to deploying nets. Intentional encirclement of dolphins is prohibited under WCPFC rules.

In addition to employing banned fishing methods, ZOF allegedly falsified official documents. The company routinely certified to US authorities that "no dolphins were killed or seriously injured" in the catches of tuna it exported as Dolphin Safe.

"We were looking at their [captain's statements], and there were many, many instances where the observer data showed a mortality event, but then their paperwork said there were no mortalities," Phillips said. "There's a lot of potential legal liability there."

Road to re-certification

To regain its Dolphin Safe status, ZOF will need to commit to ending intentional netting of cetaceans, prohibit pre-dawn net deployments, train crew in safe dolphin release methods, and consent to full data transparency, according to Phillips. 

China says foreign-backed seafood consultant punished for ‘fabricating environmental problems’

Despite the "egregious" nature of the violations, he said Earth Island hopes to work with the company to implement necessary reforms.

"Our goal is to get them back into the Dolphin Safe program," Phillips said. "But they're going to have to make the commitment to change." Such changes could take six months to a year to implement, Phillips estimated. "They've got some serious work to do." In the meantime, IMMP is working to help ZOF's former buyers find alternative sources of Dolphin Safe tuna to fill the gap.

Meanwhile, the organization is calling on the WCPFC and national fisheries agencies to strengthen regulations on the use of FADs, mandate independent observers on all purse seiners, and ramp up enforcement while calling on countries to enact stricter import laws to block tuna harvested using dolphin-deadly methods from entering their markets.

Phillips also wants WCPFC to release country-specific data as standard, noting it was an "anomaly" Chinese catches were detailed in WCPFC's December 2023 report.

He added the next report on cetacean catches based on 2023 data will be released in late 2024.

title: Royal Greenland shrimp factory in Canada destroyed by fire
content:
Police are investigating a fire that extensively damaged the Royal Greenland-owned factory at Matane, in the Canadian province of Quebec, on March 29, reports CBC News.

The fire at the Fruits de mer de l'Est Quebec processing plant was first reported around 7 pm on Friday, March 29. 

For several hours, firefighters from the small town about 350 kilometers northeast of Quebec City battled the heavy smoke and flames before extinguishing the fire Saturday morning.

Photos show some of the damage from the fire that broke out on March 29 at the Royal Greenland-owned shellfish factory in Matane, Quebec. Facebook photo by Roger Boisvert

The fire comes just a couple of weeks after Royal Greenland announced it was shutting down the factory, as previously reported by Undercurrent News. 

The company cited recent cuts to the northern shrimp quota in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, a labor shortage and low market prices for seafood among the reasons for the decision.

Kristina Michaud, the Bloc Quebecois member of parliament for Avignon-La Mitis-Matane-Matapedia, said the community had hoped another seafood processing company might be interested in buying and operating the facility.

A spokesperson for the Surete du Quebec said firefighters were initially leading the investigation into the cause of the blaze but received information that led them to transfer the case to the major crimes unit of the provincial police force.

title: Indian shrimp trade group to fight US duties, but traders relieved
content:
The Seafood Exporters Association of India (SEAI) has announced its opposition to the new US' preliminary countervailing duties (CVD) announced on March 26.

Three of four largest US shrimp source nations hit with preliminary countervailing duties

The new duties will see a CVD of 4.72% applied to Devi Sea Foods; 3.89% applied to Sandhya Aqua Exports, Neeli Sea Foods, Vijay Aqua Processors, and Neeli Aqua Farms; and 4.36% applied to all other exporters.

These preliminary duty rates went into effect from April 1, when the US Department of Commerce (DoC) published them in the Federal Register.

The SEAI intends to fight this over the rest of the process, it said, on the grounds that the Indian shrimp sector does not rely on government subsidies for its profits.

"These findings from the US DoC run counter to the well-established international principle that local duties and taxes cannot be exported and may be reimbursed," the organization wrote to Undercurrent News.

"That’s because the preliminary CVD rate for India is based on Commerce’s arbitrary findings that the reimbursements given for the Indian frozen shrimp exports on account of certain otherwise unreimbursed domestic duties and taxes were countervailable."

"However, the frozen shrimp sector of the Indian seafood industry operates entirely on competitive principles and does not rely on government subsidies for its profitability or sustenance. SEAI intends to contest Commerce’s arbitrary findings in the final determination phase of this investigation to persuade Commerce to reverse its preliminary findings."

The tariffs will be refunded if investigators determine that the countries are not guilty of providing illegal subsidies or if subsidized imports are not injuring the US shrimp industry; but any final determination -- as referred to by the SEAI -- is not expected until the fall or winter of 2024, meaning importers will likely have to front the cost for most of the rest of the year.

A fact sheet on the newtariffs.

Exporters feel it could have been worse

Several Indian shrimp traders contacted by Undercurrent were relieved, however, noting that India's base CVD of 4.36% is significantly less than the 7.55% duty faced by Ecuador, its growing export rival in the US.

India’s largest shrimp exporters go all in on value-added to take on Ecuador

"They [exporters] were expecting 6%. I think 4.3% will be okay. Moreover, it's preliminary," said the CEO of one Indian shrimp packer, who wished to remain anonymous.

He noted that although Indonesia -- the third-largest source of shrimp to the US, selling 146,250 metric tons to the country last year -- escaped inclusion in the CVD, it is still likely to be hit by anti-dumping duties when those are announced in May, as is Ecuador.

India is not part of the antidumping process and already has a rate of 1.35%.

Pervez Khan, the CEO of West Bengal-based trader SA Exports, also confirmed to Undercurrent that "we were expecting 5-6%, so it is some relief to have 4.36%."

"Now we will have some level playing field with Ecuador," he added.

Since COVID, Ecuador has begun taking a larger share of the US market, given its trade difficulties with China and rapidly growing harvest volumes.

Ecuador has begun to increase its volumes of value-added shrimp, while the country's closer proximity to the US means it saves on transit costs relative to India, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

However, the new duties will likely put a dampener on this growing trade volume, especially with Ecuador's largest farmer and processor, Santa Priscila, receiving a huge 13.41% preliminary duty.

One source involved in the process previously told Undercurrent that the subsidies were linked to the area of farms directly under a company's control. Hence, Santa Priscila, the world's largest shrimp farmer and owner of some 18,000 hectares, received an incredibly steep duty.

Of perhaps greater long-term concern now for India's shrimp sector is the fallout from the Corporate Accountability Lab and Associated Press reports of March 20, which detail allegations of labor and environmental abuses within the sector.

These were joined the same day by a whistleblower's account of life at a factory belonging to major Andhra Pradesh-based trader Choice Canning Company, which was published by the Outlaw Ocean Project. This also contained allegations of overcrowded labor conditions and antibiotic fraud, which the company has vocally denied.

Nevertheless, these reports have been seized upon by US lawmakers looking to implement a ban on Indian shrimp imports "until the situation can be further analyzed," as previously reported by Undercurrent.

title: US sticks to preliminary 13.41% CVD rate for Santa Priscila shrimp in public posting
content:
The US Department of Commerce (DOC) does not appear to be backing off its preliminary countervailing duty (CVD) rate of 13.41% for shrimp imported from Ecuador giant Industrial Pesquera Santa Priscila.

That's at least the indication from DOC's publication of four separate notices early Saturday (March 30) in the Federal Register announcing CVDs related to frozen warmwater shrimp imported from India, Ecuador, Indonesia and Vietnam -- the US' four largest source nations.

The notices are dated April 1, meaning the CVD-related deposits must begin being made on Monday. Based on language contained in the Federal Register postings, final CVD rates could be known as soon as Aug. 5, the date final anti-dumping (AD) duty rates are also expected to be decided for Ecuador and Indonesia. 

The language reads: "As noted in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum, in accordance with section 705(a)(1) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.210(b)(4), Commerce is aligning the final countervailing duty (CVD) determination in this investigation with the final determinations in the companion antidumping duty (AD) investigations of shrimp from Ecuador and Indonesia, based on a request made by the petitioner. Consequently, the final CVD determination will be issued on the same date as the final AD determinations, which are currently scheduled to be issued no later than August 5, 2024, unless postponed."

Preliminary AD rates for Ecuador and Indonesia are expected on May 22. The US shrimp industry has asked for anti-dumping duties as high as 118%.  

Three of four largest US shrimp source nations hit with preliminary countervailing duties

Undercurrent News earlier broke the news that DOC had informed all parties involved that it has determined -- pending a full investigation -- that it's likely that three of the four countries it targeted -- India, Ecuador and Vietnam -- are supporting subsidy programs that enable them to offer artificially low prices in the US market in violation of World Trade Organization rules.

Starting Monday, the Federal Register notices confirm, importers of shrimp from India will be required to deposit 4.72% of the amount paid for products supplied by Devi Sea Foods, 3.89% from Sandhya Aqua Exports, and 4.36% from all other Indian suppliers. Importers of shrimp from Ecuador will be required to deposit 13.41% for products from Industrial Pesquera Santa Priscila, 1.69% from Sociedad Nacional de Galapagos, known as SONGA, and 7.55% from all other Ecuadorian suppliers.

The Ecuador shrimp sector has expressed hope that the preliminary 13.41% CVD assigned to Santa Priscila, the country's largest farmer and exporter, is a mistake, as reported by Undercurrent. However, a well-placed industry source told Undercurrent last week that the high rate was likely intentional due to Santa Priscila's very high quantity of directly owned farms.

For shrimp from Vietnam, the deposit requirement will be 2.84% for Stapimex, 196.41% for Thong Thuan, and 2.84% for all other Vietnamese suppliers. Sources told Undercurrent that the high rate charged Thong Thuan is likely punishment for the company not cooperating fully with investigators.

DOC's Federal Register posting confirms that it has issued a negative preliminary determination for the Indonesian companies, Bahari Makmur Sejati, known as BMS (0.39%) and First Marine (0.71%), however. No deposit will be required.

"Consistent with section 703(b)(4)(A) of the Act, Commerce is disregarding the de minimis rates, and we preliminarily determine that countervailable subsidies are not being provided to producers/exporters of the subject merchandise in Indonesia," DOC said.

The CVD and AD rates are the result of a petition filed against the four countries' shrimp exporters by the American Shrimp Processors Association (ASPA), a group that represents US harvesters and processors behind roughly 85% of the US' domestic frozen warmwater shrimp production.

ASPA argued that the low prices charged for imported farmed shrimp were enabled by programs organized by the exporters' nations and have caused prices for domestic shrimp to also crash.

"Domestic landings fell by a sharp 28.6% from the first half of 2022 to the first half of 2023," ASP had advised. "Dockside prices also crashed. From June of 2022 to June of 2023, ex-vessel prices for a 26/30 size Gulf [of Mexico] shrimp fell by a staggering 44.7%."

The four source nations that were targeted for CVD and AD-related investigation accounted for 709,804 (90%) of the 788,209 metric tons of shrimp imported by the US in 2023 and nearly $5.6 billion (87%) of the $6.4bn in value, according to trade data maintained by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

India sent the US 296,243t of shrimp in 2023, 2% less than in 2023, while Ecuador sent the US 205,684t, 3% more, and Indonesia sent the US 146,258t, 12% less, the chart illustrates. Vietnam sent the US 61,516t, 13% less.

title: Bipartisan US lawmakers Graves, Peltola team up to push for ban on Indian shrimp
content:
US representatives Garret Graves and Mary Sattler Peltola, a Louisiana Republican and an Alaska Democrat, are working together to ratchet up the attack on farmed shrimp from India, asking the White House to temporarily ban the product.

Their action is just the latest in response to the bombshell investigative report dropped on March 20 by the Outlaw Oceans Project (OOP). OOP, the same journalism outfit that earlier reported on forced labor in Chinese seafood processing plants, shared evidence provided by Joshua Farinella, a former general manager at Choice Canning's Amalapuram factory in Andhra Pradesh, India, that the company allegedly mistreated its workers and shipped antibiotic-positive shrimp to the US.

The Choice Group has denied the allegations of the report, as reported by Undercurrent News.  

In their two-page letter sent to president Joe Biden on Friday (March 22), Graves and Peltola refer to the "damning evidence" provided by "someone in the industry." They note that 40% of the shrimp consumed in the US comes from India, and express concerns about the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) not adequately testing the imports.

"Even with the limited resources at our ports of entry, Indian shipments still account for 60% of all rejected shrimp," they wrote.

Indian shrimp supplier accused of labor abuse, antibiotic fraud in new report

They noted how "Congress was actively considering legislative proposals, such as HR 4547, The Laws Ensuring Safe Shrimp (LESS) Act, which would provide routine additional funding to the [FDA] to increase the testing of shrimp for banned veterinary drugs as well as fund further Sect. 32 purchases of US domestic shrimp by the US Department of Agriculture."

The lawmakers conclude: "It is imperative that your administration take swift action to protect American consumers. We urge you to implement a ban on the import of Indian shrimp until the situation can be further analyzed. Our shrimpers here at home can help fill the void and provide safe and healthy shrimp to the American market while we work to ensure the safety of our seafood supply."  

'Stop the Great Indian Shrimp Invastion'

Graves' home state of Louisiana is a major harvester and processor of US domestic wild-caught shrimp, a competitor to Indian shrimp importers. 

"Stop the Great Indian Shrimp Invasion," said the lawmaker in a press release promoting the action he and Peltola have taken.

"... We are fighting to protect free and fair trade by ensuring that foreign-farmed imports aren't given an unfair advantage while also threatening Americans's health," he continued. "Meanwhile, American shrimpers follow all the rules to keep our health and fisheries safe, and wild, healthy American shrimp are being boxed out of US markets. We need to be doing everything we can to stop bad imports from reaching consumers, especially when we have high-quality, healthy shrimp right here at home."

Peltola explained her interest in the issue, too.

"Alaska may not be a major producer of shrimp, but we rely on seafood in a similar way to communities along the Gulf of Mexico," she said in the press release. "Congressman Graves and I have spoken at length about our domestic seafood industries being hurt by a flood of imported and unhealthy seafood products – I'm proud to co-lead his letter to support American shrimpers."

Other US lawmakers have also taken action in response to the OOP investigation, as reported by Undercurrent. 

Senator Bill Cassidy, another Louisiana Republican, sent a short, one-page letter March 20 to the US Trade Representative and Customs and Border Protection, asking the agency to "urgently" investigate and guarantee Farinella full whistleblower protections, as reported by Undercurrent. 

US lawmakers seize on report of labor abuses in Indian shrimp sector

Not to be outdone, three other prominent Democrats in the House of Representatives -- Jared Huffman, Raul Grijalva and Melanie Stansbury -- have written to Farinella, requesting he present more evidence to back up his allegations by April 2, 2024. They said in their letter that Choice Canning potentially violated five laws and policies.

The Southern Shrimp Alliance, a trade association that represents domestic harvesters and processors of wild-caught shrimp in the Southeast US, applauded the letter by Graves and Peltola in a statement released Tuesday.

US wild-catch sector pushes to add Indian shrimp to child, forced labor product lists

"Once again, the shrimp industry is grateful to [representative Graves] for tirelessly fighting for shrimpers not only in south Louisiana but throughout the country," said John Williams, SSA's executive director. "We also greatly appreciate the support of [representative Peltola] and the recognition that all commercial fishermen, wherever they work in this country, face the same existential threats from cheap, unsafe seafood imports."

SSA on Monday (March 25) sent a 15-page letter to the Department of Labor seeking to get Indian shrimp added to two lists that identify products produced with the use of child or forced labor, as reported by Undercurrent.

title: Aquaculture Stewardship Council to cease operations in China
content:
The Aquaculture Stewardship Council (ASC) has decided to phase out its operations in China following a strategic review over the past 18 months.

After reviewing "internal operations and...current and future operational regions and markets," it has decided to "phase out program operations and cease investment in China," it said.

US commission urges Dep’t of State, Homeland Security to act on Chinese imports

"This will allow ASC to focus and invest in coming years in regions, markets and activities where we believe we can have the greatest impact through effective use of our limited resources."

It commented to Undercurrent News only to add that "our position may change following future business reviews."

ASC has processes in place to enable a structured approach to the phasing out of activities for companies with chain-of-custody (CoC) certification, with a scope for ASC (and potentially also a valid ASC licensing agreement for label use) in China.

These can be found in full in ASC's letter to conformity assessment bodies (CABs) here, but it noted that all existing ASC CoC certificates and surveillance audits will be maintained until certificate expiry.

Any new applicants for CoC certification with ASC scope will not be entered in the CoC database after April 19, 2024. Only ASC CoC certificates expiring in 2024 are eligible for recertification. "It is strongly recommended that CABs check all certificates that are due to expire in 2024 and engage clients regarding recertification."

"The latest ASC CoC certificate expiry shall be Nov. 14, 2027."

Asked about any similar plans it might be considering, meanwhile, the Marine Stewardship Council, told Undercurrent: "The ASC has made a business decision to carry out a phased exit from China. This is a decision for ASC alone."

Over the past half-year, an investigation by the Outlaw Ocean Project, published in The New Yorker and revealing "horrific details about abusive practices towards North Koreans forced to work in seafood processing plants" in China -- and the fact that this seafood ends up on American plates -- has prompted numerous outcries from the seafood sector.

In March, a US Congressional body created in 2000 to monitor China's compliance with international human rights standards urged the departments of State and Homeland Security to act quickly to address alleged forced labor in China's seafood industry.

The Congressional-Executive Commission on China sent a letter to Antony Blinken and Alejandro Mayorkas, the secretaries respectively of each agency, asking them to "act quickly and decisively to address forced labor in China's seafood industry and the very real possibility that US consumers of seafood are funding North Korea's nuclear saber-rattling."

A search of ASC's 'find a supplier' function on its website shows 429 companies under "China," 289 of which are currently certified.

title: Ecuador shrimp sector body hopes 13.41% US preliminary duty for Santa Priscila is ‘error’
content:
Ecuador's shrimp sector body hopes that a whopping 13.41% US preliminary countervailing duty (CVD) for Industrial Pesquera Santa Priscila, the country's largest farmer and exporter, is a mistake. 

On Tuesday, the US Department of Commerce (DOC) told a list of exporters and proponents for the tariffs that it has determined -- pending a full investigation -- that it's likely that three of four countries it targeted are supporting subsidy programs that enable them to offer artificially low prices in the US market in violation of World Trade Organization rules.

Imports from companies from Ecuador, India and Vietnam all have preliminary duties, but Indonesia got a pass.

A fact sheet on the tariffs.

As it stands, US importers will be required to deposit 13.41% of the value of shrimp imported from Santa Priscila, 1.69% from Sociedad Nacional de Galapagos (Songa), and 7.55% from all other Ecuadorian suppliers, according to the preliminary CVDs set by the DOC.

The 7.55% is an average of 13.41% for Santa Priscila and 1.69% for Songa. 

Jose Antonio Camposano, executive president of Ecuador's industry body, the Camara Nacional de Acuacultura (CNA), raised concerns over the accuracy of the assigned CVD rates.

Three of four largest US shrimp source nations hit with preliminary countervailing duties

In a statement sent to Undercurrent News, Camposano expressed skepticism regarding the discrepancy in the assigned tariffs. 

"Today, we have been informed of the outcome of the preliminary determination of the CVD case. We have only received one telephone communication regarding the assigned tariff," he said.

"This discrepancy in the percentage assigned to a single program leads us to conclude that it must most likely be an error in the calculation," said the CNA head. 

Once the CNA receives the calculations made by the DOC, "we will proceed to submit a review request for this program, in accordance with the rules of the investigation process, with the objective of correcting this margin," said Camposano in the statement. 

Other sources in Ecuador confirmed that according to the country’s lawyers, the duty set for Santa Priscilla is incorrect. Sources close to the company said that they expected a duty below 2%.

Ecuador, India shrimp packers on edge as industry awaits US anti-dumping, countervailing duties decisions

The rate seems like a "gross error," an Ecuadorian shrimp source told Undercurrent. "The number makes no sense."

If this is the rate, it will be "tough" for Santa Priscila to export to the US at all, he said. As for Songa, 1.69% is "basically zero, so they are out," he said. 

Then, this rate gives Songa a "huge advantage" over all others in Ecuador which is even more harmful than the lower rates from other countries, he said.

Duty rates will go into effect as soon as DOC is able to publish them in the Federal Register, which is expected to happen within days.

The tariffs will be refunded if investigators determine that the countries are not guilty of providing illegal subsidies or if subsidized imports are not injuring the US shrimp industry, but a final determination is not expected until the fall or winter of 2024, meaning importers will likely have to front the cost for most of the rest of the year. 

Indonesia's gets a CVD pass 

DOC said it would issue a negative preliminary determination for the Indonesian companies, Bahari Makmur Sejati, known as BMS (0.39%) and First Marine (0.71%), however. No deposit will be required.

‘Everything depends on US duties,’ says top Ecuador shrimp exec on production outlook

Starting as soon as the formal publication of the government decision, importers of shrimp from India will be required to deposit 4.72% for shrimp imports from Devi Sea Foods, 3.89% from Sandhya Aqua Exports, and 4.36% from all other Indian suppliers. 

For shrimp from Vietnam, the deposit requirement will be 2.84% for Stapimex, 196.41% for Thong Thuan, and 2.84% for all other Vietnamese suppliers.

Duty rates will go into effect as soon as DOC is able to publish them in the Federal Register, which is expected to happen within days.

The tariffs will be refunded if investigators determine that the countries are not guilty of providing illegal subsidies or if subsidized imports are not injuring the US shrimp industry, but a final determination is not expected until the fall or winter of 2024, meaning importers will likely have to front the cost for most of the rest of the year. 

Antidumping next

As for the market impact, "let's wait for the antidumping next," the Ecuadorian source told Undercurrent.

US trade panel votes to keep shrimp tariff-related investigation going

Tuesday's announcement decision follows a petition levied in October 2023 against the four nations by the American Shrimp Processors Association (ASPA), a group that represents US harvesters and processors behind roughly 85% of the US' domestic frozen warmwater shrimp production.

ASPA argued that the low prices charged for imported farmed shrimp were enabled by programs organized by the exporters' nations and have caused prices for domestic shrimp to also crash.

Being pursued on a separate track and potentially even more lethal is ASPA's petition for antidumping duties on shrimp imports from Ecuador and Indonesia. The group said it expects preliminary findings on that matter on May 22, 2024 -- potentially in less than two months. The US shrimp industry has asked for anti-dumping duties as high as 118%.

title: Blumar, Multi X mull rebuilding Entrevientos plant after fire
content:
The aftermath of a devastating fire that razed the Entrevientos plant in Chile's Magallanes region last month has left Multi X and Blumar, two large salmon producers, without processing facilities where they have farming operations.

That could change. The two firms, which jointly built and operated the plant, are evaluating whether to initiate another joint investment for the reconstruction of the facility, Gerardo Balbontin Fox, Blumar Seafoods' CEO, told Undercurrent News in a recent interview. 

Undercurrent reported last month about the devastating fire in Entrevientos, in Punta Arenas, Chile's southernmost region. The fire, which is believed to have started during routine operations, sparked by an incident in a warehouse, resulted in the total loss of the $60-million processing plant, which had been in operation since June 2020 and employed around 500 people.

Fire at the Entrevientos plant in February 2024. Photo: Radio Polar Chile.

The emotional toll of the incident was palpable in Balbontin's words when Undercurrent caught up with at Seafood Expo North America (SENA), in Boston, Massachusetts, earlier this month.

"It was a big, big plant. It was a very emotional situation," he said. "A lot of people had to stop working in a small neighborhood that was important for labor opportunities in the area. It was a complete accident, but hopefully, we can come back with a new plant there. We haven't decided yet."

The companies await the results of an investigation being conducted by their insurers and have hopes of being able to rebuild in two years, he said. 

While Blumar and Multi X evaluate the potential of a new plant, they have promptly shifted their salmon processing operations to different facilities, either in the same region or elsewhere, to maintain operational continuity, Balbontin said.

"The fire [took] place in February, and [the aftermath situation] is still heated," he remarked. "We are looking for a strategy to see what we're going to do for processing. Fortunately, we have some alternatives because production in Magallanes has decreased, and additional processing capacity exists at other processors. We are on the way to [making] a decision [on the future plan]."

Blumar, Multi X processing plant in Chile’s southernmost region reduced to ashes

Multi X is currently processing the fish it produces in the region in a small third-party plant nearby, Fernando Perez, Multi X's chief sales and marketing officer, told Undercurrent in a separate interview. Blumar is instead transporting fish on wellboats to be processed at one of its other plants.

"For now, our operational continuity is ensured as we continue to process our salmon in the Magallanes region," Perez said.

Multi X debuts new two new smoked products

While working with Blumar to make a decision about the lost processing plant, Multi X is expanding and promoting its ultra-premium, antibiotic-free, fresh, frozen and smoked salmon products from the Magallanes region to US fine dining and retail markets.

"In 2023, Multi X grew its production from 90,000 metric tons to 120,000t, almost 40%, but it expects to maintain stable production this year," Perez told Undercurrent.

Multi X, Chile's second-largest salmon producer and the Latin American country's biggest salmon smoker, sells over 60% of its production in the US. 

Fernando Perez, chief sales and marketing officer at Multi X at the Seafood Expo North America in Boston, March 2024.

The firm has expanded its range of branded smoked salmon products, debuting two new Latitude 45 branded products at SENA: smoked salmon candy bites and smoked chipotle salmon.

Multi X said the new products promise a ready-to-eat hot smoked experience, combining familiar sweet and spicy taste profiles. Multi X said the salmon used in the products is transformed from fresh to smoked within 24 hours of leaving the water, ensuring freshness. 

Alongside the new offerings in Boston, Multi X showcased its existing range of smoked and lightly smoked salmon products. Multi X has also expanded its ultra-premium, antibiotic-free ArkA fresh, frozen and smoked salmon products to sell to US fine dining and retail markets.

"ArkA is special. There is a need in fine dining for ultra-premium, antibiotic-free Antarctic salmon, and ArkA is the solution," said Jorge Goles Niemann, director of business development at Multi X. 

Blumar gets out of DTC game

In another unrelated development, BluGlacier, the Miami, Florida-based joint venture between Chilean salmon producers Blumar and Ventisqueros, has pulled the plug on its effort to sell its "Oshen"-branded Atlantic salmon product direct to consumers (D2C) after a little more than three years, Undercurrent reported at the Boston conference.

"Compared with our main activity, where we sell $500 million in salmon every year, it was a business that was growing slow and needed more attention from the organization to keep it alive than [made sense]," Sebastian Goycoolea, the CEO of BluGlacier, told Undercurrent.

However, the Oshen brand will continue to be produced for sale in retail stores, including Mariano's, a chain of 55 grocery stores located mostly around the US midwestern city of Chicago, Illinois, according to Goycoolea.

BluGlacier sells about 70m pounds overall of fresh and frozen salmon in the US annually, he estimated.

title: Three of four largest US shrimp source nations hit with preliminary countervailing duties
content:
India, Ecuador and Vietnam -- three of the four largest US sources of farmed shrimp -- learned Tuesday (March 26) that, likely as soon as the end of this week, they will be forced to pay preliminary countervailing duties (CVD) ranging from less than 2% to as much as 196%, Undercurrent News has learned.

Indonesia, the third-largest supplier of shrimp to the US, has been left off the hook, however.

The US Department of Commerce (DOC) has begun calling a list of exporters and proponents for the tariffs that it has determined -- pending a full investigation -- that it's likely that three of four countries it targeted are supporting subsidy programs that enable them to offer artificially low prices in the US market in violation of World Trade Organization rules.

Duty rates will go into effect as soon as DOC is able to publish them in the Federal Register, which is expected to happen within days.

The tariffs will be refunded if investigators determine that the countries are not guilty of providing illegal subsidies or if subsidized imports are not injuring the US shrimp industry, but a final determination is not expected until the fall or winter of 2024, meaning importers will likely have to front the cost for most of the rest of the year. 

Starting as soon as the formal publication of the government decision, importers of shrimp from India will be required to deposit 4.72% for shrimp imports from Devi Sea Foods, 3.89% from Sandhya Aqua Exports, and 4.36% from all other Indian suppliers. Importers of shrimp from Ecuador will be required to deposit 13.41% for shrimp imported from Industrial Pesquera Santa Priscila, 1.69% from Sociedad Nacional de Galapagos, known as SONGA, and 7.55% from all other Ecuadorian suppliers.

For shrimp from Vietnam, the deposit requirement will be 2.84% for Stapimex, 196.41% for Thong Thuan, and 2.84% for all other Vietnamese suppliers.

DOC said it would issue a negative preliminary determination for the Indonesian companies, Bahari Makmur Sejati, known as BMS (0.39%) and First Marine (0.71%), however. No deposit will be required.

Vietnamese shrimp. Credit: Seabina Group

The four source nations that were targeted for the investigation accounted for 709,804 (90%) of the 788,209 metric tons of shrimp imported by the US in 2023 and nearly $5.6 billion (87%) of the $6.4bn in value, according to trade data maintained by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

This chart below from the Undercurrent trade portal shows the shrimp import volume and value fluctuations by year from the four major source nations. The numbers vary slightly from those in the NOAA database but show an overall downward decline in exports to the US for three of the four countries, Ecuador being the one exception.

India sent the US 296,243t of shrimp in 2023, 2% less than in 2023, while Ecuador sent the US 205,684t, 3% more, and Indonesia sent the US 146,258t, 12% less, the chart illustrates. Vietnam sent the US 61,516t, 13% less. 

Anti-dumping duties could be more lethal

Tuesday's announcement decision follows a petition levied in October 2023 against the four nations by the American Shrimp Processors Association (ASPA), a group that represents US harvesters and processors behind roughly 85% of the US' domestic frozen warmwater shrimp production.

ASPA argued that the low prices charged for imported farmed shrimp were enabled by programs organized by the exporters' nations and have caused prices for domestic shrimp to also crash.

"Domestic landings fell by a sharp 28.6% from the first half of 2022 to the first half of 2023," ASP said. "Dockside prices also crashed. From June of 2022 to June of 2023, ex-vessel prices for a 26/30 size Gulf [of Mexico] shrimp fell by a staggering 44.7%."

Being pursued on a separate track and potentially even more lethal is ASPA's petition for antidumping duties on shrimp imports from Ecuador and Indonesia. The group said it expects preliminary findings on that matter on May 22, 2024 -- potentially in less than two months. The US shrimp industry has asked for anti-dumping duties as high as 118%.  

A Louisiana shrimper in the Gulf of Mexico. Photo: Billy Metcalf

The US International Trade Commission (ITC) voted unanimously, 4-0, on Dec. 8, to allow the continuation of the investigation that could lead to both countervailing and anti-dumping duties being charged on frozen warmwater shrimp from India, Ecuador, Indonesia and Vietnam, as reported by Undercurrent. The ITC's decision followed an all-day hearing held, Nov. 15, in which shrimp harvesters and processors described how they have suffered. 

Shrimp imports increased 15.6% from 2020 to 2022, "gaining market share at the expense of domestic producers in 2022," Elizabeth Drake, a partner at Schagrin Associates in Washington, DC, and the attorney representing ASPA, testified to the ITC. She noted how imports from the four countries for which tariffs are sought reached 1.5 billion lbs and accounted for more than 80% of US consumption.

ASPA said it documented "dozens of government subsidy programs" benefitting shrimp farmers and processors in the source countries, including subsidized loans, tax concessions, grants, export credits and the provision of land, water and other inputs. The dumping rates alleged are 9.55-25.82% by Ecuador and 26.13-33.95% by Indonesia.

US shrimp import uptick is over after six months as prices continue descent

"In 2022, for every pound of shrimp we landed in the [Gulf of Mexico] and South Atlantic, we imported more than 11 lbs from these four countries," testified Trey Pearson, ASPA's president and general manager of JBS Packing, a supplier of US wild-caught seafood based in Port Arthur, Texas.

"The flood of imports is simply overwhelming," he said. "Trends and import prices have been even more devastating as our witnesses will testify. Prices are at all-time lows and price quotes for finished frozen imports are often below our own cost of production for the same product. As a result, our processors have lost sales in production. Revenue is way down and was already low. Margins have disappeared."

Been here before

Ecuador, in particular, has been bracing for months for Tuesday's decision, placing production plans "on hold" until a ruling is known, Sandro Coglitore, the CEO of Omarsa, one of Ecuador's largest shrimp producers, told Undercurrent earlier this month. 

It's a very important issue because many small factories depend on their sales to the US. "If the anti-dumping and CVD rates are high, we must figure out if the market will absorb that increase. Or how it will affect the buying price," he said.

"If the market is unwilling or unable to pick up the tab, then there will be suffering in terms of medium and small-sized plants that depend 100% on their sales to the US. And, of course, the farmers that supply those factories will get a lower price. It will be difficult for many of them to survive with lower prices," he said.

Credit: Larisa Blinova / Shutterstock

"For the CVD, anything around 5% would be manageable," he said, adding: "If it's higher than that, it will be tough. And that's only one part; we still have the dumping."

Omarsa, which counts on the US for about 6% of its sales, stopped shipping there on March 8, he told Undercurrent.

This is not new territory. Importers of shrimp from all four source countries have confronted a countervailing duty investigation before, roughly a decade ago. In that case, it was determined that Ecuador, India and Vietnam were all guilty of subsidizing their exporters and hit with CVD rates ranging from 1.15% to 13.51%, but ITC later intervened, finding that there wasn't enough evidence of domestic shrimpers being injured by the subsidies.

title: Container destined for Indian shrimp firm’s new feed mill tested for narcotics
content:
A container of feed ingredients from Brazil destined for a new mill opened by Indian shrimp firm Sandhya Aqua Exports has been detained for narcotics testing by the country's Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI).

One of largest US Indian shrimp players brings in Marshall from Trident

On March 21, India's CBI seized a container in Visakhapatnam port which contained 1,000 bags of inactive dried yeast, each weighing 25 kilograms, which had come from Santos in Brazil. Local media reports have stated the authorities suspect cocaine is mixed in with the shipment. 

In a statement sent to Undercurrent News, Sandhya Aqua said it's totally in the dark and "never had possession of the container at any point of time."

What was ordered "is different from what might have come in the container," the company said. The dry yeast was ordered for a shrimp feed plant that Sandhya Aqua has recently set up in Kathipudi, West Godavari District.

Sandhya Aqua, which also owns AZ Gems, the second largest US shrimp importer, "is fully committed to cooperate and help the authorities' war against drugs and unfolding this conspiracy and requesting CBI to go to the deepest roots possible and identify the perpetrators involved," the company said.

Sandhya Aqua "unfortunately fell prey to this scam that commonly happens by some international drug cartels," it said. "We hope the investigations will finish soon and everything will be back to normal. We will continue to put the best of our abilities in industry-leading efforts to continue to be a pioneer and to make a positive impact in seafood space across the globe."

Owner of India’s largest US shrimp market player eyes Africa, Central America farming

CBI claimed that it had acted based on a tip-off from Interpol, and the "operation indicates the involvement of an international criminal network engaged in importing narcotics drugs by way of mixing it with other substances commonly known as cutting agents."

Nothing is conclusive until lab tests are done, said Sandhya Aqua.

"The supplier from Brazil is also in contact currently, and they have also received information as such, and they have advised our company that they will cooperate fully as well."

"The Brazilian supplier has mentioned that these happen commonly when containers come from South America where they change the contents of product at the port of loading in origin country or at transshipment point," it said.

title: Filipino investigation finds tuna fishermen exploited
content:
In the Philippines, most profits from tuna fishing go to commercial tuna boat owners and operators, while ordinary fisherfolk struggle, according to an investigation by journalism organization Bulatlat.

For months, Bulatlat analyzed in-depth dynamics favoring industrial-scale fishing fleets in the country at the expense of ordinary fishermen. Poverty is rife among fisherfolk in General Santos City, also known as the Philippines' tuna capital, with the region witnessing some 40% poverty incidence among them by 2021.

Revenues from commercial fishers in the Philippines' top-producing region increased over the last 10 years, exceeding $355m in 2022. Graph: Bulatlat

The heart of the issue lies in the opaque profit-sharing mechanisms that exacerbate the marginalization of fishers, it claimed.

With fishing vessels laden with advanced technology and resources, small-scale fishers find themselves edged out of the competition. Expensive fish aggregating devices called payaos to locate tuna also squeeze out smaller fishers and companies.

Moreover, the government's regulatory framework, ostensibly aimed at safeguarding workers' rights, falls short in practice, the report claimed. Some policies have loopholes and lax enforcement that, in fact, aid exploitation. Fishers, classified as field personnel, are deprived of basic rights and protections, perpetuating their vulnerability.

As fishers grapple with dwindling catches and mounting debts, the commercialization of tuna burgeons, thanks to tactics employed by big fishing corporations. These companies wield immense influence, stifling dissent and perpetuating exploitative practices with impunity, according to Bulatlat.

Skipjack tuna is the most abundant and valuable commercial fish caught in the Philippines over the last decade. This is due to high demand from canneries, with General Santos home to six of the country's eight tuna canneries.

Graph: Bulatlat

The province produced 1.83 million metric tons of skipjack, generating nearly PHP 130 billion ($2.3bn) from 2013 to 2022. It's a very profitable species, as over 60% of South Cotabato’s production value for the same period came from this species alone.

Despite the billions generated by the industry, Filipino fishers get poorer and poorer because profit-sharing schemes put the burden of risk on the fisher. Additionally, commercial handline fishermen struggle to compete with FAD fishing, Bulatlat wrote. 

It said the major companies it contacted did not respond.
