title: Editor’s choice: Sysco drops Indian supplier amid abuse reports; Cod shortage in spotlight
content:
EMEA editor Neil Ramsden brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week  

The news of another in-depth report of unethical labor practices in the supply chain that supplies major US buyers -- this time originating in the Indian shrimp sector -- was our most-read news last week.

Sysco Corp., the largest foodservice firm in the US, has suspended purchases from Nekkanti Sea Foods pending further investigation after reports alleging environmental and labor issues are widespread in the Indian shrimp sector. Sysco's move came after Nekkanti and other major Indian shrimp suppliers were named in an Associated Press story, which took on an in-depth report from Chicago, Illinois-based Corporate Accountability Lab, a human rights legal group. Nekkanti denies any wrongdoing. 

In fact, Sysco dropped Nekkanti as a supplier just under a week prior to the publishing of an article that clarified the Indian shrimp processor was not operating a truck photographed at a peeling shed, Undercurrent News confirmed. In the article and an on-the-record statement given to Undercurrent, Nekkanti said it does not use peeling sheds; all its processing is done within its five plants in Andhra Pradesh.

At the same time, the Outlaw Ocean Project -- the same investigative journalism outfit behind earlier findings of forced labor in China -- shared evidence linking India's Choice Canning to a flurry of allegations regarding falsified documents, knowingly shipping antibiotic-positive shrimp to the US, and worker mistreatment.

The reduced supply of Atlantic cod and total ban on Russian raw material by the US is causing headed and gutted (H&G) prices for the former to rocket to record levels, with the market desperately needing alternatives, the CEO of one of the world's largest whitefish processors told Undercurrent. Norway and Russia's 20% cut in the Barents Sea cod quota to 453,427 metric tons for 2024 was already set to send prices soaring, even prior to the US executive order from December last year banning any Russian raw material. Having almost converged at the end of 2023, Norwegian H&G frozen Atlantic cod prices are now over $2,000/t higher than Russian, with processors needing to look for other options.

China's shrimp aquaculture industry is experiencing a renaissance driven by the widespread adoption of greenhouse raceway farming systems operated by more knowledgeable farmers, according to industry experts. Robins McIntosh, an executive at Thailand-based food conglomerate Charoen Pokphand Foods, recently toured shrimp farms across China from Liaoning province in the north to Guangxi in the south. He found the new greenhouse setup to be the predominant system in most areas. 

The impending announcement of new anti-dumping and countervailing duties on shrimp products destined for the US has created significant apprehension among exporters. At the Seafood Expo North America earlier in March, shrimp packers from India and Ecuador told Undercurrent that this decision could be a game changer, depending especially on which source countries get the highest rates. 

Steve Phillips, the owner and CEO of Phillips Foods, said the work he did before making several shellfish-related acquisitions in Atlantic Canada was the most fun he's had in more than 30 years. That's roughly how long ago it was that Phillips first traveled to and explored the swimming crab fisheries of Southeast Asia, leading to the creation of a $600 million per year import sector -- in which his company remains a major player. He predicts the investment and gains his company will make in Canada's lobster, snow crab and other species will be even larger.

Last week saw something of a saga as snow crab harvesters in Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada, tried to negotiate a new pricing formula with processors. Late on Thursday, the Fish Food and Allied Workers, the union that represents inshore harvesters, said talks were over and that it now expects the matter to be decided by the Fish Price Setting Panel. Before that, amid rising tensions, the Association of Seafood Producers -- the trade association that represents the processors -- rejected the last offer made by harvesters to settle negotiations.

US importer, processor and distributor Fortune International is targeting a $1.25 billion turnover in 2024, setting sights on acquisitions to expand its reach further west and take its skin-pack production into new regions. Having snapped up East Coast skin-pack specialist Boston Sword & Tuna in 2023 to pass $1bn in revenue last year, Fortune is aiming to hit the $1.25bn goal even before any mergers and acquisitions.

Prices of Japan-bound Alaskan pollock surimi for the 2024 A season are being tentatively set for some loads, but most Japanese buyers have put their negotiations on hold, multiple sources informed Undercurrent last week. The slower market comes with Japanese buyers seeing weakened demand on the part of finished surimi product manufacturers in Japan.

Bornstein Seafoods is consolidating three West Coast US processing plants into one as part of an "optimization" drive, the company announced on Friday. The company -- which processes species ranging from Dungeness crab to albacore tuna -- has made the "difficult decision" to close plants in Bellingham, Washington, and Newport, Oregon, and move production into its site in Astoria, Oregon.

And finally, Icelandic fishing giant Samherji is changing its product and species mix in response to the drastic reduction in cod supply this year, with smaller fillets and haddock suddenly very much in vogue, according to Baldvin Thorsteinsson, son of Samherji owner Thorsteinn Baldvinsson and chair of Alda Seafood. Presenting at the North Atlantic Seafood Forum in Bergen, Thorsteinsson noted that since last summer, prices for smaller 5-8 ounce cod fillets have actually outstripped those of larger ones.

title: US lawmakers seize on report of labor abuses in Indian shrimp sector
content:
The allegations raised by a former Indian shrimp factory manager against his old employers, Choice Canning Company -- a subsidiary of shrimp exporter The Choice Group -- have garnered significant attention this week in the US Congress.

The Outlaw Ocean Project (OOP), the same investigative journalism outfit that earlier stirred Capitol Hill with its investigative series spotlighting forced labor in China, has US lawmakers again moving to action over an article published on Wednesday (March 20) in which it focuses instead on labor abuse and antibiotic fraud in the Indian shrimp industry.

OOP's latest article focuses on allegations made by Joshua Farinella, who was employed as general manager of Choice Canning's factory in Amalapuram, Andhra Pradesh, from October 2023 until resigning in February this year.

Indian shrimp supplier accused of labor abuse, antibiotic fraud in new report

In response, senator Bill Cassidy, a Republican representing the state of Louisiana, has asked the president Joe Biden administration, in a short, one-page letter sent March 20 to the US Trade Representative and Customs and Border Protection, to "urgently" investigate and guarantee Farinella full whistleblower protections. 

Cassidy, an advocate for the US domestic wild-caught shrimp industry in his home state, also has renewed calls for the passage of the India Shrimp Tariff Act, S. 2979. The bill, introduced in September 2023, calls for tariffs on Indian shrimp.

The legislation would introduce a rate of duty on imports of Indian shrimp that would escalate over time until it matched the basic tariff duty of 30% that India observes on its own shrimp imports from the US.

Currently, the US does not impose regular tariffs on shrimp imports, while the US Food and Drug Administration samples and tests less than 0.1% of seafood shipments for unsafe drug residues annually.

The Choice Canning Shrimp processing plant in Amalapuram, India, is at the heart of the latest investigative campaign from the Outlaw Ocean Project. Credit: Ben Blankenship/The Outlaw Ocean Project

"Through subsidies, sanitary cheating and dumping, Indian shrimpers are trying to drive Louisiana shrimp out of business," Cassidy said in his letter. "Specifically, the Outlaw Ocean Project's investigation, published earlier today, raises worrying concerns about the safety of shrimp imported from India into the US."

Farinella's allegations make "clear why Indian shrimp does not belong on the shelf alongside Louisiana shrimp... Indian shrimp relies on forced labor and is pumped full of antibiotics," he said in a statement accompanying his letter.

In its original response to OOP, The Choice Group described Farinella's allegations as "plainly false." It denied falsifying any documents, knowingly shipping shrimp to the US that had tested positive for antibiotics, underpaying its staff, or keeping migrant workers trapped on site against their will.

"It appears that Joshua Farinella has had a key role to bring false issues to you and to mislead you to believe Choice has engaged in conduct amounting to violations of law, regulation, or otherwise," the company's statement to OOP reads.

Meanwhile, the broader Indian export sector is already on edge regarding the impending announcement of new anti-dumping and countervailing duties on shrimp products destined for the US.

Trio of representatives ask whistleblower for evidence

Not to be outdone by Cassidy, three prominent Democrats in the US House of Representatives -- Jared Huffman, Raul Grijalva and Melanie Stansbury -- have written to Farinella, requesting he present more evidence to back up his allegations by April 2, 2024.

Grijalva, from Arizona, is the ranking member on the House Natural Resources Committee, while Huffman, from California, is the ranking member on the committee's oceans panel and Stansbury, from New Mexico, is the ranking member on the committee's oversight and investigations panel. 

In a letter sent March 18 to Farinella, the three lawmakers ask for a spreadsheet of worker headcounts and wages; text and WhatsApp messages; emails; and documents or recorded phone conversations, including those with The Choice Group's CEO and senior management in the US state of New Jersey.

They say in their letter that Choice Canning potentially violated five laws and policies, including:

Sect. 307 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which prohibits imports to the US of any good derived from forced labor;
The Lacey Act, which prohibits the import and sale of illegally obtained fish products;
The Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act, which prohibits fraudulent reporting under the Seafood Import Monitoring program.
The Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, which prohibits the illegal use of antibiotics; and
Best Aquaculture Practices certification, which attempts to ensure that producers are following best practices to deliver farmed seafood safely and responsibly.

"We are disturbed by the widespread presence of forced labor and human rights violations in the seafood supply chain," the trio wrote. "As the single largest importer of seafood in the world, the US holds tremendous market influence over the operations of global fisheries."

They continued: "The actions of US-based importers and seafood companies disproportionately affect the health and safety of all seafood products and the likelihood that seafood is not produced with forced labor or through illegal, unregulated or unreported fishing practices."

title: Norway selects DNV to carry out offshore aquaculture impact assessments
content:
The Norwegian government has chosen standards and classifications firm DNV to conduct impact assessments for offshore aquaculture in three areas.

After tendering the task to bidders, the Ministry of Trade and Fisheries has chosen DNV to assess how offshore aquaculture will impact "Norskerenna sor, Froyabanken nord, and Traenabanken."

Lovundlaks-owned offshore salmon farm targets 2028 for first at-sea release

"The interest from several major players bodes well for the development of offshore aquaculture. DNV has extensive experience with large, relevant strategic impact assessments. In addition, it provides key personnel with particularly good insight into biosecurity work which will be important in this work," said Norway's fisheries and oceans minister Cecilie Myrseth.

DNV personnel have worked on clearing SalMar Aker Ocean's offshore facility Smart Fish Farm for operations, and so have "a good understanding of the assignment...[including], among other things, the use of infection modeling and connectivity analyses as tools to be able to divide the investigation area into suitable notification areas."

DNV will be tasked with assessing the farming of salmon and trout on the environment, fish welfare, and coexistence with other marine industries.

"The overall impact assessment will form the basis for the authorities' decision as to whether all or parts of an area may be relevant for offshore aquaculture and which parts of the area should be advertised first. The deadline for the work is set for Oct. 15, 2024."

title: Bornstein to consolidate three West Coast US plants into one
content:
Bornstein Seafoods is consolidating three West Coast US processing plants into one as part of an "optimization" drive, the company announced on Friday (March 22).

The company -- which processes species ranging from Dungeness crab to albacore tuna (see picture above) -- has made the "difficult decision" to close plants in Bellingham, Washington, and Newport, Oregon, and move production into its site in Astoria, Oregon.

"We are announcing the repositioning of our operations, a move that underscores our commitment to sustainability, quality, and innovation while better serving the needs of our customers and partners in the West Coast seafood industry," said Colin and Andrew Bornstein, the top executives at the family-owned company, in a joint statement.

"While this decision represents a significant step forward for our company, we are also mindful of its impact on our valued employees," they said. "We assure our workforce that we are dedicated to supporting them during this transition period, providing job fair opportunities and access to other resources to assist them in finding alternative employment opportunities. Our commitment to our employees remains unwavering as we navigate this change together."

The company said the operational adjustment will not impact customer service and all products processed by Bornstein will remain unaffected.

The move will result in improved service of vessels, "further enhancing the company's ability to meet the evolving needs of its partners while maintaining the highest standards of quality and sustainability," Bornstein said.

At the end of January, Bornstein's plant in Iwaco, Washington, was hit with a fire just ahead of that area's commercial Dungeness crab season. At the time, investigators said the cause of the fire, which resulted in extensive damage, was not considered to be suspicious.

title: Indian export body says shrimp labor abuse report gives ‘wilfully distorted view’
content:
The Seafood Exporters Association of India (SEAI) has responded to the March 20 release of a report from the Corporate Accountability Lab (CAL) and subsequent story in the Associated Press detailing labor rights and environmental abuses in the Indian shrimp sector which it claims "leaves readers with a wilfully distorted view of Indian shrimp exporters."

Sysco stops buying from Indian shrimp supplier after reports allege environmental, labor issues in sector

The SEAI's president, Pawan Kumar, writes that the story misleadingly conflates shrimp exporters represented by the organization with smaller domestic operators, "leaving readers with the impression that major exporters are involved in the bad behavior they describe without presenting any evidence that this is the case."

The allegations raised by the CAL's report, "Hidden Harvest: Human Rights and Environmental Abuses in India’s Shrimp Industry," and subsequent article have already led Sysco Corporation, the largest foodservice distributor in the US, to suspend purchases from Indian shrimp supplier Nekkanti Sea Foods, pending further investigation.

The report alleges that forced and child labor and hazardous working conditions are prevalent in the sector, while environmental damage, including the destruction of mangroves and pollution of coastal waters, further compound the issue.

Governmental oversight of the industry is lacking, and private certification schemes, such as the Global Seafood Alliance's Best Aquaculture Practices and Aquaculture Stewardship Council, have failed to address the abuses effectively, the report states.

Yet Kumar adds that no AP reporters reached out to them for comment before publication, despite being the representative body for the sector.

The SEAI notes that it reached out to the AP, but "they flatly ignored us."

"As far as we can tell, AP never presented our association or any of our members with specific details about the infractions they alleged, making it impossible for us to examine them or indeed to establish whether they ever happened," wrote Kumar.

"But we did inform AP that none of the members they asked about had ever been found to have committed any of these kinds of infractions, and made them aware of multiple, independent channels our employees have to safely report any issues."

The AP story specifically names Wellcome Fisheries, which it says did not respond to a request for comment. Kumar's response claims Wellcome was never contacted.

"If she [author Mendoza] had, Wellcome would have provided the same details of its strong labor and environmental record that it provided to the customers to whom AP presented its unsubstantiated allegations."

title: Russian trawler fire off Kaliningrad claims one life, leaves four injured
content:
One person lost their life while four others sustained injuries in a fire that engulfed a fishing vessel off Russia's coast in the Baltic Sea, Xinhua reported.

The fire erupted aboard the Captain Lobanov trawler within the vicinity of Kaliningrad, according to a statement by Dmitry Lyskov, the press secretary of the regional governor.

Efforts were underway to tow the vessel to the safety of the Baltiysk port in Kaliningrad, with assurances from Lyskov that all injured parties would receive necessary medical attention. The cause of the fire is under investigation.

title: Daily recap: Reports of abuses in Indian shrimp; Samherji adapts to cod shortage
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Thursday, March 21:

Sysco stops buying from Indian shrimp supplier after reports allege environmental, labor issues in sector

Sysco Corp., the largest foodservice firm in the US, has suspended purchases from Nekkanti Sea Foods pending further investigation after reports alleging environmental and labor issues are widespread in the Indian shrimp sector.

Indian shrimp supplier accused of labor abuse, antibiotic fraud in new report

Choice Canning, an Indian shrimp packer and trader, is at the center of a flurry of allegations regarding falsified documents, knowingly shipping antiobiotic-positive shrimp to the US, and worker mistreatment.

Samherji turns to small fillets, haddock, saithe amid cod shortage

Icelandic fishing giant Samherji is changing its product and species mix in response to the drastic reduction in cod supply this year, with smaller fillets and haddock suddenly very much in vogue, according to Baldvin Thorsteinsson, son of Samherji owner Thorsteinn Baldvinsson and chair of Alda Seafood.

Fortune looks west for M&A, plans Illinois, Texas skin-pack expansion with $1.25bn turnover in sights

US importer, processor and distributor Fortune International is targeting a $1.25 billion turnover in 2024, setting sights on acquisitions to expand its reach further west and take its skin-pack production into new regions.

Chilean salmon sector claims NGO’s funding of Magallanes management is 'conflict of interest'

Chile's southernmost region, Magallanes, has witnessed a surge in salmon farming over the past decade, but the sector faces potential constraints due to proposed new management plans. Now, an aquaculture guild has leveled accusations of irregularities in the process of formulating the management plan for the Kawesqar National Reserve in Magallanes.

Med farmed seabass continues to get cheaper versus bream

March 2024 has seen a widening gap in the discount of the Mediterranean's farmed seabass against seabream, driven by a decline in bass prices.

title: Indian shrimp supplier accused of labor abuse, antibiotic fraud in new report
content:
Choice Canning, an Indian shrimp packer and trader, is at the center of a flurry of allegations regarding falsified documents, knowingly shipping antibiotic-positive shrimp to the US, and worker mistreatment.

The Outlaw Ocean Project (OOP) -- the same investigative journalism outfit behind earlier findings of forced labor in China -- published a new report on Wednesday (March 20) in which it shares evidence provided by Joshua Farinella, a former general manager at Choice Canning's Amalapuram factory, in Andhra Pradesh, who joined in October 2023.

It includes accounts of:

Falsified documents by Choice Canning management intended to mislead auditors about its shrimp sourcing and employee headcount;
Decisions by management to knowingly ship antibiotic-positive shrimp to the US;
Management approval of the underpayment of workers, leading to complaints to the local police;
Staff complaints of inadequate living conditions on sites, including worker dorms without sufficient bedding;
Workers being prevented from leaving the site;
Ongoing use of unsanitary off-site peeling sheds hidden from auditors; and
Repeated complaints from locals regarding pollution from the factory.

During his time running the factory, Farinella told OOP he had to make plans to hide workers ahead of inspections in order to not show overcrowding; mislead customers about the provenance and quality of their shrimp; and confront orders to send consignments of antibiotic-positive shrimp to the US.

Farinella decided to resign and go public in February, heading back to the US after just over four months at the site, and filed a formal whistleblower complaint to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), according to OOP. 

The full OOP report can be seen here.

The Choice Canning Shrimp processing plant in Amalapuram, India, is at the heart of the latest investigative campaign from the Outlaw Ocean Project. Credit: Ben Blankenship/The Outlaw Ocean Project

The factory's parent company, The Choice Group, directed Undercurrent News on Thursday to its direct response to the allegations via its law firm, Archer & Greiner, which described them as "plainly false."

"It appears that Joshua Farinella has had a key role to bring false issues to you and to mislead you to believe Choice has engaged in conduct amounting to violations of law, regulation, or otherwise," the company's statement to the Outlaw Ocean Project reads.

Choice attacked the character of Farinella, who "has an extensive criminal record," which includes "multiple guilty pleas to felony fraud and deception crimes," it continued, dating between 2007 and 2014.

"Notably, before hiring Mr. Farinella, Choice was not aware of Mr. Farinella's extensive criminal record, with multiple felony convictions pertaining to fraud, deception, and theft," it said.

The company also addressed each allegation in turn:

"Absolutely no documents have been falsified," the company has said, adding that employee counts vary from day to day as a large portion of the workforce is employed on a contract basis. The Amalapuram factory has a capacity to hold over 600 workers, it noted.

Sysco stops buying from Indian shrimp supplier after reports allege environmental, labor issues in sector

No Choice Canning shrimp shipment has ever been rejected by the FDA for testing antibiotic-positive, the company said. A WhatsApp exchange that appears to show a confirmation from management to ship antibiotic positive product has been misrepresented, it claimed, as the firm runs two screening processes for antibiotics.

These shrimp, it contended, had tested positive for the first confirmation screening, but negative on the second "more vigorous" screening.

There are also no cases of approving the underpayment of workers, the company said.

"Many of Choice's workers are temporary and are employed through third-party labor contractors," it explained. "Choice always has made every single wage payment to a contractor on time." The police investigation, it said, was of one contractor that had failed to distribute wages, not Choice itself.

Choice also pointed to a BCSI social audit, conducted by the Belgian firm Amfori, which entailed interviews of "large numbers" of Choice's workers on their quality of life. The company received an "A" grade in the last such audit, it said.

The company admitted it was aware of one case where a worker was not allowed to leave the premises at 2:30 a.m., claiming this was done for their own safety, with curfews in place forbidding workers from leaving the walled factory enclosure past 10:30 pm. It said the worker was then permitted to leave the next morning.

"Accordingly, there are not workers that are being prevented from leaving the site, such a conclusion is recklessly false," Choice said.

Choice admitted that it had used an off-site facility for a brief period of time, from January-February this year, to address a labor shortage, again relying on a contractor's facility and contract labor to provide the work. The firm provides shrimp both to BAP and non-BAP customers, and it was the latter that was targeted with this off-site work, the company said.

Sysco drops major Chinese seafood supplier; still catches heat from US lawmaker over forced labor concerns

"Thus, it naturally was not included as part of Choice's BAP audits," it said.

Choice has been leasing the Amalapuram plant since June 2022, and was not originally aware that there had been a history of complaints by local residents against the previous owner, pertaining to the smell of processed shrimp. Choice said it has since fixed the effluent treatment plant used to process shrimp.

Choice concluded that it "is prepared to proceed forward with a lawsuit filing against your organization, Outlaw, [founder] Ian Urbina, and any and all other responsible parties for any falsely published stories."

A headache for the GSA

The Choice Group sells frozen shrimp throughout the US in over 48,000 retail and foodservice locations. According to the OOP, it shipped more than $80 million worth of shrimp to the US in 2023.

New initiative aims to boost small-scale aquaculture farmers in India

Notably, the factory at Amalapuram has also been granted Best Aquaculture Practices (BAP) certification.

Last November, Choice Canning became the first Indian company to become a corporate member of the Global Seafood Alliance (GSA), the body responsible for the creation and oversight of the BAP standard. The GSA has told OOP it would "thoroughly investigate" the issues brought to light.

For his part, Farinella said he was surprised at the high number of shrimp that tested positive for antibiotics, given that the majority of farms it was sourcing from were supposedly BAP-certified -- and therefore should be antibiotic-free, OOP reported.

The company's senior quality assurance manager allegedly replied in a WhatsApp message to Farinella that Choice Canning "never buys shrimp from BAP farms," adding that "India doesn't have even 10% of the BAP farming capacity it claims."

Outlaw Ocean's review of FDA data also shows that while Choice Canning's exports to the US have never tested positive for antibiotics, the agency only tested shrimp from the firm on 21 occasions since 2003. During that timespan, the firm has shipped more than 100,000 metric tons of shrimp to the US.

In response, Choice Canning said that it is the only Indian shipping company to use a mobile lab, engaging in pre-harvesting testing at the farmer level prior to purchase -- hence the high number of positive tests.

"Ask yourself, if Choice was in fact seeking increased profits at the cost of food safety, and looking to 'gamble' that the FDA won't discover during an FDA audit or inspection of antibiotic-positive shrimp, why would Choice spend the funds to implement this pre-harvest testing procedure to establish a testing standard above and beyond any other Indian company?" it wrote to OOP.

The firm added that it conducts internal audits of BAP-certified farms, internal ELISA screening for raw material that arrives at its facility, and external screening at an accredited lab that runs a "more exacting confirmatory LCMSMS test."

On one identified occasion, where both ELISA and LCMSMS tests had failed, Choice claimed that the batch was returned to the farmer and not shipped as usual.

Equally, OOP's additional finding that "at least 730t of antibiotic-positive shrimp passed through Choice Canning's Amalapuram facility in 2023" is contested by the company, which claims the figures have been altered by Farinella.

A third-party firm that specializes in data analysis reviewed these documents and verified that they were not manipulated in any way, according to the OOP.

A tough day for Indian shrimp

The OOP report was released the same day as a separate report from the US human rights legal group Corporate Accountability Lab (CAL) into the Indian shrimp sector, titled 'Hidden Harvest: Human Rights and Environmental Abuses in India's Shrimp Industry.' 

Ecuador, India shrimp packers on edge as industry awaits US anti-dumping, countervailing duties decisions

The report was followed up with an article in the Associated Press, which prompted Sysco Corp., the largest foodservice firm in the US, to suspend purchases from Nekkanti Sea Foods, named in the story, pending further investigation.

Alongside Nekkanti, Apex Frozen Foods, Avanti Feeds, Devi Fisheries (and its subsidiary Satya Sea Foods), and Sandhya Aqua were also named in the CAL report as "generating profit off of shrimp produced cheaply at the expense of workers and the environment." So, too were such US retailers as Aldi, Costco, Hannaford, Kroger, Stop & Shop, Walmart, and Whole Foods; and such food service chains as Red Lobster and the Cheesecake Factory, as well as local restaurants that buy shrimp from Sysco, US Foods and other national distributors.

The Seafood Exporters Association of India (SEAI), which represents the sector's largest traders and processors, published a statement on Thursday (March 21) in which it charges that the Associated Press did not give the group an opportunity to respond to the CAL's report, and turned down similar outreach from the US' National Fisheries Institute.

Credit: nirapai boonpheng / Shutterstock

"As far as we can tell, AP never presented our association or any of our members with specific details about the infractions they alleged, making it impossible for us to examine them or indeed to establish whether they ever happened," the SEAI wrote. 

The SEAI said that "multiple, independent channels" exist for employees to report welfare issues within its member companies.

"They also misleadingly conflate the shrimp exporters we represent with smaller companies that operate only within India's domestic market, leaving readers with the impression that major exporters are involved in the bad behavior they describe without presenting any evidence that that is the case."

title: Chilean salmon sector claims NGO’s funding of Magallanes management is ‘conflict of interest’
content:
Chile's southernmost region, Magallanes, has witnessed a surge in salmon farming over the past decade, but the sector faces potential constraints due to proposed new management plans.

Now, an aquaculture guild has leveled accusations of irregularities in the process of formulating the management plan for the Kawesqar National Reserve in Magallanes, industry sources told Undercurrent News. 

The Magallanes Salmon Farmers Association (MSFA) has filed a complaint with Chile's general comptroller calling for an investigation into alleged conflicts of interest and violations of principles of administrative probity, impartiality, and serviceability by Chile's National Forestry Corporation (CONAF) while establishing the reserve, Salmon Expert reported.

The accused parties, which include an NGO and a university, told Undercurrent they rejected accusations as a "way to obstruct the development of management plans," thereby "facilitating the intensification of salmon farming projects."

Salmon farming association in Chile’s far south gets new head

According to the MSFA, between 2018 and 2020, framework agreements were signed between CONAF, NGO the Pew Charitable Trusts, and the Austral University of Chile, aiming to dictate the management and handling of protected areas in the Chilean Patagonia.

"Pew, a US NGO, provided more than CLP 1.9 billion [$1.96 million] to the Austral University of Chile, which would subsequently have been transferred to CONAF in an amount that we still do not know and hope will be clarified in the investigation. These funds were allocated to hiring personnel working on the formulation of the management plan for the Kawesqar National Reserve and those conducting the technical studies supporting it," claimed Carlos Odebret, president of MSFA.

"We are talking about irregular influence in the elaboration of the mentioned plan. That is, Pew -- an NGO that has expressed interest in impeding the development of salmon farming -- financing, through a network of agreements with CONAF, the development of a public policy with significant effects on third parties," Odebret said.

The manner of this financing would have allowed for direction and control over CONAF's actions in an arrangement that closely resembles a mandate contract, according to the association.

Mylthon Jimenez, a vice-chancellor at the university, defended the institution's conservation work.

He told Undercurrent the university "has collaborated with CONAF for decades, making its scientists and technical capabilities available to solve multiple issues related to nature conservation, protected area management, ecosystem services, forest production, fire control, and public policies, among others, always in line with its public role." 

He did not deny Pew's payments. According to Jimenez, the university's Pew-funded Austral Patagonia Program has collaborated in "generating and transferring new knowledge to strengthen and improve the management of Patagonia's wildlife protected areas."

"Technically managing vast extensions of (new and existing) protected territory, their species and ecosystems, is a huge challenge for the country, and the [university] has targeted its scientific and technical capabilities to meet this challenge," Jimenez noted.

Pew's Chilean office also replied to the accusations.

"Chile is one of the 10 countries in the world with the lowest investment in its protected areas. However, as part of its global commitments under the NDCs, it has pledged to develop management plans for these protected areas," Pew told Undercurrent.

"Aligned with those needs over the past eight years, Pew's Chilean Patagonia Project has collaborated with the Austral Patagonia Program [known as ProAP] at the University Austral of Chile to address these and other shortcomings in terms of capacities, training, standards, and more; initiatives are being implemented to aid in the formulation of management plans for Chile's protected areas. Thus, through ProAP, research led by some of the country's top scientists has been conducted to gather up-to-date, scientifically-based information, which has been made available to the public and relevant environmental authorities."

Within this context, collaboration agreements -- compliant with prevailing legislation and regulations -- have been established with CONAF, according to Pew.

"Historically engaged in such partnerships with NGOs, universities, and other organizations, CONAF's objective is to ensure the proper management of protected areas under its administration (national parks, reserves, and natural monuments). ProAP has assisted CONAF in enhancing processes, capacities, personnel training, and tools for effectively managing terrestrial and marine protected areas in Patagonia, in alignment with Chile's commitment to the Convention on Biological Diversity," it further said.

Pew claimed the allegations against it, ProAp and CONAF seek to "obstruct the development of management plans for unique ecosystems currently lacking regulatory frameworks, thereby facilitating the intensification of salmon farming projects -- non-native species to Chile -- by transnational corporations within the national parks and reserves of the Magallanes region."

title: Untitled
content:
Sysco Corp., the largest foodservice firm in the US, has suspended purchases from Nekkanti Sea Foods pending further investigation after reports alleging environmental and labor issues are widespread in the Indian shrimp sector.

The move from Houston, Texas-based Sysco comes after Nekkanti and other major Indian shrimp suppliers were named in an Associated Press (AP) story, which took on an in-depth report from Chicago, Illinois-based Corporate Accountability Lab (CAL), a human rights legal group. Nekkanti denies any wrongdoing. 

CAL's report, "Hidden Harvest: Human Rights and Environmental Abuses in India's Shrimp Industry," found workers face "dangerous and abusive conditions" in the sector. The report can be read in full here. You can see an executive summary here.

According to the Undercurrent News trade portal, India exported 296,400 metric tons of shrimp worth $2.47 billion to the US in 2023, up 215% in value and 125% in volume over the past 10 years (see first chart below), making it the number one player ahead of Ecuador and Indonesia (see second chart below).

However, this growth comes at a cost, with reports of widespread exploitation of vulnerable workers, including Dalit, Adivasi, and migrant communities, throughout the shrimp supply chain, the CAL report states.

Forced and child labor and hazardous working conditions are prevalent, while environmental damage, including the destruction of mangroves and pollution of coastal waters, further compound the issue, according to CAL.

Governmental oversight of the industry is lacking, and private certification schemes, such as the Global Seafood Alliance (GSA)'s Best Aquaculture Practices (BAP) and Aquaculture Stewardship Council, have failed to address the abuses effectively, the report states.

Then, antibiotic use is prevalent in the sector, the report claims. This is "not only potentially detrimental to human health, leading to increased resistance to antibiotics, but it also helps to explain the Indian shrimp industry’s focus on national markets with fewer regulations and less monitoring of imported shrimp: China and the United States," CAL states. 

Captain Fresh raises further $25m in UK gov’t, Nekkanti-led round

Indian companies like Nekkanti, Apex Frozen Foods, Avanti Feeds, Devi Fisheries (and its subsidiary Satya Sea Foods), and Sandhya Aqua; retailers such as Aldi, Costco, Hannaford, Kroger, Stop & Shop, Walmart, and Whole Foods; chains such as Red Lobster and the Cheesecake Factory, and local restaurants that buy shrimp from Sysco, US Foods, and other national sellers, "generate profit off of shrimp produced cheaply at the expense of workers and the environment," the report states.

The AP traveled in February to Andhra Pradesh in southeast India to document working conditions in the industry after obtaining an advance copy of the CAL report.

CAL and the AP both focus on reporting on the use of outsourced peeling sheds by large processors, which is prohibited by the BAP standard.  

"At one tin-roofed processing shed, AP journalists observed dozens of women working in unsanitary and dangerous conditions. The shrimp, pulled from outdoor ponds in barrels, were swished around by hand in grimy water. Once rinsed, they were dumped onto ice-covered tables, where women stood, peeling them one shrimp at a time. Many handled shrimp with bare hands. Some women had bandages on injured fingers. Some women's long hair dangled into the shrimp," the report states.

Ecuador, India shrimp packers on edge as industry awaits US anti-dumping, countervailing duties decisions

AP reporters then saw processed shrimp from this facility being loaded in large plastic crates into a truck with the brand "Nekkanti" painted on the side.

Managers at the small shed told the AP that Nekkanti and other major brands often outsource the labor-intensive peeling and deveining work to keep down costs.

Nekkanti, which is an investor in acqusitive Indian seafood player Captain Fresh, said the truck was being leased to another company, adding it does not use peeling sheds.

However, Sysco has still suspended dealings with the firm, which states on its website it's India's largest vertically integrated player with turnover of $300 million. 

"Sysco has instructed suppliers we are suspending the receipt of any products from Nekkanti… processing plants or facilities pending our investigation into allegations of human rights and labor abuses," said the foodservice giant in a statement given to the AP.

"Sysco banned packers, processors, and suppliers of Sysco-branded products from using 'peeling sheds' nearly 10 years ago when we learned about the actual and potential risk of human rights violations within this part of the shrimp supply chain," it said.

‘Everything depends on US duties,’ says top Ecuador shrimp exec on production outlook

Sysco also said it "ended its direct business relationship" with another Indian supplier, Wellcome Fisheries, in 2022 after it "refused to allow us to conduct a required social responsibility audit in their facility."

John Ducar, an advisor to the Nekkanti board, said the company had nothing to do with the peeling shed that AP visited and said their branded truck was there only because it was being leased to another company.

"Nekkanti does not outsource any shrimp processing. We explicitly refrain from conducting any business activities in processing sheds throughout India," the company told the AP.

Ducar provided a document that said Nekkanti was paid $3,600 for the four-month truck lease with the license number the AP observed.

US shrimp import uptick is over after six months as prices continue descent

"It appears that you observed the operations of an entirely separate company," he told the AP.

"We have leased 29 of our 68 trucks (which have our logo and signage permanently painted on them) to a domestic supplier during our lean season (for shrimp) and which happens to be the peak season for seafood consumption in domestic market (December to March)," reads the full statement given by Nekkanti to the AP, which you can read here. 

"Nekkanti has no involvement whatsoever in the operations of that business entity beyond the vehicle lease arrangement. Additionally, the older trucks from our fleet are regularly sold to domestic seafood industry participants, moreover, when these older trucks are sold, the company's logo is not removed."

The company named in the document did not respond to a request for comment to the AP.

Other buyers did respond to the AP.

"To be clear, we have no knowledge of Nekkanti or any of our other suppliers using peeling sheds for their products. So, accusations or concerns in such facilities come as a surprise," said Eastern Fish, a large US importer owned by Japan's Marubeni. "That said, Eastern Fish will not tolerate labor abuses of any sort at any level of our supply chain. We are taking measures to suspend purchases until we can appropriately and thoroughly investigate these claims."

Walmart, the world's largest retailer, said it's "looking into the allegations" raised by the AP.

Indian shrimp feed supplier, processor Avanti expects ‘moderate’ recovery in 2024, improvement after

Rich Products said it's "always fully prepared to investigate any allegations and take decisive corrective measures in response to any substantiated claims."

Meanwhile, Southwind Foods, which trades as Great American Seafood Import Co., said the "aquaculture practices you describe are certainly concerning and not in keeping with our interest in maintaining safe, healthy ecosystems."

"We take these matters very seriously," said the GSA, which came up with the BAP standards.

"When credible evidence of activities in violation of… [the BAP] standards are reported, they are thoroughly investigated."

title: Norwegian authorities to crack down on ‘production fish’ exports
content:
The Norwegian Food Safety Authority (Mattilsynet) has intensified its efforts to combat the export of unprocessed "production fish," a breach of the country's regulations.

Whole "production fish," encompassing farmed fish with wounds, deformities or processing errors, are not permitted for human consumption until they undergo proper treatment by domestic businesses equipped for such processes. They may then be exported as filleted salmon.

EU confirms it will raise ‘production fish’ issue with Norway after Danish complaint

The prevalence of production fish in the market has been steadily rising, accounting for 15% of fish production in 2023 compared to 5% in 2018, and numbers have been higher again in 2024, contributing to prolonged high spot market prices for fresh whole fish. This increase, particularly notable in winter, has reached over 36% in certain weeks this year, said Mattilsynet.

Daily loads of farmed salmon can range between 150 and 200 trucks destined for EU countries or terminals; Mattilsynet acknowledged its limitations in monitoring all transactions.

"We expect all businesses to follow the rules on this. Nevertheless, our inspection campaign last year showed that too many players are breaking the rules, and we are now constantly receiving reports that this is still happening," said Inge Erlend Naesset, the department director for regulations and control at Mattilsynet.

"In light of the persistent violations, we will escalate measures, including export and sales bans, market withdrawal orders, and potential police reports," Naesset concluded.

In February, Norwegian salmon farmer Masoval informed the stock exchange that an investigation into its majority-owned processing and sales company had revealed some customers were supplied with fish that were unsuitable for human consumption.

That included fish that either should have been discarded/ensiled or production-grade fish that should be elaborated in secondary processing before export.

Meanwhile, the EU Commission is to open talks with Norway after finding the latter country's policy of processing all downgraded salmon in-country should be considered a "barrier to trade."

This comes after a complaint by Denmark to the EU, Poul Melgaard Jensen of the Danish Seafood Association confirmed to Undercurrent News.

Jensen said the Norwegian export rules "seriously disrupt the market for salmon filets and processed salmon products."

"More than 36% of total production in Norway has in 2024 [as of week six] been classified as production, and the cost-price of fillets from production salmon is €3-€4 [per kilogram] below the cost-price of fillets from superior. [That] clearly in itself shows that the market distortions are unsustainable."

title: Canada makes 26 more arrests for illegal elver fishing
content:
The commercial elver fishery in Atlantic Canada is shut down, but the poaching continues.

Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) said Monday (March 18) that it had arrested 26 people so far in March on rivers in Atlantic Canada, reports CBC News. All suspects are reported to be under investigation for violating the federal Fisheries Act and Maritimes province's fishery regulations for the unauthorized harvest of elvers.

DFO officers reported seizing six vehicles, dozens of dip nets and one gun while releasing 6.5 kilograms of elvers back into rivers. 

Five arrests were announced on March 11, the day fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier officially canceled the season amid warnings from commercial harvesters and others that her action would do nothing to stop poaching.

Conservative member of Parliament Rick Perkins, who represents the federal riding of South Shore-St. Margarets, Nova Scotia, said those arrested are released and rarely face charges.

Meanwhile, commercial elver license holder Stanley King has set up trail cameras on rivers in Hubbards and Boutiliers Point, Nova Scotia, and said he has captured images of elver poachers, CBC reported.

"Given the minister felt the need to cancel the season, putting 1,100 people out of work, I hope that DFO conservation and protection [officers] will put in more effort than the token enforcement the industry has witnessed over the last four years," King wrote in a letter to the minister and DFO officials.

King told Undercurrent News recently that he doubted the closure would accomplish anything, noting that DFO "has had two previous closures to deal with rampant unlicensed fishing, and they have turned a blind eye on each occasion. We doubt this time will be any different."

title: Untitled
content:
Ecuador's shrimp production in 2024 should be stable but could drop if the US preliminary anti-dumping and countervailing duty (CVD) rates are harsh, said one of the sector's top executives.

In 2023, Ecuador exported 1.21 million metric tons (up 14% y-o-y) and produced around 1.4m, a level it should hit in 2024 unless the US anti-dumping and CVD rates are very high, Omarsa CEO Sandro Coglitore told Undercurrent News at Seafood Expo North America (SENA).

US trade investigation ‘biggest problem or threat’ facing Ecuador shrimp but rebalance possible

"I think it will be stable; the only way it's coming down is if the US market suffers if there is a setback with these suits," Coglitore said, adding that Omarsa stopped shipping to the country earlier this month.

In 2023, the US market imported 205,972t of shrimp worth $1.25 billion from Ecuador, up 5% in volume but down 8% in value. In terms of individual countries, that's behind only China, which imported 714,887t worth $3.5bn, up 21% in volume and down 2% in value.

For January, Ecuador started the year with a 6% drop in volume to 89,211t, while value was down 17%. Although exports to China dropped, the US market increased by 4% in volume to 16,675t, with a 1% drop in value to $100.1m.

As to what happens next, "everything depends on the US duties," Coglitore told Undercurrent.

McIntosh: GSMC shrimp forecast of drop from China, flat Ecuador output is bearish

It's a very important issue because many small factories depend on their sales to the US. If the anti-dumping and the CVD rates are high, we must figure out if the market will absorb that increase. Or how it will affect the buying price," he said.

"If the market is unwilling or unable to pick up the tab, then there will be suffering in terms of medium and small-sized plants that depend 100% on their sales to the US. And, of course, the farmers that supply those factories will get a lower price. It will be difficult for many of them to survive with lower prices," he said.

As Undercurrent's prices portal shows, farm-gate prices in Ecuador are already well below the levels obtained in India, Vietnam and Indonesia. 

Upgrade to Pro to view

All companies in Ecuador have plans "on hold" and are waiting to see what happens with the duties, he said.

"If the duties are too high, we will lose a significant market for value-added products. All the peeled and IQF [individually quick frozen] shrimp that the US is a huge market for, we must figure out what to do with that production," he said.

Omarsa stops US shipping, eyes April 'window'

Omarsa stopped shipping to the US market earlier in March to await the preliminary CVD rate later this month, after which there could be a window to export until the preliminary anti-dumping rate is established in late May.

US shrimp imports’ late sprint to finish not enough to salvage 2023

The US Department of Commerce (DOC) is expected to announce preliminary CVD rates for shrimp from Ecuador, India, Indonesia and Vietnam on March 25.  

Then, on May 22, the preliminary anti-dumping rates will be announced for Ecuador and Indonesia, where the US shrimp industry players are asking for 118% in their petition. Both will be preliminary rates that could change when the US government makes a final determination at the end of the year.

Depending on the CVD rate, he said, there could be an opening for Omarsa to ship after March 25 and before the anti-dumping rate on May 22. Coglitore clarified that Omarsa is only "fifth or sixth" in sales to the US, despite being number two or three in total exports. 

"The US is about 6% of our total," he said. 

Some producers continue to ship to the US. However, several importers increasingly demand delivery duty-paid shipments, where producers take the risk in case of a potential retroactive duty, sources from the sector told Undercurrent at SENA.

GSMC shrimp panel forecasts slight 2024 output drop with many farmers ‘below cost’

Omarsa is not willing to gamble in this manner.

"We stopped shipping on March 8. We are on a standby pattern to see what comes out on March 25. I don't see anybody willing to take that risk because it's a crazy risk," Coglitore said.

"Then we must see if there's a short window where we can ship again, depending on the outcome of the CVD, before the anti-dumping duty is announced, which would be May 22," he said. "It's very important, the preliminary duty, as we will know if we can take a risk before we get to the deadline that we must stop shipping to wait for the May 22 preliminary for the dumping."

He said the "window' would be after March 25 "until the end of April to early May," to reach the US before May 25.

"For the CVD, anything around 5% would be manageable. If it's higher than that, it will be tough. And that's only one part; we still have the dumping," he said.

Domestic, import shortages drive Chinese shrimp price jump

The preliminary anti-dumping rate will be layered on top of the CVD.

"So, it could be anything, in the suit, they are targeting 118%, which is absurd," Coglitore told Undercurrent. "They wanted to show a high level so the DOC would think there's merit if they asked for over 100%. If they had asked for 10%, the DOC might not care and bother putting resources into it, as they have bigger things to go after, like steel or other imports. But if they say over 100%, maybe it looks more lucrative."

There's incredulity from US importers that the law can work in this way, who will also be impacted, said Coglitore.

"It jeopardizes not only businesses from Ecuador, India, Indonesia, and Vietnam but also puts their businesses [in the US] at risk," he told Undercurrent. "Because they [US importers] can suddenly be cut out of supply, that the fishermen, the people that are suing us, will not be able to replace. They're unable to produce more, so suddenly, the price has to increase by a percentage."

'Worse than Vegas'

The situation with the duties is a guaranteed loser for Ecuador; it's just about how much. Coglitore compared the situation to playing roulette and blackjack.

"I've been telling my customers this is worse than going to Las Vegas. If you go to Las Vegas, you bet $1, and you know you will lose $1. With this one here, you get a preliminary rate. You put down $1, and maybe they come back in December when the final rate is published, and they come back for more," he said.

Boston 2024: Regal Springs asked to ‘nearshore’ Alaska processing; Canada lobster exports to China flip script

"Here, you have to spend, and the risk is paying more at the end of the year. But there's no gain. So, it's a tricky situation," Coglitore said. "Most of the customers don't understand it, so they say, this is ridiculous. It doesn't make any sense. But it's a US law. So many people can't believe that the law is so flawed."

As Omarsa is not one of the two "selected respondents," number one and two exporters Industrial Pesquera Santa Priscilla and Songa, Coglitore said his company must wait and see.

"Since we're not one of the selected respondents, I have no clue because we don't know the details on what markets will be the comparison markets and what products they're targeting. We are just bystanders waiting for our average. And no chance to get our day in court and defend ourselves," he said.

title: Whistleblower video raises concerns about fish welfare at BC caviar farm
content:
Northern Divine Aquafarms, a caviar producer located in the municipality of Sechelt on the Sunshine Coast in British Columbia, Canada, has been accused of animal cruelty.

The allegations came to light through an article first published in The Chilliwack Progress, where the executive director of Animal Justice, lawyer Camille Labchuk, said the Canadian not-for-profit group possesses a video captured by an employee that depicts what she described as "heartbreaking cruelty" towards sturgeon at the farm in Northern Divine. Labchuk did not reveal the source of the video.

Sturgeon black caviar
Photo: Northern Divine Aquafarms

In a blog post on its website, Animal Justice emphasizes the sentience of fish, asserting that despite their inability to vocalize pain, they are capable of experiencing suffering and deserve better treatment than what is allegedly provided at the caviar production facility.

Undercurrent News watched the nearly four-minute video. It shows sturgeon swimming in tanks filled with murky water and scenes of the pit tagging process, fish slaughter and egg checks. 

Animal Justice said it has filed an animal cruelty complaint with the BC Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (SPCA), urging the other organization to investigate the practices at Northern Divine Aquafarms and hold those responsible for the alleged mistreatment of the animals accountable. It's calling for an end to the exploitation of fish for caviar and for stricter regulations to protect animals in the aquaculture industry. 

According to The Chilliwack Progress article, the BC SPCA, along with biology and veterinary experts, conducted an unannounced visit to Northern Divine Aquafarms in January. While no violations of provincial legislation were observed during the visit, an investigation in collaboration with Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) is ongoing. The investigation includes a review of footage to determine if any violations are evident.

The newspaper did not get a reply to its request for comment from Northern Divine's owner, Florida-based Caviar & Caviar. It said the company acquired Northern Divine in June and expressed ambitions to increase caviar production at the facility, aiming to boost output from 18 to 25 metric tons annually. The farm is the only organic-certified caviar producer in North America, according to the BC government.

Undercurrent has also attempted twice to obtain a response from Northern Divine Caviar regarding the accusations outlined in article but has yet to receive a reply.

Northern Divine is a pioneer in recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) farming in British Columbia, having started in 1998. The company followed up with the establishment of the first RAS dedicated to growout in 2000. In 2011, Northern Divine achieved a significant milestone in its aquaculture journey with the inaugural roe harvest. It takes 11 years for sturgeon to mature and start bearing eggs.

title: US commission urges Dep’t of State, Homeland Security to act on Chinese imports
content:
A US Congressional body created in 2000 to monitor China's compliance with international human rights standards has urged the departments of State and Homeland Security to act quickly to address alleged forced labor in China's seafood industry.

The Congressional-Executive Commission on China (CECC) sent a letter to Antony Blinken and Alejandro Mayorkas, the secretaries respectively of each agency, asking them to "act quickly and decisively to address forced labor in China's seafood industry and the very real possibility that US consumers of seafood are funding North Korea's nuclear saber-rattling."

The action follows an investigation by the Outlaw Ocean Project (OOP), published in The New Yorker, exposing "horrific details about abusive practices towards North Koreans forced to work in seafood processing plants" in China, and the fact that this seafood ends up on American plates, the CECC said.

Journalist behind forced labor report to Congress, White House staff: MSC not enough; expand SIMP

OOP founder Ian Urbina appeared as a witness to a CECC hearing in October 2023 after the investigation he helped lead shook the sector worldwide.

US law prohibits imports of any goods made with North Korean labor. The Countering American Adversaries Through Sanctions Act, passed in 2017, imposes sanctions on individuals and entities associated with adversarial countries, including North Korea.

Furthermore, the employment of North Koreans violates United Nations (UN) Security Council Resolution 2397, which prohibits third countries from using North Korean laborers.

According to UN General Assembly Resolution 78/218, the UN prohibits employment of North Koreans to stop foreign currency transfers to North Korea's dictator Kim Jong Un, who uses the wages garnered from workers to fund "its illicit nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programs," said the CECC.

"North Korean labor is profitable to China's seafood industry in part because of imports to the US and other countries. Given China's footprint in the global seafood supply chain, American consumers are unwittingly exposed to products likely tainted with such labor."

As per the OOP's investigation, "seafood sold in American grocery stores and wholesalers such as Costco and delivered to military bases, school food programs, and even congressional cafeterias makes both American consumers and the US government inadvertently complicit in supporting forced labor and funding Kim Jong Un's dictatorial regime," the CECC added.

This would be a direct violation of federal law, and a coordinated US government response is needed immediately, it said.

The CECC wrote to Homeland Security in October 2023, detailing its concerns that forced labor was tainting America's seafood supply chain.

"The requests made in that letter remain relevant: Use the authorities provided by Congress to the Administration to block [Chinese] seafood imports linked to forced labor and end US government procurement of seafood caught and processed from such sources."

Now it has further laid out a list of requests it wants to see acted on as quickly as possible:

Immediately stop all imports from Chinese companies that employ North Korean labor;
Request an open briefing, or at the very least an Arria-formula meeting, at the UN Security Council, to discuss [China] 's violation of UN Security Council sanctions regarding the employment of North Koreans and the intersection of North Korea's nuclear ambitions and forced labor transfer programs;
Work with like-minded partners to insist that the UN High Commissioner for Refugees gain access to North Koreans in [China] and ensure that all North Koreans workers are given the opportunity to seek asylum;
Deepen information sharing with like-minded partners, particularly South Korea and Japan, to promote transparency and traceability in the seafood supply chain from [China];
Work through respective interagency processes to require all US federal seafood procurements to provide full supply chain disclosures, records of shipments, and forced labor prevention plans to the Seafood Import Monitoring Program and US Customs and Border Protection; and
Issue a joint interagency advisory outlining the supply chain risks for businesses and federal procurement managers in purchasing seafood from [China].

"No US business or federal agency should source seafood caught or processed with forced labor or from companies using North Korean labor, as that labor generates revenue for the North Korean government and violates US law. We look forward to continuing to work with you to ensure American consumers are no longer unwittingly exposed to products tainted by forced labor," the CECC concluded.

While OOP's initial investigation centered on the use of forced labor practices tied to the Uyghur minority people, its latest -- published earlier in 2024 -- outlined human rights abuses among North Korean laborers sent to seafood processing plants in China.

Trident Seafoods CEO Joe Bundrant called the revelations "deeply disturbing" and said his firm was committed to learning more. Trident, High Liner Foods and Sysco Corp. have all suspended business with a large processing firm in China, Dalian Haiqing Food Co., over OOP's new report.

Meanwhile, in the UK, an anonymous NGO has filed a legal petition urging the government to impose sanctions on seven Chinese firms implicated in forced labor practices tied to the Uyghur minority.

title: BAP, GAP content that Macquarie Harbour salmon producers can retain certifications
content:
Eco-label standard operators Global GAP and the Global Seafood Alliance (GSA, which owns the Best Aquaculture Practices label) have confirmed salmon farms in Macquarie Harbour, Tasmania, Australia will not be stripped of their certifications after a complaint about alleged impacts on the endangered Mugean skate population there.

SeaChoice --  a "science-based, solution-focused influencer, advocate and watchdog," according to its website -- filed formal complaints with both eco-labels. It said retailers in Australia such as Coles, Woolworths and Aldi used these certifications "as a shield to deflect criticism and to market Macquarie Harbour salmon to shoppers as ‘responsible’ and sustainable."

Tasmania’s salmon sector claims results in oxygenating Macquarie Harbour

"Right now is harvest season for Macquarie Harbour salmon, however, shoppers are unable to tell which salmon in store is from the harbor. This means supermarkets are profiting from the greenwashing of extinction while shoppers are in the dark."

It said the dismissal of its complaint added weight to a complaint filed by environmental groups in December to the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission "accusing supermarkets and certifications of greenwashing."

Environmental groups continue to claim that salmon farms in the harbor are reducing the water quality and pose a risk to the already endangered skate. 

But Global GAP told SeaChoice: "The outcome of... an evaluation by the certification body was that the producers under certification in MH [Macquarie Harbour] are still compliant with regard to the implementation of the IFA AQ v5.4-1-GFS requirements and that their farms in MH currently operate with a renewed legal environmental license, showing compliance with the local applicable environmental legislation."

"Furthermore, the involved producers demonstrated awareness of the MH situation. These producers are engaged in the implementation of additional remediation measures to mitigate identified impacts on the surrounding environment, especially the impact on the Maugean Skate population and the levels of dissolved oxygen in the area."

The industry has invested in a pilot known as the Macquarie Harbour Oxygenation Project, which teams of Australian scientists, operational crews and marine specialists have claimed goes "from strength to strength" following a successful start to stage one trials.

Aussie Greens propose worker transition plan for Tasmanian salmon farm closure

The GSA, too, said the farmers continue to meet certification standards, with the state of the Maugean skate population fully "on the radar" and having taken several steps to try and improve the situation, which are "aligned with the latest conservation advice."

It noted that salmon farming was not the only factor at play in the skate's struggles.

"GSA greatly appreciates the dedication by SeaChoice and partners to the protection of the Maugean skate and completely agree that the highest efforts must be made to prevent its extinction. We also agree with the coalition that evidence correlates the expansion of fish farming with low dissolved oxygen levels in the mid to bottom waters of the MH."

"However, the call for revocation of certifications does not account for other anthropogenic and natural impacts on water quality, nor the mitigation efforts by multi-stakeholders. Based on our investigation, these mitigation efforts could be critical to the recovery of the skate population in MH."

It will continue to monitor the results of the efforts, it said.

title: Report: Tuna caught by Chinese vessels that netted penguins, whales linked to Bumble Bee
content:
Some of the world's largest seafood brands, including US tuna giant Bumble Bee Foods, have again been linked to disturbing fishing practices and human rights abuses in China's distant water fishing fleet, including the netting of dolphins, whales and even penguins.

The report by the Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF) describes systematic illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing over a five-year period by Chinese tuna fishing giant Zhejiang Ocean Family (ZOF), a Zhoushan, east China-based firm that reportedly catches 15% of all tuna produced by China.

According to EJF, ZOF supplied over $305 million of tuna to Taiwanese tuna trader FCF, which owns the US tuna canner and brand Bumble Bee, between 2018-2021, citing public company documents.

ZOF sold another $179m in tuna to Mitsubishi Corporation and traded with Grupo Frinsa, Tri Marine Group, Maruha Nichiro and Bolton Group affiliates. EJF stressed there was no suggestion that the buyers had any knowledge of the allegations of IUU fishing or other issues documented.

The EJF report, which was released Friday (March 8), draws on interviews with 20 Indonesian crew members who worked onboard 12 ZOF fishing boats between 2018 and 2022. The crew members allege troubling practices such as shark finning, catching dolphins and whales against regulations, excessive overtime of up to 48 hours straight, lack of pay, debt bondage, and months-long isolation at sea.

A ray caught on a XIN SHI JI vessel. Source: EJF briefing Zhejiang Ocean Family Co. Ltd And Its Fishy Business.

According to EJF, interviewees described killing up to 50 protected shark species per day across the ZOF fleet for their fins, including endangered hammerhead, oceanic whitetip and thresher sharks protected by regional fisheries management organizations. One fisher aboard a ZOF vessel reported his boat would catch turtles, sharks, whales, dolphins and even penguins. The animals were netted, killed and discarded, with the teeth kept as trophies.

A megamouth shark caught by a XIN SHI JI vessel. Source: EJF briefing Zhejiang Ocean Family Co. Ltd And Its Fishy Business.

ZOF did not respond to Undercurrent News request for comment. A salesperson at the company said he'd not heard about the report.

Earth Island project director David Phillips told Undercurrent his organization has now revoked ZOF's Dolphin Safe Tuna status following its own three-month investigation into tuna fishing companies in the Western and Central Pacific Ocean. 

"The results of our analysis demonstrated that [ZOF] has failed to conform with key provisions of the Dolphin Safe Policy that they have signed on to."

"The non-conformances include the filing of false reports with our Dolphin Safe Tuna Program, as well as to tuna buyers, and violation of US tuna importation laws," said Phillips.

Entry into seafood supply chains

EJF analysis of AIS (automatic identification system) vessel tracking data revealed 39 suspected at-sea transshipments between the named Zhejiang vessels and 11 reefers that later called at ports in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and French Polynesia. EJF said this indicates potential market access for illegal catches from the fleet. Six Zhejiang vessels also directly visited ports in Korea, Singapore and French Polynesia.

The tuna caught by ZOF and that entered supply chains was then traced through subsidiaries. According to trade records from Panjiva, ZOF supplied 1,538 metric tons of precooked tuna loins to Bumble Bee through its subsidiary Ningbo Yifeng between 2018-2021. Another 2,869t was supplied by Ningbo Today Food, while a third ZOF subsidiary supplied 519t. All told, some 33,000t of tuna processed by Ningbo Yifeng was caught by ZOF vessels.

ZOF supply chain analysis by EJF. Source: EJF briefing Zhejiang Ocean Family Co. Ltd And Its Fishy Business.

Bumble Bee told Undercurrent it hadn't purchased pre-cooked loins from any ZOF entity since 2018. That year, Donald Trump imposed 10% tariffs on Chinese imports, rising to 25% in early 2019. Bumble Bee later backed a lawsuit against the US government which claimed tariffs were "devastating" for its business.

FCF later acquired Bumble Bee in March 2020 for $928m after the latter's bankruptcy. 

Trident, High Liner, Sysco suspend buying from Chinese processor over North Korean labor allegations

"The allegations related to forced labor and destructive environmental practices are issues Bumble Bee has been aggressively working to address through our leadership in the Seafood Task Force and ISSF [the International Seafood Sustainability Foundation
 ]," the Bumble Bee spokesperson told Undercurrent.

"We agree more progress is needed to address these complex challenges, and it's why we continue to work within our supply chain, with others in the industry and key stakeholders to advocate for the responsible recruitment and treatment of all workers and for the reduction IUU fishing worldwide," they said.

Other downstream companies linked with ZOF-caught tuna include Nestle Purina Petcare, Amazon, Walmart and Carrefour, EJF said. Again, EJF said there was no suggestion that any of the companies were aware of the abuses allegedly perpetrated by ZOF or that they knowingly sold from the 12 vessels investigated by EJF.

Links to Chinese government

EJF's report also raises questions about ZOF's links to the Chinese government, given its fishing activities in waters of Pacific island nations like Kiribati and its trade relationships with major seafood transnationals.

ZOF was established as a majority state-owned corporation in 2009. Private conglomerate Wanxiang Sannong Group, one of China's largest makers of auto parts, has since upped its holding to a 90% stake, with state-owned firms retaining around 20% ownership directly and indirectly through Wanxiang.  

Bumble Bee owner FCF hosts ethical recruitment task force in Taiwan

Wanxiang Sannong's ultimate beneficiary is Lu Weiding, vice chairman of the China Enterprise Confederation, China Enterprise Directors Association, and All-China Industry and Commerce Federation. Lu is also a member of the National People's Congress, China's rubber-stamp legislative body.

According to financial filings, ZOF benefited from at least $40m in Chinese fisheries subsidies between 2018 and 2021 before it canceled a planned IPO on the Shanghai stock exchange last year.

EJF CEO Steve Trent said it was long overdue for governments and stakeholders to tackle IUU and abusive labor practices in seafood supply chains. 

"The Zhejiang Ocean Family has been getting away with illegal fishing and human rights infringements for far too long," said Trent. "It is time stakeholders and governments alike finally step up to regulate the industry. The fish on our plates must not come at the cost of people, wildlife and our shared natural world," he said.

The NGO suggests implementing unique vessel numbers, public vessel tracking data, and banning flags of convenience, among other recommendations outlined in its Global Charter for Transparency.

China's supply chain under the microscope

The EJF investigation comes after Trident Seafoods, High Liner Foods and Sysco Corp. all suspended business with Chinese processor Dalian Haiqing Food Co. after another NGO reported Chinese seafood companies were using North Korean labor. 

NGO urges UK sanctions on Chinese firms linked to Uyghur forced labor

Ocean Outlaw Project found North Korean workers, who are predominately female, were subject to physical and sexual abuse, even forced prostitution, in Chinese seafood processing plants. Up to 100,0000 North Korean workers are in China, with some 80,000 in Dandong, a seafood processing hub between Dalian and the border with North Korea. The United Nations and the US prohibit the purchase of products produced by North Korea's exported workers. 

More recently, another NGO filed a legal petition urging the UK government to impose sanctions on seven Chinese firms implicated in forced labor practices tied to the Uyghur minority.

The NGO, which is seeking to remain anonymous, claims forced labor from China's Xinjiang province has been extensively used in seafood processing factories across the country. The petition has been filed under the UK's Global Human Rights Sanctions (GHR) law on March 4, and is the result of an ongoing separate investigation also by the Outlaw Ocean team.
