title: NGO urges UK sanctions on Chinese firms linked to Uyghur forced labor
content:
An NGO, which is seeking to remain anonymous, has filed a legal petition urging the UK government to impose sanctions on seven Chinese firms implicated in forced labor practices tied to the Uyghur minority.

Aldi probes Portugal supply chain after North Korean labor in China report

The submission, filed under the UK's Global Human Rights Sanctions (GHR) law on March 4, is a significant development following an ongoing investigation by the Outlaw Ocean Project.

The legal petition claims forced labor from China's Xinjiang province has been extensively used in seafood processing factories across the country, with repercussions reaching global seafood industries that rely on China's processing capacity.

Among the implicated companies are Yantai Sanko Fisheries, Yantai Longwin Foods, The Chishan Group -- including subsidiaries Shandong Haidu and Rongcheng Haibo -- The Shandong Meijia Group -- including subsidiaries Rizhao Meijia Aquatic Foodstuff, Rizhao Jiayuan Foodstuff, and Rizhao Meijia Keyuan Foods -- Qingdao Tianyuan Aquatic Foodstuffs, Rongsense Group -- including subsidiaries Rizhao Rirong Aquatic Products and Rizhao Rongxing -- and Xinjiang Zhongtai Zhihui Modern Service.

The petition aims to halt the import of seafood produced by these companies into the UK, as these products have ties to major UK importers.

EU negotiators reach provisional agreement to ban products made with forced labor

It calls for targeted sanctions to hold those involved in serious human rights violations accountable, aligning with the GHR law's objectives.

This move by the UK follows similar petitions filed in Canada and the US, demonstrating a growing international effort to address human rights abuses in China's seafood industry. 

The OOP's report is just the latest to rock the seafood industry; the group reported last fall that Chinese processors were using Uyghur forced labor and supplying major seafood companies, with products from the plants ending up in the US and EU, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

title: Trident’s Bundrant commits to investigate China’s use of North Korean labor
content:
Revelations of forced North Korean labor used at Chinese processing plants are "deeply disturbing," and Trident Seafoods is committed to learning more, CEO Joe Bundrant says. 

The Seattle, Washington-based seafood giant's leader addressed the latest findings of a report from the Outlaw Ocean Project (OOP), which outlined human rights abuses among North Korean laborers sent to seafood processing plants in China, in a letter published on the company website late last month (Feb. 26).

The report is "another black mark against a global seafood industry already reeling from allegations of supply chain impropriety," he asserted.

"Trident is doubling down on doing the right thing by making the necessary investments and improvements needed to ensure every aspect of our seafood supply chain is compliant with our standards and our customers' standards," Bundrant wrote. "The time is now for our entire industry to do the same."

OOP's investigation was originally published in The New Yorker and led to Trident, High Liner Foods and Sysco Corp. all suspending business with Chinese processing Dalian Haiqing Food Co., as reported by Undercurrent News. Previous reports have led to congressional hearings. 

US lawmakers press White House to address China forced labor in advance of WTO discussion

In the latest story, OOP -- a team of journalists led by Pulitzer Prize winning reporter Ian Urbina -- investigated the use and alleged abuse of North Koreans in Chinese seafood processing. In 2017, when North Korea launched a series of nuclear and ballistic missile tests, the United Nations and the US prohibited the purchase of products produced by North Korea's exported workers, the article explained.

The workers are sent from North Korea to other countries, such as Russia, Poland, Qatar, Uruguay and Mali, according to the report, with a portion of their wages paid to North Korea's government in Pyongyang. There are reportedly as many as 100,0000 North Korean workers in China, with some 80,000 in Dandong, a seafood processing hub between Dalian and the border with Kim Jong Un's hermit kingdom, according to the article.

Trident, High Liner, Sysco suspend buying from Chinese processor over North Korean labor allegations

Urbina's latest report contains allegations of physical and sexual abuse, even forced prostitution, of North Korean workers, who are predominately female, in the Chinese plants.

Bundrant said Trident has since launched its own investigation and is fully cooperating with OOP.

"We are focusing specifically on determining if -- or how -- we failed to detect violations of Trident’s Human Rights and Supplier Code of Conduct policies. If gaps exist in our [Corporate Social Responsibility] program and auditing process, then the answer is simple: We’ll fix them," he said.

The OOP's report is just the latest to rock the seafood industry; the group reported last fall that Chinese processors were using Uyghur forced labor and supplying major seafood companies, with products from the plants ending up in the US and EU, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

title: Europeche welcomes EU’s decision to ban products made with forced labor
content:
European fishing body Europeche has welcomed the European Union's recent decision to ban products manufactured through forced labor.

The EU's provisional deal on a regulation targeting goods produced in violation of human and workers' rights, including seafood, marks a significant step in addressing the global issue of forced labor affecting over 27.6 million people worldwide, they said.

EU negotiators reach provisional agreement to ban products made with forced labor

The agreement, which underwent substantial modifications from its initial proposal, outlines clear roles for the EU Commission and national competent authorities in investigating and enforcing the ban, according to Europeche.

The agreement came after a journalistic investigation by the Ocean Outlaw Project detailed links between alleged forced labor and illegal fishing activities in China with significant buyers in the US and EU, first focused on the Muslim Uyghur minority and then North Koreans.

In the latter investigation, published in the New Yorker, it emerged North Korean workers sent to Chinese factories were subject to enduring beatings and sexual abuse, having their wages taken by the state, and being told that if they tried to escape, they would be "killed without a trace." Some of those factories shipped their products to companies both in the US and Europe, including one that supplies the cafeterias of the European Parliament.

The association praised this development and urged swift implementation to halt the trade of fish products derived from forced labor, aligning with EU policies against illegal fishing.

Central to the agreement is establishing a database by the EU Commission to aid in enforcement, compiling updated information on forced labor risks from sources like the International Labour Organization, Europeche said.

The criteria for evaluating violations and leading investigations have also been clarified, garnering support from Europeche.

Europeche's managing director, Daniel Voces, hailed the deal as a pivotal moment in the EU's fight against exploitative labor practices. He emphasized the importance of collaboration between the EU fishing sector, the EU Commission, and member states to combat forced labor effectively, promising greater consumer confidence in ethically sourced products.

title: UK retail salmon price-fixing lawsuit pits M&S against long-time supplier Scottish Sea Farms
content:
The lawsuit from seven UK retailers against a group of farmers means Marks and Spencer (M&S) is suing Scottish Sea Farms (SSF), its main salmon supplier.

Norwegian firms Bremnes Seashore, Cermaq Group, Grieg Seafood, Leroy Seafood Group, SalMar, and Mowi were all named as defendants in the lawsuit, which Undercurrent News revealed on March 5 having first reported on Feb. 28. SSF, 50/50 owned by Leroy and SalMar, is also named along with UK divisions of Grieg and Mowi. 

Seven UK retailers allege price fixing of Norway salmon ‘cartel’ cost them over $850m

Then, M&S is named as a claimant, along with Asda Stores, Aldi Stores, Iceland Foods, Wm Morrison Supermarkets, Ocado Retail, and The Cooperative Group. J Sainsbury, which is supplied by Mowi's Scottish farms, Lidl, Tesco, and Waitrose and Partners are all not part of the legal action, which claims damages of over £675 million ($860m) from the alleged price-fixing cartel. Lidl, Sainsbury's and Tesco all previously confirmed they are not involved, as Undercurrent reported on March 1. 

M&S and SSF have one of the closest farmer-retailer relationships in the UK, along with Mowi and Sainsbury's and Waitrose and Aquascot, which doesn't own farms but sources from close partners for the high-end retailer. 

SSF -- which is even called out on M&S's website for its responsible farming -- supplies Associated Seafood with smoked supply to the retailer and Young's Seafood for natural salmon. 

Sainsbury’s, Tesco not part of UK retail damages claim over alleged Norwegian salmon price fixing

"I'm a bit mystified by that," said one European seafood source of the revelation that M&S is a claimant in the lawsuit against SSF and others. The lawsuit from the UK retailers comes after the European Commission (EC) issued a preliminary opinion on Jan. 25 stating the Norewrian companies did engage in price fixing. The EC case continues. 

M&S did not respond to Undercurrent News before publishing. 

"As with the original ongoing European Commission investigation focused on Norwegian farmed Atlantic salmon, and related class actions filed in the US and Canada, we do not consider there to be any substance or foundation to these latest claims," Jim Gallagher, managing director of SSF, said in a statement sent to Undercurrent. 

"We will, once again, engage fully in the process and expect the assertions against Scottish Sea Farms to be dismissed, just as they were in the US and Canada," he said.

title: Seven UK retailers allege price fixing of Norway salmon ‘cartel’ cost them over $850m
content:
The names of the UK retailers making a combined damages claim against Norway's largest salmon farmers for alleged price fixing have been made public, with the group stating an estimate of losses at over £675 million ($860m).

The document lists Asda Stores, Aldi Stores, Iceland Foods, Wm Morrison Supermarkets, Marks and Spencer (M&S), Ocado Retail, and The Cooperative Group as claimants. In addition, the Morrisons processing subsidiary in Grimsby, International Seafoods, is also named.

Sainsbury’s, Tesco not part of UK retail damages claim over alleged Norwegian salmon price fixing

As previously reported by Undercurrent News, Tesco, J Sainsbury and the UK arm of Germany's Lidl are not involved. Waitrose and Partners, which did not respond to a request for comment, also did not respond. 

As expected, Norway's Bremnes Seashore, Cermaq Group, Grieg Seafood, Leroy Seafood Group, SalMar, and Mowi are all named in the document filed to the UK's Competition Appeal Tribunal. 

In addition, the UK operations of Mowi and Grieg are named, as is Scottish Sea Farms (SSF) and two subsidiaries. SSF, the salmon supplier to M&S, is a joint venture between Leroy and SalMar.

The document states that the claimants' "current best estimate" of their total losses over the relevant period is £675m, excluding financing costs. The group represents over 44% of the UK grocery market with total estimated combined purchases of farmed Atlantic salmon of around £1.7 billion "during the cartel period," it continues.

UK retailers sue Norwegian salmon farmers after EC price fixing statement

In addition to the estimate of losses, the retailers also "claim damages in respect of the additional cost of financing the inflated purchase prices."

Then, the claim "compound or alternatively simple interest on the losses they have suffered," the document states. They also "reserve the right to provide further particulars of their purchases… including following further investigation and/or disclosure and/or the Defendants' responses to any requests for information."

The retailers are also claiming legal costs.

This UK claim stems from the unresolved European Union (EU) case against the Norwegians. On Jan. 25, 2024, the European Commission (EC) issued a preliminary opinion that the Norwegian salmon companies did engage in price fixing. This case has not concluded, so further clarity on the UK action will follow this, legal sources told Undercurrent.

A fine amounting to 10% of global annual turnover is the sternest award the EC can award in the case of anti-trust punishment, as previously reported by Undercurrent. 

Based on last year's revenue figures for the public companies, a 10% fine for Mowi this year would equate to NOK 6.16 billion ($588m), NOK 2.94bn for Leroy, NOK 2.91bn for SalMar, and NOK 718m for Grieg.

European Commission may take five years to pass salmon price-fixing judgement, says top lawyer

The UK retailers allege the cartel "operated in secret for at least" the period from 2011 until Feb. 20, 2019, the document states. The cartel ended when the defendants, other than Cermaq, were the subject of "dawn raids" on Feb. 20, 2019. Then, the EC opened an antitrust investigation.

Due to the retailers' "long-term contractual arrangements with suppliers and the long production cycles in Atlantic salmon farming, the effects of the Cartel are likely to have extended for a considerable time beyond the end of the Cartel Period," it states.

"The exact duration of the run-off effects will be a matter for evidence at trial, but provisionally, it is assumed to have lasted (at least) from the end of the Cartel Period until December 2020 but may have extended considerably longer; such extension is referred to as the "Run-Off Period". The Cartel Period and the Run-Off Period are collectively referred to as the "Relevant Period."

The claim form states that the effects of the alleged cartel "extended downstream through the supply chain, affecting secondary processed products" made from farmed Atlantic salmon, such as smoked, frozen, and ready-to-eat products.

Norwegian salmon shares plunge after EU anti-trust announcement

"It is anticipated that the EC investigation will culminate in due course," the claim form states, without giving a timeline.

A Norwegian competition lawyer previously estimated the EC case could take another five years to conclude.

The claim document also notes the US Department of Justice investigated Grieg, Leroy, Mowi and SalMar, although that was settled in 2023.

Then, some of the "defendants have also been sued in US class actions by both direct and indirect purchasers in relation to the cartel in Florida and have recently settled antitrust litigation in the US and Canada."

title: EU negotiators reach provisional agreement to ban products made with forced labor
content:
Negotiators from the European Parliament and Council have reached a provisional agreement on new regulations banning products made with forced labor from entering the EU market.

It stipulates that suspected cases of forced labor will be thoroughly investigated, and if confirmed, the products will be withdrawn from the market. You can read the full statement here. 

The agreement comes after a journalistic investigation by the Ocean Outlaw Project detailed links between alleged forced labor and illegal fishing activities in China with significant buyers in the US and EU, first focused on the Muslim Uyghur minority and then North Koreans. 

Aldi Portugal confirms it didn’t take product from one plant allegedly using North Korean labor, cuts sourcing ties with another

Under the proposed regulations, national authorities or the EU Commission will conduct investigations into suspected forced labor in supply chains in cases involving third countries.

If forced labor is found to have been used, authorities can demand the removal of relevant goods from the EU market, with penalties for non-compliance. However, companies demonstrating the elimination of forced labor from their supply chains may be permitted to reintroduce their products to the market.

Key features of the agreement include the establishment of a forced labor portal to enforce the rules and facilitate cooperation among authorities. Additionally, the Commission will compile a list of high-risk goods and areas prone to state-imposed forced labor, guiding investigations and import/export procedures.

Co-rapporteurs Samira Rafaela and Maria-Manuel Leitao-Marques hailed the agreement as a significant step in combating forced labor and upholding human rights in global supply chains.

The agreement awaits final approval from the European Parliament and Council before implementation, with EU countries given three years to adopt the new rules.

title: South Africa’s Premier Fishing fires CEO, pursues criminal charges
content:
South Africa's Premier Fishing and Brands has confirmed that CEO Sooren Ramdenee has been fired, and that it is pursuing criminal charges against him, over the misappropriation of funds from its Mauritian bank account.

"Premier Fishing wishes to inform the public that it has taken decisive action by formally laying a criminal case, encompassing charges of fraud, theft, and money laundering, in accordance with the Prevention of Organised Crime Act, No. 121 of 1998," it said in a statement.

Premier Fishing owner says crime uncovered last year was fraud, not cyberattack

This legal process is directed towards the individuals directly linked to the events surrounding the fraudulent transfer and theft of ZAR 15.6 million (almost $820,000).

"An exhaustive internal investigation conducted by Premier Fishing identified Sooren Ramdenee, the former CEO, as an interested party, principally owing to his close association with the events precipitating the misappropriation of funds. Premier Fishing's thorough examination further uncovered instances of negligence on Ramdenee's part, directly contributing to the loss of company assets."

In response, the company has taken swift and decisive disciplinary action, ultimately resulting in the termination of his employment, it said.

The company's findings have been relayed to the South African Police Service for further investigation.

"Regrettably, the company finds itself compelled to pursue criminal charges against, among others yet to be identified and implicated, Ramdenee and, moreover, to allow the legal process to duly unfold independently and impartially."

Premier Fishing reiterated its "relentless commitment" to recovering the misappropriated funds in their entirety, whether from Ramdenee or any other individuals associated.

The company will pursue all available legal avenues to ensure that justice is served and that the financial loss is recovered, it added.

title: Video: One fisherman dead, 24 rescued after tuna boat rescue op off Japanese coast
content:
In a dramatic rescue operation amidst treacherous conditions, Japanese coast guard helicopters saved 24 fishermen from a tilting, half-submerged vessel battered by high waves off a Japanese island southwest of Tokyo, Associated Press News reported.

The Fukuei Maru 8, which suffered engine failure shortly after departing Yaizu Port, was adrift after its engine had malfunctioned before hitting rocks and sending a distress signal.

The 379-metric-ton tuna fishing boat had onboard 20 Indonesian and five Japanese crew, Xinhua reported.

One crewmember, identified as the ship's first engineer, was thrown into the rough seas and found dead. The vessel was en route to South America for tuna fishing. The cause of the engine failure and subsequent mishap remains under investigation.

The successful rescue operation involved multiple patrol ships and helicopters.

title: Aldi Portugal confirms it didn’t take product from one plant allegedly using North Korean labor, cuts sourcing ties with another
content:
The Portuguese arm of German discounter Aldi Nord has clarified it never took product from one supplier mentioned in the Outlaw Ocean Project report on the use of North Korean labor in Chinese processing but has cut ties with another.

In the Outlaw Ocean report, two Chinese companies are mentioned as having supplied Portugal's Brasmar Comercio de Produtos Alimentares and Riberalves, who are processors selling to Aldi in the country.

Trident, High Liner, Sysco suspend buying from Chinese processor over North Korean labor allegations

The two Chinese firms are Donggang Jinhui Foodstuff and Donggang Haimeng Foodstuff, which are both based in Dongdang, a Chinese city on the border with North Korea. The Outlaw Ocean report alleges both have used North Korean labor, which the US and United Nations consider to be illegal.

On Feb. 27, Undercurrent News reported Aldi was looking into whether it'd been supplied with products produced by Haimeng.

Christian Schneider, an Aldi Nord spokesperson, said the retailer has cut ties with Jinhui, but an investigation showed Haimeng never supplied any products via Brasmar or Riberalves.

"Let us clarify: We have been made aware of two suppliers and two production sites in question by Outlaw Ocean Project: Donggang Jinhui Foodstuff and Donggang Haimeng Foodstuff," Schneider told Undercurrent in an email.

"The following applies to the Donggang Jinhui Foodstuff production facility: Our research has shown that only the supplier Riberalves has delivered one Alaska pollock article from this production facility to Aldi Portugal in the past. Following the information provided by OOP [Outlaw Ocean], it was decided to no longer source from this production site," he wrote.

"The following applies to the Donggang Haimeng Foodstuff production site: Neither Riberalves nor Brasmar have supplied goods produced there to ALDI Portugal," added Schneider.

title: UK retailers sue Norwegian salmon farmers after EC price fixing statement
content:
A group of unnamed UK retailers has issued claims for damages against Leroy Seafood Group and other Norwegian-owned aquaculture companies after the European Commission (EC) issued a preliminary opinion that they had been price fixing.

According to Leroy's Q4 and annual report, published Feb. 28, the claims were issued earlier in February 2024, after the EC's opinion on Jan. 25. Grieg Seafood's Q4 report from Feb. 22 also confirms it has been sued by the UK retailers, too. 

European Commission may take five years to pass salmon price-fixing judgement, says top lawyer

In addition to Grieg and Leroy, the EC statement included Cermaq Group, Bremnes Seashore, Leroy Seafood Group, Mowi and SalMar. 

Mowi and SalMar's Q4 reports, released on Feb. 14 and Feb. 15, respectively, mention the EC statement but not the UK lawsuit. Bremnes, Cermaq, Mowi and SalMar did not respond to requests for comment from Undercurrent News. 

"The commission has concerns that, between 2011 and 2019, the six salmon producers exchanged commercially sensitive information, relating to sales prices, available volumes, sales volumes, production volumes and production capacities, as well as other price-setting factors," said the EC on Jan. 25. "The suspected aim of this alleged conduct was to reduce normal uncertainty in the market for spot sales of Norwegian farmed Atlantic salmon into the EU."

The EC said the alleged anticompetitive conduct only concerns sales on the spot market into the EU, as opposed to sales based on long-term contracts. Spot sales are those for which prices, volumes and other sales conditions are agreed per sale, based on the market conditions on the day of the sale.

Norwegian salmon shares plunge after EU anti-trust announcement

Leroy "strongly rejects the claimants' allegations and considers such claims from customers to be baseless," it said on Feb. 28. 

"In Europe, this type of claim is first and foremost relevant if the Commission adopts a decision in its ongoing investigation and the decision is upheld," the company said. 

Leroy "understands that the claims have been issued at this stage in an attempt to interrupt the potential limitation of claims under certain laws," it said. 

On Jan. 26, Line Voldstad, a competition law partner at DLA Piper's Oslo, Norway office, told Undercurrent the case could take another five years to conclude.

title: Aldi probes Portugal supply chain after North Korean labor in China report
content:
Germany's Aldi Nord discounter chain is investigating links between its Portuguese suppliers and factories in China accused of illegally employing North Korean workers, according to a recent report from the Outlaw Ocean Project.

The German discount grocery chain has asked one local processor to halt dealings with the Chinese plant mentioned in the report until an audit can be conducted.

Trident, High Liner, Sysco suspend buying from Chinese processor over North Korean labor allegations

The use of North Korean labor has been deemed illegal since 2017 by both the United Nations (UN) and the US after Kim Jong Un launched a series of nuclear and ballistic missile tests that year. In an explosive report on Feb. 25 in The New Yorker, Outlaw Ocean director Ian Urbina presented evidence of the alleged use of North Korean labor by multiple Chinese plants based close to the border.

Two of the plants, Donggang Haimeng Foodstuff and Donggang Jinhui Foodstuff, are named in open-sourced conversations by Outlaw Ocean as suppliers to processors in Portugal, who in turn supplied Aldi Nord in the country.

Haimeng and Jinhui are both based in Dandong, right on the Chinese border with North Korea. The two companies have used North Korean labor after the December 2019 deadline for the repatriation of overseas North Korean workers required under UN Security Council sanctions, according to Outlaw Ocean. 

US lawmakers press White House to address China forced labor in advance of WTO discussion

Aldi Nord is looking at whether its suppliers in Portugal bought from Haimeng, which Outlaw Ocean said was employing hundreds of North Korean workers "as recently" as October 2023.

"We are currently conducting a data enquiry [sic] with our suppliers to get more detailed information and evaluate whether products have been sourced from the mentioned production facility. As this evaluation is still ongoing, we are unable to provide any detailed information at this time," Aldi Nord's Marina Fuhrmann told Outlaw Ocean on Feb. 5, 2024. 

Unlike many of the other Chinese processors contacted by Outlaw Ocean, Haimeng replied on Feb. 7. "Good morning: We, Donggang Haimeng Foodstuff Co. Ltd., state that we didn’t hire practices of North Korean workers. Our employment is in full compliance with SEMATA [sic, presumably SMETA, or the Sedex Members Ethical Trade Audit] standards," it said. 

According to an Outlaw Ocean email from Jan. 30, Brasmar Comercio de Produtos Alimentares, was the consignee for shipments of seafood from Haimeng back in 2021.

China says foreign-backed seafood consultant punished for ‘fabricating environmental problems’

Brasmar has supplied seafood to Aldi's brands Golden Seafood and Tesouros do Mar, according to labels on the product packaging, said Outlaw Ocean staff. Several emails to Brasmar from Outlaw Ocean asking for comment went unanswered.

Jinhui was using North Korean labor "as recently as 2023," Outlaw Ocean staff told Aldi Nord on Nov. 30, 2023.

The Chinese firm was then supplying Riberalves, a Portuguese whitefish processor and Aldi supplier, Outlaw Ocean stated. Riberalves did not respond directly to questions from Outlaw Ocean. 

On Dec. 6, Aldi Nord's Fuhrmann told Outlaw Ocean that supply from Jinhui to Riberalves had ceased.

"Consultation with our supplier has shown that the production facility in question has not been delivering goods to ALDI Portugal for several weeks," she wrote. "There is no longer any relationship with this production facility and the named supplier does not supply any other ALDI Nord countries with pollock articles."

On Feb. 5, 2024, Fuhrmann wrote that Riberalves "confirmed that they won't be purchasing any products from Donggang Jinhui until further notice."

Biden pushed by lawmakers to step up pressure on Sysco over forced labor concerns

Jinhui did not respond to Outlaw Ocean. 

Two days later, Outlaw Ocean asked Aldi Nord if Dalian Haiqing Food Co., a large processor based around 150 kilometers west of the North Korean border, was a supplier via Trident Seafoods' Pickenpack Seafoods plant. Haiqing is also accused of using North Korean labor in the Outlaw Ocean article.

Trident, High Liner Foods and Sysco have all stopped working with Haiqing pending further investigation, as Undercurrent News reported on Feb. 26.

On Feb. 12, Aldi Nord replied: "Thanks for informing us. In reference to Dalian Haiqing: we can confirm that our supplier Pickenpack did not deliver any product from this site to Aldi Nord. Thank you."

Haiqing denied using North Korean labor when asked by Outlaw Ocean.

title: Trident, High Liner, Sysco suspend buying from Chinese processor over North Korean labor allegations
content:
Trident Seafoods, High Liner Foods and Sysco Corp. have all suspended business with a large processing firm in China, Dalian Haiqing Food Co., over a new bombshell report by the Outlaw Ocean Project over the use of North Korean labor.

Having created a storm in the seafood sector last year with the revelations of Uyghur labor in Chinese processing plants, Outlaw Ocean director Ian Urbina has turned his team's focus to North Korean workers.

Trident still using Russian pollock in Europe after toasting latest US ban

The latest story, which is published in full by The New Yorker, investigates the use and alleged abuse of North Koreans in Chinese seafood processing. In 2017, when North Korea launched a series of nuclear and ballistic missile tests, the United Nations and the US prohibited the purchase of products produced by North Korea's exported workers.

The workers are sent from North Korea to countries such as Russia, Poland, Qatar, Uruguay and Mali, according to the report, with a portion of their wages paid to North Korea's government in Pyongyang. There are reportedly as many as 100,0000 North Korean workers in China, with some 80,000 in Dandong, a seafood processing hub between Dalian and the border with Kim Jong Un's hermit kingdom, according to the article.

Urbina's latest report contains allegations of physical and sexual abuse, even forced prostitution, of North Korean workers, who are predominately female, in the Chinese plants.

US lawmakers press White House to address China forced labor in advance of WTO discussion

Haiqing is the largest and most global player in the report, but Dandong Galicia Seafood, Dandong Yuanyi Refined Seafoods, Donggang Xinxin Foodstuff, and Donggang Jinhui Foodstuff are some other companies also cited. 

Galicia, Jinhui, Xinxin and Yuanyi are all based in Dandong itself, which is on the Chinese border with North Korea. Haiqing, one of the largest salmon and whitefish processors for export in China, is based in Zhuanghe City, a drive of around two hours west of Dandong and the border with North Korea. It's another two-hour drive to Dalian, the capital of Liaoning province and another seafood processing hub (see below).

Credit: Google Maps

Outlaw Ocean claims Haiqing and Galicia employed as many as 50-70 North Korean workers as recently as December 2023. Haiqing denied it employed any North Korean workers to Outlaw Ocean. Galicia did not respond.

Qu Zhenhai, the boss of Haiqing, did not respond to a request for further comment from Undercurrent News.

Trident, High Liner and Sysco all notified Outlaw Ocean they suspended dealing with Haiqing in late January while they make further investigations, having initially been contacted on Jan. 12, in communications which the NGO has made public.

According to trade records, Trident was buying from Haiqing as recently as December. The company was "the consignee for shipments of seafood, including pollock," from the Chinese company between October 2017 and December 2023.

Biden pushed by lawmakers to step up pressure on Sysco over forced labor concerns

Pickenpack Seafoods, Trident's Germany-based European processing operation, was also buying from Haiqing in 2020, 2021 and 2022, according to Outlaw Ocean. 

High Liner, meanwhile, was buying seafood from Haiqing, including cod and pollock, between August 2017 and August 2023. Sysco was buying from Haiqing between June 2018 and March 2021. High Liner dropped a Chinese supplier accused of using Uyghur labor after the previous Outlaw Ocean report. 

Suspending trade

Trident said it is "suspending trade" with Haiqing on Jan. 25 while "structuring our own investigation in collaboration with an independent third party to provide on-the-ground support," its vice president of communications, Alexis Telfer, told Outlaw Ocean.

On Feb. 23, Telfer responded to a Feb. 6 email from Outlaw Ocean, in which the NGO outlined its evidence of Haiqing's alleged use of North Korean workers, who were then subject to physical and sexual abuse.

She outlined actions taken by the company since the initial contact on Jan. 12.

"Continued investigations are somewhat hampered by our limited need to be on-site at Haiqing given their suspended trade status with Trident," wrote Telfer. "We are by no means finished with our investigations or efforts to further strengthen our CSR [corporate social responsibility] program."

After suspending dealings with Haiqing, "Trident engaged transparently with key customers -- some of whom had already been contacted directly by OOP [Outlaw Oceans] and were aware of the allegations, while others had not," wrote Telfer.

Trident "expedited an independent, unannounced audit, including external surveillance and a site walk-through, and conducted employee and management interviews prior to the Chinese New Year and Spring Festival holidays in early February," she said.

Sysco drops major Chinese seafood supplier; still catches heat from US lawmaker over forced labor concerns

The company also "engaged selected members" from its CSR and Food Safety and Quality Assurance (FSQA) teams in China "to ascertain if potential red flags had been missed either in their observations or reporting," wrote Telfer. "We are thoroughly reviewing our CSR program for gaps and improvement opportunities."

Trident also "expedited an independent, unannounced audit, including external surveillance and a site walk-through, and conducted employee and management interviews prior to the Chinese New Year and Spring Festival holidays in early February."

Now Chinese New Year is over and companies are back at work, Trident has "resumed discussions with our China teams and have dug deeper to understand if they had unrecorded observations."

Trident has "not been able to identify suspicion or evidence of North Korean workers at Haiqing," based on its analysis of the findings of the unannounced audit, previous Sedex Members Ethical Trade Audit (SMETA) audits, and reports from and discussions with Trident's on-site FSQA and CSR employees.

"There is no clear gap in our CSR program to explain how we could have failed to detect a large number of North Korean workers at the Haiqing campus," she wrote. "Regardless of our inability to independently substantiate the OOP allegations, we are proceeding on the assumption that they could be true and we're taking action accordingly. We have not resumed trading with Haiqing."

Trident said it operates an "industry-leading CSR program which includes initiatives to proactively detect possible human rights violations," he said.

UK’s Unibond purchased MSC pollock from Chinese plant accused of forced labor

"To date, our CSR audits and program initiatives have successfully detected unacceptable work conditions that periodic independent third-party audits have missed, including evidence of exploited populations (although, not at the Haiqing plant)."

The company is looking to bolster its team by increasing the number of Trident CSR officers in China "to diversify our approach and communication style with leadership and the workforce."

Telfer concluded her email by stating the company supports "the Outlaw Ocean Project's mission to advance human rights and supply chain transparency in China," saying, "we're grateful for the light that you are shining on where the industry is falling short."

She offered an in-person or digital meeting with Joe Bundrant, CEO of Trident, to Outlaw Oceans' Urbina.  

Having briefly met Urbina in Washington, DC, at the Congressional hearing around alleged labor abuses in the Chinese seafood sector, Bundrant "would welcome the opportunity to further expound on our commitment in person or on a Teams call," Telfer said.

High Liner, Sysco exchanges

The exchanges with High Liner and Sysco are not as long as with Trident.

After a back-and-forth, High Liner communications vice president Jennifer Bell confirmed on Jan. 25 that business with Haiqing was suspended "effective immediately while further information is gathered and assessed for the purposes of our investigation."

Some European, US seafood buyers dropped Chinese processors accused of forced labor this summer

Bell also asked to hear directly from the Outlaw Ocean investigator and source who visited the Haiqing plant.

She said High Liner conducted third-party audits of the three Haiqing plants it buys from in 2022 and 2023. The audit results indicated no presence of North Korean labor, she wrote.

On Jan. 26, Outlaw Ocean asked if the audits had been announced or unannounced, as well as other additional questions, to which Bell did not respond.

Ramit Plushnick-Masti, a Sysco spokesperson, also told Outlaw Ocean the company audited suppliers but did not respond on whether they were announced or unannounced.

"Sysco instructed suppliers to suspend production of our products at all facilities associated with Dalian Haiqing Food as we investigate these allegations," Plushnick-Masti wrote.

Outlaw Ocean also asked about imports made from Sysco France and Cite Marine, a European processor owned by Japan's Nissui Corp., from Haiqing. Sysco did not respond to this, however.

title: Ocean Choice scallop quota sell off preceded by vessel sinking, relationship-building
content:
Ocean Choice International's sale of its Atlantic scallop quota as part of an incredible four-Canadian company deal was made possible, in part, by a dramatic boat sinking and the relationships it helped strengthen.

St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador (NL)-based Ocean Choice on Thursday (Feb. 22) participated in a joint announcement that it was selling its offshore Nova Scotia scallop quota to Mersey Seafoods, in Liverpool, Comeau's Sea Foods, in Saulnierville, and LaHave Seafoods, in LaHave, as reported by Undercurrent News.

The agreement reduces from six to just five the number of companies that divvy up Atlantic Canada's roughly 5,000 metric tons of offshore scallop quota, including also Clearwater Seafoods and Adams & Knickle.

Based on the $23,224 paid per metric ton of exported Canadian scallops in 2023, as reported by Undercurrent's trade portal, the fishery is worth about $116.1 million annually.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view

Clearwater is till the biggest holder of Canada's offshore scallop quota, 43.8%. Prior to last week's deal, Comeau's held 16.68%, Ocean Choice held 16.77%, Adams & Knickle held 9.77%, Mersey held 7.00% and LaHave had 5.92%.

Mersey added another 6.10% of quota as part of the deal, revealed president Greg Simpson, though it is not yet known how the remaining 10.77% of Ocean Choice's quota was divvied up. 

Because "permanent" scallop quota sells for over CAD 100-per pound, the value of OCI's share was estimated to be worth about CAD 200m, the CBC reported last week.

Also, as part of the agreement, which was six months in the making, Ocean Choice is acquiring NL offshore quota for Greenland halibut and northern cod from Mersey, and Greenland halibut, cod and redfish from LaHave. A sales and marketing agreement has also been reached with Mersey that will see Ocean Choice continue to sell the scallops to its global customer base, the company said. 

Additionally, LaHave is acquiring Ocean Choice's offshore quota for Atlantic pollock, haddock and flounder, as well as the company's assets in Riverport, Nova Scotia.

"It's about a reinvestment in our home province of Newfoundland and Labrador, in our plants and in our vessels, and still staying in the scallop business through a sales and marketing agreement," said Martin Sullivan, Ocean Choice's CEO, when reached by phone on Thursday. "So, really, the business should be the same or more for us, but it's a little pivot in terms of what we see in the future."

Sullivan confirmed that Ocean Choice received some cash as part of the deal but declined to reveal the amount or any of the other financial terms, including the quota amounts that changed hands.

The other companies involved in the deal were "industry partners that are in our association, not only on scallops but on shrimp and on groundfish items," he said. "They are people we've known a long time in Nova Scotia. So we went to them as we thought it was a good fit, and we worked out a deal, and it allowed us to have a little change of direction in our business and to reinvest in Newfoundland and Labrador."

Mersey, LaHave helped catch OCI's quota

Though Sullivan reports that Ocean Choice has had good, longstanding relationships with all three of the other companies involved in its scallop quota sale, the bond with Mersey and LaHave surely grew tighter after March 2021.

That's when Ocean Choice's offshore scallop trawler, the 143-foot Atlantic Destiny, went down about 115 miles south of Nova Scotia after a catastrophic engine failure caused an explosion and fire, requiring a dramatic rescue of some 31 crew members amidst high sea swells. 

Canada's Transportation Safety Board recently released its investigation of the sinking, finding that the crew lacked sufficient training on how to handle a fire onboard, as reported by Undercurrent.

A video produced by the Defense Visual Information Distribution Service and released in March 2022 captured some of the drama.

Atlantic Destiny, a scallop trawler previously maintained by Ocean Choice International. Credit: Ocean Choice

Mersey and LaHave were among the four companies, along with Clearwater Seafoods and Adams and Knickle, that agreed to help Ocean Choice catch the remainder of its hundreds of metric tons of quota in exchange for an undisclosed fee, as reported by CBC. Ocean Choice had landed about one-fifth of its 2021 allocation when its trawler went to the bottom, leaving millions of dollars worth of quota still in the sea.

In 2021, CBC reported that Ocean Choice was in the process of designing a replacement trawler, though it was expected to take two years to build. Those plans appear to now be off the table.

Mersey's Simpson told the news service at the time that helping Ocean Choice was the right thing to do. His company was also providing work for the Atlantic Destiny crew.

"Where it's a high-risk business, we always want to work together and help each other," he said. "And we do, especially the scallop industry. We absolutely work together to manage the stock, and we want to be there for each other because … next time, it could be us. I'm 100% sure if it was the reverse, the same would happen."

A map from Clearwater Seafoods of Canada's Atlantic scallop fishery.

Simpson, on Thursday, told Undercurrent that the agreement struck with Ocean Choice was a "big deal" for his company. It owns two scallop fishing vessels: Mersey Seven and Fortune Lady, the later of which is capable of freezing scallops at sea, he said.

Mersey has been in growth mode and has made a few acquisitions in recent years, including a 75% share of Fishermen's Market, a Halifax, NS-based wholesaler, retailer and exporter of fresh, frozen, smoked and salted seafood, in 2021, bringing total employment up to 800, Simpson said.

In 2019, Mersey completed construction on a new 20,000-square-foot processing facility in Liverpool.

title: Editor’s choice: Japan’s top crab processor talks Russian supply; Canada snow crab harvesters on hook for damages
content:
EMEA editor Neil Ramsden brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week  

Our most-read story from last week came from a reporter attending the 2024 Seafood Show Osaka in Japan, where he spoke with Tsukiji Kanisho, the country's leading crab trader and processor. It expects to market 5,000t of Russian king crab globally for the 2024-25 season, an increase of 1,500t from the previous season, said CEO Noriaki Nakamura.

In a major piece of trade news, last week, US importers found out they will now have until June to bring in containers of Russian-origin seafood ordered before Dec. 22 rather than the original deadline of Feb. 21, as the Red Sea shipping crisis disrupts supply chains. 

Harvesters in the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador who refused to untie their boats in the world's largest snow crab fishery for more than a month are liable for the damages suffered by processors, a labor arbitrator has determined. Now the only question that remains is how much they will have to pay. 

Investigation revealed that while Trident Seafoods -- the largest vertically integrated firm in the US -- has been among the country's loudest voices when it comes to fighting the import of Russian-sourced seafood, it is still selling products in Europe made from Russian pollock through its German subsidiary, Pickenpack Seafoods. Pickenpack stopped purchasing Russian pollock last year, Trident told Undercurrent News. Despite this, Pickenpack was still processing Russian pollock as recently as January 2024.

Also last week, Undercurrent reported live from Aquaculture America in San Antonio, Texas. You can recap all the blog posts -- including the news that Everblue, an Israeli aquaculture startup, plans to establish land-based facilities in the US -- here. This week, we are live from Bremen, Germany, for Fish International 2024. You can follow that blog as it develops here.

Canada's Ocean Choice International is selling offshore Nova Scotia scallop quotas to Mersey Seafoods, LaHave Seafoods and Comeau's Sea Foods. A sales and marketing agreement has also been reached with Mersey that will see Ocean Choice continue to sell the scallops to its global customer base, the company said. As part of the agreement, Ocean Choice is also acquiring Newfoundland and Labrador offshore quota for Greenland halibut and northern cod from Mersey, and Greenland halibut, cod and redfish from LaHave.

The challenges and hardships currently facing the seafood industry in the US state of Alaska are significant but ultimately present an opportunity for processors and harvesters in the state to capitalize on the market in the long run. That was a main takeaway from Alaska Seafood Marketing Institute board of directors chairman Allen Kimball Thursday when he delivered over an hour of remarks, including a question and answer session, as part of a seafood market update hosted by the industry group United Fishermen of Alaska.

Acquisitive West Coast US importer and processor Santa Monica Seafood has put dealmaking on the backburner for now, with the focus on taking market share with two new plants and a restructured foodservice sales team, CEO Roger O'Brien told Undercurrent. The company, which should pass $700 million in revenue in 2024, is still in discussion with deal targets, but O'Brien told Undercurrent in a recent interview that he does not feel the time is right for mergers and acquisitions.

Last week, Thai Union Group accounts showed its share of the losses incurred by US-based restaurant chain Red Lobster Management in the fourth quarter amounted to $15.3m. At the start of this year, Thai Union announced its intent to exit its minority stake in the struggling chain, incurring a one-off charge of $530m as a result.

Colombia has firmly established its dominance in the US fresh tilapia fillet market, raising its share from 34% in 2021 to 51% in 2023, Francisco Murillo, former Regal Springs executive and current CEO of Ghana's Tropo Farms, told Undercurrent. Over the past decade, the US's demand for fresh tilapia fillets remained relatively stable, averaging 970,000 pounds per week, or 440 metric tons. he said.

After setting an all-time record for seafood imports in 2022, the US last year reduced its dependence slightly on fish and shellfish from other countries. The US imported 3.1m metric tons of seafood worth $25.8 billion in 2023, 9% less volume and 15% less value than the 3.4m tons worth $30.4bn it imported in 2022.

Norway's Grieg Seafood is to invest in a new value-added processing facility at Oslo Airport City in Gardermoen. The facility will process salmon from Grieg's production in both the north and south of the country. The investment is a part of the company's strategy to increase value creation and process more of its own fish, it said.

El Nino-driven anchovy shortages in the world's largest fishmeal producer, Peru, have led to increased production in other parts of the world to meet rising demand in China, the world's largest importer. However, this may come at the cost of sustainability.

Finally, Undercurrent conducted its latest video interview with Gabriel Luna, owner of Ecuador's GLuna Shrimp and a founding member of the Global Shrimp Council, last week. You can watch him talk about whether Ecuador shrimp prices will continue to rise here, and find the interview in full here.

title: Proximar optimistic amidst loss as first salmon harvest nears
content:
In the fourth quarter of 2023, Norwegian land-based salmon farmer Proximar Seafood reached a crucial milestone by transferring the first fish to the post-smolt grow-out facility, setting the stage for the anticipated harvest in Q3 2024.

"2024 will be a pivotal year for our company, and we are looking forward to supplying fresh Atlantic salmon to Japanese consumers, lifting the company from investing to sold revenue streams," said CEO Joachin Nielsen.

The standing biomass at the end of the quarter rose to 39.8 metric tons, a notable increase from 11.5t at the end of Q3 2023. The next operational milestone is expected in April, with the initiation of production in the second module of the post-smolt grow-out building.

Key highlights from the fourth quarter of 2023 include the private placement that raised NOK 140 million ($13.3m), with an additional NOK 25m raised in a subsequent offering in Q1 2024. The company has also ramped up its organization, totaling 33 employees, with 30 located in Japan, to prepare for the harvesting and production phase.

An incident with a tank breach in February this year, resulting in a loss of 50,000 fish, or approximately 5% of its total individuals in production, will impact harvested volumes for 2024 by approximately 250t. However, it is expected to have limited effects on the company's overall harvesting plan volumes in the medium term, between 2024 and 2025.

"We are proud of our team working effortlessly as we grow our biomass towards the first harvest later this year," said Nielsen.

"Although we've experienced issues with the tank breach following the quarter end, initiatives have been made to prevent similar incidents. This remains our number one priority," he concluded.

He also outlined ongoing investigations and prevention initiatives, including strengthening the tank foundation and the tank floor, at an estimated cost of approximately NOK 5m. 

Net loss before tax was NOK 52.96m for Q4 2023, compared to a loss of NOK 9.22m in the same period a year before; and NOK 90.7m for the full year, up from a loss of NOK 28.7m in 2022.

Operating expenses increased from NOK 8.22m to NOK 30.3m in Q4, due to operational cost increases and from NOK 25.5m to NOK 63.8m in 2023. 

According to the company, transportation costs have increased significantly following the Russian-Ukrainian conflict and recent inflation spike.

"However, with the high price levels of Atlantic salmon in Japan, also impacted by the geopolitical situation affecting import costs, the economic outlook for Proximar continues to remain attractive. Even at lower harvest levels, Proximar is expected to remain profitable, demonstrating the solidity of our business model," the company said in its financial report. 

With current price expectations, Proximar expects to be earnings-profitable even with a production of around 2,000t head-on gutted (HOG). "At the targeted long-term harvest level of 5,300t HOG per year, Proximar expects an EBITDA [earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization] cost of NOK 59 per kilogram," it added.

Mindaugas Cekanavicius, equity analyst at Norwegian investment bank Norne Securities, added that although Q4 costs might seem excessive, NOK 14m adjustments for unutilized production capacity take the results to "a decent level in line with prognosis."

"EBIT is around NOK -16m and the bottom line about NOK -30m, which would somewhat align with our expectations. Furthermore, high net financials are boosted by NOK 13.7m currency losses," he added.

title: Palermo’s ‘frozen seafood king’ arrested amid alleged tax fraud
content:
A crackdown on transnational tax fraud in southern Europe has led to the arrest of Salvatore Vetrano, dubbed Palermo's "frozen seafood king," Italian media reports.

Vetrano, a well-known figure in the seafood industry in Spain and Italy, appears on LinkedIn (see photo above) as the commercial director of the Spanish firm Pescados y Mariscos Italianna (see a photo from their website below), based in Vigo, Galicia, northern Spain.

Photo: https://pescadositalianna.com/

A total of 12 individuals are under investigation for offenses including association for criminal purposes, fraudulent transfer of assets, laundering, false declaration through the use of invoices for non-existent operations, and VAT evasion, Italian news agency Ansa reported. Vetrano is further accused of aiding Cosa Nostra, also known as the Sicilian mafia, a criminal society originating on the Italian island.

The investigation uncovered a complex network of fraudulent VAT schemes orchestrated through companies in Spain, Portugal, and Italy, with Vetrano as the hidden hand behind the operations.

The scheme involved transferring VAT debts onto "missing traders," enabling below-market prices and funneling profits abroad. The fraudulent activities revolved around fictitious transactions with shell companies in Iberian territories, ultimately defrauding both Italian tax authorities and consumers. The web involved sham purchases and sales, artificially inflating VAT credits while avoiding tax payments, Genova 24 further reported.

The tax fraud would have been carried out through a network of companies, including Pescados y mariscos italianna sl Atlasmirante, Colossatlantico Unipessoal, Pescados australia perez, Albatross dune unipessoal, which exported frozen seafood to Italy of frozen, Live Sicilia reported. Other firms that would have omitted the payment of the tax applied on the invoice to their buyers included Mondocarne, Caribian pesca, Pescado mediterraneo, Marifish srl, Sarda fish, Ittica monzese, Blau pesca and l.g. Surgelati, according to Live Sicilia. 

Photo: Live Sicilia.

The investigation, spearheaded by Italy's Guardia di Finanza, focused on aggravated tax fraud involving imported seafood products in Genoa, northern Italy. Ansa reported that five individuals have been apprehended, and assets worth over €3 million have been seized both domestically and abroad. Raids also yielded over €1m found in the Palermo residence of one of the suspects, Giuseppe Licata.

Vetrano was arrested for the first time in 1999 because he and his father had hidden in a cold room of one of his companies at the time a load of fish that had been stolen during a robbery. In 2019, Italian authorities confiscated the entire share capital and corporate assets of five joint-stock companies, including Veragel, which operated in the marketing of fish products.

title: CEO of South Africa’s Premier Fishing found guilty in cyberattack probe
content:
The CEO of South Africa's company Premier Fishing and Brands has been found guilty of negligence by local authorities following a significant theft during a cyberattack that took place last year, according to parent company African Equity Empowerment Investments (AEEI).

It did not name the individual, but said "appropriate action" had been taken. Neither AEEI nor Premier Fishing have issued news about leadership changes as of Feb. 19. 

The CEO at the time of the attack -- November 2023 -- was Sooren Ramdenee, who was appointed in May 2022.

AEEI said that on or around Nov. 15, 2023, Premier Fishing -- a 56.23% owned subsidiary -- fell victim to an alleged cybercrime fraud, resulting in the unauthorized transfer of $820,000 from its bank account to an unknown third party.

Premier Fishing filed a criminal case with the South African Police Services and launched an internal investigation.

"Additionally, and following a thorough investigation and disciplinary proceedings, the CEO of Premier Fishing was found guilty of negligence, and appropriate action has been taken in this regard."

Efforts are ongoing to reclaim the misappropriated funds, with AEEI's board of directors vowing to pursue all feasible avenues for recovery.

title: Efforts ongoing to free grounded fishing vessel in US state of California
content:
The US Coast Guard (USCG) says work is ongoing to free a commercial fishing vessel grounded near Bodega Bay, in the US state of California.

The four crew members aboard the 58-foot Aleutian Storm swam to shore after the vessel ran aground Friday night (Feb. 9), according to CW's San Francisco-based television affiliate KRON. No injuries were reported.

The vessel had 1,500 gallons of fuel on board, an unknown amount of which leaked into the nearby Greater Farallones National Marine Sanctuary during a tug operation to retrieve the vessel Monday.

The television station reports that multiple state and federal agencies have responded to the spill and grounding, including the California Department of Fish and Wildlife’s Office of Spill Prevention and Response, California State Parks, National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, Sonoma County Sheriff’s Office, Sonoma County Department of Emergency Management, Sonoma County Fire Department and California Highway Patrol. 

The cause of the incident is under investigation.

title: US trade commission rejects tariffs on tin from Canada, China, Germany
content:
The US International Trade Commission (ITC) will not impose duties on tin mill products imported from Canada, China and Germany after its investigation found that the US industry is not materially injured or threatened by them.

The decision, announced more than a week ago, follows an investigation instigated by petitions from Cleveland-Cliffs and United Steelworkers. It holds significant implications for seafood producers who heavily rely on tinplate imports for canning their products. 

The Consumer Brands Association, which opposed the petitions, said the decision was "a true victory for US consumers and manufacturers”. 

Additionally, the commission said it found the impact of similar imports from South Korea to be negligible, resulting in the termination of another anti-dumping duty investigation. 

The ITC said it will publish the results of its investigations on March 13.

title: Scientists present on paralytic shellfish poisoning’s role in Alaska’s marine die-offs
content:
Scientists, including Bruce Wright from the Knik Tribe, presented findings at the Alaska Forum on the Environment, in Anchorage, on Monday, highlighting the pervasive presence of paralytic shellfish poisoning (PSP) across various marine species and its potential impact on the food chain, reports the Alaska radio station KYUK.

While PSP has been a concern for subsistence shellfish harvesters for centuries, Wright and other scientists have begun noticing deadly marine toxins targeting animals at every level of the food chain, from plankton to whales, the report said.

Undercurrent News reported earlier that concerns are growing that the toxin is being consumed by salmon.

PSP occurs when the algae known as Alexandrium blooms in the ocean, releasing neurotoxins that accumulate in shellfish such as clams, mussels and scallops. The toxin then spreads through the food web, affecting zooplankton, forage fish and even top predators like whales.

Recent data revealed detectable levels of PSP in predatory fish like cod and salmon, raising concerns about human consumption safety and its possible contribution to declines in marine populations, such as the Pacific cod crash and the Yukon River king salmon collapse.

While the exact impacts of PSP on marine life remain unclear, ongoing research aims to understand its effects on animal fitness, reproduction, migration, and overall ecosystem health. With climate change exacerbating harmful algal blooms and warming ocean waters, the investigation into PSP's influence on Alaska's marine food web becomes increasingly urgent.

Further data collection efforts planned by scientists, like Steve Kibler from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, aim to unravel the complexities of PSP's impact and inform conservation strategies to mitigate its effects, the report said.

title: Spanish cannery enters bankruptcy proceedings after fraud investigation
content:
Conservas Plaza Chica, a Spanish cannery based in Alfaro and Cervera, in the north of the country, has recently entered into bankruptcy proceedings, Radio Arnedo reported.

The news was given to the firm's employees during a meeting to discuss the terms of an anticipated Temporary Employment Regulation (ERTE) plan.

The company came under scrutiny on Dec. 13, 2023, when Spain's Guardia Civil began an investigation into its operations related to the irregular commercialization of canned tuna products.

The investigation, conducted with the assistance of Europol and the Italian Carabinieri, led to the seizure of approximately 120,000 cans of tuna and 45,000 liters of oil. Most seized products were destined for distribution to small retailers and major food chains in Spain and Italy, particularly during the holiday season.

Following the investigation, which resulted in the detention of several company officials on suspicion of various offenses, Plaza Chica initially sent its workers home with paid leave and later proposed an ERTE plan. However, it was revealed that the company's claimed financial constraints, including the alleged blocking of its accounts, were refuted by the court, creating uncertainty around the situation.

With the company now in bankruptcy proceedings, the future is unclear for its 114 employees. The usual process involves the appointment of a bankruptcy administrator by a judge, followed by an assessment and potential sale of assets. 

Fernando Molina, the UGT union delegate for the area, highlighted the significant impact of this development on ongoing negotiations. Despite some glimmers of hope, such as potential interest in leasing the Alfaro plant, the situation remains precarious for the company.

Workers also face continued financial uncertainty, with no news on when to expect their February salaries, and facing the possibility of delayed payments if an ERTE plan is implemented.

Meanwhile, Plaza Chica is attempting to find other companies to take over its facilities, La Rioja reported.

title: Blumar, Multi X processing plant in Chile’s southernmost region reduced to ashes
content:
The massive fire that erupted Sunday (Feb. 11) at the Entrevientos salmon processing plant in Punta Arenas, Chile's southernmost region, has destroyed the plant, Undercurrent News has learned.

As reported earlier by Undercurrent, the plant, which is jointly owned by Chilean salmon farmers Blumar and Multiexport Foods, suffered from a blaze that broke out for reasons that are still under investigation. Local media reports that, based on statements from workers on site, the fire is believed to have started during routine operations, sparked by an incident in one of the warehouses.

Thanks to the immediate activation of evacuation protocols and the swift response of the region's fire department, the emergency was successfully controlled, with no reported injuries or damage to nearby residences. However, authorities have ordered a precautionary evacuation of 10 residences near the plant.

Earlier, Undercurrent reported that the fire led to the declaration of an indefinite suspension of production. However, Manuel Gallardo, Blumar's director of administration and finance, says in a statement issued subsequently that the fire has also resulted in the total loss of the processing facility.

"Given the recent occurrence of the incident, the precise economic impact on Blumar cannot be accurately determined at this time. Nevertheless, it is noted that the affected processing plant is insured against such incidents, and the insurance company has been notified," he added.

In another statement, MultiX disclosed that 15% of its production is situated in the Magallanes region. With the 'Entrevientos' plant unavailable, the company is confronted with the task of processing this volume efficiently.

"We are exploring different processing alternatives in the region and considering the potential relocation of a portion of our production to the tenth region. In terms of the processing aspect, we do not foresee any substantial losses," Multi X's executive president Jose Ramon Gutierrez said.

"Once the emergency was declared, protocols were activated, and the immediate evacuation of those inside the facility was ordered. Fortunately, there were no injuries or impact on third parties or neighboring properties. Continuous monitoring of the facilities will be maintained preventively, although the fire department has already declared the emergency as resolved," he concluded.

The $60-million processing plant has been operating since June 2020, employing around 500 people.

title: US shrimp imports’ late sprint to finish not enough to salvage 2023
content:
Additional reporting by Louis Harkell.

US shrimp imports continued their mad dash in the final month of 2023, but it wasn't enough to make up for all of the ground lost earlier in the year.

That's what the latest update of seafood trade data by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration shows. The US imported 65,467 metric tons of shrimp worth $515.9 million in December 2023, 6% more volume than in December 2022 and 5% less value. 

It was the sixth consecutive month of year-on-year volume increases after 13 consecutive months of y-o-y decreases. Eleven of the US' 20-largest source nations sent it more shrimp. 

Also, as more shrimp has been flooding the market in recent times, the overall average price has continuously dropped. The US paid an average $3.67 per pound for imported shrimp in December 2023, 5% less than the average $3.86/lb paid in June 2023 and 22% less than the average $4.73/lb paid in April 2022 when the price slide began.

The chart below, from Undercurrent New's trade portal, illustrates the recent climb in overall monthly volumes and a longer-term drop in overall average prices. (Note that the data presented by Undercurrent's Trade Portal are, like NOAA's numbers, based on US Census Bureau data but may vary by a few metric tons in some instances.)

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
US shrimp imports' late sprint to finish not enough to salvage 2023 - Undercurrent News

Even in spite of the uptick in imports over the previous six months, the US wound up importing 788,209t of shrimp worth $6.4 billion in 2023, 6% less volume and 18% less value than in 2022. The overall average price for the year was $8.17 per kilogram, 12% less than in 2022.

Another chart from Undercurrent's Trade Portal shows how US shrimp imports have been gradually decreasing since 2021 when the US took in a whopping 896,696t (nearly 2.0bn lbs) of shrimp worth $8.0bn, an all-time high. 

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
US shrimp imports' late sprint to finish not enough to salvage 2023 - Undercurrent News

Here's what Undercurrent found when it looked more closely at the US' eight largest sources of shrimp. 

India gets another trim

India again asserted its position as the dominant provider of shrimp to the US market in 2023, sending it 296,106t worth $2.3bn. That's a volume market share of 38% and a value market share of 36%, if you're keeping score. However, that was 2% less volume and 16% less value than India sent to the US in 2022.  

The chart from Undercurrent's Trade Portal shows how India's shrimp exports to the US peaked in 2021 at 341,003t but has been in gradual decline since.

Don't look for a quick turnaround in 2024 either. In a panel at the Global Seafood Market Conference, in Florida, last month, Robins McIntosh, executive vice president of Charoen Pokphand Foods, projected Indian vannamei production dropping by 1% year-on-year, from 800,000t to 780,000t in 2024, as earlier reported by Undercurrent.

Likewise, Willem van der Pijl, founder of market consultancy Shrimp Insights, who claimed to be "more positive than some others," told Undercurrent he expected "flat growth or only a small decline for vannamei" from India.

US shrimp imports' late sprint to finish not enough to salvage 2023 - Undercurrent News

The average price of India shrimp in the US finished the year at $3.56/lb, which represented a drop of 15% from the $4.20/lb price seen in December 2022, as illustrated by Undercurrent's Trade Portal.

US shrimp imports' late sprint to finish not enough to salvage 2023 - Undercurrent News
Ecuador holds 26% of market

While India lost a little ground in 2023, the US' second-largest shrimp supplier, Ecuador, gained some turf. The South American nation sent the US 205,915t of shrimp worth $1.4bn in 2023, 3% more volume and 8% less value, according to NOAA.

Ecuador finished the year with a 26% share of US shrimp volume and 22% of its value.  

Undercurrent's Trade Portal shows how Ecuador has seen its reliance as a supplier of shrimp to the US climb dramatically just since 2019.

US shrimp imports' late sprint to finish not enough to salvage 2023 - Undercurrent News

But Ecuador's rise in the US might be coming to an end, based on comments made by Sandro Coglitore, the CEO of Omarsa, one of Ecuador's largest shrimp farmers and processors, at the Global Seafood Market Conference, as reported by Undercurrent. He described an ongoing effort to have anti-dumping and/or countervailing duties levied against India, Ecuador, Indonesia and Vietnam as being his country's "biggest problem or threat" to its shrimp industry in 2024.

A shrimp processor near Guayaquil, Ecuador. Credit: Louis Harkell / Undercurrent News.

He said the increased prices threatened by tariffs could lead to a re-balancing of shrimp trade, resulting in Ecuador vacating much of its stake in the US market.

The average price of Ecuador shrimp in the US was among the lowest to begin with and has changed little over the past year. It finished in December at an average rate of $3.10/lb, an almost 3% drop from the average price of $3.18/lb seen in Dec. 2022, as shown below. 

US shrimp imports' late sprint to finish not enough to salvage 2023 - Undercurrent News
Indonesia loses ground again

Indonesia, the US' third-largest supplier, only a few years from having been supplanted in its higher position by Ecuador, fell back a bit more in 2023, NOAA data shows. It sent the US 146,259t of shrimp worth $1.2bn, 12% less volume and 26% less value. 

US shrimp imports' late sprint to finish not enough to salvage 2023 - Undercurrent News

The average price of Indonesian shrimp saw a brief rise in the middle of the year but finished in December at $3.55/lb, 16% less than the $4.22/lb seen in December 2022.

US shrimp imports' late sprint to finish not enough to salvage 2023 - Undercurrent News
US sunk Vietnam's December

Shrimp shipments to the US from its fourth-largest source -- Vietnam -- tumbled 13% by volume to 61,524t and 20% by value to $650.7m in 2023 versus the prior year, NOAA's data shows.

The year-on-year 26% drop in exports to the US in December badly hurt Vietnam, meaning it's total shrimp exports for the month were flat year-on-year, as reported by Undercurrent. The top five markets for Vietnamese vannamei in December were Japan (with 17% of the market), China and Hong Kong (16%), the US (15%), the EU (13%) and South Korea (13%).

US shrimp imports' late sprint to finish not enough to salvage 2023 - Undercurrent News

The average price for shrimp imported from Vietnam has been on a steady decline since at least August 2022, when it was $5.79/lb, with a small, quick rise in March 2023. It finished the year in December at an average $5.29/lb. 

US shrimp imports' late sprint to finish not enough to salvage 2023 - Undercurrent News
Thailand's dominance a distant memory 

Who remembers when Thailand was one of the most dominant sources of shrimp for the US? It was a long time ago. The Undercurrent Trade Portal chart shows the dramatic drop off from 2012 when Thailand sent the US 135,982t of shrimp.

Thailand shrimp exports to the US saw steep declines again in 2023. The 29,864t received represented a 24% volume drop and the $342.5m paid a 25% value slide. 

US shrimp imports' late sprint to finish not enough to salvage 2023 - Undercurrent News

Unit prices have bounced up and down all year for Thai shrimp. The final average price paid in December was $5.32/lb, just 1% down from the average $5.40/lb paid in December 2022.

US shrimp imports' late sprint to finish not enough to salvage 2023 - Undercurrent News
Mexico way off pre-COVID performance

Mexico wasn't immune to a US market loss either, witnessing a 25% plunge in its shrimp export volumes to the US last year to 15,641t coupled with a 29% drop in value to $196.3m. The chart below shows Mexican shrimp exports to the US on a downward trajectory since the pre-COVID year of 2019 when the US took in 29,508t.

Per-unit prices edged down 15% from December 2022 when they were $4.20/lb to $3.56/lb in December 2023.

US shrimp imports' late sprint to finish not enough to salvage 2023 - Undercurrent News
Argentina red shrimp sales to US down 13%

Even shrimp crossings from usually steady Argentina fell 13% by volume to 14,300t and 10% by value to $181.5m in 2023, based on NOAA data. The South American nation's wild-caught red shrimp have not been as popular as they were since the pandemic year 2020, when the US imported 17,340t, Undercurrent's Trade Portal shows. 

US shrimp imports' late sprint to finish not enough to salvage 2023 - Undercurrent News

The average price of Argentina shrimp has been one of the most erratic among all imports, as the chart below demonstrates. The average price at the end of the year was $5.99/lb, up 3% from the $5.80 paid in December 2022.

US shrimp imports' late sprint to finish not enough to salvage 2023 - Undercurrent News
Trade war continues to bite China

The US-China trade war continues to take its toll on Chinese shrimp, though its own growing consumption may also be a factor. Among major US shrimp providers, China endured some of the heaviest losses as its exports to the US virtually evaporated.

Import volumes cratered 32% to just 3,630t while import values decreased 32% to $21.4m, according to NOAA data. 

Credit: chinahbzyg / Shutterstock

But the fall has been happening since 2018, when the trade war began in July. The US imported 6,960t of Chinese shrimp that year, as illustrated in the chart below. There's little mystery behind the collapse, as importers are forced to pay tariffs of 25%. In 2023, the US paid $5.3m in tariffs on Chinese shrimp, according to NOAA data. 

China's shrimp industry has seen happier times. Its largest shrimp company, Zhanjiang Guolian Aquatic Products, has forecast significant losses for 2023, citing declining shrimp demand and prices, as reported by Undercurrent. 

Guolian said in a performance forecast on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange that losses could reach between CNY 360m and CNY 470m ($51m-$66m) for 2023. That would mark the company's biggest annual loss since its stock listing in 2009. The company lost CNY 7.58m in 2022.

On a brighter note, Vietnam's Sao Ta Foods (more commonly known as Fimex Vn) has reported a busy start to 2024, with January revenues up 26% year-on-year, as reported by Undercurrent. Its shrimp output of finished goods reached 1,250t, double the amount sold in January 2023, taking revenue to $19.2m.

As the volume-to-value ratio would suggest, prices have not recovered, but a boost in demand is a promising sign after a year of slow sales.

US shrimp imports' late sprint to finish not enough to salvage 2023 - Undercurrent News

China continues to produce the cheapest shrimp sent to the US market, but saw its average prices increase 6% from $2.83/lb in December 2022 to $3.00/lb in December 2023.

US shrimp imports' late sprint to finish not enough to salvage 2023 - Undercurrent News
