title: $14bn investor with Bregal connection is favorite to buy American Seafoods
content:
A US investment giant is being tipped as the frontrunner to acquire American Seafoods Group (ASG), with a former executive of ASG's backer Bregal Partners leading the bid, sources told Undercurrent News.

After ASG secured the long-awaited finalization of a $9.5 million settlement with the US government over alleged Jones Act breaches on Tuesday (Feb. 6), it emerged that Santa Monica, California-based Beach Point Capital Management is the frontrunner to buy the company.

Robert Bergmann, who co-founded Bregal with Scott Perekslis and worked at Centre Partners when it owned ASG from 2000-2006, is a senior portfolio manager for Beach Point, which has $14.5 billion of assets under management.

Robert Bergmann, who co-founded Bregal Partners with Scott Perekslis, is a senior portfolio manager for Beach Point Capital Management. Beach Point is seen as the frontrunner to buy American Seafoods Group. Credit: Beach Point's website

Bergmann, who joined Beach Point at some point between 2018 and 2019, is named as a portfolio manager with the Santa Monica firm, which also has offices in New York City, New York and London, UK.

He's listed as the manager of Beach Point's "tactical" distressed debt fund and is quoted in several articles about recent investments the firm has made.

Beach Point, co-founded and run by Carl Goldsmith and Scott Klein, is focused on credit, private equity (PE), real estate and structured product investments.

The firm currently has 10 companies in its PE portfolio, according to a press release from December last year on its most recent deal, for a stake in Eurofase, a Toronto, Canada-based manufacturer of lighting and heating products.

The Euroface investment was done with Bergmann's tactical fund, as were deals for controlling stakes in Wet Noses, a manufacturer of human-grade, natural and organic pet food, and Botanical Designs, a commercial landscaper, in early 2023.

American Seafoods finalizes settlement with US gov’t over alleged Jones Act breaches

Einar Gustafsson, CEO of ASG, declined to comment to Undercurrent. Bergmann did not respond to a request for comment from Undercurrent. A spokesperson for Beach Point declined to comment.

Lazard, the investment bank is running the process for ASG, also did not respond to a request for comment. New York-based Lazard, in addition to JPMorgan Chase & Co., also worked on the previous unsuccessful sale process for ASG, which kicked off in 2019.

Back in 2019, Bregal was looking at a valuation of over $1.5bn for ASG. Talks with a consortium of other players from the US pollock sector ended with no deal at the start of 2020. Then, Bristol Bay Native Corporation also couldn't get a buyout over the line. 

Perekslis, Bergmann's former partner at Bregal, who announced his exit from the PE when the ASG sale started, also did not respond to a request for comment.

According to his LinkedIn profile, Perekslis is now the founder of Stonetower Partners, a New York-based investment firm. 

Russia ban impact: Alaska pollock fillet price rise in US market will ‘lag’ due to oversupply

Perekslis was previously linked to a bid for ASG, hence his exit from Bregal, which is liquidating the fund in which the at-sea pollock processor and Blue Harvest Fisheries, another seafood company, were held.

Having sold off its once 15-strong scallop fleet to various companies, Blue Harvest filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy on Sept. 11. Blue Harvest's remaining whitefish vessels and permits were then bought by a company controlled by Cassie Canastra, whose family is well known in the seafood sector in New Bedford, Massachusetts.

Charles "Butch" Payne, a Montauk, New York-based luxury home builder and the owner of vessels that fish for southern New England species, such as whiting and squid, was Canastra's partner in the deal.

Bregal, controlled by the billionaire Dutch Brenninkmeijer family, who own fashion retailer C&A, has come under fire for being a foreign company controlling US fishing assets.

Overseas firms are only permitted to own a maximum of 25% of US fishing vessels, a level Bregal always maintained it was below.

Falling prices, settlement holdup

The emergence of Beach Point in the process comes as pollock fillet and surimi prices have been falling.

Even though the surimi outlook for the main market of Japan is uncertain, the projection is for an increase in fillet prices to the US market in the second half of 2024. The US government has moved to block pollock fillet imports from China and other countries using Russian raw materials, as previously reported by Undercurrent. 

Stalled US gov’t settlement holds up American Seafoods sale, amounts to ‘corporate purgatory’

Also, as previously reported by Undercurrent, the lack of closure on the now-finalized settlement was holding up the deal, even though ASG had agreed on it last year. 

ASG -- which has a fleet of six pollock and hake factory trawlers and a mothership vessel acquired last year -- had reached the $9.5m settlement with US Customs and Border Patrol (CBP) and the Department of Justice back last July.

"We are very pleased to have finalized the settlement with CBP and DOJ," said Per Brautaset, president of Alaska Reefer Management (ARM), one of the two ASG logistics subsidiaries involved, in a statement sent to Undercurrent on Tuesday. Kloosterboer International Forwarding (KIF) is the other.

The CBP had originally proposed fines of over $400m for ASG's alleged Jones Act abuses for use of a 100-foot railway track to meet an obscure Jones Act exemption to use cheaper foreign vessels.

FREE READ Timeline: How a 100-foot railroad put Alaska pollock sector at war with Uncle Sam

US companies are prohibited from shipping to a US port using cheaper foreign-flagged vessels unless Canadian rail is involved, which is where the "Bayside Program" came in.

Using foreign vessels, ARM/KIF shipped to Bayside, in the Canadian province of New Brunswick and just across from the US border, then put the products on the 100-foot railway. They were then unloaded from the Bayside Canadian Railway and trucked into the US market.

The settlement from KIF and ARM withdraws claims against all the other industry companies who had also been penalized for using the program to transport pollock and other seafood from Alaska to the US East Coast.

title: Norwegian fisheries alerted as storms unleash salmon escapes
content:
The Norwegian Directorate of Fisheries has received numerous reports detailing incidents at fish farms across the country in the aftermath of the recent storms.

"Up to and including Feb. 6, we have received reports of escapes or suspected escapes related to a total of 14 cages, spread over eight locations after the storm. There are three companies that have reported these incidents," the directorate stated.

The reports, predominantly from central and northern Norway, with a concentration in Trondelag, highlight damages ranging from damage to pens to holes of various sizes in nets.

Affected localities house salmon of diverse sizes, spanning from approximately 300 grams to 6 kilograms. However, the full extent of the escape has yet to be determined in any of the incidents.

The most alarming incidents appear to have occurred in Hitra and Froya, where tears measuring up to four and five meters in length have been discovered in the nets. These breaches have raised concerns about the potential impact on local marine ecosystems and wild fish populations.

In response to these reports, the directorate of fisheries has initiated an investigation to assess the extent of the damage, identify the causes behind the incidents, and implement measures to prevent future occurrences.

title: Canada wraps up three-year illegal halibut fishing investigation with more convictions
content:
Three years after Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) initially charged eight individuals and five companies with the illegal possession and sale of Atlantic halibut, the last of four trials has wrapped up.

Fish harvester Clarke Henneberry, and A.L.S. Fisheries Ltd. (ALS), a Sambro, Nova Scotia-based business that lists Wesley Henneberry as its key principal and Clarke as a director, were found guilty in a provincial court on Tuesday (Feb. 6) of violating Canada's Fisheries Act for illegally fishing and possession of Atlantic halibut. 

While DFO did not detail the penalties involved in this latest conviction, it said the individuals and companies convicted in all four trials were ordered to pay more than CAD 260,000 ($192,988) in penalties. No prison sentences were imposed, according to DFO.

The DFO investigation carried out over 24 months, saw five people and three companies convicted of 18 violations of the Fisheries Act, according to a press release from the federal agency. Charges included failing to have catch verified by a dockside observer and providing inaccurate catch information in order to land more halibut than was allowed by the conditions of the license.

This is not the first time ALS has been convicted of illegally fishing halibut.

In September 2023, the company was fined CAD 55,000 in a case that also saw Casey Henneberry, a 40-year-old fishing captain from Sambro, and another company -- Law Fisheries --  convicted of violations related to the fishing of halibut, hake and Atlantic cod. Casey Henneberry was banned for fishing for six months in Canadian and US waters.

Law Fisheries was fined CAD 10,000 and had its 50-ft longliner, the Ivy Lew, and related fishing gear seized by DFO, as reported by Undercurrent News.

During the two-year-long investigation, DFO officers also seized: two vehicles; a 28-foot enclosed trailer; a compact track loader; 7,461 pounds of halibut valued at CAD 40,000 ($31,332), including 17 undersized fish; and CAD 36,000 in cash, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

The DFO investigation also led to the conviction of four other harvesters in 2022. They were fined a total of $70,000 for illegally fishing halibut, as reported by Undercurrent.

title: AP report ties prison labor to major US food, aquaculture feed suppliers
content:
Hundreds of millions of dollars worth of food products for major brands in the US, including also grains used by aquaculture feed companies, are being produced by prison labor in the country, even while the US government seeks to ban products from other countries that use forced labor, the Associated Press reports.

The AP says it spent two years investigating how the use of inmate labor was tied to such supply chains that feed such corporations as Walmart, McDonald's, Whole Foods, Target and Costco.

It notes also how other "mammoth agriculture commodity traders," such as Cargill, Bunge, Louis Dreyfus, Archer Daniels Midland and Consolidated Grain and Barge, have "in recent years scooped up millions of dollars’ worth of soy, corn and wheat straight from prisons, which compete with local farmers." Several are involved in supplying grains for aquaculture feed.

The inmates at maximum-security facilities, like the Louisana State Penitentiary, are among America's most vulnerable laborers, reports AP. If they refuse to work, they can jeopardize their chances of parole or face punishment, like solitary confinement. They are compensated a few pennies an hour and do not have the same protections, such as workers' compensation and federal safety standards, guaranteed to most other full-time workers.

Some have even died on the job, the AP noted.

In many cases, the AP reported, they cannot file official complaints about poor conditions, though they work in industries with severe labor shortages, in some of the dirtiest and most dangerous jobs.

The 13th Amendment of the US Constitution bans slavery and involuntary servitude, except as punishment for crime. While some states -- including Nebraska, Utah and Colorado -- have ditched such language in their constitutions, more than 20 states still retain clauses that permit prison labor.

About a dozen states, including Nevada and Colorado, are pushing to eliminate involuntary servitude clauses in their constitutions this year.

Meanwhile, calls for the US to stop accepting Chinese seafood imports continue on Capitol Hill following the publication, in October, of an investigative series that spotlighted forced labor in China's commercial fishing and seafood processing industries, as reported by Undercurrent News.

The series, written by the Outlaw Ocean Project, provided haunting details about crew members being held captive, beaten and suffering from malnutrition aboard vessels in China's distant water fishing fleet. It also gave a thorough accounting of the Chinese program used to enlist and transport a large number of Uyghurs over 1,000 miles from Xinjiang, in the land-locked, northwestern part of China, to seafood processing plants in Shangdong, on the east coast.

title: Masoval appeals $2.8m misdiagnosis lawsuit against Norwegian gov’t
content:
Norwegian salmon farmer Masoval has appealed an ongoing lawsuit against the state, claiming compensation for the losses it incurred after a farm was misdiagnosed with pancreatic disease.

Masoval finds subsidiary has been selling salmon ‘unsuitable for human consumption’

Masoval has pursued NOK 29.8 million ($2.8m) in compensation for the losses it sustained when its farming site Kattholmen was misdiagnosed with pancreatic disease SAV3 in August 2019.

The case went to trial in November 2023, before an announcement was made on Dec. 29 that Masoval had been granted compensation.

The state then appealed the verdict on Feb. 2, to which Masoval has responded with an independent appeal of its own on Feb. 5.

The appeal was made the same week that Masoval informed the Norwegian stock exchange of its investigation into its majority-owned processing and sales subsidiary Pure Norwegian Seafood (PNS), which revealed some customers had been supplied with fish unsuitable for human consumption.

This included fish that should have been discarded/ensiled, or production-graded fish that should have been elaborated in secondary processing before export.

The investigation concluded that the turnover of fish not suitable for human consumption had been just under 1% of its total volume of fish and roughly 0.5% of PNS's revenue over the last three years.

These activities were halted in October 2023, Masoval said.

title: Indonesia targets new markets in face of US duties on shrimp
content:
In response to the challenges posed by potential new anti-dumping and countervailing duties on shrimp products sold to the US, Indonesia's ministry of maritime affairs and fisheries (KKP) is proactively diversifying its market access, Kontan reported.

US trade investigation ‘biggest problem or threat’ facing Ecuador shrimp but rebalance possible

The KKP is registering fish processing units to sell to Saudi Arabia, focusing on aquaculture-based products. Wahyu Muryadi, spokesperson for the minister, expressed optimism about opening market access there, particularly for shrimp, in the near future.

To expand market reach within the ASEAN region, the KKP has been collaborating with the Singapore Food Agency to facilitate virtual business matching sessions.

Indonesia is also exploring non-traditional markets through trade agreement negotiations, including the Indonesia-Tunisia Trade Agreement and the Indonesia-Eurasian Economic Union negotiations. Once these negotiations are finalized, Indonesian shrimp can be exported tariff-free to Russia, Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan.

Lastly, the KKP is also actively optimizing its presence in the Chinese market, with memorandums of understanding already in place with several of the latter's processing organizations.

title: Proximar faces NOK 6m setback as tank breach results in loss of 50,000 fish
content:
Proximar Seafood has suffered a setback with one of its four operational tanks at its recently established post-smolt grow-out facility suffering a breach, resulting in a significant loss of biomass. 

The salmon farmer, based near Tokyo, Japan, estimated the loss of approximately 50,000 fish in the tank breach, it said in a stock exchange announcement. 

The total number of fish in the Proximar facility, spanning all developmental stages, exceeded one million. Early investigations suggested that leakage from the tank washed away the soil beneath it, leading to the sudden breach.

Fortunately, a portion of the affected batch was saved and promptly transferred to another production tank, said the company.

"Proximar is currently thoroughly investigating the incident and preparing to improve all joints and sealings to prevent any future leakage," it added.

The treatment will extend to all tanks in the grow-out facility, incurring an estimated cost of around NOK 5 million ($470,476). Additionally, the expenses related to fixing the breached tank are expected to be approximately NOK 1m.

Despite the setback, Proximar emphasizes that the breach will have a limited impact on long-term harvest projections.

"The RAS [recirculating aquaculture system] technology at the post-smolt grow-out facility is demonstrating good performance regarding water treatment capacity and steady operations. Since the start of production, the company has not experienced any system-related problems, and the fish are performing very well across all the batches," it explained. 

Proximar plans to start harvesting the first batches at the post-smolt grow-out facility in the third quarter, with the breach affecting harvest volumes in Q4.

In the startup phase, Proximar strategically inserted a high number of eggs as a precautionary measure to secure excess biomass, anticipating unexpected incidents like the recent breach.

title: Daily recap: Skipjack demand soars in Ecuador; UK denies breaking Brexit deal
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Friday, Feb. 2:

Masoval finds subsidiary has been selling salmon 'unsuitable for human consumption'

Norwegian salmon farmer Masoval has informed the stock exchange that an investigation into its majority-owned processing and sales company has revealed some customers were supplied with fish that were unsuitable for human consumption.

Skipjack tuna demand soars in Ecuador amid drop in prices, Red Sea crisis impact

Ecuador's skipjack tuna industry is experiencing surging demand driven by competitive prices and the impact of the ongoing crisis in the Red Sea region on deliveries from Asia.

Scientists close in on making Atlantic salmon sea-lice resistant

Scientists might be on the verge of solving the Atlantic salmon industry's biggest problem, but it involves a technology frequently lumped together with the controversy-stirring genetic engineering used by AquaBounty.

UK denies sand eel ban goes against Brexit deal with EU

The UK's decision to permanently ban sand eel fishing in its waters does not contravene its Brexit deal with the EU, as claimed primarily by the Danish sector, a government spokesperson has told Undercurrent News.

China says foreign-backed seafood consultant punished for 'fabricating environmental problems'

The Chinese Ministry of State Security announced this week a criminal case involving a Chinese national accused of fabricating "environmental problems" in China's seafood industry and providing information to overseas institutions.

Bad weather keeps Norway salmon price flat, Chilean 'hit wall'

Storms in Norway in week five have brought farmed salmon spot prices for week six (commencing Feb. 5) back up to where they were one week prior, while Chilean levels have dived on a demand slump, sources told Undercurrent.

title: China says foreign-backed seafood consultant punished for ‘fabricating environmental problems’
content:
The Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS) announced this week a criminal case involving a Chinese national accused of fabricating "environmental problems" in China's seafood industry and providing information to overseas institutions.

The unnamed individual, referred to only as Li, allegedly established a consulting firm focused on China's fishing and aquaculture industry. According to the state security organ, Li's firm gathered data on Chinese seafood companies and later used this to falsely portray environmental and illegal fishing issues in China's enormous seafood sector.

Some European, US seafood buyers dropped Chinese processors accused of forced labor this summer

"Li...played an important role in encouraging overseas anti-China forces to introduce trade restriction bills in relevant countries," the MSS report stated.

Officials said Li enthusiastically participated in environmental activities and non-profits while studying abroad. After becoming influenced by "extreme environmentalist concepts", Li was recruited by unspecified "anti-China forces" seeking to undermine the nation's key industries.

With overseas support, Li established contacts with industry groups, multinationals, media and NGOs. After returning to China, his consulting firm quickly rose to prominence in the domestic seafood industry aided by foreign funding and resources.

The MSS alleges Li's firm established ties with some Chinese industry associations, research institutions and universities by offering funding, overseas research opportunities and other benefits. This enabled broader access to internal seafood industry data that was ultimately shared abroad.

Most critically, officials accuse Li of repeatedly fabricating evidence of environmental violations within China's seafood sector, playing a vital role in trade restriction efforts by "foreign powers". 

China’s seafood imports slow at $19.2bn but Russian crab purchases surge

MSS said Li was "punished" under national security laws, although it did not disclose the specific punishment enforced.

Undercurrent News attempted to contact sources to confirm Li's identity, but at the time of publication Chinese seafood industry associations and several companies said they were not aware of anyone named Li working as a seafood consultant.

China exported $24 billion in fish products in 2023, the largest globally. MSS claimed major importers like the EU and US have leveraged environmental concerns to introduce new non-tariff and technical barriers against Chinese seafood imports.

Trade restrictions due to unrelated matters

Currently, the US imposes restrictions on seafood imports from China produced using Uyghur labor. However, the restriction stems from widely documented mass incarceration and forced labor of Uyghur people in China's Xinjiang province rather than environmental issues.

The US also imposes punitive tariffs against over $200 billion worth of Chinese imports, including seafood, but these were enacted by former president Donald Trump on the grounds of the US' huge trade deficit with China and intellectual property theft. 

US congressional panel’s report recommends expanding SIMP for Chinese seafood

Meanwhile, the EU has so far declined to issue trade restrictions on environmental grounds, despite significant evidence of Chinese vessels engaging in illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing abroad. The EU's so-called "yellow" and "red" cards have been issued to other countries for similar violations. Past EU anti-dumping cases targeting Chinese tuna imports have arisen from state subsidies to the country's fishing fleet.

The MSS report follows an investigation last year by the NGO Outlaw Ocean Project that found Uyghur workers employed in Chinese seafood factories, which were supplying large value-added processors in Europe and North America, who were then selling to significant customers such as Albertsons, Carrefour, Edeka, Kroger, Sysco, Tesco and Walmart. The workers were allegedly moved to plants under China's "labor transfer program."

The group then reported detailed abusive labor conditions and lack of oversight on Chinese distant water fishing vessels. 

As a result of the investigations, major seafood companies in Europe and the US stopped sourcing fish from the Chinese processors. Among the companies that said they cut ties with the Chinese processors were US supermarket chains Albertsons Companies and Shaw's, and German retailers Aldi and Lidl. French retailers Carrefour and Casino and UK seafood company Young's Seafood also told Outlaw Ocean Project they were carrying out internal investigations.

title: Masoval finds subsidiary has been selling salmon ‘unsuitable for human consumption’
content:
Norwegian salmon farmer Masoval has informed the stock exchange that an investigation into its majority-owned processing and sales company has revealed some customers were supplied with fish that were unsuitable for human consumption.

Masoval acquired a 65% stake in Pure Norwegian Seafood (PNS) in June 2021 after partnering with it since 2018. Adding the Averoy-based firm made the group fully vertically integrated for the first time.

Masoval agrees deal to buy Mowi harvesting plant

"As a supplier to PNS, [Masoval] became suspicious of irregularities at PNS on Oct. 20, 2023. Prior regulatory inspections, controls, and audits had not uncovered the issues," it said.

"Through Masoval's board representatives in PNS, immediate action was taken through board instructions to completely halt the irregular activity, freeze storage was sealed, and affected products were recalled. Organizational measures were taken promptly, and new and reinforced procedures were implemented at PNS."

It then engaged Ernst & Young to conduct an independent investigation, the results of which have been passed to Norway's Food Safety Authority (Mattilsynet), after it was formally notified of the events in early November, said Masoval.

"In brief, the investigation reveals that PNS has allowed certain customers to buy frozen salmon that, according to Norwegian regulations, is not suitable for human consumption."

"Sold fish includes fish that either should have been discarded/ensiled, or production-graded fish that should be elaborated in secondary processing before export. The investigation estimates that this turnover of fish not suitable for human consumption constituted just under 1% of the total volume of fish and approximately 0.5% of PNS's revenue over the last three years."

In 2022, Masoval sold 22,141 metric tons of salmon to 33 different countries, according to its latest annual report. Some 42% of that went to Norwegian companies, mainly exporters, while 54% was sold to other European countries and 3% to Asia.

PNS sold 100% of Masoval's harvests in 2022. The group made a record turnover of NOK 1.99 billion ($190.2 million), though it did not break out PNS' revenue.

Early in January 2024, Masoval had its bid for a former Mowi harvesting facility in Ulvan in Trondelag country, west of Trondheim, accepted. It intends to use the facility to increase its own harvesting capacity, it said at the time.

Masoval said that, as a supplier to PNS, it has not gained any profit or participated in any other earnings related to these activities at PNS.

"The mentioned activities were halted in October 2023. After the investigation and other inquiries until now, there have been no indications that the irregularly traded products have affected people's health."

The revealed issues at PNS do not directly impact Masoval, it said, and they have a "marginal financial effect on the group."

"As Masoval assesses the consequences beyond this, they will primarily be related to potential public sanctions that may affect PNS."

It described the findings as a "serious and disappointing matter, both as a shareholder and supplier."

"Masoval and PNS' upmost priority is dialogue with the authorities and to facilitate government authorities' investigation activities, secondly Masoval will also consider its own contractual legal rights and possible compensation matters."

"At the same time, it is crucial for Masoval, as a responsible owner, to support PNS, its customers, and especially the employees as best as possible in this difficult situation. Despite the investigation, organizational changes, and new procedures and requirements, the production workers at PNS have delivered every day."

Taken seriously

Mattilsynet confirmed to Undercurrent News it had been told in November that Masoval and PNS had "uncovered regulatory violations concerning the export of farmed fish with errors and deficiencies, so-called production fish," and that they had taken measures to stop the activity and asked an external firm to investigate the matter.

"[We] became aware of how serious the case was this week when the results of the investigation were presented to us," said Steinar Westerberg, Mattilsynet's regional director for central Norway.

"We take this matter very seriously as the independent investigation shows that there have been exported fish that should not be used for human food and fish with deficiencies. Both are clear violations of the regulations and should not happen."

"We are following it up. Initially we are looking at the extent and assessing withdrawals of fish that should not be used for human food. We are also examining the findings of the investigation in more detail in order to assess further follow-up. We work closely with the companies. It is too early to say what consequences this will have."

Brand based on quality

In 2022, PNS launched a new brand, Pure Princess, which was well-received among high-end customers, according to CEO Helge Kvalvik.

Masoval's head of sales and processing, Eldar Arne Henden, has been head of PNS since 2004, joining the group when Masoval purchased its stake.

"PNS' sales department played a vital role in Masoval’s success in 2022," the firm said in its annual report. "The department now consists of seven skilled salespeople, three logistics personnel, one planner and one purchaser."

"[Pure Princess]'s salmon is produced to meet the requirements of customers seeking premium quality products in high-end markets. The brand is committed to ensuring the highest quality fish health, as it recognizes that superior fish health is essential to producing quality fish for the consumer."

title: Other fishermen, politicians rally to help burned out Northwest US Dungy crab harvesters
content:
The Dungeness crab harvesters who have begun dropping their bated circular steel crab pots in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of the US states of Oregon and Washington earlier this week are overcoming some adversity in the fishery, Oregon Public Broadcasting (OPB) reports.

Just days earlier -- on Jan. 22 -- a fire at the Bornstein Seafood facility in Ilwaco, Washington, destroyed an estimated 4,000 pots, as reported by Undercurrent News. 

Fire investigators wrapped up their investigation into the cause of the blaze on Saturday (Jan. 27), but have not publicly announced their findings, according to OPB. A final cost estimate has not been determined, but the fire resulted in a total loss. 

Investigators with the federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives are writing the final origin and cause report. Once the report is complete, the findings will be given to the Ilwaco Fire Department.

Meanwhile, the harvesters began dropping pots on Monday (Jan. 29) and hauling them up on Thursday (Feb. 1) to mark the beginning of the season, which sees its heaviest landings in the first few weeks.

Other crabbers from all over the West Coast have rallied to help their colleagues find replacement gear, loaning hundreds of pots for the entire season, according to the news service. Locally businesses and other groups have set up donations and other aid to get fishing families through the start of the season.

Political leaders are also pledging state and federal support over the coming months, pressing state agencies to race crab pot identification tags into the hands of the harvesters, according to the article..

title: Investigation ongoing into cause of fire at Bornstein plant
content:
Investigators say the cause of a fire that resulted in extensive damage at a facility owned by US processor Bornstein Seafoods is not considered to be suspicious, although the origin of the blaze is still unknown. 

Oregon Public Broadcasting reports that thousands of crab pots were lost in the fire, which hit the facility in Ilwaco, Washington, last week, just ahead of that area's anticipated commercial Dungeness crab season on Thursday (Feb. 1).

Fire reported at Bornstein plant ahead of Dungeness crab season

“It is basically — yeah, it’s 20 years of my life right there that just went up in smoke," Peter Nornes, a fisherman who lost 500 crab pots, told the public radio station.

No injuries were reported in the blaze.

A GoFundMe page set up last week for fishermen who lost pots in the fire had already raised just under $114,000 as of Tuesday (Jan. 30). Fishermen from other parts of the US West Coast have also donated gear.

The Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife, which manages the fishery, is also working with crabbers to quickly get proper identification tags for replacement pots ahead of this week's opener.

title: Russian crab asset seizure involves nearly 10,000t of quotas
content:
The Russian government's move to seize crab fishing assets worth some $4.24 billion in January will see it take almost 10,000 metric tons of yearly catch quotas.

That's nearly one-tenth of the country's total allowable catch. 

In two rulings released on Jan. 25, the Arbitration Court of Russia's Far Eastern Primorie region ordered the freezing of crab quotas and assets, including those of one-time "crab king" Oleg Kan. The ruling came at the request of the Prosecutor General's office.

According to the lawsuits, companies controlled by Dmitry Dremlyuga -- including Merlion, Fish Island, Crab Marin, Apella, Crab DMP, and Pacific Marin -- were involved in illegal fishing by fraudulently creating a semblance of legitimate economic activities.

Another lawsuit is based on similar claims relating to companies controlled by Kan, including Primorie Fishery Company, SevRybFlot, Moneron, Kuril Universal Complex, and Aquamarin. The lawsuits claimed that all these companies were under foreign control and, therefore, illegally acquired crab quotas.

Companies allegedly controlled by Kan had more than 8,000t per year of crab quotas, and Dremlyuga's entities had some 1,000t. Dremlyuga is a citizen of Ukraine, while Kan is a permanent resident of South Korea and not a Russian tax resident.

Russia has been mounting a case against Kan for several years.

In February 2020, the Khabarovsk Regional Court issued a warrant for Kan's arrest in absentia after he had already fled abroad. He was accused of organizing the murder in 2010 of rival businessman Valery Pkhidenko. He was tried in absentia in December 2022 on the charge of organizing a contract killing.

In 2021, authorities seized sizable real estate assets belonging to Kan. Then, in August 2023, law enforcement agencies brought charges alleging Kan had organized a criminal community that had smuggled 3,000t of crab -- worth RUB 2.6bn ($22.7 million) -- from Russia to Japan, China, and South Korea, reports The Russian Crime.

In doing so, it was alleged he had dodged applicable export duties and taxes.

Then, in December 2023, the Primorie regional court ruled to seize real estate and other assets controlled by Dremlyuga worth RUB 4.3bn.

It has also ordered the seizure of crab assets belonging to former Sakhalin regional lawmaker Dmitry Pashov. Pashov, who faced similar crab smuggling charges in June 2020, was sentenced to 4.5 years in jail. Before that, Pashov was known as the country's richest government employee with assets worth RUB 6.2bn.

The January 2023 seizure orders came when the Prosecutor General's office filed a lawsuit, case No. А51-1301/2024, requesting the annulment of crab quotas and seeking damages from companies and individuals totaling RUB 358.7bn.

Another lawsuit, No. А51-1300/2024, has requested the annulment of crab quotas operated by Dremlyuga's businesses and seeks damages from these companies and individuals totaling RUB 17.4bn.

The Arbitration Court of Primorie region ruled to impose a total ban on all defendants' business operations and freeze all their assets. Trial dates have been set for Feb. 15 and 28.

title: Editor’s choice: Shrimp outlook the big news at GSMC; EU makes move in salmon price-fixing case
content:
EMEA editor Neil Ramsden brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

Last week's top story was the team's blog from the annual Global Seafood Market Conference (GSMC) which was held this year in Orlando, in the US state of Florida. There were updates on whitefish and shrimp supply and demand outlooks, plus much more - you can find all the updates at the blog, here.

Reported from GSMC was the news that a massive shrimp glut has led to an unprecedented slide in wholesale prices, but Sandro Coglitore, the CEO of Omarsa, one of Ecuador's largest shrimp farmers and processors, doesn't see that as his sector's "biggest problem or threat" in 2024. Instead, that honor belongs to the potential of anti-dumping and/or countervailing duties in the US, he said.

Coglitore told Undercurrent News that shrimp prices will start to recover in 2024, with demand and supply more in balance, after one of the worst years the sector has seen. "It was a nightmare," he said, of a year when security concerns over the increasing power of drug gangs in the country met weak markets and low prices caused by the speed of the country's increase in production.

A private equity firm that has already made investments in the seafood sector is closing in on a deal for the Ocean Beauty Seafoods distribution business, sources told Undercurrent. According to several sources, Sole Source Capital is in the final stages of due diligence to acquire the Ocean Beauty distribution operation from the Bristol Bay Economic Development Corporation and Howard Klein, Michael Selby and Ronald Shaw.

Staying in the US, Pacific Seafood Group has filed a federal lawsuit against two former employees in Texas that it has accused of using proprietary information to steal a large percentage of its Gulf of Mexico-related sales. The lawsuit seems like just the latest escalation of an ongoing, months-long battle between the Clackamas, Oregon-based US seafood processing giant and Nello Cassarino, former CEO of the Galveston Shrimp Company, a business it mostly acquired in 2011.

And in even bigger legal news, the European Commission last week informed Norwegian salmon producers Cermaq Group, Grieg Seafood, Bremnes Seashore, Leroy Seafood Group, Mowi and SalMar of its preliminary view that they breached EU antitrust rules by colluding to distort competition in the market for spot sales of Norwegian farmed Atlantic salmon in the EU. If the commission's preliminary view is confirmed, the companies face fines of up to 10% of their annual worldwide turnover. The companies all deny the allegations and will submit their defenses.

Shares in the Norwegian salmon farmers plunged after the announcement, wiping roughly $800 million off the combined market caps of Mowi, SalMar, Leroy and Grieg, equivalent to 4% of their combined market value.

The bottom of the market for prices of pollock fillets from China, Russia and the US is seemingly yet to be reached, with multiple buyers and sellers stating that 2024 will be a rough year for the sector. As the US A season got underway on Jan. 20, there are more longer-term positives in the sector after the Biden administration updated its executive order to block imports of pollock fillets from China using Russian raw material.

Japanese seafood company Kyokuyo is expanding its overseas operations by acquiring a majority stake in Turkey's Kocaman Fisheries Export and Import Trade, a seafood processor. Kyokuyo's European subsidiary, Kyokuyo Europe, which is registered in the Netherlands, will purchase 51% of Kocaman for an undisclosed amount, the company announced on Friday.

The 2024 vannamei shrimp production forecast from the GSMC is for a 1% drop to 5.10 million metric tons after a 4.5% hike in 2023, an increase that has put many farmers globally at a loss. Robins McIntosh, of Thailand's Charoen Pokphand Foods, led the production forecast on the GSMC shrimp panel, where he said his view has "changed in the past week or two with sentiment for Ecuador having improved."

He told Undercurrent that the forecast for Chinese shrimp output to drop and Ecuador to stay flat could well be exceeded, and that a flat 2024 level of 1.45 million metric tons for Ecuadorian vannamei is "bearish."

Meanwhile, China's shrimp demand hit a soft patch in late 2023 even as full-year imports set records by volume, with growth moderating more than anticipated despite earlier predictions of a strong rebound. Newly released full-year Chinese customs data show total shrimp imports rose 13% in 2023, hitting an all-time high of 1.1 million metric tons. But momentum slowed in the second half, with volumes down 10% and values plunging 25%.

title: European Commission may take five years to pass salmon price-fixing judgement, says top lawyer
content:
A top competition lawyer in Norway has said that the European Commission could take another five years before concluding its price-fixing case brought against six Norwegian salmon companies -- Mowi, SalMar, Leroy Seafood Group, Cermaq Group, Grieg Seafood and Bremnes Seashore.

The EC announced on Thursday (Jan. 25) a "preliminary view" that the companies breached EU antitrust rules by colluding to distort competition in the market for spot sales of Norwegian farmed Atlantic salmon in the EU. It is the latest development in an investigation that began in 2019. 

Line Voldstad, Head of Regulatory and FPR (Norway) at DLA Piper. Source: DLA Piper website

In an email interview with Undercurrent News, Line Voldstad, a competition law partner at DLA Piper's Oslo office, said that these types of cases typically take around a decade from initial investigation to a final judgment. The duration depends on the complexity, scope and number of parties, "but usually these processes are very lengthy and cost and time-consuming." 

She added: "In our experience, a decade -- or more -- would not be an unusual estimate." In that amount of time, the EC's position "rarely changes materially before a final decision is reached."

You can read the full interview with Voldstad, who has worked in Brussels and London in international completion law, and before the EU and EFTA courts, below.

What is the typical timeline from the opening of a European Commission antitrust investigation to a final judgment? 

Naturally, it depends on the complexity, scope and numbers of parties, but usually these processes are very lengthy and cost and time consuming. In our experience, a decade – or more – would not be an unusual estimate. That said, several key factors, such as whether the process started with a leniency application or a dawn raid with subsequent review to attempt to establish the facts, whether and how the parties cooperate, as well as the time elapsed from the alleged breach of the competition rules etc., impact the timeline.

Norwegian salmon shares plunge after EU anti-trust announcement

The investigation itself can take years to complete, and the process before the commission with reply to a Statement of Objections and hearing before the commission can also take a long time. A subsequent process and appeal before the EU courts adds additional years.

What are the key procedural steps the European Commission follows in an antitrust investigation leading up to a final judgment?

After opening an antitrust investigation, the European Commission may conduct inspections and/or request information from the parties and other undertakings, as well as interviews with persons involved in order to attempt to establish the facts of the case. Once the EC believes it has a clear view of the case (facts and law), it will issue a so-called Statement of Objections (SO) which details the commission's views competition concerns. As mentioned, it may take several years from an opening of an investigation until an SO is issued. 

The SO is sent to the parties concerned. Subsequently, the parties are entitled to see the Commission's investigative file, submit their often extensive replies, and to an oral hearing conducted by an independent hearing officer. After considering the parties' responses to the SO, the EC will adopt a decision, where the EC may require the parties concerned to stop the infringement, impose remedies and/or impose a fine. The EC may also adopt a commitment decision in which the parties concerned offer commitments that are intended to address the competition concerns identified by the EC.

EU finds Norway’s salmon farmers breached price-fixing rules

The decisions adopted by the commission are subject to legal review by the EU courts, namely the General Court (formerly the Court of First Instance) and the Court of Justice, and the parties can object to the EC decision by application for annulment of the decision and/or reduction of fine etc. to the General Court.

Once the European Commission issues a preliminary view in an antitrust case, how often does its position materially change before a final judgment is reached?

In our experience, the EC's position rarely changes materially before a final decision is reached. These are generally very fact-heavy and complex cases; the case team has worked with an extensive number of documents and facts for a very long time during an investigation, and when an opinion of the interpretation of which documents and facts that are relevant and how they could be interpreted has developed in the case team, that conception is usually difficult to change. The parties on their side tend to have quite a different view on the relevant facts and the interpretation of the facts. And the courts may very well reach a different view and conclusion in their judgments than the view of the EC.

We understand the maximum fine in antitrust cases is up to 10% of a company's global turnover. To confirm, is "turnover" normally based on revenues in a single recent year rather than summed over multiple years of alleged violations? 

US judge OKs $85m settlement in Norwegian salmon price-fixing suit

Normally, yes, however, if the relevant year disproportionately represents the turnover of the relevant years of the infringement, it is also possible to calculate the fine differently, for example, an average. The final amount of the fine shall not, in any event, exceed 10% of the total turnover in the preceding business year of the undertaking. 

That said, it is rare for the EU to impose fines close to 10% of turnover, and on average ballpark has been 2-3%, even in fairly serious cases.

What factors and mitigating circumstances might the European Commission consider when determining the appropriate level of fines below or at the 10% maximum?

In terms of aggravating circumstances that could increase the fine, that would typically be continued or repeatedly same or a similar competition law infringement, refusal to cooperate with or obstruction of the EC in carrying out its investigations, the role of leader in, or instigator of, the infringement; the EC will also pay particular attention to any steps taken to coerce others to participate in the infringement and/or any retaliatory measures taken against others with a view to enforcing the practices constituting the infringement. 

US closes price-fixing investigation against Norway salmon farmers

Typical mitigating circumstances would be where the party concerned provides evidence that it terminated the infringement as soon as the commission intervened (this will not apply to secret agreements or practices (in particular, cartels)), provides evidence that the infringement has been committed as a result of negligence, provides evidence that its involvement in the infringement is substantially limited and demonstrates that, during the period in which it was party to the offending agreement, it actually avoided applying it by adopting competitive conduct in the market, where the party concerned has effectively cooperated with the commission (outside the scope of the leniency notice and beyond its legal obligation to do so), and where the anti-competitive conduct of the party has been authorized or encouraged by public authorities or by legislation.

Is the European Commission likely to publish details on the specific nature and mechanisms of the alleged antitrust violations and resulting consumer harm? Or does the investigative process typically remain confidential?

The investigative process typically remains confidential until the EC issues its' SO.

Could the companies' $85 million settlement in a related U.S. civil lawsuit have had any influence on the European Commission's fines or overall judgment?

In principle, no; The EC's fines are calculated based on the method of setting fines imposed under the relevant EU regulation (Article 23(2)(a) of Regulation No 1/2003). The fines and judgment is to be objectively based on the evidence of the specific case and not be influenced by other judgments.

title: Norwegian salmon shares plunge after EU anti-trust announcement
content:
Additional reporting by Louis Harkell.

Shares in major Norwegian salmon farmers plunged after the EU Commission announced on the morning of Jan. 25 its preliminary view that six companies -- Mowi, SalMar, Leroy Seafood Group, Cermaq Group, Grieg Seafood and Bremnes Seashore -- had breached EU antitrust rules by colluding to distort competition in the market for spot sales of Norwegian farmed Atlantic salmon in the EU.

EU finds Norway’s salmon farmers breached price-fixing rules

For now, this is only a preliminary view, and does not prejudge the outcome of its ongoing salmon price-fixing investigation, which began in 2019.

Nevertheless, in the hours following the announcement, roughly $800 million was wiped off the combined market caps of Mowi, SalMar, Leroy and Grieg, equivalent to 4% of their combined market value.

Of the four, Grieg's share value has taken the biggest hit, down by 6.4%, followed by Leroy (-5.3%), Mowi (-4.1%), and SalMar (-2.1%), compared with Wednesday's closing price.

The other two farmers included in the probe, Mitsubishi-owned Cermaq and Bremnes Seashore, don't trade any public shares.

In the event the final verdict made by the commission awarded its sternest anti-trust punishment -- a fine amounting to 10% of global annual turnover -- this would likely be calculated the most recent financial year, Undercurrent News confirmed with analysts.

Based on last year's revenue figures, a 10% fine for Mowi this year would equate to NOK 6.16 billion ($588m), NOK 2.94bn for Leroy, NOK 2.91bn for SalMar, and NOK 718m for Grieg.

In relative terms, Leroy stands to be the worst-impacted; a 10% turnover fine would be equivalent to 11.2% of the company's market cap, according to Norwegian analyst Carnegie Research.

This is followed by Grieg (9.2%), Mowi (6.2%) and finally SalMar (4%).

Credit: Carnegie Research

Analysts believe any fine unlikely to come to 10%

Despite this, Norwegian salmon sector analysts are doubtful whether any eventual fine will actually come to a full 10% "worst-case scenario", with the consensus being that the stock market has overreacted.

Alexander Aukner, an analyst with DNB Markets, noted that the threat of the full fine likely serves as a starting point, with reductions from cooperation.

"We have seen these cases previously where there's typically a discount to the worst-case scenario, either because you've been compliant and given information, which the farming companies have, or potentially they could be acquitted from actually doing things wrong," he said. "We think the share price drop seems like an overreaction."

Herman Alexander Dahl, an analyst with Nordea, agreed, believing that any potential fine "will most likely be less than 1% of turnover."

"According to the 2006-2023 EU cartel case statistics ~55% of the fines are below 1% of annual turnover, 70% of the fines are below 2% of annual turnover and 75% are below 3% of annual turnover," Dahl wrote. "Hence we believe the potential fine will be limited to the 0-1% range and that there is a very low probability of a fine in the range of 3-10% of global turnover."

Equally, there is the consideration that a blanket 10% fine on all global turnover would be difficult to justify when it is only fresh salmon spot sales to the EU under consideration by the probe, especially when Leroy, for instance, has its own whitefish division, Undercurrent sources said.

Dahl added that the EU case contains similar allegations to the one pursued against the six farmers by several US buyers, which ended with an $85m settlement in September 2022.

"If we assume a similar settlement/fine we believe the impact on the individual salmon farmers will be in the scope of NOK 100-250m, and have a rather limited impact on 2024 or 2025 estimates, depending on when they end the process."

EU anti-trust fines by percentage of turnover. Credit: Nordea

Will the probe affect long-term investor interest?

After seeing a substantial drop in share price on Thursday morning, it remains to be seen whether the preliminary decision will also have a cooling effect on investor demand if, as seems probable, the case drags on past 2024.

 "It had the same impact in 2019 when it [the probe] was first announced," said Aukner. "All the players fell 5-6%. So in theory, it should have been discounted by the market, but the market forgets and now it re-emerges, down 5-6% again."

Sander Lie, an analyst with Pareto Securities, noted that this is another piece of bad news for the sector after a rough 15 months of slow production growth and regulatory headwinds.

"It's hard to say," he said. "It has been a very rough year for some farmers in general in terms of the political perspective of the resource tax in Norway. Obviously, that led to a massive fall-off, especially from foreign capital, and I don't think that will be any better after seeing the headlines today."

"However, based on our first read, it seems like a scenario close to worst-case has been priced in across several of the names today."

title: EU finds Norway’s salmon farmers breached price-fixing rules
content:
The European Commission (EC) has informed Norwegian salmon producers Cermaq Group, Grieg Seafood, Bremnes Seashore, Leroy Seafood Group, Mowi and SalMar of its preliminary view that they breached EU antitrust rules by colluding to distort competition in the market for spot sales of Norwegian farmed Atlantic salmon in the EU.

"The commission has concerns that, between 2011 and 2019, the six salmon producers exchanged commercially sensitive information, relating to sales prices, available volumes, sales volumes, production volumes and production capacities, as well as other price-setting factors. The suspected aim of this alleged conduct was to reduce normal uncertainty in the market for spot sales of Norwegian farmed Atlantic salmon into the EU."

The alleged anticompetitive conduct only concerns sales on the spot market into the EU, as opposed to sales based on long-term contracts, the EC said. Spot sales are those for which prices, volumes and other sales conditions are agreed per sale, based on the market conditions on the day of the sale.

Norway accounts for over half of the production of farmed Atlantic salmon worldwide, and the EU is its main importer. The alleged conduct concerns sales of fresh, whole and gutted Atlantic salmon farmed in Norway, which accounts for nearly 80% of all farmed Atlantic salmon exported from Norway. The alleged conduct does not concern frozen farmed Atlantic salmon or processed products such as salmon fillets, loins, or smoked salmon.

If the commission's preliminary view is confirmed, this conduct would infringe Article 101 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, which prohibits cartels and other restrictive business practices.

The sending of a Statement of Objections does not prejudge the outcome of an investigation.

Previously, this group of salmon farmers was under investigation for the same allegations in the US. The US Department of Justice closed its investigation in January 2023, while the salmon farmers entered an industry settlement in May 2022for a total of $85 million.

Mowi, Leroy contest the preliminary view

Mowi confirmed it had received a Statement of Objections from the EC as a result of its inspections in February 2019 of several Norwegian producers of farmed Atlantic salmon.

"The Statement of Objections is not a final decision, but rather the commission's preliminary view that the companies under investigation may have breached EU competition rules," it stressed.

"Mowi contests the commission's preliminary view and the characteristics of the alleged behavior in the market for farmed Norwegian Atlantic salmon, and strongly believes there has been no infringement of the competition rules. Mowi will now carefully review the commission's statement and reply in writing, following standard process."

The EC will next allow the salmon farmers to exercise their rights to defence, then conclude whether the alleged behavior amounts to a violation of the EU competition rules.

Leroy said it "strongly rejects the commission's allegations," claiming to be "dedicated to ensuring compliance with relevant competition law and always competes vigorously to offer customers the best products and terms."

"The Statement of Objections [SO] is not a final decision and has been issued in accordance with the commission's ordinary procedures for such an investigation. The SO includes the commission's preliminary assessments only."

"[Leroy] has a right of response, and will, after carefully reviewing the SO, provide its comments to the commission. Leroy has cooperated with the commission throughout the commission's investigation, and will continue to work constructively with the commission."

It further noted that it is standard practice that such EC investigations last several years.

"It is not possible at this stage to make any statement on whether the case will result in sanctions or other negative consequences for [Leroy], or when the case will end."

SalMar said that it too strongly disagrees with the EC's preliminary assessment and will account for its view in a thorough reply to come.

For its part, Grieg also denied any anti-trust infringements or anti-competitive behavior by it or any of its subsidiaries, adding that it "will exercise all its rights of defence."

Fine of up to 10% of annual worldwide turnover possible

Through information received from several market players, the EC identified concerns in the market for spot sales of Norwegian-farmed Atlantic salmon in the EU, and it carried out inspections in February 2019 as part of a so-called ‘ex-officio' investigation.  

A Statement of Objections is a formal step in the commission's investigations into suspected violations of EU antitrust rules. The commission informs the parties concerned in writing of the objections raised against them. The parties can then examine the documents in the commission's investigation file, reply in writing and request an oral hearing to present their views on the case before representatives of the commission and national competition authorities, it explained.

"If the commission concludes, after the parties have exercised their rights of defense, that there is sufficient evidence of an infringement, it can adopt a decision prohibiting the conduct and imposing a fine of up to 10% of a company's annual worldwide turnover."

There is no legal deadline for the commission to complete antitrust inquiries into anticompetitive conduct.

title: McIntosh: GSMC shrimp forecast of drop from China, flat Ecuador output is bearish
content:
ORLANDO, Florida, US -- The Global Seafood Market Conference (GSMC) shrimp production forecast for Chinese shrimp output to drop and Ecuador to stay flat could well be exceeded, said Robins McIntosh of Thailand's Charoen Pokphand Foods.

McIntosh, who led the production forecast at the GSMC on Jan. 23, told Undercurrent News a flat 2024 level of 1.45 million metric tons for Ecuadorian vannamei is "bearish."

The 2024 global vannamei shrimp production forecast from the Global Seafood Market Council (GSMC). Credit: GSMC

McIntosh assumed that production in Ecuador would start to drop at the back end of 2023, with the all-time low prices, but that didn't happen. So, the production increased around 12% in 2023 to 1.45m. "There's no reason to think this can't continue, so 1.45m is bearish."

The 2024 global vannamei shrimp production forecast from the Global Seafood Market Council (GSMC). Credit: GSMC

The trend of large, integrated Ecuadorian companies buying up farms will continue. Then, the major industry players "technify" the farms with auto-feeders and aeration, which increases production dramatically and lowers the production cost.

"In the old days, they were getting 1.5-2t per hectare per crop, so maybe 4t per year. They technify the farm, going from 4t up to 20-21t per hectare per year. That's a huge jump," McIntosh told Undercurrent on the sidelines of the GSMC.

US trade investigation ‘biggest problem or threat’ facing Ecuador shrimp but rebalance possible

Then, the adjustment down for 2024 Chinese production to 1.10m metric tons from 1.15m is also something McIntosh said he could see adjusting upward, depending on the market. He also clarified the Chinese number is around 1m metric tons of vannamei and 150,000t of black tiger.

The forecast for a drop from China comes from a trip McIntosh took to China at the end of last year, visiting farmers from the North Korean border and "all the way down."

Feedback from the farmers was that the low prices of imported shrimp were hurting them, he said. "Chinese shrimp goes into the live market, and the Ecuadorian imports are frozen, but farmers asked if the imported shrimp hurts their live price. I don't know, but the Chinese farmers need $8.50/kg, and they were getting $5.50/kg," he told Undercurrent.

"Some were saying they would stop stocking, get out of the business. It was enough for me to adjust the number down," he said. "Prices have gone up again now, maybe due to Lunar New Year coming up. If that continues, production can increase."

The chart below, from the Undercurrent data portal, shows how the gap closed between farm-gate prices (converted to dollars from CNY) for vannamei in Guangdong, China, and the level in Ecuador, but it's since opened up again. 

On the GSMC shrimp panel, McIntosh gave an insight into what he saw on this recent trip to China.

"China is a country that has come on in technology, with small indoor raceways. They can do 1t per crop and two crops per year. There are 400,000 of these farms, and they can build them very fast on traditional ponds," said McIntosh.

'Resilient' farmers in Ecuador

Ecuador farmers "have been very resilient" to grow production in such a low-priced environment, said Sandro Coglitore, CEO of Omarsa, one of the Latin American country's largest producers, on the GSMC shrimp panel.

"Farmers have modified their production technology and grown despite market conditions," he said. Auto-feeders and more pond aeration have been significant production drivers.

Coglitore forecasts a drop in production in the first half of 2024, after farmers reduced stocking with the risk of an El Nino. "Farmers cut densities worried about climate change. So, the production will be lower at the start, then it could go up at the end of the year."

Black tiger growth

On black tiger, McIntosh is confident the only way is up. The 2024 black tiger shrimp production forecast from the GSMC is for a 20% increase in 2024 to 580,000t. 

The 2024 global black tiger shrimp production forecast from the Global Seafood Market Council (GSMC). Credit: GSMC

Black tiger has grown to be 10% of global production, said McIntosh. It's moving back toward the levels of 700,000t seen in 2003 and 2004. 

"If we go back to 2018, black tiger was only 8% of world production. Now it's closer to 10% and growing. Why does black tiger grow? It grows because when there are disease issues with vannamei – like China, India and Southeast Asia — farmers opt for black tiger," he said.

"Chinese farmers will tell me that the first crop, they will do vannamei, when it's a little cooler. But when vibrio starts becoming a real issue, when it's warm, they'll do a monodon [black tiger] drop and finish with a vannamei crop"” he said.

title: Russian fishing vessel stalls in the Norwegian Sea
content:
A Russian processor trawler that stalled in the Norwegian Sea is being towed back to port in Murmansk, with no casualties reported, reports 29.RU.

The vessel 'Barents Sea' reported a malfunction of its engine on the morning of Jan. 21, and had to be rescued by coastguard services.

Following the incident, the Arkhangelsk transport prosecutor's office is conducting an investigation of the vessel for signs of a crime, while attempting to establish the nature of the damage.

The vessel, which was completed in 2020, belongs to Arkhangelsk Trawling Fleet JSC. It was the first of four vessels in the KMT01 project being built in Vyborg for ATF as part of an ongoing investment project.

title: US trade investigation ‘biggest problem or threat’ facing Ecuador shrimp but rebalance possible
content:
ORLANDO, Florida, US -- A massive shrimp glut has led to an unprecedented slide in wholesale prices, but Sandro Coglitore, the CEO of Omarsa, one of Ecuador's largest shrimp farmers and processors, doesn't see that as his sector's "biggest problem or threat" in 2024.

Instead, that honor belongs to the potential of anti-dumping and/or countervailing duties in the US, he told attendees at the Global Seafood Market Conference (GSMC) on Tuesday.

GSMC shrimp panel forecasts slight 2024 output drop with many farmers ‘below cost’

But Coglitore also said he believes the industry could pivot and "rebalance" as some source nations exit some markets and move to others.

"I think there will be some rebalancing because, just for our company, we will stop shipments so that no cargo will arrive after April 1, where we expect some of the preliminary duties to be set and when we really see what's coming out," he said. "Probably other countries that don't have the risk of the duties, they might be shipping a larger volume to the US, but they will leave some places open where we have to find a place to put our product."

He gave the potential example of India sending more shrimp into the US and sending less to China for reprocessing, which could leave China open for other shrimp-producing countries, like Ecuador, to fill the void.

Ecuador, which exported 1.1 million metric tons of frozen warmwater shrimp worth $5.8 billion in the first 11 months of 2023, already counts on China as its biggest buyer. In the first 11 months of 2023, China took 654,192t – 59% of the total -- worth $3.2bn. By comparison, the US imported 187,524t – 17% of the total -- worth $1.1bn during the same period, as reported by Undercurrent News.

Sandro Coglitore, managing director of Omarsa, Ecuador's second largest shrimp exporter. Credit: Tom Seaman

Risk will factor into selling price

Undercurrent reported in December how the US International Trade Commission (ITC) had voted unanimously, 4-0, to allow the continuation of an investigation that could lead to tariffs being charged on frozen warmwater shrimp from India, Ecuador, Indonesia and Vietnam.

The decision advanced complaints brought by the American Shrimp Processors Association (ASPA) and further paved the way for the potential of countervailing and anti-dumping duties that could make shrimp from the US' four major source nations exponentially more expensive as soon as March 2024.

The vote was an indication that the commission saw enough evidence during its nearly all-day online hearing, held Nov. 15, that US shrimp harvesters and processors have suffered as a result of the low prices being paid for imports. The ITC heard from two panels, including one with about a half-dozen producers representing ASPA.

They painted a grim picture of how the price for imported shrimp was driving down the dock and wholesale prices for domestic shrimp to such low levels that they were having a hard time staying in business.

ASPA, back on Oct. 25, filed a petition with the signatures of some 850 shrimp harvesters requesting duties on foreign imports. The group reported that its members account for more than 85% of the domestic shrimp processed in the US.

A final decision regarding possible tariffs is not expected from the federal government until the Fall or Winter of 2024, sources said. The law firm Akin Gump suggests in a recent column on its website that the investigation will be completed and potential orders issued by December 2024. The law firm White & Case predicts October 2024.

Coglitore explained how two Ecuadorian companies have been selected as respondents in the investigation, referring to Industrial Pesquera Santa Priscila (“Santa Priscilla”) and Sociedad Nacional de Galapagos C.A. Songa (“Songa”). They would get hit with specific duties and other Ecuadorian companies would be charged a tariff rate that is an average number in-between, he said.

A shrimp processor near Guayaquil, Ecuador. Credit: Louis Harkell / Undercurrent News.

However, another crucial event could cause importers significant pain as soon as March 25, 2024. That's the date upon which the Department of Commerce (DOC) is scheduled to make a preliminary determination as to whether the shrimp industries in the four countries are receiving countervailing subsidies and thus can be forced to deposit funds equivalent to amounts intended to negate those subsidies. 

Most shrimp producers are now required by their importers to sell deliver duty paid (DDP), assuming much of the risk.

"So now we have to deliver the product DDP, and there will be preliminary duties somewhere in April or May, and then definite duties by the end of the year," Coglitore explained while participating on the GSMC panel. "And in between, those duties can be adjusted. So if the preliminary is lower at the end of the year, you will get a bill to pay the difference. And if the preliminary is higher, you might get some money back."

He continued: "All that risk has to be factored into the selling price to the US in the near future and it's a high risk because nobody knows which way this is going to go. So, not only will it be an issue on the market price, but I think this will be the biggest threat for the Ecuadorian industry in the US market during 2024."

Robins McIntosh, Charoen Pokphand Foods' top shrimp executive and another member of the panel, expressed sympathy for Coglitore and other shrimp exporters.

"Nothing like just running your business, and you don't know what your cost of goods is until a year or two after the fact," he said.

title: Untitled
content:
ORLANDO, Florida, US -- Shrimp prices will start to recover in 2024, with demand and supply more in balance, after one of the worst years the sector has seen, said the top executive of one of Ecuador's largest shrimp processors.

"It was a nightmare," said Sandro Coglitore, CEO of Omarsa, of a year when security concerns over the increasing power of drug gangs in the country met weak markets and low prices caused by the speed of the country's increase in production.

Shrimp expert sees 2024 global output dropping again due to disease, market uncertainties

For 2024, Coglitore expects Ecuador's production to be flat at around 1.4 million metric tons or up marginally, but other countries, such as Vietnam, to drop. With the major markets of China and the US having "hit the bottom," he's optimistic for 2024.

"Everyone is clear that in 2024, shrimp will be at a higher price and that there will be less shrimp available from certain parts of the world," Coglitore told Undercurrent News during the Global Seafood Market Conference in Orlando, in the US state of Florida. "So, the world of very low shrimp prices is over. It's not sustainable anymore."

Looking at the weekly farm-gate price data (below) for Ecuadorian vannamei on the Undercurrent data portal, prices for several main sizes have increased from the lows seen at the end of 2023.

Upgrade to Pro to view

The monthly data (see below) going back to 2011 shows prices for several sizes hit an all-time low in December 2023, at least in terms of Undercurrent's data.

"Definitely, 2023 was a very, very challenging year for everyone. In 2024, if there is a recovery in the major economies, we should see a rebound in terms of pricing despite high volumes of production. I wouldn't say production will drop dramatically, but it might not be a record year. Production levels in Ecuador will stay high," he said.

He said other countries, such as Vietnam, will reduce production due to diseases.

Then, "some countries might be impacted by duties," he said. "And if interest rates come down, demand comes back, 2024 should be the year where production can be absorbed at these price levels."

GSMC 2024: Iceland haddock hike keeps supply stable; Pollock catches up in 2024
China buyers back in after 'big' losses in 2023

The Ecuadorian shrimp sector is seeing demand pick up in China, which will remain its primary focus in 2024, especially with the uncertain situation around duties in the US market, Coglitore told Undercurrent on the sidelines of GSMC.

He said that demand from China seems to be back up again, having traveled to Orlando from Beijing, where he had been meeting with Chinese buyers.

China just published figures that show it passed 1m metric tons in shrimp imports, with Ecuador responsible for 70%. China imported 697,102t of shrimp from Ecuador, up 23% year-on-year. Yet, with prices down, values stayed flat at $3.5 billion as average import prices of Ecuadorian shrimp plunged 19% to $5.09 per kilogram. Import momentum slowed in the second half, with volumes down 10% and values dropping 25%.

China’s shrimp imports hit 1m metric tons but appetite slows

"They [Chinese importers] are starting to build new inventory and have been making money in December and January." He confirmed importers made "big losses" in 2023, but the outlook is they can make money in 2024.

Even though the cutoff point to get to the market for Chinese New Year on Feb. 10 was December, importers are buying, said Coglitore.

The US market has "definitely hit the bottom and is picking up," but the government's anti-dumping and countervailing duty investigations are casting a shadow.

"Big sales to China will continue. In the US, we must see what happens due to the anti-dumping and countervailing duty investigations. There will be new markets we have to cover if that goes south," Coglitore said.

On Nov. 15, 2023, the US Department of Commerce announced the initiation of anti-dumping investigations of frozen warmwater shrimp from Ecuador and Indonesia and countervailing duty investigations into Ecuador, India, Indonesia, and Vietnam.

US trade panel votes to keep shrimp tariff-related investigation going

The US International Trade Commission voted unanimously on Dec. 8 to allow the continuation of an investigation that could lead to tariffs being charged on frozen warmwater shrimp from India, Ecuador, Indonesia and Vietnam.  

A petition from the American Shrimp Processors Association for anti-dumping duties on shrimp imports from Ecuador and Indonesia is being pursued on a separate track.

He said there will be preliminary determinations for the anti-dumping and countervailing duty investigations in April and May, respectively. 

"So, with those preliminary rates, once they are published in the federal register, the importer has to pay cash deposits to the customs at the levels of the preliminary percentages," said Coglitore.

Ecuador’s shrimp industry ‘on edge’ as security challenges reach alarming levels

At the end of the year, there will be a determination after investigators go to Ecuador and other countries.

"Once they do the final determination, those cash deposits will be either adjusted to the new rate if it's higher, or there will be some money back if the final determination rate is lower than the preliminary," he said. "And from then on, this will be a yearly review. So, every year, there will be a continuous investigation. You have to supply the numbers, and new rates will be established based on the data, prices and information supplied."

He said the importer will have to pay the money to the US government.

When asked if this would reduce orders from Ecuador, Coglitore said he hopes not.

"We hope that the rate does have an effect and that it will be pushed through to the market and that the market absorbs the percentages."

Economic headwinds dent Ecuador shrimp exports, $1.5bn revenue hole looms large

As to what the rates could be, that's "completely unpredictable," he said.

Increased security spend

As a country suffering the rising power of drug gangs, Ecuador has a different issue to other producing nations and from the usual market worries.

"Conditions in Ecuador in terms of security and stability have been compromised. So, banking support and things are tough right now, especially for an industry struggling through 2023. It is like the perfect storm," Coglitore said.

"We've had to make lots of investment in terms of security. More workforce to fend off attacks at the farm level. At the transportation level. At the physical infrastructure. Then, you need more personal security for your human resources, workers, and everything. It's been a tough time," he said.
