title: Pacific Seafood lawsuit accuses former Texas employees of stealing 60% of Gulf Coast business
content:
Pacific Seafood Group has filed a federal lawsuit against two former employees in Texas that it has accused of using proprietary information to steal a large percentage of its Gulf of Mexico-related sales.

The lawsuit seems like just the latest escalation of an ongoing, months-long battle between the Clackamas, Oregon-based US seafood processing giant and Nello Cassarino, former CEO of the Galveston Shrimp Company, a business it mostly acquired in 2011.

In a 25-page lawsuit filed Dec. 28, 2023, in the US District Court for the Southern District of Texas, Pacific Seafood charges that Kolt DaPron and Jesus R. Estrada used confidential customer information and trade secrets in violation of provisions in their employment agreements to take sales away from Galveston Shrimp.

DaPron, an internal sales manager, and Estrada, a driver, both worked for Galveston Shrimp for 3.5 years before quitting their jobs on Dec. 4. On their way out, starting as soon as the weekend after their resignation, the lawsuit alleges, the two men "absconded with Pacific Seafood's confidential information and trade secrets, and began using the confidential information and trade secrets to operate an unregistered and competing business called Seafood Isle."

DaPron and Estrada allegedly called Galveston Seafood customers and told them they needed to update contact and payment information without disclosing that they were with a different company. Both had agreed in their employment contracts to a "one-year restriction on their ability to solicit Pacific Seafood's customers, vendors and employees," according to the complaint.

The lawsuit said the company served DaPron with a cease and desist order on Dec. 11, reminding him of the terms of his earlier agreement and demanding that he halt all contact with Pacific Seafood's clients and employees.

"Pacific Seafood has since lost six of its 25 customers to defendants, resulting in a reduction in its business by approximately 60%," the complaint says, continuing: "Prior to the defendants' misappropriation, plaintiff sold approximately 15,000 to 20,000 pounds of seafood products each month to distribution customers in the Gulf Coast region. This month, which is typically a busy season for the plaintiff, the plaintiff has sold a mere 6,300 lbs of product.

"Pacific Seafood's distribution business has completely unraveled in the Gulf Coast region because of the defendants," the complaint said.

Jumbo-sized shrimp from the Gulf of Mexico. Photograph by Elizabeth Punches on Flickr.

The lawsuit charges DaPron and Estrada with breaches of contract and fiduciary duty, misappropriation of trade secrets, and tortious interference with existing contracts and prospective business relations, as well as civil conspiracy. It doesn't spell out a specific damages amount but requests an immediate and permanent injunction.

"Money damages cannot adequately compensate Pacific Seafood, even if the defendant could respond by paying money damages," according to the lawsuit.

Cassarino seeks $1 million in earlier-filed lawsuit

Pacific Seafood's lawsuit against DaPron and Estrada is just the latest legal action involving the Oregon company in Texas, Undercurrent News found. In October 2023, Cassarino sued Pacific Seafood in a Galveston County, Texas, state court for $1 million over charges that it breached an operating agreement and its contract with him.

As described in both legal actions, Pacific Seafood acquired Galveston Shrimp in 2011 as part of an effort to expand its operations in the Gulf of Mexico region. The Galveston Shrimp website tells the story of how the company was started in 1978 as a retail operation by Rosario Cassarino, an immigrant from the Italian island of Sicily, and taken over by Nello Cassarino, his son, in 1994, who shifted its focus to wholesale.

"Over the past decade, Pacific Seafood has made the Gulf Coast an integral arm of its distribution system by investing millions of dollars into the business, hiring numerous employees in this district and training them," the Pacific Seafood complaint said.

The business specializes in the processing and sale of wild-caught US shrimp from the Gulf of Mexico, employing the brand name "Texas Wild." 

According to Cassarino's lawsuit, he continues to own 20% of Galveston Shrimp while holding firm Dulcich, the parent of Pacific Seafood, owns the other 80%.

Cassarino's lawsuit against Pacific Seafood describes how he complained to the company about its mishandling of inventory, which once resulted in a carryover of about 451,758 pounds of white shrimp worth $3m. Also, the complaint alleges that the company didn't pay its members, as required by the terms of its operating agreement, despite generating profits. 

"In 2022, GSC failed to issue a K-1 to [the] plaintiff or make any distribution to [the] plaintiff sufficient to pay all of [the] plaintiff's taxes based on company income as required by sect. 7.5 of the operating agreement," Cassarino's complaint said.  

Cassarino further alleges that he was placed on indefinite administrative leave in May 2023 pending an investigation into his business activities outside of Galveston Shrimp. However, a new employment agreement he signed in 2018 did not prohibit him from pursuing other employment. In particular, the complaint recounts how the company was concerned about Cassarino's ownership of a cold storage facility leased by Galveston Shrimp.

He also charges that Pacific Seafood seized a 2020 Hino refrigerated truck that was his property and refused to return it to him. 

Cassarino said he was notified that he was at last terminated by Pacific Seafood on July 27, 2023, after he sent the company a letter recounting how it had breached its operating agreement.

Texas Wild, a brand produced by the Galveston Shrimp Company. Image from company website.

Nello Cassarino is not named as a defendant in the Pacific Seafood complaint, but the language in the lawsuit describes DaPron and Estrada using Pacific Seafood's trade secrets "on behalf of Cassarino and Seafood Isle" and "Cassarino and Seafood Isle" using Pacific Seafoods' trade secrets to "create and to continue to operate this direct competitor."

Undercurrent could not find any articles of incorporation identifying a company called Seafood Isle in Texas.

When asked by Undercurrent to explain the reference to Cassarino in the complaint or respond to other questions surrounding the pending legal actions, a Pacific Seafood spokesperson provided little comment on Sunday (Jan. 21).

"Nello Cassarino is no longer employed by Pacific Seafood or Galveston Shrimp Company," the spokesperson said. "We cannot comment further due to ongoing litigation with Mr. Cassarino. Pacific Seafood is focused on continued investments to expand and enhance Galveston Shrimp Company to provide delicious gulf shrimp to consumers across the US for decades to come."

Chris Johnson, a partner in the League City, Texas-based law firm of Johnson & Associates, which represents Cassarino, told Undercurrent on Monday that he couldn't comment on the details of the case.

"We hope for both sides to reach an amicable solution," he said.

Undercurrent was unable to locate DaPron or Estrada for a comment, and court filings do not yet list their legal representatives.

title: No charges to be laid against OCI offshore fleet over bycatch incidents
content:
Charges were never laid against the Canadian offshore fishing giant Ocean Choice International (OCI) or its fishing vessels for catching more than their limit of Atlantic cod and American plaice during the 2022 fishing season, despite citations being recorded for such incidents.

Map showing NAFO-regulated offshore fishing areas off Canada's east coast. Republished with permission from the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization.

Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) confirmed for Undercurrent News on Thursday (Jan. 18) that while the St. John's Newfoundland and Labrador (NL)-based company was investigated for exceeding bycatch, it was determined that no further action was warranted.

OCI has been handling a steady stream of jabs on social media this week delivered by Ryan Cleary, a frequent voice of discontent on behalf of the NL inshore harvester community. Cleary, who recently resigned his role as executive director of the Seaward Enterprises Association of Newfoundland and Labrador (SEA-NL), has been blogging on the SEA-NL website and in Facebook groups about some of the details contained in the 84-page, 2022 annual report delivered by the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization (NAFO).

The report, which Cleary secured from the Canadian government with the help of an Access to Information and Privacy (ATIPA) request, identifies 11 vessels from three countries, including the Santa Christina of Portugal nd the Bordoyarnes of the Faroe Islands, that DFO identified as being cited for various infringements, including exceeding bycatch and misreporting catches, in 2022.

The report identifies four incidents involving the excessive bycatch of cod and American plaice in NL waters by Canadian vessels, three of which are owned by OCI.

Two of OCI's vessels were also each cited for "serious infringement" in fishing zone 3N for direct fishing for American Plaice, a species that is currently under moratorium.

OCI fishes for yellowtail in the offshore zone 3LNO, a prime area for groundfish trawlers regulated by NAFO.

Cleary wrongly reported that OCI was being charged in relation to the bycatch incidents but, after learning that no charges were being placed, on Thursday he called for Canadian fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier to conduct an investigation of the federal agency.

"Questions have been raised as to why the illegal fishing charges against OCI's three vessels were dropped, and DFO must explain its actions," Cleary said.

Climate changed the game

Carey Bonnell, OCI's vice president of sustainability and engagement, didn't deny the bycatch incidents involving the company's vessels took place in an interview on Wednesday (Jan. 17) with Undercurrent. But he said Cleary has been wrong about a few other things and lacked important context in his postings. 

Despite NAFO regulations allowing 15% bycatch of American plaice and 4% for cod,  for the past 6-7 years OCI's average overall bycatch of American plaice has been around 4% and the cod bycatch has been, on average, less than 1%, in the NAFO-regulated area (NRA), Bonnell noted.

The company's fishing captains focus on finding areas where they can get the best catch rates for yellowtail flounder and minimize bycatch, he said.

Carey Bonnell, vice president of sustainability and engagement for Ocean Choice International. Photo by Barb Dean-Simmons

The DFO records presented in Cleary's blog did not provide details regarding the exact amount of bycatch, but Bonnell assures the amount was minimal, not even enough to measure in metric tons.

"I just want to give you a sense of scale," he stressed. "We're talking hundreds of kilos in excess of the rules that required us to leave the  [NAFO-regulated area, or NRA]."

The handful of occurrences of infringement occurred when the company returned to the fishing area to test to see if harvest conditions for yellowtail had improved, with less bycatch, he said. When the OCI captains realized they had too much bycatch in a single tow, they "immediately followed the rules."

The conditions just didn't improve, he said, "and we left the area and basically ceased fishing that fall, at significant cost to us."

Bonnell said OCI "has developed a track record of clean fishing for yellowtail flounder in the NAFO zone." Up until September of 2022, he said, the company's performance on bycatch "had been exceptional."

So, what changed that year? Climate, answered Bonnell.

"Sea surface temperatures spiked dramatically," he said, with a nearly 3 degree Celsius increase over the previous 21-year average. "Our captains on some of our boats noted bottom temperatures in the range of about 6 degrees in September."

That's not good for yellowtail flounder fishing, he said, because those fish prefer bottom temperatures in the range of 1.5C to 4 degrees C.

Northeast Atlantic’s warming seas could harm key pelagic stocks, warns MSC

When OCI's trawlers went to their traditional fishing areas in the NRA in mid-September, they found less yellowtail than expected and ended up with a higher percentage of cod and plaice bycatch as a result.

"We had vessels that encountered elevated bycatch levels that would have exceeded the per-tow provisions," explained Bonnell.

Under the NAFO rules at that time, if a fishing vessel exceeded the bycatch limit on cod or plaice in a single tow, it had to move 10 nautical miles.

"And if you exceed it again, you have to leave the NAFO-regulated area for 60 hours," said Bonnell, noting that was the situation OCI faced with fishing trips in the fall of 2022.

"The problem is that when you hit those provisions at the beginning of a fishing trip, which is what happened to us, you are automatically in an infringement situation," he said. "It was almost impossible to avoid."

"You can't see what's on the bottom. You go to your traditional fishing grounds, where you expect to find the kind of fishing you found the previous season."

Bonnell said this is just as much a  climate change story as it is a story about fishing rules. Overall, said Bonnell, OCI is "well below the bycatch limits. But we have had those limited occurrences because of the warming climate."

NAFO cuts quotas in northwest Atlantic, sector calls for additional research

At the NAFO meetings this past fall, OCI highlighted the issue, Bonnell said. As a result, NAFO adopted new rules allowing more flexibility on per-tow bycatch while still maintaining the overall 15% limit on American plaice and 4% on cod.

Under those new NAFO measures, he noted, those per-tow occurrences OCI was cited for in 2022 would not be considered infractions today.

"So when we go out in 2024, we will have more flexibility to find those clean tows."

As for the cod and American plaice pulled back in those 2022 tows, however, DFO told Undercurrent the investigation included "fully monitored offloads of the fishing vessels' landings. ... As a result, it has been determined that no further action is warranted, and the cases have been closed."

title: FDA scallop warning draws quick response from industry groups
content:
The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is advising consumers not to eat, and restaurants and food retailers not to sell or dispose of certain whole, live scallops received from an unlicensed harvester. But harvester groups are stressing that their scallops aren't included in the warning. 

The FDA, in a statement published Friday (Jan. 12), said it was informed by the Massachusetts Department of Public Health on Jan. 5 that whole, live scallops sold by Intershell International Corp. were believed to have been harvested from a prohibited area and potentially contaminated. The scallops were incorrectly labeled as harvest location "FED 514" with harvest dates of 12/26/23, 12/27/23 and 01/01/24, according to the federal agency.

These whole, live scallops were sold to restaurants and retailers in Illinois, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York and Pennsylvania, and may have been distributed more widely, the FDA noted. The agency said it is assisting and helping to coordinate the trace-forward investigations being conducted by the states.

Meanwhile, the Fisheries Survival Fund (FSF) and the American Scallop Association say the scallops referenced in the FDA advisory are not the type typically available in markets and restaurants across North America.

"Scallops are rarely sold live or whole in North America, and they are most often harvested offshore in federal waters, not in state waters," the FSF advised in a press release. "In the United States and Canada, consumers generally purchase just the adductor muscle, the white, meaty part seen in market displays and seafood dishes.

The FDA advises that it's common for shellfish to be consumed raw and whole, but this is not true for scallops, advised the FSF, which was formed in 1998 to ensure the long-term sustainability of the Atlantic sea scallop fishery for scallop fishermen from Maine to North Carolina.

In North American cuisine, the adductor muscle is typically consumed without the roe (or coral), the group advised.

The Atlantic sea scallop "is one of the more sustainable seafood choices available, and much of the fishery has been certified as sustainable by the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC)," FSF said.

Consumers may continue to "buy and enjoy with confidence the shucked, white, meaty and sustainable scallops familiar to them in grocery cases and on restaurant menus," the group advised.

title: Norway’s 2023 salmon escapes questioned amid accuracy concerns
content:
The escape of farmed salmon from Norwegian aquaculture sites remains an ongoing challenge, with uncertainties surrounding the accuracy of reported figures, according to Norway's fisheries director Frank Bakke-Jensen. 

The lack of improvement in methodologies and routines for assessing the extent of escapes has raised concerns about the reliability of data used by both the industry and the media, he said.

"Even after dialogue with the industry, we see no improvement in methodology and routines for assessing the extent of escapes."

This means that the figures reported may not align with the actual number of escapees and are, therefore, not suitable as an environmental indicator or a measure to assess the situation. 

The precision of counting methods in major escape cases is a recurring issue, with errors linked to the number of fish in cages and the accuracy of counts.

Bakke-Jensen cited a case where a company reported approximately 185,000 fish in a cage before an incident, but post-incident counts revealed around 198,000 fish. A subsequent video review showed only 170,000 fish, highlighting a significant discrepancy.

"This means there were approximately 15,000 fewer fish than before the escape. A difference of around 28,000 fish based on the same count," he added.

Escape incidents involving rainbow trout and cod dominated the news in 2023. Reports from the public, rather than industry players, revealed these incidents, marking a shift in information sources. In 2023, 172 tips were received, compared to 114 in 2022.

Key figures from 2023 indicate 117 reported incidents, with around 18,000 escaped farmed fish distributed over 29 events. The reported escapes include 918 cod, 1,458 salmon, 15,304 rainbow trout, 400 char, and 70 seabream.

Norway's directorate of fisheries also received reports of farmed fish catches unrelated to reported incidents, prompting investigations and removal efforts in various waterways.

title: Valve failure on Canadian shrimp trawler prompts investigation
content:
Jeff Simms, the CEO of MV Osprey Ltd., a joint venture shrimp harvesting firm, asserts that his company's 260-foot trawler and its 30-person crew were never in peril off the South Labrador coast, as reported by some local media.

What concerns him the most, he told Undercurrent News, is the failure of a piece of equipment that made a recent incident much more troublesome than it should've been: an electronic shut-off valve that failed to automatically engage as expected and prevent more water from flowing into the ship.

"I'm really angered," Simms told Undercurrent News. "We will have to investigate with the classification societies to find out why this valve failed."

Transport Canada will be involved in the investigation, he said, adding he will be heading to St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador, this week to meet the ship and Transport Canada officials to start that process.

Vessel took shelter to ride out bad weather

The Northern Osprey III's recent struggles began Sunday (Jan. 7) when the crew discovered a hole in a discharge line for the fishing vessel's grey water tank, Simms recounted. In response, the Canadian Coast Guard deployed a Cormorant helicopter from the Search and Rescue base in Gander to drop off two pumps.

The Canadian Department of Fisheries and Oceans research vessel Teliost, which was in the area, was also dispatched to stand by the Northern Osprey and escort it back to St. John's.

Newfoundland and Labrador. Map from Victor Maschek / Shutterstock.

The ship did not seek shelter near Black Tickle, among the Porcupine Islands, because of the issue, contrary to press reports. The vessel's captain had earlier decided to ride out some winter weather there, and that's when the crew noticed the problem, Simms explained.

"The weather was coming down severely for 3 days, with 9 to 10 meter seas," he said.

In a situation like this, the crew usually just plugs the leak and then heads to port to make repairs, Simms said. That wasn't possible, however, in this case, because of the weather.

The captain and the company decided it would be best to "sit it out" and wait for sea conditions to improve before attempting to sail to St. John's to have the valve replaced.

Meanwhile, the crew used portable pumps to deal with the leak, said Simms, noting they chose not to use the bilge pumps because that could have caused a bigger problem with the potential of oil from the bilge water getting into the local harbor.

"We were keeping ahead of it (leak) with the portable pumps."

Also, there was no distress call, as reported by some media, Simms explained. Knowing they were going to be there for at least three days, the crew notified the coast guard.

"They felt, and we felt, it would be good to have a couple of extra portable pumps on board," he said.

After spending most of the day on Tuesday (Jan. 9) fielding phone calls from the crew's worried family members and arranging to get a dive team from St. John's, the CEO said he is determined to find out why the valve was a problem in the first place.

Divers arrived in Black Tickle on Wednesday (Jan. 10) to plug the discharge line, a process that was expected to take about 3 hours.

The faulty valve issue meant some fishing downtime for the Northern Osprey and an extra week on board the ship for the crew. The trawler was expected to set sail Wednesday evening for St. John's to have the valve replaced and then return to fishing.

"The ship was never in peril, it was never listing, it was never taking on a lot of water," Simms said. It was simply a marine incident that required some coast guard assistance.

A new piece of equipment

The Northern Osprey is a relatively new vessel, having been built in 2017 at the Tersan Shipyard in Turkey. It fishes coldwater shrimp year-round off the coast of Labrador for MV Osprey Ltd., which is a joint venture between the Labrador Fishermens Union Shrimp Company and a fishermen's cooperative in New Brunswick.

And the valve is not a big piece of equipment, Simms explained, describing it as about half the size of a 5-gallon bucket.

"It's one of those things that when you get into situations like this, you want to make sure that they work."

As a failsafe, said Simms, the crew should have been able to shut off the valve manually. But the manual shut-off did not work properly.

Coldwater shrimp. Credit: Canada's Barry Group

"You always need that safety of being able to turn that off manually, replace the valve, replace the pipe and move on," he said.

What's most concerning is that the valve that failed on the Northern Osprey was a brand-new part, said Simms.

"This ship is only five years old and only came off its latest refit in April. All these valves were all replaced new and with all classification certificates," he noted. "That's a major concern for us as an operator."

title: Belarus’ Santa Bremor switches to Turkish trout, Russian pollock
content:
Belarussian food group Santa Bremor was forced to alter its plans and strategies in 2023 after geopolitical turmoil followed Russia's invasion of Ukraine. 

With Western nations condemning Belarus' support for Russia, Santa Bremor -- which employs some 6,000 across 40 subsidiaries, many of them seafood-based -- has found itself cut off from markets and raw material supplies, CEO Alexander Moshensky told Undercurrent News.

"Our main problem today is the impossibility of expanding the number of enterprises which can supply us with raw materials for production," he said. "It means [we have a] dependence on a small circle of enterprises, existing suppliers of raw materials."

This is not only because of sanctions put in place by the West; to open a new food trade channel, Russia's Russian Federal Service for Veterinary and Phytosanitary Surveillance, or Rosselkhoznadzor, must inspect the supplying enterprises "in order to confirm the safety and quality of their products, which is currently impossible," said Moshensky. 

The strength of cooperation between Russia and Belarus has been accompanied by continuous supervision by the veterinary services of both countries, Rosselkhoznadzor has explained.

In 2022, Russian media reported that Santa Bremor's "Russian Sea" brand had disappeared from retailers' shelves because Norwegian suppliers would no longer sell to Belarus. However, the brand continues and has "maintained its market share," Moshensky told Undercurrent, and the business continues to work with other "longstanding suppliers."

Santa Bremor's website lists various trout and salmon products, including several "new" salmon items like these

"The raw material for the production of red fish products is chilled trout from Turkey. Deliveries of Norwegian salmon to Belarus have indeed been stopped today at the initiative of Norwegian manufacturers."

Likewise, the US cut off its sales of Alaska pollock to Belarus in 2022, prompting Santa Bremor to change how it produced surimi. According to public data cited by Russian publication Kommersant early this year, Russian Sea imported surimi seafood equipment from Japan's Yanagiya Machinery in October 2022.

Russian supermarkets have been selling Russian Sea surimi sticks produced in Belarus, it reported. 

"Yes, we still use pollock surimi in our production," said Moshensky. "Indeed, Russian enterprises have been actively investing in the production of pollock surimi over the past few years. There has been an almost complete replacement of American pollock surimi with Russian raw materials on the market."

Capacities in Russia continue to grow, supplying Lithuania's Viciunai Group, Russian processor Meridian, and other manufacturers, he added. Indeed, In October 2023, Russian Fishery Company signed a deal to supply around 3,000 metric tons of pollock surimi to Meridian. 

Several Russian companies -- including Gidrostroy, Okeanrybflot, Russian Fishery and Norebo Holdings -- have built and re-fitted vessels to produce fillets and surimi, but cannot obtain EU numbers and so can't export to the primary market.

"Russia remains an important sales market for Santa Bremor products; we export 58% of the total volume of manufactured products to Russia," Moshensky told Undercurrent.

"In 2020, we started modernizing the plant in Noginsk [Russia] by installing surimi production lines. However, due to the pandemic and logistics problems, the project was actually delayed for three years. No other significant investments are planned yet, because we have completely lost the markets of Ukraine, Poland and the Baltic states. We have not been able to replace these lost sales volumes so far, therefore, there is no need to expand production capacities."

Before Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Russia, Belarus, and Ukraine were Santa Bremor's key markets. It sold to 42 in total though, according to its website.

Moshensky said his group had "lost the Ukrainian market completely," with its products removed from retailers' shelves in Baltic countries and Poland too. "That led to the need to change our strategy; if earlier we strived for Santa Bremor to be a global player in the fish market, now it has become impossible due to obvious circumstances beyond our control."

He said he understood the political reasons for the seizure of Santa Bremor's assets by Ukrainian authorities, adding only that all the group's employees in Ukraine "continue to receive wages, despite the fact that the company does not conduct any economic activity."

As a result -- because of "the situation that has developed since the beginning of Russia's military operations in Ukraine in February 2022" -- Moshensky has transferred the European part of the Santa group's business to his daughter, Yana Moshenskaya.

"It is my daughter's involvement in the family business and a launching pad for the development of her competencies. Time will show how effectively Yana will be able to engage in the European direction of business and whether the right decision was made. Personally, right now, I am concentrating on projects directly related to Belarus," he explained.

As well as the Ukrainian assets -- which are now instead in the possession of Ukrainian authorities -- Moshensky has also transferred the Lithuanian trading business Santa Trade to his daughter.

The business, based in the port city of Klaipeda, trades and stores vast quantities of raw materials for the wider group, he said, with Santa Bremor producing over 100,000 metric tons of products per year.

Santa Trade often has over 10,000t of raw materials worth between €20 million and €40m in stock, he said, explaining that the logistical and positional benefits of Klaipeda made it the ideal place for such a hub. 

An extensive report by the Belarusian Investigative Center (BIC), Lithuania's LRT, and Iceland's Heimildin, published this summer, claimed Moshensky transferred Santa Trade to his daughter over fears he might be sanctioned.

It claimed he had "already taken steps to protect his business should he find himself on the sanctions list," referring to the EU's list of Belarusian businessmen sanctioned because of their close ties to president Aleksandr Lukashenko.

BIC said Santa Trade changed ownership a month and a half after the start of the war in Ukraine and is now owned not by Santa Bremor but by Newride Services of Cyprus, a company, in turn, owned by Yana Mashenskaya.

Moshensky told Undercurrent any connections between him and Lukashenko were purely official and came about due to the size of the Santa group's business. He acknowledged there had been a risk of being sanctioned by the EU but said he knew nothing about reported attempts by Icelandic politicians to shield him from any such EU action.

The BIC report also claimed Santa Trade employs only three people and has received large loans at only 2% interest rates from UK lender Max Credit Investment. Max Credit's parent company in 2016 and 2017 was Seychelles-based Alpha Mar Foundation, which was ultimately owned by Moshensky, according to BIC's investigation.

Auditor Abdulwahed Alobaly told BIC that "charging excessively high or low interest rates on intercompany loans could be an attempt to manipulate the taxable income of the companies involved, leading to tax avoidance or evasion."

In addition, sustained losses at a business also cast doubt as to whether that business was really created for economic gain, it suggested. Santa Trade has been operating with negative equity, kept afloat by loans from Max Credit, since its inception, said BIC.

However, Moshensky dismissed such claims, telling Undercurrent that from 2016 to 2022, annual audits of Santa Trade were conducted by Lithuania's Moore Mackonis, which "never had any doubts about the causes of [the firm's] losses, as well as the overall viability of the company."

Santa Bremor's 90s roots

According to official data, Moshensky controls 50% of Santa Bremor directly and another 15% through the Belarusian company Santa Servis, which he also controls, according to BIC.

The remaining 35% of Santa Bremor is held by the German company Bre Meer. From 2014 to 2018, Bre Meer was owned by the aforementioned Alpha Mar Foundation, whose beneficiary at the time was also Moshensky. Bre Meer had a change of ownership in 2018 when Alpha Mar was replaced by the Santa International Foundation, based on the British island of Jersey.

"This company is also considered an offshore," said BIC. "It does not disclose the owners of companies registered there. However, we found links between Santa International Foundation and Newride Services" -- owned, as mentioned, by Yana Moshenskaya.

Moshensky told Undercurrent his group was founded by his father, Mikhail. 

"In 1993, he created a small enterprise, Nila, which was engaged in the export of frozen fish to Europe. Soon, it was decided to expand its own business and a joint venture with the Dutch partner Lau Kok Santa Impex Brest for processing shrimp was formed."

The venture, Santa Impex Brest, developed a large international wholesale trade in fish and seafood, supplying fish from the Far East and Norway to the markets of Ukraine, Poland, the Baltic States, and the countries of the former Soviet Union.

In 1996, Mikhail Moshensky decided to begin producing herring fillets in Belarus with another buyer of such products, German company Abellman. In 1998, they built a $6m plant, using $4.5m in funds from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, he said.

After the plant began operating in 2000, the Moshensky family began buying the other shareholders out of the firm, he said.

"The creation of the fund in Jersey is not a secret. It is important for me to ensure stability and continuity in business management, to exclude the negative impact of events that may happen to me, as well as to any person, on my companies."

Such a move to safeguard companies and assets for family members is not an unusual practice, he added.

While a number of Belarusian businessmen have been sanctioned by the EU for their ties to Lukashenko, Moshensky has not. 

"I think that the explanations and arguments that I sent to the European embassies were taken into account by the representatives of European countries," he told Undercurrent. "I am glad that I managed to defend my reputation."

title: Peru’s second anchovy season at risk as reproductive peak nears
content:
Peru's ongoing second anchovy fishing season in the north-central zone has already landed over 1.2 million metric tons, comprising 72% of the total quota allocated, set at 1.6m metric tons, according to Undercurrent News sources.

Peru fishermen press gov’t for urgent closure of second anchovy fishing season

However, concerns have arisen regarding the completion of the assigned quota, primarily due to the anchovy typically reaching its reproductive peak in January -- especially in the first half of the month -- under normal conditions, reported La Republica. 

Expressing skepticism regarding the quota fulfillment, Juan Carlos Sueiro -- fisheries director with the Peruvian arm of NGO Oceana -- stated that it seems highly unlikely the quota will be achieved.

"We're already in January, and if the anchovy starts its reproductive phase, the fishing activity must cease," he said. 

Elmer Nieves, a fisheries engineer, also highlighted the significant presence of juvenile anchovy during this season, emphasizing the need for further investigation into the causes behind this abundance.

Factors include the species' survival instincts in response to abnormal weather conditions, fishing pressure and pollution, among others, warranting thorough examination by relevant authorities.

"The recommendation is to avoid catching sizes smaller than 12 centimeters, allowing environmental conditions to normalize and the resource to recover so that the industry can then resume its activities," Nieves explained.

Meanwhile, reports from onboard fishermen highlight numerous instances of juvenile entanglement, where the young anchovy gets trapped in the nets. Cleaning these nets can take up to two days, they claim.

title: SalMar denies fresh reports it knew about smuggling of salmon into China
content:
Norwegian salmon farmer SalMar has denied fresh reports that it was responsible for and knew about the illegal import of salmon to China, looking to counter claims made by newspaper NRK.

NRK has run a story on Chinese-born Norwegian citizen Yimin Dong, who is imprisoned in China, having been convicted for what NRK describes as smuggling Norwegian salmon into the country through Vietnam.

"NRK has referred to Yimin Dong as SalMar's China manager and claims that SalMar has been responsible for and knew about the illegal import of salmon to China. Both parts are wrong," SalMar said in a press release.

"Yimin Dong has never been employed by SalMar or received salary or other remuneration from the company. Until she was imprisoned, she was, for a number of years, an important customer for SalMar and other Norwegian seafood companies."

The fish she bought from SalMar was delivered and taken over by her company in Vietnam, it said; it was this company that was responsible for resale and all further handling of the goods, including ensuring that reporting to the relevant authorities was handled correctly.

"As far as SalMar knows, it has never been stated by Chinese courts or the country's authorities that SalMar should have contributed to illegalities in China."

SalMar's business relations with Yimin Dong were established in 2007 after SalMar had carried out investigations that, among other things, confirmed a "solid background with references and expertise that instilled trust."

After the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the Peace Prize to Liu Xiaobo in 2010, China introduced a series of sanctions against Norwegian businesses. A total ban on selling Norwegian salmon to China was not introduced. Nevertheless, other markets in Asia emerged as important trading partners and recipients of Norwegian salmon in the time that followed, SalMar said.

At this time, Yimin Dong conducted significant business by importing salmon to Vietnam. Her company was an important buyer and importer of Norwegian salmon, including from SalMar. According to agreements and international rules, these companies were responsible for the goods being paid for, and for further correct reporting and handling to the relevant authorities in the importing country, the Norwegian firm continued.

"Already in 2007, on the initiative of Yimin Dong, SalMar established a practice where her customers could settle directly with SalMar for fish they had bought from her companies. SalMar had confidence that Yimin Dong's companies, for its part, followed the applicable laws and regulations, and, for its own part, has naturally processed all such transactions in line with the applicable laws and regulations."

According to SalMar, NRK has pointed to documents concerning the establishment of a company by SalMar and Yimin Dong as evidence that she was the Norwegian firm's China manager. 

"These documents concern SalMar's establishment of a company together with Yimin in 2018, i.e., after the Chinese import restrictions had ended. This company never managed to become operational before Yimin was arrested."

Yimin Dong's husband, Bjorn Wikne, has expressed frustration and anger at the lack of help from SalMar to NRK.

"SalMar understands that Yimin Dong and her loved ones have found themselves in a difficult situation, and is sorry and regrets that the company was not able to establish a better communication about providing humanitarian aid to her in 2019. It was SalMar then, as now, of course, willing to, although the company, not least out of concern for Yimin herself, refused to intervene in the court case as her husband at the time wanted."

SalMar said it was pleased that dialogue has now been established to clarify whether there is anything it and Wikne can do together to remedy the situation for Yimin.

title: Fire breaks out on Cooke feed barge in Scotland
content:
On Jan. 8, a fire broke out on a feed barge operating for Cooke Aquaculture Scotland's West Fara salmon farm, reports The Orcadian. 

No injuries were reported during the incident.

The emergency response included the Longhope lifeboat and Orkney Islands Council's tug, "Freya of Scapa," attending the scene to address the situation.

A spokesperson for Cooke Aquaculture later addressed the incident, stating that the situation "was promptly brought under control, and fortunately, there were no casualties."

The company is collaborating with emergency services, and an investigation is underway to determine the cause of the fire.

title: Chilean ministers’ meeting with salmon execs sparks controversy
content:
Salmon industry leaders had an unregistered meeting with government ministers ahead of discussions around a disputed fishing law, according to an investigative article published recently.

Nicolas Grau, Chile's economy minister, and Maisa Rojas, the country's environment minister, are reported by the journalistic investigation agency Ciper to have sat down with key figures from the salmon farming industry at the home of lobbyist Pablo Zalaquett at the end of November 2023. The meeting was not officially recorded as required by Chilean laws on lobbying, Ciper said.

Both the ministers and Zalaquett declined to disclose the full list of attendees. Grau reportedly told Ciper that about eight people were present, while another participant, who requested anonymity, suggested around 10 attendees.

According to Ciper, one of the participants was Rodrigo Sarquis, a director of the seafood group Salmones Blumar. Sarquis is a cousin of Zalaquett, who is registered as a lobbyist for Blumar from meetings with various authorities during previous Chilean president Sebastian Pinera's second government.

When asked if the discussion at the dinner revolved around the new fishing law, which was presented by Chilean president Gabriel Boric on Dec. 21, Grau stated that the details of that legislation were not part of the conversation. The reformed law aims to increase transparency in the fishing sector, reduce benefits for industrial fishing, and increase quotas for artisanal fishing (see further details below).

"On Tuesday, Dec. 19, minister Rojas made public a commitment with the companies AquaChile and Cooke to carry out the first relocations of aquaculture concessions in national parks, which would leave salmon farming outside of those protected areas," Ciper wrote.

Grau was also present at the signing of that commitment, it said.

Chile halts progress of new bill threatening salmon farming in protected areas

Rojas said the dinner involved discussions of general sector-related topics, and no specific business matters or decisions of interest to any company were addressed. The journal noted that the meeting followed tensions arising from enacting the Protected Areas and Biodiversity Service Law, passed last August.

Off the record, one of the attendees mentioned that the primary focus of the meeting was the bureaucratic hurdles involved in obtaining permits from the public sector, which, in their view, hindered investment. They discussed various topics, including growth strategies and how they could assist the government in promoting economic development.

Zalaquett reportedly declined to comment on the meeting, and Sarquis did not respond to Ciper's messages. Blumar also refrained from commenting on the gathering with the ministers.

Regarding why the meeting was not registered on the lobby law platform, Grau explained, "In general, I do not register all my meals unless there is a matter of particular interest involved. However, such matters are typically addressed during working hours."

In an interview with Canal 13, Grau further explained, "We have stated as a government that the issue of having a significant portion of concessions within protected areas is a concern, and we need to explore the possibility of relocating them."

Regarding the details of the meeting, Grau admitted that he knew Zalaquett was working as a lobbyist but claimed he was unaware of the specific attendees. He expressed surprise that representatives from the fishing industry had also been present alongside salmon industry stakeholders.

Blumar declined to comment to Undercurrent News.

New Fishing law

The new fishing bill recently presented by the Chilean government and introduced in Congress for debate last week has sent shockwaves through the fishing industry, Diario Financiero reported. The bill, which consists of 213 pages and 375 articles along with transitional provisions, brings significant changes compared to the current fishing law.

It proposes reducing the duration of fishing licenses in Chile from 20 to 10 years, increasing the proportion that will be subject to auctions from 15% to 50% (meaning current incumbents would go from enjoying an 85% allocation based on "historical criteria" to just 50%), and also altering the allocation between industrial and artisanal fishermen in various fisheries across Chile.

Chilean coho salmon. Credit: Tridge

In summary, it is estimated that this would strip the industry of at least 40% of its current activity on average, with some suggesting it could be as much as 50%, according to Diario Financiero.

The industry's reaction to the project has been heated, especially among the older businesses.

Its representatives have been critical of the proposals, arguing they take away many aspects of the industry without proper compensation. The immediate loss of fishing quotas requires proper expropriation if such changes are to be made, they claim.

They also highlight the industry's significant investments in fishery sustainability in recent years.

The government has dismissed these criticisms and denies any wrongdoing in the project's development. It argued that the changes are necessary and emphasized the reduction in fishing quotas for certain companies was simply fair decision-making.

title: Escape incidents in south-west Norway spark environmental concerns
content:
SalMar-owned Norwegian processor Hardanger Seafood reported a significant incident on Dec. 29 at their Langevagen south Bomlo location, Vestland. The incident unfolded at a slaughterhouse, leading to the escape of farmed salmon weighing approximately 4-5 kg each, according to Norway's directorate of fisheries.

Over the past week, Norway's directorate of fisheries has received numerous reports of escaped farmed salmon in the surrounding area, raising concerns about potential environmental impacts, it said.

In response to the incident, Hardanger Seafood has deployed recapture nets to mitigate the situation. As of Jan. 3, they have successfully recaptured 38 of the escaped farmed fish.

Norway's directorate of fisheries said it is taking proactive measures to address the situation, including increased supervision and ongoing investigation into the incident. 

Additionally, on Jan. 4, Leroy Vest reported a recent escape incident at their Kelvesteinen site, located east of Sotra in Vestland. The incident unfolded in the midst of a de-licing operation, resulting in the escape of rainbow trout weighing approximately 2-3 kilograms each.

Leroy quickly mobilized efforts to contain the escaped fish in response to the situation. Recapture nets were deployed, and by the evening of Jan. 4, 24 farmed fish had been successfully recaptured.

The directorate of fisheries has been alerted to the incident and will closely monitor the situation through continued supervision, it added.

title: New research points to broader Bering Sea environmental shifts
content:
Warming ocean conditions in the Bering Sea from climate change have implications for a variety of marine species, including organisms that are microscopically small but have bigger implications across the ecosystem.

That's according to new research from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) published late last month (Dec. 22). It points to changes in phytoplankton booms during marine heatwaves in the Bering Sea -- particularly between 2018 and 2019 -- when sea ice was low. 

Scientists, during those years, saw more frequent open-water blooms, meaning the instances of phytoplankton that aren't coming from sea ice.

"This ecosystem is highly dependent on ice, and when ice retreats, large spring blooms provide food for zooplankton. However, when it is warm, ice melts early, and blooms in open waters (weeks after sea ice has disappeared) become more abundant," said Jens Nielsen, a biological oceanographer with the Ecosystems and Fisheries-Oceanography Coordinated Investigations Program at NOAA.

Open water blooms are less likely to send food sources to the seafloor, where bottom-dwelling species like crab live. NOAA's study notes that research has pinpointed starvation during a marine heat wave as the cause for the snow crab collapse in the Bering Sea between 2018 and 2022, however "whether increasing open water blooms increased starvation of commercially important snow crabs needs further investigation."

The research comes on the heels of the agency's Ecosystem Report Card for 2023, which noted environmental changes in fish distribution and other environmental changes, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

title: Former Zoneco CEO gets 15 years in prison for scallop scams
content:
The former chairman and CEO of Zoneco Group, one of China's largest seafood companies, has been sentenced to 15 years in prison for committing bribery and fraud during his tenure.

Wu Hougang, who led the company for over a decade until his ousting in 2020, also received a CNY 920,000 fine ($128,941), the Supreme People's Procuratorate announced on Dec. 28. 

Zoneco’s finances stabilize under state ownership

The news comes after years of controversy around Zoneco -- once China's largest listed seafood company -- centered around accusations of major accounting fraud meant to inflate profits and hide losses.

Zoneco, which farms, processes and sells seafood like scallops from Bohai Sea, first made headlines in 2018 when local media reported hundreds of millions of yuan worth of inventory for its farmed scallops had gone "missing" from seabed farming areas.

Later, Wu and others were found to have orchestrated an intricate accounting scheme over several years to falsify profits. This involved under-reporting harvesting volumes and costs to achieve paper gains, then writing down inflated asset values afterwards when regulators began asking questions.

A 2018 Zoneco earnings report claimed its scallops had "starved to death", necessitating huge writedowns. Authorities proved Zoneco vessels had been harvesting undisclosed areas outside of documented records, aided by evidence from navigation satellites.

Beyond the phantom scallops, executives also colluded on rigged contract bidding and doled out bribes to benefit the company, prosecutors said. In total, over CNY 290 million in accounting and bid-rigging occurred between 2014-2020, they concluded. 

The deceit seemed aimed partly at keeping Zoneco listed on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange. Facing likely delisting after years of true losses, the company used schemes to fabricate profits instead.

In 2020, securities regulators fined Zoneco CNY 600,000, banned Wu and three other executives for life from securities exchanges, and penalized 15 additional employees. An appeal of the October 2022 court sentencing was rejected in May 2023, finalizing prison terms for Wu and others.

Phantom die-offs

The scallop farming scandals at Zoneco engendered the moniker "running scallops" in local Chinese media. 

Zoneco faces potential ‘collapse’ of scallop fishery in Yellow Sea

Zoneco said in 2018 that starvation losses affected millions of scallops across 200,000 hectares of its seabed farming areas. Zoneco issued a writedown of CNY 722m, leading to an investigation by regulators. 

Acoura Marine, a UK-based seafood industry auditor, concluded in November 2018 that environmental factors like low rainfall and reduced plankton levels likely caused mass starvation of Zoneco's scallops, which had Marine Stewardship Council certification. Acoura predicted Zoneco's landings could significantly decline for years as a result.

However, a neighboring scallop farmer just 40 km away reported no issues during the same period. "Our scallop operations are normal," Huang Helou of Dalian Haiyangdao Fisheries told Undercurrent News that year, with ample market-size scallops still available.

The conflicting accounts fueled accusations that Zoneco fabricated both the initial scallop losses and their financial impact. Like the phantom profits from earlier periods, executives took advantage of "the difficulty in investigating underwater stocks," regulators said last week.

title: Shrimp expert sees 2024 global output dropping again due to disease, market uncertainties
content:
Global farmed shrimp production is likely to decrease again in what is expected to be a turbulent 2024, as a new disease causes some issues in China and markets globally continue to be sluggish, a sector expert told Undercurrent News.

Overall, Charoen Pokphand Foods' top shrimp executive, Robins McIntosh, is forecasting a slight decline of around 20,000 metric tons in global vannamei output in 2024 to 4.959 million metric tons, he told Undercurrent. That's after a drop of around 7% year-on-year in 2023 to around 4.97 million metric tons, according to McIntosh's numbers -- which he is always keen to reiterate are an estimate and not to be taken as gospel.

Adding black tiger volumes, McIntosh is forecasting a drop of around 107,000t to 5.379m metric tons. 

Trade insights: Ecuador shrimp export prices drop to lowest since 2011

Despite both new and old diseases, McIntosh's forecast has Chinese production of vannamei and black tiger continuing to grow, overtaking Ecuador's output, which he estimates could drop some 200,000t.

"I don't think that the trend line is going to change because the Chinese market is too strong, and the production is too strong now," he said. "I think China will overtake Ecuador again in 2024 and become the world's largest shrimp-producing country."

"It's going to be a very interesting 2024. We've got a convergence of diseases, with some new ones emerging," said McIntosh, who has worked in shrimp farming globally for Thai agribusiness giant CP and other companies.

In particular, translucent post-larvae disease (TPD), which stems from Vibrio parahaemolyticus, is a cause for concern globally, having started in China. TPD "becomes lethal to post-larvae (PL) shrimp via acquiring novel virulence factors," according to a Chinese study published on Oct. 31, 2023, in the Microbiology Spectrum journal.

China shrimp market shows positive signs at close of 2023

According to McIntosh, the vibrio has already been detected in Vietnam.

"It is more lethal than EMS [early mortality syndrome, now known as acute hepatopancreatic necrosis disease, or AHPND] was, and it's two new toxin genes," he said. "So, if this gets out into the rest of the world, that could be the next knockdown."

Then, you have a market situation where there is an oversupply, "with nobody making any money," McIntosh told Undercurrent.

"I don’t think the markets are going to rebound quickly, there's too much shrimp. Coldstores are still full, and the spigot has not been turned off. Ecuador is still increasing its production even though the increases have declined in the last four or five months," he said.

Then, the lower prices haven't been passed on to consumers in North America. "Retailers [in North America] say their costs are up. So, demand is not going to be stimulated fast. Pocketbooks are tight, and shrimp is a premium meat; it will never be chicken. Shrimp is directly in competition with beef."

Indian vannamei prices end 2023 at now familiar low

On top of all this, you have the possibility the US will hit its top four shrimp suppliers, India, Ecuador, Indonesia, and Vietnam, with duties. "It's going to be a very interesting year for shrimp, that's for sure," McIntosh said.

'Winners' have a domestic outlet

As for the winners and losers in 2024, countries with a protected domestic market, such as China and Brazil, have the best dynamics for growing production.

"Countries with domestic markets can increase, as they are not so affected by market price, which is the big force driving production down. Brazil will continue to increase. China will continue to increase because they've both got a lot of leeway in terms of domestic market," said McIntosh. "Although Malaysia's had a little bit of a hard time, but they've got the Singapore market. It's not as big as the other markets, but it's an advantage."

If you're tied into exports, as are Ecuador, India, Vietnam and Indonesia, it really comes down to market pricing, he said. "It's really messed up now in these export markets; I wish I were Chinese or Brazilian with a domestic market."

Prices for Indonesian vannamei shrimp continue down in East Java, West Nusa Tenggara

In fact, McIntosh forecasts China will grow vannamei production by around 10% to 1.050m metric tons in 2023, with around 150,000-160,000t of black tiger on top.

For 2024, his 'guesstimate' is that Chinese vannamei production will grow to around 1.200m metric tons and black tiger to roughly 200,000t, so 1.4m metric tons.

As for Ecuadorian production, McIntosh sees an 8% y-o-y increase in 2023 to 1.405m metric tons. However, he anticipates a steep drop in 2024 back to 1.200m metric tons.

"I even think that there could be a steeper drop than that, but that's conservative," he said.

The growth in China is being driven by the strong market for live shrimp, which can only be serviced by domestic production, then new raceway production systems being installed at a rapid rate in several provinces, he said.

US sees fourth straight month of y-o-y shrimp import volume improvement

Even though TPD and enterocytozoon hepatopenaei, or EHP, are causing issues for Chinese farmers, the production outlook is buoyant.

"In China, they've configured their ponds differently now. They call them small raceway greenhouses. They're individual 250–300-meter square raceways in a singular greenhouse that they run as a zero exchange," he said.

"If they get a clean PL, they can have a successful crop. They tell me that there may be as many as 400,000 of those right now. If you get 2t per raceway per year, that's 800,000t [of production] right there."

Chinese farmers are reconfiguring old ponds with the raceways, which are just used for vannamei, he said. "It's relatively quick, they say they're doing some 100,000 new raceways a year. So, that could be 200,000t of additional [vannamei] production each year."

Guangdong is the state where McIntosh said he's seen the most raceways, but it's also happening elsewhere.

Prices for Thai 60-, 70-count vannamei rise as 80s flatten

"This new culture seems to be catching on and really is the new culture that's producing the increases," said the CP executive.

Raceway systems are only used to produce vannamei, he said. "Raceways are looking for more density and fast-growing white shrimp. They seem to be able to protect the crop better than the other ponds, where they will go to monodon [black tiger] if they have disease problems."

As for Ecuador, McIntosh said there are reports of higher levels of vibrio than before, which are causing some issues.

"I think that you are starting to see some deterioration in the Ecuadorian environment. It's not catastrophic, but an issue nonetheless in a trend line that is going in the wrong direction. Then you've got the low world market. So, it would be fair to say that Ecuadorian farmers are not too happy today."

For processors, energy, labor and processing costs are higher. "I think the majority of Ecuadorian shrimp farm corporations are breaking even at best. So, it can't remain that way for them either. And that will incentivize them to start lowering their production," he said.

Global Shrimp Council launched with 20 founding companies

Then, Ecuadorian companies have much-documented issues with the reported rise in organized crime in the country, "which cost the farms money," he said.

Even China live sales impacted by imports

Ecuador's production boom has been driven by sales of head-on shrimp to China, which will exceed 1m metric tons in 2023.

Although this doesn't directly compete in the fast-growing live market where Chinese farmers sell, there's an increasing connectivity on price, McIntosh said.

"It's a different market to the imported frozen shrimp. But even they [domestic Chinese farmers] are complaining that the low prices in the world are compressing their prices. So, the cheap Ecuadorian price is pushing their prices down, and many of the farmers are not happy about that," he said.

"With China and Ecuador, we have got a head-on clash right there. Chinese production is increasing, and Ecuador is going to try to force more products in. Which will probably drop the price, which is not going to make a lot of Chinese happy," McIntosh said.

US trade panel votes to keep shrimp tariff-related investigation going

The fact China is importing around 1m metric tons on top of its estimated production of vannamei and black tiger means the growth potential for domestic farmers is massive.

"They have 900,000-1m [metric ton] expansion potential. So, the market is unlimited for the local farmers," McIntosh said.

The rising Chinese production is then being used by its importers "to beat down the prices for the Ecuadorian shrimp," he said.

Even with this situation, Ecuador's head-on-focused shrimp sector needs China, McIntosh said. "Europe is not going to blast off, and the US is becoming more difficult, so where do these big producing countries go?" 

Indian output set to return to growth in 2024

For India, McIntosh forecasted total Indian production will be around 810,000t in 2024, up from 790,000t.

He is also forecasting a 10,000t increase in vannamei for 2024 to 750,000t, but a 20,000t hike in black tiger. However, vannamei production alone was 850,000t in 2022.

Ecuadorian farmer, French supermarket partner on ‘responsible’ shrimp tails

"With India, the US duties are going to play out in ways that are hard to anticipate now," he said. "I am convinced that Ecuador will reduce production. India, I think, would like to increase production, but I don't see that happening quite yet. They still have their problems, but I also see a lot of successful ponds in India too. There are actually some very good farms going on."

For Indonesia, McIntosh forecasted a vannamei output of 320,000t and black tiger output of 75,000t in 2024, the same level as 2023 and 2022. "Indonesia will react to the market. They're on the duty list too, but I think that they're in a better position in the US than Ecuador, so I don't think they'll drop anymore. They may increase a little bit, not spectacularly, but a little bit."

Then, McIntosh has Vietnamese vannamei production diving 39% y-o-y to 430,000t in 2023, to then decline further to 400,000t in 2024. He expects Vietnam's black tiger output to increase from 125,000t in 2023 to 150,000t in 2024, however.  

"Vietnam has a hard, hard road ahead. I don't think they are competitive. They're also on the duty list in the US. Then, they've been hit with some of this transparent post-larval disease [TPD, which was first detected in China] as well," he said. "Then, they also have EHP."

As Vietnam is struggling with higher costs, has issues with TPD and EHP and is also facing US duties, "they may have the hardest time of the big four," he said.

US duties in focus

The US market could possibly become more challenging for India, Ecuador, Indonesia and Vietnam in 2024, McIntosh said.

On Dec. 8, the US International Trade Commission voted unanimously to allow the continuation of an investigation that could lead to tariffs being charged on frozen warmwater shrimp from India, Ecuador, Indonesia and Vietnam.

A final decision regarding possible tariffs is not expected from the federal government until the Fall or Winter of 2024, sources previously told Undercurrent. However, a crucial event could cause importers significant pain as soon as March 25, 2024.

US trade panel votes to keep shrimp tariff-related investigation going

That's the date upon which the US Department of Commerce (DOC) is scheduled to make a preliminary determination as to whether the shrimp industries in the four countries are receiving countervailing subsidies and thus can be forced to deposit funds equivalent to amounts intended to negate those subsidies. 

How much importers might have to set aside should the DOC decide, in March, to continue its countervailing duty investigation will depend on the level of subsidization determined, if any.

Being pursued on a separate track is a petition from the American Shrimp Processors Association for antidumping duties on shrimp imports from Ecuador and Indonesia. The group said it expects preliminary findings on that matter by May 2024.

"The politics of the whole thing are foolish. When they did this before, it was all about protecting the US wild shrimp industry, but all it did was increase the prices to the consumer," said Mcintosh.

"The US industry continued to collapse, and the imports continued to increase. It had absolutely zero effect as to the intention of it. This will be the same. It won't slow down imports. It'll just hurt the consumer because somebody's got to pay for it."

title: Kraft Industries fined CAD 1m for polluting Canadian river
content:
It is the largest environmental fine in the history of the province of Manitoba, Canada.

The Provincial Court of Manitoba ordered Canadian Kraft Paper Industries on Dec. 15 to pay CAD 1 million ($760,000) after the company pled guilty to violating the Federal Fisheries Act.

The charge stemmed from a pipe leak at the company's pulp and paper mill in The Pas, Manitoba, in February 2019.

The leak resulted in the release of 23,000 liters of black liquor, a by-product of the manufacturing process, into the mill's effluent treatment system.

Enforcement officers from Canada's Environment and Climate Change Department responded and collected samples. Through a subsequent investigation, they determined that over the course of six days, close to 181 million liters of acutely lethal effluent had been released from the treatment system into the Saskatchewan River.

That was a contravention of the Fisheries Act.

The Saskatchewan River contains many fish species, including lake sturgeon, which are listed as endangered.

In addition to the fine, Kraft Paper was also ordered to conduct an independent environmental audit within 12 months of sentencing to review its operations and make recommendations regarding the implementation of the best available technology and best practices to prevent a recurrence. A report identifying the recommendations and actions the company will take to address them will be provided to Environment and Climate Change Canada.

As a result of this conviction, the company's name will be added to Canada's environmental offenders registry, which contains information on corporations convicted of offenses under certain environmental laws.

The CAD 1m fine will be directed to a national environmental damages fund and used to support projects that have a positive impact on the environment.

title: Founders of Iceland’s Samherji set up new company in Eyjafjordur region
content:
Samherji CEO Thorsteinn Mar Baldvinsson and managing director of ship operations Kristjan Vihelmsson have unveiled Drift EA, a new venture aimed at fostering entrepreneurship and innovation within Iceland's Eyjafjordur region, near Akureyri.

Criminal cases against Samherji dropped after Icelandic tax settlement

The duo said in a statement that the new company will provide "extensive support and facilities to empower local and international entrepreneurs and businesses in developing their concepts."

"This year signifies the 40th anniversary of the acquisition of Samherji and the transformation of the vessel 'Gudsteinn GK' into the freezer trawler 'Aklureyrin EA.' Since then, Samherji has had most of its operations at Eyjafjordur, in the north of Iceland," they added.

The scope of Drift's activities -- expected to commence in the first half of 2024 -- spans domains across food production, health and medical products, biotechnology, software for the fishing industry, and "green solutions".

"Drift EA was founded to commemorate this milestone and as a gesture of appreciation to the residents and businesses within Samherji's operational area."

Samherji's reputation has taken a hit in recent years following the release of the Fishrot Files in 2019 -- a set of more than 30,000 e-mails, internal reports, spreadsheets, presentations and photos from former Samherji employee Johannes Stefansson that alleged the company had paid millions of dollars in bribes to certain Namibian cabinet ministers and businessmen in return for fishing access. 

Baldvinsson had stepped down from the helm of the company in the weeks following the files' release, but returned as sole CEO in February 2021.

Anti-corruption groups, including the UK's Institute for Public Policy Research and Transparency International, have publicly condemned Icelandic authorities and Samherji for a lack of action in the years since the file's release, with no formal charges to date brought against any Icelandic suspects.

A related criminal case covering Icelandic taxes for the period that Samherji was operational in Namibia, 2012-2018, was dropped earlier this year after the company reached a settlement with the Revenue and Customs Office in Iceland.

Nevertheless, the value of transactions flagged by Namibia's Financial Intelligence Centre as suspicious in relation to the Fishrot scheme is reportedly around $650 million, making it the largest corruption scandal in the history of either Namibia or Iceland. The trial of Namibian public officials and businessmen connected to the scandal -- the so-called 'Fishrot Six' -- is currently ongoing in Namibia.

title: US strikes EU trade deal setting 15% tariff rate
content:
The US has agreed to a trade deal with the European Union that will place a 15% tariff rate on all EU goods, including seafood.

The agreement is preliminary and its details have not yet been announced, but US president Donald Trump and European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said it had been finalized after a final round of negotiations on Sunday (July 27) in Turnberry, Scotland.

"We made it," Trump said in a joint press appearance.

The deal sets the US tariff rate on EU higher than the 10% requested by the EU negotiating team, but lower than the 20% rate EU members France, Germany and Spain had warned could trigger harsh countermeasures, including the use of its Anti-Coercion Instrument, as reported by Undercurrent News.

Under the terms of the deal, the EU will invest in the US energy sector and buy $600 million worth of US military equipment, Reuters reported.

A EU-US deal has reportedly been close for months, but on July 12, Trump unsettled negotiations when he sent a letter threatening a 30% tariff on EU goods if the bloc did not come to an agreement by Aug. 1, Undercurrent reported.

The US has been charging a 10% tariff on EU exports since April; the new 15% tariff would include those existing duties, so Brussels views a deal on those terms as cementing the status quo. 

The US imported 360,474 metric tons of seafood from the EU, worth $1.4 billion in 2024.

As you can see below from the Undercurrent trade portal, the top five US imports from the EU by harmonized system codes are fresh salmon fillets, smoked salmon fillets, frozen salmon fillets, fresh or chilled seabass fillets and frozen octopus.

title: More than half of harassment incidents of US fisheries observers not reported, researchers say
content:
Between 22 and 38% of US federal fisheries observers experienced some form of harassment while on board the vessels, according to new research published on Jan. 28 in Marine Affairs and Policy.

Furthermore, official statistics are likely an undercount due to only 45% of victims reporting incidents of intimidation, assault and coercion, researchers said.

"This is an incredibly important study that provides positive proof that official statements don't capture the whole picture of harassment rates -- it presents a new method for better accounting for non-disclosure," NOAA Fisheries acting administrator Emily Menashes said in a statement. "The work of this team is a critical step to help us focus our continuing efforts to end these types of behavior and provide a safer working environment for fisheries observers."

Scientists at the Pacific States Marine Fisheries Commission and Alaska Fisheries Science Center, and special agents at the Alaska Office of Law Enforcement, undertook the study between 2016 and 2022.

NGO raises alarm over fishery observer safety after trio of Portuguese cases

In some US fisheries, on-board observers are required to serve onboard harvest vessels for extended periods to collect essential fisheries data and report potential fishing regulation violations they witness.  

Rates of harassment were much higher for women (24-60%) than men (12-24%).

In 2023, NOAA released its Notice on Preventing Observer Harassment. The agency said it makes clear to vessel owners and operators carrying fishery observers that mistreatment is illegal and subject to prosecution.
