title: Pacific Seafood shorted US shrimpers out of millions, lawsuit alleges
content:
Pacific Seafood Group is again being accused of underpaying fishermen, this time allegedly shorting US Gulf of Mexico shrimp harvesters millions of dollars by paying them based on fraudulently created false weight and quality catch records.

The sensational charges are included in a 16-page lawsuit filed Monday (Sept. 23) in an Oregon state court by former finance director Justin Ottman against Dulcich Inc., the parent company of the Clackamas, Oregon-based seafood processing giant.

Ottman is seeking almost $2.3m for wrongful termination, violating the Oregon Family Leave Act and whistleblower retaliation.    

The complaint recounts how the former employee appeared to be favored and on the fast track, receiving multiple promotions after he was hired by Pacific in September 2018 to serve as a business development specialist. He was promoted to business development manager in 2020 and then director of finance in November 2022, answering directly to the interim chief financial officer (CFO), according to the court document.

He was told, according to the complaint, that he was "being mentored and prepared to assume the position as a financial leader at the company, with the ultimate goal being the position of [CFO]."

Dungy crab harvesters accuse wider ring of Northwest US processors of price fixing in amended suit

But that's before things went sideways for Ottman in April 2023, when he was dispatched to Galveston, Texas, "for the purpose of examining one of the brands owned and operated by Pacific Seafood, Galveston Shrimp Company," according to the complaint. 

"Mr. Ottman was sent to investigate potential concerns about self-dealing at Pacific Seafoods' Galveston Shrimp Company, [a business purchased by Pacific roughly 10 years earlier.] While Mr. Ottman found some evidence relevant to those concerns, he uncovered a much larger and more serious problem," the complaint says.

What he allegedly discovered was a "long-running scheme to intentionally misrepresent the weight and grade of catches brought in by shrimp boats, resulting in lower pay to the small businesses that operated them, and fraudulent profits for Pacific Seafood." 

Pacific's operation at the Galveston Shrimp Company performed the weighing and grading of shrimp necessary to determine a fair payment to be made to the boats at various docks around the Gulf of Mexico for their catches. But the former finance director charges that he caught the company instead using "a manipulated 'packout sheet'" to falsely represent to the harvesters smaller weights and lesser grades for their shrimp.

Shrimp boats on the Dickinson Bayou in Galveston, Texas. Photograph by Gallimaufry on Shutterstock.

"Pacific Seafood even maintained two separate accounting systems for each catch it bought: one with lower weights and grades in the packout sheet that was presented to the boat, and another reflecting what Pacific Seafood had actually received, as documented by the grading machine which reflected what was taken into Pacific Seafood's inventory," the complaint reads.

Ottman estimated that the "ill-gotten gains" totaled between $10m and $20m.

The former finance director prepared a more than 170-page report on his findings at the company's subsidiary, and presented it to Pacific Seafood senior executives, including CEO Frank Dulcich, according to the complaint. However, "instead of taking prompt action, Pacific Seafood senior leadership ignored and minimized the problem," it alleges. 

Ottman "persisted in raising the issue" regarding the fraud and then, in the weeks following, he "began experiencing severe retaliation," according to the lawsuit. He was allegedly demoted with the pretext that he "engaged in micro-management." He was then stripped of his desk and forced to work remotely from home, according to the complaint.

Pacific denied him protected leave from work related to the birth of his child, telling him he was needed as the company was performing due diligence for the acquisition of another firm, the lawsuit charges. Then, shortly after, he was told via a call on Teams, an online media, that his position was "eliminated."

His five-year stint with Pacific ended on Dec. 1, 2023.

Per the filing, Ottman suffered and continues to suffer economic damages of at least $1.75m and will continue to suffer emotional damages worth at least $500k. He's demanding a trial by jury.

Pacific issued a short response to Undercurrent's request for comment on Tuesday.

"Mr. Ottman is a disgruntled former employee who is taking his frustrations out using the legal system instead of accepting that his position was eliminated because it was not adding value to the company. His frivolous lawsuit appears intended to disparage Pacific Seafood. We are proud of our commitment to, and strong relationships with, the fleet in Galveston, Texas," the company said in an emailed statement.

Other lawsuits

The concerns about the Galveston Shrimp Company that Pacific allegedly asked Ottman to investigate no doubt relate to another series of lawsuits in Texas.

Nello Cassarino, the former CEO of GSC, sued Pacific for millions in a state court in October 2023 for allegedly breaching his contract at the business, which was owned by his family until it was sold to Pacific in 2011, as reported by Undercurrent.

Temporary restraining orders block former Pacific Seafood employees from soliciting four Texas restaurants

Pacific then sued two former GSC employees in a Texas federal court in December 2023 to stop them from allegedly stealing proprietary client information. The men, who were allegedly working for Cassarino at an unregistered Texas seafood company, were accused of causing Pacific to lose six of its 25 shrimp-buying customers, resulting in a reduction in business at GSC of 60%.

Pacific is battling other lawsuits related to the way it pays harvesters, too. 

As previously reported by Undercurrent, the company was hit with a lawsuit filed on behalf of a commercial Dungeness crab harvester in a federal court in Northern California that charged it with price fixing "monopsonization, coercion, dumping, and secret deals."

A federal judge ended up dismissing that lawsuit. However, the harvester amended and reissued the complaint this past August, alleging a "price-fixing cartel" orchestrated by Pacific, as reported by Undercurrent.

title: US judge dismisses Dungy crab price-fixing lawsuit against Pacific Seafood
content:
A federal judge has dismissed a civil lawsuit brought against Pacific Seafood Group, charging that the company used its dominant position to force other direct purchasers to fix the prices they paid to harvesters for Dungeness crabs.

Magistrate judge Alex G. Tse, in the US District Court for the Northern District of California, in San Francisco, on Tuesday (May 21) approved the requested motion for dismissal made in July 2023 by the big US West Coast processor, headquartered in Clackamas, Oregon.   

The suit was filed in March 2023 by law firm Gross Klein on behalf of commercial fisherman Brand Little, who accused Pacific of price-fixing via "monopsonization, coercion, dumping, and secret deals." Little had alleged that Pacific Seafood punished direct purchasers who didn't follow its pricing decisions or started buying from crabbers before the company. 

In his 10-page decision, Tse said he had a hard time being convinced by the harvester's arguments.

Little "alleges that all, or substantially all, direct purchasers of fresh crab on the West Coast are part of a price-fixing conspiracy," Tse wrote. "There are hundreds of these direct purchasers ... and Little must plausibly allege that Pacific Seafood coerced substantially all of them into the alleged conspiracy. He hasn't done so. He pleads only a couple of instances of coercion, impacting direct purchasers in only some geographic areas along the West Coast. From these occurrences, it's a big jump to conclude that hundreds of direct purchasers up and down the West Coast were coerced into joining a price-fixing conspiracy."

Little had alleged that Pacific Seafood retaliated against direct purchasers who didn't follow its pricing decisions by failing to "pick up the phone" when they wanted to sell crabs to Pacific Seafood for processing and denying them access to other fish products that Pacific Seafood controls.

"Antitrust discovery 'can be expensive,' and 'a district court must retain the power to insist upon some specificity in pleading before allowing a potentially massive factual controversy to proceed," said Tse, quoting another decision (Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 2007). "He needs to offer more detail before the court will allow him to proceed with a claim that could involve hundreds of non-parties in discovery." 

The judge also agreed with Pacific Seafood, saying that it was "doubtful" that Little had the standing necessary to pursue a monopsony claim because he sold to direct purchasers, who then would resell the crab to retailers and restaurants.  

The harvester has until August 20 to file an amended complaint, the judge said.

title: Indian Navy rescues Iranian fishing crew from pirates off Somalia coast
content:
The Indian Navy successfully rescued a crew of 23 on an Iranian fishing vessel hijacked off the coast of Somalia late last week, Reuters reports.

The Al-Kambar 786 was taken over by nine armed pirates while it was sailing southwest of the Yemeni island of Socotra in the Arabian Sea, on Thursday (March 28), according to the news service. The Indian Navy's INS Sumedha and INS Trishul intercepted the vessel and used tactical measures to force a surrender after more than 12 hours of intense coercion.

The fishing vessel's crew members, who were all from Pakistan, were unharmed and received medical checks before being allowed to resume their fishing activities, according to the news service. The pirates are now being brought to India to face charges.

The Indian Navy has been responding to the manifestation of the Israel-Hamas conflict in the maritime domain, especially in the Red Sea corridor -- one of the world's busiest cargo and oil transit points -- since December 2023. It reports to have carried out 18 rescue operations in the Arabian Sea since mid-December under its Operation Sankalp, launched after attacks on merchant ships in the Gulf of Oman in June 2019.

A map of Somalia. Image from Shutterstock.

title: US scallop sector fumes over Hokkaido purchase for military bases
content:
Rahm Emanuel, the US ambassador to Japan, may have pleased harvesters in Hokkaido this week when he announced that the US would be purchasing their scallops to serve American soldiers, but the US scallop industry is hopping mad.

"The US scallop industry is none too pleased with the US government buying Japanese scallops to feed US troops," Andrew Minkiewicz, a Washington, D.C.-based attorney with Kelley Drye & Warren, told Undercurrent News Tuesday (Oct. 31).

Andrew Minkiewicz. Photography from Kelly Drye website.

"The US government has never, to my knowledge, purchased domestic scallops. Our domestic prices are down, and we could certainly use the help of the US government in creating more purchasing power for US scallops. But all we get from this administration is, 'Would you like a windmill with that?'"

Minkiewicz, who has represented various companies in the US scallop sector for 17 years, was referring to the recent proliferation of windfarms, which harvesters of scallops and other species oppose for multiple reasons, including navigating difficulties, the loss of key fishing grounds and unknown biological effects.

Sources said an effort is underway in New Bedford, Massachusetts, the most common landing spot for US scallops, to communicate the industry's concerns to the president Joe Biden administration and Congress.

US to respond to China’s ban by buying Japanese scallops for military

John Murray, president and CEO of M&B Sea Products, a scallop harvester, buyer and processor based in New Bedford, said he was likewise surprised by Emanuel's announcement. 

"You would think that they would buy domestic sea scallops to supply to the commissaries," he said. "There's no reason for them to buy foreign product when there's plenty of it available domestically."

Eric Hansen, president of the Fisheries Survival Fund, a New Bedford-based group representing scallopers, feels the same way. He owns two scallop vessels and said harvesters are suffering, adding that the cost of scallop permits is "sky high."

Largest Canadian, US scallop sellers see increased interest from China after ban on Japan

Also, he noted, the administration appears to be helping one of the sources of trouble for US scallopers.

"I believe these Japanese scallops that aren't being sold to China are coming to our market and depressing our prices," Hansen said. "So, it's a little disconcerting that our government is helping the Japanese fishing industry, which is actually hurting us."

US landing prices down 9% from six weeks ago

Undercurrent has been tracking US scallop landings since the beginning of the 2023-2024 season, on April 1, and repeatedly finding prices down.

As much as $446,067 was paid for the 31,361 pounds of scallops that were landed at the New Bedford seafood auction on Tuesday (Oct. 31), an average rate of $14.22/lb. More than half of the scallops -- 17,261 lbs -- were of the most common size, 10-20s, and sold for $246,423, an average of $14.28/lb.

That's down 9% from the $15.73/lb price for 10/20s seen in week 37 of 2023 (Sept. 11-17), roughly six weeks ago, based on Undercurrent's pricing portal.

Upgrade to Pro to view

The low price is in spite of a dearth of domestic scallops. 

Based on the fishing rules contained in Framework Adjustment 36, as proposed by the New England Fishery Management Council in December and finalized by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) on April 3, harvesters were initially projected to land a combined 25.0 million lbs worth $398m during the 2023-2024 season, which ends March 31, 2024.

As much as 21.6m lbs of that amount is projected to be brought in by the big vessels in the US' limited access fleet, based on NOAA's running landings counts. That would be a 19% decrease in volume from the 26.6m lbs that was actually caught by the limited access fleet during the 2022 season, which was 11% below the original projection of 29.8m lbs.

As of Oct. 26, the limited access fleet had harvested 18.8m lbs of scallops, 87% of their annual projected landings, with five more months to go in the season. By contrast, as of the end of October 2022, the limited access fleet had landed 21.6m lbs.

More Hokkaido purchases coming

Minkiewicz, like others, has a lot of questions about the administration's Japanese scallop purchase. He wants to know how much was paid, which federal agency made the purchase and whether there was any kind of bidding competition. 

A spokesperson at the Defense Commissary Agency (DCA), the group that appears to be engineering the purchase, told Undercurrent that he was working to get answers but advised that it might take several days. 

US ambassador signals support for Japan in Fukushima conflict with China

Emanuel broke the news to Reuters on Monday (Oct. 30) about how the US was buying just under a metric ton of Hokkaido scallops (Mizuhopecten yessoensis) from Japanese companies. He said the purchase was part of a larger contract and more Japanese seafood would be acquired as part of an effort to help that country deal with a ban placed against it by the Chinese government on Aug. 30.

Eventually all types of Japanese fish will be sold in the commissaries at all 17 US installations in Japan, at farmers markets on some US bases, and served on U.S. Navy ships, Emanuel reportedly said.

The Chinese ban was a response to Japan discharging wastewater from the Fukushima nuclear plant days earlier. The plant was damaged after it was hit by a tsunami in 2011 and is reported to have accumulated more than 1m metric tons of wastewater, though scientists from Japan and the United Nations have vouched for the safety of the release.

Stars & Stripes, a newspaper read on military bases, covered the ceremony surrounding the delivery of the scallops on Tuesday to a commissary where military families shop for groceries at the US airlift hub in Western Tokyo (Oct. 31). It suggested the scallops would be made available for soldiers and their families for purchase at commissaries.

Emanuel participated in a ribbon cutting and posed for pictures with Marine Corps brigadier general George Rowell, deputy commander of US Forces Japan and several Japanese government officials as well as representatives of the Hokkaido Federation of Fisheries Cooperative Associations at the press event, based on the Stars & Stripes coverage. He made assurances that the country's seafood is safe to eat.

"I've served the products to my own children; I continue to eat the products from the Fukushima area," he reportedly said. "I've served the fish products to some of the highest elected officials in the United States government and armed forces, and we will continue to stand with our friends in Japan."

Credit: gontabunta/Shutterstock.com

China was the Japanese seafood industry's top import market, buying JPY 84.4 billion ($571m) worth of seafood in 2022, though China's imports of seafood from Japan dropped to zero in September, according to the General Administration of Customs China.

Japan exported more than 100,000t of scallops to mainland China last year, so the most recent purchase represented less than 1% of the potential loss. But the ambassador, who was appointed by Biden in August 2021, assured that much larger seafood buys are coming.

"It's going to be a long-term contract between the US armed forces and the fisheries and co-ops here in Japan," he said, continuing: "The best way we have proven in all the instances to kind of wear out China's economic coercion is come to the aid and assistance of the targeted country or industry."

The US military had not previously bought seafood from Japan, he confirmed.

title: US to respond to China’s ban by buying Japanese scallops for military
content:
A member of the president Joe Biden administration has declared the US government's intention to buy Japanese scallops to supply its military in the region as a response to China's ban on its products,  Reuters reports.

And he promises is is just the beginning.

Rahm Emanuel, the US ambassador to Japan, unveiled the initiative in an interview with the news service on Monday and said Washington was looking more broadly into how it could help offset China's ban, which he described as being part of its "economic wars."

China announced its ban on Japanese seafood on Aug. 30, the day Japan began discharging from its Fukushima nuclear plant, which is reported to have accumulated more than a million metric tons of wastewater after it was hit by a tsunami in 2011. This despite scientists from Japan and the United Nations vouching for the safety of the water release.

The G7 trade ministers on Sunday (Oct. 29) called for the immediate repeal of the ban on Japanese food.

The ban is going to be painful. Japan's ministry of agriculture and fisheries said China was the world's top importer of the country's seafood. Last year, China imported 84.4 billion yen ($571m) of seafood from its neighbor, according to the news service.

China's imports of seafood from Japan dropped to zero in September, according to the General Administration of Customs China, as reported earlier by Undercurrent.

SCALLOPS JUST THE BEGINNING

The first purchase of seafood by the US under the scheme announced by Emanuel involves just shy of a metric ton of scallops, a tiny fraction of the more than 100,000t of scallops that Japan exported to mainland China last year.

But the ambassador, appointed by Biden in August 2021, suggested much larger purchases of seafood are coming.

"It's going to be a long-term contract between the US armed forces and the fisheries and co-ops here in Japan," he said, continuing: "The best way we have proven in all the instances to kind of wear out China's economic coercion is come to the aid and assistance of the targeted country or industry."

The US military had not previously bought seafood from Japan, he said.

Asked about Emanuel's comments at a press conference on Monday, China's foreign ministry spokesperson Wang Wenbin reportedly said: "The responsibility of diplomats is to promote friendship between countries rather than smearing other countries and stirring up trouble".

More Japanese scallops likely headed to US, too

A lot of Japanese scallops (Mizuhopecten yessoensis) also could find their way to the US, thanks to the combination of the Chinese ban and another significant reduction in domestic Atlantic scallop landings, Peter Handy,  the CEO and president, and Irene Ketelaar-Moon, the vice president of sales and marketing, for Bristol Seafood, recently predicted.

Undercurrent has been reporting since before the US Atlantic scallop (Placopecten magellanicus) season started on April 1 that landings would be reduced again significantly due to the changes contained in Framework Adjustment 36, as suggested by the New England Fishery Management Council and implemented by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Conditions ripe for big jump in US import of Japanese scallops

Based on the new trip limits, harvesters were expected to land about 25.0 million pounds of scallops during the 2023-2024 season. That included 21.6m lbs landed by the US limited access fleet, a 19% increase from the 26.6m lbs that was landed by the big vessels during the 2022-2023 season, which was 11% below the original projection.

"There is a refuge in Japanese scallops – mainly 10-20 and 20-30 sizes – where unprecedented value exists fueled by a strong dollar (a bright spot of higher interest rates) and China's embargo on Japanese seafood products," Handy and Ketelaar-Moon said in a recent report for Portland, Maine-based Bristol.

Meanwhile, Clearwater Seafoods and Eastern Fisheries, the largest scallop players in Canada and the US, respectively, are seeing increased interest from Chinese buyers after the ban on Japanese seafood, as Undercurrent reported last week from the 2023 China Fisheries and Seafood Expo in Quingdao, China. 

Largest Canadian, US scallop sellers see increased interest from China after ban on Japan

Although executives with Clearwater and Eastern declined to comment on the ban itself, they both said there was more pull from the Chinese market during the Qingdao show.

"There's an increased interest in our scallops," Shawn Harding, director of international sales for New Bedford, Massachusetts-based Eastern told Undercurrent. "Historically, China has not been a big market for us. We will know more at the end of the show."

title: Chinese officials deny forced labor used in seafood factories
content:
Chinese officials are firmly denying allegations that forced labor is used within the country's seafood processing industry, calling the accusation "completely fabricated."

UK’s Unibond purchased MSC pollock from Chinese plant accused of forced labor

The accusations stem from a recent report by The Outlaw Ocean Project (OOP), which claimed some Chinese seafood processing facilities employ Uyghur Muslims under coercive working conditions tantamount to forced labor. The report prompted several US and European importers to cease shipments from a number of accused Chinese suppliers. 

In response, industry body China Aquatic Products Processing and Marketing Alliance (CAPPMA) said it conducted prompt investigations into the companies in question and contended it found "no evidence of forced labor," according to a statement released Wednesday (Oct. 18).

"Workers from all ethnic groups work in the same conditions, enjoy equal rights and equal pay for equal work," the statement read.

CAPPMA went on to say Chinese processing plants "consistently adhere to the Labor Law of the People's Republic of China and strictly follow the audit requirements of international third parties for safeguarding workers' rights and interests."

CAPPMA officials blasted the forced labor story as "fabricated" and took aim at the media outlets spreading it, though it offered no evidence of this fabrication.

"This is highly irresponsible!" the statement read. "The continuous spread of the news has resulted in some buyers ceasing shipments from Chinese processing plants."

Under Chinese law, the use of Xinjiang workers -- including those deployed via the government labor transfer program -- is legal.

However, according to the US' Uyghur Forced Labour Protection Act, imports to the US of goods produced by Xinjiang ethnic minorities at worksites located inside or outside of Xinjiang are banned.

The UN, human rights organizations and academic experts also agree that since 2018, the Chinese government has systematically subjected Xinjiang's predominantly Muslim ethnic minorities to state-imposed forced labor across the country via labor transfer programs. These use coercive methods in worker enrollment and obstruct the freedom to terminate employment.

CAPPMA's statement emphasized that employees of all backgrounds are protected by a range of labor rights under Chinese law.

"Workers of all ethnic groups enjoy a range of labor rights, including equal employment opportunities, the freedom to choose their profession, fair compensation, and access to vocational skills training," it said. "These principles also apply to employees in aquatic product processing enterprises."

Lund’s, Trident, NFI respond to report spotlighting forced labor in China

In response to the allegations, CAPPMA invited international organizations and journalists to visit Chinese facilities and judge the labor practices for themselves.

"We hope to promptly eliminate the impact of false allegations on the international fair-trade order for seafood products," the statement said.

OOP said it identified clips uploaded to multiple user accounts on Douyin -- China's equivalent to TikTok -- featuring content that indicated coercion and involuntariness among the Xinjiang ethnic minorities deployed to Shandong seafood processing plants. There is more about this on OOP's methods page.

Earlier this month, some major seafood buyers in the US and Europe suspended shipments from a number of accused Chinese suppliers following the report's publication, dealing a blow to some Chinese processors.

On Friday (Oct. 13), Lund's Fisheries, a Cape May, New Jersey-based harvester and processor of squid, scallops and multiple finfish species, declared it will not resume working with a Chinese seafood supplier identified in OOP's report.

Lund's was one of a few big names in the US seafood industry last week to make such a pronouncement following the publication in The New Yorker of the lengthy two-part series produced in collaboration with OOP.

Another large US retailer, Albertsons Companies, also said it had dropped two products from High Liner, including branded flounder and yellowfin sole, having been contacted by OOP.

High Liner has also since ceased working with the Chinese supplier accused of employing Uyghur labor.

The investigation has generated so much attention that a joint panel of Congress and White House officials has called a special hearing to learn more about the report, as reported by Undercurrent News.

title: Some European, US seafood buyers dropped Chinese processors accused of forced labor this summer
content:
Major seafood companies in Europe and the US stopped sourcing fish from Chinese processors as early as this summer after a watchdog group accused the latter of using forced labor from the Xinjiang region.

On Monday (Oct. 9), The Outlaw Ocean Project, a non-profit focused on reporting abuses within the fishing industry, published an investigation into the alleged use of forced Uyghur labor transferred from Xinjiang.

US retail giant drops High Liner products linked to Chinese supplier allegedly using forced Uyghur labor

The investigation details evidence of forced labor at Chinese seafood plants in Shandong province, where processors employ thousands of workers in whitefish and squid filleting.

The US bans imports produced with forced labor, which it considers any work conducted under threat of penalties and not voluntarily. Beijing denies any coercion and calls the program job training initiatives.

Among the companies that said they cut ties with the Chinese processors are US supermarket chains Albertsons Companies and Shaw's, and German retailers Aldi and Lidl.

Lidl France told The Outlaw Ocean Project its supplier Cite Marine, which is owned by Japanese seafood giant Nissui, had enforced a temporary suspension of all shipments from Qingdao Tianyuan Aquatic Foodstuff, after the company was informed of the accusations in early July.

Lidl France said the suspension was enacted "as a precaution."

French retailers Carrefour and Casino and UK seafood company Young's Seafood also told The Outlaw Ocean Project they were carrying out internal investigations back in July and August. Auchan did not respond to inquiries from the NGO, while Sysco's French subsidiary Davigel did not follow up on an initial response.

Outlaw Ocean reveals ‘crimes at sea’ aboard Chinese fishing vessels

On Wednesday (Oct. 11), Undercurrent News reported that Albertsons, one of the largest retailers in the US, had dropped two products from High Liner Foods, one of Canada's largest seafood companies. The retail giant stopped buying High Liner branded flounder and yellowfin sole, having been contacted by The Outlaw Ocean Project in August.

Qingdao Tianyuan's general manager, Nina Yin, sent an email to The Ocean Outlaw Project saying the accusations had led customers to refuse to buy its seafood.

In the email from Aug. 29, Yin said the accusations had "severely impacted our normal business operations... and put the livelihoods of hundreds of our employees' families at risk."

"We hope that satisfy [sic] you and you will cease the spread of negative messages immediately and retract them," Yin told the NGO in a subsequent email.

The Ocean Outlaw Project said it has publicly accessible documentation that demonstrates Chinese seafood processors' use of labor from Xinjiang.

In Qingdao Tianyuan's case, this includes multiple state media reports describing the government's involvement in transferring workers from Xinjiang to the company, and including photos of the transfers.

Report: Chinese plants using forced Uyghur labor supplying major European, US retailers

The authenticated footage confirms the presence of Xinjiang workers at Qingdao Tianyuan from as early as 2018 to as recently as May 2023, the group said.

"We have also obtained footage showing Xinjiang workers at Qingdao Lian Yang Aquatic Products Co. Ltd., a wholly-owned subsidiary of Qingdao Tianyuan, as early as April 2022 and as recently as April 2023," The Outlaw Ocean Project said in an email to Qingdao Tianyuan.

Yin defended Qingdao Tianyuan's labor practices in subsequent emails, saying the company was privately owned and did not participate in any government labor transfer programs. 

The read the full email exchange, click here.

On Wednesday, High Liner confirmed to Undercurrent News it had dropped Yantai Sanko Fisheries -- another accused Chinese company -- as a supplier.

Jennifer Bell, vice president of corporate communications, said in a written statement that this was "out of an abundance of caution, and in light of the concerning evidence and allegations included in this [Outlaw Ocean Project] article."

EU importers call for clarity on whether Chinese fillets using Russian H&G will be excluded from ATQs

"High Liner Foods is working with alternate suppliers to ensure that we minimize the impact on our supply chain," Bell said.

After hearing of the allegations brought forward by Outlaw Ocean, High Liner had Yantai Sanko audited again in August 2023, finding no evidence in either audit of the use of forced labor, she said.

title: US ambassador signals support for Japan in Fukushima conflict with China
content:
Rahm Emanuel, the US ambassador to Japan, visited the Fukushima region on Thursday (Aug. 31) and told reporters that he expected the US to support Japan in the event that China's ban on Japanese seafood develops into a World Trade Organization (WTO) dispute, Reuters reports.

Japan began releasing treated radioactive water from the wrecked Fukushima nuclear power plant into the Pacific Ocean a week ago, prompting China to impose a ban on seafood from Japan. 

Japan signals WTO action to address China trade spat following nuclear plant wastewater discharge

It's a hard punch to the gut for Japan, which exported about $600 million worth of seafood products to China in 2022, making China its largest market followed by Hong Kong, which announced its own ban on seafood imports from 10 Japanese regions after the release of the Fukushima water, according to the news service.

Japanese officials have suggested they could file a WTO complaint, arguing that China's actions are not based on scientific evidence.

During a visit to Tokyo's biggest fish market on Thursday, Japanese prime minister Fumio Kishida reportedly said his cabinet would draw up measures to help the fishing industry by early next week. The government will use tens of billions of yen (hundreds of millions of dollars), from budget reserves for this fiscal year to fund the measures, the Nikkei newspaper reported.

The Japanese government also has set up two funds worth 80 billion yen ($548 million) to help develop new markets and keep excess fish frozen until they can be sold when demand recovers, among other measures, the news service reported.

"If Japan decides to take that effort, the United States will stand by (it) not just because they're an ally, but because there's legitimacy to the case," Emanuel reportedly said in reference to the prospect of a WTO action.

He added that he could not prejudge what might happen and such support would ultimately be up to relevant US government agencies.

China claims surge in sales of domestically produced seafood after Japan ban

"The economic coercion against Japan, the robocalls of harassment and disinformation both here in Japan and around comes right out of China's playbook. This is all politics," Emanuel said.

The colorful former mayor of Chicago, who was also a member of the House of Representatives and advisor to former president Barack Obama, had lunch with Hidekiyo Tachiya, the mayor of Soma, a city near the wrecked nuclear plant, according to Reuters. They ate locally caught seafood.

Emanuel also bought seafood at a supermarket and sampled Fukushima peaches while mingling with shoppers.

title: Pacific Seafood moves for dismissal of Dungeness price-fixing lawsuit
content:
Pacific Seafood Group has moved for dismissal of a federal lawsuit alleging anti-competitive behavior in the Dungeness crab market.

The big US West Coast processor, headquartered in Clackamas, Oregon, filed a motion Friday (July 21) in the US District Court of the Northern District of California, San Francisco Division, that argues the fisherman suing it lacks antitrust standing and has failed to demonstrate wrongdoing under the Sherman Act, an 1890 measure underpinning US antitrust law.

A hearing on the motion is slated for August 11.

The lawsuit, which was originally filed March 13 by law firm Gross Klein on behalf of commercial fisherman Brand Little, accuses Pacific of price-fixing via "monopsonization, coercion, dumping, and secret deals."

Pacific counterclaimed in a July 20 statement that Gross Klein founder Stuart Gross has been manipulating media outlets since the lawsuit was filed to "inflict undue reputational harm to a business as leverage to compel financial settlement." Gross denied the allegations in a subsequent statement, as reported by Undercurrent News. 

"Plaintiff complains he does not receive a higher price for ex-vessel crab because his unidentified buyer is influenced by the price Pacific Seafood pays in a downstream market," Pacific wrote in its introduction to the dismissal motion.

"How plaintiff's disappointment becomes an antitrust violation is a mystery. Fundamentally, excess supply like that in a derby fishery leads to lower prices in a competitive market, and economically rational resellers account for expected resale prices when deciding how much to pay for inputs," it added.

"As plaintiff alleges, Pacific Seafood and other processors absorb that excess supply, which is pro-competitive, and without them, large amounts of crab would go to waste. Plaintiff's overarching theory is fully consistent with expected outcomes from a competitive market in which participants act independently in their own economic self-interest, and without exercising power over price."

Pacific argued in the motion that Little does not possess antitrust standing, as he is alleging that Pacific's actions indirectly affect his crab prices.

Pacific had made the point in its July 20 statement that the harvester is not one of the 600 independent operators from which it buys Dungeness crab, and none of those operators are co-plaintiffs in the lawsuit. 

Furthermore, Pacific argued that little did not satisfy section 1 or 2 claims under the Sherman Act. Section 1 is not satisfied because Little does not identify his buyer and thus cannot argue Pacific's collusion with them. Section 2 is not satisfied because Little does not identify a relevant market, according to the company. 

"Plaintiff's market allegations implausibly combine two distinct markets at different levels in the supply chain: an ex-vessel market, comprised of sales by crabbers to licensed ex-vessel buyers, and a downstream market, comprised of resale of crab by ex-vessel buyers," Pacific wrote.

"In response, plaintiff tries to draw a different but still facially unsustainable line," it continued. "He concedes the obvious -- that ex-vessel sales by crabbers to ex-vessel buyers is a different market than downstream resales by those ex-vessel buyers to retailers."

As of July 24, no rebuttal of the motion had been filed. Gross responded to Undercurrent via a statement. 

"Plaintiff is confident in the strength of the complaint, and its detailed allegations of antitrust violations by Pacific Seafood," he said. "We look forward to the hearing on the motion."

title: Pacific Seafood alleges media campaign intimidation in Dungeness price-fixing lawsuit
content:
Major US West Coast processor Pacific Seafood Group says a pending lawsuit filed against it regarding alleged anti-competitive behavior in the Dungeness crab market behavior is nothing more than a financial shakedown -- aided by a coordinated media campaign. 

The lawsuit, filed March 13 in the US state of California by law firm Gross Klein on behalf of commercial fisherman Brand Little, accuses Pacific of price-fixing via the "monopsonization, coercion, dumping, and secret deals." Pacific counterclaims in a July 20 statement that Gross Klein founder Stuart Gross has been manipulating media outlets since the lawsuit was filed to "inflict undue reputational harm to a business as leverage to compel financial settlement" -- a claim that he denied in a statement to Undercurrent News. 

Pacific noted that Little does not fish for Pacific and was a "controversial and vocal figure" among California fishermen, per its interviews with local fishermen. Specifically, Pacific said it had been told by the San Francisco Crab Boat Owners Association, another Gross client, that it had sent a letter to the California Department of Fish and Wildlife asking that Little be barred from participating in the California Dungeness Crab Fishing Gear Working Group "because of his self-interest and failure to represent the fleet as a whole." 

It added that none of Pacific's more than 600 independent commercial fishing vessels are participating in the lawsuit. 

Furthermore, Gross appears to be "aggressively targeting media outlets for publicity, with multiple rounds of press releases and pseudo blog posts that parrot the fabricated claims made in their complaint," Pacific said. 

"Two reporters from the AP (Associated Press) swung by the Pacific Seafood booth at the Boston Seafood Show the morning the lawsuit was filed, asking for an interview. To my knowledge, we've never had inquiries from AP reporters in Boston before," Pacific wrote.

"It is a well-known legal tactic to inflict undue reputational harm to a business as leverage to compel financial settlement. If that is what Mr. Little and Mr. Gross are doing here, I would tell them that Pacific Seafood knows we did nothing wrong and we won't be intimidated by their weak attempts to cause our business harm," it said. "We are confident that upon thorough investigation of the facts here one will find that Pacific Seafood is a great company that always has, and always will, uplift and protect the West Coast commercial seafood industry for our fleet, our employees, and our customers."

Pacific also takes issue with the complaint itself, calling it a "long, repetitive, sloppy document filled with antitrust 'buzzwords' but no substance."

"The content demonstrates a profound lack of familiarity with the commercial Dungeness crab industry and much of it does not make logical sense. The allegations about Pacific are outright lies," it said. 

"Given the timing, sloppiness, and scattershot approach of the suit, it appeared to be a rushed legal filing intended not as a legitimate grievance by a concerned party, but as a scandal intended to hit the trade headlines at a precise time to inflict maximum commercial harm on Pacific Seafood's reputation and business during a peak sales event," Pacific said, referring to Seafood Expo Global.

In a statement sent late Thursday (July 20) to Undercurrent, Stuart Gross rejects Pacific's claims on multiple fronts. His law firm did not send out multiple press releases, he said, and Pacific's statement is "riddled with false and defamatory statements."

"Pacific Seafood’s statement is a remarkable personal attack on the plaintiff and his attorney that is riddled with false and defamatory statements. This tactic is consistent with allegations in the complaint that Pacific Seafood has attained and maintained its control of the Pacific Northwest Dungeness crab wholesale-input market through illegal attacks on those it sees as threats," Stuart Gross wrote.

"Thus, fundamentally, we are gratified by the reaction, as it is indicative of the threat that Pacific Seafood sees this lawsuit posing to its illegal conduct," he added. "We look forward to proving our case in court and winning compensation for the men and women who do the work, and put their lives at risk, to put Dungeness crab on people’s plates and freeing the market from Pacific Seafood’s illegal control."

Lack of options

In the original filing, Gross Klein accuses the processor of buying out most of its rivals across the Pacific Northwest, leaving crab harvesters with few options but to accept the company's price.

Additionally, Gross Klein asserts that Pacific has made "anti-competitive agreements, coerced and otherwise, with other fish buyers whereby if those fish buyers comply with Pacific Seafood's mandates regarding the price to be paid to crabbers, Pacific Seafood will purchase those buyers' oversupply of crab for a certain amount more."

The lawsuit, which aims to eventually be certified as a class action involving similarly situated crab harvesters, also takes issue with Pacific's own Dungeness harvesting activities and what it claims is the control of "nominally independent boats."

These boats are reportedly required to sell "all the fish they catch," if they want to sell Pacific Seafood at all, the suit claimed.

"This has been a highly effective strategy given Pacific Seafood's overwhelming dominance in the wholesale-input markets for other fish," the law firm said.

It also claims that fish buyers that don't fall in line with the company's pricing are subject to the "dumping large amounts of cheap crab in portions of the wholesale-retail market."

The most recent legal filing on the case (July 19) is an approval for Pacific to exceed the standard 15-page limitation for its formal legal response.

title: Crabber sues Pacific Seafood, alleging anticompetitive behavior to ‘suppress’ Dungeness prices
content:
A Dungeness crab harvester in the US state of California has sued Clackamas, Oregon-based Pacific Seafood Group, alleging that the major US West Coast processor has engaged in a pattern of anti-competitive behavior to suppress the prices paid for their catches. 

Brand Little, who filed the lawsuit on March 13 in the US District Court for the Northern District of California, is described in the claim as an Auburn, California-based fisherman who has been fishing commercially since 2004.

Gross Klein, the law firm representing Little, accuses Pacific of having "illegally fixed the prices through a multipronged strategy of monopsonization, coercion, dumping, and secret deals", it said in a press release.

The law firm accuses the processor of buying out most of its rivals across the Pacific Northwest, leaving crab harvesters with few options but to accept the company's price.

Additionally, Gross Klein asserts that Pacific has made "anti-competitive agreements, coerced and otherwise, with other fish buyers whereby if those fish buyers comply with Pacific Seafood’s mandates regarding the price to be paid to crabbers, Pacific Seafood will purchase those buyers’ oversupply of crab for a certain amount more".

The lawsuit, which aims to eventually be certified as a class action involving similarly situated crab harvesters, also takes issue with Pacific's own Dungeness harvesting activities and what it claims is the control of "nominally independent boats".

These boats are reportedly required to sell  "all the fish they catch", if they want to sell Pacific Seafood at all, the suit claimed.

"This has been a highly effective strategy given Pacific Seafood’s overwhelming dominance in the wholesale-input markets for other fish," the law firm said.

It claims that fish buyers that don't fall in line with the company's pricing are subject to the "dumping large amounts of cheap crab in portions of the wholesale-retail market".

Pacific Seafood has not yet responded to the lawsuit in court. However, the company told Undercurrent News that it believes the suit will be dismissed quickly.

"This is a completely baseless lawsuit filed by a fisherman who doesn’t do business with us and doesn’t know our company at all. We are confident it will be dismissed quickly," Dan Occhipinti, the company's chief legal officer, was quoted as saying in a release.

This year's Dungeness season began on Dec. 31 in southern California, but harvesters were immediately met with punishing atmospheric river rains, which caused delays for weeks.

Compounding that was the worst pre-set season price, $2.25 per pound to processors and $3/lb for fresh-crab distributors, since at least 2012, Dick Ogg, a longtime harvester who participated in processor negotiations, told Undercurrent.

title: Researchers expose poor conditions for migrant workers on Scottish vessels
content:
Researchers have revealed harsh conditions and uncertainty endured by migrant crews on Scots vessels, with some not even being paid due to a legal loophole, reports The Sunday Post. 

Up to 1,000 migrant fishermen, many from Africa, Indonesia and the Philippines, and who found jobs on Scots vessels, have been exploited and abused, while some have been unpaid for months, the researchers state. 

The loophole, which involves the misuse of short-term seafarers' transit visas by some employers to bypass strict migration law, means they cannot complain and struggle to get the thousands of pounds they are owed due to their immigration status.

"The use of transit visas to employ fishing crews from the Philippines, Ghana, and Sri Lanka, among others, in the UK fishing industry is a loophole that needs to be closed but without displacing the problem offshore," said Chris Williams, a fisheries expert with the  International Transport Workers' Federation.

"The current migrant workforce in fishing are invisible, but they are here doing the work and make up most of the crew around the UK. Their lack of immigration status means they have to live on fishing vessels in UK ports and are dependent on their employer for everything, which sets a scene rife for labor exploitation and coercion due to immigration fears," he concluded.

Academics, such as Carole White of the University of East Anglia, and other organizations like the UK's Home Office or the Scottish Fishermen's Federation (SFF) have also backed the bid to strengthen the rights of the migrant crew.  

"As industry representatives, we deplore and condemn bad practices and crew members being badly or unfairly treated, regardless of their nationality or immigration status," added Elspeth Macdonald, SFF's CEO.

title: Taiwan indicts tuna vessel with Bumble Bee ties on human trafficking allegations
content:
Nine individuals affiliated with a Taiwanese tuna vessel that once supplied US canner Bumble Bee Foods have been indicted for allegedly enslaving more than 20 migrant workers in a criminal case first brought to light in 2019.

The Kaohsiung District Prosecutors' Office of Taiwan announced the formal charging of the crew of the Vanuatu-flagged, 187-foot Da Wang last week. Prosecutors found that "the captain Lin Lang and the chief mate Liang Yi had indeed exploited foreign fishermen by means of rape and coercion during their operations at sea", and charged them with violating Taiwan's Human Trafficking Prevention Law (HTPL). 

Those found guilty of HTPL violations face a maximum sentence of at least seven years imprisonment and fines of as much as TWD 7 million ($238,973).

The prosection's finding differs sharply from an earlier response to international pressure that the Chinese government called grandstanding and represents about three years of investigation and protest by the advocacy organization Greenpeace, which has also pressed Bumble Bee, and its Taiwanese owner, FCF Co, for greater transparency regarding its tuna suppliers. 

A Greenpeace spokesman told Undercurrent News that the international attention, and Taiwanese criminal investigation, were spurred by his organization's December 2019 report, "Seabound: The Journey to Modern Slavery on the High Seas" and a 2021 follow-up report "Forced Labour at Sea: The Case of Indonesian Migrant Fishers." 

The 52-page 2019 document compiles the results of interviews with 34 Indonesian migrant fishers on 13 fishing vessels. The fishers said they were the victims of deception in recruiting practices, the withholding of wages, excessive overtime and physical and sexual abuse. 

Da Wang Indonesian and Philippine crew members were kept at sea for six months straight without salary, the report states. The report quotes one crew member from the Da Wang describing how another died in his sleep after being beaten over the head.

"I witnessed horrible torture," the crew member reportedly said. "We were working even at midnight. When the fishing master was angry, he hit my friend's head near his left ear. After that, he was forced to continue working until the work was finished, and only then was he allowed to rest. In the morning when we woke up for breakfast, we found him dead in his room. The captain wrapped up my dead friend's body with a blanket and then stored him in the freezer."

The administration of US president Donald Trump announced an import-banning withhold release order (WRO) against the Da Wang in August 2020. The order allows US customs officials to seize the cargo of any transport so designated at any US entry point. The administration of US president Joseph Biden later renewed the WRO.

As named in the Greenpeace reports, the Da Wang is owned by the Taiwanese company Yong Feng Fishery and has been linked as a supplier to Taiwanese tuna trading company FCF, which owns Bumble Bee. Bumble Bee was purchased by FCF for $928 million in January 2020, as Undercurrent has reported.

Liz Conant, a spokesperson for Bumble Bee, declined to comment on the Da Wang at the time of the publication of this article, April 26. However, two days later, she sent Undercurrent an email in which she said that Bumble Bee was "not sourcing [tuna] from the vessel at the time of the report, nor have we sourced from them since."

She said that Bumble Bee works with FCF "to identify and address any health, safety, or other issues on vessels in Bumble Bee's supply chain. We remain committed to our objectives to address safety and fair treatment in the fishing industry."

Bumble Bee is "encouraged" that the government of Taiwan has a plan, due to go into effect July 1, that would require the 1,100-vessel TWN fleet and its estimated 21,150 foreign crew members to be treated more humanely. Included will be better pay, time limits at sea, Wi-Fi access, increased mandatory inspections, and requirements that harvester or crew recruiting agencies and fleets "join industry sustainability programs to help improve their environmental and social performance", she said.

In previous statements to Undercurrent, Conant has highlighted the company's attempts to work with sustainability certifiers to ensure that all of its workers are treated humanely.

"We continue to work within our supply chain, with others in the tuna industry and through the Seafood Task Force to make the responsible recruitment and treatment of all workers an ongoing top priority," she said in discussing an advocacy group's lawsuit against the canner involving allegedly false marketing claims.

Work to improve the sustainability and social standards practiced in Taiwanese fisheries and by Taiwanese fleets is ongoing.

In May 2021, Bumble Bee's Leslie Hushka, senior vice president of global corporate social responsibility, told Undercurrent that 250 of the albacore vessels that supply it would enter into Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) assessment. Those Taiwanese-flagged longliners, which had been part of a fishery improvement project (FIP) to improve data collection, are responsible for supplying 50% of the albacore Bumble Bee sells into the market, Hushka said.

Additionally, she said that Bumble Bee and FCF were implementing a "social audit" program to ensure that its vessels were protecting workers' human rights.

"I would describe that program as a 'best in class' approach to looking at workers' rights. It covers everything from training to a risk-based screening approach to third party audits for vessels to owner/officers," she said.

And, another Taiwanese fishing firm, Fue Shin Fishery and the conservation group Ocean Outcomes announced in late March that they have begun two FIPs aimed at expanding the sustainable seafood movement to include Taiwanese longline tuna fisheries.

But international efforts to eliminate slavery should involve more than the Da Wang, said J. Park, a senior oceans campaigner for Greenpeace USA, calling the indictment "indicative of a wider problem".

"The high seas fishing industry uses cost-cutting and illegal fishing tactics, forced labor, and other human rights abuses to stay profitable," Park said. "US grocery stores and consumer brands like Bumble Bee have a responsibility to ensure their products are free from human rights violations."

title: Seafood watchdog: US should’ve dropped Thailand on people-trafficking list
content:
The Seafood Working Group (SWG), a watchdog group representing 18 non-governmental organizations (NGO) that has been repeatedly critical of Thailand's handling of labor, on Friday called again for the Donald Trump administration to lower the country's ranking on the US State Department's Trafficking in Persons (TIP) Report.

The 2020 TIP report, released in June, preserved Thailand's ranking at "tier two", despite "detailed and comprehensive evidence demonstrating the weaknesses of the Thai government’s efforts in the areas of prosecution, protection and prevention of human trafficking in 2019", SWG said.

SWG, which includes Greenpeace, Fishwise and Human Rights at Sea in its coalition, has argued to have the Southeast Asia nation downgraded to the tier two "watch list" since "it does not fully meet the minimum standards set forth in the US Trafficking Victims Protection Act (TVPA) of 2000 and did not make sufficient progress to address trafficking in persons in 2019".

SWG said it did its own report, which relied on consultations with frontline worker organizations, and documented 23 potential labor trafficking cases, although it noted that even the evidence presented by State in its TIP report was "much more in line with the criteria for the tier two watch list ranking".

The TIP report is the US government’s principal diplomatic tool for engagement with foreign governments on human trafficking and is released each year, ranking countries across four tiers based on their anti-trafficking efforts. The lowest ranking, tier three, triggers possible aid sanctions; tier two does not lead to such consequences.

The 2020 TIP report highlighted five areas where the government of Thailand demonstrated increasing efforts compared to the previous year. However, SWG feels the TIP report also provided clear evidence that four of these efforts have been "weak and ineffective".

Firstly, the State Department noted serious limitations in the impact of anti-trafficking training to judges, and the work carried out with NGOs to provide trauma-informed
care training to police, prosecutors, and shelter staff, SWG observed.

"The act of conducting trainings alone, without assessing their impact, should not be considered an 'increasing effort' to combat trafficking," the group said. It also said training was largely provided with significant support from UN agencies, NGOs, and other governments; efforts that are largely funded and provided by external entities should not be used to determine tier rankings, it said.

Secondly, a focus on the rise in labor trafficking investigations is highly selective and misleading, SWG said, as the overall numbers of trafficking investigations, prosecutions and convictions all decreased, in addition to "wider patterns of ineffective law enforcement".

The TIP report stated that 76 labor trafficking cases were investigated in 2019, an increase from 43 in 2018. However, the overall number of trafficking investigations decreased, from 304 in 2018 to 288 in 2019. It further noted that "the government initiated the fewest number of trafficking investigations since 2014", SWG said.

In addition, the number of prosecutions decreased from 438 in 2018 to 386 in 2019 and convictions dropped from 316 in 2018 to 304 in 2019.

"In any case, 76 cases reflects an extremely low number of labor trafficking investigations in the context of the millions of labor migrants in the Thai economy with known vulnerabilities to trafficking."

Only four labor trafficking cases were in the fishing sector, which SWG finds to be extremely low. "The ILO Ship to Shore Rights’ study conducted in 2019 showed that 14% of fishers interviewed were in a situation of forced labor."

The US' TIP report also said "corruption and official complicity facilitated trafficking and continued to impede anti-trafficking efforts", which SWG said was a key issue
warranting tier two watch list status.

Thirdly, while compensation to victims through the anti-trafficking fund rose year-on-year, the impact fell short of supporting reintegration for survivors, said SWG. The Thai government provided THB 11.88 million ($398,990) to trafficking victims from its anti-trafficking fund, including THB 1.68m to victims residing outside government shelters, in 2019. This represented an increase from the THB 6.15m provided in 2018.

Fourthly, the TIP report noted successful restitution payments to victims of trafficking, paid by traffickers, for the first time.

"The government did not report how many restitution claims prosecutors filed on behalf of victims in 2019 (116 in 2018) but reported that courts ordered THB 3.3m in restitution for 14 victims in two cases in 2019."

However, the TIP report itself said the execution of court orders to pay restitution for victims remained ineffective, particularly for non-Thai victims.

Thailand’s 'wider failure to prevent human trafficking'

More broadly, SWG claimed Thailand did not warrant the tier two ranking in 2020 because it has "demonstrably failed to prevent human trafficking of migrant workers".

As it submitted to the US government, there are several structural issues underpinning
the risk of forced labor and human trafficking that remain to be addressed, it said.

"First, the government’s system for registering migrant workers in Thailand is insufficient and ineffective, and often leaves migrants without protection under labor laws. Second, the Thai government has failed to effectively prohibit recruitment fees and related costs, which violates the International Labour Organization [ILO]'s general principles and operational guidelines for fair recruitment and forces migrants to routinely go into debt to brokers, recruitment agencies and employers."

Third, the government has failed to remove significant barriers to changing employers, said SWG; the current policy affords workers with the limited opportunity to change employers under certain conditions but, in practice, it has been nearly impossible for migrant workers to use these provisions even when laboring under abusive
conditions, it wrote.

"These factors -- lack of labor protection, debt, and inability to change employers -- are
built into the legal framework, represent indicators of involuntariness and coercion, and are strong risk factors for forced labor and human trafficking."

The Thai government has failed to ratify core ILO Labor Conventions 87 (Freedom of Association) and 98 (Right to Organize and Collectively Bargain) or to revise its labor legislation to ensure that these fundamental, internationally-recognized worker rights are respected. As such, Thai law explicitly bans non-Thai citizens from the right to form trade unions or play leading roles in them, SWG observed.

SWG further noted that Taiwan remained at tier one in 2020 despite a "significant body of evidence documenting systemic labor trafficking in Taiwan’s fishing industry and the government’s failure to make serious and sustained efforts to eliminate it".

title: US shrimp larvae supplier’s founder faces possible life sentence for sex trafficking
content:
David Wills, the 67-year-old founder and part-owner of Global Blue Technologies (GBT), a major Rockport, Texas-based supplier of shrimp larvae, has been convicted of sex trafficking and faces a potential life in prison sentence. 

A federal jury in Corpus Christi deliberated for 10 hours following a 10-day trial before convicting Wills, now of San Antonio, on 17 different criminal counts, according to a press release from the US Department of Justice (DOJ). 

The jury heard how Wills and Maria Losoya, a 57-year-old Brownsville, Texas, woman were arrested in July 17 on charges that they started trafficking a young girl when she was only 10 years old, using their cellphones to arrange meetings where Wills could sexually assault the victim, according to the press release.

The arrangement went on from 2012 to 2015, when the victim reported the situation to the authorities.

Wills had promised to pay for the young girl's college tuition in exchange for Losoya's help, reimbursing her for gifts to the victim and expenditures she would otherwise not be able to afford, the federal prosecutors recounted. This included an iPad, Bose headphones, a flatscreen TV, Apple laptop, trampoline, swimming pool and a school trip to Washington, DC.

Image from Global Blue Technologies website.

Losoya pleaded guilty in 2017 and testified at trial.

The jury heard from a forensic interviewer, a nurse who first examined the victim, law enforcement officers and an eyewitness who described seeing the victim at a hotel where Wills and Losoya met in March 2014. It also heard from Wills’ former personal assistant, who testified he asked her to hand over a personal computer on the day the victim contacted police. Wills later admitted it was destroyed to prevent law enforcement from seizing and reviewing it.

Wills, who had a total of 12 attorneys representing him at trial, attempted to convince the jury that Losoya only wanted more money. He took the stand and said he had an affair with Losoya but denied any sexual involvement with the victim.

The jury convicted Wills of one count of conspiracy to commit sex trafficking, seven counts each of sex trafficking and coercion/enticement, one count of attempted coercion/enticement and one count of conspiracy to obstruct justice, according to the DOJ.

Previously released on a $5 million bond, Wills was taken into custody following the verdict.

Company earlier hit by hurricane

In addition to being a large-scale supplier of shrimp larvae, GBT produced vannamei under the Copano Blues brand, using Sustainable Sea Products International as its Rockville, Maryland-based marketing arm.

The company has seen its share of bad news recently.

It was one of several seafood companies to suffer from Hurricane Harvey, a category 4 storm that plowed into the Texas and Louisiana Gulf of Mexico coasts in August 2017, taking a devastating direct hit to its operations. 

More recently, in July 2019, GBT was awarded a "multi-million-dollar" contract to build a broodstock multiplication center shrimp hatchery and growout production facilities in Qatar, as reported by Undercurrent News. The grow-out modules, which will use recirculating aquaculture system technology, will include an initial capacity of 3,000 metric tons of farmed shrimp production output annually, rising to as much as 100,000t over four-to-five years, GBT said at the time.

Undercurrent has reached out to chief operating officer Lorenzo Juarez but he had not yet responded by press time.
