title: ‘Three of us have built it’; Tugushev’s take on rise of $1.5bn fishing giant Norebo
content:
"Three of us have built it... And since then we honor that agreement. One third is his."

So said Vitaly Orlov, the billionaire owner of Russian fishing giant Norebo Group, of Alexander Tugushev, one of the three co-founders of the company, on Feb. 27, 2014, in Geneva, Switzerland, the latter alleges in a recent claim document filed in the UK High Court. 

Deadline nears for Norebo CEO to challenge $350m freezing order in bitter shareholder court battle

"There is no doubt that we keep our promise that you have the benefit out of this. There is no doubt! There is no formal link. You get your benefit, you get your third,” Magnus Roth, the third co-founder of Norebo -- which Tugushev claims is now worth over $1.5 billion -- allegedly said in the same conversation. 

"My understanding having discussed with Vitaly and Magnus is that there is... it's more than a gentleman agreement. It's an oral agreement,” Nicolas Brun-Lie, a Norwegian lawyer involved with Norebo, reportedly stated.

Tugushev is suing Orlov, Roth -- who reportedly netted $330 million from selling his third in the company in 2016 -- and Andrei Petrik, a UK-based Norebo executive and “associate” of Orlov in the UK court. Orlov, Roth and Petrik, Tugushev alleges, conspired to deprive him of a third in the company.

He’s claiming his stake in the business -- which has substantial assets in Russian Atlantic and Pacific cod, haddock, pollock and herring -- is worth at least $350m. Also, he claims he’s owed millions in dividends he should have been paid going back to 2005.

A hearing in London on Aug. 23 was held in private after a judge ruled in favor of a call from Orlov to protect information on his wealth. According to Undercurrent News sources familiar with the case, subsequent hearings will be in public, unless the judge rules otherwise for a specific reason, however.

On Monday, a spokesman for Orlov confirmed to Undercurrent he will oppose the location of the case in London and the freezing order the court placed on assets up to $350m in value. Orlov’s evidence will come later in the legal process.

Tugushev -- through his lawyers Peters and Peters Solicitors -- has already made public his version of the buildup of the company by the three entrepreneurs into a business which now is the largest quota holder in the country. He also clearly states his view on his role with Norebo on his Linkedin profile (see below). 

This is, of course, only Tugushev's side of the story; a man who, as Orlov’s legal team has reportedly reminded the judge in the case, has previously spent time in prison for fraud. In fact, Tugushev -- a fishing entrepreneur who moved into a government role, then went to prison and went back into Norebo when he came out -- mentions this conviction in the claim, stating he believes it was politically motivated.

The London court case comes amid a time of transformation and investment for Norebo and the Russian fishing sector in general. The country plans to shave off 20% of its total allowable catch and allocate this to companies investing in new plants and vessels. Norebo has announced a plan to build six new 80-meter cod and haddock trawlers as part of the program, which will cost some RUB 21bn ($355m). It remains to be seen what impact this legal process will have on these plans. 

Below is a timeline of the events Tugushev describes in the claim, put roughly in order and interspersed with Undercurrent News reporting, when appropriate. 

Post-Soviet fishing entrepreneurs: 1991-2003

In the claim, it is said Orlov and Tugushev met in 1991, the year the Soviet Union collapsed, when they were working in Murmansk.

From 1989-1992, Tugushev worked for fishing firm Murmansk Trawl Fleet, before he and three other shareholders founded the Karat group of companies.

Then, the fish from Karat was sold through Orlov's then-employer, Murmansk Impex, to a Swedish company named Scandsea International, for which Roth worked. Later, Orlov was also seconded to Scandsea. By 1996, Tugushev had bought out the other three shareholders in Karat and was the sole ultimate shareholder.

Around 1997, the claim document states Roth was asked to leave Scandsea and it was agreed orally between him, Tugushev and Orlov to enter into a joint venture (JV), of which each would own one-third. 

According to the claim, the “express terms” of the JV agreement were that the three would pool their resources and share everything equally in one-third shares, and that they would work together in the fishing industry in Russia and in Norway. This business was conducted initially through Russian companies within Karat that could obtain quotas to fish in Russian waters; the fish caught would then be distributed worldwide.

World’s largest FAS cod fillet supplier sees price gap with H&G closing

Also in 1997, Ocean Trawlers was established in Norway by agreement between Orlov, Tugushev and Roth. The plan was that fish from Tugushev's Russian companies within Karat would be sold to Ocean Trawlers and distributed worldwide, according to the claim.

An actual JV agreement was written in 1998 by a written agreement between Orlov, Tugushev and Roth, but Tugushev claims he no longer has a copy.

In the claim, he states, to his knowledge, Orlov took the 1998 agreement for safekeeping. According to Tugushev, the document was “likely” drafted by a Brun-Lie, the Norwegian lawyer instructed by Norebo, and it was signed by all three parties at Ocean Trawlers' offices in Drebak, Norway.

Over time, “the fishing business of the joint venture grew very considerably and acquired very substantial value, and came to be owned and operated by the Norebo Group”, the claim states.

Further companies were incorporated offshore as the business of Norebo developed. 

According to the claim, Tugushev performed the management role of the business; Orlov acted as its CEO; Roth was “responsible for distributing the profits amongst the three parties and dealing with the tax implications”, and Petrik was responsible for managing the offshore companies, which he managed out of the UK. Petrik was also responsible for administering dividends payable by Norebo.

In 2001, the Russian operational companies in the Norebo Group were merged under the umbrella of one holding company, CJSC Almor Atlantika, incorporated in Saint Petersburg on Nov. 16, 2001.

The claim states the three agreed shares in Almor Atlantika would be divided equally between them.

The ownership of Almor Atlantika was divided as follows, according to the claim: Tugushev owned 34,828 shares (25.38%), with 12,212 shares (8.9%) held by his nominees. Then, 69,990 shares (51%) were held by a company named CJSC Norebo Invest, ultimately owned “on behalf” of Orlov and Roth. Then, 20,200 shares (14.72%) were held by Orlov's cousin Romanovskii, as the nominee of he and Roth.

Government post, prison time: 2003-2009

On Sept. 22, 2003, according to the claim, Tugushev was appointed to a Russian government position.

He took on the role as deputy chairman of the Russian State Fisheries Committee, standing down from a management role at Norebo. However, he retained his shareholding and interest.

Not even a year into this position, on June 2, 2004, Tugushev was arrested on allegations of fraud and ultimately sentenced to six years' imprisonment.

Tugushev “denies those charges and believes them to have been politically motivated”, the claim states, without giving more information.

According to a Feb. 15, 2007 article from RIA Novosti, translated to English by Sputnik News, Tugushev and three other defendants were found guilty of extorting $3.7m from the management of a fishing company based in the Pacific port of Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky to issue illegal fishing quotas in 2003.

Russian giant Norebo names new Europe, Asia top execs

However, the court cleared Tugushev of bribery charges.

When he was released on Dec. 2, 2009, he returned to work for Norebo, according to the claim.

Three Towns Capital, alleged AA 'conspiracy': 2010-2012

Following Tugushev's release from prison, a series of meetings are claimed to have taken place in Murmansk between 2010-2011, where Orlov revealed a company named Three Towns Capital (TTC) had been incorporated in Hong Kong and that this was intended to become the holding company for the entire Norebo group.

The TTC name is said to have referred to the three partners and Orlov assured Tugushev he continued to have a one-third interest in the group.

Subsequently, due to a change in Russian legislation regarding foreign ownership of Russian fisheries' assets, five holding companies were set up in Russia at the end of 2007 and the operating Russian companies were in the process of being transferred under those structures. Orlov and Tugushev discussed and took steps towards Tugushev's daughter Alisa being registered as the 33% owner of these companies, reflecting his claimed one-third interest in the group, “although ultimately this did not transpire”, the claim document states.

These meetings regarding Alisa Tugushev taking Orlov’s 33% in the company took place between 2010 and 2012, he claims.

Allegedly, under's Orlov instruction, applications were prepared to open share accounts for the five holding companies -- CJSC Flot Holding, CJSC Rybpromlnvest; CJSC Zhevenraik Holding; CJSC Norebo Holding and CJSC Soyuz Holding -- in the name of Alisa for this purpose, and sent to Tugushev for execution on Oct. 27, 2010. 

Also, meetings took place in December 2012 in Hong Kong attended by Orlov, Roth, Brun-Lie, Helge Klock, another group executive, and Tugushev and Alisa, where the possibility of her becoming the 100% shareholder in Laxagone was discussed. This course was also not adopted, however.

Russia’s Norebo to invest $350m in six cod, haddock trawlers

In 2012, Orlov is said to have informed Tugushev and Roth in a meeting in Amsterdam, the Netherlands, that, whilst the three of them were decision makers, he should be in charge of the overall day-to-day management of the group.

This request led to the execution of a written agreement, dubbed the 2012 agreement, in the claim.

Tugushev does not have a copy of the signed agreement but has an unsigned draft, which states the three have “directly and/or indirectly together full ownership control over a group of Russian fishing companies (the 'Group')".

The 2012 agreement as signed was in materially identical terms as this draft, Tugushev claims. He does not explain why he has no copy of the signed agreement.

Then, on Nov. 14, 2011, a company named Laxagone Investment was incorporated in Hong Kong by the three parties, with the intention that Tugushev would ultimately own it, according to the claim.

From 2005 to December 2011, partly over the time he was in prison, Tugushev claims he received dividends from the Norebo Group, principally in cash.

This is evidenced by dividend schedules prepared by Petrik at Orlov “and/or” Roth's instruction in around December 2011 that are part of the claim. 

Between Oct. 3, 2005, and Dec. 6, 2011, according to a table produced for Orlov by Petrik entitled "Dividend Distribution Summary", entities and individuals associated with Tugushev were paid $14,748,720.53 in dividends.

 This document also shows Roth was paid dividends totaling $25,369,948.46, Tugushev claims.

Bloomberg pins Ocean Trawlers co-founder Orlov’s wealth at $1bn

From 2012, following the incorporation of Laxagone, Tugushev claimed he received $2.07m in cash as dividend payments from Norebo at the instruction of Olga Savina, the head of the legal, accountancy and administrative services for the company.

Also, he claims to have received several other payments from Laxagone between 2012 and 2015.

In December 2012, $500,000 was paid to his daughter, Alisa; in July 2014, $1m was paid to Gavan, a company connected to Tugushev; in September 2014, $500,000 paid directly to him; and in April 2015, another $1.15m was reportedly paid directly to him.

“These payments were documented as loans but were in fact advanced in lieu of dividends owing” to Tugushev, the claim states. It was intended by Orlov, Roth and Tugushev that the loans would be repaid by the declaration of dividends once the structure for the payment of the same was in place.

On April 20, 2015, a shareholders agreement was entered into between Orlov, Roth, and two companies controlled by Tugushev, Laxagone and Foreson International. This entitled Foreson to subscribe for preference shares in Laxagone and to be paid preference dividends, according to the claim.

Foreson was a company set up and used by Tugushev to receive dividends from Norebo, such as one of $2.5m paid on June 19, 2015.

Almor Atlantika ‘conspiracy’

The claim from Tugushev goes into detail about what is termed the Almor Atlantika, or AA, conspiracy. It is alleged that between Dec. 12, 2002 and June 15, 2011, Orlov, Petrik and Roth “entered into a combination or understanding with each other” to take control of Tugushev’s shares in Almor Atlantika, the holding company he claims he understood that he controlled around a third of.

According to Tugushev, the alleged conspiracy was “hatched” in London, where Petrik has lived from at least 2001 and where Orlov lived from at least 2005, according to the claim. 

“Much of the business of the Norebo Group was conducted and administered from England. In particular, most of the office staff of the Norebo Group were based in its Maidenhead offices,” the document states.

Roth has ‘mixed feelings’ on Ocean Trawlers, Karat share sale

In 2016, Tugushev claims he discovered that, in December 2015, Orlov had “falsely informed” the main investigative directorate of the city of Moscow Investigative Committee (more on this below) -- as part of what is dubbed the IC investigation in the document -- that he’d disposed of his shareholding in Almor Atlantika in 2003.

Up to this point, Tugushev said he understood he owned a 25.4% of Almor Atlantika as shareholder and a further 9% through nominees.

Tugushev's “subsequent investigations led him to discover that his entire shareholding” in Almor Atlantika had been “misappropriated” by Orlov and Petrik, he claims.

When Almor Atlantika was incorporated, Tugushev claims his understanding was he had been allotted 34,828 shares. However, he claims that, as part of the IC investigation, Orlov alleged on Dec. 7, 2015, that 14,510 of the shares had not, in fact, been allotted to him. According to Orlov’s alleged claim, they had been returned to the treasury of Almor Atlantika on Dec. 14, 2002.

It “appears that”, the claim alleges, these shares were then transferred to Norebo Invest -- ultimately owned “on behalf” of Orlov and Roth -- on July 3, 2003. On the same day, Tugushev's remaining shares (20,318 shares, or 14.8%) in Almor Atlantika were also allegedly transferred to Norebo Invest.

“As at that time, the share register of AA [Almor Atlantika] was maintained by AA itself; and this transfer is recorded in the share register,” the claim states.

This left Tugushev with no shares in Almor Atlantika. Tugushev “did not know of or consent to these transfers of his shareholding” in Almor Atlantika, which he alleges was orchestrated by Orlov and Petrik.

A letter from Norebo Invest dated Feb. 26, 2004, reportedly stated the shareholding of the company was held by Petrik (99%) and Romanovskii (1%).

“lt is now known that the result was that by August 2008, CJSC Norebo Invest was the registered shareholder of the entire shareholding in AA,” the claim states.

Then, Tugushev claims Norebo Holding acquired a 99% shareholding in Norebo Invest. On Dec. 29, 2007.

On Feb. 2, 2011 Norebo Holding acquired the entire shareholding in Almor Atlantika from Norebo Invest.

Roth sells stake in Ocean Trawlers parent

As at that date, Tugushev claims Orlov held 76 shares in Norebo Holding and a Tsukanov held 24 shares.

Roth then allegedly acquired shares in Norebo Holding as follows: 10 on May 6, 2011, as per a share purchase agreement (SPA) with Orlov dated March 1, 2011 and 23 shares on June 15, 2011 from Tsukanov.

“Orlov produced a forged SPA showing this transaction supposedly taking place” on April 1, 2003, signed by Romanovskii and a forged signature of Tugushev, the latter claims.

In a written statement provided by Orlov on Dec. 7, 2015 as part of the aforementioned IC investigation, he alleged that he paid $30m to Tugushev in return for the transfer of his 14.8% shareholding -- equating to 20,318 shares -- in Almor Atlantika to Norebo Invest in 2003. “That was a lie and no such payment has ever been made,” Tugushev claims.

According to the claim, Orlov gave a written statement on Sept. 7, 2016, as part of a criminal investigation from the Moscow police, which was opened on Aug. 19, 2016. In this statement, he is alleged to have written Orlov alleged that the nominal value of RUB 20,318 – about $300 -- that Tugushev allegedly received for his shares “was a fair value of those shares, given the indebtedness of AA at that time. That was also a lie”, the document states.

Norebo restructure, fishing, processing investments: 2013-2015

The AA conspiracy is alleged to have taken place between Dec. 12, 2002 and June 15, 2011, with the claim also alleging another conspiracy, the Norebo conspiracy, starting in 2015. 

Between these two, from 2013-2015, Undercurrent reported on various changes in the group. 

In 2013, Undercurrent reported on a restructuring going on at what is now Norebo. 

“The purpose of the restructuring is to create one transparent group of companies, with a Russian holding on the top,” a spokesman told Undercurrent, in January 2013. “We are already today transparent, but by restructuring to one group we will also establish a more effective management."

In December, the Russian Federal Anti-monopoly Service had announced it had approved Roth’s application to buy 33% of a Murmansk-based company, ‘Soyuz Holding’ («Союз Холдинг»), which owns two Russian Far Eastern fishing companies.

This move, Undercurrent was told, was part of this restructuring. At the time, TTC was said to be 50/50 owned by Orlov and Roth. 

Then, in March of 2013, Undercurrent reported that four companies had splintered from Murmansk Trawl Fleet, part of Norebo and where Tugushev started his career. 

On March 26, an announcement by the Marine Stewardship Council said two offshoots from MTF were going it alone for MSC certification. The new companies, Strelets and Eridan, were part of four divisions that splintered from MTF in 2012, an MTF executive explained to Undercurrent, at the time. In 2012, MTF 1, 2, 3 and 4 splintered from MTF to form four separate companies, respectively called Eridan, Feniks, Taurus and Strelets, she said. These are now known as the FEST group of companies. 

Then, in June, it emerged that Norebo's MTF had bought West African fishing assets from Iceland's Samherji, know as Katla Seafood. In September the next year, Samherji revealed it made €50m on the sale. 

Towards the end of that year, Norebo's MTF's unsuccessfully tried to buy rival Arkhangelsk Trawl Fleet (ATF), which was being sold by the Russian government. On Nov. 18, 2013, a spokesman for the company told Undercurrent the Russian Federal Antimonopoly Service had withdrawn its approval to buy ATF "previously given to MTF". 

In July 2014, Undercurrent reported what was then named Ocean Trawlers -- the global sales arm of the Russian fishing companies -- had restructured the ownership of the company under Norebo Holding. 

Ocean Trawlers was integrated into Karat Group at the end of 2013, having previously been under the ownership of a TTC, it was said, at the time. 

“Transferring Ocean Trawlers under the same holding company as other companies in the Karat Group gives a clear structure of a vertically integrated group, from fishing ground to customer,” said the company, at the time. 

At the end of 2014, Norebo's fishing arm acquired Far East fishing company Sakhalin Leasing Flot, adding to the pollock quota the company controls after deals for Akroz and Roliz in 2011. At the time, it was said Sakhalin Leasing Flot had quota of around 60,000 metric tons of pollock. 

Norebo ‘conspiracy’: 2015

The document also outlines what Tugushev dubs the “Norebo conspiracy”, which he claims originated from a TTC meeting in London held by Orlov, Roth and Brun-Lie, the Norwegian lawyer, between Sept. 14-16, 2015.

After the meeting, Orlov and Roth allegedly denied Tugushev's interest in the Norebo Group and ceased payment of dividends to him.

Prior to this, in July 2015, Tugushev claims to have discovered that Roth had blocked Laxagone from making a dividend payment to him scheduled to be paid that month.

On Sept. 2, 2015, Tugushev and his lawyer, Alexander Konkov, met Brun-Lie at his offices in the Norwegian capital Oslo to discuss the payment of dividends, his interest in Norebo and the future conduct of its affairs.

At the meeting, Brun-Lie allegedly stated he was chairman of Norebo and that he acted on the instructions of Orlov and Roth.

Tugushev and Konkov requested that Brun-Lie check whether he had signed copies of the 1998 and 2012 agreements and asked him to discuss with Orlov and Roth the formal documenting of Tugushev's one-third interest in the Norebo Group and the recommencement of dividend payments to him.

Following the meeting, on the same day, Brun-Lie sent an email to Konkav, the contents of which he said had been approved by Orlov and Roth at the TTC meeting in London.

According to the claim: “The email from Mr Brun-Lie stated, 'I have discussed AT's position [in] relation to dividend with VO and MR and they do not consider the arrangement as an JO obligation to pay dividends but only a mechanism for distribution of dividends. With respect to shares VO does not recognize that [AT] has a legal right to any of his shares but that he will stand by his previous commitments to compensate AT adequately. A formal transfer of shares cannot therefore take place.'"

Following this meeting and the email from Brun-Lie, a settlement offer of $60m was made by Orlov and rejected by Mr Tugushev. No further dividends have been paid, he claims.

In November 2015, Tugushev's lawyer, Konkav, wrote to Orlov's UK-based solicitors, Macfarlanes. In emails dated Nov. 27, 2015 and Dec. 1, 2015 Konkov set out Tugushev's case as to his one-third entitlement of the Norebo Group and asked Macfarlanes to confirm:

Whether Orlov disputed that Tugushev was entitled to a one-third shareholding in Norebo and that Orlov was a nominal holder of Tugushev's shares; and whether Orlov's position was that he had no knowledge of the June 2012 agreement, or that he never signed it or that he does not have the original.

Macfarlanes' response, dated Dec. 11, 2015, stated that they did not accept the statements Tugushev made and that it was for him to identify how his alleged entitlement arose.

Russian cases: 2015-2016

After the London TTC meeting, starting in late 2015 and going into 2016, Tugushev claims civil and criminal proceedings were brought about in Russia, which Orlov was allegedly behind, in order to deprive him of his interest in Norebo.

On Nov. 24, 2015 a civil case was “purportedly” started in the Koptevskiy District Court of Moscow by Tugushev against Orlov. However, Tugushev claims he had nothing to do with these proceedings and had no knowledge of them at the time. “He only became aware of them approximately a year later (in November 2016), when one of his lawyers was searching online and, by chance, found reference to them,” the claim document states.

On Nov. 30, 2015, Orlov filed what is termed the IC complaint in the claim, with the main investigative directorate of the investigative committee for Moscow, requesting it to investigate allegations against Tugushev of extortion and coercion. Tugushev calls the complaint false and the allegations spurious. 

Those allegations included a “false complaint” that Tugushev had commenced another set of civil proceedings against Orlov and Roth in Lokhi, a small town in Karelia, Russia, “which he had not”, according to the claim document.

The complaint triggered an investigation that lasted four months before being closed, the claim document states. On April 19, 2016, the investigator in charge refused to open criminal proceedings against Tugushev and others who were the subject of the probe, it continues.

Koptevskiy proceedings

The first of the three processes which Tugushev claims Orlov engineered against him in 2015-2016, the legal action brought in his name against his co-founder he claims no knowledge of, are covered in more detail in the claim.

Those proceedings “purport” to show Tugushev “allegedly” instructing a lawyer called "Mr Dryndin" to start the proceedings on his behalf.

The purpose of what Tugushev said is a sham process was to seek a declaration that:

In 1998 Orlov, Tugushev and Roth founded a general partnership under English law
A declaration that in 2003 Orlov and Tugushev concluded a trust agreement according to which Orlov was the nominal holder of Tugushev's share in the partnership for Tugushev's benefit
To set aside the trust agreement concluded between Orlov and Tugushev in 2003
To award Tugushev against Orlov $10m in dividends that were due to Tugushev for the years 2014 and 2015 under the partnership agreement
A declaration that Tugushev was entitled to 33.3% share in Karat Holding, the Russian holding company that forms a substantial part of the overall group, was temporarily held on trust by Orlov

According to Tugushev, a “fake” power of attorney purportedly signed by him in Cyprus on Nov. 20, 2015, was submitted in the Koptevskiy proceedings claiming to show that Dryndin was authorized to act on Tugushev's behalf.

Tugushev claims he did not sign any power of attorney in favor of Dryndin, nor did he visit Cyprus at that time. 

Although, “notably”, Orlov had invited him to do so on Nov. 16, 2015, he claims.

Orlov's interests in the Koptevskiy proceedings were represented by a man named Golubev, “pursuant to a power of attorney” dated Nov. 19, 2015, containing identical wording to Tugushev's “fake” power of attorney in favor of Dryndin, Tugushev alleges.

The original of Tugushev' s fake power of attorney, together with fake seals, were found among Golubev's possessions after his arrest in connection with a separate matter on March 7, 2018, he claims, without going into more detail on what this separate matter was.

On Dec. 18, 2015, less than a month after the Koptevskiy proceedings were issued, a court judgment was awarded in favor of Orlov, allegedly unbeknown to Tugushev.

Then, on Jan. 12, 2016, an appeal against this judgment to the Moscow city court “was purportedly commenced on behalf of Mr Tugushev, but which he did not commence and of which he had no knowledge at the time”.

On March 18, 2016, the court annulled the decision of the Koptevskiy court on the basis the latter “had no jurisdiction to resolve a partnership dispute and that the appropriate forum was the arbitrage (commercial) court”, the claim document states.

On Aug. 17, 2016, Orlov filed another complaint against Tugushev with the police department for the southern circuit of the city of Moscow “in connection with a separate allegations of extortion said to arise, inter alia, from threats that he was allegedly receiving via telephone calls from one Mr Dzhamaldaev allegedly acting on Mr Tugushev's behalf between February and April 2016”, the claim document states.

The Moscow police opened an investigation on Aug. 19, 2016. Then, on Dec. 27, 2016, Tugushev was arrested in connection with this. According to the claim, Tugushev was informed by the police that the investigation had been discontinued on Dec. 11, 2017.

Roth share sale: 2016

In April 2016, Tugushev claims Roth sold his one-third share in Norebo Holding to Orlov.

The purchase price was $330m, according to a report prepared by KPMG dated April 2017 and entitled "Russian M&A Review 2016", states the claim. Tugushev "believes that the value of the Norebo Group has since increased", however. 

In June 2016, Undercurrent reported the sale by Roth. 

He later confirmed this to Undercurrent, but declined to comment on the reasons for the sale or the value.

“My feelings are mixed,” he said, of the sale, at the time. 

"I am proud of what I was a part of building from scratch and I will probably look back at this with great pleasure, with a dash of sentimentality,” he said.

“But, most things come to an end, and I am now focused on what the future holds,” said Roth. “One the one side, I will miss being a part of this organization. On the other, I am now free to pursue other possibilities in life. And that feels good, too.”

Later that year, Norebo revealed its latest investment, a new processing plant in Murmansk.

The company, which officially opened the plant on Sept. 9, had invested around RUB 1.4bn ($21.5m) in the plant at the time. 

According to a company spokesman, the total budget for the plant is RUB 2bn, with the additional funds to be used to expand the product range from frozen and fresh cod and haddock fillets.

Bloomberg billionaire, Norwegian proceedings: 2017

Prior to his arrest at the end of 2016, on Dec. 20, Tugushev's Norwegian lawyers sent a pre-action letter to Brun-Lie seeking, amongst other things, the disclosure of the 1998 agreement and other documents in the possession of the defendants relating to his ownership of the group.

However, Tugushev was arrested within seven days of this letter being sent.

He was detained by the police for two days and then placed under house arrest until March 25, 2017, following which he was released on bail subject to undertakings not to leave Moscow, according to the claim.

While this was happening, in January 2018, Orlov gave an interview to Bloomberg, which estimated his wealth at $1bn. Orlov told Bloomberg he feels the value is “much more moderate” than this, however. 

He cited “country risks” as the reason, most notably a lack of clarity about a new quota system the government is preparing to introduce favoring companies that order trawlers from Russian shipyards, a potential boon for newer, smaller businesses.

Also, Orlov told Bloomberg the company has spent about $600m in the past decade to expand its fleet.

“I never imagined I could create such a huge company,” Orlov said, in what was his first foreign media interview. “Now we want to be where the end-users are -- retail chains, food services. We see potential here.”

Bloomberg also mentioned Tugushev, who was under house arrest and charged with extortion regarding his ownership claims at the time, according to a report from TASS, the government-owned news agency. 

According to Bloomberg, Tugushev declined to discuss his legal troubles and hasn’t responded to requests for further comment since his arrest. 

In June 2017, Undercurrent also covered another expansion from the company, as it acquired a production and distribution center located in Klin, a town in the Moscow region.

Norebo uses the facility to store products from its fishing companies -- pollock, cod, haddock and pelagic fish from Far East and west of Russia -- as well as repacking products in retail packages.

Then, in September Norebo launched a new retail brand on the Russian market, Borealis (see below), produced in the plant in Murmansk. 

Later that year, on Aug. 4, Tugushev commenced proceedings against Orlov, Roth, Brun-Lie and an executive named Helge Klock in Norway, seeking disclosure of the 1998 agreement and other documents in the possession of the defendants relating to his ownership of the Norebo.

In the proceedings, Orlov “falsely” said Tugushev “does not have and never has had any interest in the Norebo Group”, the claim states. 

According to the claim, Orlov’s defense -- dated Sept. 5 -- states that, "during the period of cooperation, Tugushev never owned 1/3 of any company" and that, "Neither in 1998 nor at any other time, was there any agreement between the parties that they would own 1/3 of all prospective business created by the parties in the future".

In Roth’s defense in the Norwegian process, he states, “it is Orlov which is now the formal owner of the Fishery Group".

At the end of 2017, Norebo announced it would cease to trade under the Ocean Trawlers name, as part of a corporate rebranding which would also see its frozen-at-sea (FAS) fillets from the Atlantic and Pacific sold under one brand. 

UK-based sales arms Ocean Trawlers Europe and Ocean Trawlers Hong Kong have been renamed Norebo Europe and Norebo Hong Kong, Stephen Collyer, then Norebo’s managing director for all export markets, told Undercurrent, at the Groundfish Forum in Lisbon, Portugal.

The group’s FAS products will now be sold under new names, “Ocean Spirit” and “Glacialis”, he said.

Glacialis will be the name for FAS fillets of Atlantic and Pacific cod, haddock, saithe and pollock, which the company sells to chefs, restaurants and fish and chip shops, he told Undercurrent.

Previously, the FAS cod, haddock and saithe had been sold under the “Atlantika” brand, which did not work so well for fish caught in the Pacific, said Collyer, who left the company earlier in 2018. In 2016, the company started producing shatterpack pollock fillets on its Russian Far East fleet, and also FAS fillets of Pacific cod, he said, at the time. 

Two of the company’s fleet of eight longliners are now converted for producing FAS fillets, with the possibility of moving more over, said Collyer. The company’s whole frozen fish products and industrial blocks, sold to industrial processors and distributors, will be marketed under the Ocean Spirit brand, not Ocean Trawlers, he said. 

$35m offer, London lawsuit: 2018 

After all the above, Tugushev contends he and Orlov met on Feb. 16 of this year to discuss Norebo. At the meeting, Tugushev claims Orlov offered to pay him $35m in return for Tugushev withdrawing any claims over a share in Norebo.

Orlov proposed that this payment would be made upon Tugushev filing a claim against him in the Murmansk arbitration court, in Russia.

Tugushev did not accept Orlov's offer “and, with the benefit of legal advice”, now “considers this to have been a ruse” by Orlov to seek to confer jurisdiction upon the Russian courts and thereby to avoid the jurisdiction of the English courts and “the proper determination” of his claims.

After this meeting, in March 2018, Golubev, who Tugushev contends was used by Orlov in the Russian proceedings in 2015, was arrested.

This, according to the claim, led to the discovery of Tugushev's forged power of attorney and company seals at Golubev's house. On May 18, Tugushev's lawyer was provided with a copy of the statement made by Orlov in the Moscow police investigation dated Nov. 8, 2017 by which Orlov confirmed that Golubev represented him on the basis of a power of attorney.

“It is only now, in the light of these recent events, and with the benefit of legal advice (in respect of which privilege is not waived) that Mr Tugushev has been able to piece together the nature and extent of the complex Norebo Group Conspiracy which has been perpetrated by the Defendants as set out above in order to deprive him of his one-third interest in the Norebo Group,” the claim alleges.

On July 23, the claim used as the basis for this story was filed in the UK's High Court. The case continues.

title: Labor issues in Thai fisheries remain ‘rampant’
content:
Forced labor and other rights abuses are widespread in Thailand’s fishing fleets despite government commitments to comprehensive reforms, Human Rights Watch (HRW) has said in a new report.

The report -- “Hidden chains: forced labor and rights abuses in Thailand’s fishing industry,” -- was released with a 15-minute film at a briefing at the European Parliament on Jan. 23.

It describes how migrant fishers from neighboring countries in Southeast Asia are often trafficked into fishing work, prevented from changing employers, not paid on time, and paid below the minimum wage, claimed HRW. Migrant workers do not receive Thai labor law protections, and are denied the right to form a labor union.

Even though Thailand has received a "yellow card" warning and could face a ban on exporting seafood to the EU because of its illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing practices -- and the US has placed Thailand on the tier 2 watch list in its latest Trafficking in Persons (TIP) report -- HRW has found widespread shortcomings in the implementation of new government regulations and resistance in the fishing industry to reforms, it said.

“Consumers in Europe, the US, and Japan should be confident that their seafood from Thailand didn’t involve trafficked or forced labor,” said Brad Adams, HRW Asia director. “Yet despite high-profile commitments by the Thai government to clean up the fishing industry, problems are rampant.”

The NGO interviewed 248 current and former fishers, almost all from Burma and Cambodia, as well as Thai government officials, boat owners and captains, civil society activists, fishing association representatives, and United Nations agency staff. Of those interviewed, 95 were former fishers who survived documented incidents of human trafficking, while the other 153 were, with a few exceptions, still active fishers. The research was carried out in every one of Thailand’s major fishing ports from 2015 to 2017.

The Thai government responded to media reports on human trafficking and brutalization of fishers on Thai fishing boats in 2014 and 2015 by scrapping antiquated fishing laws, and issuing a new ordinance to regulate the fishing industry.

Some measures, such as vessel monitoring systems and limiting time at sea to 30 days, have led to important improvements for fishers, HRW acknowledged.

"However, measures to address forced labor and other important labor and human rights protection measures often prioritize form over results. The labor inspection regime is largely a theatrical exercise for international consumption. For example, under the PIPO [port-in, port-out] system, Human Rights Watch found officials speak to ship captains and boat owners and check documents but rarely conduct interviews with migrant fishers."

Despite significant resources provided to the Thai Ministry of Labour and its departments, there is no effective or systematic inspection of fishers working aboard Thai vessels, the NGO said.

For example, in its 2015 report on human trafficking, Thailand revealed that inspections of 474,334 fishery workers failed to identify a single case of forced labor. More recently, over 50,000 inspections of fishers implausibly did not find a single instance where laws on conditions and hours of work, wages, treatment on board, and other issues had been violated.

Requirements that fishers hold their own identification documents, receive and sign a written contract, and be paid monthly are frustrated by employer practices which hold fishers in debt bondage and ensure they cannot change employers. The lack of a stand-alone forced labor offense in Thai criminal law leaves a huge gap in law enforcement and deterrence, it said.

“The Thai government’s lack of commitment means that regulations and programs to prevent forced labor in the fishing industry are failing,” Adams said. “International producers, buyers, and retailers of Thai seafood have a key role in ensuring that forced labor and other abuses come to an end.”

Situation worsening?

In some respects, the situation has gotten worse in recent years, HRW found. For instance, the government’s “pink card” registration scheme, introduced in 2014 to reduce the number of undocumented migrants working in Thailand, has tied fishers’ legal status to specific locations and employers whose permission is needed to change jobs, creating an environment ripe for abuse.

“Some employers allow us to leave, but some will claim we must pay off debts first. For example, if I can pay 25,000 baht [$762] … he may allow me to leave, but if he isn’t satisfied … I would have to pay whatever he demanded" –Thet Phyo Lin, Burmese fisher

The pink card scheme, as well as practices where migrant workers are not informed about or provided copies of required employment contracts, have become means through which unscrupulous ship owners and skippers conceal coercion and deception behind a veneer of compliance. In this way, routine rights abuses go unchecked by complacent government officials who are content to rely on paper records submitted by fishing companies as proof of compliance, it claimed.

Thai labor law makes it difficult for migrant workers to assert their rights. Fishers’ fear of retaliation and abuse by boat captains and vessel owners is a major factor, but Thailand also restricts the rights of migrant workers to organize into labor unions to take collective action. Under the Labour Relations Act of 1975, any person who does not have Thai nationality is legally prohibited from establishing a union or serving as union leader.

“No one should be fooled by regulations that look good on paper but are not properly enforced,” Adams said. “The EU and US urgently need to increase pressure on Thailand to protect the rights, health, and safety of fishers.”

ILLEGAL fishing issue

Last month, a paper produced by NGO Sea Around Us -- published in the journal Frontiers in Marine Science -- claimed that "Thailand hides big numbers when it comes to its fish catches in neighboring waters".

Fish catches by Thailand’s distant-water fleet fishing throughout the Indo-Pacific are
almost seven times higher than what the country reports to the Food and Agriculture
Organization of the United Nations, the study claimed.

"In 2014 alone, the Asian country caught 3.7 million metric tons of fish outside its exclusive economic zone, but reported only 247,000t. This figure, although substantial,
represents a decline from peak numbers reached in the mid-1990s when the more
relaxed rules of Thailand’s neighbors allowed for massive catches of over 7 million metric tons per year. Back then, as much as 80% of the catch was unreported and
much of it likely obtained illegally," the study said. 

“Fishing by Thai vessels outside of Thailand’s waters takes place around the South
China Sea, the Indonesian archipelago, the Bay of Bengal as well as the Western
Indian Ocean, under both official and unofficial agreements, as well as illegally,” said
Brittany Derrick, lead author of the study and a researcher with the Sea Around Us
initiative at the University of British Columbia’s Institute for the Oceans and Fisheries.

title: Faroes ends WTO proceedings against EU following end to herring sanctions
content:
The Faroese government said the country has terminated its World Trade Organization dispute proceedings against the European Union.

The EU trade measures against the Faroe Islands were lifted this week, and the parties are no longer in disagreement, said the Faroese government in a statement on Aug. 21.

The proceedings, which it started in November last year, were suspended in June after the EU confirmed its intention to lift its ban on Faroese herring and mackerel imports.

On Aug. 16, the Faroese government also referred parts of the dispute relating to the Atlanto-Scandian herring to an arbitral tribunal under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, specifically claiming that the EU’s use of coercion is not only inappropriate conduct in international cooperation on the conservation of shared fish stocks, but is also inconsistent with international law.

But yesterday the Faroe Islands and the EU jointly requested the arbitral tribunal to terminate the proceedings.

“I am pleased that the Faroe Islands and the EU have managed to resolve the disagreement amicably, and that we can now move forward to promote a new era of stronger and broader bilateral cooperation”, said Faroese prime minister Kaj Leo Holm Johannesen.

title: Thailand downgraded to Tier 3 on US TIP report
content:
The US State Department has downgraded Thailand to a Tier 3 ranking on its 2014 Trafficking in Persons (TIP) Report, released Friday at 9 a.m. with a presentation by Secretary of State John Kerry.

The nation joins Iran, North Korea and Saudi Arabia — among 21 nations in total listed Tier 3 this year — in the ranking. This is the lowest ranking out of four tiers when including the Tier 2 Watch List — the second to lowest ranking, which Thailand has occupied for three years.

The TIP report does not contain any mechanism to impose trade barriers, and in fact, it states that any US opposition to assistance governments may face excludes trade-related assistance.

The consequences, however, could affect lending in the country. The US could decide to put pressure on international financial institutions, such as the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, not to lend to Thailand.

This could impact the seafood industry, considering the World Bank does have involvement in Fisheries Improvement Projects (FIPs) there, a source with direct knowledge of the matter told Undercurrent News.

The World Bank has also been known to lend to aquaculture projects and other economic boosting business endeavors.

Shrimp importers in the US have long been talking of the impact on the business, going back to GOAL of 2012, when the possible downgrading emerged as a big topic.

A major US buyer, speaking to Undercurrent at the time, said even being on the Tier 2 list was being “one foot in the grave and another on a banana peel”.

Now Thailand has been downgraded to Tier 3, there will surely be some impact on the sector.

Panisuan Jamnarnwej, president of the Thai Frozen Foods Association (TFFA) said a Tier 3 ranking will “definitely” affect the association members’ business.

“However, each company in the TFFA will be able to adjust themselves by, for instance, searching for other markets,” said Jamnarnwej.

Shrimp sector sources told Undercurrent at the start of the week that a downgrade could drive prices in other origins, as US buyers look to move away from Thailand.

Some sources in Thailand actually see the downgrade as a positive, as it will force some change.

Choopong Lueskprasert, managing director of Thai shrimp processor Marine Gold Products, one of the country’s largest processors, told Undercurrent in May that the situation presents a chance to "upgrade" the industry.

“Even if we are lucky and we are not downgraded, we still have to fix this and clean up the industry,” said Lueskprasert.

Overall government fails big time

It was the overall government response, not those in government that worked directly in trying to clean up Thailand’s act, that resulted in the downgrade.

“I want to be very clear — we know, and have worked with, some very good actors in Thailand who are working on the front lines who are doing a very good job,” ambassador Luis CdeBaca, from the Department of State's Office to Monitor and Combat Trafficking in Persons, told press during a conference call Thursday afternoon.

The TIP report reveals the Thai government blatantly ignored some instances of human trafficking and even ventured to punish those that tried to bring them to light.

After reports surfaced in Thai media of trafficking-related complicity by Thai civilian and navy personnel in crimes involving the exploitation of Rohingya asylum seekers from Burma and Bangladesh, the Thai navy “claimed these reports were false and responded by filing criminal defamation charges against two journalists in Thailand for re-printing these reports".

In another instance, the government let a Thai accomplice in forced labor effort go with a sentence of merely three months, having charged him for providing shelter to undocumented immigrants. The full extent of his crime was much more severe than that, considering he had held 14 victims in confinement. Meanwhile, the Burmese men he had conspired with received 30 years in prison.

The Trafficking Victims Protection Act (TVPA) minimum standards, which countries are required to meet in order to be classified as Tier 1, includes that the government prescribe punishment that is “sufficiently stringent to deter and adequately reflects the heinous nature of the offense".

Going a step further, the TIP report repeats claims -- made earlier by the media, most recently the UK's Guardian newspaper -- that the Thai government has been complicit in human trafficking in the fishing industry.

Thai officials allegedly subjected Rohingya asylum seekers, an ethnic group fleeing persecution, to forced labor in Thailand’s commercial fishing sector; yet the government reported no investigations, persecutions or convictions of public officials or private individuals on the matter, the TIP report said.

Thailand’s downgrade is classified as “automatic”, since it is required for any country that is on the Tier 2 Watch list, but it could have been avoided if the country had demonstrated “significant efforts to bring themselves into compliance” with the Trafficking Victim Protections Act (TVPA) minimum standards, which require governments to vigorously investigate and prosecute severe forms of human trafficking, as well as comply with a long and detailed list of other minimum measures needed to prevent human rights atrocities, such as identifying ways to prevent participation in international sex tourism.

Improvement, but not enough

The report does give Thailand some credit for improvement, despite the lower rating this year.

“The government of Thailand improved its anti-trafficking data collection,” the TIP report said. “It reported convicting 225 traffickers under the 2008 anti-trafficking law and related statutes in 2013.”

However, this was far from sufficient to raise Thailand to a Tier 2 status, which would have meant it was not meeting the TVPA minimum requirements but was making “significant efforts” to do so.

Human trafficking remains a big economic sector in Thailand, particularly in Thailand’s seafood industry. Approximately 17% of surveyed fishermen, who primarily worked on short haul vessels spending less than one month at sea, experienced forced labor conditions, often due to threats of financial penalty including not being fully remunerated for work already performed.

US aid loss at risk

US opposition to international banks lending is by no means inevitable — just a possible outcome.

“…Governments of countries on Tier 3 may be subject to certain restrictions on bilateral assistance, whereby the US government may withhold or withdraw non-humanitarian, non-trade-related foreign assistance,” the TIP report states. This would take effect Oct. 1.

Last year, the White House did impose full sanctions on Cuba, which has been ranked Tier 3 every year since 2007, as well as Iran and North Korea, CdeBaca told press during a conference call on Thursday. However, it chose not to impose sanctions on Russia, China and Uzbekistan when they ranked Tier 3 last year due to a desire to promote their national interests.

Froced labor hit shrimp processing too

The long-anticipated fall to a Tier 3 ranking on the report is more than just proof that being a beloved US tourist destination can’t exempt a country’s labor rights abuses with from the US State Department scrutiny.

It also shows that both Thailand and Bangladesh have human trafficking problems in their shrimp industries.

In Thailand, there were no new developments in the Thai Supreme Court’s consideration of an appeal of a 2009 conviction, upheld in 2011, where two offenders were found guilty of subjecting 73 victims to forced labor in a shrimp-peeling factory.

Both offenders remained free on bail during the reporting period for a second year in 2013.

Thailand’s shrimp industry is not alone here. In Bangladesh, families are subjected to debt bondage — a form of slavery where a worker is required to work for no pay until they have paid off a debt they supposedly owe the employer — in the shrimp farming industry in the southeast.

Cruel bosses, vulnerable people, spell disaster anywhere

The annual congressionally mandated report, put in place in 2000 through the TVPA, was created to supplement the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime (the Palermo Protocol).

It defines trafficking in persons and human trafficking as umbrella terms for the act of recruiting, harboring, transporting, providing or obtaining a person for compelled labor or commercial sex acts through the use of force, fraud or coercion.

“At the heart of this phenomenon is the traffickers’ goal of exploiting and enslaving their victims and the myriad coercive and deceptive practices they use to do so,” says the report.

Human trafficking includes sex trafficking, child sex trafficking, forced labor, bonded labor, involuntary domestic servitude and debt bondage.

It is a problem in every country in the world, including the United States. Although the US received a Tier 1 rating, it still has human trafficking problems, CdeBaca said.

“We are seeing that when you have unscrupulous and cruel bosses and vulnerable people, then you have a recipe for human trafficking, and that’s as true in Washington D.C. and the suburbs as it is in countries around the world,” CdeBaca said.

title: Thai companies questioned over cutting of working days
content:
The Thai Frozen Foods Association (TFFA) has faced questions over its commitment to seeing members pay 75% wages to employees whose working week has been cut short.

A number of Thailand's largest shrimp export companies have been forced to reduce working weeks from six days to five, due to a lack of shrimp raw material following the impact of early mortality syndrome (EMS).

In this event the companies are obliged to pay their workers at 75% normal wage for this forced second day off – something which research carried out by campaigners suggests is not happening, according to human rights activist Andy Hall.

In an email to TFFA, Hall asked what the the association's analysis and position was on the actions of, in particular, Charoen Pokphand Foods, Marine Gold, KST and “likely other TFFA members”, in changing the working week.

"What is TFFA analysis and position on the actions in particularly of CP, Marine Gold, KST and likely other TFFA members in changing the working week from 6 to 5 days and thus not paying workers compensation at the rate of 75% for additional days off caused by the EMS disease?" wrote Hall. "Do you consider this legal under existing Thai labour protection and labour relations law?"

In the email, Hall said his "significant amount of research" had shown firms are bypassing section 75 of Thailand's labor protection act by getting employees to sign consent to changing working procedures, in a process it has been suggested is not being fully explained or understood, especially by non-Thai workers.

There is also "extensive evidence" of signature forgeries and coercion to sign, said Hall.

The activist is finalizing an assessment of the situation with a team of lawyers, and has formally written to the TFFA to ask the body if it stands by a statement made in early 2013, telling companies it expects them to pay the 75% wage rate.

Research has reportedly also found illegalities in working conditions, accepting of 'recruitment fees' for work applications (which is unlawful), and laborers without work permits, he said.

title: Faroes to challenge EU in WTO over herring, mackerel sanctions
content:
The Faroe Islands have started dispute settlement proceedings against the European Union under the World Trade Organization to challenge the EU’s trade sanctions against Faroese herring and mackerel.

The sanctions, introduced on Aug. 28, ban all imports of herring and mackerel products from the Faroe Islands into the EU and also deny access to EU ports by vessels transporting these products.

The measures implemented by the EU are in clear contravention of basic provisions of the WTO agreement, said the Faroese prime minister's office in a statement on Monday.

"Contrary to claims by the EU that the measures are a means to conserve the Atlanto-Scandian herring, the coercive measures implemented by the EU against the Faroe Islands appear designed to protect EU industry interests," said the statement.

“The EU is a major trading power while the Faroe Islands is very small indeed, with an economy and income heavily dependent upon fisheries, which is ensured by the export of fish products," said the prime minister Kaj Leo Holm Johannesen.

"It is therefore crucial that when the EU takes unfair advantage of its position, the Faroe Islands has recourse to an international mechanism, such as the WTO’s dispute settlement procedures, in order to redress a situation which impairs its rights under the WTO Agreement.”

On Aug. 16, the Faroese government also referred parts of the dispute relating to the Atlanto-Scandian herring to an arbitral tribunal under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, specifically claiming that the EU’s use of coercion is not only inappropriate conduct in international cooperation on the conservation of shared fish stocks, but is also inconsistent with international law.

title: Faroese issue plea to EU over planned sanctions
content:
The Faroe Islands have issued a plea to the EU to hold off on the planned economic sanctions and instead return to negotiations, reports Shetland News.

Faroes fisheries minister Jacob Vestergaard said the EU’s plan to enforce potentially devastating economic measures was based entirely on inaccurate allegations, and asked it to return to talks so a constructive and reasoned management regime for Atlanto-Scandian herring could be agreed upon.

Last month, fisheries commissioner Maria Damanaki announced trade sanctions against the Faroe Islands would be introduced, after talks about pelagic quotas in the north east Atlantic collapsed.

In a letter to the EU commissioner, Vestergaard said the Faroe Islands remain fully committed to the long term management of the herring stock and the scientific advice on the recommended total catch level for 2013.

“I am extremely concerned that the EU’s insistence on finger-pointing and threats of economic coercion are simply a means of distracting attention from the real crux of the problem, which is the need to revise the allocation of shares of the herring stock,” he wrote.

He added that the EU’s proposed one-sided punitive action against the Faroes would circumvent a range of recognized international tools, in particular under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, that are available to coastal states to settle disputes.

In mid May the European commission gave the Faroes a one-month ultimatum in which to respond and remedy the situation - that one month is now up.

title: Russia arrests, charges Ukrainian biologist with treason over Antarctic krill research
content:
Russia has arrested Ukrainian biologist Leonid Pshenichnov, aged 70, and charged him with high treason over his research on Antarctic krill, reports The Guardian.

Pshenichnov, an expert on Antarctic ecosystems and advocate for marine protection, was detained in Russian-occupied Crimea while preparing to attend a conservation conference in Australia.

Russian authorities allege he "defected to the enemy's side" by supporting Ukraine's proposals to limit krill fishing, which they say threatens Russia's industrial interests. 

Ukraine's ambassador to Australia called the detention "illegal" and urged other countries to condemn Russia. Fellow scientists described Pshenichnov as an outstanding researcher in poor health, warning that his imprisonment is "unspeakable."

Moscow has not commented publicly.

title: US dock price-fixing lawsuit seeks millions from Florida wholesalers
content:
A group of fishermen in the US state of Florida have filed a sweeping class-action lawsuit that accuses two seafood wholesalers and processors in the state of colluding to fix prices at the docks for spiny lobsters and stone crabs.

The 47-page complaint, filed in the US District Court for the Southern District of Florida on Monday (Oct. 6), alleges that Miami-based D&D Seafood and Keys Fisheries, as well as their executives Dennis "Snake" Dopico and Gary Graves, led a conspiracy to suppress the dockside prices paid to fishermen from at least 2017 through 2025.

The scheme cheated harvesters out of tens of millions of dollars and destabilized the state's coastal economy, the lawsuit alleges.

The lawsuit identifies commercial fishing businesses Paradise Tails, based in Marathon, Florida, and Reel Faith Fishing, based in Key West, Florida, as well as fishermen Erick Bravo and Jose Hernandez, as the plaintiffs but notes that it has been filed on behalf of a proposed statewide class. It alleges violations of the Sherman Antitrust Act and Florida's Antitrust Act and seeks to recover treble damages -- or three times the actual loss -- plus equitable relief and attorneys' fees and costs.

The filing comes just weeks after Dopico, the vice president of D&D Seafood, pleaded guilty in a federal court for conspiring to fix dock prices paid to stone crab and spiny lobster harvesters, as reported by Undercurrent News.

US seafood exec pleads guilty to stone crab, spiny lobster dock price fixing

Charges against Dopico were initially filed on Sept. 1, alleging that the seafood executive engaged in a price-fixing conspiracy from July 2023 to around April 2025, working with at least four others to "depress, fix, stabilize, and maintain prices for stone crab claws and spiny lobsters purchased from fishermen," ultimately paying these fishermen at "collusive, non-competitive prices."

Prosecutors said text messages they obtained show Dopico agreeing to match prices with his co-conspirators.

"[L]et me know what you do," one message allegedly stated. "I am matching your prices. It's the one we like the most."

The lawsuit further describes the US wholesalers and processors as a "cartel" that would punish competitors who offered higher prices and "blacklisted" fishermen who tried to find higher prices elsewhere. It charges that the tactics drove down income for thousands of small fishing families from the Keys to the gulf coast, forcing some out of business entirely.

Wholesalers and processors allegedly met before each fishing season to agree on how much they would pay for every pound of stone crab and lobster. Throughout the season, they allegedly adjusted prices in unison, maintaining what one participant described in a text message as a commitment to "working together now[,] not against each other."

The civil suit filed this week refers to Dopico's recent plea agreement, which established that D&D's purchases of stone crab claws and spiny lobsters affecting fishermen in Florida totaled approximately $8 million between July 2023 and April 2025.

"Given that at least five co-conspirator firms participated in the unlawful scheme, the total commerce subject to artificially suppressed prices during this period is conservatively estimated to be around $40m on an annualized basis," the complaint states.

China trade war, low prices, immigration crackdown threaten survival of Florida lobster harvesters

The complaint further states that discovery will reveal the full scope of the conspiracy across all defendants and the entire class period, which the plaintiffs believe involves a volume of commerce exceeding $300 million.

"Plaintiffs and class members thus suffered tens of millions of dollars in aggregate economic harm," the filing states.

Florida's roughly 120 harvesters of spiny lobster and stone crabs, who were responsible for about $40 million in landings value for each species during the 2022-23 seasons, are nearly wiped out thanks to the US' trade war with China and immigration crackdown, as reported recently by Undercurrent. Sources mentioned the additional impact of the price-fixing scheme, saying they expect more arrests to follow.

title: Untitled
content:
Rough doesn't begin to describe the start spiny lobster harvesters in the US state of Florida are having to their 2025-26 season, as they suffer from low prices at the docks -- blamed on US president Donald Trump's global trade war -- and also his immigration crackdown.

It's so bad that many of Florida's remaining roughly 120 commercial fishermen that catch both lobster and stone crab will no longer be in business by this time next year, Jerome Young, executive director of the Florida Keys Commercial Fisherman's Association (FKCFA) and himself a harvester, warned Undercurrent News in a recent interview.

Young was echoing the warning given by Jorge Blanco, a third-generation fisherman from the Florida Keys, in a YouTube video titled "Lobster Fisherman Starving at $5 a Pound Ask President For Help." 

Blanco said he wouldn’t be surprised to see 30% of the commercial fishermen in Key West, one of the area's 30 inhabited islands, leave the industry this year.

"If we get a hurricane, 75%, guaranteed," he said.

The dire situation has led the FKCFA to get more vocal with political leaders. Young has issued letters to both Carlos Gimenez, a Republican representing Florida's 28th District in the US House of Representatives, which includes the Florida Keys, and also Howard Lutnick, Trump's commerce secretary, pleading for help. In particular, Young is seeking tariff and labor reforms.

"Florida's commercial fisheries are vital to the state's economy, generating $3.2 billion in income and supporting 76,700 jobs statewide," Young wrote. 

"In the Florida Keys, fisheries contribute 5-8% of total local income and employment, with stone crab and spiny lobster exceeding $80 million in dockside value. However, the industry faces mounting challenges from unfair trade practices, labor shortages and regulatory constraints," he said. 

Landing value could drop to COVID level

Just 1.7 million pounds (784 metric tons) of Caribbean spiny lobster (Panulirus argus) worth nearly $9.2m were landed in the Florida fishery between Aug. 1 and Sept. 20, 2025, the first 51 days of the new commercial season, based on data provided upon request by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FFWCC).

That's an average price of $5.31/lb. Young estimated last week that dock prices had risen slightly to a range of $5.50-$5.60/lb since.

By comparison, harvesters landed 2.2m lbs during the first two months of the 2024-25 season and got paid an average $6.70/lb. Harvesters finished last season with a below-average 4.3m lbs of landings worth just $32.0m, and a higher average price of $7.42/lb.

The 2025-26 season isn't likely to get much better, according to Young. In fact, it's shaping up to be the worst since the COVID-stricken 2020-21 season, when harvesters landed just 3.4m lbs worth $25.7m, an average of $7.51/lb.

During the first two months of that dismal season, harvesters had landed almost 1.8m lbs worth $9.7m, an average of $5.43/lb, for comparison purposes.

In better times, from 2013 to 2015, Florida lobster harvesters landed between 5.4m and 6.4m lbs worth $55m to $57m.
