China takes 80% of the landings

So, what's causing Florida's spiny lobster landings and dock prices to drop so low?

More than anything else, Young blames Trump's trade war with China. China typically imports roughly 80% of the US' landings, Young said, but it isn't buying what it normally does for US lobsters since it recently started imposing additional 35-37% tariffs on them in retaliation for the US' escalation of tariffs on Chinese products.

The latest spat is the latest in the long-running Sino-US trade war begun by Trump in 2018, during his first term in office, which has resulted in a steady erosion of bilateral trade.

"The prices are definitely down, and that's the result of reciprocal tariffs from China because most of our market was Chinese, and we haven't had a chance to pivot to other buyers," Young explained.

"Yeah, they're taking 'em, but we're not getting the price," he said. "I've heard that we might get $0.50, maybe $1.00 more, but we're usually $8.00 or more now. And we're still in the $5.00 area."

The US exported 2,170t of spiny/rock lobster worth $63.0m in 2024, down from the 2,477t worth $77.7m in 2023. That includes also California spiny lobster (Panulirus interruptus) landed between early October and mid-March of the subsequent year.

California accounted for 1,080,242 lbs (490t) of lobster landings worth $20.9m in 2024.

China was the largest destination market by far, taking as much as 1,475t worth $41.5m of the 2024 US exports, with Hong Kong serving as the second-largest market, taking 431t worth $14.2m, as the chart below illustrates.

US spiny/rock lobster harvesters saw a small surge in exports to China in late 2020 thanks to China's initiation of a four-year ban on Australia's spiny lobster, an event referred to in the sector as the "gold rush."

But with retaliatory tariffs in response to those imposed by the Trump administration, Australian lobster exports to China reopened in December 2024, as reported by Undercurrent, and Chinese importers have begun to explore other sources, too.

As noted earlier, prices paid for Florida spiny lobsters normally increase after the season begins. That relates to China showing increased interest in live Florida lobsters starting in about mid-September in advance of multiple national holidays, including the Chinese New Year celebration, which is planned this time for Feb. 17-March 6, 2026.

However, that boost in prices can't be assured this time due to the tariff situation, Young told Undercurrent.

Low dock prices are also helping to suppress catches, he said, as many harvesters are less than eager to spend the money necessary to run their boats and hire crew if they're not guaranteed a profit.

"A lot of guys either aren't fishing or are fishing much less than they normally do, like me personally," Young said. "I only put out half of my gear because of the price, and a lot of other guys did the same, and some guys didn't even put out their gear at all." 

'We can't survive on what they can survive on'

China became the primary destination for US-caught spiny lobsters because cheaper imports from other countries, including the Bahamas, Honduras, Nicaragua and Brazil largely overtook the US market, Young explained.

The Caribbean Basin Initiative (CBI), a US trade preference program established in 1983 by the Caribbean Basin Economic Recovery Act, grants duty-free access for certain imports from eligible Caribbean countries to the US market. 

"The lack of import duty on tails coming from the Caribbean is what killed our domestic market. We just can't compete," Young said.

The chart below, from UCN's trade portal, shows the US importing 8,688t of spiny/rock lobster in 2024 worth $312.5m. The Bahamas was the largest source, accounting for 2,716t worth $101.2m. 

Now the Florida lobster harvesters are hustling to get back into the US market while also trying to rebuild relationships in Europe, Young said. 

"We can't survive on what they can survive on. I would go so far as to say 90% plus, maybe 95% plus of [US] restaurants are serving imports. And that's one of the issues we're trying to address. We need some kind of a tariff or ... restrictions where they have to buy so much from us first or put some kind of a duty to level the playing field, a floor price that we can hold so we can survive off a domestic market again," Young said of the foreign spiny lobster producers. "We will go head-to-head with them on quality all day. We just don't have that opportunity."

Some harvesters have taken to throwing their lobster catch into their trucks and driving up into the middle of the state to sell it on the side of the road, Young said.

"You're keeping your head just barely above water," he said. "You're not making any money. So anything that happens to your boat, if you add into the depreciation of the boat and on mechanical devices on your boat, you're going behind at $5.00/lb."

US buyers caught in price-fixing scheme

Further complicating matters for the Florida harvesters is a recent crackdown on the fixing of prices paid at the dock.

Dennis Dopico, a vice president at Winter Haven, Florida-based seafood processor D&D Seafood Co., pleaded guilty in the US District Court for the Southern District of Florida earlier this month of conspiring to fix prices paid to stone crab and spiny lobster harvesters between July 2023 and April 2025, according to a statement released by federal prosecutors, as reported by Undercurrent News.

Dopico faces up to 10 years in prison and a $1m fine.

The conspiracy related to about $8m worth of commerce, according to the prosecutors. 

The price-fixing crackdown is just beginning, said Young. He expects prosecutors to arrest many more dealers involved in the conspiracy, further limiting the number of buyers available to harvesters.

Immigrant labor made illegal overnight

Florida's lobster harvesters are also confronting a devastating labor crisis due to a sudden shift in immigration policy by the Trump administration and a related crackdown by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), a division of the Department of Homeland Security.

ICE agents have been boarding lobster harvesters' boats since April and arresting undocumented crew. Arrests escalated in early August, when the lobster season began, Young told Undercurrent, confirming a story reported by Florida Keys Weekly.

In many cases, the arrested crew were participants in programs that guaranteed them years of legal work in the US. But unbeknownst to them, the Trump administration terminated the programs earlier this year. Young said he lost eight crew members this season to ICE raids.

In one incident, on Aug. 6, Customs and Border Patrol (CBP) and ICE agents arrested all four of his crew members, who were from Nicaragua and working in the US on the H-2B program. They had five-year work permits but the humanitarian parole program in which they were participants was canceled on July 25, a week before the season, he recounted.

The four men didn't hear or see any of the phone calls or emails that were reportedly sent to notify them of their change in status. 

"You can look at their permits and it says on there that they are authorized to work for five years from this date," he recounted. "They didn't know they were canceled and the business owners didn't know they were canceled."

Spiny lobster traps being loaded on boats in the Florida Keys. Image courtesy of "Fishing for a Living" website.

Young said his small fishing boat was loaded down with traps at the time of the raid, "which is very dangerous." They took everyone but the captain. "My guys are all still in jail," he said.

CBP boasted about the arrest in a social media post, writing, "Four illegal aliens from Nicaragua" aboard a commercial fishing vessel in Marathon, according to the Keys Weekly. 

“Don’t try it … We are watching!” the post said. “Another win for #BorderSecurity.”

While the post generated a fair show of support, other comments from Keys locals weren’t so inviting.

“Show me an American who can keep up with these guys, I’ll hire you right now, then watch you crash on the first trip,” one comment wrote.

“Safe from what? Hardworking individuals who have no prior [arrests] and have legal work permits?” said another. "Legal working permits are being revoked … and those individuals are now being deported.”

Bruce Irwin, a commercial fisherman in the Florida Keys for four decades, told the newspaper about a similar experience.

“My crew came here seeking asylum. They checked in and did everything right, got their visas and work permits, which are cleared by [DHS]. [The crew] come to work, and we’re all legal,” Irwin said. “[ICE] will do a little raid, take people off the boats, so they scare them all to where they all want to leave. If you fight it, they just detain you indefinitely. 

“It’s the most unfair thing I’ve ever seen in my life.”

Unwilling to send his crew to sea with no assurance they’d return home, Irwin said he’s back on the boat – but there’s no replacing the work he’s lost.

“The labor crisis in the Keys is huge … and we get these people, and we’re ecstatic – they’re the best people we’ve had in so long,” he said. “But my guys haven’t been on my boat. I don’t want to be responsible for you getting deported. I’m not living with that.

“It’s crippling many small businesses across the nation. If you want to take the undocumented people that never did any paperwork, then fine. But the guys who came here and did it right, why wouldn’t you want them here? One guy told me this is the best his family’s ever been in his life, and he’s so grateful for what he’s accomplished here in the country.”

So now, as a result of the dramatic loss of labor, there are a handful of workers living in Marathon, Florida, who are working around the clock and being swapped from boat to boat, Young recounted. At one point he was so desperate that he recruited five workers from Alaska, but his new hires "worked one day, said it was too hot and too hard, and then said we're going home." 

Spiny lobster tails. Photo by Florida Fish and Wildlife.

Requests include tariff reform, IUU, labeling enforcement

In his letters to lawmarkers and Trump administration offficals, Young argued the rigid employment windows of the H-2B visa program (October-March and April-September) don't align with the fishing seasons in the Florida Keys.

He suggests a shift to regionally-defined nine-month employment windows as well as a dedicated H-2B allocation for fisheries with a flexible mechanism to allow an adjustment of visa caps. 

The FKCFA leader also is seeking an amendment to the 75-25 rule that requires a crew to be made up primarily of US citizens or permanent residents, saying it's impractical for a small crew. And a requirement that of naming individual crew in waiver applications "is burdensome due to frequent crew changes," the group has advised.

Young said he got a response to his letter to Gimenez from Beatriz Viera, the lawmaker's director of community affairs and constituent services.

Recent ICE enforcement actions were a response to an executive order signed by Trump on Jan. 20 that directed the US attorney general to prosecute criminal offenses related to anyone illegally entering the US and also altered prior policies in such a way that even immigrants with work permits were being detained pending further review of their immigration status, she said.

"It’s important to know each case is different and not all shall be handled in the same way," she wrote. "Also, having a work permit does not necessarily mean they are admitted by USCIS [US Citizenship and Immigration Services] and usually means there is more to discuss on the case."

US secretary of commerce Howard Lutnick. Photo Credit: Commerce.gov

Beatriz said her office was seeking clearer guidance from federal agencies to understand the criteria and procedures being used in the apprehensions.

Tariff reform is also chief among the requests being made by FKCFA. In particular, the group is asking the White House to direct the US Trade Representative to investigate allegations of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing practices and forced labor in the Caribbean lobster trade.

The group is also seeking better enforcement of seafood labeling laws to "protect the integrity of Florida products" and assess the availability of "tariff and non-tariff barriers to ensure fair competition." It is asking for the incorporation of Florida spiny lobster into the president's "America First Seafood Strategy," a reference to an executive order issued in April, as Undercurrent reported.

title: Seven rescued, one dead after fishing vessel sinks off South Korea’s coast
content:
A South Korean fishing vessel sank off the coast of Busan on Friday, Sept. 19, leaving one person dead and another missing, according to the Coast Guard, reports The Korean Times.

The 79-meteric-ton boat sent a distress signal around noon before sinking approximately 61.6 kilometers east of Songjeong harbor. It reportedly capsized while turning to haul in fishing nets.

Of the nine crew members on board, seven -- three South Koreans and four Indonesians -- were rescued. The South Korean captain, a man in his 60s, was found in cardiac arrest and later died in hospital.

One Indonesian crew member remains missing.

Patrol ships and aircraft have been deployed to search the area. South Korea's prime minister Kim Min-seok has ordered the Coast Guard and oceans ministry to prioritize the rescue, and instructed the defense ministry to provide additional support.

title: No criminal charges for San Francisco trawler caught hocking chinook bycatch to restaurant
content:
A US fisherman could avoid jail and instead pay a $9,000 fine as part of a civil court settlement after he was allegedly caught trying to sell fileted chinook salmon bycatch stowed behind a false wall in his trawler. 

That's according to a proposed stipulated judgment obtained by Undercurrent News in the California Superior Court in San Francisco, which identified the commercial fisherman as Nicola Ingargiola, skipper of the 71-foot trawler Anna Marie moored in the bay city's iconic Fisherman's Wharf. 

California's Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) announced on Dec. 30, 2024 it had seized the vessel's load of Pacific halibut after wardens observed its skipper surreptitiously unloading an undeclared catch hidden in burlap sacks near Pier 45.

California fisheries wardens released this Oct. 1, 2024 photo of some of the undeclared fish seized by authorities after the skipper allegedly tried to smuggle bycatch off his trawler and sell it to a San Francisco eatery. (Photo courtesy of CDFW)

The arrest garnered regional media attention, though neither the name of the vessel nor the skipper was previously released by authorities, who said the unnamed fisherman had salmon fillets, sole and sanddabs in his possession. 

California commercial salmon fleet faces third consecutive closure

CDFW said the fisherman was arrested while attempting to flee after being caught allegedly trying to sell the illegal catch to an unnamed restaurant in San Francisco.

California hasn't had a commercial salmon harvest since 2023. 

The skipper's Pacific halibut catch, weighing 2,365 pounds, was also forfeited, but authorities made sure it wasn't wasted, CDFW said.

"CDFW proceeded with declaring the seized halibut the following morning, selling the fish and donating proceeds to the Fish and Game Preservation Fund," the state agency said.

Court filings obtained by Undercurrent shed more light on the incident, too. Under a stipulation between Ingargiola and the local prosecutors, the skipper has agreed to release any claim on the forfeited halibut that fetched roughly $12,000 when sold by CDFW, and be fined $9,000.

The DA's office has not commented on the case nor explained why it elected to pursue a civil case and not criminal charges concerning the alleged attempt to sell the salmon bycatch and other state fishing violations.

A state judge will need to sign off on the proposed settlement. A hearing is set for Sept. 23 in San Francisco. In the prosecutor's filing, assistant district attorney Alyce Sandbach explained why her office is moving to settle the case.

"Litigating this case would be time-consuming, complex, and would generate extensive costs and involve a significant delay in obtaining any resolution," Sandbach wrote in an Aug. 25 filing.

Ingargiola's San Francisco defense attorney, Samuel Ray, said he had no immediate comment.

Ingargiola, 69, is a third-generation fisherman whose family is from Italy. In 1972, he emigrated to San Francisco from Sicily when he was 17 years old and has worked as a commercial fisherman ever since.

That's according to an unrelated oral history he sat for with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) in 2018, recording the experiences of veteran harvesters. During the 45-minute interview, Ingargiola complained that making a living has been a struggle in recent years due to fewer fish and more regulations. 

"We don't make no money anymore," Ingargiola told the interviewers. "If it go on like this, there's not going to be no future."

title: US warmwater lobster harvesters struggle to fill labor gap created by ICE raids
content:
Bruce Irwin, a 63-year-old commercial warmwater lobster harvester in the US Florida Keys, is working more than 100 hours per week to maintain his fishing operation due to fears of his legal, documented immigrant workers being detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officers, Keys Weekly, a local newspaper, reports.

Irwin, the owner of Brutus Seafood and Irwin Inc., has made his living as a lobster harvester for more than four decades. Irwin is a member of the South Atlantic Fishery Management Council Lobster Advisory board, the Florida Keys Commercial Fishermen's Association and the Organized Fishermen of Florida.

Irwin and other fishermen throughout the Keys said that even if his workers are here legally, their documents no longer guarantee they will not be arrested and deported.

"My crew came here seeking asylum. They checked in and did everything right, got their visas and work permits, which are cleared by the Department of Homeland Security. (The crew) come to work, and we're all legal," he reportedly said. "(CBP) will do a little raid, take people off the boats, so they scare them all to where they all want to leave. If you fight it, they just detain you indefinitely. 

"It's the most unfair thing I've ever seen in my life."

Irwin cited a CBP social media post in early August boasting of an arrest of "4 illegal aliens from Nicaragua" aboard a commercial fishing vessel in Marathon, Florida, as stirring fear over his crew's well-being.

"Don't try it … We are watching!" the post said. "Another win for #BorderSecurity."

Irwin remains unwilling to send his crew to sea with no assurance they will not be detained, so he has returned to fishing on his boat.

"The labor crisis in the Keys is huge … and we get these people, and we're ecstatic-- they're the best people we've had in so long," he said. "But my guys haven't been on my boat. I don't want to be responsible for you getting deported. I'm not living with that."

title: US state’s shrimp vessel inspection leads to drug, firearm arrest
content:
A shrimp vessel inspection in the US state of Louisiana has resulted in the arrest of one subject for alleged drug and firearm violations, the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries (LDWF) reports. 

Officers with the state agency were on patrol in the Cote Blanche Bay when they observed a commercial shrimping vessel that was actively skimming for shrimp. The agents boarded the vessel, where they made contact with Peter Nguyen, 39, the captain of the vessel, and Rendal D. Jennies Jr., 42, the deckhand, according to LDWF.

Upon further inspection, the agents discovered that the skimmer nets being used on the commercial fishing vessel were oversized and did not comply with turtle excluder device (TED) requirements, the agency said. The illegal skimmer nets were seized, as well as the 1,813 pounds of shrimp that the men were allegedly in possession of.

LDWF said agents also discovered that Jennies Jr., a convicted felon, was in possession of cocaine and marijuana, as well as possession of drug paraphernalia, and "possession or dealing in unregistered/illegally transferred weapons, possession of a firearm by a convicted felon and possession of a firearm in the presence of a schedule II controlled dangerous substance."

Nguyen, who was also found to allegedly be in possession of three undersized stone crab claws, faces fines of between $250 to $500, and up to 90 days in jail for each fishing offense.

Meanwhile, Jennies Jr., who was booked into the Iberia Parish Jail, faces a fine between $1,000 and $5,000 just for alleged possession of a firearm by a convicted felon, as well as five to 20 years in jail. He also faces up to a $10,000 fine and five to 10 years in jail for alleged possession of a firearm while in the presence of a schedule II controlled dangerous substance, in addition to other fines and potential jail time.

title: US sushi restaurant owner faces deportation after being held by immigration officers for months
content:
Kelly Yu, a longtime sushi restaurant owner in the US state of Arizona, is facing deportation to Hong Kong after being held by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents since May, reports Fox 10.

The detainment of Yu has made headlines, as the owner of Kawaii Sushi, a popular Peoria, Arizona-area restaurant, has no criminal record and was an active member of her community.

Democratic Arizona senator Ruben Gallego met with Yu's family on Tuesday (Aug. 12) to hear more about the business owner's case. 

"This administration has prioritized arbitrary quotas instead of a humane process of dealing with illegal immigration," Gallego said in a statement following the meeting.

"If we're a country that values families, why are we separating families? If we're a country that values entrepreneurs, that values people that want to be part of a real American institution, why are we kicking them out of this country? "We all lose as a country when we lose the Kelly Yu's of the world." 

Yu came to the US when she was 19 years old and pregnant to escape China's one-child policy," Yu's husband, Aldo, told the news outlet. She entered the country illegally from Mexico but later married a US citizen. Her daughter, who was born in the US, is a legally protected resident. Yu reportedly sought asylum over the years but had her case denied due to the fact that she entered illegally.

During her time in the US, Yu built up Kawaii Sushi, which she expanded with a second location, and had plans for a third restaurant that was reportedly in the process of opening, according to a company website. 

She routinely checked in with ICE, which is how she ended up detained in May, despite the lack of a criminal record, according to the television station's report.

Yu's detainment is part of the president Donald Trump administration's crackdown on illegal immigrants. In the first 50 days of the Trump administration, ICE has made 32,809 enforcement arrests, the US Department of Homeland Security reports on its website. ICE has "targeted operations to remove criminal illegal aliens," the federal agency states.

title: Interpol lifts red notice for Sea Shepherd founder, anti-whaling activist Paul Watson
content:
Global police organization Interpol has lifted its red notice for Paul Watson, the 74-year-old founder of anti-whaling group Sea Shepherd, following a decision by the organization's Commission for the Control of Interpol's Files (CCF).

Watson, a Canadian-American citizen, had been wanted internationally at Japan's request over a 2010 incident in which he was accused of ramming a whaling vessel and injuring a crew member during a high-seas confrontation in the Southern Ocean.

Japanese prosecutors issued a warrant in 2012, prompting Interpol to circulate the red notice.

A spokesperson for Interpol confirmed the CCF has deleted the notice, reports Jiji Press.

Right whales trigger lobster fishing grid closures in Canadian gulf

The spokesperson said the move was not a judgment on the merits of the case or the events that occurred in 2010 but a decision based on Interpol's rules on data processing.

The commission determined that the red notice no longer met Interpol's criteria due to new developments, including Denmark's refusal to comply with Japan's extradition request.

Watson was arrested in July 2024 while traveling in Greenland, a Danish autonomous territory. He was released in December after Danish authorities rejected Japan's request, citing concerns over the age and nature of the charges.

He later returned to France, where his children attend school.

Following Interpol's decision, the Captain Paul Watson Foundation posted on X, stating
"INTERPOL RED NOTICE CANCELLED!! After being relentlessly pursued by a powerful nation with unlimited resources for over a decade... finally I am free."

According to lawyer William Julie, the CCF found the red notice action to b a disproportionate response to the allegations against Watson. He cited Watson's alleged only indirect involvement, the long passage of time since the incident, and refusals by several countries to enforce Japan's extradition request.

The commission also noted the strategic character and symbolic importance of the case, suggesting a political undertone to the notice, Julie said.

Sea Shepherd, the organization Watson founded, welcomed the decision but cautioned that legal risks remain.

"Paul Watson is no longer under a Red Notice but the Japanese arrest warrant is still active and enforceable by any country," the group stated on X.

Tokyo called the decision "extremely regrettable," and top government spokesman Yoshimasa Hayashi said it would not deter Japan from continuing to pursue Watson's arrest.

"The removal doesn't change the fact that Japan's arrest warrant for him is valid," Hayashi told a regular news briefing. "Our position remains unchanged that we will continue to call on the parties involved for his extradition."

title: Northline: Bristol Bay barge already exceeded last season’s salmon haul
content:
CLARK'S POINT, Alaska, US -- Northline Seafoods freezer barge has weathered major obstacles before returning to Bristol Bay for its second season but the US company's CEO, Ben Blakey, says so far its gambit is paying off.

"It was really hard getting up here," Blakey told Undercurrent News on Sunday (July 6) as the 400-foot floating salmon vessel offloaded pallets of frozen sockeye to a tramper bound for secondary processing in Canada.

"But it's going great. Market is strong. Volumes are huge. I think it'll be great for Bristol Bay processors -- not just Northline."

Sockeye salmon are delivered to Northline Seafoods barge Hannah on July 6, 2025 from the fishing vessel Flying Tiger. Photo Credit: Undercurrent News

The strong Nushagak Bay salmon run has helped buoy the Hannah's fortunes with more than 11.3 million fish caught since the season opened last month.

"We've already purchased more fish than in 2024, so it's been really good for us," Blakey said, without disclosing volumes.

Amidst the consolidation of processors, Northline is one of the smaller players on Bristol Bay, but is trying a new formula not seen elsewhere in the fishery. 

Northline Seafoods CEO Ben Blakey shows a freshly caught sockeye salmon delivered to the Hannah barge on July 6, 2025. Photo Credit: Undercurrent News

Rather than process wild-caught salmon as filets or headed and gutted (H&G) the massive barge is freezing whole round salmon, acting as a massive cold storage facility with a 10m pound (4,536t) capacity.

"The value of the Hannah doesn't really stop up here," Blakey said between sips of coffee in a hooded sweatshirt, surveying the calm waters and blue skies -- the first fair weather on Bristol Bay in weeks. 

Monthly cold storage rates run about $0.05 per lb, amounting to $500,000 for the volume stored on the Hannah.

"We can sit on 10 million lbs for a fraction of the cost of modern cold storage," Blakey said.

Accidental fires, threat of seizure

The Hannah's return to Bristol Bay was not a foregone conclusion. The retrofitted vessel, partly financed by a $40m US government loan, was struck by an electrical fire last season that took much of its capacity offline. 

Repairs allowed the barge to resume receiving fish until the end of the 2024 season, as Undercurrent reported.

Lienholder asks US authorities to seize freezer barge ahead of Alaska salmon season

But financial setbacks also caused a cash crunch for the Bellingham, Washington-based company, leading to vendors who helped retrofit the vessel to file liens to force payment of nearly $3m in outstanding invoices.

One welding firm asked US authorities to arrest the Hannah under maritime law over nonpayment. Northline was able to post a $1.3m bond to avoid the vessel's seizure, as Undercurrent reported.

That process is still working its way through the federal court system.

State-of-the-art freezers, automation

A tour of the Hannah's underbelly reveals a largely automated freezer operation that's unique to Bristol Bay. A relatively light crew complement -- 90 in all, with about half working in production -- allows the barge to receive and freeze around 300,000 lbs daily. 

Salmon delivered to the Hannah barge on July 6, 2025. These sockeye are sent through a spiral freezer that after two hours is designed to get the core temperature of the fish to -15 degrees Fahrenheit (-26 Celsius) before put in cold storage for up to a year. Photo Credit: Undercurrent News

The sockeye are delivered by tenders and 32-foot drift-net harvesters and put directly into slurry ice. The whole fish is then put in a spiral freezer that, after about two hours, gets the salmon's core temperature to -15 degrees Fahrenheit (-26 Celsius). 

The subzero salmon are then loaded into pallets and stored on board for eventual transhipment south.

Shoreside processor to be completed in 2025

Northline is building its own processor in the Fairhaven terminal in the Port of Bellingham, in Washington state. Scheduled to be completed in September, the 6,000-square-foot H&G line will be built over the former Arrowac Fisheries facility, which closed in 2008.

It's in a historic building that once housed Pacific American Fisheries, which, until being shuttered in the mid-20th century, boasted to be one of the largest salmon canneries on the US west coast.

Processing -- in addition to buying and freezing -- Alaska salmon will be another expansion for the relatively young company that's ambitious but pragmatic.

"One thing that I've learned is that it does make a lot of sense to take your time and do things right," Blakey said. 

Bristol Bay's robust harvest of more than 22.8m sockeye has provided Blakey optimism about the wholesale market, given the limited supply of wild sockeye globally.

"The market is very strong, even with the quantity of fish that we expect," he said. "There's significant demand, and I think that the market will absorb it."

title: North Carolina shrimp trawling ban leads to protests, death threats
content:
Shrimpers in the US state of North Carolina are not sitting back quietly as a bill that would ban commercial shrimp trawling in inshore waters and within a half-mile of the Atlantic Ocean shoreline advances.

Hundreds of protestors gathered in the state's capital in Raleigh to voice their concerns about a move they claim will kill their industry.

In a 39-2 vote, the state Senate approved House Bill 442, which would prohibit the use of trawl nets for catching shrimp, as previously reported by Undercurrent News. Because the bill was significantly changed from its original intent of regulating flounder and red snapper harvesting in state waters, it must be voted on once again by the state's House of Representatives, which approved the original bill on June 19.

The protestors, most representing the state's shrimping industry, which brings in product worth more than $4 million annually, made their presence known in the capitol building on Tuesday (June 24), as the Senate met for a final reading on a separate but related piece of legislation.

House Bill 441, which was recently rewritten and short-titled, "Shrimp Trawling Transition Program/Fees," would provide temporary transition payments to commercial fishing license holders who trawled between Jan. 1, 2023 and June 30, 2025. It must be approved by both the Senate and the House, as it was also significantly rewritten.

Shrimpers at the protest said they appreciated the aid package but opposed the bill that would severely limit the use of a gear type that many of them rely on for the bulk of their harvesting.

"I'm sure a little aid in that area would be beneficial to the fishermen because it is a pretty hefty blow," Lambert Long, a Motts Channel Seafood fisherman, told WECT 6. "All that gear, equipment, boats, that stuff with a closure like that, you know, that's a lot of investment to just try to shut down suddenly."

The ban is supported by the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission, which said it could help restore the depleted shrimp fishery, which has seen declining catches in recent years.

"There is no magic bullet that will restore depleted fisheries overnight, but reducing the impacts shrimp trawling has on the habitats that juvenile fish depend upon and limiting bycatch of those fish will make a difference," it said. 

The debate over the two bills has grown increasingly confrontational.

One individual opposed to the trawling ban, Anthony Wayne Street, 44, was arrested Friday (June 20) and charged with communicating threats to a legislative agent or court official following posts he made on his Facebook page threatening to kill lawmakers who supported the ban.

Street allegedly wrote on the social media site, "he/they be warned now you serve to lose your lives and that all senators in Raleigh need to understand what happened to Melissa Hortman and John Hoffman in Minnesota can happen here in North Carolina," according to the arrest warrant obtained by WECT 6.

Street was referring to two Minnesota lawmakers who were shot inside their homes earlier this month. Hortman was killed, while Hoffman was critically injured.

Street was charged with communicating threats to a legislative agent. He made his first court appearance on Monday (June 23), where a judge set a bond for $25,000.

title: Cargo ship captain arrested in New England for illegal lobster catch, stealing commercial gear
content:
The US state of New Hampshire Fish and Game (NHF&G) Law Enforcement division said it was responding to a tip about illegal fishing activity when it found a 44-year-old Vietnamese man allegedly using his Panamanian cargo vessel and stolen gear to illegally catch lobsters, The Union Leader reports.

Bui Cong Doai, the ship's captain, was arrested on June 6 and fined $1,269 for illegal fishing after conservation officers boarded the 400-foot Franbo Lohas, which was sailing under the Panama flag but temporarily docked in the Piscataqua River in Newington, New Hampshire.

The officers reported discovering multiple ropes extending from the side of the ship into the water and traps stolen from a licensed New Hampshire commercial fisherman. 

Lobsters, including an undersized female egg-bearing lobster, crabs, and bags of blue mussels, were also discovered on board. 

Doai was charged with three misdemeanor counts for lobster and crab fishing without a license and illegal possession of another person's lobster gear, according to state agency. He was also charged with five violations for illegal trap construction, possession of a short egg-bearing lobster and also an egg-bearing crab, as well as unlawful possession of other crabs and blue mussels.

The case was expedited due to the uncertainty of how long the vessel would remain docked, reported The Union Leader.

title: Mexican cartels threaten Texas fishing industry, Cruz tells US Senate panel
content:
US senator Ted Cruz, a Texas Republican, "sounded the alarm" over the growing threat of Mexican cartels on his state's fishing industry in an address to the upper chamber's Commerce Subcommittee on Coast Guard, Maritime, and Fisheries last week.

The panel also has jurisdiction over matters that impact oceans, coasts and inland waterways and is responsible for overseeing the US Coast Guard (USCG) and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), among other relevant government agencies and committees. 

It held a hearing Thursday (June 12), titled "Finding Nemo's Future: Conflicts over Ocean Resources," to examine US efforts to counter illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing.

While Subcommittee chairman, Alaska senator Dan Sullivan, also a Republican, was primarily focused on IUU fishing activities by Russia and China, Cruz shared concerns from his home state of Texas, which borders the Gulf of Mexico.

Texas has been facing issues with IUU fishing for years as Mexican lancha boats harvest red snapper in US federal waters. However, the USCG has been actively cracking down, as reported by Undercurrent News.

"Last year, the Coast Guard seized more than 18 tons of illegally caught fish from Mexican lanchas -- a dramatic increase from just under three and a half tons in 2017," said Cruz.

"And already this year, the Coast Guard has arrested more than 50 Mexican fishermen and seized thousands of pounds of illegally caught fish, further underscoring the need for additional measures to protect our resources."

But the issue "isn't just about fish," he said.

"Some of the very same vessels crossing into US waters to steal red snapper support Mexican cartels involved in smuggling drugs and people," he said. "These poachers are robbing from hardworking Texas fishermen, who play by the rules and rely on fishing to support their families and communities.

FREE READ US Coast Guard detains 13 Mexican fishermen suspected of illegally harvesting red snapper

The USCG is not the only government agency taking action to protect Texas fishermen. In November 2024 the US Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned five Mexican individuals associated with the Gulf Cartel, one of Mexico's most dangerous criminal organizations.

USCG continues to partner with Customs and Border Protection and other relevant agencies to make arrests and seize illegally harvested fish, the senator noted. 

"Let me be clear: our waters are not open to poachers," Cruz continued. "Texas and US fishermen deserve a free and fair market for their seafood. And Americans deserve to know the seafood on their dinner plate wasn't caught by criminal actors violating US law."

title: Untitled
content:
Four Mexican fishermen have pleaded guilty to illegally harvesting approximately 693 pounds of red snapper and four sharks in the US Gulf of Mexico, according to a news release from the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Texas.

The catch, which the men intended to sell upon their return to Mexico, has an estimated retail value of over $9,000.

Miguel Angel Ramirez-Vidal, 32, Jesus David Luna-Marquez, 20, Jesus Roberto Morales-Amador, 27, and Jose Daniel Santiago-Mendoza, 22, were detained on April 17, 2025, as previously reported by Undercurrent News. Authorities observed the crew's panga-style vessel engaged in fishing with heavy nylon line and hooks seven miles north of the US-Mexico maritime boundary line.

Santiago-Mendoza only just entered his guilty plea. Ramirez-Vidal, Luna-Marquez and Morales-Amador had previously entered guilty pleas for knowingly transporting illegally caught red snapper. 

US District Court judge Rolando Olvera is set to sentence the captain of the boat, Ramirez-Vidal, on April 13. Ramirez-Vidal had been arrested on 28 prior occasions for illegal fishing, according to the news release. He could face up to five years in prison and a maximum fine of $250,000.

The Justice Department noted that the three other men have similar previous arrests. A sentencing date for the remaining fishermen has not been announced. They remain in custody while awaiting sentencing.

Federal prosecutors say this is the first illegal fishing case in the Southern District of Texas that involves potential prison time.

title: Louisiana man arrested, charged with repeatedly stealing crawfish from farm
content:
A 47-year-old man from the US town of Echo, Louisiana, was arrested last month following complaints from a local crawfish farmer who had his traps emptied overnight on multiple occasions, according to a Facebook post by the Rapides Parish Sheriff's Office.

Tony Jake Hicks was arrested on May 11, 2025 on numerous charges related to the theft of crawfish, according to the agency. He's allegedly responsible for stealing about 400-500 pounds of the crustacean. 

Tony Jake Hicks, arrested May 11, 2025, on charges related to the theft of crawfish. Photo Credit: Rapides Parish Sheriff's Office

The resident deputy in the Cheneyville/Echo area received a complaint from a crawfish farmer of an overnight theft on April 26, 2025, according to the sheriff's office. The complaint stated that numerous traps had been emptied, and it was believed the subject was using the farmer's boat.

Another complaint from the farmer was filed on April 30 when it was reported that about 100 crawfish traps were emptied overnight.

The sheriff's office said it established a surveillance unit that observed a male subject at the pond after hours on May 10. A traffic stop was conducted later, which identified the male subject as Hicks. 

He is being held on $61,700 bond.

title: Four Mexican fishermen detained off Texas coast by US Coast Guard
content:
The US Coast Guard (USCG) intercepted a small fishing vessel and detained four Mexican nationals it claims were fishing illegally in federal waters off the coast of the state of Texas.

On Thursday (May 22), crew from the USCG Cutter Joseph Doyle seized the vessel, known as a lancha, as well as around 200 pounds of red snapper, fishing gear and equipment. The fishermen were taken into custody and handed over to US Customs and Border Protection for processing, according to a Coast Guard press release.

The arrests are the latest in a long-running battle between US authorities and small-scale Mexican fishermen who regularly cross the US maritime boundary to fish for red snapper. The Coast Guard said the illegal harvest and trade of red snapper and other fish caught in the Gulf of Mexico often serve as a revenue stream for criminal organizations and as cover for them to sneak migrants and drugs into the US.

title: US immigration dragnet snags more seafood processing workers
content:
The seafood processing sector continues to see attrition through arrests of its workers by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Two employees at New Bedford, Massachusetts-based Oceans Fleet were arrested on their way to work on May 12, according to the New Bedford Light.

Marvin Yobani Chitic Us and Justo Rufino Chitic Us, who are unrelated but both from the same small community in Guatemala, were taken into custody despite having no criminal records, the men's families told the newspaper. They said they were not informed of the arrests until hours after they found a car belonging to one of the men abandoned. 

Justo's family has still not been told by ICE of his arrest or whereabouts, but a cousin of Marvin received a call from him in the afternoon of May 12, confirming their arrests by immigration agents and their transportation to Burlington, Vermont.

Both have been employed by scallop and lobster processor Oceans Fleet for several years, according to Joshua Brightman, the lobster department manager at Oceans Fleet.

"I'm very concerned about Marvin's health. He needs his dialysis," he said.

Brightman said Marvin and Justo are not the first employees at the company to be arrested since US president Donald Trump took office on Jan. 20. 

The arrests are more evidence ICE appears to be targeting those employed in the seafood sector, according to Lisa Maya Knauer, a project manager with the immigrant community organization Centro Comunitario de Trabajadores.

"It seems that New Bedford is a target, because it appears there have been at least eight incidents since Jan. 20," she told NBC 10 WJAR. "This is something that creates fear and I think that's part of the plan."

ICE, a division within the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), previously conducted a raid on Ocean Seafood Depot's processing and distribution plant, in Newark, New Jersey, on Thursday (Jan. 23).

Trump has made it a priority of his administration to punish illegal immigration with mass deportations. Tom Homan, his appointed border czar, has vowed to undertake raids of workplaces and other gathering places for undocumented immigrants across the country, especially targeting so-called "sanctuary cities" -- US cities with local governments that have chosen to limit their cooperation with federal immigration enforcement authorities.

Through the first 100 days of Trump's second term, ending April 29, ICE arrested 66,463 people it claims entered the US illegally. 

That total includes more than 1,000 workers lacking legal papers allowing them to work in the US, according to ICE deputy director Madison D. Sheahan, who said his agency "has been zeroing in on worksite enforcement operations to protect American businesses."

Business that hired those workers have been fined more than $1 million, Sheahan said in a press release.

A 2017 research project from the New American Economy found undocumented workers made up more than 60% of the American seafood industry's workforce.

title: US court issues warrant to seize Alaska salmon barge ahead of Bristol Bay season
content:
A US federal judge has issued a warrant for the seizure of the freezer barge Hannah over outstanding debts to a vendor owed more than $1.2 million for retrofitting it in advance of last year's Bristol Bay salmon season.

The legal tussle threatens Northline Seafoods' ability to buy Alaska salmon in the world's largest sockeye fishery in 2025, though its seizure in port is not a done deal.

A flurry of recent filings in the US District Court of the Western District of Washington between the Bellingham, Washington-based salmon processor and a Seattle, Washington-based welding firm has raised questions about whether the 400-foot freezer barge Hannah would be able to sail north to Alaska next month, as reported by Undercurrent News. 

Lienholder asks US authorities to seize freezer barge ahead of Alaska salmon season

Northline has warned in court filings that seizure of its $90m seafood platform could financially cripple the company, one of the few remaining salmon buyers for the upcoming season.

Judge Lauren King noted in her Wednesday (April 30) order that Northline had argued that arresting the Hannah "would imperil the vessel's insurance coverage and its ability to participate in this year's Bristol Bay salmon season" thereby potentially eliminating its ability to earn money to repay its debts.

But she said the court is without discretion in refusing to issue a warrant.

Reached Wednesday afternoon, Northline's owner Ben Blakey declined to comment.

Uncertainties remain as sailing date nears

The judge also ordered a hearing as a last-ditch effort to agree to a settlement that would avoid arresting the 400-foot barge currently moored in Bellingham. She asked that all parties meet in advance to "confer in good faith to ascertain whether agreement can be reached" to settle out of court.

Even so, her ruling was followed by an order directed to US Marshalls -- a federal law enforcement agency -- to take possession of the vessel, using "reasonable force" if necessary.

"The US Marshal is further authorized and directed to arrest and/ or evict from the premises any and all persons who obstruct, attempt to obstruct, or interfere or attempt to interfere, in any way with the execution of this warrant," the warrant states.

The case was brought by Leo's Welding and Fabrication, which is owed more than $1.2m for work completed prior to the barge's retrofitting for the 2024 salmon season. The company's owner Leo Estrada told Undercurrent prior to bringing suit that the outstanding debt had taken its toll on his Seattle-based company.

OBI won’t run Egegik salmon cannery in Bristol Bay following Silver Bay deal

Estrada's welding firm is the largest lienholder of several totaling at least $2.8m filed against the vessel late last year. Other firms continue to have outstanding debts, while at least one has told Undercurrent it's agreed to a repayment scheme with 30% paid this month; an additional 30% payment in October, and then, in exchange for releasing the lien, 40% in January 2026.

That would allow Northline to raise revenue after the 2025 sockeye salmon season. The company has argued in court filings that even if the vessel is arrested, vendors such as Estrada's likely won't be made whole, as there is at least $40m in mortgages against the vessel secured by other creditors whose debts would take precedence in an auction.

Leo's Welding and Fabrication is being represented by the law firm of Robert Zuanich, a managing partner and co-founder of Northline's competitor Silver Bay Seafoods, which recently merged with OBI Seafoods, and is quickly rising as one of the main buyers of Bristol Bay salmon.

title: US judge weighs seizure of Alaska-bound freezer barge ahead of Bristol Bay salmon season
content:
The owner of an Alaska-bound freezer barge is asking a US judge to delay the vessel's seizure over outstanding debts to unpaid vendors lest it prevent it from operating in the upcoming Bristol Bay salmon season.

In a flurry of filings in recent days by Northline Seafoods, the Bellingham, Washington-based processor has warned that seizure of its 400-foot barge Hannah would financially cripple the company, one of the few remaining salmon buyers for the 2025 season.

"There is no time to allow for disruptions or delays aboard the vessel and still make the 2025 Bristol Bay salmon season," wrote Northline owner Ben Blakely in a sworn declaration, warning that it would be "financially catastrophic" for the company. 

"The vessel is being prepared for the 2025 Bristol Bay salmon season in Alaska and needs to begin its journey north in about one month," Blakey wrote.

As Undercurrent News has reported, Northline's 400-foot Hannah has more than $2.8 million in liens filed by multiple vendors claiming nonpayment since July 2024, with the largest lienholder filing papers to have the vessel arrested under maritime law.

Northline barge returns to Alaska for 2025 Bristol Bay salmon season

While some of the lienholders had told Undercurrent they were cautiously optimistic that Northline would have a successful 2025 season on Bristol Bay, allowing it to settle its accounts, its largest lienholder, Leo's Welding and Fabrication, is asking US authorities to seize the floating processor platform currently moored in Bellingham to prevent it from sailing to Alaska.

The Seattle-based vendor was contracted to retrofit the barge into a floating seafood processor, and it reported it's still owed $1,287,871, including $182,884 in late fees as of March 27. It has asked the US District Court of the Western District of Washington to foreclose on the vessel so it can be sold to settle its debts.

Hannah's fate uncertain ahead of 2025 fishing season

Northline doesn't deny that it still owes Leo for work completed before the 2024 salmon season, but said the exact amount is in dispute. 

On April 28, the US judge denied a motion to arrest the vessel on a technicality. It said that while most of the requirements had been met, insufficient information on the ship had been submitted in the docket and left it open for the plaintiffs to re-file their motion, which they did the following day.

Northline then immediately asked the judge for an additional 15 days to secure a bond to delay the vessel's arrest and stave off seizure of its asset, saying it's not a flight risk.

"The vessel is an unpowered barge, designed for one thing only -- to freeze salmon in Alaska," Northline's attorney wrote. "It cannot be hidden nor make an escape to international waters."

Silver Bay co-founder acting as plaintiff's attorney

The law firm representing Leo's is owned by Robert Zuanich, a managing partner of Silver Bay Seafoods, which is not a party to the action. But the company he co-founded is a direct competitor of Northline, one of the few remaining salmon buyers on Bristol Bay in a market that's seen rapid consolidation following Silver Bay's merger with OBI Seafoods, as Undercurrent has reported.

Northline has also argued in filings that if the vessel is arrested under maritime law, its proceeds wouldn't necessarily immediately settle accounts with the plaintiffs. 

That's because the Hannah was bought and retrofitted with a $40m loan that is secured as a mortgage on the vessel, "which has priority over the lien claims of Leo's Welding and Fabrication," its attorneys wrote.

It's unclear when Seattle-based US judge Lauren King will rule.

title: Mexican government arrests five involved in illegal totoaba fishing
content:
Mexican officials arrested five men on April 9 as part of an operation to protect the endangered vaquita porpoise.

Per a notice from the Mexican government, personnel from the Navy, Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection (Profepa), and the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development, through the National Commission for Aquaculture and Fisheries (Conapesca), worked together to arrest five people and seize a 26-foot boat, an 800-meter illegal fishing net, two totoaba specimens, four swim bladders (maws) and six totoaba parts.

The multi-agency operation was carried out in the Upper Gulf of California and the Colorado River Delta Biosphere Reserve.

Profepa and Conapesca work alongside the Mexican Navy to protect the vaquita and totoaba, both endangered species found in the Gulf of California.

The totoaba is highly sought after due to its swim bladder, which is sold on the Chinese black market. The swim bladder is extremely valuable because of its high collagen content and perceived nutritional benefits, which include improving brain function and reating insomnia, amongst other things, according to a research paper published in the National Library of Medicine.

There are likely just six to eight individual vaquita remaining alive, according to the Center for Biological Diversity. Vaquita are not sought out by fishermen, but can end up as bycatch in the illegal harvesting of totoaba.

title: New Jersey sushi restaurant owner seized by ICE after earlier Chinese spy conviction
content:
US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) reports that its agents have apprehended a man known as "Sushi John" in Newark, New Jersey, for the apparent purposes of deporting him after he was earlier convicted of illegally acting as an agent of a foreign government.

Ming Xi Zhang (John Zhang), 61, is the owner of Ya Ya Noodles, an Asian food restaurant in Skillman, New Jersey. The restaurant owner lawfully entered the US in June 2000 at the Los Angeles (California) International Airport, according to ICE. However, the government agency said he violated the terms of his lawful admission.

ICE agents detained Zhang on March 24, 2025.

Per a news release from ICE, the US District Court for the District of New Jersey convicted Zhang for "illegally acting as an agent of a foreign government without prior notification to the attorney general" and sentenced him to probation for a term of three years on April 30, 2024.

He was also fined $10,000 at the time, according to a newspaper account.

"Any illegal alien conducting activities related to espionage, sabotage or export control against the United States is subject to deportation," said John Tsoukaris, the field office director for ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations Newark.

Ming Xi Zhang [John Zhang], also known as Sushi John, was apprehended by ICE officers in Newark on March 24. Photo Credit: ICE

Zhang's illegal activities occurred in April 2016 when he "met with representatives of the Ministry of State Security (MSS) in the Bahamas on multiple occasions," according to court documents obtained by The Montgomery News. According to the outlet, MSS is responsible for "foreign intelligence, counterintelligence, and defense of the political security and honor of the Chinese Communist Party."

Following that incident, Zhang also hosted an individual at his Princeton, New Jersey, residence who acted as an agent of the Chinese government, the authorities charged.

Zhang's daughter, Emily, reportedly told The Montgomery News that her father has not violated the terms of his probation and that she doesn't know why he's being detained.

"How big of a secret agent could he be if he only got three years probation?" she told the outlet. "The FBI wouldn't have cooperated with him, and he would have gotten a harsher penalty if it were something more serious."

The president Donald Trump administration has put a big emphasis on cracking down on illegal immigrants. In the first 50 days of the Trump administration, ICE has made 32,809 enforcement arrests.

title: Lienholder asks US authorities to seize freezer barge ahead of Alaska salmon season
content:
A US welding company is asking a federal judge to foreclose on Northline Seafoods' freezer barge before the 2025 salmon season in Bristol Bay, Alaska.

The 400-foot Hannah has more than $2.8 million in liens filed by multiple vendors claiming nonpayment since July 2024, as Undercurrent News previously reported.

Some of the lienholders have told Undercurrent they were cautiously optimistic that the Bellingham, Washington-based salmon processor would have a successful 2025 season on Bristol Bay, allowing it to settle its accounts. 

But other lienholders have soured over the nonpayment and what they describe as poor communication. They said they were preparing to go to court. 

Payments ceased in July 2024

Leo's Welding and Fabrication, the largest lienholder, is the first to follow through in an attempt to recoup more than $1.2m for work it said it was contracted for in late 2023.

In a complaint filed Tuesday (April 8) in the Western District of Washington in Seattle, the company detailed how it had completed more than $2.8m worth of skilled work refitting the Hannah to prepare the freezer barge's maiden voyage for the 2024 Bristol Bay salmon season. 

An excerpt from the civil complaint filed on April 7, 2025 in Leo's Welding and Fabrication, LLC v. Hannah

But according to exhibits filed in court, the company only received roughly $1.7m, with the last payment made on July 9, 2024. That was barely a week after a fire broke out on board, damaging the vessel and hindering its freezer capacity, as Undercurrent reported at the time.

The Seattle-based welding firm filed a lien in December for the remaining $1.2m.

Leo Estrada, owner of the welding firm, told Undercurrent last month that attempts at securing repayment had failed, and he has had to sell off equipment and other assets to pay his tax bills to the US government.

"I owe the IRS a lot of money," Estrada said in an interview.

Request for federal officers to 'arrest' fishing vessel

The legal filing invokes a provision of maritime law enabling lienholders to "arrest" a vessel to recover debts owed for work on the vessel. It asks US Marshalls to seize the vessel currently berthed in the Bellingham Shipping Terminal so it can be foreclosed and sold to settle its accounts.

The complaint also says plaintiffs reserve the right to sue Northline Seafoods' holding company should the sale proceeds be less than the $1,287,871 plus accruing costs the Seattle-based welding company is entitled to.

2025 Bristol Bay sockeye harvest forecast ticks up to 34.84m salmon

It's unclear whether the legal challenge would disrupt the Hannah's sailing schedule to Bristol Bay. As Undercurrent reported last month, the company announced its intention to return for the 2025 salmon season.

Ben Blakey, owner of Northline Seafoods, declined to comment on Wednesday.

Under US law, Northline Seafoods has 21 days to answer the legal complaint or face a default judgment against the fishing vessel.

The Hannah was built from a repurposed Florida-based cargo barge into what the privately-held company calls its "floating seafood freezing platform." In press materials, it said the modern freezer barge was designed to improve efficiency in wild salmon processing by freezing and transporting 10m to 15m pounds of product landed by the salmon fleet. 

The Hannah was constructed with the aid of a $40m food supply chain loan backed by the US Department of Agriculture as part of then-US president Joe Biden's Build Back Better initiative.

Competitor is plaintiff's attorney

Seattle attorney Robert Zuanich, a founder and managing partner of Silver Bay Seafoods, is representing the welding firm. Silver Bay is a competitor of Northline's.

Silver Bay recently acquired Cooke's Icicle Seafoods, which had a 50% stake in OBI Seafood, further consolidating seafood processors in Bristol Bay and leading to at least one land-based facility closure, as Undercurrent reported.

Zuanich didn't immediately return a message seeking comment.

title: US Coast Guard detains 8 Mexican nationals suspected of illegally harvesting red snapper
content:
The US Coast Guard (USCG) has interdicted two more lanchas in the Gulf of Mexico and arrested eight Mexican nationals, just weeks after stopping four lanchas and detaining 16 fishermen.

USCG crew members were in federal waters off southern Texas on Friday (March 28) when a USCG air team detected two lanchas that appeared to be engaged in illegal fishing inside the US maritime boundary line in the Gulf of Mexico, the agency said.

Lanchas, which are small fishing boats approximately 20-30 feet long, are frequently used by Mexican fishermen to engage in illegal fishing in the US exclusive economic zone near the US-Mexico border in the gulf, which the administration of US president Donald Trump has ordered now be called the Gulf of America.

The Coast Guard took the eight men into custody and transferred them to US Customs and Border Protection once they were on shore. The USCG also seized the lanchas, fishing gear and equipment found on the vessels, as well as approximately 150 pounds of red snapper.

The Coast Guard interdicted and detained 8 Mexican fishermen engaged in illegal fishing and seized approximately 150 pounds of fish in federal waters off southern Texas on March 28, 2025. Photo Credit: USCG

title: Chilean fishermen protest against hake fisheries quota law
content:
Hundreds of Chilean artisanal fishermen protested outside the National Congress of Chile in Valparaiso, demanding changes to a fisheries quota bill they fear will favor large commercial fishing companies over small-scale fishers, Cooperativa reported.

The demonstration, which turned violent, saw protesters breaking a security fence and throwing objects at the government building.

The proposed legislation aims to revise the allocation of fishing rights between artisanal and industrial sectors. Fishermen argue that modifications made to the bill in the Senate reduce their share of key fish stocks, including common hake, reversing a previous decision by the Chamber of Deputies that had prioritized artisanal fishers.

"In the chamber of deputies, artisanal fishermen won 70% of the common hake allocation, while the industrial sector 30%. This was passed to the Senate, and they voted 43% for artisanal fishing, and 57% for industrial fishing. And we, as artisanal fishermen, cannot allow that. We have suffered a lot of hunger, and (we hope) that this time we can achieve what was won by a landslide in the chamber," Pedro Tono, president of the Caleta Portales workers, told Cooperativa.

Protesters also warned against a possible widening of the legality of trawling, which they claim harms marine ecosystems.

The protest escalated when some demonstrators clashed with police, resulting in four arrests. Lawmakers expressed security concerns after incendiary objects were thrown at their Senate offices.

The bill, currently under review by the Senate's finance committee, seeks to replace the controversial Longueira Law, which has been blamed for contributing to past corruption scandals. Despite the tensions, government officials have promised a thorough legislative process.

For their part, the fishermen protestors have vowed to continue demonstrating until their demands are met.

title: Unpaid vendors secure $2.8m in liens against Northline’s Alaska-bound freezer barge
content:
The freezer barge US salmon buyer Northline Seafoods is preparing to send back to Alaska has at least $2.78 million in liens against it from contractors who helped refit the 400-foot vessel purpose-built to receive and store wild-caught salmon on Bristol Bay.

That's according to interviews and US Coast Guard documents that detail the liens filed on behalf of at least seven unpaid vendors. They range from around $34,800 to more than $1.2m for work completed a year ago. 

Some of the vendors include major construction firms – some who declined comment – but also relatively small contractors who described their economic hardships to Undercurrent News. They said they sent many phone calls and emails that haven't received a response.

2025 Bristol Bay sockeye harvest forecast ticks up to 34.84m salmon

"I'm trying to sell my crane, my biggest forklift," said Leo Estrada, owner of Leo's Welding and Fabrication, a Seattle, Washington-based contractor who has been a fixture in that city's industrial waterfront for more than 20 years.

He appears to be by far the largest lienholder, with more than $1.2m secured against the vessel for work undertaken by his welding crews to ready the vessel in time for the 2024 fishing season.

"They put a really big dent in my company," Estrada said. "I'm in the middle of selling one of my houses and then selling my stuff, my equipment, so I can survive this."

Despite its owner's mounting debts, the fishing tender Hannah is preparing to return to Alaska for the 2025 salmon season, bringing the capacity to freeze and transport 10m pounds of Bristol Bay salmon, as Undercurrent reported.

"We're obviously starting to prepare and getting supplies secured and ready," Northline CEO Ben Blakey told Undercurrent. "We're looking forward to heading back up and buying fish from our fleet."

But when asked about unpaid vendors and contractors, Blakey deflected.

"I'd be interested to kind of hear which ones you're talking about before I can make a comment," he said.

Undercurrent followed up with a detailed list of liens. Blakey acknowledged receipt but has yet to respond further.

Hannah hobbled by freak fire

Part of the Northline's financial troubles are outside the Bellingham, Washington-based seafood company's control. A month after the Hannah made its maiden voyage to Bristol Bay, a blaze broke out in one of the freezers, reducing the barge's capacity to receive and store fish, as Undercurrent reported.

That cut into the privately held company's profitability, with operations hobbled at the peak of the wild sockeye run. Repairs were made, and the floating freezer barge completed the season before returning to Bellingham.

Yet payments to harvesters were delayed. It wasn't until just a few weeks ago that Bristol Bay fishermen widely reported their accounts had been settled for the 2024 season as they are gearing up for this summer.

Northline’s Alaska salmon processing barge hit by electrical fire

"We've obviously had to overcome a few challenges that happened in our inaugural season," Blakey said of the accidental fire. "We settled with our fleet and we are charging towards the 2025 season."

Letting harvesters go unpaid obviously wouldn't be an option lest Northline lose its fleet to competitors buying fish. Still, the unpaid vendors remain upset that so much time has passed with little communication from the company.

"It's been silent," Ingi Huswick, shipyard development manager for Stabbert Marine & Industrial, in Seattle. The shipyard services firm recently filed a lien for nearly $200,000. 

"That is our only avenue we have to recoup the costs for the services we have rendered," Huswick said.

Lienholders mull arrest of vessel

Under US maritime law, lienholders can invoke a rare power of arrest against a vessel for nonpayment of liens, an option some of the disgruntled vendors have reportedly discussed.

That would effectively take the Hannah out of commission just months ahead of the opening of the Bristol Bay fishing season, threatening to disrupt the wild salmon market.

But with Northline's major creditors with two mortgages totaling $60m plus a second mortgage taken out by Northline's sister company for $14.8m after the work was completed last spring, there are doubts that the unpaid vendors would be paid if the vessel was forced into default and auctioned as the banks would take priority ahead of the liens.

"The creditors still get paid off in their priority order," Jan Kallshian, president and CFO of Industrial Resources Inc. (IRI), a leading marine welder and fabricator in Mount Vernon, Washington, that reports to have unpaid accounts with Northline. 

"Unless there's something I'm missing, I don't see how that gets us any money," he added.

Northline freezer barge heads north for Alaska salmon season

In other words, the vessel could be sold -- likely cut up for scrap --  banks get paid pennies on the dollar, and the lienholders recover little more than the cost of the arrest, as stipulated in US law.

"We are hoping that they round up enough money to go fishing and then pull a rabbit out of the hat," Kallshian added. "We want them to succeed."

But he concedes that IRI is a larger firm than some of the other lienholders and has absorbed its losses – $517,371 – better than some smaller firms left holding the bag.

title: US Coast Guard detains 16 Mexican nationals suspected of illegal fishing
content:
The US Coast Guard (USCG) is continuing its crackdown on illegal fishing in the Gulf of Mexico.

USCG officers interdicted four lanchas on Tuesday (March 11), seizing approximately 2,500 pounds of fish in federal waters off southern Texas. 

Lanchas, which are small fishing boats approximately 20-30 feet long, are used by Mexican fishermen to engage in illegal fishing in the US exclusive economic zone near the US-Mexico border in the gulf, which the administration of US president Donald Trump has ordered now be called the Gulf of America. The USCG said that on Tuesday it detained 16 fishermen who were on four lanchas just north of the maritime boundary line.

"Our crews will continue to relentlessly detect and deter threats to our nation's sovereignty. These illegal activities support trafficking and other criminal activities on our nation's southern maritime border," said Lt. David Anderson, commanding officer, Coast Guard Cutter Daniel Tarr. "Our enduring at-sea presence is vital in combatting these illegal operations."

Photo by Petty Officer 3rd Class Perry Shirzad/U.S. Coast Guard District 8

Just last month the US Coast Guard caught 11 Mexican fishermen off the southern coast of Texas with more than 1,500 lbs of illegally harvested red snapper. In a separate incident, USCG officers in Texas also detained an undocumented crew member from a commercial fishing vessel. In January, another three fishermen were detained and 200 lbs of illegally harvested red snapper were confiscated, as reported by Undercurrent News.

title: Supertrawler detained off Irish coast for alleged fishing-regulation breaches
content:
A German-registered supertrawler, the Helen Mary, has been detained off Ireland's southwest coast for alleged breaches of EU fishing regulations, Irish media reported.

The European fisheries control agency's patrol vessel, Ocean Protector, escorted the 117-meter-long factory ship to Cork harbor, where it is currently docked at Tivoli Docks, Irish Examiner reported. Then, a team from the Sea Fisheries Protection Authority began an inspection, the Irish Times reported.

The Helen Mary, capable of processing its catch onboard with a storage capacity of 7,000 metric tons, was operating approximately 65 nautical miles off Mizen Head.

A man in his 40s has been arrested in connection with the alleged offenses and is being held under the 2006 fisheries and maritime jurisdiction act.

This vessel has a history of alleged fisheries breaches, including a 2019 detention in Scotland. Greenpeace has listed it as one of 20 "monster trawlers" implicated in overfishing in the Atlantic.

Under EU regulations, the Helen Mary can be detained for up to 48 hours for the alleged infractions.

title: US Coast Guard arrests 11, seizes 1,595 lbs of illegally caught red snapper in Gulf of Mexico
content:
Efforts by the US Coast Guard in Texas to end illegal fishing in the newly renamed Gulf of America resulted in the recent detention of 11 Mexican fishermen and the seizure of 1,595 pounds of illegally caught red snapper.

The Coast Guard announced on Friday (Feb. 7) that its crews, in coordination with US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officers, interdicted four lanchas -- slender fishing boats approximately 20-30 feet long -- and apprehended 11 fishermen who were engaged in illegal fishing north of the Maritime Boundary Line off southern Texas.

According to the Coast Guard, the lanchas held approximately 1,595 pounds of illegally caught red snapper, as well as nine sharks.

"Our crews will not pull back from efforts to end illegal fishing and trafficking of valuable natural resources on the maritime border," Shane Gunderson, a lieutenant and the commanding officer of Station South Padre Island, said in a statement.

Photo Credit: US Coast Guard

“Whether on the southern border or along the maritime boundary line in the Gulf of America, the Coast Guard will detect, deter, and interdict illicit activity that threatens our nation’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.”

The fishermen were taken to shore and were placed into custody of CBP for further processing.

This latest crackdown on illegal fishing comes just a few weeks after Coast Guard officers detained three other Mexican fishermen and confiscated 200 lbs of illegally caught red snapper, as reported by Undercurrent News.

title: Canadian judge denies bail in lobster extortion case
content:
A judge in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia denied bail on Friday (Feb. 7) to one of three men charged in an extortion case related to the lobster fishery, reports the CBC. 

At a bail hearing at provincial court in Yarmouth, NS, judge James Burrill ruled that Kevin Eric Langford, aged 32, should not be released from custody before his trial.

Langford was arrested on Sunday (Feb. 2) with Zacharie David Thibault, 32, and his father, Eric David Thibault, 65, and charged with extortion. Officers with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police alleged the elder Thibault hired two people to threaten a former lobster fisherman at his home in Saulnierville, NS,  and extort CAD 10,000 ($6,996), as reported by Undercurrent News.

The Thibaults also remain in jail, as their bail hearings were delayed until later in February at the request of their lawyers.

The Thibaults are alleged to be part of an organized crime family attempting to exploit the lobster industry, RCMP Sergeant Jeff LeBlanc told the CBC.

title: Criminal charges pile up for Canadian lobster dealing duo
content:
A lobster dealer in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia has been charged with extortion, reports the CBC.

Officers with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) arrested Eric David Thibault, aged 65, on Sunday (Feb. 2), alleging that he hired two people to threaten a former lobster fisherman and extort CAD 10,000 ($6,996) on Thursday (Jan. 30).

Thibuault's son, Zacharie David Thibault, 32, and a third man, Kevin Eric Langford, 32, were also arrested on Sunday.

Following a court appearance on Monday (Feb. 3), the three men remain in jail awaiting their next court appearance this Friday (Feb. 7). Canadian prosecutors opposed the release of the men, pending Friday's hearing.

The latest legal trouble for the Thibaults comes just two months after the pair were charged for threatening Geoffrey Jobert, owner of Lobster Hub in Meteghan, NS, as reported by Undercurrent News. 

The Thibaults are alleged to be part of an organized crime family attempting to exploit the lobster industry, RCMP Sergeant Jeff LeBlanc told CBC.

Legally licensed lobster harvesters and buyers in Canada's lucrative lobster industry have long complained about illegal activity in the fishery. Throughout 2024 pressure mounted on federal officials to increase efforts to crack down on criminals, as reported by Undercurrent.

The public seems to be willing to do its part to help, the RCMP said this week.

"The public is definitely tired of this going on. They know what has to be done, and co-operation -- that's crucial. And we're seeing some co-operation that we haven't seen as much in the past. It is positive," Sgt. Leblanc told CBC.
