title: Editor’s choice: Trump confirms tariffs on Canada, Mexico, China; Indian shrimp giant acquires US lobster supplier
content:
EMEA editor Neil Ramsden brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week.

Last week's most-read story was the news that AZ Gems -- controlled by the largest Indian shrimp supplier to the US, Sandhya Aqua Exports, has acquired a lobster distributor and exporter based in the East Coast state of Massachusetts. The AZ Gems "affiliate" company acquired Truefoods Premium Product from Michael Tourkistas, a legendary figure in the North American lobster sector. 

On Jan. 31, US president Donald Trump announced the country would begin levying 25% tariffs on Canada and Mexico as well as an additional 10% duty on China. The seafood industry, including US importers and Canadian and Mexican producers, has been dreading the potential of tariffs since Trump first threatened them in November.

An up-and-coming player in the US seafood industry, Fathom Seafood, plans to break ground this summer on a processing plant using state-of-the-art automation to remain competitive with overseas processors. It has thus far been known as a medium-sized processor of Dungeness crab and exporter of geoduck clams to Asian markets on the West Coast. But, in recent years, it's increased its lines by acquiring the companies Alaska Ice Seafoods, Franco Fish and Long Fisheries to expand from a shellfish specialty processor to one that produces a variety of finfish and salmon roe for caviar.

And in Europe, Norwegian salmon aquaculture business Mowi has entered into an agreement to acquire Vigner Olaisen's controlling 46% stake in Nova Sea, taking its stake in the business to a total 95%. The deal, valued at NOK 7.4 billion ($654.9 million), will be followed by a voluntary cash offer on similar terms to the shareholders owning the remaining 5% of Nova Sea for NOK 800m.

For the rest of last week's biggest stories, click the headlines below:

Pacific halibut TAC slashed 18% to 19.7m lbs for US and Canada
Canada-based conglomerate invests $42m to acquire Argentine fishing firm
Pescanova brings in Keith Decker as part of larger US restructure

Captain Fresh, Sekkingstad put together salmon JV

After 2024 losses, Norway's Kvaroy restructures, lays off some US staff

title: Catch the Current episode 2: Industry shakeups, executive orders and salmon snack sticks
content:
Industry shakeups, executive orders and salmon snack sticks -- episode 2 of Catch the Current has a little something for everyone this week.

Join hosts Amanda Buckle and Lorin Castiglione as they talk about just a few of the top-read stories of the week from Undercurrent News' team of reporters, including the latest company "reshufflings" at Pescanova USA, Kvaroy, and Pacifico Aquaculture. Plus, find out how the Los Angeles wildfires have impacted the seafood industry and what one company is doing to pay it forward.

And you won't want to miss an update on how US president Donald Trump's executive orders have hit the seafood industry so far.

There's fun to be had, of course, with a new podcast segment that is bound to be a favorite -- "Eat that fish!" And is that Oprah I hear at the end? You'll have to listen below (or scroll to the bottom of the show notes) to find out.

Subscribe now! Catch the Current is available on Apple, Spotify, Amazon Music, iHeartRadio, Pandora, and other major podcast streaming platforms. Don't see Catch the Current on your favorite app? Reach out to podcasts@undercurrentnews.com.

Don't have time to listen? Find a transcript of season 1, episode 2 of Catch the Current below:

Amanda Buckle (AB): You’re listening to Catch the Current, the latest podcast from Undercurrent News, your trusted source for seafood news, data and prices. I’m Amanda Buckle.

Lorin Castiglion (LC): And I’m Lorin Castiglione. We are back from Palm Springs, California, where we attended the National Fisheries Institute’s Global Seafood Market Conference. And I have to say, I am feeling refreshed and it’s not just because of that fresh desert air. 

AB: Agreed! GSMC is such a great way to kick off the year. For starters, it’s like one giant reunion where you haven’t seen people in months.

That must have been especially true for you as you just graduated from the National Fisheries Institute's Future Leaders Program. So it was like a reunion.

LC: Oh, it was. And I'm already missing them. We're already talking on the group chat. 
It was the best experience. If anybody has any questions about the program, I am now a self-appointed [spokesperson].

AB: Big supporters, we're big supporters. Besides the networking, again, you can't beat that. But the panels were fantastic this year.

LC: I know, I wasn’t on a panel this year, which broke my heart a little bit -- hey Richard Barry, let’s talk GSMC 2026 -- but you’re right. A fantastic lineup of speakers. Amanda and I recapped the event with our dream team of Undercurrent News reporters in the first episode of Catch the Current. So if you haven’t listened to that ... what are you waiting for?

AB: And since we’re such seafood fin-atics, we also released another episode this week -- an interview recorded while at GSMC with Cathrin Rabben and Tone Hellesvik, sales managers at Norwegian cod farmer Ode, to talk about the unique opportunities that farmed cod presents.

LC: We’re calling it episode 1.5. Be sure to subscribe and follow wherever you listen to podcasts so that you don’t miss a single episode of your new favorite podcast. Because we have another GSMC interview coming next week. Now onto the weekly recap. 

AB: There were quite a few company shakeups this week that our team reported on. Undercurrent co-founder and editorial director Tom Seaman broke the story last week during GSMC that Pescanova USA CEO Chris Maze has left the US arm of Spain’s Grupo Nueva Pescanova, a position that he held at the Miami, Florida-based subsidiary since 2019. This week Tom and I followed up with a report that Maze’s exit is actually part of a broader reshuffle. And the company has brought in seafood veteran Keith Decker to troubleshoot.

Sources told us that Decker will be in a consultancy position for a temporary period between two and six months as part of an effort to help make the US division more profitable and get it under budget. Besides Maze’s exit, those budget cuts also include a 25% reduction to Pescanova USA's already small staff of 24 full-time employees.

LC: Transcripts for episodes of Catch the Current can be found on the Undercurrent News site, which will also include a link to the original story if you want to learn more about the shakeup at Pescanova USA.

Norwegian salmon supplier Kvaroy is also restructuring. As Undercurrent News’ Cliff White reported on Wednesday, the company made a splash a few years ago with salmon hot dogs.

AB: Yeah, I remember those.

LC: Unfortunately, the past few years haven’t been great financially, with the company posting a deficit of around $10 million in 2023 and continued losses in 2024.

Undercurrent confirmed that Kvaroy laid off members of its US sales team, including its vice president of sales, Chris Cumming. The company said the layoffs were a result of difficult financial realities. With that said, Kvaroy is not reducing its US footprint, instead it is just restructuring its sales operations.

AB: Meanwhile, Ensenada, Mexico-based striped bass farmer Pacifico Aquaculture has ceased operations. Undercurrent’s Liza Mayer confirmed that the net-pen grower of non-hybrid striped bass is shutting down its operations. The decision comes after its CEO departed in November 2024.

Pacifico’s been considered a trailblazer in the North American aquaculture sector. NOAA had recognized it as the only producer of marine striped bass in Mexico and across the Western Hemisphere.

Again, links to read more about these stories can be found in our show notes. Just search Undercurrentnews.com for Catch the Current episode 2.

LC: The seafood industry found itself tangled in current events this week when US president Donald Trump’s crackdown on immigration resulted in Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, also known as ICE, raiding a Newark, New Jersey seafood plant and arresting three people.

Ocean Seafood Depot’s processing and distribution plant was raided on Thursday, Jan. 23. According to reports, ICE agents entered through the retail fish market without showing a warrant. The ICE agents then proceeded into the nonpublic warehouse, arresting three undocumented immigrants and a US citizen working at the facility. An additional four employees were issued court appearance slips. 

One of the co-owners of Ocean Seafood Depot described the employees as family people who show up to work every day.

AB: You know, Trump made all these claims about executive orders leading up to his inauguration on Jan. 20. He said he was going to do all these things on his first day in office. I know the team was keeping a real close eye on all the tariff threats -- we can talk about what happened with Colombia next -- and even the move to end offshore wind farms. But I have to admit, I wasn’t expecting an executive order like this to hit the seafood industry so quickly.

Screenshot: White House Executive Orders

LC: I agree with you. And with the Trump administration already making waves less than two weeks into office, it’s never been more critical to stay informed. 

And that’s where Undercurrent News comes in. We’re dedicated to delivering real-time, accurate, and in-depth reporting on the seafood industry -- everything from policy shifts to emerging trends -- so you’re never caught off-guard.

We’ve got a global network of reporters and analysts working around the clock to bring you the latest developments in trade, regulations, market movements and more. And when I say around the clock, I’ve only been here for four months but there is always someone, somewhere in the world keeping a finger on the industry's pulse. 

And honestly, a perfect example of our expertise here can be seen with the piece that our very own Americas editor Jason Huffman published Wednesday about how Trump’s tariffs could’ve cost US importers of Colombia tilapia more than $69m annually. 

AB: Yes, my new work BFF, Jason Huffman. You better watch out, Lorin. 

LC: I'm keeping my eyes on him. If he shows up to Boston in a matching pink suit, I'm going to be pretty upset. 

AB: Jason's piece was one of my favorite reads this week. So with the immigration crackdown, the Colombian president refused to let two US military aircrafts with 110 migrants onboard land. Trump immediately ordered an emergency 25% tariff on goods from Colombia, amongst other threats like increased inspection of cargoes. Ultimately the military aircraft were able to land and the tariff was avoided. 

LC: And just to get an idea if that tariff did get put in place, tilapia accounted for 91% of the total $151.8m worth of seafood Colombian sent to the US in 2023. 

AB: But an important thing to remember here is that the US heavily relies on seafood imports. And if Trump’s immediate reaction to not getting his way is to hit a country with tariffs on their goods ... well, we’re going to have plenty to report on this year. 

LC: You can say that again.

In our final story this week – Santa Monica Seafood gave Undercurrent News some insight into how California’s historic wildfires have hit Los Angeles-focused suppliers and restaurants hard.

Credit: Arprince / Shutterstock

Santa Monica Seafood CEO Roger O’Brien told Undercurrent’s Tom Seaman at GSMC that the company saw its LA sales drop 35% in the first week of the fires.

AB: I checked out Cal Fire’s website and the Palisades Fire, which started on January 7, is 97% contained as of Jan. 30. It’s burned over 23,000 acres.

LC: O’Brien said that, for smaller seafood companies whose sales are dependent on LA foodservice specifically, the impact of the fires could be devastating. These suppliers not only lost customers who had to close or whose businesses burned down, but he said that they sales at restaurants that are still open are also down, as people in impacted areas aren’t thinking about going out to eat.

But also interesting to note here is that O’Brien said that Santa Monica, which sells all over California and nationally, has seen an increase in sales in other areas of the state. 

AB: Yes, so he mentioned Newport Beach in Orange County. It’s funny though because that also made me think about our Uber ride from the Palm Springs airport to the GSMC conference last week. Our driver was from the Los Angeles area and he said told us that he’s experienced quite a few people who have temporarily relocated to Palm Springs either due to evacuations or to avoid the smoke.

LC: You know we also love a feel-good story too. Santa Monica Seafood has been donating seafood and meals, including $140,000 of frozen lobster, to firefighters and other California wildfire first responders. O’Brien told Undercurrent the company has already donated over 250 free meal vouchers to the Santa Monica Seafood retail store. He said that they’ve also donated over 100 fully prepared meals to groups like the Santa Monica police and fire departments and various YMCAs that are being used as evacuation centers.

Plus, the company is donating frozen lobster to Bracken's Kitchen, a nonprofit that partners with food banks, which will be used in lobster mac and cheese.

Santa Monica Seafood donated meals to first responders of the Los Angeles wildfires. Photo Credit: Santa Monica Seafood/ Facebook

AB: Love it. Bravo Santa Monica Seafood! 

Now, we’re going to end this episode with what is bound to be your favorite podcast segment of Catch the Current: Eat that fish, inspired by Jenni Davis Dresser of Sea Port Products. Thanks for the idea, Jenni! 

LC: Last week we were gifted with Salmon Snack Sticks from Surfsnax. The package is like an individual beef jerky or Slim Jim which -- as us hip workin’ moms know -- is ideal for an on-the-go snack.

[The magical banter created by Amanda and Lorin cannot be re-created in word form. You're just going to have to listen to the podcast if you want to know what they thought about the Salmon Snack Stick.]

Surfsnax Salmon Snack Stick

LC: Before we go, we have a treat for everyone! Free access to Undercurrent's pricing portal is being extended one more week!

AB: (In her best Oprah impression) You get access, you get free access, you get free access!

LC: Head over to UndercurrentNews.com and click on the prices tab up at the top and select "US wholesale" to see what we have been feverishly working on for the past few months. You’ll gain instant access to hundreds of US wholesale price assessments across shrimp, lobster, groundfish, farmed white fish, and scallops -- with salmon and crab debuting next week! 

These assessments reflect current spot market trades along with in-depth commentary to let you know exactly what is happening in the market. If you have any questions -- send them on over to pricing@undercurrentnews.com and we will gladly help you! 

AB: Thanks for listening and we’ll see ya back here next week.

AB AND LC: Bye!

title: US senators push for country-of-origin testing for red snapper, tuna
content:
Four US senators are pushing to require the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to develop testing to determine the country of origin of imported tuna and red snapper.

Republican senators Katie Britt, Ted Cruz and Tommy Tuberville and Democratic senator Brian Schatz introduced the Illegal Red Snapper and Tuna Enforcement Act on Tuesday (January 28). The bill directs NOAA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology to develop a standard methodology for identifying the country of origin of red snapper and certain species of tuna imported into the United States.

The bill will now be considered by the US Senate’s Commerce Committee. Britt, Cruz and Tuberville previously introduced similar legislation during the 118th Congress, which passed the Commerce Committee in July 2024 but did not advance to a full Senate vote before the session expired in January 2025.

"Seafood that’s caught illegally or intentionally mislabeled rips off consumers and makes it harder for law-abiding US fishermen to compete," Schatz said in a joint press release. "Our bill will help fight against pirate fishermen who try to pass off cheap foreign tuna for high-quality ahi from local Hawaii fishermen."

FREE READ US Coast Guard detains three from Mexico for alleged illegal fishing near Texas

The legislation aims to promote the creation of a field test kit to be used by federal and state law enforcement officers to identify where imported bigeye, yellowtail and bluefin tuna and red snapper were caught. If passed, the bill would require the test to be created within two years, or NOAA would have to offer an explanation as to why that timeline or the mandate for creating a portable field test was impractical.

Britt, Cruz and Tuberville's advocacy for the bill stems from a desire to curtail the illegal poaching of red snapper in the Gulf of Mexico, recently renamed the Gulf of America by US president Donald Trump.

"Cartel-backed poachers need to face consequences for their illicit activities in the Gulf of America," Britt said. "Red snapper is a core component of coastal Alabama’s economy, and our hardworking fishermen and food producers deserve fairness when fishing in the gulf. Senator Cruz’s and my Red Snapper and Tuna Enforcement Act will help protect Alabama’s fishermen."

According to Britt, Mexican fishermen cross the maritime border between the US and Mexico on small boats, or "lanchas", to illegally catch red snapper in US waters and return to Mexico. The fish are sold in Mexico or mixed with legally caught red snapper and then exported back into the United States. The US Coast Guard frequently interdicts illegal fishing operations in the Gulf of Mexico, most recently arresting 22 harvesters suspected of illegal fishing of red snapper on January 5.

The US Treasury Department identified Mexico's Gulf Cartel as a key player in illegal fishing operations targeting red snapper in the Gulf of Mexico in November 2024, asUndercurrent reported. Treasury officials said the cartel also uses lanchas fishing for red snapper as a front for drug and human smuggling operations.

Biden administration scuttled anti-IUU proposal during final week in White House

Cruz said the US red snapper fishery is one of the most well-managed and profitable in the Gulf of Mexico, but illegal fishing by Mexican lanchas puts law-abiding US fishermen and seafood producers at a competitive disadvantage. 

"Cartels and other criminal entities are illegally catching, importing, and selling red snapper and tuna to unwitting consumers then using such profits to fund other illicit activities like drug smuggling and human trafficking," he said. "I am glad to join my colleagues in introducing this common-sense, bipartisan legislation to support U.S. fishermen, and I am hopeful Congress will act quickly to stop these dangerous criminal gangs."

Due to Mexico's insufficient action to curb illegal fishing, US authorities banned Mexican fishing vessels from accessing US ports in 2022. That restriction remains in effect as of 2024.

Tuberville said he wants the country-of-origin tests to be developed so US authorities can confiscate illegally caught red snapper and tuna before it is sold commercially.

"In addition to taking business away from Alabama’s fishermen, many of the profits from these illegal fishing operations are funding the cartels. I’m proud to join Senator Cruz in introducing the Illegal Red Snapper and Tuna Enforcement Act to stop illegal Red Snapper from flooding our markets and bankrupting our great fishermen," Tuberville said.

Eric Kingma, the executive director of the Hawaii Longline Association, told Undercurrent he supported the introduction of the bill.

"It is important to have the ability to detect the origin of fish in the field, to prevent seafood fraud and avoid IUU-origin fish from coming into the country," Kingma said. 

Kingma said he was not concerned about the potential for the seafood industry to bear the cost of implementation, if and when a country-of-origin testing methodology is successfully developed.

"Hopefully it would be something that they could develop that would be available to consumers or watchdog groups, or the industry," he said. "It's a good first step."

title: US Coast Guard detains three from Mexico for alleged illegal fishing near Texas
content:
The US Coast Guard (USCG) reports that US Customs and Border Patrol (CBP) detained three Mexicans on Tuesday (Jan. 28) for illegal fishing in federal waters off the coast of Texas.

The fishermen's lancha, a 20-30 foot-long vessel often used for illegal fishing or to transport illegal narcotics from Mexico, was intercepted with 200 pounds of red snapper on board, said USCG in a press release. 

"The seized fish will be split and donated to the Harte Institute to support illegal unreported and unregulated fishing research and Sea Turtle Inc. to help feed and rehabilitate turtles," USCG said.

Coast Guard Station South Padre Island crews interdicted a lancha and seized 200 pounds of red snapper. (U.S. Coast Guard photo, courtesy Station South Padre Island)

The USCG often works with agencies like the CBP to combat illegal fishing. Since the Jan. 20, 2025 inauguration of US president Donald Trump, the two agencies have started working even more hand-in-hand, with the USCG aiding in "alien expulsion" flights as part of Trump's executive order to enforce immigration laws in the country.

Meanwhile, President Trump's immigration crackdown has hit other areas of the seafood industry, with a raid at a seafood processing and distribution plant in Newark, New Jersey, resulting in the arrest of three people, as reported by Undercurrent News.

Importers are also keeping a close eye as the president threatened to hit Colombia with tariffs and enhanced inspections of flights, private aircraft and cargo if the country didn't allow the transport plane to land. A White House spokesperson said that Colombia did ultimately agree to Trump's terms.

title: Daily recap: Pescanova brings in Decker; Chinese salmon prices jump $3/kg
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Monday, Jan. 27.

Pescanova brings in Keith Decker as part of larger US restructure

Chris Maze's exit from the US arm of Spain's Grupo Nueva Pescanova is part of a broader reshuffle that has seen seafood veteran Keith Decker brought in to troubleshoot. 

Chinese salmon prices jump $3/kg in week 5 as holiday demand spikes

Fresh salmon wholesale prices in China have surged ahead of the Lunar New Year holiday, with prices jumping CNY 15-20 ($2.06-$2.75) per kilogram in anticipation of the festive period running from Jan. 28 to Feb. 4.

US immigration agents raid New Jersey seafood plant, arrest 3

The US seafood industry has tasted its first engagement with president Donald Trump's crackdown on illegal immigration.

Vietnamese shrimp sector hopeful for continued market recovery after 2024 improvement

Vietnam's vannamei shrimp exports were up 15% in volume and 9% in value for 2024, and the hope is that improved market demand, prompted by Asian national holidays, can see that continue at the start of 2025, according to a Ho Chi Minh City-based consultancy compiling trade data for Undercurrent News.

Pacifico Aquaculture ceasing operations; CEO departs

Pacifico Aquaculture, the Ensenada, Mexico-based net-pen grower of non-hybrid striped bass, is shutting down operations, Undercurrent has confirmed.

Cod prices rebound on Peterhead, Shetland auctions, while haddock show mixed trends

Cod prices on Scotland's major auctions in Shetland and Peterhead increased in week four of 2025 (Jan. 20-26), following a notable drop in the previous week.

'Market resistance is mounting' to high scallop prices, though landing volumes remain down

There might be fewer Atlantic scallops (Placopecten magellanicus) available, but when it comes to high prices, "market resistance is mounting," warned Lorin Castiglione, Undercurrent's head of price reporting for the Americas, in her analysis of the wholesale market for week four.

title: British Navy reportedly arrests 15 Indian fishermen
content:
The British Navy has detained an Indian deep-sea fishing vessel and its 15-member crew, accusing them of poaching near Diego Garcia, the largest island of the Chagos Archipelago, part of the British Indian Ocean Territory, reports the Times of India and other local outlets.

The vessel, the Benedicta, departed on a fishing expedition from Kanyakumari, Tamil Nadu, on Dec. 29. 

According to Tamil Nadu fisheries department officials, the fishermen were apprehended on Jan. 13 while fishing for tuna, reportedly for crossing the International Maritime Boundary Line.

The boat has previously been seized twice on similar charges, according to officials, NDTV reported. The Tamil Nadu fisheries department has alerted India's Ministry of External Affairs about the incident.

Indian media said the arrest adds to the ongoing plight of Tamil Nadu's fishing communities, who frequently face detentions by foreign authorities. On Jan. 12, eight fishermen from Rameswaram were arrested by the Sri Lankan Navy, with two motorized boats impounded.

Fishing leaders across Tamil Nadu have condemned these arrests, urging the Indian government to intervene. They said 270 trawlers have been impounded by Sri Lankan authorities since 2018.

title: Anti-whaling activist Paul Watson freed from Greenland jail
content:
Anti-whaling activist Paul Watson, was released from a jail cell in Greenland just before Christmas, after the government of Denmark rejected Japan's extradition request, reports The Guardian.

Recall that Watson, 74, who heads the Captain Paul Watson Foundation (CPWF), was arrested on July 21 in Nuuk, Greenland, when his ship, the M/Y John Paul DeJoria, stopped there to refuel, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

Japan had issued an international warrant for Watson's arrest related to an incident involving a Japanese whaling research ship in 2010 when Watson was a Sea Shepherd Conservation Society member. Japanese authorities accused him of obstructing the crew by ordering the captain of his ship to throw explosives.

Japan resumed commercial whaling in 2019. 

If convicted of that crime in a Japanese court, Watson could face up to 15 years in jail.

Explaining the decision to set Watson free, Peter Hummelgaard, Denmark's minister for justice, said Japan had not given sufficient assurance that Watson's five months in jail awaiting extradition would be deducted from any future sentence.

"It has been of particular importance for the Danish Ministry of Justice to ensure that the time Paul Watson had been detained in Greenland will be fully deducted from a potential custodial sentence that he might be sentenced to in connection with the criminal case in Japan," Hummelgaard is quoted as saying by The Guardian.

Japan has officially voiced its displeasure to the Danish government over Watson's release.

Meanwhile, Watson expressed relief at being freed in time to spend Christmas with his two young sons, aged three and eight, adding that his time in jail also helped focus attention on Japan's whaling operations.

title: Lobsterman fined CAD 25,000 for breaking Canada’s fishing rules
content:
A lobster fisherman from the Canadian province of Nova Scotia has been handed fines totaling nearly CAD 25,000 ($17,645) for multiple violations under Canada's Fisheries Act.

Mikhail John Randell Pictou was convicted and sentenced by a Yarmouth provincial court way back in early October for crimes committed in 2022 and 2023 but the Maritimes regional office of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) didn't report the matter until Tuesday (Dec. 10) on its Twitter account.  

His crimes were spread out over multiple dates and handled as two separate matters in the court.

Pictou was found guilty on Oct. 7 of possessing 590 lobsters that were caught in contravention of Section 33 of the Fisheries Act and also of violating license conditions by fishing 25 untagged traps and using unbuoyed fishing gear, a DFO spokesperson confirmed for Undercurrent News on Wednesday (Dec. 11).

"The offenses that led to these convictions occurred Sept. 29, 2022, in St. Mary's Bay, NS, when fishery officers arrested Mr. Pictou and seized four crates and 25 untagged traps. The 590 seized lobsters were released live into the ocean,"  the DFO said in an email.

In a second court appearance, on Oct. 8, Pictou was found guilty of additional violations of the Fisheries Act and the Atlantic Fisheries regulations stemming from incidents that happened in November 2023. The violations included: possession of female crab; possession of undersized lobster; non-compliance of conditions of license by fishing 56 traps without tags; and possession of 692 lobsters caught in contravention of the Fisheries Act.

Fisheries officers arrested Pictou and seized his vessel, traps and catch. Some 692 illegally-caught lobsters were released live back to the ocean, the DFO official confirmed.

The court ordered that Pictou's vessel remain in the custody of DFO until all fines for the 2023 offenses — totaling CAD 12,500 — are paid in full.

Recall that commercial lobster license holders in southern Nova Scotia have complained for several years about illegal lobster fishing, particularly in the St. Mary's Bay area, and this year have accused DFO of not doing enough to enforce the rules, as previously reported by Undercurrent. 

Earlier this year, enforcement and conservation officers with the DFO in southern NS refused to work out of concerns for their safety on the job, as reported by Undercurrent.

title: Canadian fishery officers call in sick to protest suspension of colleague
content:
A veteran enforcement officer with Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) has been suspended for 10 days without pay for his role in arresting two Mi'kmaq elver fishers in the province of Nova Scotia (NS). Several DFO enforcement officers in NS and the nearby province of New Brunswick booked off on mental health leave on Wednesday (Dec. 11) to protest the punishment of their colleague, reports CTV News. 

The DFO officer was reprimanded for actions following the arrest of two Mi'kmaq men from Cape Breton who were fishing for baby eels late at night on March 26 near Shelburne, NS. The two men said three DFO officers confiscated their phones and hip waders before leaving them at a gas station, about a 45-minute drive from where they had been fishing.

The two men said they walked in the cold, without boots, along the highway for hours before they were able to borrow a cellphone to call a friend to come pick them up.

Recall that Canada's fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier launched an external review into the matter.

"The allegations brought forward regarding the treatment of the two individuals are simply unacceptable," Lebouthiller said in a statement at the time, as reported by Undercurrent News.

However, sources told media this week that many DFO officers believe the supervisor at the center of this case followed proper arrest procedures by taking the men to a location of their choice -- the gas station -- and dropping them off.

It is normal procedure for DFO officers to seize hip waders and cellphones when making arrests in suspected illegal fishing, and said the officers made some efforts to find the men's boots before leaving the scene of the arrest, the source is reported to have told the Canadian Press.

title: Canadian provincial court grants bail for lobster dealer accused of intimidation
content:
Eric Thibault, a 65-year-old lobster dealer from Nova Scotia charged with several counts of intimidation, has been granted release on CAD 20,000 ($14,249.00) bail by a court in the Canadian province, reports the CBC.

Recall that Eric David Thibault and his son, Zacharie, 32, were arrested by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police on Wednesday (Nov. 27) following an incident at Meteghan. The two are alleged to have threatened Geoffrey Jobert, owner of the Lobster Hub there, as reported by Undercurrent News.

However, the list of allegations against the Thibaults extends beyond that incident. The elder Thibault is also facing charges that he threatened a lobster fisherman who was seeking to change buyers, and three counts of witness intimidation related to an incident in January in Meteghan.

The provincial court, in Yarmouth on Monday (Dec. 2), also prohibited Eric Thibault from having contact with nine people involved in his intimidation incidents or going to their homes or workplaces. He is not allowed to contact any employee of the Meteghan Harbour Authority. He is also banned from nearly every federally-owned wharf or small craft harbor or any business in southwestern Nova Scotia that's involved in the lobster fishery.

The only exception is Wedgeport Lobster, where Thibault is employed. The president of that company, Reg LeBlanc, confirmed that Thibault worked for the company but also said the allegations against Thibault don't relate to Wedgeport Lobster, telling the CBC that Thibault is "on his own."

Thibault will return to court on Thursday (Dec. 5) to enter a plea on the charges.

Meanwhile, Zacharie Thibault remains in custody. He is charged with threatening to kill Jobert last March, trying to extort him this summer, harassing him, and intimidating him into not buying lobster from a certain fisherman, according to CBC. The younger Thibault will also be back in court on Thursday to enter a plea.

title: Father, son charged with intimidating Canadian lobster buyer
content:
Two men alleged to have intimidated and threatened a lobster buyer in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia are in provincial court in the town of Yarmouth today (Dec. 2) to begin the court process, reports the CBC.

Eric David Thibault, 65, and his son Zacharie David Thibault, 32, were arrested on Wednesday (Nov. 27) by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) in Meteghan, NS, following an incident in the village of Mavillette that day.

The two men are alleged to have approached Geoffrey Jobert, owner of Lobster Hub in Meteghan, near his home and threatened him. Recall that Jobert's home was shot a few days earlier in an attack that he believed was linked to organized criminals involved in the illegal lobster trade, as reported by Undercurrent News.

The charges against the Thibuaults don't relate to that shooting, however. The RCMP has not arrested or charged anyone in connection with that offense.

That said, the Thibualts and Jobert have had encounters before. Court records also show that the father and son have been charged with intimidation before -- involving other lobster industry members.

Last December, Eric Thibault was accused of threatening a lobster fisherman who was looking to switch to another buyer. In January, he was charged with three counts of witness intimidation. He was out on bail on those charges, pending a court hearing. A Crown prosecutor indicated on Friday he will seek to have that bail revoked.

Before his arrest on Wednesday, Zacharie Thibault had been in police custody for more than two months on unrelated charges and was just released on Tuesday (Nov. 26) after pleading guilty and being sentenced to time served and probation for offenses that included dangerous driving, mischief and uttering threats.

On Thursday, the RCMP filed additional charges against him. Those charges allege that he threatened to kill Jobert earlier this year and tried to extort the Lobster Hub owner in July.

title: Australia intercepts 14 foreign fishing boats, prosecutes Indonesian crew
content:
Australian authorities have intensified their crackdown on illegal fishing, intercepting 14 foreign vessels with 112 crew and prosecuting 19 Indonesian nationals in separate operations across northern waters, officials said.

The Australian Border Force (ABF) conducted a five-day operation between Nov. 14 and 18, boarding and inspecting the 14 vessels and seizing illegal marine products, including sea cucumber, worth up to AUD 55,000 ($36,000), the agency said in a statement on Wednesday (Nov. 20).

In related cases earlier this month, 19 Indonesian nationals pleaded guilty to illegal fishing charges at Darwin Local Court, with two repeat offenders receiving suspended prison sentences, according to court documents.

One repeat offender was sentenced to six months of suspended imprisonment with 14 days of immediate custody, while another received a three-month suspended sentence.

Fishing vessel and crew arrested by Australian Border Force. Source: Australian Border Force

The court cases stemmed from two separate incidents in October where authorities intercepted Indonesian vessels targeting sea cucumber in protected marine parks near Port Essington and Cape Talbot.

Officials confiscated substantial quantities of fishing equipment and salt used for preservation. The intercepted vessels in the October cases were destroyed under Australian biosecurity laws.

"These court outcomes reinforce that illegal fishing in Australian waters will not be tolerated," said Justin Bathurst, general manager of fisheries operations at the Australian Fisheries Management Authority.

The remaining convicted crew members were released on good behavior bonds ranging from AUD 200 to AUD 5,000, with terms between one and three years. All 19 convicted fishers will be deported to Indonesia.

Maritime border command rear admiral Brett Sonter said Australia maintains extensive surveillance and patrol capabilities to combat illegal fishing.

"Our message to illegal foreign fishers is simple: Australia does not tolerate illegal activity in our waters. We will intercept you, you will lose your catch, your equipment and possibly even your vessel," said Sonter.

Australian authorities are also conducting public information campaigns in Indonesian fishing communities to address the issue at its source.

title: Report: Up to 30% of Atlantic Canada’s lobster catch is unreported
content:
As much as 30% of lobster caught in Atlantic Canada each year goes unreported, potentially accounting for up to CAD 681 million ($488.79m) annually, according to a memo from Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO).

CBC News reported the findings, which have raised concerns about tax evasion and sustainability in the region's marine resources.

The memo, shared in August, cited an estimated 10-30% of Atlantic lobster landings that bypass the official reporting system, CBC reported. DFO is working with the Canada Revenue Agency and the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada to map out networks involved in unreported cash sales, which sidestep the daily logbooks required for commercial lobster fishing.

According to CBC News, the DFO declined an interview request. However, it did issue a statement that unreported catches create economic inequalities, jeopardize conservation efforts, and could harm Canada's reputation for sustainable fishing.

Osborne Burke, president of the Nova Scotia Seafood Alliance, told the state broadcaster that these practices add pressure on those operating legally. "It's tough for the ones that are playing by the rules to be able to compete when you have this other illegal activity occurring," Burke said.

Morley Knight, a former assistant deputy minister with DFO, told CBC that cash-based deals have attracted outside buyers who bring funds to the piers, offering fishers potentially higher prices for unreported catches. This activity challenges local buyers and risks misrepresenting the health of lobster stocks, which depend on accurate data for management, he said.

Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance president Colin Sproul issued a warning earlier this month about illegal lobster dealings, including out-of-season fishing in other areas, as Undercurrent News reported. The alliance filed a CAD 10m civil lawsuit against several parties, alleging they purchased lobsters caught illegally on Nova Scotia's southwest coast. Sproul noted that the lawsuit aims to combat illegal activities harming the regulated commercial fishery.

The issue of illegal lobster dealings led Nova Scotia to add licensing requirements for buyers and processors and increase inspections. While some officials support outlawing cash sales, the fisheries minister has suggested this does not address underlying enforcement issues.

The DFO has faced criticism for its enforcement practices in the lobster and juvenile eel fisheries. Critics argue the department has failed to fully address illegal activities, while others, including Nova Scotia fisheries minister Kent Smith, have pointed to the involvement of organized crime in the region's fisheries.

In response, the DFO said that it had initiated enforcement actions recently, including arrests and gear seizures, although the outcomes of these cases remain unclear.

title: Canadian captain convicted for fishing in marine protected area
content:
A fishing captain is the first to be convicted under Canada's Oceans Act in the Maritimes region after pleading guilty on Oct. 23 to fishing in a marine protected area (MPA), Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) reported on Twitter/X Monday (Nov. 4).

Greg MacMullin was charged in 2023 after fishery officers observed his longline vessel fishing inside the closed section of zone 1 in the St. Anns Bank MPA, a 4,264 square kilometer area off the eastern shore of Cape Breton Island, in the province of Nova Scotia.

Enforcement officers arrested the captain and seized 1,951 pounds of halibut and 123 pounds of cod, a spokesperson for the Maritimes office of DFO told Undercurrent News.

A DFO map of the St. Annes Bank Marine Protected Area. Highlighted in green, the MPA encompasses 4,264 square kilometers off the east coast of Cape Breton Island, Nova Scotia.

MacMullin pleaded guilty to the charges when the case came to a provincial court in Sydney, Nova Scotia. In the ruling handed down Monday, the court ordered that MacMullin be fined CAD 5,000 ($3,599) and his catch, valued at approximately CAD 17,745, forfeited to the government.

The court also ordered that MacMullin be required to use the national vessel monitoring system for the next decade, regardless of what area he is fishing.

St. Annes Bank, which was designated a MPA in 2017, has significant biological and ecological features. It has the highest annual sea surface temperature range on the Scotia Shelf, and provides habitat for commercial and non-commercial species, like Atlantic cod, redfish, white hake, witch flounder and American plaice, and endangered species like Atlantic wolffish and leatherback turtles, DFO explained on its website.

title: Two months without arrests: Justice sought for murder of Mexican fishing representative
content:
The Center for Development and Sustainable Fisheries (CeDePesca) has renewed its call for justice for Minerva Perez Castro, the head of the Baja California branch of the Mexican National Chamber of Fishing and Aquaculture Industry (CANAINPESCA), who was murdered in July. 

In a statement sent to Undercurrent News, CeDePesca, led by its CEO Ernesto Godelman, emphasized that impunity must not be allowed to prevail. "Impunity cannot be allowed to win. It is unacceptable that citizens who live and work honestly are prisoners of fear while the murderers walk free," the statement reads. The organization urges Mexican authorities at all levels to step up efforts in finding those responsible for the crime.

Perez had long denounced illegal extortion attempts, where criminal groups sought payments in exchange for so-called "protection." She had also urged authorities to take more decisive action against illegal fishing operations, warning of the growing influence of these criminal organizations.

Perez was assassinated on July 8. Infobae reported that her vehicle was found with bullet holes in front of the facilities of the seafood firm Atenea en el Mar, of which she was the director. Her murderer has not been identified.

title: Extortion alerts surge in Ecuador’s shrimp sector
content:
Ecuador's fishing, aquaculture, and agricultural industries faced over 900 extortion threats between mid-July and August 2024, according to a report to a report by the National Chamber of Aquaculture (CNA), Extra Ecuador reported.

The trade group said most cases occurred along coastal provinces, especially Guayaquil, Duran, Samborondon and the coastal areas of El Oro, Esmeraldas, Manabi and Santa Elena.

Citing national police and ECU 911 security data, the aquaculture chamber said the sectors saw an average of 20 daily extortion attempts. However, 75% of victims do not report incidents to police.

¡HOY 18H00! Infórmate de las cifras delincuenciales, las incidencias extorsivas en el perfil costero, los tipos de extorsión y las acciones que realiza la CNA en materia de seguridad.

SUSCRÍBETE a el Boletín de Seguridad de la Cámara Nacional de Acuacultura. ➡️… pic.twitter.com/1wzE9tulS5

— Cámara Acuacultura (@cnaecuador) September 2, 2024

Extortion takes two main forms -- virtual, with criminals posing as leaders and making threats by telephone or online, and in-person, with perpetrators familiar with targets using violent intimidation.

To combat the rise, industry groups launched surveillance networks and radio communications systems for transport vehicles. However, extortion remains an escalating threat impacting Ecuador's vital fishing and agricultural economies.

These measures aim to mitigate the growing threat of extortion in Ecuador's vital economic sectors.

In a related report, police officials said Ecuador has seen over 2,100 kidnappings and 10,000 extortion cases this year, according to an article in El Universo . The Force for Investigating Extortion (FICE), created this year, has conducted 20 operations within five days, arresting 77 people.

Authorities attribute much of the extortion to organized gangs like Tiguerones, Lobos and Aguilas. A 95% yearly increase in cases prompted the creation of a special anti-extortion police unit, which has conducted 20 operations and made 77 arrests in five days.

title: Former New York governor’s aide accused of using office to boost husband’s seafood exports to China
content:
A former aide to New York state governors Kathy Hochul and Andrew Cuomo was arrested on Tuesday (Sep. 3) on charges of using her government position to secretly promote the Chinese government and simultaneously grow the profits of her husband's seafood export business.

Linda Sun, 41, and her husband, Christopher Hu, 40, are accused of leveraging Sun's political influence to help Hu's company, Foodie Fisherman LLC, secure a foothold in the Chinese seafood market, online news outlet Gothamist reported. 

According to an indictment filed in the US District Court for the Eastern District of New York, in Brooklyn, officials with ties to the Chinese government provided crucial assistance to Hu's business, which focuses on exporting lobsters to China, starting in 2016.

The indictment outlines how Hu's seafood exports eventually led to millions in revenue, much of which prosecutors allege was laundered and went undeclared on taxes. The couple used the earnings to purchase luxury items, including a multimillion-dollar Long Island home and a Honolulu condo, according to the article.

Sun allegedly didn't disclose the financial benefits on her required state ethics forms.

In return, Sun allegedly used her roles in New York's state government to advance Chinese government interests, including blocking Taiwanese representatives from engaging with New York state officials. China, which does not recognize Taiwan as an independent country, pressures other governments to avoid official interactions with Taiwanese representatives to maintain its "One China" policy.

A more critical aspect of the allegations against the couple is the potential threat to US national security. Sun is accused of covertly promoting the interests of the Chinese government, including giving Chinese officials access to sensitive state-level discussions.

In one instance, she allegedly arranged for a Chinese official to secretly listen in on a conference call where New York state leaders were discussing their response to the COVID-19 pandemic and hate crimes against Asians. 

Sun and Hu have pleaded not guilty to the charges, including visa fraud, money laundering and violations of the Foreign Agents Registration Act.

title: Anti-whaling activist Paul Watson to remain in Denmark jail for now
content:
Anti-whaling activist Paul Watson will remain in jail in Denmark while that country continues to mull over an extradition request from Japan, reports the Associated Press. 

A Greenland district court ruled on Wednesday (Sept. 4) that Watson, who holds dual American-Canadian citizenship, will remain in custody there until Oct. 2. Greenland is an autonomous territory of Denmark, which doesn't have an extradition treaty with Japan.

Recall that Watson, 73, who heads the Captain Paul Watson Foundation (CPWF), was arrested on July 21 in Nuuk, Greenland, when his ship, the M/Y John Paul DeJoria, stopped there to refuel.

Japan issued an international warrant for Watson's arrest related to an incident involving a Japanese whaling research ship in 2010 when Watson was a Sea Shepherd Conservation Society member. Japanese authorities accused Watson of obstructing the crew by ordering the captain of his ship to throw explosives.

Japan resumed commercial whaling in 2019. 

Watson could face up to 15 years in prison if convicted by a Japanese court, as previously reported by Undercurrent News. 

Watson's vessel had been en route to the Northwest Passage as part of CPWF's Operation Kangei Maur, a mission to intercept Japan's new factory whaling ship, Kangei Maru, in the North Pacific, when he was arrested in July.

Greenland prosecutors confirmed that Watson has appealed the decision by the Nuuk district court to the High Court of Greenland. No date has been set for an appeal hearing.

title: Canadian officers refuse to work in lobster fishery over safety concerns
content:
Some enforcement officers with Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) are refusing to work in the province of Nova Scotia's big lobster fisheries out of concern for their safety, reports the CBC.

With lobster fishing season starting in just three months in lobster fishing areas 33 and 34, off the province's southwest coast, commercial fishermen are concerned about the impact of illegal fishing on lobster stocks.

Recall that at a meeting this past June in Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, between the lobster industry and DFO officials, harvesters said they were worried that the moderate livelihood fishery, which permits First Nations to fish for food, social and ceremonial purposes, would continue to cause problems in some areas, as reported by Undercurrent News.

In the summer of 2023, DFO seized over 1,200 lobster traps, arrested 15 people and released over 10,000 pounds of illegally caught lobster. Officials with DFO told the Yarmouth harvesters in June that there is an enforcement plan in place for this season, but the department couldn't commit to an increased effort.

The moderate livelihood fishery has been a long-standing point of contention ever since a 1999 Supreme Court of Canada ruling, also known as the Marshall decision, affirmed First Nations' treaty rights to fish, hunt and gather in pursuit of a moderate livelihood under the terms of the Peace and Friendship Treaties of 1760 and 1761.

Since the Marshall decision, the federal government has spent nearly CAD 1.0 billion ($731 million) buying commercial lobster licenses and transferring them to First Nations.

Those licenses require First Nations to participate in fisheries during the same seasons and be subject to the same Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) regulations as commercial fishermen.

While some First Nations in Nova Scotia have signed on to annual moderate livelihood agreements with DFO, the Sipekne'katik, who fish in the St. Mary's Bay area of Nova Scotia, in Lobster fishing area 34, have not. Although the fishery is permitted, Sipekne'katik officials have previously rejected DFO's allowable limit of 45,000 pounds.

The Canadian government and the Sipekne'katik First Nation moved to a mediation process in June in an attempt to reach agreement on what constitutes a moderate livelihood fishery, as reported by Undercurrent.

As lobster season approaches, however, licensed lobster harvesters are growing frustrated.

"There's illegal fishing occurring, and there is no enforcement staff on the road or on the water or on the wharves. And it's out of hand," Dan Fleck, executive director of the Brazil Rock Lobster Association, is quoted as saying by CBC.

In a statement to the news organization, DFO said it is "making every effort to minimize operational impacts."

The federal agency didn't elaborate on the safety concerns expressed by its officers but said it has begun investigating reports of dangerous working conditions. It also noted that enforcement work is still happening, but it would not disclose how many officers are working or if the number of officers working has changed compared to last year.

"Fisheries and Oceans Canada respects the right of employees to refuse dangerous work, and we take reports of dangerous work seriously," DFO said in a statement to CBC.

DFO officers are represented by the Union of Health and Environment Workers. The union said it is involved in helping resolve the issue, and due process is being followed.

title: Editor’s choice: Alaska salmon trollers win appeal; Live from Asian aquaculture show
content:
EMEA deputy editor Dan Gibson brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week  

In the most-read story of last week, Chinook salmon trollers in Southeast Alaska were dealt a win by the US Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals in a multi-year lawsuit brought by the environmental group Wild Fish Conservancy (WFC).

The high court ruled on Aug. 16 that a lower-level federal court had "abused its discretion" in August 2022 when it vacated the troll fishery's incidental take statement, an essential document for fisheries that might impact endangered species. The lower court had originally sided with WFC on its 2020 complaint over the impact of the troll fleet's salmon harvests on the food supply for an endangered population of killer whales in Washington state's Puget Sound.

Elsewhere, Undercurrent News was reporting live from the annual Aquaculture Roundtable Series (TARS) show, held Aug. 14-15 in the Thai capital, Bangkok. TARS brought together experts from around the world to discuss markets, price trends and feed supply developments for a variety of tropical farmed fish species such as tilapia, pangasius and pompano at a challenging time for the sector. You can read all of Undercurrent's coverage from the show here.

Back in the US, Norwegian land-based aquaculture company AquaCon announced it was shifting its plans away from building four separate recirculating aquaculture systems across the country in favor of setting up a single 20,000-metric ton facility in northern Maryland state. AquaCon estimates the capex costs of the first phase, designed to produce 10,000t of head-on gutted weight salmon, to reach roughly $300 million.

title: Daily recap: Alaska, Southeast salmon trollers win appeal; Fishmeal prices in China down
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Friday, Aug. 16: 

State of Alaska, Southeast salmon trollers win appeal over Wild Fish Conservancy lawsuit

Chinook (king) salmon trollers in Southeast Alaska have been dealt a win by the US Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals in a multi-year lawsuit brought by the environmental group Wild Fish Conservancy.

Fishmeal prices in China down $200/t but market quiet

Fishmeal prices continue to decline in China but buying activity at source in Peru remains quiet as buyers and sellers await the outcome of the upcoming second anchovy fishing season, industry sources report.

Argentina shrimp sector hopes for market boost from surging catches but fears low demand

The Argentine red shrimp industry is experiencing a resurgence in the country's national waters this season, with catches showing a significant increase compared to the previous year.

Chinese authorities uncover fake shrimp scheme, importer arrested

Chinese authorities uncovered a fraud scheme involving imported Ecuadorian shrimp, discovering that 16 shipping containers purportedly containing shrimp were instead filled with ice, according to officials.

Bumble Bee, StarKist tuna price-fixing cases to settle for $200m

The parent and former parent companies of two major packaged tuna fish giants -- StarKist and Bumble Bee Foods -- have agreed to pay more than $200 million to formally settle a long-fought class action suit that alleged antitrust violations in a conspiracy to overcharge consumers and other purchasers.

Generation change prompts drop in Norwegian salmon prices, Chile, Scots flat

Multiple industry sources told Undercurrent News they see salmon prices out of Norway falling again in week 34 (Aug. 19-25) amid an abundance of small fish, while volumes out of Scotland and Chile are continuing flat throughout August.

title: European glass eel smuggling crackdown sends prices in China soaring
content:
Additional reporting by Lewis Hu.

Wholesale prices for farmed eels in China's Guangdong province have jumped 25% from last year, reaching CNY 210,000 per metric ton ($28,930/t) for smaller grades and CNY 195,000/t for larger eels. The price surge, coupled with a 40% reduction in eel fry stocking by Guangdong farmers to only 50 million this year, may be linked to successful anti-smuggling efforts in Europe, according to the Brussels-based Sustainable Eel Group (SEG). 

"We've seen the arrests of about 800 people over the last six years," Andrew Kerr, chairman at SEG, told Undercurrent News. "And prison sentences have been doled out, three and four years. People's assets have been confiscated."  

A police raid in Portugal during 'Operation Elver' in 2018. Source: SEG website.

These enforcement actions have significantly impacted the illegal trade, which was worth as much as €3 billion ($3.2bn) in peak years. According to Kerr, the smuggling of European eels to Asia has dropped from about 300m to 350m eels annually to about 30m -- a 90% reduction. 
 
The European eel (Anguilla anguilla), a critically endangered species, has been at the center of the lucrative smuggling operation spanning continents. Born in the Sargasso Sea near Bermuda, young eels drift across the Atlantic Ocean for two to three years before arriving in European waters. It's at this stage, when they enter estuaries as transparent "glass eels," that they become targets for legal and illegal fishing. 

"We've seen the population slowly declining for several hundred years," Kerr explained. "But from 1980 to 2010, we had a period of extreme decline, going down at 15% a year." This precipitous drop led to the implementation of the EU's Eel Regulation in 2007, a piece of legislation designed to protect the species. 

Asian appetite for eel

The demand driving this illicit trade comes primarily from Asia, where eel is a popular delicacy but where local supply of Anguilla japonica is limited. Chinese farmers purchase European glass eels and stock them in freshwater ponds, raising them to harvest size after 18 months or a year. 

Eels seized during a police raid in Portugal in 2018. Source: SEG website

Suitcases used to transport European glass eels discovered during a police raid in Portugal in 2018. Source: SEG website

"To give you the scale of things," Kerr said, "the total production from European eel farms is about 6,000t a year. The biggest producer of eel from eel farms is China, producing 240,000t. That's 85% of the world's production." 

Asia's insatiable appetite -- coupled with the inability to breed eels in captivity -- has fueled a lucrative black market for wild-caught glass eels at each stage of the supply chain. "A trafficked illegal glass eel will be caught in the Bay of Biscay, and a French fisherman is likely to get about €0.05 or €0.10 to the Euro," Kerr said. "That eel landed in Hong Kong is then worth €1. Grown in an eel farm in China for a year, a year and a half, it's then worth €10." 

China's eel exports to Japan

Recent data from China underscores the economic impact of the smuggling crackdown. The shortage of wild-caught eel fry has caused a supply bottleneck in China's multi-million dollar eel farming industry. Fujian Tianma Science and Technology Group, which farms eel, reported a swing to a CNY 56.1m ($7.7m) profit in the first half of 2024, compared to a CNY 28m loss last year. The company attributed this turnaround to a 373% surge in eel farming revenue due to soaring prices. 
 
The impact has also extended beyond China. Last year, almost 90% of Japan's $529m eel imports came from China, which supplied 25,700t of live and processed eel -- the second-highest volume in 20 years. 

Further price hikes may impact demand in Japan, as the weak yen makes imported eels more expensive for Japanese consumers. Prices of Chinese farmed eels in Japan range from JPY 1,500-JPY 1,900 ($9.75-$12.35) per fish, while higher-end domestic Japanese eels cost JPY 2,500 and JPY 3,000 each, according to local Chinese media. 

According to Undercurrent's price dashboard, prices for the lowest grade imported eel, prepared in kabayaki style, are currently at their highest at JPY 4,320 per kilogram at Toyosu, Japan's largest seafood wholesale market. In US dollar terms, prices continue to rise (see below). 

Upgrade to Pro to view
Smuggling crackdown

The methods used by smugglers have evolved over time. One tactic involves using human "mules" to transport eels. "Asian people would come to Europe, theoretically on holiday, turn up at a pop-up hidden eel station, collect a suitcase full of eels, up to 100,000 in a suitcase," Kerr described. "That corresponds to 30 kilos, your baggage allowance. You put that on the airplane with you, fly back to Hong Kong with it, and then you would be taken off you by the buying team and put into the local farms." 
 
The value of a single suitcase of eels could be as high as €100,000 when landed in Hong Kong, and potentially worth €1m to the farmer after cultivation. This aligns with recent data showing that the average price of eel fry imported from Hong Kong has skyrocketed 486% since 2019 to $4,550/kg in 2023, according to Chinese Customs data (see below). 

The crackdown has been particularly intense in Spain and France, a key source of glass eels. Kerr described large-scale operations involving French law enforcement: "Sometimes 100 gendarmes from across France will converge on a river and an eel station or two, and in a sweep handle the eels in the station, check all the records, catching vehicles with eels without papers. Unbelievable amounts of attention."  

Baggage scanning technology has made it more difficult to smuggle glass eels on planes. Source: SEG website

Technological advancements have also played a crucial role in curbing smuggling. "The technology of inspecting suitcases has really improved as well," he said. "Baggage handling technology is now finding glass eels. So it's much, much harder to do." 

Evolving challenge

Despite the success in curbing European glass eel smuggling, Kerr warns that the problem has shifted. Chinese buyers have turned their attention to other eel species, particularly the American eel (Anguilla rostrata). Recent research suggests that around 300m American glass eels may now be finding their way to Asian farms annually. 
 
The challenge of eel conservation extends beyond fishing practices, too. Kerr said that the eel's decline is fundamentally an environmental problem. 
 
"WWF [World Wildlife Fund for Nature] in the State of the Planet Index describes European freshwater as the most damaged ecosystem on the planet," he noted. Habitat destruction, pollution, and the presence of barriers in rivers all pose significant threats to eel populations. "We've put 1.3m barriers into the rivers of Europe as part of our water engineering," Kerr said. "And that stops migratory fish." 

Andrew Kerr, chairman of SEG, participates in a meeting on European eel at the EU in June 2018. Source: SEG

If glass eels could be bred artificially, a key driver of demand for wild-caught would disappear. But the eel's complex lifecycle has so far defied attempts at doing so; despite success in fertilization and hatching, survival rates of baby eels -- or Leptocephalus -- in artificial settings are less than 1%. 
 
"80-90% of eggs will hatch," Kerr explained. "But we can't get them to live beyond 20-30 days and we don't know what it is that's stopping them surviving." 
 
The impact of this reliance on wild-caught fry is evident in the current supply shortage in China, which has forced some producers to adapt. Du Qihua, production manager of a grilled eel processing company in Foshan, Guangdong, told Chinese state broadcaster CCTV his firm switched to sushi slices due to the shortages. 
 
"Last year, we mainly sold whole grilled eels. This year, due to the rise in raw material prices and according to customer needs, we process them into sushi slices. One grilled eel can be cut into about 40 slices, and the price per slice is correspondingly much higher than the whole eel price," Du said. 
 
An expected drop in demand from Japan may help to cool the frothy market. Demand peaks in July for the country's traditional "Eel Day" celebrations, and the month tends to see consumption increase almost ten times compared with other months of the year.

title: Anti-whaling activist Paul Watson faces potential 15-year sentence in Japan
content:
Paul Watson, founder of Sea Shepherd and co-founder of Greenpeace, faces up to 15 years in prison in Japan if convicted on charges including accomplice to assault and ship trespass.

On July 21, 2024, Watson was arrested by Danish police upon arrival in Nuuk, Greenland, onboard the M/Y John Paul DeJoria, Undercurrent News reported last week.

Danish authorities claim that the arrest was made due to an international arrest warrant issued by Japan relating to his anti-whaling campaigns in the Antarctic more than a decade ago, according to Sea Shepherd. 

According to the organization, the Canadian-American faces the possibility of extradition to Japan, where he would serve a maximum prison sentence of 15 years.

Watson is linked to a 2010 incident in which a Sea Shepherd member boarded the Japanese whaling ship Shonan Maru 2, the Guardian reported.

The charges stem from clashes in the Southern Ocean, where Sea Shepherd's speedboat was destroyed by the Shonan Maru 2. Activist Peter Bethune boarded the vessel in response and was later arrested and sentenced in Tokyo, with charges against Watson filed soon after.

Watson's detention has sparked significant controversy. French president Emmanuel Macron has urged Denmark not to extradite Watson, who has lived in France for a year. Supporters compare his case to Julian Assange's, calling it politically motivated. Watson remains in custody in Nuuk, Greenland, pending a Danish decision on extradition by August 15.

In total, 68 members of the French and European parliaments also sent a letter to the Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen on July 24 calling for Watson's release, Euractiv reported.

Japan resumed commercial whaling in 2019, targeting whales around its waters. Watson's arrest occurs amid his efforts to intercept Japan's new whaling mothership, Kangei Maru.

Sea Shepherd has launched a petition addressing the Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, demanding Watson be released from custody.

title: Retail theft up in British Columbia suburb, salmon among targets
content:
The high price of salmon has made it a hot commodity for retail theft in Vancouver's suburb of Richmond, British Columbia alongside meat and high-end yoga attire.

Local news sources have revealed that during a focused operation by the Richmond RCMP, Canada's law enforcement agency, spanning four days in April and May, the types of goods frequently recovered, including specific food and clothing items, imply a strong resale motive among the thieves, reported The Vancouver Sun.

April witnessed a staggering 180 shoplifting reports, representing a slight decrease of one percent from March; however, this figure more than doubles the incidents reported in the same period in 2023 and significantly exceeds the average for the Richmond area, according to Richmond News.

In response to these events, local police will press charges against 23 suspects involved in the thefts, directing four juveniles toward a youth intervention program.

The crackdown led to the recovery of stolen items valued at approximately CAD 17,494 ($12,729), primarily apparel and groceries, said the Vancouver Sun.

title: Canadian lobster harvesters push for increased enforcement
content:
Lobster harvesters in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia want to see the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) crack down on illegal fishing, reports Country 100.1, a radio station based in Bridgewater, Nova Scotia.

The issue came up at a meeting Wednesday (June 12) in Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, between the industry and DFO officials.

The lobster harvesters say they are worried that the moderate livelihood fishery, which permits First Nations to fish for food, social and ceremonial purposes, will continue to cause problems in some areas.

Last summer DFO seized over 1,200 lobster traps, arrested 15 people, and released over 10,000 pounds of lobster.

There is an enforcement plan in place for this season, officials said at the Yarmouth meeting, but DFO couldn't commit to an increased effort.

Harvesters say lobster catches were low last fall in the St. Mary's Bay area, one of the areas with an active moderate livelihood fishery.

"Everybody in southwestern Nova Scotia knows why that is. I think it's incumbent on the government to act now before lobster fishing in St. Mary's Bay is a thing of the past," said Colin Sproul, a harvester who is a member of a local industry group, the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance.

title: Canada seizes more illegal elvers at Nova Scotia trucking facility
content:
Enforcement officers with Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) seized 60 kilograms of baby eels worth at least CAD 250,000 ($182,720) on Friday (May 31) in the province of Nova Scotia, reports CBC News. 

In a social media post made Monday (June 3), DFO said the elvers, seized at a transport facility in the city of Dartmouth, were to be driven to Toronto and then transported by air to overseas markets.

A Fisheries and Oceans officer with illegal elvers seized at a trucking facility in Nova Scotia on May 31. Photo from DFO social media post.

Earlier in May, DFO seized 109 kg of baby eels worth about CAD 500,000, at the Toronto airport.

As previously reported by Undercurrent News, Canada's fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier decided in March to shut down the commercial elver fishery in the Maritime provinces this year as part of an effort to combat poaching. Since then, the department says arrests and seizures are "having a significant deterrence" on illegal elver fishing. 

At the beginning of May, the department said it had made 132 arrests and seized 157 kg of elvers, 21 vehicles and hundreds of fyke nets.

title: Thousands of young Chinook salmon poisoned at Oregon hatchery
content:
Thousands of juvenile Chinook salmon have been killed in the US state of Oregon after a trespasser allegedly poured bleach into one of four tanks holding the fish at a hatchery in Reedsport, Oregon. 

In a press release Thursday (April 25), the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife (ODFW) said nearly 18,000 salmon died in the incident.

Twenty-year-old Joshua Heckathorn, of nearby Gardiner, was arrested and booked on charges of burglary, criminal trespassing and criminal mischief, according to ODFW. He could also face felony poaching charges, and other penalties for the unlawful killing of wildlife.

"In my 25 years as a game warden, this is one of the most senseless acts I have seen," said Oregon State Police Fish and Wildlife sergeant Levi Harris.

The hatchery-raised fish that were killed would have joined approximately 60,000 other fall Chinook pre-smolts in the the lower Umpqua River fall Chinook fishery, according to ODFW.

title: Jail looms for Indonesian activists protesting illegal shrimp farms on social media
content:
Greenpeace has condemned Indonesian authorities' escalating legal actions targeting four activists who protested against illegal shrimp farms damaging the ecosystem off the island of Java, reports Mongabay. 

The four activists face accusations of violating a 2008 law on online speech by posting criticisms against shrimp farms operating within the Karimunjawa National Park.

Greenpeace has criticized these legal actions as part of broader efforts by authorities to censor, intimidate, and silence environmental activism through strategic lawsuits against public participation.

The most prominent case among the activists is that of Daniel Frits Maurits Tangkilisan, charged in June 2023 for his online criticisms posted a year earlier. Although arrested in December 2023, he was released conditionally the following day.

Prosecutors are now seeking a conviction with a potential jail sentence of 10 months and a fine of IDR 5 million (nearly $320). The verdict hearing is scheduled for April 4.

Three other activists, Hasanuddin, Datang Abdul Rohim, and Sumarto Rofi'un, were reported to local police in November 2023 for posting a video opposing the illegal shrimp farms.

The activists' campaign focuses on exposing the proliferation of shrimp farms in the Karimunjawa archipelago, which Greenpeace Indonesia has documented since 2016. 

Karimunjawa National Park, spanning 1,100 square kilometers, is a vital marine reserve known for its rich coral reefs and diverse marine life.

title: DNB: Salmon farming at ‘biological ceiling,’ risks losing ‘social license’
content:
PUERTO MONTT, Chile -- Global farmed salmon supply is hitting a "biological ceiling" and risks losing its social license to operate as farmers contend with climate risk and rising sea lice levels, Norway's DNB Bank, the largest lender to the global seafood industry, has warned.

Supply growth should average 3% for the next three years, but disruptions due to warmer oceans remain a risk and output could well be lower, said Ola Trovata, DNB's main salmon analyst, at the Aquasur trade show, which is being held here, March 19-21.

Limited growth will ensure strong prices for the next couple of years, driven by the US market, which accounts for 25% of global demand, DNB has advised.

Innovation is urgently needed to improve the performance of traditional net-pen farming and to accelerate the adoption of offshore, closed containment and land-based aquaculture systems, added Anne Hvistendahl, DNB's global head of seafood.

"There's a biological ceiling to how much we can produce, and we are hitting that ceiling now," Hvistendahl said. "In a way, it's a lost opportunity. It's a good product, it ticks so many boxes, and you can get good prices. You should be able to produce more. And the incentives for technical disruption are there."

DNB predicts supply growth of 0.9% in 2024, after both Norway and Chile, the world's largest two producing countries, were impacted by production disruptions.

Trovata predicted 3.3% growth in 2025 and 2.9% in 2026. This scenario is dependent on relatively few disruptions, he said.

Chile is contending with an increase in sea lice, which weakens fish and leaves them more susceptible to pathogens such as salmonid rickettsial syndrome (SRS), which requires antibiotic treatment. One silver lining in the Chilean story is that, in 2023, salmon farmers used the lowest amount of antibiotics on record since 2011, said Jose Leal, an analyst at analytics firm Aquabench.

Chilean production fell 7% in 2023. Leal said that more Chilean farmers should adopt coho salmon farming, as the species is less exposed to problems with both sea lice and SRS.

"But there is no way that supply can meet the demand for salmon. You need new technology and to farm salmon in a different way," Hvistendahl said.

Paradigm shift

Several things need to change in order to turn around the fortunes of the sector, starting with more investment in new technologies to make production more efficient and sustainable.

Farming more salmon in closed containment units, as well as deep farming below the lice belt, are two methods that are being experimented with, but it will be a steep learning curve; many investors are waiting for environmentally friendly licenses to be approved and new technologies to be implemented.

Salmon producer Leroy Seafood Group has said that 20% of all its future investments will go into these kinds of structures on the western coast of Norway, Hvistendahl said.

Meanwhile, Norway's Salmon Evolution has completed a land-based facility using partial flow-through technology; the "proof of the pudding" of that technological concept will be when the company reaches full density at the site at Indra Havoy, Norway, Hvistendal said.

Environmental, social and governance practices are today seen as the bottom line that investors look for when analyzing a company's sustainability efforts, while regulators are increasingly tightening the environmental screw on farmers, Hvistendahl said.

Salmon farmers are combating issues presented by climate change at a time when the world is becoming more polarized and radical; Hvistendahl made reference to climate campaigner Greta Thunberg's arrest for protesting a wind farm development in Sweden.

If the salmon industry loses the support of its communities and society at large, it will be slapped with more stringent regulations from governments, she said.

Image from Aquasur 2024 website.

Mowi, the world's largest salmon farmer, is investing heavily in genetics to improve the survivability of salmon.

Other innovations, such as new freezing technology that could be used to avoid air transportation, will help the sector, she said.

"You have to grow in a sustainable way; otherwise, politicians will not allow you to grow 10 years from now," Hvistendahl said. "All industries can improve and must improve. This is a fantastic industry, but it needs to concentrate on cultivating this 'social license' to operate in order to move forward."
