title: Spanish police intercept huge drug haul in frozen fish
content:
Spanish police and Customs Surveillance (known in Spanish as DAVA) have apprehended four individuals following the discovery of a massive cocaine shipment in a frozen fish company located in Cambre, A Coruna, El Diario reported.

The cocaine delivery, which exceeds seven metric tons, was intercepted last week in an industrial warehouse. Four individuals have been confirmed as detained, and others have been questioned as part of an ongoing investigation. 

If the estimated quantity is verified, this cocaine haul would be the largest found in the Galician community this year and one of the largest ever in Spain's fight against drug trafficking in the region.

Maria Rivas, a government official in A Coruna, declined to provide further details to reporters to avoid compromising the investigation but left open the possibility of more arrests with the investigation set to continue.

title: Three Italian aquaculture producers investigated for suspected €4.5m fraud
content:
Three Italian aquaculture producers were hit with "coercive measures" following a European investigation into alleged fraud involving €4.5 million ($4.8m) in EU maritime and fisheries funds.

The European Public Prosecutor's Office decreed house arrest for one suspect and requirements to stay in their hometowns for two others after probing a string of seafood companies with headquarters near Rome and offices across central and southern Italy.

Prosecutors allege the companies defrauded EU development funds earmarked for building and upgrading fish breeding facilities. The funds were then funneled through a construction company linked to the seafood producers to inflate costs and illicitly pocket profits.

Magistrates ordered the seizure of €4.5m from six companies operated by the suspects. The Italian Financial Police executed the order.

The European Prosecutor’s independent office probes crimes against the EU budget. The allegations being investigated include criminal conspiracy, aggravated fraud to obtain public funding, money laundering and fraudulent transfer of funds.

title: Canadian lobster harvester challenges constitution, could change rules around Indigenous fishing rights
content:
An Indigenous lobster harvester from Atlantic Canada is expected to be in a New Brunswick provincial court Thursday (Nov. 30) to launch a constitutional challenge over Mi'kmaq fishing rights.

The outcome could set another precedent for First Nation fishers in the country.

The case stems from an incident five years ago when Cody Caplin and his brother, Kyle, both members of the Eel River Bar First Nation, were fishing in the province's Bay of Chaleur. It was in September and officers with Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO), who deemed the activity to be illegal, seized their boat.

Then, a year later, the Caplins were charged with 10 fishing offenses, including trapping lobster out of season.

Kyle Caplin eventually pled guilty to the charges, but his brother decided to fight in court, recounts the Canadian Press. 

Cody Caplin claims that Canada's Fisheries Act and Regulations "significantly restrict" his constitutional Mi'kmaw treaty and aboriginal fishing rights.

Canadian Senate report recommends removing federal fisheries agency from First Nation negotiations

In his application to the court, Caplin cites a 1990 Supreme Court of Canada decision regarding Ronald Sparrow, a Musqueam First Nation member in British Columbia convicted of fishing illegally in 1984. Canada's highest court quashed the conviction and agreed that Sparrow's ancestral right to fish was protected by Section 35 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which affirms existing Indigenous and treaty rights.

That decision allowed First Nations to fish outside the regular commercial season to feed their communities or to supply ceremonial gatherings. However, they can't sell what they catch during what has become known as the food, social and ceremonial fishery.

Caplin argued he had no plans to sell his catch on the day he was arrested, so his actions should have benefited from the protections offered to the food, social and ceremonial fishery. His application also mentions the 1999 Marshall case, a landmark decision regarding First Nations' fishing rights.

The meaning of the Marshall decision

The Marshall decision affirmed First Nations' treaty right to fish, hunt and gather in pursuit of a moderate livelihood. It stemmed from the prosecution of Donald Marshall Jr., a Mi'kmaq member of the Membertou First Nation in Nova Scotia.

In August 1993, Marshall caught and sold eel without a license during the fishery's off-season. He was charged under the federal Fisheries Act and the Maritime Provinces Fishery Regulations and convicted of illegal fishing by Nova Scotia's Provincial Court in 1996.

When the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal upheld the conviction in 1997, Marshall appealed his case to the Supreme Court of Canada.

On September 17, 1999, that court reversed Marshall's convictions and affirmed the hunting, fishing and gathering rights promised to Indigenous peoples in the Peace and Friendship Treaties of 1760 and 1761. 

The outcome of the Caplin case could change the legal landscape again, however.

"If we win, we could ...  make some case law for other Mi'kmaq fishermen throughout the province," Caplin told the Canadian Press.

DFO notes on its website that 34 First Nations in the Maritimes and Gaspé region, and the Peskotomuhkati, have a treaty right to fish in pursuit of a moderate livelihood.

"The Government of Canada recognizes this right and continues to work with First Nations to implement the Marshall decisions," the department stated.

Frustrations

However, recent DFO decisions have frustrated First Nations fishers.

The Mi'kmaq communities in the traditional district of Kespukwitk – Annapolis Valley, Bear River, Glooscap and Wasoqopa’q (Acadia) – met with DFO in May and outlined the First Nations' expectations for participation in the region's lobster fishery, based on their treaty rights protection (TRP).

During these discussions, the communities said they anticipated 75 TRP lobster harvesters by Nov. 27.

The lobster plan proposed in October by the Kespukwitk TRC would have see each harvester authorized to use 100 lobster traps, for a total of 7,500 traps for the season.

DFO, however, set the limit at 5,250 traps.

“This news is frustrating for the communities, as we have made several attempts to demonstrate the insufficiency of the current trap allocation, particularly within the commercial lobster season,” said chief Gerald Toney, Fisheries co-lead for the Assembly of Nova Scotia Mi’kmaw Chiefs and chief of Annapolis Valley First Nation.

The chief said requests to DFO went unanswered.

"Our Treaty Rights to harvest and sell are a constitutional priority," Toney added. "The courts said that DFO is to work with us on the implementation of the Right, not have DFO just dictate to us what they want.”

Wayne MacKay, a professor emeritus of law at Dalhousie University in Halifax, said Caplin's case and others like it are important because they are raising questions about the federal government's commitment to advance reconciliation with Canada's Indigenous population.

Several similar cases may also be going to court in Nova Scotia. DFO has charged 54 Mi'kmaq in that province with fishing violations related to the 'moderate livelihood" fishery.

Over 50 Indigenous fish harvesters in Eastern Canada face charges

MacKay noted, however, that whether it's a fishery for food and ceremonial purposes or one to earn a moderate livelihood, the critical question is whether the federal government can regulate the seasons for Indigenous people.

"The Supreme Court has been clear in saying that if conservation is an issue, the (fisheries) can be regulated and need to be regulated," he said, "but the Aboriginal people are arguing that that kind of regulation takes away from their inherent rights to regulate their own fishery."

Caplin plans to represent himself in court. However, he will be assisted by Del Riley, a member of the Chippewas of the Thames in Ontario, who led efforts in the early 1980s to entrench Indigenous rights into the Canadian Constitution.

Riley is credited with negotiating the inclusion of sect. 35 in the charter and section 25, which protects Indigenous and treaty rights from being repealed or diminished by other parts of the Constitution.

The New Brunswick court, in the town of Campbellton, has reserved three days, Dec. 14-16, to hear the case.

title: Two plead guilty to illegal smuggling of sea cucumbers in California
content:
A US woman and a Mexican man have pleaded guilty in a San Diego, California, federal court to charges that they conspired to illegally import sea cucumbers into the US and could face years in jail. 

Between May 2017 and February 2019, Zunyu Zhao (also known as Kathy Zhao), 51, from Calexico, California, and Xionwei Xiao (also known as Luis Xiao), 52, from Mexicali, Mexico, imported Isostichopus fuscus, a species protected under Appendix III of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species, from Mexico without the appropriate permits and documentation, federal prosecutors said in a press release. 

The defendants have agreed that the fair market value of the sea cucumbers was $435 per kilogram and the total value of the goods trafficked was $10,222.50, according to the press release. They also have agreed to pay restitution to the Procuraduria Federal de Proteccion al Ambiente, the Mexican governmental entity charged with protection of the environment.

A recent academic study found that Mexican and US authorities seized more than 100 metric tons of illegally caught sea cucumber worth an estimated $29.5 million between 2011 and 2021, as reported earlier by Undercurrent News. The 97 incidents involved 125 arrests.

A federal grand jury issued a sealed indictment against Zhao and Xiao in May, and the two defendants were arrested in June. Xiao is scheduled to be sentenced in September and Zhao is scheduled to be sentenced in November.

The maximum penalty for conspiracy in the US is five years and a $250,000 fine, according to the press release. The maximum penalty for illegal importation is 20 years and a $250,000 fine.

title: Canada police arrest two men after alleged assaults at Nova Scotia fishing wharf protest
content:
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) arrested and subsequently released two men after responding to reported assaults during an assembly at the Saulnierville Wharf in southwestern Nova Scotia, reports CTV News. 

The arrests occurred on Sept. 9 amid rising tensions surrounding lobster fishing disputes in the region.

Approximately 30 people gathered at the wharf's road when police officers arrived to monitor the protest. Details regarding the purpose of the gathering remain unknown.

This summer has witnessed mounting tensions in southern Nova Scotia, particularly concerning unauthorized lobster fishing. Steve Craig, the fisheries minister for Nova Scotia, intends to increase the maximum fine for buying out-of-season lobster to CAD 1 million ($734,545) from CAD 100,000.

Craig reportedly expressed his intentions following a cabinet conference on Thursday (Sept. 7) and said he was propelled into action by "industrial-scale" fishing activities being carried out beyond the federally administered season in the vicinity of St. Marys Bay, near Digby, in Lobster Fishing Area (LFA) 34.

As of week 36 (Sept. 4-10), Canada's department of fisheries and oceans disclosed that it had confiscated 464 traps for non-compliance with the Fisheries Act in two fishing areas located in southwestern Nova Scotia, LFAs 33 and 34.

title: DFO maintains it is enforcing lobster season dates in Nova Scotia
content:
Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) contends that it is working to enforce the regulations that prevent the illegal harvesting of lobster in Lobster Fishing Area (LFA) 34 despite complaints by some lawmakers and fishermen.

The Chronicle Herald, one of the Atlantic Canada newspapers owned by the SaltWire news service, said it received a written response from DFO on Friday (Sept. 1) in which the federal agency asserted that "significant enforcement resources" have been expended in the area of St. Mary's Bay, Nova Scotia, since July 17.

DFO spokesperson Debra Buott-Matheson reportedly pointed to the seizure of 434 traps along with the recent arrest, in Moncton, New Brunswick, of two men transporting 8,000 kilograms of lobster caught in the bay without a DFO-recognized commercial license. She said the lobster were released back into the ocean.

"Ensuring a safe and orderly lobster fishery has to be a primary focus, and that is why DFO will continue working with all of our partners to that effect," she reportedly wrote, adding: "We will continue to take action whenever unauthorized harvesting and other violations under the Fisheries Act are observed, while supporting the exercise of fishing rights."

Undercurrent News reported last week how Chris d'Entremont, a member of Parliament (MP) representing the western part of Nova Scotia, and Rick Perkins, an MP representing the area of South Shore-St. Margarets, on Aug. 21, sent a strongly worded letter to new fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier to complain about off-season lobster fishing in a vital part of LFA 34.

Both are members of Canada's minority Conservative Party, while Lebouthillier is a Liberal from the province of New Brunswick.

Canada is the world's leading producer of North American lobster (Homarus americanus), and LFA 34 is Canada's largest lobster fishery, accounting for 20,594 metric tons landed in 2021. The LFA 33 and 34 seasons begin every year on the last Monday in November and ends on May 31 of the following year.

St. Marys Bay, near Digby, was the scene of confrontation in September 2020 when the Sipekne'katik First Nation started a self-regulated "moderate livelihood" lobster fishery that ran outside the commercial season, leading to confrontations on the water with licensed harvesters. There were riots at two lobster pounds, one of which was later burned down in a deliberately set fire.

The Sipekne'katik, which haven't responded to a request for comment by the news service, filed a lawsuit against DFO in July over the seizure of two of its members' traps and has argued that it is running a lawful, self-regulated moderate livelihood fishery.

title: Controversial fishing ban ends in South China Sea
content:
Additional reporting by Louis Harkell

China's controversial annual summer fishing moratorium in the South China Sea ended Wednesday (Aug. 16), allowing thousands of Chinese boats to head back to the disputed waters after a three-and-a-half-month ban that drew protests from Vietnam and the Philippines.

The moratorium, which runs from May 1 to mid-August each year, is aimed at allowing fish stocks to replenish in the South China Sea. But China unilaterally imposes it across the entire waterway above the 12th parallel north, including parts of the 200-mile exclusive economic zones (EEZ) of Vietnam and the Philippines. 

World’s largest fishing country tests catch quotas as alternative to annual ban

In April, Vietnam urged Beijing not to implement the ban, calling it a violation of its sovereignty. The Philippines has also shown contempt for the moratorium, saying its fishermen can continue operating in waters it calls the West Philippine Sea.

China's coast guard said it uncovered 112 cases of illegal fishing in the South China Sea this year, seizing about 199 metric tons of catch. Thirty-three people were arrested.

Veteran Chinese fisherman Huang Yong said he spent days preparing his vessel at the port ahead of the Aug. 16 end of the ban. Huang, who started fishing as a teenager, bought his own boat six years ago for CNY 3.2 million ($440,000).

"If luck is on my side, I can catch 20-30t of fish in one trip," he told Chinese media. That could earn him CNY 300,000 to CNY 500,000 over the course of a year.

China claims virtually the entire South China Sea, conflicting with claims by Vietnam, the Philippines and other Southeast Asian countries. The waters contain rich fishing stocks and potential oil and gas deposits and are also a major shipping route.

title: Booming Bangladesh crab industry raises stock concerns
content:
The Bangladesh crab industry continues to face warnings over its unbalanced harvesting practices that have endangered local crab populations despite government bans on certain activities, reports Mongabay.

Concerns of overexploitation were first raised in 2020 when researchers found that fishing practices in the Sundarbans severely impacted biodiversity and harmed the ecological balance of mangroves at current catch rates.

Although calls are growing to increase crab hatchery volumes, only 5% of crab bought in the Bangladesh crab market is currently sourced from fishers using farms. Existing farms in the country's Satkhira district cover 321 hectares and produce close to 2,000 metric tons annually, although these still depend on extracting crabs from the wild to raise.

However, the majority of Bangladesh's crab export is caught in mangroves like the Sundarbans where crabbing is banned between January and February, and all activity is banned between June and August. 

Yet illegal crabbing continues because of the market's profitability. In the 2019-2020 fiscal year, Bangladesh exported around $35 million worth of both hard and soft-shell crabs. Because of this, it remains difficult to stop wild fishing altogether despite the regular raids, arrests, and lawsuits made against farmers who violate the bans.

title: Biden passes on $745m Mexican seafood embargo over ‘cocaine of the sea,’ vaquita porpoise
content:
The US will not impose a potentially $745 million embargo on Mexican seafood in response to that country's alleged continual trafficking of an endangered fish the Smithsonian calls the "cocaine of the sea" and the knock-on effects that catching the fish has on the also-endangered vaquita porpoise. 

In a statement issued July 17, US president Joe Biden said he would not impose trade restrictions on Mexico over the continued participation of that country in the Chinese black market for toataba swim bladders. The bladders are incredibly valuable, with a single specimen worth thousands of dollars. Though the toataba is itself endangered, fishermen targeting it with gillnets hit another vulnerable marine population -- the critically endangered vaquita porpoise, of which fewer than 10 remain. 

Following a certification of the trade as a violation of US law, Biden had until mid-July to make a decision on a trade embargo with Mexico for violating the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES). 

Instead of an embargo, the president outlined an action plan for addressing Mexico's continued participation in the toataba black market, including: holding high-level talks with the Mexican government to establish an at-least quarterly schedule of meetings concerning CITES compliance; enhanced toataba seizures, arrests and prosecutions when they cross into the US; training for Mexican personnel, if requested; and the scheduling of a new assessment with a July 2024 deadline.

"I am not directing the secretary of the Treasury to impose trade measures on Mexican products for the activities that led to the certification by the secretary of the Interior at this time because the actions outlined above are the appropriate means to address this issue," Biden announced in a statement. 

"However, to ensure that this issue continues to receive the highest level of attention, the secretary of the Interior, in coordination with the secretary of Commerce, secretary of State, and the United States Trade Representative, and other agencies as appropriate, will monitor Mexico's enforcement actions and progress and provide me with a report not later than one year from the date of this notification on whether these actions have reduced the illegal harvest and trafficking of totoaba and enhanced the conservation of vaquita," he added. "The report will be used as the basis for assessing whether additional steps, including potential trade restrictions, will be necessary."

Toataba swim bladders seized by US Customs and Border Protection

Mexico is a major seafood supplier to the US. An embargo would potentially block $745m in shipments, including 20,982 metric tons of shrimp valued at $277.8m, as Undercurrent News has previously reported.

Biden's solutions are cold comfort for the vaquita and the organizations working to save them from extinction, said the Center for Biological Diversity in a statement. 

"I'm disappointed in the US government for doing so little to save vaquitas from extinction," said Sarah Uhlemann, the center's international program director.

"These are the rarest marine mammals in the world, and yet the United States has let the Mexican government off the hook again," she added. "Mexico has a long, painful history of failed promises on protecting these little porpoises. The United States needs to apply the strongest pressure and ban seafood from Mexico until there's real enforcement on illegal fishing in their habitat. The last 10 vaquitas are at stake."

The center further noted that the vaquita population fell from 600 animals in 1997 to just about 10 now. 

"Although some evidence suggests a reduction in illegal fishing in the 'zero tolerance area' -- core vaquita habitat -- recent reports show illegal fishing continues in the Upper Gulf, including in the vaquita refuge and gillnet prohibition area," the center continued. "Mexico's September 2020 regulations, which were supposed to meaningfully address illegal fishing, have not been fully implemented or enforced. Without the removal of illegal gillnets from the entire vaquita habitat, the species will -- at best -- remain on the brink of extinction."

title: Italian police arrest 12 in tuna coloring scam
content:
The Italian police recently arrested 12 people reportedly involved in the sale of tuna that had been treated with nitrate to give it a fresh red color, reports Repubblica.

Five people have been put in jail, while seven others are under house arrest, following a police raid of owners and employees of fish companies and a private laboratory in Avellino, near Naples, southern Italy. 

Among the arrested people were top executives of two fish companies from Bisceglie, Ittica Zu Pietro and Izp processing, as well as a laboratory and a consulting and certification company from Campania, Innovatio and Studio Summit.

The charges for all include association with organized crime, adulteration of food substances, commercial fraud, and private document forgery. The investigators from the Italian Carabinieri's special unit for the protection of health, placed the proceeds of illegal activities at €5.2 million ($5.70m).

Investigations began after over 30 cases of poisoning occurred in different Italian provinces in Italy between May and June 2021. Over the last two years, several individuals in Italy have ended up in intensive care or critical condition after unknowingly consuming adulterated yellowfin tuna contaminated with nitrites and nitrates during processing.

title: Namibia’s Namsov nearly ceases mackerel fishing, processing in regulatory row
content:
Namibian seafood enterprise Namsov Fishing, now a subsidiary of Tunacor Fishing, has been talked out of ceasing its fishing and processing operations for horse mackerel, reports The Namibian.

According to CEO Gerrie Hough, the company took its decision in relation to new proposed regulations regarding fishing above the 200 meters isobath line, which has been restricted since 1997 in order to protect horse mackerel eggs and breeding grounds.

The issues stem from a change in the current fishing charts, potentially moving from an isobath line that follows natural contours to a straight one, leaving fishers unsure of whether they will be arrested for fishing below 200m depth or not.

Hough had previously written to declare that vessels would tie up and Namsov's factory would halt operations on June 23. In the same letter, Hough urged quota holders to push for a return to the status quo.

Since then, according to the Confederation of Namibian Fishing Associations, the government has now withdrawn plans to introduce new regulations, prompting Namsov to continue business as usual on June 27.

title: Bleiker’s buyer behind on deal payments with salmon plant contents up for auction
content:
The resurrection of a UK smoker that went into administration in April 2022 looks to have faltered, with the contents of its factory up for auction and its new owner behind on payments for the deal. 

Well-known seller David Smith, the self-styled 'salmon man', partnered with US firm Sixto Strategic Sourcing to buy Bleiker's Smoke House out of administration in the summer of 2022.

Smith initially rebranded the company as Salmo Group but changed the name to Seriously Fish Company on May 5 this year, then Liamedos Smokehouse and Seafood Company on June 9. The deal seems to have gone awry, however. 

Around a year after the buyout, an auction for the contents of a smoked salmon factory -- including smokers, slicing machines, a vacuum packing machine, conveyors, and more -- is currently live on the website of BPI Auctions (see below).

Three slicers up for sale on BPI Auctions. Credit: BPI website 

There are 95 lots in the auction in total, and four sources independently told Undercurrent News the items reflected the contents of the former Bleiker's plant. One of the sources is a former employee, while the other three work in the salmon sector and are familiar with the company. 

BPI also gives the location of the auction as Northallerton, North Yorkshire, which is where Bleiker's was based (see below).

Credit: BPI website 

The BPI website states the sale is driven by a "restructure." BPI declined to confirm or deny the smoker in question is Liamedos/Seriously Fish/Salmo. 

Smith claimed, despite the evidence to the contrary, that Undercurrent's sources are "incorrect" on the equipment being from his company. 

He did, however, shed some light on the name change to Liamedos. According to a letter from the UK trademarks registry, Norway's Salmon Brands -- which owns the high-end Norway brand SALMA -- disputed the Salmo name. On June 6, the Salmo application was withdrawn, according to the letter. 

Smith then did not respond to further requests for comment. FRP's administrator did not respond to a request for comment.

'Purchaser in arrears'

The latest report filed by the administrator of Bleiker's -- FRP Advisory Trading -- on May 25, 2023, details problems it has had with securing payment from the purchaser of the smokehouse's assets.

A deal was agreed in 2022 for £217,000 for plant machinery, £75,000 for stock, £4,000 each for office equipment and "fixtures and fittings," and then £1 each for various other assets like business information and intellectual property rights.

"The purchaser initially spent time disputing the balance of £75,000 and the involvement of solicitors was required to liaise with both the purchaser and its legal representatives," said FRP. "Following protracted correspondence, the purchaser has agreed that the funds are due."

In addition, the administrator wrote £50,000 of the agreed remaining sales price of £225,000 subject to deferred consideration and fell due six months from completion, or Dec. 17, 2022. "As payment was not received, we instructed solicitors to pursue collection of the outstanding balance."

Following further negotiations, the purchaser "confirmed that they had an inability to repay the balance of £125,000" -- £75,000 for stock and the £50,000 deferred consideration -- "and requested that the sum is paid in installments of £5,000" to be paid monthly.

In the period covered by this report, Oct. 29, 2022, to April 28, 2023, just £10,000 has been paid, it said. 

"The purchaser is currently in arrears, and we are liaising with our solicitors to consider our next steps," the administrator said.

In the May 25 report, FRP also said its work had been extended by a further 12 months to April 28, 2024.

The report states that "during this...period, we have continued to utilize specialist 'Relativity' software to aid our interrogation of the company's records. We have also continued to investigate certain matters brought to our attention by creditors."

"We have carried out an analysis of the company's bank statement activity and reviewed the accounting information available. We have sought feedback from our solicitors with regards to certain matters identified during the investigation."

Sixto 'not involved'

The deal from Seriously Fish/Sixto Strategic Sourcing closed on June 17, 2022, the companies told Undercurrent at the time, with Smith taking over as managing director of the new entity. 

Sixto Strategic Sourcing is based in Miami, Florida and is controlled by Felipe Eduardo Sixto, the director of a range of businesses, including Seriously Fish, of which Smith is also a director.

Felipe Sixto, who is involved with his family's food and coffee packaging business in Miami, ceased to be a person with significant control in the business in June 2022 and was terminated as a director the next month. 

Laura Morejon Sixto ceased to be a person with significant control on Oct. 1, 2022, with Smith becoming the main shareholder. 

According to Felipe Sixto, he provided a "loan to facilitate the purchase" but has had nothing to do with the company since. He referred Undercurrent to Smith for comment. 

"Laura and I haven't been part of the business in quite some time, basically when it was purchased," Felipe Sixto told Undercurrent. "I have secured loans and am a creditor. I am not an investor or shareholder. I am not involved in the business at all."

Damaged rep, tough times

Bleiker's went into administration on April 29, 2022, a few weeks after abruptly losing its main contract with Aldi. 

In May 2022, Undercurrent revealed an arrest had been made as part of an investigation from the National Food Crime Unit (NFCU) focused on alleged country of origin fraud claims before Bleiker's went into administration.

The NFCU investigated the former Bleiker's managing director, Charlie Andrew, leading to an arrest.

Bleiker's was supplying Aldi with its "Specially Selected" smoked salmon, which is supposed to use Scottish salmon approved by the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (RSPCA).  

It's thought a recording of a meeting between the management team of Bleiker's from last year about meeting Christmas supply was anonymously shared with Aldi in late March 2022.

The retailer delisted the smoked salmon supplier soon after, with the RSPCA-approved product then pulled from shelves. Former MD Andrew, former operations director Alex Mcmorran, and Dana Timsa, who was the factory manager, were all reportedly in the meeting which was allegedly recorded and shared with Aldi. 

Thus, Seriously Fish/Sixto Strategic Sourcing was left trying to restart a salmon smokehouse at a time when its reputation had likely taken a hit from the well-publicized fallout of Aldi's delisting and amid the generally tough picture for the foodservice sector last year.

title: Spain seizes Brazilian fishing boat with cocaine haul off Canary Islands
content:
Spanish authorities have seized a Brazilian-flagged fishing boat near the Canary Islands with 1.5 metric tons of cocaine in a hidden compartment in its machine room, police said on Friday as they brought the boat to the port of Las Palmas, Reuters reported.

After approaching the 25-meter (82.02 ft) vessel, called Efesios 5-20, on rough seas, a speedboat sent from the patrol ship Condor, Spanish officers arrested the crew of six people - five Brazilians and a Venezuelan national.

title: Two Japanese seafood bosses arrested over unreported bluefin catches
content:
Two Japanese fishery company presidents were arrested in February in Oma, Aomori Prefecture, for failing to report part of their catch of bluefin tuna to the prefectural government, reports Japan News.

They admitted to charges of violating fisheries law, according to the prefectural police.

According to investigators, Tadaaki Nitta, president of Uochu Co., and Kazumi Sasaki, head of Saihoku Suisan, conspired with fishermen from the town of Oma and failed to report to the prefectural government a total of about 18 metric tons of bluefin tuna caught off the coast of the prefecture and other areas from July to September 2021.

The police are also investigating about 20 fishermen who allegedly sold the tuna to the two, on suspicion of the same charges.

Bluefin tuna from Oma are sold at high prices as a luxury foodstuff. The police believe the two men illegally distributed the fish that exceeded the legal catch quotas and failed to report nearly 100t of the catch to the prefecture in fiscal 2021 alone.

As this was equivalent to almost one-seventh of the catch quota initially allocated to the prefecture, police decided to arrest the two men.

title: Editor’s choice: Sykes strikes again to create $550m shrimp giant; Brasmar snaps up UK importer
content:
Neil Ramsden, EMEA editor of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

Last week's most-read story was the news that the UK's Sykes Seafood has acquired the trading assets of The Big Prawn Co, creating a $550 million European shrimp supply powerhouse. The Cheshire-based Sykes said in a release that Big Prawn, a 100-employee supplier in Melton Constable, UK, will be united with Sykes' other shrimp-focused businesses, Ruskim Seafoods in the UK, and Klaas Puul Beeher in the Netherlands.

Another M&A scoop from last week saw Portugal's Brasmar Group snap up C.T. Holmes & Co., which trades as Holmes Seafood, a UK frozen seafood importer based in London's famous Billingsgate fish market. Holmes announced the sale in a note sent to "suppliers, partners and friends", seen by Undercurrent News. 

Staying in the UK, and Interpath Advisory has been appointed administrator of Cook & Lucas Frozen (UK), a whitefish processor which Undercurrent revealed had abruptly closed earlier in January. James Clark and Howard Smith from Interpath were appointed joint administrators to Cook & Lucas -- majority owned by Ferrari-loving ex-bankrupt Adam Croft -- on Jan. 20, 2023.

Meanwhile, what the US shellfish sector is dealing with right now is a "hangover", Rob Kragh -- vice president of category management for Thai Union Group's Chicken of the Sea Frozen Foods -- told attendees at the Global Seafood Market Conference (GSMC).

West Coast US processor and distributor Santa Monica Seafood aims to open its first East Coast operation for seafood in skin-packs in the third quarter of this year. The company has signed a lease for a 26,000-square-foot facility near Baltimore, Maryland, that will be the third location for its skin-pack operations.

Estimates put forward by six of the land-based aquaculture sector's leading players suggest they are now very much on a par with traditional salmon farmers when it comes to production costs, according to Norne Research's latest report.

The stocks of Russian king crab in the US will run out in the next few months, with no viable replacement options, said Roman Tkachenko, CEO of Direct Source Seafood, a major importer. "There are no substitutes" for the Russian king crab, especially in the large sizes, said Tkachenko on the shellfish panel at GSMC.

Judicial and law enforcement authorities in Norway and Lithuania detained five people in a day of action against a staffing network suspected of extensive tax fraud in workforce rental for fish farms in Norway. Five suspects were arrested and nine locations were searched.

Russian billionaire Vitaly Orlov has transferred control over the UK-based arm of Russia's largest seafood company, Norebo Holding, to his son, according to documents filed with the UK's Company's House. On Jan. 19, Vitaly Orlov ceased to be a "person with significant control" -- holding 75% or more of the shares -- in Norebo Europe. On the same date, his son, Nikita, became the sole "person with significant control" in the firm.

Finally, former Thai Union Group and Century Pacific executive Arnab Sengupta has joined Franco-Thai tuna broker JMB International. 

He also told Undercurrent that the economic crisis in Egypt -- the largest canned tuna market in the Middle East and a significant buyer for Thailand -- is causing capacity in several Thai plants to go unused.

title: Daily recap, Jan. 26: Egypt’s dollar crisis hits Thai tuna sector; Five arrested in Norwegian migrant labor crackdown
content:
Here's a recap of the daily seafood news from Thursday, Jan. 26:

Egypt's dollar crisis causes unused capacity in Thai tuna processing industry

The economic crisis in Egypt -- the largest canned tuna market in the Middle East and a significant buyer for Thailand -- is causing capacity in several Thai plants to go unused, according to Middle East market expert and former Thai Union Group executive Arnab Sengupta. 

Rodger May: Coho RAS farm investment about 'doing the right thing'

For Rodger May, the main reason to invest in a salmon recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) business can be summed up thusly: "Do the Right Thing". The owner of the Peter Pan Seafood Company, a Bellevue, Washington-based vertically integrated processor of wild-caught Alaska salmon, knows movies. 

Five arrested as Norway, Lithuania crack down on tax fraud, people trafficking

Judicial and law enforcement authorities in Norway and Lithuania have detained five people in a day of action against a staffing network suspected of extensive tax fraud in workforce rental for fish farms in Norway.

Trade insights: Indian shrimp exports down 5% in first 11 months of 2022

India's frozen shrimp exports have fallen 5% behind levels in the previous year due in part to a slump in sales to the US, according to the latest trade figures released by India's Ministry of Commerce and Industry.

Benchmark targets 600,000 in annual shrimp broodstock sales, pins strategy on genetic diversity

Benchmark Genetics Shrimp, a division of UK-based Benchmark Holdings, aims to ramp up shrimp broodstock sales to 500,000-600,000 animals per year as it leverages its greater pool of genetic diversity and lower costs.

title: Five arrested as Norway, Lithuania crack down on tax fraud, people trafficking
content:
Judicial and law enforcement authorities in Norway and Lithuania have detained five people in a day of action against a staffing network suspected of extensive tax fraud in workforce rental for fish farms in Norway.

Five suspects were arrested and nine locations were searched, according to the European Union Agency for Criminal Justice Cooperation, or Eurojust, which claimed it had supported the judicial cooperation and assisted the authorities in setting up and funding a joint investigation team (JIT) into the case.

After a wide investigation carried out in the fishing industry in northern Norway in 2019, the Norwegian authorities responsible for combating work-related crime identified 10 Lithuanian companies and one Norwegian company that they believe are part of the criminal network, it said. The estimated damage caused by the tax fraud amounts to approximately NOK 8 million (€800,000).

The case was opened at Eurojust at the request of the Norwegian authorities in July 2021. In addition to supporting the establishment of the JIT and providing it with funding, Eurojust actively facilitated the cross-border judicial cooperation between the national authorities involved. The agency organized four coordination meetings and facilitated the execution of several requests for mutual legal assistance.

In a coordinated action carried out in Lithuania and Norway on Dec. 13, 2022, five suspects were arrested. They are charged with extensive tax fraud or complicity in this crime. Nine locations were searched and 15 people involved were interrogated.

Norway's National Authority for Investigation and Prosecution of Economic and Environmental Crime, or Okokrim, assisted the police department of the municipality of Nordland in the investigation.

The police said four men and one woman had been arrested in Alta, northern Norway, and Vilnius, Lithuania, including a Norwegian citizen detained in Lithuania, whom Norway has requested be handed over.

"After the campaign, the Nordland police district has 13 criminal cases under investigation. These are related to 10 Lithuanian companies and one Norwegian company, which the police believe to be part of the criminal network. In the subsequent investigation, the police have aimed to discover whether one or more people can be held responsible for the criminal acts linked to this network."

The individuals are charged with extensive tax fraud or complicity in this. "Nine locations were searched and both physical and digital seizures were made. A total of 15 people involved were interrogated. The police will now review the seizure and continuously assess further investigative steps."

title: Canadian First Nation group drops lobster lawsuit
content:
Two First Nation groups, the Potlotek Band and the Assembly of Nova Scotia Mi'kmaw Chiefs, have dropped a civil lawsuit against the Canadian federal government that challenged the handling of their effort to open a "moderate livelihood" lobster fishery in the province of Nova Scotia, the CBC reports. 

The news service explained, however, that the decision represents a shift in legal tactics, not an end to the groups' battle with Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO).

The lawsuit was seeking an injunction to prevent DFO from interfering with Potlotek's self-regulated moderate livelihood lobster fishery.

The assembly said in a press release issued early in the week that it would instead put its resources into the defense of a Potlotek harvester fishing under a plan approved by the community. The assembly and Mi'kmaw communities have limited resources and cannot afford to be involved in a civil action while also defending against fisheries prosecutions, the statement explained.

DFO has insisted that moderate livelihood lobster fishing, a right of First Nation groups in Canada, must take place during commercial seasons. The federal government has continued to seize traps and arrest indigenous harvesters fishing out of season without its authorization.

Despite the legal battles, DFO reached interim moderate livelihood deals in October with four Nova Scotia Mi'kmaw First Nations in southern Nova Scotia, the article noted. DFO reports to have an "understanding" with the Acadia, Annapolis Valley, Bear River and Glooscap First Nations to fish a total of 3,500 traps during the 2022-2023 commercial season.

title: Former Namibian fisheries minister claims to have been ‘used’ in Fishrot scandal
content:
Namibia's former fisheries and marine resources minister Bernhard Esau claimed he has proof he was used by some of his co-accused in the Fishrot fishing quotas scandal, reports The Namibian.

This is stated in a list of new facts on which Esau based his latest application to be granted bail, with evidence that his "name and credentials as minister of fisheries have been opportunistically and falsely optimized by some of his co-accused" in the case, the document states.

According to the document, "the state does not have a strong case against [Esau], and he is being incriminated by association", which he will show to be untrue.

On Dec. 14, Esau testified for the first time since his arrest in late November 2019 and said he is facing "very, very serious" charges but would plead not guilty on all counts.

"I as a minister have brought peace in the industry," he said. "I opened up the industry for greater broad-based participation in ownership. The crimes I am accused of are not part of my moral and ethical chemistry."

The bail hearing continues.

title: US sanctions top Dalian, Pingtan execs over IUU, worker abuses, targets 157 Chinese vessels
content:
The administration of US president Joe Biden has expanded on its trade-related attack against Dalian Ocean Fishing (DOF), a major Chinese commercial fishing company, and added another large company to its list of targeted enterprises. 

US Department of Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on Friday (Dec. 9) announced that it has sanctioned two major figures in Chinese commercial fishing: Li Zhenyu, the chairman and general manager of DOF, and Xinrong Zhuo, the founder, chairman and CEO of Pingtan Marine Enterprise (PME).

The action also identifies their companies and eight related entities as well as 157 Chinese-flagged fishing vessels, the landings from which will be blocked from being imported into the US. 

Brian Nelson, US Treasury Department

OFAC said the actions are a response to Executive Order (EO) 13818, issued by former president Donald Trump in December 2017, which prevents the import of any goods into the US that come from a person or company involved in human rights abuses as well as travel into the country by the sanctioned individuals. The actions also build on president Joe Biden's June 2022 "Memorandum on Combating Illegal, Unreported, and Unregulated Fishing and Associated Labor Abuses", which directed federal agencies to work together to combat illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing.

"Treasury condemns the practices of those sanctioned today, which often involve the abuse of human rights, undermine fundamental labor and environmental standards, and harm the economic prospects of local populations in the Indo-Pacific," Brian Nelson, Treasury's undersecretary for terrorism and financial intelligence, said in a statement.

"These designations demonstrate how seriously we take the problem of illicit fishing and our commitment to holding the perpetrators of serious human rights abuses to account."

Crew lived off 'expired food', 'brown desalinated seawater'

The action against DOF, which owns and manages 32 commercial fishing vessels, stems from a call for action by the Environmental Justice Foundation and Advocates for Public Interest Law issued back in May 2020 after details emerged regarding the human rights abuses and deaths of Indonesian crew members working on Chinese tuna longliners in the Western Pacific Ocean, as reported by Undercurrent News. DOF was identified as the owner of the vessels in subsequent reports. 

In May 2021, US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), an agency within the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), issued a withhold release order (WRO) against DOF based on information that "reasonably indicates the use of forced labor" in its harvesting operations. The order, which was reported to be the first WRO against an entire fishing fleet, instructed CBP personnel at all US ports to begin immediately detaining all tuna, swordfish and other seafood harvested by Dalian that might be otherwise imported to the US. 

China fishing vessel (Credit: Shutterstock)

CBP told reporters at the time that the US imported $1.8 million worth of seafood harvested by DOF in 2019 and $320,808 worth of seafood in 2020. In 2021, thru April 30, the US had imported $763,115 worth of seafood caught by Dalian.

The Chinese government responded at the time by saying the Biden administration was grandstanding and charging that the action was based on a fabrication.

In its statement issued on Friday, OFAC described how DOF's Long Xing 629 went to sea to catch tuna for 13 months with a crew of 24 in February 2019 and made only one port visit. The crew worked average 18-hour days and lived off expired food and brown desalinated seawater, using at-sea refueling and transshipments of fish to refrigerated cargo vessels, or reefers, to avoid stops.

Five crewmembers died, three of whom had their bodies dumped into the ocean rather than being sent back to their homes of origin, according to OFAC.

"When the surviving crewmembers returned home, they were diagnosed with malnutrition and received only a fraction of their promised pay," the Treasury agency said. "They have since described deceptive recruiting practices, the confiscation of identity documents, punishing work and physical abuse."

While at sea, the Long Xing also reportedly engaged in illegal shark finning, taking more than 700 kilograms of fins, including from endangered sharks.  

A subsequent investigation found similar abuses occurred across DOF's fleet, OFAC said. Based on their contracts, crewmembers who left the ship would forfeit their salaries while still owing the recruiting fees they had agreed to pay out of future earnings, leading to the potential for intergenerational debt bondage.

"Other vessels stayed at sea for more than two years without a port visit, meaning no access to the outside world or any way to let others know of the oppressive conditions. Through all of this, DOF received almost $8m annually in [Chinese] government subsidies encouraging distant water fishing."

OFAC action is first against publicly traded firm

PME is registered in the Cayman Islands but operates nearly 100 commercial fishing vessels and reefers with roughly 2,000 crew members through its subsidiary Pingtan County Ocean Fishing Group, in the Chinese province of Fujian and Fuzhou Honglong Ocean Fishing Co., an affiliated company. All have been designated as producing banned goods under the OFAC order. 

In 2021, Pingtan Fishing received a $19m subsidy from the Chinese government as an incentive to develop its deep-water fishing industry to "satisfy China's demand for seafood", OFAC recounted. But its vessels have been involved in "serious human rights abuse and implicated in IUU fishing and other illegal activity in Indonesia, East Timor, and Ecuador".

Photograph from Pingtan Marine website.

This includes the 2017 seizure of a Honglong-owned vessel and the arrest and imprisonment of the vessel's crew after the Ecuadorian Navy found it had illegally transshipped more than 6,600 shark carcasses, including from endangered species, through the waters of the protected Galapagos Marine Reserve. Additionally, in 2016, an Indonesian court ordered a moratorium on PME's fishing activities and the impoundment of its affiliate vessels in Indonesia following allegations against an affiliated company that included human rights abuse.

In one case, after crewmembers reportedly contacted their families for the first time in seven months and learned they had not been paid, a crewmember's request to leave the ship was denied and food was withheld for three days, OFAC recounted. Crews that had completed their contracts, but who were forced to continue working for months in light of COVID restrictions, learned only later that they were never paid at all. Still others reported physical abuse.

On another ship, a grossly negligent response to an accident contributed to the death of a crewmember after it took over two weeks to get the seriously injured crewmember to see a doctor aboard another ship. In another case, crewmembers on one ship only learned of the global pandemic in May 2020, after they arrived in port for the first time in over a year.

Photograph from Pingtan Marine website.

OFAC also has designated, pursuant to EO 13818, the companies Heroic Treasure, Mars Harvest Co., Pingtan Guansheng Ocean Fishing Co., Fujian Heyue Marine Fishing Development Co. and Pingtan Fishing as well as the British Virgin Islands-registered Merchant Supreme Co. and Hong Kong-registered Prime Cheer Corporation for being reportedly owned or controlled by Zhuo or one of his entities.

Honglong, which is owned by Zhuo's family, has been designated as well for "having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, PME". It provided PME with millions of dollars' worth of fuel and supplies for their vessels, according to OFAC.

"PME and Honglong have used each other's vessels to collateralize loans worth hundreds of millions of dollars, and PME claims exclusive operating rights to 20 of Honglong's vessels," OFAC noted.

Among the vessels for which imports are blocked are 78 vessels in which Pingtan Fishing has an interest and 47 in which Honglong has an interest.

OFAC noted that the action marks the first it has taken against an entity listed on the NASDAQ stock exchange. Pingtan is traded under the ticker symbol PME.

title: Son of Mozambique’s former president jailed for 12 years over tuna bond scandal
content:
Ndambi Guebuza, son of Mozambique's former president Armando Guebuza, has been jailed for 12 years over an extensive $2.2 billion fishing project scandal, BBC reports. 

He was among 11 people found guilty, as he financed "his taste for luxury through embezzlement and money laundering", said Efigenio Baptista, the judge that is hearing the case. 

Others given prison sentences include Gregorio Leao, head of the Security and Intelligence Service under Armando Guebuza, and Antonio do Rosario, who became chairperson of all three newly-created state companies that took the loans.

Between 2013 and 2014, three newly established companies took on $2.2bn of debt, much of it without the knowledge or approval of the country's parliament. Despite this, the government stood as the guarantor of the loans.

The loans were issued by Credit Suisse and the Russian bank VTB, with three former Credit Suisse bankers pleading guilty to US money laundering charges over the case.

Late last year, UK authorities fined the investment bank $202m over the tuna corruption scandal.
 
The money was allegedly used to buy a large tuna factory and a maritime security fleet and finance other deals involving companies in which the state was a leading shareholder.

Mozambique officials are known to have received at least $137m in bribes during that same period. Currently, 19 individuals are on trial in Mozambique on charges of bribery, embezzlement and money laundering over the case.

Former Mozambique finance minister Manuel Chang, who originally signed off on the loans, has been in custody in South Africa since 2018. He was arrested at the request of the US -- where many investors were affected by the scandal -- but has had competing requests for extradition filed from his home country.

title: Top China whitefish boss sentenced to 30 months in prison over COVID outbreak
content:
The boss of Dalian Haiqing Aquatic Food, one of China's largest whitefish processors, has been sentenced to 30 months of prison time for violating the prevention and control of coronavirus in the country, according to reports in the Chinese media.

Qu Zhenhai, Haiqing's boss and legal representative, was sentenced by the intermediate people's court of Dalian City, Liaoning province, on Nov. 18, 2022. It followed the sentencing of Haiqing and another seafood company, and four other company executives and managers, over their roles in a COVID-19 outbreak last year.

Arrests made as China points finger at seafood firms over Dalian COVID outbreak 

Executives with the company declined to comment on the situation to Undercurrent News.

Despite the sentencing, two Undercurrent sources said Qu is not in prison and is still working.

Qu has been released, and it’s not clear if he will have to go to prison, one executive, who asked not to be named, told Undercurrent. According to sources, a further hearing in 2023 will decide his future.

Last November, Dalian suffered one of its worst outbreaks of COVID-19 during the pandemic. Earlier this year, a court determined that it was linked to contaminated imported cold chain food, frozen pollock in particular, which then spread from workers in cold storage facilities to the local community.

Chang: Another 20-30% of China whitefish plants will go under in next five years

The court said Qu was told to close all cold chain operations on Nov. 4, 2021. The order came after the city reported its first COVID-19 case just a day earlier.

However, Qu refused to execute the order and arranged for four processing factories under Haiqing, including Dalian Haikuo Food, to continue processing frozen seafood until 20:00 the next night.

Haikuo's production environment was low-temperature, humid, and poorly ventilated, the court said. In total, 76 employees became infected with COVID-19, and 41 others became infected after contacting the workers.

A Haiqing manager surnamed Liu -- who was in charge of cargo management and testing at the company -- made false health reports by bribing nucleic acid testing personnel, including a man surnamed Jiao, the court said.

Haiqing was fined CNY 800,000 ($115,011) by the court. Qu was sentenced to two years and six months in prison. Liu and Jiao were sentenced to two years and four months in prison.

Meanwhile, another whitefish processor, Dalian Keqiang Food, was fined after it failed to conduct nucleic acid testing and disinfection to save costs.

Taking advantage of the convenience of his position, Song, the company's business manager, received rebates of more than CNY 970,000 for nucleic acid testing and disinfection projects.

Unibond’s Jiang: Whitefish processed in China may no longer be cheap, but quality will improve

Keqiang was fined CNY 1 million by the court. Song was sentenced to five years in prison. The company's cold storage manager, surnamed Shao, was sentenced to two years and 10 months in prison.

The court said the two companies' actions violated China's law on the prevention and control of infectious diseases and directly led to 346 people becoming infected with the disease. 

Last September, Qu set up a UK subsidiary, Haiqing Foods UK, and listed Peter Hawkins, formerly of Sykes Seafood, as director. Back in 2016, the Chinese firm established Haiqing Foods Europe in the Netherlands, hiring Rob Van Asch from what is now Mowi, then Marine Harvest.

title: Namibian gov’t accused of failing to address Fishrot scandal’s loopholes
content:
Namibia's Institute for Public Policy and Research (IPPR) has accused the government of failing to address loopholes in the fishing industry which led to the infamous 'Fishrot' bribery scandal, reports The Namibian. 

"The government is sitting with idle hands on any improvements after the allegations of the Fishrot fishing quotas fraud and corruption case," IPPR said in a statement. "Three years after Fishrot was exposed, nothing has been done to end the secrecy that enabled the corruption scandal to take place."

Namibian gov’t demands $213m in back taxes from Samherji

The scandal, made public by Icelandic whistleblower and ex-Samherji manager Johannes Stefansson in November 2019, saw multiple Namibian government officials accused of accepting bribes from Samherji subsidiaries in return for fishing quotas.

Accused officials include former fisheries minister Bernhard Esau and former justice minister Sacky Shanghala, both of whom were subsequently arrested by Namibian authorities.

However, claiming that little improvement has been seen since then, the IPPR has called for more transparency in the fisheries sector, such as the publication of all rights, licenses, and quota details, including beneficial ownership information.

The IPPR also called for an amendment of the Marine Resources Act to remove the minister's discretionary power and introduce transparency measures, since this provision gives the fisheries minister individual power to allocate fishing quotas.

"The government will follow through on the commitments made in the Harambee Prosperity Plan II and National Anti-Corruption Strategy and Action Plan on aligning laws and practices with the standards of the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative on transparency. This means moving towards open contracting and introducing beneficial ownership registers," the IPPR concluded.

title: Louisiana cracks down on illegal harvesting
content:
Fisheries enforcement officers in the US state of Louisiana have cited or arrested two people for alleged commercial fishing violations. They have also seized one vessel and 3,850 pounds of reportedly illegal catches.

The cases all appear to be generated by anonymous tips or by agents conducting sweeps of commercial and recreational harvesting areas within state waters since Aug. 28, according to information provided by the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries (DWF) fisheries agents. Five recreational harvesters were also cited for illegal harvesting in another incident.

The largest seizure involved about 2,500lb of white shrimp taken by wardens in Terrebonne Parish on Sept. 1. They charged Hunter Daisy, 29, of Louisiana with using oversized skimmer nets, taking commercial fish without a commercial fishing license, selling commercial fish to consumers without a fresh products license, violation of license revocation, possession of more than 14 grams of marijuana and possession of drug paraphernalia, DFW said.

The agents said that they were on patrol near Oyster Bayou when they saw Daisy and a woman selling shrimp to a recreational fishing vessel. They inspected the vessel and found that Daisy had oversized fishing nets, did not possess a commercial fishing license and it was under license revocation, DFW said.

The agents seized two skimmer nets, one 46-foot shrimp vessel on a department seizure order, and approximately 2,500 pounds of white shrimp that were sold to the recreational boat, DFW said. 

Fishing while under license revocation can bring $400 to $950 in fines and up to 120 days in jail. The oversized nets, fishing without a commercial license and selling commercial fish to consumers without a fresh products license each bring $250 to $500 in fines and up to 90 days in jail, DFW said.

Another 1,350 pounds of catfish were seized when Daniel J. Wilkerson, 27, of Louisiana was cited for taking or possessing undersized catfish in Plaquemines Parish on Aug. 28. Agents said they saw Wilkerson in the Mississippi River near Buras in possession of many undersized blue catfish he allegedly harvested with hoop nets, DFW said.

The undersized fish ticket carries $250 to $500 fines and up to 90 days in jail.

title: Three charged with bilking Netuno USA of $1.3m in purchase scam
content:
Three US men have been charged with stealing more than $1.3 million in goods from Florida-based seafood importer Netuno USA by allegedly pretending to be buyers for a supermarket, the Miami Herald reports. 

Rene Hechevarria Echemend, 33, Ernesto Aguilera Baute, 36, and Jose Luis Batista Suarez, 40, face seven counts of grand theft cargo of over $50,000 and seven counts of obtaining property over $5,000, Broward County court records show. 

The theft case began in late June when a man who identified himself as Brian Gomez purchased seafood from Netuno, of Fort Lauderdale, on behalf of a supermarket, whom police declined to identify. Orders were placed on June 21, June 30, July 14, July 27 and July 29, Florida Highway Patrol (FHP) investigators said. 

After each order, Gomez was told to pick up the seafood loads at a warehouse in the town of Medley, FHP reported. About 45 days after the first purchase, Netuno contacted the supermarket and learned that Brian Gomez didn’t work there and that the email he used was fraudulent. 

FHP began conducting surveillance at the Medley warehouse and on Aug. 4, saw a truck and trailer used in the previous thefts at the warehouse. Aguilera Baute signed the order's paperwork, troopers say, and left with Echemend in the tractor-trailer carrying the seafood load. Troopers followed the truck and a red Mustang that was trailing behind it to an address in the Broward city of Weston. 

The driver of the Mustang, investigators say, was later identified as Suarez. Nearly 15 minutes after the truck backed into a bay door at the Weston facility, troopers arrested the three men.

FHP alleges that Baute and Echemend defrauded Netuno and were responsible for five of six cargo thefts. Suarez participated in last week's heist totaling about $300,000 in seafood, FHP added.

title: Mexican sea cukes pushed toward extinction by illegal fishing
content:
Despite a ban against harvesting sea cucumbers off the coast of Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula back in early 2013, they are being fished so hard today that concerns are growing about their possible extinction, reports Noticias Telemundo.

In 2020 alone, almost 1,600 metric tons of Holothuria mexicana were fished in Mexico, according to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization.

The problem is a tremendous trade demand, resulting in high prices. Mexican government data shows that 100% of sea cucumbers are exported, primarily to China, but the second largest export market is the United States.

In Hong Kong and other Chinese cities, a kilogram of large, well-processed sea cucumbers can command more than $3,500, according to the news service. The product is used in sauces, soups and traditional Chinese medicines.

"The sea cucumber was not something special, until the prices began to rise a lot," Ricardo Domínguez Cano, a Yucatán-based fisherman, told Noticias Telemundo. "Many people then came from other states and settled in Yucatán for the cucumber. And they continued fishing, despite the ban. The sea cucumber could be finished."

However, not all illegally extracted sea cucumbers are reaching their intended destination, the article noted. A recent academic study found that Mexican and US authorities seized more than 100t of sea cucumber worth an estimated $29.5 million between 2011 and 2021. The 97 incidents involved 125 arrests.

title: UK food crime probe into former Bleiker’s MD Andrew ‘ongoing’
content:
The former Bleiker's Smoke House managing director (MD), Charlie Andrew, is the focus of a UK government food crime probe, according to a report from the company's administrator.

On May 5, Undercurrent News revealed an arrest had been made as part of an investigation from the National Food Crime Unit (NFCU) focused on alleged country of origin fraud claims before the company went into administration. The Food Standards Agency (FSA), which NFCU is part of, declined to comment on who had been arrested.

The June 27 report from administrator FRP Advisory, which revealed the sale of the company to a US investor, confirmed the investigation is into the former MD and is "ongoing".

A spokesperson for the NFCU confirmed on July 6 this is still the case.

With the investigation ongoing, "we are unable to provide further details as doing so could potentially jeopardize future enforcement action", said Gavan Wafer, head of investigation at NFCU, in a statement sent to Undercurrent.

Arrest made as UK food crime body investigates former Aldi salmon smoker  

The NFCU declined to confirm or deny the focus is on Andrew, however. Andrew did not respond to a request for comment from Undercurrent.

Andrew and his wife Annabel owned 94% of Bleiker's Holdings, which then controlled the operating company outright.

In addition to the NFCU probe, FRP is also looking into the conduct of Andrew and other directors. 

FRP states "certain matters have been raised by creditors which will be investigated", without going into specifics. FRP has requested all those who have been directors of the company within three years of the insolvency complete a questionnaire to assist in preparing the statutory return to the Department of Business Energy and Industrial Strategy, "in accordance with the Company Directors Disqualification Act".

UK smoker enters administration weeks after Aldi contract loss

After this, FRP will complete the directors' conduct report. "The ongoing investigation by the FSA is also relevant to our enquiries here," the firm said.

The NFCU is looking into "a number of alleged issues including concerns about [Bleiker's] country of origin claims on some of their smoked salmon products", as Undercurrent previously reported.

FRP also notes it negotiated with the advisor of a company owned and operated by the children of the Andrews into which its trademark and branding rights had been transferred within the last 12 months, "agreeing [on] the return of all rights to facilitate the sale".

The FRP gives some details on the background to the insolvency filing of Bleiker's. FRP mentions "significant interest" in events in the pre-administration period from regulatory bodies such as the NFCU, RSPCA Assured, the environmental health department of the Hambleton District Council and the North Yorkshire Police. 

Aldi UK abruptly drops smoked salmon supplier

"Significant time has already been expended to date" dealing with these bodies, FRP noted.  

RSPCA Assured is the food labeling scheme of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, or RSPCA. As previously reported by Undercurrent, Aldi pulled a range of "Specially Selected" smoked salmon from stores in April, which led to Bleiker's insolvency filing.

According to Undercurrent sources, Bleiker's was supplying Aldi with products using non-RSPCA-approved salmon, but with the certification scheme's mark still on the packs.

The FRP report states the processor's main customer notified Bleiker's at the end of March of "concerns regarding the provenance of goods supplied and withdrew its products from sale in its stores, ceasing all orders". The customer -- which the report does not name but states accounted for around half of total sales -- was Aldi. 

Brasmar plans growth in France from acquisition, US after new hire

"Despite an ongoing dialogue and a number of audits being undertaken by the customer and its agents, no resolution could be reached." A confidential settlement was eventually agreed upon with the customer on April 26, 2022, which ended the relationship, according to FRP.

The "sudden loss" of this Aldi business, combined with the already weakened financial position of Bleiker's, meant the company was no longer viable, the report states.

Changes to cost base

Although Bleiker's reported a profit after tax of £296,000 on a turnover of £14 million for the year ending April 30, 2021, the company started to struggle to pass on higher raw material prices to customers, the report states (see below).

The higher prices, combined with difficulties sourcing temporary labor in the busy pre-Christmas period in 2021, "resulted in poor trading performance during the final quarter of 2021", according to FRP. This, in turn, placed pressure on the company's cash position, the administrator said.

It was here that the company's management "carried out a review of the business and identified some changes to the…cost base which, alongside sales price increases from customers", the report states. It does not go into detail on what the changes to the costs were, however.

As previously reported by Undercurrent, it is thought a recording of a meeting between the management team of Bleiker's from last year about meeting Christmas supply was anonymously shared with Aldi in late March 2022.

The retailer delisted the smoked salmon supplier soon after, with the products touting its RSPCA-approved raw material then pulled from shelves. 

Former MD Andrew, former operations director Alex Mcmorran, and Dana Timsa, who was the factory manager, were all reportedly in the meeting which was allegedly recorded and shared with Aldi. 

Stock issues

The FRP report also alludes to the dealings with the environmental health office (EHO) of Hambleton District Council, the local authority where Bleiker's is based, over the company's stock.

The nature of the issues with the stock is not expanded upon, however. After securing an agreement to sell the company to US-based Sixto Strategic Sourcing (SSS), FRP was contacted by the EHO of the Hambleton council "who raised various issues" regarding the stock.

FRP was unable to dispose of the stock "without a comprehensive testing program which must be approved by the EHO prior to any sales being conducted".

As a result, FRP's ability to sell the company was impacted, as "considerable time" was spent reviewing the company's records and "liaising with the EHO".

SSS -- which is teaming with David Smith, known in the sector as the "salmon man", on the deal -- confirmed it "would take on all regulatory requirements placed on the stock by the EHO and sell the stock only when the EHO were satisfied that the required testing had been completed", said FRP. 

An agreement with SSS was negotiated with the sum of £75,000 payable for the stock upon satisfactory approvals to sell being received from the EHO. In addition, SSS is paying £175,000 ($212,000) upfront for Bleiker's, with a further £50,000 to be paid six months from completion. The deal closed on June 17. 

Given the restrictions on the stock sale, the SSS offer "was favorable" as FRP was "faced with the prospect of instructing specialist advisers to liaise with the EHO and the cost of disposing of the stock securely if the relevant approvals were not required".

FSA investigation derails sale

The FRP document reveals Andrew was trying to sell the company before going into administration. 

FRP and SIA Group Asset Ingenuity contacted trade and private equity buyers but could not secure a deal.

Following FRP's appointment, two interested parties placed separate offers to purchase the company's business and tangible assets, one of which was SSS.

One interested party offered £250,000, "which was subsequently negotiated upwards to £300,000," while the other interested party offered £200,000, "which was negotiated upwards to £360,000", the report states.

Articles revealing the NFCU investigation of pre-administration activities at Bleiker's "negatively impacted the marketing process", according to FRP. 

As a result, the other party walked away, and only SSS remained interested in a deal for all of the business. However, FRP continued to receive interest in asset and stock deals.

However, as previously mentioned, the EHO issues with the stock prevented a deal for this alone.

'New' Bleiker's

The new owner of Bleiker's is based in Miami, Florida and is controlled by Felipe Eduardo Sixto, the director of a range of businesses, including the Seriously Fish Corporation, of which Smith is also a director.

Sixto's family business, Sixto Packaging, which is not involved in the deal, is a packaging supplier serving the seafood, coffee, food and beverage, and pet food sectors.

Smith is taking over as managing director of Bleiker's. Originally from Yorkshire, where Bleiker's is based, Smith is a well-known salmon seller in both the UK and the US. Most recently, he worked for Honey Smoked Fish Company, a private equity-backed salmon smoker in the US. He's since left that firm and returned to the UK, however.
