title: US investor teams with ‘salmon man’ Smith to resurrect UK smoker
content:
An investor from the US and a well-connected salmon seller have teamed up to acquire a UK smoker that went into administration in late April. 

A document filed on the UK companies' registry by administrator FRP Advisory names US firm Sixto Strategic Sourcing (SSS) as the buyer of Bleiker's Smoke House, which went under after its primary customer Aldi abruptly pulled the plug on a contract a few weeks prior.

Arrest made as UK food crime body investigates former Aldi salmon smoker  

The buyer is based in Miami, Florida and is controlled by Felipe Eduardo Sixto, the director of a range of businesses, including the Seriously Fish Corporation, of which David Smith -- known in the sector as the "salmon man" -- is also a director. Sixto's family business, Sixto Packaging, which is not involved in the deal, is a packaging supplier serving the seafood, coffee, food and beverage, and pet food sectors.

The deal from Seriously Fish/SSS closed on June 17, according to a statement sent to Undercurrent News by a spokesperson for the buyer. Smith is taking over as managing director of Bleiker's, with food executives Michael Dean coming in as finance director, Peter Person as operations director and industry veteran Stewart Atkinson as its "master smoker". 

Originally from Yorkshire, where Bleiker's is based, Smith is a well-known salmon seller in both the UK and the US. Most recently, he worked for Honey Smoked Fish Company, a private equity-backed salmon smoker in the US. He's since left that firm and returned to the UK, however.

UK smoker enters administration weeks after Aldi contract loss

"I couldn’t be prouder. We have exciting times ahead of us and we will be announcing some major partnerships in the coming weeks," he told Undercurrent. 

"I have known Dave [Smith] for 12-15 years and have a lot of faith in him," Sixto told Undercurrent. He declined to comment further. 

According to the statement, the Bleiker's name will be maintained and "essential maintenance" is underway in preparation for production to recommence in a matter of weeks’ time.

"Key employees have returned to the business bringing with them their wealth of knowledge and experience of operations. The core of every business is its team, and Bleikers is no different. We are planning to have the company back to its original staffing levels by early 2023," the company said. 

SSS is paying £175,000 ($212,000) upfront for Bleiker's, with a further £50,000 to be paid in six months from completion, according to the report on the UK company registry from FRP.

According to the report, the buyer will pay an additional £75,000 for the Bleiker's stock once approvals to sell are received from the local authority's environmental health department; £300,000 in total. The latest accounts for the company to April 2021, show Bleiker's reported an operating profit of £373,000 on sales of £14.09 million.

Aldi UK abruptly drops smoked salmon supplier

The deal includes the company's brand, which was sold in retailers such as WM Morrison Supermarkets and Tesco.

"They will be bringing this much-loved company’s products back to the customers who have loyally supported the brand over many years," the statement reads. 

According to the FRP report, the firm negotiated with the advisor of a company owned and operated by the children of Charlie Andrew, the former managing director (MD), into which its trademark and branding rights had been transferred within the last 12 months, "agreeing [on] the return of all rights to facilitate the sale".

Sixto and Smith are also directors of a UK company, Bleiker's Biotech, which was created on Sept. 21, 2021. On June 23, the company's address was changed to the one on the Leeming Bar Business Park in Northallerton, where Bleiker's factory is based.

FSA investigation spooked would-be buyers

As Undercurrent reported on May 5, the UK government's food crime arm is investigating country of origin claims made on Aldi private label products supplied by Bleiker's before its insolvency filing.

Investor sought for €250m-plus German supplier with Polish salmon plant

The FRP document reveals that former MD Andrew, now the subject of the UK Food Standards Agency (FSA) investigation, was trying to sell the company before going into administration. 

FRP and SIA Group Asset Ingenuity contacted trade and private equity buyers but could not secure a deal.

Following FRP's appointment, two interested parties placed separate offers to purchase the company's business and tangible assets, one of which was SSS.

One interested party offered £250,000, "which was subsequently negotiated upwards to £300,000," while the other interested party offered £200,000, "which was negotiated upwards to £360,000", the report states.

Honey Smoked reshuffles execs amid Costco loss

Articles revealing the FSA's National Food Crime Unit (NFCU) investigation of pre-administration activities at Bleiker's "negatively impacted the marketing process", according to FRP. Undercurrent first reported the news of the investigation and the arrest of one executive, who the FSA did not name.

As a result, the other party walked away, and only SSS remained interested in a deal for all of the business. However, FRP continued to receive interest in asset and stock deals.

The FSA has been unable to update Undercurrent on the current status of the NFCU investigation into Andrew and the insolvency of Bleiker's.

title: Washington shellfish growers fight back as invasive crabs imperil farms, ecosystem
content:
Warren Cowell was probably the first clam farmer in the US state of Washington to tackle the state's green crab invasion this year, and he did it illegally, harvesting and destroying the crabs in February, months before anybody else was out on Willapa Bay.

"I was trapping against the rules. I didn't have a permit, but I was trying to save my crop, and I figured that if they were going to come out and arrest me to take away my traps, then so be it," Cowell told Undercurrent News. "I would let them do that. I wasn't going to be stopped from trying to save my crop."

Areas where European green crabs have taken a clawhold. Map courtesy of Washington state

Cowell's irreverence is based on a bigger challenge than following the fine print in a rulebook, the growing scope of the Carcinus maenas infestation. Currently, it's the worst that Washington state -- and probably the US West Coast -- has ever seen, said David Beugli, a fisheries and wildlife scientist. 

For Cowell, the invasion is an existential threat not just to the fish and shellfish crops raised by farmers such as himself, but for the entire bay ecosystem.

"What's at stake here is the ecosystem of the bay, right? And the fact that it [the crab invasion] is going to take out the shellfish industry with it is a secondary ripple effect of what's going to happen here," Cowell said. "We need to save this bay. We have to get more people and more traps in the bay."

A nasty little critter

Also known as the European crab and discovered in or around state waters since 2012, when they were first discovered in the Salish Sea at Sooke Basin, British Columbia, the green crab didn't become an alarming nuisance until most recently, prompting Washington governor Jay Inslee's emergency proclamation of Jan. 19 that was part of a $10.9 million state effort to eradicate the nasty little critter, as Undercurrent has reported.

Graphic courtesy of Washington state

Considered among the most invasive species in the marine environment by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the green crab "Has few predators, aggressively hunts and eats its prey, destroys seagrass, and outcompetes local species for food and habitat, NOAA says on its website.

Green crab "devour juvenile king crab as well as juvenile salmon. They also destroy eelgrass habitat that larval fish use to hide from predators, and outcompete Dungeness crabs for food and habitat," according to NOAA. "Green crab could potentially damage Alaska’s multi-billion dollar fisheries industries, especially for salmon, crab, and mariculture operations."

All over the place

Exact counts are of course impossible to get, but estimates on the number of green crabs in Washington state waters range from 11,000 to 110,000. One of the state's leaders of the cleanup estimates that it has trapped as many as 40,000 since the cleanup began this spring.

Washington state fisheries officials have prioritized Lummi or Lhaq'temish Nation sea pond areas as the highest priority for the Salish Sea region and three coastal hot spots in their battle against a green crab infestation. Graphic courtesy Washington state

That would be 15,000 to 20,000 captured and destroyed from along the coast and the rest coming from Lummi Bay, said Allen Pleus, an aquatic invasive species coordinator at Washington state's Department of Fish & Wildlife. 

About 40 harvesters have been trapping the crabs.

"We're having challenges, getting all the data coming in, in real-time," Pleus told Undercurrent. "It's looking like there's going to be quite a few crab being brought in this year. We don't know exactly how many at this point, but we're expanding the scope of our trapping daily."

The effort was hamstrung by delays in securing the funding for it, and harvesters to trap the crabs. Even now, the state could use a lot more harvesters and doesn't have its efforts up to full steam, Pleus said.

A European green crah. Photo courtesy Washington state

"It's been a slower startup than what we had anticipated, and that's a lot to do with the normal COVID supply issues and the capacities within our each [state] department, like getting our hiring on time and getting the resources, the amount of crab pots, the amount of vehicles and all that sort of stuff, together," he said. 

A portion of the harvesters doing the work received funding in April, said Beugli, who is also executive director of the Willapa-Grays Harbor Oyster Growers Association. 

That's two months behind Cowell, who said he didn't see any other green crabbers out there when he was harvesting green crab.

"What we're doing is controlled trapping, basically trying to reduce the populations down to a level where they're no longer, considered a risk to the environment," Pleus said.

A big seafood state

Global warming and the warmer waters it creates are generally blamed for green crab migrating increasingly farther north since its first discovery in Canadian waters in 2012.  Washington state is ripe grounds for those creatures. 

The state is the US' largest producer of hatchery-reared and farmed oysters, clams, mussels and geoduck, with more than 300 farms accounting for 25% of the total domestic production by weight and an annual farmgate value exceeding $200 million, according to the Pacific Shellfish Institute.

In 2020, the most recent year available, NOAA placed Washington state fifth greatest in the US for value of all of its harvested seafood, $262.62m, behind top-ranked Alaska ($1.48 billion), Massachusetts ($557.47m), Maine ($520.06m), and Louisiana ($262.97m). It was the 9th-ranked state in the US in metric tonnage of seafood produced that year, according to NOAA.

As Undercurrent has reported, Washington state has enjoyed a record year in Dungeness crab harvesting. As of May 27, Washington state crabbers, including those from three coastal Native American tribes, had collected 18.3m pounds (8,300 metric tons) of Metacarcinus magister for the 2021-22 season -- 14.9m lbs for the state's fishermen, plus about 3.4m for the tribes. That's more than the amount caught in the 2019-20 season, 10.53m lbs, and in previous years. According to DFW statistics, the best poundage numbers for Washington state came in 2016-17 (16.45m), 2012-13 (13.97m) and 2009-10 (16.77m).

The Lummi area, the hardest hit by the green crab, is where the state's Native American tribes cultivate shellfish and juvenile salmon and is also part of salmon spawning runs that stretch from Washington and Oregon into Canada. Willapa Bay, meanwhile, is farther south than Lummi, just north of Portland and the Oregon line, and home to salmon spawning grounds and about half the state's Dungeness crab beds.

The state's seafood industry has never seen a natural and evolving threat like the green crab, particularly with state crabbers.

"They eat and out-compete the native species. So when you have two species overlapping with them, they're going to outcompete the native crabs brutal fast," Beugli said.

How it goes from here

Beugli wasn't sure how successful the cleanup effort would ultimately be.

"It depends on how you define success. I feel if it's to where there are no environmental economic damages, I think we can get there, based on how they populate these bays and estuaries, he said. "I think it'll be hard to eradicate them 100%, or not possible. It'll be difficult."

The green crab harvesters are doing very well, said Bill Dewey, director of public affairs at Taylor Shellfish Farms of Oregon.

"The numbers the Shoalwater tribe and shellfish growers have caught in Willapa Bay and Grays Harbor since the beginning of the year are staggering (25,000+). I believe that catch per unit effort exceeds what they are seeing in the Lummi Sea Pond. Apparently, they are also catching unprecedented numbers of gravid female green crab," Dewey said in an email. 

"These bays rarely get mentioned in green crab stories and they appear to be a real hotbed.  Besides being critically important oyster and clam-producing bays, they are key nursery bays for juvenile Dungeness crabs," he added.

State officials and harvesters are planning to meet to discuss the allocation of resources to the cleanup, which some harvesters feel is lopsided. Cowell wants to see shellfish harvesters get more funding for the cleanup since they are already on the water and experienced at harvesting.

"We've got skin in the game because financially we stand to lose the most first," Cowell said.

But more people need to be doing the cleanup now. The more doing it now, the less environmental damage the crab will do, Cowell said. The cleanup ought to be successful "if we throw enough resources at it right now, and trap them for the next at least three years."

Harvesters "need to put a stronger effort out there," said Cowell, who started a Facebook page, "Willapa Green Crab Disaster," that he encouraged prospective cleanup volunteers to join. "We've got skin in the game because, you know, financially, we stand to lose the most first."

title: Two men charged with getting early illegal jump on Florida’s spiny lobster season
content:
The eight-month commercial and recreational spiny lobster (Panulirus argus) season doesn't start until Aug. 6 in the US state of Florida, but that didn't stop at least two men from recently getting an alleged illegal early start, the Miami Herald reports. 

Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) officers reportedly watched from shore as 43-year-old Rafael Larduet Carrion allegedly caught lobster near Duck Key on Saturday (June 11), illegally separating the tails from the carapace. All harvested lobsters must be brought to shore whole, per Florida law.

Carrion allegedly pulled six wrung tails from underneath his shorts after he got out of the water and FWC stopped him on the shore. He was placed in a county jail on misdemeanor charges of possession of undersized and out-of-season lobster, wringing tails in the water and not possessing a measuring device, according to the newspaper. 

Then, on Sunday (June 12), the FWC arrested 30-year-old Randy Sanchez Tapia for allegedly harvesting out of season as many as 62 lobsters, 32 of which were undersized, while snorkeling near Whale Harbor Channel in Islamorada.

title: Seafood fraudster gets 10 years for bilking RFS, US Foods, PFG, others
content:
Paul Diogenes, a Rhode Island man who used a borrowed identity and a made up catering company to bilk several big food distributors out of nearly a million dollars worth of seafood, steak and other high-end food items, has been sentenced to 10 years in federal prison, according to a statement released Friday by US attorney Zachary A. Cunha. 

Diogenes' story reads like an over-the-top sensational crime television fiction, but it really happened.

Undercurrent News reported in August 2021 how the now 50-year-old man took the name of Paul Dejullio, someone he worked alongside as a cook at a restaurant in Fall River, Massachusetts, in 2018, to create and operate LePage Catering company.

Image from SevenMaps / Shutterstock

He then used bank information illegally taken from multiple other seafood businesses and restaurants -- over a roughly nine-month period, between November 2020 and July 2021 -- to acquire more than $831,000 worth of lobster, sea bass, shrimp, scallops, filet, rib eye steak, and wild boar, from the likes of US Foods, Performance Food Group and Reinhart Food Service (RFS). 

As part of his "sophisticated and elaborate scheme", according to prosecutors, he paid for the goods with money taken from multiple Rhode Island restaurants, including Capriccio's and the Mare, in Providence, the Riviera in East Providence, and Wilfred’s in Woonsocket.

But RFS was the biggest victim of the alleged scam, reporting that it delivered more than $531,000 worth of food products to LePage Catering without being paid, while US Foods delivered more than $185,000 worth of products and PFG delivered more than $115,000 worth of products, according to the charging documents.

Diogenes kept the food at Digger's Catch, an East Providence, Rhode Island-based business also known as East Side Shellfish, where he allegedly made himself a partner. He then resold the food, in some instances, to the same businesses whose banking information he used to pay the distributors, according to the documents.

On August 3, 2021, as FBI agents, FBI Task Force officers, and Rhode Island State Police attempted to arrest Diogenes behind an East Providence business, he rammed his car into two FBI task force vehicles, one with a task force officer and State Police trooper still inside; drove his vehicle toward an FBI agent who narrowly avoided serious injury; and rammed his car into a delivery van parked nearby before speeding away through an opening he created.

The defendant was located by the US Marshals Service and the FBI nine days later at a Middleborough, Massachusetts, hotel. He was in possession of a briefcase containing $116,404 in cash, which was forfeited to the government.

Diogenes pled guilty on December 17, 2021, to wire fraud and assault of a federal officer. He was sentenced on Friday by US District Court chief judge John McConnell, Jr., to 120 months in federal prison; three years of federal supervised release; and ordered to pay restitution totaling $831,572.

Diogenes is described in court documents as "an unrepentant and compulsive fraudster". He's been convicted in various courts and jurisdictions 34 times, including multiple convictions for fraud-related criminal activity and for charges brought as a result of his violent behavior toward law enforcement.

title: Editor’s choice: Arrest made as UK smokehouse goes under; Salmon prices ‘unsustainable’
content:
Neil Ramsden, EMEA editor with Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week.

Undercurrent's most-read stories of last week were a couple of scoops from editor Tom Seaman on the news firstly that UK salmon processor Bleiker's Smoke House had gone into administration after abruptly losing its main contract with Aldi, and then that an arrest has been made as part of an investigation into the company by the government's food crime arm.

An investigation from the National Food Crime Unit, the enforcement arm of the Food Standards Agency, relates to "a number of alleged issues including concerns about their [Bleiker's] country of origin claims on some of their smoked salmon products", its Gavan Wafer told Undercurrent.

Then, news from the previous week's Seafood Expo Global was largely the order of the day. 

Salmon farmers may be raking in bumper profits, but the current prices are unsustainable for the sector as a whole, said the CEO of Cermaq Group, the world's second-largest producer. Cermaq, which has moved into the second spot in terms of 2021 production behind Mowi, is taking a long-term view in line with its Japanese owner, Mitsubishi Corporation.

What with Ecuador's expansion of value-added production, China's delisting of multiple exporters, Europe's ongoing high sampling rate of Indian produce and the ever-present headache of ultra-high freight rates; it's a difficult time to be an Indian vannamei trader, Jagdish Fofandi -- national president of the Seafood Exporters Association of India -- told Undercurrent at the show.

Turning to the US, the parent company of major seafood distributor Fortune Fish & Gourmet has filed suit against a former sales associate over an alleged breach of a non-compete agreement and theft of the company's trade secrets. Bensenville, Illinois-based Fortune International filed a lawsuit on April 5 against Tim MacDonald in US District Court for the Northern District of Illinois. In October 2020, MacDonald, according to the lawsuit, was hired as an outside sales associate "with responsibilities primarily in the Twin Cities area of Minnesota".

And the approach to mergers and acquisitions (M&A) from Canadian food giant Premium Brands Holdings is not to focus on integration, but on openings for market expansion, CEO George Paleologou told Undercurrent, explaining that the company's strategy would mean "two plus two equals eight" for those acquired.

The Ecuadorian shrimp industry has a great interest in further market share growth in Italy, Spain and France while opening to new destinations in Europe and Asia, Jose Antonio Camposano, head of Ecuador's national chamber of aquaculture, told Undercurrent at the Barcelona show. "We made an important bet by bringing 23 Ecuadorian shrimp companies to the show, which involved an investment of over $1 million," he said. "All of them are looking to grow further in Europe, a market in which the sector expansion plans inevitably came to a halt during the pandemic, hindered by distance."

The biggest aquaculture company in the Mediterranean plans to ramp up its production of the larger-sized species "corvina" for more value-added production, said new CEO Thor Talseth. Avramar plans to produce 10,000-11,000 metric tons of corvina (also known as stone bass outside southern Europe) in 2022, compared to 5,000-6,000t last year.

Meanwhile, Turkey's seabass and seabream producers have cautioned that prices will stay at the current highs of €5.00-€6.00 per kilogram, or increase slightly, due to a limited pipeline of new farm sites.

Finally, Cousins Maine Lobster is already the US' largest lobster truck business, but four signed franchise agreements in the first quarter of 2022 and the opening of two new territories promise to grow it even larger.

title: Daily recap, May 5: Arrest made in Bleiker’s probe; Grieg set to blaze salmon trail in Newfoundland
content:
Here's a recap of the daily seafood news from Thursday, May 5: 

Arrest made as UK food crime body investigates former Aldi salmon smoker  

The UK government's food crime arm confirmed to Undercurrent News an arrest has been made as part of an investigation into Bleiker's Smoke House, a processor which went into insolvency on April 29 after losing its main contract with Aldi a few weeks before. 

Grieg set to blaze salmon trail in Newfoundland's west, dwarf Mowi, Cooke output

Grieg Seafood says it'll likely be years before it determines whether it will take advantage of the opportunity to grow 15,000 to 20,000 metric tons of salmon annually on the frontier-like western third of Newfoundland's roughly 300-mile southern coast; but even if it doesn't, it looks enthusiastically poised to move from a non-player there to supplanting both Mowi and Cooke as the dominant producer.

Brasmar plans growth in France from acquisition, US after new hire

Portugal-based processor Brasmar Group is looking to France and the US for growth in 2022 after snapping up a distributor in the former earlier this year and making a new hire in the latter.

Royal Greenland unsure whether 2021’s strong performance can go on

Royal Greenland warned the outlook for 2022 is yet again uncertain, just as the company managed to recover and adapt well to the coronavirus pandemic in 2021. 2% of the firm's 2021 revenue related to exports of shell-on coldwater shrimp to Russia. "In view of the Greenland government's appeal to stop all trade with Russia...this revenue is uncertain."

title: Arrest made as UK food crime body investigates former Aldi salmon smoker
content:
The UK government's food crime arm confirmed an arrest has been made as part of an investigation into Bleiker's Smoke House, a processor which went into insolvency on April 29 after losing its main contract with Aldi a few weeks before. 

An investigation from the National Food Crime Unit (NFCU), the enforcement arm of the Food Standards Agency (FSA), relates to "a number of alleged issues including concerns about their [Bleiker's] country of origin claims on some of their smoked salmon products", its Gavan Wafer told Undercurrent News. 

UK smoker enters administration weeks after Aldi contract loss

"The NFCU has acted on intelligence it received and which has resulted in one arrest being made," said Wafer, who is head of investigations at NFCU. 

An FSA spokesperson declined to comment on who had been arrested. She declined to comment further on the ongoing investigation, including the possibility of criminal proceedings.

Undercurrent has been unable to reach Charlie Andrew, former managing director and the company's controlling shareholder, or his wife Anabel for comment. Anabel Andrew was also a shareholder and executive with Bleiker's. 

The press team for the UK arm of German discounter Aldi referred Undercurrent to the FSA for comment.  

Bleiker's was supplying Aldi with its "Specially Selected" smoked salmon, which is supposed to use Scottish salmon approved by the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (RSPCA).  

Aldi UK abruptly drops smoked salmon supplier

It's thought a recording of a meeting between the management team of Bleiker's from last year about meeting Christmas supply was anonymously shared with Aldi in late March 2022.

The retailer delisted the smoked salmon supplier soon after, with the RSPCA-approved product then pulled from shelves. 

Former MD Andrew, former operations director Alex Mcmorran, and Dana Timsa, who was the factory manager, were all reportedly in the meeting which was allegedly recorded and shared with Aldi. 

McMorran left the company at the end of last year. He declined to comment to Undercurrent on the recording or the Aldi delisting. Timsa did not respond to requests for comment from Undercurrent. It's thought she worked for the company up until it went into administration last week.

Danish PE eyes upstream buyers as another salmon smoker goes up for sale

Alex Irvine, who was business development director for Bleiker's, also left at the end of last year. Irvine declined to comment to Undercurrent. 

"Sabotage and petty revenge" from a disgruntled former employee led to Aldi dropping Bleiker's, Andrew told his staff on April 29, the day the company went into administration. 

Andrew did not name the former employee in the statement, read out in the company's breakroom last Friday, according to an Undercurrent source who was present.  

As for the nature of the sabotage and revenge, Andrew did not go into specifics, said the former employee who was there during the speech. 

Undercurrent first contacted North Yorkshire Police about reports of an arrest relating to Bleiker's, then was referred to the FSA.  

"We would like to take the opportunity to thank North Yorkshire Police for assisting in the investigation and supporting this operation," said the NFCU's Wafer. "It is vitally important that we ensure food is safe and what it says it is and that consumers and food businesses are confident in the authenticity of food they are buying."

FRP looks for buyer 

Meanwhile, FRP Advisory Trading has been appointed as the administrator for Bleiker's and is seeking a buyer for the company's assets, as previously reported by Undercurrent. 

European salmon processor plans next step in North American market

Aldi accounted for as much as 60% of the company's turnover, which was £14.09 million ($17.6m) for the 12 months to April 31, 2021.

A spokesperson for FRP said the company's Martyn Pullin and Phil Pearce were appointed as joint administrators to Bleiker's on April 29. FRP declined to comment on the arrest or the NFCU investigation.  

According to FRP, Bleiker's employed 86 staff. "After the loss of a significant contract, the business began consultation with its employees. The business and assets were marketed for sale, but a buyer could not be found," he said. 

On April 28, 38 staff were made redundant, with the rest laid off the next day, as the business ceased trading, the spokesperson said. FRP continues to look for a buyer. 

"Bleiker’s was a family operation with a track record of supporting both major and independent retailers. The loss of a significant contract left the business in a difficult financial position. Regrettably, the insolvency has meant that the business is no longer able to continue trading and redundancies have been made," said Pullin, in a statement. 

"We are now focused on exploring options to sell the business and its assets and encourage any interested parties to come forward," he said. 

"It was one of the best jobs I've ever had. They are thoroughly nice people who tried to look after their workforce the proper way. It was a really nice environment to work in. It's going to be difficult to find something else of that caliber," the former staff member told Undercurrent.

title: Nova Scotia captain on trial for alleged illegal halibut harvesting
content:
A fisherman, a fish buyer and two related companies accused of illegal halibut landings are going on trial in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia.

Captain Casey Henneberry of the fishing vessel Ivy Lewis is accused of failing to follow license conditions in several instances between May 2019 and June 2020, including on three trips when halibut catches were reportedly unloaded without a dockside monitor present.

"The evidence will show that of the seven trips, three of those involved illegal offloads; failing to have all the weight and species of all groundfish verified by a dockside observer according to the license. There was surveillance of three trips either before or after the lawful unload," federal crown prosecutor Lee-Ann Conrod told the court.

Buyer Samir Zakhour is accused of being at the wharf to buy halibut during the last "illegal offload" in June 2020. He is also charged with misleading a fishery officer the night of his arrest.

title: Texas game wardens report finding hundreds of shark fins at restaurant
content:
Game wardens in the US state of Texas say they discovered hundreds of shark fins at a San Antonio seafood restaurant on Wednesday during a routine inspection, KSAT, a local television station, reports.

As many as 381 whole shark fins were allegedly discovered during a routine inspection, along with 29.2 pounds of frozen shark fins inside the restaurant’s commercial freezer, based on a Facebook post. 

A Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD) spokesperson declined to identify the restaurant, saying its investigation was ongoing but told the TV station that the inspection was to "determine the source of aquatic resources" used by the restaurant.

No arrests have been made.

"As an apex predator, sharks are critical to oceanic ecosystems. They maintain the food chain and serve as an indicator species. Between 70 to 100 million sharks are killed every year for their fins," the spokesperson told KSAT.

In June 2015, Texas governor Greg Abbott signed a bill into law that made the sale, trade, purchase and transportation of shark fins in Texas illegal and punishable by a jail sentence of up to 180 days and/or up to a $2,000 fine. Previously, the fins could still be imported and exported despite shark finning being illegal in US waters.

title: Canary Island bust nets $78m in cocaine
content:
Five people were arrested when a fishing boat carrying nearly 3 metric tons of cocaine was intercepted off the Canary Islands, Reuters reported.

A Spanish air patrol noticed the suspicious boat, the AKT 1, and it was stopped on April 13 by a coast guard patrol vessel about 300 nautical miles south of the Spanish archipelago as it tried to pass itself off as another fishing boat.

The cocaine, estimated to have a street value of €72 million ($78.2m), was allegedly hidden in one of the boat's fuel tanks. The name of the boat's owner was not disclosed.

Police said they were focusing on cracking down on what they call the "African route" for South American traffickers who transfer loads of drugs to fishing vessels in the middle of the Atlantic before smuggling them into Europe.

title: Dalian still yet to reach full processing capacity as COVID fears linger
content:
The Chinese seafood processing hub of Dalian is still yet to reach full capacity more than three months after the city's port officially reopened to Russian tramper vessels carrying pollock cargo, industry sources told Undercurrent News.

According to an industry source based in Qingdao, another large Chinese processing hub, just over 10 plants are processing in the Dalian area, while others are still waiting for further audits from authorities. 

UK, Germany face biggest supply shocks if Russian whitefish sanctioned

A second executive source confirmed that although 30 plus factories have been allowed to reopen, so far just over 10 are actually running due to coronavirus restrictions. "Some plants plan to reopen [but] are still waiting for government approval after lifting of broader restrictions," the source told Undercurrent. 

She added in Dalian securing raw material was also a problem, despite deliveries of Russian pollock at a seasonal high. "Though major first stop cold storages are open, Yingkou cold storage and Yi Di 1 cold storage are still closed, which has caused the plants in processing to run short," she said.

In the first two months of 2022, China imported 87,000 metric tons of headed and gutted (H&G) pollock from Russia -- its biggest supplier of the fish -- worth $106 million, according to Chinese customs. The next largest supplier was the US with just 1,270t, worth $1.92m. 

Liaoning province -- where Dalian is located -- imported 20,800t, while Shandong province -- where Qingdao is located -- imported 52,000t. The rest of China imported 17,000t. Lower imports into Dalian, while imports into Qingdao stay high, corresponds with the continued restrictions faced by Dalian processors.

Dalian-based seafood processors were forced to close in November of last year after an outbreak of COVID-19 led to a lockdown across much of the city. In December, authorities linked the outbreak to a frozen food importer. 

A third Chinese executive confirmed that plants in Dalian are still only opening gradually and that as a result processors in Qingdao have won new business from international buyers. 

He also noted more requests were coming in for Alaskan fish -- wild salmon and cod -- in place of Russian fish since the latter's invasion of Ukraine. This is despite higher prices, with Alaskan wild salmon costing $200-$300 per metric ton more than Russian fish and the difference for cod about the same, the source said.

The first executive said he thought Dalian and Qingdao's coronavirus controls would not be tightened. On April 13, two new asymptomatic cases of COVID-19 were reported in Dalian by the Dalian New Coronary Pneumonia Epidemic Prevention and Control Headquarters. On April 14, however, Dalian reopened one of the city's metro lines. 

"The coronavirus in Qingdao is well under control, life is normal," said the first executive. "So long as this remains the case I do not think there will be a lockdown.

"But both Qingdao and Dalian authorities will make their minds up based on the situation on the ground, though if there are only a few cases I do not think they will lock down cities because the cost will be much too high."

Exports also higher from Qingdao

As for exports of pollock fillets and blocks, Shandong exported 15,200t of frozen pollock fillets and blocks in the first two months of 2022, up 2% compared with the same period last year. In contrast, exports out of Liaoning slumped 41% y-o-y to 4,800t. 

Similarly, Liaoning's exports of frozen cod fillets also were down 44% y-o-y to 2,700t, while Shandong's were up 27% y-o-y to 10,200t (see charts below).

On Jan. 11, Dalian lifted a ban on Russian trampers from unloading cargo in the city's port, followed by Qingdao Port a day later. Prior to the ban, Russian fishing vessels would transship pollock to trampers which would then travel to Dalian and Qingdao to unload their cargo.

The ban meant fishing companies shipped pollock to Busan in South Korea instead, from where it was then transported to China with a South Korean health certificate. The disruption to trade was massive, with China's imports of H&G pollock down by more than 40% last year.

title: China ‘breaks’ multi-million dollar seafood smuggling rings
content:
The General Administration of Customs of China (GACC) has arrested 18 people accused of smuggling 183,700 metric tons of frozen seafood worth CNY 2.46 billion ($390m).

Chinese customs agency seizes $35.8m of smuggled black tiger shrimp

On Thursday (Feb 24), the GACC said officials from Zhanjiang Customs "broke" four smuggling rings operating in Beijing, Fujian, Guangdong, and Shandong, and seized physical evidence.  

The smuggling rings control companies that order frozen seafood such as octopus and Chinese hairtail, know as daiyu, to sell in China while falsely reporting specifications, origin and prices.

GACC said the case is under further investigation.

China cracked down in earnest on seafood smuggling from Vietnam into China from late 2017, while crackdowns increased in intensity during the US-China trade war.

title: EJF claims Chinese trawlers granted licenses in Madagascar have history of illegal fishing
content:
A fleet of Chinese vessels which was previously caught fishing illegally in West Africa has been approved for trawling by Madagascar's authorities, according to a new report by the Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF).

Under Malagasy regulations, no vessel with a history of illegal fishing should be allowed to fish in the country’s waters unless there is proof of a change in ownership. However, vessel documents used by the ships, which were obtained by EJF, appear to be forged (below), raising "major issues regarding the ownership of the trawlers".

Click to expand

EJF urged the government to "safeguard local livelihoods and food security by rescinding the licenses before the trawl season begins in March".

Madagascar’s industrial shrimp trawling season is expected to begin March 1, with exports geared toward markets in Europe, North America and China. The fleet in question, made up of eight vessels, is understood to have entered Madagascar under a license issued to Mada Fishery, a company linked to Chinese ownership that registered in Madagascar just last year.

In 2020, authorities in the Gambia arrested three of the fleet -- Gorde 105, Gorde 106, and Gorde 107 -- for fishing illegally in waters reserved for small-scale fishers, EJF claimed. Two of the three were also "double-bagging" their nets, in violation of Gambian fisheries regulations.

The vessels’ journey to Madagascar, which was facilitated in part by the Chinese navy, was punctuated by a stop in the Seychelles in May 2021, when they anchored without permission and were brought in for inspection. At the time, the captains produced documents to claim that they had legitimate business in the region; however, EJF has now found that the documents were forged, raising questions about the vessels’ true identity, it said.

Steve Trent, CEO of EJF, said: "Madagascar’s government should adhere to its well-designed fisheries code and investigate and suspend the licenses of all Mada Fishery vessels linked to illegal fishing."

"There is every indication that this company is using the woeful lack of transparency in global fisheries to obscure its history of illegal offenses. It’s crucial that vessel operators are held accountable for their fishing practices. But such accountability will not be possible so long as companies about which so little is known, like Mada Fishery, are allowed to fish in Madagascar’s waters."

title: Chinese demand for shrimp before Spring Festival hit by omicron
content:
Shrimp importers in China are in a more positive mood in the runup to Chinese New Year compared with last year, industry sources told Undercurrent News.

However, concern is mounting over cases of COVID-19 in the country and demand remains below pre-pandemic levels, industry sources said. 

In Beijing, an importer told Undercurrent both import and wholesale prices for large-sized frozen salted shrimp in China are "relatively strong, although the overall price is declining". However, the market is still "sluggish" compared to before the pandemic, when demand for imported seafood peaked.

Chinese companies lead 30 exhibitor exodus from Boston seafood show

"Market consumption is more favorable to us than last year," said the importer, who sources shrimp from Ecuador. 

"However, the large domestic wholesale market is still cautious about [imported] shrimp in original packaging. And there was a recent case of the omicron variant linked to an international post, which has caused distributors and government regulators to become more cautious," said the importer.

A recovery in Chinese imports of shrimp in November suggested an end to worries about coronavirus on packages of imported seafood. In November, China imported 70,000 metric tons of frozen warmwater shrimp, the largest volume in 16 months, according to Chinese customs data.

However, the emergence of the omicron variant and high daily cases since the start of 2022 have renewed concerns about imports. Last week, officials in Beijing urged people to wear masks and gloves when opening packages from abroad. 

It follows an outbreak of COVID-19 in Dalian in November that was linked to a logistics company handling imported frozen food and seafood, and which led to several arrests. 

Arrests made as China points finger at seafood firms over Dalian COVID outbreak 

The importer said that heightened concerns about COVID-19 in fact benefit shrimp importers currently with stock. "Many customers will consider the probability of products being contaminated when ordering from abroad. This makes it easier to win customers for those who already have stock in China," he said.

With the majority of Chinese still free to gather and celebrate Spring Festival in group settings, there are also plenty of seafood-hungry customers to sell to, he said.

"The scale of Spring Festival festivities will depend on the actual situation of the epidemic in each region. In regions without COVID-19 there will still be a big banquet, and seafood products are still a must-have item on the Chinese table."

Market for live shrimp more volatile

This week, China's effort to control coronavirus outbreaks was having a bigger impact on the market for domestically produced live shrimp, according to local media. 

According to John Hopkins University, there were 66 new confirmed cases on Jan. 19 in China. In parts of Tianjin, Anyang, Xi'an and Shenzhen residents were subject to COVID-related restrictions. 

A vendor at a wholesale market in Zhanjiang, Guangdong, said prices for wild-caught white shrimp have dropped from CNY 600 per kilogram ($94.60/kg) last year to CNY 260/kg this year, reported CCTV.

Frozen HOSO shrimp marketed on JD.com. Source: JD.com

In previous years, before Chinese New Year holidays, farmgate prices of locally produced, live vannamei shrimp in Zhanjiang were typically CNY 60-80/kg for 80 pieces per kilogram, but now have fallen to CNY 40/kg, reported CCTV.

A drop in live shrimp sales coincides with better sales of frozen products through e-commerce, it reported, suggesting consumers are compensating with more online purchases.

According to JD.com, sales of shrimp products from Zhanjiang are up 213% year-on-year, while high-end gift packages have also grown in popularity.

Suppliers are also busy preparing for online sales which dealers pick up at 8-9 pm for early shipment the next day, said JD.com.

A processor source in Zhanjiang told Undercurrent he still felt that the market was "okay", on balance. In late December, average farmgate prices in Guangdong province were clearly on the rise, according to Undercurrent's price dashboard.

Upgrade to Pro to view

"Actually we are in the low season of production so most shrimp has been harvested already. In northern China, farms have stopped producing. So there is a seasonal shortage of supply," he said.

He reckons that Chinese domestic shrimp farmers and processors ultimately are better off ahead of Chinese New Year this year. "This year ought to be a bit better," he said. "Everyone is a bit more used to the pandemic. So the market is relatively stable."

"Shrimp broodstock quality is also better, shrimp larvae is better. So shrimp production area has increased. Those businesses that produce good quality products are also doing well. They benefit from customers' recognition and because big restaurant chains and retailers want guaranteed levels of quality and supply," he said.

The importer in Beijing added difficulties importing today means potential shortages tomorrow, which could see prices rise after the holidays. "The price in the first half of 2022 will be higher than the average price in previous years due to global inflation, but after June it will be as high as in 2021," he said.

In November, Ecuador shipped 46,000t of frozen shrimp to China, up 8% compared with the same month of 2020. The figures suggest plenty of shrimp arrived in China in the month of December, before recent infections dampened market sentiment.

title: Dalian port creaks into gear after Russian pollock tramper ban lifted
content:
Additional reporting by Tom Seaman

The port in the Chinese city of Dalian is creaking into gear a week after the seafood processing hub officially reopened to Russian tramper vessels carrying pollock cargo, industry sources told Undercurrent News.

Dalian authorities have begun to allow companies to transport containers of fish to and from the port, although the movement of containers is slow due to a backlog and lack of staff, a source with a large seafood processor told Undercurrent. 

Aldi holds firm on fish finger prices with PBO pollock set for record level

"They [authorities] are allowing H&G [headed and gutted] raw material from the port into the government-controlled cold storages and then the plants," said the source. "[But] it's slow as there is not enough staff in the port," said the source.

The backlog of containers with H&G pollock held in port is estimated to have grown into "the hundreds", he said, after seafood processing plants and frozen food importers were forced to close in early November due to an outbreak of COVID-19. In December, authorities linked the outbreak to a frozen food importer. 

The main priority now is to get products manufactured before the outbreak to international buyers. "The authorities are permitting companies to move finished products out of cold storage to the port for shipping. [But] they are only allowing companies to ship out finished products produced before Nov. 3 to be transported to the port," he said.

"Nothing is moving on a big scale," he added, noting the decision to restart logistics was only taken recently.

A company based outside Zhuanghe -- the epicenter of November's outbreak -- is still awaiting confirmation fish can be moved to and from the port, a source at the firm told Undercurrent. It is currently processing local fish only.

"We've heard about this [permissions to move product]. But nothing has been implemented yet. We still haven't reopened [for international business]," the source told Undercurrent on Monday (Jan. 16). 

China jails three managers of Dalian logistics company over COVID outbreak

She added processors fear high demurrage fees given the length of time containers have been held in Dalian, although a third source reckons fees will be negotiated down. 

All eyes are on whether clearing the backlog will speed up or, given increasing rates of COVID in China, remain slow or even stop again. "I'm not quite sure when [our] plant will be really allowed to [start] processing," a fourth source told Undercurrent.

"Winter Olympics is an important event for the country. We'll need more observation of the implementation of the declaration of reopening to Russian cargo," she said.

On Jan. 11, Dalian lifted a ban on Russian trampers from unloading cargo in the city's port, while Qingdao Port followed suit a day later. Prior to the ban, Russian fishing vessels would transship pollock to trampers which would then travel to Dalian and Qingdao to unload their cargo.

As a result of the ban, fishing companies shipped pollock to Busan in South Korea instead, from where it was then transported to China with a South Korean health certificate. The disruption to trade was massive, with China's imports of H&G pollock down by more than 40% last year.

title: China jails three managers of Dalian logistics company over COVID outbreak
content:
A court in Dalian, China, has jailed three managers at a cold chain logistics company for up to four years and nine months after they allegedly broke coronavirus prevention laws while unloading frozen food in the port city. 

Sentencing the defendants, the People's Court of Dalian Economic and Technological Development Zone said the jail terms reflected "the facts, nature and circumstances of the crime committed by each defendant, as well as the degree of harm to society".

Arrests made as China points finger at seafood firms over Dalian COVID outbreak 

The names of the defendants and the company they worked for were not released.

Between Dec. 1-12, 2020, while under contract to unload and transport frozen food from an unnamed foreign vessel docked at the port of Dalian, four employees of the logistics company reportedly contracted COVID-19.

The employees then spread the disease to members of the public at a restaurant and the company's commercial premises. By Dec. 15, 2020, 83 infections had been detected in Dalian, at the time one of the largest outbreaks in the city since the start of the pandemic. 

It followed a smaller outbreak of COVID-19 in Dalian several months prior that was linked to an unspecified frozen seafood importer, and foreshadowed a third COVID-19 outbreak a year later in November 2021. A large number of port services companies in Dalian serve the seafood processing industry.

On Tuesday (Jan. 11), the Dalian court alleged that the three logistics company managers -- the firm's legal representative, its founder, and operations manager -- did not take precautions to prevent coronavirus infections, such as implementing social distancing and staff health monitoring. 

Three company managers (front row) of a logistics company in Dalian sentenced on Tuesday (Jan. 11). Source: Dalian People’s Court of Dalian Economic and Technological Development Zone

This included failing to socially distance from foreign vessel crew, failing to test employees for COVID, and failing to inform accommodation providers of the nature of their work to prevent social mixing with other guests, the court asserted.

The operations manager also reportedly "neglected his role" as supervisor, as port workers did not wear masks, protective clothing or "cotton-padded clothes", or eat meals in protective clothing, the court said. Workers were also not supervised when they left before their contracted period. Another worker who tested positive for the virus was not in quarantine when he was supposed to be.

Wechat comments under the article. One user said: “These are people who didn’t take seriously people’s health. Now they’re being dealt with seriously by the law.” Source: Wechat

The court said defendants were guilty of the "crime of obstructing the prevention and treatment of infectious diseases", and sentenced them to between three years and three months to four years and nine months in jail. The company was fined CNY 800,000 ($125,509).

"These are people who didn’t take seriously people’s health. Now they’re being dealt with seriously by the law," said one Wechat user.

The jailings follow a strict lockdown of Dalian city in November and part of December of last year after a third outbreak of COVID-19. The outbreak, which was also traced back to frozen food importers, resulted in over 300 infections and the closure of all frozen food and seafood processing companies in the city.

Last month, arrests were made at one of the Dalian-based frozen seafood importers after it was identified as the first point of infection. However, on Tuesday, signaling a relaxing of coronavirus protocols, Dalian officially lifted a ban on Russian tramper vessels docking at its port, allowing the important trade of pollock transported by trampers from Russian catcher vessels to resume after a stop of more than a year.

title: Dalian port reopens to Russian trampers in boost to pollock industry
content:
Additional reporting by Louis Harkell

Dalian officially opened its port to Russian trampers on Jan. 10 in a move that allows an important trade route bringing pollock to the seafood hub to resume operations after a ban that lasted for over a year.

"On 6:00 pm on Jan. 10, Liaoyu port resumed operations for Russian trampers carrying frozen seafood," said Liaoyu Group, a large state-owned company that operates the port, through the company's Wechat. 

Arrests made as China points finger at seafood firms over Dalian COVID outbreak 

Local media in China described the move as a significant achievement in negotiations between the Russian government and the Chinese authorities. The reopening of Qingdao, another seafood processing hub in China, is not far off, local media also reported.

The Russian fishery agency Rosrybolovstvo has repeatedly said that authorities have been working closely with Chinese customs to reopen ports for fishery products in Dalian and Qingdao.

In the fall of 2020, authorities in Dalian and Qingdao blamed outbreaks of COVID-19 on frozen fish imports, resulting in Russian trampers no longer being permitted to deliver cargo. This ended a very efficient trade for fishing companies that transhipped headed and gutted (H&G) pollock from fishers at sea and took it directly to China as bulk cargo.

As a result, Busan of South Korea became the new hub for moving H&G from trampers into containers. However, in July 2021, China stopped accepting Russian catch certificates on product transshipped via the South Korean port. So, Russian H&G is being imported and re-exported slowly with a South Korean health certificate.

The reopening of Dalian port shows that the two countries have found an effective and low-cost way to manage risks, rather than taking extreme measures, Chinese media commented. "Russian pollock trampers and Liaoyu Group will be the biggest beneficiaries," claimed the OIG Institute, a Chinese market research and import services outfit.

Russian Fishery aims to drop H&G pollock with PBO prices tipped to hit $4,500/t

It also suggests an imminent reopening of seafood processors in the city, after an outbreak of COVID-19 in the city in November was linked to a frozen food importer. On Monday (Jan. 10), an executive at a Dalian-based seafood processor told Undercurrent her company remained closed, although a source at another firm said they could process local fish.

Liaoyu's port imports more than 800,000 metric tons of aquatic products annually, accounting for 60% of the total volume in China, according to the port authorities.

The 2022 total allowable catches (TAC) of Russia's pollock fishing industry will be 1.927 million metric tons, a reduction of 3% year-on-year.

Within this figure, the TACs in the Sea of Okhotsk and western Bering Sea fisheries, two big sources of Marine Stewardship Council approved fish, will be down 10% and 1.3% y-o-y to 956,100t and 409,200t respectively, according to data shared with Undercurrent News by the Pollock Catchers Association.

title: Zoneco receives $8m gov’t cash subsidy for COVID losses
content:
Zoneco Group, one of China’s largest seafood companies, has received a CNY 50 million ($7.8m) government subsidy to compensate for losses related to the pandemic.

Zoneco, which processes sea cucumber, abalone, and scallops farmed in the Bohai Sea, said it received the amount as part of a "coronavirus supply chain impact subsidy" from the local government of Zhangzidao island, where Zoneco is headquartered.

Arrests made as China points finger at seafood firms over Dalian COVID outbreak 

On Nov. 8, food import and seafood processing plants in Dalian were forced to close by authorities, after a cluster of COVID cases was reported at two seafood processing plants in nearby Zhuanghe. Zoneco owns three companies based in Dalian, including a seafood processing plant and logistics company. 

According to Zoneco’s 2020 annual report, Zoneco's Dalian-based companies generated CNY 348m in annual sales in 2020, or roughly a third of its total revenues.

Seafood processing plants in Zhuanghe remain under a government-enforced closure, a processor source in the city told Undercurrent News on Monday (Jan. 10). However, a seafood processor based in neighboring Dalian told Undercurrent her firm is able to process local fish.

Zoneco said the subsidy would be recorded as a deferred payment and come under profits for the financial year.

Zoneco is currently being sued by shareholders who claim their investments lost value after the company falsified its scallop farming data. The firm has sold off a number of its businesses to pay fines and debts. 

This includes the recently agreed sale of a sea cucumber farm and other related assets in Zhuanghe to a local company for CNY 95m.

title: Russian Fishery aims to drop H&G pollock with PBO prices tipped to hit $4,500/t
content:
Russian Fishery Company (RFC) aims to stop headed and gutted (H&G) pollock production later this year, with prices for pin-bone out (PBO) fillets expected to soar to $4,500 per metric ton and surimi demand also strong, an executive with the company told Undercurrent News. 

If PBO prices rise as RFC predicts, that would be a hike of around $700/t, or 17%, on the ex-warehouse level shown for B season on Undercurrent's prices portal. It would also be on par with the record level hit in A season of 2009. Amid this hot market, RFC's new vessel is ramping up PBO and surimi production, and the company expects two more additions to its fleet later in 2022, in addition to having converted one H&G vessel for fillets last year.

As a result, "we are going to sharply decrease H&G production and reach a 0% share in our product mix by mid-2022", Savely Karpukhin, RFC's deputy general director for strategy and commercial, told Undercurrent. "Thanks to our ongoing investments in new fleet construction, we believe this is feasible."

Overall, RFC predicts total Russian H&G output will drop to 400,000t-450,000t in 2022, depending on how the logistical issues with shipping to COVID-conscious China progress. That forecast is way below the 540,000t of H&G produced in 2021 and close to 700,000t for 2020.

In addition, the 2022 TAC in the Sea of Okhotsk, the main Russian fishery, is down 10%. The overall Russian TAC is down 3%.

Although Russia's TAC is not down as much as the US, catching will be tough, said Karpukhin. "We expect weaker than previous years fishing conditions as well as smaller fish size in Sea of Okhotsk and very slow catch in the Bering Sea". 

So, catching 90% of the Russian quotas in 2022 "would be a victory", he said. 

"The supply shortage from lower catch in the US and Russia comes together with the strong demand for pollock fillets in the key markets, including both European and American retail, and even a higher growth in US foodservice sector," said Karpukhin.

"Combined with the well-known tough situation in China, we expect a sharp deficit on the pollock fillet market and the prices for MSC PBO blocks to be around $4,500/t, on a CFR [cost and freight] Europe basis," he said. 

The level of $4,500/t is a rough average forecast for 2022, said Karpukhin.

Will Aldi keep fish finger packs under €1.99 even as pollock prices rocket?

Although the prices for B season contracts were done in the $3,800-$3,900/t range, the spot market has moved up to $4,200-$4,300/t, as Undercurrent previously reported. However, the big contracts for A season of 2022 are still being negotiated between buyers and sellers due to the significant cut in the Alaskan TAC breaking late last year.

The impact of the 16% cut on PBO production in Alaska "shouldn't be underestimated", he said. Given the TAC reduction and the "expected fishing conditions", it's likely [Alaskan] production of regular PBO blocks will be down at a higher rate than deepskin fillets and surimi, said Karpukhin.

As previously reported by Undercurrent, US producers are likely to focus on deepskin fillets over PBO, to keep big quick-service restaurant customers such as McDonald's supplied.

Then, the growth in Russian PBO output will be backloaded, said Karpukhin.

"The growth in fillet blocks production coming from Russia, in reality, will be achieved only in B season with all the new and modernized vessels of RFC, Okeanrybflot, and Gidrostroy coming online," said Karpukhin. "In terms of physical delivery of the product to the markets, this means the very end of 2022 and Q1 of 2023."

Russia set to wipe out pollock fillet output gap with US in hot 2022 market

He said that RFC's first 108-meter new vessel, Vladimir Limanov, is already operational, but two more trawlers are expected to come online later in 2022. Vladimir Limanov was built at Tersan Shipyard in Turkey, but the next two vessels are underway in Russia, at the Admiralty Shipyard in Saint Petersburg. 

He said the company expects the first Russian-built, 108-meter trawler from the shipyard in the spring of 2022 and the second in the summer. RFC has plans to build eight more vessels in Russia, so 11 new-builds in total. 

Last year, RFC also refitted an H&G trawler, the 104.5m Pavel Batov, for PBO production. The company has "no plans, at the moment" to refit any more of its other H&G vessels for fillets, he said. RFC is looking to scrap at least four of its old H&G-focused vessels in 2022. 

Gidrostroy is also refitting two H&G vessels for fillets. Okeanrybflot has taken delivery of one new vessel from Tersan and has another coming later this year, also from the Turkish yard. 

RFC is also upping volumes from its plant named Russian Pollock in the Far East, shipping its first volumes to the EU, South Korea and the US, said Karpukhin. The plant has been "steadily ramping up" over 2021, its first year of operating, and has 500 employees working three shifts.

Russia to sail past US in MSC pollock supply amid ongoing industry turmoil

"Next year we are planning to expand the product range and launch several pilot projects with Russian retailers," he said. 

Short surimi market 

The focus in the B season of 2021 was getting Vladimir Limanov producing more surimi, with stocks also short in the market, according to Karpukhin. "In season B [of 2021], we were focusing on setting up the surimi production which was the only new part for RFC."

Even with a limited catch volume, the vessel hit daily surimi production of 45-50t and did 2,000t for the whole of B season, he said. 

"As for surimi, we see very low stocks on the key markets with stable demand and an expected drop in production from the US. We expect pollock surimi production in Alaska in 2022 to be 25,000t-35,000t lower compared to 2021, depending on the decision on the product mix by US producers," he said. In 2021, the US produced 193,690t of pollock surimi, up 9% y-o-y.

"The market will still be short and will need to rebuild stocks, so we expect an additional 5-8% price increase to 2021 levels."

H&G outlook uncertain 

Whereas Karpukhin is bullish on fillets and surimi, the outlook for H&G is murky, hence RFC's push to cut production in the second half of 2022.

Arrests made as China points finger at seafood firms over Dalian COVID outbreak 

"As for H&G, there is too much uncertainty. Any estimate or forecast would be a guess in the current circumstances," he told Undercurrent. H&G prices were around $1,450/t at the back end of last year, but both Russian suppliers and Chinese processors have been incurring very high costs relating to COVID restrictions. H&G sales in 2022 are yet to restart, sources said. 

COVID outbreaks in Chinese processing hubs Dalian and Qingdao mean Russian tramper transport vessels have been barred from unloading H&G since 2020. This has complicated the supply chain, with Russian companies having to ship H&G to China in containers from Far East ports like Vladivostok or Busan in South Korea.

In November, a COVID outbreak in Dalian saw the whole port – and all its seafood processing companies – closed. 

Although the city of Dalian has since re-opened, the main export-focused seafood processors remain shut until Jan. 15, which means they won't be able to open properly until after Chinese New Year on Feb. 1. 

Russia guides for further TAC drop in Okhotsk pollock fishery

Then, a new proposed labeling regulation from China threatens to "stop all" H&G sales from Russia unless it's changed, Alexey Buglak, president of the latter's Pollock Catchers Association (PCA), told Undercurrent in early December.

Firstly, the regulation requires all frozen food products imported by China, including frozen fish, to have labels providing information about transport vessels and cold stores where products were handled before arrival, said Buglak, at the time. "This information is unavailable when the products are produced and labeled at sea."

Secondly, the regulation requires that all bags have two labels. "One outside of the bag, the second on the inner packing. In other words, an additional internal label will be required. For fish products produced at sea, it is completely impossible."

The PCA has been pushing the Russian government to intervene. 

With Russia on its Christmas and New Year holiday until Jan. 10 and China also getting ready for its break, it seems the situation is unresolved. 

"I have not heard anything regarding labeling, but I can guess that [Russian] products of 2022 do not come to China yet," Buglak told Undercurrent on Jan. 6.

New Chinese labeling rules could ‘stop’ all H&G pollock supply next year

"We hope that clear and feasible labeling requirements will be defined by the Chinese side. We are ready to fully comply after receiving clear instructions. Let us get clear instructions first," Karpukhin told Undercurrent. 

As a result of the logistical chaos due to the COVID pandemic, RFC is "putting extra effort" into client service and has created an in-house logistics department. 

"Timely delivery of the products to our customers despite the tough global situation with container logistics is our priority for next year," Karpukhin said.

Russia, US should co-market pollock 

With Russia set to overtake the US in terms of MSC-approved pollock supply, the two countries should co-market the species, said Karpukhin. 

It's "good news for the market" that Russia has increased volumes of MSC fish, he said. "The supply of the most important wild whitefish species has become more sustainable and also more quality-focused. Joint market development efforts by Russian and American producers will secure a great future for it."

title: High-speed water chase ends with permanent fishing ban for British Columbia crabber
content:
A Canadian crab harvester has become the first in a decade to be banned from fishing for life after a high-speed pursuit in waters off the province of British Columbia (BC).

Vancouver provincial court justice Peter H. Edelmann, on Nov. 12, ordered Scott Stanley Matthew Steer, a repeat offender under Canada's Fisheries Act -- to never climb aboard a fishing vessel again, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) reported in a statement released this week.

Steer also has been sentenced to serve three years of probation, including 12 months under curfew, and provide 75 hours of community work.

The ban additionally prohibits Steer from purchasing or selling fish and fishing boats, including brokering fish sales, for five years. He must forfeit an aluminum vessel that was used in the illegal activity and was reported to be worth about $50,000.

Steer is currently awaiting two more trials in Nanaimo, BC, for alleged violations of the Fisheries Act.

As Undercurrent News has reported, the pursuit for Steer and two crew members occurred in Vancouver Harbor, in March 2020, when they were found illegally fishing for crab. Though the DFO statement doesn't say what kind of crab he was harvesting, it was likely Dungeness, the most prolific of the species off the coast of BC. 

Sammy Williams, one of the two crew members arrested with Steer, was also convicted of Fisheries Act violations on Nov. 30. He and the other crew member, Christopher Schill, who pleaded guilty in a separate trial, will be sentenced in early 2022.

Arrests made as China points finger at seafood firms over Dalian COVID outbreak

Several arrests have been made at a seafood cold storage firm at the center of a COVID-19 outbreak in Dalian, China, while executives at a major processor have also been reprimanded. Click here for the full story. 

PE-backed Daley returns to Canadian shrimp with Marinard buyout

The UK government is expected to update the coldwater shrimp sector on the situation with importing from Greenland in January 2022, a well-placed seafood industry executive told Undercurrent News. Phillips Seafood Restaurants, the foodservice part of Steve Phillips' large US seafood business, has closed its oldest and most foundational location, in Ocean City, Maryland, and is offering up the property for sale, the company announced in a Facebook posting on Monday. title: China halts customs clearances at border port with Vietnam after COVID case
content:
China has postponed customs clearances at a key inland seafood trading port with Vietnam, after a positive case of COVID-19 in the area.

Authorities in Dongxing City said on Dec. 20 the positive case of COVID-19 was detected during routine testing. Epidemiological investigations and prevention protocols, including city-wide testing, have started.

Arrests made as China points finger at seafood firms over Dalian COVID outbreak 

All citizens must suspend all customs clearance for border trade and movement of people from Dec. 21 until further notice. Emergency cargo is being given priority because of the large number of lorries and heavy goods vehicles queued at the port, it said.

Dongxing City’s public transportation services, including coaches, buses and taxis, as well as freight companies, are also temporarily suspended. All schools and libraries are also closed until further notice.

Dongxing is located in southwest China bordering Mong Cai, in Vietnam’s northeast. The border port is a key hub for imports of live, fresh and frozen seafood, as well as meat and fruit.

China’s return to purchasing sees Vietnamese pangasius exports shoot up in November

Dongxing residents are eligible for duty-free concessions on imported goods valued below CNY 8,000 ($1,256) per person per day.

In the first half of this year, more than 320,000 trucks carrying 1 million metric tons of cargo entered or exited the border trade zone, up 362% year-on-year, according to local reports. The border town has been synonymous with the grey trade of undocumented goods between China and Vietnam, which is not recorded in official data.

The situation in Dongxing comes as seafood processing plants in Dalian remain closed after a COVID outbreak in November.

title: Arrests made as China points finger at seafood firms over Dalian COVID outbreak
content:
Several arrests have been made at a seafood cold storage firm at the center of a COVID-19 outbreak in Dalian, China, while executives at a major processor have also been reprimanded. 

Local authorities said the city's recent COVID-19 flare-up was caused by "law-violating activities" of seafood cold storage and processing companies in the Zhuanghe area of the city. As a result of the outbreak, Zhuanghe's seafood companies are not expected to reopen until mid-January or after the Chinese New Year holidays.

Qingdao whitefish processors ‘can’t bridge capacity gap’ of Dalian shutdown

According to a statement published by the Dalian government on Monday (Dec. 20), five staff with seafood cold storage and processing company Dalian Keqiang Foods Co. -- where the outbreak is said to have originated -- have been detained.

Undercurrent News was unable to get a comment from Keqiang prior to publishing.

Executives and management staff at Keqiang -- described as a "first designated cold storage enterprise" in the city for the import of food products --  had "lacked management awareness, seriously violated the regulations on epidemic prevention and control of cold storages, which thus led to the outbreak of COVID-19", the statement said. 

The five employees from Keqiang, including its legal representative, were detained by the local authorities for suspected breaches of the infectious disease prevention and control law, while two were officially arrested. Shao Qingqiang is listed online as the company's legal representative. 

Meanwhile, two executives at Dalian Haiqing Aquatic Products Co. face "criminal compulsory measures" for negligence that resulted in an outbreak of COVID-19 at the company. The two Haiqing executives are its "legal representative" and its factory manager. The statement does not further clarify what "criminal compulsory measures" means, but no staff from Haiqing have been arrested or detained. 

According to the notice, Haiqing -- one of the largest processors in China of pollock and other whitefish -- failed to implement relevant epidemic prevention regulations in daily management and did not implement epidemic prevention instructions, which led to a cluster of cases at the company.

Haiqing's legal representative was not named in the government notice; according to company records, this position is held by Qu Zhenhai. 

Executives with Haiqing declined to comment to Undercurrent. 

Four staff at a medical institute also face "criminal compulsory measures" for forging nucleic acid test records, while another four employees from two disinfection and quarantine treatment companies face probes. Xiaosha Company Dalian Lianqin Fumigation and Disinfection Co and Dalian Dayi Quarantine Treatment Technology Co "falsified records, cut corners, and performed responsibilities perfunctorily, resulting in suspected obstruction of prevention and control of infectious diseases", the government notice claims.

Furthermore, the statement adds that a total of 42 government officials will also face disciplinary measures.

Shutdown of seafood processing hub

On Nov. 8, seafood processors and cold storage companies in Dalian, Liaoning province, were ordered to close by authorities following the first recorded case on Nov. 4.

Dalian's "11.03" epidemic investigation taskforce said that epidemiological investigation, serum antibody detection and cold-chain food sampling showed the virus was imported through contaminated cold-chain food products. 

Russia set to wipe out pollock fillet output gap with US in hot 2022 market

It first infected a worker at a cold storage warehouse operated by Keqiang and then spread to other workers, the task force stated. The virus was then further transmitted to local communities.

The shutdown has had a major impact on China's seafood import and re-processing industry. According to Chinese customs data, in the first 10 months of 2021, some 45% of total Chinese exports of Alaskan pollock fillets and blocks were from Liaoning province, worth around $200 million. 

On Tuesday (Dec. 21), a source at a processor in Dalian told Undercurrent that her firm had still not been permitted to reopen but expected to do so "very soon". Her company is based outside of Zhuanghe, the epicenter of the outbreak.
