title: Fake caterer pleads guilty to stealing over $880k worth of goods from major US distributors
content:
Paul Diogenes, a 49-year-old man from the US state of Rhode Island, has pleaded guilty in a federal court to using a fake catering company he created to steal nearly a million dollars worth of lobster, sea bass, shrimp, scallops, filet mignon, ribeye steak and wild boar from some of the country's biggest food distributors, Go Local Prov News reports. 

Diogenes is scheduled to be sentenced on several counts, including also wire fraud and assault of a police officer, by US District Court chief judge John J. McConnell, Jr., on March 29, 2022.

Undercurrent News reported in August how Diogenes' charging documents, copies of which were obtained by Undercurrent, read like the plot of an overly sensational television crime drama.

The man operated his fake LePage Catering company out of a legitimate seafood business, using bank information illegally taken from multiple other seafood businesses and restaurants to -- over a roughly nine-month period, between November 2020 and July 2021 -- acquire more than $831,000 worth of food from the likes of US Foods, Performance Food Group and Reinhart Food Service (RFS). 

Paul Diogenes, a Rhode Island man, has pled guilty to using a fake catering company and money stolen from several area restaurants to acquire nearly a million dollars worh of seafood from several major food distributors. This image was used by a local television station in 2018.

Doigenes used the identity of Paul Dejullio, who he briefly worked alongside as a fellow cook at a restaurant in Fall River, Massachusetts, in 2018, paying for goods with money taken from multiple Rhode Island restaurants, including Capriccio's and the Mare, in Providence, the Riviera in East Providence, and Wilfred’s in Woonsocket.

As part of his elaborate scheme, according to the documents, Diogenes kept the food at Digger's Catch, an East Providence, Rhode Island-based business also known as East Side Shellfish, where he allegedly made himself a partner. He then resold the food, in some instances, to the same businesses whose banking information he used to pay the distributors, according to the documents.

RFS was the biggest victim of the alleged scam, reporting that it delivered more than $531,000 worth of food products to LePage Catering without being paid, while US Foods delivered more than $185,000 worth of products and PFG delivered more than $115,000 worth of products, according to the charging documents.

Police first attempted to arrest Diogenes at about 8 a.m. on Aug. 3, following his gray Mercedes Benz into a parking lot behind Digger's Catch. Diogenes put his car in reverse, rammed into an FBI task force vehicle behind him, and then drove toward an agent who had to jump out of the way to avoid being hit, according to the charging documents.

Diogenes was then allegedly able to speed off through a gap he’d created by hitting the law enforcement vehicles, successfully ditching the police. He stayed on the lam for roughly nine days, moving from hotel to hotel and using different aliases, before he was arrested without incident at a hotel in Middleborough, Massachusetts, according to police.

title: Indian police arrest man accused of $26m aquaculture fraud
content:
An Indian man accused of duping fish farmers out of more than INR 2 billion ($26 million) has been arrested by police in the northwest state of Haryana, reports The Free Press Journal.

Brijendra Kumar Kashyap, managing director of the Fish Fortune Produce Company, allegedly signed contracts with multiple farmers in which they would give him INR 500,000 ($6,500). He would then promise to double this figure for them.

Kashyap, who owns eight firms altogether under the Kashyap Group of Companies, allegedly conned nearly 3,000 farmers in this manner operating in the states of Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, and Punjab, among others.

Several cases have reportedly been registered against Kashyap across multiple states. He is currently in police custody with further interrogation ongoing.

title: Editor’s recap: Ecuador shrimp harvests surge; Dalian lockdown cuts processing capacity
content:
Neil Ramsden, EMEA editor with Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

While the global shrimp sector is on course to achieve double-digit growth for 2021 and exceed that in 2022, late production data out of Ecuador has exceeded all expectations and run roughshod over the projections of the Global Seafood Alliance's annual survey. Presenting at an online event replacing the usual annual Global Outlook for Aquaculture Leadership, senior Rabobank analyst Gorjan Nikolik told listeners that global shrimp production had -- as predicted last year -- enjoyed a significant year of volume recovery, with an 8.9% production increase originally forecast for 2021.

The lockdown of seafood processing companies in the Chinese port hub of Dalian comes amid an already short market, with one executive fearing some plants may not even re-open before Chinese New Year on Feb. 1. Even though the COVID-19 outbreak in Dalian is seemingly under control and companies outside the Zhuanghe area are reportedly beginning to resume operations, there's no clarity on when export-driven processors will get going again.

One Chinese firm, Dalian Haiqing Food Co., has set up a UK entity and hired a well-respected seafood executive in the country as the COVID-19 pandemic causes chaos in the Asia-to-Europe supply chain for double frozen whitefish and wild salmon.

In the US, the town of Gouldsboro, Maine, voted in a special election on Nov. 15 to approve a six-month moratorium against all large-scale finfish farms in the area, at least temporarily delaying a planned 30,000 metric ton closed-containment salmon net-pen, according to a statement emailed by an opposition group. 

The US commercial fishing industry took its best swings yet at the Magnuson Stevens Act reauthorization bill being championed by Democrats during a hearing held Nov. 16 by the House of Representatives' Natural Resources Committee's oceans panel. The "Sustaining America’s Fisheries for the Future Act of 2021", HR 4690, introduced in late July by representative Jared Huffman, chairman of the Subcommittee on Water, Oceans and Wildlife, was the main course when the panel met. The legislation aims to modernize MSA in a way that better empowers the country's eight regional fishery councils to protect commercial fish species from the challenges of climate change.

Sunnyvale Seafood Company CEO Jeff Sedacca is to exit his role at the US shrimp importer at the end of the year to focus on advising groups that support the development of aquaculture. Sedacca has been the CEO of the Union City, California-based import arm of China's Zhanjiang Guolian Aquatic Products since 2019, and was its president for four years before that. Prior to that, he also purchased seafood from Sunnyvale for several years.

Former Bumble Bee Foods CEO Christopher Lischewski will serve his full 40-month term in a US federal prison, judge Edward Chen has ruled. Lischewski, a 61-year-old, had asked to have his sentence in the minimum security satellite camp of US Penitentiary Tuscon, in Tuscon, Arizona, converted to house arrest due to the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic. 

First-round bids are due soon for Canadian private equity's Champlain Financial Corp.'s $600 million-plus-turnover lobster and snow crab processing "rollup" C&E Seafood Corporation. According to several sources, the first round, non-binding offers are due next week to Houlihan Lokey and the National Bank of Canada, who are running the sale process on behalf of Montreal, Quebec-based Champlain.

Finally,Iceland Seafood International expects further consolidation in coming years after growing its presence in the UK seafood processing sector and the closure of acquisitions in Ireland and Spain, the firm's CEO Bjarni Armannsson told Undercurrent.

title: Judge nixes Lischewski’s request for early release from prison
content:
Former Bumble Bee Foods CEO Christopher Lischewski will serve his full 40-month term in a US federal prison, judge Edward Chen has ruled.

Lischewski, a 61-year-old with high cholesterol, had asked to have his sentence in the minimum security satellite camp of US Penitentiary Tuscon, in Tuscon, Arizona, converted to house arrest due to the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic. He is scheduled to be released from Bureau of Prisons (BOP) custody on June 18, 2023, according to the bureau. 

Chen, who presided over Lischewski's 2019 criminal trial on price-fixing charges, said that the court took into account Lischewski's medical history, vaccinated status, conditions at the prison, and the amount of time left on his sentence, among other factors.

"It finds that there are not extraordinary and compelling reasons to grant the relief requested," Chen wrote of the court's decision.

Lischewski had asked the court to weigh in on his request for compassionate release after BOP officials denied his request made to them in October.

Prosecutors lobbied the court to keep the former Bumble Bee CEO in prison.

"By any reasonable metric, defendant’s risk of contracting COVID-19 appears even lower now than it was when he entered BOP custody," they argued.

Appeal denied

Earlier this year, the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit stood by the December 2019 verdict and Chen's handling of the trial.

Among the several points that attorney John Cline raised in his client's appeal was an assertion that Chen made a "serious error" in giving instructions to the jury that ultimately found Lischewski guilty. Specifically, Cline wrote, that Chen's statement to jurors that finding the charge of conspiracy to fix prices required the government to prove that Lischewski had entered into either an "agreement or mutual understanding" with others to fix prices.

But the appeals court disagreed.

"The district court did not abuse its discretion in instructing the jury on the per se rule or prohibiting Lischewski from offering evidence about the supposed reasonableness of his price-fixing conspiracy," the court wrote.

Lischewski was convicted on a count of price-fixing on Dec. 3, 2019, a scandal for the sector that also netted guilty pleas from Bumble Bee and rival StarKist & Co, which is owned by South Korea's Dongwon Enterprise. Thai Union Group-owned Chicken of the Sea International also participated in the price-fixing, which prosecutors said occurred from 2010 to 2013, but cooperated in exchange for amnesty.

During the trial, prosecutors relied heavily on the testimony of two former Bumble Bee vice-presidents, Walter Cameron and Kenneth Worsham and a former StarKist executive, Stephen Hodge, as well as former Chicken of the Sea International CEO, Shue Wing Chan, who was protected from prosecution due to his company's amnesty agreement. The other executives were spared prison time in exchange for their cooperation with the Department of Justice.

title: Hong Kong customs chief vows to curb Aussie rock lobster trade
content:
Australia’s AUD 80-million-a-month ($60m) lobster trade with Hong Kong is on the hook after authorities declared it a national security risk, reports Sydney Morning Herald.

Australia’s monthly exports to Hong Kong have boomed by 2,000% since Beijing banned the lobsters from the mainland in October last year. The lobster is mostly smuggled into the mainland market, where it can fetch higher prices.

Louise Ho, Hong Kong’s new Commissioner of Customs and Excise, said at a press conference on Thursday night (Oct. 22) that she would crackdown on the trade. 

"On the face of it, it’s just a normal smuggling case, smuggling lobsters," she said. "But actually these smuggling activities would undermine the country’s trade restrictions on Australia. Therefore, tackling lobster smuggling activities is an important task in safeguarding national security."

Last week Hong Kong customs arrested a lobster syndicate of seven after they were found to have imported 228 metric tons of Australian lobsters worth AUD 30m, and failed to lodge the correct customs declaration forms.

title: Mozambique’s tuna bond trial underway as questions hang over ex-minister
content:
The trial for officials at the heart of Mozambique's well-publicized tuna bond scandal is underway, reports BBC News.

The scandal concerns more than $2.7 billion of loans, ostensibly borrowed by the state government to develop the African country's tuna industry. However, much of this sum was allegedly diverted to officials.

To date, 19 citizens in Mozambique have gone on trial on charges of bribery, embezzlement and money laundering. However, these only cover alleged bribes of $50m, and there are fears that the most powerful figures in the scandal are not being held responsible, according to the BBC.

Meanwhile, former Mozambique finance minister Manuel Chang, who originally signed off on the loans, has been in custody in South Africa since 2018. He was arrested at the request of the US -- where many investors were affected by the scandal -- but has had competing requests for extradition filed from his home country.

A Mozambique NGO has filed to prevent his extradition out of fears that Chang will not be prosecuted correctly by his national court. The Johannesburg High Court is expected to announce its decision on the application soon.

title: Canadian lobster firm confirms sale talks, says DFO probe wasn’t directed at it
content:
A Canadian lobster firm confirmed to Undercurrent News it's in talks to sell and said that an "ongoing investigation" from the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) that resulted in the seizure of a significant quantity of live lobster wasn't directed at it. 

However, Chris O'Neill, vice president of New Brunswick-based Raymond O'Neill & Son Fisheries, said he's unable to reveal the would-be buyer's name.

As Undercurrent reported on Thursday, ACON Investments, a US-based private equity (PE) with $6 billion of assets under management, is believed to be close to a deal for Raymond O'Neill and Suncoast Seafood, another New Brunswick-based processor. 

$6bn PE investor closes in on two Canadian lobster buyouts

"Yes, it is true we are in discussion with a potential suitor but have signed an NDA [non-disclosure agreement] which prevents us from disclosing any details," he told Undercurrent in an email. 

Undercurrent sources said the deals were set to close this week but could now be pushed into next. 

As for the "ongoing investigation" with the seized lobsters, "the incident with DFO on Tuesday was not directed towards Raymond O'Neill", O'Neill told Undercurrent. O'Neill said the company is not being accused of any wrongdoing and did not have any lobster seized. 

When asked for more comments on the investigation, he said the company does not "speculate on DFO actions". 

On Thursday, Undercurrent revealed that Raymond O'Neill is being linked to a Canadian government investigation after the seizure of some lobsters, which were then returned to the water. Raymond O'Neill's plant in Escuminac was reportedly the end destination for the crustaceans seized on Tuesday, sources in the sector told Undercurrent. 

US investment bank advises two Canadian shellfish firms eyeing sales

On Tuesday, Sept. 28, "following an inspection, fishery officers arrested, and later released two individuals", said the DFO, in a brief statement sent to Undercurrent. The officials also "seized a significant quantity of lobster, a vehicle and a trailer in New Brunswick, which originated from St. Mary's Bay", which is about 308 kilometers (191 miles) west in Nova Scotia. The lobsters were released live back into the ocean," the spokesperson said. "As this matter is part of an ongoing investigation, no further details will be provided at this time." 

 Federal officers have been enforcing regulations prohibiting lobster harvesting out of season since Bernadette Jordan, Canada's fisheries minister who recently lost her re-election bid, declared that intention in March. The enforcement came in response to reports that First Nation groups would begin fishing months early in lobster fishing area 34, where the season typically starts in early November. 

PEs investing in Canadian shellfish 

Acon and Suncoast have not responded to requests for comment from Undercurrent on the deals. The owners of Suncoast and Raymond O'Neill, are using Growthink Capital, a US-based corporate finance boutique, as an advisor on the possible deals. Avi Suriel, the Growthink executive advising on the deals, also did not respond to Undercurrent. 

If Acon closes the deals, it will be the third large PE to get involved in the Canadian shellfish sector after Champlain Financial Corp.'s deal spree and Solamere Capital's investments in the Daley family's operations last year. 

Lobster crackdown comes during Canadian supplier’s sale process

Acon's interest in the smaller Suncoast and Raymond O'Neill suggests it could take part in the ongoing sale process for Champlain's much bigger Canadian lobster and snow crab rollup, C&E Seafood Company, sources told Undercurrent. 

Suncoast and Raymond O'Neill will give Acon a solid foothold in the sector if the deals close.

Raymond O'Neill, started in 1983, has a processing site covering approximately 45,000 square feet and employs 220 staff. Raymond O'Neill is producing freshly frozen raw and cooked lobster products. The site also has a pond for live storage of lobster, located adjacent to the processing plant, the company's website states.

Suncoast, based in Grand-Digue, along the Northumberland Strait, is slightly smaller, employing around 150 in peak season, according to details published on the DFO website in 2020. The company is producing whole-cooked whole lobster, cooked lobster meat, claws and arms, and raw tails.

title: $6bn PE investor closes in on two Canadian lobster buyouts
content:
A US-based private equity (PE) firm with a strong presence in Latin America and Spain is closing in on two deals in the Canadian shellfish sector, sources told Undercurrent News.

ACON Investments, which is based in Washington, DC, and manages around $6 billion in assets, is the PE Undercurrent reported on Wednesday as negotiating deals for Suncoast Seafood and Raymond O'Neill Fisheries, sources said. Both are lobster processors based in the province of New Brunswick.

Lobster crackdown comes during Canadian supplier’s sale process

One source, who asked not to be named, told Undercurrent the closure of the deals was planned for this week but is now set for early next week. 

Earlier on Thursday, Undercurrent revealed that Raymond O'Neill's plant in Escuminac was reportedly the end destination for lobster seized by officials with Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO). 

Chris O'Neill, executive vice president of Raymond O'Neill, did not respond to requests for comment from Undercurrent prior to publishing on the sale talks or the seizure. He later responded, confirming the company is in talks to sell, but declining to reveal the would-be buyer, due to a non-disclosure agreement.

 He also stated the DFO investigation doesn't involve the company, which has been accused of no wrongdoing. The lobster was not seized from Raymond O'Neill, he said. However, O'Neill did not respond when asked if the lobster was seized by the DFO on the way to its plant. 

On Tuesday, Sept. 28, "following an inspection, fishery officers arrested, and later released two individuals", said the DFO, in a brief statement sent to Undercurrent. The officials also "seized a significant quantity of lobster, a vehicle and a trailer in New Brunswick, which originated from St. Mary’s Bay", which is about 308 kilometers (191 miles) west in Nova Scotia. The lobsters were released live back into the ocean," the spokesperson said. "As this matter is part of an ongoing investigation, no further details will be provided at this time."

The enforcement came in response to reports that First Nation groups would begin fishing months early in lobster fishing area 34 where the season typically begins in early November. 

Acon and Suncoast did not respond to requests for comment from Undercurrent in time for publishing. The owners of Suncoast and Raymond O'Neill, are using Growthink Capital, a US-based corporate finance boutique, as an advisor on the possible deals. Avi Suriel, the Growthink executive advising on the deals, also did not respond to Undercurrent. 

If Acon closes the deals, it will be the third large PE to get involved in the Canadian shellfish sector after Champlain Financial Corp.'s deal spree and Solamere Capital's investments in the Daley family's operations last year. 

PE-backed by Mitt Romney’s son emerges as latest Canadian shellfish consolidator

Acon's interest in the smaller Suncoast and Raymond O'Neill suggest it could take part in the ongoing sale process for Champlain's much bigger Canadian lobster and snow crab rollup, C&E Seafood Company, sources told Undercurrent. 

Suncoast and Raymond O'Neill will give Acon a solid foothold in the sector if the deals close.

Raymond O'Neill, started in 1983, has a processing site covering approximately 45,000 square feet and employs 220 staff. Raymond O'Neill is producing freshly frozen raw and cooked lobster products. The site also has a pond for live storage of lobster, located adjacent to the processing plant, the company's website states.

Suncoast, based in Grand-Digue, along the Northumberland Strait, is slightly smaller, employing around 150 in peak season, according to details published on the DFO website in 2020. The company is producing whole-cooked whole lobster, cooked lobster meat, claws and arms, and raw tails. 

Who is Acon? 

Acon, sources said, has been eyeing deals in seafood for some time. 

The Washington D.C.-based PE, which has not invested in seafood before, also has offices in Bogota, Columbia, Mexico City, Mexico and Sao Paolo, Brazil, and a joint venture in Madrid, Spain.

Acon has inked several deals in 2021. In July, Acon's Spanish arm acquired a controlling stake in Formacion Alcala. The company is an e-learning platform focused on education and training for healthcare professionals in Spain and Latin America.

Canadian PE buys another shellfish firm, eyes sale of ‘seafood platform’ 

In June, Acon announced a deal for Vitalis Group, a pharmaceutical manufacturer with production facilities in Colombia and Mexico. The PE completed a majority equity recapitalization of Diverzify+.

Based in Itasca, Illinois, Diverzify is a commercial flooring installation and related facility services provider selling nationally in the US. Back in May, Acon used a special purpose acquisition company to take ESS Tech, a California, US-based manufacturer of long-duration iron flow batteries for commercial and utility-scale energy storage applications, public.

Acon was founded in 1996 by Bernard Aronson, Kenneth Brotman and Jonathan Ginns.
Aronson has strong political ties. From 1989 to 1993, he was US assistant secretary of state for inter-American affairs under presidents George Bush Sr. and Bill Clinton.

In February 2015, he was asked by president Barack Obama to serve as the US special envoy for the Colombian peace process. Aronson also served as an advisor on Latin America for Goldman Sachs before founding Acon.

Before founding Acon, Brotman was a partner of Veritas Capital, a New York-based PE firm. Ginns was a senior investment officer at the Global Environment Fund before founding Acon.

content:

The lobsters were released live back into the ocean," the spokesperson said. "As this matter is part of an ongoing investigation, no further details will be provided at this time."

The news comes as Undercurrent revealed the family-owned Raymond O'Neill is in talks to sell with an unnamed private equity firm, which is also negotiating a deal for Suncoast Seafood, another processor.

title: Canada’s election means new fisheries minister to inherit tricky 8-ball seafood issues
content:
Prime minister Justin Trudeau's Liberal Party may have survived Canada's 2021 national election and retained its minority power, but that doesn't mean the country's commercial fishing industry isn't facing a lot of potential changes.

Though the Liberals kept at least 158 of the 338 seats in Canada's Parliament on Monday, one crucial member of Trudeau's Cabinet to have lost her spot is Bernadette Jordan, the minister of fisheries and oceans. The six-year member of Parliament, who represented the St. Margarets riding in the province of Nova Scotia, was defeated by Conservative candidate Rick Perkins.

Whoever Trudeau names as Jordan's successor will inherit several eight-balls, tricky seafood-related issues that could prove catastrophic politically if clumsily knocked into a corner pocket. But then the job of fisheries minister has always come with such challenges, advised Paul Lansbergen, president of the Fisheries Council of Canada (FCC), the trade group that represents the nation's commercial harvesters.

"I'm not sure if there's ever been a really easy time to have that portfolio," he told Undercurrent News in an interview Tuesday. "We always have our challenges and, certainly in Atlantic Canada, there's a lot of history and passion for the sector that always makes it difficult for the minister to manage."

As the smoke continues to clear, it appears that the Conservatives have retained 119 seats, the separatist Bloc Quebecois Party has 34, the New Democratic Party (NDP) has 25 and the Green Party has two, based on a breakdown by The Guardian. The outcome is similar to Parliament's earlier breakdown and leaves Trudeau far short of the 170 seats he needed to gain majority control.

Canadian Parliament buildings in Ottawa, Ontario. Photograph by DD Images on Shutterstock.

That means his government will again be forced to likely work with left-leaning NDPs to pass new legislation.  

Jordan was one of just two Trudeau cabinet members to have lost in their reelection bids along with Maryam Monsef, the Ontario-based minister responsible for the status of women and rural economic development.

Canada's commercial seafood industry is a dominant player in the North American lobster, snow crab and farmed salmon categories, while also producing halibut, Atlantic cod, mussels and numerous other species. It represents 90,000 jobs and CAD 9 billion ($7.6bn) in combined GDP, according to FCC. 

The sector might've expected a new fisheries minister regardless of Jordan's loss, as it's customary for prime ministers to overhaul their cabinets after an election. Jordan was named by Trudeau to replace Jonathan Wilkinson, a member of Parliament (MP) from the province of British Columbia who had served 16 months in the role, in Nov. 2019, just one month after the earlier 2019 election.

'[W]e have to be ambitious'

Lansbergen is keen to work with the new fisheries minister in helping to move forward with an "all-encompassing" new "blue economy" plan that includes maintaining the sustainability of fish resources, becoming more successful in selling to domestic and global markets, attracting more workers, improve public trust and creating better government policy and regulations.

Establishing a blue economy plan was a mandate given to Jordan in 2019, within two months of her taking her new role, and was followed by public consultations started by the Canadian Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) in early 2020, a process that wrapped up in May.

Paul Lansbergen, president of the Fisheries Coalition of Canada.

Lansbergen believes it will be no sooner than the spring of 2022 that the Canadian seafood industry sees action on the matter, maybe in elements contained in a new budget, however. Following the appointment of new cabinet positions, Parliament will resume sitting and establish new committees in the next few months, he said.

"One of the things that have held us back in Canada is that we haven't had a strong political will or support for the economic development of the sector and this blue economy strategy is, in our mind, intended to address that," he said.

"We've got a 20-year vision to become a top-three global best quality and sustainable efficient food producer, not the largest, but among the best. And if we can realize that potential, we can double the value of Canadian seafood, double the economic benefits and double the domestic consumption of seafood. But we have to be ambitious and we need the government to work with us to achieve that."

In its list of pledges leading up to the 2021 election, the Liberal Party dedicated one sentence to the issue, saying it will: "Continue working with business, academic institutions, provincial and territorial governments, and leading not-for-profits, including in freshwater economies like the Great Lakes, to ensure Canada is positioned to succeed in the fast-growing global sector of the blue economy."

In addition to the fisheries minister role, Langsbergen said FCC will be concerned about who Trudeau names to fill several other cabinet posts, including those charged with overseeing international trade, agriculture, the environment and health, as it relates to food inspections.

The Fish Food and Allied Workers (FFAW), the union representing the province of Newfoundland and Labrador's in-shore harvesters, issued a release on Tuesday, declaring that it also was eager to see Trudeau's cabinet announcements and to seek meetings "as soon as possible to reiterate the priorities identified by FFAW-Unifor members".

Keith Sullivan, president of the Fish Food and Allied Workers, in Newfoundland & Labrador, Canada.

"…In the Liberal Party's previous term in government, some progress was made on commitments made to FFAW members, including protecting the independence of inshore, owner-operator fish harvesters through the passage of amendments to the Fisheries Act that enshrined owner-operator and fleet separation policies in law," the group said. "However, there is much work left to be done when it comes to fair quota allocations for Newfoundland and Labrador harvesters, meaningful consultations, and consideration for social, economic, and cultural factors in fisheries management."

Timothy Kennedy, executive director of the Canadian Aquaculture Industry Alliance (CAIA), said in an email that his group also looks forward to working with the new fisheries minister and pointed to the Liberal pledge to advance its blue economy strategy.

"As aquaculture is the future growth of seafood production and jobs for the sector, we will continue to work with the entire seafood sector to support a sustainable growth strategy," he said.

CAIA has proposed the creation of a Canadian Seafood Development Agency to provide a more formal structure to support sustainable economic growth. 

Jordan criticized for handling of lobster fight

But a problem that might tie up the new fisheries minister appointment before he or she can address the issues the creation of a new blue economy strategy or other matters of importance to the seafood industry is one that proved particularly elusive to Jordan as it was in St. Mary's Bay, in her backyard province of Nova Scotia. It involved the Sipekne'katik, a First Nation group seeking to establish a self-regulated lobster fishery in Canada's most prolific lobster fishing area, 34, on the southwest coast of Nova Scotia, during times of the year that are otherwise offseason.

The Sipekne'katik had argued that their actions were in step with a Canadian Supreme Court ruling made some 21 years earlier that allowed fishing in pursuit of a "moderate livelihood" and said it would take less than 5% of the lobster in the area.  

A Canadian lobster. Photograph courtesy of Tangier Lobster, in Nova Scotia.

The fight turned violent in October when commercial harvesters ransacked and burned a lobster pound serving the First Nation group, leading to the arrest of 23 individuals.

Jordan declared that she would enforce LFA 34's commercial fishing dates and, in August, Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) arrested Sipekne'katik chief Mike Sack while seizing many of his band's lobster traps shortly after they were placed in the water.  

People on both sides of the LFA 34 dispute were quoted as saying Jordan's handling of the matter is why she was defeated, the Canadian Press reported.

Sack said Tuesday that he thinks Jordan didn't show enough leadership and he hoped that the federal government wouldn't keep Indigenous territories such as his in poverty.

Lex Brukovskiy, president of Local 9 of the Maritime Fishermen's Union, said he thought Jordan's loss was a clear message that commercial harvesters like himself deserve a seat at the negotiating table on the issue.

Gasoline on the net-pen fire

Also prominent on the plate of the new fisheries minister will be the prospective sunsetting of the massive net-pen salmon industry in the province of British Columbia (BC).

It was during the lead-up to the 2019 election, that the Liberals shocked the aquaculture industry by announcing what seemed like a certain death warrant for net pens in BC.  

"In British Columbia, we will work with the province to develop a responsible plan to transition from open net-pen salmon farming in coastal waters to closed containment systems by 2025," the party had pledged in its 850-page platform, an apparent response to complaints that suggested salmon net-pens were contributing to the demise of wild salmon.

However, almost immediately after, questions began to arise about what the Liberals meant in their pledge and party officials, including Jordan, later clarified several times that the 2025 deadline was for the delivery of the plan, not the actual transition.

A vessel approaches a Cermaq Group salmon farm in British Columbia. Photograph courtesy of Cermaq Canada.

Then, in November 2020, Terry Beech, a Liberal member of the House of Commons representing BC and the parliamentary secretary to the minister of fisheries, reportedly declared that the so-called "transition" the party promised doesn't even necessarily have to mean forcing fish farmers from the oceans and into land-based operations at all.

In Dec. 2020, Jordan threw gasoline on the fire, ordering the removal of all salmon from net pens in BC's Discovery Islands by the end of June 2022, a move that impacted about 30% of Mowi Canada's operation in the province and threatened a financial impact of close to CAD 200m.

The BC Salmon Farmers Association (BCSFA) last month made their case for maintaining net-pens on Canada's western coast, delivering a 30-page report that showcases more than a dozen recent innovations that make the case that they are fully capable of operating in a more environmentally sustainable way, as reported by Undercurrent. The list includes everything from the launch, in 2019, by Mowi Canada West of the CAD 35 million ($27.9m) Aqua Tromoy, a vessel equipped with a state-of-the-art non-chemotherapeutant sea lice treatment system, to Cermaq Group's current trialing of a floating, semi-closed containment system.

The sunsetting of net pens didn't get mentioned in the Liberal's pledges made leading up to the 2021 election. However, the party did commit to advance a CAD 647m Pacific Salmon Strategy, launched in June, and "make new investments to conserve and restore wild Atlantic salmon."

A North Atlantic right whale calf and its mother off the coast of Georgia. Photograph from the US' National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

The losing Conservative Party, by contrast, directly addressed issues related to aquaculture, saying it would maintain the decision to remove salmon farms from the Discovery Islands, assign responsibility for the management and sustainable growth of the sector to a department other than DFO, strengthen monitoring requirements for salmon farms; and develop a tax incentive program for the development and adoption of technologies that reduce contact between wild and farmed salmon.

It pledged to support the "sustainable development and growth of Canada's world-leading aquaculture sector", adding that it would "not take an ideological position" in regard to salmon farms on the West Coast.

"We want the aquaculture industry to succeed, but it is a simple fact that this sector can only grow as long as Canadians can have confidence in our ability to protect wild salmon," the Conservatives had said. "Therefore, any decisions related to salmon aquaculture must be based on robust science, guided by conservation, and be respectful of the communities and families that rely on these jobs."

Also among its 2021 pledges, the Liberal party has promised to "modernize the Oceans Act to explicitly consider climate change impacts on marine ecosystems and species in regional ocean management with measurable progress indicators tied to management objectives." It said it would expand a ghost gear program, cleaning up lost and abandoned fishing gear and oceans plastics.

The Liberals said they would continue protecting key marine species, including the North Atlantic right whale, another hot button issue for lobster and snow crab harvesters.

title: Second man arrested over 2020 Canadian lobster pound fire
content:
Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) have charged a second man with arson in relation to an Oct. 16, 2020 fire that completely destroyed a lobster pound in Middle West Pubnico, Nova Scotia, reported Salt Wire.

Sean Roy Messenger, 29, was arrested by the RCMP and released on Sept. 8 ahead of a scheduled provincial court appearance on Nov. 29 for arraignment, where formal charges will be lodged.

He will join Brendon Douglas James Porter, 24, of East Pubnico, Nova Scotia, who was arrested on July 14 and also charged with arson. Porter is due to appear in court on Nov. 5.

The fire occurred late in the evening and just two days after a group of about 200 non-indigenous fishermen and their supporters converged on the plant. It was storing lobster caught by members of the Sipekne'katik First Nation as part of a fishery they controversially started in St. Mary's Bay and ran ahead of the late November start date established by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans for Lobster Fishing Area 34. 

The police, at the time, said the plant was unoccupied at the time of the fire, so there were no injuries to employees. However, one unidentified man, who wasn't an employee, suffered life-threatening injuries and was taken to a hospital. That man was considered a person of interest in relation to the fire, but police refused to confirm whether or not he was one of those since arrested.

title: Man charged with using fake catering firm to steal seafood from major US distributors
content:
Police have arrested a 49-year-old Rhode Island man and charged him with using a fake catering company he created to steal nearly a million dollars worth of lobster, sea bass, shrimp, scallops, filet mignon, ribeye steak and wild boar from some of the country's biggest food distributors.

The documents used this week to charge Paul Diogenes with the felony crimes of wire fraud, aggravated identity theft and assault of a federal officer, copies of which were obtained by Undercurrent News, read like the plot of an overly sensational television crime drama. 

Diogenes allegedly operated his fake LePage Catering company out of a legitimate seafood business, using bank information illegally taken from multiple other seafood businesses and restaurants to -- over a roughly nine-month period, between November 2020 and July 2021 -- acquire more than $831,000 worth of food from the likes of US Foods, Performance Food Group and Reinhart Food Service. 

Using the identity of Paul Dejullio, who he briefly worked alongside as a fellow cook at a restaurant in Fall River, Massachusetts, in 2018, Diogenes allegedly paid for the goods with money taken from multiple Rhode Island restaurants, including Capriccio's and the Mare, in Providence, the Riviera in East Providence, and Wilfred’s in Woonsocket, according to the charging documents.

Local television stations had broadcast pictures of Diogenes in 2018 as part of an effort to locate him then in relation to the alleged identity theft.

Paul Diogenes, the Rhode Island man that police have charged with using a fake catering company and money stolen from several area restaurants to acquire nearly a million dollars worh of seafood from several major food distributors. Image was used by a local television station in 2018.

As part of his elaborate scheme, according to the charging documents, Diogenes kept the food at Digger's Catch, an East Providence, Rhode Island-based business also known as East Side Shellfish, where he allegedly made himself a partner. He then resold the food, in some instances, to the same businesses whose banking information he used to pay the distributors, according to the documents.

Wilfred's reported to police that nearly $193,000 was allegedly withdrawn without proper authorization from its bank accounts in January to pay US Food Service, LePage Catering and also Sysco, another major US distributor not identified as a victim in the documents. The Mare Restaurant was able to catch $87,700 being withdrawn from its accounts without authorization and had the amount reversed, the documents said.

RFS was the biggest victim of the alleged scam, reporting that it delivered more than $531,000 worth of food products to LePage Catering without being paid, while US Foods delivered more than $185,000 worth of products and PFG delivered more than $115,000 worth of products, according to the charging documents.

Another one of the incidents that ultimately tripped Diogenes up, according to the documents, was when a driver for PFG was told to leave his food delivery on a sidewalk. 

The driver "stated that he thought this was very odd and therefore took photographs of the product left on the street," the documents recounted. "[He] also took pictures of the white pick-up truck that the individuals from Lepage Catering were driving." Later, the license plate number revealed the vehicle was registered to East Side Shellfish.

"PFG advised that the majority of the product that was delivered to Lepage Catering was delivered to an empty parking lot or another address not associated with the business address provided on the application," the documents said.

Credit: Julianne Thomas/Undercurrent News

Also, when police approached the owner of Digger's Catch, who is not identified by name in the charging document, and showed him a picture of Diogenes, the man reportedly responded that it was instead a photograph of Dejullio, who had become his business partner in November after Dejullio was introduced to him by an employee.

Diogenes reportedly told the Digger's Catch manager that he was the owner of a group of restaurants that were forced to close by the COVID-19 pandemic. He allegedly said he had about $200,000 worth of unsold food and other products that he could sell to Digger's Catch.

The two were making about $100,000 per month by distributing food and other products to area restaurants and businesses, the Digger's Catch owner told police, adding that he paid Dejullio his half in cash, according to the documents. 

Police first attempted to arrest Diogenes at about 8 a.m. on Aug. 3, following his gray Mercedes Benz into a parking lot behind Digger's Catch. Diogenes put his car in reverse, rammed into an FBI task force vehicle behind him, and then drove toward an agent who had to jump out of the way to avoid being hit, according to the charging documents.

Diogenes was then allegedly able to speed off through a gap he’d created by hitting the law enforcement vehicles, successfully ditching the police. He stayed on the lam for roughly nine days, moving from hotel to hotel and using different aliases, before he was arrested without incident at a hotel in Middleborough, Massachusetts, according to police.

title: Canadian First Nation chief arrested over out-of-season lobster fishing, traps pulled
content:
Mike Sack, the chief of the Sipekne'katik, was arrested earlier this week in relation to his first nation group resuming its harvest of North American lobster off the coast of the Canadian province Nova Scotia in advance of the legal November start date, the CBC reports.

The Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) and Coast Guard also removed the band's lobster traps shortly after they were placed in St. Mary's Bay, according to the news service.  

Sack reportedly told the CBC he was in Saulnierville for the launch of the fishery and headed toward the town of Digby for lunch when DFO officers in an unmarked black truck pulled him over and told him he was being arrested "for promoting an illegal fishery". He was taken to the nearby Meteghan fisheries office and later released. 

The CBC reports that DFO has not provided details about why Sack was arrested or whether he could face charges under fisheries legislation.

Sack described the arrest to the news service as nothing more than "scare tactics" by the federal government. He said he was not served any papers and was not provided any conditions upon his release, so he planned to return to the wharf in Saulnierville to support his band's right to fish. 

The battle in St. Mary's Bay dates back to Sept. 2020 when the Sipekne'katik launched a self-regulated lobster fishery in the prolific Lobster Fishing Area 34, enraging other local harvesters who must wait until the last Monday of November, as reported by Undercurrent News. The Sipekne’katik had argued that their actions were in step with a Canadian Supreme Court ruling made some 21 years earlier that allowed fishing in pursuit of a "moderate livelihood" and said it would take less than 5% of the lobster in the area.

The Sipekne'katick have issued lobster licenses to 13 boats, and Sack said he believed most took to the water on Monday, according to the CBC.

Bernadette Jordan, Canada's fisheries minister, had warned in March that federal officers would enforce the regulations that prohibit lobster harvesting out of season. 

In a series of tweets early Monday afternoon, DFO said its fisheries officers were on the water in St. Mary's Bay, conducting inspections and enforcing the Fisheries Act. It warned that improperly or untagged traps would be hauled out and seized.

title: New Zealand gov’t raids eight homes in effort to shutdown illegal rock lobster ring
content:
A six-month investigation by New Zealand's Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) into the alleged poaching and black-market sales of rock or spiny lobster, referred to as "crayfish" in Australia, is the largest in recent years, Hawkes Bay Today, a local news service, reports.

The operation involved 80 officers searching eight homes, including some in the Māhia and Wairoa area, a scale that Gary Orr, the MPI director of compliance services, said was due to the large volume of crustaceans that were taken and sold illegally over a short period of time.

However, no arrests have yet been made.

"It is likely that some of these people will appear before the courts, but we are not at that stage of the investigation yet," Orr said, adding:

"We believe this was a highly organized black market ring which took in excess of 4,300 crayfish with a commercial value of over NZD 300,000 [$211,182] from the Māhia area in Hawke's Bay over a seven-month period."

MPI believes the rock lobsters were sold on the black market in the Auckland, Kawerau, Rotorua, Tūrangi, Gisborne, Napier and Blenheim areas.

title: Untitled
content:
Eighteen people have been arrested for illegally fishing a rare mollusk near Naples, Italy, reports Reuters.

Police had been investigating the group for three years for harvesting date mussels using hammers to extract them from rocks near the town of Sorrento.

Fishing for this species has been illegal since 1998 as they are classed as endangered, the report said, adding that they can reach $235 a kilogram on the black market.

The arrested people face crimes including illegal fishing, destroying the marine habitat and selling unsafe foods. The gang had also been found selling clams from a polluted area.

title: Police make arrest nine months after fire destroyed Nova Scotia lobster pound
content:
Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) have at last made an arrest in relation to the Oct. 16, 2020 fire that completely destroyed a lobster pound in Middle West Pubnico, Nova Scotia, multiple publications report. 

Brendon Douglas James Porter, 24, of East Pubnico, Nova Scotia, was arrested last Wednesday (July 14) and charged with arson, according to news services. He was held in custody Wednesday night and then released on what police referred to as strict conditions the next day.

Porter must remain in Nova Scotia under house arrest except for when he needs to go to work or attend medical appointments, the CBC reports. He must have no contact with 10 specific people, not possess any weapons, not consume controlled substances, not consume alcohol outside his home, and refrain from participating in any activity that interferes with the fishing activities of another individual, group, association, community, band or company.

He is slated to appear in a Shelburne provincial court on Aug. 25. 

The fire occurred late in the evening and just two days after a group of about 200 non-indigenous fishermen and their supporters converged on the plant. It was storing lobster caught by members of the Sipekne’katik First Nation as part of a fishery they controversially started in St. Mary's Bay and ran ahead of the late November start date established by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans for Lobster Fishing Area 34. 

The police, at the time, said the plant was unoccupied at the time of the fire, so there were no injuries to employees. However, one unidentified man, who wasn’t an employee, suffered life-threatening injuries and was taken to a hospital, police said at the time.

But RCMP spokesperson corporal Chris Marshall reportedly confirmed to the CBC on Friday that Porter was the person who was injured.

Asked why it took nine months for police to lay the arson charge, Marshall said it can take longer to investigate large fires where there is significant damage, according to CBC.

"Interviewing witnesses, gathering further surveillance, trying to gather further evidence, if there's any, and basically following up on every lead can take a significant amount of time, especially in a large incident where there's lots of damage," he reportedly said.

"Sometimes even knowing the identity of someone versus being able to gather enough evidence and gather all the facts and be able to present all that information to a prosecutor for prosecution in court, sometimes does take time."

Porter has a long list of prior charges and arrests, including several fishing-related offenses. In 2015 he was found guilty of being in possession of undersized lobster and fishing during a closed season, according to the CBC. In 2016, he was convicted of failing to return incidental fish catches and failing to comply with a recognizance or undertaking.

He was one of three fishermen fined for fisheries violations after being caught on video abusing a seal pup on their fishing boat in 2017. The pup was also killed, though that was not seen in the video, according to the CBC.

title: Former US seafood market owner charged with killing $10,000 worth of lobsters
content:
Police in the US town of Sandwich, Massachusetts, have arrested and charged 70-year-old Joseph Vaudo, a long-time, former seafood market owner, on charges that he committed felony vandalism last week when he turned off the compressor and oxygen supply to a live lobster tank at his former facility, the Cape Cod Times reports.

The incident resulted in the loss of some 2,000 pounds of lobster, costing the current seafood market owner, Superior Lobster and Seafood, about $10,000. 

The dead lobsters and shutdown power boxes were discovered early Friday morning by the manager of Superior when he was making his usual rounds. Video captured by a security camera later showed a man wearing jeans, a blue shirt and baseball hat getting out of a GMC Sierra at the property at about 9 p.m. the night before and emptying his trash into the company's commercial dumpster before moving to the compressor and oxygen supply.

Police said they identified Vaudo from the video, tracked down his vehicle registration, and recovered bags from the dumpster that included materials containing his name and address. Vaudo, who was arrested and charged Friday, pleaded not guilty in a Barnstable, Massachusetts, district court, according to a news release.

The newspaper said Vaudo, who could not be reached for comment, is well known in the local community. At one point he owned and operated three seafood markets along the marina and had served almost 15 years on the town's planning board, according to the newspaper.

His business went down in 2014 after he admitted buying stolen oysters the year before, according to the newspaper. The Massachusetts Public Health Department reportedly revoked his wholesale permit, and he lost his Food and Drug Administration certification to sell shellfish outside the state.
 
Vaudo reapplied and was approved for permits in 2017. He then opened Mr. Vaudo’s Fish Market. However, two years later, he filed for Chapter 13 bankruptcy, owing more than $1.5 million to more than 50 creditors, the newspaper recounted. He closed his fish market and vacated the building, which was taken over last summer by Superior.

title: Chinese fishing boat and crew arrested for alleged poaching
content:
A Chinese fishing boat and crew have been detailed by Taiwan following an accusation of poaching, according to Taiwan's Central News Agency (CNA).

The vessel was apprehended near the Penghu Islands, Taiwan's Coast Guard Administration (CGA) said. The Aonanao 31201 was reportedly found to be trespassing and operating illegally 20.7 nautical miles west of Penghu's Huayu islet, CNA said. The boat's crew ignored three warnings from the CGA and brandished cleavers and iron bars, it said. It was only when the coast guard patrol boat produced shotguns that the fishing boat conceded, it added.

The patrol boat found 760 kilograms (1,675 pounds) of fish on the vessel which was later thrown back into the sea. The vessel was impounded and the captain and crew were arrested.

This is the sixth time a Chinese fishing boat has reportedly been found illegally fishing in the Penghu waters since May, the CNA said.

The Penghu Islands, also known as the Pescadores, are made of 90 islands and islets. Both Taiwan and China claim sovereignty.

title: Ecuadorian shrimp prices rise further, farmers call for more control after latest robbery
content:
Ecuadorian vannamei shrimp farm-gate prices rose again across all sizes in week 24, according to the latest data available on Undercurrent News' prices portal.  

Thus, as of week 24 of 2021 (June 14-20), average farm-gate prices for head-on, shell-on  Ecuadorian shrimp rose week-on-week to $6.50 per kilogram for 20/30 count shrimp; $6.00/kg for 30/40; $5.30/kg for 40/50; $4.80kg for 50/60; $4.20/kg for 60/70; and $3.60/kg for 70/80 counts.

This means an increase of between $0.10/kg and $0.20/kg for large and medium sizes.

Prices for smaller shrimp remained flat at $3.00/kg for 80/100; $2.70/kg for 100/120; and $1.90/kg for 120/14 count shrimp, data below shows. 

Upgrade to Pro to view

However, despite ever-increasing prices allowing optimism about the future, producers are constantly concerned for their own safety on and off their farms. As a result, they are demanding that the government intensify police surveillance.

On June 17, a barge carrying several trucks loaded with shrimp from Puna Island, off the coast of southern Ecuador, was intercepted by pirates on its way to Guayaquil, the largest city in Ecuador and the country's main port, El Universo reports.

In total, 25,000 pounds of shrimp worth around $60,000 were taken by at least eight armed people at around seven in the morning that day. Even though coastguards intercepted the criminals, they only managed to arrest one of them and take back the stolen cargo.

Continued robberies, extortions, assaults, and even murders of shrimp farmers have also led the sector to make a new call for reforms to weapon policies. However, this is not the first time that producers raise their voices to demand further action.

Ecuador cops smash river crime gang, but shrimp sector fears persist

"This is a situation which, regrettably, is recurring with worrying regularity in this country," a small Ecuadorian shrimp producer, who spoke in condition of anonymity, told Undercurrent News.

"We [shrimp farmers] need to feel safe while working. Otherwise, we won't be able to carry out our work properly. Isn't this one of Ecuador's key producing sectors? Sometimes we don't feel like it really is," he added. "The government must act urgently to avert those crimes and strengthen both early-warning and monitoring systems in risk areas."

Back in March, Undercurrent also reported the sector claims for the government to guarantee a budget for river patrols, particularly in light of the lack of resources available for such patrols by the Ecuadorian navy, which has been affected by vessel maintenance issues and a lack of staff.

All this after the Ecuadorian police dismantled an organized criminal gang committing assaults on river routes in the country's southern El Oro province, one of its main shrimp-producing regions.

title: US bans entry for Namibian ministers at heart of Fishrot scandal
content:
The US government has issued a ban on entry for the former Namibian fisheries and justice ministers Bernhard Esau and Sacky Shanghala due to their alleged involvement with the Fishrot corruption scandal.

Namibia’s Fishrot scandal: Recap every development from 2020

The designation renders Esau, Shanghala and their family members ineligible for entry to the US.

Both men have spent over a year in custody following the breaking of the scandal by Wikileaks in November 2019. They are accused of laundering some NAD 175 million ($11.7m) in bribes from subsidiaries of Icelandic firm Samherji and others in return for fishing quotas.

"This designation reaffirms the U.S. commitment to supporting anticorruption reforms that are key to Namibia’s successful future," wrote the US state department. "The United States continues to stand with all Namibians in support of democracy and the rule of law, and against those who would undermine these principles for personal gain."

The US' anti-kleptocracy law applies to public officials only, and as such other members of the so-called 'Fishrot Six', such as former Fishcor chairman James Hatuikulipi, have not yet been barred from entry.

title: China Fishery trustee wants Ngs ousted for alleged ‘treachery’ over $31m claim
content:
China Fishery Group (CFG) trustee William Brandt is asking a New York bankruptcy judge for an emergency hearing to oust members of the Ng family that founded Hong Kong’s Pacific Andes International Holdings (PAIH) from their roles as CFG directors.

Brandt, who plans to hold an auction for CFG in August that could see a sale of the company for over $1.2 billion, accused Ng family members of “treachery”, “collusion” and “breach of fiduciary duty”. Brandt used the strong language after learning, he said, that members of the family had acted to commit a CFG subsidiary, CFG Investment (CFGI) into guaranteeing payment of a $14 million debt claim relating to the 2011 sale of the vessel Sheriff from a Russian firm, Morskoy Veter, to a CFG subsidiary J. Wiludi & Asociados.

"There is no sound business justification for the alleged CFGI guaranty, and the foregoing circumstances suggest activity bordering on potential collusion," Brandt wrote.

Arbitration panel

The principle of Morskoy Veter, Brandt claims, is Oleg Sizov, a long-time business associate of the Ng family and a shareholder in an affiliate company run by the family, which built PAIH into a globe-spanning seafood conglomerate with interests in pollock, fishmeal production, processing and other operations. PAIH filed for bankruptcy in 2015 and creditors, who are owed some $1.5bn, have claimed that the Ngs carried out a massive trade finance fraud that fabricated fish shipments in order to secure financing. The Ngs have repeatedly disputed those allegations. 

According to Brandt's motion for the emergency hearing, which is scheduled for Tuesday, March 25, Morskoy Veter took Wiludi before an arbitration panel in London, United Kingdom, in 2018, claiming that it is owed $14m from the 2011 sale. The arbitration proceeding is ongoing, Brandt's motion claims, and Morskoy Veter reportedly sent CFG two demand letters this year, asking for payment of the obligation they say has now grown to $31m with interest. 

In the first demand letter, sent in March, Morskoy Veter made the claim that Ng Joo Thieng, older brother of PAIH managing director Jessie Ng and a director of several group affiliates, had made an oral guarantee in 2017 to the Russian company that CFGI would pay the vessel-related debt.

The vessel itself has been sold. According to the motion, the Wiludi company later chartered the Sheriff to another CFG subsidiary, South Pacific Shipping Agency, which then reportedly sub-chartered it to PAIH's horse mackerel-catching operation in Namibia. The Sheriff was arrested in Nambia in 2017 for the alleged failure to pay $591,805 for "crew services and necessities" supplied to it. It was auctioned off for $2.5m. 

Guaranty dispute

Brandt wrote that March 2021 was the first time that he had been told of the 2017 oral guarantee and that CFGI's records don't corroborate its existence. Additionally, he recently learned that "as recently as March or April of 2021, certain Ng family members provided a written assurance of the alleged CFGI guaranty", the motion states. 

"The Ng family members have caused CFGI to execute a guaranty with no business justification for the benefit of a longtime associate, and perhaps the Ng family members themselves, thereby siphoning value from the debtors’ estates," Brandt claimed in the motion.

In a separate motion, he asked the court to remove members of the Ng family from their director positions at CFG affiliates and asked the court to approve a subpoena for documents related to the guarantee matter. Upon being asked to see a copy of the written guarantee, Brandt was told that it couldn't be found, he told Undercurrent News. He said that the guarantee could potentially add $31m to the sale price of CFG, bids for which are due by June 1.

If no bid for CFG emerges by then, Brandt has said he will support a creditor-led takeover plan for the company. 

Though he'd hoped to work with the family members and left them in place as directors, Brandt said that members of the Ng family had no authority to issue any guarantee and that it would be disputed.

"If they’re willing to do this kind of crap now, what else are they doing? So it’s time to remove them," he said.

In April, Undercurrent reported that the trustee had planned a settlement with the Ngs to pay $25m in exchange for their cooperation with the sale. That proposal is being reviewed, Brandt told Undercurrent.

"It’s certainly in a high state of abeyance, let’s put it that way," he said.

The family's response

PAIH, which remains in control of the Ng family, declined to comment for this story. Undercurrent was unable to reach Sizov. But in response the Brandt's motion, lawyers for PAIH roundly denied that any wrongdoing took place.

"Putting aside the unnecessary hyperbole, the assertions in the motion are unfounded and pure conjecture. What is certain is that the relief sought in the motion will not progress these bankruptcy cases and their upcoming sale and/or confirmation of the creditor plan proponents’ plan, but instead will cause disruption to this process," PAIH's lawyers wrote.

They added that members of the Ng family have already provided all of the documentation in their possession relating to the guarantee. 

"Importantly, the implementation of the transaction involving the vessel Sheriff was handled by personnel from the CFGI office in Peru partly due to their familiarity with the local laws and regulations with respect to the purchase," PAIH's lawyers wrote. "As a consequence, a substantial amount of the relevant documents and writings in relation to the purchase should therefore be available in the Peru office of CFGI and within the custody and control of the Peruvian management team.

The lawyers added that "each of the debtors, non-debtor affiliates and the Ng family members strongly dispute the assertions in the motion – there was no treachery, no misconduct, nothing incriminatory, and no secret intent to actively undermine the chapter 11 trustee’s efforts. To the contrary, the debtors, non-debtor affiliates and the Ng family members have been actively working towards a global settlement for the benefit of the estates and creditors of the debtors," the lawyers wrote.

title: Nova Scotia harvesters allegedly held at gunpoint, told to hand over catch
content:
Two harvesters in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia were held at gunpoint on Sunday night in the area of Terence Bay, told to hand over their catch and ordered to drive to another area to place their nets, according to a report by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP).

Jared Luben Young, a 34-year-old Mills Cove, Nova Scotia, man has been charged with kidnapping, robbery, forcible confinement, uttering threats, possession of a weapon for dangerous purposes and theft over CAD 5,000 ($4,131), according to a statement by the RCMP.

The police said the incident began when the harvesters observed a vehicle driving erratically toward the area where they had set their nets. When they arrived at their nets, they were allegedly confronted by seven men in three vehicles, who told them to give up their landings. 

"Armed with weapons, the men blocked the fishermen to prevent them from leaving," the police report said. "They then had the fishermen drive to another area nearby where they had other nets set. The men left, and the fishermen were able to call police. One fisherman was injured during the incident after being struck with a weapon. He suffered minor physical injuries."

Halifax Regional Police located one of the vehicles involved shortly after, in Halifax, arresting the driver, Young, without incident. He was scheduled to appear in a provincial court on Monday.

title: A year on, case of Kiribati fisheries observer’s death remains unsolved
content:
The suspicious death of a 40-year-old fisheries observer aboard a Taiwanese tuna purse seiner in early 2020 remains unresolved.

Groups push to protect Pacific tuna crews and observers

A year later, the case is still under investigation by local police, while the vessel returned to fish, sources told Undercurrent News.

The death of Eritara Aati Kaierua, from Kiribati, was reported on Mar. 3, 2020, in waters off Nauru, near Australia.

Kaierua, who worked for the Kiribati government and was a father of four children, was found lying on the floor of his locked cabin in the Win Far 636, a 30-year-old vessel owned by Kuo Hsiung Fishery, based in Taiwan's Kahsiung City. He had a head wound and bruising to his neck.

The agent for the vessel, which was impounded, was Central Pacific Products, a government-owned company. The Taiwanese government had alerted the multi-national regulatory body Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission (WCPFC) and the Kiribati government. 

According to the observer's log, Kaierua was seen boarding the vessel by his family on Feb. 3. However, the vessel's tracking technology was switched off, so the voyage remains unclear. Two of the vessel's Vietnamese-dominated crew were arrested upon arrival but then released after questioning. 

A year later, the family is still unaware whether or not Kaierua was murdered. It is unknown whether justice and the truth of the circumstances of his death will ever come to light.

The tragedy has sparked a call for more protection for this vulnerable workforce, who often face hostility from captains and crews. Ten observers have lost their lives in the region over the past decade with at least five of the deaths under a cloud of suspicion, but none have been prosecuted.

Following Kaierua's death last year, the Parties to the Nauru Agreement (PNA) and tuna sales organization Pacifical said they had suspended the vessel. 

The Win Far 636 was suspended from the PNA Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) scheme in 2020 as soon as it heard about the incident pending investigation, and "the vessel has not been reinstated at this point as we have no formal update", Maurice Brownjohn, the PNA office's commercial manager, told Undercurrent on April 30.

"We are not in a position to comment on the case or the status of the investigations. These are subject to Kiribati authorities and their sovereignty," Brownjohn said.

"The PNA take observer and crew safety very seriously and are continuously working to improve conditions at sea. For example, the PNA observer agency provides insurance, safety gear and two-way communication devices to all PNA observers on FSMA trips," he observed.

Brownjohn further said that, along "with wider FFA [Forum Fisheries Agency] membership, PNA members sponsored a resolution passed at WCPFC in respect of crewing standards and labour conditions as part of the regional harmonized minimum terms and conditions for fisheries access since 2019".

British NGO Human Rights at Sea has spent nine months collating publicly available evidence into the circumstances surrounding the untimely death of Kaierua.

It has recently completed a detailed report, which will be submitted to the Kiribati authorities ahead of any decision to publish noting that the "police investigation remains open but apparently stagnant", the organization's CEO David Hammond told Undercurrent.

Nonetheless, "extensive numbers of questions remain outstanding for the family of the deceased", Hammond pointed out.

"The length of time it has taken to investigate despite the restrictions of the COVID-19 pandemic has left a family in limbo without closure. This means they continue to be victims of the incident and its surrounding uncertainties, and which is completely unacceptable," Hammond noted.

This month, the MSC allocated £100,000 to help fund projects and initiatives aimed at improving the safety and welfare of fishery observers.

Since March 2020, the requirement for 100% observer coverage in the MSC-certified purse seine fishery in the western and central Pacific and PNA waters has been temporarily suspended, in response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Canada’s Jordan to include elvers in ‘moderate livelihood’ negotiations
content:
Elvers caught in the Canadian provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick are now part of that country's negotiations with the Mi'kmaq First Nation groups to implement "moderate livelihood" fisheries, the CBC reports.

"This is not just about lobster. This is about all species. So, we are going to continue to work with them in negotiations to see if there is a way for them to exercise that right as well," Bernadette Jordan, Canada's fisheries and oceans minister, reportedly said this week.

Elvers, or baby eels, are flown live to Asia where they are farmed to adult size before being harvested. With an annual quota of 9,960 kilograms, their licenses are tightly controlled in Canada as they command big dollars. Since 2011, Canada's elvers have garnered as much as CAD 3,300 ($2,640) per kilogram, on average, though their price was as high as CAD 5,200/kg in 2019, according to the CBC. 

The commercial fishery, which runs from April to early summer, is shared by just nine license holders. Each license holder is assigned a certain number of rivers and a quota. Landings are tracked via logbooks and verified by dockside monitoring.

No new licenses have been issued since 1998. Among those with licenses are members of the We'koqma'q First Nation in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia.

In 2019 the commercial fishery was valued at CAD 38 million, and each license was worth CAD 4.3m, according to a DFO economic assessment. 

Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO), a year ago, shut down the elver harvest over conservation concerns when fishing activity increased dramatically early in the season. Then, earlier this year, DFO imposed a minimum size of 10 centimeters for eels harvested by the Mi'kmaq under communal food, social and ceremonial licenses in the Maritime region with the intention of stopping their attempts to harvest elvers.

Simultaneously, Canada has been dealing with a dispute over an offseason lobster fishery started by the Sipekne'katik First Nation, part of the Mi'kmaw, in September that has led to civil unrest in the area. As in the elver case, the Sipekne'katik have claimed their right to fish for a "moderate livelihood" as guaranteed in the 1999 Marshall decision.

Jordan warned in March that federal officers would enforce the regulations that prohibit lobster harvesting out of season.

"We have to make sure conservation is the priority," Jordan reportedly said more recently in relation to elvers. "The elver is a species we are very, very concerned about. The science is still very much in development with elvers, so we have to take steps to make sure that this is a sustainable fishery."

DFO reports having arrested 14 people in connection with suspected unauthorized elver fishing so far this year, including several members of the Sipekne'katik.
