title: China, US to power ‘roaring twenties’ of global shrimp imports
content:
An Undercurrent News analysis places China, the US and emerging markets at the heart of a forecast roaring decade of shrimp consumption growth post-COVID-19.

According to the analysis of trade data, in the seven years from 2012-2019, China largely drove a near 1.1 million metric ton increase in global shrimp imports, and appears poised to drive further growth in trade in the 2020s.

Global shrimp trade set for boost amid vaccine rollout

It puts China at the center of the global shrimp industry's likely long-term plans, with the country set to surpass 1m metric tons of imports by 2027, while it could reach that threshold by 2023. 

Meanwhile, the US and emerging markets will likely boost global shrimp trade further, with the US on course to surpass 1m metric tons of imports also by 2027. Markets outside the big importers, mainly emerging economies, could hit 1m metric tons of imports by 2025.

A surprise factor longer-term may also be the falling cost of shrimp worldwide as farmers intensify production and improve efficiency, and as lower prices are transferred to the consumer. This could provide a further boost to global imports as shrimp becomes more competitive with other animal proteins.

A decade of growth

Between 2012-2019, combined global shrimp imports grew by 1.1 million metric tons, or 50% (see chart), to 3.15m metric tons in 2019, according to data supplied by International Trade Center. 

The figures include both warmwater shrimp and coldwater shrimp, in raw, cooked, prepared and preserved formats, and traded under the global harmonized system codes 030617, 030616, 160521 and 160529.

The huge increase followed the financial crisis of 2008-2009, when global imports contracted for two consecutive years. In 2020, COVID also caused an estimated 3% contraction in imports to 3.042m metric tons.

Between 2012-2020, the compound annual growth rate (CAGR) was 6.5%, greater than the growth of the global economy over the same period (2.7%, World Bank data). In 2017 alone, 234,000t of shrimp imports were added globally.

China has been key to rising global imports, with the country accounting for 70-75% of absolute global shrimp import growth between 2012-2019; its imports soared from 48,000t in 2012 to an estimated 800,000t in 2019. 

The 10-fold increase in Chinese imports followed the devastation of China's own sizeable domestic production in 2010-2012, due to the novel shrimp disease early mortality syndrome, as well as the country's expanding middle class. 

Much of the growth in imports was funneled through the "grey" trade across the border with Vietnam, which Chinese authorities began to crack down on in late 2017. Last year, most shrimp imports were imported directly via Chinese ports (see charts two and three).

Last year, Chinese direct imports contracted by 14% to 610,000t, due to consumer concerns about packages of imported seafood contaminated with the coronavirus.

However, looking ahead, should Chinese imports return to growth rates between 2012-2019, or a CAGR of 49%, Chinese imports would surpass 1.4m metric tons by 2022. By 2023, they would hit 2m metric tons. 

Even halving CAGR to 25% would see Chinese imports hit 1m metric tons by 2023 and 2m by 2026. A CAGR of 10%, which seems conservative, would see annual imports surpass 1m metric tons in 2027.

Some question whether China's import growth is the country simply replacing lost domestic production. However, others point to its huge population and culinary history of eating seafood as signs of its almost limitless market potential.

US no laggard either

The US has also been key to increasing global imports of shrimp, thanks to shrimp's popularity in US foodservice.

In 2020, the US imported 747,000t of shrimp, up from 533,000t in 2012. This represents an increase of 40% over the period, or a CAGR of 4.3%. Last year, despite the pandemic, imports grew 7%.

Looking ahead, should imports continue to grow at the current pace the US will surpass 1m metric tons of imports by 2027.

Because of US consumers' preference for processed and value-added shrimp products, growth in imports in terms of value is greater compared with other countries, including China, and so more valuable to the sector. Last week, reflecting on the country's rapid vaccine rollout, industry sources said they expect a "big surge" in US seafood demand in 2021.

Europe

The picture for Europe is less rosy for the global shrimp industry. Although imports by northern European countries held up and even grew last year during COVID-19, EU imports overall contracted by 3% in 2020 to 789,000t, according to ITC. In 2020, imports were just 5% higher compared with 2012.

Even excluding 2020 from the figures, between 2012-2019, CAGR was just 1.1%. 

As with the US, the preference for processed and prepared shrimp products in northern Europe translates into a greater value of imported shrimp per kilogram. However, shrinking populations in many European countries and slower-growing economies point to stagnating EU shrimp consumption longer-term. 

Falling Japanese sales

Indeed, Japan is a cautionary tale for the sector in Europe; since 2012, Japan's shrimp imports have fallen by 24% to 210,000t in 2020, according to ITC. 

Pound-for-pound, Japanese shrimp imports are among the highest value in the world, meaning a contraction in imports has a greater overall impact on Japan's suppliers, primarily Vietnam and Thailand. 

The contraction has been attributed to everything from Japan's shrinking population, greater market competition, and more consumption of other animal proteins among younger generations. 

However, imports by emerging markets will likely outweigh a contraction in Japanese imports. Between 2012-2020, imports by countries outside the EU, US, China, Japan and South Korea grew by 78% to 601,000t in 2020. With a CAGR of 13%, this puts the rest of the world on course to surpass 1m metric tons of imports by 2025.

During the Boston seafood show of 2019, George Chamberlain, president of the Global Aquaculture Alliance, forecast that one day shrimp would be produced "like chicken", with new technologies and investment leading to more industrialized production. 

This could see global farmed shrimp production grow to 8-9m metric tons by 2025, he said, and more affordable prices, further boosting trade.

"From my perspective, improved technology, prices rebounding from pandemic lows, improved disease management, and farm expansion and intensification all point to a steady increase in supply," Jeff Sedacca, CEO of Sunnyvale Seafood Company, a California-based seafood importer, told Undercurrent more recently, echoing the sentiment.

title: Daily recap, March 18: Santa Monica enjoys skin-pack boom; Mowi edges closer to Ducktrap deal; COVID hits Norway’s smaller farmers
content:
Here's a recap of the daily seafood news from Thursday, March 18:

Santa Monica enjoying skin-pack boom amid pandemic

Major West Coast US distributor and processor Santa Monica Seafoods got hit hard in the initial months of the COVID-19 pandemic but investments made in its skin-pack capabilities are paying off, its CEO told Undercurrent News.

Roger O'Brien, the CEO of the acquisitive Rancho Dominguez, California-based firm, one of the country's largest seafood distributors, said that before the pandemic, Santa Monica's business was roughly split 70% foodservice/30% retail. Now the ratio has essentially flipped, he said. Read the full story here.

Mowi, plaintiffs edge closer to $1.3m settlement on Ducktrap sustainability claims

Norwegian salmon farmer Mowi is drawing nearer to reaching a settlement with several US consumers who had sued it alleging that its fish are not sustainably raised and its labeling claims are false and misleading. Read the full article here.

COVID exposes ‘vulnerability’ of Norway’s small salmon farmers

Smaller salmon farmers in Norway have been made to feel vulnerable by the coronavirus pandemic, according to founding partner of Bluefront Equity, Kjetil Haga. Speaking on the latest Undercurrent webinar, he said many are considering rebranding or integration as a remedy. Haga said the coronavirus pandemic had been a wake-up call for small family-owned salmon companies. Read the story in detail here.

Tiny Canadian island processor to make big splash with skin-packed products

Labrador Gem Seafoods, a processor on the tiny, fog-blanketed island of Ramea, readies to launch nearly a dozen frozen skin-packed seafood products into the market. Read the full story right here.

India’s Apex sees profit sink in 2021, though shrimp VAP looks promising

The shrimp farmer and processor has sold less shrimp year-on-year, putting less raw material through its newly expanded plant; but its new capacity for ready-to-eat shrimp is yielding benefits. Read the full story here.

Chinese customs agency seizes $35.8m of smuggled black tiger shrimp

Chinese customs officials launched a crackdown on black tiger smuggling worth $35.8m across the country's border with Vietnam resulting in seven arrests. Read it in full here.

UK retailers threaten to pull yellowfin sourcing if IOTC stalemate persists

A group of influential British buyers of Indian Ocean yellowfin tuna will review their sourcing policies if progress to rebuild stocks is not made soon. Read the full details here.

title: Chinese customs agency seizes $35.8m of smuggled black tiger shrimp
content:
Chinese customs officials launched a crackdown on black tiger shrimp smuggling worth an estimated CNY 233 million ($35.8m) that took place across the country's border with Vietnam. Seven individuals were arrested, reported Xinhua News Agency.

The Shanghai anti-smuggling bureau of the General Administration of Customs referred the case to prosecutors on March 15.

The accused smugglers allegedly took advantage of a tax-free scheme for border residents to smuggle black tiger shrimp into China via Vietnam over a six-year period ending in August 2020.

Chinese residents living within 20 kilometers of the border area are allowed to purchase up to CNY 8,000 of goods from Vietnam every day without paying taxes and tariffs.

Chinese authorities break up $29m crab, lobster smuggling ring

A seafood buyer in Shanghai allegedly colluded with a Vietnamese supplier, falsely reporting Vietnamese black tiger shrimp that should have been imported through general trade as products for border trade. The shrimp was then reportedly smuggled via a method known in China as "ant moving" and transported to Shanghai, Qingdao and other coastal cities for sale.

Customs authorities in Shanghai and Qingdao jointly launched a special anti-smuggling operation last September. Seven were arrested in Shanghai and Guangxi.

Shanghai customs authorities said that, in recent years, the final destination of goods smuggled through border trade has shifted from the cities of Guangdong, Guangxi, and Fujian to the coastal area of Yangtze River Delta and Bohai Bay.

In addition to tax evasion, seafood smuggling through border trade reportedly causes hidden safety and health hazards. The official said the circuitous transportation route and multiple loading and unloading would cause product deterioration and disease risk.

China cracks down on smuggling, improves logistics for legal imports

China has ramped up clampdown on seafood smuggling across its border with Vietnam over the past few years. 

In 2017, the Chinese government led an anti-smuggling operation across 11 cities, specifically targeted seafood. One year later, the authorities launched another wave of crackdowns on smugglers bringing seafood into China via Vietnam, seized 1,320 metric tons of frozen seafood and arrested 66 individuals.

Moreover, the true picture of China's seafood consumption boom has also been hidden due to the 'grey trade' across the China-Vietnam border. According to an Undercurrent News analysis, Vietnam’s seafood imports were worth over $5 billion in 2016, up from $25m in 2001, with most imports transshipped to China.

title: Canada will enforce lobster fishing season dates, minister warns
content:
Bernadette Jordan, Canada's fisheries minister, warned Tuesday that federal officers will enforce the regulations that prohibit lobster harvesting out of season, responding to reports that First Nation groups might begin fishing months early in direct protest, the CBC reports.

"The number one priority for [Conservation and Protection officers] is to keep people safe — and that is to keep harvesters safe that are the non-Indigenous harvesters as well as Indigenous harvesters," Jordan said. "That is their number one priority, and they will make sure that they are doing everything they can to de-escalate situation[s]."

Jordan's comments, made to Caroll Off, the host of CBC Radio's As it Happens, follow her declaration on March 3 that the Canadian Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) will not grant licenses to any group, including First Nations, that operate outside of the commercial seasons. 

A majestic Canadian lobster. Photo courtesy of Tangier Lobster Company, in Nova Scotia.

The decision was a major development in an ongoing spat with the commercial lobster industry that started when the Sipekne'katik band, in September 2020, launched its own self-regulated 'moderate livelihood' lobster fishery in St. Mary's Bay in southwest Nova Scotia, as reported by Undercurrent News. Harvesters in lobster fishing area 34 were particularly outraged as their season doesn't begin until the end of November.

The Sipekne’katik had argued that their actions were in step with a Canadian Supreme Court ruling made some 21 years earlier that allowed fishing in pursuit of a "moderate livelihood" and said it would take less than 5% of the lobster in the area.

Jordan told Off on Tuesday that Canada will enforce the Fisheries Act.

"What happens, given that the Mi'kmaw fishermen are not going to go along with this plan to fish only within the commercial season. What will you do about that?" Off asked.

"Our fisheries officers, the [Conservation and Protection] officers will be on the water whenever the First Nations decide they want to go out," Jordan said.

"Will they be arresting people?" Off asked.

"That's going to depend on them. I don't tell the fisheries officers how to do their jobs. There's a number of different measures that they could be taking," Jordan responded. 

"Will they be seizing boats and equipment?" Off asked.

"That will be up to the fisheries officers to determine what the best approach is," Jordan answered. "Of course, we always take a measured approach. We want to make sure that we don't have the same type of situation that we had last year in the fall where we had, you know, a lot of intimidation, a lot of stand-offs. We want this to be a safe and orderly season, as well as a well-regulated one."

title: CBC: Lobster landings in Canada’s biggest zone show decline since 2015
content:
The recent decision by the Canadian federal government to allow a "moderate livelihood" lobster fishery for First Nation groups has drawn attention to a recent decline in landings off the coasts of the province Nova Scotia, the CBC reports.

The size of landings in lobster fishing area (LFA) 34, Canada's biggest zone, rose significantly between 2002 and 2015, but has been dropping since, the news service said it found. 

The issue has gained attention as a result of the ugly spat between First Nations and the commercial lobster industry that started when the Sipekne'katik band, in September 2020, launched its own off-season, self-regulated 'moderate livelihood' lobster fishery in St. Mary's Bay in southwest Nova Scotia. 

On March 3, months after a lobster pound was set on fire and 23 fishermen were arrested, minister of fisheries Bernadette Jordan attempted to settle the dispute by declaring that Canada would authorize a moderate livelihood fishery but only within the existing commercial season. 

"Lobster stocks are healthy on the East Coast and have remained that way in part because my department works to monitor biomass and determine appropriate fishing limits and practices year after year," she said in a statement. 

But are the lobster stocks healthy? To answer that question, CBC said it used freedom of information laws to request data on lobster landings for every port in LFA 34 for the years 2002 to 2020. Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) obliged, however, it held back numbers in cases that might too easily reveal individual company information.

After 2015, landings in LFA 34 fell, the data confirmed. However, landings in 2020 were still greater than in 2002 and close to the 18-year average for landing weights, the CBC said it also discovered. 

The amount of lobster landed in St. Marys Bay peaked in 2012-13, fluctuated until 2016-17, and then declined. Landings in 2020 were about half of the 18-year average.

CBC also noted that the number of boats fishing in St. Mary's Bay and the number of days fished also declined significantly between 2018-20. The number of days fished in 2020 was also about half of the 18-year average.

title: Russian crab king murder link probed
content:
The owner of Russian crab company Moneron has been arrested over his alleged links to crimes supposedly committed by a wanted man dubbed the 'crab king', reports Russia Today.

Dmitry Pashov, a businessman and lawmaker in the far east region of Sakhalin was arrested in January, accused by authorities of involvement in crimes committed by Oleg Khan, the so-called crab king.

Khan, who is believed by authorities to be the beneficial owner of Moneron, is wanted for various offenses, including the alleged killing of an entrepreneur and smuggling shellfish. 

He fled Russia in 2018 and is on an international wanted list. Khan previously told authorities that: "All the… charges against me, arrests in absentia and wanted notices are nothing but a diversion."

Pashov, who has a reported salary of $83 million and is Russia's highest-paid civil servant, is to be kept in custody for two months.

Part of the evidence against him includes a video in which he is seen pulling protected fish out of a river, according to Russia Today. Investigators then proceeded to probe his links to the Khan case.

Moneron had a catch quota of 6,000 metric tons in 2016, including red king crab, blue king crab, Opilio snow crab, Berdi snow crab. These were for the Sea of Okhotsk, and the Bering Sea fishing areas.

title: CBC: Canada to require First Nation lobster fishing during commercial season
content:
The Canadian Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) has taken a strong position in the fight over a lobster fishery launched by a First Nations group off the southwest coast of Nova Scotia. It's declared that it will not grant licenses unless the group operates during the commercial season, the CBC reports. 

The decision is a major development in an ongoing spat between First Nations and the commercial lobster industry that started when the Sipekne'katik band, in September 2020, launched its own self-regulated 'moderate livelihood' lobster fishery in St. Mary's Bay in southwest Nova Scotia.

Harvesters in lobster fishing area 34 were particularly outraged as their season doesn't begin until the end of November. The Sipekne’katik had reported their actions to be in step with a Canadian Supreme Court ruling made some 21 years earlier that allowed fishing in pursuit of a "moderate livelihood" and said it would take less than 5% of the lobster in the area.

The fight turned violent in October when commercial harvesters ransacked and burned a lobster pound serving the First Nation group, leading to the arrest of 23 individuals.

Regardless, DFO sided Wednesday with the commercial harvesters and against First Nations, declaring that it will not provide a license to any Indigenous "moderate livelihood" fishery in Atlantic Canada unless it operates within the commercial season.

"Seasons ensure that stocks are harvested sustainably and they are necessary for an orderly, predictable, and well-managed fishery," fisheries minister Bernadette Jordan said in a statement. "In effort-based fisheries such as lobster, seasons are part of the overall management structure that conserves the resource, ensures there isn't overfishing, and distributes economic benefits across Atlantic Canada."

Jordan cited part of the Marshall ruling to justify her authority, saying "treaty rights are subject to regulation provided such regulation is shown by the crown to be justified on conservation or other grounds of public importance".

The federal government "will balance additional First Nations access through already available licenses and a willing buyer-willing seller approach, protecting our stocks and preserving the industry for generations to come", she said.

Without DFO authorization, harvesters can't legally sell their catch to licensed buyers, such as lobster pounds and processors, CBC noted.

title: Namibia’s Fishcor receives 80,000t of horse mackerel quota despite financial crisis
content:
The Namibian government has allocated 80,000 metric tons of horse mackerel quota to the state-owned National Fishing Corporation of Namibia (Fishcor) despite the fact that Fishcor's bank accounts were recently frozen, reports the Namibian. 

Albert Kawana, the minister of fisheries and marine resources, defended his decision to allocate quotas to Fishcor, saying that if these quotas are still labeled as "government objectives", Fishcor is no longer responsible for implementing them.

Kawana did not explain how financially-troubled Fishcor would utilize the allocated quotas but said the normal arrangement through which Fishcor received quotas and passed them to other companies would continue.

Namibia’s Fishrot scandal: Recap every development from 2020

Fishcor, has ended its relationship with Seaflower Pelagic Processing (SPP) to facilitate the quotas. The minister terminated the cooperation as Fishcor did not utilize the quotas as per the terms of the agreement.

Among the new quotas, some would be passed on to one of Fishcor's subsidiaries at Lüderitz. The remainder would be used to sustain jobs of former SPP employees, who are currently worked for a four-month contract with Tunacor.

The Namibian government would continue to release quotas for governmental objectives through open auction as the new method, the minister said.

Meanwhile, Fishcor said the process of appointing the CEO comes close to a conclusion in days, Tunacor's chief executive Peya Hitula and Novanam chief executive Edwin Kamototo are the shortlisted candidates, while Hitula is favored for the top job, reports the Namibian.

The former CEO of Fishcor, Mike Nghipunya, was arrested last February connected with the "Fishrot" scandal. Nghipunya was charged with fraud, corruption, and money laundering involved with the payment of about NAD 75.6 million ($5.1m) from Fishcor.

title: Daily recap, Feb. 22: Indonesia, Vietnam shrimp growth; China Fishery seeks $12m lawsuit settlement
content:
Here's a recap of the daily seafood news from Monday, Feb. 22.

Indonesia and Vietnam are being eyed as the key farmed shrimp producers in the coming years, two sector experts told Undercurrent News during our latest webinar.

Southeast Asian producers — complemented by Ecuador in Latin America — are expected to drive a 2021 recovery in global shrimp volumes, said panelists taking part in "Farmed shrimp production, price outlook with pandemic now 'new normal' ". You can rewatch the webinar in full here.

"The trend for shrimp production has been an increase of 6-7% annually," Robins McIntosh — senior vice president with Charoen Pokphand Foods — told Undercurrent and the webinar's viewers.

In the US, Seattle, Washington-based Trident Seafoods has restarted operations at its major processing plant in Akutan, Alaska, after the facility was closed for weeks due to a significant COVID-19 outbreak.

Trident said that operations at Akutan restarted on Friday, Feb. 19, after a four-week shutdown. Extensive disease surveillance testing revealed that its COVID cases have been isolated. 

Thai Union Group saw its annual net profit surpass THB 6 billion ($199.7 million) for the first time in its 2020 financial year reporting, a year-on-year increase of 64%.

That came on the back of sales which were up 5%, to THB 132.4bn, thanks largely to increased demand for ambient products — likely the coronavirus pandemic's impact on consumer habits.

The firm also announced it was selling out of its Middle East retail joint venture, and that it is applying to list its feed subsidiary on the Thai stock exchange.

There is no sign of a quick end to Ecuador's problems in the Chinese market, with shrimp exports to the country languishing almost two-thirds below year-ago levels in the first month of the new year.

With Chinese consumers still worried about imported seafood's links to the coronavirus, in January, Ecuador exported 12,700 metric tons of frozen shrimp to China, 57% less than the same month in 2020, according to trade data by Ecuador’s Camara Nacional de Acuacultura, or national chamber of aquaculture. 

Specialized salmon harvest vessel the Norwegian Gannet has been given a 10-year dispensation from Norway's 'production fish' rules, allowing it to operate as intended.

The country's ministry of trade and industry stressed that its laws on 'production fish' — salmon with defects or deficiencies which are forbidden from being shipped out of Norway, in a bid to protect quality standards — still stand, and that the Gannet is a "very special case".

A year-long mediation process between China Fishery Group (CFG) trustee William Brandt and liquidators in charge of several Pacific Andes International Holdings (PAIH) affiliate companies has resulted in a settlement proposal.

Documents filed by Brandt on Friday, Feb. 19, in a New York bankruptcy court propose that as part of the settlement CFG will pay $12m in cash to several PAIH affiliates that are under the control of liquidators from the firm FTI Consulting. In exchange, the liquidators will permanently drop a lawsuit filed against CFG in Hong Kong.

And finally, four owners of a New York City seafood import business have been arrested and charged with smuggling large quantities of banned catfish into the US. If found guilty, the men each face federal prison sentences of up to 25 years.

title: Four charged in New York with smuggling catfish from Myanmar, Bangladesh
content:
Four owners of a New York City seafood import business were arrested and charged Thursday with smuggling large quantities of banned catfish into the US, according to a press release published by the US attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York.

If found guilty, the men each face federal prison sentences of up to 25 years.

The defendants include Mahmud Chowdhury, CEO and co-owner of Asia Foods Distributor Inc. (AFD), a business opened in 2014, as well as principals Shakil Ahmed, Belayet Hussain and Firoz Ahammad. They were presented on Thursday to US magistrate judge Katharine H. Parker, according to the press release.

China, Thailand, and Vietnam are the only countries from which the US deems the import of catfish and other fish of the order Siluriformes to be legal based on a federal law passed in 2015 and implemented in 2017. However, according to the 18-page complaint, signed by Adebola Awe, a special agent with the US Department of Homeland Security, a copy of which was obtained by Undercurrent News, AFD brought in at least four illegal shipments of catfish from Myanmar and Bangladesh at the Port of New York/Newark, located in Elizabeth, New Jersey, between January and August 2019.

Legally imported wild-caught catfish for sale at an H Mart in Fairfax, Virginia. Photo by Jason Huffman.

It was a refrigerated container from Myanmar, inspected at the New Jersey port on or about Jan. 31, 2019, that initially tripped up the alleged smugglers, according to the complaint.

A number of white burlap sacks were marked "Asia Foods Distributor Inc". and reported containing rohu, a species of fish more commonly referred to as carp and not subject to the Federal Meat Inspection Act. However, as the inspection continued, other burlap sacks were found bearing the same labels but also carrying a circled 'A', inside of which were found about 47 cartons of whole frozen baga ayer, a type of catfish.

Investigators later found similarly mislabeled shipments of catfish in three other containers from Myanmar and Bangladesh received in August 2019, Awe said. 

It was common for AFD to use the New Jersey port. The complaint said the company was the importer of record on at least 145 maritime shipments in Elizabeth between January 2018 and September 2019, including 32 from Myanmar and 87 from Bangladesh.

The complaint further describes inspections of AFD's warehouse and retail customers, where catfish matching the type alleged to have been illegally imported were found. Also, multiple text messages were found in which basic elements of the scheme were described by the defendants, including the use of codes on packages to identify the true source of the illegally imported catfish only to the participants knowingly involved in the scheme. 

Several of the men have admitted their part in the scheme, according to the complaint. They reportedly said they stopped and then resumed the illegal imports because they saw other import companies doing the same thing.

The investigation also involved agents from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Office of Law Enforcement (OLE) and the US Department of Agriculture (USDA), according to the press release.

"This case demonstrates the importance of our cooperation with US government partners to interdict illegal products before they enter the country", said Timothy Donovan, assistant director in OLE's northeast division. "OLE continues to work to protect consumers and fishermen from seafood fraud and the illegal importation of seafood through initiatives like our Seafood Import Monitoring Program.”

"As alleged, food safety for U.S. consumers was seriously compromised by these defendants, who disguised their importation and distribution of dangerous fish and fish products," said US attorney Audrey Strauss. "Thankfully, investigators with HSI, NOAA, and USDA-[Office of Inspector General] detected something fishy and reeled in the defendants, who now face serious federal charges."

title: Wisconsin’s ‘sturgeon general’ accused of illegal caviar consumption
content:
A fish and wildlife biologist known as the US state of Wisconsin's top sturgeon expert stands accused of having illegally obtained more than $20,000 of caviar in a single year, the Washington Post reported.

The biologist, Ryan Koenigs, has been nicknamed the "sturgeon general" by local media. He was arrested for misdemeanor theft and obstructing the investigation of a conservation warden, the newspaper reported.

Harvesting of the threatened species is generally not allowed but Wisconsin allows for a short spearfishing season during which harvesters can catch sturgeon and collect the eggs. However, selling them is prohibited and fishermen were encouraged to donate the eggs to the state for "research purposes" although state officials were simply consuming the roe instead.

Following an undercover investigation that lasted for three years, investigators found that the eggs were being consumed by officials at the state's Department of Natural Resources at occasions that included team meetings. Investigators discovered the practice after a three-year undercover investigation.

title: Fishcor CEO emptied accounts prior to arrest, documents show
content:
Mike Nghipunya, the former chief executive of Namibian state-owned processing company Fishcor, is understood to have emptied his bank accounts prior to his arrest nearly a year ago, reports The Namibian.

After arrest, only NAD 439 ($29) was found in one of the former CEO's personal accounts.

Nghipunya was involved in the payment of about NAD 75.6 million from Fishcor, believed to form part of the wider Fishrot corruption scandal.

Documents submitted to Namibia's Anti-Corruption Commission have shown that in one case, more than NAD 10.5m was moved to an account belonging to Nghipunya in the Gwanyemba Investment Trust between 2017 and 2019.

However, bank statements show that Nghipunya then rapidly moved this money out of his account in the months following the breaking of the Fishrot scandal in November 2019 and his ultimate arrest -- by that point, less than NAD 10,000 was left behind.

After his arrest in February of last year, Nghipunya was taken into police custody, where he remains alongside former fisheries minister Bernhard Esau and former Fishcor chairperson James Hatuikulipi among others.

title: SA lawyer alleges Namibian president, Fishcor partner involved in Fishrot scheme
content:
An affidavit submitted by under-fire South African lawyer Maren de Klerk to Namibia's Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) alleges Namibia's president, Haige Geingob, was fully aware of the Fishrot bribery scandal, and indeed places him at the center of it, reports The Namibian. 

Namibia’s ‘Fishrot’ investigation completed, more arrests planned

According to de Klerk's 477-page affidavit, former Investec Asset Management director James Hatuikulipi -- as well as former justice minister Sacky Shanghala -- had assured him that Namibia's governing party, Swapo, had given them permission to create an entity that could be used to funnel money towards the party.

Court documents show that approximately NAD 100 million was funneled via de Klerk and Geingob's lawyer Sisa Namandje to fund Swapo and other cronies, the Namibian reports.

Some of this figure was also used to pay politicians directly within Geingob's leadership group, such as the deputy minister of works and transport Veikko Nekundi, and Swapo Youth League secretary Ephraim Nekongo.

Previously, Geingob has denied any knowledge of the Fishrot scandal before it was broken globally by whistleblower Johannes Stefansson.

Meanwhile, De Klerk, who fled South Africa last year, is also due to be hit with corruption charges from the ACC.

De Klerk implicates Fishcor partner Louw

In a separate part of the affidavit, De Klerk also claims that he was first approached by Fishcor business partner AJ Louw regarding the Seaflower Pelagic Processing joint venture, and told that he could make obscene sums of money if he joined, The Namibian also reports.

Documents from Seaflower have shown that a group of fewer than five people was set to make NAD 3.6 billion from a partnership with Louw, who has so far denied any knowledge or involvement of the Fishrot scandal.

De Klerk would go on to establish an entity called Celax Investments Number One, which came with a 25% share in African Selection Fishing, the owner of a 60% stake in Seaflower. The ACC has said that Celax was used to funnel NAD 75m out of the joint venture and into funds belonging to Hatuikulipi, Shanghala, former fisheries minister Bernhard Esau, and Swapo's campaign.

Louw, in turn, claims that De Klerk's affidavit is factually incorrect. He claims to have no knowledge of De Klerk's involvement with the Fishrot scheme, and no involvement with any member of the Fishrot accused besides Fishcor chairman Hatuikulipi.

Louw added that he had only learned of Celax's money-laundering activities through the media.

title: Daily recap, Jan. 18: Crab price pressure; Trident’s outbreak; Cargill’s investments
content:
Here's a recap of the daily seafood news from Monday, Jan. 18:

Considerable uncertainty remains about what the state of US foodservice demand will be like in the coming months and that's complicating life for importers of blue and red swimming crab. But, for now, output from key supplier Indonesia is down and prices are rising.

As tracked by the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, American harvesters saw 29% less revenue during the first seven months of 2020 than during the same period over the previous five years due to COVID-19. Effects were keenly felt in the US state of Alaska, columnist Laine Welch reported. 

Also in Alaska, Trident Seafoods is working to contain an outbreak of coronavirus in its plant in Akutan, the largest such facility in North America. Four workers have been sickened to date, the company said.

Looking beyond the pandemic, Cargill, the world's largest agricultural company, has no intention to slow down as it expands into the global aquaculture industry.. The company believes that the Chinese economy will lead a global rebound in 2021.

Undercurrent News also recently spoke to investor Christian Lim who believes that digital advancements in farming could benefit ocean health, and within that, aquaculture. 

Additionally, Thailand's Charoen Pokphand Foods is targeting a 50% share of China’s market for imported vannamei shrimp broodstock in three years, after resuming normal sales to China this month.

Eyeing succession planning to eventually replace CEO Wally Stevens, the Global Aquaculture Alliance has named Brian Perkins, the Americas director for the Marine Stewardship Counci as its chief operating officer. GAA sister organization Global Seafood Assurances, which operates the recently created Responsible Fishing Vessel Standard, will be merged later this year with the GAA under a renamed entity, Global Seafood Alliance.

Lastly, five employees at Australian salmon farmer Huon Aquaculture Group have been arrested and charged amid a theft investigation after the company found discrepancies in stock records at the company’s Ingleburn processing plant to the tune of AUD 2.1 million ($1.6m).

title: Police arrest five workers accused of stealing salmon worth $1.6m at Huon’s plant
content:
Australian salmon farmer Huon Aquaculture Group said it identified discrepancies in stock records at the company’s Ingleburn processing plant over the six-month period to December 2020, with an estimated inventory value of AUD 2.1 million ($1.6m).

The matter revealed the possibility of coordinated criminal conduct by employees at the plant, the firm said.

The company has alerted New South Wales Police Force and five Huon employees have been arrested and charged. The employees have been terminated or stood down pending the outcome of the police investigation and ongoing court proceedings, according to the firm.

Huon confirms that whilst sales for the period ending Dec. 31 2020 were unaffected, the book value of inventory and gross margins would be AUD 2.1m lower than would otherwise be the case for that period. The company is exploring avenues to recover some or all of this amount, it said.

Huon will not be commenting further on this matter while the ongoing police investigations and court proceedings remain active, the firm said.

title: Four arrested in shooting incident near Nova Scotia First Nation group’s docks
content:
Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) this week arrested four men in connection with shots allegedly fired Sunday near the Pictou Landing First Nation's fishing docks, in the province of Nova Scotia, the Toronto Star reports.

It's not clear if the incident is related to ongoing tensions between First Nation lobster harvesters and other commercial harvesters.

The Sipekne’katik First Nation kicked a hornet's nest in September when they launched vessels from St. Mary's Bay into lobster fishing area 34, on the southwestern coast of the province, more than two months ahead of the regular season start date. The group reported its actions to be in step with a Canadian Supreme Court ruling made some 21 years earlier that allowed fishing in pursuit of a "moderate livelihood" and said it would take less than 5% of the lobster in the area. However, the group reports to have stopped its fishing efforts. 

The Pictou Landing First Nation resides instead in the middle of LFA 26, on the northwestern coast of Nova Scotia, in a combined 1,304-acre area that includes five reserves and a population of just under 500. It is one of multiple First Nation groups that is part of a deal with Canadian food firm Premium Brands Holdings to acquire Clearwater Seafoods, as reported by Undercurrent News.

Based on the police reports, officers responded to a call of gunfire in the Northumberland Strait near the port at around 5:30 pm on Sunday. Police said they were told that a man from the Indigenous band was on a small boat when he saw the crew members of a commercial fishing vessel removing lobster traps from the water. When he approached, they allegedly accelerated toward him and shots were fired.

The man was uninjured and was able to return to port, according to the police report.

A 51-year-old man from Pictou County, who isn't identified in the news service article, turned himself in Monday evening and was arrested. The other three men from the area were arrested the next morning without incident, according to the news service.

Pictou Landing Chief Andrea Paul reportedly said, in an interview Monday, that members of the First Nation were unnerved by the incident. However, police said they believe the shooting was an isolated incident and there is no threat to the public.

Corporal Lisa Croteau said Monday that no charges have been filed, but the investigation is continuing.

title: Namibia’s ‘Fishrot’ investigation completed, more arrests planned
content:
Namibia has completed its investigation into the "Fishrot" scandal, with six defendants expected to remain in prison until their trial next spring, reports Iceland's RUV, citing The Namibian.

The case is scheduled for April 22, 2021, and more arrests are expected.

Former ministers Bernhard Esau and Sacky Shanghala, former CEOs Ricardo Gustavo and James Hatuikulipi, and cousins ​​of the latter, Tamson Fitty Hatuikulipi and Pius Taxa Mwatelulo are accused of corruption, bribery and abuse of power. 

According to Ed Marondedze, the prosecutor in the case, the investigation has been formally completed. He appealed to the court to adjourn the case until March 26, 2021, but then a decision was made to transfer it to the Supreme Court. The six defendants will be remanded in custody until then, unless they are allowed to pay bail. 

An additional three are expected to be arrested in the near future in connection with the case, including lawyer Maren de Klerk.

RUV also continues to draw links between an investigation of Norway's DNB Bank and Icelandic firm Samherji, which has been connected to Namibia's Fishrot scandal by a former executive-turned-whistleblower. 

A NOK 400 million ($45.4m) fine which might be levied against Norway's largest bank is unrelated to its role in its handling of payments from Iceland's Samherji to Namibia, the latter company has said. 

Samherji has complained at RUV's reporting, which has again alleged links between Samherji and corruption in Namibia via an intermediary named Cape Cod FS. The Icelandic giant said it has "corrected" RUV on this several times, and so the Icelandic media outlet is now repeating what it knows to be false; RUV, meanwhile, simply said it was unconvinced by Samherji's explanations.

title: Benin navy nabs trawler fishing illegally near ecological reserve
content:
Armed navy sailors raided an industrial trawler in the Port of Cotonou, Benin, placing it under arrest after it was found fishing illegally on Oct. 29, according to NGO Sea Shepherd.

Some nights earlier, Sea Shepherd's crew on board the vessel Bob Barker assisted Beninese authorities in documenting the fishing boat Fada 18 as it fished inside a special management area reserved for local artisanal fishermen that extends up to five nautical miles from the coast of Benin.  

Fada 18 was caught fishing just outside the Bouche du Roy ecological reserve. The reserve consists of mangroves and lagoons critical to fish nurseries.

It’s part of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO)-listed mono biosphere reserve, home to nearly two million people in Benin and Togo, and particularly rich in biodiversity as it’s positioned in a wildlife corridor frequented by migrating tuna and humpback whales.

title: The Winding Glass: Don’t fear expansion of native seafood rights
content:
John Sackton, Seafood.com News

(The Winding Glass is the commentary and opinion column by John Sackton, founder of SeafoodNews)

The Canadian lobster industry is in turmoil over first nation fishing rights. In 1999, the Canadian supreme court ruled that Mi'qmaq and other First Nations had harvest rights that had to be recognized by the Canadian government. For decades, this was never implemented.

For that reason, the Sipekne'katik First Nation began a test case, issuing 11 licenses themselves, limited to 50 traps each, and beginning to fish lobster in southwestern Nova Scotia during the closed season.

This led to riots, the burning of lobster pounds, attacks on boats and gear, and threats to any entity that purchased these lobsters.

This is not a unique problem nor a unique response. The 1975 Boldt decision in the US, that upheld tribal fishing rights in Washington state, also saw beatings, arrests and breakups of native fishing camps.

The assertion of First Nation or aboriginal rights that had long been suppressed is happening in many countries where Europeans erased these rights over centuries. Such is the case in the United States, South Africa, New Zealand, and Canada among others. Many governments see this as a civil rights issue and are supportive of remedial action.

But in terms of fisheries, no one who has existing quota is willing to give it up without a fight. In Shippagan, New Brunswick, in 2003, a brand new Daley Bros. crab plant was burned to the ground during a riot after the company contracted with three vessels on loan to Elsipogtog First Nation. This came as the Canadian government tried to revise crab quotas.

There were also huge fights in the Gulf of St. Lawrence over the expansion of crab quotas to temporary license holders, and the efforts of the gov’t to make them permanent. Also in Newfoundland, the reduction in inshore shrimp quotas due to stock decline has sparked huge fights against offshore quota holders, even as the original expansion of inshore shrimp licenses was specifically in a last-in, first-out system.

So the violent reaction of Nova Scotia lobstermen has a long history.

But that does not mean First Nation rights should be ignored. The fact that these fishing rights have not been honored does not make them moot.

There are a number of examples of successful integration of first nation sovereignty over their fishing rights with the larger commercial fisheries community. It may be helpful to review them.

Washington State tribal fisheries

This fall is the 50th anniversary of the violent breakup of the tribal fishing camp at the Puyallup River Bridge, that sparked the lawsuit that resulted in judge Boldt’s decision upholding the fishing rights of nearly 20 western Washington tribes based on treaties signed with the federal government. 

Since then the tribes have become co-managers with Washington state, and have treaty rights to 50% of the salmon harvest. Some of the larger tribes have hired fisheries managers and have full resource and conservation departments.

However, 50% of nothing is nothing, and Washington state salmon fisheries have been decimated by loss of habitat. This led the tribes to sue the state over failure to modify road culverts so as to ensure salmon migration. This suit was successful at the US Supreme Court, and Washington has a program to upgrade road culverts over the next ten years that will cost upwards of $2 billion.

In this case, the interests of the tribal fisheries and other Washington commercial fishermen are the same: protect and enhance the resource.

The Washington tribes also participate in other fisheries, such as Dungeness crab, halibut, sablefish, etc., and sell through tribal-owned companies and non-tribal commercial buyers.

The key point is that there is a mechanism for overall fisheries management where the commercial fishery seasons are the same for tribal and non-tribal harvesters, and the ceremonial and cultural use of fish is allowed in a manner that does not infringe on the commercial harvests.

In Canada, the failure to more clearly define subsistence or non-commercial use and commercial use for economic gain has unnecessarily exacerbated the conflict.

CDQ Fisheries in Alaska

Alaska is unique in the US in that there never were territorial agreements between the US government and Native inhabitants. In 1971, congress passed the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, which extinguished aboriginal land titles and resource claims in Alaska. This was necessary to build the oil pipeline to Alaska's North Slope.

In exchange, 12 regional corporations and more than 200 village corporations were formed and tasked with dual mandates: create economic opportunities through for-profit enterprises and support shareholders through educational opportunities, scholarships, elder benefits, and social and cultural programs. The government transferred 44 million acres in direct ownership and paid nearly $1 billion in 1971.

In 2017, the 12 Native corporations had combined annual revenues of $8.4bn. The net profit from these returns is what funds many local activities.

When the settlement act passed, there was almost no Alaskan fishing in the Bering Sea and Aleutian Islands (BSAI). As the fishery developed and became Americanized, the western Alaska villages faced being shut out of the economic benefits.

The idea for the community development quota (CDQ) program was to ensure participation in the fishery by villages that historically depended on BSAI fisheries. In order to qualify for CDQ, communities had to be located within 50 miles of the coast, certified under the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, and reliant on BSAI fisheries for at least half of their fishing. The 65 villages that qualified were divided into six regional CDQ groups, who initially were allocated 7.5% of the Bering Sea pollock quota in the 1990’s. The program was very successful in improving economic conditions in these villages which suffered from extreme poverty. By 2006 the quota shares were increased to 10% and expanded to include all the BSAI fisheries, including crab, halibut etc.

Because of their quota rights they had significant negotiating leverage with partners in the Alaska commercial fisheries. Initially, they partnered by offering their quota shares to the existing companies for production and marketing. But over time, they were able to buy out a significant percentage of their partners, and now in many fisheries, CDQ-affiliated companies harvest 25% to 50% or more of the specific fishery.

During this time, Alaska fisheries have grown as well, with the pollock, crab and sablefish being especially profitable. 

The key message here is that government support for a successful economic integration led to a realistic sharing of the value of the BSAI fisheries with Alaska native groups. It was easier because it was done while the Alaskan fisheries were being developed, and not after the fact when long-established practices and historical allocations already existed.

At the time of the pollock allocation, the entire division of the pollock fishery was up for grabs between the inshore and offshore sectors, and it gave native advocates huge leverage in Washington, as all parties depended on a government resolution to the allocation questions.

Clearwater

Finally, there is the example of Clearwater. Clearwater is the largest vertically integrated Canadian fishing company focused on shellfish. Clearwater has done a better job at integrating First Nations' demands for equity in fisheries than the entire Canadian government.

The biggest weakness in the Canadian system is that until the recent fisheries reform act, there was immense pressure to settle all fisheries questions as political favors. The fisheries minister at the federal level had absolute authority over the allocation of quotas, the setting of quotas, and the annual renewal of licenses. This led to abuse. In some cases, it led to overexpansion of fisheries and or processing licenses. In others, it led to poor and non-transparent fishery decisions.

The most spectacular failure recently was the corrupt attempt to let a consortium of favored First Nations work with a straw company connected to the federal minister grab 25% of the arctic surf clam allocation from Clearwater. 

As part of its commitment to expand first nation access, the government of premier Justin Trudeau announced that it would open a bid process for a portion of the arctic surf clam quota, of which Clearwater with three clam vessels, was the only current active license holder. Clearwater put together a bid with a group of first nations that would have shared the economic value but retained the current structure of the fishery. Instead, the award was made to a company that failed on paper to meet the bidding criteria. Even worse, it involved a relative of Dominic LeBlanc, then fisheries minister, from his home riding in New Brunswick. He was later found to have violated ethics rules and is no longer fisheries minister.

The ham-handed government attempt collapsed under this cloud of malfeasance, and Clearwater then took the initiative to negotiate a 50-year agreement with 14 First Nations in Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, which provides millions of dollars of annual revenue sharing, plus access to business such as supplying the fishery. 

Chief Terrance Paul of Membertou First Nation and co-chair of the Assembly of Nova Scotia Mi'kmaq Chiefs said nothing like this has been done in the industry before at this level of collaboration between a traditional commercial player and First Nations partners.

In this case, the economic partnership, similar to those in Alaska, will provide long term benefits, structural stability to the fishery, and it can serve as a model for other collaboration.

However, it was possible because Clearwater had an existing monopoly on clam licenses. The same issue is being resolved with offshore lobster, where there are only eight licenses, all of which have been bought up by Clearwater. Now they are negotiating the sale of some of these licenses to First Nations.

However, with both arctic surf clam and lobster, these two deals involve marketing partnerships that preserve value, rather than erode value. In fisheries, secure control over a resource results in very large long term economic benefits, as can be seen in the pollock fishery in Alaska, and in the offshore lobster and arctic surf clam fisheries in Canada.

By integrating first nations into these existing structures, the value of the fishery is maintained and shared, rather than diminished.

How can this work for the lobster fishery?

The big difference between the lobster fishery and the Bering Sea and surf clam fisheries is that the lobster fishery is decentralized across thousands of harvesters and a number of lobster buyers. There is no fixed quota. And while the other fisheries require huge capital investments and are consolidated around a few companies the lobster fishery has many players, including new companies focused on sales to Asia, for example.

In the same vein, the Washington state tribal fisheries are not monolithic either. There are a large number of smaller-scale commercial fisheries in Washington, from salmon to crab to halibut and sablefish, in which there is now tribal participation.

It seems the first step needed is true integration into the management system. But in Canada, the First Nations also need to be treated as sovereign partners. The Department of Oceans and Fisheries (DFO) is not set up to do this because it is not able to share decision making. In a shared management system, there would be room at the table for existing lobster industry groups, first nations, and provincial and federal managers. At the moment, the centralized power of the DFO in lobster management is a hindrance to a resolution.

A shared management system could determine for example, whether a small-scale removal for local use was in fact a threat to the overall health of the stock, or not. Such a system could also determine that the same management system would apply across all commercial users, including first nations commercial users.

A second step would be to adopt more regulatory control over lobster. The current tools used by the DFO include closed seasons, carapace size, and trap limits. Also when there is a lobster glut, buyers have sometimes instituted trip limits.

Are these the best tools for ensuring the long term health of the lobster population? Australia and New Zealand, for example, operate on a strict individual fixed quota system. This has not prevented stock declines, but it has meant that stock declines can be better managed. The Canadian and US system is not equipped at all should lobster populations in the Gulf of Maine begin to drop due to continued warming beyond the current level.

As populations fall, some localities are hit harder than others, and this opens up the prospect of major gear conflict around access to the more productive areas. 

And, of course, there is the right whale issue. How right whale protections could impact the lobster industry is another source of tension.

First nation fishing rights are here to stay. It will be up to the stakeholders to negotiate clear paths forward for sharing and resource allocation. The more this happens in a bottom-up fashion involving local negotiations and accommodation, the better. The more it is top-down from the DFO which has a terrible track record, the more likely turmoil will continue.

The best path for the DFO is to take seriously the fact that they need to negotiate a global settlement around lobster rights that preserves both equity and fisheries management. They cannot do this behind closed doors, in a minister’s office making political tradeoffs. They must do this fully transparently in the open. That is the best hope for a resolution.

title: Crisis deepens at Namibia’s Fishcor as management, directors feud
content:
A difficult situation is brewing at the National Fishing Corporation of Namibia (Fishcor) where the relationship between upper management and the board of directors has rapidly deteriorated this year, reports The Namibian. 

Pair of Seaflower board members step down in legal spat with parent Fishcor

According to the news site, seven members of the management have accused the board of holding too much power since the departure of the latest CEO in June and gambling with the future of the state-owned processor. They claim that as many as 300 workers may go without pay this month.

"By the look of things, the company will not manage to pay salaries on 25 November 2020," the managers wrote in a letter. "This has been worsened by the fact that no fishing activities took place during the off-season month of October 2020."

In response, the board has accused the management of trying to sabotage the company by leaking information to be used against it, and ultimately excluded all senior managers from meetings due to what the Namibian claims is a lack of trust.

The management also claims to have been left out of eight separate meetings between July and September this year.

Fishcor has been heavily implicated in the Fishrot scandal, where ministers and officials allegedly accepted bribe payments from fishing companies in return for discounts on quota costs. Many of these quotas were allocated via Fishcor.

Former Fishcor chairman James Hatuikulipi, and former CEO Mike Nghipunya have both been under police custody for much of 2020 awaiting trial for their alleged roles in the scandal.

title: Namibia’s Tunacor acquires Samherji-linked fishing trawler Heinaste
content:
Namibian firm Tunacor has invested NAD 280 million ($17.9m) in the Namibian fishing industry by acquiring the Heinaste, a fishing trawler linked to Iceland's Samherji and a source of several lawsuits over the past year, Informante reports.

Tunacor's general manager Peya Hitula confirmed the company had bought the vessel from Heinaste Investment Namibia. It will be renamed the Tutungeni once it has been reflagged in Namibia.

Samherji threatens legal action over Namibia vessel seizure
 

The vessel, which has been docked in the port of Walvis Bay for almost a year after it was detained for entering and illegally fishing in Namibian waters in November 2019, is currently under vital repair and maintenance to get it ready to return to operations at sea.

"Tunacor has purchased the vessel under the conditions imposed by the office of the Attorney General because it is the authority that holds the vessel under arrest from Heinaste Investment Namibia, the owner of the arrested vessel," Hitula said.

"We understand that some minorities or individuals within the minority shareholders of the vessel may have different agendas, but the majority has legally agreed to the sale."

Besides, according to Hitula, the vessel's sale provides an opportunity for more than 100 Namibian crew members to be employed on it.

"Tunacor views the creation of employment as very important, and it would be in everyone’s interest to prevent the asset from deteriorating while docked in port for months," Hitula explained.

The firm will consider previous employees who worked on the vessel, but that process will be conducted in consultation with the government, he said.

The firm also recently recruited fishermen originally retrenched by the now-defunct Namsov Fishing Enterprises in 2015, having signed employment contracts in the last week of August.

title: South Carolina man arrested on charges of stealing shrimp trawler
content:

A deputy from Georgetown County Sheriff’s Office and an officer from the S.C. title: Pair accused in Fishrot case sued for NAD 11m
content:
Two figures at the heart of the ongoing Fishrot scandal in Namibia have been sued by one of the country's banks after failing to maintain repayments on a NAD 10.1 million ($621,000) loan this year, reports The Namibian.

Former justice minister Sacky Shanghala, as well as former Fishcor chairman James Hatuikulipi have been in police custody since the start of the year due to their role in the Fishrot corruption scandal, for which they are still awaiting trial.

The two are partners at the corporation Olea Investments Number Nine, which was granted the NAD 10.1m sum by Bank Windhoek in April 2017.

However, in a filing to the Windhoek High Court, the bank claims that Olea has failed to maintain repayments this year, in breach of its loan agreement. The corporation was in arrears with the amount of NAD 1.2m by the end of July, and the bank claims it is still owed NAD 11.07m.

Shanghala and Hatuikulipi also bound themselves as surety for the loan's repayment.

None of the defendants announced their intent to oppose the bank's legal action, and so the High Court granted a default judgement for the payment of NAD 11.07m against the two men and their corporation.

The pair will return to court on Dec. 14 for the first hearings of the two Fishrot criminal cases, according to The Namibian.

title: Untitled
content:
Iceland's Samherji Holding has taken a 50% stake in Boston, Massachusetts-based Aquanor Marketing, one of its longtime US customers, the company said.

Aquanor is an importer, distributor and marketer focused on fresh North Atlantic species including Arctic charr, cod, haddock, salmon and oysters under the Aquanor and WiAnno brands, Samherji said in a press release. 

The deal, which closed earlier this month, will increase the sales company's focus on frozen cod and Arctic charr, the release added. 

"This investment will allow us to continue our growth in the US, an important market for us that will become even more important in the future due to changes in demand related to the pandemic. Despite these tough circumstances we are looking forward to growing together with Aquanor and building on what is already a strong foundation," Thorsteinn Mar Baldvinsson, the CEO of Samherji said, in the release. 

Eric Kaiser will continue in his position as president and CEO of Aquanor, Samherji said. Orri Gustafsson will join Aquanor from Samherji as vice president of business development.

Samherji already owns a minority stake in Boston-based importer and distributor Slade Gorton & Co, which it purchased in 2016. 

Additionally, in 2018 as part of a drive to get closer to its final customers, Samherji did a deal for UK distributor Collins. 

Also, earlier on Wednesday, Samherji announced it had increased its stake in shipping company Eimskipafelag Islands (known as Eimskip), this time by 0.29%, to a total of 30.28%.

This time, it said, it intends to make an offer to other shareholders in Eimskip for their shares as required by law. Back in March, when it increased its shareholding to 30.11%, it was granted an exemption from the mandatory bid obligation. This was due to the spread of COVID-19 and the disruption that the epidemic had for the Icelandic economy at that time.

Samherji had sold shares in Eimskip when the exemption was granted, so the company's shareholding in Eimskip went below 30%.

The deals for Aquanor and Eimskip come as the company faces scrutiny for its alleged participation in Namibia's so-called "Fishrot" scandal.

Former employee and whistleblower Johannes Stefansson released thousands of emails and incriminating documents in November 2012 alleging that Samherji had paid key government officials and businessmen in order to obtain its quota holding in the country.

title: Maldives authorities arrest seven for smuggling drugs aboard tuna vessel
content:
Maldivian authorities have discovered 130 kilograms of drugs smuggled aboard a fishing vessel after making an interception at sea, reports The Edition.

The Maldives police service made seven arrests on Oct. 14 after searching the vessel, which had been intended for use in the country's yellowfin tuna fishery.

One of the men arrested was involved in a previous smuggling case aboard a drug-smuggling Iranian vessel which intercepted in November 2019. Six of the seven individuals have been remanded by the criminal court, while the seventh, a minor, has been remanded for 10 days by the Maldives' juvenile court.

One of the individuals confirmed to have planned the smuggling attempt is understood to also be a council member for the Maldives political opposition, the People's National Congress, according to the local media source Mihaaru.

title: Trial delayed for New Jersey fisherman detained in British Virgin Islands
content:
A trial for a fisherman from the US state of New Jersey accused of illegally entering the Caribbean territory of the British Virgin Islands (BVI) has been delayed without an explanation, the Ashbury Park Press reported.

The trial for Michael Foy, who has been jailed in the UK territory since June 9, was scheduled to begin on Sept. 9 but after he arrived at the courthouse he was told that the proceeding had been delayed until Oct. 5, the newspaper said, citing his attorneys.

No reason was reportedly given for the delay. The BVI director of public prosecutions Tiffany Scatliffe-Esprit did not respond to the newspaper's request for comment.

Foy's vessel Rebel Lady was carrying 7,000 pounds of tuna and swordfish when he was arrested by BVI customs officers and charged with illegal entry for violating the islands COVID-19 curfew. Officials later added the charges of unregistered and unlicensed fishing, and failure to arrive at a customs port.

Foy’s family has said that the Rebel Lady was laid-to offshore June 8, waiting for clearance to enter the BVI port of Road Town when he and his crew were approached by BVI authorities and instructed to follow their boat into port. He was arrested soon after.

title: Illegal trawlers fled Sierra Leone, says EJF
content:
Sierra Leone has urgently alerted other states in the region after three industrial trawlers escaped detention in Freetown port, according to an update from the Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF).

The Jian Mei 1, Jian Mei 4, and Hong Chang 1 had been sanctioned for violating national laws and regulations. Instead of paying their fines, the vessels reportedly fled the country. A regional search has been launched to locate the fugitive vessels and return them to Sierra Leone to face justice.  
 
Illegal fishing is a serious issue in West Africa, with trawlers devastating marine ecosystems and undermining local, small-scale fisheries industries that are critical sources of jobs and food security in the region, said EJF. In Sierra Leone, fisheries provide 9% of the economy, providing tens of thousands of jobs and the country’s main source of animal protein.

The Jian Mei 4. Credit: EJF

Authorities had arrested and sanctioned the three trawlers in recent months. Each had been documented by local fishers apparently operating in inshore waters where industrial trawling is banned. They were being held in Freetown port while the government awaited the payment of fines. However, on July 27 all three escaped port without paying. Authorities say they are unaware of their location and have appealed to neighboring states to help locate and return the vessels.
 
The nationality of the vessel owners has not been verified, though China Dialogue Ocean estimates that 75% of trawlers in Sierra Leone are connected to China. The role of Chinese vessels in West Africa has been under increasing scrutiny in recent months, with Chinese industrial trawlers making controversial efforts to fish in Senegal, Ghana and Liberia, in the face of opposition from local fishing associations.
 
In letters announcing the escape, Sierra Leone’s minister of fisheries and marine resources, Emma Kowa-Jalloh, said the vessels "were under arrest for infringing the laws and regulations of Sierra Leone [and] have left the country on July 27, 2020 illegally without fulfilling the relevant sanctions levied on them".

title: Another ‘Fishrot’ accused fails with bail appeal
content:
A bail bid by one of the men arrested and charged in one of the Fishrot fishing quotas corruption cases in Namibia has been dismissed in an appeal judgment, reports the Namibian.

Samherji dismisses watchdog allegations as ‘standard practice made suspicious’

Evidence has established that Gustavo purported to be the director of an entity called Namgomar Pesca -- which according to the state is not registered as a company -- and made misrepresentations that such an entity in fact existed, which entitled it to receive fishing quotas.

title: Former Namibian fisheries minister sees bail appeal denied
content:
The Windhoek high court has denied the country's former fisheries minister, in police custody since last December, from being released on bail ahead of his trial, reports The Namibian.

The court found that it was highly unlikely former minister Bernhard Esau was unaware of the direct benefit his son-in-law Tamson Hatuikulipi had from the allocation of fishing quotas to companies at the heart of the ongoing Fishrot investigations.

Both men's bail applications were therefore turned down by the high court magistrate.

The judge noted that based on the evidence brought before him, it appeared that the scheme to sell fishing quotas to processing firms and foreign companies in return for substantial kickbacks was orchestrated by Esau and the former justice minister Sacky Shanghala -- also in police custody awaiting trial.

Much of the state's case against Esau, Shanghala and the other members of the so-called 'Fishrot Six' at the heart of the investigation is likely to rest on the documents brought forward by original whistleblower and former Samherji employee Johannes Stefansson.

A great deal of Stefannson's account of events that led to the original arrest of the two former ministers appears to be corroborated by documents, other witness statements and the flow of money, the judge added.

title: Cornelis Vrolijk partner refutes crew charges of assault on fisheries observer
content:
A Namibian fishing company in which Dutch giant Cornelis Vrolijk is a partner has refuted charges leveled at three of its crewmembers that they assaulted and threatened an onboard fisheries observer.

The three Dutch fishermen appeared in the Swakopmund Magistrate's Court, Namibia, on July 17 on charges of assault, as well as threatening and intimidating the observer on the vessel Cornelis Vrolijk Fzn.

A spokesperson for Dutch fishing firm Cornelis Vrolijk forwarded Undercurrent News a statement from Nombili Fishing, the vessel's management firm, in which the latter said it was "highly disappointed by the unexpected charges brought against our three crew members".

"The arrests and allegations came as a total shock and surprise to the company and the crew, as no incidents occurred and/or were reported on the vessel which would remotely justify or support the charges in respect of which these crew members have now been charged."

Quarantine measures meant proper interviews with potential witnesses aboard the vessel could not be conducted by either the fisheries inspectors or the Namibian police, and Nombili said it was concerned this may have resulted in the "premature arrest of the crew in question, based on the unsubstantiated and potentially false allegations of only one fisheries observer".

The company is further investigating this case while fully cooperating with the authorities, it said.

The Cornelis Vrolijk Fzn is a Namibian vessel, working under a Namibian license with "an impeccable record and who only employs crew members who are respectable and experienced professionals", said the company.

"None of our crew have previously been charged with conduct of this nature with which these crew members have now been charged, as such conduct would never have been and will never be tolerated aboard our vessel."

Nombili stands by the rights of the accused crewmembers to defend the charges in court should the state persist with the charges once the police have been able to finalize their investigations, it said.

Local news site the Namibian specified it was the vessel's captain, chief mate, and fishing master who faced two charges: one of illegal dumping of fish at sea, and one of assaulting and intimidating the fisheries observer in the exercise of her duties. The alleged incident happened on June 26, and again on July 4.

Fisheries Observer Agency chief executive officer Stanley Ndara condemned the act.

The three Dutchmen are out on bail, with the matter postponed to Aug. 31 for further investigation.

title: Namibian court finds Fishrot firms transferred $6m via investment funds
content:
Documents submitted by Namibia's Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) have shown that two companies implicated in the ongoing Fishrot scandal transferred NAD 94 million ($6m) to a number of prominent investment firms over the past six years, reports The Namibian.

The documents, filed as part of the bail hearings for former fisheries minister Bernhard Esau and his son-in-law, Tamson Hatuikulipi, show that IJG Securities, PointBreak and Investec Asset Management Namibia received NAD 61m, NAD 23m, and NAD 10m respectively.

The funds came from the law firm DHC and Celax Investments, both co-owned by South African lawyer Maren De Klerk, who also served on the board of Seaflower Pelagic Processing, a joint venture between Fishcor and African Selection Fishing Namibia; both of whom have been accused of benefiting from ministerial corruption.

Court charges allege that both Seaflower and Celax were used as part of a money-laundering scheme, which allegedly transferred money into investment companies before returning it to Celax within the month.

Celax, which is also co-owned by South African businessman Adriaan Louw, has been accused of benefiting from NAD 75m diverted from Fishcor, whose CEO and chairman have both been arrested as part of the state investigation.

The development marks a new phase in the ACC's investigation, according to The Namibian, as the commission looks beyond the law firms allegedly used to funnel money from fishing quota sales to a number of politicians and businessmen, and places greater scrutiny on the banks and investment firms used to make the transactions possible.

title: Samherji-linked firm paid $2m to arrested Namibian minister’s son-in-law, court finds
content:
Tamson Hatuikulipi, the son-in-law of former Namibian fisheries minister Bernhard Esau, reportedly received NAD 30 million ($2m) via an owned corporation, paid by a subsidiary of Icelandic fishing giant Samherji, reports The Namibian.

Namibia’s ‘Fishrot’ scandal: from start to present

The news came out based on testimony provided by an Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) investigator during a bail hearing for both Hatuikulipi and Esau on July 7.

According to the witness testimony, Samherji's African subsidiary Esja Fishing paid the sum of NAD 29.7m to the corporation Erongo Holding and Clearing, where Hatuikulipi is the sole member.

The ACC said that Erongo Holding invoiced Esja for 'consultancy services', but an accountant with the latter claimed that no such services had ever been delivered to the firm by Erongo.

Payments were allegedly then made from Erongo to other linked companies belonging to other Namibian businessmen and ministers; Investec Asset Management managing director James Hatuikulipi -- an elder cousin of Tamson -- reportedly received NAD 1.8m, while a close corporation owned by Hatuikulipi, Grey Guard, received NAD 9.4m.

Meanwhile, the Camadara Trust, owned jointly by the elder Hatuikulipi and former justice minister Sacky Shanghala, received NAD 1m. Both men are also in police custody at present.

title: Dutch agents find €37m cocaine shipment in Colombian tuna
content:
Dutch customs officials discovered a 493-kilogram package of cocaine stashed within an import of tinned tuna arriving at the port of Rotterdam, reports NL Times.

The package, which had been shipped from Cartagena, Colombia en route to the German city of Kempen, had an estimated street value of €37 million, and has since been destroyed by authorities.

Five days earlier, Rotterdam customs officers had again discovered a package of drugs, this time a shipment of 780kg of cocaine within a container of pineapples sent from Costa Rica. The drugs on that occasion were discovered within a cooling and storage firm in Zuid-Holland, with no arrests.

In total, officials have discovered 18,000 kilograms of cocaine concealed within shipments so far this year, already just over half of the 33,732 kilos discovered at the port in 2019.
