title: Iranian flagged fishing vessels identified operating illegally in Somali EEZ
content:
Increased monitoring of the Somali exclusive economic zone (EEZ) has revealed the continuing presence of a fleet of unauthorized, Iranian flagged fishing vessels, according to Somali authorities.

Using a combination of automatic identification system (AIS) tracking, satellite remote sensing imagery and radar images Somali authorities have estimated that at least 200 vessels have been fishing illegally during the 2019-2020 fishing season. 

Between January 2019 to April 14 2020, approximately 112 Iranian fishing vessels were identified transmitting on AIS transponders from within the Somalia EEZ for a total of 2,533 days. In addition to the fishing vessels, 83 AIS net markers were also linked to Iran.

This is likely to be a conservative number due to the poor signal strength of the AIS transponders on these vessels. 

Minister of fisheries and marine resources of the federal government of Somalia, Abdilahi Bidhan Warsame, said after opening up waters through a licensing system it was a slap in the face. Since 2018, more than $2.6 million has been raised by Somalia through licence fees. 

"Having worked so hard to develop a transparent licensing system it is very concerning to see that foreign fleets are not prepared to go through the legitimate channels to gain access to fish in Somalia," he said.

Vessels identified include the FV ARESH, an Iranian flagged fishing dhow arrested in April 2015 by the Galmudug coast guard and fined $100,000 for illegal fishing and the FV SIRAJ and FV JABER, both hijacked south of Hobyo, while they were operating close to shore in March 2015. A total of 39 crew members were captured between the two vessels.

A further 43 markers could be matched to vessels transmitting on AIS, however, 17 transmitted a vessel name that was not matched to a vessel AIS and the remaining 33 were not broadcasting a discernible name. This suggests that the Iranian fleet operating inside the Somalia and Yemen EEZs consists of at least 192 vessels. 

"The AIS analysis of the AIS net markers and data from remote sensing techniques suggests the foreign fleets operating inside the Somalia EEZ is significantly larger than seen from the AIS alone and represent one of the most substantial organized illegal fleets in the Western Indian Ocean for more than a decade," said Global Fishing Watch, which helped develop the report with Trygg Mat Tracking. 

Warsame added: "We call on all distant water fishing nations to ensure they are controlling their flagged vessels and to respect our sovereignty and fisheries management regime. Our focus is on developing a safe, sustainable and fair fishing industry to benefit our nation."

Information about the licensing system, legal framework and legally licensed fishing vessels is available on the ministry website.

title: Namibia’s Fishcor sees latest CEO removed from post
content:
The CEO of Namibia's National Fishing Corporation of Namibia (Fishcor) has been removed from his post for transporting an alleged fugitive into the country, reports the Namibian.

Paulus Ngalangi was removed from his position on June 17 after the alleged South African fugitive tested positive for coronavirus.

The alleged fugitive reportedly entered the country on June 12 by crossing the Orange River in a canoe, with the aid of a police officer, before being assisted by Ngalangi in their journey to the capital, Windhoek.

Ngalangi had been Fishcor's chief financial officer since April 2015, but was moved to the post of acting CEO after former CEO Mike Nghipunya was suspended for his role in the Fishrot scandal last December.

Nghipunya was ultimately taken into police custody in February after information came to light that implicated him in the scandal involving several high profile politicians and businesses, as well as Icelandic company Samherji.

Fishcor had been one of the chief benefactors of the revised horse mackerel quotas issued by former fisheries minister Bernhard Esau from 2014 onwards, and had allegedly been used to sell many of these quotas on at discounted prices to foreign businesses.

Minister of public enterprises Leon Jooste confirmed that Ngalangi had been removed from the top job, and that the ministry was currently identifying the best individual to replace him.

title: Dalian Tianbao to delist from Shenzhen stock exchange
content:
Chinese seafood processor Dalian Tianbao Green Foods will delist from the Shenzhen stock exchange on June 30, the firm said. 

Shenzhen stock exchange informed the firm June 18 that it would terminate its listing under articles 14.4.1 (18) and 14.4.2 of the exchange's listing rules. 

In scandal’s wake, large Chinese processor posts staggering $270m loss

The delisting follows a tumultuous 18 months at the firm, during which it was deluged with lawsuits by creditors.

It also follows an invoicing scandal perpetrated by executives, including Dalian Tianbao’s chairman and majority shareholder, Huang Zuoqing. Last summer Huang was arrested over the scandal. 

According to the firm, shares in Dalian Tianbao will be transferred to China’s national market for small and medium-sized enterprises.

title: ‘Notorious’ trawler re-arrested in Ghana, says EJF
content:
A Chinese-owned trawler flying the Ghanaian flag has been detained again for the same fishing crimes as it was apprehended for a year ago, the Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF) has said.

The Lu Rong Yuan Yu 956, operated by Chinese company Rongcheng Ocean Fishery Co, was issued with a fine for using under-size mesh nets and taking fish below minimum landing size in October 2019. Despite refusing to pay, the vessel had its license renewed, said EJF. Last month Ghana's marine police apprehended it again under almost identical charges.
 
"This blatant disregard for the law is enabled by a lack of deterrent sanctions and the decision – taken by government officials in the full knowledge of these crimes – to re-license the vessel before the fine was paid," said the NGO. "If the government does not crack down on these practices it will endanger the livelihoods and food security of millions of Ghanaians."
 
The Lu Rong Yuan Yu 956 was initially apprehended in June 2019 for using nets with a mesh size below the legal minimum and taking fish smaller than legal landing size. The vessel operators had failed to declare the catches at port; according to the authorities, they planned to trade them illegally at sea in a practice known as ‘saiko’.
 
In October 2019, the owners were issued with a fine of $1 million by an out of court settlement committee, and an additional GHS 124,000 ($21,300) for the fish onboard the vessel. However, the owners refused to pay the fine and the case returned to court. Despite this, the vessel license was renewed, and the trawler put to sea again, fishing in the waters of both Ghana and neighboring Cote d’Ivoire.
 
On May 30 2020, the marine police apprehended the vessel again, and again the charges brought were nets with a mesh size below the legal limit and undersized fish. The vessel will be detained until June 16, when the case is due to come before court.
 
Around 90% of Ghana’s industrial fishing fleet is linked to Chinese ownership, an EJF investigation claimed to reveal in 2018. As Ghana’s fisheries laws prohibit foreigners from engaging in joint ventures in the industrial trawl sector, Chinese organizations operate through Ghanaian ‘front’ companies, using opaque corporate structures to import their vessels, register, and obtain a license.
 
"These repeat offenses show that the system of sanctions in Ghana is not having a deterrent effect," said EJF. "Under international law, Ghana has a responsibility to establish and implement a system of deterrent sanctions that deprives offenders of the benefits flowing from their illegal fishing activities. The fact that the vessel was authorized by the Ghanaian authorities to fish in Cote d'Ivoire, despite its failure to pay a fine for serious illegal fishing offenses, shows that Ghana's decisions on these cases have international importance."

title: Ghana retracts, bans tuna-bait fishing with artificial lights again
content:
Ghana's Fisheries Commission has reversed its previous decision to allow vessels to use artificial lights to fish for live bait, for use in tuna fishing, reports Business24.

The decision was taken in April, following pressure from the Ghana Tuna Association. The vessels used lights to catch small pelagics in the waters off Saltpond and Keta, which is against Ghanaian law, according to the Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF).

Canoe fishers, who were not allowed to use light fishing, had expressed their disagreement with the practice.

“Why was the decision made in the first place without consultation of the affected fishing communities and without basis in law? Transparency and inclusiveness in fisheries decision making is crucial to protect fish populations, livelihoods and food security in Ghana,” said executive director of EJF Steve Trent.

EJF said there was concern that the exemption for vessels could result in tensions between the navy and fishing communities.

On May 8, Ghana's navy, which is responsible for enforcement at sea, proceeded to arrest two vessels for using light to fish in the waters off Keta.

title: Editor’s recap: Grobest sees opening for small shrimp in Asia; Freight rates could tumble after hike
content:
Tom Seaman, editorial director of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

As the dust settles and the long-term impact of the global coronavirus pandemic on seafood markets around the world becomes clearer, one of the key themes emerging in many countries is the need for a renewed focus on local seafood production for domestic consumption.

According to Taiwanese feed giant Grobest Holdings, that is likely to be one of several main outcomes for Asia’s shrimp sector. “I think there’s a good lesson to learn for the whole value chain, and the main thing is most of the shrimp being produced in Asia -- except in China -- is mostly exported to other countries,” CEO Samson Li told Daniel Gibson. “So this pandemic, it’s a wake-up call for everybody.”

A rise in freight rates linked to the logjam in Chinese ports earlier in the year is adding to the issues for the frozen seafood sector, already under pressure as the spread of coronavirus globally causes havoc in economies.  

However, when the global container capacity gets back in sync and with trade likely to be down in the COVID-19 pandemic, prices could come down rapidly, sources told me. 

In a webinar organized by PricewaterhouseCoopers, executives with global food giants Archer Daniels Midland and Cargill agreed the COVID-19 pandemic has led to a customer-led transformation of food supply and demand in just a few weeks. 

More seafood plants are being impacted by the pandemic. Thai Union Group has closed its Pioneer Food Cannery in Tema, Ghana after a COVID-19 outbreak reportedly linked to over 500 cases in the country. 

Reports in the local media said the company had re-opened the cannery last Monday with reduced output, but a spokesperson for the company told me it's closed again. 

Charoen Pokphand Foods, Thailand's other global seafood giant, anticipates a better performance from its shrimp aquaculture operations in 2020, it said.

In its Q1 report, looking ahead to the year, said it expects improving overseas aquaculture performance; opportunities from a "new normal" after COVID-19 raises demand for food safety products; and a focus on efficiency improvement and "prudent investment".

Chinese customs authorities have arrested smugglers in Guangdong province, south China, suspected of illegally importing CNY 250 million ($35.2m) worth of shrimp broomstick.

Chile is the site of a substantial build-up of frozen salmon inventories at the close of the first quarter, aquaculture giant Mowi said in its Q1 report.

"The difference between supply and consumption in the first quarter 2020 of approximately 10,000 [metric tons, gutted weight] is mainly related to frozen inventory build-up of Chilean salmon," the firm wrote. "In total for the Chilean industry, frozen inventories are projected to be in the range of 40,000-50,000t."

US salmon buyers are looking to Alaska for supply this year, said Louis Anello, vice president of purchasing and support at Santa Monica Seafood. 

“Well, ultimately we have to see if the fish show up, right?” Anello said, on a salmon outlook webinar organized by Undercurrent News. “That's the unknown. If the fish show up, our hope is that we do look to our wild salmon supplies that are here within our continent. And then, with fuel prices down, and packaging prices should follow, [we hope] that we are able to drive business that way, as well as to keep our people working."

A big piece of Alaska salmon consolidation is getting closer, with Canadian seafood giant Cooke and Ocean Beauty Seafoods edging toward a deal that would merge their Alaska salmon processing operations. The deal has yet to close but has been agreed to in principle, the source confirmed. 

Lawyers for former Bumble Bee Foods CEO Christopher Lischewski have asked judge Edward Chen to sentence him to no more than 12 months' home confinement and a maximum fine of $25,000 after his December conviction on the charge of price-fixing.

At the same time, prosecutors with the US Department of Justice has asked the judge to consider a sentence of eight to 10 years and a $1m fine. A pre-sentencing report prepared in the case has called for Lischewski to receive a four-year prison sentence and a $100,000 fine. Chen, a US federal court judge based in San Francisco, California, is scheduled to sentence Lischewski on June 3.

title: Chinese authorities seize 1,600 smuggled shrimp broodstock
content:
Additional reporting by Hu Luyi in Guangzhou

Chinese customs authorities have arrested smugglers in Guangdong province, south China, suspected of illegally importing a total of CNY 250 million ($35.2m) worth of shrimp broodstock.

On May 12 customs officials and police raided premises in Zhanjiang and Maoming counties in Guangdong, seizing the smuggling ring's latest efforts -- 1,600 broodstock worth an estimated CNY 800,000. They arrested eleven individuals from six separate smuggling groups, Zhanjiang Customs Department said in a release on May 14.

The department released footage of officials examining containers filled with broodstock and suspects being placed under arrest.

Seized shrimp broodstock. Credit: Zhanjiang Customs

According to the report, the seized broodstock was brought in from the US and Thailand. It would be flown to Vietnam and then brought across the country’s northern border with Guangxi province, southwest China.

Alternatively, it was flown to Hong Kong then smuggled into Guangdong via Shenzhen. The imported broodstock then was sold on to hatcheries in shrimp farming regions such as Zhanjiang and Hainan.

The smugglers are suspected of importing 46,000 cases of broodstock in total, worth CNY 250m, Zhanjiang customs said, avoiding an estimated CNY 30m in import duties. 

Suspect is interviewed by officials before arrest. Credit: Zhanjiang Customs

The raids come amid reported outbreaks of “glass post-larvae” at Chinese hatcheries, a disease believed to be caused by a new virus. This could be increasing demand for specific pathogen-free imported broodstock.

China imports shrimp broodstock from primarily the US, Thailand, and Indonesia. In 2017, the country’s biggest supplier was Shrimp Improvement Systems, a subsidiary of Charoen Pokphand Indonesia, according to Chinese figures.

title: Firm advised by former UK politician linked to funding behind Tugushev’s Norebo case
content:
17 Arm -- a global asset tracing and corporate intelligence firm advised by former UK foreign secretary Malcolm Rifkind -- is funding Alexander Tugushev's ongoing legal bid to get what he claims he is owed for founding what is now one of Russia's largest fishing company, Norebo Holdings.

Delayed Norwegian court case to ‘shine light’ on Roth’s businesses, taxes

Tugushev's case, taking place in London, UK, sees him claiming Vitaly Orlov -- CEO and now sole owner of the firm -- and another co-founder of Norebo, Magnus Roth, have deliberately denied him his one-third (worth in excess of $350 million) of the company, which is valued at more than $1.5 billion.

The source of Tugushev's funding for the court battle has been a mystery, but now UK newspaper the Guardian claims to have revealed 17 Arm is putting up the cash. The firm told the newspaper "litigation funding is a common mechanism which empowers aggrieved people, who couldn’t otherwise afford to bring litigation, to fight their cases and win justice".

The newspaper explained that litigation funding sees a commercial firm backed by private investors pay the upfront cost of barristers and solicitors to fight a case for an individual who has a legal claim. If the individual wins, the commercial firm is rewarded with a cut of money won in court. If the individual loses, the firm gets nothing.

To avoid identification during the proceedings, those providing financial backing to Tugushev have already had to pay into court sums in excess of £3m as security for the costs which Orlov, Roth, and Petrik have incurred. This is in addition to the costs of their own legal team, plus private detectives and public relations consultants.

17 Arm is advised by two public figures in the UK; former Conservative foreign secretary Malcolm Rifkind and former director of public prosecutions Ken Macdonald, among other "establishment figures," said the Guardian.

Lord Clanwilliam, 17 Arm’s chairman, declined to respond to the news site when asked how much it would win if Tugushev were victorious in his legal claim. The company's advisory board gives advice on potential legal claims to see if, for example, they have a reasonable claim of winning.

Tugushev has, in the past, served six years in prison after being convicted of fraud in Russia. Asked if 17 Arm was giving credibility to a legal claim advanced by a convicted fraudster, the firm and its advisers told the Guardian: “We believe in the right of every individual to have their case heard in a court of law.”

The firm added: “A disputed conviction in a jurisdiction notorious for corrupt and unfair trials is no bar to bringing an arguable and admissible case in London, where a just outcome can be expected. The English high court agreed that this case was properly brought here – and its ruling was so patently correct that the court of appeal has refused the defendants’ permission to appeal against it.”

Orlov's team having none of it

Vitaly Orlov's legal team has taken umbrage at 17 Arm's suggestion that the conviction might be "disputed".

It told Undercurrent News that "whether [17 Arm's] claim [to be funding the case] should be believed is a moot point, because the newspaper reports too that the company in question...is also claiming that Tugushev is disputing his 2007 conviction, notwithstanding that he served his six-year prison sentence in full and paid a fine of one million rubles".

Tugushev’s legal team claims Murmansk ruling a blow for Orlov

"Tugushev was convicted in the face of overwhelming evidence, including a police sting, which proved beyond doubt that Tugushev had abused his position as a state official to extract bribes totaling the equivalent of $3,700,000. His guilt is beyond question, and the validity of his conviction is not in doubt," it stressed.

It called the suggestion that Tugushev’s conviction was somehow flawed "ludicrous".

"Not only has Tugushev himself committed serious criminal offenses, but he openly associates with criminals, then and now. He is moreover currently on the run from Russia, where he a warrant has been issued for his arrest in connection with yet another criminal investigation."

Murmansk's Oktyabrsky District Court arrested Tugushev in absentia on March 25, "charged with fraud on a particularly large scale". "Due to the fact that he left the Russian Federation, the accused was put on the international wanted list. 

'Wary of reprisals'

Tugushev's legal team was unwilling to confirm whether 17 Arm was indeed his financial backer.

“Alexander Tugushev’s litigation is being funded by an independent third party who has no previous engagement with the case. Receiving third-party funding for litigation is not unusual," it said.

"Given Mr. Tugushev’s previous relationship with Mr. Orlov, he is wary of reprisals if he provides Mr. Orlov with the details of this independent funder."

Tugushev remains focused on securing his substantial ownership interests in the Norebo Group, and righting the wrongs perpetrated against him by his former business partners, the team concluded.

Attending hearing from home

A case management conference (CMC) in the matter of Tugushev and Orlov, and others, will take place next month. The courtroom for the litigation will, as usual, be in the Rolls Building of London’s High Court, and although the two-day hearing (May 18 and 19) should be exceptionally busy, it is likely that not a soul will actually be in the courtroom.

Thanks to the coronavirus, every participant in the proceedings -- judge, counsel, solicitors, and press -- will be participating from their personal lockdown quarters, although the lawyers at least will be dressing, as instructed, in business attire. 

Amongst other things, the CMC will deal with the quantum of further security for costs to be paid into court by Tugushev’s anonymous backers. In this context, the Tugushev team will also be asked to provide assurances that the monies which are being paid into court originate from known and reputable sources.

The full trial of this matter is not expected to take place before Easter 2022.

title: Murder of Pacific tuna fisheries observer brings attention to dark history
content:
The death of a 40-year-old fisheries observer from a tiny island country northeast of Australia aboard a Taiwanese tuna purse seiner is under investigation by local police and causing a renewed focus on the recent dark history associated with the job.

Eritara Aati Kaierua’s death was reported on March 3 in waters off Nauru, a tiny island country near Australia, according to Stuff, a New Zealand-based online publication. Kaierua, who worked for the Kiribati government and was a father of four children, was found lying on the floor of his locked cabin in the Win Far 636, a 30-year-old vessel owned by Kuo Hsiung Fishery, based in Taiwan’s Kahsiung City. He had a brutal head wound and bruising to his neck.

The agent for the vessel, which was impounded, was Central Pacific Products Limited, a government-owned company. The Taiwanese government has reportedly alerted the multi-national regulatory body Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission and the Kiribati government. 

According to the observer’s log, Kaierua was seen boarding the vessel by his family on Feb. 3. However, the vessel’s tracking technology was switched off, so the voyage remains unclear. Two of the vessel’s Vietnamese-dominated crew were arrested upon arrival, but then released after questioning, according to the article.  

“The tragedy has sparked a call for more protection for this vulnerable workforce, who often face hostility from captains and crews,” the news service reports. “And it's brought to light the mysterious deaths of two more Kiribati monitors in the last three years.”

Ten observers have lost their lives in the region over the past decade with at least five of the deaths under a cloud of suspicion, but none have been prosecuted, Stuff reports.

title: Tugushev implies international arrest warrant is result of Norebo legal fight
content:
A Russian court in the Murmansk region has issued an international arrest warrant for fraud for Alexander Tugushev, one of the co-founders of Norebo Holding, reports TASS.

Tugushev is involved in a different ongoing court battle, taking place in London, UK, in which he claims Vitaly Orlov -- CEO and now sole owner of the firm -- and another co-founder of Norebo, Magnus Roth, have deliberately denied him his one-third (worth in excess of $350 million) of the company, which is valued at more than $1.5 billion.

Murmansk's Oktyabrsky District Court arrested Tugushev in absentia on March 25, "charged with fraud on a particularly large scale".

"Due to the fact that he left the Russian Federation, the accused was put on the international wanted list," TASS wrote. 

According to the investigation, Tugushev -- the former deputy head of the federal fisheries agency -- misled and stole more than RUB 30m rubles from Alexander Sychev, co-founder of fishing and processing firm Vostok.

Kommersant, meanwhile, reports that Tugushev arranged to create a joint venture with Sychev, fishing coldwater shrimp in the Barents Sea. "Using his contacts at the State Agency for Fisheries, Mr. Tugushev allegedly promised not only to invest his own funds in the project but also to protect the undertaking, which would guarantee its profitability," the news site wrote.

He allegedly had Sychev put up RUB 31m (nearly $400,000) for the purchase and repair of a vessel in 2017, but after Sychev had put up his half of the capital for Voskhod, he then contacted law enforcement, fearing he had been deceived by Tugushev, Kommersant added.

Tugushev's legal team told Undercurrent News he categorically denies any allegations of criminality and wrongdoing against him, and would appeal this decision.

"There are a number of close and unusual links between Mr. Orlov and this investigation, which resulted from a criminal complaint filed by Mr. Sychev," it claimed.

Orlov was in possession of a copy of Sychev’s criminal complaint long before Tugushev, his legal team claimed. "There is absolutely no reason why Mr. Orlov should be in possession of these documents, as he has no formal connection to this investigation whatsoever." Orlov has repeatedly refused to explain how he was aware of the criminal complaint at all, it said.

Further, Sychev’s lawyer in this investigation has previously appeared on a Murmansk television station to spread false rumors about Tugushev in relation to Orlov, Tugushev's team claimed.

"Mr. Orlov has well-established connections to this television station through his head of security, Mr. Prokopenko, raising questions about Mr. Orlov’s connection to Mr. Sychev’s lawyer."

Tugushev’s legal team was only provided with 24 hours’ notice before the court hearing in Murmansk, a city in which Orlov "exercises considerable influence", it added. "The fact that the court did not permit a temporary adjournment of the hearing to allow Mr. Tugushev’s legal team an opportunity to properly prepare and respond is a further indication that this is not a normal case."

It is also notable that these latest developments occurred shortly after Tugushev sent Orlov his draft amended claim in the London proceedings, increasing his claim to 45.75% of Norebo, Tugushev's team said.

"For these reasons, Mr. Tugushev strongly believes that this is yet another attempt by Mr. Orlov to interfere with his High Court claim in London through underhanded tactics.”

Orlov’s legal team told Undercurrent that neither Mr. Orlov nor Norebo was involved in this case in any way, and therefore had no comment to make. It did add, though, that it was "unsurprising that convicted fraudster Tugushev is wanted in connection with yet another fraud investigation". 

Earlier this year a Murmansk court rejected attempts by Orlov to have it disregard the jurisdiction of one of England's senior courts in his dispute with Tugushev.

In a statement, Tugushev's team said the Russian court had "rejected Mr. Orlov’s attempts to hide behind the Russian legal system to avoid decisions of the London High Court". 

However, a spokesperson for Orlov's legal representatives told Undercurrent the "application made to the Murmansk court was merely procedural", playing down the significance that Tugushev's team was lending it.

Then, one aspect of the legal disputes between the founders of Norebo took a new turn on Jan. 23 with a Hong Kong court's ruling that Magnus Roth should make a $35m interim payment as he buys Vitaly Orlov out of Three Towns Capital (TTC).

Last year high court judge Russell Coleman ordered Roth to buy the 50% share of Hong Kong holding fishing and transport company TTC, which is currently owned by Orlov. That came as Alexander Tugushev, the third founder of what is now Norebo, sought over $330m from Orlov in an equally bitter London legal process, claiming the latter and Roth swindled him out of it. 

On Jan. 23, 2020, Coleman ordered Roth to make an interim payment "from his own assets and resources (not those of TTC or the TTC Group)", according to a ruling.

title: Chile steps up COVID-19 prevention measures for salmon sector
content:
Chilean authorities have implemented new measures for the salmon sector to reduce the risk of transmission of COVID-19.

Actions are also being taken to reduce the probable impact on exports, given Chile's main salmon customers' actions to close their borders, the country's fishing and aquaculture regulator Sernapesca said.

Undercurrent reported March 19 that travel restrictions have limited the country's capacity to export salmon to the United States.

Salmon prices drop even as Chile travel restrictions limit export capacity to the US

But even as supply tightens, a massive drop in foodservice demand as the COVID-19 pandemic widens has prompted mass closings of bars and restaurants and caused US salmon prices to fall, not rise, industry sources told Undercurrent.

Sernapesca's new special measures for the sector aim to reduce the entry of people to farming centers and increase checks on authorizations to harvest, among other measures, the agency said. These and other provisions are being applied for the benefit of human health, animal health and the environment, it said.

Additionally, the country's legislature voted March 19 to postpone a much-anticipated referendum on a new constitution until October. The referendum was originally set to take place in April.

The scheduled vote to rewrite the country’s Augusto Pinochet-era constitution had calmed protests that sparked last September, disrupting Chilean salmon exports. 

A new constitution was a central demand that emerged from months of protests over inequality in late 2019. The mass demonstrations saw thousands killed, injured and arrested as well as billions of dollars’ worth of damage and losses to the country's economy.

Chile currently has over 300 confirmed cases of coronavirus, the highest number per capita in South America.

In the meantime, the Port of Miami Terminal Operating Co., an important destination for frzoen fish shipments, announced on its website that it will be closed Monday and Tuesday “due to extremely low import volumes caused by canceled vessel sailings.

title: Market turmoil breaks Norwegian seafood giants, builds them back up
content:
Norway’s largest seafood companies saw $2 billion wiped off their market value on Thursday, only for a recovery to be staged the following morning.

Violent oscillations in global stock markets saw Oslo’s Seafood Index of large market listed seafood companies fall 10% on Thursday, but then rally by 6% in early Friday morning trading.

The global outbreak of Covid-19 is disrupting seafood trade flows
Read more

Shares around the world plunged on Thursday (March 12) as investors fear the spread of the coronavirus will destroy economic growth with government action insufficient to arrest the decline.

Shares in Mowi, the world’s largest salmon farmer, fell 6%, shaving $500 million off its market value.

In early morning trading, the firm's value had recovered to parity with Wednesday’s close (NOK 179.75), then edged higher (NOK 180.95).

A sense the global economy is entering uncharted territory has left investors unsure how to grapple with the situation. "Markets are at a breaking point," Neil Wilson, chief market analyst at Markets.com, told the BBC. "No one knows what a total economic shutdown, however temporary, looks like."  

US seafood importers scramble to deal with fallout from Trump’s Europe flight limits

On Thursday the main UK index dropped more than 10% in its worst day since 1987, the BBC reported. In the US, the Dow and S&P 500 were also hit by their steepest daily falls since 1987.

In overnight trading Asian and Australian stocks staged a "dramatic comeback", reported CNBC. 

Large seafood companies' market values still remain significantly lower since the outbreak of coronavirus; Mowi's share price is down 21% from its recent peak in February.

Seafood analysts and execs told Undercurrent News on March 12 how seafood firms could be impacted by US president Donald Trump’s travel ban between European countries in the Schengen Area and the US, given the large volume of fresh seafood sent on commercial passenger planes.

title: High level Namibian panel urges creation of new quota allocation system
content:
A high level panel created by Namibian president Haige Geingob to help the country find a solution to certain economic challenges has advised for an immediate moratorium on new fishing quota allocations until a more transparent process can be created, reports All Africa.

The panel suggested implementing a ban on the allocation of new fishing rights and mining licenses for at least a year while the government introduces a more transparent procedure. According to the panel, the current processes are not beneficial to the country and must be suspended.

The government currently awards fishing rights to local industry members at a very low, discounted rate as part of its process of 'Namibianization'. However, this has seen quotas awarded to very few, select individuals, many of whom then sell off their catch allowance at a higher price to other companies.

This was the case most recently when the major government beneficiary Fishcor was alleged to have sold millions of dollars in pelagic quotas to Iceland's Samherji, which in turn created very limited jobs and value for the Namibian economy.

Often, individuals will use poor communities as a front to obtain quotas before cheating these communities of the resulting benefits afterwards, according to All Africa.

Geingob's panel has therefore recommended an open bidding process rather than the current system of opaque government assessment of business plans.

The panel also suggested the creation of a national welfare fund to help fund socio-economic projects across the country, and putting some of the proceeds from the bidding process towards this.

title: New Namibian minister Kawana refuses to reveal fishing beneficiaries
content:
The new Namibian fisheries minister, Albert Kawana, has refused to disclose information regarding the beneficiaries of fishing quotas from the past 10 years, reports The Namibian. 

Namibia’s fishing quotas for this year could be ‘illegal’

Kawana, who replaced the previous incumbent Bernhard Esau after the latter was arrested on charges of selling Namibia's pelagic quotas in return for bribes, said he would not disclose the information as it formed part of the pending trial of Esau.

It is expected that Esau, former justice minister Sacky Shanghala and four other businessmen connected to the case -- dubbed the 'Fishrot Six' by the Namibian press -- will see their case moved from the Windhoek Magistrate's Court to the High Court for trial.

The Namibian, which requested the quota information, raised concerns that the decision to use a court case could deny access to the data for years, which is seemingly counter-intuitive for a government sector now under such close public scrutiny.

According to the news site, former fisheries minister Abraham Lyambo made fishing quota allocations public every year.

This is particularly pressing, it said, as Kawana's department is set to push ahead with new long-term quota allocations this year, and there remain concerns that the formula and data being used to allocate catches remains tainted by Esau and Shanghala.

title: Spanish research manages to reduce parasite on seabream
content:
New research carried out at a Spanish institute proved that a feed additive, developed by animal nutrition firm Bluestar Adisseo is effective in reducing the impact of fish parasites on seabream.

Enteromyxosis is an important parasitic disease encountered in the farming of gilthead seabream in the Mediterranean region. This disease is caused by enteromyxum leei, a microscopic myxozoa that infects the intestinal tract, causing serious economic impacts due to arrested growth.

The Fish Pathology group at the Institute of Aquaculture Torre de la Sal (IATS, Spain), a research group in fish parasite research, has recently coordinated the EU project in this area called ParaFishControl.

“Sanacore GM has proven to be an effective feed additive to reduce the impact from fish parasites on fish performance, with observations across numerous farm trials conducted in the Mediterranean area during the last ten years," said Waldo Nuez-Ortín, lead aquaculture scientist with Adisseo.

“The experimental infection model developed by the team at IATS offered a unique opportunity to validate the efficacy of the additive to mitigate the effects of enteromyxosis in gilthead seabream under controlled conditions."

The peer-reviewed study, recently published in Diseases of Aquatic Organisms, demonstrated the dietary inclusion of Sanacore GM specifically mitigated the reduction in growth caused by the infection.

“This study confirmed field observations on the importance of an adequate feed additive program in a preventive strategy against enteromyxosis”, Nuez-Ortin concluded.

title: UK threatens to walk away from Brexit talks in June
content:
In his latest negotiating mandate, UK prime minister Boris Johnson has said he will consider leaving Brexit negotiations in June in order to prepare the country for an "orderly exit" from the transition period if insufficient progress is made in talks with the EU, reports the Guardian.

The UK government said it believes there is sufficient time over the next six months for negotiating rounds to take place by the end of June.

UK’s Brexit negotiation plan based on ‘zonal attachment’ approach to catches

"The government would hope that, by that point, the broad outline of an agreement would be clear and be capable of being rapidly finalized by September," the document reads.

"If that does not seem to be the case at the June meeting, the government will need to decide whether the UK’s attention should move away from negotiations and focus solely on continuing domestic preparations to exit the transition period in an orderly fashion."

This would set the UK on course to leave the EU on World Trade Organization terms by the end of 2020 unless both parties make major compromises over the next four months.

The UK has called for a separate agreement on fisheries allowing both parties to negotiate access and quota shares on an annual basis, while the EU is intent on keeping fishery access within the overall Brexit agreement.

Similarly, Johnson's team has said it wants regulatory freedom from the EU, with no role for the European court of justice (ECJ) in dispute resolutions. In contrast, the EU has asked for some level of regulatory alignment, with a role for the ECJ and an option to impose tariffs if either party goes back on parts of the deal.

Other disputes that will need resolution include the use of public subsidies, financial services, participation in the European arrest warrant and the UK's desire for a liberalized market for trade goods.

Earlier this week, the UK government rejected the EU's negotiating mandate, saying it saw no need for a level playing field in competition.

title: Blue Harvest completes deal for Rafael groundfish vessels, includes a few surprises
content:
Blue Harvest Fisheries has finalized its acquisition of 12 groundfish vessels and 27 related permits from Carlos Rafael, but not without a few surprises.

The company won't be paying the originally agreed upon $19.3 million, and the boats are being moved into a different New England groundfish sector, Undercurrent News has learned.

The large New Bedford, Massachusetts-based scallop and groundfish supplier announced the conclusion of its negotiations with Rafael on Thursday, nearly three months after Undercurrent first broke the news about the agreement and five months after we first reported the company's interest in the vessels.

Blue Harvest said in a press release that the move "ensures a major portion of the groundfish fishery remains in the Port of New Bedford, with vessels docked in New Bedford and crewed by local fishermen".

“Blue Harvest is committed to carrying on the best aspects of New Bedford and New England’s storied fishing traditions, and we’re excited to expand our work on the waterfront,” said Keith Decker, the company's CEO and president. “With our resources and seafood expertise, we are ideally positioned to be a productive member of the Northeast groundfish fishery for years to come.”

The terms are much the same as those reported in late November, Decker told Undercurrent in an earlier interview, just in advance of the announcement, but the company now says the original price has been renegotiated and won't reveal what the new price is, or even if it's higher or lower.

The final number of the vessels and permits obtained also has been elusive. The original agreement reported by Undercurrent identified vessels that were ultimately acquired by others as well as skiffs and permits purchased separately from the vessels to which they were originally attached.

The 12 vessels acquired by Blue Harvest include the Cowboy, Destiny, Dinah Jane, Edward Moore, Glaucus, Green Acres, Ilha do Corvo, Ilha Brava II, My Way, Nemesis,Southern Crusader and the Triunfo, the company has confirmed. It also gets permits previously associated with the Costa da Gale, Costa & Corvo I, Costa & Corvo II, Leeanne N. Zachery, Oliver, Perseus and Poseidon, according to documents obtained earlier by Undercurrent.

What took so long?

The final weeks were spent waiting for approval from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and then securing paperwork from other individuals who maintained a small percentage of ownership in the vessels and permits, including Carlos Rafael’s wife, Conceicao, and his partners, Decker told Undercurrent.

“NOAA didn’t request anything new,” he said.

An outside consulting firm was not used and Blue Harvest handled the audit of the vessels itself, Decker said.

Blue Harvest, partly backed by the New York City-based private equity firm Bregal Partners, gets millions of pounds of quota for Atlantic cod, haddock, plaice, redfish, hake, flounder and pollock. This is on top of the quota the company already owns in relation to the 21 other vessels under its command, including at least five groundfish vessels and 15 scallopers.

In combination, the company will now maintain 31 vessels in New Bedford and two in Gloucester, Massachusetts, Decker told Undercurrent. This is in addition to its upgraded, SQF-certified, 160,000 square foot seafood processing facility, where millions of dollars have been invested to install six high-capacity processing lines, direct offload capability and increased freezing capacity.

The increased number of landings is expected to increase operations at the facility, and the company said it hopes that improved processing capabilities will "improve price stability and reduce market volatility for all local operations". 

Blue Harvest also maintains facilities in nearby Fairhaven, Massachusetts, and Newport News, Virginia, as a result of earlier acquisitions.

Some vessels in ‘not such good shape’

Blue Harvest had competition in its effort to buy Rafael's vessels. Raymond and Richard Canastra, the longtime owners of the Buyers and Sellers Exchange, New Bedford’s biggest seafood auction, used their right of first refusal rule (ROFR) in Sector VII, where the Rafael vessels were members, as part of an attempt to jump in front of Blue Harvest and match the offer. The ROFR offer was withdrawn, however, after Blue Harvest filed a lawsuit in a state court.

In a press release, the Canastras explained that the lawsuit caused their financial backers to back out while also casting some shade on the condition of the Rafael vessels.

My Way, one of Carlos Rafael's groundfish vessels, which is expected to be acquired soon by Blue Harvest. Photograph by Dan Logan/Shutterstock.

“To make matters worse, the survey of the steel found the vessels to be in much worse condition than expected," they said. "These developments made obtaining sufficient financing impossible."

A quick review of the vessels acquired by Blue Harvest shows the oldest to be the 51-year-old, 74.6-feet long Green Acres, the youngest to be the 24-year-old, 83-foot Southern Crusader II, and more than half of the vessels to be at least 40 years old.

The boats are not all in great shape, Decker conceded to Undercurrent.

“The boats are in various levels of condition,” he said. “Some of them are in good shape relatively and some of them are in not such good shape, and that’s the case when you typically are buying a fleet of vessels. There is various level of conditions on them. We obviously found that there was enough value in the permits and the boats to put a deal together.”

Decker said, in advance of the deal, that four of the vessels acquired – he couldn’t say which ones -- would be made ready, fully crewed and put on the water as soon as May 1, in conjunction with the beginning of the new groundfish season in New England.

Keith Decker, CEO of Blue Harvester Fisheries. Photograph by Jason Huffman

All of the vessels will need to be properly “rigged and prepared to fish, and crews need to be hired,” he said, adding that some will also need engine and hydraulics work.

Decker was unable to give an estimate on the cost of repairs and said it was too early to tell if any vessels will need to be replaced. He said the company, in recently setting its budget for 2020,  has set aside more funds than usual for work on the vessels.

He said Blue Harvest maintains its own “very robust fleet management division” based in Fairhaven.

Rafael vessels to get new names, blue paint

Visitors trying to find the former Rafael vessels at the commercial docks in New Bedford might have a hard time.

The boats, which have previously sported Rafael's green color and his "CR" logos, are all to be painted blue “to be made part of the [Blue Harvest] organization”, Decker said, and they’ll be given new names.

The new look and identities might help to wash away the recent controversy surrounding the vessels, which were once among the nearly 40 owned by Rafael in March 2017 when the so-called “Codfather” of New Bedford pleaded guilty to mislabeling more than 782,000 pounds of fish over a four-year period (2012-2015) and evading taxes. He was later sentenced to 46 months in federal prison.

Photograph courtesy of Blue Harvest Fisheries.

The one-time fishing mogul, whose business was believed to be worth at least $100m at its height, was forced to sell all of his vessels and permits under the terms of a settlement reached with NOAA in August 2019 and had until Dec. 31, 2020 to make it happen. The agreement also gave NOAA the authority to approve any prospective buyers, including Blue Harvest.

In one of the biggest sales for Rafael, Quinn Fisheries, a 33-year-old, New Bedford-based scallop operation, in late September, bought six of his 11 scallop vessels and their related permits for about $40m. 

Though he certainly has had numerous bills to pay, including the $3m he was ordered to forfeit in civil money penalties as part of his settlement with NOAA, Rafael looks to walk away from his commercial seafood business with about $60m in proceeds from the sale of his vessels and permits, depending on what Blue Harvest paid.

'No intention' to hire former Rafael captains

Another big change that harvesters in New England will notice as a result of the Blue Harvest deal is a shift in fishing sectors.

Decker told Undercurrent just in advance of the deal that he plans to move all 12 vessels out of Sector VII, almost entirely cleaning out that sector, and into the Sustainable Harvest Sector (SHS), where Blue Harvest has its other groundfish vessels.

The former Rafael vessels previously were in Sector IX but moved into VII in March 2018 as part of an effort to retain their ability to harvest. Sector VII is managed by Cassie Canastra, the daughter of Raymond Canastra, and recently reconstituted its board after all of its former directors resigned amidst the fight over who could acquire the boats.

The SHS already includes 35 vessels as well as a few catch monitoring requirements that go beyond the federal rules, manager Hank Soule told Undercurrent. That includes hot-spot reporting for Gulf of Maine cod and minimum quota balances.

The Southern Crusader II, one of the groundfish vessels Blue Harvest now hopes to acquire from Carlos Rafael. Credit: Dan Logan/Shutterstock.

Though they may know the boats best, it seems unlikely that Blue Harvest will hire any of the 17 captains who previously worked for Rafael and were found guilty of violating fishing rules. Per the terms of their settlement with NOAA, they face suspensions and probations of various lengths and a large number of extra monitoring rules.

“At this point, we have no intention of employing any of the captains that have pleaded guilty to whatever their charges happen to be”, Decker told Undercurrent. "We would prefer to start with people who have clean records.”

Also, in response to concerns expressed about Blue Harvest being another vertically integrated company, like Rafael’s, the company has vowed to continue running a clean and transparent operation and has made commitments to both 100% dockside monitoring at its facility in New Bedford as well as equipping one of its largest vessels from an earlier acquisition with cameras to monitor catch.

Blue Harvest said in its press release that the SHS plans to hire an independent firm to conduct monitoring and ensure that all product landed from its vessels is properly reported.

“We’re committed to restoring the public trust in the New England groundfishery,” Decker told Undercurrent in its earlier interview.

Top execs have decades of experience and local ties

Opponents to Blue Harvest’s acquisition of the Rafael vessels, including a few local harvesters and their champions, also have expressed concern about the company being owned by a private equity investment firm with a parent company, COFRA Holding, based in Europe. COFRA is headquartered in Germany and tracks its history back to two brothers who founded a textile wholesaling operation in the Netherlands in 1841.

However, Jeff Davis, Blue Harvest’s founder and former CEO, and a 40-year seafood industry veteran, stressed to Undercurrent in a recent interview that only 25% of the company is owned by Bregal and the rest is primarily controlled by five US-based investors.

Davis, who is a native of nearby Acushnet, Massachusetts, and graduated from New Bedford High School in 1967, started Blue Harvest in 2014 before leading the acquisition of Virginia-based Peabody Corp. He then tacked on several other acquisitions, including Harbor Blue Seafood, in Massachusetts and Atlantic Trawlers, a Portland, Maine-based company.

The company notes other seasoned veterans in its press release, too, including a few with local ties. 

Decker, a 30-year seafood veteran, joined Blue Harvest in 2018 after serving as CEO of Canada's High Liner Foods for three years (2015-2017). The company also has chief financial officer Chip Wilson, who has more than 25 years of finance experience and previously worked in Bank of America’s investment banking division. He was CFO of Trinity Frozen Foods.

Gene Bergson, the company's executive vice president of fleet operations, has more than 35 years of experience in the fishing industry, including 11 as general manager of Harbor Blue in neighboring Fairhaven, another company acquired by Blue Harvest.

Alex Mulholland, a 30-year seafood veteran, is the executive vice president of supply chain and operations, while Rick Speed, a 20-year seafood veteran, is vice president of sales and marketing.

'[A] great deal to be optimistic about'

The Blue Harvest announcement included words of support from both Jon Mitchell, the mayor of New Bedford, and Ed Anthes-Washburn, the port director.

New Bedford mayor John Mitchell. Photo by Jason Huffman

“From the moment Rafael was arrested, our priority has been to ensure that his
fishing permits remain in New Bedford,” Mitchell said. “I appreciate that NOAA gave our arguments careful consideration in fashioning a settlement that opened the door to the acquisition announced today, which will achieve the outcome we sought. I look forward to supporting Blue Harvest’s plan to grow in New Bedford and create more jobs for our residents.”

“Today’s acquisition by Blue Harvest represents a level of investment in New Bedford and the groundfish fishery we haven’t seen in years,” said Anthes-Washburn. “The port is pleased to see that Blue Harvest is continuing to invest in vessels, processing and facilities. Combined with the port’s continued investment in infrastructure and dredging, there’s a great deal to be optimistic about on the New Bedford waterfront and with our diverse commercial fishing industry.”

title: Bluefin rancher Balfego suffers huge losses during storm Gloria, but saves facilities
content:
Spanish bluefin tuna rancher Balfego & Balfego was one of several Spanish firms to suffer huge losses in January during the powerful storm "Gloria".

The storm, which battered much of Spain's eastern coast last month for several days, affected the country's aquaculture industry, with some sources telling Undercurrent that nearly half the country's seabass, seabream and meagre production was lost.

"This January we lived through the worst storm in the history of our coast," a Balfego spokesman told Undercurrent News, adding that, during the storm, the waves reached 14 meters high, compared to a previous record high of 10m.

Among other damages, Gloria caused the escape of thousands of tuna from Balfego's marine farm in l'Ametilla, between Barcelona and Valencia. Hundreds of dead tuna appeared scattered along the beaches (see photo above) and nearby promenades following the storm, sources told Undercurrent.

The "vast majority of tuna escaped alive from the top [of Balfego's pools]", the company spokesman said, noting that this happened as the tuna farm was battered by waves "every five seconds".

"We still do not know exactly how many we have lost," he said, noting that the escape was "very important", with an estimate of about 10,000 fish. "In fact, the waters are calming down now and only yesterday we saw that we had more tuna than we thought in one of the facilities," the spokesman also said on Feb. 17.

"Despite suffering a significant loss of specimens, we have a frozen stock that will allow us to supply our customers," the spokesman pointed out. However, he stressed that Balfego's aquaculture facilities largely withstood the storm.

"It [Balfego's farm] is one of the few aquaculture facilities that survived Gloria, and storm Dana in September 2019, thanks to the excellent maintenance work of our team," he noted. 

The fact that the facilities withstood the storm allows the firm to restock for the new season, starting in May, and to operate normally, he also said.

A giant tuna at the Balfego booth, Boston seafood show in 2018
Credit: Jason Huffman, Undercurrent News

"On a commercial level, taking into account our commitment to excellence, sustainability, transparency, and food safety, we prefer to say clearly that our offer will be limited for a short period of time than to look for other types of tuna that do not meet our standards and values," he said.

Balfego would prefer to avoid partnering with other companies, for fear of inadvertently working with a firm allegedly involved in Operation Tarantelo, something that would be "unacceptable for a company like Balfego".

Operation Tantarelo refers to an investigation into a criminal network that was allegedly trading bluefin tuna illegally, with false documentation. In October 2018, Spanish police, in collaboration with Europol, arrested 79 people near Valencia, Spain, who sold more than 80,000 illegally caught tuna with sanitary irregularities, Cronica Global reported, and the trial is still ongoing.

Balfego & Balfego's general manager Juan Serrano (on the left) with Martin Berasategi Photo credit: Cronica Global

Balfego has a turnover of over €50 million, according to Cronica Global. In 2018, the firm's plant near Barcelona suffered a fire, following which the company asked the local government for help to rebuild the plant.

During the fire, Balfego, however, saved the servers with all of its documentation, including the accounting, which allowed the firm "to continue with its activity despite the deep setback", according to the firm.

Balfego has been collecting the dead or escaped tuna and said it will compensate local fishermen that fear that the dead fish will contaminate their catches, Diari de Tarragona reported.

Initially, Balfego had admitted that some escapes may have occurred from its farms due to the storms, but later realized it had lost practically all of its production, or 10,000 out of 11,000, El Pais reported. 

Ricardo Fuentes e Hijos Salazones, another Spanish bluefin tuna rancher, declined to comment to Undercurrent on Feb. 13 on the impact of the storm on its production.

Last week, on the beach of Grau de Castello, in the Tarragona province (south of Barcelona), a dead tuna was found, weeks after Gloria, El Periodico Mediterraneo reported (see photo below).

title: Suspended Fishcor boss arrested in connection with Fishrot
content:

title: Namibia hunts lawyer over $6m in ‘Fishrot’ payments
content:
Namibia's Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) is looking for a Namibian lawyer linked to NAD 90 million ($6.1m) paid out in dubious transactions from the National Fishing Corporation of Namibia (Fishcor), reports The Namibian.

Namibia’s ‘Fishrot’ scandal: from start to present

The money was allegedly paid out to individuals implicated in the "Fishrot" scandal while some of it was used to buy properties abroad.

While his name was not disclosed by the ACC, The Namibian reports lawyer Maren de Klerk from the Windhoek-based law firm De Klerk, Horn & Coetzee (DHC) was questioned by the ACC and subsequently traveled to South Africa, and has not returned. De Klerk was a close associate and lawyer of former justice minister Sacky Shanghala, who was arrested back in November.

The NAD 90m allegedly paid by Fishcor appears to have benefited the same clique that included former ministers Bernhard Esau and Shanghala, and former Investec Asset Management Namibia managing director James Hatuikulipi, who allegedly pocketed close to NAD 103m from Fishrot bribes.

title: New Namibian minister reverses Esau’s ‘Marine Resources Act’
content:
The Namibian government is set to reverse the Marine Resources Act, introduced in 2015, which gives the fisheries minister power to allocate fishing quotas as they see fit, reports Xinhua.net.

The act is to be reversed after it was allegedly used by former minister Bernhard Esau to redistribute horse mackerel quotas to firms linked to either himself or former justice minister Sacky Shanghala, as well as allegedly sell quotas to the Icelandic fishing firm Samherji in return for bribes.

Acting fisheries minister Albert Kawana, appointed after Esau's resignation and arrest in the wake of the scandal, has opted to reverse the act as of Jan. 29.

"The amendments will be reversed and other recommendations in terms of improving the act will also be implemented," he is reported to have said.

Kawana will shortly present recommendations to the Namibian cabinet, according to Xinhua.

title: Police officer latest to be charged in Fishrot investigation
content:
Namibian authorities have arrested a pair of men due to their alleged obstruction of the ongoing investigation into the Fishrot scandal, reports The Namibian.

Last week, Windhoek resident Jason Lyambo and police reservist Sakaria Kokule were arrested in relation to the case, bringing the total number now arrested and charged in connection to the scandal up to nine.

Both men are accused of attempting to bribe investigating officers from the Namibian Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC), allegedly offering NAD 250,000 ($17,000) in return for releasing evidence acquired by the ACC that had been discovered by investigators.

According to The Namibian, the pair were attempting to obtain bank cards belonging to James Hatuikulipi -- former managing director of Investec Namibia and chairman of Fishcor -- and his associate Pius Mwatelulo, as well as a handwritten note titled "allocation from the anti-corruption commission".

Hatuikulipi and Mwatelulo are both members of the so-called Fishrot six, who have been in police custody since December on charges of receiving huge, multi-million dollar bribes from foreign companies in return for awarding horse mackerel quotas.

The six men are due to stand trial at Windhoek High Court on Feb. 23.

title: China’s seafood imports surge 39% to $15bn in 2019
content:
China's seafood imports surged 39% in 2019 to CNY 106 billion ($15.3bn), according to Chinese customs data released Jan. 23, likely making China the second-largest seafood importer in the world ahead of Japan.

The import surge follows 44% import growth in 2018, in renminbi terms. It means China's seafood imports have almost doubled in value in two years.

The figures follow Beijing's announcement that China's GDP grew 6.1% in 2019, the slowest rate of economic growth since 1990, according to Reuters.

China's seafood imports rank the country only behind the US, the world's current largest seafood importer, based on 2018 import data for US and Japan (see chart one below).

In 2018, Japan's seafood imports grew 2% in value, according to International Trade Center, meaning similar growth in 2019 would take its imports to $15.4bn.

China's above import figure does not take into account seafood imported under HS codes 1605 and 1604, data for which will be released by Chinese customs at a later date. In 2018, China imported more than $315m worth of seafood traded under these codes, according to Chinese customs, which would lift its imports in 2019 to over $15.6bn.

China's fondness for seafood and increased spending power is being felt around the globe, both in the seafood industry's wild-catch and aquaculture sectors. 

It is felt most by producers and exporters of crustaceans, such as shrimp, crab, and lobster. 

This week, Undercurrent News reported Ecuador's 2019 exports of farmed shrimp to China topped 400,000 metric tons, worth over $2.32bn in exports. Farms in both Ecuador and India are expanding to meet increased Chinese demand. 

In 2019, imports of crustaceans likely surpassed imports of whole frozen fish (see chart two). (A breakdown of full-year imports by species and origin will be provided at a later date by Chinese customs.)

Whereas China's whole frozen fish imports are largely processed for re-export, imported crustaceans are mostly for domestic consumption, pointing to future growth potential as China's middle class expands. 

Live lobster, crab exporters rush to meet Chinese New Year demand

Another driving factor of China's surging imports is the continued crackdown by Chinese authorities on smuggling.

Smugglers bringing undocumented seafood into the country -- primarily across the border with Vietnam to avoid Chinese customs duties and inspection -- have been arrested and fined or thrown in jail, while processors using smuggled seafood have had product seized. In 2017, Undercurrent estimated more than $3bn worth of seafood entered China annually through smuggling.

The crackdown on smuggling means smuggled seafood previously sent to Vietnamese ports is now sent to Chinese ports and declared to Chinese customs, accounting for some of the headline growth.

title: Beijing raid poised to spur increase in direct Peru shrimp exports to China
content:
Enforcement raids and tighter border controls are poised to boost direct exports of Peruvian shrimp to China, senior Peruvian sources told Undercurrent News.

On Jan. 7 a large quantity of Peruvian shrimp was seized during raids by Beijing authorities in which 15 people were arrested in the Chinese capital.

Cartons of shrimp with 'Product of Peru' are stacked to the left of the picture. Source: Xinhua

The arrests took place during raids of several warehouses in the city's suburbs, with customs officials seizing 20 metric tons of cartons of frozen fish, squid and shrimp.

In pictures, seafood company Qingdao Ocean Fishery's name is Peru printed on cartons of frozen squid, while on cartons of shrimp is "Product of Peru". In a statement, Beijing Customs said the seafood came from Latin America and Vietnam. 

Peru started to export frozen vannamei shrimp directly to China two years ago, following a deal between the two countries.

Last November Chinese health authorities (GAAC) carried out an official visit to Peru following a visit from the Peruvian vice-minister of fisheries to China. Peru aimed to obtain an MOU between Sanipes (Peruvian sanitary authority) and GACC, which was achieved during the Chinese visit.

"So in general this is a good sign for seafood trade between Peru and China," a Peruvian source told Undercurrent.

But on the shrimp side, the protocol has not been revised yet.

"China asks Peru for some disease analyses and those cost money. So companies exporting direct to China have to pay for that," the official said.

Vietnam is more flexible, and buyers there buy everything, in terms of breakdown, sizes, colors, etc. This is likely why some Peruvian companies are still shipping to Vietnam rather than directly to China.

Peru directly exported 3,700t of shrimp to Vietnam in 2018, according to data from the International Trade Center, most of which would have been actually transshipped to China.

title: Peru shrimp seized during anti-smuggling raid in Beijing
content:
A large quantity of Peruvian shrimp was seized during raids by Beijing authorities on Monday (Jan. 7) in which 15 people were arrested in the Chinese capital. 

The arrests took place during raids of several warehouses in the city's suburbs, with customs officials seizing 20 metric tons of cartons of frozen fish, squid and shrimp.

The smuggling gang allegedly smuggled CNY 200 million ($28.8m) worth of seafood, and avoided CNY 40m in customs duties, according to Beijing Customs.

Cartons of shrimp with 'Product of Peru' are stacked to the left of the picture. Source: Xinhua

In pictures, seafood company Qingdao Ocean Fishery's name is printed on cartons of frozen squid, while on cartons of shrimp is "Product of Peru". In a statement, Beijing Customs said the seafood came from Latin America and Vietnam. 

Peru directly exported 3,700t of shrimp to Vietnam in 2018, according to data from the International Trade Center, most of which would have been actually transshipped to China.

However, Peru recently gained approval from Chinese authorities to export seafood products to the country, which reduces incentives for smugglers in China.

Meanwhile, Qingdao Ocean Fishery may have been a third-party supplier and not complicit in a smuggling operation -- it was not mentioned in the statement by Beijing Customs. The firm, which is headquartered in Qingdao, fishes in the southwest Atlantic and also has a subsidiary company in Uruguay, according to its website.

Illegal seafood trade

The raid was broadcast on TV news and indicates Chinese authorities' battle to curtail seafood smuggling remains ongoing.

China’s tariffs on imported seafood unchanged in latest revision

As recently as 2017, several billions of dollars of seafood entered China annually through the "gray trade", predominantly via Vietnam, although more recently the trade had seemingly been crimped thanks to government crackdowns. 

In the month of September last year, Ecuador shipped no shrimp to Vietnam for the first time since 2011. Previously it exported over 200,000t of shrimp into China via Vietnam annually. 

Further reducing incentives for smugglers, China has lowered import tariffs on consumer goods. A round of reductions announced by China's Ministry of Finance in late December did not affect tariff rates for seafood, however, which remain unchanged.
