title: Namibia’s ‘Fishrot’ scandal: from start to present
content:
When Wikileaks first published the documents that would later become known as the 'Fishrot' files on Nov. 13, heads were turned from around the world. The initial release had a staggering fallout across the tail end of 2019, with ramifications at the very top of some of Europe's leading fishing companies, as well as the Namibian government itself.

Samherji paid off Namibian politicians for fishing access, WikiLeaks claims documents show

The allegations made in the 30,000 or so e-mails, internal reports, spreadsheets, presentations and photos are now well-known: Samherji, one of Iceland's largest international fishing companies, is accused of paying millions of dollars in bribes to certain Namibian cabinet ministers and businessmen in return for fishing access. 

The whistleblower, Johannes Stefansson, was himself allegedly part of these deals, having served as Samherji's project manager in Namibia until leaving the role in 2016; his reliability has been repeatedly called into question by the Icelandic fishing firm.

Fishrot's claims

Samherji is widely known to have bought the fishing company Sjolaskip for ISK 12 billion ($99 million) in 2007. The acquisition, which marked the beginning of Samherji's serious business in Africa, proved lucrative for the Icelandic firm, contributing roughly a third of its revenue during its first years.

The acquisition included six trawlers, each capable of doing value-added processing at sea. Until 2010, these were primarily concentrated off the coast of Morocco, catching hundreds of thousands of metric tons worth of horse mackerel, Stefansson claimed. That year, however, the Moroccan quotas changed, and Samherji found itself without a catch and freeze at sea quota.

In search of new horse mackerel quotas, Samherji settled on Namibia, a country with a yearly total allowable catch of approximately 350,000t. In November 2011, Stefansson, together with Samherji's African manager Adalstein Helgason, allegedly met with Tamson Hatuikulipi, son-in-law to Namibia's newly appointed fisheries minister Bernhard Esau, at a hotel in Windhoek. There, Hatuikulipi reportedly agreed in writing to help deliver the quotas that Samherji was after.

In order to obtain these quotas, however, Samherji would need to pay a so-called "quota fee" to the ruling SWAPO party, which has been in permanent control of the country since 1990. The proposed Namibian gains were then openly discussed at Samherji's yearly executives meeting on March 22, 2012, according to Stefansson.

At this meeting, Helgason is alleged to have presented the company's plan to gain quota in Namibia via a "shortcut" -- paying three men with connections to Esau to obtain quotas at a lower price than was legally available to others. Indeed, the high cost of horse mackerel quotas had been putting off foreign investors for years; at the time, only South Africa's Oceana Group and Namsov Fishing Enterprises were catching them in any sizeable quantity, Undercurrent News has learned.

The men chosen by Helgason -- later referred to as "the sharks" -- were Tamson Hatuikulipi, Tamson's immediate relative James Hatuikulipi (then managing director of the financial company Investec), and SWAPO's justice minister, Sacky Shanghala.

Stefansson alleges that Samherji paid each of the men considerable sums of money, and even flew them to Iceland on three separate occasions, at a cost of millions of krone in expenses.

Samherji co-founder Thorsteinn Mar Baldvinsson -- who has stood down as CEO as the scandal broke -- is also alleged to have met Esau in person on at least two occasions in Namibia. The first is claimed to have occurred in May 2012, at Esau's ranch in the countryside, where a working relationship between the two men was established.

Shortly after the May meeting, Stefansson claims to have made the first payment to Esau of $60,000, delivered via the minister's son-in-law Hatuikulipi. According to Samherji's bank statements, there was a similar sum withdrawn at the same time, although this could not be traced by investigators.

Under Namibian law, only companies majority-owned by Namibians could be eligible for fishing quotas. As a result, Samherji became a minority part of its own Namibian subsidiary, Katla, with the rest going to a Namibian co-owner. However, Stefansson alleges that the co-owner was merely a front for the Hatuikulipis, and Samherji actually maintained its control of the company as well as a 75% economic share.

Over the course of the next four years -- until Stefansson's departure from the firm -- Samherji allegedly paid more than $10m to Esau and the 'sharks' in return for quotas, with all money reportedly going via the state-owned Norwegian lender, DNB.

The full allegations against Samherji were laid out by the Icelandic investigative program Kveikur, and can be read here.

Esau vs Namsov

Meanwhile, in Namibia, minister Esau began the process of re-allocating horse mackerel quotas in Sept. 2013, arguing that the stock management system had to be re-assessed to promote responsible exploitation of the mackerel supply. 

Namsov shareholder threatens to sell up, as parent targets sale to Tunacor

The following year, the state-run Namibian company Fishcor appointed James Hatuikulipi as its new chairman, and shortly afterwards, the company was awarded its first ever stocks for horse mackerel -- a redistribution away from the existing owners Namsov and Oceana.

That same year, in June 2014, the ministries of Namibia and Angola signed an agreement of cooperation on horse mackerel fisheries, with Namibia set to donate a sizeable chunk of its total quota to Angolan fishing firms. Namsov, it was later revealed, had written a letter to president Geingob at this time requesting 7,000t of the Angolan quota donation to reduce its own deficit of 24,000t from the quota changes. The request was ignored.

What Namsov did not realize, according to the Fishrot files, was that the Angolan quota was instead given to the joint venture Namgomar Pesca, itself a front for companies owned by Shanghala and the elder Hatuikulipi.

From there, 10,000t of annual quota allegedly went directly to Samherji, avoiding the need for a Namibian middleman. In return, the so-called 'sharks' asked for three-quarters of the price for the quota, with one quarter to be given to Namgomar for selling it on to Samherji.

Meanwhile, Namsov, alongside Emeritus and Atlantic Harvesters, would take Esau and the ministry to court after ultimately receiving only half of the mackerel quota originally agreed upon in the quota re-allocations.

Ultimately, the trial came to an end on Dec. 3, 2014, when the Windhoek high court ruled that the allocation of quotas to Fishcor had been "unlawful and irregular", although the new arrangement was not set aside.

As a result, Namsov would steadily slip further and further into decline over the next few years, with an insufficient quota to maintain its fleet and employees. Trading profit from the firm's fishing division in March 2015 was reported to be down by 23% to NAD 130.8 million ($11.1m), a figure which fell by 47.6% to NAD 66.9m by May 2016, and a further 82% to NAD 21.7m by February 2017.

Following the unexpected departure of managing director Jan Arnold from Namsov on July 11, 2016 in what is now understood to be a response to the quota cuts, Namsov would eventually fold entirely in 2018, as owner Bidvest withdrew from fishing in Namibia. Namsov's remaining assets were later bought by fellow Namibian fishing firm Tunacor.

Esau in the spotlight

Namsov's loss was Fishcor's gain, however. In December 2016, Hatuikulipi's firm announced it would be investing NAD 500m in an onshore processing site. Then, following the collapse of Namsov, Fishcor was awarded with a further 50,000t of quotas per annum in April 2018, leaving Fishcor with 16% of the country's total allowable catch. 

Opening of sub-Saharan Africa’s largest pelagic plant delayed by five months

In response, Fishcor announced it would be constructing another new mackerel processing plant in May 2018, this time with a capacity of 70,000t. The factory was completed in January 2019, following a delay of several months which was allegedly down to a lack of funding.

Esau, meanwhile, has had no shortage of investigations around his conduct during the past five years. 

In September 2014, Namibia's fisheries minister was accused of accepting a chartered jet worth NAD 1m to go and see that year's football World Cup final in Brazil. The jet was paid for by Desmond Amunyela, owner of Paragon Investment Holdings, a company with fishing rights in Namibia.

The following September, while speaking at a gala dinner, Esau claimed that Namibians continued to be exploited and deprived of their marine resources, a statement that can reasonably be said to have aged poorly.

The minister was under investigation again by the country's anti-corruption commission (ACC) in May 2017, over his decision to allocate a further 10,000t of mackerel quotas to Fishcor. It was also revealed that in 2014, Esau had contravened the Fishcor Act, personally appointing James Hatuikulipi as chairperson of the firm instead of leaving the decision to other board members as required by law.

The ACC was back in action once again in October this year, this time investigating the $10m Angola quotas. Profits from the sales of the quotas -- allegedly to Samherji, as per the Fishrot files -- had been siphoned to offshore companies in Mauritius and Dubai, with the money then coming back into Namibia via firms linked to Shanghala, Hatuikulipi, and Ricardo Gustavo, another senior manager at Investec.

And then, one month later, Wikileaks released Stefansson's documents. The fallout was immediate.

Stepping down

Given the severity of the allegations directed at Samherji, plus the wealth of incriminating evidence released by the whistleblower, it was perhaps no surprise that Baldvinsson chose to step aside as Samherji CEO on Nov. 14, a day after Fishrot's publication. 

Baldvinsson steps aside as Samherji CEO with Namibia investigations ongoing

At the time, Samherji said he would be stepping aside until the internal investigation into the company's alleged wrongdoing in Namibia had "revealed the key material facts of the matter".

Meanwhile, the company wasted no time in going on the attack, hiring Norwegian law firm Wikborg Rein to assist with the investigation. The company also laid the blame for the allegations squarely at the feet of the whistleblower Stefansson, who Samherji accused of possibly entangling it in illegal activities without the knowledge of the board.

However, other companies and institutions had also taken notice. On Nov. 15, Norway's DNB, which was alleged to have been used to transfer bribe money to key Namibian officials, launched its own internal investigation.

Meanwhile, for Baldvinsson, the increasing scrutiny and public backlash against the allegations made in the Fishrot papers saw the former Samherji CEO forced to step down from roles on the boards of other firms too: he left Framherji and Sildarvinnslan on Nov. 18; he was replaced by his son on the board of Nergard on Nov. 25; and he departed from the board of UK Fisheries, Samherji's joint venture with Parlevliet & van der Plas, on Nov. 27.

Nevertheless, Baldvinsson has continued to maintain his and Samherji's innocence in the matter. He issued a message to employees on Nov. 19 claiming the firm was unjustly "under attack", noting that the situation in Namibia had been "misunderstood".

Elsewhere at the firm, four other key executives were said by Nov. 27 to be in the process of hiring lawyers ready to defend them from any allegations of wrongdoing.

Esau in hot water

Back in Namibia, and the publication of the Fishrot files had an immediate impact on the state of the government's cabinet -- both Esau and Shanghala resigned from their positions on Nov. 13. 

Pair of accused Namibian ministers abandon bail, remain in custody until February

The following day, James Hatuikulipi stepped down from his position as managing director at Investec; one week later, he would also leave his role as chairman of Fishcor. The company's CEO, Mike Nghipunya, would also eventually be suspended on Dec. 4, as his own conduct was bought into question by the ACC.

Meanwhile, after a two-week delay, the Namibian president Haige Geingob appointed Albert Kawana to serve as the country's new acting minister of fisheries and marine resources. A government document seen by Undercurrent and dated to Nov. 25 gives Kawana the authority to assess the current state of Namibia's fisheries management system, and make recommendations to Geingob "in order to prevent and eliminate, if any, instances of maladministration, nepotism, and/or corruption."

Kawana has also been given authority to review the state's relationship with Fishcor, making "corrective measures" to the horse mackerel quotas if he deems it necessary.

At the same time, Esau was having a highly eventful November -- the now-resigned fisheries minister was arrested on Nov. 23, before being released by the Windhoek high court the following day on the grounds that the original warrant was invalid.

However, it wasn't long before the ACC was back with fresh warrants. Shanghala and Hatuikulipi were formally arrested on Nov. 26, and by Dec. 3, Esau, Ricardo Gustavo, Tamson Hatuikulipi, and Shanghala's business partner Pius Mwatelulo were also in police custody. Collectively, the six men have become known as the 'Fishrot six'.

And yet the ripples from the scandal have continued to spread, even across the Namibian border. The Angolan fisheries minister, Victoria de Barros Neto, has been implicated by the Namibian ACC for setting up the cross-border quota arrangement, which saw Namibian quotas -- ostensibly meant to help Angolan fishermen -- donated to international companies via Namgomar Pesca.

By Dec. 11, the bank accounts of Barros Neto, her husband and children had all been frozen, while Angolan authorities were said to have put out a warrant for the former fishery minister's arrest.

Meanwhile, back in Namibia, all of the 'Fishrot six' remain in police custody, although the men formally lodged an appeal on Dec. 19, on the grounds that their arrest had been politically motivated, with the intention to disrupt the government ahead of the upcoming national election.

The appeal was eventually dismissed by the judge on Dec. 30, noting that it did not meet the necessary requirements to be classed as an urgent request. As such, the six men will remain under supervision by the authorities until their hearing, set to take place on Feb. 20, 2020.

title: Something seemed fishy: 2019 in seafood sector scandals, lawsuits, investigations
content:
The final year of the decade was a tumultuous one for many seafood firms worldwide with major lawsuits, scandals, bankruptcies and arrests making the headlines in 2019.

Undercurrent News was first to report many of these stories, which you can review in our recap below. 

January

For most, the year 2019 started with off with a day’s rest for the New Year’s holiday but that didn’t apply to a group of thieves in Port Medway, Nova Scotia, Canada, who stole some 1,200 pounds of lobster on Jan 1 and Dec. 23, 2018, in separate thefts from lobster pounds. Police did not report any arrests in the case.

Then a week into the year, on Jan. 7, a Florida captain saw his fishing boat, Silvita, seized after he pleaded guilty to poaching nearly 300 spiny lobsters and stone crabs in Biscayne National Park

Troubles with lobster extended to Canadian shellfish harvester Clearwater Seafoods too when it emerged on Jan. 9 that the company had pleaded guilty to having improperly stored 3,800 lobster traps on the ocean bottom off the Nova Scotia coast for upward of two months in the fall of 2017. The company paid a CAD 30,000 ($22,600) fine, later stating that it was working with the Department of Fisheries and Oceans to eliminate at-sea storage of its lobster gear.

Additionally, one of the seafood sector's biggest legal dramas of 2019 -- a bitter fight over shares in Russia's largest fishing firm, Norebo Holding, was fought in a London commercial court. Alexander Tugushev claims fellow co-founders CEO Vitaly Orlov and Magnus Roth, who sold his shares in 2016, defrauded him of a third in the company. Lawyers for Tugushev successfully argued that the matter should be heard in London, rather than Russia, but the merits of his claim have yet to be decided. 

Also during the month, Acuinova Portugal, a Portuguese turbot farm formerly operated by Spain's Nueva Pescanova, emerged from bankruptcy, US tuna canner StarKist & Co reached a $20 million settlement with retailer Walmart over price-fixing claims, US catfish farmer SouthFresh Aquaculture filed for bankruptcy protection, and Massachusetts scallop supplier Atlantic Capes Fisheries reached a settlement of a 2017 sexual harassment lawsuit involving several female workers.

February

February began with some good news for US groundfish supplier Fishermen's Finest. The Washington state firm's 264-foot catcher-processor America's Finest left on its inaugural fishing trip Feb. 6. The move came after the vessel received authorization to fish in the US after a long legal battle, requiring a waiver that cured its violation of the 1920 Jones Act because too much foreign steel was used in its construction.

And in Europe, the European Council approved a full ban on electric pulse trawling following the European Parliament's decision to ban the contentious fishing activity in January 2018.

The day before Valentine's Day, Andreina Fenech Ferrugia, the director-general of Malta's fishing regulator, received some unwelcome news when she was suspended in connection with a Europol investigation into an alleged Spanish tuna smuggling ring. She later claimed that payments received from smuggling suspects were "entirely legitimate".

The European salmon sector was rocked by allegations of price-fixing that began when the Scottish offices of several farmers --  Mowi, Leroy Seafood Group, SalMar and Greig Seafood -- were inspected by officials from the European Commission (EC). The EC later confirmed that it had “received information – from different actors operating at different levels in the salmon market – alleging that Norwegian producers of farmed Atlantic salmon… participate or have participated in anti-competitive agreements".

The month also saw Seattle, Washington's Trident Seafoods agree to invest $23m to reduce emissions of ozone-depleting substances from refrigeration equipment on its vessels to resolve alleged violations of the US Clean Air Act.

Furthermore, US blue swimming crab importer Bonamar saw its business virtually implode and fall into receivership. The Medley, Florida-based firm, which had carried out two large acquisitions in recent years, was sued for more than $22m, the remaining balance of a $25m loan taken out in 2017. Bonamar's assets were later sold to other firms.

Additionally, Thai Union Group's John West tuna brand was prosecuted in the United Kingdom for importing fish from Ghana allegedly linked to illegal fishing. The company was later cleared of the allegations. 

March

March began with the Mozambique government suing Credit Suisse in a London, UK court over the banker's alleged role in a so-called "tuna bond scandal". The lender provided loans to Mozambican maritime security projects and the state tuna fishery between 2013 to 2016. Allegedly, many of the projects used for the funds where effectively fronts used by a trio of US bankers and others to enrich themselves through a series of kickbacks and bribes amounting to $200m, the suit alleged.

Meanwhile, in a New York court, Friedrich von Kaltenborn-Stachau, the administrator appointed to resolve the 2015 bankruptcy of European pollock processor Pickenpack, withdrew requests to recover some $283m from the companies' former affiliates, China Fishery Group. The administrator didn't state a reason for his action.

A high profile US seafood sector suit ended quietly in March when Massachusetts processor National Fish & Seafood (NFS) and Florida's Tampa Bay Fisheries agreed to settle a lawsuit that had alleged Tampa Bay executives and former NFS vice president Kathleen Scanlon conspired to steal trade secrets relating to NFS' stuffed clam production methods.

Also during the month, Indonesian security officials reported seizing four suitcases containing 125,619 lobster seeds from smugglers at Jakarta's main airport, a division of New Zealand fishing firm Talley's denied allegations that it was illegally trawling in the Tasman Sea, and Russia began a seafood sector crackdown against tax evasion. 

April

Anthony Smith, the 72-year-old businessman behind a Welsh feed startup pleaded guilty to defrauding the EU and Welsh government after claiming £4.7m ($6.2m) in grants to develop an alternative to fish feed.

US tuna canner StarKist & Co reached agreements with some of its biggest customers, retailer Target and broadline distributors US Foods and Sysco, resolving lawsuits that had alleged the companies had been damaged by the canner's price-fixing.

In Chile, large commercial fishing firms announced that they would close processing plants and lay off workers due to a law that restricts industrial fishermen from trawling for cuttlefish, limiting fishing of the species to handlines and jigging gear.

Dungeness crabbers in the US state of California saw their season cut short due to a court settlement reached between the state and a non-governmental organization over concerns about whale entanglements. The closure prompted crab prices to jump. 

Additionally, US customers filed the first lawsuits seeking damages from alleged price-fixing in the Norwegian salmon sector against farmers Mowi, Leroy, SalMar and Grieg. 

Rounding out the month, Canada's Cooke was fined $332,000 by the US state of Washington after a legal settlement ruled the firm was responsible for the escape of 250,000 salmon from a US net pen in August 2017.

May

Undercurrent was first to report that the owners of Pacific Andes International Holdings (PAIH) allegedly commited a massive trade finance scam believed to have involved more than $5.3 billion dating back some 15 years. PAIH's founding Ng family vehemently denied the allegations.

PAIH subsidiary National Fish abruptly closed its doors for good on May 10 citing " too many legacy issues" that had prevented a sale of the processor, which had struggled financially for years. The facility later reopened under new ownership.

In Thailand, a criminal court handed down fines totaling over $16m, to six defendants accused of operating an illegal vessel in Thai waters.

And Santaska, the owners of a former salmon cannery known as Wards Cove Packing Company in the US state of Alaska's Bristol Bay, put it up for sale with a $3.5m price tag.

June

Vietnamese shrimp supplier Minh Phu Seafood found itself in an unwelcome spotlight after US congressman Darin LaHood called on US customs officials to investigate allegations the company evaded US anti-dumping duties on imported shrimp from India. Minh Phu denied the charges and said it believed it would be fully vindicated. 

The US state of Maine granted a key ruling in favor of Nordic Aquafarms, the firm behind a planned 33,000-metric-ton US Atlantic salmon recirculating aquaculture system in the city of Belfast, when it ruled that the farmer had the necessary title to intertidal waterway that it needed to move forward.  

Days later, an appeals court in the US state of Illinois sided with a former employee of Mazzetta Corporation, disallowing a non-compete agreement that the company tried to use to bar him from working at Fortune International, the parent of Chicago distributor Fortune Fish & Gourmet.

And on June 21, M. Slavin & Sons, a more than 100-year-old New York City-based wholesaler with ties to the historic Fulton Fish Market, closed its doors for good after having struggled financially for years. 

Four days later, Chinese officials announced the “smashing” of a seafood smuggling operation involving the import of lobsters, snails and blue crabs worth CNY 200m ($29.1m).

July

CleanFish, a seafood wholesaler based in Northern California, sued Dale Sims, its co-founder and former part-owner and CEO, Sims' new company Buena Vista Seafood, and also one of its former major suppliers of mussels, Island Sea Farms, for at least $1.5 million in a federal court, charging that they conspired to steal trade secrets.

Days later, William Atwood, the former owner of a Maine lobster processing plant, who sold his business to Highland Park, Illinois-based Mazzetta Company sued the company seeking to void an amendment to its lease.

Also in Maine, a lobster food truck business that boomed into a national franchise after an appearance on the TV show "Shark Tank" sued a rival for allegedly infringing on its trademark. According to a 52-page lawsuit, Cousins Maine Losters' online sales were crimped when a rival firm with a lobster e-commerce business, Maine Lobster Now (MLN), registered three "confusingly similar" web domain addresses in 2013: cousinsmaineslobster.com, cousinsmainelobsters.com and cousinmainelobsters.com. 

And in Ecuador, an international dispute settlement body found for the government of Ecuador in its tax dispute with Spanish tuna firm Albacora. Ecuador had said the tuna canner owed it some $56m relating to the company's activities Posorja Free Zone.

Vitaly Orlov, the CEO of Norebo Holding, scored a victory against Alexander Tugushev, who claims he is owed $350m from his stake in the Russian fishing company. A London court ruled that a freezing order imposed on Norebo's assets should be lifted. 

And on July 30, promoters of Pebble Mine, which fishermen fear could imperil salmon stocks in Alaska's Bristol Bay, received a boost when the US Environmental Protection Agency said it would withdraw protections implemented by in 2014 under the Clean Water Act that could have posed a hurdle to the proposed development.

August

August found executives of California shrimp importer and distributor Haven Foods defending themselves against allegations made by their former employer, High Liner Foods-owned shrimp importer Rubicon Resources. Rubicon had claimed that the Haven executives stole information they gained while employed by the Canadian company's frozen shrimp division to gain an edge in taking away the lucrative business relationship High Liner had with grocer Kroger.

Thai Union Group, the owner of US tuna canner Chicken of the Sea International, announced that it had set aside some $104m to pay its bill related to its involvement in the US canned tuna price-fixing scandal. 

And on Aug. 13, Phillip Carawan, the former CEO and president of North Carolina processor Capt. Neill's Seafood, pleaded guilty to one count of falsely labeling 179,872 pounds of crabmeat with a retail market value of $4,082,841 as "product of the USA".

A week later, the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said it had reached a settlement with Carlos Rafael that will see the incarcerated fishing mogul pay a $3m civil fine, relinquish the dealer permit held by his Carlos Seafood business, permanently cease all groundfish and scallop fishing, and sell all federal fishing permits and fishing vessels he owns or controls by the end of 2020.

September

In one of the most implausible seafood stories of the year, Juan Alfaro, an affiliate of Mexican drug baron Joaquin “El Chapo” Guzman was convicted of having participated in a narcotics and money laundering conspiracy. Prosecutors said Alfaro used “front” companies to launder over $12m in drug proceeds from Buffalo to Los Angeles, including Triton Foods. and Kamora Investment Enterprises, which were located in California. Another fictitious company, Corral Seafoods, registered in the State of New York, was allegedly located in Cheektowaga, but proved to be completely fake.

On Sept. 11, US federal judge Edward Chen handed down a $100m fine to Starkist for having engaged in a price-fixing conspiracy, the largest amount paid by the US 'big three' canners that participated. The company had said that a fine of that magnitude could bankrupt it. 

And Mowi got some good news at the end of the month when the EU's General Court partially overturned a €20m fine that it had ordered Mowi -- then Marine Harvest -- to pay the European Commission in July 2014.

October

Canada's Cooke said on Oct. 3 that it was moving ahead with its proposal to farm steelhead in net-pens in the US state of Washington that it currently uses to grow Atlantic salmon. The company will partner with the Washington state-based Jamestown S'Klallam Tribe to farm sablefish, a species also known as black cod, and sterile triploid, all-female rainbow trout.

Further north, five groups active in fishing Alaska's Bristol Bay, said they would sue the US EPA over its decision to withdraw protections implemented in 2014 under the Clean Water Act that could have posed a hurdle to the proposed Pebble Mine development.

And on Oct. 12, Newfoundland & Labrador minister of fisheries and land resources Gerry Byrne suspended all salmon aquaculture licenses belonging to Mowi's Northern Harvest Sea Farms, noting non-compliance issues and a greater number of fish deaths than initially reported.

Undercurrent was first to report in October that Blue Star Foods, a Miami, Florida-based blue and red swimming crab importer and exporter, was beset by a number of issues including the acrimonious parting of its president and CEO and the gradual winnowing down of its relationship with US Foods as a major buyer.

November

The criminal price-fixing trial of former Bumble Bee Foods' CEO Chris Lischewski was the talk of the seafood sector in November. After nearly a month of testimony from witnesses who included former executives at the tuna canner as well as Starkist and Chicken of the Sea, Lischewski was convicted on Dec. 4. He has yet to be sentenced but could face a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison and a $1 million fine. His lawyers have vowed to appeal. 

In a related story, Bumble Bee filed for bankruptcy Nov. 21 citing in part a lack of a settlement with the litigants in the civil lawsuits against the company over its tuna price-fixing. Taiwanese tuna trader FCF Co made a "stalking horse" bid for the company, its longtime customer,frontpage which has yet to be approved by the court. 

And on Nov. 8, the US EPA fined major Alaska salmon processor Silver Bay Seafood $82,500 after the company reportedly violated the terms of its wastewater discharge permit at its Sitka facility in 2017.

The Norwegian salmon farmers accused of price-fixing received more bad news on Nov. 14 when it emerged that the US Department of Justice had joined the investigation against the companies. 

Additionally, the CEO of Icelandic fishing firm Samherji, Thorsteinn Mar Baldvinsson, stepped aside Nov. 25 amid allegations that the company paid bribes to Namibian politicians for access to horse mackerel quotas. 

The scandal began when Wikileaks first published the documents that would later become known as the 'Fishrot' files on Nov. 13.

December

Canadian seafood wholesaler Seven Seas Fish Co settled a five-year-old matter when it was sentenced to three years of probation in the US for re-importing frozen corvina into the US.

A week later, Canada's newly re-elected government announced it would proceed with a plan to phase out net-pen salmon farming in British Columbia by 2025 but questions still remain about how the plan will be carried out. 

And on Dec. 19, Chile's main antitrust authority announced it is seeking a combined fine of as much as $70m ($23.9m each) from three major salmon feed companies for price-fixing.

Four days later, Australian aquaculture firm Clean Seas Seafood settled its lawsuit against feed supplier Skretting, with the latter paying out AUD 15 million ($10.3m).

title: Interim Samherji CEO says partners ‘have stood with the company’ amid Namibia allegations
content:
Bjorgolfur Johansson, the interim CEO of scandal-hit Icelandic fishing company Samherji, said the company's domestic and foreign partners have "stood with the company".

On Dec. 23, Johansson, who stepped in as Thorstein Mar Baldvinsson stood down amid allegations the company paid backhanders to Namibian politicians for fishing access, wrote a letter to staff in which he said sales are "growing" and the company "is doing well in its fishing and processing operations".

Namibian ministers’ appeal rejected, will spend New Year in custody

Samherji's management "has fighting spirit on all fronts and we are convinced the future of the company is bright", he wrote in the letter, which you can see in full below. 

After Johansson's letter, it emerged the six politicians and businessmen embroiled in Namibia's ongoing 'Fishrot' scandal will remain in police custody for the New Year, after their appeal was rejected by the Windhoek high court on Dec. 27. 

The six men, including former fisheries minister Bernhard Esau and former justice minister Sacky Shanghala, have been arrested on allegations of receiving more than NAD 100 million ($6.8m) in kickbacks from the Icelandic fishing firm Samherji in return for fishing quotas, among other corruption charges.

On Dec. 19, the ministers lodged an appeal to the Windhoek high court, arguing that their detainment was politically motivated and aimed at undermining support for the government ahead of the upcoming Namibian general election.

title: Namibian ministers’ appeal rejected, will spend New Year in custody
content:
The six politicians and businessmen embroiled in Namibia's ongoing 'Fishrot' scandal will remain in police custody for the New Year, after their appeal was rejected by the Windhoek high court on Dec. 27, reports Naija 247 News.

The six men, including former fisheries minister Bernhard Esau and former justice minister Sacky Shanghala, have been arrested on allegations of receiving more than NAD 100 million ($6.8m) in kickbacks from the Icelandic fishing firm Samherji in return for fishing quotas, among other corruption charges.

On Dec. 19, the ministers lodged an appeal to the Windhoek high court, arguing that their detainment was politically motivated and aimed at undermining support for the government ahead of the upcoming Namibian general election.

They also sought to have the charges of fraud, laundering and tax evasion removed because of what they believed to be a faulty process during their arrests.

However, the acting judge Kobus Miller dismissed their claims last week as the delay in their request meant it could no longer be considered an urgent matter.

The next hearing for the six men is scheduled for Feb. 20 next year.

Esau, Shanghala, Esau's son-in-law Tamson Hatuikulipi, Shanghala's associate Pius Mwatelulo, and former Investec Asset Management members James Hatuikulipi and Ricardo Gustavo, and Samherji itself have all denied the charges set against them, based primarily on evidence from the Fishrot files released by WikiLeaks in November.

title: UCN’s top stories of 2019: 100-81
content:
2019 was another dynamic and busy year in seafood news, with Undercurrent News covering and breaking more big stories as they happened than at any time in our history.

We're looking back at the year's most-read exclusive stories. Below you can find numbers 100 to 81:

81. Boss of large Dalian-based seafood processor arrested

By Louis Harkell

Jan. 29, 2019 - Dalian Hengtai Foods, which imports an estimated 15,000 metric tons of raw material annually for processing and re-export, confirmed its boss had been apprehended

82. GSMC 2019: SIMP seen as reducing Russian king crab sales to US

By Tom Seaman, Jason Smith, Jason Huffman

Jan. 15, 2019 - Undercurrent reported live from San Diego, California, at the National Fisheries Institute's annual Global Seafood Market Conference

83. More bad news for seafood expected from frontlines of US-China trade war

By Jason Huffman

May. 13, 2019 - Seafood industry execs feared the 15% tariff increase might deal a lethal blow to some imports from China and the new list of items to be tariffed will eliminate exemptions

84. Jordan Mazzetta steps down from family business

By Neil Ramsden

Feb. 04, 2019 - One of founder Tom Mazzetta's sons, Jordan, left the firm and moved to a new venture; two others have been promoted to the position of vice president

85. Rabobank: Land-based farming set to disrupt salmon industry

By Matilde Mereghetti

Oct. 17, 2019 - Rabobank forecasts recirculating aquaculture systems have the potential to change the game over the next decade

86. High Liner charges ex-Rubicon execs with 'nefarious' theft of Kroger account

By Jason Huffman

Jun. 12, 2019 - 'This action seeks to put an end to this nefarious scheme and remedy the extreme damage caused by Haven Foods' -- lawsuit filed in California by High Liner Foods

87. MSC suspends all North East Atlantic mackerel certifications

By Neil Ramsden

Jan. 31, 2019 - The suspension came after the mackerel stock in the northeast Atlantic dropped below a precautionary threshold level, while catches remained far higher than advised by scientists

88. Four Chinese seafood firms being investigated by financial authorities

By Louis Harkell

Jun. 21, 2019 - A source at one of the companies told Undercurrent his firm had been visited by Chinese authorities asking for documents and proof of trade

89. Canada's Liberal Party pledges to replace British Columbia net-pens with RAS if re-elected

By Jason Huffman

Sep. 30, 2019 - The Liberal Party also promised to introduce Canada's first-ever Aquaculture Act if brought back; that legislation has been on the industry's wish list for some time

90. Lawsuit charges Bonamar with defaulting on $25m loan

By Jason Huffman

Feb. 19, 2019 - The fast-growing Florida seafood importer, wholesaler and processor and its founder, who acted as a guarantor, were sued for more than $22m in a federal court

91. Blue Harvest inks deal to acquire 35 Rafael groundfish vessels for $25m

By Jason Huffman

Nov. 25, 2019 - Other groundfish harvesters in the sector where Carlos Rafael's fleet worked had until roughly Christmas Day to make any competing bids

92. Young Norwegian firm aims to become the largest aquaculture group in Africa

By Maria Feijóo

Nov. 11, 2019 - The Norwegian company Willing Hands has found an opportunity to grow in Africa and aims to become the largest seafood group on the continent in the next seven years

93. World’s top seafood companies see SeaBOS shaking up entire industry

By Matt Craze

Mar. 28, 2019 - SeaBOS members disclosed more details in Boston about leadership drive that will change the seafood industry

94. Aldi trials another UK whitefish processor after Smales shift 

By Tom Seaman

Aug. 09, 2019 - The UK division of German discounter Aldi trialed two additional whitefish products from another processor after switching supply from F. Smales & Son

95. Owners of Sea Watch, US' largest clam business, in talks for sale

By Jason Smith, Tom Seaman

Jun. 26, 2019 - The owners of Sea Watch, a vertically integrated US clam business with sales of over $140m and earnings in excess of $20m, looked to sell

96. Argentina red shrimp party over as farmed product floods China, European market

By Matt Craze

Jun. 17, 2019 - A global glut in the farmed shrimp market was hurting the prospects for Argentina’s wild-caught industry, just as the most important fishing season began

97. Shrimp prices in China jump on Spring Festival demand, supply shortage

By Louis Harkell

Jan. 14, 2019 - Wholesale prices jumped 15% due to a supply shortage amid a crackdown in smuggling from Vietnam during the busiest trading period of the year, sources said

98. €400m fish finger processor up for sale

By Tom Seaman

Nov. 12, 2019 - The owners of large frozen fish processor Greenland Seafood were looking to sell the company, which has plants in Germany and France doing around 100,000t of volume annually

99. Bonamar faces multiple court challenges as recent acquisitions fall apart

By Jason Huffman

Feb. 20, 2019 - A lawsuit filed by one of Bonamar's major lenders was just the tip of the iceberg, an Undercurrent investigation revealed

100. China lifts temporary ban on shrimp imports from Omarsa

By Louis Harkell

Sep. 16, 2019 - Omarsa could resume exports of shrimp to China just one week after Chinese authorities hit it with a suspension

title: US auction owners seek to spoil Blue Harvest’s deal for Rafael groundfish vessels
content:
Carlos Rafael’s remaining fleet of as many as 35 groundfish vessels and skiffs in the US port city of New Bedford, Massachusetts, may not be under Blue Harvest Fisheries’ Christmas tree after all.

Richard and Raymond Canastra, the founders and owners of the Buyers and Sellers Exchange (BASE), a nearly 26-year-old seafood auction house, also in New Bedford,  informed the members of New England fishing sector 7 on Friday that they are taking advantage of the group's right of first refusal (ROFR) rules to seek acquisition of the vessels and their related permits, Undercurrent News has learned from its sources.

Additionally, the Canastras have filed another challenge to Rafaels' earlier sale of six scallop boats and their related permits to Quinn Fisheries, a longtime New Bedford-based scalloping company, this time in federal court.

Undercurrent reported late last month how documents showed Blue Harvest, a US scallop and groundfish supplier backed by New York City-based private equity Bregal Partners, had signed a purchase agreement to buy the Rafael fleet and all of their associated permits for nearly $25 million. The deal includes millions of pounds of quota for at least eight types of fish in the northeast multispecies fishery, including cod, haddock, American plaice, witch flounder, yellowtail flounder, redfish, white hake and pollock.

Carlos Rafael gives a demonstration on how to cut cod at a festival in New Bedford, Massachusetts, in 2010. Image is a still from a YouTube video.

The sale of the Rafael fleet promises to conclude a dark saga in US commercial fishing history. The former fishing mogul, who was believed to have once maintained a more than $100m per year operation, was convicted in March 2017 of 28 criminal counts related to mislabeling more than 700,000 pounds of fish over a four-year period and evading taxes.

Rafael, labeled the "Codfather" by the media, was sentenced to a 46-month prison term and ordered, as part of a civil settlement in August with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), to pay $3m in fines and leave the commercial fishing industry for good. The settlement gives him until Dec. 31, 2020 to sell all of his vessels and related permits.

In September, Quinn Fisheries, a 33-year-old New Bedford area scallop operation, agreed to pay nearly $46m to acquire the most valuable part of the Rafael fleet, six of his 11 scallop vessels and their related permits, as first reported by Undercurrent.  The vessels sold then included the Acores, Athena, Apollo, Gypsy Girl, Hera II and the Villa Nova Do II.

Rafael appeared poised to practically clean out the rest of his commercial fishing assets in his agreement with Blue Harvest. As reported by Undercurrent, one attachment to the 30-page agreement identified 28 vessels and skiffs reported to be worth a combined $19.3m, including the 23-year-old, 83-foot, 503 horsepower Southern Crusader II and 50-year-old, 74.6-foot, 503-horse power Green Acres.

Another attachment identified seven vessels and skiffs reported to be worth a combined $5.4m. However, it remains unclear if the second list was part of the deal.

Canastras had 30 days to match earlier offer

However, the overall agreement with Blue Harvest was not yet money in the bank. It had to survive a ROFR process, by which other harvesters in the sectors where the vessels worked had a chance to match the bid. In the case of the Rafael boats, that's sector 7, where Cassie Canastra is the manager and also the daughter of Raymond Canastra and niece of Richard Canastra.

Richard and Raymond Canastra are both owners of permits in sector 7 and members of the sector's board of directors, sources confirmed.

One of the many fishing vessels owned by Carlos Rafael . Photo by Jason Huffman

As explained by an expert on the rules to Undercurrent, any member within sector 7 had 15 days to match the offer made by the outside bidder before the opportunity was opened to members of the other sectors within the Northeast Sector Services Network for the next 15 days.

The first offer to be made within the sectors is the winner. It doesn't matter if a bidder, including the original outside bidder, tops the offer. So it's possible that the Canastra have already locked up the vessels.   

A copy of the deal Blue Harvest made with Rafael was provided to Cassie Canastra on Thursday (Nov. 21) by Stephanie Rafael Demello, Carlos Rafael’s daughter, and she had just a few days to share the purchase agreement with other potential bidders. The in-sector bidders then had until roughly Dec. 26, the day after Christmas, to act.

The original agreement with Blue Harvest required a deposit of $250,000 be made in a designated trust account managed by Rafael’s attorney, John Markey, Jr., on the date of the transaction. If the deal doesn’t close by Jan. 1, 2020, the sellers were instructed that they are responsible for securing docking space in New Bedford for the following year, the document advised.

Cassie Canastra declined to comment on the effort by BASE's owners to acquire the Rafael groundfish vessels, saying only that she was prohibited from speaking in her position as manager of sector 7. Raymond and Richard Canastra were reported to be out of the office and unavailable for the rest of the week.

Keith Decker, the CEO of Blue Harvest Fisheries, did not return a message left on his phone Monday morning.

Still fighting for scallop vessels, too

An interview the Canastras did for a NOAA publication in 2004 provided a lot of detail about their history in the New Bedford seafood industry. The two brothers -- both now in their late 50s -- said their grandfather was a whaler and, like Rafael, moved to Massachusetts from Portugal, though they were born and raised in New Bedford.

Raymond spent some of his early adult years working on scallop vessels and later served as a captain. Richard started in the snack food business before joining his brother in multiple seafood ventures starting in 1989.

As recounted by Undercurrent, the Canastras opened the Whaling City Seafood Display Auction, BASE’s former name, in September 1994, with a hole punched in a wall, an air conditioning unit bought from a salvage company and a large fan. The auction now handles roughly half of all the Atlantic scallops caught in New England as well as a considerable amount of groundfish.

Aerial view of New Bedford waterfront and New Bedford-Fairhaven bridge. Photo: Port of New Bedford

Undercurrent reported in September 2017 how the Canastras, one-time friends of Rafael, had made several attempts to buy his vessels and related permits. They confirmed, in a radio interview done shortly after, that they had a deal for at least some of the Rafael fleet, though it later fell through.

In September 2019, the Canastras made another run at Rafael's fleet, attempting to intervene in the Rafaels’ sale of his scallop vessels to the Quinns with a state court challenge. They argued that the seller didn’t handle the ROFR process correctly. The state judge, however, ruled against the Canastras, allowing the Quinn deal to go through.

The state court documents had provided details about the Canastras’ earlier effort to buy Rafael’s vessels. In an affidavit, Rafael-DeMello described how her family had dozens of talks with the Canastras about selling them their fleet before Carlos was sentenced and well after. However, during the months of conversations, the Canastras insisted that the asking price was too much.

Also, at the time, NOAA “expressed serious concerns about BASE purchasing the fleet because the violations which led to my father’s arrest took place at the unloading facility on BASE property”, said Rafael-DeMello, who continued:

“If the Canastras were proposed as purchasers, I am concerned that NOAA may not approve them as buyers of the fishing vessels and permits.”

As part of the settlement agreement with Rafael, NOAA must approve any buyers of his vessels following a review of legal history and possible relationships with Rafael.

In a subsequent conversation, the Canastras said they were unable to put a deal together because of financing issues, Rafael-DeMello said.

On November 25, the Canastras moved their efforts to the US District Court of Massachusetts, in Boston, arguing that it was the correct jurisdiction because the argument involved federally regulated fisheries. The Canastras are asking the federal court to force Quinn Fisheries and other related parties into arbitration, or alternatively nix the earlier deal and allow BASE to purchase the Rafael vessels instead.

title: Stolen lobster truck chase ends with crash, arrest, in Massachusetts
content:
The attempted theft of a truck full of lobsters in Charlestown, Massachusetts, ended Tuesday morning with the crash of the vehicle and the arrest of the thief, NBC10, a local television affiliate, reports.
 
Stephen Woodard, 29, allegedly jumped into the vehicle while it was being loaded with about $10,000 worth of lobsters at a local warehouse. A short chase ended when Woodard intentionally crashed the truck into the personal vehicle belonging to the regular driver, T-boning it, and was also rear-ended by another lobster truck, police told the TV station.

Police caught up with Woodard after he was detained by emergency medical technicians.

title: Former Namibian ministers claim ‘political motivation’ behind arrests
content:
The pair of accused Namibian former ministers alleged to have taken millions of dollars worth of kickbacks in exchange for fishing quotas have launched a fresh legal challenge in an effort to escape police custody, reports New Era Live.

Former fisheries minister Bernhard Esau, former justice minister Sacky Shanghala, and their four accused associates have claimed that their arrests were politically motivated, and have approached the country's high court regarding their continued detention.

In particular, they have accused the director-general of the country's anti-corruption commission, Paulus Noa, of "yielding to political pressure rather than carefully executing his functions."

The six men are seeking an order from the high court that would set aside their arrests, their prosecution, and the postponement of their case until February. They have also demanded to be released from custody with immediate effect.

Their application is to be heard the morning of Dec. 19, reports New Era Live.

Esau, Shanghala, Esau's son-in-law Tamson Hatuikulipi, Shanghala's associate Pius Mwatelulo, and former Investec Asset Management members James Hatuikulipi and Ricardo Gustavo, were all heavily implicated in the Fishrot files released by WikiLeaks last month.

The Icelandic fishing firm Samherji allegedly paid around NAD 150m ($10.4m) in bribes between 2012 and 2018 to politicians and businessmen -- including the six men in custody -- in return for fishing quotas.

In their affidavit, the six accused have said the release of the files was politically motivated and aimed to disrupt public support for the government ahead of the upcoming national election. They did not deny the allegations, however.

Meanwhile, a seventh man, Nigel van Wyk, allegedly a worker for one of the accused, has been arrested and charged with defeating or obstructing the course of justice, as well as for being in possession of ammunition. He too has been kept in police custody, with a trial date set for March 18, 2020.

title: Forbes pins sales of Russia’s top 10 seafood firms at almost $4bn
content:
The combined turnover of Russia’ top 10 seafood companies is RUB 238 billion ($3.80bn), according to a ranking of the top owners and firms in the sector from Forbes.

Forbes last ranked the top companies in the sector in 2017, but focused on volume then. However, for the 2019 edition, turnover is the metric used, with Norebo Holding coming out on top, with almost $1bn in turnover. Forbes also estimates 2 million metric tons of quota has been allocated to the top 10 companies in 2019.

Roth partially recognizes Tugushev’s claim in Norebo dispute, but there’s a catch

According to Forbes, Vitaly Orlov and his Norebo are the largest player in the sector, with turnover of RUB 58.2bn ($929.45m). Norebo, which is the subject of a bitter legal dispute in the UK’s High Court of Justice, spent about $600m to buy competitors in the North-West and Far East in 2011-2013, according to Forbes.

1. Vitaly Orlov, Norebo Holding 

Norebo -- which has 16 fishing companies and is 100% owned by Orlov -- is in the process of building 10 new vessels under Russia's investment quotas program. Six of these are for cod and haddock in the country's northwest and four for pollock and herring in the Far East. The company's investing some $690m on the program. 

Behind the scenes of this fishing and processing powerhouse is a bitter legal battle, however. Orlov is currently being sued in London by co-founder Alexander Tugushev, who claims he’s owed over $350m for his stake. Tugushev alleges Orlov and Magnus Roth, the third founder, swindled him out of his share.

On Tuesday, Undercurrent News reported that Roth partially recognizes Tugushev’s claim of ownership, but with a catch.

Roth said in a filing that Tugushev's claim should be offset by "a fair amount" to reflect the value that the assets grew between June 2004 to December 2009 when he was in prison on fraud charges and "failed to contribute at all" the business' operation.

Additionally, Roth's lawyers wrote in the filing that while their client admits that Tugushev is "entitled to an order that one-third of the joint venture assets shall be transferred to him", that amount should be further reduced by the value of what amounted to a major missed opportunity for the company.

Abramovich associates, Gidrostroy boss net $300m-plus Russian Far East fishing deal

According to Roth, in early 2005, Norebo's predecessor -- a joint venture between the firms Ocean Trawlers, which Roth and Vitaly Orlov, Norebo's CEO, founded, and Karat Group, which Tugushev was affiliated with -- had the opportunity to expand by purchasing a fishing business owned by Roman Abramovich, a Russian-Israeli billionaire businessman and now the owner of London's Chelsea Football Club. 

The $50m deal for that business, Chukotka Tralflot, "would have generated some $150m in profits for the joint venture partners", Roth claimed but the transaction fell apart.

"When Mr. Abramovich and/or his agents learned of Mr. Tugushev’s connection with the joint venture, they withdrew from negotiations on account of Mr. Tugushev’s arrest for fraud," Roth claimed.

2. Alexander Verkhovsky, Gidrostroy

After Orlov, Forbes has Alexander Verkhovsky and his Gidrostroy empire as the next largest player. According to Forbes, Gidrostroy has sales of RUB 34.6bn ($552.56m). Verkhovsky created the company in the early 1990s in the Kuril Islands and Forbes estimates his fortune at $800m. The company is engaged in fishing, processing and is also developing in aquaculture, according to Forbes. Gidrostroy is also the main construction contractor in the Kuril Islands, “implementing a substantial part of the federal target program for the development of the region until 2025”, according to Forbes.

Gidrostroy’s $90m pelagic, pollock plant soon to start processing using Icelandic equipment

In November, Verkhovsky and two executives linked to oligarch Abramovich inked a deal worth over $300m for a rival, adding around 22,000t of pollock, herring and cod quota to its holding. 

Sakhalin-based fishing firm Poronay, in which Abramovich-linked Efim Malkin and Irina Panchenko invested last year, acquired rival Everon, according to a report by Kommersant. The addition of Everon will take Poronay -- the rest of which is reportedly controlled by Sakhalin Island, a firm owned by Verkhovsky -- to around 82,000t in quota holding. Kommersant reported Malkin and Panchenko own half of Poronay, with Verkhovsky holding the rest. 

In July 2018, Verkhovsky’s Sakhalin Island closed a deal for Preobrazhenskaya Base of Trawling Fleet (PBTF) from the family of the Sakhalin governor Oleg Kozhemyako. No deal price was given, but Kommersant gave a level of $430m and RBC a figure of as high as $600m. A price of RUB 26.50bn (currently $423m) was touted as a valuation for PBTF at the end of 2016, when rumors of the deal first emerged.

Verkhovsky has also just opened a massive, $90m processing plant for pollock, Pacific cod and other fish in the Far East. 

3. Gennady Mirgorodsky and Dmitry Ozersky, North-West Fishing Consortium

Third in the Forbes ranking is North-West Fishing Consortium, or SZRK, as the group is known in Russia. The company, owned by Gennady Mirgorodsky and Dmitry Ozersky, has sales or RUB 32.2bn ($514.55m).

SZRK, one of the largest companies in the northwest of Russia, started in the late 1980s when Mirgorodsky -- apparently a former television director -- gained control of some trawlers as part of a debt. SZRK snapped up cod and haddock harvester Arkhangelsk Trawl Fleet in 2014, beating Russian Fishery Company in the auction process. Prior to this, Mirgorodsky and his partner Ozersky bought 100% of the quotas for crab in the Barents SeaRFC 

Impact of Russia crab quota auctions one to watch in 2020, says consultant

However, on May 1, Vladimir Putin signed into law that 50% of all Russian crab quotas were put up for auction. SZRK invested RUB 24.62bn in the auction, but still saw its total volume drop from 19,200t to 14,500t. The company repeatedly protested to Undercurrent about the validity of the auction process. However, it’s still the largest player in Russian crab fishing.

4. Igor Yevtushok and Valery Ponomarev, Okeanrybflot 

In fourth place is Okeanrybflot, owned by Igor Yevtushok, Valery Ponomarev and other partners, according to Forbes. Ponomarev and Yevtushok are, according to income declarations, among the richest Russian officials, according to Forbes.

Ponomarev represents the Kamchatka territory in the federation council and Evtushok is a member of the regional legislative assembly. The duo acquired Okeanrybflot, the largest fishing company in Kamchatka with sales of RUB 26.6bn ($424.93m). Fishing companies Vityaz-Avto, Polluks and Phoenix are also associated with Ponomarev and Yevtushok, according to Forbes.

5. Gleb Frank, Russian Fishery Company

Gleb Frank’s Russian Fishery Company (RFC) is fifth on the list, with sales of RUB 21.6bn ($344.95m). The company was created in 2011 by Maxim Vorobyov and Frank, the son of Sergei Frank, chairman and former CEO of state-owned tanker company Sovcomflot, and the son-in-law of Putin-linked billionaire Gennady Timchenko.

RFC soon acquired several companies linked to the Ng family’s Pacific Andes International Holdings -- Turnif, Intraros, Vostokrybprom and Sovgavanryba -- for some $540m. This made RFC one of the main players in Russian pollock and herring.

In 2017, Frank bought 75% of DMP-RM from Dalmoreproduct, a company founded by Dmitry Dremlyuga. In February 2018, Frank took control of the company in February 2018, buying out Vorobyov.

At the crab auctions in October 2019, RFC was one of the main buyers. According to official auction data on the Far East crab auction seen by Undercurrent, the company’s Russian Crab spent RUB 33.85bn ($534m) in the auction on 9,450t of quota. This somewhat lower than the level of RUB 38bn given in a Russian media report at the time from bne IntelliNews. Forbes reported the latter figure, also stating RFC acquired 12,000t.

Russian Crab, plans to build 10 new vessels after the auction win. The company is also in the middle of a massive pollock and herring vessel newbuild program. RFC is also setting up two cod plants with Agama Group and one in the Far East for pollock and herring, with another partner. RFC is building one 108-meter “super trawler” at the Tersan Shipyard in Turkey. The vessel is the first of 11 the company plans over the next few years, with the rest to be built in Russia. Two more should be ready by the end of 2021. 

In November, RFC abruptly parted ways with Fedor Kirsanov, who took over as CEO from Andrey Teterkin in August 2018. Victor Litvinenko, who was Kirsanov's deputy, has taken over as top executive. Prior to this, Undercurrent revealed RFC's chairman and two former senior executives had also left. 

The move came as RFC is moving its headquarters to Vladivostock, from Moscow. During the Groundfish Forum, held in Berlin, Germany in October, Kirsanov told Undercurrent he was planning to move to the Far East as a result. 

6. Kozhemyako family, Salmonica Group

After Frank and RFC is Nikita Kozhemyako and his partners, who did not leave the seafood sector after the sale of PBTF to Verkhovsky.

The Kozhemyako family control Salmonica Group, which Forbes estimates has sales of RUB 17.3bn ($276.45m). Irina Gerasimenko, the wife of Sakhalin governor Oleg Kozhemyako, his sister Olga and son Nikita own shares in companies belonging to the Far Eastern Salmonica group, which owns Tymlat Fish Factory, Sea Resources, Ozernovsky RKZ No. 55 and Rykhholkam.

Nikita Kozhemyako also owns the Voskhod company, which owns quotas for about 1,600t of Far Eastern crab, some of which were acquired at auctions in 2019, according to Forbes. The company spent RUB 3.57bn on 1,050t of crab quota in the October actions, according to data obtained by Undercurrent at the time.

Russian Fishery sister crab firm plans 10 new vessels after 10,000t auction win

7. Maxim Petrushin and Sergey Popov, Sigma Marine International

Little is known about Maxim Petrushin and Sergey Popov, who Forbes said own Sigma Marine International, Sofco and Tralflot, which have sales of RUB 14bn ($223.93).

Petrushin and Popov’s companies are fishing in the Far East, catching mackerel and iwashi, or Pacific sardines, in the economic zone of Japan. Sigma also owns about 7,600t of crab quota.

8. Yuri Prutkov, FEST-Group 

FEST-Group’s Yuri Prutkov and partners are ranked eighth on the Forbes list, with sales of RUB 12.7bn ($203.20m).

In 1992, 47-year-old Prutkov headed the Murmansk Trawl Fleet (MTF), the largest fishing company in the Northern Basin, and soon took part in its privatization. 

By 2011, MTF was a holding for a number of companies and Prutkov sold the bulk to what was then Karat Holding, which is now Orlov’s Norebo Holding. After the transaction, Prutkov retained several small companies -- Sagittarius, Phoenix, Taurus and Eridan -- which form the basis of FEST.

In 2017-2018, Russia’s antimonopoly service tried to strip Prutkov of quotas, citing the fact he and his son Vitaly are Maltese citizens. The Prutkovs, who control around 40% of the group, managed to fight back in court and hold onto the business, however, according to Forbes.

9. Ilya Klebanov and family, FOR-Group

FOR Group, which is controlled by Ilya Klebanov and partners, is ninth on the Forbes list, with RUB 11.5bn ($184.06m) in revenue.

Klebanov, a former civil servant, owns 38.9% of the group personally. One of the largest assets of the group is the Sea Star company, founded by former state Duma deputy Asan Nyudyurbegov, which Klebanov’s companies acquired in 2011 from bankruptcy, said Forbes.

10. Sergey Darkin, NBAMR

Number 10 on the Forbes list is Nakhodkinskaya Baza Aktivnogo Morskogo Rybolovstva (NBAMR), or Nakhodka Active Marine Fishery Base in English, with sales of RUB 10bn ($160.10m). The company is owned by Sergey Darkin and his family.

In 1991, Darkin created the Roliz company and led it until his election as governor of the Primorsky Territory in 2001. In 2011, Roliz was bought by Orlov’s Karat group, but the Darkin family retained NBAMR.

In 2012, Darkin left the civil service and, in 2014, created the Pacific Investment Group, known as TIGER. Darkin’s TIGER is the parent of NBAMR and a group of other companies in fishing and aquaculture in the Far East. The company spent RUB 4.08bn on 1,050t of crab quota in the auctions in October.

title: Roth partially recognizes Tugushev’s claim in Norebo dispute, but there’s a catch
content:
The bitter UK legal dispute between the three founders of what is now Russia's largest seafood company took another twist this week, with Magnus Roth partially recognizing the ownership claim by  Alexander Tugushev over a third in the company. 

In a lawsuit filed in the UK's High Court of Justice last year, Tugushev claims he's owed over $350 million for his stake in Norebo, which he alleges Roth and Vitaly Orlov, CEO and now sole owner of Norebo, swindled him out of. In Roth's defense against the lawsuit, he admits in legal documents that Tugushev has a legitimate claim to ownership in some of the assets held by Norebo Holding. But if Tugushev wants to cash in his claim, it comes with a big catch, Roth argued. 

Roth said in a filing that Tugushev's claim should be offset by "a fair amount" to reflect the value that the assets grew between June 2004 to December 2009 when he was in prison on fraud charges and "failed to contribute at all" the business' operation.

Additionally, Roth's lawyers wrote in the filing that while their client admits that Tugushev is "entitled to an order that one-third of the joint venture assets shall be transferred to him", that amount should be further reduced by the value of what amounted to a major missed opportunity for the company.

According to Roth, in early 2005, Norebo's predecessor -- a joint venture between the firms Ocean Trawlers, which Roth and Vitaly Orlov, Norebo's CEO, founded, and Karat Group, which Tugushev was affiliated with -- had the opportunity to expand by purchasing a fishing business owned by Roman Abramovich, a Russian-Israeli billionaire businessman and now the owner of London's Chelsea Football Club. 

The $50m deal for that business, Chukotka Tralflot, "would have generated some $150m in profits for the joint venture partners", Roth claimed but the transaction fell apart.

"When Mr. Abramovich and/or his agents learned of Mr. Tugushev’s connection with the joint venture, they withdrew from negotiations on account of Mr. Tugushev’s arrest for fraud," Roth claimed.

Despite those demands, a spokesman for Tugushev characterized Roth's admission as a win.

"We are pleased that Mr. Roth has confirmed that Mr. Tugushev is entitled to a third interest in the joint venture which Mr. Roth acknowledges was set up by Mr. Tugushev, Mr. Roth and Mr. Orlov.  This is a significant step forward in the case against Mr. Orlov," the spokesperson said. "Mr. Tugushev looks forward to continuing his claim in the London High Court to secure full restoration of his rights and compensation."

Orlov’s defense is due on Dec. 20. Tugushev’s reply to Roth and Orlov's defenses is due on Jan. 10 and Jan. 24, 2020, respectively. 

Then, a two-day case management conference has been listed on May 18-19, 2020, Orlov's spokesman previously told Undercurrent. According to Tugushev's spokesman, the case management conference could be in May or June next year. 

"The trial will not take place before mid-2021 at the earliest," said Orlov's spokesman, in November. 

Politically motivated charges?

Tugushev has long claimed that he was a co-founder of Norebo's predecessor, the Karat/Ocean Trawlers joint venture alongside Roth and Orlov.

Tugushev, who also says he was granted shares in 2001 of a Norebo holding company named Almor Atlantika, claims that Orlov, Roth and a third man, Andrei Petrik, conspired to misappropriate his shares in the companies while he served a five-year prison sentence beginning in 2004.

Tugushev left Norebo in 2003 and was appointed deputy chairman of Russia’s State Fisheries Committee, a post-Orlov claims Tugushev "purchased" with the intention of making money from accepting bribes. Tugushev denies this and has said his conviction on fraud charges while in the government post was "politically motivated".

According to a Feb. 15, 2007 article from RIA Novosti, translated to English by Sputnik News, Tugushev and three other defendants were found guilty of extorting $3.7m from the management of a fishing company based in the Pacific port of Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky to issue illegal fishing quotas in 2003.

According to Orlov’s version of events, Tugushev “did once have a share in a company which subsequently became a (comparatively small) part of the Norebo Group, he relinquished that share in 2003 to embark upon a misjudged and short-lived career as a corrupt government official”.

In 2018, Tugushev successfully applied to have a worldwide freezing order placed on $350m of Norebo's assets as he pressed his claim in UK courts against the defendants. Orlov challenged the UK's court's jurisdiction to hear the case, preferring instead that it be litigated in Russia. However, a judge eventually sided with Tugushev and allowed the case to remain in the UK. The freezing order, however, was later lifted, judge Sue Carr ruled, because Orlov would not sell his stake in Norebo to defeat any judgment in the ongoing case.

title: Criminal lawsuit brought against former Angolan fisheries minister
content:
A criminal lawsuit has been filed against former Angolan fisheries minister Victoria de Barros Neto due to her alleged role in the money laundering and corruption scandal that has already seen two Namibian ministers arrested, reports the Namibian.

The bank accounts of Neto, her husband and children have already been blocked by the Angolan attorney general's office, while an arrest warrant has been issued against the former minister, who was dismissed in January this year.

Teams from both Angola and Namibia are working together to investigate Neto's role in the "Fishrot" scandal -- although authorities of Angola cannot extradite an Angolan citizen for trial, as per the state's constitution.

While in office, Neto had signed the agreement with former Namibian fisheries minister Berhnard Esau permitting Namibia to donate horse mackerel quotas to Angola. It has since been discovered that these quotas were allocated to the firm Namgomar Pesca, who then allegedly sold them on to Iceland's Samherji, with profits transferred to offshore companies in Dubai and Mauritius.

From these offshore companies, profits were then supposedly funneled to Namibian firms owned by former justice minister Sacky Shanghala and former Fishcor chairperson James Hatuikulipi. Both men are now in police custody, as is former minister Esau.

One of Neto's children, Joao de Barros, is another alleged beneficiary of the redirected fishing revenue, further implicating her in the scandal, according to the Namibian.

title: Samherji-linked vessel impounded by Namibian authorities
content:
The Samherji-linked vessel Heinaste has been impounded by Namibian authorities after it was caught fishing in restricted waters near Walvis Bay two weeks ago, reports The Namibian.

The vessel was seized by the Namibian police on Nov. 22 "after it entered and illegally fished in Namibian waters," according to chief police inspector Kauna Shikwambi. 

Heinaste's captain was previously arrested by the Namibian police in relation to illegal fishing charges, and brought before a judge on Nov. 20, before being released on a bail of NAD 100,000 ($6,700)

Meanwhile, the Heinaste, which is now stateless and deregistered, is owned by Esja Fishing, which is in turn owned by Samherji's Cyprus-based subsidiary Esja Seafood. Esja Seafood has been implicated in the Fishrot files as one of Samherji's alleged routes for paying bribes into key bank accounts in Namibia, including that of Tamson Hatuikulipi, the son-in-law of former fisheries minister Bernhard Esau.

The Heinaste was previously at the center of its own legal dispute, as Esja Investment attempted to sell the vessel for NAD 280 million, to the dismay of local partners Sinco Fishing and Epango Fishing, who owned 45% of the ship. 

The judge ultimately ruled in Esja's favor, dismissing the claims made by its local partners, but the delay meant the vessel's planned sale to a Russian firm collapsed.
