title: Namibian, SA hake firms invested at least €135m in 2019 despite quota hold-up
content:
Namibia's hake industry has been at the center of a surge of investment among fishing companies this year, despite continued uncertainty regarding the future re-allocation of expired fishing rights -- a matter further delayed by the ongoing Fishrot scandal that has shaken the nation's fishing ministry to its core. 

Samherji corruption scandal may have consequences for Spanish in Namibia

In both South Africa and Namibia, the full total allowable catch for cape hake has been set for the current season, at 146,000 metric tons and 154,000t respectively.

However, full allocations of cape hake quotas in Namibia are still to be given, according to Peter Pahl, managing director of Namibian hake catcher Seawork Fish Processors.

"They’ve allocated a third of the TAC [total allowable catch], and at the moment we are waiting to see what’s happening next," Pahl told Undercurrent News.

He added that Seawork and the nation's other hake fishing companies are all expecting to see the remaining 70% of the Namibian hake quota allocated to the industry piecemeal over the next eight or 10 months.

The re-allocation of the Namibian hake quotas has been an issue of controversy over the past year -- the fisheries ministry received roughly 5,200 applications for new hake licenses after 75 fishing rights expired at the end of 2018. In May this year, the ministry was said to still be in the evaluation stage for new licenses, and Pahl confirmed that this was the most recent update the industry had received too.

The resignation and ultimate arrest of fisheries minister Bernhard Esau -- due to the now-infamous allegations that he sold horse mackerel quotas to Icelandic fishing firm Samherji in return for financial kickbacks -- has also put a halt on the quota re-allocation process, Undercurrent sources confirmed. Albert Kawana, Namibia's new acting minister of fisheries and marine resources, is believed to be making a public statement on Dec.11, which may update the industry on the plans to resume the process.

In a document released from the ministry on Nov. 25, Namibia's president, Haige Geingob, said Kawana had been given the authority "to immediately undertake an assessment and evaluation of the existing processes and procedures, relating to the management and administration of our marine resources, and make recommendations to me in order to prevent and eliminate, if any, instances of maladministration, nepotism, and/or corruption."

Geingob added that Kawana will be reviewing the affairs of the ministry and its relationship with the state-owned firm Fishcor -- the chief beneficiary of former minister Esau's sweeping horse mackerel quota re-allocations -- with Kawana given the authority to make "corrective measures" where he sees fit.

Nevertheless, Seawork and other Namibian fishing firms have been left waiting for new developments on the hake quota re-allocations from the ministry for over a year now.

"We haven’t heard anything," Pahl said. "Our news is exactly what you hear – we have all been watching Al Jazeera, but we don’t have any new information. We'll probably wait to see the new interim minister and take things from there."

Seawork among big investors in Namibian hake

Unlike horse mackerel, Namibia's hake quota allocations have remained largely pro-rata over the past 10 years, Undercurrent sources confirmed, with the consistency meaning firms can afford to gamble on major investments even when only a third of the quota is presently allocated. 

Seawork, All-Fish acquisition opens south German market to cape hake

Seawork, for instance, jointly acquired the German wholesaler Intercont Grosshandels in partnership with its German distributor All-Fish Handelsgesellschaft this November.

This investment, for an undisclosed sum, is the latest in a list of major capital expenditures by Seawork over the last couple of years.

Two years ago, Pahl said, Seawork acquired the local small-scale monkfish harvester Benguela Fishing. It has since spent considerable sums on factory upgrades at its Walvis Bay facilities -- an estimated €6 million in its most recent production upgrade, according to data from the 2019 Groundfish Forum, held in Berlin this October.

"We’ve spent a lot on factory upgrades, and besides the acquisition of Benguela, it’s just organic growth, basically. We can’t grow much beyond quota availability," Pahl said.

The 16-year-old firm, whose ownership is approximately 90% Namibian, now employs 1,700 laborers at its processing plants, where the company still requires the additional manpower for manual filleting.

Seawork also operates a fleet of five trawlers, one of which -- the 130t capacity Victory -- was refurbished this year.

"She’s ready to go to sea now basically, she’s done all the tests and so on. So that’s all been completed," Pahl confirmed.

Pahl said the company would be looking to add to its fleet in the new year, but added that "nothing's been settled yet".

"Our main focus will be in Namibia. There will be new trawlers, yes, we intend to get more, and we intend to get other factories operational; we still intend to grow a lot."

Pahl's firm is not alone in investing heavily in the Namibian seafood sector in 2019; a total of at least €135m ($150m) has been spent so far this year in Namibia and South Africa through eight different companies in the sector, according to a presentation delivered by Felix Ratheb, CEO of South African fishing firm Sea Harvest Group, at October's Groundfish Forum.

"We are asked by the government to invest, to create new job opportunities, so that's what we do"

Largest among these, the Spanish farmed and wild-caught seafood supplier Grupo Nueva Pescanova committed €30m for the construction of three 50-meter-long trawler vessels for its Namibian operations. The first vessel “Lalandii 1” was launched in July this year and will fish for cape hake in the country, where the company has more than 2,000 employees. The remaining two are then planned for launch in H2 2020.

Namibian firm Tunacor Fisheries, which acquired the remaining assets of the now-defunct firm Namsov Fishing last year, also took delivery of the country's first-ever purpose-built newbuild fishing vessel 'Oshiveli' at the end of 2018. In January 2019, during its sea trials off Walvis Bay, the vessel landed its first catch. Built for €12.5m, Oshiveli harvests both horse mackerel and hake, which is then fully-processed at sea.

Elsewhere, Hangana Seafood -- a subsidiary of the Ohlthaver & List Group -- has also committed €15m for a new processing facility and cold store in Namibia’s largest commercial port of Walvis Bay. The new facility will be operational in H2 2020 and will have an annual capacity of 25,000t once completed, as well as a cold storage capacity of 2,500t. According to the group, a further investment of €1.2m within the next five years in the plant will allow Hangana to process other fish species such as horse mackerel.

Marco Fishing completed its new factory built in Luderitz adding 1,000 square meters of floor space. This upgrade will provide with the installation of new sorting, filleting and skinning lines as well as an IQF spiral freezer.

Pescanova, Tunacor, Hangana and Marco Fishing were unavailable to comment when contacted by Undercurrent.

"I don’t think there’s anything specifically driving the investment at other companies," Seawork's Pahl told Undercurrent. "We are asked by the government to invest, to create new job opportunities, so that’s what we do."

Meanwhile, in neighboring South Africa, both Irving & Johnson (I&J) and Sea Harvest have invested in new trawlers and installations. In total, I&J committed €28m for two vessels, the wetfish trawler MFV Ferox and the freezer trawler MFV Umlobi. A further €4.5m was spent on an installation for a fresh fish processing plant, in collaboration with the Icelandic equipment supplier Marel. 

For its part, Sea Harvest also invested a total of €26m on two new freezer trawlers — MFV Atlantic Peace and MF Mzansi and €9.5m on an installation for its fresh fish operations and a value-added operation in collaboration with German tech supplier Nienstedt.

MSC certification update

South Africa's hake trawl fishery is undergoing a recertification assessment under the v2 Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certification that is expected to be completed during the first quarter of 2020. The fishery was previously certified in 2004, in 2010, and most recently in 2015 for a further five years.

Namibian hake fishery should be MSC certified early next year, Seawork estimates

Namibia’s hake fishery is also currently on its way to achieving full MSC certification, although the process has been delayed several times.

At the beginning of 2019, former fisheries minister Esau stated in his annual ministerial address to the industry that the process, which is being undertaken by their officials in collaboration with the hake association, “is progressing well”. Despite the delays, Namibia expects to finally see its certification completed by May 2020, giving its hake much greater penetration in northern Europe and the UK, according to Ratheb's presentation.

title: NOAA agent: More rules around vertical integration might foil next ‘Codfather’
content:
To stop another massive case of fish fraud like the one recently hoisted upon the New England groundfish and scallop fleets by Carlos Rafael, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) should explore adding rules around companies that operate both as harvesters and dealers, suggests Troy Audyatis, an agent in NOAA's Office of Law Enforcement (OLE).

Audyatis, who worked as part of a five federal agency effort to investigate and arrest Rafael, the so-called “Codfather” of New Bedford, Massachusetts, in early 2016, provided a few new details from the case that previously shook the region’s commercial fishing industry and also some suggestions for how to avoid a reoccurrence when he addressed the New England Fishery Management Council (NEFMC) on Tuesday, the first of a three-day meeting in Newport, Rhode Island.  

Carlos Rafael has pleaded guilty to 28 federal charges, including lying about catches and smuggling cash
Read more

“This will probably not be a popular slide,” he said at the end of his presentation, which was accessible online, before sharing a list of “possible areas for improvement.”

The list included exploring “additional restrictions on vertically integrated companies,” dockside monitoring of fish offloading, limited offloading times, increased and refined onboard observer coverage rates and electronic onboard monitoring.

Carlos Rafael gives a demonstration on how to cut cod at a festival in New Bedford, Massachusetts, in 2010. Image is a still from a YouTube video.

The commercial fishing industry in and around New Bedford won’t soon forget the Rafael saga, including how the one-time fishing mogul, whose fleet was once reported to be worth at least $175m, got caught misidentifying more than 700,000 lbs of fish over at least a four-year period, 2012-2015, in order to avoid regulatory quotas.

Rafael was arrested in February 2016 and pleaded guilty in March 2017 to 28 criminal counts, including Lacey Act false labeling violations, tax evasion and filing false reports. In September 2017, he was sentenced to serve a 46-month term in a federal prison and pay about $300,000 in fines. He is scheduled to be released on March 4, 2021, according to the US Bureau of Prisons. 

More recently, in August 2019, Rafael agreed to a civil settlement with the federal government that required him to pay a $3m penalty and leave the fishing industry for good, selling all of his remaining 46 vessels, including some skiffs, and their related permits. Simultaneously, 17 of the captains who worked for Rafael were given a combined 1,320 days of permit suspensions, 382 months of probation and are now subject to enhanced monitoring requirements, Audyatis noted.

Federal prosecutors had described how Rafael was able to get away with much of his scheme because he owned both the harvesting vessels and a seafood dealership. Rafael’s captains submitted incorrect catch reports, and the dealer reports were made to match.

“I’m not opposed to vertically integrated companies,” Audyatis stressed. “This is not a slam against vertically integrated companies, but Carlos was able to do what he did because he owned the boats and he owned the business. It’s the simple truth.”

'You'e not going to catch a crook with just more monitoring'

Tuesday's meeting was not the first time the NEFMC had heard the NOAA agent's ideas for preventing fraud in the New England groundfish fishery. They were also described in a short report delivered by OLE to the council's joint enforcement committee and advisory panel at a late July meeting, in Portsmouth, New Hampshire.

OLE, in its earlier report, recommended a "multi-species permit ownership cap", restricting the number of permits one person and or corporation can hold.

"This will restrict one entity from becoming too large of a player in the industry," the paper read. "Rafael was able to do what he did because he was vertically integrated and owned a large fleet of vessels and a federally permitted dealership to launder the misreported fish."

OLE also suggested it have "direct access to dockside monitors data" and increase at-sea monitoring coverage beyond the current 15%. It suggested mandatory offloading windows, citing vessels caught unloading their catch outside of an established period, and a "certified weighmaster program", in which OLE would certify the scales in all offloading facilities "to be true and accurate".   

The agency recommended its offshore video monitoring program be expanded from 20 vessels to all federally permitted vessels monitored through OLE. This would be in addition to the vessel monitoring system (VMS) program.

"No camera, no fish," the document reads, noting that the estimated cost of installing a functional camera system is about $12,500. 

However, at least one of the attendees at Tuesday's meeting suggested harvesters don't need more of the types of restrictions OLE suggested. During the question and answer session that followed Audyatis' presentation, longtime New Hampshire fisherman David Goethel warned that the NOAA law enforcement agent was proposing “turning the fishery into a police state”.

"You're not going to catch a crook with just more monitoring," he said.

When asked if at-sea monitoring would be necessary if port-side monitoring was sufficient, Audyatis replied: “The problem is, and we saw it in the Carlos Rafael case, when you have single species managed in separate stocks, it’s hard to tell where those fish were caught if you don’t have someone on board to verify.”

The New Bedford, Massachusetts, seafood auction. Photo by Jason Huffman.

Goethel pressed the NOAA agent on what happened to a New York dealer who also was described in charging documents as purchasing Rafael's fish. Audyatis said he was not able to talk about the matter as it was left to the federal prosecutors.

“I think a lot more emphasis ought to be put on the crooked dealer side of things than just the crooked fisherman,” said the fisherman.

“You’re not going to catch crooks with dockside monitors or at-sea monitors or any of that stuff. Turning the fishery into a police state isn’t going to catch a crook. If you want to catch a crook, you’ve got to use the right bait. Dockside monitors can be bribed. At sea monitors can be bribed”, Goethel said.

Goethel was a plaintiff in an ultimately unsuccessful 2015 lawsuit challenging a NOAA rule that required groundfish harvesters to bear the cost of at-sea observers. The rule remains valid but groundfishermen haven't had to pay for monitors in recent years as Congress allocated funds for that purpose, Ryan Mulvey, an attorney with the group Cause for Action, told Undercurrent News in March 2019.

How Rafael invited law enforcement attention

In addition to the suggestions, the NEFMC also received a more thorough understanding of the investigation that led to Rafael's arrest and conviction on Tuesday.

Audyatis recounted for the council how Rafael invited law enforcement attention on himself in January 2015 when -- angered by cuts made to his portion of federal groundfish disaster relief -- he announced that he planned to sell his more than 40 vessels and their roughly 60-related permits for cod, haddock and other groundfish as well as scallops.

"We took this as an opportunity to reach out to Carlos Rafael as interested buyers," the NOAA agent said. "We caught him using his own words."

The Whaleman statue, an iconic image of New Bedford, Massachusetts, hearkening back to when the city was focused on landing a much different species. Photograph by Lin Mei.

Audyatis described how his task force used a couple of Internal Revenue Service agents of Russian descent to pose as organized crime members interested in buying the business. Other agencies involved in the investigation were the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Department of Homeland Security and the Coast Guard Investigative Service.

"As a result of this case, we had hours upon hours of audio and video with Rafael telling us exactly what he did and how he did it. Over and over and over again. His own words, folks," Audyatis said.

Between June 2015 and February 2016, the task force conducted as many as five joint undercover operations of Rafael and his associates, uncovering evidence of “egregious fisheries violations, federal tax evasion, public corruption, bulk cash smuggling and structuring.”

The investigator presented a Powerpoint slide breaking down the illegal overfishing by year and species. It showed the behavior escalating with the Rafael business catching 37,193 pounds over the limit in 2012 to 432,536 lbs over the limit by 2015.

In all, over the four-year-period, Rafael's business illegally caught 782,811 pounds of fish over the limit, including 80,731 lbs of cod, 160,785 lbs of sea dabs, 263,851 lbs of grey sole and 277,444 lbs of yellowtail flounder.

Combined, according to Audyatis, the illegally caught fish had an ex-boat value of $1.68 million and a median estimated retail value of $5.1m.

In a separate presentation, US Coast Guard captain Kevin King said investigators identified 350 vessel trips involving the apparent misreporting of species. He said the number of trips represented less than 1% of the 60,000 trips taken by the Rafael fleet during the five-year period.

Full settlement includes trust agreement

A copy of the full settlement between NOAA and Rafael, obtained this week by Undercurrent, details more the requirements for each of the operators during probationary periods. They must notify the NOAA Office of Law Enforcement before each fishing trip, maintain haul-by-haul logs, report each species and weights of fish caught every 12 hours on vessel monitoring systems (VMSs) and set the VMS for polling every 15 minutes.

The agreement also spells out the terms of a trust created and maintained for Carlos and Conceicao Rafael, his wife, for the purpose of receiving funds from the sale of his vessels. It advises that any vessels that do not receive fair market value offers within seven months of the trust agreement, which was signed on August 1, are to be placed in a public auction process to be completed within nine months.

Such an auction might not be necessary. 

Homers Wharf, port of New Bedford. Photo: Mike Estabrook

In September 2019, Quinn Fisheries, a 33-year-old New Bedford area scallop operation, agreed to pay about $40m to acquire the most valuable part of the Rafael fleet, six of his 11 scallop vessels and their related permits, as first reported by Undercurrent.  Then late last month, Undercurrent broke the news that Blue Harvest Fisheries, a US scallop and groundfish supplier backed by New York City-based private equity Bregal Partners, has signed a purchase agreement to buy  at least 35 vessels and skiffs and all of their associated permits from Rafael for nearly $25m.

It is not yet known if any of the vessel buyers will employ any of the former Rafael fishing captains.

title: Namibia’s Fishcor suspends CEO in corruption scandal
content:
Namibia’s state-owned fishing firm Fishcor has suspended its CEO following reports he and other government officials conspired with Iceland’s biggest fishing company, Samherji, to receive kickbacks in exchange for fishing rights, reports Reuters.

Fishcor's acting chairperson Bennet Kangumu said CEO Mike Nghipunya had been sent home a week ago, following international and local media reports that he was involved in the scandal.

Fishcor has not previously commented on any role its officials might have played in the scandal.

Two former ministers -- Bernhard Esau and Sacky Shanghala -- have been arrested and now charged, accused of conspiring with Samherji to receive payments worth millions of dollars in exchange for horse mackerel fishing quotas.

Samherji and the former ministers have all denied wrongdoing.

On Nov. 29 Esau, Shanghala and three of their co-accused in the 'Fishrot' case were informed of the charges they face when they made a delayed appearance in the dock in the Windhoek Magistrate's Court, reports the Namibian.

title: Angolan nationals dragged into Samherji-Namibia affair
content:
Namibia's Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) has reportedly linked former Angolan fisheries minister Victoria de Barros Neto, and two other Angolan nationals, to the alleged Samherji bribery case, reports the Namibian.

The ACC also said de Barros Neto's son, Joao de Barros, and close associate Antonio Santos Francisco, have been linked to the investigation through investigations of payments.

Samherji execs lawyer up, as wanted Namibians return home

The Namibian news site also reported that ACC officials are questioning their director-general Paulus Noa's hands-off approach in the arrest of former justice minister Sacky Shanghala and ex-Investec Asset Management Namibia managing director James Hatuikulipi.

Noa confirmed that Shanghala and Hatuikulipi were arrested Nov. 27, a day after they arrived back from their two-week trip to South Africa. They face charges relating to corruption, money laundering, and fraud in a fishing scandal involving more than NAD 150 million ($113m).

James Hatuikulipi's relatives Tamson 'Fitty' Hatuikulipi and Pius 'Taxa' Mwatelulo were detained after they turned themselves in. Former fisheries minister Bernhard Esau and suspended director of Investec Asset Management in Namibia Ricardo Gustavo were arrested last week. Esau was released at the weekend.

They are expected to appear in court on Nov. 29, but ACC officials are apparently fuming at Noa's lack of interest in the case that he has left to his deputy, Erna van der Merwe, to lead.

title: P&P seeks distance from Samherji Namibian ops, but plans further UK JV investment
content:
A document on a proposal for a joint venture (JV) in Namibia from Parlevliet and Van der Plas (P&P) is included in the WikiLeaks Samherji “Fishrot” document dump, but the CEO of the Dutch fishing and processing giant said the companies’ cooperation is limited to the UK only, which it would like to develop further.

Unlike Iceland's Samherji, which is being accused of paying over $10 million to Namibian politicians from 2012-2018 for access to horse mackerel quotas, P&P didn’t proceed with a JV in the African country. The scandal has seen several Namibian politicians and officials resign, including its former fisheries minister, with the government investigating the alleged wrongdoing and making arrests. 

P&P was in talks with quota holders, but didn't conclude an agreement, Diederik Parlevliet, CEO of the acquisitive Dutch fishing giant, told Undercurrent News.

In the UK, the two companies own UK Fisheries, which operates two vessels, a venture Parlevliet said he’d like to build further. In Africa, however, they have essentially been in competition, sources said.

“I know the Samherji people well and they are very honest. It’s hard for me to say anything, as I don’t know [about what happened in Namibia]. We operate with them in UK Fisheries, not in Africa,” Parlevliet said.

“At that time [in 2012-2013] there were quota holders talking about making joint ventures with EU or Asian companies. We just rented the quota for a year, and during that year we were discussing with the quota holders to make a joint venture,” he said.

“The paper in Wikileaks is the description paper we made for the joint venture. But that did not happen, for commercial reasons. We did not come to a commercial agreement,” said Parlevliet. “We fished for about one year, but not under a joint venture, we had our own Namibian company and the vessel was leasing for one year from quota holders. It was many years ago, seven or eight, and since then we have not operated in Namibia.”

Sources familiar with Samherji and P&P also told Undercurrent this same story. Despite their partnership in UK Fisheries, which Samherji co-founder Thorstein Mar Baldvinsson has just stood down from, P&P was actually competing with the Icelandic firm to get into Namibia at the time, they said.

The P&P document -- which seemingly came into the possession of Johannes Steffansson, the former Samherji Namibia manager who has turned whistleblower on the company -- said annual profits from the JV could be between $18m and $21m.

In the document, which was presented at the time by Parlevliet, P&P proposed giving 51% ownership to the unnamed quota holders, and would have run from the start of 2013 to the end of 2018. The Dutch firm would have supplied a “state-of-the-art and efficient factory trawler” to the operation under the plan.

The quota requirement for a profitable operation on one vessel is 30,000 metric tons, but the preference for this vessel is 40,000t, “which makes this operation very profitable”, wrote Parlevliet.

Over the first ten months of the proposed operation, a monthly payment of $700,000 would have been paid as pre-dividend to the shareholders in the JV who are also quota holders.

At the time, P&P said it has a “long-term strategy in the Namibian fishing industry” and will support the government’s policy of “Namibianization” of the sector. P&P also said it’s “ready to discuss and to offer ownership in the fishing vessel”.

Plan to invest more in UK with Samherji

P&P would like to invest more in the UK, said Parlevliet.

This comes after Baldvinsson, the co-founder of Samherji, resigned from the UK Fisheries board on Tuesday. Baldvinsson had already stepped down from his role as Samherji CEO while an investigation into the Namibian allegations is underway.

“It’s the decision of Thorstein to step down. It’s got nothing to do with the JV itself. He stepped aside, as he did in Iceland. It’s his own decision, there’s no influence from my side”, said Parlevliet, adding he hopes Baldvinsson returns.

Samherji and P&P operate two UK-registered vessels, Kirkella, a new freezer-trawler, and Farnella, a fresh fish vessel, which catch quotas outside the country’s waters.

Then, the company is packing and also processing some volumes in the Humberside region, at Seagold, which is owned by Samherji, said Parlevliet. Samherji also owns Collins (Seafoods), a distributor to fish and chip shops, which is one customer, he said.

The companies are interested in investing further in the UK, despite the uncertainty around the UK’s exit from the European Union, said Parlevliet.

“Brexit is a black box for everyone, in Europe and the UK, so we need to wait for the elections and see what happens. But with any uncertainty, like Brexit, I always see opportunities,” he said.

This comes as Greenpeace used the Namibia scandal as a chance to blast Samherji and UK Fisheries, citing a report from 2018 on foreign ownership of UK quotas.

“As for the talk [from Greenpeace] of quotas being in the hands of foreigners, a UK fisherman has sold their quotas and got money for that,” said Parlevliet.

The two UK Fisheries vessels have “mainly British crew, land in Britain and the company is paying UK tax”, he said. “Also, we are doing a lot of investments in the Humberside region and are fully working as a UK company selling to the fish and chip market. We’d like to continue to do that. We are investing more than other companies.”

title: Namibia makes more arrests in horse mackerel quota scandal
content:
The African nation of Namibia has taken further action in its investigation of the alleged horse mackerel quota bribe scandal involving Icelandic giant Samherji, arresting Sakeus Shanghala, a former justice minister, and James Hatuikulipi, the former head of Investec Asset Management's Namibia office, the wire service Reuters reports.

Shanghala is alleged to have accepted kickbacks, while Hatuikulipi has been accused of spearheading the bribery scheme, as earlier reported.

Samherji’s Baldvinsson steps down from UK joint venture with P&P, Seagold

The scheme, which was brought to light by a WikiLeaks release of some 30,000 documents, is believed to have generated at least NAD 150 million ($10.2m).

The arrests, confirmed by Paulus Noa, an anti-corruption commission director, come as the country heads into a a presidential and parliamentary election on Wednesday (Nov. 27). The SWAPO party has ruled Namibia for three decades.

The arrests follow the detention of the former fisheries minister Bernhard Esau and another former Investec employee on Saturday on the same charges. Both were released a day later after a judge said the arrest warrants were invalid. Esau has denied wrongdoing.

Four executives at Iceland's Samherji have reportedly hired lawyers to prepare their defense against accusations of bribery and tax evasion.

title: Samherji execs lawyer up, as wanted Namibians return home
content:
Four executives at Iceland's Samherji have hired lawyers to prepare their defense against accusations of bribery and tax evasion, reports RUV, citing fellow news site Frettabladid.
 
Gardar Gislason, Samherji’s lawyer, noted neither the business nor any individuals working for it are currently official suspects in any investigation, and nobody has yet been called for questioning.

Samherji Sainsbury’s loss not linked to Namibia scandal, but M&S takes allegations ‘very seriously’

Arna Bryndis Baldvins McClure, head lawyer at Samherji; Egill Helgi Arnason, who was involved in the running of ArcticNam; Jon Ottar Olafsson, who was a consultant adviser to Samherji; and one un-named Samherji employee overseas are the four said to have hired representation.

Meanwhile, the three "so-called sharks" connected to the Samherji case are ready to give themselves up to the Namibian anti-corruption police, with two of them due home from South Africa on Nov. 26.

Sacky Shanghala, who resigned as Namibian justice minister in the wake of the investigation into the Samherji documents; James Hatuikulipi, who resigned as director of the Namibian state fisheries company Fishcor; and Tamson “Fitty” Hatuikulipi, cousin of James and son-in-law of Bernard Esau, the former fisheries minister, are the parties said to be willing to work with police.

Esau also resigned over the investigation and was arrested by anti-corruption police at the weekend, but was released on Sunday evening over a technical problem with the arrest warrant, said RUV.

Back in Iceland, fisheries minister Kristjan Thor Juliusson faced protests outside the country's parliament, calling for him to resign. He once served as chair of the board at Samherji, and is a close friend of outgoing chairman Thorsteinn Mar Baldvinsson. He said he would not be resigning.

During the same parliamentary session, finance minister and Independence Party leader Bjarni Benediktsson was accused of breaking the law by not offering additional funding for an inquiry into Samherji. He dismissed claims, stating it was up to investigators and not parliament to control where the ongoing probe went.

title: Blue Harvest inks deal to acquire 35 Rafael groundfish vessels for $25m
content:
One of the most anticipated forced sell-offs in the history of US commercial fishing – the unloading of Carlos Rafael’s fleet in New Bedford, Massachusetts -- looks to be on the verge of completion.

Blue Harvest Fisheries, a US scallop and groundfish supplier backed by New York City-based private equity Bregal Partners, has signed a purchase agreement to buy at least 35 vessels and skiffs and all of their associated permits from Carlos Rafael for nearly $25 million, documents obtained by Undercurrent News confirm.

The deal includes millions of pounds of quota for at least eight types of fish in the northeast multispecies fishery, including cod, haddock, American plaice, witch flounder, yellowtail flounder, redfish, white hake and pollock.

The roughly 30-page agreement must still survive a “right of first refusal” (ROFR) process, by which other harvesters in the sectors where the vessels worked will also have a chance to match the bid. Also, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) must approve the buyer, following a review of the company's legal history or possible relationship to Rafael.

Carlos Rafael gives a demonstration on how to cut cod at a festival in New Bedford, Massachusetts, in 2010. Image is a still from a YouTube video.

But a copy of the deal, provided to groundfish sector 7 manager Cassie Canastra on Thursday (Nov. 21) by Stephanie Rafael Demello, Carlos Rafael’s daughter, to begin the ROFR process, includes many of the details.

One attachment identifies 28 vessels and skiffs reported to be worth a combined $19.3 million, including the 23-year-old, 83-foot, 503 horsepower Southern Crusader II and 50-year-old, 74.6-foot, 503-horse power Green Acres. Another attachment identifies seven vessels and skiffs, including the 31-year-old, 81-foot, 855-horse power Bulldog, which are reported to be worth a combined $5.4m.

One point of confusion in the contract is that it refers to the $19.3m part of the deal, but the $5.4m part of the deal is included only in the attachments.

The agreement required a deposit of $250,000 be made in a designated trust account managed by Rafael’s attorney, John Markey, Jr., on the date of the transaction.  If the deal doesn’t close by Jan. 1, 2020, the sellers are responsible for securing docking space in New Bedford for the following year.

The agreement gives the sector 7 chief until Tuesday to share the purchase agreement with other potential bidders. The other prospective buyers then have 30 days to respond, so until roughly Dec. 26.

Blue Harvest CEO Keith Decker did not reply to calls for comment on Monday. Rafael’s attorney John Markey Jr., a partner with Moses Smith, Markey & Walsh, in New Bedford, said his client's family has declined to comment.

The end of a dark saga

The sale of Rafael’s groundfishing vessels promises to conclude a dark saga at the Port of New Bedford in which Rafael’s once more than $100m operation was caught mislabeling more than 700,000 pounds of fish over a four-year period and evading taxes.

Rafael was arrested in February 2016 after a sting, involving federal agents pretending to be Russian mobsters interested in buying his fleet, got him to detail his illegal actions into a hidden microphone. To get the then 64-year-old fishing mogul to talk, the agents had expressed concern about the business’s lack of profitability and, in his effort to persuade them, Rafael revealed he was keeping separate records of his operation to hide his misidentification of species.  

Rafael, who became labeled by the media as “the Codfather,” pled guilty in March 2017 to 28 criminal counts. In September of the same year, he was ordered to serve a 46-month term in a federal prison and pay about $300,000 in fines.

One of the many fishing vessels owned by Carlos Rafael . Photo by Jason Huffman

Then, in August 2019, Rafael agreed to settle the civil case brought against him by federal authorities, paying a roughly $3m penalty and leaving the commercial fishing industry for good. The settlement gave him until Dec. 31, 2020 – about 16 months – to sell all of his vessels and related permits, though NOAA maintained the authority to review and approve each transaction.

The sentence was a surprise to some as the federal agency had earlier suggested it would simply revoke Rafael’s permits, making his vessels virtually worthless.

In September, Quinn Fisheries, a 33-year-old New Bedford area scallop operation, agreed to pay about $40m to acquire the most valuable part of the Rafael fleet, six of Rafael’s 11 scallop vessels and their related permits, as first reported by Undercurrent.  The vessels sold then included the Acores, Athena, Apollo, Gypsy Girl, Hera II and the Villa Nova Do II.

Ship captains come with restrictions

All of Rafael’s groundfish vessels have been blocked from fishing, and New England's sector IX, the area his company previously dominated, has been shut down for more than two years by federal authorities, though Rafael has been permitted to lease his quota to other sectors.  

The agreement reached with Rafael states that Blue Harvest has been given adequate access to the vessels for the purpose of inspection.

Should Blue Harvest succeed in completing its deal for the Rafael vessels, it next will be forced to hire ship captains. Based on the agreement reached earlier with federal authorities, hiring back any of the captains previously employed by Rafael will mean dealing with suspensions ranging from 20 to 200 months, probationary periods ranging from 12 to 36 months, and having an observe or deck during groundfish or scallop trips.

Some of the vessels to be acquired by Blue Harvest and their previous captains played significant roles in the Rafael case.

Atlantic cod. Photograph courtesy of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Thomas Simpson was operating the Bulldog, in May 2014, when the US Coast Guard (USCG) boarded the vessel to perform a routine inspection, as a Department of Justice statement recounted. When the boarding officer asked him to reel in his net, the then 53-year-old South Portland, Maine, man instead let out more cable. After the Coast Guard officer ordered him to stop, he allowed the net to drop even more, until it became detached and sunk to the ocean floor.  

Later, USCG and NOAA hired a salvage company, at a cost of about $15,000, to retrieve the net and discovered it was using “three distinct and separate layers of netting in violation of commercial fishing regulations”.

Blue Harvest on a spending spree

Blue Harvest, like Rafael, is based in New Bedford, Massachusetts, and already maintains a base of five groundfish vessels and 15 scallopers out of two commercial ports: Fairhaven, Massachusetts, and Newport News, Virginia. It had been speculated for the past several months as one of the most likely of several possible contenders for the Rafael fleet.

The company had been on a spending spree in recent years with cash handy from its private equity backer, which simultaneously has sought to sell American Seafoods Group, a large harvester and processor of Alaska-caught pollock.

In April, Bregal announced that a second round of funding brought its total managed capital up to $1.25 billion. 

Earlier, in November 2018, Blue Harvest quietly acquired Portland, Maine-based Atlantic Trawlers Fishing and has been processing the cod, haddock and redfish caught by Atlantic’s five vessels at its New Bedford plant, which was acquired in 2016 from Canada’s High Liner Foods. The deal followed Atlantic Trawlers obtaining Marine Stewardship Council certification for the New England haddock, pollock and redfish trawl fishery in May 2018.

Aerial view of New Bedford waterfront and New Bedford-Fairhaven bridge. Photo: Port of New Bedford

Blue Harvest was seen promoting its newly acquired groundfish products at Seafood Expo North America, in Boston, Massachusetts, in March. It then announced in April, at Seafood Expo Global, in Brussels, Belgium, that it’s taking its groundfish line of products global.

The New England groundfish fisheries where Blue Harvest has been building its stake are not what they used to be. There were once 1,400 groundfish vessels in the area but the number is more like 225 to 250 today, one source estimated. 

Blue Harvest was also considered a possible buyer of Rafael’s scallop fleet, after its acquisitions in 2015 and 2016 of other scallop vessels, but the company was virtually locked out because of its existing scallop fleet.

Per federal regulation, no more than 5% of the limited access scallop vessels and permit-related quota can have the same owner. Because all of New England’s roughly 370 permitted scallop vessels have the same amount of quota, that limits their owners to 17 permitted boats each.

It’s unclear how much of a deal Blue Harvest is getting for Rafael’s groundfish operation. One source told Undercurrent some months ago that the average multiple for a groundfish vessel with permits is about five to six times earnings before interest taxes and depreciation of assets -- less than half the value of scallop permits and vessels.

title: Former Namibian fisheries minister arrested, released following court judgement
content:
In the latest twist of the ongoing Namibian fisheries corruption scandal, the country's former minister of fisheries, Bernhard Esau, was arrested on Nov. 23, before being released by the high court the following day, reports Reuters.

Esau was charged alongside former Investec Asset Management client manager Ricardo Gustavo -- who has also resigned amid scandal -- on charges of corruption. 

However, Esau was released by the Windhoek high court on Nov. 24, after it found that the warrant for Esau's arrest the previous day was invalid. Esau's lawyer argued that the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) investigators had “no power or authority in law to investigate money laundering” and issue a warrant, according to Reuters.

Under-fire Samherji co-founder steps down from SVN, Framherji boards

Court judge Hannelie Prinsloo said in his order that: “The warrant of arrest in respect of the applicant issued by the first respondent on 23 November 2019 [sic], is declared invalid and set aside." He did not add further details.

Both Esau and Gustavo are alleged to have received kickbacks after awarding horse mackerel quotas to the Icelandic fishing firm Samherji, receiving bribes in return. The scheme is believed to have generated at least NAD 150 million ($10.2m).

Esau had quit his post as fisheries minister earlier this month, alongside justice minister Sacky Shanghala, following bribery claims made in the media.

Meanwhile, South African firm Investec has denied any involvement with the scandal, although Namibian managing director James Hatuikulipi resigned two days after the ministers, following allegations that he spearheaded the bribery scheme.

Warrants of arrest have been issued to several other key Namibian officials and implicated businessmen, including Hatuikulipi and Esau's son in law, Tamson Hatuikulipi; ACC director general Paulus Noa confirmed that a new warrant of arrest would shortly be issued for Esau too. 

Back in Iceland, Samherji announced on Nov. 14 that Thorsteinn Mar Baldvinsson had stepped aside as its CEO pending an internal investigation into allegations that the company paid "millions of dollars" to Namibian officials and politicians for fishing access, as reported by Undercurrent News.

The ongoing investigation, which is being assisted by the international law firm of Wikborg Rein, stems from the release by WikiLeaks of some 30,000 documents obtained from a whistleblower, former Samherji employee Johannes Stefansson.

title: Namibia arrests Icelandic captain of Samherji-linked ship
content:
An Icelandic ship captain was arrested in Namibia earlier this week, charged with fishing illegally in Namibian waters, reports MBL.

This follows the arrest of three other ship captains in Namibia in the past two months.

Bjorgolfur Johannsson -- acting CEO of Samherji, with Thorsteinn Mar Baldvinsson having stepped aside until the pending internal investigation into the company’s alleged wrongdoing in Namibia "has revealed the key material facts of the matter" -- said the case was under control. “He is not being detained or anything like that,” Bjorgolfur said.

The captain was brought before a judge on Nov. 20. The ship he was sailing, Heinaste, is owned by a subsidiary of Samherji in Namibia, and was at the center of a recent legal dispute itself.

The Icelandic skipper and another captain, Russian by nationality, were released on a bail of NAD 100,000 ($6,700).

title: Trade insights: China snuffs out billion-dollar shrimp ‘gray trade’
content:
China’s crackdown on smuggling through Vietnam has finally ended the billion-dollar gray trade of Ecuadorian shrimp, previously described as a "threat to the global shrimp industry".

Also referred to as the 'Hai Phong route' in reference to the port in northern Vietnam containers arrive at before being smuggled across the border to avoid Chinese customs duties, shrimp and aquatic products from other origins are also transshipped through Vietnam, but the trade of Ecuadorian shrimp is the biggest. 

For the first time in eight years, an entire month went by without Ecuador exporting shrimp to Vietnam, based on September figures from Ecuador's Camara Nacional de Acuacultura (CNA), the national chamber of aquaculture (see chart one). This happened last in February 2011.

The trade took off in 2012, when Vietnam mysteriously started absorbing large volumes of shrimp. 

In December 2012, Ecuador’s monthly shrimp exports to the Southeast Asian country reached $21m; by December 2013, exports hit $50m; December 2015, $74m.

By 2017, monthly exports frequently topped $100m, and Ecuador's shrimp industry grew in tandem. The demand from Vietnam was attributed to booming Chinese demand after the country's own shrimp output slumped due to disease.

The growth in the trade led to a proliferation of smuggling groups. Chinese authorities appeared to turn a blind eye until late 2017.

In December 2017, processing factories were raided and smugglers arrested from Guangxi province bordering Vietnam north to Beijing. Meanwhile, China lowered import duties on shrimp. Subsequently, in 2018, Ecuador’s shrimp exports to Vietnam declined to $1.09bn, while direct exports to China grew to $572m. By the summer of this year, shipments to Vietnam had fallen to just a trickle.

Local industry media described the lack of September shipments as "a boon for fair competition", as importers using official import channels will no longer be undercut by smugglers.

title: Florida regulators crack down on harvest, sale of undersized spiny lobsters
content:
Kent Alexander Quinn Downs, a 33-year-old commercial spiny lobster fisherman from Marathon, Florida, was arrested Oct. 10 and charged with 11 counts of possessing undersized lobsters on his vessel as well as a felony charge related to destroying evidence, the Miami Herald reports. 

Quinn Downs and his boat, That's Right, were spotted in the East Bahia Honda Channel by Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FFWCC) officer Joshua Peters in the afternoon and hailed for an inspection. Peters said he then noticed a man dumping half a basket of undersized lobsters into the water.  

Quinn Downs later admitted there were about 15 undersized lobsters in the basket and that he dumped them when he saw the officer's blue lights, according to the arrest report.

Commercial vessels are allowed to keep 50 undersized lobsters plus one for each trap onboard, as long as they keep them in a shaded, continuously circulating live well, the newspaper explained. The smaller lobsters must be released alive and may not be sold.

Quinn Downs' vessel was allowed to have 212 undersized lobsters.

Back on Sept. 20, the FFWCC also arrested Jorge Cabrera, the owner, and Blanca Sanchez, an employee, at the Lobster Walk, a Florida Keys fish market and bait shop, on charges that they were selling egg-bearing female and undersized lobsters, the Miami Herald earlier reported.

Cabrera and Sanchez, who deny the charges, each face 12 second-degree misdemeanor counts, according to the affidavit: Three counts of possession of three undersized tails; three counts of possession of three egg-bearing tails; three counts of removing eggs from tails; and three counts of failing to return egg-bearing lobsters back to the water alive.

title: Thai, international agencies join forces to arrest IUU vessel
content:
A fish carrier with a long history of illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing was seized and put under arrest on Sept. 13 in Thai waters on the coast of Pang-nga near Phuket, the Thai department of fisheries said in a press release.

The owner of the vessel, which is named "Uthaiwan", claims that it holds a Cameroon flag. 

The vessel is associated with a history of IUU fishing in many countries around the world and was previously called “Wisdom Sea Reefer”, holding a Honduran flag.

 "This operation became a success due to a collective effort from all the parties, domestic and international, especially the [Thai] navy and the fisheries department, and the marine department, as well as INTERPOL, the European Commission (EC), and OceanMind, a non-profit organization from the UK supporting governments in the surveillance and investigation of IUU fishing," said Adisorn Promthep, general director of the Thai department of fisheries.

Before this joint seizure, officers of the Thai Fisheries Monitoring Center (FMC) and
OceanMind had monitored and received useful information on Uthaiwan from INTERPOL and the EC, confirming that it was the same vessel listed as an IUU vessel by the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC).

The vessel had entered Thai waters without notifying or asking the Thai Marine Department for permission, a requirement under Thai law for all foreign vessels.

On Sept. 14, the vessel was boarded by a combined inspection team from all of the patrol vessels. An initial examination concluded that it was an IUU-fishing vessel with eight Thai crewmen. The vessel was immediately taken back to Phuket Deep Sea Port for a full investigation. The Royal Thai government will investigate this vessel, its crew, and owners for violations of Thai law, and look to cooperate with other governments in investigating violations of their laws as well, it said.

title: State judge’s order thwarts auction owners’ apparent last stab at buying Rafael vessels
content:
Raymond and Richie Canastra, the long-time owners of the Buyers and Sellers Exchange (BASE), the New Bedford, Massachusetts-based seafood auction, have made another apparent attempt to purchase some of Carlos Rafael’s commercial fishing vessels and again have been thwarted, Undercurrent News has learned.  

This time the two brothers' effort, which involved stepping in front of another buyer, has been done in by a state judge’s order.  

Merita Hopkins, an associate judge in the Bristol County, Massachusetts, Superior Court, on Friday vacated her approval, given two days earlier, of a request by BASE for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction that would have stopped Rafael from selling seven of his 11 scallop vessels to Charlie and Michael Quinn, the father-and-son owners of Quinn Fisheries, a 33-year-old, New Bedford-based scallop operation with six vessels already harvesting, for nearly $46 million.  

The move by the Canastras, whose auction handles roughly half of all the Atlantic scallops caught in New England as well as a considerable amount of groundfish, seems to have been a prelude to them making an offer themselves for the boats, which also come with some groundfishing quota.

The Athena, one of the seven scallopers that Quinn Fisheries has a deal to buy from Carlos Rafael. Photograph by vinoverde on 123RF.

An affidavit filed in the case by Stephanie Rafael-DeMello, Carlos’s daughter, suggests she was told by Cassie Canastra, the manager of groundfish sector 7 as well as Raymond’s daughter and Richie’s niece, that BASE wanted to buy four, six or potentially even eight of the vessels that could be used for groundfishing purposes.

Though the Canastras do not own a vessel in sector 7, Rafael-DeMello said she was advised that they own groundfish permits there. 

But the judge’s ruling seems to bring an end to the Canastra’s long-running stab at acquiring Rafael’s boats and paves the way for the Quinns to add considerably to their scallop fleet.

Rafael attempted to dump groundfish quota

The series of events are just the latest chapter in the long-running saga of the so-called Codfather of New Bedford.

Rafael, who pleaded guilty in March 2017 to 28 federal criminal counts that included famously lying repeatedly about his catch to federal authorities and evading taxes, has until Dec. 13, 2020 to sell all 30 of his scallop and groundfish vessels and their 43 related permits.

That’s to make good on the civil settlement reached on August 19 with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), which also cost him $3 million in civil money penalties. As part of the settlement, NOAA retains the right to approve the prospective buyer.

And that’s on top of the 46-month prison term and $300,000 fine Rafael was required to pay to settle the criminal case against him.

Carlos Rafael gives a demonstration on how to cut cod at a festival in New Bedford, Massachusetts, in 2010. Image is a still from a YouTube video.

Rafael and his family have been working for three years, since before he pleaded guilty to federal crimes, to identify buyers capable of purchasing their vessels and permits, according to the arguments made by Rafael’s New Bedford attorney, John Markey Jr., in his defense.

Arguing on behalf of the Canastras was David S. Smith, an attorney with the Salem, Massachusetts firm of  Farrell Smith O'Connell.

On Aug. 29, 10 days after reaching the settlement with NOAA, Rafael reached an agreement to sell to the Quinns and provided a document outlining all of the material terms of the purchase and sales agreement to Cassie Canastra in her capacity as the sector 7 manager, the court documents confirm.

Undercurrent reported earlier on the disclosure of the purchase agreement, which, in unusual fashion, did not identify the Quinns. The recently filed court documents confirm them as the prospective buyers.

Per the rules of the six groundfish sectors that are part of the Northeast Sector Service Network (NESSN) (sectors 2,4,6,7,8 and 12), such information must be provided to groundfish permit holders so that they have the option of employing their “right of first refusal,” or ROFR, a 30-day period to match or outbid any offers for permits made by individuals or companies that are not already members.

However, according to Rafael’s response to the BASE complaint, the Sector 7 manager mishandled the ROFR by not making it available at the right time and disclosing too much information. Based on concerns that the deal might get botched or the Canastras might take advantage of their position, Rafael attempted to withdraw his ROFR notice, avoiding the requirement by voluntarily surrendering his less valuable groundfish permits for free, the court documents explain.

The Canastras argue in their complaint, however, that it was because of that action taken by Rafael and the improper submission of the purchase agreement, missing key information, that the sector 7 membership rules were violated and the court should at least temporarily block the deal with the Quinns.

Ultimately, the judge agreed with Rafael, based on her withdraw of the TRO, though a formal written opinion explaining her decision was not yet provided to Undercurrent at press time.

Concerns about NOAA not approving the deal

It’s no secret that the Canastras have long wanted to purchase at least some of Rafael’s vessels.    

The two brothers, who were longtime friends to Rafael, talked publicly about having a deal with him in October 2017 to buy his massive fishing fleet. Undercurrent reported at the time that they were willing to pay $93m. When the deal didn't materialize, it was widely speculated that the reason was due to concerns that the federal government might seize a number of the vessels as part of its civil case.

But the court documents made public recently in relation to BASE’s lawsuit against Canastra present a different story.  

In Rafael-DeMello's affidavit, she said her family had dozens of talks with the Canastras about selling them their fleet for months leading up to his criminal sentencing, in September 2017, and the conversations continued well after.

“After months of allowing BASE every opportunity to purchase the assets, they ultimately indicated they were not interested in purchasing the assets, and found them to be overpriced,” she said.

Also, at the time, NOAA “expressed serious concerns about BASE purchasing the fleet because the violations which led to my father’s arrest took place at the unloading facility on BASE property”, said Rafael-DeMello, who continued:

“If the Canastras were proposed as purchasers, I am concerned that NOAA may not approve them as buyers of the fishing vessels and permits.”

Attempted partnerships with Cooke, Native American group

But the Canastras, who have repeatedly expressed their desire to keep the Rafaels' groundfish quota in New Bedford, didn’t give up in their effort to buy his vessels.

Rafael-DeMello said she was approached by BASE again in 2018 about the potential of selling her father’s vessels to the Canastras, this time in partnership with Cooke, the massive Canadian-based company that’s been on an acquisition tear of late. She said she met with “BASE and representatives from Cooke in good faith”.

“During our last meeting with BASE and Cooke, BASE again claimed the assets were overpriced and they walked away from the negotiations,” Rafael-DeMello said, however.

Then, later in 2018, Rafael-DeMello said BASE visited her father in prison and put forth yet another idea.

Glenn Cooke, CEO of Cooke Inc.

“BASE proposed acquiring the fleet with a Native American tribe as a co-buyer and stated that there would be favorable tax benefits for all of the parties,” she recounted.

However, Rafael-DeMello said she was subsequently informed by BASE that they were unable to put the deal together due to financing issues. It was following the multiple, unsuccessful efforts to do a deal with the Canastras, that Rafael began to pursue talks with the Quinns, she said.

Rafael-DeMello expresses her concern about time running out on her family to finalize sales in her affidavit.

“My parents are working against the clock as it relates to our settlement agreement with NOAA, which requires that we sell all of the vessels and permits and that we cease all operations at the end of this scallop season which is only six short months away,” she said. “The Quinns are ready to close. We are ready to close. We all want to get the City of New Bedford back on the water.”

title: NOAA settlement with Rafael clears path for big scallop, groundfish vessel selloff
content:
Now that the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has settled its civil claims against Carlos Rafael and 17 of his former fishing captains, look for the wheeling and dealing to intensify for his 43 scallop and groundfish permits and a related 30 fishing vessels.

Almost two years after a federal judge sentenced Rafael to pay $300,000 in fines and restitution and spend 46 months in prison for 28 different criminal counts, including repeatedly lying about his catch to authorities and evading taxes, the 67-year-old, so-called “Codfather” of New Bedford, Massachusetts, reached an agreement on Monday to determine what civil penalties he might also pay.

NOAA budged little from the $3,356,269 it said in September 2018 that it would seek from Rafael, hitting him with a $3,010,633 civil money penalty. However, rather than revoking Rafael's many limited access permits, as some in the fishing sector desired or even expected, NOAA has given him until Dec. 31, 2020 -- about 16 months -- to sell them along with the many fishing vessels he owns or controls through transactions reviewed and approved by the agency.

Based on the estimated value of the vessels, the sales could net Rafael tens of millions of dollars, money that John Markey, Jr., his New Bedford attorney, said will be used to pay the federal authorities, repay loans and cover capital gains taxes.

Carlos Rafael gives a demonstration on how to cut cod at a festival in New Bedford, Massachusetts, in 2010. Image is a still from a YouTube video.

Rafael must also relinquish his seafood dealer permit by Sept. 1 and permanently cease all commercial fishing, except for scalloping, by Dec. 31. Scalloping must stop by March 31, 2019, the end of the current season.

“By doing it this way, their number one goal, which was to have Mr. Rafael out of the industry, was achieved, and [we achieved] our goal, which was to make sure people got back to work and these permits got used and that the hard work that Mr. Rafael has had on the waterfront for 40 years to build up the acquisition of these assets didn’t all get taken away as part of some civil procedure,” Markey, with the New Bedford firm of Moses Smith, Markey & Walsh, told Undercurrent News on Monday.

Federal limitations favor Quinn Fisheries

The tale of Rafael and his arrest dominated Massachusetts headlines for nearly two years and will forever be one of New England lore.

After coming to America in the 1960s as a 15-year-old boy from the Portuguese island of Corvo, in the Azores, Rafael climbed his way up from working as a fish cutter to become a commercial fishing mogul. His enterprise, at its height, was believed to be worth as much as $100m, including 36 vessels, a processing facility, various distribution channels and about one-fifth of the region's cod.

Rafael survived several brushes in commercial fishing, even challenging the federal authorities to catch him breaking the law, before the one mistake that did him in: attempting to sell his business. Rafael told a group of federal agents, who were pretending to be interested Russian mobsters and wearing wires, not to worry about his accounting records because of the shortcuts he took to make his real numbers much better.

In order to avoid federal limits for certain species, including cod, he had mislabeled more than 700,000 lbs of fish over a period of four years, he later admitted to the investigators, saying he did it to protect workers whose jobs were threatened.

Now the biggest question remaining for the commercial fishing industry in New England becomes who will take over Rafael's 11 limited access scallop permits and vessels or his 32 groundfish permits and 19 draggers.

New Bedford Harbor. Photo: Boviate

“We have been letting folks know that we are hoping to get a deal done with the government and that any deal we enter into with them would be conditioned upon us achieving this,” Markey told Undercurrent on Monday. “And so people have expressed interest, we have engaged in talks and discussions, and we are hopeful that we will be able to get rid of all of the boats by the deadline, which is December 2020, but we are also optimistic that some of them will be sold during this calendar year.”

An early favorite to acquire the Rafael scallop permits and vessels and maybe some of his groundfish permits and vessels, many of which can also be used as dayboats to catch small amounts of scallops, appears to be Quinn Fisheries, a New Bedford-based scallop harvesting operation since 1986.

As reported earlier by Undercurrent, Charlie and Michael Quinn, a father and son, in July, bought 14 acres of abandoned commercial waterfront property previously used by a copper mill on which the company plans to operate a shipyard and has been rumored to be negotiating with Rafael.

Michael Quinn, the business's operations manager, told Undercurrent in an earlier interview that the newly acquired property, once dredged, will likely be used to harbor the six scallop vessels already owned by the company.

The small number of scallop vessels the Quinns now own is an advantage over other potential acquirers. Per federal regulation, no more than 5% of the limited access scallop vessels and permit-relate quota can have the same owner. Because all of New England’s roughly 370 permitted scallop vessels have the same amount of quota, that limits their owners to 17 permitted boats each.

Reached by phone on Monday, Michael Quinn declined to comment about the prospect of buying Rafael's boats.

The largest player in the US scallop industry is Eastern Fisheries, which is owned by both Nordic Fisheries and the O’Hara Corporation, and thus able to maintain a combined fleet of 27 vessels. One source familiar with Eastern said the company is not likely to bid for the Rafael boats, as it is enthusiastically pursuing other species, but is not maxed out on vessels and could be quickly interested if the price was right.

Atlantic Shellfish is another large scallop operation, but president Warren Alexander told Undercurrent that he already has his 17 vessels and is also not interested in Rafael’s groundfish fleet.

Blue Harvest Fisheries, yet another large scallop operation in New Bedford, has been reported to be on a spending spree in recent years with cash handy from the global private equity firm Bregal Investments, while Bregal simultaneously has sought to sell American Seafoods Group, a large harvester and processor of Alaska-caught pollock.

In April, Bregal announced that a second round of funding brought its total managed capital up to $1.25 billion. 

But sources contacted by Undercurrent expressed skepticism about the possibility that Blue Harvest might attempt to obtain the Rafael vessels, noting in particular that the company has 15 scallop vessels now, just two shy of the limit.

Glenn Cooke, CEO of Cooke Inc.

Another company to keep an eye on, sources said, is Cooke. The Canada-based seafood giant has been extremely acquisitive of late, picking up shrimp farming operations in Central America, and was apparently enthusiastic to get more into the scallop industry after acquiring the Wanchese Fish Company in 2015. Wanchese brought with it eight US scallop vessels and licenses and two more licenses in Argentina.

Prior to acquiring Wanchese, Cooke was reported to be looking at buying all of Rafael’s scallop vessels but no deal materialized. 

A Cooke spokesperson said on Tuesday morning that the company never comments on pending acquisition efforts and so he would be unable to talk about whether Cooke has interest anymore in the Rafael fleet.

Scallop permits and vessels said to be worth about $7m each

Whoever winds up buying any of the Carlos Rafael scallop permits and vessels better be ready to bring with them several wheelbarrows full of cash, veteran sources of the New England scallop industry told Undercurrent.

As the sources explained, the going rate for a limited access scallop permit is about 12 to 14 times earnings before interest taxes depreciation and amortization (EBITDA), which works out to about $6m. The vessels themselves might sell for $500,000 to $1.5m, but are virtually worthless without the permits.

So, the overall asking price for each permit and vessel, combined, is going to be about $7m, sources estimate.

Good luck trying to separate one from the other, too. The federal fishing permits in New England come with horsepower, length and tonnage specifications to match the original vessels and changes are difficult to make, sources advised.

Also, don't look for much help from lenders, the sources warned. Banks have been somewhat skittish and loaning only about 50% of the price of a vessel, meaning buyers could be forced to come up with about $3.5m to $4m in cash for each permit and vessel combination.

One scallop industry professional suggests the Rafael vessels might be sold in a sort of reverse auction, where the price starts at the highest level and drops until one of the existing scallop companies sees an agreeable price.

"I think anybody with enough money and enough capital that knows it is a good value, if it is in fact a good value and the price doesn't get too high, might step up and buy them, as long as they don't have the restriction of too many boats," the source said.  

To maximize the value of each scallop permit, Rafael has elected to allow his vessels to fish in a very limited capacity over the past six to eight weeks, Markey told Undercurrent.

Assuming most of the quota remains, the combined more than 1.7m lbs of scallops, worth about $16.0m in dock prices, would be a generous prize to leave on the table as the 2019-2020 scallop season is shaping up as a good one with a total 62.5m lbs expected to be landed, 10% more than the previous season, which was also strong. 

Nearly 33,000 lbs of U-10/20s, the most common size of scallops, from the Georges Bank sold at the New Bedford seafood auction on Monday for $9.05 to $9.25/lb.

The groundfish permits and their related boats will be much cheaper, going for 5 to 6 times EBITDA, sources said. The vessels have been prohibited from fishing, though Rafael was able to lease out his quota to other harvesters. Putting these groundfish vessels back in the water, potentially could make them buyers of leases, driving up the value of the species, Markey suggested.

Buyers will have to decide about captains and crews

Another issue related to the sale of Rafael’s fleet will be how the buyers choose to assign captains and crew. As many as 17 of Rafael’s former captains are looking at suspensions ranging from 20 to 200 days as part of the settlement agreement. And after they’ll also be looking at probationary periods ranging from one to three years, during which time their boats will be subject to additional monitoring and reporting requirements.

Markey told Undercurrent that some captains began serving their suspensions last week and many hope to satisfy their requirements intermittently, in blocks of days between heavy fishing periods.

As one source noted, the need for experience might result in the buyers being more prone to hire the former Rafael captains.

The Carlos Seafood scallop vessel Zeus. Photo by Matt Whittaker/Undercurrent News

“These boats are all different and they don’t come with instruction manuals,” the source said.

"People make mistakes," another scallop industry professional said. "They should get another chance." 

However, a Maine-based groundfish industry source plans to ask for a list of the Rafael captains that includes the lengths of suspensions and time served to share with colleagues to avoid them being held up from fishing or subjected to extra scrutiny while on the water.

Looking forward to vacations in Portugal

Meanwhile, as the commercial fishing industry prepares to move forward and absorb Rafael's assets, many are displeased with the NOAA settlement. 

The Maine-based groundfish source told Undercurrent that harvesters there felt Rafael's quota should've been seized and redistributed to other vessels, as prosecutors suggested previously.

“So the lesson from Carlos Rafael is that crime does pay,” the source said.

Tom Nies, executive director of the New England Fishery Management Council (NEFMC), expressed a similar sentiment in a statement shared with Undercurrent. The NEFMC announced on Monday that it plans to discuss the settlement and ask questions of NOAA officials at its next meeting in Gloucester, Massachusetts, in late September.

The island of Corvo in Portugals Azores region. Photograph from Shutterstock.

“We know Carlos Rafael committed egregious fisheries violations, but the NOAA Fisheries statement is unclear about what those civil offenses actually are and whether or not Carlos Rafael has admitted responsibility for those offenses,” Nies said. “We’re pleased to learn that he will be permanently removed from the fishery once the terms of the settlement have been carried out, but we also know some fishermen will be troubled by the fact that a man who built his business through illegal activity will be allowed to financially profit through the sale of his operations.”

As for Rafael, the sale of the permits and vessels brings him one step closer to closure, his attorney said.

He reported to a federal prison in Devens, Massachusetts, on Nov. 6, 2017, and would reach the end of his 46-month term in September 2021, though he could be eligible for parole much sooner, in March 2021.

“Carlos is a strong-minded and strong-willed person,” Markey said. “That’s why he did well on the waterfront and that’s why, I think, he is doing fine where he is. All in all, he would rather be with his grandkids and his wife and be able to take vacations on Corvo in the Azores ... But he recognizes that’s not in the cards for last year and this year, but he’s hoping, once this is behind him, he will be able to enjoy some of these things.”

title: Trade insights: China’s H1 warmwater shrimp imports surpass 250,000t
content:
China's official imports of frozen warmwater shrimp grew nearly four-fold to over 250,000 metric tons in the first six months of this year compared with H1 of 2018, according to latest trade data, as the country's importers shun the Hai Phong smuggling route.

The value of China's imports increased by 223% year-on-year to $1.55 billion.

China also imported 22,597t of frozen coldwater shrimp (Pandalus borealis) over the period worth $121m, down 12% y-o-y in volume and value, data shows.

At 253,823t, China's imports grew 283% compared with H1 in 2018; since late 2017 Chinese authorities have been cracking down on undocumented imports through Vietnam, which has resulted in more shrimp being imported through official ports of entry. 

In terms of monthly imports, China imported similar volumes in June compared with May, at 46,697t (see chart one). 

A slight decline in imports from Ecuador, down 2% month-on-month to 24,076t, was offset by an increase in imports from India, up 6% m-o-m to 13,263t.

Large Chinese processing hub grows reliance on Indian farmed shrimp

China's surge in shrimp imports has coincided with a decrease in values. 

For the third consecutive month, the average unit value of China's warmwater shrimp imports fell, dropping $0.07 per kilogram compared with May to $5.88/kg in June. 

At $5.45/kg, imports from India were cheapest.

Imports from Ecuador were worth $5.55/kg. 

This was down from $5.62/kg for Ecuadorian shrimp in May, and down from $6.62/kg in June of last year, representing a decline of more than a dollar per kilogram in 12 months.

In total, China imported $274m worth of frozen warmwater shrimp in June, with $134m worth imported from Ecuador, and $72m worth from India.

In H1, imports from Ecuador were worth $669m; India, $341m; Saudi Arabia $145m, and Argentina (which supplies coldwater, wild-caught red shrimp but which is traded under the same HS code 030617), $128m (see chart two).

title: New twist in Mozambique tuna bond scandal
content:
Mozambican finance minister Manuel Chang -- who is deeply implicated in the $2 billion tuna bond scandal -- has been blocked from release from imprisonment in South Africa, reports BizNews.

On the request of the US government, Chang was arrested at OR Tambo, South Africa, en route to Dubai. The US wants Chang to be extradited to New York to face corruption charges alongside three former Credit Suisse bankers.

title: Alleged Canadian lobster thieves foiled when getaway vehicle breaks down
content:
Three men from Charlottetown, in the Canadian province of Prince Edward Island (PEI), who allegedly stole more than CAD 25,000 ($19,026) worth of lobster from a seafood storage facility,  were caught recently when their getaway vehicle broke down, the Journal Pioneer, a Canadian news service, reports. 

A Royal Canadian Mounted Police officer from the New Brunswick town of Shediac stopped to help the three men with a truck and a cube van that appeared broken down on the side of the road at about 8 a.m. on June 27 and saw something strange, the newspaper recounts. The van didn't satisfy legal requirements and also contained a large quantity of lobster that was not properly stored.

Earlier that morning LOL Seafood's storage facility in Murray Harbour, PEI, was discovered to have been broken into and was missing 48 crates of sorted lobsters.

The drive from Murray Harbour to Shediac takes about 2.5 hours under normal driving conditions.

The three men, who were not identified by the article, were arrested and their vehicles seized. Two face charges of possession of stolen property. The lobster has been returned to the owner, while the investigation continues.
