title: Europol seizes 15m endangered eels; just a fraction of €3bn illegal trade
content:
Europol has seized 15 million endangered European eels, with 153 arrests across the EU; a 50% increase in arrests for the wildlife crime since last fall, according to specialist NGO the Sustainable Eel Group (SEG).

The results were announced at a press conference held June 27 by Europol, the UK National Wildlife Crime Unit, and Spain’s Nature Protection Service (SEPRONA).

"This is our flagship operation in terms of environmental crime," said Jose Antonio Alfaro Moreno of Europol. "All the arrests mentioned are in Europe with the majority from Spain, France, and Portugal."

"The main actions have been taken by SEPRONA, they have led the way in Europe along with the Portuguese and French authorities. However, there are also five ongoing criminal cases in the USA carried out by the US Fish and Wildlife Service, involving the illegal import of eel meat coming from Asia containing DNA of the European eel."

Glass (juvenile) eels are trafficked out of the EU, put into eel farms in Asia and then sent back to the US, Canada, and the EU, which is how the DNA can be tracked.

"The development of this technology being used in monitoring the DNA of the eel has allowed us to prove that the European eel is coming from Asia. We have also collaborated with the EU Enforcement Group and the EU Food Fraud Network."

Increasing numbers of countries have joined the investigation, with Croatia, Czech Republic, Germany, Switzerland, and Macedonia helping inquiries in 2019.

"For the next season, we want to follow the line of the inquiry into eel meat production in Asia and DNA traces. With this, we expect more countries to get involved with high ambition for action. The criminal groups learn and develop their methods, so Europol need to stay one step ahead.”

The number of eels reaching Europe has declined by 90% since the 1970s. The species is now classified as critically endangered by the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES). The trafficking of European eels, however, is undermining species recovery and enforcement agencies are continually looking at ways to address the issue, said SEG.

The export and import of European eel out of and into the EU has been suspended since 2010. However, the scale of the illegal trade remains vast: according to Europol, 300m-350m European eels are illegally trafficked every year from Europe to Asia, accounting for almost one-quarter of the total number of glass eels entering European waters every year. The illicit trade has been estimated to be worth approximately €3 billion every year.

title: Chinese authorities discover over 1.2t of smuggled dried seahorse
content:
Chinese customs authorities have discovered 1.28 metric tons of dried seahorses concealed in leather hides in Qingdao, Shandong province. 

According to local media reports, the grim discovery was made by authorities after routine X-ray scans of containers unloaded at Qingdao port.

The haul is believed to be the largest of its kind in China.

Suspicions were raised when X-rays revealed empty pockets of less dense material among leather hides stacked on pallets. Chinese officials discovered the pockets, in fact, contained hidden packages containing dried seahorse.

Local media crew filmed officials cutting open packages to remove thousands of dried seahorses from 40 separate packages during one such discovery on May 20.

The packages were in a shipment from Peru, local media report. Police in Shandong have arrested the importer of the shipment.

The May 20 seizure totaled 520 kilograms, with another 200kg of dried seahorse discovered at the warehouse of the importer, which has been identified as Shandong Maojing Trade.

In April, authorities at the same port discovered 560kg of dried seahorse also concealed amongst leather hides.

Dried seahorse powder is used in Chinese traditional medicine, and is used to treat asthma, infections of the throat, insomnia, and abdominal pain. It is also believed to be an aphrodisiac.

title: Chinese authorities break up $29m crab, lobster smuggling ring
content:
Chinese media are trumpeting the “smashing” of a seafood smuggling operation involving the import of lobsters, snails and blue crabs worth CNY 200 million ($29.1m).

On June 21, 15 individuals were arrested during coordinated raids by more than 100 police across south China, local industry publication Seafood Guide reports.

Arrests took place in Fangcheng Port, a port city close to the border of Vietnam, and Dongguan, a satellite city of Guangzhou, the capital of Guangdong province, the article reports. 

According to Nanning and Guangzhou customs authorities, the group is suspected of smuggling 2,000 metric tons of seafood with a market value of CNY 200m in the nine months since September of last year.

Approximately 40t of seafood and documentary evidence were seized during the raids.

The group is alleged to have avoided paying CNY 50m in customs duties by smuggling product into China from Vietnam without declaring the shipments to Chinese customs authorities.

It marks the latest in a series of arrests of seafood smugglers which has resulted in a significant re-direction of seafood trade to official Chinese ports of entry.

title: WWF berates IOTC for failure to handle yellowfin tuna decline
content:
The World Wildlife Fund (WWF) has been heavily critical of the member countries at the 23rd annual meeting of the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC) which concluded in Hyderabad, India on June 21.

"The member countries of the IOTC have failed again to arrest the precipitous decline of the Indian Ocean yellowfin tuna population," said the WWF in a statement. "This puts at risk the livelihoods, food security and economic wellbeing of millions of people, and further erodes Indian Ocean ecosystems."

The global NGO called on the IOTC to convene an emergency session to create "a clear rebuilding strategy for yellowfin tuna". WWF added that should an agreement between member states prove impossible, then more drastic measures, including the potential closure of the fishery, should be considered until effective management is found.

Furthermore, the WWF has recommended that seafood buyers avoid the purchase of yellowfin tuna until such time as the stocks have recovered.

title: A lobster fishing dispute between two families leads to melee in Nova Scotia
content:
A long-standing dispute between two lobster fishing families in Canada’s province of Nova Scotia led to a melee involving six people and three arrests on Saturday, the CBC reports.

The article doesn’t say what the fight in the town of Little Harbour, in an area known as the Eastern Shore, was about, but the Royal Canadian Mounted Police said it involved two men going to the home of another man to confront him. The fight, which involved the use of a wrench, a golf club and a baseball bat, broke out at about 5 p.m.

Two men were taken to a hospital, and a woman was also injured but did not require medical treatment, according to the newspaper.

The newspaper did not name the individuals arrested, but said a 33-year-old South West Cove and two men from Little Harbour, ages 21 and 49, were charged with assault with a weapon among other charges.

"Since the beginning of the lobster season, the RCMP has been conducting proactive patrols with a visible police presence on the water and this will continue until the end of the season," an RCMP spokesperson said in a press release. "Building a partnership with the fishing communities and ensuring everyone safety is a priority for the RCMP."

title: Chinese aquaculture firm’s $160m deal for Okamoto condoms distributor investigated
content:
A deal which merged a Chinese fish farming company with one of the most popular condom brands in China is in jeopardy after Chinese authorities said they are investigating the transaction.

Dahu Aquaculture, China’s largest farmer of freshwater fish with revenues of CNY 1.07 billion ($154.8 million) in 2018, said Chinese authorities are investigating the firm’s deal last year to buy a 51% stake in the Chinese arm of Japanese condom manufacturer Okamoto for CNY 1.04bn.

According to the company filing at the Shenzhen stock exchange on June 6, the investigation by the China Securities Regulatory Commission pertains to “violations of stock market rules”.

China’s Sina Finance reports the investigation possibly relates to insider trading.

Okamoto China, the Chinese marketer and distributor of Okamoto condoms, ranks alongside Durex as one of the most popular condom brands sold in China. In November last year, counterfeiters were arrested with $7m worth of fake Okamoto and Durex condoms in eastern China.

Fish and condoms might make unusual bedfellows but the deal demonstrated Chinese seafood companies' interest in diversification, amid bubbly Chinese equity markets and low profitability in the Chinese seafood sector.

Dahu Aquaculture said work on the merger has now been “temporarily halted” amid the investigation and “risks potentially being called off”.

title: Two Louisiana shrimpers arrested for illegal catch, found with dead loggerhead
content:
The US Department of Wildlife and Fisheries arrested two men for commercial fishing violations in federal waters south of Terrebonne Parish, Louisiana, Houma Today, a local news service, reports.

Authorities said they found and seized a dead endangered sea turtle, two dolphin skulls and 1,626 pounds of illegally caught shrimp on their boat.

Boothville residents Nghia Van, 53, and Trang Le, 46, have been charged with violating federal shrimp permit rules, turtle excluder device regulations and the Endangered Species Act. Van was also cited for violating the Marine Mammal Act, according to the news service. 

Agents were reportedly patrolling the Gulf of Mexico when they encountered the two men shrimping in the exclusive economic zone without a federal shrimp permit. They admitted to dragging their nets for about two hours, though the law requires skimming vessels to pick up nets after 55 minutes in lieu of using turtle excluder devices.

title: Filipino canner Alliance Select endures weak Q1
content:
The Filipino seafood supplier Alliance Select Foods International suffered a weak first quarter following a poor performance from the company's two primary products, tuna and salmon.

Alliance posted a pre-tax profit of just $106,000, down 94% from last year's first quarter profit of $1.65 million. The firm reported quarterly revenues of $19.6m, down 17% from $23.7m.

The weak performance from tuna and salmon, partially down to the challenges of sourcing particular species as well as the lower prices of raw materials, could partially explain the poor results.

In a statement accompanying the posting, Alliance Select's CEO Raymond See said the company had been expecting these results.

“The first quarter results are what we had expected as we focus on delivering sustainable cash flows and long-term growth for the business,” said See. “With strong momentum of our core businesses and exciting growth prospects of new products in the pipeline, Alliance Select is targeting to ramp up performance later in the year.”

Alliance Select, based in General Santos City, has also recently invested $2m in upgrades and improvements to its facilities, the statement said. The firm hopes the investment will "provide efficiencies" in order to bolster its bottom line. 

Earlier this year, Alliance's full report for the 2018 financial year demonstrated that it had seen a 35% increase in revenue over the previous 12 months, up to $97m; a record for the company. 

In April, board members also vehemently denied allegations that they had fraudulently used shareholder funds to engage in illegal activities.

A Philippines judge had granted seven arrest warrants for Alliance board members, including vice-chairman George Sycip, late in 2018. The seven have been charged with inappropriate spending of a pool of money gathered after enticing investors, back in January 2009, to spend more than PHP 75m ($1,435,987).

title: Thai court hands out fines of over $16m to IUU operation
content:
Thailand's criminal court has handed down a guilty verdict, and fines totaling over $16 million, to six defendants accused of operating an illegal vessel in Thai waters.

The companies Green Laurel International and SVG Fisheries Development -- and individuals Supachote Saengsuk-iam, Surakan Saengsuk-iam, Wanchai Saengsuk-iam, and Prawit Kerdsuwan -- were found guilty in relation to the prosecution of the overseas fishing vessel Chotchainavee 35.

The law calls for a fine of up to THB 30m, or five times the value of the illegal catch, whichever is higher. Each defendant was therefore fined THB 131.2m ($4.1m). However, since they gave useful testimonies, the defendants’ sentences were reduced by one third, taking the fines down to THB 87.5m each. The court also ordered the seizure of the fishing vessel and its catch.

The criminal proceeding against Chotchainavee 35 was the result of a joint operation undertaken by the Command Center for Combatting Illegal Fishing (CCCIF) and the Royal Thai Police on May 2, 2015. The owner of the vessel claimed that it was registered in Djibouti, however, the Thai authorities had been keeping track of the vessel and suspected that Chotchainavee 35 had illegally fished in Somalian waters.

Since the owner of the vessel could not provide clear evidence that the catch on board was obtained legally, the Department of Fisheries subsequently issued an order to confiscate the vessel, its catch, and all assets on board. The Thai authorities also found out that the vessel was stateless since Djibouti had revoked the vessel’s registration.

Apart from the criminal proceeding against Chotchainavee 35, the relevant Thai authorities have also uncovered a connection between Chotchainavee 35 and two other vessels, namely Chotpattana 51 and Chotpattana 55. The three vessels were all formerly Thai-flagged and belonged to the same company owned by a group of Thai nationals.

Later, the vessels withdrew their registrations from Thailand and obtained Djibouti flags to fish in Puntland waters, which is part of the Federal Republic of Somalia. On Nov. 1 2018, Thai authorities led by CCCIF, anti-human trafficking investigative officers and the Special Arrest Team arrested the captains of both Chotpattana 51 and Chotpattana 55 in the Maldives on charges of trafficking of Cambodian laborers.

title: CEO: Clearwater’s China growth is organic, not US trade war driven
content:
Given that China is currently a quarter of Clearwater Seafoods sales, it's no surprise that the Canadian shellfish supplier's CEO, Ian Smith, spent most of his time on the company's first quarter 2019 earnings call reassuring securities analysts about its growth prospects there.

Although its overall sales remained flat year-over-year during Q1 at CAD 120.1 million ($89.11m), Clearwater's adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization grew 5.2% to CAD 20.1m.

Smith said while China's trade war with the US has boosted its lobster business, it's been a "very modest part" of Clearwater's overall Chinese growth.

The company said that during Q1, its Chinese sales of all species grew from CAD 11.1m to CAD 32.2m, year-on-year. 

"Most of that growth is pure organic and it’s owing to the fact that our prices have always been at a significant premium to the commodity lobster market,” Smith said.

The CEO added that clams, coldwater shrimp, lobster and turbot, a species also known as Greenland halibut, continue to be its top-selling species in China.

Still, analysts asked if Clearwater had been affected by recent Chinese-Canadian diplomatic tensions, which arose after the Dec. 1, 2018 arrest in Vancouver, British Columbia, of Meng Wanzhou, the chief financial officer of telecom giant Huawei. Canadian authorities have thus far cooperated with US officials' requests to extradite Wanzhou for trial on fraud and conspiracy charges. China, calling the charges "politically motivated", has hit back at Canada blocking imports of Canadian canola, a trade worth hundreds of millions. 

Clearwater's Smith said he's seen "no evidence" of slowing trade with China and spoke of the company’s long history in the country and many Chinese employees.

"We, of course, are doing everything that we can to ensure that we remain in full compliance with all of the food-related regulations in China and our relations with our Chinese customers have never been better,” he said.

He declined to "speculate" when an analyst asked about the Chinese government's differing postures toward seafood and canola.

Scallop prices

Smith added that Clearwater will likely be affected in the coming year by declining scallop prices brought on by higher US supply, he believes that US harvesters and processors have learned that they don't have to drop prices as far as they did last year to bring up demand. 

"So what we’re seeing this year is that while prices have come down industrywide since the American landings have started and the auction has started up, the price drops are not as significant," he said. "We have not had to take any additional pricing changes from what we had already accomplished last year.”

title: Massachusetts lobster harvester gets 47 days in jail, one day for every illegal catch
content:
Gloucester, Massachusetts, District Court judge Michael Patten has ordered a local harvester to serve a day in jail for each of 47 lobsters he caught in the US state, the Gloucester Times reports.

James Santapaola Jr., 42, was arrested Nov. 2 after local police and officials with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration saw him unloading 47 short or otherwise illegal live lobsters from his vessel, the Shearwater. The lobsters were part of a larger 600-lb haul.

Santapaola later pleaded guilty to 28 counts of possessing illegally short lobsters and 19 other counts related to the possession of 16 V-notched lobsters and three oversized lobsters.

Santapaola has a history of catching illegal lobsters, according to the newspaper. He was arrested in November 2016 after landing 183 illegal lobsters at an East Gloucester wholesaler, which never took possession of the crustaceans. As part of a plea deal in relation to that incident, he received fines that time totaling $10,050 and had his license suspended for three months in 2017.

title: Philippines tuna company Alliance fights fraud charges
content:
Members of the board at Alliance International Inc., a Philippines-based tuna canning company, expressed confidence on Tuesday that they would be found not guilty of charges that they fraudulently used shareholder funds to engage in illegal activities, The Manila Times reports.

Late last year, a Philippines judge granted seven separate warrants of arrest, naming Alliance vice chairman George Sycip and directors Jonathan Dee, Alvin Dee, Joanna Dee-Laurel, Teresita Ladanga, Grace Dogillo and Arak Ratborihan. The individuals are charged with enticing investors, in January 2009, to spend more than PHP 75 million ($1,435,987) but didn’t use the funds in an appropriate way, the newspaper reports.

The victims reportedly include several of Alliance’s foreign shareholders (Harvest All Investment, Victory Fund, Bondeast Private and Hedy SC Yap Chua). They say Alliance conducted a “wire and shut out scheme”, siphoning off funds for the benefit of Dee family owned companies.

“We are confident that the facts will bear out our innocence, and that this will hopefully lead to the eventual dismissal of the complaint,” Alvin Dee is quoted as saying by the newspaper.

The allegation that the “funds invested in the company had been involved in illegal transactions” is not true, Jonathan Dee said. “We are hopeful of a speedy dismissal of the case."

title: Chinese pangasius smuggler sentenced to 13 years in prison
content:
The Chinese ringleader of a large pangasius smuggling group has been sentenced to 13-and-a-half years in prison by a court in Ningde, Fujian province.

Lu Changji was among eight individuals sentenced for their roles in a pangasius smuggling empire based in the southeast Chinese province of Fujian, the court heard during sentencing on April 9.

Chen Dan: Chinese pangasius will be ‘hot like crayfish’

According to local media reports, the group smuggled 41,000 metric tons of pangasius products from Vietnam into China over three years, selling two out of every three pangasius fillets consumed in Fujian.

When seized pangasius products stored by the group in warehouses were auctioned off by local customs authorities, it caused a drop in local market prices, according to local reports.

In total, the company imported CNY 600 million ($89.5m) worth of pangasius products illegally and evaded CNY 107m in customs duties.

Other members of the group were sentenced to up to 11-and-a-half years in jail, while the group was fined a total of CNY 110m. In his verdict, presiding judge Lin Xueyi described the case as an "especially large customs fraud". 

The smugglers were arrested following anti-smuggling raids in late December 2017.

The raids sparked a series of arrests during 2018 which shook China’s seafood industry and resulted in a significant reorientation of trade from illegal channels to official ports of entry. 

The court heard the group, which operated under a registered Chinese company called Fujian Anxin Industrial, employed inhabitants of border towns to bring goods from northern Vietnam into China.

Those living in border towns are permitted to import small quantities of products for personal or small business use without paying customs duties but would load the products onto trucks for wider distribution. According to local media, besides southeast China the firm sold its products in Beijing, Shanghai, Chengdu, Guangzhou, and Zhengzhou. 

Court hearing in Ningde. Source: China Tingshenwang

title: Welsh feed venture owner pleads guilty to £4.7m fraud
content:
A businessman has pleaded guilty to defrauding the EU and Welsh government after claiming £4.7 million in grants to develop an alternative to fish feed, reports the BBC.

The venture was supposed to create up to 120 jobs, but Anthony Smith, 72, created seven positions and used the money for other purposes, Cardiff Crown Court heard.

Smith pleaded guilty to three counts of fraudulent trading, while two others admitted their involvement at separate court hearings.

After the hearing, Janet Potter from the CPS specialist fraud division, said Smith had "promised to make Wales a world leader in the aquaculture industry, but instead he abused the system".

The money was approved in 2006 to help develop a plant to process ragworm for bait, and ponds in which to rear them in Port Talbot and Pendine, Carmarthenshire.

Back in 2013 Undercurrent News reported that Smith -- one of the directors of what was, at the time, a new Seafresh-backed feed venture, Prochaete Innovations -- had been arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to defraud.

Smith, listed on Companies House as one of four directors of the UK-based venture, along with Lasse Hansen, David Hall, and Oddgeir Oddsen, was arrested in January 2013 in connection with the fraudulent operating of his former company, Dragon Feeds.

title: Norwegian trawler detained in Murmansk, Russia
content:
The Norwegian shrimp and cod harvesting vessel Arctic Swan has detained March 27 in the Russian port city of Murmansk on illegal fishing allegations, the Barents Observer reported.

The vessel, which is being detained by Russia's coast guard, is owned by the Alta, Norway-based company, Arctic Swan, supplies product sold by the company Coldwater Prawns of Norway.

According to the newspaper, the arrest comes days after Russian and Norwegian fishing sector players pledged closer cooperation after the Fisheries in the Arctic event in Murmansk.

Signatories to the cooperation agreement included the Norwegian Fishermen’s Association, the Russian Union of Northern Fish Industry and the Association of Murmansk Coastal and Fish Farming Industry, the newspaper said.

title: Editor’s recap: Boston blog, Cooke deals; High shrimp supply; Quoc Viet sale; Protein noodles; Kailis brothers out
content:
Tom Seaman, editorial director of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

The live coverage of the Boston seafood show from our team of four reporters dominated the most-read stories last week. 

Our Boston blog was the most-read story, with six of the rest of the top ten stories also produced at the show. 

We got the scoop on two deals from acquisitive seafood giant Cooke during the show, as the Canadian firm added to its Latin American shrimp operations and US downstream presence.

On Saturday, March 16, the day before the show started, we revealed Cooke has acquired Farallon Aquaculture de Nicaragua, a vertically integrated farmer and a supplier of frozen shrimp to Asia, Europe and the US. This comes after Cooke acquired Seajoy Group, a shrimp farmer based in Honduras and Nicaragua, in January. 

Then, during the show, Cooke inked a deal for All Seas Wholesale, a distributor based in San Francisco, California. Last year, Cooke bought JC Seafood, an importer based in Florida, as part of a drive to get closer to customers in the US. 

The low shrimp prices in the US, driven by the surge in supply, was a key talking point at the show. It looks like strong supply is here to stay. Louis Harkell reported from the Global Aquaculture Alliance's (GAA) annual shrimp forum, where George Chamberlain, president of GAA, predicted global farmed shrimp production could leap to 8-9 million metric tons within the next five years.

Advancements at all stages of shrimp aquaculture, from improved genetics of broodstock and live feed replacements for shrimp larvae in hatcheries, to better biosecurity and intensive farming systems at the farm, are “changing the face of the sector”, he said. 

The low prices for shrimp have put processors under pressure. As a result, Quoc Viet Seafood, one of Vietnam’s largest shrimp processors, is on the lookout for investment to build up the company, an executive with the company told me at the Boston show. 

The founding Ngo family is prepared to sell a majority stake in the company in order to get the working capital needed for its farm integration plan, its Ngo Quoc Tuan said. 

“It depends on who the investor is and what they offer, but, yes we would [be prepared to sell a majority],” he said. Ernst & Young has been engaged to run a sale process starting at the end of the month.

Trident Seafoods' new protein noodles were the main talking point of the show in terms of product development. The company's booth and agenda at the show was "laser-focused" on pushing the product, CEO Joe Bundrant told me. 

“What I’ve been so impressed with is the consumers buying this product are not your typical seafood consumers,” he said. The noodles have 10 grams of protein per serving and only 7g of carbohydrates and are gluten-free, using potato and tapioca starch as binders rather than flour. 

Kailis brothers depart three years after sale to China’s Legend

Last week, we revealed brothers Matthew and George Kailis have left the Australian seafood business their family built up, around three years after selling a majority stake to China’s Legend Holdings.

Legend -- the $45-billion company behind the Lenovo computer brand -- sent out a note on March 18 announcing the departures of the brothers from KB Food International Holding, the joint venture the Chinese created with the family to take control of Kailis Bros, the largest seafood processor in Australia. 

The note states David Bonomini, the company’s chief financial officer, has taken over from Matthew Kailis as group CEO. Tim Storey, who has previously worked for the company, has come back as general manager of its east coast division.

Chinese authorities arrest shrimp smuggler at Beijing airport

Chinese authorities have swooped on a Chinese shrimp importer suspected of smuggling 15,500 metric tons of seafood as he disembarked a plane at Beijing airport.

Chinese police and customs officials apprehended the suspect, named simply “Mr Zhao”, at the gate as he got off a flight from Hanoi, Vietnam, on Sunday (March 16), a CCTV News report shows.

According to the report, Zhao is suspected of a role in a smuggling ring which brought frozen seafood -- primarily shrimp -- worth an estimated CNY 890m ($133m) into China across the country's southern border with Vietnam. It is thought Zhao avoided customs duties of CNY 110m over a period of three years.

Larsen Danish Seafood sold to Latvian canner Karavela

Latvia’s Karavela fish cannery is the new owner of Larsen Danish Seafood, having taken over the German-headquartered pelagic canner's trading and production activities, said Karavela last week. 

The deal, the terms of which were not disclosed, also includes the use of the Larsen brand, and closed March 14.

Larsen Danish employs some 200 people in Harrislee, Germany, near the Danish border, according to the company's website. The company entered financial administration and was purchased by Faroese pelagic fishing firm Christian i Grotinum in 2015. 

Chicken of the Sea settles price-fixing suits with Target, US Foods, Sysco

Thai Union Group’s US shelf-stable operation reached an agreement with some of its biggest customers, retailer Target and broadline distributors US Foods and Sysco, resolving lawsuits that had alleged the companies had been damaged by the canner's price-fixing.

According to documents filed in federal court in San Diego, California, the plaintiffs and Thai Union's Tri-Union Seafoods, which trades as Chicken of the Sea International have requested that the terms of the settlement remain sealed.

title: Dungeness crab poacher banned from fishing in Canada for 10 years
content:
A British Columbia, Canada, man who went out under cover of darkness more than a year ago to poach Dungeness crabs in the Vancouver Harbor, has been banned from commercial fishing for 10 years. He had the boat he was using, which didn’t belong to him, seized by the country’s Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO), the Campbell River Mirror, a local newspaper, reports.

Arthur Michael Nelson was also given 18 months of probation, 50 hours of community work service and a mandated 25 hours of counseling by the Campbell River Provincial Court when he was sentenced roughly a week ago, according to the news service.

Sammy Williams, the owner of the vessel, the L’il Coho, has 30 days to apply for its recovery. It’s unclear if that includes the crab gear that was also seized. Williams is currently facing charges in another case related to the alleged selling of CAD 100,000 ($74,800) worth of illegally caught crab to a plant in Richmond, BC.

Nelson had earlier pleaded guilty to fishing for shellfish during a closed time, fishing without a license and obstructing a fishery officer. He was observed by a tugboat operator as he was onboard the vessel, hauling unmarked traps in an area that had been closed for decades due to safety concerns. The area, as a result, was dense with crabs.

Following a subsequent sting operation, Nelson was arrested in the early morning hours while unloading the crabs at a dock.

At the time of his arrest, DFO officers reportedly found 195 crabs, five of which were undersized, 17 crab traps, two live cages and a milk crate full of bait. The retail value of the crabs, which were returned to the water, was deemed to be CAD 2,340.

title: Scottish Salmon Company UK’s first to gain three-star BAP
content:
The Scottish Salmon Company (SSC) has become the UK’s first salmon producer to be recognized with a three-star Best Aquaculture Practice (BAP) certification, it said.

SSC was awarded a third star for sourcing its feed from BAP-certified suppliers. The company already holds two stars for its processing sites at Marybank and Cairndow, and all its marine sites throughout the West Coast of Scotland and Hebrides.

It accepted its third star at the Seafood Expo North America in Boston on March 17, where it was showcasing its "Lochlander" salmon. "The North American export market is a key focus for SSC, where demand for quality, traceability, and Scottish provenance continues to grow, with sales increasing six-fold in the last two years," it said.

“To be awarded a three-star certification within a year of our first and second recognizes the commitment and expertise of our people, and also reinforces our commitment to producing the finest quality Scottish Salmon responsibly and sustainably," said chief executive Craig Anderson.

"Fundamental to this is the quality of our feed to ensure the healthy growth and quality of our salmon."

title: Nigerian navy acquires vessels for IUU crackdown
content:
The Nigerian navy has made plans with the federal department of fisheries to acquire a number of dedicated vessels to take on the threat of illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing taking place in its waters, reports This Day.

Speaking at the three-day leadership symposium in Lagos, vice-admiral Ibok-Ete Ibas said that the situation had improved over the past year, with only 30 vessels arrested for the practice in 2018, down from 37 and 45 arrests recorded in 2016 and 2017, respectively.

As of December 2018, the Nigerian navy had submitted 247 cases to the country's prosecuting agencies, of which 51 had been successfully prosecuted.

Ibas noted the range of activities detected by Nigeria's fleet included sea robbery, piracy, crude oil theft, poaching, and human and illicit trafficking of weapons and drugs.

“In prosecuting these threatening factors, the periodic assessment of the efforts is a credible tool," Ibas said. "Accordingly, the interrogation of the implementation level of the Yaounde Code of Conduct, a major regional framework for maritime security, is unarguably overdue at over six years of existence."

Ibas also acknowledged the support provided by overseas powers such as the UK, the US, and France in helping the navy to tackle its IUU fishing problem.

title: Chinese authorities arrest shrimp smuggler at Beijing airport
content:
Chinese authorities have swooped on a Chinese shrimp importer suspected of smuggling 15,500 metric tons of seafood as he disembarked a plane at Beijing airport.

Chinese police and customs officials apprehended the suspect, named simply “Mr Zhao”, at the gate as he got off a flight from Hanoi, Vietnam, on Sunday (March 16), a CCTV News report shows.

TV news crew film Zhao as he is escorted through the airport by two Chinese officials at his side. 

According to the report, Zhao is suspected of a role in a smuggling ring which brought frozen seafood -- primarily shrimp -- worth an estimated CNY 890 million ($133m) into China across the country's southern border with Vietnam. It is thought Zhao avoided customs duties of CNY 110m over a period of three years.

The investigation was carried out by authorities in the city of Shijiazhuang, Hebei province, with 12 individuals arrested so far, according to the report. 

The arrest is the latest in a series of actions by Chinese authorities targeting smugglers who bring seafood across the border between Vietnam and China to avoid Chinese customs duties.

In 2018, Chinese seafood imports surged by 44% to $11.9 billion, as undocumented seafood imported through Vietnam was increasingly imported directly to China through official import channels. Recorded imports of frequently smuggled seafood products, such as shrimp, fresh salmon, pangasius fillets and toothfish, increased most strongly.

title: Boston restaurant chain Legal, CP Foods to co-pack shrimp for North America
content:
Boston-based restaurant chain Legal Sea Foods and Thailand's Charoen Pokphand Foods (CP Foods) are to co-pack premium shrimp products for distribution in North America, they have announced.

Within the partnership, CP Foods will produce numerous fresh-frozen items with shrimp sourced from its biosecure aquaculture farms. The products will be distributed under the Legal Sea Foods brand, and will be launched at the Seafood Expo North America, currently taking place.

"Legal Sea Foods has a long history of serving premium seafood to its more than 7 million restaurant customers annually, a success which is rooted in our fundamental belief in food safety and quality," said Roger Berkowitz, CEO of Legal.

Sujint Thammasart, chief operating officer of CP's aquaculture business, said all the firm's shrimp are raised in closed-system, environment-friendly farms and are fed with feed utilizing fishmeal certified by the Global Standard for Responsible Supply. He called Legal "the number one seafood brand in America", and said the tie-up made for a "very synergistic partnership".

title: Clearwater CEO ready for rematch with US scallop competition
content:
Given the beating Canadian scallop harvester Clearwater Seafoods took last year from the large volume and low prices coming out of the US, you might expect Ian Smith, CEO of the Halifax, Nova Scotia company, to be a bit anxious about the start of the new US season on April 1.

But he didn’t seem at all worried in a conference call with investors to talk about his company's fourth quarter and annual performance on Thursday.

Ian Smith, Clearwater Seafoods' CEO .

“We’re in a period where we started fishing in January, we’ve got good inventory positions and the market has been rather robust since the beginning of the year,” he said. “… Once the US starts fishing in anger, so to speak, and the scallops start going on to the auction, you will see some market prices in the US begin to soften.”

Clearwater made scallop sales of CAD 171.4 million ($127.4m) in 2018, a decrease of CAD 28.9m, or 14%, from the CAD 200.3m in scallop sales it saw in 2017.

As you might recall, US harvesters landed roughly 60m pounds of Atlantic scallops in 2018, including many large scallops, helping to bring prices down as low as $9 for 10/20s, the most common size, nearly all spring and summer. Similar numbers are expected in 2019, based on the limits expected to be set by the US' National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

The reduction in 2018 scallop sales, Clearwater’s most valuable species, played a significant role in the company’s overall drop in revenue and profits last year. Clearwater maintains 12 mid-shore scallop harvesting vessels in Canada and four in Argentina, according to its public filings.

In its just-published annual report, the publicly traded company (TSX: CLR) said it saw overall annual sales in 2018 of CAD 592.2m, a decrease of 5% from the CAD 621.0m garnered in 2017, and earnings before interest taxes depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) of CAD 104.4m, down 4% from the CAD 108.6m in 2017.

Clearwater wasn’t helped either by its fourth-quarter sales, which were CAD 159.8m, down 9% from the CAD174.8m it saw in the fourth quarter of 2017. It generated CAD 24.1m in EBITDA, down 15%.

Canada has yet to set its total allowable catch (TAC) for scallop in 2019, but Smith predicted "meaningful quota" across the country and "stable prices". He suggested Clearwater would have strong landings, too.  

“We expect to be in a very good position from an inventory standpoint, from a pricing standpoint and from a cost structure standpoint in 2019,” Smith said in regard to scallops.

Surf clams were left on board

As for clams, Clearwater’s second biggest source of revenue, Smith suggested the year ahead would be better as well.

Clams contributed CAD 120.2m to Clearwater’s sales figures in 2018, a CAD11.0m or 10% boost over 2017.

Helping Clearwater last year was Canada’s reversal of its decision to strip the company of 25% of its Arctic surf clam quota. Clearwater has now been guaranteed to keep the surf clam quota until at least 2020.

However, Smith said Clearwater would’ve liked to have received word from Canada’s Department of Fisheries and Oceans before August about the change of direction. He said the company was able to harvest practically all of the surf clam total allowable catch (TAC), but – as a result of the late notice -- some of the clams were left as “inventory on the vessel”.

Foot on the gas in Asia

Clearwater has continued to make moves toward expanding its business in Asia, including clams and live lobsters in China, Smith told the investment analysts.

Smith told Undercurrent in November how Clearwater had targeted “tier three” cites in China, as it launches a mandarin brand name in what has now become its largest single market. 

Smith reiterated his comments on Thursday and said Clearwater has seen no indication of a slowdown in his company’s business in China following last year's high-profile arrest of Chinese telecoms executive Meng Wanzhou in Vancouver and the apparent reciprocal arrest by China of two Canadians.

He reports to now have 30 employees placed in the communist nation, maintaining communications with Chinese buyers and various government officials. He said Clearwater's relationships with its Chinese customers are “very strong”.

He also sees a big opportunity in jumping more on the growth of e-commerce in China. 

"It's a very efficient sales platform for us because we aren't paying to have the product on the retail shelf," Smith said. "And we don't actually own the inventory in the market. It's already owned by an importer or distributor."  

Asia represented CAD 236.7m of Clearwater’s sales in 2018, with China making up  CAD 130.0m of that. By contrast, Europe represented CAD 205.7m of sales and North America CAD 249.8 in 2018.

“We’re not taking anything for granted here,” he added. “It’s eyes wide open.”

Smith also responded to a question about more possible acquisitions in the future.

Clearwater acquired Macduff Shellfish Group, a Scottish scallop harvester, in October 2015, and is looking for more deals like that one, where merger partners are well known to the company and often have deep relationships.

He said he is seeing opportunities in both North America and the United Kingdom.

Smith said Clearwater is maintaining "an active pipeline" that he “feels pretty good about”. 

"It's really about timing and price, both their price and our share price," he said.

Clearwater's stock (CLR) has bounced from CAD 5.25 per share to CAD 5.49 over the past five days, but closed at CAD 5.35 on Thursday.

title: Tugushev ‘purchased’ Russian gov’t post, intended to make money back from bribes, says Orlov
content:
Alexander Tugushev left what is now Russia’s largest fishing company after buying his way into government, with the intention of making this investment back from bribes, Vitaly Orlov, the CEO of Norebo Holding, alleges in a legal document filed in the UK court battle between the two men.

While Tugushev claims he is owed over $350 million for a third of Norebo, Orlov contends he sold his stake in 2003 when he, “despite lacking any prior governmental experience”, was appointed deputy chairman of Russia’s State Fisheries Committee.

Orlov’s claims Tugushev “purchased his office, and intended to earn his money back by using it to harvest bribes”, according to a skeleton argument filed in relation to a hearing held over four days in London’s High Court over the past few weeks, seen by Undercurrent News. In the next two weeks, a decision is expected on whether the lawsuit remains in London, as Tugushev wants and Orlov opposes, and if a $350m worldwide freezing order on the latter’s assets remains in place.  

Ocean Trawlers co-founders Roth, Orlov locked in legal battle in Hong Kong

Through a spokesman, Tugushev told Undercurrent he'd never compromise himself by taking bribes, however. 

“Mr Tugushev was one of many victims of politically motivated allegations in Russia. During his incarceration, Mr Tugushev feared for his life every day and only ‘admitted guilt’ to guarantee his safety. In 2018, the UK visa authorities acknowledged that his arrest was politically motivated, or that his circumstances had changed," the spokesman said "Tugushev will continue to rely on the facts and the law to protect his one-third interest in the Norebo Group." 

According to Orlov’s version of events, Tugushev “did once have a share in a company which subsequently became a (comparatively small) part of the Norebo Group, he relinquished that share in 2003 to embark upon a misjudged and short-lived career as a corrupt government official”.

He then lost this position in 2004 “following his arrest, conviction and incarceration for fraud”.

This “career was short-lived”, the document states.

Orlov’s team allege Tugushev demanded bribes from a company known as Pollucks in return for additional fishing quotas and, “when he did not deliver, attempted to blackmail them into silence”.

In 2004, he was arrested, convicted of fraud, and sentenced to six years’ imprisonment.

“While Mr Tugushev claims that he was falsely accused, it is clear from the judgment given at his conviction that there was a considerable body of evidence against him, including tape recordings – garnered through a police sting operation – in which he discussed the bribes paid by Pollucks, and his efforts to obtain 'scientific' quotas (i.e. fishing quotas theoretically set aside for scientific research purposes) for them,” the skeleton argument states.

Orlov’s legal team also claims Tugushev “confessed his guilt as part of an application for parole” and settled Pollucks’ civil claim against him in 2014.

“The allegations that Mr Tugushev ‘bought his way into the government and hoped to recoup the money with bribes’ is false. Mr Tugushev would not have compromised himself or his position by taking bribes,” a spokesman for Tugushev told Undercurrent.

According to Tugushev’s skeleton argument, he entrusted Orlov and Roth to look after his “ownership interests” during his time as a government official, when he could not take an active role in the management of the business.

In order to apply for parole, Tugushev also had to admit guilt, his skeleton states. “Extreme circumstances” led him to make the admission, which he goes into in a separate statement not included with the skeleton and which Undercurrent was unable to obtain.

“The admission accordingly was not in any substantive way an acceptance by Mr Tugushev of his guilt, and there was no material non-disclosure. It should also be noted that Mr Tugushev’s conviction is spent,” the argument continues.

Orlov team: Tugushev has backers with links to ‘violent criminality’

Tugushev claims he did not mislead the court about the conviction, but “explained the allegations against him, and why his position was that they were false and politically motivated”.

He concedes the conviction is relevant to his credibility, but “maintains his innocence and would have done so even if he had provided the fuller explanation that he now has”.

Crime Russia 

Orlov’s legal team also contends Tugushev has links to individuals with a reputation for “violent criminality”. One of the two is Adam Delimkhanov, a politician and member of Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party, who is the cousin of Ramzan Kadyrov, the president of the Chechen Republic.

The spokesman for Tugushev said he has never met Delimkhanov, however.

The other, a “Mr Traber”, thought to be Ilya Traber, is alleged to have links to organized crime groups in St. Petersburg in numerous stories.

Ilya Yashin, a vocal critic of Putin and one of the leaders of the liberal Russian political movement Solidarnost, mentions both Delimkhanov and Traber in a 2016 report entitled “Criminal Russia Party”. 

Traber is “well known to St. Petersburg law enforcement bodies”, the report states. “Operations reports mention Mr Traber as a crime boss nicknamed [the] Antiques Dealer. He was involved in criminal cases connected with contract killings.”

"Mr Tugushev has met Mr Traber in the past. He has not had any contact with Mr Traber since early 2016," the spokesman for Tugushev told Undercurrent. 

The case continues.

title: Maltese fishing regulator accused of seeking bribes in tuna ranching scandal
content:
The head of Malta's fishing and aquaculture regulator is accused of receiving bribes from Spanish tuna rancher Ricardo Fuentes and Sons in exchange for allowing more bluefin to be fished than the legal limits allow, Spain's El Confidencial reported.

The newspaper, covering an ongoing court investigation into the matter in Spain, reported that Malta's Andreina Fenech Farrugia met with the tuna rancher's Jose Fuentes Garcia in Bulgaria on the sidelines of a European Union meeting to discuss bribes.

"I'm in Bulgaria just for you, you have to pay me, because there is a meeting and I'm with the [director] general of Brussels," Fenech Farrugia reportedly said to Fuentes Garcia. 

The Fuentes group is under police investigation following the discovery of an illegal bluefin tuna trade that reportedly imported 2,500 metric tons of unreported fish to Spain annually, at an estimated value of $23 million.

Spanish officers have said that the traceability codes used in export invoices for many of the illegally-caught tuna led back to Maltese tuna fattening farms.

Mare Blu Tuna, the Fuentes subsidiary in Malta, denies any involvement with the trade and states that it participated in no illegal activity alongside its parent company. Mare Blu director Massimo Cappitta also stated that the information regarding the investigation of the company is untruthful. 

"The information you received is not correct and has been manipulated to cause harm to our company," he is quoted as saying in the article.

The Fuentes group also claims that only small specific purchase operations of tuna were imported from Malta, if at all. 

According to Malta Today, 79 people have so far been arrested in relation to the investigation, including brothers Jose and Pedro Fuentes -- although both have since been released with charges pending.

title: China’s direct imports of crustaceans now worth billions
content:
Booming imports of shrimp stood out amongst China’s top seafood imports of 2018, with 192,991 metric tons of shrimp worth $1.36 billion imported directly by the country last year, up 203% in volume and 187% in value compared with 2017.

The figures, published along with the latest Chinese customs data, show as Chinese celebrate Chinese New Year on Tuesday more than ever before they will likely be dining on imported crustaceans.

Undercurrent News recently reported China’s direct seafood imports ballooned 44% to $11.9bn in 2018, based on preliminary Chinese customs figures. According to the more detailed breakdown, China’s top imports consumed domestically are heavily weighted towards crustaceans, with shrimp, live/fresh rock lobster, live/fresh crab and live/fresh American/European lobster all ranked among top-five imports.

Only direct imports of fresh Atlantic salmon represented the finfish category in the top-five, coming in fourth (see table).

China's top seafood imports for domestic consumption, 2018
Product	Value ($m)	Volume (metric tons)	Biggest supplier
Warm-water shrimp	1,357	192,991	Ecuador
Live rock lobster	912	15,378	Australia
Non-frozen crab	783	56,832	Russia
Fresh salmon	652	64,798	Chile
Live American/European lobster	444	20,362	Canada
Sea cucumbers (2017 data, HK)	314	6,625	Japan
Greenland halibut	310	49,488	Greenland
Cold-water shimp	277	45,881	Canada
Pangasius fillets	268	97,479	Vietnam
Toothfish	127	4,207	France
Based on Chinese customs data compiled by Undercurrent News	© 2019 Undercurrent News

China’s imports of crustaceans are surging as domestic aquaculture production slows or even contracts, the country’s middle class expands, and smuggling routes from Vietnam into China are closed amid crackdowns by authorities.

Crustaceans’ position at the apex of China's seafood imports also reflects a culinary preference for whole, unprocessed seafood -- claws, carapaces and all -- which can be stewed, peeled and grappled with hands and chopsticks, rather than fish fillets or processed shrimp more common in the West. Moreover, China imported more lobster and crabs live or fresh by value than frozen equivalents. 

Chinese industry believes crustaceans have the best market prospects looking forward, too; in an Undercurrent poll of 16 Chinese industry figures, seven voted king crab would be one of the "hottest" seafood products in 2019; six plumped for cold-water shrimp (Northern pandulus), and five vannamei shrimp and Australian rock lobster.

Among finfish categories, only salmon scored highly, with seven votes, followed by Greenland halibut with five votes.

A table of Vietnam's seafood imports compiled by Undercurrent News and published in February 2018.

Crustaceans' are being imported directly in greater volumes than ever before in part due to a dropoff in smuggling from Vietnam to China to evade Chinese import duties and inspection. 

In February last year Undercurrent estimated Vietnam was a conduit for over $1bn worth of undocumented frozen shrimp imports alone, as well as hundreds of millions of dollars worth of live rock lobster, fresh Norwegian salmon, frozen Greenland halibut, crabs and squid (see table published in February last year).

In 2018, China’s biggest growth in direct imports was of these frequently smuggled products (see chart).

In 2018, China's direct imports of live rock lobster grew 94% to $912m, while imports of fresh Atlantic salmon grew 83% to $652m. Imports of frozen Greenland halibut, supplied mostly by Greenland, jumped 223% to $310m, while imports of frozen toothfish rocketed 514% to $127m. China's direct imports of frozen pangasius fillets, mostly from Vietnam, surged 189% to $268m.

Demonstrating the benefit of China's free trade deal with Australia, too, lower tariffs helped live rock lobster imports from the country surge to $466m in 2018. On Jan. 1 this year, Chinese tariffs on Australian rock lobster imports fell to zero.

A chart travels

Last year, at the Global Aquaculture Summit in Fuzhou, China, Cui He, the head of the China Aquatic Products Processing and Marketing Alliance (CAPPMA), gave a presentation about China’s shrimp market. In it, he included a chart of Vietnam’s imports of seafood originally published by Undercurrent.

The chart demonstrated how a huge spike in Vietnam’s seafood imports was, in fact, a proxy for a boom in Chinese seafood imports. “Shrimp exports to Vietnam are nearly all transshipped to China,” said Cui’s slide, next to the chart.  

Cui He's presentation on China’s shrimp market at the Global Aquaculture Summit last June in Fuzhou, China.

Cui estimated China’s undocumented shrimp imports from Vietnam to be roughly 360,000t in 2017.

Cui, whose orgnization CAPPMA is directed under China's ministry of agriculture, told Undercurrent in 2017 Chinese authorities were making efforts to curb grey trade of pangasius from Vietnam, by creating a register for large importers and cracking down on smuggling. In 2018, good to his word, China’s direct imports of pangasius fillets increased 189% to $268m.

title: Editor’s recap: Chinese boss arrested; US mussel farm ready to grow; MSC suspends mackerel certificates
content:
Neil Ramsden, deputy editor of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

Again we saw three big stories top our list of the most-read stories of last week.

Top was Louis' report that Chinese authorities had arrested the boss of a large Dalian-based processor suspected of import tax evasion and fraud, as authorities launch further anti-smuggling operations in seafood trading hubs in the north and south.

Zhuanghe-based Dalian Hengtai Foods, which imports an estimated 15,000 metric tons of raw material annually for processing and re-export, confirmed to Undercurrent on Jan. 29 the firm’s boss has been apprehended.

The firm said it was "unclear” what the situation is regarding the apprehension.

According to local media reports, details about the arrest of the otherwise unnamed Chinese processor in Zhuanghe include suspicion of selling over 6,000t of bonded goods for processing, worth CNY 55 million ($8.2m), on domestic markets.

The arrest occurred on Jan. 17 during raids by more than 70 anti-smuggling police officers in 12 groups in Dalian and Zhuanghe. 

Dalian Hengtai's boss' arrest preceded separate raids in other parts of the country as China’s anti-smuggling operations step up a gear. 

Both in Qingdao, Shandong province, and south China, arrests were made designed to stem the flow of goods entering the country through illegal channels. 

On Monday (Jan. 28), Chinese authorities arrested at least 38 individuals from seven “professionalized criminal smuggling gangs” across south China during co-ordinated raids. The groups are suspected of smuggling frozen seafood worth approximately CNY 298m, reports CCTV.

Read the story in full here.

Also worth mentioning here is Louis' follow-up to that story, which found Chinese processors face a “big temptation” to commit import tax fraud as domestic demand grows for processed fish such as Alaska pollock and cod.

Speaking to Undercurrent, the owner of a Chinese importer and processor said he wasn't sure if the US-China trade war had led to more avoidance, but import tax evasion by Chinese processors who both sell to the domestic market and export is “not something new". 

Sources believe China’s system of benchmarking to determine import taxes for re-processors of frozen fish and other seafood is more open to abuse by the seafood industry than other sectors. 

Read this in full here.

Over in the US Jason Huffman spoke with Phil Cruver -- founder, president and CEO of Catalina Sea Ranch (CSR).

Nearly seven years after taking the initial steps necessary to build his 100-acre Mediterranean mussel (Mytilus Galloprovincialis) farm some six miles off the coast of Los Angeles, California -- the only commercial aquaculture facility operating in US federal waters -- he is ready to make it 30 times larger and further back up his trademarked claim of operating the “Aquaculture Capital of America”, he wrote.

Now that the federal government shutdown is at least temporarily ended, CSR staff are working the telephones and will submit their application any day for a building permit to the US Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) to expand to 3,000 acres and add at least three shellfish species: 900 acres more of mussels, 1,000 acres of giant kelp and 1,000 acres of other cage-culture shellfish, including oysters, rock scallops and abalone.

Cruver’s been ready to submit his paperwork to USACE since before the congressional election, in November, in fact, he told Undercurrent, but he was waiting for an anticipated recommendation letter from Wilbur Ross, secretary of the US Commerce Department. Ross has previously expressed his support for aquaculture in federal waters as a means of reducing the US’ nearly $16 billion seafood trade deficit and has not expressed any reticence about the project.

Although USACE is part of the Department of Defense, which has been 100% funded throughout the recent federal government shutdown, Cruver said the staff he needed to work with at the agency have not been available.

Regardless, he is prepared to go forward now with or without a letter from Ross, noting the support he has from numerous other individuals and groups, he said.

Read this story in full here.

Important breaking news last week saw the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certification for all North East Atlantic mackerel fisheries suspended on March 2, 2019.

This was announced through the release of an expedited audit report for all North East Atlantic mackerel fisheries in the MSC program.

Mackerel caught on or after March 2 cannot be sold as ‘MSC certified’ or bear the blue MSC label. The suspension affects all four certificates, for fisheries across eight countries. Sources pointed out to Undercurrent it was important to note that by that time the mackerel season should be completed, meaning the first impacts of this will be delayed.

The suspension comes after the mackerel stock in the northeast Atlantic dropped below a precautionary threshold level, while catches remain far higher than advised by scientists, said the MSC. The drop in stock triggered an expedited audit by the independent certifiers in November 2018, and the report from that audit was published last week.

Dan Gibson and I followed this up with pelagic sources. Several are confident that an ongoing biomass reevaluation will show the mackerel stocks to be in much better shape than has been reported, and so they hope the suspension will be lifted before vessels return to fish mackerel in the fall. 

That said, if it is not, a mixed impact on the market is anticipated, with some hit to price.

Read that story here.

In the UK, editor Tom continued his unparalleled coverage of the Young's Seafood sale process. 

He reported that one of the three current shareholders in Young’s is being tipped as the investor looking to merge the UK’s largest processor with Sykes Seafoods, a smaller rival more specialized in shrimp and shellfish.

The UK-arm of US-based HPS Investment Partners -- which holds around a third of Young’s, with Bain Capital Credit and Lion Capital the other two shareholders -- is said to be the investment firm working on the Sykes deal. Undercurrent reported the prospect of a deal uniting Young’s and Sykes, which has turnover of around £100m and earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) of around £10m, on Jan. 16. However, at the time, it was not clear who the US-based investor was.

HPS -- which is also said to be an investor in the high-interest, payment in kind (PIK) note used to finance Young’s -- would end up with a minority stake in the new company, with Sykes holding the rest, if the deal goes ahead, sources told Undercurrent. Due diligence is thought to be underway. 

Undercurrent sources said Alan Dale, managing director and majority shareholder of Sykes, would become CEO of the combined company, if the deal goes ahead. Dale did not respond to a request for comment to Undercurrent.

It’s been said throughout the sale process for Young’s, which started last April and ended with no deal, that HPS is the most engaged investor. As a result, sources said HPS would likely try and forge on rather than sell Young’s at a low price. Private equity CapVest Partners was the last player left in the process, but Lion/Gem Luxembourg 3, the parent company of the Young’s operating business, issued a note on Nov. 11, 2018, in which it said bids were too low. Sykes was also involved in the sale process, in a combined bid with Stellex Capital Partners, a private equity, according to Undercurrent sources.

Read the full story here.

Back in the US, Undercurrent broke the news that Cooke had at last completed its acquisition of the Seajoy Group, a fully integrated Latin American shrimp producer, giving the Canada-based global seafood giant a dominant presence in yet another sector of the seafood industry.

The prospect of the deal was first reported by Undercurrent last June, but took more than half a year to reach the finish line.

By buying Seajoy from Peder Jacobson, who founded the company in Ecuador’s Gulf of Guayaquil, in 1979, Cooke is gaining Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei) farms spread across Honduras and Nicaragua with almost 3,500 hectares (8,650 acres) as well as a 6,000 square meter processing plant in Choluteca, Honduras, capable of producing 100,000 pounds of finished product daily.

About 60% of Seajoy’s production is value-added, including peeled and deveined meats, butterfly cuts, skewers, raw breaded, and cooked shrimp. Also, the factory maintains cold storage capable of holding up to 1m lbs of finished product.

“The acquisition of Seajoy is an important element in our focus on product diversification to meet our customers’ needs,” said Glenn Cooke, the CEO of Cooke, in a press release issued Friday.

Read that story here.

Awful news in Norway saw Leroy Seafood Group report an employee with a subcontracted maintenance firm was unaccounted for following a fire at a hatchery facility in Laksefjord, Finnmark on Jan. 27.

The company also lost 2.6m smolt with an average weight of 50-60 grams, it said.

"Our thoughts and prayers go out to his family circle, friends and his colleagues. Leroy Seafood Group will continue to assist the subcontractor, the police and other public bodies in conducting an inquiry into what has happened."

"Initially the focus has been to obtain an overview of the situation, and implement
mitigation measures." The firm has said it will give further updates at the end of February.

On his favorite topic of international trade, Louis reported that Pesquera Santa Priscila was just a whisker away from generating half a billion US dollars in export revenues in 2018, as exports reached 76,868t, according to data from Estadistica (Instituto Nacional de Estadistica).

Santa Priscila, which is based in the shrimp production hub of Guayaquil, generated $492m in export revenues, making it Ecuador's largest shrimp exporter. 

In 2017, Santa Priscila produced 74,000t of shrimp -- up from 56,000t in 2016 -- in addition to roughly 10,000t of tilapia.

Santa Priscila president, Santiago Salem, had targeted double-digit shrimp production growth in 2018, by investing in expanding and improving farming techniques, he told Undercurrent last year. The firm was also looking to buy farms, he said.

Omarsa and Expalsa, both also based in Guayaquil, ranked second and third with shrimp exports of 64,410t and 62,448t respectively, generating export revenues of $383m and $426m.

Read this story in full here.

Tom reported the skipjack tuna price for delivery to the processing hub of Bangkok, Thailand has likely hit the bottom, having dropped for a few months.

The price for February deliveries is around $1,260-$1,270/t, with traders looking for “a slight increase” to around $1,300/t for March deliveries, sources said. “It’s steady. If it moves at all, it will go up a little,” one source, with one of the big trading companies, said.

Prices have been sliding steadily since hitting $1,660/t in October, since the end of the ban on catching on fish aggregation devices in the western and central Pacific Ocean, which runs for three months from July 1 for the bulk of the fleet.

In Manta, Ecuador, the next largest tuna processing hub behind Bangkok, the skipjack prices have dropped to $1,450/t, with sources tipping a move to $1,500/t soon.

For Bangkok, there is some talk by canners of prices of $1,200-$1,225/t for March, but this was discounted by Undercurrent sources on the supply side.

One source told Undercurrent there have been 12 reefers unloading in Bangkok, with seven anchored or due in soon. “So, there’s no shortage of fish.”

Fishing sources, however, said catching has been slow.

You can find this story here.

Finally, Tom returned to a story he has been following a long time, and which there is more to come before long; the Alexander Tugushev/ Vitaly Orlov court argument over Norebo Holding.

The UK’s High Court has been hearing legal arguments over whether a claim regarding a $350m-plus stake in Russian fishing giant Norebo should be held in the country, as well as if a worldwide freezing order (WFO) should remain in place. 

Tugushev -- who claims fellow co-founders CEO Orlov and Magnus Roth, who sold his shares in 2016, defrauded him of a third in the company which is now worth $1.5bn -- is striving to have the case heard in London. The hearing ran from Jan. 29-31. Andrey Petrik, a Norebo executive based in the UK, is also a defendant.

You can read this initial story here.

The CEO of Norebo argues he would not be able to sell his shares in what is Russia’s largest fishing company “quickly or secretly” even if he wanted to, making a WFO on his assets in a UK High Court legal dispute with a co-founder needless.

Orlov’s legal team argued the WFO is not needed in order to preserve the value of his main asset, his stake in Norebo, a skeleton argument document claims makes up 90% of his personal wealth.

However, the document claims the value of the company is more like $718m, “possibly significantly more”, but not the $1.5bn claimed by co-founder Tugushev, who is bringing the legal action against Orlov. Orlov was served with the claim and the WFO on $350m of his assets on July 24, 2018, in the latest installment of a long-running dispute over a third of Norebo brought by Tugushev.

Orlov wants the case to be based in Russia, where both men are from and the bulk of Norebo’s assets are based, and for the WFO to be lifted.

Orlov’s stake in Norebo “is substantially more than enough to satisfy Mr Tugushev’s claim in full (which is unsurprising, given that Mr Tugushev’s claim is – for the most part – a claim for (the value of) one third of Norebo Holding)”, states the skeleton argument from his legal team, led by barrister Christopher Pymont and law firm Macfarlanes.

“The vast majority of Mr Orlov’s wealth is represented by his shares in the Norebo Group, which he neither wishes to, nor could without considerable difficulty and publicity, dissipate or divest himself of,” the argument, seen by Undercurrent, stated.

Orlov has also “been on notice” that these proceedings were coming for over two years prior to their issue. “In all that time, he has taken no steps to dissipate or dispose of his shares,” it reads.

Read the full story here, and look out for more on this.

title: As domestic sales grow, Chinese processors face ‘big temptation’ to game import taxes
content:
Chinese processors face a “big temptation” to commit import tax fraud as domestic demand grows for processed fish such as Alaska pollock and cod, industry sources told Undercurrent News.

Speaking to Undercurrent, the owner of a Chinese importer and processor said he wasn't sure if the US-China trade war had led to more avoidance, but import tax evasion by Chinese processors who both sell to the domestic market and export is “not something new". 

Boss of large Dalian-based seafood processor arrested

The assertion follows the arrest by Chinese authorities of the boss of Dalian Hengtai Foods, a large seafood processor based in Dalian, Liaoning province. In local media reports the head of the firm is named simply “Dong”.

“There surely are those like Mr Dong who chose to challenge the country’s regulation. But I’m sure most Chinese processors do not choose to do it,” a second executive with a processor in China told Undercurrent. “They are now seeing the results”.

A third Chinese executive said some Chinese processors “do take risks”.

Sources believe China’s system of benchmarking to determine import taxes for re-processors of frozen fish and other seafood is more open to abuse by the seafood industry than other sectors. 

Processors do not pay import duties or value-added tax (VAT) on raw material they import for processing and re-export. To ensure imported goods are not simply sold on the domestic market, a benchmarking system is designed to prevent this.

Under this system, Chinese customs provide processors with a “customs manual”, or booklet, to keep track of imports of raw material and exports. Processors' figures recorded in the booklet are then cross-checked by Chinese customs with a benchmark of what customs expect a whole fish would yield in fillets in terms of weight.

Hence, a metric ton of imported whole frozen headed and gutted (H&G) pollock should yield about a half a metric ton of fillets, or thereabouts.

Processors who try to cheat the system typically declare fillets with glaze uncompensated, or overuse phosphates, reporting a yield higher than the actual yield. Thus, although the pound-for-pound input and output complies with customs’ benchmark, volume is left over. Leftover volume is then sold on the domestic grey market duty-free.

Dalian Hengtai sold 6,290t of product worth CNY 55 million ($8.2m) on the domestic grey market, over a three-year period, using this approach, based on local media reports. It also mislabeled products as part of the fraud. Typically, Hengtai imports around 15,000t of raw frozen fish annually, industry sources reckon.

Dalian Hengtai Foods' website. Source: Dalian Hengtai

According to its website, the firm imports everything from Alaska pollock and Pacific cod, to yellowfin sole and pink salmon, staples of China's processing industry. 

Undercurrent was unable to reach Dalian Hengtai for further comment since it confirmed its boss was apprehended, including to confirm whether the firm is still fulfilling orders. Chinese New Year holidays mean employees have likely already left the workplace, however. 

The last contact with the company was on Tuesday (Jan. 29), 12 days after the arrest, when a salesperson answered the call.

Growing domestic demand

In 2018, China imported 569,082t of whole frozen headed and gutted (H&G) pollock, while exports of fillets and blocks were 240,309t, according to latest Chinese customs data. This amounted to a decrease in imports of 14% compared with 2017, while exports were flat year-on-year (see chart below). 

Last year, Torunn Halhjem, a senior executive with Trident Seafoods, the world’s largest pollock company, noted between 2013-2017 a growth in imports as exports shrank meant more pollock was being consumed in the country. 

“The domestic market is definitely growing at a fairly fast speed,” said a fourth source contacted by Undercurrent in relation to the arrest. “There are limited statistics available so most numbers have to be guesstimated through imports/exports over time. But Chinese consumption will definitely be the main driver in the global market going forward and already is on several species," he said, adding: "motivation to 'game the system' will always be there."

But the fact China imported less pollock but exported a similar amount in 2018 would imply less pollock stayed in the country last year, based on Halhjem's theory.

title: Convicted, former Massachusetts deputy sues Carlos Rafael for $600,000
content:
A former deputy in the Bristol County, Massachusetts, sheriffs department who was convicted of helping Carlos Rafael smuggle cash internationally has now filed a $600,000 lawsuit against the so-called "Codfather", the Taunton Daily Gazzette, a local newspaper, reports.

Antonio Freitas was convicted in July 2017, at age 47, and has already served most of his 366-day sentence for his part in helping Rafael in his much-publicized illegal catch scheme. The long-time law enforcement officer was found guilty of smuggling $17,500 of Rafael's profits to Portugal in February 2016.

Freitas denied his guilt but had an appeal of his conviction rejected by a judge in September.

According to the newspaper, Freitas' lawsuit blames Rafael for lying about his part in the incident. As explained by his attorney, Philip Beauregard, Freitas admits that he took Rafael's money with him on a personal trip to France, where he intended to propose to his girlfriend, but he was not aware he was committing a crime.

Freitas and his girlfriend had split the cash up so that both were carrying amounts of less than $10,000, and didn't report the money to federal customs.

Freitas was arrested after Rafael boasted to undercover agents about the deputy's ability to work around airport security. But Freitas didn't know he was doing anything illegal, Beauregard said. He was helping Rafael because he thought he was close with Sheriff Thomas Hodgson, according to the attorney. 

Hodgson has said he knew Rafael as a business acquaintance only and not in any social capacity, 

Rafael began serving a 46-month sentence in November 2017 after pleading guilty in March 2017 to operating a long-running scheme through which he submitted falsified records to the federal government to evade federal fishing quotas.

title: Boss of large Dalian-based seafood processor arrested
content:
Chinese authorities have arrested the boss of a large Dalian-based processor suspected of import tax evasion and fraud, as authorities launch further anti-smuggling operations in seafood trading hubs in the north and south.

Zhuanghe-based Dalian Hengtai Foods, which imports an estimated 15,000 metric tons of raw material annually for processing and re-export, confirmed to Undercurrent News on Tuesday (Jan. 29) the firm’s boss has been apprehended.

The firm said it is "unclear” what the situation is regarding the apprehension.

According to local media reports, details about the arrest of the otherwise unnamed Chinese processor in Zhuanghe include suspicion of selling over 6,000t of bonded goods for processing, worth CNY 55 million ($8.2m), on domestic markets.

Besides evading import taxes, suspects used glazing to increase yields and forged product names, reports said. Currently, China levies additional import duties of 25% on frozen fish imported from the US. 

The arrest occurred on Jan. 17 during raids by more than 70 anti-smuggling police officers in 12 groups in Dalian and Zhuanghe. 

In media reports, the boss of the firm who is arrested is named simply “Dong”.

An industry source who wished to be quoted unnamed told Undercurrent Dalian Hengtai is the firm in question in reports in Chinese media. 

Chinese authorities arrest individual linked with Dalian processor involved in import tax evasion and fraud. Credit: Seafood Guide

Dalian Hengtai sells a wide variety of processed wild-caught fish, including yellowfin sole IQF, mackerel, pink salmon, chum salmon, northern rockfish, headed and gutted and fillets of Pacific redfish, and Pacific cod fillets and loins, as well as Alaska pollock, it says on its website.

Established in 2004, it has processing capacity of 18,000t of finished products and 8,000t of cold storage capacity. It is certified HACCP, BRC, IFS, MSC and ISO 9001-2008, and also has an EU code, FDA code, Russia code and Brazil DIPOA code.

Although products are mainly exported -- to Europe, the US, Brazil, Russia, and Japan -- allowing Dalian Hengtai to claim back duties or avoid paying entirely, Chinese processors sell increasing amounts of processed products on the domestic market. 

More anti-smuggling operations

Dalian Hengtai's boss' arrest preceded separate raids in other parts of the country as China’s anti-smuggling operations step up a gear. 

China’s seafood imports balloon by 44% to $12bn in 2018

Both in Qingdao, Shandong province, and south China, arrests were made designed to stem the flow of goods entering the country through illegal channels. 

On Monday (Jan. 28), Chinese authorities arrested at least 38 individuals from seven “professionalized criminal smuggling gangs” across south China during co-ordinated raids. The groups are suspected of smuggling frozen seafood worth approximately CNY 298m, reports CCTV (see video below article). 

Officials seized more than 4,000t of frozen seafood -- including frozen squid and shrimp -- during the raids in Guangzhou, Zhuhai, Guangxi Dongxing, Fujian Zhangzhou, and Hainan Haikou.

The groups engaged in illegal import, warehousing, packaging, transportation and wholesale sales, of seafood products from Vietnam. It followed a separate anti-smuggling crackdown in Qingdao, Shandong province, on Jan. 18, in which 16 individuals were apprehended. 

In the Qingdao operation, individuals are suspected of importing CNY 200m worth of shrimp and frozen fish, also from Vietnam.
