title: China’s seafood imports balloon by 44% to $12bn in 2018
content:
China’s seafood imports ballooned by a massive 44% to $11.9 billion last year as the country continues to change the face of global seafood trade. 

In the twelve months to the end of December 2018, China imported CNY 787bn worth of seafood, according to Chinese customs data published on Wednesday. 

Chinese salmon, lobster importers charter jumbo jets for Spring Festival

In US dollar terms, the increase amounted to $3.62bn compared with 2017 to $11.91bn, Chinese customs said, a percentage increase of 43.6%.

The increase in imports was greater than for any other food commodity, Chinese figures show.

Chinese customs figures also do not include imports of fishmeal (HS code 2301), worth an additional $1.5bn-2.5bn in annual imports in a typical year. 

China’s seafood exports increased by 3% year-on-year to $21.5bn, Chinese customs show. This includes seafood traded under HS codes 03, 1604 and 1605. 

Exports grew more slowly as labor costs in China rise and aquaculture production growth slows or possibly contracts.

China is home to a huge re-processing industry, importing unprocessed fish and seafood from all over the globe and then processing it for re-export, which comprises a large share of China's seafood imports.

But Chinese imports have surged mainly down to growing direct shipments of seafood to China consumed in the country.

Arrests in China as authorities launch another seafood smuggling crackdown

In recent years, the true picture of China's seafood consumption boom has been hidden due to an illicit seafood trade across the border between northern Vietnam and southern China. According to an Undercurrent analysis, in 2016, Vietnam’s seafood imports were worth over $5bn, up from $25 million in 2001, with the majority of imports transhipped to China. 

The trade blossomed to avoid Chinese imports tariffs -- which are levied on imports for domestic consumption but not on raw material processed and re-exported -- and inspection, but legitimate importers were undercut and a large volume of seafood imports was hidden from view.

Besides a smuggling crackdown, China has also reduced tariffs on products and struck free trade agreements, with Australian exporters of rock lobster enjoying zero-tariff access as of Jan. 1 this year. 

With more seafood imported by China direct through official channels, legitimate importers will benefit from a more level playing field and a closer relationship between suppliers and consumers. 

A more detailed breakdown of China's seafood imports, such as by species and product type, will be released later this month.

title: Shrimp prices in China jump on Spring Festival demand, supply shortage
content:
Wholesale shrimp prices in China have jumped by roughly 15% in the past two to three weeks due to a supply shortage amid a crackdown in smuggling from Vietnam during the busiest trading period of the year.

Now the big question is, with the holiday festival period of Chinese New Year approaching, whether prices will continue to rise before the festival gets underway. Chinese New Year falls on Feb. 5. 

“That is the million dollar question,” an importer source based in Beijing who wished to be quoted unnamed told Undercurrent News on Sunday (Jan. 13).

“Recently the price increased very quickly, very fast. During these past two weeks, prices increased at least 15%, but I think there's a chance prices could increase by a further 25%.”

“The Spring Festival is coming and I’m curious how many containers will arrive in China before the holiday period starts. This is the main concern for me.”

China typically imports double the volume of shrimp at this time of year compared with a normal month, such as June or July, the importer said. China is the world’s largest consumer of shrimp, based on current estimates. If more containers don’t arrive soon and his understanding of inventories in China is correct, a shortage will drive further price rises.  

“We have a lot of contacts in a lot of cities and they sell a lot of volume. I was talking tonight [Sunday] with many wholesalers in Beijing and also we had phone calls in Guangzhou and Shanghai, and they don't have inventory, or not a lot of inventory. And second, they didn’t order a lot of containers. I believe the shortage amounts to about a third [of normal imports].”

“But I don't know if high prices will last until Spring Festival.”

He said another factor is whether the recent spike in prices is related to New Year’s Day celebrations in China, when selling volume by wholesalers “increased a lot”.

He also noted that although prices have risen they remain 4-5% below prices during the same period last year. According to the source, prices in Ecuador -- China's largest supplier -- have also risen (see table one). 

Ex-factory price for 1.4 kilo blocks in Ecuador

60/70	$4.70	$5.60	19.2%
70/80	$4.50	$5.30	17.8%
Source: Undercurrent News industry source
Shortage or temporary blip?

Two supply-side factors could decide whether prices in China stay high; whether Ecuador shipped sufficient volumes to China before the end of November/early December to meet demand there, and whether shrimp is still getting across Vietnam's border with China or can be re-routed in time after a smuggling crackdown.

In September, October and November, Ecuador exported a combined 22,130 metric tons, 23,860t and 29,534t respectively to China and Vietnam, according to Ecuador's National Chamber of Aquaculture (Camara Nacional de Acuacultura, CNA). This was up 40%, 8% and 61% respectively, compared with the same three months of 2017.  

Over the three-month period, of exports to both countries, 68% went to Vietnam, or 50,878t, according to CNA (see chart one).

A serious disruption in trade across the border between Vietnam and China could, therefore, significantly impact supply, given the above-mentioned large volumes of Ecuadorian shrimp to Vietnam, as well as volumes from India, Saudi Arabia, Iran, and Venezuela also shipped via the Southeast Asian country, although getting accurate on-the-ground information on the movement of goods across the border is difficult. The source said importers had “disappeared” since arrests in a wave of recent crackdowns.

“Many people have stopped processing orders with shrimp factories [in Ecuador and other supplying countries],” he said.

In a table of data from wholesalers in major trading hubs in China collated by the source, he reckoned wholesalers have sold 1,210 containers and expect another 820 to arrive before the Spring Festival, with an overall shortage of 32% (see table two).

Wholesalers who sold during the current price spike appear to have already done well, nevertheless. “Compared with last year and the year before many wholesalers made a lot of money.”

The question is whether the importer source and others with inventories can sell smarter still.

“They [some wholesalers] think this amount of profit at this price level is enough. They are getting rid of inventory. But from our data and our experience, China is short of at least 1,500 containers for the most recent month. We think there is a big shortage compared with last year.”

On Monday (Jan. 14), in a market report which supports the importer’s assessment, Seafood Guide, a Chinese industry publication, said shrimp inventories in China are currently “insufficient”, with supply through official import channels (direct imports) "still tight".

“Demand for large-sized shrimp has risen across the country in preparation for the peak season for large meals and banquets, and as many families prepare for Spring Festival,” it said.

title: Credit Suisse not off the hook over Mozambique ‘tuna bond’ scandal
content:
The Financial Times has covered the $2 billion "tuna bond" scandal with Mozambique probably more closely than any other publication and in a recent opinion piece presses the case that Credit Suisse, the Swiss bank which provided the loans, is not off the hook.

This follows the news last week that three former Credit Suisse bankers were charged by US prosecutors with alleged fraud and receiving kickbacks in connection with the loans, the FT reported. Manuel Chang, Mozambique’s finance minister at the time of the loan deals, was also arrested in South Africa on Saturday in connection with the indictment.

According to the indictment, Chang and the bankers “created the maritime projects as fronts to enrich themselves and intentionally diverted portions of the loan proceeds” to fund $200 million in bribes and kickbacks. 

Credit Suisse, however, was reported to have been given a sympathetic ear by prosecutors, FT reported separately. This is because prosecutors "seemed receptive" to the bank’s argument that it had been the victim of rogue employees.

In her opinion piece, Brooke Masters notes the Swiss bank may not be home free. 

"Two former prosecutors told me that it is standard operating procedure for an indictment to emphasize concealment efforts because that supports allegations of intentional wrongdoing," she said. What could trouble Credit Suisse is if prosecutors conclude that the bank had shoddy controls or put business interests ahead of compliance, she wrote. 

Masters concluded if prosecutors find Credit Suisse to have acted illegally, quoting a local Mozambique attorney, "it should have to pay back the investors". 

"That only seems fair," concludes the author. 

Credit Suisse came under investigation for arranging over $2bn of “hidden loans” to Mozambique, purportedly to build a tuna fishing fleet.

The money disappeared or was used to buy naval vessels and other military equipment at above-market prices. Mozambique lost International Monetary Fund funding over the scandal and has struggled to pay back the debts.

title: The top shrimp stories of 2018
content:
Deputy editor Neil Ramsden runs down some of the most-read stories in the shrimp sector for 2018. 

Generally when pulling these year roundups together I aim to avoid our price stories; they tend to be among the most-read stories for all species, but they are, of course, at their most useful when we publish them.

However, the global farmed shrimp sector was largely defined by a price dive. In May 2018 Louis Harkell reported that prices were headed down and were yet to hit the bottom as good harvests, high US stocks and China’s smuggling crackdown sent chills through the global market.

“2002, after 9/11, was the bottom for the shrimp market. We are not there yet, but we are not far off,” an executive at a large shrimp trading firm told Undercurrent at the Seafood Expo Global in Brussels, Belgium. “The bottom is close, but prices are still falling in India, Thailand, Vietnam, and Indonesia and they have gone down in China, too."

Sources said US inventories were still high after 2017’s 10% increase in imports, but it was China’s sudden and unexpected crackdown in smuggling of seafood from Vietnam that appeared to throw a spanner in global shrimp trade. According to an executive at a large Vietnamese exporter, buying activity by China “completely stopped” in January.

Others said shrimp was still being transshipped in significant quantities into China from Vietnam, an illicit trade which was estimated to be worth well over a billion dollars each year and which executives had previously warned jeopardizes the shrimp industry. On the other hand, sources – and Chinese media – said police in China were still conducting raids and making arrests; we saw more later in 2018.

Meanwhile, European buyers were biding their time, the Vietnamese executive said.

“The markets are so quiet,” he said. “And the harvests in Vietnam and other countries in Asia are also very good. It is all making the shrimp price go down a lot.” 

Read the full story here.

At the very end of December editor Tom Seaman and Louis Harkell reported that Ecuador's shrimp exports were on track to hit half a million metric tons for 2018, as the South American country swatted aside a global crash in shrimp prices with yet another extraordinary year of double-digit export growth. 

Between January-November, Ecuador's shrimp exports surged to 461,790t, according to figures from Ecuador's Cámara Nacional de Acuacultura (CNA), or national chamber of aquaculture, up a massive 20% compared with the same 11-month period in 2017. Ecuador's exports were set to surpass 500,000t if it recorded another average month of exports for the year in December, or 41,981t. 

In another milestone for Ecuador, over the 11-month period, Ecuador’s total direct shrimp sales to China passed $500 million, after a ten-fold year-on-year increase in November, according to CNA data. 

November sales to Vietnam -- much of which is then smuggled into China via the northern port of Hai Phong, a route being cracked down on -- were $105.60m, down 8% y-o-y, but up 5% in volume, to 40.19m lbs (18,229t). This would seem to suggest Ecuador's direct sales to China are increasing at the expense of the smuggling rings.

Read the full story here.

In August I covered a report by Rabobank which cast the low prices in a different light; rather than simply being a year in which prices crashed, the Dutch bank proposed the situation was indicative of a "new reality" when it comes to levels going forward.

The report -- "Keeping up with the Crustaceans" -- noted the price crash occurred during the first harvest of 2018, as a result of strong double-digit supply growth from India and Ecuador, though growth was also reported in Indonesia, Vietnam, and others.

"Currently, many farmers are harvesting their shrimp at a loss -- or at least with a far lower profit margin in the last five years -- mainly because the key elements of the cost part of the equation, such as feed, energy, and labor, have not contracted (and for some, have increased)," wrote analyst Gorjan Nikolik.

He predicted that, in addition to farmers' protests, the industry's shrinking profit pool will be redistributed throughout the value chain, with "considerable consequences".

Nikolik echoed what sources had been telling Undercurrent for much of 2018; that many farmers will reduce stocking for the next shrimp crop, or reduce feeding rates and delay harvests, or simply not stock at all. 

"Shrimp farming has a fairly short cycle, and farmers can respond quickly to changes in price, balancing the market within a few months," he wrote. "However, predicting how farmers in each region will respond to a low-price environment across a number of crops in the next few years is much harder."

India had just begun to see prices rapidly rising again in August, as packers competed for limited raw materials. However, Rabobank did not see this as the start of a full recovery.

"In our view, although a mild short-term price recovery is likely, the lower price level, in the absence of a major new disease outbreak, does represent a new reality. A reality in which price levels dictate supply trends even more than biological supply-side challenges; a shift from a supply-driven industry to a more demand-driven one."

Read that story in full here.

The graphs below, from Undercurrent's prices portal, show that Indian and Thai shrimp prices did see a second-half recovery in 2018, from all-time lows. It remains to be seen if this recovery continues in 2019.


VIEW GRAPH
Vannamei shrimp ex-farm Andhra Pradesh, HOSO, Aquaconnect, 60pcs/kg

Away from the price picture, one of the stories which most interested readers -- including, no doubt, our notable growing readership in India -- was the news that shrimp purchasers in the state of Andhra Pradesh had reportedly agreed to a minimum price on 100 count-per-kilogram harvests, in a bid to support beleaguered farmers.

Durai Balasubramanian, secretary of the Pattukottai Shrimp Farmers Association in Tamil Nadu, told Undercurrent News prices in Andhra Pradesh had fallen "below production costs" in April. This had prompted concerns that farmers would not bother stocking ponds for the next harvest cycle.

On April 12, he said the Andhra Pradesh farmers' union had met with exporters, and the latter had agreed to increase what they pay for 100-count by INR 30, "in order to protect farmers from losses".

The minimum prices reportedly agreed from April 12 were INR 380/kg for 27-30 count; INR 300 for 34-40; INR 280 for 43-45; INR 260 for 46-50; INR 250 for 53-60; INR 240 for 63-70; INR 220 for 73-80; INR 210 for 83-90; and INR 200 for 93-100. Undercurrent's prices portal shows, however, that prices dipped below INR 200 for 100 count on several occasions after April.

Find that story in full here. 

Another important story for farmed shrimp in 2018 was the first rumblings of a new, "killer" disease appearing in China.

Issues with acute hepatopancreatic necrosis disease (AHPND) -- more commonly known as early mortality syndrome, or EMS -- and other diseases were being added to by the emergence of shrimp hemocyte iridescent virus (SHIV) in China.

During the Aquaculture Roundtable Series, or TARS, conference in Chang Mai, Thailand, Robins McIntosh -- senior vice president with Charoen Pokphand Foods (CP Foods) -- flagged up SHIV, as he forecast shrimp production in China would drop in 2018 to 512,000t. At the start of the year, an increase in production in China was being forecast.

“SHIV in China… it needs to be watched, it is a killer,” McIntosh told the audience at TARS, at the end of a presentation largely about the strong production worldwide and the need for better marketing, as farmers have learned to manage AHPND/EMS, whitespot and enterocytozoon hepatopenaei, or EHP.

It is “what is known as an emerging pathogen”, McIntosh told Undercurrent. “We know it kills shrimp, we know it is in China, we don’t know it is a big deal. But, vigilance is required.”

There has been “very little testing” done, so there are few facts, he said. “I don’t know if it's outside of China. But, again, emerging pathogens require vigilance.”

In an October interview with Undercurrent, George Chamberlain, president of the Global Aquaculture Alliance, said that SHIV had been detected in southern China and Thailand, at "a very low prevalence". "We have not yet detected it in Vietnam,” he said.

Loc Tran, founder of the ShrimpVet Laboratory, speaking during the 2018 Global Outlook for Aquaculture Leadership, or GOAL, conference in Guayaquil, Ecuador, alluded to SHIV's presence in Southeast Asia.

"At this point we don’t see much, but we’re concerned and we think it’s important to have surveillance effort in place like Loc has done," the GAA president said, adding: “I think it would be wise for diagnostic labs around the world to begin surveillance for SHIV so we get a handle on exactly where it is”.

Read the full story here.

In February Louis visited India to report on the vast expansion in shrimp feed capacity which was taking place there. 

BMR Group’s new 70,000t capacity feed mill was another sign of the runaway growth in India’s shrimp sector, he wrote. As shrimp production soars, feed mills were springing up among the lush paddy fields and banana plantations all across Andhra Pradesh, India’s eastern coastal state and shrimp production hub.

The day prior to visiting BMR's new mill, Undercurrent viewed a monster, 175,000t-capacity mill then being built by Avanti Feeds, India’s largest shrimp feed manufacturer. It sits alongside a twin 175,000t mill tower built in 2015 at Avanti's Unit-4 site near Rajahmundry, Andhra Pradesh, and was scheduled to start production that month.

Meanwhile, Cargill, the world’s largest agricultural company, inaugurated a new Indian plant, which will triple output to 90,000t, in January 2018. Andhra-Pradesh-based Devi Seafoods, India’s second-largest shrimp exporter, was also building a new 50,000t-capacity plant; its third mill in as many years. 

Some wondered whether too much capacity is being built into the system. Despite plowing ahead with its own development, chairman and managing director of Avanti Feeds, Indra Kumar, said India’s shrimp feed capacity is double actual demand.

“[Shrimp feed] requirement is about 1.1 million [metric] tons. Production capacity is 2.2.-2.3m tons,” he said. But, with Indian authorities targeting farmed shrimp production of 1 million metric tons by 2020, there was no shortage of confidence among firms expanding capacity now. 

Read the full feature here.

Another top feature to come out of Louis' visit to India was on shrimp companies using technology and direct engagement at the farm level to boost yields and improve sustainability, as the country's shrimp sector undergoes a massive expansion. 

The level of engagement by firms at the farm level witnessed by Undercurrent during a recent visit to the eastern coastal state of Andhra Pradesh -- India’s largest shrimp production region -- underlines the importance Indian firms view biosecurity and good farm management, as they try to avoid some of the mistakes made by other shrimp-producing countries in the past, he wrote.

Technology is also playing a greater role; one firm in West Bengal has developed a smartphone app to help farmers monitor various parameters such as water quality in ponds. The oversubscribed Aqua India 2018 event in Chennai on Feb. 2-3, demonstrated the interest in expertise from domestic and international experts.

India may have come late to the aquaculture vannamei game, but it "has realized tremendous technical benefit from advancements developed during the sometimes catastrophic learning curve experienced earlier in this decade by Southeast Asia", said Jeff Sedacca, president of Sunnyvale Seafood. 

"Indian farming is finally maturing and moving from art to science," he said.

Find this feature here.

A couple of stories on individual companies also garnered a lot of attention in 2018.

Firstly, a deal we're waiting to see the official nod on in 2019 managed to get a huge number of hits in a short space of time last year, as Glenn Cooke confirmed the Canada-based, global seafood group that carries his family name was close to a deal for a shrimp farmer in Latin America -- which Undercurrent has previously reported is Honduras' Seajoy Group. 

Speaking at a roundtable in Saint Andrews, New Brunswick, he said Cooke is in the final stages of acquiring "one of the largest" Latin American shrimp farming companies.

"We are in the process of getting everything approved, but we have basically bought one of the world's largest shrimp operations," he said at the event, which was attended by the heads of other divisions from around the world and Karen Ludwig, a member of the Canadian Parliament representing the New Brunswick Southwest district.

Cooke said the new company will fall under Cooke Aquaculture's Chile division, which operates salmon farms and a processing plant. The deal, which still requires regulatory approvals, has been pending for months since Undercurrent first reported in June that talks were underway. 

Read this story here.

Then, back in February, Tom Seaman reported former Pescanova chairman Manuel Fernandez de Sousa-Faro, who is to face fraud charges in Spain over the crash of the company his father founded, was in a senior role at Saudi Arabian shrimp farmer National Aquaculture Group (NAQUA).

Fernandez -- who was named along with 30 other parties in a criminal proceeding by the Spanish government made public on Monday -- has been involved with NAQUA since mid-2016 and is thought to have had his contract renewed for another year, according to Undercurrent sources.

According to multiple sources, Fernandez’s hard-driving style shook things up at NAQUA and ruffled feathers, with many executives either fired or leaving of their own choice. However, one former executive, who asked not to be quoted by name, credited the Spaniard with saving NAQUA.

Read the full story here.

title: Nine stone-cold, lead-pipe locks for seafood in 2019
content:
We’re just one week into 2019 and seafood industry professionals have the same kind of nervous and excited feeling in their guts that horse racing enthusiasts might have watching the filly they bet on sprint out of the gate.

One thing is certain though. The readers of Undercurrent News will be more than a few lengths ahead of their competition, as our experienced and talented team of journalists has been monitoring developments and already knows what to expect. 

On Monday we shared with you our list of the biggest happenings we see coming in the mergers and acquisition space in 2019. Here are a few others we feel confident enough to bet the house on:

Lock #1: The US-China trade war will come to a head again early in the year

Fans of Francis Ford Coppola’s masterpiece movie about the Vietnam War, Apocalypse Now, will remember the actor Robert Duvall's character, Lt. Col. Bill Kilgore, on the beach, saying wistfully, “Someday this war is gonna end.” It was much less a prayer than a complaint.

However, as Donald Trump’s trade war with China heads into roughly its seventh month, seafood importers on both sides of the Pacific Ocean are begging for a conclusion. Sales of tilapia, tuna and red swimming crab from China and lobster and squid from the US have all suffered badly, confirms a recent analysis by Undercurrent.   

But most importantly it seems that the US president and China both want the war to end, too. Not only is it being blamed for hurting the US stock market – something that gets Trump’s attention -- but China reportedly is feeling the pain, too. China's Bureau of Statistics announced last week that manufacturing activity shrank in December for the first time in more than two years, Fox Business Network reported. 

Progress was made on Dec. 1 when Trump agreed to postpone an additional 15% tariff from hitting tilapia, red swimming crab and many other goods until March 2. The postponement was announced following reports of progress in talks between Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the G20 meeting in Buenos Aires, Argentina. 

Trump tweeted more positivity about a prospective new trade deal roughly a week ago: “Just had a long and very good call with President Xi of China. Deal is moving along very very well. If made, it will be very comprehensive”.

It was quickly followed by Lu Kang, a spokesperson for China's foreign ministry, issuing a statement: "China stands ready to work with the US to implement the important consensus reached by President Xi Jinping and President Trump in Argentina, expand co-operation on the basis of mutual benefit, manage differences on the basis of mutual respect."

Look for talks to heat up this week as a US delegation led by deputy US trade representative Jeffrey Gerrish is in Beijing for the first in-person meeting since the Buenos Aires talks. 

And note that trade deals only happen when it seems that talks could not be more fractured. It's always darkest before the dawn, as the expression goes.

Lock #2: UK will leave EU with deal, meaning fishing, seafood trade continuity

For the United Kingdom, 2019 is the year of reckoning. On March 29 at 11 p.m. GMT, the UK is set to leave the EU, its biggest trading partner. 

As the day approaches many are alarmed, in part caused by the chaos in government hub Westminster. Since the UK voted to leave the EU in a referendum in June 2016, UK politics has been gripped by Brexit. A prime minister has resigned. A general election has been fought. The opposition continues to pursue a change in government at all cost.

The consequence of no deal being struck would be a source of great joy for some and a lot of pain for others in the seafood industry. 

Credit: Bill Perry/Shutterstock.com

In a no-deal scenario, the transition deal negotiated with Brussels in late 2017, which would keep the UK in the EU single market and customs union for a further two years, would be null and void. Overnight, the UK would regain full rights to fisheries within its exclusive economic zone, currently shared with EU fishermen. 

But on the flip side, UK seafood exporters would face tariffs and customs checks on goods into the EU, and vice versa. The EU is the UK’s largest seafood export market.

Moreover, because Norway and Iceland enjoy tariff-free access to the UK market thanks to the UK’s membership in the customs union, those countries would also be severely impacted, not to mention Ireland, whose fishing industry is heavily dependent on access to UK waters. In a matter of days, the UK market would be thrown into oversupply of some seafood products and a shortage of others.

This outcome, along with fears of other far more dire outcomes for other industries, means a no-deal outcome is unlikely. Hence, after March 29, Undercurrent believes the UK will be leaving with a deal, likely the one negotiated by prime minister Theresa May, and business should continue as "normal", even despite the chaos in Westminster.

Lock #3: More investors will board land-based aquaculture train

A broad look at the recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) industry would show a map dotted with disasters, and plenty of skeptics remain. But there were lots of optimistic investors in 2018, too, a trend that Undercurrent fully expects to continue in the New Year, with the US a particular focus. 

For evidence of the growing confidence take a look at the record 250 in attendance at the Freshwater Institute’s and Conservation Funds’ Aquaculture Innovation Workshop, in Miami, in December. Several were representatives of family investment fund firms, including David Radunsky, a principal with Perot Holdings, in Dallas, Texas. He told Undercurrent in an exclusive interview on the sidelines that he has been investigating RAS as a potential equity opportunity for nearly two years and could be months from making a big move in the space. 

Helping to drive the enthusiasm around RAS last year were the announcements by Nordic Aquafarms and Whole Oceans of two new, large-scale land-based salmon farms planned for the coast of Maine. Both are expected to begin construction in mid- to late-2019, joining the Atlantic Sapphire facility where bulldozers are already plowing earth in Homestead, Florida.

Operations director Eric Meyer, talks to a crowd of roughly 500 visitors to Atlantic Sapphire's construction site in Homestead, Florida. Photograph by Eric Wuestewald.

One apparent success story that might also help to drive excitement is Ideal Fish, a Waterbury, Connecticut-based grower of seabass, or branzino. It started harvesting fish in late 2018 and recently hit a pace of 350 fish per week but plans to climb to 5,000 per week by June. The business reports having lots of orders as it is successfully making the case that the quality of its product makes it worth the 20% more it charges over the frozen imports. 

But the excitement isn’t limited to the US.

South African aquaculture company West Coast Salmon (WCS) recently unveiled plans for an Atlantic salmon farm with an annual production of 4,800 metric tons at Betty's Bay on the country's Western Cape, roughly 100 kilometers from Cape Town. Taking into account yield loss from processing the fish into a headed and gutted product, WCS believes its farm will generate an estimated 4,200t of marketable Atlantic salmon -- equating to roughly 50% of the country's total salmon imports.

And if that’s not exciting enough for you, note that Singapore-based investment firm 8F Asset Management revealed plans in November for the largest RAS facility ever built in Japan, intended to be the first of many new Atlantic salmon farms placed around the globe. The $162 million investment is expected to be operational by 2022.

The new plant is effectively a scaled-up version of the 580t “proof of concept” RAS facility in Poland, a company that 8F’s private equity fund operates as joint 50/50 partners with Israel’s AquaMaof Technologies.  

However, before anyone boards the RAS train, they should take another look at Webster City, Iowa-based barramundi grower VeroBlue. The one-time darling of the RAS movement filed for Chapter 11 protection in late September and has lawsuits filed against five former executives, though the possibility remains for the company to re-emerge in 2019 under a different structure or growing another kind of fish.

Lock #4: Net pen aquaculture will be constantly under attack

As good as the new players in RAS seem to have it at the moment, the traditional champions of net pen aquaculture, at least in North America and Scotland, are having less fun thanks to an increasing line of critics. Expect that line to get longer in 2019.

Following a vote by the Washington state legislature, in March, to phase out salmon net pens off their coast completely by 2025, the push against net pen aquaculture has focused on the coast of British Columbia, Canada. In a development that seems a harbinger of things to come, Mowi, formerly Marine Harvest, and Cermaq, in December, took the unprecedented step of reaching an agreement with First Nation groups to remove 10 of 17 net pen farms in the province’s Broughton Archipelago over the next five years to protect wild salmon runs.

On the other side of Canada, in Placentia Bay, Newfoundland, Grieg Newfoundland Salmon and Ocean Choice International are full steam ahead with their installation of a massive 33,000t salmon farming operation after receiving the final go-ahead from authorities in 2018. They expect to stock a hatchery with eggs in late 2019 and have smolt in the fall of 2020 with an initial harvest in late 2021. However, advocacy groups, which already have challenged the effort, have sworn to take whatever additional actions they can to slow or thwart the plan. 

Meanwhile, in Scotland, one of the world’s largest salmon producing regions, the aquaculture industry will be dealing this year with the fallout of an extremely critical 2018 report from the government’s rural economy and connectivity committee. Responding to high mortality rates and ongoing sea lice concerns, the panel made 65 recommendations, including the mandatory reporting of sea lice data and the possible relocation of farm sites to avoid wild salmon migratory routes.

The industry in Scotland has taken this as impetus to modernize; to look offshore for new, larger farm sites; and generally to improve the sector.

Lock #5: Shrimp prices will stay low

The price crash seen by shrimp globally during the first half of 2018 – largely the result of double-digit growth in India and Ecuador -- is the “new reality”, wrote Gorjan Nikolik, Rabobank’s associate director for animal proteins and seafood, in his August report, "Keeping up with the Crustaceans".

Although the average price of shrimp imported into the US rose from $8.24 per kilo in August to $8.46/kilo in September and $9.04/kilo in October, based on the latest import data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the market is down year-on-year. Also, late last year, US-based sources said wholesale prices had since come down, as raw material prices in India, the main supplier, came down as well. 

Shrimp cocktail. Photograph by Jessica Springer.

So, what can really be expected to happen with shrimp prices in the new year?

Undercurrent still thinks Nikolik was right and the small recent gains in price will not be sustained. Here’s why.

For starters, while some growers in India have slowed production in response to the price drops, a bunch of new processors have come on. Jim Gulkin, CEO and founder of Siam Canadian Group, a Bangkok, Thailand-based, pan-Asian frozen seafood supplier with an office in India, told Undercurrent in late November that eight to 10 new plants have been set up recently.  

Indonesia, the US’s second largest source of shrimp imports, is coming on strong, too, Gulkin said. It will see an increase of 5-10% in production over 2018.

Meanwhile, China -- the largest shrimp market in the world -- is reported to be seeing a mild recovery in its own production, a trend that will continue for the next few years, Nikolik reported. At the same time it is cracking down on illegal imports entering via Vietnam (more about that and also the rise of shrimp exports from Ecuador in a minute).

Government predictions across Asia are bullish for increased supply, and the Rabobank analyst believes at least part of this growth will be realized, given the increasing professionalization in Vietnam and the rising numbers of semi-intensive farmers. If predictions were all to materialize, the global industry would expand by over 1m metric tons in the next three to four years, he said.

The lower prices available for shrimp were expected to lead to lots of sales promotions by retailers in 2018 and contribute to demand, but that hadn’t happened by late November when Undercurrent talked to Jeff Sedacca, president of Sunnyvale Seafoods, Zhanjiang Guolian Aquatic Products’ US division.

“The US market does not need product,” Steve Brunell, a seafood buyer for Philadelphia, Pennsylvania-based importer Quaker Valley Foods, told Undercurrent late last month. “Cold storage holdings are high and product is not moving well. There is a lack of demand. While it’s true key sizes may be short, there isn’t going to be a buying rush because you can’t just get the size you want. They buy multiple sizes, and most aren’t wanted.”

Urner Barry was equally bleak on shrimp prices in its report late last month, noting how its farmed shrimp price index was approaching its lowest level in three years as global farmed shrimp production was increasing at a 6% to 7% rate per year and saturating the market.

What could make Nikolik, Urner Barry and Undercurrent all wrong about flattened or reduced shrimp prices? Answer: an outbreak of shrimp hemocyte iridescent virus (SHIV) or another disease.

SHIV, which is often fatal for shrimp, has been detected in China and is suspected elsewhere in Southeast Asia at “a very low prevalence”, George Chamberlain, president of the Global Aquaculture Alliance, told Undercurrent in September.

At least shrimp importers can look forward to one thing. On Jan. 1, the US’ National Marine Fisheries Service was to begin enforcing its Seafood Import Monitoring Program, or SIMP, standards on shrimp, requiring importers to maintain 17 new record-keeping requirements for each shipment.

Oh, did we say “look forward to”... “dread” is probably the better term.

The new regulations might further curtail demand for Indian shrimp, the Business Standard, reported recently, citing the independent investment and credit rating agency Icra.

“While most of the medium and large Indian shrimp exporters to the US and the European Union use registered farms, shrimp exports to Vietnam go both from registered and unregistered farms. This would hamper Vietnam’s re-export prospects to the US (owing to the lack of traceability), in turn curtailing Indian demand temporarily,” Pavethra Ponniah, an Icra VP and sector head, is quoted as saying.

Icra expects Indian shrimp export volume growth to slow down to 7-10% in 2019 after a period of robust compounded annual growth rate of 17% from 2013 to 2017.

Other shellfish prices are staying relatively strong. Prices for lobster, snow crab and blue swimming crab don't look to budge much in the New Year. While both snow crab and blue swimming crab remain in tremendous demand and snow crab challenged by stock assessments, the latest lobster harvests in Canada and the US seem to have been off.

Also, US lobster harvesters are fully expecting a bait crisis during their 2019 season due in particular to a shortage of herring.

Scallops recently saw another boost in their prices. However, thanks to earlier stock assessments and the related harvest to be allowed by regulatory authorities, come April look for another big haul of scallops and prices more reasonable and in line with those seen earlier in 2018.

Lock #6: China will import more seafood direct 

One significant development in 2018 that should not be overlooked, and is expected to have continued ramifications in the New Year, is the continued crackdown by China on the illegal smuggling of seafood, including especially shrimp, from Vietnam. 

Ecuadorian shrimp from Expalsa.

On top of this, free trade deals China has signed with seafood producing countries are benefiting those exporters thanks to reduced tariffs. In 2019, for instance, expect to see a big boost in Australia’s direct exports to China, after Chinese tariffs on all seafood imports from the country fell to zero on Jan. 1.

The effect of the crackdown is being felt most by Ecuador, China’s largest supplier of frozen shrimp. To avoid Chinese customs duties exporters and importers of Ecuadorian shrimp have been sending their product to Vietnam to be transhipped to China for many years. In the first 11 months of 2018, direct export volumes to China were 179.59m lbs, or 81,462t, up 492% compared with the same period last year.

One major Ecuadorian exporter told Undercurrent that all of his company’s sales to China will be done directly in 2019.

As more is shipped to China directly, the cost of Ecuadorian shrimp on Chinese markets will rise.

But the border trade with Vietnam is resilient. After previous crackdowns, smuggling has picked up again. Hence, in 2019, the border trade will still be alive and kicking. And despite the crackdown and FTAs, Undercurrent believes China will still import more seafood transhipped via Vietnam for consumption than directly from supplying countries, undercutting legitimate importers.

So, expect to see more reports of Chinese authorities arresting smugglers.

Lock #7: Norway's salmon sales to China will continue their rapid increase 

As mentioned in our earlier M&A predictions article, China really likes salmon. That’s evident in the dramatic prediction that the nation known as the sleeping giant will awaken to find that it is importing as much as 400,000t of the fish per year by 2025.

But, for that to happen, it’s going to have to rely on one country in particular: Norway.

So, no wonder the two countries are talking about the potential of a free trade agreement that could take tariffs on salmon down to zero, which just happened to be the Celsius temperature in Norway at times last week. 

Like shrimp from Ecuador, big volumes of salmon from Norway were going to Vietnam before getting smuggled over the border. An executive linked to farmer SalMar was locked up for her alleged role in a smuggling ring last year. 

Credit: ducu59us/Shutterstock.com

But direct sales from Norway to China have started to increase. Based on the latest Norwegian export data, 11,853t of salmon went to China from Norway during the first 51 weeks of 2018, up 268% y-o-y. Meanwhile, sales to Vietnam for the period were 4,896t, down 78% y-o-y. 

Norway's sales to China are also likely to be boosted by Mowi opening a plant in Shanghai and inking a deal with Alibaba Group, in October, that will "create the most effective supply chain for the distribution of salmon". 

"The best salmon in the world comes from Norway. It is not us who have determined this, it's the 600 million consumers we have on our platform," said Alibaba president Michael Evans.

"This opens very big possibilities. China is the world's most advanced internet trading market. Working together at the top level with the biggest player within this gives us great opportunities," said Mowi chairman Ole-Eirik Leroy.

Leroy said the Shanghai plant would create products intended for e-commerce, with packaging and labeling designed especially. 

Lock #8: Pollock prices will rise globally 

One seafood item that is likely to see an even better year for prices in 2019 is pollock, based on comments made to Undercurrent by sources in the US, Russia, China and Europe. A large number of circumstances are in play, including a relatively flat supply.

The Russian government approved a marginal increase in its 2019 pollock total allowable catch, but made a slight reduction in the Sea of Okhotsk (SSO) portion of the fishery. Russian vessels will have a TAC of 1.786m metric tons in 2019, up from 1.781m in 2018. For the SOO portion of the fishery, which has Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certification, the total TAC for 2019 is 964,000t, down from 966,000t in 2018.

In early December, meanwhile, the North Pacific Fishery Management Council (NPFMC) approved a 25,001t reduction in the Gulf of Alaska (GoA) pollock total allowable catch (TAC), which almost completely offset an earlier increase in the eastern Bering Sea.

The McDonald's Filet-o-Fish, made with Alaska pollock deepskin.

But Fedor Kirsanov, CEO of Russian Fishery Company (RFC), reflected on a set of other complicated circumstances that he thought would drive prices up when he talked to Undercurrent at the China Fisheries & Seafood Expo, Nov. 7-9, in a venue close to Qingdao. He predicted closures, consolidation and higher prices charged by Chinese processors. Also, he warned that a coming social tax in China would lead to an increase in prices for double-frozen fillets.

Also, the two main branded players in Germany, Nomad Foods’ Iglo and Frosta Aktiengesellschaft, are increasing prices for branded fish fingers and breaded "schlemmerfilets" as their cost for raw material has increased, sources told Undercurrent. 

Other whitefish prices are also changing amid supply fluctuations. The US Pacific cod longline sector is seeing prices drop from record highs -- $4,750/t in November -- as the volume also comes down for 2019 and, in all likelihood, in 2020 and beyond.  There is a general sentiment that prices are unlikely to go higher for both Pacific and Atlantic cod, for which the TAC in the Barents Sea is also coming down for 2019, by 7.5% to 725,000t. 

Lock #9: The US tuna price-fixing saga will head towards a close

Not much gut is needed on this one. A lot has happened since 2015 when it emerged that the US "big three" canners -- Thai Union Group's Tri-Union Seafoods, the owner of the Chicken of the Sea tuna brand, Bumble Bee Foods and StarKist & Co, owned by South Korea's Dongwon Enterprise -- were being investigated by the US Department of Justice for an alleged price-fixing conspiracy. 

All three firms have admitted to the criminal charges, with Bumble Bee and StarKist having entered guilty pleas and Tri-Union acted as a whistleblower in the case. The only major criminal aspect of the case still to be resolved involves Christopher Lischewski, Bumble Bee's former CEO who denies involvement and aims to defend himself at trial. 

The dozens of retailers, distributors and consumers who sued the canners, arguing they were damaged by price-fixing, could soon see their claims resolved not in a courtroom but at the negotiating table. 

A selection of tinned tuna. Credit: Aisyaqilumaranas/Shutterstock.com

Tri-Union has been most active on that front, reaching an accord with Walmart and talking to many other big customers about settling. 

Expect settlement negotiations with the other canners to intensify, given that the companies have admitted criminal wrongdoing. Although the pace of those negotiations is hard to gauge.

The tuna price-fixing matter has been one of the seafood industry’s ugliest court-room battles in recent decades. Keep an eye out for decisions or settlements in 2019 also in relation to at least half a dozen other court fights that Undercurrent has been following, including those related to Alaskan king crab prices, seaweed and a new hire’s alleged sharing of a competitor’s client information.  

Contact the authors jason.huffman@undercurrentnews.com, tom.seaman@undercurrentnews.com, jason.smith@undercurrentnews.com, louis.harkell@undercurrentnews.com

title: The top salmon stories of 2018
content:
Deputy editor Neil Ramsden recounts some of the most-read salmon stories of 2018.

Our most-read salmon story was, unfortunately, one of environmental concern, as farmers in British Columbia, Canada, waited with bated breath after Grieg Seafood’s toxic algae disaster in June.

Officials with Mowi, formerly Marine Harvest, might have breathed a small, collective sigh of relief, but none of the salmon farmers operating off the coast of British Columbia were really able to relax, Jason Huffman reported.

Scientists said the conditions were such that a toxic algal bloom was likely to reoccur, and it could kill more fish (happily, it did not).

The Norwegian seafood giant, the largest operator of Atlantic salmon farms in the area, was spared from the heterosigma species of algae that killed half of competitor Grieg's fish at two facilities in the Sechelt Inlet. The only operation anywhere close to the affected Grieg farms was a broodstock facility that shares the same body of water but is about 25 miles away. 

Mowi maintains about 40 of the area’s 115 farms and harvests about 45,000 of its 92,000 metric tons of fish, based on data provided by the company and the British Columbia Salmon Farmers Association.

Monitoring closely is what every salmon farming business reached by Undercurrent said they were doing following word that Grieg lost 250,000 fish – 1,000t – that were expected to be harvested in the second half of the year.   

Read the full story here.

Staying in North America, and with Jason Huffman, he reported way back in February that construction of Atlantic Sapphire's Florida-based facility was progressing as expected, meaning the US' first operational, large-scale commercial salmon farm was on track to deliver an initial harvest of 800t by mid-2020. 

The plant's location, on the southern end of Florida, about 34 miles west of Miami, will enjoy a big advantage, said CEO Johan Andreassen.

While salmon produced by competitors with more traditional sea-based farms in Chile is still in the air, flying to Miami International Airport, where they will then be loaded into trucks for the next leg of their trip, Atlantic Sapphire’s product, head-on and gutted, will already be on the road or at its final destination.

“We’ll be able to harvest here in Miami on a Monday and deliver to New York on a Tuesday without using an airplane,” he said, noting the longer shelf life this gives his fish.

Read that story here.

If onshore salmon farming saw its popularity grow in 2018 it wasn't at the expense of offshore operations, which still garner huge amounts of interest. 

One example saw the Chinese shipbuilder of SalMar's offshore salmon pen deliver a similar-looking structure to a Chinese firm that wants to farm salmon in the Yellow Sea.

Chinese state broadcaster CCTV News reported that the 60-meter wide, 35-meter-tall pen was recently delivered from a facility in the city of Qingdao operated by Wuchang Shipbuilding Industry Group, a subsidiary of state-owned China Shipbuilding Industry Corporation. The broadcaster didn't name the company that took delivery of the pen. 

The newly built pen will be transferred 130 kilometers east of Rizhao -- a coastal city in Shandong province -- to the Yellow Sea where it will be used to farm salmon. 

Unlike the SalMar unit, Wuchang Shipbuilding's new pen will not float but stand on the seafloor, the firm's general manager Chen Hao told CCTV. It will be fastened to the seabed with four large anchors to keep it stable during bad weather, he said.

Read the full story here. Louis Harkell, our reporter focused on China and Asia, also went on to document the approaches China is taking to offshore salmon farming; this sector looks set to explode, if not in 2019, then soon after. 

Louis also reported in April that Chinese customs police had uncovered smuggling rings in China which illegally imported Norwegian salmon worth up to CNY 620 million ($98.4m).

According to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV, in the early hours of March 27, customs police in Guangzhou conducted coordinated raids of suspected smuggling operations in Beijing, Shanghai, Guangdong, Guangxi, and Fujian.

During the raids, police arrested 17 individuals from seven different groups suspected of smuggling salmon, the report stated.

Guangzhou customs deputy director Zheng Jun told CCTV: “Presently this group, through avoiding customs and smuggling, and quoting low prices, imported smuggled salmon from Norway worth approximately CNY 620m.”

Other Chinese media report smuggled salmon was from other countries, too. 

In the CCTV news segment, police are filmed during one such raid inspecting fresh salmon in a cold storage facility. Several Chinese media outlets say the value of the salmon found during the raid was CNY 12.6m.

In the video, according to information printed on salmon boxes, the salmon is 7-8 kilograms, ‘superior’ grade and had been packed on March 23, just four days prior to the police operation.

Read the full story here.

It then emerged that an executive who represented SalMar in the Chinese market, and also co-owns a company in Singapore with the Norwegian firm, had been arrested over her alleged involvement in the salmon smuggling operation.

Norwegian business news site Dagens Naeringsliv (DN) reported that a SalMar-linked executive, who is a Chinese woman and holds a Norwegian passport, was arrested in China suspected of involvement in the salmon smuggling ring. 

DN did not name the executive, but Trond Williksen, CEO of SalMar, told the news site that SalMar started a company with the accused woman. He did not name her, however. 

According to documents on the Singapore companies' registry seen by Undercurrent, Yimin Dong was listed as the co-owner of SalMar Pacific, which was registered at the start of this year. She is listed on the document as a resident of Shanghai. Police had given the surname of the alleged ringleader of the smuggling group as “Dong”.

Read the full story here.

After a good deal of research, in April I wrote a feature on the "salmon pen of the future", combining the latest aquatech developments I could find (and please do let me know of any more up-to-date creations!)

 While the past few years have seen first a leap in offshore farming developments, spearheaded by Norway's development licenses, and a greater move by land-based aquaculture practitioners, both of these are in the development stages; it's likely the long-term future of offshore farming will feature an amalgamation of those designs currently being tested, while – despite some optimism now – it remains to be seen if land-based aquaculture for the full grow-out cycle will be financially viable.

In the near-to-mid-term, it seems likely that salmon farming will continue to be chiefly based in the coastal areas it has traditionally inhabited. The feature covered how various aspects of "traditional" salmon farming might change in the near future, including the pen itself; cleaning and maintenance; autonomous helpers; sea lice combat; and more. 

Find the full feature here.

Also in April, editor Tom Seaman reported that Walmart-owned Sam’s Club was moving to buy frozen salmon portions direct from farmers, which meant High Liner Foods was being cut out.

High Liner, which is seeing its Rubicon Resources shrimp business diminish as a result of the club store chain going direct to packers, was also losing the Sam’s salmon business it acquired with its 2014 deal for importer Atlantic Trading Company, sources with knowledge of the process told Undercurrent. Sources estimated the business was worth around $40m in total, which was still only a fraction of its $1.05 billion in sales High Liner made in 2017.

It was not clear if High Liner, which sells frozen salmon portions and seasoned salmon into Sam’s under the C. Wirthy & Co. brand it acquired as part of the deal for Atlantic Trading, would retain any of the business.

C. Wirthy was, at the time of writing, still in some Sam’s stores and also in Walmart. However, sources felt Sam’s would continue to increase the amount done direct, with more salmon being sold under the Sam’s “Member’s Mark” private label brand, as part of a shift in sourcing driven from the top. 

Read the full story here.

Then, in May, Americas editor Jason Smith wrote on the opening of Alaska's Copper River salmon fishing, an event which is always closely followed by our readers. 

The May Copper River salmon run is widely seen as the kick-off event to the wider Alaska season and typically attracts attention in US consumer media. Most of the run's salmon, unlike those caught during the much larger Bristol Bay season, are sold fresh to stores and restaurants in the US.

Jason wrote numerous updates in our "live blog" format. See the full blog here.

In July, Jason then followed up with the news that the bountiful 14m sockeye salmon return to British Columbia's Fraser River looked set to add commercial landings of an extra 3.4m fish on top of already strong harvests in Alaska's Bristol Bay. 

The total allowable catch for the Fraser River was set at 6.2m fish but the expected commercial catch was much smaller, 3.4m. That figure  -- about 1m fish was to come from the US with the rest to come from Canadian waters -- would be lower than it could have been as a small subset -- a stock of around 1,000 fish from British Columbia's Cultus Lake region -- had been assessed, but not yet formally listed, as "at risk", leading managers to take extra precautions this year. 

There was no directed fishery for Cultus Lake sockeye. Mike Lapointe, chief biologist for the Pacific Salmon Commission, told Undercurrent that as a result of the "at-risk" assessment and the fact that Cultus fish are often caught along with other non threatened stocks, managers were to take action to ensure no more than 20% of the Cultus biomass is caught.  

“Because it’s mixed in with these other late runs they’re going to have to forgo a fairly significant amount of their catch in order to ensure they do not catch Cultus sockeye,” he said.

Read the story in full here.

Back to China, and Louis reported in May that a Chinese media storm over “fake” labeling of trout as salmon had led the country’s fisheries industry association to ask consumers not to believe the rumors.

The China Fisheries Association was forced to issue a statement quelling internet rumors that rainbow trout farmed on the Tibetan plateau was being mislabeled salmon; was infested with worms; and painted to resemble salmon, after a soft news story by Chinese state-owned media was jumped on by Chinese netizens.

China's CCTV had reported one-third of salmon marketed in China was not imported salmon but salmon farmed on the Tibetan Plateau.

In a 12 minute film, during which reporters visited China’s largest rainbow trout farmer Qinghai Minze Longyangxia Ecological Aquaculture at Qinghai reservoir, reporters describe how the Chinese firm has expanded production to compete with imports from the world's biggest suppliers, using modern farming techniques. 

For many Chinese viewers, who mostly presume all salmon is imported, the news was a surprise, until it was pointed out the fish farmed by Qinghai Minze is not salmon but rainbow trout, a point CCTV reporters failed to mention. 

Read Louis' full story here.

After a tip at Bremen's Fish International event in March, I reported that a German engineering company was planning to farm salmon across a number of sailing vessels, operating in international waters.

Hamburg-based Next Generation Cargo aims to build five 170-meter-long sailboats by around 2023, each capable of producing 2,500t of Atlantic salmon, the firm's owner and founder Uwe Kohler told Undercurrent.

This, he added, was the firm's first plan, for a “small fleet”.

The development of the first vessel – which will operate under the name 'Quadriga' – has been completed, and building was underway at a Chinese shipyard, said Kohler.

“In the coming six months we bring the process technology on board the vessel, do all the numbers and choose partners,” he said. He declined to reveal the investment quantities involved at that stage.

The ship should take around 18 months to construct, he estimated, and the company believes it can start operating it around mid-2020. “Other types of vessel will follow, for coastal regions and local needs,” he added.

Read the full story here.

One story not strictly about salmon (yet) was the news that before leaving Cargill, Einar Wathne is going to come up with a strategy on how the US agribusiness giant can expand from feed into different areas of the seafood value chain.  

Wathne, a highly respected figure in the aquaculture sector, stood down as president of Cargill Aqua Nutrition after over three decades in the aquafeed sector. He moved into a strategic counsel role as seafood leader for Cargill Animal Nutrition. 

Going beyond feed up and downstream in the farmed salmon and shrimp sectors could figure in his new plan, which must also be driven by consumer demand, Wathne told Undercurrent.

Read the full interview here.

In further North American biological stories, Tom reported in March that two Canadian hatcheries hit with infectious salmon anemia, or ISA, were growers for Northern Harvest Sea Farms, which has been bought by Mowi, then known as Marine Harvest.

According to multiple sources, the two Nova Scotia hatcheries were Dartek and the Little Harbor Hatchery. They grow fish for Northern Harvest, which Bergen, Norway-based Marine Harvest, the largest salmon farmer in the world, was buying for CAD 315m ($244.42m), subject to approval from Canada’s competition authority.

Undercurrent sources gave a level of as many as 750,000 fish affected, higher than the 600,000 quoted by CBC. According to sources, 200,000 fish had been transferred from Dartek to Little Harbor and also had to be slaughtered, hence the total of around 750,000.

Read the full story here.

Finally, speaking of Mowi -- Marine Harvest shook the salmon world in 2018 with its decision to re-brand. 

Undercurrent reported that in changing its name and launching a new line of products under a consumer-facing brand, Marine Harvest is looking to become the "Coca-Cola" of salmon.

This turn of phrase was borrowed from Christian Nordby, analyst with Kepler Cheuvreux, who said: "With this big new strategy they want to create a strong brand, that people will pay for, globally. They want to be the brand that that category is known for; you could say like Coca-Cola."

The world’s largest salmon farmer plans to invest €35m in developing its MOWI brand over the next two years. It has also changed its name to Mowi, effective from Jan. 1, 2019.

In a presentation on the rationale for the name change and branded plans, Marine Harvest said the plan is to hit €1bn in MOWI-branded sales by 2025.

It plans to launch the brand in Europe in 2019, and then North America and Asia in 2020.

In August Marine Harvest brought in Andreas Johler, now managing director for brands. He came from a similar role with the Coca-Cola Company in Germany, and was formerly in marketing with Unilever, working with seafood.

Read the full story here.

Finally, we saw two huge Latin American deals which prove a turning point in the consolidation of the sector there.

In August, major Chilean agribusiness conglomerate Agrosuper made the unexpected announcement that it had agreed to buy two-thirds of Chile's largest salmon farmer, Empresas AquaChile, set to create a giant company with a production of over 200,00t of fish.

That would make it the second largest salmon farmer in the world after Norway's Marine Harvest, supplanting Cermaq Group and SalMar, which farmed around 123,000t and 135,200t, respectively, in 2017, according to Marine Harvest's 2018 Industry Handbook. Marine Harvest farmed 370,300t worldwide in 2017. 

Agrosuper, which raises and sells chicken, pork and turkey, and owns the salmon farmer Los Fiordos, agreed to buy AquaChile shares from its majority shareholders, it said on Aug. 6. At the same time, Agrosuper also launched a public offer of shares to acquire up to 100% of AquaChile, it said. 

It was news that shook the industry. "Awesome and unexpected," a senior executive at another Chilean salmon firm told Undercurrent. "Everyone always thinks that smaller companies will be bought out and not large ones. Even more so as AquaChile has just purchased Salmones Magallanes and Los Fiordos bought Friosur," the executive said, not hiding his surprise. "The result will be a huge company," he noted.

The deal should close in 2019. Read the full reaction story here.

Then, in November, Legend Holdings subsidiary Joyvio Group agreed to buy 94.47% of Chilean salmon farmer Australis Seafoods, in a deal valuing 100% of Australis at $880m.

Chilean salmon industry figures greeted the deal for Chilean salmon farmer Australis with enthusiastic approval – and told Norwegian salmon companies to "mind the gap". 

“This is a very good deal, not only for the companies but for all the industry," Arturo Clement, head of SalmonChile, an association of salmon farmers, told Undercurrent. “It shows the salmon industry is becoming more consolidated and generating the interest of foreign investors."

"We're very happy that Chinese group is coming to be part of the Chilean salmon industry," he said.

"It's positive news for the Chilean industry,” concurred Daniel Montoya, sales and marketing director at Salmones Blumar. “The consolidation we've seen this year, in the last months, with AgroSuper for [Salmones] Friosur, AquaChile’s Magallanes deal, and then AgroSuper for  [Empresas] AquaChile, I think the market was ready to see this process continue," he told Undercurrent.

Read the full reaction to this story here.

title: Ecuador’s shrimp exports on track to hit 500,000t-milestone in 2018
content:
Ecuador's shrimp exports are on track to hit half a million metric tons in 2018, as the South American country swats aside a global crash in shrimp prices with yet another extraordinary year of double-digit export growth. 

Between January-November, Ecuador's shrimp exports surged to 461,790t, according to figures from Ecuador's Cámara Nacional de Acuacultura (CNA), or national chamber of aquaculture, up a massive 20% compared with the same 11-month period in 2017. Ecuador's exports will surpass 500,000t if it records another average month of exports for the year in December, or 41,981t. 

Half a million metric tons would rake in over $3 billion in export revenue and is almost triple the output in 2011, when Ecuador exported 178,019t of shrimp.

The growth has confounded even Ecuador's own domestic industry in 2018, as a global crash in shrimp prices in Q2 due to oversupply caused farmgate prices in Southeast Asia and India to fall to decade-lows. 

Sources in Ecuador mooted a slowdown or even contraction of 5% in production after the crash in prices, as Ecuadorian farmers were expected to seed fewer shrimp larvae in ponds in subsequent harvest cycles. 

But in September, October and November, Ecuador's monthly export volumes were 40,188t, 44,656t and 43,927t respectively, up 31%, 11% and 36% y-o-y, while export volumes in H2 look set to surpass volumes in H1, suggesting farmers plowed on. 

Month-on-month, there were a few contractions, such as one in June (-17% m-o-m), although this is consistent with slowdowns in previous years.

Looking ahead to 2019, it would be a brave person that predicts growth will dampen, although the average unit value of exports to Vietnam, Ecuador's largest market, has fallen to $5.79 per kilogram, according to the CNA. 

Direct exports to China surpass $500m

In another milestone for Ecuador, over the 11-month period, Ecuador’s total direct shrimp sales to China passed $500 million, after a ten-fold year-on-year increase in November, according to CNA data. 

The 977% hike in sales value direct to China to $66.97 million came on lower unit values y-o-y. 

Export volumes were up by 1,141% to 24.92m pounds (11,303 metric tons), taking the total Ecuadorian shrimp sales direct to China to $508.87m, up 434% y-o-y, and 179.59m lbs, or 81,462t, up 492% y-o-y.

November sales to Vietnam -- much of which is then smuggled into China via the northern port of Hai Phong, a route being cracked down on -- were $105.60m, down 8% y-o-y, but up 5% in volume, to 40.19m lbs (18,229t).

For the year-to-date, sales to Vietnam from Ecuador are worth $1.17bn, down 8% y-o-y, with the volume at 422.89m lbs, or 191,822t, down 1% y-o-y.

Ecuador’s November shrimp sales to China were more than double its sales to the US and over $18m more than the South American country shipped to the whole of the EU in the month. Its November shrimp sales to all of the EU were 16.41m lbs, worth $48.87m; down 3% and 10%, respectively. Its sales to the US for November were 10.400m lbs, worth $30.72m, up 16% and 10%, respectively.

Sales to Vietnam and China are 67% of Ecuador’s sales volume of 96.842m lbs (43,927t) for November, worth $266.76m. For the year-to-date, sales to Vietnam and China are 60% of the total volume, which is 1.02bn lbs, or 461,790t. The total sales value for the year-to-date of all Ecuador’s shrimp exports is $2.94bn, up 14% y-o-y.

Monthly export surges correspond with reports by Ecuadorian shrimp sellers during the China Fisheries & Seafood Expo in November. 

In charts: US-China trade war hits seafood, part one

Initially, there were concerns over sales for Chinese New Year, which is on Feb. 5 in 2019, due to a crackdown in smuggling. However, sources at the show then said orders came in from Chinese buyers in big volumes.

Commenting on the increase in direct exports to China, one major Ecuadorian exporter recently predicted all of his company’s sales to China will be done directly in 2019. 

“In 2019, direct to China will be the way.” the source told Undercurrent. 

But others suggest direct exports to China could reduce Ecuador's competitiveness compared with Vietnamese and Indian shrimp packers, given Vietnam enjoys tariff-free access to China's market, while China and India are also eyeing a bilateral trade deal of sorts amid rising China-US tensions.

Currently, China levies an import tariff of 2% on imports of shrimp (HS code: 030617) plus a sales tax of 9-11%, net the value of goods. Some importers, however, insist the tariff rate is 5%.

title: Maltese police examine country’s tuna fattening pens as part of Fuentes investigation
content:
Maltese police officers are working alongside their Spanish counterparts to investigate potential tuna fattening pens that could have been used by the Ricardo Fuentes and Sons group to grow their illegally-caught produce prior to export, reports Malta Today.

The Fuentes group is under police investigation following the discovery of an illegal bluefin tuna trade that reportedly imported 2,500 metric tons of unreported fish to Spain annually, at an estimated value of $23 million.

Spanish officers have said that the traceability codes used in export invoices for many of the illegally-caught tuna led back to Maltese tuna fattening farms.

Mare Blu Tuna, the Fuentes subsidiary in Malta, denies any involvement with the trade and states that it participated in no illegal activity alongside its parent company. Mare Blu director Massimo Cappitta also stated that the information regarding the investigation of the company is untruthful. 

"The information you received is not correct and has been manipulated to cause harm to our company," he is quoted as saying in the article.

The Fuentes group also claims that only small specific purchase operations of tuna were imported from Malta, if at all. 

According to Malta Today, 79 people have so far been arrested in relation to the investigation, including brothers Jose and Pedro Fuentes -- although both have since been released with charges pending.

title: China cracks down on smuggling, improves logistics for legal imports
content:
Amy Zhong, Seafood.com News

Smuggling has been haunting China’s seafood industry for a long time, and the country's customs bureaus have decided to take stricter measures to eradicate the problem. They have recently cracked down on a series of smuggling cases through cooperation with other departments.

For example, customs bureaus in cities like Tianjin, Shenyang, Shanghai, Qingdao, Zhanjiang and Nanning have taken action together and broken up 16 smuggling gangs in China. This case involved 30,700 metric tons of frozen seafood and its value was about CNY 1.45 billion ($210 million), according to one initial estimation. These gangs are said to have sourced seafood in regions like South America since 2015, according to media reports, and smuggle them into China through border trade.

Arrests in China as authorities launch another seafood smuggling crackdown

In late October, Zhanjiang customs broke up another nine seafood smuggling gangs and arrested 25 suspects with the support of customs from cities such as Nanning, Shanghai and Qingdao. Customs officials uncovered 1,400t of frozen seafood like shrimps and dozens of documents like contracts and invoices on the spot. These gangs have been in operation since 2015 and smuggled more than 7,800t of frozen seafood worth about CNY 417 million ($60m) in total into China through border trade, according to state and media reports.

Guangxi customs also announced recently that it seized 5,993 smuggling cases involving commodities like frozen seafood and beef from January to September, for a total value of about CNY 1.78bn ($258m). It is very difficult to smuggle seafood into China through border trade now, said an anonymous manager for a logistics company in Guangxi, and the costs have grown considerably. Recently, thousands of containers were abandoned in Haiphong because their buyers have been arrested, according to media reports.

Meanwhile, some courts have initiated public prosecution against smuggling gangs. For example, a court in Jiangsu province recently tried such a case. The defendants are three local sellers who allegedly smuggled shrimp products supplied by two Vietnam companies, Cty Tnhh Anh Khoa and Trang Khanh Seafood, into China through border trade from February 2015 to December 2017. They were reported to have evaded tariffs and other taxes of more than CNY 52m. They supposedly also bought from a Malaysian supplier and then similarly smuggled them into China between July 2015 and November 2017, which resulted in tax evasion worth more than CNY 3m.

To deal with this, Chinese seafood traders have taken actions such as changing to domestic pangasius. Foreign traders, like white shrimp suppliers in Ecuador, have started to sell seafood to China through legal channels. In the meantime, the government has also taken measures to boost seafood imports in order to satisfy he demand of domestic foodies. In addition to signing free trade agreements with seafood suppliers, China has spent great effort in securing customs clearances quickly and improving logistics.

For example, one trade company in Chongqing finished customs clearance of 1.2t of white shrimps from Thailand in less than one hour this month. It used to take about three hours for the company to get seafood after it was landed, which led to survival rates of about 70%. But now the survival rates have risen about 10-20%, thanks to local customs’ one-hour fast lane for fresh food clearance. Generally speaking, local clearance periods dropped by 61.4% for cargo flights and 71.4% for those carrying both passengers and commodities now, compared with the beginning of 2018.

In five charts: Ecuador’s remarkable shrimp export growth

Apart from Chongqing, Shenzhen customs has also simplified clearance procedures, according to reports. Furthermore, importers can apply online once flights loaded with their purchases take off in foreign countries. If everything matches the relevant documents, they can get their commodities immediately without further inspection. These measures have cut clearance periods by more than one half, while also boosting fresh local imports. Earlier this month, it cleared abalones imported from Australia in about 50 minutes, which helped increase the survival rates and maintain food freshness.

China’s seafood industry has been overshadowed by smuggling gangs for a long time. Now the government is determined to break the vicious cycle before it’s too late. Its carrot-and-stick approach seems to be working well at present, media has reported. This is believed to benefit the industry in the long term, though its drastic changes may have caused some temporary labor pains.
