title: Cold Nova Scotia waters put pinch on lobster supply, drive up prices
content:
So much for the expected flood of lobsters from the southern and western coasts of Canada’s Nova Scotia province. 

Colder-than-normal water temperatures are keeping landings in the country’s two biggest lobster fishing areas (LFAs), 33 and 34, down 25% to 50% during the first two weeks of their seasons, and that’s pushing prices roughly 25% higher than expected, sources tell Undercurrent News.

“The catch is down big time,” Kevin Ross, president of the Brazil Rock 33/34 Lobster Association, told Undercurrent on Thursday afternoon. His group represents about half of the roughly 1,500 fishermen estimated to work in the two LFAs.

Water temperatures where Ross sets his traps, near Cape Sable Island off the southernmost tip of the province, were 43 degrees Fahrenheit (6 degrees Celsius) roughly a week ago, but have dropped even lower -- to 38 or 39 degrees -- late this week, he said. By comparison, at this point last year the water temperatures were roughly 10 degrees warmer.  

Lobsters respond to the cold water by staying under rocks, limiting their movements and caring little about the bait in traps, Ross said. It’s only going to get worse over the next few months as the temperatures grow colder still.

"It's not going to go up," he said. "If it does, that would be a miracle."

Fishing vessels in Fox Point, Nova Scotia, Canada. Credit: Dennis Jarvis

A lower-than-expected harvest in the first few weeks of the LFA 33 and 34 seasons, which run until the end of May, is especially bad news for lobster sellers in both Canada and the US that are trying to find supply. The two areas accounted for nearly 31,000 (a third) of the 93,000 metric tons of lobster harvested throughout Canada during the 2017-2018 lobster season, and the first three weeks of the seasons there normally account for half the catch in those LFAs.

Canada is responsible for more than 60% of the world's supply of North American lobster (Homarus americanus), as the US produces about 60,000t annually, based on the latest data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. 

Ross’s comments about water temperatures and the state of the Canadian catch confirm those made by Mark Comley, the Canadian Department of Fisheries and Ocean’s (DFO) acting area director for southwest Nova Scotia, to CBC News earlier this week.

While the beginning of the season is generally the most lucrative time for the Canadian fishery, good yields can sometimes be had in the spring, the government official told the news service. However. It’s too early to call the season a disappointment, he said.

"We really need a full six months to get a good picture of how the lobster fishing went as far as catches, and it's very important for DFO to get all the data from year to year," he said.

Recall that the harvest for LFAs 33 and 34 was scheduled to start, as usual, on the last Monday of November, on a date known as “Dumping Day”, but was delayed nearly a week due to dangerously high winds and tides. 

Sea conditions off the southern and western coasts of Nova Scotia are better than they were, but still not great. The wind there was predicted by Environment and Climate Change Canada to increase to 15 knots (17.26 miles per hour) Friday morning and then go as high as 25 to 30 knots on Saturday morning with wave heights climbing to two meters (6.56 feet). A wind of 25 knots or higher is deemed unsafe by the Canadian lobster industry.

Given their struggles, the cold weather and the increasing cost of fuel and bait, some harvesters are not hauling every day, while others, like Ross, have started to keep some of their caught lobsters in storage, which is further contributing to the limited supply. Ross noted that he’s now spending CAD 1.07 per lb for mackerel.

Thirteen days into the season and Ross said he and his fellow harvesters were still waiting for one to give them a good yield.

"We're driving it and we're getting pretty tired," he said. 

'[U]nprecedented prices at this time of year'

Lobster buyers and sellers are driving it pretty hard, too.

On Monday Ross said he received CAD 8.00 ($5.99) per pound for his catch, much better than the week before when he was getting CAD 6.50 to CAD 7.50/lb, “depending on where and who you sold them to”.

That's high compared to the price commanded by some US lobster fishermen earlier this week in Boston, Massachusetts ($5.00/lb), and Gloucester, Massachusetts ($5.25/lb).

Harvesters in Maine, meanwhile, have transitioned from working inshore to offshore where changing weather patterns can cause supply fluctuations, but the lobsters are firm shells and of good quality, sources told Undercurrent.

Stewart Lamont, the managing director of Tangier Lobster, a large Nova Scotia-based processor and exporter, confirmed that he’s paying Canadian harvesters CAD 8/lb and said others are paying even more. Last year at this time Tangier was giving up just CAD 6/lb, he said.  

“These are unprecedented prices at this time of year,” he told Undercurrent, adding: “The market did not see this coming. Neither did we or the fishers.”

Lamont, who is a major exporter, relying heavily on Asian markets, is getting a premium for his A-grade lobsters, which he said normally make up 60% of his supply, but selling his process grade lobsters, which are about 15% of his supply, at a significant loss. He said he is getting just a few cents below or above his costs for B-grade lobsters, which account for 25% of his supply,  

In the US, meanwhile, seafood wholesalers are finding plenty of smaller lobsters but struggling to locate the larger sizes. Paul DiMare, the lead lobster buyer for Boston Sword & Tuna, told Undercurrent that he is seeing wholesale prices of $8.50/lb for chix (1 lb lobsters) and quarters (1.25 lb to 1.5 lb lobsters) and $9.00/lb for halves (1.5 lb lobsters) to 2 lb. lobsters. 

But 2 to 4 lb lobsters are much more difficult to locate and going for $11.00 to $11.50/lb, he said.

The pre-holiday rush is happening now, he noted, and supply is going to get tighter heading into New Year's Day, a popular time to serve lobster in the US.

J.J. McDonnell, an Elkridge, Maryland-based wholesaler, corroborated DiMare's account this week in a newsletter sent to customers, reporting that 50% of the current run from Canada is chix size, while just 5% are 2 lbs or greater. 

Mark and Matthew Ring stand atop their lobster boat in Gloucester, Massachusetts. Photography by Jason Huffman.

“[T]he race is on to source sufficient for Christmas orders,” Lamont told Undercurrent. However, by charging overly high prices, the lobster industry risks driving consumers and institutional buyers to turn to other proteins with more certain prices for the holidays, he warned. 

“So we are between a rock and the hard place trying to buy and sell at the appropriate levels,” he said. “The next week will tell the tale as to whether higher pricing up 25% will fly this year.”

Could Huawei arrest bite Canadian lobster industry, too?

Lamont is watching another issue, too, that he told the Bloomberg Business News Network he fears could impact his business.

Though the trade war between China and the US, involving a 25% tariff implemented against US lobsters in July, has pushed a lot of buyers to Canada, Lamont expressed concerns that the arrest by Canadian authorities of Meng Wanzhou, CFO of the Chinese technology company Huawei, in Vancouver, British Columbia, on Dec. 1, could ultimately lead to retaliatory trade actions by China against Canada, he noted.

The arrest was requested by the US government which has accused Wanzhou of helping Huawei cover up violations of sanctions on Iran.

“We feel as if we may be caught in the crossfire between an America and Chinese issue,” he told Bloomberg.

On Thursday China arrested a second Canadian traveler for alleged “activities that endanger China’s national security”. So far, however, China has yet to take punitive actions that might impact the Canadian lobster industry.

title: Editor’s recap: Cooke shrimp farmer deal close; US, China trade war ceasefire; Alaska pollock, cod TACs
content:
Tom Seaman, editorial director of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

Our most-read story from last week was Glenn Cooke, who confirmed the Canada-based, global seafood group that carries his family name is close to a deal for a shrimp farmer in Latin America, which Undercurrent News has previously reported is Honduras' Seajoy Group. 

Speaking at a roundtable in Saint Andrews, New Brunswick, he said Cooke is in the final stages of acquiring "one of the largest" Latin American shrimp farming companies, the Telegraph-Journal reported. 

"We are in the process of getting everything approved, but we have basically bought one of the world's largest shrimp operations," he said at the event, which was attended by the heads of other divisions from around the world and Karen Ludwig, a member of the Canadian Parliament representing the New Brunswick Southwest district.

Though he declined to identify the company at the meeting, he said a formal announcement would come before the Christmas holiday. However, the details provided match those related to Seajoy.

Cooke said the new company will fall under Cooke Aquaculture's Chile division, which operates salmon farms and a processing plant. 

The deal, which still requires regulatory approvals, has been pending for months since Undercurrent first reported in June that talks were underway. Undercurrent reported earlier last month that the deal was close, but Cooke did not respond to a request for comment.  

At the roundtable, Cooke also said the company is focused on adding value to its products by offering more species and by getting closer to customers to better ensure the quality of its products. So, Cooke has purchased several distribution centers and a fleet of more than 100 long-haul transport trucks.

Read more here. 

US, China trade war hiatus 

The US and China have agreed to a 90-day hiatus in any escalation of the trade war between the two countries, which has caused significant disruption to seafood trade.

The temporary ceasefire was reached by US president Donald Trump and Chinese premier Xi Jinping during a bilateral working dinner and announced Saturday, Dec. 2, at the end of the G20 summit of world leaders in Buenos Aires, Argentina.

According to the terms of the agreement, the US will not ratchet up tariffs from 10% on $200 billion worth of imports of Chinese products currently to 25% on Jan. 1, as had been planned.

China, meanwhile, will buy a "very substantial" amount of US agricultural, industrial and energy products, although details were not forthcoming at the time of the announcement.

China’s state-run Global Times quoted Wang Yi, China’s foreign minister, as telling a G20 press conference: “China is willing to expand imports on the basis of its own needs, agrees to open its market and satisfy the legitimate concerns of the US as part of the process of reform and opening up.”

Over the next three months, negotiators from the two countries will discuss thorny issues such as US market access in China and China's forced technology transfer. Failure after the three months to resolve the differences will result in the implementation of new tariffs. 

Seafood trade has been one of the main casualties of the US-China trade war; US direct exports of squid and lobster to China have stalled, while US importers have either held off purchasing ahead of tariff announcements or plunged into the market to guarantee stocks prior to their implementation. In October, tilapia raw material prices in Guangdong province, China, rose to a three-year high, as US importers sought to get orders fulfilled and delivered prior to Jan. 1.

Read more here. 

Gulf of Alaska pollock TAC cut will almost offset hike in Bering Sea

The US North Pacific Fishery Management Council (NPFMC) meeting was going on all last week in Anchorage, Alaska.

At the meeting, the NPFMC followed the advisory council recommendation in an increase of 33,000 metric tons in the eastern Bering Sea pollock TAC to 1,378,411t. In the Aleutian Islands, the TAC will be 19,000t, the same as in 2018. 

Also, the NPFMC approved a 25,001t reduction in the Gulf of Alaska (GoA) pollock TAC, which almost offsets the increase in the eastern Bering Sea.

For 2019, the TAC in the GoA will be 141,227t, compared to 166,228t in 2018. For Pacific cod, the GoA TAC for 2019 from the council is 12,368, down from 13,096t in 2018. 

In the Bering Sea, the Pacific cod TAC is being cut 20,000t to 181,000t. However, the TAC in federal waters is 166,476t for the Bering Sea and 14,214t for the Aleutian Islands, as a higher portion is going to the fishery in state waters. For yellowfin sole, the TAC will be 154,000t, the same as 2018. 

Read more here. 

In pictures: China’s offshore pen designs

By 2025, the Chinese government wants 178 pilot offshore aquaculture farms built in the country, reported Louis Harkell. 

So far, taking on Beijing's ambitious target are shipbuilders and offshore oil and gas companies. Unsurprisingly, their designs resemble the large structures they build to extract fossil fuels from below the seabed.

In particular, the designs show how shipbuilders and offshore oil and gas firms are scaling down structures to account for aquaculture firms' smaller budgets.

“In China, most aquaculture farmers are small or private companies, so they can’t invest much in farming equipment," Michelle Wang Ming, account manager at CIMC Blue -- a subsidiary of CIMC Raffles, one of China’s largest shipbuilding companies -- told Undercurrent at the China Fisheries & Seafood Expo. "Who has $100 million to spend on cages?"

Blue Whale 1 by CIMC Blue is her firm's attempt to marry offshore pen design with the budgets of Chinese aquaculture firms. 

Read more here. 

Ecuador ramps up direct China shrimp sales as arrests intensify

Selling shrimp through China’s unofficial backdoor -- the Vietnamese port of Hai Phong -- could become a thing of the past as the government clamps down on the trade route, reported Matt Craze. 

One major Ecuadorian exporter predicted all of his company’s sales to China will be done directly in 2019. This represents a step change from the recent past, they said.

Chinese authorities sent a tremor through the shrimp market in early November, just as the China Fisheries & Seafood Expo was getting underway, by arresting several people linked to the China-Vietnam trade routes. Another 66 arrests were made in late November, all but snubbing out Hai Phong trade.

“This has zero effect for us”, as trade transitions to 100% direct to Chinese mainland ports starting this month, the source told Matt. “In 2019, direct to China will be the way.”

Ecuador has an existing commercial agreement with China. Traders who import directly to the Chinese mainland assume import taxes on Ecuador imports. Freight forwarders in Vietnam have been assuming the risk and earning arbitrage profits on receiving Ecuadorian shrimp tax-free in Hai Phong, and then selling it on to the Chinese market without tax.

China lowered imports tariffs on shrimp in December 2017 to 2% from 5% and lower value-added tax amid rising demand for traceable seafood from an emerging middle class. Ecuador shrimp is highly prized in the Chinese market because it is mostly sold head-on, shell-on.

That said, a lot of Ecuadorian shrimp is still disembarking in Hai Phong. Cumulative exports from Ecuador to Vietnam surpassed 150,000t by October of this year, almost on the same level as the same period in 2017, according to data from the International Trade Center.

Shrimp exports in unit value to Vietnam have slumped below $6,000/t in October, compared with prices that exceeded $6,500/t in the same month last year. Only the biggest export companies are profitable at the moment, according to another Ecuadorian senior executive who spoke to Matt. 

The biggest Ecuadorian shrimp producers, including Pesquera Santa Priscila and Omarsa, have been carrying out major expansions to their processing capacity to capture higher demand from the Chinese market. Asia currently buys about 60% of Ecuador’s shrimp. Sales to Asia were almost non-existent a decade ago as Ecuador was fully focused on the North American market.

Read more here. 

Love the Wild CEO Claudia: Price is biggest challenge for RAS products

Recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) seafood producers must overcome one big challenge if they want to be successful in the US, Jacqueline Claudia, the co-founder and CEO of Love the Wild, advised the roughly 250 in attendance at the Aquaculture Innovation Workshop conference, in Miami, Florida, on Tuesday.

They need to keep their prices competitive while dealing with a higher cost of production, even if that means temporarily subsidizing their offerings, she said at the event, from which Jason Huffman was reporting. 

“I know that the fish that we grow today is worth every single penny that you guys need for it, the money, the technology, the people that go into growing great fish the right way. But what I found is for the consumers, they talk a good game, but it comes down to price,“ she said.

The high prices being asked by RAS fish farmers is why Claudia’s frozen seafood manufacturing company relies only on traditional net-pen aquaculture producers to supply the seven species of fish she includes in her 18 different SKUs delivered to between 2,000 and 3,000 retail locations across North America, including those owned by Whole Foods Market, Claudia told Jason, following her presentation.

Until recently, Love the Wild was relying on VeroBlue Farms, a Webster City, Iowa-based RAS producer, for about half of its unspecified supply of barramundi, the manufacturer’s third-most popular species as it was providing fish at very low prices, Claudia said. Australis Aquaculture, a Greenfield, Massachusetts-based company with traditional net-pen operations in Vietnam was providing the other half and is now the only supplier, she said.

The VeroBlue barramundi product was extremely well received, “particularly by consumers in the Midwest,” Claudia said. However, the RAS company has significantly curtailed its operation while filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection and is in litigation with several former executives, as Undercurrent earlier reported. 

Claudia compared the cost of seafood to other proteins, including poultry and beef, to further make her point about price.

“We don’t start really moving the needle until we get down into free-range organic chicken price and then we can start actually substituting for other things that people eat on a regular basis,” she told attendees.

title: Ecuador ramps up direct China shrimp sales as arrests intensify
content:
Selling shrimp through China’s unofficial backdoor -- the Vietnamese port of Hai Phong -- could become a thing of the past as the government clamps down on the trade route.

One major Ecuadorian exporter contacted by Undercurrent News predicted all of his company’s sales to China will be done directly in 2019. This represents a step change from the recent past, the person said.

Chinese authorities sent a tremor through the shrimp market in early November, just as the China Fisheries & Seafood Expo was getting underway, by arresting several people linked to the China-Vietnam trade routes. Another 66 arrests were made in late November, all but snubbing out Hai Phong trade.

Arrests in China as authorities launch another seafood smuggling crackdown

“This has zero effect for us”, as trade transitions to 100% direct to Chinese mainland ports starting this month, the source told Undercurrent. “In 2019, direct to China will be the way.”

Ecuador has an existing commercial agreement with China. Traders who import directly to the Chinese mainland assume import taxes on Ecuador imports. Freight forwarders in Vietnam have been assuming the risk and earning arbitrage profits on receiving Ecuadorian shrimp tax-free in Hai Phong, and then selling it on to the Chinese market without tax.

China lowered imports tariffs on shrimp in December 2017 to 2% from 5% and lower value-added tax amid rising demand for traceable seafood from an emerging middle class. Ecuador shrimp is highly prized in the Chinese market because it is mostly sold head-on, shell-on, or HOSO.

That said, a lot of Ecuadorian shrimp is still disembarking in Hai Phong. Cumulative exports from Ecuador to Vietnam surpassed 150,000 metric tons by October of this year, almost on the same level as the same period in 2017, according to data from the International Trade Center.

In five charts: Ecuador’s remarkable shrimp export growth

Shrimp exports in unit value to Vietnam have slumped below $6,000/t in October, compared with prices that exceeded $6,500/t in the same month last year. Only the biggest export companies are profitable at the moment, according to another Ecuadorian senior executive who spoke to Undercurrent.

The biggest Ecuadorian shrimp producers, including Pesquera Santa Priscila and Omarsa, have been carrying out major expansions to their processing capacity to capture higher demand from the Chinese market. Asia currently buys about 60% of Ecuador’s shrimp. Sales to Asia were almost non-existent a decade ago as Ecuador was fully focused on the North American market.

Most of that shrimp was crossing the border without a country-of-origin label. That ended earlier this year when Chinese authorities insisted that all shrimp crossing the Vietnamese border be marked with a Vietnam country-of-origin label. The intuition with that ruling was to identify shrimp that has been entered Vietnam from other destinations.

China is shaking up the flow of shrimp imports as the market amid a price decline attributed to high supplies. The second source said that while purchasing ahead of the Chinese New Year will assure that prices don’t drop lower, he didn’t expect prices to increase either.

Some companies have been more optimistic about the level of Chinese demand. Some companies reported almost record interest arising from the China show, selling hundreds of containers in shrimp in forward contracts.

title: Maltese fish farmers appoint lawyer to follow Spanish illegal tuna investigation
content:
The Federation of Maltese Aquaculture Producers (FMAP) has appointed a lawyer to follow the ongoing investigation into the illegal Spanish bluefin tuna trade, reports Malta Today.

A raid conducted by the Spanish civil guard and Europol arrested 79 people for the sale of 80 metric tons of illegally-fished tuna in October 2018.

The investigation currently understands that overfished tuna in Italian and Maltese waters were then illegally imported by Spanish enterprises using false documentation.

FMAP have appointed the lawyer in order to follow any allegations that could lead to Maltese aquaculture being implicated. Thus far, Europol is yet to make any reference to fish harvested from Malta's tuna farms.

According to the article, the international investigation began in 2017 after Spanish police stumbled upon a 50t truckload of illegal tuna imported from Italy.

The Spanish civil guard currently estimates that the gang responsible has shipped over 1,250t of legal tuna, as well as 2,500t of illegal, overfished stock, at an estimated total value of €12 million.

According to Malta Today, while the majority of this volume was tapped from major tuna ranchers in Italy and Malta (primarily Ricardo Fuentes e Hijos, owners of Mare Blu), some has also been illegally fished in Spanish waters.

title: Editor’s recap: China smuggling crackdown; India shrimp prices fall; Cooke’s Seajoy deal nears
content:
Neil Ramsden, editorial director of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

The most-read story from last week was a breaker written by our China-focused reporter Louis Harkell. 

He found that Chinese authorities had launched another wave of crackdowns on smugglers bringing seafood into China via Vietnam, with 66 individuals arrested.

In the early hours of Thursday, Nov. 29, Chinese officials "knocked out" 16 smuggling gangs in coordinated raids at 55 locations in Tianjin and Shanghai, as well as in provinces Hebei, Liaoning, Jiangsu, Shandong, Guangdong, and Guangxi, according to the country's top customs authority.

Police seized 1,320 metric tons of frozen seafood at the scene, according to a statement on the Guangdong department website of the Customs and Excise Department of China's General Administration of Customs. The smuggling gangs are suspected of illicitly importing more than 30,000t of frozen seafood worth CNY 1.45 billion ($207 million) over three years, it stated.

476 police officers and customs officials organized into 78 task groups took part in the operation, dubbed "607".

"Since 2015 these smuggling gangs were purchasing frozen seafood in areas such as South America and shipping it to neighboring countries," said the authority.

"From there they sold it for profit after smuggling the products across the border [with China]," it said.

Read the story in full here.

Stories on Indian shrimp always get a lot of hits, both within Indian and globally, and editor Tom Seaman's latest price update was no different.

Prices for shrimp raw material in India are coming down, with the US market, the main destination for the Asian country's products, also in the doldrums, sources told him.

Industry players are hoping promotions start in retail now Thanksgiving is over, in order to stimulate the market. 

During January’s Global Seafood Market Conference, held in Miami, Florida this year, executives said they hoped the good supply of shrimp and low prices -- seen as the "new norm" by an analyst from lender Rabobank -- would mean retailers could promote.

This is yet to happen, however. “We have been hearing about promotions now, as the holiday season starts, but we haven’t seen it yet. But, historically, we have seen it. What’s happening now is, they [retailers] are making money with shrimp," Jeff Sedacca, president of Sunnyvale Seafoods, Zhanjiang Guolian Aquatic Products’ US division, told Undercurrent.

"They will continue to do so until sales slow down and the opportunity to make more money by doing more sales rather than a higher margin.” 

“We have seen it before when prices dropped and they started promoting and sales rocketed,” he told Undercurrent.

“You know how importers here are, once they have inventory they need sales and do sell cheap at times. Business should get much better after Thanksgiving [which took place on Nov. 22],” a US importer, who declined to be quoted by name, told Undercurrent.

Read the full story here.

One of the most-read read stories of last week was only published on Dec. 2 -- and sent out on Sunday to our breaking news subscribers. 

Jason Huffman reported that Glenn Cooke had confirmed the Canada-based, global seafood group that carries his family name was close to a deal for a shrimp farmer in Latin America, which Undercurrent News had previously reported is Honduras' Seajoy Group. 

Speaking at a roundtable in Saint Andrews, New Brunswick, he said Cooke is in the final stages of acquiring "one of the largest" Latin American shrimp farming companies.

"We are in the process of getting everything approved, but we have basically bought one of the world's largest shrimp operations," he said at the event.

Though he declined to identify the company at the meeting, saying that a formal announcement would come before the Christmas holiday. However, the details provided match those related to Seajoy.

Cooke said the new company will fall under Cooke Aquaculture's Chile division, which operates salmon farms and a processing plant. 

Read the full story here.

Meanwhile, I delved into the report by Scotland's rural economy and connectivity committee (RECC) on the current state of the country's salmon farms. 

In it, Marine Harvest and feed giant BioMar Group told the committee they feel land-based recirculating aquaculture systems, or RAS, are not viable alternatives to ocean-based net pens in the country. 

"Marine Harvest Scotland and BioMar identified that the move to RAS systems
may be premature, with further testing and financial viability required," the report reads.

In its submission to the RECC, Marine Harvest said a land-based tank system is often quoted as a possible replacement for farming fish in the sea, "but our extensive
research, and the experience of companies who have carried out trials, has shown that much more work needs to be done before it could be considered a viable alternative".

BioMar went a little further, stating that financially, it is not realistic to suggest that the future of Scotland's aquaculture sector is onshore. "No system to date has economically proven itself producing harvest-sized fish, where the whole life cycle has been in a recirculation system.”

The Scottish government itself is thinking along the same lines, as illustrated by a letter from the cabinet secretary for the rural economy, Fergus Ewing. He said "recirculation and closed containment is a fairly new concept to Scotland, at least in comparison to how the majority of the industry operates".

Read the story in full here.

More big breaking news from the weekend saw the US and China agree to a 90-day hiatus in any escalation of the trade war between the two countries, which has caused significant disruption to seafood trade.

The temporary ceasefire was reached by US president Donald Trump and Chinese premier Xi Jinping during a bilateral working dinner and announced on Saturday at the end of the G20 summit of world leaders in Buenos Aires, Argentina.

According to the terms of the agreement, the US will not ratchet up tariffs from 10% on $200 billion worth of imports of Chinese products currently to 25% on Jan. 1, as had been planned.

China, meanwhile, will buy a "very substantial" amount of US agricultural, industrial and energy products, although details were not forthcoming at the time of the announcement.

China’s state-run Global Times quoted Wang Yi, China’s foreign minister, as telling a G20 press conference: “China is willing to expand imports on the basis of its own needs, agrees to open its market and satisfy the legitimate concerns of the US as part of the process of reform and opening up.”

Over the next three months, negotiators from the two countries will discuss thorny issues such as US market access in China and China's forced technology transfer. Failure after the three months to resolve the differences will result in the implementation of new tariffs. 

Read the full story here.

Tom, over in our Seattle, US office currently, continued his thorough coverage of seafood M&A by reporting that Blue Harvest Fisheries, a US scallop and whitefish supplier backed by private equity Bregal Partners, has inked a deal to acquire a fishing company managing five vessels on the East Coast.

The deal for Atlantic Trawlers Fishing, based in Portland, Maine, will take Blue Harvest into the harvesting of cod, haddock, redfish and other groundfish, while adding to its fleet of scallop vessels and a processing plant in New Bedford, Massachusetts.  

The deal follows Atlantic Trawlers obtaining Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certification for the New England haddock, pollock and redfish trawl fishery in May this year. 

This is the first acquisition Blue Harvest has made under the leadership of Decker, the former CEO of High Liner Foods who came in as the top executive at the start of the year. This saw industry veteran Jeff Davis step down as CEO and from day-to-day operations at the company. 

Created by Bregal, Blue Harvest has snapped up a variety of assets on the US East Coast in recent years, including a former High Liner plant in New Bedford when Decker was still CEO of the Lunenburg, Canada-based firm. 

In November last year, Undercurrent reported that Blue Harvest had finished consolidating its processing activity into the former High Liner plant. 

Read the full story here.

In the same vein, Tom also reported that the South Korean firm US importer and processor Mazzetta Co. is talking to regarding a sale is said to be Dongwon Enterprise, the parent of StarKist & Co.

Earlier in the week, Undercurrent had reported Tom Mazzetta, CEO and founder, had been to Seoul recently to talk with a would-be South Korean buyer. CJ Cheiljedang Corp., which has inked a $1.8bn deal for Schwan’s, a large US frozen food distributor, was tipped as a possible candidate.

However, the current party Mazzetta is now said to be eyeing a deal with is Dongwon, which is one of the world’s largest players in tuna fishing and processing. 

He is said to have made a trip to South Korean capital Seoul in the past months and Dongwon executives are said to have visited Mazzetta’s east coast assets, such as the Gloucester Seafood Processing (GSP) plant in Massachusetts, which reopened earlier this year.

Mazzetta -- which is focused on importing shrimp and other seafood into the US and then sourcing and processing lobster, with its Attwood Lobster and Beach Point Processing operations, and whitefish with its GSP plant -- would be a diversification for Dongwon, which has built its business around tuna.

However, the Korean group has been branching more into shrimp in its home country, via its Dongwon F&B subsidiary, and has also added a 12.5% stake in Silver Bay Seafoods, an Alaskan salmon processor, to its ownership of StarKist in the US.

Read the story in full here.

Some sad news for The Edinburgh Salmon Company (ESCo) last week, as ultimate parent Thai Union Group announced it was having to close the plant. 

Following its announcement on Sept. 27, 2018 of the proposed sale and/or closure of the Dingwall, Scotland-based firm, it said that no feasible alternative solution to closure had been found during collective consultation. As a result, the company will cease production at the end of the year.  

"At this time, our primary concern is the future of our employees and we are now entering into an individual consultation process with each of them. We are making every possible effort to support them in their search for alternative employment," said Europeenne.

"We are exploring all opportunities and are working with the Scottish government and local enterprise and skills agencies to identify employment options in the local area."

ESCo remains ready, and will maintain the necessary employees, to fulfill all current contracted obligations which run until the end of the year, when it will cease production, the company said.

Read in full here.

Finally, another interesting find by Louis was the news that a Chinese entrepreneur from China's offshore oil and gas industry plans to build a CNY 1bn ($143.9m) offshore farm in the Yellow Sea to farm Atlantic salmon.

Wang Lingyu, who made his fortune selling subsea flexible pipes to Chinese state-owned oil and gas firms, intends to build eight semi-submersible offshore pens to produce 20,000 metric tons of Atlantic salmon annually.

It is one of three proposed offshore farms by Neptune Blue Ocean Development (NBOD), Wang's firm. In the East China Sea, NBOD proposes a farm to produce 10,800t annually of large yellow croaker, and in the South China Sea, a farm to produce 15,000t annually of golden pomfret and large yellow croaker. 

"We will start farming next year," Wang told Undercurrent at the China Fisheries and Seafood Exhibition in Qingdao earlier this month, referring to a pilot for the Yellow Sea farm.

Wang said inspiration for the idea came from offshore farms being designed and built for Norwegian salmon farmers. 

“Norway and China have built large-scale offshore pens, and we found that offshore engineering and engineering companies that used to do oil and gas services are developing in this direction," Wang said. 

The company is not hanging around; the pilot is currently under construction and targets 1,600t of salmon production by 2020. 

Following that, and depending on funding, the aim is to upscale production to the main farm -- which would have a total of 1 million cubic meters of water volume capacity (see diagram) -- to 20,000t annually. 

Read the full story here.

title: Arrests in China as authorities launch another seafood smuggling crackdown
content:
Chinese authorities have launched another wave of crackdowns on smugglers bringing seafood into China via Vietnam, with 66 individuals arrested on Thursday.

In the early hours of Thursday, Nov. 29, Chinese officials "knocked out" 16 smuggling gangs in coordinated raids at 55 locations in Tianjin and Shanghai, as well as in provinces Hebei, Liaoning, Jiangsu, Shandong, Guangdong, and Guangxi, according to the country's top customs authority.

Police seized 1,320 metric tons of frozen seafood at the scene, according to a statement on the Guangdong department website of the Customs and Excise Department of China's General Administration of Customs. The smuggling gangs are suspected of illicitly importing more than 30,000t of frozen seafood worth CNY 1.45 billion ($207 million) over three years, it stated.

476 police officers and customs officials organized into 78 task groups took part in the operation, dubbed "607".

"Since 2015 these smuggling gangs were purchasing frozen seafood in areas such as South America and shipping it to neighboring countries," said the authority.

"From there they sold it for profit after smuggling the products across the border [with China]," it said.

Earlier this month -- during the China Fisheries & Seafood Expo in Qingdao -- shrimp industry sources from Latin America told Undercurrent trade had been disrupted due to a separate recent smuggling crackdown, although they later downplayed the impact. 

Boom in ‘grey trade’ drives Vietnam’s seafood imports from $25m to over $5bn

Large volumes of seafood enter China through Vietnam -- particularly shrimp from Latin America -- as it is cheaper for smugglers to avoid Chinese customs duties and inspection than export directly to the country. Latest trade data shows the majority of Ecuador's shrimp exports to China is still being routed via Vietnam, although increasing volumes are exported directly to China. 

The crackdown appears to be similar in size and scope to one carried out in late December last year, when eight smuggling rings were "smashed" following nationwide coordinated raids. 

China's customs authority said the latest arrests would help "further regulate" China's seafood imports "ensuring the food hygiene and safety of the people". 

1,500 containers unaccounted for?

The bad news day for China's seafood smugglers could be worse if reports in Chinese media are to be believed. 

According to Seafood Guide, a Chinese industry publication, up to 1,500 containers filled with seafood destined for China currently languish in Hai Phong, a port in northern Vietnam, with importers unwilling to take delivery of the containers. 

Seafood Guide does not provide the source of this information (although other industry media in China also reported it last week claiming an unnamed industry source in India). Undercurrent's correspondent in China, Hu Luyi, said it's likely to be hearsay, although it is not unheard of for containers to be left in Hai Phong; some exporters demand large cash down payments against this risk.

title: In five charts: Ecuador’s remarkable shrimp export growth
content:
Ecuador's shrimp industry has grown remarkably in recent years generating wealth and jobs. Where has all this shrimp gone? Undercurrent News illustrates with the help of five interactive charts. 

Demand from Asia, particularly China, has driven most of the growth in Ecuador's shrimp industry. In the first ten months of this year, 60.4% of Ecuador's shrimp exports by volume went to Asian countries, according to figures from Ecuador's Camara Nacional de Acuacultura, or national chamber of aquaculture, in English. Asia's importance to Ecuador shows no sign of decreasing, on the contrary; over the period Ecuador exported more shrimp to Asia than it did during the whole of 2017. 

Most goes to Vietnam. It arrives in the northern port of Hai Phong and then is transported to China; Chinese importers use freight forwarders in Vietnam and people in border towns who smuggle the shrimp across the border to the north with China to avoid Chinese customs duties. However, chart two shows the increasing volumes of shrimp exported by Ecuador directly to China. 

Three things appear to be driving this: a decrease in Chinese import tariffs for shrimp in December 2017, from 5% to 2%, and a decrease in VAT; a crackdown by Chinese authorities on smuggling from Vietnam to China first early on this year, then again more recently; and increasing demand in first-tier cities in China for full traceability of seafood.

Direct exports are likely the future for Ecuador's exports to China, but data shows in 2018 volumes of shrimp going to Vietnam have been remarkably consistent with 2017 (see chart three).  

The vast majority of shrimp to China is head-on, shell-on (HOSO). This is because of Chinese consumers' preference for whole shrimp.

This also suits Ecuadorian packers, who have higher labor costs than packers in India. It also means prices are on average lower than to the US and Spain -- Ecuador's second- and third-largest markets respectively -- where there's a greater preference for value-added shrimp products.

In the first half of 2018, average unit values to Vietnam, US, and Spain dropped significantly following the global crash in shrimp prices. 

The final chart shows the equally impressive boom in India's shrimp exports. It also shows how the country relies more on the US market. Unlike China, US consumers tend to prefer value-added shrimp products. India also exports significant quantities of shrimp to Vietnam, which undergoes value-added processing in the country and then is re-exported to European countries. Increasingly, however, more Indian shrimp is also heading to China via the Hai Phong route.

title: Editor’s recap: China show news-fest; High Liner layoffs; Marine Harvest smolt expansion under fire
content:
Tom Seaman, editorial director of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

First of all, sorry for the delay with the newsletter this week. We had some technical issues.

Louis Harkell, Matt Craze and I have all just returned from China, where Undercurrent News had a booth at the China Fisheries & Seafood Expo. 

The blog from the show was our most-read story of the week. Matt and Louis also snagged a scoop on arrests linked to the smuggling route for shrimp into China via Hai Phong, a port in the north of Vietnam. More than 20 people linked to the trade were arrested last month, which meant shrimp entering the Chinese market through the port has been heavily restricted. 

“The trade has slowed down to a trickle,” said the owner of a large Latin American exporter on the first day of the show. “Before it was a highway.”

Ecuador’s main traders, however, were breathing easier by the end of the week. Rumors that China’s main buyers wouldn’t attend the seafood expo in fear of reprisals after the arrests turned out to be false, said one major exporter who sold 300 containers of shrimp in two days.

“Demand is huge,” a senior executive of the major exporter said. “Everyone is placing orders for main ports.”

"Main ports" is the term used for shrimp directly to the major ports of the Chinese mainland, where taxes are applied. While Ecuador has a trade agreement in place to sell to China, paying an import tariff, other producers, such as Venezuela, have no trade agreement in place and rely totally on the Hai Phong conduit to access the Chinese market.

Another main trader for one of Ecuador’s shrimp exporters also confirmed that orders ahead of the Chinese New Year (celebrated in February) have been considerable, even if more shrimp is being sold directly to China than through the Vietnamese trade route.

“The thing is that the market wants the product, and more than ever,” the trader said. “You just put it on a ship and receive the money.”

One exporter speculated that many of the arrests were not real. “One of our customers just rang us and told us that they are fine, and they only had their computer taken away from them.”

Zhanjiang Guolian Aquatic Products’ is always a company to watch at the show and has big plans for the country's domestic market. The company's new shrimp plant in Zhanjiang is set for a February opening, deputy general manager Wu Liqing told Louis, at an event the company organized. 

The Zhanjiang-based plant will do deep-processing of mainly shrimp and have an annual production capacity of 50,000 metric tons of finished products, said Wu. Back when Louis visited the plant in September 2017, workers were still digging foundations. More recent photos show the main processing building is now complete. 

Once the plant opens Guolian’s three existing plants in Zhanjiang will be closed. The new plant will offer a broader product range and be installed with labor-saving production equipment. The plant will employ about 1,000 workers.

“In China, to reduce labor costs in kitchens and canteens, more and more restaurants and foodservice operators want pre-prepared meals and finished products,” said Wu.

The firm’s chairman Li Zhong has said the plant is part of a wider strategy to re-orientate the company’s sales from exports towards the domestic market.

Li also told me the company sees crayfish as being just as important as shrimp in the future. 

The company is in the midst of a major crayfish processing and farming expansion plan, he told me. 

“We want to control the whole value-chain for crayfish and dominate the market,” he said. 

The company is promoting crayfish at the show and opened a new plant in Wuhan province earlier this year, Li said. 

Guolian’s crayfish plant has a capacity of up to 20,000t, with the company currently at around 10,000t, he said. 

Then, Guolian plans to farm up to 20,000t of crayfish in its own farms, said Li. The company is planning a push on crayfish, in online and offline retail, and foodservice.

The trade war between the US and China was a big talking point at the show, of course. 

Rob Hallion, CEO of frozen importer Crocker & Winsor Seafoods, told me the impact of the 10% tariffs from the US on some seafood products from China aren’t going to be felt until 2019, however. 

I chatted with Hallion at the Groundfish Forum in London in October, then again at the China show. 

The 10% tariffs went into play on Sept 24 and will go to 25% on Jan. 1, 2019, unless the US administration of Donald Trump and China’s government, led by Xi Jinping, reach an agreement before. However, it will be Q1, at the earliest, before the market feels the effect, Hallion told me. 

“One of the things we are kidding ourselves about is the timing of the impact of these tariffs. It’s going to take six-to-12 months for the full financial impact to be shown, as people have inventories,” he said. “I may base my prices on replacement costs, but I can’t bring up all my prices in one go, that’s not the way we operate. I don’t see the impact being felt until Q1 of 2019 and then it remains to be seen if people chose seafood, or not.”

However, the tariffs are not putting off Trident Seafoods, the largest vertically integrated seafood firm in the US, in its China plans. 

Trident plans to launch its well-known “The Ultimate Fish Stick” product in the Chinese market in the future, despite the 25% tariffs on US fish for sale to the domestic market in the country. 

The company already has a branded pollock fish finger product in Chinese retailer Yonghui Superstores, which is being produced in its joint venture plant in Weihai, Jeff Welbourn, who heads up Trident’s China business, told me. 

“The Ultimate Fish Stick is coming,” he said. The product already in Chinese retail is a single-frozen fish stick, but with a different breading formulation and flavor to the “ultimate” variety. 

Trident also displayed its frozen, skin-pack range using Alaska raw material at the show again. The range, which includes cod, pollock, salmon and sablefish products, was launched at the 2017 China show. 

Welbourn declined to go into detail on how the 25% tariffs are impacting sales. “Trident, and the Alaskan industry generally, are in China for the long-haul,” he said. 

Norway, China trade 

While trade between the US and China is shakey, Norway and its salmon farmers are very much back in favor. 

Cui He, the head of the China Aquatic Product Processing and Marketing Alliance, said he hopes to see a free trade agreement (FTA) with Norway soon. 

He said he hopes relations with Norway and China will be “deepened and further expanded” in the future. “We have a free trade agreement with Iceland and we hope will soon sign one with Norway. In the near future, we will have a result,” he said, during the Sino-Nordic Seafood Summit, held during the China expo. 

An FTA with Norway and an “ever more open China” would be a “win-win” for cooperation on aquaculture, seafood trade, processing and equipment, said He. 

On Nov. 6, at an event organized by the Norwegian Seafood Council before the start of the show, Gustav Solvang, of the Norwegian embassy in Beijing, China’s capital, said the next round of FTA talks will be after Christmas in Oslo. The aim is to conclude an FTA in 2019. 

“We hope by next autumn.” Zero tariffs on seafood are an aim for Norway, he said. This will mean more seafood going to China, at lower prices, said Solvang.

The possible size of the China market was also discussed at the summit. China will almost certainly import more than 200,000t of salmon by 2025, even as much as 400,000t, if the supply side is there to support this, said one panelist. 

High Liner layoffs 

It wasn't just news from China getting you clicking, the issues for High Liner Foods were also one of our most-read. Jason Smith, our Americas editor, who is now on his way to Australia for his honeymoon, reported on layoffs at the company. 

The new CEO, Rod Hepponstall, had told me this was coming in an interview at the Groundfish Forum a few weeks ago, which we ran earlier last week. 

High Liner Foods is continuing to struggle with falling sales volumes and earnings, which it said will continue to "face pressure" in coming quarters, he said. 

That realignment has seen 14% of its salaried workforce cut, with around 80 positions affected, a company spokeswoman told Jason. The Lunenberg, Novia Scotia company will take a $4.5m restructuring charge associated with the layoffs, it said. 

Hepponstall, a potato sector veteran who previously told me he believes the seafood industry has a lot to learn from other proteins, said in a press release that the firm's "disappointing" results reinforce "the need to realign the business".

"We started this process in July, shortly after I joined the company, focusing first on our executive realignment and have moved quickly to realign the rest of the organization. It has required some difficult decisions and we thank departing employees for their contributions to High Liner. We now have an integrated and appropriate structure that will enable us to execute on our plans to re-position the business so that we can unlock our true potential moving forward."

Marine Harvest’s 2.2m smolt expansion in Newfoundland under fire

Jason Huffman, our Americas reporter based on the US east coast, got an interesting scoop on Marine Harvest's expansion plans in Atlantic Canada. 

Andrew Parsons, the minister of Newfoundland & Labrador’s Department of Municipal Affairs and Environment, has given Northern Harvest Sea Farms (NHSF), a recently acquired division of Marine Harvest, much more than a green light to increase by 2.2m annually -- nearly 50% -- the amount of Atlantic salmon smolt that it can produce at its Indian Head Hatchery, argue a coalition of 10 wild salmon advocates, environmental groups and individuals.

Rather, it's an attempt by the Canadian provincial government official to keep all red tape to a minimum while allowing a significant expansion by the Norwegian salmon giant in the region, including the building of at least four new farms, they say.  

At least that's the case the attorneys at Ecojustice make in their 10-page letter sent Monday to Parsons, asking him to reconsider his approval in early September of a request by Marine Harvest to expand production at its smolt facility, near Stephenville, from 4.5 million fish per year to 6.7m. 

“Your decision to release the hatchery expansion project from further environmental assessment under the [Environmental Protection Act] is unlawful and must be set aside,” the letter warns Parsons. “The hatchery expansion was improperly registered... as you did not require the proponent to register the entire undertaking. To be properly scoped and registered, the undertaking must include not only the hatchery expansion itself, but also the associated increase in salmon smolt transferred to open net pens and farmed in the province’s coastal waters.”

Aker Biomarine’s new $118m vessel set for next Antarctic krill fishing season

A new state-of-the-art $118m vessel will take to the wild and inhospitable waters of the Antarctic Ocean when it departs for the 2019 krill fishing season from a shipyard in Norway.

Antarctic Endurance will be a floating showcase of “shipbuilding expertise, sustainable harvesting technology and energy efficiency” when it departs for its maiden voyage to Antarctica, Eldar Vindvik -- project manager at Norwegian firm Aker Biomarine -- told Louis. 

Ordered back in 2017, Antarctic Endurance is being built by Norwegian shipbuilder Vard Brattvag at a cost of NOK 1 billion, or just over $118m.

"The vessel has been designed and equipped in order to address the numerous challenges of Antarctic krill harvesting operations,” said Vindvik, who confirmed the vessel would be ready to start fishing krill next season, which runs from December to September. 

Skretting to cease UK production ‘due to market overcapacity’

Skretting announced on Tuesday that it has started a process of consulting with employees, a potential prelude to layoffs, with a view to ceasing production in the UK at the end of April 2019, Neil Ramsden, our deputy editor, reported last week. 

The company said the move is aimed at reducing overcapacity in the highly competitive salmon feed market and to better utilize its existing production facilities in Europe. But it stressed that it has no plans to stop production in other markets and will continue to pursue its firmly established growth strategy.

“Unfortunately, we are experiencing unsustainable market conditions in the UK. With a new large feed plant becoming operational in Scotland early 2019, the total feed capacity in the region is expected to exceed the total market by more than 50%. This is driving down prices, leading to an unsustainable commercial environment”, said Therese Log Bergjord, Skretting's CEO.

“We have therefore made the decision to start consulting with our employees on a proposal to cease feed production in the UK”.

Ocean Phoenix owner confirms Pacific Glacier purchase in works after hull repainted

A deal is indeed in the works for US pollock catcher Glacier Fish Company to sell its 84-meter factory trawler Pacific Glacier to the owner of Ocean Phoenix but the deal has not yet closed, a source confirmed to our Jason Smith. 

In an email to Jason, after I reported on the planned sale of the vessel earlier in the week, Joe Bersch, general manager of Premier Pacific Seafoods, confirmed that a deal is being pursued.

"The name is indeed changed reflecting the expectation of closing a deal between Phoenix Processor Limited Partnership, (not Premier Pacific Seafoods) and Glacier," he wrote, declining to comment further. 

The plan to offload Pacific Glacier comes as the Norton Sound Economic Development Corporation (NSEDC) reportedly plans to lease a chunk of community development quota (CDQ), which was previously fished by Glacier, to American Seafoods Group, sources told me. 

NSEDC, which owns 25% of Glacier, which is also a quarter owned by Japan’s Nippon Suisan Kaisha, the world's second-biggest seafood firm by sales, is said to be planning to lease around 30,000t of quota to American Seafoods next year, sources said. 

The switch in the Norton Sound quota would then see Premier Pacific, which also has Japanese ownership, from Maruha Nichiro, the world’s largest seafood company, take control of Pacific Glacier in 2019, sources said. However, if the plan is for this to happen -- if the deal closes -- for A season or B season. 

The move will mean Premier Pacific -- which also operates Excellence -- will be able to produce pollock fillet blocks, for which prices are firming fast, as well as surimi and headed-and-gutted (H&G) fish, sources said. Both Ocean Phoenix and Excellence can only produce surimi, H&G and mince, as well as roe and fishmeal and oil. 

This will then mean Glacier is able to consolidate its quota onto the 114m Alaska Ocean, the largest catcher-processor in the US fleet.

title: Ecuador’s shrimp exporters enjoy ‘phew’ moment as orders rush in at China show
content:
The global shrimp market started this week in a panic as news emerged of widescale arrests of Chinese traders linked to smuggling through the port of Hai Phong in northern Vietnam.

Ecuador’s main traders, however, were breathing easier by the end of the week. Rumors that China’s main buyers wouldn’t attend the China seafood expo in fear of reprisals after the arrests turned out to be false, said one major exporter who sold 300 containers of shrimp in two days.

“Demand is huge,” a senior executive of the major exporter said. “Everyone is placing orders for main ports.”

Main port is the term used for shrimp directly to the major ports of the Chinese mainland, where taxes are applied. While Ecuador has a trade agreement in place to sell to China, paying an import tariff. Other producers, such as Venezuela, have no trade agreement in place and rely totally on the Hai Phong conduit to access the Chinese market.

Another main trader for one of Ecuador’s shrimp exporters also confirmed that orders ahead of the Chinese New Year (celebrated in February) have been considerable, even if more shrimp is being sold directly to China than through the Vietnamese trade route.

“The thing is, that the market wants the product, and more than ever,” the trader said. “You just put it on a ship and receive the money.”

One exporter speculated that many of the arrests were not real. “One of our customers just rang us and told us that they are fine, and they only had their computer taken away from them.”

If the week started with a climate of panic, nerves were settled when top Chinese producer and exporter Zhanjiang Guolian Aquatic Products gave an optimistic appraisal of Chinese demand.

World’s 100 Largest Seafood Companies 2018
View report

Inviting a who’s who of the global shrimp industry to a dinner and presentation on Nov. 7, Guolian said global shrimp demand will rise to 6.5 million metric tons by 2025, compared with 5.2m metric tons in 2020 and 4.5m metric tons in 2017. The implies an annual compound growth rate of 4.75% a year, said deputy CEO Wu Liqing.

“Most Chinese companies think that demand is going to grow significantly because of the consolidation of the middle class,’ said Johnny Adum, the chief executive officer of Ecuadorian processing company Proexpo. “They prefer seafood to other protein classes. The concern of the Chinese is if they can supply this demand.”

There’s no question that China loves shrimp. They are found live in tanks, on menus everywhere and even sold individually wrapped and dried like candy. China will need all producing regions to supply projected massive demand from the world’s most populous nation, Guolian’s Wu said.

For sure, a significant chunk of China’s shrimp imports is destined for a major processing industry that re-exports shrimp out of Asia to other continents such as the United States. In that regard, the shrimp industry is wary of the full implications of the trade between China and the United States, Proexpo’s Adum said.

Right now, there is plenty of supply in the market. Southeast Asian supplies are increasing as producers overcome the presence of early mortality syndrome. Latin American farmers in Mexico and Central America also seem to have overcome supply issues related to disease, another senior industry executive said.

Ecuador as a country-of-origin gets chosen over shrimp from other producing countries, several industry executives said. The Chinese market for Ecuadorian shrimp has grown from almost nothing in the past decade to buy 70% of total exports, a senior executive said. With the scale of China’s economic development and prosperity, there’s no reason to doubt that this will continue, he said.

title: China spooks shrimp market with arrests linked to Vietnamese trade route
content:
QINGDAO, China -- Uncertainty shrouds a shrimp market entering the negotiation period for the Chinese New Year, as China arrests more than 20 people linked to Vietnamese trade.

Shrimp entering the Chinese market through the northern port of Hai Phong has been heavily restricted since the wave of arrests, which occurred late last month, industry sources told Undercurrent News at the China expo 2018 show in Qingdao, China. The arrests are allegedly linked to the labeling of shrimp of foreign origin. Chinese authorities have ordered that all shrimp crossing the border be marked with a Vietnam country-of-origin label.

“The trade has slowed down to a trickle,” said an owner of a large Latin American exporter. “Before it was a highway.”

Many producers from Latin America and other Asian countries deliver shrimp to the traders in the northern Vietnamese port of Hai Phong and sell it to the Chinese market. Ecuador, for example, can sell directly to the Chinese market and pay a tariff. Ecuadorians usually earn more profits by selling through Hai Phong as Vietnamese traders assume the risk of the resale.

Other countries such as Venezuela have no trade agreement in place and rely totally on Vietnam for access to the Chinese market. Right now, the global shrimp market is very well supplied as Ecuador and India have increased production this year.

Every producing region in the world is currently increasing supply and global output is expected to reach 5 million metric tons by 2020, an 18% increase on current capacity, according a survey compiled by the Global Aquaculture Alliance which was revealed at the Global Outlook for Aquaculture Leadership, or GOAL, conference in Guayaquil, Ecuador in September.

“There is shrimp literally everywhere,” one CEO of an Ecuadorian exporter at the China expo.

At least three officials from Ecuadorian companies said prices are trading at about $6.10 a kilogram for 40/50 counts. One trader said prices were trading in a range between $6.10/kg-$6.20/kg. Prices for 40-50 were around $7.35/kg a year ago. The only companies from Ecuador that are making money currently are those that sell value-added products and have relationships with major wholesalers and retailers.

Another Ecuadorian trader suggested that the tremor in the Vietnamese could be an opening gambit for price negotiations for shipments that enter China ahead of the Chinese New Year, to be celebrated in February.

Some exporters have long speculated that Chinese authorities turn a blind eye to shrimp shipments using the Hai Phong conduit when the market is short of supply and boosts inspections when produce is plentiful in the domestic market.

The longer negotiations go on, Ecuador’s shrimp farmers have to contend with the heightened anxiety of competing with banana and mango exporters for container space out of Guayaquil towards the end of the year.

China arrests

Chinese police and customs officials raided business premises in Zhanjiang, Nanning, Shanghai, Nanjing, Tianjin, Qingdao, and Shenyang, on Oct. 31, arresting 25, according to a statement by China’s General Customs Administration. About 1,400 metric tons of frozen seafood were inspected and cross-checked with supply contracts and import documentation, according to the statement.

“Luckily it wasn’t our clients,” one Ecuadorian trader said. “We understand that product is still going through Hai Phong.”

Anti-smuggling operations have become more frequent since a large wave of arrests at the beginning of the year. Authorities broke down a salmon smuggling ring said to be worth $100 million in late March.

However, still, huge volumes of shrimp from Ecuador enter China through Vietnam, with 105,233t of Ecuadorian shrimp exported to the Southeast Asian country in the first six months of this year.

One Indian producer consulted by Undercurrent said it preferred to sell shrimp to China directly, paying a tariff up front, or diverting product to the Russian market.

“Hai Phong is risky,” the official from the Indian company said. “We only sell if they pay cash up front.

title: WWF: Spanish tuna smuggling case exposes illegal fishing in Europe
content:
The arrest of almost 80 people involved in an illegal bluefin tuna trading ring "exposes the extent of illegal fishing and trade that continues to take place in European waters, despite European legislative measures that seek to curb these activities," the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) has said.

The arrests in Spain were carried out following a Europol investigation uncovering an illegal trade of tuna fished in Italy and Malta. The operation involved a large network of fishing companies and distributors, including one of Europe’s biggest seafood farming companies, Spain's Ricardo Fuentes and Sons Group.

“This level of blackfish and black money occurring on the European market in 2018 contravenes the leadership role that the EU is taking in the global fight against illegal fishing. Only through digitization of records to trace where fish were caught can we remove the legal loopholes and ensure each member state takes their responsibilities seriously to prevent more illegal fish entering the EU market. Without transparency on where fish were caught and how they were transported within Europe we won’t achieve a legal seafood market and sustainable fisheries governance in Europe," said Samantha Burgess, head of marine policy at WWF.

WWF stressed the European Parliament and Council "must now ensure that the revision of the EU control system effectively encourages transparency and enforces sustainable fisheries governance and seafood consumption in all EU countries".

The international investigation also provides crucial information ahead of the meeting of the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas taking place on Nov. 12-19 in Croatia, where fishing nations and the EU will agree on new international measures to manage east Atlantic and Mediterranean bluefin tuna, WWF said.

title: EU police arrest 79 in Spain as illegal tuna market dismantled
content:
European Union law enforcement agency Europol has coordinated an international operation with authorities from France, Italy, Malta, Spain and Portugal to arrest 79 individuals for their alleged involvement in Europe’s illegal bluefin tuna market, Euro Weekly News reported.

Operation Tarantelo was launched when the Spanish Guardia Civil noted irregularities involving bluefin tuna fishing in the Mediterranean Sea.

Bluefin tuna shipments were being smuggled into Spain through the French harbors after being caught in Italian and Maltese waters.

Documents from legal fishing and authorized farms were used to illegally import the fish into Spain, where insufficient inspections failed to detect the bluefin.

Unauthorized catches were also found in Spanish waters, with smugglers transporting the illegal fish in false bottoms under the deck of a vessel.

Several poisoning cases have been attributed to the unsanitary conditions in which the fish are stored when smuggled into Spain.

In total, estimated profits for 2018 amounted to over €12 million, as it is believed the illegal market has been smuggling 2,500 metric tons per year.

title: Orlov: Tugushev claim he kept Norebo shares while Russian gov’t official, then in prison ‘absurd’
content:
Alexander Tugushev's claim he retained a third of what is now Russia’s largest fishing company, Norebo Holding, while a government official, and then in prison for fraud, is “absurd”, said a spokesman for Vitaly Orlov, the company’s CEO.

Tugushev, one of three founders of Norebo, along with Orlov and Magnus Roth, is locked in a bitter legal battle in the UK’s High Court. He claims he’s owed at least $350 million for what he says is his third in the company, which is valued at over $1.5 billion, according to a statement from a spokesperson for Tugushev. This comes after the Norebo offices in Russia were raided by armed officials, in connection to another legal action previously filed by Tugushev.

Norebo offices raided by armed officials as Orlov, Tugushev fight intensifies

Before assuming office in 2003 as deputy chief of the fisheries department of the Russian fisheries ministry, Tugushev, “as an official should [have], completely divested his share in several fishing companies”, said the statement from Orlov’s spokesman, sent to Undercurrent News.

After this, Tugushev ended up being sentenced for bribery, relating to fisheries quotas.

Tugushev references this in the claim document filed in the London lawsuit, where he claims to have retained his shareholding and interest in Norebo after the government appointment on Sept. 22, 2003.

Not even a year into this position, on June 2, 2004, Tugushev was arrested on allegations of fraud and ultimately sentenced to six years' imprisonment, the claim document states. Tugushev “denies those charges and believes them to have been politically motivated”, the claim states, without giving more information.

According to a Feb. 15, 2007 article from RIA Novosti, translated to English by Sputnik News, Tugushev and three other defendants were found guilty of extorting $3.7m from the management of a fishing company based in the Pacific port of Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky to issue illegal fishing quotas in 2003.

However, the court cleared Tugushev of bribery charges. When he was released on Dec. 2, 2009, he returned to work for Norebo, according to the claim.

“Tugushev was once my friend, but prison changed him. In many respects, I do not recognize the person with whom I once had a joint business,” reads a comment attributed to Orlov himself in the statement sent to Undercurrent.

Orlov is challenging the lawsuit’s location in London and also a court order to freeze bank accounts and assets up to $350m, including his shares in the Norebo companies in the UK and Hong Kong.

Norebo CEO Orlov will contest $350m asset freeze, UK location of Tugushev lawsuit

“This is a dispute between two citizens of the Russian Federation, and its subject is a Russian enterprise that works with a Russian strategic asset… Mr. Orlov will resolutely challenge the jurisdiction of English courts, as well as a court order to freeze bank accounts,” reads the statement from Orlov’s spokesman.

London is not the place where this dispute should be resolved, especially since there are still processes with Russian law enforcement agencies, he said.

However, the statement from Tugushev’s spokesperson highlights that Orlov has “significant business interests in the UK and a substantial property in London”. Norebo “is a registered company in the UK and owns offices in Maidenhead”, the statement, sent to Undercurrent, adds. Norebo “supplies up to one in five cod eaten in the UK”, according to the statement.

The statement from Tugushev’s spokesperson came after a high court hearing which was hailed as a victory by the accuser. Orlov’s spokesman dismissed this, however. 

“The High Court’s decision marks another positive step in my battle to regain the shares in the Norebo Group that were illegally taken from me. I am very proud of what was achieved during my 17 years with the Norebo Group, and refuse to be deprived of these achievements by Mr Orlov. I will continue to fight for my interest in the company and right the wrongs perpetrated by my former business partner,” said Tugushev, in the statement.

On Sept. 19, the court rejected Orlov’s attempt to keep the worldwide freezing order (WFO) worth $350m “under wraps”, according to the statement from Tugushev.

‘Three of us have built it’; Tugushev’s take on rise of $1.5bn fishing giant Norebo

Orlov’s legal team had argued Tugushev should not be able to notify relevant third parties of the WFO without Orlov’s consent or the permission of the court, “rendering the order ineffective in practice”, according to the statement. The judge, however, rejected Orlov’s “proposed interpretation of the WFO, giving teeth to the order”.

The court also agreed with Tugushev’s legal team that the application by Orlov to rely on the privilege against self-incrimination should be expedited, so as not to impede Tugushev’s attempts to enforce the WFO in other jurisdictions, such as Russia, the statement reads. 

A hearing on this is expected to take place in November. Orlov has claimed the privilege against self-incrimination to avoid full disclosure of his assets, citing a criminal investigation in Russia and possible money laundering proceedings.

The spokesman for Orlov dismissed the statement, however.

“To describe this as a significant legal victory is absurd,” he said.

The hearing was mainly to clarify an earlier judgment, which the judge recognized was open to interpretation, he said.

“Someone has attempted to dress up day-to-day administrative business of the courts with inaccurate and unjustified hyperbole. This hearing represented an early step in Mr. Orlov’s challenge to the jurisdiction of the English courts and the continuation of the freezing order, challenges which he intends to pursue vigorously,” he told Undercurrent.

Armed raids 

This comes as armed officials raided the Murmansk offices of Norebo a few weeks ago. 

A statement from the company’s Sergey Sennikov, sent to Undercurrent in early October, confirmed the raid, which he alleged was “orchestrated by unscrupulous, criminal elements”.

Deadline nears for Norebo CEO to challenge $350m freezing order in bitter shareholder court battle

"The raids to which Norebo has been subjected were disruptive -- as they were clearly intended to be -- but they also damaged property and placed lives at risk. Although we have been able to clear up and we are now getting on with business as usual, at the time it was a deeply unsettling experience for all concerned. For example, men with guns broke down doors and forced employees to lie on the floor,” said Sennikov, in the statement sent to Undercurrent.

"All those responsible for the raid have much to answer for. Coercive tactics have no part in business nor in any law-abiding community. There must be proper respect for the law, including Norebo and its employees,” he said. “The raiders will fail. Norebo group will not be intimidated by criminals.”

A spokesperson for Tugushev said he has no connection to the authorities who carried out the raid.

In 2016, Tugushev made a criminal complaint to the Russian authorities against Orlov “for large-scale fraud”, the spokesperson told Undercurrent.

“Since that time, the complaint has been dealt with by the appropriate government authorities only, who (as reported) recently undertook a raid as part of their investigations,” the spokesperson said. Tugushev “has no connection to the investigation authorities and will continue to fight for his interest” in Norebo in the court.

title: Spanish vessel arrested off Gabon for shark finning
content:
A Spain-linked vessel has been caught fishing sharks off the coast of Gabon, despite being licensed to fish tuna, according to environmental campaign group Sea Shepherd. 

On Sept. 22, local authorities from the Central African island state of Sao Tome and Príncipe boarded the Senegalese-flagged, but Spanish-linked, long-line fishing vessel Vema, in a joint operation with Sea Shepherd and Gabonese law enforcement officers for operation "Albacore III".

Although the long-liner was licensed to fish for tuna and similar species, inspections carried out by Sao Tomean authorities working on board the Sea Shepherd vessel Bob Barker revealed their fish holds were solely filled with sharks -- predominately blue sharks that are classified as "near-threatened" by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.

Fishing line tracers (or snoods), which are the monofilament segments that support the fishing hooks, were reinforced with steel wire, thereby underlining the suspicion that the targeted species of the Vema was mainly sharks, not tuna, Sea Shephard said. Steel snoods are used to prevent sharks from biting through the fishing line to escape.

“Given how sensitive shark species are to overfishing, coupled with the fact that 15% of shark species in the Atlantic are now endangered, it is alarming that industrial fishing vessels, many from Europe, continue to massacre sharks under the guise of tuna licenses,” said Sea Shepherd director of campaigns Peter Hammarstedt.
