title: Editor’s recap: US cuts salmon fillets from China tariffs; Tesco shrimp shift; Concern over SHIV
content:
Tom Seaman, editorial director of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

On Friday, just as Louis Harkell and I were about to leave the office in London, Hu Luyi, who runs our WeChat platform in China, passed on a tip that the US had removed Pacific salmon fillets from the list of product for which tariffs will apply.

According to the notice published Sept. 28 on the Federal Register, the harmonized system (HS) codes for Pacific salmon fillets, 030.481.10 and 03.048.150, have been removed from the list of products from China Donald Trump's US government will put tariffs on. 

This amendment went into play at 12.01 a.m., on Sept. 24, according to the Federal Register. 

This comes after, on Sept. 17, the US Trade Representative excluded frozen fillets of Alaska pollock and cod from its final list of products to be hit with 10% tariffs, which went into play on Sept. 24. They will go to 25% on Jan. 1, 2019.

This will mean that salmon, cod and pollock from Alaskan fishing companies sold to China and brought back to the US as fillets will not be hit with the tariffs. It will also mean Russian salmon, cod and pollock raw material, processed in China, is exempt, however. 

In 2017, the US imported $221.87 million under the 0304.81.50 HS code, for “Salmonidae fillets, frozen, except atlantic salmon, nesoi”, according to International Trade Commission (ITC) data. For the 0304.81.10 code, the US imported $13.85m, according to ITC.

Tesco shrimp contract shift from Blue Earth to Seachill

On Sept. 25, I broke a big UK retail contract move, with Seachill UK to take on the £50m Tesco chilled shrimp supply at short notice, from Blue Earth Foods.

Blue Earth, a Redditch-based processor backed by Thailand’s Seafresh Industry, is said to be exiting the contract on “mutual consent” with Tesco, one source said.

This means Grimsby-based Seachill, the retailer’s chilled salmon and coated and natural whitefish processor, now owned by Tesco meat packer Hilton Food Group, will take on the business sometime in October, sources said. The contract covers all chilled shrimp in Tesco, including cooked and raw warmwater and coldwater products.

The circumstances around Blue Earth exiting a contract that makes up around half its business at such short notice are unclear, but they are said to have nothing to do with product quality issues, sources said.

SHIV in southeast asia

Jason Smith, our Americas editor, and Neil Ramsden, our assistant editor, were in Guayaquil, Ecuador last week for Global Aquaculture Alliance’s annual Global Outlook on Aquaculture Leadership (GOAL) conference, keeping an epic live blog ticking over. 

During GOAL, Loc Tran, founder of the ShrimpVet Laboratory, said that scientists suspect that shrimp hemocyte iridescent virus (SHIV) has arrived in Southeast Asia.

In an Oct. 1 phone interview with Undercurrent, George Chamberlain, president of the Global Aquaculture Alliance, said that SHIV has been detected in southern China and Thailand at "a very low prevalence". 

"We have not yet detected it in Vietnam,” he said.

During the recent Aquaculture Roundtable Series, or TARS, conference, held this year in Chang Mai, Thailand, Robins McIntosh, of Thai agribusiness giant Charoen Pokphand Foods (CP Foods), had said SHIV is spreading in China and is a "killer".

Tran noted shrimp farmers across Asia are already hurting from low sales prices, and the fact that bacterial disease is pushing production costs up does not bode well, he said.

He also said biosecurity, functional feeds, and replacing live feed for broodstock to prevent shrimp disease "are vital", pointing at a decline in survival rates in India. 

“In India now, survival rates are maybe 60%. They were much higher. This is mostly due to bacterial disease," he said.

GOAL shrimp outlook

The GOAL shrimp survey is a useful benchmark for supply on shrimp and farmed whitefish, although it tends to be far more bullish on Chinese production than the annual TARS conference.

According to the GOAL forecast, global shrimp production will reach as much as 5m metric tons by 2020 if the industry achieves an 18% growth rate as expected, Jason reported.

James Anderson, a University of Florida seafood economist, said that global supply is expected to rise some 5.5% from 2017 to 2018, speaking during GOAL 2018 in Guayaquil, Ecuador. 

"Between 2017 and 2020 the expectation is pretty bullish, 5.7% per year on average and that results in an expected increase in supply of shrimp globally of 18% by 2020. To me that's a big deal. That's a lot of shrimp because it's already a gigantic industry. Which really means there's got to be some effort in taking some risk out of this business and developing some market solutions to do a more creative job in marketing," he said. 

Anderson previously predicted that global farmed vannamei production would reach some 4.5m metric tons in 2018.

"Every region is expecting an upturn from 2017 to 2018," he said. That news, however, comes as the industry has suffered of late with an "oversupply" situation that has caused global prices to drop. Observers such as Rabobank have predicted that lower prices could be here to stay.

Jason also delved deeper into the forecasts by country, which suggest Vietnam shrimp output will overtake India, with Indonesia and Ecuador also growing fast.

Ecuador, Indonesia, and Vietnam are expected to reach production levels of 570,000t, 600,000t, and 700,000t, respectively, by 2020. This, according to the forecast presented at GOAL by Anderson, would take Vietnam well past Indian and Indonesian levels. 

India -- which has been the growth success story in shrimp farming over the past few years and is aiming to produce 1m metric tons -- will remain around 600,000t until 2020, according to the forecast. 

"Production in India increased substantially through 2017 but it is expected to remain stable during 2017-2020," said Anderson. A drop in 2018 Indian production, driven by low prices and disease problems, was also forecast at the recent TARS conference.

The GOAL forecast predicts that, in 2018, the output for Ecuador, Indonesia and Vietnam will reach nearly 500,000t, 550,000t, and 600,000t, respectively, with India just under 600,000t. 

The planned global output expansion extends to China, but growth there is predicted to reach just 1.3m metric tons by 2020, still far below the 2012 level of nearly 1.6m metric tons that the country produced before the early mortality syndrome crisis. 

For China, the GOAL forecast is dramatically different to the level given by Robins McIntosh, of Thai agribusiness giant Charoen Pokphand Foods (CP Foods), during the recent TARS conference. 

Virginia seafood dealer found guilty of multi-million dollar crabmeat fraud

Daniel Gibson, who has joined us as an editorial assistant, put together a nice summary of a big seafood fraud in the US.

James Casey, the owner and president of Virginia-based processor Casey’s Seafood, pleaded guilty in a federal court on Sept. 26 to deliberately mislabeling millions of dollars of foreign crab meat as US Atlantic blue crab.

Casey conspired to replace Atlantic blue crab with crab meat from Indonesia, China, Thailand, Vietnam, and Central and South America, said US attorney G. Zachary Terwilliger for the eastern district of Virginia, in a press release.

“Casey falsely labeled nearly 400,000 pounds of crab meat with a retail value in the millions of dollars. This fraud causes real financial harm to economies here in the region, and threatens to tarnish the good name of the watermen who have worked these waters for generations.”

Casey admitted to working with other conspirators to falsely labeling more than 183t of crab meat, which they then proceeded to sell to grocery stores and independent retailers.

Significant declines in Atlantic blue crab harvests began in 2010 and have made the purchase of live specimens increasingly expensive. Given the labor-intensive process of picking meat from live-harvested crabs, it has become ever more difficult for processors like Casey’s to profit from their sale.

As part of his guilty plea, Casey admitted that, because of this decline, he and his company were unable to process sufficient quantities of Atlantic blue crab to meet customer demands. To make up the shortfall, the co-conspirators used foreign crab meat to fulfill customer orders.

Bakkafrost loses 750,000 fish in mystery incident

Just as he’d landed in Guayaquil for GOAL, Neil shipped out an interesting breaking news story on Bakkafrost, as the Faroese salmon farmer revealed it lost 750,000 individuals in an incident at its A-81 Kolbanagjogv site on Sept. 20, 2018.

The fish were young, at around 500 grams each, and the total mortalities occurred within just a "couple of hours", the firm said. They were only put to sea between June and August.

"It has not been possible to confirm the cause of the incident, but algae phaeocystis, pseudo-nitzscia, and heterosigma were registered in the sea at farming site A-81 Kolbanagjogv on Sept. 20, and the algae are suspected to have caused the mortality incident," Bakkafrost said.

The company will have finished removing all the dead fish from the sea at the site on Sept. 24, and nothing abnormal has been registered since Sept. 20, it said. "Bakkafrost has people monitoring the situation closely at farming site A-81 Kolbanagjogv. The fish at [the site] are insured."

Thai Union plans to sell or close UK smoked salmon ops

On Sept. 27, Thai Union Group announced it plans to sell or close its UK smoked salmon processing operation, the Edinburgh Salmon Company (ESCo).

“Despite [the] ongoing review, significant investment and structural changes, ESCo continues to suffer heavy losses as a result of highly challenging market conditions and industry trends,” said a press release from Europeenne de la Mer, a subsidiary of Thai Union. 

Thai Union, one of the largest seafood companies in the world, will “pursue and explore all viable divestment opportunities in an attempt to avoid, reduce, and/or mitigate the potential impacts upon its valued employees”, it said.

Following the announcement to employees, the company has started the process of appointing elected workplace representatives; after which a 45-day consultation will begin.

In July, ESCo -- which Thai Union acquired as part of a deal for Merinvest, the parent of Meralliance in France -- reported a loss of £5.2m, compared to £6.9m the year before. 

The company said it lost two "major customers" last year, resulting in the loss of "approximately 1.4m [metric tons] year-on-year".

Although ESCo did not name the customers, Young’s Seafood has won contracts with sandwhich chain Pret a Manger and retailer Asda from the Thai Union-owned firm.

US live lobster ‘abundant’ in China

Chinese importers of live American lobster recently told industry media there was an "abundance" of US lobster on the market which was transshipped from Canada to avoid Chinese tariffs of 25%, Louis, our reporter focused on Asia, reported last week.

According to a report dated Sept. 8 by Seafood Guide, a Chinese industry publication, Chinese importers said large quantities of small-sized soft shell lobster -- which is typically harvested by US fishermen from mid-summer to fall -- was on the market in China, and prices were low.

"The amount of small-sized soft-shell lobster (American Boston lobster) is significant," said an importer at the time. Seafood Guide reported wholesale prices for 560-670 gram live lobster of CNY 170 per kilogram ($24.79/kg).

"But it is not easy to keep the lobster alive in tanks for very long. For importers it’s very risky,” importers said. Live prices at source were relatively high, meanwhile, exacerbating importers' problems, they said. 

"Lobster prices in Canada are ridiculous," a source at a large Chinese importer told Louis on Sept. 24. He said he'd also heard there is US product on the Chinese market which has been imported via Canada. He noted buying lobster has "been difficult this year because of the tariffs", however.

He said wholesale lobster prices in China have since increased and now are actually "too high" with demand dropping off despite mid-Autumn Festival (Sept. 22-24) and National Day (Oct. 1) celebrations. Seafood Guide also reported a more recent price jump. 

On top of possible transshipment of US live lobster through Canada, smugglers in Vietnam could also be at it to circumvent Chinese tariffs. 

Last week, China's General Administration of Customs authority said local customs officials in Dong Xing county, Guangxi province, had seized CNY 300,000 ($43,749) worth of live lobsters being smuggled into China from Vietnam.

Customs officials seized 120 cases of live lobster -- or 1.67t -- when they apprehended a wooden vessel in a local river estuary in the evening of Sept. 10. One person was arrested. 

Tariffs hit Alaska Amendment 80 fleet

US president Donald Trump's 10% tariffs are bad news for all of the US harvesters of seafood sent to China for processing, but they come at a particularly unfortunate time for the five companies with flatfish-catching vessels in Alaska’s Amendment 80 fleet, Jason Huffman, our senior reporter based on the East Coast of the US, reported last week.

Those harvesters have spent more than a combined $285m over the past six years to replace or significantly improve their 19 ships, according to Chris Woodley, executive director of the Groundfish Forum, the trade group that represents them.

Woodley told Jason that he doesn’t know how the tariffs will immediately impact his members or if any of the additional cost might make them want to hit pause on their recent recapitalization effort.

“As far as specific business arrangements with individual companies, each A80 [Amendment 80] company has got its own supply chain and its own buyers," he said. "It’s not a monolithic block. So, all we know right now is that the fish products harvested by the A80 fleet are on the list to have tariffs imposed, and that’s where we are.” 

But, he stressed, the cost will be felt. “Whenever you impose a new cost in any kind of a system, whether it's on the buyer, the seller or the producer, that cost has to get borne somewhere,” he said. “I think there are a lot of different ways that this could play out, whether that’s lower prices for us when we sell the product or a higher price paid by the consumer or somebody eats it in between.”

Among the 325,000t of different species harvested annually by the Amendment 80 fleet – nearly all of which could get more expensive soon for US consumers -- are yellowfin sole, rock sole, flathead sole, Atka mackerel, Pacific Ocean perch and Pacific cod.

In a comment letter sent to the United States Trade Representative before the agency announced its final plan for moving forward on the 10% tariffs, which graduate to 25% tariffs on Jan. 1, 2019, Woodley described how the fish caught by the Amendment 80 fleet wind up being “swept up” into the fees.

Scientists call for big cut in NE Atlantic mackerel TAC with fishing pressure ‘high’

On Sept. 28, before we broke the Pacific salmon fillet tariff story, another big story came in.

Scientists from the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (ICES) have advised a big cut in the 2019 northeast Atlantic mackerel total allowable catch (TAC) to what would be a record low, with fishing pressure high and no management plan in place. 

ICES advised a catch of no more than 318,403t in 2019, down 42% from the level of 550,948t for 2018. In 2017, ICES advised a TAC of 857,185t.

As there are no internationally agreed quotas, catches have been way above these recommended levels, however.

The unilateral quotas of countries catching the fish for 2018 amounts to 1.01m metric tons. The level ICES is recommending is the lowest ever, according to data from the group.

Concerns mount US lobster being shipped to China via Canada to avoid 25% tariffs

Vietnam is a known transshipment hub for huge quantities of seafood into China, also referred to as the ‘grey trade’, including live and fresh seafood.

Last week, Lobster Council of Canada told Undercurrent it is investigating whether exporters are sending US live lobster to China labeled as Canadian lobster, in order to avoid Chinese 25% tariffs. Geoff Irvine, executive director of the council, said he doesn’t know for sure such transshipments are taking place, but he’s concerned and plans to warn his group’s members against the behavior.

title: Editor’s recap: US move to drop pollock, cod fillets from China tariff list punishes Alaskans; Concern over lobster transshipping
content:
Tom Seaman, editorial director of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

Stories on the trade war between China and the US dominated the news agenda last week (Sept. 17-22), after we revealed on Tuesday that pollock and cod fillets have been dropped from the final list of tariffed products, which have an annual import value of around $200 billion. 

The proposed list (which you can see here), published on July 10, at the direction of US president Donald Trump, included cod and pollock fillets. However, they have been dropped by the US Trade Representative in the final list, which you can see here. The tariffs will come into play on Sept. 24 at 10%, and then go to 25% on Jan. 1, 2019.

This will mean that cod and pollock from Alaskan fishing companies which is sold to China and brought back to the US as fillets will not be hit with the tariffs. It will also mean Russian cod and pollock raw material, processed in China, would be exempt, much to the annoyance of the At-Sea Processors Association (APA). 

USTR reduced the original list of 6,031 tariff lines, first proposed on July 10, down to 5,745 full or partial lines.

One Undercurrent News source pointed out that harmonized tariff schedule, or HTS code 0304.94.90, "Alaska pollack, chilled or frozen fillets, nesoi", which means not elsewhere specified or included, is still on the list. 

According to International Trade Center (ITC) data, minimal amounts come into the US on these codes, however. 

The main HTS codes for imports of pollock off the final list are 0304755000, "Alaska pollock (theragra chalcogramma) fillets, frozen, nesoi", and 0304.751.000 (harmonized tariff schedule, or HTS, code), "Alaska pollock (theragra chalcogramma) fillets, skinned, frozen blocks weighing over 4.5 kg". In 2017, US imports of these products were worth $30.93 million and $17.20m respectively, according to ITC. 

Also off the list are the main cod codes, 0304.715.000, for frozen fillets, which were worth $288.73m in 2017, HTS code 030.471.1000, for "cod fillets, skinned, frozen blocks weighing over 4.5 kg each, to be minced, ground or cut", worth $11.25m in 2017. 

If Trump was hoping to get a pat on the back from the Alaskan pollock industry for keeping its re-processed fillets off the list of seafood products to receive additional tariffs when imported from China, he will be sadly disappointed.

Rather, thanks to some apparent confusion over the harmonized tariff codes, the administration’s exemptions appear to help the Russian pollock industry more, advises James Gilmore, the director of public affairs for the APA, one of the loudest voices for Alaska pollock producers, in an email to Jason Huffman, our senior reporter for the Americas. 

“If our interpretation is correct, Alaska pollock producers face stiff tariffs in China and Russia’s ban on US seafood imports, including Alaska pollock, remains in effect,” Gilmore said. “Meanwhile, our principal international competition—Russian pollock processed in China—enjoys tariff-free access to our domestic market.”

Gilmore's comments follow closely those made by Fedor Kirsanov, the CEO of Russian Fishery Company, one of the country's largest pollock quota holders, who told me the trade war is helping to boost his prices. 

China has retaliated against US tariffs, but seafood will be largely unaffected by its counter-measures. 

On Sept. 18, China announced it would levy new tariffs of up to 10% on imports of US goods worth $60bn, which come into play on Sept. 24.

China said the counter-measures were to "defend the legitimate rights and interests of the Chinese economy caused by the violation of international obligations by the US". Prior to the announcement in a more solemn statement, it said the US measures were "regretful". 

Among the 5,000-plus US products to be hit are smoked Pacific salmon and a type of fishmeal. No other fisheries or seafood products are affected. 

Concerns mount US lobster being shipped to China via Canada 

The Lobster Council of Canada is investigating whether exporters are sending US live lobster to China labeled as Canadian lobster, in order to avoid China’s 25% tariffs, Jason Huffman and Louis Harkell reported. 

Geoff Irvine, executive director of the council, told Jason so far he doesn’t know for sure such transshipments are taking place, but he’s concerned and plans to warn his group’s members against the behavior.

"The country of origin rules for Canada and the US are quite clear,” Irvine said. “If a live lobster came from America it must be called a product of the US, even if it goes out of a Canadian airport. Similarly, if a Canadian lobster goes out of a US airport, it is still a Canadian lobster.

"We are very proud of our brand and we don't want any other lobster to be sold under that brand."

Transshipment of US lobster to China via Canada has appeared a risk ever since the Chinese government, on July 6, slapped tariffs of 25% on some $32bn worth of US goods, including lobsters, soybeans, squid, crab salmon and multiple other items. The tariffs mean direct import of US lobster is "off the table" in China, as one US live lobster exporter put it.

But, if companies are indeed involved it would only be a matter of time before somebody gets caught, a seafood executive based in Canada, who requested anonymity, told our reporters. 

The lobster world is small and when a couple dozen employees at one Canadian company notice a large shipment of US lobsters coming in one day and going out to China the next day, people in the industry hear about it, he said.

A US-based source, who also wished to be unnamed, was emphatic: “There's plenty of that [transshipment] going on. It’s a 25% tariff; there's a big incentive. People could come down in pickup trucks to Maine and take the lobsters to Montreal or Toronto where it can be shipped by airfreight," he said, although he conceded he’d not seen it first-hand. 

Bumble Bee: Trump’s tuna tariffs ‘devastating’ 

In a letter sent to the USTR, US tuna canning company Bumble Bee Foods warned the tariffs against imports of Chinese tuna would be "devastating" for the firm.

The tariffs will hit US imports of yellowfin, skipjack, and albacore tuna loins, all of which are required by Bumble Bee's Santa Fe Springs, California factory, wrote CEO Jan Tharp.

The tariffs will hike the cost of raw materials, which in turn will "certainly lead to higher prices for US consumers", Bumble Bee's leader said.

"We are very concerned with the proposed tariff on tuna loins and the impact that these tariffs will have on our supply chain, global competitiveness, and US operations," Tharp said. "The proposed tariff on tuna loins will have a devastating effect on Bumble Bee given that our business model is to import tuna loins for further processing and canning in the US by American workers."

"The...additional costs caused by these tariffs could result in a factory closure and will certainly lead to higher prices for US consumers making a healthy, lean source of protein less affordable for those who benefit most from these products".

At the very least, the tariffs would stifle US innovation, as the firm would have to re-think plans to expand the Santa Fe Springs operation to include "certain value-added tuna products", he said.

Thai Union Group's US shelf-stable seafood operation also warned the tariffs will push up prices for both processors and consumers and may force it to move production off US soil.

In a letter to the USTR, Valentin Ramirez, CEO of Tri-Union Seafoods, which sells under the Chicken of the Sea (CoS) brand, said that additional costs in the form of tariffs -- which on Sept. 18 were confirmed, with tuna raw materials still on the list -- would "uniquely impact companies like CoS with onshore US jobs".

On the other side of the coin Dongwon Industries-owned StarKist & Co backed the tariffs in its own letter to the USTR.

President and CEO Andrew Choe wrote that it was unlikely an assessment of additional duties on the Chinese origin tuna and tuna products would cause disruption to the US economy or negatively impact US consumers, "as there are plentiful sources of supply for these products from countries other than China".

By far the main part of StarKist's operations is in Pago Pago, American Samoa, where it employs 2,400 workers. Another 100 workers are based at StarKist HQ, in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, while 65 work in Mira Loma, California, and 28 further service and sales team employees are located across the US.

Bakkafrost loses 750,000 fish in mystery incident

Faroese salmon farmer Bakkafrost has revealed it lost 750,000 individuals in an incident at its A-81 Kolbanagjogv site on Sept. 20, 2018, our Neil Ramsden reported on Sunday, having landed in Ecuador for the Global Outlook on Aquaculture Leadership, or GOAL, conference. 

The fish were young, at around 500 grams each, and the total mortalities occurred within just a "couple of hours", the firm said. They were only put to sea between June and August.

"It has not been possible to confirm the cause of the incident, but algae phaeocystis, pseudo-nitzscia, and heterosigma were registered in the sea at farming site A-81 Kolbanagjogv on Sept. 20, and the algae are suspected to have caused the mortality incident," Bakkafrost said.

"It has also been confirmed that prior to and while the incident occurred, manure has been sprayed as fertilizer onto the infield only 200 meters from the farming site. Continuous examinations are being done to confirm the cause of the sudden and short mortality incident."

There has been farming activity at this site for the past 30 years, and there has never been a similar incident, it noted. Bakkafrost has not observed any similar situations at other farming sites in recent days, it also said.

The company will have finished removing all the dead fish from the sea at the site on Sept. 24, and nothing abnormal has been registered since Sept. 20, it said. "Bakkafrost has people monitoring the situation closely at farming site A-81 Kolbanagjogv. The fish at [the site] are insured."

Tri Marine-affiliated vessel detained as lawsuits fly in captain’s death

Jason Smith, our Americas editor, who is also in Ecuador for GOAL, reported that a vessel affiliated with major tuna supplier Tri Marine International has been detained in Pago Pago, American Samoa, following a lawsuit from the family of Michael Castaneda, who captained the ship until his death in an October 2017 accident.

The purse seiner Cape Ferrat remains under arrest in the US territory following an Aug. 3 lawsuit against the vessel and two firms -- Samoa Fishing Management and Samoa Tuna Processors, a subsidiary of Bellevue, Washington-based Tri Marine.

The legal action, filed in the American Samoa High Court, alleges that the Cape Ferrat was "unseaworthy" and led to Castaneda's "wrongful death". It sought for defendants to post a $4 million bond.

William Banning, an admiralty lawyer representing Castaneda's estate, told Jason that a hearing is scheduled on Sept. 21 in American Samoa where the defendants' lawyers will argue for its release. Tri Marine declined to comment. 

US judge blocks Scanlon from working for Tampa Bay Fisheries

In the latest update in  lawsuit we have been covering for the past few weeks, Kathleen Scanlon, the long-time food quality professional accused of stealing business secrets from National Fish & Seafood (NFS) before going to work for Tampa Bay Fisheries, has now been at least temporarily barred by a Massachusetts federal judge from working for her new employer.

Judge Leo Sorokin, in the US District Court in Boston, issued an order granting Gloucester, Massachusetts-based NFS’s motion to enjoin Kathleen Scanlon from being employed by Tampa Bay and also blocking her and Tampa Bay from viewing or using any of the documents or recipes she may have copied from NFS.

Sorokin said Scanlon's claim that she kept all of her personal information on her work-related computer, email and phone because she didn't maintain such devices for personal use during her two decades of working for NFS was "plainly true".

But the judge said he didn't buy that she could not explain how "literally thousands of documents from National Fish's computer system" wound up both in her USB drive and a newly created Gmail account.

"These documents include recipes, cost analyses, policy documents, current and former product specifications, and a slew of documents regarding Whole Foods Markets, a major National Fish customer," Sorokin wrote, adding: "The Whole Food documents themselves took approximately an hour to copy on July 9."

Scanlon had agreed with Tampa Bay CEO Robert Paterson to take the new job on June 29, more than a week earlier, but didn't inform NFS of her plans to leave until July 11, two days after her massive document download, the judge noted.

NFS, a subsidiary of Pacific Andes International Holdings, in late July, filed a lawsuit against Dover, Florida-based Tampa Bay, which is part of the US seafood giant Red Chamber Group, and John Doe, an unidentified executive, for allegedly attempting to steal confidential business secrets when it hired away Scanlon, its former research, development and quality assurance director.

WorldFood Moscow 

Last week, I was reporting from WorldFood Moscow, held in Russia's capital from Sept. 17-20.  

A lot of interesting news came from the show. With regards to shrimp, Anton Churakov, an experienced buying executive, said he is seeing more offers from Ecuador of cooked shrimp. 

“I feel the Ecuadorians have a lot of shrimp,” said Churakov, who has recently joined Maguro, part of DPR Group, a Russian tuna and frozen seafood that Thai Union Group has invested in and plans to take control of. 

“They have recently started making offers of cooked shrimp, which they have not done for a long time, as they didn’t need to,” he told me, during the show. Churakov was previously with Uhrenholt Russia and, before that, Agama Group. 

Also, Argentine shrimp sources at the trade show had a matter more close to home on their mind than increasing sales to Russia. 

The technocrat government of Mauricio Macri has put in place a floating percentage tax on all products exported from the country at the start of the month. This is, of course, an issue for all of Argentina’s exports, but it comes as shrimp sellers approach their busiest time of the year. 

Macri had eradicated the 10% export tax the government of Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner had in place. However, he’s just introduced a tax related to the exchange rate with the dollar, amid the current state of economic crisis in the country. According to multiple sources, the tax is ARS 3 for every $1 exported. “This means an FOB [free on-board] for $8/kg would mean you’d pay 24 pesos (ARS) per kg,” one source me. 

The tax ends up being around 8-10% anyway, sources said. The peso has been devaluing against the dollar, which helps the exporters. However, the company’s fuel and crew costs are in dollars, which partially counteracts this. 

“It’s very bad timing, as we are coming up to the Christmas sales season [for Europe], as well as Chinese New Year. We have to go back and ask for higher prices, but customers are obviously not pleased,” another source said. 

The expansion of salmon aquaculture in Russia was also a hot topic for the show. 

Russian processor Murmanrybprom-1 has its origins in wild whitefish but sees its future in farmed salmon and trout. 

The company is processing farmed salmon and, for the first time this year, trout, from Russian Aquaculture, which is leading the development of aquaculture in the country. 

“Russian Aquaculture has big growth plans and we are part of those plans,” said Alexander Divin, the company’s managing director. Russian Aquaculture plans to hit 30,000t (gross weight equivalent, or GWE) of salmon and trout production by 2025, the company has stated. 

“We are still processing some whitefish, but it’s getting harder and harder, as you have big, vertically integrated companies that have the access to the raw material. We still plan on processing whitefish, as we want to be diversified. We are doing some plaice, for example, for export to the EU,” he told me. 

Norebo Holding, the largest quota holder in Russia, now has a processing plant in Murmansk for cod and haddock, for example. Prices for cod have been very high for the past year and a half and the outlook is for a further cut to the cod and haddock quotas in 2019. 

“Cod is a tough business to be in, as the prices have risen so much and the processors are squeezed. The big, vertically integrated firms are better equipped to ride this out,” said Divin. The outlook on salmon is very positive, however. 

“The demand for fresh salmon is very strong and currently Russian Aquaculture is the only alternative to the imports from the Faroe Islands. Salmon is on most restaurant menus and a very big product in sushi, which is huge in Russia,” he said. 

I also spoke to Norebo during the show. The company has just added coldwater shrimp to its Borealis branded range, which is set to launch in the Russian stores of French retailer Auchan at the end of the year. It’s already in X5 Retail Group and others in Russia, but Auchan is a “big step”, an executive with the company told me. She did not know, however, if Auchan would list shrimp as part of its launch. 

The addition of shrimp to the brand comes as Norebo starts fishing the crustacean, known as Pandalus borealis, in waters in west Russia with a 70.1×14.6 meter trawler bought from Iceland’s Brim. The shrimp is cooked on the vessel. 

“We control the raw material for the shrimp, so it’s a nice addition to the range,” she said. Norebo already sells cod, haddock, redfish and squid under the brand. 

The company also has chilled products for sale under the brand in Murmansk, where its main processing plant is based. 

Due to the cold chain and logistics challenges in Russia, the products are only on sale in frozen form in the rest of the country.

Defa Group, one of Russia’s largest seafood importers, has also moved into the country’s growing coldwater shrimp fishery with a trawler bought from the Faroe Islands last year. 

The company has also just got approval for export to the EU and European Economic Area (EEA) and is also in the midst of getting the official nod for sale to China, said Yulia Leontyeva, the company’s business development manager. 

This will give more options than just selling into the Russian market, she told me. Defa purchased the 60.1×12.2-meter vessel last July and she started fishing this year, under the name Arctic Lion. 

Previously, the vessel was named Havborg. Arctic Lion can produce cooked and industrial shrimp onboard. This will give Defa the ability to produce industrial shrimp for export to processors in the EU and EEA, as well as cooked sales to Russia. 

US-based Lobster Trap’s joint venture with Nederlof to increase EU sale

Fresh off the heels of a change in top managers, the US-based Lobster Trap Company struck a deal with a large Dutch buyer and distributor in a bid to increase its position in the European live seafood market.

As part of an agreement with Ijmuiden, Netherlands-based Nederlof Fish, the two companies have created a joint venture that will result in the design, construction and operation of a “world-class live inventory management system and distribution network based in the Netherlands”, according to a press release.

Lobster Trap, which maintains its headquarters in Bourne, Massachusetts, can be expected to send Nederlof plenty of lobster from Canada as well as species caught in other parts of the north Atlantic and Pacific waters.

James W. Schubauer, Lobster Trap's CEO and president, told our Jason Huffman his company "sources vast amounts of product from both US and Canadian waters and this platform will provide an array of live species to the largest and most sophisticated seafood buyers throughout the EU".

title: Tri Marine-affiliated vessel detained as lawsuits fly in captain’s death
content:
A vessel affiliated with major tuna supplier Tri Marine International has been detained in Pago Pago, American Samoa, following a lawsuit from the family of Michael Castaneda, who captained the ship until his death in an October 2017 accident.

The purse seiner Cape Ferrat remains under arrest in the US territory following an Aug. 3 lawsuit against the vessel and two firms -- Samoa Fishing Management and Samoa Tuna Processors, a subsidiary of Bellevue, Washington-based Tri Marine.

The legal action, filed in the American Samoa High Court, alleges that the Cape Ferrat was "unseaworthy" and led to Castaneda's "wrongful death". It sought for defendants to post a $4 million bond.

William Banning, an admiralty lawyer representing Castaneda's estate, told Undercurrent News that a hearing is scheduled on Sept. 21 in American Samoa where the defendants' lawyers will argue for its release.

Tri Marine declined to comment for this article.

The lawsuit, which was filed by the administrator of Castaneda's estate, Maren Miller, and the captain's wife, Tracey, claims that Castaneda's death occurred on Oct. 26, 2017, after he drowned "on a dark night after he fell from the unfit, unprotected, inadequate and unsafe gangway into the harbor water below the gangway between the vessel and the dock".

"There was insufficient or no lighting in the area where the accident occurred and no ladder or other means by which decedent could readily climb back up on the wharf or the vessel and then the rescue attempt by defendants was negligently performed," the lawsuit claims. "As a result decedent drowned."

According to a separate lawsuit filed by insurance company Endurance Risk Solutions Assurance against Tri Marine, Castaneda had been drinking at the time of the accident. He died after he fell onto a bolt in the pier that caused a hole in his skull, the suit added. 

Endurance claims in its suit that the circumstances of Castaneda's death mean that Tri Marine, not it, is liable for any damages.

"Notwithstanding the facts established by plaintiff’s said investigation, the Tri Marine defendants have made a claim against plaintiff under the terms of the policy demanding coverage for the liability of the Tri Marine defendants arising out of the death of Capt. Castaneda. Endurance has responded by denying that it has a duty to defend and/or indemnify the Tri Marine defendants in connection with claims and/or actions arising out of the death of Capt. Castaneda," Endurance stated.

Contact the author jason.smith@undercurrentnews.com

title: British Columbia protestors arrested on well boat in dry dock
content:
Six protestors found occupying a well boat in dry dock in the British Columbia, Canada, city of Victoria were arrested by police, the Times Colonist reported.

The protestors aboard the Orca Chief, a 113-foot vessel used to transfer fish between farms and the shore, were arrested on suspicion of mischief and breaking-and-entering the newspaper said. One woman duct-taped herself to boat's mast and had to be removed with help from the fire department. 

The boat was docked at Point Hope Maritime.

title: US state of Maine gubernatorial candidates to square off on seafood
content:
Maine’s commercial lobster and groundfish harvesters, processors and dealers have very little idea what their US state's four candidates for governor might do for their respective industries if elected, but that's about to change.

Three of the candidates -- Democrat Janet Mills, and independents Terry Hayes and Alan Caron – have all agreed to participate in a two-hour seafood industry forum on Oct. 4, in Rockland, Maine, and the fourth candidate -- Republican Shawn Moody -- is expected to commit shortly, the Maine Coast Fishermen’s Association (MCFA), the event's main organizer, tells Undercurrent News. 

The forum, which is also being supported by the Maine Lobster Dealers Association (MLDA), the Maine Lobstermen’s Association (MLA), the Maine Lobstering Union (MLU), the Maine Aquaculture Association (MAA) and the Alewife Harvesters of Maine (AHM), is to be held from 5 to 7 p.m. EST at the Strand Theater, an arena that seats between 175 and 200 people, and be livestreamed on the internet. (Undercurrent will provide the URL as soon as we have it.)

MCFA is careful to not call the event a debate, where candidates typically stand at a podium and are required to follow strict rules on the time allotted for answers and responses. Instead, the participants will sit comfortably in chairs on a stage along with moderator James Wright, editorial director of the Global Aquaculture Alliance, editor of the Global Aquaculture Advocate and a long-time Maine resident, and be asked to respond to a series of questions submitted by or on behalf of the various industry groups’ members, one organizer explained.

Ben Martens, MCFA’s executive director, told Undercurrent that all of the groups involved will be reaching out to their members over the next two few weeks to identify the issues they want addressed.

One topic that is likely to come up is the effort to preserve Maine’s working waterfronts, as the commercial fishing industry is increasingly losing its priority in community development and planning efforts, Martens suggested. He said MCFA has been working the past few months to inform each of the candidates about the problem and its importance to harvesters, though it has not yet recorded their views.

Lobster boats on Long Wharf, in Portland, Maine. Photograph by Jason Huffman.

The commercial fishing industry is a key contributor to the state of Maine’s economy, with landings valued at more than $569 million in 2017. Only Alaska can credit its commercial fish landings for a larger contribution ($1.6 billion in 2016), based on data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

“Strategically thinking about our state and planning for the future is something we need a little bit more of,” Martens said.

“… If a governor comes in and they say we’re going to put the spotlight on protecting our commercial fishing future, one of the most important things they can do is to make sure we have access to our oceans,” he said. “It doesn’t matter if we are talking about recreational. It doesn’t matter if we’re talking about commercial. It doesn’t matter if we are talking about aquaculture. Once you lose the access, it’s gone forever.”

The state's aquaculture industry also has concerns about preserving working waterfronts, and additionally wants to make sure its members will be able to continue leasing areas on which to operate their farms, including those used for both shellfish and finfish, Sebastian Belle, MAA's president, told Undercurrent. 

The Maine coast is the future destination of two large land-based Atlantic salmon farms, but Belle said his group has "no concerns about the new governor embracing new farms and businesses and our members look forward to welcoming new colleagues". 

Keliher could stay in job

As the governor of Maine since 2011, Paul LePage has been as polarizing a figure as the current president of the US, declaring war on the news media, while stoking fears about illegal immigrants and building racial tensions, based on multiple accounts. LePage has embraced the comparison, calling himself “Donald Trump before Donald Trump” and “Baby Donald”.

But LePage’s administration has been applauded by some of the state's business leaders, including a few in the lobster industry. And when it comes to the species that matter most in Maine, lobster is king. It accounted for $434m (76%) of the value of the state's landings in 2017, and is reported to have an overall economic impact on the state of more than a billion dollars.

“For our members, a lot of what we deal with right now, especially relative to our major trade issues, we need somebody who is supportive of our industry and who is willing to advocate for our businesses at a higher level when possible or necessary,” Annie Tselikis, MLDA’s executive director, told Undercurrent News. “Governor LePage has done a great job at that.”

Regardless, a Maine governor can’t hold office for more than eight years, so LePage will be stepping down after 2018 and giving way to one of the four candidates vying to replace him. The opening sets up one of the more interesting contests to watch in the 2018 mid-term election, which includes battles for 36 state and territorial governor jobs as well as 33 of the 100 US Senate spots and every one of the 435 House of Representatives’ positions.

Another contest for the commercial seafood industry to watch: Alaska governor Bill Walker, an independent who was elected in 2014, is considered to be one of the most vulnerable incumbents in the 2018 election, though earlier polls showed him leading Republican challenger Mike Dunleavy by 7% and his approval rating improving. Walker has been a champion for the Alaskan seafood industry, leading trade missions in recent times to Asia.

Florida, another important seafood state, is also facing a close race for governor. Tallahassee mayor Andrew Gillum, a Democrat who is supported by liberal senator Bernie Sanders, a former presidential candidate, will compete against Republican US representative Ron DeSantis, a Trump-endorsed Republican, to replace outgoing Republican governor Rick Scott, who is running for a US Senate seat. Both Gillum and DeSantis won their primary contests this week. 

Patrick Keliher, commissioner of Maine's Department of Marine Resources.

But back to Maine: Tselikis believes one of the questions her members will deem most critical at the upcoming seafood industry forum is how the candidates view their selection of the next commissioner of the state’s Department of Marine Resources (DMR), the position that could most directly influence them.

In addition to setting DMR's policies, the head of the agency sits on the fishery management councils that decide the quota for herring and other fish of importance to New England harvesters.  

Tselikis said her members have had a good relationship with Patrick Keliher, who has held the top job at DMR since 2011, and hope for the same from his successor.

Though the head of the agency has yet to discuss his plans for the future, and it’s possible that the next governor could retain Keliher. Such a move would not be unprecedented. George LaPoint was DMR commissioner for 12 years after he was appointed in 1998 by then independent governor Angus King. He was kept in the job by Democratic Maine governor John Baldacci after he was elected in 2002.

King, still an independent who caucuses with the Democratic party, is now one of Maine’s two senators.

Another key issue for the next governor, Tselikis said, is representing the state’s lobster industry in relation to labor issues. Several seafood industry groups have struggled to find enough workers as a result of the administration’s recent change of approach on the H2B visa program.

Tselikis was not able to provide the number of job openings in the US lobster industry due to H2B problems, but said that practically all of her member companies have informed her that they “don’t have enough people to do what they do” in packing or processing.

The gap could be severe this winter as the industry attempts to meet demand for the Chinese New Year, assuming a tariff dispute with China is resolved in time.

“We have not gone to heavy automation in the lobster industry because the product that we deal with is so challenging,” Tselikis said. “We are dealing with live lobsters or having to try and extract meat from a very difficult animal. It’s not like you can create a very nice machine to just cut the fish in half.

A dead heat

Maine’s governor's race is a dead heat based on a poll of some 500 state residents conducted by Suffolk University earlier this month. Moody had 39% of the vote, while Mills has 38.8%.  Hayes and Alan Caron were found to each have just 4% and 3% of the vote respectively, according to the poll, which had an overall margin of error of plus or minus 4%.

Shawn Moody, the Republican candidate for governor of Maine, from a video on his website.

Moody, a 58-year-old Gorham, Maine, resident, and owner of an auto body company, has promised to build on LePage’s policies and recruited former LePage staffers to work on his campaign. He easily won his primary contest with 56% of the vote, according to the Portland Press Herald.

In fact it was Lauren LePage, the current governor’s daughter and Moody’s campaign manager, who emailed a non-specific response to Undercurrent’s questions about any views the Republican candidate might have with regard to seafood policy or the retention of Keliher.

“Shawn Moody is committed to ensuring Maine has thriving fishing and seafood industries,” Lauren LePage said. “He believes strongly that in order to create more jobs and strengthen Maine's economy, we must continue to implement common sense regulatory reforms, lower Maine's tax burden, and reduce healthcare costs for Maine families. Shawn is the only candidate in the race with over 40 years of executive experience as a job creator, and knows what it takes to grow Maine's economy.”

Janet Mills, the Democratic candidate for governor of Maine, from the campaign's Flickr account.

Mills, a former member of Maine’s House of Representatives, has served as the state’s attorney general since 2009. The 70-year-old Farmington, Maine, resident was the top fundraiser among the original seven Democratic candidates to compete for the job, though it took her four rounds of the state's ranked choice system run-off to ultimately survive the primary.

Mills' campaign staff did not respond to Undercurrent’s call requesting her views in relation to the state’s commercial fishing industry.

Independents could be election monkey wrench

But don’t dismiss Hayes, a former state House member and currently Maine's treasurer, or Caron, a consultant who works with not-for-profit groups. They may be longshots, but there is concern among Democrats in particular that the independent gubernatorial candidates could take critical votes away from Mills.

That’s essentially what LePage opponents think happened in 2010 when the Republican candidate drew 37.6% of the vote to narrowly defeat independent Eliot Cutler, who had 35.9% of the vote. Democrat Libby Mitchell had 18.8% of the vote, while the other independent, Moody, had 5.0%.

But it’s worth mentioning that it was the independent Cutler who was in a distant third position in 2010 with just 9% of the vote when earlier polls were held.

Chris Johnson, chairman of the Lincoln County Democratic Committee, is reported to have asked his party’s members last week to attend one of Hayes’ campaign events and discourage the former Democrat from staying in the race.

Note that whoever wins the job in Maine will be the lowest paid of all US governors, making $70,000 per year, $20,000 less than the second lowest-paid governor, in Colorado.

title: Lawsuit says Maine lobster harvester ordered sinking of rival’s boat
content:
Vincent Hilt and Devlin Meklin were convicted and sentenced more than a year ago for opening up the seacocks and shutting off the bilge pumps of Oracle, a 36-foot lobster boat anchored near Tenants Harbor, Maine, in order to sink it. The boat was three-quarters submerged when its owner, Joshua Hupper, found it.

But the case isn't over.

Hupper has now filed a civil suit in a Knoxville County, Maine, court against a fellow lobster harvester, Alan Norwood, accusing him of ordering the sinking as part of an ongoing feud between the two men, the Central Maine Courier Gazzette reports. 

Earlier media accounts tell of how Norwood allegedly suspected Hupper of hauling his traps and setting his gear on top of the other harvester's gear.

Hilt, a former deckhand for Norwood, initially told police, when he sunk Oracle back on Sept. 1, 2016, that he was to receive $500 from Norwood for the deed, which led to Norwood's arrest. But Hilt recanted the statement in court, saying it was all his own idea, and a jury acquitted Norwood of all charges, based on an earlier story.  

Hilt and Meklin, who were convicted of felony criminal mischief and felony theft (they stole a skiff to reach Oracle), both received two-year prison sentences in March 2017, though Meklin had all but three months of his sentence suspended.

The damage to Hupper's boat was initially estimated at $50,000, though Hupper's lawsuit now claims the damage was at least $170,000.

title: Man accused of seafood burglary arrested in Alaska
content:
State troopers in Alaska, US arrested a man on Aug. 24 in connection with a burglary at a Ninilchik-area fish processing business.

Investigation showed that a man entered the business around 2:50 a.m. on Aug. 22 and stole food, money, and seafood from the commercial freezer in the business, Peninsula Clarion reported.

Information from the business owner and from further investigation connected the burglary to Garrett Fitzgerald, who was located and arrested in Soldotna, according to an online trooper dispatch. Some of the stolen fish was located at the scene, and investigation is ongoing, according to the dispatch.

Approximately 3,000 pounds of seafood was stolen. Fitzgerald was charged with one count of theft in the first degree, a class B felony, and one count of burglary in the second degree, a class C felony.

title: Filipino tuna canning firm exec confident he’ll be cleared following arrest
content:
An official of the Philippines-based seafood firm Alliance Select Foods International expressed confidence he'll be cleared of charges after a court ordered him and several others arrested for violations of the country's corporation code, the Philippines News Agency reported.

Former Alliance board member Jonathan Dee said he is determined to clear his name in all appropriate legal venues after two shareholder groups in the company filed two cases accusing him and others of refusal to open Alliance's books for inspection.

“The records will clearly show that there was no violation of the corporate code, and that Alliance Food board voted to allow the complainants to exercise their rights on an inspection. Unfortunately, the process was delayed by the actions of the complainants themselves, which we will show in the coming days,” Dee said in a statement.

In a series of earlier decisions, the department of justice had already cleared Dee.

title: Filipino court orders arrests of Alliance officials
content:
A metropolitan trial court in the Philippines has ordered the arrest of George Sycip, son of the late business tycoon Washington Sycip, and four other officials of a tuna processing firm for supposed violation of the country's corporation code, GMA News Online reported.

In a ruling dated July 11, the court's presiding judge ordered the arrest of Alliance Select Foods International's chairman Sycip and company officials Jonathan Dee, Marie Grace Vera-Cruz, Antonio Pacis, and Raymond See over the supposed violation of a law that provides that records of business transactions of the company should be open to any stockholder.

"Wherefore, let warrants of arrest be issued for the apprehension of the above-named accused," the ruling read.

In June the Philippines' department of justice indicted the executives for their refusal to allow certain shareholders to inspect the company books.

title: China pushes to fast track FTA with Norway as direct salmon sales rocket
content:
China wants free-trade talks with Norway to be accelerated, South China Morning Post reported. Meanwhile, Norwegian direct salmon sales to China grew, while exports to Vietnam dropped sharply, data shows. 

Free-trade talks between China and Norway should be sped up, the Chinese government’s top diplomat, state councilor Wang Yi, told his Norwegian counterpart, as the two countries continue to step up efforts to put a row over the Nobel peace prize behind them.

Beijing froze ties with Oslo and suspended discussions on a free-trade deal immediately after the Norwegian Nobel committee awarded the prize to jailed dissident Liu Xiaobo in 2010. Liu died last year while still in custody. Meanwhile, Norwegian and Chinese counterparties resumed talks on the free-trade agreement, but Norwegian salmon sales to China were still affected last year.

However, Norwegian direct sales to China rocketed this year, while sales to Vietnam -- a smuggling route -- dropped sharply, data from Norges Sjomatrad, or Seafood Norway, show. In week 30, commencing July 23, 2018, Norwegian direct sales to China totaled 387 metric tons, up from zero the previous year, while exports to Vietnam dropped to 61t, from 548t the same week a year before.

Between Jan.1-July 29, Norwegian salmon sales to China rose to 7,335t, up from 864t in the same period during 2017, while exports to Vietnam dropped to 3,447t, from 15,307t, according to the same figures. 

In April, a Chinese executive representing a Norwegian salmon company was arrested in China over alleged salmon smuggling through Vietnam into China, in the context of Chinese crackdowns on illegal seafood trade.

The woman had been instrumental in growing the market for Norwegian salmon in the region, said Atle Eide, chairman of Norwegian salmon farmer SalMar.

title: Editor’s recap: Sysco eyes Italian deal; National Fish vs Tampa Bay; Marine Harvest Chile salmon escape
content:
Tom Seaman, editorial director of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

The possibility of a massive cross-border acquisition was the most-read story on Undercurrent News last week.

Matilde Mereghetti, our reporter covering southern Europe and Latin America, picked up from sources that US broad-line distributor Sysco Corporation is eyeing a deal for Italy's largest seafood importer, MARR. 

The deal, if it goes ahead, would add a strong southern European component to Sysco’s business. Based in Houston, Texas, Sysco moved into Europe in 2016, announcing a $3.1 billion acquisition for UK-based Brake Bros.

MARR, which is listed on the Milan stock exchange and has a market capitalization of €1.59bn, is 50.4% owned by Cremonini, a family-owned conglomerate with interests in meat production, food distribution, and catering.

National Fish vs Tampa Bay 

Also, a legal scoop last week on a juicy lawsuit between National Fish & Seafood (NFS) and Tampa Bay Fisheries got a lot of interest from readers. 

US processor NFS, a US subsidiary of Pacific Andes International Holdings (PAIH), alleges a former director is joining rival Tampa Bay in order to help the latter compete for business with the likes of Whole Foods Market and High Liner Foods, having illicitly obtained “confidential information and trade secrets”.

NFS filed a lawsuit in a Boston, Massachusetts, federal court on July 20 against Kathleen Scanlon, its former director of research, development and quality assurance; Tampa Bay, which is part of US seafood giant Red Chamber Group; and John Doe, an as-yet unidentified executive with the latter.

Tampa Bay Fisheries plans to further automate its clam production process after allegedly conspiring with Scanlon. 

Salmon escape at Marine Harvest Chile farm

Norwegian multinational Marine Harvest, the largest producer of farmed salmon in the world, told our Matilde Mereghetti it has been carrying out "intensive work" to recapture some 690,000 fish that escaped a farm in southern Chile during a storm. 

Marine Harvest said it has notified all competent authorities of the incident, which happened on July 5 at a farm in Punta Redonda, in the Los Lagos region, as well as its efforts to stabilize and mitigate the matter.

Marine Harvest also reported the structures affected by the accident were built in 2017 and complied with the standards established by the manufacturer for high exposure conditions. 

Struggling Thai shrimp processors’ want end to import ban 

As shrimp raw material prices in Thailand increase again, processors in the country continue to push for the lifting of a ban on the farmed crustacean imports.

The ban, according to our sources, was put in place in September last year, with the Thai government under pressure from the strong farming lobby in the country, something processors are also wary of. This worry over inciting the wrath of the domestic farmers -- their only form of shrimp other than wild imports -- is impacting the volume of the processors' complaints, sources said.

Around the Thaifex – World of Food Asia show earlier this year, I heard Thai packers were hoping to be allowed to restart imports from the likes of India and Indonesia, which were never easy in the first place, due to strict monitoring by the country's food and drug administration. 

This came, however, at a time of heightened tension between farmers and processors, which culminated in a base price agreement that I revealed during the show. The tension in the sector means processors still want the government to allow imports again, but are wary of shouting too loudly about it, sources said. 

Prices have since rocketed up (see our prices portal), leaving processors in a tough spot.

At-risk stock to constrain 2018 Fraser River sockeye season

Jason Smith, our Americas editor, wrote an update on the Canadian sockeye fishery in British Columbia's Fraser River. 

The potential return of 14 million sockeye salmon to Fraser River during this season could add commercial landings of an extra 3.4m fish on top of already strong harvests in Alaska's Bristol Bay. 

The total allowable catch for the Fraser River is set at 6.2m fish but the expected commercial catch is much smaller, 3.4m. That figure  -- about 1m fish will come from the US with the rest to come from Canadian waters -- will be lower than it could have been as a small subset. A stock of around 1,000 fish from British Columbia's Cultus Lake region has been assessed, but not yet formally listed, as it is "at risk", leading managers to take extra precautions this year. 

FAO: Fish prices to be 25% higher by 2030

Neil Ramsden, our deputy editor, analyzed the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)'s latest State of World Fisheries and Aquaculture report. According to the FAO's modeling, fish prices are set for a rise.

The sector is expected to enter a decade of higher prices in nominal terms, it said. Factors driving this tendency include income, population growth and meat prices on the demand side; and the potential slight decline in capture fisheries production as a result of policy measures in China, the slowdown in the growth of aquaculture production and cost pressure from some crucial inputs (e.g. feed, energy and crude oil) on the supply side.

In addition, the slowdown in Chinese fisheries and aquaculture production will stimulate higher prices in China, with a domino effect on world prices.

"The increase in the average price of farmed fish (19% over the projection period) will be greater than that of captured fish (excluding fish for non-food use) (17%)," FAO said. "These higher prices, coupled with high demand for fish for human consumption, will stimulate a 25% increase in the average price of internationally traded fish by 2030 relative to 2016," FAO wrote.

US lobster prices hold steady as trade war shakes wholesalers

China’s retaliatory 25% tariff has cut several lobster exporters in the US state of Maine deep since it went into effect almost three weeks ago, but it so far hasn’t made any kind of a significant dent on prices, wholesalers told our Jason Huffman. 

The $5.25 to $5.50 per pound that they say are being charged for new shell chix (1 to 1.24 lb) and the $5.50 to $5.75 charged for quarters (1.25 to 1.49) each represent about a $0.25 to $0.50 drop since July 6, the date China’s tariffs went into effect. The prices, they say, are similar to what’s been paid in the month of July in previous years and -- so far -- there's been no indication of a panicked market.

US harvesters, meanwhile, report getting anywhere from $3.60 to $4.50/lb for new shell lobsters at the docks.

But not everyone in Maine is comfortable with the situation. The Lobster Company, in Arundel, for example, has counted on China to buy 1.5m lbs of its new shell lobster, 35% of the company’s sales, on an annual basis. Since the US’ Independence Day holiday several weeks ago, that tap of orders from China has been turned completely off, said Steph Nadeau, the company’s co-owner and sales manager.

“We haven’t shipped an order to mainland China since July 4,” she told Jason. 

Nadeau said her company is attempting to make do, maintaining relationships with Chinese buyers, and keep the harvesters she works with happy by selling lobster to China at cost, eliminating her margin. Because she has maintained a strong capital position, she said The Lobster Company and others that rely on Chinese buyers might be able to make it until the winter. After that, she's not so sure.

“We’ll just be handing the business over to the Canadians at that point,” she said.

Supply chain to bear brunt of US tariffs on China, shrimp sector will be worst hit

The Chinese shrimp sector is likely to be the most hit by the 10% tariffs from the US, with the impact likely to be mainly absorbed by the supply chain on most categories, meaning consumers could be largely insulated, sources told me.

On July 10, the US Trade Representative published a 205-page list of proposed tariffs, including nearly all categories of seafood produced or processed in China as well as many textiles, fruit, minerals, mechanical and industrial goods. In total, 6,031 tariff subheadings are included. The total is around $200 billion worth of Chinese products. The bulk of the $2.7bn of seafood the US imported from China in 2017 is included. Early October is seen as a likely implementation date. 

For tilapia and the whitefish and salmon caught in the US and re-processed in China, sources feel the impact is going to be less than shrimp, due to the current global supply glut of the latter, which is causing low prices.

“For shrimp, there is no reason for the market to accept an increase, due to the supply situation,” said Jeff Sedacca, the president of Sunnyvale Seafood, the US import arm of China’s Zhanjiang Guolian Aquatic Products, a major Chinese shrimp and tilapia supplier to the US.

“If you cut off the Chinese shrimp, there would still be more than enough to supply the US market,” he told me. 

“A tariff on shrimp could have a very negative impact on Chinese shrimp exporters,” said Peter Redmayne, whose business runs the China Fisheries & Seafood Expo -- now the world’s second largest trade show for the sector -- held every year in Qingdao.

“There’s a lot of cheap shrimp around these days and the Chinese shrimp exporters may just increase their focus on other export markets, as well as their domestic market. As far as the US consumer is concerned, it won’t change a thing when it comes to shrimp, or most other Chinese seafood imports,” he said.

Itochu aims to recoup millions as supplier’s seiners face liquidation

Jason Smith, our Americas editor, discovered Japanese tuna trader Itochu and banks that lent money to a Taiwanese fishing firm are poised to recoup some of their monies owed thanks to a court-ordered liquidation of two tuna "super seiners".

The planned sale of the seiners Fong Seong 668 and Fong Seong 696, which previously formed part of a fleet operated by Taiwan's Fong Seong Fleet Company, was ordered following creditors' lawsuits from in the Marshall Islands where the vessels were arrested in November last year.

Fong Seong is affiliated with Wee Lee International, which also owns Taiwan's Ching Fu Shipbuilding Corporation. Allegations of accounting fraud that surfaced at the shipbuilder last year, with executives accused of falsifying documents related to several hundred million dollars in loans in order to obtain a $1.2bn contract to build minesweepers for Taiwan's navy. According to media reports, those loans are now in default, which appeared to cause financial issues for other parts of the group, including the fishing arm.

According to a news summary included in the Parties to the Nauru Agreement's Tuna Intelligence publication, several creditors filed suit against the shipbuilder and the fishing company in the Marshall Islands. Itochu, one of the world's biggest skipjack tuna traders, is attempting to recover $28.9m from the companies, the summary said. Other creditors including Guam-based Hansen Helicopters and Taiwan's Bank Sinopac also seek repayment.

title: Japan’s Itochu aims to recoup millions as supplier’s tuna seiners face liquidation
content:
Japanese tuna trader Itochu and banks that lent money to a Taiwanese fishing firm are poised to recoup some of their monies owed thanks to a court-ordered liquidation of two tuna "super seiners".

The planned sale of the seiners Fong Seong 668 and Fong Seong 696, which previously formed part of a fleet operated by Taiwan's Fong Seong Fleet Company, was ordered following creditors' lawsuits from in the Marshall Islands where the vessels were arrested in November last year.

Fong Seong is affiliated with Wee Lee International, which also owns Taiwan's Ching Fu Shipbuilding Corporation. Allegations of accounting fraud that surfaced at the shipbuilder last year, with executives accused of falsifying documents related to several hundred million dollars in loans in order to obtain a $1.2 billion contract to build minesweepers for Taiwan's navy. According to media reports, those loans are now in default, which appeared to cause financial issues for other parts of the group, including the fishing arm.

According to a news summary included in the Parties to the Nauru Agreement's Tuna Intelligence publication, several creditors filed suit against the shipbuilder and the fishing company in the Marshall Islands. Itochu, one of the world's biggest skipjack tuna traders, is attempting to recover $28.9 million from the companies, the summary said. Other creditors including Guam-based Hansen Helicopters and Taiwan's Bank Sinopac also seek repayment.

Itochu and lawyers for the companies did not respond to requests for comment for this story.

The lawsuits led the Marshall Island High Court to appoint New York City-based Basil Karatzas as the vessels' liquidator. He plans to find a buyer for the vessels, which remain in Majuro Lagoon in the Marshall Islands' capital. 

Majuro is a major transshipment center where catcher vessels come to offload tuna and return to fishing, he told Undercurrent News.

“When the vessel case took place they were in Majuro and they were arrested in Majuro and that’s why the Marshall Islands' court has jurisdiction," he said.

A third vessel with links to Fong Seong, Taumoana, has also been sued by creditors in the Marshall Islands but does not currently face liquidation. 

Karatzas told Undercurrent that the deadline to make an offer on the two vessels under his oversight in July 28. A brokered sale, not an auction, is being conducted.

“It will not be an auction because I don’t think we can maximize the price we’re going to receive for the vessels with an auction process. But, effectively, it’s the same thing," Karatzas said.

Valuations

The vessels are being sold "as is, where is". He called the vessels in "good shape" but added, “they could use some maintenance”.

“Right now there is no fuel on board so the engines are not running,” he added, which will likely affect the price.

“The terms of the sale most likely would prevent buyers from coming with top dollar and we’re prepared to accept that," he said.

The replacement cost for both vessels would be around $40m combined, he estimated, and if they were operating, they might fetch as much as $30m together. However, given that they aren't running, the price will likely come in lower, he said. 

Fong Seong 668 was built in 2004. Its sister vessel was built five years earlier. Each vessel has considerable freezing capacity, helicopter decks and can accommodate a crew of 50. 

Each has around 30 to 50 years of useful economic life remaining, Karatzas said. 

He's seen interest in recent weeks in part because the tuna market remains "rather strong", he added. Interest has come in from South Korea and Taiwan. He's also marketing the vessels to potential buyers in Europe but expects that they ultimately won't go that far. 

“I think the buyer will most likely come from the Pacific Rim," he said.

title: Trump’s crackdown on immigration threatens Canadian lobster harvesters
content:
US president Donald Trump’s crackdown on illegal immigration isn't happening just on the US-Mexico border, but also in a large body of water shared by US and Canadian lobster harvesters, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation reports.

US Customs and Border Patrol has confirmed to the news agency that it has stopped as many as 21 Canadian vessels this year in contested waters near Grand Manan Island and Machias Seal Island, in the Bay of Fundy, and says it has no intention of stopping. 

The agency couldn’t say how many of the vessels stopped were fishing. It said no arrests have been made.

The contested area begins about five kilometers southwest of New Brunswick's Grand Manan and is known as the "grey zone", according to the news service. It consists of about 700 square kilometers of “lucrative lobster waters” and has been claimed by both Canada and the U.S. for decades.

A US customs spokesperson said the operation, which is being conducted by the agency’s Houlton, Maine, office, is part of a routine enforcement effort and such inspections have been made in the past. The spokesperson confirmed that the agents are enforcing "immigration laws and other violations of federal law". 

Dominic LeBlanc, Canada’s minister of fisheries and oceans, has weighed in on the matter.

"Obviously, we are concerned when Canadian fishers are intercepted by American authorities when they are practicing fishing activity that has existed positively and co-operatively with the Americans for a very long time," he reportedly said.

Concerns about illegal immigration at the border between the U.S. and Mexico should not be applied to the Canada-U.S. border, he added.
