title: FCF says tuna volumes dropping with its increased sustainability focus
content:
The volumes traded by Taiwanese tuna giant Fong Chun Formosa Fishery Company (FCF) are dropping, as the company places a stronger focus on sustainability and corporate social responsibility (CSR), said the new FCF president, as he responded to a recent damning Greenpeace report.

Max Chou, who assumed the FCF president role at the start of May, told Undercurrent News the recent Greenpeace report, report, titled "Misery at sea", is "misleading" and based on "old information".

However, Chou, in an interview with Undercurrent, was willing to accept more work needs to be done. Also, he said FCF is pushing hard on making sure illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fish does not make its way into its supply chain, as well as focusing on social issues in the sector.

Undercurrent News: World’s 100 Largest Seafood Companies 2017
View report

"We have reduced supply because of our internal control system. Because of the focus on IUU and social accountability, the volume we deal with has gone down," Chou said. 

"The initial [Greenpeace] report said we traded 700,000 metric tons, which we corrected them on. We have come down from around 700,000t to 500,000t, over time. This is as a result of being more discerning on the type of fish we deal with. Anything questionable, it's better to be safe than sorry now," he said.

Greenpeace put a lot of focus on the conditions on some vessels, which Chou said is an area of the industry that needs work.

"I do feel it's hard on the boats. That's probably a fair point that Greenpeace brings up. The Taiwanese government and the industry are looking to try and change that," said Chou.

According to Chou, this is one of the improvements in the industry the Seafood Task Force -- a group of big seafood suppliers, NGOs, and retailers -- is trying to make, he said.

Also, the purse seine fleet is ahead of the curve compared to the longliners, said Chou. "So, what we are doing on the purse seine that we think is successful, we are moving to the longliners. We're doing more audits and trying to find ways and methods where if there is a complaint, there are ways to protect them, the crew. We need to make sure the crew can have a voice and it's heard. On purse seiners in the western Pacific, it's 100% observers. It's lower on longliners."

As there are more longliners, it's difficult to have as many observers, he said.

"I think it'll take time to get more on longliners and it's a high cost. With purse seiners, they are bigger vessels and the catch rate is much higher. A lot has to do with cost," he said.

After the interview with Undercurrent, Chou's company announced a major sustainability development. On June 22, a purse seine tuna fishery in the western and central Pacific shared by the US, China, and Taiwan -- and supplying FCF -- achieved Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certification. 

The South Pacific Tuna Corporation, in conjunction with FCF and the Western Pacific Sustainable Tuna Alliance, announced the central Pacific skipjack and yellowfin free-school purse seine fishery had achieved and received the MSC standard. 

Not just Taiwan

Although he accepted some points of the Greenpeace report, he resents the focus on FCF. 

"If you read the Greenpeace report, it's as if all Taiwan vessels went through FCF," said Chou.

"Actually, only 25% or our business is from Taiwanese boats. We are dealing with a lot of vessels, such as Chinese, Korean, and Philippines boats," Chou said.

"When I talk to my staff, I tell them I want to set the bar so high above the legal and acceptable level, that in case we fall, we are still above it. We are a lot more careful with what we do. We have a tracking system where we check the catches, look at whether the licenses are valid, and if the vessel has crew contracts. For some boats, we have their VMS [vessel monitoring systems], but, for some, we won't," he said.

"It's very hard for illegal fish to come into our system, now. I'm not saying it's impossible, but it's very, very hard. If it does and we find out, there has to be some fraudulent misinformation given to us for it to come into the system," said Chou.

"In our system, with all these checks, you can't input fish that does not have all this proper documentation, as it hits a red flag and gets rejected. We have tried to set it up so there is no human error in the system and no one could go in and do something to harm the company's reputation," he said.

Greenpeace's focus on Giant Ocean, Tunago

In the report, the NGO claims to have linked FCF to both of the two main incidents it cites.

Greenpeace cites links between FCF and an incident in September 2016, when the crew of the longliner Tunago No. 61, owned by Tunago Fishing Company, murdered their captain who, it later transpired, was likely abusing them.

Then, Greenpeace mentions a link between FCF and Giant Ocean International Fishery, a recruitment agency operated by Taiwanese nationals in Cambodia with strong ties back to Taiwan.

Did Greenpeace give free pass to Thai Union to focus on Taiwan’s ‘biggest fish’ FCF?

"We have found vessels that supplied tuna to FCF connected to the Giant Ocean human trafficking case, and to the Tunago No. 61 murder case, where there are also concerns around the exploitation and abuse of crew," said Greenpeace.

The description given of both the Giant Ocean and Tunago No. 61 incidents make disturbing reading, but Chou said Greenpeace heavily overplays the FCF links.

According to the report, the Giant Ocean case goes back to 2011, when the United Nations, NGOs and the Cambodian authorities became aware of a human trafficking ring operating in the country.

In May 2013, the Cambodian government arrested a Taiwanese national, Lin Yu Shin, a Giant Ocean employee who was responsible for the recruitment of labor.

Five more shareholders and directors of Giant Ocean were also charged: Lu Tien-Te; Chen Chun Mu; Wu Fu Tsang; Huang Chun Fa; and Tsai His Hu.

In April 2014, Lin Yu Shin and the five directors and shareholders were found guilty, with each sentenced to ten years in prison. Lin was tried in person, while the others were tried in absentia, according to Greenpeace.

The five directors and shareholders are considered fugitives in Cambodia.

"In December 2017, Greenpeace identified new evidence revealing that the five convicted human traffickers were living openly in Taiwan while fugitives from Cambodian justice," the NGO said. "On top of this, two of them had officially sanctioned roles working in the recruitment of migrant crew onto Taiwanese fishing vessels, and two others appeared to be involved in recruiting for fishing vessels in Taiwan."

Lu Tien Te is listed as the contact person for the Kaohsiung Fishing Vessel Crew Services Association, which holds a license to hire 700.

Also, Chen Chun Mu is now a director with Yu Chun Enterprises, which is currently registered by the fisheries agency to employ 399.

"Greenpeace is concerned the convicted traffickers pose an ongoing risk to migrant fishers. It is difficult to understand how, when authorities in Taiwan have not reached a substantive position on the guilt or innocence of the Giant Ocean directors and shareholders, they are able to continue to ply their trade restriction unabated. Greenpeace believes Taiwan has an obligation to ensure the convicted human traffickers are not allowed to work, in any way, with migrant workers who are vulnerable to trafficking, forced labor, and exploitation," the NGO said.

"Greenpeace does try to bring focus on areas that need attention. I think that's a good thing. I am not sure I always agree with the way they do it. The incidents they use are a number of years old. The conditions and awareness in this area has changed quite a bit. Take the cases that they try to link with FCF as an example," said Chou.

Chou said FCF has worked with Giant Ocean, but a long time ago.

"After we did an internal investigation, we are now finding out one of the vessels that supplied to us used Giant Ocean as an agent seven or eight years ago. We spoke to the vessel owner and they tried using Cambodian crew twice in their history and both times the number of crews could not adapt to living on the vessel, and were repatriated before their contract ended at the owner's cost," he told Undercurrent.

"After these two experiences, the company decided not to use Cambodian crew. They never received any complaints or any outstanding issues from this crew. These are cases that happened in 2010-2011," he said.

FCF had come across Giant Ocean before the Greenpeace report, Chou claimed. 

"For two of the guys in Giant Ocean, we found out about them before the Greenpeace report. When we joined the Seafood Task Force and started doing more social accountability work, we were then trying to find out about the manning agents. One of them [Giant Ocean] is the association secretary general for the manning agents in Taiwan. That is when my staff had their first meeting with them. We had to go in and find out about the whole process and how it worked," he said.

"We knew about him and one other fellow [from Giant Ocean] due to our own research into manning agents and helping the vessels that sell to us to have a code of conduct in line with what the Seafood Task Force and FCF are doing," Chou said.

In the Seafood Task Force, FCF is involved in the tuna working group and a manning agents and workers group. "The latter is looking at hours for workers, repatriation, and if they have a complaint, making sure there are ways they can submit this so they are not punished."

Chou feels FCF is "one of the guys who are ahead rather than the guys who are getting pulled", hence his frustration with the Greenpeace report. "We want to be responsible and we are doing what needs to be done."

However, sustainability, traceability, and welfare on vessels have to be practical and possible to carry out on vessels, said Chou.

"We realize the industry is changing and we need to be at a level where the buyers, retailers, the end consumers, feel comfortable what is coming onto their table," he said.

"But, if you have regulations and rules that are so hard to achieve, it's useless. They [the vessels] will either not sign it, or they sign it and fail the task force or our audits. Then, we stop buying from them and they go out and sell to someone who does not have such high standards as us. Then, we are not helping the whole industry," he told Undercurrent.

‘No free pass' for Thai Union 

The most recent incident cited in the report is the 2016 murder of the skipper of a vessel owned by Tunago Fishery, which Greenpeace then claims to link to FCF.

The murder of Xie Dingrong, the skipper of longliner Tunago No. 61, is one of the main examples cited by the NGO in the report on alleged labor abuses on Taiwanese vessels. Just days before the captain's death, Tunago No. 61 transshipped with a Shin Ho Chun No. 102, a Panamanian flagged, Taiwanese-owned, fish carrier.

"Greenpeace have sighted records that confirm FCF has traded with both Shin Ho Chun No. 102, and its sister vessel, Shin Ho Chun No. 101," the NGO states, in the report. "FCF have acknowledged to Greenpeace that they trade with both vessels, confirming FCF's link to this tragic case."

However, according to one tuna sector source familiar with the companies, Tunago is Taiwanese-owned, but "not even affiliated" to FCF.

"Tunago was, at one time, the Fortuna fleet out of Samoa and Fiji where they delivered to StarKist and then also to Bumble Bee Foods. I understand they changed their operation and transship to their own carrier, the Shin Ho Chun, and take it directly to Bangkok to Thai Union," he told Undercurrent. "Most of the claims from Greenpeace were before 2015, except this one from Tunago, it's just strange. Why are they hiding the Thai Union connection?"

FCF's Chou confirmed he still does business with Tunago. 

"We still deal with them from time-to-time. It's unfortunate, what happened, they are a good company. We don't know the background of the whole thing and it happened over two years ago," he said.

"When we bought the fish, we did not know what had happened. When I read this [the report], I felt we were guilty by association. We were on a plane and a crime was committed by a passenger on that plane. Then, everyone on that plane is also guilty because of that. That's how I felt about this whole thing. If someone in my family did a crime, is the whole family guilty?"

The Greenpeace report also makes little mention of Thai Union. 

The report mentions Thai Union once, to state, "We encourage governments, regulators and companies to look at commitments made by Thai Union in 2017 to address such issues in their supply chains". The report came out the week after one published by Thai Union and Greenpeace on the progress made under the agreement signed by the two last year.

As Undercurrent has recently reported, Thai Union is also a customer of Tunago.

Lik FCF, Thai Union makes no secret of dealing with Tunago. Darian McBain, the company's director of sustainability, said Tunago is a very "proactive supplier" that is trialing electronic monitoring on its vessels.

"We were not aware of this incident in 2016, and are thankful that Tunago dealt with this criminal investigation professionally and in collaboration with the relevant authorities," McBain told Undercurrent.

Contact the author tom.seaman@undercurrentnews.com

title: Thailand first Asian country signing protocol to prevent forced labor
content:
Thailand's ratification of an international protocol to prevent and eliminate force labor reflects Thailand’s intention to improve labor standards, the country's government said.

The protocol, which was signed by a representative of the Thai government on June 4 in Geneva, Switzerland, will enter into force on June 4 2019, 12 months after the ratification.

Today, forced labour has evolved into complex situations that demand an updated response, the Thai government said. The 2014 protocol, which Thailand just ratified, was drafted to fill-in existing gaps, with special focus on the prevention, protection and remedy for victims of forced labor, it added.

Recently, two suspects of human trafficking on fishing vessels, were arrested in Thailand. The two suspects were accused of luring and forcing the victims to work on
board fishing vessels, the Thai ministry of foreign affairs said.

Meanwhile, Thailand's deputy prime minister emphatically stated that Thailand will be relentless in its effort to combat illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing (IUU) to reach the target of being an IUU-free country as well as to create a sustainable fisheries sector in parallel with its effort to solve the labor issues within the fisheries sector.

title: Belize strips Damanzaihao of flag, leaving it stateless
content:
In the latest setback for the colossal 50,000 metric ton vessel Damanzaihao -- the largest fish factory vessel in the world -- Belize has revoked its registration.

The International Marine Registry of Belize (IMMARBE) stripped the Damanzaihao of its flag, with NGO Sea Shepherd's legal department claiming credit. The vessel was stripped for failing to appropriately complete its vessel registration materials and notify Belize of its record of illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing, according to a statement.

Peru detains Damanzaihao over IUU allegations

The move renders the vessel stateless, according to Sea Shepherd, which has been working to get the vessel arrested and de-listed in the region.

Undercurrent News reported late last month that Peruvian authorities had detained the Damanzaihao, preventing it from leaving the country's waters until owner China Fishery Group answered to claims that the vessel previously operated there illegally.

“Sea Shepherd will work hard to ensure that other potential flag states follow suit should the Damanzaihao ever be allowed to leave Peruvian waters. If it ends up on the other side of the world, I hope it is in the form of paperclips, after it has been scrapped," declared Sea Shepherd’s Paul Watson.

The Damanzaihao, which is capable of processing 547,000t of fish per year, has been languishing in port since 2014 after having its mackerel fishing license stripped, said Sea Shepherd. It's now being held for a period of 70 days for allegedly polluting the Peruvian sea and for criminal charges relating to IUU fisheries crimes spanning from South America to New Zealand.

Ministerio Publico Fiscalia de la Nacion said fines for the vessel could be up to $7 million for the damage.

Peruvian prosecutors and ministry officials are actively working with Sea Shepherd to defend the ongoing detention of the Damanzaihao pending a criminal investigation, with a hearing on the detention status scheduled for Monday, June 14, said the NGO.

The financially troubled China Fishery said in a New York Bankruptcy Court, in April, that it would sell the controversial vessel to Singapore-based DVS-R. Sea Shepherd claimed it has received documents affirming the sale has gone ahead within Peruvian waters, despite the vessel’s intention to slip port prior to the completion of sale.

Over the past two weeks, the Damanzaihao had apparently twice requested permission to leave port in an obvious attempt to escape the tightening noose.

title: Chinese authorities bust smuggling gang over $7.8m of illegal goods
content:
Customs agents in Nanning, in southwest China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, have arrested 12 allegedly guilty of participating in a smuggling ring and seized more than 19 metric tons of seafood, reports Xinhua.

According to Nanning Customs, the suspects purchased seafood such as lobsters, crabs and squid and transported it to wharves without Customs offices in Guangxi to sell in domestic markets.

Over 500t of marine products worth about CNY 50 million ($7.8m) were estimated to have been smuggled.

The agency's anti-smuggling department identified the gang from evidence collected from several smaller smuggling cases since the beginning of the year, and arrested 12 suspects on May 28. The case is under further investigation.

title: CAPPMA: China shrimp imports worth $3.6bn, growth to slow in 2018
content:
FUZHOU, China -- China’s top seafood industry association reckons the country's shrimp imports were worth $3.6 billion in 2017, but forecasts slower import growth in 2018. 

Imported volumes amounted to approximately 400,000 metric tons of shrimp, an increase of 12% compared with 2016, according to the China Aquatic Products Processing and Marketing Alliance (CAPPMA). 

Of China's imports, about 360,000t was imported through the ‘grey trade’ with Vietnam, Cui He, president of CAPPMA, said at the Global Aquaculture Summit in Fuzhou. 

Although just a ballpark figure, he said, in 2017, "most of imports of shrimp to Vietnam were re-exported to China". He estimates 320,000t is shrimp imported by Vietnam then re-exported to China, with the rest farmed in Vietnam itself. 

Cui reckons with the clampdown on smuggling and lower tariffs, China will in future import more shrimp through official channels; three large anti-smuggling operations have taken place so far in 2018 to stem the flow, during which “a lot of criminals were arrested”, said Cui. 

Undercurrent News was first to report the huge scale of smuggling of shrimp into China from Vietnam, estimating 270,000t was smuggled in 2016. During his talk Cui also referred to an Undercurrent graph of Vietnam’s total seafood imports in 2016, which can be viewed here.

Remarking on the growth of shrimp imports, Cui said it is "worthy of our attention". 

“Ten years ago China was the biggest exporter. After ten years, China remains the largest producer, but now it's the second largest importer after the US. It is remarkable," he said.

However, this year Cui reckons Chinese shrimp demand growth will slow this year, a view shared by industry sources in the country, who recently told Undercurrent shrimp inventories remain high. Cui also pointed to the popularity of another crustacean, crayfish, as being partly behind this. 

"Consumption remains quite stable however if you look at the inland provinces, shrimp have been replaced by crayfish,” said Cui, noting that in May and June -- the peak in Chinese crayfish production -- "only a few consumers will buy shrimp". Recently, Undercurrent News reported the popularity of crayfish in China has caused problems for European importers, due to rising prices. 

According to Cui, China produced a massive 1.08 million metric tons of crayfish in 2017.

Chinese shrimp production lower

Cui said that China produced 1.2m metric tons of shrimp in 2017, down 6.3% compared with 2016. This comprised 500,000t of freshwater shrimp and 700,000t of marine water shrimp.

Chinese shrimp production. 

Another 100,000t of Chinese shrimp production is wild-caught, he said.

He said effective disease control is “still lacking”, although farming methods in north China, where there has been an increase in ‘comprehensive farming’, has helped "increase production efficiency", he said. Nowadays, most production is consumed domestically, in any case. 

"I cannot see a driver for growth of exports," he said.

Cui's shrimp production figures are considered somewhat on the high side, however, with other industry players estimating Chinese production is closer to 600,000t. 

Cui only made a brief comment on current low market prices, noting they "won't persist", forecasting that US purchases would pick up after the third quarter, as well as Chinese purchases, in time for the holiday season. "That will be the best time," he said.

title: Higher Norwegian salmon exports to China fail to offset slump to Vietnam
content:
Norway has seen exports of fresh salmon to China and Vietnam drop by just under a third, largely due to a crackdown in salmon smuggling from Vietnam into China.

Norway exported 2,811 metric tons of fresh salmon to Vietnam in the first 19 weeks of 2018, down 73% y-o-y. Although Norway's exports to China are up 840% year-on-year in the same period, overall exports to both countries are down 28% y-o-y to 7,791t, according to latest Norwegian trade data. 

In late March, Chinese authorities claimed they broke a $100 million salmon smuggling ring, which illegally imported fresh salmon from Norway into China through Vietnam. The crackdown severely curbed supply from Vietnam into southern China.

Weekly Norwegian trade data illustrates starkly the effect of the crackdown. 

In the seven weeks to the beginning of April -- prior to the crackdown -- Norway exported 1,228t metric tons to Vietnam. In the seven weeks following the crackdown export volumes slumped by two-thirds to just 404t (see graph).

Although Norwegian direct export to China have increased, prices may be less competitive than they were when the salmon was smuggled; smugglers avoid 22% in customs duties, approximately half comprising an import tariff and the other half value-added tax.

In addition, smugglers can also source from regions in Norway which remained banned from exporting to China, due to Chinese veterinary rules relating to pancreas disease in salmon. 

Indicating some market volatility presently, on Chinese wholesale markets prices have shot to above CNY 100 per kilogram ($15.70/kg) for fresh salmon from nearly all origins, with prices for Norwegian salmon (6-7kg fish) CNY 108/kg in Beijing, according to Fish First, a Chinese industry publication. Prices for Chilean product (6-8kg fish) are CNY 102/kg. 

Fresh salmon wholesale prices typically range from CNY 80-95/kg, depending on size and origin. Usually prices for Norwegian product are CNY 5-10/kg more expensive than from Chile. 

Two salmon importer sources in China this week told Undercurrent News still some quantities of smuggled Norwegian product are on the market in China. 

However, quantities are far below what they were last year; in the first 19 weeks of 2017, Norwegian fresh salmon exports volumes to China were merely one twentieth of volumes to Vietnam (see graph 2).

In their first quarter reports, neither Marine Harvest, SalMar, Grieg Seafoods nor Norway Royal Salmon provided a breakdown of their sales by country. After the crackdown, Norway's largest salmon farmers denied any connection with the trade. 

However, an arrested executive who Chinese customs allege headed the salmon smuggling ring was subsequently revealed by Undercurrent to have been in business with Norwegian salmon farmer SalMar.

Higher prices and volatile supply conditions has driven higher demand for imports through legal channels, as confirmed by Chilean sources recently.

title: ISSF calls for attention to yellowfin overfishing in the Indian Ocean
content:
The International Seafood Sustainability Foundation (ISSF) has urged tuna fishing stakeholders and regulators to address yellowfin overfishing in the Indian Ocean, ahead of the 22nd meeting of the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC), which will take place in Bangkok, Thailand, on May 21-25.

"Overfishing of the Indian Ocean yellowfin tuna stocks needs to end and effective management measures for all Indian Ocean tuna stocks -- consistent with advice from the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC) science committee -- are needed," ISSF said in a new position statement. 

In 2017, the IOTC agreed to amendments to the yellowfin tuna rebuilding plan. However, the impact of the yellowfin measure agreed in 2016, which only came into effect in January of 2017, has not yet been fully evaluated, and so it remains unclear if the amendments made will strengthen the rebuilding of the yellowfin stock. 

ISSF is concerned that while the IOTC has been progressing needed management regimes for the major tropical tuna stocks, there has been continued inaction to arrest the overfishing of other key IOTC species, including neritic tuna and billfish species that have been assessed to be either overfished or undergoing overfishing. These IOTC fisheries will experience further declines in stock status if no management actions are agreed, ISSF warned. 

ISSF called on IOTC to strengthen FAD management, including management of supply and tender vessels; ensuring full implementation of the requirement for non-entangling FADs; and the supporting of projects testing biodegradable FADs. It also asked IOTC to require 100% observer coverage on large-scale purse seine vessels.

The statement covers harvest strategies, bycatch and sharks, monitoring, control, and surveillance, compliance and capacity management.

The statement also includes ISSF’s top “asks” or requests of IOTC, along with a list of ISSF’s global priorities for all regional fishery management organizations. The full statement can be seen here.

title: Chinese salmon demand through legal channels drives price increase
content:
Prices for Chilean fresh salmon to China have been increasing in recent weeks, driven by a rise in global prices and a crackdown by the country's authorities on salmon smuggled in from Vietnam, Undercurrent News sources said.

Prices for fresh salmon (6-7 kilograms) from Chilean exporters have risen to $11-$11.50/kg in China, up from $10.70-$10.80/kg a few weeks ago, several Chilean suppliers told Undercurrent. "We are reaching record-high levels," one noted. 

Salmon prices were strengthening in all markets, including China and the US, another executive at a Chilean salmon farmer said at the Seafood Expo Global in Brussels last week. 

Brussels 2018: Chinese squid firm aims for 20-30% raw material market share

With less salmon being smuggled into China through Vietnam, demand has increased for fresh salmon through legal channels into the country, especially from Chile with which it has a free trade agreement, sources said. 

The increase in fresh salmon prices has also partially supported frozen salmon prices in the Asian market, which are rising towards $8/kg for frozen whole salmon of 6-7kg at airports in China.  

A Chinese importer said Chilean suppliers are currently quoting slightly higher prices for fresh salmon of $10.8-$11.8/kg for 5-6kg fish, and $11.8-$12.2/kg for 6kg+ fish.

On Chinese wholesale markets, in Beijing, where supply was largely unaffected by the crackdown, importer Sunkfa was offering fresh 6kg+ Chilean fish for CNY 85/kg ($13.37/kg) on Friday May 4.

In Guangzhou, where the supply of salmon has been most affected by the crackdown, Sunkfa's offer price was CNY 10/kg higher.

"This is the market price," Antuan Wang, sales manager at Sunkfa, told Undercurrent. 

The salmon smuggling scandal, which saw an executive with business links to Salmar arrested, immediately severely curtailed supply of salmon into China, sending prices for Norwegian product on wholesale markets in Guangzhou soaring to CNY 116/kg. Last week Fish First, an industry publication, said -- in order to plug a gap in supply in south China -- supply by Sunkfa and other large importers into the region had "doubled". 

An importer source told Undercurrent that smuggled salmon would be transported by truck as far north as Qingdao, but beyond this point, fresh salmon airfreighted into Beijing direct is cheaper. Qingdao is 500 kilometers southeast of Beijing.

Meanwhile, in the US, fresh salmon fillet is at around $6.10-$6.15/kg, sources said. Prices in May might stay at around this level, as Chilean offers are expected to remain stable. 

The Brazilian market, which was affected by the country's political and economic crisis, amid weakening of the local currency, remains an important market for Chilean salmon sales. In Brazil, during April, salmon of 10-12kg was priced around $7.30 "free of payment", and for May prices are expected to stay at around $8/kg, according to sources. 

Coho prices instead remained relatively stable, sources said. Headed and gutted coho of 4-6kg is priced at around $7/kg.

Chilean joint venture eyes Chinese market potential

Chilean salmon sales joint venture New World Currents (NWC) aims to increase sales to China 66% to 10,000 metric tons this year, its executive director, Eduardo Goycoolea, told Undercurrent News.

“The partners are managing to produce and offer more and the Chinese market is very demanding,” added the CEO of one of the partner companies. Marine Farm's entry into the joint venture also contributed to increases sales, another executive pointed.

“Already in the first four months of this year we are meeting the target,” he said, referring to the aim of higher sales.

“We are constantly improving logistics to china,” one of the sources also said, pointing out that transport of fresh salmon to China currently took four to five days, which is quicker compared to when the joint venture started to send fresh salmon to Asia. “One of the connections is through South Korea with Korea Airlines, but there are other routes, like through Australia or Canada,” he said.

title: Global shrimp prices continue to fall
content:
BRUSSELS, Belgium -- Farmed shrimp prices are still yet to hit the bottom as good harvests, high US stocks and China’s smuggling crackdown send chills through the global market, Undercurrent News sources said.

“2002, after 9/11, was the bottom for the shrimp market. We are not there yet, but we are not far off,” an executive at a large shrimp trading firm told Undercurrent at the Seafood Expo Global in Brussels last week. “The bottom is close, but prices are still falling in India, Thailand, Vietnam and Indonesia and they have gone down in China, too."

Sources say US inventories are still high after last year’s 10% increase in imports, but it’s China’s sudden and unexpected crackdown in smuggling of seafood from Vietnam since late last year that appears to have thrown a spanner in global shrimp trade. According to an executive at a large Vietnamese exporter, buying activity by China “completely stopped” in January.

By comparison, US shrimp import volumes were up 15% year-on-year in February of this year. 

Others say shrimp is still being transshipped in significant quantities into China from Vietnam, an illicit trade which is estimated to be worth well over a billion dollars each year and which executives had previously warned jeopardizes the shrimp industry. On the other hand, sources – and Chinese media – say police in China are still conducting raids and making arrests.

Meanwhile, European buyers are biding their time, the Vietnamese executive said.

“The markets are so quiet,” he said. “And the harvests in Vietnam and other countries in Asia are also very good. It is all making the shrimp price go down a lot.” 

India

India appears particularly exposed to a downturn, due to its greater reliance on the US market and large share of conventional, raw shrimp products sold on spot markets taking the biggest hit to prices, sources said.

“The market is really terrible,” Subbu Rajan, managing partner at VV Marine Products, a packer based in southern India exporting only raw head-on and headless shrimp IQF and frozen blocks, told Undercurrent. “Before Boston [North America Seafood Expo], around the end of February, both the export price and raw material price fell. As far as India is concerned it's a very tough market for export."

“If you're looking at basic raw material trading market, yes prices have dropped, there’s no doubt in that,” S. G. Nair, chairman and managing director of Forstar, a Mumbai-based shrimp packer, told Undercurrent.

He said those doing value-added are somewhat shielded from the fall in export prices, because more is sold according to long-term contracts, such as to supermarkets. Low raw material prices can be an advantage for some, he said.

However, the overall decrease has caused a rapid drop in raw material prices.

Farmgate prices in India have fallen to INR 270-280 per kilogram of vannamei ($4.04-$4.20/kg), 50 count, head-on, shell-on (HOSO), sources at the show said. Though this price is INR 30-40/kg higher than farmgate prices quoted by Durai Balasubramanian, secretary of the Pattukottai Shrimp Farmers Association in Tamil Nadu, earlier this month, it’s still “very low” and below costs of production, sources said.

“I think they [farmers] are losing about 20-30 rupees per kilogram,” said Nair. He said this is mostly the case for farmers in Andhra Pradesh and Orissa [Odisha] where harvesting is greatest at this time of year. “As far as a farmer is concerned that's a big sum.”

There will be no reprieve after a minimum price reportedly pledged earlier this month failed to materialize.

“[We are] very disappointed with the outcome," said Balasubramanian on Linkedin, in respect to the minimum pricing. "Most of the farmers in Andhra Pradesh suffered huge losses in the first cycle."

However an executive at a processor who wished to be quoted unnamed told Undercurrent the scheme was never likely going to take off because processors under financial strain typically will break ranks and offer lower prices than the minimum price, which farmers will accept, he said.

“I don't see any efforts being made on that front [minimum prices],” he said. “Prices are always market driven."

Vietnam

In Vietnam, raw material prices have also fallen. The Vietnamese executive said the global drop in prices has been exacerbated by the “very good” first main harvest of the year.

“It's been more and more [production] every month during the last twelve months. It's crazy,” he said. He said this was fine up to late 2017 when all the markets were buying. 

“But suddenly the volume kept increasing but the buying stopped. And smuggling problems in China stopped everything.” He estimated that since the beginning of the year at least $500 million worth of shrimp trade into China has been affected.

“Not only from Vietnam to China, but also India and Ecuador through Vietnam into China," have been affected by the smuggling crackdown, he said.

Some trade could be re-diverted direct to Chinese ports rather than Haiphong, but he noted the higher costs due to duties of around 12% -- which are avoided by smugglers -- may put off buyers. Another Chinese source importing fresh salmon told Undercurrent during the Brussels show that after years of smuggling smugglers “don’t know how to import the normal way”.

Despite Vietnam’s relative strengths in value-added production, still around 55% of shrimp exports are sold on spot markets, the executive said, exposing many Vietnamese firms to the downturn. He added both conventional and value-added shrimp products are sold on spot markets.

“Chinese mainly spot buy. They like negotiation. They like the feeling to buy cheap -- every time.”

He reckons farmgate prices for vannamei in the country are down 15% compared with the last quarter of 2017, and 10% down compared with the same period last year. Prices are “much below” the price of VND 90,000 per kilogram ($3.95/kg) of 100 count, HOSO shrimp, which he described as sustainable for Vietnam's industry.

Meanwhile, in Thailand, average weekly prices for 80 count vannamei shrimp have fallen to THB 135/kg ($3.71/kg), according to Undercurrent's prices dashboard.

Indonesia

Indonesian shrimp giant Central Proteina Prima (CP Prima) is also uncertain when global shrimp prices will bottom out. According to Arianto Yohan, director of CP Prima, US importers are asking for 10-20% discounts. 

Last year Indonesia was the US’ second-largest supplier of shrimp, meaning exporters generally follow prices received by India, the US’ largest supplier, he said.

In Indonesia, where raw material prices are typically higher, farmgate prices are currently IDR 68,000-70,000 per kilogram ($4.89-$5.04/kg) for 50 count vannamei shrimp, head-on, shell-on, Yohan told Undercurrent.

“[Global] shrimp prices are about what they were before the EMS [early mortality syndrome] outbreak in 2013. They’ve come full circle.”

Yohan attributed the price drop to high US stocks. Forecasting what will happen next is difficult, he said. 

“We tried to forecast prices last year. We thought prices would continue to go up. Actually, they came down.”

Farmers in Indonesia could reduce stocking due to lower prices although it’s unclear by how much. 

“They may seed their ponds a month later or so. Or they might reduce stocking densities,” said Irwan Tirtariyadi, president director at CP Prima. “It depends somewhat on how productive their ponds are. Areas where there are problems with disease, for those areas it may not be economical.”

However, there will unlikely be an imminent rebalancing of supply with many farmers set to harvest everything before Ramadan, which starts on May 15.

“There's a rush of volume in the system in Indonesia at the moment,” said Yohan.

title: Thailand: 11% of fisheries inspections have led to prosecution
content:
The Thai government says it has detected and prosecuted 503 cases of labor rights violations and 87 cases of human trafficking in its fisheries sector since the beginning of 2015, accounting for 11% of all the inspections carried out on vessels and in seafood processing establishments.

The numbers are part of a response provided to the group Human Rights Watch as Thailand continues to work to get out from under the cloud of a threat by the European Union, in 2015, to ban all seafood imports from the country. The advocacy group, based in New York City, had suggested Thailand needed to backup its words with more action. 

“As a result of the efforts, the overall situation of workers in the fisheries sector of Thailand over the past three years has drastically improved,” the letter says. “Nevertheless, the Thai government continues to pay close attention and try its utmost to increase the effectiveness of enforcement of those measures to ensure that workers in the fisheries sector receive full legal rights and protections.”

Thailand recounts how it has recently established special arrest teams  for fishing-related crimes at sea, which it says resulted in 50 cases of arrests between March 11 and March 22. The cases involved both Thai and non-Thai vessels, according to the letter.

Additionally, the country’s Ministry of Labor has worked with the International Labor Organization to develop a manual for labor inspections at sea, ports and seafood processing establishments. The government has promised to double the number of inspectors at its “port-in port-out” (PIPO) centers, while continuing to use new retinal scanning technology and increased inspections of employment documents.

“From 46,269 migrant workers in the fisheries sector interviewed at the PIPO Centers
in 22 coastal provinces in 2016, 3,222 workers were found to not have been treated in
accordance with the labour protection law and legal actions were taken against
the employers,” the government says.

title: Thailand sets up special arrest teams for fishing-related crimes at sea
content:
In March 2018, Thailand's deputy prime minister, general Chatchai Sarikulya, appointed five special arrest teams to inspect and arrest offenders of fishery-related and human trafficking crimes within the fisheries sector in 22 coastal provinces, according to a press release by the country's government. 

The measure aims to strengthen law enforcement in the fisheries sector.

The special arrest teams, which comprise officials from the royal Thai police, the department of fisheries and the ministry of labor, should speed up the arrests
of offenders at sea by utilizing in-depth information and intelligence.

On March 11-22 2018, the five teams arrested both Thai and non-Thai vessels conducting illegal activities in violation of the fisheries and labor laws, resulting in 50 cases that were prosecuted in both criminal courts and via administrative sanctions.

The 50 cases included 19 Thai vessels and seven foreign vessels on charges of labor and fisheries misconduct, and 24 vessels on labor-related charges.

"The special arrest teams have successfully achieved their mandate of arresting a number of offenders within a short timeframe. They will continue on this mission
and will provide further training to inspectors of the port-in, port-out control centers to strengthen their monitoring, control and surveillance capacities at port.
This is to ensure that the inspections both at port and at sea will apply the same
standard, and to deter any potential misconduct by enforcing strict inspections," the press release said.

title: National Fish’s Ventola to spend two years in prison
content:
Former National Fish and Seafood president Jack Ventola will spend two years in US federal prison on tax fraud charges, a court ruled.

Judge Douglas Woodcock handed out the sentence in Massachusetts District Court on Friday. In addition to the prison term, which was a year short of what prosecutors had sought but a blow to Ventola, who had asked for only probation, he will also spend a year on supervised release, pay a $75,000 fine and pay restitution of $1,073,470.

The sentence comes after Ventola's guilty plea to seven counts of making and filing a false tax return.

In November 2015, Ventola was first indicted on tax fraud-related charges with prosecutors alleging that he and three others -- National Fish executive vice president Richard Pandolfo, James Corbett, who headed the processor's operations and died in 2013, and Michael Bruno, an accountant who didn't work for the company but served on its board -- conspired in the 16-year scheme, which began in 1999. 

The scheme involved a temporary labor firm, Continental Labor Team, owned by Ventola and Corbett, that was used to bill Gloucester, Massachusetts-based National Fish for services never provided. The men used a network of shell companies to direct payments to a bank account controlled by Ventola, who then paid the others. Ventola, who pleaded guilty to seven counts, is accused of defrauding Hong Kong-based Pacific Andes International Holdings (PAIH) of at least $6 million during the 2007 to 2013 period alone and underreporting his income by $1m. 

Last week, Ventola's friends, relatives, employees and neighbors wrote 30 letters to a Massachusetts federal court urging a judge to sentence him to probation, not prison after his recent guilty plea.

The letters painted a sympathetic picture of a former US Marine and self-taught entrepreneur who bootstrapped his way into the seafood business and built National Fish into a 300-worker processor.

Undercurrent News: World’s 100 Largest Seafood Companies 2017
View report

Prosecutors took issue with that depiction.

"In the end, Ventola’s tax avoidance resulted in a loss to the federal government of just over $1 million. His theft from National Fish over the same period totaled nearly $6m. Ventola’s violations of the law were not occasional or opportunistic, but repeated and entitled," the memo states. 

Jessie Ng, the managing director National Fish's majority owner, PAIH, recently asked the court to consider sentencing Ventola to probation, not prison as he is a valued employee needed to restructure the business, she said.

Hong Kong-based Pacific Andes has been through tumultuous times since 2015
Read more

However, prosecutors added their own counterpoint to that request.

"Ng’s letter is carefully worded. While she notes that Ventola 'has promised to repay Pacific Andes and National Fish' and that this 'promised repayment fully addresses Pacific Andes’ concerns,' she stops short of suggesting that Pacific Andes was not, in fact, defrauded," the sentencing memo states.

Bruno, the accountant, pleaded guilty in October last year to tax fraud and wire fraud charges in connection with the schemes. He is yet to be sentenced.

Pandolfo also pleaded guilty last year. He was sentenced by US district court judge Richard Stearns to one year of probation with six months to be served in home confinement, a fine of $5,000, and restitution of $25,879.

Ventola was arrested on Nov. 23, 2015, in connection with failing to pay taxes on more than $2m in income he earned from 2006 to 2009, according to the US attorney’s office for the district of Massachusetts. He was indicted on three counts of filing false tax returns and one count of conspiracy to defraud the IRS.

title: Pacific Andes fears jailing Ventola could cause National Fish’s demise
content:
Friends, relatives, employees and neighbors of 72-year-old Jack Ventola wrote thirty letters to a Massachusetts federal court urging a judge to sentence him to probation, not prison, after his recent guilty plea to tax fraud charges.

The letters paint a sympathetic picture of a former US Marine and self-taught entrepreneur who bootstrapped his way into the seafood business and built Gloucester, Massachusetts-based National Fish and Seafood into a 300-worker processor. The letters describe him as a man of character always willing to help employees out of a jam, loyal to his community and church. 

Undercurrent News: World’s 100 Largest Seafood Companies 2017
View report

Amid those letters, one in particular stands out: a missive from Jessie Ng, the managing director National Fish's majority owner, Hong Kong-based Pacific Andes International Holdings (PAIH), which, alongside the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), was defrauded by Ventola and other National Fish employees to the tune of millions of dollars. Ng described Ventola as a vital employee for a financially troubled company in the middle of a restructuring.

Last year, a New York court overseeing PAIH's bankruptcy allowed a forbearance agreement signed between lender Cooperatieve Rabobank and National Fish's immediate parent company, the UK-registered Peaksville, to take effect. That agreement allowed Rabobank to run a sale process for National Fish after the company fell behind on $91 million in debt.

Ng didn't address that matter directly in her letter, but said PAIH has retained a restructuring firm in an attempt to tum the business around, adding that the firm lacks Ventola's seafood sector knowledge.

"Jack's continued employment as a senior executive of National Fish is, in my opinion, essential to our efforts to turn that company around. Furthermore, without Jack's presence at such a critical juncture, I am deeply concerned about the future of National Fish. The very livelihood of the many employees at National Fish is dependent on the future of National Fish being secured," she wrote.

Ventola was arrested on Nov. 23, 2015, in connection with failing to pay taxes on more than $2m in income he earned from 2006 to 2009, according to the US attorney’s office for the district of Massachusetts. He was indicted on three counts of filing false tax returns and one count of conspiracy to defraud the IRS. 

Ventola and two others, former National Fish senior sales executive Richard Pandolfo, and Michael Bruno, an accountant who didn't work for the company but served on its board, face charges that include tax fraud in connection with an alleged scheme that reportedly charged the company for labor services never provided.

Ng describes the matter differently.

"Despite the fact that "Pacific Andes and Jack have disagreed about certain items of compensation Jack received from or as a result of his employment at National Fish, Jack has promised to repay Pacific Andes and National Fish, and his promised repayment fully addresses Pacific Andes' concerns", Ng wrote.

Pandolfo and Bruno pleaded guilty. Pandolfo was sentenced to one year of probation, fined $5,000 and ordered to pay $25,879 in restitution. Bruno hasn't been sentenced but prosecutors agreed to recommend a to-be-determined fine and a prison sentence of not more than 37 months.

For the charges he admitted to Ventola could face a maximum of two-and-a-half years in prison, three years supervised release, a $250,000 fine and restitution. 

However, prosecutors will instead recommend a lesser prison sentence, a to be determined fine and $1.07m in restitution. 

Ventola's attorneys wrote in a sentencing memo that he has already paid $200,000 in restitution and is selling a vacation home to further this goal. 

Letter after letter described Ventola's good character, his attorneys wrote.

"He cared that a neighbor’s kid in college was trying to get back and forth to school and needed gas money. He cared that one of his employees had a brain tumor, and, unable to work, needed Mr. Ventola’s support. Mr. Ventola cared enough to become a mentor to a young hotel beach attendant he met while in Florida, Jason Brown, and keep in touch with him all the way from Massachusetts," the memo states. 

Scheme

Court documents suggest that the scheme Ventola and others are accused of ran from around 1999 to 2015, and while the amounts to which National Fish was billed haven't yet been provided, they could be substantial.

The indictment alleges that Ventola utilized the services of a temporary labor company called Continental Labor Team, which Ventola and a co-conspirator, who was also an executive of the seafood processor, controlled.

Ventola and an unnamed co-conspirator allegedly worked together to channel money out of Continental and into their personal bank accounts, tax free, prosecutors said.

To do this, the co-conspirator allegedly prepared fraudulent invoices for work supposedly done for Continental by a shell company Ventola controlled called International Freezing Systems (IFS). 

Ventola and an unnamed co-conspirator allegedly used the fake IFS invoices to obtain payments from Continental, which they deposited into one of Ventola’s personal bank accounts.

From there, Ventola used the funds to pay personal expenses and also wrote his co-conspirator personal checks approximately monthly.

Although the checks from Continental totaled more than $2m between 2006 and 2009, neither Ventola nor his co-conspirator reported the income on their tax returns, it is alleged.

The indictment also alleges that Ventola failed to report approximately $149,000 of other income he received in 2008 and 2009.

In a letter to the Massachusetts court from Ventola's wife of 49 years, Diane Lee, suggested thather husband's crime was mainly one of "negligence"

"As his wife, I found Jack too trusting when it came to the financials for the business. It is definitely not his strength. He would hire people to do his accounting and taxes. This decision costed him dearly," she wrote.

Ventola's lawyers too, laid most of the blame for the tax fraud at the feet of Bruno, the accountant.

"Mr. Ventola takes full responsibility for the offense to which he pled guilty. Notwithstanding, we submit it that the circumstances of the offense here, in particular Mr. Ventola’s good faith reliance on his tax preparer Michael Bruno—especially given that Mr. Ventola has only a 9th grade education, forms a just basis for a downward variance at sentencing," the lawyers wrote.

title: Editor’s recap: SalMar ties to alleged smuggler; Indian prices dive
content:
Tom Seaman, editorial director of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

The continued dive in shrimp prices in India was our most read story of the week, followed by revelations about the ties between Norwegian farmer SalMar to an executive arrested in China over her alleged links to smuggling, and Sam’s Club moving more business away from High Liner Foods.

In a break from the daily news cycle, we took a look at the innovations being developed for salmon farming, which could take the industry to the next stage in the future. 

Across the pond, we followed up on the impact of the deep cut for the total allowable catch (TAC) for the Gulf of Saint Lawrence snow crab fishery, which comes after news of a cut in the TAC for the Newfoundland and Labrador fishery.

As is often the case on Undercurrent News, news on mergers and acquisitions (M&A) also got a lot of interest. On Friday, we revealed that a buyout firm is in talks to buy Panapesca, one of Italy’s largest importers.

Earlier in the week, we reported Portobello Capital is getting ready to sell its 55% stake in Grupo Iberica de Congelados (Iberconsa), which it has built up impressively in two and a half years. According to our sources, Chinese multinational Bright Food is likely to be interested in bidding if and when the process gets underway. 

Diving shrimp prices

In India, the continued decline in shrimp prices has the industry worried.

On April 11, deputy editor Neil Ramsden reported both Thai and Indian shrimp prices are suffering steep slumps. 

India’s Andhra Pradesh pledges minimum shrimp price to protect farmers

In India, prices have been trending down through March and into April. Since the turn of the year, demand has been weak from the US, and while demand from China buoyed prices for smaller shrimp a while in February, this has not remained the case since.

Durai Balasubramanian, secretary of the Pattukottai Shrimp Farmers Association in Tamil Nadu, told Neil prices in Andhra Pradesh have fallen "below production costs" in April.

On April 12, Balasubramanian said the Andhra Pradesh farmers' union had met with exporters, and the latter had agreed to increase what they pay for 100-count by INR 30, "in order to protect farmers from losses".

He added that Andhra is currently experiencing problems "with white spot virus and vibrio", hence their early harvesting and proliferation of small sizes. "Many have made losses," he said.

Sam's goes direct on frozen salmon 

As High Liner loses more shrimp business in Walmart's club store arm Sam's, we revealed last week the chain is also going direct on frozen salmon, which means the Canada-based processor is being cut out. 

Sam’s Club cuts out High Liner on up to $40m of frozen salmon after shrimp shift

High Liner took on Sam’s frozen salmon business with its 2014 deal for importer Atlantic Trading Company, sources with knowledge of the process told me. Sources estimated the business is worth around $40m in total, which is still only a fraction of the $1.053 billion in sales High Liner made in 2017.

According to sources, BluGlacier, a US-based sales joint venture between Blumar and Productos del Mar Ventisqueros, is one of the companies Sam’s is working with. Norway-based Cermaq Group, which has farms and plants in Chile and is a significant frozen portion producer, is said to be another. Sources have also said Nova Austral could take on some business in the move.

What does the salmon farm of the future look like?

Neil Ramsden asked the above question and looked at some of the possible answers. 

Despite the push offshore and the developments with land-based farming, both of these are in the development stages. It's likely the long-term future of offshore farming will feature an amalgamation of those designs currently being tested, while – despite some optimism now – it remains to be seen if land-based aquaculture for the full grow-out cycle will be financially viable, Neil wrote. 

What does the salmon net pen of the future look like?

Then, in the near-to-mid-term, it seems likely that salmon farming will continue to be chiefly based in the coastal areas it has traditionally inhabited.

Trond Davidsen, president of the International Salmon Farmers Association, said as much earlier in 2018, noting that while closed-containment and recirculating aquaculture systems had parts to play, the most "climate-friendly" method at present was land-based post smolt production, raising juvenile salmon larger in biosecure facilities, before putting them to sea in open cages.

But that's not to say these cages will resemble those that were put to sea a decade or more ago; or even those we have now. There are numerous "aquatech" companies, established and startups, looking to make improvements to the classic net-pen formula.

Ranging from 'wrasse hotels', to flying net cleaners, lasers and microscopic water jets, the innovation in this field is truly fascinating.

Salmon smuggling scandal

The week before last, senior reporter Louis Harkell reported on a crackdown in China on a large salmon smuggling ring. Last week, I then worked with Louis to reveal the alleged ringleader of the ring is a lady named Yimin Dong, an executive closely tied and, in business with, Norwegian salmon farmer SalMar. 

Documents on the Singapore companies' registry list Dong as a co-owner of SalMar Pacific, which was registered at the start of this year. 

SalMar in business with exec at center of China salmon smuggling scandal

Dong was also listed by SalMar as the point of contact for its China office during an event organized by the Norwegian Seafood Council in Qingdao last year, before the China Fisheries & Seafood Expo, according to a document we obtained. On the document, she has a SalMar company email.

Official documents also show Dong, who owns 49% of SalMar Pacific, is a Norwegian citizen residing in Shanghai. SalMar founder Gustav Witzoe and Geir Waero, sales and marketing director, are also named as directors of SalMar Pacific. 

On April 9, Trond Williksen stepped down as CEO of SalMar, but denied this move has any relation with the scandal.

Speaking to the Financial Times, SalMar chairman Atle Eide said Dong has been instrumental in growing the market for Norwegian salmon in the region.

“She has been a close partner to SalMar . . . and well known to all in the business, as for numerous other salmon producers for more that a decade,” Eide told the newspaper, which also interview Louis for the article. 

“We believe she is innocent until otherwise proven. She has been instrumental to develop the position for Norwegian salmon in general in China and other south-east Asian markets for years and years,” he added.

Snow crab TAC cuts

Over in North America, senior reporter Jason Huffman reports that it’s decision time for prospective snow crab buyers now that Canada’s Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) has reportedly settled on an overall cut of 27% to its snow crabs.

Among others, Huffman spoke to Terry Hobbs, the owner of Kata Seafood, a snow crab seller with headquarters in Montreal, Quebec.

According to Hobbs, companies must either pay the premium $8 price now being commanded for five-to-eight ounce packages of snow crab legs and shoulders, or step to the side. But don’t expect the price to come down later, he said.

Cuts to TAC, Japan blitz pressure buyers of Canadian snow crab

That’s because Japanese buyers have reportedly already begun to pounce on the available crab, agreeably lining up to pay $7.90 to $8.00 per lb and buying four-to-eight ounce packages. American buyers who stay on the sidelines will have to compete later for whatever is left of the supply, Hobbs said. 

“They’re already here and they’re already shipping,” he said of the Japanese buyers. “There is already product going out today from [seaports] in Halifax [Nova Scotia].” 

DFO has determined it will set the snow crab TAC for the southern Gulf of St. Lawrence, including zones 12, 12E, 12F and 19, at 24,613 metric tons, a 44% cut from the 43,822t allowed there in 2017, Seafood News reported last Wednesday. A DFO official told Undercurrent to expect a formal announcement of the numbers in the next few days, though a letter sent to harvesters in recent weeks and shared with Undercurrent confirms the changes.

When added to the confirmed new 28,975t TAC for Newfoundland and Labrador area zones, a 17% decrease from 2017, and the combined 13,580t (5% less) expected to come from the Nova Scotia and northern gulf zones, that gives Canada an overall TAC of 68,275t, well below the 93,671t allowed in 2017.

PE deal, possible sale 

This week's recap ends with news of more M&A deals in seafood. 

According to our sources, a Luxembourg-based investment fund, Xenon Private Equity, is interested in purchasing 100% of Panapesca, one of Italy's largest seafood companies. The fund is said to be carrying out due diligence at present, sources told Matilde Mereghetti. 

Private equity in talks to buy one of Italy’s largest seafood importers

A deal, which is said to be contemplated at around €48 million ($59.1m), would make Panapesca the first investment in the seafood industry for Xenon, Matilde reported. 

The news comes as Madrid, Spain-based Portobello is reportedly looking to sell its 55% stake in Iberconsa, a hake, squid and Argentine shrimp catcher and processor with a turnover of close to $400m.

State-owned Chinese food conglomerate Bright Food (Group) is being tipped as a likely bidder. In May last year, Bright Food absorbed one of China’s largest state-owned seafood companies, Shanghai Fisheries (Group) General Corp.

Interestingly, Shanghai Fisheries has also been tipped as a possible buyer for a stake in Spain's largest seafood company Grupo Nueva Pescanova, which some of its bank shareholders are said to be looking to divest.

title: SalMar chairman: Exec detained for alleged smuggling key to developing Norwegian salmon in China
content:
The executive arrested in China over alleged salmon smuggling has been instrumental in growing the market for Norwegian salmon in the region, said Atle Eide, chairman of SalMar, which has established a company with her in Singapore. 

Last week, Undercurrent News revealed the identity of a woman arrested in China over the crackdown on the smuggling ring is Yimin Dong, who has represented SalMar in the market for many years.

“She has been a close partner to SalMar . . . and well known to all in the business, as for numerous other salmon producers for more that a decade,” Eide told the Financial Times. 

“We believe she is innocent until otherwise proven. She has been instrumental to develop the position for Norwegian salmon in general in China and other south-east Asian markets for years and years,” he added.

Eide said SalMar was setting up a joint venture with Ms Dong in which the Norwegian company had a majority stake.

The venture, SalMar Pacific, was registered in Singapore but had not yet begun operations.

“It goes without saying that SalMar has not been involved in any illegal export of salmon to China or to any other country,” Eide said.

SalMar’s chief executive, Trond Williksen, stepped down this week, but Eide said the decision was not related to Dong’s detention.

In its article, the Financial Times quoted Undercurrent's senior reporter, Louis Harkell. 

“'In 2001, Vietnam’s seafood imports were worth $25 million but in 2016, they were worth over $5 billion,' Mr Harkell said," the FT wrote.

title: COLTO: Arrests of illegal toothfish harvesters making a difference
content:
Richard Ball, chairman of the Coalition of Legal Toothfish Operators (COLTO), said the recent arrests of illegal toothfish harvesters is making a difference. 

“The transition over the last 20 years has been astounding. From the peak of illegal fishing in 1997, IUU fishing for toothfish has been reduced by 99%,” he said.

Ball's comments follow news that Liberia's coast guard seized the Hai Lung, a ship reported to be a “notorious Antarctic and Patagonian toothfish poaching vessel,” as it was transitioning through the West African nation’s coastal waters on March 13.

The vessel, which also has operated under the names Yele, Ray and Tropic, to name a few, has been blacklisted by a number of regional fisheries management organizations, including the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources, according to Sea Shepherd, an ocean conservation group. 

A big clue to the Liberian coast guard boarding officer that the ship was doing something illegal was that it handed him a certificate of Indonesian nationality that was allegedly issued on Aug. 8, 2017 by a senior ministry of transportation who was known to have been transferred to another position at the time, Sea Shepherd recounts.

Undercurrent News reported earlier the capture by Indonesian officials of a stateless vessel carrying 600 illegal gillnets in the Indian Ocean and believed to be employing slave labor. The vessel, previously operated by the Marine Fisheries Corporation Company and Jiho Shipping, has used multiple names, including STS-50, the Sea Breeze, Andrey Dolgov, STD. 2 and Aida.

title: Indonesia finally seizes IUU toothfish vessel carrying 30km nets
content:
Indonesia has seized an illegal toothfish fishing vessel which has evaded capture in several other countries, according to the country's fisheries ministry.

Acting on a request from Interpol, Indonesia seized the vessel and found it was carrying 600 illegal gillnets that can stretch up to 30 kilometers, Reuters reported.

Fisheries minister Susi Pudjiastuti stated the vessel was allegedly involved in organized transnational crime, based on Interpol's information. The STS-50 has also operated as the Sea Breeze, Andrey Dolgov, STD. 2, and Aida.

Based on documents published by Lloyd's List, the vessel is operated by Marine Fisheries Corporation Company and Jiho Shipping Company. Previously it has been registered to Red Star Company, Dongwon Industries Company, STD Fisheries Company, and Suntai International Fishing Company, the ministry said.

This ship is stateless, but had used eight different country flags including Sierra Leone, Togo, Cambodia, South Korea, Japan, Micronesia, and Namibia. It has been captured by the Chinese and Mozambican governments in the past, but fled each time.

When arrested, STS-50 had 20 crew consisting of 14 Indonesian citizens and six Russian citizens, including the captain. At least some of the Indonesians are thought to be victims of human trafficking.

title: SalMar CEO steps down after links to exec accused of China salmon smuggling emerge
content:
Trond Williksen is stepping down as CEO of Norwegian farmer SalMar, a few days after links emerged between the company and an executive accused of salmon smuggling in China. 

In a message to Undercurrent News, Williksen denied the China story has anything to do with his departure, however. 

"SalMar has completed a period of record results, and we have delivered a  considerable amount of value creation to the company's shareholders. I have had  a fantastic time in the company," he said, in a statement. 

"The task of heading SalMar is exciting but is also demanding. Those who know me, are aware that I have experienced a strenuous period over the past years, and I now want to focus more on myself for a period  of time," said Williksen.

According to a stock exchange note from the company, Olav-Andreas Ervik, who has served as director of farming for the company, will take over as CEO on April 10.

SalMar in business with exec at center of China salmon smuggling scandal

No mention is made of the alleged salmon smuggling operation in the stock exchange release. However, it has emerged that SalMar owns a company in Singapore with an executive who has been arrested in China, amid a crack down on the lucrative trade. 

"The board of directors regrets that Trond Williksen has asked for relief from his position as CEO. In his role as CEO, he has continued SalMar's efforts to be industry leading in biological production,” said Atle Eide, chairman of SalMar, in a statement. 

"Through his work, he has also contributed to the foundation on which to base a solid future development for the company," said Eide. 

Although the move is effective April 10, Williksen "will remain at the board's disposal" through his period of resignation, which is six months, SalMar said. 

Accused of salmon smuggling

Prior to the news of Williksen's stepping down, Norwegian business news site Dagens Naeringsliv (DN) reported Friday that a SalMar-linked executive, who is a Chinese woman and holds a Norwegian passport, was arrested in China suspected of involvement in the salmon smuggling ring. Authorities announced the bust last week, valuing the smuggling operation at CNY 620 million ($100m).

In Chinese media, the surname of the alleged ringleader of this group -- which was engaged in smuggling Norwegian salmon flown to Vietnam into China -- has been given as “Dong”.

DN does not name the executive, but Williksen told the news site that SalMar started a company with the accused woman. He did not name her, however. 

According to documents on the Singapore companies' registry seen by Undercurrent, Yimin Dong -- whose family name Dong is written with the same character "董" published in Chinese media -- is listed as the co-owner of SalMar Pacific, which was registered at the start of this year. She is listed on the document as a resident of Shanghai.

She was also listed by SalMar as the point of contact for its “China office” during an event organized by the Norwegian Seafood Council (NSC) in Qingdao last year, before the China Fisheries & Seafood Expo, according to a document seen by Undercurrent. On the document, she has a SalMar company email.

Dong, who owns 49% of SalMar Pacific, is a Norwegian citizen, according to the documents from the Singapore companies' registry. In addition to Dong, Gustav Witzoe -- founder of SalMar -- and Geir Waero, sales and marketing director, are named as directors of the company. Also, a Norwegian named Eirik Edvardsen; a British-born, Singapore based man named Stephen Fordham; and a Singaporian, Xu Lei, are also named as directors of SalMar Pacific. Williksen, however, is not a director. 

Norway salmon’s ‘big three’ deny any China smuggling links as prices rise

“SalMar Pacific is the company we were in the process of starting up together with Mrs Dong as a way to continue our cooperation,” Trond Tuvstein, chief financial officer of SalMar, told Undercurrent.

“She has been a business contact and customer of ours for many years, and she has also represented us in China on several occasions. We don’t have an office as such in China yet,” he said, despite the claim made at the NSC event last November.

Dong is “not an employee of SalMar, but she has had an account in our email system”, he said.

“As long as Chinese authorities are investigating trade of salmon and other products via Vietnam, it would not be appropriate for us to comment or answer questions publicly in this regards. You may find it useful to know, however, that SalMar has not been approached by any authority in this regard,” said Tuvstein.

title: SalMar in business with exec at center of China salmon smuggling scandal
content:
Additional reporting by Hu Luyi

An executive who represented SalMar in the Chinese market, and also co-owns a company in Singapore with the Norwegian firm, has been arrested over her alleged involvement in a salmon smuggling operation.

Norwegian business news site Dagens Naeringsliv (DN) reported Friday that a SalMar-linked executive, who is a Chinese woman and holds a Norwegian passport, was arrested in China suspected of involvement in the salmon smuggling ring. Authorities announced the bust last week, valuing the smuggling operation at CNY 620 million ($100m).

In Chinese media, the surname of the alleged ringleader of this group -- which was engaged in smuggling Norwegian salmon flown to Vietnam into China -- has been given as “Dong”.

Norway salmon’s ‘big three’ deny any China smuggling links as prices rise

“The Norwegian MFA [ministry of foreign affairs] has confirmed that a Norwegian national has been arrested in China. We will offer consular assistance in accordance with our rules. Apart from this we cannot comment on consular cases,” a spokesman for the MFA told Undercurrent News.

DN does not name the executive, but Trond Williksen, CEO, of SaMar, told the news site that SalMar started a company with the accused woman. He did not name her, however. 

According to documents on the Singapore companies' registry seen by Undercurrent, Yimin Dong is listed as the co-owner of SalMar Pacific, which was registered at the start of this year. She is listed on the document as a resident of Shanghai.

Dong was also listed by SalMar as the point of contact for its “China office” during an event organized by the Norwegian Seafood Council (NSC) in Qingdao last year, before the China Fisheries & Seafood Expo, according to a document seen by Undercurrent. On the document, she has a SalMar company email.

She is also listed as attending the NSC event as a representative of SalMar, on a separate document, which you can see below.

Dong, who owns 49% of SalMar Pacific, is a Norwegian citizen, according to the documents from the Singapore companies' registry. Her family name Dong is written with the same character "董" published in Chinese media.

In addition to Dong, Gustav Witzoe -- founder of SalMar -- and Geir Waero, sales and marketing director, are named as directors of the company. Also, a Norwegian named Eirik Edvardsen; a British-born, Singapore based man named Stephen Fordham; and a Singaporian, Xu Lei, are also named as directors of SalMar Pacific.

Chinese police uncover $100m salmon smuggling ring

“SalMar Pacific is the company we were in the process of starting up together with Mrs Dong as a way to continue our cooperation,” Trond Tuvstein, chief financial officer of SalMar, told Undercurrent.

“She has been a business contact and customer of ours for many years, and she has also represented us in China on several occasions. We don’t have an office as such in China yet,” he said, despite the claim made at the NSC event last November.

Dong is “not an employee of SalMar, but she has had an account in our email system”, he said.

“As long as Chinese authorities are investigating trade of salmon and other products via Vietnam, it would not be appropriate for us to comment or answer questions publicly in this regards. You may find it useful to know, however, that SalMar has not been approached by any authority in this regard,” said Tuvstein.

In reports online, Dong is also listed as the owner of Speed Gateway, a seafood importer. This firm imported 10,000t of Atlantic salmon in 2012, according to reports online.

“SalMar has no ownership in Speed Gateway. This company is a customer of SalMar,” Williksen, SalMar CEO, told Undercurrent.

Salmon smuggling

Norwegian salmon was smuggled into China in significant quantities as tensions between the two countries after the award by the Oslo-based Nobel Peace Prize committee to Liu Xiaobo, a Chinese dissident, in 2010, led China to effectively block direct imports of fresh salmon from Norway. 

In late 2016, China and Norway announced diplomatic relations had normalized, but direct trade did not pick up until late last year because of continued obstructions to trade.

During the first three months of 2018, Norway exported 4,482t of salmon to China, up 617% year-on-year, according to the country’s export statistics. Meanwhile, sales to Vietnam have dropped from 8,189t for January-March in 2017, to 3,454t for the same period of this year.

Also, China levies a 10% tariff on fresh salmon imports plus value added tax of 11% on net value. Importing CNY 100 worth of fresh salmon would, therefore, cost CNY 22.1 in duties. Other seafood products are smuggled when duties are less.

If convicted, Dong could face lengthy jail time. According to Chinese law, smugglers who evade duties worth more than CNY 500,000 face a minimum ten-year custody sentence, and a maximum sentence of life in jail, according to a notice published recently by Fish First, a Chinese industry publication.

Duties evaded through the salmon smuggling operation could amount to as much as CNY 137m, based on the CNY 620m estimated value of the smuggling operation. Others have been jailed for much less.

In May, 2016, a Chinese smuggler was sentenced to 12 years in jail and fined CNY 1m, for playing a key role in smuggling 212 containers of seafood into China through Vietnam in 2013-2014, evading duties worth CNY 13.9m. The Zhanjiang, Guangdong-based seafood company the smuggler was employed by also falsely claimed export subsidies worth CNY 32.9m, and was fined CNY 43m.

In March 2016, 11 smugglers from Fuzhou were sentenced to 3-14 years in jail. The group evaded CNY 35.7m worth of duties by under-reporting the value of 771 containers of seafood, and CNY 67.4m in duties by smuggling 755 containers of seafood from Vietnam. The Fuzhou-based company they were employed by was fined CNY 103m.
