title: Editor’s recap: Salmon smuggling; Pinneys fallout; China importer’s epic vision
content:
Tom Seaman, editorial director of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

Two big developing stories -- one on another UK plant closure and the second on a crackdown on salmon smuggling into China -- emerged last week.

On Tuesday, Young’s Seafood announced plans to close its plant in Annan, Scotland, which will mean the loss of 450 jobs and a major reshuffle in seafood processing for Marks and Spencer (M&S). If the plan goes ahead, several other suppliers pick up some of the M&S business from Pinneys and Young’s will also take on the retailer’s coated fish contract from Five Star Fish, which 2 Sisters Food Group plans to close.

The plan -- which will see jobs lost in Scotland and gained in England -- is already drawing ire from unions and politicians. However, sources told Undercurrent News it’ll make Young’s considerably more profitable, as the company’s investor owners are expected to kick off a sale process in the next few months.

Dawnfresh Seafoods, Blue Earth Foods and also 2 Sisters will take on business from Pinneys, if the plan goes ahead. The reshuffle comes as M&S’s chilled seafood sales are diving, as we reported April 4.

Then, on Thursday, Louis Harkell reported authorities in China claim to have busted an operation smuggling salmon worth approximately CNY 620 million ($100m) into the country. 

It’s been an open secret that a big chunk -- as much as 80%, according to some Undercurrent sources -- of the Norwegian salmon going to Vietnam was then being smuggled into China. The fish is flown to Vietnam and then smuggled into major Chinese cities on boats.

Norway’s direct sales to China have been rising and sales to Vietnam have been dropping, but it seems the authorities of the latter are keen to speed up the process of imports going direct, legally.

Marine Harvest, Cermaq Group and Leroy Seafood Group, Norway’s three largest salmon farmers, all issued denials to Undercurrent on any involvement in the trade. SalMar, however, was quiet. As reported by Undercurrent on Monday, an executive handling SalMar’s China sales has been arrested in connection with the smuggling ring. There will be more to come on the story this week.

Big Chinese importer eyes 100-year history

Prior to the salmon smuggling scandal breaking, Louis published a great interview with a senior executive of Sunkfa Group, which claims to be China’s largest seafood importer.

Louis met the firm’s Vicky Ma at the recent Boston seafood show, where she told him the company is rapidly increasing its imports of salmon and shellfish. Sunkfa has a very long-term view on the sector, Ma said.

Sunkfa claims to be the largest legal importer of salmon into China, as well as of lobster.

“In China there are not many companies which have been in the seafood sector for 30 years,” said Ma. “We are very envious of those 100-year-old companies in North America and Europe. We also hope one day to celebrate 100 years, have a brand with 100 years of history."

China’s largest lobster, salmon importer wants 100 years of history

Lobster -- Sunkfa's "biggest product", according to Ma -- is imported both live and frozen from the US, Canada, Chile, New Zealand, Australia, South Africa and Mexico. Imports of Boston lobster alone totaled 3,400 metric tons n 2017, up from 2,700t the year prior, said Ma. The firm's salmon imports -- both fresh and frozen -- totaled 8,800t. Fresh salmon imports come from six countries: Canada, Australia, Chile, Norway, the UK and Faroe Islands. 

The firm’s import share of frozen salmon can reach 10-15%, said Ma. Chile supplies close to 100% of the frozen salmon market in China. 

This year, the firm expects to import 4,500t of Boston lobster and 11,000t of salmon.

ISA at Northern Harvest

Some great reporting from our Jason Huffman on disease issues at Northern Harvest Sea Farms also got a lot of attention last week.

Marine Harvest’s deal for Northern Harvest, which would see the Norwegian giant become a big player on the east coast of North America, is also under the microscope at the moment. Not only in terms of possible competition authority issues, which Marine Harvest’s CEO told us he feels are non-existent, but also due to the infectious salmon anemia (ISA) problem at the Canadian farmer.

Newfoundland salmon farmer: ISA contained on eve of sale to Marine Harvest

Jason reported that Canadian government documents and satellite imagery suggest Northern Harvest’s recent discovery of ISA at one of its salmon facilities on the coast of Newfoundland is just the exposed point of a much larger outbreak for the St. George, New Brunswick-based company.

However, Larry Ingalls, Northern Harvest's CEO, told us this is not the case.  

"There has been multiple testing [for ISA] done on all farms over the past 60 days and all results are negative," Ingalls told Undercurrent in a brief email.

The message was the first response by Northern Harvest to multiple calls and emails after the Newfoundland and Labrador Department of Fisheries and Land Resources (DFLR), on March 30, confirmed that ISA was detected at the company's Spyglass Cove farm, near the town of Pool’s Cove.

A review by Undercurrent of DFLR records showed the nearly 50-acre site, with 15 net pens capable of holding a million salmon, likely received four transfers of smolts from three different hatcheries in 2017. One shipment from Northern Harvest supplier Dartek Hatchery, in Nova Scotia, was scheduled between Oct. 16 and Nov. 30.

As Undercurrent reported in early March, at least 500,000 young salmon had to be culled at the Dartek plant after ISA was detected there, as well as another 100,000 to 200,000 at another hatchery that had accepted a transfer from Dartek. 

The common thread means Dartek could've been the source of Spyglass’s ISA contamination, which is potentially bad news for at least three other Northern Harvest farms off the coast of Newfoundland that had permits to take transfers from the hatchery in 2017. Each is capable of holding about 1m fish, based on government records and satellite imagery.

US, China trade worries

As China cracks down on salmon smuggling, there are worries for seafood suppliers and buyers in the world’s second largest economy over the possibility of a trade way with the US.

On April 5, US president Donald Trump directed US trade officials to identify tariffs on $100 billion more Chinese imports, upping the ante in China-US trade hostilities. 

Tariffs on a further $100bn worth of Chinese goods would likely expand the scope of Trump’s attack to more consumer goods, as Reuters reported. The first round of US tariffs mostly targeted industrial goods and electronic components worth $50bn.

"The two biggest categories of US imports from China last year were communications and computer equipment, totaling $137bn according to US Census data," Reuters reported. 

Apparel and footwear, both labor-intensive industries in China, made up a combined $39bn in US imports.

Meanwhile, as Undercurrent recently reported, the US imported seafood from China worth $2.6bn in 2017.

Seafood industry smart to keep eye on US-China trade skirmish

“Hopefully they’ll just leave seafood alone,” Western Edge Seafood's long-time procurement manager Don Kelley told Undercurrent. So far, seafood has been spared in China and US's tariff tit-for-tat, although US seafood importers are closely watching the trade skirmishes.

On Wednesday last week, China announced plans to levy additional 25% tariffs on US exports worth $50bn, including soybeans. China did not say when the new tariffs would come into effect.

The US exported $12bn-worth of soybeans to China in 2017 (HS code 120190), according to International Trade Center, more than half of its total soybean exports. US soybeans are used in Chinese aquatic feed production.

China Fishery Peru sale update, anchovy quota

Several stories focused on the Peruvian anchovy fishery, on prices, volumes and the ongoing sale process for the China Fishery Group operations in the country also got a lot of interest from readers last week.

On Friday, Jason Smith, our America editor, reported that the limit on anchovy catches in Peruvian waters for the country's north-center fishing region has been set at 3.32 million metric tons.

The total allowable catch (TAC) is in line with the "very positive" forecasts that some, such as Pesquera Exalmar CEO Rosana Ortiz, have been making. Peru's marine institute has announced that the season will begin on April 12.

Undercurrent previously reported that Peruvian sources expected the north-center TAC to range between 2.5 and 3 million metric tons, most likely around 2.8m metric tons. 

During the past month or so, fishmeal buyers from China and other Asian countries have been buying large quantities of Peruvian "pre-sale" fishmeal under forward contracts for May/June delivery, sources told our Matilde Mereghetti.

Around 300,000t of fishmeal has been traded over the last month between Peruvian producers and foreign buyers, mostly from China, according to sources.

Prior to the announcement of the TAC, super prime fishmeal prices are firm at around $1,750/t, sources told Matilde.

title: Salmon prices in China spike, as prices for big fish in Norway drop
content:
Prices for fresh salmon in China have rocketed past CNY 115 per kilogram ($18.24/kg) for whole fish since the smuggling crackdown by Chinese authorities, while prices in Norway for bigger fish have dropped. 

Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou are all facing shortages of chilled salmon supplies, with severe shortages in Guangzhou, reports Fish First.

According to industry insiders, the recent salmon smuggling crackdown has been felt strongly in the market. “Some people recently have been like kites with broken strings," one industry source told Fish First. "Suppliers are no longer returning calls.”

On Sunday, April 8, whole, fresh salmon prices were no less than CNY 110/kg at major wholesale markets in Guangzhou and Shanghai (all origins), with prices as high as CNY 116/kg for 6-8.kg fish. In Beijing, prices were CNY 94-115/kg, depending on size and origin.

Early last week, salmon could still be found for CNY 88-CNY 98/kg in Beijing and Shanghai.

Meanwhile, prices for larger fish in Norway have fallen, as a direct result of the crackdown, reports iLaks.

"[Prices] have come down a lot. We have bought 3-6 kilo [fish] of NOK 67-68 in northern Norway. 6+ kilo [fish] is significantly lower, at NOK 63-65,” an exporter told iLaks, adding: "There is damn pressure on the big fish.”

Last week, Norway’s three largest salmon farmers told Undercurrent News they do not sell salmon to China via Vietnam, after a crackdown that has seen an executive linked with SalMar arrested.

title: Norway salmon’s ‘big three’ deny any China smuggling links as prices rise
content:
Norway’s three largest salmon farmers said they are not selling salmon to China via Vietnam, after a crackdown on smuggling from authorities in the world’s second largest economy that is causing prices to increase.

Marine Harvest, Cermaq Group and Leroy Seafood Group all issued statements to Undercurrent News refuting any involvement in the trade, after Chinese authorities claimed to have cracked an operation which has smuggled salmon worth approximately CNY 620 million ($100m) into the country. 

Chinese police uncover $100m salmon smuggling ring

According to a spokesman for Marine Harvest, the world’s largest salmon farmer, which is planning to establish a processing plant in Shanghai this year, the company has not been involved in selling salmon to China via Vietnam. 

“Since 2012 we have not been involved in shipping salmon through Vietnam, knowing that there was incidents of illegal export to China. This was a management decision valid for the whole group, based on our internal ethical principles,” the spokesperson told Undercurrent.

The company did not comment directly on why salmon in boxes labeled Marine Harvest were in Chinese news reports (see video below article).

Marine Harvest’s sales to Asia made up only 8% of the total in its fourth quarter, according to its recent report.

“Cermaq has not sent salmon via Vietnam to China,” a spokeswoman for the company, which is owned by Japan’s Mitsubishi Corporation, told Undercurrent.

The company’s “only sales to Vietnam are internal, last year we have sold 2 [metric] tons to Mitsubishi Corporation in Vietnam”, said the Cermaq representative.

“We have not sold any salmon to China via Vietnam,” said Henning Beltestad, CEO of Leroy. He declined to comment further.

For Leroy, sales to Asia were worth NOK 773.62m ($98.9m) in Q4, 16.9% of the total and up 12.1% year-on-year. No more detail is given on Asian sales, however.  

Beltestad also declined to comment on how salmon in boxes marked Scottish Sea Farms (SSF), which is joint owned by Leroy and SalMar, came to be found in operations in China accused of being involved in smuggling.

Jim Gallagher, managing director of SSF, told Undercurrent: “Scottish Sea Farms has been selling its premium farmed salmon to customers in China for several years now, exporting directly into the country with all the required documentation in place – both in terms of UK and Chinese customs regulation. In contrast, we have no dealings with the Vietnamese market and haven’t had since 2015."

SalMar founder Gustav Witzoe, as well as Trond Willeksen and Trond Tuvstein, CEO and chief financial officer respectively, did not respond to a request for comment from Undercurrent.

In SalMar’s fourth quarter report, the company said exports to markets in Asia rose by 19% to 12,300t. For the year as a whole, the volume of exports to Asian markets rose by 20%, the company said. 

Marine Harvest plans Shanghai plant as Norway salmon sales to China increase

The 2017 annual report for SalMar is not yet out. However, the company’s 2016 annual report states Vietnam, as well as Japan, South Korea and Singapore, is a “major” individual market in Asia for the company. Sales to Asia were 20.6% of the company’s total in 2016.

Andreas Kvame, CEO of Grieg Seafood, another large, Oslo-listed farmer which operates the sales joint venture Ocean Quality, also did not respond to a request for comment from Undercurrent.

In the Grieg Q4 report, sales to Asia are not broken out. The company’s 2016 annual report states Ocean Quality’s Asia sales were NOK 1.16 billion that year, 18% of the total and up 64% y-o-y.

Charles Hostlund, CEO of Norway Royal Salmon, the other large, stock-exchange-listed salmon farmer in the country, did not respond to a request for comment from Undercurrent. In its Q4 report, NRS said its sales volume to Asia was down 14% y-o-y.

Merete Kristiansen, sales director for Nordlaks, the largest privately owned Norwegian salmon farmer, said the company is not involved in the trade. 

“Our export to Vietnam is very limited. As you know, Nordlaks have been present at recent trade shows in China, where we have clearly stated to Chinese importers that we are not able to sell to the Chinese market before we are re-approved for export to China,” she told Undercurrent.

Last year, in total, Norway exported 23,085t of whole, fresh Atlantic salmon (HS code: 030214) to Vietnam, according to International Trade Center (ITC). This made Vietnam Norway's largest export market outside of the EU, according to ITC. 

“Around 80%” of the salmon Norway sends to Vietnam is then smuggled into China, an executive with a Chilean salmon supplier, who spoke under an agreement of anonymity, told Undercurrent.

'Hole in the market'

According to industry sources, the Chinese government crackdown on salmon smuggling has created a gap in the market that has to be filled with legally imported fish.

Chinese wholesale prices for Norwegian product have risen above CNY 100 per kilogram ($15.86/kg), reports Fish First, a Chinese industry publication, since the crackdown.

Prices for Chilean fish have risen above CNY 97/kg, industry sources told Fish First, after “big increases”.

According to Fish First, the week prior to the smuggling crackdown, prices were CNY 93/kg for Chilean product (5-6 kilogram fish), and in the mid-90s for 6-7/kg fish. Prices for Norwegian product were also in the high 90s.

Prices have not yet hit highs seen during Chinese New Year, when wholesale prices for fresh salmon jumped almost 30%. 

"It’s leaving a big hole in the market that has to be filled with legal fish," the Chilean executive told Undercurrent. "Customers are calling us for more salmon. The owners of two importers we know were arrested. Everyone knows this is happening, but they were letting it go. It seems they have decided to stop it."

A market insider told Fish First the present period is a "key time", referring to the smuggling crackdown.

For some companies "necessity knows no law", said the source, and they continue to import through informal channels, causing "market disorder". "At least half of product on the market is smuggled," the source said. 

Both higher raw material prices abroad and the smuggling crackdown were to blame for the price rises, a source at a large Chinese importer told Undercurrent.

“It’s both factors, and they interact,” the source said.

One Wechat user, presumably a buyer, commented: "Which importers use legitimate channels? How can I contact them?"  

China levies a 10% tariff on fresh salmon imports plus value added tax of 11% on net value. Importing CNY 100 worth of fresh salmon would, therefore, cost CNY 22.1 in duties. Other seafood products are smuggled when duties are less.

According to Chinese officials, smuggling groups procure salmon at source, such as in Norway, have it flown to Vietnam, use a logistics company to transport the salmon to the border with China, a smuggling group to transport the salmon across the border, and then transport it onwards to Guangzhou, Shanghai, Shenzhen, Beijing and other cities for sale.

Norwegian salmon suspected

Another industry source in China told Undercurrent Norwegian salmon is especially prone to being smuggled because of restrictions on which areas salmon can be sourced from.

As of early March, three major salmon producing provinces in Norway -- Sor Trondelag, Nordland and Troms – were still suspended from exporting to China, due to the presence of pancreas disease (PD). Chinese veterinarian authorities were due to head to inspect the three provinces last month. 

Norway salmon sales JV barred from China exports

One firm, Ocean Quality, a joint venture between Grieg and Bremnes Seashore, was recently “excluded” from sales to China, after it had expoted salmon from areas which had PD. 

The company had supplied incorrect information to Norway’s food safety regulator, said Grieg, in a note to the Oslo stock exchange in early February.

The company, which is 60% owned by Grieg and 40% by Bremnes, received a decision from the Norwegian Food Safety Authority (NFSA) “implying that Ocean Quality is excluded from exporting to China on the basis that it has been provided incorrect information to the NFSA in connection with such export”, said Grieg. 

Scottish salmon

Photos from police raids published by Chinese media showed salmon in boxes labeled Marine Harvest. The boxes carried the 'royal crest' sign unique to Scottish salmon, indicating the salmon was from Marine Harvest Scotland. 

Shanghai-based national broadcaster News24 broadcast police filmed inspecting the Marine Harvest salmon, and also salmon with SSF in product documentation (see below). 

CCTV, China's state-owned broadcaster, also broadcast the police raid.

The police investigation is ongoing.

Food safety risks associated with smuggled food were reported by both CCTV and News24. 

"Suspects often use standard containers to transport the product, causing frozen products to defrost, affecting quality. This is extremely dangerous for food safety,” said CCTV.

However, Norway's direct salmon exports to China are on the rise, on the back of improving Norway-China trade relations disrupted for several years. In the first two months of 2018, Norway was the largest direct supplier of whole, fresh Atlantic salmon to China, according to recent Chinese and Norwegian customs data.

The UK's direct fresh Atlantic salmon exports to China were worth $87.8m in 2017, according to ITC. By comparison, UK fresh salmon exports to Vietnam were worth far less at $7.3m, according to ITC.

title: Chinese police uncover $100m salmon smuggling ring
content:
Chinese customs police say they have uncovered smuggling rings in China which illegally imported Norwegian salmon worth up to CNY 620 million ($98.4m).

According to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV, in the early hours of March 27, customs police in Guangzhou conducted coordinated raids of suspected smuggling operations in Beijing, Shanghai, Guangdong, Guangxi, and Fujian.

Boom in ‘grey trade’ drives Vietnam’s seafood imports from $25m to over $5bn

During the raids, which also uncovered seafood products from Indonesia, Ecuador and West Africa, as well as beef, chicken and pork, police arrested 17 individuals from seven different groups suspected of smuggling salmon, the report states.

Guangzhou customs deputy director Zheng Jun told CCTV: “Presently this group, through avoiding customs and smuggling, and quoting low prices, imported smuggled salmon from Norway worth approximately CNY 620m.”

Other Chinese media report smuggled salmon was from other countries, too. 

In the CCTV news segment, police are filmed during one such raid inspecting fresh salmon in a cold storage facility. Several Chinese media outlets say the value of the salmon found during the raid was CNY 12.6m.

In the video, according to information printed on salmon boxes, the salmon is 7-8 kilograms, ‘superior’ grade and had been packed on March 23, just four days prior to the police operation (see photo below). 

The boxes also show an address in Shenzhen -- a large city in Guangzhou -- which Undercurrent News presumes is the delivery address. The destination country is written as People's Republic of China. 

Credit: CCTV News

The police investigation is ongoing, Chinese media report.

"We have registered the stories in Chinese media that irregularities in the trade of several products as pork, beef, chicken and seafood, including salmon from a number of countries, is currently under investigation by Chinese authorities," Norwegian Seafood Council’s China program director, Sigmund Bjorgo, told Undercurrent.

“As this is an ongoing police inquiry, we do not have any further comments on this matter."

Photos published by several Chinese news media outlets show salmon packed in boxes labelled Marine Harvest. The boxes also carry the ‘royal crest’, which is unique to Scottish salmon and suggests the salmon was from Marine Harvest Scotland, however. 

"Marine Harvest has not been involved in any smuggling of salmon to China. Since 2012 we have not been involved in shipping salmon through Vietnam, knowing that there was incidents of illegal export to China. This was a management decision valid for the whole group, based on our internal ethical principles," a company spokesman told Undercurrent. 

Direct imports increasing

Undercurrent has, in the past, identified Norwegian salmon as one of several key seafood products imported into China through informal channels -- particularly through Vietnam -- given strong evidence of this. 

However, with Norway-China trade relations improving after several years of disruption, Norway's direct salmon exports to China are on the rise. According to recent Chinese and Norwegian customs data, in the first two months of 2018, Norway was the largest direct supplier of whole, fresh Atlantic salmon to China. 

The UK also exports whole, fresh Atlantic salmon to Vietnam; last year, exports to the Southeast Asian country totaled $7.3m, according to International Trade Center (ITC).

However, UK direct fresh Atlantic salmon exports to China were worth far more at $87.8m, according to ITC.

title: China’s largest lobster, salmon importer wants 100 years of history
content:
BOSTON, Massachusetts, US -- At the Seafood Expo North America, where buying and selling of seafood takes place on a massive scale, Vicky Ma casts an envious glance at companies from North America and Europe, whose exhibitor stands tower over those from Latin America and Asia.

It is not their size which impresses -- Ma's own stand is big for a company which has turned up just to buy seafood -- but their history, Ma tells Undercurrent News.

Tales of company founders who first hauled up a lobster trap over a hundred years ago and began a fishing dynasty, or a trader who sold squid from a cart in New Jersey in the 1960s and 1970s, and whose son now imports cephalopods from all over the world, are beguiling.

Vicky Ma on the prowl for products to import to China. Credit: Undercurrent News

Certainly, China has farmed fish for centuries, possibly millennia. But despite the country’s rich history, market reforms started in 1978 meaning most present-day private Chinese companies are relatively young.

“In China there are not many companies which have been in the seafood sector for 30 years,” said Ma. “We are very envious of those 100-year-old companies in North America and Europe. We also hope one day to celebrate 100 years, have a brand with 100 years of history."

Her firm -- Beijing-based Sunkfa Group -- is well positioned to fulfill its goal.

According to Ma, vice president at Sunkfa, the firm is China's largest importer of lobster, the largest importer of salmon (when excluding trade through informal channels, she says), and one of the largest importers of crab, abalone and several other species of shellfish and molluscs. 

Last year, China imported well over a $1 billion worth of lobster (all species). Meanwhile, China is tipped to become a future salmon consumption giant.

Lobster -- Sunkfa's "biggest product", according to Ma -- is imported both live and frozen from the US, Canada, Chile, New Zealand, Australia, South Africa and Mexico. Imports of Boston lobster alone totaled 3,400 metric tons n 2017, up from 2,700t the year prior, said Ma. The firm's salmon imports -- both fresh and frozen -- totaled 8,800t. Fresh salmon imports come from six countries: Canada, Australia, Chile, Norway, the UK and Faroe Islands. 

The firm’s import share of frozen salmon can reach 10-15%, said Ma. Chile supplies close to 100% of the frozen salmon market in China. 

This year, the firm expects to import 4,500t of Boston lobster and 11,000t of salmon.

Sunkfa Group's Beijing HQ

After lobster comes crab, said Ma, another Chinese favorite, including brown crabs from the UK and France. Sunkfa accounts for 30% of the brown crab market in Beijing and the country’s north, and around 25% of the market in Shanghai and Guangzhou, she said. It has also done “very well” importing Dungeness crabs from the US and Canada.

Two other crab species -- king crab and champagne crab, from Russia and Australia respectively -- are also mostly imported by the firm. “If you eat these crabs in China, there’s a very good chance you’ve eaten those supplied by our company," said Ma, although recent global production has been "very low and prices are rising fast".

In 2016, the firm accounted for 50% of China's imports of Chile's king crab volume, she said. "At that time, the Chilean embassy in China invited our boss to talk because we imported three products from Chile and accounted for a very large share. We still make a relatively large contribution to Chile's economy."

She said Sunkfa now has several frozen products with which it has "influence in the market": frozen Canadian lobster, green mussels, Chilean king crab and frozen salmon. 

Sunkfa also sells locally-produced turbot, carp, greasy-back shrimp, and baby abalone. In 2017, baby abalone was one of its most popular domestically-produced products. "We've done pretty well with this," she said. It also recently launched sales of South Pacific bluefin tuna.

It is a big transformation for the firm considering its roots, Ma muses. 

Established in 1989, Sunkfa started out transporting seafood from the country’s aquaculture and fishing hub in the south, to the country’s north. “It was the first time people from the north could eat these sort of things. Not just beef, pork, and chicken,” said Ma, who is herself from north China. 

Because the government did not permit private companies to import goods, the firm relied on import licenses of state-owned enterprises such as CNFC Overseas Fisheries, Shanghai Fisheries Corporation, and Beijing Fisheries Corporation, she said. 

Today foreign companies come to Sunkfa to help get licenses to export to China. 

Wholesale focus

Ma said Sunkfa's strong growth is owing to its relative experience in the business and well-established distribution networks. In China's sprawling market, it knows its way around.

Sunkfa's 21 service centers

The firm has also focused on supplying the wholesale market, which still handles the vast majority of imported seafood sales in China.

Sunkfa distributes imported seafood to 122 seafood wholesale markets in China in first, second and third-tier cities, operates 21 service centers, three 'first-level cold storage warehousing' centers in Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou, and four 'second-level cold storage warehousing' centers in Wuhan, Xi'an, Fuzhou and Zhengzhou. It serves the country’s largest seafood markets in Beijing (Beijing Jingshen Seafood Market), Shanghai (Shanghai Jiangyang Seafood Market), Guangzhou (Guangzhou Huangsha Aquatic Market), and Chengdu, next to which it also has nine of its own stores for direct sales.

In 2016, Sunkfa also established its own B2B online seafood marketplace called "ewfresh". It also has a processing plant in Dalian, which opened in 2015. The plant produces salmon steaks, portions and fillets for the domestic market, sold under its own brand. At an R&D center in Beijing, Sunkfa develops new products for China’s growing middle-class.

The firm still deals mainly with wholesalers, Ma said. However, it also does some direct sales to hotel-type customers and retailers, including Hema -- the Alibaba-owned stores -- and Yonghui Superstores -- a large retailer which recently invested $85 million in Chinese shrimp company Zhanjiang Guolian Aquatic Products. Sunkfa does not presently sell directly to Chinese consumers. “Businesses have their business channels, we want to leave some space for our [wholesale] customers,” said Ma.

"We have been professionally and carefully managed," said Ma. “When China allowed private companies to import from the 1990s onwards, we were the early bird to catch the worm. We have been doing this ever since.”

Future growth

One industry source in China described Sunkfa’s market strategy to Undercurrent as “very aggressive”. But, while Sunkfa has clearly profited from China's surging seafood imports, the firm could now face its reckoning. 

Chinese e-commerce and tech giants Alibaba, JD.com and Legend Holdings are targeting the sector. Using big data, huge distribution networks and piles of cash, they've muscled in on retail and online sales, and also made upstream investments abroad. Alibaba's Hema stores -- branded part of 'new retail' -- offers to cook seafood bought by customers in-store and unique "store experiences". 

The firms source seafood direct, potentially threatening Sunkfa's business model. 

Alibaba's Jack Ma at a Hema store

Yet Ma is unfazed by the challenge. She points out that Alibaba and JD mainly do B-2-C, whereas in China seafood is still largely consumed in hotels and restaurants, which are supplied by wholesalers. 

She points to the example of lobster. "Chinese people don't really know how to cook lobster at home, they just know how to boil it,” she said. “They wouldn't know how to cook it properly, spice it, add flavor. So they prefer to eat lobster at restaurants or other foodservice outlets.”

The firm also has its own plans. Last year it spent “a huge amount of money” on an enterprise resource planning system for the entire group. On her phone, Ma draws up a wealth of data relating to the firm’s sales, profit margin, seafood pricing, including by species and regions, displayed in slick charts and graphs.

“We try to rely on science and technology to do analysis. I believe we are ahead of most Chinese seafood companies in this respect.”

Other plans for 2018 include technological advancement -- "online sales are the future in China," she said -- and centralizing the firm’s distribution networks around Zhengzhou, a hub for air cargo in and out of China.

The smuggling challenge

Sunkfa has arguably faced far tougher challenges, too. 

It is no secret China has a problem with seafood smuggling, also known as the 'grey trade', particularly through Vietnam and Hong Kong. Legitimate importers complain they're undercut by this illicit trade because smugglers don't pay Chinese customs duties and import inferior products. 

Boom in ‘grey trade’ drives Vietnam’s seafood imports from $25m to over $5bn

Cui He, head of China's Aquatic Products Processing and Marketing Alliance, recently told Undercurrent some big Chinese firms purposely avoid the seafood import business because of the problem. 

Indeed, Sunkfa has also suffered at the hands of the 'grey trade'. In the past, it was one of five companies which imported Greenland halibut.

“We originally did a great job with this product. But for a company like ours, which reliably pays import duties, which for [Greenland halibut] is 5%, plus value added tax of 13% [prior to a reduction in VAT rates in last July to 11%], we had to pay duties of 18%. So for every CNY 100 we paid CNY 18 in duties.”

“They [smugglers] didn't pay it. They certainly had to cover other small expenses, but it's very small," she said.

As a result, the firm "had no choice but to stop doing this product", said Ma. "For those who use legitimate channels it's extremely unfair." 

Shrimp trade shift hints at Chinese smuggling crackdown impact

Hence, the firm makes a conscious effort to source as much seafood from countries with free trade agreements, such as New Zealand, Australia, and Chile, "so we have no obvious disadvantage compared with informal channels". 

But Ma reckons the writing is on the wall for smugglers.

The Chinese government is “cracking down”, she said. “Every year there are arrests. It’s very risky.” Furthermore, because imports are not subject to Chinese veterinary and food safety inspection, importers using informal channels cannot guarantee quality, she added.

China directly imported $7.1bn of seafood (everything under HS code 03, not including fishmeal, fish oil or canned fish) in 2017 from top-20 origins, according to Chinese customs. Although a large portion was re-exported after being processed in Chinese factories, increasing quantities are being consumed in the country.

Top-three origins were Russia, the US and Canada.

Alfonsino (New Zealand)

title: Tax evasion sentencing delayed for former National Fish president Ventola
content:
Jack Ventola, the former president of National Fish & Seafood, was not sentenced in Boston, Massachusetts, on Monday for seven counts of tax evasion, as expected. Instead, US district court judge Douglas Woodlock granted a request by Ventola’s attorneys for more time to craft a position and submit objections to the government’s pre-sentence report, the Gloucester Times reports.

Ventola is now scheduled to be sentenced on April 27.

As Undercurrent News reported, Ventola was arrested on Nov. 23, 2015, initially in connection with failing to pay taxes on more than $2 million in income he earned from his Gloucester, Massachusetts-based company during the years 2006 to 2009. Prosecutors have dropped charges of conspiracy, wire fraud and mail fraud.

A US bankruptcy court, in October 2017, ordered Hong Kong-based conglomerate Pacific Andes International Holdings to sell National Fish after the company fell behind on its $91m in obligations to Dutch lender Cooperatieve Rabobank.

title: Shrimp trade shift hints at Chinese smuggling crackdown impact
content:
Additional reporting by Matilde Mereghetti

Chinese customs officials and police continue to arrest smugglers involved in the seafood 'grey trade' between China and Vietnam. The latest trade data suggests trade flows have been impacted.

Boom in ‘grey trade’ drives Vietnam’s seafood imports from $25m to over $5bn

Since China’s highest customs authority spearheaded raids of suspected seafood smuggling operations nationwide in late December, Chinese authorities continue to make arrests in key smuggling areas. In March, authorities announced arrests in Guangzhou and Dongxing, according to Fish First, a Chinese industry publication.  

In Guangzhou, the provincial capital of Guangdong province, police seized 20 metric tons of smuggled seafood, including de-headed vannamei shrimp from India and Ecuador (see main photo). In Dongxing, a Chinese border town with Vietnam, customs officials and police seized 6t of frozen eels and shrimp, and 10t of fresh crab, after a series of arrests in the area.

Photos of arrested individuals in front of police in Dongxing were published as a warning to existing or would-be smugglers (see photo).

The arrests come as Undercurrent News recently estimated annual grey trade between Vietnam and China of top seafood products -- shrimp, pangasius, toothfish, rock lobster, salmon and Greenland halibut -- to be worth more than $2 billion alone. Besides avoiding customs duties, smugglers also circumvent Chinese food safety inspection and quarantine.

China has lowered import duties on a range of popular seafood items to reduce smuggling incentives; import duties for shrimp are just 2%, after they were reduced from 5% on Dec. 1. The impact of both measures, although perhaps still too early to assess fully, does appear to be altered trade flows.

Still large quantities of seafood are being shipped to Vietnam, according to trade data. But, direct exports of shrimp -- the most-smuggled seafood product -- to China have increased. 

Trade flows

According to Ecuador's Cámara Nacional de Acuacultura, Ecuador exported 3,307t of shrimp directly to China in January of this year, up 246% compared with January of 2017. More up-to-date Chinese customs figures -- for January-to-February -- show China's direct imports of Ecuadorian shrimp increased 103% year-on-year to 2,356t. 

Ecuador is China's largest shrimp supplier through Vietnam. Ecuador still exported far more shrimp to the Southeast Asian country: 13,496t in January, although exports were down 7% compared with January 2017. 

China's direct imports from Argentina were also higher for January-Febuary, up 201% y-o-y to 5,833t, according to Chinese customs figures. In December, Argentina exported 946t to Vietnam, according to latest available figures from International Trade Center.

title: South Africa hopes tough jail terms for abalone poachers are deterrent
content:
South Africa’s National Prosecuting Authority is hoping tough jail terms for four abalone poachers will be a deterrent to others, reports Eyewitness News. 

The men have been handed sentences of between five and 15 years, while a fifth man was handed a one-year sentence, suspended for five years.

Sentencing was handed down on March 12, about 12 years after police arrested them at an abalone processing facility.

The men, initially part of a group of nine accused, were arrested after they were found in possession of more than 82,000 units of abalone at a coldstorage facility in Cape Town in 2006.

title: Notorious toothfish poacher arrested in Liberia
content:
An Antarctic and Patagonian toothfish poaching vessel was arrested on March 13 in waters belonging to the West African state of Liberia by the local coast guard, with assistance from NGO Sea Shepherd, the latter said. 

The F/V Hai Lung, known to the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR) by its previous name Kily, was transiting through Liberian waters when it was boarded and inspected by a Liberian coast guard team, working alongside Sea Shepherd’s patrol vessel Sam Simon.

Operating under a long list of different names -- including Yele, Ray, Kily, Constant, Tropic and Isla Graciosa -- the F/V Hai Lung is an "infamous" fishing vessel that has been blacked-listed by several regional fisheries management organizations including CCAMLR and the North East Atlantic Fisheries Commission.

As a result, the vessel has been denied port access in Togo and Angola, and unofficial sources state it was detained in Nigeria for entering its waters without authorization last year.

title: Former National Fish sales director pleads guilty to Sea Star fraud
content:
James Faro, the former director of sales for US processor National Fish and Seafood, has pleaded guilty in connection with a scheme to commit bank fraud relating to Sea Star Seafood Corporation, his previous company.

According to a statement from the US Department of Justice (DOJ), Faro and John Crowley -- who was chief financial officer for Marlborough, Massachusetts-based Sea Star -- both pleaded guilty on March 12.

In plea deal, former National Fish president likely to pay $1m in restitution

Judge Timothy Hillman scheduled their sentencing for June 8 and June 13, 2018, respectively.

Faro and Crowley were not immediately available for comment to Undercurrent News.

Although Faro is still listed on Linkedin as sales director for National Fish, Todd Provost, the company’s president, confirmed to Undercurrent he no longer works there.

Provost said Faro left between 30-60 days ago. According to Linkedin, Faro had joined National Fish -- which is majority owned by troubled, Hong Kong-based conglomerate Pacific Andes International Holdings and is now for sale -- in 2012. He’d founded Sea Star in 1983, a company previously headquartered in Marlborough, that distributed frozen seafood products.

From October 2010 until August 2012, Sea Star maintained an asset-backed loan agreement whereby a bank agreed to loan Sea Star up to $6 million pursuant to a revolving line of credit. Sea Star pledged its assets – most notably its inventory and accounts receivable – as collateral for the loan, according to the statement.

Between November 2010 and August 2012, Faro and Crowley conspired to intentionally overstate the value of Sea Star’s outstanding accounts receivable that it reported to the bank, according to the DOJ.

By doing so, Faro and Crowley fraudulently increased the level of assets against which Sea Star could borrow from the bank. In August 2012, Sea Star informed the bank that it had discovered a “discrepancy” of over $3m in its reported versus actual assets.

Sea Star discontinued its business operations approximately one week later, before Faro joined National Fish. Crowley then worked in companies outside the seafood sector. 

The charge of conspiracy to commit bank fraud provides for a sentence of no greater than 30 years in prison, five years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $1m.  

Ventola case 

In a separate case, former National Fish president Jack Ventola will likely pay $1m in restitution to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and face jail time after defrauding his former company. 

Owing $91m, court orders sale of Pacific Andes’ National Fish

Ventola was arrested on Nov. 23, 2015, in connection with failing to pay taxes on more than $2m in income he earned from 2006 to 2009, according to the US attorney’s office for the district of Massachusetts. He was indicted on three counts of filing false tax returns and one count of conspiracy to defraud the IRS. 

Ventola and two others -- former National Fish senior sales executive Richard Pandolfo, and Michael Bruno, an accountant who didn't work for the company but served on its board -- face charges that include tax fraud in connection with an alleged scheme that reportedly charged the company for labor services never provided.

title: Thai prime minister threatens arrest of migrant workers
content:
Thai prime minister, Prayut Chan-o-cha, threatened to arrest a mass of 700,000 foreign laborers who failed to register according to the government's timetable, while criticizing the labor ministry for what he called "sluggish management" of the process, the Nation reported.

“If it’s not finished by June, no more exceptions will be made [...] If they [migrant workers] can’t be registered in time, they will have to be arrested,” he said.

The verification is crucial to the registration process to legalize millions of migrant workers in Thailand so that they and their employers abide by the pending migrant worker management law.

The government has set up special monitoring centers and upgraded regulations to address IUU fishing issues, which affects Thailand’s human rights image and trade relations with the international community. The European Commission issued a yellow card to Thailand in April 2015 for not taking sufficient measures to fight illegal fishing.

title: Thailand convicts several fishermen for human trafficking
content:
Several Thai fishermen and fishing captains have been prosecuted for human trafficking, Thailand's Ministry of Foreign Affairs has said.

The convictions comes as Thai authorities try to clamp down on human trafficking amid international pressure.

Last month a Thai court imposed an 11-year prison sentence on two men who had lured two Thai fishermen aboard the vessel 'Katesuwanrat 11'. The fishermen were imprisoned and physically assaulted.

One of the men convicted was the chairman of a local fishing association and prominent local businessman. The court also imposed a fine of THB 600,000 (€16,200) on the company owning said fishing vessel.

In a separate announcement, captains of seven vessels were convicted for human trafficking after nine Indonesian crew and six Filipino crew were imprisoned and forced to work onboard vessels which docked at a port in Phuket, Thailand, in 2015. The police issued the arrest warrants for the captains and impounded all seven vessels while the criminal case was in process.

The seven fishing vessels -- all flying under the Bolivian flag -- were deemed stateless and came under the provision of the Royal Ordinance on Fisheries.

The recent convictions "demonstrate the [government's] unwavering commitment to administering the law in order to prevent and suppress human trafficking especially in the fishery sector effectively, quickly, and justly," said the ministry.

Between 2015-2017, Thai authorities prosecuted 86 cases of human trafficking offenses in fishery sector, it said. 32 cases led to convictions, while another three are scheduled to go before court by March of this year.

In 2014, Thailand was downgraded to Tier 3 on the US' TIP report, the lowest level, partly because of labor abuses in its seafood sector.

In 2016, Thailand moved up from Tier 3 to the Tier 2 “Watch List”. However, NGOs International Justice Mission (IJM) and Bangkok-based Issara Institute claim human trafficking and slavery remain "rampant" in Thailand's fishing industry.

title: Arrest made, but Maine police still investigating $230,000 lobster fraud case
content:
Maine state and local police are still trying to determine what happened to some $230,000 that J&J Lobster, in Rockland, intended be used to pay a seafood wholesaler for bait, even though they arrested the company’s dock manager in May 2017, Rockland's Courier-Gazette reports.

Chad W. Salvas, a 39-year-old Rockland man employed by the lobster dealer, claimed he was innocent when arrested in May 2017 and charged with two counts each of felony theft and felony forgery. He was arrested again in August after failing to appear for his arraignment and was released on $500 bail.

But in a summary of happenings delivered to the Rockland City Council last week, the local police department confirmed the case was not closed, according to the newspaper. The department said it “continued working with the Maine Marine Patrol on a large-scale fraud/theft investigation.” Police confirmed Monday that the case involved Salvas.

title: Chinese authorities seize, auction toothfish from foreign vessel involved in IUU
content:
Chinese authorities have seized toothfish from a foreign vessel fishing in Antarctic waters after it docked in a Chinese port, in what is being described as China's first action taken against illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing (IUU) outside its own waters. 

According to Xinhua News, a state-owned news organization, authorities in the port-city of Yantai, Shandong province, seized 110 metric tons of toothfish from a vessel owned by the firm Red Star after it docked in Yantai in May, 2016, while en route to Vietnam.

The seizure followed a tip-off from the Convention for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR), according to Xinhua, quoting a spokesperson for the fisheries bureau of China's Ministry of Agriculture. The seizure was reported after the toothfish was auctioned off by Yantai authorities earlier this month. 

Belize-registered Red Star's vessel was operating under the Cambodian flag. On inspection at Yantai port, the vessel's crew were unable to provide the required documentation for the toothfish, MoA said. 

"This is our country's first successful action taken against IUU vessels transporting illegally caught fish," said Xinhua. 

Red Star was added to the South Atlantic Fisheries Organization's list of companies involved in IUU in 2016, through its connection to the Andrey Dolgov, also known as Sea Breeze.

It's also possible the seizure occurred more recently than Xinhua reports. Trygg Mat Tracking -- a firm providing national fisheries authorities and international organisations with fisheries intelligence analysis -- reported Red Star-owned vessel Ayda was inspected in Dalian port on Oct. 22, 2017, when inspectors found toothfish. Ayda's former name was Andrey Dolgov. 

A source in China told Undercurrent News he'd heard the vessel was en route to Korea. 

Rhys Arangio, executive officer of the Coalition of Legal Toothfish Operators, said the auction was a great result. However, he said IUU problems in toothfish fisheries are "largely resolved". From a peak in IUU catch of toothfish of 32,500t in 1997, IUU catch has dropped to just 500t per year today, he said.

"Nations, CCAMLR, NGOs, and the legal industry collaborated and put multiple measures in place to eradicate this problem from within national [exclusive economic zones] in the southern oceans," Arangio told Undercurrent. "The majority of the IUU catch of Patagonian toothfish, subsequently, dried up around 2006," he said.

The remaining handful of IUU operators moved on to the high seas, or international waters, further south, to target Antarctic toothfish; in these years until around 2014 vessels were catching between 2,000 and 4,000t of Antarctic toothfish, he said.

The last big IUU fleet was called ‘Bandit 6’ -- a group of six vessels fishing including the Thunder, the Kunlun, the Yongding, the Songhua, the Viking, and the longliner Perlon. In 2015, the group was targeted by Sea Shepherd, who were "very successful", said Arangio; by 2016 all of the six vessels of Bandit 6 were either sunk, destroyed, or had their crew arrested, he said.

Nowadays there may only be "two remaining vessels hiding in the shadows, catching a small amount of Antarctic toothfish on the high seas -- under 500t per year – less than 1.5% of peak illegal catch in 1997", said Arangio. 

According to the Xinhua report, proceeds from the toothfish auction in China will go to CCAMLR. The contribution will help "support [CCAMLR's] work in the fight against IUU fishing activities, and protect the Antarctic Ocean's ecology and resources", it said, citing MoA.

title: 1,056t of seized Vietnamese pangasius auctioned off by Chinese authorities
content:
Chinese local government authorities in Fujian province have auctioned off 1,056 metric tons of pangasius products, recently seized by Chinese customs officials from a Chinese importer implicated in smuggling. 

China issues smuggling crackdown as large pangasius importer implicated

According to local industry publication Fish First, 105,556 cartons of pangasius fillets, tails, rolls and whole pangasius seized from Fujian Anxin Industrial were auctioned off online on Tuesday morning (Jan. 9) local time. Ten Chinese firms participated in the auction with Shanghai Yu Pin Fresh Supply Chain Management, a firm based in Shanghai, lodging a winning bid of CNY 15.3 million ($2.3m). 

Last week Undercurrent News reported Fujian Anxin Industrial was among the largest casualties of a nationwide smuggling crackdown by Chinese authorities. The firm was implicated in smuggling 41,000 metric tons of pangasius products worth CNY 640 million ($98.6m) into China from Vietnam, according to state-owned media organization Xinhua.

Pangasius seized by Chinese customs put up for auction. Credit: Fish First

According to Xinhua, in 2014, Fujian Anxin established a subsidiary company in Vietnam which then sent seafood products including pangasius, tuna and shrimp into China through smuggling routes. Fish First said Fujian Anxin is a partner company of the Vietnamese association Vietnam Pangasius Association (VPA), and China's largest pangasius importer.

The VPA did not respond to Undercurrent's request for comment. 

Prospective bidders were able to inspect products held in a depot in Shanghai on Jan. 3 and Jan. 4 prior to the auction. Bidding started at CNY 7.2m with incremental bids of CNY 100,000. The auction lasted 36 minutes.

Shanghai Yu Pin's winning bid equates to CNY 145 per carton, or CNY 168 per carton net auctioneers' commission (5%) and VAT (11%). 

Pangasius products seized by Chinese customs put up for auction. Credit: Fish First

The auction is concrete evidence of China's smuggling crackdown, amidst conflicting information about its impact and authorities' reputation for exaggeration and bombast; last week some Latin American exporters told Undercurrent the smuggling crackdown has had a negligible impact on shipments to the market.

But according to one source based in China, the fate of potentially "hundreds and hundreds" of containers of seafood destined for China through Vietnam is unknown, with importers afraid to collect them for fear of arrest.

title: Business as usual after Chinese smuggling crackdown, say some, others less sanguine
content:
Some Latin American exporters insist China's crackdown in seafood smuggling has had a negligible impact on shipments to the market via Vietnam, though others are less sanguine, industry sources told Undercurrent News.

Many in Latin America are not packing for China, one industry source in Ecuador told Undercurrent, pointing out that shrimp exports into the market had slowed in recent weeks. 

The source said a large packer had “in cold storage much product saved since Dec. 20. [The company] is sending one [container] via the legal route to China and three for the contraband [route], but has full storage [in Ecuador], about 15 containers". He added that the processor was “giving priority to packaging for other markets, such as Europe or US, so to continue buying head-on, shell-on shrimp” from farmers.

The Top 40 Latin American Seafood Companies
View report

The source referred to rumors that Chinese authorities had found “two Chinese importers -- two of the largest -- smuggling merchandise into China from Vietnam. They took them as prisoners". 

However, the owner of a second large Ecuadorian processor denied that exports to Asia had paralyzed, pointing out his company did not have any problem to export “to any market”.

“In addition, Ecuadorian exporters export to final ports and destinations. What the buyer or client does with that product is not our business,” he said. “Prices have decreased, but business is as usual,” he added, denying any anomaly in its shipments. 

The owner at a third large Ecuadorian shrimp processor also denied any issue with shipments to Asia. 

“Shipments to main port continue to increase heavily and demand in China [is] very strong,” he said, adding that shipments to Vietnam continue as usual.

“Prices are picking up again as demand from Europe and US is getting stronger at current lower levels and they are taking advantage of this price break,” the third source added.

However, a fourth industry source in Venezuela said that the Chinese market “stalled”, attributing lower demand to the end of orders for the Chinese New Year.

A fifth source at a second shrimp company in Venezuela said that “some customers in Vietnam are still working normally”, referring to Chinese customers asking for delivery in Vietnam. He added that “they are using the legal problems of some to [demand] lower [shrimp] prices”.

China-Vietnam seafood ‘grey trade’ hit by smuggling crackdown

However, a sixth trader source based in China was less sanguine about exporters' prospects selling into China via Vietnam.

“Many goods will not reach their final buyers. I heard that a big number of containers are left in ports... as nobody dares collecting them now,” the source, who owns a seafood company based in China, told Undercurrent on Monday (Jan. 8). "Prices have gone down as a result."

He said the crackdown was more “comprehensive" than in previous years, with those hit not just small players but also big ones, and the entire supply chain was affected.  

He added that his Ecuadorian counterparts had told him they were in fact sitting on containers filled with vannamei shrimp they “cannot move”.

“Do remember that during December and January you get the biggest arrivals in China for the Chinese New year. So, we must be talking about hundreds and hundreds of containers [affected overall into China].”

He said it would have a further impact on prices if importers do not pay the balance and goods are unsold. “The exporters will have no choice but sell off to those crazy operators taking risks [to take product via Vietnam into China] or to take back goods and add up to the inventory.”

Describing a hypothetical situation, he said Chinese importers would likely forfeit a $20,000 to $30,000 deposit on a $100,000 container-load of product if it meant avoiding jail. “Then the Ecuadorian has a choice to take it back. [But] nobody wants it... So instead of taking it back he'll accept $70,000 to a risk-taker,” meaning someone who is still prepared to try to smuggle the product into China despite the risks.

China issues smuggling crackdown as large pangasius importer implicated

“[But] the risk is very big.” He said he’d heard so far 300 operators – mainly in China’s south but also in the north and northeast – had been arrested, adding the threat of lengthy jail terms was “big stuff”.

He added the crackdown showed no signs of abating. “The only thing we know is that it started last month and continues this month. So it seems they are serious about it.”

Vietnam route

Raids of suspected seafood smuggling operations and companies using smuggled seafood have taken place all across the country. However, the trail invariably leads to Yunnan and Guangxi, the two Chinese provinces which border Vietnam.

“We saw that a lot of imported frozen seafood products were from Yunnan or Guangxi, when there are perfectly good ports near Beijing and Tianjin,” a Beijing customs official told Beijing TV. “This was not normal.”

Smugglers load trucks with goods after they're taken across the Vietnam-China border free of documentation and duties by locals. Source: Beijing TV

Chinese people living close to the border with Vietnam are permitted to import goods worth CNY 8,000 ($1,231) into China free of documentation and duties (import tariffs, sales tax) for personal and small business use, the report states. This means a full container-load of product can be transported into China by 100-200 people without paying any tax, a Chinese customs official told Beijing TV.

The report goes on to state that Chinese customs had been investigating one such smuggling ring for more than eight months, before launching a raid. 

The report did not say whether smuggling routes had been shut down. However, a seventh source in Thailand told Undercurrent on Thursday (Jan. 4) there has been a “partial closure of the border”. 

“Some traders are still very discreetly operating; others have been terminated. Communications and transactions are much more clandestine now than the past,” he said.

Last week, a source at a Vietnam-based trading company told Undercurrent that most logistics companies in China were refusing to take product from Vietnam, and would wait until the start of this week to reassess the situation.

On Tuesday, the source said trade of shrimp (origin Vietnam) had now resumed and pangasius trade was also set to resume this week. However, he said he did not know about third country border trade as it is "totally another sector of agents". 

“People don't want to comment,” the source based in China said. “People who are under suspicion will be heard on everything -- on Wechat, Whatsapp, emails."

He added that he’d not been in contact with anyone directly involved in smuggling. “It's just what you heard. There's no proof. But you criss-cross information and you get a good picture of what's happening."

He said he is “very happy” with the crackdown, however. “I must say we are very happy with this step as it will bring a more regulated market and offer a more competitive market for all. At present it is almost impossible to compete [with smugglers]."

title: Judge dismisses human trafficking lawsuit levied against High Liner’s Rubicon, Thai shrimp suppliers
content:
A lawsuit against High Liner Foods-owned Rubicon Resources and three related Thai firms -- in human trafficking as they supplied shrimp to retailers, including Walmart -- has been dismissed, court records show. 

The civil lawsuit, brought in California federal court by seven Cambodians employed outside the US, accused the companies of violating the US Trafficking Victims Protection Act and knowingly profiting from the villagers' working conditions in 2011-2012.

Undercurrent News: World’s 100 Largest Seafood Companies 2017
View report

US-based importer Rubicon, Thai exporter Wales & Co Universe, and Thai seafood companies Phatthana Seafood and S.S. Frozen Food – filed a motion in November 2017 to dismiss the case arguing that because the alleged conduct took place outside the US, the matter shouldn't be heard in a US court. 

In a Jan. 4 decision, judge John Walter granted that motion but did not detail his reasoning.  

Walmart is mentioned in the lawsuit, but is not a defendant. However, Undercurrent News sources believe Sam’s, the club store arm of Walmart, is the main customer of Rubicon.  Rubicon was purchased by High Liner Foods earlier this year, close to a year after the lawsuit was filed. Sam’s is not mentioned directly in the lawsuit.

Phatthana Seafood and S.S. Frozen Food are both part of PTN Group, according to the complaint in the lawsuit. PTN and Wales were also previously shareholders in Rubicon, before the sale to High Liner.

High Liner took over Rubicon in a $107 million deal that closed in May 2017, just under a year after this lawsuit was announced in June 2016.

As part of the deal, Rubicon and its Thai suppliers and former shareholders took a 7% stake in High Liner. Although PTN and Wales were not named directly by High Liner, they are said to be part of this deal by Undercurrent sources.

Details of lawsuit

According to the lawsuit, the Cambodian plaintiffs were allegedly recruited from their villages and employed by the defendants in Thailand.

The suit states that the Cambodian villagers paid high recruitment fees but at the Thai factory were "paid less than promised and that their already meagre wages would be further reduced by unexpected salary deductions for housing, fees, and other charges".

As one example, the complaint details the experience of Keo Ratha, a Cambodian who was reportedly hired by an "agent of CDM Trading Manpower Co for work in Thailand".

That company then reportedly arranged his travel to a Thai shrimp factory operated by Phatthana on Oct. 30, 2011. There Ratha was told be would be paid at least $250 monthly and be given free housing in exchange for eight hours of labor per day.

Ratha sold his motorcycle and paid a $150 fee to obtain a passport. He was reportedly told that $250 in recruitment fees would be deducted from his paychecks over time. However, the lawsuit claims that he was instead paid only $135 monthly and rent was deducted from that. His passport was also seized and held from him, it claimed.

"After the salary deductions and rent payments, Mr. Ratha often did not have enough
money to buy enough food to eat. He was hungry much of the time," the lawsuit claims.

Additionally, he didn't have a choice in where to live and stayed in "overcrowded and unsanitary" conditions, sleeping on a concrete floor, the suit states. He had to work around chlorine which caused him health problems, he claims.

"He asked to quit several times, but was told he could not leave. He was also told that he could not get his passport back without paying off his recruitment fee," the suit states. "Mr. Ratha was afraid that he would be arrested by the Thai police if he fled without his passport, or that he would be sold to a fishing boat as a slave—a fate, unfortunately, not uncommon in the local fishing industry."

In January 2012 he was allowed to return to Cambodia after the media reported on the situation, the lawsuit claims.

title: In plea deal, former National Fish president likely to pay $1m in restitution
content:
Former National Fish and Seafood president Jack Ventola will likely pay $1 million in restitution to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and face jail time after defrauding his former company, which is majority owned by Hong Kong-based conglomerate Pacific Andes International Holdings (PAIH).

Ventola was arrested on Nov. 23, 2015, in connection with failing to pay taxes on more than $2m in income he earned from 2006 to 2009, according to the US attorney’s office for the district of Massachusetts. He was indicted on three counts of filing false tax returns and one count of conspiracy to defraud the IRS. 

Ventola and two others, former National Fish senior sales executive Richard Pandolfo, and Michael Bruno, an accountant who didn't work for the company but served on its board, face charges that include tax fraud in connection with an alleged scheme that reportedly charged the company for labor services never provided.

Pandolfo and Bruno pleaded guilty but have yet to be sentenced. Ventola had initially pleaded not guilty but later signed a plea agreement with prosecutors that was filed on Dec. 19. As part of that agreement, Ventola admitted to seven counts of making and subscribing a false tax return while prosecutors dropped three more serious charges: conspiracy, wire fraud and mail fraud. 

For the charges he admitted to Ventola could face a maximum of three years in prison, three years supervised release, a $250,000 fine and restitution. 

However, prosecutors will instead recommend a lesser prison sentence, a to be determined fine and $1.073m in restitution. Judge Douglas Woodlock is slated to sentence Ventola on March 27.

Scheme

Court documents suggest that the scheme ran from around 1999 to 2015, and while the amounts to which National Fish was billed haven't yet been provided, they could be substantial. The processor, like its bankrupt parent company PAIH, faces financial trouble. Earlier this month, a New York bankruptcy court ordered the sale of National Fish after the company fell behind on its $91m in obligations to Dutch lender Cooperatieve Rabobank. 

The indictments also reference a fourth "co-conspirator", who was described as "co-conspirator one (CC-1)" and worked as the processor's head of operations reporting to Ventola, but that individual has not been named in court documents.

Todd Provost took over as president of Gloucester, Massachusetts-based National Fish on Friday, Pacific Andes confirmed to Undercurrent News, the same day the indictment emerged against Ventola, who the company said would stay onboard as a non-executive director.

At the time, Ventola denied that his leaving had anything to do with the federal indictment.

"My stepping down has been planned for a long time," Ventola told Undercurrent in an email, when asked if there is a link between this and the allegations.

The indictment alleges that Ventola utilized the services of a temporary labor company called Continental Labor Team, which Ventola and a co-conspirator, who was also an executive of the seafood processor, controlled.

Ventola and his co-conspirator -- who has not been named -- allegedly worked together to channel money out of Continental and into their personal bank accounts, tax free.

To do this, the co-conspirator allegedly prepared fraudulent invoices for work supposedly done for Continental by a shell company Ventola controlled called International Freezing Systems (IFS).

Ventola and his co-conspirator allegedly used the fake IFS invoices to obtain payments from Continental, which they deposited into one of Ventola’s personal bank accounts.

From there, Ventola used the funds to pay personal expenses and also wrote his co-conspirator personal checks approximately monthly.

Although the checks from Continental totaled more than $2m between 2006 and 2009, neither Ventola nor his co-conspirator reported the income on their tax returns, it is alleged.

The indictment also alleges that Ventola failed to report approximately $149,000 of other income he received in 2008 and 2009.

National Fish, which is 60% owned by Pacific Andes as well as a Hong Kong-registered subsidiary also called National Fish and Seafood, saw the $5.1m loss after earning a $2.6m profit in 2013.

The filing said that the National Fish subsidiaries experienced $236.8m turnover in 2013 and $284.2m turnover in 2014.

title: Scallops supplier pleads guilty in $3.2m tax evasion case
content:
George F. Estudante, the owner of now closed Massachusetts scallop dealer Basic Fisheries, has pleaded guilty to charges that evaded taxes by not reporting $3.2 million in business and personal income.

He pleaded guilty to three charges -- two counts of failing to file tax returns and one count of filing a false income tax return -- the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) said in a press release.

He will be sentenced on March 13 and could face a maximum of three years in prison and a $100,000 fine. 

According to the IRS, Estudante failed to file an income tax return for 2010, even though his business, Basic Fisheries, received approximately $1,418,629 in payments.  He also failed to file a tax return for 2011, although his business received approximately $1,607,726 in payments that year.  Furthermore, Estudante falsely swore on his 2012 tax return that he had received approximately $533,078 in gross receipts when his bank account reflected that he had received over $740,000.

In a related case, on July 26, the IRS announced the arrest of 44-year-old Orlando Cardoso for allegedly failing to report around $75,000 in income from scallop sales on his tax returns for 2012 and 2013. 

Cardoso's employer isn't mentioned in court records, but his LinkedIn page states he has worked as a production manager for scallops supplier Seatrade International since 2011. 

He pleaded guilty in November.  

Basic Fisheries, which is located in Marion, Massachusetts, a neighboring town of New Bedford, has since closed, according to the National Oceanic Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). The closure followed Estudante's guilty plea on Dec. 14, 2014 that he failed to report buying 2,600 pounds of scallops that exceeded a vessel's legally permitted limit of 400 pounds per trip. 

The vessel, Miss Tamera, was working undercover with NOAA investigators. The agency said Estudante would pay by check for the legal catches and pay in cash for the "overage" scallops, a violation of the federal Lacey Act, a conservation law that prohibits trade in illegally caught wildlife.

Estudante pleaded guilty to the 2014 charge in a Maryland court and received a two month prison sentence.

title: Nine men rescued from UK scallops trawlers in suspected human trafficking case
content:
UK police rescued nine African and Asian men from two scallops trawlers who allegedly worked unlimited hours at sea for very little pay, a suspected case of human trafficking, reports The Guardian.

The mens' rescue came after one of the vessels stopped in Portsmouth to treat an injured crew member. Two UK men were arrested in connection with the alleged human trafficking investigation.

The incident comes as questions have been raised about labor practices and possible exploitation in the Irish trawler fleet.

title: Clearwater fights North Korean clam counterfeiters in China
content:
Canada’s Clearwater Seafoods is not only battling to retain access to 100% of the Arctic surf clam fishery, the company is also fighting North Korean clam counterfeiters in the Chinese market, Ian Smith, CEO, told the Chronicle Herald. 

 According to Smith, the North Korean product, which is identical to Clearwater’s surf clam, has around 50% of the market.

Undercurrent News: World’s 100 Largest Seafood Companies 2017
View report

“It’s harvested by North Korean vessels that are owned or controlled by Chinese companies. The product is all processed in China and distributed throughout the Chinese market,” he told the Herald in Halifax, Nova Scotia on Friday during a tour of Anne Risley, the latest addition to Clearwater’s clam fishing fleet, which cost around CAD 70 million. 

“When the North Korean product first came to the market, they aggressively counterfeited Clearwater packaging and called it ‘product of Canada',” Smith said. “So, we spent millions of dollars over the last five years working with the Chinese government to basically stamp out counterfeit product in the China market.”

The Chinese authorities carried out simultaneous raids in three cities in early November, during which the authorities confiscated thousands of counterfeited Clearwater boxes, thousands of kilograms of North Korean clams, with more than 20 people arrested in the raids, he said.

According to Smith, the largest company involved was hit with as CAD 300,000 fine.

In an interview with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, Smith also shed some light on when the country’s Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) might decide on what happens with the 25% of the surf clam quota that will go to a First Nations group.

Clearwater is partnering with a First Nations group on an application to the DFO, which would see it retain access to 100% of the licenses, albeit with a partner. However, a sister company of Cooke Aquaculture and Ocean Choice International have also both applied, along with First Nations groups, to take the licenses on.

title: New Bedford scallop manager admits to hiding $75k in income
content:
Orlando Cardosa, a 44-year-old manager at a global scallops processor and distributor in New Bedford, Massachusetts, has pleaded guilty in a Boston federal court to not reporting $75,000 in earnings on his tax returns.

He faces up to three years in prison and a fine of up to $100,000 when he is sentenced in March, according to a press release from federal prosecutors.

Cardosa, who is identified on LinkedIn as working as a production manager for scallops with processor Seatrade International since 2011, had sworn on his 2012 and 2013 tax returns that his only income was from his employer, but he was also getting cash and checks from his employer’s supplier, according to a press release from prosecutors. 

The guilty plea is the second apparently related to an earlier federal investigation that also led to the arrest, in July, of 57-year-old George F. Estudante, the owner of since closed scallop dealer Basic Fisheries. Estudante was caught failing to report to federal fishing regulators the purchase of 2,600 pounds of scallops beyond a vessels' legally permitted limits.

Seatrade is not identified in the prosecutors' recent press release and has not been accused of any wrongdoing.

title: Canadian First Nation group plans to catch lobsters, get arrested
content:
Some members of the Mi'kmaq First Nation group planned to throw their lobster cages in the water when Canada’s most prolific fishing areas started their season this week with the expectation that they would be arrested. But that’s what they want, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation reports. 

Under a 1999 ruling by Canada’s Supreme Court, the tribe has the right to earn a ‘moderate livelihood” in Lobster Fishing Areas 33 and 34. But the definition of that terminology is not clearly defined, so Mi’kmaq activists plan on testing the boundaries by getting arrested and forcing the issue back to court, the CBC explains.

Tensions have been building in Nova Scotia since at least September between indigenous and non-indigenous fishermen, who claim their lobsters are being poached and sold on the black market. Boats have been set on fire. Illegal lobster catches have been found dumped in the woods.

The Department of Fisheries and Oceans has seized hundreds of illegal traps and recently set up a sting operation, seizing three tons of lobster at Halifax Stanfield International Airport.
