title: Leaders of Rafael’s former sector scramble to save groundfish season
content:
The leaders of Carlos Rafael’s former fishing sector remain hopeful that they can convince John Bullard, administrator of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA's) Greater Atlantic Region, to reopen groundfishing for the rest of the season, Andrew Saunders, the group’s attorney, told Undercurrent News on Tuesday.

Bullard declared Monday that he was shutting down all harvesting of groundfish by Sector IX, nearly five months before the season is due to end on April 30. The dramatic action followed the late September sentencing of Rafael, the sector’s former leader, to 46 months in prison after he got caught misreporting nearly 783,000 pounds of fish between 2012 and early 2016. 

Bullard, in a letter to Virginia Martins, the sector’s president, said the group has since “taken only minimal, insufficient steps to ensure accurate reporting and compliance with its operations plan”.

Whatever remains of the sector’s 7.22 million-combined lbs (3,277 metric tons) in annual catch entitlement (ACE) may not be transferred, Bullard's letter clarifies.

The move impacts between 15 and 22 boats that were actively fishing for catching cod, haddock, flounder, hake and other species in the area, based on different accounts, and sends somewhere between 75 and 100 crew members home for the holidays with concerns about supporting their families. Some of the ship captains had purchased ice and other supplies in preparation for fishing trips they now will be unable to take.

At an emergency 3.5-hour meeting called in New Bedford on Tuesday, the Sector IX board of directors discussed their options for convincing Bullard to change his mind, Saunders said. The group, which has not yet ruled out going to court for an injunction to block NOAA’s action, maintains that it was caught by surprise and believes the agency has the wrong impression.

The notion that Sector IX “has been sitting there like potted plants” since Rafael was arrested, convicted and sentenced is inaccurate, Saunders told Undercurrent. The group reconstituted its board in May, keeping only one of the former members, Ray Canastra, one of two brothers who own the Buyers and Sellers Exchange, in New Bedford, and have an agreement to purchase Rafael’s business. All five of the other members of the board are new.

Two months ago the board hired Saunders, a maritime attorney formerly with Kelly and Mancini, in Boston, to help it work with NOAA in a positive direction, he said, adding that the group has been trying to engage the agency in a dialogue about the changes that might be needed all along. After meeting with NOAA officials in late October, the group sought to meet again in December, for example.

The Sector IX board remains committed to cooperating and would like NOAA's further suggestions on how it might account for the earlier overfishing, Saunders stressed.

"This situation is unparalleled,” Saunders said. “If they had thought another policy perspective was needed, we would have entertained that.”

title: Oman arrests 12, seizes five vessels on suspicion of illegal fishing
content:
The country of Oman has arrested 12 Asian nationals and seized their five fishing vessels near the Khuriya Muriya Island, on the Arabian Sea, for allegedly violating labor and fishing laws, The Times of Oman reports.

The Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries recently announced that it would be tightening enforcement of its marine fisheries law following reports that illegal fishing in the country, which borders Saudi Arabia to the east, increased by almost a quarter in 2016.

title: Sea Shepherd accuses China’s Pingtan of illegal shark hunts
content:
Recent shark hunts by China-based Pingtan Marine Enterprise have highlighted the need for independent monitoring by NGOs, said Sea Shepherd in a blog post on Earth Island's website.

In Timor Leste law shark hunting is illegal, but that didn't prevent the firm from sending vessels out to the country's waters recently to illegally catch thousands of sharks, it alleged.

In September Sea Shepherd caught 15 vessels filled with thousands of sharks, using gill nets to land-internationally protected endangered species. "Banned from hunting for sharks in Indonesia's waters, these shark-hunting vessels prey on Timor Leste, an impoverished country with no resources to patrol or regulate their waters."

Pingtan Marine Enterprise, listed on the US NASDAQ exchange, has been banned in the past from fishing in Indonesian waters. The company did have fishing licenses from the Timor Leste government, but not for shark hunting, said Sea Shepherd.

It also claimed the same fleet of illegal shark fishing vessels were caught in August 2017 in a restricted marine sanctuary near the Galapagos Islands. "Though the crew was arrested, the private company still thrives on breaking international laws to feed the demand of the shark fin industry."

title: Little dent in crab prices expected from return of Venezuela
content:
Please hurry back, Venezuela! That’s what seafood wholesalers and importers can be heard pleading as they search near and far and pay exorbitant prices for more sources of the key ingredient their restaurant and manufacturing clients need to make their to-die-for crabcakes.

But even as the troubled South American country returns to the market in less than a week with its fresh Atlantic blue crabmeat, many fear it won’t make much of a dent.

Venezuela’s annual, two-month crab fishing moratorium, which ends on Oct. 15, is intended to help give its population of crustaceans a chance to rebound from heavy fishing. But the loss of production stung seafood sellers at a time when meat from blue swimming crabs has been in peak demand.

Record wholesale prices in the low- to mid-$30 range are being charged for a pound of  Indonesian pasteurized jumbo lump (from the large muscles at the backend of the crab), more than double the cost from a little over a year ago, reports Chris Phelps, a purchasing agent specializing in crabmeat for J.J. McDonnell, an Elkridge, Maryland-based distributor.

Other types of blue swimming crab meat have gone up in price, too, including lump (taken from broken jumbo lump and other parts of the crab's body), which now can be found for $16/lb, he said. Super lump is more than $21/lb, another source told Undercurrent News.

And Phelps doesn’t see a change coming soon.

"This is our slower period as the kids have gone back to school," he told Undercurrent in mid-September. "If we are going to see a change, it would have happened. I don't now think [there will be a change] before the holidays when people head to restaurants and demand is quite strong.”

Phelps’ customers are heavily in the Maryland, Virginia and Pennsylvania parts of the US that account for a high percentage of crabmeat sales, and, as a result, should be watched closely, he said.

"We are the capital for crab, so this market [dictates] what happens domestically, especially on the larger grades like jumbo lump," he said.

When the emerald lost its shine

A number of circumstances are driving prices higher on crabmeat, including a growing demand for the product in China and Thailand, countries that were traditionally thought of in the past as suppliers only. But chief among the culprits is the depressed harvest Indonesia experienced in early 2016, sources tell Undercurrent.

The crabmeat market has leaned heavily on the country nicknamed the Emerald of the Equator for its crabs ever since Baltimore, Maryland-based Phillips Seafood began shipping from there in 1994, according to the Sustainable Fisheries Partnership, an industry-supported group.

The blue swimming crab (Portunas pelagicus), referred to in Indonesia as “ranjungan,” is a cousin of the Atlantic blue crab (Callinectes sapidus) that can be found in Southeast Asia and the Philippines. Both species have noticeably flat and paddle-shaped back legs, and both are wild caught with the aid of pots, dredges, bottom gillnets and some bottom trawling.

Indonesia, which is now king among all crab exporters, shipped almost 945,000 metric tons of its crabmeat to the US in 2015, worth $24.8 billion, according to trade data collected by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). But 2016 wasn't quite as good, as the country supplied the US with 835,000t, worth $13.4bn, last year.

“Indonesia had a very aggressive couple of years with exports,” Troy Turkin, chief operating officer for Doral, Florida-based Supreme Crab & Seafood, explained to Undercurrent. “There was a lot of US inventory in the fourth quarter of 2015. Demand wasn’t absorbing all of that extra crab, and prices were not as high. But then the season never really happened. There just wasn’t as much crab.”

Supreme relies heavily on Indonesia for crabmeat, maintaining seven seafood processing plants there. 

Indonesia has bounced back in the first seven months of 2017, sending the US 1.3 million metric tons of crabmeat worth $22.9bn, more than a third of all of the crabmeat the US imported during the period, according to NOAA.

Still, Turkin also doesn’t see any let up in demand or reduction in prices coming soon, as many restaurants have already printed their menus for the first quarter of 2018. Though he said pressure is building, as buyers are growing more reluctant to pay for premium products, such as colossal or jumbo lump, and even turning to the cheaper red swimming crab.

Crabmeat price changes “will have anywhere from a 45- to 90-day timeline to truly impact things here,” he said.  “It all depends on demand and inventory levels. Most importers are keeping a tight rein on inventory to be safe.”

Don't forget about red

The high price for blue swimming crab , which is also sourced from the Philippines and India, has led buyers, almost universally, to purchase less expensive styles of meat and species, including red swimming crab (Portunus haanii), Phelps agrees.

Fished on large boats from deeper waters in the South China Sea, Yellow Sea and East China Sea by China and Vietnam, the red crab meat is discounted as it is deemed to be less flavorful and not to have as good of a texture. They reach sizes that are about 40% smaller than blue swimming crabs and come with smaller meat quantities, too.

But red crabs have one very positive quality. They represent big savings of as much as $10/lb less for their meat.

The beginning of the red crab season in China could have an impact on prices, as it brings yet another source of meat online, said Brendan Sweeny, VP of operations for Handy Seafood, a processor based in Salisbury, Md. Also, the hurricanes that hit Florida and the Gulf of Mexico -- popular destinations for crabmeat during the winter -- might impact tourism there, reducing demand, he added.

A quick look at NOAA data confirms a jump in US crabmeat imports from China that has started roughly in November and peaked in January.

Sweeny agrees that it's likely prices won't budge much in the near future, however. 

"There are so many dynamics in play, it's hard to guess," said Sweeny, whose company deals 90% in crabmeat imports despite its proximity to the Atlantic blue crab-producing Chesapeake Bay, but doesn't sell the red swimming crab. 

Red swimming crab is one of the products Shaws Southern Belle, in Jacksonville, Florida, turned to recently when Hurricane Harvey disrupted blue crab meat supplies from Louisiana and Alabama, Jason Hagen, the director of procurement, told Undercurrent. His company relies on the Gulf of Mexico states for about 10,000lbs of blue crab meat per year.

“We’re trying to find a deal out there, but it’s difficult to find. We could switch from fresh and pasteurized to frozen, but most people don’t want that,” Hagen said.

The closest thing to a Maryland crab

Venezuela’s moratorium on crab fishing is always a predictable, short-term problem, crabmeat sellers know. And typically, when the country comes back, it brings with it a good supply. A bigger concern, they say, is Venezuela's political climate, which is a “powder keg” to put it mildly.

The government of president Nicolas Maduro continues to resist calls for his ouster amidst a severe recession. Thousands of people have been arrested and more than 100 killed in the South American nation so far this year. The conflict has shaken US-Venezuela trade relations, as the US has been critical of the Maduro government and the Maduro government, in turn, has accused the US of helping the opposition.

A report published recently by the Economic Intelligence Unit predicts Maduro will not retain power beyond 2019, suggesting an economic collapse will force an ad-hoc election or a military coup. That is, unless China or Russia get involved and help the country avoid defaulting on debt, the policy group adds. The government faces due dates in the next few weeks for loans of $3-5bn, Bloomberg News reported recently. 

The story behind Venezuela’s rise in the crabmeat market goes back to 1968 – a few decades before Indonesia -- when a Louisiana oilman happened to notice large concentrations of the crustaceans at Lake Maracaibo and told his brother in the seafood business, according to a paper written in the mid-90s with the help of Sea Grant funding.

Venezuela has not been one of the top five crabmeat exporters for some time, however. It accounted for nearly 133,000t of crabmeat sent to the US in 2016, worth nearly $2bn, according to NOAA data. It already has surpassed both numbers in the first eight months of 2017, accounting for 148,000 metric tons sent to the US, worth more than $2bn --  almost two-thirds of Venezuela's combined $3.3bn in export seafood sales to the US during the period.

Still, sellers of Venezuelan crabmeat caution against underestimating its importance to the market. It’s a niche product, they say, that helps to buffer demand for Atlantic blue crabs from Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina and Louisiana.

Venezuelan crabmeat is kept and sold fresh, not pasteurized. As a result, Miami-based Bonamar – one of the largest suppliers of the product -- delivers it by airplane in styrofoam containers and heavily on ice, said Alex Cook, the company’s executive vice president of sales. It’s good for no more than 10 or 15 days after it is sold.

“It’s the closest thing we have to what’s in the Chesapeake,” he said.

Bonamar was founded by a Venezuelan family, but now sources just 20% of its crabmeat annually from the South American nation, though it continues to maintain eight processing facilities in the country, according to Cook.

Another buyer of blue crab from Venezuela is Twin Tails Seafood Corp., which sells it under the brand name of "BOSS Brand Fresh Crab Meat." Though Venezuelan crab represents just 8% to 10% of the Miami company's production, according to Paige Tilghman, Twin Tails’ executive VP.

More dependent on Venezuelan crab meat is a Maryland wholesaler who requested anonymity. He said crabmeat represents more than half of his annual sales, and he normally relies on Venezuela for 70% of his supply. It’s been a stable source of business for him in the past, he said.

“Previously, at wholesale, Venezuelan crab meat would go for $14/lb while Maryland crab would be $26/lb,” he recalled. 

What crabcake fans don't notice

The climb in price for blue swimming crab has an upside for companies still supplying Atlantic blue crab from the Chesapeake Bay and other mid-Atlantic and Gulf regions of the US. Their product is now more appealing than ever.

Fresh jumbo lump blue crab from Maryland can be found selling at wholesale for roughly $30 per pound, though its going for as high as $45/lb at retail, Phelps said.

“It’s great for us,” said Aubrey Vincent, sales manager for Lindy’s Seafood Inc., a Woolford, Md.-based processor of Atlantic blue crabs. “It levels the playing field.”

The crab supply in the Chesapeake has bounced up and down from month to month, but has been good recently, Vincent said. Lindy’s is picking 350 bushels of Atlantic blue crabs per day, generating 85,000 to 100,000 lbs of meat per week, she said.

A review of month-to-month blue crab harvests for Maryland from 2012 to 2016 confirms that July, August and September are the state’s most prolific months. Though 2017 numbers are not yet in, 2016 represented an uptick from previous years with 36.6m lbs picked in the state, 10% more than in 2015 and 51% more than in 2014.

Restaurants and retailers in the Mid-Atlantic region like to boast that they serve Maryland crab meat. However, rather than pay the high prices that such a product commands, many have taken to using less expensive lower grades of meat or meat imported from other countries, said the wholesaler who requested anonymity.

Crabcakes are now being made with a mix of meats, including a combination of Atlantic blue crab, pasteurized blue swimming crab and red crab, he said. They advertise their products instead as “Maryland-style crabcakes.”

The wholesaler, who serves more than 200 customers, including many restaurants in the area, said he knows of only four in Maryland that are serving crabcakes made 100% from Atlantic blue crab.

“They can’t afford to charge the prices it would take [to serve only Atlantic blue crab] but it would be disastrous if they took crabcakes off the menu,” the source told Undercurrent. “Customers don’t know this and think they are eating Maryland blue crab meat. If they saw Indonesian meat in a can at the grocery store, they wouldn’t buy it. But that’s what they are being served at their favorite restaurant.”

He fears the prices are going to go up another $5/lb in a couple weeks, which he said would be devastating for the market.

“Most people have no idea how tough it’s been out there,” he said.

title: Codfather fleet sale on hold as judge mulls forfeiture
content:
BOSTON, US -- Carlos Rafael may have received his prison sentence, but what happens to his massive commercial fishing operation – one of the largest in the United States -- remains to be seen.

William Kettlewell, one of Rafael’s attorneys, confirmed during Monday’s hearing in the federal courthouse overlooking Boston Harbor that Raymond and Richard Canastra have agreed to purchase at least some of his 32 fishing vessels and 44 permits, as Undercurrent News predicted late last week. However, the deal with the two brothers, who are Rafael’s long-time friends and own Buyers and Sellers Exchange, a New Bedford, Massachusetts-based electronic seafood auction firm, has hit a “hump,” Kettlewell said.

The defense attorney, with Hogan Lovells, in Boston, didn’t expound much on why the sale wasn’t being finalized. But a few major obstacles aren’t hard to miss.

For starters, the Canastra brothers have little idea what they are able to buy, given that a decision has not yet been rendered with regard to how much of Rafael’s property will be seized by the federal government. Court documents earlier revealed that an agreement between a then unidentified buyer existed to purchase the entire fleet for between $70 million and $80m, a 15% discount from the fleet’s appraised value.

Prosecutors are seeking the forfeiture of 13 groundfish vessels used in the scheme, which have a combined estimated value of $30m, of which Rafael's stake amounts to $19m. Complicating matters further is that others not involved in the crimes also own a percentage of the boats.

Young tabled a forfeiture decision until later, saying on Monday that he needed more time to consider the factors. He had pressed prosecutors during the hearing about whether they had adequately addressed the argument made by Rafael’s attorneys that they were violating his eighth amendment rights, which protect citizen from excessive fines, by taking more than allowed. Rafael’s defense team had said a forfeiture of $2.8m worth of assets would be within "constitutional bounds." 

Rafael, who was caught in a federal sting by two agents pretending to be Russian mobsters interested in buying his business, pleaded guilty in early March to 28 different federal counts, including 23 counts of false labeling and fish identification, two counts of falsifying federal records, one count of bulk cash smuggling, and one count of tax evasion. 

Carlos Rafael has pleaded guilty to 28 federal charges, including lying about catches and smuggling cash
Read more

Also still in play is a decision by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) what actions it will take against Rafael for violating its rules, which could involve civil money penalties. He misreported to NOAA nearly 783,000 pounds of fish during a roughly four-year-period, between 2012 and early 2016, telling authorities that the cod, sole and other species he was catching was instead haddock or another fish for which there were high quotas.

Rafael sold many of his illegally caught fish to a wholesale business in New York City in exchange for duffle bags full of cash and smuggled some of his ill-begotten gains to his native Portugal.

‘This is not stupid. This is corrupt’

Though he had reserved one of the largest rooms in the courthouse for a second day, US District Court judge William Young needed only a two-hour hearing on Monday to determine the sentence he would give Rafael.

Based on a federal scoring system and the time and money Rafael saved the court by agreeing to a plea bargain, Young gave him 46 months in prison and three additional years in supervised work release during which time he is banned from fishing. Rafael was ordered to pay both a $200,000 fine and $108,000 in restitution for evading federal fishing quotas among other crimes.  

The Portuguese-born businessman, who came to America with his family at 16 and worked his way up from menial jobs in fishing, has more than a month to contemplate his fate, as Young has ordered Rafael to “self-report” on Nov. 6 to a facility to be determined by the US Bureau of Prisons (BOP).  

The judge has recommended he be placed in Federal Medical Center Devens, described by the BOP as an “administrative security federal medical center” with an adjacent minimum security satellite camp. In arguing for his client to receive 24 months of home detention instead of prison, Kettlewell had described Rafael on Monday as being 65 years old and “in marginal health”.

The prison, which is sited on the grounds of a former Army post that closed at the end of the Cold War, has a population of 990 inmates at the medical center and another 127 at the satellite camp, according to the BOP.

His sentence was delivered on Monday before a large crowd made up of the fishing mogul’s family, friends, workers and reporters. No witnesses were offered by either side. The courtroom remained quiet when the judge asked if anyone would like to offer a victim impact statement.

“This is not stupid”, Young said, directing his comments at Rafael. “This is corrupt. This is a corrupt cause of action from start to finish. This is a case of extensive corruption to benefit you and to line your pockets. And that is why this is sentence is being given.”

Earlier Young had asked Rafael, dressed in a charcoal gray suit, to address the court, but the fishing mogul said he was too emotional and instead had Kettlewell read a statement he had composed in which he said he didn’t intend to hurt anyone and only was concerned for those with jobs “on the waterfront”.

Outside the courthouse after the decision, a New Bedford-area scallop fishing captain who worked for Rafael was surrounded by reporters when he told them he was now unsure about his own fate, expressing what many of the fishing mogul's roughly 250 employees must be feeling. He blamed the federal government for “squeezing people,” like Rafael, “into a position where they don’t eat” unless they break the rules.

He 'stole from his fellow fishermen'

Young’s ruling was a far cry from the one sought by Rafael’s attorneys, but several factors seemed to work against the defense team’s suggestion.

Young, at the very outset of Monday’s hearing, sided with the prosecutors on the value of the fish Rafael caught and sold. Andrew Lelling, the deputy US attorney leading the effort, described how he had employed an economist who came up with an average from multiple fish sales to suggest the illegal catch was worth between $4.9m and $5.1m at retail. The number was much greater than the less than one million dollars the defense attorneys had suggested.

“These terms are not obscure. The people who wrote them know what retail meant and what wholesale meant,” Lelling said.

Prosecutors also did their best to counter suggestions that Rafael was merely acting in the best interest of his workers and the town of New Bedford by falsifying catch records. This was not a “selfless act of attrition”, Lelling said. Rafael never mentioned keeping his fleet in New Bedford in all of the 15 hours of tape made with the federal agents, who he thought wanted to buy him out for $170m to $180m, the prosecutor noted.

Lelling also noted Rafael’s prior arrests for evading taxes, and he attacked the defense’s trivializing of the amount of fish he lied about – just 2.3% of his combined catch over the years covered. Rafael’s efforts to capture as many permits as he could had the effect of locking other fishermen out, the prosecutor explained.

“He is not a small actor,” Lelling said of Rafael. “He is the biggest actor in New England fisheries. There needs to be a precedent.”

The Conservation Law Foundation, a Boston-based group that has been among the groups pushing for a tough sentence for Rafael expressed satisfaction with Monday’s ruling. The group now wants to see some of the money used from a forfeiture of Rafael’s property used to stop future violators of catch limits.

“The sentence imposed by Judge Young today sends a strong message that systemic abuse of our fishery resources will not be tolerated,” said CLF attorney Megan Herzog. “While others played by the rules, Mr. Rafael showed brazen disregard for fishermen, their families, and the health of our ocean environment. Going forward, it is critical that we implement stronger monitoring and enforcement at sea in order to ensure New England’s fishing industry operates on a level playing field.”

The New England Fishery Management Council (NEFMC), the agency that has oversight of the fishing areas worked by Rafael, is expected to discuss Rafael's sentencing Tuesday morning at a regular meeting in Gloucester, Massachusetts.

“Carlos Rafael is a criminal who stole from his fellow fishermen and the public by intentionally misreporting his catch.  His conduct was reprehensible and the criminal penalties he received are well-deserved,” said Tom Nies, NEFMC’s executive director.

title: Vietnam fishermen killed in collision with Philippines navy boat
content:
Two Vietnamese fishermen were found dead on a fishing vessel after a collision with a Filipino navy boat near the Philippine coast, reports the Daily Mail. 

The Philippine government said Monday (Sept. 25) the encounter between a Filipino navy patrol and six Vietnamese boats fishing occurred about 34 nautical miles (63 kilometers) off Cape Bolina in the Philippine province of Pangasinan.

A Vietnamese fishing vessel initiated "very dangerous maneuvers" and slammed into a Filipino navy boat during a chase, prompting its sailors to fire warning shots, it said. The two Vietnamese were subsequently found dead onboard the vessel.

Foreign secretary Alan Peter Cayetano informed his Vietnamese counterpart, Pham Binh Minh, of the encounter that occurred early Saturday and assured him of a fair investigation.

title: $180m in seafood seized amid bust of Chinese shark fin ring
content:
A major shark fin smuggling ring was stopped by customs officers in the southern Chinese port city of Jiangmen with 50 metric tons of seafood confiscated, the news website That's Mags reported. 

The confiscated goods included shark fins, fish maws, sea cucumbers and abalone worth an estimated RMB 800 million ($180m), website said, quoting the newspaper China Daily.

Thirty-five suspects were arrested in the probe and a "dodgy" plant where the shark fins were being processed was found in Jiangmen, the website said.

The seafood was  reportedly purchased in Africa, South America and southeast Asia and transshipped to first to Hong Kong and then to Vietnam before entering China via Yunnan province. 

The bust is thought to be the largest of its kind to date. 

The news comes days after East Timorese police and activists from the group Sea Shepherd say they caught vessels from publicly traded Chinese firm Pingtan Marine Enterprise illegally fishing in the country's waters for sharks.

The UK branch of Sea Shepherd alleged that its effort with the East Timor National Police resulted in the capture of the Hong Long Fisheries fleet at anchor off the coast of Com, East Timor.

Hong Long is affiliated with Pingtan, it said.

title: Lobster quota protests turn violent in South Africa
content:
At least two arrests were made and a teenager was hit in the mouth by a rubber bullet in Cape Town, South Africa, Tuesday, after lobster fishermen clashed with police, EWN, a South African news organization, reports. Two police officers were wounded.

The fishermen were protesting an announcement by the country’s agriculture department that it was reducing lobster quotas for the six-month season from 110kg to 50kg, according to the newspaper.

The day before about 60 protesting fishermen had used a rope to barricade themselves at the Department of Agriculture‚ Forestry and Fisheries‚ insisting on a meeting with Minister Senzeni Zokwana, who is in China, according to another media outlet.

The protesters have vowed to continue demonstrating.

title: Louisiana man arrested for shrimp violations, battery of police officer
content:
A man in the southern US state of Louisiana has been arrested for commercial fishing violations and attacking a police officer on Aug. 15, prior to the shrimp season opening on Aug. 18.

According to a release from the Department of Wildlife and Fisheries (LDWF) enforcement division, agents arrested Timothy Cheramie for fishing during a closed season, resisting an officer and battery of a police officer.

Agents were on patrol in Bastian Bay when they found Cheramie actively shrimping with skimmers during a closed season. The shrimp season opened Aug. 18.

When agents boarded the vessel, Cheramie began resisting the agents by not allowing them to seize his nets.  After numerous attempts to seize the nets and dealing with interference from Cheramie, agents told Cheramie he was under arrest.

When agents attempted to place him in handcuffs he became combative and began fighting with agents as they attempted to handcuff him.  After a brief scuffle, agents were able to handcuff and arrest Cheramie.

Using skimmers during a closed season carries up to a $950 fine and 120 days in jail plus forfeiture of anything seized. 

In addition, for the first conviction of shrimping during the closed season, the court may revoke or suspend the violator's trawl, skimmer, or butterfly gear licenses for one year from the date of the conviction. 

During such revocation or suspension, the violator may be present on a vessel harvesting or possessing shrimp or possessing a trawl, skimmer, or butterfly net only if the vessel is equipped with and employs an operating vessel monitoring system which is accessible to LDWF.

title: US port of New Bedford launches seafood brand
content:
New Bedford, the leading port in the US in terms of sales in dollar value, is launching its own brand. 

On July 27, the Massachusetts port's Harbor Development Commission (HDC) officially unveiled the brand for the port, which has seen a boom in its scallop business but tough times on groundfish. 

“As America’s top grossing commercial fishing port and largest seafood processing center, New Bedford can rightfully claim the title of America’s seafood capital. But we need to do a better job proclaiming our status to the rest of the world, and that’s where this campaign comes in,” said mayor Jon Mitchell, who also serves as chairman of the HDC.

The HDC hired Moore & Isherwood Communications to develop the logo, which features the a western rig fishing vessel. 

“Outside of our region few people know how important New Bedford and our fishing industry is to providing sustainable, fresh, delicious fish to buyers and consumers everywhere,” said Ed Anthes-Washburn, port director. “The fishing industry and our waterfront is the cultural, economic and political center of our region. We think it’s important to showcase New Bedford’s seafood at the same level as other brands like Alaskan salmon or Maine lobster.”

In addition to the logo, the HDC worked with students from UMass Dartmouth’s Charlton College of Business and Moore & Isherwood to develop a website where national and international buyers can browse all of New Bedford’s processors and fish houses, and the seafood they sell.

In the future, the HDC has plans to work with local restaurants and fish markets to further identify locally-landed fish and seafood for local residents in an effort to highlight some of the underutilized species, or less popular fish, that are landed in local waters.

The project was funded by the Massachusetts Division of Marine Fisheries. It comes at a time when the port is under the microscope, with the guilty plea of local fishing baron Carlos Rafael for running a scam where he sold illegally-caught whitefish.

Several other executives in the port have since been arrested on tax evasion charges.

title: Two arrested in IRS tax evasion crackdown on US scallops sector
content:
The US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) has arrested two New Bedford, Massachusetts area scallop sector veterans in tax evasion cases that are evidence of the agency's heightened scrutiny of the sector.

On July 26, the IRS announced the arrest of 44-year-old Orlando Cardoso for allegedly failing to report around $75,000 in income from scallop sales on his tax returns for 2012 and 2013. 

Cardoso's employer isn't mentioned in court records, but his LinkedIn page states he has worked as a production manager for scallops supplier Seatrade International since 2011. 

Basic Fisheries

In a separate arrest announced July 14, 57-year-old George F. Estudante, the owner of scallop dealer Basic Fisheries, stands accused of not filing tax returns in 2010 and 2011, when his business took in over $3 million in payments, and of under-reporting his 2012 income by $207,000. 

Basic Fisheries, which is located in Marion, Massachusetts, a neighboring town of New Bedford, has since closed, according to the National Oceanic Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). The closure followed Estudante's guilty plea on Dec. 14, 2014 that he failed to report buying 2,600 pounds of scallops that exceeded a vessel's legally permitted limit of 400 pounds per trip. 

The vessel, Miss Tamera, was working undercover with NOAA investigators. The agency said Estudante would pay by check for the legal catches and pay in cash for the "overage" scallops, a violation of the federal Lacey Act, a conservation law that prohibits trade in illegally caught wildlife.

Estudante pleaded guilty to the 2014 charge in a Maryland court and received a two month prison sentence. He has not entered a plea to the recent IRS charges -- two counts of failing to file a tax return and one count of filing a false return.

Under the failing to file charges he could face up to a year in prison and a $25,000 fine. Under the false return charge he could face a three-year prison term and up to a $100,000 fine. 

The IRS has not explicitly said the arrests of Cardoso and Estudante are related, but court documents make it appear that way.

Tax evasion

According to an affidavit filed by IRS special agent David Balkcom, Cardoso "intentionally and corruptly concealed income" that he received from a "Fishery Owner" and "Fishery Owner's Employee". Those people weren't named in the indictment but Balkcom referred to "Fishery Owner" as having served a two-month prison sentence for a scallops-related violation of the Lacey Act that was part of a charge filed in 2014 in a Maryland court.

During 2012 and 2013, Cardoso's employer -- described in court documents as "Processor" but believed to be Seatrade -- "paid hundreds of thousands of dollars" to "Fishery" in exchange for scallops.

Balkcom wrote that after interviewing Cardoso, "Fishery Owner", and the owner's employee he believes that none "have been consistently truthful" about why Fishery Owner told his employee to pay Cardoso tens of thousands of dollars "first primarily by check, and then secretively by cash".

"All, however, are consistent that the payments were made, that no records were kept of their amounts or purpose, and that, as Cardoso admitted when interviewed, he did not report them either to his employer, processor, or on his federal income tax returns,"  the investigator wrote.

Seatrade is not named in the document and is not accused of any wrongdoing.

According to Balkcom, "Fishery Owner" described Cardoso as having sold him scallops even though Cardoso's employer, "Processor", is also described as having purchased scallops from "Fishery Owner".

"He did not know where Cardoso had obtained the scallops and claimed to have
destroyed any records he had concerning their purchase and the operation of Fishery," Balkcom said. "Fishery Owner further stated that he had made a number of payments to Cardoso, and that some of these payments were by check, while others were in cash. He similarly claimed to have no records of the dates or amounts of these payments."

When interviewed, "Fishery Owner’s Employee" told Balkcom that he'd delivered scallops to Cardoso's employer, "Processor" on behalf of "Fishery Owner", cashed checks from Processor and paid Cardoso.

The employee "claimed not to know where Fishery Owner got his scallops, but said he understood that Cardoso had sold Fishery Owner some," the affidavit states.

In exchange, the employee said he would pay Cardoso with cash from Fishery Owner and said "Fishery Owner sometimes told him to report a greater number of bags of scallops on Fishery’s invoice to Processor than he was actually delivering."

The employee also said he would provide Cardoso with his employer's bill of lading "for what he said were scallops Cardoso was purportedly receiving from somewhere else".

Cardoso

For his part, Cardoso in his tax return said his only income was from his employer, "Processor", Balkcom wrote. However, his bank account from Bank of America tells a different story with a series of checks and cash payments from "Fishery", the affidavit states.

"Bank of America’s records also reflect a series of large cash deposits ranging
from approximately $500.00 to $3,800.00 beginning in December 2012 and continuing through December of 2013," the affidavit states. "In December 2012 there were five large cash deposits totaling approximately $8,660.00. Then there was a break of approximately four months, during the period when Cardoso deposited checks from Fishery."

Balkcom didn't believe Cardoso's explanation for those payments -- that the transactions weren't income but payments for a man named "J.D," who Cardoso was helping to sell scallops to Cardoso's employer, which didn't buy scallops from individuals. Cardoso said he'd accepted "Fishery's" money and arranged for "J.D." to sell to it, so that Fishery could re-sell scallops to "Processor."

"Cardoso could not substantiate this story in any way," Balkcom wrote. "He stated that he did not keep any records and that he did not know how much cash he received from Fishery or how much he paid J.D. He said he thought that J.D. was no longer in the United States, and knew no way of contacting him. Cardoso also stated that he did not know where J.D. got his scallops and that no one other than him would have seen J.D. at Processor."

Cardoso told Balkcom he admitted "to keeping $10,000.00 to $15,000.00 for arranging the purported deal with 'J.D.' but said most of the money went to him." Cardoso also said that his employer, "Processor", wasn't aware of the deal with J.D.

Other cases

These arrests bring additional attention to alleged criminal activity in the New Bedford scallops sector at a time when the case of Carlos "Codfather" Rafael is making national headlines. Rafael is accused of operating a long-running scheme through which he submitted falsified records for groundfish catches to the federal government to evade federal fishing quotas. 

He has pleaded guilty but is yet to be sentenced. In addition to his groundfish business, Rafael runs a large scallop fleet.

Additionally, in an unrelated case Seatrade has made headlines of its own recently as a victim of the theft of 8,350 pounds of stolen scallops valued at $192,050. 

Two men, Antonio Vieira and Michael Caton, both of Rhode Island and both former employees of Continental Cold Storage, face charges in connection with that incident.

title: Russian court fines Norwegian vessel €1m for illegal shrimp fishing
content:
A Murmansk court has fined the Norwegian captain of a shrimp trawler €1 million for fishing illegally, after saying the vessel Remoy was catching shrimp in Russian waters without the necessary permits, the Barents Observer reported.

Captain Ketil Ervik was not present in court, but a Norwegian lawyer representing Coldwater Prawns of Norway -- the firm which owns Remoy -- and representatives from Norway’s consulate general were present.

Additionally, Coldwater Prawns of Norway was fined €2m, which the court ruling said must be paid within 60 days.

The vessel was arrested by the Russian coast guard on May 11 and taken to Murmansk. The crew had to stay on board for some weeks before being allowed to travel back to Norway.

The Norwegian fishery directorate said that an administrative error on the Norwegian side had been the reason for the detention of the vessel.

The trawler had applied for licenses to catch shrimp as part of a Norwegian quota in Russian waters. The license was issued, but the documents submitted by the directorate to the Russian side included mistakes.

The Russian prosecutors still argue that the Norwegian ship captain failed to comply with Russian regulations, and that he was personally responsible for double-checking the permissions issued.

title: Washington state company suspected of ‘high grading’
content:
US fishing company Pacific Salmon Charters' crews are suspected of habitually “high-grading,” or catching more than the legal limit of fish, and keeping only the most desirable specimens, reports the Chinook Observer.

On Thursday, July 13, officers from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife served a search warrant at the Pacific Salmon office at the Port of Ilwaco, in Washington state.

Investigators say they have evidence that Pacific Salmon Charters crews high-graded on at least two trips during the short spring halibut season.

The case is still under investigation, and no one has been arrested or charged yet.

title: UK likely to need enhanced fisheries enforcement to ‘protect’ waters
content:
UK fisheries sector chiefs have noted the need for improvements to monitoring and enforcement measures, should they get their wish for Brexit to mean only UK vessels can fish in its waters.

Speaking in London at a meeting over Brexit and fisheries, Jonathan Leake – environment editor with UK newspaper the Sunday Times – questioned whether existing fisheries enforcement was strong enough to protect UK waters.

“If you have rules they need to be enforced,” said Barrie Deas, chief executive of the National Federation of Fishermen's Organisation.

“That’s the bottom line and we need to have the resources in place to ensure that what will be our waters will be enforced.”

The UK is relatively short on enforcement vessels, but Deas noted the dramatic change which has come with satellite monitoring and “the kind of information technology and risk‐based approaches to enforcement that we’ve seen developing over the last 15 years”.

“There are also approaches like the Norwegian system which uses entry/exit notifications and gateways where vessels, fishing in UK waters, have to go through check‐in on their way back to port when they leave that country’s waters. So I think it’s certainly a valid question, but I don’t think enforcement poses insuperable challenges.”

If we set limits in our waters in access and opportunity then it behooves those other nations to behave themselves. We can take a leaf out of Norway’s book of a fairly robust enforcement system

Bertie Armstrong, head of the Scottish Fishermen's Federation (SFF), said he had been told in conversation by an EU international negotiator, “if you restrict access to your waters but give some, then all the European fishing nations will do is to enter your water for ten minutes, and misreport all the fish into their own waters that they’ve caught there”.

“In other words it would appear that on the ground inside the EU, the possibility of illegal behavior is actually openly being discussed. That would be absolutely unacceptable, as Barrie says there are electronic means and we would have to take a hard line view on widespread illegality if that were to turn out to be the other catching nation’s responses to any arrangements we put in place.”

He added the SFF did not expect widespread illegality, should the UK move to reserve its waters only for its own vessels.

“If we set limits in our waters in access and opportunity then it behooves those other nations to behave themselves,” he said. “There are electronic means to indicate when they are not, and if we can take a leaf out of Norway’s book of a fairly robust enforcement system, where arrest and fine is immediate and obvious, then I think we should be able to take charge of that.”

Unilateralism a threat to sustainability

Several speakers at the forum – including representatives from NGO ClientEarth and Daniel Owen, marine public law specialist with the UK's Fenners Chambers – raised the issue of how making unilateral management decisions could threaten fisheries.

Owen, addressing Armstrong, stated that while shared fish stocks might have an uneven distribution across different nations' waters, they remained shared stocks; the UK deciding upon its own quota for a migratory species while within its own waters, and EU nations then doing the same, could result in overfishing.

“So yes, I appreciate that there may be limits to how much the EU can actually catch in its own waters, but it doesn’t mean that it won’t fish as much as it can within its own waters, and that EU‐flagged vessels won’t, for example, fish right up to the EU side of the median line in order to fish as much as possible.”

“And so I wonder... whether there is a threat to sustainability through unilateralism – either way, by the UK or by the EU – [and] whether your point about unevenness of stock distribution is actually a natural constraint and will avoid this problem, or whether it isn’t and whether we need to look further and be very careful.”

Deas responded that science would be critical in defining shares under zonal attachment.

There shouldn’t be an argument here, it should be down to objective, agreed science on what is the zonal attachment in EU waters, Norwegian waters, UK waters, and that should be the basis of the agreement.”

Undercurrent News previously reported that common fisheries policy practices are likely to continue to play a part in the UK's fisheries management, even post-Brexit.

Earlier in 2017 the European Commission itself also warned that many member states have yet to implement EU fisheries regulations. Some countries are not properly enforcing fisheries law, either by not checking what boats or doing, or by avoiding categorising infringements as serious, added NGO ClientEarth.

NGOs have also argued that onboard electronic monitoring is an important step for the UK to take in order to maintain the sustainability of the recently Marine Stewardship Council-approved North Sea cod fishery.

title: Sea Shepherd assists Gabon in arrest of two Chinese vessels
content:
NGO Sea Shepherd has helped Gabonese authorities in the arrest of two Chinese fishing trawlers operating illegally, it said.

Its success comes one week after it announced "operation albacore II", a joint project between Sea Shepherd and the Gabonese government to tackle illegal, unregulated and unreported (IUU) fishing in central west Africa.

The two IUU trawlers, Haixin 23 and Haixin 28, flagged to China, were intercepted when five fishing vessels were observed by radar crossing the border between the Republic of Gabon and the Republic of Congo under the cover of darkness, with their fishing gear deployed and actively fishing, said Sea Shepherd.

Armed Gabonese marines boarded and secured the two trawlers without injury or incident as fisheries enforcement officers inspected the vessels. The other three trawlers escaped across the border into Congolese waters.

Upon inspection, it was discovered that neither vessel was licensed to fish in Gabonese waters, and one of the trawlers did not even have a license to fish in Congolese waters.

After a 30-hour transit, the two vessels, escorted by the Bob Barker, have been handed over to local authorities in Port Gentil to commence further investigation and the necessary legal proceedings, said Sea Shepherd.

The two 45-meter-long trawlers, with crew made up of Chinese and Congolese nationals, are the first arrests undertaken as a part of operation albacore II.

In 2016 Sea Shepherd partnered with the government of Gabon for the first operation albacore campaign, resulting in over 40 fishing vessel inspections at sea and the subsequent arrest of three IUU Congolese fishing trawlers and one Spanish long-liner. Operation albacore re-commenced in 2017 with the arrival of the Bob Barker in Gabon on July 5.

The campaign aims to expand existing monitoring, control and surveillance measures; to detect and deter IUU fishing activity while also monitoring legal compliance by licensed fishing operators.

Throughout the 2017 tuna fishing season, Gabon authorities will be stationed on board the Bob Barker, working alongside Sea Shepherd crew to patrol Gabon's sovereign waters.

title: ‘Codfather’ Rafael could exit seafood entirely with global settlement under negotiation
content:
Lawyers acting for the US government and Carlos Rafael, who owns a fleet of over 30 groundfish and scallop vessels, are negotiating a deal which could see him exit the seafood business completely, according to legal documents.

East coast US fishing baron Rafael, known as the “Codfather”, is pleading guilty to operating a long-running scheme through which he submitted falsified records to the federal government to evade federal fishing quotas. He is set for sentencing on July 28, 2017.

However, on July 13, his legal team filed a motion seeking to continue the sentencing hearing in this case to Sept. 8, 2017 “or any date convenient to the Court thereafter”.

Rafael’s council and lawyers acting for the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the regulatory agency with authority over the fishery at issue in this case, “have been discussing the possibility of a global settlement, which may involve Mr. Rafael exiting the commercial fishing business”, states the document.

“Despite diligently pursuing these discussions, the parties need additional time to resolve this issue – the result of which may be a critical component of the defendant’s argument to the Court at sentencing and may obviate the need for briefing and hearings on the forfeiture issues left open in the plea agreement,” it continues.

The document does not make any more comments on the nature of this settlement, or the implications for the rest of Rafael’s operations, or what assets he owns outside of the US to warrant a global deal.

Rafael’s lawyers, led by William Kettlewell of Collora, were not immediately available for comment to Undercurrent News.

Carlos Rafael has pleaded guilty to 28 federal charges, including lying about catches and smuggling cash
Read more

Andrew Lelling, who is leading the prosecution for the US attorney’s office, could also not be reached for comment on what could happen to Rafael's large fleet in the case of a settlement which sees him exit the sector.

Although the US government is pressing on with plans to “forfeit” 13 groundfish vessels and permits from Rafael’s large fleet, he is said to own 32 fishing vessels, controlled through independent corporate shells, as well as 44 permits.

In addition to seven more groundfish vessels to the ones set to be forfeited, Rafael owns 12 scallop vessels, which have been selling for high prices, of late. Also, he owns wholesaler Carlos Seafood, based in New Bedford, Massachusetts.

According to a letter to Undercurrent from John Pappalardo, CEO of the Cape Cod Commercial Fishermen’s Alliance, Rafael should be banned from commercial fishing forever and his quota should be redistributed to all the fishermen he harmed. "That’s what existing regulations mandate, that’s what many in the industry believe, and we agree," he wrote.

Sale plans

In 2015, Rafael had spoken to the media about selling his fleet, including both his scallop and groundfish vessels. He was tipped as being part of the deal at one point when Cooke Seafood was in the process of buying Wanchese Fish Company.

Nothing came of this and sources have since told Undercurrent Rafael may have been putting the sale talk out there, in order to scare the government into giving him disaster relief money he claimed to be owed. Sources close to Cooke said there were no direct talks with Rafael and that he was "telling stories" about being involved.

After Cooke went ahead with the purchase of Wanchese, undercover US agents posing as Russian mobsters approached Rafael about selling his business.

Rafael said he was looking to sell "the whole enchilada", including all fishing vessels and Carlos Seafood, his land-based buying and processing operation, according to an affidavit from Internal Revenue Service (IRS) special agent Ronald Mullett.

Despite having only $21 million in assets on his books, Rafael allegedly told the undercover agents posing as gangsters his business was worth $175m.

This was justified by the amount of cash he was generating through sales of illegally caught fish to a broker in New York, which was then being laundered back to Portugal, according to the legal documents.

Guilty plea

Rafael pleaded guilty to one count of conspiring to commit offenses against the US, 23 counts of false labeling and fish identification, two counts of falsifying federal records, one count of bulk cash smuggling, and one count of tax evasion.

A spokeswoman for the US Department of Justice said the maximum fine would be $7m, based on $250,000 for each of the 28 counts against Rafael.

The charges of conspiracy and tax evasion provide for a sentence of "no greater than" five years in prison, three years of supervised release, and a fine of $250,000. Twenty-three of the charges of falsifying records submitted to the federal government carry the same potential sentence, while two counts, brought under a different statute, provide for a sentence of no greater than 20 years in prison and a fine of $250,000 for each charge.

The charge of bulk cash smuggling provides a sentence of no greater than five years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of $250,000. Actual sentences for federal crimes are typically less than the maximum penalties.

He was initially arrested and charged in February 2016.

According to assistant US attorney Lelling, Rafael conspired with Antonio Freitas, a deputy sheriff from the Bristol County sheriff’s office, on smuggling a portion of the proceeds to Portugal.

Forfeiture process

Also on July 13, the US government submitted a proposed preliminary order of forfeiture for the 13 groundfish vessels, as it had previously said it would.

Even though the “global agreement” under negotiation between NOAA and Rafael’s legal team could “obviate the need for briefing and hearings on the forfeiture issues”, as the previously referenced document states, the government is pushing on with the process.

The document outlines the process here as follows:

Upon the issuance of a Preliminary Order of Forfeiture and pursuant to 16 U.S.C. § 3374(a), 28 U.S.C. § 2461(c), and Rule 32.2(b)(6)(C) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, the United States shall publish, for thirty (30) consecutive calendar days on the government forfeiture website www.forfeiture.gov, notice of the Preliminary Order of Forfeiture, notice of the United States’ intent to dispose of the Properties, and notice that any person, other than the Defendant, having or claiming a legal interest in the Properties must file a petition with the Court within sixty (60) days after the first day of publication on the government forfeiture website or within thirty (30) days after receipt of actual notice, whichever is earlier.


This notice shall state that the petition shall be for a hearing to adjudicate the validity of the petitioner’s alleged interest in the Properties, shall be signed by the petitioner under penalty of perjury, and shall set forth the nature and extent of the petitioner’s right, title or interest in the forfeited Properties and any additional facts supporting the petitioner’s claim and the relief sought.


The United States may also, to the extent practicable, provide direct written notice to any person known to have alleged an interest in the Properties that are the subject of the Preliminary Order of Forfeiture as a substitute for published notice as to those persons so notified.

title: Human trafficking lawsuit against High Liner’s Rubicon, Thai shrimp suppliers moves closer to trial
content:
A lawsuit against High Liner Foods-owned US importer Rubicon Resources and three linked Thai firms -- allegedly engaged in human trafficking as they supplied shrimp to retailers, including Walmart -- appears to be moving toward trial, according to court documents.

The civil lawsuit, brought in California federal court by seven Cambodians employed outside the US, accused the companies of violating the US Trafficking Victims Protection Act and knowingly profiting from the villagers' working conditions in 2011-2012.

Walmart is mentioned in the lawsuit, but is not a defendant. However, Undercurrent News sources believe Sam’s, the club store arm of Walmart, is the main customer of Rubicon.  Rubicon was purchased by High Liner Foods earlier this year, close to a year after the lawsuit was filed. Sam’s is not mentioned directly in the lawsuit.

US-based importer Rubicon, Thai exporter Wales & Co Universe, and Thai seafood companies Phatthana Seafood and S.S. Frozen Food – filed a motion in mid-August to dismiss the case arguing that because the alleged conduct took place outside the US, the matter shouldn't be heard in a US court. Phatthana Seafood and S.S. Frozen Food are both part of PTN Group, according to the complaint in the lawsuit. PTN and Wales were also previously shareholders in Rubicon, before the sale to High Liner.

The judge ruled in November against this motion, however.

Thai shrimp suppliers take stake in High Liner with Rubicon deal

Both parties attended a one-day mediation before judge Daniel Weinstein on June 6, a document filed 13 days later stated that those efforts did not lead to a settlement.

"The case did not settle during the mediation, but at its close, Weinstein suggested that he follow up with the parties in September 2017 after depositions have been taken," documents said.

Agnieszka Fryszman, who is working as the plaintiffs' lawyer, told Undercurrent over email that a trial has been set for Jan. 18. However, the parties may settle before then.

Undercurrent was unable to reach the defendants' lawyer in time for publication.

Keith Decker, CEO of High Liner, did not respond to a request for comment from Undercurrent. High Liner took over Rubicon in a $107 million deal that closed in May this year, just under a year after this lawsuit was announced in June 2016.

As part of the deal, Rubicon and its Thai suppliers and former shareholders took a 7% stake in High Liner. Although PTN and Wales were not named directly by High Liner, they are said to be part of this deal by Undercurrent sources.

Details of lawsuit

According to the lawsuit, the Cambodian plaintiffs were allegedly recruited from their villages and employed by the defendants in Thailand.

The suit states that the Cambodian villagers paid high recruitment fees but at the Thai factory were "paid less than promised and that their already meagre wages would be further reduced by unexpected salary deductions for housing, fees, and other charges".

As one example, the complaint details the experience of Keo Ratha, a Cambodian who was reportedly hired by an "agent of CDM Trading Manpower Co for work in Thailand".

That company then reportedly arranged his travel to a Thai shrimp factory operated by Phatthana on Oct. 30, 2011. There Ratha was told be would be paid at least $250 monthly and be given free housing in exchange for eight hours of labor per day.

Undercurrent News: World’s 100 Largest Seafood Companies 2016
View report

Ratha sold his motorcycle and paid a $150 fee to obtain a passport. He was reportedly told that $250 in recruitment fees would be deducted from his paychecks over time. However, the lawsuit claims that he was instead paid only $135 monthly and rent was deducted from that. His passport was also seized and held from him, it claims.

"After the salary deductions and rent payments, Mr. Ratha often did not have enough
money to buy enough food to eat. He was hungry much of the time," the lawsuit claims.

Additionally, he didn't have a choice in where to live and stayed in "overcrowded and unsanitary" conditions, sleeping on a concrete floor, the suit states. He had to work around chlorine which caused him health problems, he claims.

"He asked to quit several times, but was told he could not leave. He was also told that he could not get his passport back without paying off his recruitment fee," the suit states. "Mr. Ratha was afraid that he would be arrested by the Thai police if he fled without his passport, or that he would be sold to a fishing boat as a slave—a fate, unfortunately, not uncommon in the local fishing industry."

In January 2012 he was allowed to return to Cambodia after the media reported on the situation, the lawsuit claims.

Extraterritoriality

The defendants have asserted that “the conduct complained of occurred outside the US and the complaint does not allege a basis for extraterritorial jurisdiction”.

Lawyers representing the Cambodian villagers argue that the defendants’ basis for dismissal is incorrect.

Among other arguments laid out in the the response, the plaintiffs said that the defendants' failed to take into account changes that had been made to the Trafficking Victims Protection Act in 2008.

According to the filing, in 2008 the US Congress amended the act to "include accountability over the entire trafficking chain, including those at the top who financially benefit and those whose conduct occurs overseas".

The case, they said, relied "almost exclusively on a case law that predates the key 2008 amendments to the [Trafficking Victims Protection Act] and repeatedly misread the current statute, ignoring the relevant provisions enacted in 2008 that underpin the plaintiff's claims".

The Cambodians' lawyers said that "there was no extraterritorial jurisdiction provision at all [in the other case]...Congress amended the [Trafficking Victims Protection Act] in 2008 to expressly provide for extraterritorial jurisdiction over certain trafficking offenses, including the violations alleged here".

In response to the plaintiff's allegations, the defendants filed a reply on Oct. 14 agreeing that "Congress certainly has the authority to enact criminal laws with extraterritorial reach", but added that it "did not intend to allow private plaintiffs to take advantage of extraterritorial jurisdiction to seek to impose global labor standards on foreign companies".

The defendants argued that the "extraterritorial reach of the [Trafficking Victims Protection Act] extends only to criminal actions brought by the federal government, and not to private plaintiffs".

Among other complaints in the filing, the defendants also argue that the accusation that two US-based companies should be held accountable because they knowingly benefitted from alleged human trafficking is vague and can be applied to virtually any US company.

"Plaintiffs ask this court to construe the [Trafficking Victims Protection Act] to impose liability on any US company that “benefits” from doing business with foreign companies in parts of the world that have arguably suspect labor practices. If plaintiffs are right, then the litigation floodgates would open, since virtually every US company benefits from international commerce," the filing said.

title: Louisiana agents arrest man for fishing violations, drug possession
content:
A man from Bayou Dularge, a bay in Louisiana, was arrested for alleged drug and commercial fishing violations on June 27, the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries (LDWF) said in a release.

Agents with the LDWF arrested Anouda Lirette, 39, for using oversized skimmer nets as well as several other charges: possession of marijuana, possession of meth, possession of drug paraphernalia, possession of a firearm while in possession of a controlled, dangerous substance and possession of nongame birds. They found the skimmer nets were oversized and noticed some dead seagulls on the deck of his 42-foot shrimp boat.

After this, agents seized 784 pounds of shrimp, six seagulls, a rifle, drug paraphernalia, marijuana and crystal meth.

title: Norway’s ‘most modern crab plant’ closed as opilio quota launched
content:
Norway announced a 4,000-metric-ton snow crab quota on June 20, but changes to fishery access in 2017 mean the country's most modern plant lies idle, with many of its employees out of work.

Since September 2016, Seagourmet Norway's factory in Batsfjord, Finnmark has been closed, the company's chairman, Nikita Sinianskii, told Undercurrent News.

"The latest situation is the same -- the biggest and newest crab factory in Norway remains closed, and economically at the edge."

As of Jan. 1 2017 negotiations between Norway and Russia over the Barents Sea crab fishery saw the former excluded from the 'Loophole' area in which both had previously fished.

Also excluded were EU vessels, including those from Latvia which had supplied several Norwegian crab plants. It is thought Russia did this as too many vessels were fishing in the area, and it wants to come up with a management plan before the stocks are overfished.

Norwegian ministers maintain hope that once a management plan is in place, access to the fishery may be allowed again.

Seagourmet at Seafood Expo Global 2016, with Sinianaskii far right

On June 23 Sinianskii told Undercurrent the only two people working in the Seagourmet plant were he and his production manager. He claimed between 50 and 100 people had lost their jobs with the factory's closure -- "huge for a town like Batsfjord, with a population of 2,200".

"The reason [for the plant's closure] is the same as why Norwegian fishermen can no longer catch snow crab in the Loophole -- the policy of the fisheries minister, which gave all the snow crab to the Russians," he said. The Loophole is managed by the North East Atlantic Fisheries Commission.

"This question is only about Norwegian politicians. Since September 2016 we are waiting for any solutions from the Norwegian fishery authorities, but up until now all our proposals are rejected."

In 2016 -- before being forced to close in September -- the plant had handled 1,500 metric tons of live crab, he said. "The factory was designed and built specifically for crab processing, so there is no opportunity to jump for fish processing, for example."

Seagourmet's main supplier of live snow crab was Latvian firm North Star SIA, which has been unable to fish this year. It was also one of this company's vessels which was arrested by Norway in January, for the supposed illegal catching of snow crab on the Norwegian shelf in the Svalbard fishery protection zone.

Seagourmet has been able to handle some king crab instead, but this was only ever a small addition to its snow crab business, Sinianskii said. "To keep many workers only for a few hours per week or a few days in a month is economically a bad idea."

As for the possibility of buying snow crab from Norwegian vessels, he noted these are mainly processing on board, "and our attempt to attract Norwegian vessels to deliver crab to our factory have failed".

Batsfjord mayor Geir Knutsen told Undercurrent he was unsure of the government's plans in terms of fishery negotiations, but that "we hope there will be a positive solution for Seagourmet and Batsfjord".

Arctic Catch relies on its Wolf

Another Norwegian plant -- like Seagourmet, operated by Russian managers -- has also experienced issues with fishery changes in 2017, though to a less debilitating degree.

Vardo, Finnmark-based Arctic Catch had also been receiving some small volumes of snow crab from Latvian vessels, before they were disallowed.

Credit: Arctic Catch

Its most modern vessel, the Arctic Wolf, has been prevented from fishing in the Loophole region, following Russia's move to exclude other countries' vessels. "Too many vessels, mainly Russian and EU, were involved in the snow crab fishery in 2015-2016 in that small area," CFO Konstantin Vasilenko told Undercurrent.

"Catches dropped down critically, so for m/v Arctic Wolf it was not reasonable to stay with that. So for us the ban was good news, and we started operation of m/v Arctic Wolf again in 2017, but fishing in the Svalbard area."

Catches here are "twice less compared to the Loophole", but Russia's ban and a decrease in volumes from other areas, such as Canada, have pushed market prices up, said Vasilenko.

Arctic Wolf had been out of action since September 2015 as part of routine maintenance and classification, he explained.

"We actually have not stopped the factory in Vardo, because we have other activities like fish and king crab," he added. The firm's main markets are Japan, South Korea, the US and Europe.

Snow crab remains around 15-20% of Arctic Catch's total turnover. At present the firm continues to operate as it can, "hoping the Norwegian authorities will implement the regulation of snow crab fishery, that will help to have a sustainable business".

"Quota regulation is what we expected. Setting of the fishing rules, together with quota, will give an opportunity to make plans or to have better evaluation, and that is positive for a business. We expect some growth within the range of three years," he said.

title: Federal agents’ raid of processing plant remains a mystery
content:
Business appeared to be carrying on as usual at a Massachusetts processor that was recently visited by agents from the Internal Revenue Service and two other government agencies, reports South Coast Today.

It remains a mystery as to why the agents visited the plant. A multi-agency raid was conducted late morning on June 23, but officials have announced no arrests in connection with the visit.

The incident comes months after New Bedford made national headlines for unrelated law enforcement matter involving seafood.

Earlier this year, New Bedford resident Carlos "Codfather" Rafael pleaded guilty to falsifying fish quotas, conspiracy and tax evasion charges. He is scheduled to be sentenced in July.

title: Vietnam, Taiwan and the Philippines defy China fishing moratorium
content:

Chinese maritime security agencies patrol the waters and have previously arrested unlicensed vessels. However, since a United Nations tribunal declined to uphold China's territorial claims for much of the sea last year, the legality of the country's actions isn't certain.

title: Achorn says he was ‘co-operating witness’, not suspect in scallops theft
content:
Carl Achorn, a former VP of sales for Oceans Fleet Fisheries, said he cooperated with a police investigation into the recent theft of four metric tons of scallops from Seatrade International and was not a suspect.

In March, following reports of the theft of the scallops, which were valued at over $192,000, New Bedford Police asked for arrest warrants for Anthony Vieira and Michael Caton, former employees of New Bedford-based Continental Cold Storage, charging them with larceny from a building, forgery of a document, uttering a false document and conspiracy. 

Police say that the two men relied on a fake bill of landing document to transfer four pallets of U10 scallops from Continental to nearby cold storage provider Maritime Terminal International. The scallops were later sold on Vieira's behalf to Erik Orman of Tempest Fisheries. Achorn, at the time a VP of national sales at Oceans Fleet, arranged the deal for Vieira, Achorn said, according to a March 10 narrative filed by New Bedford police detective Barry Pacheco.

Police have not accused Achorn or Orman of any wrongdoing. Both men told police that they weren't aware prior to the sale that the scallops were stolen and neither man faces criminal charges. In a May 23 letter to Undercurrent News, Achorn, through an attorney, described his role in the investigation as a cooperating witness, not a suspect.

"Mr. Achorn has not been accused of or charged with, nor did he commit, any crime. The New Bedford Police Department reports show that Mr. Achorn's willing participation in the investigation assisted Detective Pacheco," Achorn's attorney, Adrienne Beauregard-Rheaume, wrote on her client's behalf.

Achorn was terminated from his position earlier this year for reasons unrelated to the theft.

When asked about the status of the scallop theft investigation, a spokesman for the New Bedford Police Department, Amancio Melo, told Undercurrent on May 24 that the "case has been closed on our end and forwarded to the district attorney's office".

When contacted, Gregg Miliote, director of communications for the Bristol County DA’s office, told Undercurrent that a pretrial hearing for Vieira and Caton is scheduled for July 10.

title: South Korean importer caught selling US lobsters as Canadian
content:
A South Korean importer has been arrested for selling American lobsters under a Canadian label for two and a half years, reports Yonhap News.

The importer, identified only as 53-year-old Kim, is accused of importing 18 metric tons of American lobsters worth KRW 2.13 billion ($1.9 million) in 321 shipments from September 2014 to March this year and selling them to local restaurants as more expensive Canadian products. 

Kim earned about KRW 2.6bn from the alleged fraud, as American lobsters are about 20% cheaper than their Canadian counterparts in the local market, the agency added.
