title: Chilean salmon convoy to Miami imperiled by modern-day bandits
content:
After a year of dealing with seaborne threats such as deadly algae and sea lice, Chile’s salmon farmers face a growing land-based problem in 2017: highway bandits.

Every day, hundreds of tons of Chilean fillets are sliced and packed onto refrigerated trucks in the country’s southern lake district, where they begin a 620-mile journey along Chile’s Pan American journey to Santiago Airport and then stowed on commercial flights bound overnight to Miami, where the product is distributed across the US.

With Chile’s salmon exports now valued at almost $4 billion a year, bandits are targeting darkly lit sections of the southern Pan American highway to flag down the trucks, assault the drivers and steal the merchandise for Santiago's black market.

Chile’s salmon farms are also fending off seaborne attacks as well, with a growing problem of thieves arriving overnight in small boats and stealing fish right out the salmon cages that are dotted around the city of Puerto Montt and the neighboring island of Chiloe, according to industry executives. The industry's growing headache isn't being addressed by the authorities, they say. 

"The level of robbery lately has been brutal: they are robbing in the sea and robbing on the highways, and nobody investigates it," said Roberto Izquierdo, the chairman of Chilean salmon farmer Invermar. "The national sport isn't soccer, it's robbery."  

Producer association SalmonChile estimates that $40 million-worth of salmon is stolen every year from land and sea-based theft, according to SalmonChile lawyer Gonzalo Mendez. The problem threatens to escalate. Prices surged last year, and Chilean salmon currently trades at near record highs in Miami.

Several individuals in Rio Negro, near Puerto Montt, were arrested in February for having robbed trucks belonging to Empresas AquaChile, with a view to selling the fish on the domestic market. The arrests are a drop in the ocean, and police need to investigate deeper to break up organized crime rackets, including the sellers of the contraband products, industry executives say.

“The police needs to devote more resources to this problem, which is affecting the industry in a significant way,” Mendez told Undercurrent News. “There is also a sanitary problem as the fish loses its cold supply chain and is distributed in conditions that are totally unsafe, something that the authorities need to take into consideration.” 

The problem would be easy to solve, as most of the illegal salmon is sold in Chile’s wealthier central region, as opposed to the poorer south. Most of the stolen fish has been put on trucks that will use the same Pan American highway to reach its final destination, Mendez said.

While Chile has one of the lowest crime rates in Latin America, there are often pockets of widespread opportunistic crime in certain areas of the country. The south of Chile has higher levels of unemployment and a lower capita-per-income than the center and copper mining rich north.

While that leads to crime, the same demographics have allowed Chilean farmers to build an entire salmon processing industry around the Puerto Montt area, unlike Norway that outsources all processing of its salmon. Chile has become the world's second-largest salmon farmer behind Norway and still has huge untapped potential, according to Marine Harvest CEO Alf Helge Aarskog and Cermaq CEO Geir Molvik. 

Chile's anchovy and sardine fishing companies based in the port of Talcahuano faced an almost identical threat more than a decade ago, when an infamous group of thieves known as "The Cats", or "Los Gatos", began to steal from open trucks of fish and fishmeal processing factories in the bay to resale in other parts of the country.

They were called The Cats as the robbers resembled cats as they scooped the fish out of open trucks before the police arrived. The Cats eventually became much more sophisticated with their methods of robbery, including purchasing high-speed yachts to intercept fishing vessels out at sea, before they were captured as part of a television investigation that was financed by the industry. 

In terms of economics, the salmon industry plunder is much more lucrative. Salmon exports rose 10%, to $3.8bn in value last year, according to central bank figures. At the same time, unemployment in the country has risen to 6.6% in the first quarter of this year, versus 6.3% a year ago, according to the National Statistics Institute. While the Los Lagos region where the salmon industry is mostly based has traditionally had low levels of unemployment, the jobless number has been rising after industry losses in 2015 that led to thousands of layoffs. 

A Multiexport Foods truck carrying salmon from the island of Chiloe to be processed at the company's main processing facility near Puerto Montt was robbed in September of last year, carrying 15 metric tons of salmon, worth about $110,000, according to radio station Bio Bio. The thieves in this case were captured shortly afterwards. 

The thefts are most difficult to handle once the fish has been processed and is on its way to Miami, Mendez explains, because producers are able to supply with their contractual clients with in the US, who are often big supermarket chains, representing a disadvantage compared with other supplies such as Canada, the Faroe Islands and Norway.

Remote salmon farmers dotted around islands in the fjords around Chile are also particularly vulnerable to pirate theft, said Invermar's Izquierdo.

Izquierdo, although an established businessman in Chile with fishery and forestry assets, has a relative newcomer to the salmon business after rescuing the company in 2015 from bankruptcy proceedings.  

"The robberies are really tough because from the investment perspective it degrades our commercial relationship with our clients in Japan and the United States," Mendez said. "We then have to call them up and tell them that we can't deliver because they robbed all the fish."

title: Stolen Seatrade scallops deal was one of several, police say
content:
(Update: This article has been updated on June 1, 2017, in part to clarify that Carl Achorn has described his role in the police investigation as a cooperating witness, not a suspect. )

The 'on the side' sale of 8,350 pounds of scallops recently stolen from New Bedford's Seatrade International was one of at least eight transactions carried out, police said.

In March, police issued arrest warrants for Anthony Vieira and Michael Caton, former employees of New Bedford-based Continental Cold Storage, charging them with larceny from a building, forgery of a document, uttering a false document and conspiracy. 

Police say that the two men relied on a fake bill of lading document to transfer four pallets of U10 scallops from Continental to nearby cold storage provider Maritime Terminal International. The scallops were later sold on Vieira's behalf to Erik Orman of Tempest Fisheries. Carl Achorn, a former vice president of national sales at Oceans Fleet Fisheries, arranged the deal for Vieira, Achorn said, according to a March 10 narrative filed by New Bedford police detective Barry Pacheco.

Police have not accused Achorn or Orman of any wrongdoing. Both men told police they weren't aware prior to the sale that the scallops were stolen, and neither man faces criminal charges. In a May 23 letter to Undercurrent News, Achorn, through an attorney, described his role in the investigation as a cooperating witness, not a suspect.

According to Pacheco's narrative, Achorn said in the March police interview that he and Vieira had previously worked together on "numerous transactions".

“Achorn began to explain that this was not the first time this had been done by Vieira and that they had done numerous transactions prior, including large amounts totaling one approximately 10,000 pounds to smaller numerous others at five to seven hundred pounds here and there”, Pacheco wrote in his police report, referring to the cash-only sale of allegedly stolen scallops.

“Achorn stated that most of these transactions were 10/20’s and not as high quality as this product, and also the size difference, not being U10’s, and the packaging material and quality were totally different than that of the 8,350-pound transaction.”

New Bedford has been the center of other allegations of crimes involving seafood in recent months. Scallop fleet owner Carlos Rafael recently pleaded guilty to charges that he repeatedly conspired to falsify records of groundfish catches and evaded taxes. He is yet to be sentenced.

And Pacheco said that the 8,350-pound transaction involving Vieira and Caton may have been one of eight deals.

"Although approximately seven other on the side scallop sales/money transactions were made by Vieira and Caton; including another large transaction of over 5,000 lbs, at this time I am only able to go by Caton statement, I am not able to locate these stolen scallops or their whereabouts," Pacheco wrote.

NEW INFORMATION

In Pacheco's report, he said Brian Cabral, president of Continental Cold Storage, had realized the Seatrade scallops were missing on Feb. 7 and began looking into the matter.

"The exact extent of the loss of Seatrade product is not known due to several more 'lots' of their product have [sic] been released without proper authorization from Seatrade," Pacheco wrote.

Seatrade told Undercurrent in a March statement that Continental is working with them to guard against future problems.

"Although this was an unfortunate incidence for everyone involved, Continental Cold Storage has assured Seatrade that they are implementing corrective actions they believe will make them a better vendor moving forward, strengthening an important link for the entire industry," Seatrade COO Bob Blais said.

Seatrade did not respond to a request for comment from Undercurrent on whether other scallop hauls have gone missing.

title: Rafael’s valuable scallop fleet ‘not for sale’, for now
content:
The fate of US fishing magnate Carlos Rafael’s scallop fleet remains unknown in the wake of his guilty plea to 28 counts of federal crimes, but, for now, a sale is not on the table, he said. 

Rafael told Undercurrent News on Monday the 12 scallop vessels, worth from $60 million-$85m, are not for sale.

When pressed on what will happen to the scallop fleet — his highest value vessels — after his June 27 sentencing hearing, Rafael said, “I have no idea. I have not even talked about what I’m going to do". 

Rafael last week pleaded guilty to 23 counts of false labeling and fish identification, two counts of falsifying federal records, one count of bulk cash smuggling, and one count of tax evasion. 

 One high level industry source, wishing to remain unnamed, told Undercurrent he anticipates the fleet will be sold, however. 

He even went as far as to say investment banks have been pitching for the business and that the fleet will likely be sold as a package. 

Rafael certainly has incentive to sell before the June sentencing, when the fate of his business and assets will become subject to the discretion of US district court judge William Young.

Young's sentencing decision will be based on the plea agreement, which stipulates fines totaling a maximum of $7m. If Rafael lacks the cash to pay the fines, it seems the assets would be next in line.

When pressed, a US Department of Justice spokesperson declined to speculate to Undercurrent on whether the assets could be used to pay the fines, indicating the answer depends on the sentencing process.

However, even if the government did seize vessels to pay those fines, that would leave a considerable amount of those vessels still in Rafael's ownership. Rafael's vessels and their corresponding permits are valued in the range of $5m-$7m, when looking at past deals for scallop vessels, and he owns at least 12 of them.

Even if Rafael does not sell the scallop fleet or have to hand it over to the government, he is unlikely to be able to continue running the business after his sentencing. He is likely to receive a prison sentence of three to four years, New Bedford mayor Jon Mitchell, a former federal prosecutor, told Undercurrent, and he faces a maximum sentence of 20 years. 

It is possible Rafael could maintain ownership but hand over scallop business management to someone while he does his prison time, although no likely candidates for such a role have arisen during discussions with Undercurrent and industry sources close to Rafael.

As for potential buyers, Cooke Seafood USA, a sister company of Canada's Cooke Aquaculture, is believed to have been the prospective buyer when Rafael attempted a scallop vessel sale in the past.

However, Rafael may have different priorities now. On the day he pleaded guilty, Rafael issued a statement espousing his loyalty to the interests of the port of New Bedford, stating his "single goal" was to protect his employees and "all the people and businesses who rely on our companies from the consequences of [his] actions" and said he would do everything he could to "make sure that the port of New Bedford remains America’s leading fishing port". 

In the event of a sale, it remains unknown whether this emphasis on the future of New Bedford means he hopes to sell to a local buyer.

Rafael valued his business at $175m in conversations with undercover US agents, who were posing as Russian gangsters interested in buying the business. Ultimately, the valuation came in an affidavit from Internal Revenue Service special agent Ronald Mullett. 

Rafael was first arrested in February of 2016 on charges of conspiracy and submitting falsified records to the US government to evade federal fishing quotas.

title: ‘Codfather’ Rafael set to give up 13 vessels as part of guilty plea
content:
US fishing mogul Carlos Rafael has agreed to give up at least 13 vessels from his fleet, according to a guilty plea filed in district court in Boston, Massachusetts on March 30.

Rafael, known as the “Codfather” due to his dominance of the New England groundfish business, pleaded guilty to operating a long-running scheme through which he submitted falsified records to the federal government to evade federal fishing quotas. 

As part of the plea, he will forfeit some of his assets. The “assets to be forfeited specifically include, without limitation” fishing vessels Athena, My Way, Hera, Hera II, Poseidon, Lady Patricia, Destiny, Olivia & Rafaela, Hercules, Sasha Lee, Drake, Bulldog, Southern Crusader II, as well as their permits.

All the vessels are for groundfish and were used in the scam, according to earlier legal documents.

"The forfeiture process begins following the conclusion of the criminal case (i.e. sentencing hearing), so there is no further public information detailing that at this time," a spokeswoman for the Department of Justice (DOJ) told Undercurrent News. 

US district court judge William Young scheduled sentencing for June 27, 2017.

It is also not clear what the fate of his seven other groundfish vessels or 12 scallop vessels will be, however.

In total, Rafael owns 32 fishing vessels, controlled through independent corporate shells, as well as 44 permits. Also, he owns wholesaler Carlos Seafood, based in New Bedford, Massachusetts. 

Guilty plea 

Rafael pleaded guilty to one count of conspiring to commit offenses against the US, 23 counts of false labeling and fish identification, two counts of falsifying federal records, one count of bulk cash smuggling, and one count of tax evasion. 

A spokeswoman for the DOJ said the maximum fine would be $7 million, based on $250,000 for each of the 28 counts against Rafael.  

The charges of conspiracy and tax evasion provide for a sentence of "no greater than" five years in prison, three years of supervised release, and a fine of $250,000. Twenty-three of the charges of falsifying records submitted to the federal government carry the same potential sentence, while two counts, brought under a different statute, provide for a sentence of no greater than 20 years in prison and a fine of $250,000 for each charge. 

The charge of bulk cash smuggling provides a sentence of no greater than five years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of $250,000. Actual sentences for federal crimes are typically less than the maximum penalties. 

He was initially arrested and charged in February 2016. 

According to assistant US attorney Andrew Lelling, who is prosecuting the case, Rafael conspired with Antonio Freitas, a deputy sheriff from the Bristol County sheriff’s office, on smuggling a portion of the proceeds to Portugal. Freitas, who has pleaded not guilty, is on unpaid leave from the sheriff’s office and is awaiting trial, according to the Boston Globe. 

A statement from Rafael, released March 30 in the run-up to the hearing by his attorneys at Collora, reads: "There have been a number of stories written about this case and about me. Some of the things that have been written are true, some are not. Here is the truth. Today I pled guilty to the charges facing me. I am not proud of the things I did that brought me here, but admitting them is the right thing to do, and I am prepared to accept the consequences of my actions."

"I started in this industry cutting fish when I was 16 years old, and it has been an honor to work with the people of the Port of New Bedford. Looking back, I’m most proud of the hundreds of jobs our businesses created, and the opportunities they created for families. Today, I have a single goal. To protect our employees and all of the people and businesses who rely on our companies from the consequences of my actions. I will do everything I can to make sure that the Port of New Bedford remains America’s leading fishing port."

title: Rafael pleads guilty, vows to protect employees from consequences of actions
content:
Carlos Rafael, the owner of one of the largest commercial fishing businesses in the US, pleaded guilty on Thursday to operating a long-running scheme through which he submitted falsified records to the federal government to evade federal fishing quotas. 

Rafael, known in the industry as “The Codfather”, due to his dominance of the New England groundfish sector, then smuggled a portion of the proceeds to Portugal. 

Rafael, 65, of Dartmouth, pleaded guilty in US district court in Boston, Massachusetts to one count of conspiring to commit offenses against the US, 23 counts of false labeling and fish identification, two counts of falsifying federal records, one count of bulk cash smuggling, and one count of tax evasion. 

The charges of conspiracy and tax evasion provide for a sentence of no greater than five years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of $250,000.  Twenty-three of the charges of falsifying records submitted to the federal government carry the same potential sentence, while two counts, brought under a different statute, provide for a sentence of no greater than 20 years in prison and a fine of $250,000. 

Carlos Rafael has pleaded guilty to 28 federal charges, including lying about catches and smuggling cash

The charge of bulk cash smuggling provides a sentence of no greater than five years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of $250,000.  Actual sentences for federal crimes are typically less than the maximum penalties. 

Rafael, owner of Carlos Seafood, based in New Bedford, Massachusetts, owned 32 fishing vessels through independent corporate shells and 44 permits.

He was initially arrested and charged in February 2016. US District Court judge William Young scheduled sentencing for June 27, 2017.

According to assistant US attorney Andrew Lelling, who is prosecuting the case, Rafael conspired with Antonio Freitas, a deputy sheriff from the Bristol County sheriff’s office, on smuggling a portion of the proceeds to Portugal. Freitas is on unpaid leave from the sheriff’s office, has pleaded not guilty, and is awaiting trial, according to the Boston Globe. 

A statement from Rafael, released Thursday in the run-up to the hearing by his attorneys at Collora, reads: "There have been a number of stories written about this case and about me. Some of the things that have been written are true, some are not. Here is the truth. Today I pled guilty to the charges facing me. I am not proud of the things I did that brought me here, but admitting them is the right thing to do, and I am prepared to accept the consequences of my actions.

"I started in this industry cutting fish when I was 16 years old, and it has been an honor to work with the people of the Port of New Bedford. Looking back, I’m most proud of the hundreds of jobs our businesses created, and the opportunities they created for families. Today, I have a single goal. To protect our employees and all of the people and businesses who rely on our companies from the consequences of my actions. I will do everything I can to make sure that the Port of New Bedford remains America’s leading fishing port."

This is not the take of the government, however.

“Mr. Rafael’s scheme not only compromised delicate fish populations, but also profited on the backs of his hard-working crew,” said US attorney William Weinreb.  “Mr. Rafael knew he was breaking the law by falsifying records, evading taxes and smuggling ill-gotten profits to Portugal.  Without Mr. Rafael and his scheme, New England fishermen who work hard for honest pay can now enjoy a more level playing field.”

The fraud perpetrated by Rafael “was motivated by greed, at the expense of the delicate ecosystem of the North Atlantic ocean”, said Joel Garland, a special agent with the criminal investigation arm of the Internal Revenue Service.

The charges arose out of an undercover investigation in which federal agents posed as Russian organized crime figures interested in buying Carlos Seafood. 

From 2012 to January 2016, Rafael routinely lied to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) about the quantity and species of fish his boats caught, in order to evade federal quotas designed to guarantee the sustainability of certain fish species. 

During that period, Rafael misreported to NOAA approximately 782,812 pounds of fish, telling NOAA that the fish was haddock, or some other abundant species subject to high quotas, when in fact the fish was cod, sole, or other species subject to strict quotas. 

After submitting false records to federal regulators, Rafael sold much of the fish to a wholesale business in New York City in exchange for bags of cash.  During meetings with the undercover agents, Rafael said that in his most recent dealings with the New York buyer he received $668,000 in cash.  Rafael smuggled at least some of that cash out of the US to his native Portugal, hiding it there to evade federal taxation on that revenue. 

“As the Nation’s federal maritime law enforcement agency, the Coast Guard has a critical role in enforcing federal fisheries regulations to protect our precious marine resources, promote sustainable fish stocks, and ensure a level playing field for all the honest fishermen,” said rear admiral Steven Poulin, a district commander in the US Coast Guard. 

Poulin said he was “proud” of the Coast Guard’s partnership with the NOAA office of law enforcement, the IRS criminal investigation division, and the US attorney's office “to help bring these illegal operations to a halt”.

According to Samuel Rauch, acting assistant administrator for NOAA Fisheries, the organization is “committed to ensuring a level playing field for honest fishermen”.

Rauch said, “Those who cheat the American taxpayers and their fellow fishermen will be found out, investigated, and brought to justice”.

title: Sales VP fired by Oceans Fleet interviewed in stolen scallops investigation
content:
(Update: This article has been updated on June 1, 2017, in part to clarify that Carl Achorn has described his role in the police investigation as a cooperating witness, not a suspect. )

Former Oceans Fleet Fisheries sales vice president Carl Achorn told police he helped arrange the sale of over 8,000 pounds of scallops valued at $192,050, but said he wasn't aware they were stolen from Seatrade International.

In March, New Bedford Police asked for arrest warrants for Anthony Vieira and Michael Caton, former employees of New Bedford-based Continental Cold Storage, charging them with larceny from a building, forgery of a document, uttering a false document and conspiracy. 

Police say that the two men relied on a fake bill of lading document to transfer four pallets of U10 scallops from Continental to nearby cold storage provider Maritime Terminal International. The scallops were later sold on Vieira's behalf to Erik Orman of Tempest Fisheries. Achorn, at the time a VP of national sales at Oceans Fleet, arranged the deal for Vieira, Achorn said, according to a March 10 narrative filed by New Bedford police detective Barry Pacheco.

Police have not accused Achorn or Orman of any wrongdoing. Both men told police that they weren't aware prior to the sale that the scallops were stolen and neither man faces criminal charges. In a May 23 letter to Undercurrent News, Achorn, through an attorney, described his role in the investigation as a cooperating witness, not a suspect.

Pacheco's narrative includes a lengthy interview with Achorn, where Achorn said he was told that Vieira was the owner of the scallops.

Achorn said Vieira was looking for cash and check in exchange for the scallops, but later changed this request to just cash. He says this cash request -- confirmed in a statement from Seaborn owner Jeffrey Lang, the first potential customer in the sale attempt -- caused him to begin asking Vieira “numerous times” whether the scallops were stolen.

ACHORN'S INTERVIEW

The narrative describes an effort by Achorn to sell the scallops to Lang, which included a transfer of the product to Lang's cold storage space.

Lang told police he never agreed to purchase the scallops due to suspicions they were stolen.

In his police interview, Achorn said that he and Vieira went for lunch in December, at which time Vieira "asked him if he would know anyone that could use some U10s, and that he, Vieira, had approximately 8,000 pounds (possibly 8,300lbs) to get rid of", the report written by the detective, Pacheco, states.

According to the report: "Achorn stated Vieira then advised him that he had had them for a while, and Achorn states he specifically remembers asking him, 'you have them?' and Achorn stated that Vieira explained to him that they belong to him and a boat owner, and that he has been holding them for him, and now has to give him money owed."

"Vieira advised him that he is selling them mainly for cash, and that although he may take some by check, he would want it in cash," the report states.

According to the narrative describing the interview with Lang, the cash request caused him to become so suspicious that he declined the purchase.

Lang “stressed that not only did the transaction not seem realistic due to the price of the scallops but the fact of the quality of them, and the fact that he would have to come up with approximately $120,000 cash; due to Achorn advising him that this was a mostly cash deal,” Pacheco wrote.

The price of the scallops, had they been sold at Achorn’s asking price of $13/lb, would have been $108,550; and the starting price of scallops at that time of year was $19.50/lb, equaling $162,825; and it could have been as high as $23/lb, equaling $192,050, Pacheco added.

Pacheco wrote that Achorn said that after Lang declined the deal, the scallops were transferred into an account called “Scallop Connection”, upon order from Vieira. Achorn claims Vieira later told him he made up the name “Scallop Connection” in order to release the scallops. 

“Achorn states that at this time, he felt skeptical, but he continued with the call to Lang, requesting the move out of his account to Vieira, aka Scallop Connection,” Pacheco wrote.

ACHORN'S EMPLOYMENT

On Monday, Oceans Fleet Fisheries CEO Lars Vinjerud told Undercurrent News that Achorn was fired two to three weeks ago. Vinjerud said this was for "performance" issues unrelated to the suspected scallop theft.

Achorn had worked for the company since 2007, according to his LinkedIn profile, aside from a year-long stint with JT Sea Products that ended in 2016. At the time he returned, Achorn told Undercurrent that Oceans Fleet “felt like home”.

Achorn's departure from JT Sea was followed by a lawsuit alleging trademark infringement over the company's "Carl’s Choice" brand of scallops -- which the company created and gave to Achorn to manage, Jim Thompson of JT Sea said.

The suit asserted that the brand was being infringed upon by Ocean Fleet’s creation of the Carl’s Select brand and was settled out of court.

title: Seatrade commends police for ‘quick and complete’ investigation into 8,350-pound scallop theft
content:
New Bedford police have identified and arrested suspects in their investigation into 8,350 pounds of stolen scallops valued at $192,050, reports South Coast Today.

The suspects are Antonio Vieira and Michael Caton, both of Rhode Island and both former employees of Continental Cold Storage, according to an affidavit from New Bedford police detective Barry Pacheco's, which the newspaper attained.

Vieira was charged with larceny from building an "utter false document" and forgery of a document and conspiracy, the newspaper said.

Caton was arrested on Thursday at the New Bedford Police Department and faces the same charges, the newspaper said. He was identified to police as a possible suspect early in the investigation, according to police documents.

"Seatrade commends the New Bedford Police Department for their quick and complete investigation," Bob Blais, chief operating officer of East Coast Seafood and Seatrade International, told the newspaper.

The theft allegedly occurred at Continental Cold Storage. Vieira, who worked there, has been fired, having worked there two decades. 

"Our integrity is of the utmost importance," Brian Cabral, president of Continental Cold Storage, told the newspaper. "These dishonorable employees have been terribly deceitful."

Caton, identified in New Bedford police detective Barry J. Pacheco's affidavit as a former "logistics manager," quit while providing three days' notice after paying back a $2,500 loan from Continental on Jan. 26, according to the police report. A press release issued by the New Bedford Police on Wednesday, the day a story on the theft appeared in The Standard-Times, says that Caton was fired.

Vieira, arrested on March 10, is scheduled to appear in court for a pre-trial hearing on May 5, while Caton's court date is April 24.

New Bedford Police haven't been able to locate the missing scallops during their investigation, which began by Pacheco on Feb. 17 with an interview of Cabral.

title: Arrest warrants issued over 8,000-pounds of scallops allegedly stolen from Seatrade International
content:
More than 8,000 pounds of stolen scallops valued at the time at $192,050 circulated through multiple seafood houses last December, reports The Standard-Times based on documents it obtained.

A warrant was issued for the arrest of Antonio Vieira and Michael Caton, claiming 8,350 pounds of scallops were stolen from Seatrade International and that Viera attempted to sell them to a number of seafood houses in New Bedford. Vieira is a resident of Tiverton, Rhode Island, and Caton -- a former Rhode Island resident -- now resides in California, the newspaper said.

New Bedford Police Detective Barry Pacheco detailed his investigation into the disappearance of scallops from Continental Cold Storage, beginning on Feb. 17 and concluding on March 10, in a 24-page narrative.

It said frozen scallops were discovered missing Feb. 6, when Continental couldn't locate four pallets of them for release to SeaTrade. He also interviewed employees at Maritime Terminal International, the closest storage facility to Continental, where Vieira emerged as a suspect. Eventually scallops landed at Northern Wind at the end of December, Pacheco said in the report.

title: US-certified shrimp trawler caught fishing illegally in Liberian waters
content:
A Nigerian-flagged fishing vessel, the Star Shrimper XXV, allegedly fished actively without a license on March 13 in the West African waters of Liberia -- the most serious offense under Liberian fisheries regulations, reports The Maritime Executive. The offense can result in a fine up up to $1 million.

The Star Shrimper XXV -- reportedly part of a fleet owned by Atlantic Shrimpers and certified by the US Department of State -- was detected by radar off the waters of Cote d'Ivoire.

A Liberian coast guard boarding team mobilized on the Sea Shepherd vessel M/Y Bob Barker and headed toward the vessel, where it was reportedly fishing with trawl gear in the water.

Star Shrimper XXV's fleet is is Friend of the Sea certified for sustainable black tiger prawn fishing, but the guidelines require the vessels to comply with legal requirements and fishing permits.

"It is not without irony that while the Star Shrimper XXV had by-catch limitation devices like turtle excluder devices on board (which they were not using during the time of their arrest), they deliberately entered Liberian waters to fish illegally without a license,” Sea Shepherd campaign leader Peter Hammarstedt told the newspaper.

“Had it not been for the intervention of the Liberian coast guard and Sea Shepherd, the illegal catch of the Star Shrimper XXV would have been sold in American and European markets as ‘sustainably-certified’. Sea Shepherd Global urges the United States Department of State to seriously review their import agreement with Atlantic Shrimpers Limited.”

title: ‘Codfather’ hearing pushed back
content:
The March 16 hearing for US fishing magnate Carlos Rafael has been pushed back to March 30, according to a court filing dated March 15.

Rafael, the East Coast US fishing magnate known as the "codfather", is expected to plead guilty to evading fishing quotas and smuggling profits to Portugal at the coming hearing, as confirmed in a tweet by the US attorney's office for the district of Massachusetts.

He had asked the court to postpone his trial in part to pursue talks with prosecutors about "resolving" the matter, as Undercurrent News reported on Jan. 23.

Rafael was arrested on Feb. 26 of last year on charges of conspiracy and submitting falsified records to the US government to evade federal fishing quotas.

Among the 27 counts Rafael faced on a federal indictment were 25 charges of falsifying records, one count of conspiracy, and a charge of bulk cash smuggling.

According to the Justice Department (DOJ), two of the 25 charges of falsifying records submitted to the federal government could fetch prison terms of up to 20 years in addition to a $250,000 fine. Another 23 counts of the charge, brought under a different statute, would carry "the same potential sentence", the DOJ said in a May release.

Rafael controls nearly a fifth of the New Bedford, Massachusetts fishing economy through his at least 36 local vessels, each with commercial fishing permits. It is not clear what the guilty plea will mean for his fleet.

title: EU snow crab fishermen expelled from Barents Sea, Svalbard waters
content:
A few EU vessels were arrested by Norwegian authorities in the Barents Sea and Svalbard waters, Europeche -- which represents the fisheries sector in Europe -- said in a release. 

Since 2013, EU vessels have been authorized to fish for snow crab in the Barents Sea and Svalbard waters, and Europeche said these vessels were carrying valid fishing license.

The Norwegian authorities "refuse to recognize the legitimate right of EU vessels to sustainably and legally operate in this area", Europeche said.

To date, 19 large boats from several EU countries remain tied up in port "out of fear of being arrested".

The snow crab fishery is a new growing business in these waters since it's considered an invasive species and becoming an important player in the Barents Sea ecosystem.

“The legal fishery conducted by EU fishermen has been harshly interrupted, forcing EU authorized crabber vessels to remain at ports, while Norwegian vessels continue catching snow crab," said president of Europeche, Javier Garat.

"We hope that the Norwegian court ruling will act as a wake-up call to the attitude of Norway, which must respect its international obligations. Many EU jobs and families directly depend on this activity and have no other alternative. We urge the European Commission services, together with Member States, to urgently find solutions to allow snow crab fishermen to resume their legal activities, since EU operators are losing an average of € 1million per month each.”

title: Untitled
content:
Nigeria's federal government will henceforth arrest, prosecute and fine illegal importers of frozen foods into the country, and seal coldstores where it is sold, reports The Nation.

Senator Heineken Lokpobiri, minister of state for agriculture and rural development, said the government would also set up a taskforce to seal and prosecute operators of coldstores who deal on those illegally imported produce.

The ministry was working in collaboration with the Nigeria Customs Service, Nigerian Navy and the Nigerian Marine Police to actualize the plan, he said.

Offenders would pay a fine of $250,000, receive five years' imprisonment, or both, in addition to the forfeiture and destruction of the produce as stipulated by the law.

Tilapia, pangassius, horse mackerel, and sardine are among the species entering the country illegally, he said. The illegal venture had resulted in huge loss of revenue, a decrease in local production, and the loss of jobs, he added.

title: ‘Codfather’ Rafael to plead guilty to evading quotas, smuggling profits
content:
East Coast US fishing magnate Carlos Rafael will plead guilty to evading fishing quotas and smuggling profits to Portugal.

The US attorney’s office for the district of Massachusetts confirmed, in a tweet, that Rafael would plead guilty on March 16.

On Jan. 23, Undercurrent News reported that Rafael had asked the court to postpone a trial in part to pursue talks with prosecutors about "resolving" the matter. 

Rafael faced 27 counts on a federal indictment. That included 25 charges of falsifying records, one count of conspiracy, and a charge of bulk cash smuggling.

Rafael was arrested on Feb. 26, then released from custody on a $1 million bond on March 2. Federal agents posed as Russian mobsters looking to buy Rafael's business in the sting.

He controls at least 36 local vessels with commercial fishing permits this year, giving him control of nearly a fifth of the New Bedford fishing economy.

Prosecutors allege that Rafael sold illegally caught fish to a wholesale buyer in New York City in exchange for tens of thousands in cash, much of which he then smuggled to Portugal through Logan International Airport in Boston with the help of former Bristol County sherif's deputy Antonio Freitas.

The March 9 tweet from the US  attorney’s office did not mention that Rafael's intention to plead guilty means for Freitas.

According to the Justice Department (DOJ), two of the 25 charges of falsifying records submitted to the federal government could fetch prison terms of up to 20 years in addition to a $250,000 fine. The other 23 counts of the charge, brought under a different statute, would carry "the same potential sentence", the DOJ said in a May release. 

Consolidation coming in US scallop fishery
Read more
The conspiracy and cash smuggling charges could each bring a maximum of five-year prison terms and a $250,000 fine.

However, "actual sentences for federal crimes are typically less than the maximum penalties", the DOJ said.

Additionally, the indictment states that if Rafael is found guilty on one or more of the counts against him, the government will pursue forfeiture of 13 of Rafael’s vessels and the associated commercial fishing permits, or property equal to that value. As well as whitefish vessels, Rafael also has a fleet of scallopers, which have been changing hands for big money of late.

It is not clear what the guilty plea will mean for Rafael's fleet.

title: Philippines’ president won’t seek sea war with China, despite successful arbitration over fishing rights
content:
The Philippines' controversial president, Rodrigo Duterte, does not want to fight with China over the fisheries dispute among the two countries, despite Manila having won an arbitration versus Beijing on the South China Sea, sources close to the government revealed to Undercurrent News.

Chinese fishing vessels continue to poach in foreign waters, including Korea’s Western Sea, East China Sea, South China Sea, Indian Ocean, Huffington Post reported last December.

Illegal fishing in Filipino waters, carried out by Chinese, Vietnamese and Taiwanese vessels, affects all fish resources, including tuna and pelagics, sources told Undercurrent.

"Duterte aims to have a new approach with China, a totally different one from the different administration, which is to talk to China," one source noted.

The new president aims to negotiate with China, prioritizing talks on trade and investments to issues related to fishing. "Philippines cannot afford a war with the major maritime power in the region, so we need to talk," one of the sources pointed out.

Fisheries issues among the two countries will be discussed at a later stage, but are not a priority for the Philippines' foreign policy.

Meanwhile, Filippino vessels have restarted fishing activity in the Scarborough shoal, which was previously obstructed by the Chinese coastguard, according to sources.

Cooperation on patrol between the two coastguards has also re-started, sources said.

At a local level, Duterte's administration prioritizes peace and order as well as the eradication of illegal drugs and corruption in the country. 

Duterte's government is not planning to introduce quotas to manage fisheries resources. The president has not forecast to change existing policies in place for fisheries management within its exclusive zone, sources also said.

South China Sea case

The problem between the Philippines and China on the West Philippines Sea and the South Chinese Sea is mainly on fisheries, sources close to the matter told Undercurrent. 

"It all started when the Philippines' government arrested Chinese fishermen intruding in the Philippines 200 miles exclusive economic zone," one of the sources told Undercurrent.

China claimed fishing rights in the north-west side of the Philippines waters, particularly on the Scarborough shoal, in line with its "nine-dash line" policy.

Chinese island building in the region, with the installation of military weapons on some islands, has seriously damaged the coral reef and the fisheries population as well as raised concerns of political insecurity for the countries in the region and also for the other maritime powers, sources said.

Last year, the Philippines asked an arbitral tribunal to rule on whether China's "nine-dash line" was a valid maritime claim and whether eight Chinese-occupied disputed features qualified as low-tide elevations, rocks or islands. These categories determine what, if any, maritime entitlements they should generate.

The Hague-based international tribunal's judgement favored the Philippines' claims, stating that the reefs and atolls on which Beijing claimed control justifying its rights in the South China Sea, were not islands, as they get submerged during high-tide.

The nine-dash line has no basis under international law, which was the position of the Philippines, according to the judgement. 

The decision was a landmark, according to Filipino sources. The decision is meant to be binding on the parties, although its implementation is still unresolved.

However, China said it would not accept the ruling, sources said. China's supreme court said last August that fishermen caught in China's exclusive economic zones would face strict legal action, the International Business Times reported.

Despite last year's arbitration proving that there are no overlapping claims between China and the Philippines and that the latter has exclusive rights over the fisheries resources in the China South Sea over its 200 nautical miles exclusive economic zone, Chinese vessels continue to fish illegally in the area.

title: High vessel, permit prices could slow US scallop M&A in 2017
content:
Long-term trends bode for additional consolidation in the US scallops sector, but high permit prices and uncertainty in New Bedford could slow the pace of M&A in 2017, sources told Undercurrent News.

The US sector, with fishing and processing concentrated in Massachusetts and, to a lesser extent, Virginia, continues to see success as prices stay elevated even as they taper down from previous highs. 

Consolidation outlook

Consolidation in the sector -- driven since 2015 to a major extent by larger players such as Canada's Cooke Seafood and Bregal Partners' Blue Harvest Fisheries -- has increased the value of permits and vessels. Vertically integrated companies that catch and process scallops are expanding, a trend that seems set to continue. 

Consolidation coming in US scallop fishery
Read more

But record prices, such as the $7 million that Greg Fulcher paid for a license and vessel in July 2015, have limits.

"There are very high valuations," Jeff Davis, Blue Harvest's CEO told Undercurrent in a interview earlier this month. "Quite honestly, the prices we have seen on the last few boats sold are at a higher price than what we are interesting in."

Fishermen looking to retire might be willing to offload their vessels, but there's not a lot of pressure otherwise, he said.

"We have not found anything out there actually for sale at the moment. No one is out there selling boats," he said.

Blue Harvest

Until the late 2010s, the US scallops sector had been largely split between individual owner-operators and some multi-vessels owners. But that balance is tilting toward the multi-vessel operators, and for good reason, Davis said.

"Globally, I think consolidation will continue in seafood. As the business becomes more complex, you need scale to make it work. I look at compliance issues today and you realize that we have to have more expertise on staff than you needed 10-15 years ago," he said.

Blue Harvest's entry into the market is a relatively recent development. The company was created when Bregal and other investors purchased Newport News, Virginia-based Peabody in 2015.  

Using Peabody's eight scallop vessels as a starting point, the firm, renamed as Blue Harvest, went on to buy Massachusetts-based Harbor Blue Seafood, taking that its vessel count to 15.

Under current law, one owner can possess up to 17 vessels, which is Blue Harvest's target, Davis told Undercurrent in September 2016. 

“We are still looking for a couple of vessels to round off our fleet. We would like 17 boats,” Davis said.

Additionally, Blue Harvest has done deals on the processing side with the purchase of Hygrade Ocean Products in August and High Liner Foods' scallop business in October.

All of this M&A will mean that Blue Harvest will land close to 12% of all US scallops and approach annual sales of $150m. 

Small fishing companies increasingly have the same compliance burdens that big firms do but aren't able to afford it, Davis said, creating a natural driver for consolidation.

"For example, when we bought Peabody and Harbor Blue, the overhead has not really changed. We need the same staff to run one company as for running both. We can do 15 boats instead of eight, with the same staff. There are efficiencies," he said. 

Other major players in the market such as New Bedford's Eastern Fisheries, the industry leader, have said little publicly about future scallops M&A.

Eastern is co-owned by Roy Enoksen’s Nordic Fisheries and by Frank O’Hara's O'Hara Corp, which own 26 vessels between them. 

The company runs two processing plants in New Bedford and two factories in northwestern China, one that processes Alaskan flatfish, and one that focuses on scallops. 

In 2015 Eastern opened a processing plant in Staphorst, Netherlands, to serve European market producing the company’s 5.5m pounds of annual sales for private label.

In a March 2016 interview, Eastern's Joe Furtado told Undercurrent that the company's future expansion will likely focus on getting closer to overseas supplies, such as in Hokkaido, Japan.

“If we can involve ourselves in the harvesting element in other parts of the world whether it’s through aquaculture or through other vessel purposes than we will certainly intend to do that," he said. "But at a minimum, at the factory level, we want to be on the ground in these areas to be as close to the source as we possibly can.”

Immediate plans

Meanwhile, Davis said though Blue Harvest still sees expansion in its future, that may not come in 2017.

"There is a point where we we’d look at west coast assets, but we are not pursuing anything now," he said. "We have to digest what we have now before we look at new ventures. I’d say we’d be pretty quiet in 2017."

Another source, who spoke to Undercurrent on condition of anonymity, said that while the pace of M&A pay pause, he predicts it to continue for the foreseeable future. The drive to create vertically integrated scallop suppliers is squeezing out firms that focus only on processing.

“It take scallops perhaps off the market that they can take off for their own customers worldwide,” he said of harvesting firms that also process. "How is the little guy going to survive if he’s going to have to buy scallops from someone else?"

The source compared the current situation on the harvesting side with what independent scallops dealers have faced since the 1980s and 1990s as broadline distributors such as US Foods and Sysco expanded into supplying fish.

“There’s very little fish guys left and I foresee the same thing happening in this market,” the source said, anticipating a day in the not too distant future when the public auctions that determine scallop prices may become obsolete. 

'Codfather'

One major question mark still looms over the New Bedford-based sector in the short-term, the fate of Carlos Seafoods' Carlos "Codfather" Rafael who current faces 27 federal criminal charges.

He controls at least 36 local vessels with commercial fishing permits this year, giving him control of nearly a fifth of the New Bedford fishing economy. This includes over a dozen scallop vessels.

Rafael was arrested on Feb. 26, then released from custody on a $1m bond on March 2. Federal agents posed as Russian mobsters looking to buy Rafael's business in the sting.

Prosecutors allege that Rafael sold illegally caught fish to a wholesale buyer in New York City in exchange for tens of thousands in cash, much of which he then smuggled to Portugal through Logan International Airport in Boston with the help of a sheriffs's deputy, Antonio Freitas.

Prosecutors have indicated they may apply to seize the company's assets if Rafael is convicted, although more recently his attorneys have floated the possibility of a settlement.

Any change to Carlos Seafoods's operations could have a significant impact on the sector, Davis of Blue Harvest told Undercurrent.

"That could be a big one," he said. "Everyone is waiting to understand what the impact of that is going to be. As you have all of his groundfish permits sitting out there. You have his scallop licenses, also. None of us know what the government’s view on that is going to be. Could they technically pull all of his licenses?"

title: Norway’s arrest of Latvian vessel on Svalbard raises conflict potential
content:
EU, Russia and the US have challenged Norway's arrest of a Latvian vessel fishing snow crab around Svalbard, the Norwegian Arctic archipelago, the Barents Observer reported.

Norway arrested the vessel on Jan. 16, which was suspected of having engaged in the illegal catching of snow crab on the Norwegian shelf in the Svalbard fishery protection zone without the permission from Norwegian authorities, the Norwegian Navy said.

The crabber, suspected of having put out 2,600 snow crab traps, was subsequently forced to set course to the port of Kirkenes, where it today is awaiting police prosecution.

Norway argues that the Svalbard treaty of 1920 gives it full sovereignty over the continental shelf around the archipelago. That view, however, is disputed by the international community, stating that all signatory counties of the Svalbard Treaty have equal rights to engage in economic activity in the waters and on the shelf.

The snow crab has the potential to become a new conflict issue in the area, according to Per-Arne Totland, a writer and expert on the Svalbard archipelago.

Regulations applying to the continental shelf for snow crab are the same applying to oil and gas, and a conflict over the snow crab could be seen as a test as to whether Norway can be subject to pressure with regard to the shelf around Svalbard, according to Totland.

title: Bloomberg pins Ocean Trawlers co-founder Orlov’s wealth at $1bn
content:
Bloomberg values the wealth of Vitaly Orlov, co-founder of Ocean Trawlers, at $1 billion, according to an article published on Jan. 23.

However, Orlov told Bloomberg he feels the value is “much more moderate” than $1bn.

He cited “country risks” as the reason, most notably a lack of clarity about a new quota system the government is preparing to introduce favoring companies that order trawlers from Russian shipyards, a potential boon for newer, smaller businesses.

Also, Orlov told Bloomberg the company has spent about $600m in the past decade to expand its fleet.

“I never imagined I could create such a huge company,” Orlov told Bloomberg, in his first foreign media interview. “Now we want to be where the end-users are -- retail chains, food services. We see potential here.”

Orlov has benefited from the “colliding forces of global trade and sanctions that today define Vladimir Putin’s Russia”, according to Bloomberg.

The interview with Bloomberg took place in Orlov’s office on Russia’s Kola Bay, across the water from a $30m factory the company has just built under its Murmansk-based Norebo Holding parent.

In the plant, Orlov plans to process 15,000 metric tons of the 500,000t the company’s fleet catches. The company has previously told Undercurrent News of its plans to expand into processing value-added products in the plant.

According to the Bloomberg article, Norebo’s fleet hauled in almost 11% of the 4.75m metric tons the Russian Federal Fisheries Agency said were caught by Russian fisherman last year.

Norebo, which had revenue of $600m in 2015, generates 60% of its sales from outside the country, wrote Bloomberg. Also, the company has seen a surge in domestic consumption as Putin’s sanctions limit food imports.

According to Orlov, Norebo also has $450m of net debt issued to fund expansion and consolidate ownership.

Orlov took control of Norebo last year when one partner, Magnus Roth, sold his share of the operation back to him, and a second was sentenced for trying to extort a stake of his own. Undercurrent first reported Roth had sold his shares.

Last month, Alexander Tugushev, who was also involved in the build-up of Ocean Trawlers, was placed under house arrest and charged with extortion regarding his ownership claims, according to a report from TASS, the government-owned news agency.

According to Bloomberg, Tugushev declined to discuss his previous legal troubles, and hasn’t responded to requests for further comment since his arrest on Dec. 30. 

Roth sold his 33% stake of Norebo to Orlov last May for an undisclosed sum. He later told Undercurrent he had "mixed feelings" on the sale.

title: Carlos ‘Codfather’ Rafael to talk with prosecutors about resolving criminal case
content:
Indicted New Bedford scallops magnate Carlos "Codfather" Rafael has asked the court to postpone his upcoming trial in part to pursue talks with prosecutors about "resolving" the matter, court documents show.

One of Rafael's attorneys, William Kettlewell, asked the Massachusetts federal court of judge William G. Young to postpone Rafael's Feb. 13 trial to at least March 20. Young granted the order.

The delay, the second in recent months, is required as Kettlewell is expected to represent a different client in a two-week trial beginning on Jan. 30, the lawyer wrote. But, that time can also be used for negotiations with prosecutors about a possible settlement.

"The short continuance requested in this motion will allow counsel time to complete that trial and complete discussions with the US Attorney’s Office regarding resolving this matter short of trial," Kettlewell wrote in the motion.

He did not respond to requests from Undercurrent News for comment.

The motion did not describe what any possible settlement or plea deal would entail. 

Assistant US attorney Andrew Lelling assented to the motion, which adds that the government is ready to proceed with trial of Rafael's fellow defendant former Bristol County sherif's deputy Antonio Freitas.

Indictment

Rafael faces 27 counts on a federal indictment. That includes 25 charges of falsifying records, one count of conspiracy, and a charge of bulk cash smuggling.

Rafael was arrested on Feb. 26, then released from custody on a $1 million bond on March 2. Federal agents posed as Russian mobsters looking to buy Rafael's business in the sting.

He controls at least 36 local vessels with commercial fishing permits this year, giving him control of nearly a fifth of the New Bedford fishing economy.

Prosecutors allege that Rafael sold illegally caught fish to a wholesale buyer in New York City in exchange for tens of thousands in cash, much of which he then smuggled to Portugal through Logan International Airport in Boston with the help of Freitas.

According to the Justice Department (DOJ), two of the 25 charges of falsifying records submitted to the federal government could fetch prison terms of up to 20 years in addition to a $250,000 fine. The other 23 counts of the charge, brought under a different statute, would carry "the same potential sentence", the DOJ said in a May release. 

The conspiracy and cash smuggling charges could each bring a maximum of five-year prison terms and a $250,000 fine.

However, "actual sentences for federal crimes are typically less than the maximum penalties," the DOJ said.

Additionally, the indictment states that if Rafael is found guilty on one or more of the counts against him, the government will pursue forfeiture of 13 of Rafael’s vessels and the associated commercial fishing permits, or property equal to that value. As well as whitefish vessels, Rafael also has a fleet of scallopers, which have been changing hands for big money of late.

title: Iceland police arrest crew of Polar Seafood vessel in connection with drugs, missing girl
content:
Icelandic police reportedly found a large quantity of drugs aboard a Polar Seafood trawler and have arrested three crew members in connection with a girl's disappearance, local media reported.

The drugs were seized aboard the Greenlandic vessel Polar Nanoq and at least three of the crew, whose names were not divulged, were arrested, the Icelandic Review reported. 

The crew members are considered suspects in the disappearance of 20-year-old Birna Brjánsdóttir.

The vessel had been halted on its journey from Iceland to Greenland and told to turn back by Icelandic police

A red Kia Rio car -- the kind the Reykjavík Metropolitan Police have been looking for in connection with the case -- has been found to be connected to the trawler.

The trawler left harbor on Jan. 14, but police have since requested a list of its crewmembers. The shoes of the missing girl were found close to where the trawler lay docked.

A Danish frigate aided in communicating with the Polar vessel, after itself being asked for help by Icelandic police. The trawler is due back in Reykjavik late on Jan. 19.

title: Former Seafish Tasmania boss charged over $260m drugs ring
content:
The former director of Australian fishing company Seafish Tasmania has faced court in Sydney after being charged over Australia's biggest cocaine haul, reports ABC.

Australian Federal Police announced it had arrested 15 men and seized 1.1 metric tons of cocaine, worth an estimated AUD 360 million ($261m).

The syndicate was allegedly using a fishing trawler to meet a "mother ship" from South America to bring the cocaine into Australia. Joseph Pirrello, 63, was arrested in Sydney on Christmas Day.

Pirello was formerly a managing director of Seafish Tasmania when the company brought the controversial super trawler Abel Tasman (later named Magiris) to Australia in 2012.

Colin Collins -- a director of fishing company Lorjona Pty -- was also arrested on Dec. 27.

Police had been monitoring the drug ring for three years.

Seafish Tasmania has been involved in a joint venture with the Netherlands' Parlevliet & Van der Plas (P&P) for some time. At the end of 2016 though, P&P pulled another supertrawler, the Geelong Star, out of the Australian fishery, seemingly for good.

The firm has been unable to achieve a "financial/commercial agreement with the local partners in Australia", it said.

"The management regrets that we cannot continue this fishing operation, partly because of the very healthy local pelagic stocks. The fisheries management in Australia is one of the most sustainable in the world."

title: Bloomberg links state-owned Chinese giant to scam bringing antibiotic-tainted shrimp to US
content:
Shanghai Fisheries Group (Corporation), a large Chinese seafood firm controlled by the government, is linked to a scam where antibiotic-tainted shrimp were illicitly imported into the US, reports Bloomberg.

According to the Bloomberg report, a group of former Shanghai Fisheries executives agreed in 2005 to create a venture that would get around antidumping tariffs on China, by routing shrimp via Malaysia.

“They would finance and control the company from China, but it would be incorporated in Texas. That was the beginning of American Fisheries,” reports Bloomberg.

Some of the same executives also controlled a Shanghai Fisheries subsidiary called Guangzhou Lingshan, a seafood packing plant in the Pearl River Delta, and the plant was buying shrimp.

“Guangzhou Lingshan built a lab inside the complex to test the quality of its shrimp, and the facility was considered one of the best in the region. Even so, former executives with the company say shrimp tainted with antibiotic traces made it into the company’s stock,” states Bloomberg.

“You know what China was like,” Lv Wei, who worked for Guangzhou Lingshan in the trade department for nine years before leaving in 2013, told Bloomberg. Almost two-thirds of the shrimp that went through the packing facility ended up with American Fisheries, she says. “They all went through Malaysia.”

Shanghai Fisheries declined to comment to Bloomberg on Guangzhou Lingshan.

Key to the scam, according to Bloomberg, is a Jun Yang, a Chinese-born entrepreneur based in Texas.

Yang was arrested in 2012 by a division of US Immigrations and Customs Enforcement, for making false claims about honey he was importing.

This honey harvested in China but passed through Malaysia, where it acquired Malaysian certificates of origin.

This illegal transshipping allowed him to avoid paying almost $38 million in antidumping duties, according to Bloomberg. “The investigators untangled a network of shell companies that seemed designed solely to deceive US regulators. In November 2013, Yang was convicted and sentenced to three years in federal prison.”

The investigators determined that Yang’s main business wasn’t honey, but seafood, as his company brokered shrimp for American Fisheries, the firm linked to Shanghai Fisheries.

At the time of Yang’s first arrest, some of the shipments were still in cold-storage facilities.

“The feds required him, as part of his cooperation, to send samples to a laboratory for analysis. Five shipments tested positive for nitrofurans, a class of antibiotics banned in the US Those tainted shrimp were eventually destroyed. All the tainted shipments had been labeled as products of Malaysia,” reports Bloomberg.

title: Profane and boastful, ‘Codfather’ reportedly told IRS of police connections
content:
In undercover recordings collected by Internal Revenue Service (IRS) agents, Carlos 'Codfather' Rafael reportedly boasted of his ability to bring cash through Boston's airport undetected.

Excerpts of a transcript of conversations that the accused scallop magnate reportedly had with two agents posing as Russian mobsters were released Dec. 12 as part of a legal motion filed by prosecutors. 

In the document, Rafael is described as discussing the movement of large sums of cash through Boston's Logan International Airport as well as his ties to a man who he told undercover agents works at the airport and can bypass security. 

Rafael: "But I guess -- I can get the money through. I have one of those guys in Boston, he is one of those f@ckin' agents who is my friend, and I give him the money before I go through security. Then I go to the bathroom."
 
Male voice three (an undercover IRS agent): "And he gives you the money."
 
Male voice four (another agent): "Nice."
 
Rafael: "Even if he is not in your port, he'll - - I call him, hey I'm flying out tonight - - because I've got like 60,000 in my - - I ain't going through the - - he doesn't go through security because he has got one of those f@ckin' badges."
 
Rafael then said that after going through security, the men would meet in the bathroom to exchange the money.
 
Prosecutors have said in other filings that they believe the man Rafael described was Antonio Freitas, a Bristol County, Massachusetts Sheriff's Deputy.
 
Freitas is charged with two counts, one for bulk cash smuggling and one for international structuring.
 
At the time Freitas worked for the Bristol County Sheriff's Department but was detailed to the Department of Homeland Security, which gave him the ability to transit Boston's Logan International Airport without having to pass through security, the indictment states.

He is currently scheduled to be tried alongside Rafael in Boston, but Rafael's lawyers sought for the trials to be severed, a request prosecutors say they won't oppose. 

The request came after Freitas reportedly made incriminating statements to investigators when asked about his involvement with Rafael. 

Codfather charges

Rafael, who is widely known by his nickname of 'Codfather', faces 27 counts on a federal indictment.

He controls at least 36 local vessels with commercial fishing permits this year, giving him control of nearly a fifth of the New Bedford fishing economy.

The charges against Rafael, who was arrested on Feb. 26, then released from custody on a $1 million bond on March 2, include conspiracy, false entries and bulk cash smuggling.

Federal agents posed as Russian mobsters looking to buy Rafael's business in the sting.

In the transcript, only parts of which have been made public, Rafael appeared to boast about his connection to the sheriff's deputy, stating that Rafael used his influence with other officials so that his friend could get a raise.

Rafael, who is from Portugal, also appears to describe making flights to his native country to deposit large sums of cash in safe deposit boxes at local banks. 

According to the recent motion made by Rafael's lawyers, Freitas detailed his role in the cash smuggling when questioned by officers. 

"During the government’s investigation of the bulk cash smuggling and structuring charges, Mr. Freitas was interviewed by FBI agents and officers of the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Inspector General, at which time Mr. Freitas made statements implicating both himself and Mr. Rafael," Rafael's lawyers wrote in the motion. 

Freitas specifically told investigators that Rafael had asked him to bring the cash on the trip, though the deputy had initially refused as the amount surpassed the $10,000 limit over which cash has to be declared. Freitas also said that he agreed to travel with the $17,500 once split with his fiance and called Rafael once in Portugal to confirm where to deposit the funds, the motion said. 

Rafael has pleaded not guilty to all of the charges but hasn't commented publicly on the case.

According to documents filed with court, the trial is expected to take one to two weeks to complete and will begin in February 2017.

title: Prosecutors not opposed to separate trials for ‘Codfather’, deputy sheriff
content:
US attorneys prosecuting scallops magnate Carlos 'Codfather' Rafael and sheriff's deputy Antonio Freitas are not opposed to holding the trials separately, court records show.

Rafael's lawyers had argued that because the deputy, Antonio Freitas, allegedly made incriminating statements to officials, trying the cases together would jeopardize Rafael's constitutional rights. They asked a judge to agree to hold the two trials separately.

Rafael, who is widely known by his nickname of "Codfather," faces 27 counts on a federal indictment. He controls at least 36 local vessels with commercial fishing permits this year, giving him control of nearly a fifth of the New Bedford fishing economy.

The charges against Rafael, who was arrested on Feb. 26, then released from custody on a $1 million bond on March 2, include conspiracy, false entries and bulk cash smuggling.

Federal agents posed as Russian mobsters looking to buy Rafael's business in the sting.

In a motion filed Dec. 8, prosecutors said that they didn't believe Freitas motion was filed in the correct way but added that they would not oppose it.

Freitas is accused of having received $17,500 in bulk cash from Rafael and on Feb. 5, 2016, allegedly divided that money between himself and his fiancé and flew to Portugal without declaring it. The funds were later deposited into a Portuguese bank account controlled by Rafael, the indictment states.

Freitas is charged with two counts, one for bulk cash smuggling and one for international structuring.

At the time Freitas worked for the Bristol County Sheriff's Department but was detailed to the Department of Homeland Security, which gave him the ability to transit Boston's Logan International Airport without having to pass through security, the indictment states.

According to the recent motion made by Rafael's lawyers, Freitas detailed his role in the cash smuggling when questioned by officers.

 

"During the government’s investigation of the bulk cash smuggling and structuring charges, Mr. Freitas was interviewed by FBI agents and officers of the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Inspector General, at which time Mr. Freitas made statements implicating both himself and Mr. Rafael," Rafael's lawyers wrote in the motion. 

Freitas specifically told investigators that Rafael had asked him to bring the cash on the trip, though the deputy had initially refused as the amount surpassed the $10,000 limit over which cash has to be declared. Freitas also said that he agreed to travel with the $17,500 once split with his fiance and called Rafael once in Portugal to confirm where to deposit the funds, the motion said.

title: Proposed Louisiana crawfish regulation could harm state’s industry
content:
Regulation proposed by a nonprofit organization could hurt Louisiana's crawfish industry, reports WWLTV.com. 

The Center of Invasive Species Prevention (CISP) recently petitioned the US Fish and Wildlife Service to asses the red swamp crawfish or Louisiana crawfish to the injurious wildlife list.

In its petition, CISP said the red swap crawfish and 42 other species don't provide any any essential economic of other benefits that outweigh their current and potential harm to the US. 

The Fish and Wildlife Service could impose punishment on those who buy, sell or trade red swamp crawfish if the species is added to the list.

US Senator David Vitter sent a letter to the service urging the agency to reject the petition.

"Ridiculously," Vitter wrote in the letter, "the inclusion of the red swamp crawfish on the list of injurious wildlife would result in the arrest and prosecution of thousands of Louisiana business owners".

title: Ecuador shrimp industry’s breakneck growth rate to slow on larvae setback
content:
Ecuador’s shrimp industry, which will break an export record in 2016, might see a slowdown next year on a vibrio-related outbreak that has reduced larvae supply.

The outbreak of vibrio occurred in the latter half of this year and affected several laboratories, reducing the availability of larvae to the industry, said a senior source at a major Ecuadorian producer. The outbreak has been isolated at the laboratory level and has not spread to farms, said the source, who asked to remain anonymous.

“The outbreak will affect export numbers from Ecuador for two-three months early next year, but no longer than that,” the source told Undercurrent News. 

The outbreak is thought to have affected several laboratories in Ecuador that supply larvae to farming companies, both among laboratories owned by producers and external dedicated suppliers, the source said.

A production blip will come after a year of bumper profits for the Ecuadorian shrimp industry. As competitors in Asia, Central America and Mexico struggled with early mortality syndrome (EMS), Ecuador’s low density farms will ramp up output to a record 800 million pounds, capturing higher prices and a bigger proportion of the massive marketplace in China.

The new export number wipes out the previous record set in 2015 at 720m pounds, which was a 17.8% gain over 2014. China has grown to become the biggest buyer of Ecuadorian shrimp, buying about a third of the total.

Chinese president Xi Jinping visited Chile, Peru and Ecuador in a Latin America in late November, in part because of the importance of growing fish and seafood exports from the western countries of South America towards the Chinese market. 

By the end of October, Ecuador’s producers had already exported 670m pounds of shrimp, a quantity that is worth $2.05 billion, according to customs statistics.

Ecuadorian larvae suppliers and farmers have struggled with unusual weather conditions this year, which has brought colder than usual nights to the Guayas Delta, where most of the country's shrimp farming industry is based, according to Jose Camposano, head of the National Aquaculture Chamber.

Vibriosis is a constant threat to both at the laboratories that produce larvae and shrimp farms for all producers in tropical countries, Camposano said, without saying if the weather setbacks would result in a drop in production.  

Pesquera Santa Priscila led production increases in Ecuador this year with an accumulated 104m pounds in the first 10 months of this year, followed by Expalsa with 91.6m and then Omarsa with 67m. 

Of the 73m pounds exported in October, 33.65m were shipped to Asia, led by Santa Priscila. The US market bought 14.2m pounds, with Propemar the biggest seller and European exports were 22.9m pounds with Promarisco the top exporter.  

Expalsa recently said it will slow its growth rate in 2017 after seeing a 15% increase in production this year to 50,000 metric tons, commercial director Juan Gomez-Behr told Undercurrent. 

Omarsa is carrying out a major expansion to its processing facilities near Guayaquil and could challenge Santa Priscila and Expalsa for the top ranking in Ecuador. The industry as a whole, which ranks among the top five shrimp exporters in the world, could expand by 10% and 15% a year by increasing density in farms, Santa Priscila founder and CEO Santiago Salem said in a July interview with Undercurrent. 

Ecuador’s exporters are hoping that a free trade agreement between the South American country and the European Union will be discussed in EU Parliament between Dec. 12-15, with a view to the FTA being promulgated by the start of 2017, said the industry source.

However, the industry is even more hopeful that an FTA can be negotiated with China. Talks for a deal are early stages and would avoid the necessity for Ecuadorian producers to use Vietnam as a conduit export route to reach the Chinese market.

Prices for shrimp that are sold through Vietnam are lower because of the risk associated with occasional spot checks by Chinese authorities, the source said. China arbitrarily increases customs checks on the Vietnamese-Chinese border and arrests smugglers when the national market is well supplied with shrimp, he said.

“With that [FTA] deal in place, we could all sleep at night,” the source said.

title: Nine arrested in China for allegedly smuggling seafood worth millions
content:
Nine suspects in a case involving 3,000 metric tons of smuggled frozen seafood worth CNY 250 million (US$36 million) have been handed to the Chinese authorities, reports Shanghai Daily. 

The 3,000t includes valuable spot prawns, lobsters and snow crab.

Chinese authorities said they began to suspect smuggling in April last year when two companies owned by the same man declared the value of the imported spot prawns at $5-$8 per kilogram, much lower than the market price.

It said the value of imports of spot prawns was normally declared at $28-38/kg. 

The smuggler, whose name was not released, was also suspected of illegally taking frozen seafood through the southern Guagnxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, which mean the shrimp sat unrefrigerated for hours. 

He is accused of smuggling 220t of spot prawns via Guangzi in 2014 using fake customs declarations.
