title: Deputy accused alongside ‘Codfather’ reportedly told officials of cash smuggling
content:
A sheriff's deputy accused of cash smuggling alongside scallops magnate Carlos 'Codfather' Rafael reportedly admitted his actions to investigators, court records show.

Rafael's lawyers argue that because the deputy, Antonio Freitas, allegedly made incriminating statements to officials, trying the cases together would jeopardize Rafael's constitutional rights. They have asked for a judge to agree to hold the two trials separately. 

Freitas is accused of having received $17,500 in bulk cash from Rafael and on Feb. 5, 2016, allegedly divided that money between himself and his fiancé and flew to Portugal without declaring it. The funds were later deposited into a Portuguese bank account controlled by Rafael, the indictment states.

Freitas is charged with two counts, one for bulk cash smuggling and one for international structuring.

At the time Freitas worked for the Bristol County Sheriff's Department but was detailed to the Department of Homeland Security, which gave him the ability to transit Boston's Logan International Airport without having to pass through security, the indictment states.

According to the recent motion made by Rafael's lawyers, Freitas detailed his role in the cash smuggling when questioned by officers.

"During the government’s investigation of the bulk cash smuggling and structuring charges, Mr. Freitas was interviewed by FBI agents and officers of the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Inspector General, at which time Mr. Freitas made statements implicating both himself and Mr. Rafael," Rafael's lawyers wrote in the motion. 

Freitas specifically told investigators that Rafael had asked him to bring the cash on the trip, though the deputy had initially refused as the amount surpassed the $10,000 limit over which cash has to be declared. Freitas also said that he agreed to travel with the $17,500 once split with his fiance and called Rafael once in Portugal to confirm where to deposit the funds, the motion said. 

 

Rafael, who is widely known by his nickname of "Codfather," faces 27 counts on a federal indictment. He controls at least 36 local vessels with commercial fishing permits this year, giving him control of nearly a fifth of the New Bedford fishing economy.

The charges against Rafael, who was arrested on Feb. 26, then released from custody on a $1 million bond on March 2, include conspiracy, false entries and bulk cash smuggling.

Federal agents posed as Russian mobsters looking to buy Rafael's business in the sting.

Debra Messier, Rafael’s longtime bookkeeper, was arrested with him, but prosecutors later dismissed those charges. 

Rafael is alleged to have falsely reported the species of more than 815,000 pounds of fish to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) between 2012 and January of this year.

The inclusion of the deputy's statements would challenge Rafael's sixth amendment rights, his lawyers argued.

"Mr. Freitas’ out-of-court statements to the government directly implicate Mr. Rafael in the charges set forth in Count Twenty-Seven of the Indictment. In light of those statements, which are likely admissible against Mr. Freitas, a joint trial presents a serious risk that Mr. Rafael’s confrontation rights will be compromised," the motion argues.

The sixth amendment protects defendants' rights, granting them the right to a public trial without unnecessary delay, the right to a lawyer, the right to an impartial jury, and the right to know their accusers and the nature of the charges and evidence against you.

Contact the author jason.smith@undercurrentnews.com

title: Three alleged attackers of Pescanova boat in Mozambique arrested
content:
The Republic of Mozambique's police have arrested three of the eight suspected assailants of Pescamar 9, a Pescanova vessel that was attacked last week by pirates off the coast of Mozambique.

The pirates had injured five crew members, rendering the captain unconscious, in an attack on Nov. 2. The pirates had stolen half a metric ton of shrimp as well as two laptops and four mobile phones from the crew and then had escaped in a small boat.

The attackers carried two pistols and machetes, La Opinion reported.

The Mozambique police has surprised three individuals driving a stolen vehicle in Munhava, a district of Beira, Mozambique's second most populous city. The three were in possess of the half-ton of shrimp that had been stolen from the fishing vessel, La Opinion reported.

Police are now intensifying the investigation to arrest the five other attackers.

Meanwhile, Pescanova’s crew has returned home to Galicia, Spain.

title: Bulgaria appoints new fisheries chief amid EU funds probe
content:
Bulgaria has appointed a new head at its Executive Agency of Fisheries and Aquaculture (EAFA), after the previous incumbent was dismissed for misusing EU funds, reports Novinite.

Valentin Valkov, who is taking over the EAFA, was previously CEO at Ribni Resursi EOOD, a company in charge of reconstruction, modernization and management of fishing ports that are public state property.

His predecessor, Yancho Yanchev, was detained in a probe into the misuse of EU funding and subsequently dismissed.

The EAFA manages a €113 million fisheries program, €88m allocated under EU programs.

Headquartered in Burgas, by the Black Sea, it also controls fisheries, aquaculture and first sale of fishery products.

title: Former head of Korean bank in hot water over $21m in loans to seafood firm
content:

title: Maine lobstermen arrested for fishing violations
content:
A 34-year-old Maine-based lobsterman has been arrested by the state's Marine Patrol after a seven-month investigation found he allegedly committed several fishing violations , the Maine Department of Marine Resources said in a release.

Duston Reed was charged with fishing with lobster traps that were not marked with a buoy, fishing untagged lobster traps, falsifying physical evidence and tampering with a witness.

The two fishing-related charges carry potential fines totaling $2,500 each. The charge of falsifying physical evidence, a class D crime, is punishable by up to 364 days in jail and a $2,000 fine. The charge of tampering with a witness, a class C crime, is punishable by up to 5 years in prison.

Reed also faces suspension of his lobster, commercial fishing and scallop licenses.

A total of 40 unmarked, untagged traps were recovered by Marine Patrol Officers after an investigation determined where they were located.

Reed also instructed his sternman, Jeremy Yeaton, to remove marine navigation electronics used to navigate and locate fishing gear, officials said.

Yeaton has also been arrested and charged with allegedly falsifying physical evidence related to removing electronics from Reed’s fishing vessel, Outer Limits. He faces 364 days in jail and $2,000 in fines for the violation.

Reed was arrested August 18 taken to jail in Lincoln County. Yeaton was arrested August 28 and also taken to the jail.

title: Phuket officials seize tuna haul from IUU fishing boats
content:
More than 2,700 metric tons of tuna were seized from boats moored off Phuket, Thailand, suspected of illegal, unreported and unregistered (IUU) fishing, reports the Phuket News.

One Phuket Fisheries official explained that his office had received the order to remove the seized tuna after the managing director of Siamtuna Fisheries -- which owns the two boats -- requested the Department of Fisheries remove the tuna as it could not afford to store the cargo any longer.

title: Protestors arrested at Cermaq’s Canada salmon farms
content:
Four Indigenous Canadian protestershave been arrested while trying to prevent Cermaq from re-stocking its sites in British Columbia, reports The Tyee.

Thiscomes after Canadian First Nation members handed Cermaq an eviction notice, calling for them to leave as they are damaging wild salmon runs.

On Aug. 22 the four people, from Ahousaht, BC, were arrested by local police for trying to obstruct Cermaq from restocking an empty feedlot with new Atlantic salmon smolts.

The protesters were arrested the following day after the company lodged complaints about the incident. Charges have not yet been laid.

Two of the protestors, Sacheen Seitcham and her husband, Joe James Rampanen, said they participated in the protest “because it is our inherent right to protect wild salmon, it is our duty and responsibility to ensure we have Indigenous food security and we are upholding our rights to do so".

The couple said they had witnessed “a noticeable decline in herring and salmon runs and the shellfish beaches as well” after fish farms were allowed into their traditional waters nearly 20 years ago.

title: Charges dropped against ‘Codfather’ Rafael’s bookkeeper
content:
The bookkeeper originally charged alongside accused fishing magnate Carlos "Codfather" Rafael has had her prosecution dismissed "in the interests of justice," court documents show.

The one page filing did not elaborate on why prosecutors used their discretion to dismiss charges against Debra Messier, who was arrested alongside Rafael after federal authorities raided the Carlos Seafood building on the waterfront of New Bedford, Massachusetts on Feb. 26.

She previously faced charges of conspiracy and submitting falsified records to the government.

A federal trial for Rafael, as well as alleged smuggling accomplice Antonio M. Freitas is slated for January 2017 at the US District Court in Boston.

Prosecutors have said that Rafael sold illegally caught fish to a wholesale buyer in New York City in exchange for tens of thousands in cash, much of which he then smuggled to Portugal through Logan International Airport in Boston with the help of Freitas.

According to court records, beginning in June 2015, two undercover federal agents posing as organized crime figures had several meetings with Rafael to negotiate the purchase of his business.

During those meetings, Rafael allegedly told the agents how he operated his business off-the-books by selling fish for cash.

This culminated in a meeting at Rafael’s office in New Bedford in January 2016, during which Rafael and Messier allegedly explained, step by step, what they called “the dance”:  the process by which Rafael and others coordinated with Rafael’s boat captains to falsify federal forms intended to track what was caught as well as forms designed to monitor the fish species purchased by Carlos Seafood.

In an affidavit made public in February, Ronald Mullett, a special agent with the criminal division of the Internal Revenue Service said that Rafael told undercover agents that Messier was well aware of the alleged scheme and "had been in the life with [Rafael] for 30 years."

title: National Fish not part of Pacific Andes chapter 11 filing
content:
National Fish and Seafood, the US processing and shrimp importing arm of Pacific Andes International Holdings (PAIH), has not directly filed for US bankruptcy protection with other parts of the group.

The filing of PAIH, China Fishery and 17 other companies linked to the group for bankruptcy protection does include National Fish, which is based in Gloucester, Massachusetts.

“There have been no filings in relation to National Fish,” a spokesperson for Pacific Andes told Undercurrent News.

National Fish is owns by Peaksville, a subsidiary of Pacific Andes based in the UK.

According to the accounts for Peaksville, it owns 60% of National Fish in the US and 100% of an entity with the same name in Hong Kong.

In turn, Peaksville is owned by PAIH, which is incorporated in Bermuda. PAIH is, in turn, controlled by N.S. Hong Investment, based in the British Virgin Islands.

Both PAIH and N.S. Hong have filed for chapter 11 in the US, however.

Along with PAIH and N.S. Hong, 14 other group subsidiaries have filed for chapter 11.

Then, three subsidiaries in Peru, CFG Investment; Corporacion Pesquera Inca (Copeinca); and Sustainable Fishing Resources have filed chapter 15 petitions with the US bankruptcy court. Under chapter 15, the representative of a corporate bankruptcy proceeding outside the US can obtain access to US courts.

In a stock exchange release in Singapore, where China Fishery is listed, the company said restructuring is underway in Peru.

The plan is to reach a "consensual restructuring or settlement of their financial obligations in a transparent and sustainable manner under the protection of relevant Peruvian laws and processes" for CFG Investment; Copeinca, which the Ng family bought for $780 million in 2013; and Sustainable Fishing Resources.

A sale process for the Peruvian assets has been put "on hold", the company said, in a press release.

Cutting losses 

On June 30, the day the Pacific Andes companies filed for chapter 11 and 15 protection in the US, National Fish's parent Peaksville filed its accounts in the UK.

The company reported a drop in turnover for its latest financial year, but reduced losses.

It had a loss after tax of HKD 20.55 million ($2.64m) for the year ending Sept. 28, 2015.

That is down from HKD 39.66m for the previous year, according to the accounts for Peaksville, the UK-based Pacific Andes subsidiary under which National Fish is held.

Annual turnover for National Fish, which sells under the Matlaw's brand, was HKD 1.97 billion ($253.89m), down 10.45% year-on-year.

After the end of the company’s last financial year, in November 2015, its then-president, Jack Ventola, was arrested in connection with failing to pay taxes on more than $2m in income he earned from 2006 to 2009, according to the US attorney’s office for the district of Massachusetts.

title: Pacific Andes US arm National Fish cuts losses
content:
US whitefish processor and shrimp importer National Fish and Seafood reported a drop in turnover for its latest financial year, but reduced losses.

The Gloucester, Massachusetts-based company, which is part of the struggling Hong Kong-based Pacific Andes International Holdings group, had a loss after tax of HKD 20.55 million ($2.64m) for the year ending Sept. 28, 2015.

That is down from HKD 39.66m for the previous year, according to the accounts for Peaksville, the UK-based Pacific Andes subsidiary under which National Fish is held.

Annual turnover for National Fish, which sells under the Matlaw's brand, was HKD 1.97 billion ($253.89m), down 10.45% year-on-year.

After the end of the company’s last financial year, in November 2015, its then-president, Jack Ventola, was arrested in connection with failing to pay taxes on more than $2m in income he earned from 2006 to 2009, according to the US attorney’s office for the district of Massachusetts.

At the time, National Fish named Todd Provost as president amid the tax fraud allegations against Ventola, who the company said would stay onboard as a non-executive director.

"My stepping down has been planned for a long time," Ventola told Undercurrent News in an email, when asked if there was a link between this and the allegations, at that time.

The indictment alleged that Ventola utilized the services of a temporary labor company called Continental Labor Team, which Ventola and a co-conspirator, who was also an executive of the seafood processor, controlled.

The Ng family is having to crisis manage on a global scale, with former ‘cash cow’ China Fishery facing liquidation amid big issues for Pacific Andes in Americas, Europe and Asia
Read more

Ventola and his co-conspirator -- who was not named -- allegedly worked together to channel money out of Continental and into their personal bank accounts, tax free.

To do this, the co-conspirator allegedly prepared fraudulent invoices for work supposedly done for Continental by a shell company Ventola controlled called International Freezing Systems (IFS).

Ventola and his co-conspirator allegedly used the fake IFS invoices to obtain payments from Continental, which they deposited into one of Ventola’s personal bank accounts.

From there, Ventola used the funds to pay personal expenses and also wrote his co-conspirator personal checks approximately monthly.

Although the checks from Continental totaled more than $2m between 2006 and 2009, neither Ventola nor his co-conspirator reported the income on their tax returns, it is alleged.

On June 9 this year, it emerged US officials have indicted Richard Pandolfo on tax charges related to undeclared income he reportedly earned at National Fish, the Internal Revenue Service said.

According to a release from the Department of Justice, Pandolfo's employer was not disclosed. However a search for the executive, who faces four charges of making and subscribing false tax returns, shows he was executive vice president with National Fish.

Now, an indictment filed against Pandolfo on June 7 in Massachusetts District Court states that his alleged acts occurred between 2009 and 2012, and concerned over $47,000 in unreported income.

Ventola steps down from Pacific Andes-owned National Fish amid tax fraud allegations

"According to the indictment, from 2009 to 2012, Pandolfo received substantial supplemental income for his work at the seafood processing company in Gloucester from the company’s president," noted the press release.

"Some of those payments were allegedly made directly to Pandolfo or his wife, but Pandolfo did not report or pay taxes on any of those payments. The indictment also alleges that other payments were made to a shell company set up in the name of Pandolfo’s wife, and were directed through a shell company controlled by the company’s president," the press release stated.

"Pandolfo allegedly did report that income, but claimed personal expenses as business expenses and deducted them, thereby improperly lowering the taxes he owed."

He could face three years in prison, one year of supervised release and a fine of $100,000.

title: ‘Codfather’ trial could hit New Bedford fishing industry hard
content:
The case of scallop fishing magnate Carlos Rafael -- who was arrested earlier this year for allegedly lying about catches and smuggling cash  -- could have significant negative economic effects for the New Bedford fishing industry, reports South Coast Today. 

Rafael, who is widely known by his nickname of "Codfather," faces 27 counts on a federal indictment of charges including conspiracy, false entries and bulk cash smuggling.

Rafael controls at least 36 local vessels with commercial fishing permits this year, giving him control of nearly a fifth of the local fishing economy.

Twelve of his vessels have high-value, limited-access scallop permits, worth tens of millions of dollars, which makes their future a vital question for the waterfront.

Given the size of Rafael’s fishing business, a significant chunk of New Bedford’s waterfront economy could be at stake if Rafael stands trail in January 2017.

Rafael was arrested on Feb. 26 but was released from custody on a $1 million bond in early March.

If found guilty the government could pursue forfeiture of 13 of Rafael’s over 30 vessels, or property equal to that value, according to the indictment against him.

The situation, including if the case will even go to trial which is scheduled for January 2017, is still uncertain.

title: Chile senator gets prison sentence in Corpesca case
content:
Ex Chilean senator Jaime Orpis has begun a prison sentence after an appeals court overturned a house arrest ruling for his involvement in the so-called Corpesca scandal

Orpis had his sentence overturned for an ongoing investigation into defrauding the state and tax evasion, and will remain in prison for the six months of the investigation into the Corpesca case, newspaper La Tercera reported.

The public prosecutor’s office accuses Orpis of having received CLP 233 million ($340,544) from Corpbanca between 2009 and 2013 in CLP 4m monthly payments, the newspaper said.

Corpesca, Chile’s largest fishing company, returned money to the tax office last year amid the investigation into illegal payments to politicians.

The funds were used to allegedly sway congress to vote in favor of a new fisheries law, which favors large companies over independent fishing companies.

title: Man arrested in $300,000 frozen shrimp theft
content:
New Jersey State police found a man who allegedly stole $300,000 worth of frozen shrimp from food distribution plant Preferred Freezer in Woodbridge, reports Woodbridge Patch. 

Police said they initially pulled over Emilce Rodriguez-Aguilar for a traffic violation but when the trooper learned that he had a criminal warrant. He was later arrested

The theft reportedly occurred on November 20 of last year, when Rodriguez-Aguilar picked up the shrimp from the plant with a valid pickup order number, but never delivered it to its intended destination.

Shrimp theft is not uncommon. And New Jersey police have already dealt with several similar cases this year.

"We've had about four frozen shrimp thefts in the past year or so," said state police Sgt. Jeff Flynn. "Mostly from supermarkets, where people are caught on camera stealing $500 or so of frozen shrimp."

The thieves generally re-sell the shrimp to people they know or to restaurants.

title: National Fish & Seafood exec Pandolfo indicted on tax charges
content:
US officials have indicted Richard Pandolfo on tax charges related to undeclared income he reportedly earned at Gloucester, Mass. processor National Fish and Seafood, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) said.

According to a release from the Department of Justice, Pandolfo's employer was not disclosed. However a search for the executive, who faces four charges of making and subscribing false tax returns, shows he was executive vice president with Pacific Andes International Holdings' US operation, National Fish.

In November 2015 the firm's president, Jack Ventola, was arrested in connection with failing to pay taxes on more than $2 million in income he earned from 2006 to 2009, according to the US attorney’s office for the district of Massachusetts.

Now, an indictment filed against Pandolfo on June 7 in Massachusetts District Court states that his alleged acts occurred between 2009 and 2012, and concerned over $47,000 in unreported income.

"According to the indictment, from 2009 to 2012, Pandolfo received substantial supplemental income for his work at the seafood processing company in Gloucester from the company’s president," noted the press release.

"Some of those payments were allegedly made directly to Pandolfo or his wife, but Pandolfo did not report or pay taxes on any of those payments. The indictment also alleges that other payments were made to a shell company set up in the name of Pandolfo’s wife, and were directed through a shell company controlled by the company’s president," the press release stated.

"Pandolfo allegedly did report that income, but claimed personal expenses as business expenses and deducted them, thereby improperly lowering the taxes he owed."

He could face three years in prison, one year of supervised release and a fine of $100,000.

According to court records, Pandolfo was granted a $100,000 bond.

Co-conspirator

Back in November, National Fish named Todd Provost as president amid the tax fraud allegations against Ventola, who the company said would stay onboard as a non-executive director.

"My stepping down has been planned for a long time," Ventola told Undercurrent in an email, when asked if there was a link between this and the allegations, at that time.

The indictment alleged that Ventola utilized the services of a temporary labor company called Continental Labor Team, which Ventola and a co-conspirator, who was also an executive of the seafood processor, controlled.

Ventola and his co-conspirator -- who was not named -- allegedly worked together to channel money out of Continental and into their personal bank accounts, tax free.

To do this, the co-conspirator allegedly prepared fraudulent invoices for work supposedly done for Continental by a shell company Ventola controlled called International Freezing Systems (IFS).

Ventola and his co-conspirator allegedly used the fake IFS invoices to obtain payments from Continental, which they deposited into one of Ventola’s personal bank accounts.

From there, Ventola used the funds to pay personal expenses and also wrote his co-conspirator personal checks approximately monthly.

Although the checks from Continental totaled more than $2m between 2006 and 2009, neither Ventola nor his co-conspirator reported the income on their tax returns, it is alleged.

title: ISSF: ‘Lack of political will’ means IOTC is still falling short on yellowfin protection
content:
The Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC) is falling short in its efforts to protect yellowfin tuna from overfishing, according to the International Seafood Sustainability Foundation (ISSF).

In the wake of IOTC meeting last week -- held in La Reunion, France -- there is judged to be a "limited political will" to change the status quo, in spite of new scientific guidance being adopted to protect tuna stocks.

"While a reduced catch of yellowfin was adopted, scientific guidance indicates that the agreed catch reductions are insufficient," said ISSF strategic policy advisor Claire van der Geest, and Wetjens Dimmlich, Indian Ocean Tuna program manager at World Wide Fund for Nature.

"The new measure amounts to a reduction in catch of about 10%, just half of the IOTC scientific committee’s recommended 20% reduction and insufficient to arrest the current declining trend in stock status or rebuild the stocks to sustainable levels by 2024."

There is also a significant risk that, without further action, these measures that are effective 1 January 2017, could result in the fishery breaching the fishing mortality limit and the stock declining below the biomass limit established by the commission.

And, with delays of up to two years on reporting of data and the high levels of non-compliance by IOTC members, the new yellowfin measure may be largely unenforceable, said van der Geest and Dimmlich, writing on the ISSF's official site.

The IOTC was, however, applauded for adopting a harvest control rule (HCR) for skipjack tuna that is consistent with scientific advice.

"The adoption of this initial skipjack HCR is the culmination of significant work, investment and advocacy by many parties – nations, industry, NGOs, scientists and retailers – and it paves the way for refinement as the management strategy evaluation work continues," said van der Geest and Dimmlich.

"Harvest strategies, which include HCRs and reference points, are an essential component of modern, science-based fisheries management."

title: Judge raises ‘Codfather’s’ bond to $2m
content:
A judge has released Carlos Rafael, the indicted New Bedford scallops industry figure known as the 'Codfather,' on a $2 million bond, a figure elevated in part due to his dual Portuguese citizenship.

He posted a vessel, his home and a property associated with his business Carlos Seafood as collateral, according to the Herald News.

The collateral for the bond, which was raised once prosecutors confirmed his dual citizenship, includes the value of the vessel Diane Jane, and its attached permit, which “exceeds $1 million,” according to Rafael's attorney, William Kettlewell.

“I’ve learned a little bit about how to put a mortgage on a fishing vessel,” Kettlewell told the court, adding that his client has "no liquid assets" available to satisfy the raised bond requirements.

Rafael was indicted earlier this week on 27 counts for allegedly lying about catches and smuggling cash to Portugal through the airport in Boston. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges.

The judge, David Hennessy, also ruled that Antonio Freitas, a sheriff's deputy who faces two criminal charges for allegedly helping Rafael to smuggle cash, will not be able to make a pre-planned trip to Canada while the criminal matter is ongoing in part because, like Rafael, he has dual Portuguese-US citizenship.

“Overall, it would be very easy for Mr. Freitas to simply leave from Canada, (go) to Portugal and not come back,” prosecutor Andrew Lelling said.

The charges against Rafael, who was arrested on Feb. 26, then released from custody on a $1 million bond on March 2, include conspiracy, false entries and bulk cash smuggling.

Debra Messier, Rafael’s longtime bookkeeper, was arrested with him, but is reportedly not named in the indictment. Federal agents posed as Russian mobsters looking to buy Rafael's business in the sting.

Rafael is alleged to have falsely reported the species of more than 815,000 pounds of fish to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration between 2012 and January of this year.

If convicted, he could face the seizure of his assets, including vessels and fishing permits, prosecutors have said.

title: Feds find 20 keys of cocaine in frozen fish shipment
content:
US federal agents have busted two alleged drug smugglers in Brooklyn with frozen fish stuffed with cocaine, reports the New York Daily News.

Triston Daniels and Troy Gonsalves were reeled in after 20 kilograms of cocaine were discovered stashed inside a shipment of frozen fish.

They were arraigned Saturday in Brooklyn Federal Court and released on $150,000 bail.

On May 4, US Customs and Border Protection officers seized an air cargo shipment of "large, frozen fish" from Suriname at Miami International Airport, according to US Homeland Security special agent Ryan Varrone.

Agents filleted the fish and removed the cocaine, which has a street value of about $600,000, according to authorities.

The fish was replaced in the shipping boxes and transported by truck to a storage facility in Queens which was kept under surveillance, Varrone's complaint states.

Daniels and Gonsalves showed up at the warehouse on Friday in a white van. They picked up the boxes and drove to another storage facility in Brooklyn where they were arrested as they unloaded the van.

Gonsalves admitted that Daniels told him that the shipment contained drugs, the complaint alleges.

The unidentified importer of the fish is located in Queens and was previously associated with a shipment of 82kg of cocaine from Guyana that was seized at the Miami airport in February, according to the court papers.

Jellyfish is very popular sliced and served as salad, particularly along China's southern and eastern coasts.

title: ‘Codfather’ Rafael indicted, gov’t could seize permits in case of guilty verdict
content:
Carlos Rafael, known as the “Codfather” in the US east coast fishing sector, has been indicted on 27 counts by federal prosecutors for allegedly lying about catches and smuggling cash to Portugal through the airport in Boston, according to local media reports.

Rafael is the owner of one of the largest commercial fishing operations in the country, with more than 30 vessels in his fleet, 44 commercial fishing permits and the Carlos Seafood business on South Front Street, according to the indictment, quoted by Cape Cod Times.

The indictment states that if Rafael is found guilty on one or more of the counts against him, the government will pursue forfeiture of 13 of Rafael’s vessels and the associated commercial fishing permits, or property equal to that value. As well as whitefish vessels, Rafael also has a fleet of scallopers, which have been changing hands for big money of late.

The charges against Rafael, who was arrested on Feb. 26, then released from custody on a $1 million bond on March 2, include conspiracy, false entries and bulk cash smuggling.

Debra Messier, Rafael’s longtime bookkeeper, was arrested with him, but is reportedly not named in the indictment. Federal agents posed as Russian mobsters looking to buy Rafael's business in the sting.

Rafael is alleged to have falsely reported the species of more than 815,000 pounds of fish to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) between 2012 and January of this year.

“On a yearly basis, Rafael’s routine falsification of dealer reports he submitted to NOAA created substantial discrepancies between the fishing activity he reported and the fish caught by his fishing vessels and acquired by Carlos Seafood,” the indictment states, according to the Cape Cod Times.

Antonio Freitas, a Bristol County Sheriff’s Office deputy, is also named in the indictment.

Freitas is charged with two counts, one for bulk cash smuggling and one for international structuring.

“Freitas assisted Rafael with smuggling cash through the airport,” the Cape Cod Times reports the indictment stating.

The US government alleges Rafael lied to the government for years about the amount and kinds of fish caught by his fleet, in order to evade federal fishing quotas. He then sold the illegally caught fish to a New York City buyer, for cash payments of hundreds of thousands of dollars, its is alleged.

The indictment refers to, but does not charge, four people involved in the alleged conspiracy. Persons A and B are employed by Carlos Seafood, person C is “an individual who owns a wholesale fish business” in New York City, and person D is a resident of Peabody, the indictment states, according to the Cape Cod Times.

Person D allegedly concealed currency at Logan and helped Freitas transport it to Portugal, according to the indictment.

On March 2, Undercurrent News reported that US federal agents are said to have seized documents from a New York City fish company who’s owner is reportedly the buyer named in the affidavit accusing Rafael of massive illegal fish sales.

Two sources said federal agents have seized documents from New York-based South Street Seafood since Rafael was arrested.In the affidavit, from IRS agent Ronald Mullett, it is alleged that despite having only $21m in assets on his books, Rafael allegedly told US undercover agents posing as Russian gangsters his business was worth $175m.

This valuation, it is alleged in the affidavit from Mullett, was justified by the amount of cash he was generating through sales of illegally caught fish to a broker in New York, which was then being laundered back to Portugal.

title: Chile fishermen’s protest intensifies, hurting salmon exporters
content:
A protest on the island of Chiloe by fishermen has spread to the mainland, effectively cutting off most of the Chilean salmon industry from exporting to the US and Brazil.

Protesters have blocked roads, including the highway that connects Chiloe with Puerto Montt, cutting off several processing plants on the mainland and access to the region’s airport, said a source at a top exporter.

“They have choked the whole industry off,” the source said. “We are being hurt by another group whose quarrel isn’t ours.”

Artisan fishermen are requesting a payout from the government to tide them over while a ban exists on seafood sales after red tide intoxicated crustaceans and other seafood.

Fishermen have set up road blocks, burning tires and old cars, and have already cut off Chiloe Island’s salmon producers from the mainland. About two-thirds of Chile’s salmon processing is located on the island in southern Chile.

The protests intensified after an official announced the government wouldn’t raise an offer to pay each fisherman CLP 100,000 for each month that the ban on seafood sales continued, according to radio station Agricultura.

There were 16 arrests on the island while the protests have reached the regional capital of Puerto Montt. The island is beginning to run of fuel and basic supplies, according to television and radio reports.

“We are clearly not in an economy that we respond in one second to whatever anyone asks for, but we are doing our maximum effort,” president Michelle Bachelet said on television.

Some of the protests have accused the salmon farming industry of causing the increase in toxins by throwing dead salmon into the sea, a theory that was ruled out by economy minister Luis Felipe Cespedes who spoke on television Thursday.

Millions of salmon fish were killed by Chattonella algal blooms, an earlier manifestation of the red tide sweeping the coast of Chile back in March.

The effect of throwing the dead fish out at sea, 130 kilometers from the coastline, has no connection with the appearance of the Alexandrium Catenella algal bloom which has appeared more recently to be the toxin affecting crustaceans on the coastline, Cespedes said.

The protest may be costing the industry $9 million a day as they unable to deliver their products to ports.

The principal damage is the loss of the fish that were recently harvested from the sea, while some exporters will have to declare force majeure on their contractual obligations with customers in the US and Brazil, the source said.

title: AP wins Pulitzer for slavery investigation
content:
The Associated Press (AP) has won the Pulitzer Prize for public service based on last year's international investigation, which linked slavery in the fishing industry in Southeast Asia to the supply chains of some of the world's largest retailers.

The reporting by Esther Htusan, Margie Mason, Robin McDowell and Martha Mendoza also freed more than 2,000 slaves, led to the arrests of a dozen people, and the introduction of legislation in the US Congress to create greater transparency from food suppliers.

AP president and CEO Gary Pruitt, addressing a staff gathering on April. 19, said it was "a significant day in the 170-year history of the AP. The series was some of the most outstanding pieces of journalism ever produced by AP -- or anyone else for that matter".

The award marks the AP's 52nd Pulitzer, but is its first for public service

title: Russia’s largest fish canner under attack by criminal gangs
content:
Eugene Gerden, Seafood.com News

Russia’s largest fish cannery may suspend operations due to state attacks possibly in collusion with criminal gangs.

The Russian Federal Security Service has started a sudden investigation against Dobroflot, on suspicion of tax evasion.

Dobroflot is the largest fish canning business in Russia, owning 15 vessels, three processing platforms, including the largest floating processor in Russia, and six transport ships.

The company has, in recent years, concentrated on fish production, although they have been in the shipping business since 1911.

The charges appear aimed at forcing a change in the ownership of the company, and in response, Dobroflot has said it may shut down.

According to some sources in the Russian Federal Security Service, the company is involved in contraband activities and suspected in failure of payment of customs duties.

The ongioing investigation and checks of the company may result in the suspension of its activities and massive cuts to its 3,500 staff.

To date, Alexander Efremov, chairman of Dobroflot, has already submitted a petition to the presidential envoy in the Far Eastern Federal District Yuri Trutnev, asking them to intervene in the current situation around the company.

According to Xenia Pisareva, head of the department of regional programs of Fishnews, one of Russia’s leading analyst agencies in the field of fishing, Dobroflot has advanced fleets, processing plants and delivery infrastructure in Russia.

The current attacks on its business may have a negative effect on the entire Russian fish canning business, as many local businessman will refuse further investments until the situation is clarified.

According to some analysts of the Russian Ministry of Agriculture, the company currently remains Russia’s largest producer of canned fish and one of the most successful in the highly competitive Far East fishing market, which is also characterized by high presence of fish and crab mafia.

According to Efremov, the current attacks could be initiated by some of the competitors of the company and criminal groups, affiliated with some corrupted Russian state officials.

The main goal of the charges is to force a sale and gain control over the activities of Dobroflot.

According to some sources close to Dobroflot, the current attacks on the company are similar to those, which took place against the management of Domodedovo airport in Moscow, the largest in the country.

This resulted in the arrest of Dmitry Kamenshik, the head of the company, who reportedly rejected some business proposals of the sale of airport to third parties, affiliated with criminal groups.

title: Marine Harvest putting ‘increasing focus’ on global downstream growth
content:
Marine Harvest will continue on its path of expansion downstream in Europe, the US and Asia, said the Norwegian group in its latest annual report.

In an introductory message to shareholders, CEO Alf-Helge Aarskog described the salmon giant’s strategic direction as predicated on developing “fish feed; salmon farming; and value-added production and sales – where the latter has become an area of increasing focus for us”.

Last year, Marine Harvest – whose topline growth was boosted by a 10% increase in sales in 2015 – set the ball rolling in this direction on several fronts, both in Europe and further afield.

This included extending the shopfloor of Polish subsidiary Morpol’s processing plant in Ustka by more than 8,000 square meters to 90,000 square meters; in Aarskog’s words,“changing the plant’s logistics to improve efficiency”, as reported in January.

The move, which is expected to be fully implemented during the first half of 2016, will add at least 10% floor space to Morpol's factory – already the biggest salmon processing unit in the world – to a capacity to process over 100,000 metric tons of salmon per year, according to Marine Harvest.

“The size of the plant in Ustka helps us achieve economies of scale in our value-added processing, and the upgrades to the plant will enable us to serve our customers even better, through dedicated production areas for the different types of products and processes,” added the group.

The announcement also coincided with Morpol opening up a sales office in Sweden, geared towards penetrating the Swedish market on smoked, marinated and fresh salmon products.

Marine Harvest to open Dallas plant, notes Rebel Fish sales ‘slower than anticipated’

"Within three years, we expect to be the market leader in VAP [value added products] salmon in Sweden," stated John Paul McGinley, Morpol’s chief operating officer, bullishly at the time.

2015 was also notable for construction being completed on Marine Harvest’s VAP plant in Rosyth, located just outside Edinburgh, Scotland.

However, Aarskog admitted that “we have had our fair share of challenges” since production got underway in September.

Some may consider the CEO’s words to be something an understatement. As reported by Undercurrent News in February, the UK venture – launched in conjunction with Marine Harvest winning the contract to supply salmon to retailer J. Sainsbury last year – is hemorrhaging money fast.

This was laid out in its Q4 results, in which losses from the plant stood at NOK 95 million in the last quarter of 2015 – noticeably more than the loss of NOK 70m the group had initially guided for in January, when it announced more than 100 jobs will be sacrificed in its Scottish operations.

While the group conceded that winning the Sainsbury’s contract had “caused more start-up challenges than previously anticipated”, the board is, however, remaining resolute, and “expects the organization to capitalize on the know-how within Marine Harvest, and streamline operations”.

“The plant has become even more important after a major UK retailer decided to make Marine Harvest their supplier of value-added salmon from November 2015,” added Aarskog in the latest report.

“Deliveries under this contract will mean a significant expansion for the plant and more local jobs. The plant is well located and will deliver high quality products to the UK market in the future.”

Morpol invests €10m in Polish plant; targets Swedish market with new office

Perhaps neglected in the noise surrounding Marine Harvest snatching the Sainsbury’s contract from Young’s Seafood last summer, and the subsequent incendiary headline over potential job losses, is that the Rosyth plant had been originally intended to play a key role in the expansion of the group’s Harbour Salmon Co. brand.

However, the range – which is stocked in The Co-operative Group and Aldi – has not suffered, said Marine Harvest, and “is still performing well, and the feedback from consumers is highly complementary”.

Burger expansion 

Last year, the Bergen-based group “continued to look for new ways in which salmon could be used” to generate greater retail appeal. This, according to the report, has mainly centered on burger products.

“We have seen that all kinds of burgers are popular in Europe,” said the group.

“Following this trend, our plants in the Netherlands and Poland developed a delicious chunky breaded salmon burger for both the fresh prepacked and frozen markets."

“The fresh prepacked version has already been successfully launched at key retailers in Belgium, the Netherlands, France, Germany and Spain.”

Presently, frozen burgers are packed in trays with modified atmosphere at plants in Bruges, Boulogne, Harsum and Burgos, while the group is aiming to launch a new line of frozen breaded salmon burgers, including sauce-topped versions, later this year.

“This product range is an example of how we create value through our integrated value chain, by combining different forces within the group such as raw materials know-how, product development, product management, marketing skills and production facilities,” read the report.

“In this way we have created a solid new product with a strong European foothold.”

That also goes for the European foodservice sector, in which Marine Harvest claims to have made positive headway, recently.

“We continue to develop existing relationships through a wider range of products, while offering category management support to our customers,” it said.

“We have consolidated and built on our strong position with the Belgian hotels, restaurants and catering channel, and are expanding into other markets. We have emphasized the development of locally specific product ranges to maximize sales opportunities and help develop long-term business growth in this important sector.”

Regarding its downstream push on the continent, Marine Harvest has been prepared to make changes at the top, also.

Marine Harvest’s Rosyth losses mount amid challenging Sainsbury start-up

In January, Maiko van der Meer, managing director of Marine Harvest Consumer Products, parted ways with the company, as part of a restructure in its downstream business.

"We are making changes in the sales structure in the group, with all the heads of regions reporting directly to me,” explained Ola Brattvoll, chief operating officer of sales, at the time.

“This is to better co-ordinate the sales of raw material and finished goods.”

Rebel Fish sales slower than expected 

Stateside, Marine Harvest has been busy making modifications to its sales and marketing strategy, including the recent reworking of its packaging for the Rebel Fish line.

The chilled, microwavable salmon range went national in the US in May 2015, and recently debuted at the Boston seafood expo – where it was nominated in the “best product” category.

However, upon customer request, Rebel Fish packaging has since undergone a reboot, with the group admitting that sales had been “slower than anticipated”.

Last year, the company also launched a range of chilled, pre-pack products in Walmart, using farmed and wild fish. The range includes farmed salmon, tilapia and steelhead trout, as well as wild cod and halibut.

“We are happy with both. They are each in a different stage, but we are very happy and are convinced this is the way to go for us to lead this game,” Gianfranco Nattero, managing director of sales and marketing for the Americas, recently told Undercurrent.

“For sure, competitors will follow, which we really want. We need to have good competitors all doing similar things to further develop the category. That would be great.”

“You are never going to hit the jackpot with the first product. Someone adds a product and it disrupts the category,” added Nattero.

US smokehouse Ducktrap River of Maine in Belfast has continued to perform strongly, too, said the group, experiencing double-digit growth in 2015 for the fifth consecutive year.

In conjunction with the acquisition of Morpol, and the introduction of Morpol products in the US, Ducktrap has helped Marine Harvest attain a stronger share in the smoked salmon market.

“This year, we expanded our sales of Ducktrap products by adding several new accounts across the country,” said the group.

“We increased our presence in the ‘home market’ on the East Coast, and had strong growth in the West Coast market.

Marine Harvest is also eyeing greater penetration of the Midwest region, and will set up a new plant in Dallas this year – as revealed in the report – although a launch date is yet to be announced.

Marine Harvest parts company with top Europe downstream exec

While business in Asia is traditionally quieter for the Norwegian player, the Mowi brand, introduced in Japan in 2014, “has been a success”, with the group adding new products to the line – including sliced Mowi sashimi – last year.

“The introduction of the Mowi brand in Japan in 2014 has been a success, not only in terms of volume growth for Mowi products, but also in driving the entire salmon category,” said the report of the brand, whose year-on-year sales were up threefold in 2015.

“We want quality in every part of this brand, and expansion is therefore taken step by step,” it continued. “In addition to increasing demand for the brand, our Narita plant is now slicing Mowi sashimi, and our plant in Oostende is producing smoked Mowi products.”

Meanwhile, across the East China Sea, March saw the opening of a third Supreme Salmon store in Taiwan.

While Marine Harvest conceded that the concept hadn’t grown quite as rapidly as it would have liked, 2015 wasn't an unsuccessful year for Supreme Salmon per se, with new products – including ready meals, fresh and ready-to-eat products – being introduced in stores.

This perhaps best crystallizes one of the main planks of Marine Harvest’s overarching downstream strategy: to get consumers to eat more, and in different ways.

But, as the group rightly identifies, for this to happen, “production capacity must also increase".

title: Ecuador shrimp prices rising as heavy rains hit output
content:
Shrimp prices from Ecuador have gone up as El Nino-fueled rain led to a production shortage, particularly for small sizes, multiple sources told Undercurrent News.

Heavy rains, expected to continue through mid-April, have hit output at a time when Chinese demand is bullish and buyers willing to pay increased prices for new orders, several Ecuadorian shrimp producers said.

Ecuador is one of the few countries currently producing shrimp -- China's shrimp season, for instance, will not resume until June -- but troubled harvests mean less volumes, so processing plants are competing for less product, which has increased ex-farm prices.

Thus, processing companies have adjusted their export prices according to the new prices for raw material.

A source said ex-farm prices in Ecuador, for HOSO [head-on shell-on] 30/40 count are between $6.40 and $6.80 per kilo; 40/50 count between $5.90/kg and $6/kg; 50/60 count at $5.5/kg; 60/70 count at $5/kg and 70/80 count between $4.15/kg and $4.20/kg.

Demand for 40/50 and 50/60 count is strong, but volumes are not enough. For 60/70 and 70/80 there is very low availability, an Ecuadorian shrimp farmer said, which was backed by two European shrimp buyers.

"All Ecuadorian shrimp plants have failed commitments [on raw material shortage]. As a country it must be 250 containers or more, so they are not taking many more orders until they catch up with production," the shrimp farmer said.

Ecuador's shortage of shrimp was reflected in US imports data for February.

US shrimp imports from Ecuador had a dip of 11.1% from 7,626 metric tons to 6,781t year-on-year, according to the latest figures from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

"While supply volumes continue affected, it's probable that prices remain firm," an executive with a major shrimp exporter said.

"I think prices will be upwards for eight weeks or more, and then it will depend on how serious are production issues in India," the previous shrimp farmer said.

Following lower international demand and last year's floods, India's export growth for frozen shrimp could fall to single digits in 2016. 

Although India is likely to increase its farming acreage this year, disease worries will have farmers harvesting their shrimp more regularly and at smaller sizes, Undercurrent sources said previously.

By the end of April, Ecuador’s shrimp output will likely have a zero growth or up to a maximum of 3%, on the back of heavy rains, Jose Camposano, the executive chairman of the National Chamber of Aquaculture (CNA, in Spanish) told Undercurrent at this year's Boston seafood trade show.

Last year, Ecuador’s shrimp exports totaled a record-high of 720 million pounds, and Camposano expected a slight growth of shrimp exports for 2016.

title: Vietnamese seafood company chief arrested for loan fraud
content:
The Vietnamese government has arrested the director of a fishing company in Can Tho city and his accountant for concealing loan fraud, reports Thanhnien News.

Phan Ba Tong, chief of Thien Ma Seafood Company, was arrested Thursday along with Tran Thi Diem for allegedly borrowing VND 700 billion ($31.4 million) from several banks in Can Tho and Hau Giang Province though their company was not eligible.

Thien Ma was formed in 2005 with a registered capital of VND 70bn. It built 12 large farms and three factories and recruited thousands of workers.

title: Prosecutors given extension of deadline to indict Rafael
content:
US federal prosecutors have been given an extension to the deadline to indict Carlos Rafael, the US fishing mogul accused of running a massive illegal fishing scheme.

Federal prosecutors initially were initially given 30 days from the day of Rafael's arrest, on Feb. 26, to file an indictment.

A spokeswoman for the US attorney's office in the district of Massachusetts confirmed to Undercurrent News the deadline has been extended, although she declined to reveal the new deadline.

"There is no additional public information at this time," she said.

Rafael -- who owns a fleet of 40 whitefish and scallop vessels and the processing business Carlos Seafood -- stands accused of running a massive illegal fishing scam, after federal authorities raided his headquarters on on New Bedford’s waterfront.

Prosecutors allege that Rafael and his accountant, Debra Messier, lied to the government for years about the amount of fish caught by his fleet, submitting falsified records to the government to evade federal fishing quotas.

The agents posed as Russian gangsters interested in buying his business.

Federal agents are also said to have seized documents from a New York City fish company, whose owner is reportedly the buyer named in the Internal Revenue Service affidavit accusing Rafael of massive illegal fish sales.

According to the two Undercurrent sources, the man alluded to by the IRS is Michael Perretti, the owner of South Street, based in New York’s Fulton Fish Market, who paid out hundreds of thousands of dollars in cash for the fish.

Rafael -- who faces up to 25 years in prison, and $500,00 in fines -- was released March 2 on a $1 million bond.

title: Bomb blasts shake Brussels in run up to seafood show
content:
The Belgian capital Brussels has been hit by bomb attacks five weeks before it is set to host the world’s largest seafood trade fair, Seafood Expo Global.

On Tuesday, there have been two explosions at the city’s Zaventem airport and another blast at the Maalbeek metro station, which is close to the main European Union buildings.

The Belgian government has raised the terror level to four across the country, the highest level. All public transport has since been suspended, and the Eurostar is no longer stopping in the city's Brussels Midi teminal. All EU meetings have been cancelled.

According to Belgian broadcaster VRT, cited by the BBC, which is posting live updates on the aftermath of the incident, at least 26 people have been killed in the attacks.

Seafood Expo Global, which runs from April 26-28 this year, was attended by 26,600 in 2015.

Diversified Communications, the US-based company that runs the show, were not immediately available for comment to Undercurrent News.

Even before the attacks, Belgium was on high alert after the capture Salah Abdeslam, believed to be the only surviving participant of the November massacre in Paris that left 130 people dead.

Abdeslam faces a Brussels court decision on Wednesday on whether to extend a Belgian arrest warrant issued on Saturday, reports Bloomberg.

title: Brazilian lobster FIP shows advances despite local troubles
content:
The Fisheries Improvement Project (FIP) for the Brazilian lobster has shown progress, despite the country's political and economic troubles.

As Brazil's Ministry of Fisheries has become a secretary within the Agriculture Ministry, the lobster fishery has not had a stock assessment since 2006.

With commercial data provided by the companies belonging to the exporter's association SINDFRIO, the Center for Development and Sustainable Fisheries (CeDePesca) started to do a stock assessment in 2013 and is going to present the third one by April 2016, before the next season starts.

Although lobster stocks are over-exploited, the assessment revealed, fishing mortality has been reduced for the last four years and the stocks have been recovering slightly, on the back of the stricter measures in the US market for not accepting lobster tails smaller than 13 centimeters.

But further reductions are needed, CeDePesca said.

“We are very aware that we need lobster stocks sustainable, that's the core of our business,” said Ozina Costa, from SINDFRIO's board.

“The partnership with CeDePesca has allowed us to understand better the situation of these stocks and the way to rebuild them, and we are working hard together to get it done with the government," Costa said.

Throughout 2015 there were significant advances on the regularity of the federal Management Committee work, and strong measures were agreed, such as only accepting live lobsters in the processing plants since 2017 onwards; prohibiting trade of lobsters at the domestic markets during the closed season; establishing a total allowable catch (TAC); and defining mandatory landings and control points.

Nevertheless, all those advances were stalled because of the institutional changes in the Brazilian government, CeDePesca said.

The Latin American NGO corroborated the low ecosystem impacts of traps based operations, which fulfilled some gaps highlighted by the initial Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) pre-assessment.

“Despite all troubles we are still optimistic. We managed to get advances, our alliance with the exporters is strong, the stock assessment has been a major contribution to the discussion, and, step by step, the decision makers are accepting the idea of substituting the current, inefficient effort control based system with a quota based one," said Rochelle Bezerra, project manager at CeDePesca.

During the recent Boston seafood show, two companies from the Brazilian state Rio Grande Norte announced their willingness to become partners of the FIP.

In the US, the Brazilian lobster FIP has got support from Tequesta Bay Seafood, Casile and Mark Foods.

title: Ecuador wild shrimp producer launches online platform for US exports
content:
BOSTON, US -- Ecuadorian producer Natluk has just launched an online platform to sell wild shrimp to the US, with the aim to focus on small volume buyers.

The company has distributed to major US suppliers but and it wants now to focus on medium to small size buyers, particularly to restaurants and hotels, Veronica Nahik, CEO of Natluk, told Undercurrent News.

"We want to focus on clients who appreciate the quality of our product, which has a premium price. The priority for big companies is to minimize costs, but there's a niche for small buyers demanding high end products," Nahik said at this year's Seafood Expo North America trade show, held from March 6-8 in Boston, US.

Natluk exports about 100,000 pounds of wild shrimp per year, of which 20% is projected to be sold via online.

"This is the goal for the first year, but the ultimate goal would be to shift distribution from big suppliers to online," Nahik said.

"This way I would remove middlemen and the company's margin would improve," she said.

Natluk's turnover last year was $5 million and it aims to double its earnings by the end of this year, partly thanks to revenues driven by the online platform but, particularly, on the back of a new line for value-added products.

"We are a medium-sized business, we cannot compete with the giant Ecuadorian processors, so we decided to specialized in value-added products, such as cooked shrimp," Nahik said.

The story behind Natluk

The company started operations six years ago in Playas, Ecuador, motivated to support the socioeconomic development of the area, Nahik told Undercurrent. 

In 2016, Natluk launched a social responsibility program with several local artisan fishing cooperatives in the region, among them Las Balsas, Punta Chopoya, Hijos del Mar and San Pedro.

For every pound of shrimp Natluk sells under the Playas Gold brand, the company gives back a percentage to the cooperatives to be invested in local communities'  health programs, schools instruments, and public works.

"We want to tell the story behind our product, which is a concern of the millennials, they want to know where the fish comes from, who is the producer or if is the product sustainable," Nahik said.

Millennials are becoming an increasingly important demographic for the food industry, and those willing to adjust to meet their needs stand to benefit, was said at a presentation about the millennials' generation at this year's Boston show.

Millennials’ decisions are increasingly driven by social justice issues.

“More than ever I think people understand that when they’re buying food, they’re not just buying calories, a meal is not longer just fuel….they have a power in that choice,” said Patricia Pinto de Silva of NOAA.

title: Police arrest eight New Bedford fishing crew for drugs at sea
content:
Police arrested eight New Bedford fishing crew members aboard six vessels for possession of heroin and other drugs, South Coast Today reported.

The arrests came after officers from the Massachusetts Environmental Police and other agencies stopped 11 vessels near Popes Island. All of the boats were outbound from New Bedford on March 15th and 16th. The operations came amid growing concern about drug use in the commercial fishing industry.

Officials said that boats were searched on a random basis and that the quantities of drugs found suggest that they were for personal use.

“There have been a number of people who have said that there’s rampant opioid use by fishermen,” said Sergeant Jason Gomes, director of port security for New Bedford police. “We also heard complaints of near-collisions at sea, and people falling asleep on watch.”

title: Tabled Russian pollock quota cut, fleet renewal plan could speed industry consolidation
content:
If the Russian government goes ahead with a recommended 14% cut in the pollock quota, it is likely to be one factor pushing smaller companies toward selling, said the CEO of the country’s largest quota holder, Russian Fishery Company (RFC).

Consolidation in the sector has already been progressing fast, with the top six firms now controlling 67% of the total allowable catch (TAC), according to a presentation from Andrey Teterkin, CEO of RFC, at the North Atlantic Seafood Forum (NASF), in Bergen, Norway.

The top six firms -- RFC; Gidrostroy; Okeanrybflot; Gidrostroy; Fisheries Holding Karat; Nahodka Active Marine Fisheries Base (NBAMR); and Preobrazhenskaya Base of Trawling Fleet (PBTF) -- controlled 55% of the total quota in 2012.

The recommended drop in quota in 2017, if it is put into place, is likely to speed consolidation. In addition, the plan being considered by the Russian government to shave 20% off the top of the TAC for companies willing to build new vessels in the country’s yards will also likely also mean smaller operators are more likely to sell, he told Undercurrent News.

Russian scientists have recommended to the government the cut in the TAC for pollock in 2017, Teterkin, said during the recent NASF event.

This will mean a drop of 15% for the industrial vessels, to 1.3 million metric tons, he said. For the Marine Stewardship Council-certified fishery in the Sea of Ohotsk, the cut is recommended at 17%. The scientists have recommended a gradual recovery in 2018-2020 to current levels.

During the conference, Teterkin said the possibility of reduced volumes is “important news” for the sector.

“The reason it is important is obvious, it is a volume factor that is going to impact the revenue stream and the profit. We have some variable costs, but the size of your business will be contracting,” he told Undercurrent, during the Boston seafood show, just after the NASF event.

If the government confirms the quota cut, which will be clear in late November or early December, “of course, it is going to create more incentives for the small players to exit”, Teterkin told Undercurrent.

“Their profit generation decreases. If this thing happens, they may think, 'why should I bother?'”

Russia plans to cut pollock A season short amid tough market

On the other hand, a lower quota is likely to be somewhat offset by higher prices.

“The reason we are going down on prices is the TAC has been going up in Russia for three years, with a stable American quota,” he said. “So, in total, the amount of flesh being offered to the market was constantly increasing.”

If the TAC is slashed, the sector “will be compensated somehow, maybe even a greater extent, by higher prices”, said Teterkin. “That is why I said we should be watching closely. For us, as a company, we don’t want either growth or a slump. We would love to have a stable, 1.8m [metric ton] total TAC, would be ideal for us.”

Who’s taking long-term view?

The second factor likely to speed consolidation is the proposed new building program, he said.

Under this proposal, which is yet to be confirmed, 20% of the TAC will be “shaved off the top” to go to those willing to build new vessels and processing plants.

Then, those who do not build will get the same percentage as before, but of a lower level.

“If you don’t build and others do, you are supposed to lose quota,” he said.

“The plan does not mean anyone is going to surrender quota, it is at the cost of everyone,” he told Undercurrent. “It is for those who are taking a long-term view. It is a good indicator of who has come to this industry for good. Those who want to build; they are the ones who are strategic investors in this industry.”

Top six dominance 

Of the 67% of the Russian pollock quota controlled by the top six companies, RFC has 221,000t of quota; Okeanrybflot has 210,000t; Gidrostroy, 191,000t; Fisheries Holding Karat, 163,000t; NBAMR, 118,000t; and PBTF, 112,000t.

The “economies of scale” the larger companies have mean their operational results are higher, “when you compare them to the “mom and pop” type of companies that we still see in Russia”, said Teterkin, speaking at NASF.

RFC, he said, has turnover of $224 million, but earnings before interest, taxes, deprecation and amortization (ebitda) of $104m.

This high ebitda-to-turnover ratio means RFC is able to handle the high level of leverage it has accumulated in a series of acquisitions, said Teterkin.

RFC’s debt/ebitda ratio is at x4, according to a slide from Teterkin, meaning it’s around $416m.

Russian Fishery not financing pollock storage in China this year

This consolidation is set to continue, he said, presenting his vision for the industry in 2018. In addition, the larger companies are more likely to renew their fleet and thus become more efficient.

According to Teterkin, between 10-20 catcher-processors are likely to be built between now and 2025, he said, as the government plans to incentivize fleet renewal by allocating more quota to those willing to invest in new-builds in Russian yards.

This will cause a shift away from headed and gutted (H&G) pollock production, which still accounts for the bulk of the fleet’s output. For February, fillet and fillet block production is already rising rapidly, due to the low H&G prices, he said.

title: Regal Springs donates 5,000 pounds of tilapia to SeaShare
content:
Tilapia producer Regal Springs reached its goal to donate 5,000 pounds of tilapia to SeaShare after serving 1,000 tilapia tacos at Seafood Expo North America in Boston, Massachusetts last week, the company said in a release.

With every taco sampled, Regal Springs pledged to donate five pounds of tilapia to SeaShare, a non-profit dedicated to supporting hunger relief efforts in the US.

“We were really happy with the response from everyone at the expo. Every person who came by our booth to sample a taco helped us reach our goal,” said Francis Yupangco, global marketing manager for Regal Springs.

“Since the beginning, philanthropy has been a huge part of Regal Springs. It’s great to see people share our enthusiasm for supporting such great organizations like SeaShare.”

Boston blog: Marine Harvest re-works Rebel Fish packaging; Rising US demand for bass attracts new exporters
Since December 2015, the company donated over 35,000 pounds of tilapia to SeaShare.

“We were thrilled to work with Regal Springs again,” said Jim Harmon, executive director of SeaShare.

“With their generosity, we are able to provide thousands of people with nutrient-rich, high quality fish that they might not have access to otherwise.”

In February, the tilapia producer appointed Soren Dalsager, co-founder of Everfish and a former exec with Royal Greenland, as its new executive vice president of global sales.

Dalsager took the role from Magdalena Wallhoff, daughter of the company’s founder Rudi Lamprecht, and is responsible for leading global sales initiatives, providing strategic direction, and connecting with key clients within the US and international markets.

title: Pangea Shellfish readies for expansion
content:
BOSTON, US -- US wholesaler Pangea Shellfish is readying itself for expansion amid increasing demand for its oysters, bolstered by the local food movement, according to president and owner Ben Lloyd.

The Boston-based, Massachusetts-based company recently purchased the building it has been leasing in its home city for the past four years to expand in the future.

"We occupy about three-quarters of the building, and down the road at some point we're going to be expanding into the rest of it, but that time frame hasn't been ironed out yet," Lloyd said.

In April 2015, Pangea told Undercurrent News it was seeing an increase in oyster demand, with 20%-30% total annual sales growth.

Lloyd said that the growth in oyster demand has "definitely been sustained, it's been the trend for the last 15, 16 years. It's been kind of a steady increase and it definitely seems to be accelerating".

Lloyd estimated growth in oyster sales to be about 20% annually, with most growth coming from restaurants, and he attributed it to the popularity of the local food movement.

"People want to know where their food is from, how it's harvested and just more information about what they're eating," he said.

A streamlined aquaculture permitting process has also played a role in oyster availability.

"Certainly the aquaculture permitting process has helped a lot of new farmers get permitted, 15 years ago you just didn't have that many choices," Lloyd said. "I think the public seems to be more open to it...I don't think there are many homeowners getting in the way of it like they used to."

The company spent time at this year's Boston seafood show speaking with foreign companies, specifically Asian companies, with the intension of expanding outside of the US, where currently it sells about 95% of its product.

Although Lloyd said he expects efforts to enter Asian markets, especially China, to increase next year, "it's nothing we've made a push on yet", he said.

Although demand for shellfish in China isn't as high as it is for finfish, Lloyd said the potential is high.

"You're looking at a country that has so many people that I think the demand is there," he said.

Although oysters make up the majority of the company's sales, Pangea also Sells oysters, clams, mussels, scallops, crab and sea urchins, and Lloyd said that growth in mussel sales has been strong.

"We're seeing overall growth, but we're seeing mussels increasing faster than oysters have," he said.

Lloyd attributed the growth, which he said was about 30%-40%, to a strong brand, "more than anything it's the result of a great product", he said.

"Honestly they sell themselves, there isn't any promotion or push."

The company also plans to expand efforts to educate consumers about oysters, something the company has been doing for six to seven years.

"The response has been great, I heard it probably 15, 20 times at the [Boston] Seafood Show, how excited our customer base was about the educational piece of it, and we definitely have plans to expand on that," he said.

Lloyd said there will be "a lot more web content" as part of its educational push, and is considering hiring more salespeople so that Pangea's marketing team can focus more of its efforts on that.

title: Boston facility adds flexibility for Maine lobster processor
content:
BOSTON, US -- Wholesaler Maine Coast Company will ease its logistical hassles in shipping live lobsters long distances and gain better flexibility when its planned Boston distribution facility is completed in June, its CEO, Tom Adams, told Undercurrent News.

The expansion Boston’s fish pier, will allow the company to hold 20,000 pounds of live lobster, adding to the 150,000-pound holding capacity the company currently enjoys with at its York, Maine headquarters.

Adams said that one major benefit of the expansion will be greater flexibility to deal with short notice orders, an important option when trading in a live product.

“We get calls from customers all the time saying, you know, I need 1,000 pounds shipped to LA, or France or wherever," he said, during the Boston seafood show.

"But they’re calling last minute and we just don’t have time to react from York even though it’s only an hour and a half away. From Boston it’s only 10 minutes away. So we’re going to capture some of those sales,” said Adams.

Due to its location within minutes of Boston’s Logan International Airport, the facility will also showcase the company’s operations in a more accessible way than transporting would-be buyers to York, Adams added.

Additionally, it will help Maine Coast better compete for business in the Boston area, he said.

Easing logistics is a key task for a live lobster shipper that is increasingly doing more of its business in China.

One common route takes Maine lobster through New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport to China via a 60-hour trip that includes a stop in Dubai, United Arab Emirates.

“That’s an incredibly tough journey in the summer,” Adams said.

title: Watch last toothfish poaching vessel get blown up by Indonesian authorities
content:
Authorities in Indonesia have sunk the last of the “Bandit 6” toothfish poaching vessels, Viking, in Pangandaran, West Java.

Representatives from NGO Sea Shepherd Global were on the ground to film the sinking (see below).

Sea Shepherd first focused its attention on the illegal operations of the Bandit 6 toothfish vessels in 2014 when it launched “Operation Icefish”; the organization’s first campaign to target illegal, unreported, unregulated fishing in the Southern Ocean.

In December 2014, the Sea Shepherd ships Bob Barker and Sam Simon departed Australia and New Zealand respectively to patrol the Southern Ocean.

On April 6, following the 110-pursuit, Thunder was scuttled by its captain and waters of Sao Tome and Principe, West Africa.

Evidence provided by Sea Shepherd later led to the conviction of the three responsible, sentences of approximately three years in jail each, and a fines of €15 million.

In May, two more of the vessels, Songhua and Yongding, were apprehended in Cabo Verde, West Africa.

Later that same month, authorities in Malaysia detained the fourth of the vessels, Perlon.

In early February 2016, the authorities in Senegal arrested Kunlun. On Feb. 26, the Indonesian navy announced the arrested of Viking.

Following two weeks of investigations, Indonesian authorities charged Viking and its crew with fisheries crimes. The vessel was subsequently sunk in accordance with Indonesian law.

The Viking’s captain, Huan Venesa of Chile, and its crew of 10 from Indonesia, Chile, Argentina, Myanmar and Peru, remain in detention in Indonesia.

title: Mexican fishermen face potential prison time for illegal fishing in US waters
content:
Four fishermen from Mexico have been indicted by a grand jury in Brownsville, Texas, for unlawfully transporting fish harvested from the Gulf of Mexico.

Miguel Angel Ramirez-Vidal, 32, Jesus David Luna-Marquez, 20, Jesus Roberto Morales-Amador, 27, and Jose Daniel Santiago-Mendoza, 22, were detained on April 17, 2025, after attempting to transport and export approximately 315 kilograms of red snapper illegally harvested from US waters, according to a press release from the office of Nicholas J. Ganjei, US attorney in the Southern District of Texas.

Authorities observed the crew's panga-style vessel engaged in fishing with heavy nylon line and hooks seven miles north of the US-Mexico maritime boundary line, according to the release.

The four men are expected to appear for their arraignment before US judge Karen Betancourt on May 22. If convicted, they could each face up to five years in federal prison and possible $250,000 maximum fines.

Ganjei's office says this is the first illegal fishing case in the Southern District of Texas in which prison time is a possibility.
