title: Three Alaska fishermen sentenced for illegally transporting crab in search of higher prices
content:
The ringleader behind a failed scheme to illegally transport more than 7,000 pounds of live crab out of Alaska for better prices has been sentenced to federal prison and banned from fishing for at least two years, the US Attorney's Office announced Tuesday (May 13).

Kodiak vessel owner Corey Potter directed his two crabbing vessels, Arctic Dawn and Gamber, to harvest Tanner and golden king crab in Southeast Alaska in early 2024 and sell their catch in Washington state.

US authorities say Potter, 64, and his son Kyle Potter, 30, who skippered the 97-foot Arctic Dawn and Justin Welch, 34, who skippered the 116-foot Gambler, bypassed reporting and landing their catch in Alaska and instead headed to Seattle, where market prices were higher.

Alaska fishermen charged with illegally transporting crab to Seattle

Alaska law requires that crab boats produce a fish ticket showing they landed their catch at an in-state processor.

The elder Potter was sentenced to one year in prison and two years of supervised release that includes a global fishing ban while on parole for violating the Lacey Act, a federal law that prohibits trade in wildlife, fish, and plants that have been illegally taken, possessed, transported or sold.

"Alaska’s fisheries are a global model of sustainable, data-driven management, made possible by the dedication of honest fishermen, strong regulatory oversight, and a commitment to upholding fairness across the industry," Benjamin Cheeseman, assistant director of NOAA’s Office of Law Enforcement in the North Pacific Division said in a statement. "This sentencing serves as a clear reminder that there are serious consequences for those who break the rules."

Welch was the first of the three to plead guilty in return for a sentence of three years of probation along with $10,025 in fines, as Undercurrent News reported.

Prosecutors say one of the crab vessels had more than 4,200 pounds of live Tanner crab aboard, while the other had over 2,900 pounds of live golden king crab aboard. 

Tanner crab tainted with BCS

A portion of the Tanner crab was infected with bitter crab syndrome (BCS), a parasitic disease fatal to crustaceans. The indictment said that several crab fishermen had reached out to the Potters expressing concern for the impact transporting crab out of state could have on the industry because of the disease. 

But despite the concerns, the Kodiak fishermen went ahead with their scheme, with nearly half of the king crab dying in transit. Since the other vessel had BCS-contaminated Tanner crab aboard, the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife seized and landfilled the entire catch. 

Corey Potter pleaded guilty in February to two felony counts of violating the Lacey Act. Welch had already pleaded guilty and was sentenced to three years of probation and fined $10,000 in June 2024

"The laws protecting this industry help ensure Alaska’s fisheries are sustainable for years to come," US Attorney Michael J. Heyman for the District of Alaska said in a statement. "My office will continue to work with state and federal law enforcement partners to prosecute federal criminal violations that jeopardize Alaska’s fisheries.”

'Deadliest Catch' connection

US authorities served a search warrant on the vessel captained by Welch, who tipped off the Potters, who deleted text messages on their phone in an unsuccessful attempt to cover up their conspiracy to sell Alaska-caught seafood in Seattle despite knowing the risk of spreading BCS.

Arctic Dawn was featured in early episodes of the TV show "Deadliest Catch" including the pilot episode in 2004. The hit series features commercial crabbing vessels in the king and snow crab fisheries in the Bering Sea.

title: ‘Legacy’ US seafood importer faces eviction from California pier as former CFO goes to trial
content:
ABS Seafood, a longtime seafood supplier in the US state of California known for its sashimi-quality products and registered as a "legacy" business in the city of San Francisco, is facing eviction after reportedly failing to pay rent.

ABS, which was established in San Francisco by Japanese immigrants and brothers Hideo and Tokihide Ichinose in 1965, supplies sushi bars, restaurants and grocery stores throughout the Bay Area. While the business originated on Keith Street, it ultimately moved to its current location at Pier 45 Shed D-1 in 2016.

However, the Port of San Francisco is trying to give the company the boot.

ABS amassed $337,258 in back rent through March 2025, according to filings made at the San Francisco County Superior Court on April 14.

The seafood supplier was reportedly served a three-day notice to "pay rent or quit" on March 11. ABS was then instructed to pay off its rent balance as well as an additional $952 per day in damages. The $22,330 rent for April 2025, a fire permit fee of $409, and a security deposit of $57,113 have also been added to ABS' bill.

Further, a spokesperson for the Port of San Francisco reportedly told SFGATE, a local news service, that the company also "filed for an unlawful detainer to protect its interest in the property only after staff spent many months with ABS Seafood seeking to resolve the growing balance due, which has reached more than $444,000."

Big eye tuna. From the Facebook page of ABS Seafood.

The company is blaming its financial struggles on a loss of business resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic, according to SFGATE.

ABS's case has a few unique circumstances surrounding it.

For starters, ABS' alleged financial troubles come a few years after a federal grand jury indicted Antonietta Nguyen, the company's former chief financial officer, of embezzling approximately $2.7 million from the company.

Nguyen, who is scheduled to stand trial in the US District Court of San Francisco on June 2, allegedly used corporate funds to cover personal expenses, including luxury items from Louis Vuitton, Hermes Las Vegas and Paris. She also is alleged to have paid tuition fees for a relative. 

Also, the company is registered with the San Francisco Office of Small Business' legacy program, started in 2015 as a way to preserve small businesses that "serve as valuable cultural assets of the city." ABS applied for membership in the program in 2021 and was officially added to the registry on June 14 of that year.

"ABS Seafood, Inc.'s combination of local knowledge, leveraging its oldest connections to local fishing boats and fishermen, and the Ichonise family's expertise in foreign markets, has allowed ABS Seafood, Inc. to remain in business over a span of 56 years and to establish a strong customer base in both the Bay Area and abroad," the company said at its legacy business application hearing in 2021.

San Francisco, California, pinned on a map. Image from Jesse Kunerth / Shutterstock.

ABS was recognized at the time for its contribution to the history and identity of the Bayview and Fisherman's Wharf neighborhoods of San Francisco. Its location within Pier 45 Shed D was also highlighted as the area is part of the historic districts, with the substructure dating back to 1926-1927.

Michelle Reynolds, the small business programs and communications manager for San Francisco's Office of Economic and Workforce Development, told Undercurrent News that the office was unaware of ABS Seafood's troubles until seeing recent local news stories. However, after finding out, she said the office reached out to the company to offer leasing support.

"We have leasing specialists who can help businesses either understand their current lease, or if they need to, find a new or different location," explained Reynolds. 

The legacy business program does run a rent stabilization grant, which is available for use by property owners to incentivize them to support long-term leases with legacy businesses. However, ABS is not currently participating in this grant because leases that are with city property are not eligible for the program. 

Reynolds confirmed that ABS received a small legacy business grant -- a one time amount of $2,575 -- for fiscal year 2021/2022.

title: Lobster shack sues US state’s port, development authorities for corruption
content:
Rye Harbor Lobster Pound, a popular New England lobster shack, has filed a lawsuit against both the US state of New Hampshire Port Authority and the Pease Development Authority (PDA), accusing it of "a campaign of extortion, intimidation and corruption."

The 32-page complaint, filed Jan. 10 in the Superior Court in Merrimack County by Nathan Hanscom and Sylvia Cheever, the father-daughter co-owners of the lobster pound and restaurant, also names Paul Brean, PDA's executive director, and Geno Marconi, the recently retired director of the Port Authority and harbors, as defendants.

The suit charges that Marconi and Brean "improperly influenced the PDA and Port Authority, using their power to harm Rye Harbor Lobster Pound." The business was specifically targeted "due to its competition with Marconi and other businesses aligned with him in Rye Harbor State Marina," it alleges.

The lawsuit lists a number of harmful policies that the business was allegedly hit with, including the removal of parking spots used by the lobster pound's customers, the cutting of the water line, and then the obstruction of efforts to install a new water line.

The business was forced to pay an "unauthorized and illegal tax, framed as a 'concessions fee' of 10% on Rye Harbor Lobster Pound's gross sales, a fee not applied to other similar businesses," the lawsuit alleges.

Rye Harbor Lobster has operated out of Rye Marine since it opened in 1996, selling live lobsters and steamer clams, the complaint recounts. However, in 2005 it began preparing and selling foods like lobster rolls and chowder.

In 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, Rye Harbor Lobster Pound "experienced a significant increase in business because it was already established as a take-out only business and was one of the only restaurants in the area that remained open," according to the lawsuit.

It was after the business' 2020 success that the PDA and Port Authority, "under the direction and influence of Marconi and with the support of Brean," began to interfere, the lawsuit continues. The timing also lined up with Marconi's planned expansion of his local family-owned business, Geno's Chowder and Sandwich Shop, the complaint says.

"The series of actions taken against Rye Harbor Lobster Pound were driven by Marconi's desire to harm a competitor to his family business and in retaliation against the Plaintiffs who were not part of Marconi's network of allied businesses and individuals who worked for or were otherwise connected with the Port Authority," the lawsuit alleges.

Rye Lobster Pound, Cheever and Hanscom are seeking general, actual, consequential, special and enhanced compensatory damages in an amount to be proven at trial.

Marconi has other problems, too. He was indicted, in October 2024, on two felony charges of witness tampering and falsifying physical evidence in relation to another case, reports Seacoastonline, a New Hampshire news service.

While he's been on administrative leave since April 2024, the PDA board of directors announced earlier this month that Marconi retired, effective Jan. 1. However, there has been some confusion about whether he has actually retired as his legal counsel told NHPR (New Hampshire Public Radio) that the PDA made its announcement without contacting or speaking to Marconi.

"Had they contacted him, they would know that he remains optimistic about resuming his role at the PDA," his lawyer reportedly told the outlet.

title: US wholesalers avoid jail time for fish fraud by turning on vessel captain
content:
Two Montauk, New York, brothers who managed the wholesale fish side of their family business, Bob Gosman Co. Inc., have avoided jail time after pleading guilty to their part in a fishing fraud conspiracy.

Bryan and Asa Gosman were sentenced by US district judge Joan Azrack at a court in Central Islip on Tuesday (Nov. 12), reports Newsday. The brothers, who had entered their guilty plea in Nov. 2021, were ordered to pay more than $247,296 each in restitution to the New York State Marine Resources account. They also each received two years of probation and $100 special assessments.

The case stems back to an April 2021 indictment that alleged Bryan and Asa Gosman, as well as Christopher Winkler, a former business partner and the captain of the F/V New Age, engaged in conspiracy to commit wire fraud and illegally overharvested fluke and sea bass between May 2014 and July 2016.

Approximately 200,000 pounds of fluke and black sea bass were overharvested during the period, with a conservative wholesale valuation of $750,000, according to the Department of Justice.

Judge Azrack said at the sentencing that the Gosmans' cooperation was "critical" in the case against Winkler, reports Newsday.

As for Winkler, in Oct. 2023, a federal jury in Central Islip convicted the fishermen of one count of federal criminal conspiracy, two counts of mail fraud and two counts of obstruction of justice.

"Fluke and black sea bass play a vital part in our marine ecosystem and quotas are designed to prevent overfishing and stabilize populations for the public good," said assistant attorney general Todd Kim of the Justice Department's Environment and Natural Resources Division in a press release at the time. "We will continue to seek justice against those who flout laws that protect fisheries and the fishing industry." 

Winkler was sentenced in July to 30 months in prison and two years of supervised probation. 

Meanwhile, Gosman's Dock, which housed Bob Gosman Co.'s wholesale business and other related businesses, has recently been sold. Stephen Deckoff and his son, Stephen E. Deckoff, bought the waterfront area, which spans 11.6 acres on the Montauk Harbor, reports the NY Post. 

The sale price has not been confirmed, but the new owners told the newspaper that they paid less than the $45 million asking price.

title: Connecticut fisherman gets one year of prison for evading $1.2m in income taxes
content:
Brian Kobus, a Durham, Connecticut, man who worked as a commercial fisherman in Massachusetts, has received a federal prison sentence of one year and one day for evading income taxes.

Kobus, who was sentenced in the US District Court for the District of Massachusetts on Wednesday (Oct.16), additionally has been ordered by judge Nathaniel Gorton to serve one year of supervised release and to pay $377,839.90 in restitution to the US government, according to a statement from the Department of Justice (DOJ). 

Kobus worked as a commercial fisherman and deckhand for various fishing companies between 2011 through 2013, and again from 2017 through 2021, the DOJ said. During those periods Kobus reportedly received more than $1.2 million in income from fishing, however, he "never filed a federal income tax return or paid the taxes that he owed," federal prosecutors said.

The fisherman is said to have regularly cashed his paychecks and "used the cash to fund his personal lifestyle" while concealing his income from the government. He was found to have caused a tax loss to the Internal Revenue Service totaling more than $377,000.

Kobus was one of seven New England fishermen charged in April 2023 with tax evasion and failing to file returns. The seven allegedly evaded taxes on income between $900,000 and $1.9m each. The other fishermen indicted included Jorge Cazarin (New Bedford, Massachusetts), Christopher Garraty (Newport and East Greenwich, Rhode Island), Wojciech Kaminski (West Warwick, Rhode Island), Rodolfo Membreno (Fall River, Massachusetts), John Doe (New Bedford, Massachusetts) and Miguel Cruz Rubio (New Bedford, Massachusetts and Elizabethtown, North Carolina).

title: Trial begins for New York fisherman charged with illegal fluke, sea bass harvests
content:
Jurors in the US state of New York heard opening arguments this week in the trial of a fishing-boat captain charged with making hundreds of thousands of dollars by falsifying logs and overharvesting fluke and black sea bass in violation of federal fisheries laws. 

The New York Times reports that 63-year-old Christopher Winkler could face years in prison if he is found guilty. He's currently out on $100,000 bail, according to the newspaper.

Undercurrent News reported in January 2022 how Winkler, captain of the New Age, a 45.7-foot trawler home-ported in Montauk, was alleged to have falsified logs as part of a $850,000 fisheries-fraud scam, earning $818,000 himself mostly for overharvesting fluke and black sea bass in violation of federal laws designed to ensure a sustainable fishery.

He was charged in a superseding indictment filed by a Long Island grand jury with one count each of conspiracy to commit mail fraud, to obstruct the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) through the falsification of fishing logs, and to unlawfully frustrate NOAA's efforts at regulating federal fisheries.

The charges resulted from what federal investigators called Operation One-Way Chandelier, a multi-year, ongoing investigation into fisheries fraud on Long Island, the US Department of Justice said in a statement.

Prosecutors announced the case in 2021, saying it was part of a conspiracy with Bryan and Asa Gosman, who managed the wholesale company Bob Gosman Inc., on the Montauk docks. The Gosmans pleaded guilty, and are expected to testify against Winkler, according to the New York Times.

title: California seafood wholesaler’s former CFO accused of embezzling $2.7m
content:
Antonietta Nguyen, the former chief financial officer of ABS Seafood, a San Francisco, California-based seafood wholesaler and importer, has been charged with five counts of wire fraud connected to the embezzlement of $2.7 million, the US attorney for the Northern District of California says in a statement. 

The indictment, filed May 31, claimed that Nguyen bought luxury items from Louis Vuitton, Hermes Las Vegas, Chanel and more on both her corporate card and a personal card that she paid for with company funds. She also allegedly used corporate funds to pay state property taxes, a relative's college tuition and personal travel. The indictment also claimed she falsified financial documents to hide the missing money. 

Nguyen faces a maximum sentence of 20 years and a fine of $250,000 -- plus restitution -- for each count if found guilty. She was released on a $250,000 bond and is slated to appear before US district judge Susan Illston.

title: Samherji disclaims fake apology website, release
content:
Icelandic fishing giant Samherji has issued a statement discrediting a fraudulent website and press release issued on May 11 that had imitated Samherji and claimed criminal responsibility for the firm.

Transparency groups slam Samherji, Icelandic gov’t for response to Fishrot scandal

"Samherji's attention has been drawn to the fact that unknown dishonest parties have sent a fake press release in Samherji's name to foreign media outlets," it said. "The same parties also seem to have set up a fake website in the name of the company hosted in the UK and, at the same time, distributed fake advertising banners."

"It should be noted that neither the website nor the press release has any connection with Samherji or the company's employees," it continued. "This appears to be a planned attack that the company takes very seriously. Samherji will request that the fake website is taken down."

The fake release made various claims regarding Samherji's conduct in Namibia, which formed the basis of the so-called Fishrot files released to Wikileaks by former employee Johannes Stefansson in late 2019, alleging the company had bribed Namibian government officials in return for quotas.

The scandal remains under investigation in Iceland, although no Samherji employees have thus far been indicted, nor are any Samherji subsidiary companies involved in the ongoing criminal proceedings taking place in Namibia.

title: Seven US East Coast harvesters charged with tax evasion
content:
Seven seafood harvesters on the US East Coast have been indicted on charges of tax evasion for allegedly hiding between $900,000 and $1.9 million each in income from the Internal Revenue Service over several years, the US District Attorney's Office in Rhode Island reports.

The harvesters worked for fishing companies out of New Bedford, Massachusetts, and Point Judith, Rhode Island, and were paid as independent contractors, the federal prosecutors said in a statement issued Sunday (April 16). The companies documented their income with Forms 1099, but the seven allegedly did not file individual tax returns or pay all the taxes owed, some for decades or more.

The seven fishermen charged are:

Jorge Cazarin of New Bedford, who faces five counts each of tax evasion and willful failure to file tax returns from 2016 to 2020;
Christopher Garraty of Newport and East Greenwich, Rhode Island, who faces three counts each of tax evasion and willful failure to file tax returns from 2016 to 2018, plus a single count of  tax evasion for taxes allegedly owed for 2007 through 2011;
Wojciech Kaminski of West Warwick, Rhode Island, who faces five counts of tax evasion from 2014 and 2016 through 2019, and four counts of willful failure to file tax returns for 2016 through 2019;
Brian Kobus of Durham, Connecticut, who faces five counts of tax evasion for 2017 through 2021, and;
Rodolfo Membreno of Fall River, Massachusetts, who faces six counts of tax evasion for 2012 and 2017 through 2021, and four counts of willful failure to file tax returns for 2017 through 2019 and 2021

One of the harvesters used another person's name and Social Security number to hide his income, according to prosecutors. Some harvesters are also alleged to have filed false income tax returns by either not reporting their fishing income or by reporting false business expense deductions.

title: Tuna giant Bumble Bee settles lawsuit with NGO over supply-chain claims
content:
One of the US' three largest tuna canners has agreed to strip from its products claims that it employs "a fair and safe supply chain" and "fair and responsible working conditions" for the next 10 years as part of a lawsuit settlement with an international NGO.

Tuna giant Bumble Bee Foods, the US' second-largest tuna canner, which has repeatedly faced scrutiny related to labor practices on the vessels that catch its fish, agreed to the deal to settle with Global Labor Justice-International Labor Rights Forum (GLJ) a lawsuit filed last year in a local civil court in Washington, DC.

According to a press release from GLJ, the plaintiff had sought to prove in civil court that Bumble Bee, owned by Taiwan's FCF Co, was in violation of DC's Consumer Protection Procedures Act.

The case was initially filed in the Superior Court of the District of Columbia, which handles civil and criminal claims for the district, but was "removed" to the District Of Columbia District Court in 2022. A federal judge then remanded the case back to the local DC court in 2022 where a settlement was recently reached.

Attempts to contact Bumble Bee spokespersons or the attorneys representing GLJ were not immediately successful.

Bumble Bee has been repeatedly accused by Greenpeace of purchasing tuna from vessels that had enslaved migrants to catch its fish. But it is also carrying out a $40 million, five-year sustainability plan to safeguard fish stocks, ocean health and labor rights, as Undercurrent News has written. 

FCF has also faced repeated scrutiny from environmental non-profit groups such as Greenpeace for its own reported practices. Specifically, it has faced allegations that worker rights abuses have occurred aboard its distant water vessels. In April 2022, nine individuals affiliated with the Taiwanese tuna vessel Da Wang that once supplied Bumble Bee Foods were indicted in Taiwan for allegedly enslaving more than 20 migrant workers in a criminal case first brought to light in 2019.

Bumble Bee is working to carry out "social audits" on all of the fleets it sources from, a company spokesman has said.

title: Greenpeace: US’ largest retailers fail human rights standards in sourcing tuna
content:
A new scorecard report published by the activist group Greenpeace claims that none of the US' 16 biggest grocers have done enough to purge forced labor and other human rights abuses from tuna supply chains -- a $42.2 billion industry.

According to the report, only two of the retailers -- Aldi and Amazon-owned Whole Foods Market-- received passing grades from Greenpeace for addressing environmental and sustainability issues in sourcing tuna.

In total, of the 16 retailers, only Aldi received an overall passing grade in the scorecard, a "D" with 61.5 points out of 100.

"Grocery retailers continue to turn a blind eye to the worst abuses at sea," said Mallika Talwar, senior oceans campaigner at Greenpeace US. "Even as customers press clothing manufacturers and other economic sectors to respect human rights and labor standards, the abuses in tuna fisheries continue unchecked. These fleets need to implement and follow much stronger labor and environmental standards -- like all others; these workers deserve safe workplaces and decent wages," she said.

Greenpeace described working conditions on fishing vessels as  "hidden" from US consumers, urging retailers to hold themselves and their suppliers to more rigorous standards.

Greenpeace pointed to a case last year that saw the leadership of the Taiwanese-owned vessel Da Wang indicted for involvement in forced labor and human trafficking.

Tuna caught by this vessel was traced to FCF Co-owned Bumble Bee Foods and made available for sale on the shelves of a Harris Teeter store, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Kroger, in Arlington, Virginia. Kroger's final score in the Greenpeace report was 27%, leading to it being ranked in 10th place. Bumble Bee, which has stopped sourcing from the vessel, said that it is working to carry out "social audits" on all of the fleets it sources from.

Of the 16 retailers Greenpeace queried for its report, 11 returned surveys, and the other five were assessed on publicly available information. Whole Foods received the highest environmental score, 84%, followed by Aldi at 78%.

Aldi came closest to receiving a passing grade on human rights, at 59.77%. Meijer scored 15% on human rights and 23% on the environment, the lowest grades in both categories. Overall, Meijer scored the worst with 16%, followed closely by Wegmans, 17%, Southeastern Grocers, 18%, and Publix, 19%.

"It's not enough to have human rights, labor, and sustainability policies -- corporations must enforce them, and they are moving too slowly," said Marilu Cristina Flores, senior oceans campaigner at Greenpeace US.

"Although many retailers have environmental sustainability guidelines in place, only five scored a passing grade in this category. And even though retailers still have a lot of ground to cover in environmental sustainability, their inaction on human rights violations is even further behind the times," she noted.

Greenpeace pointed out that very few retailers committed to respecting the International Labor Organization (ILO) Work in Fishing Convention of 2007, which provides specific guidance on minimum standards for decent working conditions on fishing vessels, including workplace safety, decent wages and working conditions, and access to food and clean water.

Only Aldi scored the maximum for commitment to these and other UN policies. According to the report, four retailers -- HEB, Publix, SE Grocers, and Wegmans -- scored zero points for this question.

Fishers in Orissa state, India.
Photo credit: Francisco Blaha.

During the latest Infofish tuna conference, held last October in Bangkok, Francisco Blaha -- a consultant for the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations -- raised the issue of human rights and labor conditions in the tuna supply chain.

Blaha, who is based in New Zealand, stressed that social requirements in the tuna fishery are often voluntary market-based initiatives. As a result, they often fail to mitigate labor abuses, he said.

He noted that the ILO's convention C188 contains a broad range of requirements relating to crewing. However, he said that only 19 parties had ratified it, which is insufficient to make it a generally accepted international regulation. 

Meanwhile, all Marine Stewardship Council (MSC)-certified fisheries and at-sea supply chain organizations are required to publicly report the measures being taken to address forced and child labor. The self-declaration is then published on the MSC website.

Blaha highlighted that human rights abuses are rife in some tuna fisheries and that more needs to be done collectively to address the issue.

He also indicated a link between harmful government subsidies, slave labor and cheap tuna, and noted that all nations should govern the high seas collectively to avoid a lack of oversight.

title: Danish magnate back in court accused of fraud with EU funds
content:
Danish fishing baron Henning Kjeldsen is back in court, this time accused of selling fishing vessels and then raising EU grant support for them, reports TV2 Nord.

Danish magnate earns $365m selling pelagic interests at home, abroad

The joint stock company Gitte Henning Konsum, where Henning Kjeldsen is the main shareholder, has, according to the indictment, sold the fishing vessel 'Myggenes' a month after paying out around DKK 300,000 ($40,223) in EU support for improvements on the vessel.

According to the prosecutor, the same applies in another case in the same company.

Kjeldsen himself pleaded not guilty to the accusations and explained that he took advice from a fisheries consultant.

"It has always been the case that if you sold, the vessel had to be within the EU for two years," he said. "There has never been anything about needing special permission to sell within the EU... I didn't read the terms, as it was something the consultant arranged. It is not something fishermen get involved in."

In response, the Danish fisheries agency, which was also called as a witness in the court, said that in the rules it is clear that vessels may not be sold before or immediately after receiving a grant. 

Late last year, Kjeldsen was successfully prosecuted and fined DKK 54 million for fishing rule violations committed between 2013 and 2019. In total, more than DKK 162.5m was also confiscated from companies he owned that were found to be "straw man companies".

Forced to exit the pelagic side of his business, he made DKK 2.4 billion from selling assets including the still-under-construction vessel Gitte Henning.

title: Lischewski back on the hook in tuna price-fixing suit
content:
A federal judge overseeing civil class-action suits from customers who say they were harmed by US tuna canners' price-fixing has ruled that former Bumble Bee Foods CEO Christopher Lischewski can again be brought in as a defendant.

The decision means that Lischewski, who in 2020 was given a three-year prison sentence after being found guilty of criminal price-fixing charges, could face liability in at least one of the civil suits.

In March, Lischewski, who served as the San Diego, California, company's CEO from 1999 until his 2019 indictment, was dismissed as a defendant in a civil suit brought by Associated Wholesale Grocers, a Kansas City, Kansas-based wholesaler.

Chris Lischewski.

Dana Sabraw, the chief justice of the United States District Court for the Southern District of California, agreed at the time with Lischewski's lawyers that the wholesaler hadn't proven that the former CEO had enough ties to the state of Kansas to establish the necessary "personal jurisdiction" to include him as a defendant.

"To be sure, some of Lischewski’s conduct was criminal and found to be so by a jury of his peers. But Lischewski’s involvement in a national price-fixing conspiracy on behalf of Bumble Bee is not sufficient to establish minimum contacts by Lischewski himself in a particular state in the absence of evidence of purposeful direction in the forum," she wrote.

But after lawyers for the grocery wholesaler filed a motion for reconsideration of the March decision, arguing that Sabraw had erred, the judge gave the case another look.

"After reviewing the parties’ briefs, the record on file, and reconsidering the case law, the court grants the motion for reconsideration, and on reconsideration, denies the motion for summary judgment based on lack of personal jurisdiction," Sabraw wrote in an Aug. 8 opinion.

The suit brought by Associated Wholesale Grocers also names as defendants Bumble Bee and its former private equity owner Lion Capital; Reston, Virginia-based canner StarKist & Co and its parent company, South Korea's Dongwon Enterprise; former StarKist owner Del Monte Corporation; and Chicken of the Sea International and its owner, Thai Union Group.

Bumble Bee agreed to plead guilty to criminal price-fixing charges in 2017 and was fined $25 million by the Department of Justice. The company, which in 2019 filed for bankruptcy and was later sold to Taiwan's FCF Co, its longtime supplier, cited those fines and the civil suits as the rationale for the bankruptcy filing.

Dongwon and StarKist continue to fight the price-fixing-related litigation, while Thai Union has largely settled the suits brought against it and its subsidiary.

Earlier this week, StarKist vowed that it will not settle some price-fixing suits, instead appealing a ruling against it to the US Supreme Court. 

Image from Shutterstock.

"StarKist has willingly and proactively settled cases with customers in situations in which there was a reasonable basis for arguing the customer was harmed," StarKist general counsel and senior vice president Scott Meece said in a statement. "On the other hand, StarKist will not settle cases, in these matters or others, if the claims are excessive or in which the complaining party was not harmed. We will continue to defend those cases, and while defense is costly, it is the right thing to do."

StarKist is challenging an earlier decision from judge Janis Sammartino to certify the hundreds of individual lawsuits into common classes. That decision, it has argued, sounds a "death knell" for the future of class-action suits they face from customers who claim they were damaged from price-fixing. Additionally, the company said that it hasn't been proven that members of the allegedly damaged classes have enough commonalities to be grouped together.

title: COO, three more VPs exit Bumble Bee as FCF restructuring continues
content:
The executive exits at Bumble Bee Foods keep coming with the San Diego, California, US-based tuna canner seeing its chief operating officer and three vice presidents depart, sources told Undercurrent News.

Sources said that the latest to leave include James Badet, a 22-year veteran who since November 2019 has served as the company's chief operating officer. Additionally, senior vice-president of sales Laura Chamberlain, senior vice-president of global corporate responsibility Leslie Hushka and vice-president of brand management Jeanine Lewis, have also departed.

According to his LinkedIn profile, Badet began working at the company in 1995 and despite a four-year absence away from the canner beginning in 1999 during which he worked at paper manufacturer Kimberley-Clark, has spent the entirety of his career at Bumble Bee. 

Chamberlain, Lewis and Hushka were more recent hires to the canner, having most previously worked at Danone, Office Depot and ExxonMobil, respectively. 

Autoresponse emails to the Bumble Bee addresses of Chamberlain, Hushka and Lewis confirmed their departures. Company representatives did not respond to Undercurrent's requests for comment for this article. Lewis, Chamberlain and Badet did not respond to requests for comment made via LinkedIn. Hushka declined to comment.

The exits follow the departures of at least nine others within recent weeks, including that of former CEO Jan Tharp, who was replaced by Jerry Chou, a shareholder at Bumble Bee's Taiwanese parent company, FCF Co. Chou stepped into his new role on July 1.

Other recent departures from Bumble Bee have included regional sales vice-president Brad Sauerzopf, Erik Engelmann, senior director of e-commerce at the company, and Dan Hofmeister, a senior vice president and general manager at the canner. As Undercurrent previously reported, the company has also bid farewell to five others, including sales executives Dan Gerlach, Allan Jackson, Scott Balog and Bryan Hutchenson, as well as purchasing officer Kevin McClain.

Many of the employees no longer with the company served under Tharp and also Chris Lischewski, who left the CEO role in 2018 after his indictment on price-fixing charges. Lischewski was convicted and sentenced to a three-year prison term in a 2019 trial that saw two former Bumble Bee vice presidents testify against him.

Damages from civil price-fixing lawsuits prompted Bumble Bee's bankruptcy and $928 million sale to FCF, its longtime albacore supplier, in January 2020, as reported by Undercurrent.

title: Bumble Bee loses three more high-level execs as FCF leadership transition continues
content:
US tuna supplier Bumble Bee Foods (BBF) has lost three more top-level executives as the company continues to transition under the ownership of Taiwanese tuna trading giant FCF Co.

Brad Sauerzopf, who has held various high-level sales positions at Bumble Bee for nearly five years, and Erik Engelmann, a senior director of e-commerce for roughly seven months, have both left the company, sources told Undercurrent News.

Also gone is Dan Hofmeister, who held a litany of positions there over an eight-year stay, including most recently the title of senior vice president and general manager where he acted as CEO of a newly created frozen food division. He's been hired by the US weight-loss service Jenny Craig to serve as its chief marketing officer, according to a statement from that company.

Jan Tharp, the former president and CEO of Bumble Bee Foods, in a video about supply chain management.

The departures follow that of Jan Tharp, who was revealed to be stepping down from her CEO post in early June after 12 years to be replaced by Jerry Chou, an FCF shareholder and former yogurt entrepreneur. Chou stepped into his new role on July 1.

As Undercurrent previously reported, the company has also bid farewell to five others, including sales executives Dan Gerlach, Allan Jackson, Scott Balog and Bryan Hutchenson, as well as purchasing officer Kevin McClain.

A 'seasoned marketing executive'

Carlsbad, California-based Jenny Craig, in announcing its hiring of Hofmeister, called him "a seasoned marketing executive and mission-minded leader with a passion for enhancing consumers' lives through strong consumer brands". 

He started his career at Bumble Bee in July 2014 as the company's director of marketing, but quickly ascended in June 2017 to the position of vice president of marketing and then in November 2018 to head of revenue management, and senior vice president (VP) of brand marketing in February 2020, based on his LinkedIn profile. 

In February 2022, he was named senior VP and general manager of the newly-created frozen food division, which he described as "scoped as the company's leading growth engine" and consisting of 125 people in five countries. 

Dan Hofmeister.

Hofmeister thanked Bumble Bee for the opportunity to work in "five amazing roles over nearly eight years" on his LinkedIn page. 

"I made the difficult decision to take a new opportunity elsewhere (more on that to come)," he said. 

Sauerzopf described a similar list of promotions at Bumble Bee from the time he was hired as a director of sales for the US mid-Atlantic and Midwest region in September 2017, promoted to regional sales vice president of the company's US mid-Atlantic region in April 2021, and then to heading regional sales for Bumble Bee subsidiary Kroger Supermarkets in June 2021. 

Hofmeister, Sauerzopf and Engelmann couldn't be reached for comment at press time. A Bumble Bee spokesperson reached by Undercurrent declined to comment.

Most of the executives who left served under Tharp and also Chris Lischewski, who left the CEO role in 2018 after his indictment on price-fixing charges. Lischewski was convicted and sentenced to a three-year prison term in a 2019 trial that saw two former Bumble Bee vice presidents complicit in price-fixing testify against him.

Complications from civil price-fixing lawsuits prompted Bumble Bee's bankruptcy and $928 million sale to FCF, its longtime albacore supplier, in January 2020, as reported by Undercurrent.

title: Bumble Bee’s Canadian efforts, tighter FCF ties fuel progress on $40m sustainability goals
content:
A specialized team of ocean mappers has spent a lot of time in the cold waters of Canada's Bay of Fundy recently, surveying its depths for lost fishing gear that's imperiling a 40,000-metric-ton Atlantic herring fishing and causing other problems for the environment.

The lost gear mapping is being carried out by workers from the Nova Scotia-based firm CSR GeoSurveys as part of a collaboration that Bumble Bee Foods' Canadian affiliate Connors Bros is taking with the Global Ghost Gear Initiative (GGGI). The bay's herring fishery was Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certified in 2016 but Bumble Bee later withdrew when concerns about the stock's health emerged.

The project is now in a fishery improvement project (FIP) and Bumble Bee hopes that the stock will eventually have rebounded enough to allow for MSC re-certification in the future, Leslie Hushka, the San Diego, California, tuna canner's senior vice president of global corporate social responsibility, recently told Undercurrent News.

"We've done a big side-scanning sonar analysis of the spawning grounds and found a tremendous amount of gear there, and within the next couple of weeks, we'll start recovery operations. So actually removing that gear out of that area to hopefully restore that fishery to strong health," she said.

Two years into a five-year plan to spend $40 million globally on improving fish stock sustainability, ocean health and labor rights, Bumble Bee has seen progress with the $14m as part of its "Seafood Future" program that it's spent to date, Hushka said.

"In two years, we've really laid the foundations for those efforts," she said, adding that the monies have been spent on a combination of internal initiatives and external partnerships such as the $1m pledged toward GGGI's work.

Recent turnover

Bumble Bee has seen extensive leadership turnover recently, including the departure of veteran CEO Jan Tharp who navigated the tuna canner through the aftermath of her predecessor, Chris Lischewski, who was jailed for price-fixing. That scandal and resulting lawsuits led to a massive shakeup that included Bumble Bee's bankruptcy and eventual sale to FCF.

Tharp, who initiated the Seafood Future program, will be replaced by Jerry Chou, the brother of FCF CEO Max Chou and Bumble Bee's board chairman. As first reported by Undercurrent, a string of other executives have left or are in the process of leaving Bumble Bee, which is filling its ranks with leaders from the consumer packaged goods sector. 

Jan Tharp, the former president and CEO of Bumble Bee Foods, in a video about supply chain management.

Hushka said that despite the leadership changes, the company remains committed to the Seafood Future program.

"This is actually a conversation that I've had with Jerry as he starts to step in behind Jan, there'll be no change in our mission and no change in our sustainability programs and so I'm confident that we're gonna have the continued support from leadership and we're gonna be able to deliver on these 2025 goals that we've set out," the vice-president said.

Continued progress

Hushka cited progress made on the program's goals, two years in. For example, 71% of the seafood volumes that Bumble Bee sources is now classed as sustainable by Global Sustainable Seafood Institute-compliant program, or is moving that way by 2025. That includes the bulk of the tuna canner's albacore stocks, processed by FCF but harvested by independent longliners. 

Last year, 250 FCF-affiliated Taiwanese albacore longliners entered into the MSC assessment process. 

"We also fully transitioned all of our albacore sourcing from FIPs at the end of 2021 along three ocean areas -- Indian, Atlantic and Pacific and resulting in meeting this species goal three years ahead of schedule. For skipjack, our transition to MSC products has begun and will continue into 2023," the report states. "Yellowfin has also been incorporated into these programs and we did not source from Indian Ocean fisheries in 2021," the report states.

Labor rights

Hushka said that the $14m spent on Seafood Future to date has also gone towards funding Bumble Bee's distribution partnership with plant-based seafood substitute maker Good Catch and efforts to improve tuna fishing crews' access to third-party grievance mechanisms to report concerns about labor conditions at sea.

FCF has faced repeated scrutiny from environmental non-profit groups such as Greenpeace over allegations of worker rights abuses aboard its distant water vessels. In April, nine individuals affiliated with the Taiwanese tuna vessel Da Wang that once supplied Bumble Bee Foods were indicted for allegedly enslaving more than 20 migrant workers in a criminal case first brought to light in 2019.

Bumble Bee is working to carry out "social audits" on all of the fleets it sources from, Hushka said and 36% of its tuna fleets have been covered to date.

Albacore tuna. Credit: Ocean Outcomes

"I feel pretty good about that considering the impacts of COVID and the difficulties we had in getting to some of the fleets based on that information, we've put in play a number of new training programs with not only FCF but with our seafood task force in terms of best practices that fleets and recruiting agencies that they work with need to adopt," she said.

In addition, Bumble Bee and FCF are working to roll out a grievance mechanism known as "Worker Voice" for its vessel crews.

"It's a simple QR code that fishers can scan on the boat and use to report any concern that they have on their working environment or their treatment or fees or wages to an independent NGO," Hushka said. "And that NGO will assist them in remedying that situation."

title: FCF parts ways with Bumble Bee seafood veterans, fills ranks with CPG execs
content:
Taiwanese tuna trading giant FCF Co is making significant changes to the top team at US subsidiary Bumble Bee Foods, with several seafood sector veterans leaving, in addition to CEO Jan Tharp.

In addition to Tharp, who will be replaced as CEO by FCF shareholder and former yogurt entrepreneur Jerry Chou on July 1, at least five senior executives have left Bumble Bee in the past few months, sources told Undercurrent News.

FCF names Chou family member, former yogurt entrepreneur as Bumble Bee CEO

Meanwhile, FCF has been adding consumer packaged goods (CPG) executives to its ranks, several from the North American operations of French conglomerate Danone, which now owns Wallaby Yogurt Company, which Chou built.

"They have replaced seafood industry execs with CPG execs," one seafood sector veteran, who is closely following the changes at Bumble Bee, told Undercurrent.

Notable exits from Bumble Bee include sales executives Dan Gerlach, Allan Jackson, Scott Balog and Bryan Hutchenson, then Kevin McClain on purchasing.

Gerlach's LinkedIn profile showed that he spent 24 years with Bumble Bee, with the final five as vice president (VP) of US sales. He declined to comment to Undercurrent.

Jackson left his sales VP role with Bumble Bee in April and is now president of a company named Centric Technology Solutions. Jackson, who joined Bumble Bee in 2010 from consumer goods giant Reckitt Benckiser, did not respond to a request for comment.

After four years with the company, Balog left a role as a regional VP for Bumble Bee, based in Cincinnati, Ohio, in March.

Bumble Bee CEO Tharp set to exit after 12 years

Hutcheson worked for Bumble Bee for 41 years, finishing as VP for sales for the West Coast region. His LinkedIn page includes a tribute from Gerlach, wishing Hutcheson all the best in his retirement.

McClain, who joined Bumble Bee in 2009 after 30 years with rival Chicken of the Sea International, has also left, sources said. McClain was VP of responsible sourcing for Bumble Bee.

Most of the executives who left served under Tharp and also Chris Lischewski, who left the CEO role after his indictment on price-fixing charges.

He was convicted and sentenced to a three-year prison term in a 2019 trial that saw two former Bumble Bee vice presidents complicit in price-fixing testify against him. Complications from civil price-fixing lawsuits prompted Bumble Bee's bankruptcy and sale to FCF, its longtime albacore supplier.

"FCF is only just starting to get under the hood and make changes. The [COVID] pandemic delayed that," one executive close to the company, who asked not to be quoted by name, told Undercurrent.

Bumble Bee hires Hicks to help run sales team

Jackson, Balog and Hutchenson and McClain all did not respond to requests for comment. A spokesperson for Bumble Bee declined to comment on the exits but highlighted the hires the company has been making.

Earlier this week, Bumble Bee added Tiffany Hicks as vice president of "specialty channels" to provide leadership for the sales team working with private label retailers, foodservice, and alternative channels. Hicks was most recently with Danone North America as its commercial restaurants and foodservice director.

In May, Bumble Bee also hired Sebastian Castro-Malaspina as vice president of national grocery accounts. Castro-Malaspina also previously worked for Danone.

Both Hicks and Castro-Malaspina ultimately work for Laura Chamberlain, Bumble Bee's senior VP of sales, who also joined from Danone, as Undercurrent reported in November 2021.

In January, Bumble Bee hired Alex Drew as VP of customer development and strategy after four years of leading category management and sales operations for JUUL Labs, an electronic cigarette company. Drew also spent more than 10 years at Anheuser-Busch InBev in sales, category management, trade marketing, pricing, and strategy positions for the global brewer.

Judge nixes StarKist’s request to have some tuna price-fixing suits thrown out

Both Drew Chamberlain report to Connie Cooper Shepherd, senior VP of strategy and business development, who joined Bumble Bee in August 2021.

Also reporting to Cooper Shepherd on the newly re-organized senior commercial leadership team are Dan Hofmeister, senior VP and general manager of Anova, Bumble Bee's frozen division, and Jeanine Lewis Canales, VP of brand marketing.

Hofmeister started with Bumble Bee in 2014 as director of marketing from Hormel Foods. From 2020 to February of this year, he was senior VP of brand marketing across the whole Bumble Bee business.

Lewis Canales joined Bumble Bee in 2020 from Office Depot, where she was senior brand and media director. She spent nine years with The Coca-Cola Company before that.

Earlier in 2021, Bumble Bee hired Leslie Hushka as its senior VP of global corporate social responsibility. Hushka had spent 23 years at energy giant ExxonMobil working on sustainability challenges across its oil and gas and chemical divisions.

title: Bumble Bee CEO Tharp set to exit after 12 years
content:
Jan Tharp, the CEO of US shelf-stable seafood giant Bumble Bee Foods, is set to leave the company, sources told Undercurrent News.

Sources said that Tharp's upcoming exit from Bumble Bee, the company she has worked for since 2010 and ran since 2018, has been communicated internally. It's thought she would stay on to transition to a successor. 

Tharp and a spokesperson for Bumble Bee were not immediately available for comment to Undercurrent.

Tharp's tenure at the top at Bumble Bee has been a tumultuous one as she immediately followed Chris Lischewski, who left the CEO role after his indictment on price-fixing charges. He was convicted and sentenced to a three-year prison term in a 2019 trial that saw two former Bumble Bee vice presidents also complicit in price-fixing testify against him. Complications from civil price-fixing lawsuits prompted Bumble Bee's bankruptcy and sale to Taiwan's FCF Co, its longtime albacore supplier.

Tharp told Undercurrent in 2020 that she felt she needed to move quickly after her predecessor's exit to reshape the "culture" at the century-old seafood brand.

Bumble Bee has parted ways with several senior executives in the past few months. The company has also been hiring of late, bringing in several executives with experience at the North American arm of French conglomerate Danone.

Earlier this week, Bumble Bee added Tiffany Hicks as vice president of "specialty channels" to provide leadership for the sales team working with private label retailers, foodservice, and alternative channels. Hicks was most recently with Danone North America as its commercial restaurants and foodservice director.

Bumble Bee also hired Sebastian Castro-Malaspina as vice president of national grocery accounts in May. Castro-Malaspina also previously worked for Danone.

Both Hicks and Castro-Malaspina ultimately work for Laura Chamberlain, Bumble Bee's senior vice president of sales, who also joined from Danone, as Undercurrent reported in November 2021.

Chamberlain followed Connie Cooper Shepherd, senior vice president of strategy and business development for Bumble Bee, who was hired in August 2021. Chamberlain reports to Cooper Shepherd. 

Before that, Bumble Bee hired Leslie Hushka as its senior vice president of global corporate social responsibility. Hushka had spent 23 years at energy giant ExxonMobil working on sustainability challenges across its oil and gas and chemical divisions.

title: US eel supplier, four employees plead not guilty in $160m smuggling scheme
content:
Four US-based employees of American Eel Depot and the company itself pleaded not guilty Tuesday (May 24) to participating in a globe-spanning $160 million smuggling scheme that relied on passing off US eels as endangered European ones.

The employees -- Yi Rui "Ricky" Huang and Fen "Emily" Liu, Chao "Kevin" Jin Shi, and Guo Tuan "Jason" Zhou -- remain out on bail, records filed with the US District Court of New Jersey show. Four China-based employees and associates of the company -- Liang "Jackie" Chen, Yundong Wei, Xiajuan Huang Zhouyi and  Hong "John" Lee -- were not arraigned.

New Jersey court records indicate that prosecutors have until June 24 to provide discovery to the defense and a status conference will be held Sept 8. to discuss if and when a pre-trial conference can be scheduled.

The US Department of Justice (DOJ) said in a press release earlier this month that American Eel, the US' largest such supplier, violated the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) treaty, which is enforced in the United States through the Endangered Species Act.

"Despite this ban", the indictment alleges, "the defendants conspired to unlawfully smuggle large quantities of live baby European eels out of Europe, to their eel-rearing factory in China. After rearing the baby eels to maturity, defendants’ Chinese facility would then slaughter and process the eels for shipping to the United States, to be sold as sushi products," the DOJ said.

The March 1 indictment goes well beyond the previously released DOJ statement in detailing the alleged scheme. It described how, in March 2013, Liu and Chen began exchanging emails discussing the CITES export ban and how to label European eels as "some other kind of fish for a US customer", the DOJ alleged in the indictment.

Then, Huang and Lee began exchanging emails regarding the logistics of moving the European eels onward to Malaysia and Thailand so they could ultimately be shipped on to Hong Kong and China, where American Eel maintained an affiliate farm, the DOJ said. The eels would be labeled as "live crabs" and sent via the Netherlands to Thailand.

In other cases, New Jersey-based American Eel would arrange for European eels to be shipped from Ukraine to Hong Kong.

"On or about Feb. 27, 2016, Person B solicited defendant Quo Tuan Zhou to send him a wire payment of $40,000.00 to a bank account in Canada, with a remaining balance to be calculated when defendant Quo Tuan Zhou and/or other employees of defendant [American Eel] visited him in Ukraine," the indictment stated.

Additionally, on several separate instances in 2015, 2016 and 2017 American Eel and its employees reportedly imported containers of eel meat into the US from China that contained European eel without having the needed CITES permits, the indictment said.

The defendants face charges of conspiracy, smuggling and false labeling of seafood under the Lacey Act.

title: US supplier, eight employees alleged to have carried out $160m eel smuggling scheme
content:
US federal prosecutors have indicted the Totowa, New Jersey-based American Eel Depot and eight of its employees and associates for their alleged roles in a four-year scheme to traffick some $160 million in endangered eels to China.

The US Department of Justice (DOJ) said in a press release that American Eel, the US' largest such supplier, violated the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species treaty, which is enforced in the United States through the Endangered Species Act.

"Despite this ban", the indictment alleges, "the defendants conspired to unlawfully smuggle large quantities of live baby European eels out of Europe, to their eel-rearing factory in China. After rearing the baby eels to maturity, defendants’ Chinese facility would then slaughter and process the eels for shipping to the United States, to be sold as sushi products," the DOJ said.

According to the DOJ, the defendants indicted are: Yi Rui "Ricky" Huang and Fen "Emily" Liu, both of Oakland Gardens, New York; Chao "Kevin" Jin Shi of Flushing, New York; Guo Tuan "Jason" Zhou of Woodhaven, New York; Liang "Jackie" Chen of Fujian, China; Yundong Wei of Fuzhou, China; Xiajuan Huang Zhouyi, 46, of Changle, China; and  Hong "John" Lee of Yuen Long, Hong Kong.

The DOJ said that the indictment, which has not been uploaded into the federal court's database, states that over a four-year period, the alleged smuggling scheme saw some 138 shipping containers with a market value of $160m imported into the US.

"The indictment focuses on six containers, seized by the government, which were determined to contain all or mostly European eel, mislabeled as American eel to avoid law enforcement detection. American eel fishing is highly regulated but still lawful in limited quantities in some areas," the DOJ said.

The mislabeling was willful, the DOJ said.

"As alleged in the indictment, the defendants knew the eels’ true species, knew what they were doing was unlawful, and intentionally lied to U.S. authorities to conceal the illegalities and avoid detection," the release stated

title: Six US harvesters charged with catching, selling 2.6m lbs of unreported herring
content:
Six US fishermen, including five from Maine and one from New Hampshire, have been charged with catching and selling millions of pounds of unreported Atlantic herring, the Bangor (Maine) Daily News reports.

The harvesters are accused of making more than 80 fishing trips in the Gulf of Maine on the vessel Western Sea between June 2016 and September 2019, and not reporting their catch to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. They were indicted Thursday on 35 counts of conspiracy, fraud and falsifying fishing records, according to the US District Attorney’s Office.

Also indicted was Western Sea, the business that owns the Rockland, Maine-based vessel used to catch the fish.

The men allegedly sold more than 2.6m lbs of herring to five fish dealers and three lobster boat captains, who are not identified in the indictment. Three of the dealers allegedly paid the fishermen more than $460,000.

Named in the indictment are: Glenn Robbins, 75, of Eliot, Maine; Neil Herrick, 46, of Rockland, Maine; Andrew Banow, 35, of Rockport, Maine; Stephen Little, 56, of Warren, Maine; Jason Parent, 49, of Owls Head, Maine; and Ethan Chase, 44, of Portsmouth, New Hampshire.

Edward MacColl, a Portland, Maine, defense attorney identified as representing Robbins and Chase, did not respond to an email seeking comment, according to the newspaper.

title: New York harvester faces expanded charges from federal sting operation
content:
A fishing-boat captain from the US state of New York faces new charges of falsifying logs as part of an $850,000 fisheries-fraud scam where he allegedly earned $818,000 himself mostly for overharvesting fluke and black sea bass in violation of federal laws designed to ensure a sustainable fishery.

Christopher Winkler, 61, of Montauk, was charged in a superseding indictment filed by a Long Island grand jury with one count of conspiracy to commit mail fraud, to obstruct the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) through the falsification of fishing logs, and to unlawfully frustrate NOAA's efforts at regulating federal fisheries.

The charges resulted from what federal investigators called Operation One-Way Chandelier, a multi-year, ongoing investigation into fisheries fraud on Long Island, the US Department of Justice said in a statement.

As Undercurrent News has reported, federal prosecutors have already charged Winkler, captain of the New Age, a 45.7-foot trawler home-ported in Montauk, for allegedly landing more than 74,000 pounds of illegal fluke and black sea bass during 70 fishing trips between 2014 and 2016.

The 18-page superseding indictment, which is dated Jan. 25, alleges that between May 2014 and February 2017, Winkler, as captain of New Age, went on at least 220 fishing trips where he caught fluke or black sea bass in excess of applicable trip limits, plus other species.

His harvests "included multiple species of fish such as black sea bass, bluefish,
butterfish, dogfish, goosefish, fluke, hake, monkfish, scup, skate, and squid," according to the indictment.

According to the indictment, from May 2014 through April 2016, Winkler was paid
$237,000 for unreported and overharvested fluke, and approximately $15,000 for
unreported and overharvested black sea bass.

Then, from May 2016 through July 2016, he received another $16,000 for unreported and overharvested fluke and from September 1, 2015, through March 7, 2017, he received approximately $550,000 for unreported and overharvested fluke, and approximately $70,000 for unreported and overharvested black sea bass. 

The New Age was mid-illegal harvest when it almost got stopped, according to the affidavit, but Winkler, "intentionally discarded and caused to be intentionally discarded
overharvested fluke when the New Age was approached by a Coast Guard vessel".

And at least some of the harvesting was done out-of-season, according to the affidavit.

At various times during the conspiracy, this fish was sold to two now-defunct companies in the New Fulton Fish Market in the Bronx and a fish dealer, Bob Gosman Co. of Montauk, plus three individuals or businesses not identified by name in the affidavit.

According to court filings, the overages of fish included at least 200,000 pounds of fluke, and the overall over-quota fish of all species were valued at least at $850,000 wholesale.

A now-shuttered federally-licensed fish dealer, Bob Gosman received at least $240,000 harvested from May 2014 to July 2016 in amounts that exceeded their allowed quotas, federal officials have said.

The New Age almost sank in February 2020, taking on water that forced the crew to abandon ship about 25 nautical miles south of Fire Island. One person was taken to the hospital, according to the East Hampton Star, a weekly Long Island newspaper. 

Not aboard at the time, Winkler was able to get onto his boat, which was still floating and drifting, and use pumps he had brought to get enough water off it to get it into port in the US state of New Jersey. 

In November, dealer owner Bob Gosman pleaded guilty in US federal court to two counts of misdemeanor Lacey Act Fish Trafficking and Bryan and Asa Gosman, also of Montauk, pleaded guilty to the illegal sales, as Undercurrent has reported.

The Gosmans originally pleaded not guilty to the charges during their initial court appearance in May 2021.

The Gosmans during a court appearance in November admitted to falsifying fishing vessel trip reports (FVTR) and dealer reports, both transmitted to NOAA, and obstructing NOAA's investigation by destroying business records rather than submit them to an ongoing grand jury investigation. 

NOAA uses the FVTRs to set policies designed to ensure a sustainable fishery.

As part of the settlement of the criminal court case, Bob Gosman Co. will pay a $50,000 fine and be placed on probation for four years. The company will also submit to enhanced monitoring, training and inspection requirements.

title: Company faces federal negligence charges in California oil spill
content:
Three US oil companies face federal indictment for several alleged areas of negligence connected to a spill of 25,000 gallons of crude oil off the state of California in October, the Associated Press reports.

Amplify Energy and two subsidiaries that operate oil rigs and a pipeline off Long Beach allegedly failed to properly respond when alarms repeatedly alerted them to a pipeline rupture that culminated with the shutdown of several areas off the coast on Oct. 3.

As Undercurrent News has reported, the spill hampered Newport Beach harvesters who were just opening their season. Operating in one of California's smaller fisheries, they hauled in 38,453 pounds of swordfish worth $232,661, 10,061 lbs of spiny lobster worth $130,631, and 10,913 lbs of shortspine thornyhead, a type of rockfish, in 2019. 

It was all part of a total seafood catch of 266,437 lbs of 51 varieties of seafood worth $722,905.

Federal prosecutors allege that the companies failed to respond properly to eight leak detection system alarms over a 13-hour period. They shut down and restarted the pipeline after each alarm, spewing more oil into the ocean. 

Amplify blamed an unnamed shipping company for displacing the pipeline with a dragging anchor and said Amplify workers responded to what they believed were false alarms because the system wasn’t functioning properly. It was signaling a potential leak at a platform where no leak was occurring, the company said.

Fishing was prohibited from Huntington Beach to Dana Point following the spill. At its apex, the spill forced the closure of some 650 square miles of marine waters, including all bays and harbors from Seal Beach to San Onofre State Beach.

The closed areas were reopened in early December. Several harvesters and processors applied for aid.

If Amplify is convicted, it can face up to five years of probation and fines that could total millions of dollars.

title: New York supplier, wholesalers plead guilty to selling illegally caught fish
content:
A 54-year-old seafood company and two part-owners from the US state of New York have pleaded guilty to receiving black sea bass and summer flounder worth at least $240,000 harvested from May 2014 to July 2016 in amounts that exceeded their allowed quotas. 

Bob Gosman Co., a federally-licensed fish dealer located in Montauk, New York, pleaded guilty in US federal court to two counts of misdemeanor Lacey Act Fish Trafficking and Bryan and Asa Gosman, also of Montauk, pleaded guilty to a single conspiracy count, according to a statement released by the US Department of Justice (DOJ).

It is part of the larger family-owned operation, known as Gosman's Dock at Montauk Harbor. None of the other family businesses are named in the indictment.

No sentencing date has been set.

The Gosmans and the business were charged earlier this year as part of an indictment alleging conspiracy to commit mail and wire fraud as well as to unlawfully frustrate the National Ocean and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) efforts at regulating federal fisheries.

As part of the plea bargain, Bryan and Asa Gosman admitted that the fish was sold to a now-defunct company, an unindicted co-conspirator in which they were part-owners, in the New Fulton Fish Market in the Bronx, New York. After the Bronx company closed, the Gosmans purchased the illegal catch via Bob Gosman Co., federal officials said.

The Gosmans admitted to falsifying fishing vessel trip reports (FVTR) and dealer reports, both transmitted to NOAA, and obstructing NOAA's investigation by destroying business records rather than submit them to an ongoing grand jury investigation. Investigators seized the forged FVTRs, federal officials said.

As part of the settlement of the criminal court case, Bob Gosman Co. will pay a $50,000 fine and be placed on probation for four years. The company will also submit to enhanced monitoring, training and inspection requirements. 

As Undercurrent News has reported, federal prosecutors have additionally charged Christopher Winkler, captain of the New Age fishing trawler, in Montauk, for allegedly landing more than 74,000 pounds of illegal fluke and black sea bass during 70 fishing trips. He sold the fish to a now-shuttered fish dealer operating at the New Fulton Fish Market, in which the Gosmans had an ownership interest. When that company closed, Winkler allegedly sold a portion of the catch to the Gosmans, federal officials said.

The Gosmans and Winkler are part of a DOJ investigation into a commercial fishing program known as a "research-set aside" that lets harvesters bid for quota above the regular limits. Prosecutors have said that some fishermen abused the program by taking fish well beyond their set-aside allotment.

The case has involved raids on the home of some harvesters, at least 70 subpoenas, seven guilty pleas and two prison sentences.

Winkler pleaded not guilty to related conspiracy and obstruction charges. His trial is pending.

title: Trial resumes for Danish fishing magnate facing fraud charges
content:
The trial against Danish fishing magnate Henning Kjeldsen, owner of the pelagic fishing firm Gitte Henning and one of Denmark's richest fishermen, resumed on June 8, reports Randers Amtsavis.

Kjeldsen has been accused of fraudulently using so-called "strawmen" companies to gain access to more fishing quotas than he is actually permitted. He has been indicted along with seven other West Jutland fishermen, an accountant and a lawyer who are alleged to have been part of the scheme.

If found guilty by the court in Holstebro, Kjeldsen and the other nine risk having DKK 210 million ($34.3m) confiscated -- the sum they are accused of gaining from the scheme -- as well as potentially receiving fines of an unknown amount.

The prosecution is also pushing to revoke Kjeldsen's licenses to fish in Denmark, which would force him to get rid of his quotas and fishing fleet.

The case began in February, having been originally postponed due to the pandemic. There are eight further court hearings to come this month before the court goes on summer recess in July.

title: New York seafood dealers fight charges of selling illegally caught fluke, bass
content:
Two of the managers of Bob Gosman Co. Inc., a 54-year-old seafood company in Montauk, New York, have entered not-guilty pleas against federal charges that they sold illegally caught fluke and black sea bass, the Long Island, New York, newspaper News Day reports.

An indictment unsealed late last month charged Bryan Gosman, 48, and Asa Gosman, 45, with a conspiracy federal prosecutors said took place between May 2014 and July 2016 involving more than $250,000 of over-quota fish. The two men allegedly submitted false fishing reports and withheld documents or emails requested in a grand jury subpoena and are also charged with obstruction.  

They were released on $100,000 bonds with their travel restricted to the continental United States.

Brian McCarthy, an attorney representing the family business, also filed a not-guilty plea on its behalf.

When that company closed, Winkler allegedly sold a portion of the catch to the Gosmans.

Winkler, 61, was arraigned last week and pleaded not guilty to related conspiracy and obstruction charges, his attorney, Peter Smith of Northport, New York, reportedly told the newspaper.

Bob Gosman Co. is part of the larger family-owned operation, known as Gosman's Dock at Montauk Harbor, according to News Day. None of the other family businesses are named in the indictment.

The Gosmans and Winkler are reportedly part of an investigation the Department of Justice has been conducting into a commercial fishing program known as a "research-set aside" that lets harvesters bid for quota above the regular limits. Prosecutors say some fishermen abused the program by taking fish well beyond their set-aside allotment. The case has involved raids on the home of some harvesters, at least 70 subpoenas seven guilty pleas and two prison sentences, according to the newspaper.

title: Three managers at Samherji’s Namibian firms charged by state in Fishrot case
content:
Managers at three of Samherji's former Namibian subsidiaries have been charged and accused of money laundering and tax evasion, among other things, by the attorney general of Namibia, reports RUV. 

Namibia’s Fishrot scandal: Recap every development from 2020

After an indictment was issued on Feb. 5, Ingvar Juliusson, Egil Helgi Arnason and Adalsteinn Helgason have been charged on 14 counts. Like the other 26 defendants, the trio will appear before the Supreme Court in the Namibian capital of Windhoek on April 22.

According to RUV, Helgason and Arnason had both been managing directors for Samherji in Namibia, with Arnason charged for his work at both Esja Holding and Mermaria Seafood.

Juliusson was a chief financial officer for Samherji in Namibia, charged with working for Saga Seafood, Esja Investment and Heinaste Investments.

Between them, Saga and Mermaria have been accused of paying just shy of NAD 170 million ($11.4m) to government officials and businessmen during their period of operation.

As per Namibian law, indictments brought against firms automatically lead to legal charges against their managers.

In a statement, Samherji said the charges brought against its personnel are "more or less all based on the statements of Johannes Stefansson" who had run the firm's Namibian operations until 2016, and whose document leak in November 2019 had precipitated the scandal.

However, the charges are also based on a separate investigation conducted by the Namibian public prosecutor, and which include bank transfers made after Stefansson's departure from the firm, as well as separate testimonies by Namibian funds which allegedly acted as middlemen.

In its statement on the matter, Samherji wrote that companies affiliated with it in Namibia had been discontinued at the end of 2019, with work underway to dissolve them "once and for all".

"Accusations against the companies in question and individuals on their behalf are no more valid now than they were before," Samherji wrote. "This case will continue and will be heard in the next months. If charges are issued against the companies, Samherji will have the first opportunity to present its defense, and the charges will be vigorously defended in court."

title: Key Antarctic krill companies agree to expand closed area
content:
An NGO-industry collaboration to protect the Antarctic Ocean has announced a big step forward with a year-round closure of a 4,500-kilometer-square area of ocean around Hope Bay in the northern Antarctic Peninsula.

The move is supported by the Association for Responsible Krill fishing (ARK) and an NGO coalition of Greenpeace, The Pew Charitable Trusts, WWF and Oceanites. 

This closure, supported by the largest krill fishing companies, will see nearly all krill companies operating in the Antarctic expanding the voluntary restricted zones that went into effect in 2018. This step would secure the year-round protection of the largest Adelie penguin colony in the region and send a strong statement of intent in support of a marine protected area in the Antarctic Peninsula from industry to the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR) and the entire Antarctic community, the NGOs said.

Studies have shown a strong population decline among the Adelie penguins within the time span they have been monitored. By closing this area, the krill industry reinforces its precautionary approach, upholding important ecosystem values and facilitating a better scientific understanding of penguin performance. 

"By creating this sanctuary around Hope Bay, the krill fishing industry is taking more action to protect the Antarctic than the governments responsible for its conservation," said Will McCallum of Greenpeace’s Protect the Oceans campaign.

"It's a shocking indictment of the failure of the Antarctic Ocean Commission to act on the scientific proposals put forward to protect this area. There is a long way to go to make sure this incredible ocean has the protection it needs and we urge governments to step up and commit to creating ocean sanctuaries in the Antarctic, free from harmful human activities. At next year’s major UN conference on biodiversity they need to agree an ambitious target to protect at least 30% of the world’s oceans by 2030."

title: Fraud charges brought against Danish fishing magnate
content:
The Danish fishing magnate Henning Kjeldsen has been indicted on charges of using "strawmen" company directors to obtain more than his permitted allowance of fishing quotas, reports DR News.

Kjeldsen, who reportedly has a net worth of DKK 1.6 billion ($241 million), has been accused of being the true owner of companies where other directors had been employed, according to the attorney general for special economic and international crime.

The attorney general -- which believes Kjeldsen has acted to circumvent rules preventing individuals from owning too much fishing quota -- has demanded confiscation of DKK 231m from Kjeldsen, as well as a future ban from commercial fishing practices.

Kjeldsen himself is reportedly Denmark's richest fisherman, making a profit of nearly DKK 130m from his main company, Gitte Henning, last year. He did not add any comments when approached by DR News.
