title: Opinion — Christopher Lischewski: ‘There was no price-fixing in the US tuna industry’
content:
(The following is a letter to the editor written by Christopher Lischewski, who served as CEO of US tuna canning giant Bumble Bee Foods until he was indicted in 2018 of price-fixing. Lischewski was convicted in Dec. 2019 and, on Tuesday, June 16, ordered to serve a 40-month prison term and pay a $100,000 fine. Regardless, the long-time seafood professional continues to assert his innocence and has vowed to file an appeal.)

My name is Chris Lischewski and I was the president and CEO of Bumble Bee Seafoods for almost 20 years. Today I was sentenced to 40 months in prison for supposedly being the ringleader of an ‘overarching conspiracy to fix the prices of canned tuna in the US from November of 2010 through December of 2013’. The problem? There was no price-fixing.

Today’s sentencing culminates a five-year saga during which the Department of Justice prosecuted the tuna industry, perhaps the most competitive category in US grocery stores, and drove Bumble Bee into bankruptcy. I was the only individual in the $2.7 billion US shelf-stable seafood category brought to trial in this purported conspiracy. I was found guilty of a crime I did not commit and a crime where there is no victim.

How can I make this statement when Bumble Bee, StarKist and several of their executives pled guilty to price-fixing and Chicken of the Sea confessed to this crime in exchange for amnesty? Let’s evaluate the facts and then look at the overwhelming power the Government has to prosecute these kinds of cases and consistently achieve guilty pleas and verdicts.

Background to the criminal investigation

The canned tuna industry is perhaps the most competitive category in all of US grocery. Gross margins are less than half of what most branded food companies earn, consumption has been declining for more than 20 years, and virtually every one of our retail customers has a business strategy to replace our brands with their own private labels.
These market conditions explain why Thai Union Group, the largest canned tuna company in the world and owner of Chicken of the Sea in the US, entered into a transaction to acquire Bumble Bee in late 2014. The merger of the two businesses was expected to achieve more than $40 million in cost synergies which would have improved the combined company’s cost structure and would have resulted in lower prices for US consumers. 

Upon completion of the transaction the canned tuna market share of the combined Bumble Bee/Chicken of the Sea entity would have been about 40% to 45%, which is similar in size to StarKist. Given the potential antitrust concern from such a high level of concentration in the US canned tuna category, both Thai Union/Chicken of the Sea and Bumble Bee expected a detailed review of the proposed combination by the US Department of Justice. 

In anticipation of this review, both companies hired outside legal counsel to assist in evaluating the feasibility of the transaction, and neither company was informed of any price-fixing concerns. Both companies entered the transaction confident that the pro-competitive aspects of the combination would lead to approval by the Department of Justice.

Following Thai Union’s announcement of the proposed acquisition of Bumble Bee in December of 2014, the government began its process to review the transaction and either approve it or challenge it on antitrust grounds. At some point, this review uncovered concerns, which led to the July 2015 announcement by the Department of Justice of a criminal investigation into price-fixing by the three major tuna companies in the US: StarKist, Bumble Bee and Chicken of the Sea. 

Within weeks of announcing the criminal investigation, it was made known that Chicken of the Sea was the whistleblower which enabled it to negotiate for full amnesty from prosecution for the company and its employees in return for its agreement to cooperate with the government in the price-fixing investigation. This was followed 18 months later by guilty pleas from two Bumble Bee executives and one StarKist executive, all three of whom were employed in sales and trade marketing (pricing) roles. The guilty pleas by their employees forced both Bumble Bee and StarKist to plead guilty in May of 2017 and October of 2018, respectively.

The per se rule

The Department of Justice conducted its price-fixing investigation, and ultimate prosecution of me, under a theory known as the “Per Se” rule. The Sherman Antitrust Act was interpreted to include the Per Se rule in 1898 when price-fixing was considered a misdemeanor with a maximum fine of $1,000. That has since evolved and a Per Se violation is now a felony crime carrying a maximum prison term of 10 years and a $1m fine.

Under the Per Se rule, the agreement to fix prices is the crime and there is no requirement to show proof of any price-fixing effect. Said another way, the government was not required to prove any financial impact or financial harm from the purported tuna price-fixing agreement. If the government could convince the jury that there was an agreement to fix prices, even if it lasted a short time, was never implemented, and had no effect on prices, the jury would be required to return a guilty verdict. 

The Per Se rule sets a very low bar for the government to overcome to achieve a guilty verdict. If it were not for this rule, there would have been no finding of a conspiracy in the US tuna industry as the evidence clearly showed that there was no financial impact of any purported price-fixing. The evidence proved that no customers were overcharged for their canned tuna – but under the Per Se rule, the fact that there was no financial harm didn’t matter.

Evidence that demonstrates an intensely competitive market

The government alleged that the tuna industry fixed prices from November of 2010 to December of 2013. During this period of time, canned tuna prices on grocery store shelves went up significantly. However, this had nothing to do with price-fixing; it was due to tuna costs which rose to unprecedented levels in 2011 and 2012. 

Unforeseen circumstances led to tremendous cost inflation. Albacore, the species of tuna used in solid white, was impacted by the tsunami that hit the coast of Japan in March 2011 resulting in the Fukushima nuclear disaster. The resulting loss of electricity throughout large areas of Japan destroyed much of the frozen tuna in Japan’s cold store facilities and longline fishing vessels that traditionally fished for albacore tuna switched to other species of tuna (bigeye and yellowfin) to rebuild Japanese inventories. 

Skipjack, the species of tuna generally used to produce chunk light, faced different supply challenges in 2011 and 2012 including a strong La Nina weather event in the Pacific Ocean and increasing conservation measures that incorporated temporary fishery closures. 

These events led to unanticipated tuna supply shortages resulting in record fish cost inflation. Albacore reached $3,200 per metric ton, up almost 50% from the end of 2010, and skipjack reached $2,270/t, up more than 130%. To put this in perspective, albacore tuna makes up about 80% of the cost of a can of solid white tuna and skipjack tuna represents about 65% of the cost of a can of chunk light tuna.

Bumble Bee attempted to pass through the higher fish costs in pricing to maintain our profit margins. However, given the intense competitive environment, we were not able to do so. This led to pressure on gross margins and our profitability suffered between 2011 and 2013. We did not regain our historical profit margins until 2014 when fish prices fell back to more normal levels and the competitive environment became more rational. 

This is demonstrated in the following charts that show Bumble Bee’s change in the average price charged to customers compared to the change in the cost of our products between March 2011 and November 2012. The price of solid white albacore to customers increased by 34.7% while costs were up 42.7%. Similarly, the price of chunk light tuna went up 45.5% while cost was up 51.3%. The inability to pass through the higher costs had a significant effect on margins and profitability.
Had the tuna industry been engaged in a price-fixing conspiracy, one would have expected to see pricing to customers exceed the increase in the cost of canned tuna.  This did not happen.

An analysis conducted by Dr. Joseph Levinsohn, an expert witness called by the defense and a long-tenured economist at Yale University, further demonstrated that there was no effect of the purported price-fixing conspiracy. Based on a 15-year analysis of actual monthly price and cost data from 2002 – 2016, Dr. Levinsohn demonstrated that prices charged during the purported conspiracy were lower than relative prices (actual price relative to actual product cost) predicted by historical data.  The conclusion of this analysis is that customers were under-charged during the purported conspiracy period. This is the exact opposite of price-fixing and is what you would expect to see in a market with robust competition.
The theory of the price-fixing offense that the government presented to the jury ran as follows. It claimed that during 2009 and 2010, the US tuna industry was experiencing intense competition which they referred to as a price war. They asserted that in an effort to meet the profitability commitments I had made to Lion Capital, the private equity group which acquired Bumble Bee in December of 2010, I instructed my executives to negotiate a ‘truce’ with StarKist in November 2010 whereby both companies would agree to price less aggressively. The government argued that this “truce” agreement in late 2010 led to inflated prices and was the beginning of the price-fixing conspiracy.

The facts don’t support this theory. While 2009 and 2010 were years of robust competition, there wasn’t a price war. These were two of the most successful years that our industry has experienced and all three tuna companies achieved record profitability.  Conversely, profitability plummeted in 2011 – the year the government claimed was the start of the conspiracy -- as both StarKist and Chicken of the Sea attacked Bumble Bee relentlessly with ultra-aggressive pricing leading to extremely poor financial performance. 2011 was not the beginning of a price-fixing conspiracy in the US tuna category, it was the beginning of rapidly escalating fish costs and intense, even irrational, competitive activity. 

During a price-fixing conspiracy you would expect to see increasing profits but in 2011, the first full year of the purported conspiracy, Bumble Bee operating income dropped 23%, StarKist was down a whopping 96.5%, and Chicken of the Sea was down by more than 75%. 

Profits remained depressed in 2012 with Chicken of the Sea performing even worse than it did in 2011. A gradual recovery began in 2013 but this had less to do with pricing and more to do with fish costs returning to normal levels. Interestingly, in 2014 after the purported conspiracy had ended, all three companies improved their profitability despite the absence of any ‘price-fixing’.
Throughout my trial, my defense team provided extensive evidence and factual data demonstrating the intense competitive environment that existed between 2011 and 2013.  One example is the following chart from a Bumble Bee board presentation that shows Bumble Bee (red line) raising its prices for solid white albacore consistent with higher fish costs in 2011 while both StarKist (blue line) and Chicken of the Sea (green line) held back their pricing so they could attack Bumble Bee and take market share. 

StarKist pricing moved from relative parity with Bumble Bee in late 2010 to a discount of 15% by the end of 2011. Chicken of the Sea, always the discounter in the tuna category, doubled its price discount from about 12% to 22%. This did not reflect a period of price-fixing, it reflected a period of intense competition.
This competitive aggression was evident in market share data.  Looking at solid white albacore – where Bumble Bee makes the bulk of its profit -- it is evident that the aggressive pricing implemented by both StarKist and Chicken of the Sea negatively impacted Bumble Bee throughout 2011 as our solid white market share dropped by 12%.

This continued into early 2012 when Bumble Bee made the decision to fight back and regain our share. Again, this was not evidence of a price-fixing conspiracy, it was evidence of an extremely competitive market.
Customer level pricing data also demonstrated significant competition. My defense team presented statistics showing the actual monthly prices that the brands charged customers for canned tuna over the purported conspiracy period. We also showed weekly market share trends. 

As would be expected in a market with vibrant competition, there were significant differences by customer and by brand. The evidence showed no pattern in customer-level pricing which is something that would have been visible if the companies were engaged in price-fixing.

To recap, the financial data that my defense team presented proved that there was no effect of the purported collusion on any retail customer during the period of November 2010 through December 2013. The government never made an attempt to introduce their own economist and didn’t present any other evidence to challenge our assertions or to support its allegation of price-fixing. That’s because under the Per Se rule, it did not need to provide evidence of any price-fixing ‘effect’.

The government's prosecution

The government’s prosecution of me was based largely on the testimony of four cooperating witnesses, Scott Cameron and Ken Worsham, formerly the senior vice-president (SVP) of sales and trade marketing, respectively, at Bumble Bee, Steve Hodge, the former SVP of sales and trade marketing at StarKist, and Shue Wing Chan, the former president and CEO of Chicken of the Sea. 

The term “cooperator” is used to describe someone who has pled guilty (or, in Chan's case, received amnesty) and has then agreed to cooperate with the government in return for a reduced sentence or some other benefit. As part of their cooperation deal they promise to tell the truth. However, the government ultimately determines how effective the cooperation has been and how it will affect the sentencing recommendation it will make on the cooperator's behalf. This gives the cooperators a strong incentive to testify in a manner that pleases the government – in this case, to obtain a guilty verdict against me.

The cooperators

Scott Cameron – SVP sales, Bumble Bee: After reviewing all of the evidence, I am confounded by Cameron’s guilty plea. Cameron met with the Government on 21 occasions leading up to my trial during which time his testimony changed substantially.  Cameron consistently stated that he colluded with Chuck Handford, StarKist’s VP of Trade Marketing from the beginning of the purported conspiracy in November of 2010 until Handford left StarKist in September of 2011. 

However, while Cameron initially stated that he did not inform me of his communication with Handford, that eventually changed to him testifying that I was the one who told him to establish the relationship in late 2010 after which he regularly kept me informed of their discussions.

Handford had worked for Bumble Bee in the past and was friends with Cameron. While it appears they talked regularly, Handford has vehemently denied any involvement in an agreement to fix prices and he was never charged by the Government. Handford stated that he always competed aggressively and this was evident not only in StarKist’s market share gains in 2011, but also in its financial performance with Operating Income plummeting by more than 95% that year. 

Bumble Bee is the only company that pled guilty to participation in price-fixing during the period of November 2010 to October 2011 (StarKist pled guilty for the period of November 2011 through December 2013 and Chicken of the Sea admitted participation in price-fixing from March 2012 through June 2013). I can only surmise that the government’s threat of prosecution resulted in Cameron pleading guilty to a crime he did not commit as I’m not sure how we could have colluded with ourselves. 
 
Ken Worsham – SVP trade marketing, Bumble Bee: Worsham testified that he colluded with Hodge of StarKist from November 2011 through December 2013. 

Hodge had added trade marketing (pricing) to his sales responsibilities in November of 2011 after the departure of Handford. During Worsham’s 32 meetings with the government leading up to my trial, he said that he and Hodge coordinated two list price increases during 2012, a year of record cost inflation, and then coordinated ‘quarterly pricing guidance’ until Hodge was terminated by StarKist in December of 2013.

Worsham said he kept me informed of his communication with Hodge in private one-on-one meetings but he could not provide details of even one such meeting. 

While evidence showed that Worsham and Hodge were in regular communication, the idea that they could fix the prices of canned tuna is unrealistic and naïve. Our principal customers, Walmart, Kroger, Costco, Albertsons, etc., are large and extremely sophisticated buyers who have tremendous purchasing leverage. 

They negotiate individually with all three brands and they all have their own private labels that they source from third-party co-packers giving them a direct insight into product cost. With canned tuna being a global commodity, our customers have the ability to verify our costs not only by comparing competitive quotes but also by looking at cost changes in their own private label products and by analyzing the numerous tuna cost indices that are readily available on the internet.

Steve Hodge – SVP sales and trade marketing, StarKist. Hodge testified for two days and my name was rarely mentioned. During the period of the alleged conspiracy, he had no contact with me of any kind and he testified that my name never came up in any conversations he had with Worsham. 

Shue Wing Chan – president & CEO, Chicken of the Sea. The real enigma was Shue Wing Chan, the former president and CEO of Chicken of the Sea (and cousin of Thai Union president and CEO, Thiraphong Chansiri). 

Chan testified that he had reached an ‘understanding’ with me to ‘not promote (discount) aggressively’ from March of 2012 through June of 2013. However, when questioned about the details, Chan admitted that the ‘understanding’ was only in his mind. Chan conceded that I never once acknowledged an agreement or understanding. Furthermore, Chan never told anyone at Chicken of the Sea about his ‘understanding’ and could not provide evidence of even one promotion he changed to adhere to our purported agreement. 

If there really was an ‘understanding’ between Chan and me it would have been identified during the antitrust legal reviews that had been carried out by Thai Union / Chicken of the Sea and Bumble Bee prior to the execution of the acquisition agreement in late 2014. My only explanation of Chan having admitted to this offense is that it enabled Chicken of the Sea to entice the Department of Justice to accept them as the ‘whistleblower’ whereby they (and their employees) were granted full amnesty from prosecution. 

Chan’s contradictory testimony aside, the evidence at trial (including the financial data discussed earlier) showed that Chicken of the Sea never stopped promoting aggressively. While Chan said he reached an ‘understanding’ with me in an effort to improve his profitability, Chicken of the Sea’s net income showed a loss in both 2011 and 2012 while only performing slightly above breakeven in 2013. 

Did justice prevail?

To sum up, my defense team proved beyond a shadow of a doubt that there was no financial data that corroborated the government’s claim of a price-fixing conspiracy in the canned tuna industry. But under the Per Se rule, the financial data didn’t matter. 

The only thing that mattered was the existence of an ‘agreement’. In addition to their assertion that I had an ‘understanding’ with Chan of Chicken of the Sea, the government argued that I was a “hands-on” CEO, and therefore must have been aware of the actions of Cameron and Worsham. The jury ultimately agreed with the government that I must have known.

I did consider myself a “hands-on” CEO and my management style included constant evaluation of performance data. Bumble Bee was a reasonably large organization with revenues of about $1 billion and I managed twelve individuals. I was not a micro-manager and I provided significant authority to my direct reports – especially ones like Cameron and Worsham who had both worked with me for more than a decade at that point in time. 

To manage the business I reviewed daily sales reports, weekly market shares and monthly financial performance. I met regularly with my executive team to discuss our business. And during the time period that the government asserted there was a price-fixing conspiracy, I saw rampant cost inflation, constant attacks on our business by StarKist and Chicken of the Sea, irrational pricing, and, for much of that time, falling profits. There was no indication of price-fixing that I or anyone else could see.   

The saga is now over and the government has won – for now. While the government argued fervently that I should spend ten years in prison for my “heinous” crime, the court has sentenced me to 40 months in prison, 40 months away from my wife and son, for a crime I did not commit and a crime for which there was no victim. It is an unjust verdict based largely on testimony from ‘cooperating’ witnesses. It is an unjust verdict that I will appeal.

Was this prosecution an effective use of five years of government effort? Was this purported crime so egregious and damaging to American consumers that it required the full force of the Department of Justice? Did it justify the massive expenditure of taxpayer funds? 

And what about the impact on the US tuna industry? Did the Department of Justice action justify driving Bumble Bee into bankruptcy? Was the $100m fine levied against StarKist reasonable? Are the plethora of civil lawsuits, lawsuits that continue to this day, warranted? I estimate that the legal fees related to this action have exceeded $100m and the only beneficiaries from this action by the Department of Justice have been the lawyers hired by those who have been accused.       

My final question is does this outcome represent ‘justice’? Maybe in the mind of some, it does but for me, the guilty verdict has shattered a 30-year career in the seafood industry, a career that I am proud of and where I feel I made a difference. For the company that I led for 20 years, it resulted in bankruptcy and the loss of investment for more than 50 managers who believed in Bumble Bee. 

And other than the lawyers, who has this prosecution by the US Department of Justice benefited? There was no harm to any customer and there was never any financial effect of this purported price-fixing conspiracy.

The legal power entrusted to the Department of Justice is capable of crushing almost any defense and is the primary reason that more than 90% of price-fixing cases are settled out of court with guilty pleas – even when there may not have been any wrongdoing. I chose to fight, and I will continue to fight because I am innocent.

Postscript -- new actions by the Department of Justice

The Department of Justice is now targeting the US beef and poultry industries. Four of the largest beef processors in the U.S., Tyson Foods, JBS SA, Cargill and National Beef / Marfrig, who are said to control more than 80% of the domestic beef processing industry, have recently been subpoenaed. 

In the poultry industry, Perdue Farms, Tyson Foods, Pilgrim’s Pride, Sanderson Farms, Peco Foods, Wayne Farms, Koch Foods, Mountaire Farms and House of Raeford Farms have been in the news for price-fixing and two CEO’s have recently been indicted. If the low bar of the Per Se rule is allowed to be applied to all of these companies, we may ultimately see our entire protein supply shift to foreign suppliers.

title: Bankruptcy, scandal behind it, Tharp ‘enthusiastic’ for Bumble Bee’s future, culture
content:
Early last year, a team of 10 of Bumble Bee Foods' 1,135 employees led a process to rewrite its corporate value statement. It was -- to put it mildly -- a busy time for the company.

Former CEO Chris Lischewski was preparing to be tried on price-fixing charges relating to a scandal that led to multiple lawsuits, a fine and eventual bankruptcy for the US tuna canner. Meanwhile, under then-interim, since confirmed CEO Jan Tharp, Bumble Bee was redoubling efforts to develop a pipeline of new seafood products that would be "relevant" to consumers. 

However, re-crafting the value statement, Tharp told Undercurrent News, was an important part of working towards creating the sort of culture that underpins everything else the company wants to accomplish.

The team, after several sessions and focus groups with coworkers, published a five-point statement at a company meeting in June 2019, settling on the values "focus forward", "come together", "act right", "find a way" and "show love". 

"One of our values is to act right. We challenge each other. When there’s decisions that need to be made and they’re tough decisions we pull out our values and we say how can we use these to guide our decisions," Tharp said. "Yes, the past is behind us and I think it really gave us an opportunity to move forward in really positive ways.”

Culture change

Over the last 18 months she's been at Bumble Bee's helm, Tharp has worked to sew the seeds of a turnaround and reinvigorate product development for the 101-year-old brand amid the price-fixing scandal's aftermath. The fallout included class-action lawsuits from customers and a $25 million fine from the US Department of Justice, both of which contributed to the company's bankruptcy and sale to Taiwanese tuna trader FCF Co. 

Jan Tharp, president and CEO of Bumble Bee Foods

"Together we have focused so much on the building of this business and all of the positive things that we have to bring to the market that that’s really how we got through the last 18 months," she told Undercurrent. "And now that everything is behind us as of Jan. 31 with the acquisition by FCF, we’re not looking backward, we’re looking forward."

In practice, that will mean a major push on new product development, additional commitments to sustainability and new partnerships outside of its traditional offerings, as seen through the recent distribution deal with plant-based seafood substitute maker Good Catch.

"We’re very enthusiastic, very proud of the work that we’ve done and I think you’re going to start seeing that spill out into the marketplace through 2020 into 2021 through our new products and innovations, some deepened commitments to sustainability and some additional joint ventures that you’ll hear about later," Tharp said.

Tharp joined Bumble Bee in 2010 as its senior vice president for global operations, shortly before the company, then-owned by private equity Centre Partners, was sold to another private equity, UK-based Lion Capital. 

A 'strategic owner'

Lion Capital's sale to Bumble Bee's long-term albacore supplier FCF, she noted, will bring an owner with a different perspective than a financial investor.

“I think having a strategic owner will definitely be something that is advantageous as we look at things, or we will be looking at things for the long term, many decades instead of a couple of years,” she said.

FCF's purchase, which valued Bumble Bee at $929m, settled the DOJ price-fixing fine and set the company on firmer financial footing. (By uniting Bumble Bee, which had revenues of $933m in 2018, with FCF, the combined company will have annual sales of over $2.6 billion, Undercurrent previously reported.) 

And, a March ruling from San Diego, California-based federal judge Janis Sammartino, who is overseeing the class-action suits filed by customers against Bumble Bee, StarKist & Co and Thai Union Group's Chicken of the Sea International (COSI) brand, means that the civil claims against Bumble Bee will be dealt with in the bankruptcy proceeding, not by her court. This has pushed the plaintiffs and Bumble Bee into settlement talks, the judge wrote. 

FCF is the latest of a long line of owners for the company. The Bumble Bee brand was founded in 1910 by a group of Oregon tuna harvesters known as the Columbia River Packers Association. After being bought by Hawaii's Castle & Cooke in 1960 and expanding into Ecuador, Puerto Rico and San Diego, Bumble Bee went through a series of owners in the 1980s and 1990s. Those changes saw the company expand beyond tuna into shrimp, oysters, smoked scallops and anchovies as well into Canada through the acquisition of the Clover Leaf brand.

Packaged foods giant Conagra Foods bought the enlarged Bumble Bee in 2000 but spun it off in 2003 to Centre Partners. Centre later added the Canadian sardine brand Connors Bros to Bumble Bee prior to Centre's 2010 decision to sell the entire company to Lion Capital. 

An 'enthusiastic' CEO

Tharp has effectively led Bumble Bee since Lischewski's May 2018 indictment. She was named by Lion Capital to serve as interim CEO and handed the post on a permanent basis following Lischewski's conviction in December. 

During the month-long trial of Lischewski, two other former Bumble Bee executives -- then senior vice president of sales Walter Cameron and then senior vice president of trade marketing Ken Worsham -- claimed that during the 2010 to 2013 period they'd had extensive communications with their counterparts at StarKist and COSI under Lischewski's direction. The men, who have yet to be sentenced, said that the companies had worked together to end canned tuna "price wars" and jointly coordinated the timing of price increases. 

Lischewski, who has steadfastly denied knowledge of price-fixing, is set to be sentenced in May.

During the 2010 to 2013 period, Worsham and Cameron reported to Lischewski directly. Tharp was not involved in setting prices during the time the criminal acts reportedly occurred, she said.  

Image from a 2018 Bumble Bee Foods commercial.

“I was not aware of the price-fixing," Tharp told Undercurrent, before stressing the company's renewed commitments to uphold its values. "As we move forward, we continue to move forward with an unwavering commitment to integrity and transparency in how we operate every part of the business.”

Tharp joined Bumble Bee in 2010 as senior vice president for global operations after a similar role at StarKist.  In 2012, she was promoted to serve as Bumble Bee's chief operating officer. In that role, she oversaw procurement, co-packing, supply chain management, planning, inventory control and customer service.

She said that the last 18 months have been difficult on the company's employees.  

"As you can imagine, as you read through the trade journals it wasn’t uplifting to read some of the things we read about," Tharp said. "But when you look at our company core and what we’ve put together as values, our values are not just things that are written on a card, they’re things that we live every day."

'Focused in on what they could control'

To keep Bumble Bee's team in the loop, the company has essentially held "monthly town hall meetings", she said.

"We’ve been very, very open with everybody in the entire company with respect to what was going on and I think that that transparency built a lot of trust with our employee base," she said. "We kept our employees really focused in on what they could control. A lot of what’s happened to the business was kind of outside of our control over the last 18 months."

Tharp, who began her career as a packaging engineer, worked in management roles at consumer packaged goods companies HJ Heinz and beverages maker Cliffstar Corporation before shifting into seafood.

According to a Nov. 21 declaration from the company's chief financial officer, Kurt McNeil, Bumble Bee is the country's second-largest tuna company -- after StarKist & Co -- and the brand is the US' leading albacore seller. It holds "leading positions in the United States in specialty seafood, sardines, and canned salmon".

The group sells sardines under the Brunswick and Beach Cliff brands in the US, chopped clams, minced clams and clam juice through the Snow's brand and raw frozen tuna through the foodservice-focused Anova brand.

The group's main US tuna cannery is in Santa Fe Springs, California, but Bumble Bee supplements its production with "strategic co-packing arrangements" in the US and 15 other countries, mostly in Southeast Asia, McNeil said.

The Snow's products are packed in a Cape May, New Jersey, plant where 70 employees can pack up to 6m clams annually, he added.

10,000 communications

Over the past 18 months, while Bumble Bee had teams working on the financial and legal issues in the aftermath of the price-fixing scandal, the rest of the company was focused on charting a path forward through new product development and revamping its core tuna offerings.

That's required an extensive market research effort, she said, which has prompted the company to develop seafood products that are "clean label" and "on-the-go protein".

"Our new marketing team has had over 10,000 individuals that they have been in correspondence with through panels, through social media," she said. "And we’ve been developing products and testing some of our packaging concepts with the consumer."

Tharp told Undercurrent she believes that tuna is fundamentally attractive to consumers in many ways but canner
s need to do a better job of "putting the customer first".

"You look at what we have to offer, we have a lean, low-calorie, high omega product. It’s high in protein, it’s affordable. It’s everything that is on-trend yet the market, when you look at it from a volume perspective, has been declining over time," she said. "It’s not declining because of a kitchen utensil, it’s declining because we as an industry really needed to focus in on giving the consumer what they want. And what they want is on-the-go protein, they want clean-label, they want a lot of the things that we have and a lot of the things that we’re developing products around."

One example of this, she said, is Bistro Bowls, a microwavable seafood ready meal, launched last year in Canada under the company's Clover Leaf brand. The product, which was named "best facilitating product" in Canada's 2020 Dux Grand Prix award, is slated to be launched in the US under the Bumble Bee brand later this year.

Some 31% of Canadians buying Bistro Bowls are new Clover Leaf customers and 21% are new to canned seafood, she said.

"We are getting incremental buys. People aren’t switching from one product to another. We are bringing new consumers into the category with relevant, convenient products," Tharp said. "So I think that’s a really good proof point that there’s still runway left in this category if you do it the right way."

Bumble Bee, she added, will also launch a "protein on the run" offering that fits into the company's "snack on the run" category.

"It’s a ready to eat, for the on-the-go consumer, high in protein, it’s got 15 grams of protein. It’s convenient, it’s portable. It’s got some great crackers in it, a nice sweet caramel and it’s going to retail for just over $2 so again the affordable side is coming in," she said.

Making products 'relevant' again

She said that she believes that Bumble Bee can do more to make the can "relevant" to consumers, noting that cans with EZ peel lids are the packaging used in the company's snack-on-the-run line. The company's can and pouch imagery will be getting a refresh, she added.

"I think we can do a whole lot more with the can with respect to decoration and making it look a little sexy, a little bit more than it is today. And at the end of the day, we are doing that. We’re rolling out a relaunch of all of our graphics and branding. And that’s going to be starting here — you’ll start to see that on pouch first but then cans will follow," she said.

She said that the type of packaging and the product's "relevance" to consumers are distinct issues.

"It is easy to blame a can or a can opener but at the end of the day I think if you're really focused in on your consumer then meeting the consumer need is what this is about and finding products that are relevant to that consumer becomes important," she said.

title: Salmofood’s likely exclusion from feed collusion case will narrow losers to Skretting, BioMar
content:
Salmofood, a group owned by Peru’s Grupo Romero, will likely win an appeal to be excluded from legal charges against Chile’s government for fixing salmon feed prices.

The Peruvian company first invested in Salmofood in 2012, paying $60 million to salmon producers Invermar and Pesquera Yadran. As the smallest competitor in a market dominated by Cargill, Nutreco’s Skretting and BioMar, Salmofood has survived by adopting a price-cutting strategy from the 'big three', a senior salmon industry executive told Undercurrent News. 

“What they would do is try and win business for one center, instead of six centers that the others would vie for, and undercut the competition,” said the executive, who has no links to Salmofood. “I strongly suspect that they will win the case to be excluded from the ongoing investigation.”

A decision by the Chilean court to exclude Salmofood from the ongoing investigation into price collusion would turn proceedings into a three-way tussle between BioMar, Cargill and Skretting. Cargill, which turned informant after it reportedly found evidence of price collusion through conducting an audit of the accounts of EWOS in 2015, is starting to win market share in Chile’s lucrative salmon market.

Skretting and BioMar have both decided to appeal against the legal investigation into collusion. Meanwhile, Cargill is offering out-of-court settlements to customers to win business, industry insiders told Undercurrent. Cargill is likely to win back market share for EWOS, which had dropped to about 20% of the Chilean market from the 33% that EWOS controlled until the 2015 acquisition.

Salmofood has scant involvement in a 22-page legal document by Chile’s antritust regulator that outlines communication between senior executives in the salmon feed industry to agree on ingredient prices to consumers, the industry source said.

Salmofood was mentioned in a solitary 2003 email in which a company executive referenced prices in a Word document. The document shows an exhaustive collection of emails and other evidence gathered from the internal records of the companies involved. 

All four companies are alleged to have shared lists showing the prices of ingredients as well as disclosing price negotiations that they were conducting with clients. These included communications with clients discussing the cost of ingredients. 

The four companies were formally charged in December after Cargill informed authorities of wrongdoing between all four companies upon buying EWOS in 2015. Cargill will face lighter charges for its role as informant. Salmofood asked Chile’s Tribunal for the Defense of Free Competition (FNE) to remove it from the indictment as it “did not participate in the conduct that forms the basis of the accusation.” The company did not respond to a request to comment for this article. 

The FNE said it will seek combined fines of up to $70m for a collusion period that stretched from 2003 until 2015. Cargill as informant has requested exemption from the fines because of its role as informant.

Both Nutreco’s Skretting and BioMar have denied wrongdoing in the collusion case and thus would not be able to offer out-of-court compensation to customers until the legal proceedings have taken place. This could take up to five years in Chilean courts, industry experts said. Salmofood, by removing itself from the legal proceedings, would also have the chance to boost market share in the lucrative Chilean salmon feed market. Chile represents about a third of the global salmon feed market.

title: BioMar’s Chinese feedmill construction delayed by coronavirus hold-up
content:
Danish feed giant BioMar Group is among the many companies to find its business directly affected by the outbreak of coronavirus, or COVID-19, in central China, according to its full year 2019 results.

BioMar’s Aussie feedmill on course for full production by mid-2020

According to the public filing by parent company Schouw & Co., construction of the firm's new aquafeed factory in Wuxi near Shanghai had been approaching its final phase when the viral outbreak began in late January. Schouw had said that the plant was due to begin commercial production by the end of 2019 in its most recent Q3 report.

The completion of the factory, constructed as part of a joint venture with BioMar's Chinese partner Tongwei Co., has now been suspended until restrictions imposed by the Chinese government to prevent the spread of COVID-19 are removed.

Once finalized, the new factory will add a production capacity for 50,000 metric tons of feed, as well as further expansion potential, Schouw said. The firm hopes that in conjunction with BioMar's existing plant in Guangdong, the new quantities of feed will help BioMar to further penetrate the Chinese market, which remains a peripheral part of the group's wider operations.

BioMar CEO, Carlos Diaz

Elsewhere, BioMar's capacity expansion for its plant in Ecuador, announced at the tail-end of 2018, remains on track, Schouw said. This will include a production line for extruded feed, which will add a further 40,000t of annual capacity to the plant.

The new line will cost an expected DKK 50 million ($7.5m) and is due to be commissioned at the end of Q1 2020.

Meanwhile, in Chile, BioMar claims to have "fully integrated" the additional capacity it gained by buying out the remaining 50% of its Chilean feed joint venture from Empresas AquaChile last June. After the acquisition, BioMar now has 60,000t more feed at its disposal in Chile, on top of the volumes already produced from its two other plants in the country.

As for BioMar's Australian plant, the firm reports no hold-ups, noting that it has effectively finalized construction and "will now commence commercial production". Providing 110,000t to BioMar's Australian clients, the factory represented an investment of DKK 300m, of which DKK 280m had been paid off by the end of 2019.

BioMar anticipates strong 2020 after expansive 2019

Looking ahead, BioMar said that this year would see further capacity come on stream, continuing to boost its market presence around the globe through all three of its divisions. 

Third quarter leads feed giant BioMar to raise 2019 earnings forecast again

In this light, the firm said it expects to generate full-year 2020 revenue of about DKK 12 billion ($1.8bn), which would represent a 7.3% increase on its 2019 earnings of DKK 11.18bn.

Based on the current currency outlook, BioMar also predicts generating earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) in the range of DKK 1bn-DKK 1.06bn next year.

Indeed, the group's earnings for 2019 were very positive, as EBITDA increased by 15% from DKK 713m to DKK 966m. The firm said this was chiefly driven by "concept development and a strong product offering", while favorable exchange rate changes are believed to have boosted EBITDA by approximately DKK 17m.

“It is a great achievement for the entire group, that we have turned an ambitious strategy into tangible results," wrote BioMar CEO Carlos Diaz. "We have during the last year expanded capacity and global presence. At the same time, we have gone through extensive structural and organizational changes."

BioMar's salmon division was the biggest driver of revenue growth, Schouw said, contributing DKK 7.8bn to the group's total revenue across both its northern and southern hemisphere divisions -- up 8.6% on 2018's results.

BioMar's other divisions in shrimp feed and European aquaculture also saw a positive year, posting revenues of DKK 3.35bn, up 7.4% year-on-year.

"We have the privilege to be 100% dedicated to aquaculture. I believe this will be an important differentiator in the future, enabling us to be agile in our customer collaboration and keeping the development of a sustainable and efficient industry as our main company purpose," Diaz said.

BioMar Chile conviction 'unlikely'

Following an industry investigation, the Chilean competition authority Fiscalia Nacional Economica (FNE) indicted four Chilean feed firms -- including BioMar -- on charges of concerted practice in December 2019. 

BioMar parent to fight Chile price-fixing charges, as Carlos Diaz email used in evidence

FNE claimed that BioMar Chile ought to be fined up to 30,000 annual tax units, which as of the end of 2019 corresponded to approximately $24m. "At the present time, the FNE has produced only a modest amount of information to support its claim, and the case is in the early stages of a process expected to last from two to four years before it can be concluded," wrote Schouw in its 2019 report.

BioMar does not acknowledge the charges and fully intends to rebut them, Schouw said when the allegations first went public.

"Based on the Chilean lawyers’ opinion in the matter and the information currently available, management believes it is not likely that BioMar will be convicted of participating in concerted practices," Schouw said in the FY 2019 report. "Accordingly, no provisions have been recognized as of Dec. 31, 2019 concerning claim submitted."

title: Cargill to win Chile market share with settlements over feed price-fixing
content:
Additional reporting from Matt Craze 

Cargill surprised the salmon industry in December by acting as an informant on 12 years of collusion in the Chilean salmon feed market. Now, the US-based company is showing the industry a chess-like business strategy, sources told Undercurrent News. 

BioMar parent to fight Chile price-fixing charges, as Carlos Diaz email used in evidence

The 155-year old agriculture giant, headquartered in Minneapolis, Minnesota, is offering out-of-court settlements in tandem with new supply contracts, industry sources with direct knowledge said.

Cargill is alone in being able to offer compensation, given that, as a whistleblower in the collusion case, the company acknowledges guilt. Cargill’s main competitors -- BioMar Group, Skretting and Salmofood, which is asking to be removed from the case -- will not be able to compensate with matching cash settlements until the legal process has run its course.

BioMar's Danish parent company, Schouw & Co., said it intends to rebut the allegations, and it will have to wait potentially five years for the legal process initiated by Chile’s competition authority Fiscalia Nacional Economica (FNE) to run its course. The Netherlands-based Nutreco, parent of Skretting, will “rebut” the charges after carefully reviewing the complaint, a spokesperson said. BioMar declined to comment. 

As none of Cargill’s competitors accept wrongdoing and Chilean legal processes are lengthy, Cargill stands to clean up in the highly profitable Chilean salmon feed market, consummating its strategy to buy Norwegian feed player EWOS Group in 2015 from its former private equity owners. Cargill also stands to win as salmon farmers who lived through a decade of losses between 2017 and 2015 choose the whistleblower over competitors. 

“EWOS is going to do extremely well out of this,” one senior industry source told Undercurrent. 

Credit: Nokwan007/Shutterstock.com

BioMar, Cargill, Nutreco and Salmofood are all privately owned and the market share of each in Chile is not public information. Skretting is the largest feed supplier in Norway, with 30% of the total, and Cargill comes third in that market with a 24% share, behind BioMar with 26%. 

When contacted by Undercurrent, a Cargill spokesperson declined to specifically say if the company was offering out-of-court compensation. Cargill's focus, the spokesperson said, "has been and will continue to be on delivering value for our customers and looking out for their best interests".

In Chile, the key insight is that salmon farming companies have often switched between the main feed suppliers in the past. This means that Cargill, through EWOS, can offer settlements to several industry players as an incentive to secure new deals. Salmon companies and potentially even US retailers may pursue damages after a final conclusion is reached, according to industry sources. 

Cargill ‘self-reported’ Chile price-fixing in January 2016

Cargill reported wrongdoing 

Authorities said they started the investigation after Cargill reported wrongdoing following its €1.35 billion ($1.47bn) takeover of EWOS Group in 2015. The FNE produced a detailed document with charges against all feed manufacturers, providing a body of evidence that included e-mails purportedly written by BioMar CEO Carlos Diaz and others. 

The allegations and evidence indicate that the companies agreed on the margins earned through the procurement of raw materials. Feed companies are under an obligation to declare some of the raw material costs to salmon farmers. 

On an emotional scale, Cargill will have a powerful appeal to salmon farming companies as a supplier of choice, the industry source said. The collusion period under review by the FNE was a time of mostly lean years for the industry. The period between 2007, a year when Chilean farms lost major clients in the US after infectious salmon anemia, until 2016, was an economically tough decade for the industry. 

"Cargill is taking market share and rightly so," a second executive contacted on the matter said. "While Cargill is out there apologizing and talking settlement, Nutreco is investing in competitors of the salmon companies. People are upset." 

The executive referred to Nutreco's planned investment in Nordic Aqua Partners (NAP), which is planning a salmon recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) in China. Nutreco has also put money into Kingfish Zeeland, a Dutch yellowtail farmer from a RAS facility that is expanding into the US.

Nutreco sees land-based farms "feeding the future", chief innovation officer Viggo Halseth told Undercurrent on Jan. 28 in reference to the Kingfish Zeeland investment. Nutreco is yet to comment on the NAP deal, however. 

Nutreco said that population growth and changing consumer needs call for "new scientific innovations that drive sustainable solutions", the company said in a statement prepared for this article and in response to the comment made by the second executive. 

"Nutreco believes that, if we are serious about ensuring that future generations have enough high-quality protein, we will require protein from all possible sources," a spokesperson said. "This includes the current aquaculture and agriculture industries, but also exploring new opportunities with the potential to drive growth." 

Skretting will work with all of its clients across all farming systems to develop feed solutions tailored to their individual needs, the spokesperson added. 

Feed is biggest cost 

Feed is the biggest operating cost in the salmon farming industry, accounting for about half of the total. Chile represents 31% of the global salmon feed market, or 1.3m metric tons, according to Mowi’s annual industry handbook.

Chile's feed market is set to grow, too, with anticipated increases in farming area. 

Cargill has set an aggressive long-term strategy of expanding in the seafood business and aquaculture, which is currently the world’s fastest-growing animal protein market category. In fact, Cargill and main competitors Archer Daniels Midland, Bunge and Louis Dreyfus are all moving into the seafood space to compensate for falling revenue margins in their core trading businesses.

Cargill plant in Wroclaw, Poland. Photo: Cargill

The "ABCD", as the four companies are collectively known, face diminishing returns from the global trade of grains and oilseeds because farmers have more control over trading information and managing inventory through the growth of the internet and silo bags that allow them to manage their own inventory levels. The response from the ABCD has been to more closely align themselves with their main customers in the animal protein industry. 

The Chilean price-fixing scandal, meanwhile, comes at a delicate time for the feed companies in the highly profitable salmon market.

Some farmers are using a prolonged period of record profits to invest in their own feed production facilities. The European salmon market has gotten tougher in the last couple of years as Mowi has opened major feed factories in Norway and Scotland. 

Agrosuper, the major poultry and chicken exporter that bought Empresas AquaChile for $850m, also plans to supply all farms with its own feed. Even though the feed business offers lower margins than farming, the biggest companies in salmon are choosing to control feed processes because nutrition is such a mission-critical element of ensuring fish health and avoiding mortalities.

title: Judge nixes Chicken of the Sea settlement as insufficient for price-fixing victims
content:
A San Diego, California-based US federal judge has rejected a proposed settlement that would have seen Thai Union Group's Chicken of the Sea International (COSI) brand pay a group of retailers and restaurant owners some $6.5 million to resolve claims related to the canner's price-fixing of canned tuna.

The judge, Janis Sammartino, ruled that it is not clear that the settlement, only $1.5m of which would be paid to the affected firms with the rest going to expenses and legal fees, is "adequate relief" to the "commercial food preparers" (CFP) damaged by the price-fixing.

"Assuming that $2m in costs and expenses includes notice, investment, and tax expenses, but not the incentive awards, a rough calculation suggests the CFP class members will collectively receive approximately 6.85% of the damages they attribute to COSI. This seems a modest amount considering that in criminal antitrust proceedings COSI admitted to price-fixing, thus essentially conceding liability in this action for civil damages," the judge wrote.

During the November criminal trial of Bumble Bee Foods CEO Christopher Lischewski, former COSI CEO Shue Win Chan testified that he believed he had an "understanding" with Lischewski not to aggressively discount COSI's tuna prices. 

COSI is the trade name for Tri-Union Seafoods, the US arm of the Thailand-based shelf-stable seafood giant Thai Union.

Sammartino said that she believed the amount of legal fees and expenses was relatively too high.

"The proposed settlement allocates $5m, or approximately 77% of the total settlement amount, to attorneys’ fees, costs and expenses. The attorneys’ fees alone are $3m or approximately 46% of the total settlement. Distribution of a disproportionate part of the settlement to counsel is one of the indicators that class counsel may not have negotiated in the best interest of the class," she wrote.

Criminal matters

Undercurrent was first to report in 2015 that Tri-Union had acted as a whistleblower informing to the US Department of Justice (DOJ) about the existence of alleged collusion between the US 'big three' tuna brands: Bumble Bee Foods, Dongwon Enterprise-owned StarKist, and COSI.

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion
Read more
 

Bumble Bee and two of its former executives have pleaded guilty to criminal price-fixing charges while CEO Christopher Lischewski was recently found guilty. 

A former executive at StarKist, Stephen Hodge, a former senior vice president of sales, also pleaded guilty.

Tri-Union confirmed in September 2017 that it had been accepted into the DOJ’s corporate leniency program, which will shield the company and its current employees from prosecution.

title: Salmofood asks to be removed from Chilean price-fixing indictment
content:
Feedmaker Salmofood Vitapro is asking a Chilean court to require prosecutors to modify an indictment accusing it of having participated in price-fxing in the feed sector, La Tercera reported.

Salmofood, which is owned by Peru's Alicorp, has asked Chile's Tribunal for the Defense of Free Competition to remove it from an indictment that also includes feed makers, EWOS Biomar and Skretting. Salmofood, the company asserts, "did not participate in the conduct that forms the basis of the accusation".

Chile's Fiscalia Nacional Economica said in December that it is seeking a combined fine of as much as $70 million ($23.9m each) from the major salmon feed companies in Chile.

Cargill has requested an exemption for EWOS Group, a part of Cargill since 2015, because it acted as a whistleblower in the case.

title: BioMar parent to fight Chile price-fixing charges, as Carlos Diaz email used in evidence
content:
An email written in 2008 by Carlos Diaz -- then BioMar vice-president for the Americas, now group CEO -- is among many being used as evidence of executives colluding over salmon feed prices by Chile's competition regulator Fiscalia Nacional Economica (FNE).

BioMar parent Schouw & Co has said it "does not acknowledge the charges brought by the FNE", and that it intends to rebut them.

Cargill ‘self-reported’ Chile price-fixing in January 2016

Chile's largest suppliers of feed have been accused of making secretive agreements among themselves to fix prices, boosting the prices of raw materials in contracts with their customers in an effort to earn additional margins.

The FNE announced on Thursday it is seeking a combined fine of as much as $70 million ($23.9m each) from three major salmon feed companies for price-fixing.

The case -- which has been brought by FNE to antitrust court, or Tribunal de Defensa de la Libre -- identifies the Chilean divisions of BioMar Group, Skretting, and Salmo Food, charging them with colluding from 2003 until 2015.

The agency has requested an exemption for EWOS Group, a part of Cargill since 2015, because the latter acted as a whistleblower in the case. Cargill has told Undercurrent News it "self-reported" as soon as it uncovered practices that went against its code of conduct, in January 2016.

BioMar Group, Skretting, Salmofood and EWOS violated article 3 [...] when concluding and executing an agreement or concerted practice that consisted in setting the sale prices of salmonid foods, traditionally known as diet, which they manufacture and sell to the salmon industry for cultivation, breeding and fattening of these fish, at least in the period between 2003 and 2015. [...]

In order to implement the "agreement", the executives of those firms -- normally their general managers or commercial managers -- made contact through email, phone calls and meetings, according to FNE.

While all four feed suppliers are said to have participated in the agreement, there were times when not all of them communicated directly, with only some of them assuming coordination in such cases, it added.

A tariff charging system

The evidence proves that at the beginning of 2003, the companies were already executing the agreement, according to FNE.

From 2003 onwards, a system of tariff charging called "cost-plus" began to be gradually implemented in the industry, affecting the way in which the companies executed their agreement, FNE claims. Under this system, the price of each diet began to be calculated as the sum of feed production costs, plus a fixed profit margin normally established by the contracts (plus). The companies also began to fix the price of macro-ingredients that have greater relevance in the composition of the diets and that had to be notified to clients under the cost-plus system, FNE went on.

In an internal email from 2003, Salmo Food's commercial director, Juan Carlos Petersen, explained each client's position in relation to the "agreement", expressly mentioning quotations made under it. In the same email, the executive said that since the agreement had been fixed, seven clients had approached him, for whom Salmo Food had not broken the "pact".

Projected price hikes for the months following the "deal" were also agreed by the firms, according to FNE. For this reason, the companies exchanged their price lists, including foreseen hikes. An example of this emerged in an email from 2003 written by Alitec Pargua's general director. Alitec is now part of BioMar.

The agreement is explained in an email written by an EWOS executive, communicating what the prices were for the fourth quarter of one year in question (see email below). It lays out the values and quantities which EWOS, BioMar, and Skretting had defined for fishmeal, fish oil, vegetable oil, gluten, soy and feathers -- raw materials that make up the diet.

An email written by an EWOS' executive, communicating  the prices for a fourth quarter: "the following are the agreed Q4 costs [...] by Ewos, Biomar and Skretting for Chilean salmon firms Camanchaca and Multiexport (...)"

Feed companies allegedly shared buyers' complaints  

The FNE is in possession of other emails from the following years proving the implementation of agreements between feed companies that violate competition rules.

It also pointed out that involved firms "exchanged confidential and sensitive information on the cost of acquiring the most relevant macro ingredients", to allow them to agree on the prices they planned to report to their customers as said "costs".

They also suggested that companies acquiring raw material at lower prices "should increase the values" on the price lists for their customers, allowing them the "appropriate additional margin". An executive said, regarding this increase, that although "there was no clear objective of how much to raise, the idea was to raise as much as possible", while another described in detail the way in which the companies continued to execute the agreement.

BioMar Group's CEO, Carlos Diaz. Between Sept. 2006 and Dec. 2009, Diaz was BioMar's vice-president for the Americas

Sometimes, feed company customers would complain about seeming deviations from "the agreement" -- that is, when a feed firm detailed a raw material or diet cost substantially lower than that of the other companies.

On some occasions, customer complaints were simply a bluff, as the feed firms found when they contacted customers to address the claim.

In an email from February 2008, BioMar's Carlos Diaz communicated directly with the general managers of Alitec (which BioMar owned 50% of at that time) and Skretting, as well as an EWOS executive in the context of a customer complaint about the alleged high prices of the diets supplied by BioMar:

An email from February 2008, written by Diaz: "Because of [EWOS executive's] prices, I think they shouldn't be pushing me so hard, and if the pigment is 0.00195, it's the same pigment I offered him, so I'd like to know right away if they offered anything less, which was not the agreement. Alitec should raise prices, as it is by far the lowest, and has room to increase. I will send a list of the centers I should have so that we are all aware and do not accept additional volumes. It has been proven that if we do put our foot down, things will work out, as long as one of us doesn't play ball. I know Skretting's proposal, and I think it will go in anyway, but not at a lower price, and it is not worth fighting that volume and lowering our margins even more. Once again, I ask you to stand firm. I look forward to your comments, and commitment (...)"


During the execution of the agreement, the companies also exchanged information on the credit conditions delivered to the salmon farms and their debt situations, in order to coordinate such conditions and avoid supplier changes by indebted customers, FNE writes.

They were also sharing info on their monthly production volumes and forecasts for the coming months. 

An Excel file from August 2009, seized from Skretting, charts how the company was aware of costs at BioMar and EWOS, in dollars and per metric ton, from an extensive list of raw materials that make up the diets. This file contains cost information for the first three quarters of 2009, FNE said, adding the commentary to the chart reads: "Although Biomar had a cost for the third quarter of $607 dollars for corn gluten, they are going to price it $700 since the replacement is close to $800. With this type of information, which they used to share before informing their price lists, the companies executed the 'agreement' and proceeded to adjust their prices for raw materials."

This agreement lasted for a long time, even through changes in some commercial managers or general managers, noted FNE, adding that those who came into their new roles continued to execute the pact.

In an internal email from BioMar in June 2013, Lisandro Encina, supply manager, explained to Martin Leon, recently appointed general manager of the company, various aspects of the operation of the industry, including that companies contacted each other before communicating their price lists to customers. This had been done up until then by Felipe Ureta, the previous general manager.

Instructions to delete emails, empty trash

The companies were aware that their behavior was against the law and tried to eliminate traces of the agreement, FNE further pointed out, noting several emails read "now you have to delete this email and empty the trash", or "so you can read it and then delete the email".  Some executives also used code words, referring to the competition as "red" (for Skretting), "green" (for EWOS) or "blue" (for Biomar), and describing members of the cartel as "Toby's club" or "Ugalde family", the agency alleges.

Although the companies left less trace of their contacts over time, the evidence shows that they continued to implement the agreement. For example, an email (see below) from December 2014 reveals that BioMar had information about the costs of acquiring fishmeal and fish oil from its competitors EWOS and Skretting before the first quarter of 2015, and that with this information it would proceed to implement the agreement. In this communication, after transmitting the acquisition costs of the competition, the BioMar executive states they could increase their prices.

An email from Dec. 2014 reveals that Biomar had information about his competitors' costs of acquiring fishmeal and fish oil

An email from BioMar's Encina, sent early in 2016 to various executives inside the company, showed the implementation of the practice had become complex due to the lack of participation of one of the companies. Cargill has said it ceased all participation in the agreements after uncovering concerning practices upon buying EWOS late in 2015.

Encina's email, sent early in 2016: "It will be increasingly difficult to make the mmpp [raw materials] game with this client. We can continue stretching the elastic but the time will come when it will snap. He is clearly well informed of the real prices of commodities and it also seems that our competition is giving him real costs and doing business on the other hand..."


Schouw & Co confirmed BioMar Chile had been "subject to unannounced inspections". "Naturally, BioMar Chile has been cooperative, responding to questions and providing the documentation requested to the extent possible."

It further confirmed that the FNE has now indicted BioMar Chile on charges of concerted practice, asking that the company be fined up to $24m. "The charges are based on isolated circumstances related to the Chilean fish feed industry in the period 2003-2015."

Credit: MARCELODLT/Shutterstock.com

"BioMar Chile does not acknowledge the charges brought by the FNE, and the company intends to rebut the charges that it has participated in concerted practices so as to restrict competition in the industry."

Skretting parent Nutreco told Undercurrent it only became aware of the allegations made by the FNE yesterday, Dec. 19. "We take competition compliance extremely seriously. We will therefore carefully review the complaint and present our case in due course."

Salmo Food has not yet replied to requests for comment.

Chilean salmon industry: 'Far from the values we promote'

Chilean salmon industry association SalmonChile said it considers the facts denounced by the FNE to be "of the utmost seriousness", adding it hopes that the situation will be clarified and that the appropriate measures will be implemented.

"For our union, the practices denounced by the FNE are far from the values we promote," it said.

title: Cargill ‘self-reported’ Chile price-fixing in January 2016
content:
As Chilean authorities seek hefty fines against BioMar Group, Skretting and Salmo Food over alleged price-fixing, Cargill has told Undercurrent News it acted as the whistleblower for the sector.

Chile's Fiscalia Nacional Economica (FNE) announced Thursday that it is seeking a combined fine of as much as $70 million ($23.9m each) from the major salmon feed companies in Chile.

Cargill has requested an exemption for EWOS Group, a part of Cargill since 2015, because it acted as a whistleblower in the case.

"Shortly after the closing of the acquisition of EWOS from Altor and Bain Capital in October 2015, our EWOS employees in Chile informed us about practices in the salmon feed industry in Chile that were inconsistent with the Cargill competition policy and possibly violated the Chilean competition law," a Cargill spokesperson told Undercurrent.

"We immediately initiated an investigation, self-reported to the FNE in January 2016, and ceased participating in the problematic conduct."

The practices -- limited only to Chile -- included contacts with competitors that violated competition policy and Cargill's own code of conduct, the firm said. "We have conducted training for all our employees in Chile about our principles and compliance policies, including our competition policy."

It added that one of the requirements of its full cooperation with FNE was complete confidentiality, adding only that "conducting business in an ethical manner is foundational to how we operate in Cargill".

Skretting parent Nutreco told Undercurrent it only became aware of the allegations made by the FNE yesterday. "We take competition compliance extremely seriously. We will therefore carefully review the complaint and present our case in due course."

BioMar parent Schouw & Co confirmed BioMar Chile had been "subject to unannounced inspections". "Naturally, BioMar Chile has been cooperative, responding to questions and providing the documentation requested to the extent possible."

It further confirmed the FNE has now indicted BioMar Chile on charges of concerted practice, asking that the company be fined up to $24m. "The charges are based on isolated circumstances related to the Chilean fish feed industry in the period 2003-2015."

"BioMar Chile does not acknowledge the charges brought by the FNE, and the company intends to rebut the charges that it has participated in concerted practices so as to restrict competition in the industry."

Salmo Food has not yet replied to requests for comment.

FNE alleges the feed firms colluded by coordinating the prices of diets and the volumes of feed supplied, and by coordinating the prices of some of the most relevant raw materials that make up the feed, and charging their customers in the price lists.

Executives coordinated via emails, meetings and phone calls and "tried to eliminate the traces of these contacts", the FNE charges. They used code words, referring to the competition as "red," "green," or "blue," and describing members of the cartel as "Toby's club" or "Ugalde family", the agency alleges.

title: Jury finds former Bumble Bee CEO Lischewski guilty on price-fixing charges
content:
SAN FRANCISCO, California, US -- After deliberating for nearly seven hours, a 12-member federal jury unanimously found former Bumble Bee CEO Christopher Lischewski guilty of price-fixing charges Tuesday afternoon, Dec. 3.

Lischewski will be sentenced by judge Edward Chen at a future date. He could face up to 10 years in prison and a $1 million fine. 

The Department of Justice's Antitrust Division, which began an investigation into the US canned tuna sector in 2015, presented 11 prosecution witnesses including four former US tuna executives who testified to the existence of a price-fixing conspiracy.

The verdict marks the end of a nearly month-long trial that began on Nov. 4. It is the final criminal prosecution in the price-fixing investigation that saw guilty pleas for Bumble Bee and StarKist & Co, which received fines of $25 million and $100m, respectively. Smaller canner Chicken of the Sea, a brand owned by Thai Union Group's Tri-Union Seafoods, acted as a whistleblower against the other two companies. The canner cooperated with the DOJ investigation in exchange for immunity for it and its employees as well as limitations on damages from the many civil suits from tuna customers who say they were harmed by price-fixing.

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion
Read more

Additionally, three US tuna executives pleaded guilty to price-fixing charges and agreed to testify against the former Bumble Bee CEO.

Two, Walter Cameron and Kenneth Worsham, were both senior vice presidents at Bumble Bee during the 2010 to 2013 period during which the government argues that the conspiracy occurred and reported directly to Lischewski.

Cameron testified that Lischewski directed him to reach out to Cameron's friend and former Bumble Bee coworker, Chuck Handford, who in 2010 was working for Starkist in an effort to broker a "truce" between the two canners' "price wars" of aggressive competition during the 2010 period. Elliot Peters, the lead defense attorney for Lischewski, contested this claim during trial arguing that pricing data and internal Bumble Bee emails from the period showed vibrant competition, not collusion. The next year, 2011, was the true "price war", and was a difficult year for all three canners as albacore and skipjack prices saw steep increases, Peters claimed. 

Handford was never charged with a crime and did not testify at trial. 

Collaborations between competitors led the way for coordinated price increases in canned tuna "list" prices, the starting point that the canners' used when negotiating with grocers and other buyers to arrive at "net" prices, prosecutors claimed.  

A third alleged co-conspirator, Stephen Hodge, a former vice president of sales at Starkist, testified that he regularly communicated with Bumble Bee's Worsham, sometimes directly and sometimes using his father, longtime Starkist executive Bob Worsham, who passed away last year. Peters, in his closing statement, argued that Ken Worsham falsified his testimony about Lischewski having knowledge of the price-fixing. Cameron, Peters added, also lied and named his former boss as a conspirator in the hopes of receiving a lesser sentence.

Cameron, Hodge and Worsham could face years in prison and major fines after their guilty pleas. They will be sentenced at a future date by judge Chen who will consider sentence reductions in exchange for the witnesses' cooperation. 

In addition to the co-conspirators, Shue Win Chan, the former CEO of Chicken of the Sea International (COSI), also testified for the prosecution as part of an immunity agreement. Chan  told the court that he believed he had an "understanding" with Lischewski that Bumble Bee would refrain from offering customers "aggressive promotions" if COSI, a chronic discounter, also did so. 

Lischewski sent Chan eight emails that referenced COSI's low prices, which prosecutors said reflected the "understanding". When he testified in his own defense, however, Lischewski said that the emails reflected his annoyance that his competitor was pricing its tuna below production costs in an effort to preserve market share. The former CEO said he felt such a practice was not good for the industry. 

On cross-examination from Peters, Chan clarified that the “understanding” he believed the men had was never explicit and that it was Chan's expectation that Bumble Bee would follow suit on promotional restraint, not a formal agreement. 

Jurors also heard from David Roszmann, a former chief operating officer at COSI, who testified that he'd had a series of encounters in 2014 where Lischewski approached him about the canner's low pricing.

The former COO and Lischewski arranged to meet and have breakfast in San Diego but Roszmann “avoided the meeting”, he testified.

“What did you tell the defendant had happened?” prosecutor Leslie Wulff asked.

“I told him I was in a car accident,” Roszmann said.

Other prosecution witnesses included two FBI employees that authenticated exhibits used in the case, Jeffrey Chang of Bumble Bee owner Lion Capital who testified as to Lischewski's bonus structure and Tri Marine International's Renato Curto.

Curto testified about an Aug. 8, 2012 email that he'd sent to members of Tri Marine's executive team summarizing a conversation he'd had the previous night with Lischewski about the tuna industry.

The men met for drinks around 8:30 or 9 p.m. but Curto testified he can’t remember if he’d had a glass of wine, a San Pellegrino water or a martini.

“I don’t remember the meeting. I don’t remember the conversation,” he said.

The email, however, describes Lischewski as saying: “His people and StarKist people were talking constantly and had good conversations about how to go to market intelligently”.

In contrast to the prosecution's 11 witnesses, the defense presented only three with Lischewski acting as the star witness. 

Taking the witness stand for over six hours Monday, Nov. 25 to make his case for innocence, he responded point-by-point to matters raised by prosecution witnesses during the past three weeks of his trial on price-fixing charges.

He contradicted testimony from Cameron and Worsham, asserting that he neither participated in any conspiracy with the men nor did he direct Worsham or Cameron to do so.

Lischewski testified that he was “shocked” when he later learned from the company’s general counsel that Worsham and Cameron had pleaded guilty.

“Scott and Kenny both worked with me for 15 years. Scott was aggressive. He was a competitor. I couldn’t imagine he was involved in price-fixing especially with his own pricing authority. Ken was an even bigger surprise,” Lischewski said. “He was one of the first guys I hired.”

Return to Bumble Bee?

Lischewski added that he was “stunned and quickly became angry” when it became clear that both of his former subordinates were claiming that he had directed them to communicate and reach agreements with competitors.

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion
Read more

Lischewski led Bumble Bee -- which has filed by Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection with main supplier FCF Co lined up as a "stalking horse" buyer --  from 1999 until his 2018 indictment and feels “personally identified” with the company, he said.
