title: Editor’s recap: Blue Harvest’s $25m deal for 35 Rafael vessels; Lischewski hopes to return to Bumble Bee
content:
Tom Seaman, editorial director of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

One of the most anticipated forced sell-offs in the history of US commercial fishing – the unloading of Carlos Rafael’s fleet in New Bedford, Massachusetts -- looks to be on the verge of completion, Jason Huffman reported last week. 

Blue Harvest Fisheries, a US scallop and groundfish supplier backed by New York City-based private equity Bregal Partners, has signed a purchase agreement to buy at least 35 vessels and skiffs and all of their associated permits from Carlos Rafael for nearly $25 million, documents obtained by Jason confirm.

The deal includes millions of pounds of quota for at least eight types of fish in the northeast multispecies fishery, including cod, haddock, American plaice, witch flounder, yellowtail flounder, redfish, white hake, and pollock.

The roughly 30-page agreement must still survive a “right of first refusal” (ROFR) process, by which other harvesters in the sectors where the vessels worked will also have a chance to match the bid. Also, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration must approve the buyer, following a review of the company's legal history or possible relationship to Rafael.

Click here for the full story. 

Lischewski trial: Defense, prosecution rest; case could go to jury Monday

The jury in the criminal price-fixing trial of Christopher Lischewski will have their say in the matter as early as Monday, Dec. 2, after the defense rested Nov. 26, with the US Thanksgiving holiday on Nov. 28 and many people off work the day after. Jason Smith, our Americas editor, is reporting live from the trial, which is being held in San Francisco, California. 

Lischewski was the defense’s final witness, one of only three that also included the economist James Levinsohn, and Stuart Kaye, the former CEO of Big Brothers/Big Sisters of San Diego County who served as a character witness. 

Judge Edward Chen told the court that the prosecution and defense will present their closing arguments Monday, expected to last at least an hour each. Chen will then instruct the jury on legal aspects of the case to consider in their deliberations.

Click here for the full story. 

Asserting innocence, Lischewski hopes to return to Bumble Bee CEO role

Taking the witness stand for over six hours Monday, Nov. 25 to make his case for innocence, former Bumble Bee CEO Lischewski responded point-by-point to matters raised by prosecution witnesses during the past three weeks of his trial on price-fixing charges.

Contradicting the testimony of two former employees, Walter Scott Cameron and Ken Worsham, and Shue Win Chan, the former CEO of rival brand Chicken of the Sea International -- all of who have admitted to price-fixing -- Lischewski said he neither participated in any conspiracy with the men nor did he direct Worsham or Cameron to do so.

Lischewski led Bumble Bee -- which has filed by Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection with main supplier FCF Co lined up as a "stalking horse" buyer --  from 1999 until his 2018 indictment and feels “personally identified” with the company, he said.

“Is it your hope to return to the company and continue to run it as president and CEO?” his attorney Elliot Peters asked him. “Yes, it is,” Lischewski said.

Click here for the full story. 

Vietnamese shrimp giant Viet-Uc looks for investor

Viet-Uc Seafood, a company that supplies one-in-three postlarvae to Vietnam’s huge shrimp farming industry, is looking for an investor, Matt Craze reported. 

The Ho Chi Minh City-based company is in talks with several interested parties after owner Van Thanh Luong decided to engage with potential buyers, a company executive confirmed to Matt. Three senior shrimp industry sources had previously confirmed they heard the company was for sale.

“There are a number of potential investors and interested parties contacting and discussing with us about the investment and cooperation opportunities,” a company source told Undercurrent.

“Everything is under consideration," he said.

Click here for the full story. 

Samherji Sainsbury’s loss not linked to Namibia scandal, but M&S takes allegations ‘very seriously’

The UK division of beleaguered Icelandic fishing giant Samherji has lost its frozen fish business into J. Sainsbury, but this came before the emergence of the scandal over alleged cash-for-quota payments to politicians in Namibia and has nothing to do with it, sources told me. 

However, the ongoing news is being monitored by Marks and Spencer (M&S), the other main UK customer of Ice Fresh Seafood, Samherji's retail packing operation in Grimsby, which had bought a larger plant in 2017 to accommodate growing demand from Sainsbury's and M&S. 

The former Seachill plant is short of work now Ice Fresh has lost the Sainsbury's frozen cod, haddock, salmon, and pollock business to two Chinese processors. Qingdao Tanford Foods has taken the cod, haddock, salmon and a plant supplying Unibond Seafood International has the pollock business, sources told Undercurrent. 

This comes as WikiLeaks released 30,000 documents on Samherji's activities in Namibia from its former manager in the African country, who claims over $10m was paid in bribes to ministers and officials for access to horse mackerel quotas. 

Click here for the full story. 

China lifts shrimp import suspensions against Santa Priscila, Expalsa

China has lifted its temporary suspensions of shrimp imports from the facilities of several of Ecuador’s largest seafood companies,  Louis Harkell reported. 

On Wednesday China's General Administration of Customs said imports of shrimp from facilities owned by Industrial Pesquera Santa Priscila, Expalsa, Congelados Y Frescos, and Winrep "can resume as normal". 

The new policy is effective immediately. 

In mid-September, the four companies and Omarsa were hit with suspensions to their export approval licenses to China on the grounds shipments carried shrimp diseases. The companies account for half of Ecuador's shrimp exports, worth over $3 billion in total in 2018. 

According to the General Administration of Customs, shipments were detected as having yellowhead disease, whitespot syndrome virus, and infectious hypodermal and hematopoietic necrosis virus.

Click here for the full story. 

Canada’s Icewater to complete plant updates over winter, in bid to compete with European processors

Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada-based cod processor Icewater Seafoods will complete its ongoing upgrade work this winter, as it looks to compete with Europe's key whitefish processors. 

The firm -- North America's largest processor of Atlantic cod, and the only to focus just on this species -- is almost at the end of a three-year, CAD 10m ($7.5m) investment program designed to ensure it remains competitive and at top quality, CEO Alberto Wareham told Neil Ramsden. 

Earlier this year, at the Seafood Expo Global in Brussels, Belgium, Wareham signed a deal with Iceland's Marel for a FleXicut automatic pinboning and portioning machine, at a cost of CAD 1.6m. 

Now, over the winter, the Arnold's Cove plant will close down for three or four months while a new, "state-of-the-art" refrigeration system is installed, he said. All of the old compressors -- some 30 or 40 years old -- are being removed, and a new, Icelandic system is being put in.

Click here for the full story. 

Judge denies Bumble Bee request to have FCF named ‘critical vendor’

Bumble Bee will be able to immediately pay nearly a fifth, $12m, of the $50.5m that it owes to its biggest creditor, tuna supplier, and possible future owner FCF Co, a Delaware judge ruled. 

However, Laurie Silverstein, the judge overseeing the company's recent bankruptcy filing, denied Bumble Bee's request that it be allowed priority over other creditors to pay the Taiwanese tuna trader the full $50.5m amount it was owed and grant it "critical vendor" status, Jason Smith reported. 

The week before last, it emerged that FCF is the "stalking horse" bidder for Bumble Bee, a company that it values at $930m. Silverstein has yet to rule on the company's proposal and it remains possible that other buyers could emerge.

Click here for the full story. 

Southeast Asia’s domestic shrimp demand puts dent in exports

The growing local demand for shrimp from customers in Southeast Asia is likely to continue curtailing export volumes, offering more attractive prices for regional producers than can be found abroad, said Fatima Ferdouse, a Bangladeshi expert and consultant on fishery trade, at the recent Infofish shrimp conference. 

For instance, Ferdouse said, one piece of giant river shrimp in Malaysia can be sold to foodservice for as much as $20. Meanwhile, in her native Bangladesh, demand for black tiger, indicus and giant freshwater macrobrachium has also shot up, Dan Gibson reported. 

“We have a lot of disposable income in developing countries for food. Maybe not much for social security, insurance, this and that, but for food security, we have a bigger budget compared to the other sectors” Ferdouse said, noting that in Bangladesh, locals are paying in the region of $30-40 for head-on macrobrachium shrimp.

Ferdouse believes that declining exports of shrimp from certain Southeast Asian countries can be linked to this increased local consumption, with better sales opportunities and higher prices available in local markets.

Click here for the full story. 

Young’s tipped to take M&S bass biz from NESI amid ‘winner takes all’ Sainsbury tender

Young’s Seafood is being tipped to come out on top in a tender of the seabass and seabream business for high-end retailer M&S currently served by New England Seafood International, as the two firms are also engaged in a “winner takes all” fight for the chilled whitefish contract for Sainsbury's.

The tender for the bass and bream business in M&S, said to be worth around £10m, is coming to a head and clarity on who has come out on top will come soon, sources told me. Although multiple sources said Young’s is the favorite to win the contract, “it’s not done until it’s done”, as one UK seafood sector veteran said.

Young’s, which private equity CapVest Partners has acquired and put under a new holding company with pork producer Karro Food Group, already does the chilled cod, haddock, and salmon for M&S and also took on the coated fish contract for the retailer in 2018. The tenders come as Simon Smith, who has joined Young’s as CEO from Seachill UK, makes changes to his top team, with Frank Green overseeing the chilled side battling with NESI. 

Click here for the full story. 

Contact the author tom.seaman@undercurrentnews.com

title: Asserting innocence, Lischewski hopes to return to Bumble Bee CEO role
content:
SAN FRANCISCO, California, US -- Taking the witness stand for over six hours Monday, Nov. 25 to make his case for innocence, former Bumble Bee Foods CEO Chris Lischewski responded point-by-point to matters raised by prosecution witnesses during the past three weeks of his trial on price-fixing charges.

Lischewski trial: After guilty verdict, sentencing set for April 8; Defense lawyers pledge to ‘continue to vigorously pursue justice’

Contradicting the testimony of two former employees, Walter Scott Cameron and Ken Worsham, and Shue Win Chan, the former CEO of rival brand Chicken of the Sea International (COSI), all of who have admitted to price-fixing, Lischewski said he neither participated in any conspiracy with the men nor did he direct Worsham or Cameron to do so.

Lischewski testified that he was “shocked” when he later learned from the company’s general counsel that Worsham and Cameron had pleaded guilty.

“Scott and Kenny both worked with me for 15 years. Scott was aggressive. He was a competitor. I couldn’t imagine he was involved in price-fixing especially with his own pricing authority. Ken was an even bigger surprise,” Lischewski said. “He was one of the first guys I hired.”

Return to Bumble Bee?

Lischewski added that he was “stunned and quickly became angry” when it became clear that both of his former subordinates were claiming that he had directed them to communicate and reach agreements with competitors.

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion
Read more

Lischewski led Bumble Bee -- which has filed by Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection with main supplier FCF Co lined up as a "stalking horse" buyer --  from 1999 until his 2018 indictment and feels “personally identified” with the company, he said.

“Is it your hope to return to the company and continue to run it as president and CEO?” his attorney Elliot Peters asked him.

“Yes, it is,” Lischewski said.

The former CEO’s explanation of some of the events earlier described by Cameron and Worsham differed in important respects.

Cameron, for instance, previously described a December 2015 meeting with Lischewski at San Diego, California’s Water Grill during which the two men had discussed the Department of Justice (DOJ) investigation into the canned tuna sector.

Cameron testified that his boss warned him “not to f#$k it up”, which he took to mean not to cooperate in the investigation.

'Like they do in the movies'

Lischewski said that Cameron brought up the subject to him over a drink.

“He asked me what was going on with the DOJ investigation,” Lischewksi testified, adding that he told Cameron not to worry about it.

“He came back and said he was worried about it. He was thinking about it all the time,” Lischewski testified.

The ex-CEO said he wasn’t worried about it “at all”, adding: “Don’t worry about it, the company has your back to an extent.”

Lischewski testified that meant that as long as Cameron continued to support the investigation and hadn’t done anything wrong, the company would continue to support him. It was meant as reassurance, not a threat, he said.

“Did you put your hand on his shoulder and hold him close like they do in the movies and say ‘as long as you and Kenny don’t f#$k it up, or words to that effect?” Peters asked Lischewski.

"I never said that," Lischewski said.

 Emails to Shue Win Chan

Cameron, Worsham and a former executive at StarKist & Co, Steven Hodge, have all pleaded guilty to participating in a conspiracy to fix canned tuna prices between 2010 and 2013. As corporations, Starkist and Bumble Bee, which recently filed for bankruptcy in large part due to legal costs stemming from the scandal, also pleaded guilty and were fined $100 million and $25m, respectively. Thai Union Group, which owns COSI through its Tri-Union Seafoods arm, received immunity from prosecution, as did the company’s employees, for acting as a whistleblower and cooperating with the investigation.

In contrast, during his three-week trial, Lischewski has steadfastly maintained his innocence. His legal team, led by Peters, repeatedly questioned witnesses pointing out that while Cameron and Worsham appeared to reference in emails that they were speaking with competitors, Lischewski was not a party to those emails.

In other cases, such as the series of emails that Lischewski sent former COSI CEO Shue Win Chan in 2013 referencing the canner’s promotions, Lischewski said it was out of concern about the damage COSI’s low pricing strategy could do to the industry.

At the time Thai Union was so concerned that COSI’s eroding market share could lead to the brand’s delisting from shelves that the Thai parent company authorized COSI an “investment” of $11m, an amount it spent on promotions to win back share.

Chan, in his testimony, suggested that he'd reached an “understanding” with Lischewski that the two canners would each cut back on “aggressive promotions”.

Lischewski testified that although he’d gotten to know Chan during this period, it was in relation to a co-packing arrangement between the firms and Bumble Bee’s sustainability initiatives and had nothing to do with pricing.

title: Lischewski lawyer to ex-Bumble Bee exec: ‘Are you just making stuff up?’
content:
SAN FRANCISCO, California, US -- Elliot Peters, an attorney for former Bumble Bee Foods CEO Christopher Lischewski, tore into Kenneth Worsham during cross-examination Nov. 18, 2019, questioning the veracity of the testimony of the US tuna canner’s former vice president of trade marketing and the quality of his memory.

Worsham previously testified that he and Steve Hodge, StarKist & Co’s former senior vice president of sales, had met for dinner at Fleming’s Prime Steakhouse & Wine Bar in La Jolla, California on May. 2, 2012.

Dinner with Steve Hodge

At that meeting, Hodge gave Worsham a thumb drive with Starkist pricing data, “hot” competitive information that confirmed that Starkist had followed through on its previous agreement with Bumble Bee to raise tuna list prices, Worsham claimed at the trial of Lischewski for alleged price-fixing. As the trial takes place in San Francisco, California, Bumble Bee is reportedly prepping a bankruptcy filing, as it faces a $25m fine from the government and big payouts to settle civil lawsuits brought by retailers, foodservice firms and other companies claiming damage by the price-fixing, as well as members of the public.

Lischewski trial: After guilty verdict, sentencing set for April 8; Defense lawyers pledge to ‘continue to vigorously pursue justice’

Worsham testified Nov. 15, 2019, that, on May 3, 2012, the day after his dinner with Hodge, he’d met at Bumble Bee’s offices in San Diego and presented the Starkist information to Lischewski and Dan Nestojko, then the company’s vice president of marketing who now serves as the canner’s senior vice president of sales.

But using 2012 records from Worsham’s Outlook calendar, Peters repeatedly pointed out inconsistencies in the executive’s testimony. Nestojko, Worsham’s calendar showed, was on vacation on May 3 didn’t come back to work until Tuesday, May 8, 2012.

Peters then asked the witness if he knew that on May 3, the day after the dinner with Hodge when Worsham claimed to have passed along the information to Lischewski, that the former Bumble Bee CEO had been traveling to New Orleans.

“Isn’t it true, Mr. Worsham, that you don’t have any more of a recollection talking to Mr. Lischewski on May 3, 2012, about your dinner with Steve Hodge than you did about your conversation with Dan Nestojko?” Peters asked

“I have a recollection about talking with Mr. Lischewski about my dinner with Steve Hodge,” Worsham replied. “If it didn’t happen on May 3, it happened the next day he was in the office. But it happened with Chris Lischewski.”

Competitive information

Lischewski stepped down from his role as Bumble Bee's CEO in 2017 after his indictment on price-fixing charges to focus on his defense. In contrast to Worsham, who like former Bumble Bee senior vice president of sales Walter Cameron pleaded guilty to price-fixing but has yet to be sentenced, Lischewski has consistently claimed he had no knowledge of collusion between the US' three largest tuna canners: Dongwon Enterprise-owned Starkist, Bumble Bee, and Chicken of the Sea, which is owned by Thai Union Group's Tri-Union Seafoods. 

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion
Read more

Worsham testified that he would typically review things with Lischewski as soon as he had access, particularly in a case where he had solid competitive information. But the lawyer pointed out that the witness had testified under oath about having the conversation on the specific May 3, 2012 date in his recent testimony.

“Are you telling us what you now in 2019 want to believe happened or are you telling us what you recall in fact happened?” the lawyer asked

“I’m telling you how my interactions with Chris Lischewski evolved after working with him for 17 years” the witness replied.

Peters paused a moment and continued.

“I’m asking you about specific meetings on a specific day and I want to know is whether you’re telling the jury what you in 2019 want to recall happened or where you have a specific recollection of this meeting? Or are you just making stuff up?” the lawyer asked.

“I’m clearly not making stuff up. All my comments are made with regards to my experience working with Chris for a number of years. Chris traveled a lot. I don’t have specific recollection of Chris’ travel dates versus in the office or out of the office. That’s a little unrealistic,” Worsham said.

He added that he specifically remembers handing Lischewski the information although he doesn’t recall the date

“When you gave that testimony were you speculating or just making it up?” Peters asked

Worsham replied simply: “no”.

Expense report

A few minutes earlier, Peters had shown the jury Worsham’s expense report that sought reimbursement for the $186 May 2, 2012, steakhouse dinner that he’d had with Hodge.

Instead of Hodge, Worsham's report claimed that he had met with Don George, then a vice president of trade marketing at Bumble Bee, to discuss "Q3 strategy".

Peters asked why Worsham lied about his dinner companion.

“Were you trying to keep your dinner with Mr. Hodge a secret from Mr. Lischewski?” Peters asked.

"No," Worsham replied.

"Then who at Bumble Bee were you lying to when you wrote this expense report?” the lawyer asked.

Worsham explained he didn't want Bumble Bee's finance department to know that he was meeting with a direct competitor.

title: Key witness in Lischewski trial ‘panicked’, lied to FBI during first meeting
content:
SAN FRANCISCO, California, US -- Stephen Hodge, one of three former US tuna executives co-operating in the US government's prosecution of ex-Bumble Bee Foods CEO Christopher Lischewski, admitted Nov. 13 that he lied to the FBI when first questioned about his role in the tuna price-fixing conspiracy.

Hodge, a former senior vice president of sales for StarKist & Co, testified during the trial at the US District Court for the Northern District of California that he lied during an hour-long 2015 meeting that occurred when a special agent from the FBI and a prosecutor from the Department of Justice showed up at his house without warning. 

“They told us that they were commencing an investigation into the tuna category in regards to conspiracy to fix prices and were interviewing me in regards to my knowledge and or involvement in the matter,” Hodge said.

"What did you tell the FBI in that meeting?" prosecutor Leslie Wulff asked Hodge.

“I told them that I did have conversations with competitors. I did not tell them the truth when it came to my involvement in the matter,” he replied.

“Why not?”

“Scared. Unprepared. They showed up at my door without any notice whatsoever. I had not ever talked to an attorney with regard to this. I panicked and did not tell the truth in the matter.”

“Why were you scared when you lied to the FBI?”

“Of being where I am right now,” Hodge said, referring to the witness stand.

He later admitted what he did because he “was guilty”, Hodge said, and agreed to testify truthfully against Lischewski, a man he acknowledged he never spoke about tuna prices with.

Under cross-examination from defense attorney Christopher Kearney, Hodge acknowledged that he could have been charged with additional crimes due to his lies during the FBI interview. Instead, Hodge was indicted with and pleaded guilty to only one count of price-fixing. 

“And you knew at the time, Mr Hodge, that it was wrong, it was a crime to not be truthful with respect to their questions?” Kearney asked.

"No, I wouldn’t say that. I didn’t know that was a crime,” Hodge replied.

"But you knew it was wrong?".

"Yes".

"You knew was improper?".

"Yes".

Regular communication

Earlier in the day, Hodge testified that during the 2010 to 2013 period he was in regular contact with Ken Worsham, who was then Bumble Bee’s senior vice president of trade marketing. Hodge also said that he regularly spoke to Mike White, director of marketing at Chicken of the Sea International, a brand owned by Thai Union Group’s Tri-Union Seafoods.

Following these conversations about the canners’ pricing movements, Hodge told the jury that he would continue to monitor the pricing agreements by watching weekly grocery store flyers across the US. Starkist bought a software package that created a report by monitoring tuna prices to watch the Bumble Bee agreement, making sure that the ads for its canned tuna were in the “proper” price points, Hodge said.

Hodge further testified that he never spoke about prices with anyone at Bumble Bee about prices other than Worsham. He never spoke to Lischewski about prices and never made any agreement with him, he said.

After Starkist fired him at the end of 2013 — this occurred because Starkist’s chairman, Ingu Park, “likes change”, Hodge said he was told — Hodge met with Worsham and Lischewski in San Diego so that he could look into a possible job at Bumble Bee. None materialized, he said.

Other than that 30 to 45-minute meeting, Hodge has never met with Lischewski, he said.

title: Curto email from 2012 suggests Bumble Bee, Starkist were ‘talking constantly’
content:
SAN FRANCISCO, California, US -- Prosecutors in the price-fixing trial of ex-Bumble Bee Foods CEO Christopher Lischewski presented the jury with a pair of emails written by Renato Curto, the CEO of Tri Marine International, written two years apart.

The emails, testified Curto, who has led Tri Marine since 1986 and been in the tuna industry for 47 years, were written to Tri Marine executives summarizing two contemporaneous conversations he had with Lischewski. Curto, who was subpoenaed to testify in the case, is in the habit of writing similar emails to document such conversations, he told the jury Nov. 12 during the proceeding at the US District Court for the Northern District of California.

He’s known Lischewski, who he called “one of the most important persons in the industry”, since the early 1990s.

“We’ve always been friends,” Curto said.

In a June 26, 2010, email to Tri Marine executives, Curto described conversations he’d had just before with tuna industry leaders including Lischewski of Bumble Bee, Don Binotto, former CEO of StarKist & Co and Thiraphong Chansiri of Thai Union Group.

Referencing the conversation he had with Lischewski, Curto informed his team at the time that Bumble Bee’s then-owner the private equity Centre Partners planned to sell the canner. Lischewski thought of moving on from the company to be succeeded by Jan Tharp, the canner’s chief operating officer. Tharp would go on to be named Bumble Bee’s interim CEO after Lischewski stepped down in 2018 after his indictment to focus on his defense.

In the email, Curto wrote that Lischewski had set an “ambitious” target of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $175 million within the next three to five years, up from $130m in 2010.

“He said that was battling Starkist for market share, especially on light meat and pouch. He said he wants to get to 25% market share in pouch,” Curto wrote, describing Lischewski’s comments.

Lischewski trial: After guilty verdict, sentencing set for April 8; Defense lawyers pledge to ‘continue to vigorously pursue justice’

Conversation over drinks

In a second email, written by Curto on Aug. 8, 2012, to Tri Marine executives, describes a meeting he had with Lischewski the day before in San Diego, California’s Grand El Mar Hotel.

The men met for drinks around 8:30 or 9 p.m. but Curto testified he can’t remember if he’d had a glass of wine, a San Pellegrino water or a martini.

“I don’t remember the meeting. I don’t remember the conversation,” he said.

The email, however, describes Lischewski as saying: “His people and StarKist people were talking constantly and had good conversations about how to go to market intelligently”.

Curto wrote that Starkist “had been very diligent” and had raised light meat prices. Bumble Bee then raised prices on albacore, Curto testified. The result, he wrote in the email, is that “margins were coming up as volumes were coming down”, Curto described Lischewski as saying.

Memory questions

However, on cross-examination, Elliot Peters, Lischewski’s attorney questioned the accuracy of Curto’s summary of the conversation.

“He didn't actually say those words. You were speculating about that weren’t you?” the lawyer asked.

“I’m certainly not saying these are his words,” Curto replied.

Peters later asked if Curto had trouble remembering things.

“In general, yes, like my hearing, my sight, everything is fading as you get older,” the 75-year-old said. He added that although his short-term memory is fine, he sometimes struggles to remember events from years ago.

Ex-Starkist exec describes close collaboration on prices with Bumble Bee

Tri Marine transition

Curto remains as CEO of the Tri Marine group, he said. However, the company is in the midst of a major transition, having been sold to Italy's Bolton Group International earlier this year. 

The deal is focused on the global tuna supply businesses of US-based Tri Marine, which includes its trading companies, processors and National Fisheries Developments, a fishing company in the Solomon Islands operating a fleet of purse seine and pole and line vessels. 

Also, the deal will see the creation of a new business unit, which Curto will "continue to separately own and lead as CEO", according to an announcement from Curto, titled "A Bright Future for Tri Marine".

This unit includes Cape Fisheries, Samoa Fishing Management, Tri Marine Fishing Management, Tri Marine Fish Co., Conservera de las Americas, Samoa Tuna Processors, The Tuna Store, Baja Marine Foods. Pesquera Tri Marine and Tri Marine SA, Curto told staff. 

Tri Marine buys tuna directly from tuna vessels and sells it to companies that process it into loins that are then sold to canners like Bumble Bee. The canner was once a major customer but reduced its volumes from Tri Marine after the tuna supplier’s largest rival, Taiwan’s Fong Chun Formosa Fishery Company, known as FCF, took an ownership stake in Bumble Bee.

Tri Marine also sells cooked tuna loins and competes in a small way to the canners by offering its own brand, Ocean Naturals, Curto told the jury. But this hasn’t worked out so well for Tri Marine.

“If you want to call a brand, I take it as a compliment. We sold maybe four cans,” he said.

Tri Marine operated its own cannery in American Samoa, Samoa Tuna Processors, but the venture incurred substantial losses and was shuttered in December 2016. Tri Marine subsequently leased the facility to Starkist.

title: Editor’s recap: Live from China; Shrimp study findings; Blue Star parts with CEO, trims US Foods biz
content:
Neil Ramsden, deputy editor of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

It was another week, another major seafood event; this time Tom Seaman, Louis Harkell, and Matt Craze were reporting live from the 2019 China Fisheries & Seafood Expo, held in a venue close to Qingdao, in Shandong Province. 

Some of the latest entries to the live blog included Canadian firms Victoria Fish and Partner Seafood joining the list of companies selling live American lobster to China; Chile's Invermar hiking salmon sales to Asia; and trader Siam Canadian’s plans to emulate its Asian model in Latin America.

Catch up on these and all the other posts, here.

The next most-read story on Undercurrent last week was a post on the findings reported by the Hatch Aquaculture Accelerator, a team of scientists based in Cork, Ireland, who recently traveled to the world's six biggest shrimp-producing countries and compared notes. They found that the densest shrimp aquaculture farms in the world are maintained in China and Vietnam, where an average of 220 to 300 shrimp share a square meter, while Thailand and Indonesia average between 70 and 130 shrimp in the same amount of space.

Indian farmers are regulated by law, meanwhile, to stock no more than 60 shrimp per square meter, and Ecuadorian farmers work at even lower densities of around 20 shrimp per square meter.

Read more on this, and their other results, here.

In the US, Jason Huffman reported that Blue Star Foods, the Miami, Florida-based blue and red swimming crab importer and exporter, was dealing with the acrimonious parting of its president and CEO and the gradual winnowing down of its relationship with US Foods as a major buyer, while simultaneously being forced to confront a less-than-glowing quarterly filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).

Carlos Faria, who joined Blue Star in January 2018, told Undercurrent recently that he voluntarily resigned from his positions on Aug. 1 over differences of opinion with his former longtime friend John Keeler, the company founder and executive chairman, in relation to growth strategy and what he said were "serious concerns" about supply management practices. 

Keeler instead maintains that Faria was fired, suggesting he was not attentive to his position, and characterized him as a "vindictive" former employee. He said Faria refused to sign a termination agreement that would've included a "generous severance package".

One of Blue Star's most recent public filings, an 8K with the SEC, states more formally that Faria was "removed" from his positions on the same date by the "unanimous written consent of the members of the company’s board of directors", which included Keeler, chief financial officer Chris Constable, and Nubar Herian, also the CEO of Monaco Group Holdings. 

Faria was further taken off the board before he was let go as an executive, explained Keeler, who has resumed the CEO title in addition to his existing chief sustainability officer role.

Read this story in full here.

While in China, Tom and Matt reported the breaking story that Russian authorities had blocked major Chilean salmon exporters on alleged sanitary concerns, leaving only a small number of firms with access to the market. 

Individual plants belonging to Mitsubishi’s Cermaq Group, Nova Austral and Productos del Mar Ventisqueros were placed on so-called red alert in October, which blocks access to the Russian market, according to Russia’s Federal Service for Veterinary and Phytosanitary Surveillance (known as Rosselkhoznadzor).

Ventisqueros was blocked for alleged traces of cadmium found in fish, Cermaq for oxytetracycline and Nova Austral for crystal violet, according to Rosselkhoznadzor. The issue was a major talking point at the China show and also came as Chilean companies face major issues getting salmon out of the country, due to the widespread protests in the country over inequality.  

Another wave of companies was also put on yellow alert, which implies that shipments will come under greater scrutiny from inspectors. These include Cermaq’s Puerto Fernandez plant, allegedly for listeria, Inversiones Cohuin for UV, Multiexport Foods for traces of arsenic and Salmones Aysen for cadmium. Being under yellow status makes it very hard to continue exporting to Russia, an industry source told Undercurrent. Pesquera Torres del Paine is under blue status for crystal violet, meaning an outcome is pending.

AquaChile was left as one of the few companies with clearance to export, a source said.

Read this story in full, here.

Louis, meanwhile, revealed plans for Pelagic Fishery City -- the extraordinary centerpiece of Zhoushan National Pelagic Fishery Base (ZNPFB), which should become the world's largest pelagic fishing base on the country's eastern seaboard.

A doughnut-shaped structure made of glass and steel, it resembles more closely a sports stadium built for a football World Cup than a traditional Chinese seafood wet market. Construction workers buzz around on motorbikes and trucks on an encircling road lined with newly planted trees.

“In two weeks’ time, we will hold the grand opening ceremony here. This will be cleared away before then,” Tina Shu, assistant manager at ZNPFB Construction Development Group, told Undercurrent, gesturing towards debris from construction scattered outside. 

An exhibition and conference center, office space and trading area, Pelagic Fishery City will handle much of the CNY 10 billion ($1.41bn) worth of seafood expected to be traded annually at ZNPFB, according to Shu. "It's the heart of ZNPFB."

Read all about it here.

Back in the US, Jason Huffman reported California’s 570 Dungeness crab harvesters were hoping to get news on Friday that would allow many of them to get back on the water within the next two weeks after a longer than usual break.

That’s when Charlton “Chuck” Bonham, director of the California Department of Fish & Wildlife (CDFW), was expected to deliver the pre-season assessment of the fishery by the California Dungeness Crab Fishing Gear Working Group, including an evaluation on the risk of future whale and other mammal entanglements with crab trap ropes. The opening dates for the 2019-2020 season should be announced soon after.

This after the months-early closure in April of both California Dungeness crab fishing zones as part of a settlement reached between CDFW and the Center for Biological Diversity over concerns about entanglements with humpback and blue whales as well as Pacific leatherback sea turtles.

Read more on this here.

In the UK, news emerged that after battling over the chilled Asda cod, haddock and salmon contracts, UK processors Young’s Seafood and New England Seafood International (NESI) are at it again.

Undercurrent understands J. Sainsbury is putting its natural, chilled whitefish up for tender, putting the UK’s first and third largest processors against each other. NESI will be vying for the roughly £25 million-£30m in cod and haddock Young’s does for Sainsbury’s, sources said.

During the long-running Young’s sale, which resulted in the company being bought by CapVest Partners-owned pig processor Hilton Food Group, Sainsbury’s did a “range review” on its whitefish, now seen as a precursor to the tender. 

The tender means a busy start defending the business for Simon Smith, who started as CEO of Young’s on Oct. 16, having left Seachill UK in the summer. 

NESI -- which has just offloaded around £10m-£15m in foodservice business from its Grimsby plant -- missed out on getting £30m in Asda salmon from Young’s in August, and is said to be aggressively looking for more volume for the factory. NESI had won around £17m in cod and haddock business for Asda from Young’s the previous year and was said to be confident about getting the salmon, but the latter held onto the business at the “11th hour”, as sources put it at the time.

However, sources said all of the Sainsbury’s whitefish business is on the table, so NESI will need to fight for its seabass and sea bream supply in the retailer, said to be worth around £10m.

Read this in full here.

Omega Protein may have succeeded in securing a Marine Stewardship Council certification last month for the Atlantic menhaden fishery, but it now faces the potential of having its ability to harvest there at least temporarily taken away or reduced.

That is, unless president Donald Trump's administration intervenes.

The Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission’s (ASMFC’s) menhaden management board voted unanimously (15-0) on Monday last week, during its meeting in Newcastle, New Hampshire, to find the US state of Virginia out of compliance with its total acceptable catch limit of 51,000 metric tons for the Chesapeake Bay in 2019.

Officials from two of the federal regulatory agencies -- the National Marine Fisheries Service and US Fish & Wildlife Service -- abstained.

Omega Protein, a Houston, Texas-based division of New Brunswick, Canada-based seafood giant Cooke, catches nearly all of Virginia's menhaden quota and voluntarily admitted, in September, that it was going to exceed the threshold. The company initially said it would stay within the 87,216t cap that the state of Virginia recognizes, but later announced that it would instead catch no more than a self-imposed limit of 67,000t.

Ben Landry, a spokesman for the company, told Undercurrent that fishing in the area under scrutiny wrapped up roughly a week prior.

Read the full story here.

Back in Europe, Matilde Mereghetti reported on the European Commission's view that Spain overfished its tuna quota in the Indian Ocean in 2017. As a result, the amount caught in excess by the Spanish fleet that year has been deducted from the country's fishing quota for 2019.

The quotas were introduced in May 2016 by the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC) as part of a recovery plan for overfished Indian Ocean yellowfin tuna stocks, which are still overfished, according to a recent report by the International Seafood Sustainability Foundation. 

In 2017, Spain exceeded its allocated fishing quota for yellowfin tuna in the IOTC area of competence by 2,465t. Only 327t could be deducted from the 2018 Spanish quota, given that year's total. The remaining quantity has therefore been deducted from the quota for 2019, the EU communicated on Oct. 15.

The EU is the only IOTC contracting party that has implemented such corrective measures, an EU Commission official stressed. The IOTC did not foresee any mechanism for paying back the overshoot, and the EU implemented such payback based on its own regulation, the EU official also pointed out.

Read this in full here.

Finally, Tom reported that a firm specializing in providing financing for seafood projects ranging from massive recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) facilities to vessel acquisitions is seeking to raise its first aqua asset-backed private debt fund for institutional investors interested in supporting sustainable seafood enterprises.

Lighthouse Finance -- which has provided funding and advisory services for some of the industry's largest players -- has received strong early interest from investors representing several billion dollars in capital to deploy, Roy Hoias, its CEO, told Undercurrent.

"The fund will also meet the top standard for sustainable investing by incorporating key sustainability metrics in its underwriting criteria," he said. 

Lighthouse plans to raise two €500m tranches for its own fund, to meet strong demand and act faster, said Hoias.

At the moment, Lighthouse is seeing unprecedented demand for capital in the sector and is involved in “five or six” RAS projects globally, as well as three big offshore projects, Hoias said. That’s not to mention the demand for “conventional” seafood investments, such as aquaculture equipment, vessels, and plants.

Read the full story here.

title: John West cleared of past IUU fishing charges
content:
UK-based Thai Union Group subsidiary John West Foods has been cleared of doing business directly connected to illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing (IUU), with which it had previously been charged.

John West indicted on eight counts of alleged past IUU fishing connections

The firm had originally been indicted on eight counts of alleged past connections to IUU fishing by the UK's Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) on Jan. 2, 2018, a story broken by Undercurrent News earlier this year.

The indictment related to events alleged to have occurred between March 1, 2012, and Feb. 28, 2014, at the major UK trading port of Felixstowe in Suffolk.

However, the lengthy legal proceedings brought at the instigation of the UK's Marine Management Organization (MMO) ultimately found John West not guilty on all counts.

The MMO's investigation became known in August 2013, when the MMO notified John West that it had begun investigating IUU fishing out of Ghana. Four years later, the MMO brought charges against John West, targeting criminal charges that could have cost the firm a considerable sum. 

The first hearing of John West's case took place before the Crown Court of Newcastle upon Tyne on Jan. 26, 2018, while the next substantive hearing was to be a preliminary hearing in October 2019 at Southwark Crown Court, the MMO told Undercurrent in March.

However, the Crown Prosecution Service reportedly offered no evidence against John West at the hearing on Oct. 30, leading to verdicts of not guilty against the firm on all counts.

“Throughout the process we have cooperated completely with the MMO and its investigators and have been fully transparent with them," said David Sankowicz, legal affairs director at Thai Union, in a release.

"We welcome the not guilty verdicts that have been recorded on all counts, Thai Union Group and all our subsidiary companies are fully committed to complying with legal codes in all of the areas in which we source our products. Legal and responsible sourcing has always been, and will continue to be, the top priority for our business.”

title: US crab importer Blue Star parts with CEO, trims US Foods biz, counters poor financials
content:
Blue Star Foods, the Miami, Florida-based blue and red swimming crab importer and exporter, is dealing with the acrimonious parting of its president and CEO and the gradual winnowing down of its relationship with US Foods as a major buyer, while simultaneously being forced to confront a less-than-glowing quarterly filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).

Carlos Faria, who joined Blue Star in January 2018, told Undercurrent News recently that he voluntarily resigned from his positions on Aug. 1 over differences of opinion with his former longtime friend John Keeler, the company founder and executive chairman, in relation to growth strategy and what he said were "serious concerns" about supply management practices. 

Keeler instead maintains that Faria was fired, suggesting he was not attentive to his position, and characterized him as a "vindictive" former employee. He said Faria refused to sign a termination agreement that would've included a "generous severance package".

Carlos Faria, the former CEO and president of Blue Star Foods.

One of Blue Star's most recent public filings, an 8K, with the SEC, states more formally that Faria was "removed" from his positions on the same date by the "unanimous written consent of the members of the company’s board of directors", which included Keeler, chief financial officer Chris Constable, and Nubar Herian, also the CEO of Monaco Group Holdings. 

Faria was further taken off the board before he was let go as an executive, explained Keeler, who has resumed the CEO title in addition to his existing chief sustainability officer role.

Seafax gave Blue Star 'high risk' payer rating in September

Regardless of who you believe, the dispute between Faria and Keeler sheds a surprising negative light on a company that was, less than a year ago, reported to be one of the five largest in the US' $700 million per year imported swimming crab industry and maintained an optimistic outlook for near-future growth.

Faria told Undercurrent in April 2018, a few months after he came to work for Blue Star, that he was there to help take it public, something that happened quietly less than a year later. He and Keeler spelled out what they said was an agreed-upon tack of buying up other companies with a diversified group of species, beyond crabmeat, and branding each new acquisition as following Blue Star's "triple-bottom-line" or "3BL" approach. 

The term, popularized in the 1990s, describes an effort by a company to satisfy social, environmental and financial goals.  

To Faria's disappointment, he said, Keeler has more eagerly pursued growth by attempting to instead acquire more crabmeat and crab-related companies.

But Faria emphasized that his differences with Keeler over acquisition strategy were not as great as many other practices he said he observed at Blue Star, including, in particular, the company's interactions with packers, where other sources also expressed concerns to Undercurrent. 

Blue Star Foods founder John Keeler poses with one of the devices used to track blue swimming crab harvests in Indonesia and the Philippines.

Seafax, a Portland, Maine-based company that's provided credit ratings on seafood buyers and sellers for more than 25 years, in September gave Blue Star a "high-risk" payer rating and chopped 74 points out of its overall pay score, dropping it to a 17 out of a possible 100 tally. Seafax, which updated Blue Star's score based on an appraisal done in July, said the company pays 23 days late, on average.

Keeler told Undercurrent this week that he is not having the problems with suppliers that've been suggested, but has been completely transparent and owes the handful of companies he secures crabmeat from in Indonesia, the Philippines, China and Sri Lanka no more than a combined $434,000, which he said was 1.4% of his projected annual revenue of roughly $30m. The average amount owed to each supplier is $50,000, he said.

Blue Star opened its new plant in Sri Lanka earlier in the year, he said.

Keeler was dismissive of the Seafax report, too, saying the credit reporting agency had a very limited awareness of Blue Star's foreign business relationships and lowered its ratings in response to the company's filings with the SEC. 

"We have purchased sporadically crabmeat when other importers are long in their inventories," Keeler wrote in an email. "We use the power of cash terms to get the best deal possible."

Blue Star’s most recent quarterly report, filed with the SEC to cover the three-month period ended on June 30, does show some apparent chinks in the company's financial armor. 

Credit: Rabbit_Photo/Shutterstock.com

Blue Star had total assets of $11.0m and total liabilities of $12.6m, during the time covered by the filing. It was operating in the red, showing a net loss of $952,796 on revenue of $7.5m, a drop of 474% in net income and 14% less in sales compared to the same period in 2018.   

The SEC report also noted, over the most recently completed six-month period, an accumulated deficit of $6.1m and a working capital deficit of nearly $2.0m with current liabilities inclusive of $2.9m in stockholder loans that are described as being subordinated to the provider of the working capital facility.

The company had $1.3m in cashflow from operating activities during the first six months of 2019, less than half the $3.1m it saw during the same period in 2018. It owed nearly $1.4m in accounts payable and accruable at the end of the first six months of 2019, compared to nearly $1m in the first six months of 2018.

All of which, Blue Star advised in its SEC filing, raise “substantial doubt as to the company’s ability to continue as a going concern”. 

But Keeler told Undercurrent that there are several elements of his company's public filings that make it look to be in much worse of a state than it actually is, including the $2.9 million loan that he said is from one of his personal holdings.

The $2.9m "is subordinated to the lender and from a practical standpoint is equity, while [generally accepted accounting principles don't] allow it to be shown that way. The true [working capital] position of the company at June 30, 2019, after considering that the loan is subordinated, is $919,236," he said.

In a statement provided by Keeler, CFO Constable further explained that the net loss includes $670,967 in non-cash expenses related to stockholder compensation. 

US Foods relationship termination explained

One of the major reasons that Blue Star, in its SEC filing, said it has dropped so much revenue recently is due to "market softness". A recent review by Undercurrent confirms that the price on blue swimming crab has been declining since at least May 2018.

Another big reason for the drop in sales, the company acknowledged, is the gradual sizing down of a relationship with a major buyer.

The SEC filing shows Blue Star in the middle of reducing the amount of crabmeat it provides Rosemont, Illinois-based distribution giant US Foods for use in its private label "Harbor Banks" products. In the latest quarterly report, the company indicates it gave up 82,000 lbs in private label business with the company during the previous three months.

Sources told Undercurrent that the US Foods relationship was even larger, accounting for between 500,000 and a million lbs. of crab annually, and was once responsible for roughly 40% of the company's annual sales. 

Keeler didn't dispute the size of the relationship with US Foods, but stressed in his call with Undercurrent that it was Blue Star's decision to gradually shrink its private label business as the margins are not as good as those achieved by the company's sale of its own brands.  

"We are ending all private label sales, including [the] Harbor Banks brand," he said in an email. "It is a corporate initiative to increase our enterprise value through our own trademarks as to [where] pasteurized crabmeat is concerned."

Keeler said he was pushed to the decision by the combination of 0.48% growth in crabmeat import volume from 2015 to 2018 and the surge in raw material and selling prices (about 30%) in 2018.  

The private label business model "has a taxing marketing dollar percentage added to the cost, resulting in [lower margins] compared to our trademarks, ultimately [causing] a higher degree of demand destruction..." 

However, private label sales remained 22% of the overall volume of crab sold by Blue Star during the first nine months of the year, Keeler said, adding: "The company continues to sell its Blue Star brand to US Food Service and other major broadliners."

Much of the US Foods' crabmeat supply relationship, meanwhile, has been taken over by Tri-Union Seafoods’ Chicken of the Sea, part of Thai Union Group, one of the US' largest crabmeat importers, and Harbor Seafood, a New Hyde Park, New York-based company, sources told Undercurrent.

An official at Harbor Seafood could not be reached at press time and Chicken of the Sea officials were prevented from talking about their supplier relationships. A US Foods spokesperson emailed a somewhat vague statement in response to Undercurrent's request for comment.

"US Foods regularly evaluates our vendor relationships based on a number of different factors and we occasionally change vendor relationships based on the evolving needs of our business or the vendor’s business," said the US Foods spokesperson, adding, when pressed by Undercurrent for more details, that the company doesn't "disclose the terms of our relationship agreements".  

Bonamar assignee drops suit

A peek under the hood of Blue Star's recent borrowing activity is interesting, too.

According to its SEC filings, the company has maintained a $14m revolving credit line with Tarrytown, New York-based ACF Finco I since late August 2016. The line of credit has been amended several times and certain financial covenants of the line were not satisfied. Prior to June 30, there was a violation of the "fixed charge ratio" and, starting in August, the default interest rate was raised by 3%.

Keeler told Undercurrent that the line remains available to Blue Star.

Filling a Blue Star Foods-labeled can. Image courtesy of Blue Star Foods.

"It is common for amendments such as these to take place with a lender over the course of the contract, mainly to adjust to the changing needs of the market, the supplier base and customer base of the borrower. The lender remains a committed partner to [John Keeler & Co]", he said, referring to Blue Star by the name given to its consolidated subsidiary.

Another loan identified in the SEC filing is one for $1 million that was made to Blue Star on March 26 by Kenar Overseas Corp., a company registered in Panama. It had a maturity date of July 26, but Keeler told Undercurrent that the loan has been extended and remains available to help the company meeting working capital needs.

The timing of when the Kenar loan was made correlates closely to when Blue Star spent some $4.4m to purchase 34,433 cases of crabmeat from the now defunct Miami crab import and export rival Bonamar Corp. The  loan was made by board member Herian and not directly related to the Bonamar crab purchase but provided at roughly the same time, Keelar told Undercurrent.

In a lawsuit filed May 8, James Howard, Bonamar’s assignee, charged Blue Star with not paying some $315,000 outstanding to close the deal. Blue Star argued at the time that the amount was held back as “retainage”, in the event that some of the crabmeat was not delivered or found to be in bad condition, for example.

The lawsuit was recently dropped by Howard, however, court records reveals.

High school friends

The acquisition of crabmeat was one of several aggressive moves made by Blue Star over the past several months under Faria’s and Keeler’s joint leadership. In April, a month after Undercurrent reported the details of the Bonamar deal, the company revealed that it was in the process of going public via reverse merger, an effort that generated about a million dollars in new capital.

It was the realization of one of Faria's goals when he joined Blue Star a little more than a year earlier.

A crab fishing boat in the Philippines. Photograph courtesy of Blue Star Foods.

At press time, Blue Star's stock was still not posted as available on the public market. Keeler said the company has applied for its ticker symbol with the Financial Institution Regulatory Authority and should have approval within months. 

Faria has known Keeler since before 1995, the year he started the company in his Miami, Florida, home. They went to high school together in Venezuela. And Faria, a financial analyst by education, worked briefly at Blue Star before, from 2005 until 2012, serving as a senior vice president. It was his first job in the seafood industry.

From 2012 until 2015, Faria was a VP of operations for Chicken of the Sea  and based in Lake Success, New York, before joining Seattle, Washington-based frozen seafood producer Aqua Star to serve as its VP of procurement for four years. It was the job he held before rejoining Blue Star.

Max Christenson, who also joined Blue Star in January 2018 – just before Faria -- to serve as its national marketing director, departed the company in May 2019 to work as the new US national director of sales and marketing for Charoen Pokphand Foods (CP Foods). He knew Faria from his time serving as a regional sales manager at Chicken of the Sea (July 2013-January 2016).

But Christenson told Undercurrent this week that his parting from Blue Star had nothing to do with the recent rift between Faria and Keeler.

'[W]e realize that we were not taking the easiest path'

Keeler on Thursday told Undercurrent that he recognized how off-putting the financials and statements in his public filings might appear, but he said that, "outside of the significant costs of building a public vehicle, the company has invested in both its business analytics and its sustainability platforms that will create value as it adds companies and species".

Blue Star Foods being presented on October 16, 2019 with the "Environmental Innovation Award" for 2019 by the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry in relation to its cloud-based traceability applications and environmental initiatives.

He estimated that Blue Star has spent nearly $500,000 in those two areas over the past 18 months, investments that he said were paying off.

He noted that the company was presented on October 16 with the "Environmental Innovation Award" for 2019 by the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry in relation to its cloud-based traceability applications and environmental initiatives. The award was presented, in Manila, to Blue Star's Ronnie Florentino and Lloyd Fernandez in the presence of Philippines vice president Leni Robredo. 

"We realize that we were not taking the easiest path by building the company in this manner, but we believe that we have a strong strategy, and are only now building the foundation of that strategy," Keeler told Undercurrent. "Once that foundation is set, and we can begin to add the bricks, we are confident that the picture to the outside world will change significantly."

title: British Columbia group self-suspends MSC certification for wild salmon
content:
The Canadian Pacific Sustainable Fisheries Society (CPSFS) has self-suspended its Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certification for the sockeye, pink and chum salmon fisheries in British Columbia, effective Nov. 27, the organization has announced.

Its members represent most processors and exporters of wild salmon.

“Everyone who cares about wild salmon in British Columbia should be worried," said the CPSFS's Christina Burridge, who is also executive director of the BC Seafood Alliance, adding in a statement that the decision means "there will now be no independent oversight of how Fisheries and Oceans Canada Pacific Region (DFO) manages these fisheries". 

“Though we are disappointed, saddened and frustrated to be forced out of the program,” she said, “we believe the fishery is sustainable and we are working on a plan to have these difficulties addressed in order to have the fishery evaluated and re-certified by the MSC at a future date.”

Worst year on record

The news of the voluntary suspension follows multiple reports of the worst year on record for sockeye salmon returns in BC, causing many in the province's fishing industry to ask for emergency relief and consumers there to instead purchase Alaskan sockeye.

According to the Fraser River Panel, 557,000 sockeye returned this year, not the nearly 5 million predicted by DFO, causing many fisheries to be closed.

Credit: Troutnut/Shutterstock.com

Climate change, overfishing and habitat destruction have all been blamed for the decline. The Fraser River water levels measured 7% lower and 2 degrees warmer than average on Sept. 5.

MSC had first certified its wild salmon fisheries, with the exception of North and Central Coast chums, in 2010, the year of a massive sockeye return, notes the statement from the CPSFS. The fisheries were re-certified in 2017, including North and Central Coast chum, with 22 conditions that require annual reporting through an audit on progress against milestones.

A year-one audit in October 2018 found nine of the 22 conditions were behind target, almost all of which were about North and Central Coast stock assessment and evaluating the effects of hatcheries on wild populations, Burridge recounted.

In late 2016, the group had agreed on a client action plan with DFO to meet the conditions and the annual milestones. The year-one targets required a plan for stock assessment and for evaluating the effect salmon enhancement, she said.

"We realized early this year that DFO was unable to deliver on those commitments so we hired external help to deliver the plans,” she explained. “But we see little practical commitment to implement those plans from DFO.  We might well pass the 2019 audit but we see little prospect of meeting the 2020 requirements.”

The self-suspension reinforces a letter sent by DFO area directors to senior management a year ago expressing concern that “the regional ability to meet well-established core salmon assessment programs is no longer possible with the allocated funding, she said.

Pain will be felt in European markets

But the Vancouver, BC-based David Suzuki Foundation issued a statement on Friday that included more stinging criticisms of DFO.

The Suzuki group noted that an independent 2018 audit of BC's wild salmon fisheries reported that the government and industry remained behind in trying to meet 40% of the conditions found wanting in 2017, including those related to improvements to fishery monitoring, better stock assessments and reducing impacts on wild salmon populations from harvesting hatchery-raised salmon. 

“A benefit of the MSC certification is that it requires the fishery to address key gaps, including lack of monitoring, dealing with the risks of hatcheries and protecting salmon biodiversity,” said Jeffery Young, senior science and policy analyst for the Suzuki group. “Despite having close to a decade to act, the government has failed to deliver on its promises to help the BC fishery meet certification requirements.”

“The inability to meet even minimum standards for sustainability is an indictment of Ottawa’s management of BC’s salmon,” said Greg Taylor, a fisheries consultant and former industry executive quoted in the statement.

He added: “The loss of MSC certification will be particularly noted in major European markets where many retailers require it. It will also mean programs like Ocean Wise, SeaChoice and Seafood Watch will no longer be able to recommend B.C. as a sustainable source of wild-caught salmon.”

The Suzuki group also took a few shots at the MSC itself, saying it "set a very low bar for wild salmon sustainability," certifying only whether management system provides for a sustained harvest and not certifying whether the fishery "meets the needs of ecosystems, bears, whales and other wildlife, or whether it is sustainable in the face of climate change”.

The low bar comment drew a response from Jay Lugar, program director for MSC in Canada. He said the MSC salmon standard was "developed over four years to bring precision to salmon management approaches" and includes the fishery's impact on the wider ecosystem and its component. 

"Only well-managed fisheries that ensure the long-term sustainability of fish stocks and keep ecosystems healthy can achieve MSC certification," he said.

title: Judge won’t allow prosecutors to use ‘FAD-free’ evidence at Lischewski trial
content:
A California judge has sided with former Bumble Bee Foods CEO Chris Lischewski's request to disallow federal prosecutors from introducing evidence at his upcoming trial that would have asserted that the tuna canner and its rivals agreed not to sell tuna caught without using fish aggregating devices (FAD).

According to a report from Law360, San Francisco, California-based judge Edward Chen granted Lischewski's motion to exclude the evidence from being introduced at the November trial.

Earlier this year, Lischewski's lawyers unsuccessfully sought to dismiss the entire criminal price-fixing case against him based on a claim that it violates his First Amendment rights but Chen declined to grant this request. 

Lawyers for Lischewski, who was indicted by the US Department of Justice (DOJ) in May 2018, argued in a March 6 brief that the prosecutors accused him of agreeing with others in industry to "limit and restrict competition" for "certain types of fishing methods".

This, the former CEO's lawyers argued, was an allusion to allegations -- described in civil suits from canned tuna buyers -- that Bumble Bee, Thai Union Group's Tri-Union Seafoods, which trades as Chicken of the Sea International, and StarKist & Co, agreed not to sell tuna products using raw material caught without using FADs.

Advocacy groups such as Greenpeace have pushed for tuna companies to discontinue the use of FADs, which would raise the price of canned tuna by some 25% and reduce consumer demand, Lischewski's lawyers wrote in a motion to dismiss the indictment.

But Chen denied the motion to dismiss in a May 24 court order, ruling that the First Amendment argument was not relevant.

"He argues it was lawful to collectively agree to not sell FAD-free tuna. As the court has explained herein, a means of furthering a conspiracy can be lawful. Defendant’s contention that his FAD agreements were protected by the First Amendment is also irrelevant," the judge wrote.

title: StarKist fined $100m for price-fixing conspiracy
content:
SAN FRANCISCO, California, US -- StarKist & Co. will have to pay a $100 million fine for having engaged in a price-fixing conspiracy, the largest amount paid by the US 'big three' canners that participated.  

Concluding a sentencing process that was prolonged by disputes between the Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania-based company and the US Department of Justice (DOJ) over how much the company could afford to pay, U.S. District Court judge Edward Chen ruled that the $100m amount was appropriate. 

Judge Edward Chen in the US District Court for the Northern District of California

The fine could have ranged between $50m and $100m. It will be paid over a five-year period with $5m due within 30 days. In 2020, the company will pay an additional $11m with four annual payments of $24m to come between 2021 and 2024. The company will also be placed on probation for 13 months. The payments will be made without interest.  

Chen said he found that StarKist did not demonstrate that the amount of the fine should be reduced from the $100m figure,

"It is my conclusion that there will be enough assets available," he said of the company's ability to pay.

'[S]peaking out of the heart'

In August, Chen had asked both parties to negotiate a payment arrangement with more "flexibility" as both had held firm to their staked out positions. The DOJ wanted StarKist to pay $100m, which StarKist claimed could "bankrupt" it or limit the company's ability to pay the $518m in claims from the distributors, retailers and other customers that sued it claiming damage from the price-fixing. 

Andrew Mast, a DOJ attorney, previously argued that paying restitution to victims of the price-fixing scheme wasn't part of the company's plea agreement with the government.

“I think that your honor has sufficient information in front of you that StarKist can pay a $100m fine and go about paying the civil claims,” he said. 

At the Sept. 11 hearing, Scott Meece, StarKist's general counsel, addressed the court, saying he was "speaking out of the heart about the company" and on behalf of its 2,600 US employees.

Credit: OoddySmile Studio / Shutterstock

"These employees have had this hanging over their heads for a long time. I've meant the majority of them. Great people and they're worried about what is going to happen to their jobs," he said. 

Meece said that StarKist "will probably have to make some kind of cuts" and could consider moving out of American Samoa to Thailand or carry out layoffs.

"Hopefully, we can find ways where we don't harm any employees but I have concerns about that," he said.

In determining the sentence, federal guidelines required Chen to start the fine at $100m and make discounts if StarKist can demonstrate by "preponderance of the evidence", that is that it's more likely than not, that the company is unable to pay the maximum.

Merger delayed

Chen said that although StarKist, which is owned by South Korea's Dongwon Enterprise, appears to have $250m in assets, the situation is complicated because around $155m of that represents its stake in Techpack Solutions, a maker of glass and plastic bottles that StarKist says it is unable to sell at this time.

Techpack is slated to be merged in the future with another Dongwon affiliate, Dongwon Systems, at which time StarKist will receive shares that it can turn into cash. But Lynch said that overcapacity in the bottle making industry means that, currently, valuations of bottlemakers are not high. 

The merger has been delayed but not for any reason related to the sentencing proceeding. Lynch said previously.

Chen added that in the future if StarKist is unable to pay the fine, it can make its argument to the DOJ which can then ask to have the fine lowered. 

StarKist's plea signals the beginning of the end of criminal proceedings that have dogged the "big three" US canners since allegations first emerged in 2015 that the firms conspired to fix prices at an artificially high level. 

Bumble Bee pleaded guilty to criminal price-fixing charges last year and agreed to pay a $25m fine to the Department of Justice (DOJ). Bumble Bee could have faced a $136m penalty if its ability to pay wasn't taken into account, DOJ officials wrote in a sentencing memorandum. Bumble Bee's fine could rise to a maximum of $81m in the event of a sale of the company.

Lischewski to face trial in November

The other big US tuna canner alleged to have fixed prices, Thai Union's Tri-Union, has avoided a criminal conviction and fine because the company acted as a whistleblower to the DOJ, informing on its rivals in exchange for leniency. 

Additionally, StarKist's Stephen Hodge, a former senior vice president of sales at the company, has pleaded guilty to a charge of price fixing. He has yet to be sentenced.

Christopher Lischewski.

Two former Bumble Bee employees, Ken Worsham and Walter Scott Cameron, both longtime sales executives have also pleaded guilty but have yet to be sentenced. 

Christopher Lischewski, Bumble Bee's longtime CEO who stepped down after he was indicted on price-fixing charges, has denied wrongdoing and pleaded not guilty. He is expected to face trial in November and could face testimony from other participants in the alleged conspiracy.

Meanwhile, the companies have been settling many of the more than 100 civil lawsuits brought against them by the distributors, wholesalers and individuals who bought tuna at reportedly inflated prices.
