title: DOJ can allege pouch tuna collusion at Lischewski trial, but not salmon or sardines
content:
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) will be able to refer to allegedly collusive communications about prices of tuna pouches at the trial of former Bumble Bee Foods CEO Chris Lischewski, but not other species, a judge ruled last week. 

As charged in the DOJ indictment, beginning in or about November 2010 until December 2013, Lischewski knowing participated in a conspiracy to fix prices of canned tuna specifically. However, the DOJ will also be able to allege collusion on pouch tuna, after an Aug. 28 order from Edward Chen, a judge in the court for the northern district of California. Chen ordered the DOJ “may introduce evidence of discussions about pouched tuna and prices, but not sardines and salmon”.

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion
Read more

Chen’s order came after a hearing on what evidence can be included in Lischewski’s trial. The order gives DOJ permission to use the evidence the former Bumble Bee CEO tried unsuccessfully to recruit David Roszmann, the former chief operating officer of Thai Union Group’s US shelf-stable operations, into the conspiracy. The DOJ, however, will need to further convince Chen it should use an email sent by Renato Curto, former Tri Marine CEO, as evidence against Lischewski. Another hearing is set for Sept. 4, where the Curto email and other matters will be covered.

The Judge's Aug. 28 order chalks up some victories for the DOJ and some for Lischewski, whose legal team has successfully omitted evidence about his ownership of tuna vessels as another driver for the alleged conspiracy and a letter sent by a former employee to owner Lion Capital, alleging collusive activity (more on this below). 

In a document filed in the run-up to the Aug. 28 hearing, the DOJ pushed to widen the evidence given from just canned tuna. At the very outset of the conspiracy, Scott Cameron of Bumble Bee, who has pled guilty to price-fixing and is co-operating with the government, talked to Chuck Handford of StarKist about the price of pouch tuna, the DOJ said.

“They agreed that Bumble Bee would not attack StarKist’s market share in pouch tuna, and that StarKist in turn would refrain from aggressively pricing canned albacore, Bumble Bee’s most important product,” the DOJ alleges. Throughout the conspiracy, the competitors continued to exchange email and verbal “jabs” complaining about each other’s retail pricing for sardines, salmon, and pouch tuna products.”

Feds push to use Tri Marine CEO’s email as price-fixing evidence against Lischewski

Although price fixing of canned tuna is the focus of the case the DOJ is bringing against Lischewski, the US government had alleged the conspiracy applied to other product categories and species.

The DOJ sought to include evidence of what it claims is collusion on other products and species outside canned tuna, such as pouches and sardines, as they are “inextricably intertwined with the charged conspiracy”.

Lischewski’s legal team argued this not relevant to the specific conspiracy he’s being charged for, which judge Chen partly agreed with.

According to the DOJ document, Lischewski is said to have confronted Shue Wing Chan, the former CEO of Thai Union-owned Tri-Union Seafoods, which trades as Chicken of the Sea International (COSI), about its cheap pricing at a Milton’s restaurant meeting in March 2012, then began to email Chan examples of low pricing he was seeing in the marketplace.

“Similarly, in May 2012, defendant emailed Chan about COSI’s sardine pricing, commenting “WOW . . . can I source sardines from you?”,” the DOJ claims.

“Evidence of competitor communications regarding the pricing of other seafood products is inextricably intertwined with the charged price-fixing conspiracy, is not unfairly prejudicial, and thus is admissible against defendant,” the DOJ alleges. “For example, conversations about pouch tuna helped maintain the price-fixing conspiracy with regards to canned tuna.”

Prosecutors get OK to argue Lischewski tried to recruit Roszmann into price-fixing 

Documents exchanged during the conspiracy refer to competitor pricing information on canned tuna as well as pricing on other items such as pouch, salmon, or sardines, the DOJ said.

The Bumble Bee, COSI and StarKist executives involved “discussed this evidence together because monitoring pricing on other products helped the conspirators monitor compliance with the conspiracy”.

However, after Chen’s ruling, only evidence of alleged collusion involving pouch tuna will be permitted at the trial.

Chen rejects DOJ’s effort to use Lischewski’s ownership of tuna vessels as evidence

The judge granted Lischewski’s motion to have mention of his ownership of fishing vessels excluded from evidence at the trail.

According to the DOJ, Lischewski’s ownership stake in fishing boats managed by South Pacific Tuna Corporation (SOPAC) gave him another reason to fix prices. The DOJ was seeking to include evidence from an August dinner conversation between Lischewski, Cameron and Ken Worsham, another former Bumble Bee executive. Worsham, like Cameron, has also pled guilty to price fixing and is set to testify against his former boss at a trial set for November.

At the August 2013 dinner with Cameron, Worsham and others, Lischewski allegedly discussed “his ownership interest in the SOPAC fishing boats, celebrated the profits his fishing boats were making due to the high market prices for tuna, and showed Cameron and Worsham financial statements and reports demonstrating this fact”.

So, “the price-fixing conspiracy allowed defendant to capture profit from high prices on both sides of the market”, the DOJ alleged. “Indeed, the evidence will show that raw fish prices increased substantially during the conspiracy period.”

Lawyers acting for Lischewski countered that the evidence is unfairly prejudicial and inadmissible, as it does not relate to Bumble Bee, a position Chen ultimately agreed with.

Letter to Lion Capital also excluded

The DOJ also granted Lischewski’s motion to exclude a letter from a “disgruntled former employee, Charlie Simmons”, sent to Lion Capital, the firm’s private equity owner, alleging price-fixing at Bumble Bee, Chen ruled.

Simmons, a former Bumble Bee salesman, alerted an executive with Lion Capital to possible price-fixing back in 2012, according to evidence the DOJ wants to introduce in the upcoming trial of long-time Bumble Bee CEO Lischewski.

The DOJ also wanted to use an email that Eric Lindberg -- a former partner with Lion who left the firm in September 2016 not long after the price-fixing allegations emerged --sent to Lischewski with an attached, unsigned letter from Simmons.  

Simmons sent the letter to Lindberg on Jan. 31, 2012, alleging “Potential Anticompetitive Activity: Emails, Meetings, Phone Calls to Competitors Suggesting to Raise Prices” among the management team at Bumble Bee and citing the Sherman Antitrust Act. The letter also named several executive positions, including the company’s then-senior vice presidents of sales, Cameron, and trade Marketing, Worsham.

Former Chicken of the Sea VP could testify against Lischewski

A number of executive positions, including Cameron and Worsham “have some explaining to do”, the letter reportedly states. “The entire company is being jeopardized”, it continues.

The email and letter were sent during the alleged conspiracy, which the DOJ claims ran from November 2010 until December 2013.

The DOJ hoped to use the Simmons letter at Lischewski’s trial, which is set for November this year, as well as the former CEO’s response, to show he was aware both of the conspiracy and Cameron and Worsham’s communications with competitors “in furtherance thereof”. The email and letter have not been submitted in the court docket.

Lischewski’s legal team argued that the email and attached letter ought to be excluded from evidence, on the grounds that it’s reliant on hearsay and can’t be properly authenticated.

“Because the Simmons letter and defendant’s subsequent email reacting to the letter show that, at a minimum, defendant was on notice of the conspiratorial activities of his subordinates, they are highly relevant to a central issue in this case: whether defendant knowingly participated in the charged price-fixing conspiracy by authorizing the actions of Cameron and Worsham,” the DOJ said.

Lischewski received a copy of the letter from Lindberg and responded to it just one week after it was postmarked, on Feb. 6, 2012.

Bolton tipped as favorite for Clover Leaf as Bumble Bee brings in turnaround adviser 

The DOJ plans to use the letter and Lischewski’s response to “show that the accusations in the letter regarding price-fixing were sent to defendant, that defendant responded to the letter but said nothing about the price-fixing allegations contained within it, and that he was, at minimum, on notice of the price-fixing conspiracy and the anticompetitive actions and communications of his subordinates”.

The government also expects to offer testimony from Cameron and Worsham that Lischewski never spoke to them about alleged antitrust violations and never told them not to talk to competitors, it said.

Lischewski’s legal team has said the fact it’s unsigned undermines its credibility, but the DOJ disagrees. “The fact that the Simmons letter was unsigned is of no consequence to its admissibility,” the government said.

As the government has included Simmons on its witness list, he can testify to the statements contained in the letter, the circumstances that led him to write it, his awareness of anticompetitive communications by Bumble Bee executives, and the defendant’s knowledge of and participation in the price-fixing conspiracy, the DOJ said.

Also, two identical copies of the letter have been produced to the government, one by Bumble Bee and another by Lion Capital, further authenticating it, according to the DOJ.

When interviewed by the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) in March 24, 2017, Simmons is said to have indicated he wrote a letter to Lion Capital but no longer had a copy. Simmons then confirmed his authorship of the letter when he was interviewed by the FBI a second time on July 30, 2019.

StarKist sentencing delayed as sale of its $155m stake in bottle-making firm mulled

The Jan. 31, 2012 postmark shows that it was sent during what the DOJ allges was “the heart of the conspiracy period”, just weeks after all three companies announced a “collusive” list price increase.

Chen also gave the DOJ the right to introduce the fact that Daniel Nestojko, a former Bumble Bee executive, is “testifying pursuant to a plea” agreement. Nestojko is on the DOJ’s list of witnesses.

However, “no mention shall be made of a corporate plea by Bumble Bee”, which has pled guilty to price-fixing and faces a $20m fine, according to Chen.

He also granted the DOJ the right to use “lay opinion” regarding Lischewski’s state of mind, “provided sufficient foundation under FRE 701 is laid”. FRE 701 is the evidence rule around the use of opinion testimony by “lay” witnesses, namely Cameron and Ken Worsham, in this case.

The testimony of Lischewski’s alleges that co-conspirators “regarding their understanding of their communications with defendant, his statements and reactions, and the meaning of codewords is helpful to determining a key fact in issue: whether the defendant knowingly participated in the charged conspiracy”, the DOJ had written in a document filed in opposition to the former CEO’s motion to omit the testimony.

Walmart drops tuna price-fixing lawsuit against Bumble Bee, Lion Capital

Lischewski’s push to have evidence on the “Tuna the Wonderfish” campaign and a co-packaging agreement with COSI was granted in part and denied in part by Chen.

The government will not assert the campaign and agreement were shams as a cover for the alleged conspiracy. “It can refer to these incidentally to show general background and fact that there were prior lines of communication and cooperation between alleged conspiracy participants.” The parties are “ordered to meet and confer regarding a limiting jury instruction if necessary”.

In the document filed prior to the hearing, the DOJ said it had no intention of arguing at trial that the “Tuna the Wonderfish” campaign or the co-packing deal was unlawful. “The evidence regarding the existence of the campaign is inextricably intertwined with the charged price-fixing conspiracy, is not unfairly prejudicial, and thus is admissible against defendant… The campaign set the stage for the conspiracy by providing an opportunity for the competitors to meet with each other and build trust in their relationships,” said the DOJ.

Also, the co-packing agreement between Bumble Bee and COSI “is inextricably intertwined with the charged conspiracy, is not unfairly prejudicial, and is thus admissible against defendant”, said DOJ.

The co-packing agreement gave Lischewski an opportunity to further the conspiracy and provided a cover for communications between him and COSI’s Chan, the government claimed.

Judge won’t dismiss charges against Lischewski on First Amendment grounds

Because of the co-packing agreement, “collusive pricing discussions were interspersed with other legitimate business discussions”, said the DOJ. It would be impossible to offer a “coherent and comprehensible story” regarding the price-fixing conspiracy without referring to the co-packing agreement, the government added.

Chen ruled against Lischewski’s push to have pre-conspiracy communications excluded, but said the DOJ would not be able to refer to allegations of simultaneous downsizing in can size by Bumble Bee, StarKist and COSI, “it shall refer to the agreement in terms of packaging generically”.

The judge granted Lischewski’s drive “in part” to have his “financial circumstances” excluded from the trial, but also denied it in part.

Evidence of his compensation -- including base compensation and bonus/incentives -- and equity in Bumble Bee potentially affected by the alleged conspiracy is relevant, as it may inform his motive during any conspiracy, wrote Chen. However, “evidence regarding general wealth and lifestyle is not”. The parties are “ordered to meet and confer regarding admissible exhibits that discuss compensation”.

title: Editor’s recap: Aldi UK’s whitefish switch; Clearwater sea cucumber plans; Haid’s global drive
content:
Tom Seaman, editorial director of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

Our top two stories last week were about a UK retail contract shift, as German discounter Aldi moved its whitefish processing from one Hull processor to another. 

On Aug. 6, it emerged from reports in the local media in Hull that F. Smales & Son (Fish Merchants) plans to close its chilled seafood division and lay off just under 100 staff after the loss of a major customer, which we confirmed is Aldi. 

We then tracked down the beneficiary of the move, Copernus, a processor based in the same city as Smales. 

Dean Simpson, managing director of Copernus, confirmed his company is putting more lines into Aldi, but declined to comment on the situation with Smales. 

Copernus, which is already a supplier to the UK arm of Aldi’s rival, Lidl, is adding cod loins and smoked haddock fillets to a cod fillet product which has been trialed in Aldi over the past few months, he said.

All three products are under Copernus’ “Hooked on Fish” brand, he said. 

Click here for the first story on the Smales loss and click here for the article on Copernus.

Clearwater CEO sees sea cucumbers as ‘multi-million dollar’ sales, profit driver

Jason Huffman reported on a plan from Canada’s Clearwater Seafoods to grow its sales of sea cucumbers. The crustacean won’t just be a small addition to the company's species mix, but rather one of the top five or six highest-margin products it offers, CEO Ian Smith told stock analysts on a call last Wednesday. 

The Bedford, Nova Scotia-based company, which is publicly traded on the Toronto Stock Exchange, expressed considerable excitement about its June move into Newfoundland and Labrador’s 3PS sea cucumber fishery in its earnings report for the second quarter. And Smith amplified the message in a conference call with analysts.

“This is a multi-million dollar top- and bottom-line new business for us,” he said. “It’s an abundant resource. The margins that we have in this species are in line with some of our more profitable species in the company.”

Click here for the full story.

Chinese feed giant eyes international breakthrough with $350m worth of investments

A relatively little-known Chinese aquatic feed company plans to spend $350m on investments abroad, after putting $240m in its foreign operations so far, Louis Harkell revealed. 

Guangzhou, Guangdong province-headquartered Guangdong Haid Group is set to expand its international footprint over the next five years with 13 new projects, including beyond its primary export market Vietnam, according to Li Yongqiang, group investment development director at the firm.

This includes projects in Indonesia, India, and Ecuador; the latter two of which were, until recently, deemed by Chinese feed firms to be too risky, on account of their unfamiliarity with those markets. 

Click here for the full story.

Salmon season delays Cooke, Ocean Beauty deal talks

Canadian seafood conglomerate Cooke still hopes to acquire major Alaska salmon processor Ocean Beauty Seafoods, but deal talks have been delayed due to the ongoing fishing season, Jason Smith reported. 

Three sources told Undercurrent that Cooke's planned takeover of the Seattle-based processor, which Undercurrent previously reported in June, is still on the cards.

One source said that Ocean Beauty's board recently voted down an acquisition proposal from Cooke, but that doesn't mean a deal isn't possible in the future. However, two other sources said that talks remain active and that the salmon season is the cause of any delay in negotiations. 

Click here for the full story.

USDA approves Cargill’s plant-based fish oil alternative

The US Department of Agriculture has approved an omega-3 rich fish oil alternative produced by agriculture giant Cargill for aquafeed use in the US, Jason Smith reported. 

Cargill has been developing its Lattitude brand fish oil alternative since 2010. Its teams in Great Falls, Montana, Fort Collins, Colorado, and Blair, Nebraska, have been busy readying to produce large-scale quantities of genetically modified canola, which will be processed into the oil for use in aquafeed.

""This approval means we are on target to deliver Latitude, our sustainable, fish oil alternative made from canola oilseeds to aquaculture farmers and feed manufacturers. It represents another key step in creating a global supply chain that can meet a critical environmental challenge," Mark Christiansen, the managing director for Cargill's specialty oils business, said in a press release. 

Click here for the full story.

Bumble Bee mulls bankruptcy filing with sales dropping, debt covenant breached

As beleaguered US shelf-stable supplier Bumble Bee Foods looks to sell its Canadian division, the company is also mulling a bankruptcy filing as one way to ease its financial burden, Bloomberg reported. 

A court-supervised restructuring under Chapter 11 is one of several options being evaluated to deal with the woes of the debt-laden company, Bloomberg reported, citing unnamed sources. Bumble Bee face a government fine and also class-action lawsuits for its role in fixing tuna prices in the US market, along with Thai Union Group's Tri-Union Seafoods, which sells under the Chicken of the Sea brand, and StarKist & Co., owned by South Korea's Dongwon Enterprise. 

Lion Capital, the private equity owner of the company, is also looking at finding a buyer, who would then have to deal with the live legal processes the company is involved in, however, the sources said. Also, the US Department of Justice (DOJ) has said the fine for Bumble Bee's role in the price-fixing would go from $25m to $81.5m if the company is sold in the next five years. Chris Lischewski, the longtime CEO of Bumble Bee, has also been indicted by the DOJ and stepped down to fight the charges.

Click here for the full story.

US fishing industry’s wind worries divide Trump camp, slow $2.8bn project

The US Department of the Interior had seemed poised to move forward with the environmental impact assessment (EIS) needed for Vineyard Wind to begin building the US's first offshore wind farm in the Atlantic Ocean as soon as this year, Jason Huffman reported. 

The New Bedford, Massachusetts-based company, a joint venture between Avangrid, a division of the Spanish wind giant Iberdrola, and Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, a Denmark-based investment firm with €6.8 billion ($7.6bn) under management, wants to erect more than 80 wind turbines that are 600-to-700-foot-tall – at least twice the height of the Statue of Liberty -- in an 118 square mile stretch of the ocean starting some 15 miles from the coast of Martha's Vineyard. It would contribute to America's goal of reducing its dependence on fossil fuels by providing at least 400,000 New England homes and businesses with a combined 800 megawatts of power, while reducing carbon emissions by over 1.6m metric tons per year.

One problem: citing concerns expressed by New England's commercial fishing industry, the National Marine Fisheries Service -- a division of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, which is part of the US Department of Commerce -- is not yet willing to give its blessing on the $2.8bn project's draft environmental EIS.

Click here for the full story.

Mackerel surveys find large stocks in north, northwest Atlantic

Pelagic research cruises of the Atlantic mackerel ecosystems have reported high biomass findings in the north and northwest of the mapped regions, according to Norway's Institute of Marine Research (IMR).

Six vessels have traveled more than 12,000 nautical miles (over 22,000 kilometers) gathering data which contributes to annual stock calculations and quota advice for mackerel issued by the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea.

"At the end of the cruise it can be seen that a few very large trawl catches of mackerel have been taken in the northern and northwestern areas of the distribution area compared to all previous years of data, and especially in the east in the Jan Mayen zone, but also southwest of Svalbard," said IMR scientist Leif Nottestad.

Click here for the full story.

Russian H&G pollock prices hit highest July level for at least 10 years

Prices for headed and gutted (H&G) pollock from Russia have cooled somewhat having hit the highest July level for at least 10 years, according to industry sources and historic data collected on the Undercurrent prices portal. 

The prices for non-Marine Stewardship Council approved 25cm+ H&G -- the size used by re-processors in China, the main market for the fish -- surged to close to $1,700/t last month, but have since come back somewhat to around $1,650/t, sources on both the buy and sell sides said.

Data from Undercurrent’s prices portal shows this is the highest level for July since at least 2008 when the data starts.

Sources are wondering if the prices for Russian H&G will stabilize, or rise again, as is the historic trend until the end of the year.

Click here for the full story.

title: Bumble Bee mulls bankruptcy filing with sales dropping, debt covenant breached
content:
As beleaguered US shelf-stable supplier Bumble Bee Foods looks to sell its Canadian division, the company is also mulling a bankruptcy filing as one way to ease its financial burden, reports Bloomberg. 

Seafood Dealmakers’ Database
View report

A court-supervised restructuring under Chapter 11 is one of several options being evaluated to deal with the woes of the debt-laden company, Bloomberg reported, citing unnamed sources. Bumble Bee face a government fine and also class-action lawsuits for its role in fixing tuna prices in the US market, along with Thai Union Group's Tri-Union Seafoods, which sells under the Chicken of the Sea brand, and StarKist & Co., owned by South Korea's Dongwon Enterprise. 

Lion Capital, the private equity owner of the company, is also looking at finding a buyer, who would then have to deal with the live legal processes the company is involved in, however, the sources said. Also, the US Department of Justice (DOJ) has said the fine for Bumble Bee's role in the price-fixing would go from $25 million to $81.5m if the company is sold in the next five years. Chris Lischewski, the longtime CEO of Bumble Bee, has also been indicted by the DOJ and stepped down to fight the charges.

Bloomberg also reported declining revenue in the first quarter sent the company's leverage ratio over the maximum allowed under the terms of its senior debt, a $650m term loan due in 2023. Lenders have, however, granted a waiver on that violation, as also previously reported by the Wall Street Journal (WSJ).

Bumble Bee declined to comment to Bloomberg and Lion did not respond to a request for comment. 

Undercurrent News previously revealed Bolton Group International is being tipped as the frontrunner to acquire Bumble Bee's Canadian operations, which includes the Clover Leaf brand, with Cooke also said to be interested. Houlihan Lokey is running the process and AlixPartners is also said to have been brought in to look at restructuring. Bloomberg also reported law firm Sullivan & Cromwell has been brought in.

A successful sale of Bumble Bee's Canadian business would go some way to easing the debt pile, but it's not clear what the Chapter 11 talk means for this. 

As well as Clover Leaf Seafoods Co., which owns the biggest shelf-stable brand in Canada for tuna, salmon, clams, oysters, mussels and other snacks, Bumble Bee also owns Connors Bros in Canada, which is the parent of the Brunswick and Beach Cliff sardine brands. The business is based in Markham, Ontario, just north of Toronto, with sales offices in Calgary, Alberta and Montreal, Quebec.

According to the WSJ, Clover Leaf generates roughly $30m in annual earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA). So, the valuation could be around $280m-$300m, 10 times EBITDA, given that the strength of the Clover Leaf brand is somewhat offset by the weaker pelagic business, according to sources. 

Clover Leaf became part of Bumble Bee in 1999 when its prior owner, George Weston, sold the company to International Home Foods, which then combined Clover Leaf with Bumble Bee. Lion acquired Bumble Bee in 2010 from Centre Partners for around $980m.

Thai Union agreed to acquire Bumble Bee for $1.5 billion at the end of 2014, but the deal collapsed a year later, as it emerged the DOJ had found evidence of price-fixing in its review of the deal. 

 Lischewski trial update 

The news on the possible Chapter 11 filing for Bumble Bee comes as it emerges the DOJ has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with John Sawyer, a former sales and marketing executive with Thai Union in the US, ahead of the upcoming trial of former Bumble Bee CEO Lischewski on price-fixing charges.

Bolton tipped as favorite for Clover Leaf as Bumble Bee brings in turnaround adviser 

Sawyer, a senior vice president of sales and marketing at Tri-Union's Chicken of the Sea brand from 2006 until August 2013, has been named in recently released court documents as a possible witness ahead of Lischewski's trial, currently scheduled to begin in November. 

Three other former executives at the US 'big three' tuna companies -- Stephen Hodge, a former senior vice president of sales for StarKist, and two of Bumble Bee's former sales and marketing executives, Kenneth Worsham and Walter Scott Cameron -- are also expected to testify. However, those men have previously pleaded guilty and their future sentencing will likely take into account their cooperation with the Lischewski prosecution. 

Sawyer, by contrast, has not been charged with a crime. His former employer, Tri-Union, acted as a whistleblower to the DOJ about the alleged price-fixing conspiracy among the canners and received amnesty from prosecution in exchange for cooperation. 

The trial of Lischewski, who was indicted in May 2018 on price-fixing charges, is slated to begin on Nov. 4, 2019, and last for nearly three weeks.

According to a previously filed motion in the case, several former tuna industry executives, who have collectively met with prosecutors over 100 times, have served as cooperating witnesses in the matter although it is unclear if they will testify.

These include Shue Wing Chan, the former CEO of Chicken of the Sea. Chan met with prosecutors some 15 times, the partially redacted document states. Lawyers for Chicken of the Sea met with the DOJ at least 36 times in the last three years.

title: Former Chicken of the Sea VP could testify against Lischewski
content:
The United States Department of Justice (DOJ) has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with John Sawyer, a former sales and marketing executive with Thai Union Group's Tri-Union Seafoods, ahead of the upcoming trial of former Bumble Bee Foods CEO Chris Lischewski on price-fixing charges.

Sawyer, a senior vice president of sales and marketing at Tri-Union's Chicken of the Sea International (COSI) brand from 2006 until August 2013, has been named in recently released court documents as a possible witness ahead of Lischewski's trial, currently scheduled to begin in November. 

Three other former executives at the US 'big three' tuna companies -- Stephen Hodge, a former senior vice president of sales for StarKist & Co. and two of Bumble Bee's former sales and marketing executives, Kenneth Worsham and Walter Scott Cameron -- are also expected to testify. However, those men have previously pleaded guilty and their future sentencing will likely take into account their cooperation with the Lischewski prosecution. 

Sawyer, by contrast, has not been charged with a crime. His former employer, Tri-Union, acted as a whistleblower to the DOJ about the alleged price-fixing conspiracy among the canners and received amnesty from prosecution in exchange for cooperation. 

"The nonprosecution agreement requires these witnesses to cooperate with the United States in connection with its investigation of the packaged-seafood industry. In exchange for that cooperation, the United States agreed not to prosecute the witness for antitrust violations involving packaged seafood. There are no other agreements that cover these witnesses’ cooperation in this case," prosecutors wrote in a July 23 motion. 

Additionally, Lischewski's attorneys have asked judge Edward Chen for a series of rulings that could limit what is said at trial. For example, they have asked the judge to exclude any arguments from prosecutors that co-packing arrangements between the US canners and a joint marketing effort known as the "Tuna the Wonderfish campaign" were unlawful.

The trial of Lischewski, who was indicted in May 2018 on price-fixing charges, is slated to begin on Nov. 4, 2019, and last for nearly three weeks.

According to a previously filed motion in the case, several former tuna industry executives, who have collectively met with prosecutors over 100 times, have served as cooperating witnesses in the matter although it is unclear if they will testify.

These include Shue Wing Chan, the former CEO of Tri-Union. Chan met with prosecutors some 15 times, the partially redacted document states. Lawyers for COSI met with the DOJ at least 36 times in the last three years.

title: Bolton tipped as favorite for Clover Leaf as Bumble Bee brings in turnaround adviser
content:
Italy’s Bolton Group International is now seen as the frontrunner to acquire Bumble Bee Foods’ Canadian operation, as it emerges the US shelf-stable seafood giant has hired turnaround consultants AlixPartners after defaulting on its debt.

After inking a deal to take control of US-based tuna raw material supplier Tri Marine earlier this month, Bolton is being billed as the favorite to acquire the Canadian arm of Bumble Bee, which owns the Clover Leaf, Brunswick and Beach Cliff brands, sources told Undercurrent News. Acquisitive and diversified Canadian firm Cooke -- which has snapped up two shrimp farmers and a US distributor already this year -- has also been linked to the sale process, which is being run by Houlihan Lokey.

Seafood’s Top Dealmakers, Q1, 2019: Flying start for M&A set to continue throughout year
View report

One source close to the process said Bolton is now exclusive for Clover Leaf, while another told Undercurrent a deal is “close” and could emerge at the end of July or in early August.

Bolton and Lion Capital, the UK-based private equity which owns Bumble Bee, declined to comment to Undercurrent. 

The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) first reported the Clover Leaf sale, before Undercurrent confirmed Bolton and Cooke’s involvement. Over the weekend, WSJ also reported Bumble Bee has brought in New York-based AlixPartners -- which is also working with High Liner Foods -- as it faces a hefty fine from the US Department of Justice (DOJ) and class action lawsuits for tuna price-fixing. Chris Lischewski, the longtime CEO of Bumble Bee, has also been indicted by the DOJ and stepped down to fight the charges.

Having pled guilty to the DOJ and agreed to pay a $25 million for its role in the price-fixing, Bumble Bee is in talks with lenders after breaching a financial covenant in its $650m term loan and revolving credit facility, according to the WSJ. 

Bumble Bee’s lenders have agreed to a forbearance period as restructuring talks continue, reports the WSJ. “They must be trying to get the Clover Leaf done to save them,” one source told Undercurrent. The WSJ reports Bumble Bee has been in default since March. 

Bolton tasks Spanish tuna veteran with running former Tri Marine operations 

Albacore link 

If Bolton is successful in buying Clover Leaf, it would be the European group’s second big tuna deal of the year, after the acquisition of the rest of Tri Marine. Undercurrent first reported the prospect of the Bolton deal for Tri Marine -- which the Milan-based firm already owned just under half of -- in April. Then, on July 6, Undercurrent revealed it was done. 

Taking control of Tri Marine gives Bolton direct sourcing of albacore, an important species for Clover Leaf in Canada, sources said. 

Then, there is the free trade agreement (FTA) between the EU and Canada, which also creates openings for supply from Bolton’s Italian, French and Spanish operations to Canada, one source said. 

Amid Ocean Beauty deal talks, Cooke vies with Bolton for Bumble Bee’s Canadian ops

“I think it [Clover Leaf] is a good fit for a number of reasons including the FTA with EU and Canada, it will tie in with the supply chain with Tri Marine for both skipjack and albacore, which is difficult to source, because there is limited supply,” one tuna sector source, who asked not to be quoted by name, told Undercurrent.

The sale is for all of the Bumble Bee Canadian business, not just Clover Leaf Seafoods Co., which owns the biggest shelf-stable brand in the country for tuna, salmon, clams, oysters, mussels and other snacks.

Bumble Bee also owns Connors Bros in Canada, which is the parent of the Brunswick and Beach Cliff sardine brands. The business is based in Markham, Ontario, just north of Toronto, with sales offices in Calgary, Alberta and Montreal, Quebec.

According to the WSJ, Clover Leaf generates roughly $30m in annual earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA). So, the valuation could be around $280m-$300m, 10 times EBITDA, given that the strength of the Clover Leaf brand is somewhat offset by the weaker pelagic business, according to sources. 

Clover Leaf became part of Bumble Bee in 1999 when its prior owner, George Weston, sold the company to International Home Foods, which then combined Clover Leaf with Bumble Bee. Lion acquired Bumble Bee in 2010 from Centre Partners for around $980m.

title: Judge rules co-conspirators can testify against Lischewski
content:
Prosecutors can use the testimony of tuna executives who allegedly conspired with Chris Lischewski to fix canned tuna prices at the former Bumble Bee Foods CEO's upcoming trial, a federal judge has ruled.

In a nine-page ruling from San Francisco, California-based judge Edward Chen, he wrote that he believes prosecutors have met their burden to present at trial that a price-fixing conspiracy existed and that Lischewski is alleged to have participated in it. Therefore, their testimony is admissible.

"However, the court did not find that the government has at this juncture met its burden of showing that the conspiracy existed prior to November 2010, the date set forth in the indictment. The court also found certain declarants were co-conspirators," Chen wrote.

The ruling states that Chen evaluated grand jury testimony made by seven individuals, whose names were filed under seal, and has ruled that six can testify.

"The government presents testimony from several participants who separately described and corroborated each other’s accounts of the price-fixing conspiracy. Not only has the government presented grand jury transcripts which paint a clear picture of the price-fixing conspiracy, the government also presents emails corroborating the testimony," Chen wrote. 

The trial of Lischewski, who was indicted in May 2018 on price-fixing charges, is slated to begin on Nov. 4, 2019, and last for nearly three weeks.

According to a previously filed motion in the case, several former tuna industry executives, who have collectively met with prosecutors over 100 times, have served as cooperating witnesses in the case.

These include Shue Wing Chan, the former CEO of Chicken of the Sea International, part of Thai Union Group's US arm, Tri-Union Seafoods. Chan met with prosecutors some 15 times, the partially redacted document states. Lawyers for Chicken of the Sea, which acted as a whistleblower in the price-fixing conspiracy in exchange for leniency from the DOJ, the document states, met with the DOJ at least 36 times in the last three years.

Additionally, Stephen Hodge, a former senior vice president of sales for StarKist & Co., the tuna canner owned by South Korea's Dongown Enterprise, has also cooperated, the motion states. Hodge, who has pleaded guilty to price-fixing but has yet to be sentenced, has met with prosecutors some seven times, the motion stated. 

Two former Bumble Bee sales and marketing executives, Kenneth Worsham and Walter Scott Cameron, have also cooperated, the motion stated. The men met with prosecutors 28 and 18 times, respectively, the motion stated.

title: StarKist sentencing delayed as sale of its $155m stake in bottle-making firm mulled
content:
A hearing to sentence StarKist & Co. on price-fixing charges has been delayed until August as a judge wants more information about whether the US canner can sell an investment in a South Korean bottle-making firm in order to help pay a fine that could stretch to $100 million.

During a June 12 hearing before San Francisco, California-based federal judge Edward Chen, prosecutors sparred with StarKist's lawyers over the company's ability to pay any fine, which will range between a minimum of $50m and $100m. StarKist, which is owned by South Korea's Dongwon Enterprise, has claimed that paying the maximum, on top of expected settlements with victims of the price fixing, could "bankrupt" the company. As previously reported by Undercurrent News, the Department of Justice (DOJ) had accused the canner of having depleted its cash reserves in order to qualify to pay a lower fine.

Each side hired experts to evaluate the canner's ability to pay, but their conclusions diverged. According to minutes of the June 12 hearing, judge Chen's attention has now turned to StarKist's $155m investment in South Korean bottle maker Techpack Solutions.

According to an article in The Korea Economic Daily, as of October 2016, Techpack was 56% owned by Dongwon affiliate Dongwon Systems and 24% owned by StarKist. A private equity firm, EQ Partners, owned the rest but planned to sell this stake to Dongwon, the newspaper reported.

The possibility of StarKist selling its $155m stake in Techpack, a manufacturer of glass and plastic bottles, came up at the hearing, the minutes state.

"StarKist claims that it cannot sell TechPack pursuant to current loan agreement absent lender’s consent. StarKist also states it would be difficult to liquidate its interest in TechPack. StarKist did not state ownership of TechPack was essential to StarKist’s continued viability as a business," the minutes state.

However, Chen asked both sides to brief the court on "whether it is possible and feasible to sell, finance or otherwise derive cash from its TechPack interest. Court reminded the parties it is StarKist’s burden to show inability to pay," the minutes state.

Sentencing has been postponed until Aug. 7, the minutes add.

Sentencing guidelines

The DOJ said in a memorandum released in May that under US sentencing guidelines, the conduct that StarKist pleaded guilty to would require it to pay a fine in the range of $120m to $240m if it weren't for a statutory cap limiting the maximum fine to $100m. The company is claiming inability to pay "based on financial projections created during pending litigation that grossly inflate its hypothetical future civil damages and substantially undervalue its estimated future earnings", prosecutors said. 

Although specific descriptions of StarKist's alleged actions were redacted, the DOJ said that the company is "depleting its cash reserves by accelerating business-related expenditures in an attempt to avoid paying a guidelines fine".

'Market leader'

The government had said that evidence suggests StarKist is "the overwhelming market leader" among shelf-stable seafood suppliers, a category that includes the company's rivals Bumble Bee Foods and Tri-Union Seafoods Chicken of the Sea brand, which is ultimately owned by the Thai Union Group.

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion
Read more

The government hired an expert consultant, Dale Zuehls, to examine the company's books.

He concluded that while the canned tuna business' prospects may be lackluster, StarKist's fortunes in the pouched chicken and tuna markets, as well as canned salmon, are in better shape.

StarKist has "more than sufficient funds" to pay a $100m fine "in reasonable installments without interest, without jeopardizing either its ability to pay restitution or its continued viability", Zuehls concluded. However, details of that allegation were redacted.

the 'big three'

StarKist's plea signals the beginning of the end of criminal proceedings that have dogged the "big three" US canners since allegations first emerged in 2015 that the firms conspired to fix prices at an artificially high level. 

Bumble Bee pleaded guilty to criminal price-fixing charges last year and agreed to pay a $25m fine to the Department of Justice (DOJ). Bumble Bee could have faced a $136m penalty if its ability to pay wasn't taken into account, DOJ officials wrote in a sentencing memorandum. Bumble Bee's fine could rise to a maximum of $81m in the event of a sale of the company.

The other big US tuna canner alleged to have fixed prices, Thai Union's Tri-Union, has avoided a criminal conviction and fine because the company acted as a whistleblower to the DOJ, informing on its rivals in exchange for leniency. 

Additionally, StarKist's Stephen Hodge, a former senior vice president of sales at the company, has pleaded guilty to a charge of price fixing. He has yet to be sentenced.

Two former Bumble Bee employees, Ken Worsham and Walter Scott Cameron, both longtime sales executives have also pleaded guilty but have yet to be sentenced. 

Christopher Lischewski, Bumble Bee's longtime CEO who stepped down after he was indicted on price-fixing charges, has denied wrongdoing and pleaded not guilty. He is expected to face trial in November and could face testimony from other participants in the alleged conspiracy.

Meanwhile, the companies have been settling many of the over 100 civil lawsuits brought against them by the distributors, wholesalers and individuals who bought tuna at reportedly inflated prices.

title: Walmart drops tuna price-fixing lawsuit against Bumble Bee, Lion Capital
content:
Major US retailer Walmart and its club store arm Sam's Club have dismissed their lawsuits accusing tuna canner Bumble Bee Foods of price fixing, court records show.

The notice of dismissal, which is typically a sign of a forthcoming legal settlement between the parties, was filed June 7 in San Diego, California federal court.

StarKist settles with Kroger, others over price-fixing claims

This comes after Bumble Bee. -- which, like rival StarKist & Co, pleaded guilty to price-fixing after the Department of Justice (DOJ) criminal probe of the sector -- has been working to settle the many claims against it. The Walmart dismissal also includes the dismissal of a suit against the tuna canner's owner, the UK-based private equity Lion Capital. 

Civil lawsuits from dozens of wholesalers, retailers and individuals across the US allege that the plaintiffs were overcharged by a long-running price-fixing conspiracy involving Thai Union Group's Tri-Union-Seafoods, owner of the Chicken of the Sea brand, Bumble Bee and StarKist. 

Those suits have all been consolidated under the oversight of San Diego, California-based federal judge Janis Sammartino.

The civil lawsuits began in 2015 amid an investigation into alleged price-fixing in the US tuna sector that spun out of the department's antitrust review of Thai Union's attempt to acquire Bumble Bee.

Under Bumble Bee's plea, the company agreed to pay a $25 million criminal fine, which will increase to a maximum criminal fine of $81.5m, payable by a related entity, in the event of a sale of the company subject to certain terms and conditions.

Two of the company's executives, Kenneth Worsham and Walter Cameron, have also pleaded guilty to price-fixing charges.

Former Bumble Bee CEO Christopher Lischewski has been indicted by the DOJ in connection with the probe but has maintained his innocence and has stepped down temporarily to contest the allegations.

title: Editor’s recap: Pentair aquaculture pullback; China factory quits tilapia; Young’s clings on to Asda biz
content:
Tom Seaman, editorial director of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

A little more than seven years after acquiring Aquatic Eco-Systems (AES), which reports itself to be the world’s leading supplier of aquatic products and systems worldwide, and just as the recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) industry appears to be taking off, Pentair is shutting down at least portions of the business, Jason Huffman revealed last week in our most-read story. 

The word was delivered last Thursday to roughly 35 employees at AES’ main operations in Apoka, Florida, informing them that their layoff will go into effect on June 5. The giant $2.9 billion water and electrical equipment manufacturer later confirmed the news in an email to Jason.

Click here for the full story. 

Large Chinese factory quits tilapia in response to US tariffs

A subsidiary of Guangdong Evergreen Group, a large Chinese vertically integrated aquatic feed and seafood company based in south China, is blaming US tariffs for a decision to refit its large-scale tilapia processing plant to instead handle species and products it can sell domestically, Louis Harkell reported. 

Leo Xie, general manager of Evergreen subsidiary Zhaoqing Evergreen Aquatic Product Science Technology, told Louis his Zhaoqing, Guangdong province-based factory previously processed 25,000-30,000 metric tons of whole tilapia fish farmed in south China. That equates to 8,750-10,500t of fillets.

But not anymore, due to the "market instability" caused by the US-China trade war, he added.

Click here for the full story. 

Young’s fights off NESI, Farne to retain Asda business at ’11th hour’

Young’s Seafood has managed to retain its large remaining business with Walmart-owned retailer Asda Stores, which had tendered the contract amid the uncertainty of the long-running sale process for the UK’s largest processor, I reported. 

The company fought off challenges from New England Seafood International (NESI) for the natural salmon part of the contract and Farne Salmon & Trout for the smoked portion, sources told me. NESI had also hoped to take on the chilled pangasius business for Asda, which did not move from Young's to NESI with the cod and haddock at the start of the year, sources said. 

It’s also thought Farne pitched to take on the smoked pelagic Asda business, done from the Young’s Fraserburgh plant, where the salmon is also processed. The companies were all informed of the decision last Wednesday. 

Click here for the full story. 

Why salmon, cod, haddock, pollock from China are now in line for 25% tariff

It may not be what the seafood industry wants to hear, but unless the US Trade Representative (USTR) changes course, frozen salmon, cod, pollock and haddock fillets previously caught in Alaska and processed in China will soon start getting hit with tariffs of 25% when re-entering the US, trade experts told Jason Huffman. 

In the US, seafood industry executives continue to express confusion and have asked the USTR for clarification to its request for comment for a proposal, published in the May 17 Federal Register, to add about $300 billion worth of Chinese products ("tranche 4") to the earlier $200bn worth of products (tranches 1, 2 and 3) that are being tariffed at a 25% rate.

Click here for the full story. 

Thaifex blog 

Louis Harkell was blogging from the Thaifex - World of Food Asia show in Bangkok, Thailand last week.

At the show, Thai shrimp packers said they could be in line to take some breaded shrimp business from China, but several said business would more likely go to Vietnam.

An executive at Marine Gold Products, which processes some 100t of shrimp produced in Thailand every day, told Louis “it’s going to be the Vietnamese”, when asked who would benefit from 25% tariffs levied by the US on imports of breaded shrimp from China. 

Last year, China supplied more than half of US breaded shrimp imports by volume, according to data from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or 30,989t. 

Click here for the full blog. 

Liquidators of Pacific Andes affiliates sue Ng family alleging fraud

A new front has opened in the long-running legal battle surrounding Pacific Andes International Holdings (PAIH), the Hong Kong-based seafood conglomerate once thought to be one of the sector's biggest firms but since beset by bankruptcy and allegations of fraud, Jason Smith reported. 

The firm FTI Consulting, acting as the court-appointed liquidators of four PAIH subsidiaries, as well as a third-party supplier, Solar Fish, have sued six members of the Ng family that founded and controls the conglomerate, as well as a dozen affiliated companies. 

The suit, filed April 18 in Hong Kong's High Court, accuses five of the defendants -- PAIH executives and Ng family members Teh Hong Eng, Joo Kwee Ng, Joo Siang Ng, Joo Puay Frank Ng and Puay Yee Annie Ng -- of having committed "dishonest assistance" that breached fiduciary duties the individuals owed to the plaintiffs.

Click here for the full story. 

China’s January-April shrimp imports surge to 160,000t

China imported 160,000t of frozen shrimp in the first four months of this year, as the country's direct imports of shrimp continue a remarkable surge, according to latest trade data, Louis Harkell reported. 

The data, which also includes imports of Argentine wild-caught red shrimp, which is not a warmwater shrimp species but nevertheless traded under the same harmonized system code, represents a quadrupling in volume of direct imports compared with the same four months in 2018. 

The value of warmwater shrimp imports surpassed $1bn, according to Chinese customs, while $245million-worth was imported in April.

Click here for the full story. 

Tuna prices expected to tumble on higher Chinese offering

Skipjack tuna prices in key processing hubs such as Thailand and Ecuador are expected to weaken in June, signaling the downtrend started last month might continue into the summer months, Matilde Mereghetti and Louis Harkell reported. 

Higher Chinese offering in key markets and lower demand in the Middle East were mentioned as the key bearish drivers, while some sources in Ecuador pointed out that price instability is hindering commissioning of new fishing vessels in Latin America.

"Skipjack prices are currently tumbling on most markets," one US-based source said, stressing prices were falling "faster than expected". 

Click here for the full story. 

Judge won’t dismiss charges against Lischewski on First Amendment grounds

A California judge has rejected a claim from former Bumble Bee Foods CEO Chris Lischewski to dismiss the criminal price-fixing case against him based on a claim that it violates his First Amendment rights, Jason Smith reported. 

Lawyers for Lischewski, who was indicted by the US Department of Justice (DOJ) in May 2018, argued in a March 6 brief that the prosecutors accused him of agreeing with others in the industry to "limit and restrict competition" for "certain types of fishing methods".

This, the former CEO's lawyers argued, was an allusion to allegations -- described in civil suits from canned tuna buyers -- that Bumble Bee, Thai Union Group's Tri-Union Seafoods, which trades as Chicken of the Sea International, and StarKist & Co, agreed not to sell tuna products using raw material caught without using fish aggregation devices. 

Click here for the full story. 

Live from Polfish 

Neil Ramsden, our European editor, was blogging live from the Polfish trade show in Gdansk, Poland last week. 

A theme that emerged at the show was increased shrimp demand for farmed shrimp in the Central European country. Neil also found several companies expanding their processing activity. 

Click here for the full blog.

title: Judge won’t dismiss charges against Lischewski on First Amendment grounds
content:
A California judge has rejected a claim from former Bumble Bee Foods CEO Chris Lischewski to dismiss the criminal price-fixing case against him based on a claim that it violates his First Amendment rights.

Lawyers for Lischewski, who was indicted by the US Department of Justice (DOJ) in May 2018, argued in a March 6 brief that the prosecutors accused him of agreeing with others in industry to "limit and restrict competition" for "certain types of fishing methods".

This, the former CEO's lawyers argued, was an allusion to allegations -- described in civil suits from canned tuna buyers -- that Bumble Bee, Thai Union Group's Tri-Union Seafoods, which trades as Chicken of the Sea International, and StarKist & Co, agreed not to sell tuna products using raw material caught without using fish aggregation devices (FADs). 

Advocacy groups such as Greenpeace have pushed for tuna companies to discontinue the use of FADs, which would raise the price of canned tuna by some 25% and reduce consumer demand, Lischewski's lawyers wrote in a motion to dismiss the indictment.

But judge Edward Chen denied the motion to dismiss in a May 24 court order, ruling that the First Amendment argument was not relevant.

"He argues it was lawful to collectively agree to not sell FAD-free tuna. As the court has explained herein, a means of furthering a conspiracy can be lawful. Defendant’s contention that his FAD agreements were protected by the First Amendment is also irrelevant," the judge wrote.

Chen also rejected defense attorneys' contention that the indictment was "duplicitous".

"The critical question is whether, under a fair reading of the indictment, the FAD agreement is alleged as merely one of the means of furthering the price-fixing conspiracy. The court has no difficulty so reading the indictment," Chen wrote.

Chen also ruled against Lischewski in a separate ruling rejecting his motion to compel the DOJ to turn over additional information related to their case.

The case is currently scheduled to go to trial in November.

title: DOJ: StarKist spent cash reserves seeking lower price-fixing fine
content:
US prosecutors allege that major tuna canner StarKist & Co. depleted its cash reserves ahead of its pending sentencing on charges that the company engaged in a price-fixing scheme in order to qualify to pay a lower fine.

In heavily redacted documents released earlier this month ahead of the company's July sentencing in federal court in San Francisco, California, prosecutors with the US Department of Justice (DOJ) have countered the canner's argument that it is unable to pay the $100 million fine prosecutors seek. Previously, StarKist's general counsel, Scott Meece, had told the court that such a fine could "bankrupt" the company or prevent it from being able to pay restitution to companies and individuals harmed by the price-fixing.

The DOJ said in a memorandum ahead of the canner's sentencing that under US sentencing guidelines, the conduct that StarKist pleaded guilty to would require it to pay a fine in the range of $120m to $240m if it weren't for a statutory cap limiting the maximum fine to $100m. The company is claiming inability to pay "based on financial projections created during pending litigation that grossly inflate its hypothetical future civil damages and substantially undervalue its estimated future earnings", prosecutors said. 

Although specific descriptions of StarKist's alleged actions are redacted, the DOJ said that the company is "depleting its cash reserves by accelerating business-related expenditures in an attempt to avoid paying a guidelines fine".

"StarKist, however, committed a crime, and should not be permitted to spend money on itself at the expense of paying the price for its criminal acts. Just as an individual defendant cannot avoid a criminal fine by transferring assets to a spouse, StarKist’s deliberate choice to spend down its cash reserves does not justify an inability-to-pay reduction," prosecutors said. 

StarKist representatives did not respond to an Undercurrent News request to comment for this story.

'Market leader'

The government said that evidence suggests StarKist is "the overwhelming market leader" among shelf-stable seafood suppliers, a category that includes the company's rivals Bumble Bee Foods and Tri-Union Seafoods Chicken of the Sea brand, which is ultimately owned by the Thai Union Group.

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion
Read more

The government hired an expert consultant, Dale Zuehls, to examine the company's books.

He concluded that while the canned tuna business' prospects may be lackluster, StarKist's fortunes in the pouched chicken and tuna markets, as well as canned salmon, are in better shape.

StarKist, which is owned by South Korea's Dongwon Enterprise, has "more than sufficient funds" to pay a $100m fine "in reasonable installments without interest, without jeopardizing either its ability to pay restitution or its continued viability", Zuehls concluded.

StarKist could afford to pay the fine in six interest-free installment payments over a five-year period, prosecutors added. Prosecutors suggested that the company pay $10m within a month of sentencing and installment of $18m thereafter.

In addition to the depleted cash reserves, StarKist "paid millions of dollars in disguised dividends to its parent company and related subsidiaries", prosecutors claimed. 

However, details of that allegation were redacted.

StarKist's view

The $100m maximum fine was determined using federal sentencing guidelines and an estimated sales volume of $600m of canned tuna during the 2011 to 2013 period.

The size of the fine has become an issue in the criminal case because, according to Meece, restitution to victims of StarKist's price-fixing has "primacy" when the judge determines the amount of the fine. 

"Now, we're not walking away from our responsibility here, Your Honor. We're agreeing to pay, at a minimum, $50m. It's just simply $100, will either bankrupt the company, or absolutely impair its ability to pay restitution to victims. And so that will be central," Meece told judge Edward Chen in October 2018.

In its own sentencing memorandum filed earlier this month, StarKist argued forcefully against the $100m figure, suggesting that even $100m would be a major hardship.

"Without a significant reduction of the criminal fine, StarKist will not be able to fully compensate all of the civil plaintiffs from its projected free cash flow, nor will it continue as a viable competitor in the market," it said.

It called Zuehls’ analysis of its finances "unreliable and fails to project accurately the amount of money available to StarKist to pay a criminal fine and civil damages". 

The company also compared its conduct in the price-fixing conspiracy and proposed fine to that paid by Bumble Bee.

"Only one former employee of StarKist has been charged, while two high-ranking executives of Bumble Bee have pled guilty and its former President and CEO has been indicted and awaits trial," the company said. "A $50 million dollar fine is more than double the fine assessed against Bumble Bee, and therefore adequately reflects the seriousness and nature of the offense and provides adequate deterrence by addressing StarKist’s position as the last remaining corporate defendant to plead guilty."

Bumble Bee pleaded guilty to criminal price-fixing charges last year and agreed to pay a $25m fine to the Department of Justice (DOJ). Bumble Bee could have faced a $136m penalty if its ability to pay wasn't taken into account, DOJ officials wrote in a sentencing memorandum. Bumble Bee's fine could rise to a maximum of $81m in the event of a sale of the company.

The other big US tuna canner alleged to have fixed prices, Thai Union's Tri-Union, has avoided a criminal conviction and fine because the company acted as a whistleblower to the DOJ, informing on its rivals in exchange for leniency.

title: Lion taps Houlihan Lokey to sell Bumble Bee’s Canadian ops
content:
UK-based private equity Lion Capital has engaged Houlihan Lokey to run a sale process for the Canadian arm of Bumble Bee Foods, which owns the Clover Leaf, Brunswick and Beach Cliff brands, according to Undercurrent News sources with knowledge of the process.

Seafood’s Top Dealmakers II: M&A spend closes on $4bn as conglomerates, PEs vie with industry giants
View report

 The Wall Street Journal first reported the sale process and involvement of Houlihan Lokey, which Undercurrent then confirmed. Undercurrent sources said the process is in its early stages and an information memorandum has not gone out yet. 

Also, the sale is for all the Bumble Bee Canadian business, not just Clover Leaf Seafoods Co., which owns the biggest shelf-stable brand in the country for tuna, salmon, clams, oysters, mussels and other snacks. Bumble Bee also owns Connors Bros in Canada, which is the parent of the Brunswick and Beach Cliff sardine brands. The business is based in Markham, Ontario, just north of Toronto, with sales offices in Calgary, Alberta and Montreal, Quebec.

Houlihan Lokey was also involved in the ongoing sale process of Young's Seafood, which Lion owns a third of. In 2017, Lion was said to be looking to sell Clover Leaf, with High Liner Foods reportedly looking at a deal. This didn't materialize, however. 

According to the WSJ, Clover Leaf generates roughly $30 million in annual earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. 

Bumble Bee, Lion and Houlihan Lokey executives did not respond to requests for comment from Undercurrent. 

Clover Leaf became part of Bumble Bee in 1999 when its prior owner, George Weston, sold the company to International Home Foods, which then combined Clover Leaf with Bumble Bee. Lion acquired Bumble Bee in 2010 from Centre Partners for around $980m. 

The Clover Leaf sale talks come after Bumble Bee has agreed to plead guilty to its involvement in price fixing in the US tuna market and is also settling class action lawsuits from customers. This came after the US Department of Justice (DOJ) started a probe of the sector amid Thai Union Group's attempt to buy Bumble Bee for $1.5 billion, a deal which collapsed at the end of 2015. 

Bumble Bee has agreed to pay a $25m criminal fine, which will increase to a maximum criminal fine of $81.5m, payable by a related entity in the event of a sale of the company, subject to certain terms and conditions. However, it's not clear what a sale of Clover Leaf would mean for the fine. 

Chris Lischewski, the longtime CEO of Bumble Bee, stood down last year to fight a DOJ indictment for his alleged role in the price fixing. Also, two senior former Bumble Bee executives, Walter Scott Cameron and Ken Worsham, have pled guilty, along with Stephen Hodge, formerly of Dongwon Industries-owned StarKist & Co.

In fact, Cameron, Worsham and Hodge, along with Shue Wing Chan, the former CEO of Chicken of the Sea International, part of Thai Union Group's US arm, Tri-Union Seafoods, look set to testify against Lischewski in his trial, which is slated to begin on Nov. 4, 2019, and last for nearly three weeks.

StarKist has also pled guilty and has tentatively agreed to pay at least $50m to the US government as a penalty for its participation in the conspiracy. But, paying the maximum $100m fine could "bankrupt" the company, its general counsel Scott Meece said, speaking at a Nov. 14, 2018, legal hearing.

title: Former Chicken of the Sea CEO, StarKist, Bumble Bee execs could testify against Lischewski
content:
Lawyers defending former Bumble Bee Foods CEO Chris Lischewski claim they still don't know enough about the specifics of the criminal case the US Department of Justice (DOJ) plans to bring against their client although it will rely heavily on testimony from former tuna executives, it has emerged.

According to a March 28 motion filed in San Francisco federal court, lawyers for Lischewski, who was indicted in May 2018 on price-fixing charges, asked judge Edward Chen to compel the DOJ to hand over more information about their extensive investigation into the US canned tuna sector ahead of his trial, which is slated to begin on Nov. 4, 2019, and last for nearly three weeks.

According to the motion, several former executives, who have collectively met with prosecutors over 100 times, have served as cooperating witnesses in the case.

These include Shue Wing Chan, the former CEO of Chicken of the Sea International, part of Thai Union Group's US arm, Tri-Union Seafoods. Chan met with prosecutors some 15 times, the partially redacted document states. Lawyers for Chicken of the Sea, which acted as a whistleblower in the price-fixing conspiracy in exchange for leniency from the DOJ, the document states, met with the DOJ at least 36 times in the last three years.

Additionally, Stephen Hodge, a former senior vice president of sales for StarKist & Co., the tuna canner owned by South Korea's Dongown Enterprise, has also cooperated, the motion states. Hodge, who has pleaded guilty to price-fixing but has yet to be sentenced, has met with prosecutors some seven times, the motion states. 

Two former Bumble Bee sales and marketing executives, Kenneth Worsham and Walter Scott Cameron, have also cooperated, the motion states. The men met with prosecutors 28 and 18 times, respectively, the motion states. 

"Mr. Lischewski is entitled to know with as much specificity as possible what was said back and forth during the nearly fifty occasions in which Mr. Worsham, Mr. Cameron, and their agents discussed their testimony with these prosecutors. To date, the government has studiously avoided any such candid disclosure," it states.

In order to prepare their defense, Lischewski's lawyers want judge Chen to compel the government to had over information related to the witnesses' plea agreements, investigators' interview notes, and "grand jury subpoenas, civil investigative demands, and related requests", the motion states. 

Last month, Lischewski's lawyers asked for the case against him to be dismissed, alleging that the price-fixing count alleges that a key aspect of prosecutors' allegation against him would infringe on his freedom of speech.

Specifically, in laying out the means and methods of the alleged price-fixing conspiracy, the DOJ alleged that Lischewski, in addition to meeting and communicating with competitors to collude on canned tuna prices, agreed to "limit and restrict competition" for "certain types of fishing methods".

This, the former CEO's lawyers argued, was an allusion to allegations described in civil suits from canned tuna buyers that the tuna canners agreed not to sell tuna products using raw material caught without using fish aggregation devices (FADs). 

Advocacy groups such as Greenpeace have pushed for tuna companies to discontinue the use of FADs, which would raise the price of canned tuna by some 25% and reduce consumer demand, Lischewski's lawyers wrote in a motion to dismiss the indictment. 

The chief argument against FAD use, the lawyers argue, is that they produce "slightly" higher bycatch rates of non-target species, some 1.7% for FADs on skipjack as opposed to 0.3% for school fishing. Additionally, school fishing relies on the use of helicopters that burn fossil fuels and undermine the method's environmentally friendly credentials, the lawyers said.

"In any event, whatever one thinks of the foregoing arguments, it is not unlawful, per se or otherwise, to assert them and convince others of their merit. On the contrary, Mr. Lischewski’s advocacy against what he believed to be Greenpeace’s unscientific “scare tactics and sensationalism” is protected by the First Amendment," the motion stated.
