title: Editor’s recap: Could price-fixing fine take StarKist under?; NESI works with ex-Young’s CEO; Mitsui eyes Santa Priscila
content:
Tom Seaman, editorial director of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

Two of our top five most-read stories from last week were focused on the price-fixing saga in the US tuna sector.

On April 10, Jason Smith revealed major US tuna canner StarKist & Co. has tentatively agreed to pay at least $50 million to the US government as a penalty for its participation in the conspiracy to fix canned tuna prices. However, the maximum $100m fine could "bankrupt" the company, its general counsel Scott Meece told San Francisco, California-based federal judge Edward Chen.

Meece was speaking at a Nov. 14 hearing during which StarKist, which is owned by South Korea's Dongwon Enterprise, pleaded guilty to the price-fixing charge and said that the company's ability to pay should be factored in when determining the amount of the fine to be paid. The $100m maximum was determined using federal sentencing guidelines and an estimated sales volume of $600m of canned tuna during the 2011 to 2013 period.

"And really, this is a $50m hearing. The low end is 50m, the high is 100m. This is really about the life or death of our company, and its ability to continue as an ongoing concern," Meece said.

Meece's statements, revealed in recently released court transcripts, have not been previously reported.

Read the full story here. 

Lischewski wants criminal case dropped on First Amendment grounds

Also on the price-fixing topic, Jason Smith revealed Bumble Bee Foods CEO Chris Lischewski would like the criminal case against him dismissed because the charge violates his First Amendment rights, his lawyers argue.

Lawyers for Lischewski, who was indicted by the US Department of Justice (DOJ) in May 2018, said in a March 6 brief that the price-fixing count alleges that a key aspect of prosecutors' allegation against him would infringe on his freedom of speech.

Specifically, in laying out the means and methods of the alleged price-fixing conspiracy, the DOJ alleged that Lischewski, in addition to meeting and communicating with competitors to collude on canned tuna prices, agreed to "limit and restrict competition" for "certain types of fishing methods".

This, the former CEO's lawyers argued, was an allusion to allegations -- described in civil suits from canned tuna buyers -- that Bumble Bee, Thai Union Group's Tri-Union Seafoods, which trades as Chicken of the Sea International, and StarKist, agreed not to sell tuna products using raw material caught without using fish aggregation devices (FADs). 

Advocacy groups such as Greenpeace have pushed for tuna companies to discontinue the use of FADs, which would raise the price of canned tuna by some 25% and reduce consumer demand, Lischewski's lawyers wrote in a motion to dismiss the indictment. 

"Labels touting the purported environmental merits of 'FAD-free' tuna are not supported by science, but are primarily driven, instead, by pressure from Greenpeace," they wrote.

Read the full story here. 

Ecuador’s largest shrimp exporter in talks to sell stake to Mitsui

According to our sources, Ecuador’s largest shrimp exporter, Industrial Pesquera Santa Priscila, is in talks to sell a 25% stake to Japanese trading giant Mitsui & Co.

The talks have been going on for several months and are advanced, the sources said. Santiago Salem, the founder and CEO of Santa Priscila, declined to comment. 

There are other keen to invest in Santa Priscila, but the talks with Mitsui are currently exclusive, the sources said.

In 2018, the Guayaquil-based firm generated $492m in export revenues from shrimp. The company's export volume reached 76,868 metric tons, according to data from Estadistica (Instituto Nacional de Estadistica). In 2017, Santa Priscila produced 74,000t of shrimp -- up from 56,000t in 2016 -- in addition to roughly 10,000t of tilapia.

Santa Priscila is totally vertically integrated, owning its own farms, six laboratories for larvae production, a feed plant and two processing plants. The company is also Ecuador’s top mango producer, according to its website. 

Read the full story here. 

With Asda salmon in sights, NESI adds Pete Ward as advisor, more Young’s execs to team

Two stories about Young's Seafood featured in the top ten. On April 10, I broke the news that New England Seafood International (NESI) is being tipped to take on the fresh salmon business for retailer Asda from Young's as it starts working with Pete Ward, the former CEO of the latter. 

As well as adding Ward as a board advisor, NESI is bringing in two executives from Young’s to its team, with the possibility of adding the Asda fresh salmon business in the future, sources said.

Asda has already moved over £30m in business away from Young's to NESI and also Lyons Seafood during the company's ongoing sale process. Asda's fresh salmon processing, worth around £34m in total, is seen as up-for-grabs, according to our sources. 

Read the full story here. 

Two offers on table for Young’s as first anniversary of sale process approaches

After the news on the NESI hires broke on Wednesday, I then reported Friday there are two offers on the table for Young's, the UK’s largest processor. 

The owners of Young’s announced a sale process on April 19 last year, with the aim of getting a deal done by the summer. An end to the protracted process, which has not been helped by Asda business losses and the general uncertainty around the UK’s exit from the EU, which has now been pushed back to Oct. 31, could finally be in sight.

One offer is for a merger with Sykes Seafoods, which would add around £100m in sales and over £10m of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization to Young’s, which owns the UK's largest seafood brand but has seen its private label business suffer in recent years, since losing £100m in salmon processing for J. Sainsbury. 

The other is from CapVest Partners, the private equity that was very close to a deal last year. CapVest is back in the mix for Young’s, having faded away in the process, with the Sykes bid being more strongly tipped at the start of the year, sources said. Sykes also reportedly bid in the sale process with Stellex Capital Management, a private equity, which is not involved now. 

Read the full story here. 

Spring-spawning herring survey finds biomass up 30%

Meanwhile, an acoustic survey of Norwegian spring-spawning herring grounds has found that biomass index is up an estimated 30% year-on-year, it emerged last week. 

The survey, conducted Feb. 13-25 by the Eros, Kings Bay and Vendla, was made during periods of very rough weather, and very few days of fine sailing, according to a report. 

"Uncertainty" levels were up compared to 2018's survey, but still low, at 10%. "As in 2018, most of the herring in 2019 were distributed in deep layers from 150-300 meters depth."

Read the full story here. 

Kiemele: Cermaq Canada won’t ‘settle for second best’ in Nova Scotia

Before Cermaq Group moves ahead with any of its plans to build salmon farms on the coasts of Nova Scotia, David Kiemele, managing director of the Norwegian company's Canadian division, said it must see two things: a public embrace and the right environmental conditions, Jason Huffman reported. 

“The social aspect has to be there,” Kiemele said. “This has to happen in collaboration and partnership with local communities, stakeholders, the big foundation of Nova Scotia, the lobster fishermen, etc., and obviously, along with that, you need to have the right environmental conditions, the right site criteria, in order for these locations to perform at their optimum. We’re starting from scratch, so we are not going to settle for second best.”

The $1.1 billion revenue Norwegian global salmon farming giant – owned by Japan’s Mitsubishi Corp. -- created quite a buzz when it announced that it has been granted exclusive six month options by the Nova Scotia government to conduct a feasibility study on four prospective Atlantic salmon aquaculture farm leases in the province, including two spots in the Chedabucto Bay region, on the eastern shoreline, and also two spots in the St. Mary’s region, south of Digby on the province’s southwestern coast.

For Cermaq to move forward, it would want to maintain between 10 and 20 farms with no less than an annual output of 20,000t, Kiemele and Linda Sams, Cermaq Canada’s director of sustainable development, told reporters at a press conference following the announcement.

Cermaq would also bring to Nova Scotia a hatchery and processing plant, creating between 300 and 350 jobs and spending between $400m and $500m, the two officials had said at the earlier press conference.

Read the full story here. 

Tri Marine CEO Curto confirms deal talks with Bolton ‘continuing’

The CEO of tuna trading giant Tri Marine confirmed deal talks are underway with Bolton Group International after I broke the story the week before last. 

Bolton, which already owns a sizeable minority Tri Marine, is in talks to take control, according to our sources. Renato Curto, CEO of Tri Marine, said, “nothing has changed as of today” in terms of the ownership structure of the company.

However, “we have also been considering deepening the relationship between our groups”, he said. Bolton -- which controls canned seafood brands such as Rio Mare, Saupiquet and Isabel -- bought just under 50% of Tri Marine in 2013.

“While conversations have been held for some time and are continuing, at this stage there is no agreement with respect to any possible change in ownership. Should the situation change, we will promptly inform our employees and business partners,” he said.

The two companies have done business for nearly four decades, said Curto.

Read the full story here. 

Switch to plant-based aquafeeds may not be as sustainable as many think, study finds

The substitution of fishmeal by plant ingredients in shrimp feed formulations could place significant extra strain on agricultural demand, according to a recent study published in the Sustainability journal, Dan Gibson reported. 

Experts from various disciplines, universities and organizations in the UK, the Netherlands, Belgium, Switzerland, Mexico, the US and Australia have collaborated to quantify the resource trade-offs involved in substituting plant ingredients for fishmeal in global shrimp feed formulations.

Their findings show that a switch to plant ingredients, often touted as the most sustainable alternative to fishmeal, would largely be shifting demand from current marine resources to "essential agricultural resources".

"We have to find a middle way," Wesley Malcorps, leading author of the paper, told Undercurrent. "It should be about the strategic inclusion of ingredients, rather than replacing one with the other."

Read the full story here. 

Mowi unable to improve average global sea lice situation in 2018

Mowi, the world's largest salmon farmer, has revealed in its annual report that measures taken to reduce sea lice levels across its many farms in 2018 ultimately failed to yield results, with average global lice levels remaining unchanged from the previous year, Dan Gibson reported. 

According to the report, 9% of Mowi farms operated with lice levels above national trigger limits at some stage during 2018. While the previous two years had seen this value fall from 12 to 9%, the megafirm made no further progress over the past 12 months.

Of particular concern will be Mowi's domestic farming base in Norway, where sea lice levels rose once again so that 12% of farms were at some stage above the national lice trigger limit during 2018, up 4% y-o-y.

Similarly, sea lice levels at Mowi's Chilean operations skyrocketed from a total of 7% to 22% over national lice limits, which Mowi attributed to "environmental challenges, limited access to non-medicinal treatment systems and high lice challenge pressure". 

In contrast, lice levels in Scotland, Canada, and the Faroes were all down significantly. In Canada and Scotland especially, not a single Mowi farm rose above national lice limits over the course of the year.

Read the full story here.

title: Lischewski wants criminal case dropped on First Amendment grounds
content:
Former Bumble Bee Foods CEO Chris Lischewski would like the criminal case against him dismissed because the charge violates his First Amendment rights, his lawyers argue.

Lawyers for Lischewski, who was indicted by the US Department of Justice (DOJ) in May 2018, said in a March 6 brief that the price-fixing count alleges that a key aspect of prosecutors' allegation against him would infringe on his freedom of speech.

Specifically, in laying out the means and methods of the alleged price-fixing conspiracy, the DOJ alleged that Lischewski, in addition to meeting and communicating with competitors to collude on canned tuna prices, agreed to "limit and restrict competition" for "certain types of fishing methods".

This, the former CEO's lawyers argued, was an allusion to allegations -- described in civil suits from canned tuna buyers -- that Bumble Bee, Thai Union Group's Tri-Union Seafoods, which trades as Chicken of the Sea International, and StarKist & Co, agreed not to sell tuna products using raw material caught without using fish aggregation devices (FADs). 

Advocacy groups such as Greenpeace have pushed for tuna companies to discontinue the use of FADs, which would raise the price of canned tuna by some 25% and reduce consumer demand, Lischewski's lawyers wrote in a motion to dismiss the indictment. 

"Labels touting the purported environmental merits of 'FAD-free' tuna are not supported by science, but are primarily driven, instead, by pressure from Greenpeace," they wrote.

The chief argument against FAD use, the lawyers argue, is that they produce "slightly" higher bycatch rates of non-target species, some 1.7% for FADs on skipjack as opposed to 0.3% for school fishing. Additionally, school fishing relies on the use of helicopters that burn fossil fuels and undermine the method's environmentally friendly credentials, the lawyers said.

"In any event, whatever one thinks of the foregoing arguments, it is not unlawful, per se or otherwise, to assert them and convince others of their merit. On the contrary, Mr. Lischewski’s advocacy against what he believed to be Greenpeace’s unscientific “scare tactics and sensationalism” is protected by the First Amendment," the motion stated.

Additionally, Federal Trade Commission regulations regarding "truth-in-advertising" would prevent the use of FAD-free tuna on environmental grounds due to the lack of benefit, the lawyers alleged.

The motion to dismiss asked for the sole count of the indictment to be dismissed or, alternatively, to apply doctrine in anti-trust law known as the "rule of reason" that the anti-FAD discussion did not unfairly restrain trade.

"The government will presumably argue that it alleged a price-fixing conspiracy, which is unlawful per se. But the government chose to allege price fixing and the purported agreement about FAD-free tuna in a single count. That count should be dismissed for duplicity—improper joinder of two or more distinct offenses in a single count," Lischewski's lawyers argued

Prosecutors responded in a separate motion that the indictment was not about the First Amendment.

"Defendant, however, attempts to challenge the indictment by ignoring the actual charge and instead converting one of the means and methods of the conspiracy into a separate offense. The court should reject defendant’s improper attempt to redraft the indictment and introduce additional facts not alleged by the grand jury," prosecutors wrote. "This case is not about Greenpeace or Federal Trade Commission regulations. Defendant was not charged for following the law and exercising his First Amendment rights."

Additionally, "because the indictment alleges a single conspiracy carried out through various means, it is not duplicitous," prosecutors wrote.

"The First Amendment does not immunize speech made in furtherance of a criminal conspiracy. Defendant’s constitutional objection to the fishing-methods allegation (which, relying again on facts outside the indictment, he asks the court to construe as an attack on protected expression) is therefore meritless," prosecutors said.

Judge Edward Chen is scheduled to consider the motion to dismiss on May 7.

title: StarKist settles with Kroger, others over price-fixing claims
content:
StarKist Co. announced a settlement agreement with a large group of plaintiffs, including Kroger, in the pending antitrust litigation over price fixing in the US canned tuna sector. 

This settlement agreement resolves antitrust claims of Kroger and 32 other retailers, that were represented in several consolidated complaints.  StarKist, which is owned by South Korea's Dongwon Enterprise, settled earlier with other plaintiffs including Target, Walmart, and Sam's.  

Seafood’s Top Dealmakers II: M&A spend closes on $4bn as conglomerates, PEs vie with industry giants
View report

"StarKist is pleased to resolve this matter with our valued customers. This settlement, together with prior ones, resolves a substantial number of the company disputes with the direct action plaintiffs," said Scott Meece, StarKist general counsel, in a statement. 

"StarKist is committed to being a socially responsible company and we are pleased to resolve this lawsuit with our customers under fair and reasonable terms," said Andrew Choe, president and CEO of StarKist. "We will continue to conduct our business with the utmost transparency and integrity, and we hope to resolve the remaining lawsuits with our other customers under similarly fair and mutually beneficial terms."

In late January, StarKist entered into a settlement agreement with Walmart valued at $20.5 million, based on a combination of cash payment and certain favorable commercial terms. 

Back in October last year, StarKist said it will plead guilty to its role in the US canned tuna price-fixing cartel, the US Department of Justice (DOJ) said. The amount of the fine to be paid could reach as much as $100m but will be determined at sentencing, the DOJ said in a release.

StarKist responded to the announcement with a press release pledging its "commitment to doing the right thing".

StarKist's Stephen Hodge, a former senior vice president of sales at the company, has also pleaded guilty but has yet to be sentenced. 

Walmart, Thai Union settle 

The StarKist settlement with Walmart comes after Thai Union Group's Tri-Union Seafoods, the owner of the Chicken of the Sea tuna brand, also settled with the retailer last year. 

Then, earlier this year, Tri-Union announced an agreement with 29 mid-sized and large retailers which accused the company of conspiring to fix prices at an artificially high level. 

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion
Read more

As per the settlement, Tri-Union will pay an undisclosed sum of cash and work with the companies on the "promotion of innovative Chicken of the Sea products", it said. 

Tri-Union representatives have said they want to settle the many price-fixing lawsuits against the company and focus on growing flagging sales of canned tuna.

When Thai Union settled the separate lawsuit brought by Walmart the company indicated that more settlements could follow. The company has set aside $44m for this purpose, it said in August 2018. 

Civil lawsuits from dozens of wholesalers, retailers and individuals across the US allege that the plaintiffs were overcharged by a long-running price-fixing conspiracy involving Tri-Union, Bumble Bee Foods -- which has pleaded guilty as part of the DOJ probe -- and StarKist. 

Those suits have all been consolidated under the oversight of San Diego, California-based federal judge Janis Sammartino.

The civil lawsuits began in 2015 amid an investigation into the US tuna sector into alleged price-fixing that spun out of the department's antitrust review for Thai Union's attempt to acquire Bumble Bee.

Tri-Union acted as a whistleblower to the DOJ informing on the alleged industry collusion in exchange for amnesty from prosecution. 

Bumble Bee, meanwhile, has entered a guilty plea to price-fixing charges. The company agreed to pay a $25m criminal fine, which will increase to a maximum criminal fine of $81.5m, payable by a related entity, in the event of a sale of the company subject to certain terms and conditions.

Two of the company's executives, Kenneth Worsham and Walter Cameron, have pleaded guilty to price-fixing charges but have yet to be sentenced.

Bumble Bee CEO Christopher Lischewski has been indicted by the DOJ in connection with the probe but has maintained his innocence and has stepped down temporarily to contest the allegations.

title: John West indicted on eight counts of alleged past IUU fishing connections
content:
Thai Union's UK tuna subsidiary, John West Foods, was indicted on eight counts of alleged past connections to illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing (IUU) by the UK's Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) on Jan. 2, 2018, Undercurrent News has learned. 

Thai Union’s John West under investigation for alleged past IUU fishing connections

According to a document from the CPS, John West has been charged with "conducting business directly connected to [IUU] fishing, contrary to Article 9(7) of The Sea Fishing (illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing) Order 2009".

The indictment relates to events alleged to have occurred between March 1, 2012, and Feb. 28, 2014, at the major UK trading port of Felixstowe in Suffolk.

The UK's Marine Management Organization (MMO) confirmed to Undercurrent that it had submitted a file of evidence to the CPS in relation to allegations of unregulated fishing in the Atlantic Ocean, which led the CPS to take action against John West.

The first hearing of John West's case took place before the Crown Court of Newcastle upon Tyne on Jan. 26, 2018. The next substantive hearing is to be a preliminary hearing in September or October 2019 at Southwark Crown Court, with no official trial date yet fixed by the CPS, the MMO told Undercurrent.

Thai Union said that "it is our policy not to comment on ongoing legal matters or audits in progress," when contacted by Undercurrent on the matter.

John West and its then-parent company, the French Thai Union subsidiary MW Brands, had also formed a partnership with WWF UK in October 2014.

When contacted for comment, a WWF UK spokesperson said: "We have been working in partnership with John West and its parent company Thai Union Europe to ensure that all seafood sold by the company in Europe will be either appropriately certified, or engaged in credible improvement projects aimed at bringing their sustainability status up to standard."

"We understand that these allegations relate to a time before our partnership and it would be inappropriate for us to comment further while an investigation is underway,” the spokesperson added.

During the period in question from 2012-2014, John West was also the target of an ongoing campaign from Greenpeace UK, which ranked the company bottom of its list of UK tuna brands in terms of sustainability in October 2015.

Greenpeace claimed at the time that 98% of John West's total tuna haul was caught using fish aggregation devices (FADs), which it claimed were "destructive".

Greenpeace UK said they were unable to comment on the current allegations when contacted by Undercurrent.

Ghanaian connection

Undercurrent first reported news of the case on Feb. 25, following the publication of an audited Thai Union report detailing the allegations. The report noted the intent of the CPS to prosecute "for alleged offenses of conducting business directly connected to IUU fishing imported from Ghana".

Prior to 2017, Thai Union had operated two subsidiaries in the West African country: the canned tuna manufacturer known as Pioneer Food Cannery, and the fishing firm TTV.

However, the TTV subsidiary was discontinued in 2016, with Thai Union taking the decision to divest the company's vessels in December of that year.

The conglomerate noted it had taken a THB 271.9 million ($7.75m) hit on its Ghanaian fleet in its 2016 financial report.

Elsewhere, Thai Union retains a 100% stake in Pioneer in Tema, which made headlines in June 2017 when an explosion and resultant fire at the plant killed two people unrelated to the company and injured five others.

The plant was not operational at the time, with the explosion believed to be caused by maintenance work that was ongoing on company premises.

Meanwhile, the West African country's fishing sector has been pushing for greater transparency over the past couple of years, as well as NGOs such as the Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF), Undercurrent reported last December.

An investigation by EJF had previously found that 90% of the country's industrial fishing fleet is linked to Chinese ownership. This is despite the fact that Ghana’s laws clearly forbid any foreign ownership or control of vessels flying its flag.

"The Chinese and Ghanaian governments must work together to eradicate the illegal fishing practices which are rife in Ghana’s industrial fleet, improve transparency and sanction those contravening ownership laws," EJF said at the time.

title: US reveals names of tuna bond scandal defendants
content:
The US has revealed three additional defendants in the Mozambique "tuna bonds" scandal, including two former government officials and an executive with shipbuilder Privinvest, reports the Financial Times.

In January the US Department of Justice indicted a trio of former Credit Suisse bankers, a former Mozambique finance minister, and another Privinvest executive in the same case. In March the government of Mozambique formally filed a lawsuit against the bank Credit Suisse at the High Court in London.

The names of three defendants had remained redacted, but now prosecutors said those defendants were aware of the charges against them. Najib Allam, the chief financial officer of Abu Dhabi-based shipbuilder Privinvest, was revealed as a defendant, along with Antonio do Rosario and Teofilo Nhangumele, two former Mozambique officials.

title: Mozambique brings lawsuit against Credit Suisse for role in tuna bond scandal
content:
The government of Mozambique has formally filed a lawsuit against the bank Credit Suisse at the High Court in London for its role in what has become known as the 'tuna bond scandal', reports BBC News.

Credit Suisse was one of the banks that provided loans to Mozambican maritime security projects and the state tuna fishery between 2013 to 2016. However, the collective sum of the loans at roughly $2 billion has helped to push the East African country into a debt crisis since 2016.

The filing at the High Court also named three Credit Suisse bankers who have already been indicted in the US, BBC News reported.

Allegedly, many of the projects used for the funds where effectively fronts used by the trio of US bankers and others to enrich themselves through a series of kickbacks and bribes amounting to $200m, according to the US indictment.

Credit Suisse did not comment for the article.

title: Bumble Bee, US Foods settle tuna price-fixing lawsuit
content:
Bumble Bee Foods has settled a tuna price-fixing lawsuit brought by US broadliner Sysco US Foods, one of a host of civil suits brought against the top three suppliers in the country and their parent companies.

StarKist settles with Kroger, others over price-fixing claims

No details of the settlement are given in a legal document filed on Feb. 25, in which both parties ask for documents filed under seal to remain so. But the agreement follows a similar move to settle with the other US major broadliner, Sysco. 

This comes after StarKist Co. -- which, like Bumble Bee, has agreed to plead guilty to price-fixing in the Department of Justice (DOJ) criminal probe of the sector -- entered into a settlement agreement with Walmart to resolve price-fixing claims at the end of January. 

The StarKist portion of the settlement is valued at $20.5 million, based on a combination of cash payment and certain favorable commercial terms, which will further strengthen the business relationship between the two companies, said StarKist, which is owned by South Korea's Dongwon Industries.

Back in October last year, StarKist had said it will plead guilty to its role in the US canned tuna price-fixing cartel, the DOJ said. The amount of the fine to be paid could reach as much as $100m but will be determined at sentencing, it said in a release.

Civil lawsuits from dozens of wholesalers, retailers and individuals across the US allege that the plaintiffs were overcharged by a long-running price-fixing conspiracy involving Thai Union Group's Tri-Union-Seafoods, owner of the Chicken of the Sea brand, Bumble Bee and StarKist. 

Those suits have all been consolidated under the oversight of San Diego, California-based federal judge Janis Sammartino.

The civil lawsuits began in 2015 amid an investigation into alleged price-fixing in the US tuna sector that spun out of the department's antitrust review of Thai Union's attempt to acquire Bumble Bee.

Walmart settlements 

The Bumble Bee and StarKist settlements come after Tri-Union also settled with the latter last year. 

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion

Then, earlier this year, Tri-Union announced an agreement with 29 mid-sized and large retailers which accused the company of conspiring to fix prices at an artificially high level.

Tri-Union acted as a whistleblower to the DOJ informing on the alleged industry collusion in exchange for amnesty from prosecution. 

Bumble Bee, meanwhile, previously entered a guilty plea to price-fixing charges. The company agreed to pay a $25m criminal fine, which will increase to a maximum criminal fine of $81.5m, payable by a related entity, in the event of a sale of the company subject to certain terms and conditions.

Two of the company's executives, Kenneth Worsham and Walter Cameron, have also pleaded guilty to price-fixing charges but have yet to be sentenced.

Former Bumble Bee CEO Christopher Lischewski has been indicted by the DOJ in connection with the probe but has maintained his innocence and has stepped down temporarily to contest the allegations.

title: National Fish’s Ventola appeals prison term
content:
From his Massachusetts cell, former National Fish and Seafood president Jack Ventola is fighting to shorten a two-year prison term he believes is unfair. 

In April 2018 after the 72-year-old's guilty plea to tax fraud charges, a federal judge sentenced Ventola, a minority owner the Gloucester, Massachusetts-based processor majority-owned by Pacific Andes International Holdings (PAIH), to prison and ordered him to pay a $75,000 fine and pay restitution of $1,073,470. He will also serve a year on supervised release.

Ventola has paid the restitution amount down to $800,012 as of June 29, 2018, but he has appealed the prison term, court records show.

According to a Dec. 28 filing submitted to the United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, Ventola believes his sentence is "substantially unreasonable" given that one of his co-conspirators in their scheme to avoid taxes, accountant Michael Bruno, was sentenced to only a year's probation, not prison. 

In November 2015, Ventola was first indicted on tax fraud-related charges with prosecutors alleging that he and three others -- National Fish executive vice president Richard Pandolfo, James Corbett, who headed the processor's operations and died in 2013, and Bruno, an accountant who didn't work for the company but served on its board -- conspired in a 16-year scheme to avoid taxes, which began in 1999. 

The scheme involved a temporary labor firm, Continental Labor Team, owned by Ventola and Corbett, that was used to bill National Fish for services never provided. The men used a network of shell companies to direct payments to a bank account controlled by Ventola, who then paid the others. Ventola, who pleaded guilty to seven counts, is accused of defrauding Hong Kong-based PAIH of at least $6 million during the 2007 to 2013 period alone and underreporting his income by $1m. 

He began serving his sentence at Federal Medical Center- Devens, an hour's drive from Gloucester, in July 2018.

According to the appeal, Ventola, like Bruno, had a clean criminal record and pleaded guilty to the charges. Both men, Ventola's lawyers argued, faced similar charges and were similarly guilty.

"For Mr. Ventola to receive a term of imprisonment in the order of years while Mr. Bruno avoids such punishment entirely – having been convicted for such similar criminal conduct – subverts natural principles of justice, undermines confidence in the criminal justice system, and ignores the Supreme Court’s mandate to correlate punishment with culpability," the appeal argues.

However, in their successful opposition to a June 2018 motion from Ventola's lawyers that sought to grant Ventola bail while an appeal was being lodged, prosecutors argued that Ventola and Bruno played different roles in the tax fraud conspiracy.

"There was a dramatic difference in the degree to which Bruno and Ventola profited from their fraud; Bruno earned around $150,000 while Ventola earned over $6 million, including both the tax and wire fraud. And their roles were different: Ventola was the leader, Bruno the facilitator," prosecutors said. 

The appeals court has yet to consider Ventola's appeal. If they do not take action he is scheduled to be released on April 15, 2020, according to the federal Bureau of Prisons.

During sentencing, Ventola's friends, relatives, employees and neighbors wrote 30 letters to the court urging a sentence of probation, not prison for the former company president.

The letters painted a sympathetic picture of a former US Marine and self-taught entrepreneur who bootstrapped his way into the seafood business and built National Fish into a 300-worker processor.

title: Twenty-nine plaintiffs reach price-fixing settlements with Thai Union’s Tri-Union
content:
Twenty-nine mid-sized and large retailers have reached a settlement with Thai Union Group's Tri-Union Seafoods, the owner of the Chicken of the Sea tuna brand, which accused the company of conspiring to fix prices at an artificially high level. 

The settlement, announced in a press release from the tuna canner, follows the plaintiffs' notice to a California federal court in December that they were dropping their lawsuits. As per the settlement, Tri-Union will pay an undisclosed sum of cash and work with the companies on the "promotion of innovative Chicken of the Sea products", it said. 

Tri-Union representatives have said they want to settle the many price-fixing lawsuits against the company and focus on growing flagging sales of canned tuna.

"We greatly value our retail partners and we are pleased this matter is resolved," Darren Parsons, Tri-Union's vice president of retail sales and business development said in a Jan 9 press release. "The agreement ensures that, together with our partners, we can continue to provide customers the healthy, sustainably sourced seafood products they expect from us."

The plaintiffs dropping the suit are: Affiliated Foods; Affiliated Foods Midwest Cooperative; Alex Lee; Associated Food Stores; Associated Grocers of New England; Bashas’; Big Y Foods; Brookshire Brothers; Brookshire Grocery Company; Certco; Dollar Tree Distribution; Greenbrier International; Family Dollar Stores; Family Dollar Services; Fareway Stores; the Golub Corporation; Giant Eagle; Kmart; K-VA-T Food Stores; Marc Glassman; McLane Company; Meadowbrook Meat Company; Merchants Distributors; Schnuck Markets; SpartanNash Company; URM Stores; Western Family Foods; Woodman’s Food Market; and 99 Cents Only Stores.

Christianna Reed, Chicken of the Sea's vice president and general counsel called the settlement a "significant achievement" in a press release.

 "We are also hopeful it will encourage any remaining litigants to put posturing aside and work with us to find pragmatic solutions that reflect the industry's challenging market realities. It is also an unfortunate reality that litigants who continue to pursue aggressive, unrealistic negotiation tactics are putting an iconic American seafood brand and American jobs at risk," she said.

In May, Thai Union settled a separate lawsuit brought by major customer Walmart and indicated that more settlements could follow.

“It’s certainly something we’re moving forward with in an aggressive manner. As we move forward in the next several months obviously this case continues on for some period,” Chicken of the Sea's vice president and general counsel for legal and risk management Christianna Reed told Undercurrent News in May.

The company has set aside $44 million for this purpose, it said in August.

Civil lawsuits from dozens of wholesalers, retailers and individuals across the US allege that the plaintiffs were overcharged by a long-running price-fixing conspiracy involving Tri-Union, Bumble Bee and Dongwon Enterprises' StarKist & Co. 

Those suits have all been consolidated under the oversight of San Diego, California-based federal judge Janis Sammartino.

The civil lawsuits began in 2015 amid an investigation into the US tuna sector into alleged price-fixing that spun out of the department's antitrust review for Thai Union's attempt to acquire Bumble Bee.

Thai Union's COSI, which in April reached a settlement in the civil lawsuit filed by large retailer Walmart, acted as a whistleblower to the U S Department of Justice (DOJ) informing on the alleged industry collusion in exchange for amnesty from prosecution. 

Bumble Bee, meanwhile, has entered a guilty plea to price fixing charges. The company agreed to pay a $25m criminal fine, which will increase to a maximum criminal fine of $81.5m, payable by a related entity, in the event of a sale of the company subject to certain terms and conditions.

Two of the company's executives, Kenneth Worsham and Walter Cameron, have pleaded guilty to price-fixing charges but have yet to be sentenced.

Bumble Bee CEO Christopher Lischewski has been indicted by the DOJ in connection with the probe but has maintained his innocence and has stepped down temporarily to contest the allegations. 

StarKist's Stephen Hodge, a former senior vice president of sales at the company, has also pleaded guilty but has yet to be sentenced. The company has also said it will plead guilty but has yet to be sentenced.

title: Thai Union, Bumble Bee push back against tuna price-fixing lawsuits
content:
Lawyers for Bumble Bee Foods and Thai Union Group's Tri-Union Seafoods are arguing that groups of civil plaintiffs banding together to wage class-action lawsuits against them shouldn't be allowed to do so. 

Civil lawsuits from dozens of wholesalers, retailers and individuals across the US allege that the plaintiffs were overcharged by a long-running price-fixing conspiracy involving Bumble Bee, Tri-Union's Chicken of the Sea brand and Dongwon Enterprises' StarKist & Co. 

Those suits have all been consolidated under the oversight of San Diego,California-based federal judge Janis Sammartino,

Earlier this year, plaintiffs in four categories or "tracks", which differ depending on how they purchased tuna from the canners, asked Sammartino to certify their individual lawsuits as joint class-actions, arguing that the facts of the cases were common enough to be treated as a group. 

This would allow the groups to have common legal counsel and pool many plaintiffs' resources together to pay the costly bills for expert witnesses, lawyers fees and other expenses that come in class-action litigation. 

However, in responding to the certification motions, Thai Union and Bumble Bee argue that there are too many differences between within some of the tracks to be treated as a class. 

The large wholesalers and distributors who dealt directly with the canners are known as "direct purchasers" with a second track of direct purchasers including large buyers such as Walmart with separate lawsuits known as "direct action" plaintiffs.

Lawsuits in two other tracks, the "commercial food preparers" including restaurants and retailers, and individual consumers known as "end-payers", include plaintiffs who purchased from the canners' tuna indirectly. 

In a motion filed Oct. 2 opposing class certification for end-payer plaintiffs, Bumble Bee said that the track must show that an anti-trust violation occurred, that all of the plaintiffs were harmed by the price-fixing and by how much.

The track's plaintiffs bought dozens of different types of tuna products from different brands from thousands of different types of different-sized stores in different states at different prices over several years. Those differences, Bumble Bee argues, mean that a joint economic model "fails" to meet class certification.

"Their failure is not surprising, given the differences among members of the 32 proposed classes," Bumble Bee's lawyers said of the end-payers.

Thai Union argued similarly, advocating against class certification for the commercial food preparers. 

"The [commercial food preparers] now acknowledge that their putative class would include members as disparate as distributors who bought the product for resale; restaurants, delis, nursing homes, and caterers who buy and use the product for commercial food preparation; and individuals who bought the product for personal consumption," the canner argued.

Judge Sammartino is expected to consider the motions in December. 

DOJ investigation

The civil lawsuits began in 2015 amid an investigation into the US tuna sector into alleged price-fixing that spun out of the department's antitrust review for Thai Union's attempt to acquire Bumble Bee.

Thai Union's COSI, which in April reached a settlement in the civil lawsuit filed by large retailer Walmart, acted as a whistleblower to the U S Department of Justice (DOJ) informing on the alleged industry collusion in exchange for amnesty from prosecution. 

Bumble Bee, meanwhile, has entered a guilty plea to price fixing charges. The company agreed to pay a $25 million criminal fine, which will increase to a maximum criminal fine of $81.5m, payable by a related entity, in the event of a sale of the company subject to certain terms and conditions.

Two of the company's executives, Kenneth Worsham and Walter Cameron, have pleaded guilty to price-fixing charges but have yet to be sentenced.

Bumble Bee CEO Christopher Lischewski has been indicted by the DOJ in connection with the probe but has maintained his innocence and has stepped down temporarily to contest the allegations. 

StarKist's Stephen Hodge, a former senior vice president of sales at the company, has also pleaded guilty but has yet to be sentenced.

title: Linked US suppliers charged with squid mislabeling fraud
content:
Two linked processing companies on the East Coast of the US were indicted on Sept. 26 for conspiracy to mislabel seafood which they then sold across the country.

The indictment accuses Roy Tuccillo Sr., 58, and his son Roy Tuccillo Jr., 31, as well as two of their Long Island, New York-based companies, Anchor Frozen Foods and Advanced Frozen Foods of purchasing Peruvian giant squid before marketing and selling it to grocery stores as octopus.

The defendants have been charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud and multiple violations of the Lacey Act, which prohibits false descriptions of fish that are transported and sold in interstate commerce. The two Westbury companies and their owners have been charged with four counts of defrauding grocery stores in Massachusetts and New Jersey.

Until trial, the indictment remains an allegation, with the defendants presumed innocent unless proven guilty beyond reasonable doubt in a court of law.

A valuable distinction

Octopus and squid have distinct differences in their taxonomy and physical appearance, but most importantly from an economic standpoint, octopus generally commands the greater retail price.

The US Food and Drug Administration allows for squid to go to market under its name or as calamari, but octopus must be labeled as such. The indictment currently leveled at the Long Island firms alleges that for three years they fraudulently imported, processed, sold and distributed 113,000 pounds of octopus that were truthfully Peruvian squid.

The case falls under the remit of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) office of law enforcement whose director, James Landon, announced the indictment. 

"NOAA "is dedicated to enforcing federal marine resource laws, including the Lacey Act and its provisions on mislabeling", said Landon, in a press release. “This investigation is a great example of how we collaboratively work with other federal partners, such as the Food and Drug Administration, to combat seafood fraud.”

title: Beleaguered Bumble Bee brings in FMCG veteran, taps consultancy to find growth
content:
Troubled US shelf-stable seafood supplier Bumble Bee Foods has hired a fast moving consumer goods (FMCG) veteran as its chief growth officer, amid a government probe of price-fixing in the sector which has also caused a wave of civil lawsuits. 

Bumble Bee -- which has pled guilty to price-fixing and is also bracing for the impact from US tariffs on seafood from China -- has hired Todd Putman, most recently with the Campbell Soup Company, in the role, according to a statement from the San Diego, California-based company. 

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion
Read more

The company is also in the middle of a "strategic transformation that will roll out over the next year", according to the statement. As part of this, Bumble Bee -- which is owned by UK-based private equity Lion Capital, also implicated in the price-fixing allegations -- will also be using San Diego-based brand and innovation consultancy, Bulldog Drummond. 

Bulldog "will help to reposition the organization for growth, build a compelling new vision and growth strategies that will guide the future of the business, develop a new product innovation pipeline that may include appropriate acquisitions and fuel a thriving company culture", the company said, as it also touted Putman's strong FMCG background. 

Before joining Bumble Bee, Putman was as general manager of Campbell Fresh -- the soup giant's consumer packaged goods business unit -- and has previous experience with Procter & Gamble, Walt Disney, and The Coca-Cola Company.

“Todd is a proven leader with the industry experience to fuel Bumble Bee’s strategic growth initiatives,” said Jan Tharp, who took over as the firm's CEO after Chris Lischewski stood down amid an indictment from the US government over his alleged involvement in the price fixing. Lischewski denies the allegations which Bumble Bee has agreed to pay a $25 million fine for taking part in. 

“I’m thrilled to join the Bumble Bee team as the company celebrates nearly 120 years as an iconic household brand,” said Putman. “Bumble Bee has all of the key components to build a contemporary growth company, and I look forward to working with the team to put a plan in place to generate both near- and long-term revenue growth.”

title: Editor’s recap: ‘Killer’ shrimp disease in China; Trouble in MSC ‘paradise’; US-China tariffs
content:
Neil Ramsden, deputy editor of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

A story on a new disease threat for Chinese shrimp production was noticeably our most-read story of last week. 

During the recent Aquaculture Roundtable Series, or TARS, conference in Chang Mai, Thailand, Robins McIntosh -- senior vice president with Charoen Pokphand Foods (CP Foods) -- flagged up shrimp hemocyte iridescent virus, or SHIV, as he forecast shrimp production in China will drop in 2018 to 512,000 metric tons. At the start of the year, an increase in production in China was being forecasted.

“SHIV in China… it needs to be watched, it is a killer,” McIntosh told the audience at TARS, at the end of a presentation largely about the strong production worldwide and the need for better marketing, as farmers have learned to manage early mortality syndrome, whitespot and enterocytozoon hepatopenaei.

It is “what is known as an emerging pathogen”, McIntosh told Undercurrent News. “We know it kills shrimp, we know it is in China, we don’t know it is a big deal. But, vigilance is required.”

Another big story last week was an investigation on the emerging issues around Marine Stewardship Council (MSC)-certified tuna in the Parties to the Nauru Agreement (PNA) islands.

An association of powerful tuna firms in Papua New Guinea (PNG), which boasts some Asian giants as members, intends to obtain its own MSC certification and terminate a collaboration with EU-based sales company Pacifical.

PNG is better off going it alone on MSC and breaking away from the PNA country group partnered with Pacifical, said Sylvester Pokajam, president and chairman of the Fishing Industry Association of PNG, which represents tuna giants Fong Chun Formosa Fishery Company, Frabelle Corp, and RD Corp, as well as a joint venture which counts Thai Union Group as a partner.

Pacifical is "not transparent with its accounts and financial operations and reporting",  Pokajam told Undercurrent, when asked why PNG has decided to obtain its own MSC certification.

Henk Brus, managing director of Pacifical, and Maurice Brownjohn, commercial manager for the PNA -- a group of tiny Pacific island nations that control the largest MSC tuna resource in the world -- refuted these allegations, however. 

In a statement sent to Undercurrent, the PNA and Pacifical rejected the non-transparency claim, referring to it as "clearly mischievous and commercially motivated". 

Live blogs

As we often are, Undercurrent was reporting live from two events last week.

It covered the Aquaculture Innovation Summit in London, which discussed current health and nutrition trends in the industry and outlined investment and innovation goals for the future. 

Venture capital investors were also attending the conference to evaluate potential financial investments or strategic partnerships.

Tom Seaman was in St. Petersburg, Russia, for the Global Fishery Forum & Seafood Expo, as the country’s major fishing and seafood companies embarked on a massive vessel and plant construction program.

The final post from that show suggested Fedor Kirsanov, CEO of Russian Fishery Company, must have been somewhat underwhelmed meeting Undercurrent for an interview; he had just arrived from the country’s Far East, where he had been at the Eastern Economic Forum, in Vladivostok. At that event, he showcased the company’s fishing and processing expansion plans to Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, the presidents of Russia and China.

Seafood sector versus tariffs

Over in the US the debate over, and fallout from, president Donald Trump's burgeoning tariff war with China continues.

Once again, reported Jason Huffman, concerns are being expressed about president Trump helping the Russians -- this time by a US seafood industry group.

Should his United States trade representative (USTR) continue on with the additional 10% to 25% tariffs it has proposed to place on 6,031 Chinese goods worth $200 billion, including reprocessed pollock and a number of other seafood products, it would be helping the Russian pollock industry gain another edge over US producers, warned Stephanie Madsen, executive director of the At-Sea Processors Association (APA), in a letter sent to the USTR.

“US trade actions that rebound to adversely affect Alaska pollock producers often strengthen our principal competition, the Russian pollock fishery, which is Russia’s largest fishery,” she said. “Chinese tariffs on US seafood products enhances opportunities in China for Russia pollock products and other seafood products, as well.”

Madsen's letter was one of more than 6,100 to be received by the USTR in response to its tariff proposals before the comment period closed on Sept. 6. 

Another saga generating a lot of reader interest is that of the lawsuit around ownership of Russian fishing giant Norebo Group. 

"Three of us have built it... And since then we honor that agreement. One third is his."

So said Vitaly Orlov, the billionaire owner of Norebo, of Alexander Tugushev, one of the three co-founders of the company, on Feb. 27, 2014, in Geneva, Switzerland, the latter alleges in a recent claim document filed in the UK High Court. 

"There is no doubt that we keep our promise that you have the benefit out of this. There is no doubt! There is no formal link. You get your benefit, you get your third,” Magnus Roth, the third co-founder of Norebo -- which Tugushev claims is now worth over $1.5 billion -- allegedly said in the same conversation. 

"My understanding having discussed with Vitaly and Magnus is that there is... it's more than a gentleman agreement. It's an oral agreement,” Nicolas Brun-Lie, a Norwegian lawyer involved with Norebo, reportedly stated.

Tugushev is suing Orlov, Roth -- who reportedly netted $330 million from selling his third in the company in 2016 -- and Andrei Petrik, a UK-based Norebo executive and “associate” of Orlov in the UK court. Orlov, Roth and Petrik, Tugushev alleges, conspired to deprive him of a third in the company.

He’s claiming his stake in the business -- which has substantial assets in Russian Atlantic and Pacific cod, haddock, pollock, and herring -- is worth at least $350m. Also, he claims he’s owed millions in dividends he should have been paid going back to 2005.

You can read editor Tom's comprehensive feature outlining the situation here.

Tampa Bay versus National Fish 

The US has its own share of legal disputes rumbling on as well. 

US processor Tampa Bay Fisheries has blasted National Fish & Seafood (NFS) as a “bankrupt company run by investors and still reeling from its top executives’ criminal convictions”, seeking to undermine the Red Chamber Group-owned firm’s success with a lawsuit over the hiring of a former NFS executive, Tom reported.

No further mention was made of NFS, which is part of Pacific Andes International (PAIH), being “bankrupt” in the document. However, PAIH, China Fishery Group and other Pacific Andes group companies are in Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the US, but not NFS directly. PAIH ultimately owns 60% of NFS, via Peaksville, a UK holding company, which actually cut losses in its latest reported fiscal year. 

Also, no more was said on “top executives’ criminal convictions. However, in April, former NFS president Jack Ventola was sentenced to two years in prison on tax fraud charges. In 2017, Richard Pandolfo, a former senior NFS executive, was sentenced to one year of probation with six months to be served in home confinement, a fine of $5,000, and restitution of $25,879.

NFS alleged Tampa Bay has stolen trade secrets in a bid to win clam contracts for Whole Foods Market and others, after poaching Kathleen Scanlon. 

However, in a document opposing NFS’ call for a preliminary injunction in a US district court in Massachusetts, Tampa Bay said NFS' lawsuit is based on a fish tale about "the one that got away".

Meanwhile, Spanish seafood company Dagustin Jaime Soriano, which also owns farms in Honduras, told Undercurrent shrimp prices from Central America have been in the process of rising since mid-July, when they touched their lowest level this year after months of decline.

From now to the end of October or beginning of November, global shrimp prices should further rise, driven by rising demand from China, for the local New Year festival, and from Europe, for Christmas celebrations, said Dagustin's Jaime Soriano Paniego.

In the US, shrimp consumption tends to be higher during the summer holiday, July 4 celebration and Super Bowl, he said. 

"Consumption in Spain has remained pretty stable since approximately 2012, while it has recently grown in China and some other Asian countries," Soriano noted, adding that the increase in global production, particularly from India and Ecuador, caused a deep price decline in the first half of the year.

Back in the US, prosecutors from the US Department of Justice have asked a California judge to delay a grocery wholesaler's lawsuit against former Bumble Bee Foods CEO Chris Lischewski, over concerns that it could complicate the criminal case against him, reported Jason Smith.

Lischewski, who was indicted on criminal price-fixing charges in May 2018 and subsequently stepped down to focus on his defense, is also the defendant in a civil lawsuit from Associated Wholesale Grocers (AWG) that claims the company was harmed by the tuna canner's price-fixing.

Prosecutor Leslie Wulff wrote in a filing that allowing the AWG lawsuit to proceed, which could involve depositions of witnesses including Lischewski, could potentially interfere with the prosecution and run the risk of violating the former CEO's fifth amendment right prohibiting self-incrimination. 

"The government’s proposed stay balances the government’s interest in protecting the integrity of the criminal proceedings, Mr. Lischewski’s fifth amendment rights, and the victims’ interest in conducting discovery and seeking restitution for the price-fixing scheme," Wulff wrote.

Snow crab, barramundi news

Jason Smith also covered the announcement that US Barramundi farmer Australis Aquaculture has sold its Turner Falls, Massachusetts recirculating aquaculture system facility to Great Falls Aquaculture, in order to focus on expanding in Southeast Asia and offshore.

Australis began farming barramundi in 2004 at Turner Falls but later expanded production overseas as demand grew. 

Great Falls will continue to produce barramundi at the facility and will retain Australis' employees there. 

“This was a strategic decision that allows Australis to focus on the expansion of our marine aquaculture operations in Southeast Asia," Australis CEO Josh Goldman said. "We will continue to operate all North American sales, marketing, logistics and finance activities from Massachusetts as we grow our global retail and foodservice business."

"We continue to believe in the importance of recirculating aquaculture technologies and it remains an integral part of our Vietnam farming systems. However, for us, we see our long-term growth in large-scale ocean farming.”

Jason Huffman, meanwhile, wrote that after "hanging out in the upper stratosphere for most of the year, the price of standard-size snow crabs from Canada has finally started hovering a little closer to Earth"; just in time for the beginning of the holiday order season.

The price of four- to eight-ounce snow crabs opened the 2018 season in Canada in April at $7.90 to $8.00/lb, as Japanese buyers lined up early and kept prices high on the odd range of sizes they typically request. 

But when the Japanese buyers departed, the market could no longer support the high prices and the drop began. “It turns out that crab is not gold, and there is a limit,” one source snapped.

Finally, the International Pole and Line Foundation (IPNLF) approached Undercurrent to reveal it had made the decision to withdraw from the MSC certification process of the Pesquera Echebastar Indian Ocean purse seine skipjack tuna fishery.

It is one of three objecting stakeholders involved in the process; NGO Shark Project is also withdrawing, project leader Iris Ziegler told me, while the World Wide Fund for Nature remains involved. The next stage of the process -- which is one of several "streamlined" MSC assessment pilot processes taking place -- will be a hearing in Seychelles, planned for Oct. 1. At present, it seems, only WWF will be there to represent objectors. 

IPNLF said the decision to withdraw was not taken lightly, but that the process "has become inconsistent with MSC’s obligations for sustainability certification".

It believes there have been unfair actions and decisions that have prejudiced its ability to participate on an even footing in the process, it said. These actions are in direct contravention of the MSC’s own core principles of transparency and accessibility for all stakeholders concerned with certification, it claimed.

IPNLF plans to submit a formal complaint to the MSC, which should lead to an internal investigation carried out by the latter, IPNLF managing director Martin Purves told Undercurrent. He was unsure as to whether this would mean a pause in the assessment process.

title: Prosecutors want suit against Lischewski stalled due to criminal case
content:
Prosecutors from the US Department of Justice (DOJ) have asked a California judge to delay a grocery wholesaler's lawsuit against former Bumble Bee Foods CEO Chris Lischewski over concerns that it could complicate the criminal case against him. 

Lischewski, who was indicted on criminal price-fixing charges in May 2018 and subsequently stepped down to focus on his defense, is also the defendant in a civil lawsuit from Associated Wholesale Grocers (AWG) that claims the company was harmed by the tuna canner's price-fixing.

Prosecutor Leslie Wulff wrote in a filing that allowing the AWG lawsuit to proceed, which could involve depositions of witnesses including Lischewski, could potentially interfere with the prosecution and run the risk of violating the former CEO's fifth amendment right prohibiting self-incrimination. 

"The government’s proposed stay balances the government’s interest in protecting the integrity of the criminal proceedings, Mr. Lischewski’s fifth amendment rights, and the victims’ interest in conducting discovery and seeking restitution for the price-fixing scheme," Wulff wrote.

Bumble Bee previously pleaded guilty to criminal price-fixing charges although Lischewski has said he was not involved in the crime. The same judge overseeing AWG's case, Janis Sammartino, ruled in April 2018 that Lischewski could not be added as a defendant in most civil lawsuits as plaintiffs had missed a deadline to add new parties. However, the AWG lawsuit is new, having been filed in August 2018 and, as such, the plaintiff was allowed to include Lischewski.

The amount of documents in the DOJ's hands relating to the criminal price-fixing case, which also involves Bumble Bee competitors Tri-Union Seafoods, the Thai Union Group owned US arm that operates the Chicken of the Sea brand, and Dongwon Industries' StarKist & Co, exceeds two million, Lischewski's lawyers have said.

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion
Read more

In a Sept. 4 filing they lamented what they called the DOJ's "voluminous, ongoing, and slow" document production.

"In total, the government has produced over 1.5 terabytes of data, totaling more than 2m documents and roughly 6m pages, and it has informed Mr. Lischewski that it intends to continue producing more documents. The discovery produced is diverse, and the government has refused to provide substantive detail regarding what that discovery includes," Lischewski's lawyers said.

title: American Seafoods adds Decker, McCabe to board
content:
US pollock harvester American Seafoods Group has added Alaska attorney Trevor McCabe and Keith Decker, the CEO of New Bedford, Massachusetts, scallop harvester Blue Harvest Fisheries to its board of directors. 

The appointments follow the departure of former Bumble Bee Foods CEO Chris Lischewski, who left in August, a move that followed his stepping down from the tuna canner to fight criminal allegations of price fixing. 

McCabe's legal work has long involved him with fisheries issues and he previously served as executive director of the At-Sea Processors Association.

Decker, the former CEO of Canada's High Liner Foods, joined Blue Harvest in January 2018. 

Blue Harvest, like American Seafoods, is backed by private equity Bregal Partners.

Lischewski, who was indicted earlier this year on allegations of criminal price-fixing in the tuna industry, joined American Seafoods' board and took an undisclosed stake in that company after its 2015 recapitalization. 

That 2015 deal, which was led by Bregal Partners, also featured a team of industry veterans: Frank Dulcich of Pacific Seafood Group; Lischewski; former Icicle Seafoods CEO Amy Humphreys; Scott Perekslis, Bregal Partners’ co-founder and managing partner; and American Seafoods’ then chairman and CEO Bernt Bodal.

With the exception of Lischewski, who was still listed as a board member as of April 2018, the others remain on the board, according to an Aug. 1 Securities and Exchange Commission filing. 

Also included as directors are Paul McGill, Charles Yoon, William Bittner and William Rosenfeld Jr. 

Lischewski, who is pleading not guilty, has repeatedly pronounced his innocence even as his company pleaded guilty to price-fixing charges last year. 

Prosecutors allege that the US 'big three' tuna canners, including Bumble Bee, Thai Union Group-owner Tri-Union Seafoods, which sells under the Chicken of the Sea brand, and Dongwon Enterprises' Starkist & Co, colluded to fix the price of canned tuna at an artificially high level.
