title: Editor’s recap: Indian shrimp prices rise fast; Rabobank says lower levels here to stay; Cargill’s seafood plans
content:
Tom Seaman, editorial director of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

As prices for vannamei shrimp raw material rise fast in India, a report from Rabobank predicted low levels for the crustacean are likely in the future, with the production outlook strong. 

These two stories about shrimp, as well as another about Cargill's aspirations to expand in this sector from its current position in feed, as well as in farmed salmon, were the top three Undercurrent News stories of last week. 

An update on the sale process for Young's Seafood, revealing bids from Mitsubishi Corporation; UK Fisheries, a joint venture between Iceland's Samherji and the Netherlands' Parlevliet & van der Plas; and CapVest Partners, also got a lot of interest. 

Other well-read stories were High Liner Foods' decision to part company with Peter Brown, a former Cargill executive who was running its US business; a controversial plan from the Chilean government around salmon production; a Dutch fishing firm's move downstream with a processing acquisition; and an analysis from our Asia reporter, Louis Harkell, on the impact of the 25% tariffs from China on US fishmeal. 

Then, updates on the price-fixing allegations against the former CEO of Bumble Bee Foods and Lion Capital, its private equity owner, as well as big retailers' efforts to get emails they claim will reveal more released, also got a lot of attention. 

Shrimp prices 

The prices for vannamei shrimp raw material in India are moving up fast.

Processors are fighting for reduced levels of raw material to fulfill orders after farmers reduced stocking due to disease issues and the weak market, sources told me. 

“Big processors are struggling to complete orders and delays, maybe major, are now anticipated. New offers from processors are now scarce,” said Jim Gulkin, managing director of Siam Canadian Group, a Bangkok, Thailand-based, pan-Asian frozen seafood supplier with an office in India.

“Raw material shortages will continue through at least October and perhaps through year-end,” he told me. 

According to Gulkin, big processors in Andhra Pradesh, the main state for Indian shrimp farming, as well as packers in other areas, “are racing to complete major year-end sales orders against rapidly-declining raw material availability”.

However, according to a report from Rabobank analyst Gorjan Nikolik, the global shrimp raw material price crash seen in the first half of 2018 is indicative of a "new reality" when it comes to levels going forward. Neil Ramsden, our assistant editor, covered the report, "Keeping up with the Crustaceans".

Gorjan Nikolik noted the price crash occurred during the first harvest of 2018, as a result of strong double-digit supply growth from India and Ecuador, though growth was also reported in Indonesia, Vietnam, and others.

"Currently, many farmers are harvesting their shrimp at a loss -- or at least with a far lower profit margin in the last five years -- mainly because the key elements of the cost part of the equation, such as feed, energy, and labor, have not contracted (and for some, have increased)."

He predicted that, in addition to farmers' protests, the industry's shrinking profit pool will be redistributed throughout the value chain, with "considerable consequences".

Nikolik echoed what sources have been telling us for much of 2018; that many farmers will reduce stocking for the next shrimp crop, or reduce feeding rates and delay harvests, or simply not stock at all. 

"Shrimp farming has a fairly short cycle, and farmers can respond quickly to changes in price, balancing the market within a few months," he wrote. "However, predicting how farmers in each region will respond to a low-price environment across a number of crops in the next few years is much harder."

India has just begun to see prices rapidly rising again, as packers compete for limited raw materials. However, Rabobank does not see this as the start of a full recovery.

"In our view, although a mild short-term price recovery is likely, the lower price level, in the absence of a major new disease outbreak, does represent a new reality. A reality in which price levels dictate supply trends even more than biological supply-side challenges; a shift from a supply-driven industry to a more demand-driven one."

Cargill's big seafood plans 

Einar Wathne, who was running the aqua feed division for Cargill, is leaving the US agribusiness giant. However, before he goes, he is coming up with a plan on how the company can expand out of aqua feed into other areas of the seafood value chain. 

Going beyond feed up and downstream in the farmed salmon and shrimp sectors could figure in this plan, which must also be driven by consumer demand, Wathne told me. 

“Salmon and shrimp are the areas we have most emphasis on for the feed side and that will clearly color our focus for the wider range. We are also a company that works to scale, so these big sectors are where Cargill works best,” he said.

“The most important thing for us is to find what fits best in our total strategy, what fits best with the rest of Cargill. We are strong in shrimp and salmon,” he said.

The bullishness on seafood from Cargill, which has operations spanning the entire value chain in other proteins, and reported sales of $114.7 billion and operating income of $3.2bn in its latest financial year, comes from the very top.

David MacLennan, Cargill CEO, told Bloomberg Businessweek a few weeks ago that the company would continue to aggressively expand in aquaculture, as part of a reboot of its strategy of being a middleman. 

P&P, Samherji JV, Mitsubishi, CapVest in mix for Young’s 

We've been working hard to break the latest news on the Young's sale process since it kicked off earlier in the year. 

The process seems to be getting closer to a conclusion, with two foreign trade players still said to be in the running, along with at least one private equity. 

Japan's Mitsubishi is still in the running to buy Young's, along with UK Fisheries, a joint venture between P&P and Samherji, as well as UK-based private equity CapVest. 

The sale process for Young's, which is being run by Stamford Partners and Houlihan Lokey on behalf of HPS Investment Partners, Bain Capital Credit, and Lion Capital, is in the final stage, with second-round -- binding -- bids already said to be in. 

The Telegraph article gives a valuation of between £170 million and £200m, but we have heard some bids came in under £150m. The news Young's will lose around £30m in shrimp and whitefish business with Asda during the process has impacted the valuation, sources told me. "It's never ideal to lose business mid-process, that goes without saying", said one. 

Undercurrent sources have also tipped Mitsubishi, which owns Princes in the UK and has been a big supplier of shrimp and pangasius into Young's, as a frontrunner in the sale process in the last few days. Mitsubishi, which also owns salmon farmer Cermaq Group, was said to be in talks to buy Young's at the start of the year, but the Japanese firm then "downed tools". The sale process was said to be driven by a desire to get Mitsubishi to speed up in its approach. 

It has also recently emerged that Mitsubishi will lose pangasius business supplying Young's, which the UK firm is going directly to Vietnamese processor Godaco Seafood on. Mitsubishi is also said to be Young's supplier for the shrimp that goes into Asda. Young's is losing this contract to Lyons Seafoods, however, meaning another loss for Mitsubishi. 

Iceland's Samherji -- which recently moved downstream in the UK with a deal for fish and chip shop-focused distributor Collins (Seafoods) -- is also a name that has been linked to the sale process by Undercurrent sources. Samherji has a long-running co-operation with the Netherlands based P&P with UK Fisheries, which operates trawlers catching cod and haddock. Samherij and P&P were also teaming up on a bid for the Peruvian assets of China Fishery Group, according to Undercurrent sources. 

Speaking about the Collins deal, Gustaf Baldvinsson, the managing director of Seagold -- Samherji's UK operation -- told Undercurrent the company is looking to go further downstream. 

On July 5 we reported CapVest, which sold Young’s and its then-parent, FoodVest Group, for £1.1bn to Lion Capital in 2008, is looking to buy the company again. 

CapVest already has money tied up in Lion/Gem Luxembourg 3, the owner of the Young's operating company, as a legacy of the sale in 2008 and, as a result, has a seat on the investor board of the company, sources told Undercurrent.

Sources familiar with CapVest, which has raised in excess of €4bn and completed over 150 transactions since being founded by Seamus Fitzpatrick and Randy Shure in 1999, said the firm would be a strong owner for Young's again.

Peter Brown gone in High Liner restructure

High Liner reported second-quarter results last week, as well as the departure of Peter Brown, the former president and chief operating officer of its US business. 

Brown left in a "North American organizational realignment" where his role was eliminated, the company announced in its second-quarter results, where earnings dropped. 

According to High Liner, Brown had been moved to a role as chief supply chain officer prior to his exit from the company, but it's not clear when. 

Rod Hepponstall, who took over as president and CEO from High Liner veteran Henry Demone earlier in the year, said more restructuring is to come. 

"The company's financial results for the second quarter of 2018 reflect continued challenges in the business related to soft sales volume, a shift in product mix from higher margin value-added products to lower margin commodity products, raw material cost increases not fully passed along to customers and inefficiencies in our supply chain," said Hepponstall. 

"The impact of these challenges in the second quarter was most acute in our US business," he said. 

"I believe significant opportunities exist for High Liner Foods, but after my first quarter as CEO, it is apparent to me that before we can fully take advantage of these opportunities, we need to operate more efficiently," said Hepponstall.

Chile salmon rule change plans

At the end of last week, Chile’s economy minister Jose Ramon Valente opted to postpone the implementation of a government measure to toughen salmon farming rules to avoid an industry crisis.

The minister set a deadline of Aug. 27 for salmon farming companies to provide a two-page memorandum putting forward their views on a measure that would make it harder for certain companies to expand by lowering permitted stocking densities.

The proposed change to density regulation rules, one of two rule options available to salmon farmers, irked a handful of companies who saw it as the only way to claw back historical production levels. 

A group that includes Norway’s Marine Harvest, Cermaq, Agrosuper’s Los Fiordos, Empresas AquaChile and Salmones Aysen were forced to stock pens at costly low densities to recover their output levels as they had been stocking sites at lower than average in the run-up to the new rules. A second group, led by Australis Seafoods, Blumar Seafoods, and Salmones Camanchaca, were happy to subscribe to a second government option called planned stocking reduction. That option imposes caps on company-wide output in exchange for the right to stock sites at the maximum allowed density.

“We are practically 50-50 between those who are the contra group, compared to those that are in favor,” Pablo Cajtak, CEO of Salmones Aysen told Matt Craze, who reports for Undercurrent from Chile. “We think that the minister understood the concerns of the contras.”

A growing conflict could lead to more companies quitting the producer association group, SalmonChile, one executive said. Marine Harvest already quit SalmonChile last year as the industry group led talks with government regulator Sernapesca to craft new salmon farming rules.

Lawsuit: Lischewski reaped ‘unlawful’ profits from numerous sales

Chris Lischewski, the former CEO of Bumble Bee, benefited from several sales of the US shelf-stable seafood giant while participating in a price-fixing conspiracy between 2004 and 2015, it is alleged in a civil lawsuit. 

According to an amended complaint from Associated Wholesale Grocers (AWG), filed in a California court on Aug. 14, Lischewski "knowingly participated in, facilitated and coordinated the conspiracy", from which he "profited substantially" in several ways, including using the firm as his "private banker". 

"He used his role to reap unlawful profits by selling Bumble Bee numerous times throughout the conspiracy period," the document alleged. Lischewski -- who stood down earlier in the year to fight criminal allegations from US Department of Justice (DOJ) --   did not respond to a request for comment from Undercurrent. 

Private equity Lion, named as a plaintiff in the AWG lawsuit, along with Lischewski, bought Bumble Bee in 2010 from Centre Partners Managment, for $980m. Lion had agreed on a deal to sell Bumble Bee to Thai Union Group -- also a plaintiff -- in 2014 for $1.5bn, but this collapsed at the end of the following year after a DOJ competition probe, which seemingly ultimately led to the criminal case by the DOJ. 

Prior to this failed deal, Lischewski was involved in several sales of the company, two involving Centre Partners. Having bought the seafood firm in 2003 when it was spun out of ConAgra Foods in 2003, Centre Partners partially exited its stake when it combined Bumble Bee with Connors Brothers -- then owner of the Canadian Clover Leaf brand -- to become the Connors Brothers Income Fund in 2004. By 2005, Centre Partners had fully exited the business through secondary offerings, according to a 2011 article by Forbes. 

Centre Partners -- which is not a plaintiff or accused of any wrongdoing by AWG -- then bought Bumble Bee for the second time in 2008 for $600m, before the 2010 sale to Lion. "Further discovery will be necessary to determine what Lion knew about the conspiracy before it bought Bumble Bee," the AWG amended complaint states. 

Retail giants push for Lion to release ‘incriminating’ Lischewski emails

Earlier last week, Kroger Company, Ahold Delhaize, and other big US retailers are calling on a judge to make Lion release documents they say could be key in proving a price-fixing conspiracy in shelf-stable seafood.

These “highly-probative” documents apparently include emails sent by Lischewski, who has also been indicted by the DOJ on criminal charges. He denies the charges. They were first mentioned in a filing from December last year when plaintiffs' lawyers said Lischewski and Lion exchanged "incriminating" emails, which were recently uncovered in the legal discovery process. However, Lion has since failed to produce the documents, according to the latest filing from the retailers. 

On Aug. 10, Kroger, Ahold Delhaize, Albertsons Companies, H.E. Butt Grocery Company and Hy-Vee filed an objection to a July 31 motion from a judge which determined it would be “unduly burdensome” to require Lion to produce “highly relevant documents” that the UK-based private equity firm had already collected and agreed to produce in 2017 in response to plaintiffs’ subpoenas.

“These documents likely contain crucial information relevant to proving the conspiracy,” wrote the retail giants’ legal team, from law firm Kenny Nachwalter.

Dutch fishing firm, fresh supplier goes downstream 

Undercurrent has long been covering the increase in cross-border, cross-sector acquisitions in the seafood sector.

It's interesting to note how this is happening with big, global players, but also on a more local level. Last week, for example, a vessel owner and fresh seafood supplier based in the Netherlands bought Belgian processor Multi-Fish and its sister companies, in a move to create “vertical integration” and move closer to the market.

Zeevishandel Mercuur, based in the port of Ijmuiden, bought Multi-Fish and several other companies previously owned by Fox Holdings, a group built up by entrepreneur Donaat De Vos.

As well as Multi-Fish, Fox also sold Verbiest, Transaqua, Daniel's Visbedrijf, Mosselman Seafood, F. Verleye and Het Viskraam to Zeevishandel Mercuur, the company confirmed to me. 

De Vos was not immediately available for comment, but a statement from Zeevishandel Mercuur cited “unexpected personal circumstances” as the driver of the sale.

The prominent position Zeevishandel Mercuur has in the fresh fish trade, as well as its own fishing vessels, will create a vertically integrated firm, the company’s Piet Spaanderman told me. 

As well as buying fresh fish from others, Zeevishandel Mercuur operates two beam trawlers, he said.

“With this deal, we get closer to the market and also we are a stronger and bigger group, for buying,” he said.

Neil Ramsden, our assistant editor, then spoke with Rosemarie van Duijn, a director of Zeevishandel Mercuur. The company hopes the deal can be a route to dealing with more retailers, she said. 

"Combined, our companies have greater knowledge of markets," said van Duijn. "We're still looking for synergies we can implement, but we expect to capitalize on economies of scale; for instance, both firms are sourcing from Iceland. There are chances to bring our costs down."

US fishmeal producers left exposed by China’s 25% tariff blow

US fishmeal producers -- including the US’ largest fishmeal producer Omega Protein -- are "certainly in some trouble” after China announced it would impose 25% tariffs on imports from the country, a fishmeal industry analyst told Louis Harkell, our Asia-focused senior reporter. 

Jean-Francois Mittaine, an analyst with 30 years' experience in the sector, told Louis Omega Protein and others in the sector will struggle to find new markets as Chinese importers turn to alternative sources. This will hit both the menhaden fisheries of the Gulf of Mexico and the pollock fishmeal industry of Alaska.

"For the Americans it is a problem," said Mittaine. “I don't see what they're going to do with their fishmeal."

On Aug. 8, China’s Ministry of Commerce said it would impose an additional tariff on imports of US fishmeal of 25% (HS code 23012010). The ingredient used in animal and fish feed was among 333 US goods worth $16bn in annual trade targeted. 

The Chinese counter-move will take effect immediately after the US imposes tariffs on the same amount of Chinese goods on Aug 23.

In 2017, the US produced around 250,000t of fishmeal, Enrico Bachis, market research director at the Marine Ingredients Organization, known as IFFO, told Louis. Of this, the US exported 61,248t to China, worth $87m, according to the International Trade Center, citing US figures. This amounted to 38.7% of its total fishmeal exports by volume. 

Chinese customs, however, report much higher imports of US fishmeal of 102,731t in 2017, worth $160m.

This would mean either China took 24.5% or 41.1% of total US fishmeal production in 2017, depending on trade figures referred to.

Bachis said he thinks it is "more appropriate to look at the imports of fishmeal reported by China", in order to understand the repercussions of the new tariff applied on US fishmeal by the Chinese. 

Mittaine, who also referred to the Chinese customs figures, described the volume as a  "very large amount".

title: Lawsuit: Lischewski used Bumble Bee as private banker, reaped ‘unlawful’ profits from numerous sales
content:
Chris Lischewski, the former CEO of Bumble Bee Foods, benefited from several sales of the US shelf-stable seafood giant while participating in a price-fixing conspiracy between 2004 and 2015, it is alleged in a civil lawsuit. 

According to an amended complaint from Associated Wholesale Grocers (AWG), filed in a California court on Aug. 14, Lischewski "knowingly participated in, facilitated and coordinated the conspiracy", from which he "profited substantially" in several ways, including using the firm as his "private banker". 

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion
Read more

"He used his role to reap unlawful profits by selling Bumble Bee numerous times throughout the conspiracy period," the document alleged. Lischewski -- who stood down earlier in the year to fight criminal allegations from US Department of Justice (DOJ) --   did not respond to a request for comment from Undercurrent News.

Lion Capital, named as a plaintiff in the AWG lawsuit, along with Lischewski, bought Bumble Bee in 2010 from Centre Partners Managment, for $980 million. Lion had agreed on a deal to sell Bumble Bee to Thai Union Group -- also a plaintiff -- in 2014 for $1.5 billion, but this collapsed at the end of the following year after a DOJ competition probe, which seemingly ultimately led to the criminal case by the DOJ. 

Prior to this failed deal, Lischewski was involved in several sales of the company, two involving Centre Partners. Having bought the seafood firm in 2003 when it was spun out of ConAgra Foods in 2003, Centre Partners partially exited its stake when it combined Bumble Bee with Connors Brothers -- then owner of the Canadian Clover Leaf brand -- to become the Connors Brothers Income Fund in 2004. By 2005, Centre Partners had fully exited the business through secondary offerings, according to a 2011 article by Forbes. 

Centre Partners -- which is not a plaintiff or accused of any wrongdoing by AWG -- then bought Bumble Bee for the second time in 2008 for $600m, before the 2010 sale to Lion. "Further discovery will be necessary to determine what Lion knew about the conspiracy before it bought Bumble Bee," the AWG amended complaint states. 

Lischewski also used Bumble Bee as his "personal private banker, authorizing loans to himself from Bumble Bee even while Bumble Bee was woefully undercapitalized," the document alleges. The next part of the document is redacted, however. 

The document claims Lion undercapitalized Bumble Bee at the time of the accusation in 2010 in 2010 and "kept Bumble Bee undercapitalized thereafter". Again, a long section on the alleged undercapitalization is redacted. 

Lischewski also allegedly sent emails about a tuna price-fixing conspiracy to executives with Lion, it is alleged in the AWG lawsuit.

He then deleted these "incriminating emails" in an attempt to thwart AWG and the DOJ's investigation "into his unlawful conduct", it is alleged. 

According to the amended complaint, Lischewski sent emails regarding the conspiracy to Jacob Capps and Eric Lindberg, then executives with the US operation of the UK-based private equity, in January 2012. 

Lischewski, Lion and its associated entities are plaintiffs in the AWG complaint, which was originally filed in May in a Kansas court, before being consolidated into the main group of civil cases alleging a tuna price-fixing conspiracy in California. 

Retail giants push for Bumble Bee parent to release ‘incriminating’ Lischewski emails

He is also said to have directly forwarded emails "regarding the conspiracy" from Ken Worsham and Walter Scott Cameron, two senior sales executives who have subsequently pled guilty in the DOJ for price fixing, to Capps and Lindberg, who both left Lion in 2016, according to their Linkedin profiles. Capps and Lindberg, who are not listed as plaintiffs in the complaint, could not be reached for comment by Undercurrent. Lyndon Lea, co-founder of Lion, also did not respond to a request for comment. 

Lischewski is said to have told the Lion executives over email that Thai Union US shelf-stable seafood arm Tri-Union Seafoods, which trades as Chicken of the Sea International, and Dongwon Industries-owned StarKist & Co. were "cheating" on pricing. Thai Union, Tri-Union, Dongwon, Starkist and Del Monte Corporation, the former owner of the latter, now named Big Heart Pet Brands, are all also named as plaintiffs in the lawsuit from AWG, along with Lischewski and the Lion companies. 

Prior to this, in October 2011, Lischewski reportedly briefed Lindberg on the "current competitive situation" before the then-Lion executive met with Dongwon executives. This, according to the complaint, is the "code" Lischewski used when discussing the conspiracy. 

The complaint notes the DOJ's criminal indictment of Lischewski for price-fixing said he used code to allude to the conspiracy. 

As well as Capps and Lindberg, a Lion executive named Jeff Chang is also named in the lawsuit. Chang was not immediately available for comment to Undercurrent and, like Lindberg and Capps, is not a plaintiff. 

Lischewski plans to file a motion stating he should be removed from the AWG lawsuit, according to a document filed earlier in August by his legal team. 

In April, Janis Sammartino, a judge for the southern district of California overseeing the civil lawsuits, ordered that lawsuits could not be modified to add Lischewski as a defendant, but that Lion and its affiliates could be added. 

However, the AWG complaint is new and not amended, so is seemingly free to include Lischewski.

Guilty pleas 

Last year, Bumble Bee agreed to plead guilty to price-fixing. As part of its guilty plea, Bumble Bee agreed to pay a $25m criminal fine, which will increase to a maximum criminal fine of $81.5m, payable by a related entity, in the event of a sale of the company subject to certain terms and conditions.

Lischewski seeks to dismiss lawsuit alleging he fixed tuna prices for over ten years

Two of the company's executives, Worsham and Cameron, have also pleaded guilty to price-fixing charges. Steve Hodge, a former StarKist executive, has also pled guilty to price fixing. 

Incriminating emails

There are also seemingly more emails between Lischewski and Lion to be revealed. Earlier this week, Kroger Company, Ahold Delhaize, and other big US retailers called on a judge to make Lion release documents they say could be key in proving a price-fixing conspiracy in shelf-stable seafood.

These “highly-probative” documents apparently include emails sent by Lischewski. 

On Aug. 10, Kroger, Ahold Delhaize, Albertsons Companies, H.E. Butt Grocery Company and Hy-Vee filed an objection to a July 31 motion from a judge which determined it would be “unduly burdensome” to require Lion to produce “highly relevant documents” that the UK-based private equity firm had already collected and agreed to produce in 2017 in response to plaintiffs’ subpoenas.

“These documents likely contain crucial information relevant to proving the conspiracy,” wrote the retail giants’ legal team, from law firm Kenny Nachwalter.

The emails sent by Lischewski should have been produced to the plaintiffs and the DOJ “long ago”, the document stated.

“They were not included in the Bumble Bee production and apparently were deleted by Mr. Lischewski, perhaps in an effort to conceal his illegal conduct,” the document alleged.

title: Retail giants push for Bumble Bee parent to release ‘incriminating’ Lischewski emails
content:
Kroger Company, Ahold Delhaize, and other big US retailers are calling on a judge to make Lion Capital, the private equity owner of Bumble Bee Foods, release documents they say could be key in proving a price-fixing conspiracy in shelf-stable seafood.

These “highly-probative” documents apparently include emails sent by Christopher Lischewski, the former CEO of Bumble Bee -- which has already pled guilty to price-fixing in the Department of Justice (DOJ) criminal case against the sector -- who has also been indicted by the DOJ on criminal charges. They were first mentioned in a filing from December last year, when plaintiffs' lawyers said Lischewski and Lion exchanged "incriminating" emails, which were recently uncovered in the legal discovery process. However, Lion has since failed to produce the documents, according to the latest filing from the retailers. 

On Aug. 10, Kroger, Ahold Delhaize, Albertsons Companies, H.E. Butt Grocery Company and Hy-Vee filed an objection to a July 31 motion from a judge which determined it would be “unduly burdensome” to require Lion to produce “highly relevant documents” that the UK-based private equity firm had already collected and agreed to produce in 2017 in response to plaintiffs’ subpoenas.

Lischewski seeks to dismiss lawsuit alleging he fixed tuna prices for over ten years

“These documents likely contain crucial information relevant to proving the conspiracy,” wrote the retail giants’ legal team, from law firm Kenny Nachwalter.

The emails sent by Lischewski -- who it has emerged is no longer on the board of American Seafoods Group -- should have been produced to the plaintiffs and the DOJ “long ago”, the document stated.

“They were not included in the Bumble Bee production and apparently were deleted by Mr. Lischewski, perhaps in an effort to conceal his illegal conduct,” the document alleged.

Lischewski maintains his innocence to the criminal allegations brought by the DOJ and also plans to file a motion stating he should be removed from a recent civil lawsuit, from Associated Wholesale Grocers (AWG), in which he is a plaintiff.

In April, Janis Sammartino, a judge for the southern district of California overseeing the civil lawsuits, ordered that lawsuits could not be modified to add Lischewski as a defendant, but that Lion and its affiliates could be added. This meant Kroger and the other big retailers were unable to add him.

However, the AWG complaint is new and not amended, so is seemingly free to include Lischewski.

Lischewski did not respond to a request for comment from Undercurrent News. Lyndon Lea, co-founder of Lion, also did not respond to a request for comment.

The Aug. 10 document notes that, on Dec. 3, 2015, Thai Union Group announced it had abandoned a deal for Bumble Bee “in the face of DOJ’s criminal investigation of them, prompting William Baer, then head of the DOJ’s Antitrust Division, to state later that day that “[the DOJ’s] investigation convinced us – and the parties knew or should have known from the get go – that the market is not functioning competitively today, and further consolidation would only make things worse”.

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion
Read more

Thai Union’s US shelf-stable operation Tri-Union Seafoods -- which trades as Chicken of the Sea International -- is the whistleblower in the DOJ case.

The requests from the retailers for information from Lion “focus on two broad topic areas: (1) the acquisition/merger between Defendants Bumble Bee and Thai Union, which alerted the DOJ to possible anticompetitive conduct and resulted in COSI applying for amnesty from the DOJ; 6 and (2) documents pertaining to communications among competitors regarding pricing and supply of tuna products as well as Bumble Bee’s inability to pay a larger fine to the DOJ”.

The legal team of Kroger and the others served two subpoenas on Lion in April and June 2017. Then, Lion agreed to produce documents in response to these subpoenas.

“They collected the documents and substantially reviewed them for production,” the document states.

Lion then “made limited initial rolling productions in response to the subpoenas”.

“In mid-October 2017, the Lion entities represented that they had completed just under half of their production by volume and would complete their production before the end of 2017 (the winter holidays notwithstanding). Soon thereafter, however, things went awry (from the Lion entities’ perspective),” the document notes.

Although the plaintiffs received less than half of the relevant documents collected by the Lion, the documents that were produced provided the factual basis for the allegations against the Bumble Bee parent, the document states.

The retailers then sought leave to amend their complaints and name the Lion and its other affiliated companies as defendants. But, shortly after the direct purchaser class filed their motion to amend, Lion informed the plaintiffs they “were suspending further production of their documents in response to the subpoenas”.

The magistrate judge denied the plaintiffs’ request for these documents, but the legal filing of the retailers said this must be an error.

The judge, however, “mistakenly found that there was not good cause for early discovery because he failed to consider: (1) that this dispute was about documents that the Lion entities have already collected and substantially reviewed, (2) that the documents contain unique and, likely, key information related not only to the Lion entities but also to other defendants, and (3) that plaintiffs will be prejudiced if they are forced to continue taking depositions without this key discovery”.

Given the “importance of the documents already produced” by Lion, the retailers claim they will be prejudiced if they are deprived of the remainder of the production during the last few months of fact discovery.

“For example, plaintiffs have already noticed depositions for TUG [Thai Union] employees, which will likely take place in Thailand in September or October,” the document said.

“If the court does not order production of the Lion documents soon, Plaintiffs may be forced to depose key witnesses without potentially crucial discovery.

Ordering production of the documents now will ensure that plaintiffs are not prejudiced by the Lion cntities’ withholding of important information during crucial depositions.”

title: Thai Union sets aside $44m for future price-fixing settlements
content:
Thai Union Group has set aside $44 million and is in active negotiations to settle lawsuits related to price-fixing in the canned tuna sector by its US arm Tri-Union Seafoods, which owns the Chicken of the Sea brand.

The group made the disclosure in a release accompanying its second quarter 2018 earnings report.

It referenced Tri-Union's recent settlement with Walmart, the world's largest retailer, involved an undisclosed cash settlement and an agreement that the companies will participate in a series of joint programs and new product promotions in Walmart stores.

More settlements could follow, Thai Union said in the release, which noted that "the company is in advanced negotiations in various other litigation discussions. As a result, Chicken of the Sea recorded a $44m one-time accrual to reflect potential risks."

Previously, an analyst with Thailand's Bualuang Securities suggested that the amount needed to settle the price-fixing claims might reach as much as $50m.

Following the Walmart settlement, an executive told Undercurrent News that more could be coming.

"This really sets us up to move toward those [other lawsuits]," said Christianna Reed, Tri-Union's vice president and general counsel for legal and risk management. "We’re fighting really hard to reach appropriate and pragmatic solutions. We just don’t have a choice. Canned tuna is a declining category with tight margins and we need to find ways to work with our customers in a forward looking way. We’re really focused on that as we move forward.”

Reed added that the company is moving toward settling the civil lawsuits against it.

“It’s certainly something we’re moving forward with in an aggressive manner. As we move forward in the next several months obviously this case continues on for some period,” she said.

But given the volume of canned tuna Walmart buys, it made sense to settle with them first, Reed said.

“Walmart is a critical retailer, a critical customer, one of the largest tuna retailers in the United States so it really made sense to start with them," she said. "We also really think about Walmart as a key partner which is why this agreement was able to focus on our partnership and distribution going forward.”

Criminal matters

Undercurrent was first to report in 2015 that Tri-Union had acted as a whistleblower informing to the US Department of Justice (DOJ) about the existence of alleged collusion between the US 'big three' tuna brands: Bumble Bee Foods, Dongwon Enterprise-owned StarKist, and COSI.

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion
Read more
 

Bumble Bee and two of its former executives have pleaded guilty to criminal price-fixing charges while CEO Christopher Lischewski was recently indicted. 

A former executive at StarKist, Stephen Hodge, a former senior vice president of sales, has also pleaded guilty.

Tri-Union confirmed in September 2017 that it had been accepted into the DOJ’s corporate leniency program, which will shield the company and its current employees from prosecution, Reed confirmed.

“The company has been fully cooperating with the government and so we do not anticipate any adverse action,” she said.

She repeated the company's assertion that participation in price-fixing was limited to Tri-Union and did not involve anyone at the parent company, which some plaintiffs in the civil litigation have alleged. 

However, the company declined to go into detail about what occurred and is focusing instead on rebuilding trust.

“Our goal is to meet customer needs with appropriate products and appropriate actions and that’s our commitment as we move forward," Reed said.

title: Lischewski off American Seafoods’ board
content:
Former Bumble Bee Foods CEO Chris Lischewski no longer serves on the board of major Seattle-based pollock supplier American Seafoods Group, a security filing indicates.

Lischewski, who was indicted earlier this year on allegations of criminal price-fixing in the tuna industry, joined American Seafoods' board and took an undisclosed stake in that company after its 2015 recapitalization. 

That 2015 deal, which was led by Bregal Partners, also featured a team of industry veterans: Frank Dulcich of Pacific Seafood Group; Lischewski; former Icicle Seafoods CEO Amy Humphreys; Scott Perekslis, Bregal Partners’ co-founder and managing partner; and American Seafoods’ then chairman and CEO Bernt Bodal.

With the exception of Lischewski, who was still listed as a board member as of April 2018, the others remain on the board, according to an Aug. 1 Securities and Exchange Commission filing. 

Also included as directors are Paul McGill, Charles Yoon, William Bittner and William Rosenfeld Jr. 

Lischewski, who is pleading not guilty, has repeatedly pronounced his innocence even as his company pleaded guilty to price-fixing charges last year. 

Prosecutors allege that the US 'big three' tuna canners, including Bumble Bee, Thai Union Group-owner Tri-Union Seafoods, which sells under the Chicken of the Sea brand, and Dongwon Enterprises' Starkist & Co, colluded to fix the price of canned tuna at an artificially high level.

title: Judge won’t allow ex-Bumble Bee CEO Lischewski’s Colombia trip
content:
A judge has denied former Bumble Bee Foods CEO Chris Lischewski's request for special permission to leave the US temporarily to attend his nephew's upcoming wedding in Cartagena, Colombia.

The US Department of Justice, which recently indicted the former Bumble Bee Foods CEO on criminal price-fixing charges, opposed the trip arguing that if Lischewski skips his $1 million bail it would be "extremely difficult and highly unlikely" to get him back to attend his trial. 

Lischewski's lawyers argued that the court should allow it because the defendant will return. 

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion
Read more

"Mr. Lischewski is not a flight risk, nor does he pose any threat to public safety. He has deep ties to California: he has raised his family, led a large company, and been an active member of the San Diego community for nearly 20 years. He would never abandon his family in an effort to evade these proceedings," the motion states.

Prosecutors, however, said that if Lischewski decides to stay, getting him back would be very difficult due to shortcomings in the US' extradition treaty with Colombia.

Lischewski, who is pleading not guilty, had to surrender his passport after his indictment. Prosecutors allege that the US 'big three' tuna canners, including Bumble Bee, Thai Union Group-owner Tri-Union Seafoods, which trades as Chicken of the Sea, and Dongwon Enterprises' Starkist & Co, colluded to fix the price of canned tuna at an artificially high level.

title: DOJ lists biggest alleged ‘corporate victims’ in tuna price-fixing case
content:
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has released a list of the US' largest food sellers and wholesalers who it says were most affected by the alleged price-fixing scheme.

In a document filed in connection with the criminal price-fixing allegations made against former Bumble Bee Foods CEO Chris Lischewski, the DOJ disclosed a list of what it said are the largest "corporate victims" that were affected by the alleged crime.

The list, which the DOJ said will allow the judge assigned to the case to determine if she or he he has a financial interest in any of the companies, includes companies such as Walmart, Target, Hannaford's, Trader Joe's, BJ's Wholesale and many others. The full list is below.

Lischewski, who is pleading not guilty, had to surrender his passport after his indictment. He is using property as security for his bail and is now out although he recently asked to have his bail relaxed to facilitate a trip to a family wedding in Colombia.

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion
Read more

On May 17, prosecutor Leslie Wulff requested Lischewski’s case be considered linked to the US government actions against Bumble Bee and its former executives, Kenneth Worsham and Walter Scott Cameron, as well as Stephen Hodge, a former StarKist & Co vice president of sales.

Lischewski “is charged with… participating in the same conspiracy to fix prices of packaged seafood products” as Bumble Bee, Worsham, Cameron and Hodge, wrote Wulff. As a result, his case should be considered related, she argued.

Bumble Bee, Worsham, Cameron and Hodge have all pleaded guilty to price-fixing, but Lischewski has maintained his innocence.

 As part of its guilty plea, Bumble Bee agreed to pay a $25m criminal fine, which will increase to a maximum criminal fine of $81.5m, payable by a related entity, in the event of a sale of the company subject to certain terms and conditions.

On May 25, Undercurrent revealed Lischewski has stepped down as CEO to fight the allegations of price-fixing from the DOJ, with Jan Tharp, chief operating officer, stepping in as interim CEO.

In an email seen by Undercurrent, he told staff of the North American shelf-stable seafood giant he will “aggressively defend myself to prove my innocence”. Lischewski also said he has not committed a crime. Bumble Bee is billing the move as temporary.

title: May’s most read: Thai shrimp sale slump, global prices dive; Canada lobster’s tough fishing
content:

Take a look down the page and recap the last month's news that got the most attention from our readers. You can also now sign up for our weekly editor's recap (as well as other new newsletters) here.

title: ICES recommends halving Baltic cod catches, halting herring fishing
content:
Responding to reports on Baltic fish stocks published on May 31 by the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (ICES), campaigners called on fisheries ministers to "end the annual cycle of overfishing" by following the lowest advised fishing limits when setting quotas for 2019.

Catches of the eastern Baltic cod stock have been falling for 30 years. From an extraordinary peak at 400,000 metric tons in 1984 to just under 57,000t in 1992, this year ICES advice recommends 16,685t -- a drastic cut of one half from last year.

ICES found that the western Baltic cod population remains extremely depleted, and below safe biological levels. A recent upward trend was entirely reliant on just one strong year class of fish in 2016, despite the fact that recruitment has been low for almost 20 years and the 2016 year-class is bookended by two of the worst recruitment years on record, Our Fish said, referring to ICES data.

“Baltic fisheries in general, and cod in particular, are fast approaching a situation when management decisions have no effect, since the stocks are not responding as would  normally be predicted by scientific models”, said Nils Hoglund, fisheries policy officer at Coalition Clean Baltic.

"For example, quotas for eastern Baltic cod have not limited fishing efforts for many years now. While fishermen have not come close to catching what they are allowed to -- because the fish are too small or simply not there -- the eastern Baltic cod stock also lacks the scientific data required to make proper assessments."

Fisheries ministers have failed to ensure there is plenty of sprat for the cod to eat in relevant areas, he said.

“Last year Baltic Sea fisheries ministers ignored scientific advice and set catch limits far above ICES advice. This year, we see the results -- eastern Baltic cod catch advice has been slashed, and western cod stocks are perched on a knife edge and illegal discarding of juvenile fish has doubled," said Our Fish program director Rebecca Hubbard. “Fisheries ministers need to note ICES' strong warnings, and set the TAC [total allowable catch] for Baltic cod at the lowest levels proposed for commercial and recreational fishers.”

Herring is fairing worse still.

According to ICES, the Baltic’s western herring stocks have been outside of safe biological limits since 2008, with low recruitment since the mid-2000’s, reaching a record low in 2016 and 2017.

Despite fishing pressure being far above maximum sustainable yield levels between 1992 and 2009, coinciding with a crash in fish stock size, fishing pressure was not substantially decreased even after 2010.

“In a damning indictment of poor fishery management, ICES recommends that catches for the Western spring spawning herring should be zero, due to continued overfishing," Hubbard noted.

"This sends a clear message to Baltic fisheries ministers that they cannot continue to ignore natures limits without repercussions. This year, fisheries ministers must end the decades of overfishing of western herring or risk commercial extinction of an ecologically important fish stock."

The Baltic plaice fishery is healthier, with fishing pressure decreasing and stock populations increasing in recent years. However, illegal discarding is now considered to be widespread in the Baltic, Our Fish warned.

“Only 7t of undersized plaice was landed in 2017, whereas researchers estimate the real figure is over 400t higher, with 100% of the catch still being discarded in some fleets. This constitutes not only a huge waste of marine resources, but illegal, unreported fishing. Baltic Sea member states -- especially Denmark, Germany, Sweden and Poland -- must start dealing with this IUU fishing in their fleets by significantly increasing monitoring and control at sea,” concluded Hubbard.

title: Tuna price-fixing plaintiffs: Little to no antitrust training occurred at US canners
content:
A US court record recently disclosed in recent class-action lawsuits suggests that employees at the 'big three' US canners had "little to no" antitrust compliance training prior to the alleged pice-fixing conspiracy.

In the document, an affidavit from plaintiffs' lawyer Peter Gil-Montllor of the New York City firm Cuneo, Gilbert and Laduca, Gil-Montllor wrote that executives at the canners were generally unaware about what types of competitive conduct were permissible under antitrust law.

"The evidence discovered thus far indicates that Bumble Bee [Foods], StarKist [& Co of South Korea's Dongwon Enterprises] and COSI [Chicken of the Sea, Thai Union Group's US brand] employees had little to no antitrust training," Gil-Montllor wrote.

Antitrust compliance

He then went on to recount, in a heavily redacted portion of the document, what several executives, including former StarKist vice-president of marketing Joe Tuza, StarKist CEO Andrew Choe, Bumble Bee vice president of private label Don Gallagher and others had reportedly said in depositions about their companies' antitrust compliance policies.

"The varying perspectives on whether conduct was legal, questionable, or illegal helps explain the anticompetitive tactics that resulted. Bumble Bee, StarKist, and COSI employees directly sent one another confidential, unannounced price increases and price guideline decisions," Gil-Montllor said. "They also directly supplied price lists occasions, Defendants leaked internal price lists or internal strategy to third parties with the understanding that the message would be passed along to competitors."

Other methods of communication among the canners reportedly involved backchannels and third parties.

"After arranging to trade information through backchannels, employees would sometimes circulate publicly-released information, providing the 'verification' which allowed them to trust that the secretly shared lists were genuine," Gil-Montllor said in his statement. "Finally, employees of the three brands communicated and confirmed each others’ attitudes towards certain price points and castigated one another for providing large discounts and being 'cheap sellers'."

The lawyer also alleged that executives occasionally attributed their "sources for competitive intelligence" to "the birds" because, Gil-Montllor claims, "the conspirators, with their loose understanding of the law, were nevertheless aware that discussing prices with competitors was almost certainly illegal."

His statement also references statements made by Marty Bellville at can-maker Impress USA, who described close-knit ties between US tuna executives.

“We all knew each other, we all had dinner together, we flew together on airplanes. Yes. In many cases we knew what we -- I include myself in the tuna family still -- we knew what everybody was doing,” Bellville is quoted as saying. 

The tuna companies are contesting the broad array of civil lawsuits against them but have not yet responded to Gil-Montllor's statements, made in support of a motion for class certification.

Class certification

The civil lawsuits from dozens of plaintiffs across the US have all been consolidated under the oversight of San Diego,California-based federal judge Janis Sammartino. The plaintiffs can be broadly characterized into four categories or "tracks" depending on how they purchased tuna from the canners.

The large wholesalers and distributors who dealt directly with the canners are known as "direct purchasers" with a second track of direct purchasers including large buyers such as Walmart with separate lawsuits known as "direct action" plaintiffs.

Lawsuits in two other tracks, the "commercial food preparers" including restaurants and retailers, and individual consumers known as "end-payers", include plaintiffs who purchased from the canners' tuna indirectly. 

Gil-Montllor's firm has asked Sammartino to "certify" the commercial food prepares as a "class", which would allow that group to have common legal counsel and pool many plaintiffs' resources together to pay the costly bills for expert witnesses, lawyers fees and other expenses that come in class-action litigation. 

The law firm Hausfeld, which represents New York-based food distributor Olean Wholesale Grocery Cooperative, the first to file a price-fixing lawsuit against the canners, is also asking Sammartino to certify the "direct action" plaintiffs as a track.

“If the judge agrees then we will pursue on a class basis for aggregate damages for the members of the direct purchaser class,” Christopher Lebsock, a partner at Hausfeld told Undercurrent News.

If the judge signs off on class certification -- a process that could take several months -- the lawsuits still need to finish legal discovery, and any motions for summary judgment in which the canners will likely argue that the plaintiffs haven’t met their burden of evidence to prove that a price fixing conspiracy occurred. 

Lebsock said that any trial isn't likely to occur before 2019 at the earliest. 

DOJ investigation

The civil lawsuits began in 2015 amid an investigation into the US tuna sector into alleged price-fixing that spun out of the department's antitrust review for Thai Union's attempt to acquire Bumble Bee.

Thai Union's COSI, which recently reached a settlement in the civil lawsuit filed by large retailer Walmart, acted as a whistleblower to the U S Department of Justice (DOJ) informing on the alleged industry collusion in exchange for amnesty from prosecution. 

Bumble Bee, meanwhile, entered a guilty plea to price fixing charges. The company agreed to pay a $25 million criminal fine, which will increase to a maximum criminal fine of $81.5m, payable by a related entity, in the event of a sale of the company subject to certain terms and conditions.

Two of the company's executives, Kenneth Worsham and Walter Cameron, have pleaded guilty to price-fixing charges but have yet to be sentenced.

Bumble Bee CEO Christopher Lischewski has been indicted by the DOJ in connection with the probe but has maintained his innocence and has stepped down temporarily to contest the allegations. 

StarKist's Stephen Hodge, a former senior vice president of sales at the company, has also pleaded guilty but has yet to be sentenced.

title: Lischewski case is rare example of CEO prosecution
content:
The US Department of Justice's (DOJ) prosecution of Bumble Bee Foods CEO Chris Lischewski is a rare example of action against an executive whose company is accused of wrongdoing, a business columnist for the Los Angeles Times wrote.  

Michael Hiltzik wrote in the newspaper that the DOJ's decision to charge Lischewski with price-fixing that the attempt to hold a CEO directly responsible for alleged criminal conduct stands in contrast to US government policy during the 2008 financial crisis when no bankers went to jail.

"One vital question in corporate crime enforcement is who's prosecuted, and that's where the tuna case may stand apart. Over a period of years the Justice Department moved away from prosecuting individual executives in favor of extracting criminal pleas, fines and civil settlements from their corporations," Hiltzik wrote. 

He said this could represent a change in DOJ policy even as white collar fraud prosecutions drop under the Trump administration.

Lischewski, who recently stood down as Bumble Bee CEO to fight the allegations, told staff of the North American shelf-stable seafood giant he will “aggressively defend myself to prove my innocence”.Bumble Bee is billing the move as temporary, while Lischewski fights these allegations, according to Undercurrent sources.

Last year, Bumble Bee agreed to plead guilty to price-fixing. As part of its guilty plea, Bumble Bee agreed to pay a $25 million criminal fine, which will increase to a maximum criminal fine of $81.5m, payable by a related entity, in the event of a sale of the company subject to certain terms and conditions.

Two of the company's executives, Kenneth Worsham and Walter Cameron, have also pleaded guilty to price-fixing charges. 

According to the DOJ indictment, Lischewski could face a maximum punishment of 10 years in prison, a $1m fine, three years of supervised release and restitution.

The indictment comes after the judge in the civil lawsuits alleging a US tuna price-fixing cartel said the plaintiffs can add the private equity owner of Bumble Bee as a defendant in the process, but not Lischewski.

The news regarding Lischewski came soon after Thai Union Group, which owns Tri-Union/Chicken of the Sea, announced a settlement with Walmart, one of the plaintiffs in the civil suits. 

After Walmart, Chicken of the Sea says more settlements could follow

Thai Union may end up spending as much as $50m on antitrust lawsuit settlements in 2018, an analyst with Bualuang Securities noted, in a report sent to Undercurrent. 

The agreement states Thai Union will pay a cash settlement, and the two companies will participate in a series of joint programs and new product promotions in Walmart stores.

title: Editor’s recap: ‘Worst-ever’ Thai shrimp slump; China buying slow; Crayfish demand booms; Lischewski goes
content:
Tom Seaman, editorial director of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

The dismal situation for Thailand's shrimp farmers and processors, slow buying of the crustacean in China and the news the CEO of Bumble Bee Foods has stepped down on a "leave of absence" after being indicted on price-fixing charges where some of our main stories last week. 

Also, our Jason Huffman was blogging from the US National Restaurant Show in Chicago, Illinois and Neil Ramsden reporting live from Aquaculture UK, held in Aviemore, Scotland. Then, Jason Smith was blogging from our US office in Seattle, Washington, giving updates on the iconic Copper River salmon run. 

I'm actually writing this from Thailand, where Matilde Mereghetti and I will be reporting this week from the Tuna 2018 and Thaifex - World of Food Asia events. The situation in the country's shrimp sector will be a big talking point at the latter. 

Thai processors are currently suffering the in the industry’s history, according Satasap Viriyanantawanit, general manager at Siam Canadian Group, which is headquartered in Thai capital Bangkok.

“I strongly suspect that most of the plants are suffering at least a 50% year-to-date sales drop compared with last year. It is the worst record in Thailand’s [shrimp industry] history,” our Louis Harkell quoted him as saying. 

China buying slow 

Louis also looked into the situation for the shrimp sector in China, where buying is slow, inventories high and farmgate prices low. Some feel the fall in global shrimp prices, which has rapidly swept through the industry and has driven farmers in India out onto the streets in protest, is thought to be close to the bottom as major North American retail buying gets underway. 

However, two importers based in China reckon Chinese buyers won’t be among those making big orders, at least in the short term. One said orders won’t pick up significantly until September.

“I think market demand is not changing so much at the moment,” a source, who wished to be quoted unnamed, told Louis. “Last year inventories [in China] were too high and now the price has dropped, so players have stopped buying and are choosing to get rid of inventory,” he said.

“In the next few months, live shrimp in China will be coming to the market. So the earliest time [for big buys] should be September, I guess,” he said.

An executive at a large Chinese shrimp company spoke similarly. “I do not expect big importing by China in the short term,” said the source. “It will take time to get a big rise in consumption."

China is one of the world’s largest importers of shrimp. Its surging imports of everything from Argentine red shrimp to Ecuadorian and Indian vannamei, have boosted global demand. Last year, the country imported 63,453 metric tons of shrimp, up 4% year-on-year, according to International Trade Center, as well as 46,774t of coldwater shrimp (Pandalus spp., Crangon crangon), up 25% y-o-y.

Approximately another 300,000t was imported via Vietnam via the ‘grey trade’, according to Undercurrent estimates based on trade data with Vietnam. In January buying through this channel “completely stopped”, one Vietnamese exporter told Louis during the Brussels show, after a crackdown in the trade by Chinese authorities.

China crayfish demand rockets 

The Chinese crayfish market is certainly not slow. The craze for crayfish which has gripped Chinese millennials shows no sign of abating, causing "headaches" for European importers who have found themselves competing for the country's supply of crustacean critters with domestic buyers, Louis reported last week. 

Billed in China as this summer’s “must have” seafood, restaurant-goers in Shanghai and Beijing are now paying up to CNY 160 ($25.11) for a half-kilogram plate of large-sized, whole crayfish, local media report. 

Prices have reached so high importers in Europe -- China's biggest export market -- are being discouraged, with one large importer saying some could pull out of the market this year.

"I think it's got to that point where prices are so high people are thinking it's time to walk away," the source, who wished not to be quoted by name, told Louis. 

India needs to build domestic market for shrimp 

Over in India, the low shrimp prices are causing a particularly grave situation in India, which had ramped up production to become the biggest exporter to the US market. One technology entrepreneur, Rajamanohar K. S, told our Neil Ramsden that the country needs to develop a domestic market. 

Rajamanohar, the co-founder of Aquaconnect -- south Asia's "largest aqua farming network" -- suggested India, the world's second most populated country, should take inspiration from Latin American shrimp producers, which have promoted their product at home, as well as a 1980s Indian campaign which pushed eggs in the domestic market.

He pointed to a 1980s campaign by the Indian National Egg Coordination Committee which, in a bid to ensure fair prices for their produce, encouraged poultry farmers to fix their own prices with the motto of “my egg, my price, my life”.

There were media campaigns in newspapers, on radio and television to try and boost consumption of eggs, educating consumers of the nutritional values they bring.

High Liner's 'Rolodex acquisitions'

The low shrimp prices are good news for the market, but not always for importers, if they have inventories bought at higher levels. One of the largest importers in the US, Rubicon Resources, which is now owned by High Liner Foods, could be impacted by this. 

We've covered extensively how Rubicon's performance has dived since High Liner spent over $100 million on it last year. Undercurrent's Americas editor, Jason Smith, and I looked into this after a source called the Rubicon and Atlantic Trading Company deals "Rolodex acquisitions", meaning the companies had no value other than their contacts. 

In both cases, the main contact in the Rolodex was Sam's Club, Walmart's club store arm, where the buyer has changed. The new buyer is moving more to direct buying, cutting out the likes of High Liner. 

Some sources even went as far to say that High Liner’s business model, that of a processor with no element of vertical integration, is going to be put more and more at risk in the future.

Still, the company stands by its "virtual vertical integration" efforts, which it says has helped the company to build its leading position in the market and will be an important part of its growth strategy moving forward.

Lischewski's 'leave of absence' 

After being indicted by the US Department of Justice (DOJ) on allegations of fixing tuna prices, Chris Lischewski stepped down as CEO of Bumble Bee on Thursday last week. 

Jan Tharp, Bumble Bee's chief operating officer, has come in as CEO on an interim basis. We broke the story, then the company confirmed the move. 

"Following the indictment, Lischewski "has taken a leave of absence to defend himself from the accusations made against him", said Jill Irvin, general counsel for Bumble Bee, in a statement. 

"Effective immediately", Tharp has taken over as CEO, said Irvin. Also, the company has "implemented new guidelines and internal policies over the past year and a half as a result of this investigation", through the leadership of its chief compliance officer. "We are committed to act with integrity and transparency in every way we operate our business."

According to the indictment, Lischewski could face a maximum punishment of 10 years in prison, a $1m fine, three years of supervised release and restitution.

In an email to all staff of Bumble Bee and Clover Leaf, Lischewski said he plans to prove his innocence. 

Lischewski said he will “aggressively defend myself to prove my innocence”.

Last year, Bumble Bee agreed to plead guilty to price-fixing. As part of its guilty plea, Bumble Bee agreed to pay a $25m criminal fine, which will increase to a maximum criminal fine of $81.5m, payable by a related entity, in the event of a sale of the company subject to certain terms and conditions.

Thai Union, Walmart settlement 

A big story broke last week on the civil lawsuits that have emerged in the US after the DOJ probe of the tuna sector. 

Thai Union Group announced a settlement with Walmart, one of the retailer's accusing the sector of damaging it with price fixing. 

The agreement states Thai Union will pay a cash settlement, and the two companies will participate in a series of joint programs and new product promotions in Walmart stores.

Thai Union may end up spending as much as $50m on antitrust lawsuit settlements in 2018, an analyst with Bualuang Securities has noted.

The settlement is as much about overcoming a price-fixing scandal as it is about finding new ways to sell a declining product, an executive with Tri-Union Seafoods, which trades as Chicken of the Sea International (COSI), told our Jason Smith. 

"This really sets us up to move toward those [other lawsuits]," said Christianna Reed, COSI's vice president and general counsel for legal and risk management. "We’re fighting really hard to reach appropriate and pragmatic solutions. We just don’t have a choice. Canned tuna is a declining category with tight margins and we need to find ways to work with our customers in a forward looking way. We’re really focused on that as we move forward.”

title: Lischewski to Bumble Bee staff: ‘I did not commit a crime’
content:
Chris Lischewski, who stood down as CEO of Bumble Bee Foods to fight allegations of price-fixing from the US government on Thursday, told staff of the North American shelf-stable seafood giant he will “aggressively defend myself to prove my innocence”.

In an email sent to all staff of Bumble Bee and Clover Leaf, its Canadian brand, Lischewski said he has not committed a crime. On Friday, Undercurrent News revealed Lischewski had stepped down to focus on his defense, with Jan Tharp, chief operating officer, stepping in as interim CEO.

Bumble Bee is billing the move as temporary, while Lischewski fights these allegations, according to Undercurrent sources.

Last year, Bumble Bee agreed to plead guilty to price-fixing. As part of its guilty plea, Bumble Bee agreed to pay a $25 million criminal fine, which will increase to a maximum criminal fine of $81.5m, payable by a related entity, in the event of a sale of the company subject to certain terms and conditions.

Two of the company's executives, Kenneth Worsham and Walter Cameron, have also pleaded guilty to price-fixing charges. 

You can read the full email from Lischewski, seen by Undercurrent, below.

Dear Bumble Bee / Clover Leaf team,

As you have likely seen, the government has levied serious allegations about me, so I wanted to reach out to you to speak as frankly as possible.

While the legal process prevents me from saying as much as I’d like at this time, I want to assure you that I did not commit a crime. I will aggressively defend myself to prove my innocence. The process will take time, but when completed, I am confident that I will be exonerated.

The process of defending myself will require substantial time in the coming months. Accordingly, during this period, I will step down from my role as President and CEO. Jan Tharp will step in as acting President and CEO.  I know she will provide seamless and strong leadership in the coming months.

Although I am very disappointed by what’s happened, I believe that we will get through this. This company is extremely important to me, as is my reputation for ethical behavior. I take my responsibility to each of you very seriously and I intend to vindicate your ongoing faith in me.

Thank you all for your continued commitment to Bumble Bee.

Chris 
Indictment follows omission from civil cases 

Lischewski was indicted by the US Department of Justice (DOJ) accused of conspiring to fix tuna prices on May 16. 

According to the DOJ indictment, Lischewski could face a maximum punishment of 10 years in prison, a $1m fine, three years of supervised release and restitution.

The indictment comes after the judge in the civil lawsuits alleging a US tuna price-fixing cartel said the plaintiffs can add the private equity owner of Bumble Bee as a defendant in the process, but not Lischewski.

In an order from April 10, Janis Sammartino, a judge for the southern district of California, said the plaintiffs can add what are termed the “Lion Entities” in the document, namely “Lion Capital LLP; Lion Capital (Americas), Inc.; and Lion/Big Catch Cayman LP” to their complaints.

However, the plaintiffs, “have not shown good cause” for the court to amend the scheduling in order to add Lischewski as a defendant, said Sammartino. They allege the big three US brand owners, Bumble Bee, StarKist & Co and Tri-Union Seafoods, which trades as Chicken of the Sea International (COSI), conspired to fix prices in the market. 

It’s a “close call” as to whether the plaintiffs “established good cause” for Sammartino to allow the addition of Lischewski as a defendant, but the judge ultimately decided enough was not done to warrant this, according to the document.

Although the court finds it is possible plaintiffs were not alerted to the “alleged detailed involvement” of Lischewski in the price-fixing until after the date to add parties had passed, they already believed he was a participant in the conspiracy, “as evidenced by the references to him in the earlier complaints”.

Also, they were in possession of documents that they believe support their position, which they could have reviewed prior to July 2017, according to the document, signed by Sammartino.

Thai Union settlement 

The news regarding Lischewski came in the same week as Thai Union, which owns Tri-Union/Chicken of the Sea, announced a settlement with Walmart, one of the plaintiffs in the civil suits. 

After Walmart, Chicken of the Sea says more settlements could follow

Thai Union may end up spending as much as $50m on antitrust lawsuit settlements in 2018, an analyst with Bualuang Securities noted, in a report sent to Undercurrent. 

The agreement states Thai Union will pay a cash settlement, and the two companies will participate in a series of joint programs and new product promotions in Walmart stores.

The US' third largest canned tuna brand's settlement with the world's largest retailer is as much about overcoming a price-fixing scandal as it is about finding new ways to sell a declining product, it then told Undercurrent. 

"This really sets us up to move toward those [other lawsuits]," said Christianna Reed, COSI's vice president and general counsel for legal and risk management. "We’re fighting really hard to reach appropriate and pragmatic solutions. We just don’t have a choice. Canned tuna is a declining category with tight margins and we need to find ways to work with our customers in a forward looking way. We’re really focused on that as we move forward.”

title: Lischewski steps down as Bumble Bee CEO to focus on price-fixing allegations
content:
Chris Lischewski has stepped down as CEO of Bumble Bee Foods, with Jan Tharp coming in on an interim basis, according to Undercurrent News sources, a move then confirmed by the company. 

According to Undercurrent sources, the move was announced to all employees of Bumble Bee and its Canadian subsidiary Clover Leaf on Thursday.

The email stated Tharp would assume the CEO role while Lischewski focuses on his case, after he was indicted by the US Department of Justice (DOJ) accused of conspiring to fix tuna prices on May 16. 

Bumble Bee’s Lischewski indicted on price-fixing charges

Lischewski and Tharp were not immediately available for comment to Undercurrent, but a Bumble Bee spokeswoman confirmed the move.

"Following the indictment, Lischewski "has taken a leave of absence to defend himself from the accusations made against him", said Jill Irvin, general counsel for Bumble Bee, in a statement. 

"Effective immediately", Tharp has taken over as CEO, said Irvin. Also, the company has "implemented new guidelines and internal policies over the past year and a half as a result of this investigation", through the leadership of its chief compliance officer. "We are committed to act with integrity and transparency in every way we operate our business."

Tharp joined Bumble Bee in 2010, from rival StarKist & Co, and was most recently its chief operating officer.

Following the DOJ decision to indict Lischewski, his lawyer has said he will be found not guilty once the facts of the case are known. 

The DOJ indicted Lischewski on one count of price-fixing, after allegations that he conspired with to sell packaged seafood at "collusive and non-competitive" prices from 2010 to 2013.

John Keker of the firm Keker, Van Nest & Peters, called his client "a decent and honorable man, who has lived a hardworking and ethical life". 

According to the indictment, Lischewski could face a maximum punishment of 10 years in prison, a $1 million fine, three years of supervised release and restitution.

The DOJ heralded the CEO's indictment as proof that they were willing to target high-ranking executives.

“The Antitrust Division is committed to prosecuting senior executives who unjustly profit at the expense of their customers,” assistant attorney general Makan Delrahim of the Justice Department’s Antitrust Division said in a press release.  “American consumers deserve free enterprise, not fixed prices, so the department will not tolerate crimes like the one charged in today’s indictment.”

Lischewski joined Bumble Bee in 1999 following an eight-year stint as a vice-president of procurement at StarKist. UK-based Lion Capital bought a majority stake in Bumble Bee in 2010 for $980m. Both parties, as well as a Cayman Islands-registered holding company, Big Catch, which directly owns Bumble Bee, could possibly have to pay millions in damages if civil suits from tuna buyers are successful. 

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion
Read more

Price-fixing

The DOJ has been engaged in an investigation of the country's packaged seafoods industry with the "big three" canners -- Bumble Bee; Thai Union Group-owned Tri-Union Seafoods, which trades as Chicken of the Sea; and StarKist, owned by South Korea’s Dongwon Enterprise.

Major companies have lodged a wave of lawsuits alleging the "big three" US tuna suppliers colluded to fix prices artificially high.

This week, Thai Union settled with Walmart over the allegations, however. 

Bumble Bee has been the first of the US tuna brands to face criminal antitrust charges, and plans to resolve the matter with a guilty plea. The DOJ announced in May 2017 that the company and unnamed co-conspirators agreed to fix the prices of shelf-stable tuna from as early as the first quarter of 2011, through at least as late as the fourth quarter of 2013.

As part of its guilty plea, Bumble Bee has agreed to pay a $25m criminal fine, which will increase to a maximum criminal fine of $81.5m, payable by a related entity, in the event of a sale of the company subject to certain terms and conditions.

Two of the company's executives, Kenneth Worsham and Walter Cameron, have pleaded guilty to price-fixing charges but have yet to be sentenced.

Shortly after its guilty plea, the company inked a deal to refinance $850m in debt.
