title: After Walmart, Chicken of the Sea says more settlements could follow
content:
The US' third largest canned tuna brand's settlement with the world's largest retailer is as much about overcoming a price-fixing scandal as it is about finding new ways to sell a declining product.

And the agreement with Walmart could be a prelude of things to come if settlement negotiations between Thai Union Group's Chicken of the Sea International (COSI) and plaintiffs in dozens of lawsuits are successful. 

COSI is the trade name for Tri-Union Seafoods, the US arm of the Thailand-based shelf-stable seafood giant Thai Union that did $3.7 billion in sales last year. 

"This really sets us up to move toward those,"  Christianna Reed, COSI's vice president and general counsel for legal and risk management told Undercurrent News. "We’re fighting really hard to reach appropriate and pragmatic solutions. We just don’t have a choice. Canned tuna is a declining category with tight margins and we need to find ways to work with our customers in a forward looking way. We’re really focused on that as we move forward.”

Reed added that the company is moving toward settling the civil lawsuits against it.

“It’s certainly something we’re moving forward with in an aggressive manner. As we move forward in the next several months obviously this case continues on for some period,” she said.

But given the volume of canned tuna Walmart buys, it made sense to settle with them first, Reed said.

“Walmart is a critical retailer, a critical customer, one of the largest tuna retailers in the United States so it really made sense to start with them," she said. "We also really think about Walmart as a key partner which is why this agreement was able to focus on our partnership and distribution going forward.”

Walmart agreement

The private settlement with Walmart, which does not require a judge's approval, will lead to the dismissal of the retailer's lawsuit in San Diego federal court. However, this has not occurred to date, according to court records.

Representatives of Walmart declined to comment. 

As described in a press release COSI sent out announcing it, the settlement will see Walmart receive a cash payment of an undisclosed sum. Additionally, the two companies will work together on joint promotions and new product development. 

Reed told Undercurrent that this will focus on its US premium canned tuna brand, Genova, as well as Chicken of the Sea light tuna across multiple sizes. Genova, Thai Union recently said,  will use Marine Stewardship Council-certified yellowfin tuna sourced from the eight-member nations of the Parties to the Nauru Agreement in the Pacific as its raw material.

Reed said that the Walmart agreement will be implemented in the “coming few months” and "over the course of the year". It will rollout nationwide “as it works in conjunction with Walmart but those details still need to be worked out”, she added. 

Other new products are forthcoming.

“We have some flavored products and some broadening product innovation coming out through the course of the year,” she said. 

Criminal matters

Undercurrent was first to report in 2015 that Tri-Union had acted as a whistleblower informing to the US Department of Justice (DOJ) about the existence of alleged collusion between the US 'big three' tuna brands: Bumble Bee Foods, Dongwon Enterprise-owned StarKist, and COSI.

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion
Read more
 

Bumble Bee and two of its former executives have pleaded guilty to criminal price-fixing charges while CEO Christopher Lischewski was recently indicted. 

A former executive at StarKist, Stephen Hodge, a former senior vice president of sales, has also pleaded guilty.

Tri-Union confirmed in September 2017 that it had been accepted into the DOJ’s corporate leniency program, which will shield the company and its current employees from prosecution, Reed confirmed.

“The company has been fully cooperating with the government and so we do not anticipate any adverse action,” she said.

She repeated the company's assertion that participation in price-fixing was limited to Tri-Union and did not involve anyone at the parent company, which some plaintiffs in the civil litigation have alleged. 

However, the company declined to go into detail about what occurred and is focusing instead on rebuilding trust.

“Our goal is to meet customer needs with appropriate products and appropriate actions and that’s our commitment as we move forward," Reed said.

title: Thai Union’s Chicken of the Sea settles antitrust lawsuit from Walmart
content:
Thai Union Group’s US shelf stable operation has reached an agreement with Walmart resolving antitrust claims brought by the retailer, according to a statement.

Under the terms of the agreement, Tri-Union Seafoods, which trades as Chicken of the Sea International, will pay a cash settlement and the two companies will participate in a series of joint programs and new product promotions in Walmart stores.

Walmart’s amended tuna lawsuit says NFI’s Connelly, Thai Union’s Chansiri, 54 others acted in conspiracy

These activities will include the launch of new innovative products across Walmart stores. Walmart is the largest retailer for canned tuna in the US. 

The settlement reflects the company’s status as the first tuna producer to engage the US Department of Justice (DOJ) as a whistleblower in the probe of price fixing in the tuna sector, Christianna Reed, vice president and general counsel, legal and risk management, said.

The revelation of the DOJ probe meant there has been a deluge of civil claims from retailers, foodservice firms, consumers and other end buyers, alleging they have been harmed by the activity. 

"We are pleased to have reached an agreement with Walmart that includes a series of continuing programs and promotions. The canned tuna industry has been and remains a low-margin business, which is particularly challenging for a player of Chicken of the Sea International's size,” said Reed.  

“This resolution is a significant achievement for Chicken of the Sea International and the newly appointed leadership team. We look forward to reaching additional pragmatic solutions to resolve the ongoing litigation. Our partnerships with retailers are important to the success of our business," said Darren Parsons, vice president, retail sales and business development.

Last May, Walmart filed an amended complaint against Thai Union and its US operation, as well as Bumble Bee Foods and StarKist & Co, as well as others. 

In the class-action lawsuit, the retailer also listed 56 major industry players who allegedly took part. 

Lischewski indictment 

The settlement between Thai Union and Walmart comes after, on May 17, the DOJ indicted Bumble Bee's CEO Chris Lischewski on allegations that he conspired with others to fix tuna prices from 2010 to 2013. 

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion
Read more

The indictment, filed in San Francisco federal court, charges Lischewski with participating in a conspiracy to fix prices of packaged seafood beginning in or about November 2010 until December 2013.  

Lischewski's attorney, John Keker of the firm Keker, Van Nest & Peters, called his client "a decent and honorable man, who has lived a hardworking and ethical life". 

"He has been a leader and beacon within the seafood industry for more than 25 years.  And most significantly on this dark day, he is innocent of any wrongdoing," the lawyer said. "We are disappointed by the DOJ’s decision to charge him with criminal conduct.  When the facts are known and the truth emerges, Mr. Lischewski will be found not guilty, and that vindication will rightfully restore his good name.”

According to the indictment, Lischewski could face a maximum punishment of ten years in prison, a $1 million fine, three years of supervised release and restitution.

title: Editor’s recap: Lischewski indicted; Bottom ‘close’ for shrimp; Mexican mortalities; Cooke in for Miami processor
content:
Tom Seaman, editorial director of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

A big development in the tuna price fixing scandal, Jim Gulkin of Siam Canadian Group's views on the bottom being near for shrimp prices and several stories on mergers and acquisitions (M&A) in seafood dominated the agenda on Undercurrent News last week. 

On May 17, in a long-anticipated move, the US Department of Justice (DOJ) indicted Bumble Bee Foods' CEO Chris Lischewski on allegations that he conspired with others to fix tuna prices from 2010 to 2013. 

The indictment, filed in San Francisco federal court, charges Lischewski with participating in a conspiracy to fix prices of packaged seafood beginning in or about November 2010 until December 2013.  

Jason Smith, our Americas editor, broke the story, then followed up with a statement from Lischewski's attorney, John Keker of the firm Keker, Van Nest & Peters. The statement called his client "a decent and honorable man, who has lived a hardworking and ethical life". 

"He has been a leader and beacon within the seafood industry for more than 25 years.  And most significantly on this dark day, he is innocent of any wrongdoing," the lawyer said. "We are disappointed by the DOJ’s decision to charge him with criminal conduct.  When the facts are known and the truth emerges, Mr. Lischewski will be found not guilty, and that vindication will rightfully restore his good name.”

According to the indictment, Lischewski could face a maximum punishment of ten years in prison, a $1 million fine, three years of supervised release and restitution.

Bottom close in shrimp 

Over the past few weeks, our coverage of falling shrimp prices has got a lot of interest. 

Gulkin, CEO of shrimp and frozen seafood supplier Siam Canadian, told us the bottom is “very close”, as major purchases for the year-end get underway and more are expected to start in the weeks ahead. 

Gulkin, whose Bangkok, Thailand-based frozen seafood company has offices across Asia, said the bottom will come as an abundance of small shrimp hits the market, due to early harvesting. 

“We are seeing substantial volumes of both raw and cooked 71/90 across Asian origins. Many more small sizes are being landed in Thailand, Indonesia, India and Vietnam," he said. The volume of small sizes is “particularly unusual” in India, Indonesia and Vietnam, he told us.

A halt to dropping prices will be welcome relief for shrimp producing countries who've suffered a price rout. Farmgate prices for vannamei shrimp in major producing countries have plummeted (see our prices dashboard for more), due to several key factors. 

Minimum price talk 

As shrimp prices have continued to fall, there has been talk in Andhra Pradesh, India -- the main production province in the country -- of a minimum level. 

However, shrimp processors in Andhra reportedly failed to implement a minimum price guarantee, after a pledge to do so was reportedly made in April.

This means the state government of Andhra Pradesh may now be stepping in.

Mexican mortalities 

A factor which could impact shrimp prices in Mexico is higher mortality levels, caused by disease. 

This is expected to cause an 11-18% year-on-year drop in the Mexican shrimp production this year, sources at local companies told us. 

However, a local news story and rumors about disease outbreak in Mexico have "exaggerated" the issue, Aldo Villasenor Camacho, president of the AHOME aquaculture association, told Matilde Mereghetti, our senior reporter for Latin America and Southern Europe. 

"We have a small delay in the seeding [of larvae], about 70%," Villasenor said, pointing out that Mexico's three largest producing states, Sinaloa, Sonora and Baja California -- which represent 80% of the shrimp production in Mexico -- were experiencing mortalities of about 20-30%. 

More deals from Cooke 

Barely a week goes by without an M&A story on Undercurrent, with Canada's Cooke Aquaculture very active on this front. 

On Friday, we revealed Cooke has agreed a deal for JC Seafood, a foodservice-focused processor based in the US state of Florida.

Miami-based JC closed on a sale to Cooke on Thursday, one of its founders, James O’Hanlon, told us. 

O’Hanlon said he won’t continue with the company after the deal, but Carlos Sanguily, one of the other founders, would.

The deal fits in with Cooke's stated acquisition plans. During the recent Brussels show, Glenn Cooke, CEO of the Canada-based, global wild and farmed seafood group, told Undercurrent he was on the lookout for processors and distributors in the US to buy, as well as upstream assets. 

On May 17, the day before the news of the JC deal broke, we also revealed the wild catch sister company of Cooke has made an offer for a 39.43 meter Argentine shrimp trawler currently owned by Grupo Continental Armadores de Pesca (Conarpesa). 

Cooke, which operates in wild catch with its Cooke Seafood company, hopes to buy Alvarez Entrena I, subject to court approval, three sources told us. 

The process could conclude in July, they said. Cooke hopes to pay around $7m for the Conarpesa vessel.

Global bank brought into Young's sale 

Cooke is also being tipped as a possible bidder in the Young's Seafood sale process, which we revealed a global investment bank has been brought in on. 

London-based M&A advisory boutique Stamford Partners has been previously reported to be working on the sale, but we revealed on May 16 that bankers from Houlihan Lokey will also be involved in the process. 

According to multiple sources, the teaser for Young’s -- the largest seafood company in the UK -- has contacts for both Stamford Partners and Houlihan Lokey.

The rationale for bringing in Houlihan Lokey, which is based in Los Angeles, California and has offices across the US, Europe and Asia, is to “cast the net wider” in the process, as one Undercurrent source put it.

The thinking of the owners of Young’s -- HPS Investment Partners, Bain Capital Credit and Lion Capital -- is to combine the food sector expertise and familiarly with the Young’s business of Stamford Partners with Houlihan Lokey’s global clout, according to sources.

Macknight US sale 

Another scoop on a sale process got a lot of reads last week, when we revealed Jonathan Brown is using two advisory firms, one in France and one in the US, to run a sale process for the US-based Macknight Food Group (MFG) operations.

A sale teaser for a US smoked salmon operation, which Undercurrent sources said matches MFG's profile, has been circulating since the start of May. The investment banks running the process are Paris-based Messis Finance and Generational Equity, based in Dallas, in the US state of Texas.

The idea behind using the French and US firms is to tap possible buyers on both sides of the Atlantic, a source, who asked not to be named, told us. Also, there could be interest in the business from Asia and Latin America, he said. 

China's aqua billionaires 

China's wealthiest aquaculture and aquatic feed entrepreneurs include at least three  billionaires, according to an analysis of market-listed firms by Fish First, a Chinese industry publication.

As the world's largest producer of farmed fish, China has spawned aquatic feed and aquaculture firms which have seen their empires expand on the back of consolidation within their respective markets, in particular the sector for aquaculture and livestock animal feed. The analysis reveals continued large shareholdings in the firms has turned many founders into hugely wealthy individuals.

Among the leading entrepreneurs is 48-year-old Xue Hua, chairman and CEO of Guangdong Haid Group, one of China's largest manufacturers of aquatic feed, swine feed and animal health products. Hua entered the billion-dollar club last year after an increase in value of his shareholding propelled his worth to CNY 9.1bn ($1.43bn). 

Alibaba summit 

Another piece of news on China got a lot of interest last week, as executives from international seafood companies convened in the home city of Alibaba, Hangzhou, as the Chinese tech giant seeks the "world's best, freshest food" for its online and offline retail ventures.

Food companies from 13 different countries, including meat, fruit and vegetable and seafood companies, convened for Alibaba's 'global fresh food summit' at the firm's campus in Hangzhou on May 11. Executives from Clearwater Seafoods, Thai Union Group, Vinh Hoan Corporation, Cargill and Danish Crown, Europe's largest pork processor, were present. 

Bill to give endangered species power to Interior advances 

Over in the US, a bill to give the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's job of protecting wild salmon, steelhead trout and other species that move between freshwater and seawater over to the Department of Interior was approved, by a 22-14 vote. 

The measure is opposed by a dozen environmental advocacy groups and also several US fishing groups, including the Pacific Coast Federation of Fishermen’s Associations (PCFFA), a group that collectively represents some 750 harvesters that fish for salmon, halibut, albacore tuna and Dungeness crabs among numerous other species on the west coast of the US.

In an interview with Jason Huffman, Undercurrent's senior reporter for the Americas, moments before Wednesday’s vote, Noah Oppenheim, PCFFA’s executive director, expressed skepticism about the ability of Interior’s Fish and Wildlife Service to participate in the management of salmon populations off the coast of California.

“The pace at which we deal with calculating what our impacts to winter run salmon will be when we fish or design a season, is up to the minute," he told Jason. "If Fish and Wildlife had to run things up the chain, while we design fishing parameters in real time, it would be impossible. It would destroy the way we manage the fishery and it’s just simply a bad idea.”

Lischewski guilt or innocence on this and perhaps other allegations swirling around the Tuna industry is to be determined in a court of law. The rhetoric coming from his attorney and the group he was and still is a fixture in (the NFI) is to be expected. What has already been determined is the decline in US per capita consumption of Tuna since 2006 when the mercury myth began. In my opinion the Big 3, the Tuna Council and NFI did a horrible job in addressing the mercury hysteria and the effect social media would have in spreading the information.

The $20 Million that is reported to have been spent on the misguided “Wonderfish” debacle did not help. Parents were afraid to give tuna to their kids and the Big 3 thought a cartoon character would change their minds… stunning. Wild tuna is one of the world’s great protein sources yet those controlling it could not figure out an intelligent way to market it. It can be reasoned that failure started a race to the bottom prompting allegations of short weights, price fixing, fraud and perhaps other issues against the Big 3 that continues today.

As an industry that is allowed to profit from producing protein derived from the world’s oceans and waterways we should all learn from what we are seeing with this unnecessary fiasco by some of our largest companies. We must do better at policing our industry and we all know who are the offenders and enablers.

title: Untitled
content:
US shrimp sector veteran Jeff Sedacca, Rick Reeder and a Texas shrimp packer were involved in a "kickback" scheme to enrich themselves and executives at National Fish and Seafood, prosecutors say. 

Neither Reeder nor Sedacca stand accused of any crime, court records show. But a memorandum that the US Attorney's Office filed in Massachusetts District Court on April 20 ahead of Friday's scheduled sentencing of Jack Ventola, National Fish's former president, describes the men's alleged involvement in a scheme that saw millions diverted away from the Gloucester, Massachusetts-based processor, which is majority owned by Pacific Andes International Holdings (PAIH). 

A 2017 indictment accused Ventola and three others -- two National Fish vice presidents and an accountant -- of defrauding PAIH and the federal government using several methods. The charges, however, related to tax avoidance and not theft from PAIH, although this was alleged in the indictment. 

As part of the fraud, prosecutors also alleged the existence of a scheme running from 2007 to 2014 involving a then-unnamed shrimp repackaging company, North Texas Packing, that provided services to National Fish.

Ventola, prosecutors said, directed the co-owner of the shrimp repackaging firm, a National Fish employee called Individual A in a previous indictment, to increase the fees it charged National Fish. The men then entered into a "kickback arrangement" that saw the repackager issue checks totaling $411,927, half of the increased fee, to Alpine Investments, a company controlled by Ventola. 

Individual A, identified in the April 20 sentencing memo as Sedacca, who at the time headed National Fish's shrimp sales, shared the other half of the increased fee with Individual B, Rick Reeder, the memo states. It adds that the men co-owned North Texas, which, according to Reeder's LinkedIn profile, closed its doors last year. 

"In the wake of that agreement, Reeder began to write checks in matched pairs—each issued on the same days in the same amounts—to 'Alpine Investments' (a fictional entity) and to JBS Management, a company registered to Sedacca," the sentencing memo states. "That pattern continued unbroken until 2012, when the payments from North Texas to JBS dropped off." 

Sedacca then paid Reeder using JBS, the sentencing memo states.

Undercurrent News' attempts to reach Reeder for comment were not immediately successful. Sedacca, who left National Fish in 2016 to become president of Sunnyvale Seafoods, the US operation of China’s Zhanjiang Guolian Aquatic Products, did not respond to requests for comment.

Jason Freeman, an attorney who previously represented North Texas, declined to comment.

According to the sentencing memo, Ventola offered investigators another explanation for the payments from North Texas: that they were "legitimate consulting fees". Prosecutors argued that this contention is "false on its face".

"To accept that contention would requiring believing that it was simply coincidence that, for five uninterrupted years, Ventola’s 'consulting fees' — unsupported by invoices or an IRS Form 1099, and unreported on Ventola’s tax returns — matched, to the penny, the amount of money North Texas independently paid its majority owner, who also happened to be Ventola’s colleague in National Fish’s Gloucester office," prosecutors wrote. "And it was just coincidence that, beginning in 2009, JBS Management nearly always paid Reeder exactly half the amount JBS had received from North Texas Packing each year."

Neither Sedacca nor Reeder face criminal charges in connection with the matter, according to court records. 

A spokeswoman for the US Attorney's Office declined to comment on the decision not to charge the men, citing a policy of not commenting on charging decisions. 

Fraud scheme

In November 2015, Ventola was first indicted on tax fraud-related charges with prosecutors alleging that he and three others -- National Fish executive vice president Richard Pandolfo, James Corbett, who headed the processor's operations and died in 2013, and Michael Bruno, an accountant who didn't work for the company but served on its board -- conspired in the 16-year scheme, which began in 1999. 

The scheme involved a temporary labor firm, Continental Labor Team, owned by Ventola and Corbett, that was used to bill National Fish for services never provided. The men used a network of shell companies to direct payments to a bank account controlled by Ventola, who then paid the others. Ventola, who pleaded guilty to seven counts, is accused of defrauding PAIH of at least $6 million during the 2007 to 2013 period alone and underreporting his income by $1m. 

Bruno, the accountant, pleaded guilty in October last year to tax fraud and wire fraud charges in connection with the schemes. He is yet to be sentenced.

Pandolfo also pleaded guilty last year. He was sentenced by US district court judge Richard Stearns to one year of probation with six months to be served in home confinement, a fine of $5,000, and restitution of $25,879.

Ventola's friends, relatives, employees and neighbors recently wrote 30 letters to the court ahead of his sentencing, urging for a sentence of probation, not prison. 

The letters describe him as a man of character always willing to help employees out of a jam, loyal to his community and church. Included in those letters is one from Jessie Ng, PAIH's managing director, who described Ventola as a vital employee for a financially troubled company in the middle of a restructuring.

Hong Kong-based Pacific Andes has been through tumultuous times since 2015
Read more

Last year, a New York court overseeing PAIH's bankruptcy allowed a forbearance agreement signed between lender Cooperatieve Rabobank and National Fish's immediate parent company, the UK-registered Peaksville, to take effect. That agreement allowed Rabobank to run a sale process for National Fish after the company fell behind on $91m in debt.

Ng didn't address that matter directly in her letter, but said PAIH has retained a restructuring firm in an attempt to tum the business around, adding that the firm lacks Ventola's seafood sector knowledge.

"Jack's continued employment as a senior executive of National Fish is, in my opinion, essential to our efforts to turn that company around. Furthermore, without Jack's presence at such a critical juncture, I am deeply concerned about the future of National Fish. The very livelihood of the many employees at National Fish is dependent on the future of National Fish being secured," she wrote.

title: Former EWOS exec on trial for accepting bribes
content:
A former executive of fish feed supplier EWOS Group -- now owned by Cargill Animal Nutrition -- is on trial in Norway under charges of gross corruption, the country's economic and environmental crimes unit, Okokrim, has said.

He is accused of having sought or received bribes from suppliers, amounting to NOK 2.7 million ($347,100).

"This has been a widespread investigation, and the corruption proceedings described in the prosecution extend over a period of more than ten years," said senior attorney Elisabeth Harbo-Lervik of Okokrim.

A further two men were indicted in January 2018 for gross corruption, having allegedly offered bribes of over NOK 2m in one case, and over NOK 1m in another.

In August 2016 Sor-Trondelag district court sentenced a 52-year-old man to prison for 11 months, for gross corruption in the same case.

His sentence reflects the fact that he confessed, Okokrim noted. He had admitted to paying more than NOK 690,000, seemingly to the Ewos executive now on trial, as a bribe.

Cargill told Undercurrent News it was "not party to this case".

"We have been subjected to an unfaithful employee who is now charged in a corruption case. Corruption or unethical behavior is, of course, completely unacceptable. The former employee left Cargill in 2015 after our own internal investigation revealed breaches of our internal guidelines. We now see that the police think he has also broken the law. Since the case is ongoing and Cargill may have suffered damages, we will monitor how it evolves and assess all our options."

title: Bumble Bee gave DOJ 1.2m pages of documents for price-fixing probe
content:
Bumble Bee Foods has handed over one million pages of documents to the US Department of Justice (DOJ) in its probe of price fixing in the US shelf-stable seafood sector, according to a legal document.

California-based Bumble Bee -- which has pleaded to guilty for its involvement in the alleged cartel -- handed over 1.2m pages of documents it has produced for the DOJ to the plaintiffs in the civil lawsuits accusing the US tuna giants and their foreign owners of price fixing.

Walmart’s amended tuna lawsuit says NFI’s Connelly, Thai Union’s Chansiri, 54 others acted in conspiracy

This revelation on the scale of documentation the DOJ has on the alleged cartel was made in an April 10 order from Janis Sammartino, a judge for the southern district of California. In the order, Sammartino ruled the plaintiffs in the civil price-fixing suits can add Bumble Bee’s private equity owner Lion Capital and other linked entities to the lawsuits, but not Chris Lischewski, the seafood firm’s CEO.

According to the document, the documents Bumble Bee had given to the DOJ were given to the plaintiffs on March 31, 2017. Then, in May, the plaintiffs in the civil cases filed amended complaints, containing a raft of new allegations. 

A May 2017 amended complaint from retail giant Walmart listed 56 seafood industry executives, including senior figures from the big canners and their parent companies, as well as the president of the National Fisheries Institute, as alleged co-conspirators in the price fixing. 

DOJ probe 

Thai Union Group -- which owns Tri-Union Seafoods, which trades as Chicken of the Sea International -- has admitted its US arm was the whistleblower to the DOJ. 

No Thai Union executives have been accused by the DOJ, but two from Bumble Bee and also one from StarKist & Co, which is owned by Dongwon Enterprise, have. 

Meanwhile, Bumble Bee entered a guilty plea for its role in a price-fixing cartel. Last August, Bumble Bee pled guilty to violating the Sherman Act in California federal court, in line with what the company announced in May 2017. 

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion
Read more

Bumble Bee admitted to its role in a conspiracy to fix the price of canned tuna and agreeing to pay a reduced fine of $25m.

In July 2017, Undercurrent reported that prosecutors say fining Bumble Bee more than $25m would "jeopardize" firm's future and suggest giving company a $111m reduction in penalty from what federal guidelines otherwise suggest.

Bumble Bee is the first and only company so far to be indicted in the DOJ's probe of the US packaged seafood sector. Two former Bumble Bee executives, Ken Worsham and Walter Cameron, have pleaded guilty, as has Stephen Hodge, formerly of StarKist.

At the time, Thai Union, which had planned to buy Bumble Bee for $1.5 billion, announced that the investigation prompted it to cancel a share offering it would have used to finance the merger.

That prompted a wave of litigation. Lawsuits filed against the canners allege that the price-fixing conspiracy ran for years and involved years of close cooperation between the companies.

The suits have alleged that the joint “Tuna the Wonderfish” advertising campaign, co-packing of Thai Union and Bumble Bee; and the companies' participation in the International Seafood Sustainability Foundation also presented chances to collude.

The “Tuna the Wonderfish” advertising campaign, which ran from early 2011 through early 2012, was designed to stem the tide of declining sales.

The deal was eventually cancelled in December 2015 amid cheers from the DOJ.

title: Report critical of NMFS won’t be allowed in fluke trial
content:
A Long Island, New York, fisherman charged with over-harvesting fluke would like to use a report showing “overzealousness” by the US National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) in his defense, but a federal judge has disqualified it, News Day reports.

Thomas Kokell faces the possibility of prison time if he’s convicted in a trial that is set to begin this week at a US District Court in New York. The Northport man is charged with conspiracy, mail fraud and the falsification of federal records in connection with the alleged illegal harvest of more than $400,000 worth of fluke, also known as summer flounder, according to the newspaper, which serves the Long Island area.

Kokell is the only one of multiple defendants in the case to fight in court, according to News Day. The Justice Department already has reached plea agreements with seven Long Island and New York City fishermen and dealers charged in connection with a six-year probe. Five received prison time or home detention with fines ranging from $150,000 to $932,000.

Kokell’s defense team had hoped to present, as evidence, a report issued by the NMFS’ Inspector General in 2010 that found “systemic, nationwide issues” at the agency. The IG noted a disproportionate number of cases and larger fines against fishermen in the Northeast. However, prosecutors argued against allowing the report as evidence, noting that none of the agents who charged Kokell in the 2016 indictment were cited in it, and U.S. District Judge Joseph F. Bianco agreed.

“I’m not saying a case is a fishing contest, but the case could completely get derailed if the propriety of the government’s investigation in terms of enforcement practices or things like that is put before the jury,” the judge said, according to a transcript seen by News Day.

title: Philippines DOJ indicts Alliance Select officials
content:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) of the Philippines has found probable cause to indict several officers of publicly listed tuna canning firm Alliance Select Foods International, reports abs-cbn.com.

According to the news site, the DOJ indictment is over alleged violations of the country’s corporation code, stemming from its stockholders' plea to inspect the firm’s books and records.

The case originated from two complaints filed by Alliance stockholders Harvest All Investment Limited, Victory Fund Limited, and Bondeast Private Limited, which wrote Alliance on January 15, 2014 to invoke their right to inspect the firm’s corporate books and records due to “substantial financial downturn… which was adversely impacted its share price in the market”.

title: Alleged 16-year tax scam may have cost Pacific Andes’ National Fish big
content:
A long-running tax fraud allegedly committed by some of its employees may have compounded financial woes currently felt at processor National Fish and Seafood, court records suggest.

At least three people affiliated with the Gloucester, Mass., processor majority owned by the Hong Kong-based Pacific Andes International Holdings (PAIH), face charges in connection with an alleged scheme that reportedly charged the company for labor services never provided.

Court documents suggest that the scheme ran from around 1999 to 2015, and while the amounts to which National Fish was billed haven't yet been provided, they could be substantial. The processor, like its bankrupt parent company PAIH, faces financial trouble. Earlier this month, a New York bankruptcy court ordered the sale of National Fish after the company fell behind on its $91 million in obligations to Dutch lender Cooperatieve Rabobank. 

Hong Kong-based Pacific Andes has been through tumultuous times since 2015
Read more

What role, if any, the alleged fraud in the processor's current financial troubles hasn't been detailed publicly. PAIH spokesman Geoff Walsh and former National Fish president and minority owner Jack Ventola did not respond to requests seeking comment.

The three individuals charged -- Ventola, former senior sales executive Richard Pandolfo, and Michael Bruno, an accountant who didn't work for the company but served on its board, according to the US Department of Justice (DOJ) -- face charges that include tax fraud.  

The indictments also reference a fourth "co-conspirator", who was described as "co-conspirator one (CC-1)" and worked as the processor's head of operations reporting to Ventola, but that individual has not been named in court documents.

According to the DOJ, in addition to their positions at National Fish, Ventola and CC-1 were officers of a Massachusetts company, Mass Labor Force, which was later renamed Continental Labor Force. At the behest of those two individuals as well as Bruno, Continental was hired to provide workers for National Fish, the DOJ said. 

"At their direction, the seafood processor paid Continental a markup over the hourly wages of the temporary workers  -- typically sending the money to Continental via wire transfers in interstate commerce -- purportedly in exchange for the services Continental rendered," Bruno's indictment states. "In fact, however, it was employees of the seafood processor who recruited the temporary workers, handled their employment applications, and otherwise dealt with issues relating to their employment."

The indictment states that CC-1 then created "fraudulent invoices" from a company known as International Freezing Systems (IFS), which had no operations and no bank accounts. Upon receiving IFS' invoices, Continental would pay that company. Those payments were reportedly deposited into Ventola's bank accounts, from which he would pay CC-1 and Pandolfo, the DOJ said. Bruno reportedly helped Ventola prepare his tax returns. 

The defendants allegedly used several other companies that lacked operations -- such as Timatt and TP Consulting Interior Design Group -- to mask payments received in the scheme.

According to the DOJ, Ventola received payments totaling $441,927 between 2008 and 2014 from an unnamed Texas-based seafood packaging company. Those payments were made out to Alpine Investments, which had a bank account controlled by Ventola, the DOJ said.

Ventola has pleaded not guilty to the charges. He stepped down from his position at the company on Nov. 23., 2015, the same day that he was indicted on three counts of filing false tax returns and one count of conspiracy to defraud the Internal Revenue Service (IRS).  

He is slated to go on trial in Massachusetts federal court on Feb. 5, 2018. The trial is expected to last two weeks, court records state.

Pandolfo pleaded guilty to participating in the scheme and was sentenced to a year of probation with six months to be served in home confinement, a fine of $5,000, and restitution of $25,879. The IRS claims that he failed to pay $25,879 in taxes, which he was ordered to repay in restitution.

Bruno has pleaded guilty and is scheduled to be sentenced on March 8, 2018. He could face a maximum of five years in prison, three years' supervised release and up to a $250,000 fine.

title: Owing $91m, court orders sale of Pacific Andes’ National Fish
content:
A US court has ordered the sale of Pacific Andes-owned processor National Fish and Seafood after the company fell behind on its $91 million in obligations to Dutch lender Cooperatieve Rabobank. 

The Oct. 3 order from New York bankruptcy judge James Garrity means that a forbearance agreement signed between the lender and National Fish's immediate parent company, the UK-registered Peaksville, can take effect. That agreement allows Rabobank to run a sale process for the embattled importer and processor, which, together with a Hong Kong trading unit, lost $2.3m in its latest fiscal year off sales of HKD 1.67bn ($213m), which ended Sept. 28, 2016.

National Fish now has 10 days to hire an investment bank and put itself up for sale.

Sale process

Gloucester, Massachusetts-based National Fish is one of several assets ultimately owned by bankrupt Hong Kong-based seafood conglomerate Pacific Andes International Holdings (PAIH).

Hong Kong-based Pacific Andes has been through tumultuous times since 2015
Read more

The group, which was founded in 1986 as a small seafood trading firm and generated $1.6bn in sales in 2014, is enmeshed in a massive bankruptcy proceeding under judge Garrity's supervision. Unlike PAIH's other assets such as its pollock trading business and the lucrative fishmeal and fish oil production arm China Fishery Group, in Peru, National Fish has never filed for bankruptcy.

According to a filing made by Rabobank's lawyers, the bank has extended trade finance to the firm for years. But National Fish has been behind on its repayments since July 28, 2015 and owes about $91m in principal, Rabobank said.

In addition to the difficult environment for value-added seafood processors worldwide and the financial troubles at its parent company, National Fish also suffered a severe blow in 2016 when shrimp sector veteran Jeff Sedacca left the company to join the US operation of China’s Zhanjiang Guolian Aquatic Products, Sunnyvale Seafoods. National Fish's shrimp business with mega-retailer Walmart followed Sedacca. 

Peaksville's owners

Repayment of the debt is the obligation of Peaksville's owners: PAIH, which owns a 60% stake; and Jack Ventola, National Fish's former president, who owns the rest. 

According to Rabobank's filing, the forbearance agreement means that the bank will continue providing National Fish with "the working capital necessary to continue as a going concern".

The agreement paves the way for a sale of the processor and, in exchange, PAIH and Ventola can be cleared of their obligations as guarantors on the $91m debt if the sale amount is higher than a specified "release price". That price is listed in the filing but redacted.

Ventola stepped down from his position at the company on Nov. 23., 2015, the same day that he was indicted on three counts of filing false tax returns and one count of conspiracy to defraud the Internal Revenue Service. The indictment alleges that he failed to pay taxes on more than $2m.

Ventola told Undercurrent News at the time that the indictment and his resignation were not related and that he had planned to step down for some time. He was replaced by Todd Provost, the company's chief operating officer.

The indictment alleged that Ventola utilized the services of a temporary labor company called Continental Labor Team, which Ventola and a co-conspirator, Richard Pandolfo, who was also an executive vice president at National Fish, controlled.

Tax charges

Ventola and Pandolfo allegedly worked together to channel money out of Continental and into their personal bank accounts, tax free.

To do this, Pandolfo allegedly prepared fraudulent invoices for work supposedly done for Continental by a shell company Ventola controlled called International Freezing Systems (IFS).

Ventola and Pandolfo allegedly used the fake IFS invoices to obtain payments from Continental, which they deposited into one of Ventola’s personal bank accounts, the indictment said.

Pandolfo pleaded guilty to tax-related charges involving $47,000 in unreported income. He was sentenced to one year of probation with six months to be served in home confinement, a fine of $5,000, and restitution of $25,879.

Ventola pleaded not guilty to all charges. He is slated to go on trial in Massachusetts federal court on Feb. 5, 2018. The trial is expected to last two weeks, court records state.

title: Advocacy group looking beyond Rafael to overhaul New England fishery practices
content:
If the Conservation Law Foundation (CLF) had its way, none of Carlos Rafael’s relatives or business associates would get to keep any of the 13 groundfish boats he used to violate federal catch limits, and big changes would be made to the way quota-sharing allowances are handled in the Gulf of Maine.

On Wednesday, less than two weeks before U.S. District Court Judge William Young, in Boston, decides how much time New England’s largest fishing vessel owner, also known as the “Codfather,” spends in prison, the local advocacy group held a nearly one-hour panel session to discuss what it would like to see happen. The group, an advocate for more sustainable fishing practices on the New England coast of the US since 1989, has played a vocal part in the Rafael case.

Peter Shelley, CLF’s senior counsel, said he doesn’t want to ever see Rafael back in the fishing business.

Carlos Rafael has pleaded guilty to 28 federal charges, including lying about catches and smuggling cash
Read more

“All of his fishing privileges should be revoked, in our opinion," Shelley said of Rafael Wednesday. “I think all of the assets that were associated with Mr. Rafael should be forfeited. And the allegations by a number of people that they have innocent interest in Mr. Rafael’s boats and therefor the forfeiture should not go forward we think are just transparently hollow, and hopefully the judge will reject all those. And then we want to see [the National Marine Fisheries Services] take aggressive action against Mr. Rafael civilly.”

Rafael, who reportedly once valued his scallop and groundfish business at $175 million, could get up to 76 months in prison when he is sentenced following his hearing, which is scheduled for Sept. 25-26. However, prosecutors have recommended a 46 month sentence as part of an agreement in which Rafael pleaded guilty, in March, to 28 criminal charges, including conspiracy to evade fishing quotas, profiting from the sale of misreported fish and tax evasion.

The date of the sentencing follows just a few days after Rafael’s youngest daughter is to be wed, according to court documents. The documents reveal that the troubled fishing mogul has asked for permission to be temporarily released from prison to attend the event and stay the weekend with family in Massachusetts.

Rafael, reported to be in his mid-60s, was caught in a sting, in 2015, by undercover IRS agents posing as Russian criminals. He detailed to them how he’d been cheating the federal government for three decades, catching cod and reporting it as a cheaper species with greater quotas.  

Though Judge Young may order Rafael to pay some form of restitution, especially in relation to his non-fishing related crimes, federal authorities are expected to also render some type of ruling in relation to divvying up at least parts of Rafael’s fishing empire, which includes the 13 vessels used for cod fishing and their associated permits.

Questions remain about how the administration will handle Rafael's sizable scallop operation, which was not part of the case brought against him. But many have an opinion on how his assets should be distributed.

Conceicao Rafael, Carlos’s wife, late last month filed a petition in a Massachusetts federal court arguing that she owns 50% of eight vessels and three fishing companies. She says she didn’t know the boats or companies were being used to do anything illegal. Joao Camara, an associate of Rafael’s, has made a similar claim for one of the vessels.

Jon Mitchell, the mayor of New Bedford, Mass., where Rafael based his operation, has argued that the permits should stay and continue to support the economy there. However, a Maine congressional delegation has asked Commerce Department secretary Wilbur Ross to redistribute the permits outside of the city.  

“The folks in New Bedford, Mass., are concerned that if those permits don’t stay associated with New Bedford, well that New Bedford will lose a lot of its infrastructure,” said Togue Brawn, the owner of Downeast Dayboat, a Portland, Maine-based scallop seller and another member of Wednesday’s panel.

“And I certainly feel sympathy for them, but part of the reason I feel sympathy, or maybe it’s empathy, is because I see what happened in Maine. Those permits wound up in New Bedford at the expense of other ports in Maine.”   

‘Worst fears’ were realized with fish diversity amendment

But more than punishing Rafael and carving up his empire, CLF also sees an opportunity to fix what it believes are inherent flaws in the New England groundfish management plan. The ability of fisherman to bypass catch limits by buying each other’s permits has contributed to an excessive amount of consolidation in the industry, the group maintains.

It’s believed, for example, that Rafael controls more than 15.5% of the fish coming into New England docks thanks in large part to that allowance, Shelley said.

“Catch shares are known to consolidate fisheries,” said Patrick Shepard, a fisheries and seafood associate for the Maine Center for Coastal Fisheries and another participant on the panel. “They are not a very good way to preserve small-scale fishing.”

But Shelley clarified to Undercurrent Thursday that CLF isn’t looking to eliminate catch shares, the current system for which has been used in New England since 2010. Rather, it wants to see more restrictions placed on them. He said the New England Fishery Management Council blew its chance to do something positive when it recommended changes to NMFS known as the 18th amendment, or the “fish diversity amendment,” the rules for which went into effect in May.

“The worst fears I think by everyone have been realized in relation to the fish diversity amendment,” he said.

A proposal to maintain a 20% cap per fishing operation on each species was declined and instead NMFS went with a 20% aggregate cap, Shelley explained to Undercurrent. Because the nets used to catch all 13 of the stocks of fish available off the New England coast don’t discriminate, by owning all of the cod-related permits Rafael has had the ability to dictate fishing for the entire region, Shelley said.

“If I have deep pockets and I have four friends with deep pockets, we can own the entire fishery,” he said in the panel discussion.

But Shelley also hopes Rafael’s permits, which include some not in use, are not fed back to the existing fishermen in New Bedford.

“If we do that with these 13 fishing permits, or 32, or whatever the number ends up being, we’re actually going to cause more consolidation in this fishery,” he said. “The rich are going to get richer. The folks who are arguably following in the footsteps of Carlos are just going to end up with more.”

100% monitoring of catch limits

Another change Shelley said he wanted to see was that all of the fishing vessels in New England be electronically monitored for compliance with catch limits. As it is, just 14% of the 300 commercial boats in the area are required to carry a human observer, he noted. He believes the money made by the federal government in seizing Rafael’s assets could be used to pay for such a program that would employ cameras on every boat.

“The New England fishery is hundreds of years old. The notion of having a government person sit there with a clipboard is alien to 300 years of fishing history. So, I think that’s a problem,” he conceded, but added: “The belief that an observer watching 14% of the fleet would get an accurate reading [of the whole fleet is wrong].”

Fishermen are going to be more careful to follow the rules when someone is watching, he said, adding: “If you don’t have 100%, I don’t know how fishermen are going to trust each other.”

But the monitoring of catches has to be “scale appropriate,” Shepard added.  Small boats and large boats shouldn’t have the same level of monitoring. 

Shepard believes some other positive changes could come from Congress as a result of the Rafael case, too.

“We have a huge opportunity with the reauthorization of [the Magnuson Stevens Act] to put some of this language in, and if we can use this case as the rational for putting some of that language in, that would start to get us there," he said.

title: NOAA slow to punish ‘Codfather’, public records show
content:
The US’ National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has yet to discipline New England fishing mogul Carlos Rafael since he was indicted in May 2016 for mislabeling hundreds of thousands of pounds of fish, a public records request by a Massachusetts state lawmaker reveals.

Rep. William Straus, a Mattapoisett, Massachusetts, Democrat, had requested from NOAA all charging documents involving Rafael, referred to in the media as “the Codfather,” reports South Coast Today, a New Bedford, Massachusetts, newspaper. However, the request returned no documents.

Rafael, who pled guilty in March of falsely labeling fish quotas, tax evasion and smuggling money, is scheduled for sentencing on Sept. 25 and 26.

NOAA told the newspaper that it doesn’t comment on pending cases, but said it is common for the agency to issues penalties after criminal proceedings.

title: Bumble Bee enters guilty plea for tuna price fixing, agrees to pay $25m fine
content:
US shelf stable seafood giant Bumble Bee Foods entered a guilty plea on Wednesday for its role in a price fixing cartel, agreeing to pay a fine of $25 million.

According to a report from Law360, Bumble Bee pled guilty to violating the Sherman Act in California federal court Wednesday, in line with what the company announced in May. 

Seafood’s Top Dealmakers: Cross-border, cross-sector consolidation gathers pace
View report

Bumble Bee admitted to its role in a conspiracy to fix the price of canned tuna and agreeing to pay a reduced fine of $25m.

Jill Irvin, Bumble Bee's general counsel and senior vice president, entered the guilty plea in court on Aug. 2. According to Law360, she told judge Edward Chen that it was true the company had colluded with other seafood producers.

Undercurrent News was unable to obtain a copy of the plea agreement, which has been filed under seal. 

In July, Undercurrent reported that prosecutors say fining Bumble Bee more than $25m would "jeopardize" firm's future and suggest giving company a $111m reduction in penalty from what federal guidelines otherwise suggest.

The firm will have five years to pay the $25m under a proposed sentencing agreement filed with the court.

DOJ: Bumble Bee should get $111m reduction in fine for ‘substantial’ cooperation, inability to pay more

Bumble Bee could have faced a $136m penalty if its ability to pay wasn't taken into account, Department of Justice (DOJ) officials wrote in a sentencing memorandum. 

According to the memo, Bumble Bee will follow a five-year payment schedule for the fine: $2m within 30 days of sentencing; another $2m each at the sentencing's first and second anniversaries; $4m after year three; $6m in the fourth year and a final payment of $7m in year five.

After reviewing the company's books and taking into account financial analysis performed by two experts -- one hired by the government and a second hired by Bumble Bee -- both parties agreed to cap the proposed fine at $25m.

"As a result of information presented by the company, the parties agree that $25 million without interest represents the fine that Bumble Bee can pay without substantially jeopardizing its continued viability," the agreement states.

The total fine will rise to a maximum of $81.5m, payable by a related entity in the event of a sale. It remains unclear if this additional penalty will be triggered if Bumble Bee's Canadian operations are sold, for which High Liner Foods has been tipped as a possible interested party, as sources have told Undercurrent. 

Judge Chen has final approval over the firm's sentence and whether to accept any plea agreement but typically prosecutors' recommendations carry a lot of weight. In arriving at the $25m figure, prosecutors began by assessing the tuna canner's sales from 2011 to 2013.

The criminal charges cover only that period. Lawyers representing the grocers, distributors, retailers and customers who have sued Lion Capital-owned Bumble Bee -- and fellow US 'big three' canner Thai Union Group-owned Chicken of the Sea and Dongwon Industries's Starkist -- claim the conspiracy began as early as 2004, however.

Bumble Bee is the first and only company so far to be indicted in the DOJ's probe of the US packaged seafood sector. Two former Bumble Bee executives, Ken Worsham and Walter Cameron, have pleaded guilty, as has Stephen Hodge, formerly of Starkist.

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion
Read more

At the time, Thai Union, which had planned to buy Bumble Bee for $1.5 billion, announced that the investigation prompted it to cancel a share offering it would have used to finance the merger.

That prompted a wave of litigation. Lawsuits filed against the canners allege that the price-fixing conspiracy ran for years and involved years of close cooperation between the companies.

The suits have alleged that the joint “Tuna the Wonderfish” advertising campaign, co-packing of Thai Union and Bumble Bee; and the companies' participation in the International Seafood Sustainability Foundation also presented chances to collude.

The “Tuna the Wonderfish” advertising campaign, which ran from early 2011 through early 2012, was designed to stem the tide of declining sales.

The deal was eventually cancelled in December 2015 amid cheers from the DOJ.

title: Massachusetts alleged bluefin tuna smuggler found not guilty
content:
A Marblehead, Massachusetts tuna broker has been cleared of federal charges that he had allegedly orchestrated a scheme to illegally catch and export bluefin tuna, reports Salem News. 

Robert Kliss and his Lynn-based business North Atlantic Traders were found not guilty of charges that included conspiracy, smuggling and falsifying records, by a US District Court jury on Friday. 

Kliss, his business and a captain-for-hire, John Cafiero, were indicted in April following a four-year investigation by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and federal prosecutors. 

Investigators alleged that Kliss then arranged to export the tuna to Japan, netting $135,000 from the sales.

title: DOJ: Bumble Bee should get $111m reduction in fine for ‘substantial’ cooperation, inability to pay more
content:
Prosecutors say fining Bumble Bee Foods more than $25 million would "jeopardize" firm's future and suggest giving company a $111m reduction in penalty from what federal guidelines otherwise suggest.

The firm will have five years to pay the $25m under a proposed sentencing agreement filed with the court.

Seafood’s Top Dealmakers: Cross-border, cross-sector consolidation gathers pace
View report

Bumble Bee could have faced a $136m penalty if its ability to pay wasn't taken into account, DOJ officials wrote in a sentencing memorandum. The company, which recently pleaded guilty to participating in a long-running conspiracy to fix the prices of shelf-stable tuna, is scheduled to appear before San Francisco judge Edward Chen to be sentenced on Aug. 2.

According to the memo, Bumble Bee will follow a five-year payment schedule for the fine: $2m within 30 days of sentencing; another $2m each at the sentencing's first and second anniversaries; $4m after year three; $6m in the fourth year and a final payment of $7m in year five.

After reviewing the company's books and taking into account financial analysis performed by two experts -- one hired by the government and a second hired by Bumble Bee -- both parties agreed to cap the proposed fine at $25m.

"As a result of information presented by the company, the parties agree that $25 million without interest represents the fine that Bumble Bee can pay without substantially jeopardizing its continued viability," the agreement states.

Fine's calculation

The total fine will rise to a maximum of $81.5m, payable by a related entity in the event of a sale. It remains unclear if this additional penalty will be triggered if Bumble Bee's Canadian operations are sold, for which High Liner Foods has been tipped as a possible interested party, as sources have told Undercurrent News.

Judge Chen has final approval over the firm's sentence and whether to accept any plea agreement but typically prosecutors' recommendations carry a lot of weight. In arriving at the $25m figure, prosecutors began by assessing the tuna canner's sales from 2011 to 2013.

The criminal charges cover only that period. Lawyers representing the grocers, distributors, retailers and customers who have sued Lion Capital-owned Bumble Bee -- and fellow US 'big three' canner Thai Union-owned Chicken of the Sea and Dongwon Industries's Starkist -- claim the conspiracy began as early as 2004, however.

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion
Read more

To calculate the proposed fine, prosecutors first determined how much shelf-stable tuna the company sold from 2011 to 2013: $1.389 billion. That range was reduced by more than half to $567.7m after "Bumble Bee provided two important categories of self-incriminating information that were previously unknown to the government".

The public portion of the heavily redacted sentencing memo did not detail what those categories are. Much of the document remains under the court's seal due to the ongoing investigation.

Sentencing guidelines

The $567.7m figure, described by the sentencing guidelines as "the volume of affected commerce" was then used as a baseline to calculate the "base fine". The law states that the fine should be the highest amount determined under one of three methods: the $1.2m fine listed in a sentencing table; calculation of Bumble Bee's "pecuniary gain" achieved through the conspiracy as determined by expert economic analysis; or taking 20% of the volume of affected commerce, seen as a proxy for determining damages.

Prosectors said that relying on economic analysis would "unduly complicate" sentencing and therefore used the 20% estimate. That brings the "base fine" to $113.5m.

The sentencing guidelines then take in account the details of the crime in order to assign a "culpability score" to which multipliers are applied. Bumble Bee started with a five point score and three points were added due to "involvement in and tolerance of criminal activity". Two points were subtracted for cooperation leaving a score of six points, which meant multipliers of 1.2 and 2.4 were used along with the base fine to create a range of $136.2m to $272.4m.

Bumble Bee should be assessed toward the bottom of that range because of its cooperation, prosecutors said.

"A downward departure is appropriate here because Bumble Bee provided substantial assistance. The government relies heavily on insider cooperation to break up cartels which, by their nature, are secretive," the sentencing agreement states.

Ability to pay

But even using the bottom of the range as the maximum fine, Bumble Bee still would have had to pay $136.2m but because of its "substantial assistance", which appears to have been detailed in the redacted portion of the document, prosecutors are suggesting that the company face a maximum fine of $81.5m, which will only occur in the case of a sale.

Taking into account Bumble Bee's inability to pay the full fine if no sale occurs, prosecutors and defense lawyers agreed that the company should pay $25m.

Complicating matters further is that United Kingdom-based private equity Lion cannot be fined, the document states.

"Lion Capital cannot be held criminally liable for Bumble Bee’s corporate acts since it is a separate legal entity. Therefore, the financial condition of Bumble Bee, not Lion Capital, should be used to assess the company’s ability to pay a guidelines range criminal fine," it states.

Plea agreement

Bumble Bee is the first and only company so far to be indicted in the DOJ's probe of the US packaged seafood sector. (Two former Bumble Bee executives, Ken Worsham and Walter Cameron, have pleaded guilty as has Stephen Hodge, formerly of Starkist.)

At the time, Thai Union, which had planned to buy Bumble Bee for $1.5bn, announced that the investigation prompted it to cancel a share offering it would have used to finance the merger.

That prompted a wave of litigation. Lawsuits filed against the canners allege that the price-fixing conspiracy ran for years and involved years of close cooperation between the companies.

The suits have alleged that the joint “Tuna the Wonderfish” advertising campaign, co-packing of Thai Union and Bumble Bee; and the companies' participation in the International Seafood Sustainability Foundation also presented chances to collude.

The “Tuna the Wonderfish” advertising campaign, which ran from early 2011 through early 2012, was designed to stem the tide of declining sales.

The deal was eventually cancelled in December 2015 amid cheers from the DOJ.

title: New Bedford seafood wholesaler indicted for tax evasion
content:
A former New Bedford seafood wholesaler was indicted on July 13 for failing to file tax returns and filing a false tax return for his business’s income, according to a release from the US Department of Justice (DOJ).

Fifty-seven-year-old George Estudante allegedly failed to file an income tax return for 2010 even though his business, Basic Fisheries, received approximately $1,418,629 in payments, according to court documents.

He also failed to file a tax return for 2011, although his business received approximately $1,607,726 in payments that year; and he falsely swore on his 2012 tax return that he had received approximately $533,078 in gross receipts when his bank account reflected that he had received over $740,000, the DOJ release said.

Estudante, formerly of Marion, Massachusetts, faces two counts of failing to file tax returns and one count of filing a false income tax return.

The former charge provides for no greater than one year in prison, one year of supervised release and a fine of $25,000. The latter charge provides for three years in prison, one year of supervised release and a fine of $100,000.

Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge, based on the US sentencing guidelines and other statutory factors.

title: National Fish veteran Pandolfo sentenced in federal court for tax evasion
content:
A senior sales executive at US-based National Fish and Seafood in Gloucester was sentenced in federal court in Boston for tax fraud, the District of Massachusetts said in a release.

Richard Pandolfo, age 71, of North Andover, was sentenced by US district court judge Richard Stearns to one year of probation with six months to be served in home confinement, a fine of $5,000, and restitution of $25,879.

Pandolfo was indicted by a federal grand jury in June 2016 on tax charges related to undeclared income reportedly earned at National Fish, which is part of the beleaguered Asian seafood giant Pacific Andes group.

In April 2017, Pandolfo pleaded guilty to one count of making and subscribing a false tax return.

From 2008 to 2012, Pandolfo received substantial supplemental income for his work at a seafood processing company in Gloucester from the company’s president.  Some of those payments were made directly to Pandolfo or to his spouse, but Pandolfo did not report or pay taxes on any of those payments.

Other payments were made by a corporate entity controlled by the seafood processor’s president to a purported interior design company set up in the name of Pandolfo’s spouse.  Pandolfo did report that income, but improperly deducted personal expenses from that income as business expenses, thereby improperly reducing the taxes he owed.

In total, Pandolfo failed to pay $25,879 in taxes, which he agreed to pay in restitution to the Internal Revenue Service as part of his plea agreement.

title: Migrant rights activist to launch litigation against Thai state prosecutors
content:
British labor rights activist Andy Hall has announced he will file litigation against Thai state prosecutors, the police, and a canned fruit company that previously accused him of defamation.

Lawyers representing Hall — who specializes in migrant rights and is also a researcher — will on May 31 file criminal litigation against Thailand's attorney general, nine Thai state prosecution officials and one senior police officer at the central criminal court for corruption and misconduct cases, in the Dusit District of Bangkok, Thailand.

Hall's lawyers will then file further criminal litigation at Prakanong Court, in Prakanong District of Bangkok, against Natural Fruit Company; a board member with legal authority to act on behalf of the company; a senior company management official; and the company's lawyer — altogether four additional persons.

The litigation concerns a criminal defamation charge relating to an interview Hall gave to Aljazeera English in Myanmar. The charge was filed against him by Natural Fruit in Bangkok in July 2013. Thailand's attorney general, investigating the complaint, recommended the case for prosecution. Following this, officials prosecuted Hall, who was then in May 2014 indicted for a full criminal trial at Prakanong Court.

Hall's passport was confiscated, curtailing his freedom of movement overseas. Natural Fruit requested that it become a joint prosecutor in the case alongside the attorney general.

In October 2014, following a six-day trial, Prakanong Court dismissed the prosecution by the attorney general and Natural Fruit as unlawful on the grounds of an alleged flawed police investigation and interrogation procedures.

Despite the dismissal, Hall claims judicial harassment against him continued as both Natural Fruit and state prosecution officials continued to pursue this case, appealing the legality of the dismissal first to the appeals court and then on to the supreme court.

In November 2016 Thailand's supreme court delivered its final verdict on the appeals, dismissing the case once and for all on both procedural and investigatory grounds.

"I am launching these litigations consisting of two sets of criminal prosecutions today with a heavy heart, and not out of anger or with any desire for revenge," said Hall, adding, "it is regretful that things have reached this stage".

Hall said he was encouraged to initiate litigation by migrant workers whom he continues to support in Thailand; many in the tuna and shrimp processing sectors. 

"After my criminal conviction, many workers and rights defenders in Thailand and even globally told me they hesitate to voice concerns on exploitation, or report fully on abuses, due to fear of negative repercussions," he said.

Hall said he and human rights lawyers advising him hope the litigation can help to reform the Thai justice system.

"Such reform through litigation can enhance the rule of law and ensure meaningful accountability for victims of the unlawful and unacceptable abuse of state police investigatory and prosecutorial powers," Hall added.

Andy Hall continues to fight his previous conviction on criminal defamation and computer crimes charges, also initiated by Natural Fruit, in which he was found guilty and handed a suspended three-year prison sentence in September 2016. This guilty verdict met with wide-ranging international criticism from civil society, trade unions, business enterprises and the UN, International Labor Organization, and EU.

The launch of criminal litigation by Hall coincides with the Thai prime minister's launch of Thailand's national action plan on business and human rights.

Finnish labor rights charity Finnwatch; the Thai Tuna Industry Association; and Thai Union Group have all contributed towards Hall's legal fees, fines and bail costs at the various stages of his struggles. At his trial hearings, Finnwatch and Thai seafood associations and companies also testified in Hall's defense.

title: Marine Harvest’s sea lice fight costs rise 32%
content:
Marine Harvest saw the costs of fighting sea lice across its global operations rise in 2016, as Norway and Scotland in particular struggled with the pest.

In Norway alone, the firm noted, “the exceptional cost related to sea lice mitigation amounted to €78.5 million in 2016, compared to €59.2m in 2015, an increase of 32.5%”.

In Norway, “other seawater costs” per kilogram of fish harvested were 26% higher in 2016 due to “higher sea lice pressure contributing to an increased number of treatments, and the harvesting of fish at a lower average weight”, the firm said in its 2016 annual report.

Scotland felt the impact of sea lice to an even greater degree, with “other seawater costs” per kg harvested rising by 36.8% compared to 2015.

This increase was again mainly due to costs associated with biological challenges, specified as increased sea lice treatment and mitigation costs. Marine Harvest did not break down the figures involved in sea lice mitigation for Scotland.

The company also revealed data showing that the percentage of farming sites which exceeded national sea lice “trigger levels” or lice limits – on an average monthly basis – rose in 2016.

“Disappointingly, several factors, including abnormally high water temperatures
for extended periods; insufficient cleaner fish capacity; limited access to non-medicinal
treatment systems; and extraordinary lice pressure, singly or in combination, precluded optimal control and hampered full application of our strategy in Scotland," wrote Marine Harvest. 

“The increase in losses associated with delousing interventions highlights the need to strengthen our efforts to further develop integrated approaches and optimize non-medicinal treatment systems,” the company added.

Scotland had the worst showing, with the percentage of sites exceeding limits rising from 50% to 69%. Norway saw the number of sites double, from 4% to 8%.

Elsewhere the mitigation efforts led to a better result; in Ireland the number of sites exceeding national levels fell from 18% to 4%, in the Faroes they fell from 12% to 3%, and in Canada they fell from 25% to 13%.

Across the group, the total sites exceeding sea lice limits rose from 14% to 15%.

Scotland aquaculture's 'dirty man'

The Salmon and Trout Conservation of Scotland (S&TCS) has seized upon these numbers, suggesting they show Scottish salmon farms “lag very far behind its operations elsewhere in the world” in terms of controlling the parasite.

“The situation in Scotland compared to other countries is truly shocking and a damning indictment of Scottish Government’s failure to regulate salmon farming effectively,” said Andrew Graham-Stewart, S&TCS director.

“This is incontrovertible proof that Scotland really is the dirty man of global aquaculture. It lays bare Scottish government’s complacent mantra that the industry here is well regulated and sustainable. Ministers must surely now cease peddling ‘alternative facts’ when it comes to the industry’s environmental performance.”

While Marine Harvest itself is obviously disappointed with the figures, it's worth noting that it owns 122 sites in Norway, and only 50 in Scotland, so percentage shifts appear far more drastic in the latter than the former.

S&TCS pointed to Marine Harvest CEO Alf-Helge Aarskog's own assertions in the annual report, which state, “poorly managed fish farming systems can lead to a high frequency of diseases and increased use of antibiotics or other medicines, including medication to combat sea lice, the industry’s main challenge at present". 

“We know that two important drivers in this regard are a too high density of fish farms and too rapid growth in a small area.”

This warning against too-high a density of farms and too-rapid growth makes the Scottish government’s growth targets – of doubling the size of the industry by 2030 – look increasingly dangerous to the environment and to the industry, said Graham-Stewart.

This discounts the potential for improvements; a potential which Marine Harvest – and other salmon farmers – are investing much to try and achieve.

“Sea lice remain our number one challenge, and as such will continue to be our top R&D priority for the foreseeable future,” said Marine Harvest.

“Although we still have a way to go, we increased our use of non-medicinal tools in 2016 and expect to reap the benefits of our efforts going forward.”

The company spent €51.3m on R&D in 2016, an increase of 95% on 2015.

R&D focus areas include prevention, as well as further development and optimization of non-medicinal treatments, cleaner-fish farming and the optimization of cleaner-fish
use, as well as biotechnological solutions.

Diagram showing where the Neptun cage is intended to sit in relation to the coast

“Our zero-adult-female strategy, rolled out in the group in 2015, remains in focus. In 2016, we decided to further increase our resources within this field and will therefore establish an internal 'lice action team' which will run and coordinate all lice projects
and activities in which we are involved.”

This team will be strengthened through the addition of engineering competence, it added.

Marine Harvest is also searching for opportunities to better protect the fish from becoming infected during the marine phase of farming.

It is currently testing the second batch of fish in its semi-closed floating facility, Neptun, which is helping it to develop more sustainable production regimes, it said.

“Since the floating semi-closed technology is still very new, we are focusing on testing several different concepts, to be sure we select the best one once the technology is taken to a larger scale.”

title: New Bedford fishing industry anxious over Rafael’s permits
content:
The New Bedford fishing industry is waiting anxiously to see what will happen to vessels owned by Carlos Rafael, the indicted fishing magnate whose business supports a long chain of industry jobs in what is the nation's largest port.

Rafael, also known as "The Codfather", recently pleaded guilty to 28 counts of federal crimes, agreeing to give up at least 13 vessels from his fleet as part of his guilty plea agreement.

The big question is what becomes of these groundfish 13 vessels -- whether they will be auctioned off on the open market, held by an entity such as the city of New Bedford and removed from circulation, or kept in the Rafael family, the newspaper said.

Jon Mitchell, who was a federal prosecutor before becoming mayor of New Bedford, told the newspaper that Carlos's groundfish business represents 75% of the city's total groundfish value. 

Brett Tolley, a community organizer with the Northwest Atlantic Marine Alliance in Gloucester, told the newspaper the government should distribute the permits in a way that does not create a "Carlos 2."

"The level of consolidation and corruption and impact that Carlos Rafael has had has put fishing businesses out of business in Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and you name it," says Tolley, who belongs to a fishing family dating back four generations.

In total, Rafael owns 32 fishing vessels, controlled through independent corporate shells, as well as 44 permits and his wholesale business Carlos Seafood.
