title: ‘Codfather’ Rafael’s trial date approaches
content:
The trial of New Bedford fishing magnate Carlos 'Codfather' Rafael is getting near – scheduled for March 20 – and as yet there has been no further mention of a potential deal between he and federal prosecutors, reports The Gloucester Times.

The Rafael case, already postponed twice, will see the fishing boss accused of 25 counts of lying to federal fishing regulators about the value and species of his seafood landings, and selling portions of those landings off the books.

The indictment accuses Rafael of falsely reporting to NOAA Fisheries the species of about 815,812 pounds of fish in the four-year span between 2012 and 2016 in an alleged scheme to circumvent federal fishing quotas and “profit from the sale of misreported fish.”

He also is charged with one count of conspiracy and another count of bulk smuggling of cash out of the country.

In a January filing, Rafael’s attorney William Kettlewell indicated to the court that Rafael was speaking with federal prosecutors about a potential deal that might resolve the matter before it goes to trial.

Neither side, however, has commented on those negotiations other than the singular mention in Kettlewell’s filing.

Before that, on March 7, the federal appeal by New Hampshire fisherman David Goethel and the South Dartmouth-based Northeast Fishing Sector 13 is set to begin.

They appeal an initial defeat n the summer of 2016, as they seek to reverse a ruling which granted summary judgment to the federal government, effectively allowing it to continue imposing the costs of at-sea monitoring on federal permit holders.

title: North Carolina captain pleads guilty to illegal striped bass fishing
content:
A 71-year-old North Carolina faces sentences of up to a $250,000 fine and a five-year prison term after pleading guilty to illegally fishing for and selling Atlantic striped bass, officials said.

Ralph Craddock of Manns Harbor, North Carolina was indicted in January 2015 and accused of violating the Lacey Act by catching, transporting and selling illegally caught fish and making false statements to investigators from the National Oceanic Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) about the catches, court records show.

The US Department of Justice said in a press release that the infractions stem from a February 2010 investigation by NOAA agents who were looking into suspected illegal bass fishing from 17 commercial vessels. 

After intercepting one vessel, Lady Samaira, the captain of which was not named in the press release, officials' attention focused on Craddock's vessel, Captn Ralph.

After analyzing Craddock's electronic data and written logs, NOAA alleged that Craddock harvested over 12,000 pounds of striped bass, a species on which a moratorium has been in place on since 1990. 

"Further analyses revealed that between February 1, 2010, and February 4, 2010, Craddock, harvested 1,750 pounds of Atlantic Striped Bass from the exclusive economic zone, with an estimated fair-market retail price of approximately $14,000, which he sold to a dealer in Wanchese, North Carolina," the release stated. 

When confronted, Craddock allegedly lied to NOAA officials "concealing the true location of the harvest in his federal vessel trip reports," the release said.

He is scheduled for sentencing on March 27, 2017.

title: Omega Protein faces 2014 explosion lawsuits; probation hearing delayed
content:
Three men who say they suffered psychological and physical injuries from a 2014 explosion at an Omega Protein manufacturing plant say the company failed to warn them of the risks of their work.

Civil court records show that former Omega contractors Clay Davis and Rusty Gabel sued the fishmeal and fish oil maker in Mississippi federal court earlier this month, joining contractor Joshua Walls, who sued in May.

Those suits were preceded by claims brought by the relatives of Jerry Taylor who was killed in the explosion and sued Omega for wrongful death. His family entered into a confidential settlement with the company earlier this year, court records show.

Additionally -- in a separate proceeding -- a Virginia judge has granted Omega a 90-day delay of a legal proceeding that could see the menhaden catcher face new criminal charges related to wastewater dumping.

Explosion

The civil suits stem from a July 28, 2014 incident at Omega's Moss Point, Mississippi processing facility. The men were working with welding equipment on a 32-foot high 300,789 gallon steel tank, number 10, that contained "stickwater," a slurry of water, chemicals, and cooked fish that was a manufacturing byproduct.

Because of the rotting fish waste inside, the stickwater produced flammable gases such as hydrogen sulfide, methane and methanethiol, which the plaintiffs said is a "known scientific fact in the fish processing industry."

The men, all contractors of the firm Accu-Fab & Construction or the staffing agency Global Employment Service that the company hired, were welding as part of an effort to build a catwalk across the top of the tank, according to their similarly worded lawsuits.

On the morning of the explosion, according to the claims, contractors were cutting piping off the top of the tank. Walls and Taylor were on top of the tank while Davis was near the bottom and Gabel was on a stairway welded to the tank.

The explosion was caused when the welding work heated the stickwater inside, the lawsuits claim.

"The force of the explosion shot Walls' body some 100 feet to the southwest of tank #10, where he impacted and tore through the corrugated metal roofing of an adjacent building," Walls' lawsuit states. "This fortuitous circumstance likely saved Walls' life by preventing him from falling farther to the ground below."

He suffered "numerous severe personal injuries, many of which are permanent in nature," the suit states.

Taylor, who was working alongside Walls at the top of the tank, was also thrown more than 100 feet but landed with force on the metal top of another tank and died from "blunt force impact," his family's legal claim states.

Davis was blown eight feet into some pipes and "has suffered physical and severe permanent mental/emotional problems," his lawyers claim.

Gabel too, suffers from "unbearable fear" after the incident due to having watched coworkers die and be injured, the suit states.

Negligence?

The plaintiffs suits claim that Omega is at fault for the explosion in part because the tanks were allegedly not properly labeled as to the risk of flammable materials. Additionally, the suits claim that Omega engineer Alan Stewart told Accu-Fab employee Joey Norman that the stickwater tank was cleared for welding work.

"On information and belief, Stewart, acting on behalf of Omega, refused to use a combustible gas detector to test Tank #10 for flammable gases and failed to otherwise eliminate the flammable gases inside Tank #10," Gavel's suit states.

Investor group won’t push for Omega Protein CEO’s ouster

When contacted for comment for this story, Omega spokesman Ben Landry declined to speak in detail, citing the ongoing legal matter.

However, he said the company has increased internal and external audits of its safety procedures.

"It’s an unfortunate situation and I think we've done our best to ensure that it doesn't happen again," he said.

Wastewater dumping

Omega also faces criminal liability stemming from allegations of wastewater dumping that reportedly occurred at its Louisiana plant.

The menhaden catcher has been on probation since 2013 after pleading guilty to a two count indictment for criminal violations of the Clean Water Act related to wastewater discharge from several of its vessels. Omega paid $7.5 million in fines and penalties related to that sentence and was placed on a three-year probation.

Prosecutors, though, are asking a judge for permission to revoke that probation after a Dec. 8, 2014 video allegedly showed an Omega supervisor at its Abbeville, Louisiana plant reportedly using a pump to improperly discharge wastewater from a holding pond into a canal.   

Eastern Virginia-based federal judge Raymond Jackson was previously scheduled to rule on the matter on Sept. 8 but six days earlier he granted Omega's request for a three-month delay.

In addition to facing new charges related to the 2013 guilty plea, which concerned discharges of oil and fish waste from several of the company’s fishing vessels between 2008 and 2010, Omega may face a separate investigation into the 2014 incident.

According to a court document Omega filed asking for the delay, investigators from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) have been interviewing the company's employees and on Aug. 29 asked to speak with seven more workers on Sept. 13 and 14.

The ongoing investigation would make it difficult for Omega to make a response in court to prosecutors' requests to have its probation revoked "without waiving fundamental constitutional rights and protections," the company said.

The judge granted the request but noted that "a further request for a continuance is disfavored."

Landry, the Omega spokesman, declined to comment on the matter until the investigation was concluded.

title: Vietnam’s Phuong Nam in bank buyout; new farms, plant in works
content:
HO CHI MINH CITY, Vietnam -- Vietnamese shrimp processor Phuong Nam Seafood – which has been in recovery mode since a $36.7 million fraud scandal sent it bankrupt in 2012 – has been restructured, renamed, and is close to a full takeover.

One of the banks to which money was owed in bad loans – Lien Viet Post bank – lent its financial support to the firm. After restructuring and taking the name Khai Minh Seafood, the firm “is ready to participate in Vietnam's aquaculture industry” again, CEO Timothy Tan Yuen told Undercurrent News.

Khai Minh is now “in position to negotiate with creditors of the Phuong Nam factory to take over the plant shortly", he said. The firm is already managing the site in terms of finances, production and sales.

On top of this, it already has plans to establish another factory, “nearby a strategic farming area”, he said. The current factory is located in Soc Trang province, and Khai Minh will look to buy and renovate a plant either in Ca Mau or near to Ho Chi Minh City next, said Yuen.

The company also has ambitious plans for a new 'shrimp farming city' in Soc Trang, for which it has just received approval from the People's Committee of Soc Trang province.

The first phase of this project will cover 1,000 hectares, and see Khai Minh invest in indoor farming, farmers' housing, a market, clinic and school, said Yuen.

“This project will then be extended to Ca Mau province in 2017. The purpose is to secure clean, non-antibiotics raw materials for our factories starting 2017.”

In the meantime the company intends to balance its own production with imported raw material to fill its processing capacity, likely to the tune of a 50:50 ratio, he said.

Under its previous name, Khai Minh had been researching indoor shrimp farming for two years, and has settled on a farming method which sees postlarvae raised indoors, before moving to outdoor ponds on the same site. It had looked at the feasibility of 100% water recirculation, but found it unviable, he said.

The Top 40 Farmed Shrimp Exporters in Latin America and Asia
View report

The new strategy – which at present can produce four growout cycles per year according to tests – balances intensive and extensive farming methods. It will also produce both vannamei and black tiger.

Currently, said Yuen, 60% of Khai Minh's sales go to the US. In the past, at least, (and under the name Phuong Nam) it claims to have supplied Costco and Walmart, among others. It has Aquaculture Stewardship Council certification, and four Best Aquaculture Practice stars, so it intends to target a higher-end market, said Yuen.

The plant in Soc Trang is already geared towards value-added products, and when Undercurrent visited it in 2014, around 80% of its output was this type of product.

Turnaround plan

Under the ownership of Lien Viet Post bank, Khai Minh is hoping to achieve quite a turnaround after being at the heart of what is thought to be one of the country's most serious corruption cases.

In August 2015, 25 bankers were sent to jail for their parts in illegally lending nearly VND 800 billion to Phuong Nam, which went bankrupt in 2012, owing more than VND 1.6 trillion ($75m).

The crime was uncovered in 2012, when Phuong Nam chairman and director Lam Ngoc Khuan fled to the US, leaving his firm with the VND 1.6tr debt. In the first week of August, 2015, 25 bank executives were handed jail terms of between two and seven years for their parts in illegally lending to Phuong Nam.

They had orchestrated a loan scam to give Phuong Nam nearly VND 800bn. The Soc Trang People’s Court also sentenced Phuong Nam deputy director Trinh Hong Phuong to 12 years, and chief accountant Lam Minh Man to 14 years, for fraud.

According to the indictment, between 2008 and 2010, Phuong Nam chairman Khuan instructed his subordinates to forge documents to attest to the company's solvency to secure loans worth trillions of dong from the five banks.

title: Prosecutors want Omega Protein’s probation revoked over alleged wastewater violations
content:
Prosecutors are asking to revoke the probation of menhaden catcher Omega Protein, which could mean further penalties related to alleged violations of waste water discharge laws after more violations were subsequently uncovered.

The Texas-based fishmeal and fish oil producer has been on probation since 2013 after pleading guilty to a two count indictment for criminal violations of the Clean Water Act.

The company was ordered to pay a $5.5 million fine and fund an additional $2m in community service projects.

Additionally, Omega Protein was sentenced to serve a three year term on probation, update its environmental compliance processes and agree to supervision.

The violations stemming from the 2013 sentence occurred between 2008 and 2010 related to discharging oil and fish waste from several of the company’s fishing vessels into the sea. 

However, in June of this year, prosecutors from the US Attorney's Office for the eastern Virginia district asked a judge to hold a hearing to give Omega Protein a chance to argue why its probation shouldn't be revoked. 

The lawyers referenced a video of a Dec. 8, 2014 incident taken from a special agent of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) at the company's Abbeville, Louisiana plant as the impetus to revoke the probation.

"The video shows the shift supervisor utilizing a portable gasoline pump to discharge wastewater out of a holding pond into a canal which is a 'water of the United States'," prosecutors alleged in court filings.

When confronted by the EPA agent, a plant supervisor "explained that he made the discharge because he was told to do so by the plant manager," the filing states.

According to prosecutors, even if the discharge was just storm water as the plant's general manager later suggested, Omega Protein did not file a required monitoring report for December 2014 with the Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality, which would put it in violation of the terms of the company's federal permit to discharge wastewater.

A hearing in the case is set to be heard on Sept. 8 in a Norfolk, Virginia courtroom.

Omega Protein disclosed the possible revocation -- which would potentially allow prosecutors to reopen the 2013 case and levy more fines and penalties -- in its Q2 2016 quarterly report but said it's unable to determine the "potential outcome or its effects" at this stage.

But in addition to reopening the 2013 case, Louisiana prosecutors may bring charges related to the 2014 incident, the company said.

"In addition, if the United States Attorney in the Western District of Louisiana were to file new criminal charges regarding the waste water disposal operations of the Abbeville facility as a result of that office’s investigation, then Omega Protein could be subject to additional criminal penalties or prosecution in that district," it said.

That would potentially lead to increased compliance costs and the inability to receive government contracts or loans, it said.

title: ‘Codfather’ Rafael expanding fishing fleet despite indictment
content:
Indicted fishing magnate Carlos 'Codfather' Rafael appears to be expanding his fishing fleet despite the ongoing criminal case against him, records suggest, according to a report from Food Republic.

The publication cited a May 16 filing made with the Massachusetts Secretary of State that showed that Rafael's wife Conceicao formed the company Nemesis LLC to engage in fishing. A month later Nemesis bought a vessel previously called the Jamie & Ashley, the publication said. 

The publication spoke to the US Attorney's office, which is prosecuting Rafael on charges of conspiracy and submitting falsified records to the government, which said that the arrangement is legal.

“Rafael can continue to work while under indictment as he was released on conditions following his arraignment in federal court,” said Elizabeth McCarthy, a spokeswoman for the US attorney’s office.

McCarthy notes that her office is aware that Rafael recently added his wife’s name to his business but adds that the recent boat purchase doesn’t break any court-imposed rules related to the case.

“The indictment seeks forfeiture of boats and permits involved in the conspiracy we charged, and we have obtained a civil restraining order preventing him from liquidating those assets,” she said.

A federal trial for Rafael, as well as alleged smuggling accomplice Antonio M. Freitas is slated for January 2017 at the US District Court in Boston.

Prosecutors have said that Rafael sold illegally caught fish to a wholesale buyer in New York City in exchange for tens of thousands in cash, much of which he then smuggled to Portugal through Logan International Airport in Boston with the help of Freitas.

According to court records, beginning in June 2015, two undercover federal agents posing as organized crime figures had several meetings with Rafael to negotiate the purchase of his business.

title: Lawyer in tuna price fixing suits: DOJ focuses on ‘most culpable’ execs
content:
A plethora of executives are named in amended civil lawsuits accusing the top three US tuna brands of market collusion, but the focus of the US Department of Justice (DOJ) will be on the most culpable, said a lawyer involved in the civil lawsuits.

The DOJ previously requested a pause on discovery in the civil lawsuits accusing Bumble Bee Foods, Thai Union Group-owned Tri-Union Seafoods, parent of Chicken of the Sea; and Dongwon Industries-backed Starkist of engaging in price fixing.

Despite this, amended complaints were filed in late May in the civil lawsuits, expanding on the allegations contained in the lawsuits last year. In one of the lawsuits, in the “track” for complaints from retailers and wholesalers who have opted to be outside a class action, it is alleged top executives from Bumble Bee, Chicken of the Sea and Starkist were involved.

In the amended complaint, Chris Lischewski, CEO of Bumble Bee from 1999 to the present day; Don Binotto, Starkist CEO from the 1990s through November 2010; John Signorino, Chicken of the Sea CEO from January 2005 to October 2007; and Shue Wing Chan, Signorino’s successor, are all named.

In another of the amended complaints, Andrew Choe, CEO of Starkist, is also named. None of the executives named are defendants in the civil suits, however, and the lawyers on the civil side are in the dark as to what the DOJ intended to do.

“DOJ does not tell civil litigants what its intentions are with respect to charging any person or entity with violating antitrust laws,” Christopher Lebsock, of law firm Hausfeld, which is overseeing the class action track for direct buyers, such as Olean Wholesale Grocery Cooperative, told Undercurrent News.

Lebsock, however, was able to give a general idea of how the DOJ process works.

“Company executives are not immune from prosecution. However, DOJ often limits prosecutions to the executives who are most culpable and in control,” he said.

He also gave a sense of what would happen next, if the DOJ does indeed decide to proceed with actions against individuals or companies.

“Generally, DOJ would advise a target that it intends to seek indictment. The target then needs to decide whether he/she/it is willing to enter a guilty plea or fight the indictment,” he said.

“If the latter course is decided, then once the indictment is issued, the target, now a formal criminal defendant, would have all procedural and substantive defenses available to him/her. Basically, there would be pretrial efforts to have the charges dismissed, then discovery, and trial. In the US, there must be a unanimous verdict of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt,” Lebsock said.

The DOJ is investigating the leading tuna brands for alleged collusion
Read more

A trial would take place before a jury, unless the government and the defendant waive the jury, he said. “The jury would hear evidence and decide whether the target participated in a conspiracy beyond a reasonable doubt.”

Speaking to Undercurrent in September last year, Andre Barlow, a partner with the Washington. D.C.-based law firm Doyle Barlow and Mazard, said US regulators have also shown a willingness to go after firms that collude.

“The antitrust division has been real aggressive and people have been put in jail,” he toldUndercurrent.

According to DOJ statistics, in 2014, 10 people were sent to prison as a result of criminal antitrust probes and US officials collected $1.4bn in criminal fines. Over the past five years, judges have handed out jail terms that are an average of 25 months long.

The new information behind the more detailed complaints came from outside of formal discovery, said Lebsock. In addition, Tri Marine has been removed as a defendant.

"The pause on discovery is still in place. The additional allegations set forth in the amended complaints are based on the plaintiffs’ continuing investigation,” he said.

Grand jury convened 

Although what exactly is going on with the DOJ probe is not clear, the class action lawsuit from the direct buyers stated the San Francisco office of the antitrust division of the DOJ has confirmed it is conducting an investigation into anticompetitive practices in the packaged seafood sector in the US. The DOJ has convened a grand jury in the northern district of California.

In its motion to intervene in the civil litigation, DOJ stated: “Both the civil and criminal cases pertain to allegations of collusive conduct among packaged seafood manufacturers” in violation of the Sherman Act.

The complaint for the direct buyers' section of the class action, which Lebsock’s firm Hausfeld are representing, indicates the DOJ likely has an amnesty applicant.

“Typically, the DOJ gets documents and other information from an amnesty applicant, and then goes to the other companies. This can result in guilty pleas if the DOJ believes that there is enough evidence to justify a prosecution,” said Lebsock. “When deciding on the level of a fine, the DOJ will look at how culpable was a company, how co-operative they were and also how solvent the company is.”

In one of the civil lawsuits filed last year, Starkist was named as being the likely amnesty applicant. Then, latter lawsuits stated it is likely to be Chicken of the Sea.

The amended complaints, however, hedge their bets somewhat. They all state that Thai Union, the owner of Chicken of the Sea, and Bumble Bee have publicly stated they have been subpoenaed by the DOJ, but Starkist has not.

The class action from the direct buyer plaintiffs stated it has been publicly reported Chicken of the Sea is the amnesty applicant.

Lawsuits: US brands colluded on not selling FAD-free tuna

For the amnesty applicant, whoever it is, the benefits are clear. The US Antitrust Criminal Penalty Enhancement and Reform Act (ACPERA) provides leniency for a participant in a price-fixing conspiracy that voluntarily discloses its conduct to the DOJ, according to the class action complaint by the catering plaintiffs.

In most recent cases in which guilty pleas for price-fixing conduct have been obtained, there has been a cooperating party that has been accepted into the DOJ’s ACPERA program as an amnesty applicant, the document stated.

One of the leniency benefits for a conspirator that is accepted into the ACPERA program is that he or she is not charged with a criminal offense and is not required to plead guilty to criminal charges.

“In light of the intervention and request for stay by the DOJ, it is reasonable for this court to infer that there is a criminal investigation and an ACPERA "amnesty applicant" in this case,” it is stated in the complaint.

As indicated on the same DOJ webpage, the leniency applicant must also establish the “confession of wrongdoing is truly a corporate act, as opposed to isolated confessions of individual executives or officials”.

Thus, a whistleblower would be an admission of a corporate-level conspiracy.

The lawsuits also refer to the DOJ comment on the cancellation of Thai Union's deal for Bumble Bee.

“Consumers are better off without this deal,” said assistant attorney general Bill Baer of the department’s antitrust division, at the time. “Our investigation convinced us – and the parties knew or should have known from the get go – that the market is not functioning competitively today, and further consolidation would only make things worse.”

What next?

After the deadline on the stay of discovery expires, which is Dec. 31, 2016, discovery can "take place in earnest", said Lebsock.

“The DOJ might come in with a criminal complaint before January, or they might ask for more time. January is when discovery can start [on the civil side], presuming the DOJ does not ask for more time,” said Lebsock.

Lawsuits: US brands colluded on not selling FAD-free tuna

“In 2017, if the deadline of January is enough for the DOJ, we will get going with a flurry of written discovery and depositions,” he said. “The submissions for class classification are due in September.”

After the hearing in January, when judge Janis Sammartino approved the call for a stay on discovery from the DOJ, these lawsuits were divided down into four “tracks”.

Three of these tracks are class actions, with the fourth encompassing lawsuits from direct tuna buyers -- retailers and wholesalers -- alleging they have been damaged by overpaying.

On May 23, the bulk of the amended complaints were filed, containing much more detail.

In addition, it is also alleged Dongwon, parent of Starkist, and Thai Union, owner of the Chicken of the Sea brand, were also involved.

The three class action tracks allege the conspiracy started in 2008. The lawsuit from the direct buyers not part of the class action also alleged the conspiracy started in 2003, which means Del Monte Foods, the owner of Starkist from 2002-2008 before the sale to Dongwon, is also included as a defendant.

One of the class action complaints is from direct purchaser plaintiffs, namely wholesalers, retailers and other direct buyers; another is from indirect purchaser commercial food preparer plaintiffs, catering companies who bought tuna; and the third is from indirect purchaser end-payer plaintiffs, namely American consumers.

By Jan. 30, 2017, the defendants need to have provided all documents produced in connection with the DOJ’s packaged seafood antitrust investigation and all parties shall serve initial disclosures, according to a document filed on May 31 on the case management order.

Earlier in May, amended complaints were filed in the multitude of civil lawsuits alleging abuse in light of the revelation of the DOJ probe of the shelf stable seafood sector in the US.

Looking further forward, by July 1, 2017 the plaintiffs need to have identified any additional class representatives or defendants. Additional plaintiffs or defendants can be added after this deadline, with leave of the court after showing “good cause”, the document on the case management stated.

By Sept. 15, the plaintiffs will need to have filed and serve any motions for class certification.

Jan. 26, 2018 is the deadline for the defendants to file and serve any opposition to the motions for class certification.

The plaintiffs’ motions for class certification will be heard on or about April 13. By May 18, the parties shall complete fact discovery.

By March 8, 2019, the parties will have to file and serve any dispositive motions, with April 26 the deadline for oppositions. By May 31, 2019, any party having filed and served a dispositive motion shall file and serve any reply to opposition, it is stated in the document.

“Dispositive motions are, effectively motions for summary judgment.  Defendants will file a summary judgment motion arguing that the civil plaintiffs cannot establish one or more elements of their claim,” said Lebsock.

“The motion will ask the judge to rule in the defendants’ favor on the entire case or on a subset of issues.  Assuming that the summary judgment motions are denied in whole, or in part, then the case will proceed to trial,” he said.

title: Skretting gets approval for NZ finfish research facility
content:
Approval for Nutreco-owned aqua feed firm Skretting to construct a finfish research facility in New Zealand has been granted, despite opposition from locals.

A 71-page decision document was signed off on July 7 by the Marlborough district council outlining the conditions pertaining to land, water and coastal use of the area, reports Stuff.co.nz.

The council initially received 219 submissions in relation to the application, of which 10 were in support and 209 were opposed.

Okiwi Bay resident of 20 years, Paula Holder, said she was "devastated" by the decision, reports the news site. "It's just a sad indictment for New Zealand to think that this could go ahead in our little bay and that a multinational company can come in and pollute our bay - because that's what they're going to do, and we get no gain."

She said the decision was made in the interests of bolstering "big business" rather than those of local residents.

title: Judge extends ‘Codfather’ curfew during summer
content:
A judge has granted a request from scallops magnate Carlos 'Codfather' Rafael to stay out past his court-mandated curfew in order to manage his fishing business, the South Coast Today reported.

Rafael, whose federal trial on conspiracy and bulk cash smuggling charges is scheduled for January, asked for the time during the summer, documents filed with the court state.

“With daylight extending to past 8:30 p.m. throughout the summer months, the present conditions of release prevent Mr. Rafael from working until sundown as is his usual practice,” the document states.

Currently he is required to be at home every night by 7 p.m. and wear an electronic monitoring bracelet. A judge extended the curfew to 8:30 p.m.

title: Carlos Rafael trial set for January 2017
content:
The trial of indicted fishing magnate Carlos Rafael and alleged smuggling accomplice Antonio M. Freitas is scheduled for January 2017, reports South Coast Today.

This would be nearly a year after US federal authorities raided Rafael’s seafood business on New Bedford’s waterfront.

The two defendants’ cases have progressed side by side so far. Neither appeared in US District Court on Wednesday in Boston, where District Court Judge William G. Young scheduled their trial to begin on Jan. 9, 2017, in a brief status conference.

Neither a federal prosecutor nor lawyers for Rafael and Freitas commented afterward.

Rafael, a 64-year-old Dartmouth resident who owns one of the largest commercial fishing operations in the US, including scores of New Bedford-based vessels, faces 27 counts on federal charges including conspiracy, false entries and bulk cash smuggling, according to the indictment filed last month.

Freitas, a 46-year-old Taunton resident and Bristol County Sheriff’s Office deputy, has been suspended without pay. He faces two federal counts; one for bulk cash smuggling and one for international structuring.

Prosecutors allege that Rafael sold illegally caught fish to a wholesale buyer in New York City in exchange for tens of thousands in cash, much of which he then smuggled to Portugal through Logan International Airport in Boston with the help of Freitas.

title: Norway authorities appeal decision not to remove NRS subsidiary rights
content:
Norway's National Authority for Investigation and Prosecution of Economic and Environmental Crime (Okokrim) has filed an appeal against a court decision not to sentence a Norway Royal Salmon (NRS) subsidiary to a loss of farming rights.

Nord Senja Laks, a subsidiary of NRS, was ordered by an appeals court to pay a NOK 5 million fine for misreporting sea lice occurrences. The Halogaland Court of Appeal passed sentence on the firm on May 25, upholding the verdict passed by Senja District court in October.

However, Nord Senja Laks -- which was indicted of offences back in February 2015 -- was not sentenced to loss of rights. Consequently, the verdict had no effect on the licenses held by the company and future operations.

However, now Okokrim has filed a notice of appeal regarding the fine and the
decision not to sentence Nord Senja Laks to loss of rights, presumably believing the offences warrant restrictions to be imposed on its license to farm.

title: Trial of migrants’ rights activist Andy Hall to begin this week
content:
The trial of British migrants rights activist Andy Hall is scheduled to go ahead in Bangkok on May 19.

At Southern Bangkok Criminal Court, Hall will go on trial facing criminal defamation and computer crimes charges. Over three years since an original criminal prosecution was filed against Hall, the first three days of this criminal trial in May will hear testimony of prosecution witnesses. Defense witness testimony will be over eight days in June and July.

This criminal case, with multiple charges filed, is the most serious of all the four cases brought by a Prachuap Khiri Khan province-based pineapple processing company -- Natural Fruit Company -- against Andy Hall.

The charges were brought following publication of a Finnwatch report, "Cheap Has a High Price", in January 2013. Whilst this case was the first and most serious to be filed against Hall back in February 2013, it is the second case to actually reach a full criminal trial in Thailand's courts.

The criminal charges in this case carry a maximum combined penalty of seven years' imprisonment in addition to potential fines.

Hall was indicted on these charges in January 2016 when, pending trial and following granting of temporary release on bail, his passport was confiscated and permission to leave Thailand restricted without clearance from the court.

"Andy Hall's work in defence of migrant worker rights in Thailand is internationally recognized," said Sonja Vartiala, Finnwatch's executive director.

"This campaign of judicial harassment against him has been condemned by civil society and responsible businesses all around the world. Finnwatch continue to stand by Andy Hall."

'Cheap Has a High Price' alleged labor rights violations at Natural Fruit's processing plant in Southern Thailand, as reported from interviews with migrant workers from Myanmar. The interview data was analyzed, assembled and a report was published by Finnwatch, whereas Andy Hall only coordinated the field research and, with a help of a team of others, conducted worker interviews for the report.

Vartiala will travel to Bangkok in July to give testimony as a defense witness at the Court. Another key defence witness will be from retail chain S Group, one of the biggest companies in Finland.

The defence will also call migrant workers formally employed at Natural Fruit, leading figures from export companies also featured in Finnwatch's reports on migrant conditions in Thailand as well as migrant rights, consumer and media activists, unionists, lawyers and researchers.

"What is the most worrying thing about this campaign of intimidation against Andy Hall is the impact it has on other people – activists, journalists, whistleblowers and victims of abuse – who may be silenced in fear because of it," said Vartiala.

title: BP drops bid to avoid paying $1bn to seafood industry
content:
Oil company BP has dropped its bid to avoid paying almost $1 billion in oil spill damages to Gulf Coast shrimpers, oystermen and seafood processors, reports Bloomberg.

The company's subsea gusher pumped over 4 million barrels of crude oil into the Gulf of Mexico in 2010, which closed fisheries and blackened the shores of five states.

BP claimed lawyers negotiating on behalf of the seafood industry wrongly inflated the number of Southeast Asian immigrant fishermen and boat hands claiming damages from the spill. The overstatement jacked up BP’s settlement by hundreds of millions of dollars, the company claimed.

BP had paid about $1bn of its $2.3bn seafood compensation fund when it balked at paying the rest after finding irregularities in one law firm's client list.

Mikal Watts, a Texas attorney, was indicted last year for allegedly lying about representing more than 40,000 mostly Vietnamese-American boat captains and crew members in spill claims against BP. Watts will face trial in July.

BP held onto its civil fraud claims against Watts and his San Antonio law firm, while dropping the rest of the fight against the seafood industry payout.

The seafood payout is part of a larger BP settlement related to its 2010 spill.

title: Worries in New Bedford over impact from Rafael’s arrest on groundfish sector
content:
Stakeholders in the US east coast port of New Bedford, Massachusetts fear a major impact from the charges against Carlos Rafael, the largest operator in groundfish and also a major scallop fleet owner.

Rafael and his bookkeeper were arrested Friday on charges of conspiracy and submitting falsified records to the US government to evade federal fishing quotas.

“Carlos Rafael is a dishonest guy -- he's already served time for tax evasion and been convicted of falsifying his fish landings. But does Carlos’ story show you can’t make a living fishing anymore without cheating?” wrote Jack Spillane, in an opinion piece for South Coast Today.

“And what will happen to all the valuable fish quotas Carlos controls? Will the government let Rafael continue to fish while under indictment for a crime that could put him away for 20 years? Will it let someone else buy up his quota? Does anyone even have that kind of money for ground-fishing when it’s so hard to make money doing it?”

With Rafael owning the biggest groundfish fleet in the harbor, James Kendall, a seafood sector consultant, also expressed concern for what might happen to the boats and the fishermen.

Rafael’s boats, he told South Coast Today, have been leasing quota from boat owners who own too little to make it possible to fish for a profit.

“If they don’t rent to him who is going to rent it?" he asked. “The impacts would be a lot wider than what you see first hand.”

Rafael valued business $154m over book level due to illegal fish sales, feds allege

Jon Mitchell, mayor of New Bedford and a former federal prosecutor, told South Coast Today he has read the affidavit from an undercover agent on the case.

“Based on my experience if the allegations are true, then he’s going to federal prison for a long time,” he told the website.

A worry for Mitchell is the impact on Rafael’s employees.

“His business has been disrupted, understandably, but there are livelihoods that depend on the operation of that business. If there is any assistance we can offer them, we’ll make sure to follow through,” he said.

One way the city might be able to help would be to expedite the transfer of quota from the Rafael boats to other boats to keep up the level of fishing.

As for a widespread negative effect, Mitchell wasn’t quite as pessimistic as others. “We’re a very big port and although (Rafael) has a controlling share of the groundfish sector in the region, the port is a lot bigger than him," he said.

30-year alleged scam 

Rafael was arrested on Friday, after allegedly told undercover agents from the US Internal Revenue Service (IRS), posing as two Russian mobsters and a broker, that he had been running the fish fraud scheme for 30 years.

Feds: Rafael told undercover agents he’s been running fraud scheme for 30 years

Rafael justified a valuation of $175 million for his business, allegedly due to the money made illegally.

According to a spokeswoman for the IRS, Rafael pleaded not guilty.

"He's being held until Wednesday when a detention hearing will take place," she told Undercurrent.

Portugal-born Rafael, a US citizen who owns over 40 fishing vessels ported in New Bedford and Gloucester -- 12 for scallops and the rest for groundfish -- allegedly detailed the scheme to the undercover IRS agents, who had approached him about buying his business.

According to an affidavit from IRS special agent Ronald Mullett, seen by Undercurrent News, Rafael’s ownership of both the vessels and the buyer, the company Carlos Seafood, enabled him to commit the fraud. In selling the fish, he reportedly received cash payments from a buyer in New York named as "Michael" in the document.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) requires all dealers to submit, on a weekly basis, electronic reports, known as dealer reports, detailing information about the fish they buy, usually from incoming vessels, according to the affidavit.

To submit reports, the dealer must log onto a NOAA website and enter the data.

Dealer reports include data about the date a catch was landed, the name of the vessel that brought it in, the grade, species, price and weight of the fish, and the number of the trip report that corresponds to the catch.

NOAA uses the dealer reports as a check on the information vessels submit on trip reports. In a given instance, if the species and weight listed on the dealer report do not match the corresponding trip report, the discrepancy may be evidence of fraud on one or both reports.

“Therefore, to perpetrate an ongoing fraud regarding the weight or species of a given catch, the vessel operator and the dealer must collude. This is easier when the vessel and the dealer are owned by the same person, here Carlos Rafael,” Mullett’s affidavit states.

During the talks between the undercover IRS agents and Rafael, the agents reportedly asked him specifically how he prevents accurate records of fish from being reported after they are weighed at the auction house.

“We call them something else. It’s simple. We’ve been doing it for over thirty years,” Rafael replied, according to the affidavit.

title: Reports: Protests as Thai exporter forced to close doors
content:
Shrimp processor Crystal Frozen Foods, which has long feared for its survival due to early mortality syndrome (EMS) and the EU-issued Thai yellow card, has apparently been forced to shut down.

Labor rights activist Andy Hall, tweeting to Undercurrent News from Thailand, said on Jan. 29 that employees at the factory were outside protesting. The company had run out of money to pay wages, and had been forced to close, he said, citing contacts with Migrant Workers Rights Network (MWRN) on-site.

The protest ended soon afterwards, peacefully, said Hall. Company and labor officials at the site agreed with MWRN that laid-off workers would be taken to file for claims of compensation on Monday morning, he added.

Crystal experienced labor disputes in February 2015, when it allegedly failed to pay minimum legal wage and the appropriate dismissal compensation. The exporter moved to take a loan in order to pay the legal amount required, Crystal’s managing director, Pornchat Achakulwisut, told Undercurrent at the time.

On Feb. 5, some 150 Myanmar migrant workers reportedly submitted complaints to the Labor Protection Office at Mahachai, Samut Sakhorn province, accompanied by migrant rights groups.

@undercur Worker protests erupt again Crystal Food. Company fails to pay workers, announces factory now closing down pic.twitter.com/HPASMmgoV8

— Andy Hall (@Atomicalandy) January 29, 2016

The complaint, echoed by a reported 200 protesting outside the factory on Feb 2, concerned how the factory has allegedly continued to fail to meet the minimum legal wage of THB 300 per day and provide an eight hour working day to its migrant employees, according to Hall's Facebook page.

“Our business operation is based mainly on farmed vannamei shrimp which has been affected by the EMS crisis during the past two years, causing high mortality rates of farmed shrimp in Thailand,” said Achakulwisut.

“The loss of GSP [EU Generalized System of Preferences tariffs] privileges for Thai products has also eroded our price competitiveness further, and we have been struggling to keep our customers for value-added products with vannamei-based raw materials. Our efforts seem to be in vain after we completed all pending orders for the Christmas season in Europe last October 2014,” he said.

Two months later he told Undercurrent that his firm -- a member of the Thai Frozen Foods Association -- could not pay its suppliers, and was pessimistic about its chances of survival.

“[Now] Crystal Frozen Foods is going downhill in all directions, since we do not have enough cashflow left to manage our operation properly,” said Achakulwisut in April. “Our major raw materials suppliers have stopped delivering to us, after we failed to pay them on time, and we have no choice as paying compensation to workers is the top priority.”

“I do not see any light at the end of the tunnel for my company yet, and it is just a matter of weeks before this plant has to be closed down permanently,” he said.

Achakulwisut suggested that, at a time of economic crisis such as that facing Thai shrimp processors during the supply shortage caused by EMS, companies needed some time to restructure.

“During economic crisis, companies like Crystal need time to restructure, especially on the financial side, and in Thailand we do not have a law like chapter 11 filing, which will give a company opportunity to recover," he said.

“More and more Thai seafood processors will run into business problems as more workers will lose their jobs, and under the depressed economic situation it won't be easy to find new jobs for large numbers,” he warned.

Two other Undercurrent sources in Thailand agreed that job losses through this combination of circumstances had been seen, and remained a risk.

“It is a terrible shame to see good people, as I believe Khun Pornchat to be, facing impossible odds and possibly going out of business as a result,” said on source.

Undercurrent was not able to reach Achakulwisut before publishing this story.

Yellow card the final nail?

By the end of April -- after the European Union's decision to yellow-card Thailand during the Seafood Expo Global trade show in Brussels, Belgium -- Crystal was facing pressing challenges.

“The latest yellow card ban by the EU is also putting pressure on our squid and fish fillets line, which we have relied on to run the plant after being forced to stop vannamei shrimp processing a few months ago,” he said.

“If we can’t export the sea-catch products to EU too, the end is not very far off for CFF operations.” Speaking in April 2015, he forecast Thailand gaining a red card, because "there are labor issues behind the scenes" of the whole sector.

Andy Hall -- who as of Jan. 14, 2016 is on bail from Thai courts in advance of indictment over a criminal defamation and computer crimes case, brought by pineapple exporter Natural Fruit Company -- has recently spoken out over the risks to employees as seafood firms go under.

He has accused Thai shrimp peeling sheds of laying off staff without compensation or protection. This, he said, puts workers -- principally from Myanmar -- at risk of being "sold" to other employers, as Thai seafood companies scramble to clean up their supply chains in the wake of reports of slavery, human trafficking and other labour violations.

"It's unacceptable the way they've handled it," said Hall. "We heard from the workers that they got absolutely no compensation. They just got moved to another workplace, and this is very risky behaviour."

Even for companies not having to close, this could be an issue, as Undercurrent reported on Jan. 28. A new Thai regulation, entering into force on Jan. 13, meant a Thai shrimp exporter with supply links to major UK retailers has had to lay off workers in its Chumphon plant aged below 18; which it apparently did without any further compensation.

title: Court imposes travel ban on Andy Hall, bail posted by Thai tuna firms
content:
A Thai court has imposed a travel ban on British Migrant rights activist Andy Hall,  following a temporary bail request submission.

Hall has also had his passport confiscated, as ordered by the Bangkok South Criminal Court on Jan. 14. His bail surety costs of THB 300,000 were shared between Finnwatch, the Thai Tuna Industry Association and Thai Union Group.

The bail request was made in advance of Hall’s official indictment next week on Jan. 18 for an internationally monitored criminal defamation and computer crimes case brought against him by Thai pineapple exporter Natural Fruit Company.

Hall cannot now leave Thailand before the case has been ruled on by the court, unless permission is granted on a case by case basis.

The activist has said he will now petition the British Embassy to Thailand for assistance in requesting diplomatic officials to seek the return of his passport.

"The confiscation of Andy Hall's passport and the limitations placed on his ability to travel freely are a form of harassment and intimidation," said said Sonja Vartiala, executive director of Finnwatch.

"Ever since the beginning of this campaign of judicial harassment, Andy Hall has shown nothing but respect towards the rule of law and the judiciary in Thailand, alongside his willingness to respond to allegations against him in a court of law. For this reason, there seems to be no reason to treat him as a flight risk, confiscate his passport and prevent him from travelling in and out of Thailand."

Hall is scheduled to speak at next month's SeaWeb Seafood Summit in St Julian's Malta. There's a chance this may not happen now, although Hall confirmed to Undercurrent News that "I will ask permission to go to Malta still".

title: Activist Andy Hall to seek bail ahead of indictment hearing
content:
Migrant rights activist Andy Hall is to to formally surrender himself to a Thai court on Jan. 13, ahead of his formal indictment on defamation and Computer Crimes Act charges, brought by Thailand's Natural Fruit Company.

In doing so, Hall will request temporary release on bail, although, on condition, this may entail the confiscation of his passport and a travel ban on his entering and leaving Thailand.

Finnwatch, the Thai Tuna Industry Association and Thai Union Group have prepared THB 300,000 between them for submission to Bangkok South Criminal Court  in support of Hall’s and as a bail surety.

The charges in this case relate to publication of a 2013 Finnwatch report, "Cheap has a High Price", detailing alleged human rights violations at Natural Fruit's pineapple-processing plant in Prachuap Kiri Khan province. Hall coordinated the field research for the report and conducted interviews with workers.

This case is only one of four, which were first filed by Natural Fruit against Hall in February 2013. The other criminal defamation case, related to an Aljazeera new interview given by Hall in Myanmar, was dismissed by the Appeal Court in September, but will be appealed to the Supreme Court.

Hall will plead to innocent to the charges, which carry a maximum penalty of seven years in prison.

'This case is just one in a long series of cases that consist essentially of judicial harassment," Hall told Undercurrent News. "I am confident that eventually, although surely after many years of merit-less appeals by the company or prosecutors, all cases against me shall be dismissed."

"Its just a shame the cases can impact negatively on my ability to commit all my spare time to work to address migrant rights abuses in Thailand. But key is that I manage my team and legal defence in a way that has as little impact on my work as possible.'

Hall, working alongside the Migrant Workers Rights Network, has played a prominent role in exposing labor abuses in the Thai seafood industry, and mediating in ongoing disputes between Burmese workers and companies -- most notably, that of tuna canner Golden Prize.

title: National Fish: Traceability software will reduce slavery in Thai supply chain
content:
Pacific Andes International Holdings-owned US importer National Fish and Seafood is implementing traceability software at shrimp farms in Thailand to ensure slavery is not used in its supply chain, the company said.

By using the Farmforce and SourceTrace software at the Thailand shrimp farms which supply it, National Fish believes it can avoid any connection to forced labor, a practice that is reportedly common in the country's seafood industry.

The software will help the company "tap into the benefits of a cloud-based platform so farmers, processors, importers and buyers can all benefit from a transparent, traceable supply chain ensuring social and environmental compliance with international standards," National Fish said in a press release.

In 2015, James Baros, the company's aquaculture and sustainability manager, joined the Thai Shrimp Sustainable Supply Chain Task Force, a group which aims to crack down on labor abuses and illegal fishing in Thailand.

The task force is focused on three main ways to combat Thailand's seafood slavery problem. First, it aims to implement "track and trace" systems, which will be verified internationally.

The Ng family is having to crisis manage on a global scale, with former ‘cash cow’ China Fishery facing liquidation amid big issues for Pacific Andes in Americas, Europe and Asia
Read more

Secondly, the group wants to spearhead the use of internationally recognized codes of conduct in Thai ports.

Finally, it hopes to push forward with fisheries improvement projects in the Gulf of Thailand and the Andaman Sea, two areas where labor abuses have reportedly taken place previously.

National Fish said that the company is committed to preventing human rights violations in pre-processing facilities. Earlier this year, the company helped a Thai supplier construct a feed mill to ensure that the company knew what was in its supply chain.

"This undertaking successfully further secured our supply chain, giving us increased control over all inputs ensuring legality and fair labor practices of our fishmeal suppliers and affiliated fishing vessels," Baros said.

The efforts toward combatting longstanding accusations of slavery and human rights abuses in Thailand comes as National Fish has endured a difficult few months.

Human trafficking and slave labor allegations against the Thai industry are escalating
Read more

Its parent company, Pacific Andes, faces an effort to wind up its major China Fishery Group subsidiary and Pacific Andes managing director and vice-chairman Joo Siang Ng resigned in December.

Amid the corporate turmoil, the companies are beginning the process to sell off several subsidiaries, including its operations in Peru.

Additionally, Pacific Andes and China Fishery faces regulator investigations in Singapore and Hong Kong.

National Fish has also faced troubles of its own and recently changed executives amid tax fraud allegations against its longtime president, Jack Ventola.

Todd Provost took over as president of the company on Nov. 20, the same day the indictment emerged against Ventola, who the company said would stay onboard as a non-executive director.

Ventola was arrested on Nov. 23 in connection with failing to pay taxes on more than $2 million in income he earned from 2006 to 2009, according to the US attorney’s office for the district of Massachusetts. He has been indicted on three counts of filing false tax returns and one count of conspiracy to defraud the Internal Revenue Service.
