title: 2015 timeline: A year in Thai labor scandals
content:
Arguably no topic has stirred as much as emotive debate across the seafood sector in 2015 than the situation over human rights and labor abuses in Thailand.

As can be seen below, hardly a week passed without a report -- both on Undercurrent News and in the wider international press -- on the escalating problem in the southeast Asian nation.

While human rights' organizations have sought to redress gross inequalities suffered by migrant workers -- mainly from Myanmar -- some of the country's largest companies have found themselves in the firing line.

Thai Union Group, in particular, has been the subject of much unfavourable scrutiny over the transparency of its supply chain -- or perceived lack thereof -- with Greenpeace waging an especially fervent campaign against the tuna canner.

Some of the world's biggest retail brands have also found themselves implicated, after a report published in November by the Associated Press revealed that several supply chains could be linked back to an illegal peeling shed in Thailand, manned by slave workers.

The Thai government's response to such accusations has been divisive. Just as the EU slammed the country for its sluggishness in tackling illegal, unregulated and unreported (IUU) fishing activities -- resulting in the issuing of a yellow card -- pockets of the international community have been unimpressed by its inability to crack down on offences.

Despite various promises issued by Thai prime minister Prayuth Chan-ocha to clean up the sector, including the first upgrade of the country's fisheries act since 1947, many remain unconvinced that such pledges are nothing more than lip service.

With several labor disputes between workers and their employers still in full flow -- with NGOs and activists fighting for the former -- it is unlikely this geopolitical crisis will ease for some time yet.

Below you can scan the year of scandals, accusations and refutations in full, with links to the full, original stories.

January

On Jan. 12, Thailand announced plans to implement new regulations to address concerns of forced labor in its fishing industry.

Among the new regulations -- approved by the National Legislative Assembly -- was a requirement for at least ten hours of rest per working day and 30 days of leave per year, as well as the registration of migrant workers and their families. Enforcement was set for within 60 days. 

But only two days later, on Jan. 14, Thailand was again the focus of international condemnation over plans to use prisoners in its fishing industry.

In total, 45 human rights organizations -- including Greenpeace Southeast Asia sent a letter to Thai Prime Minister Prayut Chan-o-cha,  asking him to end a pilot project to recruit prisoners from Thailand's correctional facilities to fill a labor shortage in the fishing industry.

The petition worked. Less then a week later, on Jan. 20, the Thai government scrapped its plans to put prisoners to work on understaffed fishing boats

On Jan. 15, the US State Department -- having named Thailand one of the world's worst centers for human trafficking the previous June -- called for Thailand to empower victims of trafficking and forced labor to complain, and to crack down on corrupt officials.

February

On Feb. 6, shrimp processor Crystal Frozen Foods, a member of the Thai Frozen Foods Association (TFFA), announced it had moved to take out a loan to pay compensation to underpaid migrant workers, who were assisted by the Labor Protection Office and the NGO Migrant Worker Rights Network (MWRN).

Thai human rights abuses were the focal point of a tense discussion on supply chain management at the SeaWeb Seafood Summit, held on Feb. 10, New Orleans.

On Feb. 17, the Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF) called for Thailand to remain downgraded on the US State Department’s Trafficking in Persons watch list.

The NGO said the Thai Government had made "inadequate improvement" in fighting widespread human rights abuses in the fisheries sector to be returned to Tier 2.

Thailand's Ministry of Affairs responded, saying it was deeply disappointed with EJF's report, and claimed it had overlooked Thailand’s ongoing intensified anti-human trafficking efforts and positive results yielded.

“In 2014, the Ministry of Labour took legal actions against 156 labor brokers who violated labor laws. 107 illegal brokers were also arrested,” it said in a press release.

However, there was more to come from from the NGO, which added -- as reported on Feb. 25 -- that overfishing, pirate fishing and people trafficking/slavery needed to be addressed as interconnected issues in Thailand. 

“Producers and consumers of Thai seafood are embroiled in one of the most outrageous social and ecological crimes of the 21st century. Ecosystem decline and slavery exist in a vicious cycle,” said EJF executive director Steve Trent.

March

Amid rumors of a potential European Union yellow card for Thailand, Charoen Pokphand Foods (CP Foods) detailed efforts on its supply chain labor visibility.

On Mar. 11, human rights groups Finnwatch and MWRN announced a three-year collaborative project, in a bid to empower migrant workers in Thailand to negotiate better working terms and conditions, and improve their quality of life in Thailand.

US critics continued to apply pressure on the Thai government to clean up the exploitation of workers in the tuna sector.

On the back of a year-long investigation, on Mar. 25 the Associated Press published a report linking fish caught by trafficked Myanmar workers back to Thailand.

Unwitting buyers of such seafood included Thai Union -- Thailand's largest seafood company and one of the biggest in the world -- which subsequently dropped supplier Niwat Co. from its supply chain, after the latter was implicated in the AP report.

On Mar. 26, Thai Union said it was confident that the AP report would have little impact on $1.5 billion deal to acquire US firm Bumble Bee Foods.

Directly addressing the AP report, Thai prime minister Prayuth Chan-ocha vowed to take legal action against companies found using forced labor.

April

The month kicked off with Thai Union executives meeting with the country's military government over the issues of slave labor in the seafood supply chain.

On Apr. 2, officials from Thailand -- along with Indonesian delegates -- journeyed to the the island of Benjina in Indonesia to investigate how foreign fishermen -- mainly from Myanmar -- wind up in bondage.

The AP had revealed that the men had been lured into leaving their countries to go to Thailand, where they were used as slave labor on boats and brought to Indonesia.

However, the Thai delegation found no proof of mistreatment and found all crews to be Thai.

Four days later, on Apr. 6, it was revealed that some 320 fishermen that had been used as slave labor on fishing boats were given their freedom back, following a "dramatic rescue", ordered by Indonesian officials. 

Thai Labor abuses also carried ramifications for European players, with a report by Fairfood International stating shrimp sold in some European supermarkets, including Lidl, was peeled and processed by exploited Asian shrimp workers on poverty wages.

Having seemingly moved quickly to solve the dispute with migrant workers in February, on Apr. 13, it was reported that Crystal Frozen Foods was facing closure, and unable to pay its suppliers.

On Apr. 18, a documentary feature film 'The Ghost Fleet' -- telling the story of some of the lucky few to have escaped forced labor on Thai fishing vessels -- was released.

Three days later, Thailand's worst fears came true when it was finally awarded a yellow card by the European Commission for not taking sufficient measures in the international fight against IUU.

"Thailand is deeply disappointed with the EU’s decision,” Thailand’s Department of Information from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a press release on the same day.

Thai Union also responded, claiming that a “minimum” of its seafood supply was sourced from Thai vessels. The company said it was confident of avoiding legal implications or restrictions for it or its customers related to the yellow carding.

Crystal Frozen Foods, on the other hand, said it was already feeling the strain from the EU ruling, with managing director Pornchat Achakulwisut telling Undercurrent News: "“If we can’t export the sea-catch products to EU too, the end is not very far off for CFF operations.”

On Apr. 23, the Thai seafood industry came under fire yet again at a congressional hearing on Wednesday at a House Foreign Affairs subcommittee meeting.

Amid the fall-out, Thailand announced it had partnered with Indonesia to form a fisheries working group to tackle IUU.

On Apr. 28, Thailand’s Commerce Ministry revealed plans to send a mission to the European Union to brief authorities there about the Asian nation’s attempts to remedy illegal labor practices.

May

On May. 13, seven people from an Indonesian fishing firm -- including five Thais -- were arrested in Benjina in connection with human trafficking and slavery.

Two days later, Satien Ngernanek, the co-owner of a Thai fishing trawler allegedly involved in human trafficking in Indonesian waters, turned himself in at the Department of Special Investigation (DSI).

On May.18, Thai PM Prayuth Chan-ocha reiterated to broadcaster CNN that his country was in the midst of clamping down on human trafficking and slave labor in the seafood sector.

24 hours later, 40 Burmese slave workers were freed from an illegal shrimp peeling shed  in Samut Sakhon, a coastal Thai town near Bangkok. Some of the rescuees said they had been trapped in the facility for as long as three years, despite having paid back so-called debts to employment brokers.

Labor issues subsequently cast a long shadow over the Thaifex-World of Food Asia trade show, held in Bangkok in the same week.

On May. 25, it was reported that the MWRN had expressed concerns to members of Thailand's 'Shrimp sustainable supply chain task force' over its lack of "on-the-ground" domestic experience.

“A task force made up of consultants, international rights or consumer/conservation groups and industry representatives, as well as buyers, is not sufficient to move forward sustainably on the labor issues the task force also seeks to address,” human rights campaigner Andy Hall wrote in an email to the companies involved.

June

On Jun. 1, Thailand's government adopted IUU sanctions in the first update to its fisheries act since 1947.

A follow-up report by Finnwatch called for a ban on recruitment fees for migrant workers entering Thailand from Myanmar through the official Memorandum of Understanding process. Workers were said to have paid hundreds of euros in various fees in order to take up employment at Unicorn factories -- which are part of Sea Value -- said the NGO.

On Jun. 17, it was reported that anti-slavery private donor fund, the Freedom Fund, had pledged to spend $5 million on an initiative to encourage global retailers and producers to tackle forced labor in Thailand by developing tools to boost supply chain transparency.

Andy Hall, the human rights campaigner, and affiliate of MWRN, welcomed an announcement made by TFFA, committing to traceability measures in a bid to "clean up" the sector.

The measures were a “stronger standard and mechanisms” than before, human rights campaigner Hall told Undercurrent.

On Jun. 23, more than 3,000 mid-sized Thai vessels were warned by the government that they would have to stop fishing on Jul. 1 under measures designed to curb IUU.

July

Trawler operators in some of Thailand's coastal provinces claimed to be facing crew shortages, in light of new regulations geared towards curbing IUU, which came into play on Jul. 1.

The fishermen requested the government to begin another round of migrant registrations to curb the problem.

A joint task force of Thai police and anti-human trafficking personnel arrested five accomplices and the leader of a human trafficking ring near Bangkok.

Thailand remained on Tier 3 in the latest US Trafficking in Persons (TIP) report, published on Jul. 27,

“Although Thailand took steps to improve trafficking-related laws and coordination between agencies working to combat human trafficking, Thailand did not undertake sufficient action during the reporting period required for tangible progress on its formidable human trafficking problem,” read a statement on the website of the US embassy in Bangkok, in response to the report.

The decision to retain Thailand on Tier 3 was supported by labor rights groups in a joint letter sent to US secretary of state John Kerry on Jul. 27.

Thailand’s Department of Provincial Administration, however, disputed part of the TIP report's findings.

The portion in question said: "Due to proactive efforts by some officials, 900 hilltribe members received citizenship. While national-level officials seemed to have a greater understanding that statelessness may be a risk factor for trafficking, this understanding had not necessarily become a standard at the municipal and regional levels.”

In response, the director-general of Thailand’s Department of Provincial Administration said that any request for Thai citizenship was made via local officials and that from January 2014 through June the government had granted citizenship to 10,551 hilltribe or stateless people.

Thai Union said it was no longer buying fish from motherships manned by slave workers, as exposed in a New York Times report, published on Jul. 27.

Sasinan Allmand, the head of corporate communications for Thai Union, told Undercurrent the company stopped buying from brokers sourcing from motherships at the start of the year.

The group added that it hoped to have 100% of its supply chain independently audited by 2016.

August

In continuation of its well publicized efforts to clean up its supply chain, Thai Union revealed it had dropped a number of suppliers.

“We have cut down to dealing with 51 ships and five ports. Then, we now have five fishmeal factories we are dealing with,” Scott Solar, the company's director of culinary development and responsible sourcing, told Undercurrent. 

“This has come down from over 200 vessels. The number of fishmeal factories was 22. I don't have the exact number of ports.”

The US State Department sought to clarify the part of its recent TIP report under contention from Thai authorities (see above).

A State Department official told Undercurrent that the 900 figure (relating to hilltribe members) was for the number of people assisted by one NGO, and not the total number of hilltribe members or stateless people who were granted citizenship from January 2014 to June.

Despite its remonstration regarding its Tier 3 downgrade, the TTIA said it had accepted the ruling as a challenge to further improve areas in the seafood sector that are not in compliance.

On Aug. 19, in the US, a California woman filed a class action law suit against US retailer Costco Wholesale alleging the company misled consumers over the shrimp it sells from Thailand.

"This case arises from the devaluing of human life," stated the plaintiff, Monica Sud, in a suit document filed in the Northern District of California.

The following day, CP Foods -- which Sud accused, among other Thai companies, of knowingly relying on slave labor -- said the accusations were "without merit", retorting that its fishmeal came from certified manufacturers and legal vessels.

Brokerage Asia Plus Securities predicted CP Foods' results would not suffer a negative impact from the lawsuit.

On Aug. 24, migrants' rights activist Andy Hall was indicted by a Bangkok court relating to defamation case brought by pineapple processing company, Natural Fruit Company.

On Aug. 28, Thai Union joined CP Foods in its own litigation battle, and was named in a slavery lawsuit filed against Swiss food company Nestle. 

The suit, filed by the law firm Hagens Berman Sobol Shapiro LLP, alleged that Nestle violated three California laws prohibiting false advertising and unfair competition because Thai Union had knowingly used forced labor to harvest fish used in the cat food.

Nestle responded in a statement, saying "forced labor has no place in our supply chain", but stopped short of denying the allegations.

September

On Sep. 11, in a seminar at Chulalongkorn University, activists argued that stringent labor protection measures were required alongside ongoing efforts to combat IUU.

"The measures issued by the government are a step in the right direction, but they fail to protect workers," said Pantima Tungpuchayakol, from the Labour Rights Promotion Network Foundation.

An article published in the New York Times on Sep. 14 claimed more steps were being taken to end forced labor in fishing, in light of its investigation into abuses in the Thai seafood sector.

However, on the same day, a report drafted by the non-profit Asia Foundation and the United Nations' International Labor Organization (ILO) revealed that over a quarter of Thailand's child workers in the fishing industry were regularly exposed to fire, gas or flames -- more than twice the level of their counterparts in other sectors.

Petfood suppliers Mars and Proctor & Gamble became the latest high-profile brands to find themselves subjected to lawsuits over slave labor in their supply chains linked back to Thailand -- namely Thai Union subsidiaries Songkla Canning and Thai Union Manufacturing.

On Sep. 18, the Thai Appeal Court threw out -- for the second time -- the Attorney General and Natural Fruit's appeal on one of the cases filed by the pineapple company against Finnwatch researcher Andy Hall.

The European Commission rejected claims coming out of Thailand that a delegation had secured an extension on its deadline on yellow card talks for the end of October.

“Despite differing accounts, no decision has been made by the Commission yet on this,” Enrico Brivio, speaking on behalf of the Commission, told Undercurrent.

On Sep. 22, a US law firm confirmed it was investigating a further allegation that Costco Wholesale relied on fishmeal producers used by its Thai shrimp supplier, which used slave labor in its supply chain.

Speaking during a webinar on human rights issues in the supply chain -- ahead of the Innovation Forum, to be held in London in November -- activist Andy Hall said that in ten years of working in Thailand, no US company had ever approached him for his views of how things are on the ground.

“Debates over what we do are happening in boardrooms and over the phone, away from where they need to. It's time to start getting stakeholders together and actually starting some measures, to gain some practical learning experiences on the ground," said Hall.

On Sep. 25, a lawsuit was filed in California accusing Thai Union Group and its US subsidiaries of selling products to consumers from a supply chain containing slave labor.

This was the first lawsuit over alleged slave labor filed directly against Thai Union and its Chicken of the Sea US subsidiaries.

In the same week, the under-fire tuna canner revealed a new ethics and labor code of conduct, aimed at attaining a higher level of accountability and transparency throughout its supply chain across all its member companies.

October

Thai Union found itself the subject of more unfavourable scrutiny at the start of the month when NGO Greenpeace launched a global campaign against the group over its perceived labor abuses -- as well as harmful fishing methods.

The canner, however, went some way to mending its reputation by partnering with the MWRN to give formal training to employees across its operations in Thailand on labor and social welfare regulations -- all with the aim of having its migrant workers properly educated on labor and social welfare rights according to Thai law by the end of 2016.

While singled out as a notable exception -- along with CP Foods -- as a company taking a stance against labor abuses, Andy Hall wasn't so complimentary over other players, claiming abuses were a daily occurrence, even in certified, audited factories.

Greenpeace remained unconvinced as to This Union's efforts, ramping up its campaign to include labor unions -- representing five million people -- who called for the group to reform its social and environmental practices.

On Oct. 26, Andy Hall spoke out again on the “new low of confusion and chaos”, as to Myanmar continuing to record laborers for a registration system unacknowledged by Thai authorities.

“In a sign of how poor relations and coordination between Myanmar and Thailand continued to be on migration issues, no solution to this disagreement could be found between the two countries,” wrote Hall.

Having had its review postponed until the end of the year, Thailand reiterated its confidence in avoiding a red card from the EU over IUU fishing problems.

Following a lawsuit issued against it on Oct. 12, US-based pet food supplier Big Heart Pet Brands announced it was conducting "aggressive" review of all its suppliers, after being accused of supplying shoppers with products from a supply chain containing slave labor among its partners -- including This Union.

On Oct. 28, Greenpeace held a day of global protests against Thai Union's subsidiaries.

November

CP Foods -- employer of more than 3,400 Cambodian worker at its processing plants in Saraburi and Nakhon Ratchasima -- underlined its commitment to establishing fairer conditions for migrant workers.

Having been granted the highest level of Thai Labour Standard Accreditation (Thai Labour Standard 8001-2553), senior vice president Suchart Sitthicha insisted the company adhered to non-discriminatory principles, in line with international standards denouncing all forms of exploitation -- child labor, forced labor and human trafficking.

Held in collaboration with the Labour Rights Promotion Network Foundation, Thai Union put on a training workshop for its migrant employees in order to create awareness about their children’s rights with regards to education.

On Nov. 4, the International Labor Organization hosted a workshop in Bangkok to tackle illegal forms of employment in Thailand's fishing and seafood sector.

The multi-stakeholder consultation meeting on “Strategies for Addressing Unacceptable Forms of Work in Thailand’s Fishing and Seafood Industry” included government officials, trade unions, industry figureheads, NGO partners and academics.

But on the same day, Greenpeace claimed it had uncovered new incidents of forced labor on Thai operated vessels, with This Union once again condemned.

The report by Greenpeace Southeast Asia featured new interviews with survivors of trafficking and forced labor in Indonesia, who had faced abuse and food deprivation on Thai-operated fishing vessels.

The MWRN called on TFFA to deliver a promised list of shrimp peeling sheds working with its members. According to Andy Hall the information had been pledged for July.

The MWRN did, however, again reserve praise for CP Foods' migrant worker policy, which it said was the "only factory in Thailand to currently commit to cover a substantial or total amount of the Thailand based fees involved in memorandum of understanding migrant recruitment from neighboring countries".

Migrant workers at Golden Prize Canning -- a member of the TTIA and signed up to the ILO's good labor practices program -- revealed their fears to MWRN of a military presence presiding over a labor dispute with their employer.

Golden Prize was alleged to be working its employees at long hours, and below minimum wage in a debate dating back to July.

The TTIA said it was hoping for a swift resolution to the dispute, having sent an eight-point letter of demands to Golden Prize.

On Nov. 7, Thai officials arrested eight people -- including Sompol Jirotemontree, the head of the Trang Fishing Association--  in connection with human trafficking allegations.

On Nov. 11, as 1,500 Golden Prize migrant workers turned out force to protest against their employer once more, the MWRN blasted the TTIA as "woefully insufficient" and "having failed to save the problem".

The protest did, however, end peacefully, with workers agreeing to return to work the following day.

Back in the US, lawyers representing Costco accused Monica Sud -- woman who alleged in a class-action lawsuit that the chain sold her shrimp linked to human trafficking violations in Thailand -- of lying.

Costco reviewed its membership records and didn’t find evidence that Sud ever purchased “Thai-farmed prawns”, Costco lawyers said in a Nov. 16 court filing.

On Nov. 23, Nestle released an ambitious action plan aimed at dispelling doubts that parts of its supply chain for pet food relied on human trafficking in Thailand.

The six-page policy, entitled “responsible sourcing of seafood - Thailand,” aimed to have a series of measures put into place by the end of 2016 to resolve all labor issues.

The following day, it was revealed that the Thai labor protection office -- aided by MWRN -- had stepped in to investigate Golden Prize over alleged labor abuses.

In a new investigation, the Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF) named one of the most powerful individuals in the region of Kantang -- the owner of the Boonlarp Fishing company, Pompon Jirotmontree -- as having run his operations using forced and slave labor, while also claiming many workers were murdered by his security guard.

December

On Dec. 1, it was revealed to Undercurrent that under-fire Golden Prize Canning had relinquished its membership of the TTIA, opting to move over to the Thai Food Processors Association (TFPA) -- also the subject of criticism from the MWRN.

"It’s very worrying that Golden Prize has been accepted so quickly by the TFPA, especially given how little it has done to improve its workers’ rights,” lamented a MWRN source.

KCF Seafood then became the latest Thai seafood player to find itself accused of migrant workers' rights abuses.

On Dec. 8, the group, an exporter of tilapia, rohu and pangasius, was hit by a protest of over 140 workers from Myanmar, claiming to have been subjected to illegal debt bondage and thinly-veiled death threats.

On Dec. 14, a new investigation from the Associated Press revealed that a number of global retailers -- including Wal-Mart, Kroger, Whole Foods, Dollar General and Petco -- were selling shrimp linked to an illegal peeling shed in Thailand, manned by migrant slave workers.

“It comes as no surprise whatsoever” was the verdict of Andy Hall in response to the allegations.

No less than 24 hours later, Thai Union revealed it had severed tied with two shrimp pre-processing sheds -- one in December and one back in May.

On Dec. 10, it announced its intention to have cut external pre-processors, or peeling sheds, from its supply chain by the end of 2015.

Spurred on by the AP report ,Global Aquaculture Alliance (GAA) pledged to exclude any firms outsourcing to peeling sheds utilising child or forced labor from holding its Best Aquaculture Practices (BAP) standard -- to come into play on Jan. 1 2016.

Olive Garden and Red Lobster -- two US restaurant chains mentioned in the AP report -- spoke out against slavery in the seafood sector. Both groups claimed they were unaware of labor abuses in their respective supply chains.

Thailand's prime minister Prayut Chan-ocha also joined the chorus, vowing to take action against slavery in the country's shrimp processing facilities.

But his pledge appeared to fall on deaf ears in the US, where human rights groups and politician called for a boycott of fish and shrimp products linked to slave labour in Thailand.

Supermarket chain Whole Foods -- mentioned in the AP report -- denied that it sold shrimp connected to slave labor.

A truck tracked AP staffers had been discovered to transfer shrimp from slave-manned facilities to a subsidiary of Thai Union, a Whole Foods supplier.

However, the retailer refuted this, tweeting that "after thorough investigation, we’re confident Thai Union shrimp at our stores did not come from [an] illicit processing facility".

On Dec. 17, the American Shrimp Processors Association (ASPA) said it welcomed the latest investigation into slave labor in the Thai seafood sector.

"it is more important than ever to know where your shrimp are from," said David Veal, executive director of ASPA.

Karmenu Vella, the EU fisheries commissioner, also warned Thailand needed to address its issues with human rights and slavery fast, as well as the issues with IUU fishing.

In the wake of the exposé, the Thai Royal Police launched a renewed crackdown on human trafficking.

Focused on the central province of Samut Sakhon -- where the documented abuses were said to occur -- the enforcement measures included checks of licenses and labor permits.

Taking Thai Union's lead, TFFA moved to eradicate third party pre-processing operations from the shrimp supply chain of its members, effective at the end of December 2015.

On Dec. 23, it was reported that Golden Prize had shut down negotiations around back-payments apparently owed to migrant workers, stating it would only speak to the the country's Department of Labour Protection and Welfare.

Following Thailand announcement of a crackdown on labor abuses earlier in the month, the Royal Thai Embassy in Washington, D.C, said the peeling shed accused of using slavery had been shut down by authorities on Nov. 9, and the owner of the shed as well as three other individuals had been charged with several offenses.

In a press release, it also claimed 20 workers, as well as 11 children under the age of 18, had been rescued during the inspection of the shed and identified as human trafficking victims.

On Dec. 28, in a letter addressed to Undercurrent, Tom Mazzetta, the CEO of US shrimp and seafood importer Mazzetta Company criticized the boycotting of Thai shrimp by consumers as wrong, arguing "that in a global environment it takes steadfast commitment to ensure your supply chain is solid and your vision for corporate responsibility is being realized".

On Dec. 30, a group of activists revealed their plans to protest human trafficking conditions in Thailand's seafood sector outside a Washington, D.C. Walmart.

At a meeting of the Samut Sakhon Seafood Processing Club, the owners of several shrimp peeling sheds in the region disputed claims of slavery in their establishments, in response to the AP report.

"I fully support and am ready to work with the government to stamp out human trafficking and illegal practices in the shrimp industry. Not all of us violate the law," Akhom Krueawan, the club's president, said.

title: Ventola steps down from Pacific Andes-owned National Fish amid tax fraud allegations
content:
A new top executive has been named for Pacific Andes International Holdings' US operation National Fish and Seafood, amid tax fraud allegations against its longtime president, Jack Ventola.

Todd Provost took over as president of Gloucester, Massachusetts-based National Fish on Friday, Pacific Andes confirmed to Undercurrent News, the same day the indictment emerged against Ventola, who the company said would stay onboard as a non-executive director.

Ventola was arrested on Nov. 23 in connection with failing to pay taxes on more than $2 million in income he earned from 2006 to 2009, according to the US attorney’s office for the district of Massachusetts. He has been indicted on three counts of filing false tax returns and one count of conspiracy to defraud the Internal Revenue Service.

"My stepping down has been planned for a long time," Ventola told Undercurrent in an email, when asked if there is a link between this and the allegations.

The indictment alleges that Ventola utilized the services of a temporary labor company called Continental Labor Team, which Ventola and a co-conspirator, who was also an executive of the seafood processor, controlled.

Ventola and his co-conspirator -- who has not been named -- allegedly worked together to channel money out of Continental and into their personal bank accounts, tax free.

To do this, the co-conspirator allegedly prepared fraudulent invoices for work supposedly done for Continental by a shell company Ventola controlled called International Freezing Systems (IFS).

Ventola and his co-conspirator allegedly used the fake IFS invoices to obtain payments from Continental, which they deposited into one of Ventola’s personal bank accounts.

From there, Ventola used the funds to pay personal expenses and also wrote his co-conspirator personal checks approximately monthly.

Although the checks from Continental totaled more than $2 million between 2006 and 2009, neither Ventola nor his co-conspirator reported the income on their tax returns, it is alleged.

The indictment also alleges that Ventola failed to report approximately $149,000 of other income he received in 2008 and 2009.

The charge of filing a false tax return provides for a penalty of no greater than three years in prison, one year of supervised release and a fine of $100,000.

The conspiracy charge provides for a sentence of no greater than five years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of $250,000 or twice the gross gain or loss from the offense.

‘Long-term plan’

National Fish, in a statement sent to Undercurrent, claimed the promotion of Provost is in line with the long term succession plan on which Provost has been working closely with the board for several years.

Provost has been with the company since 1997 and was previously its chief operating officer.

“I am very proud of NFS [National Fish] and what we have accomplished to this point,” said Ventola, in the statement.

“From our products to our capabilities and culture, I could not be more enthusiastic about our development as a seafood company. At this time, I am looking forward to pursuing some family and personal interests,” he said.

In its latest reported financial figures for 2014, National Fish incurred a HKD 39.6m ($5.1m), loss despite a 20% rise in turnover.

National Fish, which is 60% owned by Pacific Andes as well as a Hong Kong-registered subsidiary also called National Fish and Seafood, saw the $5.1m loss after earning a $2.6m profit in 2013.

The filing said that the National Fish subsidiaries experienced $236.8m turnover in 2013 and $284.2m turnover in 2014.

title: NRS Q3 hit by high costs; guides for lower 2015, 2016 salmon harvests
content:
Norway Royal Salmon (NRS) has reported improved third quarter 2015 results when compared with Q3 2014, and with Q2 2015, though investment bank Nordea notes a “substantially lower ebit [earnings before interest and tax] than expected”.

Operational ebit came in at NOK 23 million ($2.64m), when consensus had put it at NOK 64m, and Nordea had expected NOK 83m, wrote senior seafood analyst Kolbjorn Giskeodegard.

This was an improvement on Q3 2014, when NRS lost NOK 15m, and on Q2 2015, when ebit came in at NOK 19m.

The reason for the deviation was higher than expected costs; in its northern farming region, where 95% of its salmon for the quarter was harvested, NRS saw costs of NOK 30.4, meaning an ebit per kilogram of NOK 9.69.

Harvesting in the south was very low, costs were above NOK 40, and ebit came close to NOK 0 per kg.

“The underlying cost level has been substantially elevated by higher feed costs,” wrote Nordea. “For this quarter a NOK 25m one-off from ISA outbreak has also impacted both overall ebit and 2015-16 volume guidance negatively.”

For 2015, NRS has lowered expected harvests by 2,500 metric tons (8.2%) to 28,000t – still 25% up on 2014.

Its estimated harvest for 2016 is 27,500t – surprising, according to Nordea, “although they are very confident that they will be in place with full MAB utilization also on the ten new licenses by end 2016, hence reaching their full new capacity (our estimate is 38,000t) during 2017”.

“The company has aimed to break the 30,000t threshold since 2014; now they have postponed this to 2017. This is a more realistic target; we do however expect a negative 3-4% market reaction today.”

Nordea also notes that as more companies guide down volumes for 2016, the tighter the overall salmon market becomes, and the higher the salmon prices (all other factors constant). This should benefit NRS, and the other names in the sector, the bank said.

Higher sales, but at higher costs

NRS posted sales revenues of NOK 743.9m in Q3, up 45% year-on-year. This was in part thanks to prices averaging NOK 40.71 per kg gutted weight, 7% higher on Q2 2015 and 16% higher compared with the Q3 2014.

The sales operations experienced an increase in sales volumes of 29%, at 16,333t, compared with the corresponding prior-year period.

The sale of some Aquaculture Stewardship Council-certified salmon also added to higher selling prices, NRS noted.

Crucially, production costs for harvested fish in NRS's northern region were NOK 1.28 higher than in the second quarter of 2015, and NOK 1.73 higher than in the corresponding period last year.

This increase was mainly a result of higher feed cost per kg harvested due to higher feed price and higher feed conversion rates. The fish disease infectious salmon anemia was detected at two sites in the quarter, and all fish at both sites have since been destroyed, the firm noted.

In the southern farming region production costs were NOK 5.18 per kg higher than in Q3 2014, with feed prices driving costs up.

Nord Senja Laks could still be hit

The Norwegian National Authority for Investigation and Prosecution of Economic and Environmental Crime (Okokrim) has recently announced it has appealed the sentence made against NRS subsidiary Nord Senja Laks, for misreporting sea lice.

The company was fined NOK 5m and NOK 400,000 in confiscations in October, after being indicted of offences back in February.

Nord Senja Laks was not sentenced to loss of rights. Consequently, the verdict had no effect on the licenses held be Nord Senja Laks and future operations.

However, Okokrim has now filed a notice of appeal regarding the fine, and the decision not to sentence Nord Senja Laks to loss of rights.

title: Norway Royal Salmon subsidiary found guilty of sea lice misreporting offences
content:
Norway Royal Salmon subsidiary Nord Senja Laks has been found guilty of misreporting sea lice occurrences.

The company, indicted of offences back in February, has been sentenced by Senja District court to pay of a fine of NOK 5 million, and confiscation of NOK 400,000.

However, it was not sentenced to a loss of rights - which consequently has no effect on the licenses held be Nord Senja Laks' future operations - which some had predicted.

The Norwegian government had reserved the right to take away the green licenses awarded to company, upon the first allegations of giving wrongful information to the Norwegian Food Safety Authority as to its handling of sea lice.

Nord Senja Laks - of whose shares Norway Royal Salmon owns 66.67% -  has not decided whether to appeal the verdict. Any appeal must be filed on or before Nov. 6, 2015.

title: Thai criminal case against migrants rights’ activist dismissed again
content:
A Thai Appeal Court has dismissed the Attorney General and Natural Fruit's appeal on one of the cases filed by the pineapple company against Finnwatch researcher Andy Hall.

The case concerned an interview Hall, who has been prominent in his work to improve the lives of Thai and migrant laborers in the Thai seafood sector, gave to Aljazeera in Myanmar.

The Appeal Court decision was read at the Prakanong Court - the same court that dismissed the alleged criminal defamation case in the first place on Oct. 29, 2014 due to a flawed interrogation process.

The Attorney General and Natural Fruit cannot now appeal further to the Supreme Court.

"We are relieved and glad about today's Court decision and that the legality of the previous dismissal has been upheld. Case is now closed," said Sonja Vartiala, Finnwatch's executive director.

The case heard in this event was just one of four cases filed by Natural Fruit against Hall. Hearings on the other criminal case will continue on Oct. 19, when he will be formally indicted for criminal defamation and a computer crime on a case that relates to the publication of a Finnwatch report apparently exposing labor rights violations at the Natural Fruit pineapple processing plant. This second criminal case is the most serious of the four, and carries a maximum penalty of seven years' imprisonment.

In addition to two criminal cases, National Fruit has also filed two damages claims against Hall.

Finnwatch and hundreds of other civil society organisations have appealed for the criminal proceedings against Andy Hall to be dropped, and for the Thai authorities to bring Natural Fruit to justice for the alleged labour rights violations at their pineapple processing plant.

title: Walmart, Costco shrimp supplier aiming high after $36m fraud scam
content:
Vietnamese shrimp company Phuong Nam Seafood has ambitious plans for expansion and growth by the year 2020, as it recovers from the blow of a $36.7 million fraud scandal.

The processor – which lists Costco, Walmart, and Mitsubishi among its customers – is planning to boost turnover and push to become a vertically-integrated shrimp firm by 2020.

This is something of a turnaround plan for the company, which a few years ago was at the heart of what is thought to be one of the country's most serious corruption cases. In August 2015, 25 bankers were sent to jail for their parts in illegally lending nearly VND 800 billion to Phuong Nam, which went bankrupt in 2012, owing more than VND 1.6 trillion ($75m).

Undercurrent News visited Phuong Nam's processing plant in October 2014, when it had an estimated turnover of $40m, according to general manager Nguyen Thi Bach Lien. Its aim at that time was to bring more shrimp raw material through, and utilize more of its capacity.

At that stage, operating at 50% capacity was a good result for peak production periods, said Lien. In October it sourced all of its shrimp from Vietnamese farmers, with no farms of its own.

That is all set to change, however. At the recent Vietfish event in Ho Chi Minh, Phuong Nam said it was due to begin harvesting from its own, new, shrimp farm in 2016, and that is just the beginning of its plans.

Over the next five years it intends to grow into one of the country's leading shrimp exporters, it says in its company brochure, and apparently hit a $1bn turnover mark.

Whereas in October 2014 it was hoping to invest in and start up one farm, its long-term plan now includes 1,000 hectares of shrimp farms, utilizing recirculation aquaculture system (RAS) technology. The farm it intends to begin harvesting from in 2016 should supply the Soc Trang plant to the tune of 50% capacity on its own, said Lien.

At present there are 110,000 square meters of shrimp farms undergoing testing of the technology, to improve quality and productivity. Phuong Nam is working with what it calls a “world leader” in water treatment, Norwegian firm Kruger Kaldnes -- part of the global water and energy firm Veolia Group -- on the RAS.

The $1bn turnover target may be a mis-communication. They have been operating now just under a year; they have walked out of the darkness, and I think maybe they are looking at $100m in 2015 or 2016

The company also claims to be building “the most modern shrimp laboratory in Vietnam” as part of its quality assurance procedures.

The firm claims to have some major customers around the world: High Liner Foods, Costco, Walmart, Sysco and Loblaw in North America; Metro [though the retail group told Undercurrent it "has no ties" with Phuong Nam], Lyons Seafood and Rud. Kanzow in Europe; and Mitsubishi, Kyokuyo, and Hanwa in Japan.

UPDATE: Mitsubishi too told Undercurrent it has not had business with Phuong Nam for the past few years.

Realistic aims?

It remains to be seen just how the fraud situation has affected Phuong Nam's plans for the future. While the crime was uncovered in 2012 – Phuong Nam chairman and director Lam Ngoc Khuan had fled to the US, leaving his firm with debts of VND 1.6tr – the impact seems to be ongoing.

“Supposedly the company, or factory, has been closed for the last two weeks, and they are trying to sort everything out with the banks,” one source in touch with employees of Phuong Nam told Undercurrent.

One employee at the firm believes it can still manage and pull through, but “it will be very difficult for them to grow due to the financial constraints”, he added.

Phuong Nam was at one time in the top three shrimp exporters in Vietnam, but after this corruption case it was declared bankrupt, and production ceased until the firm was taken over by a group of banks.

“I think the $1bn turnover target may be a mis-communication,” said another Vietnamese source familiar with the company. “They have been operating now just under a year; they have walked out of the darkness and I think maybe they are looking at $100m in 2015 or 2016.”

Phuong Nam had a turnover in 2007 of $88m, and employed 3,200 people.

Him Lam's CEO is determined to move Phuong Nam back to being a top seafood factory in Vietnam, and to focus on the US market, like in the past

On the farming side, Phuong Nam did have production sites in Soc Trang, which even a few years ago were advanced, this source said. He believed these may have been around 200 or 300ha at that time, but after the bankruptcy the company stopped farming – something its general manager told Undercurrent in 2014.

It seems that under the new banking ownership Phuong Nam is planning to restart its farming, on larger and more technologically advanced sites.

“In our last meeting with them, Phuong Nam was talking about the indoor farming that it already started this year. By 2016, they may reach 200ha, and expand to 1,000ha in 2020,” he said.

“They are very positive on this ambitious plan, and all is under tight controls by the bank. By 2016, there will be 200 indoor farms for black tiger and vannamei; by 2020 they expected to reach 1,000 farms; but this all in the planning stages.”

Through more modern technology the firm hopes to be able to harvest seven shrimp crops per year, he believes. “The factory aims very big; they also want to liaise with US customer to back up the project.”

The source also believes Phuong Nam intends to buy a second plant, which can handle 5,000 metric tons of raw material per year after a refit.

The company's management did not respond to requests for further comment on the topics of the scam or the firm's recovery.

25 bankers jailed; still more take over

In the first week of August, 2015, 25 bank executives were handed jail terms of between two and seven years for their parts in illegally lending to Phuong Nam, reports Thanh Nien News.

They were convicted of “violating loan regulations at credit organizations” while working at the Soc Trang, Bac Lieu, and Hau Giang province branches of LienVietPostBank, Vietnam Development Bank (VDB), Sacombank, Vietcombank, and An Binh Bank.

They had orchestrated a loan scam to give Phuong Nam nearly VND 800bn. The Soc Trang People’s Court also sentenced Phuong Nam deputy director Trinh Hong Phuong to 12 years, and chief accountant Lam Minh Man to 14 years, for fraud.

They were ordered to pay the bank a total of VND 392m, and the court ordered the confiscation and sale of the company’s properties and stocks to compensate the five banks to the tune of VND 40bn.

According to the indictment, between 2008 and 2010, Phuong Nam chairman Khuan instructed his subordinates to forge documents to attest to the company's solvency to secure loans worth trillions of dong from the five banks.

The company had actually been loss-making every year until 2012, when Khuan moved to the US with his family.

As of August 2015 -- click to enlarge

Now Phuong Nam is owned by the banks to which it owes money; Undercurrent's source believes Lien Viet Bank might have plans to take over all the debts, and take sole ownership. Indeed, in the shrimp firm's latest brochure it lists Lien Viet Bank as the sole creditor.

Lien Viet's CEO is also CEO of Vietnam's second-largest property and real estate firm, Him Lam Corporation. Him Lam is listed by Phuong Nam as its investor. “Him Lam's CEO is determined to move the company back to being a top seafood factory in Vietnam, and to focus on the US market, like in the past.”

Even in 2012 Phuong Nam was swapping its debts to banks for equity, Thanh Nien News reports. This was when Khuan left the firm in the lurch; new owners Agribank Soc Trang brought in Tran Van Tri, CEO of Tri Viet International Investment Corp., as the CEO of Phuong Nam.

Tri Viet Corp. had experience in the field of rescuing seafood companies, after restructuring Vietnamese pangasius firm Bianfishco. Tri himself had been CEO here, only stepping down after the firm reported an improvement in its debt situation.

In September 2013 Phuong Nam settled its debts and began selling to international clients once more. Tri told local news the clients were the same ones who had bought from them previously, returning after hearing the good news.

title: Thai court indicts migrants’ rights activist Andy Hall
content:
A court in Thailand indicted a prominent human rights activist, very active in the country's seafood sector, in a defamation case brought by a pineapple processing company on Aug. 24.

The Bangkok South Criminal Court indicted migrants' rights researcher and human rights defender Andy Hall in a criminal defamation and computer crimes act case filed against him by a pineapple processing company, Natural Fruit Company.

Hall (pictured), a prominent campaigner for human rights in workers in Thailand's seafood processing sector, has been ordered to appear to plead on Oct. 19, where he will plead not guilty on Oct. 19, he told Undercurrent News. He will then face detention, official charging and can request bail.

"The Bangkok South Criminal Court had an opportunity to put an end to a saga of intimidation already lasting 30-months aimed at nothing but gagging a human rights defender. Regrettably the Court chose instead to press on with a trial of these unfounded charges," said Sonja Vartiala, executive director of Finnwatch, an NGO Hall has worked with on reports on labor practices in Thai food and seafood processors.

Natural Fruit has filed altogether four cases against Hall following the publication and dissemination of a Finnwatch report "Cheap Has a High Price" in early 2013.

The report, which Hall contributed research to, was based on information gathered through interviews with the workers of a Natural Fruit pineapple processing factory and exposed labor rights violations at the plant.

Natural Fruit did not comment on the research findings prior to the publication of the report, although given ample opportunity to do so, states a press release from Finnwatch.

The criminal defamation and computer crimes act case, to which today's decision to indict relates to, is the most severe of all the cases filed against Hall, and carries a maximum penalty of seven years imprisonment.

"To equate someone's reputation with another person's liberty is always disproportionate. Thailand should abolish its criminal defamation laws as they infringe on freedom of expression," said Vartiala.

At this point, the prospects for Hall to receive a fair trial are looking grim, she said.

Of the other three cases, one is for criminal defamation and the other two are civil defamation cases where damages of THB 400 million are being claimed by Natural Fruit.

Prakanong Court heard the first criminal defamation case already in 2014.

"The hearings were marred with the prosecution’s failure to make full disclosure to the defense of all evidence available to them, Thai authorities' failure to provide critically important information to the defense when requested and witness intimidation among other issues. Subsequently, the Prakanong Court dismissed the charges," Finnwatch states, in the press release.

The office of the attorney general has appealed the decision, urging the case to be reopened. A decision on this appeal is expected on Sept. 25, 2015.

The hearings for the civil defamation cases have not been scheduled yet. To date, no one has been held accountable for the labor rights violations at the Natural Fruit pineapple processing plant, states Finnwatch.

In July, Thailand was kept on Tier 3 in the latest US Trafficking in Persons (TIP) report. Thailand was downgraded to Tier 3 on the 2014 TIP report, partly because of labor abuses in its seafood sector.

title: ‘Wicked Tuna’ star pleads not guilty to fraud charges
content:
A fisherman featured on the National Geographic channel reality show ‘Wicked Tuna’ has pleaded not guilty to charges stemming from allegations that he claimed over $44,000 in government disability benefits despite being able to work, television station WCVB reported.

Paul Hebert, a Gloucester fisherman, was seen on the show harpooning large fish and manning big fishing rods, prosecutors said. They alleged that during the period he was filmed, he simultaneaously claimed he couldn’t work, lacked an income and did not possess other assets. Those claims were false, prosecutors said.

If convicted on the fraud-related charges, Hebert could receive a five-year prison term and a fine of up to $250,000 for each count on the four-count indictment.

title: Star of ‘Wicked Tuna’ TV show indicted on federal fraud charges
content:
A star of US television's 'Wicked Tuna' show has been indicted on federal fraud charges, reports Fox News.

The indictment says Paul Hebert claimed to be disabled and unable to work while he was catching fish and appearing on the National Geographic Channel reality show.

The four-count indictment against the 50-year-old from Gloucester, Massachusetts, alleges that Hebert accepted a little more than $44,000 in Social Security and Medicaid benefits between 2010 and 2013.

The indictment says that while claiming disability, Hebert was "capable of arduous physical labor." Beginning in October 2010, it said, "he earned money through fishing and later through his television work."

title: Silver Bay, Copper River leave MSC hopefuls out in cold
content:
The Alaska Seafood Processors Association (ASPA) is leaving major Alaska salmon processors without easy access to the suddenly hard-sought Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) approval this summer.

“We do not believe it [the group attempting to re-join] is presently consistent with the ASPA’s above stated purpose to admit your group into the client group, ” ASPA leader Rob Zuanich wrote in a letter sent to Trident Seafoods government relations and sustainability director Stefanie Moreland on Tuesday, having already stated the ASPA’s purpose is to promote the interests of those who have demonstrated a commitment to maintain MSC certification.

The ASPA -- including Silver Bay and Copper River among its large-scale members -- is willing to re-visit the discussion in September,  Zuanich said in the letter seen by Undercurrent, but at this point, "We note that the 2015 season is now upon us, and we have our businesses to run.”

The Trident-led group attempting to re-join includes Peter Pan Seafoods, Icicle Seafoods, Ocean Beauty Seafoods, North Pacific Seafoods, Alaska General and Leader Creek Fisheries. On May 8, the group offered to pay the full cost of the assessment incurred by the current and previous client groups to date.

Under MSC rules, these companies can opt to form their own client group instead of waiting to resume discussions -- an option unlikely to enable them to carry the MSC eco-label for product caught during the 2015 salmon season, which kicks off with the Copper River opener on Thursday with Copper River Seafoods set to be the only MSC certified company on the water.

The MSC requires new client groups to complete their own fisheries assessments. Although these are shorter for already-certified fisheries such as Alaska salmon, the minimum time they take is three to four months, according to the MSC.

The seven page letter, available here,  was largely a damning indictment of large processors' actions since their exodus from the MSC program in January of 2012, when processors representing 80% of the Alaska salmon supply left the program. It chronicles years of MSC-bashing from major processors and the Alaska Seafood Marketing Institute (ASMI).

The letter concludes: "We see a group of large processors who attempted to destroy the MSC certification of Alaska salmon through almost any means possible. We also see that when this group of larger processors were members of past MSC salmon client groups they gave no consideration to the views of the smaller processors or Alaska's salmon fishermen."

Among the ASPA's specific grievances is the way the re-join attempt was made – through an email with a deadline rather than a request to discuss the situation face to face, the ASPA said.

Trident did not immediately respond to request for comment from Undercurrent on the manner it engaged with the ASPA on its request in mid-April, when the company told Undercurrent it was in talks to rejoin the client group.

The ASPA says it does not necessarily think the processors forming their own client group is the preferred approach.

It was more explicit on its stance on the history of the Alaska salmon MSC status than the future in its letter.

It alleges signs of opposition to the program from the Alaska industry that did not remain involved in the MSC, including processors reaffirmation of their withdrawal from the MSC in a letter sent out by the Alaska Seafood Marketing Institute in 2012, which cited “confusion in the marketplace” caused by the MSC brand.

The ASPA notes that Alaska salmon processors have had other opportunities to re-join, including the invitation by the Purse Seine Vessel Owners Association (PSVOA) in 2012 inviting every Alaska salmon processor to rejoin.

“Regrettably, the PSVOA decision to move forward did not lessen determination by your clients and others to stop any further MSC certification,” the ASPA said.

It closes the letter with a note to major processors that there are other certifications companies can seek.

title: Norway Royal Salmon Q1 harvest up 38% as lower prices, higher costs hit earnings
content:
Norway Royal Salmon (NRS) harvested 38% more volume in the first quarter of 2015, but lower prices and higher production costs hit the company's earnings for the period.

The salmon farmer's operational ebit (earnings before interest and tax) saw a decrease of NOK 17.8 million ($1.4m) or 20.4% to 69.3m in Q1, year-on-year.

Its farming business harvested a total of 7,514 metric tons gutted weight in the quarter, compared to 5,435t in the same period last year. This is 900t higher than previous estimations, due to "good growth" and "accelerated harvesting" caused by biological challenges in the quarter, NRS said.

Including allocated margins from sales, the division achieved an operational ebit per kg of NOK 10.31, down from NOK 17.04/kg in Q1 2014.

Reduced price achievement in region north affected the result from the company's farming business in Q1, but also higher production costs.

"Due to a previous ISA outbreak in region north, causing higher mortality and low average harvesting weights, as well as accelerated harvesting at one site due to winter wounds, operational costs in the region were they had 84% of their volumes this quarter increased," said Nordea senior seafood analyst Kolbjorn Giskeodegard.

NRS, however, posted 9% higher operating revenues to NOK 760.1m, on the back of an increase of sold volumes to 16,959 metric tons, up 21% year-on-year.

"The growth in sold volumes [...] was driven by a growth of more than 40% in the Asian market," NRS said.

Asia accounted for 20% of the export volumes from NRS in the first quarter, while the share of exported volume to Western Europe ha increased to 70%. The share to Eastern Europe was 8% and North America 2%, the company said.

The sales business achieved a record high operational ebit of NOK 12.4m in the first quarter, the company said.

High supply growth and the loss of the Russian market, though, put salmon prices under pressure.

The spot price (NASDAQ) for superior quality during the quarter was NOK 40.79 per kg gutted weight, an increase of 4% from the fourth quarter of 2014 and a decrease of 14% year-on-year, NRS noted.

For 2015, the company projects a global supply growth ranging from 1% to 5%, while in the longer term global growth is expected to be low.

"This provides the basis for a positive market outlook for both 2015 and in the long term for the industry," the company said.

Production growth up 40% on green licenses

NRS is forecasting an increase in harvest of 43% for 2015, to 32,000t year-on-year.

Owing to the 10 new licenses awarded in 2014, the company can potentially have a capacity growth of 40%, it said.

Increased volumes to 45,000t on the back of added green licenses will be running in late 2017, Nordea noted.

"A large part of the production of the group is based on green criteria, which gives a more sustainable production, as well as strengthens the group's position in region north further. We are working with full force to implement this growth," said Charles Hostlund, NRS CEO.

title: Maine man fined in cross-border pesticide case
content:
A judge on Monday ordered Maine store owner Clyde Eldridge to pay a $5,000 fine and serve a year on probation for lying to US investigators about sales of pesticides to Cooke Aquaculture subsidiary Kelly Cove Salmon, reports CBC News.

The maximum penalty for this offense is five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, the newspaper said.

Assistant US attorney Jim Moore told the newspaper Eldridge received a more lenient fine due to his decision to wave his indictment and plead guilty.

The case involved a toxic chemical known as cypermethrin can kill sea lice, which also kills crustaceans. Environment Canada was notified tests revealed the presence of the chemical in late 2009, when fishermen discovered dead lobster traps off Grand Manan and Deer Island, the newspaper said.

Moore told the newspaper Eldridge initially lied, telling investigators he sold the chemical to different people over time but did not keep detailed records; but later it was revealed all 10 or 11 transactions of he product went to a product manager of Kelly Cove Salmon, the newspaper said.

Cooke Aquaculture spokesperson Nell Halse told the newspaper steps have been taken to ensure "this situation would never happen again."

Eldridge expressed remorse to the newspaper on Tuesday. "It was a mistake on my part, we all make mistakes, and this is one that I made," he said.

title: Norway salmon farmers’ Q4s confirm sea lice as key driver in 2015 supply
content:
Salmon supply – and so prices, margins and capital expenditure capabilities – boil down to the biological management of Norway's farmers in 2015.

This time last year, at the North Atlantic Seafood Forum in Bergen, Norway, CEOs pointed to sea lice as the single biggest issue facing the salmon farming industry, and that has been borne out through 2014.

A year on, speaking at Marel's salmon ShowHow in Copenhagen, February 2015, Rabobank analyst Gorjan Nikolik suggested sea lice management will continue to define the global salmon picture this year.

It will dictate supply growth, which in turn will dictate prices; presently a supply growth of 3.7% is expected for 2015, just behind demand, he said.

After a year of strong growth in Chilean salmon supplies – an estimated 24%, three or four times greater than analysts predicted – it is Norway that is back in control when it comes to supply growth in 2015, with Chile once more constrained by its own biological situation.

Still, in Norway, capacity growth is hard to come by. Maximizing existing MAB (maximum allowed biomass) levels will involve managing all sanitary conditions, including pancreas disease (PD) and amoebic gill disease (AGD), which affect feeding and so lower harvest weights.

Currently the main factor in possibly growing salmon volumes in Norway is the awarding of 'green licenses' – which, by definition, will depend on the farms' ability to control sanitary conditions.

A second option on the table is the chance to buy a 5% expansion to any existing license but, like the green license, this comes with strict biological criteria: at a cost of NOK 1.5 million for the expansion, the farmer must also keep sea lice levels at under 0.1 lice per fish.

Early in 2015 Marius Gaard, author of Mysalmon.no, analyzed sea lice levels over 2014 in Norway. Data show average sea lice levels in 2014, measured by adult female sea lice per salmon, was just over 0.2.

In 2013 a low level of 0.15 was achieved, while 2010 and 2011 were tough years, at over 0.3. This shows that maintaining a level of below 0.1 sea lice per fish is likely to be tricky, especially in the south of Norway where sea temperatures tend to be warmer.

His recent article for Undercurrent News shows the sea lice number breakdown in greater detail, by region.

$40m on combating sea lice

The fourth quarter results of Norway's salmon farmers have shown that sea lice and sanitary conditions were, and are, a chief concern when it comes to supply.

At the NASF a year ago, Marine Harvest CEO Alf Helge Aarskog joked, “whoever solves sea lice, come and see me, because we need help”. In its Q4 report it noted higher sea levels in western Norway, Scotland and Chile than a year previously.

It also detailed what it spent on sea lice mitigation, as a group, in 2014. This was NOK 53m in Q1, NOK 80m in Q2, NOK 74m in Q3 and NOK 96m in Q4, for a year total of NOK 303m, or $40m.

“The future biological development in Norway is to a large extent in the hands of the politicians,” the company said in its Q4 report. “A modest and sustainable increase in capacity going forward is a prerequisite for improving control of issues such as sea lice, pancreas disease and amoebic gill disease.”

"The cost of medication per kg harvested was 70% higher in the fourth quarter of 2014 than in the corresponding period in 2013"

Extensive stocking of cleaner fish (wrasse) has been carried out in Norway by the farmer, and it continues to test non-medicinal tools and approaches in collaboration between its Global R&D and Technical and the operating units in Chile, Norway and Scotland.

Overall Marine Harvest saw an operational ebit margin (earnings before interest and taxes) of NOK 9.2 per kg. It noted NOK 199m total in exceptional items relating to sea lice mitigation and extraordinary mortality.

“As in previous periods, sea lice mitigation costs have been high for the harvested generation. The higher sea temperatures have resulted in a challenging sea lice situation (more treatments and significant treatment losses),” the firm said of its Norwegian operations.

“The cost of medication per kg harvested was 70% higher in the fourth quarter of 2014 than in the corresponding period in 2013, while the estimated exceptional cost related to sea lice mitigation amounted to NOK 117m (versus NOK 62m ). Quarterly and year to date exceptional sea lice mitigation costs were NOK 1.67 and NOK 1.38 per kg harvested respectively (NOK 0.90 and NOK 0.70 respectively).”

All in the same pest-ridden boat

Most of Norway's largest salmon farmers reported similar stories in their Q4s.

Salmar reported “a challenging situation with respect to salmon lice and PD” in its central Norway region, though did add it had the situation under control in the fourth quarter.

“More frequent delousing of fish held at sea accumulates the salmon lice cost per kg, and this is expected to affect the overall cost picture in 2015,” it further added.

With an overall ebit per kg of NOK 12.21, its Rauma segment’s biological situation was especially difficult, with costs of delousing rising. PD too contributed to an ebit per kg of NOK 8.74 in this region.

Salmar is planning an open-ocean fish farming facility, which it hopes will be “highly escape-proof, and its design – along with its positioning in more exposed offshore locations – will lead to reduced levels of disease and salmon lice”.

Norway Royal Salmon noted its production cost for fish harvested in Q4 was NOK 4.86 per kg lower than in the third quarter. Despite this, it said, the production cost was still high as a result of costs associated with AGD and PD.

“Region South experienced good growth in the quarter. The fish health situation in the region is still demanding.” Its overall ebit per kg in Q4 was NOK 11.4.

NRS recently heard its subsidiary Nord Senja Laks had been indicted by the Norwegian government, over misreporting of sea lice numbers. As a result the government has reserved the right to take away the 'green licenses' awarded it in 2014.

The company is forecasting an increase in harvest of 43% for 2015, to 32,000t, driven by the awards of new green licenses. However, analysts with Nordea believe the firm holds the potential of becoming a 55,000t salmon farmer following the final nomination of the nine green licenses, combined with a 5% growth scenario in Finnmark.

Grieg's Q4 costs were up as a result of lice treatment, and mortality due to gill disease in Shetland, as well as fish that had been affected by PD in Norway's Rogaland region. Its ebit per kg came to NOK 8.8.

Compare all of these ebit per kg numbers to Faroe Islands-based Bakkafrost, which did not mention sea lice in its Q4 except to say its new wellboat (coming June 2015) would enable it to use freshwater treatment to fight the pests.

It achieved ebit per kg in Q4 of DKK 14.34 (NOK 16.4) – down from the previous quarter. The Faroes have tended not to suffer from sea lice as badly as Norway, either through a less intense stocking density or less propensity to have lice in the first place, with colder sea temperatures.

title: Norway Royal Salmon subsidiary indicted over sea lice misreporting
content:
The Norwegian government has reserved the right to take away the green licenses awarded to Norway Royal Salmon subsidiary Nord Senja Laks in 2014, after an indictment for misreporting sea lice occurrences.

Nord Senja Laks has by indictment dated Feb. 17, 2015 been charged for violating the rules on the reporting and handling of occurrences of sea lice, for giving wrongful information to the Norwegian Food Safety Authority (Mattilsynet) and with one account of omission of ensuring proper supervision and care when placing fish in waiting cages for harvesting.

The indictment concerns the company's aquaculture facility in Lenvik municipality in the period June 2012 to February 2013.

The indictment reserves the right to also request that the court confiscates dividend for saved costs by not implementing sea lice reducing measures, according to a notice to the Oslo stock exchange.

It also holds the power to remove the rights to exercise awarded green licenses to farm salmon, trout and rainbow trout of April 11, 2014, and the right to exercise co-localization of green licenses belonging to NRS Feoy of Dec. 17 2014. Nord Senja Laks was in 2014 awarded two green licenses.

Norway Royal Salmon owns 66.67% of the shares in Nord Senja Laks.

“Nord Senja Laks has only received the indictment, but we will acquire an overview of the case which covers the period June 2012 - February '13,” said Charles Hostlund, CEO of Norway Royal Salmon.

“The company does not have any further information and has therefore no possibility to have any considerations about this issue. Regardless of the outcome of this case, we regard it as very serious that such charges are brought against one of our subsidiaries. We await further handling of the case.”

title: Casson Trenor leaves Greenpeace
content:
Casson Trenor left his post at Greenpeace as seafood campaign leader on Friday after five and a half years with the NGO.

"I'm taking a month or so to myself to spend the holidays with family. After that, I haven't decided yet. There are a lot of opportunities," Trenor told Undercurrent News.

Trenor plans to stay in the ocean conservation field but said he is open to possibilities inside or outside the world of NGOs, and left the question on his plans somewhat open ended.

"I'm more interested in the specifics of any position than its category, so no promises either way," he said.

The timing is right, as one of Trenor's many side projects expands. As co-owner of San Francisco sustainable sushi chain Tataki, Trenor is planning to open another sustainable sushi restaurant with his partners soon. Called Shizen, it adds a fourth restaurant to Trenor's collection, which include Tataki, Tataki South and Tataki Canyon.

Yet Trenor said his move from Greenpeace would have happened with or without its opening.

Trenor is also author of the book Sustainable Sushi and described by Wikipedia as "an American environmentalist, social activist author, restaurateur, blogger and media personality."

He has held a number of hats at Greenpeace, having switched to his current role a year ago from his former title of seafood team leader. Prior to Greenpeace, he worked for Fishwise.

Although Greenpeace is most known for taking a hard-line stance against even small sustainability violations, Trenor came out in industry's defense in May of 2013, when he told Huffington Post blogger and Trader Joe's critic Evelyn Iritani that the company was making “tremendous progress” toward saving the oceans.

Yet Trenor's main role of campaigning for ocean conservation inevitably involved industry criticism throughout the years. In the case of the Tuna 2014 conference in Bangkok, Thailand in May, Trenor said tuna regional fisheries management organizations were not doing their part to protect tuna.

It remains to be seen whether Trenor's next venture incites the level of industry criticism that Greenpeace has. Most recently, even the Marine Stewardship Council joined the National Marine Fisheries Service in criticizing its indictment on the seafood industry, its "Carting Away the Oceans" report.

title: New book claims to expose modern slavery in New Zealand waters
content:
New book tells story of abuse and modern slavery on boats fishing for New Zealand quota, publisher Awa Press said in a press release.

"The Catch", a book to be released in August, is set to present "a powerful indictment of conditions endured by crew on foreign charter vessels fishing in New Zealand waters", and examines "the destructive practices threatening many of the world’s fisheries", according to the publishing house.

The author, Michael Field, is a senior journalist for The Sunday Star-Times and a Radio New Zealand Pacific affairs correspondent.

He says he first became interested in the fishing industry in 2008 when a Taiwanese boat, Tai Ching 21, was found near Kiribati with no one on board and lifeboat and life-rafts missing. None of its 29 men -- Chinese, Indonesian and Filipino crew and Taiwanese officers -- has ever been found.

Field’s search for the men’s identities led him into "a dark world of foreign-flagged vessels fishing as far south as ice-bound Antarctica".

In "The Catch" he said he reveals what he discovered: "Horrifying examples of modern slavery in which men from poor countries are trapped on filthy, unsafe ships, treated brutally by captains and officers, and receive little or no pay; and fishing practices that are wasteful, environmentally damaging, and often illegal."

Since the introduction of the quota management system in 1986, some of New Zealand’s largest fishing companies have increasingly used foreign charter vessels to fish for their quota.

Field claims irresponsible fishing practices of such vessels are not only endangering crews but stripping the world’s seas and threatening the food supply of people everywhere, propelling us towards one of the environmental tragedies of our times.

Field’s revelations have been backed by independent studies from researchers at the University of Auckland Business School, and by foreign journalists and organizations, said Awa Press.

The publicity led to a 2013 ministerial inquiry and a bill, currently before Parliament, that would require fishing vessels to be flagged to New Zealand.

title: NFI: TIP report not an indictment of entire industry
content:
National Fisheries Institute (NFI) president John Connelly is asking consumers to see Thailand's downgrade, released today, as 'a snap shot of challenges that need ongoing Thai government attention'.

Connelly sent his public response to Thailand's downgrade to Tier 3 on the US Department of State's Trafficking in Persons (TIP) report just minutes after it came out on Friday, demonstrating the extremely close watch the industry has on this issue. NFI previously said a boycott of the Thai shrimp industry would be counterproductive, as it would undercut efforts by buyers to drive change in their supply chains.

Here is Connelly's letter in full:

Unfair and illegal labor practices are abhorrent, and NFI members distinguish themselves through their commitment and actions to eradicate them.

Most NFI members have required rigorous third-party audits of their supply chain in order to ensure it is free of labor abuses. In fact, NFI itself has conducted the only comprehensive analysis of the leading global social responsibility standards in order to assist our members in finding the most thorough and credible labor systems.

The TIP report illustrates that there is a need for increased and sustained prosecution of trafficking violators worldwide. That understanding is a core component of NFI members’ ongoing communications to foreign governments, law enforcement and regulators.

Consumers should not misunderstand today’s report as an indictment of the entire industry but rather as a snap shot of challenges that need ongoing Thai government attention.

NFI members have also directed NFI to work with organizations providing credible information regarding labor abuse at specific plants or organizations.  NFI stands ready to assist in investigations of such allegations.

NFI recognizes and appreciates Thailand’s renewed focus on stamping out labor challenges in the seafood sector. NFI members continue to work with committed suppliers and partners there, to lead the way in not only pushing for change but providing products that are produced through safe, fair, ethical labor practices.

John Connelly

President, National Fisheries Institute
