title: Marubeni guilty plea came from scheme to pay bribes to Indonesian officials
content:
Marubeni's guilty plea to violating the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) and the $88 million fine attached to it, made public last week, came as a result of its participation in a scheme to pay bribes to government officials in Indonesia, the Justice Department said in a release.

“Marubeni pleaded guilty to engaging in a seven-year scheme to pay – and conceal – bribes to a high-ranking member of Parliament and other foreign officials in Indonesia,” said acting assistant attorney General Raman. “The company refused to play by the rules, then refused to cooperate with the government’s investigation. Now Marubeni faces the consequences for its crooked business practices in Indonesia .”

As part of the plea agreement, Marubeni has agreed to maintain and implement an enhanced global anti-corruption compliance program and to cooperate with the department’s ongoing investigation.

Acting U.S. attorney Michael J. Gustafson added that the company worked with a Connecticut company and others to bribe Indonesian officials in order to secure a contract to provide power-related services in Indonesia.

The plea "is an important reminder to the business community of the significant consequences of participating in schemes to bribe government officials, whether at home or abroad," Gustafson said.

The guilty plea included one count of conspiracy to violate the anti-bribery provisions of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) and seven counts of violating the FCPA.

The FBI is working with its international law enforcement partners to ensure that companies are held accountable for their criminal conduct, said assistant director in charge Valeria Parlave.

The plea agreement cites Marubeni’s decision not to cooperate with the department’s investigation when given the opportunity to do so, its lack of an effective compliance and ethics program at the time of the offense, its failure to properly remediate and the lack of its voluntary disclosure of the conduct as some of the factors considered by the department in reaching an appropriate resolution.

Frederic Pierucci, who was the vice president of global boiler sales at Marubeni’s consortium partner, pleaded guilty on July 29 of last year to one count of conspiring to violate the FCPA and one count of violating the FCPA. David Rothschild, a former vice president of regional sales at the consortium partner, pleaded guilty on Nov. 2 of 2012 to one count of conspiracy to violate the FCPA. Lawrence Hoskins, a former senior vice president for the Asia region for the consortium partner, and William Pomponi, a former vice president of regional sales at the consortium partner, were charged in a second superseding indictment on July 30 of last year. The charges against Hoskins and Pomponi are merely allegations, and the defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty.

According to court filings, Marubeni and its employees, together with others, paid bribes to officials in Indonesia – including a high-ranking member of the Indonesian Parliament and high-ranking members of Perusahaan Listrik Negara (PLN), the state-owned and state-controlled electricity company in Indonesia – in exchange for assistance in securing a $118 million contract, known as the Tarahan project, for Marubeni and its consortium partner to provide power-related services for the citizens of Indonesia.

To conceal the bribes, Marubeni and its consortium partner retained two consultants purportedly to provide legitimate consulting services on behalf of the power company and its subsidiaries in connection with the Tarahan project. The primary purpose for hiring the consultants, however, was to use the consultants to pay bribes to Indonesian officials.

As admitted in court documents, Marubeni and its co-conspirators retained the first consultant in the fall of 2002. However, in the fall of 2003, before the Tarahan contract had been awarded, Marubeni and its co-conspirators determined that the first consultant was not bribing key officials at PLN effectively.

One e-mail between employees of the power company’s subsidiary in Indonesia described a meeting between Marubeni employees, employees of its consortium partner, and PLN officials during which the PLN officials expressed “concern” that if Marubeni and its consortium partner win the project, whether the agent would give the officials “rewards” that they would consider “satisfactory,” or “only give them pocket money and disappear. Nothing has been shown by the agent that the agent is willing to spend money.”

Shortly thereafter, a Marubeni employee sent an e-mail to other employees at Marubeni and its consortium partner stating that “unfortunately our agent almost did not execute his function at all, so far. In case we don’t take immediate action now now [sic], we don’t have any chance to get this project forever.”

As a result, Marubeni and its consortium partner decided to reduce the first consultant’s commission from 3% of the total contract value to 1% and pay the remaining 2% to a second consultant who could more effectively bribe officials at PLN. In an e-mail between two employees of Marubeni’s consortium partner, they discussed a meeting between Marubeni, an executive from the consortium partner, and the first consultant, stating that the first consultant “committed to convince [the member of Parliament] that ‘one’ [percent] is enough.”

Marubeni and its co-conspirators were successful in securing the Tarahan project and subsequently made payments to the consultants for the purpose of bribing the Indonesian officials. They paid hundreds of thousands of dollars into the first consultant’s bank account in Maryland to be used to bribe the member of Parliament. The consultant then allegedly transferred the bribe money to a bank account in Indonesia for the benefit of the official.

FBI agents from the Washington Field Office regional FBI as well as the Criminal Division’s Office of International Affairs. It also received support from law enforcement colleagues in Indonesia at the Komisi Pemberantasan Korupsi (Corruption Eradication Commission), the Office of the Attorney General in Switzerland and the Serious Fraud Office in the United Kingdom.

Assistant chief Daniel Kahn, of the Criminal Division’s fraud section, and assistant U.S. attorney David E. Novick of the District of Connecticut, are prosecuting the case.

title: Untitled
content:
The current CEO of US scallop supplier Mar-Lees Seafood is cited in legal documents as being involved in deals in which seafood was allegedly sold to the company at inflated prices, before Mar-Lees bought his company and he became CEO.

Ziad ‘Zeke’ Shahin and his former company TAF Enterprises -- which was acquired by Mar-Lees with Shahin taking over as CEO in early 2013 -- are named as being involved in alleged “kickback” deals, in a document accusing the company’s co-founder and former CEO John Lees and others of fraud and racketeering.

Shahin, who was indicted for a fraud himself in 2001, could not be reached for comment to Undercurrent News.

In 2001, Shahin “fraudulently transferred an annuity investment from the Great American Life Insurance Company on behalf of the victim to a fish company for his own personal benefit”, according to public documents from the Essex Superior Court.

He is not, however, one of the accused in the Mar-Lees case and the document does not make any allegations of wrongdoing against him, or TAF. Undercurrent understands he is still CEO of the company, as listed on Mar-Lees’ website.

TAF and Shahin, however, are cited as being involved in the transactions in which the owner of 80% of Mar-Lees, listed in the legal document as Seafood Development Partners, allege were one of several frauds committed by Lees and others.

Lees “used his insider executive position at Mar-Lees to carry out a series of fraudulent schemes via which Lees obtained kickbacks” and other companies, such as TAF, made additional profits, allege the document from Seafood Development Partners, believed to ultimately be controlled by Julius Numavicius, a businessman from one of the wealthiest families in Lithuania.

Each of these kickback schemes consisted of a basic pattern, the document claims.

“Lees would purchase, using his own funds, a large volume of tilapia fish, which would be held in storage. The tilapia would be held in the name of Blue Sea or another straw [company], rather than of Lees.”

After approximately a month, Shahin’s company TAF would purchase the tilapia from the straw entity at a price higher than paid originally by Lees, the document claims.

“Lees would receive a pre-arranged approximate 8% kickback built into the higher price paid by TAF; and TAF would then sell the tilapia to Mar-Lees at an additional markup, funding both the kickback to Lees and the additional profits to Blue Sea [Products, a company listed as a defendant] and TAF,” it states.

In a deal described on Dec. 22, 2011, Lees allegedly bought 20,000 cases of tilapia from TAF, and held the fish in the name of Blue Sea, owned by Thomas Jacob, also a defendant.

“Lees sent an email to Shahin at TAF and Jacob at Blue Sea informing them as to how the transaction would work, stating: “[a]s I mentioned, I will be running this thru [sic] Bluesea Products.... He will be the customer of record on this transaction,” alleges the document.

Lees then personally wired $1.02 million for the purchase, alleges the document, but the tilapia was held in the name of “Global Sourcing Alliance Inc. c/o Blue Sea Products LLC”.

On Dec. 22, 2011, Jacob sent an email to Lees attaching an executed “purchase order contract” for $1.02m worth of tilapia.

The purchase order specified that “Global Sourcing Alliance Inc. is acting purely as custodian on behalf of John A. Lees in this transaction”.

The terms of the purchase were that TAF would pay Lees back $1.10m by Jan. 31, 2012, and Lees would return the tilapia to TAF, it states.

Lees, Jacob, Blue Sea, and TAF completed the transactions as described, according to the document.

Lees received $80,000, the difference between $1,10m and $1.02m, as a kickback, alleges the document. “On information and belief, TAF then sold the 20,000 cases of tilapia to Mar-Lees at a price high enough to cover the kickback and generate a profit for Blue Sea and Jacob.”

Lees recommended and approved the transaction in his capacity as co-chief executive officer, it states.

Similar transactions took place in January 2012, with 10,000 cases of tilapia; and in March 2012, with 20,000 cases, again.

“In each transaction, Mar-Lees could have directly purchased the  seafood products at the original, lower price, rather than the later inflated price at which Lees arranged for Mar-Lees to purchase the products,” the document alleges.

The company was “deceived into purchasing the seafood products at an artificially increased price”, it states.

Shahin is also mentioned in the document as being involved, before selling TAF to Mar-Lees and becoming CEO, in an alleged attempt from Lees to compete with Mar-Lees using a new entity, called ZJM.

In the spring of 2012, the document claims, Lees introduced Shahin and his company TAF to the owners of Mar-Lees, representing that Lees knew Shahin from the industry and thought he would make a good CEO.

In approximately May or June of 2012, Lees met with Shahin and the owner of 80% of Mar-Lees, believed to be Lithuanian businessman Julius Numavicius, in Boston to discuss the possibility of hiring Shahin as an executive and acquiring TAF, claims the document.

At this time, Lees was serving as co-CEO of Mar-Lees under a consulting contract and was responsible for the company’s sales efforts, according to the filing.

“On May 16, 2012, Lees sent an email to Shahin, copying Sweeney, in which Lees provided extensive advice to Shahin as to how best to position himself and Lees with Mar-Lees’ owners and how Lees wanted Shahin to protect Lees’ position, including telling Shahin “I am counting on you to land this plane. Once they [New Mar-Lees owners] announce you then they are stuck to make this work”.”

In or about June and July of 2012, Mar-Lees was in discussions to purchase a seafood business, variously known as “Captain Carl’s” or “Carl’s Gourmet Foods,” from Carl Masiello.

According to the document, “in or about July 2012, Lees and Sweeney were simultaneously making plans with Shahin to set up yet another separate company to compete with Mar-Lees, including by acquiring Captain Carl’s”.

On July 14, 2012, Sweeney emailed Lees and Shahin about setting up “a new LLC to take over the Carl’s assets and existing business”.

“The email refers to the new company as “our new ‘clam’ venture” with equity to be split 25% for Carl [Masiello], 30% for Zeke [Shahin] 30% for John [Lees] and 15% for MFS [Michael F. Sweeney],” the document alleges.

“The July 14, 2012 email makes clear that Lees and Sweeney were planning to set up a company to acquire TAF or, if Mar-Lees acquired TAF, to do business as a separate entity and compete directly with Mar-Lees while hiding Lees involvement from plaintiffs,” it alleges.

On July 31, 2012, Sweeney allegedly sent an email to Lees, with a copy to Shahin, about promoting business for their new venture.

The same day, Lees responded in an email to Sweeney with a copy to Shahin, making  ”clear the plan to compete in the seafood business by selling to a major supermarket”, it is alleged in the document.

“Mike, once we open the new co then Zeke will get the new co set up at [a specific Mar-Lees customer prospect],” Lees is alleged to have written, in an email.

“The supermarket chain referenced in the email was one that Mar-Lees was actively seeking as a customer,” the document states.

Sweeney was “actively involved” in the business planning for the new ZJM venture both as counsel and as a principal, and in the efforts to have ZJM acquire the Captain Carl’s business, the document alleges.

The defendants’ “competitive plans for ZJM were ultimately foiled when Mar-Lees hired Shahin as Mar-Lees’ CEO and acquired Shahin’s and TAF’s customer lists and relationships, and hired Masiello and acquired Captain Carl’s”, the document states.

title: Major MSC clients demand formal apology on MSC video
content:
Commentary by John Sackton, Seafood News 

The biggest group of Marine Stewardship Council client fisheries have demanded that the MSC immediately remove a video attacking their fisheries from Youtube and from the Loblaws' Facebook page.

The video, by attacking trawl fishing, attacked 84% of the MSC's clients.

The group, Alaska Fisheries Development Foundation, sent the letter (pasted below) to MSC CEO Rupert Howes on Tuesday. A second group of Alaskan fisheries, represented by the Alaska Fisheries Development Foundation, also sent a letter to the MSC protesting the video.

The video has been removed from Youtube and from Loblaws' Facebook page.

This incident will further the anger that many in the Alaskan industry remaining MSC certified fisheries feel towards the dishonesty of the organization.

The MSC reacted with alarm to the video, produced and funded by Loblaws and WWF Canada, which attacks more than 80% of the suppliers of MSC fish.

The video shows just how bankrupt is the call for ‘MSC’ labels that also condemn trawl fisheries.

The video was first posted to Youtube on Sept. 10, and began to be noticed by the many MSC client fisheries that were attacked.  It is a professionally made video with 39 different people listed in the credits.  This video was not a ‘mistake’.

Many MSC clients have reacted with outrage, and that is why the MSC quickly pressured WWF Canada to take down the video.

But the video exposed a real truth: MSC governance procedures allow stakeholders with no scientific credentials or understanding to influence changes to the MSC standards.

This has happened over and over again with Greenpeace, SFP, WWF and other NGO’s. Often the NGO’s themselves don’t speak with a unified voice.

WWF, for example, has a fairly decentralized structure, and WWF Canada can do things that WWF International might not fully support. The MSC also has a problem with NGO’s using its logo to represent things that may be more than the MSC wants to make public.

But the issue behind this video won’t go away. The video makes the case that trawl fisheries should be banned. Yet over 80% of the tonnage of MSC certified fisheries - including those sold at Loblaws, comes from trawl fisheries.

Seafood.com News chart from lists of certified fisheries on MSC website. The trawl category includes both mid-water and bottom trawls.

The consequence of the lack of formal rules in MSC governance means that these ‘stakeholders’ who want to ban trawling -- which include portions of the WWF that is one of the primary sponsors of the MSC -- will be given a hearing regardless of the scientific merits of their case.

The MSC claims that the reason it is a superior standard is that it keeps raising the bar for sustainable fisheries. The 84% of MSC clients that are trawl fisheries should take careful note of this, and plan for a future where MSC stakeholders call to ban trawling.

Their alternative is to change to an FAO backed sustainability certification where the governance rules require that changes to standards be based on scientific analysis and evidence.

What is wrong with this video?

It gets backward the actual impacts of farming and fishing. Farming is not a undisturbed ecosystem, as depicted in the video. Most farmland comes from clear cutting forests, destroying the entire original ecosystem, and then replacing it with a monoculture that has far less species diversity and ecological richness.

By contrast, wild capture fisheries, although they do reduce the size of fish populations, leave ecosystems intact and maintain the historical mix of species. Obviously there are some areas with benthic ecosystems that cannot be trawled - coral reefs, and other fragile vertical benthic environments like kelp forests. But this is not where the industry trawls.

A recent example of this whole problem came up in Alaska with the Greenpeace campaign over the Bering Sea Canyons. It was supported by SFP which went so far as to threaten pollock producers that unless they adopted SFP’s approach to protecting the Bering Sea Canyons, SFP would ask their partners not to purchase pollock from this area.

The problem?

There is no scientific evidence that these habitats are different than any other habitat on the Alaskan continental slope, and after studying the issue, NOAA determined that the ‘canyons’ contained no special benthic habitat, and therefore the existing level of protection through the legal framework of Essential Fish Habitat would suffice for long term protection.

These MSC stakeholders -- such as SFP, WWF, and those who support this type of video -- will continue to escalate their demands to constrain trawling not with scientific arguments over specific issues, but with consumer scare tactics that imply the opposite of the truth.

There is no room for a sustainability standard that rejects science in this manner. That is the upsetting message in this video -- that those who proclaim themselves the guardians of sustainability actually are putting their own fundraising, gatekeeper, and ideological biases ahead of a scientific investigation of the facts.

The great contribution that the US Magnuson Act made to global fisheries management was to insist that fishery management decisions be based on sound science, and to provide a public framework for that to happen.

This video is an example of how WWF Canada, the MSC, the SFP, and other NGO’s are willing to undermine this essential principle in order to maintain their own influence and relevance in the global seafood industry.

Fifteen years from now, the MSC is likely to be a footnote, while the fisheries that sustain global food production will continue to be strong, their sustainability certified by a more objective and formal international benchmarking process.

Below is the letter from the Alaska Fisheries Development Foundation, followed by that from the ASF.

Letter to MSC from Alaska Clients:

Alaska Fisheries Development Foundation, the MSC client group for the BSAI and GOA Pacific Cod fisheries , is outraged at the video in the link below , which was apparently produced by the World Wildlife Fund (WWF).

We believe that the MSC owes AFDF and other MSC fishery clients an apology, as well as a full explanation of how the MSC logo was included in this video, and what action you are taking with WWF to ensure it never happens again. When WWF implemented its "Stinky Fish" campaign a few years ago, we were assured by MSC that WWF had hijacked the MSC logo for an unauthorized purpose . We were also told, by you personally , that it would not happen again.

Either MSC is party to this misguided and vindictive assault on certified gear groups, or you have allowed your logo to be used without your permission by WWF for a campaign that damages both certified and non-certified fisheries. We hope you will take whatever action is necessary to see that this video is withdrawn by WWF , and at the very least, you prohibit them from further using the MSC logo in this video. Finally, we strongly encourage you to publicly disavow any association with the video .

AFDF began work on MSC certification for the Alaskan P cod fishery in January 2006, and completed the certification in January 2010, after considerable expense. We signed up for the certification process because we wanted to feature the sustainability of our fishery management , as well as the four gear types that are used to harvest cod. This video shows a complete absence of knowledge of the fishery or the industry. It also shows some management issues on the part of MSC, particularly after the Stinky Fish and Scarlet Letter debacles.

This video comes at a time when all the groundfish fisheries in Alaska are looking at the cost/benefit ratio of MSC certification versus other sustainability certifications.

AFDF is one of the only two remaining fishery development foundations authorized by the Magnuson Act in 1976, and has been conducting fishery and seafood research , and product development for 36 years ..... and represents not only all of the participants in the Pacific cod fishery off the coast of Alaska , but a large cross section of participants in most U.S. ground fish fisheries off of Alaska. Thank you for your attention to this matter , we are awaiting your response.

All 13 Board members , representing primary processors, large and small, support sector companies and the fishing communities of Alask a agree that this is an assault on the industry .

James Browning Executive Director

Alaska Fisheries Development Foundation

 

Letter from ASF:

Dear Rupert Howes:
As you know, the Association of Sustainable Fisheries (ASF) represents Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certified and in assessment fisheries. Its members account for a significant percentage of the tonnage and value of fisheries in the MSC process.Our members are dismayed that MSC would lend its name to the silly, offensive video produced by WWF Canada for Loblaw. A VP of WWF Canada has told one of our members that it was a Loblaw initiative in partnership with WWF and MSC.

The problem should have been obvious to anyone in MSC. To consumers, it sends the message that only pole and line fisheries are acceptable while demonizing the mobile gear used by many of your certified fisheries. Meanwhile the farming analogy is just plain dishonest. As Ray Hilborn - and even Oceana’s Andy Sharpless - have pointed out farming does precisely what the video claims it doesn’t. It removes biodiversity on a grand scale in favour of crops and animals.

My own fishery, where costs for MSC certification of three BC salmon species have hit almost C$1 million, finds the video with its vaguely West Coast reference to salmon plain insulting since it implies that the purse seines used to catch the majority of that salmon are the equivalent of clear cutting rather than a selective, sustainable means to put food on the tables in Canada and around the world. Our other members are equally exasperated and angry.

We thought the MSC might have learnt something from the rather similar Stinky Fish fiasco. But apparently not.

We ask that you insist that Loblaw and WWF Canada remove the video from You Tube and the Loblaw Facebook page and that you, as the MSC CEO, disown such a tiresomely stupid exercise.

Yours sincerely,

Christina Burridge,

ASSOCIATION OF SUSTAINABLE FISHERIES

title: Damm wins Pescanova war by landslide at crucial shareholder meeting
content:
The sword-rattling of interest groups could be heard even hours before the 12:30 pm extraordinary shareholder meeting kicked off in Pontevedra, near Vigo, Spain, at Pescanova's headquarters this Thursday.

Presiding the assembly was an old hand of the company, Jose Maria Perez-Carasa, in what observers noted as an ominous sign for investors seeking a full turn of page.

After a few "painfully tense" hours, a new board line-up emerged from the clash between Pescanem, the Cartesian-led block, on the one hand and former board members Damm, Luxempart and Iberfomento on the other. With an initial control over 15.76% of the corporation's capital, the latter were the final winners of the encounter. Votes equivalent to 11.03 million shares, 70.82% of the participants in the meeting, conceded their support to the Catalan beer producer.

The success of the Damm-led bid means a seven-member board will be set up at Pescanova, replacing the current 11-member board. Juan Manuel Urgoiti, former independent director at Galicia-based Inditex and former president of Banco Gallego, will be appointed chairman at Pescanova. Urgoiti was the preferred candidate of the Damm camp, who insisted the new chairman should be independent.

With him on the board will be Jose Carceller of Damm, Francois Tesch of Luxempart, Fernando Harce Melendrez of Iberfomento (replacing Jose Antonio Perez-Nieva Heredero, who is being investigated for use of insider information), Yago Enrique Mendez, Luis Angel Sanchez and Alejandro Legarda Zaragueta.

In an exchange with Undercurrent News, commercial lawyer Nasif Hamed, who attended the shareholder meeting, described the atmosphere surrounding the assembly as "very troubled".

Unsurprisingly so, considering Pescanova will struggle to find a viable future under the weight of its many eye-watering figures: after half a century of history and having conquered a seat among Spain's most esteemed household staple meals, its chairman of 33 years Manuel Fernandez de Sousa-Faro stepped down in July leaving the company with its shares suspended, €3.67 billion of debt and a €1.67bn equity hole in a balance sheet still under investigation.

During 2011 and 2012, up to a staggering 80% of all sales were found to be linked to special purpose vehicles void of any economic content, according to findings by Pescanova's bankruptcy administrator, Deloitte.

But if Fernandez remains accused of fraud and hiding data from the official regulator of the Spanish financial markets CNMV, high court judge Pablo Ruz indicted earlier on Thursday morning Demetri Carceller, the president of the brewery Damm --which owns a 6.18% stake in Pescanova-- for his alleged involvement in his father's €72-million money-laundering scheme.

Can Pescanova really move on and shake the dirt off its shoulders? In Vigo, analyst Jose Beiras told Undercurrent that there's a "mighty reason why shareholders, creditor banks and the Spanish government should come together" to start afresh: the company's liquidation would imply value losses of 75% to 77%.

Fund manager Alberto Roldan pointed out in the aftermath of the vote that Damm's was "the most judicious option". But, he added: "A new management should not mean that all the fraud committed can be forgotten."

The Spanish association of minority shareholders Aemec supported the Cartesian fund, proprietor of a 5% stake, in a radical proposal to elect board directors one by one from an open list. But more than an hour into the meeting, no voting system had yet been agreed, and only a closed-list choice was offered later.

The Cartesian lobby intended to renew Pescanova's board in its entirety. Madrid-based attorney Javier Cremades said it was "a credible, professional and truly independent bid. Everything has failed in Pescanova, from auditors to the official watchdog, to the whole former board. There's future only if the next phase is one where transparency reigns."

The 613 shareholders who traveled to Galicia welcomed the confirmation that former chairman Fernandez was not putting forward his own candidacy, as it had been rumored during the previous weeks. Fernandez may have been the reason of Cartesian's failure, though, as he talked in his public intervention of "change of faces" in reference to the minority stockholders' bid.

Less than two hours after the assembly started, the confederation of businessmen in Galicia CEG sent participants a message appealing to their "intelligence and sense of responsibility". CEG said "positive thinking" is needed to "keep the company alive, and save its 11,000 jobs." And investors listened.

Auditor PriceWaterhouseCooper will publish its research on the company in October.

title: Capitaine Houat embezzled funds found in New Caledonia
content:
More than €200,000 in funds said to have been embezzled by Capitaine Houat's former financial director Stephane Ringot have been traced back to New Caledonia, reported Ouest France.

The funds were found in bank accounts belonging to an IT entrepreneur, who was arrested on Monday in New Caledonia. He has now been transferred to Lorient, western France, and indicted for complicity in fraud.

Ringot is accused of having embezzled €286,000 from Capitaine Houat, the fish processor which supplies almost exclusively the Intermarche supermarkets.

€66,000 of that amount had already been found, but until now, the remaining €220,000 were missing.

It is that amount that has now been found in New Caledonia, transferred across several company accounts and partly reinvested into properties.

Ringot has been indicted for fraud and was jailed on April 12.

title: Capitaine Houat ex-financial director indicted over fraud charges
content:
The former financial director of Intermarche's processing affiliate Capitaine Houat has been arrested over charges that he embezzled €286,000 from the company, reported Ouest France. 

Capitaine Houat noticed anomalies in its accounts earlier this year and fired Stephane Ringot in February for gross misconduct, said the newspaper.

Last week Ringot was imprisoned by police over charges of fraud, and is now being held in remand in prison, it said.

Based in Boulogne-sur-mer, western France, Capitaine Houat is France's largest fresh fish processor and supplies almost exclusively the supermarket chain Intermarche. It is part of the Mousquetaires group of companies that owns Intermarche.

Only three weeks ago, another former Capitaine Houat employee was arrested after admitting to having started the fire that decimated Capitaine Houat's factory and warehouse in Lorient in August 2011.

title: Sushi chefs await whale smuggling verdict
content:
Two sushi chefs in Santa Monica in the US have been charged by a federal grand jury for smuggling and selling protected whale meat, according to Santa Monica Patch.

Kiyoshiro Yamamoto, 48, of Culver City, Susumu Ueda, 39, of Lawndale, and Typhoon Restaurant, are accused of illegally importing and selling the meat of sei whales.

It is illegal to sell any kind of whale meat in the United States. Sei whales are protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act of 1972 and are listed as endangered in the Endangered Species Act of 1973.

Ueda's attorney, James Spertus, said his client was "behind a counter making sushi" and would have had "no idea where the meat came from", reports Santa Monica Patch.

"If you buy some oranges from the store, you do know where they came from," Spertus said. "Ralphs knows—you do not."

According to the indictment, the whale meat was ordered through a seafood dealer named Ginichi Ohira.

Yamamoto is charged with concealing the purchase of whale meat and the restaurant's source, and instructing other sushi chefs to do the same. Ueda is charged with lying to a federal agent about the source of the whale meat. Yamamoto could face a maximum sentence of 67 years in federal prison while Ueda could face a maximum of 10 years.

Sentencing will be announced in the next few weeks.

title: Hearing day for Russian pollock catchers
content:
The Russian pollock association and eight Far Eastern fishing companies are due to attend a hearing today over alleged cartel activities.

The hearing is held by the Federal Anti-Monopoly Service and will take place this Tuesday, Oct. 23.

The pollock association, which represents 45 fishing companies in the Russian Far East, has vehemently denied the charges and says the anti-trust agency has failed to specify how the association finds itself in breach of competition rules.

The documents received by the FSA include no details about the charges, said the association.

Another eight Far Eastern fishing companies are also facing charges in the same indictment.

title: Five accused of Trident Seafoods embezzlement
content:
Five people have been charged with embezzling almost half a million dollars from the Trident Seafoods plant in Kodiak, Alaska, in the US.

The financial discrepancies were discovered some time after bookkeeper Isa Wolfe was fired in 2010, reports Alaskan radio station KMXT.

“She’d been there a very long time, and actually was there years before the embezzlement started," said US Attorney Aunnie Steward.

"And when she was terminated the folks that came in to take over discovered that a lot of fraudulent accounting had been going on for quite some time," Steward is quoted as saying.

The US Attorney's office has accused Wolfe of using the company accounts to write 52 cheques to four friends, and the under-age son of one of them, between January 2008 and August 2010.

Jeremy Smith and Jamie Fathke of Kodiak, Anne Wilson of Kent, Washington, and Valerie Olivares of Corpus Christi, Texas, have also been indicted, with Wolfe and Smith having been taken into custody.

The maximum total sentence for each count of embezzlement is 20 years imprisonment, a fine of $250,000, or both, as well as repaying the amount embezzled, said Steward.

Under federal sentencing statutes, the sentence actually imposed will take into account the seriousness of the offences and any prior criminal convictions.

Anchorage federal court is expected to set court dates soon after the accused make their initial appearances for arraignment.

title: Norway’s male king crabs fetch higher prices in week 44, females fall
content:
In week 44 (Oct. 27-Nov. 2), Norwegian king crab prices diverged. Prices for all four sizes are provided below in NOK and USD.

Data from the Norges Rafisklag auction, also available on Undercurrent News' prices portal, shows a rise in live male crab prices, while female crab prices moved downward.

Weekly volumes for live male king crab weighing over 3.2 kilograms rose week-on-week. Landings rose to 4.8 metric tons during the period, up from 3.9t the week and from 2.9t in the same week last year.

The price of the 2.2-3.2kg live male king crab also increased w-o-w. This size category also saw a slight volume increase, with weekly landings up w-o-w to 9t, up from 8.7t in week 43 and from 4.5t in the same period the year before.

For live female king crabs in the 800g-1.6kg size bracket -- the larger-volume category -- volumes stayed flat w-o-w at almost 1t, while their price fell by NOK 5/kg. 

Finally, prices for the larger 1.6-2.2kg female king crab also fell w-o-w by NOK 7/kg, as did sales volumes of this size range to 432kg.

US wholesale prices flat

The red king crab market continued flat this week following several weeks of strong upward momentum in prices, according to the latest assessment from Undercurrent News.

After a series of steady gains across all size categories two weeks before, Norwegian red king crab prices are now holding firm at elevated levels.

Market participants describe current conditions as "defined by tight supply and solid demand," with product movement remaining consistent but without further price increases.

According to Undercurrent data, 6–9 count crabs averaged $84.00 per pound, while 9–12 count crabs stayed at $80.00/lb. The mid-size 12–14 count and 14–17 count categories also continued at $75.00/lb and $72.00/lb, respectively, as did the 16–20 count at $66.00/lb.

title: Untitled
content:
Vietnamese pangasius farm-gate prices took a downturn for the largest harvest sizes, and continued climbing on the medium and smaller fish as October ended, according to updates from a Ho Chi Minh City-based consultancy commissioned by Undercurrent News to gather and analyze data.

Fingerling prices, too, have dropped from their precipitous high, according to this data -- see the subheading below. 

However, Le Thi Thuy Trang, sales manager with Siam Canadian Group in Vietnam, told Undercurrent the company hadn't seen any such fall.

Farm-gate prices for all harvest sizes reached a summer low in weeks 29 and 30, then rose since. But in week 40 (Sept. 29-Oct. 5), prices for 1.2 kilogram-plus fish began to drop, while 1.0-1.2kg and 800 gram-1.0kg continued to steadily rise.

That meant that, as of week 43 (Oct. 20-26), the largest fish -- preferred by the Chinese market -- were slightly cheaper to buy than the smaller ones for the first time since weeks 10-12, according to this data:

VIEW GRAPH
Pangasius Vietnam - Farm Gate, UCN
© 2025 Undercurrent News
To view the full datas
GO PREMIUM
Upgrade to Pro to view

"Farm-gate prices of large-sized fish have fallen because the demand has weakened (while supply remains steady), with new orders to China in early November remaining sluggish," a source at the consultancy told Undercurrent.

But as mentioned, Trang told Undercurrent: "I haven’t observed any drop in prices for either large-sized fish or fingerlings. Due to unfavorable farming schedules and market differentiation, prices are now clearly defined by size."

"Smaller sizes (3-5 ounce and 5-7oz) are currently unavailable, as farmers are refusing to sell at this stage, while larger sizes (14oz and up) -- mainly for the China market -- are in short supply and fetching higher prices."

She added that, in her experience, "prices tend to rise after the Qingdao show [China Fisheries and Seafood Exhibition, or CFSE], as this is typically when Chinese buyers finalize purchases in preparation for the Chinese New Year (in February)."

Trang has previously warned that raw material supply was "critically scarce" heading into the fourth quarter of 2025.

Meanwhile, for fish weighing 800g-1.0kg and 1.0-1.2kg, it has been a steady climb in farm-gate price up to week 43, with both reaching around VND 29,900 ($1.14)/kg.

The smaller fish sizes are the preferred range for producing fillets sent to the EU and US, with the US preferring the larger end of that range. 

Prices for the largest fish have crept above levels seen at the same time in 2022 to be October's highest in the past six years:

Prices for smaller fish also hit their highest October levels in at least six years:

Farm-gate pangasius prices rose by 3% for the 800g-1.0kg and by 1% for the 1.2kg+, the consultancy told Undercurrent.

"With production costs down to VND 25,000/kg due to lower feed prices, farmers' profit margins have improved markedly year-on-year, prompting immediate restocking after harvest," it wrote.

"However, fingerling supply has fallen by an estimated 20% over the past nine months, posing a risk of raw material shortages in late 2025 and early 2026."

At CFSE, a director at Vietnamese pangasius producer Vinh Hoan Corporation told Undercurrent the industry faces supply shortages starting in early 2026 after typhoons disrupted fingerling production.

Recent typhoons lowered water temperatures by several degrees Celsius, hurting fingerling mortality rates and growth in the fourth quarter, said Tien La. The impact will materialize in the first quarter following the typical eight- to 10-month grow-out period, with more pronounced effects expected in Q2.

The shortage compounds existing supply challenges as Vietnamese farmers increasingly favor harvesting larger fish for more profitable markets, particularly China. This has already created a shortage of smaller-sized raw material.

Meanwhile, export demand from key markets remains solid, though most imported slightly lower volumes month-on-month in September. The free on board price of pangasius fillets treated for the EU, 100% net weight, has been stable and high since July:

The US wholesale market for Vietnamese pangasius was steady in week 44, according to Undercurrent's latest assessment, with standard- and low-moisture IQF products steady at $2.15-$2.40 per pound.

Market participants continue to describe the tone as balanced but subdued, with comfortable inventory levels cushioning any immediate price movement.

Despite flat downstream pricing in the US, upstream sentiment is mildly firm. Some lower-priced offers circulating in the US market this week were reportedly tied to liquidation sales rather than reflective of current production economics.

Fingerling prices still historically high

The prices farmers pay to restock their ponds with juvenile fish have been high in 2025, and historically so since late summer.

The consultancy's data shows a steep downturn in prices since week 40's peak at over VND 63,000/kg (for 30-count/kg fish), easing below VND 54,500/kg by week 43.

"The fingerling prices declined due to a decrease in purchases," the consultancy told Undercurrent. "While companies continue to purchase fingerlings for restocking, given the large number of vacant ponds, overall stocking activity remains limited due to persistently high prices."

"In contrast, small-scale farmers are temporarily suspending new stocking because of flooding and expectations that prices will decline once fingerling supply begins to recover."

However, Siam Canadian's Trang said fingerling prices had not eased.

"The price of pangasius fingerlings currently stands at VND 60,000/kg, compared with VND 57,835/kg two weeks before. Prices remain at historically high levels and continue to trend upward," she said.

Before that, for September, the consultancy reported limited fingerling supply had pushed prices up sharply, by some 24% m-o-m.

title: New land-based steelhead project takes shape in BC as open net-pen phaseout looms
content:
A new land-based steelhead trout farming venture is emerging in Salmon Arm, British Columbia, led by a fish farming entrepreneur betting on a simpler, modular recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) design.

William Vermeer, founder and CEO of Aquameer Innovations, said he quietly began testing his prototype system two years ago and incorporated the company in June 2025 with a local business partner, Lorne McNeilly. The pair is now building a 25-cubic-meter tank to demonstrate the concept to investors and regulators.

"We've had fish in the prototype for over two years," Vermeer told Undercurrent News on Tuesday (Oct. 28). "The system's been running great. It's a small-production prototype, but it proved the fundamentals."

William Vermeer, co-founder and CEO, Aquameer Innovations. Photo: Aquameer

Vermeer's first RAS test unit -- a roughly four-cubic-meter "Franken-tank," as he calls it -- sits on his property in Salmon Arm, where he also runs a small hobby farm and greenhouse. The system raises steelhead trout sourced from Miracle Springs Hatchery in Mission, BC, using freshwater recycled at about 99%, he said.

Over the past six months, the company has raised about CAD150,000 ($107,600) in pre-seed investment from family and friends. Vermeer said the funding is being used to scale Aquameer's new aquaculture system, expanding from the original 4-cubic-meter tank to a 25-cubic-meter version. 

The 25-cubic-meter version is designed to hold roughly 1.5 metric tons of fish and feed up to 20 kgs per day. Vermeer expects this will allow Aquameer to gather performance data -- feed conversion ratios, energy profiles and growth rates -- before pursuing a full-scale build.

He has applied for a new federal aquaculture licence with the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) after letting an earlier one lapse. He hopes to secure approval within a year.

Lorne McNeilly, co-founder and CFO, Aquameer Innovations. Photo: Aquameer

Salmon Arm lies roughly 500 kilometers east of Vancouver and about 400 km southeast of Campbell River, the hub of BC's salmon-farming industry.

'Ready to scale'

Aquameer's website declares the company "ready to scale," a phrase Vermeer said reflects its shift from tinkering and prototype phase to actively seeking investment and moving toward commercial phase. He expects to seek about CAD 5 million in equity capital early next year to finance the commercial deployment of the modular system.

"The goal is to build a 1,000t farm within five years," he said. "We've already had interest from two ag-tech venture firms we met through my day job in robotics. They want quick build times and lean operations, and that's what this (proprietary) design delivers."

That aligns with a broader shift toward smaller, modular land-based aquaculture projects that Undercurrent observed at RASTECH 2025. Industry players describe this as a more disciplined "phase 2.0" of RAS development -- focused on demonstrating viability at 1,000-2,000t before scaling, rather than pursuing the mega-farm ambitions that defined the sector's earlier years.

Aquameer's model, which Vermeer called independent production units (IPUs), emphasizes factory-built modules that can be assembled on site with minimal specialized labor -- an approach he pursued after finding commercial RAS systems prohibitively expensive.

"It is simple, scalable and redundant," he said. "If we can prove it works at this scale, we can replicate it fast."

A sector in transition

Vermeer's startup arrives as British Columbia's salmon-farming sector faces sweeping change. In June 2024, then-fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier confirmed Ottawa's plan to ban open net-pens by 2029, as Undercurrent reported. She renewed existing licences under stricter conditions at that time, giving operators five years to shift into closed-containment or land-based systems.

Vermeer argues that steelhead trout could help fill the gap left by open net-pen Atlantic salmon as Canada moves to ban the practice in British Columbia by June 30, 2029.

"Steelhead are hardier and more disease-resistant than salmon," he said. "When you feed them a salmon diet, the fillet looks and tastes the same; some say it is even better."

Aquameer's initial production will focus on whole fish, weighing around three kgs, but Vermeer said the company will experiment with various sizes to gauge market demand. He envisions sales to local retailers and foodservice buyers. The farm's modular footprint could be replicated near other BC communities or First Nations interested in on-land aquaculture, he added.

Vermeer acknowledges the road ahead won't be easy.

"I'm not coming into this thinking it's going to be easy," he said. "Licensing is a big thing, raising the capital will be a challenge, and the logistics of building a large-scale farm are complex. But if we can pull it off once, we can replicate it many times."

title: Canadian seafood company fights back on temporary foreign workers penalty
content:
A New Brunswick shellfish processing company that was slapped with a CAD 1.0 million ($716,954) fine for violations of Canada's Temporary Foreign Workers (TFW) program is asking Canada's federal court to review the case, reports CBC. 

The penalty issued by Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) on Sept. 17 against Bolero Seafood Processing, a division of Montreal, Quebec-based Sogelco International, was the largest ever issued by the government agency for violations of the TFW program, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

The Bolero processing plant is located in Saint Simon, a small town on New Brunswick's Acadian Peninsula, about 75 kilometers east of Bathurst.

In its application for a judicial review, the company argues, among other things, that the penalties imposed by ESDC have caused it to "suffer considerable stigma akin to a finding of guilt in a criminal proceeding without any right to a trial or a hearing," reports CBC.

The lobster and sea cucumber processor failed to provide proper wages and working conditions, failed to comply with federal and provincial labor laws, and failed to provide a workplace that was free of abuse, ESDC stated in an Oct. 6 new release on its website.

"These measures go well beyond a mere regulatory response and have the effect of significantly damaging the company's reputation and operations, and are grossly disproportionate to the … allegations," Bolero stated in its application for review, noting that ESDC officials "reversed the onus of proof" when it presumed the company had violated TFW regulations.

If the application for leave is granted, Bolero wants the Sept. 17 decision quashed and the matter remitted to the federal department for reconsideration. The company is also seeking a public retraction of any statements by federal officials, including the Oct. 6 news release by ESDC.

title: Untitled
content:
When the Nova Scotia aquaculture review board wrapped up its four-day hearing Friday (Oct. 10), the story that emerged was less about a farm's expansion and more about the uneasy intersection of science, livelihoods and coastal identity on the province's southern shore.

At the center of it all stood Kelly Cove Salmon, a subsidiary of Canadian seafood giant Cooke Aquaculture, seeking permission to add six cages to its long-running Coffin Island site in Liverpool Bay. The change would bring the total to 20 cages and boost production capacity to about 660,000 Atlantic salmon.

The company calls it a modest, logical expansion. Opponents see it as one more step toward industrializing a bay that, in their view, has already given enough.

Scaling back ambitions

Kelly Cove has held the Coffin Island lease for over 15 years, but this application has roots in something much larger. Cooke once envisioned three farm sites across Liverpool Bay that would have tripled local output to nearly 1.9 million fish. That plan shrank this year after six years of bureaucratic stalls and political pushback, including a 2024 statement by premier Tim Houston declaring Liverpool Bay unsuitable for new aquaculture sites.

By the time the hearing opened in Bridgewater last week, the scope had narrowed to a single boundary amendment at Coffin Island. Still, it drew an audience of residents, fishers, conservation advocates and lawyers who have become familiar figures in Atlantic Canada's aquaculture debates.

A courtroom-like setting

On one side of the hearing room sat Robert Grant K.C. and David Barry, lawyers from the Halifax firm Stewart McKelvey, representing Kelly Cove. On the other side sat attorneys from Ecojustice, the environmental law organization representing the Protect Liverpool Bay Association.

Counsels for the parties and attendees at the Nova Scotia Aquaculture Review Board hearing on Kelly Cove Salmon's Coffin Island expansion, held in Bridgewater from Oct. 7-10, 2025. Screen grab from ARB video

Early in the proceedings, several lay witnesses described what they feared the expansion would mean for their lives along the shoreline.

One witness, a local Airbnb host who operates a coastal property, expressed worries the expansion could bring increased noise and nighttime lighting, undercutting the area's aesthetic qualities and the commercial value of his business.

Company counsel, in turn, noted that most locals had purchased or renovated their homes years after the Coffin Island site was already established.

Lobsters and livelihoods

Economist Chris Milley of Halifax-based Nexus Coastal Resource Management -- hired by local lobster harvesters -- argued that even small expansions can unsettle fisheries through "passive" displacement and perception. But as the questioning continued, Milley admitted that his predictions were based on general averages rather than specific local details and that adding six cages "would not displace many lobster traps."

Kelly Cove's lawyers countered that fishers already work inside the lease grid outside of anchor lines, and that DFO's own tagging and underwater footage show lobsters present beneath the existing cages.

Challenging the critics

Marine biologist Inka Milewski, a longtime critic of open net-pen farming, faced her own test on Friday. Testifying at the request of Jamie Simpson, counsel for intervenor group 22 Fishermen of Liverpool Bay, Milewski was pressed on the strength of her conclusions about the potential impacts of salmon aquaculture expansion at Coffin Island.

Grant reminded the board that Milewski had previously argued aquaculture should be moved out of public waters and emphasized that much of her Coffin Island analysis came from reviews of academic literature, rather than direct field data from Liverpool Bay.

Under cross-examination, Milewski acknowledged her report relied heavily on external studies and testimony, admitting there was no direct evidence of negative impacts on the local lobster fishery in her submission.

Milewski appeared uncertain at times, needing to check her language and clarify whether her conclusions pointed to negative impacts as likely or merely possible. At one point, she struggled to identify any locations that might be suitable for marine-based salmon farms.

Grant then cited peer-reviewed research showing no clear link between fish farming and lobster declines, challenging Milewski's assertions and highlighting the ongoing debate within the scientific community.

The hearing's most intense exchanges, however, revolved around wild Atlantic salmon. Jonathan Carr, representing the Atlantic Salmon Federation (ASF), fielded questions about whether ASF's policy against open net-pens shaped his testimony.

Carr was also asked about the Atlantic Salmon Federation's relationship with its funders during cross-examination. Counsel referenced outdoor lifestyle company Patagonia founder Yvon Chouinard -- a major ASF donor, as Carr has acknowledged -- and an advocacy advertisement placed by "Patagonia 50" (an environmental campaign from the company) on the back cover of the Atlantic Salmon Journal, ASF's publication. The exchange was used to illustrate Patagonia's public opposition to open net-pen salmon farming and to probe potential influence over ASF's communications.

"I would think much of it would align with the Atlantic Salmon Federation," he told the board. "But again, this was done as a non-biased report in terms of looking at what impacts aquaculture operations have on wild populations."

Kelly Cove Salmon's Coffin Island site in Liverpool Bay, Queens County, Nova Scotia. Photo: Cooke Aquaculture

Carr later clarified that he does not consider open net-pens safe for wild salmon or the environment under current conditions. "I would concur with that statement under the current conditions we have," he said. But he also underscored ASF's push for "responsible aquaculture… done in a more sustainable manner."

"I wouldn't say that we're advocating for aquaculture completely out of the ocean. We're advocating for a more responsible way of doing things," Carr added.

His careful phrasing hinted at something rarely acknowledged in these hearings -- that the idea of sustainable open-net farming is not impossible; it is just not yet realized.

Eddy Halfyard, a research scientist with two decades in salmon conservation and a former Nova Scotia Salmon Association biologist, spoke next. Halfyard appeared as an expert witness at Simpson's request.

Halfyard's testimony was measured and dense with technical detail. She spoke of how acid rain, land use and underlying geology combine to acidify rivers, and why liming and restocking programs need constant monitoring. In instances where she didn't have current data, she said so.

The company's case

By the end of the week, Cooke's lawyers had hammered home the same point: this isn't about building new farms, just extending an existing one. They argued that the opponents' evidence -- however passionately delivered -- lacked site-specific data tying Coffin Island to measurable harm.

Under Nova Scotia's aquaculture regulations, those factors are defined broadly and require the board to weigh impacts on fisheries, navigation, wild salmon sustainability and other marine users.

"We're confident Kelly Cove Salmon demonstrated that the expansion presents no unacceptable risk and satisfied the factors to be considered in decisions related to marine aquaculture sites," Joel Richardson, vice president of Cooke Aquaculture, told Undercurrent News following the hearing.

The board will reconvene on Oct. 31 to hear Kelly Cove's remaining witnesses, after which written submissions are due. A decision is expected within 30 days after the close of submissions, likely in early December.

title: Genetic testing at Alabama shrimp festival exposes state labeling law violations
content:
Genetic testing firm SeaD Consulting uncovered multiple instances of mislabeling of foreign product as domestic at the National Shrimp Festival, according to Gulf Coast Media.

The festival is a four-day event that celebrates wild-caught shrimp from the Gulf of Mexico. The event took place Oct. 9-12 in Gulf Shores, Alabama, attracting a crowd of around 300,000 seafood lovers.

The festival announced it would partner with Houston, Texas-based SeaD to ensure that all shrimp sold at the event complied with Alabama's new seafood labeling law. It appointed Chandra Wright, the director of environmental and education outreach at The Lodge at Gulf State Park, to the newly created role of "chief shrimp investigator," as reported by Undercurrent News.

The chief shrimp investigator found "several" violations, thought the festival did not specify the number of vendors out of compliance with their contractual obligation to serve domestic shrimp.

"Over the past two days, we have found several apparent violations of mandates that domestic shrimp be served," Wright told Gulf Coast Media. "We are now reasonably confident that each of the 18 shrimp vendors are in compliance with our contract."

SeaD conducted on-site DNA testing of shrimp -- a process it said takes about two hours. Flagged vendors had their inventory and receipts examined by festival organizers. One vendor reportedly admitted to selling imported shrimp and was fined $500, according to local news publication AL.com. That vendor could not serve shrimp until he could prove to festival organizers that it switched to domestic shrimp.

Each vendor with a violation was issued a list of local suppliers, and Wright said that all vendors found out of compliance had switched to domestic product by the festival's end.

In week 40 (Sept. 29-Oct. 5) of 2025, the largest size grade of Norwegian king crab saw ex-vessel prices ease, while other size grades increased a little week-on-week, data from the Norges Rafisklag auction shows.

Weekly volumes for male king crab weighing over 3.2kg lifted a little w-o-w, but remained down from the highs of recent weeks. Landings rose to 4.7 metric tons during the period, also up from 3.9t in the same week last year.

title: Canadian seafood processor fined CAD 1.0m for temporary worker violations
content:
A seafood processing company in the Canadian province of New Brunswick has been handed a CAD 1.0 million ($716,954m) fine and banned from hiring temporary foreign workers for 10 years.

The penalty issued against Bolero Shellfish Processing, a division of Montreal, Quebec-based Sogelco International, on Sept. 17 is the largest ever issued by Employment and Social Development Canada (ESCD) for failing to comply with the rules of Canada's Temporary Foreign Workers (TFW) program.

The lobster and sea cucumber processor failed to provide proper wages and working conditions, failed to comply with federal and provincial labor laws, and failed to provide a workplace that was free of abuse, ESCD said on its website.

"Any mistreatment of workers or misuse of the program will not be tolerated," the federal agency said.

Bolero Shellfish in Saint Simon, New Brunswick. Photo screenshot from Google Street View

Bolero is owned by and employs up to 85 workers, in season, at its plant in Saint Simon, a small town on New Brunswick's Acadian Peninsula, about 75 kilometers east of the city of Bathurst.

Sogelco president Gabriel Elbaz could not be reached for comment by Undercurrent News at press time. However, the company plans to challenge the ESCD decision in court, reported Global News.

"Bolero Shellfish categorically rejects the conclusions of the federal government, which do not reflect the reality of its practices nor its commitment to the well-being of employees hired under the Temporary Foreign Worker Program," the company is quoted as saying by Global News.

title: Australian tuna fishers struggle to compete as ‘costs soar, access shrinks,’ exec claims
content:
Australia's highly regulated, sustainability-certified tuna industry is facing an uncertain future, as rising operating costs, labor shortages, and shrinking access to fishing grounds make it increasingly difficult for fishers to stay afloat.

Speaking virtually at the XII ANFACO World Tuna Conference in Vigo, Spain, Tuna Australia CEO David Ellis issued a blunt warning: "The current operating environment is becoming unsustainable, even for a sector that is widely recognized for doing everything right."

Ellis, a veteran of over 30 years in the tuna sector, described a fishery that has transformed itself through years of investment in environmental stewardship, crew safety, traceability, and product quality.

Vigo tuna conference 2025: Future bright as new markets open in China, Latin America

Yet despite these advances -- including full Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certification across several key species -- Australian tuna operators are now battling what he called a "marine spatial squeeze," with nearly 40% of the nation's waters effectively off limits to commercial fishing.

"Decades ago, most of our exclusive economic zone (EEZ) was open to fishing," he said.

"Now we're seeing that space eroded by a growing number of competing uses: marine parks, offshore wind farms, aquaculture expansion, shipping routes, oil and gas exploration, and even rocket launches. It's death by a thousand cuts," he added.

Because longline gear cannot be precisely confined to narrow zones, Ellis noted that no-fishing areas -- particularly marine reserves -- create significant buffers around themselves, "which further reduces usable space."

He estimates that when indirect exclusions are factored in, as much as 39% of the Australian EEZ is inaccessible to tuna fishers, especially in the east, where multiple management regimes overlap.

"We're not just being squeezed physically, but politically and economically."

And that squeeze comes with an economic cost.

According to Ellis, Australian tuna fishers find competing on the global market increasingly difficult. While Australia positions itself as a premium, boutique supplier of sashimi-grade fish to the US, Japan, and other Asian countries, producing those products is expensive.

"Our deckhands are earning around $50,000 a year, and they should. It's hard, skilled work," Ellis said. "But it puts us at a disadvantage when we're competing against fleets operating with vastly lower wage bills."

Labor is only part of the cost equation, though.

Fuel prices remain volatile, bait is becoming more expensive, and insurance and compliance costs continue to rise. At the same time, young Australians are showing little interest in maritime careers, forcing fishing companies to rely heavily on imported labor," he explained.

"When I started out, the industry was competitive and full of talent. Now, we're struggling to get crew, engineers, even captains. The next generation is looking elsewhere," he also noted.

As if the economic and workforce pressures weren't enough, Ellis also pointed to what he sees as a growing burden of regulation that threatens to undermine the very sustainability the industry has worked so hard to achieve.

Australian tuna fisheries are subject to overlapping governance by three regional fisheries management organizations -- the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission, the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission, and the Commission for the Conservation of Southern Bluefin Tuna, he mentioned -- in addition to a dense web of domestic laws and reporting obligations.

"Each of these bodies has its own conservation and management measures. The duplication is staggering," Ellis said. "And it's not just unnecessary, it's expensive. Every new rule means more reporting, more monitoring, more admin. We're not saying don't regulate. We're saying be smart about it."

Ellis emphasized that Australian tuna fisheries are among the most heavily monitored in the world. Longline vessels operate year-round and use electronic logbooks, onboard cameras, and real-time catch documentation.

Additionally, advisory committees regularly assess catch volumes to ensure sustainability, and Australia is actively pushing for science-based harvest strategies at both national and international levels. "We're selective, we're traceable, we're transparent. We do things properly."

But Ellis also questioned whether sustainability certifications, even those as respected as MSC, are now multiplying to the point of diminishing returns. "There are over 160 certifications in the marine space," he noted. "Each one costs money to apply for, audit, and maintain. What's the net gain? Are we just doing it to tick boxes? MSC was a great initiative and still is, but we need to ask whether adding layers of labels is helping or hurting."

That skepticism doesn't mean the industry is turning its back on innovation. On the contrary, Ellis shared a range of initiatives currently underway to drive improvements in safety, efficiency, and environmental impact.

"These include new protective gear to reduce injury during longline retrievals, artificial bait alternatives to reduce costs and reliance on wild baitfish, and efforts to eliminate bycatch of seabirds and other non-target wildlife," he explained.

"Tuna Australia is also investing in circular economy strategies, turning waste into usable products, and encouraging fleet operators to explore value-added product lines to reach new markets," he added.

Ellis concluded his remarks by calling for stronger recognition of high-performing fisheries through certification, broader policy and market support.

"We've proven that sustainable fishing is possible. We're living it. But how do we survive if we're constantly being crowded out, overregulated, and under-rewarded? MSC showed what was possible. What's the next big step for NGOs, governments, and the market?" he said.

"We've done everything we were asked to do. Now we need a system that lets us keep doing it, and makes it worth doing," he concluded.
