title: Untitled
content:
Scottish fishing groups have reacted the most angrily to the news on Sept. 30 that the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (ICES) has advised a dramatic reduction in landings of northeast Atlantic mackerel for 2026.

From advised landings of 576,958 metric tons in 2025, ICES has said catches in 2026 should be no more than 174,357t; down some 70% year-on-year.

The Scottish Pelagic Processors' Association (SPPA) warned a cut of this magnitude will have a "devastating impact" on the Scottish mackerel processing sector if implemented.

ICES advises dramatic 70% cut to northeast Atlantic mackerel advice for 2026

"The mackerel processing industry in Scotland employs around 2,500 people, mainly in Peterhead, Fraserburgh and Lerwick, and jobs would be put in jeopardy if such a draconian cut were implemented," said Robert Duthie, chair of the SPPA.

"There is a healthy domestic market for canned and smoked mackerel, and it is also a major export product, including to premium markets in Asia, which would also be put at risk," he added.

The advice from ICES uses a revised methodology on how many young fish enter the spawning stock biomass -- "an arbitrary figure and [one] we are certain doesn't reflect the true situation of the mackerel stock and adopts a 'worst-case' scenario."

"There are, of course, ongoing issues with mackerel management that need to be resolved, most notably the failure of coastal states to reach a comprehensive international agreement, which is something both UK catchers and processors have long been calling for. But despite this, the catch advice by ICES is unnecessarily harsh and is based on doubtful science. We urge for a common-sense approach when it comes to deciding upon the final quota allocations for 2026."

This comes hot on the heels of ICES' advice that cod catches in the North Sea, the west of Scotland, the eastern English Channel and Skagerrak should be cut from 15,000 metric tons in 2025 to zero for 2026. Different fisheries and situations, but equally painful for fisherpeople in the relevant coastal states.

In response to the mackerel news, Elsepth Macdonald -- chief executive of the Scottish Fishermen's Federation (SFF) -- said: "While SFF recognises ICES authority and expertise on leading on the complex science behind the stock assessments, we are increasingly concerned about what seems to be a growing trend of ICES stepping out of their remit of providing scientific advice and stepping into fisheries management, which is not their role -- that is for governments. We have seen this twice recently, first on northern shelf cod and now on northeast Atlantic mackerel."

"The over-precautionary approach being used by ICES when formalizing their advice appears to be them seeking to influence governments on how stocks should be managed. But fisheries managers -- governments -- must take a number of factors into account in their management decisions, of which science is an important one, but not the only one," she added.

Managers must take into consideration all three pillars of sustainability -- the environmental, but also the social and socio-economic implications of management decisions, she argued. "Stock assessors in ICES are not equipped to deal with these wider issues that extend far beyond ICES's remit and expertise."

And Ian Gatt, chief executive of the Scottish Pelagic Fishermen's Association (SPFA), said the advised 70% reduction was "a hammer blow to the industry because of bad assumptions and, frankly, guesswork."

"It seems that absurdly cautious assumptions have prevailed over hard evidence. ICES advice has been highly variable in the past few years, and we understand that this year it reflects an arbitrary choice of a recruitment period into the fishery. It is unacceptable that the viability of our industry should be jeopardised by an ICES best-guess decision plugged into a computer model. In short, the same science with better assumptions would lead to a much better outcome for our industry."

Richard Williamson, a Shetland-based second skipper and chair of the SPFA, claimed the new advice bore no resemblance to what he and other fishermen were seeing right across the mackerel fishing grounds in the northeast Atlantic.

"We don't disagree that the stock is not as high as it was back in 2015-16, for example, but we believe that the stock is in better shape than it was two years ago. We wouldn't disagree either that a comprehensive, long-term sharing arrangement binding all players in the international mackerel fishery, based largely on zonal attachment combined with a long-term management plan for this important stock, is long overdue."

"Fishermen are custodians of the sea. We have no interest whatsoever in demanding excessive quotas that would end up crippling our businesses and the communities that depend on them. That is why we have objected to ICES advice in the past when we felt it was too high, as we did when  the ICES advice for North Sea herring was increased by 32% in 2024, for example."

Simon Collins of the Shetland Fishermen's Association added that the pelagic fishing fleet had itself become a major and credible contributor to hard scientific data in recent years.

He said: "We believe in scientific guidance on catch limits when it is backed with real data and a rigorous scientific process. We utterly reject this new approach by ICES, in which reckless guesswork and fag-packet choices in analysing serious data result in recommendations that threaten a critical part of the UK's fishing fleet and all the onshore businesses that depend on it. This is not how any scientific institution should conduct itself."

ICES was not able to respond to a request for comment from Undercurrent News in time for publication.

'Massive lack of precision?'

In Norway, fishing industry association Fiskebat questioned the scientific methods and the data behind the advice.

"A methodology revision was carried out this winter, where the reference points for mackerel were changed. A new critical level for the spawning stock of mackerel (Blim) was defined. What was the background for this adjustment, and is it scientifically well-founded?"

"When an upward adjustment of the critical action point for the spawning stock is combined with a very pessimistic estimate of future year classes, it quickly gives a picture of the mackerel stock that is far more negative than what the fishermen themselves experience, which stands in stark contrast to ICES' quota advice."

Princes shifts to MSC Chilean jack mackerel after dramatic Atlantic catch advice cut

It claimed this was not the first time Norway has experienced dramatic changes in quota advice, "which have later proven to be incorrect."

"Mackerel stock research over the past 15 years has been characterized by a massive lack of precision, uncertainty in methodology, belief or not in egg surveys and larval measurements, belief or not in acoustic measurements, belief or not in tag-recapture as a method, retrospective stock assessments, write-ups, write-downs and retrospective adjustments to estimates, mortality and taxation pressure."

The end product, claimed Fiskebat, is a research history that leaves the impression of "science in the dark."

It pointed to 2018's advised catch reduction of 40%, which prompted the industry and Norway's Institute of Marine Research to push back. "A new methodological revision was carried out, and the result was a significant upward adjustment of the spawning stock and quota advice in the spring of 2019."

"Fiskebat generally supports the quota advice from ICES. However, there is reason to raise serious questions about a revised model that gives dramatic results in the quota advice for a stock that has not historically been particularly volatile, and where we know that some of the premises that are decisive for the estimates are discretionary and very difficult to anchor scientifically. When the quota advice will also have such major consequences for an entire industry, the professionalism must be unassailable and the trust in the process high."

At Fiskebat's request, the Norwegian government is convening a meeting between administration, research and industry organizations, it said.

Shocking -- but not surprising

The North Atlantic Pelagic Advocacy Group (NAPA) -- a market-led coalition of over 50 global retailers, foodservice companies and suppliers -- expressed its deep concern after ICES' research showed that the mackerel stock has reached its lowest level for over 20 years, which it added corresponds to decades of excessive catches.

In addition, it said, Atlanto-Scandian/ Norwegian spring spawning herring and northeast Atlantic blue whiting have also seen substantial stock declines after "entrenched periods of unilateral quota setting by coastal states for all three species."

Catches have been higher than the scientific advice in every year but one since 1998, and have been 33% beyond what science considers safe limits each year on average for the past decade.

In 2024, the UK, Norway, and the Faroe Islands signed a tripartite catch-sharing agreement that commits to reducing their catches and adhering to specified percentages of the recommended limits. However, this agreement excludes other coastal states: the EU, Iceland, and Greenland. 

NAPA "is calling urgently for international quota sharing agreements to bring mackerel catches back into line with scientific advice and reduce pressure on the struggling species," and the companies that are part of the coalition have been vocal about shifting their sourcing away from the beleaguered fisheries. 

Indeed, UK canned food firm Princes Group has announced it has shifted the sourcing of its mackerel, halting its purchases from the northeast Atlantic and instead buying Marine Stewardship Council (MSC)-certified Chilean jack mackerel.

"The latest update on the state of the mackerel stock is shocking, but not surprising," said Aoife Martin, NAPA's independent chair. "As the voice of the marketplace, NAPA has been calling for action to address this issue for five years. In that time, excess catches have totalled over 1 million [metric tons] above scientific advice. It has proven inevitable that there would be stark consequences not only for the species, but for all who depend on it for their livelihoods."

NAPA is leading a fishery improvement project (FIP) that aims to drive political action towards a comprehensive sharing arrangement, keeping total catches within scientific limits. Success could see the fishery regain the MSC certification it lost in 2019, it said.

It has also identified interim steps that all coastal states can take to reduce fishing pressure while working towards an agreement, in recognition of the time needed for international political negotiations. This includes limiting high seas catches to 10% of total catches, focusing on human consumption for the use of whole mackerel, and limiting banking and borrowing -- in which countries bring forward or push back certain amounts of quota between years -- to 10% of the annual total. 

Martin said it was clear from coastal state discussions last week that there is a willingness from the parties involved to find solutions, to the extent that there are several proposals on the table -- although not yet any one proposal that all states endorse. 

"The severity of the state of the stock should serve as a jolt to get the next round of negotiations on track towards a meaningful compromise, and an agreed position for sustainable fishing," she said.

The FIP ends in April 2026. If coastal states have not delivered sufficient improvements in management by then, NAPA warns that more of its members will be forced to seriously reconsider their pelagic sourcing decisions -- potentially looking to other species and regions with a more dependable future. 

The European Association of Fish Producers Organisations (EAPO), which represents multiple businesses across the relevant coastal states, said it was "greatly concerned about the state of the mackerel stock in particular, as well as the huge impact on fisheries, the value chain and coastal communities."

Tim Heddema, chair of EAPO's Northern Pelagic Working Group, said: "As always, industry and NGOs will make shared recommendations through the Pelagic Advisory Council. These recommendations and the EU industry position will be published on Oct. 3."

Erin Priddle, MSC's director for northern Europe, added: "Today's advice is a stark warning: without urgent action, mackerel stocks are at very real risk of collapse."

"The science is clear, and now, after years of inaction, governments must put aside political deadlock and work together to agree quotas in line with scientific evidence for the long-term sustainability of this critically important species."

title: Japanese aquatech launches first commercial farmed salmon roe amid supply crunch
content:
Japanese aquaculture startup Smolt Co. is preparing to roll out the first commercial volumes of salmon roe (ikura) produced entirely from farmed cherry salmon (Oncorhynchus masou), positioning the move as a step toward rebuilding Japan's domestic supply chain for one of its most iconic delicacies.

The Miyazaki-based company said Monday (Sept. 22) it will begin taking orders in October for deliveries scheduled from November 2026, targeting an initial output of 10 metric tons.

Products such as green roe, soy-marinated roe, and salted roe will be available, with traders, processors, restaurant chains, and retailers among the expected buyers.

The move comes as wild-sourced supply tightens at home and abroad.

Japan sees early Hokkaido chum catch rebound, long-term decline persists

Hokkaido, Japan's largest salmon-producing region, is bracing for one of the weakest autumn chum runs on record, with just 11.4 million fish forecast to return in 2025 -- 35% below last year's already historic low and more than 60m under past norms, as reported by Undercurrent News.

Japan's traditional suppliers in Alaska and the Russian Far East also see limited availability and elevated prices, adding further strain to the country's ikura supply chain.

Smolt is pitching its farmed cherry salmon roe as a partial solution to the supply shortfall.

Since its founding in 2019, the firm has refined full-cycle aquaculture of cherry salmon, developing heat-tolerant strains through six generations of selective breeding and optimizing spawning and egg quality.

Earlier pilot products under the "Tsukimi Ikura" brand laid the groundwork for the current commercial launch, the firm said.

The company highlights cherry salmon roe's mild flavor and consistent quality as advantages, alongside full traceability and independence from volatile wild fisheries.

Volumes will remain small compared with Japan's domestic ikura production, which industry sources estimate at about 1,600t in Hokkaido in 2024.

Smolt, however, said the project will contribute to domestic food security and stabilize prices by reducing reliance on imports.

It added that the initiative also opens the door to new production hubs across Japan through partnerships with aquaculture and processing companies.

title: Untitled
content:
The Norwegian government's latest aquaculture regulations have put a greater emphasis than ever on data and precision -- a move which looks likely to have knock-on impacts for mergers and acquisitions (M&A) in the sector.

"I think we are at the crossroads; the new proposed regulations are very much focusing on the farmers being much more precision-oriented," Jorgen Horntvedt -- partner with M&A firm Seafood Corporate Advisors -- told Undercurrent News at Aqua Nor in Trondheim recently.

Aqua Nor 2025: Nordly touts huge potential of alternative plant-based aquafeed ingredients

"The stick is really coming over [the farmers] to show the government that they are doing the right thing in order to have a license to operate. The new regulations will cater to everything that has to do with data collection. The farmer must be at the level that he knows how the area performs, how he deals with sea lice and de-lousing, how he deals with the sludge, how he deals with product after it's been harvested. The rest of the material will probably also be a focus area, to utilize more value."

"So for the farmer, it's kind of skewed now with more CAPEX [capital expenditure] in technology upfront before the farming cycle starts, preparing everything so that they know exactly how their biomass will perform through the cycle. Then afterwards, there will probably be a lowering of the OPEX [operating expenditure] going forward."

The current low selling prices for farmed salmon in Norway show that this new picture can't be taken lightly, he said. "You have to come down on the OPEX side, and you have to show the regulatory authorities that you're actually doing something to contribute to making the regulation work as intended."

Horntvedt's hypothesis is that this could see a "bundling" of aquatech businesses in Norway as the hub of this sector's innovation.

"A lot of the technology companies are now so small that they are not really making money, or don't have a lot of customers, or are at an early stage. There will probably be room for a bundling of more technology companies, and these companies will end up as larger platforms, brought into an established unit or a new platform setting that will continue to grow."

New regulations essentially amount to a license to operate, meaning the leading farmer in each area -- with the greatest analytical capacity -- will be well-placed to head discussions with other farmers as to how to meet rules, or to buy smaller farmers that are more "on the fringes." Hence, "the continued M&A and consolidation on the farming side will continue to be relevant going forward," he said.

Processing, feed are hot topics

Horntvedt previously told Undercurrent that he felt the US' ongoing tariff measures could prompt Norway's salmon farming giants to invest in enhancing their processing operations, alongside ongoing spending on efficiency and supply growth, and that remains the case, he said.

"I think farmers will see more M&A activity around either cooperating or coming into investments in value adding of their product. Today it's all about getting their product out at the right price, at the right time, and making sure that the raw material focus is the key focus. But I think that many of the farmers will be more keen going forward to put more value on the product and aligning this with the huge capacity that there is in Europe for value-added products."

"Some of the farmers will probably think it's interesting to go down downstream in that sense, and other farmers will favor doing this in Norway, as we've seen with Kvaroy," he said, referring to 1814 Salmon, a company led by salmon farmers Kvaroy Salmon and Fram Seafood and investment company Nyhamn.

New global tariff era could prompt Norway’s salmon farmers to invest more in processing

Then, Mowi's decision to sell its feed division has made the aquafeed sector a hot topic, said Horntvedt. 

"I wouldn't comment on that deal in particular, but in general -- who would win this profitability race going forward? Because fish feed producers historically have been on the fringe of margin upside, not really having a position to negotiate up on their margins. But with this precision farming and more stringent regulatory requirements, the fish at sea need to be stronger and need to be followed more closely -- a key is to supply the right fish feed for the different stages of the development."

Traditionally, he said, competition between feed producers is quite fierce. Mowi selling its feed assets will mean a highly significant contract will go, probably, to one of the other big suppliers.

Then, there is the growing importance of alternative protein firms in the aquafeed sector, he added.

"I think it's going to be even clearer that the Norwegian hub of aquaculture is going to be the hotspot for global tech aquaculture innovation. Now, how are we going to get to a level where the technology providers will be able to take away some of the systematic risks in the biology?"

"The hubs and companies that are already set up to do this, and those that could invest in them, are all more or less from Norway, and I think there is an awareness of how important this technology shift is in the aquaculture industry. This symbiosis with the farmers is happening here, and I think that's the shift we want to see going forward."

In recent "Fishy Friday" updates from DNB's senior vice president for seafood, Dag Sletmo, the analyst welcomed the news that the Norwegian Food Safety Authority (Mattilsynet) has established a "regulatory sandbox" for digitalization and development in aquaculture. 

"The aquaculture industry is innovative and rapidly evolving. Technological developments in the industry provide new opportunities, but also new issues," said Mattilsynet in its announcement. "The possibilities for sharing data are also developing. The [authority], and the regulations we administer, must be equipped for the future. Therefore, we invite cooperation on testing technical solutions, digitalization and new ways of receiving data from the industry -- within the framework of a regulatory sandbox."

Sletmo said the success of digital technology in aquaculture would depend on good regulations, which would either slow progress down or speed it up.

"I think there is a structural change in the market, which is good for suppliers [to the aquaculture sector]," he said. "New technology opens a lot of new opportunities. More diverse technology should allow for stronger pricing power as value-based selling can grow at the expense of head-on price competition."

"Walking around Aqua Nor...was also a good reminder of how sophisticated technology has become and how wide the range."

Manolin -- itself a technology business focused on improving salmon farming through data and machine learning -- said when the new regulations were announced that it expected to see them shift investor thinking.

"At the heart of [Norway's] proposal is a bold question: What if we stopped regulating how much fish a farm produces, and started regulating how much impact that production has? If enacted, this would fundamentally alter how growth is permitted, how value is measured, and who gets to thrive in the next generation of salmon farming."

Previously, growth potential was defined by license volume, it noted. Large operators with multiple sites and extensive biomass allowances had the edge. But in this new framework, growth is a function of performance:

"This realignment is likely to shift investor focus, too. Markets that once valued salmon companies based on production output may soon weigh on-farm metrics -- lice counts, mortality trends, escape incidents -- as key indicators of future earnings."

title: Nissui eyes new value in pollock with study linking protein to muscle growth
content:
Japanese seafood giant Nissui Corp. has announced clinical trial results showing that protein derived from pollock can enlarge fast-twitch muscle fibers in humans, the first time such an effect has been demonstrated in a human study. 

Conducted with Juntendo University, the 12-week pilot trial provided evidence that pollock protein can alter muscle fiber morphology, improve body composition and potentially enhance functional performance. 

FREE READ Recap GAPP meeting: Alaska’s US senators take measures to help pollock industry; Surimi prices climb after supply shock

The Tokyo-based group said Monday (Sept. 22) that the findings were presented Sept. 19 at the 79th annual meeting of the Japanese Society of Physical Fitness and Sports Medicine.

Nine healthy adult men were enrolled, with eight completing the protocol. Each consumed one fish sausage fortified with 4.5 grams of pollock protein every morning for 12 weeks. Muscle biopsies showed that fibers responsible for quick and powerful movement became thicker after the intervention. 

The researchers also reported improvements in overall body composition, with increases in skeletal muscle and fat reduction, alongside a trend toward greater strength in high-speed movements.

For Nissui, one of the world's largest pollock processors, the breakthrough represents an opportunity to create new value from a species that has defined its business for decades. 

Pollock was once considered a highly perishable fish used mainly for roe and surimi in Hokkaido, but Nissui's development of frozen surimi technology in the 1960s -- in collaboration with the Hokkaido Fisheries Research Institute -- transformed it into the foundation of Japan's surimi industry. 

After pioneering surimi factory trawlers in the 1960s, Nissui established UniSea in Dutch Harbor in 1974, building a land-based plant in Alaska as the 200-mile fisheries jurisdiction limited access for Japanese vessels.

FREE READ New monthly UCN China, Russia, US pollock fillet block prices go live

The company later expanded downstream with the acquisitions of Gorton's in the US and Cite Marine in Europe.

The moves allowed Nissui to build a fully integrated pollock value chain spanning raw material supply, industrial surimi, and consumer brands across North America, Europe and Asia.

The pollock protein research now signals a new frontier. 

Since 2009, Nissui has marketed pollock domestically under the "Sokkin Protein" brand -- literally "fast-twitch protein" -- promoting products such as sausages, bars and soups, highlighting pollock's high proportion of fast-twitch muscle. 

Nissui said the new research could strengthen the campaign with scientific backing and position pollock as a commodity raw material and a differentiated functional food ingredient for sports nutrition and healthy aging.

title: Enforcement blitz in British Columbia nets 34 fishery violations
content:
A recent enforcement blitz in British Columbia waters, spanning four months and involving eight coordinated patrols, uncovered numerous violations -- but all were committed by recreational fishers, according to Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO).

The enforcement sweep consisted of four separate patrol operations, each lasting two days, for eight patrol days spread over June through September. The patrols were timed to coincide with peak vessel traffic and covered waters from the Southern Gulf Islands to Port Renfrew on Vancouver Island.

Dubbed "Operation Sea Dog," the Canadian participants included DFO's Conservation and Protection (C&P) branch, the federal agency's enforcement arm; the Canada Border Services Agency and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The US agencies involved were the US Coast Guard and the Washington State Fish and Wildlife Police.

"None of them were commercial fishing violations," Jamie McEachern, C&P area chief, told Undercurrent News in a phone interview on Thursday (Sept. 18).

"The majority of people out on the water during our patrols were recreational fishers. We would have checked commercial fisheries if the opportunity presented itself, but the focus ended up being on recreational violations simply because those were the vessels present."

Inspections during the patrols included 336 vessels and 753 individuals, resulting in 34 violations. Offences included fishing without a licence, using barbed hooks, retaining undersized crabs and illegally keeping wild chinook and coho salmon.

McEachern said one of the most common violations relates to coho salmon retention. Hatchery coho are intentionally marked by fishery managers through the removal of their adipose fin, making them distinguishable from wild coho, which often must be released. He said officers regularly encounter cases where anglers unintentionally keep wild coho during hatchery-only openings.

"There are specific times of the year that you can only retain hatchery coho," McEachern said. "It is a common violation because people are excited, they're catching a fish, but they're not taking the extra time to properly identify whether it is a hatchery coho or a wild coho, and they're unintentionally retaining wild coho when it's not open for retention." Hatchery coho can grow to around 12 pounds, making them especially appealing to anglers, he added.

McEachern said these kinds of errors underscore the importance of compliance education. "We found throughout the summer that compliance was lower than we had hoped, signaling that people are not doing their full research before going fishing," he said.

Penalties this year ranged from CAD 575 ($417) to CAD 1,000. In a separate case from last year's blitz, three individuals were sentenced just this year to CAD19,000 in fines for fishing in a rockfish conservation area and retaining 32 rockfish, two cabezon, a greenling and a sole species.

While McEachern confirmed that some seizures involved significant quantities of fish, officers did not find evidence of commercial intent. "All these circumstances were for personal consumption by recreational harvesters," he said.

DFO announced the conclusion of the blitz in a LinkedIn post on Wednesday (Sept. 17), highlighting its collaboration with US agencies and the role of aerial and intelligence support in the patrols.

McEachern noted that C&P continues to conduct inspections across all fisheries -- indigenous, commercial and recreational -- throughout the year. Commercial patrols are generally coordinated with openings like the June-July shrimp fishery.

"Vancouver Island is a huge area with only 40 fishery officers to cover it," he said. "We use aerial surveillance and collaborate with the Canadian Coast Guard to help fill those gaps."

Earlier this year, two commercial fishers in British Columbia were fined a combined CAD 40,000 for illegally harvesting shrimp during a seasonal closure off Vancouver Island, as Undercurrent reported.

title: US Alaska pollock sector touts reduced carbon footprint
content:
SEATTLE, Washington, USA -- New data suggests the US Alaska pollock industry has reduced its carbon emissions by nearly a fifth since 2018, making the wild-caught fish even more environmentally friendly than meat proteins like beef, chicken and pork.

Genuine Alaska Pollock Producers (GAPP), the industry's marketing agency, released preliminary research results on Thursday (Sept. 17) that show Alaska pollock caught in the US last year produced 3.09 kilograms of carbon for every kilogram of protein, a fraction of competing land-raised protein sources, including plant-based meat substitutes.

GAPP's 2025 meeting in Seattle, Alaska. Photograph courtesy of Craig Morris.

That's 18% less than the last time a similar study of US-caught Alaska pollock was undertaken, showing it produced 3.77 kg of carbon per protein kg between 2016 and 2018.

GAPP president Craig Morris has called the results "staggering" and has encouraged the US pollock industry to incorporate its findings in product messaging. 

Dalhousie University researchers Peter Tyedmers and Michelle Mann are working on an updated "life-cycle assessment" (LCA) of the US pollock sector similar to a study undertaken in 2021, as Undercurrent News reported at the time.

"The results of an LCA allow us to understand how we might reduce the environmental burdens and support sustainable decision making," Mann told attendees.

(Source: GAPP)

GAPP uses the research to underscore the environmental advantage over other protein sources, such as beef, which in 2021 was found to have 115.75 kg of carbon dioxide per kg of meat. Similarly, pork meat was responsible for 15.75 kg of carbon per equivalent protein. Chicken fared the best of the terrestrial animals with 12.5 kg per kg of protein.

Maruha accelerates solar panel installation to reduce CO2 emission by 23,000t over three years

That's according to a survey conducted by the Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada-based university in conjunction with the Monterey Bay Aquarium in California. 

The researchers have cautioned that the data was only received last month, and the model is still being refined. A full report isn't expected until early next year, with publication still nearly a year away.

"I want you to note that final transportation [carbon emissions] has been excluded from our preliminary results, but they will be included in the final report," Mann said.

Professor Tyedmers said that carbon savings are not from less consumption of fossil fuels.

Dalhousie University professor Peter Tyedmers and graduate student Michelle Mann delivered preliminary findings on Sept. 18, 2025 at the GAPP meeting in Seattle. The pair of researchers are working on an updated "life-cycle assessment" (LCA) last undertaken in 2021. (Photo by Jacob Resneck/UCN)

Rather, he posits that the change comes from the previous researcher’s assumption in 2021 about the type of refrigerant used by the industry with a relatively high climate impact.

“We have much better resolution on the refrigerant losses, both in their quantities and their types,” Tyedmers said.

But he said that doesn’t mean the industry hasn’t improved its environmental performance.

“If we were to model the way they did [in 2021], it would have the effect of further reducing the greenhouse gas emission contributions associated with the human food,” he said.

title: Tuna category gains ground in Spain, as culinary trends, inflation reshape EU dining habits
content:
VIGO, Spain -- Tuna is steadily gaining prominence in the Spanish culinary world, fueled by evolving dining trends and the growing popularity of innovative dishes, according to some local analysts.

Central to this rise is the role of sushi and poke, among other presentations, where tuna has become a star ingredient, appealing particularly to younger generations who are reshaping traditional dining categories, said Edurne Uranga -- vice president of Foodservice Europe at market consultancy Circana -- during the XII ANFACO World Tuna Conference that took place last week in Vigo, Spain.

In restaurants, tuna is no longer confined to niche menus. Its versatility has allowed it to expand across a variety of preparations, from fusion plates to high-end gastronomy, according to Uranga. The analyst suggested that this is only the beginning, with tuna expected to cement its position as a staple in modern dining experiences.

A tuna dish at a restaurant in Vigo, Spain. Photo: Undercurrent News.

This evolution reflects broader shifts in consumer behavior. People are visiting restaurants less frequently due to new lifestyles, yet when they do, they are willing to spend more, Uranga said. Diners demand higher quality, authenticity, and creativity, leading them to embrace ingredients like tuna, she claimed.

On the retail side, the trend diverges. According to NielsenIQ analyst Miguel Barreiro, consumers are becoming more price-conscious, buying fewer items per visit and prioritizing "rationalized consumption."

This contrast highlights how the restaurant channel, rather than supermarkets, is emerging as the key arena where tuna's popularity can flourish.

Global foodservice spending hits $1.6 trillion

Uranga said the global foodservice industry's consumer spending reached over $1.6 trillion over the past year, growing 2.7% year-on-year.

This gain was driven not only by inflation but also by a rise in traffic and consumption occasions, she said. 

"This isn't just about price hikes," she stated. "What's most interesting is that growth comes from more 'eating-out' occasions. Even in difficult economic times, consumers are visiting restaurants less frequently due to new lifestyles, like for example the post-pandemic work-from-home habit, but spending more, she pointed out.

In Europe alone, of the €900 billion ($1.1tr) spent on food and beverages last year, 40% went to foodservice and immediate consumption, including restaurants and delivery, but also vending and hot food counters. 

Uranga also explained that while pre-COVID-19 pandemic traffic hasn't fully recovered, it is not due to a slowdown in demand but a shift in routine. 

"Our daily lives have changed. Hybrid work and fewer commutes have altered when and where we eat. We spend more per visit now, even if we go out slightly less," she said. "This is the new normal, not a temporary dip."

Private label canned tuna continues to surge

Barreiro highlighted the resilience of Spain's private label canned tuna market amid shifting consumer habits and economic pressures. 

Volume growth remains modest, driven by demographic changes such as smaller households and an aging population. Barreiro noted that these trends are reshaping food baskets toward smaller, more affordable formats.

Private labels now account for 51% of retail food sales in Spain, one of the highest levels in Europe, outpacing even Germany. 

Promotional activity has increased, though efficiency remains limited, with only 32% of promotions delivering meaningful volume gains. While still small at 7.1% of total sales, online retail is expanding rapidly with 18% growth, offering fresh opportunities for distribution brands.

Barreiro stressed that affordability remains top of mind for Spanish retail sector consumers. Despite slower price growth, food basket costs are still 8% above 2022 levels. He noted that many households are trading down to retailer brands and lower prices.

Looking ahead, innovation and omnichannel development will be critical, according to Barreiro.

Despite the challenging environment, with canned tuna benefiting from renewed demand and health-conscious consumers seeking sustainable, convenient options, Barreiro forecasts steady organic growth for 2025-2026 if the industry can align with evolving consumption moments and lifestyle shifts.

title: Untitled
content:
American millennials are helping turn salmon into an everyday protein, not just a special occasion dish -- a trend that could add 300,000 metric tons of demand in the United States alone, according to one industry veteran.

Gianfranco Nattero, a former longtime Mowi executive who now oversees international sales for Chilean exporter Sea Garden, told investors at the IX Aquaculture Investment Workshop in Panama City, Panama, last week that global producers are unprepared to meet the surge.

Import data underscores that trend. US purchases of Atlantic salmon have climbed steadily over the past decade, with Chile, Canada and Norway the dominant suppliers.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view

Per-capita consumption in the US has doubled since 2010 to nearly 2 kilos, but still trails European markets, where consumption averages about 3 kilos. "That's one kilo more per person, and with 300 million people, it's an additional 300,000t," he said.

Global production is unlikely to keep pace, however. Expansion faces limits across major producing countries: Norway is constrained by resource taxes and site restrictions; in Canada, government-mandated farm closures have driven a 41% decline in British Columbia, once the country's main salmon-producing province; and Chile continues to struggle with relocation and regulatory hurdles. Indigenous and coastal community opposition also weighs heavily in both Chile and Canada. Forecasts show global salmon supply growth slowing from 27% in the previous decade to just 17% over the next six years, Nattero noted.

Compounding the squeeze are tariffs ranging from 10% to 50%, which Nattero said are driving up consumer prices and forcing some companies to absorb the added cost. While a few have passed on the increases, producers are seeing thinner returns at comparable price levels.

"We don't know what Mr. Trump can come up with tomorrow," he said, cautioning that US trade policy could suddenly shift supply flows.

Budding alternative markets

If tariffs continue to pressure the US market, exporters from Norway, Scotland, Chile and Canada may redirect volumes to alternative destinations such as China, Brazil, Russia and Mexico. Those markets, he said, have the scale to "move the needle" in global trade.

Technology is often cited as a solution, but Nattero emphasized that land-based RAS, offshore cages and confined systems are "not to replace conventional farms" but to supplement existing capacity. Whether they can scale fast enough to close the demand gap remains uncertain.

Price volatility will persist, he added, given the mix of consumer growth, policy risks and uneven supply expansion. Nattero likened the outlook to "reading a crystal ball." Producers and exporters, he said, must navigate daily swings in prices, demand and politics.

title: FAO panel rejects EU push to list eels on CITES
content:
The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) Expert Advisory Panel has concluded that a European Union proposal to list all Anguilla eel species, including Japanese and American eels, in Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) does not meet the convention's scientific criteria.

Appendix II includes species that may become threatened without trade regulation.

Reacting to the report, an official at Japan's Fisheries Agency told Undercurrent News, "FAO's assessment supports our position." However, the official cautioned that previous CITES meetings have seen listings approved even when expert panels concluded that the criteria were not met.

"We cannot afford to be complacent," the official said, adding that Japan will "continue to lobby contracting parties at every opportunity."

In its assessment of the 20th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CoP20) Proposal 35, the FAO panel found that neither Anguilla japonica nor A. rostrata satisfies the biological thresholds required for inclusion.

"The Expert Panel assesses Proposal 35 not to meet the CITES listing criteria," it stated, noting that the two commercially significant species show medium inherent productivity, large effective population sizes, and low extinction risk based on recent population viability analyses.

The panel added that "the suggested direct linking of international trade to population declines across the genus is not well supported by the evidence."

It highlighted that East Asia's national and regional management measures are "extensive and demonstrably effective," pointing to cooperative frameworks and practical species identification methods to support sustainable trade monitoring.

While acknowledging that a CITES listing might benefit regulatory harmonization, the panel cautioned that "the risks of unintended negative consequences -- including increased illegal trade, market distortions and the disruption of successful management cooperation -- are considerable."

It said that targeted conservation actions and strengthened species- and region-specific management would be more effective than a premature genus-wide listing.

For the American eel, the panel also concluded that Proposal 35 "does not appear to meet the listing criteria for CITES Appendix II."

Fisheries for glass eels and elvers are concentrated in Nova Scotia and Maine (Canada and the US), and parts of the Caribbean, while the species' range spans from Greenland to northern South America.

Because of this, the panel said, "it is likely that A. rostrata is resilient to exploitation by fisheries occurring in only a small portion of its range."

Although yellow and silver eel abundance in North America has declined by more than 50% in some areas, the population overall remains large.

"The risk of extinction posed by international trade is low," the panel concluded, warning that a CITES listing could disrupt legal fisheries and "result in increased illegal trade and hence reduced resources for population and fishery monitoring, market disruptions, and economic harm to artisanal and small-scale fishers."

Japanese eel data dispute

The panel cited comprehensive stock assessments for the Japanese eel, indicating that populations are currently at 22–24% of carrying capacity, above precautionary thresholds defined under CITES criteria, and showing signs of recovery since the 1990s.

The panel estimated the effective population size at about 20,000, which it said is sufficient to avoid immediate genetic risks.

It criticized the EU proposal for "selective reliance" on localized studies while omitting more robust regional assessments, saying "the proposal fails to offer robust evidence demonstrating a clear, documented link between trade and stock decline."

EU proposal, Asian opposition

The FAO review comes after the European Commission formally adopted a proposal in June to seek international trade restrictions for all 18 eel species under CITES.

If adopted at the upcoming CoP20 in Uzbekistan, the listing would require export permits for all eel shipments, likely restricting trade in glass eels and processed products such as kabayaki, a style of grilled eel glazed with a sweet soy-based sauce.

Japanese officials told Undercurrent earlier this year that the measure would "severely impact East Asia's eel industry and threaten the availability of a culturally significant food."

In 2024, Japan's consumption reached about 63,000 metric tons, with roughly 70% sourced from China as live eels or grilled kabayaki.

The Fisheries Agency estimated mature biomass at around 17,000t, or 22% of the original stock size, exceeding the CITES listing threshold of 5–20%. Officials said the extinction risk is less than 0.02%, calling it negligible.

Japan has disputed EU claims of sharp stock declines, saying reported glass eel catch reductions are due to improved aquaculture survival rates, industry consolidation and changes in statistical definitions rather than resource depletion.

It also rejected the EU's concerns about illegal trade, saying "European and Japanese eels have completely separate habitats and do not mix. Glass eels have unique morphological features that are verified when they are stocked."

Since 2014, Japan, China, South Korea, and Taiwan have managed glass eel stocking under a joint framework. At their most recent meeting in Shizuoka in June, the four sides agreed to keep the 2025–26 quota unchanged at 78.8t, with allocations of 36t for China, 21.7t for Japan, 11.1t for South Korea and 10t for Taiwan.

In a joint statement, they reaffirmed commitments to conservation and scientific research, endorsed plans to continue traceability improvements and warned that the EU plan "might risk undermining" the region's existing framework.

title: Canadian shrimp vessel fined CAD 40K for illegal fishing in glass sponge reef
content:
A fishing vessel owner has been fined CAD 40,000 ($28,900) for illegally setting shrimp traps in a marine refuge area off the coast of the Canadian province British Columbia.

Lien Bich Thi Dang, 66, the Vancouver, BC-based license holder and owner of the BC Spirit, was sentenced last week in North Vancouver Provincial Court after pleading guilty to two violations of Canada’s Pacific fisheries regulations, local news outlet North Shore News reported.

Investigators found that, in May and June 2022, crew members set shrimp traps on seven occasions in two marine refuges in Howe Sound, a fjord located north of Vancouver. The areas are closed to bottom-contact fishing to protect fragile glass sponge reefs -- ancient reef-building organisms once thought extinct that were rediscovered off the Pacific coast in the 1980s.

A glass sponge species, Venus flower basket. Photo: NOAA

In submissions to the court, federal prosecutor Nick Elson said the reefs filter billions of liters of seawater and store carbon in ways comparable to old-growth forests. Because they are made of silica, they can take up to 200 years to recover, he said. A shrimp trap hitting a reef “virtually always” causes harm, he said.

In addition to the fine, Dang received a one-day fishing ban on the opening day of the 2026 commercial shrimp season, which is typically the most lucrative day of the short three-week harvest.

Authorities noted that, while Dang had instructed the crew to avoid the closure zones, the vessel’s GPS had not been updated to show them.

title: Ex-Pacific fisheries commission bookkeeper jailed over $211K embezzlement
content:
A US federal judge has sentenced Pamela Kahut, the former chief financial officer of the Pacific States Marine Fisheries Commission (PSMFC), to eight months in prison for embezzling funds from the interstate agency that helps manage Pacific fisheries.

Kahut, 68, of Wilsonville, Oregon, had worked at the PSMFC for decades and pleaded guilty to stealing roughly $211,000 over six years to pay for her spouse's long-term care annual premiums, repay pension loans and consumer debt, according to a statement from the US Attorney's Office. 

US District Court judge Karin Immergut for the District of Oregon also ordered Kahut to repay the amount in full, fined her $10,000 and ordered her to spend three years of probation following her scheduled release from a federal prison.

The Portland, Oregon-based PSMFC is best known for distributing federal disaster funding to commercial harvesters and processors. But it also monitors fishing activities and collects data for the seafood industry in the US states of Alaska, Washington, Oregon, California, Idaho and Hawaii.

Barry Thom, executive director of the PSMFC, said at the sentencing hearing that Kahut's theft had eroded trust among commission employees as he urged the judge to send her to prison as part of her sentence, The Oregonian newspaper reported.

Thom added that the organization officials went through a period of disbelief that a longtime and respected employee would break their trust, the newspaper reported, followed by anger when evidence of the breach became impossible to deny. 

He said commission leaders also had discovered another $400,000 missing this spring, suggesting her embezzlement activities could be wider than investigators had succeeded in uncovering, the newspaper reported.

The newspaper reported that Kahut told the court she will feel "shame and guilt" for the rest of her life. She reportedly said her crime stemmed from "a personal situation" that had gotten out of control. 

"I always thought I could solve things on my own," the newspaper quoted her as telling the judge.

title: Nordic startup Ocean Next to transform fish waste into gourmet products
content:
Sweden's Ocean Next, a newly launched company under the Ocean Collective group, has announced plans to commercialize a new line of sustainable seafood products made from traditionally discarded fish parts.

Salmon Evolution strikes Swedish smokehouse partnership

In partnership with Finnish foodtech pioneer Superground, Ocean Next will turn undervalued fish components -- such as bones and hard tissues -- into products like fish nuggets, burgers, and fish balls.

The initiative is part of a wider push to reduce food waste and accelerate sustainable production across the Nordic region.

Production will be based in Falkenberg, Sweden, drawing on the craftsmanship and heritage of Korshags Food, another subsidiary of the group. 

"During the past year, we've explored how this novel method can unlock new value from what was once considered waste," said Jorgen Bergqvist, CEO of Ocean Collective and executive chairman of both Korshags Food and Ocean Next.

"We see real potential in turning these refined materials into tasty, cost-effective products that don't compromise on quality or sustainability," he added.

A long-term goal for Korshags and Ocean Next is to make seafood production fully regenerative within a few years, a step beyond sustainability, aimed at restoring ecosystems and improving overall ocean health.

"We're excited to scale this innovation with Ocean Next," said Jaakko Kaminen, CEO of Superground. "Our shared mission is to make a tangible impact, not just in the Nordics, but eventually in global markets as well."

title: Aquaculture Stewardship Council grants timely reprieve on sustainable feed requirements
content:
The Aquaculture Stewardship Council (ASC) has approved a variance allowing aquaculture farms more breathing room to meet its aquafeed standard. The decision comes after industry complaints about difficulties sourcing sufficient ASC-certified feed.

Originally rolled out in 2022 and formally launched in 2023, ASC's feed standard is used to certify aquafeed-producing feed mills and their ingredient suppliers. In February 2025, ASC extended a deadline requiring ASC-certified farms to use ASC-conforming feed from January 2025 to the end of October 2025. 

The variance, approved June 16, allows aquaculture firms a one-time exemption for sourcing feed not certified by the ASC beyond its original Oct. 31 deadline, with several caveats, ASC senior communications manager Gaynyr Dickson told Undercurrent News.

"The variance should not be considered as an extension of the Oct. 31, 2025, deadline but provides specific non-conformity closure timelines for different circumstances," Dickson said.

Applicants for certification face a cascading series of consequences if they remain short of 100% compliance following the cutoff date, but penalties have been scaled back as a result of the variance.

If applicants for ASC certification hit the 75% conformity threshold for sourcing ASC-feed, they now have 18 additional months to reach full compliance, or they receive a minor non-conformity (NC) warning.

If they are under 75% compliance, they receive a major NC warning if they haven't not made any effort to engage non-certified feed suppliers to ascertain the possibility of obtaining ASC-certified feed. Companies can submit a variance request showing evidence of limitations of the commercial availability of ASC-certified feed, which must include proof of an agreement by their feed supplier to pursue ASC certification.

If their request is approved, companies are awarded another 24 months to reach compliance before facing a minor NC penalty. If their variance request is rejected, they only receive 12 months to comply before being hit with a minor NC.

Multiple minor NCs can be upgraded to major NCs by certification bodies, and companies are typically given three to nine months to resolve major NCs before their ASC certification is suspended.

"If non-conformities are not closed in the defined deadlines and conformance is not demonstrated, the sanctions will escalate until the suspension of the farm certificate," Dickson said.

While 35 feed mills in 14 countries are now ASC-certified, as Undercurrent has reported, including plants operated by Skretting, Cargill, BioMar and CP Foods, Dickson acknowledged there is not enough ASC-approved feed to satisfy demand.

"The publication of the variance request recognises the challenges in some species and geographies in achieving the requirement," she said.

Brian Ahlers, the technical sales manager for sustainable seafood at certification body SCS Global Services and a longtime seafood sustainability specialist, praised ASC's move in a LinkedIn post.

"One of things I appreciate about the new ASC feed standard is that it meets the aquafeed industry where they are at, while offering a framework for continuous improvement. Given the current challenges of auditor shortages, raw material shortages, meeting market demand will remain a challenge for the foreseeable future, and this variation request offers much-needed flexibility," Ahlers wrote.

title: Cooke Chile CEO ramps up criticism of SMA salmon farm sanctions, calls them ‘illegal,’ damaging to industry trust
content:
Cooke Aquaculture Chile CEO Andres Parodi has escalated his company's criticism of Chile's (Superintendencia del Medio Ambiente, or SMA) for its recent closure of two salmon farms and $1.4 million fine. 

SMA on Aug. 22 added the fine to its earlier decision to close the farms in the Aysen region after finding that the Canadian seafood giant broke several environmental laws. It said it found Cooke committed a combined eight environmental violations at its Punta Garrao, Huillines 2 and Huillines 3 farm site sites.

The ruling led to a strongly worded response from Cooke last week, as reported by Undercurrent News. But that wasn't the last word from the company on the matter.

In a series of public statements issued this week, including several detailed posts on LinkedIn, Parodi, the Canadian seafood giant's head of its Chilean operations, accused the SMA of acting as "judge and party" in a flawed process that, he claimed, disregards evidence and violates the company's legal rights.

"It was quite obvious that we would be sanctioned, since in this process the SMA acts as both prosecutor and judge. A flawed system," Parodi wrote. "This sanction is, in our view, expropriatory, arbitrary, illegal, discriminatory, ideological, disproportionate, and divorced from science and the law."

Cooke decries Chilean gov’t order to close two salmon farms, add $1.4m environmental fine

Cooke has vowed to appeal the SMA decision, and Parodi pushed back on the regulator's claims, insisting that the farms were operating legally under concessions granted in the 1990s and that Cooke had never caused environmental harm.

"The Cooke team acted in good faith, always with 100% of the necessary sectoral permits, without causing damage to the environment, and always willing to cooperate with authorities," Parodi said.

"We will keep appealing and trust that at some point, justice will be served, because we are in the right," he added.

He also rejected what he described as regulators' and environmental organizations' misuse of the term "environmental damage," claiming that expert reports commissioned by the SMA itself found no ecological harm.

"What a misuse of the word' environment.' They want to suggest the company caused damage, which simply isn't true," he wrote. "According to experts selected by the SMA itself, no harm occurred, but we are still guilty, it seems."

Parodi's LinkedIn post reflects growing frustration within Cooke, which has already threatened to reconsider its future in Chile if the current regulatory environment continues.

He warned that the SMA's approach could set a dangerous precedent for Chile's entire aquaculture sector.

"With the same argument, the SMA could shut down 30% of Chile's aquaculture concessions. This is an ideologized institution, blinded by unchecked power, while other authorities remain silent in the face of this arbitrariness," he said.

Cooke accuses Chilean regulator of overreach in salmon farm suspension

Parodi also took aim at the environmental NGOs that supported the sanctions, criticizing what he described as a lack of transparency about their funding and motives.

"They have clearly succeeded in permeating state institutions with their anti-business agenda, twisting the concept of environmental protection to position themselves on one side and companies on the other."

Cooke again reiterated that its operations at the Huillines sites were based on valid concessions defined by specific geographic coordinates and challenged critics to prove that the farms were within the park's boundaries. It also emphasized the firm had reached an agreement with Chilean authorities in 2023 to relocate the concessions voluntarily, but the SMA's sanctions disregarded both that agreement and the company's regulatory compliance.

"What is truly illogical? Our reaction of shock and disappointment, or a 200-page sanction, full of ideology and vendetta, imposed despite our full compliance and a good-faith agreement to leave the area?" Parodi stated.

He then concluded by urging the Chilean government to step in, particularly Chile's finance minister, Nicolas Grau, who was part of the original agreement to coordinate state agencies and respect acquired rights while relocation processes unfolded.

"How can anyone invest in Chile if a formal commitment signed by four ministers and undersecretaries means nothing in the SMA's of SMA's abuse? Now, as finance minister, Grau has the chance to show that the pledged word still has "value," he said.

title: FDA approvals in hand, US lab-grown salmon startup looks for partners
content:
SAN FRANCISCO, California – There's a modern miracle at work inside a former 13,000-square-foot microbrewery in this city's "Dogpatch" neighborhood on an industrial waterfront.  

A towering stainless steel 3,500-liter fermenter is no longer used to brew ales and lager. Instead, it's mixing the liquid diet of cell-cultivated coho salmon destined for dinner plates in upscale restaurants.

Wildtype produces the nation's first -- and so far only -- lab-grown seafood approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for human consumption, something that happened in May, as Undercurrent News reported.

The steel tanks from the Magnolia Brewery -- shuttered in 2022 to make way for the seafood tech startup -- are still in use, growing coho salmon cells. The brewery's once busy sports bar has been repurposed into a demonstration kitchen.

A Wildtype lab technician prepares a feeding solution on Aug. 20 at the San Francisco, California, startup's facility producing the first "cell-cultivated seafood" approved for sale in the US. Photograph by Jacob Resneck.

"We didn't actually have to do too much to the space, which was cool," co-founder Justin Kolbeck told Undercurrent during a recent visit. "We added some nautical themes to make it less sportsbar-y. But it had great bones that you could build on."

Co-founded by Arye Elfenbein, a cardiologist, and Kolbeck, a former US diplomat, the fledgling company initially made waves when it reported raking in more than $120 million in seed money from a slew of investors that included such Hollywood celebrities and business titans as Leonardo DiCaprio, Robert Downey Jr. and Jeff Bezos, as Undercurrent reported. 

But Wildtype is keeping the door open to finding manufacturing partners or licensing its technology to firms that can bring lab-grown salmon to a larger market.

"We need bigger scale so we can spread our fixed costs over bigger sales volumes," Kolbeck said. 

"We're really proud of this place," he continued. "But this is not our core strength, like building manufacturing plants. Other companies are probably better than us at that."

Now that the company has regulatory approvals and recently added a fourth restaurant that has agreed to use its "cell-cultivated" coho sashimi and lox, it needs to prove it can produce on an economic scale, Kolbeck said.

"The price that we're selling to the restaurant, we are losing money, partially because we're just not at full capacity yet," he conceded. 

But that's because production is limited to just 5-10 metric tons annually in this converted former microbrewery as part of a proof-of-concept effort rather than in a full-blown production facility, he said.

Resistance to lab-grown meats from ag interests

Wildtype boasts plenty of other market advantages in addition to its federal approval.

By not having to cast nets in the ocean, the company is able to brag that it promotes the conservation of species. It also discards no animal byproduct or waste, a key differentiator from aquaculture or cloning, according to the company.

"We will take the cell and rather than growing it into a fish, we just grow it into sashimi or a fillet -- and that's the main difference," Elfenbein said

Still, domestic political headwinds exist, with Indiana recently becoming at least the sixth US state to ban lab-grown meat and seafood, joining Florida, Mississippi, Nebraska, Alabama and Texas, as Undercurrent has reported.

Bans in US states threaten to stifle cell-based seafood before it reaches market

Even though these laws target meat producers, Wildtype's FDA-approved cultivated seafood is included in the new bans.

"We've gone to speak at these legislatures," Elfenbein said. "This is a totally different thing."

A law recently passed by the Texas legislature will force sushi restaurant Otoko in the state capital, Austin, to stop serving Wildtype seafood when a two-year ban takes effect next month. Lawmakers in the Lone Star State approved the ban because of concerns that the nascent lab-grown meat industry could disrupt traditional livestock markets, family farms and product labeling, the Texas Tribune reported.

The political clout of the US beef and pork industry is formidable in agricultural states in the US heartland. The governor of Nebraska's family controls one of the largest pork producers in the state, for example.

"So he's not interested in having more competition," Kolbeck said.

'We're not going to be precious about it'

Meanwhile, expansion continues with Wildtype's coho salmon being added to the menu at The Walrus and the Carpenter, an upscale eatery in Seattle, Washington, the unofficial capital of the Pacific Northwest fishing industry, as Undercurrent reported.

Its coho salmon cells are raised from specimens collected at a fish hatchery in Washington state. But unlike hatchery fish, which are ranched in the open ocean, or aquaculture-raised fish grown in net-pens over their two-year life-cycle, Wildtype's coho fillets are grown in weeks.

Wildtype supplies in-house smoked coho salmon lox raised from the cells cultivated in a laboratory in San Francisco, California, USA to upscale eateries following its approval by US regulators certifying its seafood as fit for human consumption. (Photo courtesy of Wildtype)

But even that quick turnaround doesn't allow Wildtype to compete with wild-caught salmon or farm-raised coho due to the company's modest scale. 

Widltype has refined its production methods -- its signature liquid feed costs have plummeted a hundredfold to around $1/liter. However, the founders believe it is time to expand by constructing a purpose-built production facility or licensing its methods.

"We're not going to be precious about it," Kolbeck said. "If there are other seafood companies that want to use this tech, we're really happy about that."

Kolbeck said that's because the co-founders are under no illusion that they can produce commercial seafood at scale inside the confines of a small craft brewery.

"It's hard to make money as a microbrewery," Kolbeck said. "The same thing is true for a microfishery."

title: The RAS ecosystem is still growing and attracting multi-industry suppliers
content:
If the AquaNor conference in Trondheim feels busier this year, we might have land-based aquaculture to thank. Investment in the industry exceeded $1.3 billion during the first half of 2025 and could top $2 billion by the end of the year, according to the Land-based Aquaculture Report published by Spheric Research.

Renewed investor interest in a sector whose viability was heavily questioned just a few years ago is underpinned by encouraging results at a new generation of producers.

Norway’s Hima Seafood started harvesting fish at its 8,000 metric ton per year trout farm, while Danish Salmon and Nordic Aqua Partners are operating at close to full capacity, according to recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) consultant Ivar Warrer Hansen. 

Money and early signs of success are attracting more suppliers including specialized aquaculture players and companies from related industries like water treatment. The Land-based Aquaculture Report’s supplier database swelled to 212 companies, from 144 in last year’s edition.

Western Europe and North America are home to more than two thirds of suppliers. Norway tops the list with 46 companies or 22% of the database thanks to a domestic salmon farming industry that spent heavily on land-based smolt production and a cluster of RAS-focused integrators, engineering firms, and equipment providers.

Asian suppliers have yet to establish a significant presence in the land-based aquaculture space but that could quickly change.

China is rapidly becoming a force in aquaculture equipment and services just as it has in other industries. At least six suppliers currently hail from China, up from just one last year.

Four of those companies specialize in filtration and water treatment equipment, which should come as no surprise given Beijing is enforcing strict discharge and recycling rules for water-intensive industries like aquaculture.  

South Korea is also on our radar with the number of suppliers tripling, admittedly from a low base, to three firms amid a flurry of RAS investments in the last two years.

Multi-industry companies -- municipal water treatment, industrial automation, etc -- that adapted their products and services for land-based aquaculture totaled 90 firms or 42% of suppliers. Their influence is particularly strong in areas like filtration and water treatment, flow solutions, construction, and oxygenation.  

Companies dedicated almost exclusively to RAS technology accounted for almost a third of the database with 68 firms of which 38 are integrators that deliver turnkey RAS post-smolt and grow-out facilities. RAS post-smolt used to be the most lucrative business, but that is changing now that investors are committing billions of dollars to grow-out projects.

Multi-aquaculture suppliers -- those with a broader aquaculture portfolio but a defined RAS offering-- represented 25% of the total with 53 firms. They are most visible in mature categories such as feed and genetics where established aquaculture suppliers are adapting their traditional products for land-based farms.

The growing number of suppliers should lead to a stronger and more robust supply chain with multiple benefits.

Competition is rarely a bad thing. Integrators will have a larger choice of supporting infrastructure to choose from when designing turnkey facilities. The opportunity to adapt existing technologies with a proven track record in other industries should lessen the need to develop expensive boutique solutions.

All of that should benefit the cost-structure of land-based projects through skilled labor and commodities prices will remain wild cards.

At the end of the day land-based producers will need to show they can operate profitably at or near full capacity to keep money and suppliers flocking to the sector.

title: ISSF finds minimal lift in large-scale tropical tuna purse seine capacity
content:
A new report from the International Seafood Sustainability Foundation (ISSF) has found only a marginal lift in the global large-scale tropical tuna purse seine (known as LSPS) fishing fleet year-on-year.

The authors estimate that, as of June 2025, 675 LSPS vessels are fishing for tropical tuna species -- an increase of 3.8% compared to last year -- with a combined fish hold volume (FHV) of 864,700 cubic meters, representing a less than 0.2% increase from last year in overall fishing capacity. 

Tuna sales boost Bolton’s turnover, profit in 2024

"ISSF is the only organization that aggregates and analyzes global capacity data for these fleets year over year,” said Victor Restrepo, ISSF's vice president of science. "Our snapshot series provides science-based insights to support RFMO [regional fisheries management organization] and industry decision-making on sustainable tuna fishing capacity management -- an issue central to long-term ocean health.”

LSPS vessels, defined as those with at least 335 cubic meters in FHV, account for the majority of the world’s tropical tuna catch. To update the report, ISSF compiles data from RFMO vessel registries and other sources, focusing on vessels targeting skipjack, yellowfin, and bigeye tuna.

There were 47 LSPS vessels built after 2012 added to RFMO-authorized vessel lists since the 2024 report, including 11 newly built in 2024 and 2025. More than half are flagged to Indonesia and hover near the 335-cubic-meter threshold, said ISSF.

Nine LSPS vessels were removed from the fishery due to scrapping or sinking between 2024 and 2025, underscoring the need to account for vessel removals alongside new additions when evaluating fleet capacity, it said. 

Then, 498 of the 675 LSPS vessels (74%) are now listed on ISSF’s independently audited ProActive Vessel Register, representing 83% of the total FHV. The register is a voluntary transparency tool highlighting vessel practices that support sustainable tuna fisheries. 

South Korea’s Dongwon to ramp up overseas pet food capacity, eyes StarKist Samoa hub

For the first time, the report presents a trend analysis of flag state designations over time, showing that LSPS vessels flagged to developing or emerging economies now outnumber those flagged to developed ones by a ratio of 3.47 -- more than double the ratio in the first snapshot released in 2012.

The estimated total number of all tuna purse-seine vessels worldwide rose by 9%, from 1,939 in 2024 to 2,106 in 2025. The Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission region continues to host the largest number of LSPS vessels (332).

ISSF recommended that vessel owners and RFMO expand their International Maritime Organisation Number use; adoption of the system has grown from 12% in 2011 to 99% today.

It also said greater quality control in RFMO vessel registry submissions is needed to address data gaps, and that all RFMOs should maintain not only lists of authorized vessels but also records of vessels actively fishing each year.

You can find the report here.

title: Spain’s Jealsa part of Cape Verde tuna plant takeover
content:
Spanish canning giant Jealsa Foods is reportedly considering investing in a tuna plant in Mindelo, Cape Verde, formerly owned by Vigo-based Atunes y Lomos (Atunlo).

Frescomar, part of the Ubago group, took over Atunlo's plant in Mindelo early in 2025, with Atunlo facing imminent bankruptcy as it struggled to secure enough support for its restructuring plan.

Atunlo has since been liquidated, ending an 18-year run as one of Spain's largest tuna suppliers.

Jealsa's move would be made in collaboration with Frescomar in a bid to reinforce its presence in West Africa and secure access to a key raw material supply hub.

But Jealsa told Undercurrent News that Ubago is leading the project, and declined to add any additional details, stressing that at this stage, it is only "a project." 

Spain’s largest tuna seller to liquidate as debt restructuring fails

Ubago also told Undercurrent it was premature to explain any details at this stage. "At this time, the project is not fully defined," it said.

The plant spans 7,190 square meters and can handle vessel unloading, sorting, and re-shipment. Production could focus on frozen raw tuna and raw tuna that is gutted and filleted, with a daily capacity of 80 metric tons of whole fish, according to sources.

The facilities would be managed by a consortium of companies led by Frescomar, "along with two other Spanish companies," according to Cape Verde publication A Nacao.

The project would create 200 direct jobs, primarily benefiting local women, Voz de Galicia reported earlier this year.

Spain’s Atunlo liquidated, Tunagrove moves to take over remaining assets

In Cape Verde, Atunlo operated a government-owned meatpacking and tuna processing plant employing around 350 people, according to Voz de Galicia. By February 2025, workers had gone four months without pay or social security contributions. Atunlo owned 51% of the plant, with Frescomar and Frigove holding 33% and 16%, respectively.

To address the crisis, state-owned Portos de Cabo Verde (Enapor) stepped in to cover the workers' six months of back wages and social security. Enapor is expected to continue paying salaries until a new private operator takes over. The company is also suing Atunlo's insurer for €650,000, according to Voz de Galicia.

Enapor has stated that a new operator will soon take over. Government teams have begun inspecting the long-shuttered plant, which reportedly needs some investment to restart operations.

title: Greenland’s cod stocks show positive signs
content:
Greenland's cod stocks are showing signs of recovery and stability, with both inshore and offshore populations assessed as healthy and well above biological reference points, according to the Greenland Institute of Natural Resources (GINR).

Newspaper Sermitsiaq has reported that GINR and the government have set higher quotas for 2025, reflecting improved stock health and advances in scientific assessment methods.

Iceland’s new position as world’s top cod supplier sees EU buyers flooding domestic auction

For West Greenland, the inshore cod quota has been set at 27,572 metric tons, including 2,000t reserved for recreational fishing.

Offshore quotas have also seen a significant bump, with West Greenland at 6,500t (up 2,100t from 2024) and East Greenland at 35,000t, divided between the Dohrn Bank and Southeast Greenland.

These increases come after more refined stock assessments based on genetic data and improved geographic modeling.

Then, the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea has released its 2026 advice, offering more cautious recommendations of 4,336t for West Greenland's inshore-spawning cod, 4,708t for West Greenland's offshore cod, and 23,518t for the East Greenland and Iceland offshore cod.

Greenland has also adopted a new cod management plan as of January 2025, aimed at improving long-term sustainability, especially in the context of mixed-stock fisheries.

GINR credits genetic stock identification and spatial distribution modeling with sharpening its ability to distinguish between overlapping cod populations -- a major challenge in recent years. These tools are now integrated into the government's fisheries decision-making framework.
