title: Morrisons’ supplier Falfish back in black, stable profit at other processor
content:
The seafood operations of Myton Food Group -- UK retailer Wm Morrison Supermarkets' food manufacturing business -- enjoyed a good 2024 financial year, with one factory increasing its profit after tax and the Falfish operation turning from a loss to a profit.

Morrisons reorganized its food manufacturing and processing assets, including its fish-processing plant in Grimsby and fruit-packing facilities, into a newly defined standalone entity called Myton Food in 2023.

Cornwall-based Falfish, which Morrisons acquired in 2021, sources and processes fish and shellfish from auctions and partner vessels, as well as importing.

The 52 weeks ended Oct. 27, 2024, saw turnover stable at £49.6 million ($65.9m), though cost of sales rose to the extent that gross profit was £1.9m, down year-on-year from £4.9m.

Still, administrative expenses were dramatically reduced, with profit before tax rising from £578,000 to £1.7m. Profit after tax was £303,000, compared to a 2023 loss of £92,000.

It does appear that this change has come, at least in part, from a change in account, with the company noting:

"For the periods covered by these financial statements, the group [meaning Morrisons and its subsidiaries] managed its manufacturing business using a cost center model. Goods sold between the manufacturing and retail operations were transferred at cost plus a standard margin; this reflects the way the business was operated."

"It is anticipated that it will transition to a profit center model in the future. As part of the ongoing transition, a review of the cost allocation methodology has been performed in the period, resulting in costs in the profit and loss account being reclassified compared to the presentation in previous years, particularly between cost of sales and administrative expenses."

Then, at Grimsby-based processor International Seafoods, there was a similar drop in administrative expenses in return for a hike in cost of sales.

Turnover lifted from £151.2m to £159.1m, while gross profit fell from £7.9m to £4.0m as a result of the higher costs of sales.

Operating profit rose from £2.0m to £2.7m, while profit after tax was £2.8m, up a little from £2.2m in 2023.

Late in 2024, Morrisons -- which has been owned by US private equity Clayton, Dubilier & Rice (CD&R) since 2021 -- parted with seafood veteran Phil Nickells, who had been running buying for International Seafoods. He said on LinkedIn that the role had been made redundant.

He recently resurfaced in a short-term role as an operations consultant for New England Seafood International. His exit came the year after CD&R's Morrisons launched Myton Food.

title: Untitled
content:
Capelin suppliers in the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador (NL) are asking East Asian buyers to pay record-high prices for frozen roe-bearing fish from the 2025 season, citing reduced competition from Iceland and Norway as justification for offers that multiple importers describe as "unrealistic."

 A major packer began approaching buyers in early July with initial cost-and-freight (CFR) offers, which have since been followed by other processors.

Icelandic mackerel packers push record high prices amid quota cuts, tight inventories

According to multiple sources, the initial offers, quoted on a CFR basis, stand at $6.00 per kilogram for sizes under 40 fish/kg, $5.60/kg for 41–45, $5.20/kg for 46–50,  $4.80/kg for 51–55, $4.40/kg for 56–60 and $4.00/kg for 61–65.

The prices assume a 100% female ratio and are subject to downward adjustment depending on actual female content, which typically ranges between 70% and 100%.

The offers represent a substantial increase from the previous season, when prices ranged from the upper $2.00s to the mid-$3.00s per kilogram, depending on size, according to the sources.

This year's landings are unusually weighted toward larger sizes, particularly 46/50 and 51/55 count, a Tokyo-based Japanese buyer told Undercurrent News.

Canadian producers are marketing their product into a tightening global supply environment.

Norway has not opened its capelin season in recent years, and Iceland set a quota of just 8,589 metric tons for the 2024/25 season.

As a result, prices for Icelandic roe capelin -- particularly "high-grade mix" lots with around 80% female content -- have surged to between $4.10/kg and $4.20/kg CFR, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

East Asian demand

Newfoundland's roe capelin is primarily exported to East Asia.

In Japan, it is processed into salted-dried products for retail and foodservice. In China and Taiwan, the fish is also sold frozen in small cartons for use in barbeque and street food.

"While larger fish are preferred in some markets, budget-conscious buyers are largely opting for smaller sizes this season," said the Tokyo-based buyer source.

Referring to the Canadian offers, the same buyer described them as "asking for what doesn't exist," adding that prices at these levels are "beyond reach" for most buyers, including in Japan, and that drawn-out negotiations and eventual price corrections are likely.

"Most companies here are sitting on leftover low-cost raw material from last season and are simply waiting for the Iceland season to start again," he said. "No one wants to -- or can -- commit to the high Canadian offers at present."

A second Japanese buyer was more blunt, calling the Canadian offers "wishful thinking."

"These are not prices that Japan or many other countries can realistically afford," he said. "This is shaping up to be a long game toward price correction."

A third source in Japan pointed out that a large volume of Icelandic capelin remains in cold storage, removing any urgency to actively procure NL fish at current prices.

"Most of the current Icelandic stock has low female ratios and is unsuitable for the Japanese salted-dried market," said the second source, however.

Icelandic roe capelin prices hit record high on tiny supply

The prospect of a new anticipated supply also encourages East Asian buyers to hold back, as Iceland's Marine and Freshwater Research Institute (MFRI) has issued a preliminary recommendation of a 46,384t quota for the 2025/26 season.

The figure by MFRI is only an early advisory and will likely change depending on upcoming resource assessments, the second source said. 

A Chinese secondary processor echoed the concerns, telling Undercurrent that "it might be more cost-effective to buy the fish from other importers in the country."

He cited recent cases where Icelandic prices declined after domestic resale, saying, "This might happen to Canadian fish too."

Regarding the cost of procuring Newfoundland capelin for the Japanese market, the second Japanese buyer told Undercurrent that "both importers and end-buyers are limited, so we are unable to disclose any information about procurement costs at this stage."

The UCN trade portal shows that Canadian capelin ranks as the third-largest source of Japan's capelin imports, following Norway and Iceland.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view

Meanwhile, dock prices for NL's 2025 capelin fishery have also increased sharply.

According to the Fish, Food and Allied Workers Union (FFAW), which represents fishermen in the province, harvesters secured a minimum dockside price of CAD 0.40 per pound for grade A fish.

That grade is defined as 55 count or smaller, with no more than 10% feed content and a minimum of 40% usable females, with females under 5.25 inches counted as males for grading. Capelin must also contain at least 23% roe.

The minimum guaranteed dock prices by specification for Newfoundland and Labrador capelin in the 2025 season. Screenshot from the FFAW's website

This marks a significant increase from the CAD 0.25/lb minimum set in both 2023 and 2024.

Last year, six processors -- Barry Group, Beothic Fish Processors, Golden Shell Fisheries, Labrador Fishermen's Union Shrimp Co., Bay Roberts Seafood, and Happy Adventure Sea Products -- voluntarily paid CAD 0.30/lb, with two others reportedly committing verbally, according to a FFAW statement.

Status quo quota for 2025

The season in the Canadian province is now winding down, with some major fishing zones officially closed by late July.

Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) rolled over the 2024 quotas for 2025, with a total overall quota of 24,758t.

The largest portion of that quota, 14,533t, was allocated for fishing zones 2J3KL and 3Ps, which extend from Fortune Bay on the province's south coast and the entire north east coast to the mid-Labrador shore.

As of July 26, the fishing season had wrapped up in most of that zone.

DFO reports that Bonavista Bay landed 1,883t against a quota of 543t, while Trinity Bay landed 2,142t against a 1,712t limit.

Cape Fox to Hampton and Notre Dame Bay also exceeded their allocations and closed. Only North Head to Dog Bay Point in Division 3K remained open, with 78% of its 1,323t quota harvested in late July.

The 3K and 3L divisions landed 8,961t, surpassing their joint quota of 7,408t by more than 1,500t.

Capelin harvest in Newfoundland and Labrador through July 26. Screenshot from DFO's website

The remaining 10,225t of the overall quota comes from zones 4RST, which includes the west coast of NL and the Gulf of St. Lawrence around the provinces of Prince Edward Island and the lower north shore of Quebec.

The season in that zone opened June 4 and is now closed.

title: Canadian man gets CAD 1m fine, six years in jail for illegal fishing
content:
A fisherman from the Canadian province of British Columbia (BC) with a history of violating federal fishing regulations will spend the next six years in jail, and pay a fine of over CAD 1.0 million ($730,000) for illegal fishing and the sale of sea cucumbers, reports Nanaimo News Now.

Scott Stanley Matthew Steer was sentenced in a BC Supreme Court in Nanaimo on Friday (July 25). The sentencing hearing came six months after Steer was found guilty of eight charges, including fishing without a license and fishing out of season.

Steer's wife, Melissa Larocque, was also fined as the sole operator of a numbered company tied to the operation and will also be responsible for paying the million-dollar fine.

BC Supreme Court judge David Crerar said it was well-established during the trial earlier this year that Steer orchestrated every aspect of the illegal sea cucumber operation and that Laroque was also fully involved.

The CAD 1.0m fine imposed on the couple was proportional to the CAD 1,105,718 they reportedly received through the illegal sales of the sea cucumbers, the judge noted. They were given 20 years to pay it.

This was not Steer's first brush with the law.

The 47-year-old had received several shorter jail sentences and a lifetime fishing ban long before the newest charges came to court, Crerar noted.

In 2013, Steer was convicted of landing fish without a licence and defrauding crew members and the vessel owner, and given a 10-year fishing ban and a six-month jail term.

Steer considered himself "unbounded by the laws," and a long-term jail sentence was not only appropriate, but necessary, Crerar said, reported Nanaimo News.

"His deliberate deception in illegal fishing shows contempt for the fragile, finite marine resources and ecosystems. The only way to stop Mr. Steer from ravaging the ocean and flouting the law and court orders is to remove him from the sea for a long period of time," Crerar is quoted by Nanaimo News.

title: Maine lawmaker seeks to use draft marine mammal bill to delay lobster rules
content:
US representative Jared Golden, a Maine Democrat, used a congressional hearing on Tuesday (July 22) to make his case for delaying new lobster trap rules for another seven years with the help of a bill soon to be introduced by an Alaska lawmaker.

An unnamed 32-page draft bill being worked on by US representative Nick Begich, an Alaska Republican, got its 15 minutes of fame and then some on Tuesday at the Natural Resources Committee's oceans panel.

The bill would overhaul the Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA) of 1972 in several ways, including making significant changes to section 101 of the law regarding the process for incidental take -- the unintentional or accidental injury or death of marine mammals during otherwise lawful activities authorizations, as explained in the synopsis presented to the panel.

Currently, incidental take regulations can be authorized for five years for non-military readiness activities and seven years for military readiness activities. The discussion draft removes those timeframes.

As currently written, this discussion draft would amend MMPA in multiple ways, including removing the requirements for consultation under the National Environmental Policy Act, and adding a new section on "objective application of the best available scientific and commercial data."

MMPA was passed more than 50 years ago with good intentions, Begich said at the hearing, adding: "As the decades have passed, though, the use of vague or overly precautionary standards has led to confusion, delay and unintended harm."

Nick Begich. Image from 2024 campaign.

Begich, who was elected in 2024, replacing Democrat Mary Peltola, also stressed that his legislation is a discussion draft, not a final bill. The draft will be refined in the weeks and months ahead, he said.

"I fully expect and welcome further input and collaboration. I am committed to working with colleagues on both sides of the aisle to make these reforms common sense and bipartisan," said Begich, adding the discussion and input would include coastal communities, tribes, fishing groups, developers, scientists and anyone else who might be impacted by the MMPA amendments.

'Serious concerns'

While many Democrats and a slew of conservation groups, including the International Fund for Animal Welfare, Oceana and Earth Justice, are cautioning against wide-reaching changes to the MMPA, as reported by Politico, Golden fully supports a review.

In particular, he's concerned about new lobster fishing regulations that are due to be implemented by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) in 2028 that would require use of modified fishing gear and seasonal closures of lobster fishing areas to avoid entanglements of the endangered North Atlantic right whale.

Traps, ropes, whales and gavels: A chronology of the battle over the US Gulf of Maine lobster fishery

The rules were set to take effect in 2024, but were delayed by Congress in a provision contained in a massive omnibus budget bill passed in December 2022, as reported by Undercurrent.

In June 2023, lobster fishermen won another battle when an appeals court ruled that NOAA erred in a biological opinion that was used to promulgate stricter new trap rope rules for the fisheries. The 33-page decision reversed US District Court judge James Boasberg's earlier summary judgment that suggested harvester practices placed further risk on endangered North Atlantic right whales and ordered NOAA back to the drawing board, as reported by Undercurrent.

The US lobster industry’s very big day on Capitol Hill

"I have serious concerns with the MMPA and I believe that changes need to be made to the law to ensure that it cannot be used to shut down entire fisheries and the communities they support," Golden said at the hearing.

"Simply put, the federal government should not be in the business of destroying the lives of hardworking Americans and thousands of small family-owned businesses based on assumptions that are not grounded in sound data," he said.

Golden suggested that, with the MMPA amendments under consideration, the current moratorium on rules to protect right whales in the lobster fishing state should be extended past 2028.

"Based on my conversations with fishermen, more time is needed to incorporate the research and data collected during the pause into future right whale regulations. I am grateful to congressman Begich of Alaska for working with me on this discussion draft and for including a much-needed extension of the regulatory pause until 2035 to ensure that any future actions taken to protect right whales are informed by a greater volume of data," Golden said in a press release on Wednesday (July 23).

US representative Jared Golden at a hearing Tuesday to discuss multiple bills. Image is still from video.

Lawsuits piling up in Alaska 

In Alaska, court challenges are ongoing over seal habitat and trawling.

The government of Alaska has launched a legal challenge against NOAA on the agency's 2022 decision to allocate160 million acres, an area the size of Texas, as critical habitat for bearded seals, which are listed as "threatened" by the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

Alaska has argued that's too much and the federal agency didn't consider the economic impacts of the designation, especially whether areas along the state's North Slope should be excluded. The state also has argued the species are not threatened since the seals also are found in other arctic waters outside of the US.

The Alaskan midwater trawling fleet has also come under fire for marine mammal bycatch. 

The global environmenal group, Oceana, filed a lawsuit against the US government in December 2024, alleging federal fisheries managers are failing to adequately track marine mammal entanglements in commercial trawl gear in Alaska waters, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

That case is still winding its way through the courts.

Tribes join lawsuit over withheld documents of marine mammal bycatch in Alaska groundfish fleet

The current MMPA has held up essential projects in Alaska, like energy development, port construction and fishing operations, not because of clear science, but because of uncertainty and subjective interpretation of the Act, Begich said.

"This draft aims to bring clarity, objectivity and balance back to the implementation of the MMPA," Begich told the committee.

"It focuses on updating key definitions like harassment and negligible impact, so that we're regulating based on real measurable effects, not hypothetical ones. It makes sure that decisions are based on the best available science, not assumptions or exceptionally conservative modelling," he said.

title: US wholesale: Alaska pollock market enters transitional B season
content:
Click here for trial access to our US wholesale seafood pricing platform, where you can find proprietary assessments for farmed and wild salmon, crab, shrimp, scallops, farmed and wild groundfish/whitefish, live and frozen lobster and octopus, with more soon on the way.

The 2025 Alaska pollock fishery is positioned for another high-output year, supported by robust and well-defined quotas across both the Gulf of Alaska and Bering Sea. In the gulf, harvest allowances are split evenly across two periods, with 85,607 metric tons allocated for Jan. 20-May 31 and again for June 1-Dec. 31.

In the Bering Sea, quotas continue to emphasize B season landings, which run from June 10 through Oct. 31:

B Season (June 10-Oct. 31):
Inshore: 330,875t
Catcher-Processors: 264,700t
Mothership: 66,175t
CDQ: 76,670t

A Season (January 20-June 9):
Inshore: 270,715t
Catcher-Processors: 216,572t
Mothership: 54,144t

With these allocations in place, the Bering Sea fleet has entered the second half of the year amid a biological transition, strategic harvest pacing and evolving product strategies.

As of July 12, B season harvest volumes were tracking at approximately 88% of the same period in 2024, according to the Genuine Alaska Pollock Producers (GAPP). While this initially appears sluggish, UCN sources note it aligns with typical patterns during transitions between dominant year classes.

Genuine Alaska Pollock Producers (GAPP)

The 2018 year class, known for its above-average size and yield, is beginning to taper off. In its place, fleets are encountering more mixed schools of younger, smaller fish, a shift that impacts both catch rates and product yields. Vessels are spending more time locating optimal schools with the aim of maintaining catch quality and efficiency, but the extra effort is slowing the pace of early harvesting.

Still, signs of rising catch totals are emerging. For the week ending July 12, landings outpaced the same week in 2024 for both inshore and catcher-processor sectors, an encouraging signal that fishing activity is ramping up.

Genuine Alaska Pollock Producers (GAPP)

Despite the slower B season start, frozen production is up 2% year-over-year. This counterintuitive trend is attributed to a stronger A season: in 2025, the Bering Sea A season quota rose from 568,611t to 604,161t, with actual catch climbing from 544,203t to 585,844t. The resulting early-year surge in biomass provided processors with a stronger raw material base heading into summer.

Sources note this production uptick is not being driven by a shift from fresh to frozen output or yield changes, but by the overall increase in catch volume across the calendar year.

Average fish size this season remain mixed and location-dependent, with younger cohorts weighing down the average in some areas. This trend affects recovery rates for fillet and surimi production, as smaller fish produce lower yields and can impact processor economics.

So far, processors appear focused on surimi and pin bone out (PBO) fillet production for the B season. Surimi demand is reportedly strong, particularly from domestic and Asian buyers, while PBO fillets remain a staple for US retail and foodservice programs.

Genuine Alaska Pollock Producers (GAPP)

If the trend toward smaller fish persists, fillet recovery could become a more pressing concern, potentially influencing both production costs and wholesale pricing. Strategic inventory planning and customer flexibility will be critical in adapting to these shifts.

US wholesale prices for Alaska pollock were mostly stable through Week 29 (July 14–20). Single-frozen Alaskan fillets remain flat and Chinese-origin twice-frozen fillets are similarly unchanged after weeks of steady increases. Industry contacts have reported upward pricing pressure building amid stronger inquiries since the B season's start.

At the same time, reprocessed pollock blocks have trended higher, with firmer pricing reported for both fillet blocks and minced product. Continued demand and broader tariff uncertainty are helping to support these gains.

Buyers are closely monitoring supply variability, particularly as smaller fish sizes and selective product focus could tighten availability. Some market participants anticipate stronger pricing ahead, should demand remain firm and trade dynamics continue to evolve.

Export markets and trade policy remain key watchpoints in the second half of the year, especially as pollock competes with other global whitefish species amid mixed demand trends and volatile currency conditions.

Overall, the 2025 B season is shaping up as a year of recalibration. As the fishery moves away from the high-yielding 2018 class and adapts to new biological realities, the focus is shifting to strategic harvesting, yield optimization and flexible product planning.

While current yields and pace differ from past seasons, quota volumes and recent landing gains suggest the industry remains well-positioned to meet market demand, provided harvest conditions remain stable.

The Alaska pollock sector is navigating a natural inflection point, not a crisis, but a strategic adjustment. As B season progresses, maintaining balance across biological supply, processing strategy and global market demand will be key to preserving price stability and supply chain confidence.

title: Cooke accuses Chilean regulator of overreach in salmon farm suspension
content:
The Canadian seafood giant Cooke has launched a formal legal challenge against Chile's environmental regulator, the Superintendency of the Environment (Superintendencia del Medio Ambiente, or SMA).

It accuses it of exceeding its powers by suspending two long-running salmon farming operations in Patagonia.

The case, heard Wednesday (July 9) by Chile's Third Environmental Court, could have significant implications for the regulatory oversight of the country's aquaculture industry, one of the largest in the world.

Cooke files legal complaint against Chile regulator over fish farm suspension order

The dispute centers on the Huillines 2 and Huillines 3 salmon farms in the Aysen region, which SMA ordered to halt fish stocking in March and April 2025. The regulator imposed the shutdowns as provisional measures, citing potential environmental risks and alleged overproduction in violation of technical limits.

Cooke Aquaculture Chile, a division of the larger partner company, argues that the shutdowns are "unjustified, unlawful, and based on flawed technical reasoning." In oral arguments presented by attorney Martin Gutierrez, the company accused the SMA of "acting arbitrarily and retroactively" applying environmental criteria to concessions and technical projects approved more than two decades ago.

"These farms have operated for over 25 years with no record of environmental harm. There is no evidence of any imminent risk to the environment, which is a legal requirement for such a measure," Gutierrez told the tribunal.

He further argued that both centers consistently meet environmental standards, as confirmed by reports from the Universidad Austral and routine certifications by national fisheries and aquaculture service, Sernapesca.

A major point of contention is the SMA's interpretation of production limits.

The regulator alleges that Huillines 2 and 3 exceeded their authorized output by thousands of tons, triggering mandatory entry into the Environmental Impact Assessment System (or SEIA, in its Spanish acronym).

Cooke counters that the original technical projects for these farms, approved before SEIA came into force in 1997, set minimum -- not maximum -- production levels, and that the authority lacks jurisdiction to reinterpret that baseline.

Cooke says Chilean environmental ruling may lead to over $30m in losses

The SMA's position, Gutierrez added, "contradicts the views of other Chilean authorities, including the Undersecretariat for Fisheries (Subpesca) and the ministry of economy."

He also accused the agency of "selectively omitting evidence" and failing to conduct its own on-site inspections before ordering the shutdowns.

Adding further legal complexity, Cooke contends that the farms are located outside the boundaries of the Laguna San Rafael National Park, a designation the SMA used to justify heightened environmental precautions.

Cooke insists they are not and that the boundaries of maritime areas have never been legally defined. 

"The SMA is basing its argument on a hand-drawn line from 1983," Gutierrez said. "The park's maritime limits are not clearly defined by law, and the ministry of defense granted the concessions in 1999 and 2000 with full awareness of the surrounding geography."

The Salmon Council, a trade group representing major aquaculture companies in Chile, joined the case to support Cooke and warned of broader implications for the industry.

Its legal representative, Edecio Carrasco, told the tribunal that the SMA's actions "undermine legal certainty and threaten dozens of other concessions granted before environmental regulations were modernized."

"There's a risk here of setting a precedent that changes the rules for an entire sector retroactively," Carrasco said. "This is not just about Cooke. This is about trust in how Chile regulates long-standing economic activity."

He also criticized what he described as a regulatory "loop" in which provisional measures are imposed, expire, and are reissued before courts can issue substantive rulings. "We're stuck in an endless loop where environmental shutdowns are challenged, expire, and are then repeated without real judicial review."

Cooke seeks recusal of environmental judge over Chile salmon farm suspension

The SMA defended its actions, arguing that the farm production increases were substantial and required environmental reassessment under existing law.

"Shutdowns were a precautionary measure based on known risks associated with intensive aquaculture operations, particularly in ecologically sensitive areas," said attorney Katharina Buschmann, representing the SMA.

She also added that the agency's decisions "had already been reviewed and authorized by the environmental tribunal earlier in the year," and cited a 2024 ruling from the SEIA that affirmed the farms should have entered its system due to production changes.

"The regulator is not required to wait for environmental damage to act. It is enough to demonstrate a credible risk, and that threshold has been met," Buschmann told the court.

Both sides cited conflicting interpretations of environmental, administrative, and sectoral law. The tribunal's decision is expected to set a legal and political precedent in a country where salmon exports are second only to copper.

Cooke has also noted that it began relocating the farms over two years ago under a government-backed plan. However, it argues that while that process plays out -- a timeline that could take years -- "it should be allowed to continue operating under existing authorizations."

A ruling from the tribunal is expected in the coming weeks.

title: Conservation groups sue Pacific Seafood alleging Clean Water Act violations at Columbia River steelhead trout farms
content:
The Center for Food Safety (CFS) and Wild Fish Conservancy (WFC) filed a lawsuit in the US District Court for the Eastern District of Washington against Pacific Seafood Group on July 2, alleging multiple Clean Water Act violations at its three commercial net-pen steelhead trout farms since 2020.

Citing records gleaned from Freedom of Information Act requests, the two nonprofit groups accused Pacific Seafood of exceeding its farming permits' effluent limits, neglecting to monitor and report discharges, and failing to develop and implement plans for best management practices to reduce pollution.

"These confined industrial fish farming operations have been unlawfully and egregiously polluting the Columbia River for years," CFS legal director George Kimbrell said in a release. "Fish feed, fish waste, chemicals, pharmaceuticals and other contaminants released by these facilities threaten water quality and native fish populations. We're taking this action to ensure compliance with environmental laws designed to protect our waterways and the species that depend on them."

Pacific Seafood’s BC operation fined CAD 25k for pollution

Pacific's subsidiary, Pacific Seafood Aquaculture, operates three net-pens in Nespelem, Oregon, grow rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss), which Pacific markets as steelhead. 

San Francisco, California-headquartered CFS and Duvall, Washington-based WFC, both environmental non-governmental organizations, said Pacific has been violating its National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permits, overseen by the Environmental Protection Agency, since they were reissued in April 2020.

Specifically, Pacific did not conduct required monitoring or adhere to other requirements of its permits, resulting in unlawful pollution that had the potential to harm wild fish and the Columbia River ecosystem, which is home to several animals listed under the Endangered Species Act, according to the lawsuit. Daily discharges of pollution including fish feces, uneaten fish feed, fish carcasses and chemicals used to treat fish diseases also negatively impacted human recreation, including fishing, in the area, the lawsuit said.

"Despite 'sustainable' marketing claims and third-party certifications, government records tell a different story -- one of chronic noncompliance and ecological harm," WFC executive director Emma Helverson said. "Local communities and economies should not be left to shoulder the costs of cleanup and ecological damage while a billion-dollar corporation cuts corners on basic environmental protections." 

The lawsuit requests an injunction enjoining Pacific from operating the farms, as well as asking that Pacific pay for an evaluation of damage caused to the environment and any remediation deemed necessary. It also demands Pacific pay civil penalties up to the maximum authorized by the Clean Water Act for each violation proved and for remuneration of litigation expenses.

Pacific Seafood joins US West Coast processing group PSPA

A Pacific spokesperson denied the lawsuit's allegations. Since the company purchased the farm sites in 2008, it has invested millions of dollars to rebuild much of the infrastructure at the sites, including the net-pens and moorings, and it installed a state-of-the-art camera monitoring system, the company said.

"We stand firmly by our tireless efforts to comply with our permits and our long-standing commitment to sustainable practices. We've made clear to the plaintiffs that their claims are based on inaccurate and grossly incomplete information, but they apparently decided to file it anyway," the spokesperson said in an email sent to Undercurrent News. "We remain committed to transparency, environmental responsibility, and working with regulators and stakeholders to protect our shared ecosystems."

The spokesperson described Pacific's farming operations in Nespelem, which are co-managed with the Colville Confederated Tribes, as "a model of environmental stewardship" and noted they each carry four-star Best Aquaculture Practices certification.

"This type of lawsuit is unfortunately used by an entire industry of environmental groups and their lawyers to extract attorney fees and settlements from even the most environmentally upstanding companies and to exert political pressure on industries they don't like," the spokesperson said.

Both CFS and WFC have filed numerous previous lawsuits against seafood companies in the US Pacific Northwest. 

Last month, CFS sued in federal court to invalidate permits for nine shellfish aquaculture operations in Washington state.

In May, WFC sued the federal government over it missing a deadline to rule whether chinook salmon should be listed as threatened or endangered across the Gulf of Alaska.

title: Land-based aquaculture investors ditch salmon megafarms for modular ecosystems
content:
Capital is still flowing into land-based aquaculture in 2025, but where -- and how -- it is being deployed is changing.

While headlines have focused on the collapse or downsizing of several high-profile projects, investors and strategists say the shift marks a deeper reckoning with what business models are truly viable. The push now is toward modular, replicable systems targeting local markets and consumer-driven product formats, and increasingly, not just for salmon.

A report released three weeks ago by Peritus Capital, a boutique investment firm based in New York, helps clarify that pivot. Authored by Kimberley Player, a former principal at US private equity firm Equilibrium Capital and now an industry consultant, the paper "Selling Food, Securing Capital," outlines how investor priorities are evolving away from vertical integration and scale for its own sake.

Peritus, which has backed projects including Pacifico Aquaculture's striped bass operation in Mexico, argues that future winners in the RAS sector will emerge from "ecosystems" of specialized players rather than single companies attempting to master everything from hatch to harvest to sales.

Rather than tying up capital in large, vertically integrated builds, the report suggests early-phase investment is shifting toward system integrators, contract operators, and platforms that offer technical services or modular capacity. The next generation of winners, it argues, may be defined more by partnership and adaptability than by control over the entire value chain.

It's evident from both the RAStech floor discussions and the Peritus report that RAS in 2025 has evolved beyond just representing 'salmon megaproject.' It has become a more diverse and experimental sustainable sector. Photo: Liza Mayer

That sentiment echoes what Undercurrent News reported earlier: that capital hasn't vanished from the land-based sector -- it is just moving differently, with more caution and closer alignment between technical strategy and market realities.

Kimberley Player of Peritus Capital. Photo: Liza Mayer

Beyond just salmon

The renewed focus on downstream feasibility dovetails with what industry observers noticed at RAStech 2025, held in San Diego in June. While salmon RAS once dominated the conference, attendees this year noted a sharp decline in salmon-centric participation and a broader range of species and project scales represented.

 "There's very few salmon people here. I've seen someone from Salmon Evolution -- maybe one or two others -- but there's not a lot of other people," one attendee remarked. The shift, the attendee added, was positive: "It is great for networking. You're not just talking to the same salmon crowd anymore."

One senior investor said they're now looking at species like trout, yellowtail, barramundi and shrimp not just for their market appeal but for how they allow for operational phasing and localized branding.

Family offices step in

The Peritus report said a rebalancing of risks and expectations is underway. Some institutional capital is pulling back, but family offices and specialist funds are stepping in, often closer to the end markets and more willing to support hybrid or phased business models.

According to Player's analysis, many early RAS failures weren't solely about technology but mismatched investor expectations and a lack of integration between production and the real-world demands of seafood distribution.

Those views echo takeaways from this year's RAS Investors' Forum, where several panelists stressed that viable models going forward are unlikely to mimic traditional protein production.

"It's not about small versus large," said Peritus Capital CEO Howard Tang during the forum. "It is about what fits the site, the market and the species."

title: Pacific Seafood’s BC operation fined CAD 25k for pollution
content:
A seafood processor in Ucluelet, British Columbia, owned by the Pacific Seafood Group, has been fined CAD 25,000 ($18,394) for charges that it repeatedly exceeded pollution limits in wastewater discharged into Barkley Sound, reports the National Observer.

The BC Ministry of Environment cited Ucluelet Harbour Seafoods for 33 alleged violations between May 2023 and August 2024. During that period, the company is alleged to have repeatedly pumped harmful contaminants like ammonia, oil, grease and other fish offal well above permitted levels into the ocean.

In 28 cases, the effluent exceeded allowable levels by more than 50%, according the provincial agency. One sample contained ammonia 4,600% above permitted levels. Other samples showed fish oil and grease exceeded limits by over 17,000% and fish waste solids by 3,000%, the ministry noted.

Ucluelet Harbour Seafoods, a division of Pacific Seafoods, is located on the western side of Vancouver Island, British Columbia, Canada. Photo is screenshot from Google Maps

Pacific Seafood said it has made infrastructure and procedural improvements to prevent future incidents.

"We have made significant improvements at our UHS facility to strengthen environmental performance, including better dock procedures to reduce lost product, new water systems that speed up solids removal, and upgraded wastewater treatment that prevents overflows and improves efficiency," Amy Wentworth, the company's senior environmental director, reportedly offered in a statement, reports the National Observer. 

Pacific Seafood operates 40 facilities across North America and Chile.

title: Protectionist Mississippi seafood labeling law to take effect in July
content:
A law taking effect in Mississippi on Tuesday (July 1) requires seafood sellers in the US state to label their products as domestic or imported.

The law mandates that restaurants, markets, wholesalers and online retailers place "domestic" or "imported" labels on all menus, signage, packaging and online listings. It was signed by Mississippi governor Tate Reeves in April, as Undercurrent News reported.

Enforcement duties will be split between the Mississippi Department of Marine Resources (MDMR) in coastal counties and the Department of Agriculture and Commerce in northern Mississippi, according to WDAM7. Violators will be fined $500 for their first offense, with penalties rising to $10,000 or more for repeated infringements.

In advance of the law's enactment, restaurant owners have expressed concern over its vagueness.

One restaurant owner asked if they could signify imported and domestic items using an "I" or "D," but lawmakers she contacted weren't sure and the MDMR said it "depends on the context and intent."

MDMR chief of operations Patrick Levine said enforcement will be lenient at first and will focus on whether there is a good-faith effort made to inform seafood buyers about the origin of the seafood they're purchasing.

"If you're not trying to deceive them, we're not trying to hurt you," he said. "If you're trying to deceive someone, that's when you're going to get hurt … if our officer walks in and says that, they're gonna listen and say, 'Yeah, this makes sense. Now try to correct it as quick as you can.'"

But even after a pledge from state authorities that first-time violators will receive a three-day window to correct any labeling that breaks the law, the restaurant owner responded by saying the bill "is not very clearly written."

"That's the problem with this bill; it's up to your interpretation or your interpretation," the restaurant owner said.

title: Two men fined CAD 40K for illegal shrimp fishing off western Canada’s Vancouver Island
content:
Two commercial fishers in British Columbia have been fined a combined CAD 40,000 ($29,137) for illegally harvesting shrimp during a seasonal closure in waters off Vancouver Island, on Canada's west coast -- an incident that occurred in 2022 but was reported only last week.

Scott Castle and Terry Lorenz were found guilty in separate court proceedings in Nanaimo for fishing in a closed section of Stuart Channel during the commercial shrimp fishery shutdown on May 30, 2022, reported The Vancouver Sun.  

The pair also failed to complete the required catch documentation and were found to have sold the illegally harvested shrimp.

Castle was fined CAD 30,000 for the harvest and licence violations, plus an additional CAD 8,228 from proceeds of the sale. Lorenz received a CAD 3,000 fine and a five-year fishing ban.

Fisheries and Oceans Canada said such actions threaten conservation efforts and could undermine the province's CAD 50-million shrimp industry. The illegal catch could have impacted female shrimp critical to reproduction, which typically spawn between January and April in British Columbia, the publication reported.

title: Massive quota boost requires change at Canada’s biggest cod processor
content:
It was a watershed moment for a Canadian company that relies solely on Atlantic cod and managed to survive through a 32-year-long moratorium on what used to be the world's largest stock for the species.

"This is the most Canadian cod we've had access to since 1992," Alberto Wareham, president of Icewater Seafoods, based in the province of Newfoundland and Labrador (NL), told Undercurrent News following the announcement by Canadian fisheries minister Joanne Thompson on Tuesday (June 18) of a huge quota bump.

The total allowable catch for the 2025-26 season is 38,000 metric tons, more than twice the 18,000t quota set last season, which was the first official commercial fishery since 1992, as reported by Undercurrent.

With 30,400t TAC assigned to the inshore, the challenge now is logistics, said Wareham.

Normally, the fishing season for the inshore boats begins the third Sunday in July and runs until the last of September, or early October, he noted.

Last year the season was a little later starting, said Wareham, recalling how Icewater saw the first landings from the inshore on July 28. All of the 15,000t allocated to the inshore fleets in 2024 was landed by the end of September, he added.

This large, headed and gutted cod came from the Canadian offshore, caught by Ocean Choice International trawlers, frozen at sea and delivered to Icewater Seafoods in Arnold's Cove for processing on Feb. 23, 2024, marking the first time in 32 years that Icewater has processed northern cod. Photo by Barb Dean-Simmons

With a higher TAC this year it will mean more fishing weeks, and a steady pace of cod coming to processors.

"To catch 30,000t, we'd need about 15 good fishing weeks, and that's with perfect weather, no delays, and everyone buying," he said.

Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) has not yet provided details about season start dates in the various fishing zones around NL, but Wareham said, in order to accommodate the extra quota, the season should open as early as possible in July.

However, DFO is allowing midshore fleets to use mobile gear this year, which should help ensure the full quota can be landed, he added.

"The small day-boats can safely fish from mid-July through September. But if we want to keep going into October and November, it's going to be the midshore boats and larger inshore vessels doing the work," said Wareham.

"This much cod hasn't been caught in the inshore since 1991, so we're navigating new ground," Wareham added.

Assessing logistics and market opportunities

For Icewater, the increased quota also means more weeks of operation this year.

In 2024, with the commercial quota bumped to 18,000, following years of a stewardship fishery that set a maximum allowable harvest of 12,999t, Icewater spent 10 weeks processing inshore cod, and 14 weeks handling the cod landed by Canadian trawlers for the first time since the 1992 moratorium.

With the new quota, which also allows 3,693t for the offshore fleets, three times the 1,000t allocated for the 2024 season, Icewater could be running for 35 to 40 weeks, Wareham noted.

"That's approaching full-year employment," he said.

The northern cod range from zone 2J, off the coast of Labrador, to zones 3LNO, off the east coast of the island of Newfoundland. Photo screenshot from DFO map

"And it's all Canadian cod. We won't need to import," Wareham said, referencing the fact that, prior to 2024, Icewater had to source frozen-at-sea cod from the Barents Sea to feed its production.

While logistical planning is underway at home, Wareham is also setting his sights abroad. Icewater has been long-time supplier of frozen cod loins and fillets to European markets. One of its main customers is the UK-based Marks and Spencer, although it also supplies US customers.

Quota cuts in the Barents Sea is also driving demand, he noted.

The Barents Sea cod stock, which feeds fleets in Norway, Russia and Finland, has been in decline in recent years, leading to the TAC for 2025 getting slashed by 25% to 340,000t, as previously reported by Undercurrent. 

"We had customers last year that wanted more cod than we had for them," said Wareham, who is heading to Europe next week to secure orders with long-standing buyers and find new markets.

Alberto Wareham, president and CEO, Icewater Seafoods. Photo courtesy of Icewater Seafoods.

And that's good news for NL cod harvesters as well, said Wareham, noting that the inshore harvesters union, the Fish Food and Allied Workers (FFAW), and the processors, through the Association of Seafood Producers, recently negotiated a dock price for Grade A cod at CAD 1.18 ($0.86) per pound, to take effect after Aug. 1.

That's a 12% increase from last season's negotiated price, said Wareham.

Legal challenge still in play

The FFAW also welcomed the quota announcement and the share for the inshore harvesters.

"We're certainly thrilled to see a substantial increase going to the inshore northern cod fishery this year, which is reflective of the robust inshore catch rates," said FFAW president Dwan Street, in a press release.

"These improvements by the minister show a keen willingness to work with our members and ensure that fishing decisions are reflective of the needs of our coastal economies," Street said.

Canadian court denies harvesters’ injunction to stop cod fishery

However, the union is still pressing forward on a legal battle over the DFO decision to allow Canadian offshore fleets to participate in the fishery.

The union claims the federal government promised during the moratorium that only inshore fleets only would be permitted in a commercial fishery, as long as the total quota was less than 115,000t.

The case was filed in federal court last July, as reported by Undercurrrent. Formal hearings are scheduled to begin this December, the union said in its press release.

NGOs: Quota hike ignores science, risks collapse

Meanwhile, the quota hike announced June 18 did not impress two non-government, environment watchdog groups.

Thompson has defied science advice and legal obligations under Canada's Fisheries Act, Oceana Canada said in a press release.

Despite signs of weak productivity, poor age structure, and food scarcity, DFO has overlooked precautionary management, said Rebecca Schijns, fishery scientist at Oceana Canada, an environmental charity based in Toronto, Ontario.

Scientists at DFO have indicated there's a 71% chance that the cod stock will decline further within three years — risking a return to the critical zone by 2028, Schijns noted.

"This wasn't a science-based decision — it was political. It trades long-term recovery for short-term gain." Schijns said.

Canada’s fisheries minister ignored staff cod advice, court documents reveal

Oceans North, an Ottawa-based conservation group, shares that concern.

"Northern cod remains a vulnerable stock," said Gemma Rayner, fisheries and special projects advisor for the conservation group, in a press release. "Rebuilding it requires patience and ecological responsibility, not short-term economic decisions."

Despite DFO's claims of stock improvement, Oceans North said the change stems from a redefinition of the Limit Reference Point (LRP), not actual population growth.

The LRP determines when a stock is in the "critical zone," where fishing should be minimized. 

In October 2023, Canada made a significant change to how it accounts for northern cod biomass by implementing a new limit reference point model that lifted the stock from the critical to the cautious zone under the precautionary approach framework, as reported by Undercurrent.

"This adjustment creates a misleading picture of recovery. The stock has not grown since 2017 and was still classified as in the critical zone as recently as 2023," Oceans North stated.

The quest for MSC certification

Meanwhile, full validation of the fishery through Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certification is still a work in progress.

"We're getting closer, but two things are still missing: a defined upper stock reference point and harvest control rules," said Wareham, adding DFO has committed to the industry to complete those by the end of 2025.

If that's accomplished, the information would be added to the 2026 science update, and the industry could apply for MSC certification.

Gaining MSC certification would boost market access in Europe, where some countries require the MSC stamp of approval for fish imports.

"We have a chance to rebuild this fishery — and to make cod the backbone of Newfoundland's economy again," offered Wareham.

title: Canadian harvester fined CAD 37K for fishing in protected waters
content:
A commercial fisherman from coastal British Columbia, Canada, has been fined nearly CAD 37,000 ($27,300) for illegally fishing in a protected area often referred to as "Canada's Galapagos," local publication Richmond News reported last week.

Stefan Grega, 79, who operates in the Richmond area near Vancouver, pleaded guilty to five charges under Canada's Fisheries Act, including fishing in a closed zone within the Gwaii Haanas National Park Reserve, possessing and selling the catch and operating in contravention of conservation rules.

The violations took place in May 2022, when Grega made six fishing sets in Gwaii Haanas, a federally protected area off the coast of Haida Gwaii in northern British Columbia, according to the news service. The area is ecologically sensitive and co-managed by the Haida Nation and Parks Canada.

At his sentencing hearing, federal crown prosecutor Chloe Sauder described the region as a pristine marine ecosystem "designed to be untouched." She pressed for CAD 62,000 in fines and penalties, including the full commercial value of the catch.

However, judge Derek Mah imposed a lower amount, accepting the defense's argument that Grega earned only a portion of the sale proceeds and entered the conservation area accidentally due to bad weather and outdated navigation charts.

Still, Mah emphasized that the sentence must serve as a deterrent, noting Grega's past warnings and a previous conviction. "The public must know there's a significant penalty for fishing in closed areas," the publication quoted the judge as saying.

Grega has until April 2026 to pay the full amount.

title: UN Conference ends with High Seas Treaty almost in force, but NGOs filing legal challenges over MPAs
content:
The third UN Ocean Conference (UNOC) ended with 19 additional countries depositing their ratifications for the High Seas Treaty, meaning the total number that count towards entry into force has now reached 50.

Only 10 more are needed to cross the critical 60-country threshold that would trigger the treaty -- officially know as the BBNJ Agreement -- coming into effect, said NGO group the High Seas Alliance.

As of Friday (June 13), 19 additional instruments of ratification were deposited by countries at the UN during the conference, and 20 more countries signed the treaty, signaling their intent to ratify. Additional countries that ratified during UNOC: Albania, Bahamas, Belgium, Croatia, Cote d'Ivoire, Denmark, Fiji, Malta, Mauritania, Vanuatu, Greece, Guinea-Bissau, Indonesia, Jamaica, Jordan, Liberia, Solomon Islands, Tuvalu, and Vietnam.

UK to ban bottom trawling in 41 MPAs, says environment secretary

The EU has also deposited its instrument of ratification. However, as a regional economic integration organization, its ratification does not count toward the total, only ratifications by its individual member states.

Additional countries that signed during UNOC: Andorra, Armenia, Burundi, Cambodia, Equatorial Guinea, Guinea, Guinea Bissau, Jordan, Lebanon, Lesotho, Montenegro, Niue, North Macedonia, Papua New Guinea, Peru, Senegal Serbia, South Africa, Saint Kitts and Nevis, and Yemen.

"The journey towards a High Seas Treaty has been nearly as long as the great migrations of whales, sharks and turtles, but the wave of new ratifications at UNOC shows we are in the final straight," said Matthew Collis, senior director of policy at the International Fund for Animal Welfare.

In addition to the boost in ratifications, the number of countries signing the Treaty also surged. An extra 20 countries added their signatures during the week, bringing the total number to 136. This is an encouraging sign, as widespread ratification will be crucial to ensuring the Treaty's full effectiveness.

Rebecca Hubbard, director of the High Seas Alliance, emphasized the urgency to maintain momentum: "We must keep our foot on the #RaceForRatification accelerator. The treaty's power lies in the number of countries that join, so while we celebrate this incredible progress, we urge all remaining nations to ratify without delay and help drive this Treaty past the first 60 to make it a truly global force for ocean protection."

Around 60 heads of state and government attended the meeting, reflecting a significant high-level attention for the plight of the ocean, said the alliance. The momentum on High Seas Treaty ratification showed what is possible when the world comes together with urgency and purpose.

Attention is now also turning to how the Treaty will be implemented once it enters into force. Several major announcements were made last week, including the re-launch of the High Ambition Coalition for BBNJ and the €10 million that has been made available through the EU's €40m Global Ocean Programme to provide technical assistance to developing countries for both ratification and implementation.

Private philanthropy also stepped up with the Minderoo Foundation pledging an additional $6.5m to support high seas protection, and funding was confirmed to create a secretariat for the "first movers initiative," which will help advance early proposals for high seas marine protected areas (MPAs), said the alliance.

"Focus is intensifying on building strong bodies and processes under the treaty to ensure it functions effectively, as well as identifying critical high seas sites for protection once the treaty is operational through an ongoing preparatory committee process at the UN. Efforts to build the case for high seas MPA proposals submissions under the treaty were also showcased at the conference, profiling a number of areas including the Salas y Gomez and Nazca Ridges, the Lord Howe Rise and South Tasman Sea and the Costa Rica Thermal Dome in the Pacific."

Anger over general MPA progress

Meanwhile, fellow NGO Seas at Risk expressed its anger at the pressure on Europe's existing MPAs, which it said have been "left to fend for themselves by European leaders" at UNOC in Nice, France.

"Despite scientific evidence and citizen pressure, the Nice Action Plan that outlines the commitments made at UNOC confirms that only a handful of EU member states took steps towards protecting MPAs, while the vast majority took no decisive action to prevent destructive fisheries such as bottom trawling in these precious marine habitats."

The "underwhelming lack of ambition" on EU MPAs was "tone deaf given the EU's recent publication of the European Ocean Pact, which was presented by European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen at UNOC."

The pact prioritizes the protection and restoration of ocean health, which is in line with existing EU commitments including the marine action plan, which calls on member states to phase out bottom trawling in MPAs.

"While some countries -- including the UK -- are taking the right steps and banning destructive bottom trawling from MPAs, EU countries have failed to take action. Mild progress was made in Portugal, where the expansion of its MPA network was announced, although the management plan for these areas is yet to be defined."

Denmark reaffirmed its commitment to banning bottom trawling in parts of its waters and to continuing the designation of strictly protected areas -- aiming to reach 8% by 2028 and 10% by 2030. Similarly, Sweden referred to its preexisting plan to introduce a future ban on bottom trawling in some MPAs.

Some countries showed "sheer confusion in their stance," such as Spain, which publicly defended harmful bottom trawling while simultaneously announcing a fishing ban to protect a unique deep-sea reef in the Alboran Sea, said Seas at Risk.

"In a pure box-ticking exercise, French president Emmanuel Macron announced a ban on bottom trawling in 4% of French waters where absolutely no trawling takes place."

French NGO Bloom -- which was up in arms about Macron's perceived deception -- has pledged to take legal action over the issue.

Seas at Risk added that it, together with its member Danmarks Naturfredningsforening and NGOs ClientEarth and Oceana, has also launched a legal complaint to the European Commission, to call for infringement action to be taken against countries that "continue to flout EU nature laws, including the EU Habitats Directive."

"The legacy of EU countries at this conference on ocean protection can be summed up as: 'Do as I say, not as I do'," said Seas at Risk senior marine policy officer Tatiana Nuno. "While the Commission president spoke on one stage about the importance of ocean health, EU leaders took to others to give industrial trawlers a free pass to destroy the seabed and the precious life it supports. Our ocean cannot take any more. Europe has the most trawled seas in the world, which makes the EU's inaction on protecting its seas even more damning."
