title: Catch the Current episode 21: Where in the world is Undercurrent News? Industry event highlights
content:
It's that time of the week! Don't miss an all-new episode of Catch the Current as members from the Undercurrent News team call in from around the globe to give updates on their recent event live blogs. 

We're looking to 90s computer game "Where in the world is Carmen Sandiego" for inspiration as we welcome Jacob Resneck, reporting from the North Pacific Fisheries Management Council meeting in Portland, Oregon; Liza Mayer, reporting from San Diego, California, for RASTECH 2025; Barb Dean Simmons, reporting from Fredericton, New Brunswick, Canada, for the Aquaculture Canada Conference; and Masa Takeuchi, reporting from the Seoul Food & Hotel trade show in South Korea.

Listen now on YouTube below!

Subscribe now! Catch the Current is available on YouTube, Spotify, Amazon Music, iHeartRadio, Pandora, and other major podcast streaming platforms. Don't see Catch the Current on your favorite app? Reach out to podcasts@undercurrentnews.com.

Don't have time to listen? Find a full transcript of season 1, episode 21 of Catch the Current below:

Amanda Buckle (AB): You're listening to Catch the Current, the coolest seafood podcast out there from the team at Undercurrent News, your trusted source for seafood prices, news, and data.

I'm Amanda Buckle, and if you're a 90s child like me, you may remember a computer game/game show called "Where in the World is Carmen Sandiego?" Players had to figure out where in the world Carmen and her henchmen were hiding.

Well, this week, we're playing our own version called "Where in the World is Undercurrent News?" Because we've got a team of reporters live-blogging from all over.

But before we check in with them, this week the big story was out of Alaska with our very own Jacob Resneck breaking the news Wednesday evening that some Dutch Harbor pollock vessels are sitting out the B season over a price dispute.

Maritime tracking, as of Wednesday, showed at least five Alaska trawl vessels tied to the dock at Westward Seafoods plant in Dutch Harbor. Westward Seafoods is owned by Japanese giant Maruha Nichiro and part of a cooperative of eight catcher trawl vessels.

Some Dutch Harbor pollock vessels sit out B season opening over price dispute

Its partners claim the Japanese conglomerate has still not finalized pricing for the recently concluded A season, and that Maruha did not tender a preseason price for B season, which opened this past Tuesday. Westward Fishing CEO Greg Baker told Undercurrent News that he decided to tie up his vessels in response to a disagreement over Maruha's price transparency. Baker also said that vessel operators and their crew remain unpaid for fish delivered months ago.

The stand down is not a coordinated effort across the fleet. One US trade industry group exec confirmed to Undercurrent that the stand-down is the independent actions of some captains who are waiting out the processors over dissatisfaction with prices.

Meanwhile, Maruha's competitors have released preseason B prices, which the vessel owners would not disclose to Undercurrent. But they did say that the offers are historically low and don't cover breakeven costs.

The full story from Jacob Resneck, plus ongoing coverage on the subject, can be found in the show notes.

Now, on to our very first installment of ....."Where in the world is Undercurrent News?"

First up is Jacob Resneck, reporting from the North Pacific Fishery Management Council.

Jacob, where in the world are you for this event?

Jacob Resneck (JR): Well, it was controversial because this North Pacific Fishery Management Council meeting, which is responsible for regulating federal fisheries off the coast of Alaska, was in Oregon this month. By law, they're supposed to have a meeting once a year down in Washington state or in Oregon because a lot of the fleet's there.

But it was controversial because there was a big thing on the agenda about redefining what mid-water trawl gear, pelagic trawl gear actually means. And they decided to do this down in Oregon, where a lot of the fleet is based, but where it's hard for a lot of the Alaska fishermen to get to.

It's also right when salmon season is kicking off. And so there was a lot of pushback from the salmon fleet and others about the timing and the choice of place for the meeting to talk about this controversial trawl issue.

AB: How many people usually attend this event?

JR: You know, it's hard to say. You have your industry groups. It's in the hundreds, usually, but then you have a whole host of people calling in, attending virtually as well. It was a mixed thing.

There were a lot of Alaskans that I recognized who had come down for the event. There were a lot of people who called in. But there was also criticism from Tribal groups because this is when the subsistence harvest and hunting, fishing, trapping really is going in earnest.

So there was a pretty limited call-in from the more rural coastal villages this time around.

AB: What do you feel is the big takeaway from this year's meeting?

JR: Well, the council's been under a lot of pressure to redefine what is pelagic trawl, midwater trawl. The dictionary definition would mean keeping your nets off the bottom.

Alaska pollock sector prevails over attempt to restrict pelagic trawl gear

The last time they actually defined this in the regulation was back in 1993. People didn't agree on a lot of things, but one thing everyone did agree on is that 1993 definition no longer reflects reality.

The pelagic trawl fleet has been out of compliance for years and a lot of for good reasons because there's been innovation, changes in the technology, like these salmon excluders and things that are designed to reduce bycatch, to let salmon escape the nets while catching a lot of pollock and other groundfish.

But it runs afoul of the 90s regulation. So the council had to go back and retool that regulation. Now they were under a lot of pressure. There was over 90 comments, written comments came in, the majority saying, "Hey, if it's gonna be called pelagic trawl, that should mean off the bottom. If it's not gonna be off the bottom, call it something else."

The council ultimately did not do that. They basically grandfathered in the status quo of what more reflects the facts on the ground in the water, what the fleet is doing now. 

But looking ahead, they're gonna come back early next year and try to kind of fine tune some of the definitions and see how the nets are performing. That left a lot of the crab harvesters, crab industry, salmon industry dissatisfied because they felt that that was letting the trawl industry off a little too easy. No one ever comes out of these meetings fully satisfied, but that's how the council went.

AB: There's gotta be winners and losers. I don't see a meeting where everyone comes out a winner, right?

JR: Right. The main thing that's going on with this fishery council and the other regional fishery management councils that regulate US fisheries in federal waters is all this uncertainty in what's happening with the federal government. Agencies aren't getting the money released from Washington, D.C., like they're used to.

And so we just heard this morning that a lot of the funding is still held up and it's uncertain if it will be released. So the council has all these really, really important things to do at their upcoming meetings.

In December, they have to set the groundfish specifications. They have to report back to the International Pacific Halibut Commission to set their halibut harvest specifications.

North Pacific council faces funding crunch, delegates Cook Inlet salmon harvest to feds

But they also had promised to come back to the chum bycatch issue, which is so huge for Western Alaska for the subsistence users who are concerned about large amounts of chum salmon caught in trawl nets.

They talked about how they just don't have time to fit all these in December. But beyond all that, since the money is still frozen, they don't even know if they have money to have a meeting at all.

So there's a lot of high-level discussions going back and forth saying, how can we even plan something when the money is being withheld? And they're having a hard time getting answers from the administration of US president Donald Trump.

So, that's something we're reporting on now. There's so much to do, a long way to go and no time to get there and there might be no money either. So stay tuned because we have to see how this shakes out, because without the money, without the meetings, the US government cannot legally open these fisheries.

Alaska freezer longline fleet seeks reg changes to forestall observer shortage

AB: And I was going to say, I'm like a nine-day meeting seemed really long. But talking to you for a few minutes about just a few of the things that were discussed, I feel like, yeah, that's definitely not even enough time. That's wild.

JR: There is so much else going on that they have to do by law. There's all these specifications and things.

Just a little background. We heard this presentation. There are over 500 fishery stocks that are managed by these different regional councils. And the Trump administration has come back to the agency, NOAA, that does this, the National Marine Fisheries Service, and says, "Going forward, don't expect to be able to manage these fishery stocks the way you have been." So there's a lot of retooling and rethinking and they don't know what else they can do because this is all defined by law and statute.

So we don't really know what the future holds.

AB: All these stories and more will be linked back in our show notes. You can read all of Jacob's coverage from the North Pacific Fishery Management Council's meeting right there.

We just heard from Jacob Resneck. Now joining us from San Diego, California, from the RASTECH conference is our very own Liza Mayer.

Liza Mayer (LM): Hello, everyone, from San Diego, California, where RASTech 2025 just wrapped up on June 11.

RASTECH 2025: Why small-scale RAS is gaining ground in a post-hype market

I've been coming to this event since it launched in 2019. And this year certainly felt different for me -- in a good way.

What stood out for me was the conversation around smaller RAS operations.

Having covered the space for years, the focus was on 10,000-[metric] ton mega-plus farms or mega farms, especially for salmon. I felt that tone has shifted. You can think about modular species, diverse and built around 500 to 3,000 [metric] tons, with some even smaller.

So two big things came up again and again, especially yesterday during the investors forum. One, the technology is better. Water treatment is more efficient and more species are proving viable in land-based systems.

Number two, the market is catching up. There's now a consumer segment, these experts told me, especially in Europe and parts of Asia, who are willing to pay a premium for local, sustainably-raised fish. And it's not just theory.

The trend is showing up in projects that were first announced during the hype of the RAS hype cycle. If you remember when the sector was just starting, conference rooms were filled with some just looking, trying to learn about the space. I'm talking about national events even before RASTech conference was born.

But now these ideas are being reworked with more modest, achievable goals. For example, I just broke this morning the news about Whole Oceans. It's a long-delayed salmon project in Maine, originally unveiled in 2018 as a 20,000 metric ton facility. It's now being scaled down to 3,000t.

AB: That's a big difference.

LM: Anyway, all the details are in my report.

Another project, Aquacon, a Norwegian-backed venture in Maryland, followed the same path. Originally, it aimed for a 20,000t facility. Now, it plans to develop a 10,000t facility, starting with just 6,000t initially.

So in the east, in Japan, we're seeing land-based farms operating from 16 to 900t a year. So you can imagine 16t a year. That's very focused. That's very small, but very close to consumer markets.

So are we in RAS phase two? That was the question I floated around to experts at the conference. They answered me. Read my latest blog. Many are agreeing that this is now the next phase of RAS. I talked to venture capital guys, fish farmers, RAS technology suppliers. It offered a different angle on what this post-hype market really looks like and where it's headed next.

AB: And we'll link back to that in the show notes. So definitely check that out.

Thanks, Liza. All right. Moving along in our "Where in the world is Undercurrent News?"

Aquaculture Canada 2025: Aquaculture industry sees need for smarter public engagement

We're in Fredericton, New Brunswick, Canada, now with Barb Dean-Simmons, who has been reporting live from the Aquaculture Canada Conference. Barb, it's day three. You just wrapped up.

Tell us what's been going on for these past few days.

Barb Dean-Simmons (BDS): Jam-packed conference, you know, three days of back-to-back-to-back sessions. Three sessions at a time. So my challenge was to pick which one I'm going to sit in on to hopefully get a story.

Day one, very sciency, lots of academics presenting their research papers on a variety of topics. Everything from the growth and survival of mixed sex diploid and all female diploid and triploid rainbow trout in variable temperature seawater to the optimal marker density and genotyping tool choice for long-term genetic success in aquaculture breeding programs.

But I also learned that there's no such thing as too much science and innovation because science has helped the aquaculture industry develop some strong broodstock in the salmon farming industry and trout farming. They've helped develop new vaccines and continue to work on that.

And science is helping the industry plan for and tackle challenges around climate change. You know, in Atlantic Canada, we've seen some hurricanes come through. And so people are measuring water temperatures, watching weather and figuring out what that means for the farmers that need to operate on the water in those challenging weather conditions.

Glen Cooke, CEO of Cooke. Photo provided by Cooke

And science can also help combat some of the rhetoric and misinformation about the aquaculture industry. That's the word from Glenn Cooke. He's considered to be the godfather of aquaculture in Canada, of course, and a world leader in the industry.

And he was the much-anticipated special guest for a fireside chat on day two of the conference. So everybody, every delegate, I think, was in the room for that one, all 350 to hear what he had to say.

So, Amanda, that's the first time I've met Glenn Cooke.

So, did I ask him about salmon since he is the godfather of salmon? Of course not. I decided to tackle him on cod. And more specifically, whether Cooke might be thinking about adding cod farming to its lineups.

Cooke hints at possible return to cod farming

AB: I'm sure that caught him off guard.

BDS: Oh, you can check out that story on our blog and the full story on our website, of course. And side note, just what I found interesting about seeing him in the room and meeting him, he seems to be a rather low-key kind of guy. I mean, he's not a three-piece suitor.

So it was kind of fun, too, after his talk to watch the conference delegates kind of gather around and mob him for just a handshake or say hello and grab a selfie. It's kind of like a rock star moment.

AB: The rock stars of seafood. I love it.

BDS: So final thoughts. The conference theme was "Aquaculture is agriculture."

And that's a theme that the industry has been pushing for several years now, trying to convince governments, provincial and federal, to place oversight for aquaculture into the hands of the folks who regulate agriculture.

But I would say the secondary theme, the thing that kept popping up more so through day two and day three, was the chat about the public perception of the industry and how the industry needs to fight disinformation in order to change public opinion.

Very interesting chat on that this morning with a panel discussion hosted by the Young Farmers Association of [British Columbia]. And I heard that theme repeated through the last couple of days.

So to wrap it up, it was a jam-packed three days with sessions happening simultaneously every day. And along the way, I learned that: algae can be a low-cost solution for land-based fish tanks; Underwater robots come with cool attachments that can cut tangled ropes and put a patch on a torn net; and young people who are involved in the aquaculture industry like their jobs. They want to see the industry grow and are always willing and eager to talk to anyone willing to listen about the importance of aquaculture to food security and the economy. 

AB: I love those takeaways. Barb's stories, her blog, everything can be found in our show notes. So definitely check that out. Thanks, Barb.

Last but not least, our "Where in the world is the Undercurrent News team?" continues with Masa Takeuchi.

Masa, where are you now? Because you've been reporting from two major food trade shows in Asia.

Masa Takeuchi (MT): Hi, Amanda. Over the past few weeks, I've been reporting from two major food trade shows in Asia -- Thaifex Anuga Asia food show in Bangkok, Thailand, and Seoul Food & Hotel 2025 here, in South Korea. The Thaifex was held at the IMPACT convention center in Bangkok from May 27 to 31.

Thaifex 2025: US stockpiling sees Thai canned tuna exports jump; Norway mackerel prices on track for new high

And one of the main themes of the show was, you know, again, US tariffs. Especially for Southeast Asian exporters. Countries like Thailand, Vietnam and Indonesia are facing the risk of higher US import duties under the Trump administration's tariff policy. As you know, Thailand is a major canned tuna exporter in the world, and the US is its largest market.

According to the Thai Union Industry Association, which represents the whole tuna sector in Thailand, during the first quarter of this year, Thailand shipped out around 141,000t of canned tuna worth $6 million, which is up 5% in volume and 1% in value year on year.

But and then also exports to the US alone rose 14% as buyers placed early orders ahead of possible Thai hike. But that window may close unless a deal is reached by July 9. The current duty of 22.5% for canned tuna for human consumption could jump up to 48.5%.

Tuna can. Photo: VICUSCHKA / Shutterstock

That's a huge rate.

So, the Thai Union Industry Association president told me this could slash Thai tuna exports to the US by as much as 60% by 2026. He also warned that Thai tuna would no longer be competitive if the new tariff hits and raw material could shift to processors in other countries.

AB: So moving on to your latest live blog.

Seoul Food 2025: K·FISH chef expedition to promote South Korean seafood globally

MT: This week, I'm reporting from Seoul Food & Hotel, South Korea's largest international trade fair for food, beverage and hospitality. This event runs from June 10 to 13 at KINTEX, just outside of Seoul. And it features 1,600 exhibitors from 51 countries.

AB: Pretty hefty event.

MT: Yeah.

AB: And now what is seafood's presence like there?

MT: For example, the Alaska Seafood Market Institute had run a booth for the first time this year. And also the Norwegian Seafood Council. But this is kind of the general food trade show. So the seafood is just one portion, but its presence has been expanding in recent years.

AB: Did tariff and trade talks kind of control the conversation at that event as well?

MT: According to the South Korean Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, between January and April this year, South Korea exported $1.05 billion worth of seafood. That's still growth.

But the most noticeable slowdown from previous years' shipment to the US rose 7% to $187m. But that's down from 12% growth last year. The slowdown is being felt mostly clearly in dry seaweed or gim in Korean, which accounted for nearly 45% of the total of Korea's seafood export to the US last year.

And also in the first quarter of this year, gim exports surged to $58 million dollars. But the growth itself slowed in April. April was the first full month under the new 10% baseline tariff.

So, that means the tariff has impact on one of the biggest seafood exports to the US.

AB: Well, that does it for us this week. I hope you enjoyed "Where in the world is Undercurrent News." Don't forget to check the show notes for links back to these event blogs and we'll see you here next week. Bye!

title: US wholesale: Norwegian salmon prices surge, Chilean frozen fillets slide as market focus shifts
content:
Two key storylines defined the US wholesale salmon market in week 24 of 2025 (June 9–15): a sharp price rally for fresh Norwegian fillets following a holiday-shortened production week, and steep declines for frozen Chilean fillets as suppliers shift more product away from a sluggish fresh market.

Fresh Norwegian fillet prices rallied this week, increasing $0.85–$0.90 per pound, with US wholesale values landing at $7.10/lb (2–3 lb), $7.20/lb (3–4 lb) and $7.25/lb (4–5 lb). The surge follows a reduced harvest linked to Norway's June 9 "Whit Monday" religious holiday and builds on earlier supply tightening after an algal bloom triggered emergency harvesting in Nordland. 

VIEW GRAPH

Upgrade to Pro to view

Though full-year output remains robust, temporary constraints are reshaping availability and pricing. Importers who froze fish earlier this year in anticipation of firm summer pricing now face margin pressure, as fresh prices undercut frozen inventory.

Steep correction for Chilean frozen fillets

With fresh demand muted and inventories elevated, Chilean suppliers are increasingly pushing product into the frozen channel, and prices are reflecting that pivot. Frozen Chilean fillets saw significant declines in week 24, with reported trades dipping into the low-to-mid $5/lb range.

Fresh fillet prices also softened for a third consecutive week, down $0.42–$0.45/lb across sizes. US wholesale levels averaged $5.33/lb (2–3 lb), $5.45/lb (3–4 lb) and $5.58/lb (4–5 lb), as sellers work through heavy inventory while demand remains seasonally weak.

Despite the broad softening, frozen portions, particularly 8 oz cuts, continue to command premiums due to tight availability.

Looking ahead, Q3–Q4 production will be critical: These quarters account for roughly 60% of Chile's annual harvest, and without a meaningful recovery in demand, oversupply risks may intensify.

On the trade side, despite reports of increased production out of Norway, Chile remains the leading supplier of fillets to the US by far. Monthly import volumes from Chile consistently exceed those from all other origins, with April 2025 totals approaching 33.5 million pounds, more than double the volume shipped by Norway.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view

Even as Norwegian exporters ramp up shipments and gain share, Chile's dominance in the US market underscores its entrenched position as the primary supplier of fresh and frozen salmon fillets.

As the global salmon market moves deeper into summer, the outlook remains split. Chilean suppliers are leaning heavily into frozen product to manage weak fresh demand, raising concerns that Q3-Q4 volumes could oversaturate the market if consumption doesn't rebound.

In contrast, Norwegian salmon continues to find pricing support, buoyed by seasonal demand in Asia, reduced harvest volumes tied to holidays, and the lingering effects of earlier emergency harvests. Still, with tariffs set to rise in the US and trade tensions looming, both origins face an uncertain second half of the year that will test buyer appetite and pricing resilience across wholesale markets.

title: The US lobster industry’s very big day on Capitol Hill
content:
The US lobster industry enjoyed a few glorious hours on Capitol Hill Wednesday (June 4) when champions for the sector made their points of view on stifling regulatory limits and tariffs known to both the White House and Congress.

US senator Susan Collins challenged commerce secretary Howard Lutnick to address trap rope-related restrictions aimed at better protecting North Atlantic right whales that are threatened to go into effect on January 1, 2029 and also tariffs on Canada in one room of the Dirksen Senate Office Building. The US Senate Appropriation Committee's Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies panel was holding a two-hour hearing to review the president's budget proposal.

Simultaneously, just three blocks away in the Longworth House Office Building, Dustin Delano, chief operations officer for the New England Fishermen's Stewardship Association (NEFSA), was also educating the House Natural Resources Committee's oceans panel about the trap restrictions and numerous other issues that he said gave Canadian harvesters an advantage.

Lobsters being unloaded at a wharf in Maine. Photograph by Jason Huffman.

At the Senate hearing, Collins, a Maine Republican, described to Lutnick how, in 2022, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), under former president Joe Biden, proposed regulations that threatened to dramatically limit harvesters' ability to use ropes on traps. The NOAA ruling was required by a federal court decision.

Democrats divert hearing about Trump’s commercial fishing EO to instead focus on DOGE cuts at NOAA

"So, Mr. Secretary, I know there's a new executive order that attempts to establish much higher standards for scientific research," Collins said to Lutnick. "It emphasizes rigorous evidence-based methodologies to inform federal regulations. Can you talk to us about how you believe that this new approach to regulation based in science will help protect the Maine fishing industry and our lobster industry from arbitrary and capricious regulations, as the court found was done in the previous administration?"

Lutnick responded: "This administration views the Maine lobster industry as an American treasure, and we need to protect it. ... We think this capricious lack of rigor in our science has got to end. So, the gold standard executive order saying only real science, not opinion-based science, has to be the rule, so we protect our fishermen, we protect our ranchers. These are key things that this administration is going to drive for.  So, I completely agree with you. We will protect the great Maine lobster industry, because it is a treasure for America."

Commerce secretary Howard Lutnick during a Senate hearing held on June 4, 2025. Image is still from video.

Lobster industry's fate depends on next proposal

Maine's congressional delegation, including Collins, worked as a team, in late 2022, to get a six-year delay of the rules included in a budget bill, she recounted. Until the beginning of 2029, the current rules are deemed sufficient to satisfy the Endangered Species Act and the Marine Mammal Protection Act under the legislation. 

Subsequently, the Maine Lobstermen's Association (MLA) sued NOAA, its National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) and the Department of Commerce, winning a favorable decision by a US Appeals Court in June 2023. The three-judge panel described the methodology used by the federal agency as "very likely wrong" based on assumptions made, as reported by Undercurrent News.

So, does the expiration of the NOAA rule suspension at the end of December 2028 mean the US lobster industry needs to then get in compliance with new trap rules?

"NOAA is beginning the process of writing new regulations," one MLA staffer told Undercurrent this week. "But the simple answer is, 'yes,' it will all depend upon what the federal government proposes when it releases its new set of proposed regulations (perhaps next year?)."

Coincidentally, a delegation from the MLA spent this week in Washington, D.C., visiting lawmakers and members of the administration, hoping to persuade them more to their causes. 

Six years not enough

Over in the Longworth building, Delano articulated to the House oceans panel how continuous pressure on lobster harvesters to better protect right whales was a major source of difficulty and creating dangerous conditions.

He was one of five witnesses called to address president Donald Trump's executive order (EO 14276), "Restoring American seafood competitiveness." 

"No one questions the need to protect the species," said the New England fisherman. "Fishermen have made enormous sacrifices to help. We've modified our gear, reduced our lines, increased trawl lengths to reduce entanglements, but these changes come at a cost financially and physically."

He continued: "The longer trawls we now use create dangerous working conditions. The weak links in our ropes can snap under tension, sometimes in our faces, creating serious safety risks."

A map shows the proximity of the US Capitol to the buildings where both Senate (Dirksen) and House (Longworth) hearings took place on June 4, 2025.

Delano expressed a low amount of confidence in the remaining four years being enough time for NOAA and the lobster industry to produce enough data to hold off future trap rules in 2029.

"[U]nless the current regulatory process is extended, these restrictions will return before the science is ready," he warned the subcommittee.

Later, during questions and answers, he expounded.

"I do not think that six years is enough time," Delano said. "I think what was asked in the first place was 10 to 12, and that is because here we are two-and-a-half years after that legislation, and we're finally able to get the funding and able to get started on collecting the data. And it takes a significant amount of time to get through the TRT process, and so that's why they're already starting in that direction."

Delano advocated for non-invasive whale tagging, which he said has been tried successfully in the southern hemisphere with "real, real-time location data," adding: "We could avoid conflict zones more accurately instead of relying on broad closures that don't reflect reality."

Much of Wednesday's hearing in the House was consumed by Democrats attacking the dramatic cuts made to NOAA made by the Department of Government Efficiency and future cuts threatened by the Trump 2025-26 budget proposal, as reported earlier by Undercurrent.

Canadian advantages in gray zone

But the right whale concern wasn't the only one addressed by Delano. He also managed to register a complaint about the way Canadian harvesters are operating with less regulatory limitations in the "gray zone," a 277-square mile area off the coast of Maine and Canada claimed by both countries since the Revolutionary War.

"For years, the contested waters produced a modest lobster catch; now there is an abundance of lobster," he wrote. "In the gray zone, Americans must toss back any lobster with a carapace longer than five inches. Canadians have no such limits. Canadians can catch 'jumbo' lobsters while Americans cannot. Canadians will continue to dominate the market while they catch the most popular lobster without interference." 

"It's not just unfair, it's unsustainable," he said at the hearing. "Our fishermen are playing by strict US rules while Canadian-caught seafood can enter our markets unchecked. We need to move toward co-management at the very least, but ideally assert full US sovereignty and resolve this dispute with Canada."

He continued: "We're not asking for a free pass. We're asking for fairness because, when regulation erases your ability to fish, to plan to provide, you're not just losing your job, you're losing your identity, your future, and your community, and that's a loss this country can't afford."

Dustin Delano, chief operations officer at the New England Fishermen's Stewardship Association, at a House hearing on June 4, 2025. Image is still from video.

Additionally, Delano talked about unfair advantages Canadians have with regard to groundfish rules.

"Canadian fishermen can trawl with a 5.2-square-inch mesh, while American fishermen in the Gulf of Maine are restricted to a 6.5-square-inch diamond mesh," he noted, adding: "While the differential sounds small, at only 1.3 inches, the practical difference is enormous. The smaller mesh lands a much higher yield."

The "gray zone," a prolific lobster fishing area disputed by both Canada and the US. Image courtesy of Portland Press Herald.

Lutnick: Lobster covered by USMCA

Collins also hit Lutnick on trade-related concerns Wednesday, asking him for a brief update on where the administration stood with regard to tariffs on Canadian products.

She described how the Maine economy is integrated with Canada, relying on the other country to process much of its lobster, as well as potatoes, blueberries and lumber before importing the finished products back into the US. She noted how 95,000 Mainers get their electricity from Canada, while the state relies on its northern neighbor for 95% of its refined petroleum products and 90% of its potash, which is used as the fertilizer for potatoes.

Lutnick answered: "Sure, so, the overriding principle is [the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or USMCA]. So, if the products are actually made in Canada and actually made in the United States, they come back and forth, and it's easy for them to fall under the USMCA, and that has no tariff. Things that are outside of that, where companies chose to be outside of those rules, and those rules, as you know, have been in place quite a long time."

He said: "They have the fentanyl tariffs, right?  Because we needed to close the border and make sure fentanyl was not coming into the country.  And people say, oh, Canada doesn't do much in fentanyl, but if you look at the fentanyl rings in Canada, they're often manned by Mexican cartels…"

Fears ran rampant for months that the lobster industry would be severely damaged by an emergency declaration signed by Trump in February to impose 25% tariffs on goods from Canada and Mexico. 

A Maine lobster. Photograph by Jason Huffman.

In March, Collins and senator Angus King, a Maine independent, and representative Chellie Pingree, a Maine Democrat, sent a letter to Lutnick calling on the administration to work with Canada to address issues of shared concern and foster economic cooperation. Then, in April, she delivered remarks on the Senate floor in support of a resolution authored by senator Tim Kaine, a Virginia Democrat, to end the emergency declaration and cosponsored the Trade Review Act of 2025, a bipartisan bill to reaffirm Congress' constitutional role in setting and approving US trade policy.

Worries have subsided since Trump, in April, clarified that items determined to be in compliance with USMCA, like lobster, would not be tariffed after all. But the lobster and snow crab industry maintains nervous pits in their stomachs about tariffs being threatened again.

title: Italian construction giant enters offshore farming sector with Aqualoop partnership
content:
Italian construction giant Saipem, which provides engineering and construction services for the energy sector, has entered the aquaculture space after agreeing to "a strategic collaboration" with Norwegian offshore farming pioneer Aqualoop.

Iceland takes first steps towards offshore salmon farming

According to Saipem, the partnership will look to "overcome the limitations of current confined water farming systems," making use of Saipem's long experience designing and building oil rigs and other offshore energy installations.

"In the context of the collaboration, Saipem would be specifically responsible for the construction of offshore cages, submersible down to a depth of 20 meters or more below the sea surface and about 160m in diameter, for the farming and growth of fish in the open sea according to Aqualoop's technology."

Saipem is already involved in Norway through its subsidiary Moss Maritime, which offers design and engineering services for both the offshore energy and maritime sectors.

Aqualoop currently offers a floating, submersible fish cage it calls the 'Big Dipper', which has built-in fish tanks and mechanisms for sorting and fish logistics between the pens.

The base version of the Aqualoop Big Dipper has a total grow-out area of 500,000 cubic meters divided between eight submersible cages, bigger even than the Ocean Farm 1 concept created by SalMar Aker Ocean.

It has been designed for harsh environments in areas with a water depth in excess of 200 meters, and can be customized for other conditions and other species besides Atlantic salmon.

The company took investment from Icelandic consultancy Marko Partners during a fundraising round in March 2023, and the two have invested in a new entity they call Icelandic Offshore Salmon, which they believe will be Iceland's first offshore aquaculture project.

title: UK monitors shellfish aquaculture amid exceptionally warm spring ocean temperatures
content:
The UK's marine scientists are monitoring the conditions for shellfish aquaculture amid exceptionally high spring ocean temperatures.

Temperatures in the seas around the UK and Ireland soared by mid-May, with some areas 4 degrees Celsius warmer than normal, with potential implications for marine life, the BBC reported.

Sea temperatures in April and the first half of May were the highest recorded during those months since monitoring began 45 years ago. Climate change is causing oceans to warm around the globe and is making marine heatwaves more likely.

A marine heatwave is defined as sea temperatures that exceed the seasonal threshold for more than five consecutive days. In the UK, the marine heatwave threshold for May is 11.3°C. On May 19, the average sea surface temperature reached 12.69°C.

When it comes to aquaculture, "it's difficult to generalize about shellfish, as responses will vary depending on each species' thermal tolerance, period of acclimation etc.," Dr Mairi Cowan of the Scottish Association for Marine Science (SAMS) told Undercurrent.

"My main concern would be increased susceptibility to disease (bacterial, viral, parasitic), with the elevated temperatures stressing their immune systems, accelerating pathogen growth, and allowing disease-causing organisms to expand their range/persist longer."

Native oysters (Ostrea edulis) in the UK are at the cooler end of their thermal range and may be less adversely affected by heatwaves than species closer to their upper thermal limits, she said.

"However, their performance is still compromised during short periods of elevated temperatures."

One study from the northwest coast of Spain found that gill tissue begins to function anaerobically above 26°C, with cardiac dysfunction occurring at 28°C, and mortality at 36°C, she continued.

"Although these temperatures wouldn't be experienced in subtidal habitats, for intertidal shellfish species, this could be an issue. Elevated temperatures can also accelerate gametogenesis, potentially affecting larval quality and leading to a mismatch between larval release and favourable environmental conditions, and can skew adult sex ratios."

In February, SAMS reported that a new study in Nature Climate Change had found there were nearly 3.5 times the number of marine heatwave days in the summers of both 2023 and 2024 compared to any other year on record.

Geoff Robinson, aquaculture technical officer at Ireland's seafood development agency Bord Iascaigh Mhara, said the organization was "acutely aware of the issue of sea temperature rises associated with climate change and is working closely with aquaculture producers to adapt to these effects."

As well as shellfish, salmon is the main species farmed around the coast of the UK.

"Fish are highly sensitive to any changes in water quality parameters such as changes in temperature, oxygen concentration, salinity, turbidity and phytoplankton. BIM deploys real-time monitoring in aquaculture sites across Ireland to help producers mitigate variations, including higher-than-average water temperatures. The data collected is available to aquaculture producers and allows them to adapt their husbandry as needed," said Robinson.

Research institute confirms algae bloom affecting north Norwegian salmon farms

In the case of an oyster producer, this can mean reducing or temporarily stopping oyster handling while surface water temperatures remain high to protect the shellfish, he continued.

"Or for a salmon farmer, changing a husbandry practice in the short term to reduce fish stress. For example, feed rations can be reduced to allow for lower levels of oxygen in the water."

Dr Iain Berrill, head of technical at industry body Salmon Scotland, told Undercurrent that since the start of 2025, the Scottish salmon sector has access to "rigorous water temperature and quality monitoring and keeps a close eye on environmental conditions."

Despite the climate concerns, the industry has recorded the "highest monthly survival rates on record, and 2024 was the best year for survival since 2020. Sea lice levels are the lowest ever recorded. This is due to the almost £1 billion investment by our salmon farming producers in measures to maximize animal health and welfare."

Higher sea temperatures can contribute to algae bloom development, the likes of which have threatened northern Norway this spring.

title: Nueva Pescanova quadruples earnings, cuts loss to €38m in shortened fiscal 2024
content:
Spanish multinational Nueva Pescanova significantly improved its financial performance in 2024, posting a fourfold increase in earnings and returning to operating profitability.

Despite substantial debt repayment costs, the company posted a net loss of €37.9 million in the nine months ending Dec. 31, 2024, an improvement of over €90m compared to the previous year's loss of €131m (see profit and loss statement at the bottom of this article), according to its latest financial report.

Total revenue during the nine-month period reached €770.6m, bringing the full-year turnover to €982m, up 1.2% from the like-for-like period of €969.8m in 2023, as shown in the second graph below.

Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) rose to €40.1m, more than four times the €9.8m recorded in the previous financial year, despite the current reporting period covering only nine months (see graph below). This reflects stronger operational efficiency and cost control, even as financial expenses, including €33.84m in debt repayments, weighed the bottom line.

According to the firm, profit margins increased significantly due to improved efficiencies in aquaculture and processing, reduced overhead costs, and targeted commercial efforts in markets with higher returns.

"The recovery in sales during the fiscal year, along with cost reductions, drove the increase in EBITDA. On the commercial front, the group has focused its attention on higher-margin operations to optimize profitability," Nueva Pescanova said.

Operating profit, excluding depreciation and non-recurring items, turned positive at €1.4m compared to a loss of €90.5m in the previous period. 

Sales gains were observed in markets such as France and Portugal, where the company's seafood offering and refined channel strategies contributed to better performance. Meanwhile, the US and Asian markets maintained steady contributions to overall revenue, according to the group.

The group's 2024 turnover reached €982m, up 1% from €970m in 2023. Source: Nueva Pescanova's calendar 2024 results vs. 2023.

These results mark a turnaround aligned with the business transformation plan launched in late 2023.

The plan focuses on four pillars: sharpening the commercial strategy, optimizing performance across the supply chain from fishing and aquaculture origins through to processing plants and final destination, restructuring the organization, making it more agile and adapting to the market environment, and driving cross-functional projects to capture value.

"By implementing this business plan, the group will strengthen its position as a leader in the marketing of seafood products, based on an agile and dynamic organizational structure that draws on the group's knowledge and experience in all the activities that make up its value chain," Nueva Pescanova said.

The group said its brand remains the most recognized for seafood in Spain. According to data from a survey firm, Ipsos retains the number-one spot in brand awareness, with 95% total recognition and the highest top-of-mind positioning among consumers. The brand also leads the sector in brand equity, holding an 18% market share, outpacing its closest competitor by over six points.

Backed by its majority shareholder, Abanca, Nueva Pescanova maintains sufficient financial autonomy to continue executing its transformation plan and long-term growth strategy, the firm said.

Source: Nueva Pescanova's April-December 2024 results.

title: Alaska startup pitches ‘iron fertilization’ to Trump to reverse fishing declines
content:
A US businessman claiming direct access to the Donald Trump administration is working to gain support for rebuilding Alaska's fish stocks through a controversial form of geoengineering that would be authorized by the US president's declaration of a "national emergency."

Russ George wants to use iron to generate a giant plankton bloom, tending the sea as if it's a massive saltwater aquarium.

George worked as chief scientist to the Haida Salmon Restoration Corporation, which in 2012 controversially spread 100 metric tons of iron sulphate and 20t of iron oxide off the west coast of Canada in an attempt to stimulate phytoplankton blooms to feed salmon when they would return to the Frazier River.

Company behind ‘rogue’ ocean fertilization loses court bid to block charges

Canadian officials quickly condemned the project after it became public, contributing to an international outcry and criticism from the 87 nations signed up to the London Convention. The 1975 treaty prohibits dumping in international waters except for legitimate research.

But reporting in the Vancouver Sun suggests that Canada knew about the scheme as early as 2011 and only began investigating the CAD 2.5 million ($1.8m) project after the bad publicity that also led to acrimony between George and his former partners.

George believes the media coverage was unfair.

"It got ravaged by the green media," he told Undercurrent News on the sidelines of ComFish Alaska, a seafood expo held in Kodiak in mid-April. 

Revelations also surfaced that George sought to profit from selling carbon credits to a Swiss company, but that never materialized, the Vancover Sun reported in late 2012.

US gov’t report highlights impacts of Russia, plant closures on Alaska seafood industry

George told Undercurrent in a recent interview that his ambitions for Alaska would be "basically a clone of that" and that he's in touch with the Trump White House to draft an executive order to revitalize America's fishing grounds. It would employ the same controversial methods, could boost ocean productivity and raise revenue by selling so-called blue carbon credits, he said.

"I want to focus on the fact that there's an ocean emergency here," George told Undercurrent at ComFish. "The most important and least contested executive orders ever issued by any president are the emergency declarations following natural disasters."

Plans for executive order

George divides his time between California and Alaska and founded a startup, OPR Alaska, in 2020, state business records show. He recently pitched his iron fertilization idea directly to Alaska's congressional delegation, arguing that policymakers can't be passive amidst a record $1.8 billion decline in Alaska's seafood revenue.

"I got a call from the White House on Thursday (Jan. 23) asking me to help write this executive order for ocean restoration," George told US senator Dan Sullivan, an Alaska Republican and Trump ally, during an April 16 question-and-answer session at ComFish.

Sullivan, who participated in the event via a web link, thanked George for his "hard work" and said he'd research the issue with the Trump administration.

"Let me get back to you on that," Sullivan said.

Nearly a month later, Sullivan's office has not responded to a request from Undercurrent for an update. 

It's not George's first attempt to interest the US government in an ocean fertilization scheme. He worked with US representative Buddy Carter, a Georgia Republican who, in 2024, introduced HR 7797, a bill that would authorize $33m annually over five years to develop a pilot program on ocean fertilization and restoration research and development.

The legislation received no co-sponsors and quietly died with the end of the 118th Congress.

George said the executive order route would be preferable "because that will cut through the red tape" rather than working through the standard federal agencies.

'Dangerous to go around dumping things like iron'

Geoengineering would likely appeal to Trump: a relatively cheap technological fix to adverse ocean conditions that could offer quick results. But ocean researchers have misgivings. 

"There are a lot of scientists who think it's dangerous to go around dumping things like iron in the open ocean and have spent quite a lot of time trying to find ways to regulate this so it's not just a free-for-all," University of Victoria oceanography professor Ken Denman told the Canadian Press in 2016 when a similar project was proposed in Chile. 

Marine scientists have also found correlations between historic iron fertilization and neurotoxin domoic acid, which can make commercial species like crab unfit for human consumption.

"Given that iron fertilization in iron-depleted regions of the sea has been proposed to enhance phytoplankton growth and, thereby, both reduce atmospheric CO2 and moderate ocean acidification in surface waters, consideration of the potentially serious ecosystem impacts associated with (domoic acid) is prudent," researchers wrote in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2010.

When George pitched his idea to federal fisheries scientists, they were skeptical.

Bob Foy, science and research director at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Alaska Fisheries Science Center, said George's pronouncement that the US is in the "throes of this catastrophic ocean health decline" is overstating the problem.

"I wouldn't go as far as to say the entire ocean's health is in absolute decline – it's changing," Foy told George at ComFish. "For all of the stocks that we've mentioned that have been negatively impacted by heat waves or changes, we've also seen other stocks [like] Bristol Bay sockeye salmon [reach] highest production that we've ever seen."

He said climate change, marine heat waves and ocean acidification are real challenges, but fertilizing the ocean likely won't help.

"The reasons for these changes are not likely something you can restore back to. You're not going to bring a species back if it has changed because of changing temperature or changing sea ice or changing ocean conditions," Foy said. "So I think it would be a mistake to think that we need to work backwards to restore ocean conditions to something that they might have been."

Russ George, founder of Ocean Pasture Restoration (OPR), told attendees of ComFish in Kodiak, Alaska that he's in touch with the White House to draft an executive order to authorize geoengineering to stimulate declining seafood stocks. Photograph by Brian Venua.

George declined to share documented evidence of his contacts with the White House. However, the US president has been known to sign far-reaching executive orders whose ambition and reach are regularly tested in the courts.

Republican US senator Lisa Murkowski, also representing Alaska, told George at ComFish that she's skeptical of executive actions that lack oversight. 

"Emergency orders can be opportunities," said Murkowski, who was present at the meeting. "But as one who is a strong believer in the role that we play in Congress, as representatives for those in our states, I want to make sure that it's not just executive authority that is leading us, but that Congress is in sync and working towards that."

Ocean revitalization or carbon trading gambit?

OPR Alaska's pitch is ocean restoration, but during a meeting with the Alaska Seafood Industry Task Force late last year, George also revived the idea of raising revenue through selling so-called "blue carbon" credits which he said had been received favorably by the office of Alaska governor Mike Dunleavy.

Blue carbon, as defined by NOAA, is carbon dioxide from the atmosphere absorbed and stored in the world's oceans.

Ultimately, he believes his firm could generate a profit by selling carbon credits for this process.

"Fish are for everybody. We have no way of laying claim on the fish value," George said at the Sept. 19, 2024 meeting. "But we have the privilege of laying claim on the blue carbon."

He brushed off any concerns that dumping iron filings in the marine environment could have unintended consequences like harmful algae blooms.

"There'll be academics who will want to say, 'Well, I can imagine a hundred reasons why it's not safe,' but that's just their imagination," George said. "You have to do the test. If you don't do the real work, you'll never know."

title: Global salmon consumption hits record Q1 high as Mowi lifts 2029 production goal
content:
Global salmon consumption reached a new all-time high for a first quarter in 2025, hitting 590,000 metric tons -- up 5% year-on-year, according to aquaculture business Mowi, which also cited Kontali.

Consumption exceeded supply by approximately 7,000t on good market development, releasing some stock from an already low inventory, it said in its Q1 report.

Click to enlarge

European consumption increased by 4.6%, mainly driven by strong retail demand, particularly within the natural fresh category. Key markets such as France, Germany, the UK, Italy and Spain all showed positive developments. Foodservice demand was stable during the quarter.

Consumption in the US increased by 6.2% y-o-y in Q1, with growth again mainly driven by the retail channel.

"The fresh pre-packed category continued to drive volume growth, reflecting a broader market shift towards higher-value product categories. The positive development was further supported by Mowi's strong growth in skin-pack sales of 24% y-o-y."

The online grocery segment also maintained solid momentum, with significant increases in e-commerce sales compared to the previous year, it added.

US growth was strongest within delivery services, driven by broader offerings and promotional activities from major retailers. "Overall, consumer behaviour continues to favour home consumption, supported by inflationary pressures and changes in shopping patterns," said Mowi.

Regarding the tariff upheaval that has defined Q1 for the US, Mowi said the rates it currently faces are 10% for Norway, Scotland, Chile, Ireland, the Faroes and Iceland, and 0% from Canada.

Click to enlarge

"Based on this, the current weighted average US tariff rate for imported salmon based on market share per origin is 9%. The situation is fluid and Mowi is continuously monitoring developments. The company is redistributing volumes from our seven origins with respect to prevailing trade policies at any given time to best serve our customers."

"Based on the US salmon market's global share of approximately 20% and an estimated price elasticity of 1.0, the temporary negative global demand effect is projected to [be] 2%. Indirect effects related to a potential general economic slowdown come in addition," it added.

In Brazil, consumption declined by 8% in Q1, primarily driven by lower supply availability, as higher demand from the US market absorbed volumes, particularly from Chile. Underlying demand in both retail and foodservice segments remained solid.

Finally, in Asia, consumption grew significantly, increasing by 13% y-o-y. Growth was particularly strong in China/Hong Kong, where consumption rose by 28%.

As the Norwegian Seafood Council has noted, Norway's salmon exports to China jumped 188% in April alone compared to the same month last year, making China the third-largest market globally for Norwegian salmon. The Q1 surge pushed Norway's market share in China to 62% as of March, exceeding the 50% threshold for the first time in over a decade of gradual market expansion.

"The positive development was mainly driven by better availability of larger-sized salmon, aligning with strong demand from the foodservice segment. All key markets in the region showed positive consumption trends, reflecting continued robust underlying demand for Atlantic salmon."

Strong demand means good result for Mowi in Asia

All of this good demand has meant a strong performance for Mowi's downstream sales division, "Consumer Products," where operating revenues were down just marginally y-o-y at €893.3 million, but earnings before interest and tax rose from €23.1m to €33.0m.

Sales volumes came to 57,564t, up from 55,999t in Q1 2024.

Click to enlarge

Improvements were led by Asia, where volumes and earnings lifted enough to result in Mowi's best first quarter ever. Volumes lifted from 7,408t to 9,566t -- overtaking the Americas as a segment -- and sales revenue there rose y-o-y from €110.6m to €130.8m.

In Europe, volumes reached just under 40,000t in Q1 -- down a little y-o-y -- and operational revenues eased to €620.0m. 

"Operational performance was good, including yield improvements," Mowi noted. "Developments were particularly good in the fresh segment. Volumes were relatively stable. These effects led to increased earnings, and underlying demand in Europe continued to be good. Average prices were somewhat down, influenced by mix effects."

Then, in the Americas, volumes for skin-pack products improved by 24% compared with Q1 2024. For the fresh category as a whole, volumes were relatively stable, and this was also the case for the chilled segment, it said.

"Average margins improved versus Q1 2024 on positive mix effects. Compared with Europe, the US retail market is still somewhat behind on the recovery curve, and the introduction of tariffs is also challenging. However, we expect demand to work itself out in due course."

title: Nissui bets on Europe to offset Americas slowdown, targets record $6.1bn sales
content:
Japanese seafood giant Nissui Corp. plans to increase its consolidated sales 2% year-on-year to a record JPY 900 billion ($6.1bn) for the fiscal year ending March 2026, marking a fifth consecutive all-time high, as its solid growth in Europe is set to offset a projected slowdown in its North and South American operations amid headwinds caused by US tariff policies.

The Tokyo-based seafood giant flagged concerns Wednesday (May 14) that higher whitefish and shrimp raw material costs and weaker US demand for China-processed seafood could squeeze its North American business. Nissui said it will "leverage its 'global links' to expedite a shift in procurement sources."

In the earnings materials published Wednesday, Nissui highlighted the outlook for its three key North American subsidiaries, which are most exposed to what it called the "Trump risk."

F.W. Bryce is expected to be the most heavily impacted, as the Gloucester, Massachusetts-based seafood distributor sells frozen Pacific cod, flounder, sole, and North Atlantic cod in the US market.

"Sales of whitefish products processed in China may decline in the US," said Nissui. "It also takes time to consider alternative processed products," it added.

King & Prince Seafood, based in Brunswick, Georgia, produces value-added seafood for the foodservice sector. Nissui expects higher shrimp procurement costs from Southeast Asia. 

Maruha plans $410m investment to lift sales to record $7.3bn

"Considering a change in suppliers is also risky," the company said. It also warned that "it will be difficult to pass on the prices due to the price difference with other proteins, such as chicken."

Gorton’s expects 'minimal' impact

Gloucester, Massachusetts-based Gorton's is the US retail market leader in breaded seafood, including fish fingers. 

"Procurement in the US is the primary source, and the impact is minimal," said the group. It added, however, that "consumption trends are uncertain," citing concerns about weaker demand amid an economic slowdown.

As previously reported by Undercurrent News, the manufacturer is investing $98.3 million to build a new processing plant in Indiana.

Nissui's earnings materials state that the new plant will begin operations in the second half of this year. The company aims to "improve our in-house production ratio and logistics efficiency."

Pacific Seafood eyes bankrupt Peter Pan’s largest Alaska plant

Nissui's Alaska pollock business, which has been struggling since 2023, includes its processing operation via UniSea in Dutch Harbor, Alaska, and its minority stake in at-sea processor Glacier Fish Co.

Despite a recent upward trend in fillet and surimi prices, Nissui stressed in a separate filing that "prices remain low." 

The group plans to raise the fillet production ratio by around 5%, capitalizing on its relatively stable high prices compared to surimi, Nissui said. It will also enhance collaboration with fishing vessels to ensure timely raw material procurement aligned with processing operations.

EMDEPES faces fleet downsizing

In South America, Nissui's whitefish business, including hake and hoki, is operated by Chilean subsidiary Empresa de Desarrollo Pesquero de Chile, also known as EMDEPES, with two factory trawlers, "UNZEN" and "UNIONSUR."

Nissui plans to consolidate operations to a single vessel, UNIONSUR, a Nissui spokesperson told Undercurrent. 

The Chilean harvester aims to increase the fillet production ratio over surimi, following the same strategy as in Alaska. The company noted that while it will incur lay-up costs until UNZEN is sold, it expects the unit to "return to profitability from fiscal 2026."

Maruha’s Seacon closes deal for Van der Lee to move past €800m revenue
Expansion in Europe

To offset the slowdown in North and South America, Nissui is increasingly relying on its European operations.

Since 2023, its Danish-based Nordic Seafood has expanded upstream by acquiring Maxima Seafood in the Netherlands and Denso in Denmark, both with fresh seafood processing functions. In 2024, Nordic launched Pesca Nordica to handle processed farmed fish. 

Downstream, France's Cite Marine has expanded production capacity while developing the chilled coated seafood market in Spain and Italy, alongside tapas products placed next to seafood sections.

Starting early this year, Nissui is also expected to ship refined fish-oil-derived pharmaceutical raw materials produced in Japan to the European market, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

Nissui expects its European business to continue growing, projecting a 9% y-o-y rise in overall operating profit to JPY 34.5bn in fiscal 2025, another record for the fifth straight year.

For the fiscal year 2024, which ended March 2025, the company reported consolidated sales of JPY 886.1bn, up 7% from the previous year, with an operating profit of JPY 31.7bn, up 7% y-o-y.

After adjustments for internal eliminations, overseas sales rose 7% to JPY 357.5bn, with North America up 8%, Europe 11%, and Oceania 22%. South America declined 7%, however.

The company's segment matrix showed continued struggles in Japan's marine and food products businesses, North America's marine operations -- Unisea, F.W. Bryce, and Glacier Fish -- and South America's marine operations (see below).

Chilean coho and trout salmon farmer Salmones Antartica swung to a JPY 2.6bn profit from pond-stock valuation in fiscal 2024, compared to a JPY 2.8bn loss a year earlier, as selling prices recovered. 

Kyokuyo targets record $2.3bn revenue amid global trade uncertainty

Nissui said the farmer expects performance improvement further in the second half of the fiscal year 2025, though first-half results will still reflect last year's poor survival rates.

In Japan, the purse-seine fishery posted solid catches of skipjack tuna and mackerel, but weak sardine landings weighed profits. 

The aquaculture business saw overall declines in sales and profit, hit by weak tuna prices, reduced shipments and slow growth for yellowtail, and smaller-sized coho salmon due to early harvesting, the company said.

In the food products segment, frozen food for the retail and foodservice sectors, fish sausages performed strongly, while rising raw material procurement costs driven by a weak yen led to an overall decline in profitability.

title: Previously convicted US lobsterman changes state, gets caught with V-notched female lobsters
content:
A US lobsterman who left his home state of Maine after recent illegal fishing convictions has now been charged with new violations in the neighboring state of New Hampshire.

The New Hampshire Fish and Game Department Law Enforcement Division shared on Facebook on May 4 that Rodney Genthner of Friendship, Maine, has been charged with multiple violations related to an April 23 inspection of his vessel, For The Win.

Per the post, New Hampshire conservation officers had been surveilling For The Win for the past month "due to infractions of licensing and required equipment regulations while engaged in fishing in federal waters and harvest landings" in New Hampshire. Upon boarding the vessel in the early hours of April 23, officers reported discovering the following violations: 

• Possession of V-notched female lobsters (marked, breeding females that are illegal to possess);
• Short lobsters (carapace length less than 3 1/4");
• Unlawful dumping of fish in state harbors;
• Unlawful possession of wolffish (a state and federally protected species);
• and failure to operate a vessel monitoring system.

In November 2022, Genthner was fined in Friendship, Maine, for numerous fishing violations, including violating protected resources; possessing mutilated unmeasurable lobster; taking, transporting, selling, possessing egg-bearing lobster; and molesting or disturbing lobster gear. In August 2023, he was fined for engaging in activities while his fishing license was suspended.

title: US wholesale: Single-frozen Icelandic cod fillet prices keep rising as Pacific level out
content:
The single-frozen groundfish market in the US remains firm through week 18 (April 28-May 4), with elevated pricing levels sustained across major categories including Alaska cod, Iceland haddock and Alaska pollock. However, only one product, Icelandic cod, posted an upward revision this week.

Undercurrent News' US wholesale price assessments show Icelandic cod fillets increased by $0.10/lb this week across all sizes, pushing the average to $8.78/lb, up 1.15% week-over-week and now at the highest level of 2025. This marks the fourth-consecutive week of gains, reflecting continued tight raw material availability, firm European demand and a strong auction environment in Iceland.

According to Undercurrents's index of all sizes of ungutted cod on Icelandic auctions, cod prices remain historically elevated, supported by Iceland's status as the primary quota holder following harvest cuts in Norway and Russia.

In April 2025, prices reached $4.11/kg, among the highest levels ever recorded and up over 60% from historical averages. While there was a slight 1% dip from the previous update, the broader trend reflects multi-year highs driven by supply constraints and robust demand across both European and North American markets. 

Despite steady demand from the US, limited export availability has kept the pressure on, making Icelandic cod a premium but increasingly strategic option for tariff-conscious buyers.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view

The United States and United Kingdom are Iceland's top export markets for frozen cod fillets, consistently leading in both value and volume. The UK shows steady demand, supported by its strong preference for cod and close trade ties with Iceland.

The US often surpasses other markets in volume and value, especially during seasonal peaks, and remains a key destination due to favorable trade conditions. Compared to France, Spain and the Netherlands, which show smaller and more variable imports, the US and UK offer scale, stability and premium pricing, making them a strategic focus for Icelandic suppliers.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
US wholesale: Single-frozen Icelandic cod fillet prices keep rising as Pacific level out - Undercurrent News

In early 2025, US imports of frozen cod fillets (Gadus morhua, HS code 0304715000) spiked to their highest levels in over a year, with China continuing to dominate as the primary supplier. However, US Census import data only runs through February, and a shift in import patterns is likely in the coming months due to the sharp tariff increase on Chinese-origin product.

Iceland remains the second-largest source, supplying a steady share, while other countries like Vietnam and Indonesia contribute modest volumes. The January surge likely reflects pre-tariff stockpiling as buyers moved to secure product ahead of rising costs.

Haddock historically high

While Icelandic haddock prices remain historically high, no change was recorded at the US wholesale level this week. Average pricing across all sizes held at $7.22/lb, with offers mostly within prior ranges. This marks a pause following sharp gains earlier this spring.

US buyers continue to lean on Iceland as the key source of low-tariff Atlantic haddock, as Chinese-processed supply remains constrained under the weight of a 145% tariff. That pressure is expected to intensify, with anxiety building around the possible expiration of Section 301 tariff exemptions. If not renewed, the cumulative tariff on Chinese haddock would rise to 170%, effectively sidelining most Chinese-origin product from the US market and further concentrating demand on single-frozen Icelandic supply.

Single-frozen Alaska cod remained flat from the previous week, with average prices ranging from $5.45–$5.95/lb, depending on size. Pricing reflects stable A-season landings and moderate domestic demand, as buyers seek substitutions amid premiums on Atlantic cod. However, tight supply at origin and inflation-adjusted cost pressures have tempered any potential downside movement.

Demand remains solid even post-Lent, driven by tight inventories and the continued exclusion of Russian-origin supply. Still, purchasing behavior is measured, with buyers closely evaluating margins in an environment of elevated operating costs and uncertain tariff policy.

Despite the rising cost base, Pacific cod continues to trade at a significant discount to Atlantic cod, depending on size, offering a more economical alternative for buyers squeezed by pricing on Norwegian and Icelandic product.

Pollock fillets from Alaska held firm in week 18, with 2–4 oz fillets averaging $2.88/lb and 4–6 oz at $3.58/lb, according to Undercurrent's wholesale assessments. With pricing still well below Atlantic cod and haddock, pollock remains a cost-effective substitute across retail and foodservice channels, particularly in the face of inflationary pressure and rising tariffs on other whitefish species.

The 2025 A season was marked by a strong and productive harvest, with pin-bone out (PBO) fillet output surging on the back of larger fish, improved yields, a 6% quota increase and a strategic shift away from surimi toward higher-value fillet production.

Despite robust output, market sentiment remains supportive, bolstered by tight substitution options in other whitefish categories and strong performance in global roe and surimi segments.

For now, the single-frozen market remains defined by tight quotas, rising replacement costs, and limited alternatives, with US buyers left to weigh price premiums against supply reliability.

title: Japan’s Kawasaki harvests first fish from new chemical-free aquaculture system
content:
Japan's Kawasaki Heavy Industries has launched the MINATOMAE System, a chemical-free aquaculture system that controls water quality and oxygen levels in fish farming, it announced.

"Designed to address global food security challenges, Kawasaki's system helps secure Japan's food supply amid rising population and environmental pressures. It also revitalizes local economies by supporting coastal fisheries and creating new jobs," it said in a statement.

The system is currently undergoing trials near the Port of Kobe and is being refined ahead of a broader commercial rollout. From January to April 2025, the company successfully farmed rainbow trout, harvesting 900 fish weighing between two and three kilograms.

Looking ahead, Kawasaki plans to incorporate renewable energy sources -- such as cold energy from liquefied natural gas and waste heat from industrial processes -- into future system upgrades.

title: Western Pacific council highlights limits of Trump’s marine monument reopening
content:
The reopening of the Pacific Islands Heritage Marine National Monument (PIHMNM) to commercial fishing will only apply to waters between 50 and 200 nautical miles offshore, the Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council (WPRFMC) has clarified.

US president Donald Trump, on April 17, issued executive order (EO) 10918, "Unleashing American Commercial Fishing in the Pacific," restoring legal fishing in the PIHMNM, as reported by Undercurrent News. The area is rich in skipjack, albacore and yellowfin tuna, and areas of it can now be fished by US vessels based out of Hawaii and American Samoa, which has an economy that is heavily dependent on the tuna industry. 

However, while the monument covers around 770,000 square miles of ocean, the EO will only impact areas around three US islands: Wake, Johnston and Jarvis. Marine areas around the main Hawaiian Islands or the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands, as well as Howland and Baker islands, the Palmyra Atoll and Kingman Reef will not be affected, the council clarified.

A map of the marine areas covered by the Pacific Remote Islands Marine National Monument. Image courtesy of US Fish and Wildlife Service.

The WPRFMC, one of eight regional councils that provides guidance to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration in managing US commercial fisheries, had previously fought the president Joe Biden administration to prevent the expansion of the PIHMNM, which was formerly known as the Pacific Remote Island Marine National Monument.

In particular, the council has expressed concern about the impact conservation efforts might have on the American Samoa economy, which is 90% dependent on the tuna industry, as reported by Undercurrent News.

The WPRFMC, this time around, cited research by University of Washington fisheries expert Ray Hilborn and others showing marine-protected areas with static boundaries "do not effectively conserve highly mobile species such as tunas or reduce bycatch."

"These areas are well beyond the reach of fishing gear or shallow reef-dependent species. US fishing activities targeting migratory tunas occur near the surface (maximum 400 meters) using gear such as deep-set longlines, which do not contact the seafloor or sensitive habitats," WPRFMC executive director Kitty Simonds said in a statement.

Near-shore coral reef ecosystems and protected species that populate them, such as green and hawksbill sea turtles and red-footed boobies, "continue to thrive in areas unaffected by the proclamation," Simonds said.

US fisheries management under the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act "is among the most comprehensive and conservation-based in the world" and that the EO is primarily targeted at "ensur[ing] American fishermen -- not foreign fleets -- can responsibly access US waters, while upholding the rigorous conservation standards that have defined US fisheries for decades," she asserted.

The PIHMNM was created by US president George W. Bush in 2009 under the US Antiquities Act and was subsequently expanded by US president Barack Obama in 2014.

The WPRFMC opposed that expansion, and a considered expansion by US president Joe Biden that he eventually abandoned.

Trump has vowed to push to reopen other US marine monuments to commercial fishing, including the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands and the Northeast Canyons and Seamounts Marine National Monument on the US East Coast, as Undercurrent has reported.
