title: IOTC approves 15% bigeye tuna TAC increase, introduces skipjack catch limits
content:
The Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC) has approved a significant increase in the total allowable catch (TAC) for bigeye tuna, raising the limit from the current 80,583 metric tons to 92,670t for the years 2026-2028, Japan's fisheries agency announced on April 21.

IOTC members reject tuna fishing closure proposals at annual meeting

The decision was made at the 29th annual meeting of the IOTC, held April 13-17, 2025, in Reunion, an island in the Indian Ocean that is an overseas department and region of France. The new quota represents a 15% increase for all fleets.

The increase follows recommendations from IOTC's scientific committee, which reported a recovery in bigeye tuna stocks. Based on the committee's findings, the IOTC concluded that the 15% increase in the TAC would be sustainable under the current management procedure.

The procedure automatically adjusts the TAC based on predefined data, ensuring that decisions are made with minimal exceptions and enabling more dynamic resource management.

Yellowfin and skipjack measures

While the IOTC decided to keep national catch limits for yellowfin tuna unchanged, it will continue monitoring the resource status.

China challenges Indian Ocean tuna quotas as yellowfin stocks rated ‘green’

Initial assessments had raised concerns about the overfishing of yellowfin tuna, but the most recent stock assessment, conducted in December 2024, concluded that the species was no longer being overfished and was maintaining levels consistent with the maximum sustainable yield.

This was seen as very positive news from stakeholders in the region, as the Indian Ocean yellowfin tuna stocks have been overfished for years, while measures to limit the quotas caused tension among IOTC members in the recent past.

For skipjack tuna, the IOTC introduced a new TAC and national catch limits for the first time. Countries that exceeded 10,000t in average annual catches between 2021 and 2023 will face gradual reductions over the next three years.

According to the French tuna fishing association Orthongel, these measures complement those already in place for yellowfin tuna and will bring the three main tropical tuna species in the Indian Ocean under quota regimes.

Major advances, but challenges remain

Orthongel welcomed the "major advances in tropical tuna management in the Indian Ocean" and praised the "return to a climate of cooperation and dialogue between the parties."

"These decisions now provide IOTC with a comprehensive management framework for tropical tuna in the Indian Ocean," Orthongel said, referring to the adoption of the two resolutions concerning skipjack and bigeye tuna.

European fishing association Europeche also said that adopting catch limits for skipjack and bigeye marks a "notable advancement towards an efficient, science-based management framework for tropical tunas."

"This is a milestone for the region," said Anne-France Mattlet, director of the Europeche tuna group. "We now have the tools to ensure the long-term sustainability of skipjack, bigeye, and yellowfin; now we need consistent, inclusive implementation across all fleets to make it happen," she added.

Orthongel also said that the "calmer climate" has enabled significant progress on previously divisive issues, such as shark conservation. The adopted measure on sharks strengthens the fight against shark finning and improves shark management, according to Europeche.

Despite acknowledging progress, Orthongel remains concerned about ongoing unequal obligations and regulatory exemptions that hinder fair competition and consistent regulation, it claimed.

"There has been no quota increase for yellowfin tuna despite the improvement in the stock endorsed by the scientific committee during its last assessment at the end of 2024, the IOTC preferring to focus on management measures and wait for confirmation of the stock's recovery before deciding on a quota increase."

This will be one of the issues at the next session, which is scheduled to take place in the Maldives in May 2026.

According to Europeche, adopting the skipjack measure through a voting procedure rather than consensus reflects a "broader shift that could challenge the effectiveness of future IOTC measures."

"Although voting is foreseen in the IOTC rules, the increased use of this mechanism risks a rise in formal objections, weakening the cohesion and enforceability of conservation measures," it said. Europeche also raised concerns on the decision to exempt Indonesia from the requirement to deploy IOTC-certified independent observers on at-sea transhipments.

"More generally, once again, discussions on high-seas boarding and inspection, shark finning bans, and improved monitoring of gillnet fisheries failed to advance, largely due to persistent opposition from a small group of countries," it said.

"The growing divide between fleets bound by strict oversight and those operating with minimal controls is extremely worrying," claimed Xavier Leduc, president of the Europeche tuna group.

Europeche also noted that, despite the EU proposal, crew labor standards were absent from the discussions. The retailers' group Global Tuna Alliance (GTA) called the IOTC delegates to demonstrate greater urgency in setting labor standards at future sessions.

It said it was positive that the  IOTC had agreed to benchmark current labor standards, an initial move toward potential future regulations. Despite that, progress was limited due to resistance and delays in managing tuna stocks, according to the GTA. The organization emphasized the need for urgent reforms and broader industry support on this issue.

"Despite disappointing resistance from some IOTC members, we were pleased that the
commission responded positively to a proposal by the European Union and tasked the secretariat with benchmarking the current Indian Ocean labor standards. It is expected that the results of this study will inform the tasking of a working group by the commission in 2026," the GTA said.

title: US importer Supreme Crab announces first major package redesign in 10 years
content:
Supreme Crab & Seafood, a Weston, Florida-based importer of swimming crabmeat, frozen yellowfin tuna and other items, has redesigned its cans for a "fresh, cleaner look" that "reflects the brand's commitment to quality, transparency, and delivering the finest hand-picked, wild-caught crab meat to customers," the company announced in a recent press release.

It's the 16-year-old company's first major packaging redesign in 10 years, according to CEO Troy Turkin.

Half of the new lid design includes to-scale images of the product inside, which gives customers "a clear idea of what to expect when they open the can," the company said in a statement. A refined aesthetic highlights each crab variety.

"Our new can design enhances our brand identity while maintaining the integrity and premium quality our customers expect," said Alyssa Chowdhury, the company's manager of brand assurance. "We're proud to showcase this fresh new look while keeping the same great-tasting crab we are known for."

The company has undergone several key changes since promoting 30-year seafood professional Turkin from chief operating officer to CEO in September 2024, as reported by Undercurrent News. The move was made as part of a succession plan, so that Andy Walton, who held the top post, could focus on developing retail products. Turkin has been with Supreme since March 2016.

Other changes include two new hires and a new operating system, which begins integration this month and is estimated to be ready to go in July or August, Turkin said. The company has also consolidated its warehouse use, worked on SKU rationalizations and launched a few new product items. It joined the Science-Based Targets Initiative, an effort to help companies cut their greenhouse gas emissions.

title: Confusion reigns over tariffs on Asia-processed fillets using US raw material
content:
US seafood companies that send their raw materials to foreign countries for processing before returning the finished product for sale in the US are asking the Department of Homeland Security's Customs and Border Patrol (CBP) for a clarification on how much they have to pay under president Donald Trump's new "reciprocal" tariffs.  

Some believe they have to pay nothing, while others believe the goods are fully subject to the tariff and yet others believe the tariff amount is subject to a more complicated formula. But everyone agrees that an expert opinion is needed.

"I do not believe [such items are exempt from the tariffs]," wrote one executive at a big US seafood company potentially impacted by the matter. "I believe it is subject to country of origin, which is defined by substantial transformation. However, they write this so hard that the final verdict should be from experts."

US customs alert: Imports have until May 27 to arrive to avoid Trump’s 10% tariffs

The seafood industry, like many other industries, are still scrambling to deal with the announcement made by Trump in the White House Rose Garden on April 2 that goods from nearly every country in the world will be slapped with a general 10% tariff rate when imported by the US and goods from several dozen countries will get hit with even higher rates, as reported by Undercurrent News.

Seafood from Vietnam will now face a US tariff of 46%, while all products from Indonesia face a 32% tariff. Products from China will confront a 34% US tariff, Trump announced, and that's on top of the combined 45% tariff most Chinese seafood already faces coming into the US. 

All three are countries used by US seafood companies to process their raw materials before importing them back into the US.

The president's executive order (#14257) and a subsequent cargo systems message service (CSMS) alert from CPB (#64649265) clarify that there is an exemption for goods that involve raw materials being sent to foreign countries to be transformed and then imported back into the US.

As explained in sect. 9903.01.34 of the memo: "For articles in which at least 20% of the value of article is US originating, the US content will not be subject to the reciprocal tariff. The reciprocal tariff will be assessed on the non-US content."

Trade expert Jessica Rifkin, a principal attorney at the law firm Olsson Frank Weeda, also would like to get clarification from CBP, but she believes the correct reading is the more complicated approach.

"So the way I would read that is you're taking the entire customs value of whatever you're importing," Rifkin offered. "That would include any transaction value of something that's being imported. It's the bill of materials, the cost of the components that were used to make that article plus whatever processing or whatever went in and on top of it, profit, all of that, whatever the supplier's total price would be. You back out the US content and you pay the duty on what remains."

Rifkin believes tariffs on the item would be easier to assess if a company was importing something like a seafood potpie from China.

"I can subtract out the fish that is of US origin," she said. "I think it becomes more aggressive when you've got the entirety of the raw material that's US origin. I don't know. I still think there would be a tariff due on the value of the processing."

The CBP memo goes on to instruct how importers should include separate lines in forms related to the import: one for the value of the US-origin part of the good; and the other for the value of the non-US origin part of the item.

For some rough idea on how much this approach could mean to US companies, consider Alaska pollock sent to China, mostly for processing. It had an average value of $1,749 per metric ton in January 2025 upon import by China. 

The average value of frozen Alaska pollock imported by the US from China in February 2025, by contrast, was $3,484/t, a difference of $1,735.

Confusion reigns over tariffs on Asia-processed fillets using US raw material - Undercurrent News

Should the US apply both of the two earlier 10% tariffs ordered by Trump in recent months along with the new 34% tariff, for a combined 54% in tariffs, the logic would suggest a tariff of $936.90/t in this scenario.

title: NPFMC may still consider Gulf of Alaska trawl closures to conserve Tanner crab despite advisory panel punt
content:
The North Pacific Fishery Management Council (NPFMC) Advisory Panel has delayed action again on considering measures to expand closed areas of the Gulf of Alaska to trawling to conserve Tanner crab stocks.

"I certainly think a more refined area closure would need to be considered for me to support this moving forward," panel chair Shannon Carroll, a Trident Seafood executive, said before the advisory panel voted 12-9 to send the proposal back for further study.

Bering Sea crab harvesters say decision to nix proposed protections is another setback

Advisory panel member Julie Kavanaugh, a Kodiak fisherman, had brought a motion to advance closures of two statistical areas that would be considered by the full council.

"This has been an ongoing concern for 20 years," she said.

The issue pits groundfish trawling interests against crabbers in the waters off Kodiak Island, Alaska. Crabbers have expressed frustration the NPFMC has repeatedly punted on advancing closures to reduce bycatch in the trawl fishery. 

Last year, the advisory panel declined to take action on the same measure, instead sending it back for more study, Undercurrent News reported at the time.

However, since the advisory panel's actions aren't binding and only the NPFMC can conduct a formal vote on fishery management issues, some crabbers are holding out hope the closures will be considered by the full council at its Sunday (April 6) meeting.

Testimony to the advisory panel from competing fishing groups urged starkly opposite outcomes.

Advocates for closing statistical areas 525702 and 525630 to the trawl fleet said the move will reduce bycatch, an important move to conserve Tanner crab stocks, worth doing even at the cost of lost opportunities for catching groundfish.

"We know that there will be winners and losers from these changes," Kodiak fisherman Alexus Kwacha wrote. "Move this paper to initial review, and let's proactively protect these crab in this well-defined habitat."

But trawl advocates argued there is not enough data to justify closures and questioned the effectiveness of static closures on a species that migrates along the seafloor.

"Fishery management decisions must be grounded in robust, up-to-date scientific data," wrote Julie Bonney of the Alaska Groundfish Databank.

title: Trump tariffs: Chile, Ecuador get off lightly while other major US seafood suppliers hit hard
content:
US president Donald Trump's 10% general tariff announcement on Wednesday (April 2) threatens to impact importers of seafood from all nations as soon as Saturday morning (April 5), but seafood from some nations will be hit with much higher fees.

Vietnam will now face a US tariff of 46%, while all products from India will get hit with a 26% rate and those from Japan will be slapped with a 24% rate. Goods from the European Union will have to overcome a 20% rate.

Products from China will confront a 34% US tariff, Trump announced, though it remains unclear if that amount is in addition to the roughly combined 45% tariff most Chinese seafood already faces coming into the US.

Those countries were among the dozens identified by Trump as the "worst offenders" in erecting trade barriers to US products. The tariffs he imposed with an executive order on Wednesday equate to roughly half of what his administration claims these nations were charging US products in entrance fees.

Two major seafood source-nations for the US -- Chile and Ecuador -- will escape with relatively light tariffs, with their goods soon to face the baseline 10% rate.

The 10% tariffs will take effect on Saturday at 12:01 a.m. ET, while those impacting the worst offender list will go into effect on April 9 at 12:01 am ET, CNN is reporting.

The lists

For days leading up to the event, Trump promoted his coming action as "Liberation Day," but he did not provide details of his plans. The Office of the US Trade Representative provided a few hints about what to expect in a 397-page report delivered Monday (March 31) that singled out multiple countries for their trade barriers, as reported by Undercurrent. 

The two documents below show the reciprocal tariffs Trump has suggested he will charge different nations (columns on the right), based 50% of the tariffs his administration claims they have set for American goods (columns on the left). 

Several of the countries identified as being among the worst offenders and hit with higher tariff rates, like India (26%), Indonesia (32%), Vietnam (46%), China (34%) and Thailand (36%), are among the US' largest suppliers of shrimp and numerous other seafood items. 

The list below, compiled by Undercurrent, ranks the countries that garner the most value out of their seafood exports to the US.

Questions remain about Canada, Mexico

It remains unclear what will happen to the 25% levies Trump previously announced against products from Canada and Mexico, starting April 2, in response to their perceived lack of response to Trump's request they do more to stop fentanyl and undocumented immigrants from being trafficked into the US. Recently, Trump declared that goods from those countries that were compliant with the US-Mexico-Canada-Agreement will not be penalized, while non-compliant goods will continue to be charged at a 25% rate. 

The National Fisheries Institute (NFI), the US' biggest seafood industry group, believes it's the case that the Canadian and Mexican products have escaped the higher tariffs. It issued a statement after Trump's speech in which NFI president and CEO Lisa Wallenda Picard said she was "encouraged by exemptions on reciprocal tariffs for some countries, like Canada and Mexico."

But she added that "tariffs will raise the cost of seafood, making the healthiest animal protein on the planet less available and more expensive." She warned that Trump's tariffs "could threaten many of the 1.6 million American jobs that, according to the federal government, US commercial seafood companies support."

Trump's actions followed an effort the same day by a group of US senators, including some Republicans, to rally support for a joint resolution to block his planned tariffs on Canada. The legislation, which was passed by a 51-48 vote on Wednesday evening, criticized Trump's efforts to use the International Economic Emergency Powers Act (IEEPA) as its authority for the tariffs by citing its efforts to combat fentanyl smuggling and illegal crossings of the Canadian border by migrants.

However, the bill, which was introduced by US senator Tim Kaine, a Virginia Democrat, has no companion measure in the US House of Representatives, where House majority leader Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, is said to block any such effort.

US senator Susan Collins, a Maine Republican, spoke for more than 13 minutes in support of the resolution during open floor time Wednesday. She described how her state's economy is "integrated with Canada," its most important trading partner.

Maine senator Susan Collins making her case for legislation to block Trump's planned tariffs on Canada. Image is still from C-Span video.

"From home heating oil, gasoline, jet fuel and other refined petroleum products, to Maine's paper mills, forest products businesses, agricultural producers and lobstermen, the tariffs on Canada would be detrimental to many Maine families and our local economies.

She said she supported using tariffs on Mexico and China. She said she shared Trump's goal of "stemming the tide of dangerous fentanyl that flows in the United States" and commended him for "taking far stronger actions to halt this dangerous and deadly flow than did the previous administration," but she said did not agree with his invoking his IEEPA powers. 

"The fact is, the vast majority of fentanyl in America comes from the southern border," she said. "In fiscal year 2024, less than 1% of fentanyl seizures occurred at our northern border, and our Canadian neighbors are working collaboratively and cooperatively with our government to stop that trafficking."

Collins described how products are processed back and forth across the border, including between $200m and $400m worth of lobster sent to Canada each year for processing.

"There are 240 lobster-processing plants in Canada, but only 15 in the United States," she said. "I share the president's goal of getting more of that manufacturing done in the state of Maine, done in the United States, but the fact is that if we impose these tariffs on Canadian processing, it's going to be our Maine lobstermen who will bear the cost; it's going to be consumers who bear the cost."

She warned that the US aquaculture industry would suffer, too.

“In Washington County, in far-eastern Maine, Cooke Aquaculture is one of the largest employers, with more than 200 direct jobs throughout the state," she said. "While they have a processing plant in Machias, Maine, the first step of their salmon processing occurs in Canada before reentering the United States for finishing. At a time when the Maine aquaculture industry is growing, these tariffs on Canada would jeopardize current jobs and also block future ones."

US senators Mitch McConnell and Rand Paul, both representing Kentucky, were among the Republicans to have supported the bill. Trump, late on Tuesday (April 1), blasted all three of the GOP lawmakers in a TruthSocial post.

Executive order declares 'national emergency'

Following Trump's speech, the White House published his executive order to execute the new tariff plan. It restates the history of trade policy in the US dating back to 1934, arguing that despite the "country's previous commitment to the principle of reciprocity, the trading relationship between the United States and its trading partners has become highly unbalanced, particularly in recent years."  

In the order, the president relies again on the authority granted by the IEEPA. And to justify the new tariffs, he declares a national emergency.

The order reads: 

"I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of America, find that underlying conditions, including a lack of reciprocity in our bilateral trade relationships, disparate tariff rates and non-tariff barriers, and US trading partners’ economic policies that suppress domestic wages and consumption, as indicated by large and persistent annual US goods trade deficits, constitute an unusual and extraordinary threat to the national security and economy of the United States. That threat has its source in whole or substantial part outside the United States in the domestic economic policies of key trading partners and structural imbalances in the global trading system. I hereby declare a national emergency with respect to this threat."

title: Oyster farmers pan Alaska bill to add farmed seafood to ASMI portfolio
content:
A bill introduced in the US state of Alaska by its governor, Mike Dunleavy, to allow a state marketing agency to promote shellfish in addition to wild-caught finfish has received pushback from shellfish farmers hostile to the prospect of helping to pay for the effort.

Alaska's mariculture sector is divided – primarily between shellfish and seaweed farmers – whether it would be worthwhile to levy an assessment of between 0.1% and 0.6% of their product's value to pay for the state's promotional efforts, as Undercurrent News reported.

"Shellfish farmers feel that this could really burden us," Weatherly Bates, co-owner of Alaska Shellfish Farms, which raises oysters and mussels and also grows kelp, told the House Fisheries Committee at its first hearing on HB135/SB131. 

"The Alaska Seafood Marketing Institute (ASMI) markets wild-caught fish for years, disparaging us as farmers," added Bates, who is also president of the Alaska Shellfish Growers Association.

Dunleavy administration pitches farmed fish

Dunleavy's administration has already drawn fire from the commercial fishing sector for attempts to relax Alaska's ban on farmed fish production, as Undercurrent reported.

His latest initiative would allow ASMI to market shellfish and seaweed production, although it's unclear how this would be paid for. His administration has pitched the idea of putting ASMI's muscle behind the US state's growing mariculture industry.

"Alaska already produces more than 50% of the seafood in the United States, and it's a natural progression for Alaskans to expand mariculture as a renewable resource that Alaska can add to its economic portfolio," Anna Latham, deputy commissioner at the Department of Commerce and Economic Development, told lawmakers at the March 27 hearing.

ASMI's board, appointed by the governor, voted in February to support adding mariculture to its wheelhouse.

"It gives the ASMI board the powers to market mariculture products produced in the state of Alaska," ASMI executive director Jeremy Woodrow told the committee. 

But because mariculture is narrowly defined in Alaska law, it would take another change in statute to bring farmed salmonids under its umbrella, a political landmine in a state that's banned finfish aquaculture since 1990. 

"The definition of aquatic farm products as currently written only includes shellfish and seaweed in aquatic farm products," Woodrow said. "It does not include finfish of any type."

'I'm a farmer, not a fisherman'

Around a half-dozen oyster farmers testified that bringing their farmed products under the Alaska wild-caught seafood brand would be inappropriate.

"I am not fishing for oysters; I am harvesting my crop, just as if I grew peas or potatoes, which the state of Alaska is not currently promoting," Seawan Gehlbach, an owner of Simpson Bay Oyster Company in Cordova testified.

She added: "I'm a farmer, not a fisherman."

Other longtime shellfish farmers argued they have already built their own markets and have no need of ASMI's assistance.

"We have done everything on our own through direct marketing and building relationships with our customers," Katie Bode, co-owner of Tommaso Shellfish on Prince of Wales Island, told the committee.

The Alaska Mariculture Alliance (AMA), the industry organization that advocates for the shellfish and seaweed sectors, said its board was not briefed on the legislation. 

Its membership would support the initiative only if the separate sectors were allowed to vote in a binding election whether to opt in to ASMI and be taxed accordingly, it told the committee.

AMA executive director Jason Lessard told lawmakers that there's no consensus between shellfish farmers, who have been marketing their products directly to consumers for decades, and kelp growers, who are part of a nascent industry more friendly to state-supporting marketing.

"We acknowledge that while both shellfish and seaweed are products of ocean farming, they're very different, and they're in very different places right now," Lessard told the committee.

The bill did get a boost from Southeast Conference, a regional civic and business group based in Juneau, which is stewarding a $49 million "Alaska Mariculture Cluster" federal grant awarded in 2022, as Undercurrent reported.

"ASMI is the gold standard for marketing," Southeast Conference executive director Robert Venables said. "Their guidance and expertise is going to serve the maritime culture sector very well."

'We are the rising tide'

Lawmakers also quizzed ASMI leadership on the wisdom of adding to the state marketing board's workload without providing additional resources.

ASMI receives US gov’t grant to promote Alaska seafood overseas

Alaska House speaker Bryce Edgmon, an independent from Bristol Bay who is co-chair of the fisheries committee, posed that question directly.

"This bill would purport to increase your workload but not come with additional money," he queried ASMI's executive director.

"Any time we have an opportunity to market the brand Alaska, we lift that rising tide," replied Woodrow. "We are the rising tide."

The committee took no action on the bill. Its companion bill in the Alaska Senate has yet to have a hearing scheduled.

title: Chilean fishing firms threaten lawsuits over horse mackerel quota changes
content:
Several Chilean and Norwegian-owned fishing companies have announced their intention to file lawsuits against the Chilean state, citing economic devastation caused by proposed legal changes in the fishing industry, El Mercurio reported.

The "fractionation" law seeks to reduce Chile's fishing quotas for industrial companies -- in force until 2032 -- and increase those for artisanal fishermen.

Industry leaders claim the proposed legislative changes could lead to company closures, job losses, and a significant downturn in economic activity.

Chilean firms Camanchaca, Austevoll Seafood-owned FoodCorp Chile, Blumar Seafoods and Landes represent nearly 60% of the horse mackerel industry in south-central Chile and approximately 80% of fish production for direct human consumption in the Latin American country.

Their representatives have expressed concerns that the adjustments will create instability and unpredictability in the sector.

The companies argue that modifications to the fishing quota system will severely impact their operations, particularly in Chile's central and southern regions. They claim that the new regulations disrupt long-term investments and could lead to legal disputes over property rights. 

Chilean fishermen protest against hake fisheries quota law

"It's a very bad law based on a purely ideological principle. Acquired rights are being violated," Gerardo Balbontin, general manager of Blumar, told El Mercurio. According to the executive, the most significant impact of the signing of the fractionation law is the horse mackerel fishery. He said that it's likely that the firm would need to stop an operational vessel and stop the project to build, with permits, a new plant in Coronel, where the company had aimed to hire 450 people.

Ricardo Garcia, general manager of Camanchaca, defined the project as an "expropriation without paying the corresponding compensation." Andres Fosk, general manager of Landes, added the law was "unconstitutional" since those fishing rights were authorized in 2012 when the fishing permits were switched for transferrable fishing licenses.

The fishing sector's opposition centers on what they see as a lack of consultation and transparency in the decision-making process.

title: Nissui introduces upcycled fish leather from farmed yellowtail
content:
Japanese seafood giant Nissui Corp. will launch trial marketing of a new sustainable material called "namino leather," made by upcycling the skin of farmed yellowtail, known as Kurose Buri, the company announced Monday (March 24).

Produced from fish raised by Nissui-owned Kurose Suisan Co., the leather is crafted from yellowtail skin that would otherwise be discarded or used for fertilizer. The company plans to introduce the product this spring to apparel manufacturers in Japan and environmentally conscious markets in Europe and North America.

The yellowtail used for the leather is farmed entirely in-house, encompassing artificial breeding, hatching, rearing and spawning, without relying on wild juvenile fish.

Nissui to tap EU market with fish oil-based pharma shipments

Once matured in sea pens off the coasts of Miyazaki and Kagoshima prefectures, the fish is harvested and processed into fillets while still fresh.

"By-products such as heads, bones, tails and skin, typically used for fertilizer, are now being repurposed," the company said. "The skins are tanned and finished with the help of Japanese leather artisans to create a refined, functional material for fashion and design."

Nissui aims to harvest 3 million individuals annually -- about 15,000 metric tons -- by 2030 under its Kurose Buri brand, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

Namino leather is Nissui's response to increasing ethical and environmental concerns in the fashion industry, where traditional animal leathers face growing scrutiny, Nissui said. The fish leather provides an alternative that reduces reliance on petroleum-based materials while offering a lower environmental impact, it added.

Characterized by a delicate pattern formed by the yellowtail's fine scales, the fish leather has a smooth surface and refined appearance, Nissui said. 

Nissui-backed Three Oceans parts ways with UK foodservice sales veteran

Each piece of namino leather typically measures between 35 and 45 centimeters wide, with a height ranging from approximately 15 to 20cm near the head and five to 10cm near the tail.

The leather is tanned using either natural tannins or chrome-free synthetic alternatives and finished with various surface treatments.

Options include urethane coatings, metallic finishes and foil stamping in gold or silver. Custom finishes are also available for different applications.

title: Just 18 months, two meetings, to sort quota-sharing deal for key farmed salmon feed ingredient
content:
BERGEN, Norway -- Northeast Atlantic coastal states have 18 months before the Marin Trust fishery improvement project (FIP) for blue whiting -- which currently allows the pelagic fish to be used as a key ingredient for farmed salmon -- fails without a comprehensive quota-sharing agreement.

Before the deadline of October 2026, there are only two coastal state meetings scheduled -- one in October 2025, the other perilously last-moment for October 2026. This is a hard and fast deadline; Marin Trust will not risk any damage to its brand by seeking another extension, it has been made clear.

Norway salmon farmers feel the fear as vital feed ingredient sustainability deadline looms

As Undercurrent News reported from the North Atlantic Seafood Forum (NASF) early in March, blue whiting is an ingredient for some 50% of Norway salmon's feed. Jorgen Skeide, feed manager at Leroy Seafood Group, and Grieg Seafood's feed and nutrition director, Tor Eirik Homme, were clear that blue whiting -- which lost its Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certification late in 2020 but can still feature in farmed salmon diets as long as it is part of a recognized FIP -- would be off their fishes' menu if the FIP ends without resolution.

William Davies, group corporate social responsibility (CSR) manager for Sofina Foods Europe -- which operates the Young's Seafood brand, as well as supplying most retailers with private label salmon -- illustrated the problem for the supply chain.

"The Young's CSR policy extends to the sustainability of [aquaculture] feed, plus Young's, like most UK processors, is part of the Sustainable Seafood Coalition, which extends to marine ingredients in feeds. Within that policy, there's not a lot of room to maneuver when the NAPA [North Atlantic Pelagic Advocacy Group] FIP ends."

He also warned the industry "would see environmental NGO activity when they get hold of that story -- '[recently] historically high stock levels collectively overfished.'"

There are alternatives for salmon diets, but as Dave Robb -- Cargill Aqua Nutrition Group’s sustainability lead and chair of the NAPA blue whiting subgroup -- told Undercurrent News, "the shuffle of resources to accommodate changes will add complexity and cost to supply systems for fishmeal users, and I think probably we see a degradation of value for fishers as they sell to different markets."

More on the alternatives below, but first -- what is the problem?

Click to enlarge. Blue whiting data, courtesy of Erling Kare Stenevik, Norway's Institute of Marine Research

Essentially, years of a failure on the part of the coastal states to agree to a quota-sharing agreement mean the combined fishing efforts of the EU (mostly Danish vessels), the Faroe Islands, Iceland, Norway and, more recently, the UK (post-Brexit) have regularly exceeded the advice given by the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (ICES).

"There were two year-classes, 2020 and 2021, which were the highest numbers in the whole time series" when it came to spawning stock biomass (SSB) recruitment, explained Erling Kare Stenevik of Norway's Institute of Marine Research. That raised the SSB to a high level but essentially disguised the problem of overfishing.

"The fishing pressure is high on this stock, much higher than the FMSY [fishery maximum sustainable yield]. The fishery is really dependent on two year-classes now; some 70-80% of the fishery is expected to be on those two."

"And from history, we can see that following an increase, if you don't have new strong year-classes coming in, there will be expected also a large decrease in the SSB in the coming years, especially with high fishing pressure."

In other words, years of overfishing may be about to take their toll. 

"The 2025 fishing advice is still high, 1.45 million metric tons, following the management strategy," said Stenevik. "That's a reduction of around 5% year-on-year, and the SSB is expected to decrease slightly in 2026 if the advice is followed -- the decrease is going to be stronger if it's not followed."

The coastal states last agreed to and obeyed a quota-sharing agreement in 2013. 

The seafood sector has largely placed the blame for the failure to agree on a comprehensive quota-sharing agreement at the feet of coastal state governments. Several speakers over the course of NASF called it embarrassing, with Heidrun Lind Marteinsdottir, CEO of Fisheries Iceland, stating the North East Atlantic Fisheries Commission (NEAFC) meetings have, in her experience, been "superficial" at best.

NASF 2025: High Liner woos young North Americans to replace red meat, poultry with seafood

"There are no working groups besides the science groups. The talks do not go on into the evenings. There is no discussion of the economic values or the jobs at stake," she said. "Informal talks between the heads of delegates have yielded little."

Marteinsdottir is part of Iceland’s delegation as an industry representative, but she noted: "the industry reps are largely left in the kitchen, nibbling on British biscuits."

Esben Sverdrup-Jensen, CEO of the Danish Pelagic Producers Organisation, agreed. 

"The NEAFC talks have maybe even been toxic. As a negotiating environment, there's little trust or respect; there's little contact, even. As an industry representative, I almost stopped coming to the meetings. When we stopped sharing beers as negotiators, it became hard."

The NEAFC is not equipped with a dispute resolution mechanism, and any provision for such a situation under the International Foundation for the Law of the Sea is "fluffy," he said, casting doubt on any path to resolutions via that route.

Tarjei Eide, managing director at Cargill Aqua Nutrition, had a stark take during an NASF panel. 

"We need this win -- there are harder issues ahead. If we cannot solve this, how are we solving other more complex matters later? We have to show as an industry that we can do it because this is not the most complex challenge we have."

And Sofina's Davies said the challenge would only get harder: "This is to help the fishing sector, too. If a FIP is needed when stocks are low, this will be a much harder road. If they need to be rebuilt, it's a lot of pain for a longer time."

Dynamic shares or a 'shadow government'?

So, with little faith in NEAFC meetings to agree on quota shares for the first time in years, what's the answer?

The question was posed several times during NASF, and the general consensus -- while it, of course, won't be easy -- was for the industry to take the lead.

As an audience member neatly summed up: "I'm warming to the idea of the industry getting together and forming a 'shadow government' representing their countries, and presenting a plan to negotiators that they agree on. If they did that, you'd be hard-pressed to not take that seriously."

Sverdrup-Jensen agreed this was an interesting idea, with some past precedence in the blue whiting fishery, though he noted that for the EU, selecting representatives to speak for 27 countries was quite a task.

It's perhaps worth noting that Denmark's FF Skagen and TripleNine Thyboron are involved in the Marin Trust FIP for blue whiting, as are Bio-Marine Ingredients Ireland and Pelagia Killybegs (the latter part of the Norwegian pelagics giant, Pelagia).

He proposed it was clear that trying to agree fixed shares of the blue whiting quota had failed and that it was time to look instead at "dynamic shares." Management of the herring fishery in the North Sea (still MSC-certified) sees catches distributed differently depending on the size of the SSB, with smaller players keeping fixed shares and bigger players benefiting when stocks are at their most plentiful.

"It's different, but fixing shares, it's clear, hasn't worked. It also risks moving the difficult decisions from the negotiating table to the scientists... but maybe it's a way."

Several audience members at NASF suggested the quota-sharing arrangement needed to be escalated beyond NEAFC meetings, to government foreign office-level or higher. 

For Norway's government especially, a failure to act on the issue will look poor. It has a "targeted mission" on sustainable feed; that by 2034, all feed for farmed fish and livestock in Norway should come from sustainable sources and contribute to reducing greenhouse gas emissions in food systems. It also wants to increase the proportion of Norwegian-produced raw materials in feed for farmed fish from the current 8% to 25%.

If blue whiting fails its FIP, Norway will be starting from 4% instead.

While blue whiting has been broken out on its own for the Marin Trust FIP, there are also mackerel and Norwegian spring-spawning herring stocks in the northeast Atlantic which are in the same boat, having lost MSC certification. 

Fisheries Iceland's Marteinsdottir proposed the negotiating parties widen their scope to include all three, acknowledging that while that make the issue more complicated, it could also offer the opportunity for more "cards to play" and room to maneuver. 

Protein alternatives: Latin America, plant-based?

If NEAFC does fail to agree a quota-sharing agreement and blue whiting fails its FIP, aquaculture feed firms supplying Norway's salmon farmers will need to look for alternative sources of protein.

Click to enlarge. Credit: Marin Trust

The bulk would likely come from Marin Trust-certified or approved FIP fisheries in Latin America or off Africa; 15.9% of global fishmeal and oil between 2019 and 2023 was certified and of Peruvian origin, and 6.7% certified and from Chile.

Marin Trust is currently running FIPs in Panama, Ecuador, Mauritania, India, Thailand, and Vietnam.

The issue for Norway's salmon farmers, and the feed firms that supply them, would be the cost and optics of sourcing those. As Leroy's Skeide said: "How does it sound that the Norwegian industry will have to source raw materials from Peru for us to be responsible farmers while Norwegian-produced fishmeal is sent to China to feed piglets?"

"When blue whiting fell out of the [MSC] certification in 2020 and before the FIP, Norwegian and Scottish feed companies unilaterally stopped buying any caught after the certification ended," Dave Robb, Cargill Aqua Nutrition Group's sustainability lead, told Undercurrent. The feed sector was only able to make that decision with nine months of planning -- "it’s that complicated."

Marin Trust FIPs

"We had to be certain our customers wanted it, and that we could supply alternative proteins."

Then, there are the alternative proteins that have been worked on already including insect meal and plant-based proteins; "there's a protein digestibility in the amino acids that we need at the right price," said another source in the feed sector, wishing to remain anonymous.

"That's always the block, is the price. If you change the dynamics in the market -- like we saw with fish oil from Peru and El Nino a few years ago -- suddenly that can unlock availability for other options to come in that had been too expensive. But what happens when that market comes back upstream again? Unless the economics have been changed, they'll slide out again. That's the risk of those alternative supply chains."

Feed companies continue to work with developers of alternative proteins, but pricing remains the block.

"Unless they can fit into our formulations without cost impact, then our customers are reticent to buy them, because there's no commitment from the retailers to take them. If the fish increases by a small percentage in cost, the retailers aren't going to pay for it, we've heard that very clearly from the retailers."

February saw French insect protein producer Ynsect essentially go under after failing to secure financing under its safeguard plan, but Undercurrent's feed sector source said insect meal could still be regarded as a "great opportunity."

"What we've got to do is find the right food stock for the insects so that it's viable. [The sector] has been growing insects, because of the regulations, on quite refined protein sources, some of which could be used directly almost for human consumption. That's been great to learn about the production of insects, but what's exciting about insects is to use them to recapture lost protein sources, so move them more towards true waste streams rather than by-product streams."

Obviously keeping food safety front-and-center, changing what the insects are fed on should bring the price point of the protein down and allow for serious scaling up.

Finally, Leroy announced earlier this year it was adopting chicken by-products as an ingredient in fish feed, in collaboration with Cargill/ EWOS -- a move which, "if you put one and one together, you can see is us gearing up for alternatives to fishmeal," said Skeide at NASF.

Poultry by-products have been allowed for farmed fish diets for over a decade -- the only barrier to adoption was whether markets would accept it, Cargill's Robb told Undercurrent. 

Leroy is framing it as a move that can lower the carbon footprint of Leroy's feed by up to 16% and support "circular economy principles."

"I think this is an area where, as we get to a place where the feed sector is challenged on resources and pricing and sustainability metrics, it's really good to review our options. It will be down to a market decision," he said. 

"That protein [poultry by-products] is being used for other things at the moment, it's not being landfilled. But this would be a more efficient use of that protein, I think, and it definitely brings a cost opportunity as well, which could allow us to do other things on sustainability elsewhere with that same value. That would be my aspiration, as a sustainability manager!"

They fit well into feed formulations in terms of nutrients and pricing, he added.

"So, we'd still see a future where we would use a portion of fishmeal, but it could be reduced by having these other animal-based proteins included where the amino acid profile of those animal-based proteins is more favorable to what we need in the feeds compared to using, for example, plant-based ones."

title: Acquisitive Nordic group buys Salma brand from Bremnes Seashore
content:
Norwegian salmon producer Bremnes Seashore has reached an agreement to transfer the ownership of the premium Salma brand to acquisitive seafood group Insula.

With this acquisition, Insula takes on the responsibility of further developing and distributing one of Norway's "most recognized brands for fresh salmon," said the companies in a joint statement. The firms did not disclose the terms of the deal.

Production of Salma products will now take place at Insula's sister company, the farmer and processor SalMar. Kverva owns 45.4% of SalMar and 95.7% of Insula.

FREE READ 100 jobs impacted as Norway’s Bremnes Seashore ends premium Salma brand

The ambition is to reintroduce the products to Norwegian grocery stores by the fall of 2025.

Bremnes had discontinued the brand due to mounting losses and challenging market conditions, affecting more than 100 jobs, it said at the end of 2024. The Salma division has been operating at a loss in recent years, with projected annual deficits running into tens of millions of Norwegian kroner. Rising raw material costs and increased operational expenses have made it difficult to achieve the volumes necessary for profitability. 

"Salma has played a significant role in the history of Bremnes Seashore. We take great pride in having built a brand that has set the standard for quality and freshness in the Norwegian market," said Linda Litlekalsoy Aase, CEO of Bremnes, regarding the transfer to Insula.

"This journey has been defined by innovation, courage, and the contributions of talented individuals at every stage. Now, we are pleased that Salma has found a new home with Insula -- a company with strong brand expertise, a robust distribution network, and, most importantly, dedicated and experienced professionals who understand this industry well."

Insula views this acquisition as an opportunity to preserve and further develop a brand with a unique market position and strong consumer recognition, it said.

Sigvald Rist, managing director of Insula Norway, said Salma was a flagship in the Norwegian seafood industry, the result of impressive brand building and product development over many years.

"We hold great respect for the work Bremnes Seashore has done and would like to extend special thanks to Olav Svendsen for his role as founder and driving force behind Salma. We also want to acknowledge all those who have contributed to making Salma what it is today -- from production to marketing."

The completion of the transaction is subject to approval by the relevant authorities. Pareto Securities served as the financial advisor for the transaction. 

Bremnes maintains the Bomlo brand.

title: Untitled
content:
A major US seafood processor is chafing under the state of Oregon's environmental regulations, claiming will require costly upgrades to comply with the state's new wastewater permitting rules, the Lincoln County Leader reports.

Pacific Seafood Group operates five separate plants in Newport, Oregon. The company says that new permitting requirements by the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) will require the company to construct a new wastewater treatment system for each facility or to link them together for centralized processing. 

"In the last couple of years, we started to see that the expectations of the DEQ regulation would require seafood processing locations to invest in treatment systems that range anywhere from $1 million to $5 million," Amy Wentworth, Pacific Seafood's director of environment, health, and safety said at a Feb. 25 meeting of the Port of Newport Commission, the newspaper reported.

Pacific Seafood plant fined for wastewater discharge

The millions in required upgrades have caused the Oregon seafood industry to become concerned it might have to move its processing operations either south to California or north to Washington.

Port of Newport executive director Paula Miranda said she's been working with Pacific Seafood and local business groups to keep the West Coast processor from pulling out, including exploring ways to apply for grant funding.

"We started having this conversation with Pacific Seafood," she said. "We have been brainstorming to figure out the best way to go about this."

But she said that a public agency can't apply for grants on behalf of a single private enterprise, but rather must shape its application so to any funding it receives helps to improve overall regional infrastructure.

"It would be unusual for the port to apply for something for one sole user," she said, 

Port Commission president Gil Sylvia acknowledged the complexities of the challenges ahead as her group works with state regulators tasked with ensuring the quality of public water supplies

"We want to help," Sylvia said. "But [we] recognize that there are financial issues, legal issues and uncertainties with what DEQ will or won't accept."

title: Nissui to tap EU market with fish oil-based pharma shipments
content:
Japanese seafood giant Nissui Corp. is set to begin shipping its refined fish-oil-derived pharmaceutical raw materials to Europe in early 2025, aiming to tap into growing international demand, a company spokesperson told Undercurrent News.

The move follows regulatory approvals from the European Medicines Agency and the UK's Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency. The Tokyo-based company will start shipments to Europe in the January-March quarter of 2025, the company revealed in its financial presentation for the April-December 2024 period.

"The initial shipment is scheduled for the first quarter of the year, but as of now, shipments have not yet begun," the spokesperson confirmed to Undercurrent.

In addition to its sales of eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid, the seafood company plans to expand its overseas market by offering functional ingredients that utilize advanced fish oil refining techniques.

Nissui's financial presentation for the April-December 2024 period released in February. Credit: Nissui Corp.

These include stability-enhancing technologies such as deodorization, emulsification, and antioxidant treatments, allowing for the expansion of products like gummies and jellies, the company said in the presentation.

The group also plans to resume exports to the US market once buyers clear its existing inventory, the company said in its 2024 integrated report.

In Asia, the Nissui Group is pursuing growth, with approvals for high-purity EPA formulations in Thailand and China and ongoing applications in Vietnam.

Nissui's Integrated Report for Fiscal 2024. Credit: Nissui Corp.

Its fine chemicals business, which includes producing and selling pharmaceutical and functional ingredients derived from fish oil, is one of three core growth drivers outlined in the Tokyo-based giant's long-term vision, "Good Foods 2030," alongside its overseas and aquaculture businesses.

Peruvian seafood exports soar with canned tuna, fish oil leading charge

The company's 2024 integrated report highlights the fine chemical sector's leveraging of strengths through its "Global Links, Local Links" strategy, which aims for steady growth while managing risks and opportunities.

"An increase in cardiovascular diseases is anticipated, particularly in advanced nations like Europe and the US," the seafood company stated. "Our EPA-based pharmaceutical ingredients uniquely contribute to addressing these global health issues."

Nissui also seeks opportunities in the market for EPA intermediates, particularly EPA ethyl ester, which is concentrated in pharmaceutical formulations.

The seafood company plans to leverage multi-channel sales strategies to boost revenue and operating profits, growing through raw materials and intermediate product sales.

Expansion into fine chemicals

Originally focused on the seafood industry, the group expanded into fine chemicals in the 1960s, particularly producing essential fatty acids derived from fish oil.

By the early 2000s, it had integrated advanced purification technologies for EPA production, securing its position in the global pharmaceutical market as demand for cardiovascular disease treatments increased.

With a focus on sustainable practices and high-purity products, the Tokyo-based company has refined its raw material procurement, production methods, and global distribution strategies.

Nissui's Integrated Report for Fiscal 2024. Credit: Nissui Corp.

The US Food and Drug Administration approved its domestic production facilities in 2021. However, the integrated report states that stricter-than-expected technical requirements in the application process have delayed overseas expansion.

Despite these hurdles, the seafood giant remains confident in its quality and technological capabilities in EPA production, particularly in EPA ethyl esters, which are concentrated to intermediate levels for pharmaceutical manufacturing.

China’s fishmeal imports hit record 1.96m metric tons as Peruvian supply rebounds
Stable procurement and supply chain

The group's approach to raw material procurement has been a cornerstone of its success in the fine chemicals market. Its strength lies in its integrated system, which focuses on securing sustainable, high-quality raw materials while ensuring smooth sales operations in domestic and international markets.

The Tokyo-based company sources anchovy and sardine oil from Japan and Peru through its procurement arm, Nissui America Latina Peru.

The company said the dual-source approach helps mitigate foreign exchange risks and reduces reliance on any single supplier or region, ensuring a stable and cost-effective supply chain.

Stable procurement has allowed Nissui to expand its pharmaceutical raw material production. The increasing sardine catch in Japanese waters in recent years and reliable sourcing from Peru support this growth, directly contributing to fish oil availability.

The group manages procurement through direct sales channels while maintaining an efficient supply chain that minimizes inventory costs and product availability. Its strategic sales operations ensure a steady supply of high-purity EPA production, even during market fluctuations.

The approach allows Nissui to guarantee production timelines and meet domestic and international demand, it said.

World-class storage and production facilities

Nissui operates advanced storage and processing systems across multiple locations in Japan.

Maruha Nichiro invests $21m to expand US surimi seafood capacity by 3,400t

In Hokkaido, it maintains a stockpile of raw fish oil composed of 19 tanks, each capable of holding 1,000 kiloliters. This storage system, one of the largest globally, ensures a continuous and reliable supply of fish oil for production.

The company's production capabilities are concentrated in its Kashima and Tsukuba facilities. Its Kashima No. 2 Plant, which specializes in pharmaceutical manufacturing. The facility adheres to the strictest current good manufacturing practices, ensuring high-quality and safe products. Its Tsukuba Plant enhances the group's production capabilities by refining and concentrating raw oil into high-purity EPA.

For the April-December 2024 period, Nissui's Fine Chemicals segment experienced a 6% year-on-year decline to JPY 107 million, with an operating profit of JPY 1m, compared to breaking even in the same period a year earlier. All segment earnings currently come from its domestic operations (see below).

 'Single A' issuer rating 

Nissui announced on Wednesday (March 5) that it has received a "Single A" issuer rating from Rating and Investment Information (R&I), a Japan-based credit rating agency, with a "stable" outlook.

R&I said the rating reflects Nissui's well-balanced business portfolio, geographically diversified revenue sources that support stable profits, and the growth potential of its overseas food business.

Based on the issuer rating, R&I assigned Nissui a commercial paper rating of "a-1," stating that it believes the company has secured the necessary liquidity for CP redemption.

Nissui said it sought the rating "to enhance the diversification and stability of financing by acquiring an objective evaluation from a third-party institution."

title: Weakness in global shrimp markets weighs on Benchmark’s turnover, margins
content:
Benchmark Holdings, a UK aquaculture biotechnology company, saw its Q1 (Sept. 1-Dec. 31) revenue drop 30% year-on-year to £17.7 million ($22.31m).

The decline was attributed to its advanced nutrition division, which was impacted by ongoing weakness in global shrimp markets and a shift in product mix. Health revenues also reflected the restructuring of this division and the pause in sales of Ectosan Vet and CleanTreat as the company pivots towards a new land-based business model, it said, 

Benchmark agrees to sell genetics division in deal worth up to £260m

Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization showed a loss of £200,000, compared to a £3.5m profit in Q1 FY24, Benchmark said. Operating costs fell by 15%, to £7.3m, reflecting strict financial discipline ahead of the genetics disposal, according to the company. Net debt increased to £62m from £49m at the end of FY24.

The company's unaudited Q1 results refer to the three months ending December 2024, which constitutes the first quarter of its fiscal year (FY) 2025. The quarter marks a transition period, with the company advancing towards completing its genetics business disposal and streamlining its operations, the company said. 

Benchmark's nutrition division focused on operational efficiency, expanding its product range, and driving innovation. The recently launched shrimp diet tailored to the Ecuadorian market sold out in its first period, and the European marine fish sector showed strong performance.

"The strategy in place and the steps we have taken over the last 18 months to mitigate the impact of soft shrimp markets have placed Advanced Nutrition in a strong position for market recovery and for its longer-term future," said Benchmark. 

Meanwhile, the health division focused on its new business model for Ectosan Vet and CleanTreat through a joint venture with Water. The restructured health division, now centered on Salmosan Vet, reported cash-positive operations. "Sales of SalmosanVet of £1.6m (Q1 FY24: £2.1m) were driven by sales in Norway and Chile, which experienced high sea lice levels, offset primarily by lower sales in the Faroe Islands compared to last year," the firm said.

Benchmark said that the sale of its genetics business is on track for completion by the end of March 2025. Proceeds will be used to return capital to shareholders and reduce company debt.

Benchmark said its performance aligns with management management's expectations.

The latter part of Q1 showed improving trends in advanced nutrition, while health remains a profitable unit. CEO Trond Williksen defined the quarter as a "stepping "stone" for the company. He expressed optimism about the company's focus post-genetics disposal, highlighting opportunities for shareholder value creation.

"Q1 FY25 has been a stepping-stone quarter for us, representing a period of transition for Benchmark ahead of the completion of the genetics disposal and streamlining of the continuing business. Our reported performance reflects ongoing weakness in the global shrimp markets for advanced nutrition coupled with a temporary change in product mix and a solid performance in health," Whealthe" said.

"Looking forward, we expect an improvement in trading conditions and margins, and we have two well-positioned businesses capable of delivering attractive shareholder returns. Our restructured Health business performs well as a cash-generative business and is advancing towards a relaunch of a new land-based business model for Ectosan Vet and CleanTreat," he added.

title: Newfoundland aquaculture sites removed from proposed marine sanctuary
content:
A revised boundary for the proposed marine sanctuary on the south coast of Newfoundland and Labrador has been released, confirming that aquaculture sites are no longer within its footprint.

However, fishing industry stakeholders remain wary of the pending sanctuary designation, arguing that the South Coast Fjords National Marine Conservation Area (NMCA) could still disrupt their livelihoods and should be scrapped entirely.

The proposed NMCA overlaps with the Bays West area, which the provincial government has identified as a key zone for aquaculture expansion. The region is expected to increase Newfoundland's annual Atlantic salmon production by 15,000 to 20,000 metric tons, creating jobs and boosting the local economy.

It is also a vital area for fisheries. Lobster, halibut, scallops, and redfish are all commercially important species fished in the affected waters. With the updated boundary still encompassing critical fishing grounds, industry representatives remain wary of how it will impact operations.

Last month, Parks Canada -- the federal agency overseeing the NMCA process -- told Undercurrent News a revision of the proposed sanctuary's boundary would exclude salmon-farming sites. At the time, many stakeholders responded with skepticism, saying they would only believe it when they saw the final map. The agency's statement has proven accurate with the updated boundary now public, though fish harvesters say some of their concerns remain unaddressed.

Proposed updated South Coast Fjords NMCA boundary

Pushback despite aquaculture carve-out

Jamie Baker, who represents Fish, Food and Allied Workers (FFAW) members from fishing zone 3PS in the Placentia and Fortune Bay areas, confirmed to Undercurrent on Monday (Feb. 17) the union received the updated boundary information late last week.

Baker said the labor union is reviewing the changes with its members alongside responses from Parks Canada to fisheries-related questions that have been outstanding since November 2024.

"There is no doubt our members in the region have some very clear and valid concerns about how this proposal would affect their livelihoods, especially at a time when those harvesters, after years of struggles, are finally on the verge of seeing some real solid potential for strong, sustainable inshore fisheries development in a few key species," Baker said.

Jason Sullivan, a fisherman and vice president of FFAW, told Undercurrent much of the aquaculture area initially included in the sanctuary's boundary has been removed from the updated sanctuary map. But despite the alterations, the sanctuary will still harm fish harvesters, Sullivan said.

"Looking at the boundary map, it's clear that most of the aquaculture-affected areas have been removed. The revised NMCA boundary is a bit smaller and has shifted further east," said Sullivan, who spoke to Undercurrent as a fisherman. "Those harbors and bays where aquaculture takes place are no longer included, but the open-water areas remain, which means fisheries like lobster and halibut are still going to be impacted."

Sullivan warned the NMCA could lead to additional fishing restrictions, particularly if protected species are found in the area. "If a right whale moves through the NMCA, everything shuts down. If a sea otter gets caught in a lobster pot, that could mean a permanent closure. These marine closures always seem to come at the expense of fishermen," he said.

Mayor Steve Crewe of Hermitage-Sandyville, a vocal critic of the marine sanctuary, acknowledged the revised boundary had spared aquaculture sites but maintained that the NMCA should be scrapped entirely.

"The boundary has gone farther right as we were asking, so yes, I guess it addressed that (concern). But as for the NMCA itself, I still think that it should be pulled. I believe the fishermen up there are pretty concerned about it now. What does it mean for them?" Crewe told Undercurrent in a phone interview on Monday.

He indicated that he would wait to see if the steering committee contacted the group for further discussions and would provide input again if they did.

Revised boundary follows objections

The boundary was revised after sustained opposition from Newfoundland's fishing and aquaculture industries. In December 2024, the NMCA steering committee was directed to redraw the map after Newfoundland and Labrador premier Andrew Furey and his government responded to mounting concerns from industry representatives, including Newfoundland Labrador fisheries minister Elvis Loveless.

As Undercurrent reported at the time, Loveless, who represents Fortune Bay-Cape La Hune in the Newfoundland and Labrador House of Assembly, said the province was taking steps to ensure the livelihoods of coastal communities would not be harmed.

"We want the area designated in current discussions redefined," Loveless posted on Facebook in the Newfoundland Fisherman's Forum. "When the future of the fishing industry and livelihoods are threatened, I will not stand for it. This is too important to all of us."

The NMCA feasibility study is governed by a memorandum of understanding (MOU) between the province of Newfoundland and Labrador, Qalipu First Nation, Miawpukek First Nation and the Town of Burgeo. Its goal is to assess whether a protected area should be established in the South Coast Fjords region.

Cooke remains opposed

Joel Richardson, vice president of public relations for Cooke Inc., which operates numerous salmon farms in the area, reiterated the company's opposition to the NMCA. The seafood conglomerate's CEO, Glenn Cooke, has been one of the leading voices urging the Newfoundland government to withdraw from the agreement assessing the sanctuary's feasibility.

"Our position on the federal Liberal government's proposed NMCA is unchanged -- we urge the provincial Furey government to oppose any NMCA that restricts commercial and recreational fishing and imposes new federal rules around included or adjacent aquaculture farming and vessel operations," Richardson told Undercurrent.

"NMCAs negatively impact jobs in the seafood industry, which severely damages the viability of rural coastal communities. Our hundreds of Newfoundland employees, suppliers, and their families are fully opposed to a South Coast NMCA," he said.

What's next?

The NMCA steering committee is expected to finalize recommendations in the coming months, but Sullivan said the steering committee still has not officially communicated with fishermen about the revised boundary despite it being circulated among other industry groups. He warned that the opposition would only grow without a meaningful response to fish harvesters' concerns.

"This isn't over," Sullivan said. "The people fishing in this area need to come together and fight back. They're looking to destroy our livelihood, and where does it stop? Whose fishing area will be next?"

Baker said FFAW is fully committed to ensuring harvesters receive the most up-to-date and accurate information, and that FFAW's membership will determine how the union responds.

"The singular aim of our current process is to ensure our harvesters can fully and clearly understand any and all implications of the NMCA proposal for their fisheries," he said. "We feel a lot of this may have been avoided had harvesters been adequately invited to participate as a full member of the steering committee right from the start."

Parks Canada has not yet responded to requests for comment as of publication.

title: Major US shrimp importers unite as Captain Fresh’s CenSea buys Ocean Garden
content:
India's Captain Fresh has acquired US shrimp importer Ocean Garden Products via its Illinois-based subsidiary Central Seaway Company (CenSea).

The acquisition adds the Ocean Garden, Compass, Asian Garden, and Pride of Mexico, brands to CenSea's portfolio, Captain Fresh said on Tuesday.

Koral to be included in Captain Fresh, Sekkingstad salmon JV, with ‘more to come’

Undercurrent News first reported a deal was in the works for San Diego, California-based Ocean Garden last week. In addition, Captain Fresh is reportedly in talks to acquire Blue Sea Products, another shrimp-focused US importer based in New Jersey, on the East Coast. 

Captain Fresh founder and CEO Utham Gowda has set an ambitious goal of reaching $1 billion in sales in its next fiscal year.

The company's latest acquisition unites two large US seafood importers and distributors with complementary businesses under its umbrella, its statement said. 

While CenSea is "a leader in Asian shrimp and other seafood products from around the world," Ocean Garden focuses more on Mexican and Ecuadorian shrimp. 

The integration brings Ocean Garden's team, led by president and CEO Celso Lopez, into the CenSea organization under the leadership of co-presidents Nate Torch and Jeff Stern.

"Ocean Garden has been a well-respected brand and household name with respect to Mexican shrimp, both wild-caught and farmed, as well as other origins produced for their array of brands. We are excited to leverage the strength of their brand and product portfolio to provide a stronger basket and a greater variety of products to our customers," said CenSea's Torch. 

Captain Fresh in talks to buy US importers Blue Sea, Ocean Garden

 "We at CenSea are committed to enhancing Ocean Garden's operations by expanding product portfolios and enabling new markets access while upholding their core values," said Stern. "We are preserving their legacy and enhancing it -- ensuring that customers continue to receive the premium-quality seafood they trust, now with even greater efficiency and broader offerings."

"Our customers will continue to receive the same exceptional service and quality seafood that has defined Ocean Garden's success since 1957," said Ocean Garden's Lopez. "What's most exciting is that with our synergies with CenSea and Captain Fresh group's technology-driven approach, we now have the opportunity to set new standards for excellence in seafood sourcing and distribution."

Salmon JV, Blue Sea deal in works 

Captain Fresh is aiming for $1 billion in revenue in its financial year starting April 1 with the various expansion projects it has underway, with an initial public offering also on the agenda. 

Captain Fresh eyes spot in seafood’s top 10, targets $1bn sales for next year

One such push is a salmon supply and processing joint venture with the owner of Norway's Sekkingstad, which includes the latter's Skagerak Processing plant in Hirtshals, Denmark, and Captain Fresh's Koral factory in Poland. 

Another is a CenSea-led buy-out of Perth Amboy, New Jersey-based Blue Sea, which is also in the works. 

Blue Sea -- which is owned by Thomas Jacob, a veteran seafood entrepreneur originally from India -- would make a complementary fit to CenSea, sources told Undercurrent. Jacob's company is focused on shellfish such as shrimp, crab, lobster and scallops, but also finfish and squid, but with strong sales channels in the US East Coast compared to the Midwestern CenSea.

title: Icelandic cod, haddock prices jump in week six
content:
Icelandic auction prices for both ungutted cod and haddock have jumped in week six (Feb. 3-9) of 2025, echoing developments in Norway, the latest data added to Undercurrent News' price portal shows.

Pricing data from Reiknistofa Fiskmarkada (RSF) -- a business that connects 11 fish markets at 45 locations on one auction network -- shows that index ex-vessel prices for ungutted cod are up more than ISK 30/kg relative to just a week ago.

It's the second-highest weekly price point of the last year, beaten out only by Christmas week. Notably, total ungutted cod volumes on the auction did drop off somewhat compared to the previous week.

Upgrade to Pro to view

By weight, it appears larger sizes are seeing more of an increase than sizes under 2kg.

RSF puts the current prices of large cod over 5g in weight at ISK 648/kg; 3-5kg cod at ISK 588/kg; 2.7-3.5kg cod at ISK 541/kg; and 2.0-2.7kg cod at ISK 492/kg. For all but the very largest fish, it's the highest weekly average of the last 52 weeks:

Prices in US dollars are provided below:

In the 3.5-5kg category specifically, there has been a clear drop in volume, with only 8,564t sold in week six, prompting the sudden rebound:

When compared with the same week of last year, it's clear that prices are are more than ISK 100/kg higher for the same-sized cod, likely a product of international supply reductions:

Gutted cod -- which is produced on longer journeys out to sea over several days -- remains out of season, and as such only ~34,000t were sold in the latest week, at an average of ISK 600/kg.

It's down on the levels of the previous fortnight, but still not back to the levels seen before prices began to climb from September onwards last year:

The limited supply on the auction, which doesn't usually pick up until March, makes it hard to draw any firm conclusions on different weight categories. Nevertheless, once again all but the smallest fish are coalescing in value around the range of ISK 450-550/kg.

Looking at the main 3.5-5kg category, prices are now a little lower than they were at this stage last year, having slumped to ISK 464/kg on average:

Haddock prices also climbing

Following very much the same trajectory as cod of late, auction prices for ungutted haddock are also on their own steady upward march, with week five's small downturn being almost immediately cancelled out on the latest week.

For week six, RSF recorded 106t of ungutted haddock sold, at an average of ISK 427/kg. In volume terms, this was less than half of what had been sold the previous week, and markets adjusted up ISK 30/kg w-o-w as a result:

Across weights, the same pattern as in cod is evident, with the largest fish very much in demand and rising in value fast.

For the latest week, RSF gave average values of ISK 527/kg for the biggest ungutted haddock over 2kg in weight, while the 1.6-2kg category was trading a little lower at ISK 515/kg.

In both cases, prices had jumped roughly ISK 90/kg on where they had been in week five:

For the 1.6-2kg weight, usually the benchmark category for the auction, ungutted haddock prices are at their highest level in over a year, just as the 20t sol in week six is unusually low; 166t were sold in the same week of 2024.

It means that ungutted haddock is once more matching the price peaks of early 2023, rather than the lower levels that defined the end of that year and the start of 2024:

For head-on gutted haddock, average prices have also risen, up to ISK 363/kg, now just a little below the New Year spike of ISK 375/kg.

Here again, sales volumes are lower than at the same stage of 2024 -- just 93t were sold across all sizes in week six, compared to 210t last year:

By weight category, once more, it's the largest fish that are in the highest demand.

Most gutted haddock sizes are continuing to sell between ISK 320-400/kg; however, the largest haddock over 2kg is now trading up near ISK 600/kg and rising fast:

That huge jump in price for the largest sizes is offset by more modest w-o-w changes elsewhere, though.

For 1.8-2kg gutted haddock, the average price remains somewhere in between the levels of 2023-2024:

Finally, other major species from RSF's auction are also available on Undercurrent's data portal.

Below, you can see the latest price and supply data for the main size category by volume for each of the next five biggest commercial species sold on the RSF auction after cod and haddock: redfish, plaice, saithe, catfish, and ling.

Much like cod and haddock, week six has seen auction prices for all major alternative species: redfish, saithe, catfish and ling. For most species, week six was an astoundingly low week for sales volumes, however.
