title: Indian shrimp giant acquires North American lobster supplier from industry veteran
content:
A company controlled by the largest Indian shrimp supplier to the US has acquired a lobster distributor and exporter based in the East Coast state of Massachusetts, Undercurrent News has confirmed.

An "affiliate" company of California-based AZ Gems has acquired Truefoods Premium Product (TPP) from Michael Tourkistas, a legendary figure in the North American lobster sector. TPP aims for a turnover of over $100 million for 2025, Tourkistas told Undercurrent. 

FREE READ US wholesale: Surprise sentiment on North American tails despite limited inventory

AZ Gems and Wanaka USA, the affiliate used to do the TPP deal, are all ultimately part of India's Sandhya Aqua Exports, a large, family-owned farming, processing and export group based in shrimp hub Andra Pradesh. 

Executives with AZ Gems and TPP confirmed the deal to Undercurrent, which is being billed as a "strategic partnership with Wanaka USA."

The deal is an alliance of two entrepreneur seafood families, with AZ Gems/Sandhya Aqua led by Kunam Kotaiah Chowdary, son of the group's founder, who studied in California before taking over the reins of the company.

Greece-born Tourkistas -- who founded and built up lobster and scallop supplier East Coast Seafood Group (ECSG), which he sold to Forum Capital Group in 2015 -- and his team will stay on after the deal.

In 2020, Undercurrent revealed that Tourkistas had created Truefoods and bought back the former ECSG live lobster-focused business from Forum. "I failed at retirement," Tourkistas said at the time.

Whole, cooked, North Atlantic lobster. Credit: Truefoods Premium Product

"I'm still very much involved with Truefoods and excited about what's ahead. My focus remains on supporting our customers and partners while continuing to grow the business alongside Wanaka USA and AZ Gems," Tourkistas told Undercurrent on Thursday. "We've built something great, and I'm looking forward to keeping that momentum going. This is truly a win-win for all involved."

Customers and suppliers can expect "business as usual, with no operational changes at TPP," he said. "Instead, the partnership strengthens TPP's market reach and enhances its ability to navigate the evolving seafood industry."

Matthew Tourkistas, Michael's son, is chief operating officer of Truefoods, which is based in the former ECSG office in Topsfield, Massachusetts.

US shellfish dealers need to be ‘boxers and ballerinas,’ GSMC panel advises

Truefoods sells live lobster, in addition to frozen whole, tails, fresh and frozen meat in North America, Europe and Asia, with French, Spanish and UK contact numbers given on its website.

The deal with AZ Gems "marks an important step in TPP's continued growth, enhancing its ability to serve customers in North America, Europe and Asia with high-quality seafood," said a statement from the buyer. "TPP will maintain its strong relationships with long-term Canadian partner plants and global customers, ensuring the same commitment to quality, service, and reliability that has defined the company."

AZ Gems, which has a turnover of over $600m and ranks number 63 on Undercurrent's upcoming top 150 global seafood company report, has strong sales channels and a team in the US market for Truefoods' lobster.

Kunam, AZ Gems' founder and CEO, added former Trident Seafoods executive Jamie Marshall to his US team in 2022 as executive vice president (VP) of sales. Marshall has since added two more former Trident sellers, Tom Dorwart and Matthew Flinchum, to the AZ Gems US team.

Frozen, raw, North Atlantic lobster tails. Credit: Truefoods Premium Product

Mary Mabey-O'Rourke also joined Thai Union Group's US frozen seafood arm in 2023 as a sales VP. Ned Ligenza, another US seafood sales veteran, is the company's VP of business development.

"What makes it even better is the incredible team I've had the pleasure of working with for years, both in the US and Europe. And for the past five years, having my son Matthew involved in building the business has been really special. The opportunity for him to work alongside Jaime Marshall -- who's been a personal friend for years -- makes the future even more exciting," Tourkistas told Undercurrent. 

"This partnership allows us to leverage Wanaka USA's extensive distribution network while continuing to do what we do best -- delivering premium seafood products to our valued customers," said Tourkistas. "We remain dedicated to our partners and are excited about the opportunities this collaboration brings."

In the US, AZ Gems has sister sales companies, Zalo Fresh and Select Source, Canada. In Europe, a key market for Truefoods, the company has "affiliates" such as Bonmea in the UK and Germany and Wanaka Seafood in France.

title: Fish oil prices fall as Peruvian producers fret over carried stock
content:
Fish oil prices have dropped significantly in early 2025, with producers in Peru selling at around $2,600 per metric ton to China, cost and freight, down from December highs of $3,190/t, free on board (FOB), according to Undercurrent News industry sources.

Prices for 25% EPA+DHA food-grade fish oil to China are currently trading at approximately $2,575-$2,600/t FOB Callao (Peru), reflecting a sharp decline from late 2024 levels reported by the Marine Ingredients Organisation, known as IFFO.

VIEW GRAPH

© 2025 Undercurrent News
To view the full datas
GO PREMIUM
Upgrade to Pro to view

"There is still a lot of oil in Peru, and weather conditions for fishing are fine," Roland Erausquin, director of Erausquin International Consulting, told Undercurrent. "The next fishing season will start in April or late March, so availability is not going to be a problem."

The price volatility follows the market's lurch down in the second half of last year after Peruvian producers entered the second fishing season with carried stock from the first. This caused average fish oil trades to fall to $2,750/t, FOB, in October, according to IFFO data, down 62% year-on-year.

Then Peru announced an above-average second-season quota, keeping prices low in November.

Fish oil market sentiment shifted again when results from early second-season fishing revealed lower-than-usual levels of omega-3 content, sources said. This quality issue particularly impacted sales to European buyers, who require a minimum of 28% EPA+DHA content for food-grade applications.

"In December, there was a lot of production of 24-27% EPA+DHA that got some people nervous and moved the market [upwards]," Jorge Garcia, a Peru-based fish oil trader, told Undercurrent. Peru's "normal spec" fish oil is 27%-and-over DHA+EPA content, he said.

The more recent price weakness comes after oil yield and fishing concerns eased, according to Erausquin, with fishing conditions recovering and oil yields stabilizing.

"What a great feeling to look back on this season's over 90% fulfillment of the fishing quota," reflected James Frank, managing director at Peruvian fishmeal and fish oil trading outfit MSICeres, in a recent market report. "Although there were plenty of mini bans, and at times stoppages for rough seas, the pipeline was always skillfully filled."

While MSICeres' report highlighted an unusual scarcity of super prime fishmeal, "whose absence had to do with the nature of the fish along with its distance from the plants," fish oil yields were described as "a winner this season."

Exports recover

The price movements come against the backdrop of significant Peruvian fish oil exports in 2024, which totaled 97,740 metric tons. The majority of this volume -- 76,448t or 78.2% -- was exported as crude fish oil, while refined fish oil accounted for 21,292t (21.8%).

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view

Europe emerged as the largest market, taking 45,105t or 46.1% of total exports, followed by the Americas at 38,553t (39.5%). Asian markets, despite China's dominant position in fishmeal trade, accounted for just 13,150t (13.5%) of fish oil exports, with Oceania receiving the remaining 927t.

Erausquin said Chinese buyers have recently been more active in the market, as they can blend lower EPA+DHA oils with other sources. Deals have quickly trended down, starting at $3,000 before falling to $2,900 and, lately, $2,600/t.

He added that producers are anxious to clear inventory before the next fishing season begins. Carrying stock into the new season could be "very risky, especially with the omega-3 oil yield profile as it is," he said.

Pharmaceutical sector

Despite the price volatility of the past two years, Erausquin said the global market for fish oil remains strong, with good demand from the pharmaceutical and nutraceutical sectors. Consumption of fish oil supplements is growing worldwide, particularly following increased health consciousness during the COVID-19 pandemic.

This premium market segment has seen recent spot trades at $4,000-$5,000/t for higher EPA+DHA content oils, though volumes are relatively small compared to the feed and more standard food-grade markets, he said.

"Koreans or Japanese will go for high-grade pharmaceutical oils. But this is a small volume sold on the spot market," said Erausquin. While food-grade demand is split between European and Chinese buyers, the European market continues to dominate the feed industry segment, he added.

title: Daily recap: China shrimp market still weak; US Dungy supply tight, prices high
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Tuesday, Jan. 14.

Week 3 farm-gate shrimp roundup: Chinese market weakness persists despite Lunar New Year approach

Chinese farm-gate farmed vannamei shrimp prices remain depressed despite the approaching Lunar New Year festivities on Jan. 29, traditionally a period of peak demand and strong pricing, while prices from other origins softened or stayed firm.

Supplies tight, prices high as US Dungy crab season underway in Oregon, Washington

Commercial crabbing in portions of the US northwest coast will open on Wednesday (Jan. 15) along a 57-mile stretch from Cape Falcon, Oregon, to Klipsan Beach, Washington. 

Vietnamese pangasius farm-gate prices highest since 2022

Farm-gate prices for Vietnamese pangasius have risen sharply at the turn of the year on limited supplies, according to the latest updates from a Ho Chi Minh City-based consultancy commissioned by Undercurrent News to gather and analyze data.

US appeals court rules against Alaska cannery workers seeking overtime during COVID-19 lockdown

An Alaska salmon processor did not need to pay overtime wages to workers confined to their bunkhouses during the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic, a US appeals court in San Francisco, California, has ruled.

Scotland's Peterhead auction sees cod, haddock prices up as Shetland values diverge

Prices for fresh cod and haddock increased across several categories at Scotland's Peterhead auction in week two (Jan. 6-12), reflecting strong demand for both species in the early weeks of the year.

Ecuador's Aquagold signs another supply deal with Chinese partners

Ecuadorian shrimp exporter Aquagold has signed a private-label deal with Chinese firm Jinfulin, expanding in northern China after an earlier distribution agreement with one of China's largest shrimp processors in the south.

title: Untitled
content:
An Alaska salmon processor did not need to pay overtime wages to workers confined to their bunkhouses during the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic, a US appeals court in San Francisco, California, has ruled.

Alaska General Seafoods had required workers at its seasonal processors in Naknek and Ketchikan, Alaska, stay on the company's premises in April 2020 due to restrictions stemming from the COVID-19 pandemic.

OBI, Ocean Beauty Seafoods ordered to pay $2.1m in COVID-19 wage quarantine settlement

The 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals, in San Francisco, California, held Friday (Jan. 10) that the US District Court in Anchorage, Alaska, was correct when, in November 2023, it ruled that the Kenmore, Washington-based company keeping its workers off-the-clock despite their movements being restricted during free time was lawful.

"Although plaintiffs resided on their employer's premises and were confined to company property due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the undisputed evidence shows that plaintiffs were called in to work infrequently and were able to engage in a range of personal activities while on call," the appeals court found.

The workers in Flaherty v. Kanaway Seafoods, Inc. had alleged their employer violated state and federal wage-and-hour laws when it implemented the pandemic lockdowns. They claimed they were effectively confined to their workplace and not compensated.

The lower court had ruled in favor of the Alaska processor, saying the workers could still use their time for personal activities and also held that the unionized workforce's collective bargaining rights only extended to actual work hours. 

"In any event, the undisputed evidence shows that plaintiffs were called in to work infrequently and did not have their sleep regularly interrupted," the appeals court ruled.

title: Week 3 farm-gate shrimp roundup: Chinese market weakness persists despite Lunar New Year approach
content:
Additional reporting by Dan Gibson, Lewis Hu and Neil Ramsden. 

Chinese farm-gate farmed vannamei shrimp prices remain depressed despite the approaching Lunar New Year festivities on Jan. 29, traditionally a period of peak demand and strong pricing, while prices from other origins softened or stayed firm.

Latest data from Undercurrent News shows Guangdong, China prices for 60-count vannamei recovering slightly to $4.64 per kilogram in week three, up from $4.38/kg. However, this remains well below historical norms for the pre-festival period and trails Thai prices at $4.69/kg.

While now above Vietnamese prices, which softened to $4.58/kg in week two from $4.83/kg, the current Chinese price levels remain unusually weak for a market that typically commands a premium due to its live domestic sales.

Upgrade to Pro to view

Indian prices in the Nellore region registered a third week of decline, with 60-count vannamei shrimp easing to $3.81/kg in week three from $3.87/kg. Meanwhile, Ecuadorian prices showed some weakness in smaller sizes, with 60/70-count grades slipping to $3.30/kg while 50/60-count maintained $3.85/kg.

Indonesian material in week three stood at $3.46/kg for 60-counts, down from $3.62/kg, positioning it among the more competitively priced origins in the global market. It means a spread of approximately $1.39/kg between the highest-priced origin (Thailand) and lowest (Ecuador's 60/70-count) in the market.

China's shrimp market struggles

A modest uptick in Guangdong province has done little to ease farmer concerns ahead of the Lunar New Year celebrations on Jan. 29.

After hitting historic lows for the period in the first week of January, Guangdong's 60-count vannamei prices edged up CNY 2 to CNY 34/kg ($4.64/kg) in week two. However, the limited recovery -- confined to 60-count and larger sizes -- has offered little comfort to farmers.

Both Jiangsu and Fujian provinces also remain stuck at CNY 28/kg, while Guangxi and Shandong continue to hold at CNY 32/kg. There remain particularly high inventory levels in Jiangsu and Fujian, sources report.

"We may be going through an era where the biggest holiday in China won't be able to raise prices," a farmer told Undercurrent this week, noting rising anxiety levels as the Lunar New Year festival approaches. The sentiment marks a sharp contrast to traditional seasonal patterns, where the holiday's approach typically drives stronger farm-gate prices.

"The New Year's market can be described as miserable," another farmer noted last week. "Greenhouses are producing so much shrimp that the market is in turmoil, and few trucks are coming from Yangjiang to buy our shrimp."

It's a significant reversal from last year when 60-count shrimp prices in Guangdong commanded CNY 61/kg in week two. The situation has become particularly frustrating for Chinese producers watching price trends in other countries, sources report. 

Prices soften in Andhra Pradesh

In India, shrimp prices declined across major farming regions in the third week of January, marking the third consecutive week of declines, although prices still remain elevated for the period.

In the Nellore region, 40-count shrimp prices moved down to INR 400 ($4.62)/kg from INR 403/kg the previous week. Other sizes followed suit, with 50-count shrimp reaching INR 360/kg, 60-count INR 330/kg, and 70-count INR 310/kg.

Andhra Pradesh markets showed comparable adjustments, with 40-count vannamei shrimp easing to INR 400/kg from INR 410/kg in week two. Prices settled lower across all sizes, with 50-count at INR 360/kg, 60-count at INR 330/kg, and 70-count at INR 310/kg.

"The main driver of the uptrend in prices is the reduced inflow of supply material, particularly in Andhra Pradesh, which is the largest market," a source familiar with the farming situation told Undercurrent last week. "This reduction has created a scenario of high demand and limited availability, pushing farm-gate prices up steadily over the past few weeks."

The supply situation has been further complicated by processors from Odisha sourcing material from Andhra Pradesh, as supply in Odisha is also quite low, the source added.

The price surge has been particularly pronounced in black tiger shrimp in past months, with 30-count sizes jumping from INR 430/kg to INR 520/kg since June, while 20-count grades now command INR 610-630/kg.

Looking ahead to the summer crop cycle, industry observers anticipate changes following Makar Sankranti, a Hindu festival celebrated on Jan. 14.

"We may see a surge in material inflow after Sankranti, as we may begin partial harvests," the first source noted. "Regarding summer crop stocking, as it is the largest crop cycle across the nation, we may see widespread stocking across the production regions."

The current market conditions present a different scenario from last year's challenges.

"Last year, the major concerns were reduced farm-gate prices and increased production costs. At this moment, it appears positive, but we will have a clearer picture closer to Sankranti, given the price levels at that time and weather conditions," the source explained.

Large sizes still firm in Vietnam

Vietnamese vannamei shrimp prices slipped back across most size categories in the second week of January 2025, though larger sizes held firm amid tight supply.

High-value 20-count shrimp held steady at VND 219,000 ($8.63)/kg, while 30-count sizes showed minimal change at VND 152,000/kg, suggesting continued demand for bigger shrimp. However, mid-range sizes faced softened, with 40-count dropping to VND 127,200/kg from VND 131,143/kg the previous week.

The decline was more pronounced in smaller grades. Prices for 60-count shrimp decreased to VND 116,200/kg from VND 121,714/kg, while 70-count fell to VND 112,200/kg. The smallest 80-count category settled at VND 104,200/kg, down from VND 108,143/kg.

"At the moment, the prices stopped climbing, and some also lightly declined. For shrimp of bigger sizes, the prices are still high, on high demand and less quantity; for smaller sizes, the prices are more attractive, they've reduced, and [farmers] still have volumes," a source with a Vietnamese processor told Undercurrent last week.

Small sizes slip in Ecuador

Ecuadorian shrimp prices are diverging in early 2025, with larger sizes maintaining their stability while smaller grades face downward pressure in week two.

Large and mid-size grades continued their steady run, with 20/30-count holding firm at $5.00/kg for a fifth consecutive week. This extended through 30/40-count at $4.70/kg, 40/50-count at $4.35/kg, and 50/60-count at $3.85/kg.

However, smaller sizes slipped. The 60/70-count category dipped to $3.30/kg from $3.40/kg, while 70/80-count saw a more substantial decline to $2.80/kg from $3.10/kg. The smallest 80/100-count grade maintained its level at $2.40/kg.

The mixed price trends come after a year of market challenges in 2024. "We will close the year at the highest levels [of prices]," an industry source previously told Undercurrent. "However, 2024 has not been a good year. It hasn't been bad either if we consider previous years' situations, but it could have been better."

East Java prices tick up

Indonesian shrimp prices continued their ascent at the start of week three of 2025, with East Java reporting gains across all size categories.

Larger sizes set the pace, with 30-count grades reaching IDR 75,000 ($4.60)/kg, while 40-count climbed to IDR 70,000/kg. The 50-count category advanced to IDR 64,000/kg from IDR 62,880/kg the previous week.

Mid-sized grades showed similar strength, with 60-count shrimp moving up to IDR 61,000/kg from IDR 60,000/kg. The 70-count category reached IDR 59,000/kg from IDR 57,240/kg, while 80-count sizes rose to IDR 58,000/kg from IDR 56,240/kg.

Smaller sizes maintained the positive momentum, with 90-count advancing to IDR 56,000/kg from IDR 54,120/kg and 100-count moving up to IDR 54,000/kg from IDR 53,000/kg.

Thai maintain gains

Thai shrimp prices continued to rise in week two of 2025, building on momentum from late last year.

The benchmark 60-count shrimp climbed to THB 162.50 ($4.68)/kg, advancing from THB 160/kg the previous week. Meanwhile, 70-count sizes held steady at THB 155/kg, while 80-count grades moved up to THB 142.50/kg from THB 140/kg.

title: California labor union takes aim at Pacific Seafood Group’s environmental record
content:
A labor union has taken aim at US processor Pacific Seafood Group's checkered environmental record by creating a website that highlights the company's string of permit violations.

UNITE HERE Local 49, a Sacramento, California-based service workers union, announced on Wednesday (Jan. 8) that it had launched pacificseafooddirtysecret.org. The website catalogs discharges in the US states of California, Oregon, and Washington that had exceeded permit limits, triggering action by state and federal regulators.

(Screenshot by Jacob Resneck/UCN)

Pacific Seafood representatives don't deny the violations yet say they are puzzled why the labor union has decided to target its company with a negative publicity campaign.

"They're positioning it like it's a secret or something," Pacific Seafood communications director Lacy Ogan told Undercurrent News. 

As Undercurrent has reported, the Oregon-headquartered company was fined $220,000 by regulators in Washington state over discharges at its Westport plant. It was at least the third time the plant had been fined by state or federal regulators since 2020.

Union's ties to fish processor unclear

The most recent filings with the US Department of Labor shows the Sacramento-area labor union branch represents about 4,900 workers in hotels, casinos, airports and food service in California.

The company operates a distribution center in Sacramento -- where UNITE HERE Local 49 is active -- but Ogan said the company is unaware of any organizing campaign among the company's workforce.

"It's very odd," she added.

UNITE HERE coy on campaign tactics

Aamir Deen, UNITE HERE Local 49's president, wouldn't say why his union had decided to run a negative publicity campaign against the seafood company's well-documented permit violations.

"We're the union that represents workers in the hospitality and food service industry. So we care about the environment," Deen told Undercurrent. "Pacific Seafood is a vendor in the industry, and so we believe that the public has a right to know about this stuff."

Pacific Seafood pays EPA $74,500 to settle California wastewater case

He added: "I would point you to the website for anything further, but that's really all I can say right now."

Pacific Seafood, which operates about a dozen facilities across the US, said it's been upfront about wastewater regulations that "have been challenging for the seafood industry" as a whole.

"Violations such as these are widely covered by media and Pacific Seafood has been vocal about the challenges we and the rest of our industry face," Ogan wrote in a statement. 

"In situations where our environmental protocols and robust treatment equipment fail to achieve perfect environmental compliance, we immediately investigate, learn from each failure, and apply corrective actions to mitigate future issues," the statement concluded.

title: Chinese region’s tilapia production costs to rise on tightened rules
content:
Additional reporting by Louis Harkell.

China's tilapia farming industry in Hainan province will face stricter environmental protection protocols from this year onward, which looks set to increase costs for processing plants.

The Hainan local government has issued a notice to farmers, requiring all aquaculture operations to comply with "Discharge Standard DB 46," a local standard specifically targeting aquaculture's impact on water standards.

Sampling inspections will be conducted at pond drainage points, and penalties ranging from CNY 100,000 to CNY 1 million ($13,647 to $136,470) will be imposed for violations. In severe cases, operations may be ordered to cease by the government.

According to Chinese customs, Hainan exported 14,836 metric tons of frozen tilapia fillets in the first 11 months of 2024, almost double the volumes from the other major tilapia farming hub, Guangdong province (7,804t.) Some 3,219t was shipped by other Chinese provinces (see below).

The inspection parameters include total suspended solids (≤ 90 milligrams per liter), chemical oxygen demand (≤ 20 mg/L), total nitrogen (≤ 5.0 mg/L), and total phosphorus (≤ 0.8 mg/L).

The government stated that the new regulations comply with China's Environmental Protection Law, Water Pollution Prevention and Control Law, and Fisheries Law.

The government also requires farmers to sign agreements with processors, stipulating that processors may only purchase tilapia raw materials meeting environmental standards for export. Compliant raw materials are expected to cost CNY 0.2/kg more than previously.

Hainan province's regulations came into effect on Jan. 1. Guangdong implemented mandatory environmental policies two years ago, increasing farmers' costs for managing discharge.

"In the short term, the new regulations will impact prices due to the rise in costs," an executive of a Hainan-based factory told Undercurrent News. "If viewed from a long-term perspective, this is also a good thing, as it allows the industry to develop in a more regulated manner," the executive said.

As of the first week of 2025, the price of 500-800g tilapia delivered to factories in Hainan was CNY 9.60/kg, while the price for 300-500g tilapia was CNY 7.60/kg.

Upgrade to Pro to view

The prices in Hainan have remained unchanged compared to late December 2024.

In Guangdong, during the first week of 2025, the price of 500-800g tilapia increased to CNY 9.60/kg, up from CNY 9.40/kg in late December 2024. The price for 300-500g tilapia rose to CNY 7.60/kg, up from CNY 7.20/kg in late December.

Another source in Hainan said that some farmers have already been fined for violations.

"As far as I know, some people have already been fined, and now everyone is being very cautious," Liu Zhili, general manager of Hainan Gengift Aqua-Technology -- China's second-largest tilapia fry supplier -- told Undercurrent.

"Farmers must manage discharge according to government requirements. Even if discharge is necessary, they must apply to the government. In general, discharge will not occur unless in special circumstances," Liu said.

"The initial impact is big, but over time, everyone will gradually adapt," he said.

title: Canadian fisherman penalized for catching undersized lobsters
content:
A fisherman from the Canadian province of New Brunswick has been fined CAD 10,000 ($6,950) for catching undersized lobsters, reports the Telegraph Journal. 

The charges were laid against Lance Francis in September 2024 after fisheries inspectors boarded his boat at the Richibucto wharf on Sept. 13 to inspect his catch. Among the 515 pounds of lobster, inspectors found 217 crustaceans with a carapace shorter than the 79-millimeter minimum.

All of those smaller lobsters were tossed back into the water except for a couple that were kept as evidence, according to the article.

Prosecutor Guylaine Basque told the court she couldn't find another case from the Moncton area involving such a high number of undersized lobsters. She asked provincial judge Ronald LeBlanc to impose a CAD 10,000 fine and also issue an order for probation and community service. LeBlanc agreed with the fine amount but said he didn't see the need for probation and community service.

title: Trident completes sale of Kodiak operations to Pacific Seafood
content:
US giant Trident Seafoods announced Wednesday (Dec. 18) that it has completed  the sale of its Kodiak, Alaska, processing operations to Pacific Seafood Group.

As Undercurrent News has reported, Clackamas, Oregon-based Pacific Seafood is already a major player in the Northwest US seafood sector with existing operations in Kodiak and ties to harvesters in the region.

Trident Seafoods launches new retail, club store packaging

The deal, first announced in October, includes three processing plants -- Star of Kodiak, Alkod and Kodiak Near Island -- as well as the Plaza bunkhouse apartments for worker housing. 

Trident's Kodiak employees are to be kept on by Pacific Seafood, ensuring continuity and stability for the team and the local community, the two companies said in a joint statement.

Ashton Meier, Pacific Seafood's vice president of processing, will be in charge of the combined operations, the two privately-held companies said.

"Kodiak is home to some of the most abundant and sustainable fisheries in the world, and we are honored to partner with our new, very talented team members, the fleet and the community to unlock new opportunities for this region," Meier said in a statement. "With Pacific Seafood's vertical integration, global market access, and value-added capabilities, we are ready to deliver unmatched value and stability for Kodiak's hardworking fishermen and our customers worldwide."

Pacific Seafood began as an independent local retailer in Portland, Oregon, in 1941. It remains a family-owned and operated company with over 40 facilities across the U.S. and Canada, employing more than 3,000 team members and distributing products worldwide, the company said.

Pacific Seafood has been in the news recently over a lawsuit accusing the company of underpaying harvesters in the Gulf of Mexico shrimp fishery, as reported by Undercurrent. It company has denied any wrongdoing. It was also fined $220,000 earlier this year for repeated wastewater discharge violations at its plant in Washington state.

Trident restructuring in Alaska 

Seattle, Washington-based Trident sold its Alaska plants in Ketchikan and False Pass  to Seattle-based Silver Bay Seafoods, as Undercurrent also reported. Its Petersburg, Alaska, facility was sold to regional processor E.C. Phillips & Son.

Trident's presence in the Aleutian Islands remains. However, the company has also discussed plans to wind down operations in Akutan by building a new processor in Dutch Harbor, but those plans are currently on hold, as Undercurrent previously reported.

title: Editor’s choice: AquaBounty shuts down; Espersen fleshes out plan to mitigate cod supply ‘crisis’
content:
EMEA editor Neil Ramsden brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week.  

The most-read story from last week was the sinking of the Canadian fishing vessel Knot Too Shore, 36 nautical miles west of Seal Island in the province of Nova Scotia. The four crew were rescued safely.

Meanwhile, a lobster fisherman -- also in Nova Scotia -- was handed fines totaling nearly CAD 25,000 ($17,645) for multiple violations under Canada's Fisheries Act.

In more commercial news, AquaBounty Technologies -- the US company that developed the world's first genetically engineered salmon -- has announced it's shutting down its remaining farm operations and saying goodbye to its CEO. "AquaBounty will immediately begin to wind down its Bay Fortune operation, its only remaining operating farm, including the culling of all remaining fish and a reduction of substantially all personnel over the course of the next several weeks," said David Frank, the chief financial officer and interim CEO, in a statement.

And fisheries managers in the US state of Alaska have announced a 341,500 pound (155 metric ton) harvest for golden king crab in Southeast waters in 2025 -- a 25% increase over the previous season.

In Europe, the rocketing prices for Atlantic cod, which look set to continue into 2025 with a further 25% reduction in supply from the Barents Sea, mean Denmark's A. Espersen must change its strategy, its new CEO told Undercurrent News. Espersen expects Atlantic cod prices to continue rising in 2025. The quota will come down 25% to 340,000t after a 20% cut in 2024, presenting a "crisis" for the processing sector. Meanwhile, prices for frozen, headed and gutted Norwegian and Russian for delivery to China have hit record levels. 

And last but not least, last week, Undercurrent unveiled its new US seafood wholesale pricing platform, which launches with benchmark assessments for farmed shrimp and Argentine reds, frozen lobster tails and meat and scallops, as well as wild and farmed whitefish.

title: Canadian minister warns marine sanctuary threatens Newfoundland fishermen
content:
Canadian lawmaker Elvis Loveless, a minister in Newfoundland and Labrador (NL), says the provincial government is taking steps to address mounting concerns from fishermen and aquaculture advocates regarding the proposed South Coast Fjords marine sanctuary.

Loveless, who represents Fortune Bay-Cape La Hune in the Newfoundland and Labrador House of Assembly, said in a Facebook post on Tuesday (Dec. 3) that premier Andrew Furey and members of the feasibility study's steering committee met on Dec. 2 to discuss redrawing the proposed marine sanctuary boundaries.

The feasibility study, or National Marine Conservation Area (NMCA), is governed by a memorandum of understanding (MOU) between the province of NL, Qalipu First Nation, Miawpukek First Nation, and the Town of Burgeo. It aims to assess the feasibility of establishing a protected area in the South Coast Fjords region.

Loveless, who was in the meeting, emphasized the importance of safeguarding the livelihoods of coastal communities.

"We want the area designated in current discussions redefined," he posted on the Newfoundland Fisherman's Forum on Facebook. "As such, meetings will reconvene in the new year with a new area considered for an NMCA. When the future of the fishing industry and livelihoods are threatened, I will not stand for it. This is too important to all of us."

Loveless is weighing in on the issue because the proposed marine sanctuary will affect his constituency, Fortune Bay-Cape La Hune, as many residents fish in the area under consideration and rely on its resources for their livelihoods.

Mayor Steve Crewe of Hermitage-Sandyville confirmed to Undercurrent News that the meeting occurred, stating he was informed on Tuesday morning. Crewe, a vocal critic of the proposed sanctuary, expressed cautious optimism about the development.

"The premier told the steering committee to go back to the drawing board, figure it out, and then come back in the new year. If not, he's withdrawing their signatures from the NMCA MOU feasibility study," Crewe said.

Aquaculture and fishing industries at stake

The proposed sanctuary overlaps with the Bays West area, identified as a prime zone for aquaculture expansion. The region is expected to significantly increase Newfoundland's annual Atlantic salmon production by 15,000 to 20,000 metric tons, creating jobs and boosting the economy, particularly on the island's southwest coast.

The area is also economically crucial for fishermen. Jason Sullivan, a Newfoundland fisherman and vice president of the Fish, Food and Allied Workers (FFAW) union, estimates the combined economic impact of the fishing and aquaculture industries in this region to be over $100 million. Sullivan emphasized the importance of this southern fishing area, mainly due to its rich lobster habitat.

"This is how we make our living, and this is how we keep our coastal communities alive," Sullivan said.

Speaking as a fisherman himself -- though not from the contested area -- Sullivan questioned the rationale behind the sanctuary, arguing that local fishermen have been stewards of the ocean for 500 years and that the area remains pristine. "We can't have any more marine protected areas around our fishing grounds," he said. "If they bring this in, it will be a snowball effect. What's next? Where do they stop?"

Crewe echoed Sullivan's concerns, highlighting the lobster fishery's recent success in the region.

"The past few years have been great for the lobster fishery, especially in Virgil, where it's booming. Economically, it would be disastrous if they couldn't do lobster fishing anymore," Crewe said. He warned that if the aquaculture industry also closes, the region would be "done."

Glenn Cooke, CEO of Cooke Inc, the largest seafood company in Canada, has been at the forefront of opposition to the sanctuary proposal. In a letter to Premier Furey last month, Cooke urged the provincial government to withdraw from the MOU.

Responding to the latest developments, Cooke told Undercurrent, "People across the south coast greatly appreciate that mayor Steve Crewe, minister Elvis Loveless and premier Andrew Furey are pushing Ottawa to redraw the NMCA boundaries so that fishing and aquaculture outport communities are not negatively impacted. It's vital to rural coastal communities and our nation's food security that governments defend livelihoods and families in the seafood sector." 

What's next?

Loveless announced that public consultations in St. Albans and Harbour Breton have been postponed. Discussions are set to reconvene in early 2025. The steering committee will revisit the proposed boundaries to address stakeholders' concerns while balancing economic and environmental priorities.

"This is a start," Sullivan said. "But if it doesn't lead to something reasonable, there will be pushback."

Crewe expressed similar sentiments. "This is good news, but no one is celebrating yet. We'll wait and see what they come back with in the new year"" he said.

title: Canadian aquaculture industry blames DFO for losing salmon markets to foreign competitors
content:
The Canadian aquaculture industry last week let its frustrations out regarding the performance of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) before an important parliamentary panel.

"The DFO, if they're an advocate of our sector, have done a really bad job," Tim Kennedy, president of the Canadian Aquaculture Industry Alliance (CAIA), told the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Oceans (FOPO) in an impassioned five-minute testimony about the agency on Wednesday (Nov. 20).

Canada has the world's largest coastline, at 202,080 kilometers, but it has failed to capitalize on its natural advantages due to DFO's shortcomings, he said.  

"Since 2018, our peak was 148,000 [metric] tons of Atlantic salmon, and last year we were down to just 89,000t," he said. "Meanwhile, the Faroe Islands, with just 1,000 kilometers of coastline, now produce the same amount of salmon as all of Canada."

In stark contrast, Norway, a leader in aquaculture, has set a goal of increasing the value of its salmon sector five-fold by 2050, Kennedy noted.

Tim Kennedy. Photo: Screenshot from Senate of Canada proceedings

"Since 2002, we haven't seen any significant increase in our aquaculture production," he told the committee. "This is a clear indication that DFO, as the regulator and advocate for our sector, has not done a good enough job in promoting the industry's potential."

Kennedy's testimony to the FOPO was part of a five-year review outlined in Canada's Fisheries Act. In a session that ran over an hour, Kennedy used his five-minute allotted time to advocate for the industry.

Kennedy's criticism stems from the perceived conflict of interest inherent in DFO's dual role as regulator and advocate for the aquaculture sector. He argued that this has hindered the industry's ability to thrive and expand.

To improve the situation, Kennedy repeated his proposed idea of moving responsibility for aquaculture from the DFO to Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada. A department focused solely on aquaculture would provide better support and development, he argued.

Kennedy also called for changes to the Fisheries Act to clearly define "aquaculture" as a food-producing industry. The only mention of aquaculture in federal law appears in the Bank Act, and it is defined inaccurately, he said. A proper definition, he argued, would clarify the role of aquaculture in legislation, helping to establish it as a legitimate food sector alongside traditional agriculture rather than being overlooked in federal legislation.

Yes to transition, no to ban

One central discussion point was the June 30, 2029 ban on open-net pen salmon farming in British Columbia.

As Undercurrent News reported, fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier announced in June that the ban aims to transition salmon aquaculture on Canada's west coast to more sustainable practices that better protect wildlife.

Kennedy remarked about the evolution of the salmon farming industry over the years, distinguishing between legitimate concerns from its early days and outdated criticisms that no longer reflect current practices. He acknowledged that the industry once needed significant improvements due to its infancy but emphasized that substantial progress has been made.

Many of the criticisms directed at the sector today are "recycled" complaints about issues that have already been addressed, he said.

"Change has happened," Kennedy said, pointing out that while public perceptions often lag, the sector has adapted to meet modern standards.

He also emphasized that the industry remains open to evolution but remains against an outright ban, stressing the need to balance environmental concerns with the protection of jobs and the communities that depend on the aquaculture sector.

"We are for transition," he said. 

Photo: Cermaq Group

Laurel Collins, a New Democratic Party member of Parliament for Victoria, British Columbia, raised concerns about job losses resulting from the ban on open net-pen salmon farming in her province.

Kennedy agreed that once the BC ban takes effect in June 2029, many areas will have few job opportunities. He stressed that there would be areas with almost no other job opportunities once the ban was in place.

"There are good, well-paid jobs in small and First Nations communities across Vancouver Island that could disappear," he said. While he supports transitioning to better practices, he reiterated opposition to an abrupt shutdown, which would harm workers and communities that rely on these jobs.

Frozen investment

Investment in the aquaculture sector also came under scrutiny. Robert Morrissey, a Liberal member of Parliament for Egmont, a federal electoral district in western Prince Edward Island, questioned why the industry had not made significant capital investments despite its ability to implement "dramatic changes," as noted by Kennedy.

Cermaq's floating, semi-closed containment system, shown here, represents the industry's last significant innovation—an investment made over four years ago. Photo: BC Salmon Farmers Association report

Mia Parker, secretary of the CAIA and an executive at Mowi Canada West, explained that uncertainty surrounding the transition has deterred investments.

"The transition process has chilled institutional investment in aquaculture in Canada, so we haven't received any funding in four years," she said.

Parker argued that this lack of investment has left the Canadian aquaculture industry "four years behind every other salmon-producing region in the world" in terms of adopting new technologies and innovations to mitigate environmental impacts.

She emphasized the industry's readiness to evolve if provided with a clear and supportive legislative framework.

Undercurrent has contacted the DFO for comment but it asked for more time to respond.

title: New Brunswick lobster processor joins growing crowd looking for buyers
content:
The "For Sale" sign has just gone up for LeBreton Fisheries, a major family-owned lobster company in the Canadian province of New Brunswick (NB), and reportedly for multiple other lobster-related holdings in Atlantic Canada as well.

LeBreton is on the Acadian peninsula in northeastern NB, adjacent to lobster fishing areas (LFAs) 21, 22, 23 and 25 in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. It maintains its headquarters in Grand-Anse.

If the name sounds familiar, that's because the company was fined more than CAD 365,000 ($254,994) and banned from hiring temporary foreign workers for two years in May after it was found, by Immigration Canada, to have maintained work and pay conditions that didn't match workers' contracts, as reported by CBC. The company also didn't make information about workers' rights available in two official languages or keep documents for the required amount of time, according to the article.

The ban expires on April 15, 2026.

The fine is the highest one handed a New Brunswick employer of temporary foreign workers, and it was the second fine for LeBreton, according to CBC. The company was penalized CAD 30,000 in 2023 for failing to provide a work environment free of harassment and reprisal.

The properties for sale, Undercurrent News has learned, include a 21,000-square-foot factory equipped to process raw and cooked lobster in Val Comeau, NB, about 249 kilometers (155 miles) north of the capital city of Fredericton. Another structure available in Val Comeau is a 21,600 square foot tank house with a capacity to hold 260,000 pounds of live lobster.

Two more buildings are for sale in Grande-Anse, NB, about 300 km north of  Fredericton. One is a 23,150-sq-ft processing plant that can process 60,000 lbs of lobster daily. The other is a 10,562-sq-ft production area that includes holding tanks with a capacity for 100,000 pounds of live lobster.

Credit: SevenMaps / Shutterstock

The business has been listed with TriNav, a major marine brokerage firm headquartered in St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador. The listing notes that the business owners are willing to sell the commercial assets as one package or separately.

Kevin LeBreton, one of the owners of the family business, could not be reached for comment. An asking price has not been published.

Riverside on market, too

LeBreton is not the only lobster company up for sale in Atlantic Canada.

Riverside Lobster, based in Meteghan, Nova Scotia, about 45 km west of Yarmouth, on the province's south shore, has been seeking a buyer since February, when the parent company, Champlain, announced it would be permanently closing the factory, as reported by Undercurrent.

That decision came just a few months after the company announced it would temporarily cease operations at the location over fear of low catches again during the fall-winter 2023-2024 lobster season in Southwest Nova Scotia, which includes the mammoth lobster fishing areas (LFAs) 33 and 34.

LFAs 33 and 34 landed a combined 21,405 metric tons of lobster in 2023, based on data shared with Undercurrent by the Lobster Council of Canada. It was 8% less than the 23,274t landed in 2022 and 30% less than the 30,637t landed in 2021.

TriNav is also handling that sale, confirmed Kerry Hann, the NL marine broker's manager of sales and corporate development.

Hann said a handful of lobster pounds are also for sale around the Maritimes. It's not unusual to see some of those smaller operations being bought and sold, he added.

"There's always people snapping up those smaller operations, and that's usually done quietly," Hann said.

Beyond lobster processing, Hann added, TriNav also has a lobster boat-building operation for sale in southwest Nova Scotia, as well as some lobster fishing enterprises.

"So it seems that everything for sale in the Maritimes right now seems to be lobster-related. But I don't want to speculate why that is," said Hann.

Contentious times

It's no secret that the lobster industry in Atlantic Canada has been contentious, and perhaps no more so than this year, with allegations and evidence of illegal lobster fishing dominating the news.

Earlier this year, the provincial government in Nova Scotia implemented new regulations to curb the illegal lobster trade, as reported by Undercurrent.

In October, officials from Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans raided a lobster pound in Shelburne County, in the province's southeast region, and seized CAD 100,000 worth of lobsters.

Earlier this month, the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance, a non-profit group that represents lobster fishing throughout the provinces of NS, NB and Prince Edward Island, filed a notice of action in the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia against Independent Fisheries Limited of Sable River, in Shelburne County. It alleges that Independent Fisheries bought lobsters caught illegally in St. Mary's Bay, on Nova Scotia's southwest coast, as reported by Undercurrent.

title: Italy’s Newlat Food completes Princes’ integration ahead of schedule
content:
Italian food corporation Newlat Food said it has successfully integrated Princes Group, one of Britain's biggest ambient food firms, within its group, solidifying its position in the food market with a restructured global operation.

Princes' acquisition, completed in Aug. 2024, has driven Newlat's revenues up by 49% in the first nine months of 2024, also boosting its net profit, according to the Italian group.

Mitsubishi completes £700m sale of Princes to Italy’s Newlat

Under the leadership of its president, Angelo Mastrolia, Newslat has implemented "an efficient organizational overhaul to fully capitalize on the Princes' acquisition," the company said.

"The integration process with Princes exceeded expectations and the timing of our plan," Mastrolia said as the group released its Q3 results.

The company has centralized its procurement around Mastrolia's leadership. "Starting from Oct. 1, the purchasing function has been centralized under Mastrolia, with the aim of optimizing processes and strengthening the strategic management," Newlat said.

Photo: Newlat Food.

The group has been reorganized with three business units: the UK and Ireland, Italy, and continental Europe and the rest of the world. Newlat will adapt its strategies according to the demands of each region.

"This subdivision will ensure effective and targeted management on all markets, allowing commercial strategies to be adapted to the specific needs of each country, improving the relationship with customers and increasing the ability to respond quickly to the needs and dynamics of each reference market," it said.

Headquartered in Liverpool, Princes has a presence across continental Europe, managed from the Netherlands. There are also dedicated sales and marketing offices in Poland, tuna processing facilities in Mauritius, tomato processing in Italy and edible oils production in Poland.

In Italy, Princes Italy, traditionally focused on the tomato sector, is set to merge with Newlat's broader portfolio of pasta, baked goods, and specialty products by Jan. 1, 2025. The Italian integration is expected to yield operational synergies, boosting flexibility and enabling Newlat to present a single point of contact for customers across multiple product categories, according to the group.

Newlat also owns Symington's, a Leeds-based branded meal and snack manufacturer in the UK, which it acquired in 2021.

In the UK, the integration of Symington's production and corporate operations into Princes Group, will be completed by March 31, 2025, aligning with the close of the UK's fiscal year, Newlat said.

According to the Italian group, this consolidation will create a unified structure aimed at maximizing efficiencies and more effectively meeting retailer requirements.

"The same integration will concern Symington's business -- which has already been done commercially merged under the direction of Princes, led by Simon Harrison --, with the aim of unifying the activities in the British market, maximizing operational synergies between the two companies. The completion of the integration is expected by March 31st, in line with the traditional closing of the UK financial year, to ensure a smooth transition and meet deadlines British retailers," Newlat said. 

Simon Harrison was appointed CEO of Princes Group in April 2024. The ex-Coca-Cola manager has been with Princes since 2021, first as chief commercial officer and later as deputy managing director. 

Simon Harrison, Princes Group's CEO. Photo: Princes.

"The Princes acquisition has generated remarkable value across all metrics, demonstrating the strong cash flow generation and growth momentum within Newlat. These strategic initiatives lay the groundwork for significant future growth," Mastrolia said.

He emphasized that the guidance for 2025 reflects Newlat's financial strength, allowing for debt cost optimization and enabling growth-oriented investments. He noted that the integration process with Princes has been more efficient than expected, benefiting from a streamlined procurement process and the recent reorganization into three macro-regions tailored to each market's specific needs.

Earlier this year, Harrison defined Newlat's acquisition as an "exciting prospect for Princes". "We are delighted that Newlat share our confidence in the Group's strategic growth plans, brand strategy, operational excellence and people culture".

While geopolitical instability in regions such as Israel, Palestine, and Ukraine continues to cast uncertainty over global markets,

Newlat's diversified portfolio, strengthened by the Princes acquisition, has proven resilient, the group said. The company's management has prepared for potential impacts but remains cautiously optimistic, citing the group's strong financial and operational standing as buffers against significant adverse effects.

Financial results

Newlat's consolidated revenue for the first nine months of 2024 reached €896m, up 49% year over year, according to the group. Princes' consolidation contributed significantly to the growth trajectory, the group said.

"The first nine months of 2024 represent an extraordinary milestone, with our combined revenue reaching a record €2.03 billion and net profits exceeding €170m," Mastrolia said.

"The results of the first nine months demonstrate the enormous value generated by the acquisition of Princes in every aspect: turnover grew by 49.2%, net profit by 840%, the net worth by 133%, and the net financial position proved to be decidedly better than any prediction. These data confirm that the acquisition of Princes has created, in just two months, value well beyond that every rosiest expectation for all shareholders, laying solid foundations for significant growth in the years to come," he further said.

Meanwhile, the details of Princes' director were changed to Angelo Mastrolia, the firm communicated to the UK company house.

title: Controversial consultancy company outs another US seafood festival for selling imported shrimp
content:
A second US shrimp festival is embroiled in controversy after a genetic testing company says it found imported shrimp being passed off as a product of the Gulf of Mexico, AL.com reports.

SEAD Consulting made headlines last month when it said it had uncovered widespread use of imported shrimp at the Louisiana Shrimp and Petroleum Festival, as Undercurrent News previously reported. SEAD followed up by testing shrimp from several vendors at the Annual National Shrimp Festival held in Gulf Shores, Alabama, earlier this month. 

SEAD Consulting founder Dave Wiliams said in a statement that the company's tests can identify shrimp species in two hours, faster than other genetic tests, thus ensuring "that fraudulent practices are caught in real-time." The company reported that it had tested five dishes at the Annual National Shrimp Festival, and that only one, served by Rouses grocery, featured authentic wild-caught Gulf of Mexico shrimp. 

The others were farm-raised shrimp from other countries, he said.

Major seafood restaurants issued letter by US Federal Trade Commission about ‘misleading’ customers

SEAD's announcement quoted Jeremy Zirlott, identified as a boat owner and processor from Bayou La Batre, Alabama, who said the results were "not surprising but incredibly disheartening."

The announcement also stated that the vendors broke a state law that, as of 2024, requires merchants to disclose the country of origin of seafood sold to patrons, including whether it's wild or farm-raised.

Festival organizers fired back, saying that they had a stipulation that imported seafood should not be sold.

"We have had our domestic provision in our vendor contracts for years," festival co-chair Ginny Barnas said in a statement, AL.com reports. "There are monetary penalties for violating the contract, and repeat violators can be removed from the Festival."

Activist genetic testing company advocates for US fleet

The controversial Texas-based genetic testing company caustically suggested the Annual National Shrimp Festival in Alabama should be called the "International Shrimp Festival."

Organizers criticized the testing company for going public but not reporting which vendors it claimed were selling imported products.

"If he refuses to release the alleged violators' names to us, there's very little we can do to ensure these vendors are penalized or asked not to come back to our Festival," Ryan Moberly, a spokesperson for the Coastal Alabama Business Chamber told the news outlet. 

SEAD says its goal is to defend US harvesters in the Gulf of Mexico. 

"As more festivals and restaurants are put under the microscope, those doing the right thing will be publicly acknowledged, while fraudsters risk being exposed and potentially fined," he said in the company's report.

title: Daily recap: Chilean salmon industry hits back at NYT; Larger US lobster gauge nixed
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Monday, Oct. 21:

Chilean salmon industry blasts critical NY Times report as ‘flawed,’ ‘unethical’

The Chilean Salmon Council (CSC), the group that represents eight of the Chilean salmon industry's 12 biggest players, has at last responded to a highly critical New York Times (NY Times) article published two months ago, calling the reporting "flawed" and "unethical."

US lobster panel votes to again delay higher gauge requirement 

The American Lobster Board of the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission (ASMFC) voted Monday (Oct. 21) to again delay the implementation of a new rule that would raise the minimum allowable catch size for North American lobsters in the US.

H&G haddock prices surge during Groundfish Forum; cod also on rise 

Prices for headed and gutted (H&G) haddock from Russia and Norway increased sharply, and cod was also increasing as the top executives in the trade met in Copenhagen, Denmark, last week for the 2024 Groundfish Forum.

Iceland’s Laxey likely to seek funds early in 2025 for phase two of land-based salmon plan 

Land-based salmon farming project Laxey is likely to seek the next part of its fund-raising early in 2025, chairman Larus Asgeirsson told Undercurrent News.

Iberconsa advances fleet renewal plans in southern Africa, hake catches disappoint 

Spanish firm Grupo Iberica de Congelados (Iberconsa) is moving ahead with its fleet renewal plans in Namibia and South Africa. 

Canadian First Nations receive blessing to continue in-season lobster fishing 

For the fourth year in a row, four aboriginal groups on Canada's east coast have permission from the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) to pursue a moderate livelihood fishery for lobsters during commercial seasons in lobster fishing areas (LFAs) 33, 34 and 35 off the coast of the province Nova Scotia.

Russia adopts new regulations to permit unilateral quotas 

The Russian authorities have approved a new regulation governing procedures around the unilateral approval of the total allowable catch (TAC) in areas previously defined by international treaties.

New approach to BC salmon farming transition raises hopes, concerns 

British Columbia's salmon farming industry is cautiously optimistic about the Canadian government's "whole of government approach" in the process to transition the sector.

title: Russia adopts new regulations to permit unilateral quotas
content:
The Russian authorities have approved a new regulationgoverning procedures around the unilateral approval of the total allowable catch (TAC) in areas previously defined by international treaties.

Russia's federal government adopted a decree dated Oct. 9 that sets out rules to approve TAC levels in the areas of international treaties, including within the country's exclusive economic zone.

The new regulation applies in the absence of relevant decisions by multilateral bodies usually enforced by international treaties signed by Russia, the fishery agency Rosrybolovstvo said in a statement. While the federal government of Russia would approve the TAC levels in these areas, Rosrybolovstvo would approve lists of marine species available for fishing in them, it said.

Rosrybolovstvo must approve the lists for the upcoming calendar year by Dec. 15, the statement said.

The new regulations followed recent legislative amendments applicable to TACs.

Previously, on May 29, the authorities officially amended Russia's laws on fisheries, adding a new provision -- Article 67 -- that allows the federal government to approve TACs in international waters for Russian fishery businesses. It's a provision that takes effect from Dec. 1, 2024.

Earlier this month the Russian government approved the new TAC levels for next year, envisaging increases year-on-year for pollock and crab species, as well as decreasing cod TACs. Russia's Agriculture Ministry adopted Order No. 567, dated Oct. 2, 2024, to approve the country's total TACs for 2025 at 3.61 million metric tons or a 4.9% increase year-on-year.

Within that figure, the pollock 2025 TAC is set at 2.46m metric tons, up 7.2% on the previous year. The new regulation has set the 2025 TAC for all species of crab at 109,800t, up 3.4%, including 50,000t for opilio crab, up 5% y-o-y. Lastly, next year's Pacific cod TAC is set at 140,600t, down by 3.2% on this year's levels.

title: Ecuador, Central America, Seychelles aim to draw investment from Spanish fishing firms
content:
MADRID, Spain -- Representatives from Ecuador, Seychelles and Central American nations are urging Spanish fishing firms to increase investment in their fishing sectors.

This call to action came on Oct. 10 as representatives gathered in Madrid during Spain's IV National Tuna Congress, organized by OPAGAC, the Spanish frozen tuna shipowners association. The congress underscored the vital role of Spanish fishing investors in bolstering these regions' economies and industries. 

"For us in Ecuador, we truly feel that the Spanish industry and fleet are part of us. The investment from Spanish companies generates jobs and resources in our country, strengthening the trade relationship between Spain and Ecuador," said Maria Rafaela Hurtado, Ecuador's vice minister of aquaculture and fisheries.

According to her, Ecuador exported some 162,000 metric tons of fish and seafood products to the EU in 2023, translating into approximately $900 million in revenue. She also highlighted that 19% of these exports were directed specifically to Spain, illustrating the increasing importance of the Spanish market for Ecuadorian seafood. 

"These figures are not just numbers; they reflect our growing partnership and the mutual benefits derived from this collaboration," she pointed out.

Ecuador's Vice Minister of Aquaculture and Fisheries, María Rafaela Hurtado. Photo credit: National Tuna Congress

Hurtado also stressed the importance of collaborative efforts to combat illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing, which remains a significant threat to marine ecosystems worldwide.

"Our countries, with large fishing fleets, have a unique opportunity to set a standard for responsible fishing practices," she said. "If we work together -- governments, industry, and stakeholders -- we can ensure the health of our oceans and the viability of our fishing industries for years to come."

The Ecuadorian government actively promotes investment by offering tax incentives and fiscal benefits to foreign companies that establish operations in the country, particularly those that create jobs and contribute to the local economy. "This approach is central to our strategy for attracting foreign investment and promoting economic growth," she concluded.

Bernal Chavarria, who coordinates fisheries management and policy for the Central American Fisheries and Aquaculture Sector Organization, OSPESCA, also echoed the sentiment of collaboration.

"Effective collaboration is essential for navigating the complexities of fisheries management within Central America, which includes countries such as the Dominican Republic, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Belize," he said.

"However, the synergies we seek go beyond direct investments; they impact the regulation of resources and sustainability efforts within regional fishing organizations. We now have a more defined framework for responsibility, prioritizing sustainability and the combined economic, social, and environmental benefits," he added.

Chavarria also highlighted the successful cooperation established through the EU's association agreements with Central America, which have led to significant advancements in the region's fishing industry. "These agreements have enabled us to engage collaboratively in various fisheries management organizations," he stated.

Finally, Jean-François Ferrari, Seychelles' minister of fisheries and blue economy, reflected on the longstanding relationship between Spain and his country, particularly emphasizing the 42-year fishing agreement with the EU. He also called for enhanced scientific support to help combat illegal fishing activities.

In #CongresoDelAtun2024 Mr Jean François Ferrari, minister of Fisheries and the Blue Economy in #Seychelles highlights European fishing companies investments : "The local community see the Spanish and European fleets as partners, not as companies that come to fish and go."
Photo: Europêche Tuna Group/ X.com

"You [the EU] set the rules. Help us continue fishing sustainably and fight against illegal practices," Ferrari urged, highlighting the ongoing challenges posed by security issues in the Indian Ocean and the need for sustainable management of resources.

"We have opened our doors not only to investments in the fishing sector but also in agriculture," he also stated. "However, we're currently seeing limited appetite for investment, primarily due to the unreliability of supply chains and the impacts of El Nino."

However, Ferrari also expressed hope that momentum could shift positively, particularly with support from the EU. "There needs to be a broader European commitment to recognize fishing nations like the Seychelles as essential partners, not as competitors."

He pointed out that current perceptions in Brussels often portray these countries as threats to the EU fishing industry due to their lower production costs.

"Fishing is a global industry, and we all benefit when it is managed sustainably," he continued, stressing the importance of the fishing community advocating for its interests amidst rising environmental concerns. "I encourage everyone in the fishing industry to make their voices heard, or risk being overshadowed by other, more politically influential groups."

Looking ahead, Ferrari expressed optimism about the future of foreign investment if the fishing sector effectively communicates its achievements and sustainability efforts. "If we market our industry well and tell our positive stories, there will be opportunities for investment in our companies," he concluded.

title: Trident inks deal to sell Kodiak plant to Pacific Seafood
content:
Trident Seafoods has reached an agreement to sell its Kodiak, Alaska, fish processing plant to another Northwest US giant, the Pacific Seafood Group, the two companies announced Monday (Oct. 14).

The two privately-held companies "are currently completing the due diligence process" and expect to close the deal next month, they said in a joint statement.

Seattle, Washington-based Trident last year announced a restructuring plan that included offloading four processing plants as the sector reckoned with major challenges from climate change and market forces, as reported by Undercurrent News. 

Trident close to deals on three Alaska plants; Kodiak will take longer

Monday's announcement reiterated that Trident was not winding down operations by selling a major year-round facility that processes pollock, salmon, Pacific cod, halibut, flatfish, rockfish, crab and herring. 

"Our top priority is to reassure employees and the fleet that this is a handoff, not a shutdown," Trident CEO Joe Bundrant said in the release. "We are committed to a smooth transition with Pacific Seafood, so they are well prepared to operate for the 2025 A season."

Clackamas, Oregon-based Pacific Seafood is already a major player in the Northwest US seafood sector with existing operations in Kodiak and ties to harvesters in the region. CEO Frank Dulcich said he planned to retain the Kodiak plant's existing workers.

"We are excited about this opportunity to expand our Kodiak operations and leverage our diverse national and international distribution channels to provide even more opportunities for Kodiak team members and the fleet," he said in the joint statement. 

The combined operations will be led by Pacific Seafood's vice president of processing, Ashton Meier, who, according to the release, has more than 20 years of experience in global seafood markets.

According to a recent US government report, Alaska's seafood sector has been beset by challenges, with an estimated loss of $1.8 billion. Trident announced last year that it was actively seeking buyers for four of its Alaska plants as part of a restructuring effort.

Trident restructures Alaska operations

Undercurrent reported earlier this year that Trident sold its Ketchikan and False Pass plants to Seattle-based Silver Bay Seafoods. Its Petersburg facility was sold to regional processor E.C. Phillips & Son.

Trident's presence in the Aleutian Islands remains. However, the company has also discussed plans to wind down operations in Akutan by building a new processor in Dutch Harbor. But those plans are on hold as they hit stumbling blocks in securing affordable energy from the island's geothermal sources, as Undercurrent previously reported.

Pacific Seafood has been in the news recently for other reasons, including a lawsuit accusing the company of underpaying harvesters in the Gulf of Mexico shrimp fishery. The company has denied any wrongdoing. It was also fined $220,000 earlier this year for repeated wastewater discharge violations at its plant in Washington state.

The company declined further content in relation to its acquisition of the Trident facility in Kodiak.

title: Russia now plans to pass 160,000t pollock surimi output in 2029, not year before
content:
Russia is still on track to pass 160,000 metric tons in pollock surimi production, but a year later than initially forecast, the sales director of the sector's largest player told Undercurrent News.

Some delays to the construction of Russian Fishery Company (RFC)'s new-build vessels mean the company has adjusted its country-wide forecast from 163,000t in 2028 to the year after. Earlier this year, Savely Karpukhin, the CEO of RFC, made the 163,000t-by-2028 forecast.

"There is a slight delay in vessels going into operations," Oleg Moskvin, sales director for RFC, told Undercurrent during the 2024 Surimi School Europe, held Oct. 8 in Barcelona, Spain. "Thus, next year, we expect around 80,000t across all Russian vessels and factories. By 2029, we will come to 163,000t, not 2028."

A forecast for Russia's surimi production from Oleg Moskvin, sales director of Russian Fishery Company, during the 2024 Surimi School Europe event, held on Oct. 8 in Barcelona, Spain. Credit: Tom Seaman

RFC is anticipating countrywide production growth of 14% to 80,000t in 2025, before two years of "spikes" in growth as new vessels start operating, said Moskvin. The forecast earlier in the year was for an output of 124,000t in 2025 and 80,000t in 2024.

Moskvin told the Surimi School audience that two new RFC "super-trawlers" arriving at the end of 2025 with surimi capacity should increase country-wide production to 100,000t in 2026 and then 120,000t in 2027.

Global 2024 surimi output set for 4% drop to 905,000t; US pollock, tropical in decline amid rise of Russia

He said that only around 20,000t of that 120,000t can go to the Russian market, "so the rest will be exported."

As new Russian vessels and plants cannot get EU licenses due to the invasion of Ukraine, the target markets are in Asia. RFC is the largest producer, but Gidostroy also has vessels and plants with large surimi capacity, with RK Lenina a smaller producer.  

In the US, producers are increasing fillet production and reducing surimi as much as possible due to the low prices, which have just increased slightly for Japan. Russia is doing the opposite due to the EU market being closed to the new vessels; around 90,000t of fillets will be produced in 2024, down 22% year-on-year.

A forecast for Russia's pollock production from Oleg Moskvin, sales director of Russian Fishery Company, during the 2024 Surimi School Europe event, held on Oct. 8 in Barcelona, Spain. Credit: Tom Seaman

A stable Russian fillet production of 90,000t is forecast for 2025; the same for headed-and-gutted and whole-round output at 751,000t and 150,000t, respectively.

TAC hike doesn't mean higher catch

In addition, reports of slow catching in the west Bering Sea are part of the cause of the lower-than-expected surimi output this year and could also impact 2025, even though the government will hike the total allowable catch (TAC) 7% to 2.46 million metric tons.

"The TAC is defined by the government structures. Though the TAC is important, in reality, the catch may be different. There are plenty of concerns among fishery companies that the situation in the Bering Sea may repeat next year [in 2025]. This will result in catch utilization at about 83-84%. Eventually, there will be less pollock supplied to the market," Moskvin told Undercurrent.

Russia's pollock catch and total allowable catch, as presented by Oleg Moskvin, sales director of Russian Fishery Company, during the 2024 Surimi School Europe event, held on Oct. 8 in Barcelona, Spain. Credit: Tom Seaman

In 2024, the forecast is that Russia will catch 2.04m metric tons of a 2.29m TAC due to the issues in the west Bering Sea fishery.

"This year, we are facing difficulties in the Bering Sea. We anticipate the same catch as 2024 in 2025," said Moskvin.

"The scientific data shows there is [a] significant [quantity of] fish in the sea. So, the Russian government wants to increase the TAC. But we have had difficulties catching the fish," said Moskvin, adding that this applies to all companies.
