title: US seafood firm rebrands to take bigger bite of New York’s gourmet market
content:
The Lobster Place, a New York-based seafood processor and distributor, is rebranding to LP Seafood & Specialty, to reflect its growing focus on specialty food distribution alongside its core seafood business.

The 50-year-old company, led by second-generation owner and CEO Ian MacGregor, has built a competitive advantage in the New York City market by optimizing its logistics and infrastructure to rapidly fulfill late-night seafood orders for restaurant clients. This capability is now being leveraged to expand the company's specialty food offerings.

The Lobster Place Warehouse. Photo: LP Seafoods & Specialty

The expansion into specialty foods is largely a result of LP Seafood & Specialty's 2021 acquisition of Gourmet Cargo, a small boutique specialty food distributor.

"Gourmet Cargo was sort of a startup distribution arm of a larger import-export business called Fine Sailor. When the pandemic hit, they were really struggling as a new company," MacGregor told Undercurrent News.

"I knew the principal, and when the whole industry was reeling here in New York City, I thought this might be a good opportunity to put the businesses together."

"When we folded the Gourmet Cargo business into our operations three years ago, it became clear that we could apply our expertise in just-in-time delivery to a wider range of premium specialty products," said MacGregor.

"In the New York City foodservice market, customers typically place orders for seafood late in the evening, around 9 or 10 pm, and want delivery between 6 and 9 am the next morning," said MacGregor. "Our entire logistics and infrastructure are built around satisfying this very short order window."

He added that the company's 30,000-square-foot processing and distribution facility efficiently handles tasks like hand-cutting fish fillets to order, enabling it to provide customers with this rapid, precise fulfillment service.

Photo: LP Seafood & Specialty

"We're proud to be the only SQF-certified (Safe Quality Food Certification) seafood distributor in the New York City market," MacGregor said. This third-party food safety certification is recognized worldwide and is typically required by major customers like cruise lines and supermarket chains.

Since the merger, LP Seafood & Specialty has doubled the size of its specialty foods segment, growing it from around $1.5 million to $3m in sales.

LP's gourmet foods segment now represents 10% of the company's overall business -- double its previous size before the merger with Gourmet Cargo.

"Our business is still 90% seafood, and we've been able to leverage that expertise to grow our specialty foods offerings," MacGregor explained. "But seafood will always be the foundation of what we do."

MacGregor said the company's former name, The Lobster Place, had become "both a blessing and a curse over the years," adding to the reasons for the name change.

CEO Ian MacGregor joins team at LP Seafood and Specialty

While it carried substantial brand equity and recognition in the local market, it also perpetuated the misconception that the business only sold lobster.

"We've dealt with that misnomer for years," he said. "The time was right for us to shift our identity and stake out mindshare as a full-line seafood and specialty foods distributor."

Challenges, opportunities

MacGregor said one of the key challenges facing LP Seafood & Specialty is "occupying mindshare" in the marketplace. Large broadline distributors like Chef's Warehouse and Baldor Specialty Foods have such a wide range of products that chefs and buyers often think of them first when sourcing specialty items.

"We have to be out in the marketplace every day, reminding people what we have, showing people what we have, because the chefs aren't necessarily in a place where they're thinking, 'Hey, I really want some cool olive oil. I should get in touch with LP Seafood & Specialty'," he said.

To address this challenge, the company plans to leverage its sales team and marketing efforts to actively promote its specialty food offerings and build awareness among its customer base.

However, the last 18 months have presented significant challenges for the restaurant industry, particularly in New York City. MacGregor cited data showing that the city has faced more acute customer traffic declines than other major markets. As a result, many operators have become more price-sensitive and willing to switch suppliers over even slight cost differences, he said.

Photo: LP Seafood & Specialty

"Where we had enjoyed the best gross margins in 2022, we've now seen significant price competition and margin compression come back with a vengeance," MacGregor noted. "Chefs and buyers are shopping harder than ever to find the best deals."

Despite these headwinds, LP sees growth opportunities. The company now serves accounts as far as 175-200 miles from its Manhattan base, capitalizing on the dispersion of people and businesses in the broader New York metropolitan area.

MacGregor said the intention is to continue increasing market share in the city while gradually expanding the delivery radius.

Mowing forward

While the company has rebranded to LP Seafood & Specialty to better reflect its expanded product offerings, MacGregor said that preserving the core values that have defined The Lobster Place remains a priority for him.

"The relationships and the core values that have guided this business for decades will stay intact," assured MacGregor, who took over from his father as CEO in 2002. 

"People will still know us as Lobster Place, but they'll also come to understand that we're a full-line seafood and specialty foods distributor -- one that can deliver the same high level of service and expertise that we've built our reputation on."

title: Shetland aquaculture sees major gains after SSF takeover
content:
Three years after Scottish Sea Farms (SSF) acquired Grieg Seafood’s Shetland salmon farming operations, the region is seeing significant improvements in performance and productivity, according to the firm.

SSF completed the acquisition of Grieg Seafood's Shetland salmon farming operations in a deal worth £164 million ($227m) in December 2021. SSF regional production manager Richard Darbyshire credits major investments in infrastructure, technology, and personnel for driving a “game-changing” turnaround. 

FREE READ Global salmon industry is dodging downturn because of RAS smolt investments

"Farm managers are accountable not only for biological performance but minimizing production costs too, which was new to those joining from Grieg," Darbyshire said. "The changes have led to lower production costs, better fish survival rates, better growth, and improved employee satisfaction."

The company has upgraded marine sites and onshore facilities, adopted innovative netting and water monitoring systems, overhauled biosecurity measures, and implemented a new management structure focused on accountability and communication, he said. A new management structure, which added two area managers and implemented weekly meetings with farm managers, has also improved focus and communication. 

Among the best-performing farms was Coledeep in the Gonfirth area, with an average live weight increasing from 4.99 kilograms per fish to 5.5kg between 2022 and 2024. 

Coledeep's farm manager, Laurie Manson, praised the enhanced connection between management, farm teams, and health specialists for driving the improvements.

"Investment in infrastructure has been a critical part of the transformation. Farms have been expanded, new pens and moorings installed, and a bespoke double netting system introduced to reduce seal-related fish deaths," said Manson. By mid-2025, this system will be rolled out across the region. 

FREE READ Scottish Sea Farms successfully recovers sunken landing craft

Shore facilities have also seen upgrades, with new buildings and equipment making operations more efficient and comfortable for staff.

Keith Fraser, Shetland engineering manager, noted that upgrades to the fleet and shore bases have reduced third-party costs and improved productivity. Meanwhile, a new base on Trondra has provided modern amenities for the team, enhancing working conditions.

Several innovations from Grieg Seafood have been retained and refined, such as the water analysis laboratory in Lerwick, which provides daily monitoring of water conditions. This, combined with a more decentralized feeding system, has given farm managers greater control over their operations.

The integration has also facilitated a "knowledge exchange," with SSF adopting Grieg's freshwater treatments for AGD and sea lice, while adding advancements such as reverse osmosis systems to improve efficiency.

"There's always room for improvement. But we've come a long way, and the two teams are working as one to deliver some of the region's – and company's – best results yet," said Darbyshire.

title: Canadian steelhead farm fined CAD 350k for operating outside license
content:
West Coast Fishculture Ltd., a steelhead trout grower in Lois Lake, British Columbia, has been hit with a CAD 350,000 ($258,103) fine after pleading guilty to operating without a license under Canada's Fisheries Act, the news service chek News reports.

The Powell River, BC-based company, which was bought by Agrimarine in 2013, initially reared its steelhead in net-cages near the center of the lake but in recent years switched to a system of semi-closed, solid-walled, floating rearing tanks in a slightly different location. The switch was part of the company's move to enhance production. But it also moved the fish outside of its license.

Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) has been documenting the company's illegal operations since June 2021 when officers discovered that West Coast Fishculture was operating outside of its tenure, according to the news service. A second inspection in September 2022 found that the company had continued to stock fish in illegal pens.

In 2023, when the company was not supposed to have any fish in the lake, WatershedWatch Salmon Society submitted footage to the DFO showing fish in the semi-closed containment fish farm, as well as photos of the farm's product for sale in a nearby store with a recent packaging date. 

West Coast Fishculture is also required to remove any remaining infrastructure from Lois Lake by Aug. 31, 2025.

Federal prosecutor Molly Greene celebrated the win on Thursday, telling the Powell River Provincial Court, "what's really important here is the need for a deterrent effect on others in the industry, and it has to be more than the mere cost of doing business."

title: Mowi dodges heavy fines for sea lice numbers
content:
The Norwegian Food Safety Authority notified Mowi of a fine of NOK 465,526 ($43,847) per day if it did not reduce sea lice levels at its Skipningsdalen facility in Flekkefjord municipality by Sept. 9, reports E24.

The warning came after the lice level was reported at 0.93 adult female lice on average per fish -- almost twice as much as the maximum limit of 0.5 lice. Mowi's communications director, Ola Helge Hjetland, said the firm was back under the limit again within the deadline.

"Unfortunately, we had a surprising outbreak of lice, but the employees handled the situation very well and got the level below the limit quickly. There are now very low lice levels at the facility," he said.

A week earlier, SalMar was threatened with fines of NOK 570,867 per day if the lice levels at Hosenoyan in Trondelag did not fall back to accepted levels by Sept. 3. It was experiencing levels of 1.6 adult female lice per fish, putting it down to warmer sea temperatures.

"In the last month, more exceedances of the lice limit have been reported than in previous years, and we see a number of facilities with a lot of lice. It may be related to higher sea temperatures," said Janne Kandal, case manager with the Norwegian Food Safety Authority.

title: Spain’s WOFCO ups turnover 16% even before Conarpesa, Fandicosta deals
content:
Spanish seafood firm Worldwide Fishing Company, also known as WOFCO, saw increased turnover and profit margin in 2023, even before it consolidates its deal for nearly 50% of Argentine shrimp supplier Continental Armadores de Pesca (Conarpesa).

According to its financial report, WOFCO's revenue for the year 2023 rose by 16% to €382.7 million ($427m), as shown in the table below.

This growth reflects WOFCO's successful efforts to enhance its market presence and product offerings, according to the firm, which was founded in 2016 and has grown quickly to become one of Spain's largest seafood processors and distributors.

WOFCO's increased income was driven by a hike in exports and a rise in sales within the EU, which domestic sales were down: 

Source: WOFCO's 2023 results.

The company's net profit after taxes also showed a notable improvement, rising 29% from €17.2m in 2022 to €22.2m in 2023.

WOFCO's financial health remains solid, with key indicators showing stability and strength, it said. The company's leverage ratios are well below the thresholds defined by the European Central Bank for highly leveraged companies, it pointed out.

A significant highlight for WOFCO in 2023 was the completion of the acquisition of 47.82% of the shares in Conarpesa. The payment to sellers was completed in January 2024, meaning the transaction will be consolidated in the 2024 fiscal year; this acquisition strengthens WOFCO's position as a global leader in wild shrimp processing, the firm said.

WOFCO also said that, in December 2023, Aldan Pacific, a company 40% owned by WOFCO, secured a loan from Globalbank, allowing it to recover €4.9m that had been advanced for the purchase and repair of the vessel Ria de Aldan (formerly Manapany); a 90-meter tuna fishing vessel destined for tuna fishing in the Pacific, specifically in Ecuador.

Moreover, WOFCO successfully concluded negotiations in the first half of 2024 for the acquisition of Fandicosta, which also included the assumption of control over Bonfrig FDC Ultracongelados and Astilleros Varaderos Domaio, companies that were wholly owned by Fandicosta.

WOFCO told Undercurrent News earlier this year that "2023 [was] an exceptional year for WOFCO," with the company achieving its best financial result to date.

The company's main product lines continue to be Argentine red shrimp, Patagonian squid, tuna, and swordfish, with a portfolio exceeding 40 products.

WOFCO finalizes deal to buy Spanish processor Fandicosta out of bankruptcy

Looking ahead to 2024, WOFCO said it expects continued growth driven by the integration of Conarpesa and the acquisition of Fandicosta. These strategic moves are expected to strengthen the company's market position and further expand its global presence.

"In terms of markets, we are maintaining a continued rise in North America as well as expanding into other areas through greater commercial penetration and an expansion of our product range," it said.

WOFCO previously told Undercurrent that it had no immediate plans to acquire additional shares in Conarpesa, where it currently holds a minority stake.

It also told Undercurrent it continues to expand its market reach and product range, particularly in North America and other emerging markets.

title: British Columbia man fined CAD 33k for harvests in protected sponge reef area
content:
A commercial halibut fisherman from British Columbia, Canada, has been ordered to pay CAD 33,596 ($24,498)  by a provincial court judge for illegally fishing in a protected marine area.

The CBC reports that Brent Belveal, who owns and operates the vessel Gypsy Soul, pleaded guilty to illegally fishing in the Hecate Strait Queen Charlotte Sound Glass Sponge Reef Marine Protected Area back in April of 2020. Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans said in a statement last week that Belveal was issued the fine in May of this year.

The CBC reports that the incident was captured through electronic monitoring data.

The area has been protected as a sanctuary since 2017, according to the news service, due to its location as the largest living example of glass sponge reefs that are estimated to be 9,000-years-old. Fines for illegal fishing there were increased for both commercial and recreational fishermen in 2021.

title: Foreign workers vital to Canada’s seafood processors, immigration consultant warns
content:
An immigration consultant who's helped businesses across Atlantic Canada find workers through the nation's temporary foreign worker (TFW) program says seafood processing companies would struggle to find workers without it, and that would have a trickle-down effect for other parts of the industry.

"Given the recent increases in crab quotas in Newfoundland [and Labrador], even hiring every Canadian applicant would still result in the need for night shifts and harvester trip limits," said Marilyn Clark, founder of Port to Port Inc., an immigration consulting company based in Halifax, Nova Scotia.

The reliance by seafood processors on the TFW program has garnered more scrutiny since Courtney Glode, a communications director for the Fish Food and Allied Workers (FFAW), the union that represents inshore harvesters and plant workers in NL, alleged misuse of the TFW by Ocean Choice International (OCI) and Royal Greenland in a letter to the editor published by the local news site SaltWire on July 19.

Glode said the two big processors should be investigated for abuses, charging that they haven't replied to applications for jobs from local workers, yet complain they can't get anyone local to work.

OCI has rejected the accusations and asked the FFAW for an apology, as reported by Undercurrent.

The FFAW's allegations are "unfounded and defamatory," Clark told Undercurrent this week. For one thing, companies must submit a labor market impact assessment (LMIA) to Service Canada to show it could not find a qualified Canadian to fill the job, she said.

"Because the program prioritizes Canadians, job ads must be posted at median or union wages for one to three months. And even with an approved LMIA, Canadians are given every opportunity to seek full-time employment," she said.

The cost of hiring a foreign worker is also the more expensive option, she added.

"None of the companies I work with would prefer hiring TFWs over Canadians. In truth, an LMIA is expensive, time-consuming, and a logistical nightmare," she said.

Marilyn Clark is the owner of Port to Port Inc. Photo from Port to Port Enterprises website

In addition to the CAD 1,000 ($727.50) fee to Service Canada for the labor market assessment, companies must also foot the bill for each worker's travel costs —including airfares and hotels — to and from Canada. That could add up to CAD 4,000, or more, for each foreign hire, Clark said.

A recent report from a Canadian Senate committee that spent two years investigating the issue noted that some companies had to buy or build accommodations in some rural areas where housing is limited. Others had to compete with the tourism industry, renting properties for their workers during peak tourism times when accommodation costs were higher.

"One company shared that to build regulated worker housing can cost CAD 25,000 to CAD 40,000 per suitable space," the committee reported.

"So it's not cheap to get foreign workers," said Clark.

TFW system failing employers and workers

The Senate committee investigating temporary and migrant labor in Canada heard from businesses, labor unions, academics and other interest groups from across the country.

"Employers in Atlantic Canada confirmed that the region is facing challenging demographics due to an aging population, declining birth rate and outmigration," the committee noted in its final report, issued in May.

The committee said it was told that the Atlantic region will need to retain 18,000–22,000 immigrants per year to meet projected labor market needs in 2030.

"Every single employer in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, from construction to seafood processing to dairy farming, told members of the committee that they could not continue operating without their international workforce," the report noted.

The committee's final report concluded that the current system is failing workers and the employers who depend on them.

The report, Act Now: Solutions for Temporay and Migrant Labor in Canada, noted that, under the current structure, foreign workers coming to Canada receive what is known as a closed, or tied, permit that requires them to work for specific employers.

That not only can make them more vulnerable to "abuse at the hands of bad actors," but it can also be a disadvantage for well-intentioned employers because they have no flexibility to move workers where needed, to staff higher-skilled occupations or to recognize good work with promotions, the report warned.

Canadian lobster processor banned from hiring foreign workers, fined CAD 365k

"Fifty years of piecemeal change has created a labyrinth of programs, streams and pathways to temporary and permanent work, with different levels of government and departments duplicating and complicating efforts. This is confusing for workers and employers and costly to Canadian taxpayers," the report stated.

The report made six recommendations to improve the system to protect workers while allowing Canadian businesses to thrive. The key recommendation was a "Migrant Work Commission" to spearhead the creation of a better system. Other recommendations included phasing out employer-specific work permits, exploring sector- or region-specific work permits, and reforming lax enforcement and compliance measures.

On Wednesday (Aug 7), Canada's minister of Employment and Workforce Development told food industry associations that the government is considering a policy change that would refuse TFW applications for jobs that pay below the median hourly wage in each province and territory, CBC reported.

The median wage varies by jurisdiction, ranging from CAD 24.00 per hour in Prince Edward Island to CAD 39.24 per hour in the Northwest Territories.

However, representatives of the food and beverage manufacturing industry, who attended the meeting with environment minister Randy Boissonnault, are worried about the impact of such a policy on their operations.

"If that applied to food and beverage manufacturing, it would be a crisis," Kristina Farrell, CEO of Food and Beverage Canada, is quoted as saying by the CBC.

Program is essential

Canada's temporary foreign worker program was created in 1973 as a last-resort measure to fill jobs for which qualified Canadians were unavailable.

The recent Senate report shows that, among the seafood processing industry in the Atlantic provinces, Nova Scotia hired the most TFWs in 2023, employing 2,645. The other four Atlantic provinces hired a combined 2,540 TFWs, with Prince Edward Island employing the most, 905. The Quebec seafood processing sector applied for just 20 TFW permits in 2023.

This graph from a recent Canadian Senate committee report shows how many temporary foreign workers Atlantic seafood processing companies hired in 2023.

In recent years, more and more Canadian companies are finding workers through the program.

Federal government statistics show that 239,646 applications were approved under the program in 2023, twice the 108,988 approved in 2018.

"It is now clear that this program is essential and entrenched; it is, therefore, time to recognize this reality and adapt Canada's migrant labor infrastructure accordingly," the Senate report states.

"The next five to 10 years will be critical, especially for the industry in Newfoundland and Labrador," said Clark, adding that many of the processing operations are in very small communities in remote areas.

"A lot of these facilities just can't find people to work," she said.

Labor shortages could impact others in the industry, she added, noting if processors don't have enough people to process crab, for instance, it could mean fish harvesters might have to reduce their fishing trips to allow time for plants to finish product.

It's an issue that impacts everyone in the industry, she said, suggesting labor groups like the FFAW, should be collaborating with the processing to find solutions, rather than slinging accusations.

"You need fishermen, you need workers, you need people that's going to market the resource. One side shouldn't be against the other all the time. The clear goal is to get the resource, harvest your renewable resources, get it to market, and get the money flowing into the province and into the pockets of people in these rural, coastal communities," Clark concluded.

title: Herring quota cuts threaten Canadian cannery future
content:
North America's leading supplier of canned herring says the Canadian government's decision to slash the fish's quota by nearly 25% in the Bay of Fundy could have a devastating impact on its operation.

"We've modified our business significantly over the past few years to cope with quota reductions, but this latest cut will mean the plant, as it operates today, could struggle moving forward," Matt Walsh, director of marine resources at the Connors Brothers factory in the province of New Brunswick, told Undercurrent News.

Connors Brothers, which has been in the canned herring business for 165 years, is owned by FCF Americas, one of the world's largest marine industry supply chain companies. Taiwan-based FCF acquired Connors Brothers and Clover Leaf Foods in Canada when it bought their parent company, US-based Bumblebee Foods, for $928 million in 2020 after Bumblebee filed for bankruptcy protection, as reported by Undercurrent.

Bankruptcy, scandal behind it, Tharp ‘enthusiastic’ for Bumble Bee’s future, culture

Herring is the only business for the Connors Brothers factory and cannery, located in Blacks Harbour, about 70 kilometers south of the provincial capital of Saint John. It is the staple for the Brunswick brand, a line of canned, smoked and flavored sardines made from herring. The product is sold in 40 countries, Walsh noted.

Recall that Canada's fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier announced on July 5 that the total allowable catch (TAC) for the Southwest Nova/Bay of Fundy herring fishery, from fishing zones 4W and 4X, would be 16,000 metric tons for each of the next four seasons (2024-2028) as reported by Undercurrent.

This particular herring stock was declared to be in the critical zone in 2018. Since then, the annual TAC has been cut by over 50% under the Canadian Department of Fishery and Ocean's (DFO's) precautionary framework for fisheries management. It was reduced from 42,500t in 2018 to 35,000t in 2019. In 2022, DFO cut the TAC to 23,450t and reduced it further to 21,000t in 2023.

The company, which maintains its own fleet of three purse seiners, usually fishes most of the quota, taking about 42% of the TAC each year, said Walsh.

The fishery opened on June 1. In previous years, Connors Brothers' seiners usually fished until mid-October, he said.

Connors Brothers herring seiners at Blacks Harbour, New Brunswick. Photo from Connors Brothers

"But with the TAC now, we're trying to slow walk it a little bit, but we'll probably be done by the end of August or mid-September this year," said Walsh.

"I'm looking out the window here now, and I've got our three purse seiners tied to the wharf," Walsh told Undercurrent on July 18. "They didn't go last night, and they're not going tonight. We'll have to pick and choose our days a little bit to try and drag it out."

'A relatively large biomass of fish'

Much of the data behind the DFO assessment of herring stocks comes from the industry, noted Walsh. The Herring Science Council (HSC), founded in 2003 to work collaboratively with DFO on herring research and management, funds research for the Bay of Fundy stock. 

Gary Melvin, who was a herring scientist with DFO for 25 years, is now a science advisor to the HSC.

While the overall stock spawning biomass of herring in Southwest Nova Scotia and the Bay of Fundy is lower than its historical high of around 500,000t in the mid-1980s, there's still a lot of spawners in the system, Melvin said.

The Bay of Fundy herring stock encompasses fishing zones 4W and 4X along the southern coast of Nova Scotia. Screenshot of Fisheries and oceans map

"If you take the analytical models and look at the biomass estimate, you're looking at somewhere between 180,000t to 220,000t. This is still a relatively large biomass of fish," said Melvin.

While no one is disputing that the biomass has decreased, what is being challenged is whether the stock should be classed as "critical," said Melvin.

"We (HSC) are saying 'no' because if you look at it using standard international approaches, it is not," said Melvin.

One of the problems is that DFO does not use the global standard to determine maximum sustainable yield (MSY), said Melvin. In fisheries science terms, MSY is defined as the maximum catch (in numbers or mass) that can be removed from a population over an indefinite period, to ensure the stock can continue to grow.

The international standard is that the Limit Reference Point (LRP) -- a point in time when the estimated biomass is such that growth of that stock will be challenging, or even impossible, if fishing is not decreased  -- is roughly 40% of the biomass at MSY, he noted.

"If you use the DFO definition of the [LRP], stock is in the critical zone. However, if you use the MSY, a [LRP] that is an international standard used in many other fisheries in Canada, the stock is in the cautious or healthy zone," said Melvin.

A Herring Science Council employee tags herring on board a herring seiner in 2022. Photo from Connors Brothers' Facebook page

So this is a real mixed message that needs to be addressed," he said, adding, "We have been trying for two years to get DFO to sit down at the table and discuss it."

The HSC even hired an international expert on management strategies to evaluate the options on the herring stock, noted Melvin.

Doug Butterworth, professor emeritus with the University of Cape Town in South Africa, has authored and co-authored numerous scientific papers on fisheries management. He currently heads the Marine Resource Asset and Management group and has provided fisheries management advice to several countries.

The PEW Charitable Trust Foundation has described him as "one of the world's most influential fisheries scientists."

Butterworth's calculations using DFO herring data showed a quota cut wasn't necessary, said Melvin.

"It showed you could still meet the goals of rebuilding by 2030 by leaving the catch at status quo," said Melvin. "So rather than making radical changes when there's so much at stake, that would give time for the department and the industry to sit down and work this out."

DFO stands by its science

Meanwhile, the DFO stands by its science on the Bay of Fundy herring stock.

"Science advice informing TAC decisions for the southwest Nova Scotia/Bay of Fundy Atlantic herring fishery is sound and indicates that the stock is in the critical zone and has been since 2018," DFO stated in an email to Undercurrent.

"The science advice also indicates that TAC reductions are needed to rebuild the stock out of the critical zone," the federal agency said, adding that stock assessments are based on multiple indicators for the stock, noting the at-sea surveys conducted by the industry and independently analyzed by DFO scientists.

"Setting a TAC for the next four years (2024-2027) provides predictability for harvesters and processors," DFO officials added.

"This decision was made in consultation with industry, stakeholders, rights holders and the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick," DFO stated, adding that the agency "takes concrete steps to ensure transparent, impartial and evidence-based peer review and scientific advice for decision-makers."

Atlantic Canada herring stock continues to struggle

However, both Melvin and Walsh say that, in stock assessment meetings with the industry, DFO never mentioned the possibility of adopting a management plan for four years. They said they were blindsided by that decision.

DFO said it will "continue to collaborate" with the industry, stakeholders and the provincial governments, and "decisions will continue to be to be based on the best available science, and we will continue to monitor the stock of Atlantic herring in southwest Nova Scotia and the Bay of Fundy."

The HSC maintains that DFO's conclusion that the stock is in the critical zone needs to be corrected.

"Based on accepted international standards and practices, this stock does not fall into the critical zone category, which means catches at or above the 21,000t TAC could be supported," said Melvin, who also pointed out that recent surveys in the Scots Bay area show the SSB at the highest level observed in the last seven years.

"In a good year, our boats would do 10 surveys at Scots Bay and get a 300,000t SSB," Melvin said.

From three surveys conducted by the HSC this year, the SSB was calculated at around 200,000t, he said.

"So this year was looking exceptionally good," said Walsh.

Rebuilt Canadian herring stock could be worth CAD 402m, report advises

But if there's a sense that there's more herring out there, there could be another reason for that, DFO offered.

"The herring fishery . . . is conducted in areas that Atlantic herring aggregate, which can give the perception that the stock is more abundant than it actually is," DFO officials stated in the email to Undercurrent.

Challenges ahead

While HSC and Connors Brothers will continue to pressure DFO to reassess its Bay of Fundy herring decision, Walsh isn't hopeful the TAC will change for this season.

That creates immediate concerns for the company's 500 employees at Blacks Harbour. Most work in the processing plant, while 65 work in the cannery. A few others crew the company's three purse seiners.

Workers at the Connors Brothers herring processing plant in Blacks Harbour, New Brunswick. Photo from Connors Brothers

The question is whether they will all accumulate enough hours and weeks of work to qualify for benefits through Canada's Employment Insurance system.

Benefits are based on average weekly income and the number of hours and weeks worked. Workers in the southwest region of New Brunswick, where the unemployment rate is currently around 6.4%, require at least 650 hours of work — equivalent to 16 40-hour weeks — to qualify for benefits.

"People are very upset, questioning the future of employment here, which is likely to change," said Walsh. "It's just very uncertain times for our particular company."

While the company also sources frozen herring from a supplier in the nearby province of Newfoundland and Labrador, it can't operate solely on importing frozen fish.

Getting fresh herring from the Bay of Fundy is just more economical for the operation, said Walsh.

"Unless we can modify the plant for additional species, our future is in serious jeopardy," Walsh said.

That's why the company, in collaboration with the HSC, will continue to lobby DFO to rethink its science on this stock and re-evaluate the quota recommendation.

"We've accepted previous cuts because we're firmly committed to ensuring a sustainable fishery for years to come. Unfortunately, the minister decided not to follow the process we've all invested in and instead made decisions that don't reflect what the science and global experts have told us," Walsh said.

title: AquaBounty’s Indiana farm fire sale is cautionary tale, RAS investor believes
content:
AquaBounty Technology's recent agreement to sell its Albany, Indiana, farm at below its original acquisition cost is a cautionary tale for others in the recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) industry, believes the CEO of one firm that invests in aquaculture.

AquaBounty, the world's first producer of a genetically engineered salmon, announced the sale of its 122,000 square foot RAS facility for $9.5 million last week to Hixton, Wisconsin-based Superior Fresh, as reported by Undercurrent News. The deal is expected to close by the end of July.

The price was significantly below the $14.6m AquaBounty paid for the facility in 2017, which serves to highlight the company's pressing financial struggles, Howard Tang, CEO of Peritus Capital, told Undercurrent in a recent interview.

The New York-based investment firm, known for backing aquaculture, alternative protein and renewable energy sectors, emphasizes the transaction is a stark indication of AquaBounty's urgent need for capital, notably to repay a $10m loan it has with Los Angeles, California-based JMB Capital Partners Lending, which matures on July 31.

Howard Tang, CEO of Peritus Capital. Photo: Liza Mayer

"I'm unclear whether this is 'low' or simply market price for these assets today. But it definitely shows a need for liquidity, likely to address its JMB loan," Tang said.

He suggested that the reduced sale price of AquaBounty's farm reflects current market conditions, where share prices for major land-based farms are declining.

The significantly lower sale price of AquaBounty's farm sends a cautionary message to both current and potential investors in the land-based aquaculture sector, especially those interested in RAS facilities focused on Atlantic salmon, he said. It highlights the challenges and risks of investing in such ventures and advises stakeholders to carefully assess asset valuations.

"Be cautious of overpaying. Atlantic Salmon RAS grow-out remains a tough sell," Tang cautioned.

Tang noted that the acquisition by Superior Fresh, the first commercial-scale RAS Atlantic salmon farmer in the US, suggests thorough due diligence and a realistic assessment of the facility's value, rather than a simple bargain purchase.

"Superior Fresh, as a well-regarded strategic player, would have a robust diligence and understanding of the value of this facility," he said.

A photograph of the Superior Fresh campus in Hixton, Wisconsin, shot in the fall of 2019.

However, Tang emphasized that the industry's outlook is not defined by isolated events.

He said: "It's essential to remember that individual projects and the industry's future are not determined by a single event. Projects live and die on their own merits – even Atlantic salmon! This (AquaBounty sale) is a bad 'comp' (comparable) for the sector, but one data point doesn't determine the future of an industry.

"It will always come down to the plan, the players and the potential. Look at the buyer, Superior Fresh (raising) Atlantic salmon in an all-freshwater process combined with an aquaponics system for leafy greens. That's a differentiated model, and I'm pretty sure they wouldn't be expanding if they weren't doing well."

Salmon RAS company Superior Fresh to buy AquaBounty’s Indiana farm

As for AquaBounty's decision to sell at a loss, Tang sees the move as strategic one, as the company had already acknowledged that the Indiana facility wasn't meeting its needs. It has been working to raise funds for the construction of a new facility in Ohio.

"It's far better to focus resources on where they think they have the best chance of scaling and reaching profitable production," he said.

"The project must demonstrate scalability and profitability," he said. "This will attract investors. Demonstration farms aren't enough. Investors know that RAS can grow fish. Investors don't know that RAS can grow fish profitably."

With ongoing improvements and a sharpened emphasis on operational efficiencies, he expects the impending years to solidify the industry's prospects.

"I believe in the next few years, the success stories will start to outshine the tough ones," he said.

title: Mysterious disease threatens US East Coast oyster farms
content:
A mysterious disease is causing trouble for oyster farmers in the US state of Virginia.

Dubbed "sudden unexplained mortality syndrome" (SUMS), the perplexing issue first emerged in 2015. However, Chesapeake Magazine reported on Monday (July 8) that oyster farmers in the Chesapeake Bay have recently noted a significant rise in mortality rates, especially during the warmer months.

Bruce Vogt, president of Big Island Aquaculture in Gloucester County, Virginia, explained that his farm's mortality rate has climbed from the expected 30% to a concerning 50%. He said that the spike in deaths is hindering business growth and delaying investments.

Source: Shutterstock

Despite this, the magazine reports that Virginia's oysters remain safe to eat, with the state still leading oyster production on the East Coast.

Unlike previous oyster diseases caused by single pathogens, SUMS is thought to result from a mix of stress factors. These include changes in water temperature, dissolved oxygen levels and genetic vulnerabilities in oysters.

To tackle this issue, researchers at the Virginia Institute of Marine Science (VIMS) have brought experts from eight universities to study the problem.

The team is working on several fronts: collecting data from oyster growers; analyzing genetic samples from both healthy and affected oysters; and testing different oyster seed genetic lines in various environments.

The researchers are also investigating how different algae species in oysters' diets and environmental stress might contribute to the mortality rates. Additionally, they are conducting experiments to enhance the resilience of oyster larvae by exposing them to sudden environmental changes, improving their ability to adapt and withstand various conditions.

A fishing boat on Chesapeake Bay. Photo: David Kay/ Shutterstock

Virginia has been deeply involved in oyster cultivation for over a century. However, modern methods of farming oysters in confined spaces like bags and racks have introduced new challenges. The VIMS report emphasizes the need for ongoing collaboration between scientists and farmers to solve SUMS.

Vogt, while realistic about the challenges ahead, is hopeful that supporting scientific research will eventually benefit oyster farmers. "It's tough to keep going if the losses keep increasing, so I'm committed to helping the scientists find a solution," he told the publication.

title: Mowi Scotland worker’s death in 2020 highlights safety risks
content:
A Scottish inquiry has highlighted how routine tasks on fish farms can pose life-threatening risks following the death of Clive Hendry in February 2020, the BBC reported.

Hendry was crushed while transferring from a moving work boat to a salmon feed barge near Kyle of Lochalsh. His employer, Norwegian salmon farmer Mowi's Scotland division, was fined over £800,000 last year for health and safety violations.

During the fatal accident inquiry, sheriff Gary Aitken noted the emotional impact on witnesses and stressed the need for careful planning in routine activities. Hendry, an assistant manager, died after falling into the water during a touch-and-go transfer. Despite efforts to rescue him, he could not be resuscitated.

The sheriff emphasized that Hendry's death underscored the importance of safety in everyday tasks. Mowi Scotland has since ceased the practices involved in the incident.

title: New Maryland aquaculture law expands ‘shellfish’ definition
content:
The US state of Maryland has expanded its definition of "shellfish" in a legislative update to include live mollusks, molluscan bivalves and bivalve shells, a move that is expected to encourage new ventures by simplifying regulatory processes for aquaculture businesses.

Previously, the term was defined as "live oysters, seed oysters, oyster shells, live hard-shell clams, live soft-shell clams and clam shells," a narrow definition that excluded such shellfish species as bay scallops.

Senate Bill 303, introduced to the Maryland Senate on Jan. 10, 2024, and passed recently, however, changes the game, said Matt Parker, an aquaculture business specialist at the University of Maryland Extension.

Parker said the law would likely reduce administrative burdens for Maryland's Department of Natural Resources, as the state agency won't have to make special exceptions each time someone wants to grow a different species. But it may have only a minimal economic impact on existing shellfish growers, he added.

"We currently have one scallop farm in Maryland, and there is interest in other species besides oysters and hard clams. It should have very little economic impact on any grower since the scallop farm was already in operation," he told Undercurrent News this week.

Brian Russell, president of the Southern Maryland Shellfish Growers Association, echoed Parker's sentiment.

"I had heard there was some interest from growers on the lower Eastern shore of the (Chesapeake) bay to try farming bay scallops and I believe that is where the legislation stemmed from," Russell told Undercurrent. "(But) for the majority of Maryland shellfish aquaculture, it does not change anything because we are limited by salinity to only growing oysters." 

Lee Beauchamp, the owner of the bay scallop farm, Bay Water Seafood, however, told  WMDT 45, a local ABC television affiliate, that the change was a long time coming and will help the entire area.

The [Code of Maryland Regulations] was a little antiquated, and it was very specific to oysters and clams, and this bill is an update that allows us to be able to aquaculture other species, including bay scallops… It helps everybody because its going to allow other species to be brought into the aquaculture operations in Maryland," he said.

Oysters represent the largest shellfish sector in Maryland, bringing in an estimated $97 million in economic impact to the state's economy over the 2012-2023 period, according to data from the University of Maryland Extension and Maryland Seagrant.

title: Peru plans emergency anti-IUU measure
content:
The Peruvian production ministry, also known as Produce, has announced forthcoming regulatory reforms to combat illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing by foreign vessels.

This decision comes after revelations that a Chinese vessel, Tian Xiang, was fined a mere PEN 250 ($65) for illegal fishing within Peru's 200 nautical miles of territorial waters.

The announcement was made by Sergio Gonzales, Peru's production minister, following numerous alerts from organizations like the National Society of Industries and the National Society of Artisanal Fishing of Peru, also known as SONAPESCAL. These groups had highlighted the unchecked entry of over 150 foreign vessels into Peruvian ports in 2023, raising concerns about the lack of satellite monitoring and control.

The proposed emergency decree aims to strengthen oversight and impose stricter penalties on foreign vessels violating Peruvian fishing regulations. The reform includes a significant investment of PEN 27.5 million ($7.2m) for acquiring two new patrol boats to enhance maritime surveillance.

Elsa Vega, president of Sonapescal, said the initiative emphasized the need for strong enforcement of rules requiring foreign vessels to have a national ship monitoring system (SISESAT). The regulation will also enable Peru to report offenders to international entities like the South Pacific Regional Fisheries Management Organization (RFMO-PS), potentially leading to the revocation of their fishing permits.

Alfonso Miranda Eyzaguirre, president of the Fisheries and Aquaculture Committee of the National Society of Industries, also praised the move as a positive step towards ensuring sustainable fishing practices and protecting the interests of Peru’s artisanal fishermen.

"This is a first step and we hope that this reform, and those that may be taken in the future, contribute to better control of the vessels that capture squid on the high seas, which severely impact the sustainability of the species and compete unfairly with our artisanal fleet," said Miranda.

title: Editor’s choice: Canada aquaculture ban, Espersen CEO out, G7 concerns over Russia
content:
EMEA editor Neil Ramsden brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week  

Our most-read stories of last week concerned supply issues in North America. The first was about the imminent sockeye salmon season in Alaska's Bristol Bay, where this season's run forecast is 12.1 million fish. Signs point to salmon numbers on the rise, with the fishery likely to begin within a week.

The second was the news that commercial capelin harvesters in the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador (NL) have threatened to tie up this season unless they get a better dock price. They say they are upset that the fish price setting panel has chosen the CAD 0.25 per pound ($0.18/lb) offer by the Association of Seafood Producers over the CAD 0.40/lb suggested by their union, the Fish Food and Allied Workers.

Also last week, Undercurrent New was live from Aquaculture Canada 2024, held at the Delta Hotel & Prince Edward Island Conference Center in Charlottetown. You can recap all that coverage here.

Staying in North America, US seafood giant Pacific Seafood Group's processing operation in the coastal town of Westport, Washington, was last week fined $222,000 for repeatedly discharging polluted wastewater into Half Moon Bay, according to the state's environmental management agency.

And with Canada expected to make an announcement very soon on a plan for a northern cod fishery this year, the union that represents fishers in NL is pressing prime minister Justin Trudeau to keep a promise made in 2021 by his Department of Fisheries and Oceans -- to see offshore draggers eliminated from the fishery until the total allowable catch reaches 115,000 metric tons per year.

For the rest of last week's biggest stories, see the list below:

Canada to ban open-net pen salmon farming in British Columbia by 2029
Klaus Nielsen steps down as CEO of Espersen after 25 years in charge
53 big US seafood associations, companies ask Peltola to withdraw 'bottom-trawling' bill
Nestle-backed $200m fund nixes massive RAS builds, bets on small-scale, distributed facilities
G7 leaders issue joint statement expressing concern about Russian seafood practices

Scientists recommend 31% cut in 2025 Barents Sea cod quota
New England's Aherne sees 'very tough few months' ahead on cod, haddock
Legal action on behalf of UK consumers seeks £382m from salmon giants for price fixing
Logistics firm takes on global shipping giant over spoiled seafood container
India's Jeelani becomes latest to add VAP shrimp offering with 10,000t factory

title: Norway salmon prices ease again, but Chilean stable, Scots bump up
content:
Spot prices for farmed Norwegian salmon look to be down again for week 26 (June 24-30), canceling out week 25's modest jump.

Meanwhile, Chilean salmon are stable in price and Scottish have seen their own small rebound after sustained declines, said Undercurrent News sources.

Salmon prices at a glance, week 26 of 2024:

Chilean trim-D 3-5lbs sold to the US: Unchanged at $5.75-$6.20/lb
Norwegian 4-5kg: Down around NOK 5, back to NOK 75/kg
Scottish 4-5kg: Back up to around £7.00/kg

Several sources told Undercurrent Norwegian salmon prices are expected to dip again after a brief break in the declines that have continued since week 20.

An executive at a Norwegian farmer said prices on the producer's end were down roughly NOK 5 per kilogram week-on-week, back to a rough range of NOK 74-78/kg for the most commonly traded 3-6kg sizes.

On June 21, NOK 75 equates to €6.63, $7.11, or £5.60.

An executive with a second Norwegian farming business said Friday (June 21) had begun with farmers pushing for a small w-o-w increase, but that by early afternoon the reality was instead a slight decrease. "It seems to be down now, very mixed signals," he said.

Then, a source with a large processor in Europe said he was being quoted €6.80/kg for 2-3kg salmon, €7.05/kg for 3-4s, €7.20/kg for 4-5s, €7.40/kg for 5-6s, €7.55/kg for 6-7s, and €7.40/kg for 7-8s, delivered duty paid to the port in Continental Europe.

That's down quite sharply from €7.50/kg for 3-4s, €7.75/kg for 4-5s, and €8.00/kg for 5-6s in week 25.

A source with another European processor, buying smaller salmon in the 2-3kg size range, also saw an as-yet-undefined easing in prices for week 26 after they'd lifted to just under €7.00/kg the prior week.

A trader had "superior" grade Norwegian salmon at €7.30/kg for 3-4s, €7.70/kg for 4-5s, and €7.80/kg for 5-6s for delivery on June 24.

Upgrade to Pro to view

Undercurrent has also recently added wholesale salmon pricing data from France's Rungis International, the principal wholesale market in Paris and the second-largest market in the world.

The latest daily data from Rungis (second chart, below) shows fresh, whole, gutted 2-3kg Norwegian salmon trading at €9.80/kg, unchanged from the previous week; 3-4kg salmon still at €10/kg; 4-5s at €10.40/kg; 5-6s at €10.80/kg; and 6-7s at €11.20/kg.

In China, the same price slump that's been felt for the past fortnight in Europe has also continued to make its presence felt in the Far East, as can be seen in salmon wholesale prices from markets in Beijing, Guangzhou and Shanghai -- all now also available on Undercurrent's price portal.

The price of head-on, gutted 6-7kg fresh Norwegian salmon delivered to Guangzhou flattened out at CNY 97/kg in week 25. That was as Chilean supply eased a littler more to CNY 90/kg, and Faroese salmon -- now re-entering the Chinese market after a prolonged period without shipments due to industrial action -- came down in price to CNY 105/kg.

Over in Chile, a source with a salmon producer told Undercurrent the Urner Barry report for June 20 showed prices were unchanged at $5.75-$5.95 per pound for 2-3lb fish; $5.90-$6.05/lb for 3-4lbs; and $6.05-$6.20/lb for 4-5lbs, trim-D fillets destined for Miami, the US.

The source has described the steady downward pressure as "typical" for this time of year.

Undercurrent now carries Chilean salmon pricing from Skills, which has acquired DataSalmon. It supplies Chilean salmon price indexes to the Brazilian, Chinese and US markets, based on weekly data from 15 producers representing 80% of the fresh supply from Chile.

As can be seen in the first chart below, the current price level and softening to the US is almost identical with the same period of 2023. If the trend continues to follow suit, the next month will see significant further declines in price, although 2022's data suggests last year's summer drop was extreme.

Chilean salmon prices to the Brazilian and Chinese markets, on the other hand, are well below the levels of 2022 and 2023, according to the latest data from Skills, which extends up to and including week 23 (June 3-9):

Finally, prices for medium-sized 3-5kg Scottish salmon have seen a lift for week 26, according to a source with a processor.

After giving a rough average of £7.25/kg "or just under that" for Scottish salmon in week 24, he told Undercurrent that values had dropped another £1/kg in week 25.

However, "they're back up at nearly £7.00/kg next week," he said, adding that he also saw that pricing for Norwegian salmon delivered to the UK -- also a rise w-o-w.

The European wholesaler trader had "superior" Scottish salmon at €7.80/kg for 3-4s, €8.35/kg for 4-5s, €8.55/kg for 5-6s, and €8.30/kg for 6-7s and 7-8s for delivery on June 24.

That is again slightly up from €7.70/kg for 3-4s and €8.30/kg for 4-5s, but down from €8.80/kg for 5-6s and €9.40/kg for anything larger.

Pricing data from the Rungis International market also shows the current trading levels for fresh, whole, gutted salmon from Scotland for both label rouge and standard fish.

Notably, while Scottish 2-3kg label rouge salmon have been traded at €13/kg since the start of the year, standard quality fish of the same weight have slipped to €11.60/kg in value as of week 21. Both values were unchanged in week 25:

title: Canadian lobster dealer gets five years for defrauding processor of more than a million dollars
content:
Terry Banks, a 58-year-old lobster dealer in Nova Scotia, was handed a five-year prison sentence on Wednesday (June 19) for defrauding Independent Fisheries, a processor in the Canadian province, of more than a million dollars, the CBC reports.

The decision by Nova Scotia Supreme Court justice Pierre Muise follows a case that has reverberated throughout the Canadian lobster industry since charges were first laid in 2017, according to the news service. The judge convicted Banks in January following a trial.

The judge said Wednesday that Banks has not shown any remorse. He noted other convictions, including a 2008 case where Banks was imprisoned for defrauding a local bank of CAD 2.5 million, money that still hasn't been repaid.

Muise ordered Banks, from the town of Brooklyn, to pay CAD 800,000 in restitution, and fined him CAD 800,000.

Standing outside the Halifax courtroom, prosecutor Rick Miller reportedly described the Canadian lobster industry as one that still relies on trust, honesty and handshake deals.

"When you allow someone like Terry Banks to get into this industry and take advantage of that, then there's a real detriment, because people go out of business, people lose their property, people lose their homes, their boats and everything," he said.

title: Pacific Seafood fined $222,000 for water quality violations at Washington plant
content:
US seafood giant Pacific Seafood Group's processing operation in the coastal town of Westport, Washington, has been fined $222,000 for repeatedly discharging polluted wastewater into Half Moon Bay, according to the state's environmental management agency.

The Washington Department of Ecology announced the fine for the Oregon-headquartered seafood processor on Thursday (June 13).

The agency alleged that the Westport facility had violated its water quality permit 58 times over the past two years, consistently exceeding pollution limits for acidity, bacteria, oil and grease.

In a press release, Vince McGowan, Ecology's water quality program manager, emphasized the unacceptable nature of these violations, especially since other similar facilities comply with permit requirements.

The Pacific Westport facility received citations for failing to monitor water as required, in addition to citations for discharging wastewater with high levels of organic matter, solids, acidity, oil and grease and fecal coliform bacteria.

McGowan stressed the need for Pacific Westport to upgrade its wastewater treatment system to meet regulatory standards. The facility has made short-term fixes but has yet to invest in substantial improvements, he alleged.

Allegations are 'misleading'

In response to the fine, Pacific provided a statement to Undercurrent News over the weekend highlighting its commitment to environmental protection and its efforts to comply with regulations.

"We are disheartened by Ecology's approach to sensationalizing information and intentionally misleading the public instead of working with our team," said Lacy Ogan, communications director for Pacific.

"For example, their press release alleges we are 'polluting Half Moon Bay with water that is too acidic,' giving the impression that pH violations are ongoing and regular when the truth is, there was only a single pH violation, which resulted from a broken pH meter."

Ogan said the Westport facility has made significant technological investments and has a team dedicated to environmental health. Its initiatives include collaborating with Ecology, hiring third-party engineers and investing in wastewater treatment improvements -- actions that align with an engineering report and a scheduled plan reviewed by Ecology, she noted.

"Our company prides itself on our commitment to the environment and has been recognized as leaders in pollution reduction by the EPA," she said.

History of violations

Ecology pointed out that the Pacific Westport operation has a history of similar infractions, including penalties from the US Environmental Protection Agency in 2020 and additional fines from Ecology in 2022.

"Before issuing this most recent penalty, Ecology conducted two technical assistance inspections at the facility to help the facility get back into compliance. When followed, these permit requirements help protect aquatic life and human health," the agency said.

Ecology allocates the water-quality penalties to the state's coastal protection fund, which supports water-quality restoration projects by public agencies and Tribes.

Pacific said it will appeal the penalty.

title: AquaBounty names Melbourne as CEO, replaces Wulf
content:
AquaBounty Technologies' Sylvia Wulf on Friday (June 7) announced that the land-based grower of the first genetically engineered salmon has named David F. Melbourne, Jr., as its new CEO, replacing her, though she will remain as the non-executive chair of the board of directors.

The Harvard, Massachusetts-based company has been struggling financially and, in early February, announced a plan to sell its Albany, Indiana, facility, which is 122,000 square feet and capable of raising 1,200 metric tons of fish, as reported by Undercurrent News. This despite the construction of a new, larger facility in Ohio being only 30% complete.

The company declared on May 15 that it had emptied out its tanks in Albany, harvesting more than 320t of fish, in preparation for a new company to take over the facility, as reported by Undercurrent.

In late April, AquaBounty had reported success in obtaining a $10-million term loan that involved offering both of its US farms as collateral.   

AquaBounty, publicly traded on NASDAQ under the ticker symbol AQB, reported seeing a net loss of $11.2m during the first quarter of 2024, which ended on March 31, 72% worse than the $6.5m loss it reported in the first quarter of 2023. 

AquaBounty Technologies CEO Sylvia Wulf speaks to reporters at the company's groundbreaking in Pioneer, Ohio.

Wulf has been the CEO and chair at AquaBounty since January 2019 (5.5 years), according to her LinkedIn profile. Previously she spent about 7.5 years as the president of stocks and senior vice president of merchandising for US Foods.    

Prior to taking the president role in August 2023, Melbourne had served AquaBounty as its chief commercial officer for more than four years (2019-2023). Prior to that he was the senior VP of marketing and corporate responsibility for Bumble Bee Foods for nearly 14.5 years (2005-2019). 

Wulf said in a statement that Melbourne's ascension to CEO has been part of a "long-term succession plan for the leadership team" since his earlier promotion.

"Over the last year, Dave has led day-to-day business functions for the company," she said. "The board recognizes the outstanding contributions and leadership he has provided over the last year, including his role in the efficient shutdown of our Indiana farm. With his promotion, he will take on the additional responsibilities for the business including leading our pursuit of a range of financing and strategic alternatives, as well as investor relations and strategic initiatives to achieve AquaBounty's growth plans. Dave is a transformational leader and I have full confidence in his ability to take the reins at this critical point in time. I look forward to working with him in my continued role as board chair."

Dave Melbourne from LinkedIn.

Melbourne said he is "excited for the opportunity" and plans to focus most immediately on securing the required financing to maintain liquidity and support current operations.

"Working in conjunction with our investment banking partner, we will prioritize completing the sale of the Indiana farm and aggressively push forward on identifying and finalizing financing and strategic alternatives," he said.

Melbourne added: "We have made great progress over the last five years across all areas of our business. We have leveraged our advantages of vertical integration; refined and improved our operational expertise and technical capabilities; made important strides forward in our breeding, genetics, and fish health and nutrition initiatives; and successfully launched our salmon into the US and Canadian markets. AquaBounty has a bright future, all supported by a strong, experienced and committed team. Together, we will face the challenges and look forward to driving continued progress."

title: Charity asks UK competition authority to probe ‘sustainably sourced’ scampi
content:
Scottish charity Open Seas has asked the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) to investigate UK retailers that claim their scampi is "responsibly sourced," reports the BBC.

Open Seas has been campaigning for supermarkets to stop purchasing the products, which come from the UK's nephrops fishery -- one which the charity claims causes "extensive environmental damage" by trawling the sea bed.

The British Retail Consortium said retailers were working closely with suppliers to "ensure products meet customer expectations on sustainability."

UK nephrops FIP asked to provide evidence backing claims of progress

It added: "Retailers are committed to sourcing scampi responsibly." However, Open Seas claimed describing the product as "responsibly sourced" breaches CMA guidance.

A spokesperson for Whitby Seafoods, the UK's largest supplier of scampi, said: "We strongly dispute the claims made by Open Seas" and that it has "a strong track record in building on the work of the scampi fishing industry in driving improvements to sustainability."

Whitby is involved in the nephrops fishery improvement project, which is now inactive having "failed to meet social responsibility policy" requirements by April 2024.

In its complaint to the CMA, Open Seas said supermarkets' claims that their fisheries were "responsible" was ambiguous, due to the term being "defined by a self-interested industry group without reference to international norms for defining responsible seafood."

Whitby Seafoods said: "The claim that scampi is ‘responsibly sourced’ is used in line with strict third-party guidance from the Sustainable Seafood Coalition [SSC]."

The SSC was founded by companies including Marks and Spencers, Waitrose and Partners, and Young's Seafood. Edward Whittle, Whitby Seafoods' sustainability director, sits on its steering committee alongside other seafood producers, including Young's and supermarket J. Sainsbury.

title: US states look to diners to curb blue catfish problem
content:
An invasive fish that's become a problem in rivers in two US states is becoming a sales opportunity for fishermen and fishing companies.

Wild blue catfish (Ictalurus furcatus) — introduced to Virginia and Maryland in the 1970s for the sports fishing industry — have increased to the point that they now account for as much as 80% of all fish species in some river systems.

"It's eating our crab, striped bass, herring and other finfish," Mike Hutt, executive director of the Virginia Marine Products Board (VMPB), told Undercurrent News at Seafood Expo Global (SEG), in Barcelona, Spain, in April.

Mike Hutt, executive director of the Virginia Marine Products Board. Photo by Barb Dean-Simmons

"They have taken over, and they will continue to take over if we don't do something about it," said Hutt, who was representing the Southern US Trade Association on Seafood (SOUSA) at SEG.

Population up 500% in 10 years

Blue catfish were initially introduced by Virginia's Department of Wildlife Resources (DWR) into the James and Rappahannock Rivers in 1974. More were released into the York River watershed in 1985, with about 300,000 blues released over those 11 years. 

At the time, populations of striped bass — a prized trophy fish for sports fishermen — were declining throughout the Atlantic. Blue catfish were meant to replace them.

It was originally thought that the blue catfish would remain confined to the rivers where they were introduced and would not venture beyond the salty boundary of Chesapeake Bay. However, the fish adapted to the salt water and swam further.

By the late 1980s, they appeared in the Potomac River, eventually moving on to the Nanticoke and Patuxent Rivers.

Both Virginia and Maryland have classed the blues as an invasive species.

While there isn't extensive data on the number of blue catfish in these states' rivers, Maryland's Department of Natural Resources (DNR) uses harvest data as a measure. In the Potomac River and other Maryland waters, commercial landings of blue catfish skyrocketed from 609,525 pounds in 2013 to 4.2 million pounds in 2023, an increase of more than 500%, the DNR notes on its website.

Surveys of the James and Rappahannock rivers in Virginia show that blue catfish comprise about 75% of the total fish biomass. Three out of every four lbs of fish biomass is blue catfish.

Data from Maryland Department of Natural Resources show how commercial harvests of blue catfish have increased since 2012. Screenshot from DNR website.

Solving the blue catfish problem with consumer appetite

Hutt believes one of the best solutions to the blue catfish problem is putting more of them on dinner tables. Finding markets for the fish allows commercial fishermen to at least make some income while trying to bring the rivers back to balance, Hutt pointed out.

"We've got commercial fishermen behind it, knowing that it provides jobs and money for fear and fuel," he said, adding that as markets for the blue catfish grow, it will also create opportunities for packaging and distribution companies.

"It could be a big industry, and we are working to build it," he said.

Fortunately, blue catfish has an excellent flavor, thanks to its diet of other seafood, Hutt added.

Unlike other catfish that forage for food on muddy bottoms, blue catfish grab their food throughout the water column, feeding on crab, American eel, herring, seabass and whatever else they can find.

"It tastes like what it feeds on," Hutt said.

Last year, fishermen in Virginia harvested 3m lbs of blue catfish from state rivers, but "the government feels that's not even putting a dent in the stock because the biomass is steadily growing," he said.

Currently, most blue catfish is sold fresh in the US domestic market to some grocery stores, restaurants and independent retailers, he said.

Blue catfish at a seafood market in Jessup, Maryland. Photograph by Jason Huffman.

"But we need to get it to club stores, where you can sell the higher volumes in individual quick-frozen packs," said Hutt.

For the past two years, the VMPB has also been seeking markets further afield, featuring the blue catfish in its booth at seafood expos like the SEG.

"It's been very well received," said Hutt, adding: "I think we're on the verge of really opening up a good market for that product."

Virginia created a grant program last year to support blue catfish processing infrastructure. The original quest was for $4m, but the budget was slashed to $250,000 just before the bill was adopted, reported Chesapeake Bay Magazine.

In February, Virginia governor Glenn Youngkin announced that Sea Farms Inc. of Hayes, Virginia, would get a repayable grant of $250,000 to buy a blast freezing system and expand freezer storage capacity to handle blue catfish.

title: EU delays vote on closing 10% of fishing grounds
content:
A vote on a proposal to fully close 10% of EU fishing areas has been postponed until October 2024, the EU's Marine Strategy Coordination Group (MSCG) announced.

The MSCG, which oversees the implementation of the EU's Marine Strategy Framework Directive aimed at protecting marine environments, opted to delay the vote to allow more time for discussion and input from fishing industry stakeholders about the potential impacts of the closures.

Ivan Lopez, chairman of the European Bottom Fishing Alliance, welcomed the postponement, saying his organization appreciates "the MSCG's decision today to delay the vote."

"The European Commission cannot use a backdoor, such as the implementation of ill-defined objectives of an EU Directive, to adopt measures that have such a huge impact on our fishers," Lopez said. "Decisions as such must be checked by the elected institutions of the EU."

With the European Parliament currently on hold due to elections, Lopez said the delay "provides valuable time for stakeholders to further engage in constructive discussions with our administrations to achieve a balanced approach."

title: UK’s Seafish begins formal industry consultation to revise levies
content:
UK public body Seafish has started formal consultation with levy payers and the wider seafood industry on proposals for a new levy model. 

During its 2021 strategic review, the seafood industry recognized the need for a review of the levy system, given it had not changed since 1999, it said. Once this formal consultation process ends, Seafish will make formal recommendations to the government, which will be considered by relevant ministers across the UK and devolved administrations (Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland).

Levy is due on the first sale of seafood, both domestically landed and imported, in the UK. It is not charged on farmed salmon, trout, and freshwater fish species because these species are excluded by primary legislation. Nor is it currently charged on canned, bottled and pouched seafood products.  

The levy collected is used by Seafish to provide support, advice and services across the whole UK seafood supply chain.  

The review in 2021 saw general agreement that an improved levy model was needed to ensure Seafish had a stable financial model and could continue to provide the support industry needs in the future, it said.

The Seafish board held informal consultations with the seafood industry in spring 2023 on proposed changes to the levy system. Now, a statutory consultation on the proposed changes will be open for 12 weeks until Aug. 9.

Information on the consultation, which consists of the Formal Consultation Paper (available in Welsh and English), the draft Regulation, and an Economic Impact Assessment, can be downloaded from the Seafish website here.  

The proposed changes to the Seafish levy include: 

The current sea fish levy rate of 0.903 pence per kilogram will be increased to £0.01/kg. This will be renamed the 'category 1' levy.
The current levy rate that applies to mussels, cockles, and pelagic fish (as defined in regulation) will increase from 0.258p/kg to 0.5p/kg over a three-year period.
The current levy rate for whelks will increase from 0.4515p/kg to 0.5p/kg
The levy for mussels, cockles, pelagic fish (as defined in regulation) and whelks will be renamed the 'category 2' levy.
The levy rates for manufactured fishmeal and "fish destined for" fishmeal will also increase, as follows:
Manufactured fishmeal will increase from 0.175p/kg to 0.315p/kg.
Fish destined for fishmeal will increase from 0.035p/kg to 0.05p/kg.
For the first time levy will apply to canned, bottled, and pouched seafood products,
for those species within the scope of the levy.
The levy for all seafood and seafood products would be adjusted annually, subject to a cap on the annual adjustment of 2%. 
Minor changes to the administration of the levy to make collection and payment more efficient. 
 

"After our informal consultation last year, we have taken industry feedback on board and made further revisions to refine the proposed levy adjustments," said Mike Sheldon, chair of the Seafish board. "It is our priority to make the levy fit for purpose, fairer for all and ensure we can continue to deliver the support industry have told us they need, now and in the future."

"While we appreciate that the seafood industry is under financial pressure, our proposed changes strike a good balance, minimizing impacts on the industry while allowing us to effectively support the seafood sector as an organization."

title: Canadian lobster processor banned from hiring foreign workers, fined CAD 365k
content:
A lobster processing plant in the Canadian province of New Brunswick has been fined more than CAD 365,000 ($254,994) and banned from hiring temporary foreign workers for two years, reports CBC News.

Immigration Canada said it found, in April, that the work and pay conditions at LeBreton Fisheries, in Grand-Anse, did not match the workers' contracts, according to the news service. Also, the federal agency said the company didn't make information about workers' rights available in two official languages or keep documents for the required amount of time.

The two-year ban will expire on April 15, 2026.

The fine is the highest one handed a New Brunswick employer of temporary foreign workers, CBC reports, and it's the second fine for LeBreton. The company was penalized CAD 30,000 in 2023 for failing to provide a work environment free of harassment and reprisal.

The company said the sanctions are unjustified and is evaluating its legal options.

One of the owners, Kevin LeBreton, said the company has hired no foreign workers this year and plans to hire locals. Last year, LeBreton employed 80 temporary foreign workers. 

For the past month, the company has been advertising job openings on its Facebook page, seeking workers to fill various positions at its lobster factories in Grande Anse and Val Comeau, New Brunswick.

title: Mowi issues green bonds raising nearly €300m
content:
Mowi has issued a total NOK 3.5 billion (€298 million) of new unsecured green bonds, it announced in a stock filing on the Oslo Bors exchange.

Mowi refinances with another sustainability-linked facility

The bonds are split between two tranches, one of NOK 2.5bn with a tenor of five years, and another of NOK 1bn with a tenor of eight years.

The entire issue amount and coupons will be swapped into floating euros, the firm said, adding that the transaction was "well oversubscribed."

Furthermore, the proceeds from the green bond issues are to be used in green projects as defined by Mowi's 'green and sustainability-linked financing framework,' which the firm released in May last year.

The settlement date is set to May 3 for both tranches, when an application will be made for the bonds to be listed on the Oslo stock exchange.

Danske Bank acted as Mowi's green bond advisor, while DNB Markets, Nordea and SEB served as joint global coordinators on the transaction.

ABN Amro, Credit Agricole Corporate and Investment Bank, and Rabobank also all acted as joint lead managers on the transaction.
