title: High Liner ‘well prepared’ for expanded Russia ban, may still bring in some haddock
content:
BARCELONA, Spain -- Canada's High Liner Foods is prepared for the expanded US ban on Russian seafood processed in third countries that takes effect on June 1, CEO Paul Jewer told Undercurrent News at Seafood Expo Global (SEG).

"We feel like we're well prepared to deal with the challenges on the supply front. Frankly, we've been preparing for years," he said.

FREE READ Live from SEG: ‘Dire times’ in pollock surimi; Farmed salmon supply outlook

"There could be some impact on raw material costs as we look forward on a couple of key species where demand may exceed supply," said Jewer about the current rocketing prices for headed and gutted (H&G) Atlantic cod from Norway.

"We see changes in prices all the time in raw material costs, and it's our responsibility to manage that and figure out how we can still find the best value for our customers," he said.

High Liner is buying more US pollock to replace volumes of Chinese double frozen made from H&G Russian pollock, as well as looking to increase volumes of alternative species like southern blue whiting from New Zealand, or Cape hake from South Africa.

Products made from southern blue whiting are already in Canadian and US retail, and it's now about educating the customer, he said.

Sea Harvest adds vessels to harvest higher hake quota as cod cuts, geopolitical issues drive demand

High Liner could also continue to import small volumes of double-frozen haddock products using Russian H&G for some parts of its business, said Jewer.

"I think some of that may continue, but haddock is not a big part of our business," he said. Haddock -- not an Alaskan species like cod, crab pollock and pollock -- was not included on the list of Russian products processed in third countries to be banned from June 1 under the executive order.

"But, of course, we'll see what happens as folks look at other species," he said.

Move away from China processing continues

High Liner is also continuing to reduce its reliance on re-processing in China and eyeing moving production back closer to home.

The company, which generates around two-thirds of its sales from the US market, has been moving processing out of China and into Indonesia and Vietnam in the past few years, Jewer told Undercurrent at SEG.

"The percentage of product that we have coming through China would be less than half of what it was four or five years ago. And we have seen very solid growth in both Indonesia and Vietnam," he said.

The High Liner exec declined to give exact figures but said the percentage of re-processing being done for his company is under half of its total now.

Trident’s Pickenpack back in market for Russian pollock

Then, High Liner is looking at other countries in Asia, Latin America and Eastern Europe to further "diversify its supply chain," he told Undercurrent.

"Near-shoring," so moving processing back from Asia to North America, is also "very much on the agenda," said Jewer.

"We think we'll continue to be a diversification of where processing occurs. We remain hopeful that we'll be able to find some opportunities for nearshore processing as well. We look forward to more processing work being done in North America, obviously supported by automation, that'll be critical," he said.

How exactly this near-shoring process evolves is yet to be defined, however, he added.

title: Stable expenses, increased sales with Mercadona drive Profand’s 2023 earnings
content:
Vigo, Spain-based firm Profand Fishing Holding, a key supplier to the country's largest retailer, Mercadona, maintained a stable revenue in 2023 but saw a slight decline in profit.

The firm's turnover last year was €930 million ($990m), almost on par with the previous year's figure of €932m. In 2022, its turnover was equivalent to over $1 billion at the time; however, the euro has depreciated against the US dollar since then.

Its earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization demonstrated significant growth, reaching €68m, a 14% increase from the previous year. This improvement was attributed to stabilized operating expenses, such as freight and electricity, following recent inflationary trends.

Despite strong operational performance, adjusted attributable profit for 2023 saw a decline, amounting to €12.3m, 21% lower compared to €15.6m in 2022. This reduction was primarily influenced by increased financial expenses, driven by rising global interest rates to curb inflationary pressures.

Profand's Zaragoza plant. Photo: Profand.

According to Profand, its strategic investments remained robust, totaling €63.3m during the year. The company's investment plan was designed over the past two years to enhance industrial capacity and bolster vertical integration strategies.

Last year, the firm acquired a new processing plant in Boston. Thus, Stavis Seafood, Profand's US wholesale wing, has relocated to the former Legal Sea Foods building in the Boston Seaport area. 

Additionally, the firm, already a significant player in wild Argentine shrimp, in addition to fish and cephalopods, bought an aquaculture farm for Pacific white shrimp in Ecuador, establishing a subsidiary in the country. Profand purchased a small farm there with the objective of moving into processing in the country.

In a statement sent to Undercurrent News, Profand defined the capital expenditure executed last year as "the culmination of a strong investment plan implemented over the past two years with the strategic objective of expanding and strengthening Profand's industrial capacity and promoting the group's vertical integration strategy, accompanying Mercadona in the development of its new fish model."

In terms of production volume, Profand sold a total of 67m trays in 2023, with 59m produced in Spain alone, a 14% increase attributable to Mercadona's commitment to the new fish sales model. By the end of the year, Profand had sold a total of 112,000 metric tons of fish, it said.

"In 2023, the group exceeded compliance targets for sustainable fishing, workers in centers audited for human rights compliance, use of electricity from renewable sources, and recycled materials in plastics," Profand added.  

The Spanish business said it uses high-pressure processing technology in its plants, which allows the company to extend the shelf life of its products without using additives while retaining all their nutritional properties. According to the firm, this results in a significant reduction in food waste and, therefore, CO2 emissions.

It increased its global workforce by 267 employees in 2023, focusing on creating jobs in Spain, where it generated 504 new positions over the last two years.

title: Danish biotech venture Unibio names new CFO
content:
Danish biotechnology firm Unibio International has appointed Spencer White as its chief financial officer, effective April 29, 2024.

Unibio is one of the leaders in the production of single-cell proteins which can be used in aquaculture feed.

With three decades of experience in financial services and investment management, White will join Unibio from TWL Pacific, where he served as a founding partner.

Bringing a wealth of expertise in corporate finance, capital raising, and strategic advisory, White will play a pivotal role in Unibio's financial operations and global investment strategy, according to the firm. He will collaborate closely with CEO David Henstrom and the board to explore diverse investment opportunities for the company. 

"His extensive experience in corporate finance, investment strategies, and proven success in helping companies raise capital will undoubtedly play a pivotal role in steering our company towards sustained growth and success," said Henstrom.

White defined Unibio as a company with "a noble mission to feed the planet through innovation and sustainable protein production."

Unibio aims to become the world market leader in protein production based on methanotrophic bacteria, partly by own production and partly by licensing the production technology to international investors wishing to establish large-scale production plants of Uniprotein using surplus gas.

Its U-Loop technology converts natural gas into a highly concentrated protein product, marketed as Uniprotein, which can be used as a direct supplement in animal feeds. According to the firm, it can be a substitute for fishmeal, a traditional feed component and an increasingly scarce resource.

title: Chilean authorities confirm $950,000 fine for Nova Austral
content:
A Chilean court of appeal has confirmed the salmon farmer Nova Austral will be fined CLP 900 million (now $947,421) over damage caused to the seabed in the Punta Arenas area.

The sanction was originally imposed by the Superintendence for the Environment (known under its Chilean acronym SMA) in the summer of 2022. 

Latest lawsuit against Chile’s Nova Austral could force closure of four farm sites

Nova Austral appealed the decision, calling it "unjustified and disproportionate given the background information in the process, including the defenses presented by the company." 

Undercurrent News reported at the time that the combination of fines the company faced was capable of forcing it to close four farming sites.

Chile's Third Environmental Court had annulled the initial decision to hit the farmer with a fine of 1,300 "annual tax units," or more than CLP 900m. 

The SMA appealed that, and has now won its appeal.

Still pending a decision are appeals regarding the SMA's decision to revoke several farming licenses for Nova Austral sites in the Alberto de Agostini National Park, Magallanes Region.

Again, in this case, the aquaculture business was successful in appealing the decision to the Environmental Court. The SMA has appealed to have the license revocations upheld.

title: Inquiry over Mowi Scotland worker’s death adjourned until June
content:
An inquiry into the death of Mowi employee Clive Hendry has been adjourned by the courts until June 2024, Stv News reported.

Hendry, 58, was crushed between two vessels at Mowi Scotland's Ardintoul site on Loch Alsh four years ago, leading to what an Inverness sheriff described as "a significant incident with a tragic outcome."

Mowi fined £800k over death of employee in Scotland

Scheduled for further hearings on June 12, the inquiry will assess written submissions from legal representatives of The Crown, Mowi, and Hendry's partner.

Key aspects to be determined include the cause of death, potential preventive measures, and strategies for future safety enhancements.

This development follows Mowi Scotland's admission of guilt to health and safety breaches in May 2023, resulting in an £800,000 ($1 million) fine imposed by the Inverness Sheriff Court.

title: German seafood giants cooperate on Bremerhaven net zero project
content:
Three of the largest seafood companies based in the German port of Bremerhaven are cooperating on a project to become carbon neutral by 2030.

The project, which is in the planning stage, involves Deutsche See, Frosta Aktiengesellschaft and Nomad Foods' Frozen Fish International plant in the port. In addition to the seafood firms, Holz Cordes, a wood supplier, and Nord Ceram, a tile maker, are involved in the project.

Frosta drops Russian pollock from brand, private label ‘up to customers’

"The basic idea is to get to net zero by 2030," Felix Ahlers, CEO of Frosta, told Undercurrent News. "You need to group energy demand and cover geothermic, wind and solar."

The companies are currently evaluating the best approach, having all submitted their energy usages, said Ahlers.

"When you put all the demands together, it's rather stable, over seasonality, day and night. So, it was a very interesting process, to talk to your competitors and to agree that on this issue, we are not in competition," he told Undercurrent.

"We realized it's much more efficient to do together rather than each company on its own," said Ahlers. "When we started to look, we realized that when we do our own energy solutions, it's not so efficient, and the paybacks are not good. In many situations, when the wind blows a lot, you can't use it, maybe overnight. So, there's a lot of potential when we put everybody together."

World’s largest pollock buyer Nomad notes difficulty of replacing Russia, anticipates more sanctions

Frosta is also working on its own solar parks and wind energy projects in addition to the group initiative, said Ahlers.

The companies have hired two managers to oversee the project. Other than this, the financial commitment required has not yet been defined.

"We don't know how much we will need to put into the whole project yet," said Ahlers told Undercurrent.

title: Camanchaca on verge of ‘biggest acquisition for 25 years’
content:
BERGEN, Norway: Chilean seafood group Compania Pesquera Camanchaca is on the verge of completing a deal for the remaining 30% of pelagics fishing operation Camanchaca Pesca Sur (CPS) that it doesn't already own, CEO Ricardo Garcia Holtz revealed at the North Atlantic Seafood Forum.

Chile’s Camanchaca opens new $30m facility for frozen jack mackerel processing

The business is a joint venture between it and Germany's Stengel family, formed in 2011. Camanchaca owned 70% of the firm at its formation, and the minority shareholder -- the Stengel-linked Grupo Bio Bio -- had 30% with a PUT option, which it exercised in 2022.

"We've been negotiating in 2023 the terms of the transaction -- precisely the price -- and that process is being completed as we speak," said Garcia. "The price is going to be defined by two investment banks, and the valuation of that range for the company is between $107 million and maybe $300m, so a wide range."

The transaction should be taking place within the next two-to-four weeks, he said on March 7, describing it as a "game changer, a very substantial acquisition -- the major acquisition of Camanchaca for the last 20, 25 years."

CPS is a fishing operation in the south of Chile, where the most valuable resources for Chilean fisheries are located, he said. It is focused on jack mackerel.

"The cash generation capacity of this fishing operation is substantial. We've been generating more than $50m in cash over the last few years and EBITDA [earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization] of $200m in the last five years."

Excluding Camanchaca's salmon farming operations, its enterprise value (EV) -- the market value of Camanchaca plus its net interest-bearing debt -- is approximately $100m; "very, very low," said Garcia.

"This transaction, we believe, which is going to be public in the next few weeks, will show the gap between the fair value of the stock and what the market value is. We think that will be very substantial as we do the numbers, we come up with a negative valuation for everything that is not salmon and the pelagics business in the south. That is, all the pelagics in the north and all the mussels business. At the moment, the EV EBITDA of Camanchaca is about three times traded in the market."

He noted that it could be asked why investing in fisheries is a wise move during "turbulent times."

CPS is "precisely located" in the Chilean sector to serve the African market, he continued.

"More than 85% of our production in CPS, the frozen fish goes to the African market at the moment."

Over the coming years, Africa's population is set to grow more than any other continent's, he added.

CPS' landings have been climbing, from 130,000 metric tons to more than 200,000t in the year ended September 2023, he said. It also purchases raw material on the international market to keep its recently completed (in 2022) facility near Coronel topped up.

"That processes between 650t and 700t per day -- that's a very substantial production capacity on a daily basis that allowed us to process last year more than 80,000t of frozen fish."

title: SalMar Aker Ocean eyes new offshore sites globally, early harvests show strong promise
content:
BERGEN, Norway: Offshore salmon farming firm SalMar Aker Ocean (SAO) has looked at a host of other countries and has a shortlist drawn up for the most promising opportunities for international expansion, said CFO Trine Romuld at the North Atlantic Seafood Forum (NASF).

"We have the ambition of being present not only in Norway but also internationally. We have four key defined factors we are considering: First, of course, all biological conditions are needed."

"Second, it would be beneficial to have access to a value chain already in place. Third, it needs the regulatory framework, so we know what to plan for; and it needs to be close to the market."

The company has looked at 30 different countries and has a shortlist that it is now looking at "more deeply," she said.

That comes as Norway continues to develop its own regulatory framework for offshore aquaculture, to the impatience of some in the sector.

Click to expand

Speaking elsewhere at NASF, Cermaq Group CEO Steven Rafferty noted how anticipation of offshore aquaculture has completely stalled.

"The Norwegian government has killed the potential for offshore investment at the moment because there's no clarity on the regulation," he said. Indeed, with no certainty over whether or not offshore salmon will be included in the resource tax, it leaves significant risk for any would-be investors.

Click to expand

"The offshore knowledge is here in Norway, so we have to start here and then move it on to other countries," added Rafferty.

"But now it's stopped in Norway, and I'm afraid I'm quite negative for the foreseeable future."

SalMar chair Gustav Witzoe said in September 2023 that the Norwegian salmon farmer was keen to develop offshore aquaculture but that this won't happen until the government clarifies the new ground rent tax regime.

Just a few days after he was quoted saying that, SAO was given the green light to establish a Smart Fish Farm -- a vast, fully offshore salmon production unit -- in the Norwegian Sea.

Norway's directorate of fisheries gave SAO subsidiary Mariculture site clearance for a location roughly 45 nautical miles outside what Norway calls its "baseline" (the innermost of its ocean demarcation borders). The site clearance has been granted for 19,000 metric tons of maximum permitted biomass of salmon.

SAO CEO Roy Reite said the next important milestones would be the clarifications relating to ground rent tax and the regulatory framework for offshore aquaculture.

In February 2024, Norway's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Fisheries announced the initiation of a commission tasked with conducting a "comprehensive" public impact assessment for offshore farming. The areas under consideration include Norskerenna Sor, Froyabanken Nord and Traenabanken. 

Strong results at existing sites

Biological performance at SAO's Arctic Offshore Farming (AOF) sites — bought from Norway Royal Salmon last year — has looked even stronger than at the more established Ocean Farm 1 as the first harvests come to fruition, said Romuld.

The first harvests at AOF are taking place as March 2024 begins, she said, while Ocean Farm 1 has recently harvested its third cycle of salmon.

As shown in the first image below, growth at Ocean Farm 1 exceeded expectations in the second generation and continued to do so in the third. This time out, a sea lice treatment was needed — still likely far less than at other traditional farms.

Click to expand

Survival rates are high, though SAO is aiming for 97% — it's not there yet at Ocean Farm 1.

At AOF — which operates two offshore cages — there have been zero sea lice treatments in this first cycle.

Click to expand

Growth rates have again been good, and survival rates have been higher at 96.4%.

"It's very promising, and we also have some things to learn, some improvements for the next generation, but it's a very good start," said Romuld.

SAO's long-term goal is still to produce 150,000t of salmon offshore.

title: EU opens door to fishing innovations in bid to improve ‘discard ban’ application
content:
The EU has clarified that member states can trial and implement innovative new fishing gears without first getting the approval of the Scientific, Technical and Economic Committee for Fisheries (STECF).

The news comes ahead of a seminar on innovative fishing methods to be held in Brussels, Belgium, on March 7, run by the North Sea Advisory Council (NSAC) and the European Association of Fish Producers Organisations.

The EU's common fisheries policy has required that all fish caught must be landed since 2019. This has caused a variety of issues, including the phenomenon of "choke species" (vessels using up all their by-catch quota before they've fully utilized another quota for a species that's swimming with said by-catch), and in general, is still not fully adhered to.

A "commitment to fully manage fish stocks by output -- total allowable catches (TACs) -- should be followed by a removal of prescriptive rules governing how the fishers conduct their fishery," said Mogens Schou, an independent fisheries policy adviser who has planned and will moderate the aforementioned seminar for NSAC.

"By the European Commission's own admission, the reform does not work; unaccounted discarding continues, and the recent revision of the EU Control Regulation is not going to change that."

In a November 2023 letter that Schou shared with Undercurrent News, the EU's Directorate-General for Maritime Affairs and Fisheries explained that:

"The general rule is that if a member state develops a new technical measure which is at least as good as the existing one, then it can implement these measures directly via national legislation, without having to agree it prior with other member states in a regional group via a joint recommendation."

"Therefore, in implementing the new technical measures, regulation any member state can implement a new gear based on national trials that have proven its effectiveness. Only if the Commission has doubts about the effectiveness of a new gear would we ask STECF to assess it after its implementation. The difference is hence that it is no longer necessary to get STECF assessment prior to the implementation of the new measure."

As Schou noted, transitioning from optimizing catches through discards to do it by selective fishing practices and flexible quota management remains a largely unexplored option. However, this may now change.

The opportunity for EU members to implement a free choice of gear based on national trials, provided the gear proves effective, offers an opportunity for a more flexible and selective approach within defined effectiveness boundaries, he said.

Member states could approve a new gear based on selectivity concerning fish sizes and species, aligning with EU Technical Regulation -- the traditional approach to trying to reduce discards of unwanted catches.

"However, managing fish stocks based on fishing mortality, rather than merely fish sizes, presents a more relevant approach in line with the objective of obtaining a maximum yield from fish stocks," he said. "Effectiveness should be measured by mortality rates comparable to those used by ICES [the International Council for the Exploration of the Seas] to calculate TACs."

Schou pointed to New Zealand's "Precision Seafood Harvesting" (seen in the featured image above) gear as an example of a trawl that "lets the fish swim freely in the bag, without being squeezed in the codend and which allows the undersized fish to swim freely out of the bag."

"The fish is brought live on deck and unwanted catches are released alive. The result is perfect selectivity, better fish welfare -- no stress, and high fish quality and price."

The technology was tested over 10 years and is now approved by the New Zealand government.

He acknowledged that the main hurdle for innovative gears at the moment was the requirement of a fully documented fishery via remote electronic monitoring (REM).

"Given that the proof of [gear] 'effectiveness' now lies with the member state, it will be up to them to establish REM coverage, mandatory or voluntary, as they wish. I am quite certain that the incentive to apply REM on a voluntary basis will be strong."

More details about the March NSAC seminar can be found here.

title: Canadian processor fined CAD 40,000 for undersized Dungies
content:
Tenshi Seafood Limited, a seafood processor in the Canadian province of British Columbia (BC), has been fined Can 40,000 ($29,606) for possession of undersized Dungeness crabs, Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) reports.

DFO made the ruling public on Monday (Feb. 20), though the fine was handed down on Dec. 6 by a Richmond, BC, provincial court. 

Tenshi, which is based in Richmond, was charged in January 2023 following a routine inspection of its processing plants and later pled guilty in court. 

The harvest of undersized Dungeness crabs is the largest threat to the conservation of the stocks, which is a traditional food source for indigenous communities and important for the livelihood of commercial crab harvesters, DFO said. In British Columbia, it is illegal to retain female Dungeness crabs and male Dungeness crab with a carapace size of less than 165 mm. 

This is the second significant fine in three years for Tenshi. In 2021 Tenshi was fined CAD 75,00, and its co-owner, Dishi Liu, was fined CAD 25,000 for selling undersized Dungeness crabs, as reported by Undercurrent News.

title: NZ King Salmon 30-year veteran resigns from board, firm wins open-ocean approval
content:
Paul Steere, who has been part of aquaculture company New Zealand King Salmon (NZKS) for three decades, has announced his resignation from the board.

Steere took charge as the firm's inaugural CEO in 1994 and, following his departure as CEO in 2009, he joined NZKS' board as an independent non-executive director. He has most recently been the chair of the audit, finance and risk committee.

NZ King Salmon settles appeals in boost for offshore plan

He also spent almost 14 years as director at Clean Seas Tuna, from 2010 to the present day, according to his LinkedIn profile.

NZKS announced the appointment of Paul Munro to the board, taking over as an independent non-executive director on March 1, 2024, and as chair of the audit, finance and risk committee on March 31.

Steere will step down from the board on March 31.

Meanwhile, NZKS has also been told of a positive decision regarding its "Blue Endeavour" open-ocean aquaculture plan made by Fisheries New Zealand, part of the Ministry for Primary Industries.

"Fisheries New Zealand assesses the effects of proposed marine farm areas on fishing through the undue adverse effects test. A proposed marine farm cannot proceed if it would have ‘undue’ adverse effects as defined by the process," the company explained.

The decision will be "gazetted" on Jan. 16, 2024, followed by a 30-working day judicial review period. A judicial review would require a judge of the High Court to examine whether the way the decision was made was in accordance with the law and no other matters, it said.

Should the judicial review period pass without issue, NZKS "can give effect to its already granted resource consent."

The company has been pursuing the project since 2018. If constructed, the proposed Blue Endeavour salmon farm would be the first of its kind in New Zealand, located seven kilometers north of Cape Lambert in Cook Strait.

Salmon producers are increasingly exploring the possibilities of farming cooler, open-ocean waters as climate change warms the waters.

In 2021, New Zealand King Salmon had to fallow three farms in the Pelorus Sounds in the Marlborough region of New Zealand after early elevated seawater temperatures in these three farms wiped off 28% of the company's fish, as Undercurrent News reported. Because farming is currently limited to just six farms, the company is expected to harvest only 6,500 metric tons of salmon in the 2024 fiscal year.

Following two challenging years for the salmon farming company, it announced a return to profitability in the first half of 2023-24 financial year, as Undercurrent reported.

The Blue Endeavour project could potentially bring an additional 10,000 metric tons of production for the company.

title: Former Cooke manager gets three years for CAD 2.8M copper-wire fraud
content:
Patrick Brennan, a former manager at Cooke Aquaculture subsidiary Kelly Cove Salmon in New Brunswick (NB), Canada, has been sentenced to serve three years in prison and fined CAD 100,000 ($74,719) for his part in a copper wire fraud scheme, Saltwire News reports.

Brennan was charged along with three others in August 2023 by a St. George, NB, detachment of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP). Together the group is alleged to have purchased and sold some CAD 2.8 million worth of copper wire, which they used to buy drugs.

Brennan, who served as saltwater manager at Kelly from 2012 until 2021, authorized more than 1,000 purchases of bare copper wire, according to the article. The company became aware of the irregularities through an internal review in 2021 and reported the findings to the RCMP. 

Cooke CEO Glenn Cooke described the incident as a "significant financial loss for the organization" that affected construction projects, damaged supplier relationships, and potentially harmed the company's reputation in the Charlotte County community, according to the article. In a victim impact statement, he expressed the company's disappointment in Brennan's misconduct and expressed gratitude that justice was being served.

Alongside Brennan, the other individuals charged in connection with the scheme include Andrew Peters, Melanie Pirie and Leonard Totten. The charges against them include conspiracy to commit fraud, fraud over CAD 5,000, possession of proceeds of crime property, and transporting the proceeds of crime.

Brennan changed his plea to guilty on the fraud charge, while Peters pleaded guilty to possessing stolen property and taking the copper wire for resale. Peters is scheduled for a disputed-facts sentencing hearing in October. The remaining two individuals are set for a five-day trial this month.

title: Trident: Sale of majority stake in Japan salmon roe JV ‘unrelated’ to US restructure
content:
Trident Seafoods' Japanese operation has sold its majority stake in a salmon roe joint venture (JV) to its local partner, a move the US industry giant told Undercurrent News is not connected to its ongoing domestic restructure.

On Dec. 29, 2023, Trident Seafoods Japan sold off all its shares in Trident Niigata Foods to the wholesaler Niigata Reizo. Trident Niigata Foods is a fish roe producer, established in 2015 as a JV with 3,000 shares held by Trident Seafoods Japan and 1,500 shares from Niigata Reizo. The company primarily produces salmon roe products, such as ikura, sujiko, and masuko, utilizing Trident's channels in raw product procurement and final product sales.

Trident selloff highlights uncertainty surrounding turbulent 2023 market

"The sale of Trident's share of Trident Niigata Foods to Niigata Reizo was under consideration for more than a year, and the deal finally closed," Alexis Telfer, vice president for Trident, told Undercurrent.

"The transaction is unrelated to our current initiatives in Alaska," said Telfer when asked if the deal was linked to Trident's wider US restructuring. The Trident restructure broke on Dec. 12, with the Seattle, Washington-based company announcing plans to seek buyers for Alaskan shore-side plants in Kodiak, Ketchikan, Petersburg and False Pass.

Trident is also retiring or seeking buyers for other assets, such as its historic South Naknek Diamond NN cannery facility and support facilities in Chignik, Alaska. The restructuring effort is not confined to Alaska; Trident said it is also streamlining and optimizing its head office support functions, resulting in a 10% reduction in headcount.

Russians see Alaskan pollock ‘monopoly’ the only result of new US trade ban

The Trident Japan JV share sale and US restructure come with prices for pollock and salmon set low, putting the whole Alaskan industry under pressure.

Niigata Reizo hopes Trident cooperation can continue

Niigata Reizo hopes to continue to work with Trident even after the parting of ways on the roe JV.

"We have a long-term business partner with Trident Seafoods and try to keep up a cooperative relationship even after the transaction," an official of Niigata Reizo told Undercurrent. However, Trident Seafoods Japan and Niigata Reizo have agreed in the stock purchase agreement to exclude the Trident brand from the company name.

US importer blasts Alaskans ‘masquerading’ monopolism as patriotism over stricter Russian tariffs 

Takashi Mizushina, a logistical management executive for Niigata Reizo, was named president of the roe sales venture at an extraordinal general meeting held on Dec. 29, 2023.

Following the transaction, Trident Seafoods Japan is expected to focus on more pollock and salmon operations to boost sales and explore new business in the Asian country, sources said. 

The company currently runs a plant in Choshi, Chiba Prefecture, for salmon products, while its subsidiary Mangokunotsubu produces surimi seafood products in Onagawa, Miyagi. Then, Trident Osabe Foods, a JV with Osabe Foods, is involved in pollock processing.

title: Iceland’s proposed aquaculture fees would smother growth, industry fears
content:
Iceland's Ministry for Food, Agriculture and Fisheries has pushed back the deadline for submitting views on its new aquaculture regulations by one week to Jan. 10, 2024.

"In the bill, a new comprehensive law is proposed on marine farming, land-based farming and offshore farming. The goal of the bill is to create legal conditions in Iceland for increased value creation guided by sustainable utilization and an ecosystem approach," the government said.

Embracing land-based, offshore farming, Icelandic aquaculture can become new economic pillar

It wants to see Iceland's aquaculture laws based on "defined parameters that prevent the industry from having a negative impact on its environment, whether on ecosystems or wild populations. In addition, animal welfare and disease prevention will be the best in the world."

The Association of Fisheries Companies (named SFS for its Icelandic name, Samtok fyrirtaekja i sjavarutvegi) had revealed its displeasure at the initial deadline of Jan. 3, stating: "There is very little time for such an extensive and impressive matter, during the holidays. This is very disrespectful to the consultation process."

One week further is likely to be scant consolation.

SFS backs the government's aims in hoping to see aquaculture grow sustainably, and to bring land-based farming the dedicated regulations it needs. However, its response to the bill consultation is unlikely to be glowing. 

"Such punitive punishments and sanctions are proposed for certain matters that the operational basis of companies in salmon farming in Iceland is seriously weighed," it said.

"The minister goes against the guidelines of a detailed Boston Consulting Group report prepared for the Minister of Food last year. It recommended both moderate fees in a growing industry as well as forward thinking for the future, as there are many opportunities. The minister proposes both high and burdensome taxes and considers the operating basis of the companies."

The new bill proposes banning aquaculture in Eyjarfjordur and Oxarfjordur in order to protect the fjords -- but SFS argues that such plans were not present in any mooted plans this year, so no scientific examination of the areas has been carried out to determine whether they need protection or not.

SFS further noted that the proposed new tax and fee environment is comparable to other salmon farming nations as they are now; "these plans go significantly further than what is done in the countries we compare ourselves to, where the growth of the sector was supported with a reasonable fee environment in the early days of development."

Iceland's sector is still in that early growth phase, it argued, and so should be helped.

As Norway's companies have said all year, higher taxes and fees reduce the scope for companies to invest in new technologies or solutions.

"Despite that, the minister makes increased demands on companies in salmon farming to invest in more environmentally friendly solutions for food production. [...] There is a great desire on the part of companies in aquaculture to look for the most environmentally friendly ways in their operations, but this requires a lot of long-term funding."

title: Canadian Indigenous lobster harvesters upset over fines for fishing out of season
content:
Two Mi'kmaw fishermen from the Pictou Landing First Nation in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia, convicted of fishing lobsters in closed season, are not happy with their CAD 7,000 ($5,245) fine following a sentencing circle hearing earlier this month, reports Kukukwes News, an independent Indigenous news outlet in Canada. 

William Nicholas and his son, Zachary, were charged with fishing lobster in Lobster Fishing Area 26, near Pictou Landing, in October 2019, months after the season.

Both men had originally pled not guilty and initially intended to challenge the charges on constitutional grounds, arguing that Canada's Fisheries Act violates their treaty right to catch and sell fish to earn a moderate livelihood. However, they withdrew their challenge in September, reportedly because they could not afford the legal fees needed to bring in expert witnesses.

William Nicholas also claims they were unable to get legal support from the Pictou First Nations chief and council.

"We didn't have enough money to fight for, you know, to take it to a higher court," he reportedly told Kukekwes News. "We had no choice."

The case was heard in a sentencing circle, an Indigenous restorative justice hearing tribunal sometimes chosen as an alternative to the formal criminal court system. It involves a collaboration with members of the community and the criminal justice system.

Zachery Nicholas was fined CAD 750 for each offense, for a total of CAD 3,000, while his father was fined CAD 1,000 for each offense, totaling CAD 4,000.

More than 50 Mi'kmaw fishers have been charged with illegally fishing lobster or elvers and 19 of them indicated they will fight the charges on constitutional grounds. Only two of those 19 are supported by Mi'kmaw leadership in Nova Scotia, according to Kukekwes News.

The Millbrook First Nation and the Assembly of Nova Scotia Mi'kmaw Chiefs have each retained lawyers on behalf of the two men.

title: Environmentalists express concern as Asian vessels gather outside Argentine waters
content:
Conservationist Milko Schvartzman has issued a warning about the recent influx of a massive fleet of Asian vessels that have congregated near mile 200 of the Argentine exclusive economic zone (EEZ).

This development has raised concerns about the environmental impact and regulatory challenges posed by these vessels, according to Schvartzman, who is responsible for the conservation and fishing program of the Environmental Policy Circle, a digital platform that focuses on policy.

Argentinean illex squid prices still elevated in China

In an article he posted on his LinkedIn page, Schvartzman said that approximately 100 Chinese ships are en route to the edge of the Argentine EEZ, originating from the Pacific Ocean. Furthermore, he pointed out that -based on satellite images- there will be a total of at least 400 Chinese vessels, in addition to 200 vessels from other nations, including Koreans, Taiwanese, and Spanish. All those vessels are engaged in fishing activities that appear to lack proper regulation and oversight in the South Atlantic region, according to Schvartzman.

The article doesn't specify which species is being pursued by so many harvesters, however, the area is known as a major squid fishery.

"This foreign fishing mega fleet assembles annually with substantial predation, encroaching upon mile 200 of the Argentine EEZ, a situation that is unparalleled anywhere else in the world," he said. "Nowhere else globally do we witness such a large concentration of vessels operating without adherence to any regulations, all within such a confined area. This stretch of sea where the fleet operates inflicts severe environmental harm on the South Atlantic marine ecosystem and negatively impacts the economies of coastal nations that rely on the same species targeted by this fleet," he continued.

Schvartzman stressed that it is crucial to recognize that the ecological impact inflicted by a fishing vessel operating at mile 201, in an unregulated context, is no different from that of a vessel fishing at mile 199, which would be deemed illegal.

The distinction lies only in the legal terminology, but the ecological consequences for the marine environment remain the same.

He emphasized the need for governments to seek solutions proactively and called for collaboration with neighboring countries like Brazil and Uruguay to coordinate monitoring efforts.

This year, Argentina's squid season, which is meant to restart in January, has been characterized by low catches.

title: Spain sanctions vessels for disabling tracking devices off Argentina
content:
The Spanish government has investigated and sanctioned 25 Spanish-flagged vessels for infractions while fishing on the high seas, based on a 2021 analysis from NGO Oceana, which you can read here. 

These fishing vessels were fined up to $65,000 (€60,000) for repeatedly turning off their automatic identification systems (AIS) on multiple occasions without cause, which is illegal for Spanish-flagged fishing vessels.

The sanctioned vessels were fishing near Argentinian waters between 2018 and 2021. Around 90% of the Spanish-flagged vessels cited in Oceana's analysis appeared to turn off their public tracking devices at least once. Spanish-flagged vessels spent nearly twice as much time with AIS devices off as they did visibly fishing.

Mediterranean states moves to combat overfishing with sanction system

"Oceana applauds this admirable step taken by the Spanish government to take action against vessels that openly flout the rules as if they are above the law," said Max Valentine, Oceana campaign director. "Mandating and enforcing the use of AIS devices is crucial to increase the transparency of fishing at sea."

These sanctions directly result from Oceana's analysis, which was shared with the Spanish Directorate-General for Merchant Shipping and highlighted ships navigating with their AIS devices allegedly turned off. 

Oceana analyzed the activity of fishing vessels along the border of Argentina's national waters from Jan. 1, 2018, to April 25, 2021, using data from Global Fishing Watch, an independent nonprofit founded by Oceana in partnership with Google and SkyTruth. AIS devices transmit a vessel's name, flag state, and location. 

"We welcome the decision of the Spanish administration to take another step in favor of transparency in the fishing sector," said the advisor of Oceana's illegal fishing and transparency campaign in Europe, Ignacio Fresco Vanzini. "Those who do not respect the rules should know that their actions have consequences; in this case, it is in the form of sanctions. The use of Automatic Identification Systems is key to the safety of fishermen, for states to know what is happening in their waters, and to ensure that fishing activities are carried out within the law."

Vessel tracking made compulsory for all EU fishing vessels

While turning off AIS devices without legitimate security concerns is illegal in places like the European Union, few countries have AIS requirements like Spain and rarely take action against fishing vessels for this violation, said the NGO. 

Any fishing vessel flagged to a European Union (EU) country greater than 49 feet (15 meters) in length must be equipped with an AIS device that transmits the vessel's location, direction, and speed at sea. 

Navigating without AIS is considered an infringement of EU and Spanish law, as vessels can only turn off AIS legitimately in exceptional situations and while following specific rules, like when navigating in areas where piracy could be a problem.

The sanctioned vessels repeatedly turned off their AIS without legitimate reasons more than 1,200 times for at least 24 hours. In contrast to the EU, the US only mandates AIS usage for fishing boats over 65 feet (20 meters), which comprise only 12.4% of the country's fishing fleet.

This small portion of ships is only required to have AIS turned on within 12 nautical miles of shore, which covers less than 8% of the country's exclusive economic zone, with no AIS requirements while operating on the high seas, said Oceana.

title: Trident plans to sell four Alaska shoreside plants, cut staff in ‘comprehensive restructuring’
content:
Trident Seafoods announced Tuesday (Dec. 12) that it's begun a "comprehensive restructuring initiative" that involves seeking potential buyers for four of its Alaska shoreside plants among other moves.

The news coming from the vertically integrated, Seattle, Washington-based giant may be unsettling as it suggests financial woes at one of the US seafood industry's oldest and largest players. Trident has been operating continuously in Alaska for more than 50 years and maintains a significant presence in the Alaskan whitefish and salmon arena while also operating processing plants globally. 

"Bold action today is necessary to deliver fair value to fleet, communities, and all stakeholders into the future," said Joe Bundrant, the company's CEO, in a statement.

The company will be a bit smaller not long after Tuesday's announcement.

Among the changes being discussed is a plan to seek buyers for its diverse operations in Kodiak, Alaska, and move to a significantly scaled-back winter season. The Kodiak plants operate nearly year-round and support multiple species, including primarily pollock, salmon, Pacific cod and crab, the company noted.

"Our Kodiak operations are integral to the Gulf of Alaska fisheries," noted Jeff Welbourn, senior vice president of Alaska operations, in the statement. "They are highly efficient, multispecies plants, and we are working diligently to find a new owner to support the fleet and the Kodiak community."

To round out the Alaska operations strategy, Trident said it's retiring or seeking buyers for other assets, such as its historic South Naknek Diamond NN cannery facility and support facilities in Chignik.

Trident said it's also assessing its overall company-owned vessel strategy.

The restructuring effort is not confined to Alaska either. Trident said it is also streamlining and optimizing its head office support functions, resulting in a 10% reduction in headcount.

Undercurrent News reported in late September how Trident had been on an executive hiring spree, adding multiple blue-chip names to its ranks. The company doesn't say in its statement where it plans to reduce its labor force.

Pollock fillet prices follow surimi down

Trident also announced that its regional salmon strategy would refocus operations in Southeast Alaska and Area M. The move will see the company seeking buyers for its seasonal plants in Ketchikan, Petersburg and False Pass.

"These are all well-maintained operations that align better with other operators’ strategies," Welbourn said. "We are optimistic the combination of new ownership and our continued service to the fleet through our other locations will mean little to no disruption for regional salmon fleets."

Trident said its restructuring effort enables it to execute its strategic drive to modernize its processing plants throughout Alaska. In August, it announced a delay to the three-year plan to build a new, state-of-the-art processing plant in Unalaska’s Dutch Harbor to replace its aging plant in Akutan, Alaska. Construction is likely to resume once the restructuring activities are complete, the company said.

Trident Seafoods' plant in Akutan, Alaska. Credit: Trident

"We are modernizing and re-tooling the remaining Alaska plants to be more efficient, effective and sustainable operations," said Welbourn. "This will allow us to continue supporting as many fleets and communities as possible across Alaska for the long term."

Trident, like other Alaska-based harvesting and processing companies, has been struggling this year with both low pollock and salmon prices among other issues, as reported by Undercurrent. Bundrant spoke to the matter in August in announcing the delay of its new Unalaska plant.

"I've been in the industry a long time, and I've never seen markets like this," he said at the time. "The rate and pace at which markets are collapsing across our key species is staggering. Not only are global inventories and operating costs high, but demand is low, and some are selling at or below cost just to generate cash."

With a projected three-year build plan, the new timeline means the plant would be operational no sooner than 2028, Trident said in a statement sent to Undercurrent at the time. 

The company addressed its struggles again in Tuesday's statement, noting how "foreign competition has driven prices down, squeezed margins, and displaced US producers from markets that they developed over decades."

Trident delays build of new Unalaska plant amid ‘collapsing’ markets

Bundrant is quoted as saying: "We are competing against producers in other countries that do not share our commitment to or investments in environmental sustainability, social responsibility, and product quality. Many of our foreign competitors operate with minimal regulatory costs and oversight, inexpensive infrastructure, and exploitive labor practices."

He added: "Overall, I remain confident in the Alaska seafood industry and our role in it. These are significant changes, and we are focused on treating our impacted employees and communities with the respect and compassion they deserve. Embracing these changes and operating a more streamlined company will allow us to reinvest in the communities, people, processes, and assets that enable us to continue our mission of responsibly sharing wild Alaska seafood with the world."

title: Untitled
content:
Prices for small headed and gutted (H&G) frozen cod and saithe have continued to drop on Norway's auctions in recent weeks, with the usual pre-Christmas upturn still yet to appear in week 49 (Dec. 4-10), according to the latest data from domestic auction house Norges Rafisklag.

With H&G haddock prices now holding firm (see below), the price gap between similar sizes of the two species has shrunk to NOK 22 per kilogram, the smallest since the summer.

In euro terms, the average value of smaller frozen cod has been on a steady downward trajectory since August and now sits at a weekly average of €3.51/kg, down a whole euro from €4.53/kg in the same week of 2022 (second chart, below):

Upgrade to Pro to view

For H&G frozen cod, volumes have picked up a little in recent weeks, but the majority of the volume remains fish from the smallest size category, 1-2.5kg.

As a result, average auction prices for frozen cod have now fallen below NOK 45/kg to a weekly average of NOK 44.49/kg:

Over the last two weeks, cod from the lowest defined weight category have comprised 2,387 metric tons of the 3,400t total sold on the auction.

This bump in supply has prompted prices of 1-2.5kg frozen cod to slump from NOK 44/kg down to NOK 41/kg in just three weeks:

For other sizes, it's very much as you were. Prices for the medium size category, 2.5-4kg, have actually seen a small uptick to NOK 51.96/kg, although only 184t were sold, a far cry from 636t in the same week of 2022:

Finally, with the largest 4-6kg frozen cod in short supply all year, it is no surprise that prices refuse to budge from the current height of NOK 65/kg, with only 60t sold on the auction in week 49.

For fresh cod, prices have leveled out after the spike and drop seen through October and early November. Norges Rafisklag put the latest weekly average prices across all sizes at NOK 41.28/kg for the small 126t volume sold.

Typically, volumes of fresh cod do not begin to truly pick up again until the fishing season starts in late January:

While Norwegian krone prices have now very much returned to the level of 2022, the relative weakening of the krone in that time means that they are lagging some €0.20/kg below the same week of 2022 when measured in euros:

Haddock settles as huge volumes of saithe hit market

It appears that this year's non-stop price downturn for frozen haddock has finally come to an end, at least on Norges Rafisklag's auction.

Values for H&G frozen haddock over 0.8kg have stabilized in the last couple of months, and week 49 saw little change as prices held at NOK 19.91/kg on average despite volumes dropping to 289t.

Frozen haddock prices remain some 39% lower than the same week of 2022, but that gap is now shrinking at last:

For smaller frozen haddock under 0.8kg in weight, average prices are a little lower, at NOK 17.94/kg on average -- although volumes are negligible at present:

The same cannot be said of frozen saithe, which saw another week of huge volumes on the auction.

In the main commercial size category of 1.2-2.3kg frozen H&G saithe alone, 1,424t of fish were sold on the auction at an average price of NOK 15.44/kg.

Curiously, this is a slightly higher price than the previous week, when only 188t were sold at a rock-bottom NOK 14.83/kg. It remains to be seen whether the huge volumes of week 49 will have a knock-on impact on demand in future weeks:

It was a similar story for larger, 2.3kg frozen saithe -- volumes surged to 513t, the second-highest week of the year, while prices also saw a small uptick back to NOK 18/kg.

Sales of smaller frozen saithe under 1.2kg in weight remain low, however, with just 235t sold in the latest week, at a nadir of NOK 14.62/kg.

title: UK, EU, Norway trilateral fishery talks conclude, several quotas hiked
content:
The UK fishing industry will have access to 420,000 metric tons worth of fishing opportunities worth up to £700 million ($878.2m) after agreements were reached with the EU and Norway, the UK government claimed.

That brings the total fishing opportunities secured for the UK fleet in 2024 in the main negotiating forums to 750,000t -- 80,000t more than in 2023 -- worth up to £970m based on historic landing prices.  

The deal with the EU has secured UK fishermen access to opportunities of 130,000t for 2024, worth up to £340m, it said.  

The trilateral deal with the EU and Norway secures access to opportunities for 290,000t of North Sea stocks, worth around £360m. 

This is on top of 330,000t, worth around £270m, from catch limits agreed earlier in the year on widely distributed stocks with coastal states in the northeast Atlantic, it added.

As a result of quota share uplifts agreed in the post-Brexit Trade and Cooperation Agreement, the UK has up to 120,000t more quota from the 2024 negotiations than it would have received as an EU member state, the government claimed.

In the fourth year of the UK operating as an independent coastal state in the negotiations, catch levels were agreed for over 80 important total allowable catches. This included key commercial stocks across the industry, including northern shelf cod, North Sea saithe, and nephrops stocks in the Celtic/Irish Sea.

"These significant deals give UK fishermen access to important fish stocks worth £970m and take advantage of our position outside the EU to independently negotiate in our fishing fleets' best interest," said UK fisheries minister Mark Spencer.

"They are based on the latest scientific advice and support a sustainable, profitable fishing sector for years to come while continuing to protect our marine environment and vital fishing grounds. Sustainability has been at the heart of the UK's approach to negotiations, pushing for decisions based on the best available science to protect key stocks and support the long-term viability of the UK fishing industry. Advice from scientists at the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (ICES) is the starting point for the UK's approach and, where possible, catch limits have been set at or within these advised levels."

A provisional estimate is that the same number of jointly managed stocks have been set in line with or lower than the levels advised by ICES scientists compared to last year, despite challenging advice for a number of stocks, the UK said. A full and independent review of the sustainability of negotiated outcomes will be published early in the new year. 

The full outcome of annual fisheries negotiations is to be published in the Secretary of State's determination of fishing opportunities for British boats by the end of the year.  

"Our agreement with the UK secures important fishing opportunities for our fishers and was reached thanks to the goodwill demonstrated by both parties during the negotiations," said Luis Planas Puchades, Spanish minister for agriculture, fisheries and food, on behalf of the EU. "We have ensured that our fishing rights in the Atlantic and the North Sea will continue to be protected in the coming year and we are living up to our sustainability commitments."

The EU also stressed that it had stuck to ICES' advice where it could, and had worked with the UK to improve data availability where needed.

That meant total allowable catch (TAC) cuts for haddock in the Irish Sea (-14.5%), haddock in the Celtic Sea (-30.6%), whiting in the Celtic Sea (-50%), and plaice by-catches in the English Channel (-42%). 

It also allowed for lifts in TACs for whiting in the West of Scotland (+20%) and megrim in the North Sea (+9.6%). The full table of TAC figures can be found here.

During the Agriculture and Fisheries Council meeting, which will take place on Dec. 10 and 11, EU ministers will aim to reach a political agreement on the overall fishing opportunities in the Atlantic and the North Sea for 2024 and, in some cases, also for 2025 and 2026.

The figures for the EU-UK shared stocks will become part of that political agreement.

Norway happy with 'balance'

The Norwegian government noted the exchange of quotas with the EU has a long tradition, but in recent years has been more demanding than before, since Norwegian vessels have traditionally fished for quotas that are now in the British zone.

"It is good that we now agree with the EU on these agreements. We have had a good tone in the negotiations and the result is balanced. Getting agreements in place with those we share stocks with, well in advance of Christmas, is a priority task for the government," said Norway's fisheries and oceans minister Cecilie Myrseth.

"With quota swaps in place, it means that Norwegian fishermen can fish on the quotas Norway has swapped for Greenland, including prawns [coldwater shrimp], blue halibut and redfish, and in the EU zone, such as pollock."

The EU, for its part, has switched to a cod quota in the Barents Sea of ​​9,981t.

"With these agreements in place, Norwegian fishermen have predictability, and the opportunity to fish the quotas contained in the agreements when it is rational and economical. It was important for both parties to now get this in place and I am very satisfied with it," said Myrseth.

Norway spent a lot of time discussing the management of cod and North Sea herring with the UK, it said.

As a result, the parties have agreed on a total quota for 2024 of 31,301t, which is an increase of 15% compared to the quota for 2023. This quota includes cod west of Scotland. The quota set aside for the North Sea is 24,900t, with the Norwegian share coming to 4,233t.

Changes in ICES methodology have complicated quota determination, and there is a need to look more closely at how this will be done in the future, Norway noted. "The method for setting the quota for cod for 2024 is therefore temporary."

The parties also agreed to continue closing the spawning grounds for cod in 2024. The closures will take place in the first quarter. Norway will, as in previous years, consider closing fields in the Norwegian zone to protect small cod later in the year. 

For North Sea herring, Norway and the UK have adopted a TAC of 532,166t, up 28.3% compared to 2023. The Norwegian quota is 147,994t.

For pollock, the two parties have adopted a total quota for 2024 of 73,815t, up 25%, with a Norwegian quota of 34,776t.

For haddock, they agreed a total quota of 101,420t, an increase of 17.8%. The Norwegian quota is 23,327t.

Oceana unconvinced

However, environmental NGO Oceana warned the negotiations on yearly fishing catch limits between the EU and UK have "again ended with a significant number of fish populations put at risk of overfishing and collapse, including key species such as cod."

In the agreement for next year's 71 catch limits for shared fish populations, the UK and the EU have continued to ignore scientific advice for a significant proportion of fish populations, it said.

Preliminary analysis of the agreement indicates that there has been no breakthrough in terms of increasing the number of catch limits in line with scientific advice compared to previous years, with many severely depleted populations remaining at grave risk, said Oceana.

"Yet again, where is the 'gold standard' of fisheries management that our [UK] government claims to be striving for? As the worrying outcome of these catch negotiations show, we are struggling to reach bronze standard, or even make it to the podium at all," said Hugo Tagholm, executive director at Oceana in the UK.

"These piecemeal adjustments -- one step forwards, two steps back -- threaten our ability to safeguard our seas, our fish populations and our coastal communities. The simple fact is that the EU and UK could end overfishing tomorrow by following independent scientific advice and setting sustainable limits. We should seize the opportunity to let our seas bounce back to thriving good health, rather than playing a shameful part in their destruction."

Vera Coelho, deputy vice president at Oceana in Europe, said this new agreement "quite simply goes against the law."

"This irresponsible decision by the EU and the UK to continue overfishing severely depleted populations of much-loved species, like cod, herring, and horse mackerel is putting their future at risk. Preserving these populations is our shared responsibility, vital not only for the health of our ocean but also for the viability of coastal fishing communities."

Over a quarter (26%) of northeast Atlantic fish populations are still overfished, a report this year by the Scientific, Technical and Economic Committee for Fisheries of the European Commission revealed. Less than half (40%) of UK catch limits were set in line with scientific advice in 2023, according to a report from UK government advisors, the Centre for Environment Fisheries and Aquaculture Science.

Scotland: Science supports increased quotas

The Scottish government noted the UK/EU/Norway trilateral agreement includes quota increases for all six of the jointly managed North Sea stocks: cod, haddock, whiting, plaice, saithe, and herring.

"This reflects positive advice from [ICES], with all TACs set at levels consistent with the maximum sustainable yield approach. These opportunities are worth an estimated value to Scotland of £199m, an increase of £68m compared to 2023 quotas."

It said UK/EU bilateral negotiations to set TACs for more than 70 stocks, including the North Sea and West of Scotland, have also concluded, with an estimated value to Scotland of £194m. Among the stocks covered by this agreement are North Sea and West of Scotland nephrops, hake, monkfish and ling, as well as Rockall haddock and cod, and West of Scotland whiting and cod.

"These agreements include a number of positive outcomes for Scotland, providing key opportunities to vessels and coastal communities, and building on the successes of last year's negotiations," said Cabinet Secretary for Rural Affairs, Land Reform and Islands Mairi Gougeon.

"I am particularly pleased that agreement has been reached to set quotas for North Sea and West of Scotland cod at levels reflective of the latest science. This is the first step in transforming the way in which we manage this iconic stock, and I look forward to the continuation of that important work in 2024."

Establishing appropriate catch limits for North Sea and West of Scotland cod was Scotland's top priority in this year's negotiations, and the increases in these quotas for 2024 reflect an extremely positive picture of the health of the newly defined north-western stock, said the Scottish government.

Credit: Scottish government

"This represents a step change away from the previous zero TAC advice for the West of Scotland. Discussions to further develop the management of this stock, in light of the latest scientific information will take place in 2024. Scotland's priority will be to ensure an appropriate and evidence-based approach to these management changes as we move to a new set of area-based advice and subsequent sharing discussions with Norway."

Bilateral discussions with Norway and the Faroe Islands on additional exchanges of access and quota opportunities are ongoing.

title: New Icelandic aquaculture legislation goes up for consultation
content:
The Icelandic government has submitted its new bill on aquaculture reform for consultation, proposing stricter regulations and a change in production fees.

Food minister Svandis Svavarsdottir's proposed bill is the result of extensive policy work that began at the beginning of 2022, the government said.

"The goal of the bill is to create legal conditions in Iceland for increased value creation guided by sustainable utilization and an ecosystem approach. It is also emphasized that aquaculture will be managed based on defined parameters that prevent the industry from having a negative impact on its environment, whether on ecosystems or wild populations. In addition, animal welfare and disease prevention will be the best in the world."

The main changes and innovations proposed in the bill that relate to open net-open farming are:

Waste and sea lice infestation in pens have a direct impact on production potential
Production allowances are to be limited in the event of escapes from pens
The percentage of sexually mature fish in a sea pen may not exceed 1%
The production fee will be "more in line with the producers' income generation"
An ecosystem approach and animal welfare will be prioritized through the introduction of infection control zones
Eyjafjordur and Oxarfjordur will be protected from farming and the current conservation areas will be formalized in law
Genetic risk assessments will be based on the number of fish instead of biomass
The transfer of breeding permits for fertile salmon between regions will be possible
The predictability and independence of municipalities should increase under changes to the current Fisheries Fund
The Marine Research Institute's advisory role is clarified
The supervision and control powers of the food safety authority Matvaelastofnun will be strengthened

Land-based aquaculture will, for the first time, be specifically addressed in legislation. Discussion on this topic is focused on infection control and animal health.

Aquaculture further offshore is not yet practiced in Iceland, but there has been increased interest in the activity in recent years, the government noted.

"In order to find out if and where offshore farming is promising in Icelandic jurisdiction, it is necessary to undertake detailed research, which needs to be framed. A framework for the licensing process also needs to be created, but it is very important that predictability and clear legislation exist to support the first steps of the industry."

The consultation will run until Jan. 3, 2024, and the documents (in Icelandic) can be found here.

title: More gov’t action needed to drive Norway’s great feed shift, says Wathne
content:
TRONDHEIM, Norway -- It's no great secret that the Achilles' heel of Norway's enormous salmon sector is its dependence on foreign sources of aquafeed.

Nofima launches Cargill-backed project to optimize algae, insect ingredients for aquafeed

So, in a year when global fishmeal and fish oil prices have soared to eye-watering heights, the Norwegian government has accelerated its ambitious intent to source 100% of the nation's feed from sustainable sources by 2030, with a heavy emphasis on domestic production.

Longtime industry veteran and former EWOS CEO Einar Wathne, now a member of the government's advisory committee overseeing the mission project, detailed its sweeping ambition to Undercurrent News.

"It is a fantastic opportunity on the feed side, as the Norwegian government has created one or two missions for developing sustainable feed programs, where all feeds for both the green and blue sectors in Norway will come from sustainable sources," he said.

"We want to reach a 50% reduction in LCA [life cycle assessment carbon emissions] -- but such an ambitious change cannot be done only with the help of the market and the dynamic between suppliers, farmers and consumers."

According to a report published earlier this year by Norwegian research institution SINTEF, only 180,000 metric tons of the 1.05 million metric tons used across both terrestrial and marine farming is produced in Norway. Of this figure, 110,000t is actually grain raw material intended for livestock, not aquaculture.

Presently, 92% of the aquaculture sector's feed is imported from elsewhere, in some cases from environmentally dubious sources, and dependent on supply chains at the mercy of geopolitics and climate. The report claims that feed ingredients account for roughly 70% of the salmon sector's carbon footprint.

It's obvious that something dramatic needs to happen if the country intends to pursue its long-term annual production target of 5m metric tons of farmed fish by 2050, a goal that SINTEF estimates will require 2m metric tons of aquafeed. It's not a gap in future supply so much as a yawning chasm.

Einar Wathne in 2019. Photograph courtesy of Cargill.

Of course, growing the share of sustainable feed production and growing Norwegian feed production are two different prospects. Wathne said one of the first goals of the advisory committee is to define which imported feed ingredients are actually sustainable.

"We will probably not go greenfield, but the criteria needs to cover LCA, it needs to cover biodiversity, land use, etc," he told Undercurrent. "So we will propose then to set down a new sustainability standard, and that will be defined to imported ingredients first."

With this classification to hand, the Norwegian government could use taxes and other incentives to drive farmers to change their sourcing policy where needed, Wathne said.

"Then, in the longer run, we would hope they can develop a scaled-up production in Norway, but the first phase is to work with the 92% imported ingredients and really put up standards so we can make that shift."

There is also the cost issue; traditionally, novel feed ingredients entering the market, such as algal oil and insect meal, come at a higher price than conventional ingredients like fishmeal and fish oil.

2023's feed prices, of course, have been anything but traditional, yet Wathne believes standard market dynamics are still insufficient to drive change on the scale that the committee is after.

"If we have a really transactional business as we have in feed at the moment, we will not reach those results. The push is there from the retailers, but it's not strong enough to make a substantial shift; this change doesn't come without help," he said.

"As we have done with changing to electric cars, it was incentivized. We've got a tax relief on your electric car, you didn't need to pay the toll road, all these good things. That's why more than 50% of the cars in Norway are now electric."

What could Norway's future feed sector look like?

Naturally, beyond incentivizing farmers to adopt more sustainable feeds, the end goal here is that Norway may one day produce the majority of its own feed and reduce dependence on erratic production and prices from other countries.

Nofima launches Cargill-backed project to optimize algae, insect ingredients for aquafeed

At the most basic level, this means better use of fish waste streams, such as using more fish byproducts to make fishmeal instead of selling mackerel, herring or salmon whole, with heads and backbones that will eventually go to waste, Wathne said.

"Then we have green renewable energy and a lot of hydroelectric power, which is a great input into any process," he told Undercurrent. "So if we could have fermentation where we don't need to bring feedstock from sugar but use other feedstocks instead, then we can combine that with our industrial efficiency to build concentrated fermentation plants. But I think that one will take a bit longer."

There are other seafood products that could be grown as a feed source while working in tandem with the existing salmon farms, he added.

"It's also about using our fjords for feed growing. So blue mussels, tunicates, even macroalgae that can't be used directly, but maybe parts of it can," Wathne continued. "And they will enable nutrient balance because they would take out nutrients that the salmon is loading."

Already, he claimed, some salmon farmers have begun using mussels adjacent to their farms to reduce the local nitrogen and phosphorus load produced by the salmon pens.

"So there is a clear win-win here, but again, if you're going to make feed with it, you need to be scaled up. So one of the political issues will be allocating big areas for fields of blue mussel growing or other species."

"Objectively, science-based, we can do it -- but we need a willingness to go for it."

Therein lies another potential roadblock: will the political ambition to push a fully sustainable feed industry within Norway remain if, as polls currently suggest is likely, the incumbent Labour government is replaced by Norway's Conservative party at the next election in 2025?

For his part, Wathne is unconcerned.

"I think they are investing so much, and it has such a long horizon that it will probably be discussed, but it would be very strange for a new government to completely change it; the theme has broad political support," he told Undercurrent. 

"I hope we can get actions in place soon; some of those big inventions and sustainable fuel programs have been well supported, so it's not really where the big political discrepancy between the blue and red side is."

The newly introduced ground rent tax has been a far more divisive, headline-grabbing issue, but with feed, Wathne believes there is an opportunity for the government to soften the blow for the aquaculture sector.

"If they take tax money in, we haven't yet seen how they are going to make this pay back. So maybe this is where the government could show some support if they are willing to reinvest some of that tax in bringing the industry in the desired direction."

"Sometimes it may seem that there is polarization in the political discussion, but it's not that big. The political system in Norway broadly supports the growth of aquaculture, which is a bit different from other producing countries, and I think this sustainability focus is a supported shift."

title: New Canadian fishing vessel’s design fine-tuned during ocean voyage
content:
A new fishing vessel is taking shape at the Chantir Naval Forillon shipyard in Gaspé, in the Canadian province of Quebec. The 27-meter-long boat will be delivered to Pecherie Turbide in the Magdalen Islands, on Canada's East Coast, in the spring of 2024.

The multi-purpose vessel, temporarily named Optimum, will be able to fish for snow crab in the spring, before its on-board equipment is modified to gear up for trawling in the fall, reports La Presse.

The vessel was designed by Navanex, a company launched in 2019 as a division of Chantier Naval Forillon. 

Engineers Hubert Simard and Jean-Nil Poirier Morissette spent 10 days in the North Atlantic in January on a fishing vessel they had designed, to get a deeper understanding of life at sea. They faced winds of up to 55 knots and swells of up to 7 meters (23 feet), not to mention regular doses of nausea.

"We had a good understanding of how fishermen fish, but we decided to do a field experiment to really understand it and feel it," Simard, project manager at Navanex, told La Presse. "... It took us a couple of days to get over [the trip], but after that we knew what we were talking about."

As a result of their sea voyage, the engineers identified a number of ways to improve the safety and ergonomics of operations on the fishing deck. They improved visibility from the control station by eliminating blind spots.

They also refined the shape of the hull, and its bow bulb, to reduce flow resistance, added a recessed stabilizer fin and included a ballast water system enabling the trim of the vessel to be configured to suit different fishing conditions.

An energy-efficient exhaust gas treatment system as well as a liquid ice "slurry" generating system will be among the modern features on the new vessel, which was specifically designed with the resurgence of the redfish fishery in the Gulf and Atlantic in mind.

In a press release, Navanex touted its design as "the best large vessel under 24 meters ever built," adding the design would be available for sale and build by other shipyards.

title: Court slams Canadian province for severe punishment of lobster seller
content:
It was overkill.

That's how Nova Scotia Supreme Court justice Pierre Muise described the two-year ban imposed by the Canadian province on a lobster pound owner caught with crustaceans harvested under an Indigenous license that does not permit selling the catch, CBC News reports.

Tyler Nickerson, who owns Fisher Direct in Shag Harbour, was charged in 2018 after fishery officers from Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) raided the pound and found 47 lobsters that had been tagged for Indigenous food, social or ceremonial (FSC) purposes. An FSC license does not permit the sale of the catch.

Nickerson pleaded guilty in March 2022 to violating the federal Fisheries Act and was fined CAD 20,000 ($14,602).

After that, Steve Craig, who was a fisheries minister for Nova Scotia at that time, imposed a two-year ban on Fisher Direct.

"The grossly disproportionate severity of the sanction imposed in the case at hand, and the lack of any discernible reasonable justification for it, make it such that the minister's decision was arbitrary," said Muise in his decision, released Tuesday (Nov. 21). 

For comparison, Muise cited the 2021 case of Atlantic ChiCan, a lobster pound business operating on Cape Sable Island. That company pleaded guilty to exporting 63,000 pounds of lobster from the US, falsely labeled as a product of Canada.

Nova Scotia's fisheries minister only imposed a two-week ban on that operation.

"It is clear and obvious that Mr. Nickerson's offending behavior was far less serious than that of Chican," Muise wrote, noting that there was no evidence that Nickerson knew the shipment he had received was involved in the purchase of FSC lobster.
