title: Opening briefs filed in US Supreme Court challenge at-sea monitor fees
content:
The New Civil Liberties Alliance (NLCA) filed an opening brief on Monday (Nov. 20) in the US Supreme Court, challenging a federal government rule that requires fishermen to pay for observer coverage at sea.

The litigants in the Relentless v Department of Commerce case are Rhode Island-based companies Relentless Inc., Huntress Inc. and Seafreeze Fleet. NLCA is arguing on their behalf that the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) rule on fees for at-sea monitors violates the US Constitution.

At the heart of the issue is a 40-year-old court decision from a case that pitted the Chevron oil company against environmentalists. That 1980 case established that federal court judges should defer to government agencies, like NOAA, to interpret ambiguous rules.

However, lawyers for the Rhode Island companies argue that Chevron violates the Constitution by compromising the independence of judges when interpreting the law.

"The Constitution establishes the independence of the judiciary from the political branches to ensure that judges will exercise this core interpretive function impartially, without fear or favor," their brief states.

Chevron "defies these principles by telling judges to defer to inferior-but-tenable agency interpretations of ambiguous federal statutes, they contend.

"Acquiescence is mandatory so long as the agency's interpretation falls within an ill-defined zone of reasonableness -- even if the judge believes the agency's interpretation is 13 wrong. ... Chevron thereby forces judges to abdicate their most important duty: to faithfully apply the law."

Oral arguments are expected to be heard on Jan. 17, 2024.

title: Alaska senator’s amendment to block Russian seafood from US school meals makes it into appropriations bill
content:
US senator Dan Sullivan, an Alaska Republican, is celebrating his inclusion of an amendment in a fiscal 2024 budget bill passed by the upper chamber last week that would further prevent Russian seafood, even when it's processed in China, at least from being served in school meals.

The amendment is contained in one of three appropriations bills addressing agriculture, military and veterans affairs and transportation spending that were grouped in omnibus legislation and passed by the Senate on Wednesday (Nov. 1) by an 82-15 vote. 

It would close a loophole that allows Chinese seafood or Russian seafood processed in China, altering its defined "country of origin," to be purchased by the US National School Lunch Program (NSLP), explains a statement from Sullivan's office.

Russian pollock fishing. Credit: Russia's federal agency for fisheries

Sullivan previously championed a "Buy American" provision in the 2018 Farm Bill that requires the NSLP only to purchase domestically landed and -processed fish, but local or regional school food authorities (SFAs) have the discretion to bypass this requirement when a foreign bid costs less than a domestic bid. 

The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) doesn't purchase foreign seafood in general, and it remains unclear how much of the seafood consumed by children in schools comes from other countries, as no one has tallied the amount. However, it is believed to be a substantial amount, a source explained to Undercurrent News on Monday.

USDA already has put forward a rule to limit the discretion to buy foreign-sourced seafood to just 5% of a purchasing budget, but Sullivan's amendment would remove that discretion entirely.

Murkowski, Sullivan double down on Russian seafood ban at US pollock event

"In 2018, we fought for and delivered a 'Buy American' provision in the Farm Bill to give our students fresh, delicious, sustainable seafood caught by American fishermen," he said in a statement. "Unfortunately, a loophole allows [NSLP] purchasers to keep buying foreign fish -- possibly even Russian-sourced fish breaded and pumped with phosphates in China that we thought we'd already banned -- if they can demonstrate it saves even one percent of the cost relative to domestic fish. This has to end once and for all. 'Buy American' should mean 'Buy American.'"

The legislation, including Sullivan's amendment, now goes to the House of Representatives for consideration.

Congress has until Nov. 17 to pass legislation to continue funding the federal government in the current fiscal year, which began on Oct. 1, 2023. A total of 12 appropriations bills must be passed by both chambers.

Back in late September, Congress passed a continuing resolution to keep funding in place for a limited time, and many expect similar short-term stopgap legislation to be passed again. 

The earlier continuing resolution led a small group of hardline GOP members to oust then-speaker of the House Kevin McCarthy, replacing him with representative Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican. Johnson is expected to ask for another "clean" CR, meaning no changes like the one proposed by Sullivan,  to keep the government running until at least January. 

The history of Sullivan's efforts to ban Russian seafood dates back to 2014, when Russia invaded the Crimean Peninsula in Ukraine. In response, the US and its allies imposed sanctions, not including Russian seafood imports. Russia then enacted retaliatory sanctions, including against US seafood imports, creating the imbalanced seafood trade relationship that exists today between the two countries.

Alaska lawmakers continue push for more restrictions on US imports of Russian seafood

In February 2022, senators Sullivan and Lisa Murkowski, also an Alaska Republican, introduced the US-Russian Federation Seafood Reciprocity Act, a bill that would impose a ban on the import of all Russian seafood products into the US. He attempted to pass the bill by unanimous consent but was blocked by Ed Markey, a Massachusetts Democrat who expressed concern about how it would impact processors in his state.

Then, in March 2022, president Joe Biden issued an executive order that banned the import of all Russian seafood starting on June 23, 2023.

title: New study outlines climate change threats for North Pacific right whales in Bering Sea
content:
Ship collisions and gear entanglements with North Pacific right whales in the Bering Sea could become more common as warming waters push the species and fishing fleets further north, advises a study published recently in the journal Ecological Applications.

The University of Duke (North Carolina) researchers found that "as rising global temperatures push Arctic icecaps into retreat, large and small sea creatures and the commercial fishing boats that follow them are also migrating northward" into the narrow Bering Strait, according to Alaska Native News, which recently reported on the study.

That includes ice shelves that foster zooplankton, which is a critical food source of North Pacific right whales -- a species with a population currently estimated to be 30 animals in the wild.

North Pacific right whales have had a critical habitat designation in the waters off the US state of Alaska's coast since 2007. Earlier this year, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration announced it would review a request to expand the area, which was filed by environmental groups.

The study's authors said the findings are "an important step toward having grounds for strategic, refined protections and management" as ocean conditions change.

title: Spain’s Froxa cautious while exploring new international markets, sustainable innovations
content:
VIGO, Spain -- Spanish frozen processor Froxa is cautiously optimistic about the future on the back of "a successful" first half of 2023 in sales, the firm's co-owner and CEO, Jose Javier Fernandez, told Undercurrent News.

"We have had a great first half of the year in sales. Maybe one of the best we ever had," he said. "However, this is not a time for great celebrations, even though things could be moving in the right direction for Froxa. We cannot make any predictions on how we will end the year since we are still in a difficult economic environment with high market volatility."

Fernandez and his team have several concerns about the global economic landscape, particularly how Spain's large processors and suppliers will cope, which have left them wary about the coming months. 

"There are many rumors surrounding the sector now, and in the end, we are also dealing with a turbulent industry," said Ana Castanedo, the firm's marketing director, of the tough outlook. "Ultimately, even if we are doing well in every aspect and are financially stable, the very turbulent environment we live in could end up affecting us too." 

Conxemar 2023: LatAm sector faces decreased investment amid political turmoil; Oceano’s cephalopod consolidation

The company reached over €42 million ($44.6m) in revenue in 2022, continuing the steady growth seen since 2021 after a 30% drop in 2020. 

Regarding 2024, Fernandez and Castanedo also expressed concerns about the potential challenges, citing the decreasing purchasing power among consumers and a continuous decline in per capita consumption over the past decade.

"Despite a positive first half of 2023, we anticipate a sustained decrease in consumer spending due to rising inflation and economic uncertainty," Fernandez told Undercurrent. "That is why we are also exploring new markets abroad."

Froxa plans to attend the Seafood Expo North America in Boston next year. "In an aim to establish a presence in the North American market while continuing to strengthen our position in Latin America, we will be attending the show for the first time," Castanedo said.

Froxa is already present in Mexico, Colombia, Chile, the Dominican Republic and Peru, and could be also looking to explore the African market, in which it is already present via Ceuta and Melilla -- Spain's enclaves sitting on the northern shores of Morocco's Mediterranean coast and Europe's only landmasses in continental Africa.

Addressing the challenges posed by the Chinese market, where Froxa already has a presence, Fernandez and Castanedo discussed the market's cautious approach due to prolonged lockdowns and uncertainties.

"The aftermath of the pandemic has left people in China cautious and apprehensive. Many had been confined to their homes for an extended period, relying on government-issued rations for essential supplies. This experience has instilled fear, prompting individuals to save money rather than spend it, uncertain about what the future holds," explained Fernandez.

Spain’s Froxa sees new growth opportunities in LatAm, Africa, as Chinese demand stays low

In addition to the pandemic's effects, he highlighted the consequences of the Fukushima water discharge in Japan.

"Despite the currents carrying it towards the US, Chinese consumers have shown a sharp decline in their consumption of Japanese products, plummeting by a staggering 70%. Also, while there was an initial anticipation for an increase in imports from other sources, this trend is not materializing as expected," he added.

According to Castanedo, the firm is "actively engaged" in sustainable practices and product innovation to counter all potential impacts. "We are closely monitoring the situation there and exploring innovative solutions to adapt to changing consumer behaviors."

"This way, we recently introduced new products like MSC [Marine Stewardship Council]-certified dab and a new precooked item under our gourmet line, the 'gamba cristal,' or lightly floured Mediterranean shrimp," he shared.

"We are committed to maintaining our high-quality standards whatever the current context and investing in new sustainable initiatives such as expanding our photovoltaic installations and developing projects for water reuse," Fernandez added.

At the firm's Cartes facility in Cantabria, Spain, a significant expansion of 50 kilowatts has been implemented, boosting the installed "clean energy" capacity to 450 kW. Similarly, a 110 kW expansion on the rooftop has been completed at the Mercasantander installations, resulting in a total installed photovoltaic capacity of 310 kW.

"It is a commitment to a continuous improvement process that not only reduces expenses but also contributes significantly to a more sustainable future. A more conscientious approach optimizes costs, which is undeniably crucial for any business, and aligns with our broader mission to be environmentally responsible," Castanedo concluded.

title: Iceland to embrace stricter aquaculture policies following escapes
content:
Iceland's government has proposed new, stricter, legal frameworks on the country's salmon farms following an escape that made headlines even in Europe.

The Minister of Fisheries, Svandís Svavarsdottir, on Oct. 4 presented the draft, which proposes increased monitoring of fish farms and requiring license holders to pay "a fair price" for the use of natural resources.

Arctic Fish deals with salmon escape in Iceland

"Fee collection from the sector must reflect that [fish farming] is a matter of utilizing limited resources," said Svavarsdottir. "It is fundamental that those who profit from the use of the country’s natural resources pay a fair price for it. But it is equally important that we set ourselves ambitious, measurable goals in environmental matters and set a timetable on the way to those goals."

The objectives and strategy in the draft extend to the year 2040, and the action plan to the year 2028.

At a press conference for the proposals, Kolbeinn Arnason of the Food and Agriculture Ministry stated that the new regulations would be enforced through the introduction of both positive and negative incentives, reported Iceland Review.

"With tax incentives on the one hand, positive incentives so that people invest in equipment so that the risk [of escaped fish] will be lower. Then we have negative incentives, which include that the company will bear responsibility for escape incidents. The consequences for a company of such an escape will be in the form of the government stripping that company of a permanent fish farming license."

Arctic Fish, a rapidly growing salmon farmer in the Westfjords of Iceland that's majority owned by Norway's Mowi, has been working "systematically" to clean up the escape of an unspecified number of fish, first discovered in August.

The event made the news in the UK, where The Guardian also noted Arnarlax had been fined £705,000 for not reporting an escape of 81,000 fish in 2021.

title: Four British Columbia Dungy crab harvesters hit with CAD 287,000 in fines
content:
Four British Columbia Dungeness crab fishing captains have been hit with CAD 287,000 ($212,740) in combined fines for illegal harvesting practices in Boundary Bay, according to Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO).

DFO recounted the cases in a recent press release. 

Han Van Lam, master of the fishing vessel John Lam, on August 4, pleaded guilty in a provincial court in Surrey, BC, to illegally fishing in US waters during the 2019 and 2020 commercial seasons, according to the federal agency. He was fined CAD 50,000, forced to forfeit 96 traps that had been seized as evidence, and has been prohibited from fishing for the first 14 days of the annual commercial season openings in 2024 and 2025.

This is the first time that this prohibition has been imposed by the courts, according to DFO.

In another ruling, also made on Aug. 4, Michael Hau, master of the Muoi H, pleaded guilty to failing to scan his traps during the 2018, 2019 and 2020 crab fishing seasons, as per the conditions of his license, according to DFO. He was fined CAD 20,000 and forced to forfeit a catch reported to be worth CAD 19,030.68.

Earlier, on June 27, Hoan Trung Do, master of the Bounty Hunter, pleaded guilty to fishing in US waters and setting more traps in 2018, 2019 and 2020 than allowed under the conditions of his license. He was fined CAD 160,000.

On June 23, Viet Dam, master of the Pacific Falcon, also pleaded guilty to illegally fishing in US waters and fishing more traps in 2019 than allowed. Dam was fined CAD 38,000 and forfeited 83 traps.

title: Icelandic salmon farmer to list shares on country’s ‘First North’
content:
Icelandic Salmon -- the parent company of Arnarlax -- has published a "company description," a requirement as it works towards the admission of its shares to trading on Nasdaq First North Growth Market Iceland.

The First North Growth Market is a registered SME growth market operated by an exchange within the Nasdaq group, said the aquaculture firm, which is 51% owned by Norway's SalMar.

"Issuers on Nasdaq First North Growth Market are not subject to all the same rules as issuers on a regulated main market, as defined in EU legislation... Instead, they are subject to a less extensive set of rules and regulations adjusted to small growth companies."

The risk in investing in an issuer on this market may, therefore, be higher than investing in an issuer on the main market, it admitted. 

This would be a dual listing, with Icelandic Salmon's shares already listed on the Euronext Growth Oslo Market in Norway.

"[Icelandic Salmon] considers that a listing of the company's affiliated shares is an important milestone for the company and its operations," it said. "The aim of the listing is to support the operational ambitions of the company by enabling new local investors to participate in the company’s growth story and value creation."

"A First North listing is expected to contribute to an increased interest in the affiliated shares and the company among investors, as well as among suppliers, media and other stakeholders. Additionally, a First North listing provides increased liquidity in the trading of the affiliated shares, which is advantageous for existing shareholders. Overall, the company assesses that a First North listing...will benefit the company's future development."

As part of its company description, issued ahead of the listing, Icelandic Salmon said some 88-92% of its revenue for the six months ended June 30, 2023, came from exports. 

It "derives a significant portion of its revenues from its top five customers and the loss of any of these as a customer, or default by any of these customers, could result in a significant loss of revenues and cash flows," it said, as one potential risk factor.

These customers were Poland's Suempol, Norway's Seaborn, the UK's Severn and Wye Smokery, Premium of Iceland, and French processor Mericq. Together, they represented 28% of Icelandic Salmon's total revenues for the period in question.

All issuers with shares admitted to trading on the First North Growth Market have a certified adviser who monitors that the rules are followed. Icelandic Salmon's is Arion Bank.

title: Canadian fishing vessel owners fined CAD 6,000; nearly 32,000lbs of tuna confiscated
content:
Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) reports that the owners of the  commercial fishing vessel Ocean Provider have been slapped with a fine of CAD 6,000 ($4,445) and had 2,250 albacore tuna, amounting to 31,956 pounds, seized for fishing without a license off the coast of the province of British Columbia in 2022.

The company, which was identified as 1269039 BC Ltd., admitted to the illegal fishing activity between July 22 and Aug. 15, 2022 before it was sentenced in the Port Alberni Provincial Court. The illegal catch was valued at CAD 127,824.

DFO said its investigation of the company arose from customary inspections of the Canadian-United States fishing fleets undertaken by fishery officers aboard the Canadian Coast Guard's vessel Tanu. The officers boarded the Ocean Provider at sea, 42 nautical miles off Barkley Sound on the West Coast of Vancouver Island, near Bamfield. The crew was actively fishing at the time, but DFO officers ascertained that the vessel lacked the appropriate authorization. The ship was escorted to port where the catch was offloaded for further processing and confiscation.

title: Scotland’s Ace Aquatec eyes full fish lifecycle coverage after camera launch
content:
TRONDHEIM, Norway -- The most striking aspect of Ace Aquatec's new A-Biomass camera, launched during last month's Aqua Nor show in Trondheim, Norway, is how light it is. 

Scotland’s Ace Aquatec names new chief tech officer

At just 8.5 kilograms, the device packs in two stereoscopic cameras, low light sensors, and an AI computer to comprehend what it sees into a box small enough to pick up with one hand.

According to new chief technology officer (CTO) Keith Davidson, the camera represents the output of a five-year R&D process initiated by an aquatech company that finally wanted to cover the rest of a fish's life cycle, not just its harvest.

Davidson, who only started at the firm in July, comes with a wealth of technology experience outside the realm of aquaculture, whether in oil and gas, as a product engineer at Hewlett Packard Enterprise, and most recently, as the director of global 'over-the-top' platforms at British broadcaster Sky.

"I've always wanted to work in a field that uses technology for good," Davidson said. "Doing something that has a benefit, that takes a humane approach to aquaculture, was a big plus for me. There's also not many times that you get to work right across the technology spectrum."

Founded in 1999, Ace Aquatec chiefly manufactures humane stunners for fish harvesting, as well as hydroacoustic and electric fence predator deterrents. Now, the company is adding a third element to its portfolio with a 'growth' range for monitoring fish health.

The new device, initially aimed squarely at salmon farmers, will use AI and a camera that's accurate to 1-2 millimeters to assess the length and weight of fish in a pen, sharing real-time information with the farmer's data portal.

The aim is to enable farmers to monitor and grade fish in the most unobtrusive manner possible, Davidson said.

"A lot of approaches about estimating weight are quite invasive to the fish," he explained. "So we've adopted a camera and a particular monocle stereo that allows us to capture their dimensions and accurately sample without disturbing them and creating stress among the fish themselves."

"That's one of the reasons we've stepped into this side of production, because if you start linking that to the harvesting systems where we're processing with in-water electric stunners, the idea is that we can ultimately follow the weight and the biomass of the fish all the way through from the pens to the harvest site in the most humane way possible."

Ace Aquatec CTO, Keith Davidson

The sales team at the show confirmed to Undercurrent that as with the stunners, Ace Aquatec's ambition is not constrained to salmon; similar systems for trout, seabass and tilapia farmers will be released next year.

From a hardware perspective, nothing about the camera will need to change for different species, Davidson noted -- it's just a question of training the AI model inside what to look for in different species.

"As we develop the product, we will obviously look for any improvements we can make to the physical camera, but even right now that technology has the ability to pick up different species. It's really just the software that has to be modified for release to customers."

In line with the new product launch, Ace Aquatec also secured financial backing from Earth Capital in June, aimed at accelerating the commercial rollout of the camera. Earth Capital joined Aqua-Spark and Chroma Ventures' Chris van der Kuyl -- co-owner of the UK game developer 4J Studios -- as participants in Ace Aquatec's £10 million ($12.46m) series A investment round.

"I can't go into specific details of what Earth Capital is looking for, but they are coming because of the biomass camera system," Davidson told Undercurrent. "They are an active member of our board to help us move the business forward, same as Aqua-Spark came in for the in-water electric stunners; that's the kind of model that Ace Aquatec has been running."

The firm's goal is to have roughly 2,000 camera units in the water by the end of 2024, and a large part of Davidson's initial role will be to optimize the production line. Beyond that, he said, the firm will be looking to add more digital functions linking to its data portal to the rest of its portfolio.

"I'm lucky that I'm a CTO coming into an organization with a suite of products, and we'll be looking across that suite as we take the next step," he said. "We want to move these to the digital realm so that we can bring data and informational benefits to our customers, and we will be looking at the plans for that over the next couple of months."

Donald Sutherland, head of digital R&D and one of the main brains behind the A-Biomass camera, at Ace Aquatec's stand at Aqua Nor 2023. Credit: Dan Gibson/Undercurrent News

Chile sales booming

Also speaking to Undercurrent at the Aqua Nor Ace Aquatec's chief marketing officer Tara McGregor-Woodhams noted that the new piece of kit is expected to be in high demand from Chilean farmers who have been all over the company's fish stunners this year. 

Scottish fish stunning tech finds distributor for Americas

"For us, the welfare aspect in Chile has definitely changed, and the level of inquiries we've had from Chile for our HSU (Humane Stunner Universal) has been off the scale," she said.

"That's the biggest demand we've had this year, to the point where, although we've got an office in Chile anyway [since Sept. 2020], we've got a new general manager starting in September."

The stunners have taken off in the country, she said, as Chilean farmers such as Empresas Aquachile are trying to cut down significantly on the handling of the fish during harvest.

"And on the back of that, because it's for salmon, people have asked, 'when is your biomass camera coming?'" she continued. "So I think we'll probably deploy quite a lot to Chile, is my feeling."

The new camera will use a winch system to move around within a pen in order to get a good dispersal, she said, which the firm believes will be invaluable to Scottish farmers facing tight stocking density quotas.

"By being able to put the camera in and have it for 24 months, you can make sure you are within those limits and not get fined, which is a big thing," McGregor-Woodhams said. "It's good for farmer transparency, as they get very worried about that."

Designed to operate with one unit per pen, the camera is expected to attract interest primarily from the largest farmers, she added, though the company did not wish to disclose any details on price.

"We're aiming big at the moment, and from the inquiries we've had, it's the big players looking for a solution," she said. "But there are different markets like Chile, where smaller farmers have come back to us and said biomass and welfare are a big thing for us, Canada too."

title: Atunlo exec claims lack of controls on frozen tuna at some EU border points
content:
VIGO, Spain -- Jose Pernas, general manager at vertically integrated tuna firm Atunlo, used his presentation at the recent XI ANFACO World Tuna Conference to raise a red flag over a lack of control at certain European borders when it comes to the import of frozen yellowfin tuna.

In his presentation, Pernas emphasized the significant value that frozen tuna brings to the fishing and processing sectors but claimed discrepancies in regulations across European countries that have led to a concerning rise in unregulated imports.

Yellowfin frozen at -18°C is a highly sought-after product in the seafood industry due to its quality and versatility. Pernas explained that in Spain, the price of pre-cooked yellowfin loins currently ranges between €6 and €7 per kilogram, depending on factors such as product quality, cleanliness, and destination. In contrast, a kilogram of raw tuna loin can fetch between €7 and €9 in the market, depending on the product type and processing method, all stemming from a similar raw material, he said.

The yellowfin tuna market for direct human consumption grew 10-12% annually until 2020. Sales volume in Europe average 130,000t-150,000t per year of yellowfin and bigeye weighing more than 10kg.

Freezing and handling tuna at -18°C incurs higher costs than fish destined for brining, Pernas said, expressing his concerns about the varying sanitary regulations within the European market. He said Spanish authorities now require certificates of freezing in tanks and a sworn statement from the skipper or shipowner certifying the product's intended destination for the import of frozen tuna at -18°C.

This has led to a significant surge in imports of tuna loins into Europe from other countries via Portugal and the Netherlands, according to Pernas. These countries allow the dispatch of this fish with a simple health certificate, indicating whether the product is intended for human consumption, without rigorous checks on how the fish has been frozen, he said.

Countries such as Vietnam and Ecuador have substantially increased their frozen tuna exports to Europe in recent years. Vietnam's Association of Seafood Exporters and Producers reported a 68% increase in frozen tuna exports to Europe in January and February this year.

However, Undercurrent News' trade portal doesn't show a particularly strong trend:

EU imports of frozen yellowfin and general tuna products, HS codes 030342 and 160414

Pernas said this has come despite Vietnam exporting almost no frozen tuna at -18°C to Europe.

He said a shipment declared as frozen tuna at -18°C with a corresponding health certificate from Vietnam was blocked and rejected in the port of Vigo, Spain, earlier this year. The authorities requested freezing temperature certificates for the tanks and a letter from the ship's owner or skipper. Unable to provide these documents, the cargo was refused.

Spanish health authorities contacted their Vietnamese counterparts, who quickly realized the shortcomings in their documentation and control procedures.

Pernas called for standardized sanitary regulations and controls across European borders, particularly for high-value products like frozen tuna.

Imports of -18C frozen yellowfin tuna loins from Ecuador to several European countries.

Without uniform regulations, the industry remains vulnerable to unregulated imports, posing potential risks to consumers and legitimate businesses alike, he stressed. It is up to European authorities to address these concerns and ensure the safe and fair trade of frozen tuna within the region, according to Pernas.

Last year, Atunlo's freezer vessels caught about 85,000 metric tons of tuna. The firm has three sites in Spain -- in Grove, Cambados and Santona -- one in Mindelo, Cape Verde, and another in Vilanova Ferrer, Portugal. It processes about 250t of tuna per day, both for canning and for direct human consumption.

Atunlo produces loins and steaks for distribution for foodservice and retail loins for the industrial sector. 

steaks, burgers growing in popularity

The primary products in the tuna market for direct human consumption are natural or marinated and flavored loins. There are also vacuum-packaged products in various forms for supermarkets or distribution, along with other emerging products like tuna tartare and traditional delicacies like mojama.

Products such as tuna burgers and pre-cooked tuna have gained prominence recently. Notably, these products must be made from tuna frozen at -18°C, following EU regulation 853/2004, said Pernas.

The executive observed that the market for these products experienced substantial growth starting in the early 2010s, primarily in Spain.

Spain is a major producer of natural, processed, flavored, and mojama tuna products. However, he admitted that until 2017, there was a lack of continuous supervision in the extraction and processing phases. This changed when a meeting was convened in Brussels in 2017 to address the transformation of tuna and flavored marinades, focusing on the ingredients used and the sourcing of raw materials, according to the executive.

After this meeting, the EU Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety (DG Sante) expressed concerns in a presentation in September 2017, stating that the tuna treatment procedures were inadequate and the tuna used was unsuitable. This raised significant issues and led to inspections of various Spanish industries, even threatening closures.

In response, various interprofessional associations, especially ANFACO and industry operators, worked intensively to resolve the problem and align with DG Sante's regulations. Notably, they banned nitrates and nitrites and regulated the use of antioxidants up to 300 parts per million.

However, in May 2019, the industry faced another challenge when a company presented research indicating that the tuna used for processing was still unsuitable. It argued that tuna fishing vessels and third-party freezers in brine couldn't reach -19°C. This triggered a new round of intensive efforts by the fishing sector and various associations to demonstrate that tuna fishing vessels could indeed freeze at -18°C, as required.

In Spain, for instance, the definition of a freezer tuna fishing vessel specifies its capability to reach -18°C, as defined by regulation 853. However, the ability to achieve -18°C varies among vessels due to their technical specifications, refrigeration capacity, compressor power, brine lines, the condition and maintenance of the vessel, and the volume of the catch. Freezing 200t differs from freezing 30t, and the refrigeration requirements vary accordingly.

Pernas explained that by 2019, the market for -18°C tuna had become more regulated, with clear guidelines for freezing temperature records, freezing time, and temperature verification at transshipment. Quality and product differentiation received greater attention in the fishing industry. The processing sector also effectively regulated additives, histamine levels, and shelf life for refrigerated products. However, certain aspects, such as what constitutes a transformed product and the use of carbonates for sanitary control, still require clarification.

Since 2021, the EU has implemented two types of sanitary certificates: one for direct human consumption and another for products preserved at -20°C. These certificates specify the intended use and freezing temperature on board for non-community fleet products.

In Spain, additional requirements include tank temperature freezing records and a sworn statement from the skipper or shipowner certifying the -18°C freezing process. Operators in Spain are also subject to continuous monitoring of -18°C tuna shipments and histamine levels, ensuring compliance with the optimal standard of under 25 ppm, according to Pernas.

title: Nova Scotia captain, two fishing companies fined CAD 125K over halibut, hake, cod catches
content:
Casey Henneberry, a 40-year-old captain from Sambro, Nova Scotia, and two companies, ALS Fisheries and Law Fisheries, have been fined a total of CAD 125,000 ($92,470) for fisheries violations made while pursuing halibut, hake and Atlantic cod, CBC News reports.

Henneberry also has been banned from fishing for six months.

The case involved the misreporting of trips made by Henneberry's vessel, the Ivy Lew, between May 2019 and June 2020, and a secret, middle-of-the-night offload of halibut, valued at CAD 40,000, during which Henneberry fled from Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) officers, according to the article.

"Mr. Henneberry's offending conduct is that he inaccurately logged and hailed weight of groundfish on four trips over approximately one year and on one of those trips, he illegally off-loaded CAD 40,000 worth of halibut, intending to sell it," Halifax provincial court Judge Elizabeth Buckle said in her written sentence.

ALS Fisheries and Law Fisheries were found guilty of failing to ensure that license conditions were complied with and were fined CAD 55,000 and CAD 10,000, respectively. ALS Fisheries owns the Ivy Lew, which has been held by the DFO for the past three years.

title: Israel’s Pure Blue Fish just months from beginning construction of land-based yellowtail farm in South Carolina
content:
Israeli aquaculture company Pure Blue Fish has revealed plans to begin construction of its land-based kingfish yellowtail farm in the US state of South Carolina before the end of the year.

CEO Igar Avrech and partner/chief technology officer Ehud Brill told Undercurrent News this week that the company aims to produce 600 metric tons of fish in the first phase, an increase from the originally planned 340t.

The company expects the design phase of the recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) facility to be completed within the next three months, with the groundbreaking of a facility in the Matthews Industrial Park, in Orangeburg County, anticipated in early December. 

Both executives expressed confidence in a swift permitting process aided by a positive relationship with local authorities.

Avrech said he visited with officials from South Carolina's Department of Agriculture just last week. Back in June, Undercurrent reported that Hugh Weathers, the state's agriculture commissioner, made a trip to the company's corporate headquarters in Israel.

Pure Blue Fish also is developing its first land-based yellowtail farm in the Haifa district of Israel, where significant progress is underway in its construction. The inaugural batch of fingerlings will arrive on Nov. 15.

Construction of Pure Blue Fish's yellowtail RAS farm in the Haifa district of Israel is well underway. Photo: Pure Blue Fish

"Obtaining the building permit in an industrial park, where regulations are very clear, will be straightforward," said Brill about the South Carolina facility. "As for the biological permit, our facility uses a fully closed [RAS], so the facility is very environmentally friendly. We don't see problems with the biological permit. We're doing something good for everyone and the ocean." 

The company's utilization of what it has described as the world's first "zero-discharge" RAS facility as an interesting backstory, originating from the now-defunct Local Ocean, a land-based yellowtail farm in Greenport, upstate New York.

Brill served as the COO and manager of Local Ocean, which was initiated by a consortium of Israeli and Mexican entrepreneurs. However, the investors pulled out of the project, leading to its closure in 2013 and the property was foreclosed by the lender.

The former Local Ocean site is now occupied by steelhead producer Hudson Valley Fisheries (HVF). However, HVF has no affiliation with Local Ocean, its management, or investors, as the site was acquired by HVF from the property owner.

Brill, a marine biologist, explained how the RAS technology being used initially emerged from research conducted at the Hebrew University's Faculty of Agriculture in Israel and he was recruited to implement it in the Local Ocean facility in upstate New York during its transition to the commercial phase.When the project's investors discontinued their involvement, he said he returned to Israel and his group decided to pursue the technology independently, securing its rights and subsequently making substantial improvements.

Ambitious targets

Pure Blue Fish has outlined an ambitious expansion plan to reach 5,000t of annual production in a little over eight years in the same site in South Carolina. The expansion will be executed in modular phases, ensuring scalability and operational efficiency. Once operating at full capacity, the farm will employ between 100 and 150 workers.

"Our initial 600t production is budgeted at approximately $10 million, excluding working capital. We are fully funded for this phase. As we progress toward our 5,000t capacity target in the same location, the capital expenditure will be roughly $60m," said Avrech.

Avrech highlighted the strategic location of the South Carolina farm, just six hours away from consumer markets in the state and around it. He said this proximity allows for efficient delivery to an estimated 50m potential customers.

Brill outlined the company's forward-looking strategy to build farms in different locations each year.

"We plan to have eight locations in the next four years," he said. "However, each site will grow in four stages to reach a total of approximately 5,000t eventually (per site). This means that it will take about eight years in each location to reach full capacity.

According to Brill, Houston, Texas, is the probable location for the company's second US facility in 2025. The allure lies in the substantial market of 40-50m consumers within the city and surrounding areas. Additionally, Las Vegas is another potential contender for expansion, given its significant tourist influx of around 40m visitors annually. However, the management will evaluate market expansion to align with its overarching strategy, said Brill.

The company's expansion isn't confined solely to geographical reach but extends to the diverse range of species it aims to cultivate. Notably, red drum and white seabass from California are among the species also under consideration.

Avrech, the CEO, elaborated on the company's approach: "We will commence our operations with kingfish yellowtail. As we establish ourselves in South Carolina and embark on our expansion journey, we will gather more insights to determine the additional species we will venture into."

In terms of production during the initial phase, Pure Blue Fish is strategically positioning itself for market entry. Avrech revealed that the company had inked a letter of intent with two distributors boasting extensive nationwide distribution networks. 

"We have already secured letters of intent with two distributors for our phase 1 production of 600t," Avrech said.

He highlighted the company's commitment to delivering the freshest produce to consumers:

"Our fish is six hours away from farm to table – that's a safe bet," Avrech said. "Our fish will be with the clients in six hours from harvest time. That's the beauty of it. We can, daily, supply fresh fish to the market."

title: Icelandic fisheries report submitted ahead of new law draft
content:
The final report drawn up by Icelandic working group "our Audlindin", looking in part at the future of the fishing sector, has been presented to the government.

The report, in Icelandic, has been published for comment on the government's consultation portal, here. Reviews and comments will be taken up to and including Sept. 26, and these will be taken into account during the drafting of a bill for a comprehensive law on the utilization and management of marine resources, planned to be submitted to Iceland's parliament in the spring of 2024. 

Largely concerned with sustainable and efficient fisheries management, part of the report also addresses quota ownership and competition within the sector -- an area that routinely comes up as a topic for reform.

Icelandic companies' share of quota in cod-equivalent metric tons and percentage of the total, as of May 2023. Click to enlarge.

Currently, the combined catch share of individual and related parties may not exceed 12% of the total value of the catch share of all species. The rules as to how "related parties" are defined have allowed the biggest companies, like Brim and Samherji, to reach the size they are.

While the report acknowledges the strengths and appropriateness of companies looking to consolidate and build, it adds: "It is wise to make changes to the current laws on fisheries management with the goal in mind that individual companies cannot become so large that it directly hinders normal competition in fishing."

With regards to the biggest companies gaining political strength within their sectors, it said: "This primarily means setting rules to ensure that those already in operation remain not so powerful that they can with their organizational power prevent new parties from entering the industry."

"The strong control of a few parties over the fishing resource can lead to...the person in question getting a lot of power in society and the position of those who control the shipping companies can become too strong towards the government, credit institutions and employees. Those who were in the sector could, in fact, determine who could enter it, and thus could prevent normal competition."

Iceland's minister for food, Svandis Svavarsdottir, said the work that had gone into the new report was "an important step to create the conditions for greater harmony in the fishing industry."

"The interests of the public are put in the foreground and are reflected, for example, in a strong environmental focus and proposals for increased transparency and an increase in fishing fees in accordance with the financial plan."

Meanwhile, Iceland's Samtok fyrirtaekja i sjavarutvegi (SFS) -- the seafood sector's industry association -- expressed its regret that the report had not focused "on what is most important; the competitiveness of the Icelandic fishing industry and its position in competition with the fisheries of other nations."

"Therein lies the biggest challenge now and in the future. The oft-mentioned reconciliation in the fishing industry will hardly be discussed if the Icelanders lose in a difficult away game and there will be no value for the exchange."

It felt the report delivered little new information, but noted it had praised the existing system of catch quotas and transferable fishing permits as the one that was "considered the best and has delivered great value to Icelandic society."

Finally, in a fairly damning comment, SFS said:

"In the minister's open presentation today, it was wrong that the minister intends to present bills that in two cases are not in accordance with the contents and conclusions of the report. On the one hand, the minister intends to propose an increase in the fishing fee, and on the other hand, she intends to experiment with the auction of fishing permits. Neither is suggested by the experts who chaired the working groups and wrote about the relevant topics in the report. For that reason, there can be doubts that the minister ever intended to abide by the results of a report that were not in accordance with the minister's political vision."

title: US judge unconvinced Lion Capital exec, Dongwon founder Kim didn’t discuss tuna prices
content:
Former Bumble Bee Foods owner Lion Capital is set to face a federal trial in a class action lawsuit for its alleged involvement in collusion in the US tuna sector following an Aug. 21 order from a California judge.

Dana Sabraw, a chief in the US District Court for the Southern District of California, said she's unconvinced pricing wasn't discussed in meetings held in 2010 and 2011 between a top executive with the UK private equity and the founder of South Korea's Dongwon Industries (click here to read the order).

World’s 100 Largest Seafood Companies, Tenth Edition
View report

The meetings between Eric Lindberg, a former Lion executive, and Jae Chul 'JC' Kim, Dongwon's founder and then-executive chairman (pictured below), form a crucial part of why Sabraw rejected Lion's claim it can't be held liable for price fixing during its ownership of Bumble Bee.

Although the US tuna giant was bought from bankruptcy protection by FCF Co. after pleading guilty to conspiracy and its former CEO served prison time, Lion denies any awareness of price fixing. Sabraw's order favoring the plaintiffs in the suit -- four groups alleging harm by the pricing fixing, classes of direct purchasers, end-payers, commercial food preparers and direct action plaintiffs -- means the legal process can continue, and Lion could face a trial.

Lion "had the authority to stop Bumble Bee's anticompetitive behavior" but instead seemingly turned a "blind eye to Bumble Bee's collusion," which "enabled the conspiracy to continue," the judge stated.

New testimony suggests US tuna price-fixing began earlier than previously thought

Lion's possible US trial for its alleged role in the price fixing is one of the final pieces of a scandal that first surfaced at the end of 2015 when Thai Union Group canceled its planned $1.5 billion deal for Bumble Bee.

The US Department of Justice (DOJ) issued a statement at the time that "consumers are better off without this deal," adding the "market is not functioning competitively today, and further consolidation would only make things worse."

A wave of civil lawsuits followed the DOJ investigation, which were categorized into the four groups of plaintiffs. 

It was later revealed that Thai Union -- which operates in the US tuna sector with Chicken of the Sea International (COSI) -- was the whistle-blower on the price fixing, meaning it was exempt from fines. However, it's shelled out big in civil settlements. 

Bumble Bee was fined $25 million for its role in the price fixing. W. Scott Cameron and Ken Worsham, two former senior Bumble Bee sales executives, pled guilty and testified against Chris Lischewski, the company's long-time CEO, at a 2019 trial in San Diego, California, from which Undercurrent News reported live. 

US Supreme Court declines to hear StarKist appeal in price-fixing lawsuits

Stephen Hodge, a senior StarKist sales executive, also pled guilty and testified. Dongwon-owned StarKist Co. was fined $100m for its role. 

Neither Dongwon/StarKist nor Lion responded to requests for comment from Undercurrent. Kim and Lindberg could not be reached for comment. 

First meeting

Two meetings between Lindberg, then leading Lion's deal team on Bumble Bee, and Dongwon's JC Kim are discussed in detail in Judge Sabraw's order. Lion and Dongwon deny any pricing discussion took place, and before both meetings, Kim -- who stood down as top executive of Dongwon to make way for his son in 2019 -- asked if a lawyer should be present. In both cases, Lindberg said no, as pricing was not to be discussed.

Lindberg first met Kim, whose company owns StarKist, the largest US tuna brand, on Nov. 15, 2010, prior to Lion's deal for Bumble Bee in December that year.

"Despite Lindberg's denials, this evidence is sufficient to raise a genuine issue of whether Lindberg and Kim discussed prices. Discussing prices with a competitor in the context of this case is an act in furtherance of Bumble Bee's price-fixing conspiracy," she wrote, referring to meetings that took place on Nov. 15, 2010, and Nov. 28, 2011.

Bumble Bee CEO Tharp set to exit after 12 years

Before meeting Kim and Thai Union chairman and CEO Thiraphong Chansiri as part of a final stage of due diligence, Lindberg received some guidance from Lischewski, who was found guilty of price fixing. 

Lischewski impressed upon Lindberg that one "key message [was] to ensure Dong Won [sic] that Lion will support rationale [sic] market behavior by Bumble Bee," the judge wrote. 

Lindberg has stated he could "not recall whether [he] read that sentence, among many emails [he] received [and could] not recall it making any impression on [him] at the time."

Jake Capps, another then-Lion executive, who was not copied on Lischewski's email to Lindberg, testified that had he "learned that Chris Lischewski had asked a member of the deal team to convey to Dongwon that Lion will support rational market behavior by Bumble Bee," he "would have considered that a red flag," wrote the judge.

COO, three more VPs exit Bumble Bee as FCF restructuring continues

Before the first meeting, Lindberg consulted an attorney "to ensure that the meeting would be permissible under the US antitrust laws" and emailed Dongwon stating that there was no need for an antitrust attorney because "[p]rohibited topics under US competition laws are quite narrow, such as sharing detailed cost information and discussion of pricing strategy and collusion, and we certainly will not discuss those topics."

Dongwon prepared a detailed memo of the meeting summarizing each participant's statements as the meeting unfolded. At the beginning of the meeting, Lindberg stated that "as the industry's two most-leading companies come together, there may be a concern that this violates the Anti-Trust Law."

Lindberg then summarized the topics he wanted to discuss and closed with, "as a major shareholder, I will preface this meeting by saying ... there will be no mention of pricing or strategies," the judge wrote.

Despite this, the plaintiffs in the lawsuit point to other parts of the memo on the meeting and Lindberg's statements after the meeting to argue that pricing was discussed, however, wrote Sabraw.

Kim asked Lindberg how Lion "was planning to increase Bumble Bee's value before divesting it and suggested a preference for increasing prices rather than cutting costs, can downsizing, or reducing product quality," she added.

Lischewski trial: After guilty verdict, sentencing set for April 8; Defense lawyers pledge to ‘continue to vigorously pursue justice’

After the meeting, Lischewski informed Lindberg that Kim fired former StarKist CEO Don Binotto and excoriated the management team for "extremely aggressive" pricing, the judgment reads. "Lindberg responded, 'he made allusions to his displeasure with Binotto in my discussion Monday. [H]is stated displeasure at price cutting sounded good to me...'"

Second meeting

After the deal had closed, in August 2011, Lindberg reached out to Kim for another meeting, stating, "I consider this an 'owner to owner' meeting."

Ultimately, they met on Nov. 28, 2011, with Lindberg and another executive representing Lion.

Again, the parties vigorously dispute whether pricing was discussed at the meeting, wrote the judge. Kim again inquired if Lindberg would "be accompanying a lawyer."

Lindberg responded he would not and noted they would "not discuss anything so specific about the US market that we should be concerned about anti-competitive/price collusion issues." Lindberg denies that he discussed collusion or price agreements with Kim.

Sabraw's order, however, notes the plaintiffs point to Lindberg's statements after the meeting to argue that competition was discussed.

Lindberg's request for a second meeting with Kim came on the heels of blocking a plan from Lischewski to attack StarKist's market share by lowering prices, she added.

On July 28, 2011, Lischewski shared with Lindberg and others concerns that Bumble Bee was losing market share to StarKist and COSI, commenting that their attacks on Bumble Bee "were not rational."

COO, three more VPs exit Bumble Bee as FCF restructuring continues

Bumble Bee intended to counter-attack StarKist in their tuna pouch segment to "send a very strong signal... and while that will have an impact on our margins, it will have a bigger impact on [StarKist]." Lindberg immediately responded to stop Bumble Bee from cutting prices: "under no circumstances do we want any negative price signaling."

"Lindberg's statements about the second meeting [with Kim] imply that prices were again discussed," wrote Sabraw.

The day after the meeting, Lindberg messaged the CEO of FCF. Lindberg reportedly told FCF's CEO, who is not named but was W.H. Lee at the time, that Kim had told him StarKist would "act rational if no one try [sic] to challenge their share."

On March 30, 2012, Lindberg commented to Lyndon Lea, the founder of Lion, that although StarKist and COSI's attacks had been "completely unreasonable, we may be on the verge of an important shift. Jae Chul Kim at Dongwon hinted at this when I met him in December."

Lindberg had no further meetings with Kim.

title: PEI fisherman fined CAD 8k for catching undersized, egg-bearing lobsters
content:
A harvester from the eastern part of Prince Edward Island (PEI), Canada has been fined over CAD 8,000 ($5,876) for catching both undersized and female lobsters with eggs attached.

Thang Quoc Tran, 66, pleaded guilty to the charges under the federal Fisheries Act, reported Saltwire.

Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans officers discovered 77 undersized lobsters and three female lobsters with eggs when inspecting Tran's fishing vessel, the news service reported. The DFO officers seized the lobsters and released them back into the water.

Tran's lawyer and the federal prosecutor recommended a joint fine of $100 for each undersized lobster and $250 for each female lobster with eggs.

The harvester's fishing license will be suspended at the start of next year's season for 96 hours – or five to eight days. He also has the option to buy back six of those days in the form of a fine of CAD 7,748.72 for each day.

Judge Nancy Orr accepted the joint recommendation and fined Tran a total of CAD 7,700 for the undersized lobsters and CAD 750 for the three female lobsters bearing eggs.

title: Canadian crab harvesters fined CAD 17,500 for leaving gear in water
content:
Two snow crab harvesters from the Cape Breton area of the Canadian province Nova Scotia were sentenced last month to paying fines of CAD 17,500 ($12,964) for leaving their fishing gear unattended for longer than 72 hours, Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) reported recently on its Facebook page. 

In this case, the traps were left in the water for more than three weeks, according to DFO, which did not name the individuals.

Additionally, 40 traps, ropes and buoys, valued at CAD 40,000, were forfeited, and one individual had their personal fishing license suspended for four months, between Sept. 1, 2023 and Dec. 31, 2023.

"Leaving gear unattended longer than the limit harms fish habitat and kills both the targeted species and bycatch," the federal agency advised.

title: Ammonia leak builds on woes surrounding East West’s 77-year-old catcher-processor
content:
The Pacific Producer, a 77-year-old catcher processor vessel that normally operates off the coast of Alaska, is leaking ammonia while sitting in a dock in Tacoma, Washington, the US Coast Guard (USCG) has reported.

The federal agency and Washington Department of Ecology crews were working in HAZMAT suits to locate the leak on Wednesday (Aug. 16), USCG said in a Facebook posting Wednesday (Aug. 16). A USCG communications official told Undercurrent News on Thursday (Aug. 17) that the effort remained ongoing but that the leak poses no immediate threat to the public as it appears to be limited to inside the vessel.

US Coast Guard investigates ammonia leak aboard Pacific Producer on Aug. 16, 2023. Image from USCG Puget Sound Facebook page.

Air quality is being monitored in the area, the USCG official said.

The 169-foot, 472-metric ton vessel, which has been docked in Tacoma for about a year, is reported to have a checkered history, including a long string of health and safety violations.

The US Department of Labor's Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), in February, cited the operator, Seattle-based East West Seafoods, and owner, Christos Tsabouris, for 20 violations and proposed $208,983 in penalties, as reported by Undercurrent News at the time.

A statement published by the federal agency in February recounts how an inspection by OSHA was initially opened in July 2022 in Kodiak, Alaska, but was delayed when the Pacific Producer departed the port. Through coordination with USCG's Puget Sound, Washington, operation, a joint inspection resumed when the vessel arrived in Seattle in October.

"Inspectors found murky, brown water in the ship's drinking water system; crew members being served expired food; water used to process fish leaking into dry food storage and the galley's dining area; and other unsanitary conditions throughout the vessel," OSHA reported.

"In addition, OSHA discovered employees exposed to dangerous electrical hazards throughout the vessel, including damaged and improperly installed electrical equipment, broken outlets and outlets near water, ungrounded extension cords and exposed wiring. Inspectors also found the vessel had no fire suppression system as required, which exposed the crew to fire hazards.

The USCG has invalidated the Pacific Producer's certificate of compliance, halting the employer's continued operations until repairs are made, according to the OSHA statement.

Ammonia gauges were 'painted over'

A USCG internal email shared Thursday with Undercurrent sheds more light on the latest incident.

It describes how the USCG received a report from the Tacoma Fire Department (TFC) that it was doing an inspection of the vessel when it "sensed a high concentration of ammonia." TFD reportedly tested the air closest to the vessel and, after finding 89 parts per million of ammonia, instructed its personnel that they should not enter the vessel unless wearing special gear.

"Two ammonia tanks on the deck are severely degraded and the gauges are painted over," the USCG said an inspection found. "The ammonia tank below deck is reported to be in a similar condition."

On Tuesday morning (Aug. 15), the US Environmental Protection Agency's Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA) fund was accessed to contract the company US Ecology, according to the USCG email.

"US Ecology set up air quality monitoring devices in areas near the vessel," the USCG email said. "The current readings have shown there is no immediate threat to the public and the devices continue to be monitored."

The contractor boarded the vessel on Thursday and found the leak in the engine, but had not yet been able to secure it, the email continued. The vessel remains "locked up and sealed." 

US Coast Guard investigates ammonia leak aboard Pacific Producer on Aug. 16, 2023. Image from USCG Puget Sound Facebook page.

A 'blatant and continued disregard for crews' 

The Pacific Producer's history of trouble goes back even further.

In 2012, 2014 and 2018, OSHA inspections identified similar sanitation, electrical and fire hazards, and other dangers related to a lack of lockout/tagout, machine-guarding and fall protections, the federal agency noted in February. Also, there was an ammonia leak in 2018.

On top of that, in 2017 the US Department of Justice found East West Seafoods intentionally discharged oily bilge water and raw sewage into the ocean within three miles of the Alaskan coast four years earlier. It later presented false records to the USCG. A federal court in Alaska sentenced the company and its owner to five years of probation and $50,000 in fines.

"Alaskan fishing industry workers depend on their employers for vessels that don't jeopardize their safety and health," OSHA acting regional administrator Jack Rector said in February. "For more than a decade, our inspectors have found disgusting and dangerous conditions aboard the F/V Pacific Producer, and the wellbeing of crews aboard the vessel are at great risk because of its owner's failures.

"This employer's blatant and continued disregard for crews aboard the F/V Pacific Producer must end before tragedy strikes," Rector said. "The U.S. Department of Labor and its federal partners will use their full enforcement powers to hold East West Seafoods and Christos Tsabouris accountable for their callous neglect and contempt for federal workplace safety standards."

title: Sekkingstad almost doubles profits in tough 2022
content:
Norwegian salmonid exporter and processor Sekkingstad upped its sales and profits in 2022, despite a tough year of volatile markets.

Its turnover rose 24% year-on-year to NOK 2.77 billion ($270.9 million), thanks to increased income on all product types, including whole salmon and trout and further-processed fish.

Costs also rose y-o-y, from NOK 2.76bn to NOK 3.43bn -- a significant step up, but not enough to prevent operating profit from rising 52% to NOK 29m.

The bottom-line result for the year was a profit of NOK 19.7m, up from NOK 10.7m in 2021.

Sales of whole salmon and trout remained by far Sekkingstad's most important product and, in fact, became more important; it went from making up 82% of the firm's sales in 2021 to forming 84% in 2022 (NOK 2.9bn).

"Refined" products saw sales rise from NOK 352.6m to NOK 390.9m, but as a share of overall sales, fell from 12.7% to 11.3%.

In terms of geographical markets, the "rest of world" segment increased in importance at the expense of the domestic Norwegian market. Sales to Norway fell year-on-year to NOK 241.9m, going from 13% to 7% of total sales, while those to the rest of the world rose to NOK 1.28bn, going from 32% to 37% of all sales.

The European market was the largest for Sekkingstad, with sales rising to NOK 1.94bn in 2022; 56% of all income, compared with 55% the year before.

Late in 2022, the firm's sales director, Jannicke Johansson, told Undercurrent News it was seeing salmon buyers stock up on frozen fish in anticipation of short supply in the first half of 2023 -- a prediction that came true.

Prices at that time (early September 2022) were the lowest they'd been all year, and they would soon fly up again in 2023.

Johansson also said the company was considering reducing air cargo to send more salmon frozen by sea, though she added it would need the help and understanding of customers in order to take this carbon footprint reduction step.

"You cannot ship fresh salmon to overseas destinations like China or South Korea, which want fresh produce, because they are too far away and shipping times are inconsistent. On the contrary, these countries are not that far away if we ship the salmon frozen," Johansson explained.

From March 1, 2023, Sekkingstad's CEO, Even Hopland stepped down to "seek new challenges," with Bard Sekkingstad -- the company's owner -- moving into the top spot.

Hopland had been with the group since May 2019, when he joined as CEO of its subsidiary Skagerak Salmon, based in Denmark. Before that, he spent nearly three years as CEO of Norway's Fjord Processing.

Sekkingstad turns 100 years old in 2023 and will "celebrate fully" come September, the company said.

title: Russia eyes increased fishery cooperation across Africa
content:
Russia's fishery agency Rosrybolovstvo has pledged to further develop fishery cooperation with a number of African states.

"The fishery partnership between Russia and African nations dates back to the Soviet time, and now we have to give it a new boost," Rosrybolovstvo's head, Ilya Shestakov, was quoted as saying in an agency statement.

The dynamically growing population of Africa indicates an increasing demand for the supply of seafood products, while Russia has the export potential to meet this growing demand, he said.

During the recent Russia–Africa Summit in St. Petersburg in July there were top-level bilateral talks between the president of Russia and the heads of state of Senegal, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau. The agenda of these meetings included the development of fishery cooperation, Shestakov said.

"We plan to increase cooperation with Nigeria, Ghana, Senegal, Morocco, Mauritania, Cote d'Ivoire, South Africa, Mauritius, Mozambique and other countries," he said. 

Rosrybolovstvo has long prioritized fishery cooperation with African states. Russia already has agreements in place with Morocco, Mauritania, Senegal, Guinea-Bissau, Sierra Leone and Namibia, while the country eyes agreements with Angola, South Africa and Guinea.

The eastern-central Atlantic's highly productive pelagic resources of sardine and mackerel are important to the Russian fishing sector, and the country's fleet has a catch potential of 300,000 metric tons in the central-eastern and south-eastern Atlantic regions, according to the agency.

In February 2023, Russia and Mauritania agreed to develop bilateral fishery cooperation. The pair signed a fishery agreement in 2003 that allowed Russian fishing vessels to use Mauritanian harbor facilities.

According to Russian estimates, the total commercial fish stocks near Mauritania are estimated at about 4 million or 5m metric tons per year, and Russian fishermen annually catch more than 100,000t of horse mackerel in Mauritanian waters.

In December 2020, the Moroccan government adopted a maritime fisheries cooperation agreement with Russia. The agreement defined the cooperation in the preservation and
exploitation of fishery resources in Moroccan waters, including conditions for Russian fishing vessels in the areas off the Atlantic coast where Morocco exercises its sovereign rights and/or which are within its jurisdiction. The deal replaced the 2016 agreement that expired in March 2020. The new agreement, the eighth of its kind since 1992, lasts four years.

Russia and Guinea, meanwhile, signed a cooperation agreement on fisheries and aquaculture in September 2018. Under the deal, Russian fishing vessels can fish in Guinean waters. The two countries pledged to combat illegal fishing and develop and implement scientific and technical programs.

The agreement remains effective for five years with the option of a further automatic five-year extension. This agreement also replaced the 1981 agreement.

However, Russia has had bumpy fishery relations with some African states, including Senegal.

In January 2014, the Russian-owned factory trawler Oleg Naydenov, which regularly fishes off the West African coast, was boarded by armed Senegalese commandos near the maritime border with Guinea-Bissau and escorted back to the port of Dakar. The Senegalese government reportedly demanded $1.2m in fines for the vessel's alleged illegal fishing in the exclusive 12-mile fishing zone, releasing the vessel a few days later. 

In February 2023, Greenpeace Africa noted the presence of a Russian factory trawler, Vasiliy Filippov, in Senegalese waters, with an estimated storage capacity of more than 2,000t. According to Greenpeace Africa, foreign trawlers are only worsening Senegal's overexploited fish stocks.

Senegal has estimated that 300,000t of fish are taken illegally from its waters each year.

In the meantime, Russia's ambitious vision for fishery cooperation with African states may face strong Chinese competition.

In February 2022, the Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF) found 90% of fishing vessels operating in Ghana are owned by Chinese companies. EJF blamed the depletion of fish stocks in Ghana on Chinese trawlers, the owners of which use complex schemes to create front companies in the country, it claimed. Ghana's small pelagic fish
populations, such as sardinella, have dropped 80% in the past two decades.

The issue is common among West African countries, where illegal fishing is estimated to account for more than one-third of all catches, costing the region nearly $1 billion a year, according to EJF, which estimates that Ghana itself loses up to $50m a year.

Up to a fifth of illegal wild catches worldwide are believed to come from waters off Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Mauritania, Senegal and Sierra Leone. Most of the fish are believed to be caught by vessels from China, amounting to more than 2m metric tons a year in the region.

Russia also views African countries as markets for its seafood products.

In June 2019, the Russian Fishing Company indicated plans to export more pollock and herring to Nigeria, Ghana and other African countries. In 2018, it sold around 10,000t of Pacific herring to Nigeria, it said.

In June 2023, Russia's seafood industry group outlined ambitious plans to increase fish exports to Africa. Russian exports of seafood products to Africa can quadruple to 200,000t a year from the current 50,000t, according to the All-Russian Fishery
Association.

title: Benchmark faces fine of up to $9.8m for Chilean environmental impact
content:
Benchmark Chile Genetics and Exportadora Los Fiordos both face fines for environmental impacts at Chilean salmon farming operations, according to a press release from the country's Superintendencia del Medio Ambiente (SMA).

The government agency has confirmed that a Curacalco fish farm owned by Benchmark's Chilean subsidiary and an Estero Peuco farm belonging to Los Fiordos have caused "unforeseen environmental impacts," specifically a "proliferation of microorganisms" in discharges.

SMA has filed charges against the pair. Benchmark faces fines of up to 11,000 "annual tax units", or CLP 8.34 billion ($9.78 million). Los Fiordos could be fined up to 1,000 tax units, or CLP 758m.

Benchmark has been accused of three offenses; one minor and two serious. Los Fiordos' one charge is minor.

After the formulation of charges, each company has a period of 10 business days to present a compliance program and 15 business days to formulate their disclaimers, SMA said.

A spokesperson for Benchmark told Undercurrent News:

"Benchmark acknowledges the findings from the recent audit conducted by SMA. We are reviewing the findings and are committed to working closely with the relevant authorities and institutions to resolve the points raised in order to achieve full compliance, thereby removing the basis for any fine to be imposed.  As a responsible operator, Benchmark is committed to addressing any identified findings in an effective, transparent, and timely manner."

Los Fiordos did not reply to a request for comment before publishing.
