title: Valsecchi: Outlook for tuna canneries ‘no worse’ than current situation
content:
Streamlining production and optimizing efficiency to reduce costs are two ways that canneries should look to adapt in the face of rising costs and declining consumption, Adolfo Valsecchi, CEO of Italian cannery Generale Conserve, told Undercurrent News.

The group he developed, which produces the canned seafood brand Asdomar, has been looking to reduce the amount of olive oil used in each can.

He also stressed the importance of new processing technologies and automation in boosting yields.

Adolfo Valsecchi, CEO of Italian cannery Generale Conserve.

Last year, the Italian tuna market experienced a 2-3% decline in sales. Progress in negotiations between producers and distributors on increased prices in the face of higher costs has been slow, leading to the persistence of old pricing structures during the early months of 2022, Valsecchi said.

Then, in 2023, price increases from the previous year were compounded by further hikes.

According to Valsecchi, sales volumes in Italy have declined by 9% over the past two months, reflecting a significant slowdown in the market's growth. In contrast, over the last decade, the tuna market in Italy and Europe generally has maintained an average growth rate of 2-3%, making this recent downturn particularly noteworthy.

Italy's Generale Conserve owns the As do Mar tuna brand. Credit: The company's Facebook page.

Canneries in Italy and the rest of the world are in a precarious situation as they navigate the complexities of negotiating price increases for tuna cans with retailers. Despite efforts to secure higher prices, it is unclear whether they will achieve further growth at this stage, as consumption has dropped over the past two months, according to Valsecchi.

Private labels taking advantage 

In this context, private label producers have gained some ground in the Italian market at the expense of the "branded market," even if they also suffer under the cost increases, he said. 

Generale Conserve also produces tuna for private labels, accounting for about 35% of the group's total output, including jars and cans.

He said that this helped the firm to "stay in closer contact with its customer" and that clients appreciated the possibility of supplying third-party brands. Producing private labels also means the company handles additional volumes, and so supports company initiatives like investing in innovation and cost reduction.

Tuna cans in an Italian supermarket earlier this month.

"Since we ask them [our clients] for good placements and promotions for our brand, we believe that if we are collaborative and have a good reputation for meeting specifications and producing quality products, they are happy to have their brand made by us at competitive prices, and they show their appreciation by treating our brand well," he said.

Valsecchi said the Spanish are Italy's main competitors for private label supply.

"At the same time, half of the Italian brands are produced by Spanish companies, and the Spanish also produce private label products," he observed, claiming Italian retailers prefer an Italian supplier "because of higher trust."

His company specializes in producing yellowfin tuna, as well as small quantities of skipjack produced in the firm's second plant in Vila do Conde, Portugal, where it also makes tuna, mackerel and salmon in glass jars. 

Yellowfin price trend

Valsecchi believes the recent decline in yellowfin prices is driven by good catches in the Indian Ocean, which usually peak between January and July, and slower demand.

Catches significantly improved after French canneries had already bought the majority of the raw material they needed for the peak summer season, buying fewer quantities than usual. According to Valsecchi, it is too expensive for shipowners to store all the fish landed during this period and keep them in a cold store, so most of those volumes are reaching the market at weaker prices.

However, he doesn't expect tuna prices to fall as low as has been seen in the last four or five years over the next year and a half.

"For the second half of this year and next year, we shouldn't expect significant discounts or a return to prices from the last four or five years. The fishing vessels have obligations to respect the fishing effort and justify compliance with the allocated catch quota for each ship, so there are limits; they cannot fish as much as they want," he said.

Valsecchi noted that over 50% of European tuna canneries had shifted their production to skipjack, which was cheaper and more abundant than the yellowfin his firm focuses on.

He did state the yellowfin steak market has expanded significantly and "pays more" because the product is sold in the fresh channel.

"[The shift from cans to steak and other value-added products] is a segmentation that will happen [for yellowfin tuna]," he noted. "It remains the most prized tuna among the different varieties," he added. 

Expecting a loss

Generale Conserve, which reached a turnover of about €150 million ($165.2m) last year, is expected to increase its total sales further this year due to increased sales prices.

However, profit is likely to swing to a loss due to the increase in production costs. This trend is likely to impact most tuna canneries, even the most "solid," according to the tuna industry veteran.

"We expect a higher turnover than last year due to the increase in the product cost of the raw material generating sales inflation. But margins are very tight, and we think the whole sector has a hard time breaking even this year," Valsecchi said. He noted that last year the firm managed to achieve a "slight profit."

Generale Conserve is not planning to launch new products or expand into new markets outside of Italy as "in difficult times, focusing on new projects or different goals is even more difficult," Valsecchi said.

"It is wise to focus on the adventure we have known all along, not having new adventures and keep all attention on the experience gained in the markets we know."

The company continues to prioritize Friend of the Sea and Marine Stewardship Council-certified tuna when available; the executive said he had not encountered a significant price difference between tuna carrying different certifications.

The company's key objective in the short term is to defend its market position, despite the challenging environment.

"Last year, we maintained a profit, but this year is a more difficult situation. We will do everything not to lose our market share," he said.

"As a strategy for canned products in general, we aim to maintain a high-quality product. We are a premium brand and a leader in the premium segment, which is a well-defined niche that is not easy to enter or maintain. So for now, we aim to focus on defending this position," Valsecchi said.

"As a premium company, we have focused our promotions on premium products, such as glass jars, fillets, and similar items. We have concentrated our promotions on the smaller formats, the ones that customers encounter at the checkout counter, and we believe that consumers will be wise enough to consume tuna as a specialty, as a healthy, genuine product with great organoleptic properties. So we expect them to pair it with side dishes that cost less."

Valsecchi concluded that he expects the following year to be "no worse" than the last two.

"It should not be worse; there will be an adjustment, and when there are difficult moments, there is also a push forward to improve technologies, contain costs, and research efficiency."

title: US senators’ offices in talks over bill to better block Russian seafood imports
content:
Negotiations are happening between US lawmakers' offices over a bill that would better stop the import of Russian seafood by eliminating a loophole for product processed in China or other countries, Undercurrent News has learned.

Senator Ed Markey, a Massachusetts Democrat, put the kibosh on Alaska Republican Dan Sullivan's effort on June 22 to seek unanimous consent for the US-Russian Federation Seafood Reciprocity Act of 2023, S. 2011, as Undercurrent earlier reported. Sullivan's bill, which is also supported by Alaska Republican Lisa Murkowski, would block Russian seafood from getting around president Joe Biden's March 2022 ban if it's processed in China or another country. 

Though Markey said last month that he supported efforts to punish Russia for its invasion of Ukraine, he said Sullivan's bill would do too much damage to seafood processors in his home state, causing sourcing-related disruptions and job loss. He named Gorton's Seafood, a Gloucester-based division of Japan's Nissui Corp, as one of the companies that's most worried.

Still of C-SPAN 2 broadcast showing senator Ed Markey debating senator Dan Sullivan's bill to ban Russian seafood.

But Markey also said at the time that he and others in the Massachusetts delegation would be willing to work with Sullivan to "find a commonsense pathway" through problems with the legislation. 

That appears to be what's happening, as a staffer in Sullivan's office confirmed Thursday (July 13) that the two offices are now talking.

It wouldn't be the first time the two lawmakers have attempted to work out differences over Sullivan's efforts to ban the import of Russian seafood.

Sullivan made an unsuccessful effort to gain unanimous consent of S. 3614, a similar bill, in February 2022, before Biden issued executive order 14068 accomplishing much the same feat. Markey stood up to oppose Sullivan's bill then as well, advising that he had concerns about Massachusetts processors, as reported by Undercurrent.

The two sides reportedly worked out their differences on the 2022 legislation, but S. 3614, which was also supported by Murkowski, never made it out of the Senate Finance Committee before the end of the 117th Congress.

Markey argued this time that the new bill has different provisions that have yet to be studied.

Alaska senator Dan Sullivan pleading for support in his effort to ban Russian seafood. Image is still from C-SPAN 2 broadcast.

S. 2011 "would go against how seafood origin has been considered under longstanding US law and defined through the United States Treasury Department," Markey said. "So, as a result, while Customs and Border Protection [CBP] attempts this difficult enforcement task, processors could see major disruption, workers could lose their jobs. Consumer good costs for Americans could rise significantly."

Unlike Biden's executive order, S. 2011 -- as currently worded -- would include under the ban any product "of Russian Federation origin, including any such product incorporated into another product or substantially transformed in a country other than the Russian Federation." The legislation would go into effect 90 days after passage, giving processors little time to make changes.

Also different is how the ban contained in the bill would only terminate 90 days after the date on which the president "determines and certifies to Congress that the government of the Russian Federation has terminated its prohibition on the importation of seafood products from the United States." Its expiration is not tied to the Russian occupation of Ukraine.

As reported earlier, Sullivan's effort to stop the import of Russian seafood isn't as much about the invasion of Ukraine as it is about Russia's ban on US seafood, which dates back to at least 2014 when Russia responded to sanctions inflicted in relation to its invasion of the Crimean Peninsula. 

This time around, a companion bill, HR 4165, has been introduced in the House of Representatives' Ways and Means Committee by Garret Graves, a Louisiana Republican. It's been co-sponsored by Mary Sattler Peltola, an Alaska Democrat. However, the lower chamber bill also has yet to gain additional co-sponsors.

title: Fishing industry raises alarm on unlicensed Chinese vessel’s entry into Peruvian waters
content:
The recent entry of an unlicensed Chinese industrial vessel into Peru's 200-mile exclusive economic zone is worrying the country's fishing industry.

On July 2, a Chinese vessel reached Paita, a fishing hub in northern Peru, with an injured crew member who needed medical attention.

The vessel, named "Han YI 3," allegedly disregarded control regulations for extracting resources, including squid, from Peru's coast, according to the committee for the sustainable management of the South Pacific's giant squid, known as Calamasur.

Alfonso Miranda Eyzaguirre, Calamasur's president, told Undercurrent News he was "deeply concerned" over the event.

He called for stricter controls and inspection measures on the Chinese fleet to determine the vessel's compliance with Peruvian maritime regulations.

Miranda stressed the importance of verifying the government's registration of the vessel's entry and ensuring that inspections, as defined by the Port State Measures Agreement and the Regional Organization for Fisheries Management of the South Pacific (RFMO-PS), have been conducted according to the appropriate protocols.

Calamasur highlighted the recurring pattern of Chinese vessels entering the 200-mile zone with crew members in poor health. According to the association, Chinese vessels take advantage of crossing into Peruvian waters to explore stocks in the areas. 

Miranda argued that this practice allows them unrestricted access to monitor the productive areas where marine species such as giant squid reside.

According to the association, Peruvian authorities have not carried out an inspection on the human rights situation of the vessel that landed in Paita.

The entry into Peruvian waters rings an alarm bell after a recent incident occurred in Montevideo, Uruguay, where a desperate crew member sent a message in a bottle, claiming to be held captive and pleading for help. The case raised awareness of a "new kind of slavery" where the crew is not paid and not let off the boat for long periods, one source that preferred to remain unnamed noted.

Last month, a woman found a message in a bottle near the Sauce de Portezuelo area in Maldonado, Uruguay. It contained a message in Chinese from a crew member claiming to be held captive, titled SOS. Following an investigation, Uruguayan authorities discovered the crew had been at sea without touching port for over two years. Their contract expired in June 2021, and they have not received salaries since. The crew members intended to change ships.

Uruguay's prefecture recently completed an investigation into the request for help found inside the bottle on the coast of the Maldonado area and concluded that it was not a "criminal situation" but a problem of "labor relations," La Nacion reported. As a result, it did not assist since the issues were related to labor issues and financial compensation to the crew, according to Infobae.

Chinese squid vessels dodge Peru monitoring

In 2020, over 300 Asian vessels operated in international waters close to Peru's EEZ. According to Calamasur, inspections have helped to reduce their number, with about 20 operating at present near Peruvian waters. The group aims for these controls to become stricter.

"In the case of Peru, we are uncertain if labor and human rights verifications have been conducted on this vessel, considering that this is an ongoing issue that affects the Chinese fleet and is consistently denounced," stated Miranda. He further emphasized the negative impact of the Chinese vessel's presence on the livelihoods of Peru's artisanal fishermen, creating an atmosphere of anxiety.

Hundreds of ‘dark’ vessels fishing illegally off Argentine coast in March

Calamasur has urged the Peruvian government to provide transparent and concise reports regarding this "suspicious entry," as it has caused discomfort and concern within the fishing community. Miranda highlighted the reluctance of the distant water fleet to undergo stricter inspections, both within Peru's jurisdictional waters and in international waters.

He noted that the proximity of Chinese vessels to Peru's 200-mile (see map below) area has raised alarm, as artisanal fishermen have repeatedly reported the illegal extraction of over 50,000 metric tons of squid and concluded by emphasizing the importance of regional cooperation in addressing the issues stemming from illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing practices.

Calamasur's concerns align with Peru's significant contribution to global squid landings, accounting for over 50% of the world's production. According to data from 2020 provided by Peru's production ministry, between 2010 and 2019, the average annual squid landing was approximately 430,000t, peaking at 556,000t in 2014.

The dominant role Peru plays in squid production underscores the urgency of tackling issues related to illegal fishing practices.

Peru's cuttle fish, squid exports. Source: UCN trade portal.

China cuttle fish, squid exports.

Last month, Peru participated in the fifth meeting of the Latin American Alliance for Sustainable Fishing, also known as Alpescas, where the protection of fishing resources and the fight against hunger and malnutrition were vital topics.

The meeting emphasized the need for strengthened national legislation, enhanced monitoring and control measures for distant water vessels, and collaborative efforts among countries to uphold responsible fishing principles advocated by the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO).

According to Miranda, the concerns raised by Calamasur and the initiatives undertaken by Alpescas demonstrate the commitment of multiple stakeholders toward ensuring sustainable fishing practices and preserving marine resources in Latin America.

title: Blumar fined $40,000, has production cycle at Aysen site suspended
content:
Chilean salmon farmer Blumar has been sentenced to pay a fine of 500 'annual tax units' -- equivalent to around CLP 31.6 million, or $40,000 -- and told to suspend its operations for one production cycle at its 'Dring 2' site in Aysen, reports AdPRENSA. 

The ruling was made after an investigation by Chile's national fisheries and aquaculture service, Sernapesca, which found discrepancies between the company's reported information and what was verified. 

According to the information provided to Sernapesca, Blumar declared the sale of 4,561 metric tons of Atlantic salmon to three processing plants and three storage points. However, it was found that the firm's 'Dring 2' site exceeded its authorized limit for farming by 657t.

In addition, the company provided inaccurate and late information to the regulatory body, declaring the stocking of 9,067 fewer fish than recorded at the beginning of the cycle in 2015. It was also discovered that the company exceeded the authorized fish limit in seven of the 24 cages on the site. 

Blumar has a period of 10 business days to appeal the sentence. If no appeal is made, the company will be required to comply with the provisions of the ruling.

title: Markey thwarts effort to close loophole in Russia seafood ban, identifies Gorton’s as part of opposition
content:
US senator Ed Markey on Thursday (June 22) shot down an effort by fellow lawmaker Dan Sullivan to gain quick passage of a bill intended to block a loophole that allows Russian seafood to get around president Joe Biden's ban if it's processed in China or another country.

Markey, a Massachusetts Democrat, said the measure would do too much damage to seafood processors in his home state, causing sourcing-related disruptions and job loss, and he named Gorton's Seafood, a Gloucester-based division of Japan's Nissui Corp, as one of the companies that's most worried.

Sullivan was attempting to gain unanimous consent of the US-Russian Federation Seafood Reciprocity Act of 2023, S. 2011, a speedy way to advance the bill he introduced on June 15 in the Senate Finance Committee, as reported by Undercurrent News. The legislation is also supported by senator Lisa Murkowski, another Alaska Republican, and has a companion bill.

Credit: flysnowfly / Shutterstock

HR 4165 was also introduced on June 15 in the House of Representatives' Ways and Means Committee by Garret Graves, a Louisiana Republican. It's been co-sponsored by Mary Sattler Peltola, an Alaska Democrat.

Markey said he and others in the Massachusetts delegation would be willing to work with Sullivan, an Alaska Republican, to "find a commonsense pathway" through problems with the legislation. 

"But right now, Gorton's of Gloucester is very concerned about this bill," he said. "You know, one firm has 450 workers, another has 350 workers, and we have dozens of other companies up in Massachusetts with employees that are potentially jeopardized by this bill."

In the nearly one-hour back and forth between the two lawmakers, which is available on C-SPAN, Sullivan responded by suggesting the solution was simply for these processors to source US-harvested seafood. He shared some harshly critical words for Gorton's.

"But at least my colleague is being honest, right? This is about Gorton's of Gloucester," he said. "That's kind of what we knew by the way. To Gorton's of Gloucester, here's my message: You continuing to import Russian seafood is a bad business idea ... Funding the Putin war machine is a bad business idea. Most American business companies have realized that. So Gorton's of Gloucester, here's my idea for you. Buy more Alaskan seafood, buy more Massachusetts seafood. Get off your addiction to Russian war machine seafood that is laundered through China. It's an unsustainable business model. And at some point, even your US senator is not going be able to defend you."

Undercurrent emailed a request for comment to Kurt Hogan, Gorton's CEO, on Friday morning, but didn't hear back before press time. 

Alaska senator Dan Sullivan pleading for support in his effort to ban Russian seafood. Image is still from C-SPAN 2 broadcast.

Old adversaries

This is not the first time Sullivan has tried to pass legislation to stop the US from importing Russian seafood and Markey thwarted the effort.

Sullivan made a similar unsuccessful effort to gain unanimous consent of S. 3614, a similar bill, in February 2022, before Biden issued executive order 14068 accomplishing much the same feat. Markey stood up to oppose Sullivan's earlier bill as well, advising then that he had similar concerns about Massachusetts processors, as reported by Undercurrent.

The two sides reportedly worked out their differences on the 2022 legislation, but S. 3614, which was also supported by Murkowski, never made it out of the Senate Finance Committee before the end of the 117th Congress.

Markey argued this time that the new bill has different provisions that have yet to be studied.

S. 2011 "would go against how seafood origin has been considered under longstanding US law and defined through the United States Treasury Department," he said. "So, as a result, while Customs and Border Protection [CBP] attempts this difficult enforcement task, processors could see major disruption, workers could lose their jobs. Consumer good costs for Americans could rise significantly."

New bill has different language

The language for S. 2011 was made available this week. Unlike Biden's executive order, Sullivan's bill would include under the ban any product "of Russian Federation origin, including any such product incorporated into another product or substantially transformed in a country other than the Russian Federation."

The legislation would go into effect 90 days after passage, giving processors little time to make changes.

Also different is how the ban contained in the bill would only terminate 90 days after the date on which the president "determines and certifies to Congress that the government of the Russian Federation has terminated its prohibition on the importation of seafood products from the United States." Its expiration is not tied to the Russian occupation of Ukraine.

As reported earlier, Sullivan's effort to stop the import of Russian seafood isn't as much about the invasion of Ukraine as it is about Russia's ban on US seafood, which dates back to at least 2014 when Russia responded to sanctions inflicted in relation to its invasion of the Crimean Peninsula. 

The Alaskan lawmaker described Thursday how he appealed unsuccessfully to every president to ban Russian seafood after he took office in 2015, including Barack Obama and Donald Trump. Biden, he said, was the first to act on his concern.

Credit: Russian Fishery Company

"But the Biden executive order has a loophole," he said. "It's got a massive loophole that of course the Russians are taking advantage of. The vast majority of Russian seafood is harvested and frozen in simple product forms. And then, guess what, it's shipped to which country? That other great dictatorship in the world. I'm joking when I say 'great.' It's a brutal dictatorship, China.

"So Russian fishermen now send all their fish to China to get it reprocessed, laundered essentially. They fill it with phosphates. And guess where they ship it, to the United States. Hundreds of millions of dollars of Russian seafood now gets sent to China, another dictatorship. And they send it back to the US, almost duty-free. So that's a giant loophole. It's happening every day. It's an outrage."

He said the consumption of the allegedly inferior product is turning Americans off from eating seafood.   

"The Russian war machine benefits from this. The Chinese, of course, benefit from this, and American fishermen are getting screwed," he said.

Sullivan said he's been informed that the loophole can also be closed by the Biden administration, in advance of an act of Congress, and enforced by CBP. He said he also has reached out to the deputy secretary of the US Department of Treasury, Wally Adeyemo, and was awaiting a callback.

How much Russian seafood is US still importing?

Russia was the eighth-largest beneficiary of US seafood imports in 2021, sending 48,867 metric tons worth $1.2 billion, a 12% increase in volume and 34% increase in value over what it sent the US in 2020, Undercurrent found when it studied National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) data. That was topped only by Canada, India, Chile, Indonesia, Vietnam, China and Ecuador.

Russian seafood exports in 2021 to the US included roughly 80 items, but the most valuable were frozen snow crab, 18,799t worth $509.2m in 2021, and frozen red king crab, 8,486t worth $419.7m.

Even after Biden's ban, which went into effect in late June 2022, Russia managed to send the US 23,730t of seafood worth $922.8m over the course of the year.

Russian caught pollock Credit: Gidrostroy

So far, in 2023, according to NOAA, the US has not imported any seafood from Russia. 

But of course that doesn't include Russian seafood that has managed to get around the ban by being processed in other countries, changing its country of origin. It's difficult to measure how much. However, according to an International Trade Commission report, the US imported $300 million in salmon and pollock from China in 2022 -- some caught in the US and reprocessed in China, but a majority likely originating from Russia.

It's also difficult to know which US seafood processors or other businesses are still relying on Russian product imported from China. However, among companies to have recently written the US Department of Treasury to argue for preserving exemptions on many of the species imported from China, including Alaska pollock fillets, were: Gorton's; the New Hampshire-based office of Canada's High Liner; Endeavor Seafood, in Newport, Rhode Island; King & Prince Seafoods, in Brunswick, Georgia; The Nordic Group, also in Gloucester; The Hadley Company, in Wareham, Massachusetts; Southstream Seafoods, in Warwick, Rhode Island; Channel Fish Processing, in Braintree, Massachusetts; Maritime Products International, in Newport News, Virginia; Slade Gorton, in Boston, Massachusetts; FW Bryce, in Gloucester; Arctic Fisheries, in Buffalo, New York; and Captain D's, in Nashville, Tennessee.

A shot at MSC

Sullivan also used his time on the Senate floor Thursday to rip the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) for continuing to certify Russian fisheries as sustainable.

As reported recently by Undercurrent, Doug Vincent-Lang, the commissioner of Alaska's Department of Fish and Game, wrote a four-page letter last month to MSC CEO Rupert Howes that was sharply critical of the not-for-profit sustainability organization for making what he said were special allowances so that Russian pollock, salmon and crab can continue to carry the blue tick. MSC responded that the letter was off-base, as reported by Undercurrent.

"Now, unfortunately, we are seeing some certification efforts such as the Marine Stewardship Council," he said. "Shame on them, allowing themselves to be pulled into a profit-driven mindset that is focused on one thing, money and benefiting Russia."

Certifying the Russian fisheries as sustainable "is a joke," he declared. "It is ridiculous. Shame on MSC for helping to fund the Putin war machine."

title: Australis to ‘lower or stop’ farming in Aysen, Magallanes to offset overproduction
content:
Chilean salmon farmer Australis Seafoods plans to compensate for its self-denounced overproduction in 33 grow-out sites in the Aysen and Magallanes regions by producing 91,376 metric tons less in coming years.

"This figure corresponds to the total compensation committed to by Australis Seafoods in the sanctioning procedures initiated by the Chilean environmental authority (known as the SMA) on the occasion of the firm's self-report presented on October 27, 2022," said Australis in the documents presented to the SMA.  

This would mean stopping production at some of those sites if approved by the SMA or in additional compensation sites other than those object of the self-report in compliance with all applicable sector and health regulations. 

In total, the company has presented 21 compliance programs in the last few weeks, including close to 300 different actions -- some of which have a timeline extending until 2028 -- with a cost of approximately CLP 64 billion ($79.4 million), Undercurrent News learned. 

"Change to the company's controller, which materialized at the end of the year 2022, and given the charge formulations for overproduction in Australis grow-out sites, the need for a global production adjustment in the company has been defined," it added. "This can be seen in Australis' voluntary and collaborative participation in the SMA's compliance pilot program, being the first in the sector to join."

As mentioned in Australis' self-report, 21 sanctioning procedures were initiated, which included 52 serious infractions, all for the overproduction of 85,000t of salmon in different production cycles ranging from 2014 to 2022, as well as six minor charges for other environmental breaches.

Australis initiated the SMA-required compliance programs the same day it provided its overproduction reports to the agency. Thus, the financial impact would come from those compliance plans, which include stopping production for several complete cycles and producing less in some centers. 

Australis' reporting on its overproduction was accepted in most cases since the SMA's investigation for two of them was already in progress.

Another five charges prior to the self-reporting must be included, too. Those charges, amounting to another 12,000t of overproduction, ignited the conflict between the firm's parent company, China's Joyvio Foods, and former owner Isidoro Quiroga over whether the Chinese company was aware of them before the buyout in 2019.

The calculation of the self-reported production was determined by estimating the biomass value declared in harvest declarations -- the number of harvested fish multiplied by average weight -- minus the biomass declared in the seeding declaration. The declared mortality reported to Sernapesca in the aquaculture monitoring information system was also included in the calculation, according to the company. 

"If approved by the SMA, Australis Seafoods' proposed compensation programs will serve as a significant step towards addressing the overproduction issue and ensuring compliance with environmental regulations. The company's efforts to self-report and take corrective actions demonstrate its commitment to responsible and sustainable salmon farming practices," Australis also stated. 

The Chinese owners denied having any knowledge of this in advance, though, and filed civil and criminal lawsuits against the company's former owner and others, demanding over $1.2bn in compensation, as Undercurrent also reported. 

However, internal emails involving top Australis Seafoods and Joyvio Food executives between 2021 and 2022 throw doubt on claims they had no idea about overproduction prior to buying the firm and current CEO Andres Lyon taking over at the Chilean salmon farmer. 

Table shows Australis plan to compensate for its self-denounced overproduction in 33 grow-out sites in the Aysen and Magallanes regions by producing 91,376t less in coming years. The first column corresponds to each sanctioning procedure (21 in total) and the second to the total tons it should compensate.

title: OSHA memo targets New England processors, wholesalers for inspections
content:
It's well established that commercial fishing is a hazardous occupation, but so too is working at a seafood processing plant.

At least that's what the US Department of Labor's Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) believes based on a policy directive issued late last week by its Region I (New England) office. The 14-page memo, which can be found here, instructs OSHA officials in five offices to begin conducting "programmed inspections, emphasis programs and compliance assistance and training" at area seafood processing operations and related merchant wholesaler operations.

The list includes OSHA offices in Braintree and Andover, Massachusetts, as well as those in August and Banger, Maine, and in Providence, Rhode Island.

"The intent of this local emphasis program is to increase awareness of the significant health and safety hazards in this industry that can cause or have caused severe injury or death to employees, and to encourage employers to take steps to correct these hazards, thus reducing potential injuries and deaths," the memo reads.

The New England seafood processing industry sector has a problem with injuries and illnesses, notes the memo, which was distributed by Region I administrator Galen Blanton. In the past seven fiscal years (fiscal 2016-2022), there have been two fatalities and four finger amputations.

"Fall hazards continue to injure employees on and around the docks," the OSHA memo added. "Employees in these industries continue to be exposed to ammonia and cooling system hazards, resulting in three general duty clause violations and one hazard letter. The general duty clause violations include one willful serious and two repeat serious violations."

According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), seafood processors experience an injury and illness rate of 6.8 per 100 full-time equivalent employees, which is 2.5 times higher than the national average of 2.7. Additionally, seafood wholesalers see an injury and illness rate of 4.5, which is 1.6 times higher than the norm for their category, and seafood packaging and processing firms maintain an average DART (days away, restricted and transfer) rate that's 3.3 times higher than the national average, the report noted.  

In one of the most dramatic incidents, an employee was fatally strangled at a processing plant in New Bedford, Massachusetts, in January 2019 when his jacket sleeve got caught in a rotating shaft, tightening his jacket and shirt around his neck, according to the OSHA memo. The agency said the company, which is not named, failed to implement a lockout procedure prior to maintenance employees being exposed to active machinery.

Some 11 months later, in November 2019, the owner of a cleaning company was killed when he was unable to exit a spiral freezer at a different unnamed seafood processing company's plant in Braintree, Massachusetts, after the hot water and steam cleaning cycle began, according to the memo.

In yet another incident, in October 2019, a worker from an employment agency was attempting to clear a jam on a bag sealer machine in a Gloucester, Massachusetts, plant when his finger got caught in the pulley, according to OSHA. He suffered a severe laceration and/or amputation. The guard had been removed from the machine a week before and not replaced.  

Some 50 inspections, conducted by OSHA's Region I offices between fiscal 2016 and fiscal 2022, resulted in 82 serious citations, five repeat citations and one willful general duty clause citation. The most frequently cited citations were for failing to follow elements of the lockout-tagout standards (18) and inadequate or missing machine guarding (14), the memo instructed. Unsafe operation of powered industrial trucks and failure to follow elements of the confined space standard were both cited seven times.

The new program, which was scheduled to be initiated on June 1, 2023, is set to expire within five years unless renewed by the agency.

title: Zoneco’s finances stabilize under state ownership
content:
China’s Zoneco Group, previously the country's largest listed seafood company, is no longer considered a delisting risk after reporting a third consecutive year of profits.

The improvement comes after state-owned enterprise Dalian Yanhua Group, a conglomerate mainly involved in salt production, became Zoneco's largest shareholder last year, according to the company. 

State-owned Chinese firm promises to increase holdings in Zoneco

Dalian Yanhua outbid rivals for a 15.5% stake in Zoneco, which it acquired in CNY 343 million ($54.3m) in March 2022, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

The bid boosted Yanhua’s shareholding above that of former controlling shareholder Changhai County Zhangzidao Investment and Development Center (ZIDC), whose share fell to 7% from 22.5%.

On July 26, 2022, ZIDC entrusted its 7% equity to Dalian State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission, which is the indirect controlling shareholder of Yanhua. Hence, the state-owned enterprise controls 22.5% of the shares in Zoneco.

According to Zoneco's 2022 annual report, the company's net profit was CNY 3.93m, a 46.4% decrease from 2021 but the third consecutive year of profits. The company's sales revenues came to CNY 2.02 billion, stable with 2021. 

Zonceco told the Shenzhen Stock Exchange on May 26 that the company’s operating conditions have improved significantly, and its liabilities have dropped from more than CNY 3bn at their peak to CNY 2bn as of the end of 2022. Moreover, under the coordination of the Dalian Municipal Government, banks offer preferential interest rates for corporate loans. It added there were no overdue loans last year.

In addition, the company recovered some CNY 570m by strictly controlling costs and selling non-main business assets, it said. As of the end of last year, the company's cash flow was CNY 479m, enough to guarantee 12 months of operations, it said.

In 2020, Zoneco was fined CNY 600,000 over a long-running "scallop saga" involving accounting fraud and missing scallops. Hougang Wu, Zoneco's former chairman, was given a lifetime ban from public securities markets following the scandal. 

The company still faces a number of civil litigation cases and is seeking to reach a settlement with the plaintiffs, which is not expected to affect its continuous operation.

title: Salmon companies talk Italian growth plans in face of inflation pressures
content:
MILAN, Italy -- The Italian expo Tuttofood, which took on May 8-11 in Milan, highlighted what seemed like a thriving salmon industry with a plethora of exhibitors representing the whole production chain.

Despite the downstream salmon market in Italy and elsewhere currently facing a significant challenge with soaring raw material prices and the simultaneous impact of inflation on consumers' buying power, suppliers were hopeful they could stimulate consumption.

Several aim to promote value-added products, including smoked salmon and other ready-to-eat and ready-to-cook dishes, in the everyday diet of Italian consumers, not only during the Christmas holiday as has traditionally been the case. The trend is already moving, partially driven by a love of Japanese food and other cuisines.

(Note, for the graph below, EUMOFA warns that initial figures for the latest datapoints are often revised after a short time, so the spike illustrated at time of publishing may mellow.)

Upgrade to Pro to view

Despite rising inflation, demand for salmon products has remained relatively strong compared to other products, according to executives attending the show. Salmon suppliers fiercely compete to position their new convenient and value-added offerings.

Some salmon companies attended the event for the first time, like Faroese farmer Hiddenfjord, which aims to diversify its sales after it stopped supplying the Russian market in February last year.

Norway's Seaborn and Bremnes Seashore attended the Milan event, the latter promoting its sashimi brand SALMA. Bremnes has production at its factory of nearly 50,000 metric tons per year, of which around 35,000t come from its own farming locations.

Salma focuses on the sale of branded products such as burgers and sashimi to retailers, which can be stored in the fridge and have a shelf life of 11 days, according to export director Johnny Haberg. 

Haberg told Undercurrent News that Salma's turnover reached about NOK 435 million ($37m) in 2021 and is expected to be higher this year thanks to the passing on of high salmon prices. Figures for 2022 have not been finalized and audited yet.

"Even if prices go up, demand [for our branded products] grows around the world," Haberg noted. He claimed that the growing demand for salmon in some relatively new markets in Asia and some more mature markets like the US, combined with stalled global production growth, has contributed to boosting prices of salmon in general and hence also for Salma's branded premium products.

Among other exhibitors, Mowi's Italian sales office was showcasing the Norwegian multinational's products for retailers and discounters on the Italian market.

The firm has historically produced private label products for big Italian shops such as Ikea or Coop and had only one branded line, under the name Harbour, produced exclusively for supermarket chain Esselunga. However, since May 2021, Mowi has launched its own, MOWI-branded, products in Italy's large-scale retail, promoting itself as a brand that has a strong focus on raw material quality and sustainability, brand specialist Lorena Maria Faustini told Undercurrent at the show.

"We started out [sales of our branded products] with very few clients but have expanded into large-scale distribution, as it [the brand] is appreciated by consumers," Faustini said.

Mowi has progressively expanded its range of value-added products available in Italy and is planning to launch new lines that are already on sale in Germany or other European countries later this year.

The range includes smoked salmon with a new tomato and basil flavor, and Mowi "infusion fillets" are now available in one-portion packs for individual consumers. The fresh salmon "infusion" packaging can be put in the microwave, according to Faustini, who defined these products as "dinner saving" since they are ready in only 2.5 minutes of microwave cooking.

This year, Mowi also launched branded sushi, which -- according to Faustini -- will be followed by other products to cater to consumers who enjoy other world cuisines. It also has a barbecue, escalope, and a "cartoccio" product, which includes a bag to cook the salmon in the oven with all its sauces.

All of Mowi's value-added line sold in Italy is processed in Poland. 

Meanwhile, Lanef, an Italian distributor of smoked salmon and other seafood products, claims to be one of the firms investing more in the marketing and branding of salmon products on the Italian market, together with Mowi, on TV and via social media campaigns.

Lanef has two main salmon brands, Re Salmone and Coda Nera. Its products -- all branded and not including any private label -- are positioned in supermarkets, restaurants and stores. 

Last year the company made €57m in turnover, about 10% up on the previous year. Lanef expects to continue growing by investing in high-quality products, according to the marketing manager.

Lanef's Ti Amo branded salmon.

In recent years, Lanef has launched the TV campaign Ti Amo (I Love You), which as of this year, has also become an inscription on the packaging window of their Re Salmone's smoked salmon packs.

This year the firm also plans to launch fresh salmon fillets for high-end restaurants, which will be part of its "luxury line". Lanef's campaign targets young, nutrition-conscious consumers who want ready-to-eat products. 

Local smokers also exhibited at Tuttofood.

Scandia, based in the mountain region of Valtellina in northern Italy, produces smoked salmon and mushrooms. The firm, which achieved a revenue of about €20m last year, has been growing its salmon business by about 8-10% compared to the previous year, according to sales executive Ferdinando Colombo. It buys whole salmon and smokes it in-house in its factory in Morbegno.

Italian firm Fjord has expanded its portfolio of smoked fish products after being acquired by the country's largest caviar maker, Agroittica.

It sells salmon from different origins and with added flavors. Since the acquisition, Agroittica has worked to improve the quality to match the expectations of its caviar customers, according to the firm's commercial director Stefano Bottoli.

He said that the integration between Agroittica and Fjord took time due to a "different vision" and "quality standard."

As a result, Agroittica has made investments in technology to produce Italy's "best [smoked] salmon." He said quality improvement is ongoing after achieving a "very high" level.

"There is a strong will on the part of all management to increase the qualitative aspect of the company, which is very high right now. Our goal is not to be good but to be the best possible," he claimed. 

Starlaks, which has a processing capacity of about 1,000t, and FoodLab are two other Italian firms specializing in the sale of smoked salmon for the foodservice sector.

Among the other smoked salmon brands promoted at Tuttofood were Spanish names such as Brasmar's La Balinesa and Iceland Seafood International's Ahumados Dominguez.

title: NGOs urge EU to back new law protecting marine areas
content:
Several NGOs are urging EU institutions to vote for a "nature-based solution to climate breakdown."

A new law on nature restoration, if voted in during the coming months, will establish legally-binding rules for European member states and strengthen measures to effectively tackle the triple crises of climate change, biodiversity loss and environmental degradation.

The measure could include at least 20% of the EU land and sea areas restored and protected by 2030, depending on the text agreed.

This week, on May 24, the European Parliament's fisheries (PECH), agriculture and rural development (AGRI) and environment, public health and food safety (ENVI) committees will vote on amendments to the European Commission's proposed EU Nature Restoration Law.

PECH's work on the opinion was led by member of European Parliament Caroline Roose. ENVI has led the work, with PECH and AGRI providing opinions that ENVI will consider before the EU Parliament votes in plenary to adopt its final position in July.

The report adopted in plenary will reflect the European Parliament's agreed position during the subsequent trialogue negotiations with the European Commission and Council -- representing member states -- to finalize the EU Nature Restoration Law. 

Negotiations on this file are particularly challenging given the political context, which includes inflation, the energy crisis, and the rise of polarising populism in the run-up to the 2024 European elections.

Several political group members in the PECH committee, including those in the center-right European People's Party, the Eurosceptic European Conservatives and Reformists, and the liberal Renew Europe, are threatening to reject the Nature Restoration Law proposal in full or to weaken its level of ambition and scope significantly, according to the NGOs.

Nicolas Fournier, campaign director for habitat protection at Oceana in Europe, said the nature restoration law could be a "game-changer" for the ocean and EU fishers relying on productive seas.

The EU Commission's proposal ignored the need for coherence between fisheries management under the common fisheries policy and new restoration objectives, for instance, tackling destructive fishing in restoration areas, he added. According to him, the European parliament could fill that gap.

Tatiana Nuno, senior marine policy officer at Seas At Risk, defined the law proposal as a "once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for the EU to respond to the climate and biodiversity loss crises."

title: Rising demand, erratic supply boost fish oil prices, enhance appeal of other omega-3 sources
content:
MADRID, Spain -- Global demand for omega-3 is growing faster than production volumes of fish oil, which is still the main source of healthy omega-3 fatty acids, said Aldo Bernasconi, vice president of data science at the Global Organization for EPA and DHA Omega-3s (GOED).

"Based on preliminary figures, omega-3 ingredient production grew by 1.7% to 117,746 metric tons in 2022," Bernasconi said during the International Marine Ingredients Organisation (IFFO) members meeting in Madrid, Spain.

"Growth is expected to continue at an annual average growth rate of 2% to reach over 125,000t in 2025."

With demand for EPA and DHA omega-3s growing faster than that -- by 2.6% in 2022 -- record fish oil prices due to the El Nino phenomenon affecting production in Peru and a trend toward cheaper algal oils are helping make new sources more desirable.

Fish oil prices in Peru have already exceeded the $6,000/t mark, doubling the price levels of late 2021, according to data presented by Fernando Norambuena, global sourcing category manager for novel ingredients with BioMar Group.

"Multiple companies are trying to bring to market genetically engineered seed oils with EPA and DHA," he added. "Also, a general public interest in plant-based foods and a larger variety of compositions are helping to bring algal oil-based supplements out of their niche markets -- vegetarian or vegan, or consumers with fish and seafood allergies."

According to data presented by Bernasconi, the demand for crude fish oil was 232,539t in 2022, up 2.2% year-on-year from 227,543t in 2021, and is expected to grow by 2.5% annually to hit over 250,000t in 2025.

"The main source of crude fish oil will continue to be the pelagic fisheries, as well as by-products from the fish processing industry, which contributed approximately 152,432t of the total sourced in 2022," he explained. "The rest will come from new alternatives."

However, he added, consumer resistance and the many regulatory issues make the expansion of genetically modified oils difficult, and major expansions in capacity are needed before algae can become a larger player in the supplement market. 

"Of course, things are changing and there is huge potential for GMO oils. However, there is still great cultural resistance against their use for human consumption in Europe and the US, which are, by far, the markets with the largest demand for omega-3 ingredients," Bernasconi pointed out.

"Nobody sees algal oil being a viable replacement for fish oils in the short term, even though there are many companies turning to invest in these now that fish oil prices have gone over the roof. Algal oil production still needs to be scaled manyfold before we get to the point in which it can be considered as a real alternative."

Omega-3 products are used in various applications, from dietary supplements to pet foods and pharmaceuticals. Recently, the sector that is pulling the most demand is that of dietary supplements, followed by pet foods, while the pharmaceutical sector grew slower than in previous years, according to Bernasconi.

Additionally, most of the gains in ingredient demand were driven by increases in concentrates, as these oils gradually replace refined oils in the larger, more established markets, he pointed out.

Regarding volume growth, the fastest-growing regions are in Asia and in developing markets in Latin America. The more established markets -- the US and Europe, mainly, grew modestly, "returning to more normal levels after the large corrections of 2021," he concluded.

title: Mowi fined £800k over death of employee in Scotland
content:
Mowi has been fined £800,000 ($1.01m) after an employee was crushed and drowned when he fell into the water during a boat transfer at its Scottish operations.

According to the UK's Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service (COPFS), the company pled guilty to health and safety breaches at Inverness Sheriff Court on May 9, 2023.

This comes after a three-year fight for justice by Catriona Lockhart, partner of Clive Hendry, the 58-year-old fish farm assistant manager who died at the firm's Ardintoul fish farm on Feb. 18, 2020.

He drowned after falling into the water from a feed barge access ladder during a boat transfer, according to a Marine Accident Investigation Branch report.

Report finds failings at fault in 2020 death of Mowi Scotland worker

He stepped from the deck onto the ladder while the Beinn Na Caillich was still moving forward and was crushed between the boat and the barge. A fish farm technician on board the barge attempted to stop the injured man from falling into the water by holding onto the back of his personal flotation device and oilskin jacket, but he slipped out of them.

Despite Hendry being recovered from the water and the efforts of the fish farm workers, emergency services, and medical staff, the assistant manager could not be resuscitated.

Mowi -- named Marine Harvest at that time -- failed to provide employees with the necessary supervision to ensure lifejackets were properly tightened and secured. Since Hendry's death, wearing restraining straps has been made compulsory, and a more effective lifejacket design has been introduced.  

"Had these been in place at the time, then Mr. Hendry's transfer from the Beinn na Cailleach to the Sea Cap would have taken place without incident, and he would be alive today," Debbie Carroll, who leads health and safety investigations for the COPFS, said. "Hopefully, this incident should prompt other employers to consider their duties and that failing to keep their employees safe can have fatal consequences for which they will be held accountable."

Hendry's partner Catriona Lockhart called for a fatal accident inquiry to be held into his death, the BBC reports.  

"I am just devastated to have to relive it again and just sit and hear all the failings again. The fine was never ever relevant. There is never a decent fine. There are no winners here, just losers," she said. "Myself and Clive's family and friends are heartbroken about the loss of him. You can never put a pound sign on anybody's life."

title: Poor Argentine illex catches, El Nino boost Peruvian giant squid prices
content:
BARCELONA, Spain -- Poor catches of illex squid in Argentina and changing water conditions in Peru have affected giant squid prices, several Peruvian suppliers at the Seafood Expo Global show in Barcelona, Spain, told Undercurrent News last week.

Victor Quillay, general manager at Peru's Spring Valley Fruit in the Barcelona show in 2023.

"In January and February, giant squid catches were good. But now they are [relatively] bad again," said Victor Quillay, general manager at Peru's Spring Valley Fruit, a giant squid processor. 

Last month, water temperatures in Peruvian waters near the coast rose following heavy rains brought by Cyclone Yaku, according to another source. 

The latter executive noted that Peruvian water temperatures near the coast are currently 2-3 degrees Celsius above average. He defined the situation as a "moderate or mild" coastal El Nino. He said that, however, it is probable that a more intense El Nino would impact Peru from June onwards. The starting date, duration and intensity are still unknown. It could affect giant squid catches in the coming months, he stressed. 

According to Peruvian firm Perupez's president, Dario Alvites, El Nino might be good for giant squid catches, depending on when it starts and its intensity.

Peruvian giant squid. Photo: Capecal.

On April 26, the United Nations' Food and Agriculture Organization issued a report stating that El Nino was forecast to return from June 2023 onwards, following three years of La Nina. Dry weather conditions are expected in "key cropping areas of Central America, Southern Africa and Far East Asia." At the same time, "excessive rainfall and possible flooding" is foreseen in Near East Asia and East Africa.

"Giant squid prices had dropped in January and February but have returned to rise," Spring Valley Fruit's Quillay said. 

According to sources, giant squid fillet prices have jumped over $300 per metric ton since February to about $2,050/t. 

"Peruvian giant squid is always a substitute for illex squid. Asia is one of our major buyers. If the illex season goes badly, prices could increase further, and if the fishing in Peru also worsens, they could go even higher," Quillay said. 

The Argentine fishing season is still ongoing, but catches have been poor. According to one Argentine source, Argentine illex squid catches this year might be half or less than half of last year's. Prices for the species have jumped well above $3,000/t. But higher prices do not compensate for much lower volumes, the latter noted.

Product scarcity has cleared Argentina's illex squid inventories out, and fishermen are almost empty-handed this year, according to Spanish wholesaler Cabomar Congelados' marketing director Tania Lage.

Peruvian giant squid's improvement project

The Peruvian squid chamber, Capecal, also presented its fishery improvement project at the Barcelona seafood expo.

During a presentation on the side of the show (see photo on the left), industry representatives pointed out that this resource is of vital importance for Peru, as it is the sector that generates the most significant amount of employment among artisanal fishermen in the country.

Capecal, launched last year, comprises 17 companies, including some of the essential processors and exporters of the fishing sector for human consumption. Soon, it will reopen for new members to join amid interest from other firms.

The association participates in the monitoring and research on the species, supporting the Institute of the Sea of Peru (IMARPE), promoting the process of formalizing the fishing fleet
artisanal, combating illegal fishing and its various variants, and working to strengthen relationships in the production chain of the giant squid, according to Gerardo Carrera, Capecal's president.

Carrera presented a new institutional seal to mark involved member companies at the event.

It "will be an excellent means to distinguish the members of this organization that make an important effort to periodically report on the progress of the fishing improvement project [FIP] that we are promoting to achieve sustainability certification," he said.

According to Carrera, Peru's giant squid fishery might obtain the Marine Stewardship Council certification by December 2025. 

Alfonso Miranda Eyzaguirre, Capecal's vice president, pointed out that it is necessary to work hand in hand. "Essential agreements" with IMARPE and the Humboldt marine research institute had been achieved to carry out permanent biomass monitoring and evaluation, he said. 

Artisanal fishermen are being trained to collect and analyze biological information, fisheries and oceanography of scientific quality aligned to the commitment to respect the environment and ecosystem sea, promoting research to find positive impacts of underwater life, through continuous technological improvement, according to Capecal.

title: Untitled
content:
The Seafood Ethics Action Alliance (SEA Alliance) -- a group of 31 leading UK retailers and seafood businesses that have "come together to ensure the prominence of human rights and labor standards as a consideration in developing truly sustainable seafood supply" -- is urgently calling on labor ministers of key seafood sourcing countries to make progress in ratifying and implementing the ILO Working in Fishing Convention (C.188).

Despite being in force since 2017, C.188 has so far only been ratified by an extremely limited number of countries, it said.

The international agreement aims to protect the rights of fishers and ensure that they are working safely. It sets out binding minimum requirements relating to occupational safety and health, rest periods, written work agreements, and social security protection, as well as providing for regulation of the recruitment process and investigation of complaints by fishers. With only a few countries having ratified the convention, many workers in supply chains for SEA Alliance member companies are not yet covered by these essential protections.

Spain, a major supplying country for international seafood markets and host of this year’s Seafood Expo Global, became the 21st country to ratify the convention earlier in 2023. Now the SEA Alliance is calling on other countries to urgently follow suit in order to provide a basis for effective regulation and enforcement of minimum labor standards in the global fishing sector.

The SEA Alliance is attending the Global Seafood Expo in Barcelona not only to advance advocacy efforts around the ratification of C.188, but also to drive forward action amongst its membership and other companies. It will be convening a meeting of retailers, seafood businesses, trade union representatives, and NGOs to launch the development of a set of powerful, co-designed commitments that will be refined and finalized over the next 12 months alongside its existing work program, it said.

title: Matorka accelerates fundraising plans, rebrands to showcase Icelandic origins
content:
Land-based arctic char farmer Matorka is set to embark on an ambitious fundraising plan to double its 3,000-metric-ton hybrid flow-through system (HFS) facility in Grindavik, Iceland, as the company also unveils a new brand logo to support its expansion efforts.

Matorka CEO Christo du Plessis told Undercurrent News that the company has demonstrated the system's effectiveness and the market demand for its premium Arctic char, making them confident that the time is ripe for expansion.

Christo du Plessis

"I see land-based farming as a promising investment opportunity for suitable projects," said du Plessis.

"The sector, especially in Iceland, is witnessing significant interest in new projects emerging. Our established track record and comprehensive understanding of the system make us stand out, as we have successfully produced Arctic char at commercial scale for more than five years. We know the system inside and out. Our experience set us apart from other projects that may lack such expertise."

Hybrid flow-through gaining traction

The industry sees HFS as a promising alternative to conventional flow-through systems and recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS). The company plans to capitalize on the growing interest and support for HFS projects, which have gained traction in aquaculture, especially in Norway.

"A hybrid flow-through system is perceived as lower risk and potentially requires lower operational costs. In our case, that's certainly the case. Our capital expenditure (CAPEX) per kilogram is only a fraction of full RAS systems [less than €8/kg in 2017-2018 when the company built the current facility, it says]."

"Additionally, these systems require less energy and fewer qualified staff to operate, as they do not have complex biological filters with short reaction times in case of issues. Unlike RAS systems, which require higher stocking densities per cubic meter to maximize productivity and profitability, hybrid flow-through systems are more like natural ponds for fish, with oxygen being the main requirement. This lower capital expenditure also reduces the pressure on stocking density per cubic meter of water, further mitigating risk in our operation," he said.

Du Plessis said the crucial factor in their decision to proceed would be their advisers' advice, assessment of potential investors' readiness to move forward, and the overall market mood. They plan to launch the fundraiser in mid- or late August if the signals are positive.

The amount they need to raise is "modest and not in the hundreds of millions of euros range," he said. He added that their farm's efficient construction approach and low CAPEX/kg make adding 3,000t a manageable goal. While du Plessis doesn't have a final figure at this stage and doesn't want to speculate, he is confident in the firm's ability to raise the necessary funds for expansion.

He acknowledged that inflation may impact the CAPEX, but he does not expect the cost to double "given the current inflationary environment."

Rebranding

Matorka's new logo unveiled on Monday, April 24

As the fundraising plan gains momentum, Matorka has unveiled Monday (April 24)  a business-to-business rebranding that aims to launch a refreshed logo and brand story to better showcase the unique qualities of its Icelandic origin.

Du Plessis said the new brand story and logo will focus on how Iceland's rugged landscape, with its winter storms, ice, volcanoes, and lava, produces a refined salmonid that is less fatty than salmon but still full of flavor.

"Along with the rebranding, there will be a renewed effort to reach out more directly to customers, whether through intermediaries or not, and establish a closer relationship with buyers in the foodservice and retail sectors. Matorka aims to have a more open policy, inviting buyers to visit their farms and understand the entire process from egg to filleting," he said.

The CEO emphasized the competitive landscape for Matorka in the Arctic char segment, citing Iceland's dominant position in sales and exports, with the company being the second largest producer in the country.

"Iceland is responsible for a significant portion, estimated at around 75%, of the global trade in Arctic char, as per FAO [Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations] data," said du Plessis. "With many other countries not actively exporting, Iceland is a major player in this market. Additionally, within Iceland, we are the second largest producer of Arctic char."

Moving forward, Matorka plans to leverage its refreshed brand story and logo, showcasing the unique qualities of its Icelandic origins, and foster closer customer relationships to maintain its competitive advantage.

title: France objects to Indian Ocean FAD measure, EU rejects Indonesia’s interpretation
content:
France has lodged its objection to the resolution restricting the use of drifting fish aggregating devices (dFADs) in the Indian Ocean by tuna purse seine vessels. Its objection is the seventh to have been submitted so far.

Resolution 23/02 mandated the creation of a 72-day dFAD ban in the Indian Ocean, among other measures.

"France, on behalf of its overseas territories, considers that the conservation and management measures provided for in this resolution do not take sufficient account of scientific advice. Furthermore...[it] regrets that this resolution has not been the subject of more thorough consultations, which would have enabled it to reach a decision by consensus, more in line with the spirit of the commission’s work," it said in a letter sent to the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC).

"Through its objection, France...therefore intends to object to a resolution which sets a precedent considered irrelevant for the proper functioning of the commission to enable it to meet its objectives pertaining to the conservation of living marine resources."

France's objection comes after the EU objected to the measure, citing a "worrying precedent" of adoption.

The EU said it would instead propose a revised tuna management measure with the aim of 'addressing loopholes' at the May meeting of the IOTC.

In a letter to the IOTC, Marco Valletta, head of the European delegation at the IOTC, also replied to a claim that the EU had misinterpreted the adopted measures. He denied the suggestion the EU had misinterpreted rules around registering dFADs on a newly established register.

According to Indonesia, it was clear from the wording of resolution 23/02 that lost FADs can be deleted from the FAD register and replaced with new ones, according to the limits set out in the resolution.

"The proposed interpretation by Indonesia seems to be based on the combined reading of paragraphs four, five and eight of the resolution 23/02," said Valletta in response. "It is clear from the reading of paragraph eight that contracting parties have the right to modify the information provided under the register and referred to in paragraph four. However, there is no indication, under paragraph eight or any other part of resolution 23/02, of any specific procedure to deregister lost, stolen or destroyed FADs. Paragraph eight refers solely to paragraph four (concerning the information contained in the register), but it does not refer at all to paragraph five (concerning the FAD limits established by the resolution)," Valletta wrote.

"This interpretation is strengthened by the fact that a specific approach is instead explicitly defined to qualify -- under paragraph 64 -- the way in which reactivated instrumented buoys shall be counted against the 'original' dFAD limit defined by the register," he added.

In any case, Valletta said the text of the resolution was ambiguous and could lead to a double interpretation, making its implementation difficult.

"By following the path of the majority rather than the consensus, the IOTC adopted a text that is unclear, unfair and not implementable in many respects. We believe that the next IOTC meeting will be an opportunity to take the needed remedial actions and to adopt a coherent, science-based and effective management framework for the use of DFADs in the Indian Ocean," he wrote.
