title: Canadian land-based salmon farmer sets sights on US as it nears full commercial scale, profitability
content:
Canada's Sustainable Blue is on the cusp of a remarkable feat in the small world of land-based Atlantic salmon farms: achieving profitability.

The Nova Scotia-based company is on pace to reach a 1,000 metric tons per year production goal by September or October of 2023, while simultaneously staying in the black, CEO Kirk Havercroft told Undercurrent News in an interview this week. This while the company also simultaneously explores potential expansion sites in the US, including especially in Washington state.

"We are already seeing promising results from the farm's performance as a whole, and we are confident that this is a commercially scalable project," he said. "Our immediate goal is to make sure that we hit our production target, and then focus on achieving targets while exploring expansion opportunities."

Kirk Havercroft

Sustainable Blue made headlines last week when it was reported that the company had inked a deal with Washington's Department of Natural Resources to identify state lands that could best host future recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) operations. The state has effectively ended net-pen fish farming by earlier refusing to reauthorize two net-pen farm leases owned by Canadian aquaculture giant Cooke.

Havercroft said it was the company's success with its zero-discharge RAS (zRAS) that has been the catalyst for its recent expansion efforts.

"We're excited by this because it feels like a real endorsement for the development work that has gone into our zero-discharge technology."

Start small and steady

In the North American RAS realm, two distinct camps have emerged. Some advocate for a "go big" approach, the likes of Atlantic Sapphire, the Homestead, Florida-based Atlantic salmon farm that has set an ambitious target of harvesting 220,000t per year by 2031. They believe that large-scale RAS facilities are the key to success.

Then there are those like Sustainable Blue who advocate for a different strategy: building smaller-scale RAS facilities that can produce salmon in smaller quantities but in multiple locations. They argue that distributed RAS facilities, strategically located in various locations, offer advantages such as increased resilience, reduced risk of disease outbreaks and improved market access.

With differing perspectives on scale and distribution, the debate continues among stakeholders in the RAS community as to which approach holds the most promise for the future of salmon farming. As for who will reach profitability first, Sustainable Blue says it's nearing that goalpost this year.

The company was established in 2007 as a land-based producer of European seabass and transitioned to Atlantic salmon production in 2012. Its inaugural harvest entered the market in 2015, a milestone that positions the company as the longest-continuously operating RAS salmon farm in North America, according to Harvecroft's assessment.

He said Sustainable Blue sells its salmon predominantly to a national retail chain in Canada. While the product is currently limited to the Atlantic Canada region, the retail chain has plans to expand distribution across the country as volumes increase.

No plan to sell technology

Havercroft stated that the company has dedicated considerable effort over the years to develop its zRAS platform, which includes features such as 100% recirculation of saltwater and zero discharge to local waterways and communities.

One of the key differentiators for Sustainable Blue is its proprietary RAS filtration process, developed in-house, showcasing its unique approach to technology development. Havercroft said the engineering has been carefully designed around this process and has been refined and fully commercialized at the Nova Scotia facility, resulting in a fully closed system.

He further highlighted that Sustainable Blue built the Nova Scotia facility in increments to test new ideas and fine-tune the technology. The company began producing salmon in 2012, but it was only last year that it commissioned its fully commercially scaled aquaculture module, which now represents the final module size and engineering for all future developments.

Sustainable Blue's facility in Nova Scotia, Canada will reach it 1,000t full production target before the year-end. Photo: Sustainable Blue

"This (full-scale) facility has just come online, and it's the key to reaching a profitable scale," he said. "With increasing volumes and biomass on site, we anticipate reaching full production and profitability by September/October of this year."

The company's long-term goal is to achieve annual production volumes of 20,000t to 25,000t, which would likely be attained through different developmental stages and possibly in various locations. The CEO believes that the market on the West Coast can support such production volumes.

Havercroft emphasized that selling the zRAS technology to other farmers is not currently in the plan.

"We are salmon farmers," said Havercroft. "Selling our technology is not the plan at this stage."

On the expansion radar

The state of Washington is a key market on Sustainable Blue's radar for immediate expansion plans, Havercroft confirmed.

The company aims to capitalize on the growing demand for sustainably-produced seafood in the region and is actively exploring opportunities to establish its land-based salmon farming operations there, he said. At the same time, Sustainable Blue also has plans to increase production in Canada, leveraging its success in Nova Scotia to expand its operations domestically.

Seattle landscape. 'The state of Washington is very much on our radar in the immediate term,' says Sustainable Blue CEO Kirk Havercroft. Photo: Debannja/Pixabay

He said the reason for prioritizing expansion outside of Canada initially is rooted in the company's overarching goal to produce salmon across North America. 

"We have always aspired to develop our operations on both the East and West Coasts, which includes expanding within Nova Scotia and Eastern Canada while simultaneously pursuing plans in Washington state," he told Undercurrent. "While we acknowledge the potential for further growth within Canada, our ambition has always been to establish a presence throughout North America."

Havercroft said Sustainable Blue saw an opportunity to align its technology with DNR commissioner Hilary Franz's stance on aquaculture, and representatives of the company residing on the West Coast initiated a dialogue with her office.

Franz welcomed the partnership in a statement published Wednesday (April 12).

"I'm excited to bring this partnership to Washington. This agreement represents an important step toward restoring finfish aquaculture in a sustainable, healthy way that does not pit farmed fish against the native salmon we all work so hard to sustain," she said.

Havercroft told Undercurrent that Franz has plans to visit Sustainable Blue's operations in Nova Scotia.

What's next?

The next step in the Washington state process would involve a feasibility study, which would begin with a detailed program and discussions between Sustainable Blue and the DNR to establish specific and detailed siting criteria, Havercroft explained. Once the state has these criteria, it can review all available lands for potential lease to Sustainable Blue's facility.

Site exploration is expected to begin this spring. 

Havercroft further stated that the company would then visit and evaluate each site to determine its highest priority and the closest fit to the criteria, outlining how the process would evolve.

He said his company has yet to reach out to Indigenous Nations in Washington, though it's part of the roadmap to explore opportunities for collaboration and participation in sustainable aquaculture initiatives.

A map of Washington state. Image from Shutterstock.

Sustainable Blue's zero-discharge technology will give the company an advantage during the permitting and regulatory process, as it does not require a permit to discharge effluent, unlike conventional RAS farms, Havercroft said. 

"One of the most controversial elements of regulating conventional RAS farms is getting a permit to discharge effluent, which conventional RAS facilities need to have. We don't need that; we won't be applying for a discharge permit. So when we do get to permitting and regulatory, I think our project will be at an advantage compared to a conventional RAS farm," he said.

The timelines are not yet set in stone due to the uncertainty of the feasibility stage. Havercroft said however that the company aims to start the feasibility work quickly, ideally before the summer, in collaboration with Franz's team.

He estimated the typical timeline for feasibility work, design, financing, and construction to be nine to 12 months, with construction potentially starting in approximately 18 months, assuming all goes smoothly.

title: Trident pollock factory trawler on fire in port
content:
A pollock factory trawler owned by US industry giant Trident Seafoods has suffered a fire while moored in Tacoma, Washington.

The Kodiak Enterprise caught fire early on Saturday morning, April 8, while alongside the Hylebos Waterway in Tacoma, according to a statement from the US Coast Guard.

The fire has progressed throughout the ship and was last reported approximately 100 feet from the vessel's freon tanks, according to the Coast Guard, which has been involved in the response along with the Tacoma Fire Department, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the Washington Department of Ecology and other agencies.

"We want to thank everyone for their prompt response and support," said Joe Bundrant, CEO of Trident. "This has been a challenging containment issue and we appreciate the ongoing efforts over this Easter weekend."

The crew on Fire Boat Zenith captured photos of their efforts to extinguish the flames on the vessel fire in Tacoma. pic.twitter.com/wrLKpWFFlk

— South King Fire (@Southkingfire) April 9, 2023

 

The cause of the incident is under investigation. Additional updates will be released as they become available, the Coast Guard said.

Kodiak Enterprise reportedly has an estimated 55,000 gallons of diesel and 19,000 pounds of freon onboard. The heat from the fire can cause pressure to build in the freon tanks.

The freon tanks are designed with built-in heat-activated pressure relief valves, which are designed to release pressure in an emergency. While freon can be toxic if inhaled in large quantities or in a confined space, the release of freon into the atmosphere is not expected to pose any health and safety risks to the public, the Coast Guard said.

As a precautionary measure, the EPA has been conducting air monitoring to assess air quality in the surrounding areas.

To ensure the public's safety, the Tacoma Fire Department issued a temporary shelter-in-place order for neighborhoods close to the vessel.

In addition, the Coast Guard has closed the Hylebos Waterway for all commercial and recreational vessel traffic via a vessel traffic service special measure. The Coast Guard has deployed the Coast Guard Cutter Osprey and Station Seattle to enforce the closure.

"The safety of the public and responders is our top priority," said the Coast Guard's Youngmee Moon, the on-scene coordinator. "The unified command is working closely to leverage each agency's capabilities to respond to this incident as effectively as possible and keep the public safe."

There are no reported signs of maritime pollution. As a preventive measure, responders have deployed three layers of containment boom around the vessel to protect the marine environment. Authorities have also deployed three skimmers and three boom boats.

title: US-created, AI-based mortality monitoring tool among finalists in European contest
content:
Concern may be growing about the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in multiple industries, but it's being heralded as a possible game changer in the aquaculture space. 

All five of the finalists in the NewTechAqua Award Challenge that were announced last week, in Belgium, employ AI technology. They were selected from a list of 47 proposals in the most recent edition of the contest.

The only finalist from the US was the Conservation Fund's Freshwater Institute (FI), which created something called MortCam to provide real-time monitoring and alerts for fish health and welfare. FI developed the tool with funding from the US Department of Agriculture's Agricultural Research Service. 

MortCam, which uses both AI and internet-of-things technology, enables farm managers to make better-informed decisions regarding mortality management and maintaining good fish health, according to Brian Vinci, FI's director. He said it was the first year that FI participated in the NewTechAqua challenge.

FI research scientist and precision aquaculture team leader Rakesh Ranjan explained how the technology works in a statement.

"Mortcam consists of an imaging sensor integrated with an edge computing device customized for underwater applications," he said. "Images acquired are used to train and optimize a machine learning model for resource-constrained edge devices with limited computation capability to detect and count dead fish accumulated near the drain plate. The model is deployed on the MortCam to log the mortality data at a user-defined frequency. The system generates an email and text alerts to notify operators of mortality events. In this way, real-time mortality alerts may aid in proactively initiating procedures to prevent potential additional mortalities."

The MortCam, developed by the Conservation Fund's Freshwater Institute. Image courtesy of Freshwater Institute.

Other NewTechAqua finalists included:

Seaducer (France): It involves a cutting-edge technology to produce outstanding oysters all year round by reducing tiresome tasks and optimizing production costs;
Findit (Norway): It uses a cloud-based platform for precision farming;
Noah Genetics (Switzerland): It uses tools to prevent the loss of genetic diversity and to optimize animal AI, particularly in the aquatic ecosystem; and
Bioceanor (France): It provides predictive analytics for water quality.

The finalists will now participate in a two-month coaching program, run by expert members of the NewTechAqua group and other partner organizations, and aimed at improving the viability and marketability of their solutions. They will then be invited to present their solution at the NewTechAqua final conference at the end of the year, where a promotional video will be presented as a prize for the top candidate.

Concerns raised

The encouraged use of AI in aquaculture comes in the wake of AI experts and tech heavyweights, including Tesla founder Elon Musk and Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak, calling for a six-month pause in the development of powerful AI tools last week.

In an open letter citing potential risks to society, they aired their concerns about powerful AI tools easily being weaponized. The letter raised concerns about the potential for machines to spread propaganda and false information, the potential for job automation leading to unemployment, the development of non-human intelligence that may eventually surpass and replace humans, and the risk of losing control of society to these advanced systems.

They want AI labs to resume development only when there's a confidence that their effects will be positive and their risks will be manageable. The open letter has so far collected over 50,000 signatures, of which over 3,000 have been vetted as real as of the time this article was published.

Regardless, Vinci sees opportunities emerging from the use of AI in aquaculture, should it be harnessed correctly.

"AI is a powerful tool that will result in improvements throughout the aquaculture industry. But it is still just a tool. We need people who know how to use that tool effectively to produce the improvements desired," he said in an email to Undercurrent.

"I look for improvements to start on the production side with improved feeding, fish health monitoring and biomass measurements," he added. "Longer term, I anticipate improvements will occur in all aspects of the business from financial projections to optimizing sales and distribution."

title: 15 tuna stocks currently would not meet MSC fisheries standard
content:
An increasing number of tuna stocks worldwide are failing to meet the minimum requirements on harvest control rules set by the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) due to their failure to implement controls before rebuilding is required.

As a result, up to 15 tuna stocks currently do not meet the MSC fisheries standard criteria, according to the International Seafood Sustainability Foundation (ISSF) 's latest report on the sector.

The report concluded that only eight of 23 major commercial tuna stocks worldwide would achieve passing scores on MSC principle one, avoiding overfishing and maintaining target stock biomass levels when measured against the MSC standard.

Those stocks include Western Atlantic skipjack, North Atlantic albacore, South Atlantic albacore, Eastern Atlantic bluefin, Western Pacific skipjack, Eastern Pacific yellowfin, Eastern Pacific skipjack and Indian Ocean skipjack. Six of those stocks also have fully implemented well-defined harvest control rules.

Most tuna regional fisheries management organizations (RFMOs) score well on MSC principle three for fisheries management, ISSF added.

Under the standard's principle three, "effective management," the RFMOs scored well overall, with the four tropical tuna RFMOs receiving passing scores. Most tuna RFMOs exhibited similar weaknesses in compliance and enforcement, while other weaknesses varied between RFMOs, the ISSF said.

The organization's report, which first began in 2013, aims to evaluate the sustainability of global tuna stocks against the MSC standard. The scores in the report focus on stock status (MSC principle one) and the international management aspects relevant to RFMOs (part of MSC principle three) and are based on publicly available fishery and RFMO data. 

One tuna RFMO, the Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission (IATTC), received unconditional passing scores for all seven performance indicators under principle three. The other three tropical tuna RFMOs (the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas, Indian Ocean Tuna Commission, and Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission) received overall principle-level passing scores from the report's authors.
 
The full report highlighting stocks that received passing and failing scores can be read in full here. 

Last October, the MSC published the third edition of its fisheries standard following a four-year consultation and review of the industry.

title: Scottish salmon industry dismisses claims sea lice levels breach guidelines
content:
The Scottish salmon industry has rejected a report accusing the sector's farms of failing to meet their own guidelines on sea lice.

A new report from the campaigning charity WildFish claims that the Scottish salmon and trout farming industry is allowing parasitic sea lice levels to reach over five million lice on a single farm at one time, with up to two billion sea lice being emitted over a week, risking fatal spread to wild fish.

The report, 'Breaching the Limits', analyzes industry-reported sea lice data, Fish Health Inspectorate records and reported chemical usage on Scottish marine fish farms.

It reveals that 40% of sea lice counts submitted by open-net salmon companies last year were either in breach of the industry's own guidelines, or not reported. "Part of the industry’s Code of Good Practice (CoGP), these guidelines are five times more lenient than neighboring Norway; additionally, they are unverified," WildFish said.

However, Tavish Scott, chief executive of the industry's body Salmon Scotland, has hit back, calling the report "yet more conjecture from a group of anti-salmon activists with a long history of misrepresenting the facts", adding that sea lice are naturally occurring and affect both wild and farmed salmon.

"Scotland’s salmon farms consistently demonstrate low average levels of lice, thanks to farmers, vets and fish health specialists, with fish health and welfare as our farmers’ top priority," Scott claimed.

According to Salmon Scotland, the code of good practice provides guidance on sea lice management, not defined thresholds, meaning the claim that fish farms "breached sea lice thresholds" is incorrect.

Salmon Scotland also notes that the sector is compliant with the legal controls and requirements overseen by the Fish Health Inspectorate. It alleges further that WildFish's figures have been based on a vast range of assumptions, leading to overestimates.

Sea lice spread hitting wild salmon numbers

A key part of WildFish's report looked into the impact of sea lice on populations of wild salmon along Scotland's coastline and rivers.

The Scottish government last year declared that the wild Atlantic salmon population is in crisis, while catches for wild salmon and sea trout in Scotland in 2021 were the lowest on record, the organization said.

During young salmon migration, when salmon are most vulnerable to sea lice due to their small size, the Scottish salmon and trout industry reported sea lice levels that exceeded the industry limits on one in four occasions, WildFish added.

"This analysis of industry sea lice data from last year is yet another demonstration of why the Scottish government needs to take urgent and strong action to tackle sea lice infestations on salmon and trout farms in our coastal waters," said Rachel Mulrenan, Scotland director for WildFish.

In one such case, the Norwegian company Mowi recorded sea lice levels as high as 8.2 lice per fish on one of its farms, 16 times the industry limit, and 40-80 times higher than what would be permitted in the company’s home country of Norway, WildFish reported.

The NGO also noted that Loch Duart was the worst-performing producer where sea lice numbers are concerned. "Over a third of sea lice counts provided by the company in 2022 were above the industry thresholds; one of its farms breached Marine Scotland’s 2.0 sea lice limit a total of 19 times -- far more than any other producer."

Following the publication of a report by the Scottish government’s salmon interactions working group in 2020, the Scottish Environment Protection Agency (SEPA) was tasked with monitoring and reducing the impact of sea lice spreading from fish farms to wild salmonids (salmon and trout). However, progress on the framework has been slow, and it will not initially address the risk posed by sea lice on Scotland’s 200+ existing salmon and trout farms, claimed WildFish.

title: Salmon Scotland raises concerns about proposed marine activity ban
content:
Salmon Scotland, the trade body for Scottish aquaculture, has written to all three first ministerial candidates to seek continued support for the sector and to raise concerns about a proposed ban on marine activity in stretches of water.

The winner of the contest to replace Nicola Sturgeon as the leader of Scotland's biggest political party is set to be announced on March 27. Humza Yousaf, Ash Regan and Kate Forbes have been campaigning for weeks.

Salmon Scotland CEO Tavish Scott urged the members of Scottish parliament to recognize the economic contribution of salmon farms, address the nation's rural housing crisis, and take action to streamline the aquaculture licensing regime.

Addressing the consultation currently underway on highly protected marine areas (HPMAs), which would see around 10% of coastal waters around Scotland closed to human activity, Scott said a "thorough understanding of the impact on business, livelihoods and communities is essential".

Scottish National Party leadership candidate Forbes has pledged to scrap the proposal, and has also said she would consult on which of Marine Scotland's statutory responsibilities could be "more effectively delivered by local authorities".

Scott welcomed her comments and said: "Kate Forbes looks open-minded on further reforms, and if she becomes our first minister, we would welcome an early discussion with her on these important policy developments and how they could benefit the sustainable growth of the sector."

In his letter to all candidates, Scott wrote: "As a key contributor to the economy, our sector recognizes the importance of collaboration and dialogue with government."

He also praised rural affairs secretary Mairi Gougeon for being a "tireless champion for Scottish salmon".

Scottish salmon adds £760 million ($931.4m) a year to the country's economy; is the UK's biggest food export; and the sector employs more than 2,500 people in fragile, coastal communities across rural and island Scotland, with a further 10,000 Scottish jobs dependent on the supply chain, he reminded the candidates.

On the rural housing crisis, Scott reiterated calls for £10m of the rents paid by salmon farmers to Crown Estate Scotland to be ringfenced for direct investment in rural housing. 

And more than one year since the independent review of aquaculture by Russel Griggs for the government, Scott added:

"Professor Griggs published his conclusions in February 2022, stating that the current set-up needs urgent change to deliver on the full potential of the blue economy. We agree. The consents and licensing process for salmon farms is unnecessarily long and complex, with several regulatory bodies involved, leading to delays, uncertainty, unnecessary cost and bureaucratic procedures."

"If the system is streamlined, as Prof. Griggs recommends, our sector can be more competitive on the global arena. Our ask is for faster progress on implementing Prof Griggs' recommendations, which have already been accepted by the Scottish government."

Scottish Sea Farms speaks out on behalf of Orkney

Continuing the theme, Orkney's seafood sector has united against Scottish government conservation proposals that "could threaten the future of critical coastal businesses and the communities they support", according to a press release from salmon farmer Scottish Sea Farms.

Fishermen, fish farmers and companies in the extended supply chain have warned that the introduction of HPMAs "will destroy aquaculture and commercial fishing activities, which are cornerstones of the Orkney economy". 

The proposals prevent any form of fishing or aquaculture within or close to an HPMA, including cessation of existing activity.

Ministers have pledged to designate at least 10% of Scottish seas as HPMAs within three years, on top of the 37% of Scottish seas which are already protected under law. They claim that the strictly enforced new zones will conserve marine ecosystems while continuing to provide economic and social benefits.

"But Orkney seafood representatives said a lack of baseline data, combined with an absence of defined tools and methodologies to measure the success of the HPMAs, undermines the ability of the policy to achieve its environmental objectives."

There are fears that the government’s 2026 deadline will see HPMAs rushed through without proper scrutiny of how they will work in practice or an understanding of the significant socio-economic impacts resulting from the proposed restrictions.

title: Last chance saloon? Coastal states to talk mackerel in London before March 31 deadline
content:
The Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) and the North Atlantic Pelagic Advocacy (NAPA) have called for the coastal states that harvest northeast Atlantic mackerel to make good on their commitment to secure a long-term quota sharing agreement by March 31, 2023.

With delegates meeting in London next week and the deadline fast approaching, the long-term sustainability of this iconic species remains uncertain, MSC said.

An agreed management framework including harvest control rules and harvest strategies would enable fisheries managers to ensure the long-term sustainability of these stocks. It would also open the door for mackerel to regain MSC certification, helping to secure important markets, said the ecolabel organization.

Northeast Atlantic #mackerel was #overfished by 42% in 2021. This was driven by #CoastalStates walking away from joint management negotiations & setting their own quotas.

Fish stocks aren't infinite. #ShareItBeforeItShuts #TakeYourFairShare

Learn more 👉 https://t.co/iCPuLeczAa pic.twitter.com/G507mGNAHE

— North Atlantic Pelagic Advocacy Group (@NAPAfisheries) March 23, 2023

"In the absence of this framework, nation states have been able to set total allowable catches [TACs] in line with their own national interests, rather than following internationally set limits defined by the International Council for the Exploration of the Seas. This is a fundamental reason why mackerel lost its MSC certification back in 2019, with blue whiting and Atlanto-Scandic herring following in 2020."
 
The loss of these MSC certificates is being felt in markets all over the world, with the MSC label disappearing off retail shelves for mackerel and AS herring, the ecolabel claimed.

More than 40 retailers, foodservice companies and suppliers that form NAPA have made sourcing statements as part of their commitment to its fishery improvement projects (FIPs). "With just one year left for these FIPs to be completed, now is a critical moment to secure a quota share agreement in line with science for mackerel, with herring and blue whiting following suit."
 
Erin Priddle, regional director for the MSC in North Europe, warned that without a long-term management plan and agreed quota-sharing agreement, the risk to the future sustainability of the mackerel stock remains high, even if the stock biomass remains stable.

"We urge coastal state delegations to raise their ambition in next week's negotiations and finally put an end to the deadlock that has robbed these fisheries of long-term and lasting sustainable management for over a decade."

The MSC told Undercurrent News that after the March 31 deadline, coastal states may continue their talks, but that there are no further planned meetings until the annual negotiation in October 2023.

This is the meeting where they set their TACs, which are then rubber-stamped at the North East Atlantic Fisheries Commission annual meeting. If a quota allocation and long-term management plan are not agreed upon by March 31, then coastal states will declare their TACs in the spring without regard to the scientific limit and set TACs once again as per their own national interests.

The last meeting between the delegations -- held March 8 in Nuuk, Greenland -- brought promising news, according to Oli Samro of Fishfacts, who presented at the North Atlantic Seafood Forum.

He claimed that Norway, the UK, the EU, and the Faroe Islands had broken mackerel out for separate discussions and were close to an agreement. It would not be a full "coastal states agreement", as Iceland, Russia, and Greenland were not involved, he said.

"Norway and the Faroes realize that any deal must be 'paid for', that they will likely to have give up some of their share," he said. "The deal has progressed, and they are talking about technical details now, some of which will involve access to each others' waters."

Samro did not believe a deal would be in force for 2023, but that 2024 looked likely.

title: Canada fines three in BC over CAD 100k for illegal fishing
content:
Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) has fined three men a collective total of more than CAD 100,000 ($73,164) in the province of British Columbia for illegal fishing practices, Global News reports.

The most penalized was Adrian Slavko Kern, who was fined CAD 49,705 for illegally deploying fishing gear to catch halibut and sablefish in the Chatham Sound area near Prince Rupert in September 2018. The area was closed to fishing at the time.

Kern, who had three previous convictions for violating the Fisheries Act, has pleaded guilty to the latest offenses, according to the article. He is also banned from applying for a new commercial fishing license for eight months.

DFO also has fined commercial crab harvester Sou Tac Ma CAD 44,000 after he was found guilty in December 2022 for a pair of Fisheries Act violations aboard his vessel Golden Phoenix. Ma was caught crab fishing twice in Rivers Inlet during a closure in the spring of 2019.

Another commercial crab harvester, Truc Hoang Le, was convicted of "numerous" Fisheries Act violations, including failing to comply with his license in the Chatham Sound area during the spring of 2018. Le, owner of fishing vessel Marine Hunter, was fined a total of CAD 20,000, according to the DFO.

title: Russia lists WWF as ‘foreign agent’
content:
On March 10, Russia added the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) to its register of "foreign agents", reports AP. 

Explaining the decision in Moscow, the Russian justice ministry said the organization "under the guise of protecting nature and the environment...tried to influence the decision of the executive and legislative authorities and hindered the implementation of industrial and infrastructure projects". 

Russian law requires individuals and organizations determined to have received foreign funding and engaged in loosely defined "political activity" to identify themselves as "foreign agents". This label brings additional government scrutiny and carries a strong pejorative connotation in the country. 

WWF representatives, however, said this decision was unfounded and promised to take it to court.

title: US wholesaler Elite Sky fined $250,000 for false labeling on seafood sent to China
content:
US seafood wholesaler Elite Sky International was fined $250,000 and put on five years probation for exporting falsely-labeled lobster and shark fins from Florida to China.

United States Southern District of Florida judge K. Michael Moore sentenced Elite, of Marathon, Florida, after finding that the company had reexported approximately 63,000 pounds of lobster Elite imported from Nicaragua and Belize and falsely labeled the product in shipping documents as "Live Florida Spiny Lobsters, Product of USA" from November 2018 through October 2019.

The company also bought shark fins from a licensed local fisherman in Florida and exported approximately 5,666 lbs of them, falsely labeling them as "Live Florida Spiny Lobsters, Product of USA" or "Frozen Fish", according to a statement released by the officials from the US Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida.

Moore set special conditions of probation for the company, requiring it to form a corporate compliance program and retain third-party independent auditors to oversee its activities, officials said.

title: Mozambique ordered to open files in Credit Suisse, Privinvest ‘tuna bond’ case
content:
A London judge ordered the Mozambique government last week to grant access to documents held in state offices or risk derailing a blockbuster London lawsuit against Credit Suisse, shipbuilder Privinvest and others over the $2 billion "tuna bond" case, Reuters reported.

Judge Robin Knowles told the High Court in London that Mozambique had failed in its disclosure duties, describing this as a "really serious matter", and ordered access to relevant documents from entities such as the State Information and Security Service (SISE) and office of the president.

"If I need to exercise my powers for strike-out to ensure compliance with the Republic's (of Mozambique) duties and the obligations of this litigation, I will, because that is my duty and the fairness of the trial I wish to deliver to the Republic and all parties is at stake," he told the High Court.

But he stopped short of ordering a deadline ahead of a three-month trial expected in October.

Between 2013 and 2014, three newly established companies took on $2.2bn of debt, much of it without the knowledge or approval of the country's parliament. Despite this, the government stood as the guarantor of the loans.

The loans were issued by Credit Suisse and the Russian bank VTB, with three former Credit Suisse bankers pleading guilty to US money laundering charges over the case.

In 2021, UK authorities fined the investment bank $202 million over the tuna corruption scandal.

title: Norway gov’t proposes regulation changes to fund marketing, research on seaweed
content:
The Norwegian government proposed classifying seaweed and kelp as seafood to encourage further sector development.

The Norwegian ministry of trade has proposed that it be defined as seafood, bringing seaweed under the focus of the Norwegian Seafood Council (NSC) and the fisheries and aquaculture industry's research funding (FHF). 

"The FHF should be able to direct funds for the research and development of Norway's seaweed and kelp industry, which should benefit from the NSC's services, such as marketing abroad," it said in a statement. 

"This is an industry with great potential, which has long shown a strong need for access to marketing and research funding resources. We have listened to these demands and will work on meeting them," said Norway's minister of fisheries and oceans, Bjornar Skjaeran.

The ministry is also proposing to extend the scope of the export duty for fish and fish products to include seaweed and kelp, meaning that marketing and research fees will be charged for both. 

"We are working hard to improve the opportunities for Norwegian exports abroad, also for new marine products. This work is part of a larger and long-term goal to ease activities along the entire coast and create more opportunities for the Norwegian seafood industry," Skjaeran concluded.

title: UK designates new highly protected marine areas; fishing group hits out
content:
The UK government has announced the first highly protected marine areas (HPMAs) in English waters triggering strong criticism from both fishing organizations and environmental groups. 

On Tuesday (Feb. 28), the UK's department for environment, food and rural affairs (DEFRA) said three sites would be designated HPMAs before July 6. The three sites are Allonby Bay in the Irish Sea, Dolphin Head in the Eastern Channel, and North East of Farnes Deep in the northern North Sea. 

UK fishing bodies raise alarm over ‘spatial squeeze’ for marine resources

DEFRA said the designated areas would prohibit all harmful activities, including fishing, construction and dredging, creating a "haven for marine life". 

The three designated sites are down from five sites originally proposed, after Lindisfarne and Inner Silver Pit South were struck off plans for HPMA designation. The decision followed further consideration of the socio-economic impacts and consultations with stakeholders, the government said.

UK environment secretary Therese Coffey said the HPMAs were a "vital step forward".

"HPMAs are a vital step forward in enabling our ecosystems to thrive, increasing climate resilience and ensuring we have a healthy and productive marine environment for generations to come," said Coffey.

The first three HPMAs include inshore and offshore sites, and will complement the existing network of marine protected areas (MPAs) covering 40% of English waters.

Their introduction follows recommendations in the Benyon Review to "help achieve clean, healthy, safe, productive, and biologically diverse oceans and seas", and drives forward the government's commitment to protect at least 30% of the global ocean by 2030.

"This is a crucial next step to aid marine ecosystem recovery in our waters and I'm delighted to see my recommendations become a reality today," said marine minister Lord Benyon. "Not only will the first of these HPMAs protect important species and habitats, but they will propel the UK forward in our mission to protect at least 30% of the global ocean by 2030." 

NFFO hits back

However, the announcement received a less than warm reception from the National Federation of Fishermen's Organisations (NFFO), which represents fishing groups in the UK.

NFFO CEO Barrie Davies told Undercurrent News that in its pursuit of HPMAs, the government was failing the fishing industry, while environmental benefits were less than clear.

Scottish fishing body slams gov’t proposals for highly protected marine areas

"Our view is that the government's policy on marine protected areas has lost its way," said Deas. "MPAs are important and necessary but they should have clear conservation objectives, be based on clear evidence following meaningful dialogue with those whose livelihood will be affected.

"HPMAs meet none of these criteria. They have no clearly defined purpose and are part of a wider program to expand the MPA network at a speed that precludes collating the necessary evidence or meaningful dialogue."

Above all, there was an absence of a "coherent, joined up government policy" in relation to the scale of fisheries displacement that the expansion -- in combination with the accelerated expansion of offshore wind -- implies, he said.

"The report commissioned by NFFO/SFF [Scottish Fishermen's Federation] by ABPmer suggests that in the worst case scenario, the UK will lose 50% of its fishing grounds over the next few decades. This has implications for fishing businesses, fishing communities, fisheries management, and marine ecology outside MPAs."

'Not enough'

Unsurprisingly, the UK environmental group Marine Conservation Society saw things in a different light. According to the organization, the HPMAs fall short of an ambitious and meaningful change in marine protection, although they represent a step in the right direction.

"These sites represent less than 0.5% of English seas, and the latest announcement needs to go further in responding to the climate and nature crises. Two of the originally proposed five sites have been dropped from designation," noted the group. 

Defra to propose UK ‘highly protected marine areas’

"Our marine habitats must be given the opportunity to recover and provide the maximum benefits to us -- including biodiversity restoration, carbon storage and supporting fisheries recovery. The UK government cannot continue to underachieve and must show much greater ambition and initiative to build a network of HPMAs – or No Take Zones – covering at least 10% of English seas by 2030 to allow our seas to thrive," added Jean-Luc Solandt, principal specialist of MPAs at the NGO. 

The group said it would continue working with the UK government and others, including coastal communities, to achieve at least 10% of English seas as HPMAs by 2030. "There is precedent in the UK -- the Scottish government has already committed to designating at least 10% of Scotland's marine area as HPMAs by 2026," it said. 

"The Office for National Statistics has estimated that the UK's marine natural capital assets are worth £211 billion. To maximize the incredible benefits that we can get from our seas, they must be protected to recover and flourish," the group added. 

Ecological protection and climate resilience in the limelight

The results of the HPMAs will likely be seen soon. DEFRA said Allonby Bay contains honeycomb reefs and blue mussel beds, which can provide water purification and important protection from coastal erosion, and are relatively fast-growing. It also contains 'blue carbon' habitats that capture and store carbon. 

"Nursery and spawning habitats for a range of commercial species including cod, plaice, sole and herring will also be protected," it said.

Meanwhile, Dolphin Head has been degraded following the impacts of human activity. HPMA designation, therefore, presents an opportunity to fully recover habitats and species, including feeding and nursery grounds of many important commercial fish species such as cod, herring, and plaice, said DEFRA.

Lastly, North East of Farnes Deep has high levels of biodiversity. The large areas of muddy habitats benefit storage of carbon as well as a range of species including birds, marine mammals and fish. "This includes spawning and nursery habitats for up to ten commercially important species such as angler fish, surmullet, whiting and haddock," said DEFRA.

title: Maine aquaculture resilient despite hurdles in land-based salmon sector
content:
Maine's land-based salmon aquaculture faces obstacles, but Sebastian Bell, executive director of the Maine Aquaculture Association, believes they won't hinder the state's growth or status as an attractive destination for aquaculture investment.

"Our growth rate has been about the same over the last 20 years, slow but steady," he told Undercurrent News at the sidelines of the Aquaculture America conference on Sunday.

Sebastian Belle, Maine Aquaculture Association.

Citing the latest data from the US Department of Agriculture, Belle said aquaculture has a $136 million total impact on Maine's economy. The annual farmgate value ranges between $80 million and $100m. Aquaculture currently employs approximately 700 full-time workers, which is an increase of nearly 23% from the figure of 571 reported in 2017 by the University of Maine.

Maine is home to the Canadian seafood conglomerate Cooke Aquaculture's only Atlantic salmon farm in the US, making the state the largest producer of Atlantic salmon in the US. Maine's other primary seafood products include oysters, blue mussels, Atlantic sea scallops and seaweed.

Strict regulations

Belle credits Maine's strict regulations and strong brand recognition for keeping investors interested.

"If somebody gets through the permitting process and builds a facility, then they can be very sure that it will be a very defendable facility from an environmental point of view, from a sociological point of view," he said. "That, combined with the fact that Maine is close to a huge market, the east coast of the United States of America, and the Maine brand is a solid brand in the marketplace for seafood, keeps investors coming and trying to build projects."

He added that challenges are not unique to land-based salmon using recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS) but are present in every form of production and every species grown. There's always a learning period, he said.

"We need some projects to be built and operated for some time," he said. "Certainly, Atlantic Sapphire in Florida is the biggest project in the United States, and they've had challenges. Will they be successful? We don't know yet, but there are certainly some very clever people designing systems, investing in that sector, and people are learning as they go just as everybody does in aquaculture."

Belle advises potential investors to spend a considerable amount of time and effort explaining their proposal to the community they plan to invest in. He emphasized the importance of doing their homework upfront to understand the community's concerns and to avoid misleading them. 

He said investors should spend time on the ground, listen to the community's concerns, and be truthful about their proposals. He suggested that some of the previous projects in Maine encountered resistance because they needed to do more work in the communities they wanted to invest in.

Outlook

Belle foresees a positive future for aquaculture in Maine. "We anticipate a rise in employment figures in the coming years since some of the small farms are transitioning into mid-sized farms and hiring more workers, in addition to establishing new farms," he stated.

Photo: Maine Aquaculture Association

The state will need up to 80% more workers by 2030, according to the 2020 report, "Maine Aquaculture Workforce Development Strategy," from the Gulf of Maine Research Institute and Maine Aquaculture Association.

Maine is addressing this by developing occupational standards for the fish farming industry, making it the only state in the US with such standards. Having well-defined occupational standards can help to standardize training and education programs for workers in the industry. In addition, occupational standards can lead to a more skilled and knowledgeable workforce, which can improve productivity and efficiency in the industry, Belle said. 

The Maine aquaculture leader said one of his staffers, Christian Braid, spent two years developing the standards, which are now the basis for a US Department of Labor apprenticeship program.

"It is the first of its kind in the country, and we will have our first seven apprentices in the program this year. So we're very excited about that kind of feeding system for workforce development in the state," he said.

Belle mentioned that Maine has been conducting training programs for new farmers for nearly two decades, noting that more than 400 people have participated. Around 60% of the individuals who completed the training program went on to start their farms.

"So that's what's fuelling the growth in Maine. The growth in Maine is really in small farms. And as those farms grow and mature and get bigger, they will employ more people and broaden the choice of products we will have to sell under the Maine brand," he said.

title: NGO warns EU objection to IOTC’s dFAD-ban would ‘jeopardize a rare victory’ for the ocean
content:
The EU still has time to object to the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC)'s decision to introduce a ban on the use of drifting fish aggregating devices (dFADs), but French NGO Bloom has warned that any such objection would be a "denial of democracy" in fisheries management.

The NGO has sent a letter to the EU commissioner for environment, oceans and fisheries, Virginijus Sinkevicius, to formally ask that the EU Commission not object.

Photo: Bloom.

During a special session of the IOTC held in Kenya on Feb. 3-5, a proposal introducing a 72-day dFAD closure period was adopted to protect yellowfin stocks by reducing the catch of juvenile fish. Among the members that attended the meeting, 16 voted in favor, seven against, and one abstained. 

Bloom defined the decision as a "rare victory for the ocean". "These floating and drifting rafts [...] are responsible for the capture of huge numbers of juvenile yellowfin and bigeye tuna -- two species considered overfished -- as well as many fragile species of marine animals such as turtles and sharks," it said. It added that the dFAD ban was a crucial first step for the regeneration of the Indian Ocean's health.

According to the IOTC's rules, a state objecting to a measure does not have to apply it to its own fleets.

The IOTC secretariat confirmed to Undercurrent that contracting parties have 120 days to object to the two resolutions recently adopted at the February meeting.

According to Bloom, the EU Commission will decide in "a few days’ time whether or not it will object" to the introduction of a dFADs ban. The Council of EU member states must approve the European Commission's objection procedure.

According to Bloom, if the EU objects to the IOTC prohibition, the ban on dFADs will become useless as these devices are mainly used by European vessels.

Bloom has also requested to see all communications between the European Commission and the tuna sector, hoping to gain some clarity as to what it says is industrial lobbying.

It has claimed in a report on the size of the EU delegation to IOTC meetings that the number of people attending has risen on average from 22 to 40, claiming this as evidence of lobbying.

title: World’s largest distant water fishing fleet caught 2.25m metric tons in 2022
content:
China's distant water fishing fleet (DWF), operating mainly on the high seas, caught 2.25 million metric tons of fish in 2022, just short of its annual target production of 2.3m metric tons by 2025, according to the country's Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs (MoA).

Last year's catch amounted to around 30% of the country's total marine fisheries production, which includes catch from China's exclusive economic zone (EEZ), according to a local media report. 

Chinese listed seafood companies more positive as profits recover

Zhou Wei, a senior oceans campaigner at Greenpeace in Beijing, told Undercurrent News that when it comes to sustainable fishing, China is "generally moving in the right direction, but more efforts are still needed to ensure long-term sustainability".

Last year's catch was mainly from international waters, and in the EEZs of 30 or so countries China has fishing agreements with, according to the MoA.

It comprised vast quantities of tuna and Pacific mackerel in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean, and squid and cuttlefish in the Indian Ocean and Southwest Atlantic. Off the coast of West Africa, Chinese vessels also netted sardines used for fishmeal.

Zhou said the Chinese government is seeking to "stabilize" catch at 2.3m metric tons, referring to an "opinion" policy on the 14th five-year plan announced in February of last year.

It comes after the country announced a cap on the DWF fleet size at 3,000 vessels by 2020, back in 2018.

"China wants to continue to control the fleet; it is combatting IUU [illegal, unreported and unregulated] fishing, generally continuing on from the 13th five-year plan," said Zhou.

"[However,] we don't have further information about how much in subsidies were distributed last year. That's not available to the public. There's no comprehensive, regular data release relating to the distant water fisheries," she said.

In December of last year, Shanghai Kaichuang Marine International, one of China's largest distant water tuna fishing companies, announced it received CNY 39.8m ($5.76m) in subsidies from the government. The subsidies were allocated by the "2022 National Special Fund for Foreign Economic and Trade Development", it said.

Regarding IUU fishing, Zhou said China showed a willingness to "punish" those caught, after a succession of high-profile incidents. This includes the sinking of a Chinese vessel caught illegal fishing by Argentina in 2016.

In 2018, Greenpeace reported China fined companies or withdrew subsidies for illegal fishing in West Africa.

Zhou added that more could be done with better communication between coastal countries' governments and China.

"It is important for the Chinese government and the coastal countries' governments to enhance communication and collaboration, to regularly exchange information on combating IUU fishing, and to ensure that the fishing practices are environmentally sustainable, socially beneficial and equitable," she said.

Last summer, China was a co-signatory of a World Trade Organisation agreement to curb the use of subsidies in the fishing industry.

The agreement is deemed essential, according to environmental campaigners, in order to "stop wasting money on harmful subsidies and instead free up funding for a better management of fishing resources".

title: Nissui builds $180m war chest for international M&A drive
content:
Japan's Nissui Corporation, the world's second-largest seafood company, has amassed a JPY 25 billion ($180 million) war chest mainly for foreign mergers and acquisitions (M&A) as it seeks to hit JPY 1 trillion ($7.4bn) in sales by 2030.

According to the company's integrated 2022 report, the seafood giant aims to ramp up its foreign investment to create more equal weighting between its Japanese domestic business and its foreign enterprises.

Global seafood giants sent M&A spending past $7bn in 2022, but 2023’s outlook uncertain

It has earmarked JPY 120bn for business investment this decade, largely funded by the cash-making activities of its fishing, processing and fine chemicals businesses. Of this amount, JPY 25bn is allocated for M&A, "most" of which will be spent on acquisitions outside Japan, it said.

"[We will build] a platform for sustainable growth on a global basis through outside Japan M&As and the restructuring of our outside Japan locations," the company said in its report, which was published in November. "[This will be in addition] to keeping an eye on changes in the external environment."

The M&A largesse comes after the company has already expanded its seafood processing and raw material sourcing in North America and Europe. In the Humber region, in the northeast of the UK, it owns controlling stakes in several processors in England's biggest seafood industry hub.

Nissui's global seafood empire, which you can click to enlarge. Credit: Nissui

Nissui, which is listed on the Tokyo stock exchange and has a market capitalization of JPY 169bn, or $1.26bn, said it is targeting "American and European markets". Plans for the latter involve growing in the Spanish, German, and Benelux markets, in particular.

Framing its strategy is a target to grow international sales from 34% of group sales in fiscal 2021, to 50% by 2030 -- more than double its full fiscal year 2021 international revenues of JPY 236bn, according to the report. By comparison, it expects its domestic sales to grow by just 9% over the same period, from JPY 459bn in fiscal 2021.

In March 2022, to oversee its international business expansion and its full year 2030 target, the company established an "international business department". The department will "strengthen the auditing of outside Japan subsidiaries" and ensure "reinforcement of group governance [which] will be essential for accelerating global growth in particular", it said.

Nissui 2030 sales split target. Source: Nissui integrated report 2022

Nissui already looms large over the global seafood industry. In 2021, it generated JPY 694bn in revenues, handling roughly 2.71m metric tons of wild-caught fish and crustaceans alone in 2019, according to its figures, or 2.7% of total global wild catch.

European expansion appears to be a key geographic focus to grow further. In 2021, the company generated JPY 115bn in revenue in the region -- including from fisheries, food products and fine chemicals sales -- its biggest source of revenue outside Japan.

Most recently, in November of last year, Nissui's Grimsby, UK-based processor Flatfish acquired Regal Fish Supplies, which has a fleet of vans delivering seafood directly to consumers in England and North Wales.

It followed Nissui's acquisitions of Humber seafood businesses Three Oceans Fish Company in 2020, and 75% of the shares in Flatfish in 2019. Also, last year, its Cite Marine subsidiary acquired Agromousquetaires, a seafood, poultry and vegetable product plant in Brittany, northern France.

Nissui’s Cite Marine plans new coated whitefish plant to target German market

In its previous quarterly report, Nissui said it had plans to build a new Cite Marine plant with an eye on the German market. The plan to move into the German market via Cite Marine comes after Nissui missed out on buying AliSa International, the parent of the French and German coated pollock plants which trade under the Greenland Seafood Europe name. Young's Seafood came out on top in this sale process in late 2020, but Nissui had been involved earlier. 

"As well as being areas with market growth potential, these businesses are domains in which we will be able to demonstrate our strengths in the technologies and expertise we have cultivated to date," it said.

J.P. Klausen & Company (JPK), a Denmark-based global seafood supplier owned by Nissui, has also been investing. At the end of 2022, Undercurrent News revealed JPK has moved into the pelagic sector in the Faroe Islands, with a vessel 20% owned by the firm having started fishing in February last year. 

Nissui’s Flatfish inks deal for UK home delivery seafood supplier

Nissui-owned JPK and its majority partners in the Faroe Islands own Vestmanna Seafood, a processing plant, which added Vestmenningur, a 100-meter pelagic trawler, to its operation last year, managing director Jens Peter Klausen told Undercurrent last December.

Vestmenningur is harvesting around 20,000 metric tons of blue whiting, herring and mackerel quota the company now owns. Producing surimi from blue whiting is a development project JPK is evaluating. JPK also owns 20% of the Vestmanna Seafood operation, which has an active land-based pelagic operation and a whitefish factory that is not in use, Klausen said.

Nissui's Nordic Seafood, which is the parent company of JPK and is focused more on foodservice, was also in the running to buy UK coldwater shrimp specialist Northcoast Seafoods. Seafood Connection, the Dutch subsidiary of Nissui's larger rival Maruha Nichiro, came out on top in this process, with a deal announced in May 2022. 

Breakdown of Nissui business categories by sales. Source: Nissui integrated report 2022

By consolidating companies across species and the supply chain, Nissui believes it can leverage "synergic effects".

In North America, where it generated JPY 108bn in sales, it reported more cooperation between UniSea and Glacier Fish Company, US land-based and at-sea pollock processors, respectively, and frozen, value-added seafood processors Gorton's and King & Prince Seafood Corp. 

Nissui’s JPK teams with Faroese partners on pelagic trawler, eyes blue whiting surimi

"We want to create the kind of synergies and value that only Nissui Group can realize, by leveraging those business foundations to deliver innovative food solutions," it said.

In Nissui's third quarter report, published at the start of February, the company said it's "considering capacity expansion and M&A to increase production volume" in North America. 

Tied in with its vision is "innovating productivity" and advancements in technology. It says "much room for improvement" in seafood businesses lies simply through digitization, with "still many analogue operations on the ground in production and in our administrative divisions".

It also expects the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to come into play for demand forecasting and improving the efficiency of supply chains in the short- to medium-term. 

Shrimp, salmon growth

In terms of species categories, Nissui identified farmed salmon and shrimp as categories where it sees particular growth potential.

While the company does not break down its sales by species, salmon, shrimp and whitefish are its main products in the foods products business, which generated JPY 328bn in sales, and JPY 15.4bn in operating profits in 2021. 

To further drive sales growth in shrimp, in the US, it has entered the household frozen category with the launch of popcorn shrimp under its brand Gorton's, the US' biggest brand in frozen seafood. Although Gorton's is mainly a frozen whitefish business, the addition of popcorn shrimp represents further growth of its range using the farmed crustacean.

"The market size of marine products has been growing for household and commercial use in the US. [But] the markets for processed whitefish and shrimp still have significant room for expansion," it said.

Meanwhile, in Asia, it has tied up with Thailand-based company Thai Delmar -- a supplier of Marine Stewardship Council-certified fried whitefish to global hamburger franchises such as McDonald's -- to expand fried shrimp and fried whitefish businesses to the fast food industry. 

Then in salmon, while it currently markets and sells coho salmon and trout farmed by its Chilean subsidiary Salmones Antartica through its Five Star brand, mainly on the Japanese market, it has been increasing production at its Chilean operation of Atlantics.

In refined fish oils, mainly involving production of EPA, or eicosapentaenoic acid, an omega three oil, it is also preparing for the European Medicines Agency certification to sell EPA in the European pharmaceutical market.

"Today, drivers for our growth include business expansion in Europe, profitability of aquaculture in Japan, and overseas rollout of the EPA business," it said.

Aquaculture future

In terms of supply-side strategies, Nissui, which has its roots in Japan's deep sea fishing industry, signaled greater focus on aquaculture as it seeks to cater to a growing global population in the context of limited resources.

Maruha Nichiro ups overseas sales to record levels after EU, US acquisition spree

It expects growth in land-based farming, in which it has invested in production for several species, including vannamei shrimp, salmon and chub mackerel and trout. In Denmark, it has invested in land-based salmon venture Danish Salmon, one of the world's few proven land-based salmon farming operations, which produces 2,570t of fish a year. 

"We will aim to become a company capable of earning JPY 1tn in sales and JPY 50bn in operating profits by 2030, by accelerating growth and differentiation of aquaculture and fine chemicals businesses," it said.

Separately, it said that by 2030 it aims for "100%" of wild-caught fish it sources to be from "well managed" or "managed" fisheries, based on criteria by the NGO Sustainable Fisheries Partnership, up from 71% in 2019.

Nissui said to reduce exposure from deals, the company is considering obtaining an external credit rating to help secure "flexible financing at stable low-interest rates".

Australia’s Seafarms pulls funding plug on Nissui-backed land-based shrimp project

It is also in the process of improving oversight. Earlier this year, Australian shrimp mega-project Project Sea Dragon, in which Nissui owns a 15% stake, was put into administration by its owner. Nissui, which had invested AUD 25m in the project near Kununurra in Western Australia, appeared sold on the vision of serving growing Asian demand with up to 180,000t of black tiger shrimp annually, although ultimately had a backseat role in the project. 

Nissui vowed it would not hesitate to divest from businesses that were underperforming or didn't align with high growth and high investment efficiency. Last year, the company sold its listed subsidiary, Nissui Pharmaceutical, due to "limited synergies" with the rest of the group.

"By proceeding with action such as the sales of businesses that have little potential synergy with the group, we will pursue the transformation to a more appropriate business portfolio," it said.

title: Icelandic Salmon expects no supply growth in 2023
content:
Icelandic Salmon, the Westfjords-based farmer majority owned by Norwegian giant SalMar, expects a year of no production growth before it anticipates ramping up harvests again in 2024.

Weak farming margins, M&A costs bring SalMar’s earnings in below expectations

The company forecast harvests of 16,000 metric tons of Atlantic salmon in 2023, level with last year's output, which grew by 40% compared with 2021.

The growth pause comes as the company awaits license approvals for 4,500t of additional biomass in Arnarfjodur, one of three fjords farmed in the Westfjords region, on top of a 10,000t farming license in Isafjardardjup. 

Arnarlax fined by Iceland’s MAST for overstocking salmon pens

It follows a record year of earnings and revenues on the back of last year's strong production output.

In 2022, the group grew operational earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) to €36.15 million ($38.5m), up from €7.3m in 2021. This came on an operating income of €157.6m, up from €90.8m in 2021.

On a quarterly basis, the group's operating income amounted to €51.7m compared with €35.8m in the corresponding quarter of 2021. Icelandic Salmon does not provide its revenues in its quarterly income statements.

"The second half of 2022 has followed the strong results we achieved in the first half of the year," said Bjorn Hembre, CEO of Icelandic Salmon and Arnarlax, the salmon farming unit of the group. "We are starting to reap the benefits of our expanded operations and achieved significant growth in the final quarter and last year."

He added Iceland Salmon was in a "strong financial position" and was a "proud contributor to the Icelandic economy and society".

Slow license approval

Trumpeting its economic benefits may be a strategy to impress license authorities as the company seeks more approvals.

It also comes after the company was fined ISK 120m ($858,000) by the Icelandic food and veterinary authority (MAST) in November, due to incorrect information about the number of fish stocked in the company's sea pen in Westfjords.

An investigation by MAST found the company could not account for the fate of at least 81,564 Atlantic salmon after a visit by the body initially to investigate salmon escapes.

So far -- while not specifically related to the fine -- applications for increasing biomass in Arnarfjordur by 4,500t remain under review. Its 10,000t application for a farming license in Isafjardardjup is also still in progress, but it, too, has been delayed -- this time due to "updates on white beams and sailing routes".

The company remains upbeat about its long-term farming opportunities. Under the country's current risk assessment issued by Iceland's Marine Research Institute, 106,500t maximum allowable biomass of fertile salmon is permitted in the country.

"Of the 106,500t, licenses have been issued for 86,800t," it said in an earlier report.

US sales push

In the fourth quarter, Icelandic Salmon's biggest market for its salmon was the US.

Source: Icelandic Salmon Q4

This had gifted it a key selling point into the market -- low emissions transport due to Iceland's proximity to the country.

In Q4, it shipped 82% of its salmon to North America by sea, compared with just 18% by air. With the US Icelandic Salmon's biggest market, this makes it a lower-carbon emission supplier than other countries from Europe, it said.

"The majority of salmon is transported by air into this market, resulting in high carbon footprint and cost. This, along with rapid growth of the market in the last few years and relatively low, but growing, seafood consumption per capita, offers an interesting opportunity for Icelandic Salmon."

title: Alaska processing vessel fined $208,983 for alleged unsanitary conditions
content:
A seafood processing vessel in the US state of Alaska is facing heavy fines for alleged health and safety violations for the fourth time since 2012, Alaska Public Media reports. 

The US Occupational Safety and Health Administration fined 169-foot factory fishing vessel Pacific Producer $208,983 on allegations that include murky, brown water in the ship’s drinking tanks, serving expired food to crew and fish processing water leaking into dry food storage and dining areas. Electrical hazards such as damaged equipment, broken outlets, outlets near water and exposed wires, as well as no forms of fire suppression, are also alleged.

Chris Tsabouris, the owner of East West Seafoods, which owns the vessel, declined to comment when contacted by KMXT-TV.

As Undercurrent News has written, Tasbouris and Seattle-based East West were fined $12,654 for operating in waters from 2009 to 2012 without an approved oil spill readiness plan in 2013.

title: Untitled
content:
New civil lawsuit testimony from some familiar faces in the US' long-running canned tuna price-fixing scandal suggests that the conspiracy began earlier than 2011, the year prosecutors previously said marked its start.

The testimony, a Feb. 6 "status report" about the case filed by lawyers for plaintiff Associated Wholesale Grocers, comes from depositions taken in recent weeks of former Bumble Bee Foods executives Walter Cameron and Ken Worsham as well as Stephen Hodge, formerly of StarKist & Co. 

All three men avoided jail time for their own participation in the scandal after agreeing to testify in the criminal trial against former Bumble Bee CEO Christopher Lischewski, who prosecutors said led the conspiracy. When deposed previously in the civil suits Cameron, Worsham and Hodge exercised their Fifth Amendment rights against self-incrimination, but after the criminal cases against them ended, gave new depositions.

"This is the first time these executives have testified in depth about emails, phone records, and concealment efforts in the pre-conviction period. The evidence obtained since the original briefing shows the involvement of StarKist executives (and a consultant) during this period. And it provides evidence of Mr. Lischewski’s participation and direction of his co-conspirators to exchange competitive future pricing information with Bumble Bee’s competitors, including StarKist in the pre-2011 period," the status report stated.

The customer lawsuits initially focused on the US' three-largest tuna canners -- Bumble Bee, Thai Union Group's Chicken of the Sea International and Dongwon Industries-owned StarKist. But they were later amended to add Lischewski and former Bumble Bee owners Del Monte Foods Company and UK-based private equity investor Lion Capital. Thai Union, which has settled the class-action lawsuits against it, and Bumble Bee, which declared bankruptcy in 2019 and was later purchased by Taiwan's FCF Co, are no longer defendants in the cases.

Lischewski, who was sentenced to prison in the case, has long denied his involvement and suggested that price-fixing did not occur. 

StarKist, which in 2019 pleaded guilty to criminal price-fixing charges and ordered to pay a $100 million fine, continues to fight the civil cases. The company's general counsel and senior vice president, Scott Meece, said previously that while the company is willing to put an end to the civil lawsuits from customers, it will not settle "cases, in these matters or others, if the claims are excessive or in which the complaining party was not harmed".

The other defendants have also denied that they knew the price-fixing was taking place. According to the plaintiffs' status report, however, the testimony from Hodge, Worsham and Cameron suggests otherwise. 

"The additional evidence disputes StarKist’s claim that the conspiracy was confined to a few actions by Mr. Hodge affecting the price advances in 2011 and 2012. It contradicts StarKist’s claim that its actions were independent. It also undermines StarKist’s claim that the collusion had no impact on pricing. Importantly, the evidence includes testimony on emails, phone records, and concealment efforts by the conspirators in the 2007 to 2010 period," the report states.

StarKist had asked San Diego, California-based judge Dana Sabraw, who is overseeing the case to throw out the plaintiffs' claims that price-fixing occurred before the 2011 period. The company's defense efforts suffered a major blow last year when the US Supreme Court decided not to review its appeal of judge Janis Sammartino's 2019 decision to certify the hundreds of individual lawsuits from customers into common classes.

That decision, the canner has argued, sounds a "death knell" for the future of the litigation, as it essentially forces it to settle. Additionally, the company said that it hasn't been proven that members of the allegedly damaged classes have enough commonalities to be grouped together.

title: LatAm body urges controls of giant squid fishing parties in the south Pacific after Chinese vessels refuse inspection
content:
Latin America's Committee for the Sustainable Management of Giant Squid (CALAMASUR) has urged the regional fishery management organization (RFMO) watching over the South Pacific to implement "effective" controls on all parties to avoid illegal practices.

The request was brought up at the meeting of the technical and compliance committee of the South Pacific RFMO, which is currently taking place in Manta, Ecuador, where CALAMASUR is participating as an observer. It comes after two Chinese vessels fishing in the area refused to be inspected, the conservation group said.

LatAm body baffled by lack of will to protect giant squid

CALAMASUR's president, Alfonso Miranda Eyzaguirre, said that, without exception, all vessels fishing in the commission's area have the obligation to ensure compliance with management measures, particularly through at-sea inspections. He stressed that flag states must avoid any doubt of complicity in illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing activities.

All parties, "without excuses or delays", must implement "effective compliance of all the resolutions in force, especially those related to control and surveillance of fishing," he said.

Previously, Miranda has told Undercurrent that 631 Chinese vessels are "irregularly fishing" giant squid in the South Pacific, "to the detriment of Peru, Ecuador and Chile".

Latin American parties suggested at the meeting that the possible breach of China's obligations as a flag state should force the RFMO to propose an improvement plan that would specifically address this. However, representatives from China objected to the proposal even being considered, as the country refuses to be considered as "non-compliant".

Miranda has in the past claimed that Chinese fishing vessels complete only about 1% of fishing trips with a scientific observer onboard, compared to up to 100% for other flag states in other fisheries.

At the previous meeting of the South Pacific RFMO -- which took place last October in South Korea -- China opposed an increase in observer coverage, and a CALAMASUR proposal for a reduction in fishing efforts and for science-based management in the area.

In 2017, Ecuador's naval forces intercepted the Chinese vessel Fu Yuan Yu Leng 999 while sailing illegally within the Galapagos marine reserve. Some 300 metric tons of fish were found in its holds, including vulnerable species such as hammerhead and silky sharks, which are in danger of extinction.

Undercurrent News reported that the crew received jail time of between one and four years and were fined $5.9 million.

Poor start to Argentine illex season feeds into rising squid prices in China

Chinese vessels fishing near Ecuador's Galapagos Islands turn off their satellite-based automatic identification systems and use "twin vessels" to enter the Latin American country's exclusive economic zone, according to marine conservation specialist Milko Schvartzman. 

Every year, a vast fleet of Asian vessels fish off the South American seas. It repeats a route that goes from the South Atlantic, off Argentina, to the outskirts of the Galapagos, in the Pacific, passing through Chile and Peru. In their trajectories, some vessels have been caught fishing illegally and have also been accused of human rights violations.

According to an investigation carried out by the Argentine NGO OceanoSanos, the region's main port used by the Chinese fleet in Latin America is Montevideo, in Uruguay.

A recent investigation carried out by Mongabay revealed that a firm called Verny in Uruguay is the principal maritime agency in assisting Chinese-flagged vessels, some of which have a history of illegal fishing and human rights violations.
