title: Iceland’s government pledges action on aquaculture sector after report
content:
A government review of Iceland's salmon aquaculture sector has painted a damning picture of the industry's oversight, though the industry itself has responded to its findings positively.

The Icelandic National Audit Office (INAO) found the administration and supervision of open-net fish farming in Iceland are weak and fragmented; that fish farming regulations are an unclear patchwork. The government has pledged to act on the report’s findings, reported Iceland Review.

The report, commissioned by the ministry of food, fisheries, and agriculture, paints a picture of a fish farming industry that has grown rapidly over the past decade, noting that changes in legislation that were intended to promote the growth and development of the sector have not been followed up by strengthening administration or supervision.

Farming areas have grown with little input or action from the government, and there are examples of aquaculture zones overlapping with sailing routes, protected areas for telecommunications and electricity cables, and obstructing navigational lighthouses.

According to the INAO report, monitoring of the sector needs to be strengthened. The Marine and Freshwater Research Institute has pointed out that it does not have the resources required to define fish farming zones. The report says that the Icelandic Food and Veterinary Authority did not consider additional monitoring necessary despite uncovering serious and repeated deviations from existing regulations.

“It is quite clear that the regulatory framework around this is a patchwork, is unclear, ineffective, and so on,” said the minister of food, fisheries and agriculture Svandis Svavarsdottir.

“We’ve been chasing an industry that has grown very quickly.” She said changes to laws would require considerable preparation, but that there were also many suggestions in the report the government would act on immediately.

The industry -- represented by Samtok fyrirtaekjai sjavarutvegi, or SFS -- took a positive view of the report, noting that it too has been warning that aquaculture administration was not fit for purpose.

"There have been irregularities in the administration of sea salmon farming and the respective authorities have not been guaranteed sufficient strength, framework and resources to deal with the increased activity of the sector in recent years," it said.

"In the report, there are various problems and, among other things, defined suggestions for improvement are presented to the institutions that manage fish farming."

Most of these aim to ensure uniform legislation, but "there are also suggestions related to maximizing the overall utilization of aquaculture areas", it said. "It is clear that these suggestions will prove to be an important contribution to the ministry of food's proposed strategy for the future of aquaculture."

The report inevitably focused on where legislation has fallen behind as the sector has grown, and no on its successes, SFS said.

"That was necessary; now that increased knowledge and experience have been built up within the administration, it is important to correct what has gone wrong and look ahead. It will bring little success to lie in the trenches, and surely it is worth remembering that he who makes no mistakes usually does nothing. In the long run, fish farming will become a powerful primary industry and an important pillar in the country's economy and prosperity."

Aquaculture company Arctic Fish -- now majority owned by Mowi -- agreed with SFS, stating that complex and inconsistent regulations have "plagued" the sector.

"License applications that are many years in the making are the clearest example of how the situation is," it said. 

"The positive thing, of course, is the fact that despite this, there have been many powerful companies in seafood farming in Iceland that have created a lot of work for many. The government has gotten a new tax agency that has already started to make sense for the nation's population and communities that have been sick are now thriving. This has been done without harming nature and sea salmon is a sought-after product that we proudly sell worldwide."

It said it would be happy to take part in consultations on future administration.

title: Untitled
content:
The Norwegian government's resource tax plan could re-shape the focus of leading aquaculture companies' investments in the sector in the medium term, Gorjan Nikolik, chief seafood analyst at Dutch agri-bank Rabobank, told Undercurrent News.

Gorjan Nikolik, senior industry analyst, Rabobank Photo credit: Aquaculture Alliance

In the short term, Norway's plans for an additional resource tax on aquaculture -- whether it is introduced at 40%, as proposed, or a lower level as is now being rumored -- will likely support prices and benefit other producing nations, he said.

While the final details of the tax proposals still need to be agreed upon, the plan has already impacted the global salmon sector, Nikolik noted.

Some of the top salmon producers in the country -- such as Mowi, Leroy Seafood Group, and Cermaq Group -- froze their investments back in October last year, soon after the new tax proposals cast a shadow of uncertainty over their future. More than NOK 35 billion ($3.53bn) worth of investments were postponed or reduced, according to an analysis produced by the Norwegian seafood federation, Sjomat Norge.

DNB: Tax plan can further hit Norway salmon sector’s growth, after $3.5bn investments put on hold

Nikolik pointed out that investments in bigger smolt have been the driver for better utilization of Norwegian licenses, which has led to reasonable volume growth in recent years. As a result of the current freeze in investments in this field, Norwegian salmon supply growth could be cut to 3% per year rather than the 4-5% that it had been on track to reach, according to Nikolik.

This remains dependent on the final details of the plan approved by the government, which is currently considering the feedback received during a recent public consultation. When ready, the government will present a proposal to the parliament, a spokesperson from the Norwegian ministry of fisheries told Undercurrent.

Since the tax's retroactive beginning date of Jan. 1, 2023, some Norwegian banks have speculated that the tax could yet be set at a gentler rate than the 40% previously proposed, perhaps between 15% and 25%. 

This phase of uncertainty, until the government clearly defines the tax proposal, "has already had a heavy impact on the future growth of the sector. And there is already some kind of a risk premium to invest in Norway because of the unreliability of the policy", the analyst told Undercurrent.

The short-term beneficiaries of this fallout are the other producing countries: Chile, Ireland, Iceland, Canada and the Faroe Islands, Nikolik said. 

Those countries will take advantage of a higher salmon spot price in the short term, he said. Slower production growth in Norway, driven by the tax proposal, will be a support factor for prices for the next two-to-three years. However, other drivers, such as biology, temperature and water, will also continue to play a role.

"In 2022, some major players delivered below expectations. This tax proposal is some of the best news that the [global] industry could receive [from a price point of view] since Norway is seen as the [country with the most] potential long-term supply growth," Nikolik noted. 

Upgrade to Pro to view

Meanwhile, some investors could divert their funds from Norway into other salmon-producing regions. Nikolik said that, however, there isn't "much room to grow salmon production in other states", a factor that the Norwegian government might have considered.

Mowi: Iceland can be ‘new Faroes’ in 10 years’ time

In the longer term, the producing country with the highest taxes is likely to see lower, or even negative, supply growth as other regions find ways to grow with technology. 

Higher salmon prices could lead Chilean farmers to invest in more hatcheries and to grow their smolt sizes, Nikolik predicted. He noted that, in the last four or five years, Chile hasn't really grown much in salmon production. 

updated Proposal: work in progress

The Norwegian government is still to hammer out the details of its tax plan, which will be further elaborated on and discussed in the political arena in the coming months. 

Depending on the final plan, Nikolik forecasts that Norwegian farmers could reduce investments in at-sea operations and potentially radically change their farming systems in the long term.

He pointed out that if the new resource tax plan does not cover smolt and new offshore projects, the industry could reduce its overall investment, but channel a greater proportion of funds into those segments.

For example, they could move production from traditional, coastal areas to instead utilize land-based post-smolt facilities before growing salmon to harvest size further offshore, mitigating the higher tax brackets, Nikolik said.

Mowi plans salmon broodstock, egg facility for Scottish operation

He said that if recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) developments are not included in the tax plan, there could be a rise in those investments in Norway or elsewhere. So far, no traditional salmon farmers or family-owned companies in Norway have embraced RAS significantly since it has involved higher risks; but the tax plan could potentially push the industry to emerge as a greater supporter of RAS, the analyst suggested.

"They [farmers] would have less cash flow availability to invest from [farming] operations. So they would either have to raise new capital to do this, or it could be that the legislation is defined in such a way that some of these investments are actually tax deductible. And that's another big part of the debate," Nikolik said. "The decision on what is going to be tax deductible will drive considerably how investments are going to look," he added.

Another potential outcome of the new tax is that Norwegian farmers invest in other parts of the value chain, such as feed production or processing, he went on. This could prove attractive to salmon farmers if they feel they can increase the profitability of those operations, merging them with the production phase for greater integration.

"It could be that we find ourselves with much more post-smolt [growth], which is the best result for the Norwegian government. That means that the value chain remains in Norway, and it continues to grow, maybe not as fast as it did, but with a higher price," he explained.

However, this would only be a medium-term solution; in the long term, the tax will likely create a movement of salmon farming outside of Norway, according to Nikolik.

title: Untitled
content:
After Nova Austral argued that the company had not committed any more infractions since 2017, Chile's superintendent of the environment, or the SMA, revealed new lawsuits against the firm for the 2019-2021 production cycles.

On Feb. 2, the Chilean salmon producer asked for the annulation of the SMA resolution to apply sanctions that resulted in the loss of environmental permits for Nova Austral's Aracena 10, Cockburn 14 and Cockburn 23 farms in July 2022.

They were all subject to the same sanction -- the toughest the SMA can deliver -- for overproduction of fish by 25%, 15% and 30%, respectively, between October 2015 and late 2017.

At the hearing before Chile's third environmental court, Nova Austral argued that the alleged environmental damage that the SMA said justified most serious sanctions didn't occur. 

Also, it said that from when the overproduction that gave rise to the sanctions would have been verified, there had been "no subsequent breaches by the company" that could justify classifying it as a persistent offender. 

"This is disproportionate and discriminatory," said Nova Austral's lawyer, Julio Recordon. "The SMA is exceeding its sanctioning powers and also assuming land management powers that are not in the law."

In July, the SMA also fined the company CLP 900 million ($929,176) for artificially altering the seabed of the Aracena 14 site near the city of Punta Arenas.

On behalf of Nova Austral, Recordon reiterated that those sanctions would lead to an unsustainable adverse financial situation and "quite possibly" to the closure of its operations in Chile. "Nova Austral is a radically different company from what it was five years ago," he stated. 

The SMA, however, assured that Chile's national fisheries and aquaculture service, Sernapesca, made two new complaints against the salmon farmer, this time in the Aracena 1 and Aracena 13 farms in the Alberto de Agostini National Park for periods between 2019 and 2021. 

Sernapesca denounced the overproduction of fish by 11% in Aracena 1 and 24% in Aracena 13, said SMA's lawyer Khatarina Buschmann. 

Nevertheless, the two new complaints mentioned have not yet been informed, in any case, through the SMA's national environmental control information system.

title: ‘Lack of compromise’ at IOTC special session worries ISSF
content:
The International Seafood Sustainability Foundation (ISSF) has said that the "lack of compromise" at a recent meeting of the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC) sets an "unwelcome precedent", even though some enhanced measures were agreed upon.

The IOTC concluded a special session on Feb. 5, adopting a conservation and management measure on fish aggregating devices (FADs) for Indian Ocean tuna fisheries. During the special session, which was called last year due to inaction on this topic, two FAD resolutions were successfully adopted. 

India proposes full ban on drifting FADs in the Indian Ocean

A proposal on drifting FADs (or dFADs) -- used by industrial purse seine fleets, including those of the EU -- was put forward by 11 coastal states and was adopted by a two-thirds majority following a vote by secret ballot in the final hours of the three-day meeting in Mombasa, Kenya. The proposal, which will come into effect on Jan. 1, 2024, included a phased reduction in the number of drifting FADs permitted per vessel, from 300 to 250 in the first year and to 200 in 2025.

It also mandated the creation of a dFAD registry. According to the International Pole and Line Foundation (IPNLF), this will allow for increased transparency and monitoring of the controversial man-made devices used to attract tuna, a large proportion of which can be juveniles.

Additionally, the adopted proposal puts in place a 72-day closure period for dFADs. This aspect of the proposal received the most opposition from the EU, which threatened to object to the proposal in its entirety, according to IPNLF.

Another proposal on anchored FADs, put forward by Maldives and Kenya, was adopted by consensus.

In a position statement issued before the IOTC session, the ISSF urged enhanced, science-based FAD management provisions.

ISSF acknowledged the commission's progress in adopting some of the improvements it has called for, including FAD marking guidelines, a timeline for transition to biodegradable FADs, and access to FAD position data for the IOTC scientific committee for science needs.  
 
However, it said it is "concerned by the lack of a shared effort by all IOTC delegations in working together toward the realization of scientific advice. The general breakdown of communication and negotiation that was evident at the IOTC special session sets an unwelcome precedent for future meetings and, ultimately, the sustainable use of Indian Ocean tuna fisheries," it said.

It stressed IOTC parties are beholden to the United Nations Fish Stocks Agreement, the core provisions of which require cooperation and consultation amongst all coastal states and states fishing on the high seas.

"Both practices are critically important in managing highly migratory fish stocks like tuna, and both practices seemed to have been unfortunately lacking at this meeting," noted ISSF president Susan Jackson.

"We therefore remain cautious in our assessment of the effectiveness of the new FAD measure, especially in helping rebuild the yellowfin tuna stock. And we urge all parties to recommit to working together for the long-term sustainable management of Indian Ocean resources," Jackson added.

Other reactions: Europeche, IPNLF

Meanwhile, European fishing association Europeche said the decision against dFADs was "inapplicable" and that it severely threatens coastal developing states' economies. 

"Purse seine fishery's existence in the Indian Ocean is at stake after an inapplicable decision against drifting FADs was imposed by vote in the IOTC," it said.

It pointed out that the IOTC's decision had a "clear target" to "end FAD fisheries and expel Europeans from those waters". Europeche noted it had been approved by 11 states, including "recurrent objectors to important management and conservation measures" such as Somalia, Pakistan, Indonesia, Madagascar, India, Iran and Australia. 

The organization stressed that the decision to "rapidly phase out drifting FADs" will destroy the purse seine fleets and undermine the economies of the developing states that depend on it. "For instance, Seychelles and Mauritius' canneries might not survive this decision, which is binding, since their supply depends on the landings from these vessels," it said.

"Mauritius is not a big fishing nation yet. It is a processing nation. For that, Mauritius needs raw material. The purse seine fishery contributes 20,000 jobs and guarantees access to the EU market, which brings good opportunities to Mauritius, to enhance its economy," said the Mauritian delegate in the meeting.

The representative from Comoros also opposed the Indonesian proposal and claimed its preference for the European one, which was to improve traceability, transparency and biodegradability while protecting local economies.

"Comoros supports the EU proposal because it has an industry that must function. Small countries are also waiting for supplies brought by these large boats," he said.

The delegate from Seychelles also strongly opposed the approved measure. "Having a moratorium on one particular gear, without any scientific advice, is unfair and discriminatory," he said.

According to Europeche, while other fishing fleets catch more than half of the total tuna catches in the IOTC area, the whole burden is placed on purse seiner fleets.

"This is, 46 vessels which employ hundreds of sailors, including from Africa and create employment in processing plants, shipyards and port facilities in the Indian Ocean," it said.

It stressed that the EU, Seychelles, Mauritius, Comoros and other contracting parties were not opposing the introduction of further FAD measures. "These countries were only requesting specific scientific advice, to be delivered in the next scientific committee in December 2023, for the IOTC to take a science-based decision in 2024," it said.

Anne-France Mattlet, director of the Europeche tuna group, regretted the IOTC outcome.

"No science to base the decision on, no consideration for local economies, and above all, no possibility given to the EU and other opposed developing countries to discuss and find a compromise," she said.

Mattlet said that the proponents only agreed to meet once for less than two hours in three days and pointed out the vote imposed measures that will threaten the whole EU long-distance tuna fleet and the purse-seine-dependent economies of the region.

"Can it be something else than a geopolitical issue? We are strongly asking the EU to challenge this decision, in line with the affected developing countries, to save the purse-seine fleet and support its developing partner states. The contrary will hand over our tuna supply to non-EU fleets and foreign interests".

Europeche said it was concerned about the influence exerted by the IPLNF. "UK companies represented by this organization are close to acquiring a monopoly on [Marine Stewardship Council] certified tuna in the UK market. An attractive market for the EU purse seine fleet which is also certified," it said.

Meanwhile, Jess Rattle -- head of investigations at the NGO Blue Marine -- defined the IOTC's outcome as a "landmark decision" and a "giant step forward for the conservation of tuna stocks in the Indian Ocean" that had been three years in the making.

"In the face of immense pressure and opposition from powerful actors from the EU, the 11 coastal states and the other supporters of the drifting FAD measure showed true leadership and dedication to protecting the Indian Ocean's tuna stocks and the countless coastal communities that depend on them," she said.

Martin Purves, the IPNLF's managing director, congratulated the coastal states who "worked so hard to secure this important victory for tuna stocks and coastal livelihoods throughout the Indian Ocean region".

"While acknowledging that significant concessions were made to accommodate small island developing states during the negotiation process, the new measure on harmful drifting FADs will have a significant impact on controlling the damage caused by industrial purse seine tuna fleets," he said.

title: Trident Seafoods fined $25,000 over environmental damage from vessel fire
content:
The US state of Washington has issued a $25,000 fine to Trident Seafoods, alleging a hydraulic oil spill, negligence and a failure to adequately report an all-night fire that destroyed a seafood processing ship in 2021,  The News-Tribune of Tacoma said.

The state Department of Ecology (DOE) said that 20 to 30 gallons of hydraulic oil spilled into the Hylebos Waterway while firefighters fought the blaze aboard the Aleutian Falcon.

"Even small amounts of oil can severely injure or impair mammals, fish, birds, and other animals," DOE said in a statement. "Oil can also adversely affect the habitats that wildlife depends on for survival."

As Undercurrent News has written, the Falcon was moored on Feb. 17 at Trident's Tacoma facility between its time in Alaska supporting summer salmon fisheries. When operating, the 230-foot vessel with a crew of 120 supplemented Trident's shore-based and more extensive processing vessel operations throughout Alaska.

No injuries were reported.

The company has 30 days to appeal the fine.

title: Chilean aquaculture law reform proposals loom over Magallanes projects
content:
Chilean salmon producers are likely to pause investments in new projects in the country's southernmost region until there is more clarity on how the country's aquaculture law may change.

That's the sense that Carlos Odebret, president of the Magallanes salmon producers' association, gets from his talks with industry participants.

Last year, Chile's undersecretary of fisheries discussed the need to develop a new law for aquaculture. 

"We interpret this news [on the upcoming discussion in a new aquaculture law] as a sign of the state's interest in developing the [salmon] industry in the long-term," Odebret told Undercurrent News during a recent interview.

The executive pointed out that even if the aquaculture reform proposal's objectives haven't been fully defined, salmon producers have interpreted this move as a sign that the government intends to "define the rules of the game [for the salmon industry] in the long-term".

He observed that beyond the specific objectives that the law will have, he disagreed with the notion that the government plan intends to eventually phase out the salmon farming industry.

It "projects the industry for the long term, and this is good news, despite the pressure that some NGOs have raised in Chile", Odebret further observed.

He also noted that a second element for the upcoming discussion on aquaculture will likely center on the locations of farming sites.

"There has been a lot of discussion about the location of the salmon industry in competition with protected wildlife areas. And what we have seen is that the government has taken action to relocate concessions that are in national parks. This distinction between parks and other protected wilderness areas is essential because national parks are the most protected category, and it makes a lot of sense to relocate [salmon concessions]," Odebret said.

He pointed out that a recent law established that the development of the salmon industry in the national reserves had to be combined with the protection of these regions.

"This is a path that we hope the government will maintain, especially in the Magallanes region," he noted.

Odebret pointed out that the presence of salmon farms within the national reserves doesn't exceed 0.06% of the total area. He stressed that it is possible to develop aquaculture in a way compatible with protecting wild areas, particularly with the national reserves.

According to Odebret, deciding where the appropriate location for salmon sites is a matter of land management, which is the state's responsibility. He noted that a long-term plan was necessary, considering that 92% of concessions in the national reserve in Magallanes were authorized before the creation of the reserve.

The new law will require a "long discussion, not only with salmon producers but also with the regional governments, civil society and workers", Odebret added.

Recently, Chile's congress continued discussion on a bill that establishes the biodiversity and protected areas service and the national system of protected areas.

Despite some legislators pushing to disallow salmon farming concessions inside these zones, the bill moved forward with a provision that allows aquaculture concessions to operate in protected areas with a management plan, Salmon Expert reported.

Chilean salmon farmers’ Magallanes investments begin to bear fruit

Investments made in recent years to develop the salmon farming industry in Magallanes are paying off, according to Odebret.

The region harvested a total of 170,000t last year, roughly flat compared to 2020 and up to the 140,000 metric tons reached in 2021. The year-on-year change of the past two years is driven by salmon's long production cycle and limits in production growth set by the latest regulations. Mortality level has decreased to below 4% on average, Odebret noted.

The region's salmon output more than tripled from 47,000t in 2015 to 175,000t in 2020. With an investment of over $200 million in recent years, Chilean salmon producers have been able to build a regional salmon production hub. They are still keen to invest further in the region.

title: Badinotti adds new EMEA top exec, eyes growth through M&A
content:
Italy's Badinotti Group, a maker of cages and nets for the fishing and aquaculture industries, has appointed Sergio Biancheri as its new general manager for the EMEA region.

Biancheri -- with over 20 years of experience in leading sales and operations teams in the automotive and home automation sectors -- will be responsible for the company's commercial operations in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa (EMEA), the firm said.

Sergio Biancheri. Credit: Badinotti

"We are very excited about Sergio's arrival. His experience and track record will be essential for implementing the company's 2025 strategy and thus be able to consolidate our leadership position in all the units and countries we have defined as objective," said Christian Torres, Badinotti's CEO.

According to Biancheri, the firm's target in the EMEA region will be "to enlarge Badinotti's local presence to be closer to customers". 

"As we have recently done in Croatia, growing organically and through acquisition," he said. 

In 2020, the group partnered with Croatian aquaculture firm Cromaris for a project to which it provided engineering services, mooring design, selected equipment, and installation.

The agreement also included providing equipment -- 40 new floating cages of 120-meter circumference in four rafts -- with installation services off the coast of Zadar, Croatia.

It has also made several deals in recent years, including Croatia-based Pensito Adriatik, Scheel Marine, and Chilean net loft V&V.

title: Greater jack mackerel catches help Chilean fishing industry to achieve growth, diversification
content:
A significant increase in landings of jack mackerel in Chile, combined with significant commercial efforts to diversify sales markets beyond Africa, has helped the Latin American fishing industry to achieve outstanding growth in recent years.

The jack mackerel stock in Chile, which in the past was threatened by overfishing, has recovered, according to industry sources. This has allowed fishing quotas there to be increased over the past five years.

Jack mackerel stocks have recovered thanks to conservation measures defined by the South Pacific Regional Fisheries Management Organisation, which manages Chile's jack mackerel fishing resources, according to the Chilean fishing industry association Asipes.

Retailer group notes Chilean jack mackerel taking market share in Europe

A spokeswoman with the association told Undercurrent News that good resource management has allowed it to increase its quota year after year and receive the Marine Steward Council certification in 2018. 

In 2020, Chile's jack mackerel quota totaled 439,000 metric tons, up 15% year-on-year. It rose further to 504,000t in 2021 and 570,000t in 2022, according to sources.

European supply chain representative group the North Atlantic Pelagic Advocacy Group (NAPA) has even written to politicians there to highlight the growing market share being won by Chilean jack mackerel.

It claimed fisheries management failures in Europe have propelled major brands to turn to Chilean jack mackerel as a sustainable alternative to overfished northeast Atlantic mackerel, which no longer carries the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certificate -- unlike Chilean product.

Orizon

Chilean cannery Orizon Seafood, which belongs to Empresas Copec, is one of Chile's largest producers of jack mackerel, mackerel, sardine and anchovy. It has the largest quota for jack mackerel in Chile, 180,000t, accounting for nearly 30% of the total for this year, according to Gabriel Sanchez, an export manager with the firm.

It sells frozen fish, cans and fishmeal and fish oil. The group's turnover totals about $200 million per year. 

Gabriel Sanchez, Orizon's export manager, at Conxemar 2022.

The firm plans to launch a new jack mackerel burger next year in the US.

It has expanded sales in Africa and Asia, promoting its value-added products like frozen jack mackerel fillets and burgers and other canned products. Logistical issues during the pandemic and the rise in transport costs have also encouraged the company to further diversify its markets into Europe and the US in recent years, with positive results, Sanchez said.

Blumar's fishing division 

Blumar Seafoods is another of Chile's largest fishing companies. Beyond its salmon production, Blumar also processes pelagics (mainly sardines and anchovy) into fishmeal and fish oil. 
It also sells jack mackerel for human consumption.

Over the last five years, Blumar's fishing division has been able to diversify its jack mackerel sales beyond Africa into Europe and Asia.

Thanks to a recovery in Chilean jack mackerel quotas, Blumar's volume for the species totaled about 90,000t last year and could rise to 100,000t in 2023.

Through its Vigo office, Blumar has opened sales in eastern Europe this year. Blumar's office in Shangai was in charge of sales of jack mackerel to Asian customers.

title: Canadian harvester granted retrial after conviction for not keeping log
content:
A herring harvester from the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador will stand trial again after winning an appeal of his conviction for allegedly violating the Fisheries Act by failing to complete a general fishing log, SaltWire reports.

Justice Peter Browne released his written decision on the matter on Jan. 6, granting Lindsay Crocker a new trial on his conviction on the charge in a provincial court in Corner Brook on December 2018.

Crocker was convicted along with Todd Young and Gauvin and Noel Co. Ltd. for fishing without a proper license and using a vessel without a registration card. They were fined CAD 2,000 ($1,492), and Crocker's skiff was forfeited.

Browne rejected several points of an appeal from the three after a hearing held in November 2022 but said that the trial judge erred in the general fishing log decision against Crocker. The justice ruled that the earlier judge relied on an online dictionary definition of a "tuck seine" when finding that Crocker "purposely and intentionally completed his logbook to cover up the illegal fishing" instead of allowing the parties to make further submissions on the distinction between a tuck seine and purse seine.

The three had argued in their appeal that there was nothing unlawful about their arrangement and that any perceived violation was technical, which Browne seemed to agree with. 

The original incident occurred in November 2016.

title: Nova Scotia harvesters forced to pay CAD 70,000 for smuggling halibut
content:
As halibut landings and prices have improved off the coast of the Canadian province of Nova Scotia, so too have illegal fishing enforcement efforts by Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO), the CBC reports.  

DFO this week made public the convictions and sentencing this fall of four men for a halibut smuggling case that dates back to 2019. Combined fines totaling CAD 70,000 ($51,243) were levied in a Shelburne provincial court.

CBC reports that the case involved a lobster boat trying to flee fishery officials at about 2 a.m. on a morning in May 2019 and was found to be hauling illegally caught halibut. Authorities reportedly seized some CAD 34,000 worth of the flatfish and a truck and trailer used in the crime. 

Among those convicted and sentenced was Johnny Penney, who pleaded guilty to unlawful transport of halibut and obstructing a fishery officer. He was fined CAD 25,000 and may not fish any species except lobster for a period of three years. Dean Goreham pleaded guilty to unlawful transport of halibut and possession of undersized halibut and was also fined CAD 25,000, while Devin Peterson pleaded guilty to unlawful transport of halibut and obstructing a fishery officer and was sentenced to pay CAD 10,000. All three must pay their fines by April 20, 2023.

A fourth man, Dustin Kenney, pleaded guilty to unlawful transportation of halibut and obstructing a fishery officer and was sentenced to pay CAD 10,000 by May 24, 2023, according to the article.

title: Iceland gov’t stalls on demands to close open net pet farming
content:
The Icelandic government has stalled a petition from more than 20 sports fishing and environmental organizations to ban open net-pen salmon farming in the country, reports Fish Farmer Magazine.

The group's ire was originally raised by the escape of 80,000 salmon from a pen owned by the farmer Arnarlax last year. Arnarlax was fined ISK 120 million (£700,000) for the escape in November, but has appealed.

The fine is the largest ever imposed on any Icelandic salmon company following an escape.

However, Iceland's minister of food Svandis Svavarsdottir said she wasn't ready to take a position regarding the group's demand, although she added that it was proving a challenge to create a sustainable aquaculture industry. 

Svavarsdottir also said she would take the group's views into account when creating new aquaculture policy, and that Iceland's National Audit Office is looking into the regulations and legal implications of any adjustments.

The government is also understood to be looking at new ways to raise tax from the sector, following Norway's own 40% resource tax proposal.

title: Trial of Cermaq’s game-changing fish management tech advances
content:
Testing a technology that could revolutionize fish health management is well underway at Norwegian farms owns by Cermaq Group, with fish stocked for the third time in the iFarm net pens.

The iFarm technology uses artificial intelligence and machine learning to identify each fish in a net pen. Monitoring fish individually means only the sick individual -- rather than the whole stock -- would be treated.

The Mitsubishi Corp.-owned salmon producer said the focus in this phase is on machine learning, sensors, data collection, and further development of the mechanism that sorts out fish.

And this time, the iFarm is set up in the net pens at the sea site Hellarvika in Steigen.

"With the first version of iFarm, everything was new, and we had an incredibly steep learning curve, but as we got started with operations, we think it worked out quite well," said site manager Tor Hansen at Hellarvika.

The goal is to make the sorter eventually become autonomous so that together with the sensor system in iFarm, it can make its own decisions based on defined criteria, such as the discovery of lice or wounds, said the company.

title: Camanchaca, Grupo Bio Bio disagree on Pesca Sur pelagic division value
content:
Chilean salmon farmer and fishing company Camanchaca and Grupo Bio Bio will head to arbitration to resolve a disagreement regarding the latter's sale of its 30% stake in Camanchaca's Pesca Sur pelagic division.

Camanchaca currently owns the remaining 70% of the shares, and it is obliged to acquire Grupo Bio Bio's full stake in Pesca Sur if it finally decides to sell. 

On Sept. 15, Grupo Bio Bio informed Camanchaca of its intention to do so.

Following the price-setting procedure established in an agreement signed by both parties back in 2011, on Oct. 18, Grupo Bio Bio and Camanchaca simultaneously disclosed their respective price determination for the shares. 

Grupo Bio Bio valued the division at $27.05 per share, or a total of $93.3m, while Camanchaca offered $13.92 per share or a total of $48m.

Given that the valuations made by each party differ by more than 10%, the sale price of Grupo Bio Bio's 30% stake in Pesca Sur will now be adjudicated by an investment bank or a mutually agreeable expert.

Currently, there is still no defined bank or expert, and Camanchaca and Grupo Bio Bio are analyzing how to implement the price determination mechanism mentioned above.

Pesca Sur is headquartered is in Coronel, Region del Bio Bio. It operates several canning, fishmeal and fish oil production plants, and also has a fleet of purse seiners and several crustacean fishing vessels.

title: Arnarlax fined by Iceland’s MAST for overstocking salmon pens
content:
Icelandic salmon farming company Arnarlax has been fined ISK 120 million ($858,000) by the Icelandic food and veterinary authority (MAST) due to incorrect information about the number of fish stocked in the company's sea pen in Westfjords, reports Stundin.

An investigation by MAST found the company could not account for the fate of at least 81,564 Atlantic salmon, after a visit by the body initially to investigate salmon escapes.

Arnarlax declined to comment to Undercurrent News, noting it is appealing the decision and so the case remains ongoing.

title: China’s online seafood sales still booming, especially fresh, high-end imports
content:
China's seafood e-commerce market has entered a new period of development, with high-end categories such as imported salmon and cod growing rapidly, according to Yang Guang, director of Alibaba's B2C fresh food segment.

Since 2017, China's online trade of aquatic products has boomed, with compound annual growth reaching 23%. In 2020, online retail sales were CNY 34.5 billion ($4.83bn), Yang said at China Seafood Summit on Nov. 16. 

Lack of China trade hammering Australian lobster harvesters this Christmas

Alibaba is the largest e-commerce platform in China -- it owns Taobao and Tmall, which serve the low-end and high-end e-commerce markets respectively.

Sea cucumbers, hairy crabs and shrimp (including frozen and headless) are the most popular seafood products on Taobao and Tmall.

Sales of salmon, cod, and swimming crab are also growing fast. Among them, salmon -- as a high-quality deep-sea protein rich in omega-3 -- has become a more fashionable choice for Chinese consumers. Cod is more popular among children and mothers because of its high nutritional value (in China, cod is a general term for pollock, Pacific cod, Atlantic cod, haddock and other whitefish products).

Yang said that the online seafood market is relatively fragmented, and there is still an opportunity for new players to enter the sector. Companies with strong supply chains operating in categories with barriers to entry tend to perform better in terms of growth, though.

China's first-tier and second-tier cities account for nearly half of online seafood consumption, while more than 60% of buyers are female and 60% are between 30-49 years old.

Some 45% of online consumers have relatively high purchasing power, providing more opportunities for high-quality, high-premium products, Yang said. 

Ecuador shrimp prices continue free fall as farmers threaten protests, strikes

"Among the high-consumption groups, urban mothers, white-collar workers and senior middle-class people are the key groups, as they have higher education and higher income, and have higher requirements for product quality, taste, nutrition and health," said Yang.

Young consumers aged 25-34 tend to buy imported seafood such as salmon and cod online, while middle-aged and elderly people prefer freshwater fish, canned food and other products.

The "freshness" of seafood is the most important factor for online consumers. The more mature the freshness preservation technology, the better the quality and taste of goods traveling via long-distance transportation can be maintained.

In addition to freshness, safety, hygiene, nutrition, and third-party certification have also become factors that high-end consumers pay attention to. Low fat, low sodium, high protein, and zero additives are also becoming important selling points.

Yang highlighted the success of Guolian, one of China's largest seafood companies, selling its products through e-commerce. 

Guolian quits aquaculture amid processing push

"Since Guolian landed on Tmall in 2016, it has started to build a full product supply chain, including the establishment of product selection, warehousing and transportation, and refined operation services, to provide consumers with the best shopping experience," said Yang.

Guolian has also invested heavily in product innovation for the B2C market. It has launched successive best-selling products, which gained market recognition through popular short videos and live broadcasts.

For instance, on June 18, 2022, the day of an e-commerce promotion, Guolian sold more products by volume in just two hours than during the whole corresponding day a year previously, Yang concluded.

title: Millions of tilapia lost in Kenyan cages on Lake Victoria
content:
Kenyan fish farmers on Lake Victoria have suffered enormous losses following the death of their stocks in early November, reports The Observers.

Experts have attributed the losses to "upwelling and pollution". More than 364 million fish are believed to have died, with an estimated value of KES 1.4 billion ($11.4m).

In a bid to cut down on losses, the cage owners are now harvesting the dead fish to sell as dried fish. On Nov. 13, Kenya's Marine Fisheries Research Institute cautioned the fish farmers to check for signs of contamination.

The institute's experts put the mortality event down to upwelling, a natural phenomenon that involves temperature changes and oxygen depletion. Upwelling usually takes about an hour, but fish confined in cages are often deprived of oxygen during the process.

title: High court acquits Danish fishing magnate, clears him of $7.4m fine
content:
A Danish high court has overturned a ruling previously made by the district court that had prosecuted fishing magnate Henning Kjeldsen for appropriating more quotas than was legal, reports DR.

Danish magnate Kjeldsen in hot water again over accounting change

He had been fined DKK 54 million ($7.4m), but the question argued by both courts was whether there was a legal case to punish at all. The high court said not, and swept the case aside, including punishments for several co-accused.

Defense lawyer Olaf Koktvedgaard represented Kjeldsen. "The high court has ruled that there was no authority to punish Henning Kjeldsen, which is what we have said all along," he said. "This is a case of people who got caught up in the system and who should never have been charged."

He is now waiting to see if the prosecution chooses to appeal the verdict. DR said it expects the case to end up with Denmark's supreme court, as tends to be the case when two of the country's courts interpret legal positions in completely opposing fashions.

title: Tuna in the WCPO risks losing MSC without progress on harvest strategies
content:
The Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) has called on member governments of the Western Central Pacific Fisheries Commission (WCPFC) to pass necessary the conservation management measures for tuna stocks at their upcoming session, which will place in Da Nang, Vietnam, from Nov. 27 to Dec. 3.

These measures would safeguard the long-term sustainability of the world's most crucial tuna stocks by committing fishing nations to pre-agreed actions for protecting them should they ever decline below sustainable levels, MSC said. It added that progress in agreeing on harvest strategies is increasingly critical to the ongoing certification of these fisheries.

In a separate release, MSC congratulated the Commission for Conservation of Atlantic Tuna (ICCAT) on reaching a landmark agreement to adopt a harvest strategy for Atlantic bluefin tuna. It also stated that ICCAT's breakthrough for bluefin "should inspire progress in the Western Central Pacific".

MSC pointed out that the lack of progress in delivering work plans for implementing harvest strategies is eroding the rationale for tuna fisheries in the Western Central Pacific Ocean (WCPO) meeting minimum requirements of MSC certification for available harvest control rules (HCRs).

"To ensure ongoing MSC certification, WCPFC delegates must reach an agreement on two key conservation management measures, which would result in the implementation of a harvest strategy for skipjack tuna and demonstrate progress towards delivering harvest strategies for other tuna stocks within the region," it said. 

According to the certification, the conformity assessment bodies responsible for the certification of MSC fisheries in the region will collectively consider the outcomes of the meeting to determine whether they provide the evidence needed to support ongoing certification.

There are 33 MSC-certified tuna fisheries in the WCPO.

"Failure by the WCPFC to implement harvest strategies would jeopardize the long-term health of these stocks and undermine the progress made by WCPO fisheries, which have worked hard to improve their sustainability and meet the MSC's global standard for environmentally responsible and sustainable fishing," said Rupert Howes, the MSC's chief executive.

In addition to continuing to meet minimum requirements, all tuna fisheries in the WCPFC have timebound conditions to implement more robust harvest strategies with well-defined HCRs by June 2023 to remain certified to version 2 of the MSC fisheries standard.

An agreement to adopt harvest strategies for skipjack at the upcoming meeting could close this condition for MSC-certified skipjack fisheries. For certified fisheries targeting other tuna species, convincing progress towards agreeing HCRs could provide the opportunity to remain certified beyond June 2023 by adopting requirements within the new MSC standard. These new requirements allow an additional five years for fisheries to implement state-of-the-art harvest strategies while adopting the other improvements included in the new standard.

Tuna stocks in the WCPO are currently healthy, and the stocks are not overfished.

However, the green status and the MSC certifications may not last without robust management, noted Tom Pickerell, executive director of the Global Tuna Alliance, a network of over 50 seafood companies responsible for 30% of the world's tuna catch.

"The current situation can be likened to having a house without a roof: everything is fine when the sun is shining, but it's bad news once it starts raining. Without harvest strategies, the stocks are at risk. Being in the green now doesn't mean they will necessarily stay that way; long-term management is needed to avoid complacency," Pickerell wrote in an article on the issue published on the World Economic Forum's website.

Pickerell urged the WCPFC to adopt a harvest strategy for skipjack and agree a revised work plan for setting a harvest strategy for South Pacific albacore and setting target reference points for bigeye and yellowfin in 2023.

"To support this, we are calling for the establishment of science-manager dialogue meetings that bring together scientists and delegates outside of the main regional fisheries management organization (RFMO) meetings to discuss the details relating to long-term management," he said.

The use of science-manager dialogue meetings is essential to progressing the small print that makes up the harvest strategies, so it's paramount the WCPFC utilizes them. All other tuna RFMOs already use these forums, Pickerell added.

"If we don't make progress on establishing robust management measures for tuna this year, many MSC-certified tuna fisheries could face difficulty meeting their conditions and may be suspended from the program," he said.

Should all western central Pacific tuna fisheries see their MSC certificates suspended, over 2 million metric tons of tuna would have to be sold without the certification into the supply chain, and brand owners would no longer be able to use the MSC ecolabel on products made from this catch.

The Pew Charitable Trusts pointed out that "the Pacific Ocean remains the last region of the world without any management procedures governing fishing vessels that target an internationally managed stock".

It stressed this could change after next week's WCPFC meeting in Vietnam. It urged the commission's members to "adopt and immediately implement a management procedure for Pacific skipjack tuna, which makes up 35% of the world’s total commercial tuna catches and is a critically important source of food, livelihoods, and government revenue".

title: Bolton to source all tuna from MSC-certified fisheries, ‘comprehensive’ FIPs by 2024
content:
Italian company Bolton Group has committed to sourcing 100% of its tuna from Marine Stewardship Council (MSC)-certified fisheries or "credible and comprehensive" fishing improvement projects by 2024.

Tri Marine pulls bigeye tuna fishery from MSC certification

The group's global sustainable development director, Luciano Pirovano, said that vertical integration is a competitive advantage to achieve its planned sustainability objectives. The group acquired Spanish and Latin American cannery and fishing Grupo Conservas Garavilla in 2018 and completed the acquisition of US-based fishing and processing firm Tri Marine in 2020.

Despite criticisms following the fast growth of the eco-label, Bolton recognizes the MSC as the best available standard for sustainable fisheries. 

"We support MSC as the best eco-labeling for sustainable fisheries, even though it can further improve, particularly including the social aspects of the fisheries. The standard, the only one [for tuna] approved by the GSSI [Global Sustainable Seafood Initiative], is well recognized in all markets, so we aim for that," Pirovano told Undercurrent News. 

Bolton Group owns canned tuna brand Rio Mare, among others. Photo: Rio Mare

"The industry needs a high standard with a comprehensive approach that makes continuous upgrades and improvement efforts. The MSC fisheries standard offers concrete companies concrete goals to work on fisheries," he said.

Major tuna firms back NGO calls for safety-at-sea mechanism

GSSI recognizes a total of five fisheries standards. Those include MSC, Marine Ecolabel Japan, Alaska Responsible Fisheries, Iceland Responsible Fisheries and Audubon GULF.

"These five fisheries standards have shown alignment with the GSSI global benchmark tool framework, which is based on the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations code of conduct for responsible fisheries and the FAO ecolabeling and aquaculture guidelines," GSSI said in a statement sent to Undercurrent. 

According to Pirovano, even though the MSC standard needs to move forward with social issues for workers at sea, it is so far the "most comprehensive tool we have as a company to raise the [sustainability] bar in the market", offering "concrete goals on fisheries".

He pointed out the International Seafood Sustainability Foundation (ISSF), of which Bolton is a member, aims to certify all fisheries with MSC without conditions.

MSC has recently launched a new version of its fisheries standard.

"MSC's effort to continuously evolve is complex and exhausting, but it is critical," Pirovano said. He pointed out MSC had launched its new standard following a well-done stakeholder engagement process.

Bolton backs calls for ICCAT to establish new tuna harvest strategies

According to the MSC's fisheries standard, regional fisheries management organizations must meet harvest control rules and harvest strategies requirements, agreeing on and implementing effective harvest strategies to end overfishing.

In the upcoming Western and Central Pacific Fishery Commission (WCPFC) meeting, which will be held in Vietnam from Nov. 27-Dec. 3, stakeholders will discuss the possibility of introducing new harvest control rules for all tuna species, including yellowfin and bigeye. Tuna fisheries operating under the WCPFC risk having their MSC certification suspended from June 2023 if they disagree on the introduction of well-defined harvest control rules or practical tools to control catches, as required by conditions set by the MSC.

Pirovano explained that the Western and Central Pacific is a strategic area for Bolton, given that a significant portion of its sourcing comes from Indonesia's artisanal fishing areas and the Solomon Islands.

On the upcoming decision to implement harvest strategies in the WCPO, Pirovano pointed out Bolton believed the correct way to go forward was the "more gradual approach that doesn't create a shock". He explained that Bolton's sustainability team had recently hired a compliance officer to work on advocacy to further push in this direction.

Watch: ISSF’s president on the state of sustainable tuna fishing in 2022

He said he was optimistic about the possibility that the WCPFC would find an agreement.

The executive also mentioned the resurgence of the bluefin tuna stocks in the Mediterranean sea, following the introduction of quotas that were hard to agree on, as a successful example in which stakeholders managed to find an agreement to protect tuna stocks.

He also mentioned recent efforts by a group of players, including retailers, to push towards an agreement of involved countries that would enable the North Atlantic mackerel to regain its MSC certification.

Pirovano said Bolton sourced only relatively small quantities from the Indian Ocean, where yellowfin tuna stocks have been overfished for a few years. Total catches are far more than the recommended level to ensure maximum system yield is maintained, despite some large buyers threatening to cut their catches from the region if overfishing did not end. On this point, Pirovano said Bolton believed it was essential to maintain a presence to put pressure on implementing conservation measures.

Bolton confirms deal for US tuna brand Wild Planet

On the difficulties in finding an agreement in the Indian Ocean to reduce yellowfin catches, Pirovano said it was perhaps necessary for involved governments to engage with coastal countries such as Oman, Iran, and Yemen to build pressure in the context of high-level trade negotiations.

Partnership with Tri Marine as a competitive advantage

Pirovano stressed Bolton's vertical integration is helping Bolton to progress faster in its sustainability improvements.

He pointed out that vertical integration with Tri Marine was a natural move after 25 years of partnership. "The partnership with the Tri Marine has been one of Bolton's reasons for success since the latter focused on the supply chain and Bolton on promoting its brands," Pirovano said.

Spanish ‘responsibly fished’ tuna label cleared for US, Italian markets

He noted that the acquisition of Tri Marine allowed Bolton to access raw materials with desired quality and sustainability.

Tri Marine just received a green light for the bigeye scope extension for the MSC certification of its Solomon Islands longline fishery, which now covers albacore, yellowfin and bigeye. The fishing firm, however, voluntarily withdrew the Solomon Islands bigeye tuna purse seine and pole and line fishery from the MSC assessment.

The MSC certifications for Tri Marine's Solomon Islands' skipjack and yellowfin tuna purse seine and pole and line and longline albacore and yellowfin fisheries remain unaffected.

title: Tri Marine pulls bigeye tuna fishery from MSC certification
content:
Tri Marine International has withdrawn the Solomon Islands bigeye tuna purse seine and pole and line fishery from Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) assessment.

The company had previously applied for a scope extension of its MSC certification to include bigeye tuna, which was not previously covered under the certification. 

Ruling holds up expansion of PNA’s MSC tuna certification to extra 300,000t

The MSC certifications for Tri Marine's Solomon Islands' skipjack and yellowfin tuna purse seine and pole and line and longline albacore and yellowfin fisheries remain unaffected.

According to an announcement from certification body SCS Global Services, the withdrawal is effective as of Nov. 4, 2022. 

Tri Marine cited the cost of certifying what is a small component of our broader skipjack and yellowfin fishery as the reason for the withdrawal. 

"Bigeye represents a minimal percentage of total tuna catch from our Solomon Islands purse seine and pole-and-line fishery, the majority of which is sold locally," Juan Corrales, CEO of Tri Marine, told Undercurrent. 

"Given the significant cost and effort involved in MSC independent adjudication, a decision was made to voluntarily withdraw bigeye from the MSC scope extension," he said. 

Tri Marine's decision to withdraw from the MSC certification process for bigeye in the Solomon Islands was voluntary. 

However, the Coalition for Transparent Tuna Fisheries (CTTF), an NGO which contests the MSC certification of industrial tuna fisheries, claimed the move as a victory.  

"The good news is that by default, we just won another objection. The ripple effect from our successful PNA [Parties to the Nauru Agreement] objection last month has evidently played a part in Tri Marine's decision to withdraw their bigeye tuna scope extension," CTTF's Alex Hofford wrote to Undercurrent. 

"Everyone knows that drifting fish aggregating devices (FADs) are a complete disaster for marine ecosystems, and so Tri Marine's climb down on their bid for an MSC scope extension for bigeye in the Solomon Islands can only be interpreted as good news for Pacific ocean biodiversity," Hofford added. 

PNG to review its rebate, vessel day schemes to offset rising energy costs

Tri Marine further clarified that its fishery is predominately an anchored FAD fishery, not a drifting FAD fishery. It also noted there were no objections to the bigeye scope extension for its Solomon Islands longline fishery, which now covers albacore, yellowfin and bigeye. "This scope extension was undertaken simultaneously with our SI PS/PL scope extension," it said in a statement sent to Undercurrent.

On Sept. 30, 2022, MSC received a notice of objection from CTTF to the final draft report and determination of certification body SCS in respect of the scope extension to include bigeye in the Solomon Islands' tuna purse seine and pole and line fishery.

In an MSC document notifying the independent adjudication on Solomon Island's certification scope extension dated Oct. 12, independent adjudicator John McKendrick pointed out there were only a few months ahead of the "June 2023 deadline for a harvest strategy and harvest control rules to be implemented".

Tuna fisheries operating under the Western and Central Pacific Fishery Commission risk having their MSC certification suspended from June 2023 if they do not agree on the introduction of well-defined harvest control rules or effective tools to control catches, as required by conditions set by the MSC.

Major tuna firms back NGO calls for safety-at-sea mechanism

Italian tuna giant Bolton Group acquired Tri Marine in 2019. The fishing group has a Solomon Islands factory, which supplies Bolton's facilities in northern Italy.

Bolton's global sustainable development director, Luciano Pirovano, commented that bigeye tuna "is not a relevant species [for the group's tuna supply], weighing [about] 4% on our total tuna supplies". 

A decision to uphold an objection to the scope extension of the PNA's tuna fishery's MSC certification last month has set back the PNA's proposed application to an additional 300,000 metric tons of catch.

title: Thai Union sets another sales record in Q3 as bullish 2022 continues
content:
Thai Union Group has posted another set of record quarterly results for Q3 2022, just three months after breaking its previous sales record in Q2, continuing what has been a very successful year for the seafood conglomerate.

Thai Union sees ‘exceptional’ quarter for pet care, value-added

Quarterly sales came to THB 41 billion ($1.09bn), surpassing the THB 40bn mark for the first time in the company's history. It marks a 14.6% year-on-year increase in revenue, while sales volumes increased by 8.1%.

Sales growth was predominantly driven by a 55.9% y-o-y improvement from the pet food and value-added division, which has been the group's standout performer this year.

"The PetCare and value-added business grew exceptionally, thanks to continued strong demand in PetCare business, low baseline comparison after last year's temporary factory closure during the pandemic, higher selling prices, higher volumes to support customer's marketing activities, and favorable FX [currency exchange]," Thai Union said.

Elsewhere, the ambient seafood segment -- covering canned and pouched tuna, sardines, mackerel and salmon -- also recorded a 13.6% growth in turnover, achieving all-time high Q3 sales of THB 17.0bn, supported by high prices and strong demand for canned seafood from Asia and the US. 

"Sales increased in both branded and private label, despite concern of recession," the group commented.

Lastly, Thai Union's frozen and chilled seafood divisions "remained stable", the company added, despite exceptional US performance in the corresponding period of 2021. In Q3, this "normalization" was offset by market recovery in Europe and Asia, the group claimed.

What this means is that quarterly gross profit came to a record high of THB 7.4bn -- up 15.8% y-o-y -- while net profit amounted to THB 2.5bn. This marked a 30% y-o-y improvement, driven by a growth in sales volumes and favorable currency rate changes, even as it was partially offset by a higher share of loss-making US foodservice subsidiary Red Lobster.

After the first nine months of 2022, Thai Union's sales by region are generally similar to 2021, with 43% stemming from the US, 26.1% from Europe -- down two percentage points -- 5.8% from Japan, 10.5% from Thailand and 14.6% from regions defined as 'other'.

title: Untitled
content:
The price crisis hitting India's shrimp farming sector in the second half of 2022 has only deepened in recent weeks, despite local government efforts to cut feed rates and set minimum prices, Undercurrent News sources said.

India’s main farming state steps in to reduce feed costs, raise shrimp price

On Oct. 14, a new committee formed by the main farming state of Andhra Pradesh announced it would reduce the cost of feed inputs by INR 2.60-INR 2.80/kg ($0.03/kg), while also setting a minimum price of INR 240 ($2.90)/kg for 100-count shrimp in order to mitigate the ongoing slump in the market.

However, there has been little discernible success from the committee's efforts so far, with the latest prices provided by data suppliers Aquaconnect and Aqua Exchange showing rates across most sizes to be well below the norm for the time of year (see below).

"The meeting really wants to stem the fall in prices," Sheraz Anwar, CEO of major seafood packer Abad Fisheries, told Undercurrent. "But if the market does not accept higher prices, then naturally no intervention can help."

Indian shrimp farmers this year have been struggling with sharply increased production costs due to the rising price of inputs such as feed and fuel.

Now, with many working at a loss, Durai Murugan, owner of vannamei producer Sea Gem Aqua Farm claimed on LinkedIn that "no one will touch vannamei culture in the short term if there will not be a reversal in prices".

"Government efforts to stabilize prices gone in vain. Prices [have] dramatically fallen," he told Undercurrent. "Current price scenario, farmers will opt not to stock coming months ahead."

Given that export volumes are roughly on par with 2021, and the rupee has depreciated in value, it "remains a mystery" why prices have fallen so much, Murugan added.

Anwar explained that, from the exporter's perspective, many of the issues affecting the sector are the same as has been the case all year, just more acute.

"The main issue is low demand all over the world in major markets," he told Undercurrent. "[The] US has so little demand with high-cost inventory, any new orders for small quantities are being well serviced from Ecuador with shorter delivery periods."

"China has also slowed down tremendously with other issues such as factories not able to apply for renewals, [and] Europe is also slow, with 50% inspections for imports from India still in place for over five years, even with much lower rejection rates."

Likewise, there is little relief for farmers moving to black tiger shrimp, where a similar price slump has occurred over the past couple of months.

Manoj Sharma, owner of Gujarat-based farmer Mayank Aquaculture and a strong proponent of black tiger culture, noted sadly that farmgate prices for the species have fallen by 35% recently.

Murugan agreed that black tiger does not currently represent a viable alternative for farmers. 

"Black tiger current prices are way lower than vannamei, so they won’t be doing black tiger at all," he said. "Some farmers produced in [a] recent crop, many failed to sell; there is zero demand from exporters, especially for black tiger."

Anwar also noted that the current market price for large black tiger shrimp in India is roughly INR 100-120/kg lower than it was at its peak earlier this year.

Low October

The latest farmgate prices from Aquaconnect for vannamei in week 44 (Oct. 31-Nov. 6) still make grim reading for farmers, despite a small uptick across medium and small-sizes.

Large, 30-count shrimp are still at INR 430/kg, with 40-count at INR 380, 60-count at 310, 80-count at INR 270 and the smallest 100-count at the government-defined minimum of INR 240 -- itself still lower than the current cost of shrimp production.

Vannamei shrimp ex-farm Andhra Pradesh, HOSO, Aquaconnect, 30pcs/kg

The current slump is even more pronounced for prices in US dollars, which have slipped further over the last month as the rupee has depreciated:

Week 44's price of INR 430/kg for the large 30-count shrimp is lower than the same week of any year since 2017, and effectively INR 110/kg below week 44 of 2021.

For medium 60-count shrimp, week 44's improvement to INR 310/kg means the gulf with 2021's value is not quite as vast, but it remains lower than usual for this time of year:

Finally, the new baseline of INR 240/kg for 100-count is roughly standard for October, but still well below the highs of INR 280/kg that small shrimp were fetching this summer, when demand from China was at its greatest:

Fellow Indian data provider AquaExchange shared prices very similar to those of Aquaconnect's for week 44, albeit INR 10/kg lower for 40, 60, and 80-count product:

Murugan also shared the latest minimum prices set by the Seafood Exporters Association of India in the smaller farming state of Odisha, effective from Nov. 2, as evidence of the rock-bottom state of the market.

The current going rate for larger 30-count shrimp in Odisha is INR 370 ($4.50)/kg, while mid-sized 60-count are just INR 250/kg and 100-count a deeply loss-making INR 180/kg.

Farmgate prices for vannamei out of the secondary farming state of Gujarat are also at an impossibly low level for farmers to turn a profit, having fallen since the summer.

Aquaconnect's data for the state puts 30-count shrimp at INR 410/kg, 40-count at INR 350/kg, 60-count at INR 280/kg, 80-count at 240/kg and 100-count at just INR 210/kg in week 44:

title: Untitled
content:
The overall Russian pollock total allowable catch (TAC) for 2023 will be down marginally this year, with a further increase in the western Bering Sea not entirely offsetting continued drops in the Sea of Okhotsk (SOO).

FREE READ Recap Groundfish Forum 2022 coverage 

In total, the TAC for 2023 is 2.06 million metric tons, compared to 2.08m for this year.

The original TAC for 2022 was 1.93m metric tons before a mid-year adjustment in the west Bering Sea from 409,700t up to 559,000t, Alexey Buglak, president of the Russian Pollock Catchers Association, told Undercurrent News.

Russian's west Bering Sea TAC "was revised and increased due to new scientific data through the year", Buglak told Undercurrent.

Russia's pollock quota development. Credit: Pollock Catchers Association

The bulk of the west Bering Sea is now Marine Stewardship Council (MSC)-certified. As previously reported by Undercurrent, Russia will likely surpass the US fishery in terms of MSC pollock volume in 2023.

In the SOO, which has long been MSC approved, the TAC for 2023 is 1.01m metric tons, down 7% year-on-year. 

During the recent Groundfish Forum in the US Pacific Northwest city of Seattle, Washington, the talk was of a likely hike in the US pollock TAC for 2023. The forum's supply forecast is for a US catch of 1.32m, up from 1.25m in 2020.

Credit: Groundfish Forum

The forum's forecast for Russia, which came out before the TAC was announced, was for a drop to 1.77m, from 1.83m.

As for prices, Russian headed and gutted (H&G) pollock for delivery to China is firming, as the chart below from the Undercurrent prices page shows. Although Russia has been producing much higher volumes of pin-bone out (PBO) fillets in 2022, production of H&G is bouncing back in recent weeks, sources told Undercurrent.

VIEW GRAPH

Russian PBO prices are languishing some $500/t below the US level due to the market turmoil rippling out from the invasion of Ukraine, sources at the forum claimed.

Other approved TACs for 2023

Along with pollock, the Russian agriculture ministry released confined several other TACs. 

The new regulation set the TAC for the 2023 Kamchatka crab season in the Barents Sea at 12,690t, which is unchanged this year. In the west Kamchatka subzones, the TAC for Kamchatka crab is set at 13,608t or up from 11,883t this year.

The TAC for Baltic herring was set at 24,200t or down from 27,200t in 2022. The TAC for Baltic sprat was set at 45,100t or up from 44,200t in 2022.

In the Far East, the TAC for Pacific herring is set at 290,000t, or down from 310,000t this year, for the Northern Sea of Okhotsk subzone. For the Karaginsky subzone, the Pacific herring TAC is set at 36,900t, or down from 39,500t. In the west Kamchatka subzone, the 2023 TAC is 32,300t, or down from 43,000t. 

The Pacific cod TAC for the west Bering Sea zone is set at 84,500t, or down from 90,000t in 2022. For the Karaginsky subzone, the Pacific cod TAC is at 18,100t, or down from 19,100t, and at 14,900t in the Petropavlovsk-Komandorsk subzone, up from 13,400t this year.

title: Ruling holds up expansion of PNA’s MSC tuna certification to extra 300,000t
content:
A decision to uphold an objection to the scope extension of the Parties to the Nauru Agreement (PNA)'s tuna fishery's Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certification will set back the PNA's proposed application to an additional 300,000 metric tons of catch. 

The recent decision by the independent adjudicator might have a further knock-on effect on the PNA and other certified tuna fisheries operating in the Pacific Ocean if the Western and Central Pacific Fishery Commission (WCPFC) does not agree on new harvest control rules at its upcoming meeting.

PNA, which was the first tuna fishery in the Western and Central Pacific Ocean to obtain  MSC certification in 2011, had applied to extend the scope of its certification to include bigeye tuna and catching on fish aggregating devices (FADs). The proposed extension would allow PNA to get the MSC certification for an additional 300,000t of tuna, according to PNA.

Earlier this month, adjudicator John McKendrick ruled the PNA's fishery should not be MSC-certified for two points, bigeye, and FADs. The objection had been lodged through the MSC's own objection process.

"At this stage, the decision won't affect the supply of MSC tuna from PNA waters to consumers who value the high standards of PNA tuna management," PNA said in a reaction sent to Undercurrent News on Oct. 24.

"Those consumers will still have access to over 600,000t of high-quality sustainably caught skipjack and yellowfin catch that can be provided from PNA MSC-certified free school fishery," they said.

PNA pointed out the decision will "mean a delay in expanding that supply to cover catches from FAD-associated schools and bigeye while the necessary adjustments are made by the WCPFC and PNA to address the issues raised by the decision".

PNA also said it supports the view of the MSC that the "outcome demonstrates the checks and balances in place to ensure the rigor of MSC certification within the dynamic and complex context of fisheries management".

The certification expansion would "have large implications on many families, businesses, and communities engaged in supplying MSC-certified sustainably harvested tunas, and it is important that the process is seen to be scrupulously fair," PNA added.

Next steps

In the upcoming meeting of the WCPFC, which will be held in Vietnam on Nov. 27-Dec. 3, stakeholders will discuss the possibility of introducing new harvest control rules for all tuna species, including yellowfin and big-eye.

"An agreement on harvest control rules for skipjack at the December meeting of the WCPFC would strengthen the evidence presented by CABs [conformity assessment bodies] that tuna fisheries in the region meet the MSC’s minimum requirements for available HCRs," an MSC spokesperson told Undercurrent.

Tuna fisheries operating under the WCPFC risk having their MSC certification suspended from June 2023 if they do not agree on the introduction of well-defined harvest control rules or effective tools to control catches, as required by conditions set by the MSC.

Representatives of 38 tuna fisheries gathered on the side of the Infofish 2022 tuna conference in Bangkok, Thailand, earlier this month to discuss those measures, but Undercurrent understands that consensus was still far away from the needed 50%.

Adopting the new version of the new MSC fisheries standard would allow fisheries more time to implement new harvest control rules.

MSC introduces stricter requirements for certified tuna fisheries

Since PNA obtained its certification, over 30 other fisheries operating under the WCPFC have obtained the MSC blue label. Several of those fisheries have applied or are in the process of applying, like Micronesia, for the expansion of their certification to the PNA waters. However, those fisheries are not managed by the PNA but by individual companies or countries.

So far, these certifications and their scope extension haven't been impacted by the independent adjudicator's ruling. However, the recent independent adjudicator's ruling could have a ripple effect on other of some of these certifications.

In the case that no new measures are agreed upon at the upcoming WCPFC meeting, the CABs could, for example, announce new audits of those certifications, according to industry sources.

The issues raised by the independent adjudicator in relation to the FAD-associated catches reflect the importance of strong evidence to support MSC certification, according to the MSC spokesperson.

"The independent adjudicator’s decision relates to the evidence presented in the assessment of the FAD-associated component of the PNA fishery to the MSC’s requirements on habitat management. For example, the evidence presented during the objection process post-dated the original assessment and could, therefore, not be used to justify the original scoring," the MSC spokesperson wrote to Undercurrent. 

MSC also confirmed that this has no bearing on the MSC certification of other FAD-associated fisheries in the region.

Independent adjudicator's ruling

The adjudicator's decision comes after a long dispute process, following criticism of the approval of the scope extension to PNA's FAD catches.

The Coalition for Transparent Tuna Fisheries (CTTF) submitted a total of 15 points of objection before an MSC adjudication hearing was held in Dubai, the United Arab Emirates, in April 2022. There, the representative for the CTTF met with fishery managers from the PNA and their CAB, Lloyds Register. 

The objection was upheld due to a lack of bigeye tuna harvest strategies set by the WCPFC. The WCPFC represents the interests of 26 member states, mostly in or around the Pacific region.

"I am simply applying the [MSC] standard, and on the fact, the CAB have not been able to show the management body has committed to introducing harvest control rules before bigeye tuna stocks decline below BMSY [biomass at maximum sustainable yield]," McKendrick said.

According to the MSC objections process, even if only one point is upheld, the fishery under assessment cannot be certified as sustainable.

In light of its objection being upheld, CTTF called on the MSC to "immediately halt any new drifting FAD fisheries being proposed for MSC certification to save its own reputation as a responsible certification body with integrity".
