title: Swedish PE Altor buys Bain’s stake in Chilean salmon farmer Nova Austral
content:
Altor Equity Partners, a private equity firm based in Sweden, has bought out Bain Capital's stake in Chilean salmon farmer Nova Austral.

On Oct. 17, Altor announced the closing of the acquisition of US-based Bain's stake in Nova Austral, a mid-sized farmer that has faced financial and regulatory troubles for years. 

Nova Austral suffers terrible Q2 with sales, earnings plummeting

The two PE firms took control of Nova Austral in 2014, buying the salmon farmer from bankruptcy protection with EWOS Group, the aquafeed supplier Altor and Bain owned at the time. Nova Austral, which went into bankruptcy as part of the Pescanova debacle, was retained by the two PEs after Ewos was sold to Cargill in 2015. 

Nova Austral has been having a tough time of it recently. In September, the company reported a disastrous second quarter, with revenues plummeting, proof that the lingering effect of 2021 mortalities and regulatory action against it are still being felt.

The Puerto Montt-based company said in an earnings release that its Q2 2022 revenues amounted to $16.7 million, half of the $28.6m seen a year earlier. Furthermore, its pre-value adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) came to a negative $11.3m in Q2 2022, twice the negative $6.1m EBITDA seen in Q2 2021.

A series of infectious salmon anemia outbreaks in December 2020 cost the company 4.8m smolt and $3.8m and led to the lack of a Q2 2021 harvest. 

Then, during Q4 2021, the company disclosed "a new mortality incident at the hatchery" of one of its farming sites that killed about 1.4m smolts.

Nova Austral argues license revocations, fines could sink it

"The reason for this mortality was contamination with H2S [hydrogen sulfide] generated by the wrong functioning of biofilters," the company said.

Additionally, the company also faced $1.23m in regulator fines in September 2021 over four charges relating to the company's past participation in a 2019 mortality misreporting scandal.

Furthermore, in July, Chile's federal environmental agency, known by its Spanish abbreviation SMA, revoked licenses for three of Nova Austral's salmon farming sites in the Magallanes region and fined the company nearly a million dollars over charges that it exceeded its production authority and damaged the seabed at one of the locations.

The fines and revocations are under appeal. And a lawyer representing the company said previously that it could be forced to shut down if the penalties stand.

title: Barramundi Group’s CEO resigns
content:
Andreas Von Scholten has resigned as CEO of Singapore-based Barramundi Group after three years in the role.

FREE READ Watch: Barramundi Group CEO talks Oslo listing, future plans

Von Scholten, who joined the company in November 2019, has joined the company's board and will transition to a new role as a company director effective Jan. 1, 2023.

He will be replaced by James Kwan, who has been part of the group as a member of the executive team since December 2019, first in a role as chief marketing officer, and from June 2022, also overseeing the farming and processing operations in Singapore.

"It has been a privilege to serve as CEO of Barramundi Group since November
2019, and I look very much forward to continuing working with James and the
company in my new role as director," Von Scholten said. "The company has been through a major transformation in recent years and is now progressing well on the strategy leading to profitability."

Earlier in 2022, Kwan took on a concurrent role as general manager in Singapore, with responsibilities spanning broodstock, grow-out, processing and commercial operations. 

"I thank the board for the trust placed in me to lead the company at a juncture where it is continuing to execute strategic and tactical operational changes that will lead us towards profitability," said Kwan. "On the commercial front, we need to re-assert our brands, innovate and excite the market once again with creative offerings that have defined our earlier successes."

The group boasts a commercial reach across key markets including Singapore, Australia, China, Hong Kong, South Korea, and the US.

title: MSC introduces stricter requirements for certified tuna fisheries
content:
The Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) launched new data showing steady growth in tuna catch and products certified to its standards for sustainable fishing. 

Currently, MSC-certified tuna catches exceed two million metric tons, making up close to half (47%) of the global wild commercial tuna harvest, according to the data included in an update to the MSC's 'Sustainable Tuna Handbook'. 

As a result, the number of brands selling tuna with the MSC label now exceeds 430, up from 126 in 2015, said the MSC. "However, challenges remain in ensuring the long-term sustainability of tuna fisheries." 

Improvements of particular relevance to tuna fisheries include stronger requirements on fish aggregating devices (or FADs), shark finning, endangered, threatened and protected species and effective monitoring, control and surveillance.

The revised standard, to be launched in late October, also sets new requirements for harvest strategies for fisheries managed by Regional Fisheries Management Organisations (RFMOs), including purse seine and long-line tuna fisheries.

"The new MSC Fisheries Standard will ensure that certified fisheries remain world leaders in sustainable fishing. Certified tuna fisheries will now be required to deliver a set of defined milestones aimed at securing agreement between multiple national governments to implement state-of-the-art harvest strategies derived through open and fair negotiations," said Rohan Currey, MSC's chief science and standards officer.

"These requirements represent a significant increase in expectations of fisheries managed by RFMOs and will create a unified and powerful push towards ensuring vital protections are agreed that ensure sustainable management of tuna stocks in perpetuity," he concluded.

For more on this, see Undercurrent News' live reporting from the Infofish World Tuna 2022 conference and exhibition, held in Bangkok, Thailand from Oct. 11-13.

title: Louisiana mulls rule change after latest Omega Protein fish spill
content:
The US state of Louisiana is cracking down on menhaden harvester and processor Omega Protein after a net spill released some 900,000 mostly-dead fish near a popular beach known as the Cajun Riviera.

The Louisiana Wildlife and Fisheries Commission (LWFC) voted during its Oct. 6 meeting to tentatively approve a new state regulation that would press civil fines on harvesters who dump large numbers of fish, fail to report to fisheries police such spills within two hours or leave gear in the water for more than 48 hours. 

Commissioners said they were responding directly to an incident where an Omega Protein vessel apparently gathered too many fish and was forced to cut its 1,500-foot net off the southwestern shore at Holly Beach on Sept. 8. Commission member Brandon DeCuir rejected Omega spokesperson Ben Landry's statement during the meeting that the company took full responsibility for the accidental spill.

"There's a historical track record for you guys in this industry," DeCuir told Landry during the meeting. "What I tend to find in a certain industry, in certain aspects, is that if the fine is only 'X', but your ability to make money is three or four times 'X', you're willing to absorb that fine as part of your [industry] and you'll just keep doing the same behavior over and over."

Landry disputed that characterization.

"I think you have the wrong idea about us. I mean, we're not criminals," Landry responded. "We're not bandits out on the water. We're responsible commercial fishermen."

Many mishaps through the years

As Undercurrent News has reported, this was not the first time the Cooke-owned menhaden harvester has come under fire for accidental spills or other environmental contaminations. The company spilled more than 400,000 dead fish off Virginia in two incidents last year.  

The Reedville, Virginia-based division of Cooke also admitted in September 2019 to violating a federal harvesting cap set by the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission in Virginia.

Additionally, Omega pleaded guilty to criminal charges that it improperly discharged wastewater near its Abbeville, Louisiana plant in 2016  and agreed to pay $1.2 million in fines and serve three years on probation. 

According to a separate plea agreement the company signed in 2013, from 2008 to 2010 two Omega vessels regularly collected "bail water" from its Reedville plant and other vessels and discharged it too close to shore instead of going further out to sea as is required.

The bail water, fresh water used to pump fresh fish from the vessels to the plant, contained fish waste such as fins, scales and excrement as well as pollutants produced in processing.

The Louisiana spill last month was the third in recent months for Omega. A commercial menhaden fishing vessel owned by Ocean Harvesters, which supplies Omega Protein, inadvertently killed "many" red drum when a spotter plane directed the crew onto a school of menhaden that likely had another school of red drum beneath it off the coast of Virginia on July 25. The vessel's captain noticed the netted red drum and immediately ordered their release, Omega Protein said at the time.

A fishing vessel employed by the company had what might have been a sizeable fish kill when a net entangled and tore about a mile off Silver Beach, Virginia on July 5. Virginia Marine Police told Undercurrent that their investigation determined both spills were accidental. 

What the new regulation would do

As part of their vote, the Louisiana commissioners approved a notice of intent that allows comment on the proposed law until Jan. 5. The commission is expected to approve the new regulation from 90 days to a year after that date, according to the commission's meeting notice. 

When reached by Undercurrent, Landry said in an email that the company welcomed Louisiana's new restrictions.

"This [notice of intent] in many ways reflects the current policies and procedures that the menhaden industry has been following for decades, and also continue today," Landry said. "We look forward to working cooperatively with the LDWF [Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries] in years to come to minimize unfortunate incidents like our net tear in early September."

According to the meeting notice, the proposed rule would:

Prohibit abandoning menhaden purse seine gear and establish a 48-hour window to remove all gear before it is considered abandoned;
Establish the use of marking tools that are released when gear gets cut away or lost to facilitate the gears' retrieval and warn of the navigational hazards the gear represent;
Require purse seiners to make "all reasonable attempts" to retrieve menhaden and bycatch in a net release and to notify LDFW within two hours of any release, and;
Define releases as "a waste of a fishery resource subject to civil fine and restitution and abandonment of gear shall constitute a commercial littering violation".

The amount of the fine is not specified in the documentation, but Joseph Orgeron, a Louisiana state representative, said it would be $0.11 per pound.

Might revive a fight

The accident might revive a simmering conflict between recreational harvesters and commercial fishermen of menhaden, said Orgeron. Earlier this year he led the unsuccessful attempt earlier this year to set the state's first annual manhaden catch limit, 260,000 metric tons. Louisiana is the last state in the Gulf of Mexico that doesn't cap its menhaden hauls. 

Omega was lucky to not be fined over the September incident, Orgeron said.

"We didn't realize that we didn't have it [a fine] anywhere in our regulations," Orgeron told Undercurrent. "Because this happened while there was no regulation, I don't believe it could be retroactively enforced."

As Undercurrent has written, menhaden, also known as "pogies", are heavily sought for their omega-3 fatty acid content, which is useful in fishmeal and dietary supplements. They're also used in feeds for poultry and pigs and are a popular source of bait for commercial lobster, crab and crawfish harvesters. 

Nationwide, Louisiana does far and away the most business in menhaden harvesting in the US, according to the latest NOAA data. From 2017 to 2021, it led the nation in menhaden harvests, averaging 318,773t annually worth an average of $67.68 million. Mississippi and Virginia have typically vied for 2nd place after Louisiana, harvesting not much more than a third of the amount that the Cajun state collected.

Over that time period, its highest catch was 2018's 387,923t worth $90.31m, with 2021's 267,334t worth $60.40m on the other end of the scale. By way of comparison, Virginia's greatest harvest in those years came in 2019, when it harvested 150,826t worth $90.32m. That was also Mississippi's best year -- 150,763t worth $41.99m -- over the five years, as Undercurrent has written.

OP, the largest harvester of menhaden in Louisiana, was sloppy in its handling of the accident, Orgeron said. The company immediately notified an LDWF biologist of the accident, but didn't tell the department that the net remained on the water, or describe the incident very thoroughly, for several days, he said.

The accident will probably make it easier for Orgeron to renew his push to set a catch limit, he said. He complimented LDWF for pushing the NOI so quickly.

"I just wish that they would be more helpful in providing a little bit more guard rails to the industry as a whole on them fishing so close to shore," Orgeron said.

title: Salmon is seafood’s biggest winner in FDA’s new ‘healthy’ labeling proposal
content:
It's not hard to spot the seafood industry's biggest winner in relation to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) proposed change to the definition of "healthy" on food packages. It's salmon, including both wild-caught and farm-raised.

Though seafood is mentioned 54 times in the more than 80-page proposal published on Sept. 29 in the Federal Register, salmon is the only seafood species called out separately. It's identified six times, mostly as an example of a food item that would be newly qualified for use of the positive marketing term should FDA go ahead with its rule change.

That's in part due to salmon being rich in beneficial omega-3 fatty acids and protein while being low in saturated fat and cholesterol, reports the New York Times. Under the current definition, salmon isn’t considered to qualify because it's high in fat, even though it's the good kind of fat, the article goes on to explain.

As for other seafood, the FDA labeling change may seem pretty ho-hum but it's still a very positive development, Brandon Phillips, senior director of communications and advocacy at the National Fisheries Institute (NFI), told Undercurrent News in a recent email exchange. The majority of seafood, he said, already is eligible to carry the "healthy" moniker under the current definition. 

The proposed change "will open the door for even more species because the focus will shift from restricting certain nutrients to encouraging whole, healthy foods", he added.

Sockeye salmon fillets. Photograph by Miro Vrlik Photography on Shutterstock.

"Public health experts already regard seafood, in general, as the healthiest animal protein on the planet," Phillips said. "There’s essentially no debate about that. In fact, the Dietary Guidelines for Americans have long recommended Americans eat two to three servings of nutritious, wholesome seafood every week. Efforts that support this recommendation in a meaningful way should have an impact on encouraging people to eat seafood." 

The US government has determined that as many as 94% of children and 80% of adults are not eating the recommended amounts of seafood, he noted.

"Increasing consumption of seafood should be a public health priority, regardless of category or species," he said. "The proposed change to what can be labeled 'healthy' is focused on specific food categories that the Dietary Guidelines have targeted as foods to encourage. Any successful plan to highlight and promote 'healthy' food should have an effect on seafood consumption in order to be called a success." 

Phillips assured that NFI's nutrition, scientific and regulatory staff would make the FDA's Dec. 28 deadline for submitting a comment letter.

At press time the FDA had received just 29 comment letters, but none yet from the seafood industry. The National Association of Egg Farmers has written in support of the proposal, saying shell eggs have been established as healthy and the changes are "in keeping with FDA's nutrition-related strategic goals". 

'Any kind of Frankenstein food'

FDA's proposed change is a long time in coming.

The current definition of "healthy", established in 1994, allows food manufacturers to voluntarily use the term on packages only if the products inside possess limited amounts of total fat, saturated fat, cholesterol and sodium and provide at least 10% of the daily value of one or more of the following nutrients: vitamin A, vitamin C, calcium, iron, protein or dietary fiber.

As recounted by Auburn University history professor Xaq Frohlich in an article published recently on his college website, the FDA began to reconsider its policy in 2015 after it called out the Kind Snacks food company for using "healthy" on snack bars that had a fat content above the FDA’s threshold. The fat came from nuts, which is, today, generally seen to be a healthy source.

FDA quickly backed down from its complaint against Kind, which was backed by the likes of the Center for Science in the Public Interest (CSPI) and other consumer advocacy groups that rallied to the snack company's cause.

"Critics pointed out the perverse logic of the current rule, which allows sugary ready-to-eat breakfast cereals and fat-free puddings to use 'healthy' on their labels but doesn’t permit its use on healthy basics such as nuts, avocados or salmon, all of which are high in good fats," Frohlich recounted. "Nor could 'healthy' be used for cooking oils such as olive oil, which didn’t meet the definition’s threshold of providing certain vitamins."

Kind praised the FDA for its recent proposal in a Sept. 29 posting on its website.

"We applaud the FDA in taking the long-needed step to update the definition of "healthy" so that it reflects current nutrition science and the Dietary Guidelines for Americans. We are incredibly proud that Kind helped catalyze this progress," said Daniel Lubetzky, the company's founder and chief impact officer.

Image from a 2016 Snack Food & Wholesale Bakery article.

In 2016, FDA updated its guidelines to allow for some foods to contain more total fat and to include some that provide at least 10% of the daily value of vitamin D or potassium. However, there is still no limit on added sugars, an omission the agency now believes is inconsistent with today’s nutrition science.

The recently proposed rule, by contrast, would limit added sugars to no more than 2.5 grams per serving, although this could vary depending on the food. It also would restrict the amount of sodium to no more than 230 milligrams per serving and provide limits for saturated fat, which similarly could vary.

A six-ounce serving of yogurt, for example, would not qualify as "healthy" if it contained more than 2.5g, or 5% of the daily value, of added sugars, and a frozen dinner of salmon, green beans and brown rice would not qualify as "healthy" if it contained more than 4.0g of saturated fat. 

"This plan is strong enough to exclude huge swaths of supermarket products from self-identifying as 'healthy'," said Marion Nestle, a professor of nutrition, food studies and public health at New York University and one of the most famous nutritionists in the US, in her newsletter Food Politics. 

"Products bearing the 'healthy' symbol will have to contain real food and be low in saturated fat, salt, and sugar, as called for by federal dietary guidelines," she said. "The new rules won’t stop 'healthy' products from being loaded with additives and artificial sweeteners. And the FDA won’t require warning labels for unhealthy products, which work better than other symbols. But these proposals are a marked improvement over the current situation."

Dariush Mozaffarian, a cardiologist and professor of nutrition at the Tufts Friedman School of Nutrition Science and Policy, in Boston, Massachusetts, also sees big strides being taken.

"The old rule was really outdated -- you could create any kind of Frankenstein food that met the nutrient criteria and label it as healthy," he is quoted by the New York Times as saying. "This is a major advance."

The White House in Washington DC, US. Credit: THONGCHAI.S/Shutterstock.com

Overcoming 'entrenched interests'

This is not the first time FDA has struggled to define a term. In 1992, the FDA went after Florida orange juice makers for their use of the term "fresh" on frozen concentrated orange juice, Frohlich pointed out. In 2016, it also proposed rules to define "natural", an initiative that has gone nowhere.

"Part of the slowness of updating these guidelines reflects the entrenched interests of the food industry, who have designed their food products for the current guidelines, and this results in a status quo bias for those rules," he said. 

US Food and Drug Administration logo

But the latest proposal does mark progress.

At one time, the FDA didn’t even allow health claims on foods, the Auburn University professor noted. It was worried about misinformation and fraud that was common in drug markets. But then medical associations, in the 1960s, became concerned about the health consequences of overeating and started promoting the notion that eating low-fat foods would prevent future risk of heart disease. 

By the 1970s, the FDA shifted direction and introduced a "voluntary" nutrition label. Food companies that wanted to make health claims could now do so, as long as they put the FDA’s "Nutrition Information" label on their packages. The result was a dramatic explosion of new diet products, especially low-fat dairy substitutes and high-fiber cereals, Frohlich said.

However, by the 1980s there was a proliferation of health claims on food and new diet foods that "tested the boundaries between what is classified as a food versus drug" and led to the passage of the 1990 Nutrition Labeling and Education Act as well as the agency's development of new guidelines, including the 1994 definition of "healthy", he added.

Other winners and losers

The FDA said in its proposal that about 34,000 UPCs (universal product codes), or 14% of total UPCs in grocery stores, qualify for the existing "healthy" nutrient content claim, but only 5% of UPCs carry the label, reported food policy journalist Helena Bottemiller Evich recently for her newsletter Food Fix.

"My guess is that a major chunk of the UPCs that qualify are things like fresh produce, which don’t tend to be packaged or loaded up with marketing labels, ostensibly because consumers already know they are healthy," she said.

Bottemiller Evich recounted how she made a trip to a Washington, DC-area Safeway recently and came away thinking the FDA's 5% estimate was high.  

But Peter Lurie, CSPI's executive director, told Undercurrent that he believes that percentage could grow under the proposal.

"It could increase because the old definition had this total fat requirement, so you could find products, and seafood might be one of them, where even though total fat might have been high, you could still meet a saturated fat requirement," he said, adding: "It's also possible that you would see people availing themselves of [the 'healthy' claim] more because it's now more clearly defined than before."  

Photograph by Zoriana Zaitseva on Shutterstock.

The New York Times has suggested that nuts, avocados, seeds and certain oils also could be among the big winners. 

The biggest losers, the newspaper reported, would include many sugary cereals, granola bars, highly sweetened yogurts and white breads. They might currently qualify as "healthy" under the current definition but wouldn't under the proposed rule.

Lurie said CSPI agrees with the notion that Americans should eat more fish as it is recommended by the Dietary Guidelines.

He said his organization also agrees with the FDA's latest proposed change to the definition of "healthy", though it wishes that the labeling requirement would be mandatory instead of voluntary, and on the front of the package where it "would also be interpretive with respect to certain nutrients".

Consumers might erroneously think that any foods without a "healthy" label are automatically deemed unhealthy, he said.

"As a result, it might be difficult for a consumer to know what the absence of a healthy claim means," he told Undercurrent. "Is it something that can't meet the criteria or something that the marketing people have decided is not beneficial to the product. The voluntary aspect of this places inherent limits on what can be done." 

Part of a larger strategy

The FDA released its proposed new definition for "healthy" foods on the same day as the White House Conference on Hunger, Nutrition and Health, in Washington, DC. As reported by Undercurrent, the all-day event on Sept. 28 was used to promote the president Joe Biden and vice president Kamala Harris administration's "National Strategy on Hunger, Nutrition, and Health".

See page 22 of the national strategy for the administration's plan to make sure foods labeled as "healthy" align with current nutrition and the Dietary Guidelines for Americans among other steps.

Diet-related chronic diseases in the US are the leading causes of death and disability, the FDA noted upon announcing its change.

"Healthy eating patterns, which include fruits, vegetables, lower-fat dairy and whole grains, are associated with improved health, such as reduced risk of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, certain types of cancers, and being overweight or obese," the agency said. "Providing informative and accessible food labeling empowers consumers and may help foster a healthier food supply for all if some manufacturers include more fruits, vegetables, dairy and whole grains and limit saturated fat, sodium, and added sugars in their products, to qualify to use the updated claim."

FDA is also researching a symbol to illustrate the "healthy" claim on the front of packages, proposing research on the effort in March.

"Having a standardized graphic to show that a food qualifies for the 'healthy' claim would further support the FDA’s goal of helping consumers more easily identify packaged food products that help them build healthy eating patterns," the agency said.

Some of the possible stickers FDA could use to help bring attention to its newly defined "healthy" label. Image courtesy of Marion Nestle's Food Politics newsletter.

title: Chinese seafood vendor jailed for role in COVID-19 outbreak in Beijing
content:
A Beijing court has sentenced a Chinese seafood merchant and his colleagues for obstructing the prevention of infectious diseases linked to last year's COVID-19 outbreak, Beijing News reports.

According to a judgement document of the Beijing Fangshan People's Court, a merchant surnamed Yang was sentenced to one year and six months in prison and fined CNY 200,000 ($27,680). Three colleagues were sentenced to one year in prison.

Between April 2021 to November 2021, Yang imported frozen hairtail fish from Thailand and stored the fish in a rented cold storage in Fangshan district, Beijing. Before entering the cold storage, Yang did not submit a COVID-19 test and disinfection certificate, court documents said.

Warehouse shelves were not disinfected regularly, and domestic and imported foods were not stored separately. Yang also instructed his colleague, surnamed Xue, to replace the imported label with the label of a domestic company, the court papers show.

Court papers revealed that Yang's colleague Xue tested positive for COVID-19, the first positive case in the city's Fangshan and Fengtai districts during the outbreak in January and February 2022.

Environmental samples taken from Yang's cold storage also tested positive for traces of the coronavirus, including samples from outer packaging of fish products and the surrounding environment.

The court said that Yang's illegal storage of imported cold chain food and failure to follow COVID protocols directly led to the spread of COVID-19. 

He was found guilty of committing the crime of obstructing the prevention and treatment of infectious diseases under China's Law on the Prevention and Control of Infectious Disease. The company's two deputy general managers were found guilty of the same charge.

The court said it considered Yang's guilty plea and cooperation in the case when sentencing, considering his sentence relatively light.

title: Hatch Blue ready to invest in novel aquafeeds, high-value species
content:
Hatch Blue's second fund, "the Blue Revolution Fund", has closed its first funding round and hopes to bring third-party verified impact investing to the aquaculture sector, it announced.

As a result of the first closing, Hatch Blue is ready to make investments -- typically with an initial ticket of €500,000 to €5 million ($4.95m) depending on the company's needs. Investments will be sourced globally and made in the form of equity or equity-like instruments, it said.

Hatch launches €50m investment plan for ‘regenerative’ aquaculture

The fund focuses on investing in impactful sectors, such as next-generation farming systems, regenerative farms, alternative seafood, aquaculture ingredients, nutrition, farm software/hardware, health and genetics.

"We are looking for novel feed ingredients that are significantly more sustainable but cost-competitive when compared to existing ingredients," said Georg Baunach, managing partner and co-founder of Hatch Blue.

"In the regenerative farming sections, we are searching for companies that align well with venture-type returns. An area of 'next-generation' farming systems we are especially keen to explore are high-value species that typically have a challenging environmental footprint when farmed conventionally."

"Technologies, health or genetic solutions that improve feed conversion ratios or survival rates are also of high interest to us given the current rise of input costs and the close alignment with reduction in scope three emissions," he said.

The current aquaculture market is valued at over $200 billion. Large multinationals entered the space in the mid-2010s and professionalized its upstream industries. Those feed, pharma and equipment companies depend on inorganic growth to maintain their competitive advantage. The Blue Revolution Fund aims to support the growing demand for innovation in the aquaculture sector while actively working to develop more sustainable and regenerative industry practices, it said.

"The fund has sector-specific knowledge and focus, which includes an industry-experienced fund management team along with a unique and high-quality dealflow."

Hatch has set fund-level targets that were defined before knowing the portfolio composition. This was intended to provide investors with confidence that the team is selecting companies that can positively impact the aquaculture industry.

To verify the impact, the fund is working with an independent third party to assess the investment before financing is approved and will continue to monitor and report on the investment's progress. "This is, to our knowledge, a first in the industry for a global fund like ours."

The fund has set 10-year targets, and will measure the following impact metrics:

Portions of sustainable seafood produced
Metric tons of carbon sequestered or CO2 equivalent avoided
Hectares of habitat-forming area
Hectares of coastal area impacted by existing farms with a focus on improved environmental outcomes
Tonnes of nitrogen removed from coastal waterways
New jobs created in coastal communities

"Even though I have full trust in our own motivations to positively impact food systems, ocean health and coastal communities, best practice should be to have a third-party watchdog and involve them in a meaningful way," said Baunach.

title: Spain fines fishing vessels for turning off mandatory location trackers
content:
The Spanish government has fined two Spanish fishing vessels, Releixo and Egaluze, €20,000 for turning off their mandatory automatic identification systems (AIS) on several occasions without due cause.

During the four-year period between 2012 and 2016, the two vessels appeared to disable their AIS devices for over 1,000 hours, said NGO Oceana, which provided the data for the government to act upon.

"This exemplary sanction of €20,000 to punish two fishing vessels for switching off their AIS is an important step towards having more transparency in the fisheries sector," said Oceana's senior policy advisor for illegal fishing and transparency, Ignacio Fresco Vanzini.

"With this action, the Spanish administration is sending a clear message to the fishing industry: even if monitoring of fishing is based on vessel monitoring systems, it is not acceptable to navigate without being visible to other vessels or control authorities, and risk putting fishers' lives in danger. We hope these sanctions become the norm and other EU member states feel compelled to act."

Oceana analyzed Global Fishing Watch data to identify vessels with apparent gaps in their AIS transmissions. "The Global Fishing Watch map helps advance ocean governance through increased transparency of human activity at sea, empowering anyone to view or download data and investigate global fishing activity in near real-time for free," it said.

title: Son of Atlantic Sapphire CEO re-brands, expands former Platina USA ops
content:
Norwegian expatriate Emil Andreassen -- the son of Atlantic Sapphire founder and CEO Johan Andreassen -- is stepping out of his father's shadow to carve his own niche in the North American seafood processing sector, reports SalmonBusiness.

The younger Andreassen, who took over the processing operation at Platina Seafood USA in 2020, buying it from his father, who is no longer involved in the business. The company purchased a new 26,000-square-foot processing facility in Miami, Florida, during the winter of 2021 and moved its headquarters to the same location in the spring.

Andreassen has renamed his company "NovoMar", while preparing it for expansion. In fact, work at the Miami processing facility is in full swing to prepare the business for production during the late fall. New graders, filleting machines and assembly lines will all be installed.

NovoMar launched its new NOVO brand in the spring, debuting its refined products for consumers in thousands of stores across North America. The assortment consists primarily of salmon, but also of mahi, hake, tuna and shrimp.

The processing plant will carry out filleting, pin-bone deboning, as well as portioning, vacuum packing, skin packing, freezing and glazing. The facility has the capacity to process 20 million pounds (9,000 metric tons) annually in phase one and will graduate to 40m lbs annually in phase two by Q2 of 2023, said the company in a press release.

From a turnover of $55m in 2021, NovoMar is projecting a lift to $80m in 2022.

"We will refine from pin bone in A-trim down to, among other things, portions in skin-pack or frozen IVP," Emil Andreassen said. "We will soon finish phase one. Initially, we have capacity for around one-and-a-half or two vehicles of raw material per day in one shift. Phase two will bring in a new line and double the capacity."

Platina was originally established as a large import and distribution network in North America in 2012. The company's main focus has been Atlantic salmon, and it is now one of the largest independent importers of salmon in the US, with a reported presence in over 15,000 stores and hundreds of foodservice distributors.

The younger Andreassen was born in Alesund, Norway, and raised in Vestnes, Norway, before studying, living and working in the US for the last 10 years.

title: IFFO: Global fishmeal production trending slightly lower in 2022
content:
Global fishmeal production has fallen slightly below last year's levels after good output in North America, India and the North Atlantic failed to offset a drop in Peru, the world's largest producer, according to the Marine Ingredients Organisation (IFFO).

In the first seven months of 2022, total cumulative fishmeal production was down compared with the same period in 2021, despite the US, India, the Iceland/North Atlantic area and the African countries reporting an increased cumulative production. 

Fish oil buyers for omega-3 supplements suffer as high prices hit demand

Enrico Bachis, IFFO’s market research director, said that the main reason was a smaller Peruvian anchovy quota.

"The drop in Peru, both for fishmeal and for fish oil production, is due to a lower quota granted to the north-center of the country in the last quarter of 2021, which resulted in fewer catches in the first quarter of 2022," said Bachis.

Last year, Peru's anchovy quota for the second season -- which started in November and ended in January of this year -- was cut by 26% compared with 2020. Then catches were down 4% in Peru's north-center region between April-June 2022 compared with the same period in 2021. 

Meanwhile, Chinese domestic production of marine ingredients remains "subdued" and confined to the south, although activities are expected to pick up in all areas in September. 

As for fish oil, IFFO said the 2022 total cumulative production is in line with that of 2021. A drop in output in Peru, Chile and India has been offset by rises in European countries, the US and Africa above 2021 figures during the first seven months of the year.

So far, this has failed to offset a surge in Peruvian fish oil prices to record highs, as Undercurrent News recently reported, due to tight global markets for other agri-oils.

On the demand side, aquafeed production in China, the world's biggest importer of fishmeal, remains at high levels compared with 2021 despite the series of heatwaves. However, COVID-19 lockdowns continue to limit consumers' access to both the retail and the foodservice facilities within locked down areas, said IFFO.

Pig and piglet prices also showed some weakness in August after a four-month hike.

"[Pig] supply is expected to grow larger than forecast by the authorities in 2022 while imported pork meat has continued to decline. High costs of feed ingredients and the weak demand explain the annual drop in the cumulative pig feed output," said IFFO in its market update.

Chinese imports of foreign fishmeal have also decreased during the first seven months of the year. However, important tonnages are expected to reach Chinese shores in the coming weeks.

title: Danish magnate Kjeldsen in hot water again over accounting change
content:
Fishing magnate Henning Kjeldsen has once again drawn the ire of the Danish Business Authority after it unearthed dubious accounting practices by his fishing company, reports TVMV.

Now, the authority has threatened to forcibly dissolve the fishing baron's holding company, Henning Kjeldsen Holding, which has already been in a lengthy legal battle over the size of its quota share.

On this occasion, the issue is the documented value of Kjeldsen's fishing quotas. The firm's 2020 accounts record them as having a fair value of DKK 2.5 billion ($335 million), a sharp increase in value of DKK 1.9bn compared to the previous year.

The company changed its accounting principles that year to reflect what it believes the quota would be worth if sold on the market. While not illegal, the authorities believe that quotas are not traded often enough for any official value to be set in this way.

As a result, Henning Kjeldsen Holding has been ordered to submit new accounts for 2020 without the revaluation, or make the change in its accounts for 2021; it has 30 days in which to do so.

Kjeldsen, who was last year prosecuted and fined DKK 54m for fishing rule violations committed between 2013 and 2019, currently owns two vessels and a share of a third, after selling off his pelagic vessels and quota.

title: Canadian lobster industry: Seafood Watch rating system used to ‘depress markets’
content:
The Lobster Council of Canada (LCC) has responded to last week's announcement by the Monterey Bay Aquarium's Seafood Watch program that it has lowered the rating it gives North American lobster (Homarus americanus), snow crab (Chionoecetes opilio) and other species to red or "avoid" by saying the new scores for lobster do "not accurately reflect significant action by Canadian lobster harvesters and the Department of Fisheries, Oceans, and the Canadian Coast Guard (DFO) and Transport Canada".

Seafood Watch said its rating changes were made due to the risk of endangered North Atlantic right whales getting snared in trap ropes. Previously all Canadian lobster and snow crab were rated yellow or "good alternative".

The ratings were released after "an extensive consultation period" where the LCC, the Canadian lobster industry's largest trade association, Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans and others provided up-to-date resource management and North Atlantic Right Whale (NARW) mitigation measure information, LCC said. Seafood Watch was informed about numerous measures taken, including dynamic closure protocols that identify individual whales and quickly close geographical grids to all fixed gear fishing activity, universal gear requirements, defined lobster seasons with trap limits, ongoing whale safe gear trials and implementation and mandatory speed reductions for shipping.

"The justification for the new 'avoid' rating does not reference any of this significant action by Canadian lobster fishery stakeholders, does not identify any pathway toward achieving a better evaluation and only tells the fishery to 'do more'", wrote Geoff Irvine, LCC's executive director, in a statement. 

"This type of rating scheme seeks to use the power of their ratings to depress markets to force changes within fisheries," he added. "While programs of this nature can be helpful if a fishery is not acknowledging a problem, the lobster sector and government of Canada understand the importance of this issue and have invested millions of dollars annually to reduce risk and potential harm to the endangered North Atlantic Right Whale. ... Depressing markets for lobster will not make the sector move faster, it will only take resources away from those who are working on the problem."

Following the Seafood Watch rating changes, both HelloFresh and Blue Apron, two of the biggest direct-to-consumer meal services serving the US, pledged to drop North American lobster from their menus, as reported by Undercurrent.

title: Nova Austral suffers terrible Q2 with sales, earnings plummeting
content:
Chilean salmon farmer Nova Austral saw a disastrous second quarter in 2022 as expected with revenues plummeting, proof that the lingering effect of 2021 mortalities and regulatory action against it are still being felt.

The Puerto Montt-based company said in an earnings release that its Q2 2022 revenues amounted to $16.7 million, half of the $28.6m seen a year earlier. Furthermore, its pre-value adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) came to a negative $11.3m in Q2 2022, twice the negative $6.1m EBITDA seen in Q2 2021.

"Revenues decreased 42% vs 2Q21 mainly due to lower volumes sold (2,100 metric tons, whole fish equivalent [WFE], -51%), offset by higher average prices per kilogram WFE (+19%). In turn, [costs of goods sold] decreased in line with the volume reduction," the company said.

The company harvested 8,800t in Q2 2022, a 22% improvement year-on-year, although the company did not harvest any fish in Q2 2021.

Nova Austral has been struggling for months. A series of infectious salmon anemia (ISA) outbreaks in December 2020 cost the company 4.8m smolt and $3.8m and led to the lack of a Q2 2021 harvest. 

Then, during Q4 2021, the company disclosed "a new mortality incident at the hatchery" of one of its farming sites that killed about 1.4m smolts.

"The reason for this mortality was contamination with H2S [hydrogen sulfide] generated by the wrong functioning of biofilters," the company said.

Additionally, the company also faced $1.23m in regulator fines in September 2021 over four charges relating to the company's past participation in a 2019 mortality misreporting scandal.

Furthermore, in July, Chile's federal environmental agency, known by its Spanish abbreviation SMA, revoked licenses for three of Nova Austral's salmon farming sites in the Magallanes region and fined the company nearly a million dollars over charges that it exceeded its production authority and damaged the seabed at one of the locations.

The fines and revocations are under appeal. And a lawyer representing the company said previously that it could be forced to shut down if the penalties stand.

title: US antitrust regulators block $987m deal between rival shipping giants
content:
US federal antitrust regulators forced China International Marine Containers (CIMC) to end its tentative $987 million purchase of rival shipping giant Maersk's refrigerated container building business, Freight Waves reports. 

The purchase would have combined half of the world's four suppliers of insulated container boxes and consolidated control of more than 90% of the market in Chinese entities, as the top three manufacturers worldwide are Chinese. And CIMC is already the world's largest builder of ocean-shipping containers, the US Justice Department said in a statement.

Under the tentative deal, AP Moller-Maersk would have sold its Maersk Container Industry subsidiary and its Qingdao, China factory to CIMC for $987m.

As Undercurrent News has reported, Maersk was among 23 shipping operators fined a total of $81m for "fixing" freight rates on the South Korea to Southeast Asia route between 2003 and 2018.

title: Louisiana effort to set commercial catch limits on menhaden falls short
content:
The US state of Louisiana will start collecting harvest data from menhaden purse seiners every month starting in May 2023. But, for now, legislators have stopped short of imposing catch limits on the state's largest commercial fishery.

Lousiana's Act No. 759 went into effect on Aug. 1 after governor John Edwards signed it into law on June 18. It requires the Louisiana Wildlife and Fisheries Commission to set requirements for monthly harvesters' reporting of "location data in degrees, minutes, seconds, with a defined datum, determined by global positioning satellite navigational instrument reading; estimated volume of harvest; length of the menhaden estimated based on a sample of the harvest", according to the act's text.

The act is a watered-down version of what would have been the first annual catch limit,  260,000 metric tons, applied to the menhaden harvest in the waters of Louisiana, the last state in the Gulf of Mexico that doesn't cap its menhaden hauls, District 54 Republican state representative Joseph Orgeron told Undercurrent News.

"It's a compromise with the menhaden industry," Orgeron said.

Edwards' administration, Orgeron said, merely wanted to collect catch data, a point seconded by Rene LeBreton, public information director at the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries (LDWF).

"This act does not establish a quota," LeBreton said in an email to Undercurrent.

Menhaden is a fish to fight over for almost anybody interested in the Gulf of Mexico and the US East Coast. While they are not directly consumed by humans, commercial harvesters catch them because they are valuable fishmeal, fish oil and pet food. Recreational anglers like them because they are a bait of choice for sportfish, and conservationists want them protected because endangered species are also among those that feed on them.

A valuable fish for recreational and commercial anglers 

Some of the law's opponents wonder why the state's commission or LDWF would want to collect the catch data. Harvesters already supply that information to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, said Ben Landry, spokesperson for Omega Protein of Reedsville, Virginia. The US' largest menhaden harvester and processor and a subsidiary of Canada's Cooke, Omega harvests the fish in the gulf states of Louisiana, Mississippi and Texas and has processing facilities in Louisiana and Mississippi.

"Don't let it get lost in the shuffle that we've been providing this data every time our nets hit the water since the 1970s and the state can get it at any time from the federal government," Landry told Undercurrent. "They have an NDA [non-disclosure agreement] with NOAA to get our data; we've signed off on that. So this is not a situation where the biologists at wildlife and fisheries in Louisiana say, 'We have no idea what they're catching because we can't get their data.' That's not what this is about."

"This is about recreational anglers, wanting the state to get it directly from us, as opposed to having to go through NOAA," Landry said. 

Orgeron authored a version of a bill that passed by a 75-to-22 margin in the House in April but a companion bill died in the Louisiana Senate, replaced by the weaker initiative. If Orgeron's bill had made it into law, it would have also required menhaden fishing vessels to report daily locations and catch amounts to the state, he said.

Orgeron agreed with Landry that he had recreational anglers partly in mind with the bill, but he also likes the idea of LDWF gathering its own data. Orgeron said that despite it being removed from the final bill that became law, he wants to see a catch limit on commercial harvesters.

Orgeron also wants to have them kept out of some portion if not all of the three miles of state waters off the coast because the percentage of their catch within state boundaries has increased within the last several years.

A recent study funded by the Science Center for Marine Fisheries found that over two-thirds (67.7%) of the overall gulf menhaden catch coastwide occurs within three miles of shore, generating $638m in economic impacts, as Undercurrent has written.

That reduces the amount of fish that recreational anglers can catch, Orgeron said.

Landry disagreed. The recent closure of an Omega processing plant in Cameron inadvertently skewed the percentage because that plant was charged with harvesting fish deep in federal waters. Its absence, therefore, increased the percentage of in-state fishing along the coast in a misleading way, Landry said.

As Undercurrent has written, menhaden, also known as "pogies", are heavily sought for their omega-3 fatty acid content, which is useful in fishmeal and dietary supplements. They're also used in feeds for poultry and pigs and are a popular source of bait for commercial lobster, crab and crawfish harvesters. 

Nationwide, Louisiana does far and away the most business in menhaden harvesting in the US, according to the latest NOAA data. From 2017 to 2021, it led the nation in menhaden harvests, averaging 318,773t annually worth an average of $67.68 million. Mississippi and Virginia have typically vied for 2nd place after Louisiana, harvesting not much more than a third of the amount that the Cajun state collected.

Over that time period, its highest catch was 2018's 387,923t worth $90.31m, with 2021's 267,334t worth $60.40m on the other end of the scale. By way of comparison, Virginia's greatest harvest in those years came in 2019, when it harvested 150,826t worth $90.32m. That was also Mississippi's best year -- 150,763t worth $41.99m -- over the five years.

Good food for some very endangered species

Menhaden also draw interest from environmentalists who say that the fish is a valuable forage for other, and in some cases, endangered species -- osprey, eagles, whales, porpoises, striped bass, bluefish, sharks and mackerels.

The Atlantic menhaden (Brevoortia tyrannus), which live 10 to 12 years and grow 14 to 18 inches in length, are listed by the Chesapeake Bay Program, a watchdog group that has helped engineer the restoration of that important US mid-Atlantic coast ecosystem, as one of the bay's most important sea creatures.

Efforts to tighten harvesting controls on menhaden commercial hauls have been controversial, but The Times-Picayune, a New Orleans-based newspaper, reported that Texas has managed to prohibit menhaden fishing within a half-mile of its coast. Florida has eliminated large-scale net fishing in its waters. Mississippi and Alabama have set one-mile buffer zones, as Undercurrent has written.

New York state passed a law in April 2019 ending menhaden harvesting in state waters to preserve it as a forage fish except as part of efforts to prevent overpopulation of the pogies. Other efforts to preserve menhaden include Maine legislators being asked by the state's fisheries managers this spring to consider limiting the number of commercial menhaden licenses issued there to prevent possible overfishing.

And Omega was recently investigated in Virginia for a bycatch incident involving what it called "a rare and unexpected encounter with a school of red drum" that resulted in large numbers of dead fish washing ashore at a Virginia state park late last month. Landry said the company has been cleared of any negligence.

'The resource is not overfished'

A report earlier this month from the Atlantic State Fisheries Commission sparked further contretemps by claiming that menhaden are not being overfished along the US East Coast.

The commission said that the 2022 Atlantic Menhaden Stock Assessment Update "indicates the resource is not overfished nor experiencing overfishing relative to the current ecological reference points (ERP). In 2021, population fecundity, a measure of reproductive capacity, is above both the ERP threshold and target and total fishing mortality is below both the ERP threshold and target."

The Gulf of Mexico and Atlantic menhaden fisheries won Marine Stewardship Council certification in 2019 for achieving the group's standards for sustainable fishing. 

Looking ahead, no one should expect Louisiana's new law to change much of the situation's dynamics. The Louisiana Wildlife and Fisheries Commission will meet in September to start the process of creating a catch-count system as described in the new law, LeBreton said.

Omega looks forward to cooperating with the state in harvesting the data the state seeks, Landry said. Meanwhile, Orgeron said that he probably won't push the issue again with a bill next year, but hopes that the state's counts will lead to the state performing a bycatch study that will help protect recreational fishing interests.

title: Germany’s Bluu Seafood launches first two cell-based seafood products
content:
German food tech company Bluu Seafood has unveiled its first two market-ready products made from cultivated fish cells, as it prepares to begin the regulatory approval process for key markets in Asia, Europe and the US.

The company launched fish fingers and balls made from cultivated fish cells and enriched with plant proteins, a process intended to optimize how they cook and taste.

In this first phase, Bluu Seafood is targeting initial approval and market launch in Singapore by the end of 2023, as the regulatory process there is already well-defined, it said in a statement.

"With the completion of our first products, we can demonstrate visible and edible results after less than two years of operational work. This officially makes us the first company in Europe to produce cultivated fish," said the firm's founder and CEO, Sebastian Rakers.

"We are now working closely with regulatory agencies to clear the way for market launch and are using the time to focus on scaling," he added.

In addition, Bluu Seafood has also developed first prototypes of more complex products such as fillets and sashimi. It is focused on Pacific and Atlantic salmon, as well as rainbow trout and carp. 

The company combines cell and food technology to grow a variety of seafood products directly from animal cells, without compromising animal welfare and with a significantly smaller environmental footprint than conventional fishing, the firm also stated.

"With Bluu Seafood, we can make an important contribution to the supply of animal protein that allows us to manage our oceans in a way that conserves resources and hopefully also promotes biodiversity in this habitat that is so important to all of us," Rakers concluded.

title: Pacific Seafood gets water quality fine reduced
content:
Pacific Seafood Group agreed to a reduced $92,000 fine with Washington state regulators after the major US West Coast processor made a series of unauthorized wastewater discharges into Gray's Harbor, The Associated Press reports.

The processor's Pacific Seafood Westport unit was originally fined $123,000 after it was accused of 48 violations relating to the outfall pipe it shares with the City of Westport, according to the radio station KXRO. The outfall pipe reportedly released wastewater containing fecal coliform, grease, oils, and other solids above thresholds allowed in its permit from the period of April 2020 through November 2021, according to the Washington Department of Ecology.

"Half Moon Bay, within Grays Harbor, contains wetlands and open marine water. The area is popular for recreation, and is home to numerous species of fish, crab, and shorebirds. Excess effluent from seafood processing can harm aquatic life and reduce water quality. Maintaining water quality standards and eliminating pollution is critical to protecting the health of this important ecosystem," the department said in a statement.

The company agreed to the reduced penalty, according to a statement. The remaining $31,000 of the original $123,000 penalty will be waived if the facility remains in compliance with its water quality permit for one year.

title: StarKist takes tuna price-fixing fight to US Supreme Court
content:
US tuna canner StarKist & Co is not backing down from a protracted legal battle in its defense of lawsuits brought by customers who say they were harmed by price-fixing in the canned tuna sector.

The Reston, Virginia-based tuna canner, owned by South Korea's Dongwon Enterprise, has appealed a lower court's decision in class-action lawsuits against it to the US Supreme Court. The company's general counsel and senior vice president, Scott Meece, said that it will not settle some lawsuits.

"StarKist has willingly and proactively settled cases with customers in situations in which there was a reasonable basis for arguing the customer was harmed. On the other hand, StarKist will not settle cases, in these matters or others, if the claims are excessive or in which the complaining party was not harmed. We will continue to defend those cases, and while defense is costly, it is the right thing to do."

StarKist is challenging an earlier decision from judge Janis Sammartino to certify the hundreds of individual lawsuits into common classes. That decision, it has argued, sounds a "death knell" for the future of class-action suits they face from customers who claim they were damaged from price-fixing. Additionally, the company said that it hasn't been proven that members of the allegedly damaged classes have enough commonalities to be grouped together.

However, in April 2022, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals voted nine-to-two to uphold the certification decision, which applies to three distinct types of customer groups: direct purchasers, indirect purchasers and end consumers. But on June 23, in a 134-page "writ of certiorari" to the US' highest court, the tuna canner claimed that the lower courts' decisions missed the mark.

"Members of the three putative classes purchased different volumes and types of packaged tuna from different sellers at different points in the supply chain through different channels and procurement methods, creating highly individualized leverage and pricing among class members. The direct purchasers’ own expert admitted there was no proof that 5.5% of the proposed direct purchaser class had suffered any injury—and, according to applicants’ expert, that number is as high as 28%. The other putative classes suffered from similar flaws," Starkist said.

Customers have alleged that the tuna price-fixing scandal occurred roughly from 2011 to 2013 and involved StarKist as well as Bumble Bee Foods, which is now owned by Taiwan's FCF Co, and Thai Union Group's Chicken of the Sea International.

In 2018, StarKist pleaded guilty to criminal price-fixing charges and was fined $100 million.

title: Nova Austral argues license revocations, fines could sink it
content:
A lawyer representing Chile's Nova Austral as it appeals significant fines and the revocation of three farming licenses believes that the salmon farmer could be forced to shut down if the penalties stand.

In July, Chile's federal environmental agency, known by its Spanish abbreviation SMA, revoked licenses for three of Nova Austral's salmon farming sites in the Magallanes region and fined the company nearly a million dollars over charges that it exceeded its production authority and damaged the seabed at one of the locations.

Nova Austral then challenged the regulator's decision to a Chilean appeals court.

Julio Recordón, a lawyer for the company, said during arguments at appeal that the penalties could lead "quite possibly to the closure of its operations in Chile", the publication SalmonExpert reported.

The revocations applied to the company's Cockburn 14, Cockburn 23 and Aracena 10 farm sites, which Nova Austral has said are key to the entity's financial sustainability. Nova Austral has lost money for years, accruing a $81 million loss in 2020 and a $54m loss in 2021

Nova Austral produced 15% more than allowed at its Cockburn 14 farm between the months of October 2015 and May 2017, 30% more than allowed at its Cockburn 23 farm between January 2016 and November 2017, and 25% more than allowed at its Aracena 10 farm during a 2016-2017 cycle, according to the press release.

The SMA said it applied a fine of CLP 900m ($929,176) to the company for artificially altering the seabed of the Aracena 14 site near the city of Punta Arenas.

title: Untitled
content:
US menhaden processor Omega Protein is being investigated for a bycatch incident involving what it called "a rare and unexpected encounter with a school of red drum" that resulted in large numbers of dead fish washing ashore at a Virginia state park.

A crew from a commercial menhaden fishing vessel owned by Ocean Harvesters, which supplies Omega Protein, inadvertently killed "many" red drum when a spotter plane directed the crew onto a school of menhaden that likely had another school of red drum beneath it on Monday (July 25), the company, which is owned by Canada's Cooke, said. The vessel's captain noticed the netted red drum and immediately ordered their release, Omega Protein said in a statement on Wednesday.

"It is a rare event for menhaden nets to interact with red drum, or any other species. In fact, we have no record of an incident of this kind occurring in the recent past," Omega said in the statement. "The most likely explanation is the unusual situation in which a school of red drum swam beneath a school of menhaden, making them unobservable to the spotter pilot."

"Our captain and crew, in deciding to immediately open their nets and release both the red drum and menhaden, were following company policy adopted out of respect for the species, and our commitment to their conservation and protection," the company added.

The Virginia Marine Resources Commission (VMRC) and Virginia Marine Police (VMP) are investigating the incident, which occurred a mile offshore of Kiptopeke State Park on the southern end of the Eastern Shore of Virginia and the Delmarva Peninsula in Northampton County, near Cape Charles.

A cleanup has been underway at the park since Monday. The total number of fish killed has not been announced. VMP blamed net stress and water temperatures for killing the fish. VMRC spokesperson and commissioner's assistant Michele Guilford did not immediately return telephone messages and emails left by Undercurrent. 

Ben Landry, a spokesperson for Ocean Fleet Services and Ocean Harvesters, declined to comment Wednesday on the status of the cleanup and police investigation except to say that "we have been in constant communication" with the agency "and we will continue to assist in any way that we can."

'More and more people are being concerned'

Omega Protein and Ocean Harvesters have come under fire previously for dead-fish spills involving menhaden in Virginia. Monday's incident was the second this month. A fishing vessel employed by OP had what might have been a sizeable fish kill when a net entangled and tore about a mile off Silver Beach, Virginia on July 5. 

"Many" menhaden "were alive and swam away, but we acknowledge that many were already dead at the time of the tear," Landry said in a statement.

Dead fish also washed ashore at Silver Beach as a result. A cleanup began July 6 and was expected to take several days, Landry said in the release, which was dated July 6.

Another pair of incidents occurred in September, resulting in more than 400,000 dead fish being accidentally released near the community of Hampton Roads, as Undercurrent has reported. Those spills were estimated to involve some 121.6 metric tons of menhaden.

One of the spills was reportedly caused by the company snagging the net on a submerged anchor. That drew a letter from Steven Bowman, then VMRC commissioner who reminded Omega that harvesters had reached 75% of the year's 51,186t menhaden fishing limit within Virginia waters of the Chesapeake Bay. Future spills could be deducted from the limit, he warned.

Omega Protein had exceeded the cap previously, which resulted in the first-ever moratorium on the commonwealth's menhaden fishery in the Chesapeake -- one of the two largest in the US.

Chris Moore, senior regional ecosystem scientist for the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, a non-profit that closely monitors the health of the many species in the world's third-largest estuary at 4,479 square miles, told Undercurrent that vessels affiliated with the menhaden supplier have been linked to multiple incidents in the past.

"I think we've had these spills just about annually over the last couple of years and obviously this is at least the second one [in a] year. Due to their timing of when they happen and the location they're having, I think more and more people are being concerned, not only for the ecological impact that we see with basically having these fish go to waste," Moore told Undercurrent.

There is also "the economic impacts and the recreational impacts for people who can't recreate because the fish are washed up on the beach, or also obviously turning away who may come to visit certain areas," Moore added.

OP takes 'full responsibility'

Omega Protein said in a statement that menhaden harvesters actively avoid game fish and other species such as red drum. Catch of non-targeted species comprises less than 1% by volume of menhaden harvesters, with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration calling the menhaden fishery "one of the most selective and effective fisheries, with little bycatch". 

The company said it immediately notified VMRC of the incident and takes "full responsibility."

"We quickly developed a strategy for retrieving any fish floating in the water or washing ashore in the area. By early morning today, additional fishing vessels and crewmembers from our fleet were on site and working to remove any fish floating in the water.  Our third-party, on-call emergency response crew is on-site to remove any fish that come ashore. These additional fishing vessels are not harvesting fish but are actively assisting the fish clean-up and removal," the company said in the statement, which is dated July 26. 

"We acknowledge the impact and inconvenience Monday’s incident may have on the Eastern Shore community and will continue to focus our collective efforts on the situation until it is remedied. We anticipate that most fish will have been removed by nightfall. However, our fishing vessels will anchor offshore overnight to monitor the situation at sunrise. Should more fish appear in the morning, our fishermen will be there to continue the cleanup."

The company also took responsibility for the net spill on July 5 and paid crews for the cleanup there.

A division of Cooke of New Brunswick, Canada, Omega Protein describes itself as a century-old nutritional product producer that develops and delivers foods, dietary supplements and animal feeds to processors and retailers, including highly-refined specialty oils, specialty proteins products and nutraceuticals. The processor has seven manufacturing facilities located in the US, Canada and Europe.

Omega has what it describes as a long-term supply contract with its independent fishing partner, Ocean Harvesters. The company is headquartered in Reedville, Virginia after being located for several years in Houston, Texas. Ocean Harvesters owns 30 vessels that harvest menhaden in the Atlantic Ocean and Gulf of Mexico.

A representative who answered the phone at Ocean Harvesters declined to comment on the incident.

title: Credit Suisse agrees $23m payout in Mozambique tuna bond scandal
content:
The investment bank Credit Suisse has agreed it owes investors $22.6 million in restitution for its part in a corruption scandal involving 'tuna bonds' in Mozambique, reports Reuters. 

Prosecutors asked US district Judge William Kuntz on Tuesday (July 26) to order Credit Suisse's European subsidiary to pay restitution to 18 investors in Mozambican bonds the bank arranged. Much of the bond proceeds were diverted via kickbacks to Credit Suisse bankers and Mozambique officials, prosecutors have said.

The subsidiary, Credit Suisse Securities Europe, agreed to the amount, according to the filing. It pleaded guilty to conspiracy last year as part of a $475m settlement with US and UK authorities.

Last October, the investment bank was fined £147m by UK legal authorities for its role in the tuna bond scandal. 

The UK's Financial Conduct Authority claimed Credit Suisse had failed to properly manage the risk of financial crime, with staff alleged to have taken and paid out bribes as they arranged $1.3 billion of loans ostensibly intended for Mozambique's tuna sector.

In one case, a Mozambique government contractor paid kickbacks in the region of $50m to staff on Credit Suisse's legal team from 2012 to 2016 to receive loans at favorable rates.

A Russian investment bank, VTB Capital, also reached a settlement of its own pertaining to the bond scandal.

title: Judge bemoans small fines for Canadian snow crab harvesters caught underreporting
content:
Four snow crab harvesters from the Canadian province of Prince Edward Island pleaded guilty last week in a Georgetown court to underreporting their landings and received relatively small fines, the CBC reports.

Jason Ahearn, James Gavin, Earl MacRae and Jeffery MacLeod are among 13 harvesters who were charged following a Department of Fisheries and Oceans investigation called "Operation Gannet" conducted in 2019 and 2020. In most cases, the fines amounted to CAD 1,500 ($1,166) per offense. 

The investigation involved comparing landing estimates made by harvesters to those recorded by monitors. In at least one case, the difference was as great as 20,000 pounds. 

Judge Nancy Orr expressed frustration at the low fines set out in the sentencing guidelines, saying they aren't much of a disincentive if someone ends up being able to sell 20,000 lbs of snow crab that didn't get reported as counting toward their quota.

The remarks were in relation to the sentencing of Gavin, who was reported to have an extensive record, with convictions dating back to 1995, according to CBC. He was fined CAD 2,500.

Defense lawyer Clifford Hood had argued that his clients failed to fill out the proper paperwork but maintained that they didn't exceed their overall share of snow crab quota. He said it's not unusual for crab crews to shift quota from boat to boat.

title: StarKist claims price-fixing didn’t extend to private label tuna sold in Costco, Walmart, Target
content:
StarKist & Co has claimed that its participation in the decade-old, US sector-wide tuna price-fixing scandal extended only to its branded products and not its tuna sold under private label. However, a judge overseeing class-action civil suits against the company has struck down a request to limit the scope of the litigation due to that argument.

The Reston, Virginia-based tuna canner, owned by South Korea's Dongwon Enterprise, continues to defend itself from lawsuits from customers who say they were damaged from price-fixing that reportedly occurred from 2011 to 2013. In 2018, the canner pleaded guilty to criminal charges and was fined $100 million. But as the civil suits linger on, the company has claimed that although it admitted to price-fixing, the scope of the conspiracy was limited and there is no proof that private-label tuna sold under retailers' brands such as Walmart's Great Value, Target's Market Pantry and Costco's Kirkland was part of the price fixing.

"Defendants argue their private label tuna products comprise a 'discrete segment' of their business (on average about 13% of their net sales)," Dana Sabraw, the chief judge of the Southern District of California, recounted in a July 19 opinion.

StarKist had asked for Sabraw to grant the company summary judgment, which would have tossed the price-fixing claims involving private label and limited potential damages in the suits. But Sabraw turned down the request. She ruled that the company's 2018 guilty plea didn't address the matter explicitly.

"Because the plea agreements reference tuna products in general terms, do not specify any particular product and do not speak to the scope of the conspiracy, the court declines to find that defendants admitted in their plea agreements to a price-fixing conspiracy that included private label," she wrote.

However, the contention that StarKist's private label sales made up a distinct market separate from its branded products is one for a potential future trial, the judge added.

"But even assuming defendants’ premise was correct and there were two markets, plaintiffs have presented evidence of a linkage between those markets sufficient to withstand defendants’ motion," the judge wrote.

The tuna price-fixing lawsuits, which also involve Thai Union Group's Chicken of the Sea International and Bumble Bee Foods, were previously being litigated in the courtroom of judge Janis Sammartino but she recused herself from the case late last year shortly after it emerged that one of her family members owned stock in two of the plaintiffs who say they were damaged by the tuna canners' price-fixing.

title: British Columbia man fined as part of Dungeness poaching case
content:
A man from the province of British Columbia will pay an additional CAD 6,000 ($4,634.81) after Canadian officials seized his boat, which was allegedly used for illegal Dungeness crab harvesting, North Shore News reports.

Judge Lyndsay Smith fined Sammy Alvin-Raymond John Williams, 32, of Gold River, B.C., on July 13, in North Vancouver provincial court.

Smith found Williams guilty in November of several fishing offenses including setting gear in Burrard Inlet during a closed time, fishing for Dungeness crab in waters during a closed time, fishing without a license and possessing crab in contravention of the Federal Fisheries Act.

Fisheries officers netted three men on fisheries charges following a high-speed chase of a fishing boat in Burrard Inlet on the night of March 1, 2020.

The trio had been fishing at night, with no navigation lights on, using unmarked crab traps, a prosecutor said. When officers boarded the boat, they found 250 Dungeness crabs as well as four commercial crab traps. 

The judge noted that Williams, a member of the Muchalaht First Nation, lives in a remote community where employment is limited.

Another man accused in the case, Scott Stanley Matthew Steer, was sentenced to a six-month jail term and lifetime crab fishing ban for his repeated and flagrant flouting of fisheries laws, including five offenses stemming from the same incident.

A third man aboard the boat, Christopher Robin Shill, was fined  CAD 5,000 for obstruction of a fisheries officer in connection with the case in December.

content:

Chile revokes three Nova Austral salmon farm licenses for overproducing, levies fine of nearly $1m

Chile's federal environmental agency has revoked licenses for three of Nova Austral's salmon farming sites in the Magallanes region and fined the company nearly a million dollars over charges that it exceeded its production authority and damaged the seabed at one of the locations.

Demand drop in overheated whitefish market would be 'no bad thing'

As inflation on whitefish raw material gets passed through to the end consumer in the UK, a drop in demand is likely. "In some ways, that's probably no bad thing, just to take the heat out of the market," said Ryan Scatterty, whose family controls the chilled and frozen coated seafood specialist Thistle Seafoods.

Espersen in talks to sell Russian plant

Denmark's A. Espersen is in talks to sell its plant in Russia, which was supplying the Filet-O-Fish to McDonald's restaurants before the US foodservice giant pulled out. 

Cargill investment part of Multi's shift from salmon' commodity traders to marketers'

Chilean salmon farmer Multi X's selling of just under 25% to US agribusiness giant Cargill is part of the company's shift to a value-added focus, said its chief financial officer.

Apex Frozen Foods, one of India's largest shrimp processors, aims to ramp up production at its newest plant in Andhra Pradesh after two years operating mostly below half capacity.
