title: Chile revokes three Nova Austral salmon farm licenses for overproducing, levies fine of nearly $1m
content:
Chile's federal environmental agency has revoked licenses for three of Nova Austral's salmon farming sites in the Magallanes region and fined the company nearly a million dollars over charges that it exceeded its production authority and damaged the seabed at one of the locations.

The Superintendence of the Environment (SMA) said in a press release issued Wednesday (July 6) that this is the first time it has revoked an environmental permit under new rules, noting that it was left with little option.

"The decision is adopted after sanctioning procedures, with various evidentiary measures such as sediment analysis, sampling and underwater filming, proved that the company caused environmental damage in the Alberto de Agostini de Magallanes National Park, after exceeding the maximum authorized production in the Cockburn 14, Cockburn 23 and Aracena 10 Salmon Farming Centers," SMA said.

Nova Austral produced 15% more than allowed at its Cockburn 14 farm between the months of October 2015 and May 2017, 30% more than allowed at its Cockburn 23 farm between January 2016 and November 2017, and 25% more than allowed at its Aracena 10 farm during a 2016-2017 cycle, according to the press release.

The SMA said it applied a fine of CLP 900m ($929,176) to the company for artificially altering the seabed of the Aracena 14 site near the city of Punta Arenas.

An environmental court must now review the case. 

"[T]he SMA was forced to make a historic decision, delivering a clear signal," said Emanuel Ibarra, Chile's superintendent of the environment. "It is not possible to generate these levels of overproduction that cause environmental damage in protected areas such as the Alberto de Agostini National Park. We are facing a persistent offender, who already has a series of serious procedures in the SMA. With this, we hope that the owner can improve his environmental behavior in all the centers that he still has."

He added: "I want to emphasize that it is the first time that an environmental permit has been revoked since the creation of the new environmental institutionality, and now the Third Environmental Court must resolve the consultation process, that is, whether or not to approve it".

The case originates from inspections made in response to a complaint filed by the National Committee for the Defense of Flora and Fauna (CODEFF) and a complaint filed with the National Fisheries and Aquaculture Service (SERNAPESCA), according to the SMA press release.

SERNAPESCA national director Fernando Naranjo said it was a documentary review that resulted in the detection of overproduction. On-site inspections then detected new irregularities.

"As a state auditing institution, we ratify our commitment to continue the face-to-face, documentary and remote control of these centers, convinced that aquaculture is an activity of relevance for the country that must be developed in harmony with the environment to consecrate its sustainable development," Naranjo said.

title: Argentina’s red shrimp fishery closes in on MSC
content:
Argentina's red shrimp fishery has moved closer to achieving the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certification with the country's institute of fisheries, INIDEP, developing a limit reference point for the stock.

This is the point at which fishing is no longer considered sustainable, and a step that is a very much-needed requirement for MSC certification.

"It would serve as a trigger threshold for implementing immediate measures to reduce the fishing effort defined by the Federal Fisheries Council (FFC)," stated INIDEP. "Said point consists of taking 60% of the average number of shrimp surveyed during the INIDEP's March campaigns as the trigger for these measures."

Also, Argentina's FFC incorporated an abundance criterion in the decision to open and close fishing zones. At the same time, the country's undersecretary of fisheries, through its "supervision directorate", has achieved almost total coverage in unloading inspections, with barely 6% presenting infractions. 

According to the non-governmental organization CeDePesca, "all these developments strengthen the prospects of having a sustainable shrimp stock and, therefore, increase the probability of obtaining the international recognition that the European and US markets increasingly require, through independent certification".

Modifications to management measures of the resource have also been adopted, a capture by unit of effort (CPUE) criterion that aids in the decision-making on opening and closing zones to fishing. INIDEP recommended considering a different CPUE limit for each month, basing the numbers on historical data to avoid recruitment overfishing.

Finally, although the overall shrimp stock abundance has decreased since its peak in 2017, it has not reached concerning levels yet. The INIDEP report emphasized that "the population yield has been maintained at excellent levels, around 200,000 [metric] tons in recent years".

title: New CEO Rafferty lifts lid on ‘black box that is Cermaq’
content:
BERGEN, Norway -- Every few months there is a flurry of activity on the Oslo Stock Exchange as the largest Atlantic salmon producers in the world file their quarterly financial results in quick succession. Mowi. SalMar. Leroy Seafood Group. Grieg Seafood. Bakkafrost.

NASF 2022: If cod is the new salmon, is pollock the new cod?; Chances of full NE Atlantic pelagic quota sharing agreement ‘slim’

But not Cermaq Group, still -- at the time of writing -- the second-largest salmon farmer in the world by volume before the fulfillment of SalMar's deal for NTS.

Since its acquisition by Japanese conglomerate Mitsubishi Corporation in 2014, Cermaq has been a highly private company, keeping its results firmly to itself while holding them up for scrutiny against those of its public competition.

Still, times change, and new CEO Steven Rafferty -- appointed to the post to replace the outgoing Geir Molvik in March this year -- was present at the North Atlantic Seafood Forum (NASF) in Bergen, Norway last week to offer a little more color on the company's activities.

"We don't normally communicate our results at all," Rafferty explained. "I'm presenting a bit of information today that's perhaps more than Cermaq would normally provide because I think it's good to open the black box that is Cermaq for many people."

Altogether, Cermaq produced 223,400 metric tons of salmon last year, he said, a figure that consisted of 22,900t out of the Canadian province of British Columbia, 98,400t from Norway, and 102,100t in Chile.

While not willing to offer an exact figure for Cermaq's regional margins, Rafferty showed how the company's performance held up versus a rolling 12-month average of its peers in each farming country (below).

"So if you look at Norway, we're consistently above the peer group, that being Mowi, Grieg, SalMar and NRS [Norway Royal Salmon] -- and it's consistently above. But you can never say never, that this won't be maintained, and we're very practical and humble about this because we're constantly trying to improve our results and not be complacent."

Then in Canada, Cermaq is once again generally outperforming the profit margins of its neighbors, albeit with far more fluctuation year-to-year.

"The one you can see is very different is Chile, where we were a very underperforming operation for many years, going back to 2015 actually," said Rafferty. "We were well behind the competition, and it's only in the last few years we caught up. But Chile is a constant challenge."

For 2021, the group as a whole reported sales of $1.25 billion, and a profit of NOK 2.6bn ($263 million), the largest in the company's history, fuelled by "the biggest ever margin in Norway" alongside the turnaround in Chile.

"But just to put it into perspective, for Mitsubishi NOK 2.6bn puts us at only 3% of the total Mitsubishi result," Rafferty continued. "They're very happy with Cermaq, so they want us to grow, they see it as a big growth industry and a megatrend."

Noting wryly that Japan's insistence on a mere two weeks of holidays for employees gives Mitsubishi staff "a lot of time to visit us", Rafferty added that Cermaq was unusual in the Mitsubishi portfolio due to its lack of a Tokyo HQ.

"And the reason is because Norway is an innovation hub of salmon; I think the other countries have to step up to come close to Norway, but we have a consolidated R&D team, technical experts, all sorts of scientists based in Norway that support the global operations of Cermaq, and Mitsubishi recognize they could not fill that gap in Tokyo."

Norway regulation slick, Canada' extremely stressful'

Taking into account Cermaq's rare perspective in salmon farming nations across the globe, Rafferty feels criticism of Norway's aquaculture regulations is seriously misplaced.

BC salmon farmers satisfied with gov’t reprieve, license renewals

"A lot of people complain about the traffic light system, but for me, it's extremely easy to understand, well thought through, and it's been done a lot in consultation with the industry," the Cermaq CEO shared. "So the current regulations are not loved by everyone, but in my view they're a standard-bearer compared to a lot of other countries."

As if to illustrate the point he turned to the current, difficult situation in Canada, where the government has taken a stance against the salmon industry two years ago, ordering an end to conventional cage farming in British Columbia by 2025.

"Right now, we're waiting for an announcement any day about if the licenses of ours or our competitors will be renewed in Canada," Rafferty said. "It's an extremely stressful time for our colleagues in Canada."

"It's an extremely intolerable and unacceptable stance that they [the Canadian federal government] have taken against an industry that's reasonably sustainable. Certain politicians are listening to NGOs who just want the industry closed."

Fortunately, from Cermaq's point of view, the firm's Canadian licenses are believed to be among those renewed later the very same afternoon as Rafferty's appearance at NASF, for a period of two years.

Mowi and Grieg, two of the other major salmon farmers operating in the province, each issued optimistic yet guarded statements as they await further details on the terms of the renewals, and disclosure on whether all existing licenses will be included.

Chilean regulations' not suitable for purpose'

Lastly, Rafferty broke down what he considers to be some of the industry's misconceptions about the state of Chilean aquaculture. 

"There is a misunderstanding of the Chilean industry in my view," said Rafferty. "I've got many comments from other farmers, other suppliers that say that Chilean companies just make a mess of it in Chile. Of course, I'm one of those farmers, so I take it a little bit to heart, but it's not true."

Chilean salmon farms, he said, are in form and function almost identical to their counterparts in Norway.

Cermaq CEO Steven Rafferty presenting at NASF 2022. Credit: Dan Gibson/ Undercurrent News

"It's got great natural advantages in Chile, but the issue is the regulations are not suitable for purpose," he explained.

"I think a lot of people in Chile would say we grew too quickly at certain times in an unsustainable way. There were ISA [infectious salmon anemia] issues, there was an earthquake, volcanic eruptions, algae blooms, all sorts of external factors, and we grew a little bit too quick." 

"And what the government tried to do with good intentions is put restrictions on the growth to make it sustainable, but what they've managed to do is make regulations that are a bit contradictory to each other and it makes it very, very hard."

According to Rafferty, certain regulations are directly contradictory to other rules, meaning the Chilean industry faces higher costs trying to comply.

"And then in the western or northern hemisphere, you'll read that another Chilean company was fined for doing this or that, but it's nothing intentional -- it's a misinterpretation of the legislation," the Cermaq CEO continued. "Even the government bodies and the Chilean companies interpret it differently."

Following the appointment of the new president, Gabriel Boric, earlier this year, Rafferty said that he hoped a new, less opaque set of rules could be established.

"Cermaq will definitely help to support anything that can be learned from Norway to make the whole thing more simple. Chile's dear to my heart and I'd really like to say in 10 years' time that Chile has a much more sustainable way of working without the current legislation."

title: Western Pacific council committee pans proposed expansion of national monument
content:
A committee serving the Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council (WPRFMC) has rejected a proposal to ban fishing within waters under its remit west of Hawaii and effectively turn it into the largest marine protected area in the world. 

The WPRFMC panel that heard the proposal, its scientific and statistical committee (SSC), dismissed the plan to expand the Pacific Remote Islands Marine National Monument (PRIMNM) as unnecessary and scientifically dubious.

The Pacific Remote Islands Coalition (PRIC) initially made the recommendation for the monument's expansion, saying it would help fit the goal of US president Joe Biden's America the Beautiful initiative to conserve 30% of US lands and waters by 2030, according to a statement released by WPRFMC officials. 

Map of the proposed expansion of the US western Pacific Economic Exclusion Zone courtesy of Pacific Remote Islands Coalition

 

Self-defined as a community-driven effort to expand the protections for PRIMNM, the coalition wants to extend it to cover waters surrounding Howard and Baker Islands, Kingman Reef and Palmyra Atoll from 50 to 200 nautical miles, council officials said.

The PRIC coalition fears that mining and general human interference, including fishing, would further harm threatened, endangered, and critically endangered species including sharks, rays, whales, seabirds and turtles, and more, according to its website.

The unprotected areas of PRIMNM contain 98 seamounts, known to be ecological hot spots with yet-to-be-discovered species, according to the website. Many Native Hawaiians support protecting those areas, said Sol Kaho'ohalahala, a Native Hawaiian Elder.

"The Pacific Remote Islands hold precious connections to our past and promise for our future as Pacific peoples. In the same way these waters are at the nexus of cross-cultural voyaging pathways across Polynesia, they likewise are an intersection of climate change mitigation, cultural practice and scientific discovery. We must protect these waters," said Kaho'ohalahala, a PRIC representative said in a statement.

However, SSC members said that the PRIC proposal doesn't make sense scientifically, doesn’t protect diverse habitats and it creates unbalanced regional representation, leading to strong socioeconomic impacts that undermine biodiversity goals, council officials said.

The SSC suggested the council request a comprehensive evaluation of the unintended consequences of the proposed expansion and that any measures be evaluated through a transparent and public process prior to implementation.

SSC members added that unintended consequences of the expansion range from the displacement of US fisheries by competing foreign fisheries to a reduced supply of US-caught fish to the American Samoa tuna cannery run by StarKist & Co,

A marine ecology researcher, University of California professor Douglas McCauley, told a council panel that deep-sea miners searching for polymetallic nodules -- also known as manganese nodules -- will hurt Pacific fisheries, including in waters near Hawaii, if the area isn't protected, the Hawaii Tribune-Herald reports.

All of the US' Economic Exclusion Zones. Graphic courtesy of National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration

The mining and its noise will dislodge sections of previously unexcavated ocean floor, causing plumes, and plumes created by wastewater dumping from mining ships that could contain copper, cadmium, iron, cobalt, chromium, nickel and zinc could contaminate fisheries, McCauley said.

He said computer modeling done by researchers from the University of Hawaii and Massachusetts Institute of Technology to determine the plumes' impact could affect 8% to 16% of US fisheries, including encroachment of 11.3% into skipjack tuna fisheries, the Tribune-Herald reports.

The SSC noted, however, that the western Pacific is the largest managed ocean area (~1.7 million square nautical miles) in the US, and more than 60% of its waters already meet America the Beautiful criteria.

Their region alone already meets 29% of the initiative’s goal, councilofficials said.

PRIMNM was established in 2009 by US president George W. Bush and expanded in 2014 by president Barack Obama under the Antiquities Act.

title: NTSB: Autopilot malfunction doesn’t relieve US captain of fault in shrimper sinking
content:
A captain’s decision to leave the wheelhouse of a shrimping vessel unattended while transiting a river in the US state of Georgia on autopilot is what led to its grounding and sinking, the National Transportation Safety Board declared in an eight-page report issued this week. 

The 78.7-foot-long, wooden-hulled, single-propeller commercial fishing vessel the Sage Catherine Lane was on its way to harvest offshore when it left anchorage in Cumberland Sound and began heading down the St. Marys River on June 9, 2021, according to the report, which was covered recently by the shipping news service gCaptain.

The location of the sinking of the Sage Catherine Lane in June 2021. Image from NTSB report.

The vessel grounded on the north jetty of the St. Marys entrance channel, south of Cumberland Island. The three-person crew abandoned the vessel, after it began to flood, and were rescued by a nearby good Samaritan vessel.

The Sage Catherine Lane broke apart and sunk following a thunderstorm three days later. It was holding about 2,300 gallons of fuel, engine oil and hydraulic oil on board. 

A crewmember sustained a minor injury during the hasty departure and the vessel was declared a total loss at $1 million, according to gCaptain.

The report described how problems had earlier been detected with the autopilot system and a rudder on the vessel. The captain had left the wheelhouse to answer a phone call  but, shortly after, he felt the vessel turn abruptly to port, it said. Returning to the wheelhouse, the captain attempted to turn away from the north jetty, but he was too late.

"Autopilot use does not relieve the operator of responsibility to conduct a proper navigation watch," the report said. "Use of autopilot should not be a justification for an operator to leave the wheelhouse or bridge unattended in confined waters. Navigating in channels and harbors requires quicker reaction times due to traffic, currents encountered, and frequent course changes, and more rudder due to slower speeds. Therefore, autopilot use is often discouraged or prohibited in a harbor entrance or narrow channel."

title: Daily recap, May 9: Norway waits to pass on higher cod prices; Thai Union names new chair
content:
Here's a recap of the daily seafood news from Monday, May 9: 

Cod becoming 'new salmon' as Norway waits for higher prices to hit consumers

It’s been a strange year so far for cod processors in Norway; demand from Europe has never been higher, but issues with exchange rates, freight costs, and quota cuts are squeezing company margins like never before. For Insula’s chief operations officer for whitefish, Morten Hyldborg Jensen, it's proving a headache.

Amid record Q1 sales, Thai Union CEO adds chairman role after father’s exit

Thirapong Chansiri, the current president and CEO of Thai Union Group, has been named as chairman of the company's board of directors following the resignation of his father Kraisorn, who was recently fined for insider trading.

Last imports of Russian king, snow crab trickle into US market

The US effort to import Russian king crab may have seemed red hot in January and February -- before a presidentially ordered ban went into effect -- but shipments have since slowed down significantly, reveals the latest update of seafood trade data by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Spain's offshore fleet 'strangled' by high fuel costs, could stop operating soon

High energy prices and fuel costs are beginning to suffocate Spain's offshore fleet, said the general assembly of the Spanish fishing confederation, known as Cepesca. The sector may have to stop operating before the end of June if support is not provided, Javier Garat, president of the European fishing industry body Europeche and the International Coalition of Fisheries Association, told Undercurrent News.

Mexico's Del Pacifico pushes blue shrimp to Europe with Frime tie-up

A Mexican wild-caught shrimp company will bring its homespun story of small-scale artisanal fishers to Europe through a tie-up with Spain's Frime, one of Europe's largest processors of yellowfin tuna steaks.

title: Amid record Q1 sales, Thai Union CEO adds chairman role after father’s exit
content:
Thirapong Chansiri, the current president and CEO of Thai Union Group, has been named as chairman of the company's board of directors following the resignation of his father Kraisorn who was recently fined for insider trading.

Thai Union said in a statement that the company has also appointed Nakorn Niruttinanon as a company director and Kirati Assakul as "lead independent director" and vice chairman of the board.

The vacancies occurred at the global seafood giant in April when the Stock and Exchange Commission of Thailand fined nine individuals at the company, including several senior executives, for insider trading in an incident that reportedly occurred in 2017.

In addition to the new board members, Thai Union announced record-high sales in the first three months of 2022 as prices improved, volumes increased and exchange rates worked in the group's favor. 

Thai Union's revenue rose 16.5% year-on-year to THB 36.3 billion ($1.05bn). At the same time, however, the group's earnings before interest and taxes fell 17.1% year-on-year to THB 2.018bn mainly due to losses at its US restaurant unit investment, Red Lobster Seafood Company.

"Red Lobster’s operations in 1Q22 was at THB 335m share of loss (THB 243m loss from operations and THB 92m loss from lease accounting adjustment)," Thai Union said.

However, the group said that stronger shelf-stable seafood demand worked in its favor.

"The ambient seafood business sales growth was thanks to higher tuna sales across all regions., after last year’s normalization from a high base in 1Q20, which was from pantry-loading during the first wave of COVID-19, as well as higher selling prices," it said.

The company also enjoyed a recovery in frozen and chilled seafood sales.

"The frozen and chilled seafood business continued recovering from strong demand of food service businesses after facing impacts from restaurant closures since 1Q20 during the pandemic, as well as from higher selling prices," the company said.

The pet food and value-added seafood businesses also remained strong it said.

"The PetCare and value-added business continued to deliver strong PetCare sales growth from new and existing products and a broadening portfolio of new customers, as well as higher sales of value-added products and packaging businesses," it said.

It added that inflation continues to be a major challenge for the company.

"We faced unprecedented levels of inflation in Q1 2022, both from key costs and ongoing logistics issues. We saw total impact of THB 710m from freight price increase in Q1 2022, vs ~THB 200m in Q1 2021,"

In order to compensate, the group plans to increase the efficiency of its inventory management and reap benefits from economies of scale, better negotiate to pass on some costs, increase automation and better manage its own expenses, it said.

title: Untitled
content:
A Dutch beam trawler faces a DKK 527,000 ($74,508) fine after it was caught fishing in Danish waters in an area protected for flatfish, according to the Danish Fisheries Agency.

The fisheries agency said the vessel was caught fishing in a "plaice box" in Rodspaettekassen, an area along Denmark's west coast protected from large fishing vessels. According to the agency, the vessel was caught last autumn fishing in the plaice box with illegal gear, its AIS signal turned off and its fishing logbook littered with errors. 

The case was assessed together with the European Commission and other authorities before its handing over to the police. 

It comes after another Dutch beam trawler was fined DKK 375,000 by Danish police for fishing with illegal gear in April. 

"It is completely unacceptable that Dutch beam trawlers sail in Danish waters and fish illegally," said Rasmus Prehn, Denmark's minister of fisheries. "Therefore, I am very pleased that the Danish Fisheries Agency, after a long period of hard work, has once again got hold of another Dutch beam trawler and reported him to the police for serious violations of the fisheries legislation."

title: US surimi maker Shining Ocean fined $56,000 for COVID death
content:
The Sumner, Washington, US-based surimi maker Shining Ocean has been fined $56,000 for a COVID-19 death due to what state authorities called knowingly putting workers at risk of exposure to the virus.

The Washington Department of Labor and Industries (DLI) issued the fine due to a Nov. 4, 2021 staff meeting where it said the company was "purposely ignoring the workplace coronavirus safety requirements … [which] resulted in 16 workers becoming infected, one of whom died".

Only three or four of the 23 attendees were reportedly wearing a mask, and "the president of the company wasn't one of them", DLI said in a statement. It did not identify the president. 

The company also failed to systematically track or verify worker vaccination status, and when asked, the owner, who was not identified in the statement, told DLI inspectors that "he didn’t feel like there was a reason to", the agency said.

From the Shining Ocean website.

"Employees said the company president told them it's their personal choice whether or not to wear a mask," DLI officials said. 

DLI assistant director Craig Blackwood placed the blame for the death of the worker, whose name was not disclosed, squarely upon the company's management.

"This happened when COVID rates and hospitalizations were high and the requirement to wear masks was still in place," Blackwood said in the statement. "Management got complacent about workplace safety and it cost a worker his life."

A Shining Ocean representative declined to comment on the case when reached by Undercurrent News.

The company did not appeal the citation and paid the fine in full. That money goes into the state's workers' compensation supplemental pension fund, helping workers and families of those who have died on the job, officials said.

The Nov. 4 meeting came two days after Undercurrent reported that Aquamar Holdings, which is backed by Huron Capital and Salt Creek Capital, was negotiating a deal for Shining Ocean with then-owner True World Group.  

Undercurrent reported that True World -- which owns the largest sushi sector distributor in North America, True World Foods  -- completed the deal on Dec. 10, 2021. It also sold International Seafoods of Alaska to Silver Bay Seafoods in early 2020. 

With the deal still pending, Aquamar did not own the company at the time of the incident, Daryl Gormley, CEO of Aquimar, told Undercurrent.

True World did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Today, the company is in compliance with all required pandemic safeguards, Gormley said.

Founded in 1985, Shining Ocean sells in retail under the Kanimi, Seafarer and Crab Smart Natural brands and pre-made seafood salads and sushi rolls offered in delis and restaurants.

Aquamar's acquisition of the surimi maker consolidated its position as the second-largest surimi supplier in North America after Trident Seafoods. As of December, the sector had six North American players: Trident's Minnesota plant and Ontario, Canada's Ocean Foods, and four plants in Washington: Maruha Nichiro-owned Trans-Ocean Products; Nippon Suisan Kaisha-owned King & Prince Seafood; and Sugiyo USA, owned by a Japanese group with the same name.

title: Editor’s choice: China rejects Ecuador shrimp; Sanctioned Russian oligarch linked to PE selling East Coast
content:
Neil Ramsden, EMEA editor with Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week.

Our most-read story of last week was the news that hundreds of containers of frozen shrimp from Ecuador have likely been rejected by Chinese authorities due to positive tests for COVID-19 in samples from packaging, according to a senior executive with one of the country's largest shrimp importers.

Also published recently after weeks of work was a special report conducted with help from the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project. Undercurrent found that a Russian billionaire just sanctioned by Canada and Australia is linked to tens of millions of dollars in transactions with the US private equity currently trying to sell East Coast Seafood Group, one of the country’s largest lobster and scallop processors.

After being fined for insider trading, Kraisorn Chansiri -- the chairman of Thai Union Group -- resigned, as did Chuan Tangchansiri, a director of the company. 

In India, outbreaks of disease, not least white spot syndrome, have blighted the start of the first harvest season of the year and caused a temporary glut of smaller sizes on the market, multiple sources confirmed to Undercurrent.

The US state of Maine has terminated the applications submitted by American Aquafarms to build a closed pen Atlantic salmon farm in an area of water near Acadia National Park. The reason given was that the company "failed to fulfill its legal obligation to demonstrate an available source of fish to be cultivated at its proposed salmon farms in Frenchman Bay".

AquaBounty Technologies, the US company famous for growing the world's first genetically engineered salmon, confirmed in an email to Undercurrent that it has discussed selling conventional Atlantic salmon eggs to American Aquafarms, after the news was revealed by the rejection from Maine's Department of Marine Resources.

A group of creditors of Peru's China Fishery Group (CFG) continues to work to complete the legal procedures necessary for them to take control of the fishmeal and fish oil maker so that it can emerge from a nearly six-year-old bankruptcy proceeding in the US. However, legal actions from Sun Securities, which appears to be an affiliate of the Hong Kong-based Pacific Andes International Holdings, CFG's parent company, appear to be holding up the resolution of the CFG case, US court records show.

Market analyst Ernst & Young, in its latest report on the Norwegian aquaculture sector, found there are currently 88,529 metric tons worth of biomass attached to development licenses issued by the country's government in the pipeline.

Finally, this week marks the return of Seafood Expo Global, the world's largest seafood trade fair, from which Undercurrent will be reporting in force. Last week, the event had about 1,560 exhibits registered – 77% of its 2019 record show. Stay tuned for stories from the show all week.

title: Maine terminates closed salmon pen application over egg sourcing issues
content:
The US state of Maine's  Department of Marine Resources (DMR) announced late Wednesday (April 20) that it has terminated the applications submitted by American Aquafarms to build a closed pen Atlantic salmon farm in an area of water near Acadia National Park.

The reason given by DMR in a short statement is that the company "failed to fulfill its legal obligation to demonstrate an available source of fish to be cultivated at its proposed salmon farms in Frenchman Bay." American Aquafarms had proposed to source from a hatchery reported to be managed by AquaBounty, in Newfoundland and Labrador (NL), Canada, according to DMR.

"Additionally, American Aquafarms failed to provide documentation demonstrating that the proposed source of fish/eggs could meet genetic requirements in law (§6071(4))," the statement read, concluding: "No further action will be taken on these applications."

American Aquafarms can submit an entirely new application, but a restart would likely add years to the permitting process, sources told Undercurrent News.

American Aquafarms has faced opposition and controversy almost since it first announced its plans in late 2020 to build a salmon farm with as many as 30 pens, each 150-feet wide, off the coast of Maine's Mount Desert Island. The US company had hoped to have all of its applications completed by the summer of 2021 and, by 2024, be growing as much as 30,000 metric tons of salmon annually.

A map, used in a presentation given to the Gouldsboro, Maine, town government, shows the two locations where American Aquafarms intends to place its salmon netpens. The prospective salmon farms are marked as green boxes. The other locations marked in green denote national park land.

The company was established by the founders of Norcod, a Norwegian cod farmer, including CEO Mikael Roenes, who was convicted in early 2008 in Norway of multiple counts of fraud, forgery and gross financial infidelity, as reported by Undercurrent.

In November, the town of Gouldsboro, Maine, voted in a special election to approve a six-month moratorium against all large-scale finfish farms in the area, at least temporarily delaying American Aquafarms' plans.

Just weeks earlier, the company announced that it had hired Keith Decker to serve as its new CEO, taking him away from Blue Harvest Fisheries, a scallop and groundfish harvester and processor based in New Bedford, Massachusetts.

On Tuesday, Gouldsboro’s planning board held a public hearing on a proposed ordinance to create a local aquaculture licensing program, in addition to the state, which currently processes all aquaculture projects along the coast, the Bangor Daily News reported.

Company was notified of hatchery concerns in September

American Aquafarms has known since at least September 2021 that its plan for sourcing smolts was not okay with DMR.

That's when Marcy Nelson, director of DMR's aquaculture division, notified the company in a letter, a copy of which was obtained by Undercurrent, that the AquaBounty facility listed as the proposed source of Atlantic salmon (Salmon salar) eggs or smolts was "not currently considered a “qualified source/hatchery” in accordance with standards defined in [regulations].

"MDMR has never reviewed or provided an import permit for Atlantic salmon originating from AquaBounty," the letter said. "With limited exceptions for import into approved quarantine facilities, the commissioner may not issue an importation permit for salmonid finfish that do not meet the requirements of Chapter 24."

It's not clear that AquaBounty is producing any salmon or smolts in NL, though it maintains a hatchery in the Canadian province of Prince Edward Island that is producing genetically engineered salmon for grow out in another facility in the US state of Indiana, as previously reported by Undercurrent. 

An AquaBounty spokesperson directed Undercurrent to a company website that lists only the Rollo Bay, PEI, operation, the Indiana facility and a future facility planned for the US state of Ohio. 

Keith Decker, CEO of American Aquafarms. Photograph courtesy of American Aquafarms.

Crystal Canney, executive director of Protect Maine's Fishing Heritage Foundation, one of several groups to formed the coalition Frenchman Bay United in opposition to the salmon farming project, said Thursday that her members "couldn't be more pleased with this result."

"This is a blow to industrial scale aquaculture in the water and it will result in protecting Maine's future," she said, adding: "There is a lot more work to be done so this doesn't happen anywhere along the Maine coast."

Henry Sharpe, president of Frenchman Bay United, said his coalition was "grateful that DMR came to this conclusion" and said they are now asking American Aquafarms to "end this ill-conceived project now".

Undercurrent has reached out to a spokesperson for American Aquafarms but had not yet received a comment by press time.

title: Camanchaca’s fishing unit fined $14,700 for shrimp bycatch
content:
Chilean fishing and aquaculture regulator Sernapesca has fined Pesquera Camanchaca some $14,700 for exceeding the amount of dwarf shrimp it is allowed to take as bycatch when fishing for anchovy.

According to the news service Aqua, a Chilean court in the city of Iquique accepted the complaint that alleges that Camanchaca violated the country's principal law on fishing and aquaculture. The company's vessel Abrimer reportedly landed 65.5 metric tons of anchovy and 14.5t of dwarf shrimp on June 26, 2021. The shrimp landing constituted 18.1% of the catch, over the maximum amount allowed amount of 3%, or about 5t, the complaint states.

The skipper of the boat was fined $2,072.

title: Thai Union chairman Kraisorn Chansiri resigns after insider trading fines
content:
Kraisorn Chansiri, the chairman of Thai Union Group, has resigned weeks after being fined for insider trading, the Stock and Exchange Commission of Thailand (SEC) announced.

Additionally, Chuan Tangchansiri, a director of the company, has also resigned, the SEC said in a filing.

In a statement published online, Thai Union, one of the seafood industry's biggest giants, said it has "seriously conducted [its own] fact-finding investigation and found no evidence indicating any insider-trading activities." Thai Union said it "would like to emphasize that [it] has adhered to the good corporate governance of the listed company and always continued to maintain our corporate governance standard including uplift and update our corporate governance system to be aligned with international standards."

Earlier this month, the SEC announced it had fined nine Thai Union officials for suspected insider trading.

Those fined include the group's chairman Chansiri, fined THB 3.43 million $102,348). The SEC also fined eight others: Dispol Chansiri (THB  551,809); Chan Hon Kit (THB 2.41m); Chan Tin Shu (THB 891,809); Cai Nguyen Chu (THB 806,809); Chuan Tangchansiri (THB 1.7m); Chen Yu Zhen (THB 551,809), Chan Hon Hung (THB 2.16m) and  Hui Pui Wah (THB 861,809).

According to the agency, Kraisorn Chansiri, Chan Hon Kit and Tangchansiri obtained inside information about Thai Union's third-quarter 2017 performance, which saw a "significant increase in profits". Others then bought shares or benefitted from them, the SEC said. All nine will be prohibited from being a director or executive in a securities issuing company or securities company for at least a year, the SEC said.

title: Here we go again … Another lawsuit filed in US to end Atlantic Ocean fishing ban
content:
The first legal step has been taken to again challenge, before the US Supreme Court, prohibitions against commercial fishing in a nearly 5,000-square mile part of the Atlantic Ocean.

The Pacific Legal Foundation (PLF), a law firm that does pro bono work for libertarian causes, on Tuesday (April 12) filed a 41-page lawsuit in the US District Court for the District of New Jersey that charges president Joe Biden, commerce secretary Gina Raimondo and interior secretary Deb Haaland with exceeding their authority under the Antiquities Act of 1906 when the White House issued presidential proclamation 10287 in early October.

That’s the executive order (EO) that reinstated the commercial fishing prohibitions contained in former president Barack Obama’s September 2016 proclamation, EO 9496, which designated 4,913 square miles of water and submerged lands where the Atlantic Ocean meets the continental shelf as the Northeast Canyons and Seamounts Marine National Monument, as reported by Undercurrent News.

The triangular space is about 150 miles southeast of Cape Cod, Massachusetts, in the fishing rich Georges Bank area of the North Atlantic Ocean, and is reported to be the home to at least 54 species of deep-sea corals as well as toothed whales, such as the endangered sperm whale, and many species of beaked whales. Fin and sei whales, two additional endangered species, have also been observed in the canyon and seamount area.

Obama’s order allowed fishing for red crab and lobster to continue until Sept. 15, 2023, and recreational fishing to continue indefinitely.

In the game of executive order ping pong, Biden’s order reversed EO 10049, issued by former president Donald Trump, which reversed Obama’s prohibitions against commercial fishing in June 2020.

Biden’s and Obama's EOs were seen as particularly bad news for the harvesters of swordfish, big-eyed tuna, yellowfin tuna and mahi-mahi, who reported having lost millions of dollars and seeing their fleet shrunk by dozens of vessels as a result of 9496.

PLF’s suit is filed on behalf of Patrick Fehily, a New Jersey-based commercial fisherman with four boats harvesting scallops, tuna and swordfish, and David Malley, a 50-year seafood industry professional from Massachusetts who recently bought his first vessel to fish for tuna and swordfish.

It seeks immediate injunctive relief and lists five counts in its claims for relief, including that the Antiquities Act doesn’t allow the president to declare national monuments in areas that are not on land or not controlled by the federal government. The national monument doesn't include "historic landmarks" or historic and prehistoric structures", which is what the Antiquities Act was meant to protect, and Biden's EO violates the Articles 1 and 2 of the Constitution, which deals with the separation of powers in US government, the lawsuit argues.

"Unless a permanent injunction is issued to forbid the implementation of proclamation 10287's fishing ban, plaintiff's will be irreparably harmed," the lawsuit advises. "The fishermen are suffering and will continue to suffer a diminution of income, reduced fishing opportunities, and depletion of value in their fishing vessels and permits because of proclamation 10287 and its ban on commercial fishing."

"The creation of the Northeast Canyons and Seamounts Marine National Monument violated the core requirements of the Antiquities Act to limit protections to specific monuments," PLF attorney Frank Garrison said in a statement. "Most fundamentally, the act gives the president authority to create monuments on federally owned or controlled land. The ocean is not land. Presidential action that goes beyond laws passed by Congress undermines the democratic process and the Constitution’s separation of powers."

Garrison is joined in arguing the case with other PLF attorneys Damien Schiff and Paige Gilliard.

A 'bull's eye around the right case to be made'

It likely will take several years of lower-level federal court challenges to reach the US’ highest court. But once there, the commercial fishing industry has good reason to have confidence in the outcome.  

That’s because of the way chief justice John Robert earlier rejected a request by PLF to review the constitutionality of Obama's executive order, field on behalf of the Massachusetts Lobstermen’s Association and four other fishing groups, as reported by Undercurrent. Roberts wrote a four-page explanation in which he said the request didn't meet the standards necessary to warrant a Supreme Court review, but he added that he was receptive to the argument.

Frank Garrison. Photograph from Pacific Legal Foundation website.

“Which of the following is not like the others: (a) a monument, (b) an antiquity (defined as a 'relic or monument of ancient times', Webster's International Dictionary of the English Language 66 (1902)), or (c) 5,000 square miles of land beneath the ocean?," the chief justice wrote.

Roberts practically drew a bull's eye around the right case to be made next time, seafood industry attorney Andrew Minkiewicz, a partner at the firm Kelly Drye, in Washington, DC, told Undercurrent at the time. 

"This doesn't happen every day or even in a lifetime," Minkiewicz said of the apparent opportunity for the industry. "The chief justice really outlined his skepticism of the way presidents are using the power that is, or is not, granted to them in the Antiquities Act."

The chief justice's language was such an indication of the conservative-dominated court's true leaning that the Boston Globe called the decision to ot hear the case a "Pyrrhic victory for conservation groups in New England".

Reached by email on Wednesday, PLF attorney Garrison told Undercurrent, "We are confident that we will prevail at the district court, but if the case is appealed, it is hard to say how long it will take to get to the Supreme Court. It will depend on how long the case takes at the district court and circuit court levels."

When asked how PLF might avoid the mistake that prevented the case from being heard previously by the Supreme Court, Garrison answered: "We believe we were right on the law in the previous case and the chief justice of the US Supreme Court recognized the president’s overreach under the Antiquities Act. We continue to believe the president is exceeding his authority under the act and the Constitution."

title: New Bedford awards $27m port improvement project
content:
New Bedford, Massachusetts, the US' most valuable commercial fishing port, has awarded a construction contract worth $27.9 million as part of a 150,000 square foot expansion project. 

DW White Construction of Acushnet, the lucky recipient, will build a north/south bulkhead at the North Terminal in the upper harbor.

"The project is designed to spur significant investment in the Port of New Bedford in the years to come by meeting the infrastructure needs of commercial fishermen, the offshore wind industry and other port users to ensure economic growth and increased efficiency", the port authority said in a statement. 

The project will also:

Backfill the new bulkhead with approximately 97,000 cubic yards and create 150,000 square feet of upland terminal space across the area backfilled landward of the bulkhead;
Complete the new, designed and permitted confined aquatic disposal (CAD) cell -- a storage system that helps prevent the spread of contaminated sediments -- with 480,000 cubic yards, and;
Increase infrastructure to support the offshore wind industry and provide much-needed berthing space for commercial fishing vessels.

New Bedford Mayor Jon Mitchell said the project "represents a major step in our effort to modernize the Port of New Bedford. It will enhance the long-term competitiveness of our maritime industries and help create quality jobs for our residents."

As Undercurrent News has reported, the port generated $451m worth of scallop landings in 2019, according to data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. 

Most recently, the port lost its executive director, Justin Poulsen, last month after only eight months on the job. As reported earlier by Undercurrent, Poulsen joined the port authority in late July 2021 after serving previously as vice president and executive director of the PortNYC for the New York City Economic Development Corp. The announcement came more than five months after Ed Anthes-Washburn left the position to join the private sector.

The port generated economic activity worth in excess of $11 billion, according to a 2018 economic study, and has a fishing fleet of 500 vessels that lands over 122m pounds of product annually leveraging $322m in direct sales, according to the city's website.

title: Two convicted in Canadian lobster sales scam
content:
Two men have been convicted in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia for illegally buying and selling lobster caught under an Indigenous food, social and ceremonial (FSC) license, CBC News reports.

License conditions prohibit the sale of the catch.

Terry Dale Banks and Tyler David Nickerson were fined a total of CAD 55,000 ($43,600) in Shelburne provincial court Wednesday (April 6). Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) said the charges stemmed from a September 2018 inspection of a Shag Harbor lobster pound.

The department was under immense pressure at the time from commercial lobster fishermen in southwestern Nova Scotia to stop illegal sales of FSC lobster, seen by many as cover for a growing black market fishery.

A month before the Shag Harbor bust, DFO officers seized 100 crates of lobster worth CAD 50,000 from a pound in New Edinburgh. It suspected those lobsters were caught and retained under an FSC fisheries license.

As Undercurrent News has reported, Banks was charged for allegedly being part of a scheme that stole about CAD 3 million from four different seafood companies. Banks is currently on trial in the Nova Scotia Supreme Court for the alleged fraud.

In 2020, he was convicted and fined CAD 45,000 on three charges relating to falsified export certificates for live lobster.

title: Daily recap, April 1: Norway salmon prices push NOK 100/kg; Thai Union execs fined
content:
Here's a recap of the daily seafood news from Friday, April 1: 

Norway salmon prices push NOK 100/kg, with Scottish, Chilean still high

Spot prices for Norwegian farmed salmon are pushing the NOK 100 per kilogram level this week -- week 14 of 2022 -- while Scottish are either flat or up, and the dip in Chilean prices could flatten or even rebound, sources told Undercurrent News.

Thai Union executives reportedly fined for alleged insider trading

The Stock and Exchange Commission of Thailand (SEC) has fined nine Thai Union Group executives for suspected insider trading. According to the agency, company chairman Kraisorn Chansiri, Chan Hon Kit, and Chuan Tangchansiri obtained inside information about Thai Union's third-quarter 2017 performance, which saw a "significant increase in profits". Others then bought shares or benefitted from them, the SEC said.

April skipjack raw material prices rocket to nine-year highs

April skipjack tuna raw material prices are surging up to over nine-year highs in processing hubs in Asia and Latin America, with fuel prices rising and fishing slow, sources told Undercurrent.

Fishin' founder's new Ren plant follows Beaver Street into Walmart skin-packs

Manish Kumar, the founder of US-based frozen supplier The Fishin' Company, is entering the chilled, skin-pack fish sector for Walmart and other customers from a new plant, sources told Undercurrent. Fishin’-linked Ren Seafoods is just starting processing at its new plant in Mobile, Alabama, and is taking on some distribution in the south of the salmon and whitefish skin-pack range for Walmart.

Vietnam's pangasius farmers urged to avoid heavy stocking while prices are high

Vietnam's pangasius sector has long operated in something of a boom-bust cycle; Duong Nghia Quoc -- president of the Vietnam Pangasius Association -- has warned farmers that the current high price levels will correct, and not to go "all in" on producing as much as possible.

title: Thai Union executives fined for alleged insider trading
content:
The Stock and Exchange Commission of Thailand (SEC) has fined nine Thai Union Group executives on suspected insider trading.

Those fined include the group's chairman, Kraisorn Chansiri, fined THB 3.43 million $102,348). The SEC also fined eight others: Dispol Chansiri (THB  551,809); Chan Hon Kit (THB 2.41m); Chan Tin Shu (THB 891,809); Cai Nguyen Chu (THB 806,809); Chuan Tangchansiri (THB 1.7m); Chen Yu Zhen (THB 551,809), Chan Hon Hung (THB 2.16m) and  Hui Pui Wah (THB 861,809).

According to the agency, Kraisorn Chansiri, Chan Hon Kit and Tangchansiri obtained inside information about Thai Union's third-quarter 2017 performance, which saw a "significant increase in profits". Others then bought shares or benefitted from them, the SEC said. All nine will be prohibited from being a director or executive in a securities issuing company or securities company for at least a year, the SEC said.

In a release, Thai Union acknowledged the fines.

Thai Union, it said, "would like to inform that the company has acknowledged the announcement of the SEC and processed on further investigation in order to ensure that the company is complied with all relevant law and regulation including corporate governance principle. Nevertheless, such matter shall not affect the business operation of the company and the company shall update to SET [Stock Exchange of Thailand] once there is further information".

title: Cermaq running tests with world’s first in-cage salmon sorter
content:
Mitsubishi-owned salmon farmer Cermaq claims to have successfully sorted swimming fish within a net pen using a new tool developed for its iFarm concept. 

Cermaq equips entire sea site with ‘iFarm’ AI for first time

The new salmon sorter, developed by technology company BioSort in collaboration with Cermaq, will allow farmers to separate fish within the pen to allow for follow-up treatment of specific individuals, Cermaq said.

It's a necessary feature for the iFarm project, which aims to improve fish health through artificial intelligence and machine learning.

The sorter in action. Credit: Cermaq

"To my knowledge, no-one has previously sorted swimming fish in a net pen before, so this is a big step towards individual-based handling of fish," said Geir Stang Hauge, managing director of BioSort.

The tech company has been working on the development of the sorter for two years. Controlled by a number of underwater electric motors, the new iFarm sorter was first tested in BioSort's lab and pool at their offices in Oslo, then in the sea outside Oslo, before it was installed and tested in net pens at Cermaq's sea site in Vesteralen in Northern Norway.

Currently, the sorter is controlled manually, but the goal is for it to be autonomous so that it, together with the sensor system in iFarm, can make its own decisions based on defined criteria, BioSort said.

"Now that we have shown that it is possible to sort out swimming fish, the work will be intensified," added Hauge. "The development team takes the learnings from this test to the development of the next-generation prototype of the sorter that will be able to function under even more conditions."

title: Bumble Bee’s former PE owner back on the hook for tuna price-fixing claims
content:
A federal judge overseeing civil class-action suits from customers who say they were harmed by US tuna canners' price-fixing has reversed a previous decision that shielded Bumble Bee Foods' former US-based private equity owner, Lion Capital, from potential liability.

The Monday (March 21) decision by Dana Sabraw, the chief justice of the United States District Court for the Southern District of California means that Lion could potentially be ordered to pay damages in the litigation, which has been ongoing since 2015.

The sprawling class-action litigation was previously overseen by judge Janis Sammartino, who recused herself from the matter in August 2021 after it emerged that an unnamed relative of hers had owned stock in broadliner Sysco Corp and retailer Target, two members of the "direct purchaser plaintiffs". Following that recusal, several plaintiffs asked Sabraw to reconsider Sammartino's January 2020 decision to exclude the private equity and Bumble Bee holding company Big Catch (Cayman) from the litigation because plaintiffs' lawyers did not present "new plausible allegations of direct participation by Lion Capital" in the conspiracy.

But upon review, Sabraw disagreed with Sammartino. 

"Plaintiffs alleged sufficient material facts to support a reasonable inference that Lion Capital learned prior to completing the acquisition that Bumble Bee’s profits were the product of pricing actions which would be untenable in a competitive market and were in fact the product of anticompetitive agreements. Lion Capital proceeded to acquire Bumble Bee anyway," Sabraw wrote.

San Diego, California-based Bumble Bee agreed to plead guilty to criminal price-fixing charges in 2017 and was fined $25 million by the Department of Justice. The company, which in 2019 filed for bankruptcy and was later sold to Taiwan's FCF Co, its longtime supplier, cited those fines and the civil suits as the rationale for the bankruptcy filing.

 

"The allegations of Lion Capital’s involvement in the conspiracy are underscored by Bumble Bee’s Plea Agreement, which suggests that Lion Capital was not merely passively involved but had meaningful information to contribute to the then-ongoing investigation," Sabraw wrote.

However, Lyndon Lea, the founder and managing partner of Lion, told Undercurrent News that he and Lion had no knowledge of the price-fixing.

"Lion Capital is very disappointed with the new ruling, which we believe is fundamentally inconsistent with what has been established in this case and in other, related tuna matters in which the US Department of Justice stated that the price-fixing conspiracy was concealed from Lion Capital.  We will vigorously defend ourselves from these revived, and still baseless, civil allegations," Lea said.

Former Bumble Bee CEO Chris Lischewski was convicted on price-fixing charges in 2019 and remains in prison. Dongwon Enterprise-owned StarKist & Co continues to fight the litigation, while Thai Union Group-owned Chicken of the Sea International has largely settled the suits brought against it.

The litigation remains ongoing.

title: Ghana’s Tropo Farms courts investors as it forges ahead on tilapia market ambitions
content:
BOSTON, Massachusetts, US -- It's one thing to ramp up production, but it's quite another to build the market and distribution channels to consume it; this is the problem facing Ghanaian tilapia business Tropo Farms as its lofty expansion project picks up steam.

Ghana’s Tropo Farms outlines plan to triple tilapia volumes in next three years

Tropo Farms needs additional capital, and over the past few months it has begun to court outside investment -- a growing trend across the continent's biggest aquaculture projects.

Speaking to Undercurrent News at the recent Seafood Expo North America show in Boston, company CEO Francisco Murillo said the firm was confident it would have a deal sorted with new investors within the next few months, suggesting Q3 as a likely deadline for completion.

"We are working on bringing investors into the company -- talks have already started," said Murillo, who joined Tropo last year.

"Now that we have a more robust management team the company is a lot better prepared to go into conversations with investors; those conversations are currently ongoing," he continued.

At present, there remains no defined structure to the prospective investment deal, whether it will mean selling a minority stake in the company, forming a partnership, or setting up a funding round.

"It depends who you talk to," he said. "We're talking to three different opportunities; some of them like to do it a certain way, others like to do it a different way. So we're working with them to see what makes sense, and at the end of the day what's the best overall deal for them and the company going forward."

Tropo Farms does not currently have any outside investors with a significant stake in the business, Murillo said, making it unusual among large tilapia farmers in Sub-Saharan Africa.

"That's also an advantage because it gives us a clean slate," he explained. "It's not like you have to make sure that whoever is coming in has compatible objectives with somebody that might have already been there."

Murillo did not disclose the names of the prospective investors in discussion with Tropo Farms. Similarly, Murillo confirmed that company founder and owner Mark Amechi has hired a financial advisor for the deal, but did not say who.

Developing Ghana's market

Last year, Murillo explained to Undercurrent the ambitious growth project that he had joined at Tropo. 

Sub-Saharan Africa’s tilapia sector could be about to come of age

The company operates farms around the shores of Lake Volta and has set itself the target of tripling its total production capacity from roughly 8,000 metric tons to 24,000t in the space of just three years.

"We ended last year with a harvest of about 7,400t, and our plan for this year is 12,000t," he told Undercurrent in Boston.

"We're talking about a 60% increase -- and the reason why I never thought that this was unreasonable is that I always expected, and now I'm confirming, that in reality the market was under-served."

Tropo Farms sells its fish entirely on the domestic market, and primarily to Ghana's capital and largest city, Accra. It opened a new distribution center in the area last month, further broadening its market outreach.

"There is an underlying demand there that was not being properly satisfied, and we were able to produce more, so we've been able to see that fully absorbed basically -- even though 60% year-on-year is not something anybody takes lightly."

The company is on track to meet its 12,000t annual target as of the end of Q1, a position that Murillo described as "very satisfying".

When talking to investors, the company is looking at two potential growth scenarios for this year, one rapid and centered on "very fast, aggressive growth", the other less so.

"The main issue there is how fast we think we can develop the market for that extra volume, because producing the fish -- as challenging as it gets -- is a little bit more under our control," he continued. "But if we don't have the market to sell that extra product, then it becomes very expensive very quickly."

This year, Tropo is exploring several options for expanding its domestic market. On the one hand, the company is looking to broaden its geographic coverage around the country. It is also looking at using e-commerce, trying to go "direct to wet markets where distributors don't usually go".

"Right now, we're covering the south part of the country only," he said. "But Ghana is a very big country, which is an advantage in terms of potentially developing consumption, and the challenge is that it does not have so good infrastructure."

"The foundation for developing the demand is there, we just have to figure out a way to get to those people on a progressive plan.

title: Skretting’s new sustainability policy gives NE Atlantic blue whiting the all-clear
content:
Skretting and parent firm Nutreco have adopted a new responsible sourcing policy which gives it the all-clear to continue sourcing blue whiting from the Northeast Atlantic.

The new policy represents a shift in approach compared to 2020, when it had said at the North Atlantic Seafood Forum, "if you lose MSC [Marine Stewardship Council's certificate], you lose us as a customer".

"Certified marine ingredients aren't a goal for us anymore, they're a requirement," he had added. Blue whiting represents one-sixth of the fish the firm uses in the production of marine ingredients, and one-quarter of fish used in the production of fishmeal.

When blue whiting had its MSC certificate suspended -- not withdrawn -- in 2020, Skretting sustainability manager Trygve Berg Lea told Undercurrent News it was the firm's goal "to source 100% certified marine ingredients globally by 2025".

"The suspension of blue whiting can result in the MSC certification being withdrawn. If that happens, blue whiting will no longer be a MarinTrust certified marine ingredient, and we will look to source alternative fishmeal that does not include blue whiting."

However, its new policy has changed tack:
A Skretting spokesperson confirmed that Northeast Atlantic blue whiting now registers as an "A-" on the above policy.

"The Northeast Atlantic pelagics fishery that we consider here is blue whiting, which is accepted by the MarinTrust Improvers Programme and we buy from a MarinTrust site," she said.

The new responsible sourcing policy will be used as a practical guide to decide on the type of marine ingredients that can be sourced for Skretting's global operations, the firm said in a press release.
 
"The document builds into the ambitions set in Nutreco's Sustainability RoadMap 2025, which aims to ensure that by 2025, Skretting sources marine ingredients that are 100% certified or coming from a fishery improvement project (FIP) for its global operations, as well as ensuring that all the fishmeal and fish oil used to produce feed originate from fisheries that are managed according to the FAO code of conduct for responsible fisheries."
 
The policy is built on a risk-based approach and was developed through internal collaboration within Nutreco and Skretting (sustainability, procurement and quality teams) at a global and local level to reflect the realities in the markets and included comments and revisions from external stakeholders, it said.
 
Important areas addressed in the policy include:

Specific criteria on what to buy according to five sustainability classes of marine ingredients coming from whole fish, by-products from wild fish catch and by-products from aquaculture, aligned with the most important fishery management certifications in the industry.
Clear purchasing targets for each sustainability class defined, both the relative share of purchases and a defined timeline to reach the ambitions set in Nutreco's Sustainaiblity RoadMap 2025.
Mapping of countries identified with a high risk of IUU fishing activities. Marine ingredients from these countries cannot be sourced unless they come from the highest sustainability classes. The policy in this area supports Nutreco and Skretting's commitment and work in SeaBOS (a collective of the world's largest seafood firms grouped in a bid to drive better sustainability).
Mapping of countries identified with a high risk of forced labor on board fishing vessels. For these countries, there are additional requirements to marine ingredient manufacturers. "Skretting is the first company in the world that communicates open and transparent criteria towards marine ingredient suppliers in this area."

In 2021, 80% of fishmeal and fish oil originating from whole fish and by-products that were purchased by Skretting came from fisheries certified according to the MarinTrust or MSC programs, or from fisheries that were part of a MarinTrust FIP, which the firm described as important progress compared to the 69% reported in 2020. 

"We're taking a critical step forward in outlining a clear path to attaining our RoadMap 2025 targets for marine ingredients. This marine ingredient sourcing policy sets a milestone in industry transparency and traceability in the very complex value chain of sourcing marine ingredients," said Jose Villalon, corporate sustainability director at Nutreco.

"The responsible use of marine ingredients is under constant scrutiny and we have an important role to play to contribute with more transparency in the industry," added Jorge Diaz, sustainability manager at Skretting. "Through this policy we're open about the criteria that we will use to source our ingredients and we want to be accountable for that. Reaching our targets is not something that we can do alone and it comes with challenges, but we will not shy away from them and will keep collaborating with all the relevant stakeholders to identify and mitigate the risks of our operations."

Alex Warrington, senior coordinator for the feed standard with the Aquaculture Stewardship Council (ASC), said ASC knows from developing its feed standard that greater transparency is a key step towards reducing the impacts of marine ingredients in aquafeed.

"The aquaculture industry has made progress in this area, by increasing the use of bycatch for example, but there is plenty of room for more progress towards responsible sourcing. Transparent, accountable sourcing policies such as Skretting's can play an important role in this."

Half of the marine ingredients produced worldwide are certified by independent certification bodies against the MarinTrust standards, said Libby Woodhatch, executive chair at MarinTrust.

"They assure that marine ingredients are sourced in fisheries championing best practices. Certified plants must comply with national environmental and social regulations and approved raw materials are properly segregated. Looking at the other 50% share of the industry, MarinTrust believes in FIPs as a preliminary multistakeholder approach aimed at helping drive change in fisheries around the world. Nutreco's Sustainability RoadMap 2025 validates our vision."

TripleNine, as a supplier to Skretting, added that the responsible sourcing policy gives it a "clear and practical guideline to Skretting's current and future demand when it comes to sustainable raw materials and their documentation".

title: EU fleet faces stoppages, collapse as fuel price rises to record high
content:
Additional reporting by Louis Harkell

The EU fishing sector has demanded urgent aid from the European Commission (EC) in the face of the sudden rises in energy, fuel and logistics costs as a result of Russia's invasion of Ukraine. 

"Operating costs are skyrocketing, mainly because fuel prices are through the roof," Javier Garat, president of European fishing industry body Europeche and the International Coalition of Fisheries Association, told Undercurrent News.

Fuel already accounts for over 50% of the EU fleets' operating costs.

"Since late 2020, the price has more than tripled in the EU, from €0.306 per liter to over €1.16/l on March 9. €0.60/l was already the price limit for our vessels to remain profitable. The situation is even worse than the fuel crisis of 2008," he said. "Never in history had the price exceeded the euro."

Russia-Ukraine fallout: Ukraine invasion thought to be behind increased dolphin deaths

In the last two weeks, the price has risen by 69%, and it continues to rise on a daily basis by some 10% per day, as the data below shows. 

As a result of the COVID-19 pandemic, the sector saw fuel prices increase by over 58% in 2021, which adds to the 107% increase from Jan. 1 to today.

"The high fuel costs are keeping fishermen in the harbor and this will limit supply and push up prices," Guus Pastoor, chairman of the Dutch Fish Processors and Traders Federation, told Undercurrent.

"[Seafood] prices are already high, and consumers can react when prices go up further," he said.

"The impact of the increase has been such that many vessels have been forced to stop operating. Fishing is no longer profitable," concurred Garat. 

"The inactivity of a fleet supposes not only economic losses but also many difficulties for the future of that fleet if it wanted to resume its operations," he added.

The industry has requested emergency face-to-face meetings with the EU commissioner for the environment, oceans and fisheries, Virginijus Sinkevicius, Garat said.

Additionally, the Spanish fishing sector has requested a meeting with the country's minister of agriculture, fisheries and food, Luis Planas, for extra aid to come from the national government, Basilio Otero -- president of Spain's national federation of fishermen's associations -- told Undercurrent. 

However, according to Otero, while the European fisheries sector met on March 14 with Sinkevicius, Planas has yet to answer. 

"We need him [Planas] to receive us [Spanish sector]," he said. "We need first-hand information on what our country is planning to do to mitigate the impact of the invasion that is negatively affecting our industry."

If no answer is received or solutions provided, the EU fishing sector plans to call all vessel owners to go on strike this week, Garat and Otero also told Undercurrent. 

"There are no collective actions planned yet, but I am sure our fleets will end up stopping their operations completely if there is no response to their demands," Garat explained. 

"If this ends up happening, the stoppage could last forever, depending on when urgent aid arrives," Otero commented. 

At the meeting with Sinkevicius, the fishing sector -- represented by Europeche and the European Association of Fisheries Producer Organizations -- reiterated the need to adopt urgent measures given the turn of events.

Sinkevicius emphasized that the EC takes the situation very seriously and is working around the clock on solutions. He committed to studying the measures urged by the sector and proposed to hold another meeting once the package of measures is more clearly defined.

What the industry wants

According to Europeche, the sector has already asked the EU commissioner to restore the exceptional measures adopted in 2015, right after Russia invaded and annexed the Crimean peninsula from Ukraine, to soften the blow of the crisis.

One request relates to an increase in the interannual fishing quota flexibility from 10% to 25%, which would allow organizations to transfer up to 25% of unused quotas this year to 2023.

Spain threatens to close ports to Russian vessels, encourages EU to follow suit

Likewise, the industry considers it essential to increase the aid caps per company within the framework of 'de minimis' aid -- only up to €200,000 for each undertaking over a three-year period -- to the amount of €300,000 per vessel.

Also, it claims that the current situation adds to the impact of both the pandemic and Brexit and, although they very much welcomed the creation of the Brexit Adjustment Reserve, they reminded the EU that the funding has not yet been activated. 

"That further limits the ability to deal with the current situation, compared to other affected sectors," Garat told Undercurrent. "Unfortunately, not everyone in the sector will survive this crisis, but with these or other proposed aids, they could at least leave with dignity."

According to Otero, the Spanish sector is also asking the national government for additional measures, including reducing social security contribution rates, the temporary suspension of port charges, an extension of COVID aid, or a VAT reduction on fish and seafood products.

"Which is nothing more than what other EU members have already asked their respective governments," he concluded.

title: Untitled
content:
SAN DIEGO, California, US — The long effort to modernize the offshore aquaculture permitting regime in US federal waters is advancing with a "refined" version of the latest legislative effort circulating before several Congressional committees.

Sara Brenholt, the campaign manager behind the group Stronger America Through Seafood (SATS), said at the recent Aquaculture 2022 conference said that the version of the Advancing the Quality and Understanding of American Aquaculture (AQUAA) Act introduced in 2021 is identical to a version introduced in 2020. That bill didn’t progress before the 2020 presidential election.

The latest iteration of the effort, still enjoys bipartisan support — from senators Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi), Marco Rubio (R-Florida) and Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) — and in the House by Steven Palazzo (R-Mississippi) and Ed Case (D-Hawaii). The bill has been referred to the three House committees: the Committee on Natural Resources, the Committee on Agriculture and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee. The Senate version continues to be referred to the Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee of which Wicker is the ranking member, Bernholt said.

"It is critically important to note that all AQUAA co-sponsors are working in lockstep together to make sure that there is no daylight between their offices," Brenholt said.

She urged audience members "Including those in the seafood supply chain, the environmental community, commercial fishing communities and small aquaculture farmers operating in state waters" to support the bill.

"We believe that the time is now to grow an American aquaculture industry that sets the global standard for environmental sustainability, provides economic benefits and jobs to communities up and down the seafood supply chain and opens up the US to compete on the world stage," she said.

Permitting certainty 

The AQUAA Act aims to improve the offshore aquaculture permitting process for US federal waters, which is currently an uncertain, lengthy affair with duties split between three main agencies the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the Environmental Protection Agency and the US Army Corps of Engineers with several other federal agencies contributing input. While the pathway was eased somewhat by a 2020 executive order from the administration of president Donald Trump, AQUAA Act proponents believe that the legislation is needed to provide the needed amount of regulatory certainty that investors need to put their money into offshore aquaculture.

The legislative effort has a long history. Bernholdt said that efforts to improve permitting began with the National Aquaculture Act was passed in 1980. It was followed by a series of aquaculture legislative bills set to improve upon it beginning with the Marine Aquaculture Act of 1995, which was co-sponsored by three Democratic senators, she said.

"The bill was relatively small and sought to develop a pilot project with funding, research and development opportunities and outlined a permitting system through NOAA and the Department of Commerce," Brenholt said.

While there wasn’t "significant movement" on the bill, it became a "catalyst for a flurry in activity" in the mid-2000s.

In 2005, then-Senators Daniel Inouye (D-Hawaii) and Ted Stevens (R-Alaska), reintroduced the measure in 2006, which was accompanied by a similar House companion bill.

This faltered but in 2010, the effort resurfaced with an initiative from former representative Lois Capps (D-California).

"These bills stressed elements such as determining appropriate locations, issuing regulations to prevent impacts on marine ecosystems and fisheries and supported research to guide the development of offshore aquaculture," Brenholt said.

The modern AQUAA Act includes provisions of all of the previous bills and was first introduced in the 115th Congress by senators Wicker and Rubio. It was then introduced in the House by representatives Palazzo (R-Mississippi) and Collin Peterson (D-Minnesota), the former head of the House ag committee who was defeated in the 2020 election.

In 2018 after the mid-term elections, the AQUAA Act went through a series of discussion drafts involving "considerable consultation from the aquaculture industry and the environmental community, regulatory agencies and other aquaculture stakeholders," Brenholt said.

SATS then worked to find a Democratic co-sponsor in the Senate as the bill went through further refinement.

"Senator Wicker’s staff worked closely with the commerce committee staff to create new language addressing some of the environmental concerns they received on the first iteration of the bill. The concept of the Aquaculture Opportunity Areas was developed as well as refining the national standards and creating a set of feed standards that were workable for both the eNGO [environmental non-governmental organization] communities and the industrial feed manufacturers," the SATS representative said.
