title: Zoneco ownership at stake as shares slated for auction
content:
Chinese seafood company Zoneco Group will no longer be controlled by its major shareholder, as the latter's shares are auctioned off to pay defaulted debts, reports Zhihui Haiyang.

Zoneco informed investors on Feb. 23 that Beijing Equity Exchange will auction 110 million shares held by Changhai County Zhangzidao Investment and Development Center (ZIDC), Zoneco's major shareholder, resulting in a new controlling shareholder.

Zoneco receives $8m gov’t cash subsidy for COVID losses

As of Feb. 23, ZIDC held 160m outstanding shares in Zoneco, accounting for 22.5% of
the total share capital.

The auction will take place on March 25, from 10:00 am until 0:00 am the next day, with a starting bid of CNY 343m ($54.3m).

If the auction is successful, ZIDC's stake will be reduced to 7%, resulting in the loss of its controlling shareholder status.

Zoneco, a Dalian-based farming, processing and trading company, forecast a net profit of CNY 6m-9m in 2021, down from CNY 14.8m in 2020. This, however, is largely thanks to the sale of its Dalian property and government grants.

This is not the first time that Zoneco's shares have been auctioned.

On May 2021, the court of Suzhou, Jiangsu Province ruled that the company must auction off approximately 58.79m shares, or 8.27% of the company's share capital, to repay debts.

Meanwhile, Zoneco has been contending with multiple lawsuits related to accusations of fraud by over 100 plaintiffs, including investors, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

Zoneco harvests scallops farmed in the Bohai Sea and imports raw material for processing. The company was China's largest market-listed seafood company by sales until 2017. However, it has been better known for its "running scallops" fiasco.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission later used historical satellite log data of seeding and harvesting activities to expose Zoneco's financial fraud, by showing the numbers had been "plucked from thin air".

Eventually, Zoneco was fined CNY 600,000 over the long-running saga. Hougang Wu, Zoneco's then-chairman, was given a lifetime ban from public securities markets.

title: Editor’s choice: SalMar outbids Mowi for NTS; Beaver Street seeks investor
content:
Neil Ramsden, EMEA editor of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week.

Arguably the biggest news story of the past seven days was the announcement that salmon farmer SalMar has made a voluntary offer for all the outstanding shares in Norwegian aquaculture group NTS, outbidding rival Mowi, which subsequently pulled its offer. If the deal goes ahead as planned -- and SalMar has the backing of over half of NTS' shareholders -- it would see it leapfrog Leroy Seafood Group to become Norway's second-largest salmon producer by a clear margin.

One of the largest family-owned US seafood companies is out in the market looking for an investor, sources told Tom Seaman last week. Beaver Street Fisheries, based in Jacksonville, Florida, has tasked Antarctica Advisors with running a process to sell a stake in the company, which is a major supplier to Walmart and other North American retailers and foodservice operators, sources said.

Staying in the US, and rumors surrounding the good health of the snow crab population in one of Canada's two largest fisheries are true, which bodes well for an increase in supply in the year ahead. Amelie Rondeau, who heads the fisheries and ecosystem sciences group at Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans told Undercurrent on Friday that her team estimates, based on last year's surveys, that there is 80,000 metric tons of commercially harvestable snow crab biomass in the southern Gulf of Saint Lawrence.

The return of Chinese demand is likely to absorb much of 2022’s expected shrimp boom, Jim Gulkin, founder of Thai-based frozen seafood supplier Siam Canadian, told Undercurrent. With demand at unprecedented levels in key markets, and suppliers scrambling to keep up, prices are soaring as farmers in major producing countries look to drastically increase their output. Estimates from Thai producer Charoen Pokphand Foods and other industry members suggest international harvest volumes could increase by as much as 10% this year, driven by Ecuador, Indonesia, India and Vietnam.

Legislation introduced last week by Alaska senators Dan Sullivan and Lisa Murkowski that would prohibit the US from importing seafood from Russia could cost the Russian seafood industry more than $1.2 billion annually and hit the snow crab sector the hardest. That's what Undercurrent found when it reviewed the latest US seafood import figures compiled by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration; read our update here.

Seattle, Washington, US-based Trident Seafoods announced Friday that it has named Thomas Scherer as the new managing director of its European operation, replacing Stephan Kleemeyer in the role. Scherer will also continue to maintain his current role as managing director of Pickenpack.

And another 15 seafood companies and organizations have withdrawn their exhibits from the coming Boston seafood show, including such well-known firms as Ready Seafood, Regal Springs Tilapia and the Kingfish Company. These companies join a group of 68 others that have pulled their exhibits amidst COVID-19-related worries since Jan. 11, as determined earlier by Undercurrent. 

After being prosecuted by Danish authorities for owning too great a share of the country's fishing quotas via "straw man companies", Henning Kjeldsen has made DKK 2.4 billion ($365.1 million, excluding VAT) from selling his pelagic assets to Swedish, Danish and Russian buyers. Late last year he was successfully prosecuted and fined DKK 54m for fishing rule violations committed between 2013 and 2019. In total, more than DKK 162.5m was also confiscated from companies he owned that were found to be these so-called 'straw man' firms.

title: US RAS depuration firm weighs its options, seeks partners
content:
A young US company that has developed technology to more efficiently remove off-flavor compounds from fish raised in recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS) has bagged salmon farmer Superior Fresh as a customer and the Norwegian firm AquaCon as a research partner.

Now that four-year-old, Verona, Wisconsin-based Exciton Clean has refined and proven its depuration technology, it's weighing its strategic alternatives, CEO Chris Haughey told Undercurrent News. Those potentially include seeking a partner, looking for strategic acquisitions -- or to become one -- while also applying its Exciton AOP (advanced oxidation process) reactors to more species grown in RAS, he said.

"We are not as a business exclusively based in seafood," Haughey said. "We are not exclusively focused on salmon. There are several companies in the US raising sturgeon in RAS for caviar."

That's just one interesting opportunity for the company, he said.

"Sturgeon is interesting because it is a very cold-water fish," Haughey added. "These fish also have issues with off-flavor."

Off-flavor, or what is typically a muddy or earthy taste in fish, is probably the largest hurdle RAS salmon farmers must overcome to achieve widespread commercial success, said John Davidson, a research scientist with The Conservation Fund's Freshwater Institute, which helps develop aquaculture solutions.

"It is something that we get questions about more than any other topic," Davidson told Undercurrent.

Exicton's depuration process is among several in the RAS world competing to solve this problem. Among the difficulties with depuration is that it generally involves a great deal of water flushed through the fish and at least a week in order to work, Davidson said. 

The water, plus the depuration equipment and utilities to run it, cost money, and, usually, the fish lose valuable weight before they are slaughtered, although the weight loss is sometimes overemphasized, Davidson said.

"It's not a large amount of weight loss -- 4% to 6% is pretty standard, but if you begin to multiply that by millions of fish harvested by commercial application, then it does become a relatively sizeable issue," Davidson said. "It takes more water that you may not have available to you on a commercial scale."

Davidson said he wasn't familiar enough with Exciton's technology to discuss its effectiveness, but said that the company is known within the aquaculture industry and the dozen or so RAS farms in the US under development, in construction or operational.

Haughey said that his company's process reduces typical RAS depuration times by half – anywhere from 40% to 60% of the time usually needed to improve fish taste.

"By using our technology in the depuration process, you can save a huge amount of water," Haughey said. "We estimate savings of 70 to 90% of the water needed to depurate fish."

Shortening depuration time and limiting fish weight loss are both vital to RAS success, Davidson said.

Exciton at this point in its development represents the fruit of about $4 million in self-raised and outside investment. Besides its sales to Superior Fresh of some depuration equipment in April 2020, the company is working with one large RAS operator that Haughey declined to name.

The company is also involved in research projects at the University of Maryland's Baltimore County Institute of Marine and Environmental Technology with Yonathan Zohar, a longtime professor at the university and one of the US' leading scientists specializing in aquaculture biotechnology, recirculating marine aquaculture, fish reproductive physiology and hatchery platforms. 

Exciton and the university are working with Norwegian Atlantic salmon producer AquaCon to improve the depurator company's ability to depurate fish in brackish water environments and to test its AOP against other depurators, Haughey said.

As Undercurrent has reported, AquaCon is planning to build three new salmon recirculating aquaculture system facilities on the Eastern Shore of the US state of Maryland and has signed a memorandum of understanding with the university's Aquaculture Research Center (ARC) to develop aquaculture technology.

Haughey came to EC as its CEO slightly more than a year ago with a degree in mechanical engineering from Stanford University and nearly 10 years as a co-founder of Tegu Toys of Honduras, which manufactures wooden, magnetized building blocks. 

He expressed confidence that the fledgling RAS salmon industry will soon find its feet.

"We are seeing RAS Atlantic salmon operators getting to break in or better even at relatively small scales," Haughey said. "Superior Fresh's recent expansion has taken them to about 700 metric tons a year and our understanding of them is that they are happy with the results."

title: Tuna vessel, catch seized as owner refuses to bring observer on board
content:
Wayne David MacFarlane, director of New Zealand's Tuna Fishing Company, has been fined NZD 7,800 (a little over $5,000) and had his vessel and catch seized after refusing to bring a fisheries observer on board, Stuff reports. 

The vessel, named the Northern Odyssey, left Dunedin -- the second-largest city in the South Island of New Zealand -- with an observer aboard on Apr. 9, 2021, and the vessel returned to unload its catch on Apr. 15. 

Back at port, MacFarlane told the observer the vessel would not return to sea without him, yet the crew left port on Apr. 19 to go fishing again without him. Fishery officers contacted him to come back to port and pick up the observer, but he refused.

During the trip, however, the crew experienced mechanical problems that needed to be repaired, so the vessel returned to port on Apr. 26, when the catch -- valued at over NZD 64 million -- and the vessel were seized. 

This was the second time in less than a year that MacFarlane was convicted and sentenced under the Fisheries Act. In February, he was fined NZD 15,000 for not deploying tori lines [seabird scaring devices] while fishing as required.

title: Danish magnate earns $365m selling pelagic interests at home, abroad
content:
After being prosecuted by Danish authorities for owning too great a share of the country's fishing quotas via "straw man companies", Henning Kjeldsen has made DKK 2.4 billion ($365.1 million, excluding VAT) from selling his pelagic assets.

‘Tired’ Danish magnate sells vessel, quotas after 2021 prosecution

Late last year he was successfully prosecuted and fined DKK 54m for fishing rule violations committed between 2013 and 2019. In total, more than DKK 162.5m was also confiscated from companies he owned that were found to be so-called "straw man companies".

On Facebook, he then declared he had had enough of negative attention and had sold all his pelagic fishing rights, including the still-under-construction vessel Gitte Henning.

The ceiling for ownership of Danish fishing rights is 10% of the overall total, an Undercurrent News source familiar with the industry there explained. Thus, what Kjeldsen sold was a fraction less than 10% of the country's individual transferable quotas (ITQ).

He sold two vessels in total. The 64-meter Gitte, built in 2003, was sold to a Russian buyer; no Undercurrent sources have been able to say which company was the buyer, however. 

Then, the 87.7m Gitte Henning -- still being constructed at Spain's Zamakona Yards -- has been sold along with quotas to Denmark's Rederiet Isafold, owned by Niels Jensen & Co. 

Shipbroker Atlantic Shipping revealed the vessel would replace the Isafold, which was built in 2006 at Karstensens Skibsvaerft, and which will be sold later this year, when the new vessel is delivered.

Information from the Danish Fisheries Agency supplied to Undercurrent shows that Kjeldsen also sold pelagic quotas worth DKK 472.7m to Rederiet Isafold. A rough calculation would suggest that Isafold therefore bought just under 20% of Kjeldsen's pelagic assets.

In full:

Isafold bought DKK 472.7m worth of quota; Themis Fiskeri bought DKK 500.1m; Astrid Fiskeri acquired DKK 1.2bn worth; Skagen Fiskeri DKK 126.3m; B-C Pelagic Danmark bought DKK 42.9m; and Rederiet Geysir DKK 52.4m.

"Kjeldsen was required to sell either his pelagics quotas or his whitefish business as a result of the prosecution," Undercurrent's source said. "I think he would have chosen the pelagics because he was at the ownership ceiling -- there was not a lot more he could do there. But in whitefish there is still room to develop."

On its own Facebook page, Themis Fiskeri confirmed it had bought pelagic quotas in the sell-off, stating they would grant the firm the flexibility to fish other species and thus operate year-round.

"It allows us to optimize the operation and utilization of the S144 Themis," the firm said. "Themis has fished absolutely amazingly and deserves to be at sea as much of the year as at all possible."

Denmark’s Astrid Fiskeri swaps vessels with Norwegian firm as part of fleet overhaul

"We have long had a strong desire to engage in the fisheries on Atlantic herring, not only because it is exciting for both skipper and crew, but also because it makes the business far more stable and independent, by spreading it across more fisheries."

In the past, its exposure to sand eel and sprat quotas has meant some volatility in terms of fishing resources, it added.

Swedish fisheries blog Svenssons Nyheter took a deep look into Danish quota ownership on Feb. 15 and found that Astrid Fiskeri -- owned by Sweden's Johansson family -- is now Denmark's single-largest quota holder, with 9.86%. 

Next is Asbjorn, with 9.62%; Isafold is now number three, with 9.27%; Beinur, 7.39%; Rederiet Ruth, 7.04%; Fiskeri AB Ginneton, 6.5%; Themis Fiskeri, 5.89%; John Anker Hametner Larsen, 4.66%; Tor-on Fiske, 4.09%; and AB Ocean, 3.99%.

It also ranked the companies by 2020 gross profit, which looks like this:

Astrid Fiskeri, DKK 222.1m; Rederiet Ruth, DKK 193.7m; Isafold, DKK 164.6m; Gitte Henning Pelagic (now sold up), DKK 151.2m; Asbjorn, DKK 122.4m; Beinur, DKK 118.7m; Cattleya, DKK 77.5m; Themis Fiskeri, DKK 61.3m; Rylo Fiskeri, DKK 60.7m (has now sold its business to Tor-on Fiske); Lingbank, DKK 52.5m.

title: New Zealand’s Sanford warns of Omicron impacts on supply chain
content:
New Zealand seafood company Sanford has reported improvements in sales volumes and prices for the first quarter of 2022, consistent with its expectations, it said.

Still, looking ahead, it warned of additional challenges posed by coronavirus' Omicron variant.

Q1 saw good results, said CEO Peter Reidie, showing that things are improving "in a way that is meeting our expectations."

"We continue to face supply-side challenges around access to labor and freight costs. Looking ahead, there are additional challenges posed by Omicron. These challenges will likely be operational, where the last two years have been defined by suppressed demand."

"Now demand is recovering in many of our markets, but we are preparing for further disruption in local supply chains and labor issues in a tight labor market."

Sanford is focusing on the challenges the company can control, which includes having a fully vaccinated workforce, operating teams in bubbles wherever practicable and having plans in place to manage the absence of key individuals, said Reidie.

Sanford also acknowledges challenges outside of the pandemic, such as rising ocean temperatures, which can impact aquaculture operations.

"We have seen warmer-than-usual waters in our Big Glory Bay salmon farm for January. This has had some impact on salmon mortalities, although these were not outside the previous three year's average for this month," said the CEO.

"We are managing this carefully with lower stocking densities and additional aeration in all our salmon pens. However, the period ahead from March to May is traditionally a critical one for oxygen levels and algae, so we will continue to monitor and manage carefully."

For Q1, Sanford's sales volumes were up 11% year-on-year.

The wild-catch division saw pricing improvements but lower sales volumes on the prior comparable period (pcp), down 12%. Volume impacts in the wild-catch division were offset by favorable pricing, up 24%.

Strong customer demand for greenshell mussels saw pricing in this division up 12% versus pcp and sales volumes up 30%.

Strong demand in key markets saw salmon sales volumes up 47% on the pcp. Sanford has also cleared its remaining frozen stock in this period, it said.

"Sanford is exploring options for its crayfish quota, which it fishes and manages through third parties, which may result in its sale. It intends to reach a decision before the April start of the quota year for that species," it added.

Sanford also confirmed it was on track to communicate the results of its "strategy refresh" by June.

title: Statt Torsk happy with farmed cod sales at over NOK 60/kg
content:
Norwegian cod farming operation Statt Torsk has completed its third pilot-scale production run, producing a total of 420 metric tons of "excellent quality" fish.

Around 70% of that -- so, almost 300t -- was sold to "one of the largest Spanish food retailers at gross prices at the level of NOK 60+ per kilogram", it said.

The company now enters a new phase -- industrial-scale production, said CEO Gustave Brun-Lie.

"As from September this year, we will deliver more than 3,000t of fresh and high-quality products, aiming at everyday deliveries in accordance with a defined and predictable schedule throughout January 2023. We will then have some pause, and from May 2023 we shall be able to deliver whole year around."

As previously reported, Leroy Seafood Group handled the sales for this pilot run, with processing taking place at third-party business Per Stave.

title: Northern Australia adds rock oyster ‘brand’ to federal species database
content:
Northern Australia now officially has its own 'brand' of tropical rock oyster after the black-lip rock oyster was formally added to the national fish names database, according to a missive from the state government.

Being added to the database means that all species of Saccostrea echinata produced or sold in Australia must now be identified as black-lip rock oyster.

According to Matt Osborne from Australia's department of industry, tourism and trade, by establishing a standard naming convention, the industry can remove ambiguity around the species.

"There are many different species of tropical oysters across Northern Australia and they are often difficult to visually tell apart," he said in the release. "To add further confusion, the naming of tropical oyster species is not well defined, with confusing taxonomy and inconsistent use of common names. This lack of consistency has created challenges for regulators, farmers and hatcheries."

Meanwhile, Northern Australia's tropical rock oyster R&D project is at its midpoint according to the release, with researchers in multiple states working on new hatchery and farming techniques to improve grow-out performance of two native tropical rock oyster species. Their work has reportedly culminated in record hatchery production at Darwin's aquaculture center and Hillary's marine shellfish hatchery near Perth in Western Australia.

title: As 2022 begins, 17 tuna stocks fail MSC standards, says ISSF
content:
The latest report from the International Seafood Sustainability Foundation (ISSF) found that 17 of 23 major commercial tuna stocks worldwide are not meeting the criteria of the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) standard.

Multiple Pacific tuna fisheries face certification loss by 2023, MSC warns

Its latest evaluation of tuna fisheries against the MSC criteria found that only six are successfully avoiding overfishing and maintaining target stock biomass levels, it said.

These stocks include North Atlantic albacore, South Atlantic albacore, Eastern Atlantic bluefin, Western Pacific skipjack, Eastern Pacific yellowfin, and Indian Ocean skipjack, all of which earned a passing score for the MSC fisheries standard on its principle 1: "Sustainable Fish Stocks". Under principle 3, "Effective Management", most tuna regional fisheries management organizations (RFMOs) scored well.

In the February 2021 edition of the report, seven stocks passed principle 1. In this year's report, one less stock received a passing score, specifically South Pacific albacore. Principle 3 evaluations remained unchanged for the most part.

The report attributes 17 other tuna stocks’ inability to pass MSC principle 1 to poor stock status, the lack of well-defined harvest control rules (HCRs), and/or the lack of effective tools to control harvest.

Those fisheries that failed the principle 1 test were: yellowfin, bigeye, Western skipjack, Eastern skipjack, Western bluefin, and Mediterranean albacore in the Atlantic; Western yellowfin, Western bigeye, Eastern bigeye, Eastern skipjack, Northern albacore, Southern albacore, and Pacific bluefin in the Pacific; and yellowfin, bigeye, and albacore in the Indian Ocean; and lastly, the Southern bluefin tuna fishery.

title: IOTC cuts Seychelles’ tuna quota due to overfishing
content:
The Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC) has reduced the yellowfin tuna catch quota this year for the Seychelles as payback for overfishing by that island nation's industrial longline fleets, the Seychelles News Agency reports.

The principal secretary for fisheries, Roy Clarisse, told SNA that Seychelles lodged a formal objection to the IOTC chairperson on Jan. 5. That appeal is pending.

Under IOTC Resolution 21/01, Seychelles qualified for a total yellowfin tuna allocation of 35,871 metric tons, a reduction of 8,331t for 2022. That covers catch from all fleets registered in the island state -- purse seiners, industrial longliners and semi-industrial longliners. 

The Seychelles' fishing fleet had been granted in June 2021 an increase in their yellowfin tuna catches for 2022 by 7% in 2022, following a new IOTC interim resolution, Undercurrent News has reported. 

The article doesn't indicate why the quota was cut, but the Seychelles has had difficulties with illegal activities in its waters. The captain of a Sri Lankan harvesting vessel was fined SCR2.5 million ($167,000) for illegal fishing in Seychelles waters in August, Undercurrent has reported.

The vessel was the third since May 2021 caught illegally fishing in the Seychelles' 1.4 million square kilometers of exclusive economic zone.

The quotas have been set since at least 2015, when the IOTC's scientific committee established that the Indian Ocean yellowfin tuna stock is being overfished. Consequently, resolution 16/01 adopted an "interim plan for rebuilding the Indian Ocean yellowfin tuna stock in the IOTC area of competence". The resolution was revised in 2017, 2018, and 2019.

According to an IOTC circular published on December 31, 2021, if a given fleet over-caught fish in 2020, it has to pay back 200% of that amount they over-caught -- 100% for 2021 and 100% for 2022.

Seychelles, an archipelago in the western Indian Ocean, has three fleets that are comprised of 13 purse seiners, which are mainly Spanish and French-owned vessels, as well as 61 industrial longliners and 39 semi-industrial longliners vessels targeting yellowfin tuna.

title: ‘Tired’ Danish magnate sells vessel, quotas after 2021 prosecution
content:
Danish fishing magnate Henning Kjeldsen has announced the sale of his pelagic vessels and quota, reports TV2 Nord.

Danish prosecutors aim to take $32m from fishing magnate in court

Late last year he was successfully prosecuted and fined DKK 54 million for fishing rule violations committed between 2013 and 2019. In total, more than DKK 162.5m ($24.6m) was also confiscated from companies he owned that were found to be "straw man companies".

Now, on Facebook, he has declared he has had enough of negative attention and has sold all his pelagic fishing rights, including the still-under-construction vessel Gitte Henning.

"I'm tired. Not tired, as in tired. But tired of the political hetz [witch-hunt] that has been on me and my shipping company as well as family," he wrote on Facebook, according to the news outlet.

It is still unknown to the public who bought the quotas, but regardless, it is a loss for the Danish port of Skagen, said John Jakobsen, chairman of the Skagen Fisheries Association.

"This means that there are fishermen in Skagen who are without a job. It is a great asset for the city that is disappearing."

Kjeldsen still owns two vessels and shares in a third, but the sale of the other vessels and rights means that fishing for him will be on a different scale in the future.

title: US research team might have found way to make biofuel from algae
content:
Researchers at a university in the US state of Montana are exploring a potential breakthrough in producing biofuel from algae.

A $3 million grant from the US Department of Energy will help the Montana State University research team -- which also includes scientists from the University of Toledo and University of North Carolina -- in the early stages of a three-year project aimed at developing a biofuel process for algae, the university said in a statement.

Like soybeans, camelina and other crops, algae contain oily substances that can be extracted and refined into biodiesel, which differs from ethanol and other alcohol-based liquid fuels produced by fermentation.  But the costs associated with supplying the algae with supplemental carbon dioxide from sources such as coal-fired power plants have discouraged commercial production.

Now, the researchers think that a recently discovered strain of algae could be cultivated using only the ambient carbon dioxide of the atmosphere. The algae, called SLA-04, was discovered by the project's University of Toledo researchers in an eastern Washington lake containing high levels of carbonate minerals similar to baking soda.

As part of the grant, the team will sequence the algae's DNA and then use a process called metabolic mapping to identify which genes correspond with the algae's biochemical strategies.

title: Korea fines shipping companies $81m for rate collusion
content:
The Korea Fair Trade Commission (KFTC) has fined 23 liner operators a total of $81 million for 'fixing' freight rates on the South Korea to Southeast Asia lane between 2003 and 2018, reports Loadstar. 

Most of the major liner operators and a number of regional carriers were among those fined, including HMM, SM Line, Korea Marine Transport (KMTC Line), Pan Ocean, Sinokor, Maersk, Evergreen, Yang Ming, Wan Hai, SITC and Cosco.

KMTC received the heaviest penalty, $24.86m, while HMM, South Korea's flagship carrier, must pay around $3m.

Investigations began in July 2018, after timber importers complained to the KFTC that liner operators had simultaneously increased freight rates along the South Korea to Southeast Asia route.

title: California issues first $5K fine for poaching under new law
content:
A sportfishing company became the first to pay increased poaching fines and penalties that went into effect in the US state of California when he pleaded guilty to working in a marine protected area (MPA).

Helgren's Sportfishing of Oceanside Harbor, California, owned by Joseph Helgrens, was fined $5,000 and ordered to stay out of Swami’s State Marine Conservation Area for one year in a San Diego county courthouse recently. Both are penalties under Assembly Bill 2369, which prohibits banned activities in California’s MPAs, and went into effect in January 2019, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (DFW) said in a statement.

The vessel Electra was caught in Swami's State Marine Conservation Area, one of many MPAs along California's coast, in December 2020. DFW game wardens were responding to a tip about illegal fishing in the MPA when they saw the boat, DFW said.

The wardens board the boat and documented commercial passenger fishing activities, DFW said.

"The $5,000 minimum fine imposed in the Electra case is the first of its kind since the law was passed," stated David Bess, DFW chief of the law enforcement division. "We hope the Electra case disposition will send a message that commercial fishing in an MPA will be stopped by wildlife officers and will result in substantial fines."

title: Judge rules California gas company liable for 119-year-old pollutants in herring fishery
content:
A US federal court order might clear the way for a natural gas utility company cleaning up 119-year-old pollution damaging a herring fishery in the state of California's San Francisco Bay.

Federal judge William Orrick found in a decision released this week that Pacific Gas and Electric (PG&E) of San Francisco is liable for natural-gas pollutants left behind by its predecessor, San Francisco Gas & Electric (SFG&E). 

Basing his ruling on sections of the federal Clean Water Act (CWA) and Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA), Orrick found that when it purchased the former SFGE, PGE assumed liability for pollutants dumped at the Cannery Manufactured Gas Plant that were still there from late 1903.

"The parties do not dispute that SFGE removed some parts of the Cannery MGP; the only issue is the impact of that act," Orrick wrote in his decision. "Without evidence to the contrary, I agree that by removing the gas generators and gasholders from the Cannery MGP, SFG&E necessarily handled or transported waste, again establishing direct liability for PG&E under the RCRA."

Dan Clarke, a former San Francisco resident, filed the civil lawsuit seeking a court order that would force PG&E to investigate and clean up the contamination. Though not directly connected, Clarke's effort is similar to a lawsuit filed by a group of 33 commercial crab fishermen who sued the city of San Francisco for a fire at a pier-side warehouse in December 2020, said attorney Stuart G. Gross of Gross & Klein of San Francisco, who represented both plaintiffs.

Gross called Orrick's order a victory for Clarke and herring harvesters who still work the area near the old gas plant, which is east of the Golden Gate Bridge. He called the ruling a "starting point of proving what that contamination is and what they [PG&E] have to do to clean it up."

"The San Francisco herring fishery is the only urban commercial fishery in the US. It is conducted entirely within San Francisco Bay, one of largest population centers in the world, and herring are highly sensitive to [refined hydrocarbon] contamination," Gross told Undercurrent News. "When you get these environmental assaults, they [herring] are the first to go."

A PG&E spokesman told the Courthouse News Service that the utility is committed to addressing environmental impacts from historic gas plant operations but maintains that it should not be held legally responsible for alleged contamination from the former Cannery gas plant.

"PG&E respectfully disagrees with the court’s ruling, and believes the evidence demonstrates that PG&E is not the corporate successor nor has ever operated the former Cannery MGP and is therefore not responsible for the alleged contamination," PG&E spokesman Jeff Smith told Courthouse News in an emailed statement.

It is unclear whether PG&E will appeal the order. The company has settled three similar gas-plant cleanup lawsuits over the past few years, according to Courthouse News.

As Undercurrent has reported, the San Francisco herring fishery, at one time, was one of the most lucrative in the world. Recently, the San Francisco Herring Association cut checks totaling more than $1.7 million to hand out to about 50 fishermen in exchange for retiring their herring permits.

Both sides will hold a pre-trial conference in February to determine the next steps to the ongoing litigation, Gross said.

title: USDA awards $500,000 to build aquaculture workforce training in Maine
content:
The US Department of Agriculture's National Institute of Food and Agriculture (NIFA) has awarded a $500,000 grant to the Gulf of Maine Research Institute (GMRI) to help establish an aquaculture workforce training system, US representative Chellie Pingree, a Maine Democrat, reports. 

Pingree, who serves on both the House of Representatives Appropriations Committee's agriculture subcommittee and the House Agriculture Committee, was a proponent for the funds, which, according to her press release, will be used to: 

"Help GMRI develop and pilot a Maine Department of Labor (ME DOL) Aquaculture Aquaculture Apprenticeship Program where participants will gain valuable experience, receive mentoring, get trained and tested on defined occupational competencies, and learn to use cutting-edge technology at Maine's most sophisticated commercial shellfish and sea vegetable farms;
"Develop and administer a series of stackable, credentialed, aquaculture short courses at Southern Maine Community College (SMCC) that form the basis of an Aquaculture Certificate;
"Update the Maine Aquaculture Occupational Standards for Shellfish and Sea Vegetables, Recirculating Aquaculture Systems, and Marine Finfish to ensure that aquaculture workforce training remains relevant to Maine's rapidly evolving and growing industry;
"Coordinate program development and delivery between SMCC, Washington County Community College, the Mid-Coast School of Technology (K-9 Career Technical Education High School), and ME DOL apprenticeship to establish matriculation pathways and dual-credit programs that enable fast-tracked degree completion. The programming developed will have the potential to be expanded to other community colleges in Maine and throughout the Northeast."  

"Maine’s aquaculture industry is vital to our state’s economy but needs a skilled workforce to continue to grow and innovate," Pingree is quoted as saying. GMRI "has developed a forward-thinking solution. ... This substantial NIFA award will help ensure Maine’s aquaculture industry reaches its full potential now and in the future."

In April 2021, the Maine Aquaculture Innovation Center, in Walpole, was awarded $500,000 from NIFA to develop an aquaculture workforce training pilot in partnership with Washington County Community College, Pingree also noted.

title: After 52 years in the seafood industry, GSA’s Wally Stevens leaves with few regrets
content:
Wally Stevens retired from the Global Seafood Alliance (GSA) last month having helped the nonprofit through its greatest period of transition and growth. While he says he leaves the organization feeling well-satisfied, he does have a complaint.

"When I started working here, they promised me one day [of work] a week," Stevens told Undercurrent News. "They lied."

He's joking, of course.

But that wry, faux put-upon humor is a good example of Stevens' personal style and an element to his position as one of the stalwarts of seafood sustainability. For nearly 15 years with GSA and its predecessor, Global Aquaculture Alliance (GAA), Stevens mixed self-deprecation with warmth, patience and gravitas. It has a way of leveling the playing field, making people feel like they are, or can be, part of something larger and better than themselves, said Steve Hedlund, GSA's communications manager, who worked with Stevens for about nine years.

"Wally's ability to bring people together is incredible. We operate in a pre-competitive space where collaboration and inclusion are paramount. Without it, there’s no credibility or integrity in the work that we do, whether it's standards development or the dissemination of information through media and events," Hedlund told Undercurrent.

With Stevens, "everyone has a seat at the table, and I've always admired Wally for that", Hedlund said. "He also values the power of education and networking as much as anyone in this great industry, which a lot of people, myself included, have benefitted greatly from. So many people look up to him."

As Undercurrent News has reported, GSA announced Stevens' retirement and his successor on Dec. 16. Brian Perkins, who joined the Portsmouth, New Hampshire-based GSA as its chief operating officer on March 1, assumed Stevens' post effective Jan. 1. Stevens said he leaves the presidency of the organization satisfied with where it is.

Getting people 'to understand the vision'

"Sustainability in seafood is fairly new. It's probably been around 25 years," Stevens told Undercurrent. "Everything [with sustainability] is unfolding and getting better."

Cui He (right), president of the China Aquatic Products Processing and Marketing Alliance, met with Wally Stevens when the latter was president of Global Aquaculture Alliance.

Stevens' collaborative skills served him well at the helm of GAA, the name it assumed earlier this year when it merged with sister organization Global Seafood Assurances to become Global Seafood Alliance earlier this year, as Undercurrent has reported. 

The merger occurred partly to reflect that the new organization straddles traditional and non-traditional seafood providers with its Best Seafood Practice (BSP) and Best Aquaculture Practice (BAP) certifications, which denote the achievement of greater sustainability, which is generally defined as the conservation of natural resources and global ecosystems. 

Helping to formulate and update the standards for the BAP and BSP, and getting seafood industry members to pursue certification, required all of Stevens' listening and persuasive skills, Hedlund said. That process started in-house when Stevens joined the organization in 2007 and was Stevens' biggest challenge, Stevens said.

"It really was getting everybody within the organization to understand the vision -- where we were going. Getting, as with any business, silos merged into one big thing, in one big mission, as opposed to four or five views as to what the world should be like, was the difficult thing," Stevens said.

According to the most recent count provided by Hedlund, more than 3,100 seafood processing plants, farms, feed mills, hatcheries in 39 countries have earned BAP certification as of this year, up from 2,918 BAP certificate carriers in 2020. The BAP program issued 15 certifications in 2004 and broke the 1,500 mark in 2016.

GSA awarded its first Responsible Fishing Vessel Standard (RFVS) in mid-January to the Antarctic Discovery, which belongs to harvester Australian Longline Fishing of Tasmania. RFVS is a new program that applies sustainability standards to fishing vessels.

"The type of people who are good at bringing together are important here. You need to be very patient and understanding and listen very well," Hedlund said. "If you are defensive and protective, you will struggle to address the major challenges facing the industry."

"At the time Wally joined, we weren't collaborating enough with academia, the conservation industry and members of the industry," he added.

Stevens was positioned well to provide those connections when he joined GAA. He had some seafood bona fides. Stevens had worked for Boston-based seafood distributor Slade Gorton for 17 years, resigning as president of the company to go to GAA. Prior to Slade Gorton, he was president of salmon aquaculture provider Ocean Products and a senior vice president of Booth Fisheries, where he started in the seafood industry in 1970.

Stevens was also connected with the academic world through the National Fisheries Institute (NFI). He served as its chairman in 2001 and in 1988, co-founded the organization's Future Leaders program, in which attendees take a year enhancing their knowledge and leadership skills by focusing on seafood industry issues in production, sales and other areas.

"One of my proudest legacies is to think that we moved forward the assurance that [consumers] should come with seafood to a better place," Stevens said. "We want people to eat more seafood. To the extent that we provide reassurances [to consumers] about the seafood coming into them, we have accomplished that."

'All seafood is good if it's done responsibly'

One of those who attended the NFI Future Leaders program credits it, and Stevens, with opening his eyes to how the seafood industry has an obligation to the wider world.

Attending NFI "was probably for me one of the most impactful periods in seafood," said Dana Bartholomew, until recently the executive vice president in charge of business development at US traceability vendor Legit Fish.

"The whole premise behind it was Wally looking around the room and seeing a whole bunch of gray-hairs. He wanted to create a next-generation in the industry that would create a network that they [in the network] could lean on and turn to each other," said Bartholomew, who worked with Stevens at Slade Gorton for several years. "What Wally understood is that through people's interaction, cooperation and respect for each other, we -- not just in a company or a country -- would be able to talk openly about challenges and issues."

"He was somewhat disarming because he was just such a kind man. You felt genuine warmth and kindness with him," Bartholomew added. "He was able to get people to see things that maybe they hadn't seen before."

GSA claims it is the "world’s only third-party certification program capable of providing credible third-party assurances linking responsible wild-capture fisheries to ... RFVS-certified vessels and Seafood Processing Plant Standard (SPS)-certified facilities through the chain of custody (CoC) standard".

Stevens is proud of that but quickly recognizes that there are other players in the sustainability world. The Marine Stewardship Council, Aquaculture Stewardship Council, Global Gap, Global Food Safety Initiative and Global Sustainable Seafood Initiative are among the other sustainability efforts pushing seafood industry members to follow more or better environmental and social practices. 

Some sustainability organizations have folded, while others have merged, but Stevens believes that they can all work together because they have all worked to avoid overlap.

"Benchmarking has done a lot to separate the players from non-players. The benchmarking activity … has really brought parity and a level of credibility to the work of what we do, to the work that others do," he said.

Stevens won't be stepping out entirely as he leaves the presidency. He will remain a member of GSA's board of directors and its executive committee and he looks forward to letting others have the reins.

"That's what I am seeing in the proliferation of people who are looking for solutions or to get them going in that direction," Stevens said. "Whether they are in the industry, the NGO (non-government organization) community or governments, wherever they may be, we have gone from protecting the status quo to doing things better and doing things smarter and better. All seafood is good if it's done responsibly."

title: Fleury Michon’s former CFO fined for insider trading
content:
France's Financial Markets Authority (AMF) has sanctioned the former financial director of agri-food group Fleury Michon, Jean-Louis Roy, for using inside information relating to the significant deterioration of the firm's annual results to sell assets, reports Capital. 

The AMF noted that Roy had sold "all of the redeemable share subscription and/or acquisition warrants" in March 2017. However, the deterioration in the company's results wasn't made public until April 2017.

For his part, he had argued that he had sold his bonds because of their limited validity period and a need for liquidity to repay a debt. He left the group last year under a contractual termination agreement.

The AMF's sanctioning decision, which could amount to €60,000, may be appealed against.

In July 2021, a similar case took place between the stock exchange and the former CEO of Fleury Michon, Regis Lebrun. They reached an agreement to close an investigation into an insider breach over the same period.

The AMF also suspected Lebrun of having sold shares and share subscription warrants at the end of 2016 and early 2017 when he was aware of the significant drop in the group's results, which had not yet been made public.

Under the agreement between the two parties, the former CEO pledged to pay €225,000 to the public treasury, without admitting his guilt.

title: Canada charges nearly CAD 46k for breaking new whale proximity rules
content:
The Canadian government handed out nearly CAD 46,000 ($36,230) in combined fines in 2021 to alleged violators of its new distance-related measures designed to protect endangered southern resident killer whales, the Vancouver is Awesome website reports. 

The government announced in early 2021 that vessels are now prohibited from approaching within 400 meters (1,312 feet) of a killer whale in British Columbia coastal waters between the Campbell River and Ucluelet until May 31, 2022. Canada's marine mammal regulations, which apply year-round, already enforced a minimum distance requirement of 200 meters.

Transport Canada explained in a press release that, between June 1 and Nov. 30, 2021, three "sanctuary zones" were maintained where fishing and boating was not permitted with some exceptions. These zones were created to reduce underwater noise and physical disturbance so the whales could better socialize, forage and rest. 

In October, five environmental groups called on Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans and other enforcement bodies to ramp up patrols, prosecutions and penalties. The groups cited a report from the marine mammal surveillance group, Straitwatch, which documented whale-watching operators "routinely violating" legally established buffer zones.

In one 12-day period in 2020, whale-watching operators allegedly breached the 400-meter buffer 84 times, according to a Straitwatch report. Another 51 recreational fishing vessels were observed within 400 meters of southern resident killer whales; of those, 28 came closer than 200 meters.

"Enforcement actions" resulted in 11 penalties in 2020, totaling CAD 45,750. It's not clear from the article how many of those fined were commercial seafood harvesters.

title: Fish Factor: Salmon research task force announced; LEDs from fish; Seafood grants
content:
Undercurrent News is featuring 'Fish Factor', a weekly column featuring the reporting and perspective of Alaska seafood journalist Laine Welch

An Alaska Salmon Research Task Force Act was recently introduced in the US Congress last week by Alaska Republican senators Lisa Murkowski and Dan Sullivan that, if passed, aims to gain better understanding about causes of salmon declines, especially in the state's northwest regions.

The task force of up to 19 people would conduct a comprehensive review of salmon science and management in Alaska. The bill also would establish a working group specifically focused on salmon returns in the Arctic-Yukon-Kuskokwim (AYK) region of western and interior Alaska.

The group would include members from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the North Pacific Fishery Management Council, the  Pacific Salmon Commission, between two and five Alaska representatives including subsistence, and commercial or recreational users, five academic salmon experts and one state representative appointed by the governor.   

Within one year, the group would publish a report identifying knowledge and research gaps and advance policies that might result in more salmon abundance and stability. 

The action follows a salmon roundtable discussion the Alaska Congressional delegation hosted earlier this month with tribal leaders and state fishery managers and scientists.

Many agreed there is a need for better data - but most called for action.

"We don't have time to sit on our hands and wait for these research projects to start and finish. Precautionary management needs to happen now. Adaptive management needs to happen now," said Mary Peltola, director of the Kuskokwim Inter-tribal Fish Commission.

Managers need to look at salmon habitat in rivers and oceans in a more holistic way, Peltola said, pointing to policies that allow large ocean vessels to capture Chinook and chum salmon as bycatch while local river residents are not allowed any fish. 

"We have got to find a way where we manage as a whole system and not these silly, man-made jurisdictional issues," she added. "And the fact that the Department of Fish and Game says their hands are tied when it comes to salmon bycatch in the Bering Sea, because that's under the purview of the North Pacific Fishery Management Council - having both agencies pointing at the other is unfair to all of the users."

Senator Sullivan also called for change. 

"Our existing management system, with the state’s authority to manage Alaska’s salmon harvest and the federal government managing federal fishery salmon harvest and much of the at-sea research, has created a clear gap in research and research prioritization that urgently needs to be addressed," Sullivan said. 

Senator Murkowski has dedicated a line and a questionnaire for public comments through Jan. 14.

Meanwhile, a group of Alaska tribes and groups representing Bering Strait communities has filed an emergency petition with the US Secretary of Commerce to eliminate Chinook salmon bycatch and cap the number of chums taken by trawl gear.  Under current rules, the pollock fleet in 2022 is allowed to take up to 45,000 Chinook salmon and an unlimited number of chum salmon while no salmon is available for local subsistence harvests.

"Our salmon runs and our communities are at the breaking point. We can’t risk the chance of high bycatch in these dire times. We need to do everything possible to save our Chinook and chum salmon runs, and we all need to do our part to restore our salmon runs, and eliminating bycatch is critical," said Brooke Woods of the Yukon River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission.

Petitioners also include Nome-based Kawerak, the Association of Village Council Presidents, the Aleut Community of St. Paul Island, the Bering Sea Elders Group, and the Kuskokwim River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission.

Salmon sperm spawns plastic, LEDs

Salmon sperm is being used to make biodegradable plastic cups in China.

Researchers at the country's Tianjin University created the item by extracting DNA from salmon sperm and dissolving it in water with molecules commonly found in adhesives. It produces a gel that can be made into various forms and freeze-dried.

The DNA-based bio-plastic can be created from genetic material from any living thing, the researchers said. Other applications for the substance include uses in electronics and packaging.

Salmon sperm also made headlines a few years ago for its ability to intensify LED lights that are used today in digital clocks to home lighting and electronics.

Andrew Steckl, one of the world’s leading experts in photonics at the University of Cincinnati, collaborated with US Air Force scientists to make a pioneering bio-LED device.

Steckl said the magic stems from the double helix shape of salmon DNA.

"The double helix has some interesting properties in regard to light emission which is not well known by the general public but is known by some practitioners," he explained. "Because of the way it is shaped, you can insert light-emitting molecules within it  that operate more efficiently than in other host materials."

The sperm comes from wild salmon from Japan, where it is widely harvested for its DNA, Steckl said. In the case of LEDs, it is refined into pure fibers and made into thin films of tightly controlled dimensions that produce light. 

Steckl said the organic material is abundant and readily available for other uses.

"To me it is a powerful argument that we have one of the biggest and most competitive industries in America in agriculture and fishing and it produces a huge amount of biomaterials which can be used in many different ways," he said, adding that they also reduce the need for heavy metals or other hazardous materials.

"This is not the sort of material that people have a lock on - in other words, it’s not a mine somewhere in some country that produces a particular metal," he said. "People in the semi-conductor and in flat panel display industries are quite concerned that certain specialty metals that are critical to device fabrication are going to begin to run out. And this is not 100 years from now, this is maybe less than 10 years from now."

Fish grants

NOAA Fisheries/Alaska Region has launched a new webpage dedicated to sharing Alaska Aquaculture Grant Opportunities.

The page will provide up-to-date information on funding opportunities for aquaculture stakeholders in many categories. Also included on the new webpage are writing resources to help improve grant applications.

title: Washington state court rejects Cooke appeal of lease termination
content:
A second civil court in the US state of Washington has affirmed the termination of a lease on Cooke's net-pen farm in Port Angeles following a 2017 escape of Atlantic salmon, reports the Orcasonian, a news service serving the state's San Juan Islands. 

The decision upholds a lower court ruling that approved the Washington Department of Natural Resources (DNR) decision to terminate the lease, which concluded a nearly four-year appeal process that began in 2018 when Cooke filed suit against DNR. Cooke argued that DNR had wrongfully terminated the lease ahead of its 2025 expiration date.

As Undercurrent News has reported, the state canceled the lease following the August 2017 escape, fined Cooke and banned the farming of non-native fish in Washington waters. 

The appeals court rejected Cooke's opinion that the termination was arbitrary and capricious, finding DNR's decision "was based on facts supported by substantial evidence, pursuant to plain terms of the contract, was well reasoned and made with due regard to the facts and circumstances."

Cooke is phasing out salmon farming in compliance with the law. The company now seeks to raise native steelhead and sablefish in Washington state, including at Port Angeles, with the Jamestown S'Klallam Tribe.

title: Loch Duart suffers £3m loss in grim COVID-afflicted year
content:
Scottish salmon farmer Loch Duart has reported a bleak set of annual results for the financial year ended March 31, 2021.

Loch Duart takes COVID hit after profits surge under new US owner 

With a business model heavily dependent on both exports and foodservice sales, the farmer claimed its ultimate £3.13 million ($4.1m) loss was an inevitable consequence of mass national and global lockdowns during the 12-month period.

Full revenue for the year came to £31.2m, down 22% from £40.3m. Moreover, gross profit was more than halved, dropping from £9.8m to just £4.1m year-on-year.

Salmon prices fell during the year, adds Loch Duart -- now majority-owned by a US fund managed by Vision Ridge Partners, who acquired its stake in the farmer last June. Meanwhile, the company was either denied entry to key markets or forced to pay an increased cost to access them.

"As a result, the company had to develop an alternative sales strategy for the period, which, although challenging, has resulted in an acceleration of changes which will see improved sales performance in future years."

Loch Duart also continued to implement strategic plans so as to be better placed at the end of the pandemic, it said. This included the June 2020 acquisition of the Black Isle processing plant, which previously belonged to the Edinburgh Salmon Company, or ESCo. Europeenne de la Mer -- itself a subsidiary of Thai Union Group -- closed ESCo in November 2018 as its losses mounted.

The plant's acquisition "has improved capacity, quality and reliability as well as opened opportunity for product development to better service the post-pandemic changing customer requirements".

In Scotland, Loch Duart continued its "significant investment" in farming infrastructure and training in support of its ongoing refined farming strategy. 

Meanwhile, the market disruption that followed the UK's exit from the EU also reduced the volume the company was able to export in the year.

"Despite that setback, the prices at the end of the year started to return towards more normal levels," the firm said. "Year end stocks placed the company in a credible position from which to start the following year."

Efforts to explore the potential for utilizing its licenses on the east coast of Canada are continuing, the company added, "but any such possibility is not yet predictable in timing or scale". Loch Duart confirmed that it still retains the necessary licenses to operate in the country.

title: US Amendment 80 fleet fears $86m revenue hit, idle vessels after NPFMC vote
content:
A steep reduction in the amount of halibut bycatch that members of the US Amendment 80 fleet can catch would end up costing them millions and likely lead to some vessels being tied up at the dock, harvesters fear.

Chris Woodley, the executive director of the Groundfish Forum, which represents the cooperative of 19 trawl catcher/processor vessels in the Amendment 80 fleet, said that the Dec. 13 recommendation from the North Pacific Fishery Management Council (NPFMC) will have major ramifications if implemented by the National Oceanic Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). The NPFMC voted eight-to-three to recommend the adoption of "final action" on "alternative three" under the proposed Halibut Abundance-Based Management system for Amendment 80 vessels in the Bering Sea and the Aleutian Islands. 

The proposal, which involves lowering limits on halibut bycatch caps, technically known as "prohibited species catch" (PSC), will see the existing cap of 1,745 metric tons annually reduced by as much as 35%, Woodley told Undercurrent News.

"That is going to result in $86m or so in losses to our companies and could cause some of our companies to shut down or just go out of business," Woodley said.

He clarified that the $86m revenue loss is related to a potential 25% cut from the current PSC cap. A 35% cut in the cap could cause lost sales of as much as $110m annually. 

His group represents five companies -- O’Hara Corporation, Fishermen’s Finest, United States Seafoods, Ocean Peace and North Star Fishing Company -- that are based in the state of Washington but trawl for soles, flounders, rockfish, Atka mackerel, Pacific ocean perch and Pacific cod in Alaskan waters.

The consequences of the NPFMC recommendation, which still needs to be formally adopted by Gina Raimondo, the US secretary of Commerce, would likely be felt in 2023. But it will likely complicate fishing plans and reduce catching effort, leaving some vessels idled during the season.

"It depends on how much halibut we encounter out on the fishing grounds," he said, adding that he believes the measure will have "no conservation benefit" on halibut spawning stock biomass.

The measure would drop the fixed cap of PSC in favor of an amount that is adjusted annually based on biological indices. 

The measure, the NPFMC said in a "need statement" that the abundance-based management proposal "links the Amendment 80 sector PSC limit to halibut abundance and provides incentives for the fleet to minimize halibut mortality at all times. This action could also promote conservation of the halibut stock and may provide additional opportunities for the directed halibut fishery."

The matter attracted hundreds of public comments, many from those who want the practice of trawl fishing stopped entirely.

"I'm a Alaskan power troller, if I keep one undersized king salmon to eat I get a $1,000 fine. Trawlers slaughter thousands of king salmon, halibut, crab, etc, and dump them overboard, they should be subject to wanton waste laws or heavily fined," a commenter identifying as Michael Dunn said.  "What is/has been happening is unsustainable and will collapse our fisheries if allowed to continue."

Another commenter, identified as Chris Hanna, questioned the economic value of trawling at all. 

"Trading king salmon, crab and halibut stocks for eight cents/pound Pollak [sic] and Arrow tooth flounder is ludicrous and only can be justified by a small handful of individuals in a very small sector of the industry that gains financially from it," Hanna said. 

Next steps

Speaking hours after the vote, Woodley declined to speculate if his group would seek legal action or directly lobby secretary Raimondo.

"This action is unprecedented by the council in terms of not, you know, providing a fleet with tools to achieve a new fishery management goal. So, at this point I think all options are on the table and that's just where we are," he said.

Woodley added that the fleet already works to limit bycatch using the tools it has available and has adopted "halibut avoidance plans" to minimize losses. Other reduction measures include the use of excluders, and deck sorting to return live halibut back to the ocean if it ends up in trawl nets.

title: Canadian wholesaler fined CAD 50k for mislabeling US lobster
content:
Chinese-owned seafood wholesaler Atlantic ChiCan (AC) in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia has been fined CAD 50,000 ($39,062) for mislabeling US lobsters as Canadian and shipping them to China, CBC News reports.

Between May and October 2019, AC imported 63,000 pounds of live US lobster and mislabeled it, thereby avoiding a 49% tariff on lobster imported into China from the US state of Maine, but Canadian prosecutor Max Kruger said there was no proof that tariff avoidance motivated the scheme.

"The evidence that we did have, including statements given by plant staff, was they were trying to satisfy insatiable market demand from their Asian customers, in particular, China", he said.

Canadian authorities detected the ruse in September 2019 and found that AC exported mislabeled lobster 286 times between June 1 and Sept. 30, 2019.

Atlantic ChiCan lawyer Victor Goldberg said the Chinese owners were unaware of the scam. Those operating the plant have left or were fired, consultants were brought in for spot audits and the company no longer imports US lobster, he said.

title: Shetland fishing group blasts floating offshore wind plans
content:
The Shetland Fishermen's Association (SFA) has called for greater scrutiny of proposals for a floating wind farm designed to provide low-carbon electricity to oil and gas installations.

UK fishing industry takes fright over offshore wind energy boom

SFA said the proposals under the Innovation and Targeted Oil and Gas (INTOG) leasing round threaten fishing grounds to the west of the islands and are "being rushed through without proper consultation". 

The INTOG program is independent of ScotWind, a program managed by Crown Estate Scotland, which will provide low-carbon electricity for domestic and commercial uses.

"The Shetland fishing industry depends on these rich grounds to the west of the islands for catching, and is hugely concerned that proper assessment of the potential impact of INTOG offshore wind on fishing is not being made," said Sheila Keith, SFA's policy officer.

"While the fishing industry will always support the aim of lowering carbon emissions, the INTOG consultation is being rushed through with scant attention to detail, unlike ScotWind which involved widespread and detailed consultation."

In charts: Where UK offshore wind projects overlap with fishing

SFA claims data on current and historical fishing activity in the areas under consideration is limited to bottom trawling and excludes seine netting, pelagic hauls, gillnetting and longlining. The data is also confined to the activity of Scottish vessels, missing out fleets from the rest of the UK, the EU, Norway and Faroe. 

Keith wants more time allotted to scrutinize proposals before leases are signed. "These are vast areas, with water depths of up to 200 meters. Floating wind technologies are in their infancy for those sorts of conditions and developers readily concede that technological solutions will not be available until after 2030.  

"The whole process should be slowed down so that the industry can gather and fully assess fishing data from these areas. That way, existing fishing opportunities and activities can be safeguarded as required in the National Marine Plan."

title: Top execs at Chinese seafood processor fined by regulator
content:
China’s securities regulatory body has fined top executives at a listed Chinese seafood processor over financial irregularities.

On Nov. 30, the China Securities Regulatory Commission (SRC) fined executives at Shandong Oriental Ocean Sci-Tech CNY 100,000-CNY 1.2 million ($15,705-$188,462) after a financial probe uncovered "major omissions" in disclosures to investors.

China’s first RAS salmon farm sold for $32m to fund behind Qingdao show venue, Baiyang deal

Oriental Ocean, a seafood processor and former owner of one of China's first land-based recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS) for salmon, borrowed hundreds of millions of yuan from third parties to repay debts and for external guarantees, said SRC. It then failed to disclose asset transactions, external guarantees, major litigations and arbitrations to investors in a timely manner, it said.

SRC said unusual financial activity also surrounds the sale of its RAS salmon facility in Yantai, Shandong province, to state-owned asset manager Qingdao Conson Financial Holdings in early 2020. It added that Oriental Ocean's multiple litigations and arbitration cases in relation to contract disputes total as much as CNY 700m.

Oriental Ocean, which is listed on the Shenzhen stock exchange, was fined CNY 1.3m, while its holding company Oriental Ocean Group was fined CNY 1.2m. It also fined Che Shi -- chairman and general manager of Oriental Ocean -- CNY 1.2m and banned him for life from securities markets.

Yu Yanbing, chief financial officer of Oriental Ocean, was fined CNY 600,000 and banned from securities markets for ten years. Five other executives of the company were handed smaller fines and were not banned from securities markets.

Other Chinese seafood industry executives have faced similar punishments in the recent past due to financial irregularities at listed companies. Last year, Wu Hougang, the former chairman of Zoneco Group, formerly China's largest listed seafood company by seafood sales, was fined CNY 300,000 and banned from securities markets after the company falsified its inventories of scallops grown in Bohai Sea. The firm is now facing multiple lawsuits from shareholders.

Meanwhile, Dalian Tianbao Green Foods, a whitefish processor, was fined and eventually delisted from the Shenzhen stock exchange last year, after it hid massive debts while its founder and biggest shareholder cashed in on the firm's inflated market valuation.

Che and Yu have now resigned from their positions at Oriental Ocean, according to a Dec. 1 filing by the board of directors. The board emphasized that the company is currently safe from delisting.

title: Cermaq Canada fined $500K for 2017 diesel spill
content:
The Canadian subsidiary of Norwegian salmon farming giant subsidiary Cermaq has been fined $500,000 (US $389,535) for a spill of more than 500 liters of diesel fuel into the coastal waters of the province of British Columbia (BC) in 2017, CBC News reports.

The company was sentenced this week by a provincial Canadian judge because the subsidiary pleaded guilty to a charge under the Fisheries Act of unlawfully depositing a deleterious substance into Raleigh Passage in Campbell River, BC. 

"I conclude that the consequences of this incident to Cermaq to date, including the monetary cost and damage to its reputation, go a long way to impress upon Cermaq the need to ensure its systems and training are sufficient to prevent similar offenses in the future," judge Catherine Crockett said in her sentencing.

Crockett rejected prosecutors' motion for a CAD 1.4 million fine for Cermaq, which is ultimately owned by Japan's Mitsubishi, saying that no proven harm to wildlife occurred and Cermaq has accepted full responsibility.

"Nevertheless, I must impose a fine in keeping with Cermaq's corporate size and relative financial means, so the fine could not be seen by Cermaq, or other companies that operate in the marine environment, as simply the cost of doing business," according to her decision.

As Undercurrent News has reported, the federal fisheries department said in a statement the fuel overflowed into the water when a fuel pump was left on overnight. No farmed salmon were killed in the spill, and tests showed there was no impact on their health and little impact upon the ocean.

All the fish were processed and sold.

title: Better supply outlook for US Pacific cod as Russia cuts TAC
content:
The US Pacific cod quota looks set to increase in 2022 as Russia reduces its total allowable catch (TAC).

Alaskan production has been on the decline over the past few years as Russia has increased its TAC, but the reverse looks set to happen in 2022.

Russia's 2022 TAC will be 186,600 metric tons, a reduction of 12% year-on-year, or 26,280t, according to government data.

The TAC in the main Russian fishing zone, in the western Bering Sea, is down 14% y-o-y to 90,000t. The total of Russian production that is Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certified for 2022 will be 42,135t.

Although the US Pacific cod TACs have not been set, the outlook is for an increase.

The plan team of the North Pacific Fishery Management Council (NPFMC) is recommending an acceptable biological catch (ABC) level of 153,383t in the eastern Bering Sea fishery for 2022, an increase of 24% y-o-y. In 2021, a TAC of 111,380t was set from the ABC of 123805t.

In the Gulf of Alaska, the NPFMC plan team is recommending an ABC of 24,043t, marginally up on the 2021 level of 23,627t. A TAC of 17,321t was set from this ABC level for 2021. All of the US fishery is MSC certified.

The plan team's ABC's will be discussed at a meeting of the NPFMC scientific and statistical committee (SSC) held from Dec. 2-9. At the meeting, the SSC will decide what ABC to recommend at the Dec. 8-16 NPFMC meeting where the TACs will be defined.

Pacific cod is the second most significant groundfish in the Bering Sea and Gulf of Alaska behind pollock. The NPFMC plan team is proposing an ABC 19% down on the 2021 TAC for the eastern Bering Sea, as reported by Undercurrent News on Nov. 30. In Russia, the 2022 TAC will come down 3% y-o-y, but the Sea of Okhotsk fishery will be reduced 10%.

Main Atlantic cod TACs down

In the Barents Sea and Iceland, the two biggest volume Atlantic cod fisheries, the TACs are down for 2022.

On Oct. 15, the Joint Norwegian-Russian Fisheries Commission (JNRFC) agreed to a 20% cut in the 2022 Atlantic cod TAC to 708,480t. The cut is in line with the latest advice from the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (ICES) issued on June 15. 

JNRFC has also agreed to a carryover of 15% in uncaught cod quota from 2021, up from the 10% previously permitted.

For Barents Sea haddock, the JNRFC cut the TAC 23% to 178,532t for 2022, in line with the management rule. ICES' advice had been 180,003t. Norway's quota for 2022 will be 88,130t. For haddock, the possible carryover will be 10%, as normal. 

In Iceland, the cod TAC has been reduced 13% to 222,373t for the 2021/2022 fishing season, which started on Sept. 1.

 Iceland's haddock quota was increased by 11% to 50,429t for the 2021/2022 fishing year.

title: Fire destroys lobster pound in Nova Scotia days before season starts
content:
Fire has destroyed a lobster pound in New Edinburgh, in Nova Scotia, a few days before the beginning of the season, which opens on Nov. 30, CBC reports. 

The staff sergeant of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) Marc Rose explained that the emergency call came in at around 10 pm on Nov. 25. saying the plant was on fire. "Flames could be seen from a great distance away," he said.

Firefighters extinguished the fire shortly before 3 a.m. on Nov. 26 with no injuries. "Right now the scene is being guarded for further investigation," Rose added. However, he was unable to say whether the fire is suspicious or not.

Additionally, the same lobster plant was vandalized back in 2020 when hundreds of commercial fishermen and their supporters raided two facilities where Mi'kmaw fishermen stored catches.

The owner was later charged for making false statements to fisheries inspectors and fined CAD 20,000 ($15,662) for failing to disclose lobster sales.

title: Maryland seafood processor fined $240,000 for visa fraud
content:
A seafood processor in the US state of Maryland was fined $240,000 for illegally employing as many as 142 undocumented, foreign temporary workers as part of what a prosecutor called "a calculated pattern of visa fraud" over five years, WBOC-TV 16 reports.

Capt. Phip's Seafood (CPS) of Secretary, Maryland was fined and sentenced to three years of probation. Its owner, Phillip J. "Jamie" Harrington III, 50, of Dorchester County, Maryland, will serve one year of probation and has paid a $10,000 fine, a $5,000 special assessment and will perform 100 hours of community service.

Harrington and CPS must also participate in an employee verification program and were debarred from participating in a federal visa program.  They entered a guilty plea in September, according to an announcement by acting US attorney Jonathan F. Lenzner. 
 
"Over a five-year period, Capt. Phip's Seafood and its owners engaged in a calculated pattern of visa fraud that not only deceived the government but also resulted in lower wages to their employees," Lenzner said. "Rather than play by the rules that other businesses follow, the defendants manipulated the H2-B visa program for the sole purpose of increasing their profits at the expense of their employees and the fair market."
 
CPS, which produces and distributes ice and seafood, had from 2013 through 2018 sought prevailing wage determinations for several job descriptions and filed petitions for visas for only the jobs with the lowest wages, regardless of the employees' actual work, Lenzner said.
 
CPS submitted false job descriptions and used workers who were only supposed to produce ice in oyster processing, maintenance, truck driving and as drivers' assistants, but only paid them for ice production, among other violations.

Most of the workers were Mexicans.

title: Aussie gov’t permits offshore aquaculture research near Tasmania
content:
The Australian government has passed legislation permitting research projects into offshore aquaculture off the coast of Tasmania.

The island state is the country's largest producer of farmed seafood, and now the current government has approved research into offshore production of finfish, shellfish and seaweed in Commonwealth waters -- more than three nautical miles out to sea.

"The Tasmanian government is taking a considered approach, including only allowing projects that are for a fixed-term, of limited scale and in a defined research area," reads a statement from Tasmania's minister for primary industries and water, Guy Barnett.

Research is to be undertaken by Launceston's Blue Economy Cooperative Research Centre. They will work to understand what kind of projects will be both feasible and sustainable, as well as what policies will need to be in place before moving to commercial-scale activity.

The Tasmanian government is also developing a 10-year salmon plan over the next year, Barnett wrote, which will include prospects for the salmon aquaculture industry to expand further in offshore waters.
