title: Opinion: Biden’s executive order raises monumental questions
content:
(The following is a letter to the editor written by David Frulla and Andrew Minkiewicz, partners in the Washington, DC, law offices of Kelley Drye & Warren.)

The landlocked state of Utah may not be known for commercial fishing but seafood harvesters in the US should pay close attention to one of the latest actions taken there by Sean Reyes, the state's attorney general.

As reported by the Salt Lake Tribune, Reyes has issued a request for proposals, or RFP, for legal assistance to challenge president Joe Biden's Oct. 8 executive order reinstating boundaries for Bears Ears and Grand Staircase Escalante national monuments, adding back some two million acres stripped out four years earlier by former president Donald Trump.

Biden's order, which was expected, simultaneously reinstated commercial fishing prohibitions in the Northeast Canyons and Seamounts Marine National Monument.

David Frulla. Photograph from Kelly Drye website.

Altogether, the later ocean-related monument occupies about 9,950 square miles, equal to the size of Maryland. That's tiny, though, when compared to the central Pacific's Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument, spanning from Hawaii west past Kure Atoll.  Billed by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) as the world's largest conservation area, that monument includes 583,000 square miles, greater than the size of Alaska's land area. 

Presidents created all of these monuments, and over 120 others, pursuant to the Antiquities Act of 1906. All told, monument areas comprise 1.5 times the size of the Louisiana Purchase. While over half the monuments are under 10 square miles, over 95% of all monuments by area are marine monuments.  

The Antiquities Act contains two main legal elements: The president may designate "objects" to be protected, but must draw the boundaries around these objects that are "confined to the smallest area compatible with the proper care and management of the objects to be protected." For their part, "objects" include "historic landmarks, historic and prehistoric structures, and other objects of historic or scientific interest."

This past March, chief justice John Roberts explained that, "A statute permitting the president in his sole discretion to designate as monuments' landmarks', 'structures,' and 'objects' -- along with the smallest area of land compatible with their management -- has been transformed into a power without any discernible limit to set aside vast and amorphous expanses of terrain above and below the sea."

The chief justice then observed, "The scope of objects that can be designated under the act, and how to measure the area necessary for their proper care and management, may warrant consideration …." Chief justice Roberts wrote these words in a "concurring" judicial opinion agreeing with rest of the Supreme Court not to hear the Massachusetts Lobstermen's appeal of lower court decisions dismissing their lawsuit challenging the Northeast Canyons monument.

Fishing groups awaiting president Biden's decision on the Northeast Canyons and Seamounts monument took heart from the chief justice's concurring opinion. However, fishermen were not the only ones to read that opinion. President Biden's team apparently did, too. 

Andrew Minkiewicz. Photograph from Kelly Drye website.

President Biden's proclamations last month differ from his predecessors' original monument declarations. His terrestrial designations describe, in far more detail, the dozens, if not hundreds, of objects these expanded monuments protect. The proclamations describe the monuments' every geologic, cultural, and paleontological facet in precise detail, even describing why the night sky is unique. 

Indeed, these proclamations read like lavish hikers' guides. Regarding Grand Staircase-Escalante, for instance: The landscape is "akin to a nesting doll of objects of historic and scientific interest …  It is rare and unique in today's world to encounter a place where one can wander and ponder undisturbed, and explore and discover at one's own pace."

The marine monument proclamation goes so far as to identify the ecosystem function of "plankton and fecal detritus."

The designations then provide additional analyses why the areas containing this collection of objects purportedly represent the smallest area compatible with protecting those elaborately described objects.

Regarding the Northeast Canyons and Seamounts proclamation:

·       The monument boundaries need to protect a series of marine ecosystems, and these ecosystems themselves are protectable objects;

·       The marine environments and their processes are complex and interconnected, and need to be protected as a whole to avoid "cascading negative effects"; and

·       Open-ocean boundaries need to be squared off whenever possible to be enforceable.

US Supreme Court chief justice John Roberts during his confirmation hearing in 2005. Photograph by Rob Crandall from Shutterstock.

Roberts explained that monument designations have included an "ecosystem" before. Yet it's notable how broadly president Biden's phraseology is in knitting, via "ecological linkages", a collection of ecosystems together into a monument. 

Questions remain, however: Should and does a president, however nobly-inclined, have the power, by himself or herself, to declare entire ecosystems (plural) as "objects" to protect? Can ecosystems be patched together into "the smallest area compatible" via "ecological linkages"?  Is there any review of a president's decision that the Magnuson Stevens Act, Endangers Species Act, Marine Mammal Protection Act, and a host of other environmental laws passed by Congress over decades are insufficient to protect an important marine area? 

At this point, we have to ask, are there any limits or checks on the president's power under the Antiquities Act? Does the law impose no realistic limits on the executive?  And, if the law imposes no limits, how does a law of this nature operate within our democracy?

title: Finnish rainbow trout farmer invests €45m to scale up to 3,000t
content:
Finnish aquaculture company Finnforel plans to invest €45 million ($51.6m) in its next growth phase, as the company aims for rapid expansion both at home and in global markets.

"Over the next decade, the mission of the Finnforel team is to bring Finnish genetics and fish farming know-how to the world. In the future, fish will be farmed where consumers are," the firm claimed.

Its rainbow trout products are currently sold in more than a thousand grocery stores in Finland under the Saimaan Tuore brand. Finnforel achieved a significant breakthrough in November 2020, when its 1,000-metric-ton production plant in Varkaus achieved maximum capacity level, it said.

Pekka Viljakainen, chairman of the board and one of the founders of Finnforel, said the firm's "highly refined model, which works without antibiotics or environmental emissions", can claim a significant part of the future seafood market.

With this investment, Finnforel will expand the production capacity of its Varkaus plant from 1,000t to 3,000t. The resulting facility will cover the entire fish farming process, from juvenile fish to consumer-ready products, it said.

Construction work on the extension, which will cost approximately €25m, will begin immediately.

In December 2021, Finnforel will begin exporting its fish products to the UK, Germany, and the Netherlands, it said. At the same time, the company is entering the design phase for several similar 3,000t projects in Europe, Russia and the Middle East.

A significant part of its expansion plans is to introduce "industrial-scale broodstock and fry production suitable for recirculating aquaculture systems" to Finland.

At present, most of the eggs used in fish farming in Finland are imported. Finnforel is building a €12m genetics and fry plant in Hollola that, upon completion, will have the capacity to produce eggs for six Finnforel plants around the world.

"According to the business model created by Finnforel, fish will be processed from eggs to consumer packaging. By securing the entire production chain, we create an easy way for consumers and retailers to buy and sell fresh and delicious fish," said Max Alfthan, managing director.

"The consumption of fish is growing internationally, and I firmly believe that more vigilant consumers will increasingly favor organically produced alternatives that are easy and quick to prepare."

Finnforel is financing these investments through a €34m share issue, plus €4.5m from the European Maritime and Fisheries Fund and €6m in loans from banks.

The share issue will make some significant Finnish and international institutional investors shareholders in Finnforel, it said. These include Ahlstrom Invest, Finnish Industry Investment, the European Investment Bank (European Fund for Strategic Investment), The Good Investors (Ireland/France) and other European family enterprises.

title: Scottish Salmon Co denied expansion on Isle of Arran
content:
The Scottish government has rejected an appeal process by the Scottish Salmon Company (SSC) as the firm sought to expand its operations on the Isle of Arran.

Bakkafrost details plans to invest almost $1bn by 2026

Bakkafrost-owned SSC was seeking permission to construct an Atlantic salmon farm comprising 12x120-meter fish pens, and an accompanying feed barge. The application was first denied in March 2021, prompting SSC's appeal.

On Nov. 9, the government reporter filed her decision, dismissing the appeal and refusing planning permission.

On its website, SSC wrote that it was looking to develop its operations in Arran with a new site of the northeast coast, in the Firth of Clyde.

"All pens will be painted dark grey or black in color to minimize visual impact. The project has innovation at its heart, ensuring robust fish health and welfare and environmental sustainability," it said, writing before the application process had begun.

This, seemingly, wasn't enough to satisfy the reporter, who said:

"In this case I find the proposal is an unacceptable incursion into an isolated, locally and nationally valued area of landscape and seascape. Whilst I recognize the benefits of the proposal and that other significant effects would be avoided I do not consider this to be an acceptable location."

"I find that the significant landscape and visual effects of this proposal are not outweighed by its social and economic benefits...Whilst aquaculture as a whole is a significant and important contributor to the Scottish economy I do not consider this single proposed fish farm is of a scale or nature that could be considered nationally important."

A spokesperson for SSC told Undercurrent News the company was disappointed by the decision, but said "it’s pleasing to note that the reporter for the Scottish government largely agreed with the environmental assessment that any environmental impacts would have been confined to the landscape and visual impact from the proposed fish farm site".

"We will continue to work with the Scottish government to play a prominent role in the sustainable growth of the aquaculture industry, which is crucial to the country’s economic recovery."

SSC added that it takes its environmental responsibilities and stewardship extremely seriously, and is working hard on this as a business through its "Healthy Living" plan, guided by core values in its goal to become the "leading and most sustainable salmon producer in Scotland".

"We have strong links with Arran stretching back over 30 years and our existing operation there continues to provide long-term employment for people on the island and is a key driver in the local economy."

title: Peru’s second anchovy season likely to start in coming days
content:
Peru's production ministry, Produce, is now preparing for the second anchovy fishing season in the main center-north fishing area, which is likely to start during the coming days, reports La Republica. 

Produce is currently evaluating the authorization of the start of 2021's second anchovy fishing season for indirect human consumption.

Following exploration work carried out by the country's Institute of the Sea, Imarpe, Produce explained that historical fishing quotas from recent years will be respected to make the conservation of the species sustainable over time. 

Additionally, the fishing season is set to end when the maximum allowable catch limit has been reached, which Produce has not yet defined.

title: Spain’s Froxa sees sales surge close to pre-pandemic levels
content:
After a 30% revenue drop in 2020 due to the pandemic, Spanish frozen processor Froxa has seen 2021 ending with "good growth" approaching pre-pandemic levels, the firm's co-owner and Asia-Pacific director, Jose Javier Fernandez, told Undercurrent News. 

According to him, this would be mainly thanks to a tremendous increase in consumption and sales since April and May, when foodservice channels -- representing around 75% of the firm's total sales -- started to show their first signs of reactivation. 

Iberconsa set to hit profit target this year after tough 2020

"Retail sales have also grown quite significantly, but the company is still very reliant on foodservice, not only in Spain but also internationally. We see demand through this channel going back to being what it was before COVID or going beyond, even," he said during the Conxemar 2021 show that took place in Vigo, Spain, between Oct. 5 and 7. 

Froxa's sales amounted to around €43.8 million ($50.7m) in 2019, up 15% year-on-year from $38m in 2018. 

"Moreover, the company is gaining additional share in its main markets. Many companies in the sector did not see this increase in consumption coming this soon and were not stocked up with enough product." Fernandez also explained. "Luckily, we were so we could supply our clients and also competitors."

Following this trend and despite current supply problems caused mainly by skyrocketing freight prices and short availability of shipping containers, the firm expects to see demand increasing further this year and through 2022. 

Froxa has all its Christmas supply secured as it believes demand will also be strong during the season. "People are eager to eat out now with restrictions easing. We have been locked up for almost two years, and I believe consumption will reflect our wish to turn the page on this chaos."

Nevertheless, Fernandez doesn't see container shortages improving in the short term, with low availability and increasingly high prices, until early 2023 the soonest. 

Cabomar sees booming EU retail demand for MAP since COVID

"This information is publicly available everywhere, so all parties in the sector are aware of the situation. However, even though Froxa is trying to increase its prices slowly, it is what it is, and consumers will also feel it in their pockets." 

In the meantime, Froxa's plans include further expansion in Latin America, where its presence has grown steadily in the last few years, he also told Undercurrent, as well as investing in new production lines to deliver on the increasing demands for its products. 

"We do not yet have a defined strategic plan for the next few years as we prefer to wait for our end-of-year results first and see how exactly we have done in 2021," he said. "However, we aim to continue growing healthily and launching new products soon."

title: French authorities detain British scallop trawler as rights row escalates
content:
A pair of British scallop trawlers have been fined, and one detained by French authorities as the ongoing dispute over post-Brexit licenses continues to cause strife in the Channel, reports The Evening Standard.

One was fined for initially refusing to allow crew from a fishery control vessel on board. The second was detained after it was found to not possess a license to catch in French seas; it now faces the possibility of having its catch seized and its captain may receive a ban from French waters.

French maritime minister Annick Girardin said the measures were customary during the scallop fishing season and formed "part of the tightening of controls in the Channel, in the context of discussions on licenses with the United Kingdom and the European Commission".

title: Seafood’s biggest firms move to next phase of sustainability efforts
content:
SeaBOS -- or Seafood Business for Ocean Stewardship -- a partnership between ten of the largest seafood companies in the world and leading sustainability scientists, has agreed during its annual CEO meeting to move to the next phase of its sustainability efforts.

This will see the companies involved continue activities designed to eliminate illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing and forced labor throughout their operations and supply chains, to protect endangered species, to phase out their use of antibiotics, reduce plastic pollution, and to continue efforts to limit their greenhouse gas emissions.

Since its launch in 2016, the partnership between seafood companies and scientific partners has developed into a "powerful model of cooperation to advance ocean stewardship not only in their own operations, but throughout the entire seafood sector", it said. Sweden's Princess Victoria has also been an active supporter of the initiative from the start. 

Henrik Osterblom, director of science at Stockholm Resilience Centre, said "the science of SeaBOS and concept that led to its formation is now moving into the next phase as members implement and meet specific goals towards achieving their original commitments".

FIPs ‘on verge’ of offering 1m tons more sustainable tuna to choose from

"This is exciting, and particularly as there are other industry sectors following the learnings of SeaBOS, and developing science-based solutions to global challenges," he added.

SeaBOS companies confirmed that individual risk assessments of their own operations showed no IUU fishing or forced labor activities. Members will now extend efforts to assess the risk of IUU fishing and labor abuse across their entire supply chains.

"Given the endemic nature of these issues throughout the seafood sector, members recognize that risks remain high of either or both being found in seafood operations. Members committed to working with relevant actors to continue to assess and reduce their risk and should any indication of IUU fishing or labor abuse be found to act upon them swiftly and transparently."

To assess and help address these risks, several science-based and operational solutions have been and will continue to be applied, including a global effort to map risks of IUU fishing and forced labor; electronic monitoring and use of novel technologies to extend traceability; and "voluntary procurement actions alongside a tool kit of policies and procedures, and third-party certification approaches".

SeaBOS members will engage in new efforts to minimize impacts on endangered species, with an initial focus on elasmobranchs (sharks and rays) and seabirds.

"SeaBOS members will identify global ‘best practice’ measures to reduce their impacts on endangered sharks and rays, as well as endangered seabirds, and extend science-based solutions to more species groups in future," said Therese Log Bergjord, chair of SeaBOS and CEO of Skretting.

Amid the risks of antimicrobial resistance, working towards reducing the use of antibiotics in aquaculture is one of SeaBOS’ key commitments. Surveys within SeaBOS companies have revealed the complexity of antibiotics use in aquaculture with differing international, national, and regional legislative requirements along with multiple different ‘codes of conduct’ and ‘farming standards’ already in existence.

During the 2021 meeting, SeaBOS members agreed to an "antibiotics stewardship roadmap". To begin they agreed to form a SeaBOS antibiotics code of conduct by October 2022; surveys of operations; a workshop in early 2022, and that there would be zero use of HPCIAs and CIAs (high priority critically important antimicrobials and critically important antimicrobials for human health, as defined by the World Health Organisation) in aquaculture operations unless there are national jurisdictional or region-specific regulations already in place permitting that to occur.  

Science-based alternatives (eg vaccines) will be developed to replace those antibiotics, including through collaborations with relevant experts and governments.

While the agreement last year to establish science-based greenhouse gas reduction goals by October 2021 was not fully met, nine out of the 10 companies have already set their own emissions reductions targets. Members agreed that by May 2022 they would all have emissions reduction goals that align with the aim of the UN framework convention on climate change to limit global warming to well below 2, and preferably to 1.5 degrees Celsius.

Since 2018, SeaBOS companies have achieved an estimated 131,117 metric tons of absolute CO2 reductions, the organization said.

"The critical role of sustainable seafood in human health and nutrition, and the opportunity to mitigate climate change impacts through innovative approaches in the seafood sector, are both key elements for SeaBOS inputs to the 2021 UN food systems summit and the United Nations climate change conference."

Members emphasized the importance of industry-policy-science collaboration to have lasting positive impacts on sustainability and ocean health, and to ensure regulatory measures at a global level were supporting positive change. "SeaBOS members will develop a more strategic approach to help build and promote better ocean governance, with added resourcing in the coming year to address those issues specifically," said Thiraphong Chansiri, vice-chair of SeaBOS and CEO of Thai Union Group.

SeaBOS committed in 2016 to reduce the use of plastics in seafood operations, and encourage global efforts to reduce plastic pollution. Multiple members participated in the 2021 international coastal cleanup program, and plan to extend that amongst members and their subsidiaries as a mechanism to raise awareness and understanding of the challenge.

They reinforced the SeaBOS "city to sea" strategy implemented in 2020 and agreed to report on plastics footprint assessments, as well as efforts to reduce or replace plastics in their operations by October 2022.

title: Untitled
content:
The investment bank Credit Suisse has been fined £147 million ($202m) by UK legal authorities for its role in the Mozambique tuna bond scandal, reports the BBC. 

Credit Suisse to face London trial over Mozambique ‘tuna bond’ scandal

The bank must also write off $200m in debt owed by the African country that has been tainted by corruption, according to the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). The pair of financial settlements form part of a $475m figure arranged by UK, Swiss and US regulators.

The FCA claimed that Credit Suisse had failed to properly manage the risk of financial crime, with staff alleged to have taken and paid out bribes as they arranged $1.3 billion of loans ostensibly intended for Mozambique's tuna sector.

In one case, a Mozambique government contractor paid kickbacks in the region of $50m to staff on Credit Suisse's legal team from 2012 to 2016 to receive loans at favorable rates.

Mozambique officials are known to have received at least $137m in bribes during that same period. Currently, 19 individuals are on trial in Mozambique on charges of bribery, embezzlement and money laundering over the case.

VTB Capital reaches settlement with SEC

A Russian investment bank, VTB Capital, also reached a settlement of its own pertaining to the bond scandal this week.

While the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) did not find that VTB engaged in intentional misconduct or fraud relating to the scandal, it has held the bank responsible for disclosure failures relating to a 2016 public offering.

"Specifically, the SEC has found that VTB was negligent because the offering materials contained misleading statements by Mozambique and omissions that VTB failed to prevent," VTB wrote in a statement. "These alleged disclosure failures, the SEC found, relate to (1) the full nature of Mozambique’s indebtedness, and (2) VTB’s role as a lender on two earlier transactions."

Although it did not admit or deny allegations made by the SEC, VTB has ultimately agreed to pay a penalty fine of $4m and disgorge $2m in fees.

"The settlement reached today marks the end of the SEC’s investigation into VTB’s role in the Mozambique transactions," the bank continued. "As we have previously said, VTB took significant steps to ensure the accuracy of the Eurobond disclosure, which were met with resistance and pressure from a number of other parties engaged in the deal, as the SEC recognized."

"We’d like to emphasize that throughout the numerous international litigations and investigations related to the Mozambique loans, none of our employees have been charged with unlawful conduct."

title: Murkowski opponent fined for using commercial fishing gear in campaign ad
content:
A Republican challenger opposing US senator Lisa Murkowski in a race for a senate seat in the US state of Alaska has been fined $270 for commercial fishing without a commercial fishing license during the taping of a campaign advertisement, the Anchorage Daily News reported.

Republican candidate Kelly Tshibaka, running in next year’s race against Murkowski, was featured in a July ad using commercial fishing gear but had no license for it. 

Tshibaka said she will not contest the citation but said that state officials misapplied it to her. She denied trying to pass herself off as a commercial harvester. 

“Under no circumstances could I have been defined as commercially fishing. I was not paid, I did not materially assist in the operation, and the fish I touched were not sold,” she said in a statement.

Murkowski mentioned Tshibaka's legal fishing snag in an interview with CNN, and Tshibaka answered by saying that Murkowski's “campaign team, her minions in the media, and her political pals have unjustly tarnished my name by falsely accusing me of getting the wrong sport fishing license. It was all a lie."

title: Biden to restore Atlantic monument prohibitions, setting stage for high court battle
content:
Now that president Joe Biden has pledged to use his executive order authority to reinstitute prohibitions against commercial fishing in a 5,000-square mile part of the Atlantic Ocean, another Supreme Court showdown with the commercial fishing industry seems inevitable. 

But don't count on it happening for several years, sources told Undercurrent News.

The White House announced Thursday (Oct. 8) that Biden soon would be signing proclamations to restore protections for three national monuments that were removed by former president Donald Trump: Bears Ears, Grand Staircase-Escalante and -- of most consequence to the commercial fishing industry -- the Northeast Canyons and Seamounts.

The actions, the White House said in a statement, are "consistent with recommendations from secretary of the interior Deb Haaland, who -- with the support of the Departments of Agriculture, Commerce, and Justice, and the White House Council on Environmental Quality -- reviewed the actions of the previous administration that drastically reduced protections for these places."

"Under the restored protections, commercial fishing in the [Northeast Canyons and Seamounts] national monument will be prohibited, with fishing for red crab and American lobster to be phased out by Sept. 15, 2023," the White House statement continued. "Consistent with president [Barack] Obama's proclamation 9496, recreational fishing in the national monument may continue."

The industry had breathed a sigh of relief when Trump, in June 2020, signed proclamation 10049 to allow commercial fishing in the Northeast Canyons and Seamounts protected area, reversing part of Obama's Sept. 2016 order, which had been executed under the authority given him in the Antiquities Act. Obama's order made a seven-year exception for lobster and red crab harvesting.

In particular, Trump's action was seen as good news by the longline harvesters of swordfish, big-eyed tuna, yellowfin tuna and mahi-mahi. They reported having lost millions of dollars and seeing their fleet shrunk by dozens of vessels as a result of 9496.

Not part of the conversation

The ocean conservation group Oceana was one of the first to celebrate the White House announcement.

The triangular space included in the national monument, the first in the Atlantic Ocean, is about 150 miles southeast of Cape Cod, Massachusetts.

"The canyons and seamounts are home to at least 54 species of deep-sea corals, which live at depths of at least 3,900 meters below the sea surface," the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) says on its website. "The corals, together with other structure-forming fauna such as sponges and anemones, create a foundation for vibrant deep-sea ecosystems, providing food, spawning habitat, and shelter for an array of fish and invertebrate species. 

Also, toothed whales, such as the endangered sperm whale, and many species of beaked whales are strongly attracted to the environments created by the area's submarine canyons, NOAA said. Fin and sei whales, two additional endangered species, have also been observed in the canyon and seamount area.

"The United States -- and New England -- has its marine monument back, and ocean life in these New England waters are safer because of it," said Gib Brogan, the group's senior campaign manager, in a statement sent late Thursday to Undercurrent. "Protecting the New England marine monument is a win-win for both fishermen and healthy oceans, sustaining strong fisheries for years to come."

The Northeast Canyons and Seamounts Marine National Monument. Image courtesy of NOAA.

The commercial fishing industry has reacted with outrage, however.

"This is an unfortunate decision that is opposed not only by those affected in the commercial fishing industry, but by all eight fishery management councils and [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration] Fisheries," said Bob Vanasse, the president of Saving Seafood, a domestic seafood industry advocacy group, in a statement sent to Undercurrent. "There is no scientific justification to prohibit commercial fishing while allowing recreational fishing. While the Biden-[Kamala] Harris administration has claimed decisions will be based on science, and not on who has the stronger lobby, this decision shows otherwise."

In particular, the industry has taken exception to what it feels is the administration not giving it enough of an audience on the matter. 

Undercurrent reported in June how Haaland had recommended in a confidential report that Biden restore the prohibitions against commercial fishing in the giant marine reserve.

Deb Haaland. Photograph from her campaign website.

"In March, before secretary Haaland was confirmed, industry members were given just one hour with staff to express their concerns," Vanasse said. "We have since requested an opportunity to meet with the secretary — as we did with her two predecessors — but our request, though acknowledged has gone unanswered."

Vanasse said the Mid-Atlantic and New England fishery management councils "have already done their job", and have protected the deep-sea corals in the region with public input using their authority under the Magnuson-Stevens Act.

"Marine sanctuaries should be created with public input as outlined in the National Marine Sanctuaries Act, not by the stroke of the presidential pen via a misuse of the Antiquities Act," Vanasse said, continuing:

"Anyone who likes fresh local swordfish, tuna, lobster and crabmeat should be very angry with the Biden-Harris administration today.  And I know some environmental advocates will claim that the statistics show that no harm has been done to the fisheries from this closure.  They think that because they don't understand fisheries and misunderstand the statistics. We could have explained that to secretary Haaland if she had bothered to listen."

Jim Budi, a founder and vice president at American Sword and Tuna Harvesters (ASTH), told Undercurrent in January that the US only catches 30% of its international quota of swordfish. The Endangered Species Act already exists to protect them against harm, he said.

In 2020, while under the exemption made in Trump's executive order, ASTH's members were able to fish in the national monument area and had one of their best trips in years, he said. This year the convergence of ocean currents resulted in 13 harvesters in his group finding 80% of their catch in the monument area, he reported. 

"The monument achieves no conservation gain," Budi told Undercurrent on Friday. "The pelagic longline fishery is a 100% sustainable surface fishery that targets highly migratory species. [ASTH] targeted surface fish concentrate in the area of the fishing ban as they migrate through. Our fishery is already successfully and over regulated by a myriad of existing laws. [ASTH] members have the same effect on the benthic environment of the monument as a bird flying over the Grand Canyon. The monument eliminates a vibrant, fertile coastal fishery forcing U.S. consumers to eat more imported fish and U.S. fishermen to travel dangerous distances to less productive fishing grounds."

Chris Brown, president of the Seafood Harvesters of America, sent a statement to Undercurrent on Friday morning, too.

"We were very disappointed to learn about the Northeast Canyons and Seamounts decision late last night," he said. "The Biden-Harris administration had the opportunity to revisit this issue and empower science, a true public process, and be guided by the principles contained in both the MSA and the Monuments Act to come up with a better process and a better solution. 

"Additionally, disregarding the carbon footprint and the impact of the recreational sector fishing in these distant waters seems profoundly unwise and inconsistent with the direction best suited to our national interests," he said.

The chief justice's bull's eye around the case

How long Biden's new executive order stands remains to be seen, as the level of protection surrounding the Atlantic marine monument has changed with every administration. Also, there's the threat of the order being thrown out eventually by the US Supreme Court.

Chief justice John Roberts seemed to hint at so much in a four-page explanation he wrote to go along with the court's opinion in March when it rejected a petition of certiorari filed by the Massachusetts Lobstermen's Association (MLA) and four other fishing groups as part of an effort to overthrow the Obama action.

Roberts practically drew a bull's eye around the right case to be made next time, seafood industry attorney Andrew Minkiewicz, a partner at the firm Kelly Drye, in Washington, DC, told Undercurrent at the time. 

US Supreme Court chief justice John Roberts during his confirmation hearing in 2005. Photograph by Rob Crandall from Shutterstock.

"This doesn't happen every day or even in a lifetime," Minkiewicz said of the apparent opportunity for the industry. "The chief justice really outlined his skepticism of the way presidents are using the power that is, or is not, granted to them in the Antiquities Act."

The Pacific Legal Foundation, a libertarian public interest law firm, had argued on behalf of MLA and the other fishing groups that president Barack Obama overstepped his bounds in Sept. 2016 when he used the 1906 antiquities law and proclamation 9496, an executive order, to create the Northeast Canyons and Seamounts Marine National Monument. Roberts said the request didn't meet the standards necessary to warrant a Supreme Court review, but his explanation indicated he strongly agreed with the sentiment.

"Which of the following is not like the others: (a) a monument, (b) an antiquity (defined as a 'relic or monument of ancient times', Webster's International Dictionary of the English Language 66 (1902)), or (c) 5,000 square miles of land beneath the ocean?," the chief justice wrote.

Andrew Minkiewicz. Photography from Kelly Drye website.

The chief justice's language was such an indication of the conservative-dominated court's true leaning that the Boston Globe called the decision a "Pyrrhic victory for conservation groups in New England" who would like to restore the bans against commercial fishing in the national monument area. The newspaper said it was a "potential roadmap for a legal challenge" and "seemed to signal that the court would be willing to consider truncating or invalidating the 5,000 square miles of federally protected waters".

Minkiewicz on Friday told Undercurrent that it would require a whole new legal action to challenge the Biden action, however, and it could take years for the matter to reach the Supreme Court. The only other course would be for the country to elect a new president to issue yet another executive order in order to reverse the decision, a slightly more difficult undertaking that would take another three years to see through. 

Regardless, Vanasse hinted in his statement to Undercurrent late on Thursday that more high court action could be coming soon.

"Now all we can do is hope that the full Supreme Court takes heed of chief justice Roberts, who recently expressed concern that presidents have been exercising 'power without any discernible limit' when they create new national monuments," Vanasse said.

title: New Zealand company, director fined $1m for black market scam
content:
A New Zealand company and its director have been fined NZD 1.5 million ($1.04m US) for an alleged scam that left unreported more than 12 metric tons of seafood worth NZD 900,000, Sunlive reports.

Michael Vernon Weaver, 42, and his company, Southern Ocean Seafoods, owe NZD 525,000 each in fines after he pleaded guilty during a criminal trial in July. Authorities identified both this week. He faced 19 charges under the Fisheries Act of 1996. Two harvesters were sentenced last year.

The New Zealand government seized more than 1.6m metric tons of crayfish quota shares valued at over NZD 1.2m as part of the settlement.

Investigators found that Weaver gave another company, Snapper Seafoods, the illegal pāua and crayfish, which came from the Chatham Islands, between January 2017 and March 2018. He and the harvesters agreed to false amounts of fish to declare for the record, authorities said.

Snapper was unaware of the illegalities and was not charged, authorities said.

title: Mowi Scotland seeks permanent injunction against anti-salmon campaigner
content:
Mowi's Scottish division is seeking a permanent interdict (injunction) against anti-aquaculture campaigner Don Staniford on health and safety grounds.

Staniford, despite repeated requests not to do so, has continued to put himself and the company’s employees and animals at risk, the company claimed. 

Scotland’s largest salmon aquaculture company has commenced proceedings seeking orders preventing Staniford from entering onto, attaching vessels to or approaching within 15 meters of all structures, docks, walkways, buildings, floats or pens at its salmon aquaculture farming sites. Following the service of court papers, Staniford has given undertakings to court to not act as complained of, pending a full determination of the proceedings.

Canadian court dismisses Staniford’s appeal over Cermaq defamation ruling

"This person’s behaviors and actions that we have borne witness to over the past two years gives cause for great concern and is not something that our staff should have to endure whilst going about their daily work," said Mowi Scotland's chief operating officer, Ben Hadfield. "Everyone should be able to go to work and expect their workplace to be free of harassment and intimidation."

While Mowi has been concerned at Staniford's "lack of respect toward...employees", the basis for these court proceedings is to ensure the safety and wellbeing of employees, fish and Staniford and his associates, the company said.

"Our business also receives much oversight from licensed professionals, government regulators and third-party auditors, and therefore does not require the services of self-appointed individuals."

Mowi’s writ cites the regular site visits and audits conducted by professionals trained in such areas as fish health, safety, and environmental management. The Scottish salmon sector -- the country’s largest food export -- is recognized as one of the most highly regulated and transparent, it said.

Mowi Scotland’s salmon aquaculture farms were inspected 316 times in 2020 by third-party organizations that included Marine Scotland, the Scottish Environment Protection Agency, and the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (RSPCA), with much of its data provided online for the public to access, it continued.

"We have not wanted to pursue legal recourse, but we cannot stand by and watch any person risk injury to themselves or for them to intentionally or unintentionally bring harm to our employees or our fish. These incursions are dangerous, unauthorized, risk our strict health protocols and have an unacceptable impact on our dedicated employees."

Staniford told Undercurrent News he would be defending Mowi's legal action "in the strongest terms". 

He claimed film shot inside Mowi's salmon farms in July revealed welfare abuse, "mass mortalities and lice infestations", and said he was not surprised the Norwegian firm wanted to prevent the public from finding out "the ugly truth about Scottish salmon". 

"Thankfully, the truth always wins out in the end and I look forward to debating these vital legal issues in open court," he added. The RSPCA went on to clear Mowi of the allegations made, finding no evidence to support them.

Mowi referred back to a case from 2012, when Staniford was -- eventually -- successfully sued for defamation by Cermaq-owned Canadian farmer Mainstream Canada.

His conduct during the trial was viewed poorly by the judge -- the Honourable Madam Justice Adair (Supreme Court of British Columbia) -- who in her written judgment pointed to Staniford mocking the physical appearance of three women who provided testimony, and described Staniford as "akin to a zealot" who will "twist facts to conform to his own personal view".

In that case, though the activist’s comments were seen to be defamatory and motivated by express malice toward Mainstream, the court initially accepted his fair comment defense.

However, a court of appeal later overturned that decision and ruled that Staniford was not eligible for protection under a fair comment defense because he failed to adequately provide facts to back up his claims.

title: New Zealand’s Sanford fined after crewman death
content:
New Zealand's largest fishing company Sanford has been fined NZD 375,000 ($263,218) and ordered to pay NZD 121,860 reparations and NZD 35,000 costs to the family of a crew member who died on one of its fishing vessels, reports Stuff.

Steffan Antony Stewart, 26, of New Plymouth, died after becoming entangled in machinery on the factory fishing vessel, San Granit, on Nov. 14, 2018.

Stewart had entered part of an automated freezer system to clear a blockage. When the system activated he became caught and was fatally injured by moving parts of the system.

Sanford pleaded guilty to one charge under New Zealand's Health and Safety at Work Act of exposing workers to risk of death or serious injury.

The 67-meter long San Granit was designed for operation in the Southern Ocean. The newest addition to Sanford's fleet of deepwater trawlers, the vessel was built in Norway and launched in 2015.

title: Pollock truckers on the hook for some $94m in US Jones Act fines
content:
The shipping, cold storage and logistics firms involved in the use of the so-called "Bayside" program that relied on a 100-foot section of Canadian rail to ship frozen pollock from the US state of Alaska to the "lower 48" aren't the only ones in the supply chain facing substantial enforcement penalties from the US government.

Also ensnared in the US Customs and Border Protection's (CBP) efforts to enforce the Jones Act, which mandates that shipping between US ports be done with US-flagged and crewed vessels, are nine third-party trucking companies used to transport the frozen fish.

These firms face an estimated $94 million in proposed fines, according to a statement made by Jennifer Adamski, the director of operations and logistics for Kloosterboer International Forwarding (KIF) and Alaska Reefer Management (ARM).

"And as a result, as of August 28, 2021, sixty-one truckloads of seafood product owned by KIF's shipper-customers and destined for delivery to their Eastern U.S. end-customers by the end of August, have been held in Bayside for final transport to the Calais, Maine border crossing," she wrote.

ARM and KIF are two subsidiaries of American Seafoods Group (ASG) that have asked an Alaska-based federal judge for a temporary restraining order and injunction to allow for the reopening of the Bayside program, which involves the use of the Bayside Canadian Railway (BCR), and sees pollock shipped from Dutch Harbor in Alaska to Bayside in New Brunswick Canada, via the Panama Canal. Before being trucked into the US market via the border crossing at Calais, Maine, the frozen seafood goes up and down a 100-foot train track outside the Kloosterboer Bayside Cold Storage.

According to Adamski, the trucking companies hit with the $9.8m in proposed fines shipped the fish from the Canadian city of Bayside to the US city of Calais, Maine, after the pollock took the short trip via rail on BCR. CBP officials are assessing the fines with respect to trucking trips made in late 2019 that relied on pollock shipments from the Bahamas-flagged vessel Duncan Island.

On Aug. 28, CBP issued "notices of penalty" (NOP) to some 14 individual entities related to the Duncan Island shipments, Adamski wrote. The seafood involved in the shipments had an assessed value of $14.7m, she wrote, adding that the proposed fines total some $80.4m. CBP claims that the Bayside program's use of the short rail line does not qualify it to use a Jones Act exception known as the "Third Proviso".

"Based on the NOPs that KIF is currently aware of concerning this shipment, CBP collectively has fined KIF and the other thirteen separate entities more than five times the value of the products transported," she wrote.

As previously reported by Undercurrent News, Dutch Harbor cold storages are currently over capacity with frozen pollock while US shippers are unable to cope with the big volumes caused by the sudden closure of the Bayside program. 

ARM and KIF as well as CBP will each have 20 minutes to present their arguments in federal court in Alaska on Sept. 17. According to a statement made in a court filing made by Andy Pillon, terminal manager of cold storage provider Kloosterboer Dutch Harbor (KDH).

Because of the stalling of the Bayside program, "KDH now is operating at full capacity", said Pillon. "Product that otherwise would have been destined for Bayside, Canada and then Calais, Maine and delivered to customers throughout the Eastern United States currently remains on hold in Dutch Harbor."

American Seafoods: Gov’t push to keep Bayside program closed is ‘unconstitutional’

He added that the capacity constraints in Dutch Harbor have "become so severe that KDH has been forced to work with KIF and ARM to contract with vessels with refrigerated container capacity for emergency and temporary cold-storage capacity".

Normally, anyone ARM vessel on a regular schedule would call KDH and be loaded full of product stored in the cold storage in one call to the berth and then sail to its destination, he said. The stalling of the Bayside program is creating a logjam, however.

"This has the additional effect of limiting available berth space for the regular fishing vessel offloads at KDH, said Pillon. In the remote port of Dutch Harbor, the main Alaska pollock landing hub, shippers deliver large volumes of seafood each day during the A and B seasons, he said. "The products must be stored before they can be timely transported, thereby making available storage capacity for new, incoming seafood products. But Dutch Harbor, Alaska is a remote area with limited cold storage facilities. There are approximately three cold storage facilities that together can store approximately 53 million pounds [24,040 metric tons] of frozen seafood."

The average amount of pollock products landed in Dutch Harbor during B season is roughly 457m pounds, he said.

Approximately 1.5m (680t) pounds of ASC products will be overdue for delivery to customers by the end of September and approximately 3m pounds (1,361t) likely at risk for October requirements, said Andreassen, in support of ARM and KIF's response to CBP. Then, several million pounds due in November and December, "for which plans are unknown at present", he said.

title: UK Sustainable Seafood Coalition endorses GDST
content:
The UK Sustainable Seafood Coalition (SSC) has endorsed the Global Dialogue on Seafood Traceability (GDST) and will now encourage the wider adoption of the standard by individual businesses.

The SSC is a coalition made up of UK retailers and seafood businesses that specialize in global seafood commerce. Its endorsement "amplifies the reality that these standards are attracting global recognition and are already changing the way that seafood traceability can be accomplished", said the two organizations in a press release.

The SSC codes of conduct currently include a commitment to robust traceability measures. The GDST 1.0 standard represents "significant progress in collaboratively defined standards of what such measures should include".

The SSC will establish a traceability working group to update its codes of conduct and guidance documents to reflect best practices, in collaboration with GDST colleagues. In addition, several members have already chosen to individually adopt and implement GDST 1.0 within their own supply chains. 

A number of SSC members have already adopted the standard, including J. Sainsbury’s, Lyons Seafoods, New England Seafood International, Youngs Seafood, Wm Morrison Supermarkets, Hilton Seafood UK, The Cooperative, and Seafresh Group. At the SSC members' meeting, the coalition agreed to encourage the wider adoption of the standard by individual businesses.

"The GDST standards provide an invaluable framework for aligning seafood traceability standards and we look forward to wider recognition and adoption across the seafood industry," said Joe Prosho from Morrisons. 

William Davies from Hilton Seafood UK added that "responsible sourcing of seafood involves ensuring the integrity of the product, along with relevant data flows in the supply chain".

"Hilton Seafoods support  and encourage the wider role of out of the GDST within seafood supply chains and the alignment of  data points within the agreed KDEs for wild and farmed products."

title: UK’s T Quality eyes acquisitions after ‘untold pressures’ of COVID
content:
UK fish and chip shop supplier T Quality was able to lift its sales and profits for the year ended Dec. 31, 2020, despite the period featuring nine months of coronavirus lockdown measures.

Sales rose 2.2% to £85.6 million ($118.5m), "despite a selling price of block fish decline of 8% on a like for like basis". Profit after tax rose from £1.09m to £1.6m year-on-year.

"The business has redefined how it approaches challenges and opportunities presented by the rapidly changing food and drink industry, and we are innovating as a consumer-first fast food business," it said. "This strategy has become even more pertinent as a result of the coronavirus pandemic."

T Quality brought in contingency measures to combat the impacts of COVID-19 lockdowns, and accessed government funding under the "job retention scheme". 

"It is a point of pride a to how colleagues and the business has continued to progress whilst begin readily focused on feeding the nation despite untold pressures across our depots and call centers," it said.

It is now reviewing an acquisition strategy, and is in talks with "several opportunities to give greater coverage throughout the whole of the UK whilst also reviewing new markets," it said. T Quality is part of Saria, a UK food firm with operations spanning the whole supply chain and with a turnover approaching £280m. That, in turn, is part of the global Saria Group.

T Quality said it remained focused on margin per invoice in 2020, resulting in another year of "line count per invoice increase and an ongoing change in products offered to customers".

Its market was challenging, with a further 5-6% decline in the number of fish and chip shops trading, it said. "Overall account numbers grew slightly, which in a declining market can only represent an increase in market share."

It increased its business into UK pubs, and launched into the care home industry "where many of the company's products comfortably sit", it said.

title: Environmental regulators fine Nova Austral $1.23m over mortality misreporting scandal
content:
Chilean regulators have fined salmon farmer Nova Austral $1.225 million over four charges relating to the company's past participation in the 2019 mortality misreporting scandal.

The farmer, which raises its fish in Chile's southerly Magallanes region, was previously fined $215,000, the statutory maximum, by fishing and aquaculture regulator Sernapesca and also prohibited it from using a farming site for one production cycle.

This stemmed from 2019 claims that Nova Austral, under the leadership of ousted CEO Nico Nicolaides, had underreported salmon mortalities in 2019 and allegedly adulterated the seabed to cover up anaerobic conditions.

The new fines were determined by Chile's federal environmental regulator, known by its Spanish acronym SMA. The agency laid five charges against the salmon farmer relating to covering up the salmon deaths, breaching waste handling procedures and failing to comply with preventative measures, among other charges. 

Nova Austral now has five days to appeal the fine, the SMA said.

The farmer said last month that is continuing to see its bottom line hurt by low harvest volumes and resulting costs that "are not sustainable" even as the salmon farmer pledged to increase harvests by year-end.

Owing mainly to a series of infectious salmon anemia outbreaks in December 2020 that cost that cost the company 4.8 million smolt and $3.8m, Nova Austral didn't harvest any fish during the second quarter of 2021, it said. Further compounding matters was the delayed stocking of the company's A11 farming site, which will now see its fish brought to market in January and February of 2022.

However, Nova Austral said in August that it will stock some 7.5m to 8m smolt this year, which will allow it to carry out harvests of 9,500 metric tons, whole fish equivalent, in 2021, significantly lower than 2020's 15,000t.

title: Untitled
content:
The US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agency never approved the "illegal" use of a 100-foot rail track in transporting pollock and other seafood from Alaska to the US East Coast, lawyers for the government argue in court documents.

On Friday, CBP's lawyers filed a response in a US federal court in Alaska to a lawsuit from two logistics subsidiaries of American Seafoods Group (ASG) requests for a temporary restraining order (TRO) and preliminary injunction to re-start the so-called "Bayside program".

Customs lays out Jones Act case against American Seafoods subsidiaries

In its response, the CBP labeled the transport model used by ASG's Alaska Reefer Management (ARM) and Kloosterboer International Forwarding (KIF) since 2012 as "flagrantly illegal", hence the level of the proposed penalties. The complaint from ARM and KIF states the industry has received over $350 million in proposed penalties from CBP, but the amount listed adds up to over $460m, with ASG companies on the hook for $330m.

ARM and KIF are requesting "a license to break the law" by asking the court to "permanently enjoin CBP from collecting penalties for what CBP believes was years of flagrantly illegal conduct", with the push for a TRO and restraining order, the government's lawyers said. Both sides will have 20 minutes to state their cases in a hearing on the TRO and injunction on Sept. 17.

As previously reported by Undercurrent News, ARM and KIF have been using foreign vessels for shipping seafood from Dutch Harbor in Alaska to Bayside in New Brunswick Canada, via the Panama Canal. Before being trucked into the US market via the border crossing at Calais, Maine, the frozen seafood goes up and down a 100-foot train track outside the Kloosterboer Bayside Cold Storage (KBB).

Some Jones Act-compliant producers want to see US pollock sector punished

CBP said the Bayside Canadian Railway (BCR), the name of the 100-foot track (pictured above, from Google Maps), does not meet the Jones Act exception named the "Third Proviso" and has not been approved.

The Third Proviso specifies foreign-flagged vessels -- cheaper and more plentiful than US-registered ones -- can be used in the transport of products from one US location to another if Canadian rail is involved on the route. Also, tariffs for the route must be recognized and approved by the Surface Transportation Board (STB).

ARM and KIF, two ASG-owned logistics firms, switched from a Jones Act-compliant shipping method in 2012 to the "illegal" Bayside program without telling CBP, its lawyers claim.

Contrary to what ARM and KIF claim, CBP said it only became aware of the Bayside program and the short BCR track in 2017 after receiving a letter from a tipster.

FREE READ Timeline: How a 100-foot railroad put Alaska pollock sector at war with Uncle Sam

The switch in 2012 from the New Brunswick Southern Railway (NBSR) -- a route approved by CBP with an STB tariff on record -- took place as ARM and KIF "believed the NBSR was too costly", the government alleges. No new tariff was filed with the STB for the route, according to the CBP. Nor did or ARM/KIF seek a ruling letter from CBP for the new route.

ARM and KIF's claim that it is their "understanding that CBP was apprised of the change from NBSR to the BCR rail trackage in 2012" is false, said CBP. "The only 'disclosure' in the record of this new manner of transportation is via various bills of lading, which are submitted to CBP at the time of entry of merchandise into the United States. Bills of lading are commercial documents (not CBP forms) that should be included in all shipments."

ARM and KIF provided an example of a bill of lading that they claim notified CBP of their change in operations with their complaint.

"This bill of lading lists the 'routing' of the shipment which takes place after it is unladen from the cargo vessel. The example indicates that the shipment moves from 'Kloosterboer Bayside to Bayside Canadian Railway North,' then from 'Bayside Canadian Rail to Bayside Canadian Railway South,' then from 'Bayside Canadian Rail' to 'New Bedford, MA'. In fact, the shipment does not go from the Bayside Canadian Rail to New Bedford, but rather, the final transportation to New Bedford is done by the tractor-trailer, in this example, operated by John Cook trucking."

The bill of lading also "misleadingly suggests" the Bayside Canadian Railway North and Bayside Canadian Railway South are discrete stops on the railway. "It fails to disclose that the train reverses itself and returns with the merchandise to its original position", CBP alleges.

American Seafoods: Use of 100-foot railroad in East Coast shipments driven by lack of alternatives

"The bill of lading does not provide any other factual details about the nature of the railway in use. CBP does not expect it to, because that is not the purpose of the document; CBP does not use a bill of lading for the purpose of understanding the detailed facts about the rail being used," the government said. "Instead, CBP utilizes the bill of lading to know what merchandise is in the shipment, the quantity of the merchandise in the shipment, the entities involved in the transportation of the shipment, from where the shipment and merchandise originated, and to where and to whom the shipment is to be delivered."

Railroad to nowhere

To qualify for the Third Proviso, there must be "transportation of merchandise" over a "through route". Secondly, this must be "in part over Canadian rail lines".

The BCR does not meet the requirements of the Third Proviso, as going up and down a 100-foot track is not "transportation" over a "through route", said CBP.

The term "through route" has been defined by the US Supreme Court as "an arrangement, express or implied, between connecting railroads for the continuous carriage of goods from the originating point on the line of one carrier to a destination on the line of another".

The Supreme Court's definition of a "through route" requires a "continuous carriage of goods" from one point to another. This definition is accepted by ARM and KIF, said CBP.

Pollock set for US could be shipped to Europe if ‘Bayside program’ not reopened

However, using the BCR, "the merchandise does not travel the BCR 'from one place to another,' it begins and ends in the same place, never leaving the Bayside port. So, the BCR is not part of a 'transportation' over a 'through route'."

CBP also cites the Oxford English Dictionary's definition of continuous as being: "Characterized by continuity; extending in space without interruption of substance; having no interstices or breaks; having its parts in immediate connection; connected, unbroken;" and "In unbroken connection with; joined continuously to; forming one mass with".

However, the movement of merchandise via the BCR "is not part of a continuous carriage of goods", said CBP.

A video of the process, which has now been deleted from the KBB Facebook page, shows "the rail cars with the merchandise go by rail from point A, to point B, then back to point A, all within the Bayside Port, before the merchandise is offloaded from the rail cars and transported by truck to the United States".

According to CBP, "there is nothing about the movement along the BCR that resembles a continuous carriage of goods along a route. The merchandise also does not move "without interruption" in a "connected, unbroken" manner. The BCR does not connect to any destination."

American Seafoods firms could be on hook for over $330m in US gov’t fines

"Even without focusing on the dictionary definitions of each word in the Supreme Court's definition of a through route, there is no question that the movement of merchandise back and forth on the BCR is completely unlike what the Supreme Court described."

The movement of goods via the BCR "defies the concept of "transportation"," CPB said.

Approved systems to 'illegal BCR

In 2001, Sunmar Shipping got a ruling letter in favor of transporting frozen seafood from Dutch Harbor into Bayside before it went on trains for "approximately 34 to 91 miles or more" on the New Brunswick Southern Railway (NBSR) before being trucked into the US market.

CBP later issued a similar ruling letter to American Seafoods Company (ASC), which also identified the NBSR as the Canadian rail carrier used to transport frozen seafood from Dutch Harbor to Maine via Bayside.

ARM and KIF then took over the shipping on behalf of ASC. Until 2012, they used the NBSR as a through route over Canadian rail lines to transport their product from Alaska to Maine and other US destinations, CBP states.

Big US pollock catchers confirm fines, deny culpability in alleged Jones Act violations

Plaintiffs knew CBP had previously issued a "ruling letter" to ASC concluding that the NBSR route met the requirements of the Third Proviso. "There was also a rate tariff on file with the STB for this route. All was good," the response from CBP states.

However, as they "believed the NBSR was too costly", ARM and KIF "radically changed their method of transporting seafood" in 2012 to use the 100-foot railway.

The companies "experienced difficulties in reliably providing timely delivery to end-customers and extremely high transportation fees" with NBSR, hence the 2012 shift which CBP claims it was unaware of, the document states.

However, the "commercial soundness of the BCR is irrelevant, as "the BCR was constructed solely as an attempt to make otherwise impermissible coastwise traffic appear to fall within the statutory exception", said CBP.

title: Could Peter Pan’s PE backer be solution to Silver Bay’s Dongwon exit issue?
content:
Private equity McKinley Capital Management is tipped as a possible interested party in the 12.5% stake in Silver Bay Seafoods that South Korea's Dongwon Enterprise and its US subsidiary StarKist & Co. are exercising a put clause on to sell back, sources told Undercurrent News.

Alaskan salmon processor Silver Bay will have to pay around $26 million to buy back the stake as per the put clause, with $6m in interest on top of the $20m paid for back in 2014, as previously reported by Undercurrent. It's though Dongwon/StarKist -- which is paying back $100m in fines for tuna price-fixing back to the US government in installments -- has given Silver Bay several months to pay.

Amid $100m price-fixing fine, Dongwon asks Silver Bay to return $26m

McKinley, which started its investment in seafood in the US state of Alaska by backing the buyout of Peter Pan Seafood from Maruha Nichiro, is one company Silver Bay has approached as a possible buyer, sources said.

Rob Gillam, CEO and chief investment officer of McKinley, didn't rule out interest to Undercurrent.

"We also read about the Silver Bay development [Dongwon/StarKist exercising the put clause, as reported by Undercurrent] … in the news", when asked for comment on reports McKinley is one firm Silver Bay has approached.

"I have a lot of respect for Silver Bay's team and their business. I'm sure there are lots of people who heard the news and are interested in taking a closer look at this great company," he told Undercurrent.

"McKinley Alaska is active in seafood with our Na'-Nuk Investment Fund's investment in Peter Pan. We are continually evaluating Alaska-themed opportunities that meet our investment criteria across many industries and sectors," said Gillam.

Peter Pan follows suit after OBI lifts Bristol Bay base price

Silver Bay is considering finding a buyer for the stake "as one option", one Alaska-focused executive, who spoke under an agreement of anonymity, told Undercurrent.

Another, familiar with the Silver Bay plans, said the company will easily have the financial firepower to repurchase the stake, if needed.

However, Troy Denkinger, the fishermen co-founder and president of Silver Bay, is said to prefer getting another investor in.

"Troy's preference seems to be to get in a new investor rather than buy the stake back," one Alaska seafood sector veteran, who asked not to be named and is familiar with the plans, told Undercurrent.

"I'm sure Troy will not want to write a $26m check," said another Alaskan seafood sector veteran.

"I'm not sure why they don't just repurchase it; they must have had a good salmon season and would have plenty of cash," he told Undercurrent.

Peter Pan continues to build leadership team with new retail VP

Executives with Dongwon, Silver Bay and StarKist did not respond to requests for comment from Undercurrent. 

Back in 2014, StarKist invested $12m for a 7.5% stake, with its direct parent Dongwon F&B putting in $8m for 5%. The put option in the deal gave Dongwon and StarKist the right to ask for the money back after a pre-agreed period of time which expired earlier this year.

The move to recoup the investment comes as StarKist faces a fine of $100m from the US government over its part in fixing the prices of canned tuna along with Bumble Bee Foods and Thai Union Group's shelf-stable US operations.

In addition to the price-fixing fine, the rationale for the investment at the time from Dongwon didn't really play out, Undercurrent previously reported. 

"They were looking to partner up with a supplier in Alaska and get bigger in salmon in Korea, as well as for raw material for the StarKist pouches. But I don't think they really ended up buying enough to make it worth it," one said. "Then, StarKist is facing these big payments. So, it just makes sense to get that money back."

For Silver Bay, which was only eight years old at the time, the deal was about partnering up with a big player to project strength to the market, he said.

At the time of the investment, Silver Bay had four plants. The company now has seven plants, six in Alaska and another in California for squid.

Canada’s Canfisco reportedly close to deal for Marubeni’s North Pacific

Undercurrent understands Dongwon asked for the money earlier in the year. Silver Bay, however, requested an extension to make payments after the ongoing Alaska salmon season has finished, sources said. 

The exercising of the put option by Dongwon and StarKist comes in a year of comings and goings for Silver Bay. 

Silver Bay lost Jon Hickman, who was its chief operating officer (COO), at the start of the year to Peter Pan. Silver Bay promoted Branson Spiers to the COO role to replace Hickman. More recently, Silver Bay brought in Colin Tippet, an executive formerly with Icicle Seafoods, as its vice president of plant operations. 

The company also added Libby Moore to its management team as its chief administrative officer, effective March 1, from OBI Seafoods. Moore joined as Undercurrent revealed the exit of Michael Guy, who was brought in as chief financial officer in January to replace Larsen Mettler, who has since surfaced at venture capital firm S2G Ventures. 

At the end of 2020, Ocean Beauty Seafoods veteran Tom Sunderland joined Silver Bay after a spell at rival Trident Seafoods.

title: Zoneco suffers first half losses as investment income declines
content:
Chinese seafood firm Zoneco Group reported losses of CNY 39.4 million ($6.1m) during the first half of 2021.

Zoneco has turned its profits of CNY 40m in H1 2020 into losses in this period, down 198.58% year-on-year, according to the company's interim report filed on Shenzhen Stock Exchange.

Meanwhile, the firm recorded overall revenues of CNY 1.05 billion in the first six months of this year, up 3.65% y-o-y.

Losses continue for China’s biggest seafood firms

Zoneco said there had been a significant decline in investment income and asset disposals, as the firm sold shares in Dalian Zhangzidao Central Refrigerated Logistics Co. and transferred the use of its sea area off Guanglu Island in the Yellow Sea in the same period last year.

Based in Zhangzidao, Dalian province, Zoneco harvests scallops farmed in the Bohai Sea and imports raw material for processing.

With the effective control of the epidemic and the recovery of consumption, Zoneco has seen a gradual rebound in domestic sales. In particular, sales of sea cucumber increased by 54.25% y-o-y, while revenues from sea urchin products were up 96.44% y-o-y. Its main product -- scallop -- also recorded a sales growth of 4.3% in this period.

However, sales of abalone products slumped by 85.11% y-o-y as the trade of fresh abalone has been suspended since the second half of 2020.

In May, Suzhou Intermediate People's Court in Jiangsu Province ruled that Zoneco must auction off approximately 58.79 million shares to pay defaulted debts. The company has also been facing numerous lawsuits related to accusations of fraud by its investors.

China court orders Zoneco to auction off shares to repay debt

In a company filing issued to the stock exchange on Sept. 2, Zoneco revealed it had accumulated about CNY 10.66m of litigation costs in the past 12 months.

Meanwhile, Zoneco's board has agreed to sell its wholly-owned subsidiary Zhangzidao Group Changdao Aquaculture Co. to Shandong Changfeng Ocean Technology Development Co. for CNY 20m last month (Aug. 28).

Zoneco was China's largest market-listed seafood company by sales until 2017, and it has been renowned for its "running scallops" fiasco.

The Chinese regulatory body used historical satellite tracking data to expose Zoneco's financial fraud by showing log data of its vessels' seeding and harvesting activities had been "plucked from thin air". Eventually, Zoneco was fined CNY 600,000 over the long-running saga involving missing scallops.

The case was transferred to the public security bureau for criminal investigations, while Zoneco's major shareholders were prohibited from selling their stakes in the company.
