title: Pollock set for US could be shipped to Europe if ‘Bayside program’ not reopened
content:
US catchers will be forced to re-direct Alaska pollock destined for domestic customers on the East Coast to other countries unless a temporary restraining order (TRO) is granted allowing the so-called "Bayside program" to restart, said a senior American Seafoods Group (ASG) executive in a court document.

If a TRO is not approved to allow the transport of pollock from Alaska to the US East Coast via the Canadian port of Bayside again, ASG "will be compelled to divert the seafood products slated for its American business customers to Europe… letting our US customers down", said Inge Andreassen, president of ASG's harvesting subsidiary American Seafoods Company, in a statement supporting the TRO.

American Seafoods firms could be on hook for over $330m in US gov’t fines

A hearing on the TRO will take place on Sept. 17, in 11 days, as companies race to complete the US pollock B season. The industry will argue the program -- where a 100-foot piece of railway at the Kloosterboer Bayside Cold Storage is used to tick the box of going on "Canadian rail" before trucking to the US -- meets a Jones Act exception.

The raw material supply chain is already jamming up after the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) federal agency started slapping hundreds of millions of dollars in fines on all parts of the supply chain involved in shipping from Dutch Harbor, Alaska, to Bayside, in the Canadian east coast province of New Brunswick, in mid-August. The additional logistical disruption in pollock comes as 2021 Alaska pin-bone out production is way down, and the Russia-to-China route for headed and gutted pollock is also severely disrupted due to the pandemic.

As of Sept, 2, approximately 26 million pounds (11,793 metric tons) seafood of valued at around $41m is on hold at Bayside awaiting transport into the US, said Jennifer Adamski, director of operations and logistics for ASG-owned firms Alaska Reefer Management (ARM) and Kloosterboer International Forwarding (KIF). This equates to more than 550 truckloads, she said, in her statement in support of the TRO. 

Close to 17,000t of ASG pollock is either stuck in the Kloosterboer Bayside facility, on the way to the East Coast, in storage in Dutch Harbor, or on ASG vessels, said Andreassen.

ASG has 11.54m (5,235t) pounds of product held in cold storage in Bayside. There is also 13.28m (6,024t) pounds is in transit or set to be received into the Canadian cold storage, said Andreassen. An additional 10.38m (4,708t) pounds of product is being held in cold storage in Dutch Harbor. A further 2m (907t) pounds of fish are currently on-board ASC fishing vessels scheduled for trans-loading into Dutch Harbor.

Hearing date set for Sept. 17 on pollock industry’s Jones Act restraining order request

Statements from the top executives of Arctic Storm Management Company and Glacier Fish Company (GFC), two large pollock catchers, also reveal they have product stuck. However, they did not reveal the quantities.

"We have product remaining in cold storage at Bayside for our domestic customers in the eastern US that we cannot ship to them without risk of additional customs penalties," said Doug Christensen, president of Arctic Storm, which owns two factory trawlers, in his statement supporting the TRO.

"This will likely mean that we will be unable to timely fill the delivery orders these domestic customers have placed with us and that we will instead need to divert this product to foreign customers," he said.

GFC, which also operates two factory trawlers, has "significant quantities of frozen products" remaining in cold storage in Bayside pending shipment to domestic customers, said the company's president, Jim Johnson, in his statement.

The product cannot be shipped into the US "without exposing GFC to the risk of additional CBP penalties and/or seizure of the products", said Johnson, whose company also operates two factory trawlers.

Big US pollock catchers confirm fines, deny culpability in alleged Jones Act violations

"This disruption is occurring in the season when value-added seafood processing factories substantially "increase their operations" in preparation for next year's Lent, said Andreassen. ASG customers are "in jeopardy due to demands from their downstream customers, which have increased substantially since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic", he added.

As previously reported by Undercurrent News, companies such as Channel Fish Processing and Eastern Fisheries warned they would run out of raw material and be forced to lay off staff if a TRO isn't granted.

As well as shorting ASG's US customers such as Channel Fish and High Liner Foods, moving the product overseas "opens the door" to foreign-sourced fish, said Andreassen, namely double frozen pollock from China and single frozen from Russia.

"The financial threat to our business is real and sizable both in terms of fines, but also in terms of customer service. Our customers depend on us and this route for the timely delivery of frozen seafood cargo that is designed well in advance each year around our fishing season, and the Lenten season when fish consumption rises in the US," he said.

Other than shipping the fish in Bayside overseas, ASG and others could transport the goods relocate goods back to Dutch Harbor for reshipment into the US market. However, this will create a "log jam" in Dutch Harbor, which has limited capacity, said Andreassen.

Alaska pollock’s Jones Act crisis threatens East Coast US processors, school lunches

Also, every company will be competing to send products back from Bayside, he said.

Or, companies could delay and pay for transport to carry goods back to the US mainland from Bayside at a time when temperature-controlled shipping containers are running short, said Andreassen.

In addition to the possibility of finding new customers for the pollock in Bayside or on the way to the East Coast, ASG, Arctic Storm, GFC and other impacted pollock companies will need to find new supply routes for the fish in Alaska.

"CBP's penalty notices have also necessitated that we find alternative refrigerated transportation for our products currently held in Alaska cold storage facilities and for future shipments of domestic-bound products," said GFC's Johnson.

"We have concerns whether potential alternative arrangements in total will be adequate to support the entirety of the displaced cargo and may negatively impact GFC through significantly delayed transit times, increased handling, decreased service quality, and higher costs," he said.

As Arctic Storm completes the pollock B season, a "substantial portion" of the product on vessels or in storage in Alaska is destined for domestic customers, said Christensen.

Lawsuit reveals broad scope of Jones Act crackdown on US pollock industry

"We must now find alternative refrigerated transportation for this product. Although there are some limited alternative transportation options available, it is doubtful that those alternatives offer the capacity needed to transport all of the pollock industry's domestic-bound product in a sufficiently reliable, timely and cost-effective manner," he said.

So, Arctic Storm will be "competing with other pollock producers for the limited capacity of those alternative transportation options", said Christensen.

The story so far

The industry has been dealing with a surprise crackdown on its efforts to ship frozen product from Dutch Harbor to Bayside since at least Aug. 9, according to a lawsuit filed on Sept. 2 against CBP by ARM and KIF, the logistics firms ultimately owned by ASG.

Undercurrent reported early last week how -- with no apparent warning and at the end of the sector's important B season -- CBP had begun slapping US companies with massive penalties for using foreign-owned tampers to haul their frozen catch from Dutch Harbor in Alaska to New Brunswick in Canada, in violation of the 100-year-old law that requires the use of US-owned, built and crewed vessels for US port to US port shipments.

The vessels travel down the US West Coast, through the Panama Canal, and up the US East Coast. The federal agency is apparently ignoring an exemption to the law, known as the "Third Proviso", that had been used by the industry with CBP's blessing for at least 20 years. It requires pollock shipments to be transported over Canadian rail lines as part of their journey back into the contiguous US.

Biden initiative, short track possible factors in US pollock industry’s Jones Act crisis

In their complaint filed last Thursday, ARM and KIF describe in detail how they've used a mere 100-feet section of rail lines in New Brunswick to qualify for the exemption, moving a container full of frozen fish up and down the tracks, before having it trucked the rest of the way to its destination in the US. The process is dubbed the "Bayside program" in the documents.

The complaint document from ARM/KIF states CBP has issued more than 170 penalty notices, proposing fines of at least $350m, 35 times more than the largest Jones Act penalties ever collected, against companies involved up and down the supply chain of the Bayside program.

However, the complaint and other linked legal documents seemingly reveal fines totaling $462m. ASG and its lawyers did not respond to requests for clarification on this discrepancy.

ASG and subsidiaries ARM and KIF could be on the hook for at least $330m of this, according to Undercurrent's calculations.

According to the documents, the fines dished out by CBP to ASG companies directly add up to $71m. ASG's fishing subsidiary American Seafoods Company is liable for $46m and KIF hit with $25m. However, companies fined a further $259m intend to hold ARM/KIF responsible for the penalties they have received, taking the total ASG could be hit with to $330m, Undercurrent has determined, based on details in the complaint.

But it could be even worse. There's a further $132m in penalties for cold storage and trucking firms, for which the document does not state if ASG-owned companies will be held liable.

According to the complaint, the additional $259m in possible fines that companies intend to hold ARM/KIF responsible for breaks down as follows.

"At least nine" of KIF's shipper customers -- other pollock catchers using the so-called "Bayside program" -- have informed KIF of penalty notices issued to them, totaling approximately $139m. In addition to ASG, other fishing and processing firms used the ARM/KIF transport service to take pollock from Dutch Harbor to Bayside.

US pollock sector battles more than $300m in Jones Act fines, questions where exemption went

"All of these KIF shipper customers contend that KIF is liable for the penalties issued to them by CBP," the complaint states. Arctic Storm and GFC confirmed CBP fines, in separate statements supporting the TRO. The presidents of both Arctic Storm and GFC stopped short of stating ASG/ARM/KIF are financially liable but said they used the shipping in service in good faith of its legality.

ARM -- which, along with KIF, organizes the logistics of shipping pollock from Dutch Harbor, Alaska -- is not seemingly being fined directly, according to the complaint document. However, ARM is being held liable by other companies for at least another $120m in fines.

Five ship owners that ARM contracts to use vessels to deliver seafood from Dutch Harbor to Kloosterboer Group's cold storage in Bayside have collectively provided to ARM nine notices of penalty, totaling approximately $55m. The ship owners "contend that ARM is responsible for payment", according to the document.

"In addition, to date, ARM has received notices concerning ship owners and charters who have been assessed penalties totaling" over $65m. The ship owners and charters intend to object to the penalties and holding ARM liable for any fines from the CBP, as well as defense costs. The ship owners and charters' insurance policy carriers have also been advised of CBP's notices, the complaint states.

The complaint also states CBP has issued $37m in penalties to two cold storages it contracts to store its customers' seafood in Dutch Harbor and Bayside.

The statement from Adamski, director of operations and logistics for KIF and ARM, clarifies these firms are Kloosterboer Dutch Harbor (KDH) and Kloosterboer Bayside Cold Storage (KBB). KDH and KBB are part of Kloosterboer Group, which US giant Lineage Logistics acquired from its former Dutch owners earlier this year. ASG seemingly owns a piece of KDH, but it's not clear how much. ASG and Kloosterboer Group executives were not immediately available to clarify this.

The complaint also states that two importers and nine trucking companies contracted by KIF have received penalty notices totaling approximately $95m. The document does not name any trucking firms or clarify if they intend to hold ARM/KIF responsible.

title: American Seafoods firms could be on hook for over $330m in US gov’t fines
content:
Editor's note: An earlier version of the story reported the total penalties American Seafoods Group companies could be liable for is $136 million, but further analysis suggests it's $330m 

American Seafoods Group (ASG) and subsidiaries involved in pollock logistics could be on the hook for at least $330 million in fines from the US government amid a crackdown on alleged breaches of the Jones Act related to the transporting of fish from Alaska to the US East Coast.

Big US pollock catchers confirm fines, deny culpability in alleged Jones Act violations

The fines dished out by US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to ASG companies directly add up to $71m, according to legal documents filed in support of a lawsuit, temporary restraining order (TRO) and an injunction to both cancel the fines charged by federal authorities and allow the previous transportation practices to resume. A judge ruled on Sept. 3 that a hearing on the TRO will take place on Sept. 17.

According to the documents, ASG's fishing subsidiary American Seafoods Company is liable for $46m and Kloosterboer International Forwarding (KIF) hit with $25m. KIF is a logistics firm owned by Alaska Reefer Management (ARM), which is part of ASG. Per Brautaset, president of ARM, confirms in his statement that -- despite still using the Kloosterboer name -- his ASG-backed firm acquired KIF in September 2018.

However, companies fined a further $259m intend to hold ARM/KIF liable for the penalties they have received, taking the total ASG could be hit with to $330m, Undercurrent has determined, based on details in the complaint.

But it could be even worse. There's a further $132m in penalties for cold storage and trucking firms, for which the document does not state if ASG-owned companies will be held liable. Although the complaint says the total fines have hit $350m, the penalties listed add up to $462m.

Executives with ASG and their legal team were not immediately available to clarify this apparent discrepancy.

Hearing date set for Sept. 17 on pollock industry’s Jones Act restraining order request

ASG and the other industry players are hoping to get the fines nixed and the trade re-opened again.

"The financial threat to our business is real and sizable, both in terms of fines but also in terms of customer service," said Inge Andreassen, ASG president, in a statement filed in support of the court actions. "Our customers depend on us and this route for the timely delivery of frozen seafood cargo that is designed well in advance each year around our fishing season, and the Lenten season when fish consumption rises in the US."

As a result of the penalties issued against KIF and the ship owners to date, ARM faces "imminent destruction" of its business, if an injunction is not granted, said Brautaset. ARM's average net income for the two prior years is only $1.6m, he said.

"If ARM is found liable for such penalties, despite any ARM arguments opposing such claims, it will not be able to indemnify such losses," he said.

Likewise, ARM cannot provide any aid or coverage for the penalties sustained to date by KIF. CBP also continues to issue penalties related to the co-called Bayside program, "and the amounts of those penalties continue to accrue", said Brautaset.

The additional $259m in possible fines that companies intend to hold ARM/KIF responsible for breaks down as follows, according to the complaint.

Alaska pollock’s Jones Act crisis threatens East Coast US processors, school lunches

"At least nine" of KIF’s shipper customers -- other pollock catchers using the so-called "Bayside program" -- have informed KIF of penalty notices issued to them, totaling approximately $139m. In addition to ASG, other fishing and processing firms used the ARM/KIF transport service to take pollock from Dutch Harbor, Alaska, to Bayside in the east coast Canadian province of New Brunswick, then into the US.

"All of these KIF shipper customers contend that KIF is liable for the penalties issued to them by CBP," the complaint states. Arctic Storm Management Group and Glacier Fish Company (GFC) confirmed they have been fined by the CBP, in separate statements supporting the TRO. The presidents of both Arctic Storm and Glacier stopped short of stating ASG/ARM/KIF are financially liable but said they used the shipping in service in good faith of its legality. 

ARM -- which, along with KIF, organizes the logistics of shipping pollock from Dutch Harbor, Alaska -- is not seemingly being fined directly, according to the complaint document. However, ARM is being held liable by other companies for at least another $120m in fines. 

Five ship owners that ARM contracts for the use of vessels to deliver seafood from Dutch Harbor to Kloosterboer Group's cold storage in Bayside have collectively provided to ARM nine notices of penalty, totaling approximately $55m. The ship owners "contend that ARM is responsible for payment", according to the document.

Lawsuit reveals broad scope of Jones Act crackdown on US pollock industry

"In addition, to date, ARM has received notices concerning ship owners and charters who have been assessed penalties totaling" over $65m. The ship owners and charters intend to object to the penalties and holding ARM liable for any fines from the CBP, as well as defense costs. The ship owners and charters' insurance policy carriers have also been advised of CBP’s notices, the complaint states.

The complaint also states CBP has issued $37m in penalties to two cold storages it contracts to store its customers' seafood in Dutch Harbor and Bayside. 

A statement from Jennifer Adamski, director of operations and logistics for KIF and ARM, clarifies these firms are Kloosterboer Dutch Harbor (KDH) and Kloosterboer Bayside Cold Storage (KBB). KDH and KBB are part of Kloosterboer Group, which US giant Lineage Logistics acquired from its Dutch former owners earlier this year. ASG seemingly owns a part of KDH, but it's not clear how much. ASG and Kloosterboer Group executives were not immediately available to clarify this. 

The complaint also states two importers and nine trucking companies contracted by KIF also "received substantial notices of penalty" totaling approximately $95m. The document does not name any of the trucking firms or make it clear if they intend to hold ARM/KIF responsible.

Bayside program

Undercurrent reported early last week how -- with no apparent warning and in the middle of the sector's important B season -- CBP had begun slapping US companies with massive penalties for using foreign-owned tampers to haul their frozen catch from Dutch Harbor in Alaska to New Brunswick in Canada, in violation of the 100-year-old law that requires the use of US-owned, built and crewed vessels for US port to US port shipments.

The vessels travel all the way down the US West Coast, through the Panama Canal, and up the US East Coast.

The federal agency is apparently ignoring an exemption to the law, known as the "Third Proviso", that had been used by the industry with CBP's blessing for at least 20 years. It requires pollock shipments to be transported over Canadian rail lines as part of their journey back into the contiguous US.

In their complaint filed last Thursday, ARM and KIF describe in detail how they've used a mere 100-feet section of rail lines in New Brunswick to qualify for the exemption, moving a container full of frozen fish up and down the tracks, before having it trucked the rest of the way to its destination in the US. The process is dubbed the "Bayside program" in the documents.

title: Lawsuit reveals broad scope of Jones Act crackdown on US pollock industry
content:
The scale of the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) crackdown on the US pollock sector in relation to its alleged Jones Act violations is even broader than many in the seafood industry may have realized, also hitting cold-storage facilities, foreign-owned shippers and trucking companies, a lawsuit filed recently by the industry reveals.

CBP has issued more than 170 penalty notices since Aug. 9, when the crackdown began, accounting for combined proposed fines of at least $350 million, 35 times more than the largest Jones Act penalties ever collected. 

Biden initiative, short track possible factors in US pollock industry’s Jones Act crisis

Undercurrent News reported late Thursday how Alaska Reefer Management (ARM) and Kloosterboer International Forwarding (KIF) had filed a lawsuit and motions for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction in an Anchorage, Alaska, federal court. A review of the court documents confirm many of the sensational facts earlier reported by Undercurrent about the massive Jones Act case being brought against the companies that dominate US' largest commercial fishery.

They also provide many more details previously unknown.

Undercurrent reported early in the week how -- with no apparent warning and in the middle of the sector's important B season -- CBP had begun slapping US companies with massive penalties for using foreign-owned tampers to haul their frozen catch from Dutch Harbor, Alaska, to Bayside, New Brunswick, Canada, in violation of the 100-year-old law that requires the use of US-owned, built and crewed vessels for US port to US port shipments. The vessels travel all the way down the US West Coast, through the Panama Canal, and up the US East Coast.

The federal agency is apparently ignoring an exemption to the law, known as the "Third Proviso", that had been used by the industry with CBP's blessing for at least 20 years. It requires pollock shipments be transported over Canadian rail lines as part of their journey into the contiguous US, also known as the "lower 48".

US pollock shippers head to federal court to stop Jones Act enforcement

The dispute was revealed in a memo circulated in Washington, D.C., by the At-sea Processors Association, a group that represents six seafood companies that maintain interest in or operate 16 US-flagged high-tech trawl catcher/processor vessels in the Alaska pollock fleet.

In their complaint filed Thursday, ARM and KIF describe in detail how they've used a mere 100-foot section of rail lines in Bayside to qualify for the exemption, moving a container full of pollock up and down the tracks, before having it trucked the rest of the way to its destination in the US. 

Undercurrent had suggested that the seemingly nonsensical use of such a small piece of train track by the industry was likely key to CBP's enforcement effort, but was not able to get a pollock industry source to confirm the practice. 

More shocking, however, are the court documents' detailed breakdown of the penalties being issued. They relate to offenses that allegedly occurred as long as five years ago. 

The lawsuit said KIF had been served directly with two penalty notices, combining to total $25m, while the owners of five ships that contract with ARM said they had received nine notices of penalties totaling about $55m, which they contend ARM is responsible to cover. Other ship owners and charters have been assessed penalties for more than $65m, which they also maintain ARM is responsible for.

At least nine of KIF's shipper customers say they have been hit with more penalty notices amounting to a combined $139m. Two cold-storage facilities with which KIF contracts in Dutch Harbor and Bayside report to have been hit with fines totaling about $37m. And two importers and nine trucking companies contracted by KIF said they are being fined about $95m.

US pollock sector battles more than $300m in Jones Act fines, questions where exemption went

As a result of the crackdown, the lawsuit advises, the "entire supply chain is at a complete standstill".

"Because of the notices of penalties levied on third-party trucking partners -- essential to transport the frozen seafood products into the United States -- two of KIF's primary trucking partners have informed KIF that they will no longer transport goods via the Bayside program absent assurance they will not incur further penalties, which are directly linked to the value of their seafood cargoes," the complaint continues.

The scale of the Alaskan pollock industry can't be overstated. It produced 1,520,712 metric tons of fish in 2019, more than twice the size of landings of the US' second-largest commercial fishery, menhaden, according to data recorded by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. It was worth $387.6m.

However, the ARM and KIF lawsuit said: "the scope of the penalty notices assessed to date is more than twice the annual value of all frozen Alaskan seafood transported through the Bayside port to US destinations". 

The KIF and ARM lawsuit request a ruling that the pollock industry's mode of delivering fish into the US complies with the Jones Act, that CBP improperly modified or revoked a prior agency ruling and that due process and Eighth Amendment rights were violated. They seek an immediate injunction against further Jones Act enforcement actions and unspecified compensatory damages as well as legal fees.

title: Fresh from gate, Atlantic Sapphire suffers $51.5m net loss during first half
content:
Atlantic Sapphire (AS) suffered a net loss of $51.5 million on combined sales of $10.9m during the first six months 2021, the Norwegian-based company with Atlantic salmon recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) operations in both the US and Denmark, reported Thursday. 

AS has been the RAS company to watch in North America ever since it announced its plans, several years ago, to build a land-based facility in Homestead, Florida, and later upped its goal to project producing as much as 30,000t of Atlantic salmon annually by 2023. The industry knows that AS' performance could weigh heavily on investors' enthusiasm for other projects in the sector. 

The company, which is publicly traded on the Oslo Bors Stock Exchange (ASA), began harvesting salmon at its US operation in Oct. 2020, as reported by Undercurrent News. However, there have been more than a few hiccups since AS came out of the gate, as are evident in its latest report.

In a presentation delivered Thursday, AS said its first batches of fish "have been exposed to suboptimal conditions, which has negative trickle-down effects later in the life cycle", and it's now estimating that half of the 3,000t of head-on and gutted salmon that it planned to harvest in the second half of 2021 will be pushed into 2022. 

Atlantic Sapphire's financial statement for the first half of 2021.

However, it also said that phase 1 conditions now are "stable after [a] long period of commissioning efforts and construction challenges" and it has started the third quarter of 2021 with good water quality parameters and biological performance. Steps are being taken to minimize risk and reduce oxygen consumption, including a controlled harvest of some 100,000 fish at sub-optimal weights and also a paused feeding, the company said. 

Also, on the bright side, demand is strong for locally raised salmon in the US, the company said. AS CEO Johan Andreassen declared in May that the conditions were ripe for high prices, a prediction that proved omniscient.

"In my 20 years in the industry I have never seen a stronger outlook for high salmon prices than now. Buckle up!" he tweeted, as reported by Undercurrent. 

AS also revealed Thursday that it's trying out rainbow trout as another potential species to sell, noting that the fish is robust and tolerates higher temperatures and densities than Atlantic salmon. No modifications would be needed to AS' infrastructure, it said. Also, trout commands high prices in Europe, similar to salmon, with room to develop the market and command even better rates, the company noted

AS reported that its combined harvest out of both the US and Denmark was 1,275t of head-on gutted salmon during the first six months of the year, up from 989t during the first six months of 2020. 

The US operation was responsible for $7.5m in sales during the first six months of 2021, up from $172,000 during the first six months of 2020, while the Denmark operation contributed $3.3m, up from $2.8m during the earlier period, according to AS' financial statements.

Its financials show that it had a combined 4.5m fish accounting for 3,037t of live weight at both operations as of June 30, up from 2,020t on June 30, 2020. As many as 1.1m of the fish, accounting for 2,876t, were at a harvestable size at the time.   

Atlantic Sapphire is one of three land-based farmers to have been given a buy rating by Fearnley Securities. Credit: Atlantic Sapphire

AS's consolidated earnings before interest taxes depreciation and amortization during the recently completed six-month period was a negative $42.2m, worse than the negative $21.9m EBITDA experienced during the first six months of 2020.

Delivering news about unfortunate developments at its two plants is not a new experience for AS. 

More than half – 60% -- of the undisclosed number of salmon in production at the Norwegian company's Homestead plant as part of its first batch developed gonads well in advance of their scheduled harvest, Andreassen and chief financial officer Karl Oystein Oyehaug told investment analysts during an earlier presentation, as reported by Undercurrent.

The company experienced an "internal chiller plant breakdown" and a massive mortality event in Homestead on March 23, claiming some 200,000 salmon, or 500 metric tons, roughly 5% of the company's expected 9,500t phase-one harvest volume. It said Thursday that the incident cost it $7m in lost sales, though the insurance and claim process is ongoing.

In April, the company was forced to rescue three contract company workers from a large tank in Homestead after they passed out, saying later that they were not following "confined space safety protocols".

Then, in July, it reported another mortality event in Denmark, which it attributed to human error, causing it to lose some 400t of fish.

AS' stock closed at NOK 75.40 ($8.54) on Thursday, down 50% from the NOK 150.0 high it hit in late February.

title: Untitled
content:
South Korean seafood giant Dongwon Enterprise and its US subsidiary StarKist & Co. are exercising a put option on the 12.5% stake they bought in Silver Bay Seafoods in 2014, demanding $20 million and interest back, sources told Undercurrent News.

With the interest, the total Alaska-based wild salmon processor Silver Bay will have to pay is around $26m, sources said. Back in 2014, StarKist invested $12m for a 7.5% stake, with its direct parent Dongwon F&B putting in $8m for 5%. The put option in the deal gave Dongwon and StarKist the right to ask for the money back after a pre-agreed period of time which expired earlier this year.

Dongwon, Starkist to own 12.5% in Silver Bay

The move to recoup the investment comes as StarKist faces a fine of $100m from the US government over its part in fixing the prices of canned tuna along with Bumble Bee Foods and Thai Union Group's shelf-stable US operations.

Undercurrent understands Dongwon asked for the money earlier in the year. Silver Bay, however, requested an extension to make payments after the ongoing Alaska salmon season has finished, sources said. 

Executives with Dongwon, Silver Bay and StarKist did not respond to requests for comment from Undercurrent. 

"They [Silver Bay] will have had a good salmon season, so it should not be a major issue to pay back," one Alaska seafood sector veteran, who asked not to be named, told Undercurrent.

Value-added in focus ahead of Peter Pan’s first season under new owners

In addition to the price-fixing fine, the rationale for the investment at the time from Dongwon didn't really play out, he said.

"They were looking to partner up with a supplier in Alaska and get bigger in salmon in Korea, as well as for raw material for the StarKist pouches. But I don't think they really ended up buying enough to make it worth it," he told Undercurrent. "Then, StarKist is facing these big payments. So, it just makes sense to get that money back."

For Silver Bay, which was only eight years old at the time, the deal was about partnering up with a big player to project strength to the market, he said.

At the time of the investment, Silver Bay had four plants. The company now has seven plants, with six in Alaska and another in California for squid.

DOJ: StarKist spent cash reserves seeking lower price-fixing fine

A hefty fine

Since its October 2019 sentencing by San Francisco, California-based federal judge Edward Chen, StarKist has long said that it would not be able to a $100m fine, the maximum allowed by law. That amount would prompt the company’s bankruptcy, as was the case with rival US canner Bumble Bee, StarKist’s lawyers said at the time. They argued it would also force StarKist to relocate its canning operations from its longstanding base in the US territory of American Samoa to Thailand where labor is cheaper, potentially putting thousands of people out of work.

This has yet to occur.

While StarKist lawyers argued in 2019 that although the company appeared to have $250m in assets, the situation was complicated because around $155m of those assets represents its stake in Techpack Solutions, a maker of glass and plastic bottles that StarKist said it was unable to sell.

Techpack was slated to be merged in the future with another Dongwon affiliate, Dongwon Systems, at which time StarKist would receive shares that it could turn into cash. But StarKist attorney Niall Lynch said that overcapacity in the bottle-making industry meant that valuations of bottle makers are not high. Department of Justice prosecutors accused StarKist of deliberately lowering its cash reserves so that it would not be able to pay the fine.

Chen ruled in 2019 that StarKist’s $100m fine was be paid over a five-year period with $5m due in November 2019, $11m to be paid in 2020 and additional annual payments of $24m to follow. 

Lynch had asked judge Chen to lower the $100m fine to $50m so that the company could use its future cash flows to pay damages from civil lawsuits filed by customers who say they were damaged from price-fixing. Those suits are still ongoing and StarKist has objected to a San Diego, California-based judge's decision to grant the plaintiffs class certification. 

Dongwon move comes amid turbulent year 

The exercising of the put option by Dongwon and StarKist comes in a year of comings and goings for Silver Bay. 

Silver Bay lost Jon Hickman, who was its chief operating officer (COO), at the start of the year to the "new" Peter Pan Seafood. Silver Bay promoted Branson Spiers to the COO role to replace Hickman. More recently, Silver Bay brought in Colin Tippet, an executive formerly with Icicle Seafoods, as its vice president of plant operations. 

The company also added Libby Moore to its management team as its chief administrative officer, effective March 1, from OBI Seafoods. Moore joined as Undercurrent revealed the exit of Michael Guy, who was brought in as CFO in January to replace Larsen Mettler, who has since surfaced at venture capital firm S2G Ventures. 

At the end of 2020, Ocean Beauty Seafoods veteran Tom Sunderland joined Silver Bay after a spell at rival Trident Seafoods.

title: Norwegian krill harvester fined over ‘inside information’
content:
Norwegian Antarctic krill harvester and supplement maker Aker Biomarine has been fined NOK 500,000 ($55,902)  by the country's stock exchange for rules violations, the exchange said.

The Olso Bors fined the firm NOK 350,000 for "breach of the duty to disclose inside information" and another NOK 150,000 for "failure to disclose information" to the exchange, it said in a release.

The charges are linked to Aker Biomarine's launch of an initiative the company is calling Lysoveta, which it describes on its website as a "new process" to produce lysophospholipid-bound long-chain omega-3s eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA). 

"Lysoveta achieves more targeted delivery and greater uptake of DHA/EPA in specific organs, such as the brain and eyes. EPA/DHA are vital nutrients to support healthy structure and function of these organs across the human lifespan," Aker said on its website. 

However, the Oslo Bors said that it considered the company's Nov. 24 announcement about the Lysoveta launch to be "inside information" for the company.

"Oslo Bors considers that this information constituted inside information no later than in the evening of 19 November 2020 and that the duty to disclose the inside information arose at the same time," the exchange said. "Furthermore, Aker BioMarine has breached its duty to provide information to Oslo Bors by not providing the exchange with information about certain matters in connection with the exchange's inquiries about the matter."

The krill harvester has yet to respond publicly to the matter.

title: Malta fish farm operators ordered to clean up slime
content:
Three fish farm operators in Malta have been ordered to clean up slime that had entered swimming zones, reports The Times of Malta.

The Environment and Resources Authority (ERA) ordered the farms to clean up slime that was found in the St Peter's Pool, St Thomas Bay and other areas of the Marsaskala coastal region.

According to one bather, rocks were "covered in an oily white and sticky slime".

"This is the worst I've experienced it because it stuck to my skin, and equipment and wouldn't wash off. Yuck. It felt like I was slimed in Ghostbusters," the report said.

The unnamed operators were cooperating with the authorities and immediately began the cleanup operation, along with the ERA and the police, the report added.

Slime produced by Malta's tuna farming industry has been a regular problem.

In 2019 Malta's Mare Blu Tuna Farm was temporarily shut down and fined after a routine inspection found a consignment of bait fish feed that had not been properly thawed, sources within the environmental regulator said.

This could have resulted in excessive fatty residue forming an oily slick on the sea surface once it was lowered into tuna pens.

title: SPAC craze expected to soon be part of seafood finance
content:
A new global financing craze is providing hundreds of millions of investment dollars for indoor farming systems, indicating that investors could be willing to take risky bets on new aquaculture systems. 

Special purpose acquisition companies (SPAC) were an obscure alternative financing mechanism to an initial public offering (IPO) or traditional debt finance routes to market before the coronavirus pandemic. With a ban on travel affecting the roadshow process of IPOs and a massive amount of capital or "dry powder" held by private equity firms and other institutional investors, a SPAC boom emerged in 2020.

Share offering to mean new markets, likely M&A for Barramundi Group

There were 34 SPAC deals last year, after an average of about five a year between 2010 and 2019, according to S&P Global Intelligence. More than 90% of those deals were to finance early-stage tech ventures in the US. But the SPAC boom continued its exponential rise in 2021 and branched into high-risk yet lucrative areas such as biotech and indoor farming. There were 94 SPAC deals recorded in the first half of the year, according to S&P. 

Four food-tech SPACs emerged this year, including three indoor farming companies, Aerofarms, AppHarvest and Local Bounti, funneling more than a billion dollars into ventures to sell herbs and tomatoes raised in heated farms from Kentucky to New Jersey. A fourth company, Benson Hill, comes even closer to the doorstep of the $250bn aquaculture industry as a provider of ultra-high refined soybean concentrate for fish feed. 

It could only be a matter of time before SPAC financiers start to look at tough-to-finance projects such as land-based fish farms or major insect protein processing facilities to replace marine ingredients.

"I see no reason why not, assuming it would involve a sufficiently attractive buy-out offer to shareholders," an executive involved in the land-based fish farming industry told Undercurrent News. "SPACs can be formed based on different market risk profiles."  

The tolerance for risk in SPACs was sky-high earlier this year. At least eight electric-vehicle (EV) companies went public in 2020 through SPAC-financed deals. The Economist wrote in an April editorial that the SPAC trend is "a giant experiment with a different way to take firms public." 

Meet the RAS investors: Devonian Capital looks for more US partners

The model allows favorable terms for the originators of the SPAC, often known as the sponsors of the investment vehicle. Other (retail) investors buy shares in the SPAC on less favorable terms without knowing the eventual target of the SPAC management team. They are effectively betting on the business acumen of the sponsors, who are often revered investors. One example is celebrity hedge fund manager Bill Ackman, whose SPAC Pershing Square Tontine Holdings traded at a 50% premium to its cash value earlier this year. The eventual acquisition of a target results in a so-called de-SPAC deal, where the target is merged with the SPAC and goes public in an IPO. 

SPACs and their sponsors usually start out with a pre-ordained acquisition target. Big agriculture companies Bunge and Cargill participated in the Benson Hill and Local Bounti deals, respectively. Ag-focused S2G Investments, which is investing in seafood companies, also participated in the Benson Hill deal. 

Part of what might be holding back investments in the next Atlantic Sapphire in the recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) space could be the lack of industry expertise and valuation models known to instructional investors for companies operating in the space. S2G Investments is one of the few known companies with that level of expertise, as is aquaculture-focused private equity firm Aqua-Spark, which has now invested in almost 20 companies. These are two of a very small pool of investors equipped with due diligence skills to evaluate an aquaculture investment fully. 

"Aquaculture has yet to see the same transition to next-generation technologies that have occurred in the indoor farming sector," Adam Bergman, managing director of EcoTech Capital and the former head of agtech and food tech lending at Wells Fargo, told Undercurrent. "Indoor farms, particularly vertical farms, are integrating AI, automation and robotics, data analytics and AI, which have yet to have the same adoption levels in aquaculture." 

RAS IPOs 

A handful of RAS start-ups have successfully carried out IPOs on the Oslo bourse, following in the footsteps of Atlantic Sapphire, the earliest of companies in this segment to raise the finance to build an industrial-scale facility in the US state of Florida. Andfjord Salmon, Nordic Aqua Partners, Proximar Seafood and Salmon Evolution have all navigated the traditional IPO route to develop land-based projects. But outside of the Nordic finance bubble, RAS start-ups have struggled to raise finance. 

Atlantic Sapphire: Land-based farms can learn from aircraft industry de-risking

The Land-based Salmon Handbook published jointly by Spheric Research and Undercurrent News last year identified about 80 projects to grow salmon on land in the world, and several new initiatives have arisen since then. In the US, only AquaBounty Technologies, which has developed a bioengineered salmon, is listed on the Nasdaq exchange. Blue Star Foods, a Miami company that owns a salmon RAS facility called the Taste of BC in British Columbia, will test the US market's resolve with a planned conventional IPO on the Nasdaq exchange. Outside of Norway and the US, finance is scarce. 

Investors are intrigued by the RAS model, which offers a lower carbon footprint and eliminates coastal salmon farming problems such as sea lice and disease issues, said Maggie Fried, the head of ocean, seafood and aquaculture for a family-office investor consortium known as CREO. But they are also scared off by the lack of an existing industrial-scale facility and studies that show projects require a price premium to be profitable, she said. 

Spin-offs, private equity 

SPACs are also likely to enter the seafood space by buying spun-off assets from existing companies or by PE firms looking for an exit strategy. PE firm Bregal Partners was in talks with at least two SPAC companies to divest its stake in Alaskan pollock fishing company American Seafoods Group, sources told Undercurrent at the time. Bregal has rejected several bids from fishing companies to buy the fishing assets for under $1.4bn, sources said. 

Bregal in talks with ‘blank-check companies’ for American Seafoods deal

The lack of a deal may have something to do with a dampening of the SPAC space since April when the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) said it would tighten regulations governing the use of SPAC instruments. 

However, the model offering an alternative to the IPO process has shown its worth and will probably regain momentum this year. It is also becoming popular in other countries outside of the US, Joseph Shaposhnik, CEO of TWC Special Purpose Acquisition Corp., said in a webinar organized by S&P Global Intelligence. 

"More high-quality businesses will enter the market," Shaposhnik said. "That will put more and more emphasis on companies that have real revenue and real cash flow." 

The SPAC is likely not done in so-called CleanTech and companies with environmental, social and governance credentials, including seafood, said Adam Bergman. 

"There will be a longer-term opportunity around cleantech and sustainability," he said.

title: Les Hodges: Russian king, snow crab supply caught in severe Asia bottleneck
content:
The world is desperate for more snow and king crab, but Russia -- the only game in town -- is having a hard time getting its crustaceans into several markets, reports renowned crab sector veteran Les Hodges. 

Russian snow and king crab "replenishment product" has been hampered by a "severe supply bottleneck in Asia", the longtime, Washington state-based consultant said in his most recent monthly newsletter sent to clients. Crab is arriving every week in a transit point in South Korea, but importers can't get containers to ship it.  

"It is currently taking 4-6 weeks to obtain a container, freight rates have quadrupled, and there is a 2-3 week delay in offloading on the US west coast," he said. "The South Korea container squeeze has simply created gridlock for not only crab and seafood, but everything from furniture to clothing is delayed."

The problem is expected to continue for some time, Hodges warned.

The tragedy surrounding Russian king and snow crab is happening just as the two other large sources of snow crab, Canada and Alaska, have wrapped up their seasons, and retail demand and the growing number of opening restaurants have virtually wiped out inventory. Many categories and sizes are unavailable, and prices are moving up almost every week, Hodges noted.

The US economy is in a good position to pay the hefty prices sought for king and snow crab as well as lobster and other premium seafood, as long as they can find a supply, he added. 

The US gross domestic product grew at an annualized 6.5% rate through the second quarter of 2021, lifting it above its pre-pandemic peak and clearly demonstrating a V-shaped recovery, defined as a period of economic decline with a trough and then a rapid recovery, Hodges said.  

The labor market is strong, too. Employers added 943,000 jobs in July, higher than expected, and unemployment dropped from 5.9% to 5.4%. Consumer spending in the second quarter advanced at a solid 1.8% pace topped only by the fast-paced rebound in the third quarter of 2020.

Hodges said representatives of his consulting firm, Les Hodges and Associates, visited various supermarkets in several parts of the US in late July to evaluate the presence of crab in fresh counters. Eight out of 10 had king crab or snow crab in their "fresh counters" even if not on promotion, he noted. 

Comparing the Jan. 1, 2021 crab market to July 31, 2021, the price increases of king and snow crab have continued and are now up over 65% depending on size.

"The inability of marketers to adequately replenish inventories, combined with increased demand, has strained the crab supply chain," he said. "The challenges faced by marketers are substantial as they compete for crab in world markets and face quotas on crab that are finished or close to the same."  

Individual Russian harvesters' quotas maxing out

Alaska finished its 2021 snow crab (Chionoecetes opilio) season in mid-May with 44.5m lbs (20,185t) fully harvested, but its catch has mostly disappeared from the US market with many of the sales made early to Japan, Hodges noted.   

The Canadian snow crab season started one month early, on April 3, to avoid entanglements with North Atlantic right whales, and hit its total allowable catch (TAC), among the largest fisheries at 71,756t (158.2m lbs) by the end of July.

"There was intense initial demand by US buyers and market prices started 50% higher and never looked back," he said. "Today 5-8 size snow crab is being quoted at more than $16.00/lb [in the US city of Boston, Massachusetts]. Larger sizes are even higher. Exports to the US have been strong following the same delivery pattern as the last five years except it occurred one month earlier." 

Snow crabs. Credit: Vintagepix/Shutterstock.com

In Russia, the TAC for 2021 is more than 100,000t, with harvesters close to reaching their individual quotas on some species based on a utilization report delivered on July 28, Hodges said. Though the Russian processors and their customers are looking forward to the red king crab season that starts Sept. 1 with a 27,000t quota.

The latest fishing report showed a continued significant effort on snow crab in the Northern Okhotsk fishery. Of the 62 vessels reported, 29 are fishing for snow crab with the majority processing cooked, followed by eight harvesting live and four producing raw frozen. Inspection reports from Northern Okhotsk shows large sizes with excellent meat infill, Hodges reported.  However, a number of inspection reports showed some levels of sea lice on shells. 

South Korea has imported 4,001t of Russian live snow crab and 2,013t of Russian and Norwegian live king crab through the first six months of 2021, Hodges also noted. Average import prices for the year to date are $45.59/kg on king crab and $28.15/kg on snow crab. 

However, live king and snow crab imports by South Korea retreated from earlier levels in June in both volume and price, he added, based on Korea Customs Service data. King crab imports were 252t in June vs. 412t in May with the price dropping to $36.52/kg on Russian and increasing to $50.60 on Norwegian.  Russian snow crab deliveries in June were also lower at 616t compared to the 912t imported in May.  The average price was $20.23/kg. 

More of Hodges' report on the state of the snow and king crab markets can be found here.

title: Bolton set to buy high-end US tuna brand
content:
Italy-based Bolton Group International is closing in on a deal for a high-end US tuna brand, Wild Planet Foods, sources told Undercurrent News.

The percentage of the stake Bolton is set to take in Wild Planet under the deal is unclear, but it appears it will give the Italian firm control.

Sources were unsure if the deal has closed, but it is said to have been agreed upon. "I think it's a live item," one told Undercurrent.

Bolton Group: Discounters, private labels win retailer race during pandemic shopping boom

Bill Carvalho, president and founder of Wild Planet, based in McKinleyville, California, declined to comment to Undercurrent.

Luciano Pirovano, sustainable development director for Bolton's food division, also declined to comment.

Carvalho is set to stay on after the deal closes, sources said.

Wild Planet, which is sold in the likes of Costco Wholesale, Target, and Whole Foods, has grown from a tiny niche brand founded in 2004 by Carvalho to the fourth-largest in the US, according to its website.

"It's a great fit for Bolton. The quality of the [Wild Planet] products is very high and they're also very into the story. They are basically southern European [products] in terms of quality," one source, who asked not to be named, told Undercurrent.

Credit: Wild Planet Foods

The company's core product is pole-and-line and troll-caught albacore tuna in cans and pouches. As well as albacore, Wild Planet's tuna range includes skipjack and yellowfin. The company also sells shelf-stable anchovies, mackerel, salmon, sardines, yellowtail, and even beef and chicken. In April, Wild Planet launched a range of ready-to-eat tuna salad bowls in Whole Foods.

Wild Planet is regularly ranked by Greenpeace as having the most sustainable sourcing in the US. In 2019, the company won global supplier of the year and environmental stewardship awards from Whole Foods.

Bolton's North American aspirations

Bolton, who owns the Rio Mare brand in Italy, Isabel in Spain, and Saupiquet in France, was looking to move into the North American branded market in 2019 with a deal for Bumble Bee Foods' Canadian business, which owns the Clover Leaf, Brunswick and Beach Cliff brands for shelf-stable seafood.

US tuna price-fixing case seen as example of ‘aggressive’ antitrust enforcement

The sale process, however, collapsed amid the uncertainty around Bumble Bee, which ended up filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection at the end of the year. Taiwan's FCF ended up buying Bumble Bee from Chapter 11 for $928 million, creating an industry giant with sales of around $2.6 billion.

FCF's main competitor in tuna trading, Tri Marine, was fully acquired by Bolton in 2019.

Bumble Bee's Chapter 11 filing came about due to a $25m fine from the US government for its role in price-fixing in the sector, along with StarKist & Co and Thai Union Group's Chicken of the Sea International (COSI). The government fined StarKist $100m but COSI, as the "whistle-blower" on the price-fixing, evaded punishment.

title: US tuna price-fixing case seen as example of ‘aggressive’ antitrust enforcement
content:
The United States Department of Justice (DOJ) is stepping up its policing of criminal antitrust violations and the recent tuna price-fixing scandal could be a harbinger of what's to come, a law firm believes.

"DOJ's success in the packaged-seafood investigation will further embolden its attorneys to scour through merger documents for signs of potential criminal antitrust violations. DOJ credited its civil attorneys' keen eyes during the merger review, leading to the discovery of materials that resulted in the criminal investigation," lawyers from the Washington, DC-based law firm Arnold & Porter wrote in a recent article published on the firm's website.

The news that executives US tuna canners StarKist & Co, Bumble Bee Foods and Thai Union Group's Chicken of the Sea International (COSI) engaged in price-fixing in the early part of the last decade rocked the seafood sector.

The DOJ investigation of the canned tuna sector arose in 2014 as part of a pre-merger review when COSI's US parent, Tri-Union Seafoods, planned to acquire Bumble Bee. That merger was called off the next year as the investigation widened.

The Arnold & Porter lawyers who wrote the article: Andre Geverola, Sonia Pfaffenroth and Javier Ortega, said that companies across all industries should be mindful of criminal antitrust risks when pursuing mergers given the significant potential impacts.

"As the packaged-seafood case study makes clear, failing to account for criminal antitrust risks can result in significant financial losses for companies and their investors, and individual liability for corporate executives," the attorneys wrote.

The tuna price-fixing scandal led to an amnesty application from whistleblower COSI, as well as guilty pleas from StarKist and Bumble Bee and three executives there. In 2019, prosecutors convicted former Bumble Bee CEO, Christopher Lischewski, after a five-week trial. He was sentenced to serve three years in prison but has maintained his innocence.

StarKist was fined $100 million for its role and Bumble Bee was fined $25m. The weight of the scandal prompted Bumble Bee to file for bankruptcy and enabled its purchase from its longtime albacore supplier, Taiwan's FCF Co.

Recently, the administration of US president Joe Biden indicated that it would step up its antitrust enforcement efforts generally. 

On July 9, the White House issued an "Executive Order on Promoting Competition in the American Economy". That order did not mention seafood but made particular reference to agriculture.

 "Consolidation in the agricultural industry is making it too hard for small family farms to survive. Farmers are squeezed between concentrated market power in the agricultural input industries -- seed, fertilizer, feed, and equipment suppliers -- and concentrated market power in the channels for selling agricultural products," the order states.

In their article, the Arnold & Palmer lawyers noted that the two executive branch agencies entrusted with antitrust enforcement will be emboldened by the lead taken by the administration.

"The DOJ Antitrust Division and the Federal Trade Commission quickly followed with an announcement that they would jointly launch a review of merger guidelines with an eye towards a more aggressive enforcement approach," the lawyers wrote.

title: Skipper fined, vessel confiscated in Seychelles for illegal fishing
content:
The captain of a Sri Lankan harvesting vessel has been handed a SCR2.5 million ($167,000) fine for illegal fishing in Seychelles waters, according to the Seychelles News Agency.

Mahalingam Kanapathi, 32, pleaded guilty to the offense of fishing without a license under the country's fisheries act following a ruling Wednesday by a Seychelles Supreme Court, a mid-level federal court that hears more complex and high-value civil claims and more serious criminal cases. He has 14 days to pay the fine or face two years in jail. During that time he cannot leave the country.

His fishing vessel, Sampath 7, which was intercepted in June by the patrol boat Topaz, was ordered by the court to be confiscated by the federal government.

It was the third vessel to be caught illegally fishing in Seychelles' waters since May, the report added, citing the complex challenge the island nation faces in policing 1.4 million square kilometers of exclusive economic zone.

The article doesn't indicate what kind of fish Kanapathi was harvesting illegally.

title: Fish Factor: Crab shell textile treatments; Seafood council scholarships; Bristol Bay’s record
content:
Undercurrent News presents 'Fish Factor', a weekly column featuring the reporting and perspectives of Alaska seafood journalist Laine Welch

Most people are unaware that the yarns and fabrics that make up our carpets, clothing, car seats, mattresses, even mop heads, are coated with chemicals and metals such as copper, silver and aluminum that act as fire retardants, odor preventors, antifungals and antimicrobials.

Now, crab shells from Alaska are providing the same safeguards in a bio-friendly way. The metals and chemicals are being replaced by all-natural Tidal-Tex liquid treatments derived from chitosan molecules found in the exoskeletons of crab shells.  

The bio-shift stems from a partnership between Leigh Fibers of South Carolina and Tidal Vision, the proprietary maker of the crab-based product which it began making in a 20 foot Conex van in Juneau six years ago. The company, which now operates near Seattle and has 22 full-time employees in three production facilities, expects to put up to 60 people to work within two years.

In July, Tidal Vision opened its newest facility within Leigh Fibers’ headquarters, bringing its earth-friendly technology into the heart of the US textile industry. Leigh Fibers is one of North America’s largest textile waste and byproduct reprocessing businesses. It dates back to 1866 and now services 25 countries.

"Partnering with Tidal Vision is a win-win for our company, our customers, and the environment," said Eric Westgate, a senior vice president at the company. "Their Tidal-Tex product line delivers the key benefits that our customers look for in textiles at a lower price and is made from sustainable materials in the USA. At Leigh Fibers, we’re committed to advancing sustainable innovation and repurposing textiles for a cleaner, healthier planet."

Tidal Vision CEO Craig Kasberg echoed those sentiments.

"Having a partnership with Leigh Fibers was really strategically advantageous for us because they produce the fibers that then get turned into yarns that then get turned into all sorts of woven or non-woven textiles for everything from the automobile industry to the carpet industry to the acoustic sound insulation industry to the mop head industry to the furniture industry. They are at the top of the supply chain and treating those fibers was the easiest way to have the biggest impact in the textile industry," he said.

Most of the raw product comes from snow crab and red king crab delivered to St. Paul Island in the Bering Sea where they are processed into frozen leg clusters. The shells are transported to the mainland where they are put through Tidal Vision’s zero waste, proprietary extraction process that produces chitosan in a flake form and is then made into the ready to use, liquid Tidal-Tex product.  

Kasberg said it provides the same fabric protections as the manmade agents at far less cost.

"Our costs are minimal. They're basically just tied to the logistics and some of the freezer storage costs but it’s nearly a free input material," he said.

All crustaceans have chitosan, a polysaccharide that is the second most abundant organic compound in the world next to cellulose. Because of its unique molecular makeup, Kasberg calls it a "turnkey chemistry solution" to displace often toxic synthetic methods.

"All these heavy metals need to be mined and refined, and then modified into these metal-based chemicals. Whereas we're taking an abundant and even problematic byproduct from the seafood industry and with a really low-cost extraction method, producing a biochemistry solution that can provide the same properties in these industries. Our inputs are tied to a byproduct," Kasberg said.

Tidal Vision has tested a lot of crustacean "inputs", Kasberg said, but Alaska crab shells pack the best chitosan punch.

"The starting molecular weight of the chitosan is higher," he said.

Tidal Vision hopes to build more partnerships and expand to other countries within the next few years.

The company also features a line of other chitosan-based products including water clarifiers and a game animal spray that prevents spoilage and keeps insects away.

"Our goal as a company is to create positive and systemic environmental impacts with our chitosan technologies," Kasberg said. "We're still on the ground floor of Tidal Vision’s potential today."

Seafood scholarships

Scholarships are being offered to small and medium-sized seafood businesses to help shape and launch a new National Seafood Council. Its mission is straightforward: to provide a unified voice for the industry to encourage Americans to eat more seafood. 

A task force was formed in April 2021 led by the Seafood Nutrition Partnership (SNP) to get things underway.

"Some of the tasks include designing the governance of the National Seafood Council and the makeup and responsibilities of the board members. We want to make sure that the task force is representative of size of companies, gender, geography around the US and points all along the supply chain," said Linda Cornish, SNP's president.

Nominations are wanted from six to eight seafood-related companies whose annual revenue are less than $20 million. The scholarships, backed by the Walton Family Foundation, will be based on those revenues multiplied by .00025, or a minimum of $2,500.

A National Seafood Council was created in 1987 as part of a Fish and Seafood Promotion Act but fizzled after five years. In May 2021 a group of over 60 US fishing companies, groups and medical professionals asked Congress to provide $25m in seed money to revive the group to develop a national seafood marketing and education program. The seafood council would eventually become industry-funded, similar to other food industries.

"Seafood is probably one of the healthiest foods that people can eat and there's just not enough funding to get that message out," Cornish said. "The milk industry has about $300m a year to market their product, pork about $70m a year, avocados about $50m. Seafood doesn't have that. So for us to tell our story to the consumers in a more cohesive and unified way, we need some help to get this council started, and provide that resource to have a marketing campaign to do the same as other food groups have."

Cornish said the idea has been well received in Congress.

"Right now we're looking for some champions in Congress to spearhead that request on this group's behalf," she added. "There's a lot of priorities being discussed on Capitol Hill and we need to make sure that the needs of this National Seafood Council are heard by Congress."

Americans overwhelmingly turned to seafood during the Covid pandemic and Cornish said the time is right to advance the health message.

"We're still fighting this COVID-19 pandemic and seafood supports immune health and also is great for brain development and heart health," she said. "I think the industry is ready to work together in a more collaborative way to get this unified message out to the consumers. And I really think we have the right window of time to do so."

Eating seafood also tops the list in new US dietary recommendations that Americans eat two servings per week, starting with kids at six months.

The deadline to apply for a task force scholarship is Aug. 13.

Bristol Bay breaks it!

The reds are still rolling in at Bristol Bay where a run topping 64m has officially broken the record for all-time sockeye returns since 1893! The previous record was set in 2018 at 62.9m fish. 

"Large numbers can be hard to comprehend, so consider this," wrote Andy Wink, executive director of the Bristol Bay Regional Seafood Development Association which is funded and operated by driftnet fishermen. "If lined up nose-to-tail, this year’s Bristol Bay sockeye run would stretch on for roughly 20,000 miles, enough to encircle all the lower 48 states… twice!"

It’s natural abundance on a truly epic scale, Wink added.

"It’s important to highlight just how special the Bristol Bay salmon resource is. These records aren’t being set while overfishing. All escapement goals were met to propagate strong future runs. Despite all the bad news about environmental degradation and destruction, Bristol Bay is a shining example that healthy ecosystems can and still do still exist. It’s really an ecological treasure. We ask that state and federal government protect Bristol Bay salmon and the natural habitats that allow it to thrive."

Processors have increased the base price at Bristol Bay to $1.25 per pound. At an average fish weight of 4.5 pounds and a catch so far at nearly 39.5m fish, back of the envelope calculations put the value of the sockeye haul to fishermen so far at over $222m.

Bristol Bay sockeye currently represents 82% of the statewide sockeye landings of nearly 49m and 56% of all salmon harvested so far across Alaska (80.4m). 

"The boats aren't even dry yet and interest in Bristol Bay drift permits is beginning to trickle in. Permits are popping up for sale, with preliminary asking prices between $200,000 and $240,000," said the Fish Ticket report by Alaska Boats & Permits in Homer.

title: Scottish association’s scallop chief out after prosecution for illegal fishing
content:
The former head of the Scottish Whitefish Producers Association (SWFPA)'s scallop committee, John MacAlister, no longer holds the role after a vessel he owned was prosecuted this year for illegal fishing, BBC television program Countryfile has reported.

NGO ‘out of patience’ with Scotland’s scallop, nephrops FIP

David McCandless, a chief officer with the North Eastern Inshore Fisheries and Conservation Authority, told the BBC's Tom Heap the vessel Star of Annan -- owned by MacAlister -- had been observed scallop dredging out of season; operating with its automatic identification system switched off; and damaging local lobster pots to free its dredge.

This took place in North Yorkshire, he said. The skipper at the time was fined over £3,500, but MacAlister received a record fine of more than £200,000 ($272,000).

Adding insult to injury, MacAlister had spoken to Countryfile in March 2019 as the head of the SWFPA's scallop committee, assuring Heap that no professional fisherman under the association was fishing illegally in marine protected areas. The offenses for which he was prosecuted took place that same month, and continued for several months more.

Confronted by Heap in 2021, he told the program the skipper in charge of the Star of Annan was not the company's regular skipper, and suggested the legal action around the incident was ongoing. He threatened the journalist with legal action should he continue to accuse MacAlister personally.

The SWFPA told Countryfile that MacAlister was no longer chair of the scallop committee but remained a member. Click here to view the piece on the BBC iPlayer in the UK (beginning around nine minutes in).

title: US offers Ecuador support in deterring IUU fishing off Galapagos
content:
The US' consul general in Ecuador, Brian Quigley, pledged his full support to the Latin American country in the fight against illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing following the recent arrival of foreign vessels near the Galapagos Islands' fishing grounds. 

"The US and Ecuador are close friends and allies, and we stand united against IUU fishing," Quigley said during a forum hosted by the US consulate's public affairs office on illegal fishing with Ecuadorian media.

Ecuador spots 294 foreign vessels near Galapagos, deploys naval, air forces

During his intervention, he also recalled that, among the support already provided to Ecuador, the US helped the local prosecutor's office intercept a massive Chinese fishing vessel, the Fu Yuan Yu Leng 999, in August 2017.

Back then, authorities discovered the Chinese vessel inside the Galapagos marine reserve with around 300 metric tons of endangered marine species, including more than 6,000 sharks killed for their fins. The crew received jail time of between one and four years and were also fined a total of $5.9 million. 

Quigley also highlighted that an expert in illegal fishing is about to finish her three-month research mission in the Galapagos archipelago. "We are waiting for the end of the month to come when she finishes her investigation period so that we can learn about her recommendations and all the material she collected." 

Additionally, Fernando Rey, a researcher working for the WWF in Ecuador, also spoke at the meeting and stressed that there are still some outstanding issues on the part of the Ecuadorian governance, and more specifically, "within legal frameworks, which urgently need several improvements and corrections," he said.

China, Ecuador hold talks amid Galapagos fishing fears

Against this background, the Ecuadorian coordinator of organizations for the defense of nature and the environment, CEDENMA, in its Spanish acronym, demanded that Ecuadorian authorities take preventive action in the face of the imminent arrival of these vessels.

"IUU fishing doesn't only happen once foreign fleets operate in the waters of an exclusive economic zone but also when they catch species protected by international treaties, such as the hammerhead shark," CEDENMA's president, Gustavo Redin, said. 

"What happened in 2017 is just the precedent that shows that the international fleet fishing outside our EEZ may also be fishing for these protected species," he added. 

Finally, Bruno Leone, president of Ecuador's national chamber of fisheries, explained that IUU fishing is the third-largest illegal activity in Ecuador, after drug and arms trafficking, and highlighted the importance of the fishing sector for the Ecuadorian economy. 

According to him, Ecuador's fisheries sector exported around $5.5 billion worth of products and employed 108,000 people directly in 2020.
