title: NGO ‘out of patience’ with Scotland’s scallop, nephrops FIP
content:
Environmental NGO Open Seas is "out of patience" with Scottish fishery improvement projects (FIPs) set up to try and increase the sustainability of the country's scallop and nephrops fisheries, it has said.

Scottish gov’t under pressure to impose real-time tracking on all inshore fishing vessels

For five years or more it has warned that dredging and bottom trawling have been taking place in marine protected areas (MPAs), with regulations and traceability requirements too weak to stop the proceeds of this fishing from reaching the market.

The nephrops are largely processed by some of the UK's biggest players into scampi sold through pub chains and most retailers. The scallops occasionally get sold in the UK, but are more often exported to EU markets. 

"We are now recommending consumers take more concerted public action to put pressure on the sourcing of some of the most environmentally damaging fisheries operating around Scotland and the UK. That is why this month we have launched the #EndSeafoodGreenwash campaign," it said.

"Unfortunately, government regulation has been weak and for the past few years we have held out hope that good leadership within the seafood industry would help to resolve these issues -- sadly this has not happened."

Back in 2017, said Open Seas, it contacted businesses selling scallops dredged from Scottish waters and scampi (the main product created from nephrops catches in the UK) caught in Scottish bottom trawls, noting that several of these fisheries were "red-rated" (according to the Marine Conservation Society "good fish guide") yet sold under the guise of "responsible" or "sustainable" marketing, it said.

Many of these businesses recognized the concerns but noted that they were only following a precedent set out by the Sustainable Seafood Coalition -- a coalition of food businesses who have defined a code of practice that aims to set criteria for the term "responsibly sourced" as a fishery which is either not red-rated, or which is red-rated but for which there is an improvement plan, it went on.

"This is a relatively low bar and not what most people would consider responsible sourcing. However, it was not in fact being met by these fisheries in several locations. So, within a few months of setting out our concerns, the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) explained their intention to establish FIPs for both nephrops and scallops fisheries."

Open Seas said it tried to participate in the FIP as it was put together, only to be ignored for long periods of time by the MSC and the steering group that was put together.

When the FIP plans were released they "were not great", it said. "They contained either mistakes or factual errors, but by this point they were finalized and not open to discussion. Of specific concern to us, they downplayed issues of illegal and damaging dredging in protected and sensitive areas of seabed and the damage caused to fish stocks by ongoing, illegal discarding – two issues we believe are the most important to resolve."

Open Seas presented evidence illegal discarding to the FIP group; "the group updated their action plan to state: 'In the absence of real-time, at-sea data, it is very difficult to ascertain fully whether vessels are complying or not'. This seemed to be a refusal to acknowledge a problem; at the same time a parliamentary inquiry concluded that discarding continues."

By Feb. 5, 2021, claiming to have discovered more evidence of illegal dredging in the fisheries supposedly being improved, the NGO was losing patience and again contacted the MSC asking for its position on illegal fishing, it said. It was told to submit a formal request to the group, and did so on March 26, 2021.

"This was made more pertinent when we learned that the head of the scallop committee of the Scottish Whitefish Producers Association (SWFPA) had been prosecuted for illegal scallop dredging (more on this below). The SWFPA is a member of the FIP and involved in actions of the FIP relating to 'compliance'. We received a response to our concerns on May 13 which shows no real acceptance of responsibility for this issue nor leadership in addressing it."

Open Seas' concern is that retailers and others have been selling scallops and scampi as "responsibly sourced" seafood despite them potentially coming from red-rated fisheries, simply because this FIP process exists. Retailer Tesco has also sold bottom-trawl-caught langoustine (another nephrops product) as "responsibly caught" which doesn't comply with the code established by the Sustainable Seafood Coalition, the NGO said.

ClientEarth, which hosts the Sustainable Seafood Coalition, told Open Seas a FIP should be considered "inactive" if it reports no improvement in fishing practice or management or improvement on the water within three years of launch.

It cited the first steering group meeting of Project UK – an MSC initiative to establish 12 fisheries within eight FIPs – in June 2018 as the launch of the FIP in question.

"It is now three years since June 2018 and we have seen no change of fishing practice or improvement on the water – damage, illegality and discarding have continued throughout the three years," said Open Seas. "We therefore consider the FIP stalled and ineffective, if not actually inactive."

Sustainable Seafood Coalition (SSC) coordinator Oliver Tanqueray told Undercurrent News: "The SSC was set up to tackle greenwashing in seafood supply chains. Our codes of conduct help seafood businesses to provide clear, consistent and accurate claims to their customers.

"These codes include commitments to actively engage with fisheries where environmental improvements are needed. The SSC recognizes credible fisheries improvement plans as an important tool through which these commitments can be met. Responsible sourcing often requires businesses to collaboratively support a fishery on a pathway to sustainability."

Television program corners scallop committee head

In an episode of BBC documentary Countryfile, television producers tracked down John MacAlister, the abovementioned head of the SWFPA's scallop committee whose vessel – just days after speaking to Countryfile for a piece on this topic in March 2019 – was caught breaking restrictions on dredging in MPAs.

He said the vessel's skipper was not registered to the SWFPA, and suggested the legal action around the vessel Star of Annan was ongoing, though the documentary crew said the prosecution had found MacAlister's company guilty and fining it over £200,000 ($276,000).

The SWFPA said MacAlister was no longer chair of the scallop committee but remained a member. Click here to view the piece on the BBC iPlayer (beginning around nine minutes in).

MSC left disappointed

George Clark, MSC's UK and Ireland program director, told Undercurrent it was disappointed to see Open Seas' campaign launch just as Project UK publishes its annual report, "which highlights all the progress made within this past year".

"We disagree with their conclusion of the status of the Project UK FIPs, which are all transparent, publicly reported, and rated A-C by the globally accepted independent ratings provider for FIPs, FisheryProgress.org."

The UK has well-established and supported frameworks for defining and agreeing definitions around environmental claims for fish and seafood, that go above and beyond legal requirements, he continued.

"We are proud to work alongside stakeholders across the seafood supply chain and marine science community, who share our values in driving forward improvements in UK fisheries and supporting progress towards a sustainable future for UK seafood."

It wished to clarify that while the first meeting of the "round two steering groups" was indeed June 2018, this was when the pre-assessment was commissioned, and is considered by FisheryProgress.org and the Conservation Alliance for Seafood Solutions (CASS) as a 'prospective FIP'.

"Prospective FIPs have one year to undertake a pre-assessment and agree on appropriate actions, before being launched as a 'comprehensive FIP'. The FIP has only now just completed the second year as a comprehensive FIP. The round two FIP action plans were agreed and signed off by the respective steering groups on March 25, 2019 for scallops and May 1, 2019 for nephrops."

MSC also said it does not "lead" on the Project UK FIPs, but facilitates them and acts as secretariat.

"The advice comes from independent consultants (Poseidon) and the actions and decisions related to the FIP are all agreed by the relevant steering groups. The MSC has been careful to ensure neutrality throughout Project UK and that steering group members have full responsibility of the direction and delivery of the project."

title: EJF warns of systemic shark-finning in Taiwan after vessel suspension
content:
The Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF) has applauded the actions of Taiwan's fisheries agency, which this week fined the owners of a vessel engaged in illegal shark-finning, but warned that a systemic problem remains in the country.

EJF's evidence was used to convict the owners of the Dong Cheng 368, who were fined TWD 10.25 million ($370,000) and had their license suspended for 11 months. They had been engaged in both shark-finning and the capture of prohibited species, including the highly endangered oceanic whitetip shark.

During EJF’s investigation, crew from the vessel also alleged that they were made to work for extremely long hours -- sometimes 14 hours with only a three or four hour rest before the next shift -- but although the Dong Cheng is still under investigation by the authorities, no further sanctions have been made.

Back in 2018, EJF included evidence in their submission for more than 60 other vessels engaged in similar practices.

The NGO believes from its investigations that shark-finning practices are more widespread than originally thought and that more systemic changes, such as making the use of CCTV mandatory onboard vessels alongside more extensive port inspections, are necessary.

Over three-quarters of overseas ports used by Taiwan’s fishing fleet have no Taiwanese inspectors, the EJF warned, while out at sea, in the absence of CCTV, there are no reliable mechanisms to enforce the laws or verify their catch.

"It is good to see that our evidence was useful for the Fisheries Agency in apprehending and sanctioning the perpetrators of these environmental crimes, but equally it is disappointing that the government is not actively uncovering these abuses itself," said Steve Trent, CEO of EJF.

"Our investigations indicate that these practices, and the human rights abuse that often accompanies them, are widespread within the Taiwanese distant water fleet, not restricted to a few badly behaving vessels," he continued. "To tackle this systemic problem, I strongly recommend that the fisheries agency push ahead with electronic monitoring including CCTV, with a view to making this mandatory for all distant water vessels and adopt the measures in EJF's 'Charter for Transparency' without further delay."

title: 415,000t more Russian pollock gains MSC
content:
With no objections filed to the Western Bering Sea pollock Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certification process, certifying body Lloyd’s Register has said the fishery has gained the blue tick ecolabel.

"Subject to successful outcomes from surveillance audits, Western Bering Sea pollock is certified under the MSC requirements for sustainable fisheries from the date of certification [July 6, 2021] and for five calendar years following this date," it said.

The fishery can use the MSC's logo on all products defined within the public certification report.

The fishery's 2021 total allowable catch (TAC) amounted to 415,000 metric tons.

As usual when a fishery becomes certified, the certifier implemented several conditions that must be met -- in this case by the fourth year of certification. It also filed a non-binding recommendation that the fishery's client group -- Russian Pollock Catchers Association -- looks to develop an onboard information recording system, "using the existing logbook or electronic recording systems".

This should record the depth profile of the gear on each trawl; the lowest proximity of the gear to the seafloor; if at any point the gear touches the seafloor or fouls any submarine feature; and if in the event that fouling of the seafloor or any submarine feature occurs, that any benthic organisms that may be found are recorded as well as any lost or abandoned gear noted or recovered.

"To facilitate this, an identification guide should be developed for use aboard vessels to help with the identification of species and any features of significance and that might support the development of measures needed to avoid possible vulnerable marine ecosystems that might be identified as present in pollock fishing areas."

This news comes as an additional portion of the Russian Sea of Okhotsk (SOO) fishery, where the TAC in 2021 is 126,000t, met the MSC standard earlier this year.

That portion of the fishery was absorbed into the wider SOO MSC fishery. The TAC in the main portion of the SOO fishery is 1.06 million metric tons. So, the Russian total of MSC-approved fish became 1.187m metric tons.

Including this latest MSC certification then, that MSC-approved quota rises to 1.6 million metric tons.

title: Untitled
content:
Chilean salmon farmer Multiexport Foods aims to reduce the use of antibiotics on its farms by 60% by 2025 and use more sustainable raw materials in fish feed. 

The company said that last year its use of antibiotics was 24.5% less than 2017, which itself was 56.8% down on 2013. In total, the use of antibiotics went from 458 grams per metric ton of harvested salmon in 2017 to 336g/t in 2020, as the image below shows. 

"As part of the strategy Multiexport Foods defined back in 2016, the company seeks to decrease the use of antibiotics in a sustained way," the firm stated. "Furthermore, their use is restricted solely and exclusively to situations where diseases occur, always under the supervision of qualified professionals."

Also, the salmon farmer is committed to producing 25% antibiotic-free salmon in 2021.

"We are proud to say that all of our harvests in the Magallanes region have been free of antibiotics and antiparasitics," the company said. "In 2020, 19.3% of our salmon has been produced with no use of antibiotics and we aim to increase that figure further in the coming years."

Additionally, Multiexport also pledged to ensure the fish feed they use is made from more sustainable raw materials. 

Thus, the company aims to use 100% RTRS-certified soy by 2024, as well as 100% certified fishmeal and 50% certified fish oil by 2022.

Credit: Multiexport Food's 2020 Sustainability Report

title: Fish Factor: Soaring crab demand; Weathervane harvest opens soon; Salmon health benefits
content:
Undercurrent News is now featuring 'Fish Factor', a weekly column featuring the reporting and perspective of Alaska seafood journalist Laine Welch

Crab has been one of the hottest commodities since the COVID-19 pandemic forced people in 2020 to buy and cook seafood at home, and demand is even higher this year.   

Crab is now perceived as being more affordable when compared to the cost to enjoy it at restaurants, said global seafood supplier Tradex, and prices continue to soar.

That’s how it’s playing out for Dungeness crab in Kodiak, Alaska, and, hopefully, in the southeast region where the summer fishery got underway on June 15.

Kodiak’s fishery opened on May 1 and 76,499 pounds have been landed so far by just eight boats, compared to 29 last year. The Kodiak price this season was reported at $4.25/lb for the crab that weigh just over two lbs on average. That compares to a 2020 price of $1.85/lb for a catch of nearly 3 million lbs, the highest in 30 years, with a fishery value of nearly $5.3m.

The pulls are skimpy though, averaging just two crab per pot. Kodiak’s Dungeness stocks are very cyclical and the fishery could be tapping out the tail end of a peak. Managers say this summer should tell the tale.  

Southeast’s summer Dungeness could see 190 or more permit holders on the grounds. Crabbers won’t know until June 29 how much they can pull up for the two-month fishery after managers assess catch and effort information. The fishery, which occurs primarily around Petersburg and Wrangell, will reopen again in October.

Last season’s combined summer and fall fisheries produced nearly 6.7m lbs at the Panhandle, just shy of the Dungeness record of 7.3m lbs set in 2002 and more than double the 10-year average.

Southeast crabbers averaged just $1.72/lb last season, down by more than $1 for a 2020 fishery value of $11.49m.

Elsewhere, California crabbers fetched record prices for their Dungeness crab in a fishery that saw low landings and a shortened season that ran from Jan. 11 through early May.

The fleet of 359 crabbers fetched a record $6.02/lb for a catch of just 3.6m lbs, down 10m lbs from the previous year. The value of this year’s California fishery was $18.7m, down from nearly $46m in 2020. 

In Las Vegas, Nevada, a major crab market for the hotel and casino industries, television station KTNV said that Dungeness and snow crab legs have gone up between 17% and 33% in the past three months, reported Undercurrent News.

Alaska king crab legs have climbed 90% said John Smolen, owner of the Crab Corner Maryland Seafood House in Las Vegas

"We used to sell our Alaskan king crab legs for $34.99/lb and we’re currently selling them for $59.99/lb, which is still a very tight margin," Smolen said, adding that he believes the rise is the result of the pandemic depleting wholesale inventories. 

"Until we can get our production way back up ahead of our usage and build up a reserve supply, I don’t see the prices changing anytime soon," Smolen said.

Crab market expert Les Hodges added that "in order to maintain their gains, retailers must compete with the rapid opening of the foodservice sector in addition to a strong international demand for a resource that is limited in supply. Prices have been driven to all-time highs with more increases coming in the future for crab."

Scallops are coming

One of Alaska’s smallest and priciest fisheries gets underway on July 1 – weathervane scallops.

The fleet size is limited by federal licensing to nine permits, but just two boats take part in the fishery which spans from Yakutat to the Bering Sea and can run through February.

"It’s pretty specialized and it’s not something you can get into easily," said Nat Nichols, area shellfish manager at the Alaska Department of Fish and Game in Kodiak. "It takes a fair bit of institutional knowledge and also specialized gear. Lots of people have some Tanner crab pots lying around in their back yards, but not many have a 15-foot New Bedford scallop dredge."

The scallop fishery also is very labor-intensive as it includes catching and processing.

"It takes a lot of manpower, with crews of 12 people that are shucking by hand. Every Alaska scallop you’ve ever seen was shucked by hand," Nichols said.

This year the two boats will compete for a slightly increased catch of 345,000 lbs of shucked meats, which are the adductor muscle that keeps the shells closed. Scallops are a wildly popular delicacy and can pay fishermen over $10/lb, depending on size and grade.

Weathervane scallops are the largest in the world and it takes them about five years to reach a marketable shell size of about five inches. Some can measure 10 inches across!

The boats drop big dredges comprising four-inch rings to keep out smaller sizes. They make tows along mostly sandy bottoms of strictly defined fishing regions. The fishery is co-managed with the federal government and has 100% observer coverage.

The total first wholesale revenue for Alaska scallops last season was estimated at nearly $2.36m meaning an average crew share of $41,274.   

That pales in comparison to the Atlantic sea scallop fishery, the world’s largest and most valuable. In 2019, landings at ports in primarily Massachusetts, Virginia and New Jersey totaled over 60.6m lbs of shucked meats valued at nearly $570m. 

This year’s Atlantic harvest is projected to decrease to around 40m lbs. Prices for the largest sizes (U10s and U12s, meaning the number of meats that make up 1lb) topped $30/lb at recent New Bedford auctions, according to National Fisherman. 

Salmon helps healthy hearts

A global study concludes that there are some big differences between eating farmed salmon and wild, and the way it’s prepared really matters.

The Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) pooled data from four international studies of nearly 200,000 people to make the connection between eating fish rich in omega-3 fatty acids and the risk of getting and dying from heart disease.

For those with a bad heart, JAMA concluded that eating two to four, four-ounce servings of salmon a week reduces the risk of dying by a whopping 36%. The researchers touted salmon as delivering some of the highest doses of omega-3’s along with protein, selenium, B12 and vitamin D.

And they noted some big differences between farmed and wild salmon.

A wild salmon fillet has 131 fewer calories and half the fat as the same amount of farmed fish. While farmed salmon can have slightly more omega-3s, they also have 20% more saturated fat.

The JAMA study also referred to the wide use of antibiotics in most farmed fish growing operations, citing higher levels of "persistent organic pollutants" that are resistant to biodegrading. Levels of polychlorinated biphenyls or PCBs, for example, are five to 10 times higher in farmed salmon than in wild fish. 

The adverse effects of PCBs were so widespread the chemical was banned in the US in 1979, but most farmed fish comes into the US from other countries that don’t have the same restrictions.

How the fish is cooked also really matters. The JAMA study said a weekly diet of fried fish increases heart attack risk by 17% as it cancels out the healthy fat benefits of the fish.

It's more proof that you are what you eat.

Seafood votes

Weathervane scallops, king salmon, pollock and king crab are the four seafood favorites selected in a mock election that the state Division of Elections is using to give Alaskans a chance to practice the new ranked-choice voting method next year.

Voters next November will get one ballot and rank several candidates for a given office by their preference; the top four will advance and the one getting the majority of votes will win.

To test the new system from June 1-15, nearly 4,000 Alaskans voted from a selection of 18 seafood choices to determine the top four favorites. 

The winner will be chosen in the final seafood election on June 30.

And just as in the national elections, the seafood election faced allegations of vote tampering.

Read a great write=up of the attempted seafood skewering by Liz Ruskin of Alaska Public Media called "Nice try, pollock: How Alaska’s most prolific fish almost won the state’s ranked-choice mock election".

title: Scots want buying boycott as Faroes follow Norway in setting mackerel quotas
content:
The Faroe Islands and Iceland have followed Norway's lead and set 2021 unilateral fishing quotas for mackerel, prompting further outcry from the market.

Pelagics market condemns Norway’s unilateral mackerel quota

Jacob Vestergaard, the Faroese minister of fisheries, has set a quota of 167,048 metric tons, or 19.6% of the 852,284t catch level recommended in September 2020 by the International Council of the Exploration of the Sea (ICES).

"The Faroe Islands have decided to raise their share in the same proportion as that of Norway," he said. Between 2014 and 2020, the Faroes' share had been 12.6% of the total coastal states' landings.

Vestergaard said he hoped and expected that negotiations between coastal states would continue. 

Iceland too has announced its 2021 mackerel quota, but it has stuck at 16.5% of the North East Atlantic Fisheries Commission quota -- which followed the ICES advice -- as it had in 2020. This means Iceland's quota is down year-on-year, from 152,000t to 140,627t.

The table below shows that the unilateral quotas already set have surpassed the ICES advice for 2021, before Greenland and Russia have had chance to set theirs:

Mackerel quotas 2021
 	Mackerel quota 2021 (metric tons)	2021 quota as a share of ICES advice	2020 quota as a share of ICES advice
Norway	298,299	35.00%	22.50%
UK	222,228	26.10%	n/a
EU	200,279	23.50%	49.30%
Faroe Islands	167,048	19.60%	12.60%
Iceland	140,627	16.50%	16.50%
Greenland	Undecided		6.50%
Russia	Undecided		14.10%
Total	1,028,481	120.70%	121.50%
ICES advice	852,854		
Source: Coastal states governments and sources
Scottish anger

Scottish fishermen, represented by the Scottish Pelagic Fishermen's Association (SPFA) and the Shetland Fishermen’s Association (SFA), have called on retailers and food suppliers to stop sourcing Norwegian and Faroese mackerel after the two countries unilaterally increased their quota shares. 

It demanded action by members of the North Atlantic Pelagic Advocacy Group (NAPA), which is committed to sustainable quota shares and operates the fishery improvement project (FIP) which seeks to get Northeast Atlantic mackerel's Marine Stewardship Council certificate reinstated. 

Within the last week, Norway and the Faroese have both increased their mackerel quota shares by 55%, said the Scottish bodies.

"Norway is an advocate of zonal attachment, where fishing quota is associated with where the fish actually are. But in recent years Norway has been catching less mackerel in its own waters and more in UK waters, as our members can testify from the increased presence of Norwegian vessels," said Ian Gatt, chief executive of the SPFA.

"Norway's own figures show that in 2017, it caught just over 69% of its mackerel in its own exclusive economic zone (EEZ) and 21% in the UK EEZ. In 2020, those figures were 15.7% and 84.3% respectively – a very large swing. On that basis, it should be reducing its quota share, not increasing it."

Simon Collins, executive officer of SFA, added that the Faroese catch a bigger proportion of their mackerel in UK waters than in its own (52% to 45% last year).

"It has also transferred or swapped around a fifth of its mackerel quota for other fish stocks in the past four years so can have no need for additional fish. This is an outrageous move by these countries, and it needs to be addressed urgently by NAPA and by government at the highest level.

"Since its inception, NAPA has confined its actions to writing letters to coastal states. With this escalation by Norway and [the Faroese] we are way beyond the point of letters having any impact. It is now time for NAPA members to come off the fence and take direct action by ending the sourcing of mackerel from these two countries in their retail supply chains."

NAPA told Undercurrent News it had already publicly condemned the unilateral quota increase by Norway, and takes the same stance on the Faroes.

"The NAPA policy FIP for NE Atlantic mackerel and Atlanto-Scandian herring is the vehicle we are using to drive towards cooperative, long-term and science-based management of these stocks. It is built around an acknowledgment that this requires political will from all sides, and that is what the supply chain wants to see. NAPA will continue advocating with all coastal states engaged in the management of these stocks across the three-year period of the FIP."

The FIP enables NAPA partners -- which include over 50 retailers, foodservice companies, and suppliers -- to continue sourcing from these stocks, despite the Marine Stewardship Council certificate loss, it said.

"Individual members are free to source from whomever they choose. NAPA cannot and will not discuss any collective buying arrangements to fully adhere to antitrust/ competition laws."

title: Thai Union’s ‘dairy-style’ business gets closer to 100% utilization of tuna
content:
Thai Union Group's focus on innovative uses for more and more parts of the tuna which might, at one time, have been considered waste has seen it near 100% utilization of each fish landed, it told Undercurrent News.

Only around 50% of each tuna is utilized as the canned shelf staple that has boomed in sales over the past year, with most of the remainder traditionally used for fishmeal and oil. But Thai Union is betting on those by-products eventually becoming more valuable than the canned meat.

Thai Union plans crude tuna oil plants in Ghana, Seychelles

Thai Union Ingredients (TUI)'s managing director, Leon Coolen, joined the firm from the dairy industry in 2018, and sees earnings potential on a par with that sector, he told Undercurrent.

"Profitability potential is definitely there. I often make the comparison with the dairy market, where ingredients were a waste outlet before as well, especially when it comes to whey, coming from cheese. Now it's the 'powdered gold' of milk; dairy companies don't earn money with milk and cheese, they earn money with the ingredients ending up in all kinds of fancy applications."

That's very much the direction he aims to take TUI, he added; "from a general perception that the company is dealing with waste, to changing that".

"We actually have a lot of value at hand, but at the same time, it will take time to build a supply chain, and a reputation, and to have the research fully aligned with the ambition. After three years working over here, that's progressing very well."

For now, TUI remains a tiny drop in the ocean for what is a $4.1 billion sales group, but it's the profit margins of things like refined tuna oil, bone powder, and new proteins -- as compared with the "old" uses like fishmeal and oil -- that are the focus.

"Again, I can make the comparison with dairy where the ingredients business normally makes up maybe 20% or 25% of sales, but it can even be over 50% of profits."

That won't necessarily be replicated in the tuna industry, he said, but the signs are that tuna-based proteins for medicinal and cosmetic applications have good "functionality".

"My roadmap is pretty clear for the next two or three years, and that is basically to roll out the supply chain and make sure everything properly works; that the quality of the products is as we predict. And that takes me well into 2022 or 2023.

"In the meantime, Thai Union is working hard to see if we can have lift off from these ingredient platforms, which are very interesting nutritionally, very interesting concepts. That's why I think for the next 10 years Thai Union will continue to invest in these areas."

Low-hanging fruits are picked

Utilization of 100% of each tuna may not be something that's on the cards even in the future, as some of the "least useful" parts of the fish may not have functionality, and could even dilute the efficacy of other products were they included. 

"With tuna oil, bone powder, collagen, and fish protein hydrolysis, we have basically picked the low-hanging fruit," said Coolen. "These are fairly 'me too' products [similar to other products that already existed from other manufacturers] that we have fine-tuned towards tuna. Collagen peptides are already abundantly available, but they are predominantly from cow and pig, which come with some religious issues."

Fish proteins come with ready-made healthy associations and perceptions, he noted. "So, the fish collagen peptides market is growing fast, and there's a shortage now, so we want to get into the market as soon as possible.

"As for other [tuna] body parts, we have roughly a third of the GIC [Thai Union's Global Innovation Center] working on ingredients, and they see a lot of opportunities to move beyond the 'me too' products, with the focus on pharma and medical."

As previously reported, Thai Union is preparing to build new facilities alongside its tuna primary processing plants in Ghana and Seychelles with the aim of becoming the world's largest supplier of tuna oil. These facilities will produce crude tuna oil for shipping to its refinery in Rostock, Germany, for further processing.

It is also planning to begin pilot-scale production of collagen peptides and tuna-protein hydrolysis this June at its largest tuna processing plant in Songkhla, Thailand.

title: Chilean hake trawling ban proposal voted down
content:
A move to ban hake trawling in Chile has been narrowly voted down by the country's parliament, El Mostrador reports.

As well as a ban, the proposal also sought to make sure Chilean fishers could only use this fishing gear type in certain areas defined by the country's fishing authority.

Chile’s proposed hake trawl ban would compound COVID-19 pain, trade group warns

The voting results, which took place in Chile's chamber of deputies on May 25, were as follows: 74 votes for, 41 against and 12 abstentions. A total of 78 votes in favor were needed for the proposal to go through.

Those in favor argued the ban is necessary to guarantee the conservation of hake and appealed for greater cooperation within the fishing sector.

However, Chile's minister of economy, Lucas Palacios, said this could lead to the closure of eight processing plants and the loss of 1,150 jobs and CLP 3 billion ($4m) in tax revenue.

As Undercurrent News previously reported, the country's National Fisheries Society, Sonapesca, also said that going ahead now with this law could devastate the country's fishing industry, which has already been badly affected by COVID-19.

"Something similar also happened in August last year when the cuttlefish trawling ban law came into force. However, if the bill goes ahead, the consequences will be even greater this time," Sonapesca general manager Hector Bacigalupo said.

In addition, the ban would also tighten hake inventories, which would cause prices "to double or triple, as it happened with cuttlefish prices," Bacigalupo said. 

"Many small- and medium-sized enterprises had to shut down after that and those remaining cannot absorb all the demand on their own," he said. "It has now been demonstrated that industrial fishing is still important for the artisanal fishing sector, whose captures of cuttlefish have been reduced by two-thirds."

title: Thai Union plans crude tuna oil plants in Ghana, Seychelles
content:
Thai Union Group is preparing to build new facilities alongside its tuna primary processing plants in Ghana and the Seychelles, with the aim of becoming the world's largest supplier of tuna oil. 

This was according to Leon Coolen, managing director of Thai Union Ingredients (TUI), who gave Undercurrent News an exclusive interview in May 2021.

It already has one such crude oil plant in Thailand, built at its largest tuna processing facility, in Songkhla. Here, around 50% of each fish is canned as a cupboard staple across the world, while the other half, traditionally, has gone for pet food, fishmeal and oil, and other uses.

Thai Union is looking to maximize the value it gets from every fish though, and brought in Coolen in 2018 from the dairy sector, where he was used to turning "by-products" into the industry's "gold".

The Songkhla plant has shifted from cooking entire tuna, and then cutting it up, to a more automated procedure by which the parts to be canned are removed and then cooked, leaving the "by-products" in their raw form to be processed into crude tuna oil.

This is then shipped to Rostock, Germany, where Thai Union has been formulating products such as UniQDHA tuna oil and UniQBONE. The Rostock plant began operating in April 2021, and plans to launch commercially later this year, when it will begin selling to the infant formula and supplement sectors.

The group is already looking larger scale, knowing it does not want to ship tuna heads and other parts from the Seychelles and Ghana to Thailand, said Coolen. Hence, the tuna plants there will be modified, as Songkhla was, and crude oil facilities built.

"In the case of Ghana, we are now commissioning that factory. We need a lot of licenses and permits, but we expect to start up in the third quarter of this year," he said.

"In the Seychelles we don't know exactly yet when that will materialize. We want to go step by step."

While he declined to give a figure at this stage as to the investment going into TUI, he said it was fair to say it was in the "tens of millions of dollars".

The Rostock plant represents an investment of between €23 million ($27m) and €24m, he said, so "altogether, yes, it will be tens of millions".

A booming marketplace

Authorities in the EU, US, and China require that a certain minimum level of omega-3 DHA oil content is included in infant formula milk, and the two largest sources of these are tuna oil and algae oil, Coolen explained. 

Tuna oil remains the single-largest volume supply still, as it is lower in price than the algal equivalent, with the same functional benefits. For market value comparison, a Global Market Insights report from October 2020 said the global DHA algae oil for infant formula market was estimated at $245m in 2019, and was slated to surpass $435m by 2026.

The same company estimated the omega-3 ingredients market in general -- including supplements and other uses -- was expected to cross $3.8 billion by 2026.

"Thai Union is the biggest tuna processor in the world, so it stands to reason we can also be the biggest oil producer," said Coolen. "Let's say with the volume of fish that we process, we can supply more than 50% of the global demand for tuna oil. That's quite considerable."

This is still essentially in the start-up phase -- Coolen talks about a 20-year timeframe for this enterprise to ramp up -- but Thai Union's "Pet Care and value-added sales" increased by 20.8% year-on-year for Q1, on the back of increasing volume (up 16.1%), "attributable to a focus on higher-margin products, new products launched, and people spending more for their pets since the pandemic".

Volumes sales in this division were up 16% at 73,000 metric tons, and their value reached THB 5.5 billion ($174.8m). The majority of this will have been from its pet care range.

The firm has said its crude tuna oil has a "very high refining yield that delivers a DHA content of 28% to 30%", while the refined oil has similar DHA levels to those found in fresh fish.

"For both products, the TUI manufacturing process uses less fish to produce the same amount of oil, uses fewer chemicals, consumes less energy, and produces less waste -- all helping preserve the environment."

UniQBONE tuna calcium powder, introduced earlier this year, has been sold into business-to-business channels in Q1, it said.

title: China court orders Zoneco to auction off shares to repay debt
content:
The financial status of the Chinese seafood firm Zoneco Group is once again in question, as Suzhou Intermediate People's Court in Jiangsu Province ruled that the company must auction off approximately 58.79 million shares to pay defaulted debts.

The amount is 8.27% of the company's share capital and the online auction will take place from June 9-12, according to the company's notice filed to Shenzhen Stock Exchange on Wednesday (May 12).

The stock, which belongs to the company's major shareholder Changhai County Zhangzidao Investment and Development Center, have been judicially frozen due to the dispute over the pledged securities repurchase.

Zoneco’s major shareholders prohibited from selling amid criminal investigations

On April 9, 2020, Suzhou Intermediate People's Court ruled freezing the shares and other immovable property of Changhai County Zhangzidao Investment and Development Center after Soochow Securities applied to the court for property preservation.

In the latest notice, Zoneco claimed the auction will not have a significant adverse impact and will not cause any changes in the company's control. The company's production and operation are normal at the moment, it said.

Meanwhile, Zoneco has been facing multiple lawsuits related to accusations of fraud by over 100 plaintiffs, including investors, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

On Tuesday (May 11), the company revealed it has accumulated about CNY 10.4 million ($1.61m) of litigation costs in the past 12 months. The amount accounted for more than 10% of the absolute value of the company's most recent net assets.

Zoneco said the possible impact on its profit is still uncertain since certain court cases have not been closed. The company "will attach great importance to relevant lawsuits and safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of the company and all shareholders", it added.

Based in Zhangzidao, Dalian province, Zoneco harvests scallops farmed in the Bohai Sea and imports raw material for processing. The company was China's largest market-listed seafood company by sales until 2017. However, it has been better known for its "running scallops" fiasco.

China’s Zoneco expects loss-making quarter having returned to black in 2020

The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) later used historical satellite tracking data to expose Zoneco's financial fraud by showing log data of its vessels' seeding and harvesting activities had been "plucked from thin air".

Eventually, Zoneco was fined CNY 600,000 over the long-running saga involving missing scallops. In addition, Hougang Wu, Zoneco's ex-chairman, was given a lifetime ban from public securities markets. After his resignation, Wu initiated an administrative lawsuit against the CSRC's ruling.

The CSRC had transferred the case to the public security bureau for further investigations on criminal responsibility.

Last month, the firm reported it was expecting a loss of CNY 30m to 50m for the first quarter of 2021, having returned to black last year.

The company recorded a full-year profit of CNY 14.81m in 2020. However, after deducting non-recurring gains and losses, it suffered from losses of CNY 143.9m.

title: Atlantic wind project opposed by harvesters gets final approval
content:
The administration of US president Joe Biden on Tuesday announced that it has given the final approval necessary for the building of some 84 turbines over a 118-mile stretch of ocean located roughly 12 nautical miles off the coast of Martha Vineyard, Massachusetts.

Nothing short of a possible legal challenge now stands in the way of the $2.8 billion Vineyard Wind Project, which is strongly opposed by commercial seafood harvesters concerned about their ability to navigate waters around turbines and the potential impact they might have on squid and fish. 

Joe Biden. Photograph by Gage Skidmore on Flickr.

The 100-page "Record of Decision", which was issued jointly by the US Department of Interior's Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM), U.S. Army Corps
of Engineers (USACE), and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), includes the Final Environmental Impact Statement (FEIS) for the project's construction and operations plan.

The wind farm, which is a joint venture of the energy firms Avangrid Renewables and Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, is expected to generate about 800 megawatts of electricity, enough to power about 400,000 homes while creating about 3,600 jobs.

The Responsible Offshore Development Alliance (RODA), a group that represent 185 fishing-dependent businesses and associations in 13 states and more than 30 different fisheries, was among the first to respond on Tuesday.

"For the past decade, fishermen have participated in offshore wind meetings whenever they were asked and produced reasonable requests only to be met with silence," said Anne Hawkins, RODA's executive director, in a statement. "From this silence now emerges unilateral action and a clear indication that those in authority care more about multinational businesses and energy politics than our environment, domestic food sources, or US citizens."

There was little question the Biden administration expected to move fast to approve the building of wind farms after his 22-page executive order, issued in January, within days of his inauguration, included language that required the not-yet-confirmed secretary of the interior to review siting and permitting processes on public lands and in offshore waters in order to identify ways in which the US can double its use of such power by 2030. 

The US currently has only five wind turbines in Rhode Island state waters generating 30 megawatts of power and two turbines offshore nearest Virginia generating another 12mw, so the commitment wasn't too threatening for the harvesters. But it was an indication of bigger changes to come.  

The offshore wind energy trade association, meanwhile, was in full celebration mode on Tuesday.

"This is a historic day for clean energy and for our country that has been over a decade in the making," said Heather Zichal, CEO of American Clean Power. "...Now is the time to push forward on offshore wind, catch up to global competitors, and decarbonize our electric grid, so that the U.S. can deliver economic and environmental benefits to our citizens and combat climate change."

Annie Hawkins, RODA

RODA doesn't share the same point of view, however, saying the decision is an example of BOEM continuing to "abdicate its responsibility to the public and leave all decisionmaking to large, multinational corporations". It included no mitigation measures to offset impacts to critical ocean ecosystems and commercial fisheries, the group argued. 

"To the best of our knowledge BOEM did not even consider any mitigation measures recommended by RODA or any fisheries professionals, scientists, or natural resource managers, despite having clearly defined requests available to them," RODA said.

"In one pen stroke, BOEM has confirmed its scattershot, partisan, and opaque approach that undermines every lesson we’ve learned throughout environmental history: the precautionary principle, the importance of safety and environmental regulation, the scientific method and use of the best available data, and adaptive management policies. It is shocking that NMFS could sign off on a decision so inexplicably adverse to its core mission and the research, resources, businesses, and citizens under its jurisdiction."

title: Norway police fine Mowi more than $450,000 over 2018 escape
content:
The police force of Trondelag, Norway, has fined salmon farmer Mowi NOK 3.75 million ($455,593) over a 2018 escape incident, according to the country's directorate of fisheries.

Aquaculture equipment supplier Egersund Net was also fined NOK 750,000 for the event. Around 54,000 fish escaped Mowi's Geitryggen site in February 2018.

The directorate reported Mowi for violating "provisions regarding the requirement to exercise special care to prevent fish escapes", including that facilities and equipment used for aquaculture must be properly designed, have sound properties, and be used with the necessary care, and that the operation must be technical, biological and environmentally sound.

Egersund Net was fined in the same case for supplying aquaculture equipment that was not "properly designed and has justifiable properties", and for failing to notify the directorate of "deviations in products or services that may lead to deviations".

The directorate also reported a company named Ilsvag Holding had been fined NOK 500,000 and "confiscated" a further NOK 200,000 by Sor-Vest police, for "operation without a valid construction certificate, violation of the requirement to exercise special care to prevent fish escapes and violation of the requirement that the operation must at all times be technically, biologically and environmentally sound".

title: Vinh Hoan still pushing on collagen, VAP, as pangasius sales to EU surge
content:
Vietnamese pangasius giant Vinh Hoan Corporation continues to expand its capacity in value-added processing, collagen and gelatin production, and by-products, as it strives to maximize the value gained from every fish.

Vinh Hoan to complete new feed plant this year as part of $80m investment

Tam Nguyen, CEO, told Undercurrent News the company has lifted its total pangasius product processing capacity from 800 metric tons of raw material per day early in 2020, to 1,000t by the end of the year -- and at present. There are no plans to increase this capacity again by the end of 2021, she added.

It has also more than doubled its value-added processing capacity by renovating its lines, taking output from 2,000t of final product per year up to 5,000t, she said. 

Late in 2020 it completed an expansion to its gelatin production at Vinh Hoan Collagen, part of its "wellness" division, which meant it can now produce up to 3,500t of finished products per year. 

At the same time, it completed its wellness research and development center, which will focus on developing new products for the firm. It reiterated a target set last year, for collagen and gelatin sales to grow 40% and reach $35 million.

Its Thanh Binh subsidiary -- its second-largest processing site after the firm's headquarters -- will this year operate an expanded factory for pangasius fillets, as well as a new production line for value-added products such as breaded and flavored items. 

"Revenue from value-added products is expected to continue to grow with nearly 10 products successfully developed and accepted in 2020," it noted.

At the same site is Vinh Phuoc Foods, which produces fillets, but has seen an expansion to its fishmeal and oil production. As more processing capacity comes online here and at nearby Thanh Binh, more fresh by-products are available for use in this growing segment, Vinh Hoan said.

"Therefore, we expect strong growth in fish oil and fishmeal sales. In addition, the refined fish oil product line from Vinh Phuoc Foods will bring increased profits for the group, as fish oil can now be sold in the food segment at a higher price."

Nguyen told Undercurrent that two new lines at Thanh Binh and Vinh Phuoc had been added, and were for "other products that we can't disclose details for the moment".

Finally, its headquarters now also contains a newly renovated value-added product processing factory, together with a new product development area. This will meet the "growing demand for ready-to-prepare products, as global consumers begin to prepare more seafood at home during a period of social isolation", the company said. 

Expansion of value-added capacity at Vinh Hoan had taken something of a back seat in favor of its wellness and by-product divisions in recent years, but 2020's coronavirus pandemic has shown the value of producing lines aimed at the home delivery channel.

Early in 2021 it bought a majority stake in domestic-market-focused food firm Sa Giang Import and Export, and has also launched a new brand -- BASAmaster -- aimed at the home market, which should find some synergies with the Sa Giang name, Vinh Hoan CEO Tam Nguyen told Undercurrent News. The brand will hit shelves in Vietnam during the second quarter of 2021, it said.

Vinh Hoan's revenue fell 11% in 2020 to VND 7.04 trillion ($305 million). Frozen pangasius exports made up 69% of that, while value-added goods made up 2%, unchanged since 2018. However, revenue from by-products and collagen were up, "showing that the exploitation of value from Vinh Hoan's product chain has been brought into full play".

EU market surged in 2020

Once a European market staple, pangasius has had a tough time in the EU over the last decade or so, put in large part down to highly unflattering television programs aired in some important importing countries. 

Seabass, pangasius enjoyed booming 2020 at UK retail

Over the last year or so China's appetite for Vietnamese pangasius has soared, making it the country's single largest market, and Vinh Hoan's second-largest market after the US.

But in 2020, Europe came surging back. By the end of the year Vinh Hoan had sold to 47 different countries -- nine more than in 2019 -- with Europe (including the UK) accounting for 18% of exports. 

"The market's bright spot for 2020 was the growth of the European market," it said. "The Europe-Vietnam free trade agreement [EVFTA] helped reduce pangasius tax rates in Europe, increasing the competitive advantage. Vinh Hoan has taken good advantage of this opportunity to grow sales in Europe."

"The UK market recorded impressive growth, up 63% thanks to the main consumption channel of pangasius in the UK being the retail channel. Other European countries such as Belgium, the Netherlands, Italy, and Spain, all saw sales growth compared to 2019."

Overall, Vinh Hoan's EU sales rose 35% to VND 1.24 trillion ($53.7m).

You can find the fully interactive version of this trade data at Undercurrent's trade flows page, here.

The EVFTA has initially removed tariff barriers on industrial pangasius fillet "blocks" exported to Europe for further processing into finished goods. "Although the initial export volume is not high, this product is of great significance in production efficiency at our filleting factory, because it can optimize the utilization rates of different fish sizes to help save costs," the company noted.

Vietnam as a whole saw its pangasius sales to the US slip 14% in value in 2020, with the strongest decline registered in Q2, due to the coronavirus outbreak there.

Upgrade to Pro to view

Vinh Hoan saw its own sales there fall 21% last year, to VND 2.44tr. It remained its largest market though, accounting for 51% of all pangasius product sales.

Its sales to China fell 24% in 2020, to VND 1.21tr.

Vinh Hoan saw China and the US begin to recover in February and March 2021, restocking inventories as foodservice began to reopen. At the same time, demand from retail customers in Europe and the Americas has remained stable, it added.

title: Ex Bumble Bee executives given probation, not prison for tuna price-fixing
content:
Two former executives at US tuna canner Bumble Bee Foods will pay $25,000 fines and perform community service for their roles in the sector's price-fixing scandal but will avoid prison time.

On Wednesday, April 28, San Francisco, California-based federal judge Edward Chen handed down the sentences against Walter Cameron and Kenneth Worsham, who previously served as Bumble Bee's senior vice presidents of sales and trade marketing, respectively. The sentences of both men, like their former counterpart Stephen Hodge, a former senior vice president of sales at StarKist & Co, were reduced given their testimony at the 2019 trial of former Bumble Bee CEO Christopher Lischewski.

Lischewski, who is serving a 40-month prison sentence at Arizona's United States Penitentiary Tuscon, has roundly denied involvement in price-fixing and is appealing his sentence.

At the former CEO's trial, Cameron testified that Lischewski had directed him to enter into an agreement to fix canned tuna prices. Cameron had told jurors that, working with Chuck Handford, his counterpart at StarKist at the time, the canners agreed to end the "price war" of 2010 and raise list prices throughout 2011. Handford was never charged with a crime and did not testify at trial. 

In dozens of letters to the court, Cameron's friends, former coworkers, relatives and others praised his character and the way that he had owned up to his role in the price-fixing scandal. Prosecutors agreed with the downward departure from federal sentencing guidelines due to his "substantial cooperation".

They used that phrase as well to describe the cooperation of Worsham, Cameron's former coworker. Worsham described his own involvement in price-fixing during Lischewski's trial.

Worsham testified that he and StarKist's Hodge met for dinner at Fleming's Prime Steakhouse & Wine Bar in La Jolla, California on May 2, 2012. At that meeting, Hodge reportedly gave Worsham a thumb drive with Starkist pricing data, "hot" competitive information that confirmed that Starkist had followed through on its previous agreement with Bumble Bee to raise tuna list prices, Worsham claimed. The account was disputed by Lischewski.

In an April 14 letter to the court, Worsham spoke of the impact his crime has had on his life.

"What I did, many years ago at Bumble Bee, has completely redefined who I am now. I was proud of my career, proud of my accomplishments, and proud of my family. I am left without a career, my accomplishments are negated, I have lost the respect of my previous peers and have remaining only the support of my family, even though I have embarrassed them and myself beyond belief," he wrote.

He added that he deliberately did not solicit letters of support.

"None of these people helped me get into this predicament and I don't feel good about asking them to spend one second of their time asking for their support. I own this issue," he wrote. 

The sentences of the two former Bumble Bee vice presidents will mean that Lischewski is the only tuna exec to serve prison time for the price-fixing scandal.

title: Vinh Hoan to complete new feed plant this year as part of $80m investment
content:
Vietnam's largest pangasius exporter, Vinh Hoan Corporation, has budgeted over $80 million in investments for 2021.

It has three main projects on its slate: the completion of its new feed factory, the finalization of its hatchery, and acquiring and preparing land for a new farming complex. The total capital expenditure for these projects amounts to VND 1.9 trillion ($82.3m), over several years.

Vinh Hoan ups stake in Sa Giang for $6.8m

In 2021 the company plans to spend VND 700 billion on these projects, as well as VND 200bn for factory renovations and VND 400bn on miscallaneous investments, CEO Tam Nguyen told Undercurrent News.

Vinh Hoan's new feed plant, which it established in 2020 and expects to be operational by the end of 2021, is designed to have a production capacity of 350,000 metric tons per year. Built over six hectares, it will use the most modern and automated technology possible, the company said. Nguyen told Undercurrent the feed mill investment would come to a total VND 500bn.

"This feed mill will not only contribute to revenue and group profitability but also facilitates research and development of new animal husbandry formulas," it said.

At the turn of the year, sources told Undercurrent that increasing feed costs were likely to be one of the key challenges facing the pangasius sector in 2021. By April, the first feed cost hikes had been implemented, estimated by one source at 10%.

In its own 2020 annual report (released in April 2021), Vinh Hoan acknowledged a "sharp increase in feed costs". 

"The global feed market is still in a bull market, we still have to be prepared for the cost of farming to increase in 2021," it warned. "Hence, we focus on controlling and improving farming efficiency to be competitive in both cost and quality of raw materials."

The new plant, once operational, should help to save on some input costs and increase revenue from trading aquatic feed, it added.

Nguyen told Undercurrent the feed mill would serve the company's farms first, but it would likely continue to buy feed during the first construction phase. "Then we can increase the feed manufacturing volume to be more self-sufficient. In the other words, we are not sticking to strictly self-sufficient or targeting any external sales. We leave it flexible."

But it warned that expected reductions in fingerling and administration costs for 2021 harvests would only partly offset the increased feed costs, and it has guided for lower profits year-on-year, despite higher turnover.

"​Feed cost can be low and high from time to time -- we invest in feed not only because of cost but also to serve our other initiatives in farming innovation," the company's CEO said.

To be precise, its target is net sales of VND 8.6tr, up 22%, and consolidated net profit after tax of VND 700bn, down 2.6%.

Pangasius business to boom

While Vinh Hoan has now diversified itself into value-added products, healthcare and wellness, and even some other foodstuffs, pangasius remains its core, and its outlook for 2021 is decent.

Vinh Hoan invests $25m in tech, growth

"The effects of the COVID-19 pandemic have shown signs of significant decline worldwide, especially as many countries have successfully produced vaccines," the firm noted. "Facing this positive sign, we expect most pangasius export markets to fully recover."

Throughout 2020 it worked on increasing its processing capacity, and by the end of the year this was up 20%, it said, leaving it "ready to accommodate the order increase".

"The recovery of raw fish prices will ease the pressure on export prices. Therefore, pangasius revenue is expected to increase both in volume and price, 15% higher than the same period [in 2020]."

Last year Vinh Hoan invested in its farming facilities, increasing efficiency and capacity, and bringing its raw material self-sufficiency up to 70%, it said.

Fingerling quality has long been a limiting factor for Vietnam's pangasius sector, and Vinh Hoan has been putting money into Vinh Hoan Fish Hatchery Company, located in An Giang province. In 2020, it said, the firm has "perfected the technique and process of effective incubation, which can be applied as soon as the new hatchery is ready for stocking in the third quarter of 2021".

This will go a long way towards improving its farming over time, it said.

Then, the company intends to pursue and invest in "digitizing production management system technology" this year, with the digital transformation of its operations regarded as a trend it must "catch up" with.

It wants to develop a "cyclical model" for farming that sustainably creates a value chain for several other agricultural products, it continued.

"Digital, biotechnology, governance innovation, and cyclic economic model will be key programs that will take Vinh Hoan further."

It already looks to maximize the value of processing offcuts and other parts of the fish traditionally thought of as waste, launching its pangasius skin-based collagen and gelatin projects in 2015 and breaking ground on a new food-grade fish oil factory in April 2020.

Its "cyclical model" will be complete as various ongoing projects come into full operation, but this includes a new high-tech farming area that will produce rice and fruit alongside pangasius, with various waste products being used elsewhere in its production chain, it said.

"​It is actually the model of re-using waste from one area to add value and create new products in the other," explained Nguyen. "We have been doing it already with the collagen business using fish skin, fishmeal and oil/refined oil using fish scraps, and fertilizer using waste from the fish fillet factory."

"We are now just expanding the model to other areas including planting and fruit processing, which will be our new business. We are also expanding it to a more circular farming model reducing waste and water usage."

Early in 2021, Vinh Hoan established a new 100%-owned subsidiary, Thanh Ngoc Agricultural Products Company, that will focus on producing dried and frozen fruits. Construction on a plant under this firm's name will be started in the second half of 2021 on 5ha of land next to its fish processor -- and the site of its fish oil facility -- Vinh Phuoc Foods.

title: China’s Zoneco expects loss-making quarter having returned to black in 2020
content:
Chinese seafood company Zoneco Group is expecting a loss of CNY 30-50 million ($4.62m to $7.70m) for the first quarter of 2021, having returned to black last year. 

Based in Zhangzidao, Dalian province, Zoneco harvests scallops farmed in the Bohai Sea and imports raw material for processing.

Zoneco said in its filing to the Shenzhen Stock Exchange that, looking ahead, it will focus on its main business, market, and customers. It will also try to reduce risks associated with the business.

Zoneco returns to black as more investors file fraud claims

Nevertheless, the company's financial prospects are uncertain as it has been facing multiple lawsuits related to accusations of fraud by over 100 plaintiffs, including investors, who are claiming about CNY 54.3m in total, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

Meanwhile, Zoneco revealed its full-year revenue declined by 29.4% to CNY 1.926 billion ($296.8m) for 2020.

The company said the coronavirus pandemic had hit exports, logistics and sales, causing its income from the seafood trade to drop by 40%, as well as a 27% decline in seafood processing products, and a 65% slump in cold chain transport. 

The firm's product gross profit decreased by CNY 30,55m year-on-year. It also incurred losses due to foreign exchange movements and loan interest repayments.

The firm returned to black in 2020 as it recorded a full-year profit of CNY 14.81m, an increase of 103.78% compared with the previous year. The result was within the range between CNY10-15m that the company previously predicted.

It turned the small profit after it transferred rights to use sea areas, sold equity in subsidiaries, and received government subsidies, Zoneco said.

However, the firm recorded losses of CNY 143.9m after deducting non-recurring gains and losses in 2020.

Zoneco, which until 2017 was China's largest market-listed seafood company by sales, has been renowned for its "running scallops" fiasco.

The Chinese regulatory body used historical satellite tracking data to expose Zoneco's financial fraud by showing log data of its vessels' seeding and harvesting activities had been "plucked from thin air". Eventually, Zoneco was fined CNY 600,000 over the long-running saga involving missing scallops.

The case was transferred to the public security bureau for criminal investigations, while Zoneco's major shareholders were prohibited from selling their stakes in the company.

title: Norway’s Bremnes plans near-$50m investment in new processing site
content:
Norwegian salmon farmer and processor Bremnes Seashore aims to invest over NOK 400 million ($47.8m) in a new cold store and processing facility as its existing site in Kvednavikjo, Bomlo municipality, it has announced.

The new site will cover some 14,000 square meters and allow the firm -- producer of brands including Salma and Bomlo -- to produce larger volumes via the most up-to-date processing methods, it said.

"We see that consumers demand more refined product, and we will deliver," said Bremnes' CEO Einar Eide. "The new factory enables us to process significantly larger volumes than today, while at the same time expanding the number of products."

The new plant will result in new product development and research, said factory manager Geir Ivar Adnanes. Its goods will be sold by the whole "Seashore Group", which includes Sjor -- the new name for Ocean Quality, which was previously a joint venture between farmers Bremnes and Grieg Seafood.

Phase one will include the construction of a new cold store, before moving on to the processing facility. Its existing plant will continue with full capacity throughout the building works, it said.

Bremnes said the new factory would mean better utilization of raw materials, and an improved carbon footprint, with only the finished products being shipped out of the area.

"Bremnes Seashore believes we must process more of the salmon locally in Norway, and we must take our share of responsibility for strengthening the basis for value creation, jobs and ripple effects," said the firm's development manager, Simon Nesse Okland.

"If we are to increase processing here and thoughout Norway, we need a production regulation throughout the year that ensures manageable access to raw materials. Through the development, we will provide work to local and regional suppliers. We will also facilitate cooperation with other actors."

Bremnes operates 23 fish farms, and the entire group -- including Sjor and Salmon Brands -- had a turnover of NOK 3.1 billion in 2020, it said.

title: Avramar workers quarantined after COVID outbreak at Greek plant
content:
Mediterranean aquaculture group Avramar, formerly known as Andromeda Group, has had to quarantine some employees at its facilities in Argolida, Greece, following an outbreak of COVID-19.

Mediterranean bass, bream giant launches new identity, growth plan

A workers' union has staged a protest following some COVID-19 cases at a plant in Argolida belonging to Avramar, formerly known as Andromeda Group, 902.gr reported.

The union asked the firm to take "all the necessary measures to track and avoid the spread of the virus under the responsibility of the employer".

"According to the complaints [we received from workers], there are several confirmed cases of workers in the packaging plant of Selonda [Aquaculture, which currently belongs to Avramar] in Nea Epidavros," the union said.

The firm confirmed to Undercurrent News that it identified "positive cases of COVID-19"  at its Argolida facilities, following regular rapid COVID-19 testing for all personnel.

After the detection, and despite being checked with a rapid test, the entire work shift has been placed in a 14-day preventive quarantine for precautionary reasons, according to the instructions of the occupational physician who supervises the facilities.

Avramar told Undercurrent that "in the critical period of a global pandemic that we are running, our company applies all the necessary measures defined by the Greek law and health and safety protocols for the protection of its employees in all of our facilities and in all the locations that we operate".

Such measures include the gradual arrival and departure, thermometrical measurements, use of personal protective measures as masks and face covers,  avoidance in synchronization of shifts, tactical cleaning and disinfection of the facilities,  constant information of our employees regarding safety measures, regular testing (rapid tests), etc, it also said.

In addition to all the above, our company conducts twice-weekly rapid testing for COVID-19 in all of its facilities that employ over 40 people.

The correct application of the above-mentioned measures is also confirmed by the inspections carried out by the labor inspection body on a frequent and undisputable basis and relevant reports are made, the group said.

title: Editor’s choice: Atlantic Sapphire woes; Labeyrie brought into smoker’s suit; Snow crab demand; Shrimp’s roaring twenties
content:
Yannick Guerry, editor of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

For Atlantic Sapphire, Q1 represented a "lost quarter" for biomass gain, as the mortality incident on March 23 coupled with other smaller losses means the firm actually has 300 metric tons less biomass than it began the quarter with. The results saw the company's share price tumble, with approximately $220 million wiped off its market cap in just 24 hours. In a bad few days for the business, three contract company workers had to be rescued from a large tank at Atlantic Sapphire's Homestead, Florida, Atlantic salmon recirculating aquaculture system after allegedly not following "confined space safety protocols", the company said.

A US court has cleared the way for Santa Barbara Smokehouse to obtain a Labeyrie Fine Foods executive's testimony that the two were in deal talks until the California smoker's former salmon vendor, AquaChile, reportedly cut off its fish supply in 2019. According to a court order, the US government has officially approved the smokehouse's request to France's ministry of justice to obtain testimony from Alexandre Pavion. Pavion has served as Labeyrie's mergers and acquisitions director since 2017.

Seafood wholesalers, restaurants and retailers are climbing over the top of each other in a mad quest for snow crab legs and prepared to pay handsomely to anyone who can supply them. One wholesaler said he was prepared to pay suppliers what he charged retailers last year and some restaurant managers said they were eliminating their all-you-can-eat snow crab offerings or increasing their prices at buffets.

An Undercurrent News analysis places China, the US and emerging markets at the heart of a forecast roaring decade of shrimp consumption growth post-COVID-19. According to the analysis of trade data, in the seven years from 2012-2019, China largely drove a near 1.1m increase in global shrimp imports, and appears poised to drive further growth in trade in the 2020s.

Canada's Ocean Choice International told Undercurrent that it may look at acquisitions to move further downstream in Europe as it ramps up contract processing in several plants, the company's CEO said. The addition of Helgi Anton Eiriksson, the former CEO of Iceland Seafood International, to the management board of OCI's new downstream company in Europe is part of a strategy to get closer to customers, Martin Sullivan told Undercurrent.

title: Chicken of the Sea proposes $20m settlement for tuna price-fixing
content:
Thai Union Group-owned Chicken of the Sea International (COSI) hopes to settle a large chunk of the outstanding price-fixing class-action lawsuits against it for $20 million, court documents show.

The proposal between COSI and members of the "end-payer" class of plaintiffs, customers who purchased tuna from the company indirectly, does not apply to the other defendants in the suit: Dongwon Enterprise-owned StarKist & Co, and Lion Capital, the former owner of canner Bumble Bee Foods.

According to an April 9 statement from plaintiffs' attorney Betsy Manifold, judge Janis Sammartino will consider the COSI settlement during a May 20 hearing. Some $5m of the COSI settlement will go to pay claims administration costs. And lawyers expect that settlements from the other defendants will be forthcoming, she wrote.

"Settlement class counsel anticipate a recovery from the remaining nonsettling defendants, given their admissions about liability and damages, and the criminal guilty pleas and convictions related to this case. Accordingly, at this point in the case, giving notice of the COSI Settlement and approving a plan to distribute its settlement funds along with those from future recoveries is the most streamlined and economical approach," she wrote.

Earlier this year, COSI announced a $13m settlement with a group of tuna buyers known as the "direct payer plaintiffs". As first reported by Undercurrent News, as a "whistleblower" to the US Department of Justice in the criminal antitrust case, COSI and Thai Union received amnesty from criminal prosecution. The protections also limit the damages in the civil cases against COSI, Manifold wrote. 

"However, if no other monies are received (which we believe to be unlikely), settlement class counsel estimates that on average a settlement class member who purchased a can or pouch of tuna on a weekly basis during the settlement class period (about 200 cans) will receive approximately $10.50," she wrote.

The class action litigation, which kicked off in 2015, appears to be winding down. Plaintiffs were sorted into four "tracks" depending on how they purchased tuna from the canners and the class certification ruling allows each track to have common legal counsel and pool many plaintiffs' resources together to pay the costly bills for expert witnesses, lawyers fees and other expenses that come in class-action litigation. 

The large wholesalers and distributors who dealt directly with the canners are known as "direct purchasers" with a second track of direct purchasers including large buyers such as Walmart with separate lawsuits known as "direct action" plaintiffs. Lawsuits in two other tracks, the "commercial food preparers" including restaurants and retailers, and individual consumers known as "end-payers", include plaintiffs who purchased from the canners' tuna indirectly.

Thai Union has been active in settling many of the suits, which have already had a significant impact on the industry. The company set aside some $104m to pay for its part in the price-fixing.

In November 2019, Bumble Bee filed bankruptcy in Delaware and was purchased by its longtime tuna supplier FCF Co. Bumble Bee has cited the class action suits as well as a $25 million fine from the Department of Justice as two major factors behind the bankruptcy. 

Additionally, Starkist, which judge Edward Chen fined $100m in 2019 after its guilty plea to price-fixing charges, indicated at the time that it too could file for bankruptcy or move its operations from American Samoa, which would result in mass layoffs.
