title: Atlantic Sapphire reports Q1 price drop after ‘lost quarter’ for biomass growth
content:
The Danish recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) salmon farmer Atlantic Sapphire reported in its latest operational update that the average price achievement for fish from its Florida "bluehouse" in the US domestic market dropped by 27% during the first quarter of 2021, compared to the previous three months.

Fearnley: 500,000t of land-based salmon by 2030 on a cost-neutral basis

The firm produced 421 metric tons of salmon during the quarter, which were then sold to market at the average price of $6.8 per kilogram, down considerably from the $9.4/kg average it had been achieving at the tail end of 2020.

However, it is worth noting that the price achievement for the firm's "superior" 3kg+ fish has remained equal, at $12/kg -- it is simply that Atlantic Sapphire produced a lower proportion of these fish than previously due to maturation issues, the firm said.

The feed conversion ratio of the first batch of fish at the Miami site was also higher than expected, with roughly 60% of fish maturing early. In this regard, the second batch is showing significant improvement, with less than 10% maturation at present.

Q1 also represented a "lost quarter" for biomass gain, as the mortality incident on March 23, coupled with other smaller losses means the firm actually has 300t less biomass than it began the quarter with.

With empty tanks available, Atlantic Sapphire noted that it would utilize some of the additional capacity to grow the fish to larger harvest weights, and operate with reduced densities for the next few months.

Christopher Vinter, an analyst with Sparebank 1 Markets, added that in the fourth quarter, Atlantic Sapphire's JEA Index -- an indicator of biomass growth -- had been on budget, and the farmer had remained on budget when the Q1 system had been fully operational and stable. In its Q1 update, the firm reiterated its plans to return to that level.

To this end, Atlantic Sapphire has outlined a number of construction and commissioning-related issues that were responsible for the reduced growth and increased cost it experienced during the quarter (below).

In terms of construction, all phase one growout systems are now ready to take in fish, with five of the six growout systems successfully split. Once this process is completed, Atlantic Sapphire will have 19 independent RAS systems, it said.

New center drains are set to be installed for each of the systems over the next two to three months, as these were identified as a key design weakness responsible for the March 23 incident.

Meanwhile, the construction of the firm's filleting facility has also been completed, and is due to be in operation shortly, pending final permits. The need for external processing capacity during Q1 was another cause for higher costs, the firm said.

Focus has now shifted instead towards phase two construction, which is due to commence in the next quarter. It claims that the second phase will be significantly more efficient, with many lessons learned from issues that delayed the first phase of construction, and much greater in-house capability now available -- 150 employees as opposed to five before.

US engineering firm Hazen & Sawyer has been contracted with full design responsibility, while Wharton-Smith, a US firm specializing in water treatment projects, has been elected as general contractor. Once complete, Atlantic Sapphire plans for the second phase to give it 25,000t of head-on-gutted production from 2023 onwards.

Three rescued contract workers 'not following protocols'

On the evening of April 14, there was a separate incident at the Miami bluehouse site, as three contract workers had to be rescued from one of the tanks, an accident first reported by Channel 4 CBS. 

Atlantic Sapphire: Three contract workers rescued from tank weren’t following safety protocols

Two of the three workers have since been released and the third is in stable condition, Atlantic Sapphire reported. The firm claims that the three were not following confined space safety protocols.

In a statement released later, Atlantic Sapphire said the employees were working for a contractor and were cleaning out the bottom of an empty, dry and unused tank. The company didn't say which specific protocols were not followed, whether cleaning solutions were involved, or whether there was a lack of sufficient oxygen. 

Similarly, Atlantic Sapphire did not identify the contractor or the names of the workers.

"The company's emergency procedures were immediately activated and our safety and health personnel, together with Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, evacuated the tank," the company said. "All three individuals were immediately transported to Homestead Hospital to receive medical attention and they are in stable condition."

title: Atlantic Sapphire: Three contract workers rescued from tank weren’t following safety protocols
content:
The three contract company workers, who had to be rescued from a large tank at Atlantic Sapphire's Homestead, Florida, Atlantic salmon recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) operation and hospitalized, were not following "confined space safety protocols", the Norwegian company said.

Two of the three workers have since been released and the third is in stable condition, Atlantic Sapphire reported. 

Channel 4 CBS, a Miami, Florida-area television affiliate, first reported on the incident Tuesday, even flying a helicopter over the scene.

"They were in there in one of these tanks used to raise fish for routine maintenance and there was some type of fume released and they were overcome by it," Miami-Dade County Fire Department chief Jason Richard told the TV station.

In a statement released later, Atlantic Sapphire said the employees were working for a contractor and were cleaning out the bottom of an empty, dry and unused tank. The company didn't say which specific protocols were not followed, whether cleaning solutions were involved, or whether there was a lack of sufficient oxygen. 

Similarly, Atlantic Sapphire did not identify the contractor or the names of the workers.

"The company’s emergency procedures were immediately activated and our safety and health personnel, together with Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, evacuated the tank," the company said.  "All three individuals were immediately transported to Homestead Hospital to receive medical attention and they are in stable condition.

"The safety of our employees and contractors is our primary concern," Atlantic Sapphire said. "In compliance with the company’s protocols, the respective investigation was initiated to determine the root cause of the accident. 

"The company has determined that the contractor’s employees did not follow confined space safety protocols," it said. "Furthermore, the affected contractors did not fall into the relevant tank or otherwise face any impact-related injuries."

Atlantic Sapphire, which is publicly traded on the Oslo Bors Exchange (ticker symbol: ASA)  has had a bad run of luck in recent times just a few months after it had its first commercial harvest on its way to becoming what it hopes will be a 10,000 metric ton per year operation in its first phase of construction.

Late last month it suffered another massive salmon mortality, losing some 500t (head-on, gutted) fish, equivalent to about 5% of its annualized phase one harvest volumes, as reported by Undercurrent News. The fish that died had an average weight of approximately 1 kilogram. The company’s preliminary analysis indicated an identified design weakness from its RAS that caused significant amounts of particles to flow from the drum filters into the biofilters and trickling filters, resulting in "elevated turbidity and possibly gasses".

title: Canadian processor fined CAD 100,000 for undersized Dungies
content:
Tenshi Seafood Limited, a seafood processor, distributor and exporter based in the Canadian province of British Columbia, and its co-owner, Dishi Liu, have been found guilty and fined for violating Canada's Fisheries Act for selling undersized Dungeness crabs.

The company was ordered to pay a CAD 75,000 ($60,000) fine and Liu required to pay another CAD 25,000.

Additionally, Dishi Liu has been ordered to provide Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) with a list of its customers from the past two years and publish a letter, addressed to all of its customers, setting out the facts related to the case.

The rulings, made public this week, were rendered by judge Bonnie Craig in the Richmond Provincial Court back on March 4. Earlier, on Jan. 17, 2020, the court found Thuong Nguyen, owner of the commercial fishing vessel Dream Chaser, similarly guilty and ordered him to pay a CAD 10,000 fine. 

The charges stem from a routine inspection of Tenshi's operations in Richmond, BC, on Sept. 8, 2018, by a DFO fishery officer who "observed a man running from the building and speeding away with what looked like a crab crate in the back of his vehicle", DFO said in a press release. 

"Once inside the plant, the owner, and some staff, actively obstructed the fishery officer from conducting an inspection, would not answer questions, failed to provide the necessary paperwork, weights or volume figures from the previous sale, and attempted to destroy evidence," according to DFO. "Several undersized crabs were found discarded in the processing plant."

title: Definition of ‘mutual understanding’ at issue in Lischewski appeal
content:
The meaning of two innocuous-sounding words has become a central issue that a panel of US appeals court judges will consider in deciding whether Christopher Lischewski should be released from prison early.

On June 16, lawyers for Lischewski and the US Department of Justice's Antitrust Division, who convicted the former Bumble Bee Foods CEO on price-fixing charges in Dec. 2019, will have 20 minutes each to make their case before the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. 

Among the several points that attorney John Cline raised in his client's appeal was an assertion that trial court judge Edward Chen made a "serious error" in giving instructions to the jury that ultimately found Lischewski guilty. Specifically, Cline wrote, that Chen's statement to jurors that finding the charge of conspiracy to fix prices required the government to prove that Lischewski had entered into either an "agreement or mutual understanding" with others to fix prices.

The distinction is vital and the error is serious enough to have the verdict overturned, Cline argued.

"In the context of this case, the latter meaning had crucial significance; during the period of the alleged conspiracy, fish costs skyrocketed, and it was 'mutually understood' by everyone in the industry that prices had to rise accordingly. Such a commonly held view falls short of the 'agreement' that forms the heart of conspiracy," he wrote, according to a Sept. 25, 2020, filing.

DOJ prosecutors disagreed.

"This instruction was clear and correct. Agreement and understanding are synonymous terms, and the jury would have understood them as such," prosecutors wrote.

They also took issue with another major element of the appeal regarding an aspect of the Sherman Antitrust Act, one of the country's principal laws regulating competition. The Sherman act prohibits "unreasonable" restraints on trade but it also includes a "per se" rule that defines some acts like price-fixing as "conclusively proven to be unreasonable", the appeal states. 

Lischewski's attorneys repeatedly argued at trial that there was no evidence that price-fixing occurred in the sector. Additionally, any collusion between other tuna executives -- which his lawyers said Lischewski lacked knowledge of -- did not cause harm to consumers, they said. But Chen's decision to allow the use of the "per se" rule meant that even if no harm occurred, the jury couldn't consider the "reasonableness" of the accusation against him. And that was a violation of Lischewski's constitutional rights, the appeal argued.

Lischewski argued similarly in a June 2020 opinion piece written for Undercurrent News.

But DOJ prosecutors defended the application of the per se rule to the case.

"The district court correctly adhered to this court's precedents upholding the per se rule and requiring intent to conspire for price-fixing offenses. Lischewski's contentions flout longstanding antitrust law," prosecutors wrote.

Price-fixing trial

After a month-long trial, Lischewski was convicted on a count of price-fixing on Dec. 3, 2019, a scandal for the sector that also netted guilty pleas from Bumble Bee and rival StarKist & Co, which is owned by South Korea's Dongwon Enterprise. Thai Union Group-owned Chicken of the Sea International also participated in the price-fixing, which prosecutors said occurred from 2010 to 2013, but cooperated in exchange for amnesty.

During the 2019 trial, prosecutors relied heavily on the testimony of two former Bumble Bee vice-presidents, Walter Cameron and Kenneth Worsham and a former StarKist executive, Stephen Hodge, as well as former Chicken of the Sea International CEO, Shue Wing Chan, who was protected from prosecution due to his company's amnesty agreement. The other three executives pleaded guilty to price-fixing charges but Cameron and Worsham have yet to be sentenced.

Hodge is serving a sentence of three years probation, six months home confinement with a curfew, 120 hours of community service and a $25,000 fine. 

During Lischewski's trial, Cameron testified that the CEO directed him to reach out to Cameron's friend and former Bumble Bee coworker, Chuck Handford, who in 2010 was working for StarKist in an effort to broker a "truce" between the two canners' "price wars" of aggressive competition during the 2010 period.

Elliot Peters, the lead trial defense attorney for Lischewski, contested this claim, arguing that pricing data and internal Bumble Bee emails from the period showed vibrant competition, not collusion. The next year, 2011, was the true "price war", and was a challenging year for all three canners as albacore and skipjack prices saw steep increases, Peters claimed. 

Handford was never charged with a crime and did not testify at trial. In addition to Lischewski's own testimony that he was not aware of his subordinates' collusion, the defense also presented evidence from Yale University economist Joseph Levinsohn, who presented data that prices charged to consumers during the conspiracy period were lower than what they had been previously when the higher production cost of tuna was taken into account. 

Lischewski could have faced a $1 million fine and up to 10 years in prison but Chen sentenced him to three years and four months and fined him $100,000. Lischewski is currently incarcerated at United States Penitentiary Tuscon in the state of Arizona, according to prison records. Without an appeal to shorten his sentence, he is currently expected to be released on June 18, 2023, prison records show.

One thing this article omitted was the fact that the DOJ used 26 ‘unindicted co conspirators” as leverage against a proper defense for Lischewski. These individuals, if called as witnesses for the defense, would have exposed themselves to the DOJ filing criminal indictments on them regardless of evidence to the contrary. These such threats are common tactics in the DOJ playbook to ensure the balance of power is tilted in their favor entering trial. In layman terms it is a legal loophole they have at their disposal which would otherwise be considered witness tampering. The jury in this case was not permitted to be told by the defense of these unindicted co-conspirators as it would add to them potentially believing an alternative reality. That the acts of two tenured executives could possibly go undetected by the CEO in hopes of them enriching themselves. It it of note that today the court records show Ken Worsham is asking the court to seal all documents related to his upcoming sentencing. Effectively if the Judge agrees, it would permit Worsham from ever having to disclose to future employers that he was convicted of a crime. It is notable that Worsham and Cameron still have yet to be sentenced, Hodge was given a walk, while Lischewski, has now served 8 months in prison, for a crime he continues to vehemently plead not guilty to, but for a crime these three government turned witnesses themselves plead guilty to 5 years ago. It is astonishing the lengths that our own US Justice Department will go to to put innocent citizens in jail for while giving amnesty and whistleblower payments to foreign agents operating on US soil. title: Fish Factor: Vessel mask rules; Russian trade dispute; Hatchery hauls
content:
Undercurrent News is now featuring 'Fish Factor', a weekly column featuring the reporting and perspective of Alaska seafood journalist Laine Welch

The mask requirement for all persons aboard fishing vessels still stands and Alaska’s US senators are trying to use their clout to have it removed.

A Coast Guard Marine Safety Information Bulletin issued March 22 states its authority to restrict vessel access to ports and operations if they fail to follow the rules as defined by the Center for Disease Control (CDC).

"Vessels that have not implemented the mask requirement may be issued a Captain of the Port order directing the vessel’s movement and operations; repeated failure to impose the mask mandate could result in civil and/or criminal enforcement action," the bulletin says.

The CDC mask requirement has been interpreted by the Coast Guard to apply to "all forms of commercial maritime vessels",  including cargo ships, fishing vessels, research vessels and self-propelled barges. It requires "all travelers" to wear a mask, including those who have been vaccinated, according to National Fisherman which added, "Why commercial fishing vessels have been included in a requirement written for airplanes, trains, subways, buses, taxis, ride-shares, trolleys, and cable cars has yet to be explained by the Coast Guard".

"Senator [Lisa] Murkowski and I have been pressing this relentlessly on a call with the Coast Guard commandant, a call with the White House guy who's supposedly in charge of all the CDC issues, we had a meeting with the head of the CDC, we are trying to explain to them how, no offense, but just how stupid this is and how uninformed it is," senator Dan Sullivan said last week at a ComFish forum. "And it could be a safety issue, not with regard to COVID, but with having to wear masks when you're out on the deck of a ship in 30-foot waves trying to bring in gear or pots. So, we're going to continue to work on that one."

"The CDC has planted their heels on this one as I understand it," echoed Doug Vincent-Lang, commissioner of the Alaska Department of Fish and Game. "Certainly, from a realistic standpoint, it makes no sense. So we're on the front side of that conversation."

Vincent-Lang added that he is speaking with members of other coastal states and hopes to garner support to overturn the mask requirement.

"I think to the extent that we can form some kind of a unified position on this issue across more states, we stand a better chance of changing it. Because this is a CDC guidance which can be changed depending upon how they get policy direction from the White House. And if they hear from other coastal states in addition to Alaska, they'll probably be more inclined to do it," he said.

Feedback on the masking rule can be given at wearamask@uscg.mil.

Trade talk

Alaska’s senators also spoke candidly about ongoing trade policies with Russia that hurt the U.S. seafood industry and expressed hope for change under the new administration.

Russia stopped purchasing any foods from the US and other nations that imposed sanctions on Russian individuals and businesses after its illegal land-grab of Crimea from Ukraine in 2014. Meanwhile, US purchases of seafood from Russia have increased every year.

Russian seafood imports to the US in 2020, for example, topped 97.5 million pounds valued at nearly $1 billion, compared to 80.2m lbs in 2019 valued at nearly $698m.   

"I think it was the one area where the Trump administration was kind of weak. I thought we could have done more," said senator Sullivan, calling the lack of action "a disappointment".

Sullivan said he raised the issue "front and center" in a recent meeting with new US Trade Representative Katherine Tai and called her "'very impressive".

"I said, look, it's just ridiculous. Six years! I mean, that embargo started at the end of the Obama administration and the whole Trump administration. Meanwhile, most of their fish comes in almost duty-free, and they're taking market share from our fishermen in America.  She's going to look hard at this."

Senator Murkowski added that she intends to raise the trade imbalance with new secretary of state Antony Blinken and encourage him to include it in diplomatic discussions with Russia. 

"The fact that this has been in place for as long as it has, the fact that it has caused harm to our fisheries is something that the education needs to continue at different levels. You've got US trade, but you've also got the State Department with regards to the relationship that you have with Russia. This is one thing that I think we all agree we have got to have addressed. It has been going on for far, far too long, and quite honestly, it's untenable."

Both senators also said they spoke with the secretary of state and the national security advisor when they recently passed through Anchorage on their way to China and "pressed them hard to work on tariffs that the Chinese have put on our exports".

Murkowski and Sullivan also addressed many more topics at ComFish, including actions they are taking to mitigate climate change. View the full presentation at www.comfishak.com/

Hatchery hauls

Last year nearly 31m salmon that got their start in Alaska hatcheries were caught in commercial fisheries, or 27% of the statewide harvest. The dockside value of $69m comprised 23% of the state’s total salmon value.

That’s according to the annual salmon enhancement report newly released by the Alaska Department of Fish and Game.

There are 30 hatcheries producing salmon in Alaska, of which 26 are operated by private, nonprofits funded primarily from sales of a portion of the returns, called cost recovery. There also are two state-run sport fish hatcheries, one research hatchery operated by National Oceanic Atmospheric Administration Fisheries, and one hatchery operated by the Metlakatla Indian community.

At Prince William Sound, where six hatcheries operate, about 15m hatchery salmon were harvested in 2020. Those fish accounted for 70% of the total commercial catch that was worth nearly $27m at the docks, or 67% of the total value for the region.

At Southeast Alaska, 14 hatcheries operate, split between northern and southern regions. Last year, fewer than 4m hatchery salmon were caught accounting for 45% of the total harvest and 52% of the value to fishermen at $18m.

Two hatcheries operate at Kodiak where last year nearly 5m salmon were harvested worth about $5m, or 11% of the total dockside value. Nearly all of the fish were pinks.

The three hatcheries at Cook Inlet produced just under 200,000 salmon valued at $585,000, or 6.9% of the region’s total to fishermen.

Alaska’s combined hatcheries released 1.7bn juvenile salmon in 2020 and are projecting a return this year of nearly 66m fish.

Get schooled!

A first-ever, field-based Alaskan Aquaculture Semester in Sitka is being offered this fall to a dozen students from Alaska and across the nation.

It’s part of the University of Alaska/Southeast Fisheries Technology Program that has been preparing students for jobs throughout the industry since 2009 with classes focusing on aquaculture and salmon enhancement and fisheries management.

The aquaculture semester adds in more direct training on the water.

"Students will come here and be able to get 13 credits of instruction with courses in salmon culture and mariculture, and also in cold water survival," said Angie Bowers, assistant professor with the Fish Tech Program. "And they're going to learn how to drive boats and fix motors and tie knots and how to be safe. They will also be able to do an internship based on whatever they're interested in. We'll tour processors, they will be able to help out at local hatcheries and shadow fishermen."

There are three salmon hatcheries in the region where students will help with egg takes and learn about fish pathology and rearing prior to the tiny salmon heading out to sea. Bowers said students also will be introduced to shellfish and kelp farming.

"Because of the timing of the semester, that's not the typical growing season for kelp, but we will be able to identify species of kelp and make the seed string that gets out-planted on a kelp farm. We will be visiting an oyster farm and we'll try to incorporate as much of that mariculture experience as we can," she said.

Students also can get certified in SCUBA diving within the university program that trains scientific divers across the entire system.

The Fish Tech Program is the university’s only one and two-year, entry-level applied fisheries program. There has been a 10-fold growth since it began 12 years ago in Ketchikan and graduates now work for agencies or organizations across Alaska and in the Lower 48, said director Joel Marcus. Part of the program’s success, he said, is that nearly all classes can be taken remotely.

But the new Aquaculture semester will focus on being out on the water.  Only 12 students will be accepted for the fall semester that starts on August 23rd and runs through December. Visit Salmon Culture Semester to learn more or email Angie Bowers at abowers4@alaska.edu

title: Chicken of the Sea close to $13m settlement in tuna price-fixing case
content:
Thai Union Group-owned Chicken of the Sea International (COSI) has reached an agreement to settle a class-action lawsuit from a group of customers that claimed damages from the US canned tuna brand's participation in a price-fixing scandal earlier in the decade.

The tuna buyers in the suit are known as the "direct payer plaintiffs" and include the companies Olean Wholesale Grocery Cooperative, Pacific Groservice, Piggly Wiggly Alabama Distributing Co, Trepco Imports and Distribution and Benjamin Foods.

They will share in $13 million, according to the settlement.

"The settlement provides the settlement class members with significant relief. And this relief is comparable, if not superior, to other publicly reported settlements," plaintiffs' lawyers wrote in support of the proposed settlement. "The settlement class members are mostly comprised of smaller companies, with other larger retailers having effectively opted out of the class by filing their own suits or separately settling with COSI."

The settlement does not include the two other main defendants in the price-fixing case, Dongwon Enterprise-owned StarKist & Co and Bumble Bee Foods.

Plaintiffs have been sorted into four "tracks" depending on how they purchased tuna from the canners and the class certification ruling allows each track to have common legal counsel and pool many plaintiffs' resources together to pay the costly bills for expert witnesses, lawyers fees and other expenses that come in class-action litigation. 

The large wholesalers and distributors who dealt directly with the canners are known as "direct purchasers" with a second track of direct purchasers including large buyers such as Walmart with separate lawsuits known as "direct action" plaintiffs.

Lawsuits in two other tracks, the "commercial food preparers" including restaurants and retailers, and individual consumers known as "end-payers", include plaintiffs who purchased from the canners' tuna indirectly.

A large number of the suits have been settled. The class-action suits have already had a major impact on the US canners. In November 2019, Bumble Bee filed bankruptcy in Delaware and was purchased by its longtime tuna supplier FCF Co. Bumble Bee has cited the class action suits as well as a $25 million fine from the Department of Justice as two major factors behind the bankruptcy. 

Additionally, Starkist, which judge Edward Chen fined $100m in 2019 after its guilty plea to price-fixing charges, indicated at the time that it too could file for bankruptcy or move its operations from American Samoa, which would result in mass layoffs.

Thai Union, which escaped criminal liability because it acted as a whistleblower to the Department of Justice, has set aside some $104m to pay for its part in the price-fixing. Most of the related lawsuits have now been settled, the company has said.

title: US panel to ask Biden to open Pacific island monument to commercial tuna fishing
content:
The most important panel for recommending policy related to America's tuna-focused fleets of the Pacific -- including Hawaiian- and American Samoa- based longliners and US-flagged purse seiners -- will ask president Joe Biden this week to let harvesters back into a large part of the ocean designated as a national monument.  

The Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council (WPRFMC), one of eight powerful regional panels created by the Magnuson-Stevens Act (MSA) to advise the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), voted unanimously Thursday, March 25, to request the removal of commercial fishing prohibitions in the massive Pacific Remote Islands Marine National Monument (PRIMNM), Kitty Simonds, the executive director, told Undercurrent News via email.

It was at the end of two weeks of virtual meetings and the final third day of deliberations on important fisheries issues, she said.

The restrictions were set by former president George W. Bush but expanded upon by former president Barack Obama, under which Biden served as vice president, using the Antiquities Act. Recreational fishing continues to be allowed.

Kitty Simonds.

In a letter to be sent to the White House as well as recently confirmed secretaries of the interior and commerce, Deb Haaland and Gina Raimondo respectively, WPRFMC will ask for the removal of "fishing prohibitions in the [PRINMN] to allow fishery resources to be managed within the authority of the [MSA]," Simonds said.

It's an action that is likely to also be welcomed by tuna giant Starkist & Co., the US-based division of South Korea's Dongwon Enterprise, which maintains an important cannery in the area. 

The request could get more attention following the strongly worded, four-page opinion shared early last week by US Supreme Court chief justice John Roberts that suggested presidents have overused the Antiquities Act to create marine national monuments. As reported by Undercurrent, Roberts seemed to be inviting another challenge by the industry, suggesting the court would be more likely to uphold a future appeal.

The restrictions set around the Pacific monument could be additional grounds for just such an argument to be made.  

Bigger than Texas

It was in Jan. 2009, the final days of Bush's second term as president, that he used the Antiquities Act and an executive order to establish protections for the Pacific Remote Islands. It was his fourth marine national monument proclamation, which included also the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands.

The area sustains many threatened, endangered and depleted species, including the green and hawksbill turtles, pearl oysters, giant clams, reef sharks, coconut crabs, groupers, humphead and Napoleon wrasses, parrotfish, dolphins, and whales, according to NOAA.

The original area of the protected Pacific Remote Islands was about 83,000 square miles, but was significantly expanded by another executive order in Sept. 2014 by then-president Barack Obama to cover 490,343 square miles, including seven islands and atolls, larger than the size of Texas (268,597 sq. miles). 

Like Bush, Obama also relied upon an executive order and the Antiquities Act, a bill signed into law by former president Theodore Roosevelt in 1906 in response to the defacement of Pueblo ruins in the US state of New Mexico. 

"Our council's argument has always been about the 'size' of the Pacific marine monuments around the US Pacific Remote Islands, the Hawaiian Islands, American Samoa and the CNMI and the Marianas Trench, of course," Simonds said in her email to Undercurrent. 

The US Pacific region comprises 1.4 billion acres of ocean, though the monuments in the area, when combined, comprise a total of 759.3 million, more than 51%, she said. The Pacific Remote Islands national monument makes up 316.9m of that.

'This doesn't happen every day or even in a lifetime'

While the WPRFMC's request relates to US Pacific waters, the timing of the vote seems to have at least been partly inspired by happenings related to the US Atlantic Coast. 

The Supreme Court, on March 22, announced that it was denying certiorari to an appeal made by the Massachusetts Lobstermen's Association and four other fishing groups regarding Obama's use of the Antiquities Act to create the Northeast Canyons and Seamounts Marine National Monument, a nearly 5,000 sq mile part of the Atlantic Ocean protected from both drilling and commercial fishing.

However, while chief justice Roberts said in his opinion that the MLA-related request didn't merit high court review, he took a shot at the presidents' use of the Antiquities Act to declare national marine monuments. The "issue in this case demonstrates how far we have come from indigenous pottery", he said.

Seafood attorney Andrew Minkiewicz, a partner at the firm Kelly Drye, in Washington, DC, was among several sources to suggest to Undercurrent that the chief justice practically drew a bull's eye, in his opinion, around the right case to be made in a future appeal.

US Supreme Court chief justice John Roberts during his confirmation hearing in 2005. Photograph by Rob Crandall from Shutterstock.

"This doesn't happen every day or even in a lifetime," Minkiewicz said. 

The MLA lawsuit was filed in 2017, three years before former president Donald Trump issued proclamation 10049 on June 5, 2020, a new executive order reversing some of the earlier Obama order in the Atlantic by making an allowance for commercial fishing. However, proclamation 14008, an executive order issued by Biden on Jan. 20, seemed to crack open the possibility that the ban will be restored.

The order, among other things, gave the Department of Interior (DOI) 60 days (until March 21) to issue a report recommending whether the new administration should reinstate the commercial fishing ban in the New England monument area or maintain Trump's exemption while also addressing other changes by the previous administration.

A DOI spokesperson told Undercurrent last week that the report has yet to be delivered to the White House, per the deadline, but will likely make its way there sometime in April after Haaland completes a trip to Utah where she will visit other, land-based national monuments.

Watching with intense interest will be the US' longline harvesters of swordfish, big-eyed tuna, yellowfin tuna and mahi-mahi in the Atlantic. They reported having lost millions of dollars and seeing their fleet shrunk by dozens of vessels as a result of Obama's earlier executive order, which also protected the area from drilling activities.

Should Biden respond to the report by reinstating the commercial fishing ban in the Atlantic, that could lead to another lawsuit that makes its way to the Supreme Court, Minkiewicz has suggested.

But commercial harvesters banned from large sections of the Pacific may already have the standing necessary to file such a suit.

Joe Biden. Photograph by Gage Skidmore on Flickr.

Simonds said in one of her emails to Undercurrent that she was not aware of another lawsuit being planned by the commercial fishing industry there but noted that the council "would be very interested in learning about such a challenge".

"The chief justice focused his statement of March 22 on size -- 'confined to the smallest area compatible with the proper care and management of the objects to be protected'," she said. "He mentions '3.2  million acres of submerged land' as the area of the New England monument." 

"I agree that the chief justice appears to be open to further consideration," she said, referring to the suggestion being made in Undercurrent's earlier article. "He says in the last sentence of his statement, 'The scope of the objects that can be designated under the act, and how to measure the area necessary for their proper care and management, may warrant consideration'."

US tuna purse-seine fleet evaporating

Trump had promised to answer prayers by the commercial tuna fishing industry and grant a similar exemption in the Pacific while still in office. But he never delivered.

Simonds and WPRFMC chair Archie Soliai had requested Trump's attention to the matter in a letter they sent him in May 2020. The restrictions in the Pacific often force tuna-focused fleets in the region to fish outside the US exclusive economic zone (EEZ), they said. That pushes them into high seas areas or the waters of other Pacific island-states where fishing access is costlier.

"For example, US purse seine vessels, unable to access productive fishing grounds in the US EEZ must pay $13,000 per day for access to the EEZs of Pacific Island States. The US tuna purse-seine fleet has dropped from a recent high of 39 vessels to currently 24 licensed vessels," the letter stated.

The fleet has since lost another six vessels and is now down to 18, according to the American Tunaboat Association (ATA), which represents the group and also appealed to Trump.

American Samoa, a US territory in the Pacific, is home to tuna company Starkist. Credit: Bryan Chernick/Shutterstock.com

William Gibbons-Fly, a former 15-year State Department staffer who serves as ATA's executive director, advised Trump in his own letter that Obama's "ill-considered and ill-conceived decision to close huge areas of the US fleet's historical and most productive fishing grounds" was helping to put a lot of his members out of business.

The ATA leader also blamed China's subsidization of vessel construction, financing, fuel and other operating costs, as well as the lack of compliance by several countries' fleets with international fishing standards for his fleet's woes. 

Lifting the fishing restrictions in the Pacific marine monuments would also specifically benefit the Pago Pago, American Samoa cannery run by StarKist & Co, which generates some 4,000 direct and indirect jobs and is the island's largest employer,  Gibbons-Fly and others advised.

Aumua Amata, a Republican delegate for the US House of Representatives from American Samoa, joined in the plea with a separate letter in March 2020 to Trump. She said eliminating the fishing restrictions was a matter of food security during the pandemic and noted how demand for canned tuna had spiked 30% in just a week.  

"Now is the time to reopen American waters to ensure an American supply chain with American boats fishing American waters and having American manufacturing plants processing essential staple foods for the American people," she said.

Pacific bluefin tuna (Thunnus thynnus) schooling, Mexico.

Regardless of whether the Supreme Court might reverse the executive orders that earlier granted national monument status to parts of the ocean, Simonds hopes the new administration doesn't use the Antiquities Act in an attempt to expand further on commercial fishing prohibitions.

"I hope this administration does not contemplate using the Antiquities Act to expand 'protection'," she said in one of her emails to Undercurrent. "The tools for managing area closures in US zones are in the toolbox of the Regional Fishery Management Councils [RFMCs] found in the Fishery Conservation and Management Act of 1976 and three subsequent reauthorizations -- now known as the [MSA]."

More than 72% of US oceans already protected

The WPRFMC's coming request of the Biden administration will be just the latest in a series of actions by NOAA's eight regional councils intended to keep conservation under their purview.  

The Council Coordination Committee (CCC), the senior leaders of all eight RFMCs, on March 12, wrote to Haaland and Raimondo requesting they encourage the administration to keep relying on the existing regulatory scheme rather than create artificial goals.

In particular, the panel was addressing another Biden executive order, 14008, which directs the two cabinet members to "submit a report to the National Climate Task Force by April 20 recommending steps to work with state, tribal and territorial governments, fishermen and other key stakeholders to achieve the goal of conserving at least 30% of our lands and waters by 2030"

Deb Haaland. Photograph from her campaign website.

"The MSA gives the US the strongest statutory framework in the world for the management of sustainable fisheries and associated ecosystems and the US is recognized as a world leader in marine conservation and sustainable fishery management," the CCC wrote.

The letter argues that the RFMCs "have already made significant progress" in achieving the administration's so-called "30-by-30 goal" and could continue to be a valuable asset. 

"More than 1,000 individual spatial habitat and fisheries conservation measures have been implemented, protecting more than 72% of the nation’s ocean waters from fishing
impacts, which helps to ensure preservation of ecosystem functions," the council leaders said in their letter.

"[T]he entire [EEZ] under authority of the MSA should be classified as a conservation area for marine fishery resources, and at least 72% of that area should be classified as protected," they argued.

title: US chief justice’s remarks set up likely showdown with Biden over fishing bans
content:
Did US Supreme Court chief justice John Roberts throw down the gauntlet for president Joe Biden and invite another lawsuit by the commercial fishing industry earlier this week when he expressed his disdain for past use of the Antiquities Act to block off certain parts of the ocean?

That's what it looks like to seafood attorney Andrew Minkiewicz, a partner at the firm Kelly Drye, in Washington, D.C. 

"This doesn't happen every day or even in a lifetime," Minkiewicz said of the apparent opportunity for the industry. "The chief justice really outlined his skepticism of the way presidents are using the power that is, or is not, granted to them in the Antiquities Act. And he raises questions a lot of us have had, like, 'How did we go from trying to protect ancient dwellings from people robbing their artifacts to now 580,000 square miles of ocean being locked up with the stroke of a pen?"

Andrew Minkiewicz. Photography from Kelly Drye website.

In his four-page explanation, issued Monday, March 22, for why the high court rejected the petition for certiorari filed by the Massachusetts Lobstermen's Association (MLA) and four other fishing groups as part of an effort to allow commercial fishing on nearly 5,000 square miles in the Atlantic Ocean, Roberts practically drew a bull's eye around the right case to be made next time, Minkiewicz and others believe.

The Pacific Legal Foundation, a libertarian public interest law firm, had argued on behalf of MLA and the other fishing groups that president Barack Obama overstepped his bounds in Sept. 2016 when he used the 1906 antiquities law and proclamation 9496, an executive order, to create the Northeast Canyons and Seamounts Marine National Monument. Roberts said the request didn't meet the standards necessary to warrant a Supreme Court review, but his explanation indicated he strongly agreed with the sentiment.

"Which of the following is not like the others: (a) a monument, (b) an antiquity (defined as a 'relic or monument of ancient times', Webster’s International Dictionary of the English Language 66 (1902)), or (c) 5,000 square miles of land beneath the ocean?," the chief justice wrote.

"If you answered (c), you are not only correct but also a speaker of ordinary English," he said. "In this case, however, the government has relied on the Antiquities Act of 1906 to designate an area of submerged land about the size of Connecticut as a monument -- the Northeast Canyons and Seamounts Marine National Monument."

Roberts noted that the Antiquities Act, which was signed into law by president Theodore Roosevelt, originated as a response to the defacement of Pueblo ruins in the US state of New Mexico and provided a means for the "preservation of prehistoric antiquities". Roosevelt, a staunch advocate of the measure and champion of preserving America's natural landmarks, later used the power again in 1908 to reserve more than 800,000 acres of land when he created the Grand Canyon National Monument.

The Northeast Canyons and Seamounts Marine National Monument. Image courtesy of NOAA.

However, the marine monument "at issue in this case demonstrates how far we have come from indigenous pottery," Roberts wrote.

He said the courts have yet to rule on how limits to a monument's size apply to "such an imprecisely demarcated concept as an ecosystem. … The scope ... may warrant consideration -- especially given the myriad restrictions on public use this purely discretionary designation can serve to justify."

The chief justice's language was such an indication of the conservative-dominated court's true leaning that the Boston Globe called the decision a "Pyrrhic victory for conservation groups in New England" who would like to restore the bans against commercial fishing in the national monument area. The newspaper said it was a "potential roadmap for a legal challenge" and "seemed to signal that the court would be willing to consider truncating or invalidating the 5,000 square miles of federally protected waters".

The article even quoted one of the biggest advocates for the national monument as expressing apparent worry.

Theodore Roosevelt. Photograph from the US Library of Congress.

"It's concerning any time you get a statement like this from a justice, especially from the chief justice," said Peter Shelley, senior counsel at the Conservation Law Foundation (CLF), in Boston, Massachusetts. "The tea leaves of this statement are going to be read closely by people with very different perspectives."

The commercial fishing industry, meanwhile, is in a more upbeat mood.

"I think it's encouraging that chief justice Roberts understands the situation so clearly, and he has made the point speaking from the most exalted seat on the most exalted bench of any court in the land," said Bob Vanasse, the founder of Stove Boat Communications and Saving Seafood, a group that communicates the interest of the commercial fishing industry.

"He absolutely understands this perfectly, which is that a statute passed in 1906 for the explicit purpose of protecting Pueblo antiquities has been expanded unchecked over decades -- and most rapidly in the past two decades -- to give the president unrestricted authority to prohibit any activity in any location, no matter how large, and whether or not it's even technically US territory."

DOI's report to be delivered to White House in April

One of the challenges associated with trying to take on the use of the Antiquities Act to declare marine monuments is that former president Donald Trump, on June 5, 2020, issued proclamation 10049, a new executive order reversing some of the earlier Obama order in the Atlantic by making an allowance for commercial fishing.   

"To bring a case, you have to show actual harm," Minkiewicz explained. "There are lines out there that are designated a monument, but are they harming you? You can't really argue that right now. There is no Damocles sword hanging over your head."  

However, that could change if Biden follows up on his own executive order, 13990, "Protecting Public Health and the Environment and Restoring Science to Tackle the Climate Crisis", issued Jan. 20, 2021, as reported by Undercurrent. Among other things, it gave the Department of Interior 60 days (until March 21) to issue a report recommending whether the new administration should reinstate the commercial fishing ban in the New England monument area or maintain Trump's exemption while also addressing other changes by the previous administration.

Atlantic deep sea red crab. Photograph courtesy of NOAA.

But the turnaround time was incredibly short, given that new interior secretary Deb Haaland wasn't confirmed until March 15. Also, the order required her to consult with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS).

Asked Wednesday by Undercurrent whether the agency made its March 21 deadline, DOI press secretary Tyler Cherry responded that Haaland "is looking forward to visiting Utah in April to meet with stakeholders, Tribes, and elected leaders". 

Based on multiple newspaper accounts, she will use the opportunity to tour Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante, two land-based national monuments created with the help of the Antiquities Act, but no specific dates have yet been provided.

"The Interior Department's report to the president on national monuments, as called for in executive order 14008 [sic], will reflect those conversations and will be transmitted to the White House following the trip," Cherry said, though he apparently used the wrong EO number in his response.

DOI officials were joined by representatives from NMFS in an online, one-hour listening session March 12 to hear the concerns of a dozen commercial fishing industry representatives. They included officials from Lund's Fisheries, a Cape May, New Jersey-based harvester and processor of both squid and Atlantic scallops, and Town Dock, a Narragansett, Rhode Island-based harvester and processor of squid, as well as the Blue Water Fisherman's Association, a trade group whose members harvest swordfish, tuna and sharks, and the Atlantic Red Crab Company, a New Bedford, Massachusetts-based harvester and processor.

Katie Almeida, Town Dock's senior representative for government relations, told the DOI and NMFS officials how her company was already threatened with the loss of important squid fishing grounds due to the planned building of offshore wind farms.

"So the threat of losing additional acreage is a major economic concern for us and the workers that depend on our ability to fish for squid," she said. "Our fleet is commercially dependent upon access to these areas. ... We need to continue to access the historical fishing grounds we have come to depend upon."    

"What the Interior Department recommends to president Biden on this issue really matters, not only to the environment but to the fabric of a number of coastal communities and minority ethnic groups," said David Borden, executive director of the Atlantic Offshore Lobster Association.

"These concerns are not partisan. Both Democratic and Republican presidential candidates supported the creation of five marine monuments through the Antiquities Act. Several large coastal cities, with large minority populations, will be negatively affected by any closure of the area to fishing."

Joe Biden. Photograph by Gage Skidmore on Flickr.

What would trigger the lawsuit

If Biden responds to the DOI report by restoring the prohibition against commercial fishing in the Atlantic national monument, as some expect he will do using yet another executive order, however, that could be the trigger that leads to another round of challenges from the commercial fishing industry, said Minkiewicz.

Among the groups that could be injured and have grounds to sue should Trump's exemption be negated are the longline harvesters of swordfish, big-eyed tuna, yellowfin tuna and mahi-mahi. They reported having lost millions of dollars and seeing their fleet shrunk by dozens of vessels as a result of Obama's earlier executive order, which also protected the area from drilling activities.

Another group that could potentially bring a case would be one of the many prevented from fishing in the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument, located in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Hawaii. Obama had expanded protections for that area by 442,781 square miles as part of an executive order issued in August 2016, creating the world's largest marine protected area.

Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument. Image from NOAA.

Trump had promised to answer prayers by the commercial fishing industry and grant a commercial fishing exemption in the area while still in office but never delivered.

Presidents have designated five large underwater areas as national monuments since 2006. The Papahanaumokuakea, Rose Atoll, Mariana Trench and Pacific Remote Islands were all originally designated by president George W. Bush.

It would take several years for any case to make it back through the district court and appeals court before being eligible for consideration by the Supreme Court, Minkiewicz added.

Recall that the case denied certiorari by the Supreme Court on Monday was first brought in 2017 by MLA and also the Atlantic Offshore Lobstermen's Association, the Long Island Commercial Fishing Association, the Garden State Seafood Association and the Rhode Island Fishermen's Alliance. It was dismissed by a federal court in October 2018 and had that decision affirmed on appeal in December 2019 before it was sent to the Supreme Court for possible review in June 2020. 

But should Minkiewicz get the chance to take on the use of the Antiquities Act to prohibit fishing, it wouldn't be the first time. He and David Frulla, another Kelly Drye partner, already represent the Atlantic red crab harvester Williams as an intervenor on the side of the Trump administration in a lawsuit brought against it by CLF, the National Resources Defense Council and the Center for Biological Diversity, in June 2020, to challenge the commercial fishing exemption granted in the Atlantic national monument.

title: US Supreme Court won’t review presidential authority on marine monuments
content:
The US Supreme Court on Monday declared that it will not review the US president's authority to use the Antiquities Act to establish marine national monuments.

The court has denied a request for certiorari made by the Massachusetts Lobstermen's Association (MLA) and four other fishing groups to reverse the protected status given the Northeast Canyons and Seamounts Marine National Monument -- a 5,000-square-mile piece of the Atlantic Ocean, off the coast of New England -- established in 2016 by president Barack Obama.

Chief justice John Roberts said, in a statement, that while the case potentially posed interesting legal questions, it did not do so in a way that was appropriate for high-court consideration. 

New president Joe Biden, on Jan. 20, signed "Executive Order on Protecting Public Health and the Environment and Restoring Science to Tackle the Climate Crisis", among other things, ordering the secretary of the Department of the Interior to conduct a review of changes president Donald Trump made, via his own executive orders, to the boundaries and conditions of several US locations designated as national monuments. 

The Northeast Canyons and Seamounts Marine National Monument. Image courtesy of NOAA.

That includes proclamation 10049, signed by Trump on June 5, 2020, to modify the Northeast Canyons and Seamounts Marine National Monument, granting an exemption to allow for commercial fishing. 

Trump's action was seen, at the time, as good news for the longline harvesters of swordfish, big-eyed tuna, yellowfin tuna and mahi mahi. They reported having lost millions of dollars and seeing their fleet shrunk by dozens of vessels as a result of executive order (9496) issued by Obama in September 2016. It declared the area a national monument in order to protect the sea life there from both drilling activities and fishing.

Monday's decision by the Supreme Court relates to a lawsuit brought in 2017 by the fishing industry groups, including also the Atlantic Offshore Lobstermen's Association, the Long Island Commercial Fishing Association, the Garden State Seafood Association and the Rhode Island Fishermen's Alliance. The suit, which sought to abolish the monument, was dismissed by a federal court in October 2018. The decision was then affirmed on appeal in December 2019, before it was sent to the Supreme Court for possible review in June 2020. 

Roberts makes apparent Sesame Street crack

Roberts made an apparent Sesame Street reference in his opinion, lacing it with more than a hint of sarcasm.

"Which of the following is not like the others: (a) a monument, (b) an antiquity (defined as a 'relic or monument of ancient times', Webster’s International Dictionary of the
English Language 66 (1902)), or (c) 5,000 square miles of land beneath the ocean?," he wrote.

"If you answered (c), you are not only correct but also a speaker of ordinary English," he said. "In this case, however, the government has relied on the Antiquities Act of 1906 to designate an area of submerged land about the size of Connecticut as a monument -- the Northeast Canyons and Seamounts Marine National Monument."

US Supreme Court chief justice John Roberts. Photograph from RHRealityCheck.org on Flickr.

The chief justice continued: "We have never considered how a monument of these proportions -- 3.2 million acres of submerged land -- can be justified under the Antiquities Act. And while we have suggested that an 'ecosystem' and 'submerged lands' can, under some circumstances, be protected under the Act ... we have not explained how the Act’s corresponding 'smallest area compatible' limitation interacts with the protection of such an imprecisely demarcated concept as an ecosystem. The scope of the objects that can be designated under the Act, and how to measure the area necessary for their proper care and management, may warrant consideration—especially given the myriad restrictions on public use this purely discretionary designation can serve to justify.

"Despite these concerns, this petition does not satisfy our usual criteria for granting certiorari," he concluded, however. 

NRDC: Fishing industry attacks 'failed at every level'

The Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC) was among the first to respond on Monday. The decision means the appeals court’s ruling affirming the legality of the monument stands, the group said. 

"The Supreme Court’s rejection of this case is a victory," said Kate Desormeau, NRDC senior attorney. "The commercial fishing industry’s attack on Northeast Canyons and Seamounts has now failed at every level of the federal courts."

"The chief justice’s solo statement raised questions about the size of national monuments in the abstract," she said. "But there is ample scientific support for Northeast Canyons and Seamounts’ boundaries, developed through a year-long process during the Obama administration, In recent years that rationale for the monument has only gotten stronger. NRDC suggests in its press release that Biden "should restore full monument protections to Northeast Canyons and Seamounts with a new proclamation right away", saying his administration has heard an outpouring of public support.

NRDC, the Conservation Law Foundation, the Center for Biological Diversity, and Zack Klyver, a whale-watching naturalist based in Maine, filed a separate suit against the Trump administration in June 2020 to reverse his changes to the national monument status.

title: Wild-caught organic talks excite big US seafood players, draw out opponents
content:
The Alaska commercial fishing industry and several other US seafood industry groups made their case Thursday for why the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) should move forward with an organic label for wild caught-seafood and allow their products, including especially pollock, to be among the first to earn the honor.

"We acknowledge that the considerations and potential trade-offs are complex, but we believe that the program will be strengthened considerably if a decision is made to advance standards that can apply to wild-caught seafood," the groups say in a five-page letter sent to Jenny Tucker, deputy administrator at the USDA's Agricultural Marketing Service (AMS).

"Americans rely on and trust the USDA organic seal. Its complete absence from the seafood sector is an enormous missed opportunity."

The letter is signed by top executives and policy experts at the Genuine Alaska Pollock Producers, the At-sea Processors Association, the Alaska Seafood Marketing Institute, the Pacific Seafood Processors Association and the National Fisheries Institute.

The USDA organic label. Unfortunately, there are currently no organic seafood standards approved by the USDA that might allow for its use.

The letter followed a one-hour, online listening session held the same day in which Tucker invited some 160 participants to offer their comments on the prospect of establishing organic standards for wild-caught seafood in the US.

The meeting was held by USDA on the same day and even overlapped the times of two other important seafood-related online meetings, including one dealing with how the agency would divvy up $1.5 billion in COVID-related relief to the agriculture and seafood industries. Yet participants in the organic labeling meeting included representatives from some of the biggest players in the seafood industry, such as Trident Seafoods, the O'Hara Corporation, StarKist Tuna (part of South Korea's Dongwon Industries), Lund's Fisheries, American Seafoods, Gorton's Seafood, Icicle Seafoods, the Groundfish Forum and even the Maine Lobster Marketing Collaborative, as well as at least one notable seafood buyer, BJ's Wholesale Club.

"[A] pathway for organic designation of wild-caught fish will significantly benefit domestic harvesters and processors by increasing the value [of their catch], and ensure that US consumers are getting the healthiest and most nutritious seafood on the market," said Annika Saltman, charged with handling fisheries management and regulatory affairs for Fishermen's Finest, a Kirkland, Washington-based commercial harvester.

Also in attendance were outspoken stakeholder groups in the US organic space,  including the Organic Trade Association, the Center for Food Safety, the National Organic Coalition and the Cornucopia Institute. Some expressed opposition to the notion of an organic standard for wild-caught fish.

There "are much more urgent matters within the organic standards" that should get attention ahead of creating standards for wild-caught fish, including protecting native ecosystems and establish organic standards for the origin of livestock, said Marie Burcham, policy director for the Cornucopia Institute.

"We understand this is an ask from Congress," Burcham commented, adding: "How would inputs be controlled? How would ecosystem health be tracked, especially with migratory fish? There are lots of problems to tackle here."

'[A] picture of failure'

Undercurrent News reported earlier this month how the new administration of US president Joe Biden had re-opened the conversation about creating an organic labeling standard for US-produced seafood, surprising many by focusing first on wild-caught seafood instead of aquaculture.

The effort has been fought for since at least 2003 by Alaska senator Lisa Murkowski, a Republican, who has tried several times to introduce legislation that would allow Alaska salmon and other wild-fish products to be labeled organic food. Her language in a fiscal year 2021 appropriations report requested "serious dialogue" about such a measure, the Alaska seafood groups advised in their letter.

"We believe that the values underpinning Alaska seafood – and the messages we have long sought to convey to consumers – strongly aligned with organic producers and the [National Organic Program]," the groups said. "We also believe that specific features of Alaska seafood, harvested from the pristine waters of Alaska, overwhelmingly share the core characteristics of organic food produced in accordance with existing USDA standards."

Alaska pollock. Credit: Alex Coan/Shutterstock.com

The Alaska groups point to "one particularly egregious example of how the lack of a USDA organic certification for wild-caught seafood plays out," noting how US-based certified organic livestock operations eschew Alaska-produced fish meal and fish oil in feed, because it lacks organic standing, and instead import these products from other countries.

"This is a picture of failure, with domestic organic livestock missing out on a pristine and premium feed ingredient; imports needlessly displacing a domestically produced product; and the environmental goals of the program undermined by market distortions that increase transport-related carbon emissions," the letter continued.

'Not a need to consider certifying all wild-caught fish'

AMS' Tucker opened Thursday's online listening session by advising participants that "Congress has urged the National Organic Program to assess the feasibility and appropriateness of developing organic production and labeling standards for wild-caught seafood".

The agency is required to deliver a report to Congress on its progress, Tucker confirmed. She then asked participants in the online chat to respond to eight questions.

What is the industry's definition of wild-caught fish?
What is your feedback about the development of organic production and handling regulations for wild-caught fish?
What types of provisions might differentiate organic wild-caught fish from conventional wild-caught fish in the production phase? During the processing/handling phase?
What would the impact of organic production and handling regulation be on the wild-caught seafood industry?
How could wild-caught fish be regulated and enforced for organic labeling?
How does the wild-caught fish industry control the origin of harvested fish, control what is fed to their harvested fish, and treat medical conditions of their harvested fish?
What location would an inspector use for announced and unannounced inspections?
What could an organic system plan look like for wild-caught fish production or wild-caught fish processing?

From Thursday's presentation by the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service.

The comments given in response provided the champions of organic labeling for wild-caught seafood a sense of who their friends and enemies will be in the upcoming fight as well as what the biggest challenges could be.

Dennis Moran, the president of Fisherman's Finest, who was also in the online meeting, noted how agricultural crops are required to be grown in organic conditions. But "with fish, there are organic parts of the water and non-organic, so it seems there should be a distinction between organic wild-caught, which means an area of pristine waters as opposed to wild-caught in an area that might be less pristine, like certain rivers, lakes, etc.," he added.

Joseph Logan, the food safety and quality assurance global director for Trident Seafoods, suggested a method for organizing the standard to make it more manageable and not wash out the meaning of the label.

"Organic system plans and organic labeling would be specific fishery-dependent and there is not a need to consider certifying all wild-caught fish," he suggested. "Once a fishery is certified, then [the] industry within that fishery could join the program. Examples: Oregon Dungeness crab, Alaska pollock, Bristol Bay salmon. None of these utilize hatchery, ranching or other human interventions."

Another group that's sitting on the sidelines of the organic wild-caught debate but with a significant amount of interest is the US aquaculture industry. They were on the verge of seeing USDA publish a proposed organic labeling standard before the regulation was yanked from the Federal Register in the final days of the president Barack Obama administration, as reported by Undercurrent.

They were ignored by the Donald Trump administration and, especially given that much of the policy work has already been done, they had hoped to be the first to get consideration under Biden.

"If USDA develops standards for wild-caught seafood BEFORE aquaculture, It will seriously undermine the 'organic brand' because of all the scientific work that was done on aquaculture standards and because it will be responding to political pressure," commented Sebastian Belle, executive director of the Maine Aquaculture Association and representative of the National Aquaculture Association.

'Not a controlled/defined environment'

Steven Summerfelt, the chief science officer at Superior Fresh, a recirculating aquaculture system grower of Atlantic salmon in Wisconsin, was one of several participants to raise the traditional and one of the most difficult questions regarding the idea of sticking an organic label on wild-caught seafood. 

"Knowing the environment where a wild fish has lived and the feed that it has eaten is impossible," he commented. "The wild fish can be tested for contaminants, but otherwise it doesn't seem to me that wild fish can be audited with any degree of certainty. This is not a farmed animal raised in a controlled/defined environment with defined inputs. With these limitations, how can it be certified organic?

The labeling employed by Wisconsin-based salmon RAS company Superior Fresh.

With no organic label available, Superior Fresh recently worked to have its salmon products certified as "non-GMO", as it sources feel that is not genetically engineered.

Steve Etka, policy officer for the National Organic Coalition, raised a similar concern.

"Since organic is a processed verified label, it’s unclear how you would verify the production process for wild seafood," he said. "You can certainly verify the catch procedures and the processing, but how do you determine anything about the conditions under which the fish was born and grown? [The Organic Food Production Act] requires the use of organic feed for all organic livestock. If a fish is wild, how do you verify what they eat?"

"I am concerned about oversight on a product where the full life of the fish, what it ate, and what environment it had been exposed to, would not be known," said Harriet Behar, who identified herself as an organic farmer and advocate. "I have followed this issue for many years, and the organic price premium in the marketplace should be reserved for products where consumers are assured that all aspects of production and known and follow the foundational principles of organic.  I do not see a way that wild fish can meet this requirement."

Evelyn Drawec, an organic program consultant for the National Biosecurity Agency of Seychelles, a country in East Africa, raised similar points.

"Due to the nature of organic certification, the fact that fish live in a volume of water that accumulates runoff materials such as pesticides and chemicals from land activity, and that fish are mobile and not contained in this body of water, how would it be possible to enforce the principles of organic?" she asked.

title: US firm hit with fine for selling illegal oysters
content:
Louisiana, US-based seafood wholesaler Indian Ridge Seafood has been fined for illegally selling oysters. 

The New Orleans company earlier admitted in federal court to selling 14,346 sacks of oysters worth more than $650,000 to out-of-state buyers without reporting the transactions to the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries.

Louisiana seafood company failed to report sale of $650k worth of oysters

This was a violation of the Lacey Act, a law that bans trafficking in illegal wildlife, US district court Judge Susie Morgan ruled. She slapped Indian Ridge with a $10,000 fine for the transgression of "knowingly selling and transporting [illegal] oysters in interstate commerce with a market value in excess of $350.000".

The judge said Indian Ridge should have realized the oysters were bought and owned in violation of Louisiana state law, and failed to report it to the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries.

The company, which is owned by Walter Guidry, Jr., has held a seafood wholesaler and retail license in Louisiana's Terrebonne Parish since 2015.

title: Daily recap, March 5: Farmed salmon prices on rise; Pollock prices near record highs; Nova Austral legal issues go on
content:
Here's a recap of the daily seafood news from Friday, March 5:

Norway, Chile, Scots salmon prices remain on upward trend

Norwegian farmed salmon spot prices look set to remain above NOK 60 per kilogram this week -- week 10 of 2021 -- while Scottish and Chilean continue to trend upwards. Read the full story here.

Pollock fillet, surimi prices near record highs as pandemic hits production

Prices for US pin-bone out pollock fillet blocks and surimi are rising close to record levels as production in Alaska is being hampered by the coronavirus pandemic, sources told Undercurrent News.

Adding to the market uncertainty is a drop in Russian supply, as catching in the Sea of Okhotsk is hampered by small fish and poor weather. The logistical challenges caused by the coronavirus crackdowns in the Chinese processing hubs of Dalian and Qingdao are also disrupting production, sources said. Russian 'tramper' vessels cannot efficiently transport headed and gutted pollock from the fishing grounds to the Chinese ports, leaving suppliers needing to resort to less efficient alternatives. Read the full story, with plenty of data and infographics, here.

Legal issues lumber on for Nova Austral

The legal fallout from its 2019 misreporting scandal continues to affect Chilean salmon farmer Nova Austral, which also suffered a costly loss of smolt late last year. The company's CEO, Nicolas Larco, told investors on a recent earnings call that regulator Sernapesca had fined it $215,000, the statutory maximum, and also prohibited it from using a farming site for one production cycle. Read that in full here.

Superior Foods acquires Black Pearl trademarks after Martin shutdown

US Midwest distributor Superior Foods Company has acquired the Black Pearl Seafood trademarks and intellectual property after Martin International closed down the business at the end of last year due to the coronavirus pandemic. Superior, based in Grand Rapids, Michigan, confirmed the deal to Undercurrent on Friday. Read more here.

Harrison looks for UK shellfish role after short spell in smoked salmon

UK retail sales specialist Craig Harrison is looking for a new role and a return to the shellfish supply arena after a brief stint with smoked salmon, he said. Since 2009 he has spent time with several companies, including the former Young's Seafood operation Pinneys of Scotland. He then spent 10 years as sales and product development director with Norfolk-based The Big Prawn Co. Read this in full here.

Maine closed pen aquaculture developer lures marketer away from Hofseth

Finally, American Aquafarms, a Norwegian company looking to build an ocean-based closed pen Atlantic salmon aquaculture operation off the coast of the US state of Maine, has hired its new marketing director from the ranks of the Hofseth family of companies.

Teodor Strand-Johansen announced on his LinkedIn page recently that he has been serving since January as a partner and marketing director for American Aquafarms where he reports his new employer to be "establishing the future of eco-friendly aquaculture in coastal Maine". Read that in full here.

title: Legal issues lumber on for Nova Austral; Firm remains confident in new smolt
content:
The legal fallout from its 2019 misreporting scandal continues to affect Chilean salmon farmer Nova Austral, which also suffered a costly loss of smolt late last year.

The company's CEO, Nicolas Larco, told investors on a recent earnings call that regulator Sernapesca had fined it $215,000, the statutory maximum, and also prohibited it from using a farming site for one production cycle.

This stemmed from 2019 claims that Nova Austral, under the leadership of ousted CEO Nico Nicolaides, had underreported salmon mortalities in 2019 and allegedly adulterated the seabed to cover up anaerobic conditions.

Larco said there are some legal aspects stemming from the scandal that still need to be resolved.

"There are still some cases that haven’t moved at all and that remain the same as they were before. And we don't have any additional information on that," he said.

He struck a more positive tone regarding the planned restocking of several of the company's farm sites with salmon smolt. The company took a $3.8 million hit to its earnings in the fourth quarter of 2020 after losing 4.8m smolt during a series of mortalities in December.

"We’re not expecting these levels of mortality in the sites we are harvesting going forward," he said on March 3. "We have today, as we speak, two sites that have been stocked 100% with our own smolts. One of them was stocked nine months ago and so far we have a mortality rate of 4.4% so we are very happy with that performance"

The company said previously that the mortalities occurred in "four out of eight departments" due to "intoxication of water". Nova Austral had intended to stock those smolts for grow-out in the first six months of 2021, it said.

Additionally, the company stated in its Q4 release that it also had to contend with the detection of infectious salmon anemia (ISA) at farm sites belonging to a joint venture it runs with Salmones Austral.

Larco added, however, the company is once again receiving Navarino Law subsidy payments -- cash granted for operating in the remoteness of Tierra del Fuego at the southernmost tip of Patagonia. These had been suspended due to the misreporting scandal.

Nova Austral is owned by the equity funds Altor Fund III and Bain Capital, which are thought to be mulling their exit strategy from the farmer. The funds planned to maximize value from the company in part by negotiating with the Chilean government to relocate several farm sites presently located in the Alberto de Agostini National Park. This would improve efficiency and reduce criticism from environmental groups, sources previously told Undercurrent News. 

However, talks stalled in 2019 after the misreporting scandal emerged. 

They remain in early stages, Larco said.

"In the future, we will try to negotiate the relocation of those licenses but it’s still very early in the legal process to do something like this. We continue dealing with the legal procedures and afterward, there is the possibility we can move those licenses," the CEO said.
