title: Key Chilean region plans $280m in investments to grow salmon sector
content:
Chilean farmers active in Magallanes aim to further develop the salmon cluster in the southern region, following years of exponential growth.  

Magallanes saw its salmon output more than triple from 47,000 metric tons in 2015 to 175,000t in 2020, according to Carlos Odebret, the president of the Asociacion de Productores de Salmon y Trucha de Magallanes, said.

Carlos Odebret, president of the Chilean salmon producers' association in Magallanes. Credit: Asociacion de Productores de Salmon y Trucha de Magallanes

Now farmers' strategies will turn away from further increasing production as in previous years and focus instead on maintaining current efficiency, Odebret told Undercurrent News.

Those goals include keeping feed conversion ratios and fish mortalities low while maintaining strong output and good harvest weights.  

The executive said Magallanes, Chile's southernmost, largest, and second-least populated region, has significant competitive advantages with regard to fish health. Producers aim to develop the salmon cluster, maintaining those sanitary conditions "as much as possible", he explained.

Between 2020 and 2023, a total investment of $280 million is planned in the region.

Some of the largest investments aim to further process the fish locally, developing the region's processing capacity. By doing so, salmon farmers will be able to export value-added products directly from Magallanes with a shorter production cycle.

One example of this is Australis Seafoods' $70m investment in the Dumestre plant in the city of Puerto Natales. Additionally, Salmones Blumar and  Multiexport Foods invested a total of $50m investment in their joint processing plant in the region, which has been operating since last year.

To start operations there, the two firms were able to hire 300 people in the middle of the pandemic, an action that helped to offset the region's losses in tourism income.

A third processing capacity investment is Landes' environmental project in Punta Arenas, which will process salmon by-products to obtain fishmeal and fish oil.

Additionally, some freshwater hatchery projects are in the environmental review stage. Two of those, planned by firms Sealand and Bluriver, have already received permits.

However, a recent ruling by Chile's supreme court stated that the director of the country's environmental assessment service, must annul the permit granted to Sealand as the project must undergo further consultation with local indigenous communities.

Empresas AquaChile, Cermaq, and Nova Austral each operate hatcheries in the region. Additionally, some farmers rely on smolts transferred in from elsewhere in Chile.

Logistics improvement

Another area in which Magallanes' salmon producers are focusing is the development of the logistics in and out of the region, a key challenge for farmers. Odebret pointed out transport within the region and to the rest of the world has so far developed at a slower pace than salmon production. Investments in this field will allow lowering logistics costs in this region.

"Most of the actions that will be seen in Magallanes in the coming years will be aimed at strengthening the salmon cluster in the region and seek degrees of construction of closed circuits in the same region, seeking autonomy from other regions," he said.

He pointed out that Magallanes is located at the remote southern end of the world, far away from the traditional salmon farming and feed production hubs in Chile such as Los Lagos.

Therefore, investments in local ports are being made to increase connections with Los Lagos and other hubs. The development of processing plants will increase the need for logistics development within the region so wellboat suppliers will likely expand their presence in Magallanes, Odebret added.

Presently, salmon is shipped to different markets mainly by truck from Puerto Natales or Punta Arena via Argentina to the city of Ezeiza or directly to Brazil.

Odebret said farmers in the region are in talks with the local government to develop direct flights from Punta Arenas airport to the US. This would require an expansion of the airport but would significantly speed up exports. For 2021, however, truck transport will remain dominant, according to Odebret.

Credit: Magallanes Salmon Farmers Association

Future development

In 2016, the Chilean government closed off Magallanes to new aquaculture concession applications. This limits the applications under evaluation to the 140 submitted before the cut-off date, which could be added to the 140 already approved. According to Odebret, 40 concessions are likely to be approved, depending on their environmental assessments. This could occur within three and 10 years from their submission to the authorities.

"The space available is quite exhausted," Odebret said. He noted that the region had a production limit due to its delicate environmental balance, although more studies on the production capacity could be needed.

The region's fish mortalities remain below 5 to 10% levels.

"Sanitary conditions are very good so far. But salmon farming growth is limited to these new 40 concessions," he said.

He added it was not known when concessions would be approved and that some relocations of Nova Austral and other projects had been approved in 2020.

Odebret, who is originally from southern Chile and has been in the local salmon industry for 15 years, was named president of the Magallanes' salmon producers association in 2019. 

Credit: Magallanes Salmon Farmers Association

Sanitary conditions

The executive pointed out that progress on issues such as smolt transport as regulations have worked to reduce infections. New sanitary programs require vaccination of bacterial kidney disease, infectious salmon anemia, and other diseases to protect the heritage of the region from a fish health point of view, he explained.

Farmers are implementing sustainability strategies for the different areas and trying to minimize the use of antibiotics while achieving sustainability seals of approval such as Aquaculture Stewardship Council certification. 

Odebret stressed Magallanes' pristine waters have a significant competitive advantage over other regions from a fish health point of view. Still, an emerging problem has been detected with sea lice, which is mainly concentrated in production areas with higher salinity, according to Odebret.

The Magallanes region defined its salmon production zones in 2012, much later than the rest of the country. This has allowed keeping production areas apart from each other. In most zones, there are no more than two companies operating, according to Odebret.

But he admitted that sea lice was an emerging problem and has to be taken care of. Coordination is essential to achieve this and the fact that fewer actors operate in isolated areas in Magallanes helps, according to Odebret.

The executive pointed out sustainability and conservation of the region were of fundamental importance for the development of the aquaculture industry. He also said maintaining good relationships with indigenous communities was also an objective for the association. 

Referencing the Nova Austral scandal, Odebret said the company had admitted its error and that authorities had sanctioned with the highest fine applied for situations of this type. 

Covid impact

As in other countries or regions, the coronavirus crisis restricted the ability to travel within the region, which forced producers to make relevant adjustments in terms of operation, movement, and care of people, Odebret said.

Out of about 3,500 that work in the salmon sector in Magallanes, about 500 travel via charter planes from other regions.

Salmon farming in Chile was named an essential sector and the activity was allowed with certain sanitary protocols, including preventive examinations and COVID-19 tests every time someone enters the region. This led to some delays in the harvest, which caused fish to grow larger than planned, Odebret said. Additionally, delays and restrictions complicated logistical and productive processes.

Another consequence of the pandemic was the drop in foodservice sales, which accounted for about 40-60% of Chilean sales. This, combined with a rise in Chilean production planned before the pandemic, caused a collapse of US salmon prices last year, a trend that has reversed this year.

Odebret forecasts salmon consumption will increase because those who ate in restaurants during the pandemic "found out how simple it is to cook salmon at home".

title: ISSF: 16 tuna stocks don’t meet MSC criteria
content:
A new report commissioned by the International Seafood Sustainability Foundation (ISSF) found that 16 tuna stocks are currently unable to pass the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC)'s sustainability criteria.

Uncontrolled catching puts several tuna fisheries at risk of losing certifications

Criteria analyzed in the evaluation included MSC principle one (sustainable fish stocks), poor stock status, the lack of well-defined harvest control rules (HCRs), and/or the lack of effective tools to control the harvest. A stock would pass if its overall score was 80 or above, and no single score is less than 60.

This comes after two other NGOs warned last year that the lack of well-defined HCRs or effective tools to control catches put several tuna fisheries at risk of losing their sustainability certifications.

Failing scores

Failures were due to the poor status of the stock, the lack of well-defined HCRs in place, and/or the lack of effective tools to control the harvest, ISSF pointed out. Three of the 23 stocks have fully implemented well-defined HCRs, and the report identified some progress towards this aim by all regional fisheries management organizations. ISSF, however, pointed to slow progress -- exacerbated in some cases by the COVID-19 pandemic -- and failure to implement controls before rebuilding is required has led to stocks failing to meet minimum requirements.

Fisheries that received principle-level failing scores included in the Atlantic Ocean including yellowfin, bigeye, western skipjack, eastern skipjack, western bluefin, and Mediterranean albacore. In the Pacific, six stocks received overall principle-level failing scores: western yellowfin, western bigeye, eastern bigeye, eastern skipjack, northern albacore, and Pacific bluefin. In the Indian Ocean, yellowfin, bigeye, and albacore all received overall principle-level failing scores. Southern bluefin tuna also received an overall P1 failing score.

The evaluation found that seven out of 23 major commercial tuna stocks worldwide are "successfully" avoiding overfishing when measured against the MSC fisheries standard and maintaining target stock biomass levels. These include the north Atlantic albacore, south Atlantic albacore, eastern Atlantic bluefin, western Pacific skipjack, eastern Pacific yellowfin, south Pacific albacore and Indian Ocean skipjack.

These seven stocks earned a passing score -- two of them without conditions -- for the MSC fisheries standard on its P1. Most fisheries also scored well under principle three, effective management, ISSF said. 

In the March 2020 edition of the report, four stocks passed P1, indicating a slight improvement explained by the new stock assessments conducted in 2020, as well as good scores by one of the bluefin stocks newly incorporated in this version, ISSF noted. Principle three evaluations remained unchanged for the most part, it said.

title: Argentina’s southern king crab fishery undergoing MSC review
content:
Organización Internacional Agropecuaria (OIA) this week announced that its draft assessment of Argentina's southern king crab (Lithodes santolla) fishery has been made available for review, taking it one step closer to certification by the Marine Stewardship Council.

The fishery, which includes the Central Patagonian stock, is located in the Argentine Sea, a body of water extending from Montevideo, Uruguay, southward to Tierra del Fuego, and about 500 miles north of Antarctica. The assessment was requested by Argentinian fishing companies Centomar, Bentonicos de Argentina and Crustaceos del Sur, according to OIA.

The draft assessment identifies as a strength how the target stock has been subject to a "permanent and comprehensive monitoring ... generating a great deal of information as biological and fishery features". The fishing gear (a conical trap) has been improved and demonstrated "an adequate selectivity and efficiency".

As for weaknesses, the assessment identified a "lack of an explicit and well-defined harvest control rule, which states actions that will be taken in response to change in the biomass of stock and the non-establishment of a limit reference point".

A virtual site visit has been scheduled for April 26-30, as physical meetings have been restricted by the Argentinian government due to concerns about the COVID-19 outbreak.

title: Chilean Salmon Council firms certify COVID-safe operations in processing plants
content:
The companies in the Chilean Salmon Council -- Empresas AquaChile, Cermaq, Mowi and Salmones Aysen -- now have approval from the Chilean Security Association, ACHS, which supports the management plan for the prevention of COVID-19 infections in the country, reports Mundo Acuicola. 

The ACHS seal also certifies that all the protocols established by the Chilean health authority are met, and the best practices and international recommendations are correctly applied to deal with the pandemic.

"Our main goal is to protect the health of our workers by complying with strict protocols to protect them and maintaining safe operations," says the executive director of the Salmon Council, Joanna Davidovich. "The ACHS seal allows, through an expert third party, to guarantee and reassure everyone that their operations comply with the highest standards defined by the authority and experts in complete safety."

Agrosuper's Empresas AquaChile certified its seven processing plants in Cardonal, Calbuco, Quellón, Cailín, Chonchi, Ancud and Magallanes in January this year, as Cermaq also did in its Chinquihue and Quemchi plants.

Additionally, salmon farming giant Mowi also certified its plants in Chacabuco and Cabulco in late January and early February, respectively. Meanwhile, coho salmon farmer Salmones Aysen certified its two plants in Puerto Montt, Salmones Aysén and Sea Flavors, on Feb. 12.

title: Untitled
content:
The news her firm could no longer send farmed mussels to the EU came as a shock to Nicki Holmyard, co-founder of Offshore Shellfish, a firm based in Brixham on the southwest coast of England.

The business-owner, who founded Offshore Shellfish with husband John, had just managed to get the firm's second load of the year shipped out to its customer in the Netherlands, albeit with the added frustration and cost of new post-Brexit paperwork and delays.

"We were feeling quite good about ourselves," Holmyard told Undercurrent News. Then the next day she received a call from the Shellfish Association of Great Britain (SAGB).

Offshore Shellfish vessel. Credit: Offshore Shellfish

They told her that what her firm was doing was illegal and it would have to stop, relaying a message from the European Commission. It confirmed what everyone in the industry had feared since the EU referendum vote; that as a third country, the UK would no longer be able to export certain types of live bivalves, such as mussels, to the EU. 

"We’ve effectively shut down," said Holmyard, whose firm employs more than 15 people.

The ban on exports of certain live bivalves has sent shockwaves through the UK shellfish industry, which counts the EU as the biggest market for mussels, cockles, oysters and scallops, both farmed and wild-caught. While organizations such as the SAGB say they warned the UK government that EU rules on imports of live bivalves from third countries could lead to a ban, the UK government had assured them otherwise.

Last week, amid accusations of government incompetence, opposition MPs called for the resignation of UK environment minister George Eustice. For his part, Eustice said his department was only relaying what the EU had said themselves.

On Feb. 8, Eustice wrote a letter to the EU Commissioner for Health and Food Safety, Stella Kyriakides, calling for the ban to be lifted. During a parliamentary session, he added that he believed the UK’s interpretation of EU law is correct. 

UK shellfish exporters mull registering EU firms to reduce Brexit paperwork

For Holmyard, the blame game does nothing to resolve the fact her firm’s mussels lie six meters below the waterline rather than on dinner plates on the Continent. "There’s talk of a legal challenge. But we need this resolved now," she said.

With the UK now outside of the EU, Offshore's mussels must be depurated before entering the vital European market. But because the UK lacks its own suitable depuration facilities, the firm is unable to do so, meaning it has shipped no mussels to the EU since the second week of January, when normally it would ship 80-100 metric tons a week.

The ban affects the firm's sales during six months of the year when her firm’s mussels are harvested from waters defined as "class B", requiring depuration. Only mussels produced in "class A" waters can be consumed directly. According to Holmyard, 70% of her firm's sales are during the period under the ban.

According to Sarah Horsfall, SAGB assistant director, the ruling affects both producers of wild-caught and farmed mollusks. However, mollusk farmers in England and Wales stand to lose most because of the predominance of class B waters. "That’s slightly different from Scotland. They do have quite a lot of class A areas and so are much more fortunate," said Horsfall.

UK public body Seafish estimates that the UK's export of live bivalve mollusks to the EU was worth around £15 million in 2019, or 12,000t by volume. According to information from UK's Centre for Environment Fisheries and Aquaculture Science and EUROSTAT, the weight of sea mussels production by UK aquaculture sector in 2018 was 14,200t, valued at around £16m.

"I'm extremely angry," said Holmyard. "We'd asked the UK government to negotiate so this trade could continue. We'd been shouting at the government for 18 months, two years about this. They kept saying, ‘no, it'll be alright, no, it'll be alright’. But the [European] Commission’s point is very clear."

"The industry feels badly done by," said the SAGB executive. "And absolutely yes, there have been calls for the government to rectify the situation and to compensate the industry because they've had absolutely no time to prepare at all."

Tending a lost crop?

Companies like Offshore Shellfish now face having to tend a crop of mussels that they may not be able to sell.

Like their terrestrial counterparts, aquaculture farmers must contend with changing seasons and lifecycles of living organisms that do not bend to the will of their human cultivators.

It means that although Offshore Shellfish can begin to sell to Europe again from around the beginning of April, when its waters are reclassified as class A, that is the start of the spawning season. "By the time you get to the other end [in Europe], they’ve all spawned and lost all their meat," said Holmyard. 

Offshore Shellfish mussels. Source: Offshore Shellfish

Then, during the summer months, Offshore Shellfish would normally begin re-tubing, a process that involves seeding tubes with mussel spat for the following year’s harvest. Re-tubing also helps redistribute mussels on ropes to avoid spat growing in large clumps.

The heavy work of lifting ropes with mussels from thousands of meters of lines is carried out by Offshore Shellfish’s vessel and crew. "We do this during summer months because we are constrained by weather in terms of days that we can get access," said Holmyard, leaving it just one month of normal harvesting and sales. In some years summer algal blooms mean the company also has to halt harvesting during this period.

She said building a depurator in the UK would not necessarily solve her company’s problems.

When the firm had previously investigated the idea, it found the local harbor had limited space and water of the right quality. Moreover, when mussels are placed into tanks for depuration, which can take a minimum of 42 hours, they begin to cling onto the tank, and so require grading again.

"You have to grade them to get them out of the tanks. Then when they go to Holland, they would go through that process again," which leads to higher costs and mortalities.

Nicki Holmyard, of UK-based Offshore Shellfish, accepts the Animal Welfare award on behalf of M&S.
Credit: Phil Wilkinson

She added to depurate the volume of mussels her firm harvests and sells each week would require a facility with some 20 metric tons of holding capacity. "It would cost several million. You can’t do that overnight."

Benefits of depurating on the Continent also include being able to hold the stock in tanks close to markets, said Horsfall. "They can keep it live for quite some time if they want to, and then distribute it as required. They have the infrastructure there because that’s where the market is."

She said although her organization has run numerous campaigns over the years to try to grow UK sales of mussels, they’ve largely failed to make inroads. "Compared with the amount that people consume it on the Continent, it's really very low. So it’s a really difficult one."

Holmyard said she finds it hard to fathom what the company will do without a resumption in trade. The firm’s farms are installed in seas owned by the UK’s Crown Estate, and it would take several years to remove the gear.

Before the current crisis, the company was mulling expanding its farming production capacity from 2,500t a year to 10,000t a year in an investment worth "millions".

"We’ve got 15 people’s jobs on the line here. We’ve got our life’s work on the line. This is all the stupid game of brinkmanship and we are the little guys in the middle. It's been so badly handled," she said.

title: Fish Factor: USCG mask rules; Fish board meetings; GE salmon debut nears
content:
Undercurrent News is now featuring 'Fish Factor', a weekly column featuring the reporting and perspective of Alaska seafood journalist Laine Welch

Fishermen must wear masks while they are underway, even while sleeping, and the US Coast Guard (USCG) intends to enforce it.

That’s an edict issued as a public health emergency by the Center for Disease Control (CDC) in a Marine Safety Bulletin issued on Feb. 1. It requires the wearing of masks at all times in US waters on all commercial vessels "when boarding, disembarking, and for the duration of travel" to prevent the spread of the COVID-19 virus.

The action states that "conveyance operators traveling into or within the US may transport only persons wearing masks and must use best efforts to ensure that masks are worn".

Best efforts include allowing entry to a vessel only to those who wear masks, instructing persons that failure to comply constitutes a violation of federal law, and removing any person who refuses to comply.

Exemptions apply to children under two years, a person with a disability who can not safely wear a mask or a person for whom wearing a mask would create a risk to workplace health, safety or job duty, or if an operator is "the sole occupant of the vehicle".

Exceptions to the rule apply while eating or drinking, or communicating with a hearing-impaired person or if a person is unconscious.

National Fisherman editor Jessica Hathaway was the first to break the news on Feb 11, and said she was advised by the Coast Guard that fishing vessels are included under the rule "at this time".

When she requested further guidance, Hathaway was directed to the CDC.

"Enforcing this rule would certainly be difficult," Hathaway wrote. "However, it clearly opens the door for being boarded and fined. The Coast Guard has clarified that the rule will be enforced."

The mask requirement will remain in effect "unless modified or rescinded based on specific public health or other considerations, or until the Secretary of Health and Human Services rescinds the determination".

Fishermen and others can submit comments and questions via email at wearamask@uscg.mil/

Fish Board bumps

The state Board of Fisheries will meet online on March 8 to decide when, where and how to fit in a double slate of meetings upended by the COVID-19 pandemic that spans from Southeast Alaska to the Arctic.

The board would normally be wrapping up a roster of 275 proposals for Southeast, Prince William Sound and statewide shellfish next month. But those regions are likely to be bumped to next winter or mixed in with already scheduled meetings for other regions this fall.

"We currently have the work session in October and then that's followed immediately by a Pacific cod meeting, which is for the Alaska Peninsula, Aleutian Islands, Bering Sea and Chignik. So those are currently slated for this coming October," said Glenn Haight, the board's executive director. "And Bristol Bay will happen in December. It's possible you could put in a Prince William Sound or Southeast meeting in November, and then continue on into January with some of the other ones. It's just a matter of putting things in the right places so people have a chance to react to them and we have time to do all the factors that go into it."

The call for fishery proposals for Bristol Bay, the Alaska Peninsula, Chignik, the Arctic, Yukon, Kuskokwim and Bering Sea regions has been extended from April 10 to May 10. 

"The board did not reopen the call for proposals for Southeast, Yakutat, Prince William Sound and shellfish statewide." Haight said. "So what we currently have for proposals is what the board will take up next year. There was a note though, that if there are some conservation issues or if there are other kinds of pressing matters, people from those regions can submit an agenda change request by Aug. 23 and the board will review those requests at their October work session."

Public comments for the special March 8 meeting are accepted through March 2.

Meanwhile, four of the seven board members, only one who hails from a coastal community, have yet to be confirmed by the Alaska legislature even as they are making decisions.

Genetically modified salmon arrives

It’s taken nearly three decades but genetically tweaked salmon is set to hit supermarket shelves in a month or two.

The fish, derided by some as  "Frankenfish", is the first animal to get approval from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). It is manmade from an Atlantic salmon with genes spliced from Chinook and an eel-like ocean pout. The faster-growing fish can go from egg to 11 pounds in 18 months, 10 months faster than normal salmon.

Once the market normalizes after the COVID-19 pandemic, Massachusetts-based AquaBounty Technologies plans to produce nearly 3 million pounds annually at its recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) facility in Indiana, the company told Undercurrent News.  Another land-based farm is planned in the US and a smaller farm at Prince Edward Island in Canada already is selling the genetically modified salmon there. 

Pushback to the manmade fish has been fierce, even before it was approved by the FDA in 2015, and it has steadily increased. 

Recently, major foodservice supplier Aramark said it will boycott the fish, joining the ranks of Compass Group and Sodexo. Also, more than 80 retailers have said they won’t sell the salmon, including Costco, Walmart, Target, Albertsons, Kroger and Whole Foods Market.

The US green light on genetically engineered salmon has opened the door for other creatures. At least 35 other species of fish— as well as chickens, pigs and cows engineered to fit in factory farming systems — are currently under development.  

Meanwhile, Undercurrent reported that AquaBounty announced last week it has raised over $127m in a public offering of stock that included 14,950,000 shares at a price to the public of $8.50 per share.

Fish info for all

One unexpected plus to the pandemic is how it has brought fishing industry information, workshops and training to far more people through web-based events, no matter where they are located.

Two are in the upcoming pipeline:  Up first is the annual Fishermen’s Expo on Monday, Feb. 22 hosted by the Alaska Longline Fishermen’s Association (ALFA) in Sitka.

"We're going to focus more on loan programs for folks that are interested in getting involved in fishing. We have a speaker from the Commercial Fishing and Agriculture Bank that provides financing for fishermen, and we’ll also have a loan officer from the Department of Commerce, Community, and Economic Development to talk about some of the loan programs that they have for commercial fishermen," said Natalie Sattler, ALFA's communications director.

Emergency skills will be featured by the Alaska Marine Safety Education Association along with ALFA’s crew apprentice program. Also, updates on years of local ocean floor mapping, called bathymetry, that helps fishermen target catches better and avoid harmful fishing practices.

Go to www.alfafish.org to register for expo links and updates.

Then, on March 4 and 5, a who’s who of big names is in the lineup for the Southwest Alaska Municipal Conference (SWAMC).

It will feature mariculture, regional broadband, fish forecasts, marketing updates, legislative leaders and commissioners, Senator Lisa Murkowski, Covid relief programs, community roundtables and much more. Find links to register for the SWAMC Summit at www.swamc.org/

Topics at both virtual events will appeal to anyone interested in Alaska’s seafood industry as well as those far removed from fishing.

title: Report claims ‘hidden cost’ of salmon farming reaches $50bn since 2013
content:
The "short-term pursuit of profits" by salmon producers is creating significant unaccounted environmental and social costs, which include growing mortality rates, damage to local ecosystems, pressure on wild fish stocks and poor fish welfare, claims a new report by Just Economics.

Its analysis into the negative impacts of salmon farming puts the cumulative costs to economies, society and the environment since 2013 at almost $50 billion. More than half of these costs are falling to producers ($28bn), with the rest ($19bn) being "passed on to society" in the top four salmon-producing countries of Norway, Scotland, Canada and Chile, it said.

The "Dead Loss" report was commissioned by The Changing Markets Foundation, which previously attacked the use of marine ingredients in salmon feed.

"Salmon farming is a prime example of a broken food system: every year, it hoovers up millions of [metric] tons of wild-caught fish for feed, mortality rates on farms are soaring, and pollution is harming pristine ecosystems and wild salmon," said Natasha Hurley, campaigns manager with Changing Markets. 

"This analysis shows that disregard for good fish husbandry is not just bad for the environment and fish welfare, it’s also a business risk: companies are squandering money and resources and if they carry on like this, the industry won’t be able to sustain itself in the long-term. Sooner or later it will hit environmental limits and a refusal by tax-payers to keep footing the bill for pollution and other losses."

Pre-harvest mortalities account for the highest proportion of the costs -- $15.5bn -- to the four countries’ economies, the report found.

Of the four countries, only Scotland and Norway publicly release mortalities data. In Scotland, deaths have increased two-fold since 2013, from 10,329 metric tons in 2013 to 25,772t in 2019. This represented 6% of harvests in 2013, and 13.5% in 2019.

The report claimed Mowi -- the world’s largest farmed salmon producer -- accounted for half of overall mortalities from the top ten companies over the period. The report finds that unexplained and unexpected deaths at all of Mowi’s farms worldwide, over the period 2010-2019, totaled approximately 50m salmon (252,521t) with a cost of $1.7bn.

Mowi told Undercurrent News that, looking into the report, Changing Markets did conclude that "when considering the full range of benefits and impacts, the business of salmon farming demonstrates overall positive benefit" -- something Mowi, of course, agreed with.

"This conclusion echoes other third-party reports, such as the Coller FAIRR Protein Producer Index (the world’s only comprehensive assessment of the largest animal protein producers on critical environmental, social and governance issues), which ranks Mowi as the world’s most sustainable animal protein producer," the company said.

It also agreed with Changing Markets that there are opportunities for continued improvements for the salmon farming business. "Our commitment to continual sustainability improvements is not just words, it is detailed and actioned through our Blue Revolution Plan."

"This said, we do not agree with Changing Markets’ core agenda of shifting consumption of sustainably-caught fish meal which includes small pelagic fish such as sardine and anchovy. The inclusion of small amounts of fishmeal and oil in our salmon’s diet is certified sustainable by third parties and integral to a salmon’s health and welfare. The consumption of pelagic fish by humans and fish is the most responsible use of a global commodity, and shifting this market to less efficient uses does nothing to improve sustainability."

The report claimed the environmental cost of "unsustainable farming" over the same period is estimated at $14.5bn, "through the pollution of seas and freshwater lakes, damage to wild salmon stocks and biodiversity, and the generation of CO2 emissions".

It added that "transparency and accountability in salmon farming are extremely weak and that legislation is needed for the industry to meet higher standards".  

A spokesperson for the Scottish Salmon Producers Organisation said: "Farmed salmon has a great environmental story to tell -- it has the lowest carbon footprint of any main livestock protein, it is a nutritious and healthy food and, as the United Nations and other international experts have acknowledged, aquaculture provides one of the best solutions to feeding the world's burgeoning population in the years to come. It is a shame that the authors have chosen to ignore these undeniable benefits when publicizing this report."

And Grieg Seafood told Undercurrent the Changing Markets report "appears to be advocacy masquerading as analysis", and that some areas of it needed clarification and correction. 

Still, it confirmed the company is intent on reducing its impact on nature, improving fish health and welfare, developing new feed ingredients -- both marine and protein-based -- reducing carbon emissions, and recycling more resources.

"The report rightly states that long-term economic profitability goes hand-in-hand with reduced impact and better fish welfare," it said. "Grieg Seafood has a long-term, systematic and preventative approach to solving our sustainability challenges."

It pointed to large investments in reducing the time salmon spends in the sea, as well as digitalization, machine learning and artificial intelligence.

"We have set science-based targets to achieve net zero carbon emissions by 2050, in line with the Paris agreement, and we aim to certify all farms according to the strict sustainability standard Aquaculture Stewardship Council by 2023."

title: Zoneco returns to black as more investors file fraud claims
content:
Chinese seafood company Zoneco Group expects full-year profits of CNY 10 million to CNY 15m ($1.5m-2.3m) for 2020, but the firm's financial situation is uncertain as investors filed claims to the court for fraud.

Zoneco suffered CNY 100m-150m in losses after deducting non-recurring gains and losses but turned the small profit after it transferred rights to use sea areas and sold equity in subsidiaries. It also received government subsidies. 

Based in Zhangzidao in Dalian province, Zoneco harvests scallops farmed in Bohai Sea, and is also a seafood importer and processor. The firm said market prices of inward processing export products fell during the pandemic year causing it to build up some raw material inventories.

Zoneco chairman resigns over ‘running scallops’ saga

Zoneco also faces multiple lawsuits from investors. According to the company's filing to Shenzhen Stock Exchange on Jan. 30, the Dalian Intermediate People's Court has notified Zoneco of 69 plaintiffs suing the company for fraud, with claims totaling CNY 13.3m ($2.1m).

Zoneco said the cases have not been heard and its impact on the company's profits is uncertain.

This has been the fourth time that Zoneco revealed such notices since last November. On Nov. 21, Dec. 2 and Dec. 19, the firm announced it was accused of fraud by 44 other investors claiming CNY 41m ($6.3m) in total.

Under the court ruling three of the company's bank accounts in China with more than CNY 36m in deposits were frozen, Zoneco reported on Dec. 29. The firm stated only 7% of its funds were frozen, which does not significantly impact its operations. 

Zoneco, which until 2017 was China’s largest market-listed seafood company by sales, is known for its "running scallops" fiasco.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) later used historical satellite tracking data to expose Zoneco's financial fraud by showing log data of its vessels' seeding and harvesting activities had been "plucked from thin air.".

Last June, the CSRC fined Zoneco for CNY 600,000 over the long-running saga involving missing scallops. The case was then transferred to the Chinese Public Security Bureau for further criminal investigations, with Zoneco's major shareholders prohibited from selling their shares in the firm.

title: Sanford risks losing $14m vessel after fishing in protected zone
content:
New Zealand’s largest fishing company Sanford could lose a NZD 20 million ($14.4m) vessel after it was found trawling in a protected fishing area off the country’s southern island, reports Stuff.

Sanford, which has pleaded guilty to the charges, said the incident was "utterly unintentional".

Skipper Grant Clifford Walker, 50, and first mate William Dessiou Lash, 45, also face fines of up to NZD 100,000. The firm could also be fined NZD 100,000.

Sanford's San Waitaki was caught in the protected habitat, called a benthic protected area (BPA), fishing for orange roughy on Nov 5, 2018.

Data showed the vessel -- a deep-water stern trawler with processing factory and freezer facilities onboard -- trawled the seabed in the protection area numerous times.

Fish taken by the vessel in 2018 were seized and sold, with the proceeds of NZD 150,720 being held by the New Zealand government. In addition, the company could be ordered to forfeit the San Waitaki, valued at NZD 20m, also to the government.

"Frankly, we feel embarrassed and disappointed with ourselves about what happened," said the firm. "We have, for a long time, been one of the New Zealand fishing companies supporting BPAs and helped to bring them into existence. To then accidentally miss one and unintentionally fish inside it is unacceptable to us and we are very sorry," it said.

title: EU cod fleet fishing halted amid confusion over Svalbard, Norway quotas
content:
The EU cod fleet is experiencing great uncertainty at the start of 2021 due to Norway's unilateral decision to cut the European quota in Svalbard. 

In addition, a quota transfer to the UK in the Brexit deal for this specific area is adding to the uncertainty, sources told Undercurrent News. 

All this adds to the sector's concern that neither Norway nor the EU has yet expressed their intention to reach a bilateral agreement; one which is in great demand since it could clarify the situation of a sector whose operations depend entirely upon it.

"The EU cod fleet is currently at a standstill. We still don't have access to Norwegian waters, since the Nordic country already stated its position and will not negotiate anything bilaterally until a trilateral agreement with the EU and the UK is reached," Ivan Lopez, spokesperson for the European Fisheries Alliance (EUFA) -- a coalition of EU fishing fleets that fights for continued access to British waters after Brexit -- explained to Undercurrent.

The trilateral consultations between the EU, Norway and the UK, which commenced on Jan. 12, are still ongoing, according to Norway's government.

Furthermore, on Feb. 2, an important meeting of the EU Agriculture and Fisheries Council, or AGRIFISH, will occur in Brussels, where the European Commission (EC) is expected to confront Norway and demand a prompt response from the Nordic country to all these issues, said Lopez, who is also director-general of fishing company Pesquera Ancora. 

"We believe that there should already be a plan drawn up for 2021 in these areas, and here we are still waiting for it," he added. "However, perhaps most worrying -- more worrying even than all of this -- is that Norway seems to be acting in bad faith as the country is perfectly aware that delaying our access to their waters will do us a great deal of harm."

Norway claims access and quota exchanges have to be negotiated separately in bilateral consultations with the UK and the EU; talks which have not yet concluded with either the EU or the UK for North Sea stocks, according to Halvard Wensel, communication advisor to the Norwegian ministry of trade, industry and fisheries. 

"In accordance with traditional practice, reciprocal access to fish in each other's waters will only be granted on the basis of an agreement. Norway has not yet concluded bilateral agreements with neither the EU nor the UK for North Sea stocks," Wensel told Undercurrent. 

"Norway and the EU did, however, agree to a limited access agreement for the month of January only, allowing a few vessels from the EU and Norway to fish in Skagerrak. Access is only permitted for vessels that have previously been active in this particular area in the same period in 2020."

However, on Dec 22, Norway's minister of fisheries -- Odd Emil Ingebrigtsen -- reduced the EU's quota off the archipelago of Svalbard by more than 17,000 metric tons. This came as a surprise since Norway had already decided to set aside 34,864t of cod for the EU from this zone, as announced in the Norwegian-Russian Fisheries Commission that took place in October.

This meant a quota reduction of around 37% compared to what Norway had agreed with Russia a few months earlier, EUFA's Lopez told Undercurrent.

Therefore, the EU will be given a cod quota of only 17,885t in Svalbard's waters for 2021, while the UK had been given its own quota of 5,500t. "This bewildered us as we don't believe there is an explanation behind such a cut taking place now," he said. 

"Also, we have seen in Brexit's agreement annex 2E [see image below] that the EU has given 25% of the quota to the UK in this area too when it historically has always had between 11% and 13% only," Lopez said.

"Why did the EU do that? It is not their competence, but Norway's, which has not spoken out on the matter. Apart from that, nobody in the sector understands the legal criteria by which this has been reached either." 

Norway, for its part, declined to comment on this as Wensel claimed this is an issue that has to be addressed by the EC or the UK government. 

According to the EC, the UK and EU fishing shares for cod in Svalbard reflected in Brexit's agreement are based on recent track records for between 2012 and 2016.

"Consequently, and in line with the negotiation directives, the relevant fisheries activities by the concerned EU member states have been upheld," an EC spokesperson told Undercurrent. 

"The available EU fishing quota will be distributed amongst the member states on the basis of the existing allocation keys, that is, the percentage proportions for each member state, defined under the common fisheries policy (CFP)," she said. 

From the trade and cooperation agreement between the EU and the UK, page 897

Svalbard has the world's northernmost international waters, sovereignty over which was granted to Norway via the Svalbard Treaty, signed in 1920 in Paris, France. Half a century later, in 1977, a fisheries protection zone around Svalbard was introduced when Norway extended its exclusive economic zone to 200 nautical miles.

"The EU has established fishing opportunities for Arctic cod in international waters for 2021 in line with this long-established procedure. Norway has so far never disputed the establishment of the autonomous TAC [total allowable catch] by the EU," the EC's spokesperson said. 

"We regret the decision taken by Norway to break with this well-established approach by unilaterally fixing fishing opportunities for the European Union that are substantially lower than what the EU should have," she said. "The Commission is currently analyzing the decision by Norway and appropriate measures to counter it."

According to Lopez, the treaty makes Norway the only country with the right to regulate the exploitation of mineral and natural resources in the archipelago and its territorial waters.

"However, all the signatory countries of this treaty must be treated as an equal. There can be no country with a most-favored-nation status. Not even Norway, which seems to be the case now, with the country making no-sense decisions unilaterally," he added.

Acceptance by the EU of fishery regulations set by Norway in the waters around Svalbard is therefore conditional on the regulations being applied in a non-discriminatory manner, based on scientific advice and respected by all interested parties.

Norway unilaterally accords a quota for third parties in the fishery protection zone (FPZ), an activity that dates back to the establishment of the zone in 1977, Wensel told Undercurrent. 

"Based on the actual fishing activities undertaken by third parties that had habitually fished in the FPZ-area prior to the establishment of the zone, Norway unilaterally accorded a quota to such third parties. As a result, the EU was accorded a quota, which allowed for the continuation of the ongoing fishing activities from before the establishment of the FPZ by union vessels," Wensel said. 

After the UK's withdrawal from the EU and subsequently the EU's CFP, the UK is no longer part of EU fishing activities, he said. "The EU will therefore no longer benefit from fishing activities carried out by UK-flagged vessels prior to the establishment of the FPZ when Norway determines third party quotas for the zone."

Cut in provisional TACs for 2021 also

According to the provisional TACs published by the EU Council for 2021, the EU's provisional TAC for cod fishing in Svalbard (zones 1 and 2b) in 2021 is 6,004t, down 75% year-on-year from 24,009t in 2020, as the image below shows. 

"In 2020, the EU could fish around 6,000t in the NAFO area, over 20,000t in Svalbard's EEZ, and a total of around 27,000t in Norway," Ivan Lopez also told Undercurrent. "Currently, we [the EU cod fleet] can only count with those 6,004t since, as I said before, we still cannot fish in Norwegian waters."

On Jan. 26, UK Fisheries, the distant water fishing venture jointly owned by Parlevliet & Van der Plas (P&P) and Iceland's Samherji, said it expected its £35 million lead trawler Kirkella at last to fish in the waters of Svalbard.

P&P, Samherji’s UK venture’s flagship trawler finally sets off for Svalbard

"Does that mean the danger to distant waters fishing is over? Not at all, unfortunately. This trip is a sticking plaster," Trevor Datson, a press officer for the firm, wrote in a statement. "Yes, we have a license for it, but this isn't enough to keep distant waters fishing afloat. It's about 10% of what we would have been allowed to fish under the pre-Brexit regime. Right now we are 90% worse off than we were at this time last year." 

The vessel can only do a single trip on the quota it has been given, which is less than a tenth of what it would normally have to fish for a whole year, Undercurrent also reported. 

P&P and Samherji's UK Fisheries owns Pesquera Ancora, which Lopez runs. According to Lopez, it also seems like the EU thought that Norway could recognize the TACs for the previous year for the first quarter of 2021 while negotiations between them were taking place.

"However, Norway does not, so the provisional TAC in Norwegian waters that appears in the document does not even exist in practice," he said.

“Furthermore, we also do not know what percentage of the supposed 6,004t that we can fish in Svalbard waters corresponds to each EU country, something that we should know by now as well [see the second image below]", he added. "So, in practice, all our boats are still moored in port. Devastating."

In response to this, Wensel told Undercurrent that while the EU has decided to set preliminary TACs for the first quarter of this year on the basis of TACs agreed for 2020, Norway has, in the absence of fisheries agreements for 2021, set preliminary TACs on the basis of scientific advice from the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea for 2021.

Credit: EU Council

2020's cod TAC in Svalbard waters was 27,295t, of which 5,038t corresponded to Germany, 11,687t to Spain, 2,255t to France, 2,244 to Poland, 2,418t to Portugal, 3,286t to the UK, and 366t to other member states. Credit: Spanish version of the EU's Official Journal

title: Former StarKist SVP Hodge given probation, not prison for tuna price-fixing
content:
Stephen Hodge, a former senior vice president of sales at StarKist & Co, will not serve prison time for his participation in a conspiracy to fix US canned tuna prices, a judge ruled.

Instead, Hodge, San Francisco, California-based federal judge Edward Chen has ruled, will serve three years probation, six months home confinement with a curfew, perform 120 hours of community service and pay a $25,000 fine. That falls in line with what federal prosecutors had asked for given Hodge's "cooperation and substantial assistance to the government" in the prosecution of former Bumble Bee Seafoods CEO Christopher Lischewski, according to prosecutors' sentencing memorandum for Hodge.

In 2017, Hodge pleaded guilty to a charge of conspiring to fix the prices of shelf-stable seafood, the first non-Bumble Bee executive to do so, the US Department of Justice (DOJ) said.

Hodge is a former senior vice president of sales with Starkist, which is ultimately owned by South Korean group Dongwon Enterprise. He was charged with one count of price-fixing by the DOJ, according to a document filed in the US district court of northern California. 

According to May 30, 2017, criminal information filed with the court, Hodge conspired with executives from other companies to fix prices, from early 2011 until 2013.

Although no companies are named in the document, Hodge was with Starkist, one of the "big three" in the US tuna sector, along with Thai Union Group-owned Tri-Union Seafoods, which trades as Chicken of the Sea, and Bumble Bee. In early 2014, Undercurrent News reported Hodge had left Starkist.

Hodge was the third executive to be charged by the DOJ with price-fixing, after Ken Worsham and Walter Scott Cameron, both longtime Bumble Bee sales executives. Neither Worsham nor Cameron have been sentenced in connection with the crime. All three men testified against Lischewski at his trial in November 2019. He was sentenced to 40 months in prison and fined $100,000.

title: Former processing plant co-owner jailed for tax evasion
content:
The former part-owner of a New Bedford, Massachusetts seafood processing plant has been sentenced to serve three years in federal prison after failing to pay his taxes for a decade.

The US Department of Justice (DOJ) said in a press release that Billie Schofield a former part-owner and employee of processor Northern Pelagic stopped filing his annual tax returns with the Internal Revenue Service in 2009.

"Between 2008 and 2018, Schofield obstructed IRS efforts to assess and collect his taxes by filing fraudulent forms, advancing frivolous tax arguments, creating and using a nominee entity and bank account, negotiating income checks to cash, and creating and submitting fraudulent checks to the IRS in an attempt to extinguish his tax liabilities. Including penalties and interest, Schofield caused a tax loss of more than $350,000 to the United States," the DOJ said.

Schoefield ceased working for the company more than six years ago and ceased to be an owner four years ago, an attorney for Northern Pelagic said.

In addition to the prison term, Schofield will serve three years of supervised release, was fined $5,000 and ordered to pay $364,200.22 in restitution.

title: SalMar applies for next step in offshore farming
content:
Norwegian salmon farmer SalMar has taken the plunge on its next planned offshore aquaculture unit, filing an application to build an exposed-water site in the Norwegian Sea.

Offshore division SalMar Ocean has applied for a site capable of holding 19,000 metric tons of maximum allowed biomass, "corresponding to the calculated capacity for offshore aquaculture unit Smart Fish Farm to be established in the open sea", it said.

The fisheries directorate of Norway will hear public comment on the plans for four weeks. 

The application has been made under Norway's development license scheme, which grants temporary farming permits to innovative projects. SalMar was granted the development licenses in 2019, but has waited until 2021 to make an investment decision.

The 760,000-cubic-meter Smart Fish Farm is capable of holding 3 million salmon, twice the number of the Ocean Farm unit the company is already operating. The application is filed for a region defined by Norway as "area 11", off the coast of the islands of Hitra and Froya:

title: Zoneco’s major shareholders prohibited from selling amid criminal investigations
content:
Chinese seafood company Zoneco Group's major shareholders are prohibited from selling stakes amid criminal investigations by Chinese authorities.

Last June, the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) penalized Zoneco by imposing a CNY 600,000 fine over a long-running saga involving missing scallops. The CSRC later transferred the case to the Chinese Public Security Bureau for further investigations on criminal responsibility.

Zoneco Group's risk disclosure statement on Jan. 8. Source: Shenzhen Stock Exchange

In a risk disclosure statement issued last Friday (Jan 8), Zoneco said the company recently received a notice from Dalian Public Security Bureau for taking evidence regarding the suspected securities cases.

Given the company is currently under investigation, "major shareholders" must retain their stakes, Zoneco said.

Shares in Zoneco, listed on Shenzhen Stock Exchange, declined by 5.22% and closed with CNY 4.18 on the day of the announcement made.

Wu Hougang, Zoneco's ex-chairman, along with other executives, overinflated the scallops' value at Zoneco's Marine Stewardship Council-certified sea ranches in the Yellow Sea. Wu was fined CNY 300,000 and given a lifetime ban from public securities markets. He resigned after the CSRC's ruling.

Zoneco chairman resigns over ‘running scallops’ saga

Wu has recently initiated an administrative lawsuit against the CSRC demanding the penalty to be revoked, reports Tencent News.

Wu's successor, Tang Yan, who was a Zoneco's executive previously, was also fined by authorities for her involvement in the corporate fraud.

The Chinese seafood supplier, which until 2017 was China’s largest market-listed seafood company by sales, reported four large-area scallop losses in six years. The firm's fiasco was widely known as "running scallops".

In early 2018, Zoneco reported a CNY 723m ($102m) loss for the previous financial year, after writing off inventories of scallops that had "starved to death". Zoneco called in experts to conduct a hydrodynamics model of the northern part of the Yellow Sea, to ascertain the die-off cause. 

Chinese securities regulator used historical satellite tracking data to expose the firm's financial fraud by showing log data of Zoneco vessels' seeding and harvesting activities had been "plucked from thin air", reports Chinese state-owned broadcaster.

title: Norway sees whitefish, coldwater shrimp exports fall in 2020
content:
While Norway's overall seafood exports were stable for 2020, it saw overseas sales of whitefish and coldwater shrimp drop, according to data from the Norwegian Seafood Council (NSC).

Cod, the largest species for the country's catching sector by value, saw volumes fall 4% to 172,000 metric tons, and value fall 4% to NOK 9.6 billion ($1.13bn). 

"After a fantastic start to the year, with price growth for most products, it looked like 2020 would be a promising year for cod exports. During the corona crisis, however, demand fell, which has resulted in falling prices for most products. Had it not been for the weak Norwegian krone, the fall in prices would have been significantly steeper," said NSC analyst Ingrid Kristine Pettersen.

The loss of the restaurant segment was the main reason for the declining demand.

"At the same time, we saw a growth in home consumption and increased demand for frozen products in several markets. This is probably one of the reasons why frozen fillets of cod have seen a price increase in 2020, measured both in Norwegian kroner and in euros."

Saithe and haddock also saw declines.

Saithe, the second-largest species in whitefish, saw 2020 exports fall 14% to 99,400t, while value fell 5% to NOK 2.4bn. 

Haddock saw export volumes fall 2% to 58,700t, and by 8% to NOK 143 million.

It was a tougher year for clipfish, with export volumes down 9% at 83,400t, and value down 10% at NOK 4.3bn. 

"The main reason is a significant reduction in exports to Brazil, but reduced demand in Portugal as a result of the corona crisis and closed restaurants have also contributed negatively," said NSC analyst Ingrid Pettersen.

Brazil has been hit hard by the coronavirus pandemic at the same time as low oil prices led to a weakening of the Brazilian real against the dollar. Declining stocks and an early Easter, which is the most important sales period for Norwegian clipfish in Brazil, have, however, contributed to increased clipfish exports of cod and saithe in December 2020, compared to the same month in 2019, said Oystein Valanes, NSC's representative in Brazil.

Christmas is traditionally the main season for clipfish consumption in Portugal, and over 25% of clipfish sales take place in December.

"Although total consumption has fallen in 2020, Christmas sales in the grocery trade have exceeded all expectations. Several of the chains report better December sales in 2020 than in 2019. The main reason is probably aggressive price campaigns in stores," said Johnny Thomassen, NSC envoy to Portugal.

At the same time, the value of saithe clipfish has been fairly stable in 2020 compared to 2019. This is despite the fact that Brazil is also an important market for saithe clipfish.

"The reason is strong demand in the Caribbean during the corona crisis. Norway has never before exported so much clipfish to the Dominican Republic as in 2020, neither measured by volume nor by value", said Pettersen.

Mixed shellfish picture

Coldwater shrimp saw significant declines year-on-year, with volumes falling 25% to 12,000t and value falling 16% to NOK 909m. The decline in value was primarily driven by lower demand in the main European markets.

"The impact of closed restaurants has mostly impacted frozen peeled prawn, which makes up 79% of the export value," said the NSC's Josefine Voraa, manager for shellfish.

"Increased sales of frozen peeled prawn in the retail trade have not managed to cover the loss of the restaurant and canteen segment." On top of that, sales to the UK market -- the second-largest export market for Norwegian shrimp in 2019 -- halved. 

"This is largely due to the corona crisis and uncertainty associated with Brexit," said Voraa. "To our largest prawn market Sweden, which accounts for 36% of the export value, exports in 2020 are in line with 2019. Also, lower demand has led to lower prices, reduced prawn catches in Norway and fewer exports of industrial prawn for processing in other markets."

It was a brighter story for Norwegian crab, with king crab experiencing its best-ever year. Export volumes eased 1%, but value was up 4%, to 2,000t and NOK 668m respectively.

Strong demand growth in the fall, combined with a weak krone measured against the dollar and adaptable Norwegian players, led to the export value of red king crab being the highest ever.

"Challenging logistics at the start of the corona crisis and closed restaurants put a damper on exports of red king crab in the first half of the year, with a decrease in value of 20%, or NOK 52m, compared to 2019", said Voraa.

With the logistics challenges resolved, there was strong growth in exports of red king crab in the second half of the year, with an increase in the export value of 21%, or NOK 80m.

"Measured in dollars, prices have been relatively stable in 2020. For live red king crab, there has been an increase in export value of NOK 63 million, which has been driven by volume growth in markets such as Vietnam, Hong Kong SAR and South Korea. This autumn, we also experienced strong growth in demand for frozen red king crab in the USA, France and Japan," she said.

Snow crab, meanwhile, saw export volumes stable y-o-y at 2,500t, and value up 10% at NOK 362m.

"Snow crab exports have had a very exciting development in 2020, with increased prices and increased sales of snow crab in the retail trade in the USA and China," Voraa said.

title: COVID-19 recap, Dec. 31 to Jan. 3: Santa Monica acquisition; Ecuador shrimp challenges; Brexit worries
content:
The novel coronavirus COVID-19 continues to upend the global seafood trade, reducing foodservice demand and complicating supply chains. If you have any stories on how your company is dealing with the crisis, please email us, editorial@undercurrentnews.com. Here's a recap of pandemic-related seafood news from Thursday, Dec. 31 to Jan. 3:

California-headquartered US processor and distributor Santa Monica Seafood has bought out its joint venture partner and taken 100% control in Ethos Seafood Group, it announced, a prime example of dealmaking despite the pandemic.

Santa Monica said it had closed a purchase agreement for the equity interest in Ethos Seafood that had been owned by the privately-owned investment and management company Blue Earth Group.

Ecuadorian farm-gate shrimp prices fell across almost all sizes in the final week of 2020 after a few weeks of increases, data tracked by Undercurrent News' prices portal show.

Meanwhile, in Indonesia, prices for head-on, shell-on, farm-gate vannamei shrimp from Indonesia rose in week 52 (Dec. 21-27) across all sizes.

Good news may soon be coming for Australian rock lobster exporters who have long relied on China as a lucrative market. The business was hit hard first by the COVID-19 pandemic and more recently by a trade dispute between the two countries. 

In salmon, Norwegian spot prices have taken a steep downturn for the first week of 2021, reports news site SalmonBusiness.

And the weekly export volume of Norway's fresh salmon dropped by 43% week-on-week to 14,183 metric tons, according to the latest data published by the Norwegian Seafood Council.

Lastly, in the UK and EU, seafood industry representatives are finding much to grumble about in the recently reached Brexit deal. Sources told Undercurrent News that the EU fishing sector feels misled by the outcome of the Brexit deal after four years of continuous negotiations.

The new fisheries arrangement, defined under the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement, sees 25% of fish quota in UK waters (by value) held by European fishing fleets returned to the UK over a phase-in period of five-and-a-half years.

Jimmy Buchan, chief executive of the Scottish Seafood Association, has welcomed the Brexit deal but urged the UK government to sort out a replacement for the European Maritime and Fisheries Fund scheme soon, in addition to the £100 million ($`136.7m) that has been promised to support the seafood sector and take advantage of the increase in some fish and shellfish stocks.

title: IPNLF urges IOTC members to adopt new conservation measures at one-off 2021 meet
content:
The International Pole and Line Foundation has urged members of the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC) to adopt new proposed conservation measures for yellowfin tuna at their next meeting, scheduled for March 2021.

IOTC meeting agenda omits yellowfin overfishing issue

Although IOTC members met as usual in November -- albeit using video conferencing technology -- the pressing issue of yellowfin tuna conservation was not discussed as it was deemed the constraints of holding a virtual meeting made it too challenging to effectively negotiate new conservation measures among members.

Instead, a special IOTC session was scheduled for March 2021, devoted solely to the yellowfin issue.

Ahead of the meeting, the IPNLF has defined what it believes to be four crucial measures that IOTC members should adopt:

At a minimum, the IPNLF believes all IOTC members should commit to a total catch reduction of 20% for yellowfin tuna, as recommended by the IOTC’s scientific committee.
Amendments to the existing conservation plan -- Resolution 19/01 -- should focus on the already agreed catch reduction ratios by different fishing gears, and the relative contributions these gears make to the overfished stock status of yellowfin, instead of adding new measures.
Doubling all of the currently agreed catch reductions by fishing gear as stated in 19/01, with exemptions applying only to artisanal fleets catching less than 2,000 metric tons per year.
Phasing out all supply vessels that assist purse seiners in the deployment and retrieval of fish aggregating devices (FADs) by the end of 2021, reducing the number of operational FADs assigned to any one purse seiner from 300 to 200, and ensuring full transparency of FAD deployment and tracking.

"The long-term viability of the region’s tuna fisheries is at risk," said Shihan Adam, IPNLF's director of science.

"The consequences of Resolution 19/01 continuing to be ineffective will be felt most critically by small-scale tuna fisheries, especially those in developing coastal states that provide critical livelihood support to coastal communities. We all have a duty to ensure that effective management measures are adopted at the special session in March."

title: Chicken of the Sea, large US grocers settle tuna price-fixing suits
content:
Thai Union Group-owned Chicken of the Sea International (COSI) has settled a class-action lawsuit from several major grocers that claimed damages from the US canned tuna brand's participation in a price-fixing scandal earlier in the decade.

The terms of the settlement were not disclosed. However, according to a Dec. 3 filing made to San Diego, California-based federal judge Janis Sammartino, a group of large grocers known as the "direct action" plaintiffs -- Kroger, Albertsons, Hy-Vee and H. E. Butt --have sought the dismissal of their suit against the canner "with prejudice". This means that the suit can not be refiled. 

According to the filing made by the grocers' lawyer William Blechman, an attorney for the Miami, Florida-based firm Kenny Nachwalter, the parties "previously agreed to resolve Plaintiffs’ claims against the COSI defendants only". 

The plaintiffs represent the largest grocers in the US. Kroger and Albertsons operate nearly 5,000 stores combined whereas midwest-focused chain Hy-Vee owns 265 stores and H-E Butt, known as H-E-B, operates 340, mostly in Texas. 

 The first civil suits against Bumble Bee Foods, Dongwon Enterprise-owned StarKist & Co., and Chicken of the Sea, a brand owned by Thai Union Group's Tri-Union Seafoods, began in 2015 as allegations emerged that the companies had engaged in a scheme to fix canned tuna prices.

Plaintiffs have been sorted into four "tracks" depending on how they purchased tuna from the canners and the class certification ruling allows each track to have common legal counsel and pool many plaintiffs' resources together to pay the costly bills for expert witnesses, lawyers fees and other expenses that come in class-action litigation. 

The large wholesalers and distributors who dealt directly with the canners are known as "direct purchasers" with a second track of direct purchasers including large buyers such as Walmart with separate lawsuits known as "direct action" plaintiffs.

Lawsuits in two other tracks, the "commercial food preparers" including restaurants and retailers, and individual consumers known as "end-payers", include plaintiffs who purchased from the canners' tuna indirectly.

A large number of the suits have been settled. The class-action suits have already had a major impact on the US canners. In November 2019, Bumble Bee filed bankruptcy in Delaware and was purchased by its longtime tuna supplier FCF Co. Bumble Bee has cited the class action suits as well as a $25 million fine from the Department of Justice as two major factors behind the bankruptcy. 

Additionally, Starkist, which judge Edward Chen fined $100m in 2019 after its guilty plea to price-fixing charges, indicated at the time that it too could file for bankruptcy or move its operations from American Samoa, which would result in mass layoffs.

Thai Union, which escaped criminal liability because it acted as a whistleblower to the Department of Justice, has set aside some $104m to pay for its part in the price-fixing. Most of the related lawsuits have now been settled, the company has said.
