title: Canadian lobster poised to hold long-lasting MSC label edge over US
content:
Now that Canada's lobster harvesters, processors and exporters hold the advantage of a Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certification over their US rivals, don't look for them to give it up any time soon.

That's because independent auditor SAI Global, back on Nov. 25, issued a 324-page draft assessment that suggests all five of the Canadian lobster fisheries should be able to keep using the little blue MSC labels on boxes and bags containing its crustaceans for another five years. The only task remaining, according to the auditors, is to develop and complete a plan that spells out how to better protect and conserve endangered North Atlantic right whales.

"During the review and analysis of available information and data, the team did not identify any issues that could prevent the fishery from continuing to conform with the MSC Fisheries Standard," the SAI auditors said in their brief summary of the report, which is now available for comment until Dec. 25.

The US lobster fishery, meanwhile, has lost its MSC certification and is looking at a much bigger job in front of it in order to recover its right to use the label.  

In August, the MSC suspended the US lobster fishery's certification permission, which it had held for seven years, in a response to a federal court ruling that found the sector in violation of the US' Endangered Species Act. Based on what sources told Undercurrent News about what needs to happen to restore the certification and the progress being made, it could be at least a year before anything changes. 

"There's no way the US lobster fishery is going to be able to regain use of the MSC label any time soon. Based on what has to happen and the progress being made, anything less than a year would be extremely optimistic," said one source, involved in the efforts for reinstatement, who requested anonymity. 

'[N]ot a terribly difficult condition'

The rivalry between the Canadian and US lobster fisheries goes back dozens of years and continues today in earnest as both sectors pursue many of the same buyers and export markets. Canada is the world's largest producer of North American lobster (Homarus americanus), nearly 100,000 metric tons annually, and reports to generate as much as $2 billion per year in export sales. 

The US is a strong second, harvesting roughly 60,000t and maintaining annual exports of roughly $550 million, not to mention lots of domestic sales.  

Because the US has many more airports near its harvesting and processing facilities in the Northeastern US, its lobster sector enjoys a distinct transportation advantage over the Canadians'. However, in recent times, the US has been playing catchup with Canada on trade deals and continues to suffer hefty tariffs in the major market of China thanks to an ongoing trade war.

Canada now also holds the advantage of MSC certification, though it used to be something both nations' lobster industries enjoyed. The US Gulf of Maine lobster fishery obtained MSC status in 2013 and Canada's Bay of Fundy, Scotian Shelf and Southern Gulf of St. Lawrence lobster trap fisheries all obtained MSC certifications separately from late 2014 to early 2015. 

In its draft report issued late last month, SAI Global said it was combining all five of Atlantic Canada's lobster fisheries, including also the fishery operating around Prince Edward Island, under one review and recommending them for a single certification. SAI's team of four auditors seem to find little concern in the stability of Canada's North American lobster stock, which is worked by a combined 5,500 license holders. 

"For lobster populations in all the [units of assessment, or UoAs], the current high landings reflect high levels of recruitment associated with consistent favorable environmental/ecological conditions, and the scores and rationales for all [performance indicators] reflect the strong influence of environmental conditions on recruitment," the auditors wrote.

A North Atlantic right whale calf and its mother off the coast of Georgia. Photograph from the US' National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

The fishery has a "minimal impact on other bycatch species, because there are low bycatch rates and high survival of any discarded bycatch,"  the auditors wrote.

The one criticism: "However there is a potential impact of the UoAs and other MSC UoAs on the recovery of North Atlantic right whale (NARW) populations and it may be necessary to raise a condition against PI 2.3.1," the auditors added, referring to one of the standards being scored and the need for further measures to be explored. 

The group explains further that lobster traps are set very close to the shore in shallow waters. That was verified by the assessment team during its visits, which took place between Sept. 30 and Oct. 2, 2019.

Most entanglement interactions cannot be traced back to gear because they leave only scars, though some scars are severe and lead to health impacts, the auditors added.

Some entanglements have been traced back to US lobster gear because it is marked, except for coastal Maine gear, while Canadian gear is not marked, "which hinders any ability to determine where those cases that do have attached gear came from", they said.

Geoff Irvine, executive director of the Lobster Council of Canada, told Undercurrent on Tuesday that the request made by the SAI auditors won't be a difficult one to satisfy.

Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO), since 2018, has introduced multiple new measures in both the snow crab and lobster fisheries aimed at reducing trap rope entanglements with right whales, he noted. They included static closures for when whales are spotted in particular fishing areas, new gear-marking requirements, added rules for harvesters to report lost gear, and increased surveillance of fishing areas by aircraft, drones and underwater gliders.

The changes Canada has made to improve its protection of North Atlantic right whales.

The changes followed a slew of right whale deaths in the Gulf of St. Lawrence in 2017 and 2019.

To satisfy the auditors and MSC, Irvine said, the harvest sector will merely need to uniformly document all of the changes and make sure they are harmonized across different species and fisheries. 

"I mean our plan is to work with DFO and continue to improve the mitigation measures that keep us away from right whales," Irvine said. "That's going to be our plan. No, it's not a terribly difficult condition."

'The window to save this species is closing'

The preservation of right whales has long been a difficult issue for both the Canadian and US lobster fisheries. 

A petition filed by the Conservation Law Foundation (CLF), the Center for Biological Diversity (CBD) and the Defenders of Wildlife (DOW) with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) on Dec. 3 reports that the right whale population is now down to 356 animals, only about 70 of whom are breeding females. That's nearly a 25% population loss in less than a decade, the conservation groups say is a trend for which entanglements share much of the blame. 

A big banded "select" lobster on a wharf near the US town of Rockland, Maine. Photograph by Jason Huffman.

The petition seeks to have NMFS issue an emergency declaration that would close both New England groundfish and lobster fisheries until better conservation plans can be put forth.

“At least 32 right whales have been killed by human activities in the last three years alone, yet the federal government is still sitting on its hands,” said Erica Fuller, a CLF senior attorney, in a press release announcing the petition. “The window to save this species is closing. We’re left with no other option but to file this petition. The federal government must declare this situation what it is – an emergency – and take action to protect these animals now.”

It was a lawsuit filed by CLF, CBD and the Humane Society of America that ultimately resulted in a ruling in April 2020 by US District Court judge James Boasberg, in Washington, D.C., that NMFS failed to properly include an "incidental take statement" for right whales in its management plan for lobster. Boasberg gave NMFS until May 31, 2021, to issue a new biological opinion and to craft new rules.

NMFS did not respond to Undercurrent's request for an update on the effort as the president Donald Trump administration is in the midst of a transition to the future administration of president-elect Joe Biden.  

It was Boasberg's ruling that caused the MSC, in August, to suspend the US Gulf of Maine lobster fishery's certification. MSC gave the Maine Certified Sustainable Lobster Association (MCLSA), a 14 company group that sponsored the US lobster fishery's certification process, until Jan. 29, 2021 -- less than two months from now -- to provide its plan for restoring its status.

Unloading a lobster boat in Rockland, Maine. Photograph by Jason Huffman.

Should MCLSA fail to meet the deadline, the group could lose its MSC status altogether and have to start from scratch, MSC spokesperson Jackie Marks confirmed for Undercurrent this week.

“Although we don’t have any direct role in the outcome of this federal case and the ultimate impact to our industry, we are confident we will regain MSC certification through our ongoing efforts to uphold the highest standards of sustainability,” MCSLA president Craig Rief said at the time of the MSC announcement. “We will actively participate with the upcoming biological opinion and provide any necessary resources to assist NOAA, MSC, and our stakeholders in our steadfast commitment to protect threatened and endangered marine life while providing the highest quality product to all consumers.”

Among the companies that make up MCLSA are some heavyweights in the lobster processing sector, such as Thai Union Group's Chicken of the Sea Frozen Foods, Luke's Lobster, Maine Coast Shellfish, Cape Bald Packers, Cozy Harbor Seafood, East Coast Seafood Group and Inland Seafood.

Neither Rief nor John Whiteside, MCSLA's general counsel, could be reached for comment for this article. However, a representative for one of the MCSLA's member companies told Undercurrent this week that the group is scuffling to solve the problem. It's waiting for some advanced word from NMFS on its biological opinion, that that's not due for another few months, before releasing its plan to MCS. 

Also, the source said that the group lacks members who are harvesters, the ones who will likely have to execute any of the changes suggested. In addition, he said, any future MSC certification efforts are going to have to include "harvest control rules", or HCR, measures to be taken in the event of unexpected concerns about the health of the stock. It was an issue raised as a condition in previous assessments of the fishery.

"The client must provide evidence that well-defined HCRs, taking into account main uncertainties, are in place and ensure that the exploitation rate is reduced as limit reference points are approached," an assessment of the fishery published in November 2016 advises.

The view of Owl's Head Lighthouse from a lobster boat in Maine. Photograph by Jason Huffman.

Meanwhile, as the US lobster industry awaits the return of its MSC certification, it is forced to continue defending itself to its buyers and the media.

"I think the important thing to point out here is that the Maine fishery has had whale protections in place for over 20 years," Marianne Lacroix, executive director of the Maine Lobster Marketing Collaborative, told Undercurrent this week. "And they've been continually putting in place new regulations in order to further protect the right whales. So this current suspension wasn't the result of a lack of effort by the Maine fishery. It's related specifically to this legal action."

Meanwhile, sources gave different answers about how damning the issue will be for future sales. A top executive at one large seafood processor and exporter told Undercurrent that he thinks the lack of an MSC label will do little to discourage the sale of US lobster products, while another said the lack of a label will matter significantly in markets where Canadian lobster is a competitor and consumers are more selective, noting the European Union as an example. 

"There are some markets that are more sensitive to this kind of thing than others," Lacroix said. "And they'd like to see some kind of label or status."

Clearwater dropping MSC on offshore lobster fishery

In a related matter, Clearwater Seafoods announced more than a week ago that it's dropping the MSC certification for its Canadian offshore lobster fishery, calling it "a voluntary decision driven by business considerations", CBC reported.

Clearwater's offshore lobster fishery, off the coast of southern Nova Scotia, was the first lobster fishery on the Eastern Seaboard to receive MSC certification in 2010. The current five-year certification expires at the end of the month.

"Clearwater is confident in the ability of this fishery to meet the MSC standard today, but has chosen not to initiate recertification at this time given the internal resources required to support recertification," Clearwater vice-president Christine Penney said in an email statement to CBC.

Environmentalists, meanwhile, are questioning the company's motives, the news service reported.

Two years ago, Clearwater was determined to be illegally storing thousands of lobster traps on the ocean floor even after it had been repeatedly warned by Canadian authorities to stop the practice because it was a conservation risk. The discovery triggered an MSC audit and new conditions were imposed to demonstrate compliance.

"The question comes to mind whether they're unable to show that evidence and therefore they wouldn't pass the certification," Shannon Arnold with the Ecology Action Centre in Halifax is quoted as saying. "And so, by just walking away from it, they're not forced to show that to the consumers that they're actually fishing within the law."

Clearwater, however, has asserted that its lobster fishery will continue to maintain sustainable harvesting practices.

"While Clearwater has chosen not to enter into recertification of the offshore fishery MSC program at the end of 2020, the sustainability measures that were in place for 10 years of successful certification continue to be in effect," Penney reportedly told the CBC. "The offshore lobster fishery remains sustainable. The fishery has not been suspended or failed, and it maintains its current certificate until December 2020."

title: PNG supports introduction of harvest control rules in western Pacific, crew welfare
content:
Members of Papua New Guinea (PNG)'s fishing association (known as the FIA) support the implementation of new harvest control rules by the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission (WCPFC). 

Additionally, at the WCPFC meeting this week (Dec. 9-15), they aim to show their progress in implementing crew welfare and labor conditions, the association's sustainability director, Marcelo Hidalgo, told Undercurrent News.

Members of the PNG's FIA include Majestic Seafood, IFC, RD tuna canners PNG, and RD fishing, Nambawan, South Seas Tuna Corporation, Frabelle processing PNG, Frabelle fishing, and others.

PNG achieved Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certification in May, since becoming the ecolabel's third-largest tuna fishery by volume, behind Dongwon Industries' tropical yellowfin and skipjack tuna fishery in the Western and Central Pacific Ocean, and the Parties to the Nauru Agreement.

Conservation and management measures (CMM) for the three tropical tuna species -- bigeye, skipjack, and yellowfin -- are expected to take center stage at the meeting. 

The lack of well-defined harvest control rules or effective tools to control catches has put several tuna fisheries at risk of losing their sustainability certifications, two NGOs warned during the virtual Infofish 2021 tuna prelude event earlier this year.

In 2014, the WCPFC committed to transitioning its management approach from short-term quotas to a long-term methodology using harvest strategies.

This science-based, precautionary approach is designed to meet a set of agreed objectives for the management of a fishery, such as preventing overfishing, by automating catch limits that have the best chance of meeting those objectives.

That transition is not yet complete, so this year the WCPFC should focus on taking the important next steps to develop harvest strategies while ensuring that healthy stocks don’t deteriorate and that unhealthy stocks are at least put on the path to recovery, the Pew Charitable Trusts has said.

PNG supports the implementation of new harvest control rules, Hidalgo noted.

Crew welfare

"PNG also aims to demonstrate it is leading on crew welfare and implementation of social standards in the tuna supply chain," Hidalgo added. He pointed out the island nation is making strong efforts to "align with market and retailer sourcing policies as well as with regional fisheries bodies".

Marcelo Hidalgo

In 2018, the PNG's fishing association committed to implementing with a responsible sourcing policy (RSP) that included a pillar focused on crew welfare, labor, and social requirements for the tuna fleet.

In 2019, the FIA tuna fleet began a crew welfare and social requirements audit program to assess on-board conditions against the International Labour Organization's C188 and various other standards and regulations, he said.
 
"Until today 35% of the MSC certified FIA tuna fleet has been audited, assessed, and is complying with these requirements. This is a journey and FIA is moving ahead in this area," Hidalgo said.
 
FIA tuna processing members have, since 2012, complied with labor and social standards like the BSCI agreement, he added. The FIA extended this commitment to the fishing operation to ensure a comprehensive approach to human rights and workers' welfare.
 
"The FIA RSP does not aim to reinvent the wheel when it comes to labor on-board and social labor standard, [but it] harmonizes all current standards, guidelines, and regulations to ensure that FIA tuna fleet members comply with them," he said.

PNG has opted to maintain the requirement for its purse seine tuna vessels to carry fisheries observers this year, even though the MSC has allowed the practice to be suspended until the end of January 2021, due to the COVID-19 outbreak.

The PNG fishery is the first to be certified across all gear types, including fishing aggregating devices, Hidalgo said. As a result, PNG is already aligned with the new MSC standard version 2.2 which was launched in March of this year.

title: Sweden’s 100,000t land-based salmon project signs up feed supplier BioMar
content:
Feed producer BioMar Group has signed an agreement to supply Lighthouse Finance-owned Quality Salmon with feed solutions for its 100,000-metric-ton land-based Atlantic salmon facility once production begins in 2022.

"At BioMar we have been working with feed solutions for RAS [recirculating aquaculture systems] for more than 20 years and we are excited to partner with Quality Salmon Sotenas to join them on their journey," said Ole Christensen, vice president of BioMar and head of the EMEA division and the RAS segment.

Swedish region signs land lease for Europe’s largest RAS salmon farm

"We have a strong focus on finding innovative and sustainable feed solutions and being a part of a project that has a focus on circular economy and adoption of new raw materials, makes it a good match with the way we do our business," he added.

"We believe projects like Quality Salmon Sotenas will be significant for meeting the demand for food in the future and look forward to cooperating with the companies behind the...project in Sweden as well as for similar projects in other places around the globe."

In June Quality Salmon secured a lease from the city of Sotenas for 140 hectares (345 acres) of land, as reported by Undercurrent News. At an estimated investment of SEK 17-20 billion ($1.8bn-$2.1bn), the RAS facility, which is due to begin construction in 2021, intends to be Europe's largest land-based salmon farming project.

The signing of a letter between the firm and neighboring Munkedal municipality means Lighthouse has been able to confirm its logistics timeline, aiming to produce 100,000t of Atlantic salmon by 2026, Undercurrent also reported. 

"Investing SEK 17bn-20bn in the industrial park and aiming for future production of 100,000t of salmon per year demonstrates our level of ambition pretty clearly. We want to do more than just framing and producing salmon. That is why we have chosen to partner with BioMar, as we share a mutual vision that sustainability and innovation are the key drivers for success," said Roy Hoias, CEO of Lighthouse and co-owner of Quality Salmon. 

Lighthouse was in talks with multiple "big farmers", Hoias told Undercurrent, who had each expressed an interest in using the new facilities, once fully built.

"We are working on that as we speak now, and hopefully we will have this defined and sorted by the end of this summer."

The appeal to industry members, he said, was Sweden's unique trading position, giving it an attractive edge over Norway for export purposes. As a member of the EU, for instance, Sweden can trade salmon with other EU members duty-free, while it also has a strong trade deal with China, as well as remaining one of the few countries still able to trade salmon with Russia.

The establishment is expected to create thousands of job opportunities, growing
demand for new housing, and improvements to infrastructure in the region. In order to create efficient transportation, a logistics center for electric trucks is planned at Haby, in Munkedal.

To this purpose, Quality Salmon also signed a collaboration agreement with Sekkingstad, Skagerak parent firm Trient on processing and a letter of intent with iCell Sustainable Nutrition, to have the Shanghai, China-based company construct and operate their water cleaning and nutrient recovery system.

title: Latest proposal to reduce quota for Iceland’s biggest harvesters might do opposite
content:
The latest proposed change to how Iceland governs its largest fishing group quotas would have minimal impact for Samherji, and might actually allow the other two biggest quota owners to get even larger, according to Kjarninn, an Icelandic news service.

Earlier this year Undercurrent News reported on the previous bid to curtail the largest fishing companies in the country; a draft bill which gave them until the end of the 2025/26 fishing year to bring their total quota holdings down below a new statutory limit. The legislation did not progress through parliament, however.

Experts foresee Icelandic salmon consolidation, big fishing firms to go on growing

The latest proposal, by Pal Magnusson of Iceland's Independence Party, seeks further restrictions on the allocated quota share for Iceland's "fishing blocs", as Kjarninn calls them: Samherji, Utgerdarfelag Reykjavikur (UR)/ Brim, and firms linked to Kaupfalag Skagfirdingar. The current ceiling for total quota ownership is 12%.

Under Magnusson's proposals, Samherji -- which owns 49.9% of Sildarvinnslan, which in turn owns Bergur-Huginn -- would have to sell almost 1.2% of its quota ownership over the next almost six years.

According to the calculation rule in this bill, UR would hold a share of 8.6% of the catch, and could therefore add about 3.4% of the total quota without going too high.

Kaupfelag Skagfirdinga owns FISK Seafood, which in turn holds 32.9% of Vinnslustodin I Vestmannaeyjar, which again holds shares in other firms. Under Magnusson's proposal, FISK would be defined with a 7.4% catch share and "could add significantly to reach the ceiling", Kjarninn reports.

title: Grieg eyes further NOK 500m in green funding
content:
Norwegian salmon farmer Grieg Seafood is contemplating a "tap issue" of up to NOK 500 million ($56.4m) under its existing senior unsecured green bond, with maturity date June 25, 2025, subject to market conditions.

The current outstanding amount is NOK 1 billion, and the borrowing limit is NOK 1.5bn, it said.

A tap issue is a procedure that allows borrowers to sell bonds or other short-term debt instruments from past issues, according to Investopedia. The bonds are issued at their original face value, maturity, and coupon rate, but sold at the current market price.

The proceeds from the potential tap issue will be used for green projects as further defined by the green bond framework, Grieg said. The firm successfully raised NOK 1bn in green bonds back in June. 

DNB Markets and Nordea have been engaged as arrangers for the contemplated issue.

title: Sainsbury’s, Mowi rebut attack over salmon feed sustainability
content:
UK retailer J. Sainsbury claims its "bespoke diet" for farmed salmon is "designed to protect our natural resources from over-fishing", but has failed to live up to its commitments, according to campaigners from Changing Markets and Feedback.

Scottish salmon sector pledges to source 100% of feed from sustainable sources

In the pair's own report, published back in March, they ranked Sainsury's sixth -- behind Tesco, The Co-operative, Waitrose & Partners, Marks and Spencer, and Lidl -- on a scorecard assessing supermarket chains’ sustainability policies for farmed seafood.

Feedback calculates that in 2019, Mowi used 880,000 metric tons of wild fish in its global operations, sourced from countries such as Mauritania and Peru, to produce 436,000t of farmed salmon. It claims this goes against Sainsbury's intention to feed salmon a bespoke diet "designed to protect our natural resources from overfishing".

The campaigners note more sustainable feed options, such as using non-fish ingredients or by-products from fish that was caught for human consumption, do exist, "but neither Mowi nor Sainsbury’s has adopted a policy to phase out wild fish in its salmon feed".

It should be noted that feed giants BioMar Group and Skretting do not believe marine ingredients will ever completely disappear as a feed ingredient.

The campaigners also raised concerns about mortalities on Mowi farms in Scotland, where Sainsbury’s sources its salmon. Between January and September 2020, Mowi reported over 1.1 million salmon mortalities to the Scottish government fish inspectorate.

"This is the second-highest figure of all large salmon farming companies operating in Scotland, though reporting standards varied between companies. In addition, Mowi’s Scottish farms have seen high numbers of farmed salmon escapes, 124,000 in two separate incidents this year, raising concerns for further impacts on Scotland’s dwindling wild salmon population, which is suffering the effects of inter-breeding with escaped farmed salmon."

Natasha Hurley, campaign manager at Changing Markets, said Sainsbury's claim that its farmed salmon diets help prevent overfishing was "demonstrably untrue": "the reality is, hundreds of thousands of tons of wild fish -- which could feed millions of people -- are ground into fishmeal and fish oil just to feed farmed salmon on Mowi farms."

"Fishing communities in Asia and Africa are deprived of valuable protein just so that wealthier consumers in the UK can buy cheap salmon. Salmon farming is big business, but while the Sainsbury’s-Mowi partnership may be lucrative for both sides, it is a terrible deal for the health of global fisheries."

Sainsbury's eyes ASC standard

Sainsbury's told Undercurrent News all the fishmeal and fish oil in its salmon feeds was certified to the MarinTrust standard (formerly IFFO RS). "We are committed to the responsible sourcing of fishmeal and fish oil for aquaculture feeds and believe that the use of these ingredients in feeds is responsible when sourced from well-managed fisheries."

BioMar, Skretting: Marine ingredients won’t totally disappear from salmon feed

The retailer also plans to adopt the developing Aquaculture Stewardship Council feed standard, which has a defined improvement pathway for marine ingredients with Marine Stewardship Council certification as the ultimate goal for fisheries, when it becomes available for audit in 2021. 

Regarding a lack of policy around alternative feed ingredients, Sainsbury's said it recognized the need to develop new raw materials for animal feeds to complement existing sources of protein and omega-3 in particular, such as insect meals and oil from microalgae. It has an active dialogue with its salmon feed supplier as to the opportunities for assessment and the potential inclusion of these materials in feeds in the future.

It is also a member of the Innovate UK funded REACT-FIRST consortium which aims to develop a novel single-cell protein from waste carbon dioxide for aquaculture and chicken feeds, it added.

Finally, it said its salmon feeds do not include fishmeal or oils sourced from Asian or African fisheries.

A Mowi Scotland spokesperson told Undercurrent the company shared Feedback’s interest in ensuring the global food supply is most efficiently utilized, and "agreed with the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations that to ensure a food secure future for all, the fisheries and aquaculture sector is key".

"The fact is, our oceans cannot naturally supply the demand for fish, and aquaculture is a very important and carbon-friendly solution to increasing the yield of healthy and appetizing seafood."

Mowi's meeting with Feedback confirmed a difference of opinion on the role of livestock farming in food security and the appeal of forage/small pelagic fish as a primary food source for humans, it said, but "we do agree on the importance of sourcing sustainable feed ingredients and ensuring minimal food waste throughout the value chain".

On the issue of Mowi's mortalities in Scotland, the firm said:

"Mowi acknowledges the need to continually improve salmon survival and to develop solutions to biological and/or environmental health challenges – all of which are a natural part of farming in nature. All farmers share this concern as each man and woman works very hard during an animal’s lifetime to ensure the product makes it to market."

"Fish survival is a key focus for our farmers and our animal health team, and Scotland’s '10 year farmed fish health framework' that sets out a number of key sustainability measures for the salmon farming sector is an example of this focus."

This comes just as a new sustainability charter issued by the Scottish salmon farming industry set out a roadmap for future "green" strategies, including several pledges on feed.

'A Better Future For Us All', which encapsulates all aspects of aquaculture, features environmental promises including a commitment to becoming net-zero in greenhouse gas emissions before 2045, and being 100% reliant on renewable energy.

title: Canadian activists take up fight for First Nation lobster harvesters against Clearwater
content:
Group Solidarity Kjipuktuk/Halifax, an Atlantic Canada-based activist group that states opposition to capitalism as its major cause, is taking on Clearwater Seafoods on behalf of lobster harvesters with the Mi'kmaw First Nation. The group has organized a demonstration in front of the Clearwater Seafood Market, in Bedford, Nova Scotia, Thursday morning, the Canadian news service Global News reports.

In a statement posted on its Facebook page, the group says it opposes the "special treatment that Clearwater Seafoods receives from the Canadian government" in relation to the special lobster fishing license it maintains, which allows it to harvest year-round from a large area of water.

It points to an incident, in 2019, when Clearwater was found to be in “gross violation” of lobster fishing regulations and fined because it left its traps unattended on the ocean floor. It says Clearwater has continued to lobby Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans to be allowed to leave traps for longer than the current limit of 72 hours.

"Just by existing, Clearwater’s massive operation poses a serious threat to both Mi’kmaw livelihoods and lobster conservation," the Facebook statement says.

Clearwater, Canada's largest shellfish harvesting company with clams, coldwater shrimp, scallops and lobster in its massive portfolio, has been in talks to be acquired by British Columbia-based Premium Brands Holdings in partnership with the Membertou First Nation of Nova Scotia and a deal is close, as reported by Undercurrent News. The Miawpukek First Nation of Newfoundland and Labrador is also thought to be in the mix.

In September, Clearwater announced that it would be selling two of its eight lobster licenses in an $18.9m deal with the Membertou First Nation. 

"We recognize that Clearwater sold a minority share of its offshore lobster licenses to Membertou First Nation in September 2020," Group Solidarity says in its Facebook posting. "Our opposition is not to Mi’kmaw participants in commercial fishing. Clearwater’s move from monopoly to near-monopoly in offshore lobster fishing doesn’t mitigate the company’s dismal track-record or significantly change the company’s industry consolidation."

Simultaneous to Clearwater seeking a buyer, the Sipekne’katik First Nation, on Sept. 17, opened an offseason lobster fishery in Canada's most prolific lobster fishing area (LFA 34), an area off the southwest coast of Nova Scotia. It resulted in widespread protests by commercial harvesters still waiting for their season to open on the last Monday of November, as usual. The backlash recently included the burning down of a pound being used to hold the First Nation group's lobsters.

Last week, Sipekne’katik chief Michael Sack announced that his band has decided not to participate in the upcoming lobster season due to safety concerns.

title: Irish court to hear challenge against EU’s alleged unsustainable fishing
content:
The Irish High Court has granted leave for environmental charity Friends of the Irish Environment (FIE) to apply for a judicial review aimed at challenging the EU regulation setting 2020 fishing quotas under the common fisheries policy (CFP), because of its alleged failure to "meet a legally defined deadline of ending overfishing in all stocks by 2020".

"This legal action aims to challenge the short-term political decision-making process which in the long term is destroying the Irish fishing industry," said FIE spokesperson Kate Ruddock. "If this challenge is successful it will push politicians to take decisions that allow stocks to recover to a level where fishing can be guaranteed into the future."

"However, no request has been made to suspend the implementation of the 2020 decision on TACs [total allowable catches] because we do not want to harm fishing activities – in fact, the motivation behind this case is to protect the Irish and European fisheries from collapse."

In 2013, as part of the last reform of the CFP,  the Council of the European Union and the European Parliament agreed in article 2(2) of the CFP regulation to end overfishing by 2015 "where possible" and by 2020 "at the latest". 

Every December fisheries ministers from across the EU meet to set the fishing limits for the next year, with advice from the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (ICES) to work from. 

"Yet around half of the TACs set by the Council in December 2019 exceed the scientific advice provided by ICES, according to an analysis by the environmental law charity ClientEarth who are supporting Friends of the Irish Environment in bringing this case. This habit of endorsing overfishing is jeopardizing the long-term economic, social, and environmental sustainability of European fishing activities."

A recent ClientEarth study on which member states have been lobbying for higher than scientifically advised TACs in the period from 2017 to 2019 shows that Ireland is among those that have most actively advocated for higher TACs, along with others like Spain and France, claimed FIE. Moreover, in the challenged regulation, Ireland benefits significantly from unsustainable TACs by having considerable shares in 13 of the stocks that exceed the scientific advice.

FIE is asking the Irish Courts to refer the case to the European Court of Justice.

title: Premium, First Nations edge closer to Clearwater deal
content:
Canadian food group Premium Brands Holdings and some First Nations groups are close to a deal for Clearwater Seafoods, the largest shellfish harvesting company in the country, sources told Undercurrent News.

Premium is in exclusive talks to acquire Clearwater and the announcement of a deal agreement could come in the next couple of weeks, they said. Membertou First Nation of Nova Scotia is involved in the Premium bid for Clearwater, a big player in species including clams, coldwater shrimp, scallops and lobster. The Miawpukek First Nation of Newfoundland and Labrador is also thought to be in the mix, too, as Undercurrent previously reported. 

Premium Brands, First Nations bid seen as frontrunner for Clearwater

At the start of October, Undercurrent reported Richmond, British Columbia-based Premium was seen as the favored bid, but some sources said Cooke and the Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan (OTPP) were also in the background. However, it's now thought Premium and the First Nations are exclusive in the process and a deal is being worked out, sources said. 

Both Clearwater and Premium -- which counts Starbucks as a major customer of its large sandwich business -- are in quiet periods ahead of third-quarter results. So a statement on a possible deal, if it gets over the line, could coincide with these, sources said. 

Clearwater, North America's largest vertically integrated shellfish harvester, processor and distributor, is yet to announce a date for its Q3 earnings call. Premium's Q3 earnings report and call will take place on Thursday, Nov. 5.

The involvement of First Nations groups has been considered essential for any successful buyer of Clearwater.

"It takes care of a lot of the political risk for any would-be buyer, after what happened with the surf clams," said one source, who asked not to be quoted by name. 

Clearwater briefly lost its surf clam monopoly in 2018 when the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) created a fourth license. This license was then controversially awarded to Five Nations, an entity comprised of First Nations from Quebec, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Labrador, Prince Edward Island, and New Brunswick.

PE-backed by Mitt Romney’s son emerges as latest Canadian shellfish consolidator

This entity had partnered with Premium Seafoods Group to harvest, process and market the catch. But in August 2018, the license was canceled after it emerged the partnership was formalized after it was awarded, that participants had family ties to the federal Liberals, including then-fisheries minister Dominic LeBlanc, and were unable to secure a vessel to harvest the quota.

In March 2019, Clearwater inked a 50-year surf clam license deal with 14 First Nations groups, including both Membertou and Miawpukek. Membertou then agreed on a separate deal Sept. 8 to buy two of Clearwater's eight lobster licenses for CAD 25 million ($18.9m). 

Terry Paul and Mi'sel Joe, the chiefs of Membertou and Miawpukek respectively, could not be reached for comment by Undercurrent. Nor could Ian Smith, CEO of Clearwater. 

Brendan Paddick, a Clearwater director who is heading the committee undertaking the strategic review/sale process, declined to comment. RBC Capital Markets, which is running the sale process along with Antarctica Advisors, a seafood-focused firm, declined to comment to Undercurrent. Antarctica's Ignacio Kleiman declined to comment.

"The company continues to advance the strategic review process with its financial advisors to identify, review and evaluate a broad range of potential strategic alternatives available to it with a view to continuing to enhance shareholder value," said a Clearwater spokesperson. 

"The process is continuing in earnest and no timeline for its completion has been currently defined. There can be no assurance that any such strategic alternatives will ultimately lead to a transaction. As a general policy, Clearwater does not publicly comment on potential transactions unless and until a binding legal agreement has been signed."

Deal ready 

In June, Premium raised $300m in new capital, partly to fund more deals. These funds "will further strengthen our balance sheet as well as our ability to pursue our pipeline of acquisition opportunities," said George Paleologou, president and CEO of Premium, in a statement from the time. 

Paleologou and William Kalutycz, the longtime chief financial officer of Premium, were not immediately available for comment to Undercurrent. 

When the sale process for Clearwater kicked off in March, Undercurrent sources said interest from Premium might well have been the driver. 

First Nation chief in Clearwater talks steps away from lobster mediation

Premium has acquired the likes of Ready Brothers Seafood and Maine Coast Shellfish in the last two years as part of a plan to build CAD 1 billion turnover seafood division. Most recently, Premium inked a deal to buy Toronto, Ontario-based Allseas Fisheries, one of the largest seafood distributors in the country. Premium paid CAD 139m ($106.7m) for Allseas and Canadian soup and fillings maker Global Gourmet but did not break out the specific purchase price for each deal.

Clearwater will be a considerably more expensive catch for Premium, which has snowballed through acquisitions to CAD 3.8bn in sales and CAD 290m in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) for the 12 months to the end of June 2020.

The company's share price is CAD 6.94 on the Toronto stock exchange on Nov. 3, giving a market capitalization of CAD 452.13m. That's an increase of 22% since the start of the year, but down 53% from the CAD 14.70 that Clearwater hit in June 2016, before the surf clam license debacle. 

Premium, by contrast, commands a lofty valuation on the stock market. The company's share price is CAD 98.53, giving a market capitalization of CAD 4bn. 

Undercurrent sources and analysts covering Clearwater previously said a sensible valuation for the business would be in the eight to12x EBITDA range, so CAD 900m to CAD 1bn mark. 

John Risley and Colin and Mickey MacDonald control around 60% of Clearwater's shares. Risley and the MacDonald brothers built the company up from selling Nova Scotia lobsters from the back of a truck. Risley and the MacDonald brothers could not be reached for comment to Undercurrent. 

Antarctica Advisors and RBC Capital Markets, who are running the process for Clearwater, also did not respond to requests for comment. 

Royal Greenland CEO: We have been good neighbors in Newfoundland

Canadian shellfish consolidation 

If Premium gets a deal done for Clearwater done, the group will be the latest entrant to the consolidation going on in the Canadian shellfish sector. 

Earlier in October, Undercurrent revealed a US private equity (PE) backed by the son of Mitt Romney, the Bain Capital co-founder and former presidential candidate, is making deals in the sector. 

Documents seen by Undercurrent show a firm linked to Taggart "Tagg" Romney's Solamere Capital, a $1bn-plus PE firm based in Boston, Massachusetts, has purchased undisclosed stakes in several seafood processing companies in eastern Canada owned by the Daley family, which trades as Daley Seafoods.

Following these deals, Terry Daley, president of Daley Seafoods, has acquired another shellfish plant, with unspecified US-backing. Undercurrent seafood sector sources said Solamere is also behind this deal, however.

In August, the Canadian government approved a deal from a US-backed company named 11656520 Canada for a lobster plant in Pointe-Sapin, New Brunswick, from the Island Fishermen's Co-operative Association. Documents show Terry Daley as the only director, but the company is listed as US-owned on the Canadian government's website.

Private equity-backed Champlain Seafood buys Canada’s Captain Dan’s

Companies including Champlain Financial Corp., OTPP, and Royal Greenland have all inked deals in the sector in the past few years.

Royal Greenland, a state-owned fishing and processing group, moved into Canada with a deal for shellfish processor Quin-Sea Fisheries a few years ago. Earlier this year, Royal Greenland also inked a deal for Quinlan Brothers, formerly a sister company of Quin-Sea. Royal Greenland has also done a deal with Clearwater for a joint venture coldwater shrimp plant.

In 2017, OTPP, which has CAD 170bn of assets under management, acquired the Canadian mussel farmer Atlantic Aqua Farms Partnership (AAF) from Encore Capital, a US-based PE. Cooke was also in the running for AAF, which had snapped up two rival Prince Edward Island-based mussel firms and a US shellfish distributor in December 2016.

Then, Montreal, Canada-based PE Champlain has embarked on an aggressive series of seafood deals, with former Sobeys CEO Marc Poulin at the helm.

Champlain acquired Captain Dan's Seafood, a processor based in St. Dieppe, New Brunswick, in October 2019. The deal was done in partnership with the family office Claridge, which manages the wealth of the billionaire Stephen Bronfman and his family and is invested in industries including food, technology, renewable energy and real estate.

Champlain burst onto the scene in 2017, buying Riverside Lobster International and Pecheries Cheticamp Fisheries International. In 2019, Undercurrent reported Champlain had also acquired Downeast Cape Bald Packers and US distributor Boston Lobster Company. The deals came before fires at Cape Bald's plants in New Brunswick.

Undercurrent also confirmed Champlain made a deal in 2018, acquiring crab processor and distributor Petit de Grat and the live lobster and crab brokerage business of related company Premium Seafoods.

title: Editor’s recap: Sealaska buys NESI; Maruha Nichiro sells Peter Pan; Diseases hurt Asian shrimp ops
content:
Neil Ramsden, deputy editor of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

There were two big pieces of M&A news late last week, both with links to the US state of Alaska.

First, Sealaska -- an Alaska Native Corporation -- has acquired a majority stake in UK processor New England Seafood International (NESI).

Fred Stroyan, founder of NESI, will retain a minority stake in the salmon, tuna, and whitefish processor, with key members of its management team staying in place, according to a statement on the deal. He will continue on the board and Dan Aherne will remain as CEO of NESI, which will "remain independent and continue its three-decade journey".

The companies said that joining forces will offer both businesses increased access to resources, broader product and category capabilities and deeper market access. Sealaska also has alluded to more possible deals in the future, noting the "enlarged seafood group and enhanced management capacity provide an opportunity for further investments".

Then, this past weekend, Maruha Nichiro agreed on a deal to sell Peter Pan Seafoods to US seafood entrepreneur Rodger May and Alaskan private equity McKinley Capital Management. 

Back in July, Undercurrent reported McKinley and May, who already owns Alaskan seafood distributor Northwest Fish Company, were in exclusive talks to acquire Peter Pan. The deal has now been agreed upon and is set to close at the end of the year. 

"As local owners and operators, we bring strong leadership and a commitment to Alaska," said May and McKinley, in an announcement on the deal seen by Undercurrent dated Nov. 1. 

"We are excited to be a part of this 100-year-old seafood processing company's growth, and to combine it with Northwest Fish Co.'s rapidly growing sales and value-added processing seafood business. We believe in the value and strength of the Alaska seafood brand and are committed to providing more wild Alaska seafood to consumers," they said.

Read that story in full here.

The combination of Enterocytozoon Hepatopenaei (EHP) and white feces disease (WFD) has been a devastating cocktail for South Asian shrimp farmers this year, reported Dan Gibson, citing panelists on a recent webinar led by The Aquaculture Roundtable Series (TARS). 

As a result of the growing prevalence of EHP and WFD, survival rates in India, Indonesia and Thailand have dropped significantly, meaning farmers are harvesting more small sizes, TARS panelists said.

According to Loc Tran, the director of Vietnam's ShrimpVet Laboratory, the two present such a damaging combination because they work in tandem. A pre-infection of EHP, which is only detectable on a microscopic level, makes shrimp more susceptible to contracting the far more visible WFD.

Read that in full here.

A new study of the coronavirus outbreak that took place in the Chinese capital Beijing earlier this summer, led by Beijing's Center for Disease Prevention and Control (CDC), has ultimately pointed to environment-to-human transmission via contaminated imported salmon as the most likely source. 

This is a turnaround from the CDC's original position in June, when it denied there was any evidence linking imported salmon to the outbreak. It will come as a blow to seafood suppliers in the country.

The study, published on Oct. 23, investigated the circumstances of the cluster of coronavirus cases reported in Beijing in June at the city's Xinfadi food market. You can read more on this here.

Dutch cold storage and logistics company Kloosterboer told Undercurrent it was "100% not possible" that seafood packages contaminated with the coronavirus in China came from its warehouse in Harlingen, Netherlands, as it has not shipped seafood to China in over six months.

On Wednesday of last week, China's General Administration of Customs said authorities detected coronavirus on packages of seafood from Kloosterboer's Daalimpex Harlingen warehouse. The warehouse is registered under the number 6614EG. 

Chinese authorities also identified three Russian fishing vessels as the source of seafood packages contaminated with the coronavirus. As a result of the positive finding, all consignments from Daalimpex and the three Russian vessels will be subject to increased Chinese import inspections for a week. After this, import inspections will return to normal.

Read this in full here.

At roughly the same time, Dutch authorities stopped issuing health certificates for exports of seafood destined for China in cases where the product originates from a third country such as Norway and Russia, Undercurrent sources told Louis Harkell.

The decision is set to disrupt the significant trade of frozen headed-and-gutted (H&G) cod and haddock shipped to China from Russia and Norway via Holland.

On Tuesday, Oct. 27, two industry sources based in Europe confirmed the change. According to a note from a company seen by Undercurrent, the decision followed pressure from Chinese authorities who complained about imported seafood from third countries carrying Dutch health certificates.

"From one day to the next the Chinese started to criticize this [practice]. According to them, Russian fish should be covered by a Russian export health certificate," the note said.

Read more on this here.

The lack of well-defined harvest control rules or effective tools to control catches put several tuna fisheries at risk of losing their sustainability certifications, two NGOs warned during the recent virtual Infofish 2021 tuna prelude event.

According to the Pew Charitable Trusts, harvest strategies, or "management procedures," represent the latest generation of science-based approaches to effective fisheries management.

Of the 19 global tuna stocks, only four achieve a passing score for "principle one" relating to the status of the stock, according to Tom Pickerell, the executive director of the Global Tuna Alliance, a group of major retailers.

Read more on this here.

In more M&A news, Dutch fishing giant Cornelis Vrolijk reached an agreement to buy the shares of processors Haasnoot Vis (which trades as Polaris) and Neptunus Seafood, based in Katwijk and Enschede respectively. Both have been sold by Haasnoot Food Family.

Cornelis Vrolijk has strengthened its position in the fishing chain in recent years, via the acquisition of several fish processing companies in the Netherlands and Belgium.

Haasnoot Vis and Neptunus are "excellent additions to these companies’ existing activities", Cornelis Vrolijk said. Read more here.

Lawyers for former Bumble Bee Foods CEO Christopher Lischewski argue that he didn't receive a fair trial in 2019 for price-fixing charges in part because one of the laws that the Department of Justice used to prosecute him reportedly violated his rights.

Additionally, among other claims, Lischewski's appellate attorney, John Cline, argues in a 70-page filing before the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit that district court judge Edward Chen erred in the instructions he gave the San Fransisco, California-based jury before their deliberations. 

The appeal takes issue with an aspect of the Sherman Antitrust Act, one of the country's principal laws regulating competition. The Sherman act prohibits "unreasonable" restraints on trade but it also includes a "per se" rule that defines some acts like price-fixing as "conclusively proven to be unreasonable", the appeal states. 

You can read this in full here.

As UK salmon brand Sea Smoked launches what it says is the UK's first completely plastic-free, commercial smoked salmon line this month, co-founder and managing director Dan Pawson told Undercurrent it expects to see rapid sales growth.

While its initial launch has been with high-end UK retailer Booths, it is already in talks with "most of the major retailers", who are "all very interested", he said. "Right now all supermarkets are having to pledge to move to become more plastic-free, so it's a big opportunity."

Sea Smoked is backed by industry veteran Jonathan Brown and, like snack product Sea Chips, is produced at Brown's Grants Smokehouse plant in Cumbria, using materials designed by Pawson's firm and to its specifications. Read more on this here.

And finally, Norway's Stolt-Nielsen has sold its loss-making US caviar farm to an upcoming rival in the state of California.

Eugene Fernandez, president of Hyde Road Agricultural Associates, confirmed to Undercurrent he closed a deal to acquire the Elverta, California-based Sterling Caviar farm earlier this week.

Stolt, an Oslo stock exchange-listed shipping group with an aquaculture division, listed Sterling Caviar for sale in its recent Q3 results.

Sterling Caviar, which is reportedly the largest caviar producer in North America, had assets of $7.44 million and liabilities of $2.19m, according to the Stolt Q3 report. Stolt reported an impairment loss of $8.66m on Sterling.

title: In appeal, Lischewski argues 2019 trial violated his constitutional rights
content:
Lawyers for former Bumble Bee Foods CEO Christopher Lischewski argue that he didn't receive a fair trial in 2019 for price-fixing charges in part because one of the laws that the Department of Justice used to prosecute him reportedly violated his rights.

Additionally, among other claims, Lischewski's appellate attorney, John Cline, argues in a 70-page filing before the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit that district court judge Edward Chen erred in the instructions he gave the San Fransisco, California-based jury before their deliberations. 

The appeal takes issue with an aspect of the Sherman Antitrust Act, one of the country's principal laws regulating competition. The Sherman act prohibits "unreasonable" restraints on trade but it also includes a "per se" rule that defines some acts like price-fixing as "conclusively proven to be unreasonable", the appeal states. 

Lischewski's attorneys repeatedly argued at trial that there was no evidence that price-fixing occurred in the sector. Additionally, any collusion between other tuna executives -- which his lawyers said Lischewski lacked knowledge of -- did not cause harm to consumers, the said. But Chen's decision to allow the use of the "per se" rule meant that even if no harm occurred, the jury couldn't consider the "reasonableness" of the accusation against him. And that was a violation of Lischewski's constitutional rights, the appeal argued.

"By precluding Lischewski from presenting evidence of reasonableness and deciding the 'unreasonable' element as a matter of law, the district court violated Lischewski's Fifth Amendment right to due process and his Sixth Amendment right to have a jury determine each element of the offense," the appeal stated.

Lischewski argued similarly in a June opinion piece written for Undercurrent News.

Additionally, the appeal also argued that Chen "erred" in the instructions he gave to the jury.

"Unlike most offense instructions, standard conspiracy instructions emphasize what the government does not have to prove and what does not constitute a defense," the appeal stated. "The district court instructed the jury on these usual points. But the court went further."

Chen should not have read additional instructions discussing possible defenses to the charge, the appeal argues.

"None of these instructions should have been given. In the absence of a contrary defense argument, there was no need to tell the jury, again and again, what the government did not have to prove and what did not constitute a defense. The instructions served only to suggest that the government's burden was easily satisfied," the appeal stated.

The Department of Justice has not yet responded to Lischewski's appeal.

Price-fixing trial

After a month-long trial, Lischewski was convicted on a count of price-fixing on Dec. 3, 2019, a scandal dor the sector that also netted guilty pleas from Bumble Bee and rival StarKist & Co, which is owned by South Korea's Dongwon Enterprise. Thai Union Group-owned Chicken of the Sea International also participated in the price-fixing, which prosecutors said occurred from 2010 to 2013, but cooperated in exchange for amnesty.

During the 2019 trial, prosecutors relied heavily on the testimony of two former Bumble Bee vice-presidents, Walter Cameron and Kenneth Worsham and a former StarKist executive, Stephen Hodge, as well as former Chicken of the Sea International CEO, Shue Wing Chan, who was protected from prosecution due to his company's amnesty agreement. The other three executives pleaded guilty to price-fixing charges but have yet to be sentenced.

During the trial, Cameron testified that Lischewski directed him to reach out to Cameron's friend and former Bumble Bee coworker, Chuck Handford, who in 2010 was working for StarKist in an effort to broker a "truce" between the two canners' "price wars" of aggressive competition during the 2010 period.

Elliot Peters, the lead defense attorney for Lischewski, contested this claim, arguing that pricing data and internal Bumble Bee emails from the period showed vibrant competition, not collusion. The next year, 2011, was the true "price war", and was a challenging year for all three canners as albacore and skipjack prices saw steep increases, Peters claimed. 

Handford was never charged with a crime and did not testify at trial. In addition to Lischewski's own testimony that he was not aware of his subordinates' collusion, the defense also presented evidence from Yale University economist Joseph Levinsohn, who presented data that prices charged to consumers during the conspiracy period were lower than what they had been previously when the higher production cost of tuna was taken into account. 

Lischewski could have faced a $1 million fine and up to 10 years in prison but Chen sentenced him to three years and four months and fined him $100,000. Lischewski is currently incarcerated at United States Penitentiary Tuscon in the state of Arizona, according to prison records.

title: Uncontrolled catching puts several tuna fisheries at risk of losing certifications
content:
The lack of well-defined harvest control rules or effective tools to control catches put several tuna fisheries at risk of losing their sustainability certifications, two NGOs warned during the recent virtual Infofish 2021 tuna prelude event.

According to the Pew Charitable Trusts, harvest strategies, or "management procedures," represent the latest generation of science-based approaches to effective fisheries management.

Of the 19 global tuna stocks, only four achieve a passing score for "principle one" relating to the status of the stock, according to Tom Pickerell, the executive director of the Global Tuna Alliance (GTA), a group of major retailers.

During his presentation at the online event, Pickerell showed a table produced by the International Seafood Sustainability Foundation (ISSF) to visualize the issue:

The Global Sustainable Seafood Initiative (GSSI)'s managing director, Herman Wisse, agreed that the lack of harvest strategies and controls is a risk to the fisheries' sustainability status.

During his presentation at the same virtual event, Wisse pointed out that "if these measures are not implemented within the next two-to-three years, many of the tuna certification stocks that are certified will lose their certification", referring to the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC)'s criteria regarding harvest strategy and control.

Those standards indicate that stocks are managed responsibly, ensuring the robustness and resilience of those stocks to the future, Wisse also said.

Pickerell said the assessment of many tuna fisheries to the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) fishery standards had identified the need for improvements to or adoption of well-defined harvest strategies and harvest controls.

Many MSC certified fisheries have a condition in place to adopt well-defined harvest controls, he added. These grant the certification but stipulate that conditions must be met within certain timeframes.

"If deadlines [on implementing harvest control rules] are missed, then the whole set of certified fisheries are at risk of losing their certification. And that would have a significant impact on the market, which is looking for these products," Pickerell also said. He referred to the December 2021 deadline for the large skipjack fisheries in the western central Pacific Ocean. 

"We need to enforce and implement those and get good management systems in place so that we can ensure the resilience of the supply. [...] And here is where we see that many of the fisheries are currently not meeting the requirements as outlined in the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)'s guidelines and reflected in these sustainability certification standards that are recognized by GSSI," Wisse said. He stressed that in 2015, less than 25% of the global tuna supply was certified. 

Wisse agreed with Pickerell that having good harvest strategies and harvest control rules in place is key to ensure that the stock status remains at a good level.

Wisse said it was important for industry groups to align their effort in pushing the regional fisheries management organizations (RFMOs) to implement strategies including harvest control bycatch mitigation measures and more. This year, GSSI had agreed with the ISSF and the GTA to align efforts in pushing the RFMOs to implement these strategies, Wisse noted.

Pickerell highlighted that the pandemic had caused most tuna RFMO meetings this year to be postponed to November or December and to take place virtually. "So it is very important for us to set out what we're calling an agenda-setting letter to remind the delegations that we understand the practicalities, we understand the challenges, but the fisheries are continuing, and sustainability is not stopping for anyone," he said.

title: Canadian harvesters march to challenge First Nation’s off-season lobster fishery
content:
Hundreds of commercial fishermen and their families gathered in downtown Yarmouth, a small coastal town in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia, on Friday to draw attention to their desire for a meeting with Bernadette Jordan, the country's fisheries minister, reports CTV News.

Tensions have been brewing in Nova Scotia since Sept. 17 when the Sipekne' katik, a Canadian First Nation group, launched a first-of-its-kind, rights-based lobster fishery in the middle of the country's most prolific lobster fishing area (LFA 34) during the offseason. The new fishery's launch follows some 21 years to the day after a Canadian Supreme Court ruling that affirmed a treaty right to hunt, fish and gather in pursuit of a "moderate livelihood", a term that was problematically not defined. 

The Sipekne' katik's fishery, which is about 250 kilometers west of the city Halifax, is granting licenses to band members who meet management plan requirements. Each Sipekne' katik license authorizes 50 traps per fisher, which are to be monitored. 

The group said it plans to take less than 5% of the lobster in the area.

Chief Mike Sack said he met with Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) Monday to discuss a moderate livelihood fishery plan, according to the news service.

"We went into discussions with the federal government and we showed them our plan," Sack said. "We weren't there to make a plan with them. We have a plan we're working towards self-governance and that's our focus and we're striving towards that."

But other harvesters are not thrilled. They marched peacefully on Friday with their families from the DFO office to town hall, where they met briefly with Yarmouth mayor Pam Mood, according to multiple news services.

"We've all fished in peace with the Mi'kmaq for 20 years and we all want the same issue, we want DFO at the table, to help us know what the future of our fishery is going to look like," harvester Joel Comeau reportedly said.

"We're not challenging rights, we're not challenging the Marshall decision, we just want to know, we want to know what our fishery is going to look like."

title: Another Chinese seafood firm warns of delisting risk
content:
Chinese seafood company Shandong Oriental Ocean risks being delisted by the Shenzhen stock exchange after a recent rule change.

Under new rules listed companies that have been "publicly condemned" by the exchange three times in the past 36 months could be delisted, the firm said in a filing last week.

It follows the delisting of Dalian-based seafood processor Dalian Tianbao Green Foods in June, due to fraud. Another firm, Zoneco Group, had its chairman and several executives fined for inflating assets in May.

Oriental Ocean, which is a seafood processor in Yantai, has been condemned twice by the Shenzhen stock exchange authority for financial irregularities, including losses of CNY 743m ($108m) on total revenues of CNY 725m, according to its financial filings.

The company's board of directors and management said the firm would "earnestly learn lessons and strengthen corporate governance".

In May of this year, Oriental Ocean sold China's first land-based salmon farm with recirculating aquaculture systems to Qingdao Conson Financial Holdings, Qingdao's state-backed investment fund, for CNY 226 million ($32m).

title: Editor’s recap: Trident shakeup; Clearwater sale frontrunner; Gorton asks Congress for aid
content:
Neil Ramsden, deputy editor of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

Our most-read stories last week all came from North America. 

Firstly, a shakeup at the top level at Trident Seafoods contained a few surprises to sources in the US sector, especially on the Alaskan operations side.  

Joe Bundrant, CEO of $2 billion-plus-turnover Trident, is making some significant changes in the management of the company's operations and also downstream on sales, sources told Undercurrent. Bundrant, who is the son of company founder Chuck, could not be reached for comment.

On the commercial side, Allen Kimball and Jeff Thompson, the head executives for Trident's international and domestic sales respectively, will be replaced by one person, a chief commercial officer, sources told Undercurrent. This hire is yet to be made, however. 

Vic Scheibert, Trident's veteran Alaska operations chief, is being replaced by Bob Masching, who joined the company from outside the seafood sector earlier this year. Scheibert, who was set to retire in 2021, will continue as an advisor to his replacement, who does not have experience with the Alaska seafood sector.

Read more here.

Late on Friday last week, Undercurrent broke the news that acquisitive Canadian food group Premium Brands Holdings is being tipped as the frontrunner for Clearwater Seafoods in a bid said to involve First Nations groups.

Cooke and the Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan (OTPP) are said to be the other two players who were in the mix for Nova Scotia, Canada-based Clearwater, North America's largest vertically integrated shellfish harvester, processor and distributor. When a process kicked off in March this year, Undercurrent sources said interest from Premium might well have been the driver. 

Clearwater has declined to comment. Read this story in full here.

Kim Gorton, the CEO of Slade Gorton, a Boston, Massachusetts-based processor, made the seafood industry's case on Wednesday for the US Congress to get a new stimulus bill done.

"We estimate that the seafood industry has about $2.2bn in outstanding bad debt, and other distributors have about $10bn," she told members of the US House of Representatives' Committee on Small Business during a hearing that started at 10 a.m. 

"Small businesses cannot absorb a deficit of this magnitude.  We need help to fix this," she added.

Democrats in the US House of Representatives this week rolled out yet another version of their coronavirus-related stimulus bill, calling it the HEROES Act again, and again asked for payments of $1,200 per individual or $2,400 per married couple who file jointly, plus $500 per eligible dependent. 

Recap this story here.

Shrimp packers in India have been forced to deal with a considerable shortage of raw material supply over the past month as a result of mass mortalities and early harvests in the country earlier in September, reported Dan Gibson.

The prices for larger shrimp, which have been steadily rising since the start of August, began to rise sharply over the past week as the country faces a raw material shortage.

"Since last two weeks there [has been] a drastic drop in raw material landing and pricing going up," Sebastian Jacob, CEO at Indian firm Continental Seafoods told Undercurrent. Find his take in full, and others', here.

US land-based farmer Atlantic Sapphire continues to grab headlines, this time by making its first commercial Atlantic salmon harvests from its facility in Homestead, Florida.

The amount of the harvest from its recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) "bluehouse" was not disclosed but the company said that it will ramp up volumes on a weekly basis to include Chef's Warehouse, which supplies restaurants, and grocers Giant Eagle, H-E-B, New Seasons Market, Publix, Safeway, Sobey's, Sprouts Farmers Market and Wegmans.

"Today we’re proud to finally start serving Americans delicious bluehouse salmon with quality and freshness they have not experienced before," CEO Johan Andreassen said in a press release. You can find out more on this here.

The US state of California's spiny lobster season will begin in less than one week, as planned, despite a request by some harvesters to close or postpone the fishery over fear of low prices caused by the US-China trade war and pandemic, reported Jason Huffman.

In an email sent to harvesters early last week, a copy of which was obtained by Undercurrent, three officials at the California Department of Fish & Wildlife (CDFW) advised that they don't have the authority to keep the fishery from its traditional start date of the first Wednesday in October (Oct. 7 this year). Nor do they have the ability to quickly authorize the sale by harvesters of processed tails.  

"Such a change would require action by the Fish and Game Commission that will likely require about a year to complete," wrote Jenny Hofmeister, an environmental scientist, Tom Mason, a senior supervisor, and Sonke Mastrup, a program manager, at CDFW's invertebrate management program.

This full story can be found here.

Bucking the trend for global shrimp production, Ecuador's output should be flat or even up by the end of 2020, believes consultant Gabriel Luna, of GLuna Shrimp. 

Speaking on a webinar held by India's Society of Aquaculture Professionals, Luna gave his "optimistic" outlook, proposing that projected exports should rise somewhere between 0% and 3% this year, to a maximum of around 1.44 billion pounds (653,626 metric tons).

Exports in 2019 were up 25% from the prior year, and for January through August 2020, they were up again, though only by 6%.

"When we look at this it looks like, okay, 'Ecuador is up 6%', but the reality is that we were on our way to being up 25% again. So even though we are still up, 6% is because, in the first two or three months of the year, we carried a lot of overproduction or a lot of extra volume that is still decreasing as the months go by."

Read the full story here.

Back in Europe, a court ruled Hendrik Nienhuis, the former CEO of the shrimp processor now known as Heiploeg International, should pay €13 million for orchestrating the North Sea shrimp price-fixing cartel that pushed the company into insolvency.

The court found the 83-year-old Nienhuis responsible for the illegal price agreements made by Heiploeg, Klaas Puul Beheer and some smaller buyers with fishermen between 2000 and 2009. Klaas Puul blew the whistle on the cartel, avoiding a fine. Heiploeg was fined €27m, going into administration and then being snapped up by Parlevliet and van der Plas in a controversial pre-pack deal.

Read the full story here.

Russian "tramper" transport vessels are no longer able to unload fish in the Chinese port of Qingdao due to coronavirus contamination concerns, sources told editor Tom Seaman.

The port of Qingdao, a major seafood importing and processing hub in the northeast province of Shandong, is closed for bulk cargo vessels carrying frozen food after local authorities detected two asymptomatic COVID-19 infections in port workers. This closure covers trampers used to transport pollock, salmon, and other fish from Russia to China, two suppliers, and two Chinese processors told Undercurrent.

Qingdao's port remains open for containers, sources said.

The "chaos" in Qingdao means Russian companies are having to re-route shipments of headed and gutted (H&G) pollock to Dalian, another significant northeast China seafood hub in Liaoning province, they said.

Read this in full here.

A vessel owned by Norebo Holding has been blocked for a month by China after traces of coronavirus were linked to packages of pollock and pelagic fish.

Fishing vessel Vladimir Starzhinsky, a 105-meter trawler owned by Norebo's Far East subsidiary Roliz, was suspended on Saturday by Chinese customs in the eastern coastal province of Shandong. A transport vessel not owned by Norebo, Crystal Africa, was also suspended. 

Sergey Sennikov, the Russian fishing and processing giant's head of external relations and sustainability, told Undercurrent the contamination likely happened in China, however -- read it here.
