title: Premium Brands, First Nations bid seen as frontrunner for Clearwater
content:
Acquisitive Canadian food group Premium Brands Holdings is being tipped as the frontrunner for Clearwater Seafoods in a bid said to involve First Nations groups, sources told Undercurrent News.

Coronavirus could disrupt Clearwater sale, but doesn’t change founders’ intent

Cooke and the Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan (OTPP) are said to be the other two players who were in the mix for Nova Scotia, Canada-based Clearwater, North America's largest vertically integrated shellfish harvester, processor and distributor. When a process kicked off in March this year, Undercurrent sources said interest from Premium might well have been the driver.

Premium, which has acquired the likes of Ready Brothers Seafood and Maine Coast Shellfish in the last two years as part of a plan to build CAD 1bn turnover seafood division, is said to have teamed with two First Nations groups on its bid. 

The two groups linked to the Premium bid are the Membertou First Nation of Nova Scotia and Miawpukek First Nation of Newfoundland and Labrador, sources said. Membertou, based on Cape Breton Island, agreed on a separate deal Sept. 8 to buy two of Clearwater's eight lobster licenses for CAD 25m ($18.9m). 

There has also been speculation that OTPP is or was working with First Nations on its bid, although Undercurrent has been unable to get more information on this. Sources have even linked Membertou to also working with OTPP earlier in the process. 

It's not clear if Premium is in exclusive talks for Clearwater, which is being advised on the sale by RBC Capital Markets and Antarctica Advisors. One source said Premium is, indeed, exclusive. Another, however, said other parties are still in play. It's thought Cooke and OTPP were still in the process until recently. A selection of the bid to go exclusive with supposed to take place this week. 

Clearwater’s Risley open to foreign buyers as Canadian interest grows

It's thought bids are in the CAD 1 billion ($750 million) range, sources told Undercurrent. In 2019, Clearwater reported sales of around CAD 620m and adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) of CAD 104m, so a multiple of around 10x.

The acquisitive Premium, led by CEO George Paleologou, is said to have been interested in buying Clearwater for several years. So has Cooke, one of the most proactive dealmakers in seafood. In 2011, Cooke tried a hostile takeover of Clearwater. 

Spokespeople for Cooke, Premium, Membertou and Miawpukek did not respond to requests for comment from Undercurrent. Ian Smith, CEO of Clearwater, also did not respond to a request for comment. Brendan Paddick, who heads the committee advising Clearwater's shareholders on the deal, declined to comment.  

A spokesperson for OTPP, which moved into seafood with a deal for Candian mussel farmer Atlantic Aqua Farms in 2017 and has $131bn of assets under management, declined to comment. 

John Risley and Colin and Mickey MacDonald, who control around 60% of Clearwater's shares, did not respond to requests for comment. Risley and the MacDonald brothers built the company up from selling Nova Scotia lobsters from the back of a truck.

Quin-Sea, Clearwater JV processing plant wins necessary approval in Canada

Following the publication of this article, Clearwater issued a press release stating that the company "continues to advance the strategic review process with its financial advisors to identify, review and evaluate a broad range of potential strategic alternatives available to it with a view to continuing to enhance shareholder value.

"The process is continuing in earnest and no timeline for its completion has been currently defined," the company said. "There can be no assurance that any such strategic alternatives will ultimately lead to a transaction."

Run of seafood deals 

Premium has been on a run of seafood deals of late. Most recently, it inked a deal to buy Toronto, Ontario-based Allseas Fisheries, one of the largest seafood distributors in the country. Premium paid CAD 139m ($106.7m) for Allseas and Canadian soup and fillings maker Global Gourmet but did not break out the specific purchase price for each deal.

Clearwater will be a considerably more expensive catch for Premium, which snowballed through acquisitions to CAD 3.8bn in sales and CAD 290m in EBITDA for the 12 months to the end of June 2020.

The Canadian fishing company, a big player in species such as clams, coldwater shrimp, scallops and lobster, traded at CAD 6.05 on the Toronto stock exchange at the opening on Oct. 2. This is the highest level since early 2008 and gives a market capitalization of CAD 394.15m.

However, Undercurrent sources and analysts covering the company previously said a sensible valuation for the business would be in the 8-12x EBITDA range, so around the CAD 1bn mark.

title: Court rules former Heiploeg boss should pay €13m over shrimp price-fixing
content:
A court has ruled Hendrik Nienhuis, the former CEO of the shrimp processor now known as Heiploeg International, should pay €13 million for orchestrating the North Sea shrimp price-fixing cartel that pushed the company into insolvency.

Bencis in talks to sell Shore EU shrimp ops to Sykes, Costa Rica organic arm to local team

On Monday, a court found the 83-year-old Nienhuis responsible for the illegal price agreements made by Heiploeg, Klaas Puul Beheer and some smaller buyers with fishermen between 2000 and 2009, RTL Nieuws reported.

Klaas Puul blew the whistle on the cartel, avoiding a fine. Heiploeg was fined €27m, going into administration and then being snapped up by Parlevliet and van der Plas (P&P) in a controversial pre-pack deal.

“The liability procedure against Nienhuis is the final piece in the bankruptcy of Heiploeg,” said Pieter Lettinga of Dorhout Advocaten, the law firm acting as the Heiploeg bankruptcy trustee.

Nienhuis is appealing against the verdict, his lawyer Peter Hoekstra told RTL Nieuws. Ultimately, the court will determine what Nienhuis has to pay. Undercurrent News could not immediately reach Nienhuis for comment.

Heiploeg owed over €100m to creditors before the pre-pack deal with P&P, according to the report from RTL Nieuws.

In an attempt to recover money for creditors, Lettinga and colleague Gerard Breuker have gone after Nienhuis and eight Heiploeg directors and commissioners who they held responsible for the cartel and subsequent bankruptcy. The trustees reached a settlement of €3m with the other eight, RTL Nieuws reports.

Cornelis Vrolijk enhances focus on machine-peeled shrimp with stake in Dutch firm

Lettinga and Breuker see Nienhuis as the driver of the cartel, so did not want to settle. The €13m amount is around half the total fine for Heiploeg, as Nienhuis was Heiploeg's chairman for roughly half of the cartel period, until 2004.

The trustees already seized assets worth several million euros from Nienhuis last year.

Pre-pack case also not resolved  

An appeal over the bankruptcy and pre-pack sale of Heiploeg to P&P is also ongoing.

Around 90 employees ended up out of work and those who returned did so on less favorable terms, RTV Nord reports.

The unions objected to the bankruptcy process, which took place without their knowledge. After the Supreme Court approved the flash bankruptcy, this judgment will now be reviewed by the European Court of Justice.

Shore-backed Dutch shrimp supplier in administration after ‘perfect storm’

Telson administration

It's not been a good year for Nienhuis. Earlier this year, Telson, a venture focused on machine-peeled North Sea shrimp he was involved in with his son, Onno, went under. 

On March 11, Undercurrent reported Telson had gone into administration amid tough times in North Sea shrimp. Telson was 50% owned by Bencis Capital Partners under its Shore shrimp group. 

In May, Dutch seafood giant Cornelis Vrolijk acquired the former Telson plant from administration for its Kegge Garnalenhandel shrimp subsidiary. Then, on June 16, Cornelis Vrolijk nabbed an undisclosed stake in Garnalenpelcentrum (GPC) Kant, a company making and operating machines for peeling North Sea shrimp. 

GPC Kant rented space in the former Telson plant. The company had been contract peeling shrimp for Telson until March, when the latter firm went under.

title: CP Foods’ US-farmed shrimp will need to establish ‘premium’ niche
content:
With renewed interest in domestic production as a result of the pandemic, the entrance of Charoen Pokphand Foods (CP Foods) into the US with a land-based facility in Florida -- announced last September -- would appear to be well-timed.

CP Foods building land-based shrimp farm in Florida

However, as Robins McIntosh, senior vice president with CP Foods told Undercurrent News on its 'Global Shrimp Market Outlook' webinar, this domestically-produced shrimp will never be able to compete with Asian imports on price.

McIntosh told Undercurrent that CP Foods would be marketing its new shrimp as a fresh product, never frozen, in order to set apart as a separate commodity in the eyes of US consumers.

"It’s got to be separate," he said. "I don’t think, given all of the intricacies of working in the United States you’re going to be able to compete on price in the near future, and maybe even outside of the near future."

Even in the semi-tropical areas of the US, he noted, temperatures can be highly seasonal, meaning any shrimp farm will have to be contained indoors, along with the necessary expensive insulation.

"And then you’re having to create very intensive systems," he continued. "Today, there’s no super-intensive systems that don’t get chronic mortality and die-off during the cycle. We’re trying to create a system that will handle that, but it would have to be super intensive to cover the cost of the building to make it economical."

Compared to intensive poultry farming, where it's possible to produce one kilo per square meter per day within the building, with shrimp the best that can be achieved is 200 grams.

"But the building cost is the same. So it’s the building and then the intensification, and a lot of other technologies that still need to be refined," he said.

Nevertheless, McIntosh is hopeful that by cutting the time it takes to get vannamei to market from 120 days to just 50 days, improving feed conversion ratios and reducing mortalities, CP Foods will be able to significantly slash the cost of production.

"I think we can put a shrimp into the market at much lower prices than US-grown shrimp are being put there now -- $40 a kilo – so I’m hoping we can make a profit at maybe $15-$16 a kilo," he told Undercurrent. "But that’s not like the $5 a kilo that we would produce in Southeast Asia."

Jeff Sedacca, CEO of Sunnyvale Seafood Co -- a US division of China's Zhanjiang Guolian Aquatic Products -- agreed with McIntosh, noting their own difficulties at trying to get a price premium for vannamei shrimp produced in Texas.

"I completely agree with Robins – the key to this is you’re creating a new item or a different item," Sedacca said on Undercurrent's webinar. "The Kobe beef buyer is not comparing the price they’re paying for Kobe beef with the price they pay for a steak at Wallmart."

"So this [domestic shrimp] business will pick up, the customer is out there, but it’s not going to be a factor affecting the normal vannamei market."

CP's urban ambitions

At present, CP's Florida farm, built by subsidiary Homegrown Shrimp USA, remains just a pilot project for the Thai conglomerate. 

‘Exciting’ with the chance of ‘burnout’: CP Foods’ McIntosh details US shrimp plans

Currently, Homegrown has built one recirculating aquaculture system farming unit with a capacity for approximately 200 metric tons of vannamei shrimp a year, he said. With the 20 acre plot of land available, CP Foods is capable of building five such units capable of growing 1,000t of shrimp in total.

"The idea would be that this type of technology can go anywhere -- so it’s not on the coast, it can be on 20 acres near any urban center, and you could produce 1,000t of shrimp to produce fresh to an urban center and try to gain that premium," he told Undercurrent.

Further plans for this design would include building similar farms close to other urban centers in the US and Europe, producing shrimp at a price "that’s not competing with an import, but certainly at a price where a consumer would not mind paying it for a premium shrimp," he added.

Design for Charoen Pokphand Foods pilot land-based shrimp farm in Florida, US. Source: Presentation by Robins McIntosh, senior vice president at CP, at Infofish 2019, Bangkok, Thailand.

Earlier this year, McIntosh told Undercurrent CPF's initial investment in the Florida project would be in the range of $6m to $8m, though he hoped that it would produce cash flow quickly.

The shrimp will be grown in round tanks in a manner similar to the ones that CP uses for broodstock, as it expects the dynamics of water movement to be easier at a larger scale.

The first of these 500t tanks were understood to be on target to start stocking in May, while expansion will be dependent on how successfully the first unit surmounts biological and environmental challenges.

"If the biological test passes, the profitability is really outside our control. It depends on the market price, it depends on how its sales go. It will depend on things we really need to learn as we go," McIntosh told Undercurrent in February.

title: New court ruling sanctions Chilean salmon firm for delivery of false sea lice count
content:
The Court of Appeals of Puerto Montt has confirmed a ruling made by the Castro Court that fined salmon farmer Invermar with UTM 500 ($32,680) for delivering "unreliable information" to the Servicio Nacional de Pesca y Acuicultura (Sernapesca) regarding its sea lice count.

This comes after the same court confirmed last July a ruling by the Castro Court that issued a record fine of UTM 3,000 (approx $196,085) to another Chilean salmon farmer -- Nova Austral -- for delivering "unreliable information", Sernapesca noted.

For the national director of Sernapesca, Alicia Gallardo Lagno, "these judgments confirm the relevance of providing accurate information to Sernapesca so that we can take control measures that guarantee the sustainability of aquaculture in Chile".

She added the suspension of operations for up to two consecutive growing cycles could also apply.

title: Atlantic Sapphire plans to raise $100m to repay debt, expand
content:
Norwegian land-based salmon farmer Atlantic Sapphire plans to issue a private placement of its Oslo, Norway-listed shares in order to raise around $100 million to repay debt and fund its expansion, the company said.

The farmer said that the net proceeds of the private placement will be used to partially repay and cancel $50m existing credit facilities with DNB Bank, strengthen its balance sheet and fund "general corporate purposes" and finance the "acceleration of further expansion. 

The bookbuilding period to participate in the private placement opened today, Sept. 9, and closes Sept. 10 at 8 a.m. CEST. 

"The managers and the company may, however, at any time resolve to close or extend the bookbuilding period at their sole discretion and on short notice," the company said. 

Several members of Atlantic Sapphire's management team, including CEO Johan Andreassen, company co-founder Thue Holm, chief infrastructure and development officer Svein Taklo, chief operating officer Dharma Rajeswaran and board members Alexanders Reus, Andre Skarbo, Tone Bjonrnov have committed to buy shares in the private placement. 

At present, Atlantic Sapphire has about 4m fish swimming in its "bluehouse" under development in Homestead, Florida, and another million fish in its Denmark facility, adding up to a combined standing biomass of about 2,200 metric tons.

Atlantic Sapphire recently posted a loss of $31.58m during the first half of 2020, compared to $9.44m over the same period of 2019, as reported earlier by Undercurrent. The company had $10.81m in cash at the end of the period, compared to $65.71m at the end of June 2019.

Last month, the company said that the coronavirus pandemic is disrupting its US market launch but it plans to harvest fish in September for a "10,000+ store footprint".

Atlantic Sapphire said that the construction timeline for its Homestead recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) facility "has gradually extended" due to COVID-19 and "other unforeseen delays".

The company has seen immigration and labor access interruptions due to the pandemic but does not expect a long-term impact. The "delayed ability to operate the farm at full capacity" has pushed the company's "steady-state" phase one production level into the first quarter of next year.

At its Danish RAS site, the company expects to get to "steady-state" in the fourth quarter of 2020. Steady-state is defined as the equivalent of 9,500t (in head-on, gutted, or HOG) of annualized harvest volumes in phase one in the given period in the US, and 2,400t HOG annualized harvest volumes in Denmark. Atlantic Sapphire plans to harvest 1,000t (HOG) of salmon in the Florida RAS during the fourth quarter.

title: Lawsuit could make cod even more of a choke species for New England groundfish
content:
Groundfish harvesters in the Northeastern United States already face some of the lowest limits ever set in relation to how much Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua) they can catch in the Gulf of Maine and Georges Bank, but a lawsuit filed last week in a federal court could reduce them further and threaten fishing for other species, too.

The 46-page complaint, filed Aug. 28 in the US District Court in Washington, D.C., by the Boston, Massachusetts-based Conservation Law Foundation (CLF), charges commerce secretary Wilbur Ross, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), NOAA assistant administrator for fisheries Chris Oliver and NOAA’s National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) with having violated the Magnuson-Stevens Act (MSA) and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) when they approved and implemented “Framework Adjustment 59 to the Northeast Multispecies Fishery Management Plan”.

The final rule, published July 30 in the Federal Register, sets the combined acceptable catch limit (ACL) for Atlantic cod in the Gulf of Maine at 523 metric tons for the 2020, 2021 and 2022 seasons, 21% lower than what was allowed in the previous two years. It allows an ACL of 1,234t for cod in Georges Bank during the same periods, 29% less than the previous limit.

The Gulf of Maine. Map produced by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

But CLF instead would have NMFS reduce the limits to incidental bycatch only, thresholds that would still need to be defined but could result in the closing of all other groundfish harvests should they be quickly met.

Note that the 13 species in the New England groundfish fishery, including also haddock, Acadian redfish, yellowtail flounder, pollock, American plaice and white hake, accounted for nearly 180,000 metric tons of combined quota in 2020.

NMFS' rule was based on the recommendations of the New England Fishery Management Council (NEFMC), which was following the suggestions of its Scientific and Statistical Committee (SSC), a group of 16 mostly university scientists. The CLF argued that the panel wrongly put its okay behind Option A, a regulatory approach taken when stocks are healthy, and that hasn’t been the case for Atlantic cod stocks for a long time.

One of the SSC members, in a minority opinion, had argued instead for the use of Option C on Gulf of Maine cod, the approach that’s more appropriate for a troubled stock and consistent with allowing only an incidental bycatch limit. The council member suggested an allowable biological catch (ABC) – the number on which ACL is based -- of 450t for cod in the Gulf of Maine, roughly 100t less than the ABC relied upon in the final rule (552t). The minority opinion did not suggest an ABC for Georges Bank.

CLF’s complaint asks the court to give the agency six months to respond and to also force it to cover the cost of its lawsuit.

Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua). Credit: Podolnaya Elena/Shutterstock.com

 Bad timing

CLF’s lawsuit is not the first to challenge NMFS’s approach to managing the cod stocks in New England, and -- though one regulatory source maintained that the federal agency has previously prevailed -- the conservation group pointed Undercurrent to at least three important victories, in 1991, 1993 and again in 2014. 

Regardless, commercial harvesters in New England are none-too-pleased with the timing of the conservation group’s latest effort, given the challenges they’re facing in relation to the tight pandemic-afflicted seafood market.

“It’s a really difficult time,” said one of the members of the Sustainable Harvest Sector (SHS) who talked to Undercurrent under condition of anonymity. “Is the fishing of 100t really going to make or break Gulf of Maine cod?”

The source warned that reducing the amount of cod that can be caught to a bycatch limit would make it much more likely to accidentally reach the threshold and stop all commercial fishing in the area. Because there is such a small ACL for cod now, harvesters already are avoiding the species, focusing instead on more plentiful haddock and redfish, the source asserted.

The Carrabassett, one of the groundfish vessels acquired by Blue Harvest Fisheries from Carlos Rafael and refitted. Photograph courtesy of Blue Harvest Fisheries.

The SHS, which counts Blue Harvest Fisheries, a large New Bedford, Massachusetts-based groundfish harvester, among its members, includes two groups (SHS1 and SHS3), and both have rules intended to protect cod, explained Hank Soule, the sectors' manager.

Boats in both groups must maintain a minimum of 250lbs of cod quota to go fishing in the Gulf of Maine and they're also required to report back when any “hotspots”, or cod concentrations, are encountered, he said. The sectors then broadcast a notice to all member vessels to alert them of the location to be avoided.

SHS3 has a further requirement, said Soule: All boats in that sector are prohibited from fishing west of 70 degrees in the Gulf of Maine, covering the inshore fishery, as the area is where more than 75% of the Gulf of Maine cod is encountered.

Also, harvesters will often use special trawling nets with holes on the bottom to catch haddock and allow cod to escape, said Undercurrent's source, though Soule said the practice is neither encouraged nor discouraged in the SHS groups. 

"We just help ensure our fishermen are using and documenting gear types and catches with those gears as the law requires," he clarified.

Erica Fuller, one of the two CLF attorneys involved in the complaint, told Undercurrent  this week that her organization recognized that it was a tough time for New England’s commercial fishing industry, especially given the challenges inflicted by the COVID-19 pandemic, and it was not thrilled to be filing a lawsuit at this moment. She explained, however, that the MSA allows only 30 days to challenge new catch limit settings, and NMFS started that clock ticking with its publication in the Federal Register.

“We have empathy for the fishing industry,” Fuller told Undercurrent. “But if we don’t act now [against Framework 59], we’ll never be able to challenge it.”

Cod abundance was 'legendary'

CLF, meanwhile, has been focused on preserving Atlantic cod for more than 30 years, noting in its lawsuit how Peter Shelley, its senior counsel and vice president, has been a member since1983 and likes to fish for the species recreationally with his grandchildren.

The prosecution of Atlantic cod in New England is a long and sordid affair, as the complaint recounts.

Cod abundance in the area was “legendary” when the Europeans first arrived on North American shores, and early explorers told tales of how a fisherman could catch the fish by simply dipping a basket in the water. The species is believed to have driven colonial settlements, including the creation of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, and major industrial growth in the area for several hundred years.

However, the industrialization of the fishing fleet in the early 20th century led to a sharp and unhealthy increase in catches, and landings grew even further in the late 1950s when foreign distant-water fleets arrived.

“At the peak of foreign fishing in the 1960s, Northwest Atlantic groundfish removals reached around 2.5m metric tons per year, much of which was Atlantic cod,” the lawsuit recounted.

Then, in the 1980s, fishing mortality rates were two to three times the levels associated with maximum stainable yield, CLF said. “This meant the fishery was removing 50-70% of all adult cod each year.”

But it got even worse.

“The ‘historic lows’ in biomass of the 1980s identified at the time of the early stock assessments now, in hindsight, represent historic highs in the time period, and the most recently accepted assessment models estimate biomass in both Atlantic cod stocks to be less than 10% of target levels,” the complaint states.

Carlos Rafael gives a demonstration on how to cut cod at a festival in New Bedford, Massachusetts, in 2010. Image is a still from a YouTube video.

Atlantic cod is also notably the species that is believed to have been targeted the most by Carlos Rafael, the infamous “Codfather” of New Bedford, Massachusetts, was caught mislabeling some 782,000 fish between 2012 and 2015 in order to avoid catch limits. Rafael pled guilty to criminal charges and was sentenced to 46 months in federal prison, before later agreeing to a civil settlement that forced him to sell all of his commercial fishing vessels.

Keith Decker, the CEO of Blue Harvest, the company that purchased most of Rafael’s groundfish vessels, told Undercurrent in January that he has zero interest in catching cod until the stock is revived and would avoid the choke species as much as possible.

"Our vessels are specifically focused on haddock and redfish," he said at the time. "Most of the cod quota will remain in the water this year. We intentionally try not to catch cod."

Under MSA, passed in 1976, NMFS has a “mandatory duty” to rebuild fisheries in a time period that is “as short as possible” but “’not [to] exceed 10 years’, except where the biology of the stock, environmental conditions or an international agreement dictate otherwise”, CLF said in its lawsuit. That would require the Gulf of Maine cod stock to be rebuilt by 2024, and the Georges Bank cod stock by 2026, results that are not possible under the current course of actions being taken, the group argued.

title: Spanish tuna fleet enters full MSC assessment
content:
Spain's tuna fleet, grouped under the Association of Large Tuna Freezers (or AGAC) has entered Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) assessment.

AGAC also includes OPAGAC, or the organization of associated producers of large tuna freezers. There are 48 freezing tuna vessels linked to the association in all, fishing tuna in all the oceans where tropical tuna can be found. 

The associations represent companies including Grupo Albacora, Grupo Calvo, Jealsa, Grupo Garavilla, and five others.

Their vessels use purse seine gear to catch up to 8% of the world's total yellowfin, bigeye and skipjack tuna catches, from the Indian, Atlantic, and Pacific oceans, MSC said.

The fishery has been in a fisheries improvement project for five years, before deciding to enter MSC assessment. The audit will be carried out by independent assessor Lloyds Register in four distinct geographic areas covered by the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas; the Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission; the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission; and the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission.

The assessment will cover 12 different units defined by species, stock, and fishing area. Any units that pass the assessment process and are recommended for certification will be eligible to be licensed to use the MSC’s blue fish ecolabel, MSC explained.

"This will contribute to the achievement of the environmental objectives of the common fisheries policy and the international commitment of Spain towards sustainable exploitation of these important marine resources by the Spanish tuna fleet which is present in all the oceans," said the country's general fisheries secretary.

Laura Rodriguez, director of the MSC in Spain and Portugal, said AGAC was the first to ask for its entire global catch across three oceans to be assessed simultaneously.

"The assessment process will provide invaluable information which we have not had before on the sustainability levels of each of the tropical tuna species in each ocean. We are very pleased about AGAC’s decision to steadily improve its fishing practices over the years, and for now committing to a rigorous assessment process for environmental sustainability," she said.

AGAC managing director Julio Moron said that MSC assessment could now take more than a year, and that his organization knows "there is work yet to be done".

"We believe that reaching this far demonstrates the commitment of the fishers and shipowners of AGAC towards preservation of the marine environment on which depend our livelihoods and employment. We are fully committed to do whatever is in our hands to preserve our fishing activity with the least environmental impact possible and protecting the health of the tropical tuna stocks."

title: Camanchaca loses over 100,000 salmon in southern Chile
content:
An escape of salmon has taken place at a collection center in San Jose, in Chile's Los Lagos region, belonging to salmon farmer Salmones Camanchaca, the country's National Fisheries and Aquaculture Service (Sernapesca) said after carrying out an inspection.

According to the information collected by Sernapesca, the event occurred during the early morning of Aug. 27, with one cage affected. An estimated 124,309 salmon, weighing around 500 grams each, are thought to have been lost.

Sernapesca is verifying the state of the cage structures and nets through filming with the use of underwater equipment, fish count, and other means to determine the exact number of escaped fish. It has been monitoring the company's actions from the day the event was reported, as well as the application of contingency plans, it said.

Sernapesca also said it will determine the possible responsibilities and legal actions as appropriate.

Last month, Chile's Superintendencia del Medio Ambiente (the country's environmental superintendency, or SMA) fined Mowi CLP 5.3 billion ($6.68 million) over an escape that the company -- then named Marine Harvest -- suffered in the Los Lagos region back in 2018.

In the meantime, Chile's Undersecretariat of Fisheries and Aquaculture (Subpesca) has announced new regulations to prevent the sinking of cages and reduce the number of fish escapes in salmon farming. 

The decision came after Blumar Seafoods reported a mass escape at its farm in the Seno Reloncavi, also in Los Lagos, in late June, with 16 farming cages out of 18 affected due to adverse climate conditions.

The new regulations -- which should be released to the public soon -- will take into account all the elements that may damage or impact negatively salmon net cages, such as tides and tidal currents, winds and waves, among others.

title: Pandemic disrupts Atlantic Sapphire’s US launch
content:
The coronavirus pandemic is disrupting land-based salmon farmer Atlantic Sapphire's US market launch, but the company plans to harvest fish in September for a "10,000+ store footprint".

Atlantic Sapphire's first-half update, published to the Oslo stock exchange on Friday, states the construction timeline for its Homestead, Florida, recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) facility "has gradually extended" due to COVID-19 and "other unforeseen delays".

COVID-related delays of foreign workers behind Atlantic Sapphire’s early salmon cull

The company has seen immigration and labor access interruptions due to the pandemic but does not expect a long-term impact. The "delayed ability to operate the farm at full capacity" has pushed the company's "steady-state" phase one production level into the first quarter of next year.

At its Danish RAS site, the company expects to get to "steady-state" in the fourth quarter of 2020. Steady-state is defined as the equivalent of 9,500 metric tons (in head-on, gutted, or HOG) of annualized harvest volumes in phase one in the given period in the US, and 2,400t HOG annualized harvest volumes in Denmark. Atlantic Sapphire plans to harvest 1,000t (HOG) of salmon in the Florida RAS during the fourth quarter.

On the plus side, the COVID-19 "reality highlights [the] advantages of local production and lean, integrated operations", said Atlantic Sapphire.

The Land-based Salmon Handbook
View report

The company is "well-positioned" for the market trend towards value-added products versus traditional fish counter retail. Atlantic Sapphire is making additional investments to produce value-added and ready to eat products in addition to HOG and fillets. Also, the company has inked a supply deal with Acme Smoked Fish Corp, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

Atlantic Sapphire also expects the cost of airfreight from Europe and Chile to the US to remain "higher for longer", adding to its cost edge over traditional farmers.

The company expects to get a premium from its "egg to plate" traceability. Its "differentiated" product, which it is branding as produced in a "Bluehouse", will achieve pricing "decoupled" from pandemic-related spot market volatility, the company said.

The company posted a loss of $31.58 million for the first half of 2020, compared to $9.44m over the same period of 2019. Atlantic Sapphire had $10.81m in cash at the end of the period, compared to $65.71m at the end of June 2019.

Atlantic Sapphire boss announces RAS smoked salmon line with Acme

Emergency harvest review

Atlantic Sapphire's first-half report also addresses the July 28 "emergency harvest" at the Florida RAS facility. As a result of the event, approximately 200,000 salmon with a total weight of approximately 400t (HOG) were harvested.

Other grow-out systems in the RAS facility were unaffected. "The exact chain of events is still under investigation and preliminary findings do not indicate intoxication or disease as the cause of the event," the company said.

Atlantic Sapphire believes "disruptive construction work close to the operating environment acutely stressed the fish through loud sounds and severe vibrations".

The "challenges of delayed construction and commissioning of critical components", in part because of the coronavirus pandemic, have resulted in increased operational risk and limit the tools the company "has to deal with non-conformities", it said.

Atlantic Sapphire emergency harvest spooks market ahead of launch

Atlantic Sapphire "believes that the event would have likely been mitigated if the permanent fish movement system would have been fully commissioned", it said. The company is still assessing the complete financial impact of the event, including insurance proceeds.

Re-fi for phase two?

Atlantic Sapphire plans to develop the design and capital expenditure budget in Q1 of 2021, with construction starting in Q2.

In light of the phase one construction and "steady-state" harvest delays, Atlantic Sapphire is looking into options to refinance its long-term debt with DNB at more favorable terms for phase two.

This includes replacing the $30m short term debt facility before its Nov. 30, 2020 expiry date "through either a loan facility, bond issue, or any other type of debt or equity capital market transaction", the company said.

On April 21, 2020, the group amended the credit facility with DNB to increase the aggregate amount from $86m to $210m. A lot of financing will be needed for Atlantic Sapphire to hit its goals, it said.

Atlantic Sapphire plans to scale up to the production of 90,000t of salmon a year on its current site (see below), which would supply almost a quarter of the current consumption in the US, according to Kontali statistics. Further on, the company plans for output of 220,000t by 2031.

title: Consumer groups square off against US canners in tuna price-fixing appeal
content:
A trio of consumer groups has waded into a long-running legal fight between the 'big three' US canners accused of price-fixing and the distributors, wholesalers, restaurants, retailers and end-users who bought tuna from them.

In amicus briefs filed Aug. 21 with the San Francisco, California-based United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, three groups -- Public Citizen, the American Antitrust Institute, and the Committee to Support the Antitrust Laws (COSAL) -- arguing against the canners' appeal of a lower court judge's decision to certify the hundreds of individual lawsuits into common classes. 

The canners have argued in their appeal that the July 2019 decision from district court judge Janis Sammartino to certify the classes -- accepting that the facts of the hundreds of individual cases against the canners are common enough to be treated together -- sounds a "death knell" for the future of the ongoing class-action lawsuit.

The canners have said Sammartino's ruling was made in error, in part because the overcharges that the different members of the classes say they experienced "differed wildly" and the economic models used to estimate them were flawed. Additionally, it hasn't been proven that every member of each class suffered damages, which is needed before class certification is granted, the canners' lawyers have argued.

However, in their amicus briefs, the consumer took issue with those assertions.

"Were this court to reverse the District Court’s grant of class certification, it would not only affect the members of the certified classes but could also thwart the ability of consumers and other victims of future anticompetitive violations from seeking redress," COSAL stated in its brief.

It added that "US competition policy could be seriously undermined if antitrust plaintiffs could not use representative evidence but were required to show harm to every class member under [civil procedures] at the class certification stage". 

Costly suits

The first civil suits against Bumble Bee Foods, Dongwon Enterprise-owned StarKist & Co., and Chicken of the Sea, a brand owned by Thai Union Group's Tri-Union Seafoods, began in 2015 as allegations emerged that the companies had engaged in a scheme to fix canned tuna prices.

Plaintiffs have been sorted into four "tracks" depending on how they purchased tuna from the canners and the class certification ruling allows each track to have common legal counsel and pool many plaintiffs' resources together to pay the costly bills for expert witnesses, lawyers fees and other expenses that come in class-action litigation. 

The large wholesalers and distributors who dealt directly with the canners are known as "direct purchasers" with a second track of direct purchasers including large buyers such as Walmart with separate lawsuits known as "direct action" plaintiffs.

Lawsuits in two other tracks, the "commercial food preparers" including restaurants and retailers, and individual consumers known as "end-payers", include plaintiffs who purchased from the canners' tuna indirectly.

The class-action suits have already had a major impact on the US canners. In November, Bumble Bee filed bankruptcy in Delaware and is set to be bought by its longtime tuna supplier FCF Co. Bumble Bee has cited the class action suits as well as a $25 million fine from the Department of Justice as two major factors behind the bankruptcy. 

Additionally, Starkist, which judge Edward Chen fined $100m last year after its guilty plea to price-fixing charges, indicated at the time that it too could file for bankruptcy or move its operations from American Samoa, which would result in mass layoffs.

Thai Union, which escaped criminal liability because it acted as a whistleblower to the DOJ, has set aside some $104m to pay for its part in the price-fixing. Most of the related lawsuits have now been settled, the company has said.

title: Mowi looks to divest 50% stake in wellboat firm
content:
Mowi is looking at divesting its 50% stake in wellboat owner DESS Aquaculture Shipping, it has announced.

In 2016 Mowi entered into an aquaculture shipping joint venture with Deep Sea Supply (DESS). "Mowi’s reason for entering into aquaculture shipping was a response to the growing demand for wellboat capacity and to reduce cost," it said.

DESS Aquaculture Shipping has developed into a highly competitive wellboat company with 10 vessels in operation, two under construction, and another two to be contracted shortly, it added.

"Mowi’s stake in DESS Aquaculture Shipping has from the start been defined as a non-core asset. [It] has now reached a critical size and is well-positioned for further growth."

Mowi's board has therefore initiated a potential divestment of the 50% stake, it said.

In July 2020, DESS Aquaculture Shipping took delivery of the new wellboat Aqua Havsoy, which will start on a charter with Mowi's northern Norway region. The vessel has a capacity of 3,900 cubic meters.

DESS Aquaculture Shipping also owns and operates the Aqua Tromoy, the “largest and most technologically advanced vessel to ever serve the Canadian aquaculture industry”.

That 77-meter ship has a hold capacity of 3,000 cubic meters of water, and serves Mowi Canada West, a 45,000 metric ton per year operation, "moving fish from site to site and to provide environmentally friendly fish health treatments".

title: Chile fines Mowi record $6.7m over 2018 Los Lagos escape
content:
Chile's Superintendencia del Medio Ambiente (the country's environmental superintendency, or SMA) has fined Mowi CLP 5.3 billion ($6.68 million) over an escape that the company -- then named Marine Harvest -- suffered in the Los Lagos region back in 2018.

SMA said this was the highest fine that has been issued for a single incident, and claimed the escape was deemed "very serious due to the fact that irreparable environmental damage was found as a result of the massive escape of salmon".

The body claims Mowi's facilities were not up to scratch, a fact which allowed more than 690,000 farmed salmon to escape.

SMA chief Cristobal De La Maza said the fine "closes a long and complete investigation process on our part".

"We want to give the signal that all those companies that do not respect the regulations and, in addition, infringe them causing environmental damage, as in this case, will be sanctioned in a proportional manner."

However, Mowi does not consider the case closed, with the firm planning to appeal the decision. 

It has noted the public prosecutor's investigation of the accident concluded there was no evidence of negligence or omission by the company. The escape was caused solely by unusual weather patterns, it said.

"With respect to this preliminary pronouncement by the environmental authority, Mowi Chile once again reiterates its firm conviction that the accident and fish escape did not cause any environmental damage. This is shown by the background information and numerous scientific studies performed after the accident, and which was confirmed by the health authority."

Mowi also pointed out that a large number of the escaped salmon were caught by third parties and sold on the informal market, "which unfortunately was not recorded by the
authorities".

"Mowi Chile did everything within its reach to recapture the fish, in addition to the captures by the informal fishing sector. It must also be considered that there was a decrease in the number of salmon as a consequence of natural predators, particularly the well-known overpopulation of sea lions in the area."

After the escape, follow-up investigations continued for over a year and found there were "practically no Atlantic salmon in the area or adjacent rivers", Mowi added.

The public prosecutor’s office also concluded there was no background information revealing fault or omission by the company. It therefore recommended dropping the case against Mowi in August 2019, a suggestion approved by courts.

"Mowi Chile will continue to participate actively in the areas where it operates, especially during these difficult times faced by the world and the country as a result of the public health crisis. Mowi Chile will continue to work on being a good neighbor and
creating jobs for the communities in southern Chile."

title: Editor’s recap: Walton behind VC on seafood push; The future of small-scale RAS; Ocean Fish plans retail growth
content:
Neil Ramsden, deputy editor of Undercurrent News, brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

In a refreshing change, several of the most-read stories of last week didn't revolve around COVID-19. 

Our top story, by editor Tom Seaman, was on the fact that the billionaire grandson of Walmart founders Helen and Sam Walton is a backer of a venture capital fund looking to invest over $100 million into sustainable seafood companies.

Lukas Walton, the 33-year-old son of John and Christy Walton, is listed online as the owner of S2G Advisors, which is doing business as S2G Ventures.

Lukas -- who Bloomberg ranks as the 53rd most wealthy person in the world with a net worth of $20.8 billion -- is listed with Chicago's Department of Business Affairs and Consumer Protection as S2G's owner. Walton is also listed as the president of another entity based in the city named Education, Agriculture and Technology.

Meanwhile, the rise of land-based aquaculture over the past 10 years is a trend that looks likely to accelerate following the pandemic, as more consumers turn to local sources of food production. And while Atlantic salmon is currently grabbing the headlines, the relative ease with which land-based systems can be altered to suit different species begs the inevitable question: what's next? 

Dan Gibson sought to answer this. While the pandemic has seemingly demonstrated the case for huge recirculating aquaculture systems farms in pivotal markets, veteran Canadian RAS designer John Holder and US equipment manufacturer Henning Gatz believe there is a clear need for smaller, more flexible farming facilities.

Then, I wrote about a UK processor making its bid to be the latest in the country to grow and consolidate into a major player. 

UK fishing and processing company Vistgate -- which trades as Ocean Fish -- has significantly expanded its production facilities with the purchase of a new factory, managing director Leigh Genge told me.

"We've been wanting to build a second facility for several years -- not just for the increased capacity, but also to streamline and to separate our bulk wholesale and retail businesses more efficiently," he said.

However, opportunity knocked last year when a meat processing unit on the same industrial estate as Ocean Fish's St Austell, Cornwall-based facility became available. The factory had passed from 2 Sisters Food Group to meat firm Kepak in 2018, then in 2019 it was divested again by the new owner. The plant had mainly served retailer Tesco, and Ocean Fish was able to snap it up. 

Maria Feijoo continued her excellent coverage of Ecuador's farmed shrimp picture, reporting that Ecuador's average export volume is expected to fall to 90 million pounds per month during the second half of 2020, which would be 40-50% less than during the first half of the year.

"Ecuador exported about 120m lbs of shrimp in June, a fall of about 20% in comparison with May figures. Besides, the country exported even less volume of this product in July, about 95m lbs of which only 20m went directly to China," said the head of Ecuador's national chamber of aquaculture, Jose Antonio Camposano.

"This means that only between 20 and 30% of our production ended up in the Asian country in July, when China is often the leading importer of this product, accounting for between 62% and 65% of our shrimp exports."

Maria also wrote that small Ecuadorian suppliers expect prices to increase in the coming weeks gradually, now that China has lifted the ban it imposed on the last of three whose export licenses were suspended since July.

"This ban has had an equal or larger impact than the COVID-19 crisis had in our businesses all this time. It has negatively affected our products' reputation and drove a sharp fall in prices, which are still very low," a small Ecuadorian shrimp producer, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told Undercurrent. 

Thai Union Group-backed restaurant chain Red Lobster Seafood Co is facing the "most challenging time" in its history, its CEO has said.

The Orlando Sentinal reported that Kim Lopdrup described 2020 in a statement as the most challenging time "Red Lobster has faced in our 52 years of operation". 

The 700-restaurant operator borrowed $380m and still has $355m outstanding, which comes due in July 2021, ratings agency Moody's Investor Service said in a June statement. Earlier this year, Moody's cut Red Lobster's credit rating to Caa1, defined as "poor".

A subsidiary of Aleutian Pribilof Island Community Development Association (APICDA) has filed a lawsuit against Trident Seafoods over the latter's alleged refusal to buy a 25% stake of a salmon and whitefish processing joint venture in the US state, editor Tom revealed last week.

The lawsuit, filed in court for the Western District of the State of Washington, alleges Trident first overspent on renovating the False Pass Seafoods JV and then refused to purchase APICDA Joint Ventures' remaining chunk of shares in the plant for close to $6m.

Trident has not operated the plant in the COVID-19 pandemic-hit 2020 salmon season, working instead with Peter Pan Seafoods on a contract processing arrangement, as first reported by Undercurrent. Silver Bay Seafoods has also built a massive plant in the remote community of False Pass.

Lower than expected landings of pink and chum salmon in Russia and the US state of Alaska have greatly tightened supply and are throwing up uncertainties for markets, sources told Jason Smith.

The combined pink catch from Russia and Alaska, by far the world's largest producers, totaled some 523,000 metric tons in 2019 and 576,000t in 2018, a veteran salmon sector source said. As of Aug. 5, roughly 152,000t of pinks had been landed in both countries, although that figure has somewhat improved since, particularly in Alaska where 12 million pinks were landed in the past week. 

"Because both Russia and Alaska have had such strong pink runs the past two years, many people, unfortunately, do not believe or know about the current situation," the source said.

In the UK, Gordon Blackshaw, the longtime foodservice sales director of Sykes Seafood, has left the company. Sykes has been forced to make changes in its foodservice department due to the coronavirus pandemic, the company's CEO Alan Dale told Undercurrent.

Finally, the administration of US president Donald Trump did more than raise questions about forced labor in the South Pacific Ocean's tuna fishing industry on Tuesday last week when it announced an import-banning withhold release order (WRO) against the Da Wang, a Taiwan-owned distant water vessel. 

It gave Greenpeace another device with which to continue pressuring tuna canning giant Bumble Bee Foods into being more transparent about its suppliers.

All three of the tuna longline vessels that have been slapped with WROs by US Customs and Border Protection since February 2019 are Taiwanese-owned or flagged, and two of the three were linked either directly or indirectly to the Fong Chun Formosa Fishery Company, the Taiwanese tuna trader that bought San Diego, California-based Bumble Bee out of bankruptcy in January for $928m.

title: Red Lobster sees its ‘most challenging time’ as $355m loan looms
content:
Thai Union Group-backed restaurant chain Red Lobster Seafood Co is facing the "most challenging time" in its history, its CEO has said.

The Orlando Sentinal reported that Kim Lopdrup described 2020 in a statement as the most challenging time "Red Lobster has faced in our 52 years of operation”. 

The 700-restaurant operator borrowed $380 million and still has $355m outstanding, which comes due in July 2021, ratings agency Moody's Investor Service said in a June statement. Earlier this year, Moody's cut Red Lobster's credit rating to Caa1, defined as “poor”.

Red Lobster has responded to the crisis by ramping up COVID-19 prevention measures to make diners feel safe in its restaurants and offering free delivery on orders larger than $30 placed on the company’s website or app Monday through Thursday, Lopdrup said.

“Our priority is to make sure Red Lobster is one of the survivors of this crisis,” Lopdrup said. “While there are many unknowns, I am optimistic about Red Lobster’s future. We have a great team, and I’m proud of how nimbly they reacted to a fast-changing situation.”

Earlier this month FSR Magazine reported, citing Debtwire, that Red Lobster had hired advisor Guggenheim to explore strategic options.

In May three analysts covering Thai Union told Undercurrent News the company's 25% stake in Red Lobster was set to go on eating away at its profits.

The Thai giant saw increased sales, but a fall in earnings and profits, for Q1 2020 -- with its stake in Red Lobster pointed to as significant negative. Income from investments in associates swung from a Q1 2019 gain of THB 347m ($10.8m) to a 2020 loss of THB 18m -- "mainly due to Red Lobster, along with other businesses in the US, being ordered to close down all of its outlets during the COVID-19 pandemic".

title: Nomad to spend $500m buying up its own stock, ‘sharpen M&A focus’
content:
European frozen food giant Nomad Foods -- owner of the Iglo, Findus and Birds Eye brands -- plans to purchase up to $500 million of its own ordinary shares, suggesting the move will precede a flourish of new M&A activity.

The UK-based company, which is publicly traded on the New York Stock Exchange, announced its strategy along with the results of its second quarter, in which it garnered €599m ($711m) in revenue during the three-month period that ended June 30, an increase of 11.4% over the same period in 2019.

Nomad is talking about launching what it called a "modified Dutch auction" tender offer in which the bidder indicates the number of shares of common stock it wants to buy, and the price range it would be willing to offer. The company has said it expects to buy at a range of $23.00-$25.50 per share, and "as soon as reasonably practicable".

The quantity represents 11% of its market capitalization.

"We are pleased to announce our intended return of capital to shareholders which underscores the board's confidence in the growth prospects of our business and our commitment to pursuing a disciplined, value-enhancing capital allocation strategy," said Noam Gottesman, Nomad Foods’ co-chairman and founder. "In addition, we are accelerating investments behind key organic growth initiatives, including the expansion of our European plant protein sub-brand, Green Cuisine."

Martin Franklin, another co-chairman and founder, added the company was also sharpening its M&A focus "behind a targeted pipeline of European frozen food acquisitions".

"This refined strategic approach creates an opportunity to drive long-term shareholder value through the accretive return of excess cash while retaining financial flexibility to pursue our growth ambitions."

The terms and conditions of the tender offer will be described in an offer to purchase and related letter of transmittal that will be sent to Nomad's shareholders shortly, the company said. The tender offer will be held open for at least twenty business days following its commencement, and tenders of shares must be made prior to the expiration of the tender offer period.

Double-digit organic revenue growth

Nomad has cash to burn. While the coronavirus has hit large parts of the food industry in Europe and the rest of the world with a lethal punch, it has thus far been good for the bottom line of the UK company, its latest quarterly filing shows. 

Organic revenue growth was 12.3%, including 9.9% growth in volume/mix and 2.4% attributed to price increases during the three-month period. For comparison purposes, consider that organic growth was just  2.1% in all of 2019.

The company also saw earnings before interest taxes depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) in the second quarter of 2020 of €119m, an increase of 21%. The results were enough for Nomad to raise its adjusted EBITDA guidance to more than €460m from its earlier prediction of €450 to €460m. It's now expected see more than €1.27 earnings per share.

Nomad said its "full year guidance now assumes organic revenue growth at a high-single digit percentage range versus the prior expectation of mid-single-digit organic revenue growth".

Stéfan Descheemaeker, Nomad's CEO, had optimism to spare in a statement released by the company.

"Frozen food has proven to be one of the most durable consumer categories throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, a testament to its role in offering families quick and nutritious meal solutions at home," he said. "These are values which we believe will transcend beyond this acute period and appeal to a broader set of consumers in a post-COVID-19 world."

Nomad said it will spend about €10m on incremental strategic investments to fuel brand building activity, drive targeted retention of new consumers, and further accelerate the growth of its Green Cuisine products.

After combining first-quarter results, Nomad saw revenue of €1.28 billion during the first half of 2020, a 10.9% increase, and organic revenue growth of 9.8% (7.9% in volume/mix and 1.9% in price increases). Adjusted EBITDA increased 8% to €239m during the first six months.

Nomad said its gross margin declined 70 basis points to 29.7% as pricing, promotional efficiencies and mix were more than offset by cost of goods inflation during the six-month period. Also, adjusted operating expenses increased 7% to €176m as double-digit growth in indirects was offset by a decline in advertising and promotion.

The company will "accelerate strategic investments to convert the unprecedented adoption of frozen food and trial of our brands into permanent consumption behavior”, Gottesman said.

title: Study finds Pacific suppliers of canned tuna too lax on slavery policies
content:
Major corporate suppliers of canned tuna from the Pacific to European supermarkets are too lax on human rights policies, according to a study conducted by Deloitte.

The research, released by the European tuna fleet -- headed by Spain's Organizacion de Productores de Atun Congelado (OPAGAC) -- found only half of 35 surveyed companies had no defined processes for taking action regarding human rights, and only 17% had complaint mechanisms for their employees.

"The major corporate suppliers of western Pacific-fished canned tuna for European supermarkets are especially lax in watching out for and prosecuting violations of workers’ human rights in their tuna production chain, and their processes include no mechanisms of any kind for identifying modern slavery onboard tuna vessels, even though such practices are becoming more and more frequent, especially in Asian fleets," claimed OPAGAC.

The study found that only 11% of major canned tuna marketing groups -- mainly from the US, Australia, Thailand, Canada, and the Philippines -- have internal policies and monitoring procedures to detect the risk of slavery.

"In the case of fishery products...big food distributors are focusing more on environmental and biological sustainability than the kind of sustainability that involves human rights and working conditions, " said OPAGAC. "This would explain why some major European chains are certifying the sustainability of their fishery products with various seals, but none of them are making it mandatory to have observers on board to verify certified fishing activities."

title: New Zealand’s foreign visa clampdown threatens hoki, blue whiting catches
content:
New Zealand's government is not issuing visas for fishing crews to come into the country over concerns about importing cases of coronavirus, creating a significant issue for catchers of hoki and southern blue whiting (SBW), sources told Undercurrent News.

Many of New Zealand's large fishing companies use mostly -- sometimes entirely -- foreign crew on six-month-plus visas to operate their vessels. New crew would usually be coming out from Russia, Ukraine and other countries around the world for the primary hoki season, which is just getting underway. But the government, which faces an election in September, is reportedly not issuing new visas.

These issues with getting replacement crew come as the hoki total allowable catch (TAC) has been cut and the sector is bracing for another reduction in the 2020/2021 season. The pandemic has also impacted prices.

The visa clampdown "has potentially dire consequences" for both the hoki and SBW seasons, especially the latter, one senior New Zealand sector executive who asked not to be named told Undercurrent. The SBW fishing starts when hoki finishes, around September/October. Around NZD 100 million ($66.5m) is generated from the three-month hoki season, with SBW earning around NZD 50m, sources said.

The global outbreak of Covid-19 is disrupting seafood trade flows
Read more

"There are 12 vessels in New Zealand that use 100% foreign crew. Many, many more vessels, including freshers, use a mixture of both NZ and foreign crews. All will be affected over time," a second top New Zealand seafood executive told Undercurrent. "We are still trying to get a resolution, even though the outlook looks grim."

The timing for allowing an influx of foreign workers into the country is sensitive for the center-left government, led by prime minister Jacinda Arden, which faces an election on Sept. 19. With the election, the last thing Arden's Labor Party-led coalition wants is for any media attention on foreign workers importing COVID-19 and then being seen to take jobs from locals put out of work by the pandemic.

"The more they can stall and delay the better, even though locals can fill very few of these positions," the second executive told Undercurrent.

"The fact that New Zealand doesn't have qualified seafarers or workers willing to work at sea is irrelevant in this political climate," a third New Zealand seafood sector executive, who also did not want to be named, told Undercurrent. 

Seafood New Zealand, an industry body, is lobbying the government.

"There are ongoing discussions with the New Zealand government about getting skilled crew into the country. At present, seven New Zealand-flagged deepwater vessels need a changeover of their crew. These crew are not available in NZ," Jeremy Helson, chief executive of Seafood New Zealand, told Undercurrent.

"Industry has proposed that the foreign crew needed for these vessels would be flown into New Zealand, primarily by charter, and transferred directly to the vessel, posing very low COVID-19 risk; however, the government will not allow quarantine onboard the destination vessel," said Helson.

Sealord turns to other New Zealand businesses amidst COVID-19 worker shortage

"Government-established quarantine facilities are operating at capacity and we are working with [the] government to understand the guidelines and criteria for setting up an alternative quarantine facility for [the] foreign crew, at our cost," he said.

If these crew cannot be transferred to the vessel, around 500 land-based Kiwis will lose their jobs as there are no fish to process, and there will also be significant financial losses to New Zealand, he said. "The industry is actively engaged in trying to recruit and train New Zealanders into at-sea jobs. But, as everyone knows in the primary production area, this is neither quick nor easy."

The seven vessels mentioned by Seafood New Zealand as needing a crew change are the 104-meter, Ukraine-built, Bolshoy Avtonomniy Trawler Morozilniy (BATM) class fleet operating under the New Zealand flag. 

Two of the BATMs are owned by Independent Fisheries, with a third chartered by the company. The New Zealand-based arm of Japan's Maruha Nichiro owns one and charters another. Sealord charters two. Sanford, New Zealand's largest seafood company in revenue, does not operate BATMs, but has a charter arrangement with South Korean companies. Talley's Group, another major hoki harvesting firm, is said to use a higher percentage of New Zealand workers. However, sources said all of the significant fishing firms would be impacted, if the situation is not resolved.

None of the companies responded to requests for comment in time for publishing. 

"The bar for being granted an exception to the border restrictions is set high to help stop the spread of COVID-19 and protect the health of people already in New Zealand. Individuals' requests for exceptions to the border restrictions are considered against the strict criteria as set out in immigration instructions," a spokesperson for Immigration New Zealand [INZ], part of the country's Ministry of Business, Innovation & Employment. 

"Requests for a border exception for 'other critical workers' must be submitted by ship owners, authorized agents or employers through the INZ website, on behalf of the workers they are seeking exceptions for. Requests from individual workers will not be considered," she told Undercurrent. "Requests for approval of 'other critical workers' made by employers are considered on a case-by-case basis by senior Immigration New Zealand officials."

Uncertain resource, price outlook adds to issues

Even without the issue of the visas, the uncertain resource picture and outlook on prices in the COVID-19 dominated world would be a cause for concern for New Zealand's big fishing firms.

Sealord’s Paulin: Hoki cut in line with what industry planned anyway

The hoki TAC for the 2019/2020 fishing year, which started on Oct. 1, has been cut 23% to 116,190 metric tons. The sector is bracing for a further cut in 2020/2021, with some sources talking of as much as 30%.

Also, prices "have certainly softened for all forms of hoki", due COVID-19, said source B.

Prices for headed, gutted, tail off (HGT) hoki, considered the benchmark, have softened somewhat, but from a bumper level, said the first executive. Last year, HGT hit $3,000/t, an all-time high, but has come "back a little in early small volume sales this year so far", he said. 

However, significant volumes have not yet hit the market. "If the catch rates continue to be poor, there may not be much on the open market," he told Undercurrent.

Worse for SBW

The lack of visas will impact the hoki season but will be a big issue for SBW, due to the later start.

"Certainly, for the SBW season, it will be a big problem. We are not sure yet how many vessels will go but looks like many will be tied up by late August or early September," the second executive told Undercurrent.

SBW is a very seasonal fishery, with most of the 49,000t TAC taken in a six week season. "So, it looks like most of the fish will be left in the water," the first source said. 

For hoki, all vessels "are still here and fishing", with the season set to finish in late August, he said.

"Catches are down on hoki, though," he said. "Also, productivity is down as some crew has left vessels to go home."

The crew still on the vessels have never fished hoki before, which will impact productivity, said the first executive. 

"They are normally back home by now after the squid season," he said. "Some crew have been on-board for eight months. They all have families in Europe and are desperate to return. So much so, that some have abandoned the vessels when they have been in port. On a humanitarian basis, the fishing companies have agreed enough is enough and they will fly them home in chartered planes after the hoki season."

The third executive agreed. 

"The trapped crew in NZ do not have experience targeting the hoki or SBW fisheries and have proven to be less effective without the decades of knowledge their opposite crew has," he told Undercurrent. 

"The crews are also mentally and physically fatigued, resulting in the hoki catch by these vessels being down for the same time last year. Once commercial flights, although limited and unreliable, started up, the vessels have lost up to 20% of the crew each. This further reduces production capabilities and the making of secondary products, like hoki roe," he said. 

As many as 12 vessels could be impacted for the hoki season, which is about 40% of the catching capacity, including the seven-strong BATM fleet,  the sources said. 

"If crew continue to sign off following port calls, some of the seven BATM fleet will have to stop operating," said the third sector executive. 

"Many of the crew will sign off at the end of August 2020 and it is expected five or six of the seven [BATM] vessels will stop and go into hibernation. This will mean up to 17,000t of SBW will not be caught and turned into headed and gutted product for export," he told Undercurrent. 

New Zealand cuts hoki TAC 23% amid concern over stocks

There is also not enough space in New Zealand's ports to take the BATM vessels, he said. "Even if space could be made available, ports are reluctant to have vessels tied up blocking wharves for an undefined period. Companies operating the vessels are majorly concerned that without the goodwill of the crew that the vessels will be abandoned in port or worse at anchor."

Source B was marginally more positive on the hoki season, but only slightly.

"Hoki looks set to be under caught, because of poorer productivity from vessels with short crew and the resource being not so strong," he told Undercurrent.

"Not having these vessels' fish affects the entire industry eventually because it will mean a lot of uncaught quota," said source A. 

This will, in turn, mean lease values for these species will dive. "That directly affects the Maori quota owners who generally lease their quota to vessel owning companies. No money from fishing for Maori means a major social problem for the government."

This could lead to forced quota sales at knock-down prices, he said.

It might also force a change in the sector, with the foreign-crewed vessels needing to be replaced. 

"If it continues, it means that there will be an urgent need for vessel construction to replace the foreign crewed vessels. My personal view is that it's going to be a train smash unless they let these crews in," the first source told Undercurrent. 

If a resolution is not found, all the foreign-crewed vessels will have to stop operating by Oct. 1, 2020, "with no plan or path as to when they can start operating again", said the third executive. 

"This will not only lose jobs for the 1,200 foreign crew but will lose NZ jobs in the fishing companies, supply companies and service providers. Over NZD 500m will be lost from the NZ economy and 126,000t of fish will not be caught. This is 25-30% of the fishing industry."

title: Nuseed secures Canadian feed, food approvals for omega-3 canola
content:
Nuseed Americas, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Nufarm, a publicly traded agricultural chemical company headquartered in Melbourne, Australia (ASX:NUF), announced this week that it has received confirmation from the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) that its omega-3 canola meal has been determined to be safe for use in fish and livestock feeds.

Also, Health Canada has determined that the highly refined oil derived from Nuseed’s omega-3 canola is safe for human consumption as or in foods in Canada, according to the company.

Nuseed group executive Brent Zacharias said the Canadian regulatory approvals are an
important milestone in the development and commercialization of its omega-3 canola product.

“Canada is the third-largest producer of farmed salmon globally," he said. "These approvals position Nuseed to supply the Canadian market with an oil that has been shown to deliver fish health benefits and to enable industry sustainability goals; particularly in reducing the reliance on scarce marine ingredients.

“Given Canada’s position as the largest canola production country, approval also ensures our future scalability, giving us access to a key expansion market.”

title: Atlantic Sapphire emergency harvest spooks market ahead of launch
content:
An emergency harvest at land-based salmon farmer Atlantic Sapphire's under-construction US facility has wiped about $55 million off the company's market capitalization, with the share price dropping 5.7%.

The news the company had initiated an emergency harvest from a grow-out system in its Homestead, Florida, recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) facility saw its market cap drop NOK 500m ($55m) to NOK 8.27 billion at the close of trading on Norway's Oslo stock exchange on Wednesday.

The company was preparing for its first harvest of fish at the facility to hit the market at some point in Q3. 

The system in question "had been recently stocked despite not being fully commissioned", the company said, in a stock exchange notice. "The exact chain of events is still being investigated, however, disruptive construction work close to the operating environment, including loud sounds and severe vibrations, stressed the fish."

Close to 200,000 Atlantic salmon with a total weight of approximately 400 metric tons (ahead-on and gutted, or HOG) are expected to be harvested, of which approximately 150t are planned to be sent for processing and will be sold.

The 200,000 fish account for approximately 700t (HOG) of projected harvest, "or three to four weeks of US phase one annualized revenue".

The incident matters most for near-term financing and the direct impact is minimal, Christian Nordby, equity research analyst with Kepler Cheuvreux, told Undercurrent News.

"Atlantic Sapphire wants to prove that their case is as 'safe' as it can be -- the fewer risks the better. This was a risk we did not think so much about," he said.

"So when the share price is now down 7.5%, this is driven by that cost of financing raises; equity costs more, bank debt costs more, etcetera." (The share price had recovered slightly by the close of trading in Norway.)

Atlantic Sapphire needs a considerable amount of financing to attain its target levels of 220,000t by 2031, he added.

It has said that of the 400t of salmon which needs to be harvested, 150t will be sold for processing, implying 250t will not. With these 400t salmon harvested at 40% below optimal size, Atlantic Sapphire should now be looking at around 5,500t of salmon in the second half of 2020, rather than 6,000t, said Nordby.

"The forced harvest is also likely to incur higher costs and lower price achievement but the company needs to assess the damages."

The analyst also pointed out that this is the first time construction work has been seen to have caused a severe incident like this, and that "as Atlantic Sapphire is expected to do construction for the coming decade, we might experience more of these incidents".

The RAS company has already stated the incident demonstrates the importance of having multiple independent systems to diversify biological risk; the incident was confined to one of its systems only.

Upon completion of phase one at the US facility, Atlantic Sapphire will have a total of 12 independent grow-out systems, "limiting the risk and financial impact of any systemic contamination to below 10% of total output and revenue", it said. The 12 systems will have an expected annual production of around 10,000t (head-on gutted) salmon per year.

Perhaps as a show of confidence, Johan Andreassen -- Atlantic Sapphire chairman -- invested $18,591 in 1,500 shares on July 29. He now holds 14.8% of the company's total shares, via two different holding firms.

He told Undercurrent he believed the company's stakeholders understand the "extreme challenge" of operating an incomplete facility with ongoing construction work, and delays which have "become more challenging due to the COVID situation".

"We know that we can produce fish in Miami that has high quality and taste perfect and we will still commence harvest in Q3. Once we have phase one completed, we will have a very different risk picture."

"As we go into phase two and beyond, we will have a mature existing infrastructure and organization in place, and we expect the build-out of these phases to be less painful than phase one," he added.

The fish at the heart of this incident are Atlantic Sapphire's "frontrunners", and have, throughout their entire lifecycle, been moved into brand new systems that, to some extent, have had construction work going on at the same time, he told Undercurrent.

"In other words, this fish group has always been the closest one to the construction work. We have had multiple situations where stress has been observed due to construction, but we have been able to avoid significant mortality as a consequence."

title: New Zealand’s Sealord ordered to forfeit $16m vessel over illegal deep-sea trawl
content:
Sealord Group, one of New Zealand's largest seafood harvesters and processors, has been ordered to forfeit Ocean Dawn, a $16 million vessel, and pay a $16,000 fine for an illegal deep-sea trawl in a protected zone, 1 News, an Auckland, New Zealand, television news service, reports.  

The incident reportedly happened over a two-day period in late October 2018, when the vessel fished for hoki in the lower buffer zone of a benthic protection area about 200 nautical miles east of Christchurch. The area is one of 17 that was closed to dredging and bottom trawling by the New Zealand government in 2007, covering a 1.1 million square kilometer area, according to the news service.

Earlier convicted, Sealord vessel master Bolen Terric Goomes was fined NZD 7,500 ($5,010) and first mate Thomas Adrian Pope was fined NZD 5000 ($3,340), according to the article. 

Sealord has said it will continue to operate Ocean Dawn while an appeal process is underway.
