title: New Zoneco CEO is executive previously fined for fraud
content:
Chinese seafood company Zoneco Group's new CEO is a company executive previously fined by authorities for her involvement in corporate fraud at the firm.

This week, Tang Yan was unanimously elected as Zoneco's new CEO and chairperson of the board. Tang, who was previously joint executive CEO, replaces disgraced former CEO Wu Hougang, who departed last month.

Zoneco chairman resigns over ‘running scallops’ saga

Tang was among those fined CNY 80,000 ($11,401) by the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) last year for her involvement in the fraud at Zoneco, a large scallop farmer, seafood importer and processor based in Liaoning province. Last month, Zoneco lost an appeal against charges of corporate fraud worth some CNY 600 million.

Wu was fined CNY 300,000 by CSRC and given a lifetime ban from public securities markets, while several other executives were also fined. Zoneco itself was fined CNY 600,000.

During a shareholder meeting Tang made no mention of the issue, expounding instead on strategies to return the company to profitability. These include "trimming fat", or selling off assets, she said.

Liu Ming, also previously joint executive CEO, was elected to director of the board.

Beijing Jirongyuan Tongfang, Zhangzidao's second-largest shareholder, welcomed the two appointments.

"The company is currently in a difficult time, and the two bravely shoulder heavy burdens. On behalf of Zoneco's second-largest shareholder, we would like to express our gratitude and will give our full support," said a spokesperson.

title: Untitled
content:
At least 260 vessels, mainly from China, have been spotted fishing within the 188-mile limit of the Ecuadorian archipelago's exclusive economic zone (EEZ) for several days, according to authorities from the Latin American country's navy forces. 

Through satellite monitoring and continuous maritime surveillance carried out by Guayaquil's naval forces, it was determined that the fleet is made up of fishing, supply and reefer vessels, similar to fleets also sighted in the area during previous years.

Daniel Ginez, Ecuador's chief of naval operations, explained that there are permanent and uninterrupted operational joint surveillance patrols in the area to prevent any violation of Ecuador's national sovereignty. 

"There is a possibility that these vessels could enter our country's EEZ at any time and, therefore, we have sent several patrol vessels to the area, which are still there," he said.

"Additionally, we are currently carrying out several explorations by air to make sure that our jurisdictional waters are not subject to any type of illegal fishing by any of these foreign vessels."

According to the Galapagos' maritime authorities, every year in summer, a greater presence of foreign fishing vessels is observed, so it is usual that closer monitoring and follow-up in the area is carried out 24 hours a day from both Ecuador's mainland and the archipelago.

In 2017, the Latin American country's naval forces intercepted the Chinese vessel 'Fu Yuan Yu Leng 999' while sailing illegally within the Galapagos marine reserve. Some 300 metric tons of fish were found in its holds — including vulnerable species such as hammerhead and silky sharks, which are in danger of extinction.

The crew received jail time of between one and four years and were also fined a total of $5.9 million, Undercurrent News previously reported.

title: COVID-shrimp link: Deadly threat or dangerous hype?
content:
China's crackdown on three Ecuadorian shrimp exporters after positive tests for coronavirus on packaging and inside a shipping container is causing chaos in the shrimp industry. 

It's stoking public fears of imported seafood, led to mandatory inspections and congestion at ports, and caused a crash in Ecuadorian shrimp exports and prices. But is China's apparent war with imported shrimp an overreaction?

Can food outer packaging really carry a deadly payload of coronavirus, after a transoceanic journey in a refrigerated shipping container? Or is there no risk contaminated packaging could spark a new outbreak in a country free of the disease?

To understand if there is any scientific basis for China's actions, Undercurrent News spoke with the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the UK's Food Standards Agency (FSA), seafood industry bodies, health industry insiders, as well as professional translators.

First, is it correct that China reported 'positive tests for coronavirus' on outer packaging of imported Ecuadorian shrimp?

Reuters, Bloomberg, China Daily and Xinhua News, all reported that samples taken from outer packaging of shrimp "tested positive for coronavirus", when China's General Administration of Customs (GAAC) first announced the findings on Friday, July 10. This is how Undercurrent also reported the announcement.

Bi Kexing speaking at the July 10 press conference. Source: CCTV

But was GAAC's announcement lost in translation, given it was in Chinese, as were subsequent reports of other positive tests by local authorities?

One professional translator reckons media got it wrong, although another translation agency took an opposing view.

Bi Kexin, head of the Import and Export Food Safety Bureau of GAAC, qualified that positive tests were for "coronavirus RNA", according to Phylls Ang, a translator based in Switzerland. At GAAC's July 10 press conference and in subsequent reports of findings, positive tests were all for "coronavirus RNA", based on Ang's translation. RNA, or ribonucleic acid, are strands of DNA matter from the virus, not a whole, live coronavirus.

A translation of the same passage by TransPerfect, the world's largest translation agency, does not disagree with Ang, but says the media version is not incorrect either. 

July 10 press conference. Source: CCTV

This is because RNA tests, also known as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests, are nearly always used to detect coronavirus. When a laboratory finds coronavirus RNA in a swab taken from a patient, that patient is reported as having tested positive for the coronavirus.

TransPerfect's interpretation is that Bi said this was a positive RNA test for coronavirus, but because RNA is not a widely understood scientific word, the acronym can be dropped.

"'Coronavirus detected with RNA tests', 'positive RNA test for coronavirus' are both correct, but 'positive new coronavirus test' is the most simple and concise," said TransPerfect.

Okay. So did China find live coronavirus or not?

This is unclear. As mentioned above, when checking for coronavirus on a surface, authorities use a PCR test to detect the RNA left behind by the virus' presence. 

According to the British National Health Service (NHS), when a sample is returned to a lab, a reagent is added. If the virus is present, it will trigger a chain reaction producing billions of copies of the genetic material, sufficient for detection by scientists.

A PCR testing machine used to detect the coronavirus. Credit: Chin Savuth, Flickr

However, the PCR test cannot easily establish whether the virus is 'live' -- capable of multiplying and growing inside a cell, and therefore, infectious. So a positive result may merely be the detection of trace RNA left behind by a virus that has long since deteriorated; only specific laboratories at research institutions with suitable biohazard protection measures can determine either way.

Still, detections can provide valuable information for medical authorities on how the virus has spread, and how it may have entered a space. Moreover, scientists can analyze viral RNA from different locations so that as it mutates, they may be able to trace particular samples back to their point of origin.

As yet, Chinese authorities have not said whether positive samples were live or not.

Okay. But Chinese authorities said the positive sample was not transmissible, right, which is pretty much the same?

This is another point of contention. Jose Campasano, president of Ecuador's industry body Camara Nacional de Acuacultura (CNA), is adamant that during the Friday press conference, Bi said the samples tested were not transmissible.

He told Undercurrent Ecuador is expanding safety protocols "although the RNA detected by the PCR test at the outside packaging and container wall wasn't contagious". 

Ecuador’s shrimp sector announces ‘severe contraction’ in production, exports

Ang reckons Bi's phrasing was somewhat ambiguous, however. 

According to Undercurrent's translation of the press conference, which Ang says is correct, Bi said: "Experts judged that the positive detection did not mean the [sampled virus] was transmissible".

"Reading the segment of the press conference in its entirety, it looks to me that Bi was saying that the positive results in this particular case do not mean that the samples were infectious or can transmit the virus," said Ang. "However, while he is saying that the possibility is very low, he is not directly ruling it out. This might be why more vague terms were used."

"In my opinion, it's a fairly diplomatic way of phrasing it so that he can have an 'out' later if it turns out that the virus can indeed be transmitted via food," said Ang.

Okay. But this is all academic because there is no evidence coronavirus can be contracted by eating food, right?

Correct. World health and food safety organizations are in agreement that there is currently no evidence of foodborne transmission either of COVID-19 or its similar respiratory predecessor, SARS. 

According to a direct response to Undercurrent from the EFSA, "as of today, we have not been able to source any data (epidemiological or otherwise) that shows that food or food packaging is a primary risk factor for illness".

"Evidence shows the virus seems to be transmitted mainly via small respiratory droplets through sneezing, coughing, or when people interact with each other in close proximity," it said.

In its own risk assessment, the UK's FSA lists the probability of seafood being infected by coronavirus as "negligible" -- effectively, a risk so low that it does not merit consideration.

Chinese customs officials test containers filled with seafood for the coronavirus. Source: WeChat.

However, FSA conservatively estimates the risk of exposure to coronavirus via cross-contamination from both domestic and imported food products as higher than negligible, describing it as "very low".

"Although the likelihood in some steps with pathway B [cross-contaminated foodstuffs] is considered negligible, due to the high volumes of food and FCM (food contact materials) and food packaging produced both domestically and internationally a conservative estimate of very low is assigned," the FSA writes.

For its part, China's GAAC also noted the lack of evidence of foodborne transmission of coronavirus, citing the World Health Organisation (WHO), EFSA, the German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment, and the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (USCDC).

"Up until now, there is no evidence of the spread of the new coronavirus through food. These views can be found on the WHO website and the websites of these [above] agencies. They are publicly available. Up until now, with more than 10 million cases diagnosed globally, and more than 80,000 cases reported in our country, there has been no reported case caused by food intake," said Bi at the July 10 press conference.

But what about in chilled or frozen conditions, as later suggested by China's CDC?

This is an area where China appears more concerned.

The FSA noted that relatively few studies had been conducted to investigate the survival of coronavirus in cooler conditions. "But, we do know that, in general, virus inactivation occurs more slowly at cold temperatures."

One such study published in The Lancet scientific journal in early April found the virus to be "highly stable at 4 degrees centigrade, but sensitive to heat," detecting only a minor deterioration in infectiousness by day 14 of testing.

Table adapted from the findings of Chin et al. (2020) defining the time taken at different temperatures for coronavirus to reduce in titer below detectable levels. Credit: UK FSA

The same report also noted that, at room temperatures, the virus survived for longer on smooth surfaces such as glass (up to four days) and stainless steel and plastic (up to seven days in both cases).

On cardboard surfaces -- such as those used by Ecuadorian companies to pack shrimp -- coronavirus has been found to drop below the detectable limit at room temperatures after 24 hours. 

Other forms of food preservation, such as drying, have been found to reduce coronavirus activity significantly. 

Ben Chapman, professor and food safety expert of North Carolina State University, described the survival of coronavirus on different surfaces -- including food and packaging -- and temperatures as a "big one". 

"There are a few studies out there that address this, but there are still a lot of unanswered questions. We need to know how long the virus remains viable not only on different materials, but under various temperature and humidity combinations. Another line of questioning involves the extent to which heat, disinfectants, UV light and pressure can inactivate the virus. Understanding these issues will provide scientific evidence upon which we can make better recommendations for controlling the spread of the virus," he said in a blog post.

Wu Zunyou, chief epidemiologist for China's Center of Disease Control (CDC), told CCTV on July 11 the positive findings on the outer packaging of shrimp "showed the possibility imported seafood could carry coronavirus into China". "Whether such [an] introduction can cause a new outbreak requires further scientific discussion and verification." 

Chinese authorities seal off shrimp from Ecuadorian companies hit by ban

In the meantime, precautions should be taken, including banning imports if necessary, Wu said. "For imported goods, especially from countries with epidemics, and especially imported packaged products frozen or preserved in low temperatures, inspections should be strengthened, or imports should be banned altogether. These measures can reduce risks."

In regards to the risk posed by imports, the FSA told Undercurrent: "Existing rules on certification and imports are enough to ensure imported food products are not contaminated with COVID-19 at a level representing a risk to consumers; we do not believe that measures limiting free trade of food products are necessary." 

It is a stance agreed on in principle by the EFSA, the WHO, and the US FDA, which reiterated an earlier statement on the threat of coronavirus entering a country via food imports when contacted by Undercurrent.

"The United States understands the concerns of consumers here domestically and around the world who want to know that producers, processors and regulators are taking every necessary precaution to prioritize food safety especially during these challenging times," the FDA said, in a joint statement with the US department of agriculture.

"However, efforts by some countries to restrict global food exports related to COVID-19 transmission are not consistent with the known science of transmission."

The US CDC did not respond to comment when contacted by Undercurrent.

Is this the same as the salmon chopping board incident which linked imported salmon to an outbreak of COVID-19 in Beijing?

This is not the same. The main difference is the positive sample was taken from a salmon chopping board in a busy open-air market in Beijing, meaning verifying how the virus got there was next to impossible.

China's CDC also said there was no evidence the salmon was contaminated with coronavirus before entering the market. 

In this case, however, Chinese customs officials swabbed the outer packages of shrimp and inside the shipping container transporting the shrimp when the consignments arrived at two separate ports in China (Dalian and Xiamen).

Assuming the inside of the containers was not tampered with between leaving Ecuador and arriving in China, and there was no contamination by the Chinese officials taking the samples, the positive samples indisputably came from Ecuador.

Chinese exec calls salmon ‘collateral damage’ in coronavirus outbreak

Following the salmon incident, many port authorities in China introduced mandatory checks on all imports of fresh salmon, a measure extended to imports of shrimp. Other food products also face mandatory checks at ports, albeit at a lower frequency.

From July 3 to the end of July 9, Chinese customs tested a total of 227,934 samples taken from imported goods; this included 43,964 product samples, 47,568 internal and external packaging samples, and 36,402 environmental samples. Aside from the five positive samples from Industrial Pesquera Santa Priscila, Empacreci, and Empacadora Del Pacifico Sociedad Anonima Edpacif, there were no positive tests for the coronavirus. 

Are food processing plants and packaging centers more at risk?

Given their crucial role in the supply of food and other essential items, food processing plants and other packaging centers enjoy special provisions to stay open during lockdowns. 

However, these are busy environments with people handling lots of goods. An NHS insider told Undercurrent that a "high frequency" of the outbreaks currently being reported in the UK are at such facilities. 

American Seafoods, Iberconsa hit with COVID-19 outbreaks on trawlers

"Many of the local outbreaks we are currently dealing with are in warehouses and food processing plants. The confined working spaces, a predominantly young workforce and a lack of following strict social distancing and hand hygiene measures make it easier for the virus to spread."

The seafood sector has reported its fair share of outbreaks. In June, Chilean salmon farmer Blumar significantly cut output at its Talcahuano processing plant after five COVID-19 cases were confirmed. The same month, Pacific Seafoods, a US seafood processor, temporarily closed its plant in Newport, Oregon, after an outbreak. Meanwhile, American Seafoods and Iberconsa both recently reported outbreaks of COVID-19 on trawler vessels.

China has suspended imports from food processing plants in other sectors that have reported outbreaks; last month, China suspended imports from a Tyson Foods' chicken processing plant in the US and a German pork processing plant. Some Brazilian meat plants have voluntarily suspended exports to China for fear of being put on a banned list.

In response to suspensions, CNA said Ecuador is "taking this situation very seriously and acting according to the WHO recommendations and new Chinese standards... The industry is reinforcing protocols with PCR testing for plant workers, reinforced protocols at packaging material reception, storage and handling, and container cleaning and disinfection."

Is China doing this to drive down shrimp prices?

It is unlikely China is doing this to punish Ecuador, benefit from lower prices, or to protect its shrimp farmers (latest reports in China indicate domestic farmed shrimp prices are also falling, perhaps because consumers have conflated imported shrimp with all shrimp).

However, there is no doubt this is hugely damaging for Ecuador's shrimp industry, which is heavily dependent on the Chinese market.

Latest projections show Ecuador is on track to export just 4,990 metric tons of shrimp to China in July, or only 9% of May's exports to the country. Ivan Ontaneda, the country's minister of production, foreign trade, investments and fisheries, also said the industry has not "experienced such a profound price crisis like this one in more than a decade".

title: Fish Factor: Alaska seafood left out of federal trade data; cost of China trade war; ‘honey bucket’ warnings
content:
(Fish Factor' is a weekly column featuring the reporting and perspective of Alaska seafood journalist Laine Welch.)

Most Alaskans are surprised to learn that seafood is by far Alaska’s top export, the source of the state’s largest manufacturing base and its top private employer.

More surprising is that those simple-to-find facts are not included in the official trade sheet for Alaska provided by the office of the US Trade Representative (USTR).

The information on the USTR website, for example, incorrectly claims that petroleum and coal were Alaska’s top exports in 2018. But seafood has been the state’s top export by far for decades. 

“Seafood comprises over half of Alaska’s annual export value, averaging $3.3 billion annually over the past decade, averaging $5.6bn from 2017-2018,” reports the Alaska Resource Development Council (RDC) on its fisheries page.

The USTR states that “Alaska goods exports in 2016 (latest year available) supported an estimated 37 thousand jobs.”

Wrong again.

Laine Welch, the founder of Alaska Fish Radio.

Alaska’s seafood industry alone supports nearly 60,000 direct jobs and an additional 10,000 secondary jobs. And, as the RDC points out, “seafood processing is the largest manufacturing sector in Alaska, accounting for 70% of Alaska’s manufacturing employment.”

But the federal trade reps have a different take.

Under the USTR category "Made in America Manufacturing Exports from Alaska and Jobs", it states: “Other top manufacturing exports are transportation equipment ($68 million), food & kindred products ($23m), computer & electronic products ($23m), and machinery, except electrical ($23m).

Who knew?

For the category "Agriculture in Alaska Depends on Exports", the USTR claims that: “Alaska is the country’s 50th largest agricultural exporting state, shipping $17m in domestic agricultural exports abroad in 2017.” 

Alaska’s top agricultural products listed are “other plant products” ($14m), “other livestock products” ($1m), followed by “feeds and other grains, processed grain products, and beef and veal” ($326,000).

But Alaska is not alone in the seafood snub.             

Credit: Peter Hermes Furian/Shutterstock

A review of other states’ official trade pages shows contributions by the industry are not mentioned for fishing powerhouses like Maine, Massachusetts, or Louisiana and more.

And Hawaii will be surprised to learn that, according to the federal trade office, its largest exports also are petroleum and coal – although it has no reserves of either!

Overall, the USTR state trade data is poorly defined, loaded with incorrect facts and figures, provides no attribution, and each page looks like a sloppy cut and paste job tossed together with no expertise or interest.

Hopefully, the issue will draw the attention of Robert DeHaan who on Friday was appointed to the Agricultural Technical Advisory Committee that covers trade in animal products. 

DeHaan is the vice president for government affairs at the National Fisheries Institute (NFI) and has worked at the senior government level in both trade and transportation. The committee advises the government on policy matters including existing trade agreements and the negotiation of new ones.

“This is a great opportunity for the seafood community to have a seat at the table where trade decisions are made,” DeHaan said in an NFI press release. “I’m thrilled to be able to bring our industry’s perspective and guidance to the people in charge of trade policy.”

China tariffs tank Alaska seafood

It’s been two years since president Donald Trump started a trade war with China by imposing taxes on seafood coming from that country, including US seafood processed in China – taxes that are paid by Americans and not the Chinese, as he would have you believe -- while China imposes tariffs on US seafood.  

Seafood comprises well over 30% of Alaska’s export volume and the ongoing tariffs have added up to huge losses from our biggest trading partner.

An analysis by the Alaska Seafood Marketing Institute (ASMI) shows that exports to China reached the highest level ever in 2017, at nearly $1bn ($988m).

By 2018, Alaska seafood exports dropped by $204m, the largest year-over-year decrease ever. And by 2019, sales to China were at the lowest level since 2010 at $702m.

That’s a drop of more than $250m in two years.

During the same time, China saw a 91% increase in seafood imports from other nations, going from $8.1bn to $15.4bn.

While the exact amount varies by species and product, ASMI said the average tax on Alaska seafood entering China is 38%.

For comparison, it’s 8% for Norway, Russia and Canada; Chile and New Zealand pay zero seafood tax to China.

There’s been explosive growth among Chinese seafood eaters since the tariffs were enacted, ASMI said, with sales jumping from $8.1bn to $15.4bn since 2018. But that growing appetite is being filled with seafood from elsewhere than Alaska or the US.

Added to the trade squeeze with China, the US seafood industry also continues to compete with less expensive imports from Russia. Trade data show the US imported nearly $700m worth of Russian-caught seafood in 2019, although that country has embargoed all seafood US imports since 2014.

Combine US trade policies that are clearly at odds with backing the seafood industry, mix in crippling and ongoing market impacts from COVID-19 and it adds up to a triple whammy for Alaska’s fishermen and coastal communities.

The trouble with 'honey buckets'

Don’t be dumping your doings overboard is a message from the state of Alaska to fishing vessel operators.

A letter sent out last week by the Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) reminds fishermen that it is illegal to dump sewage within three miles from shore.

“It is common practice, obviously, for folks to use a honey bucket on their boat and to just throw it overboard," DEC commissioner Jason Brune told KDLG in Dillingham, Alaska. "There is no doubt it is an ongoing practice. So, we are working to educate folks operating in our waters about the Clean Water Act. I would encourage folks to think about the water in general, think about being good stewards, and to bring that to our proper disposal on shore.” 

Dumping sewage violates the Clean Water Act and can net you a fine up to $2,000.

Brune’s letter also said the dumpings damage the nearshore environment by contaminating shellfish beds and fish habitat and can spread diseases to other people.

Alaska pollock.

All boats with onboard bathrooms must use Coast Guard-approved sanitation devices with storage tanks that are emptied at a pump station on shore or beyond three miles. Boats with honey buckets also can use the pump stations or bag style camp toilets that can be sealed and disposed of at approved collection areas.

Along with the dangers of contamination, Brune pointed out that dumping sewage in nearby waters simply sends the wrong message.

“We have environmental standards that we want to hold folks to to make sure that we’re being protective of our marine resources, of our fish and of the environment that we love here in Alaska.” he said.

Fish board find

A public records request to Alaska governor Michael Dunleavy’s office of boards and commissions produced a redacted resume for his elusive Board of Fisheries nominee, McKenzie Mitchell.

Alaska governor Mike Dunleavy. Image is a still from a video on the governor's website.

Since 2019 she has been a professor of economics and “recreation business leadership” at the University of Alaska Fairbanks, and a “contract economist for [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration] constructing market demand models for fisheries prevalent in Alaska”, it says.

Mitchell’s resume says she has been a boat captain and sport fishing guide at lodges on Kodiak Island for several years, presently at Raspberry Island Remote Lodge. She also is an assistant big game guide at Afognak Wilderness Lodge at Kodiak and Midnight Sun Safaris and Lazy J-Bar-O Outfitters at Healy.

A hearing on the fish board nominees is set for Sept. 3 in Anchorage. Public comments are being submitted to state representative Louise Stutes at rep.louise.stutes@akleg.gov.

title: Untitled
content:
The court order that gave Indonesia and other countries that supply the US with blue or red swimming crab (BSC and RSC) more time to avoid a Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA)-related ban might have helped ease tensions, but it has done little to reduce wholesale prices.

On jumbo lump in particular, BSC (Portunus pelagicus) wholesale prices are up 28% since the third week of the year (Jan. 13-19) and climbed another 0.6% just this week, reports Undercurrent News' senior price analyst Gary Morrison in his latest review. Meanwhile, wholesale prices for RSC (Portunus haanii) jumbo lump are up 46% since mid-January. 

And those prices have only continued to move up since Oct. 31, when the positive MMPA news was published, as reported by Undercurrent.

The delta between the prices for jumbo lump BSC and RSC remains $10.00, much more than the $7.12 difference seen in week 3.

"While there was a reprieve for implementation of the [MMPA], there are still some regulatory hurdles to climb," commented Morrison in his latest review of the market. "Most importers are working as they had previously, and harvesters are setting traps as if there is no issue. But the impact won't be felt for some time. The structural issues of higher costs and supply constraints are firmly set in place." 

Troy Turkin, the CEO of Supreme Crab & Seafood, a Weston, Florida-based importer, offered similar sentiments when asked recently for swimming crab importers' current state of mind.

"I would tell you if you asked that question more than two weeks ago, there would've been a high level of nervousness related to the industry because not only about just prices keep going up and we're at or near COVID levels," he replied. "Now there's more of a sense of relief in relation to the MMPA, but not necessarily from a pricing perspective, because overseas the numbers are still going up, at least on blue swimming crab."

Dialogue still needed

Price relief might've been expected after the US Court of International Trade, late last month, granted a temporary stay on the MMPA-related import restrictions that threatened to sharply curtail imports of BSC from key Asian fisheries, starting on Jan. 1, 2026. 

Issued on Aug. 28, NOAA's MMPA bans were set to block an estimated $3.6 billion worth of seafood from 46 nations, including also tuna, shrimp, squid, lobster, grouper, conch and dozens of other commercially important species from such countries.

The ruling followed a lawsuit brought against the US Department of Commerce and the National Marine Fisheries Service on Oct. 9 by 10 importers, along with the National Fisheries Institute and the Restaurant Law Center.

The most recent court's decision stays the enforcement of the ban on five BSC and RSC fisheries with specific gear types, including: Indonesia gillnets and entangling nets (Fishery ID 12391), Vietnam gillnets and entangling nets (ID 2988), Philippines pots/traps (ID 2129), Philippines gillnets and entangling nets (ID 2130) and Sri Lanka crab nets, gillnets, and entangling nets (ID 2705).

Blue swimming crabs in Indonesia. Photograph by Travis182 on Shutterstock.

Under the agreement, NMFS was given 60 days to initiate a new review of the affected fisheries, starting from Thursday (Nov. 13), the date the 43-day federal government shutdown ended. That gives foreign governments until roughly Jan. 12 to respond and submit more documentation with a reapplication in order to have a potential comparative finding that is more favorable.

Instead of Jan. 1, importers will have until at least June 2026 to prepare for a new ruling, Turkin explained.

"There's still the need for us to try and help and assist our stakeholders on the ground overseas to educate properly their trade associations so that those people can be having dialogue with their own governments, because this isn't officially over," he said.

"So we could be right back at this in the next six months. But we're optimistic that we'll be able to get everything in and properly communicated in the timeframe we've been given."

This impacts only gill nets or other kinds of entangling gear, not pot- or trap-caught products, he stressed. Also, a few crab-producing nations, such as China, do not face a potential ban.

Meanwhile, are crab supplier countries trying to beef up their presence in other markets to compensate for the threat of a US ban in the future?

"I don't think so, because of the sheer size of the US market and how much is bought here," Turkin said. "But there has always been a concern that improper application of the [MMPA] could push suppliers to countries that don't care about marine mammal protection. We don't want to be in the business of developing less sustainable markets for crab."

Indonesian BSC exports to US off 7% through August

Indonesia is the US' largest source of swimming crab by far. It sent the US 12,860 metric tons of BSC worth $332.1 million in 2024, 16% more volume and value than in 2023, as illustrated by the UCN trade portal chart below. 

Indonesia accounted for 46% of the 27,705t of combined BSC, RSC and blue crab imports last year.

Because US import data hasn't been updated since July, due to the government shutdown, it's impossible to know how much has been delivered since then. Indonesia BSC export data, which trails import data and is available via UCN's trade database, shows it sent the US 8,746t worth $214.8m in the first eight months of the year, 7% less volume and 9% less value than in the first eight months of 2024. 

However, multiple sources interviewed by Undercurrent say the acquisition of Indonesian BSC by importers in September and October, after the initial MMPA-related announcement was made, was voracious. As a result, they expect to see bigger numbers for those two months when import and export data is updated again, which is expected to happen this week, followed by a much smaller amount of volume imported in subsequent months. 

Loss of Venezuelan crab to create void

However, one major source of crab looks to be knocked completely out of the US market. Venezuela, which sends the US blue crab (Callinectes sapidus), the same species as is harvested domestically in the US, failed to ever submit paperwork in response to the NMFS' MMPA investigation. It was not included in the temporary stay.

Simultaneously, the president Donald Trump administration has been directing missile strikes against vessels off the Venezuelan coast, accusing them of attempting to deliver illegal drugs to the US. It has continued to escalate the US military's involvement, too, appearing to make the US less inclined to peacefully overlook the MMPA-related concerns for one major import product.

Two Venezuelan blue crab importers Undercurrent interviewed this week seemed resigned to the notion that there is little that can be done to rescue their supply.

"It doesn't look good," one importer commented, stating the obvious.

Blue crab from Venezuela.

Venezuela sent the US 2,659t of blue crab worth $61.4m in 2024, making it the fourth-largest source of a swimming crab product for the US behind Indonesia, Vietnam and China. That was 20% less volume but 4% more value than in 2023. 

Over the first seven months of 2025, Venezuela sent the US just 1,452t worth $37.9m, 27% less volume and 14% less value than the same period in 2024, based on its export data. The country, on Oct. 15, came out of its annual, 60-day crab harvesting moratorium.

More pressure on Vietnam, China

Without Venezuelan crab in the US market, more pressure will fall on RSC from China and Vietnam, which are somewhat constrained in their ability to deliver more crab to the US, importers told Undercurrent.

That is a recipe for higher prices, they advised. 

Vietnam, the US' second-largest source of swimming crab in 2024, sent it 3,569t of RSC worth $73.2m, 9% more volume and 10% more value than in 2023. 

However, imports of RSC from Vietnam have declined in 2025, based on export data. Over the first seven months of the year, Vietnam sent the US 1,838t worth $36.8m, based on its latest export data. That's 24% behind last year's volume pace and 26% behind its value pace. 

Vietnam has largely moved in front of China as the US' biggest source of RSC. China, in 2024, sent the US 3,353t worth $68.6m, 13% more volume but 11% less value than in 2023. 

But over the first nine months of 2025, China sent the US 1,593t worth $34.9m, 32% less volume and value than the first nine months of 2024, as illustrated in the charts below.

Tariffs sting, too 

It wasn't just the MMPA-related ban that helped to drive up blue, BSC and RSC prices, advised Morrison and Turkin. Additional challenges include the 19% tariff facing Indonesian products since Aug. 7, the rate set as part of a trade deal with US president Donald Trump, which is up from the 10% rate Trump slapped on most countries in April.

BSC from the Philippines has been slapped with a 19% tariff. RSC from Vietnam faces a 20% tariff, while Chinese RSC is getting hit with a 45% tariff. Importers are paying 15% for blue crab from Venezuela.

The tariffs are being passed along in prices, as margins aren't big enough to absorb the extra costs, Turkin said.

What could bring prices down in the near future?  

"Normally, this is the time of year for Indonesia when the heavier rains start and the supply is more ample over the next 90 days," Turkin said. "If that happens, I certainly do anticipate prices overseas coming down."

Reimbursement challenge awaits seafood industry if Trump tariffs overturned

Also, the US Supreme Court held a hearing on Nov. 5 to debate the constitutionality of Trump's tariffs, firing several difficult questions at his legal team, as reported by Undercurrent. A decision is expected no later than June 2026 but could come much sooner and force the administration to refund tariff amounts. 

"Nobody's talking about tariffs as much right now because of the severity of the MMPA, but I'm anxious to hear what's going to happen with the Supreme Court ruling," Turkin said.

He said he's not counting on a refund even if the court rules against the tariffs.

Regardless, Turkin remains hopeful that his company's biggest product remains available.

"We, as Americans, do not consume enough seafood. And we don't have enough availability locally to be able to satisfy the American demand for crab if these Asian imports aren't available," he said. "So I certainly want to see the pricing be affordable for people, and this market cannot sustain $50 a pound."

"Distributors have to make some money too, to be able to get it to the consumer. Restaurants have to be able to cover their overhead to get it to the person eating it. So this is just the beginning of these higher prices and it's just not going to be a sustainable price point, at least during this time period to remain that high."

Turkin said he is starting to see restaurants take crab cakes off the menu due to the high prices. 

"People have started to switch species, people have started to buy less. People have started to consider whether to take it off menus. We haven't fully felt it yet, but the process is underway and it's coming."

"Crab is a healthy protein option for us and we need to protect marine mammals. We need to support the MMPA, but we also need to make certain that we're not cutting off supply of such a healthy option for American consumers to have access to."

US president Donald Trump announcing his nation-specific tariffs on April 2, 2025. Photo Credit: The White House/ Facebook

title: Untitled
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Monday, Nov. 10:

Mowi: September harvest 'inflection point' bodes well for 2026 salmon price

After a weak three quarters for Norwegian farmed salmon spot prices, the world's largest producer expects Q4 and 2026 to see increases based on constrained supply and continued strong demand.

Maruha Nichiro shifts focus from raw material to consumer amid Umios rebrand

The rebrand of Japan's Maruha Nichiro as Umios is part of a broader strategy to shift focus to a consumer-driven, bottom-up approach, from a raw material-driven, top-down one, the company's second-in-command told Undercurrent News.

Chilean salmon prices to Brazil again drop below $6 per kilo

Chilean salmon prices to Brazil for delivery in week 46 of 2025 (Nov. 10-16) declined sharply week-on-week, falling again below $6.00 per kilogram, market sources told Undercurrent on Monday (Nov. 10).

Alaska Wildlife Troopers confirm trawl bycatch at center of criminal probe

The raid of an Alaska groundfish industry group's offices conducted by wildlife-related law enforcement officials in the US state last week has been confirmed as being in relation to allegations of bycatch being sold by processors.

Clearwater Macduff write-down, poor Maine lobster catch take glimmer off Premium Brands' Q3 results

The Canadian food giant Premium Brands is celebrating much-improved third-quarter results, but not because of anything its seafood-related holdings contributed.

Atlantic salmon prices fall in China amid weaker foodservice demand

Atlantic salmon prices at Chinese wholesale markets declined in week 46, as demand from the foodservice sector weakened. 

US gov't shutdown threatens to disrupt 2026 groundfish harvests

The US federal government shutdown -- now the longest on record -- threatens serious ramifications for the upcoming groundfish harvests in the Bering Sea and Gulf of Alaska, including the pollock A season, Undercurrent has learned.

Hiddenfjord expands salmon processing, hatchery facilities to meet export demand

Faroese salmon producer Hiddenfjord is investing in expanded infrastructure to meet growing international demand, adding new capacity to both its processing and hatchery operations.

title: Editor’s choice: US crab importers granted respite from trade ban; Live from Busan, Alaska
content:
EMEA editor Neil Ramsden brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week.

Last week, Undercurrent News reported live from Busan, South Korea, and Anchorage, Alaska, the US, for two big events in the seafood calendar.

Korea held the Busan International Seafood & Fisheries Expo from Nov. 5-7. Hosted by Busan Metropolitan City, the show ranks among Asia's top three seafood and fisheries trade fairs and is Korea's largest, featuring 430 exhibitors from 22 countries. You can recap our coverage of that here.

And Anchorage was home to the annual Alaska Seafood Marketing Institute's All Hands on Deck meeting on Nov. 6-8. The meeting is a decades-long tradition that's traditionally held in late fall or early winter after the busy summer salmon season but before the winter groundfish and crab harvests get underway. You can find coverage of that here.

Then, last week, the US Court of International Trade granted a temporary stay on upcoming Marine Mammal Protection Act import restrictions that threatened to sharply curtail imports of blue swimming crab from key Asian fisheries. The court's approval of a settlement between crab importers and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration pushes back an import ban that was set to take effect Jan. 1, 2026, on swimming crab fisheries that were denied comparability findings.

Staying in the US, law enforcement agents in Alaska raided the downtown office of a long-established trawl industry group in Kodiak on Nov. 4, seizing electronics as well as devices belonging to its executive director. Alaska Groundfish Data Bank, an organization that represents the commercial trawl fleet and shoreside processors in the Gulf of Alaska, notified its membership earlier this week that Alaska State Troopers had served a search warrant at its downtown office while its executive director was off-island for a medical appointment.

A snow crab processing plant owned by St. Mary's Bay Fisheries on the south coast of the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador appears to have been destroyed by fire on Nov. 4. The fire began at about 9:00 p.m., breaking out in the middle of hurricane-force winds of 106 miles per hour, according to Environment Canada.

Prices continued to rise to new record levels on frozen Russian and Norwegian headed and gutted (H&G) Atlantic cod and haddock, with offers rocketing during the China Fisheries & Seafood Expo in Qingdao. Undercurrent adjusted up its week 45 price assessments on H&G cod and haddock from both countries, with sources describing a situation where offers rose by as much as $1,000 per metric ton.

Peru announced a surprisingly small provisional fishing quota late Saturday (Nov. 1) for the world's largest anchovy fishery, setting off alarm bells in the country's fishmeal industry. The 500,000t limit for the year's second north-center fishing season -- starting Nov. 7 -- is roughly one-fifth of last year's quota and the lowest in over 10 years.

Atlantic mackerel prices show no sign of cooling, as expectations of a steep supply drop next year drive East Asian buyers into a raw material scramble. Across Japan, South Korea and China, importers are now rushing to secure substitutes, sending Pacific mackerel prices soaring as well. The market may appear to be a bubble, but voices of concern are already growing that a painful correction could be on the way.

US seafood industry: Hold on to your receipts. If Donald Trump's tariff agenda gets blitzed, they may come in handy. The US Supreme Court on Nov. 5 heard heated oral arguments in a case that will decide the legality of the US president's tariff agenda. The case, Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, is the first of at least seven legal challenges to Trump's tariffs to reach the top US judicial body.

And as much as 37% of the salmon at one Cermaq Canada site off the coast of British Columbia died in September, but the federal agency responsible for aquaculture oversight only disclosed the losses recently. Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans did not specify how many salmon were being stocked at Cermaq's Bawden site, located in northern Clayoquot Sound off the west coast of Vancouver Island, about 40 miles north of Tofino. Without that figure, the scale of the mortality event is difficult to verify.

For the rest of last week's top stories, click the headlines below.

Week 45 US wholesale prices: Fears of bans propel octopus upward; Looming Canada openings sink live lobster
Seafood Connection hires experienced EU pollock sales exec from Trident
Chinese shrimp processors struggle to launch Ecuador operations amid raw material squeeze
'Somebody has to say no'; Europe's cod sector grapples with relentless price spike
Indian shrimp exports to US fall to lowest since COVID, move to other markets
Maine lobster industry warns against overreacting to 'overfishing' language in stock assessment
Six big things that happened to US seafood prices after global trade war started
Alaska salmon season posts strong returns with $541m dock value
Russian, US pollock sellers bullish on A season 2026 PBO fillet block prices
Russian pollock sellers push for higher H&G spot prices, Q1 2026 contract levels

title: Daily recap: Alaskan producers raise concerns over federal shutdown; Europe cod sector grapples with price spike
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Friday, Nov. 7:

ASMI All Hands on Deck 2025: Groundfish producers raise concerns in public, private over federal gov't shutdown

The ASMI All Hands on Deck meeting is a decades-long tradition that's traditionally held in late fall or early winter after the busy summer salmon season but before the winter groundfish and crab harvests get underway. Catch all the updates here.

'Somebody has to say no'; Europe's cod sector grapples with relentless price spike

How do you survive as a cod processor in a world where stocks are in a race to the bottom, the threat of unilateral Barents Sea quotas looms larger with each passing day, and there's a six-month delay between the deal for raw material and the sale to the end-buyer?

US wholesale: Sourcing risks, high costs drive up prices for value-added shrimp

The US wholesale shrimp market is struggling to cope with challenges wrought by policies enacted by US president Donald Trump. US tariffs on shrimp-producing nations, and now a fight over funding of food subsidies for low-income Americans, are driving pricing movements in Undercurrent News' latest shrimp assessment for week 45 of 2025 (Nov. 3-9).

Alaska trawl group targeted in apparent criminal probe

Law enforcement agents in Alaska raided the downtown office of a long-established trawl industry group in Kodiak on Tuesday (Nov. 4), seizing electronics as well as devices belonging to its executive director, Undercurrent has learned.

Norway salmon spot prices remain under pressure, Scottish flat or climbing

Spot prices for Norwegian farmed Atlantic salmon have seen just a small decrease for week 46 (Nov. 10-16) of 2025, while Scottish salmon are either stable or on the rise, sources told Undercurrent.

Russian wild salmon prices hold steady after harvest exceeds forecast

Russian wild salmon prices are holding firm after this summer's harvests exceeded initial forecasts, industry sources told Undercurrent. Russia's Far East region landed 333,000 metric tons of Pacific salmon by Sept. 22, when authorities closed the season, according to the Russian Federal Research Institute of Fisheries and Oceanography.

US wholesale: Lack of deals has buyers questioning whereabouts of Alaska's wild salmon catch

US wholesale wild salmon continues to move at exceptionally low levels on the spot market. Some of Undercurrent's price assessments for the fish, reported here for week 45 (Nov. 3-9), may have to be temporarily removed in the coming weeks due to a dearth of reported deals, in keeping with Undercurrent's price reporting methodology.

title: US swimming crab importers granted temporary reprieve from marine mammal-related ban
content:
The US Court of International Trade has granted a temporary stay on upcoming Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA) import restrictions that threatened to sharply curtail imports of blue swimming crab from key Asian fisheries.

The court's approval of a settlement between crab importers and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), issued Friday (Oct. 31), pushes back an import ban that was set to take effect Jan. 1, 2026, on swimming crab fisheries that were denied comparability findings, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

"Happy to report we settled the case. We got the time we think we need to earn a finding of comparability in the fisheries that were banned," Brice Phillips, vice president of sustainability and business development for Baltimore, Maryland-based Phillips Foods, told Undercurrent via email.

Wholesale prices had skyrocketed

Issued in August, NOAA's MMPA bans were set to block an estimated $3.6 billion worth of seafood from 46 nations, including tuna, shrimp, squid, lobster, grouper, conch and dozens of other commercially important species from such countries.

Blue swimming crab fisheries appeared to be hit hardest, with importers estimating the bans would eliminate 89% of imports by volume (45.3 million of 51.1m pounds). US wholesale prices for swimming crab have skyrocketed in response, Undercurrent reported.

US importers warn of potential closures in lawsuit challenging US swimming crab ban

The case was initiated by 10 importers, along with the National Fisheries Institute and the Restaurant Law Center, which together sued the US Department of Commerce and its related agencies, NOAA and the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), as well as the US homeland security and treasury departments, on Oct. 9.

They argued the bans were issued "without reasoned explanation, fishery-specific evidence or consideration of economic consequences," Undercurrent reported.

On Oct. 14, the industry representatives asked the court for a preliminary injunction, seeking to delay the imposition of the ban beyond Jan. 1, 2026.

"We are, on behalf of all the plaintiffs, pleased with the outcome and commend the Department of Justice for working during a difficult period to bring this to a successful resolution and avoid irreparable harm to some of the most storied American seafood companies," NFI chief strategy officer Gavin Gibbons told Undercurrent via email.

"The parties made the decision to settle the case in order to ensure the responsible implementation of the Marine Mammal Protection Act, which was our goal all along. This action will help safeguard the sustainability of both the fisheries and the US businesses that rely on the raw material." 

Government shutdown complicates matters

The most recent court's decision stays the enforcement of a ban on US imports from five blue swimming crab fisheries representing the bulk of US supply sourcing. They include: Indonesia gillnets and entangling nets (Fishery ID 12391), Vietnam gillnets and entangling nets (ID 2988), Philippines pots/traps (ID 2129), Philippines gillnets and entangling nets (ID 2130) and Sri Lanka crab nets, gillnets, and entangling nets (ID 2705).

Under the agreement, NMFS will initiate a new review of the affected fisheries within 60 days, although it has granted an extension of that timeline, so the countdown will begin only when Congress restores NMFS appropriations. The US government has been shut down for more than a month as Republican and Democratic lawmakers have been unable to agree on funding legislation.

The US Department of Justice cited the shutdown in a bid it made on Oct. 21, asking the court to delay proceedings due to the lapse in federal appropriations, but US Court of International Trade Judge Joseph A. Laroski Jr denied the motion, citing the "immediate and compounding harm" alleged by plaintiffs.

Blue swimming crab from Indonesia. Photograph by Jason Huffman.

During that 60-day period, NMFS will consult with the governments of Vietnam, the Philippines and Sri Lanka and allow them to submit additional information demonstrating actions they have taken to ensure the protection of marine mammals in their fisheries. Other interested parties, including plaintiffs and other industry stakeholders, may also submit information to NMFS.

The court mandated NMFS issue new comparability findings for the five fisheries within 180 days after the end of the 60-day submission period.

Any of the five fisheries that receive positive comparability findings will be permitted to continue exporting product to the US, while fisheries with negative comparability findings will have their crab banned from US export. They can then reapply for another comparability finding but must demonstrate equivalency with US MMPA standards before they receive approval.

The Environmental Defense Fund has been building an adaptive management plan for the blue swimming crab fishery in Lampung Province, Indonesia. Photo courtesy of EDF.

Opposition from US fishermen

Not all US seafood industry representatives are opposed to the MMPA bans. In fact, the Hawaii Longline Association and the Southern Shrimp Alliance, which represent domestic fisheries, both told Undercurrent NMFS must do more to ensure domestic US fisheries are competing fairly with foreign interests.

The two groups, along with the Commercial Fisheries Center of Rhode Island, New England Young Fishermen's Alliance, Maine Coast Fishermen's Association, Cape Cod Commercial Fishermen's Alliance, Alaska Marine Conservation Council and the Alaska Longline Fishermen's Association filed for permission to file an amicus brief in the case on Oct. 22. However, the settlement achieved in the case rendered their filing moot.

title: US lawmaker’s bill seeks to expand rigs-to-reefs efforts in Gulf of Mexico
content:
A bill introduced in the US House of Representatives aims would give states more flexibility to convert decommissioned offshore oil and gas platforms into artificial reefs.

The Marine Fisheries Habitat Protection Act, HR 5745, introduced on Oct. 14 and announced this week by US representative Troy Carter Sr., a Louisiana Democrat, would amend the National Fishing Enhancement Act of 1984 to expand federal support for "rigs-to-reefs" programs in Gulf Coast states.

The measure, which has bipartisan support from US representatives Mike Ezell, a Mississippi Republican, and Marc Veasey, a Texas Democrat, has been referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.

The bill would permit the US Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement to allow certain retired offshore structures to remain in place as artificial reefs, rather than requiring their complete removal, provided they pose no threat to navigation or the environment. Supporters say the initiative could help preserve fish habitats while reducing decommissioning costs for operators.

Carter said, in a press release from his office, that the measure represents a "science-backed solution that turns yesterday's energy infrastructure into tomorrow's marine sanctuaries."

Carter has been active in seafood and fisheries policy. Earlier this year, he co-introduced the Destruction of Hazardous Imports Act (HR 2715) with Louisiana Republican Clay Higgins, which would grant the US Food and Drug Administration authority to destroy imported seafood deemed unsafe for consumption, as Undercurrent News reported. He also supported HR 9226, a bill introduced in 2024 by US representative Mary Peltola, an Alaska Democrat, to ban offshore fish farming.

title: Shrimpers say Newfoundland marine protection plan puts key trawl grounds at risk
content:
Shrimp harvesters say Canada is moving ahead with plans to establish a marine conservation area off northern Newfoundland and Labrador without meaningfully consulting the industry, warning that key fishing grounds could be lost under the proposed boundaries.

The 15,800 km² Torngat Area of Interest has been under review since 2022 and is now in the negotiation phase between Parks Canada, the Nunatsiavut Government and Makivvik. The goal is to create an Inuit Protected Area/National Marine Conservation Area (NMCA) connecting land and sea from the Torngat Mountains to offshore Arctic waters.

While federal officials adjusted the boundaries in 2023 (see map below) to exclude about 979 km² of shrimp trawl grounds, harvesters say the change falls short and that industry concerns continue to be ignored.

A 979 km² reduction made to avoid shrimp trawl grounds "isn't enough," according to Bruce Chapman, executive director of the Canadian Association of Prawn Producers.

"Yes, we asked for the adjustment," he told Undercurrent News. "No, it's not enough. We continue to have no role in the process. The government has lost our trust through this failed process."

Source: Parks Canada

In a December 2023 letter that Chapman shared with Undercurrent, the group said the small boundary change "did not address" concerns and warned that the plan could restrict access to productive trawl grounds and constrain future shifts in shrimp distribution as ocean temperatures rise.

Parks Canada confirmed to Undercurrent last week that the Torngat initiative is now in the negotiation phase, focused on finalizing the boundary, developing a co-management structure and concluding agreements needed for designation. Fisheries within the proposed NMCA would remain regulated under the Fisheries Act by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO).

Parks Canada said consultations with Labrador and Nunavik communities are planned for the coming months as part of an ongoing engagement. The agency described the area as home to Arctic char, walrus and several species at risk, including beluga whales and wolffish. Officials added there is no fixed timeline for formal designation, which will follow negotiations between Ottawa, Makivvik and the Nunatsiavut Government.

Located north of the Inuit community of Nain, the area encompasses Arctic fjords, seabird colonies and feeding habitat for whales, seals, walrus and Arctic char. Parks Canada said it would link coastal and marine ecosystems while protecting Inuit cultural and subsistence use of the region.

The Fish, Food & Allied Workers union, representing more than 14,000 harvesters and plant workers across Newfoundland and Labrador, said the site is too remote to affect most of its members.

"It's in the middle of nowhere in terms of population," said Jason Sullivan, the union's vice president. "Those who it could potentially affect are Aboriginal, and an NMCA isn't enforceable to them."

While the Torngat plan has drawn less controversy than the proposed South Coast Fjords NMCA, which faces opposition from fishers and salmon farmers, both initiatives illustrate the strain between Canada's conservation ambitions and working-water access.

Canada has committed to conserving 30% of its land and ocean areas by 2030 -- a goal not based on science, according to a DFO admission during a recent parliamentary hearing early this month, as Undercurrent reported.

For Chapman and his members, this makes Ottawa's continued push to expand marine protections even more difficult to accept.

"We don't yet know the full extent of the longer-term impact," he said, "but it's clear this process hasn't been handled in good faith."

title: Peru enforces nationwide fishing ban to protect jumbo flying squid during reproductive season
content:
Peru's ministry of production, Produce, has imposed a nationwide ban on the capture of jumbo flying squid to protect the species during its reproductive season.

The restriction will remain effective from Oct. 26 to Nov. 25, 2025.

During this period, all fishing, transport, processing, and sale of jumbo flying squid are prohibited, unless it can be proven that the product was caught before the ban began.

The measure is based on scientific recommendations from the Peruvian Sea Institute, the Imarpe, to ensure the species' sustainability and the long-term stability of the fishing sector.

The duration of the ban could be adjusted if Imarpe detects changes in the squid's reproductive activity.

title: ‘Here we go again’: Pacific Seafood shrugs off fresh allegations of water pollution at US fishmeal plant
content:
US conservation groups have signaled they intend to sue Pacific Seafood Group (PSG) over discharges at a West Coast fishmeal and crab and shrimp shell products plant near the Columbia River.

The Center for Food Safety and Northwest Environmental Defense Center wrote in a Tuesday (Oct. 14) letter to state and federal regulators that the Warrenton, Oregon, facility operated by PSG subsidiary Pacific Bio Products has exceeded its state discharge permits for chlorine by more than 4,000% with recent levels much higher.

California labor union takes aim at Pacific Seafood Group’s environmental record

It attached pages of tables, which it said showed exceedances of chlorine from April 2022 to June 2025. The 79-year-old plant produces a number of agricultural products, including pet food, aquaculture feed and fertilizers. 

"Pacific has violated the permit's monitoring and reporting requirements by failing to monitor effluent and the receiving stream and by failing to report the results to [Oregon regulators] as required," attorneys for the groups wrote.

"The Columbia River and Oregon Coast are already burdened by pollution and habitat destruction from multiple sources," Center for Food Safety staff attorney Kingsly McConnell wrote in a statement. "When the government fails to enforce our environmental laws, the people have both the right and the responsibility to respond."

PSG denies allegations

The Clackamas, Oregon-based West Coast seafood giant fired back, saying the legal action was being brought by "the same cast of characters" intent on smearing the company's reputation.

"Folks like this will throw around a lot of false statements to try to make a splash with the media," PSG spokesperson Lacy Ogan told Undercurrent News via email. "We deny their bogus allegations."

Pacific Seafood settles with former Texas driver accused of stealing shrimp secrets

The fast-growing company is a major player in West Coast crab, shrimp, Pacific wild-caught finfish and more recently, aquaculture. One of the groups involved in the latest legal action brought a lawsuit alleging water pollution violations on the Columbia River at a Washington state steelhead and trout farm, as Undercurrent reported.

The intent-to-sue letter is a legal precursor requiring a formal 60-day notice before filing a lawsuit in a US federal court over violations of the US Clean Water Act. 

Ogan, the company representative, said the seafood company isn't worried.

"Here we go again," she said. "The fact is no one cares more about protecting the marine environment than Pacific Seafood because our business and the livelihoods of our team members depend on healthy and sustainable waterways now and in the future."

Aside from allegations of water pollution, the company is also embroiled in litigation over alleged price-fixing in the Dungeness crab market, as Undercurrent reported.

title: US importers warn of potential closures in lawsuit challenging US swimming crab ban
content:
For several of the 10 US importers that sued the US government on Thursday (Oct. 9), the fight is existential.

The lawsuit, filed in the US Court of International Trade, targets the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and its National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), as well as the US departments of commerce, homeland security and treasury, as Undercurrent News reported.

The 141-page suit alleges NOAA "imposed bans without reasoned explanation, fishery-specific evidence or consideration of economic consequences."

It demands NMFS reverse its ban on products from 240 foreign fisheries due to noncompliance with the US Marine Mammal Protection Act and redo its comparability findings for each fishery "using a results-based approach."

For the companies involved, the stakes couldn't be higher. The bans, scheduled to come into effect Jan. 1, 2026, will prohibit approximately $3.89 billion in seafood imports from entering the US annually, representing 13% of the total 2024 US seafood import value of $27.5bn and 16% of the total import volume (1.09bn of 6.8bn pounds).

The impact is especially acute for blue swimming crab (BSC) importers, as the denials will eliminate 89% of imports by volume (45.3 million of 51.1m pounds). US production of canned crabmeat was a mere 29,000 pounds last year, showing there is no adequate domestically sourced substitute.

That disappearance of product from the market will demolish over $200m in combined annual revenue from the affected companies, the lawsuit claims.

Baltimore, Maryland-based Phillips Foods, which owns a 20-25% market share of US swimming crab sales, said its business derived from the affected fisheries represents $180m in annual revenue.

"The resulting supply disruption will force Phillips to shut down certain operations by Oct. 15, 2025, to avoid stranded inventory. No commercially viable substitute source exists. US BSC landings would have to increase by over 500 million pounds to replace imports," it said.

As a result, Phillips said it will be unable to fulfill existing customer programs and will be forced to shut down several of its overseas processing facilities, leading to layoffs at home and abroad. It also faces the loss of financing tied to affected product lines and "permanent erosion of market share as products are removed from menus and retail placements."

"The longer the restrictions remain in effect, the more difficult it will be for Phillips to reestablish customer relationships and restore its market position," it said.

Newmarket, New Hampshire-headquartered Heron Point Seafood claims it faces a loss of over $50m in annual revenue as a result of the ban and has up to $10m in incoming inventory that could be stranded if it arrives after Jan. 1. Sister companies Cebu Pacific and Byrd International, both of Salisbury, Maryland, said they will lose a combined $40m due to the ban. Katy, Texas-based Crustacea said more than $10m of its business is derived from the sale of crab products set to be banned.

Newport International, based in Saint Petersburg, Florida, will lose approximately half its crab supply as a result of the ban, which is worth around $40m in annual revenue. Moreover, it will be forced to shutter its overseas processing plants and lay off thousands of employees, and it may lose lines of credit tied to financial projections and covenants. 

"Newport also anticipates layoffs of US employees beginning in early 2026, permanent loss of skilled labor both domestically and overseas, loss of market share, and reputational harm from its inability to fulfill customer obligations," it said in the suit.

Gastonia, North Carolina-based 3Fish said it will lose $40m in annual revenue and may be forced to halt all production.

Salisbury, Maryland-headquartered Handy Seafood said it will cease production of its beloved crab cakes on Oct. 15 and will be unable to supply key US customers once its finished goods inventory is depleted.

Shaw's Southern Belle Frozen Foods, of Jacksonville, Florida, depends on imported BSC for around $10m of annual revenue.

"The restrictions therefore pose a direct threat to Shaw's business viability, given its substantial dependence on products originating from the denied fisheries," it said.

Supreme Crab and Seafood, based in Weston, Florida, said imported crab represents a substantial portion of its total revenue and it has no recourse or alternative sources for the imported product it will no longer have access to after the ban comes into effect.

NFI speaks out

The National Fisheries Institute (NFI), a trade group representing the US seafood industry, is the lead plaintiff in the suit. 

The parties to this lawsuit are strong proponents of the MMPA but "want to see it responsibly and sensibly applied," according to NFI chief strategy officer Gavin Gibbons.

NFI's Crab Council, a 26-member panel that includes some of the plaintiffs in the suit, has worked for years to improve the sustainability of the world's swimming crab fisheries, Gibbons said.

But no US crab importer was ever contacted by NOAA during its comparability findings to determine the economic impact of the ban, neglecting its legal requirement to consider "reliance interests," which involves investigating how its policy affects businesses and the market, according to Gibbons.

"NOAA implemented these comparability findings and excluded these stakeholders from its assessment process, in the process violating the Administrative Procedures Act," Gibbons told Undercurrent News. "How can you determine how stakeholders might be affected by policy if you never talk to the stakeholders?"

While the ban impacts a range of commercially important seafood species imported into the US, the plaintiffs chose to focus their lawsuit on swimming crab because of the willingness of crab importers to share the impact NOAA's action is having on them.

"We are able to show the impact on the blue swimming crab community pretty readily," Gibbons said. "But we're asking for relief for any affected fisheries."

By denying market access based on regulatory gaps rather than proven impact on marine mammals, NMFS exceeded its statutory authority, Gibbons said.

"NOAA has replaced science-based evaluation with a bureaucratic checklist," he said. "These fisheries aren't banned because they're actively harming marine mammals. The failures come from data deficiencies, lack of observers, gear types that NOAA doesn't like, claims of inaccurate or inadequate reporting … So many of the deficiencies have nothing to do with documented marine mammal interactions."

NFI also takes issue with the short timeline between NOAA's decision and the ban's implementation. While NOAA faced a court mandate to enact stricter enforcement of the MMPA under the terms of a January 2025 legal settlement it reached with the Natural Resources Defense Council, the Center for Biological Diversity and the Animal Welfare Institute, its setting of a Jan. 1 implementation date is causing severe damage to importers, who face legal risks for accepting product that is already en route to the US.

"It's a bureaucratic straw man that if we don't implement this right now, there's going to be this emergent impact on marine mammals," Gibbons said. "There's scenarios where they're saying things there aren't observers, or there aren't logbooks documenting marine mammal interactions. And then you dig into the fishery, and the fishery says, 'Well, we don't see any marine mammals. Why would we be keeping logbooks and having observers?' Any interactions are either so rare or nonexistent, but they're still failing."

The ultimate consequence of NOAA's actions, besides harming the seafood industry, could actually be more harm to marine mammals, Gibbons said.

"Banning these products is very likely to do more harm than good," said Gibbons. "Shutting off commerce with fisheries gives up leverage and actually encourages selling to countries with little or no marine mammal protections. Fears about unintended consequences are very real."

title: Untitled
content:
New import rules in the European Union (EU) set to come into force in January 2026 have the Canadian lobster industry worried about losing access to the market unless harvesters can quickly improve their documentation on catches.

The EU now wants data for individual harvesters, including details about which boat made the catch, where it was caught and under what circumstances, Stewart Lamont, managing director of Tangier Lobster, a Nova Scotia-based exporter, told Undercurrent News on Friday (Oct. 10).

"It's essentially an initiative by the EU to crack down on IUU [illegal, unreported and unregulated] fishing," he said, but requiring a "a level of specificity" not seen before by the industry.

It could be a logistical nightmare for both live and processed lobster exporters, Lamont said, while also acknowledging that the Canadian industry has been plagued by illegal and unreported lobster fishing, which needs to change.

"Canada has international commitments on IUU activity. And if we are turning a blind eye to undocumented cash transactions, we're not living up to our commitments. We're not properly managing our resources," he said.

Canadian lobster industry unimpressed by latest DFO enforcement report

However, with just three months to go to set up a system that details how and where each lobster was caught, and provide that information for each shipment to the EU, the task ahead is challenging, said Lamont.

"We used to identify lobster landings by port," he said. "Now we'll need to track boat-by-boat, day-by-day. The documentation required will be enormous."

No option but to adapt

The EU rule is not singling out Canadian lobster, Geoff Irvine, executive director of the Lobster Council of Canada, told Undercurrent on Friday.

"The EU is asking all of its trading partners for the same additional traceability," he said. 

The EU regulation to prevent, deter and eliminate IUU entered into force on Jan. 1, 2010.

The rules have been updated since to make it compulsory for EU operators and importers of fish products to use CATCH, a digital system to record landings information to verify that products entering the EU market have not originated from IUU fishing, as explained on the EU website.

Under the new system, lobster buyers and exporters will be required to provide specific vessel numbers and catch locations, in digital format, for the EU CATCH certificates, which will be necessary for export, Irvine explained. Each landing will also require a captain's signature.

"Most of the recordkeeping will take place on shore by the first buyers and processors," Irvine said, adding that his group was working closely with Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) to respond.

Lobster traps stacked on a vessel in preparation of setting day in Canada's largest lobster fishery, LFA 34, a major lobster fishing zone on Nova Scotia's southwest coast. The season there begins in November. Photograph courtesy of Coldwater Lobster Association.

Such a detailed catch reporting system is not a new concept within the Canadian fishing industry, Irvine added, noting that such a system has been in place for 15 years to handle northern cod landings in the province of Newfoundland and Labrador. It was created while the fishery was under a moratorium and a limited stewardship fishery was allowed.

The dockside monitoring program, managed by the Fish Food and Allied Workers (FFAW), the union that represents fish harvesters, also verifies landings volumes for crab, pelagics and other species.

However, there is no dockside monitoring program in any of the other Atlantic Canadian provinces, even though a study of illegal fishing by the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Oceans recommended that such a system should be adopted for all fisheries.

The 2024 report by the parliamentary panel recommended that DFO implement modern technology and computer systems for data collection, such as a digital and standardized catch register for all Canadian fishers, so that reporting requirements are more standardized across the country, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

"For lobster, we just haven't had to fully embrace it until now. But if we want to sell to the EU, we simply have to do it," said Irvine.

Canada has no option but to adapt, both Lamont and Irvine agree.

The EU has become a growing market for Canadian lobster, but it's still a distant third in importance to the US and China.

In 2024, Canada exported 3,446 metric tons of live lobster worth $72.2 million to the EU while sending 19,658t worth $355.1m to the US and 15,991t worth $345.8m to China. Over the first eight months of 2025, Canada has exported 2,447t of live lobster worth $52.6m to the EU.

 "Our industry has done this many times before. We are already providing digital traceability to US buyers. This just adds a few new elements we need to figure out," Irvine said.

"Can we rise to the challenge? We'll see in three months. But we may have no choice," added Lamont.

High-level Canada seafood trade panel brainstorms solutions to US dependence during time of Trump

However, the challenge may be greater than some lobster processors can cope with, and not all firms might get on board with the EU rules, Lamont said. Some might instead decide the European market is not worth the hassle and continue to focus on the US or Asian markets.

That won't be Tangier Lobster. It has longstanding relationships with importers across the EU, and it's not something they want to give up, he said.

He hopes there might be some "middle ground" whereby a live lobster exporter would not have to vouch for every single lobster in every shipment. But he's already started to try to figure out how to collect the data that will be necessary to clear EU customs.

It won't be simple, he said, noting that Tangier buys from 30 different lobster dealers across Atlantic Canada, who buy from multiple harvesters.

"They have a relationship in their communities with individual fishermen," Lamont said. "So we will talk to our dealers, and they will talk to their fishermen. They already have a lot of data, so it's not a great burden on the fishermen. But it is a burden on the buyer, who must segregate and document what comes from whom, when and where. That's where the burden will be."
