title: Half of UK’s key fish stocks on brink of collapse amid gov’t inaction, report warns
content:
Half of the UK's top ten commercial fish stocks are in peril, with many either critically depleted, being overfished, or both, according to a new report released by Oceana UK.

The report, "Deep Decline: State of the UK's Fish Populations 2025", covers 105 species and reveals that just 41% of these stocks are considered healthy, while over a quarter (27%) are critically low in numbers and 25% are currently being overexploited.

Alarmingly, one in six stocks falls into both categories -- critically low yet still fished beyond sustainable limits -- pushing them towards the risk of total collapse.

Among the worst affected are North Sea cod and herring, North East Atlantic mackerel, and Southern North Sea edible crab. North Sea cod, in particular, has been highlighted as critically depleted, with the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea recommending a zero catch quota in 2025 to prevent its collapse.

Despite this, government-set catch limits for these stocks have repeatedly exceeded scientific advice.

"This crisis is not an unavoidable tragedy but a political failure," said Hugo Tagholm, executive director of Oceana UK. "Five years after becoming an independent coastal state, the UK continues to set fishing quotas that ignore science, jeopardising marine ecosystems, fishing livelihoods, and food security. Ministers must act now to end overfishing and rebuild fish populations with legally binding targets."

The report also highlights stark regional differences. The Irish Sea is the worst affected, with overfished stocks rising from 27% in 2020 to 41% in 2025, while the Celtic Sea also faces critical depletion. In contrast, the West of Scotland maintains the healthiest fisheries, with 62% of stocks considered healthy.

Despite the bleak outlook, Oceana UK points to examples of sustainable management working well. Stocks like West of Scotland haddock, Western Channel sole, and North Sea plaice have remained healthy due to catch limits aligned with scientific recommendations since 2020, demonstrating that recovery is possible when policy follows science.

However, industry representatives have criticised the report's findings.

Daniel Lawson, executive officer of the Shetland Fishermen's Association, called Oceana an "anti-fishing group" that "sensationalises" data and ignores the complexity of marine ecosystems, including climate change and offshore developments.

Similarly, Elspeth Macdonald, chief executive of the Scottish Fishermen's Federation, accused Oceana of "oversimplifying fisheries science and setting unachievable targets that could undermine practical solutions."

Oceana UK is urgently calling on the UK government and devolved administrations to adopt a comprehensive strategy to end overfishing by 2026.

This includes legally binding deadlines to rebuild stocks, aligning all catch limits with scientific advice by the end of 2025, publishing annual audits scrutinised by Parliament and supporting fishermen through the transition to sustainable fishing practices.

New leadership in Europe

The report's release coincided with the announcement that Vera Coelho has been appointed executive director and vice president of Oceana Europe.

Coelho has played a pivotal role in securing over 20 policy victories for European waters, including the establishment of marine protected areas and the enforcement of sustainable fishing regulations.

"I'm honoured to lead Oceana's team in Europe at such a critical moment," Coelho said. "Strong, science-based policies can deliver real results for our oceans and communities, but urgent action is needed."

title: Untitled
content:
The old site of southern China's largest seafood wholesale hub, the Huangsha seafood market in Guangzhou, is set to officially close this month, with all vendors required to relocate to the newly built facilities across the river.

The new complex, named Huangsha Seafood Center, opened on Sept. 8 and is intended to replace the decades-old market as the region's main seafood trading venue.

However, some vendors have yet to move due to various reasons and continued operating at the old market during China's Golden Week holiday (Oct. 1-8).

Market operator Guangzhou Port Group has announced a series of restrictive measures to accelerate the transition. Starting 10:00 a.m. on Oct. 15, seafood trading vehicles — including logistics and wholesale trucks — will be barred from entering the old market.

From Oct. 22, further restrictions will take effect, including limits on water supply and the closure of facilities, with the operator ceasing all services.

All vendors have been instructed to settle rent and utility fees up to Sept. 30 and complete exit procedures, as business operations will no longer be permitted after Oct. 15.

Guangzhou Port Group said it will enforce a "no entry, only exit" policy to ensure that, once the old market withdraws from seafood wholesale activities, no seafood-related operations continue on the site.

The old Huangsha Market has been in operation for over three decades, hosting more than 200 varieties of fresh and live seafood from over 20 countries, with an annual trading volume exceeding 270,000 metric tons and a transaction value of more than CNY 10 billion ($1.39bn).

title: National Fisheries Institute, swimming crab importers sue US over marine mammal rules
content:
A coalition of major seafood importers, processors and restaurant industry groups has filed suit against the US government, challenging a recent move by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to block seafood imports from hundreds of foreign fisheries under the Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA).

The National Fisheries Institute (NFI), Restaurant Law Center and 10 seafood companies, including Phillips Foods, Newport International and Supreme Crab and Seafood, filed the complaint Thursday (Oct. 9) in the US Court of International Trade. The complaint targets NOAA and its National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), as well as the US departments of commerce, homeland security and treasury.

Other plaintiffs include 3Fish, Handy Seafood, Heron Point Seafood, Shaw's Southern Belle Frozen Foods, Cebu Pacific, Byrd International and Crustacea Seafood.

At issue is NOAA's Sept. 2 "comparability findings" determination, which denied import eligibility to 240 fisheries across 46 nations for allegedly failing to meet US standards for protecting marine mammals, as Undercurrent News reported.

The bans are scheduled to take effect Jan. 1, 2026, impacting billions of dollars in seafood trade and choking the supply of pasteurized blue swimming crab meat sourced from Southeast Asia and Venezuela.

"After a decade of assessing fisheries, without stakeholder input, NOAA has given affected members of the seafood community only four months to come into compliance or face complete shutdown," NFI chief strategy officer Gavin Gibbons said in a press release. "We are talking about US processing and distribution businesses working with imported, raw materials that can't be sustainably harvested at this volume in our own waters."

The plaintiffs argue NOAA violated the Administrative Procedures Act by not consulting "reliance interests" to determine how its policies might affect the market. 

US foreign fisheries ban threatens ‘death punch’ to swimming crab importers

The bans could cripple the US crab industry. Phillips Foods, one of the two largest swimming crab importers, reported $180 million in annual revenue tied to affected imports and warned it would be forced to shut down operations by mid-October to avoid stranding inventory. Other plaintiffs described similar risks of layoffs, plant closures and market losses.

Brice Phillips, vice president of sustainability and business development for the Baltimore, Maryland-based company, told Undercurrent in early September NOAA's move represents a "death punch" to the swimming crab sector.

The plaintiffs are seeking an injunction to halt enforcement of the bans, along with an order directing NOAA to revisit its decisions using a results-based approach.

"Banning these products is very likely to do more harm than good," said Gibbons. "Shutting off commerce with fisheries gives up leverage and actually encourages selling to countries with little or no marine mammal protections. Fears about unintended consequences are very real."

title: Australis dispute escalates as former owners’ family group seeks to void arbitration outcome
content:
The family group behind the former owner of Chilean salmon farmer Australis Seafoods, Isidoro Quiroga, has filed a petition to annul a recent arbitration ruling, sharply escalating a long-running legal battle with current owner Joyvio Group.

Asesorias e Inversiones Benjamin (AIB), representing Quiroga, submitted the nullity motion to the Santiago Court of Appeals on Oct. 3, arguing that an award issued by the Santiago Arbitration and Mediation Center (the CAM, in its Spanish acronym) in the Australis case is "aberrantly defective" and in direct violation of Chilean legal standards.

As Undercurrent News previously reported, the CAM found that the former owners of Australis Seafood violated an equity acquisition agreement by failing to make "complete and accurate representations" about the company's status and "not disclosing key information related to environmental regulations."

The Aug. 1 ruling orders the respondents to pay $217.2 million in principal damages plus $80.4m in interest accrued since July 2019, with additional interest continuing to accumulate until full payment is made.

In the filing to which Undercurrent News has had access, AIB claims the award ordered a partial price refund, neither requested by either party nor discussed during the proceedings, a ruling they say effectively nullifies a valid and binding contract.

China’s Joyvio awarded $298m in Chilean salmon farmer Australis acquisition dispute

"It seriously and manifestly violates the fundamental principles of Chilean law," the petition reads. "Its defects strike at the heart of due process, legal certainty, and public confidence in arbitration as a system for resolving business disputes."

Years-long issue

The case centers on Joyvio's 2019 acquisition of Australis for nearly $1 billion, one of the largest transactions in Chilean aquaculture history.

In 2023, Joyvio initiated arbitration, alleging the sellers misrepresented production capacity and other financial details.

The tribunal ruled in Joyvio's favor this year, granting partial compensation, a decision the Quiroga family is now seeking to overturn.

In response, Quiroga's legal team also argued the tribunal's own findings undermine the damages awarded in the high-stakes salmon industry dispute.

"The arbitral award confirms this is a 100% commercial and civil dispute," Cristobal Eyzaguirre, Quiroga's attorney, told El Mercurio in his first media interview in 35 years of practice.

"The majority vote is completely incoherent. On one hand, it categorically rules out any fraud by the sellers, reaffirms that no information was hidden, recognizes that in 2021 -- two years after the sale -- the SMA [Environmental Superintendency] changed its criteria on overproduction," he added.

Additionally, in a legal opinion submitted with the petition, Gary Born, chair of the International Arbitration Practice Group at WilmerHale, stated the CAM award was "one of the most aberrantly defective decisions" he had seen in his career.

"Annulling the award is necessary to discourage similar rulings in the future and to preserve confidence in Chile as a credible arbitration venue," Born wrote.

$300m Australis award blasted by former owner’s attorney as ‘incoherent’; appeal coming

Other experts also echoed that view.

Yves Derains, former secretary general of the ICC International Court of Arbitration, wrote that such an award "would not pass scrutiny" in international institutions. Josa Maria Alonso, president of the Madrid International Arbitration Center, said the decision "should be annulled under the Model Law" and would likely not be recognized or enforced in Spain.

AIB's petition also warns that if the ruling is allowed to stand, it could damage Chile's reputation as an international arbitration hub and undermine legal predictability in cross-border commercial transactions.

The Santiago Court of Appeals is expected to consider the nullity motion in the coming weeks.

"A decision to overturn the award could have wide implications for foreign investment in Chile's aquaculture sector and for the use of arbitration in large-scale M&A disputes," AIB concluded.

title: US shrimp festival partners with genetic testing firm after mislabeling controversy
content:
One year after exposing shrimp mislabeling at a seafood festival in the US state of Alabama, genetic testing firm SeaD Consulting has found itself as a partner of this year's event.

"In an effort to ensure all shrimp sold at the 52nd annual National Shrimp Festival complies with new state seafood labeling laws, we have established a partnership with SeaD Consulting to DNA test shrimp sold at the festival," the organizers announced in a press release.

The National Shrimp Festival, in Gulf Shores, Alabama, has been held the second week of October since 1971. The four-day annual event -- which features shopping, music and "fresh seafood from the Gulf of Mexico" -- attracts around 300,000 people.

But in 2024, it also attracted a lot of unwanted attention when Houston, Texas-based SeaD Consulting exposed that, through its genetic testing of five shrimp dishes from the festival, only one dish contained authentic gulf wild-caught shrimp.

An Alabama state law that went into effect on Oct. 1, 2024, requires that foodservice establishments notify consumers of the country of origin of their seafood and whether it was farm-raised or wild-caught. 

FREE READ Latest shrimp mislabeling probe finds restaurants flouting Alabama disclosure law

While the festival organizers reportedly had a $500 fine in place for those selling imported farm-raised shrimp, SeaD Consulting said at the time that "enforcement" at the festival "appears to be lacking."

Festival organizers appear to have a special focus on enforcement this year, though.

Thanks to sponsorship from the Organized Seafood Association of Alabama (OSAA), a group that festival chairman Rob Barnas said in a press release has been absent as a sponsor for "several years," event organizers were able to bring in SeaD Consulting.

SeaD will be working alongside Chandra Wright, the director of environmental and education outreach at The Lodge at Gulf State Park, who was recently appointed to the newly created "chief shrimp investigator" role.

Photo Credit: Screenshot/ Chandra Wright

Wright, who previously worked as a tourism specialist at the Mississippi-Alabama Sea Grant Consortium, will be aiding SeaD in a volunteer capacity to ensure that food vendors at the 2025 festival are following Alabama state law.

One thing that Wright will be looking for is to ensure that the origin of the shrimp or other seafood item is on the vendor's sign as part of their menu in "large letters." In a video explaining her role, she also said that she would be working closely with vendors to check invoices, boxes and products to ensure that they are wild-caught.

Another aspect that's seemingly new this year is a booth to educate attendees about local seafood and its impact on the community.

"It's important that we do everything we can to make sure the hard-working men and women from our state who bring in the tastiest shrimp anywhere get their just due. It's not right and just plain dishonest to advertise Alabama wild-caught shrimp when you're serving imported shrimp grown on a farm," commented Ernie Anderson, OSAA's president. "With SeaD's new testing, we can make sure these bad actors are found out in a short time."

The National Shrimp Festival is not the only seafood event that SeaD has partnered with to end mislabeling. The company shared on its Facebook page last week that it will be speaking at the upcoming Louisiana Shrimp Festival and Shrimp Aid event the weekend of Oct. 18-19 and testing dishes at the festival for accuracy.

title: US gov’t shutdown threatens lots of new hurdles, obstructions for seafood industry
content:
The US federal government shut down on Wednesday (Oct. 1) amid a political impasse over health care subsidies, and that has plenty of consequences for the seafood industry.

The shutdown, which will continue until at least seven Democratic senators join the Republican majority to approve a continuing resolution with adequate funding to run the government, will result in the cessation of most activities undertaken under the executive branch of government.

The impact for seafood will grow the longer the shutdown drags on.

A plan issued on Monday (Sept. 29) by the US Commerce Department, which oversees the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and its National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), also known as NOAA Fisheries, confirms many of the operations of the agency in charge of fisheries regulation will be suspended through the shutdown.

NOAA Fisheries cuts to force radical restructure of Alaska office, FOIA response reveals

Exceptions include law enforcement, facility maintenance, seafood inspection and activities funded by mechanisms other than NMFS' annual congressional appropriation.

The document clarifies NMFS must ensure the enforcement of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act, Marine Mammal Protection Act, Endangered Species Act and continue with all other operations "required to protect life and property (and) avoid irreparable harm to US trust resources."

That means commercial fisheries management and the deployment of onboard observers will continue through the shutdown, as will all programs funded through cost-recovery fees paid for by industry.

However, work on all fisheries-related projects, including natural resource and infrastructure projects, funded by current-year annual appropriations, has ceased.

Legal work on "active litigation related to NMFS actions for which there are imminent or near-term court-ordered deadlines that are unable to be suspended during a lapse" will continue, according to the document.

US representation at "international meetings where fishing privileges or the allocation of fishing rights will be determined/voted on, including international regional fishery management organization meetings, such that lack of representation would harm US trust resources," will also continue.

Staff responses to environmental disasters that could threaten US fisheries commerce or aquatic environments, such as oil spills, may be authorized as needed, the document confirms.

An email sent by a senior Commerce Department official to NMFS employees, seen by Undercurrent News, further outlines the steps being taken by the agency in response to the shutdown, including furloughs of most employees.

"A funding lapse will result in certain government activities ceasing due to a lack of appropriated funding. In addition, designated pre-notified employees of this agency would be temporarily furloughed," the document instructs.

"The agency has contingency plans in place for executing an orderly shutdown of activities that would be affected by any lapse in appropriations forced by Congressional Democrats. Further information about those plans will be distributed should a lapse occur."

Friends of NOAA fear continued cuts, uncertainty as fiscal 2026 approaches

The email also contains some loaded language that could comprise a violation of the Hatch Act, which bars most government employees from engaging in partisan political activity while performing official duties to ensure a politically neutral civil service.

"President Trump opposes a government shutdown, and strongly supports the enactment of HR 5371, which is a clean Continuing Resolution to fund the government through Nov. 21, and already passed the US House of Representatives," the document reads. "Unfortunately, Democrats are blocking this Continuing Resolution in the US Senate due to unrelated policy demands. If Congressional Democrats maintain their current posture and refuse to pass a clean Continuing Resolution to keep the government funded before midnight on Sep. 30, 2025, federal appropriated funding will lapse." 

Legislative roadblock

The shutdown has ground to a halt most work on legislation affecting the US seafood industry. 

Bills that are under consideration in the US Senate and House of Representatives include:

Fisheries Modernization Act of 2025 (HR 4800) -- proposes a Magnuson-Stevens reauthorization, with amendments to some fisheries management programs;
FISH Act of 2025 (S 688) -- combats illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing and targets foreign seafood that undermines US supply chains; 
Supporting Equity for Aquaculture and Seafood Act "SEAS Act" (HR 4898) -- includes measures to support and expand domestic aquaculture, access to capital and equity for aquaculture businesses; 
Imported Seafood Quality Enforcement Act (HR 2776) -- contains amendments to the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act to tighten screening of imported seafood; 
Imported Seafood/Shrimp inspection & promotion (HR 512) -- creates a shrimp inspection/consumption fund and imposes enhanced inspection duties for shrimp products; 
Sustaining America's Fisheries for the Future Act (HR 3718) -- reauthorization/amendments to Magnuson-Stevens; fisheries sustainability, bycatch and regional management reforms; 
Save Our Seafood Act (S 1292) – permanently authorizes exemption of fish processors from H-2B visa cap;
Protecting Global Fisheries Act (S 1369) -- measures to strengthen US policy to protect global fish stocks and seafood supply chains; and 
Northeast Fisheries Heritage Protection Act (HR 674) -- prohibits commercial offshore wind development in Lobster Management Area 1 in the Gulf of Maine. 

Additionally, Congress was considering changes that would weaken the Endangered Species Act and Marine Mammal Protection Act, as reported by Undercurrent News, as well as a pullback of management of the Gulf of Mexico red snapper fishery (HR 260), a bill funding the development of a test to determine the origin of wild-caught fish include red snapper (S 283); a provision that would close a loophole to stop the recently renamed Department of War from buying imported seafood (HR 3838), and a bill that would extend the data reporting requirements beyond ocean vessels to aircraft, truck and rail shipments (S 1259).

A pair of Maui dolphins. Photograph by Laura Boren for the Department of Conservation.

Could lead to mass NMFS layoffs

Additionally, the shutdown could advance the Trump administration's efforts to reduce the size of the federal workforce by converting temporary furloughs into permanent layoffs.

The White House Office of Management and Budget issued a memo that a shutdown would give the administration the opportunity to issue "reduction in force" notices to people who work on programs that are "not consistent with the president's priorities," Politico reported last week.

Federal agencies could later modify those reduction-in-force notices to keep only the minimum number of necessary employees, effectively giving the Trump administration a way to dismiss many workers it has so far lacked the authority to fire.

Since taking office in January, Trump has targeted NOAA for cuts. His administration has proposed a 17% reduction in the federal agency's 2026 budget, which could eliminate an additional 2,000 of the agency's 12,000 remaining employees.

NOAA has lost over 1,000 workers during a round of firings of temporary employees in February and March and a voluntary buyout over the summer, as Undercurrent reported.

title: Aquaculture belongs in Canada’s nation-building strategy, crowd told
content:
"If we did not have fish farming, we would now be inventing it," Ken Coates told a packed room at the 30th annual Cold Harvest convention in St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador, this week.

Coates, professor emeritus at the Johnson Shoyama Graduate School of Public Policy at the University of Saskatchewan, attempted to help ease some of the underlying anxiety in the aquaculture industry that they aren't being appreciated or given enough priority in Canada. Contributing significantly to the worry is the planned sunsetting by 2029 of net-pen salmon aquaculture in the other-coast province of British Columbia.

"The world needs food. Canada needs food, good food, high-protein food. We need what you guys produce," said Coates, who was the keynote speaker at the Newfoundland Aquaculture Industry Association (NAIA) conference on Wednesday (Sept. 24).

In a wide-ranging, hour-long address to about 200 attendees that touched on everything from the urban/rural divide on resource issues to the scourge of social media, Coates argued that the debate around aquaculture has been hijacked by an urban, activist-driven narrative that ignores rural realities and economic needs.

"What we actually need, really need on a national scale, is evangelists for rural and small-town life," he said,

Ken Coates, professor emeritus at the University of Saskatchewan, was the keynote speaker at the Cold Harvest conference on Wednesday, Sept. 24, 2025. Barb Dean-Simmons photo

Public attitudes have been molded by distrust of science and the politicization of resource development, he charged.

"In the last 10 years, we had a government that was very much focused on the conservation environmentalist side, and didn't pay very much attention at all to the economic consequences," said Coates, who published an academic paper, Swimming Against the Tide, in February 2025, that criticized Canada's BC-related decision.

Aquaculture in BC is regulated by the federal government, unlike in Atlantic Canada where provincial governments are the lead regulators for the industry.

No tolerance for intimidation

Although several Indigenous groups in BC have backed salmon farming as a way to strengthen their economies and protect wild stocks, they have been drowned out by well-funded, media-savvy activists, who use emotion and the political power of social media to influence public attitudes, Coates said.

"Activists play a vital role in our society. They help us identify problems. They challenge us to go with better solutions," he said.

However, they should not have the final word on aquaculture, or any other resource policy, he stressed.

"You're going to have protestors as long as you have an industry and you just have to sort of accept that as part of the price of working in any kind of environmentally sensitive area," Coates said.

What cannot be tolerated are tactics rooted in harassment and intimidation, he said.

"I am mortified, absolutely mortified at the personal attacks against supporters of the fish farming industry. I don't know how many of you have dealt with this yourself, with people attacking you on social media, sometimes making death threats like they did against Indigenous people on the west coast," he said.

NAIA 2025: Canada’s BC plan cools aquaculture investor appetite nationwide

Industry and government should expose the bad behavior, let the public know about the levels of intimidation and harassment from the anti-aquaculture groups, he argued. There also needs to be more transparency about activists' funding sources, and Canada needs to improve and enforce the rules around lobbying and public advocacy.

"We actually, as a country, need more public engagement, but it has to be more open and fair," he said.

Tailor-made solution 

The debate over aquaculture is playing out against a shifting political and economic backdrop in Canada.

Earlier this month, prime minister Mark Carney unveiled a "nation-building" strategy to revive Canada's resource and infrastructure sectors. Projects such as a liquefied natural gas plant, a copper and gold mine, and an expansion of the Port of Montreal were among the first to receive federal backing.

"We used to build big things in this country, and we used to build them quickly. It's time to get back at it and get on with it. That starts with getting out of the way," Carney said at an event in Edmonton, Alberta, on Sept. 10, as reported by the CBC. 

Aquaculture needs to be on that list, said Coates.

"Canada needs great industries right now, and if Carney and his government want to prove that they want to get the economy going, they have one tailor-made opportunity," he said.

"Get rid of the fish farming ban on the west coast. Allow the industry to expand in a careful and constructive way," Coates urged.

Canada's Department of Innovation, Science and Economic Development (ISED is preparing a report on the impact of the BC decision. That report, which is expected to be finished very soon, will guide the future of aquaculture in the west coast province, Canada's fisheries minister Joanne Thomson said recently, as reported by Undercurrent News. 

Thompson, who represents a ryding in St. John's in Parliament, has given no hint of where she stands regarding BC aquaculture, or whether she has any desire to change or reverse the 2024 decision made by her predecessor Diane Lebouthillier.

Canada's fisheries minister Joanne Thompson appeared at the 30th annual Cold Harvest aquaculture conference in St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada, via pre-recorded video message on Thursday, Sept. 25. Photo by Barb Dean-Simmons

"The file sits with ISED, and they will come out with their report, then it will move to me. But I am waiting, as many others are, to read that report, and I think our conversations will go from there," she said at a press conference on Aug. 29.

Meanwhile, the aquaculture industry has learned that the ISED report will confirm that the decision to ban net pen farming will cost the federal government CAD 9.0 billion ($6.5bn) and that no closed containment technologies currently exist that can feasibly replace the open net pens, a source told Undercurrent at the Cold Harvest conference.

Fight 'like you've never fought before'

Coates on Wednesday pressed the sector to stand its ground more forcefully in the face of opposition.

If aquaculture were a brand new concept right now, it would likely be hailed as a great idea for producing a lot of good food, with jobs and economic benefits for small towns, he suggested.

Canada’s plan for British Columbia salmon farming in ‘final stages’

"You have a great industry. It's ecologically sound. It's scientifically based. You're constantly committed to constant innovation and constant development, and you're doing things right. You create lots of jobs, stable jobs in rural areas and small towns," he said.

"it is just bizarre that we're at this huge moment where we need the food globally and we're sort of fighting against it here."

With Canadian leaders pledging support for nation-building projects, there's no better time than now to promote aquaculture as a solution for Canada's economy and food security, he said.

"This is your chance to stand up, fight for your communities like you've never fought for them before, fight for your industry like you've never fought before. Canada needs you to succeed," he said.

title: Untitled
content:
Vietnam's pangasius sector continues to show resilience, with export values up year-on-year in 2025 even as sales to the US continue to slide since May, according to the Vietnam Association of Seafood Exporters and Producers (VASEP) and the latest data.

VASEP said cumulative turnover from pangasius exports had reached over $1.4 billion as of the end of August, up 10% from 2024. August alone saw export value reach $200 million, up 5% y-o-y.

That has come as a result of stronger pricing; a consultancy commissioned by Undercurrent News to gather and analyze customs and production data reported that volumes were stable at 88,104 metric tons, down 0.7% month-on-month and 1.0% y-o-y.

That means volumes have been stable and high since June, despite the fact that sales to the US have eased since a rush to get product shipped to that market before new tariffs came into force. You can see the breakdown by markets at the subheading below.

August exports to the US and ASEAN markets declined by 5% and 11% in volume terms, respectively, but this was offset by increases to China and Hong Kong (5%), the EU (4%), Brazil (4%), Mexico (31%) and the UK (23%).

The average export price across all pangasius products -- from the most heavily glazed fillets up to Aquaculture Stewardship Council-certified, zero-glaze items -- was unchanged m-o-m at $2.14 per kilogram for August.

August Vietnamese customs data on pangasius, from the consultancy

"Leading companies are ramping up processing volumes, not only to meet Q4 export orders but also to proactively boost capacity for inventory build-up," the consultancy told Undercurrent. "The strategy serves as a necessary preparation in the face of tightening raw material supply, sustained high farm-gate prices, and the anticipated rise in import demand from multiple markets during the year-end peak season."

VASEP added that the first eight months of 2025 had shown the pangasius sector was maintaining a "steady recovery momentum," albeit with uneven markets.

"While China & Hong Kong stagnated, CPTPP [the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership bloc], ASEAN and Brazil became new drivers, while the US and EU continued to be stable pillars. This reflects a clear trend: Vietnamese pangasius is gradually repositioning itself in the global trade flow, by diversifying markets, increasing deep processing and strengthening its brand in high-value segments," VASEP claimed.

As reported by VietnamNet, VASEP is leaning hard into creating greater domestic demand for pangasius as well. 

Export items like pangasius should not be reserved solely for foreign markets; winning the hearts of local consumers first creates a stronger, more sustainable launchpad for global success, was its message at a recent Hanoi event.

US exports ease again

The pangasius sector expected sales to the vital US market to decline once new tariffs against Vietnamese goods were enforced, and they have -- but August saw volumes a little higher y-o-y still. 

That said, at under $3.00/kg, the average export price of all products to this market is lower y-o-y.

VASEP said this year's exports had been worth $234m, up 3.7% y-o-y and "quite stable."

"Despite the modest growth rate, the US is still the most important market due to its high value, strict requirements and global influence. Maintaining growth in the context of complex tariffs and technical barriers shows that Vietnamese pangasius is consolidating its position in the mid- to high-end segment. This is also the driving force for businesses to continue to promote standardization and brand building in this market," it said.

Vinh Hoan Corp., the country's largest exporter of pangasius fillets and the biggest exporter to the US, reported a strong July (the last month for which it has filed an unaudited update), with total revenue up 13% y-o-y at VND 1.27 trillion ($48.1m). 

While the rest of the world and Europe segments saw strong growth for Vinh Hoan y-o-y, so did the US:

Credit: Vinh Hoan

And as shown at Undercurrent's trade portal, US imports from Vietnam have been stronger this summer than last: 

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view

Meanwhile, volume shipments to China & HK also stayed firm in August, up a little m-o-m though down y-o-y:

The average price across all products shipped slipped 1.5% m-o-m, but remains a few cents better per kilogram than a year ago. VASEP said August sales to China reached $55m, down 4% y-o-y.

The CPTPP bloc continues to be an important growth region for Vietnam’s pangasius sales this year.

Exports have now reached $242m, up 36% y-o-y. "Japan, Canada and Mexico are important markets in the bloc, with diverse needs from frozen fillets to processed products," said VASEP.

"The tax incentives from the [free trade agreement] and the change in consumer trends towards convenient and safe products are opening up great opportunities. CPTPP is therefore not only a short-term bright spot, but also a long-term strategic area for the pangasius industry."

Mexico, a major importer in the bloc to which VASEP has previously noted sales are encouraging, saw sales of 3,084t in August -- only the fourth time they've surpassed 3,000t in the past year. Prices slipped 3.7% to $2.11/kg.

After a strong first half to 2025, Brazil's import volumes continue to be higher y-o-y.

August saw it bring in 3,400t -- around 400t higher than August 2024 -- and prices also bounced back by 3.2% to $2.87/kg.

The EU, too, is performing a little better y-o-y, with volumes a slightly mixed bag but prices largely higher than in 2024.

August saw volumes rise to over 6,000t, and prices lift 3.9% to $2.40/kg, much-improved from August 2024.

So far this year, pangasius exports to the EU reached $120m, up 6% y-o-y, said VASEP.

"Although the growth rate is not high, the EU is a valuable market and has a strong brand influence. Stable demand for high-standard pangasius fillets, especially in Germany, the Netherlands and Spain, shows the potential for long-term consolidation. However, to exploit it to the fullest, the industry needs to focus more on sustainability certification, traceability and green consumption trends -- increasingly strict criteria of the EU."

The ASEAN markets have been promising and stable for Vietnam this year, and August saw another month of volumes that were up y-o-y, if down m-o-m, at 10,600t.

The average price across all products was down 1.1% m-o-m at $1.77/kg.

Finally, July saw volumes shipped to the UK lift again after July's dip, to 1,700t. Prices, meanwhile, were as high as they've been in a year, up 10.6% m-o-m at $2.92/kg.

title: Week 39 farm-gate shrimp roundup: China prices firm ahead of holiday, India extends gains on tight supply
content:
Additional reporting by Lewis Hu and Neil Ramsden.

Chinese farm-gate vannamei prices firmed across all major producing regions in week 39, while Indian values continued their upward momentum and Indonesian prices faced pressure from ongoing US market access issues.

The broad-based increases in China is driven by farmers waiting for peak holiday pricing ahead of the extended National Day holiday running Oct. 1-8, creating tight supply conditions, according to market sources.

As a result, Undercurrent News' global index for 60-count vannamei edged up to $3.67 per kilogram in week 39, though values remain marginally below year-ago levels:

Upgrade to Pro to view

Indian prices in Andhra Pradesh extended gains on larger sizes amid continuing raw material shortages and solid exporter demand, building on the strong momentum from the previous week despite the ongoing 50% US tariff on Indian seafood imports.

Meanwhile, Indonesian prices held steady as over 600 farming businesses grapple with reduced market access following the US ban on processor Bahari Makmur Sejati (BMS), with regional disparities persisting.

Elsewhere, Ecuador maintained flat pricing for a second consecutive week amid uncertainty over potential transport strikes and diesel subsidy impacts, while Thai values saw modest movement. Vietnamese processors raised prices for larger sizes to attract supply amid ongoing production constraints.

Following the changes, farm-gate prices for 60-count shrimp from China, Vietnam and Thailand continue trading at substantial premiums -- roughly 30% higher -- compared to material from India, Indonesia and Ecuador, according to Undercurrent's price tracking data.

Prices pick up in China 

Vannamei shrimp prices increased across all major producing regions in China during week 39, with most areas seeing CNY 2.0 ($0.28)/kg gains for the benchmark 60-count size, according to pricing data on Undercurrent's price portal.

Guangdong, Shandong, Jiangsu and Guangxi provinces all recorded CNY 2.0/kg increases, while Fujian posted a more modest CNY 1.0/kg rise, reversing the price stability seen in previous weeks.

The broad-based price increases come as farmers withhold inventory ahead of China's National Day holiday running Oct. 1-8, market sources told Undercurrent.

"Farmers are unwilling to harvest and are waiting for the highest price during the holiday," one source said, adding that this year's National Day break will be longer than in previous years, providing more time for consumption.

The strategy has created tight supply conditions, with relatively few shrimp in circulation and large-sized shrimp particularly scarce, according to market participants.

The price rally marks a turnaround from week 38, when prices remained flat across most regions despite predictions of increases tied to the approaching holiday period.

Weather concerns continue to influence market dynamics, with meteorologists warning that a strong typhoon could reach southern provinces this week. Late September is a period of frequent typhoon activity, potentially disrupting harvest and transportation operations.

The price gains also align with typical seasonal patterns in China's shrimp market, where prices tend to strengthen in fall months as production decreases, signalling additional rises in the weeks ahead.

Indian prices edge up again

Vannamei shrimp prices in India's main farming region of Andhra Pradesh continued their upward trajectory in week 39, with larger sizes posting INR 5.0 ($0.06)/kg increases, according to Aquaconnect pricing data on the price portal.

The benchmark 30-count size, along with 40-, 50-, 60- and 70-count categories, all rose INR 5.0/kg week-on-week, building on the strong gains recorded in the previous week. Smaller sizes from 80-count through 100-count held steady at week 38 levels.

The sustained price strength reflects ongoing raw material shortages and robust demand from exporters anticipating improvements in US market conditions, according to industry sources.

"Prices are increasing due to various factors, including slow stocking and material availability," Durai Murugan, owner of Sea Gem Aqua farms, told Undercurrent last week. "Demand is solid among exporters looking for further increases in upcoming weeks. There are strong rises in US wholesale price indexes, too."

Farmers remain cautious about production commitments following the implementation of the 50% US tariff on Indian seafood imports on Aug. 27. The tariff uncertainty has left farmers hesitant to commit to longer and riskier production cycles needed to grow shrimp to larger US-preferred sizes.

A veteran trader last week attributed the ongoing price increases to "raw material shortages, pending orders to be completed and expecting some favorable news on tariffs."

However, industry sources have previously warned that low prices could discourage farmers from growing shrimp to the larger US-preferred sizes during the monsoon harvest season, potentially exacerbating supply constraints.

Prices stable in East Java

Vannamei shrimp prices in East Java remained unchanged across all size categories in week 39, despite ongoing market disruptions from the US red-listing of major processor BMS.

The benchmark 30-count size held flat for a second consecutive week, along with all other sizes from 40-count through 100-count, according to pricing data on Undercurrent's price portal, even as the market digests new developments in the radiation contamination case that has blocked Indonesia's largest exporter from its biggest market.

New details emerged last week about the scale of the US enforcement action, with the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) revealing it denied entry for 139 lines of BMS shrimp on Sept. 10 across four of its five regional import divisions. The FDA allowed BMS to recover 18 rejected refrigerated containers -- totaling more than 600 metric tons of shrimp -- for potential distribution to other countries.

The incident has drawn sharp criticism from US domestic producers, with the Southern Shrimp Alliance calling the redistribution of rejected containers "shocking" and warning about potential "port-shopping" where refused products could re-enter the US market through different entry points.

Indonesian farmers in areas with high concentration of BMS buying power have seen farm-gate prices 25-30% below Java levels, although in areas like Banten and Makassar, prices have steadied due to alternative processing options.

Ecuador prices stable

Vannamei shrimp prices in Ecuador remained unchanged across all size categories for a second consecutive week in week 39, according to pricing data on Undercurrent's price portal.

The benchmark 50/60-count size held steady, while premium 20/30-count material also maintained its level, continuing to command a premium exceeding $1.00/kg over 30/40-count shrimp.

Market participants remain concerned about president Daniel Noboa's elimination of diesel subsidies for the transport sector, a policy change that follows the shrimp industry's earlier loss of fuel subsidies.

However, farmers have noted that current levels remain improved compared to earlier in the year, particularly for larger sizes.

Vietnam prices still high

Major processing plants in Vietnam have raised purchase prices again for larger vannamei shrimp sizes to attract supply, with farm-gate prices for 30-count shrimp posting slight increases while smaller sizes remained unchanged in week 39, according to market sources.

The selective price increases reflect ongoing supply constraints in farming areas producing 30-count/kg shrimp and larger specifications, industry participants told Undercurrent.

"The purchase volume of vannamei shrimp by major processing plants has remained fairly stable," a Ho Chi Minh-based consultancy previously told Undercurrent, though it had warned that farming areas producing larger sizes would remain limited in the coming weeks.

Small uptick in Thailand

Vannamei farm-gate prices in Thailand saw modest movement in week 39, with the benchmark 70-count size rising THB 2.50 ($0.08)/kg while other categories remained unchanged, according to pricing data on Undercurrent's price portal.

The 60-count and 80-count sizes held steady w-o-w, maintaining their positions at the highest levels since April.

The slight uptick in the benchmark size breaks several weeks of complete price stability, though levels remain approximately 2-3% below year-ago prices.

title: US fishing groups contend foreign fishery bans don’t go far enough
content:
An industry-shaking decision by the US National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) to ban products from as many as 240 fisheries it determined violate the Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA) did not go far enough, two US fishing groups argue.

The bans, set to go into effect on Jan. 1, 2026, will impact around 15% of US seafood imports, or approximately $3.6 billion worth of trade, according to NMFS, a division of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). A review conducted by Undercurrent News of the banned fisheries determined they could have catastrophic consequences for dozens of seafood-exporting nations.

But the Hawaii Longline Association (HLA) and the Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA), which represent domestic fisheries, contend NMFS could have done more. Additional fisheries that NMFS deemed to have equivalent marine mammal protections to the US should not have received that designation, they say.

"Many nations don't have the monitoring levels to accurately assess impacts nor any real enforcement of their fisheries," HLA executive director Eric Kingma told Undercurrent. "For NOAA to find that foreign nations are comparable to US standards is not accurate and it appears NOAA failed to consider the actual standards to which specific US fisheries are held, such as the US longline fisheries in Hawaii and the Atlantic."

A regulatory body also has weighed in.

On Thursday (Sept. 18), the Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council called on NOAA to strengthen its MMPA import provisions and create a clear public and stakeholder input process. The council requested that NMFS evaluate the amount of tuna imports impacted by its bans. 

NMFS' assessments do not hold tuna longline fisheries in the Western and Central Pacific up to the federal MMPA standard, the council said in a press release.

Kingma said countries with fleets competing for billfish and tuna with US vessels in the Western and Central Pacific don't mandate abundance estimates for marine mammal populations, establish potential biological removal levels, assess their fisheries impacts against those levels or implement measures to mitigate those impacts.

"You're telling me that foreign distant-water longline fisheries operating around Hawaii, in the same proximity and same fishing grounds as us, are removing hooks from false killer whales without causing serious injury? To me, that is absolutely inaccurate," he said in testimony before the council.

Hawaii Longline Association executive director Eric Kingma. Photo courtesy of Eric Kingma.

Unfair competition

If Hawaii longline vessels leave a hook in a false killer whale after an interaction, without any trailing gear, that's deemed a 'serious injury' and treated as a mortality, even if the animal swims away alive after release, Kingma told Undercurrent.

"If we have more than three of those interactions observed in the US exclusive economic zone (EEZ) around Hawaii, the whole southern EEZ area -- around 130,000 square miles -- is closed to our fishery, which has occurred," he said. 

Hawaii-based fishing operations are required to use weak circle hooks to promote hook-straightening out of the mouths of false killer whales, which Kingma said "is very dangerous to crew due to potential fly-backs from weighted branch lines."

In the Atlantic, US vessels must also use weak circle hooks and face restrictions on mainline length.

"No other nations are employing these measures," Kingma said.

Kingma said competition is fierce on the high seas of the Pacific, where the Hawaii fleet does 85% of its fishing. 

"We know these foreign nations' pelagic longline fisheries don't use the same (or similar) monitoring or mitigation measures that are used in the Hawaii fleet and those fisheries simply do not meet the standards to which our longline fisheries are held under US law," he said.

"NOAA needs to perform a genuine, detailed, and accurate assessment of these foreign fisheries for the exercise to actually reflect whether those fisheries meet the standards to which US fisheries are held. If they do not, then NOAA should force them to do so through the power of the US seafood market, as the MMPA and NMFS's regulations require."

Concerns over foreign shrimp fishing standards

Similarly, SSA executive director John Williams said the NMFS decision "lets foreign fishermen off easy."

"The announcement continues the application of weaker standards to foreign seafood suppliers compared to what is required of American fishermen," he said in a Sept. 5 release. "Foreign fleets are permitted access to the US market while operating under conditions that would shut down US commercial fisheries."

US foreign fisheries ban threatens ‘death punch’ to swimming crab importers

NMFS has delayed conducting MMPA comparability findings on foreign fisheries for years and only did so after being ordered to do so by a federal judge, after being sued repeatedly by environmental groups.

"The MMPA's intent is clear: If American fishermen can't do it, neither can foreign fishermen," Williams said. "After 50 years of non-enforcement, NOAA finally acts -- only to rubber-stamp foreign operations that would never pass muster for a US fishery."

NMFS provided positive comparability findings for numerous fisheries with documented adverse impacts on marine mammal populations, questionable or missing observer programs and claims of zero interactions with marine mammals "that simply cannot be true," Williams said.

"The largest foreign wild-caught seafood suppliers who compete with American fishermen for sales in the US market [are] mostly getting a pass from NOAA Fisheries with standards far below what must be met by US commercial fisheries," he said.

SSA said it had substantial concerns about the standards applied to foreign shrimp fisheries. It said NMFS granted positive comparability findings to nearly all fisheries providing wild-caught shrimp to the US, "even when those same fisheries have been documented as harming marine mammals."

It called out the Argentine red shrimp fishery, Mexico's gulf shrimp fisheries and Peru's marine shrimp fishery for having documented issues that NOAA did not address in its positive comparability findings for each fishery.

For the Argentine fishery, it said the Monterey Bay Aquarium has issued an "avoid rating" due to its adverse impact on marine mammal populations. The government of Mexico has made "the unbelievable claims" that there are no interactions with marine mammals in its trawl fishery, SSA said.

Peru's commercial shrimp fishery has known adverse impacts on marine mammal populations, and no observer program is in place, SSA said.

Argentina accounted for 61.3% of US wild-caught shrimp imports in 2024, while Mexico provided 25.4% and Peru sent 2.3%. Ecuador (4.9%), Panama (1.8%), Nigeria (1.5%) and Guyana (1.0%) accounted for most of the remainder, and all received approvals except for Mexico's blue shrimp and yellowleg shrimp fisheries.

Fishing vessels in Puntarenas, Costa Rica. Photo courtesy of Shutterstock.

SSA pointed to US president Donald Trump's "Restoring American Seafood Competitiveness" executive order (14726), issued April 17, as further justification for NMFS to take harsher action against foreign seafood suppliers.

"The imbalance between what NOAA Fisheries demands under the MMPA from US commercial fisheries versus foreigners supplying our market is inconsistent with the goals of the executive order," Williams said.  

In its original Aug. 28 announcement, NMFS cited the same executive order to support its decisions.

"These import provisions align with president Trump's executive order to restore American seafood competitiveness, protect American jobs and ensure fair trade practices that prioritize the domestic market. By holding foreign fisheries to the same rigorous standards, NOAA Fisheries is safeguarding the integrity of American seafood while creating a level playing field for US fishermen," NMFS said.

But Blake Price, SSA's deputy director and former gear development fisheries biologist for the NMFS harvesting systems unit, said the agency had fallen short.

"American fishermen who operate under strict restrictions imposed to protect marine mammals should not be forced to compete for sales in the US market against foreign fishermen who face no similar limitations," Price said. "Protecting migratory marine mammals from harm in US waters, but welcoming seafood from foreign commercial fishing industries that kill those same marine mammals while outside of US waters makes little sense."

US trade court weighed in

SSA cited a ruling from the US Court of International Trade, which found earlier this month that NMFS improperly granted New Zealand approval last year to import seafood products from two fisheries that imperil the critically endangered Maui dolphin, as Undercurrent reported.

The court found that NMFS failed to establish New Zealand's government had regulated commercial fisheries with the MMPA's zero mortality goal or employed the law's negligible impact standard, SSA said. 

The judge in the case ordered NMFS to more thoroughly reevaluate whether programs adopted by New Zealand to prevent Maui dolphin bycatch are comparable to US standards.

title: Editor’s choice: Latest on US’ Indonesian shrimp block; NOAA bans a blow to US source nations
content:
EMEA editor Neil Ramsden brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week.

Last week, Undercurrent News reported from the annual Genuine Alaska Pollock Producers meeting, held in Seattle, Washington. You can recap all the news from the event here.

Readers continue to closely follow developments after US authorities blocked Indonesian shrimp from entering the US over radiation contamination concerns. The US Food and Drug Administration revealed on its recently launched food import database that it denied entry for a massive 139 entry lines of shrimp produced by Bahari Makmur Sejati under two codes for "adulteration." 

In Alaska, US tug crews worked to regain control of a Circle Seafoods salmon barge that broke its mooring on Sept. 15 amid heavy winds.

A coming US ban on fisheries determined to be out of compliance with the US Marine Mammals Protection Act will have potentially catastrophic consequences for dozens of seafood-exporting nations, Undercurrent reported last week. Products from as many as 178 fisheries that the National Marine Fisheries Service has listed as out of compliance with the law will not be permitted to enter the US beginning Jan. 1, 2026. You can read a breakdown of the impacts for various source nations here.

And Spain's Grupo Profand -- one of the largest seafood processors in the country, traditionally focused on species such as squid, octopus, shrimp, hake, and lobster -- has entered the tuna sector for the first time this year with a new line of frozen products.

Two of Undercurrent's weekly stories on price assessments were among the most-read last week. First, UCN adjusted its price assessments on frozen Norwegian headed and gutted cod and haddock up again, with the latter moving rapidly in response to the latest US trade announcement that will see Russian-origin haddock -- which had been viable for sale to the US even as cod, pollock and salmon have been banned since June 1, 2024 -- now also banned from Jan. 1, 2026.

And Indian vannamei farm-gate prices strengthened across all size categories last week, despite the ongoing 50% US tariff on Indian seafood imports, while prices in Ecuador held flat and Vietnam showed mixed movements as processors adjusted buying strategies.

The consortium that owns Mexican tuna-ranching firm Baja Aqua Farms has acquired its primary aquafeed supplier. The acquisition, first reported by Undercurrent in April, includes Baja Marine Foods and its subsidiaries Pelagicos de Baja California and Pesquera Baja Marine. Antarctica Advisors was the sell-side advisor on the deal.

US pollock fisheries in Alaska's eastern Bering Sea are entering the final stretch of the 2025 B season with mounting concern that as much as 20% of quota may go unharvested, particularly in the inshore plant sector, Undercurrent heard from multiple sources.

For the rest of last week's most-read stories, click the headlines below.

$9.5bn Danish meat supplier launches salmon brand
Ecuador shrimp gets imported by US at lower rate even when peeled in Asia
US wholesale: Fresh, frozen wild salmon prices rise as Alaska season closes
Week 38 US wholesale prices: Tariffs push shrimp, cod into new territory; Chilean salmon climbs higher
Aqua Bridge signs framework agreement to acquire Avramar's Greek assets
High Liner open to using M&A to grow business with immediate impact
EU spot prices for US pollock fillet blocks move up; Chinese, Russian sellers push for more
US appetite for Canadian snow crab pushes imports closer to records
