title: Catch the Current episode 35: Vigo tuna recap, market insights, creating a seafood wishlist
content:
Where in the world is Undercurrent News? In this episode of Catch the Current, hosts Amanda Buckle and Lorin Castiglione catch up with reporters Mati Mereghetti and Maria Feijoo, who are back from Vigo, Spain, where they covered the XII ANFACO World Tuna Conference.

Plus, the whole price reporting gang jumps on the pod to share what's going on across their respective markets. Don't miss a recap of the major seafood headlines of the week, and stick around for some fun at the very end as Amanda decides she's ready to start a seafood wishlist.

Don't forget to subscribe so you don't miss an episode. Next week we'll be welcoming Undercurrent's Tom Seaman and Jacob Resneck to share highlights and some insight from the annual Association of Genuine Alaska Pollock Producers meeting in Seattle, Washington.

Thank you to our sponsor: Wisefish.

Listen now on YouTube!

Subscribe now! Catch the Current is available on YouTube, Spotify, Amazon Music, iHeartRadio, Pandora, and other major podcast streaming platforms. Don't see Catch the Current on your favorite app? Reach out to podcasts@undercurrentnews.com.

Don't have time to listen? Find a full transcript of season 1, episode 35 of Catch the Current below:

Amanda Buckle (AB): You're listening to Catch the Current, the coolest seafood podcast out there, from the team at Undercurrent News, your trusted source for seafood prices, news and data. I'm Amanda Buckle.

Lorin Castiglione (LC): And I'm Lorin Castiglione.

Before we dive in, a quick shoutout to our sponsor Wisefish. With over 30 years in the seafood industry, they're powering aquaculture, fisheries, processors and seafood sales with one integrated platform that makes managing complex operations simpler. Check them out at wisefish.com/catch-the-current.

AB: So where in the world is Undercurrent News?

This week, Undercurrent New editor-in-Chief Tom Seaman and reporter Jacob Resneck were in Seattle, Washington, for the annual Association of Genuine Alaska Pollock Producers meeting. Unfortunately, due to time constraints, we weren't able to catch up with them for this episode.

Vigo tuna conference 2025: Future bright as new markets open in China, Latin America

LC: But don't worry, we'll get them back on next week. But this week we're excited to hear from Undercurrent's Mati Mereghetti and Maria Feijoo, who reported from the World Tuna Conference in Vigo, Spain, which took place Sept. 11-12. Mati and Maria will be joining us in the second half of the pod to share some of their highlights from the event. So stick around for that.

AB: For now, let's kick off with some of the big headlines from this week, like the rescue of a Circle Seafoods barge that broke its mooring on Monday amid heavy winds around Annette Island near the southern tip of Southeast Alaska.

The National Weather Service issued a high wind watch for the area, with winds expected between 25-35 miles per hour and possible gusts up to 60 mph. The bulletin warned that high winds could blow around unsecured objects and damage property. 

And sure enough, according to a series of public notices, the stormy weather caused the 382-foot freezer barge to break free. Fortunately, less than four hours later, a pair of tug boats had attached moor lines and were towing the unmanned barge to a sheltered location. 

Circle Seafoods’ salmon barge returned to Alaska port by tugs after hours adrift in storm

There were no reported injuries. Undercurrent reporter Jacob Resneck spoke to Circle Seafoods co-founder Eren Shultz who said that the barge's crew and processing workers had safely left the vessel before it broke free. He also added that, based on visual inspections from the tug crews, it does not appear to be taking on water.

The barge, which freezes pink salmon, is in its first season and has a cold storage capacity of around 10 million pounds.

LC: That sounds like an exciting first season for it. Check the show notes for a link to the full story.

Meanwhile, an upcoming US ban on fisheries determined to be out of compliance with the US Marine Mammals Protection Act is still top of mind for dozens of seafood-exporting nations.

Undercurrent editorial director Cliff White reported in late August that products from as many as 178 fisheries that NOAA Fisheries has listed as out of compliance with the law will not be permitted to enter the US beginning Jan. 1, 2026.

NOAA’s marine mammal-related fisheries bans deal blow to US seafood source nations

The ban extends to seafood that's processed and reexported by third nations, a NOAA spokesperson confirmed to Undercurrent. 

NOAA Fisheries public affairs team lead Rachel Hager told UCN that National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) is working with US Customs and Border Protection to enforce the seafood import restrictions upon entry into the United States. Further, the earliest countries with banned fisheries can reapply for a positive comparability finding if after Jan. 1, 2026, the date the ban goes into effect.

In total, the new regulation, which NMFS was forced to impose as part of a January 2025 court settlement with conservation groups, is expected to upend some $3.6 billion of the US' roughly $25.8bn in annual seafood imports.

AB: Some of the US' top suppliers impacted include Chile, which is the US' second-most valuable source of seafood at 286,000t worth nearly $3.1bn in 2024. Chile has two fisheries impacted by the bans, its longline and gillnet fisheries targeting jack and chub mackerel and hake.

Our pal Cliff crunched the numbers and Chile's total US mackerel exports surpassed $3.5m in value in 2024. Its hake and whiting exports exceeded $4.2m. He said it's not clear how much of this product will be blocked by the US' ban on fisheries. But also important to note is that it's a relatively minor total impact on the country's overall US seafood exports, which are overwhelmingly comprised of farmed salmon.

LC: Indonesia, which has a huge swimming crab export business to the US is another one set to be slammed by NOAA's ban on its gillnet and entangling net crab fishery.

Of that country's 217,121t of seafood worth $1.9bn that was exported to the US in 2024, ranking it fourth most valuable, crabmeat accounted for $242.4m. And that's not Indonesia's only fishery to be impacted. You'll have to check Cliff's story to see what else.

Vietnam is another country set to be hit by the ban. In a statement, the Vietnam Association of Seafood Exporters and Producers said the ban will impact nearly $512m worth of its exports, including tuna, crabmeat, mackerel, and mahi.

AB: And you can't forget about Ecuador, which will have its gillnet and entangling net fishery banned. The fishery targets skipjack, bigeye and yellowfin tuna and mahi, among others.

I highly recommend you check out Cliff's deep dive into NOAA's marine mammal-related fisheries bans. Again, link in the show notes.

High Liner Foods has acquired the Mrs Paul's brand from Conagra. Photo courtesy of Keith Homan/Shutterstock.

Moving along ... Canada's High Liner Foods remains on the lookout for mergers and acquisitions that can strengthen its supply chain long term and make an immediate impact on its sales. And that's after it acquired US retail brands Mrs Paul's and Van de Kamp's from Conagra Brands this summer at the adjusted purchase price of $42.4m.

LC: CEO Paul Jewer told Undercurrent News during an interview at the recent Aqua Nor show that the company is happy with the investments its made so far and that the real focus now will be looking at ways that the company will grow its business immediately. He said the Conagra deal fits well into that and that High Liner is very open to more deals like that.

UCN's Neil Ramsden has the full story. Check it out in the show notes.

AB: Aquaculture is evolving fast, and managing fish farming alongside processing, sales and logistics means handling complex data daily. Wisefish offers an integrated platform built specifically for aquaculture and seafood businesses. It collects data from farms, linking biological and financial insights, so you can track costs and yields clearly.

The system captures for example feed and medication usage, biomass increase, mortality, labor and equipment costs to give a full picture of profitability. It also supports planning across harvest, sales and deliveries, helping you make smarter decisions with accurate, up-to-date info. By replacing spreadsheets and siloed systems, Wisefish reduces manual work and errors, freeing time to focus on growth.

Whether scaling or optimizing workflows, Wisefish helps improve efficiency and control costs without disrupting your existing systems. Learn more at wisefish.com/catch-the-current.

Alright, let's welcome some Undercurrent friends on to talk about what's going on in the markets. 

Ben Fisher, we haven't had the pleasure of sharing the mic with you in some weeks. What's going on in your markets.

Ben Fisher (BF): Well, the wild salmon market continues to be hot. We discussed the lackluster pink salmon catch a few weeks ago. But now that the commercial Alaska season is wrapped up, we know from the Alaska Seafood Marketing Institute's harvest reports that actually none of the five species hit their preseason harvest targets this year.

Even sockeye, which saw a very impressive run in Bristol Bay, fell a couple of percentage points short of the annual projection. At this point of the year, as fresh salmon becomes increasingly difficult to find, the remaining species which are out there are coming up a bit in price. So we reflected a small rise in fresh coho and king pricing.

US wholesale: Fresh, frozen wild salmon prices rise as Alaska season closes

And now that the commercial season in Alaska is done, what does that mean for frozen volumes? It means that all of the species are in very high demand.

For example, this is the case to such a degree that it appears there's just no 2-4 lb sockeye on the spot market. So we temporarily removed that price a few weeks ago on Undercurrent's wild salmon price assessment.

And you know when you're reporting a price, that says something about the market. But when you're removing a price, because of no spot deals being done -- even though those fish exist out there somewhere -- that says something about the market as well.

We received reports from contacts that some producers are beginning to allow limited amounts of frozen H&G 4-6 lb sockeye trickle out a little bit. That price is there, and it remains steady this week, but it's definitely higher than what it was when frozen sockeye started hitting the market.

My other market which is moving considerably and has been doing so for a few weeks now is the Mediterranean sea bass, or bronzino. Undercurrent tracks bronzino from Greece and Turkey, and traditionally Greek-sourced fish has been more expensive. However, price increases by Turkish producers has brought the fish from both origins to near parity, according to one buyer in the US.

Farmers in the Mediterranean have had to deal with heat-related mortality events for two consecutive summers now, and the US' 15% tariffs are being felt as well. As a result, our assessment for bronzino has come up in recent weeks, and what used to be a somewhat affordable fresh option is less so now. 

LC: Thanks, Ben. Also joining us on the pod today to share some insight into his markets is Gary Morrison. Gary, what do you got for us this week?

Gary Morrison (GM): Well, I think we're going to start off with shrimp again. I think that's where we've been talking and focusing a lot of our time and energy here on the pod the last couple weeks. And I'll make it brief.

The market is still in the same trend. Prices in wholesale week 38 have surged again, and the cost structures are what's driving it. If you look at where prices are moving the fastest, it is still focused on the areas that US consumers want.

US wholesale: Another big rally hits shrimp prices as buyers weigh market

They look for convenience, they look for ease, and that means peeled shrimp and cooked and breaded. And those are the product forms that you can't really origin shop. Peeled and deveined, you do have Ecuador making a big push. But we talked about it previously, they're at capacity, and they're pushing prices right up to Asian origin tariff rates.

If you look at the US wholesale market, P&D, 16-20, Tail-on, both Latin origin and Asian origin, they're at parity now. So that tells you how Latin producers are pushing prices.

Where people can't origin shop, when you're talking cooked and breaded, the Asian origin countries are also pushing prices and pushing them fast, and the US buyer is absorbing them.

There is some pushback, but importers are able to sell into the rally, so it's going to be pretty consistent as cost structures rise, cheaper inventory is being removed from the market, prices are being raised by importers.

And we'll focus quickly on the lobster meat market because that market continues to be pretty stout as well.

We entered the year with limited inventory. Landings in Maine were probably subpar, according to the boats there. And certainly Canada is not starting off as robust as they thought.

So there is supply risk, and demand for lobster rolls continues to be strong. Prices are reset on a weekly basis.

This week we saw some prices edge up, but the trend is still squarely in place. The product is tight, product is wanted, and prices are moving higher.

LC: Thanks, Gary. On my end, let's talk salmon. So the US farmed salmon market is caught in kind of a push and pull right now. We've got fresh prices firming, frozen values are softening, and supply growth is tightening.

So we're seeing seasonal disruptions, shifting trade flows, and tariff uncertainty that are all adding layers of volatility right now. In the US, Chilean salmon prices firmed in week 38, reversing last week's slight dip. Fresh fillets and whole fish pricing increased on the back of the short production week during Chile's Fiestas Patrias holiday, which is curbing supply and leaving buyers with higher replacement offers.

On the frozen side, the picture is softer, however. Chilean fillets ease, and we're just beginning to see some additional 6-8 ounce size portions becoming available, and adding some downward pressure there. However, the bulk of trade remains within the quoted range on Undercurrent's price portal.

The Norwegian salmon continues to rally. So we've got fresh whole fish gaining about $0.40 per pound this week, and that is driven by strong Chinese demand for larger fish, and compounded by logistical disruptions that we've seen from recent landslides. So export volumes are lower, but average prices have risen. China is now paying premiums above NOK 100 per kilo for larger sizes.

Stepping back, global output growth is slowing sharply compared to the last decade, but US consumer demand remains resilient. Salmon continues to hold its unique role as both a premium and everyday protein, though producers are entering Q4 facing the twin challenges of tariffs and tightening supply.

AB: Thanks, Lorin. And as always, links to these analysis pieces in the show notes.

As promised, we've got two final UCN friends joining us on the pod, Mati Mereghetti and Maria Feijoo joining us now to share all the scoop from Vigo.

Welcome, Mati and Maria. Mati, why don't you start off with telling us a little bit about the event you covered last week.

XII Anfaco world's tuna conference 2025. Photo: Undercurrent News.

Matilde Mereghetti (MM): Hi, everyone. Yes, so last week, Maria and I were in Vigo to attend the ANFACO World Tuna Conference.

It was especially busy this year.

So in addition to local executives from canneries and fishing companies, the event drew strong international participation this year, with delegations from Vietnam and Thailand, the Philippines, China, as well as Papua New Guinea and various Latin American countries, particularly from Ecuador.

For me, one key takeaway was the growing focus of Asian suppliers on boosting European exports, largely in response to challenges in the US market amid rising reciprocal tariffs.

And the conference was not without controversy, with moments of tension reflecting the realities of an intensely competitive market.

Maria Feijoo (MF): The conference definitely had its tense moments, especially when Juan Alonso, vice-president of Spanish tuna giant Jealsa, took the stage. He actually opened with a video showing the aftermath of a massive fire that destroyed 60% of the facilities just a few years ago. And he said they thought that was the worst crisis they'd faced until now.

So, according to him, what's coming with the new EU trade agreements, it's even more dangerous for the European tuna industry. He directly pointed to deals with countries like Thailand, Ecuador and Papua New Guinea, which allow them tariff-free access to the EU market, but without meeting the same labor, environmental or regulatory standards that European producers are held to.

Basically, Ecuador, for example, are processing way more tuna than they catch, and no one really knows how.

The concern isn't just about losing market share, it's about competing on completely uneven ground. So he definitely made it clear: European producers aren't afraid of competition, but they want a level playing field.

His message to the EU was quite simple. If you're going to drop tariffs, then make sure everyone's following the same rules. So otherwise, he warned this hurricane, he called it, of trade deals could do more damage than the fire that nearly wiped them out.

MM: Jealsa was referring to the free trade deal that is being negotiated between Thailand and the European Union, but Jealsa's accusation again is that some of its competitors are operating under lower standards. It immediately prompted a firm reaction from representatives of suppliers, of tuna suppliers, from Ecuador and Papua New Guinea.

For example, various Ecuadorian executives highlighted the country's leadership in tuna lendings across the Eastern Pacific. They stressed that between last year and this year, favorable oceanic conditions have been marked by a neutral climate scenario between El Nino and La Nina boosting tuna availability in the region, causing record lendings in Manta, Ecuador, and they highlighted their commitment to sustainability and compliance with European rules.

MF: So to wrap up on a positive note, there's a lot of excitement about the future of the tuna industry.

Roberto Alonso, secretary general of ANFACO-CYTMA, pointed to growth in places like China and Latin America, and the industry is becoming more sustainable, with most tuna stocks now being managed responsibly. Also, consumers are shifting toward healthier and more ethical products. And things like AI and digital trustability are going to help fight illegal fishing, as well.

And the EU's new forced labor regulations are actually seen as a chance to show leadership and build trust. So the conference ended with a call for more global cooperation and fair trade, and hopefully we'll be back in Vigo in 2027.

Yes, definitely, the conference ended on a positive note, and it was highlighted that market trends show rising demand for tuna, sushi and other fresh and frozen products in Spain and Europe, while canned tuna continues to expand in Latin America and the Middle East.

AB: And actually, you ladies will be back in Vigo in a few weeks, is that correct?

MM: Yes.

MF: Yes, Conxemar.

MM: And we are looking forward to it, Maria and I. I feel like at home in Vigo now, we've been so many times. It's a really nice place.

AB: So if you haven't already checked out Maria and Mati's coverage from Vigo, the tuna conference, we have the link in the show notes, and again, they'll be in Vigo, reporting from Conxemar from October 7-9. So just a few weeks away. Thanks again ladies for joining us.

AB: Before we go -- some fun and light news.

LC: Hit me.

AB: Our pals at Echo Falls have expanded their salmon caviar product line.

LC: Tell me more.

AB: Let me just say one word: Wasabi.

Echo Falls expanded its salmon caviar product line with a new wasabi flavor. Photo Credit: Echo Falls

LC: I'm sold.

AB: That's right, capitalizing on the current flavor trend, Echo Falls is introducing a new wasabi-flavored salmon caviar.

Listen to this description: "Developed for those consumers who enjoy complex and bold flavors, the wasabi caviar layers the rich, briny flavor of salmon roe with the fresh, clean punch of wasabi. Perfect on its own, the wasabi salmon caviar can also be incorporated as a complement or garnish in numerous appetizers and entrees, including seafood boards, poke bowls and sushi hand rolls."

LC: You've got their commercial right there. But that sounds awesome. 

AB: And if wasabi is not your thing, then Echo Falls still has a traditional salmon caviar. They're sold in a newly designed 2-ounce retail pack, so add it your shopping list.

LC: And to our "Listen To Us Eat."

AB: There you go.

And in other fun product news, Spanish group Grupo Profand -- one of the largest seafood processors in the country, traditionally focused on species such as squid, octopus, shrimp, hake and lobster -- has entered the tuna sector for the first time this year with a new line of frozen products.

The move comes as sales of frozen tuna products are reportedly increasing in Spain, opening new opportunities in the competitive sector. The Atun 360 range uses tuna "coproducts" such as trimmings and small cuts, raw material which is often left outside the premium market for loins and steaks. 

LC: And the products are really unique. At the moment, the new frozen line includes fusilli pasta with tuna and Mediterranean vegetables, tuna tabbouleh with bulgur and mint, teriyaki tuna bowl with rice and vegetables, and a tuna fajita kit with marinated fish and accompaniments. 

Photo: Profand.

Profand will target the Atun 360 range initially at European markets like Spain, Italy, France and the UK, sourcing fish particularly from Spanish vessels harvesting yellowfin tuna in the Atlantic and the Eastern Pacific Ocean.

AB: I want these in our grocery stores. Besides the sushi section, I can't think of a single ready-to-eat or ready-to-cook tuna option. 

LC: I can't either, and all of these sound incredible.

AB: I know, yeah, they're different. Because you have, I'm trying to think ... we do have bowls, and usually it's shrimp in, like, a pasta bowl, shrimp in a fajita bowl.

We could go for that all day long, but it is nice to do something different, and I feel like tuna is also a fish that people are very familiar with.

LC: Right, and it's very versatile, and everyone's comfortable with it. 

AB: Actually, you know, my girls already started their Christmas wish list. Did your kids start doing that, Lorin?

LC: No, not yet. Oh, gosh.

AB: I think I'm going to start my own list this year, and it's going to be a seafood wishlist.

LC: Oh, I have one -- crispy shrimp bites at McDonald's Japan.

A heart-shaped shrimp nugget appears in McDonald’s Japan’s “Puri-Puri Ebi Purio,” promoted as a lucky find. Credit: McDonald’s Japan

AB: Don't get me wrong, I love the Filet-O-Fish, but it would be so fun to have different seafood limited-time offerings to try. 

LC: Agreed. And especially this one, because some lucky customers can find a heart-shaped crispy shrimp nugget. McDonald's stressed that not every box will contain a heart-shaped piece, turning it into a game of chance.

AB: I would just keep buying, just for the chance.

LC: I got it!

AB: One time -- this is such a silly story, but I remember as a kid, getting I think it was from Burger King, but just getting a thing of the french fries, and inside was one single onion ring.

LC: Oh, yes, the lucky onion ring.

AB: And everyone was like -- And everyone being my entire family --  was like, oh my god, you got it! And it was very exciting.

LC: Simpler times.

AB: Yeah, but I could see the same thing happening with this heart-shaped shrimp bite. That seems, really cool. So, I want it.

Well,  my stomach's growling so we should probably wrap this up.

From roe to plate, Wisefish supports seafood businesses across aquaculture, fisheries, processing, and sales with one integrated platform. Trusted by companies around the world like Tassal, Nils Sperre, and others. Wisefish helps control costs, improve margins and enable smarter financial decisions, replacing spreadsheets and siloed systems. Learn more at wisefish.com/catch-the-current.

LC: And see everyone back here next week for a recap of GAPP's annual meeting.

AB: Bye!

title: ICCAT signals ‘inevitable,’ tougher tuna regulations ahead if overfishing continues
content:
VIGO, Spain -- The future of Atlantic tuna stocks is hanging in the balance, with the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT) signaling that tougher regulations and deeper catch reductions are "inevitable" unless overfishing is urgently addressed.

Ernesto Penas, president of ICCAT, delivered the news that years of warnings about unsustainable fishing practices, particularly involving bigeye tuna, have gone largely unheeded, and the consequences will be severe if corrective action is not taken immediately.

Vigo tuna conference 2025: Future bright as new markets open in China, Latin America

"We've been lucky so far, but that luck is running out," Penas said during the XII ANFACO World Tuna Conference, which ran in Vigo, Spain, on Sept. 11 and 12.

"If overfishing continues at the current pace, total allowable catch cuts and harder quotas are inevitable. We cannot afford to delay any longer," he added.

Bigeye tuna, a species prized in both fresh and canned seafood markets, is at the heart of the crisis. Scientific assessments have shown that its population is at critically low levels, yet fishing fleets continue to exceed recommended catch limits.

Some fleets associated with the canning industry have repeatedly flouted ICCAT rules, pushing the species closer to collapse, he said.

"The canning sector has a responsibility -- and a lot to lose -- if these trends continue," Penas stated. "They are not just passive recipients of tuna; they influence how and where fishing happens through their demand. Continued overfishing driven by these fleets threatens not just the fish, but the entire industry's future."

Despite repeated calls from ICCAT and scientists for stronger enforcement, quota violations persist. The lack of accountability has frustrated regulators who worry that these breaches will force the Commission's hand toward stricter measures, including steep catch reductions that could deeply impact fishing communities and supply chains worldwide.

 

Sustainability status of Atlantic bigeye tuna. Credit: ICCAT

Catches by gear vs. TAC of Atlantic bigeye tuna. Credit: ICCAT

But the pressure isn't limited to bigeye tuna.

Penas also warned that skipjack tuna, a species often viewed as abundant and the backbone of much of the global canned tuna market, is also experiencing rising catch rates without adequate management.

"We're seeing the same dangerous patterns that preceded past stock collapses," he said. "Just because skipjack stocks are currently in better shape, does not mean they are immune. Without robust management, they too could be pushed to the brink."

The canning industry, which processes a large portion of Atlantic tuna, has faced increasing scrutiny as a key player in this unfolding crisis. Penas criticized the disconnect between sustainability claims made by many major canners and their actual sourcing practices.

"We hear a lot of rhetoric about sustainability from canners, but what matters is what happens on the water and in the supply chain. Responsible sourcing, traceability, and pressure on suppliers to follow ICCAT rules must become the norm, not the exception," he pointed out.

Sustainability status of Atlantic yellowfin tuna. Credit: ICCAT

Contrasting the precarious state of many stocks, he also highlighted successes to illustrate what is possible when management works. He praised North Atlantic albacore, calling it "the best-managed fishery I've ever seen," with consistent enforcement of scientifically grounded quotas that have maintained stock health.

Sustainability status of North Atlantic albacore tuna. Credit: ICCAT

Similarly, the remarkable recovery of Atlantic bluefin tuna stands as a testament to what political will and strict enforcement can achieve. Once on the verge of collapse due to rampant overfishing, bluefin stocks have rebounded thanks to rigorous catch limits and international cooperation.

"Bluefin was a wake-up call for the entire tuna world," Penas explained. "It showed that recovery is possible with strong leadership, science-based management, and industry cooperation. But it also taught us how fragile that recovery is. We cannot afford to repeat the mistakes that nearly wiped out bluefin."

Sustainability status of Atlantic bluefin tuna. Credit: ICCAT

ICCAT's challenge now is enforcing compliance among its more than 50 member countries, many of which face political and economic pressures that complicate regulation. The persistent quota violations reveal gaps in monitoring and enforcement mechanisms, fueling concerns that voluntary adherence is insufficient.

"We are prepared to take stronger action if necessary," Penas warned. "If governments and industry actors fail to uphold their responsibilities, ICCAT will have no choice but to impose stricter quotas, enhanced monitoring, and tougher sanctions. These are not threats; they are realities we must face to protect the future of these fisheries."

The situation unfolding in parts of West Africa adds urgency to that challenge. In Ghana -- a key tuna-producing and processing country -- economic pressure, foreign competition, and governance gaps have damaged the sector.

"Ghana should not be seen just as one of the tuna-producing or processing countries," said Anthony Kim, CEO of Ghana's Pacific Wide, during the event. "Ghana must be recognized as a ready partner that plays an important role in ensuring food security across the country."

Kim confirmed that Ghana's tuna fishery has "worsened a lot in recent years." Pole-and-line fishing has nearly disappeared, and just two purse seiners remain active, both of which are expected to stop operations by the end of 2025.

He warned that unless international partners engage with countries like Ghana through cooperation and capacity-building -- rather than just control -- the collapse of local industries could become a reality.

"This is not just a business issue; it's a question of national development," Kim said. "If international partners want sustainable tuna, they have to invest in the systems and communities that produce it."

Ghana has previously been hit with trade sanctions -- including a "yellow card" from the EU in 2013 due to illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing -- and although the country has implemented reforms, the sector still faces reputational and structural challenges.

Ghana tuna vessels status. Credit: Pacific Wide

As global demand for tuna continues to rise, fueled by both canned products and fresh seafood markets, the risks of stock collapse extend far beyond environmental damage.

Economic shocks, disrupted supply chains, and price volatility could ripple through communities and countries reliant on tuna exports.

"We've seen what happens when we wait too long. The cost of inaction is much higher than the cost of immediate reform. The clock is ticking, and the time to act is now," Penas concluded.

title: Barramundi Group finalizes private placement as part of restructure
content:
Singapore-based aquaculture company Barramundi Group has taken a step toward financial stability by completing a significant private placement and share offering, raising nearly SGD 3.9 million ($3.1m) as part of its ongoing restructuring efforts.

On Sept. 15, 2025, Barramundi signed a share subscription agreement with United Overseas Bank (UOB), its secured creditor, and several existing shareholders.

Barramundi creditors vote in favor of debt restructure

The agreement formalizes the issuance of up to 135m new ordinary shares, including shares allocated to UOB through a debt-to-equity swap, priced at SGD 0.0289 each. This private placement alone is expected to bring in SGD 3.4m in gross proceeds.

Key insiders also played a major role in raising equity. Board member Andrew Kwan Kok Tiong subscribed for over 41m shares, increasing his stake to about 26% of the company's outstanding shares.

Similarly, Warif Holdings -- closely linked to another board member, Khairuddin Abd Hamid -- subscribed for an equal number of shares and also held roughly 26% of voting rights.

Alongside the private placement, Oslo-listed Barramundi conducted a subsequent offering in early September to eligible shareholders who did not participate in the initial placement. The offer allowed shareholders to purchase shares on similar terms, with about 5.9m shares allocated and raising approximately NOK 1.35m ($137,895).

Payments are due later this month, with share delivery expected by the end of September.

These combined efforts will increase Barramundi's total share capital to approximately SGD 157.9m, or around NOK 1.2 billion, spread across 175m shares.

The company's equity raise is a central part of its wider restructuring strategy aimed at overcoming recent financial difficulties.

As Undercurrent News previously reported, Barramundi has been grappling with operational setbacks caused by a virus outbreak at its Singapore farms and environmental challenges that affected its Australian operations, which were sold in 2023.

Facing legal pressure from UOB and potential receivership, the company has sought to restructure its debt and shore up liquidity through this equity issuance.

Under the restructuring plan, UOB is set to receive 16m shares and a scheduled repayment of SGD 1m within five months, along with a share in any profits from the lease or sale of Barramundi's farm site on Saint John's Island, Singapore.

Following creditor approval, Barramundi has now applied to the court to formally approve its restructuring scheme and an extension of the existing moratorium order that currently protects it from enforcement actions.

A court hearing date has yet to be announced.

title: Vigo tuna conference day one recap: Spanish sector confronts trade policy, harsh fishery mangement
content:
Undercurrent News is reporting from Vigo, northern Spain, where the XII ANFACO World Tuna Conference runs Sept. 11-12.

You can read all the news from the first day of the event below:

Thai Union: French tuna market recovers after NGO mercury report shock

France's canned tuna market is regaining ground after a slump triggered by an NGO report on mercury levels, according to Alexis Jacquand, managing director of brand Petite Navire, owned by Thai Union Group.

World's tuna supply under threat without urgent investment in processing, says FAO

The world's growing appetite for tuna is on a collision course with processing bottlenecks that threaten future supply, said William Griffin, consultant at the United Nations' Food and Agriculture Organization. 

EU to enforce world's toughest forced labor import ban by 2027

The European Union will enforce a sweeping ban from December 2027 on all products linked to forced labor, marking the world's toughest import restriction of its kind. 

Private label canned tuna continues to surge as Spanish consumers shift to value

NielsenIQ analyst Miguel Barreiro highlighted the resilience of Spain's private label canned tuna market amid shifting consumer habits and economic pressures. 

Global foodservice spending hits $1.6 trillion as consumers prioritize eating out despite economic strains

The global foodservice industry reached over $1.6 trillion in consumer spending over the past year, growing 2.7%, said Edurne Uranga, vice president of Foodservice Europe at market consultancy Circana.

MSC-certified tuna fishery numbers continue to grow, challenges in stock management remain

The Marine Stewardship Council has reported significant growth in the number of tuna fisheries achieving certification under its program, while cautioning that weak enforcement of harvest control rules remains a pressing challenge for sustainable management.

Conservative tuna management becoming the norm, says ISSF

Victor Restrepo, the chair of the International Seafood Sustainability Foundation's scientific advisory committee, highlighted a growing global trend toward conservative tuna fishery management, noting that while there is biological room to increase catches, precaution and sustainability continue to drive policy decisions. 

Experts call for urgent reform as tuna fleets face operational crisis in the Atlantic

Despite healthy stock assessments for tropical tunas in the Atlantic, some fishing fleets are struggling to maintain operations, and experts say the problem isn't the fish, but the system. 

ICCAT: Canning industry must act now to prevent Atlantic tuna stocks collapse

Atlantic tuna stocks are under mounting threat, with key species facing overfishing and quota violations, and the canning industry is largely to blame, warned Ernesto Penas, president of the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas.

Skipjack holds strong in Ecuador as Indian Ocean prices weaken

Tuna prices remain a pressing concern across major markets as sector executives traveled from one industry event to another over the past seven days.

Galician tuna industry goes high-tech with government-backed digital revolution

Galicia's tuna canning industry is undergoing a digital transformation, fueled by strong support from the Spanish government. 

Marine Instruments, Grupo Profand win top honors at 2025 Tuna Awards

Spanish marine tech specialist Marine Instruments and seafood company Grupo Profand were awarded top honors at the 2025 Tuna Awards.

title: Untitled
content:
As Undercurrent News adjusted its price assessments on frozen Russian and Norwegian headed and gutted (H&G) cod and haddock up again to new record levels in week 37 (Sept. 8-14), yet another trade quirk in the US emerged, which seems likely to move prices on the latter species.

VIEW GRAPH
CIF China prices for 1-2.5kg Norwegian (blue) and 1-2kg Russian (green) frozen H&G Atlantic cod
© 2025 Undercurrent News
To view the full datas
GO PREMIUM
Upgrade to Pro to view

While the cost, insurance and freight (CIF) prices for frozen and trawl-caught H&G cod from Russia (1-2kg benchmark size) and Norway (1-2.5kg) are at a spread of around $750 per metric ton, haddock has been much tighter. In the week 37 UCN assessment, there's only a gap of $200/t between Norwegian 800g plus trawl-caught and frozen H&G haddock and Russian 500g-1kg, as you can see below.

The narrow gap on Russian and Norwegian H&G haddock compared to cod is driven by the fact that fish from the former can still go to China and other processing hubs, then be sent to the US as fillets and other products. Cod, pollock, and salmon have all been banned in the US since June 1, 2024, after an executive order passed by previous president Joseph Biden which Donald Trump kept in place.

NOAA advances import bans on 46 nations’ fisheries

However, this loophole on H&G haddock looks set to end on Jan. 1, 2026, as Russia is not on the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) list of countries that adhere to the Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA), according to an Aug. 29 announcement.

Although nothing is certain in the Trump regime, two major US importers said they are operating under the assumption that no haddock finished products using Russian raw material can come into the country after Jan. 1, 2026.

As a result, H&G Norwegian haddock will be more in demand, which could support prices even though the quota for the fish could increase 18% in 2026 to 153,293t, if scientific recommendations are followed.

"Due to the MMPA being enforced, there will be no more Russian haddock allowed in from a third-party country," one US importer who wished to remain anonymous told Undercurrent. "Norwegian haddock should go up in the next few weeks."

Significant volumes of finished haddock products based on Russian raw material have been coming into the country, he said.

"We use Russian almost exclusively -- or at least we did," he told Undercurrent.

With no new entries after Jan. 1, 2026, the deadline to order raw material is coming up fast, with 10 weeks to deliver the H&G to China and then as much as 60 days to the US East Coast and 20-30 days to Los Angeles, he said.

Prior to this NOAA move on MMPA emerging, the general view was that haddock prices could come under some pressure, given the high levels and fact Norway has 18,410t left to catch as of week 36, 5,395t more than the same week of 2024, according to government data.

As for cod, only 37,683t is left to catch for Norway, compared to 45,169t at week 36 of 2024.

Cod supply is reported to be scarce, hence the ever-rising prices.

"There is just not much about, so prices seem to be rising $150/t a week," one European trader said. "People don't want to buy, but they do as they are worried the price will be more next week."

Russia gives Norway a month to lift sanctions before banning it from EEZ

According to this source, there could be processing casualties in Europe as a result, which could then see the market adjust. "I do think people will go under; they are producing at a loss," he said. "Maybe this cools prices. But then the quota will be cut, and you have the issue with Norway and Russia."

Russia has given Norway until Sept. 26, 2025, to revoke its sanctions on two Russian fishing companies -- Norebo Holding and Murman SeaFood. This deadline was set during an extraordinary session of the Joint Russian-Norwegian Fisheries Commission held on Aug. 26, 2025, where Russia gave Norway one month to reconsider its position. 

The sanctions in question were initially imposed by Norway in July 2025, following the EU's decision from May 20, 2025, to include these companies in its 17th package of sanctions against Russia. European companies can no longer pay Norebo or Murman, excluding them from the market.

The sanctions were imposed due to alleged involvement of these companies' vessels in espionage and sabotage relating to critical infrastructure, including underwater cables -- allegations which the companies deny. 

If Norway does not lift the sanctions by the deadline, Russia has threatened to:

Close its exclusive economic zone to Norwegian fishing vessels
Conduct fishing and distribute fishing quotas in the open waters of the Barents and Norwegian Seas based on Russian national interests 

However, Russia's fishery head Ilya Shestakov has recently stated that if Norway cancels its sanctions, Russia will not take any retaliatory measures. 

If this happens, it will be an end to Marine Stewardship Council-certified Russian cod, creating more turmoil in the markets, the European source said.

title: Argentine province orders Red Chamber to hand over former Alpesca assets
content:
The provincial government of Chubut in Argentina has ordered US fishing firm Red Chamber to hand over the former assets of Alpesca, which it has been leasing and operating.

In a letter seen by Undercurrent News, the government of Chubut notified Red Chamber's Argentinian subsidiary, RCA, that it had rejected its appeals, terminating the lease and charter contract with the province of Chubut.

US-based Red Chamber alleges espionage as it vies for control of Argentine firm’s assets

It demanded that Red Chamber return all assets belonging to Alpesca and AP Holding to the province of Chubut by Sept. 30 or face legal action.

The vessels Promarsa III (currently inoperative) and Cabo Virgenes will not be able to operate beyond Sept. 30, 2025, "by which time they must be at dock in order to incorporate the on-duty crew or use the existing ones if they belonged to Alpesca."

Chubut has also asked Red Chamber to pay ARS 2.52 billion ($1.8 million) in outstanding rental fees.

The Argentinian fisheries secretariat terminated the contract in February, and after a hierarchical appeal for reconsideration, the government's legal advisory office recommended dismissing it and terminating the 10-year lease with RCA, reported Parte de Pesca.

Spain's Grupo Profand will take over the running of the assets, Revista Puerto reported, citing Luis Emilio Nunez, general secretary of the Food Industry Workers' Union in the province.

Chubut is drafting contracts for Profand, although nothing will be formalized until the transition is complete, sources told Undercurrent. Red Chamber is expected to file lawsuits against the state of Chubut, but there is no official confirmation yet, sources added.

As Undercurrent has reported, RCA had been operating the former Alpesca processing plant, employing 400 people, along with seven national fishing permits and five provincial fishing permits.

It had filed a criminal complaint in local courts alleging a case of corporate espionage linked to the expropriation process of the assets, while confirming to Undercurrent that its contract with Chubut remained legally valid and fully enforceable.

Profand and Red Chamber Argentina did not reply to a request for comment in time for this article.

title: Oceana flags certification risk for Philippine tuna exports after court ruling
content:
Philippine tuna exports could face the loss of key sustainability certifications following a recent Supreme Court ruling that allows commercial fishing vessels to operate in waters traditionally reserved for small-scale fishers, environmental group Oceana has warned.

The decision by the court's First Division opened municipal waters -- the 15-kilometer coastal zone managed by local governments -- to larger commercial boats. Oceana cautioned that the move could undermine international sustainability standards such as those set by the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC), jeopardizing the country's access to high-value export markets.

Industry stakeholders and local fishing groups have also expressed concern that increased pressure from commercial fleets will erode fish stocks and weaken the resource management systems central to securing certification.

"Allowing commercial vessels in municipal waters raises serious questions about stock management and environmental enforcement," cautioned Veronica 'Jinky' Rabano of Jarla Trading, a member of the Philippine Association of Tuna Processors.

According to community leaders cited by Oceana, tuna catches have already declined sharply in recent years, with handline fishers reporting that daily hauls that once reached 100 kilograms now often fall below 50kg.

The Philippine Tuna Handline Partnership earned MSC certification in 2021 after years of preparation and significant investment.

Oceana noted that this progress is now at risk of being undone. Losing certification, it said, could mean exclusion from premium markets that demand proof of sustainable sourcing.

The Department of Agriculture and the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources have filed motions challenging the ruling, emphasizing the importance of protecting municipal waters to safeguard small-scale fishers' rights and maintain the tuna industry's sustainability credentials.

title: Editor’s choice: All the news from the Global Shrimp Forum; US to further disrupt trade with NOAA bans
content:
EMEA editor Neil Ramsden brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week.

Our most-read story of last week was our coverage of the Global Shrimp Forum, held in Utrecht, the Netherlands -- you can recap the news from the event here.

Meanwhile, US swimming crab importers are expressing grave concern that a move by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to ban products from 240 fisheries worldwide could be catastrophic to their businesses. NOAA has announced a tightening of its enforcement of the Marine Mammal Protection Act that will result in full or partial bans of seafood imported from 46 nations beginning Jan. 1, 2026.

Some 1.7 million Atlantic salmon were impacted by warm waters and low oxygen at Mowi's farms in Newfoundland and Labrador (NL), Canada, last week, but the firm was at pains to note mortalities came to around 400,000 fish. "The 1.5m figure is a gross overstatement," managing director Gideon Pringle told Undercurrent News. "This is not an incident anywhere close to [the] scale of [September 2019's fish deaths]."

Mayonna, a Dutch retail-focused seafood processor, is to shut down by mid-October 2025, drawing the curtain on more than two decades in business. Mayonna was part of the Kennemervis Group, a collection of seafood businesses that also included Dutch fish trader FishPartners and Danish herring processor Werner Larsson Fiskeeksport. But that group has now ceased to exist -- an automated reply from Kennemervis CEO Jeroen Kiers' email account stated that the group "is no longer in operation."

Global aquaculture giant Cooke Aquaculture has asked the Canadian Transportation Agency for emergency permission to contract two US-flagged delousing vessels as the company battles a spike in sea lice on its salmon farms in NL. Cooke operates five delousing vessels in Atlantic Canada equipped with thermal lice systems -- mechanical, chemical-free treatments that use warmwater baths to remove parasites from fish. Usually, that fleet is sufficient, but this summer's prolonged hot, dry spell has stretched capacity.

Japanese giant Kyokuyo Co. has agreed to acquire a controlling stake in a Danish processor and distributor, marking its latest step to strengthen its growing European operations and accelerate global expansion. Kyokuyo Europe, the Tokyo-based group's Dutch subsidiary, signed a basic agreement with Engelsviken Canning Norway to purchase 90% of shares in Engelsviken Canning Denmark, making it a consolidated subsidiary.

Russia's agricultural watchdog, Rosselkhoznadzor, has indicated plans to suspend imports of Chilean fish, citing alleged labeling and paperwork violations. It claimed to have repeatedly recorded inconsistencies in the accompanying documentation for these products. There have also been discrepancies in the information indicated on the labels and stated in veterinary certificates, it said.

Polish smoked salmon processor Suempol, the oldest producer of its kind in the country and one of the largest in the world, is entering shrimp for the first time in 30 years with a deal for a Belgian processor. The company has acquired 100% of the shares in Belgium's Van Biesen & Pieters.

title: Catch the Current episode 33: A plea for pumpkin spice lobster rolls amid another seafood ‘death punch’
content:
Tariffs, import alerts, die-offs ... what else can the seafood industry get tossed its way?

Undercurrent News editorial director Cliff White joins "Catch the Current" hosts Amanda Buckle and Lorin Castiglione this week to talk about the latest, potential "death punch" being experienced by swimming crab importers in particular.

Meanwhile, Maine lobstermen are dealing with their own gut punch in the form of low landings as well as a whole lot of other nuisances. Undercurrent's Barb Dean-Simmons jumps on the pod to talk about how the lackluster 2025 lobster harvest has led to consumers "hemming and hawing" over high prices.

But it's not all doom and gloom in this week's episode. Lorin's got a market update. And Amanda's freshly back from the Netherlands, shouting from the rooftops about "The Happy Protein" campaign and making a plea for someone to add a pumpkin spice lobster roll to their fall menus. And there's even some potential good news regarding the "radioactive shrimp" import alert.

Thank you to our sponsor: Wisefish.

Listen now on YouTube!

Subscribe now! Catch the Current is available on YouTube, Spotify, Amazon Music, iHeartRadio, Pandora, and other major podcast streaming platforms. Don't see Catch the Current on your favorite app? Reach out to podcasts@undercurrentnews.com.

Don't have time to listen? Find a full transcript of season 1, episode 33 of Catch the Current below:

Amanda Buckle (AB): You’re listening to Catch the Current, the coolest seafood podcast out there, from the team at Undercurrent News, your trusted source for seafood prices, news and data. I’m Amanda Buckle.

Lorin Castiglione (LC): And I’m Lorin Castiglione.

AB: Before we dive in, a quick shoutout to our sponsor Wisefish. With over 30 years in the seafood industry, they’re powering aquaculture, fisheries, processors and seafood sales with one integrated platform that makes managing complex operations simpler. Check them out at wisefish.com/catch-the-current.

Welcome back from the Netherlands, Amanda. Tell us all about your trip to the Global Shrimp Forum.

AB: Yes, it was a quick trip due to the first week of school, but still a great one.

I flew in for the first day of the Global Shrimp Forum on Tuesday and was able to catch the wild-caught shrimp side event, which was sponsored by the Marine Stewardship Council and the Worldwide Fishing Company.

FREE READ GSF 2025 day one recap: US shrimp tariffs to hit shrimp consumption soon; Global Shrimp Council launches new campaigns

You and I talk about this often. But it's truly insane how much there is to learn about the seafood industry. So, this trip, eight years into my career in seafood journalism, I learn that they're harvesting shrimp in Utah! 

Did you know that, Lorin?

LC: No, I did not know that.

AB: It's so cool! I was not familiar with brine shrimp, or Artemia. It's not something I've reported on in the past, but it was really interesting to hear from Timothy Hawkes, chairman of the board at Great Salt Lake Brine Shrimp Cooperative, who was one of the panelists at the event.

I want to actually share some of my knowledge, my newfound knowledge with you.

LC: Oh, please.

AB: Great Salt Lake Artemia or GSLA, it's a collection of member companies working together to harvest and distribute Great Salt Lake Artemia.

But brine shrimp is essential in farm seafood and Great Salt Lake Artemia provides nearly half of the global supply of brine shrimp cysts, or eggs, harvested each year. It's exported to 55 countries around the world and 10 million tons of marine shrimp species rely on it.

So, Utah is full of surprises. I've never been. Have you, Lorin?

LC: No, but this sounds like we need to make a trip. 

AB: Exactly. But now onto the reason why I flew to the Netherlands -- the Global Shrimp Council!

I had the honor of being the co-chair for the Global Shrimp Council Update and Outreach Meeting that took place Tuesday afternoon. It was sponsored by the Global Shrimp Forum Foundation and gave attendees -- both current and prospective members of the Global Shrimp Council -- an update on the "Global Shrimp - Happy Protein" marketing campaign. 

And Lorin, it is fire!

LC: I feel like you sound like my elementary school kids talking about the latest lingo when you say that.

AB: You got to be hip. You got to be cool. But I mean, it was a lot about social media. So yes, you got to be hip with the times, Lorin.

Miguel Barcenas, the strategy and marketing consultant for the Global Shrimp Forum, debuted the promo video for the campaign at the event. And I think it's got the potential to start a real shrimp movement. It was just a fantastic video.

It was just lively. It was exciting. I'm going to see if it's online, if I can link back to it.

The video they have of shrimp cooking and being thrown onto the grill. It had families in it, and they're trying to push that... eat shrimp. It's nutritious. And it just overall just makes you feel happy.

LC: You know, nobody sad is eating shrimp.

AB: No, but it's true. Like, I mean, I'm a pescetarian, so I don't eat other things, but I've never had shrimp and then afterwards sat down and been like, oh, I feel disgusting.

You know, I do... I think of shrimp, and I do smile.

It built a lot of excitement and you got to hear from companies and people with the companies that have been with the Global Shrimp Council since it started and hear why they're so passionate about it and why they want people to join.

And its companies throughout the supply chain. Anybody could be a part of it, but who has their hands in the shrimp supply chain should join the Global Shrimp Council and it should help promote shrimp consumption.

It's just... it's shrimp, you know? And these guys, they're the guys behind the [singing] "Avocados from Mexico." So they obviously know what they're doing.

LC: And that's always in my head, especially at 3 a.m. when I'm trying to sleep.

And my kids love saying it, too.

AB: You're never just like "say" avocados from Mexico. You [sing] "avocados from Mexico."

That was nice. OK.

LC: Yeah.

AB: Anyway, we're actually going to have a Catch the Current bonus episode.

We had a whole gang out in the Netherlands because I wasn't the only one that got to co-chair an event. Gary [Morrison] was also up on stage as a panelist.

I think he'll be traveling. So I'm not sure if we'll have him on, but we'll have the rest of the team who was reporting from the event who could share just the highlights and all the big takeaways.

GSF 2025: US shrimp buyers find India dependency difficult to break; Disease outbreaks drive consolidation in Vietnam

And of course, we have the blog up, too. So if you haven't checked that out, we'll link back to that.

But it was my first time at the Global Shrimp Forum and I only got just a taste and... Lorin! I didn't even talk about the food I ate there. Oh, my gosh.

LC: Yes. Yes. Please tell us.

AB: The best part about, of course, all these events is the food. And the Global Shrimp Forum had a walking dinner on Tuesday night. So they had like different stations up. So you just got to go walk around...

LC: Like a cocktail party.

AB: And take a little plate to go and grab a drink. They had little tables set up. And so you just had to get up and keep going to try different things.

I tried Madagascar shrimp for the first time.

One of the dishes offered during the "walking dinner" during the 2025 Global Shrimp Forum in Utrecht, Netherlands. Photo Credit: Undercurrent News

LC: Are those the huge like banana-sized ones?

AB: Well, mine wasn't nearly...it was taken apart. So it could have been. It was big. It was pretty big. It was delicious. But they had a bunch of different suppliers send in shrimp for these dishes and it was curated specifically for the event.

And as a bonus, in the swag bags, they had postcards with illustrations of each of the dishes and the sponsoring company. So it was creative and fun and delicious. So I'm hoping to be able to go back one day.

LC: Me too. We got to take Gary out of there. I'm going to start covering the shrimp market.

AB: Speaking of the markets, Lorin, why don't you break down what's going on in some of your markets this week?

Week 36 US wholesale prices: Atlantic cod, Norwegian salmon rally after Labor Day; New reporting for larger live lobster sizes

LC: All right. So this week in the US groundfish market, things are tightening up again another notch.

Atlantic cod is still leading the charge, but Pacific is following closely behind. And that's pushing buyers to focus more on making sure they've got supply covered rather than worrying about cost. Haddock also moved higher as raw materials stay tight and a lot of sellers are still keeping customers on allocation, which tells you just how snug supply is.

Pacific cod is still acting as the fallback for price-sensitive programs that don't want to pay the Atlantic premiums. But it's not exactly cheap either there. Haddock really stood out.

We saw notable premiums out of both China and Iceland. Both origins are dealing with limited raw materials and strong program demand, which is keeping the market firm.

US wholesale: Cod climbs again, haddock tight on supply in week 36

Policy is also playing a role. The US trade representative extended Section 301 tariff relief until November 29, which is key for twice-frozen products like haddock and yellowfin sole, for example. That gives buyers some breathing room in the short term, but there's still a lot of uncertainty heading into the end of the year.

So overall, cod and Haddock remain very supported. Atlantic is expensive, but buyers are still pulling it in. Pacific is acting as more of a pressure valve and Haddock is staying strong on tight supply. So unless something shifts in tariffs or quotas, the trend into Q4 looks steady to firm pricing across the board.

AB: Lorin, we are lucky to work with some of the best of the best. So let's invite a few of our Undercurrent friends on to chat about some of the big news to break this week. Joining us now to talk about the lackluster 2025 lobster harvest in the US state of Maine is reporter Barb Dean-Simmons.

Barb Dean-Simmons (BDS): Well, when it comes to Maine, the lobster season this year is not doing so well. Landings again are down by about 20% compared to 2024, which was the worst season in 16 years. So here's your flashback.

In 2024, Maine lobstermen caught about 86 million pounds worth, about $528m at the docks last year, and that was well below the 97m lbs landed in 2023. And sources tell us that the landings are down by 20%. So if you do that math, we're looking at about 70m lbs for this season.

Of course, final data from the 2025 season won't be available until early 2026. The bright spot is there's a lot of small lobsters in the mix. One source told us that traps are coming up full of small lobsters.

Now, they're too small of course to bring ashore this year. They're going back in the water. But hopefully with a bit more growing, they'll be at market size in about three years.

So hopefully that will turn out well in terms of supply over the next few seasons to come.

AB: And now another issue for the lobster industry are underwater pests. Is that right? 

BDS: This season, and I think it's typical for some seasons, but sea fleas. That's those small shrimp-like scavengers. They love dead things. So they like dead fish, dead meat.

And they're really attracted to the herring- and menhaden-filled bait bags that are used in lobster traps. And one source told us they're going right through our bait before the traps can actually catch a good-sized lobster. Sometimes the bait, there's nothing left in the bag except for bones once those sea fleas get at that bait.

The other nuisance that's come back this summer is sea squirts. And that's those filter-feeding marine invertebrates that are also known as tunicates. And they just attach themselves to the lobster traps in colonies.

And they get really heavy with water. So when lobstermen are trying to haul their lobster traps that have been inundated by the sea squirts, it's really heavy. That makes today's work a whole lot harder.

Sea pests, low landings, sticker-shock further challenge Maine’s lobster harvest

And apparently, sea squirts have been more prolific because of warming waters. Since 2000, they're seeing more of them. So that's two things that are really making this season more challenging than they really want them to be for the lobster fishermen.

AB: You know, it's really crazy when you think about how lobster gets to your plate, what some of these struggles are that these fishermen are dealing with. So that's really interesting.

You got low landings. And so that's equaling high dock prices. So what does that mean for consumers? What can you tell us there?

BDS: Well, yeah, when something is in short supply, the theory is that people want more of it. And certainly the price of that limited item usually goes up. And that's been the case for dock prices. Fish harvesters are getting a pretty good deal on their catches this year. I think it's even a little bit higher than last year.

And I've got those details in the story. But the shortage of live lobsters for meat and tails means also high prices at wholesale for that meat. And that means, you know, the ticket price at the restaurant and at the food truck is a little bit higher.

And that's leaving consumers hemming and hawing over whether or not they can afford to buy that lobster roll.

So Bret Taylor, Taylor Lobster, in Kittery, Maine, he told me that demand is not gang busters, but it's not terrible either. It's just OK. And he says that he thinks consumers are being very cautious about their dollars.

Now, the big question is whether consumers will continue to gobble up those lobster rolls after the Labor Day weekend, when the summer fun subsides.

And Paul DiMare over at Boston Sword and Tuna told me that he thinks that people will after Labor Day, they're going to hunker down, try to save some money. And he says he thinks that will cause prices to come down. And his quote was, "I'm not an economist, but that's just the way I feel, given the current economy."

AB: It does seem like that. It doesn't like, right. You get that feeling. I get that feeling, too.

BDS: Yeah, we all have a limited, you know, we all have a budget, a household budget, and we all like to have the nice stuff every now and then. But I guess there comes a time when you have to, you know, save money for the for the next thing that you're going to really need.

AB: And by Labor Day, lobster rolls are done unless someone introduces pumpkin spice lobster rolls.

So if anyone's thinking of ideas on how to keep a lobster roll thing going, pumpkin spice, I will take royalty checks. Thank you very much.

BDS: Maybe there's a sea squirt in there somewhere. Who knows?

AB: Oh, gosh, Barb, that does not sound delicious at all.

NOAA advances import bans on 46 nations’ fisheries

LC: Thanks Barb. Now joining us on the pod is Undercurrent editorial director Cliff White, who reported last week on how the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, also known as NOAA, took a big step towards banning seafood imported from 46 nations, putting a 2026 deadline for countries to adhere to the US Marine Mammal Protection Act, also known as MMPA.

Can you go a little bit into the specifics of what items might be impacted?

Cliff White (CW): Yep. Swimming crab, for sure. Tuna, shrimp, wild-caught shrimp. Wild catch fisheries in general. Anyone who's dealing with wild products should look at this list.

NOAA put out a list on Thursday of around 240 fisheries that are now banned from exporting products to the US. They're from 46 countries, 12 of which all products are banned, including Venezuela and Russia. And 34 of which have some fisheries banned, at least one fishery.

Some of these fisheries are really obscure, probably don't send any exports to the US, but there are some that send tens, potentially even hundreds of millions of dollars of products to the US.

The species I spent the most time looking at this week was swimming crab. And this, I think, is going to be the number one species impacted. Swimming crab fisheries in Indonesia, Vietnam, Sri Lanka and India are all affected by this, not to mention Venezuela, which is another huge exporter of blue crab. So Venezuela's stuff is entirely banned.

Not a single piece of seafood from Venezuela can enter the US legally starting January 1. So that's huge. All this is effective January 1.

And not all fisheries from those big exporting nations that I mentioned from Asia are affected, but many significant fisheries are.

AB: So do you think we're going to see a push now with an increase in Venezuelan swimming crab coming in before the end of the year?

CW: I wouldn't be surprised, yeah. There's only a few importers that deal in Venezuelan swimming crab.

I've spoken now with five different seafood executives, and everyone's trying to figure it out. And it's going to vary by species and vary by importing country or country that sends exports to the US. But it could be anywhere from no impact at all, depending on the fishery, to devastating, crushing. I think one executive called it a "death punch" to the US swimming crab import sector.

So it could be really bad. But I have questions into NOAA to try and figure out the impact of this, and they haven't gotten back to me yet. They say they will by the end of the week.

I have questions into NFI. They're looking into it. They had an emergency meeting yesterday to discuss this.

US foreign fisheries ban threatens ‘death punch’ to swimming crab importers

So it's complicated, and there's not a lot of answers out there right now. It sounds like from what I'm hearing from the industry, that the earliest they'll be able to appeal is after this goes into effect January. And knowing government being government, it'll take at least a couple of months to get any answers back, whether the appeal can be successful.

This all stems back to NOAA being forced by several lawsuits filed by environmental NGOs challenging their enforcement of the Marine Mammal Protection Act. All these environmental NGOs challenged NOAA's regulatory equivalency. So they weren't, in effect, treating foreign fisheries with the same stringency that they were treating domestic fisheries.

So there was what the Southern Shrimp Alliance, which is the US domestic wild-caught shrimp industry, has called an unfair disadvantage put on US fisheries and fishermen who are facing much more stringent regulations.

So NOAA was forced by a court settlement made earlier this year to publish this list of fisheries, and they studied each fishery that they could in depth. Over 2,500 fisheries worldwide, and determined for each one whether they met Marine Mammal Protection Act levels of regulation or not.

The vast majority, they said, did. And that's also being still criticized by environmental NGOs. But 240 failed, did not pass this test that NOAA did. And those are the ones that I'm looking at to see how that's going to impact US imports starting in 2026.

AB: You know, that's really interesting, too, because you said Russia was also on there. And with Trump opening up conversations again with Putin. There was some speculation that they might reopen trade. And so now that kind of, at least for seafood, dampers that, if that was ever an option, I guess.

CW: Yeah, totally. It's another huge angle of this. So Russia did not respond to NOAA's request for information. So it was put on a list of total ban.

It's totally banned, starting January 1, 2026, from exporting any products to the US. There's another separate ban that president Biden put in place in 2023. So that's still in place. President Trump hasn't rescinded that, but he has floated in vague terms, as Trump does, the possibility of easing sanctions on Russia in exchange for some kind of ceasefire in Ukraine.

That hasn't happened yet. But now it can't happen because there's this other ban in place. So there's this redundancy now on Russian products.

And Russia was a top 10 exporter to the US before this ban was put in place. Now zero products came in last year and zero products can come in under this new regulation, even if Trump wants them to. He doesn't have the authority to change this.

It's going to be NOAA that's going to have to decide it.

AB: And again, it's just it's for the foreseeable future. It's indefinitely starting January 1. I think, from what I'm hearing from the industry, that the industry can file for a new consideration or review of each individual fishery.

It'll be done on a fishery-by-fishery basis. I think the home country needs to be involved in that as well, wherever that fishery is located. These reviews involve close contact between governments and regulators to try and find out what's actually being regulated, whether these are paper regulations or whether they actually have teeth in these local fisheries.

And yeah, it looks like NOAA did a really exhaustive job looking at these fisheries, but the review would have to find that something has changed in between when they did the initial study and now, basically.

So any of these fisheries that fail need to do something to fix what's going on, what caused them to fail in order to get a passing grade and to begin exporting again or being allowed to get permission to export to the US.

LC: And all of that happened in less than three months.

CW: The executives I spoke to in the swimming crab industry think that the industry will be more or less shut down for at least eight months.

So because the supply chain is so long, they're going to stop shipping Nov. 1, because they don't want to get caught with any product coming in after Jan. 1. They're going to shut down. They haven't finalized this decision.

They're still waiting for confirmation from NOAA, this is what's going to happen. But they're going to shut down a lot of their imports from Indonesia, which is the primary exporter of swimming crab, but also India, Vietnam.

China has 55% tariffs. India, which is another producer, has 50% tariffs. So even though those don't face bans, they're still bloody expensive with these huge tariffs. Not to mention all these other Southeast Asian countries have 20% tariffs.

It's too expensive for them to produce. So there's still going to be some product coming into the US. They're estimating maybe half of all product will be, or the total will be halved by 2026. And that the earliest they'll be able to get a new decision is four or five months into the new year.

Then you still have to restart your factories, restart all your sourcing. That's another two, three, six months.

So it's going to be a very difficult 2026 for swimming crab importers next year.

LC: That all collides at the end of the year when we see a major push for exports into the US, right on the tails of Lent in the beginning of the year. So not an optimal time at all.

AB: And I just want to say is that if you do not have a subscription to Undercurrent, what are you waiting for? Because this is the type of information that we've got that you need. So check out Cliff's full story in the show notes.

CW: Thanks guys.

Importers push to limit FDA alert for radioactive shrimp from Indonesia

AB: Before we go, just an update on what's going on with the radioactive or so-called radioactive shrimp. An interesting development.

Gunster, a major US law firm with 340 attorneys, is pushing the FDA, to edit its import alert that blocks all the shrimp from Indonesia's Bahari Makmur Sejati or BMS.

So Gunster was hired by two US companies that import Indonesian shrimp that are very concerned, they say, about the targeting of BMS. And they've asked Peter Quinter, a Boca Raton, Florida-based attorney and shareholder at Gunster and the chair of the firm's US Customs and International Trade Law Group, to look into this.

So what he's doing is, because FDA issued import alert 99-51, which states that BMS's products are contaminated with radionuclides such as CS-137, what Quinter wants to do is he wants the FDA to remove the general import alert against BMS and instead edit it to specify that only the shrimp from one problem facility is banned.

So we've got the full details on that story. Like I said, a really interesting development. They made the request to the FDA.

We'll have to see if the FDA is willing to grant it. So check that out.

LC: Well, that does it for us this week. Be sure to check out the bonus episode of Catch the Current coming out Monday for all the scoop from the Global Shrimp Forum.
