title: Untitled
content:
US swimming crab importers are expressing grave concern that a move by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to ban products from 240 fisheries worldwide could be catastrophic to their businesses.

NOAA announced last week a tightening of its enforcement of the Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA) that will result in full or partial bans of seafood imported from 46 nations beginning Jan. 1, 2026, as Undercurrent News reported. The fisheries that will be banned do not meet the US standard for protecting marine mammals, according to individual determinations made by NOAA.

Among the impacted fisheries are tuna, shrimp, squid, lobster, grouper, conch and dozens of other commercially important species from such countries as Bangladesh, Brazil, Chile, Ecuador, Ghana, Malaysia, Mauritania, Mexico, Oman, Peru, Saudi Arabia, Senegal, South Korea, Taiwan and Turkey.

NOAA estimates the value of trade that could be impacted at approximately $3.6 billion.

NOAA advances import bans on 46 nations’ fisheries

The hardest-hit seafood sector by total US import value is likely swimming crab, including blue swimming crab (BSC) (Portunus pelagicus), red swimming crab (Portunus haanii) and blue crab (Callinectes sapidus), overwhelmingly sourced from six nations: Indonesia, Vietnam, the Philippines, Venezuela, China and India.

But starting in 2026, crab caught by gillnets or entangling net fisheries in Indonesia, Vietnam, the Philippines and Sri Lanka, and those caught with pots or traps in the Philippines, Sri Lanka and Vietnam will be banned from entering the US. Also banned will be crab caught with single or pair trawls or trap nets in Vietnam.

NOAA said the fisheries potentially threaten numerous marine mamals, including the pantropical spotted dolphin, long-snouted spinner dolphin, short-beaked common dolphin, Indo-Pacific humpbacked dolphin, Indo-Pacific finless porpoise, short-finned pilot whale, killer whale, Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphin, rough-toothed dolphin, Irrawaddy dolphin, finless porpoise, Risso's dolphin, Fraser’s dolphin, Bryde’s whale and Chinese humpback dolphin.

Also, all seafood from Venezuela, including blue crab, will be prohibited from being sold commercially in the US as that country did not respond to NOAA's request for information.

NOAA's move is a massive problem for the US swimming crab industry, Brice Phillips, vice president of sustainability and business development for Baltimore, Maryland-based Phillips Foods, told Undercurrent in a recent interview.

"With these bans, no one's going to be producing product after Nov. 1," he said. "We're going to need to stop production on Nov. 1, because otherwise we run the risk of putting several million dollars' worth of crab on the water that's not going to be allowed in after Jan. 1."

Phillips chairs the National Fisheries Institute (NFI) Crab Council, a 26-member panel created by the US' largest seafood trade group. Together, the council's members account for nearly all US swimming crab imports.

The combination of NOAA's MMPA-related bans and tariff rates of 19% or higher on all Asian suppliers imposed by US president Donald Trump represent a "death punch" to the swimming crab sector, Phillips said.

"This is a disaster of nightmarish proportions for me and for all the crab council members," he said. "It's going to mean either a total lack of availability of crab products to the American consumer, or drastically increased prices."

Tharakan: Crab cakes will 'vanish' from menus

NOAA's back is relatively up against the wall thanks to a deal reached in January 2024 by the former president Joe Biden administration with the Natural Resources Defense Council, the Center for Biological Diversity and the Animal Welfare Institute.

NOAA agreed to the Jan. 1, 2026 implementation deadline in order to settle lawsuits brought by the conservation groups, which had accused the federal government of being in violation of its non-discretionary duty to impose import bans on foreign nations' fish and fish products that have been harvested in violation of the MMPA standards.

Anjan Tharakan, the president of St. Petersburg, Florida-based crab importer Newport International, said the new regulatory requirements will result in "higher prices and fewer choices at the dinner table."

"Staples of American cuisine such as crab cakes, sushi (and) fish tacos could vanish from menus nationwide or become unaffordable for the average diner," he said.

Domestic crabmeat production meets only a small portion of US demand, with 80-90% of the crabmeat consumed in the US being imported. The US imported 27,732 metric tons (61.1 million pounds) of swimming crab worth $655.9m in 2024, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

Banning millions of pounds of crabmeat from entering the US will result in job losses for processing facilities and restaurants, and will cost the US treasury millions of dollars in tariff revenues, Tharakan told Undercurrent via email.

"Coastal communities in Maryland, Delaware, Virginia, the Carolinas, Louisiana and Florida rely heavily on imports to supplement their limited domestic blue crab supplies. In Maryland, for example, nearly every restaurant serves a crab cake," he continued. "If import bans take effect on Jan. 1, 2026, only about 1 in 10 may be able to keep it on the menu, and likely as a seasonal or limited offering."

Tharakan said Newport supports marine mammal protection but strongly opposes blanket import bans, as they punish fisheries working hard on self-improvement.

"These measures ignore the real progress many foreign fisheries are making through fishery improvement projects," he said. "The MMPA standards are based on US fisheries, which benefit from greater resources, technology and enforcement. Expecting developing nations to meet these standards without assistance is neither realistic nor equitable, especially given their socioeconomic constraints."

Newport International sells the Jack's Catch brand of crabmeat. Photo courtesy of Newport International.

Indonesian harvesters will have to fish harder

Indonesia is responsible for the largest share of swimming crab coming into the US by far, sending it 12,860 metric tons (a 46% share of the total import volume) valued at $325.7 million (a 50% share of the total import value) in 2024. 

The chart below shows how the US has become more dependent on Indonesia as a source of BSC since 2012.

US foreign fisheries ban threatens 'death punch' to swimming crab importers - Undercurrent News

Indonesia's BSC fishery is relatively evenly split between gillnetters, traps and pots, Phillips said. However, if the NOAA ruling forces fishermen in Indonesia to use collapsible traps, they will likely convert, he added.

It will take time, and most crab fishermen in Southeast Asia are poor and cannot easily invest in new gear, he said.

The conversion will cause additional headaches, since collapsible traps take up more deck space and most of the boats in Indonesia's fishery are very small. That will mean fishermen will have to conduct more fishing trips per day to get the same amount of production, he said.

Crab fishermen in Indonesia. Photo courtesy of EDF.

In the meantime, Phillips said his company and others will likely have to shut down some or all processing in Indonesia.

The industry will ask NOAA for a new finding of comparability, but the earliest that can be done is after Jan. 1, and it could take months for the government to process the request, according to Phillips. Applicants must then prove their fishery actually meets MMPA standards, which is also not a given since it just failed NOAA's most recent audit.

"Best case, we're probably looking at a bare minimum of an eight-month outage, but it could be far worse," Phillips said.

During that time, fishermen will have to find other work and may sell their gear, and local crab-cooking stations will have to lay off staff. If and when the comparability finding is approved, it will take an additional three to six months to bring factories back online, between rehiring thousands of workers and ensuring regulatory and legal compliance. 

"So even if we get a finding of comparability sometime next spring and we have product coming out of our plants by July 1, it's not going to arrive in the US until Sept. 1," Phillips said. "There is just going to be a complete, total and drastic reduction in supply coming into the US."

Phillips Foods operates four processing facilities in Indonesia, one in Vietnam and one in India. It also has a regional office in Bangkok, Thailand. 

"I'm going to have to make calls sometime this week and let them know that we run the very real risk of not having product for them anymore and that they may need to sit around for eight months," Brice Phillips said.

Phillips estimated Indonesia's 30m lbs of crab exports may be halved in 2026. Phillips Foods and Thai Union's Chicken of the Sea own a combined 40-50% market share of the US swimming crab market, with the remaining players, including Handy, Harbor Seafood, North Coast, Supreme Crab and Newport making up the remainder. It's possible not all will survive the crisis, he speculated.

"You'll probably see the smaller guys just disappear," he said. "Most of them are primarily in Indonesia, with maybe some side hustle business in other Asian countries. The tariffs were already driving prices up around 20% and nobody would like that, but we could all probably handle it. But this is a totally different story, with just the outright ban on some of the imports. There's no way around it.

"The most realistic outcome is companies decide it's just not worth it to be involved in swimming crab, and they drop it altogether," Phillips said.

Phillips Foods' vice president of sustainability Brice Phillips. Credit: Tom Seaman

Just as bad elsewhere in Asia

While Indonesia is the epicenter of the swimming crab universe, Vietnam (2,992t worth $62.8m), the Philippines (2,799t worth $72.5m), China (2,356t worth $34.7m) and India (1,871t worth $51.8m) all represent critical secondary sources for US importers. Sri Lanka contributed another 926t worth $18.6m.

Check out the charts below for a year-by-year illustration of how much the US depends on other Asian nations for BSC and RSC imports.

US foreign fisheries ban threatens 'death punch' to swimming crab importers - Undercurrent News
US foreign fisheries ban threatens 'death punch' to swimming crab importers - Undercurrent News
US foreign fisheries ban threatens 'death punch' to swimming crab importers - Undercurrent News
US foreign fisheries ban threatens 'death punch' to swimming crab importers - Undercurrent News

But with partial bans hitting Vietnam, the Philippines and Sri Lanka (in addition to 19-20% tariffs on all three countries, as well as Indonesia), and sky-high, 50% tariffs now in place on Indian goods and 55% tariffs on Chinese seafood, US importers have no good alternative options.

Phillips described the swimming crab market across Asia as a "scorched earth."

"If I look at each of the fisheries affected by the (NOAA ban), the only place that I see that we would have the ability to continue production, as-is, will be in Indonesia," he said. "Even if I could funnel product around to other countries -- which we can't do because we just don't have the infrastructure -- it's going to face a tariff anywhere it goes."

US red swimming crabmeat importers face trouble from both major sources

Further exacerbating the industry's problems is an Indonesian regulation implemented in 2023 that requires any company exporting containers with natural resources worth more than $250,000 to place a cash equivalent to 30% of the value of the cargo in an Indonesian bank's escrow account for up to three months. That rule ties up hundreds of thousands of dollars in cash for months for each container of swimming crab exported, as Undercurrent has reported.

As a result of the rule and the sector's long supply chain, it operates at very high debt levels. The coming changes could mean Phillips Foods' cash flow will be reduced by up to 80% to 90%, Brice Phillips said.

Venezuela, the one non-Asian supplier of swimming crab to the US, sent it 2,615t worth $56.6m in 2024. The blue crab species landed there is the same species as that fished in the Gulf of Mexico and along the US East Coast, including in the Chesapeake Bay. It is primarily shipped fresh from Venezuela to the US city of Miami, Florida, where it receives high-pressure pasteurization. 

Paige Tilghman, the executive vice president of Doral, Florida-based Twin Tails Seafood, a major importer of Venezuelan crab, said he was still working to determine the impact of the NOAA decision and how it will impact his company.

Below is a chart showing the annual fluctuation of Venezuelan blue crab imports received by the US.

US foreign fisheries ban threatens 'death punch' to swimming crab importers - Undercurrent News
Impact on local communities, sustainability

While the NOAA decision could prove to be highly damaging to US importers, it will be an unmitigated disaster for local fishing communities in Indonesia and elsewhere in Asia, Phillips said.

Each of Phillips Foods' Asian plants employs 500 to 1,300 people, many of whom may lose their jobs.

"The human element of this is just heartbreaking," Phillips said. "There are human beings picking this crab meat. It's arduous work. And the fishermen, a lot of these guys have been with us for 30 to 40 years, when we first started doing business over there." 

A Phillips Foods plant in Indonesia. Source: Phillips Foods.

Small-scale harvesters, who aren't financed by big banks, catch just 40 lbs at a time, he said. They save for years to afford their boats, and many build their own vessels. 

"The socioeconomic destruction that is going to flow downhill into these rather poor fishing villages has got to be recognized," he said. "We're talking about thousands of people who are going to be affected by this decision. And it's going to happen practically overnight."

Phillips also fears for the demise of the NFI Crab Council's sustainability efforts, which are funded by a $0.03/lb rate paid by its members. 

"[P]eople facing an existential threat are going to be thinking about saving every penny, so I'm worried we might see an exodus from the council, or even its complete dissolution, which would turn the clock back 15 years on all the great work we've been doing," he said.

The Environmental Defense Fund has been building an adaptive management plan for the blue swimming crab fishery in Lampung Province, Indonesia. Photo courtesy of EDF.

On the positive side, less fishing pressure will improve the health of Asian swimming crab populations, which Phillips said are currently being fished at maximum levels. But the NOAA ruling isn't about fishing pressure. Rather, it's about a lack of documented evidence that the fisheries don't threaten marine mammals.

"I just keep coming back to the fact that we haven't had any findings of non-comparability in any of our blue swimming crab production countries, at least in modern history, and now all of a sudden we've got them for four major producing countries," Phillips said. "We've been blessed with a species that's purpose-built to handle a lot of fishing effort, but we're doing so much to ensure it stays sustainable. And this (NOAA decision) could blow those efforts right out of the water."

NFI takes action

NFI called an emergency virtual meeting of the crab council on Wednesday (Sept. 3) to discuss NOAA's move. NFI chief strategy officer Gavin Gibbons told Undercurrent his organization is working on a plan of action.

"We've seen the announcement and we're looking more into it," Gibbons said.

Troy Turkin, the CEO of Supreme Crab & Seafood, a prominent US importer of swimming crab and crab council member based in Westin, Florida, said he was hoping to hear that NFI was commencing a lobbying effort in support of the swimming crab sector.

"I'm choosing to remain optimistic. There are just too many moving parts. I'm waiting (to panic) until the facts are clear. Is it possible for crab to be excluded? Can the (impacted) countries negotiate and submit more documentation? Right now, I have no clue," Turkin said. "But this is extremely scary."

Troy Turkin speaking on a trade regulation panel at the 2025 Boston seafood show. Photograph by Jason Huffman.

Asked on Aug. 29 for additional information about whether the countries or fisheries facing US prohibitions have any recourse or whether the bans will definitely come into effect on Jan 1., a NOAA spokesperson said she was not able to comment until Friday, Sept. 5 at the earliest.

Representatives of other crab council members did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

title: Untitled
content:
European farmed shrimp importers are not as relaxed as Indian exporters about the September 2026 deadline for India to meet the European Commission (EC) requirements for its new EU regulation regarding the use of antibiotics.

India is still absent from the approved country list, which could mean "buyers may start adjusting purchase strategy from early 2026 already," said Willem van der Pijl, managing director and co-founder of the Global Shrimp Forum (GSF), held Sept. 2-4 in Utrecht, the Netherlands, during the export and import session at the event.

Looking at EU import data for the first half of 2025, India is the second largest shrimp source for the bloc, with imports under the three main customs codes for frozen and processed shrimp at 42,803 metric tons, up 8% year-on-year.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view

As in the US market, India is under pressure from Ecuador. The EU imported 115,674t from Ecuador in the first half, up 19% y-o-y.

 On Thursday, Sept. 4, a closed-door meeting took place on the sidelines of the forum to discuss the issue, organized by GSF and the Dutch Fish Federation, with representatives from the Indian embassy in Brussels, Indian exporters and processors and the European association AIPCE-CEP.  

A slide on the outlook for India from Willem van der Pijl's Global Shrimp Forum (GSF) presentation. Credit: GSF

The meeting was focused on "getting a clear picture of the current state of affairs and discussing it with the EU industry, to decide what we could do to increase pressure and where that effort should be concentrated," one European source present at the meeting told Undercurrent.

Letters will then be sent to both the EC and the Indian government to communicate the need to resolve the issue speedily, sources familiar with the meeting told Undercurrent.

According to sources, the Indians have given all the required documents in mid-August and are awaiting a response.

"The ball seems to be in the court of the EU," the first source told Undercurrent.

For India, the main challenge is giving the EC a level of comfort that enforcement will take place once the list of prohibited antibiotics and other substances has been locked in.

"I think the main challenge is that there are two parts [to the regulation]. First, you forbid the substance. The second is how do you enforce that it's actually not used? The first one is easy, the second one is less easy, especially in a country like India which is so big," said van der Pijl in a panel discussion at GSF.

Indonesia, another major global farmed shrimp supplier which is looking to grow its EU sales, is also not on the list. Sri Lanka and Nigeria were also omitted, said van der Pijl on the panel.  

"I think Indonesia did well in terms of the speed at which they managed to deliver the documentation that the commission wanted," when the issue came to prominence a few months ago, he said.

As for India, there was more of a delay; but geopolitics means there's a renewed sense of urgency.

The situation comes after Donald Trump's US government slapped 50% extra tariffs on India (see rates below) in its main market.

A rundown of the US tariffs, from the Global Shrimp Forum (GSF). Credit: GSF

Unlike Ecuador, Indonesia, and Vietnam, India does not have a free trade agreement (FTA) with the EU. The latest round of negotiations will take place next week (week 37, Sept. 8-14).

"There is increased importance for India to maintain competitiveness in the EU market," said van der Pijl in light of the Trump tariffs.

"I saw Willem's slide on India not being on the list," said G. Pawan Kumar, president of trade body the Seafood Exporters Association of India and owner of supplier Sprint Exports, on the panel.

"India's Export Inspection Council has to give a guarantee. The paperwork is in process. It should happen in the next couple of weeks. We don't have to go beyond September 2025. We still have one year until the deadline," he said.

India's YTD total shrimp export growth to major markets. Europe has been its fastest-growing sales market this year, with exports up 21% in H1. Credit: GSF

MPEDA shrimp exec says India will comply with new EU antibiotic rules, repeats call for lower sampling rate

The good news is that "there is a serious negotiation between the EU and India," said Kumar regarding the FTA.

"The trade deal is on the way. Hopefully, it'll be signed in October; that is what we gather from the Indian government," he said.

Van der Pijl was somewhat less bullish.

"I'm a cultural anthropologist, and there is a big cultural problem in the perception of situations between European and Indian authorities, I would say. And that means I am still not 100% convinced this will all play out," said van der Pijl.

An Indian executive, who asked not to be quoted by name, was blunter.

"The Indian mentality is such that, if the deadline is September, we will start working on it in August," he told Undercurrent on the sidelines of the conference.

"There's a lot of need for open conversation between those authorities to make sure that it does [get rectified]," said van der Pijl. This was the purpose of the meeting, which van der Pijl mentioned during the presentation.

Indonesia adopts GDST standard for seafood data platform, hopes move will appease EU

The new regulation supersedes a previous one in which India was included.

"So, we had a regulation on [antibiotic] residue monitoring plans that every country needs to have in place and regulates how you, as an authority, deal with the use of antibiotics in agriculture," said van der Pijl.

"Then, there is a new regulation, regulating which antibiotics cannot be used in all edible protein products. This new regulation has a new country list which overrules the previous one," he said.

"The EU wants a list of antibiotics or growth stimulators, which are used to farm shrimp or any animal, which should not be there. When we talk about India, there are about 37 items listed. I think that has been sorted out for most of them," said Kumar.

title: Fallout from BMS red listing in US, Trump tariffs will hit Indonesia shrimp exports in H2
content:
UTRECHT, the Netherlands -- Indonesian shrimp exports will slow in the second half of the year, due to the fallout in its main US market from tariffs and the shock red listing of major supplier Bahari Makmur Sejati (BMS) over concerns about radioactive isotope contamination.

While the 2025 outlook may have signaled a recovery to around 230,000 metric tons in Indonesian exports, tariffs and the BMS situation will slow growth in H2, said Willem van der Pijl, co-founder and managing director of the Global Shrimp Forum (GSF), during the GSF export and import session, held Wednesday (Sept. 4). 

Van der Pijl is forecasting a 9% increase in 2025 to 219,848t. However, Aris Utama, head of sales and marketing at Bumi Menara Internusa (BMI), another large Indonesian exporter, is slightly more bearish.

A forecast for 2025 Indonesian shrimp exports given at the Global Shrimp Forum (GSF). Credit: GSF

The increase seen in the first half was driven by US importers bringing in as much as they can before the tariffs hit, so it will not continue in the second half, said BMI's Utama on the export and import panel. The US is responsible for close to 75% of Indonesia's shrimp exports, as you can see below. 

A summary of Indonesian shrimp exports by market given at the Global Shrimp Forum (GSF). Credit: GSF

"Everyone is aware of all the issues for Indonesia. I would like to be somewhat optimistic, but I'd probably take around 210,000t. That would be my rough guess. There's also a lot of disease issues on farms, which are hitting production," he said.

Indonesia breathed a sigh of relief to get a 19% additional tariff on its good entering the US, down from a threatened 32%, with the Southeast Asian country also committing to significant purchases of US commercial aircraft, energy, and agricultural products in exchange.

Indonesia also has an additional 3.90% of anti-dumping duties, taking the total to 22.90%, as you can see below.

A rundown of the US tariffs, from the Global Shrimp Forum (GSF). Credit: GSF

Then, on Aug. 14, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) made the unprecedented move of putting Indonesian processor BMS on its red list over concerns about contamination from the radioactive isotope Cesium-137 (Cs-137). This blocks imports from the company, the largest Indonesian seller to the US. 

No products have tested positive for Cs-137 in the US market at this time, and no illnesses have been reported to date, according to FDA. But shrimp in Walmart and others supplied from various processors has been recalled as a result.

While this only applies to shrimp from BMS, "the perception that this is a countrywide alert is still not dismissed yet at this stage," said Utama of the market impact.

A multi-government agency effort is underway in Indonesia to get to the root of the possible cause of the contamination.

"Indonesia is not a nuclear country; we do not have nuclear power plant anywhere; we're not developing any of the kind of nuclear technology. So, it's very strange to see this happen," said Utama.

As a result, he's not worried about the impact on BMI. "We have no worry whatsoever. Because we have never had anything like this in our farms or facilities."

Indonesia seeks further export diversification

Although Indonesia got a reprieve on the US tariff level compared to what it could have been, the country is still seeking to boost exports to Asia and Europe and reduce its dependence on the US, which currently takes close to 75% of its shrimp.

"We would definitely like to export to more markets outside of the US, like Europe," said Utama.

Data presented by van der Pijl showed Indonesia's exports are growing to other markets, albeit from low bases. For the EU, Indonesia is working toward meeting the EU's requirements on demonstrating no antibiotics are used in shrimp farming.

Credit: Global Shrimp Forum

Indonesia is not currently on the EU's list of countries that have provided "sufficient evidence and guarantees" regarding antibiotic prevention in seafood exports. 

If Indonesia is unable to convince EU authorities that adequate oversight and enforcement measures are being taken, companies in the country will be unable to export shrimp to the EU after the deadline of Sept. 3, 2026, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

According to van der Pijl, Indonesia's government has been fast to deliver documents to the European Commission in order to hopefully get on the list.

"Indonesia did well to deliver the documents to the EU they wanted," he said.

Meeting requirements of US deal is 'dicey proposition'

Looking back at Indonesia's preliminary agreement with the US to get the reduction to a 19% additional tariff, Utama said it's not going to be easy to meet the requirements. 

The text of a preliminary agreement includes Indonesia's commitment to purchase $15 billion worth of liquified petroleum gas, crude and gasoline from US exporters.

"The current rate for the past few years has been about $3bn. So it's five times more," he said. 

Then, it stipulates the building of oil refineries in the US "when Indonesia doesn't have enough in our country," said Utama. 

"If you look at the proposal from the US, it's a pretty dicey proposition. I'm not saying what our government is capable or incapable of doing, but it's quite a stretch to fulfill that," he said. "But I'm pretty sure the government would consider doing everything possible to secure and maintain trade with the US."

title: Daily recap: Scotland to enforce new MPAs; China’s wholesale salmon prices surge
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Monday, Sept. 1:

Scotland to enforce new protected sea areas from Oct. 16

The Scottish government has announced that new fisheries management measures for marine protected areas within offshore waters between 12 and 200 nautical miles from the coast will come into effect from Oct. 16, 2025.

China's wholesale salmon prices see early September boost

Salmon wholesale prices in China's first-tier cities have surged sharply for week 36 (Sept. 1-7), driven by reduced supply from Norway, market sources told Undercurrent News.

Trade talks to continue despite high court ruling against seafood industry-injuring tariffs, USTR assures

The US president Donald Trump administration is still working to negotiate trade deals in spite of a ruling by an appeals court that found many of its seafood industry-crippling tariffs are illegal, US trade representative Jamieson Greer said Sunday (Aug. 31).

Trade insights: India shrimp exports rise 22% to $2.6bn in H1 before US tariffs hit

India's shrimp exports rose 22% to $2.63 billion in the first half of 2025, trade data showed, with strong US demand preceding steep tariffs implemented on Aug. 27 that are expected to radically shift trade flows.

Canada's plan for British Columbia salmon farming in 'final stages'

The final version of a plan to guide the future of salmon farming in the Canadian province of British Columbia will be released very soon, fisheries minister Joanne Thompson told reporters Friday (Aug. 29).

Icelandic whitefish prices pick up at high levels as new season kicks off

Prices on Iceland's domestic whitefish auction have picked up in week 35 (Aug. 25-31) meaning that cod and haddock markets begin the new fishing season on Sept. 1 at a level well above each of the past two years, according to price and supply data shared with Undercurrent.

US extends Section 301 tariff exclusions on China to Nov. 29, including key seafood items

The Office of the US Trade Representative last week extended Section 301 tariff exclusions for another 90 days, moving their expiration from Aug. 31 to Nov. 29, according to a Federal Register notice issued Aug. 28. The action covered 178 exclusions, of which 10 are seafood products.

title: Scotland to enforce new protected sea areas from Oct. 16
content:
The Scottish government has announced that new fisheries management measures for marine protected areas (MPAs) within offshore waters between 12 and 200 nautical miles from the coast will come into effect from Oct. 16, 2025.

Specifics on the plan will be made available at 5.00 pm on Sept. 1, here. 

But the government said that site-specific measures being introduced include restrictions on certain fishing activities that could damage these habitats and species, such as bottom-towed gear.

"These measures have been developed through collaboration with industry, scientists, environmental organisations and communities and are based on the best available evidence – they will help protect biodiversity, support sustainable fishing, and build resilience to climate change," said the government.

Scotland's cabinet secretary for climate action, Gillian Martin, added that "Scotland's seas are an integral part of our national identity, and this is a major milestone in protecting our marine environment."

"It's important, now, more than ever, that we address the twin crises of biodiversity loss and climate change and these new measures will help to support and enable marine ecosystems to flourish and build climate resilience."

With these new protections in place, Scotland's marine environment will be better equipped to support thriving marine industries, protect food security and secure the ecosystem services that the country relies on, she said.

The Joint Nature Conservation Committee (JNCC) marine species team leader Declan Tobin said: "This is a landmark moment for MPA protection, following fifteen years of collaboration. JNCC is proud to have supported Scottish government in developing these measures, turning science into action for a brighter and more sustainable future for our seas."

The Scottish government's response to the consultation and fisheries assessments will also be available on the website from 5 pm, Sept. 1. Corresponding impact assessments are available at the same link from tomorrow.

Meanwhile, the UK government -- through the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs and the Marine Management Organisation -- launched a 12-week online consultation on June 9 proposing new byelaws to prohibit bottom-trawling and, in some cases, static gears (like traps and nets) in an additional 30,000 square kilometers of English waters.

This would expand total bottom-trawling restrictions to about 48,000 square kilometers, according to the National Federation of Fishermen's Organisations (NFFO).

The proposed byelaws are tailored to each MPA's specific habitat sensitivities (e.g., sandbanks, gravel beds, muds) and species protection needs.

Approximately 1,303 UK fishing vessels are expected to be directly impacted by these gear restrictions; the eight ports facing the highest estimated revenue losses are spread across different counties, with around 50% of the total losses concentrated in the South West of England, said the NFFO.

title: Newfoundland salmon producers stunned by timing of new aquaculture requirements
content:
Atlantic salmon farmers in Newfoundland and Labrador say they were blindsided to learn last week that sweeping new aquaculture regulations issued by the Canadian province have been in force since Aug. 7, despite having been consulted on the policy groundwork.

"Industry participants were aware that new aquaculture regulations were soon to be released as they had been consulted on the policies and new legislation; however, when informed on Aug. 20 that they were in effect since Aug. 7, they were surprised," Keith Sullivan, executive director of the Newfoundland Aquaculture Industry Association (NAIA), told Undercurrent News on Thursday (Aug. 28).

Grieg Seafood Newfoundland also said it only became aware of the rules nearly two weeks after they were in effect. The company has asked to meet with provincial government officials to clarify the new requirements and enforcement processes.

"Grieg Seafood Newfoundland takes its responsibilities and accountabilities very seriously. After careful review, we are confident that we have remained in compliance under the new regulations," said Gaitane Villeneuve, the company's communications director, in an email.

Mowi Canada East and Cooke Aquaculture declined to comment.

Below is a summary of the new requirements.

Transparency requirements raise concerns

The new regulations, enacted under the authority of NL's Aquaculture Act, passed in 2023, impose sweeping changes on salmon farmers.  

The most notable is a requirement to disclose to the public within 24 hours information on escapes, confirmed diseases, quarantine or depopulation orders, mass mortality events, and monthly sea lice counts. NL's Department of Fisheries, Forestry and Agriculture must approve reports before they are posted on company websites or released through an industry association.

Members of the Canadian salmon farming community, who spoke to Undercurrent anonymously, said this could create practical challenges for farmers in managing crises.

"The 24 hours [reporting requirement] can cause some issues for farmers as they struggle to prepare plans to deal with the situation, and the media is already on top of them. The notice period should be longer to give the farmer time to properly assess the situation and plan to execute a good solution," one salmon farming executive said.

A salmon farming veteran noted that in British Columbia, similar information is reported to government regulators, which then decide what to publish.

Mowi sea site in Newfoundland. Photo: Mowi

"There have been attempts to create transparent, live reporting portals in Canada, but these have faced technical and regulatory challenges," the person said, adding that Norway's model of real-time public reporting is often cited internationally.

Stocking rules formalize existing practices

Together with the transparency provisions, the new rules also formalize how farms are stocked and fallowed.

They restrict farms to a single species and a single year-class of fish per site, with mandatory fallowing between production cycles -- a practice that industry sources note is already widely used in salmon farming.

"The rule requiring each site to stock only one species and one year class at a time is a good biosecurity practice already followed by salmon farmers in British Columbia, even before it was mandated," one industry source said. "It helps break disease cycles and is standard in responsible farming."

Another observer echoed that fallowing sites between cycles is standard in most salmon-farming regions globally and described it as "neither new nor surprising."

The regulations do not specify how long sites must be kept fallow; instead leaving the decision to the fisheries minister or chief veterinarian. Industry sources said this could be problematic.

Photo: Grieg Seafood NL

"If the decision on fallow periods is left to a government official, it could create real problems for farmers; if there's a delay, fish can't be moved from the hatchery on time, leading to overcrowding and stress. In aquaculture. Timing is everything," said one.

What's next

NAIA has begun follow-up discussions with provincial officials to gain clarity on the new requirements, Sullivan said.

"NAIA has since had initial discussions with provincial government officials and has commitments for detailed follow-up to ensure as much clarity as possible around the regulations," he said.

Producers continue to emphasize responsible practices, pointing to waste recycling initiatives, shoreline cleanups, and the sector's record-high value in 2024 as indicators of its broader role in the province, he stressed.

Grieg said it appreciates the government's efforts to update regulations to address priorities like fish health, welfare, environmental protection and transparency. It also noted that regulators had been managing "multiple emergency situations" this summer, including an unprecedented wildfire season, which may have contributed to communication gaps.

Undercurrent has requested comment from DFFA but has yet to hear back.

title: China aligns with UN treaty to enforce stricter fishing vessel inspections
content:
China has issued new guidelines to strengthen port inspections and combat illegal fishing, following its recent accession to the UN's Agreement on Port State Measures, reports China Daily. 

The directive, released by China's Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs along with five other agencies, mandates tighter controls on foreign fishing vessels entering Chinese ports.

Measures include stricter "entry reviews," expanded reporting requirements, and denial of access to vessels linked to illegal activities.

The policy underscores a "zero tolerance" stance on illegal fishing and promotes sustainable use of marine resources. It also calls for improved coordination, standardized port services, and enhanced international cooperation in fisheries enforcement.

title: US senators ask Trump administration to sanction Chinese seafood, repeating request made to Biden
content:
Two US lawmakers are urging US secretary of commerce Howard Lutnick to impose "the toughest possible sanctions on seafood from Communist China" in response to human rights abuses on the high seas.

It's a repeat of requests made by other members of Congress nearly two years ago.

Republican senators Rick Scott, from Florida, and Katie Britt, from Alabama, sent a letter to Lutnick last week highlighting the ongoing -- and they say "escalating" -- illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing. 

"The United States must no longer tolerate the exploitation of our markets by regimes that flagrantly violate human rights, ravage our oceans, and destroy American jobs," Scott and Britt wrote to Lutnick on Aug. 21.

They are calling for Lutnick to use the High Seas Driftnet Fishing Moratorium Protection Act, which empowers the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to prohibit the importation of certain fisheries products in the case of IUU fishing.

The three-page letter accuses China's fishing fleet of depleting fish stocks and destroying habitats, all while engaging in human rights abuses, including forced and child labor. 

"In the United States, nearly 11% of all seafood imports -- worth an estimated $2.4 billion in 2019 -- stem from IUU fishing," the letter continues. "This illegal trade steals tens of thousands of American jobs and deprives our economy of over $1 billion in potential revenue each year."

In addition to the full enforcement of the high seas driftnet law, the senators are also calling for "a total ban on seafood imports from nations that engage in or support these abuses."

The requests made of the Trump administration by members of Congress are similar to those made of former president Joe Biden in late 2023 following the investigative series written by the Outlaw Ocean Project, a group led by Ian Urbina, a former 17-year reporter for the New York Times and the winner of a Pulitzer Prize.

Published in The New Yorker on Oct. 9, the series provided haunting details about crew members being held captive, beaten and suffering from malnutrition aboard vessels in China's distant water fishing fleet.

The series also provided a thorough accounting of the Chinese program used to enlist and transport many Uyghurs over 1,000 miles from Xinjiang, in the land-locked, northwestern part of China, to seafood processing plants in Shangdong, on the east coast.

US Senate bill would ban Chinese seafood within year of passage

The Ban China's Forbidden Operations in the Oceanic Domain (C-FOOD) Act, S. 3417, introduced in the US Senate in December 2023, was the most extreme response from lawmakers to an investigative series showing Chinese harvesters and processing companies using forced labor.

The bill, from senator Tom Cotton, an Arkansas Republican, would -- within a year of enactment -- ban all Chinese seafood, including both wild-caught and aquaculture products, from entering the US until Congress gets reports from the US secretary of state that neither China's fleets nor its aquaculture industry are "meaningfully using forced labor"; the commerce secretary "that the Chinese government is not subsidizing its fishing fleets beyond international norms"; and the defense secretary that "the Chinese fishing fleet would not be used in an invasion of Taiwan."

The legislation, which was co-sponsored by Scott and fellow Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith, from Mississippi, was not able to advance beyond the Senate Finance Committee, however.

title: Untitled
content:
California authorities have revoked the commercial licenses and permits of two commercial harvesters for regulatory violations in the US state's Dungeness crab and lobster fisheries, officials announced Wednesday (Aug. 27).

The revocations were made official at the June 2025 meeting of the California Fish and Game Commission.

The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) said 68-year-old Christopher James Miller had committed numerous violations over the past decade, including abandoning 156 lobster traps around Santa Barbara and the Northern Channel Islands, leaving gear in the water after the season closure, failing to retrieve baited traps and filing inaccurate catch records.

A voluminous record of citations and warnings stemming back to the 2010-2011 spiny lobster season indicates that Miller, who lives aboard his boat Dolly Dagger in the port of Santa Barbara, has "possible psychiatric and mental health issues, as well as substance abuse issues," and was often confused about the gear he'd set for lobster and crab, according to written reports by investigating wardens.

California warns Dungeness crab harvesters: Don’t cheat

"Respondent has not demonstrated he can be trusted to operate as a lobster fisherman in compliance with applicable laws and regulations," wrote Erlinda Shrenger, an administrative law judge who oversaw complaints against the veteran fisherman earlier this year.

In the Dungeness crab fishery, 45-year-old Ronald Ghera of the Gerry B., based out of Fortuna, California, repeatedly abandoned crab traps in 2023 and 2024, according to CDFW.

"Ghera abandoned around 100 Dungeness crab traps in the Pacific Ocean two seasons in a row, necessitating the removal of the traps," CDFW Law Enforcement Division chief Nathaniel Arnold wrote in a briefing to the California Fish and Game Commission. "Not only did Mr. Ghera put migrating wildlife at risk of entanglements, he also put the Dungeness fishery at risk by abandoning his traps." 

State fishery wardens had contacted Ghera "numerous times, only to have him ignore their requests" to remedy the violations, Arnold wrote.

The majority of California commercial harvesters are law-abiding and follow the rules, Arnold said in a media release.

"There are a few individuals, however, who choose to partake in commercial poaching," Arnold wrote in a statement. "These individuals will eventually be caught and will likely lose the privilege to commercially fish in this state through either criminal or administrative actions."

title: Profits slip for Chile’s Camanchaca fishing division in Q2 as global fish oil prices halve
content:
Chilean company Camanchaca saw profits from its fishing division fall in the second quarter of 2025, as higher landings were not enough to counter sharp declines in international fish oil and fishmeal prices.

The unit generated earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) of $23 million in Q2, down 29% from the $32.4m seen a year earlier, while revenues slid 9% to $97.7m.

Camanchaca’s Q2 revenue drops 26% as sales slow, profit slightly slips

Net income from fishing dropped to $10.9m, compared with $17.4m in Q2 2024, Camanchaca said in its quarterly results.

Volumes, however, were strong: Pelagic catches rose 33% year-on-year to almost 110,000 metric tons, including 68,000t in the south and 42,000t in the north.

The increase was driven by larger jack mackerel and mackerel landings, as well as a surge in purchases from artisanal fleets, which more than doubled compared to the same period last year.

But prices told a different story.

Fish oil averaged $2,119 per metric ton in the quarter, down 53% from Q2 2024, following Peru’s recovery in its key anchovy fishery. Fishmeal prices also weakened, down 18% to $1,536/t, while frozen jack mackerel slipped 8% to $833/t.

For the first half of 2025, fishing revenues were steady at $180m as larger catches offset price weakness. Total pelagic landings jumped 42% year-on-year to 283,000t.

Additionally, fishmeal output rose 53% to over 41,000t and fish oil production more than doubled to nearly 10,000t. Frozen jack mackerel output reached 76,400t, up 3%, while canned jack mackerel production grew 3% to 752,000 cases.

Even so, EBITDA for the segment fell 12% in H1 to $44.5m, representing 55% of group earnings. The company attributed the decline to the accumulation of inventories at lower prices rather than weaker operations.

Fish oil inventories at the end of June stood at 8,900t, versus 2,600t a year earlier, while canned jack mackerel inventories climbed to 590,000 cases from 453,000.

Camanchaca emphasized that the fundamentals of its fisheries remain sound.“The recovery of stocks such as jack mackerel and shrimp reflects a decade of stricter fisheries law enforcement,” the company noted in its report.

Looking ahead, Camanchaca expects sales from existing inventories to boost second-half results, though market conditions remain volatile.

The company said it is also facing “regulatory threats from the government, which appear to be seeking to hinder growth and efficiency,” but maintained that its 2026 outlook is more favorable both in terms of volumes and pricing.

title: Forensics device to help in US seafood fraud fight as part of Trump agenda
content:
Do we see a new seafood "Law & Order" spinoff in the future?

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) said this week that agents with its Office of Law Enforcement (OLE) have completed their second deployment of a forensics device capable of identifying falsely labeled seafood.

The operation is in line with US president Donald Trump's Executive Order (14276) for "Restoring American Seafood Competitiveness," issued in April, as reported by Undercurrent News. A 45-day public comment period closes on Oct. 14.

Pilot testing of the rapid polymerase chain reaction (PCR) device first began at the Port of Newark in the US state of New Jersey in November 2024, NOAA said in a statement. However, last month, NOAA Fisheries -- more properly known as the National Marine Fisheries Service -- brought the device to the US state of California, where officers conducted a week-long enforcement operation at the Port of Long Beach and the Los Angeles International Airport.

Eight imports of fresh and frozen shark and tuna meat were inspected as part of the pilot and training operation, which ultimately revealed the mislabeling of imported bigeye, yellow fin, blue fin, albacore, and other tuna species. 

"The new device is proving to be a valuable tool that helps officers examine more shipments in less time, with rapid results that also help clear the way for legal seafood to reach the market counter," said Bryan Landry, OLE's assistant special agent in charge. 

"These devices assist us in protecting US consumers from seafood fraud and to combat illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing, which remains a high priority for NOAA Fisheries," added OLE director James Binniker.

title: Mystery clouds discovery of pilotless fishing vessel off US West Coast
content:
US authorities are baffled over the apparent disappearance of a veteran Pacific Northwest fisherman whose pilotless vessel was discovered after steaming south for several days on a steady course off the West Coast.

Fishing gear was set up on the deck of the trolling vessel. A half-finished cup of coffee was found sitting at the helm, and the skipper's oatmeal was left unfinished, as if fisherman Joel Kawahara suddenly disappeared in the middle of his meal, a longtime friend who had been housesitting for him in Quilcene, Washington, told the Los Angeles Times.

His friend Heather Burns told the newspaper that Kawahara's life jacket was found still hanging in the boat.

The 39-foot Karolee was intercepted by the crew of a US Coast Guard cutter on Aug. 13 and towed into Humboldt Bay, California, the Lost Coast Outpost reported. Maritime tracking showed that the troller had remained on a steady course of four knots for days, but didn't stop to set gear in the fishing grounds. 

Attempts by Coast Guard watchstanders to hail the Karolee before boarding went unanswered, authorities said.

Joel Kawahara, seen in this undated photo, went missing on or around Aug. 8, 2025 off the coast of Oregon or Washington. His fishing vessel, Karolee, was discovered several days later with no trace of Kawahara on board. (Photo courtesy of Ever Loved memorial site)

On Aug. 12, a Coast Guard C-27 fixed-wing aircrew from Air Station Sacramento in California responded to the vessel's position and unsuccessfully attempted to make contact.

The aircrew visually noticed the vessel was rigged for fishing, its lights were energized and a life raft was observed in its cradle. Yet there was no trace of the 70-year-old skipper, who had been fishing commercially alone.

"It's a strange case," Coast Guard petty officer Steven Strohmaier told the LA Times. "There were no signs of distress, no signs of debris."

Coast Guard crews searched for over 18 hours, scouring an area of 2,100 square miles, including over 430 miles of trackline, but found no sign of the veteran salmon, tuna and halibut fisherman, who has long been active in the West Coast and Alaska fishing communities.

Kawahara was a board member of Save Our Wild Salmon Coalition, president of the Coastal Trollers Association and member of the Pacific Fishery Management Council, the LA Times reported.

"He was one of the smartest people I ever met," Jeremy Brown, a fellow fisherman who knew Kawahara for 35 years, told the newspaper. "He's just incredibly open, lively and intellectually curious."

Coast Guard officials said the agency was not investigating how Kawahara went missing, and there has been no indication any other law enforcement agency is looking into the incident.

FREE READ US fishing vessel sinks, one missing as Oregon Dungy season comes to close

The only clues as to what may have happened, Burns told the LA Times, are the last few messages Kawahara sent to friends the morning of Aug. 8, remarking on whales passing close to his vessel.

In a text message early that morning, he reported watching a group of murres (black and white sea birds) fishing near him.

"All of a sudden this whale comes up and boils the water less than 50 yards ahead of me," Kawahara texted Burns just before 7:30 a.m. "I slowed down and turned but boy it was kind of close. The good news is lots to eat for whale and birds."

Half an hour later, he texted another person he knew to be fishing in the same region, his last known contact with the outside world.

With no additional reports of distress or responses to callouts, the Coast Guard suspended its search for Kawahara on Aug. 13 and impounded the vessel in Eureka, California.

"Suspending a search for someone is the toughest decision we make in the Coast Guard," commander Chelsey Stroud, search and rescue mission coordinator for the Coast Guard's Northwest District, said in a statement. "We send our deepest condolences to the family, friends, and loved ones of the missing man."

A memorial service is being planned, according to a web page set up to honor his legacy and memory.

title: Cooke decries Chilean gov’t order to close two salmon farms, add $1.4m environmental fine
content:
Chile's Superintendency of the Environment (Superintendencia del Medio Ambiente, or SMA) has added a $1.4 million fine to its earlier decision to close two salmon farms in the Aysen region after finding that the Canadian seafood giant broke several environmental laws.  

SMA said, in an announcement published Friday (Aug. 22), that it found Cooke committed a combined eight environmental violations at its Punta Garrao, Huillines 2 and Huillines 3 farm site sites. The last two, located in Laguna San Rafael National Park, have been shut down.

The environmental regulator ruled Cooke exceeded the maximum authorized production at Punta Garrao, where the company produced 3,068.9 metric tons of salmon between September 2017 and February 2019, 22.72% above the legal limit.

SMA ruled Cooke installed farming-related structures outside of the concession area and did not have contingency plans in place for oil spills or protection of an endangered local otter species.

SMA found that Cooke had modified its Huillines 2 and Huillines 3 sites without undergoing environmental assessment and increased production at both farms without obtaining the required environmental permitting. It ruled Cooke had built structures outside its concessions and found aquaculture industry waste on the coastline adjacent to the farms.

As the next step in the regulatory process, SMA's sanctions will be reviewed by Chile's Third Environmental Tribunal, which has already begun deliberating other sanctions previously issued against Cooke, as Undercurrent News has reported.

In statements provided to Undercurrent News, Cooke vice president Joel Richardson said the company was disappointed by the ruling.

"Cooke Chile has been operating for nearly 20 years in Chile with a commitment to sustainability and respect for the environment. We are disappointed by the ruling issued by SMA, which reflects a biased, anti-business stance, and is outside the spirit and letter of current legislation. Clear evidence was presented during the hearing to support the fact that our operations do not harm the environment. The SMA disregarded the expert evidence it itself ordered, which ruled out any environmental harm," he said.

Cooke Chile intends to appeal the decision to the highest court necessary, Richardson added.

The Blacks Harbour, New Brunswick, Canada-headquartered seafood giant, which operates salmon farms across four continents, has been fighting against environmental sanctions related to the Huillines farms for months, after SMA ordered to halt fish stocking at the sites in March and April 2025. 

The company has threatened to pull its business from Chile altogether, arguing the Chilean government is jeopardizing regulatory stability and investor confidence in Chile's aquaculture sector through unfair enforcement of its laws, Undercurrent reported.

The Chilean Salmon Council, which represents major export companies including AquaChile, Mowi, Cermaq and Cooke, has also contested SMA's decision.

title: Untitled
content:
Namibia is moving to transform its fishing industry from a raw fish exporter into a value-added seafood economy, aiming to double local processing and boost exports of higher-value products, Chinese news agency Xinhua reported.

Agriculture, fisheries, water, and land reform minister Inge Zaamwani announced that the government's new national development plan targets increasing locally processed catch from 23% to 45% within five years. The shift could create 15,000 jobs, reduce raw fish exports by 60%, and expand Namibia's presence in international seafood markets.

Fishing quota holders will be subject to mandatory processing requirements and stricter bycatch rules. Bycatch thresholds are set at 2%, while penalty fees will more than triple from 15% to 50%.

The sector's GDP contribution slipped from 4.5% in 2023 to 4.1% in 2024, mainly due to lower allowable catches of hake and horse mackerel. 

Namibia also plans tighter enforcement against illegal fishing, including new monitoring systems and joint naval-police patrols.

title: Peru to resume jumbo flying squid fishery after two-month ban
content:
Peru's ministry of production, Produce, has announced that the fishing season for jumbo flying squid (Dosidicus gigas) will officially resume on Aug. 25, following the end of a ban that began on June 30.

The decision to reopen the fishery was shared during a meeting with artisanal fishermen in the southern port city of Ilo, reports Baird Maritime.

Officials explained that the move is based on findings from a recent scientific and monitoring campaign conducted by the Peruvian marine institute, IMARPE. The campaign assessed the availability and biological conditions of the squid population to ensure its sustainable management.

Jesus Barrientos, vice minister of fisheries and aquaculture, emphasized that the reopening will be carried out "responsibly," with a strong focus on preventing overexploitation.

"Our goal is to avoid any scenario that could threaten the availability of this important resource in 2026," Barrientos said. "All decisions are grounded in scientific evidence and guided by a management model that balances productivity with long-term conservation."

IMARPE's data will inform the final quota for artisanal fishermen in this new season phase.

Produce also noted that, for the time being, "it is not appropriate to set a differentiated quota for Peru's southern region," as the country continues to build its own scientific case regarding the status of the squid stock.

title: Salmon fraud more rampant than study reveals, US state officials say
content:
Salmon lovers are getting duped more often than a recent study suggests, warn officials in the US state of Washington's Department of Fish and Wildlife Police 

They say the problem goes well beyond the findings of a Seattle Pacific University (SPU) study, with some restaurants knowingly selling cheaper farmed Atlantic salmon as premium wild-caught chinook, reported The Seattle Times on Thursday (Aug. 14) 

The state fisheries officers believe the study's numbers are "far too low" compared to what they see in the field, according to the article.  

While the seafood industry insists the issue is overblown, the enforcement officials caution that salmon fraud is "getting worse" -- especially when the fish is served with sauces or glazes that make it harder to spot the difference.

As Undercurrent News reported in November 2024, the 18-page peer-reviewed study in PLOS One examined 119 samples from sushi restaurants and grocery stores in Seattle, finding that 18% were mislabeled.

Diners may be losing an average of $8.85 per pound when cheaper farmed fish is sold as more expensive wild-caught salmon, with the gap reaching $12.31/lb when farmed Atlantic salmon is served in place of chinook, one of the highest-priced wild species.

Sushi restaurants had a significantly higher mislabeling rate of 23.1% in the study compared to grocery stores' 13.5%, and 100% of substitutions in sushi restaurants financially favored vendors.

The paper's interviews with local sushi chefs, grocery executives and trade groups revealed a mix of vigilance and skepticism about the problem.

Some told the paper they rely on vendor trust and staff training to prevent mislabeling. University of Washington fisheries scientist Ray Hilborn called for blockchain traceability to ensure consumers "get what they are paying for."

Hilborn also recounted spotting fish labeled as wild sockeye salmon at Seattle's Pike Place Market that he believed were clearly farmed. The fishmonger later changed the sign, the paper said.

Fishermen in the US state of Louisiana, eager to get a head start on the 2025 fall inshore shrimp season before its official opener on Monday (Aug. 11), are in hot water with the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries (LDWF).

Tran faces a fine of between $400-$950 and up to 120 days in jail.

Just days before that incident, on Aug. 5, LDWF agents cited two other subjects for commercial fishing violations: Jessie Voisin, 78, and Paul Verdin, 68, both of Grand Caillou, Louisiana. The fishermen allegedly had 306 lbs of shrimp in their possession, which was seized and sold to the highest bidder.

On Aug. 1, agents cited Julienne G. Creppell lll, 56, of Buras, Louisiana, and seized 544 lbs of shrimp in his possession.

Like Tran, the other parties also face fines and jail time.

title: $300m Australis award blasted by former owner’s attorney as ‘incoherent’; appeal coming
content:
Former Australis Seafood owner Isidoro Quiroga will appeal a $298 million arbitration award to Chinese conglomerate Joyvio, with his legal team arguing the tribunal's own findings undermine the damages awarded in the high-stakes salmon industry dispute.

The Santiago Arbitration and Mediation Center ruled Aug. 1 that Quiroga and other former shareholders must pay $217.2 million plus interest for incomplete representations during the 2019 sale of Australis to Joyvio for $920m. However, the tribunal also found no fraud occurred and confirmed that Chilean environmental authorities changed their interpretation of salmon production limits in 2021 -- two years after the transaction closed. 

China’s Joyvio awarded $298m in Chilean salmon farmer Australis acquisition dispute

"The arbitral award confirms this is a 100% commercial and civil dispute," Cristobal Eyzaguirre, Quiroga's attorney, told El Mercurio in his first media interview in 35 years of practice. "The majority vote is completely incoherent. On one hand, it categorically rules out any fraud by the sellers, reaffirms that no information was hidden, recognizes that in 2021 -- two years after the sale -- the SMA [Environmental Superintendency] changed its criteria on overproduction."

The ruling has significant implications for Chile's salmon industry, as it appears to validate long-standing industry claims that regulatory interpretation of production limits shifted after numerous farms had already been operating under previous guidelines. Under the earlier interpretation, farms that stocked the authorized number of fish were compliant, regardless of the tonnage ultimately harvested.

Eyzaguirre said the tribunal found that Australis had always operated under this previous interpretation, which counted fish at stocking rather than final harvest weight. The regulatory shift to counting total biomass harvested only occurred in 2021, according to the tribunal's findings.

The arbitrators awarded damages based on their conclusion that some Australis executives had "suspicions" that regulatory interpretation might change in the future, and that these suspicions should have been disclosed to buyers. This reasoning has raised concerns among Chilean M&A practitioners about setting precedents for disclosure obligations in future transactions.

"It would be absurd to think that after a complete analysis of the company, Joyvio did not know the production limits of the salmon industry," the tribunal stated, according to defense documents.

The case centers on allegations that Quiroga concealed information about overproduction at Australis farms during due diligence. Joyvio originally sought nearly $2 billion in damages and termination of the purchase agreement, but the tribunal rejected the contract termination request and awarded approximately 15% of the amount sought.

Quiroga's team plans to file for annulment with Chile's Court of Appeals, arguing the arbitrators exceeded their mandate by creating a novel "price adjustment" remedy not requested by Joyvio and by ignoring contractual provisions that capped damages at 5% of the purchase price and excluded liability for post-sale regulatory changes.

The dispute has roiled Chile's salmon sector since 2023, with parallel criminal proceedings ongoing against Quiroga for alleged fraud and mismanagement, charges his defense says should now be dropped given the tribunal's findings.

Joyvio has stated it will pursue enforcement of the award in multiple jurisdictions where Quiroga holds assets.

The US farmed whitefish market entered week 32 of 2025 (Aug. 4-10) in a holding pattern, with only minor price adjustments across the main traded species. Tilapia and pangasius both saw limited movement at the wholesale level, but origin conditions tell a different story, marked by farm-gate pricing shifts, persistent oversupply and mounting trade headwinds.

US wholesale prices for frozen Chinese tilapia fillets were steady in most sizes, with only larger 7-9 ounce fillets easing by $0.05/lb. The adjustment extends the mild downward pressure seen in recent weeks, even as weaker farm-gate prices in China show the first signs of recovery since late May.

In Guangdong, Guangxi and Hainan, farmers have been under pressure from peak seasonal harvests, rising regulatory costs and prolonged below-breakeven returns. Now, with the harvest season winding down, large processors have begun raising purchasing prices, helping to establish a floor for raw material values.

Farmers remain reluctant to sell at a loss, and raw fish availability is starting to tighten as supply in ponds diminishes.

Despite firmer origin prices, the US market remains quiet. Importers continue to work through elevated inventories, with retail demand subdued and no immediate supply shortage expected. Chinese processors have been leaning on DDP deals and incentive pricing to maintain export momentum.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
US wholesale: Pangasius tops tilapia as imports shift in 2025 - Undercurrent News

US imports of frozen tilapia fillets fell sharply in Q2 2025, marking one of the lowest quarterly volumes in more than a decade, according to the latest data available on Undercurrent's trade portal.

Despite some monthly spikes earlier in 2025, year-to-date figures suggest the sector is on track for the lowest annual total since at least 2012. The data reinforces the long-term contraction in the category, with current volumes now a fraction of the peak levels seen between 2012 and 2015.

Pangasius exporters front-load shipments ahead of tariffs

Vietnamese pangasius pricing in the US also held steady in week 32, but, like for tilapia, origin markets are showing signs of early recovery after months of downwards pressure. Farm-gate prices for most sizes are beginning to tick higher, particularly for 800-1,000 gram and 1000-1,200g fish, after bottoming out in late July. Only the largest size category (1,200g+) edged slightly lower last week.

Prices had been sliding for months, with larger fish, typically sold into China, underperforming as Chinese demand softened. Meanwhile, domestic procurement slowed as processors leaned on in-house farming. But with pond supply thinning and pressure on farmers building, a modest rebound is emerging.

Vietnam's top pangasius exporter, Vinh Hoan Corp, also posted strong Q2 results, reflecting margin improvements and operational efficiency. While net revenue was flat at VND 3.2 trillion ($121.6 million), gross profit rose 33%, and after-tax profit surged 53% to VND 522.5 billion, the company's highest quarterly result since Q2 2022.

Vinh Hoan's scale and performance underscore its importance in the global seafood industry; it currently ranks #112 on Undercurrent News' Seafood Titans 150, an annual report profiling the sector's largest seafood companies worldwide.

Still, questions linger about demand in H2 2025. Much of Vietnam's first-half export strength was tied to front-loading shipments to the US ahead of new tariff enforcement. With that window closed, it remains to be seen whether export momentum can hold.

US pangasius imports surged in June 2025, reaching their highest monthly volume since June 2022. The spike underscores Vietnam's front-loaded export strategy, with many suppliers rushing shipments ahead of increased US tariff enforcement.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
US wholesale: Pangasius tops tilapia as imports shift in 2025 - Undercurrent News

The recent reduction of US tariffs on Vietnamese pangasius, from the original 46% to 20%, has eased some cost pressure, but buyers remain cautious, working through inventory built ahead of the tariff update. Short-term demand in the US is muted, though some improvement is possible later in Q3 as stocks are drawn down.

Vietnamese exporters are also leaning into the EU market, where volumes are slowly recovering but remain below historical norms. Domestically, procurement has slowed as processors increasingly rely on company-owned farms, contributing to the ongoing downward trend in farm-gate prices.

The balance of supply and demand in the US farmed whitefish sector remains fragile. For tilapia, high inventories and soft retail movement are likely to keep a lid on pricing despite lower origin costs. For pangasius, stable US values mask significant weakness at origin, where farmers face sustained pressure from low procurement activity and subdued export demand.

Yet, the US import picture tells a different story: Pangasuis has now overtaken tilapia in volume, a reversal of the typical trend.

Despite a strong start to the year for tilapia, Q2 saw a sharp contraction, while pangasius surged to its highest monthly volume in over two years. As Vietnam capitalizes on tariff relief and an aggressive front-loading strategy, pangasius is positioning itself as the market's dominant force, at least for now.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view

With Vietnam’s tariff relief now in place, pangasius could gain further ground, but for now, buyers remain focused on managing inventories, not making bold commitments.
