title: Catch the Current episode 29: The USDA is making it rain Alaska pollock
content:
Alaska pollock is practically falling from the sky on this week's episode of Catch the Current.

Hosts Amanda Buckle and Lorin Castiglione talk about the eye bulging story of the week: the US Department of Agriculture's commitment to purchase a whopping $100 million of Alaska pollock products. When you hear how it compares to the previous record-setting number, you'll be picking your jaw off the floor. 

Meanwhile, Undercurrent News reporter Jacob Resneck joins the pod to give an update on Alaska's salmon season. Plus, following a recent trip to the Alameda, California, Coast Guard base, Jacob shares some insights on how the US maritime law enforcement agency is navigating the Bering Sea with Russian and Chinese vessels.

But that's not all! US president Donald Trump keeps the tariff curveballs going and much more.

Thank you to our sponsor: Wisefish.

Listen now on YouTube!

Subscribe now! Catch the Current is available on YouTube, Spotify, Amazon Music, iHeartRadio, Pandora, and other major podcast streaming platforms. Don't see Catch the Current on your favorite app? Reach out to podcasts@undercurrentnews.com.

Don't have time to listen? Find a full transcript of season 1, episode 29 of Catch the Current below:

Amanda Buckle (AB): You're listening to Catch the Current, the coolest seafood podcast out there, from the team at Undercurrent News, your trusted source for seafood prices, news and data. I'm Amanda Buckle.

Lorin Castiglione (LC): And I’m Lorin Castiglione.

AB: This episode is brought to you by Wisefish, a business solution built for the seafood industry. Whether you're in farming, fishing, processing, or handling seafood sales, Wisefish helps you manage your entire value chain in one connected system. Learn more at wisefish.com/catch-the-current.

LC: Well, Aug. 1 finally arrived and US president Donald Trump updated all his country specific tariffs. But ... surprise! Trump has thrown another curveball. This week he announced in an Executive Order that the US will increase the tariff on Indian imports by a further 25%, on top of the previously announced 25%.

Trump adds further 25% import tariff to beleaguered India

AB: India's full additional tariff rate to the US -- including pre-existing countervailing and anti-dumping duties [on shrimp] -- will now rise to 58.26%. 

The penalty issued by Trump ties into the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war. Trump has accused the government of India of directly or indirectly importing Russian oil.

LC: India is the single largest supplier of frozen shrimp to the US, accounting for roughly 40% of the country's total shrimp imports last year. The country generated roughly $2.35 billion in export revenue just through sales of shrimp to the US last year. 

And before this new tariff rate -- just to give you an idea of India compared to other Asian exporters -- Vietnam has a combined tariff rate of 48.6%, Indonesia 22.9% and Thailand 19%. 

But looking at India's main rival for the US market, Ecuador has a combined tariff rate to the US of just 18.78%.

AB: Right now the US is buried in imported shrimp, with UCN Americas editor Jason Huffman noting this week is largely in thanks to the tariff deadlines set by Trump.

US shrimp imports surge higher still in race to beat larger Trump tariffs

The US imported over 413,000 metric tons of shrimp worth $3.4 billion in the first six months of 2025. That's 18% more volume and 28% more value than the 351,025t worth $2.7bn that was imported in the first six months of 2024. 

Jason reports that the US has now seen year-on-year shrimp volume increase for eight consecutive months, dating back to November 2024.

But June specifically had a pretty crazy showing, and it's not hard to see why. There was the earlier deadline of July 9, on which Trump threatened a tariff jump from the generalized 10% rate he set in April to much higher nation-specific rates. He later postponed the new tariff deadline until Aug. 1, and then this Thursday, Aug. 7. He also adjusted the rates for several countries that agreed to deals, which, as we just spoke about, he continues to adjust.

LC: Jason reports that the current import levels are on pace to nearly match the records set in 2021, when shrimp imports spiked following the pandemic.

However, Undercurrent News senior price analyst Gary Morrison doesn't believe that's likely to happen. 

AB: What's Gary's hot take, Lorin?

LC: He predicts a second-half lull in US shrimp imports. His reasoning is that so much of it is sitting in US cold storage from the earlier rush.

With its global team of reporters, Undercurrent News is the source to go for daily tariff updates and how it impacts the seafood industry. Check out the show notes for links to more insight into the impact of the tariffs on the shrimp market and more in UCN's ongoing trade war blog. 

AB: Tariffs continue to dominate the daily conversation and likely will continue to for a while. But for me, the big story this week involved Alaska pollock.

USDA announces intent to buy massive $100m of Alaska pollock using tariff funds

The US Department of Agriculture announced that it's looking to make a massive $100 million investment in Alaska pollock, using funds made available to it by previously collected tariffs.

US agriculture secretary Brooke Rollins announced late last week that the USDA intends to purchase up to $230m in fresh seafood, fruits and vegetables from American farmers and producers to distribute to food banks and nutrition assistance programs across the country through Section 32.

And Lorin, I got to tell you, when I usually see these notices and seafood is mentioned, it's usually a tiny slice of the pie.

LC: Yeah, this is huge.

AB: Yeah, exactly. I scrolled all the way to the bottom of this announcement and I swear my eyes bulged out of my head.

Of that $230m, the USDA carved out $100m worth of Alaska pollock products and...

LC: Pollock! Pollock! Pollock!

AB: But on top of it, catfish, farm-raised catfish also got carved out $20 million.

So $120 million out of that $230 million is for seafood, which is wild.

LC: That's great. 

AB: Yeah, really exciting, especially when you consider it's Section 32, so it's going to food banks and nutrition assistance programs.

So it's really a great win, not just for pollock, but for ...

LC: Anybody.

AB: The $100m specifically is just really crazy because when you look at fiscal year 2019, which currently holds the record as the biggest year by value ever for USDA purchases of Alaska pollock, 2019 was at $76.3m.

LC: Wow.

AB: Now they want to buy $100 million, but they've already bought $58.3 million. So if, or once they fully award this $100 million, the USDA for fiscal year 2025 would in total have bought $158.3m, which blows fiscal year 2019 out of the water.

LC: That's incredible.

AB: It truly, truly is.

The other really interesting thing about Section 32 is that USDA Section 32 allows access to 30% of the gross receipts from customs duties collected in previous years. So I never really thought about the connection to tariffs. And, of course, the money for the $100m and $20m for catfish isn't coming from tariffs collected from Trump recently. They are previous tariffs. But it'll be really interesting to see if these recent tariffs will result in even more seafood purchases under Section 32 in the future.

LC: The one thing that you can look forward to from these tariffs.

Back-to-back salmon die-offs hit Cooke’s Newfoundland sites

Now onto UCN's top story of this week: back-to-back salmon die-offs at Canadian seafood conglomerate Cook Aquaculture's Newfoundland and Labrador sea farms. 

The company reported a combined loss of more than 56,600 fish in a span of just two days.

AB: Undercurrent's Liza Mayer reported earlier this week on the story. The company's local operating arm, which is Cold Ocean Salmon, filed public notices with the province's Department of Fisheries, Forestry and Agriculture, confirming the mortality events at its Grip Cove and Olive Cove sites. The most recent report was made on Thursday, July 31, and they report that 17,662 smolts died during transfer operations.

Cold Ocean Salmon attributed the losses to mechanical issues during transfer from a well boat causing increased acclimation strain. And just two days earlier on Tuesday, July 29, the company reported a larger mortality event at its Olive Cove site where 38,942 fish died. That site had been actively harvesting when the die-off began earlier in July.

More on Liza's story in the show notes.

LC: Despite these mortality issues, there is still plenty of salmon going around in the global salmon market. And let me dive into it. So the first dramatic movement that we saw this week was out of Norway.

US wholesale prices for fresh Norwegian fillets dropped sharply this week, down about $0.30 to $0.35 a pound across key sizes. That puts Norwegian pricing on par with Chilean products for the first time in months. It wasn't just fillets, whole fish slipped around $0.10 a pound and frozen portions also dropped $0.15 a pound, landing fresh market values at some of the lowest levels we've seen this year.

The driver there: heavy harvest pressure. Norway's July exports hit a record 136,000t, and that was up 28% from last year. The US still took a good chunk of that volume, but price growth was sluggish.

Now turning to Chile, a softer story but still important, fillet prices were mostly flat to down a little bit, easing about $0.05 on core sizes like 3-4s and 4-5s. Seasonal demand remains quiet, and Chilean offers are facing stiff competition from both Norwegian product and the US domestic wild salmon harvest.

Eastern Canadian salmon farms double harvest pace in battle against heat, sea lice, low prices

One segment that held firm are frozen portions, particularly 6-8 oz. sizes. Spot inventories are very tight, and there's no new production expected until at least September there. And then there's Canada, where we've seen a recent rebound after wholesale prices dropped sharply last week. That was due to processors rushing harvests ahead of warm water threats and sea lice issues, and that flooded the market, driving prices down.

This past week there was a holiday in Canada, so that shortened the production week and prices have rebounded a bit there.

If you want to check it out Barb Dean-Simmons also wrote a story on what's happening in Canada, a bit of a deeper dive, and she did an excellent job, so we can link that in the show notes as well.

But depending on which origin, things are definitely moving in the global salmon markets.

AB: A quick word about Wisefish, proud sponsor of Catch the Current. Wisefish is a business solution, purpose-built for the seafood industry, backed by over 30 years of experience. Whether you're in farming, fishing, processing, seafood sales, or doing all of the above, Wisefish helps you work more efficiently across the entire value chain, from daily workflows to cost control, traceability and sustainability. As seafood businesses scale, operations become more complex. Wisefish replaces spreadsheets and removes siloed systems, enabling scalable growth, compliance, and making faster data-informed decisions. Learn more at wisefish.com/catch-the-current.

Now joining us on the pod to talk about what's going on in the world of wild salmon is our pal, UCN reporter Jacob Resneck.

Jacob, you published a story this week that the salmon harvest in Alaska is at its halfway point of its projected 2025 landings. Can you break it down for us?

Alaska’s wild salmon season at 50% of forecast with more than 106m fish landed

Jacob Resneck (JR): Yeah, I mean, we're at the halfway point overall with over 106 million fish caught.

That's across five species, but they come in at different times. But the lion's share and really what we're talking about, the big ones, is the wild sockeye. And Bristol Bay really went gangbusters this season. They're wrapped up and done. And they were up quite a bit.

McKinley Research puts out a really helpful harvest update every week for the Alaska Seafood Marketing Institute. What they've shown is we've broken 106 million fish across five species. The big driver of this, of course, has been the Bristol Bay wild sockeye. That's been a real success story this year.

And year over year, they're up 29%. Well, they had a pretty lackluster year. So this is something they really needed.

So overall, I think Bristol Bay, they've broken over 40 million fish. And this time last year, they were at not even 32 million. So it's a really good thing.

There's been a lot of concern about too much sockeye, too quick on the market. What will that do with prices? The shorter answer is we don't know yet.

When I talk to people who track this sort of thing, they tell me that since there was such a low harvest last year, there really isn't any inventory left over from 2024.

So there's a lot of demand right now. And wild sockeye is a pretty niche item when it comes to salmon, since it really can't compete in volume with like farmed Atlantic salmon, things like that. So there's a lot of optimism that the market will be able to absorb the product.

The deals are being made right now with the middlemen, the distributors, between the producers and the distributors, when it ultimately gets to the end consumers, restaurants, supermarkets, things like that. The dust has not settled yet. But we're gonna be watching that really closely to see what happens with the actual wholesale salmon markets. That's just too soon to tell. All right.

LC: Well, anytime anybody has any optimistic news on a market, we are all for it. So thanks for that update, Jacob. I also wanted to ask you about a fun little field trip that you got to go on last week involving the Coast Guard.

US Coast Guard captain Jim O'Mara, commanding officer of the Munro, reflects on his vessel's 121-day Bering Sea patrol during an Aug. 1, 2025 interview with Undercurrent News. (Photo by Jacob Resneck/UCN)

JR: Yeah, I don't live that far away from one of their largest West Coast bases. It's down in Alameda, California. And the national security cutter, Munro, had just gotten back on board. They were up in the Bering Sea for about four months.

And, you know, the US Coast Guard, they're kind of the traffic cops of the EEZ, the federal waters and fisheries. And they do regular boardings of US fishing vessels. And they also patrol up there to watch what other countries are doing, make sure there aren't any foreign fishing vessels coming into the EEZ because it's a 200 nautical mile exclusive fishing zone.

I got to sit down with the commander to see what they saw up there. They say the good news is the US fishing fleet is largely -- like 95% -- in compliance with all that health and safety kind of thing. They do regular boardings for these large harvesters, processors, long liners, everything up there.

And it was just kind of interesting to see their perspective of being the highway patrol, if you will, of the high seas. They didn't have any trouble up there. You know, they see the Russians, they see the Chinese, things like that.

You know, we get a lot in the news about Russian and Chinese vessels up in the Arctic, because there is a lot of posturing, geopolitical posturing. And it's usually not about fishing. It's usually about oil and gas exploration and stuff like that.

What the Coast Guard's been telling me is there they didn't see anything provocative. I mean, it is still international waters. So foreign vessels can go through. They can transit. They can't fish, though.

They have to make sure they didn't see any foreign fishing vessels in US waters. And there hasn't been anything that we need to worry about so much. But they said that it's important that they have that presence because they meet presence with presence is kind of their tagline. And if they weren't there, well, then it wouldn't be so exclusive because there would be no one to patrol those waters.

We're going to have a feature story about the perspective of the US Coast Guard up in Bering Sea coming up on Undercurrent shortly.

The US Coast Guard Cutter Munro’s 26-foot over-the-horizon cutter boat returns to the fantail notch after conducting a boarding of a commercial fishing vessel in Dutch Harbor, Alaska on May 2, 2025. (Photo by Lt. j.g. Samika Lewis/USCG)

AB: Thanks, Jacob. Before you go, I'm going to ask you to join Lorin and I in this final conversation. But first, I have a question for you both.

How many oysters have you ever eaten in one sitting?

LC: Oh, gosh. In one sitting, maybe like a dozen, a dozen and a half.

What about you, Jacob? I feel like it's got to be more.

JR: I would say similar. I don't think I've ever been able to afford more than two dozen in a sitting.

We usually shuck them ourselves. I was just looking on Facebook, you know, here's a picture of your kids when they wanted to hang out with you. Five years ago, when my kids were like two and three, slurping down raw oysters in 2020.

AB: You know, my youngest does seem to like boogers, so I feel like I might be able to get her to enjoy some raw oysters.

JR: My son still, he loves, loves raw oysters. But I think the most I could probably do would be two dozen.

AB: I don't think I've ever honestly eaten more than a dozen oysters. I'm not going to go out and just get oysters. I want to get something else for dinner. So I'm not probably getting more than that. I would split, you know, like a dozen, two dozen oysters.

LC: Well yeah, you order some for the table, and then you go through those a little bit quick and then you're like, does anybody want any more? And then you keep adding to it.

AB: All right, fine. One more round, one more round. OK.

One restaurant in Louisiana is challenging people to eat 180 raw oysters.

LC: Oh no.

AB: With an hour on the clock.

LC: That's too much.

AB: So the restaurant is called Acme Oyster House. It's in New Orleans. Supposedly, breaks are permitted, but bathroom trips are closely supervised.

LC: Ew.

JR: Are they small? Are they like Miyagis?

LC: Yeah. What kind of oysters are we talking about here?

AB: You know, I didn't, I didn't look into it. I'm just going to assume it's like the biggest,  meatiest thing you could find.

OK, let's compromise on something in the middle.

Either way, even if it was small ones, do you think you could handle 180?

LC: No, no.

AB: How many people do they have shucking those things?

LC: This is counteractive to increasing seafood consumption, because if you do that, I feel like you'd never want to see another oyster in your entire life.

JR: I don't think I could do it, but I would be game to try.

AB: That's what I was going to say. You could, you could order actually, you could order from this website. It ships through Gold Belly. So we could reach out so you could participate in the challenge virtually.

LC: What do you win?

AB: The glory, Lorin. The honor. The bragging rights...

JR: More oysters.

AB: The bragging rights of being a part of the honorary 15 Dozen Club. There's already 159 people currently in it.

LC: You should have queued up somebody who is in this 15 Dozen Club to be a guest on the podcast this week. Maybe next week, see if we can do it.

JR: Do they comp you if you if you eat them? 

Photo Credit: Acme Oyster House

AB: I don't think so... these are all great questions.

There's 159 people that did this, that ate 15 dozen. But there's actually some overachievers. Do you guys want to guess how many Brad from Uniontown, Pennsylvania, ate to claim the title of the leader of the house.

LC: Wait, people have gone above and beyond 180?

AB: Yes, yes. There's people that have ate more than that. More than 180. Take a guess.

LC: 207.

JR: 230.

AB: 516 oysters! That's 40 dozen!

LC: Get Brad on the line right now. I have questions.

JR: It's like the John Candy movie. There's a John Candy movie, "The Great Outdoors," where he eats the 96 ounce sirloin.

AB: Just imagine like Brad out with his wife and kids visiting Louisiana and he sees this competition and his wife's like, "Don't do it, Brad. The kids want to go do this thing." He's like, "Let me just he gets up ..."

LC: Does the "Frank the Tank" motion.

AB: And then this table starts showing one more round. And then he's at 516 oysters passed out in the parking lot. His wife, Jeannine, is so upset. The holiday's ruined.

[Editor's note: This is a fictionalization of eating 516 oysters and not actually how the iconic Brad claimed his title.]

JR: I think Undercurrent should probably sponsor us to try it.

AB: If anybody wants to see Jacob, Lorin and I eat 180 oysters in one sitting...

LC: I'm the wing woman. I will get your waters. I will get the napkins, but I will just be watching that.

AB: Well, that does it for us. Thanks for tuning in to Catch the Current. title: Spain raises 2025 Mediterranean red shrimp quota
content:
Spain’s fisheries ministry has increased the country's 2025 catch limit for the Mediterranean red shrimp fishery by 45.9 metric tons for authorised vessels, Baird Maritime reported.

The change applies to 286 vessels in the Mediterranean bottom trawling system with a record of targeting the species. The additional quota comes from two sources: 35.9t obtained through a quota exchange with France, following what the ministry described as intensive negotiations, and 10t drawn from Spain’s national reserve.

Officials said the increase will benefit the trawling sector during peak demand periods in summer and Christmas, enabling shipowners to plan operations more effectively.

The government has also authorised the pooling of catch limits, allowing individual vessels and fishing associations to share quotas to more efficiently use available resources. The ministry said the adjustments "reaffirm its commitment to the responsible management of fishery resources."

title: Indonesian harvesters’ attorneys fight to keep alive forced labor suit against Bumble Bee
content:
Two law firms that represent four Indonesian harvesters, who filed a lawsuit against canned tuna giant Bumble Bee Foods accusing the company of benefiting from forced labor, are now fighting an effort to dismiss the case.

The law firms for the fishermen, who are backed by the environmental advocacy group Greenpeace, filed their response on Thursday (July 31) to the motion for dismissal filed by Bumble Bee Foods in early June in the US District Court for the Southern District of California.

The group's lawsuit, filed in March, alleged that the fishermen experienced human trafficking and forced labor onboard vessels that caught tuna the company eventually sold in the US, violating the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act (TVPRA) and California negligence law, as reported by Undercurrent News.

TVPRA was created to combat human trafficking, including forced labor, which the court filing states that the plaintiffs "meet all the TVPRA statutory requirements," argues the response submitted by Cohen Milstein Sellers & Toll, a Washington, D.C.-based firm, which is arguing the case along with Schonbrun Seplow Harris Hoffman & Zeldes, in Hermosa Beach, California.

"Bumble Bee knew, recklessly disregarded and/or should have known that it was sourcing tuna from vessels engaged in obtaining labor by force, physical restraint, and other means," the attorneys argue. "Bumble Bee received reports over a decade focused specifically on the vessels that supply tuna to Bumble Bee -- reports that highlighted the specific abuses suffered by Plaintiffs here -- and was aware of US law enforcement action finding forced labor on a Bumble Bee supplier vessel."

Bumble Bee, in its argument for dismissal, said staffing agencies that placed the fishermen on board the vessels should be held accountable for any incidents of forced labor. While it doesn't believe it is legally at fault for any abuse allegedly suffered by the fishermen, the company said it's making efforts to improve its business practices to ensure workers in its supply chain are not taken advantage of, citing its "Trace My Catch" traceability tool and supplier code of conduct as evidence of its efforts to mitigate labor risks.

title: Catch the Current episode 28: ‘A great day for America’…but what about for seafood?
content:
Trump's trade war deadline has arrived -- again. For real this time, sort of. There is a lot to unpack ... but Catch the Current is on the case!

Host Amanda Buckle is joined by Undercurrent News editorial director Cliff White and EMEA deputy editor Dan Gibson to talk about all things Trump and tariffs in the hours leading up to the much-anticipated Aug. 1 trade deadline, which got extended to Aug. 7, as reported by Undercurrent.

Plus, UCN reporter Masahiko Takeuchi calls in to share details on Nissui's big move.

Listen now on YouTube!

Subscribe now! Catch the Current is available on YouTube, Spotify, Amazon Music, iHeartRadio, Pandora, and other major podcast streaming platforms. Don't see Catch the Current on your favorite app? Reach out to podcasts@undercurrentnews.com.

Don't have time to listen? Find a full transcript of season 1, episode 28 of Catch the Current below:

Amanda Buckle (AB): You're listening to Catch the Current, the coolest seafood podcast out there, from the team at Undercurrent News, your trusted-source for seafood prices, news and data. I'm Amanda Buckle.

This episode is proudly brought to you by Wisefish, a trusted seafood business solution with over 30 years of experience. Based in Iceland, which is once again dealing with an active volcano right now, Wisefish helps companies worldwide manage everything from fishing and farming to processing, sales, traceability, and carbon accounting, all in one integrated solution. We're excited to have Wisefish as the first-ever sponsor of Catch the Current. Learn more at wisefish.com/catch-the-current.

FREE READ Trump tariffs fallout: US imports drop 5.1% in August as trade policies hit home

Well, August 1 -- "a great day for America," as president Donald Trump has posted on his Truth Social platform -- has finally arrived. And as expected, it's been one chaotic ride.

My co-host Lorin Castiglione has somehow duped me again and scheduled some work travel around Trump's "Liberation Day" tariff deadline, but I've got Undercurrent's very own editorial director Cliff White and EMEA deputy editor Dan Gibson joining me on the pod this week to talk about all the major trade news.

So, this is basically like that old game show "Deal or No Deal" with Howie Mandel...if it had a baby with that Brad Pitt and Morgan Freeman movie, "Seven."

"What is the tariff rate?!?!"

Cliff, let's start with India. What did Trump have in that briefcase/box?

Cliff White (CW): It's a 25% tariff!

Well, that's not exactly what the Indian shrimp exporting industry is saying. Those are not their exact words.

US hits largest shrimp source India with 25% tariff

Dan will have more on this, but the tariff rate was higher than India expected. I think they were looking around at what other Asian exporting nations had received, and it was 19% for Indonesia, 20% for Vietnam. And especially the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, has a special relationship with US president Donald Trump. So I think there's surprise in India that 25% was the number that came out yesterday.

That said, it sounds like the two parties are still negotiating. But Dan can talk about the impact here.

Dan Gibson (DG): The response in India has been one of bemusement and a certain degree of bewilderment, I think, as you rightly say there, Cliff. The expectation was that it would be something similar to Indonesia's and Vietnam's rates, if not better. But instead, he's just gone to Truth Social and announced 25%.

And this presents a problem as a headline writer, because normally when the US president announces something, that's official, right? But it doesn't really seem to work that way these days. So it's unclear as yet whether that is going to be the final, final, final rate, or if that's just another negotiating tactic that may be reversed in the next few days.

But India is hugely dependent on the US -- 40% of all of its shrimp exports go to America. You're talking $2.3-2.5 billion a year trade flow right there.

Indian shrimp sector reels from 25% US tariff threat

Let's put that into comparison. Last week, the UK signed its own free trade agreement with India. And India does $100 million to the UK. And they're thinking, oh, we can get a 70% increase to $170m, which, again, you put that up against the behemoth of their trade with America, it's a drop in the ocean.

So realistically, they have been in competition with Ecuador for the US market. And I think having such a big gap between their tariff rate and Ecuador's tariff rate is less than ideal, to put it mildly.

So they are going to be looking, I would imagine, to diversify to anywhere else that can take this extra volume that they have. And I could well see, within the next few years, Ecuador surpassing them to become America's biggest supplier of shrimp. If this holds.

I think otherwise, in the short term, just looking at farm-gate prices earlier this week, they've been coming up the last couple of weeks because it's the end of peak harvest season. So there's a bit of a raw material shortage.

And I think at the same time, they were expecting, as I say, a better deal with America. So effectively, the 10% drop that they had in prices when the "Liberation Day" tariffs -- I'm using air quotes here -- "Liberation Day" tariffs were first announced, basically had that initial drop.

And that's been wiped out in the last couple of weeks. And the people I spoke to yesterday and today have told me they fully expect that the market will sag once again if this holds.

L. Vannamei. Credit: nirapai boonpheng / Shutterstock

AB: The Southern Shrimp Alliance, an organization of shrimp fishermen, shrimp processors in the US states of Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Louisiana -- a whole list that goes on -- they are extremely happy with this announcement.

They put out a press release applauding Trump's move for the additional 25% tariffs because India is the single largest supplier of foreign shrimp to the US markets.

Now, the 25% tariff on India announced Wednesday is bad, especially considering the amount of shrimp imports to the US, as I just spoke about. But it could always be worse.

Remember that in early July, Trump slapped Brazil with a 50% tariff, effective Aug. 1. On Wednesday afternoon, the White House announced that Trump signed the Executive Order implementing the additional 40% tariff on Brazil, bringing the total tariff amount to 50%.

Trump signs executive order to finalize 50% tariff on Brazil

CW: No surprise here. But it's a finalization of that 50% rate. The surprise is the justification that Trump used for this tariff. Number one, he cited the political persecution of former president Jair Bolsonaro.

And that's a little unusual to cite political persecution. And also some of Bolsonaro's supporters have been banned or censored on social media, or been requested by the Brazilian government to be censored. So that was mentioned by Trump.

These are unusual reasons for tariffs. Usually they're economic reasons. So that might not fly legally, especially because the law that Trump is citing for these tariffs, there are seven lawsuits challenging the president's ability or right to implement tariffs under this law.

One is actually being heard right now, oral arguments in an appeals court in US federal court. It is likely to proceed to the Supreme Court within months. And if that happens to go against Trump, if the Supreme Court rules against him -- which you never know with the Supreme Court these days -- that could nullify pretty much all the tariffs that Trump has been talking about for months and months here.

So that's kind of the big Occam's razor hanging over this whole situation. But it's interesting that Trump mentioned political stuff in this tariff announcement because that's the justification needed under this law -- a threat to the US national security. And he's trying to get there with this. Whether the Supreme Court agrees, we'll find out.

US president Donald Trump signing an executive order. Photo courtesy of The White House.

AB: So now Brazil is the US's 19th most valued source of seafood. When you look by the numbers, it accounts for over 39,000 metric tons worth $232m in 2024.

In particular, the new tariffs threaten U.S. imports of tilapia, red snapper and rock lobster. So our very own Maria Feijoo reported Thursday that Brazil's seafood industry is urgently seeking relief after the US imposed a 50% tariff. And Maria is joining us now on the pod to share more on how the new tariff has triggered a sector-wide crisis.

Maria Feijoo (MF): Well, this is actually pretty serious. Just like that, no warning, no negotiations. And it sent shockwaves to the entire sector in Brazil.

This is an industry where around 70% of all exports go straight to the US. So a move like this is more than just a disruption. It's a full-blown crisis.

The Brazilian Association of Fish Industries, known as Abipesca, says roughly 300m reais worth of seafood is currently sitting at ports, on vessels or waiting inside processing plants.

That is roughly around $54m at the moment. A lot of this product is highly specialized for the American market, like specific tilapia cuts, which make up nearly 90% of Brazil's fish exports to the US. So there's just no easy way to pivot that back into the domestic market. Which is already oversupplied and cannot absorb the volume.

Brazil’s seafood sector seeks $160m bailout as 50% US tariff paralyzes exports

So now, exporters are running out of working capital. They're calling on the federal government for an emergency bailout of 900m reais, or around $160m, with a grace period and a two-year repayment plan. Without that support, around 35 companies could shut down and 20,000 jobs are at risk.

Now, what's especially interesting is the political backdrop. This all started with a letter from Trump accusing Brazil of undermining US democratic institutions. No real evidence was provided, but it was enough to justify the massive tariff, it seems.

In the meantime, some states in Brazil are stepping up. Goias, for example, which is a major seafood exporter, has announced its own emergency credit program. And on the federal side, finance minister Fernando Haddad has said Brazil will keep talking to the US, but also that the government is preparing its own emergency measures as well.

There's also pressure building to reopen the European market, which has been closed to Brazilian seafood since 2017 due to sanitary restrictions. So that's now looking like a critical opportunity for diversification, because right now the industry is just too dependent on a single market: the US.

AB: Trump was very busy in the lead-up to the tariff deadline. He also announced that his administration reached a new trade agreement with South Korea featuring $350bn in Korean investment and a 15% tariff on the country's exports to the US. 

DG: South Korea is the US' 17th most valuable source of seafood. It sends nearly 28,000t worth approximately $306m last year. Predominantly, this includes toothfish, which I believe is a very popular product over there.

So the 15% tariff, to be clear, it matches the rate that's previously been announced for Japan and the EU. And it's currently the rate that I believe is in place for Norway as well.

US strikes EU trade deal setting 15% tariff rate

CW: The list of deals coming in is changing by the minute here.

It's currently Thursday afternoon as we're recording. We're seeing reporting of deals with Thailand, which is a big seafood exporter to the US, as well as Cambodia and Taiwan, another seafood exporter, though its US market is somewhat smaller. And yeah, we're kind of waiting for the shoe to drop on a lot of these deals before the Aug. 1 deadline.

The one country that seems to have avoided that deadline is Mexico, which just got a 90-day extension of its current tariff rates, which are pretty much nil.

There are some products that fall outside of the US-Mexico-Canada (USMCA) trade agreement that are being tariffed, but for the most part, including all seafood, there's zero tariffs on Canadian goods for the next 90 days now as they continue to negotiate a deal, the US and Mexico.

And Canada, still facing no tariffs, but it's not looking likely they're going to get a deal after Trump blasted the country on Truth Social this morning for its decision to support Palestinian statehood. Trump posted that Canada's decision will make it very hard to make a deal.

So we will see what happens there.

AB: "Oh, Canada."

That is definitely something we'll be watching, and I'm sure something will be breaking in our off hours, because that's always when these things from Trump seem to happen.

CW: There are no off hours, Amanda.

AB: There are no off hours.

That's actually what I was just about to say, if I had just followed my own script.

So the Aug. 1 deadline has been looming for some time, and Undercurrent has been posting updates on the US trade war as quickly as they come in, thanks to our global team. If you're not subscribed to Undercurrent News... what are you waiting for?

AB: A quick word about Wisefish, our very first sponsor here on Catch the Current.

Wisefish is a modern business solution built specifically for seafood companies.

Whether you're in farming, fishing, processing, seafood sales, or doing all of the above, Wisefish helps you manage the full value chain in one place. They've been around for over 30 years, and fun fact, about 80% of Iceland's seafood exports are managed through the system today. Seafood businesses around the world use Wisefish to bring efficiency to their operations -- improving everything from daily workflows to cost control, traceability and sustainability. It's an integrated solution that replaces spreadsheets and removes siloed systems.

You can learn more at wisefish.com/catch-the-current.

AB: I refuse to let the tariffs of terror dominate all the talk this episode. Another big story to break this week was Japanese seafood giant Nissui Corp.'s plans to build a new processing factory to boost its frozen seafood and surimi output. Joining the pod to talk about Nissui's big plans is Undercurrent's very own Masahiko Takeuchi.

Masa, we were talking a bit about this while preparing for the show. You were telling me that this new processing factory comes at a pretty interesting time because Japan's surimi consumption is down, but fish sausage demand is growing.

Nissui plans huge new facility to boost frozen seafood, surimi output 50%

Masahiko Takeuchi (MT): Yes, exactly, Amanda. As you said, overall demand for surimi products in Japan is weak.

Traditional items, like kamaboko and chikuwa, are not selling well, especially with younger people. But fish sausage, which is also made from surimi, like pollock surimi, is different. It's doing surprisingly well.

According to point of sale data, that means checkout data from supermarkets and convenience stores, fish sausage sales rose by 11% in volume and 13% in value in the first half of 2025. This happened even though prices also went up by 2%.

So why is this happening?

First, product is easy to keep and use. You don't have to refrigerate it and you can eat it straight away. That makes it popular for busy people and even for emergency storage at home after the COVID-19 pandemic.

Second, it's seen as healthy.

Surimi-based fish sausage sold at a retail chain in Japan. Photo: Masahiko Takeuchi

Some types include added nutrients like DHA or calcium. This also promotes the fast-absorbing protein from pollock in their fish sausages.

And third, fish sausage is getting attention online.

As surimi sales slump, Japan’s fish sausage stages remarkable comeback

Social media users and influencers are posting recipes and some TV programs have featured it recently. So it's reaching a new generation of consumers.

Nissui is responding to this shift. The company plans to build a new factory in Takyushu city, Fukuoka prefecture, western Japan. Construction begins in August and the factory is expected to be ready by the end of next year. This will be a large modern plant with a huge investment.

It will replace two existing factories in the same area and significantly boost the company's production capacity by more than 50% compared to the current level. The new plant will focus on making more fish sausage and frozen seafood. Some production will also move from Nissui's Tokyo Hachioji factory.

Nissui says the new factory will use automation and digital tools to improve efficiency and safety. It will also be designed to lower energy use and reduce fiscal strain on workers.

This investment is part of Nissui's long-term food business strategy in Japan called "Good Foods 2030." The company wants to grow its domestic sales by focusing on products that are convenient, healthy, and suitable for today's lifestyle. So the fish sausage might sound like an old-school product for Japanese consumers, but it's actually playing a central role in Nissui's strategy.

AB: Thanks Masa.

Now, before we go there's one last story I want to talk about. And when I saw this I just couldn't wait to talk about it with Lorin because Lorin and I have this obsession with Red Lobster, despite being deprived of the iconic limited edition insulated Cheddar Bay Biscuit fanny pack.

Dan, have you ever seen this thing?

DG: I'm afraid not.

AB: I'm going to insert this into the show notes. It's the most glorious fanny pack you've ever seen. It's insulated, Dan, just strapped to your stomach.

The Holy Grail of fanny packs. (Circa a 2019 promo that Amanda and Lorin never got over.) Photo Credit: Red Lobster

DG: It is not something I've considered. Is food hygiene a problem with a fanny pack?

AB: You know what? This is the problem with you. Lorin doesn't question the motives or anything. So forget it.

Cliff, Dan, I was going to ask you to be my BSF -- my best seafood friends --  and gab with me on this final story.

DG: I'm happy to. I'm just worried my accent will be a bit of a downgrade.

AB: Well, an egg-bearing lobster ended up in a Red Lobster restaurant in the US state of Utah last week.

Female egg-bearing lobsters, they're illegal to harvest or sell under federal law in the US. So the lobster, the staff at the Red Lobster, lovingly named it Claudia, packed up a newspaper and gel packs and shipped it back to Maine in the hope of saving it from a culinary fate.

But unfortunately, the story does not have a happy ending. Claudia died in transit back to Maine.

CW: I'm not going to be able to fill in for Lorin because I can't even imagine what she would respond to this story with. So I just have to fill in my own response, which is WTF?

Like, why are we sending a lobster back to Maine? Just eat it. Okay? It's all the way in Utah.

AB: It had the eggs!

An example of what an egg bearing lobster looks like.
Photo Credit: NH Fish and Game Law Enforcement Division and Operation Game Thief

CW: Don't name it, eat it!

AB: Yeah, I wish there was ... like there had to have been another way instead of shipping it. It was like a four-hour flight.

Actually, I gotta backpedal. Dan, have you ever eaten at a Red Lobster?

[Editor's note: Dan lives in London where they are deprived of Red Lobster restaurants.]

DG: No, I haven't actually. In fact, I remember early when I first started at Undercurrent, I'd never even, like, been to or was aware of Red Lobster.

So I remember once filling in to help out with the US newsletter and doing a pickup on, I think they were closing a store somewhere, and I thought, "oh no, this small family-run operation in Florida, they're closing a store, ye olde Red Lobster." That's terrible.

AB: Oh, ye olde Red Lobster, the small family-run business, that's cute.

We're going to have to take you next time you're in Jersey. We have one by us.

Maybe you're right, Cliff. Maybe the better solution here would have just been to eat it. Right? The lobster died anyway. But I do like that...

DG: Sorry to butt in here. Are we absolutely sure that this lobster, like, the pilot just didn't sort of take a break and then come back, sort of picking bits of the lobster out of his teeth going, "Oh no, you won't believe what's happened. It's Claudia. It's not looking good for her. She appears to have been boiled."

AB: Sir, you have the lobster bib still tied around your neck.

CW: I'm just putting it on the record. I would eat Claudia. 

DG: Just go back and get another one. Call this one Claudia. Say it was this one the whole time.

FREE READ Red Lobster staff at Utah restaurant discover egg-carrying crustacean, attempt to return it to Maine

AB: Oh my goodness. No, but I do want to say is that I do think it's really great that they educate their wait staff and their managers about sustainability efforts because I think it is really important to share that. And especially now, it's spreading awareness.

Now people know that Maine lobstermen v-notch these female lobsters and toss them back. And the issue with this one was that it wasn't notched and they think that it wasn't showing its eggs when it was caught and shipped to this Utah restaurant. What's really crazy is that this actually happened once before in Utah.

I don't know why these pregnant lobsters keep getting sent to Utah of all places.

CW: Mormon lobsters.

You're right. I like the sustainability angle, the fact that these folks that work at Red Lobster can talk so knowledgably about it.

I'm a Maine resident. I have a lot of pride for the lobster fishery here that is a sustainably operated fishery because of regulations like the one that Red Lobster did its best to go above and beyond even to adhere to, throwing the female, the pregnant females back. But that said, you're already in Utah.

This one snuck through the cracks. Just don't send it back. Just eat it.

AB: Just apologize.

Oh, my goodness. Well, Cliff, Dan, I appreciate you keeping me company on the pod today and talking lobster. And we'll see what tariffs of terror await us next week.

CW: Can't wait, Amanda. This is gonna be a fun one.

DG: Fun is one way of putting it, yeh.

AB: Thanks for tuning into Catch the Current. The seafood business is complex, but Wisefish makes it clearer and more connected, helping companies keep everything flowing smoothly. Whether it's aquaculture, fisheries, processing, or seafood sales, Wisefish powers smarter decisions, better traceability and clearer insights every day. Find out how at wisefish.com/catch-the-current.

title: Trade group representing US domestic shrimp industry backs Trump’s tariffs
content:
A group representing American shrimp fishermen and processors in eight southern US states has praised the wave of tariffs announced by US president Donald Trump on Thursday (July 31).

Trump placed double-digit tariffs on every major shrimp-producing country, as reported by Undercurrent News. Those include a 25% tariff on India, which supplied 38.4% of US shrimp imports by volume last year; a 15% tariff on Ecuador, which accounted for 26.9% of US imports in 2024; and a 19% tariff on Indonesia, which shipped 17.4% of US imports. Vietnam, which supplied 9% of US shrimp imports in 2024, agreed to a 20% US tariff and Thailand, which sent 3% of all US shrimp imports, received a 19% tariff. Many of these countries also must pay additional antidumping and countervailing duties.

Southern Shrimp Alliance president John Williams, a longtime proponent of the US federal government taking more active measures to help the domestic industry, said he expected the move to spur a revival of the domestic shrimp sector, which has suffered significant losses in recent years and seen many lifelong shrimpers decide to give up the trade, as Undercurrent has reported.

US shrimp industry celebrates Trump tariffs on competitors as ‘crucial lifeline’

"President Trump's bold actions provide real hope that not only can America's shrimpers get back to work producing a superior-tasting, local seafood but that, after years of watching friends and neighbors leave the industry, we will start to see new investment in the world's most sustainable wild-caught warmwater shrimp fishery," Williams in an Aug. 1 press release.

In 2024, the US imported 93% of the shrimp it consumed. Williams said domestic product could take more market share as Trump's tariffs take effect.

 "For decades, we've made it difficult for our fishermen to operate while foreign suppliers, who aren't held to the same high standards, enjoyed unfettered access to American consumers," Williams said. "Most seafood importers, retailers, and restaurants went after the cheapest possible supply they could find, increasing their margins no matter how unethically this seafood was produced or brought to market." 

The Southern Shrimp Alliance claims cheap imported shrimp is the product of generous government subsidies, weaker environmental laws and unregulated labor practices. 

"Over the last 30 years, the US market has been a dumping ground for seafood produced overseas. Overcapacity in particular sectors of aquaculture production has been propped up by the ease with which excess seafood could be sold into the United States," Williams said. "These issues have not only undermined American producers but also negatively affected consumer demand for shrimp products. The tariffs are expected to increase US food security and provide consumers with greater access to well-managed US wild-caught shrimp."

The tariffs "fundamentally change this dynamic," Williams said, as they slow imports while the Trump administration addresses harmful trade policies and enforcement deficiencies.

For example, Indonesia's recently signed US trade deal includes commitments to adopt laws prohibiting the importation of goods produced through forced or compulsory labor, improve enforcement of its labor laws, and combat illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing, according to the Southern Shrimp Alliance.

title: Federal appeals court reviews Maine lobster harvesters’ petition over 24/7 GPS tracking rule
content:
More than eight months after their case was dismissed, a group of five Maine lobster harvesters is back in court this week to challenge a state rule that requires 24-hour GPS tracking on federally permitted lobster boats.

Attorney Alfred Frawley,  representing harvesters Frank Thompson, Joel Strout, Jason Lord, Christopher Smith and Jack Cunningham went before the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit in Boston, Massachusetts, on Monday (July 28) to make oral arguments. Frawley, a partner in the Portland, Maine, law firm of McCloskey, Mina, Cunniff & Frawley, is trying to get the three-judge panel to overturn a decision by federal judge John Woodcock, in November 2024.

Wookdcock had dismissed the harvesters' lawsuit, which charged Maine's Department of Marine Resources (DMR) and former commissioner Patrick Keliher with violating their Fourth Amendment rights when the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission introduced DMR's new monitoring rule in 2022. The rule was intended to gather spatial data to further aid in the protection of endangered North Atlantic right whales.

The harvesters had argued that the tracking system is an invasion of privacy in that they don't solely use their lobster boats for harvesting.

Woodcock said the state's interest in preserving the lobster resource outweighed the privacy concerns raised by the fishermen.

"Given the choice between the overaccumulation of data and the accumulation of inadequate data, the law favors preservation of the resource over the lobstermen's rights of privacy," Woodcock wrote.

However, Frawley, on Monday, told the court that the mandate amounted to "a warrantless GPS search of people in their private lives."

He emphasized that the rule applies regardless of whether the vessels are being used for fishing, transport, or personal reasons and argued that such sweeping surveillance exceeds the bounds of what courts have previously allowed for regulated industries.

Maine assistant attorney general Jack Dafoe countered that the regulation serves a "special need" beyond law enforcement, including fishery management and species protection. He maintained that the lobster fishery is a closely regulated industry in which participants have diminished expectations of privacy.

The appeals court judges pressed both sides on whether the DMR rule is overly broad. One judge raised the US Supreme Court's 2018 ruling in Carpenter v. United States, which found that long-term location tracking without a warrant violates the Fourth Amendment. Another questioned why the GPS requirement could not be limited to fishing trips.

Contact the author liza.mayer@undercurrentnews.com

title: Indonesia adopts GDST standard for seafood data platform, hopes move will appease EU
content:
The Indonesian government has launched a new mandatory digital reporting system for members of the country's biggest seafood supply chains, Undercurrent News confirmed at the recent Shrimp Summit in Bali.

Last month, the country adopted the standardized entry format used by the Global Dialogue of Seafood Traceability (GDST) for its digital industry data platform, Stelina.

Since last year, it has been a legal requirement for supply chain actors working with the country's three biggest seafood export species -- shrimp, tuna, and blue swimming crab -- to enter specific product details (below) for all sales transactions.

This is a requirement for fishers, fish farmers, distributors, processors and sellers, according to Berny Subki, director of Indonesia's directorate of logistics.

The full outline of mandatory data points now required from fishermen, fish farmers and distributors in Indonesia. Credit: Dan Gibson/Undercurrent News

"Starting from 2014 and 2015, the ministry of marine affairs and fisheries emphasized more needed to be done to connect the upstream to the downstream through SLIN (Systems Logistics International)," he explained to Undercurrent at the summit.

"Then, beginning in 2020, we started to build the digitization at that time, because we had too much data. The actors of the fisheries in Indonesia are mostly micro- and small enterprises."

So began the digital 'Stelina' platform, which moved data records from paperwork to an online database. The second, upgraded version of the platform was launched by the Inodnesian government in April this year.

"Then we have been in discussion with the GDST for one and a half years, and we now have a strong commitment that Stelina will adopt the GDST standards," Subki continued. 

In practice, with the domestic industry now entering data under the same standardized GDST-compliant format, it means that information can be entered into the Stelina database without double entry.

Moreover, the new system will see transaction data entered in real time with every purchase or sale. 

"When the product moves, they make a report; when the fish changes from raw material into loins, they make a report; and this has to be approved finally by QR codes for export, they can check and approve," Subki explained.

Berny Subki, director of Indonesia's directorate of logistics. Credit: Dan Gibson/Undercurrent News

Currently, the system has a straightforward focus on essential traceability details, from vessel IDs to input origins and harvest weights. 

The GDST's executive director, Huw Thomas, confirmed to Undercurrent that Indonesia had become the first country to implement a national seafood traceability system compatible with the GDST standard.

As the platform develops, additional data elements on labour and animal welfare can also be added, depending on what buyers need.

"At the end of the day, the GDST's job is to get data elements for everything about the global seafood trade that people want to know, and then it's up to businesses, governments, certification schemes and brands to decide what it is they want to use from those data elements," Thomas said.

Indonesia's urgent need to diversify seafood markets

According to data presented at the summit by Tornanda Syaifullah, director general of product competitiveness at Indonesia's ministry of maritime affairs and fisheries, Indonesian seafood exports as a whole bounced back in 2024.

Last year, the country shipped $5.95 billion worth of seafood overseas, an increase of 5.7% year-on-year, well ahead of Indonesia's average growth rate across all exports (up just 3.7%).

While still not back to the high point of $6.24bn recorded when seafood demand peaked in 2022, it's still the country's second-highest seafood export value ever recorded, according to government data.

Shrimp accounted for $1.68 billion of the total, followed by skipjack tuna ($1.03bn), cephalopods ($870 million), crabs ($510m) and seaweed ($340m).

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
Indonesia adopts GDST standard for seafood data platform, hopes move will appease EU - Undercurrent News

Data on Undercurrent's trade portal shows that the US remains its number one export market, although sales to China have been growing rapidly in recent years.

That said, exports to the EU and other ASEAN markets have also been steadily increasing in the last couple of years as Indonesian businesses begin to diversify away from their current US dependence.

Subki told Undercurrent that Indonesian authorities hope the mandatory Stelina system will also help to make the country's shrimp more appealing to European buyers -- where traceability requirements and testing regimens are more stringent than in the US -- and to appease the EU's latest antibiotic crackdown.

The EU's current list of countries whose governments have provided "sufficient evidence and guarantees" regarding antibiotic prevention was released earlier this year.

Indonesia, alongside India, was notably absent, and if unable to convince EU authorities that adequate oversight and enforcement measures are being taken, they will be unable to export shrimp to the EU after the deadline of Sept. 3, 2026.

Indonesia adopts GDST standard for seafood data platform, hopes move will appease EU - Undercurrent News

Nowhere is Indonesia's need to diversify stronger than in shrimp. Indonesia sells roughly two-thirds of all its shrimp to the US (see below), generating over $1bn in trade revenue every year, while Japan ($259m last year) represents the country's only other significant shrimp buyer.

So while the industry will no doubt be relieved to have agreed a trade deal that reduces the additional tariffs on Indonesian goods from the threatened 32% to 19%, this will still be highly damaging for its export demand if Ecuador remains at 10% and India cuts its own deal with the US at a lower rate.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
Aqua Star becomes 100th GDST member

Meanwhile, for GDST, this year's Shrimp Summit also marked a milestone, as it welcomed Washington, US-based Aqua Star into the fold as its 100th partner since its foundation in 2017.

In a statement, Aqua Star's vice president of sustainability Corey Peet noted the importer's goal is to provide seafood "that is always sourced ethically and responsibly."

"Partnering with GDST underscores this dedication. Traceability across supply chains is not the future; it's right now and we want to be part of the solutions developing across all of our supply chains."

title: Chilean salmon council disputes environmental order against two Cooke farms
content:
Chile's Salmon Council formally contested the decision by the Superintendency of the Environment (Superintendencia del Medio Ambiente, or SMA) to shut down two Cooke Aquaculture farming operations in the southern region of the country.

The Salmon Council, which represents major export companies including AquaChile, Mowi, Cermaq, and Cooke itself, is acting as a third-party coadjutant in the case under review by the Third Environmental Tribunal.

Cooke accuses Chilean regulator of overreach in salmon farm suspension

The case centers on SMA's order to suspend operations at Cooke's Huillines 2 and Huillines 3 centers based on alleged non-compliance with environmental regulations.

However, according to the Council, the order is flawed and sets a dangerous precedent for the entire Chilean aquaculture sector.

During a public hearing held before the Tribunal on July 22, the Council's attorney, Edesio Carrasco, argued that the SMA's interpretation of the applicable legal framework is incorrect and retroactively imposes standards on projects that were legally approved before Chile's Environmental Impact Assessment System (SEIA) came into force.

"These centers were authorized under a different regulatory regime, and their operation did not require an environmental qualification resolution when they were approved," said Carrasco. "The SMA is now trying to enforce modern environmental limitations on historical projects, which violates principles of legal certainty and regulatory continuity."

Carrasco also emphasized that the Council's concern goes beyond the interests of Cooke Aquaculture alone.

"This decision affects not just one company but the foundation of the salmon industry in Chile," he said. "It creates uncertainty around hundreds of concessions that were lawfully granted before the current environmental system was implemented."

The Salmon Council contends that the SMA's interpretation "undermines decades of stable regulatory practices that have enabled the growth of salmon farming into Chile's second-largest export sector after copper."

According to Carrasco, the original framework did not impose maximum production caps. Instead, it established a minimum utilization threshold -- typically 50% of permitted stock -- to prevent speculation and promote economic activity in the southern fjords where most salmon farms operate.

Citing a legal opinion from the Comptroller General of the Republic, Carrasco noted that an increase in production is not necessarily subject to SEIA approval, provided the expansion is carried out in a technically and environmentally sound manner.

Cooke files legal complaint against Chile regulator over fish farm suspension order

"The key obligation was not to overproduce, but to produce enough to validate the concession. That's very different from what the SMA now claims," he explained.

He also pointed out that companies, including Cooke, have respected key environmental parameters such as the aerobic capacity of the seabed and density limits for fish stocking, which are seen as crucial to avoiding environmental degradation in aquaculture zones.

The Council now requests that the Tribunal issue a formal ruling on the legality of the SMA's decision, asserting that the enforcement action was arbitrary and inconsistent with Chilean administrative law.

The outcome of the case could redefine how historical aquaculture permits are interpreted across the country, and may influence the future regulatory model for one of Chile's most economically and environmentally sensitive industries.

"This case is about more than just Huillines 2 and 3," Carrasco said. "It's about whether we still have a reliable, coherent framework for sustainable aquaculture in Chile."

The Tribunal has yet to issue a decision.

title: Untitled
content:
Chinese farm-gate prices for tilapia continue to fall in week 30 (July 21-27, 2025) as Typhoon Wipha -- the strongest typhoon to hit southern China this year -- made landfall in Guangdong on July 20.

The storm compounded challenges for an already oversupplied market, forcing many farmers into panic harvesting.

Prices for 500-800 gram tilapia delivered to processors in Guangdong dropped by $0.20/kg week-on-week to a new low, as shown in the first chart -- from Undercurrent News' prices portal -- below. In Hainan and Guangxi, prices also declined by between CNY 0.2 and CNY 0.4 on Monday.

Upgrade to Pro to view

Some farmers reported actual transaction prices in Guangdong of below CNY 7.00/kg, driven by the urgent harvest before the typhoon hit.

"Today (July 20), the farm-gate price (to the local market) was only CNY 7.20/kg, as mid-buyers continued to push prices down. The actual transaction price was just CNY 6.96/kg," a Guangdong farmer commented under Undercurrent's WeChat post.

It was noted that tilapia sold to local wet markets was about CNY 0.40/kg cheaper than to processors, as export farms face higher costs due to government registration and required discharge treatment facilities.

"If I don't sell the fish, I'm afraid the farm will be flooded when the typhoon hits. It's really tough being in aquaculture this year," he said.

On the demand side, Chinese processors have yet to receive new orders from the US, prolonging market uncertainty. 

There is still no news from the US so far," a processor owner in Hainan told Undercurrent.

An executive from a Guangdong company echoed this, adding that the industry is now going through its toughest period.

"Everybody is struggling, as we don't dare to buy more fish because there are no sales," he said. "I really hope US buyers can place some orders soon to help the industry get through this crisis. The next crop's production will decrease for sure, but we need to ensure the sustainability of the industry."

US wholesale unchanged in week 29

US wholesale prices for frozen Chinese tilapia fillets were unchanged in week 29, with standard moisture levels ranging from $3.20–$3.50/lb and chem-free offerings holding between $3.40–$3.70/lb. While pricing at the wholesale level remains stable, underlying market dynamics are under increasing pressure.

Inventories in the US are reported as fully adequate to ample. With cold storage facilities full and domestic demand, particularly at retail, remaining muted, buyers are largely unable to capitalize on falling replacement costs.

To manage peak harvest volumes, Chinese processors are actively offering delivered-duty-paid deals and price guarantees. Still, concerns persist about sustained below-cost pricing and mounting regulatory burdens, including newly enforced environmental compliance measures. These factors are expected to prompt reduced pond stocking for the next production cycle, potentially tightening the market later in the year.

title: US Senate rushes passage of bill to require testing of red snapper caught in Gulf of Mexico
content:
A bill that seeks to better protect US fishermen in the Gulf of Mexico from Mexican cartels smuggling illegally caught red snapper into the country was passed in rapid fashion by the US Senate this week.

The Illegal Red Snapper and Tuna Act, S. 283, advanced by unanimous consent in the upper chamber on Monday (July 14) after it was introduced back in January 2025 by senator Ted Cruz, a Texas Republican. It now awaits a vote in the US House of Representatives.

The bill was sent to the House on Tuesday (July 15), where -- as of 12:12 p.m. -- it was being "held at the desk."

While the US Coast Guard has been actively cracking down on illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing in the Gulf of Mexico, Cruz's bill, if passed by the House, would seek to develop a field test that could determine whether a fish was caught in Mexican or US waters.

US Senator Ted Cruz at an event in 2021. Photograph by Gage Skidmore on Flickr.

The legislation was sponsored by three other Republicans -- senators Katie Britt and Tommy Tuberville, both of Alabama, and senator Roger Wicker of Mississippi --  and one Democrat -- Brian Schatz of Hawaii. Per the text, the bill would require the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to develop a standard methodology for identifying the country of origin of red snapper or tuna imported into the US.

It's unclear how scientists will be able to distinguish which part of the gulf red snapper (Lutjanus campechanus) has been caught in, but the champions of the bill are expressing confidence that it can be done. The bill states that a standard methodology, "based on chemical analysis, for identifying the country of origin," would be jointly developed by "key agency leadership."

"Technology exists to chemically test and find the geographic origin of many foods, but not for red snapper or tuna," said a press release from Tuberville's office.

"With the help of machine learning, NIST scientists are currently able to chemically determine the geographic origin of foods, including strawberries, apples, cherries, ginseng, ginkgo, beef, honey and rice," the release continued. "Using those same methodologies, these scientists believe it would be possible to determine the geographic origin of red snapper, allowing law enforcement to have a better understanding of the networks that support illegal fishing."

According to Tuberville, the test would ultimately allow "federal and state law enforcement officers to identify the origin of the fish and confiscate illegally caught red snapper or tuna before it is imported back into the US."

Mexican cartels threaten Texas fishing industry, Cruz tells US Senate panel

Cruz made an impassioned plea to the Senate's Commerce Subcommittee on Coast Guard, Maritime and Fisheries during a hearing held June 12 to discuss the more general concern of how to use ocean-related resources, as reported by Undercurrent News.

Eliminating IUU targeting reef fish, a category that includes grouper and red snapper in the US, would increase the domestic commercial fishing and seafood processing industry's operating income by $3.71m, said Nathan Rickard, a partner at law firm Picard Kentz & Rowe, in his testimony before the panel. 

"Hardworking Texas fishermen in the Gulf of America are being undercut by cartel-backed entities who illegally catch and smuggle red snapper into US markets, using profits to fund other illicit activities," Cruz said more recently about his bill. "I am proud to lead the fight on this bipartisan legislation to crack down on these corrupt operations, stand up for Texas fishermen, and protect our communities. Now, it's time for the House to act and help us put an end to this illegality."

IUU fishing has been taking place in Texas waters for years, with small Mexican lancha boats often used to harvest red snapper in US federal waters, as has been documented by the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS). 

Further, according to DHS, these same boats that illegally catch snapper are also being used by the cartels to smuggle drugs and people into the US.

In 2024, the US imported 4,464 metric tons of red snapper worth $46.6 million from Mexico. In the first five months of 2025, 2,560t of red snapper worth $25.0m were imported.

title: Pacific bluefin talks collapse as Japan, US split on new harvest rules
content:
International negotiations over a new management procedure for Pacific bluefin tuna ended without agreement, reflecting a sharp divide between Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, which favor expanding quotas, and the US, which is calling for more restrictive measures to protect the stock.

Japan's Fisheries Agency said Tuesday (July 15) that the outcome of the talks was a deferral of any final decision to next year.

Pacific bluefin tuna talks stall, decisions postponed to next year

Delegates from more than 10 nations met in Toyama, Japan, from July 9-15 under the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission (WCPFC) Northern Committee and the Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission (IATTC).

The agenda centered around agreeing harvest control rules (HCRs) that would underpin a new management procedure to automatically set annual catch limits based on scientific stock assessments.

According to Japanese officials, 16 management scenarios were presented -- comprising eight candidate HCRs evaluated under two different "East-West impact ratios" that define how quotas are split between the Western Pacific, dominated by Japanese and Korean fleets, and the Eastern Pacific, where US and Mexican fisheries operate.

The impact ratios under discussion were 80:20 and 70:30, respectively.

"Details of the new management measures require unanimous agreement among the parties, and a consensus could not be reached," an official at the Fisheries Agency told Undercurrent News. "As a result, the conclusion has been postponed beyond 2026."

"On the premise that resource management must be thorough, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan were positive about increasing catch limits, while the US remained cautious," the official added. "There are also voices from Japanese coastal fishers calling for further quota expansion."

AP: American Samoa tuna fleet rarely used protected Pacific waters re-opened by Trump

Meanwhile, the US delegation has argued that the substantial quota increases agreed last year -- which raised the WCPFC's large fish quota by 1.5 times and small fish quota by 1.1 times -- have already contributed to fewer bluefin migrating into American waters, requiring stricter limits.

In contrast, Japan and other Western Pacific nations maintain that the stock has recovered enough to justify gradual increases under clear rules.

Negotiators also discussed proposals for a unified catch documentation scheme to improve traceability, prevent illegal fishing, and strengthen monitoring and enforcement measures. However, no agreement was reached on these areas either.

"The WCPFC had already agreed in 2024 that the current measures would be reviewed again in 2026," the agency official noted.

The Toyama meeting closed without resolution, leaving the debate to continue at the WCPFC annual session in December in the Philippines and the IATTC annual meeting in September in Panama.

title: Trump to impose 35% tariff on Canada, largest US seafood trading partner
content:
US president Donald Trump on Thursday evening (July 10) announced a 35% tariff on goods imported from Canada to take effect Aug. 1, again threatening billions of dollars worth of seafood imports and exports on both sides of the border.

The tariff news was delivered by Trump, per his new mode of operation, in a letter sent to prime minister Mark Carney and shared in a Truth Social post at about 8:30 p.m. Eastern Time. The letter references the earlier conflict that Trump used to threaten tariffs against Canada, allegations that the country is not doing enough to block the illegal flow of the drug fentanyl across the northern border, and suggests the tariffs will be dropped if Canadian companies move some of their manufacturing into the US.

"As you will recall, the United States of America imposed Tariffs on Canada to deal with our Nation's Fentanyl crisis, which is caused, in part, by Canada's failure to stop the drugs from pouring into our Country," he said in the letter. "Instead of working with the United States, Canada retaliated with its own Tariffs. Starting August 1, 2025, we will charge Canada a Tariff of 35% on Canadian products sent into the United States, separate from all Sectoral Tariffs. ... As you are aware, there will be no Tariff if Canada, or companies within your Country, decide to build or manufacture product within the United States and, in fact, we will do everything possible to get approvals quickly, professionally, and routinely -- in other words, in a matter of weeks."

Trump makes no indication in the letter about the prospect of again exempting products in compliance with the US Mexico Canada Agreement (USMCA), a deal he signed in late 2020, as he did during earlier trade spats, when US and Canadian seafood industry executives both believed they were going to get hit with 25% tariffs, as reported by Undercurrent News at the time.

Canada was even made exempt from the 10% generalized tariff Trump declared would apply to goods from most other nations on April 2, his so-called "Liberation Day."

The US counts Canada as both its biggest seafood import source and its biggest seafood export market. It imported 308,117 metric tons worth almost $4.0 billion from Canada in 2024, while exporting to Canada 160,041t worth $1.0bn.

The North American lobster industry can expect to pay a heavy price if the tariffs are enforced as a large amount of lobster caught in the US is sent to Canada for processing before being trucked back to the US for sale to consumers. Also in danger are large amounts of snow crab and Atlantic salmon exported by the US to Canada.

 

Contact the author jason.huffman@undercurrentnews.com
