title: Untitled
content:
With the world’s single largest shrimp purchasing nation imposing sweeping reciprocal tariffs on four of the five largest producing countries in the world, you could be forgiven for thinking that farmed vannamei production would dive this year.

2025 Shrimp Summit: Loc Tran aims for 100,000t from ambitious eco-farm project; India will comply with new EU antibiotic rules

In reality, according to analysts from Norwegian consultancy Kontali and Dutch bank Rabobank, every major shrimp producing nation is expecting significant year-on-year volume growth.

"The numbers for H1 are up by 8% compared to last year, and a large part of this is what we see happening in exports from Ecuador," Kontali's Erwin Termaat told listeners at the recent Shrimp Summit in Bali, Indonesia.

For the first five months of the year, total exports from Ecuador are up 18% and responsible for the majority of the global volume hike year to date.

That said, analysts are far more bearish where the second half of 2025 is concerned.

"For H2, uncertainty remains with the US tariffs, Vietnam facing anti-dumping duties, and other things. So we think that H1 has been an outlier in that sense, and that growth is going to come down during H2," Termaat continued.

In its own second-half global aquaculture update, Rabobank took a similar view.

"Ecuador, which saw strong export growth in early 2025, may face a slowdown in production later in the year if US tariffs are enforced, as some early shipments were likely accelerated in anticipation," the bank writes.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view

Kontali's final projected global production forecast for 2025 -- in 'live shrimp equivalent' (LSE) terms -- is for 5.8 million metric tons of farmed vannamei, which would represent just a 6% y-o-y increase on last year's total.

"But we believe that the demand is still there, the main markets still want shrimp, so there is a need to supply that and therefore growth is still possible," Termaat added.

After all, as Kontali was keen to remind listeners, as big as it is, the US still only accounts for 20% of global shrimp consumption.

Kontali's 2025 shrimp production forecast in a nutshell. Credit: Dan Gibson/Undercurrent News

Ecuador makes big gains in H1, shifts more focus to US

In 2024, Ecuador's booming vannamei production growth machine slowed down for the first time since COVID.

Following a colder than expected summer and electricity shortages in the second half of the year, the country only recorded a 2% increase in production volumes.

"Last year, exports to China were down, so they were losing a bit of share in their main market and had to look more into diversification," Termaat added. "That's something that we also see happening in 2025, and will probably happen in the coming years as well."

Rabobank likewise sees the favorable 10% duty rate on Ecuadorian shrimp as a strategic advantage for the country over its Asian competition, opening the door to expanded value-added exports and reducing dependence on the increasingly unpredictable Chinese market.

Indeed, Sandro Coglitore, CEO of Omarsa, told listeners that frozen raw head-on, shell-on shrimp are set to represent less than half of Ecuador's total shrimp exports this year for the first time ever, a sign of the times.

"Ecuador had a huge advantage at the first stage [of the US Liberation Day tariffs], so that opened up the door for most of the US importers to be present in Ecuador," he said on a summit panel discussing the figures. 

"There has been a trend to have long-term retail contracts, and if this issue on the tariffs is not sorted, there will also be more importers choosing Ecuador because of the transit times. We traditionally have a very good relationship with the US, so we’re in a very good position to grow our peeled and value-added production to them, and of course, the head-on."

For its part, Kontali has Ecuador down for a stunning 10% increase in vannamei production this year, even after the likely H2 slowdown.

Credit: Rabobank

Caution surrounds India's winter crop

The first four months of this year saw an explosion in production growth out of India following a record fourth-quarter stocking, incentivized by high farmgate prices at the tail-end of 2024.

"So India is also on a good growth trajectory for the first half of the year, especially the first three or four months which have been amazing -- exports are up 30% when we look at LSE," said Termaat.

"But we know that stocking for the winter crop has been much lower, so this is going to come down. We believe that India will end the year with a 5% increase." This would see the country end the year with 1.1m metric tons of shrimp.

Rabobank also notes that India has so far performed better than expected under the new tariff regime -- although this is likely to change if no deal is negotiated before Aug. 1 and the proposed 26% rate comes into play.

"Indian exports have remained resilient, continuing to outperform expectations despite higher duties," it said, adding that India has managed to partially reroute some of its shrimp to China as a means of relieving US tariff pressure.

The bank also agrees that India has entered its summer production cycle cautiously, constrained by high temperatures, rising feed and fuel costs, and trade uncertainty.

Harvest cycles in the country have become more spread out over the last year, however, with more farmers moving away from traditional peak stocking periods in pursuit of better off-season prices.

"There's also more ready demand from importing markets for value-added Indian shrimp, who need supply ready at any given moment," Kontali's Termaat said at the show. "So last year's 5% increase in supply from India came as a welcome to the US market, which saw increased demand for value-added product during 2024."

Credit: Rabobank

China approaches 1m metric ton harvest

While China remains hard to pin precise figures on, Kontali believes the country's vannamei harvests will fall just shy of 1m metric tons this year.

"Last year we projected that Chinese production would increase just 2%. We had heard a lot about disease incidents as well as a relative slowdown in production from the greenhouses, but what we saw is that this relative slowdown did not happen as we expected."

"Therefore, China ended up at approximately 5% growth instead of the 2% we had planned for."

This year, the spread of intensively farmed greenhouse shrimp is expected to bring another 5% hike, which by Kontali's estimate would leave the country with roughly 992,000t.

Kontali's China shrimp production figures up to 2024. Credit: Dan Gibson/Undercurrent News

Most of this volume is intended for the domestic market, and Luo Guozhi, a professor with Shanghai Ocean University, explained that demand within China continues to grow.

"The growth rate has slowed down but the market's really tremendous," she said. "In 2023, the consumer ate 2.25kg per capita, in 2024 it increased to 2.5kg per capita, but it's only focused on people on the coastal area. We have the largest area inland that also wants to consume more, and eat much more shrimp."

"In the production stage, this means the shrimp should have a higher tolerance for transport, but that, I think, is a challenge for the farmer."

As a result of its increasing domestic production volumes and the country's own economic uncertainty, Rabobank adds that Chinese import demand is expected to stay soft for the foreseeable future.

Chinese shrimp import growth by month. Credit: Rabobank

Indonesia to follow Vietnam's diversified strategy

Finally, Termaat said that Vietnam and Indonesia, the two largest shrimp-producing nations in Southeast Asia, are also projected by Kontali to see 5% and 6% volume increases this year despite facing in theory the biggest tariff hikes.

For Vietnam, the country has both seen impressive export growth as well as a burgeoning domestic market for live shrimp in recent years.

"Therefore, we saw our 5% increase expectation lead into +6% last year," Termaat said. "Even though the trade data showed an 18% increase during the year, we believe that some of this already came from production volumes at the end of 2023, with a spillover into 2024 trade."

"The domestic market has since decreased, but it's still viable, and at this point in 2025, they're still operating at the same level [as last year]."

Hence, Kontali believes that Vietnam will continue to grow production volumes at the same rate as last year, tariffs or no, projecting a final output forecast of 704,000t.

The country has already negotiated a 20% tariff rate with the US, down from the originally proposed 'reciprocal' tariff of 46%. Still, Vietnam is far from dependent on US sales, with significant shrimp export volumes also going to the EU, Japan, South Korea, and China every year.

Credit: Rabobank

Finally, Indonesia was the only country to see a downturn last year. Originally projected to be a 5% drop in harvest volume, the drop was ultimately just 3%, Termaat said, with strong sales reported during Q4.

This improvement is also being borne out in 2025, he added, and as such Kontali is projecting a 6% uptick in volumes this year, back to around 380,000t of farmed production.

"Still not at the numbers that Indonesia saw in 2021/22, but really the rebound is there, and if the main markets still demand more shrimp, there is the opportunity to grow further for Indonesia with market diversification on their mind."

Rabobank takes a similar view, noting that Indonesia is far more dependent on the US than Vietnam, and more vulnerable to contractions in demand from price inflation.

At the Bali summit, Hendi Efendy, head of international business development at Indonesian aquaculture service company CP Prima, said the country has begun looking in earnest at diversifying shrimp sales into other markets this year.

The country faces an additional 32% tariff on all exports to the US from Aug. 1; as such, Effendy believes the country's future strategy lies in "expanding our markets in Europe, Japan and probably China."

"Our market share in Europe and Japan is not as big as what we expected, but it should increase significantly in the coming years," he added.

Data presented by Kontali showed that of all major shrimp consumption markets, the EU (+14%) and Japan (+11%) were the only two to see double-digit import volume growth last year.

Effendy himself was more bullish on what the world can expect from Indonesia's shrimp sector in 2025, saying the country could produce 10% more vannamei in 2025, which would return harvests to just under 400,000t.

Credit: Rabobank

title: Untitled
content:
The European Commission (EC) has failed to answer the "core question" over the application of the sanctions on Russia's Norebo Holding and Murman Seafood to double-frozen fillets from China, despite clarifying some points. 

On June 26, the EC's department for Financial Stability, Financial Services and Capital Markets Union (FISMA) responded to a June 2 letter from Europe's top seafood processing and importing association, AIPCE-CEP, asking for clarification on the impact of the sanctions on trade. It made it clear that no payments, direct or indirect, to Russia's Norebo Holding and Murman Seafood for the products can take place after May 20, even if a contract had been agreed before that date.

EU importers seek clarity on whether Chinese fillets from Norebo, Murman H&G off limits under sanctions, stocks can be released

The sanctions, for alleged involvement in espionage, were announced on May 20, and this is the last date money can be transferred directly or indirectly to the companies from an EU buyer, the FISMA letter to AIPCE-CEP makes clear. So, any contracts signed before May 20 but not paid "can no longer be fulfilled," FISMA states.

"Contracts to import fishery products agreed before the designation can no longer be fulfilled from the date of designation as long as this fulfillment would result in making funds or economic resources available, directly or indirectly, to or for the benefit of the designated companies," said FISMA.

What is not clear from the response, however, is whether an EU company can buy fillets from China based on raw material from these companies if the processor in China had paid before May 20. In this case, no benefit is flowing back to the two companies after May 20 -- that already happened.

CIF China Norway, Russia H&G cod prices hit new record in week 27 as 21% quota cut looms for 2026

China is the largest buyer of pollock from Russia, much of which is then processed and exported to the EU and especially Germany.

"We don't know, but it is precisely the core question we need a precise answer to. This is not clarified," an executive involved in AIPCE-CEP told Undercurrent News on July 2.

Looking at Chinese data on the Undercurrent trade portal, 292,229 metric tons of frozen pollock, 22,142t of cod, and 7,614t of haddock have been imported from Russia from January to April, the first quarter of 2025.

A chunk of this would be from Norebo and Murman, especially on cod and haddock -- and it's now unclear how much could come back to the EU.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view

The supply chain to China for these products is complex. Sometimes, a European trader will buy headed and gutted (H&G) cod, haddock or pollock from a Russian company, send that to China for processing and pay a cost, then bring back to Europe.

In other cases, Chinese processing companies will buy the H&G based on EU contracts or the assumption of getting them, then sell the fillets on.

The EC's response states that buying products from China or other third-party processing hubs based on cod, haddock or pollock raw material from Norebo and Murman, even bought before May, could constitute an "indirect" payment to the sanctioned companies and may therefore also be prohibited going forward.

"Sourcing fishery products from third-country suppliers (presumably not designated themselves) that themselves sourced those products from the designated companies before their designation has to be assessed against the prohibition to make funds or economic resources available, directly or indirectly, to or for the benefit of the designated companies," the EC stated in response.

EU buyers resist Chinese processors’ push for higher pollock fillet prices as Norebo sanctions add fuel to H&G market

"For instance, does paying the third-country supplier result in part of the payment being subsequently transferred to the designated companies? If yes, EU operators could be considered as making funds indirectly available to the listed persons, which is prohibited by the sanctions," said the EC.

If the H&G was purchased before May 20 by a processor outside the EU, then a company in the bloc buys finished products, the money would not have been "subsequently transferred" back to Russia -- hence the AIPCE-CEP confusion.

FISMA also has a warning for those who could seek to get around the sanctions.

The circumvention prohibition laid down in an EC regulation against Russia from Oct. 8, 2024, "can also be relevant here," the EC said. 

This states: "It shall be prohibited to participate, knowingly and intentionally, in activities the object or effect of which is to circumvent the measures referred to in this Regulation, including by participating in such activities without deliberately seeking that object or effect but being aware that the participation may have that object or effect and accepting that possibility."

The letter constitutes the "informal views" of FISMA, the letter states, and "only the European Court of Justice can provide [a] binding interpretation of EU law."

Russian firm Murman looks to navigate EU sanctions with direct China sales

FISMA states: "On specific cases, we would recommend that you reach out to your national competent authority for sanctions, as member states are in charge of the implementation and enforcement of EU sanctions."  

AIPCE-CEP also asked if European businesses continue to provide "ancillary paid services (including, but not limited to, processing, storage, logistics, and quality control) to third-country suppliers concerning goods that were contractually obtained and fulfilled by those suppliers after May 20, 2025 -- maybe a reference to contract processing in China.

Bombshell sanctions  

There has been much uncertainty in the sector since the EC announced the sanctions on May 20, effective that day, and then did not issue any clarification to industry or Undercurrent.

Since May 20, H&G cod prices have been driven to new record levels since the sanctions, with haddock also on the increase (see below, from the Undercurrent prices portal). On top of this, Norwegian and Russian scientists recommended a 21% cut in the 2026 cod quota on July 1. For haddock, the recommendation is an 18% increase in 2026, which could give some relief to the trade.

Also, on haddock, the main markets are Canada, the UK, and the US -- which are not impacted by the sanctions.

Then, on pollock, in which Norebo is -- or was -- a player in delivering fillets to Europe, fillet and H&G prices were rising anyway (see H&G below). This will likely accelerate due to Norebo being removed from the market, and EU buyers also being unable to trade in finished products produced from H&G bought after May 20.

It's thought Norebo had product in storage for European customers and also on the way which had not been paid for. The company will have to sell this into the Russian market, with other producers then focusing more on exports to Europe, sources said.

Norebo and Murman will likely be forced to shift sales to Russia, China, Brazil, and the UK, Undercurrent previously reported.

Following the EU sanctions, Murman's CEO, Vladimir Khizhnyakov, said the company is pursuing alternative sales strategies. Having previously sold via European traders, the company is "consulting" with other businesses that have experience in direct sales to China for processing, he said.

"The main thing here is that there are potential buyers and sellers for goods. And it is already working," Khizhnyakov said.

Murman claims the sanctions against them are "totally unfounded" and based on misunderstandings, as is the position Norebo has taken.

title: The truth about American seafood, according to those fighting to promote consumption
content:
The US Dietary Guidelines for 2025-2030 are under construction but it's unlikely its seafood-related guidance will vary much from the previous version, covering 2020-2025. That version recommended Americans eat at least eight ounces of seafood per week, or roughly two servings per week. 

One problem: Few Americans are doing that.

What's happening instead, according to the 421-page report delivered in December 2024 by the 2025 Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee (DGAC):

"[The] mean [average] intake of seafood is 0.5 oz equivalent per day for individuals ages 1 year and older and 89% have intakes below the weekly recommendations. 10% to 21% of adults ages 31 years and older have intakes at or above the recommendations while 10% or less of individuals ages 1 through 30 years have intakes at or above the recommendations. Additionally, 34% of non-Hispanic Asian individuals are at or above the recommendations for Seafood compared to 11% of the total population ages 1 year and older."

Efforts to reverse the trend are gaining traction, however.

The Fall in Love with Seafood campaign, led by the nonprofit Seafood Nutrition Partnership (SNP) and rolled out nationwide in February 2024, shows a $4.52 return on every dollar invested, according to updated data shared with Undercurrent News. The nonprofit's Summer Seafood Challenge encourages Americans to commit to eating seafood twice a week for 60 days as part of a broader effort to shift consumer behavior.

With demand for seafood outpacing domestic supply, industry leaders say both wild and farmed sectors must grow together to meet consumer needs and strengthen the US seafood system. Photo: Linda Hughes on Shutterstock.

SNP has a good product to promote, too.

Like beans, "seafood and fish are not only lower in saturated fat, but also higher in omega-3 fats," relative to meats and dairy products, noted DGAC, a panel made up of 20 nationally recognized scientists appointed by the US Department of Health and Human Services and the US Department of Agriculture, in its December report. "Higher omega-3 fat intake from seafood/fish is associated with cardiovascular disease benefits."

"There hasn't been a generic seafood marketing campaign in this country and it shows," Linda Cornish, the founder and president of SNP, told Undercurrent in a recent interview. "Americans love seafood; they just forget about it."

Her group works with retailers to increase seafood's presence in stores while encouraging industry leaders to promote consumption among their communities. "Let's walk the walk and talk the talk," she said.

Capitol Hill event brings attention

Still, improving US seafood consumption will require more than marketing, argued the participants of Capitol Hill Ocean Week, an event held June 3, in Washington, D.C., to discuss ocean-related policies.It brought together officials from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the US State Department, and commercial harvesters and aquaculture producers.

Though consumption is strong, the US is heavily reliant on imports to satisfy demand. Panelists emphasized that stabilizing and growing local production -- through better infrastructure, labor investment and regulatory reform -- is essential to narrowing the gap between what Americans eat and what is produced domestically.

US seafood landings have fallen by about 1 billion pounds annually compared to historical averages, said Emily Menashes, NOAA's deputy assistant administrator for operations, at the event. She pointed to aging infrastructure, labor shortages and international competition as key stressors on the US commercial fishing sector.

Fishing vessels docked in the Northeast US. NOAA officials say aging infrastructure and declining landings are contributing to mounting pressures on the American seafood industry. Photo: NOAA

"Sustainability is about more than just fish populations -- it's about the communities and economies that depend on them," Menashes said.

A recent executive order signed by US president Donald Trump directs federal agencies to develop an "America First Seafood Strategy" focused on modernizing fisheries data, boosting aquaculture and strengthening the domestic supply chain. But speakers at one session emphasized that no strategy will succeed without addressing the human side of the industry.

"You can't build a US-based seafood economy without people," said Imani Black, founder of Minorities in Aquaculture, whose nonprofit trains women and underrepresented groups for aquaculture careers. "There are thousands of jobs going unfilled -- on boats, in hatcheries, in processing facilities."

She added that visibility is a key barrier. "Too few young people see seafood as a viable or visible career path."

Black said engaging new audiences may require new messengers. "Not every waterman wants to be on TikTok," she said. "But if we give creators the tools and the science, they can help tell the story truthfully and effectively." 

Also on the panel was third-generation commercial fisherman Buddy Guindon, founder of Katie's Seafood Market, in Galveston, Texas, who said rebuilding trust starts with transparency. His cooperative, the Gulf of America Shareholders Alliance, runs a tagging program that lets buyers trace seafood back to the boat and crew that caught it. 

Growing farmed, wild sectors

But it's not only about wild-caught seafood. In fact, panelists at the Capitol Hill event rejected the notion that wild and farmed seafood are in competition.

"We have more demand for seafood than we can supply," Menashes said. "We can grow both sectors if we invest in infrastructure, education and workforce."

Dave Hogan, director of the Office of Marine Conservation at the US State Department, said the US is also working to enforce stronger global standards for sustainability and labor practices. "If we want a level playing field, imports must meet the same expectations," he said.

While no single solution will fix the system, panelists said the tools for recovery already exist; what's needed now is coordination and commitment, the panelists said.

"This is a moment of possibility," Menashes said. "We have the science. We have the values. Now we need to build the systems that connect all of that to the market."

Or, as Guindon put it: "People will choose American seafood -- if they know it exists."

title: US Senate panel debates bill to curtail illegal seafood imports
content:
US Senator Dan Sullivan gave his bill to curb illegal seafood imports at a hearing last week of the Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Subcommittee on Coast Guard, Maritime, and Fisheries.

The panel heard testimony on Thursday (June 12) from Alaska Bering Sea Crabbers president Gabriel Prout; Southern Shrimp Alliance trade counsel Nathan Rickard; Center for Strategic & International Studies Southeast Asia Program and Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative director Gregory Poling; and Stephenson Ocean Security Project director Whitley Saumweber.

"US fisheries are the most sustainable fisheries in the world, but sustainably sourced, legally caught, high-quality seafood can't compete with illegally sourced seafood that is being plundered from our oceans," said Dan Sullivan, an Alaska Republican and the panel's chair, in the opening of the hearing.

His bill, the Fighting Foreign Illegal Seafood Harvest (FISH) Act (S. 688), introduced Feb. 24, would create a blacklist of vessels linked to illegal, unreported and regulated fishing activity, increase US Coast Guard enforcement efforts and encourage greater US contributions to the global fight against IUU fishing.

The bill received unanimous approval from the Senate Commerce Committee on April 30 and is to be considered next by the full legislative body. It has six co-sponsors, including three Republicans (Alaska's Lisa Murkowski, Mississippi's Roger Wicker and South Carolina's Lindsey Graham) and three Democrats (Rhode Island's Sheldon Whitehouse, Oregon's Jeff Merkley and Delaware's Lisa Blunt Rochester).

Democrats divert hearing about Trump’s commercial fishing EO to instead focus on DOGE cuts at NOAA

IUU fishing accounts for up to 20% of all fish caught annually, resulting in between $10 billion and $50bn in annual losses for legal operators, Sullivan said at the hearing. China is by far the largest culprit, with a subsidized fleet of approximately 57,000 fishing vessels, backed by its military and implicated in forced labor practices, accounting for 44% of global fishing activity, he said, citing statistics provided by Global Fishing Watch.

"China is ravaging our oceans," Sullivan said.

Prout called out Russia for providing subsidies to build out its fishing fleet and subsequently routing crab through North Korean smuggling networks for eventual processing and relabeling in China. That crab is entering global markets and distorting prices, he said.

"It has heavily subsidized its seafood industry to deliberately undercut US competitors; flooded international markets with underpriced seafood following its 2022 invasion of Ukraine to help fund its war; and contributed to an estimated $1.8bn in losses for the Alaska seafood industry during 2022 and 2023," Prout said.

A US ban on Russian seafood that was tightened in 2023 to include imports of product processed in third countries has helped stabilize Alaska crab-fishing industry, according to Prout.

"This past season, myself and my family, and all the rest of the fishermen who participated in [Alaska's red king crab fishery this season] experienced record prices at the dock for their catch. I can confidently say that I believe that wouldn't have taken effect had there still been a large importation of Russian product coming into the domestic market," Prout said.

Prout and Saumweber praised Sullivan's bill. Saumweber also urged passage of the Illegal Fishing and Forced Labor Prevention Act, introduced previously in the US House of Representatives by California Democrat Jared Huffman. 

Democrats point to NOAA cuts

The Democratic Party's ranking member on the subcommittee, Blunt Rochester called out deep cuts to the budget and staff of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), which is the chief regulator of US fisheries, as harmful to efforts to combat IUU fishing.

"Unfortunately, the administration has fired about 18% of NOAA's Fisheries staff and is looking to cut the budget by 30%. To make matters worse, cuts to the rest of the agency are undermining this work even further," she said. "Due to the ongoing hiring freeze, 30% of NOAA's research ships will not leave the dock this summer. Fewer research ships in the water will result in fewer assessments and surveys, opening the door for illegally caught and fraudulently labeled products to flood the market."

However, Sullivan said the administration of US president Donald Trump should be credited for his "Restoring American Seafood Competitiveness" executive order, which he said contains mechanisms to fight IUU fishing and for his funding increase for the US Coast Guard. 

The order contains language that could potentially result in the expansion of the Seafood Import Monitoring Program, directing it toward species at the highest risk of being tainted by IUU fishing, he said. It also could mandate country-of-origin labeling, which could increase transparency and reduce the amount of illegal seafood sold in the US.

title: EU aims to tighten oversight on IUU by third countries
content:
The EU has reached a provisional deal to strengthen its response to unsustainable fishing practices by third countries.

The updated regulation, which still needs to be approved by the EU Council and Parliament before it can be formally adopted, introduces stricter definitions, deadlines, and enforcement tools to ensure greater international accountability.

The provisional agreement, struck by the pair of bodies, aims to protect marine resources and support EU fishers facing unfair competition.

"The aim is to safeguard the long-term sustainability of shared fish stocks, while also ensuring fair competition for European fishers and protecting EU fishing interests," the EU said in a press release.

If non-cooperative countries fail to comply with EU standards, they could face trade penalties, including seafood import bans.

Key updates include precise criteria for identifying non-compliance, such as excluding other nations from consultations or disregarding shared conservation efforts. Regional fisheries bodies are now formally covered under the EU's enforcement scope.

The European Commission must regularly report on its interactions with third countries to boost transparency. A new 90-day deadline also requires faster responses to EU notifications, encouraging swifter diplomatic solutions.

"Today's agreement gives us stronger tools to tackle non-sustainable fishing practices allowed by third countries and to encourage responsible fishing," said Jacek Czerniak, Polish state secretary for agriculture and rural development.

Currently, the EU regulation 1026/2012 sets out a framework for the EU to adopt measures against non-EU countries that allow non-sustainable fishing practices. These measures can include identifying a country as such, as well as imposing restrictions on imports of fish and fishery products from that country.

title: EU court upholds Atlantic bottom fishing ban amid industry backlash
content:
The EU's General Court has upheld a controversial regulation banning bottom fishing in parts of the northeast Atlantic, rejecting a legal challenge brought by the Spanish government and several fishing industry groups.

The ruling affirms the European Commission (EC)'s 2022 decision to prohibit bottom-contact fishing methods in 87 areas identified as potentially hosting vulnerable marine ecosystems (VMEs).

The court stated that the EC was not required to assess the fragility of ecosystems in relation to specific types of gear -- such as demersal longlines used by many of the affected Spanish fleets -- nor to evaluate the socioeconomic impact of the closures in detail.

The decision has drawn strong criticism from the European Bottom Fishing Alliance (EBFA), representing 20,000 fishers and 7,000 vessels across 14 EU coastal nations.

"This decision, while legally binding, disregards the scientific and technical realities of bottom fisheries," said EBFA chair Ivan Lopez. "The ban has already caused severe disruption to responsible longline fleets, including a 30% drop in catch for some operators within 50 days of implementation."

Lopez added that while the EU legal system must be respected, "it offers few effective options to challenge regulations perceived as disproportionate or harmful to local economies."

He also called on EU lawmakers to review and amend the existing Deep-Sea Access Regulation to better balance environmental protection with the viability of traditional fishing communities.

In contrast, environmental groups welcomed the ruling as a crucial win for marine conservation.

"There is now too much evidence about the damage wrought by wide-scale, repeat bottom trawling to ignore," said Francesco Maletto, an ocean lawyer with ClientEarth, one of several organizations supporting stronger protections for VMEs.

"The court's ruling confirms that precautionary protection of sensitive marine areas is both legal and necessary," he added.

This is the second and third time within a month that EU courts have ruled in favor of ecosystem protection over industry concerns. ClientEarth and other NGOs are also pursuing legal action against several EU member states for failing to enforce bans on harmful fishing practices in marine protected areas.

The issue has gained increased public attention following the release of Ocean with Attenborough, a documentary series featuring footage of bottom trawling that sparked global concern.

title: Wave of support pushes High Seas Treaty closer to enforcement
content:
On June 9, 18 countries ratified the High Seas Treaty during the UN Ocean Conference in Nice, France, marking a significant step in international efforts related to ocean governance.

An additional 17 countries signed the treaty -- marking their intention to ratify it in the future -- bringing the total number of signatories to 134. The 18 new ratifications propel the agreement to a total of 49, just 11 short of the 60 needed for it to enter into force.

The treaty, formally known as the BBNJ agreement, provides the first-ever legal framework to conserve marine biodiversity in areas beyond national jurisdiction, which cover nearly half the planet. It is key to achieving global goals like protecting 30% of the ocean by 2030.

"This is a tidal wave of hope," said Rebecca Hubbard, director of the High Seas Alliance. "With just 11 more ratifications needed, we're on the verge of transforming ocean governance."

New funding pledges, including AUD 10 million ($6.5m) from the Minderoo Foundation and support from Bloomberg Philanthropies for a new marine protected areas (MPA)-focused secretariat, aim to accelerate implementation.

"Protecting the high seas is essential to advancing the 30x30 goal," said Melissa Wright, senior member of the environment team at Bloomberg Philanthropies. "The surge of ratifications today is historic, and we are proud to help accelerate the creation of the first high-seas MPAs."

In another major announcement, French Polynesia revealed plans for the world's largest MPA, covering nearly five million square kilometers, including 1.1m fully or highly protected. 

"This level of ambition is what the world needs to turn the tide in favor of a healthy and productive ocean," said the president of the International Union for Conservation of Nature, Razan Al Mubarak. "French Polynesia has set a new standard for marine conservation leadership."

However, several Peruvian industry associations, including Comex Peru, the Sociedad Nacional de Industrias and the Sociedad Nacional de Pesqueria, said they disagreed with Peru's signing of the BBNJ treaty, arguing that it threatened national sovereignty and undermined the country's control over marine resource management.

They claim the treaty imposes unnecessary restrictions, weakens effective regional fisheries management organizations, and is driven by NGOs with anti-productive agendas. 

"This agreement is being pushed by NGOs seeking to destroy productive sectors such as fishing in our country, which generate thousands of jobs and are an engine of decentralized development," the associations said in a joint statement.

"We reject the government's signing of agreements that affect food security, destroy formal jobs, and undermine private investment. It is surprising that no technical information has been requested from key sectors such as the environment ministry, the production ministry, the Peruvian Marine Institute, business associations, and workers in the sector, among others, for a consensual decision that benefits the national interest."

title: Untitled
content:
Skipjack tuna prices in the Bangkok and Manta processing hubs have softened further, and may have hit their bottom, while various sources at canneries and European supermarkets expressed optimism for the canned tuna sector, noting demand for the category is growing.

In Bangkok, Thailand, canneries are reportedly worried about US tariff uncertainty and Ecuador's intense competitiveness, which has led large buyers in the Asian processing hub to now demand prices below $1,500 per metric ton.

Thai tuna exports to US could fall 60% if tariffs hit 48.5%, says industry chief

In a recent interview with Undercurrent News at the THAIFEX-Anuga Asia trade show, Chanintr Chalisarapong, president of the Thai Tuna Industry Association, said Thailand's tuna exports to the US could drop by as much as 60% if the Trump administration's reciprocal tariffs are enforced at the currently proposed level, raising the total import duty to 48.5%.

"Exports to the US could fall by approximately 50-60% by 2026. If the 36% tariff remains in place long-term, it will become increasingly difficult for Thai exporters to access the US market."  

If no agreement is reached by July 9 or no extension is granted, the reciprocal tariff will rise, bringing the total duty to 48.5%. There have been no updates on negotiations at the time of writing.

In this context, some large Thai canneries have reportedly been able to achieve some deals below $1,500/t for June delivery in Bangkok. One source reported a deal done by a Thai cannery at $1,490/t, while another said the current price in Bangkok is around $1,500/t. Other buyers in the region are believed to be paying slightly more, around $1,520/t and up to $1,550/t.

One Asian source pointed on June 5 to a price range of $1,470-$1,550/t for prices in Bangkok, Thailand. He said that the current level was making it harder for suppliers to push for deals with large canneries at $1,500/t, but this remained the target for June deliveries. Another source in Asia pointed to a range between $1,480/t and $1,550/t in Bangkok and added Thai canneries were "using tariffs as an excuse to push the market down in the face of poor fishing in the Western Pacific Ocean".

Meanwhile, in General Santos City, the Philippines, non-GSP (generalized scheme of preferences) skipjack prices are around $1,500/t.

Ecuador: Competitive edge eroding as fuel subsidy ends?

Meanwhile, according to sources, in Manta, Ecuador, good catches and lower offers from various regions have pressured prices below last month's level of $1,650/t. In mid-May, Undercurrent assessed prices in the Latin American hub at a range of $1,600-$1,650/t.

"Until last week, I was closing deals at $1,600/t. However, some factories are now considering offering $1,550/t to shipowners," one source with an Ecuadorian cannery told Undercurrent on June 5. However, a source from a European cannery stressed that prices in Ecuador remained between $1,600/t and $1,650/t, being supported by strong demand from the local canneries.

"In Ecuador, there is a large amount of yellowfin being caught this year; it might be a historic record. The ex-vessel price for yellowfin has dropped to about $2,100/t for the large fish, plus 10 (size)," the latter source further said. Another source in Ecuador agreed to this price level for yellowfin, although he added that there were offers at various levels.

Earlier this week, the Ecuadorian government ended its diesel fuel subsidy. The move, part of a broader fiscal tightening effort, has sparked concern across the local industry, where fuel represents nearly 36% of operational costs.

One source noted that this move might push Ecuadorian shipowners to refuse deals for skipjack at a price below $1,600/t, and instead support prices in the short term.

Ecuador's government has also pledged $42 million in fleet renovation funding to modernize its aging vessel fleet, most of which are over 50 years old. However, this long-term investment may not immediately offset the cost increase from lost fuel subsidies. 

Indian, Atlantic Oceans

Fishing activity in the Indian Ocean has "slowed down very much" over the last two weeks, with current conditions resembling June's traditionally lean catch periods. Tuna vessels report difficulty finding viable fishing grounds, following a strong May that saw heavy unloadings, particularly at ports in Mauritius and Seychelles.

Despite the catch downturn, prices for skipjack tuna remain stable at around €1,300/t, while yellowfin sits just below €2,000/t, reportedly around €1,950/t. Local canneries in the region, including Seychelles, Mauritius, and Diego Suarez, are using this period to process existing large inventories, and no new unloadings were reported in Seychelles this week.

The lack of immediate price movement is attributed to the still-ample inventories and the usual slight lag between catch trends and market pricing.

In the Atlantic, particularly in the waters off Gabon, catches have been described as "reasonable," although not abundant. Spanish vessels are operating in Mauritania, Dakar (Senegal), and other areas.

Pricing in West Africa remains largely flat. Skipjack prices in Abidjan, Ivory Coast, are steady at around €1,350/t, with buyers aware of competitive offers from the Indian Ocean. Yellowfin prices for smaller grades (20-40kg) are reportedly around €2,250/t, while large yellowfin is scarce due to limited recent catches.

Large Spanish canneries quietly pressure CIF skipjack, yellowfin prices

In Spain, sources said a Spanish cannery quietly secured some yellowfin deals at €2,100/t CIF, with one unconfirmed deal as low as €2,050/t.

Sellers, possibly also from Spain, are believed to have discreetly offloaded some older inventory at these levels. One source said these lower figures are being kept under wraps by buyers to avoid pushing broader market prices down, and by sellers reluctant to publicize steep discounts. 

However, the majority of sources quoted yellowfin prices in Spain at €2,250-€2,300/t in Spain and Italy. One source stressed that the lowest deal done was at €2,150/t, but most deals in Spain have been done between €2,200/t and €2,300/t.

"There were a few particular deals, very specific ones, below €2200/t, but the majority was bought between €2,200/t and €2,300/t," one source said. In Italy, a deal was reportedly done at €2,250/t, but most deals remain slightly above that level, sources said.

Sources also pointed out that skipjack prices delivered in Spain have slightly dropped below last month's level of €1,550/t. However, sources said skipjack prices delivered in Spain remain at €1,500/t-€1,550/t.

"Prices in Spain are between €1,500-€1,550/t for fish from the Atlantic, and between €1,600/t and 1,655/t for fish from the Indian Ocean. Fish from the Indian Ocean are usually a bit more expensive than the ones from the Atlantic, because the size is slightly better. The average size of skipjack from the Indian Ocean is larger than that of the Atlantic, so it commands a slightly higher price," one source said.

Industry sources also told Undercurrent that loin prices delivered into Spain from duty-free origins like Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, or Ecuador are currently around $5,500/t for skipjack and $6,600/t for yellowfin.

title: US recording artists Dolly Parton, Kid Rock enter seafood space with separate retail, foodservice ventures
content:
Two US recording artists entered the seafood space last month in separate ventures targeting both retail and foodservice. 

Country legend Dolly Parton has grown into a global icon known for more than her hit songs "Jolene" and "9 to 5." In 2022, she entered into a partnership with American consumer packaged goods holding company Conagra Brands to get her name and face on a line of baking mixes and frostings. 

Fast-forward to 2025, and Parton's retail food line with Chicago, Illinois-based Conagra has expanded. In May, she and Conagra announced the launch of a new line of single-serve frozen meals, including a shrimp and grits dish.

"I've always believed in the power of a warm, hearty meal, and now with these offerings, I'm bringing a little taste of my own Southern favorites to you," Parton said in a press release. 

Conagra vice president and general manager Tim Nangle elaborated that the expansion into frozen foods was a "natural next step" due to the singer's "genuine love for home-cooked meals and deep connection with fans."

Although Conagra's got a long line of brands in its portfolio, in the frozen seafood space its primary offering is the Mrs. Paul brand of breaded fish products

Other than that, the consumer goods company has some shrimp sprinkled throughout single-serve and skillet-ready frozen meals. Conagra brands include Bertolli and Evol, which both offer different shrimp with pasta options, and Healthy Choice, which has a shrimp fajita power bowl and a cajun-style chicken and shrimp dish.

The new shrimp and grits dish from the Dolly Parton line pairs "succulent" shrimp and cherry tomatoes with creamy white cheddar grits in a "bold, spicy Southern-style sauce." The single-serve dish has a suggested retail price of $4.49 and can be heated in either the microwave or oven.

'The Detroit Cowboy'

But, as noted above, Parton's not the only country artist dabbling with seafood.

On the foodservice side, country rocker/rapper Kid Rock is expanding his presence in the restaurant business with a new seafood-focused dining establishment in Nashville, Tennessee, called The Detroit Cowboy.

Music artist Kid Rock outside his new restaurant in Nashville, Tennessee. Photo Credit: The Detroit Cowboy

The restaurant, which had its grand opening on Tuesday (June 3), is in partnership with the Joe Vicari Restaurant Group, the owners of Joe Muer Seafood, which has two restaurants in the US state of Michigan. A third Joe Muer Seafood location has been open for two years in Nashville, but the restaurant is transitioning into the new Detroit Cowboy.

Kid Rock, whose real name is Robert James Ritchie, opened his first Nashville restaurant, Kid Rock's Big Ass Honky Tonk Rock N' Roll Steakhouse, in 2018. The live music bar, which Ritchie developed in partnership with Ryman Hospitality Properties, specializes in grilled meats and burgers.

Ritchie also had a restaurant in Detroit that he opened in 2017, but that closed in 2020 as a result of backlash from inappropriate comments he made about media personality Oprah Winfrey.

The newest restaurant venture with Joe Muer Seafood, which Ritchie was drawn to as a Detroit native, is being touted as a fine dining experience.

"The Detroit Cowboy by Kid Rock and Joe Muer Seafood seamlessly blends the rich traditions of Joe Muer Seafood's fine dining experience with the soul of both Detroit and Nashville's music scenes and histories, creating a unique destination for lovers of exceptional seafood, steaks, and stories," the restaurant's website boasts. 

"The Detroit Cowboy isn't just a restaurant -- it's a culinary ride like no other, where like-minded folks who love this country can dine in style," Ritchie said of his new venture. "The Detroit Cowboy is the only place on earth where Detroit grit and Nashville swagger collide for the finest dining hangout. The Vicaris and Joe Muer know fine dining, I know how to hang pictures, create a vibe, and make things fun!… all while still holding two middle fingers up high for the haters!"

Shoutout from Trump

The restaurant even got a shoutout from US president Donald Trump on his Truth Social platform this week

"Congratulations to my friend, Kid Rock (I call him Bob!), on the Grand Opening of his new Nashville restaurant, 'The Detroit Cowboy,'" Trump posted. "I hear it is a very friendly MAGA establishment, and look forward to going there sometime soon!"

MAGA, of course, stands for Trump's campaign slogan of "Make America Great Again." Trump could be referring to Ritchie's comment about it being a place for "like-minded folks who love this country." Or he could be referring to one of his many MAGA initiatives.

A post made by US president Donald Trump on TruthSocial June 3, 2025.

Since entering the White House for a second term, Trump has signed an executive order to "restore American seafood competitiveness," which includes boosting US seafood production, sales and exports.

Described as a seafood and chops house, the Detroit Cowboy menu does have a wide assortment of US-sourced seafood, including a Rhode Island fried calamari appetizer, and entrees like the roasted Alaskan halibut, Alaskan king crab legs, lobster pot pie with Maine lobster and Georges Banks seared scallops.

But at the same time, the menu also highlights imported seafood items, including Wester Ross Scottish Salmon and Tristan da Cunha lobster tail. The menu also doesn't provide the sourcing for every seafood item, like the deviled crab cake or the saffron mussels.

Seared Scallops from The Detroit Cowboy, the new restaurant from Kid Rock in Nashville, Tennessee. Photo Credit: The Detroit Cowboy

Another one of Trump's MAGA initiatives has been an immigration crackdown. And Kid Rock's Honky Tonk restaurant had to temporarily close last month when US Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents began conducting raids. One employee of the restaurant said that the manager "came back and told anyone without legal status to go home," reported the Nashville Scene.

Ritchie responded in a post on X: "Clearly I do not have anything to do with day to day operations at my Honky Tonk - but it's good click bait, I get it. That being said I 100% support getting illegal criminals out of our country no matter where they are. I also like President Trump want to speed up the process of getting GREAT immigrants into our country - LEGALLY!"

title: China expands access for marine ingredients but raises bar on compliance
content:
China is becoming more open to global marine ingredient imports, while simultaneously tightening its regulatory grip at home, according to Maggie Xu, China director for IFFO, the Marine Ingredients Organisation.

Speaking at IFFO's members meeting held in Madrid, Spain, on May 12-14, Xu laid out the country's evolving strategy for marine ingredients: encouraging innovation and international trade while enforcing stricter oversight at home.

"Generally speaking, China's market is turning to become more open to imported marine ingredients and novel feed, but law enforcement by Chinese authorities is being more rigorous," Xu said.

"Improved availability and declining global fish oil prices are squeezing domestic profits, so exports of fish oil for animal feed may be restricted. But fish oil for human use is expected to keep growing," she added.

Sustainability targets ‘too ambitious’ as fishmeal sector struggles to certify supply

A significant change is the ongoing revision of the country's Feed Ingredient Catalogue, which now includes enzymatic, highly soluble insect protein and single-cell protein, a major development for global feed innovators.

"These new programs...all require an import license from the ministry of agriculture," Xu explained, indicating that while the door is open, it's heavily guarded.

Labeling requirements are also being updated in tandem with China's national standard for fishmeal. For example, crude fat is now exempted from labels for all fishmeal types, but histamine content must be declared in red fishmeal.

"Administrative measures are being streamlined and made more transparent," she noted. "But members are reminded to ensure consistency of your registration information at both MARA [Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs] and GACC [General Administration of Customs of China]."

Imports climb as local output plummets

Domestically, production of marine ingredients is shrinking. Xu reported China's fishmeal output in 2024 is expected to fall to 400,000 metric tons, a 34% year-on-year decrease, while fish oil output is down 31%, estimated at 82,000t.

This drop is due in part to shrinking profit margins for producers, fewer available raw materials, and the more favorable pricing of imported products.

"The significant decrease is a result of profit decline for domestic fishmeal producers and better fishmeal import improvement," Xu said.

In contrast, imports are surging. Fishmeal imports hit a record high close to 2 million metric tons, up 19% y-o-y. Xu credited a strong rebound from Peru and a price drop that revived demand.

"During the first three months of this year, the trend remained unchanged and fishmeal importation to China increased again by 18% y-o-y," she said.

Fish oil imports have grown even faster. In 2023, they were up 54% y-o-y, and early 2025 numbers show a further 22% increase.

China's sourcing strategy is expanding geographically, with Brazil and the Faroe Islands approved for export, and new African partners such as Mauritania and Gambia now eligible under China's zero-tariff policy for least-developed countries.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
Aquaculture still dominates, but landscape is shifting

Aquaculture remains the backbone of China's marine ingredient consumption. In 2024, aquaculture accounted for 97% of fishmeal and 55% of fish oil usage, according to Xu.

"The national aquaculture output last year was over 60m metric tons, which was up by 4.3% y-o-y," she reported.

"Snakehead fish production was high in 2023, with feed demand expected to stay strong in 2024. Large-mouth bass farming saw increased profitability and is expected to expand by 10%. Japanese amberjack farming declined last year but is recovering, with improved fry availability and increased imports in early 2025," she explained.

Fishmeal prices in China steady with Peruvian anchovy season at halfway point

Offshore and inland aquaculture are growing, with coldwater species such as salmon and trout gaining ground in inland provinces like Heilongjiang.

However, feed production across the sector fell 3.5% last year, reflecting market hesitation. Xu said, "The agricultural sector in China was lacking confidence at the beginning of 2024," though indicators now point toward recovery.

However, one of the most notable shifts is in the fish oil segment for human consumption, known as direct human consumption (DHC). This accounted for 41% of China's fish oil usage in 2024, up significantly due to growing health awareness and China's aging population.

"Compared with the slow increment in feed, the DHC segment demonstrated a larger increase," Xu said. "More attention is being paid to health."

Pet food also grew modestly, taking up around 4% of fish oil consumption.

Geopolitical uncertainty still looms

China's growing openness comes amid ongoing geopolitical tensions. In particular, new tariffs from the US government have impacted bilateral trade in marine ingredients.

"Extra-territorial duty measures adopted by the US government triggered another round of trade wars," Xu warned.

However, a recent US-China economic summit brought hopeful news. Both sides agreed to slash tariffs by 91%, with a temporary 90-day suspension or reduction of others.

"Although limited impact is expected in the short term, a stable and sustainable trade and economic relationship is always welcomed," she concluded.

title: US regional council kicks off meeting by revisiting pelagic trawl rules for Alaska pollock fleet
content:
NEWPORT, Oregon, USA – The US North Pacific Fishery Management Council (NPFMC) is taking baby steps this week toward updating midwater trawl regulations amidst complaints that pelagic gear routinely scrapes the seafloor with impunity.

At stake at the group's nine-day meeting, which started here on Monday (June 2) with advisory panel discussions, is the multi-billion-dollar US pollock industry's ability to maintain the status quo as the largest fishery by volume and a major economic powerhouse in the North Pacific.

But a chorus of critics, from crabbers to salmon harvesters who have found common cause with conservationists, have been building momentum for NPFMC, one of the US' eight regional councils, to more clearly define whether pelagic trawl should be able to come into contact with the bottom.

Alaska pollock industry reports successful A season, but chinook bycatch spiked

Even those charged with enforcing the law admit that the definition of pelagic trawl – last updated in 1993 – isn't clear-cut for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) officers charged with enforcement.

"There's a lot of ambiguity to the way that the current definition can be interpreted," Alex Perry, compliance liaison and analyst with NOAA's Office of Law Enforcement, told the advisory panel on Tuesday (June 3).

The debate in recent years has seen international campaigners call for reform, as Undercurrent reported, with frustration building over the pace of the NPFMC's work on the issue. Its roots are, more recently, in a 2022 motion in response to the collapse of Bristol Bay red king crab stocks that closed that fishery for two successive seasons.

Red king crab. Photograph courtesy of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

The issue was revisited in October 2024 when the NPFMC resolved to update the rules to consider commonly used components in codends, bycatch excluder devices in pelagic gear, and allow monitoring devices.

But the possible solutions being discussed are narrow options and don't address the larger conflict between pollock trawlers and critics demanding stronger enforcement of what constitutes midwater gear.

Commercial crabbers have been among the most vocal, calling for reform of the US trawl sector, complaining that the bycatch and seafloor habitat destruction are taking a toll on Bering Sea fisheries. They say the NPFMC's actions don't go far enough.

"We are concerned with the overall health of Alaska's crab stocks, and the potential impacts mobile bottom contact gears could be having on vulnerable crab on the seafloor and on their habitat," wrote veteran crabber Gabriel Prout, president of  Alaska Bering Sea Crabbers, in one of more than 90 comment letters overwhelmingly critical of the status quo.

Many of the commenters are critical that US regulators allow a gear type to label itself pelagic, used at the midwater, above the seafloor, even though, like its non-pelagic cousin, it routinely makes contact. In February 2022, 2.7% of the North Pacific seafloor showed signs of habitat disturbance from commercial fishing gear.

"If the intended function of pelagic trawl gear is to operate near the seafloor, potentially with seafloor contact," Prout wrote, "then a new gear definition, category, or name that reflects that behavior would be appropriate."

Pollock industry sounds the alarm

But the NPFMC has so far resisted tackling that question head on. Instead, the council has folded in efforts to update the rules to take into account current practices with recent innovations designed to reduce bycatch.

No matter which alternative the council chooses under the current alternatives, it won't alter the status quo or address critics' core demand of keeping pelagic gear off the seafloor.

"There's really no change at all to any fishery management program, management regime for the fisheries, for [total allowable catch (TAC) settings], for bycatch management, any of that," NOAA fisheries management specialist Caleb Taylor told the advisory panel.

The US pollock industry has it could be damaged if the rules are rewritten without care and support.

"A one-size-fits-all approach will not work," Andrea Keikkala, executive director of United Catcher Boats, which represents pollock vessels in the Bering Sea and Gulf of Alaska, wrote in a comment letter.

"The Alaska pollock fishery is the largest in the nation, tasked with feeding the world and supporting coastal economies, while also serving as stewards of marine ecosystems," she added.

Alaskan pollock displayed at the Alaska Seafood Marketing Institute booth at Seafood Expo North America 2024. Credit: Masahiko Takeuchi

Innovations such as salmon excluders are designed to reduce chum bycatch but are currently operated under experimental permits, as Undercurrent reported.

Other designs are already in service, and veteran trawlers warn that if the rules are altered without considering industry advances over the past 32 years since the pelagic gear definition was written, it would be a step backward.

"A lot has changed," said Kodiak trawler Patrick "Paddy" O'Donnell, a member of the advisory panel. He remarked that explicitly limiting the design of nets could preclude technological advances. 

"If we're not careful and too prescriptive here about what we can and can't do, then we're handicapped," O'Donnell added. "We can't move ahead with gear innovation in the future, and we don't know what the future is going to bring."

Alaska crab, pollock fisheries headed for showdown over midwater trawls

That apparent unwillingness to consider cracking down on pelagic gear hitting the seafloor has created tension within the panel and the greater Alaska fishing community. 

"This process shouldn't use word semantics to favor the pollock fishery," wrote Kodiak fisherman Kevin Suydam, who owns crabbing, seining and longlining vessels. 

It has been a slow-burning issue with the US trawl sector coming under increased scrutiny not only from conservationists and global campaigners but also from other gear types.

Hannah Heimbuch, director of Under Sixty Cod Harvesters, representing smaller Pacific cod harvesters in the Gulf of Alaska and Bering Sea, said that until relatively recently trawlers denied that pelagic gear contacted the seafloor.

In recent years, NPFMC reported, on-board observer data and testimony from the trawl fleet itself have made it clear seafloor contact is a routine occurrence despite the 1993 definition.

"That's not a minor technical issue  – it's a major management gap," Heimbuch told the panel. 

The NPFMC has come under criticism from salmon fishermen for scheduling the pelagic trawl debate outside Alaska in early summer when the wild harvest is just getting underway, but during a lull between the pollock A and B seasons.

"We are in the midst of our fishing season, especially the tribal subsistence sector," panel member Mellisa Maktuayaq Johnson, a Tribal member of the Nome Eskimo Community, said during the deliberations.

Below the surface a mystery

Regulations require at least one NPFMC meeting to be held annually in Oregon or Washington, typically in Portland or Seattle. The choice of Newport, a relatively remote coastal town hours from the nearest passenger airport, resulted from urban venues being expensive in June, NOAA planners told Undercurrent.

NPFMC staff have explained how the current rules need attention. Alaska state law prohibits seafloor contact for pelagic trawling. Federal regulations in the Gulf of Alaska say that seafloor contact can't exceed 10%.

Alaska tribes appeal dismissed US pollock lawsuit to higher court

But vessels aren't equipped with monitors, and enforcement agents often can't tell what's happening below the water's surface.

"Without any regulatory requirements for bottom contact sensors and associated data and lack of current technology for enforcement, there is no way to determine whether vessels are meeting the standard," NPFMC fishery analyst Anita Kroska told the AP. 

The advisory panel – which is a mixed group of commercial interests representing pollock, salmon, crab harvesters – will issue its recommendation. After that, the full NPFMC will deliberate this weekend on whether to update the pelagic trawl gear rules.

title: Spanish tuna sector claims 24% drop in tuna catches is down to rising Asian competition
content:
Asian fishing fleets, particularly from China and South Korea, are increasingly dominating key Atlantic fishing grounds, forcing European vessels -- especially those from Spain -- out of their traditional zones due to mounting regulatory burdens, claims a recent article published in El Economista.

The European tuna sector has claimed multiple times that without urgent policy action, the continent risks losing its strategic fishing capacity and becoming entirely reliant on imports.

Fishing body backs new EU commissioner’s pledge amid sector crisis

The Spanish tuna fleet, represented by the industry association of large tuna freezers OPAGAC, raised concerns over what it describes as an unsustainable imbalance.

Since 2016, the European purse seine fleet operating in the eastern Atlantic has shrunk by 38%, from 21 vessels (including 14 Spanish and French) to just 13. Over the same period, their tropical tuna catches fell by 24%, while Asian-flagged vessels operating under third-country registries in African nations such as Ghana, Senegal, and Guinea have increased catches by 68%, it said.

OPAGAC attributes this trend to "discriminatory" enforcement of sustainability rules. While European fleets comply with strict environmental and labor regulations, including limits on catches, mandatory observers onboard, and seasonal bans on fish aggregating devices (FADs), Asian fleets face minimal oversight, it argues.

This has allowed them to expand rapidly in West African waters, where, according to OPAGAC, European vessels have operated since the 1960s and contributed to local development through job creation and infrastructure investments.

The European Commission's regulatory push, combined with measures from the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT), is cited as a key driver of declining competitiveness. Although ICCAT recently agreed to shorten the FAD ban from 72 to 45 days starting in 2025, OPAGAC considers the move insufficient and is calling for stricter, verifiable enforcement across all fleets in shared waters.

Data underscores the shift: while European catches of key tuna species such as yellowfin and bigeye have fallen by 38% and 36%, respectively, since 2016, Ghana alone has increased total tuna catches by 80%, including a 151% surge in bigeye tuna.

Amid growing concern over Europe's declining fishing footprint, the sector is hopeful that newly appointed EU commissioner for fisheries and oceans, Costas Kadis, will prioritize fair competition and sustainability. 

OPAGAC argues that aligning trade access in the form of the EU's autonomous tariff quota system with sustainability criteria is essential to maintaining regulatory coherence, ensuring a level playing field.

title: Untitled
content:
Undercurrent News is reporting live from the Thaifex Anuga Asia food show, held at the IMPACT Muang Thong Thani events hall in Bangkok, Thailand, from May 27 to 31.

Recap all the news from days four and five below, beginning with two originals from reporter Masahiko Takeuchi, posted Friday (May 30):

Thai tuna exports to US could fall 60% if tariffs hit 48.5%, says industry chief

Thailand's tuna exports to the US could drop by as much as 60% if the Trump administration's reciprocal tariffs are enforced at the currently proposed level, raising the total import duty to 48.5%, according to Chanintr Chalisarapong, president of the Thai Tuna Industry Association (TTIA).

China, Japan agree on phased lifting of seafood trade ban

The Chinese and Japanese governments have reached an agreement on procedures to resume seafood exports, paving the way for shipments from 37 of Japan's prefectures -- excluding Fukushima and nearby areas -- to restart once facilities are re-registered, the latter announced on May 30.

Thai canned tuna exports jump in Q1 on US tariff stockpiling

Thailand's canned tuna exports got off to a solid start in 2025. From January to March, the country shipped 140,762 metric tons worth $599 million -- up 5% in volume and 1% in value year-on-year, according to the TTIA.

Reduced quota set to push Norwegian mackerel prices to another record high

Prices for Norwegian mackerel for the upcoming season, which begins in August, will "no doubt" exceed the record levels seen in 2024–25, driven by intensified competition due to a reduced quota, multiple sources told Undercurrent.

Thai importer Todokeru Foods targets regional growth for Japan's premium seafood

Bangkok, Thailand-based importer and distributor Todokeru Foods is working with a major wholesaler from Toyosu Market in Tokyo -- home to the world's largest seafood trade volume -- to expand sales of premium Japanese seafood in Thailand and neighboring countries.

Vinh Hoan launches pangasius instant noodles to maximize fish use

Vietnamese pangasius giant Vinh Hoan Corp. has begun selling a new instant noodle product featuring pangasius surimi noodles in a kimchi-based soup, targeting Asian and European markets.

Chinese buyers rush for Hokkaido scallops ahead of Japan seafood ban reversal

Chinese seafood processors are scrambling to secure Japanese scallops, particularly from Hokkaido, following signs that Beijing will soon lift its ban on Japanese seafood imports, multiple sources told Undercurrent.

Maruha Nichiro expands ultra-low temperature tuna sashimi sales in Thailand

Maruha Nichiro Corp., the world's largest seafood company, is expanding its sales of ultra-low temperature tuna in Thailand as part of a broader push to tap growing seafood demand in Southeast Asia.

title: Daily recap: More from Thaifex 2025; China to lift Japanese seafood ban; Trump’s tariffs switched back on
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Friday, May 30:

China, Japan agree on phased lifting of seafood trade ban

The Chinese and Japanese governments have reached an agreement on procedures to resume seafood exports, paving the way for shipments from 37 of Japan's prefectures -- excluding Fukushima and nearby areas -- to restart once facilities are re-registered, the latter announced Friday (May 30).

Thaifex 2025: Chinese buyers race to lock in Hokkaido scallops ahead of ban lift

Undercurrent News has been reporting from the Thaifex Anuga Asia food show, held at the IMPACT Muang Thong Thani events hall in Bangkok, Thailand, from May 27 to 31.

Trump's tariffs switched back on by federal appeals court

The US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit has paused a ruling that nullified most tariffs imposed earlier this year by US president Donald Trump.

Pace of crab landings in Newfoundland expected to increase with better weather, regulation change

Poor weather, coupled with trip limits, has slowed the pace of landings in the world's largest snow crab fishery since April. However, a regulation change on June 1 will see the pace of landings pick up, an industry source told Undercurrent on Friday (May 30).

Vietnam sees pangasius demand from US, China continue strong

Vietnamese exports of pangasius were stable in April 2025, though Chinese demand remained good and shipments to the US lifted month-on-month again as companies look to beat the tariff deadline, according to data from a consultancy commissioned by Undercurrent to gather and analyze customs and production data, and to the Vietnam Association of Seafood Exporters and Producers.

Thai tuna exports to US could fall 60% if tariffs hit 48.5%, says industry chief

Thailand's tuna exports to the US could drop by as much as 60% if the Trump administration's reciprocal tariffs are enforced at the currently proposed level, raising the total import duty to 48.5%, according to Chanintr Chalisarapong, president of the Thai Tuna Industry Association.

Argentina illex squid landings hit multi-year high, improved Peru supply triggers price drop

Argentina's domestic shortfin illex squid fishery has delivered its strongest performance in years, landing over 170,000 metric tons in the first five months of 2025, as a rebound in Peruvian catches also triggers price declines, according to Undercurrent News industry sources.

Spain's Marfrio reels in hope as jumbo flying squid returns to Peruvian waters

After nearly a year of halted production and supply chain strain, Spanish seafood group Marfrio is cautiously optimistic about the months ahead as the jumbo flying squid (Dosidicus gigas) makes a steady return to Peruvian waters.

Norway salmon prices see modest recovery in short week, but Chile, Scots slump

Spot prices for Norwegian farmed salmon to be delivered in week 23 of 2025 (commencing June 2) have seen a small rebound in value after the drastic fall of the previous week, a period where both Chilean and Scottish prices also took a pounding, sources told Undercurrent.

title: SEA Alliance creating ‘worker voice directory,’ commits to impact review
content:
Fresh off the delivery of a landmark study of migrant labor recruitment practices in global tuna processing, the Seafood Ethics Action Alliance (SEA Alliance) has committed to an impact review and a two-year effort to build a network of seafood industry worker contacts for its membership.

The SEA Alliance -- a group of 39 retailers and seafood businesses that collectively account for 95% of grocery sales in the UK -- is a precompetitive organization dedicated to supporting human rights due diligence in the seafood supply chain. SEA Alliance is supported by UK public body Seafish and funded by the David and Lucile Packard Foundation and the Walton Family Foundation.

Its Responsible Recruitment Tuna study, presented at the 2025 Seafood Expo Global, sought to identify ways to encourage responsible recruitment practices in the tuna shore-based processing sector and to provide mechanisms for improving labor standards for migrant workers.

FREE READ Study spotlights migrant labor recruitment practices in tuna processing

The study found a gap between stated labor policies of tuna buyers and their actual due diligence practices. It placed the blame on complexities in seafood supply chains that impeded buyers from being able to conduct sufficient labor rights enforcement, and a lack of commercial and regulatory pressure resulting in underfunding of mechanisms required for adequate oversight.

Julia Black, SEA Alliance's chair and group ethics and social sustainability senior manager at Hilton Foods, said the report was an example of the organization's commitment to progress on human rights due diligence.

"One of the cornerstones of how we operate is creating a safe space where members can come with these thorny issues and really explore how they can be approached, and how to implement change in the supply chain," Black told Undercurrent News after the presentation of the study.

The next step for member organizations is figuring out how to operationalize the report's recommendations, which include providing incentives for suppliers to streamline supply chains and enforce contractual safeguards, Black said. 

"These changes will be implemented through human resources teams on the supplier side, taking these high-level human rights discussions and tangibly putting checks and balances into how they recruit migrant workers," Black said.

FREE READ Labor activists criticize MSC for enabling abuses in fisheries

One of the biggest challenges facing suppliers is the issue of recruitment fees, Black said. The report urges UK seafood companies to partner with zero-fee recruitment agencies or pay recruitment costs upfront and to implement more active monitoring of recruitment practices.

"The cost of recruitment has traditionally been borne by the worker, but we want to reveal the true cost of recruitment and how it's linked to the true cost of goods. Hopefully that leads to recruiting costs becoming borne by the employer," Black said.

Through the report and its future work, SEA Alliance hopes to create new buyer-supplier collaboration models, Black said.

SEA Alliance is now beginning its next project of building out what it is calling a "worker voice directory" to allow its members to directly contact worker organizations, such as fishing unions, to get information about how laborers are being treated.

"A lot of our members are asking … how they can engage meaningfully with worker organizations," Black said. "[The directory] is about bridging that gap between, for example, a processor in the UK and a union in Ghana, to drive change things for the workers on the ground in these plants and on these boats."

The creation of the directory will be a powerful tool in SEA Alliance's efforts to improve worker rights and support businesses "who actually want to engage on that journey," SEA Alliance head Georgia Worrall told Undercurrent.

The two-year project will be "a massive piece of work," involving global outreach, but will serve to fulfill a demand from SEA Alliance members for direct contact with workers to help them better understand the issues workers are facing.

"What we're missing is that relationship is an actual channel of communication from a retailer to speak to the workers in their supply chain," Worrall said. "We're finding there's a difference in making contacts with workers and then in building those relationships. And I don't think we get that deeper level of information without having conversations on a day-to-day basis."

SEA Alliance has also launched a "commitment to progress" initiative, through which it will engage with an independent third party to complete a 12-month assessment of the organization's results. The organization will then develop a three-year strategic plan based on recommendations provided by the evaluation.

"We want to know if the initiatives we are putting out there are impactful and are successful," Worrell said. "A lot of the time, it's not that businesses don't have the desire to make improvements, they just might not have the tools or support they need. I think our results are really impressive in terms of delivering for our members, but I do think we could have delivered more. For the future, I hope for SEA Alliance is able to provide whatever tailored support our members need to be able to achieve their goals, and that's what we're working toward."
