title: Pacific Islands crack down on IUU fishing to protect tuna stocks
content:
Pacific Island nations have concluded a major regional enforcement operation, targeting illegal fishing activities to safeguard critical tuna stocks.

During Operation TUI MOANA 2025 (OPTM25), a two-week regional operation targeting illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, 10 members of the Pacific Islands Forum Fisheries Agency (FFA) coordinated patrols across their exclusive economic zones and nearby high seas.

The operation led to 76 vessel boardings, nine vessels of interest identified, and one confirmed apprehension for suspected illegal fishing. Authorities also logged 31 vessel sightings and nearly 5,000 satellite detections.

Australia, France, New Zealand, and the US supported the operation, which showcased strong regional cooperation and advanced surveillance capabilities.

Jason Raubani, FFA's officer overseeing the fisheries operations division, praised the effort, calling it a "clear sign of unity and commitment to protecting the region's tuna resources."

"The success of OPTM25 highlights the continued strong regional cooperation that is in place, and the commitment to protecting the rights of members and their valuable tuna resources," he said.

title: Untitled
content:
Fortune International and Vikenco are in settlement negotiations over a lawsuit filed by Fortune subsidiary Boston Sword and Tuna (BST) alleging its former chief financial officer and current Vikenco CEO Chris Marchese stole confidential business information and trade secrets.

Judge Richard G. Stearns of the US District of Massachusetts has given the companies until June 30 to come to an agreement, according to an order issued Wednesday (May 21).

While negotiations are ongoing, Marchese has been placed on "garden leave," during which he will be paid his normal salary but will refrain from working at Vikenco. 

Also on Wednesday, Stearns gave Vikenco until June 12 to respond to BST's complaint, filed April 29, which alleges it caught Marchese violating confidentiality, non-solicitation and non-competition agreements by sending incriminating emails to senior executives at Vikenco. 

Chris Marchese. Photo courtesy of Boston Sword and Tuna.

Marchese and Vikenco used stolen information to set up a competing business selling salmon to US customers and to solicit BST clients, the lawsuit contends.

Marchese joined Vikenco as CEO of its North American subsidiary in December 2024 following a 13-year tenure at BST, which Fortune acquired in May 2023.

Vikenco was a longtime supplier of Boston, Massachusetts-based BST. The lawsuit claims information provided by Marchese allowed it to successfully conduct a planned scale-up of its US business, partially at the expense of  Bensenville, Illinois-headquartered Fortune BST, which claims to have proof it lost several customers as a result.

Earlier in the year, Undercurrent News reported BST had lost a chunk of skin-pack business with retailer Trader Joe's, although that's not mentioned in the lawsuit. 

Vikenco responded to the suit by saying it is an attempt by Fortune to escape fixed-rate contracts for tens of millions of dollars worth of salmon. It argues Marchese's non-compete agreements were voided by BST and are unenforceable.

Vikenco is also pushing for the dispute to be heard in Massachusetts state court rather than federal, per a stipulation in Marchese's employment contract.

Fortune is seeking a restraining order to prevent Vikenco from using BST's trade secrets, the return of any misappropriated information, monetary damages, including punitive compensation and attorneys' fees.

"We are pleased that the court entered the parties’ stipulation that will ensure that there are no further violations of Mr. Marchese’s post-employment restrictions, and that he will be placed on mandatory 'garden leave.' We believe our complaint details compelling evidence of premeditated and brazen actions that directly threaten Fortune’s business, our clients, and the security of our trade secrets, and it is our intent to take the steps necessary to protect our company and the best interests of our customers going forward," a spokesperson for Fortune International told Undercurrent.

Boston Sword and Tuna's headquarters in Boston, Massachusetts. Photo courtesy of BST.

While the two parties work on a settlement, Marchese has agreed not to solicit business from customers he worked with at BST and is forbidden from providing services to Vikenco.

Additionally, Vikenco has agreed not to pursue business from companies that have conducted business with BST in the past 12 months.

However, Vikenco may fulfill orders through mid-June with any businesses that did not have prior relationships with BST or Marchese, as well as a limited set of four customers not identified by name in the court documents.

Vikenco has also been ordered to preserve all data on company computers, phones and other electronic devices, including emails, that may contain confidential information related to Marchese's business activities with BST or its clients."

Vikenco representatives did not respond to a request for comment on the settlement negotiations.

title: US aquaculture industry seeks to strike four rules it says hamper trade, raise costs
content:
The US aquaculture industry has jumped onto the deregulation train being driven by the new president Donald Trump administration, formally requesting the elimination of four rules it claims create unnecessary burdens for live animal trade.

The National Aquaculture Association (NAA) laid out its efforts in an announcement shared Wednesday (May 21) on its LinkedIn page. The group requested changes to four rules in response to a call for public feedback on regulatory updates from the White House Office of Management and Budget. It said the rules are outdated or excessive.

Three of the measures focus on US Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) regulations, while the fourth challenges a transportation requirement enforced by the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration.

For starters, the NAA is challenging federal health inspection rules for imported salmonids, such as trout and salmon. The group said the US Department of Agriculture is now recognized as the national authority for aquatic animal health and that overlapping inspections by USFWS duplicate existing protections under the Animal Health Protection Act.

Another request targets US Department of Transportation rules that limit hours of service and require the use of electronic logging devices for truck drivers. The group said these rules don't work well for transporting live animals, such as fish, because drivers can't stop for long without hurting the animals' well-being.

In one that doesn't seem as related to aquaculture, NAA is asking USFWS to undo its 2016 decision that labeled several salamander species as "injurious wildlife" under the Lacey Act. This classification restricts the import and movement of these species across state lines because they are thought to potentially harm agriculture, forestry, wildlife or human interests.

The North-American lungless Red-backed salamander (Plethodon cinereus) on green moss. Photograph by HWall on Shutterstock.

Salamanders do not play a direct role in aquaculture. However, the NAA appears to be using this case to address a broader legal and policy concern regarding the expansion of federal authority, particularly under the Lacey Act. By naming native species based only on their disease risk, the agency might create a rule that could later impact important aquatic species for farming, like certain fish or shellfish.

The group argues that Congress did not intend for the Lacey Act to include native species, highlighting that 20 of the listed salamanders are originally from the US. They also argue that using the possibility of these salamanders carrying diseases, like Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans (Bsal), as the only reason for their listing is beyond what the law was meant to cover.

Yet another request seeks to eliminate USFWS' overtime and premium inspection fees for processing wildlife shipments outside regular business hours at ports of entry. The group has argued that these fees are not aligned with the 24/7 nature of international trade and impose unnecessary costs on businesses that move live animals, whether dead or alive.

US seafood exporters have done better than regain ground in Ukraine more than three years after Russia first launched its military invasion of the European country, based on the latest report from the US Department of Agriculture.

Vietnamese pangasius farm-gate prices remain firm at five-year high

Vietnamese pangasius farm-gate prices remained firm and at a five-year high through April and into the first week of May, according to the latest updates from a Ho Chi Minh City-based consultancy commissioned by Undercurrent to gather and analyze data.

title: Cooke says Chilean environmental ruling may lead to over $30m in losses
content:
Cooke Aquaculture has filed a new complaint against Chile's Superintendency of the Environment (Superintendencia del Medio Ambiente, or SMA), claiming a recent enforcement order could cost the Canadian seafood giant $30.8 million in combined direct and projected losses.

In a formal filing submitted to the country's Third Environmental Court, Cooke's legal representative, David Cademartori Gamboa, alleged that a resolution issued by the SMA on March 31 is unlawful.

Cooke mulls exit from Chile over disputed suspension of salmon farm operations

The resolution ordered the immediate suspension of salmon stocking at the company's Huillines 2 fish farm in southern Chile, citing potential environmental risks.

Cooke argued the SMA's claims of imminent environmental harm "are unsubstantiated and contradicted by evidence in the agency's own administrative files."

It also claimed that expert opinions from SMA consultants, the ministry of economy, the undersecretariat for fisheries and aquaculture (or SUBPESCA), and the national fisheries and aquaculture service (SERNAPESCA) all conclude that Huillines 2 does not pose a risk to the environment.

"The alleged risk is a fabrication," the filing reads. "There is no technical, legal, or scientific basis for this provisional measure. The supposed danger is no more than a specter conjured by the SMA's own narrative."

Cooke's complaint emphasized the financial consequences of the SMA's decision, detailing an estimated $3.3m in direct losses and $27.5m in lost profits. Beyond the financial impact, the case sets a dangerous precedent for Chile's regulatory framework and investment climate, the company warns.

"If a Chilean court endorses such an unfounded administrative act, the message it sends to the industry, the economy, and the country is disastrous," Cooke said. "This is not just about money. It's about legal certainty."

The Canadian company further criticized the SMA for what it called "a deliberate omission and distortion of key evidence," and accused the regulator of breaching its legal obligations under Chile's administrative procedures law and public service ethics rules.

Cooke seeks recusal of environmental judge over Chile salmon farm suspension

Cooke is asking the court to declare the resolution "illegal, annul it, and strike down any future measures issued on similar grounds." The company is also seeking an exemplary condemnation of legal costs to underscore the seriousness of the matter.

The Third Environmental Court has not yet ruled on the admissibility of the complaint, and the SMA has not commented on the legal challenge.

As Undercurrent News previously reported, the case also involves a second salmon farm, Huillines 3, which was subject to a provisional measure in 2022 ordering Cooke to halt the imminent seeding of 170,000 Atlantic salmon specimens.

This suspension was based on allegations of potential environmental harm, despite an earlier authorized stocking of over 432,000 fish at the same site. 

Cooke also challenged this decision through a judicial appeal, claiming "procedural irregularities and a lack of legal basis."

"According to recent reports, including one commissioned by Chile's SMA, the Huillines 3 farm complies with applicable environmental standards and has not caused appreciable adverse effects on surrounding natural resources," said Cademartori.

"The rule of law has failed the company, a foreign investor that trusted in the country's regulations," he stated.

title: Peruvian jumbo flying squid catch rebounds after tough year as anchovy season achieves 50% of quota
content:
Peru's jumbo flying squid fishery has seen a slow recovery in the first months of 2025, following a significant downturn that left many processing companies struggling for raw material throughout much of last year.

"Catches are recovering; however, sizes being caught are much smaller," one industry source told Undercurrent News during Seafood Expo Global (SEG), noting that while catches have improved, squid being landed are generally smaller than usual. "It is too small to make some products such as rings, or other [value added products] that need bigger sized fish, so we are selling whole fish to China.

"After last year's lack of jumbo flying squid, today we at least have something to do; it's much better than nothing," one source with a large processor noted. "There's progress, but not so much in added value. It's more of a quick-turnover business and about shipping whole [product]," he added.

One of the sources noted during SEG that the price for jumbo flying squid fillets has risen sharply in the wake of the renewed catches. It is currently hovering around $4.50/kg and above, up significantly from the last price of $2.70/kg when the resource was available last year.

Peruvian squid exports dropped year-on-year in 2024. China is one of the largest export markets, as shown in the second graph below.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view

Meanwhile, anchovy catches in the country's centre-north fishing area have surpassed 51% of the allocated 3 million metric tons quota this week, sources told Undercurrent.

Peruvian processors struggle

Last year, Peruvian seafood processing firms endured around six months of severe difficulties due to the lack of jumbo flying squid, one of the country's main export species. This has caused a crisis in Peru's seafood for human consumption.

In response, some processors sought to diversify their product lines, turning to species such as swordfish, scallops, mackerel, and jack mackerel, among others, to keep operations running.

Oceano Corp.'s owner, Ignacio Tirado Melgar, said the company's strategy focused on a renewed commitment to its US and Peruvian operations.

"We are consolidating in Peru, and indirectly, we are also participating in the United States,  with Sea Fresh and The Town Dock. Now, we are going to focus solidly on the United States and operations in Peru," he told Undercurrent at SEG.

A company majority controlled by the owner of Peru's Oceano Corp. has acquired a US East Coast squid company earlier this year, having snapped up Rhode Island's Sea Fresh U.S.A. in 2023.

Francisco Via, Seafrost's business development manager, at the Seafood Expo Global 2025 showing the firm's canned tuna products. Photo Credit: Undercurrent News

Seafrost, one of Peru's largest processing companies, used its canned tuna business last year to expand substantially.

The firm has successfully secured private label contracts with both European and US retailers, pushing its tuna operations to now account for about 50% of its total annual sales, according to Francisco Via, Seafrost's business development manager.

Before the pandemic, tuna comprised only 20-30% of Seafrost's business.

In 2018, Seafrost bought a tuna processing plant in Paita, Peru, from Tri Marine's Peruvian subsidiary Conservera de las Americas, which had acquired it in 2014 from Austral Group for $10m, Undercurrent had reported. Despite not confirming the transaction's value, Seafrost's general manager, Antonio Bologna, had told Undercurrent back then that the acquisition would allow the firm to almost double its canned tuna production capacity and increase its turnover this year by 30%.

IUU fishing control

Meanwhile, Peru is enforcing strict controls on the Asian squid fishing fleet operating near its waters, according to the Peruvian industry association Calamasur. 

Peruvian authorities have asked those vessels to use their satellite tracking system (SISESAT) to access Peruvian ports. Due to this requirement, many Chinese vessels have opted not to comply and are now turning to Chilean ports like Iquique and Talcahuano instead.

Nearly 20 Chinese vessels have sought shelter in Chilean shipyards in recent months, with two currently awaiting approval to dock, despite having records of illegal fishing. Notably, vessels such as Fu Yuan Yu 7872 and Hua Ying 819 have been previously sanctioned by US, Peruvian, and Chinese authorities for illegal fishing and labor violations.

Alfonso Miranda Eyzaguirre, head of Calamasur, praised Peru's firm stance, noting a significant reduction in the presence of Chinese vessels since the 2024 enforcement of the satellite tracking requirement. However, he expressed concern that Chile may now be absorbing these vessels without similar controls, potentially weakening regional efforts against illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing.

Chilean representatives, including Pascual Aguilera of the National Alliance for the Defense of Artisanal Fishing, echoed these concerns, warning that Chile could become a new haven for vessels with questionable practices unless stricter regulations are adopted.

Both Peruvian and Chilean officials are calling for bilateral cooperation to create a unified regional standard for maritime monitoring and enforcement in the South Pacific.

title: US wholesale: Mixed trends for farmed whitefish as tariffs roll-back
content:
The US farmed whitefish market continued to show mixed signals in week 20 (May 12–18), with frozen tilapia prices holding steady, fresh fillet values easing and pangasius and catfish markets moving in opposite directions.

US wholesale pricing for frozen Chinese tilapia fillets remained flat this week, with 3–5 oz moisture-added product averaging $3.35/lb and chem-free fillets of the same size holding at $3.55/lb. However, some low-end offers re-emerged following the May 14 US–China tariff rollback, which lowered the headline tariff from 145% to 30% for 90 days.

That said, the longstanding 25% Section 301 duty remains in place, leaving the effective rate at 55%, a level that industry sources still describe as "semi-functional but painful."

Chinese supply remains limited, with producers in Guangdong, Guangxi and Hainan still navigating production disruptions. However, the 90-day tariff relief is expected to ease some pressure on processors, while alternative routes via Vietnam and Thailand are being explored to reduce exposure to high US duties.

Meanwhile, the fresh tilapia market softened as supply from Brazil and Colombia continues to improve. Brazilian exports have surged, while Colombia and Honduras are also staging recoveries following earlier biological setbacks. Average prices for fresh 3–5 oz fillets dropped to $4.48/lb, down $0.20 or 4.18% week-over-week, according to Undercurrent pricing assessments.

With volume recovering and seasonal demand stabilizing, market participants are warning of a potential price squeeze, particularly if inventories continue to build. Margins remain under pressure, especially for smaller-scale producers.

Pangasius Slips as Supply Outpaces Demand

The pangasius market softened in week 20, with US wholesale prices for Vietnamese 3-5 oz fillets down $0.10 to $2.10/lb, a 4.55% weekly drop. Inventory levels on smaller-sized fillets remain elevated, and demand, particularly in the foodservice sector, has not kept pace with availability.

Buyers remain cautious amid uncertainty surrounding tariffs. Pangasius currently benefits from a temporary 10% US tariff, but that could jump to 46% after July 9 if no new agreement is reached. The looming hike is discouraging forward bookings and creating additional hesitation in the market.

In contrast, Chinese catfish prices rose sharply this week, with average wholesale values up across all sizes. 3–5 oz fillets increased by $0.12 to $3.95/lb, a 3.13% gain, while 7–9 oz fillets reached $4.10/lb, up 4.59% week-over-week.

The price surge reflects tight supply, as imports remain suppressed by the same 55% cumulative tariff affecting tilapia. Buyers looking for alternatives are struggling to find viable options, and sellers report limited flexibility in sourcing. Some importers are delaying orders, while others are securing any available stock amid growing concern that relief will not come quickly.

As trade policies evolve and summer demand patterns take shape, the farmed whitefish market continues to reflect a highly segmented landscape. While the tariff rollback has introduced short-term optimism, uncertainty around Section 301 exemptions, tariff enforcement and production recovery timelines will keep pricing dynamics fluid in the weeks ahead.

title: Untitled
content:
Click here for trial access to our US wholesale seafood pricing platform, where you can find proprietary assessments for farmed salmon, crab, shrimp, scallops, farmed and wild groundfish/whitefish, live and frozen lobster, and octopus, with more soon on the way. 

The US groundfish market maintained a steady-to-firm tone in week 20 (May 12–18), with most key categories holding or building on recent gains despite ongoing trade and pricing uncertainty. While the recently announced 90-day pause on reciprocal tariffs has prompted some cautious optimism, the reality on the ground, particularly for Chinese twice-frozen product, remains largely unchanged.

As part of the US–China agreement announced May 12, reciprocal tariffs have been reduced across the board for 90 days. China's overall tariff rate dropped from 145% to 30%, which includes 10% under the paused reciprocal tariff regime and 20% from earlier fentanyl-related duties.

However, Section 301 tariffs remain in place, meaning key Chinese-processed products like twice-frozen haddock and sole could still face a cumulative 55% tariff if no exemption is renewed by May 31.

Despite this rollback, buyers remain cautious. Most are still hesitant to commit to Q3 and beyond, citing limited clarity on future enforcement, and logistical timelines that may not allow product shipped under the lower rate to arrive before the tariff window closes in August.

Chinese-processed twice-frozen cod and haddock fillets held steady this week, with industry sources saying the rollback is unlikely to meaningfully change buying patterns until more is known about Section 301 outcomes. The effective 55% tariff is still too high for many US importers, particularly on 2x haddock, and buyers are avoiding long-term commitments in the current climate.

On the other hand, single-frozen Icelandic cod and haddock continued their upward trajectory, buoyed by strong European demand, firm raw material pricing and limited inventories in the US. With Iceland enjoying a stable 10% tariff rate, US buyers are increasingly shifting to this origin despite prices creeping above historic norms. As of week 20, pricing levels for Icelandic fillets were described by some traders as entering uncharted territory.

Pacific cod held full steady, continuing to benefit from substitution dynamics as buyers seek relief from rising Atlantic cod costs. Demand for P-cod remains solid, but sellers are struggling with margin compression due to elevated replacement costs and tight raw material availability. Still, it remains a favored option among cost-sensitive buyers navigating inflationary headwinds.

The yellowfin sole market held firm, particularly on larger fillet sizes. Buyers are positioning ahead of the May 31 Section 301 tariff exemption deadline, which, if not extended, could push the cumulative tariff back up to 55%.

While lower than the previously feared 170%, that rate would still pose a material cost burden. Many importers are focusing on landed and tariff-safe inventory until the regulatory picture becomes clearer.

Alaska pollock pricing remained stable in both single- and twice-frozen segments. Substitution appeal, solid retail demand and moderate A season landings are helping manage short-term needs.

However, twice-frozen inventory remains constrained, and replacements are not expected for another four to six weeks. With no immediate relief in sight, pricing for July arrivals is expected to remain firm, and many distributors are securing what they can.

In the head and gutted (H&G) trade, Norwegian 1–2.5kg trawl-caught cod reached record highs, with CIF China prices reported as high as $7,700–$7,750/t in week 20, up $50–100/t from the previous week. Some traders said they had heard H&G offers pushing toward $8,000/t, driven by speculation that US demand could resume amid reduced tariffs, as reported by Undercurrent News.

But whether these levels are sustainable remains unclear. One Chinese processor cautioned that logistics timing and tariff expiration windows may limit how much of this demand materializes in time. US buyers may still face high tariffs on finished products arriving too late to qualify under the 90-day window.

The week 20 groundfish market reflects a sector in wait-and-see mode. While headline tariffs have temporarily dropped, Section 301 and shipping timelines remain the critical variables that will shape US demand. For now, tariff-favored origins like Iceland and Alaska continue to outperform, while China-processed product remains sidelined until deeper clarity on policy and pricing emerges.

title: Vikenco claims Fortune’s ‘invalid’ lawsuit tied to $80m salmon contract dispute
content:
Norwegian salmon processor Vikenco is fighting back against claims made by a US seafood distributor that it conspired to steal confidential business information and trade secrets.

Vikenco said a lawsuit filed by Fortune International is an attempt to escape fixed-rate contracts for tens of millions of dollars worth of salmon.

"[Fortune] agreed in a series of binding contracts to purchase about $80 million worth of salmon from Vikenco in 2025 – contracts BST [Boston Sword and Tuna] now seeks to renege on, using this lawsuit as leverage," the suit said. 

In a May 13 response to a lawsuit filed by Fortune on April 29, Vikenco argued against the validity of Fortune International's claims that its former employee, Chris Marchese, violated noncompete and nondisclosure requirements after he joined Vikenco's US division as CEO in December 2024, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

$500m Norway salmon processor sets up US operation with former Boston Sword exec

Fortune, which acquired BST in 2023, backed by an investment from Bahrain-based Investcorp, claimed in its lawsuit that Marchese, who worked at BST for 13 years, had secretly coordinated the launch of Vikenco's US operations while still employed at BST. Fortune said it had obtained emails that revealed Marchese and Vikenco illegally coordinated a plan to undermine BST's business and give Vikenco an unfair head start in launching into the US market.

Vikenco said Marchese was demoted by BST from chief operating officer to director of salmon and key accounts in late 2024 and lost as much as $100,000 in annual compensation when BST eliminated his regular bonuses. The several non-competition agreements he signed related to his job and bonuses "are unsupported by consideration, were invalidated by numerous material changes in Mr. Marchese's employment (including a significant demotion and reduction in compensation), or were superseded by subsequent agreements," Vikenco alleged.

Marchese met with Fortune chief operating officer Mark Palicki on Oct. 29, 2024, and complained that cost-cutting forced by the company's private equity ownership was negatively impacting BST's customer service and employee morale. Marchese was demoted the next day and left the company by the end of December.

"Marchese's resignation from BST was not a genuinely voluntary separation, but rather it was a constructive discharge, where he felt forced to leave the company where he had built his career in the seafood industry in response to intolerable conditions created by BST and Fortune," Vikenco said.

Because of that, Fortune's non-competition covenants are unenforceable, and "even if one or more of the agreements containing non-solicitation and confidentiality covenants were enforceable, plaintiff's claims would fail for lack of breach or damages," Vikenco said.

Fortune accuses $500m Norwegian salmon giant’s new US entity of unlawfully going direct to Boston Sword customers

Vikenco said none of what Marchese did after he switched firms caused Fortune or BST any irreparable harm and communications he had with BST's customers were not unusual for competitors in the salmon sector. It argues that any communications or materials BST identifies as "confidential" are standard industry documents -- equipment layouts, customer purchase orders, and supplier correspondence -- were either previously known to Vikenco as a BST longtime supplier or are not trade secrets under state law in Massachusetts, where BST is based, or federal law.

"There is nothing unusual or nefarious about these communications. It was business as usual," Vikenco said. 

Marchese has not solicited BST customers, and former customers that ceased working with BST "left of their own volition," Vikenco said.

"The movement of that business reflects the poor business decisions and management imposed on BST after private-equity backed Fortune bought BST, which degraded the quality of BST's customer service," it said.

Vikenco also claims the dispute, if litigated, should be heard in Massachusetts state court rather than federal district court, per a stipulation in Marchese's employment contract.

Fortune is seeking a restraining order to block Vikenco from using BST's trade secrets, a return of any misappropriated information, monetary damages including punitive compensation and attorneys' fees.

title: US shrimp import bill gains company amid wider push for oversight
content:
One of multiple bills aimed at applying more oversight on shrimp imports gained a companion on Tuesday (May 13).

US representative Mike Ezell, a Mississippi Republican, announced the introduction of the Safer Shrimp Imports Act (HR 8364) in the House along with joint sponsors Julia Letlow, a Louisiana Republican, and Troy Carter, a Louisiana Democrat. 

The legislation pairs with S. 667, introduced by senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Mississippi Republican, in February, as reported by Undercurrent News. 

Both bills would prohibit shrimp imports from countries that either lack a formal agreement with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to facilitate facility inspections, or do not operate a food safety system that the FDA deems equivalent to US standards. The FDA would be directed to establish agreements with foreign governments to enable inspections of shrimp processing facilities.

They also would direct the secretary of Health and Human Services to begin negotiating such agreements within 180 days of enactment.

The Food and Drug Administration's White Oak, Maryland, headquarters. The agency has come under scrutiny from lawmakers and industry groups over its oversight of shrimp imports, which account for the vast majority of US consumption.

Shrimp from countries found out of compliance would be classified as adulterated under US law and refused entry into the US market.

The bills also would require annual reports to Congress on the law's implementation, beginning one year after enactment.

SSA points to regulatory gaps

Supporters of the legislation say the current system leaves imported shrimp subject to far less scrutiny than other seafood. Unlike catfish and pangasius, which fall under US Department of Agriculture jurisdiction and must pass equivalency checks before reaching US markets, shrimp imports are not subject to any such pre-approval process.

The Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA), which represents US shrimp fishermen, processors and other domestic industry stakeholders, highlighted this gap in a press release on Tuesday. It argued domestic producers operate at a disadvantage while hundreds of exporters are able to ship shrimp into the US without prior review.

In March 2025, the FDA reported rejecting a shipment of shrimp from a Chinese company named Rudong Zhengxiong Trade Co., SSA noted. Weeks later, it rejected three more entry lines from Zhengxiong (Rudong) Trade Co. Such slight name modifications can allow non-compliant exporters to continue operating under limited oversight, the group contended.

In contrast, the European Union requires Indian and Vietnamese exporters to test shrimp for banned antibiotics or veterinary drugs before the product leaves port, SSA noted. Because the US lacks these requirements, contaminated shrimp may be diverted from stricter markets like the EU to more permissive ones like the US, it warned.

As of Tuesday, neither version of the Safer Shrimp Imports Act has advanced beyond committee. The Senate bill remains before the Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions, with no co-sponsors at the time of introduction.

Just one of three pending bills

The Safer Shrimp Imports Act is one of three bills currently before lawmakers aimed at responding to pressure from domestic shrimp producers. The two other proposals take aim at separate policy gaps: foreign subsidies and the handling of non-compliant imports.

The Save Our Shrimpers Act, introduced on March 11 by US representative Troy Nehls, a Texas Republican, would bar US contributions to international financial institutions if those funds support foreign shrimp farming or processing. It would also require the US Government Accountability Office to report annually on whether these institutions are complying with laws that prohibit support for projects competing with domestic industries, as Undercurrent News reported in March.

The Destruction of Hazardous Imports Act of 2025 (HR 2715) was introduced on April 8 by US representative Clay Higgins, a Louisiana Republican, and co-sponsored by Louisiana Democrat Troy Carter. The bill would give the FDA explicit authority to destroy seafood imports found to contain banned substances or drug residues. It is intended to prevent rejected shipments from being re-exported under slightly altered company names, a tactic that has enabled some exporters to evade enforcement, as Undercurrent reported in February.

Major industry associations, including the Southern Shrimp Alliance and the American Shrimp Processors Association back all three bills. Supporters say the proposals would ensure a more consistent set of food safety and trade rules for shrimp imports.

FDA's capacity to enforce new mandates remains a significant concern. Under current law, the agency is tasked with inspecting more than 19,000 foreign food facilities annually, yet it conducts fewer than 1,000 such inspections per year, as Undercurrent reported.

But none of the bills noted above have progressed beyond committees.

title: Study spotlights migrant labor recruitment practices in tuna processing
content:
With concerns about human rights violations within the seafood sector continually rising, The Responsible Recruitment Tuna study -- launched at Seafood Expo Global in Barcelona, Spain -- marks a significant step in tackling challenges within the sector, and highlights the value of collective action, according to the coalition that has commissioned it.

"A study into the implementation of responsible recruitment practices and the Employer Pays Principle (EPP) in the global tuna processing sector" was co-launched at an event hosted by the Seafood Ethics Action Alliance (SEA Alliance).

The document and its recommendations aim to identify ways to encourage responsible recruitment practices in the tuna shore-based processing sector, to provide mechanisms for improving labour standards for migrant workers.

At the launch event -- chaired by Julia Black, group ethics and social sustainability senior manager at Hilton Food Group and chair of the SEA Alliance -- Georgia Worrall, head of SEA Alliance, outlined how the group of 39 leading UK retailers and seafood businesses, along with a consortium of seafood groups, sought to respond to industry concerns by commissioning the independent study, carried out by Impactt.

That consortium included the British Retail Consortium, Food Network for Ethical Trade, Global Tuna Alliance, and the Seafood Business for Ocean Stewardship. The study was funded by organizations representing participants across the length of the supply chain.

The authors of the study, David Rousseau and Priyanka Kanani -- principal consultants at Impactt -- outlined how the findings highlight both the challenges in establishing enforceable labor standards for migrant workers in tuna processing around the world and explore how the seafood industry is working to improve labor conditions and tackle human rights violations.

With a focus on five countries -- Maldives, Mauritius, the Philippines, Seychelles and Thailand -- the study centres on migrant labour used in tuna processing, building a picture of practices in each country by reviewing regulatory frameworks and conducting interviews and surveys.

It uses inputs from external stakeholders as well as industry members to offer tailored recommendations to buyers, suppliers, and industry associations seeking to ensure that responsible recruitment is implemented throughout supply chains, said the coalition.

"SEA Alliance members are actively seeking a deeper understanding of the issues arising in recruitment in the tuna sector and practical actions that can be taken towards resolving them," said the body. "The study highlights the urgent need for coordinated action between industry associations, governments, and the private sector to eliminate recruitment issues and increase fair treatment of all workers."

Daniel Suddaby, executive director of the Global Tuna Alliance, added:

"The Global Tuna Alliance warmly welcomes this important study and will be promoting its recommendations to strengthen responsible recruitment in the tuna sector. We see this as a valuable contribution to ongoing efforts to ensure fishers' rights by sourcing from socially responsible States and promoting the implementation and verification of best practice social standards throughout the supply chain."

title: Progress at IOTC welcomed, but ISSF calls for stronger action
content:
The International Seafood Sustainability Foundation (ISSF) has welcomed progress made at the recent Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC) meeting, applauding new conservation measures for skipjack, bigeye tuna, and sharks.

IOTC approves 15% bigeye tuna TAC increase, introduces skipjack catch limits

The ISSF welcomed the "cooperative spirit" of IOTC members and noted improvements in quota systems and harvest strategies.

Despite these gains, ISSF emphasized the need for more decisive action. "ISSF remains concerned about weak compliance, diluted conservation measures, and insufficient focus on monitoring and bycatch mitigation. For the IOTC to fulfill its mandate, CPCs must continue to enhance their efforts for science-based management and effective monitoring," ISSF said.

While the skipjack and bigeye measures mark important steps, loopholes could allow overfishing, according to ISSF.

On skipjack, "reaching agreement required provisions that, if fully utilized, risk catches that exceed the TAC, as in previous years. This outcome weakens the potential impact of the new measure and may undermine the integrity of the skipjack MP," ISSF pointed out.

On bigeye, amendments were adopted to apply the new bigeye TAC under the MP and to allocate the catch by countries. ISSF noted, however, "catch limits were not applied across all fleets and, as a result, if all CPCs maximize their fishing opportunities, the new measure may run counter to effective catch controls and operation of the MP."

On shark conservation, a new measure requires shark fins to be naturally attached (FNA) for all landings. However, like similar shark measures in other tuna RFMOs, the new measure includes the option for FNA alternatives, ISSF noted. The organization said that, therefore, it "remains concerned that allowing for these alternatives could undermine the effectiveness of such measures."

The foundation also criticized the lack of discussion around boosting observer coverage and electronic monitoring, calling it a missed opportunity for greater transparency. Small steps forward on vessel monitoring and transshipment oversight were acknowledged.

ISSF concluded by urging contracting and cooperating non-contracting parties to build on this momentum with firmer, science-based management and better enforcement to ensure the long-term sustainability of Indian Ocean fisheries.

title: Report claims global gaps in seafood import controls let IUU goods through
content:
A new report from the EU IUU Fishing Coalition has highlighted critical flaws in global seafood import controls.

It warns that illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing continues to threaten oceans, livelihoods, and food security, said environmental NGO WWF.

The study finds that while catch documentation schemes (CDS) are essential to stop illegal seafood at borders, inconsistent standards between major importers leave gaps.

The report analyzed the EU, US, Japan, and South Korea, which together account for over 60% of global seafood imports, and shows stark differences in their systems.

South Korea leads, meeting all 17 key data requirements (KDEs) but for only three species. The EU will soon meet 16 KDEs with its digital CATCH IT system. The US and Japan trail has weaker requirements and missing key details like vessel IDs.

The report calls for urgent harmonization of CDS, full adoption of the 17 KDEs, digitalization to speed up verification and cut fraud, and expansion of coverage to all wild-caught species. Illegal fishing will keep slipping through without aligned global action and more vigorous enforcement, it said.

The coalition urges countries to collaborate to build interoperable, binding systems that finally close the door on IUU seafood.

title: US Coast Guard detains 12 Mexican fishermen accused of illegally catching red snapper, shark
content:
The US Coast Guard (USCG) is continuing to crack down on illegal fishing in US waters, confirming in a news release that on April 21 it detained 12 Mexican fishermen found allegedly engaged in illegal fishing in federal waters off Southern Texas.

USCG said it detected three lanchas -- 20-30-foot long boats used by Mexican fishermen -- engaged in illegal fishing north of the maritime boundary line in the Gulf of Mexico, which is also being referred to as the Gulf of America under the US president Donald Trump administration.

In addition to taking the 12 fishermen into custody, the USCG also seized approximately 550 pounds of red snapper and 850 lbs of shark.

"The Coast Guard remains unwavering in our mission to protect and defend our nation's maritime borders," lieutenant commander Lisa Motoi, chief of enforcement for the USCG's eighth district, said in a press release. "With highly trained teams aboard our cutters, boats and aircraft, we will continue to aggressively target illegal fishing and the criminal networks it fuels. Our presence at sea is a critical line of defense for the nation's sovereignty."

USCG's latest action comes about a month after it detained eight Mexican fishermen on two lanchas near the US maritime boundary line. Approximately 150 lbs of red snapper were seized during that search. Also, just a few weeks before that, 16 Mexican nationals suspected of illegal fishing were detained, with the USCG confiscating approximately 2,5000 lbs of fish, as reported by Undercurrent News.

Red snapper and shark were seized by the US Coast Guard during a recent search of lanchas off the coast of Texas. Photo Credit: USCG

title: Russian antitrust regulator mulls seafood price, foreign control measures
content:
The Russian antitrust regulator has pledged to introduce an exchange-based system to tighten pricing controls in the domestic seafood market, despite objections from industry groups.

The watchdog has also indicated plans to expand measures against foreign control in the seafood sector.

The Russian Federal Antimonopoly Service (FAS) has determined that long chains of resale transactions have inflated the retail prices of food products, including seafood. It has submitted proposals aimed at stabilizing the price situation to the Federal government, while some cases of improper price hikes have been reported to law enforcement agencies, it said. 

In April, FAS suggested developing exchange-based trading rules for seafood products so as to reduce the length of the supply chains and allow retailers to purchase directly from seafood businesses. The agency's proposal was based on its analysis of domestic pricing and price-setting patterns for pollock, cod, haddock, herring, and pink salmon.

FAS argued that intermediaries between seafood businesses and retail chains are the primary contributors to price inflation. In some cases, the supply chain may include up to six intermediaries with surcharges of up to 50%. As a result, the retail prices of seafood products are increasing by up to 3.5 times, the agency said.

It advocated reducing supply chains and limiting the number of intermediaries by developing exchange-based trade and other alternative sales channels, including fairs and fish markets. The agency also suggested adopting mandatory requirements applicable to exchange-based fish trade, including specific volumes of seafood products to be traded on exchanges. 

The All-Russian Fishery Association (known under its Russian acronym VARPE) said seafood prices might be rising at retail, but not to the fishery sector.

The Russian Shipowners Association said FAS' proposals would not shorten supply chains, but rather could create yet another intermediary and adversely affect existing trade links, pushing retail prices up further.

Russia completes nationalization of Murmansk port

Meanwhile, FAS has also reiterated pledges to crack down on illicit foreign ownership in seafood businesses. Legislation on the size of foreign investments in certain sectors deemed to be "strategic," including the seafood industry due to its importance for the country's food security, has been proposed.

In February, FAS released a draft bill aimed at extending restrictions on foreign involvement in the seafood industry through amendments to existing legislation on investments.

According to the bill, any acquisition by a non-Russian of a stake in a domestic company involved in processing, storage, or transportation of seafood would be subject to approval by a government commission. Previously, this requirement only applied to fishing, while processing, storage, and support services remained open to foreign involvement.

In recent years, sizable seafood assets, including the Murmansk port and Far Eastern crab assets, have been nationalized following claims of "illicit foreign control."

title: Chile’s SMA charges Cermaq with major environmental breaches at two salmon farms
content:
Chile's environmental enforcement authority, the Superintendency of the Environment (Superintendencia del Medio Ambiente, or SMA), has filed serious charges against Cermaq Chile for environmental breaches at two of its aquaculture sites.

The charges stem from significant salmon overproduction at facilities in the Magallanes and Los Lagos regions, actions that breach national environmental regulations and, in one case, threaten protected marine ecosystems.

The first case centers on Cermaq's Punta Islas farm, located within the Kawesqar National Reserve in the Magallanes Region.

Between September 2020 and May 2022, Cermaq produced 4,364 metric tons of salmon at the site, 780t over the maximum authorized limit of 3,584t.

According to SMA documents, the overproduction was confirmed by data from the National Fisheries and Aquaculture Service (SERNAPESCA) and environmental monitoring reports. It revealed "anaerobic seabed conditions, a red flag for environmental stress often caused by excess organic waste and low oxygen levels."

The environmental organization Fundacion Terram, which filed the initial complaint, pointed to the high ecological value of the reserve and called the breach "especially serious" due to its impact on a protected area.

The SMA echoed these concerns, noting that "unauthorized overproduction in such zones not only violates permit conditions but also represents an unpermitted activity in a state-protected area, an aggravating factor under Chilean environmental law."

The second case involves Cermaq's operations at CES Quicavi in the Los Lagos Region, where the SMA identified two instances of overproduction.

The first occurred during the 2018–2019 cycle, when the farm produced 4,022t of salmon, 272t over the authorized limit of 3,750t. A more egregious breach was detected in the 2021–2022 cycle, when production soared to 5,423t, exceeding the legal cap by 1,673t, or 44.63%.

Though not situated in a protected area, the Quicavi site is located in a biologically rich marine channel, and the SMA warned that such levels of overproduction "pose considerable environmental risks."

"Overcrowding and increased organic waste in salmon farms can lead to eutrophication, low oxygen levels, disease outbreaks, and the disruption of benthic ecosystems," it said.

The regulator also stressed that overproduction undermines the assumptions of environmental impact assessments, which are based on specific biomass limits deemed safe for local marine environments.

Both cases have been classified as "serious" infractions, a designation that enables the authority to impose severe penalties. These include the revocation of environmental permits, temporary or permanent closure of facilities, or fines of up to 5,000 annual tax units (UTA), which could amount to several million dollars.

However, if the company proposes and successfully executes an approved compliance plan, it may avoid administrative sanctions altogether.

title: IOTC’s new tuna deal called incomplete without stronger enforcement, labor standards
content:
The 29th session of the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC) concluded on April 17 with the adoption of a management framework for tropical tunas, setting new catch limits for skipjack, bigeye, and yellowfin species.

The newly adopted measures bring all three major tropical tuna species under catch limit regimes for the first time, a move towards sustainable management of these fisheries. A separate measure addressing shark finning was also approved.

"This is a milestone for the region," said Anne-France Mattlet, director of the Europeche Tuna Group. "We now have the tools to ensure the long-term sustainability of these stocks -- but we need consistent, inclusive implementation across all fleets."

The session revealed significant divisions among members, with the skipjack catch measure adopted through voting rather than consensus, raising concerns about the commission's cohesion.

Indonesia's exemption from requirements to deploy IOTC-certified independent observers on at-sea transhipments sparked criticism. These observers are considered essential for monitoring compliance and preventing illegal fishing.

"The growing divide between fleets bound by strict oversight and those operating with minimal controls is extremely worrying. We are witnessing the emergence of a two-speed IOTC," said Xavier Leduc, president of the Europeche Tuna Group.

The commission failed to progress on high-seas boarding and inspection, crew labor standards, and management of minor tuna and billfish stocks, despite scientific recommendations about the poor status of some species.

title: Entangled gray whale freed by NOAA Fisheries team off California coast
content:
An adult gray whale that was found entangled in a gillnet off the US coast of Southern California's Palos Verdes Peninsula has been freed by a National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) team. The incident occurred on April 9.

Responders with NMFS, part of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) also known as NOAA Fisheries, discovered that the gillnet was caught on a rock crab trap on the bottom, which was ultimately "tying the whale in place."

"The whale was anchored in place because of the trap about 100 feet down on the sea floor and was having difficulty coming to the surface to breathe," Justin Greenman, assistant California stranding coordinator for NMFS' west coast region, explained in a news release.

Responders say that the rock crab trap was set near Newport Beach in Orange County. The whale had "dragged" the gear "some distance" before it became caught on the sea floor. 

Efforts to free the whale from the gear took about two hours, with responders requiring specialized tools to cut most of the gear. NOAA said that the whale swam away rapidly upon being freed.

"It wasn't going anywhere because of the way the net was caught," added Justin Viezbicke, California stranding coordinator for NOAA Fisheries, who led the response. "Without our response, the chances of this whale surviving were very low."

NOAA's response to the whale entanglement comes as the administration of US president Donald Trump seeks to drastically scale back the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Under the newly proposed definition, endangered species would only be protected from intentional killing or injury caused by activities such as hunting, trapping or harassment.

If interpreted broadly, the change could dramatically alter US fisheries management and regulation. Enforcement and regulation of ESA has shaped US commercial fishing regulation, and fights over the interpretation of the law and how it protects species like the North Atlantic right whale along the Atlantic coast, humpback and gray whales along the Pacific coast, and marine turtles in the US Southeast have resulted in numerous lawsuits, as reported by Undercurrent News.

title: Untitled
content:
The deadline for getting seafood or other products into the US to avoid the higher, country-specific tariff rates threatened but suspended for 90 days by US president Donald Trump is July 9, a growing consensus of trade attorneys and shrimp industry professionals interviewed by Undercurrent News agree.

That means the product must have already arrived in the US by that date, not be on the water or otherwise in transit to the US, believes trade attorney Jessica Rifkin, a principal with the law firm of Olsson Frank Weeda, among others.

The confusion relates to language contained in executive order (EO) 14266, issued by Trump issued on April 9 to modify his EO 14257, issued on April 2.

The earlier EO applied a generalized 10% tariff on goods from nearly all countries and hit several dozen countries with much higher "reciprocal" tariffs, including such major seafood sources as Vietnam (46%), Indonesia (32%), India (26%) and the European Union (20%). EO 14266 declared that the generalized 10% tariffs remain on all countries but it suspended the higher tariffs for 90 days, until July 9 at 12:01 a.m. eastern time.

Though relieved to have more time, seafood exporters and importers were confused by the additional language contained in EO 14266 regarding shipping. Some argued that it meant the product had to be in a shipping container en route to the US by 12:01 a.m. eastern on July 9 while others argued it meant the product must've already arrived in the US by that time.

"I read it as an arrival deadline," said Rifkin. "There is no automatic exception from tariff actions for goods that are in transit at the time the new tariffs go into effect. The exemptions for in-transit merchandise are specifically provided or not provided by the executive orders for each tariff action."

And that didn't happen in EO 14266, she emphasized.

Tariff-hit Asian packers scramble to make US shipments amid confusion over July 9 deadline

Rifkin gave the examples of the earlier fentanyl-related EOs that Trump issued in February and March.

The first one, EO 14193, was issued Feb. 7, hitting China with a 10% tariff starting on Feb. 4. It made an exception for goods that were in transit to the US by Feb. 1. The second, EO 14228, issued on March 7, raised the tariff on China to 20% but gave no additional transit grace period. It simply hit Chinese goods entering the US after March 4 with an additional 10% duty.  

"You really have to be kind of guided by what's in the executive order or not," she advised, noting that so far, there are no new instructions from Customs and Border Patrol to suggest imports will have more time.

'I could read it 10 times and still not know ...'

The specific language in EO 14266 that has everyone confused is in section 2. It reads:

"Sec. 2. Suspension of Country-Specific Ad Valorem Rates of Duty. Effective with respect to goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on April 10, 2025, enforcement of the second paragraph of section 3(a) of Executive Order 14257 is suspended until 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on July 9, 2025.  Effective at 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on April 10, 2025, and until 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on July 9, 2025, all articles imported into the customs territory of the United States from the trading partners enumerated in Annex I to Executive Order 14257 shall be, consistent with law, subject to an additional ad valorem rate of duty of 10%, subject to all applicable exceptions set forth in Executive Order 14257." 

"Never in my career have I seen this level of chaos," said one shrimp company executive, who has decades of experience in the sector, in relation to the administration's handling of the tariffs.

A top executive at another large shrimp importer expressed anxiety when Undercurrent caught up with him this week. 

"I do not know if I should scratch my watch or wind my a**!" he said. "It is still difficult to get answers and interpret how to move forward on the 90-day exclusion. Each day the clock closes in on the 90 days, and it is going to take some work for everyone to understand and move forward with confidence."

Additionally, Trump keeps changing direction.

"It can change again on a moment's notice as we have seen numerous times with this administration," the top shrimp company exec said. "Truthfully, everyone is still confused with dates and times on the initial order, let alone the 90-day terms. ... Your section 2 statement has no clarity. I could read it 10 times and still not know for certain what it means."

Imported Indonesian shrimp in a Safeway grocery store in Silver Spring, Maryland, in March 2025. Photograph by Jason Huffman.

However, two major suppliers of shrimp from Asia interviewed by Undercurrent shared the same opinion as Rifkin. They are among many in the industry racing to get product on the water to the US to avoid the higher tariff rates. 

It takes five to eight weeks to ship from India and Southeast Asia to the US, depending on the origin and final port in the US.  The July 9 deadline is not an issue for Ecuador, however, as the South American country was only hit with 10%.

US shrimp wholesale prices rocket up amid buying surge in advance of bigger tariffs

From India, US East Coast ports take around 40-50 days, with a shipping time of 36-38 days to the West Coast, sources said. Then, to Houston, Texas, a large port in the south of the US, it's 50-55 days.

US shrimp importers are raising their prices across the entirety of the category again this week, protecting their current inventory and advancing imports ahead of a critical deadline, as reported by Undercurrent. 

"They have clearly said shipping to arrive" before the July 9 date to get the 10% tariff, an executive with a major Indian shrimp supplier told Undercurrent, asking not to be quoted by name.

India is the number one supplier of shrimp to the US, followed by Ecuador, Indonesia, Vietnam and Thailand, as the data below from the Undercurrent trade portal shows.

title: China ratifies Port State Measures Agreement
content:
China, the world's largest fishing nation, has officially become a member state of the Port State Measures Agreement (PSMA), signing to ratify it on April 16, 2025.

Led by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations, the PSMA entered into force in 2016 as the first binding international agreement targeting illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing through port state measures.

China submitted its instrument of accession on March 17, 2025, and formally joined the agreement one month later, according to China's Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs (MOA).

"China's accession to the PSMA is a milestone in the global effort towards responsible governance and sustainable development of fisheries," said Qu Dongyu, director-general of the FAO. "This step reflects the growing strong commitment of all the states that preceded and those who will follow China in joining hands to combat IUU fishing through the PSMA framework."

"China is a major fisheries nation and also a responsible one. When it comes to combating illegal fishing, we have always maintained a stance of zero tolerance," added Liu Xinzhong, MOA director-general for the fisheries and fishery administration bureau.

"Combating illegal fishing is the most important measure for conserving resources," Liu continued. "For a long time, the international community has been exploring effective approaches -- some focus on law enforcement, others on penalties. However, using ports to restrict, combat, and govern illegal fishing is likely one of the best solutions."

Regardless of how the catch is obtained, it must eventually be landed and sold, and ports are the only gateway for that, he said. Therefore, implementing port state measures to fight illegal fishing is widely recognized by us as one of the most effective approaches.

According to the MOA, in 2024, China operated 167 approved distant-water fishing enterprises and over 2,470 overseas fishing vessels. These fleets operated across the high seas of the Pacific, Indian, and Atlantic Oceans, the Southern Ocean, and within the exclusive economic zones of partner countries with an total annual catch reached approximately 2.19 million metric tons. Despite this vast scale, China claims to maintain a generally stable distant-water fishing fleet under its control policies.

To align with the PSMA and strengthen legal enforcement, China is actively advancing the revision of its Fisheries Law.

"In fulfilling our obligations under the PSMA, we have been taking action in the past, and there is still a long way to go. The core issue lies in the legal and regulatory framework -- every policy must be supported by laws and regulations," Liu said.

On Oct. 18, 2024, a draft revision of the Fisheries Law of the People's Republic of China was approved by the State Council. The draft includes provisions that align with the PSMA, providing the legal foundation necessary for enforcing port state measures, Liu added.

In 2025, China plans to launch at least 10 fishery enforcement campaigns.

These include initiatives supporting the decade-long fishing ban, the seasonal moratorium on marine fishing, and the inspection and supervision of foreign-flagged fishing vessels operating in Chinese waters. The government also aims to strengthen enforcement capacity by training law enforcement personnel and assembling expert teams for review, assessment, and negotiation efforts, he concluded.

Research commissioned by The Pew Charitable Trusts has identified China as having the top 10 busiest ports in the world based on the total number of fishing and carrier vessel visits. That same research also ranked China as one of the countries in Asia with the highest risk in terms of its ability to effectively combat IUU fishing, due mainly to low governance levels.

"While the PSMA predominantly focuses on foreign-flagged fishing vessels visiting another country's ports, the treaty also contains a critical requirement that parties investigate their own vessels when wrongdoing is suspected and punish them if it's confirmed. To date, most countries have focused on implementation as it relates to foreign vessels, which has led to many distant-water fishing vessels returning to domestic ports to avoid PSMA-triggered inspections in foreign ports. China, which has both the largest distant-water and domestic fleets in the world and has approached PSMA adoption very seriously, can help change that narrative," it said.

title: Trump moves to weaken Endangered Species Act by redefining ‘harm’
content:
The administration of US president Donald Trump is seeking to drastically scale back the Endangered Species Act by tightening the definition of the word "harm."

Under the newly proposed definition, endangered species would only be protected from intentional killing or injury caused by activities such as hunting, trapping or harassment, according to a joint press release issued by the US National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) and the US Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS).

The change is intended to scale back protections against the destruction of critical habitat for endangered species, said Conservation Law Foundation senior attorney Erica Fuller.

"It's probably the first of many direct assaults on the Endangered Species Act, and I'm sure it will be challenged," she told Undercurrent News.

The change in interpretation could undermine the Endangered Species Act's (ESA's) current legal prohibition on habitat modification or degradation that kills or injures wildlife by significantly impairing essential behavioral patterns including breeding, feeding or sheltering, Fuller said.

US president Donald Trump speaking at the White House. Photo courtesy of the White House.

But if the Trump administration pushes its reinterpretation further, it could undermine protections provided under the ESA's "take" restrictions, which forbid harming or harassing endangered animals themselves.

If interpreted more broadly, the change could dramatically alter US fisheries management and regulation. Enforcement and regulation of the Endangered Species Act has shaped US commercial fishing regulation, and fights over the interpretation of the law and how it protects species like the North Atlantic right whale along the Atlantic coast, humpback and gray whales along the Pacific coast, and marine turtles in the US Southeast have resulted in numerous lawsuits.

In a recent high-profile case, the Maine Lobstermen's Association (MLA) sued the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), arguing it went too far in setting stricter trap rope rules to prevent entanglement of right whales. MLA won that case in 2023 when the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia overturned a judgment by US district court judge James Boasberg, as reported by Undercurrent.

In their joint statement, NMFS and FWS said the change comes in response to the US Supreme Court's decision in the Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo case, which overruled the so-called "Chevron deference." Chevron had given federal agencies wide latitude to interpret vague edicts from Congress and craft regulations based off their best understanding of scientific consensus.

"This proposed rule aims to align the definition with the plain text of the ESA, as informed by historical and legal interpretations of 'take' as an affirmative act directly affecting wildlife," they said.

The federal agencies said their interpretation of the ESA will now "match the single, best meaning of the statute—not an agency's own preferred interpretation."

"FWS and NMFS propose that the statutory definition of "take"—encompassing actions like harass, pursue, hunt, or kill—is sufficient without further elaboration of 'harm' by regulation," they said.

The proposed change could also impact US seafood imports.

The ESA prohibits the importing, exporting, transporting or selling of endangered species of fish, wildlife, and plants in interstate or foreign commerce, and several countries have been prohibited or limited in their ability to export some seafood to the US due to the US government's declaration they have not done enough to protect marine endangered species.

For example, the US considered banning all seafood imports from Mexico after determining the country was not adequately protecting the critically endangered vaquita porpoise or totoaba fish. 

A vaquita porpoise. Credit: WWF

Public commentary on the proposed alteration is now open for the next 30 days. If adopted, the change will not apply retroactively and will not affect existing permits, the agencies said.

The ESA, signed into law in 1973 by then-president Richard Nixon, was aimed at protecting threatened and endangered fish, wildlife and plants from extinction, and created civil and criminal penalties for violations.

The move to curb its reach aligns with Trump's stated goals of increasing commercial development and eliminating regulations.

Industry groups and some congressional Republicans have pushed for years to gut the ESA, said Drew Caputo, vice president of litigation for lands, wildlife and oceans at environmental law organization Earthjustice.

"[They] want to get rid of this definition so they can make the argument that unless you actually put a gun to a species and kill it, your activity is perfectly legal under the Endangered Species Act," he told The New York Times.

The change would repeal a rule upheld by the US Supreme Court in 1995, in Babbitt v. Sweet Home Chapter of Communities for a Great Oregon. In that case, the court ruled against property owners who claimed the ESA should not prevent them from building on a habitat deemed critical for endangered species, as any harm caused to them would be indirect.

A NOAA spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request from Undercurrent for clarification on how the proposed change would impact fisheries management. 

Noah Greenwald, endangered species director for the Center for Biological Diversity, named logging of Alaska's Tongass National Forest, which Trump unsuccessfully attempted to initiate in his first term, as a potential repercussion of the change in interpretation. The area's streams and shorelines provide habitat for all five species of Pacific salmon, as well as other animals that are endangered, including fin and sperm whales.

"We'll absolutely challenge this," Greenwald said.

title: ‘You’re (re)fired!’ NOAA scientists sacked after appeals court nixes US judge’s reprieve
content:
A US appeals court earlier this week overruled a lower judge's order that kept federal agencies from terminating thousands of "probationary" employees lacking civil service protections. 

A day later, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Agency (NOAA) employees were informed that they had again been fired.

"The NOAA probationary employees who were fired and then reinstated and put on admin leave have just been re-fired," an unnamed NOAA scientist told Undercurrent News on Thursday (April 10).

Trump administration begins implementing mass firings at NOAA

US states had sued the federal government, arguing that cutting thousands of employees without notice had put unreasonable hardship on the states.

A judge issued a temporary injunction in mid-March, and the federal agencies reversed course on March 17. As Undercurrent reported, NOAA informed hundreds of federal fisheries employees that they were back on the payroll but would be placed on leave, preventing them from returning to duty. 

'Some great new hires'

But that court-enforced limbo is apparently over, with the Trump administration free to enforce its terminations, according to a four-sentence letter dated April 10 obtained by Undercurrent. 

Immediately affected are hundreds of federal scientists and other support staff within NOAA Fisheries, which regulates harvests in the US' exclusive economic zone (EEZ).

Those let go included "some great new hires, some with extensive non-federal experience, or who had changed federal jobs within the last year," NOAA's top administrator in Alaska, Jon Kurland, recently told the North Pacific Fishery Council during last week's regulatory briefing.

As Undercurrent reported, the capacity of the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) is strained by the loss of its workforce, with agency leaders warning of uncertainties ahead for science-based fisheries management. 

"I don't currently know the full aggregate numbers, but NMFS will need to adjust to this new reality," Kurland said on April 3.

Asked for comment, NOAA's public affairs would not address the unfolding situation.

"Per long-standing practice, we are not discussing internal personnel and management matters," Sally Martinelli of M2 Strategy, a private firm contracted to do media relations for the federal agency, wrote to Undercurrent in an email.

NOAA staff on leave dismissed

The notice to the fired probationary employees, who had been in a state of limbo since at least March 17, added that the federal government would not be paying them beyond the day they were initially fired.

US fishing groups ask Trump administration to ‘prioritize stability and predictability’ in fisheries management

"The Department will waive any indebtedness created by the court's order that you be paid beyond your termination date," John Guenter, the US Department of Commerce's acting general counsel, wrote to individual employees on April 10.

Seafood industry leaders have reacted to the reduced federal fisheries staff with growing alarm. 

As Undercurrent reported, before the mass firings began, many within the US seafood industry expressed their private worries that the Trump administration's zeal for reducing the federal bureaucracy could threaten the bedrock of the Magnuson-Stevens Act.

The US government's regulatory regime relies on stock assessments conducted by federal scientists that are used to set sustainable and economical harvest levels. There have long been fears they could be a casualty upending science-based management.

Beyond the cutback to federal fisheries management, there are other fears of losing federal services. NOAA also runs the National Weather Service, which mariners rely upon for navigational safety.

Martinelli, the public relations contractor, said the federal agency's work continues.

"NOAA remains dedicated to its mission, providing timely information, research, and resources that serve the American public and ensure our nation’s environmental and economic resilience," she wrote.

title: Chinese squid fishing vessels near Peru again as local prices fall
content:
Concerns over illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing have resurfaced in Peru as Chinese squid fishing vessels once again approach the Latin American nation's waters.

In 2024, 400 unauthorized foreign squid fishing vessels reportedly entered Peruvian ports. This came as jumbo flying squid [also known as giant squid] catches sharply declined.

Peru's production ministry, also known as PRODUCE, issued Supreme Decree No. 014-2024-PRODUCE. The decree aims to tighten oversight of foreign fleets, particularly those targeting jumbo flying squid and requires these vessels to install Peru's satellite tracking system, known as SISESAT, to use national ports.

The regulation has had an immediate effect, according to Alfonso Miranda Eyzaguirre, president of the South Pacific Giant Squid Management Committee (CALAMASUR). Since its implementation, no foreign squid vessels have entered Peruvian ports except for one medical emergency.

However, although the law mandates foreign vessels install the SISESAT tracking equipment, none have done so, according to Calamasur. Instead, several ships have opted to dock in Chile, bypassing Peruvian controls altogether.

To address implementation challenges, Calamasur, in collaboration with the Universidad Científica del Sur, released a policy paper analyzing the decree. The study praises Peru's officials for closing oversight loopholes but highlights potential new vulnerabilities. Notably, a provision in the final decree version allows foreign vessels to transmit tracking data from their home country's approved system as compatible with SISESAT rather than installing the Peruvian device.

This clause could open gaps in enforcement if not managed strictly, Piero Rojas, a legal expert and co-author of the paper, warned. The homologation process allows foreign tracking signals to be accepted without public consultation or impact assessment, raising red flags for transparency and technical reliability, he said.

Fisheries engineer Ivan Gomez further cautioned that foreign tracking systems might lack the robust alarm and alert functions built into Peru's artisanal fleet devices, which are critical for real-time intervention in case of illegal activity.

Miranda emphasized the issue's urgency, noting that foreign squid fleets approach the South Pacific each year around this time.

"This decree is a step forward," Miranda said, "but it must be implemented with transparency, technical rigor, and collaboration."

Peruvian prices 

Meanwhile, jumbo flying squid prices dropped by 30% in just days, falling from PEN 7 to 5 per kilogram ($1.88-1.35/t), reports the Peruvian news service Infobae. 

Peru’s Society of Artisanal Fishing, also known as Sonapescal, called this drop abrupt and unjustified, blaming it on alleged price-fixing by freezing companies, not market conditions.

This sudden fall threatens the livelihoods of thousands of coastal families, it said.

Sonapescal denounced speculative practices, lack of state regulation, and internal disorganization among fishers as structural issues worsening the crisis. The group urged fair pricing, transparency, and stronger coordination across the sector to ensure sustainable, equitable fishing.

Peru's squid exports drop last year can be seen in the graph below.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
Chilean catches recover 

While squid catches in Peru dropped last year, in neighboring Chile they have recovered.

Chile's jumbo flying squid [jibia in Chile] exports have experienced a dramatic 211% increase between 2019 and 2024, driven by a rise in artisanal fishing and strong international demand, especially from countries like South Korea, Spain, Japan, and China, Chilean news service Emol reported.

This growth comes despite initial concerns following the implementation of the so called jibia law, which banned industrial trawling and limited jibia fishing to artisanal methods (hand lines and jigs). The law caused significant job losses in the industrial sector, including the closure of six processing plants and the loss of 1,700 jobs, most of them held by women.

While exports initially dropped post-law, things have changed since 2022, as small and medium enterprises (SMEs) ramped up their exports. In 2024, Chilean exports reached $178 million, a 56% increase from 2023. Early 2025 data shows a 923% year-on-year growth in January and February alone, as shown in the graph below.
