title: US domestic shrimp industry continues to back Trump tariffs, even at lower rate
content:
The Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA), a trade organization representing the US domestic shrimp industry, continues to praise global tariffs implemented by US president Donald Trump, even after he lowered rates for many of the world's largest shrimp producers to 10% on Wednesday (April 9).

"It is encouraging that the Trump administration's tariffs have prompted countries to show a new willingness to address trade policies disadvantaging American producers. We want to compete in a market where competitors cannot use intolerable practices like forced labor and banned antibiotics to undercut us," said SSA executive director John Williams. 

For over a decade, SSA has called for the US government to take action against India, Ecuador, Indonesia and Vietnam -- the countries responsible for the vast majority of US shrimp imports -- alleging unfair trade practices. On April 2, the day Trump delivered his reciprocal tariffs, Williams said the move would slow imports and "prevent Americans from becoming completely dependent on foreign shrimp producers while the administration addresses harmful trade policies and enforcement deficiencies," Undercurrent reported.

US shrimp imports increase for four straight months in advance of new tariffs

Despite Trump dropping the rates on India, Indonesia and Vietnam from above 30% to the lower 10% rate it placed on Ecuador, Williams said his group still backed the president.

"For shrimpers, tariffs respond to an urgent need to offset unfair trade. After decades of US-supported investment in foreign shrimp aquaculture, it's time to support our well-regulated, healthful, sustainable domestic shrimp industry instead," he said. "Failing to act immediately risks outsourcing America's most consumed seafood to industries that engage in horrible practices and losing our commercial domestic shrimp industry."

Support from the shrimp industry

The US shrimp industry has received high-profile coverage of its support for the tariffs from The New York Times and NBC News.

Billy Nungesser, the lieutenant governor of Louisiana, called the tariffs "good news" for his state's shrimp industry. 

"We will continue advocating for increased regulation and inspection of foreign seafood while promoting wild-caught shrimp from off the Louisiana Gulf Coast as the healthiest and tastiest in the world," he told Axios.

Imported products represent 94% of all shrimp consumed in the US -- and 90% of that total comes from India, Ecuador, Indonesia and Vietnam.

The total value of the domestic shrimp fishery fell from $522 million in 2021 to $268m in 2023, and US shrimp prices remain near historically low values, according to NOAA Fisheries.

Even though the industry has shrunk by around 40% in the past few decades, it still employs an estimated 15,000 people, SSA claims.

Jeremy Zirlott, the founder and owner of Coden, Alabama-based Zirlott Trawlers, is a third-generation fisherman and SSA board member. He told Undercurrent News many shrimping businesses in the US South have closed because they've been unable to compete with cheaper imports.

"In the last 25 years, it's probably 40% of what it was, and we've seen a 60% loss in infrastructure. Boats captains and crews are disappearing -- you almost cannot find a good, young captain anymore," he said. "It's definitely got tougher and tougher, and without some major intervention, we're going to go away."

Jeremy Zirlott/Photo courtesy of Jeremy Zirlott/Facebook

Zirlott said he thinks the tariffs will help preserve the domestic shrimp sector, but he'd like the Trump administration to provide further help by directing some of the funds collecting through tariffs back into the industry.

"The tariffs are going to collect a lot of money for the US Treasury, and I would like to see some of that money through either the Saltonstall-Kennedy Act … maybe we could develop some legislation to get some of that money back to the industry for infrastructure or maintenance, just to keep keep the industry viable," he said.

Zirlott understands the US industry alone cannot supply nearly enough shrimp to satisfy domestic demand, and said he doesn't want shrimp to become an unaffordable luxury for US consumers. But he said imported product is artificially cheap due to subsidies, inadequate environmental and labor regulations and international aid for aquaculture-focused economic development programs abroad.

"I'm all for a free-market approach, but that's not what we have right now. The market has become so manipulated over the years that US consumers don't even know what they're getting right now." 

Zirlott said he's not against imports, but said he hopes the Trump administration can help create policies that reverse the erosion of the viability of the US shrimp industry.

"We just want to maintain our niche. I don't think the industry will ever come back to what it was in the 1970s, '80s and even '90s. But if we can just slow down the losses and maintain what we have, that would be a victory."

The tariffs, he said, are "a good start" on that project.

"The public's going to have to decide, do they want American-produced shrimp, or do they want inferior-quality shrimp imported from other countries? If they want American-produced shrimp, they have to be willing to pay more for it. If they're not willing, then we're going away."

title: Vendors in New York’s famed Fulton Fish Market ticketed for multiple undersized fish violations
content:
The US state of New York's famed Fulton Fish Market has been ticketed for multiple violations of fishing conservation practices following an inspection of vendors.

Law enforcement officers from the New York Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) partnered with officers from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration on March 21 to inspect the Fulton Fish Market, one of the oldest and largest seafood wholesalers in the nation. Per a notice from the DEC, 48 undersized black sea bass, four undersized fluke and one oversized striped bass were confiscated.

The Fulton Fish Market, which was established in 1822, was issued tickets for multiple commercial marine violations. The famed co-op, which features over 25 companies in  400,000 square feet of space, moved to the Bronx in 2005 from its former location in the financial district waterfront of lower Manhattan.

Officers with the fish they confiscated at Fulton Fish Market. Photo Credit: NY DEC

New York's DEC has been cracking down on undersized fish and shellfish. Last month, officers also seized 168 undersized North American lobsters found during an inspection by a wholesale seafood dealer in the Bronx, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

title: Cooke mulls exit from Chile over disputed suspension of salmon farm operations
content:
Cooke Aquaculture is considering pulling out of the Chile salmon farming business following a decision by a federal agency to suspend its Huillines 3 operation in the Aysen region.

The Canadian company, one of the largest players in Chile's aquaculture industry, has accused the nation's Superintendency of the Environment (Superintendencia del Medio Ambiente, or SMA) of overstepping its authority by halting the farm's operations without substantial evidence or legal justification. 

At a hearing before Chile's Third Environmental Court on April 1, David Cademartori, Cooke Aquaculture's legal representative, presented the company's case, describing the SMA's actions as "arbitrary" and harmful to Cooke's operations.

"The rule of law has failed the company, a foreign investor that trusted in the country's regulations," he stated, also calling on the court "to reverse the suspension and prevent further damage to the business."

If the suspension is upheld, it could result in substantial financial losses for Cooke Aquaculture, which has made significant investments in the region. The company stated that the SMA aims to impose a limit, reducing the farm's production from its current output of up to 4,000 metric tons to just 125t.

The Aysen region of Chile. Map from Wikimedia.

"The impact on our operations has been severe. This suspension is disproportionate, and if this decision is not reversed, there is a real risk that we will have to withdraw from the country," Cademartori warned. 

The controversy began with an SMA resolution -- Ex. No. 303 -- issued on Feb. 25, which ordered a procedural suspension of salmon planting activities at the Huillines 3 farm.

The SMA claimed that Cooke was operating outside of the Environmental Impact Assessment System (SEIA, in its Spanish acronym), alleging that the company "had altered its operations without proper environmental review."

However, Cooke Aquaculture disputes these allegations, insisting that its activities have remained unchanged since 1997, when it began following the same technical project, which stipulated only a minimum production level, not a maximum.

Cooke Chile accuses environmental authority of unfair persecution

"This [the suspension] is a misguided attempt by the SMA to enforce rules that do not apply to Cooke's operations, as the farm's activities predate the SEAI law," said Cademartori. 

"The company has been operating under the same technical project for nearly three decades," he emphasized, arguing that projects initiated before the SEIA's implementation should not be subject to modern regulatory requirements.

The 'imminence of harm'

Cooke's legal dispute in Chile centers around whether the Huillines 3 farm is subject to the SEIA or if it should continue to operate under its original project plan.

Cademartori described the SMA's decision to cap the farm's production at 125t as "an arbitrary shift in policy." During the hearing, he noted that the original technical plan never specified a maximum production level, only a minimum, and the company has adhered to these guidelines for years.

Cooke also criticized the decision for being based on a presumption of environmental harm rather than proven damage. The company referenced technical reports from experts, including one from the University of Austral, which found "no evidence of anaerobic conditions at the farm."

Cooke appeals suspension of operations at nine sites in Chile

This contradicted the SMA's claims of environmental risk, which were based on the assumption that the farm's operations were contributing to significant pollution in the surrounding marine environment.

However, despite Cooke's claims, SMA argued that all salmon farming operations in Chile, including those predating the SEIA, must comply with modern regulations if their activities are modified in ways that could affect the environment.

The environmental regulator argued the suspension of the Cooke operation was not due to proven environmental damage but rather the "imminence of harm."

"This pollution, attributed to uneaten feed, feces and other waste produced by the farm, poses a threat to the fragile ecosystem of the Laguna San Rafael National Park, a nearby protected area," SMA said.

As the Third Environmental Court prepares to issue a decision, Cooke's legal team is pushing for the suspension to be lifted and for the farm to resume operations.

The case also involves two third-party supporters: industry association SalmonChile, which advocates on behalf of the aquaculture industry, and NGO Greenpeace, which has aligned with the SMA and is urging the court to uphold the suspension.

title: Rapid genetic testing helps NOAA crack down on IUU fishing, imports
content:
Law enforcement officers with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) are now using a new, rapid ​polymerase chain reaction (PCR) device to help tackle illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing (IUU).

The agency says that the device helped them identify more than 27 tons of fish at the Port of Newark, New Jersey, in November 2024, that were illegally harvested and prohibited from entering the US for commercial trading.

NOAA agents are responsible for conducting inspections at ports. The agency said that it could take weeks to process a sample sent to a forensic lab, which it said can slow seafood products moving through US ports.

However, the PCR device, which researchers at Florida International University developed, can significantly cut back on the testing time it takes to identify a fish species, according to Diego Cardenosa, the lead researcher on the project.

"The idea is to make this technology available to everyone so that it becomes routine to do genetic testing in the field," said Cardenosa. "Then it becomes a regular part of evidentiary support in law enforcement. This novel technology brings a lot of value to cases that law enforcement needs to handle." 

The device is similar to the PCR tests that were developed to detect COVID-19 in humans, but can identify more than 100 species of fish, Cardenosa said.

title: Untitled
content:
The whitefish sector is entering a period of high tension as importers and suppliers brace for the implementation of steep new tariffs announced by president Donald Trump on April 2.

Tilapia and pangasius, two of the most widely-consumed aquaculture species in the US market, are now in the crosshairs, with Chinese-origin tilapia facing a cumulative tariff of up to 79% and Vietnamese pangasius set to encounter a 46% duty starting April 9.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view

The tilapia market has been under mounting pressure for months, but US wholesale prices have remained surprisingly steady.

Currently, Chinese-origin tilapia is subject to a 25% Section 301 tariff, which has been in place for several years as a result of the trade war with China started by Trump in 2018. Earlier this year, two additional rounds of 10% tariffs were introduced under new trade measures, followed by an additional 34% under the "Liberation Day" tariff announcement, bringing the potential total tariff burden to 79% if fully enforced.

VIEW GRAPH

© 2025 Undercurrent News
To view the full datas
GO PREMIUM
Upgrade to Pro to view

Despite this significant cost exposure, domestic prices have yet to fully reflect these increases. Several factors are contributing to the disconnect, including moderate inventory levels, buyer reluctance to absorb higher costs and ongoing uncertainty around enforcement, particularly regarding how and when the additional tariffs will be applied, who ultimately bears the cost and how specific shipments are classified.

As a result, many importers are holding pricing steady for now, awaiting further clarity before adjusting market offers.

Industry contacts report that suppliers in Guangdong are willing to make modest price concessions to keep production lines moving, while plants in Hainan are less flexible due to tighter supply. The key factor now is urgency as many importers are shipping what they can before April 9, while others are choosing to hold product in cold storage and wait for clarity on tariff enforcement and possible negotiations.

The pangasius (swai) market has held firm, with pricing near the upper end of the quoted range. Vietnamese processors continue to face tight raw material supply, with constrained harvests expected through at least June.

Larger fillets or preferred specs are already commanding slightly higher offers, but most market participants expect volatility in Q2, depending on how the harvest progresses and how much inventory remains in the US.

What complicates matters further is the lack of a clear path forward on trade negotiations.

While Vietnam is expected to push aggressively to reduce or eliminate the 46% tariff, the current US administration has shown little willingness to engage, adding another layer of uncertainty to the market. With the US serving as one of Vietnam's largest pangasius customers, the implications of losing access could be severe for Vietnamese producers.

Some exporters are pushing product out before the April 9 deadline, while others are holding off, unsure how the situation will evolve. Importers, for their part, are working closely with customers to delay price shifts until more clarity is available, many speculating and hopefuly that this could all be part of a broader, short-lived negotiation strategy.

title: Alaska senators introduce bills to allow more foreign seafood workers, impose sanctions on Russia
content:
Alaska's US senators are taking separate tacks to protect and boost their state's seafood industry.

US senator Lisa Murkowski, an Alaska Republican, and US senator Tim Kaine, a Virginia Democrat, have re-introduced The Save Our Seafood (SOS) Act, exempting processors from the H-2B visa limit to address labor shortages being experienced by the US seafood industry.

The H2B guest-worker program allows US employers to temporarily hire foreign nationals to perform non-agricultural labor or services if they document the vacancies cannot be filled by US citizens. 

"Alaska's seafood industry is a delicate chain – and when processors don't have the workforce to meet demand, the whole industry can fall apart," Murkowski said in a statement. "Through this legislation, I'm working to ensure that the industry has a dependable workforce that can process and deliver the highest-quality seafood in the world."

US seafood sector warns Alaska could be casualty of Trump’s trade war
Seafood industry decries barriers to recruitment

The US seafood industry is rallying behind the bill, which faces political headwinds as the administration of US president Donald Trump cracks down on immigration. Trump's administration has pursued an aggressive enforcement agenda, with even legal visa holders caught up in dragnets set to deport undocumented immigrants.

"This legislation would help ensure enough workers will be available to support Alaska's seafood sector," Julie Decker, president of the Pacific Seafood Processors Association said in a joint statement with Murkowski. "Alaska produces nearly 60 percent of all U.S. seafood. In order to do this, Alaska seafood processors need a workforce in our highly remote coastal communities."

Ben Bale, chief financial officer of Ocean Companies, a US West Coast seafood processor, fishmeal producer and logistics firm, said uncertainty about the H-2B visa program is a major challenger for US employers in the seafood sector.

It’s almost an annual thing: Maryland presses for more H-2B visas

"Making the H-2B program cap-exempt would eliminate this uncertainty, enabling us to plan production more effectively, support the local fishing industry, and enhance economic stability for our business, our employees, the community and the guest workers who depend on these opportunities," Bale said in a statement.

Atlantic processors in the US have also thrown their weight behind liberalizing the H2-B visa regime. Jack Brooks, president of the Chesapeake Bay Seafood Industries Association, said guest workers are vital for the industry's health.

"These hardworking people who come to Maryland every season under this very important program support thousands of jobs of American citizens and small seafood businesses around Maryland's Chesapeake Bay that also support seafood processors," Brooks added.

Sullivan silent on H2-B visa reform

The bill – introduced in 2024 – currently has four Democratic co-sponsors and three other Republicans aside from Murkowski. But absent from that list is US senator Dan Sullivan, a fellow Alaska Republican. 

He's championing a bill – co-sponsored by Murkowski – to impose punitive tariffs on Russia, a country that was notably absent from US president Trump's list of nations targeted under a sweeping global tariff policy that's sent shockwaves through world markets, as Undercurrent News has reported.

US gov’t adds 20,000 H2-B visas amid worker shortage

As currently written, the legislation would impose a 500% tariff on imported goods from countries that buy Russian oil, gas, uranium and other products. Sullivan said the goal is to force Russian president Vladimir Putin to the negotiating table to end his country's war with Ukraine.

"A bipartisan majority of my Senate colleagues and I are working to provide a comprehensive sanctions package against Russia that puts Putin on notice and gives the administration additional tools and leverage to end this war and find a workable peace," Sullivan wrote in a statement.

The US sanctions would be imposed if Moscow refuses to engage in good faith negotiations for a lasting peace with Ukraine or initiates another effort, including military invasion, that undermines the sovereignty of Ukraine after peace is negotiated, the bill's sponsors said in a statement.

title: US shrimp industry celebrates Trump tariffs on competitors as ‘crucial lifeline’
content:
US president Donald Trump's decision to place tariffs on more than 100 countries, including all of the top exporters of shrimp to the US, has been praised by the trade group representing domestic producers.

The Southern Shrimp Alliance has long fought what it calls the unfair trade policies of countries including India, Ecuador, Indonesia and Vietnam -- the countries responsible for the vast majority of US shrimp imports, which account for 94% of all shrimp consumed in the US.

Now those four countries face tariffs of between 10-46%, and John Williams, executive director of the Southern Shrimp Alliance, is celebrating.

"We've watched as multigenerational family businesses tie up their boats, unable to compete with foreign producers who play by a completely different set of rules," Williams said in a press release. "We are grateful for the Trump administration's actions today, which will preserve American jobs, food security, and our commitment to ethical production."

The US shrimp industry has suffered significant losses in recent years, and as a result, many lifelong shrimpers have decided to give up the trade, according to Williams. 

"Since 2021, the prices of imported shrimp have dropped significantly, decreasing their value by more than $1.5 billion. This economic downturn has led the US shrimp industry to lose nearly 50% of its market value, forcing many shrimping businesses to close. Despite the falling wholesale prices, retail shrimp prices have remained historically high for consumers, highlighting the disconnect between wholesale and retail markets," he said.

The Southern Shrimp Alliance disseminated a chart showing the new tariff rates being placed on the top shrimp exporters to the US.

The Southern Shrimp Alliance claims cheap imported shrimp is the product of generous government subsidies, weaker environmental laws and unregulated labor practices. It also asserts US-funded international financial institutions have invested billions into aquaculture development abroad, "helping multinational companies rapidly displace the well-regulated US shrimp industry."

"The total number of shrimp and aquaculture development projects increased significantly in the past decade, primarily in India and Ecuador, which supply nearly 70% of all US shrimp imports and are the largest competitors to the US shrimp industry," it said. "Ecuador alone received over $550 million in development funding for shrimp farming since 2000, with $195m going directly to private companies competing with US shrimpers. This investment helped fuel a staggering 150% increase in Ecuadorian shrimp exports to the US in just four years. Similar funding has gone to other major producers like India, Indonesia and Vietnam, creating a global shrimp oversupply."

US wholesale: Tariffs on shrimp producing countries vary widely, impact disparity even greater with Vietnam hit hardest

The Southern Shrimp Alliance has also warned of widespread use of banned antibiotics in foreign shrimp aquaculture. 

"Despite these concerns, many US retailers continue sourcing large volumes of shrimp from the most problematic countries, often relying on inadequate industry certification programs," it said.

Trump's tariffs come "at a critical moment," with the US shrimp industry at a tipping point of potentially disappearing entirely, Williams said.

"Our government has been outsourcing our food supply to companies engaged in practices we would never accept on American soil," Williams noted. "Without quickly addressing unfair trade, we are choosing a food supply chain that is fully outsourced to industries that engage in horrible practices. If we wait for systemic reforms, we will lose our domestic shrimp industry."

The trade group said the tariffs are "aimed at protecting American jobs and ensuring food security."

"The new duties are expected to slow imports and prevent Americans from becoming completely dependent on foreign shrimp producers while the administration addresses harmful trade policies and enforcement deficiencies," it said.

That will be a huge benefit to the domestic shrimp industry and US consumers, Williams said.

"Today's demand for shrimp is met at a massive human, environmental, and public health cost," said Williams. "When we outsource our seafood production to industries that use forced labor and environmental shortcuts, we're making a choice about the kind of world we want to support."

title: Untitled
content:
Agents with the US state of Louisiana's Department of Wildlife and Fisheries (LDWF) have issued citations to four fishermen who were caught engaged in illegal fishing in Terrebonne Parish on March 26.

Luis Martinez, 39, Darrel Luke, 60, Tyler Melancon, 23, and Tyler Luke, 42, were all issued citations by LDWF law enforcement officials during a patrol in the Bayou Chauvin Area late last month.

Per the LDWF, the four men were in four separate crabbing vessels. Agents found that Martinez was in possession of four crates of crabs, 5% of which were immature female crabs. LDWF agents returned the crabs to the water. Darrel Luke, as well as Tyler Luke, were also found to be in possession of immature female crabs on their separate vessels. Licensed crab fishermen are not allowed to exceed 5% of incidental take of immature female crabs. Agents also returned those crabs to the water.

Meanwhile, the fourth man, Melancon, was found to not possess the required commercial fishing licenses while actively commercial crabbing.

The men who possessed more than their limit of juvenile female crabs face fines up to $950 and up to 120 days in jail. Melancon faces a fine up to $500 for failing to possess a commercial fishing license while engaged in commercial fishing activities.

title: Untitled
content:
Regal Springs is bullish on both recovering its tilapia production in 2025 and its traction in the US market, but US president Donald Trump's planned April 2 tariffs on Mexico are a possible headwind, executives told Undercurrent News at the recent Seafood Expo North America (SENA) show.

The Switzerland-based global company, which farms in Indonesia, Honduras and Mexico and generates most of its sales in the US, could benefit from Trump's tariffs on China, which include a 45% tariff on frozen tilapia. However, the 25% tariffs on Mexico, which Trump has threatened, would be detrimental to the firm's business, the company's Todd Raasch and Vernon Bradley told Undercurrent at SENA.

Regal Springs launches fajita-ready tilapia fillets in Mexico

Indonesia and Honduras could face unspecified tariffs on April 2, what Trump is dubbing "Liberation Day," delivering a threat to place reciprocal tariffs on every country that also has them on US exports.

Raasch, the company's managing director for North America, said Regal is concerned about a potential 25% tariff on Mexico.

"The level we're at for our normal weekly business, Honduras can't do it all. We need both fresh plants to be able to fill our customer's needs," said Raasch. "We have customers on the [US] East Coast and West Coast. So, it's important that all of them are running at full capacity so we can make our commitments."

Although they told Undercurrent the company had its "best-ever" SENA regarding product demand, the tariffs are "totally disruptive," as Bradley, global head of business development and marketing, put it.

"The conversations with almost all the customers are around you can't plan. It [the 25% tariff] was on, and it was off, it's coming back on, but we don't know for how long," Raasch told Undercurrent.

FREE READ US wholesale: Farmed whitefish balance tariffs, tight supply, tepid demand

"If it's a value item, like tilapia, any increase kind of takes it out of whack," he said of the market impact of the 25%.

"We can switch from one source, but you can't do it overnight. It takes eight weeks to get the product over from Indonesia," said Bradley.

Obviously, Canadian salmon could also get 25% tariffs on April 2, which could benefit Regal's tilapia, he said.

"We may see people trading down from salmon to tilapia. Maybe tilapia people go down to pangasius," Bradley told Undercurrent.

Some customers who are buying Chinese tilapia are now looking to Regal, as the 45% tariff means "we might be a little closer on prices," said Raasch.

With the 45% on China, the level between frozen fillets from Indonesia, are "going to be super close," he said. "We're still going to be higher, but much closer."

A stronger dollar could help offset this, "but it might take a bit to see that come to fruition," he said.

"All we can do is navigate our way through it. There are a lot of rocks in the way, but we'll navigate accordingly," said Bradley.

Fresh tilapia fillet prices have been rising in the US wholesale, as Undercurrent's latest assessment for week 13 shows. 

VIEW GRAPH

Upgrade to Pro to view

Frozen tilapia fillet prices from China are also up in US wholesale, although not as much as might be expected with the 45% tariff. 

"Market conditions for tilapia appear steady, though cost pressures from the recently enacted 45% tariff on Chinese-origin product remain top of mind. Despite this significant increase in landed costs, US wholesale prices have not shown a corresponding rise. This disconnect seems to be driven by cautious buyer behavior, moderate inventory levels and uncertainty around enforcement timing and logistics," said Lorin Castiglione, Undercurrent's head of price reporting for North America, in her latest market pulse. 

"For now, importers appear to be holding pricing in place, though some are reevaluating sourcing strategies. Fresh tilapia from Central and South America continues to attract interest as a potential hedge against tariff exposure. However, supply remains limited, and most of the region's capacity leans toward whole or fresh formats, not frozen fillets," she added. 

US expansion plans

Amid this uncertainty, Regal is seeing strong demand in the US and is looking to get production back on track in 2025.

The company launched a fajita-ready range of tilapia fillets into Walmart and its Sam's Club subsidiary in February, with the range set to hit the US market later this year, said Bradley.

In addition, Regal is getting traction with its premium coated range and also its "Filetitos" – mini fillets for all the family, as Bradley put it.

As a result, the company is looking to double or even triple its sales staff, adding four to eight positions in 2024.

Raasch and Bradley said Regal's Mexican and Honduran operations should recover production in 2025. In Honduras, the company faced high fish mortality rates in 2022 and 2023. Additionally, the Honduran government's initiative to eliminate industrial activity on Lake Yojoa led Regal to consolidate operations solely on Lake El Cajon.

In Mexico, record-high water temperatures in Lake Malpaso resulted in reduced oxygen levels, adversely affecting tilapia production. To address this, Regal Springs explored new technologies to enhance oxygen supply. After resting Lake Malpaso for a year between 2022 and 2023, operations resumed in 2024, leading to a gradual recovery in harvest capacity.

Tthe drop and then recovery over 2024 from Honduras can be seen on Undercurrent's trade portal, looking at the country's exports on a quarterly basis. 

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
Possible US tariffs on Mexico cast shadow over Regal Springs' expansion plans - Undercurrent News

Then, the impact of the production drop in Mexico can be seen on US imports. The Mexican domestic market also consumes a lot of the tilapia the country produces, so US imports do not tell the whole story. 

Possible US tariffs on Mexico cast shadow over Regal Springs' expansion plans - Undercurrent News

Looking at the overall US imports of fresh tilapia in pounds, the drops from Honduras and Mexico have given a window to Brazil and especially Colombia fill the gap. 

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view

Regal's production in Indonesia is going well, as shown in the country's exports. In 2024, Indonesia exported 12,371t of frozen tilapia fillets worth $92.26m, up 15% y-o-y in value and volume. The bulk of this goes to the US, and Regal is the main exporter.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
Possible US tariffs on Mexico cast shadow over Regal Springs' expansion plans - Undercurrent News

"We've got Indonesia operating at full capacity," said Bradley.

Regal's Latin American production is recovering, he said.

"In Mexico, we've got a lot of fish coming back on stream in the second half. It dropped, and now we are over our problems and back onstream. It takes a year to grow the fish, so there will be a lot more fish from Mexico in the second half," he said.

"Honduras is all about fresh, and that slipped. But that's come back too, so we believe we've got the capacity to go forward," he told Undercurrent.

"If this really takes off, we just have to manage it carefully," he said of the supply relationship with the new product programs.

title: Untitled
content:
In a move aimed at averting potential trade retaliation from the US, Ecuador has announced a temporary reduction of import tariffs on shrimp products to 0%.

The resolution, made by Ecuador's foreign trade committee (or COMEX, in its Spanish acronym), officially took effect on March 29, 2025.

It is seen as a preemptive step to maintain favorable trade relations with the US amid shifting policies under president Donald Trump's influence on trade regulations. It came in response to concerns that Ecuadorian shrimp exports could face increased tariffs from the US government. 

The tariff reduction applies to multiple subcategories of shrimp products, classified under Ecuador's tariff code 0306.17, which previously carried a 30% import duty.

This includes whole shrimp, peeled shrimp tails, and other derivatives. The new 0% tariff rate will remain effective until Dec. 31, 2025.

COMEX stated that the measure aligns Ecuador's trade policies with the US "Fair and Reciprocal Plan," a framework linked to Trump's previous trade strategy. Authorities in Ecuador hope this move will help exporters avoid potential economic setbacks and maintain competitive access to the US market.

The shrimp industry has responded positively to the decision, highlighting its potential to boost export stability and global competitiveness.

Ecuador's national customs service, SENAE, has been assigned to oversee the enforcement of the new tariff policy. Additionally, COMEX has mandated the vice ministry of foreign trade to conduct a full assessment by the end of 2025 to evaluate its effectiveness and any necessary adjustments.

title: US wholesale: Farmed whitefish balance tariffs, tight supply, tepid demand
content:
The US market for farmed whitefish, including tilapia, pangasius/swai and catfish remains in flux as importers navigate a volatile mix of elevated tariffs, shifting supply fundamentals and soft demand. While tariffs are theoretically inflationary, the actual impact on wholesale pricing has been muted to date, exposing a complex tug-of-war between rising global costs and cautious US buyer sentiment.

One of the most pressing issues in the current market is tilapia, where the total tariff rate on Chinese-origin product has now ballooned to 45% following an additional 20% imposed earlier this year. Despite this, US wholesale prices have remained flat in March, raising questions about the disconnect between rising landed costs and market pricing.

VIEW GRAPH

© 2025 Undercurrent News
To view the full datas
GO PREMIUM
Upgrade to Pro to view

Industry sources suggest that this could be due to several factors, including moderate inventory levels in the US, uncertainty around how the tariffs will be enforced and general caution across the supply chain. Many buyers appear to be in a holding pattern, continuing to move existing product while waiting for clearer direction on logistics, tariff enforcement and demand trends.

Further complicating matters is the implementation guidance from US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), which introduced an unexpected deadline. In addition to departing China before Feb. 1, shipments also had to enter the US by March 7 to avoid the surcharge. This caught many importers off guard, especially those shipping to the East Coast, where longer transit times made compliance nearly impossible.

In China, raw material prices have remained firm, with 500–800g fish trading at approximately CNY 9.8/kg in Hainan and CNY 9.2/kg in Guangdong, levels that have seen little fluctuation since January, Undercurrent News reports. Processors and farmers continue to face high internal costs, including new environmental regulations that require significant investment in discharge treatment facilities. Production disruptions from a 2024 typhoon are still affecting supply in southern provinces.

At the same time, Chinese exporters are reportedly reducing shipments to the US, consolidating operations and exploring sales opportunities in other markets such as Europe and Africa. Some uncertainty also surrounds whether historically low FOB China prices are still sustainable, given today's elevated farming and processing costs.

Fresh tilapia from Central and South America is gaining attention as an alternative, although frozen fillet capacity remains limited, and most production in the region leans toward whole/gutted or fresh product.

Pangasius has also begun to show slight signs of firming, though pricing remains largely within prior ranges. Vietnam-based suppliers have flagged shortages in raw material supply that are expected to continue through June. A strong harvest is anticipated before the flooding season, which may ease prices temporarily, but firmer trends are expected again by fall.

Higher offers have been observed in some quarters, largely tied to rising farming and processing costs in Vietnam. These increases have not fully filtered through to US pricing yet but could do so in the coming months, depending on the strength of domestic inventories.

Catfish pricing remains relatively steady, with some light firming pressure noted during the Lenten season. Post-holiday replacement costs and normal seasonal shifts in production are supporting pricing, but there are no signs of sharp upward movement.

Tariff turbulence

Despite higher import costs, demand remains cautious in the US. Buyers are still assessing the real-world impacts of tariff hikes while managing through a broader market environment that has yet to show significant signs of recovery. Several importers are evaluating alternative sources of supply, but regional capacity, product format limitations and the risk of future trade actions remain hurdles.

With raw material costs holding steady or rising in both China and Vietnam, and inventories being drawn down across the US, the second quarter of 2025 could prove pivotal. If demand picks up, particularly around Easter and other retail-driven periods, pricing pressure may build quickly.

Until then, the farmed whitefish market continues to hover in an uneasy equilibrium, stable on the surface, but highly vulnerable to policy shifts, inventory depletion, and supply-side volatility.

title: New York inspects Bronx seafood dealer, finds more undersized lobsters
content:
The US state of New York's Department of Environmental Conservation's (DEC) Division of Law Enforcement reports in a press release to have seized 168 undersized North American lobsters found during an inspection of a wholesale seafood dealer in the Bronx, one of New York City's five boroughs.  

The crackdown was done in partnership with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's National Marine Fisheries Service.

While the Bronx wholesaler has not been identified, the DEC said that on March 13 it issued the business owner a notice of violation and confiscated the undersized shellfish. The lobsters were then donated to Bowery Mission in Manhattan, a non-profit that helps provide hot meals to New Yorkers in need.

Officers with lobsters seized during routine compliance inspections of wholesale seafood dealers in Bronx County. Photo Credit: NY DEC

The latest update from DEC comes about a month after officers seized an additional 97 undersized lobsters from two other wholesalers in the state, as reported by Undercurrent News. During that inspection officers also found clams that had been "placed in water without a valid permit and unlawfully possessed tautog tags."

title: Canada initiates dispute at World Trade Organization over Chinese tariffs
content:
The Canadian government has asked the World Trade Organization (WTO) to launch dispute consultations over China's decision to impose 25% tariffs on seafood and agriculture products.

The tariffs, which took effect on March 20, apply to 49 seafood items from Canada, including lobster, coldwater shrimp, Greenland halibut as well as certain crab species and other shellfish, as previously reported by Undercurrent News. 

China indicated its actions were a response to Canada's decision to levy a 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles beginning Oct. 1, 2024, and a 25% tariff on Chinese steel and aluminum products starting Oct. 22, 2024.

The Canadian government, in its March 20 letter to the WTO, argues that China did not follow its obligations under the provisions of the WTO when it imposed the tariffs.

"China's measures are tantamount to a unilateral determination that Canada's measures violate Canada's WTO obligations. China failed to make such a determination through recourse to dispute settlement in accordance with the rules and procedures of the DSU," Canada claims, among other things, in its letter.

Canada is also asking for the consultation process to begin within 10 days from the date of the letter.

"The Government of Canada considers that this consultation request concerns a matter of urgency relating, inter alia, to perishable goods," Canada's letter points out.

Canadian companies test waters in new markets at SENA 2025

Bilateral consultations between the parties are the first stage of formal dispute settlement under WTO rules.

"Consultations give the parties an opportunity to discuss the matter and to find a satisfactory solution without resorting to litigation," the WTO explains on its website. 

Even if consultations fail to resolve the dispute, it remains possible for the parties to find a mutually agreed solution at any later stage of the proceedings, the WTO also stated.

"A majority of disputes so far in the WTO have not proceeded beyond consultations, either because a satisfactory settlement was found, or because the complainant decided for other reasons not to pursue the matter further," the organization said. "This shows that consultations are often an effective means of dispute resolution in the WTO and that the instruments of adjudication and enforcement in the dispute settlement system are by no means always necessary."

Tariffs would cost $308m

If the Chinese tariffs on seafood remain in place, it would be costly for Canadian producers.

Based on the 2024 figures, China's introduction of a 25% tariff on 49 seafood items from Canada would cost $308 million ($216.15m).

The UCN trade portal below shows that China imported 94,712 metric tons of seafood from Canada in 2024, valued at $1.23 billion under the 49 categories.

Canada initiates dispute at World Trade Organization over Chinese tariffs - Undercurrent News

Lobster would be among the most impacted Canadian seafood, with China importing 26,920t worth $614m in 2024, a record high in value, as the UCN trade portal shows below.

US agrees to Canada's WTO request for consultation

Canada filed a similar request to the WTO on March 4, requesting consultations with the United States over the 25% tariffs president Donald Trump has threatened to impose on Canadian goods. 

Trump had initially signed an executive order to impose the tariffs on March 6 but then decided to delay the action until April 2, as reported by Undercurrent.

The president previously said the tariffs would be imposed in relation to the influx of undocumented immigrants and fentanyl coming across US land borders, but in his speech to the joint session of Congress on March 4  -- which was not technically a state-of-the-union address -- he talked more about trade imbalances and fairness, as reported by Undercurrent.

In its letter to the WTO, Canada said the tariffs are "inconsistent with the US obligations under several provisions of the 1994 General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT)". The GATT is an international treaty binding on all WTO members.

World Trade Organization chief urges more dialogue between US, trading partners

In its letter of response on March 14, the US argued that the matter was not subject to WTO review because it was related to the US Emergency Measures Act.

"Issues of national security are political matters not susceptible to review or capable of resolution by WTO dispute settlement. Every Member of the WTO retains the authority to determine for itself those measures that it considers necessary to the protection of its essential security interests, as is reflected in the text of Article XXI of the GATT 1994," the letter stated.

However, the US said it would accept Canada's request to enter into consultations but did not accept Canada's view that this is a "case of urgency."

Canada boosts quota more than 9% in world’s largest snow crab fishery

Canada is the US' largest source of seafood and also its biggest export market. It sent the US 308,117 metric tons of seafood worth almost $4 billion in 2024 and it took 160,041 metric tons of seafood worth about $1bn the same year.

The UCN trade portal shows that US imports of Canadian shellfish was the highest valued, worth nearly $2.1bn in 2024.

Canada initiates dispute at World Trade Organization over Chinese tariffs - Undercurrent News

title: Fiji eyes Korean developments in sustainable tuna fishing
content:
Fiji, in the South Pacific Ocean, is reinforcing its commitment to sustainable tuna fisheries by addressing marine pollution, according to the country's deputy secretary of fisheries, Netani Tavaga.

As a member of several regional fishery management organizations, Fiji is obliged to adhere to strict conservation rules, including reporting minor oil spills and fishing line cuts.

Tavaga highlighted challenges in waste disposal at sea, as fishermen struggle to store and manage waste on vessels. Efforts are underway to collect garbage and bring it back to ports in Suva, though maintaining vessel hygiene for fish storage remains a concern.

To tackle these issues, Fiji is exploring solutions used by Korean fishermen, including biodegradable fishing mainlines that deteriorate within seven years. Tavaga said this advancement could help reduce marine pollution from discarded fishing gear.

Fiji also faces billions of dollars in economic losses from overfishing in the high seas. In response, the country's ministry of fisheries is tracking tuna migration patterns to enforce sustainable fishing practices and mitigate the impact of overfishing, he said.

title: Untitled
content:
The tariffs applied on Chinese goods by the US mean that current price quotes for double-frozen pollock fillets are about the same as those for the A season level for Alaskan single-frozen, executives told Undercurrent News at Seafood Expo North America (SENA), in Boston, Massachusetts, last week. 

In US president Donald Trump's first term (January 2017-January 2021), double-frozen fillets from China were exempt from the 25% tariffs put in place by US president Donald Trump during his first term (January 2017-January 2021), using his Section 301 authority. However, no such exemption has been put in place for Trump's two new 10% tariffs, and Alaskan flatfish and Atlantic haddock even face a combined 45% increase when the Section 301 exemptions expire on May 31.

US importers face possible 45% tariffs on China-processed Alaskan flatfish, Atlantic haddock from June 1

With the combined 20% tariff, recent quotes on pollock blocks out of China are currently on par or even above A season prices for single frozen, pin-bone out (PBO) fillets from the US, Thomas Zaffiro, CEO of Channel Fish Processing, a large processor based in Braintree, Massachusetts, on the US East Coast, told Undercurrent.

"I think that will correct. I think the pollock market will edge up in B season," he said. 

Zaffiro noted, however, that the levels out of China are offers and deals have not yet been committed. 

One Chinese processing executive, who asked not to be quoted by name, agreed – giving around $3,400-per-metric-ton, free-on-board (FOB) for double frozen using Alaskan headed and gutted (H&G) raw material as the current quoted level. Adding shipping and 20% in tariffs probably takes this above the $3,700-$3,800/t delivered East Coast level for US PBO agreed in A season, further supporting the premise this price is set to rise for B season.

B season deals for US PBO fillets were under discussion at the SENA show, which is much earlier than in the past few years. Alaskan fishing and processing companies are looking to increase prices, but even buyers accept the market is likely to move up.

FREE READ Boston 2025 in 5: How Pacific Seafood is using new workplace tech to double size

PBO prices could settle in a broad range of $3,700-$4,000/t, delivered East Coast, for B season, ranging from land-frozen to sea-frozen, sources at the show told Undercurrent, with deepskin 20% above this. Zaffiro agreed with this range.

"The situation has totally changed in a year," one US pollock supplier told Undercurrent, comparing the climate to last SENA when the situation was tough outside of the US market, where Russian pollock is banned.

"We were still uncommitted on prices in Barcelona [for Seafood Expo Global] in April last year," the seller, who asked not to be quoted by name, told Undercurrent.

"Even though we don't have any unsold volume, if we had, I think the price would be around $100-$150/t over A season," where the market price was $3,600/t ex-coldstore in Europe and $3,700-$3,800/t, delivered East Coast for the US, he told Undercurrent.

For double frozen pollock fillets using Russian H&G, for Europe and other markets, FOB prices of around $3,000/t are being quoted, sources said. Again, with $150/t of freight and a 13.7% duty, the level would be around the $3,600/t, ex-coldstore Europe, agreed for A season for US PBO.

VIEW GRAPH
Single-frozen US pollock fillet blocks, PBO, ex-coldstore Europe, UCN
© 2025 Undercurrent News
To view the full datas
GO PREMIUM
Upgrade to Pro to view

The dramatic premium for the double frozen fillets using US raw material stems from the US ban on Russian fish, even when processed in China and other third countries. China's pollock fillet exports illustrate the trend, with the US going from trading below the EU in average price to rising 4% to $3,379/t for 2024, while the EU dropped 22% y-o-y to $2,446/t due to the ongoing use of cheaper Russian H&G.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
Wholesale price gap remains

Looking at Undercurrent's week 12 (March 17-23) US wholesale price assessments on single and double frozen fillets, a 5.5% gap remains, as you can see below, or on Undercurrent's data portal.

"Historically, tariffs have not led to instant price increases upon implementation at the wholesale level. Instead, the market typically experiences a gradual and measured adjustment, as companies take time to assess trade agreements, inventory positions, and current demand trends before adjusting pricing strategies," said Lorin Castiglione, Undercurrent's head of price reporting for North America, who makes the weekly assessments. 

Given discussions at SENA, there is a growing consensus that B season pricing will edge upward, she said.

"While buyers acknowledge that market conditions support some upward movement, pricing adjustments depend on negotiations, inventory levels and overall demand dynamics. It's also important to note that added costs tend to get passed along to consumers at a faster rate for value finfish like pollock, as the smaller margins leave less room to absorb price fluctuations."

FREE READ Recap day three from Boston 2025

Pollock pricing is positioned to be more immediately impacted by changes in trade policy, tariffs and supply chain disruptions than premium seafood categories at higher price points, said Castiglione.

"With the lack of tariff exemptions that were previously applied to double-frozen fillets using US raw material, this lays the foundation for further price alignment between domestic and imported options in the coming months, a situation we have seen in the past with single and twice-frozen haddock when tariff exemptions weren't at play, resulting in inverted pricing for a period of time," she said.

"Uncertainties still lie around the currently banned Russian product, adding another layer of complexity to the market. If the US reopens its doors to Russian pollock exports, it could significantly alter supply dynamics, potentially increasing competition and putting downward pressure on prices," said Castiglione. "Conversely, if the ban remains in place, the market will continue to adjust within the existing supply constraints, reinforcing stronger demand for domestic and alternative imported options."

If the ban remains in place on Russian fish going into the US, even when processed in third countries, it could even become economical to process the headed and gutted fish in the US, said Channel's Zaffiro.

"We think, with some investment in technology, we can cut it [H&G] for the same price in the US" if there's 20-25% added from tariffs, he said.

Effort to shift from China

The uncertainty surrounding Trump's duties on China, including whether US-caught seafood will become exempt, has seafood executives considering their options.

"I feel like I spent more time [at SENA] talking about tariffs than fish," a Chinese processing executive who spoke under an agreement of anonymity told Undercurrent at the show.

Beaver Street eyes national US skin-pack footprint, spiny lobster boost from Canadian tariffs

"Everyone wants the Chinese companies to set up processing in Vietnam, Indonesia, India, but there are no credible volumes for the foreseeable future – aside from the long-established options," he told Undercurrent.

Channel, for one, is currently buying two cod items from China but is looking to move production to other countries, Zaffiro told Undercurrent.

The company bought in extra volume before the additional tariffs on China came in, and then it is in the process of shifting production to India and Vietnam.

"There was already a plan in place to move it to Vietnam and India," after accusations of labor abuse of the minority Uyghur workforce in China emerged in 2023.

"That forced a lot of people to move. Then, the looming tariffs are always a good reason to think about getting out. Other countries like Vietnam, Indonesia, and India are picking up with their capabilities."

However, there are concerns the US could tariff India next.

"We're trying to figure it out at this point, which is going to be difficult," he said.

Another upcoming issue for US importers is the possible additional 25% tariff on Alaskan flatfish and Atlantic haddock processed in China from June 1 on top of the 20% already added since Trump took office.

FREE READ Week 12 US wholesale prices: Tilapia, salmon edge higher; scallop pressure mounts amid potential Framework 39 delays

The so-called Section 301 exceptions from the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) expire on May 31, 2025, on 164 products, including haddock, founder and sole fillets. The relevant seafood products, which haddock fillets are the main trade flow, were worth $115 million in 2024 and totaled 20,563t. 

The USTR gave exemptions for the products from 25% tariffs after the trade war with China in Trump's first term, then Joseph Biden's administration kept rolling them over.

US industry body the National Fisheries Institute (NFI) has been attempting to communicate with the USTR around clarity on a further extension, but this is proving difficult under the Trump administration, sources said.

So, as it stands, the tariff on the products will go from the current level of 20% to 45% on June 1.

Alaskan cod, pollock and salmon were totally exempted from the 25% at the time, so they will remain at the current 20%, sources at SENA told Undercurrent. Tilapia and some other Chinese products have gone to 45%, as they were hit with 25% tariffs by Trump in his first term, which were extended by Biden.

"Working with the NFI, in the past, we've had a direct line to the USTR," one senior US seafood executive and NFI member told Undercurrent.

"But, with how much is going on in [Washington] DC, they can't even get a conversation with them. So, we don't know what's going to happen with that," he said of the efforts to get clarity from the USTR.

title: Blumar CEO looks forward to rebound year as political change, trade worries circle
content:
BOSTON, Massachusetts, US -- Blumar is on track to do better in 2025 after a down year in 2024, but the big Chilean seafood producer has plenty of potential challenges ahead, CEO Gerardo Balbontin told Undercurrent News this week on the sidelines of the Seafood Expo North America.

He called 2024 unlucky for Blumar, which lost an entire farm's worth of Atlantic salmon production to an algae bloom and suffered a fire that destroyed its Entrevientos plant in southern Chile.

"It was a challenging, difficult year. But fortunately, we have passed 2024 and we are looking forward," Balbontin said in an exclusive interview.

The Talcahuano, Chile-based firm, which farms Atlantic and coho salmon, as well as mussels, while also processing pelagics into fishmeal and fish oil, has yet to publish its Q4 2024 results. Blumar's production volumes rebounded in the second half of 2024 while costs decreased, hopefully boosting the underwhelming figures it saw in Q1, Q2 and Q3 of 2024, Balbontin said.

In 2023, the group achieved profits of $13.1 million, down 79% compared to the previous year, but recorded $674.4m in sales in 2023, 2% more than in 2022. Its annual production total in 2023 ranked it the ninth-largest Atlantic salmon farmer in the world that year.

For 2025, Balbontin said Blumar's bottom line will be further lifted by a new, three-year efficiency program dubbed "Project Contracorriente/Countercurrent" that is aimed at streamlining the company's operations. 

"We are growing much more from what we produced this year, and we think it's going to be a good year," he said. 

Playing right song at right time helped Chile grow US Atlantic salmon market dominance

Blumar is still deciding what to do about its Entrevientos processing plant, eight kilometers north of Punta Arenas, Chile, which it jointly operated with Multi X until it burned in February 2025. As a temporary measure, it has leased another facility owned by Australis and invested around $1m in upgrading it.

"The plant was in very good condition, so all we had to do was put the machinery [in] that was needed, which we did in three months. The plant is working, and we are processing all our raw material coming from Magallanes there," Balbontin said. 

Political challenges in Chile

Blumar has not firmed up its long-term plan in Magallanes, with Balbontin saying his firm is waiting until after the November 2025 presidential election to decide.

"The Magallanes region has demonstrated to have a lot of advantages in terms of salmon farming," he said. "We don't have sea lions there. We don't have SRS. Fish grows very well there. There are a lot of other challenges operating there, such as logistics and weather, but it's a fantastic area overall to grow salmon.

"But we need to see how the future looks, especially after the new government is elected and signals its intentions with the industry. Thereafter, we can think on the long future. Today, we are just in wait-and-see mode."

Blumar struggled in 2024 after a ratcheting up of environmental enforcement ordered by Chilean president Garbriel Boric cost the company, along with many other Chilean salmon farmers, millions of pesos in fines.

"The Chilean government has been difficult. It has been very difficult for salmon producers, and not only for salmon. There have been difficulties for many other sectors also. It has become very difficult to produce and to operate, especially if you are involved with the environment."

Blumar, AquaChile call for comprehensive reform in aquaculture law

After three years in office, Boric has arrived at a better comprehension of the industry and its economic importance in rural areas of Chile, Balbontin believes. But, as Boric cannot be reelected, Balbontin is putting his hope into Chile's electorate choosing a more business-friendly candidate to be the country's next president.

"You never know if the new administration will be better or not, but we wish to have a more pro-economic growth president who really understands that the country cannot focus only on conservation, especially a poor country like Chile, that they need to produce and export. So we are hopeful things will change," Balbontin said.

Trade worries

Chile's next president will likely have to deal with a deteriorating trading relationship with the top consumer of Chilean salmon, the United States. US president Donald Trump has threatened tariffs on a host of countries his administration deems to have implemented trade barriers against US goods. Balbontin said he can't fathom why the US would want to place tariffs on Atlantic salmon, which it does not produce at significant volumes, and said he hopes tariffs can be avoided.

"I think it's not good for anyone to have tariffs, but if it happens, we will have to look at alternatives. It won't be easy because, of course, the American market for us is by far the biggest," Balbontin said. "But it cannot be predicted, so we have not put scenarios into our business model with tariffs."

Until tariffs become a reality, Blumar will keep its focus on the US, where Balbontin said it has found growing success in the fast-growing sushi market.

"The US is by far our main market, so we put a lot of effort in to understand it. It is changing every year," Balbontin said. "Despite demand decreasing a bit, the US is still a huge market and has huge potential. The most important thing we have perceived is that [Chilean] product is still a super product and still the demand is there. Now we are just trying to find out what are the products customers are requesting."

title: Untitled
content:
Additional reporting by Lewis Hu, Dan Gibson, Neil Ramsden and Maria Feijoo

Farm-gate shrimp prices declined in India during week 11 (March 10-16), narrowing the gap with Ecuador, while markets in China continued their remarkable recovery with further price gains, according to the latest data compiled by Undercurrent News.

The Chinese market maintained its upward trajectory, with 60-count vannamei in Guangdong province rising to CNY 40 ($5.51) per kilogram in week 10, up from CNY 38/kg the previous week.

This continues the dramatic recovery from January's near two-year lows and positions Chinese shrimp prices above those from Thailand, where 60-count prices fell to THB 160 ($4.73)/kg from a recent high two weeks earlier.

Chinese, Thai, and Vietnamese shrimp are now commanding premium prices compared to other origins. Indonesian prices remain stagnant, however, with the country Asia's lowest-priced supplier.

Meanwhile, the price gap between comparable sizes of Indian and Ecuadorian vannamei has continued to narrow. Medium-sized 60-count shrimp in Andhra Pradesh held steady at INR 330 ($3.78)/kg in week 11, while Ecuador's 50-60 count stood at $3.40/kg.

VIEW GRAPH
Vannamei shrimp ex-farm Andhra Pradesh, HOSO, Aquaconnect, 60pcs/kg
© 2025 Undercurrent News
To view the full datas
GO PREMIUM
Upgrade to Pro to view
Early harvests drive India prices lower

Farm-gate prices for Indian vannamei shrimp are declining earlier than usual this season, with a significant drop in medium and large sizes as the first harvest of 2025 arrives ahead of schedule.

According to data from seafood trading platform AquaConnect, prices for larger 40-count shrimp in Andhra Pradesh fell sharply from INR 410/kg to INR 380/kg in week 10, maintaining this price into week 11. Medium-sized 60-count shrimp dropped from INR 350/kg to INR 330/kg, while 70-count fell to INR 300/kg, the lowest level since November.

"Yes, [the first harvest] has started, but it won't last for a long time," an industry source familiar with India's farming situation told Undercurrent. "Prices are reducing due to the US tariff and the risk weightage given to this phenomenon by exporters."

The source confirmed that the threat of new tariffs from the Trump administration is impacting market dynamics. "Also, the tariffs being enforced on other countries like China and Vietnam can have an impact on Indian raw material prices, as China and Vietnam reprocessors are big consumers of small-sized shrimp," he said.

Despite the early price drop, medium-sized shrimp are still trading approximately INR 20/kg higher than at the same time last year.

Sheraz Anwar, director of shrimp and cephalopod processor and trader Abad Overseas, said earlier this month that only the earliest vannamei farmers and late-season black tiger producers had completed harvests.

"Prices were very high due to shortage of raw material in the last few months, now it's more or less manageable," he told Undercurrent at the time. "Seeding on vannamei (70%) and black tiger (40%) is complete, and the rest should be seeded in March and April, respectively," he added.

He said markets fell to rock bottom from April through July last year, and farmers will be keen to avoid the same fate this year:

China shrimp prices continue recovery

Chinese vannamei shrimp prices have surged dramatically in recent weeks, continuing their recovery from near two-year lows reached in January and puzzling many industry participants who had expected continued weak market conditions after Chinese New Year.

According to the latest data, 60-count shrimp prices in Jiangsu province climbed to CNY 56/kg in week 10, up from CNY 54/kg in week nine and CNY 46/kg in week eight -- effectively doubling from the CNY 27/kg recorded in week three. Meanwhile, Guangdong province saw prices rise to CNY 40/kg in week 10, up from CNY 38/kg the previous week.

"The sharp price drop in January almost caused all farmers in Jiangsu to incur losses, yet now the price has doubled. This is truly a rare occurrence," an executive from a feed company told Undercurrent. The source added that traders from Fujian and Guangdong are transporting shrimp to Shanghai due to severe shortages in Jiangsu, which serves as the largest live shrimp supplier to the Greater Shanghai area.

The rapid price recovery has been most pronounced in northern provinces, with Shandong seeing a CNY 8/kg increase from week eight to week 10, stabilizing at CNY 46/kg. Fujian, however, saw a slight week-on-week correction in week 10, easing to CNY 43/kg from CNY 44/kg.

Despite the rising prices, Chinese farmers remain cautious about increasing production. "The price of post-larvae has not yet increased, which suggests many farmers are still holding back. There has not been a large-scale stocking yet," a spokesperson from Tongwei, China's second-largest shrimp feed manufacturer, reported.

Slight correction in Vietnam for large sizes

Vietnamese shrimp prices saw a modest correction in week 10 after several weeks of steady increases, with larger sizes suffering as processors adjusted buying strategies.

Data provided by aquatech platform Tomota shows chilled 30-count vannamei at VND 158,500/kg ($6.22/kg) for the latest week, down from VND 160,000/kg in week nine. Meanwhile, medium sizes remained relatively stable, with 60-count rising slightly to VND 119,000/kg from VND 117,000/kg the previous week.

"Large processing plants tend to maintain stable vannamei shrimp prices for the primary purchase sizes of 50-80 counts/kg to ensure a consistent supply of raw materials," an industry source told Undercurrent. "However, a considerable reduction in farm-gate price has been implemented for the 30-counts due to a current lack of urgent demand."

The source noted that farm-gate prices were VND 176,000/kg for 30-count, VND 134,000/kg for 50-count, and VND 112,000/kg for 80-count whiteleg shrimp.

In the black tiger market, prices for all major sizes saw slight reductions. Prices for premium 10-count black tiger fell to VND 386,000/kg from VND 391,143/kg, while 20-count decreased to VND 191,000/kg from VND 196,143/kg.

The adjustments come amid continuing supply challenges, with the source reporting that "new vannamei shrimp stocking area in the first two months of this year remained low (9% per month), and disease outbreaks were complex (approximately 30-40% discard rate)."

Disease problems persist in March, particularly in the important Mekong Delta region, where stocking progress has been slow to improve. Despite these challenges, most processing plants are maintaining relatively stable raw material prices for black tiger shrimp amid limited supply and transaction volumes.

Prices stable in Ecuador

Ecuadorian vannamei shrimp prices held steady in week 10 for the fourth consecutive week following a significant market correction in early February.

Premium 20-30 count shrimp maintained their price at $4.60/kg, while 30-40 count held at $4.05/kg. Medium 40-50 count and 50-60 count remained at $3.75/kg and $3.40/kg respectively.

Despite the recent market correction, current prices remain notably higher than those seen a year ago. Premium 20-30 count shrimp are trading $0.60/kg above last year's levels, while medium-sized 50-60 count have seen a substantial year-on-year increase of $1.33/kg.

Prices steady in Indonesia

Indonesian vannamei shrimp prices continue to position the country as Asia's lowest-priced supplier, with the market showing minimal movement in recent weeks.

According to data from platform Jala, East Java saw prices for 90-count shrimp recover slightly to IDR 55,000 ($3.36)/kg in week 11. Similarly, 100-count shrimp rebounded slightly to IDR 53,000/kg.

The Indonesian market has remained largely flat since the beginning of 2025, despite minor week-to-week fluctuations across various size grades.

Significant price drop in Thailand

After strong gains earlier in the year, Thai shrimp prices reversed course in weeks nine and 10, with substantial declines across all major size categories.

According to the latest market data, ex-farm prices for benchmark 60-count vannamei fell to THB 160/kg in week 10, down from THB 165/kg in week nine and a recent high of THB 175/kg in week eight. This represents an 8.6% decline over just two weeks.

title: Untitled
content:
South Africa's Sea Harvest Group expects the industry to harvest all of its increased 2025 hake allocation of 151,700 metric tons due to fleet upgrades, a senior executive with the company told the whitefish panel at the North Atlantic Seafood Forum (NASF).

The total allowable catch was increased 4% for 2025, after a year in which the total was not fully utilized, but exports of frozen fillets and whole -- as well as fresh -- fish hit a record level of $192 million.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view

South Africa's export volume across all three main product types was 41,223t, of which frozen fillets make up the biggest portion.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
South Africans upgrade hake fleet to catch bumper 152,000t quota with demand strong - Undercurrent News

"It's at a peak for this season, and we expect that to remain stable in the next two to three years, then reduce again to levels of about 135,000-140,000t," Konrad Geldenhuys, the chief operating officer of fishing and processing firm Sea Harvest Group, told the NASF panel audience in a video presentation from Cape Town.

Although the smaller total allowable catch (TAC) in 2024 was not fully caught due to "lower catch rates and also insufficient capacity," companies are adding new capacity for 2025 in the Marine Stewardship Council-certified South African and Namibian fisheries, he said during the session at NASF, held every March in Bergen, Norway. 

Sea Harvest has acquired two headed and gutted (H&G) freezer trawlers from Spain to replace two lost in 2024. In May last year, a Sea Harvest trawler sunk, with the loss of 11 of the 20 crew. Then, in October last year, another vessel suffered a fire, with all the crew rescued.

Konrad Geldenhuys, the chief operating officer of fishing and processing firm Sea Harvest Group, covered the outlook for Cape hake supply at NASF. Credit: Tom Seaman

One of the new H&G freezers arrived in early 2025, with the other acquired in January and set to arrive in May.

"The first should start fishing by the end of March," Geldenhuys said.

According to Geldenhuys, the two vessels are larger than the ones they will replace, so they will increase Sea Harvest's capacity.

In 2024, the company also added Harvest Cap Nord, a hake freezer trawler, and Isabella Marine, a hake wet fish trawler, to its fleet.

"The industry is currently building capacity to catch the TAC, which is at a peak. Once the TAC reduces, that additional capacity will be applied as a vessel renewal strategy," said Geldenhuys.

For Namibia, the 2025 TAC was cut 9% to 140,000t for 2025. "That was fully caught in 2024," Geldenhuys said.

Global markets strong amid Russian restrictions 

Looking more closely at South Africa's exports of frozen/fresh whole hake and frozen fillets on the Undercurrent trade portal, you can see sales were up in value to most of its main markets.

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view
South Africans upgrade hake fleet to catch bumper 152,000t quota with demand strong - Undercurrent News

Felix Ratheb, CEO of Sea Harvest, said the outlook on demand for 2025 is robust in a post dated Feb. 26, 2025, on the website of the South African Deep-Sea Trawling Industry Association (SADSTIA).

Ratheb said the market for Cape hake is strong, and it stands to benefit from the gaps left in Western markets by the reduction in Atlantic cod catches and the diversion of Russian catches to Asian markets.

"The ongoing war in Ukraine has had a significant ripple effect on global groundfish supply, with Russia accounting for a substantial 36% of global groundfish production," said Ratheb.

Russian H&G pollock prices drop as supply recovers; cod, haddock rise

"This includes 56% of the world's pollock catch and 30% of Atlantic cod production.

In response to Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the US imposed a ban on all Russian seafood imports in March 2022, which was later extended to include seafood processed in third countries such as China, he said.

"Simultaneously, the European Union imposed a 13.7% tariff on Russian seafood imports, while the United Kingdom enforced an even higher tariff of 35%. These sanctions reduced the flow of Russian-origin groundfish to traditional Western markets, especially the EU," said Ratheb in the SADSTIA post.

In response, Russia has promoted its domestic seafood market and is ramping up exports to Asia, particularly China and other nations in the BRICS (Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa) bloc, said the Sea Harvest CEO.

"There's a very big push by the Russians to consume their catch of pollock internally," says Ratheb, "this is quite a big change in the market. It creates new opportunities for Russian producers, but it also reduces the supply of groundfish to traditional markets in the EU and the US."

The most significant impact on the global market for groundfish has been a sharp decline in Atlantic cod production. Quotas have been cut dramatically, said Ratheb.

US wholesale: Twice-frozen cod, haddock prices keep rising

"For example, quotas for Northeast Atlantic cod have been cut by more than 30% in response to lower-than-expected recruitment. The 2025 catch forecast of 650,000t represents a 40% reduction from the 2022 high of 1.1m metric tons."

He said cod is considered a premium groundfish species, and Atlantic cod accounts for roughly 17% of the global groundfish supply.

"The steep decline in Atlantic cod supply, coupled with no expected quota increases until at least 2028, has already started to drive prices up," said Ratheb. 

As Undercurrent's prices portal shows, Russian and Norwegian frozen cod and haddock raw materials are at record levels, looking at delivered China levels.
