title: Trump doubles down on seafood industry-punishing tariffs in speech to Congress despite bad market reaction
content:
US president Donald Trump, in his record-long, 99-minute speech given to a joint session of Congress Tuesday night (March 4), didn't give any sign he might withdraw the 25% tariffs imposed on all goods from Canada and Mexico, or the additional 10% tariff just placed on Chinese products.

The seafood industry looks to pay a dear price in the newly reignited trade war, as the US imported a combined 738,180 metric tons of seafood worth more than $6.1 billion Canada, Mexico and China in 2024, while exporting 518,176t worth $2.2bn to the three countries the same year.

A 25% tariff on Canada and Mexico alone would cost seafood importers more than $1.1bn. 

Trump previously said the tariffs would be imposed in relation to the influx of undocumented immigrants and fentanyl coming across US land borders, but in his joint session speech -- which was not technically a state-of-the-union address -- he talked more about trade imbalances and fairness.

Canadian lobster, snow crab sectors fear US consumer backlash as tariffs push prices 25% higher

"We have been ripped off for decades by nearly every country on Earth, and we will not let that happen any longer," Trump said. "Much has been said over the last three months about Mexico and Canada, but we have very large deficits with both of them."

Just hours before Trump's speech, US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick suggested in an appearance on the Fox Business News show "Kudlow" that Trump might announce a compromise with Canada and Mexico on Wednesday. He said he had spoken to both countries on the phone Tuesday (March 3), and they told him "they'll do better."

"I think he's going to work something out with them," Lutnick said, adding: "It's not going to be a pause — none of that pause stuff — but I think he's going to figure out, you do more and I'll meet you in the middle someway and we're going to probably be announcing that tomorrow. Somewhere in the middle will likely be the outcome, the president moving with the Canadians and Mexicans but not all the way."

Lutnick's comments came following another down day for US stock markets. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 both finished Tuesday off a little more than 1% while the Nasdaq exchange finished the day down slightly under 1%. Each exchange had seen previous days of declines in apparent response to Trump's tariffs, among other issues.

Trump had previously set tariffs to take effect on Feb. 4, but delayed them a month for Canada and Mexico while allowing a 10% tariff to begin for China. Chinese seafood imports, already facing 25% tariffs in the US as the result of tariffs put in place by Trump during his first term as president, in 2018, are now facing combined tariffs of 45%. 

Much of the costs associated with tariffs are passed along to US consumers, making seafood from other countries, including lobster, snow crab, Atlantic salmon, tilapia and red swimming crab, more expensive.

But Trump described tariffs as a "beautiful word" during his address, crediting them for pushing car companies to set up manufacturing plants in the US. He also credited his tariffs on Mexico for getting that country to hand over "29 of the biggest cartel leaders in their country," adding that Mexico wants "to make us happy, first time ever."

He said more tariffs are coming, including reciprocal tariffs that he plans to put in place on April 2. 

Hundreds of US seafood products on Canada’s list for potential retaliatory tariffs

"Other countries have used tariffs against us for decades, and now it's our turn to start using them against those other countries," he said. "On average, the European Union, China, Brazil, India, Mexico and Canada, have you heard of them? And countless other nations charge us tremendously higher tariffs than we charge them. It's very unfair."

He continued: "We have been ripped off for decades by nearly every country on Earth, and we will not let that happen any longer. Much has been said over the last three months about Mexico and Canada, but we have very large deficits with both of them."

Farmers, who count on exports to sell many of their goods, can look forward to tariffs being imposed by other countries in retaliation, too, but Trump assured them that his "new trade policy will also be great for the American farmer."

He said: "I love the farmer, who will now be selling into our home market, the USA, because nobody is going to be able to compete with you. Because there's goods that come in from other companies, countries and companies. They're really, really in a bad position in so many different ways. They're uninspected. They may be very dirty and disgusting, and they come in and they pour in and they hurt our American farmers."

Trump said tariffs will go on agricultural imports starting on April 2.

USMCA review in the works

Trump's comments on Tuesday night were in keeping with his 2025 trade policy agenda, published Monday (March 3) by Jamieson Greer, the recently confirmed US trade representative.

"President Trump alone recognized the role that trade policy has played in creating these challenges and how trade policy can fix them," a five-page summary of the policy reads. "Since he first took the oath of office in 2017, president Trump has reshaped the trade policy landscape to prioritize the national interest. He has built a new consensus that tariffs are a legitimate tool of public policy. He has demonstrated the imperative for tough trade enforcement against countries who think they can take advantage of the United States and get away with it. He has shown that the United States has leverage and can negotiate aggressively to open markets for Made in America exports, particularly for agricultural exports. He has proven that a robust and realist trade policy can create jobs, promote innovation, strengthen the national defense, raise wages, support farmers and foster the manufacturing renaissance that many elites long thought was impossible for the United States to achieve."

Greer further noted that USTR is planning to conduct a statutorily required public consultation process of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement in order to "assess the impact of the USMCA on American workers, farmers, ranchers, service providers and other businesses" in preparation for a mandated review of the agreement in July 2026.

title: US bill would require foreign shrimp producers satisfy equivalency standard
content:
A new bill from US senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Mississippi Republican, would require foreign shrimp facilities to satisfy inspection standards that are equivalent to those required of US shrimp producers if they want to keep exporting to the US.

The Safer Shrimp Imports Act (S.667), introduced Feb. 20, is in its early stages and has been referred to the Senate Committee on Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions. It has no co-sponsors yet. But Hyde-Smith, in a statement published Tuesday (Feb. 25), argued that the bill is needed because 90% of the shrimp consumed by Americans comes from foreign sources.  

"There are three key reasons why this bill is urgently needed," she said. "First, it would give American consumers greater confidence that the imported shrimp they're eating isn't contaminated with drugs. Second, it aligns with the president's Make American Healthy Again goals to eliminate harmful chemicals in the food supply. And third, it will help level the playing field for American shrimpers who suffer because foreign governments dump their subsidized and tainted shrimp on the US market."

The bill would create regulations similar to those championed by late US senator Thad Cochran, also a Mississippi Republican, to level the playing field for domestic catfish producers with importers of pangasius from Vietnam. Thanks to a measure he had included in the 2014 farm bill, since 2015 imported pangasius has had to comply with food safety standards enforced by the US Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service.  

Hyde-Smith's legislation would instead lean more heavily on the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). It would require foreign governments with shrimp facilities seeking to export shrimp to the US to demonstrate to the US agency an equivalent food inspection system.

US senator Cindy Hyde-Smith at a hearing in 2019. Photograph from USDA on Flickr.

Any shrimp imported or offered for import into the US from a country that has not been established to have met such a standard would be deemed to be adulterated, meaning it couldn't be sold or consumed in the US. 

The bill also would require regular reporting by the FDA to Congress on its implementation. 

Hyde-Smith echoed critical sentiments being expressed by the president Donald Trump administration in her statement, suggesting the FDA isn't currently doing a good enough job of stopping the import of contaminated shrimp.

"The FDA has been lackadaisical about seafood inspection for far too long, contributing to a silent public health crisis in America," she said. "I look forward to working with the president and [Health and Human Services Department] secretary [Robert F.] Kennedy [Jr.] to make shrimp healthy again."

"International equivalence" is considered the leading standard for evaluating different countries' food safety inspection systems, the statement continued.  

The legislation is supported by the American Shrimp Processors Association (ASPA), a group that reports to represent harvesters and processors behind roughly 85% of the US' domestic frozen warmwater shrimp production. It was ASPA's petitions in October 2023 that led to antidumping and countervailing duties being brought against the imports of shrimp from companies in four of the US' biggest shrimp source countries in 2024.

"We are thrilled that senator Hyde-Smith has taken a great step in the direction of ensuring that foreign producers conform to the same requirements as our domestic producers," ASPA counsel Edward Hayes, also a partner at the New Orleans, Louisiana, law firm of Leake & Andersson, told Undercurrent on Tuesday.

title: US judge allows Oregon lawsuit over cold-water salmon refuges to proceed
content:
A US judge is allowing the latest lawsuit to improve water quality for salmon and steelhead in Oregon's Columbia River to proceed with government agencies forced to ensure there's enough cold water for the endangered fish species.

That's after attempts of a negotiated settlement apparently failed last year, sending the complex environmental and legal case back to the courts. 

Litigants want more time to solve Columbia River salmon problem

US District Court of Oregon judge Amy Baggio noted that Northwest Environmental Advocates (NWEA) has filed a string of lawsuits to compel the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to ensure water temperatures in the state's largest river are below 68 degrees Fahrenheit (20 degrees celsius) to prevent die-offs.

"This case is the fourth in a series of cases involving Oregon's rivers and the survival of its cold water fish," Baggio wrote in her Feb. 11 order denying the EPA's request to limit the scope of the agency's involvement.

The latest lawsuit accuses the NMFS of relying on a flawed 2015 biological opinion "that will bring no real protection to threatened or endangered salmon and steelhead listed under the Endangered Species Act."

The cold-water refuges outlined in the NMFS biological opinion envision cold-water refuges for the endangered fish but lack any enforcement allowing state and federal environmental regulators to ignore them.

NMFS declined to comment citing the pending litigation.

"Columbia River salmon and steelhead are not protected one iota from the dangers of unsafe water temperatures by the mounting number of paper plans," NWEA executive director Nina Bell said in a statement announcing the 2021 lawsuit.

The complaint seeks to compel the court to throw out the old plans that it says haven't proven successful after two decades of litigation and require "EPA to prepare new cold water refugia plans that will set out steps/actions to remedy existing temperature conditions that are adversely affecting migrating salmon and steelhead" to be approved by the court.

FREE READ US Pacific Northwest sees huge Columbia River sockeye salmon return

"Every day that passes with these unsafe water quality criteria in place poses more risk of injury and lethal harm to the imperiled species and thus more injury to NWEA and its members," wrote the attorneys for the Portland-based environmental advocacy group.

Oregon state officials reported huge die-offs in 2024 following hot weather on the Columbia River where about 700,000 sockeye salmon were projected to return to fresh water but were imperiled by high water temperatures, as Undercurrent News reported.

Wild salmon on the Columbia River have been imperiled by hydroelecric dams and other human activity for more than a century. But as Undercurrent has also reported, the federal government has invested hundreds of millions in recent year to help restore the runs.

title: Royal Greenland affiliate Quin-Sea claims defamation by Canadian processor group
content:
Add a defamation lawsuit to the months-long fight between Quin-Sea Fisheries, a division of Royal Greenland, and the Association of Seafood Producers (ASP).

Quin-Sea, a snow crab processor based in the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador (NL), has filed a statement of claim in the Supreme Court of Newfoundland and Labrador against the ASP and its executive director, Jeff Loder. It charges that the organization, which serves as a trade group for processors in NL, made false statements to Undercurrent News and AllNewfoundland, a St. John's (NL)-based news service, indicating Quin-Sea and Royal Greenland both violated the Fishing Industry Collective Bargaining Act (FICBA).

"The combined effect of Loder's media comments gives the reader an unambiguous impression that Quin-Sea has intentionally broken the law," said Quin-Sea, which has called the statements "slanderous" and "made with malice."

Jeff Loder, executive director of the Association of Seafood Producers. Picture courtesy of ASP.

The bad blood between Quin-Sea and the ASP is rooted in a deal brokered during the 2024 snow crab season between the ASP and the Fish Food and Allied Workers (FFAW), the union representing fish harvesters in NL.

To get the 2024 snow crab season underway in NL, after fish harvesters refused to fish for two weeks at the start of the season in April, the ASP reached a deal with the union for a dock price of CAD 3.00 ($2.15) per pound. The deal ended a two-week harvester tie-up in the world's largest snow crab fishery, which has a 2024 quota of 57,568 metric tons.

As part of that deal, the ASP agreed to have an independent third party, the accounting firm of Deloitte Touche, conduct a review at the end of the season to assess the market prices paid to processors for frozen 5-8 ounce snow crab sections and determine whether harvesters should get an additional rebate for their catches for the season, as reported by Undercurrent.

However, Quin-Sea claims in its Supreme Court filing that the deal between the ASP and FFAW was signed "under duress" and "contrary to the spirit and intent" of the province's Fishing Industry Collective Bargaining Act (FICBA).

"The revised 2024 crab schedule was the result of backroom dealings between ASP and the FFAW, held without transparency to ASP members, and without the proper representation of at least three processors, as required by the FICBA," Quin-Sea wrote in its application to the court.

"Even if the deal had been a legally-enforceable part of the collective agreement, it contained no requirement for any processor, including Quin-Sea, to disclose its confidential business records," Quin-Sea contended.

When Quin-Sea refused to share its sales data with Deloitte, the FFAW's then-president Greg Pretty, said the union would not accept any report on settlement payments to harvesters without the Quin-Sea data.

Royal Greenland’s Quin-Sea withdraws from Newfoundland processors group

That prompted the ASP to file a grievance against Quin-Sea with the province's labor board in October 2024, requesting that the board order the company to provide the information required about the value of its 2024 sales of 5-8 oz crab sections, as per the collective agreement signed by all ASP members with the FFAW.

However, Quin-Sea also claims that the ASP made "blatantly false" statements in that grievance to try to compel the company to produce confidential business records.

By December, the FFAW had a new president, Dwan Street, and the union and ASP agreed to work without the Quin-Sea data to settle the final crab prices. The ASP withdrew its grievance application but continued to chastise Quin-Sea/Royal Greenland.

"From the perspective of the ASP, Royal Greenland broke the 2024 collective agreement. Those behaviors will not be tolerated," Loder was quoted as saying by media.

"if one processor can decide what the rules are in Newfoundland, there's no sense in negotiating anything," Loder emphasized, adding: "[T]his will be the last time a processor or a harvester deliberately breaks the collective agreement and undermines a broader arrangement."

Quin-Sea claims Loder's statements were slanderous, made with malice and diminished the company's reputation.

Canadian processor group in fight with Royal Greenland over crab harvester bonus

The company, which canceled its membership in ASP in January, is seeking general and aggravated damages against the ASP and Loder, jointly and severally, as well as court costs related to the action.

The company has declined requests for interviews regarding its legal claim.

"Quin-Sea Fisheries is fully cooperative with, and respectful of, local laws and regulations. As a matter of principle and out of respect for the legal process, including those involved therein, the company does not comment on legal proceedings," offered Patrick Hickey, strategy and impact advisor with Quin-Sea, in an email to Undercurrent.

The ASP has not offered a public statement regarding Quin-Sea's claims, but a spokesperson for the group said it would file a statement of defense.

No court dates have been set for the matter.

title: Peru tightens fishing regs for jumbo flying squid, targets MSC certification
content:
Peru's government has implemented a new regulation to protect artisanal fishermen impacted by sustainability concerns facing Peru's jumbo flying squid (pota) fishery.

Peru's production ministry issued a resolution on Feb. 9 mandating that squid fishing in Peruvian waters must be conducted exclusively using manual and passive techniques, such as jigging lines, so as to guarantee a "capture without significant negative impacts." The decision aligns with the scientific recommendations of Peru's Sea Institute, a governmental agency also known as Imarpe.

Peru’s giant squid sector faces worst crisis as concerns over Chinese IUU practices mount

Peru's jumbo squid fishery is crucial to the nation's economy. It employs over 20,000 artisanal fishers and generates up to $850 million in revenue annually, accounting for approximately 30% of the country's seafood exports by value.

However, concerns have grown over the resource's sustainability due to the use of non-selective fishing methods such as purse-seine nets and curtains, which can harm the marine ecosystem and create unfair competition for artisanal fishers.

The graphs below from UCN's trade portal show that giant squid and cuttlefish exports last year (broken down by the top 10 partners in the second graph) dropped until June 2024, according to the latest available data. Meanwhile, prices sharply increased.

Peru tightens fishing regs for jumbo flying squid, targets MSC certification  - Undercurrent News

The graph below also shows Peruvian exports of seafood for human consumption (including jumbo squid but also other species) until Nov. 2024.

Industry representatives have welcomed the new regulation as a step toward more sustainability. As a further measure, some of the country's squid industry associations said they are aiming to obtain the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certification for the fishery.

Alfonso Miranda, president of the fisheries and aquaculture committee of Peru's National Society of Industries, said the measure guarantees artisanal fishermen will continue to use less-harmful methods of fishing.

"The ministerial resolution reaffirms three key principles: exclusively artisanal fishing, predominance of manual methods and use of selective gear such as the jigging line," he said. "The next step for better fishery management is the publication of the Squid Fisheries Management Regulation (ROP)."

Squid prices rise as supply squeeze hits key commercial species

Javier Querevalu, president of the Yacila fishers guild, noted Imarpe has classified jumbo squid as fully exploited, meaning that limiting non-selective fishing is crucial to prevent overexploitation. Gerardo Carrera, president of the Peruvian jumbo squid chamber, also known as CAPECAL, underlined the need for further regulatory improvements to advance toward MSC certification, an internationally recognized sustainability standard.

"Today, Peru shows the world that sustainability is not a slogan but a practice," said Jorge Jacinto, a leader of the San Jose Artisanal Fishers Association. He said the Imarpe must now work to maintain and strengthen the reforms, particularly the ROP, to secure the fishery's future.

Crackdown on illegal foreign fishing operations

Peru's government has also initiated a crackdown on the monitoring of foreign fishing vessels operating near its exclusive economic zone, particularly those from China, which have frequently been accused of crossing into Peruvian waters.

Between May 2023 and September 2024, government enforcement of satellite monitoring regulations was inconsistent, leading to approximately 400 unauthorized entries of Chinese squid vessels into Peruvian waters, according to the Committee for the Sustainable Management of the Jumbo Flying Squid, also known as Calamasur. This sparked outrage among local fishers, who accused authorities of not taking action against the illegal foreign incursions into local waters.

Peru’s fleet to compete with Asian fleet on high seas amid giant squid shortage in EEZ

In response, in September, the government reinstated the installation of a mandatory satellite tracking system (SISESAT) for all foreign squid vessels entering Peruvian waters, and made it clear all foreign vessels in Peruvian waters must abide by the same regulations as Peruvian ships, which include severe penalties for tampering with or disabling satellite tracking.

A Chinese source writing on Undercurrent's WeChat noted a Chinese vessel that entered Peruvian waters for an emergency recently had complied with Chinese government regulations, though it had installed China's navigation system rather than SISESAT.

China's largest squid trading platform, Huacai Zhaoyu, said Chinese fishing vessels near Peru are operating legally.

"Fishing vessels strictly adhere to Chinese laws and regulations and, most of the time, operate in international waters outside Peru's exclusive economic zone (EEZ). Even when entering Peru's EEZ, they follow Peru's regulations and procedures meticulously," Huacai said.

However, Calamasur said satellite reports indicate that not a single Chinese vessel has complied with the SISESAT requirement since its implementation.

Alleged refuge in Chilean ports

According to the Peruvian group, some foreign squid-fishing vessels have diverted their operations to Chilean ports, where monitoring regulations are less stringent.

According to Calamasur, in January 2025, the Chinese vessel Lu Rong Yuan Yu 608 avoided Peruvian controls by detouring over 2,200 km to Iquique, Chile, instead of entering a closer Peruvian port. The association said this effort doesn't make financial sense, as the cost of fuel, crew expenses, and lost fishing time for a diversion to Chile --estimated at $250,000 -- far outweighs the $200 cost of complying with Peru's satellite monitoring.

Lu Rong Yuan Yu 608. Photo: Calamasur.

Eight Chinese vessels have already opted for Chilean ports, where satellite monitoring is less strict. The trend raises questions about hidden costs or undisclosed incentives driving these vessels to avoid Peruvian oversight, according to Calamasur.

Miranda, who is also Calamasur's president, said that enforcing satellite monitoring is crucial to combating illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing. He urged Peruvian authorities to impose sanctions on non-compliant vessels and uphold Peru's leadership in fisheries transparency.

However, legal experts have warned that gaps in the new Peruvian regulations could allow foreign vessels to circumvent monitoring.

Piero Rojas Vasquez, legal advisor to the Peruvian Society of Artisanal Fishing, also known as Sonapescal, pointed out that a provision allowing foreign vessels to "homologate" their satellite signals with Peruvian systems could lead to reduced transparency, as it would rely on data filtered through technology operated by foreign authorities rather than direct tracking by Peru.

Rojas Vasquez said the provision was added to the final legal framework without transparent regulatory analysis or public consultation, raising legitimacy and legal concerns. He called for stricter regulatory oversight to prevent Peru's new system from being exploited as a loophole allowing continued IUU fishing.

title: Long-time NOAA staffer Menashes named acting leader of NMFS, replaces Coit
content:
The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has a new leader of its National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), the branch of government that oversees regulation of domestic fisheries, which is also known as NOAA Fisheries.

Emily Menashes, a nearly 25-year NOAA staffer who has been NMFS deputy assistant administrator for operations since 2023, has been appointed as the agency's acting assistant administrator, as well as NOAA's acting assistant secretary for oceans and atmosphere, confirms a recently published organizational chart.

Menashes was tapped to fill the vacancy resulting from the departure of Janet Coit, who was appointed to head NMFS by the previous US president, Joe Biden, in 2021. Coit left NOAA in January 2025 upon the inauguration of current US president Donald Trump.

In her new position, Menashes will oversee NMFS' 4,800 employees spread across five regional offices, six science centers and 20 laboratories in 15 states and US territories. Menashes will also head up US recreational and commercial fisheries management in federal waters.

Fishing groups laud Trump’s choice for NOAA administrator, Neil Jacobs

Menashes has retained her previous title as deputy assistant administrator for operations, a role that provides oversight of the NMFS budget and its facilities, including NMFS' headquarters offices of Human Capital Management, International Affairs, Trade and Commerce, Law Enforcement, Aquaculture, Policy and Communications.

However, her position is likely to be reviewed by US president Donald Trump's pick for commerce secretary Howard Lutnick or his NOAA administrator nominee Neil Jacobs if and when they are confirmed. Menashes would report to Jacobs if he is confirmed, and Jacobs in turn would report to Lutnick.

Lutnick's nomination was advanced by the Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee on a 16-12 vote, and his confirmation awaits a vote of the full Senate, which is expected within the next week. Jacobs' nomination has not yet been voted on by the committee.

NOAA employees have been told to expect deep reductions in staff and budget cuts under the Trump administration, as Undercurrent News previously reported, though Lutnick has vowed not to dismantle the agency entirely, as envisioned by Project 2025, a conservative strategy for reducing the size and scope of the federal government, which has been largely adopted by Trump.

Previously, Menashes was a senior policy advisor and acting NOAA deputy chief of staff, chief of staff at NOAA's Ocean Service, and deputy director in NOAA's Office of Sustainable Fisheries. From 2023 to 2024, she played a role in the crafting and implementation of the National Seafood Strategy.

Menashes grew up in Pennsylvania and Connecticut and has a master's degree in marine resource management from Oregon State University and a bachelor's degree in biology and environmental studies from Bowdoin College.

She reported pursuing a career in fisheries management after working on a research project studying groundfish fisheries in New England.

Trump’s commerce secretary pick, Howard Lutnick, vows not to dismantle NOAA

"I knew I wanted to pursue a career that involved the ocean after doing my college capstone research on the interaction between ecology and economics in the management of the New England groundfishery," she said in a 2022 interview. "The fascinating and challenging interplay between the environment, people, and decision-making is what drew me to NOAA and what continues to excite me about the work we do."

In 2023, Menashes outlined the goals she set in her new position as NMFS deputy assistant administrator for operations.

"My immediate goals are to continue the outstanding work underway to build and nurture an inclusive and engaged workforce and do everything I can to break down organizational barriers to make it easier and more efficient to fulfill our mission while we face the growing impact of climate change."

title: US lawmaker asks Trump for 100% tariffs on Asian seafood
content:
US representative Clay Higgins, a Louisiana Republican, has asked president Donald Trump to levy tariffs of up to 100% and increase trade enforcement for seafood imports from China, Ecuador, India, Indonesia and Vietnam.

"Domestic shrimpers, fishermen, and crawfish producers in Louisiana and across the country face significant challenges competing against foreign seafood industries that are heavily subsidized and engage in illegal dumping into the United States," Higgins wrote in a letter sent Tuesday (Feb. 11).

"These unrighteous trade practices artificially drive down prices, disrupt fair market conditions, and threaten the livelihoods of hardworking American seafood producers. Without strong and consistent intervention, our seafood industry will remain vulnerable to these illegal trade tactics that erode the competitive market," Higgins added.

 "I respectfully urge your administration to use all available enforcement tools, such as imposing antidumping and countervailing duties, implementing stricter testing protocols, and taking decisive actions, including levying tariffs of up to 100% or destroying shipments that fail to meet US health standards, to ensure a level playing field for American producers," Clay requested.

The letter comes as the new president has issued and threatened to issue a slew of executive orders to tariff goods from different countries, including a new, additional 10% tariff on products from China.

Seafood imports also are under attack by state legislatures. A new law went into effect in Louisana on Jan. 1 requiring restaurants to disclose the origin of all seafood listed on their menus, as reported by Undercurrent News.

title: Wild salmon group demands pause in Newfoundland farm expansion until marine debris removed
content:
A wild salmon advocacy group says it's discovered salmon-farming debris in additional sites in the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador and is calling for a halt to the industry's expansion until pollution concerns at existing sites are addressed.

The Atlantic Salmon Federation (ASF), which advocates on behalf of the preservation of wild salmon populations, this week said its staff flew over multiple locations on Feb. 2 and observed deteriorated and sunken sea cages beyond "The Locker," a cove near Gaultois where salmon producer Cooke Aquaculture was ordered to remove aquaculture debris by Jan. 31.

"[A]ll visible aquaculture waste appears to have been removed" from The Locker, ASF acknowledged. However, the nonprofit said it has since identified additional sites in the province where abandoned farming equipment remains in the water, including sites leased to Cooke subsidiary Cold Ocean Salmon and Mowi-owned Northern Harvest Sea Farms.

In response to ASF's claims, Cooke vice president for public relations Joel Richardson defended the company's operations.

Joel Richardson, spokesperson for Cooke.

"Our Newfoundland and Labrador farming division, Cold Ocean Salmon, always has ongoing operations to replace, repair, remove and recycle cages. It's how responsible fish farming is done," Richardson told Undercurrent News on Wednesday. "Sea cages are engineered and designed for use in the ocean without harm to native species and marine habitat."

Richardson criticized ASF for taking money from outdoor clothing apparel company Patagonia owner Yvon Chouinard.

"ASF would be wise to focus on the decades of microplastic pollution created globally by one of its biggest donors," Richardson said. "Plastic Patagonia apparel is known to shed microplastics and microfibers into watersheds through residential washing machine discharge, which endangers wild salmon."

Mowi managing director Gideon Pringle also denied ASF's allegations.

“Mowi Canada East has no 'abandoned' equipment at sea. Disappointingly, images of Mowi assets have been misrepresented to media by ASF. In reality, the images show normal equipment at active and fallow (temporarily inactive) licensed farming locations," Gideon told Undercurrent.

"Contrary to ASF claims, damaged pens do not sink. Furthermore, any storm-damaged fish pens will be repaired or recycled in due course and prior to salmon restocking.”

ASF said it is working with an image analysis firm to conduct a satellite survey of all salmon farm sites in Newfoundland and Labrador. With 115 active fish farming licenses in the province, the organization believes the recently documented sites represent only a small part of a larger problem.

Illegal dumping in the province can result in fines of up to $1 million for companies, but ASF said it is unaware of any financial penalties imposed on Cooke in the case of The Locker.

New sites identified

Among the locations where ASF said it has documented salmon farming debris are:  Harvey Hill, Northeast Arm (Licenses #AQ15-LIC-0991, AQ15-LIC-0993), leased to Mowi's Northern Harvest Sea Farms, where ASF claims images show deteriorating and sinking sea cages.

A concentration of unused sea cages at Harvey Hill, Northeast Arm, near Harbour Breton on Feb. 2, 2025. Photo: Jake Dicks/ASF

ASF also claims photos taken on Feb. 2 of the farm site at Manuel Arm, Bay d'Espoir (License #AQ15-LIC-0842), leased to Cooke subsidiary Cold Ocean Salmon, show partially submerged, broken-down net pens (see photo below).

A screen grab from video shot on Feb. 2, 2025, showing boats working in the vicinity of the sunken debris. Credit: Google Earth, Jake Dicks/ASF

And ASF alleges images taken on Feb. 2 show a boat hauling away broken sea cages at the  Northwest Cove, Hermitage Bay (License #AQ15-LIC-0836) site, also leased to Cold Ocean Salmon.

A photo ASF said was taken on Feb. 2, 2025, showing a boat hauling away farm-site debris. Credit Google Earth, Jake Dicks/ASF

ASF is calling for provincial authorities to investigate these sites and to enact stricter enforcement of environmental regulations before approving any new aquaculture expansion in the region.

Industry response

Keith Sullivan, executive director of the Newfoundland Aquaculture Industry Association (NAIA), dismissed ASF's claims, arguing that the organization presents misleading information.

"The Atlantic Salmon Federation's campaign is an intentional attempt to mislead. They are presenting out-of-date pictures, while current pictures show equipment on sites licensed to the farming producers in Newfoundland and Labrador," Sullivan told Undercurrent in an email.

Keith Sullivan, NAIA executive director

"Floating aquaculture cages are an example of normal and safe equipment for ocean use. This is a thinly veiled attack by this activist group on the people, the jobs, and the coastal communities that farm the ocean. The aquaculture industry is strictly regulated by government agencies," Sullivan said.

Sullivan noted that all salmon producers, as members of the Canadian Aquaculture Industry Alliance (CAIA), have committed within their 2024 sustainability reports to ensuring that no farming equipment is released from farm sites and that there is prompt recovery of marine debris in the case of an accident.

"Seafood farmers in the province are proud to provide premium seafood to the world and be leaders in building strong and resilient coastal communities. Aquaculture is the economic engine for many of the towns on the south coast of Newfoundland," he added.

title: Labor activists criticize MSC for enabling abuses in fisheries
content:
NGO Global Labor Justice (GLJ) and allies in the Seafood Working Group (SWG) have issued an open letter to the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC), calling on the certification body to address labor abuses in certified fisheries.

The letter, signed by several SWG members, including the International Transport Workers' Federation, Humanity United, Freedom Fund, and Greenpeace US, asked the MSC "to take responsibility for the role of its social policies and processes in enabling the abuse of workers in certified fisheries and its attendant role in instances of certifying fish produced under conditions of labor exploitation."

According to the letter, at least 128,000 fishers are subjected to forced labor, while over 100,000 lose their lives annually due to hazardous conditions.

"Many fishers face grueling hours, withheld wages, abusive conditions, and extreme isolation, often with little to no protections or recourse. Despite these alarming conditions, seafood from such fleets continues to enter European and US markets. This systemic disregard for fishers' labor rights in the seafood sector is unacceptable and must urgently be addressed," the letter reads.

Due to increasing attention to the exploitation of migrant fishers and recent reports of forced labor incidents in MSC-certified fisheries, the MSC is facing scrutiny for failing to take responsibility for how its social policies and processes contribute to unchecked labor abuse in certified fisheries, according to the NGOs.

The SWG called on the MSC to be transparent about its ecolabel's limitations in protecting labor rights.

"Member organizations within the SWG have called on the MSC to be transparent, ensuring that all stakeholders -- including consumers -- understand that the MSC ecolabel does not, and cannot, safeguard against labor rights violations. Additionally, the letter demands that MSC must inform companies that relying solely on the MSC ecolabel for sourcing decisions without considering labor standards enables labor exploitation of workers and exposes companies to significant reputational risks."

"As the MSC does not provide adequate assurance for the protection of labor rights, the letter recommends that the MSC clearly acknowledge the label's limitations, actively and publicly endorse legally binding solutions to effectively protect fishers' labor rights, and promote other mechanisms that allow workers to assert their collective agency to monitor, enforce, and remedy labor rights violations."

You can read the full letter here.

Whole Foods’ latest seafood code update takes on labor standards, Wi-Fi access

An MSC spokesperson told Undercurrent News: "The presence of forced labor anywhere in the world is deeply distressing and unacceptable. As this letter highlights, widespread labor issues in the seafood industry are a significant challenge for the sector. We support efforts to address them and have requirements aimed at doing this."

Fisheries engaged in the MSC program must describe measures in place to prevent forced labor, and any fishery convicted of this, on vessels or in their supply chains, are excluded from being part of the MSC program, they continued.

"However, the MSC standard is an environmental one, rooted in the science of fisheries management, and the ecolabel makes no social claims. Our labor eligibility requirements are pre-entry requirements that entities have to meet before they are allowed to be audited against MSC's fisheries and chain of custody standards."

"A global survey of more than 20,000 people, carried out in 2024 by research organization Globescan, found that 99% of consumers do not associate the MSC ecolabel with working conditions and social responsibility," the MSC added.

"We recognise this is a rapidly changing space, and we are currently reviewing our requirements to see if they can be adapted to support businesses to meet their obligations for emerging due diligence legislation. We intend to continue working in partnership with experts on this issue to help the seafood sector make progress."

title: Spain’s fishing sector navigates turbulent waters with tightened quotas, post-Brexit talks
content:
As 2025 unfolds, Spain's fishing industry faces a tumultuous period, marked by new regulations, ongoing protests and challenging negotiations both within the country and on the international stage.

According to Javier Garat -- president of Europeche, the organization representing the European fishing industry, and secretary-general of Cepesca, the Spanish Confederation of Fisheries -- the sector is grappling with numerous challenges but also recognizing opportunities arising from these difficult circumstances.

Fishing body backs new EU commissioner’s pledge amid sector crisis

A central issue for the fishing industry now is the recent introduction of strict regulations in the Mediterranean, designed to curb overfishing.

Among the most impactful measures is a dramatic 79% reduction in fishing days, which Garat warned could have "severe economic consequences," he explained in a recent interview with RTVE.  

"The impact will be felt across the Mediterranean. The challenge is not just economic but also practical," he explained. "New total allowable catches and quotas and fishing regulations are seen as an attempt to regenerate fish stocks, but they also mean fewer catches for fishermen."

To mitigate the effect of these restrictions, the Spanish government has allowed changes to the mesh size of fishing nets, with coastal fishing nets increasing from 40 to 45 millimeters and deep-sea nets shifting to a square design.

"While these adjustments are intended to allow juvenile species to escape and regenerate fish populations, they come at a financial cost," Garat pointed out. "In many parts of Spain, there will be less catch, and this will directly affect income levels."

However, despite the government's efforts to introduce compensatory measures, such as a new subsidy program for nets, Garat expressed skepticism. "They're offering to provide nets to help with the transition, but what we need is a long-term solution."

Tensions have been high, especially after Spain's ministry of agriculture, fisheries, and food "painted the new rules in a positive light," with Garat describing the minister's public statements as "triumphalist" in contrast to the realities on the ground.

"It felt like the situation was being painted in a positive light when it's far from that," he claimed.

Thus, the government's measures have been met with resistance from the fishing community. In a dramatic response, 95% of the Mediterranean fleet went on strike in early January to protest the regulations.

Although some vessels returned to work after further compensation measures were announced, protests persisted, highlighting the frustration and uncertainty within the industry.

Spain leads Falklands squid stock assessment after 2024 season suspension

Additionally, the Spanish government has begun evaluating its fishing fleet to determine whether to implement a subsidized scrapping plan.

The assessment aims to identify fleet segments with excess capacity, particularly in the Mediterranean and Gulf of Cadiz, where imbalances have been noted. The fishing sector is requesting more substantial compensation to scrap their vessels than was provided in 2015. 

Beyond the immediate regulatory concerns, Garat also pointed to two key issues that will shape the future of Spain's fishing industry in 2025: post-Brexit negotiations and the reform of the common fisheries policy (CFP).

The transitional period for access to UK waters will end in 2026, and Spain is preparing for new negotiations with the UK. "We believe that the UK fleet has a strong dependency on European markets, and that will continue to be a key negotiating tool," said Garat.

Additionally, Garat highlighted the need for an overhaul of the CFP, particularly the "discard ban" regulation, which has proven difficult for fishermen to follow.

"The discard ban was a poorly drafted regulation, and we've been advocating for a more realistic approach for years," he explained. "Ensuring that future reforms are practical, enforceable, and aligned with the realities of fishing operations is very important now."

Another area of focus for Garat was the European Commission (EC) 's "Pact for the Oceans," an initiative that aims to align fisheries policy with broader ocean management efforts.

While he expressed cautious optimism about the pact's potential to reduce bureaucracy and promote sustainability, he noted that "the real test would be whether the EC's promises are effectively implemented."

"The fishing sector is one of the most regulated industries in the world. It's not as simple as people might think, with many layers of complex legislation," he said. "This underscores the need for greater understanding and support for the fishing community, which faces increasing environmental and regulatory pressures."

Despite the current challenges, Garat remained determined and pragmatic about the future of Spain's fishing industry.

"We [the Spanish fishing sector] are going to have to work with the changes, accept them with resignation, and try to make the best of it. However, even though we are determined to continue fighting for a better future for our fishermen, we need a government and an EC that will truly listen and support the sector in the long term," he concluded.

As Undercurrent News previously reported, Europeche and other representatives held a first meeting on Jan. 29 with new commissioner Costa Kadis to address the future of the EU fisheries sector under the legislative term 2024-2029. 

Europeche emphasized the urgency of addressing challenges such as shrinking fleet sizes, job losses, rising costs, and increasing access restrictions. The association once again called on the EC to creat" a "level playing f"eld" by ensuring imported seafood meets the same sustainability standards as EU-caught products -- something it has long argued is not the case.

title: Daily recap: US-EU tariffs would hit $1.4bn in seafood; Threat of NOAA staff cuts worries industry
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Friday, Feb. 7.

US tariffs on EU would hit $1.4bn in seafood imports


Salmon, octopus, fresh seabass and seabream, and cod fillets -- four categories the European seafood industry is fretting about as US president Donald Trump flirts with levying more tariffs.

US seafood industry concerned by threat of staff reductions at NOAA

The seafood industry is concerned about reports of disruptions at the federal agency that oversees the regulation of commercial fishing in the US.

Koral to be included in Captain Fresh, Sekkingstad salmon JV, with 'more to come'

Captain Fresh's Poland-based salmon smoking plant Koral will be included in the formal joint venture (JV) between the Indian firm and the owner of Norway's Sekkingstad with "more to come," the JV's new CEO said.

Red Lobster sets goal of profitability by 2026

Red Lobster is forecasting a $51.8 million loss for its 2025 fiscal year but a return to profitability in 2026.

Spain leads Falklands squid stock assessment after 2024 season suspension

Spain has sent a scientific expedition to assess squid stocks in the Falkland Islands following the suspension of the region's second fishing season in 2024.

title: Catch the Current episode 3: Trump’s tariffs and what the seafood industry should be watching next
content:
"You're tariffed."

US president Donald Trump started off the week doling out tariffs to Canada, Mexico and China -- and then pausing tariffs on Canada and Mexico after the two countries agreed to enforce border protection. What happens next? Undercurrent News' team of reporters are breaking it all down on the latest episode of Catch the Current.

Hosts Amanda Buckle and Lorin Castiglione are joined by Undercurrent News co-founder Tom Seaman, editorial director Cliff White, Americas editor Jason Huffman and head of growth and strategy Gary Morrison as they discuss where the seafood industry currently stands with Trump's tariffs and what could possibly be in the pipeline.

Listen below!

Subscribe now! Catch the Current is available on Apple, Spotify, Amazon Music, iHeartRadio, Pandora, and other major podcast streaming platforms. Don't see Catch the Current on your favorite app? Reach out to podcasts@undercurrentnews.com.

Don't have time to listen? Find a transcript of season 1, episode 3 of Catch the Current below:

Amanda Buckle (AB): You’re listening to Catch the Current, the latest podcast from Undercurrent News, your trusted-source for seafood news, data and prices. I’m Amanda Buckle.

Lorin Castiglion (LC): And I’m Lorin Castiglione. 

We love boasting about out global team at Undercurrent. We’ve got our headquarters in London and reporters all around the world. What some of you may not know is that Amanda and I are based out of New Jersey. This week we were able to host a couple of fellow staffers who are not local to the area -- Americas editor Jason Huffman and Undercurrent’s new editorial director, Cliff White. 

AB: So of course we had to record a podcast together! Jason, Cliff -- welcome to Catch the Current, the most informative -- and who are we kidding, coolest -- seafood podcast in the world! 

Cliff White (CW): Thanks for having us.

Jason Huffman (JH): It's good to be here.

LC: We also have one more Undercurrent expert lurking in the background -- Gary Morrison, our head of growth and strategy, as well as reporter on the lobster, crab, and shrimp markets. Man, what can’t he do. 

Gary Morrison (GM): Thanks Lorin.

AB: And we also have Undercurrent co-founder Tom Seaman.

Tom Seaman (TS): Hello, good to be on the pod again.

LC: We didn’t plan it like this, but your visit is very convenient because there is so much going on with US president Donald Trump’s tariffs.

Photo Credit: Whitehouse.gov

AB: Our team of reporters have been knee-deep in the coverage. There are a lot of moving pieces here -- and things are changing every day -- so your first stop every morning should be to check UndercurrentNews.com for the latest updates, but we’re going to do our best to cover the immediate impacts here. 

LC: That's right. On Saturday, Trump signed an executive order that placed 25% tariffs on products imported from Canada and Mexico, while adding another 10% to the 25% tariffs already paid for Chinese goods. Trump’s tariffs were supposed to take effect on Tuesday, Feb. 4, leaving no time for the seafood industry to prepare.

AB: But then… a twist! Snip snap, snip snap. Trump paused the tariffs on first Mexico and then Canada! The proposed tariffs are paused for at least 30 days.

I'll let you all fight over this first question: Did the seafood industry just dodge a bullet? Or did it just buy more time to prepare?

JH: I think they dodged a bullet. But we don't know until he actually permanently removes the tariffs. They're still hanging out there. He gave them 30 days, and he may come back later on and try to leverage this into something else. But will he? Given the circumstances, I feel kind of like he won't.

AB: Cliff, similar thoughts?

CW: TBD.

AB: The safest answer on a podcast.

FREE READ Unlock seafood impact of Trump trade war with UCN portal

CW: I mean, it's always TBD with Trump, right? Like, he changes his mind every day, every hour, and depends on what he ate for dinner and how his last conversation went. So, no one's safe with Trump. I think that's his biggest leverage point.

That's the art of the deal is you can always get a better deal. And his word is not as important as his swagger. And we'll see how that plays out.

He's got a lot more swagger in his first term than he did in his second.

AB: I would agree with that. We're already heading in strong. I think Lorin and I joked in the first couple of podcasts that we're going to have an endless supply of content to publish this year.

It's been nonstop since he came into office on Jan. 20.

Gary, as a market reporter, are you seeing some contacts concerned about this delay? Or are they seeing it as it's not going to be an issue?

GM: Initially, there were some people that reacted pretty swiftly. And certainly when I'm talking about Canadian crab and lobster, where they reacted with price increases pretty quickly.

But as that tariff was removed and they put a pause on it, cooler heads have prevailed. I think most people seem to think that we did dodge a bullet in the fact that if the negotiations and what was agreed upon during those conversations happened, that they would not have the tariffs imposed in the 30 days. So right now a little bit more level-headed pricing is happening.

LC: And just to play off of Gary's level-headed answer and his contacts, being cool, calm and collected -- my contacts, I think, are more like me, where we're spiraling and thinking of every possible situation that could happen. So, for example, on salmon, where the 25% tariff on Canadian farmed salmon that could push US buyers to alternative sources. And that's probably going to be from Chile or from Norway.

FREE READ US wholesale: Week 6 seafood price assessments live

In a perfect world it could give more opportunity to the US salmon industry, but we produce a limited farmed product and our wild-caught harvest is highly seasonable with volumes that can't support current US demands alone.

Something else one of my contacts brought up that I think wouldn't ... sway the administration obviously, but I think it's interesting to point out, is that, for salmon especially, there's potential environmental impacts.

Canada regionally trucks all of its salmon down to the East Coast or the West Coast while Chilean products fly in the bellies of planes and then transfer to trucks and...

AB: It's spiraling, basically, is what you're saying, because I wouldn't have thought about that aspect either.

LC: Right. It's funny to chat with my contacts and we're kind of going through every different scenario. But again, it's a wait and see.

TS: To your point, Lorin, about alternatives on salmon. I mean, obviously, the main export from Europe into the US is salmon -- that's the bulk of it.

There are other products, but it's the bulk of it -- and I think, generally, the Norwegian salmon goes to Denmark, Holland; countries like that for processing. And a lot of it will come to the US that way. Some of it does come directly from Norway, but obviously, it's very high-cost processing in Norway.

Fresh salmon fillet on ice. Credit: Jukov studio/Shutterstock.com

So, if there are tariff supplies to Europe, which Trump is threatening, that could impact one of those other supply sources that you mentioned, Lorin.

And then, I think a lot of people feel that if Europe is tariffed, it's very unlikely that Norway would escape that. I'm sure it would be sort of swept up in that in some way.

But it's going to be interesting to see because, you know, Europe is not... Europe and China are not Mexico and Canada. You know, they're very, very large economies on their own rights and will be much harder to sort of push around. Which is a bit different with Canada in particular due to its incredible reliance on the US for trade. And obviously, I think the most interesting thing so far is the Chinese situation.

I'd be interested, Lorin, to hear what your contacts are saying on that in terms of that causing further inflation, particularly on cod, which is already going up in price. That 10% tariff is going to products exported from the US to China processed and coming back. It's just going on everything.

LC: China is a huge reprocessing hub, especially for groundfish. And what we've seen in the past on items like haddock, where exemptions came into play and then exclusions came into play. It was all back and forth. That caused so much price volatility. Right now, twice frozen supply is already constrained with premiums continuing to develop week after week.

In addition to the added tariff or the potential of tariffs, just put so much more pressure on the markets already.

US tariffs on EU would hit $1.4bn in seafood imports

CW: Trump's just going to look for the next thing, man. He is rapid firing announcements, executive orders.

He is the aggressor. He's always looking for the next thing to push on. And he's already mentioned the EU.

TS: And the UK. He mentioned the UK.

CW: Yeah, once it's in his head. It's just when.

AB: Now, do you want to talk about shellfish? We talked about salmon's impact, whitefish... you know what about lobster out of Canada?

JH: We already have supply issues with shellfish. Gary can talk about this as well. The prices have gone up on a number of these. The supplies of both items are limited. We're about to head into the new snow crab season.

So we're going to have some more snow crab soon. But lobster is very limited. I mean, it's not like they needed pressure to drive up prices. We're already there.

Fresh, cooked North Atlantic lobster meat. Credit: Truefoods Premium Product

GM: To Jason's point, you know, the lobster inventory here in the US right now is pretty limited. Prices have been firming.

The one thing that we did see over the last couple weeks prior to this tariff initiation was people assumed that it was coming. So they did shift some inventory into the United States from Canada in advance, but that only allowed sellers here to discount prices, which was opposite of the sentiment that we probably would have thought because carrying costs like cold storage becomes a lot more expensive here in the US than it is in Canada. So they wanted to move some of that inventory that they were holding.

And in crab, we're seeing prices firm. Inventory ... it's basically non-existent here from Canada as well. So we're seeing a shift in buying patterns.

Norway is really stepping in and buyers in the US have continued to pay higher prices, sometimes significantly higher for both red king crab and snow crab out of Norway. That season is starting to come to an end as well. Inventory is a little bit tight.

AB: Do you think that trend is going to continue since we now have a month?

GM: Yeah, diversifying suppliers. I think Tom brought it up. Canada is so dependent on the US for all their trade. I think 77% of their GDP comes from the US and they're certainly looking to diversify their customer base.

Buyers here now want to diversify their supplier base just in case things are unsettled and you can't get it from one place where it becomes more expensive.

US gov’t scientists chafe at Trump admin’s offer of severance, threats against disloyalty

AB: Jacob Resneck just published a really fantastic -- two pieces --  this week talking just about what NOAA's dealing with right now and how there's just so much confusion in that agency. What other things are you seeing within the industry that Trump is having an impact on that doesn't even have to deal with tariffs?

JH: Jacob's articles this week were really compelling.

One of them dealt with this regulatory freeze, the idea that maybe we could get into a position where the fisheries can't be regulated because of the limits on what can get through NOAA and the regional councils. Then there's the employment issue.

Federal employees are having to worry now about the security of their jobs and what positions that NOAA will be affected and how that will affect the commercial fisheries going forward. So those are issues.

AB: It's lot of confusion and this is getting relayed to these fishermen and these groups outside of NOAA that we don't know what's happening and that can't be good for anybody overall either to have all this confusion and chaos right now.

And that's kind of just what it feels like. It's a chaos bomb.

Photo Credit: White House

JH: It's kind of mind-blowing.

I mean, when have we had a new administration come in that put this much concern and worry into a market because of regulatory changes. Will this kind of get normal at some point?

TS: I also think there's obviously implications for the Marine Stewardship Council certification of the pollock fishery or lots of the Alaska fisheries when it relies on very robust fisheries management. And if all that's thrown out then it's going to have some knock-on effects on things like that if it's not resolved.

So that's something to watch too because the MSC requires certain levels of management that -- if potentially aren't in place -- everybody's losing their job.

So, the situation at NOAA is in flux.

AB: I just want to circle this back to Tom. You're in London. So you're the only one here not based in the US, which gives you a unique perspective as an outsider looking in. So how is this impacting Europe right now? Is this impacting Europe at all?

TS: Well, not at the minute because it's all just kind of threats so far. But the Europe stuff's all theoretical.

I agree with you Cliff, it is going to happen. But the China stuff is happening and they are obviously going to as soon as this happens with China.

They then start doing not only actual trade barriers, but they'll also start doing like they did with the Ecuadorians in Covid where they were just inspecting every containers for traces of Covid and it was all completely nonsensical. Everyone knew that but it was a trade barrier. It was kind of a flex and they are more than likely.

I've asked Lewis, our reporter in China to be on the case with this because I can see that suddenly there'll be, you know, delays on containers. They'll be detained for customs inspections because that's kind of the way it works.

Obviously, the US is very reliant on China as a reprocessing hub. They've tried to diversify to, say Vietnam, Indonesia, other countries successfully, but China is still the main hub.

And then a lot of that's coming back to the US as well. So there's kind of potential destruction, I think, on US exports to China. It remains to be seen, but this has happened in the past. And then the 10% tariff on -- at the minute -- trying to process products using US fish coming back to the US and obviously I think that will get an exemption like what happened before, but none of that's happened yet. So it's very interesting to see.

Credit: Miro Vrlik Photography / Shutterstock

CW: I wanted to ask Gary because we're having an interesting discussion and I think both of us agree that Trump's strategy here -- and it is a strategy. I mean, he laid this out, Americans voted on it. It can be really effective. He can get a lot from it. Where do you see this going from his standpoint, if you can get in Trump's head?

GM: We heard it at GSMC, you know, quite a bit that tariffs are used as policy, right? Not as a negotiating tool in foreign policy.

So it's more about foreign policy and things that he wants to benefit the US and, you know, his big thing was securing the border. And I think that's what tariffs are being used for. They're not being used as a punitive tool or as a tool to, you know, raise money to enact border security, whatever that may be, whether they already agreed upon it and have not enacted what they agreed upon or he got a little bit more, but I think it's more about border security and, you know, preventing drugs [from coming] into this country.

JH: I think the outcome was we had two of those countries with tariffs threatened against them drop, right? Or at least postpone, and then one kind of went through. Did Trump actually win or did he lose? Because those countries threatened to retaliate and then they offered him something that they had already given him and then he paused the tariffs. Is that a retreat, a surrender, or is it because the threat is still out there? Is he winning? I mean, I don't know how to view it.

And then if he won, is he encouraged to do it again with other countries? Or if he lost, does this give him a defeat? And he goes, he's got to think about it the next time. I mean, I can't say if he won, lost, or anything. I mean, that's going to be determined, right? Or what his motivation, you know, certainly was, but I'll liken it to, you know, things like accords where people are not living up to their obligations, right? So you can agree to anything that you want.

You also have to live by those obligations or contracts. And certainly in other countries, there have been entered into contracts with the U.S. that they said they've been doing something, whether that be reducing CO2 and it just doesn't happen. So if he won or lost, I can't answer that.

title: Fishing body backs new EU commissioner’s pledge amid sector crisis
content:
Europeche, the body representing the European fishing industry, has expressed strong support for the new EU fisheries and oceans commissioner Costas Kadis' commitment to shaping a "resilient, competitive, and sustainable" EU fisheries sector.

Europeche said that in their first meeting under the legislative term 2024-2029, discussions centered on securing "balanced" policies that support the industry, maintain access to traditional fishing grounds, and ensure fair market competition.

This comes as some EU fleet representatives stressed that the sector is at a crossroads.

The first meeting between the EU fishing sector and Costas Kadis, the EU Commissioner responsible for fisheries and oceans, took place in January 2025. Photo: Europeche.

Europeche emphasized the urgency of addressing challenges such as shrinking fleet sizes, job losses, rising costs, and increasing access restrictions. The association once again called on the European Commission to create a "level playing field" by ensuring imported seafood meets the same sustainability standards as EU-caught products --something it has long argued is not the case.

Javier Garat, president of Europeche, welcomed the meeting with the Commission.

"We are very pleased with the Commission's active engagement today. Commissioner Kadis has shown a strong commitment to maintaining an open dialogue and developing practical policies and regulations for the sector," he said.

"This is just the first of many meetings needed to tackle the significant challenges facing our industry. Our discussion with Commissioner Kadis represents an important step towards shaping a competitive and sustainable future for the EU fisheries sector. We look forward to a shift in policy direction, and the CFP [common fisheries policy] evaluation presents a crucial window of opportunity. Europeche remains fully committed to working closely with the Commissioner and his team," he further said.

Europeche called for a "more balanced approach" to fisheries management that prioritizes environmental concerns as well as socio-economic and food security objectives. Among their key proposals were revising restrictive policies, such as the landing obligation, and addressing broader challenges, including climate change, Brexit, and the energy transition. The association also advocated for reducing the administrative burden on fishers by simplifying complex regulations.

Europeche claimed there was mounting pressure from marine protected areas and offshore renewable energy projects, stressing the need for a science-driven approach to marine protection that respects traditional fishing grounds. The organization also pushed for greater flexibility in multiannual management plans, particularly in the Baltic and Mediterranean, and called for an urgent revision of the Western Mediterranean regulation.

Decarbonization was another focal point, with Europeche reaffirming its commitment to transitioning to zero-emission fisheries. However, it stressed the necessity of adequate EU funding, fleet modernization, and innovation to achieve this goal. The association advocated for increased financial support in the next funding program and the introduction of an EU fleet renewal plan.

Post-Brexit negotiations were another pressing topic, with Europeche calling for clear political directives and early agreements to ensure stability in shared waters. The association emphasized the importance of securing a fisheries agreement by the end of 2025 to maintain resource management and safeguard EU interests. Additionally, Europeche advocated for linking market access to fisheries access and compliance, proposing tariff and trade measures to counter unsustainable practices by neighboring countries like Norway.

EU fishing sector crisis

Executives from several fishing firms told Undercurrent News that keeping their businesses profitable, attracting young fishers, and securing access to fishing grounds is becoming increasingly difficult, while other nations such as China or Russia are actively supporting their fleets.

The EU fishing sector is facing a perfect storm of rising operational costs driven by inflation, soaring energy prices, growing regulatory and bureaucratic burdens, and increased competition from imports, claimed Daniel Voces de Onaindi, managing director of Europeche, during an interview with Undercurrent in late 2024.

"The reality is that the EU fleet is frustrated, and quite a few companies in Europe are reconsidering their future in the industry," said Voces. He noted that numerous vessel owners are waiting for national governments to introduce scrapping schemes with financial compensation, reflecting growing uncertainty in the sector.

Julio Moron Ayala, president of the Spanish confederation of fisheries, also known as Cepesca, previously also emphasized the challenges local fisheries face in the Mediterranean, particularly issues related to engine power and increased downtime for fleets.

He also discussed the "dire situation" in the Atlantic Ocean's tuna fishing industry. He cited various factors contributing to "this disaster," including the three-month fishing ban and claimed an influx of Asian vessels under African flags that has undermined European operators.

Moron, who is also the director at the tuna fleet representative body OPAGAC, claimed "unfair competition" regarding operating and social costs between European and extra-European vessels, as well as lax regulation enforcement, especially regarding the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas' fish aggregating device closure compliance. 

Economic conditions are worsening, leading many fishing companies to bankruptcy, he said, adding that increased fishing of smaller species, such as sardines, by non-European fleets off the African coast is negatively impacting local populations and tuna availability.

Although scientific reports indicate the recovery of certain tuna species in the Atlantic region, economic performance remains difficult, he said.

subsidized scrapping plan in Spain

Meanwhile, local media reported that the Spanish government has begun evaluating its fishing fleet to determine whether to implement a subsidized scrapping plan.

The assessment aims to identify fleet segments with excess capacity, particularly in the Mediterranean and Gulf of Cadiz, where imbalances have been noted. The fishing sector is requesting more substantial compensation to scrap their vessels than was provided in 2015. 

The longline fishing fleet has proposed an organized decommissioning, with up to 45 vessels potentially being scrapped. Challenges such as the EU's ban on bottom fishing, unfair competition, and declining fish prices have worsened the sector's situation, La Opinion A Coruna reported.

Previous government aid proposals have been criticized for offering lower subsidies than those granted in Ireland and France, which introduced scrapping plans after Brexit.

The industry remains divided; some advocate for government support to fight fishing restrictions, while others seek financial aid to exit the sector. The European Maritime, Fisheries, and Aquaculture Fund plays a key role in financing these measures.

title: Trump regulatory freeze ties hands of US fisheries managers
content:
A blanket freeze on regulations by US president Donald Trump is – perhaps unwittingly – preventing federal agency officials from managing fisheries for conservation, Undercurrent News has learned.

A presidential order issued within the first hours of the Trump administration entitled "Regulatory Freeze Pending Review" directs agencies to withdraw any draft rules issued by the administration of former president Joe Biden and prohibits federal agencies from issuing new ones pending review by the new president's political appointees.

US gov’t scientists chafe at Trump admin’s offer of severance, threats against disloyalty

But in practice that means federal fisheries managers can't issue binding closures of fisheries since they are unable to publish in the Federal Register. 

Veteran staffers at the National Oceanic and Administration (NOAA) National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) say science-based management is a casualty of power politics thousands of miles away in the US capital.

"Some guy in (Washington) DC doesn't know the intricate ramifications of these things," a NOAA Fisheries biologist told Undercurrent. 

That's because federal fishing season openings are often set in harvest plans but fisheries managers close the fisheries when the total allowable catch (TAC) is met by issuing rules that have to be published.

Three Pacific cod fisheries in Alaska and an Atlantic herring possession limit were quietly withdrawn from the register in keeping with the US president's directive.

"We have a crew of in-season managers who are tracking these fisheries, and they're reaching their catch limits and without being able to submit anything to the Federal Register," the NOAA official said. 

In their place, NOAA issued "information bulletins" ordering the closures. But without being published, they are just advisory.

"They don't have a regulatory or statutory basis to close those fisheries," the official added. 

Language has been added to bulletins that warns NMFS will report violations to "the North Pacific Fishery Management Council on any fishing activities that occur after the federal agency announces that harvest levels have achieved their TAC."

But there's skepticism within industry that the regulatory body has the authority to mete out justice or is in any way equipped to enforce catch limits.

Alaska processor says quotas being followed

One Pacific cod processor in Alaska told Undercurrent there's no immediate danger of over-fishing since the fishery is rationalized and the industry is keeping within its quotas. The executive suggested that the bulletin would be followed as if it were a regulation.

But there are fears that derby-style fisheries that are less organized might not be self-regulating. There's a Pacific cod pot fishery with vessels from different ports in Alaska that without clear direction could turn into a free-for-all.

"They're in King Cove and Sand Point and Kodiak and a little bit in Homer, and they're not organized at all," the agency source said, "and so that would probably be the greatest concern."

So far there's no indication that commercial fishermen or processors are taking advantage of the political dysfunction. 

Industry group walks tight-rope

A veteran fishing industry organization leader said it's communicating closures to its gear group without the nuance that managers are operating in a legal grey area. But the longer this goes on, the industry source told Undercurrent, the more likely harvesters might not abide by the advisories.

Eventually there could also be federal fisheries, like sablefish, that cannot legally open without a notice in the Federal Register. Managers also reallocate quotas by publishing in the official journal.

All questions to NMFS staff in the Pacific Northwest were directed to the agency's headquarters in Washington.

Agency officials didn't respond by late Tuesday.

title: PNG example makes case for private certifications in social accountability
content:
The Fishing Industry Association of Papua New Guinea (FIA PNG) has disclosed non-conformities identified during a crew welfare certification process, collaborating with Australian universities to analyze data and discuss the real-life conditions of tuna fleet workers.

The case study -- a first for the industry, according to the FIA -- compares government enforcement roles with certification programs, particularly the International Labor Organization's Fishing Convention (ILO C188). It can be found in full here.

The research, conducted in partnership with the Australian National Centre for Ocean Resources & Security and the University of Wollongong, examines lessons from third-party audits on social accountability certification and its role in improving fishing crew welfare.

The findings suggest that, while formal governance is essential, private certification programs like the Fairness, Integrity, Safety, and Health (FISH) standard can complement regulatory efforts. The study highlights common compliance challenges, industry responses, and areas requiring further scrutiny by policymakers and industry players.

There are areas where data about living and working conditions onboard and tuna industrial players remains unavailable, said FIA.

"The aim of sharing this paper is not just to highlight the good performance of the FIA PNG tuna fleet has achieved regarding ILOC188 and labor rights; it is also to highlight the gaps so that tuna Industry players can directly invest in improvements," said FIA PNG's COO, Marcelo Hidalgo.
