title: Vietnam’s surimi product exports see strong Q4 despite annual decline
content:
Vietnam's exports of fish paste and surimi products grew steadily in the final quarter of 2024, though full-year exports fell slightly, the Vietnam Association of Seafood Exporters and Producers (VASEP) announced on Jan. 31.

Total annual exports reached $298 million, a 2% decline from 2023. However, demand picked up in key markets during the last three months, with notable increases in Thailand, China, and Taiwan.

Taiwan saw the sharpest rebound, with surimi imports from Vietnam surging 301% in the fourth quarter after two consecutive quarters of decline.

Vietnam exported fish paste and surimi products to more than 43 markets in 2024. The eight largest buyers -- South Korea, Thailand, China and Hong Kong, Japan, the EU, Indonesia, Malaysia, and the US -- accounted for 90% of the total export value.

Despite the late-year recovery, exports to most major destinations remained lower than in 2023, according to VASEP.

Vietnam's surimi industry has faced challenges due to new government regulations introduced to address the European Commission's illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing "yellow card" warning.

VASEP said port authorities and local fisheries management agencies have struggled with implementation, and inconsistent enforcement has caused delays in issuing export certifications.

Domestic raw material shortages and tighter restrictions on imported ingredients have further hampered the industry's recovery. While most major markets reported lower year-on-year imports, Vietnam's exports to Thailand, the EU, and Taiwan remained relatively strong by the end of 2024.

title: First of 3 new US Coast Guard cutters arrives in Alaska
content:
The first of three new US Coast Guard (USCG) vessels that will conduct federal fisheries enforcement in Alaska arrived at its new homeport of Kodiak on Tuesday (Jan. 28), the agency announced.

The John Witherspoon (WPC 1158) is one of three modern 154-foot Fast Response Cutters (FRCs) that will be homeported in Alaska and conduct patrols and enforcement in the Bering Sea, Gulf of Alaska and Arctic Ocean.

The three new FRCs in Alaska have a range of 2,500 miles and are designed to replace the service’s fleet of 110-foot cutters that are on track to be decommissioned in 2025, the USCG said. 

The USCG is currently scheduled to have six FRCs operating throughout Alaska by the end of the year to patrol federal fisheries within the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), conduct search and rescue and respond to vessels in distress. 

The USCG announced in 2019 that the vessel would be named for Witherspoon, an African-American officer who died in 1994. He was the first African-American officer to command both cutters and an onshore unit in his career.

Born Aug. 26, 1939, in the North Carolina foothills of the Blue Ridge Mountains, John G. Witherspoon enlisted in the US Coast Guard in 1963 and went on to rise to the highest ranks at the time for an African-American officer commanding both vessels and onshore units. He died in 1994. (Wikimedia Commons)

In a statement announcing the vessel's arrival, lieutenant commander Cmdr. Adam Young, commanding officer of the Witherspoon, called the late officer "a trailblazer who found enjoyment and purpose in leading and mentoring others." 

The Jan. 29 announcement did not specify that Witherspoon was an African-American. Past military histories catalog how his career broke color barriers by advancing to ranks not previously achieved by African-American officers in the USCG.

The administration of president Donald Trump has forbidden federal agencies from any mention of racial, ethnic and other forms of diversity in its materials or policies. 

A formal commissioning ceremony is planned for April, the USCG said.

title: Canadian First Nations reject Ottawa’s offer of CAD 260m to acquire lobster licenses
content:
First Nations chiefs in Atlantic Canada have rejected an offer from the federal government that would have provided almost CAD 260 million ($181m) to help them purchase fishing licenses, boats and gear.

The Assembly of Nova Scotia Mi'kmaw chiefs fear the offer from the Canadian government could threaten their Treaty Rights, said Wilbert Marshall, Chief of the Assembly, in a press release on Friday (Jan. 24)

The proposal by Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO), pitched by minister Diane Lebouthillier in a letter to the Assembly on Dec. 3, 2024, would have seen First Nations negotiate directly with willing sellers to purchase DFO-sanctioned fishing licenses, particularly for the highly-valued lobster fishery in the province of Nova Scotia (NS), where dock prices in recent years have climbed to CAD 7.00 and higher.

However, the Mi'kmaw chiefs, representing 11 of the 13 First Nations communities in NS, have panned DFO's offer.

"This proposal raises serious alarms," said Marshall, co-lead of the Assembly's fisheries portfolio. "DFO's approach reminded us of earlier initiatives from the 2000s, which failed to respect and uphold our inherent Rights. Our Treaty Right to fish is not a commercial fishery."

Canadian court grants more time for mediation over lobster fishing rights

Since 1999 Canada has spent over CAD 1.0 billion to buy up commercial lobster licenses around Atlantic Canada, primarily in the province of Nova Scotia, and transfer them to First Nations, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

A 1999 decision by the Supreme Court of Canada -- known widely as the Marshall decision -- affirmed First Nations' rights to fish, hunt and gather in pursuit of a moderate livelihood under the terms of the Peace and Friendship Treaties of 1760 and 1761.

The moderate livelihood fishery permits First Nations groups to fish for lobsters during commercial seasons, under the terms of memorandums of understanding with the Canadian government, as reported by Undercurrent.

In 2024, for instance, DFO announced the continuation of authorizations for four First Nations in Nova Scotia to fish for and sell lobsters during open commercial seasons. For the current lobster season in Lobster Fishing Areas (LFSs) 33, 34 and 35 -- the largest lobster fishing areas in Atlantic Canada, which delivered 23,581 metric tons of lobster in 2023 -- the First Nations are authorized to use 6,300 traps in LFAs 33 and 34, and up to 1,000 traps in LFA 35.

However, the moderate livelihood fishery has been a long-standing point of contention, especially in the lobster fishery in Atlantic Canada, where commercial license holders say some First Nations have been carrying out an illegal and unregulated lobster fishery under the guise of a moderate livelihood fishery.

Lobster harvesters not impressed by Canada’s enforcement efforts

The United Fisheries Conservation Alliance (UFCA), which represents several lobster harvester groups in the province of Nova Scotia, filed a notice of action on Friday (Aug. 23) in the Nova Scotia Supreme Court against the Sipekne'katik First Nation, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

The UFCA is asking the court to declare the First Nation's self-regulated lobster fishery in St Marys Bay illegal and demand regulation under the federal Fisheries Act.

That case has yet to be proven in court.

Meanwhile, the Assembly of Mi'kmaw Chiefs said the recent DFO proposal was simply another attempt by Canada to ignore the rights-based fishery by continuing its efforts to force Mi'kmaw Treaty harvesters into the same license-based system as the non-Indigenous commercial fishery. This has been long rejected by Mi'kmaw leadership in favor of emphasizing a Mi'kmaw-led process, the two chiefs stated in the press release.

"We have built a better way forward and the trust we have built within our communities and with our harvesters, through our community-based harvest plans, would be jeopardized if we even entertained these new agreements with DFO under this proposal," said Chief Gerald Toney, co-lead of the Assembly's fisheries portfolio.

Many Mi'kmaw communities in Nova Scotia have already invested significant time and effort in developing comprehensive plans that prioritize conservation, sustainability, and safety, while also recognizing our inherent Treaty Rights, self-governance and the court-affirmed right for Mi'kmaq to fish for a livelihood, the chiefs offered.

"We want to make it clear; our rights are not for sale," said Chief Marshall. "We will advocate for a fisheries governance framework that honors our Treaties, respects our inherent rights, and is based upon Mi'kmaw law and Mi'kmaw jurisdiction."

title: Canada cancels plan to add more licenses, divvy up elver quota
content:
Canada's Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) is canceling a pilot project that would have taken quotas from established commercially licensed elver operations in Atlantic Canada. This would have allowed up to 150 more people to access the fishery.

An official in Diane Lebouthillier's office revealed the decision in a statement on Thursday afternoon (Jan. 23).

"Minister Lebouthillier is proud to have spearheaded the successful effort to add stronger regulations and enforcement mechanisms to the toolbox available to DFO for this fishery. However, the 2025 elver fishing season will not include the pilot program to expand commercial access to this fishery," said Richard Anderson, the acting director of communications in Lebouthillier's office.

"Consultations are an important factor when making fishery management decisions, and the minister has listened to the feedback when arriving at her decision. We sincerely thank all those who participated in the discussion," said Anderson.

The short, one-paragraph announcement did not provide any further details about a management plan for the 2025 elver season, which begins in March.

Elver license holders welcomed the news.

"This is absolutely the right move. It's one of the rare circumstances when the minister and DFO have listened to feedback, considered it and considered the sage advice of the most knowledgeable people in the industry, which are the people that founded it," Stanley King, spokesperson for the Canadian Committee for a Sustainable Eel Fishery (CCSEF) told Undercurrent News minutes after the DFO announcement.

The three-year pilot project that DFO had proposed would have allowed 150 new commercial licenses to enter the fishery in 2025. That would have meant an 80% to 90% reduction in quota for existing commercial license holders, with no compensation for the loss of quota.

That amounted to nothing more than a government "smash and grab," King said in a previous interview with Undercurrent.

Currently, nine businesses in Canada's Maritime provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick hold commercial licenses to harvest juvenile American eels. Those companies employ about 200 people to fish the rivers to collect the valuable elvers, which are primarily sold to China, where they are grown in aquaculture facilities to supply the sushi market.

Though the combined elver quota for Nova Scotia and New Brunswick is small, around 9,860 kilograms annually since 2006, the value of the catch has been sky-high in recent years, ranging from CAD 3,000 ($2,225)/kg to CAD 5,000/kg in the past decade.

For the past couple of years, the fishery was estimated to be worth about CAD 19 million ($14.9m) annually in NS.

"All CCSEF members are tremendously relieved by the minister's decision not to pursue her proposed pilot project," King said.

"With so many changes for this coming 2025 season, including new regulations and the addition of several hundred Indigenous fishers, the potential for more chaos and premature (seasonal) closure was just too high," he said.

Still, CCSEF members continue to be concerned about enforcement this coming season and have deep reservations about having quota expropriated without compensation to satisfy obligations to First Nations, King added, noting that DFO has already decided to allocate a little more than 50% of the elver quota to First Nations.

title: Biden administration scuttled anti-IUU proposal during final week in White House
content:
The administration of outgoing US president Joe Biden quietly withdrew a controversial rule proposal designed to crack down on illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing and forced labor on commercial fishing vessels in his final days in the White House.

The National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) gave notice with little fanfare on Jan. 16 that it was pulling its 2022 proposal, saying it had insufficient time to finalize the rule before the changeover to US president-elect Donald Trump on Monday (Jan. 20).

"Combating IUU fishing has been a top priority for NMFS," the agency wrote in the Federal Register. "Despite its best efforts, NMFS does not have sufficient time to finalize before the end of this administration a revised version of the regulation that would appropriately address the statutory changes or to seek public input on those potential changes."

As Undercurrent News has reported, some of the provisions designed to combat forced labor had come under fire from the second-largest tuna canner in the US.

Bumble Bee Foods, which has repeatedly faced scrutiny related to labor practices on its harvest vessels, had urged the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) not to conflate forced labor with illegal fishing.

SIMP, IUU, sharkfin provisions buried in just-passed $858bn US defense spending bill

"Our view is that the problems of forced labor and IUU fishing are different and require different solutions and approaches. To eliminate forced labor throughout the supply chain, measures must be taken by governments that apply to all its vessels regardless of where they fish," Bumble Bee wrote in a comment letter opposing the NOAA proposal in 2022.

After the rule was proposed in July 2022, Congress passed an omnibus piece of legislation for defense spending that contained changes that required the rule to be revised. 

As Undercurrent reported, the defense bill amended the law to expand NOAA's Seafood Import Monitoring Program (SIMP) to include protections for marine resources imported from countries that don't have comparable regulations in the US. 

NOAA details plans to include ‘country of harvest’ in SIMP expansion

The battle over SIMP expansion predates the rule and has actually been going on since the program was first rolled out in 2016. It requires catch documentation and traceability for multiple items of seafood deemed at risk of IUU practices for some 13 species of imported seafood, including Atlantic cod; blue crab; grouper; king crab; mahi mahi; Pacific cod; red snapper; sea cucumber; shark; swordfish; and tuna, including albacore, bigeye, skipjack, yellowfin and bluefin.

Most of the concerns over SIMP expansion were from seafood importers rather than US domestic producers, as Undercurrent reported. Even so, prominent trade associations, including the National Fisheries Institute (NFI), representing US seafood processors, wholesalers and importers, had raised concerns to the agency. 

"NFI is pleased to see a continued focus on important fisheries issues including IUU but expansion of a program that NOAA itself has said, 'does not prevent or stop IUU fish and fish products from entering US commerce', is not a good use of limited resources," Gavin Gibbons, then vice president of communications at NFI, told Undercurrent at the time.

Conservationists incensed by climbdown

Oceana, the international campaigner often critical of industrial-scale fishing, released a blistering statement on Tuesday (Jan. 21) criticizing the US government agency for caving to pressure.

"After dragging its feet for years, NOAA failed to finalize a new rule that would have strengthened the United States’ ability to combat illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing and recognized the link between IUU fishing and forced labor," Oceana campaign director Max Valentine wrote in a statement. "This rule would have ensured that the United States could take strong action against other countries engaged in IUU fishing and that ignore human rights abuses in their fleets."

She added: "Oceana encourages president Trump and his administration to put this rule back on the table to help ensure that all seafood sold in the US is safe, legally caught and honestly labeled"

NOAA updates seafood inspection regs to reflect current practices

Oceana released the results of a survey it commissioned in 2024 in which 90% of 1,053 registered US voters said that imported seafood should be held to the same standards as US products. 

The US government's scuttling of the rule is unlikely to be the end of the debate over IUU regulations and the SIMP program. The US agency included boilerplate language alluding to the fact that the rule could be re-filed by the next presidential administration.

"If, in the future, NMFS decides it is appropriate to issue regulations on this topic, it will do so via a new notice of proposed rulemaking," the agency added.

title: Somalia’s tuna stocks still threatened by illegal fishing, report finds
content:
Somalia's fisheries, including yellowfin tuna, are under severe strain from illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing, according to a new report by ENACT Africa, an EU-backed initiative addressing transnational crime.

This exploitation, primarily by foreign vessels from countries such as China, Iran, and Pakistan, is depleting fish stocks, harming ecosystems, and costing Somalia an estimated $300 million annually.

The report highlighted the country's weak maritime governance, corruption, and ineffective enforcement of fishing laws, which allow destructive practices like bottom trawling and fish-aggregating devices. Without urgent intervention, yellowfin tuna faces a potential 70% population decline within a decade, it claimed.

Somalia's long-standing governance challenges, exacerbated by civil conflict, have made monitoring its waters difficult. Conflicting interests between federal and regional authorities further complicate regulation. For example, controversial agreements with foreign fleets, including a 2018 deal with Chinese companies, illustrate systemic issues, according to the report.

"In this context, a 2019 report revealed that the Liao Dong Yu fleet (a Chinese foreign vessel) was not operating within the 2018 stipulated law. Instead, the fleet had obtained fishing licenses from Puntland authorities through questionable means. This was reportedly facilitated by businessman and senator Dahir Ayande, a close ally of Puntland president Said Abdullahi Deni, pointing to the influence of political associations in undermining the governance of Somalia's fishing industry," the report explained.

"In the meantime, Chinese vessels continue to be involved in illegal tuna fishing off the Somalia coastline, using prohibited and destructive methods. These include using large purse seines and longline vessels to catch immense volumes of tuna, bottom trawling, selective equipment that can capture certain fish while excluding others, and even dynamite fishing -- using explosives to kill and collect fish," the report further reads.

title: Parliamentary report opts against moratorium on new Scottish salmon farm sites
content:
The slow rate of progress in improving the regulation and enforcement of the Scottish salmon aquaculture industry needs to be addressed as a matter of urgency to future-proof the industry and to enable it to grow sustainably, according to Holyrood's Rural Affairs & Islands Committee.

This was the overarching conclusion of a report published after several rounds of evidence-giving held over recent months. The report concludes the committee's scrutiny of the salmon farming industry in Scotland and the extent to which recommendations made by its predecessor committee in 2018 have been implemented.

Mowi exec urges gov’t help as Scottish salmon farmers bid to cope with climate change

Calling for stronger leadership from the Scottish government, the committee requests a clear timetable be provided setting out how both the outstanding 2018 recommendations, and its own recommendations, will be implemented within the next year.

The committee also asks the government to set out how implementation will be measured and for dedicated ministerial oversight of the workstream involved to drive delivery.

It will revisit progress made on issues raised in the report in one year and may make further recommendations at that time.

Crucially for the salmon aquaculture sector, the committee has decided not to call for a halt on new farm sites or expansions to existing farms.

"The committee seriously considered whether calling for a moratorium, or pause, on new sites, or the expansion at existing sites, would be appropriate -- especially given the view held by some about the lack of progress in addressing high mortality rates since 2018," it said. 

"However, given the lack of certainty around the impact a moratorium on production would have, especially on those directly employed on farms or living in local communities, the committee is not currently in support of a moratorium or pause on production."

Members of Scottish parliament (MSP) Ariane Burgess (of the Scottish Greens) and Emma Roddick (Scottish National Party) dissented from paragraph 312 of the report, which stated the committee was not in support of a moratorium or pause.

Committee convener Finlay Carson, MSP, said: "We recognize the importance of the salmon farming industry to the Scottish economy and the jobs it supports in many rural and island communities. We also realize the efforts made by the industry to invest and innovate to overcome the new and unpredictable challenges it faces."

"But further progress should have been made in implementing the [2018] committee's recommendations...as well as anticipating the impact of climate change and rising sea temperatures on the industry. This would have helped address some of the polarised views the industry is currently facing in relation to the production process."

Ultimately, he continued, it is the Scottish government's role, as well as the industry's, to drive the change agenda required to allow science, research and the regulatory landscape to keep pace with the rapidly changing marine environment.

"That is why we are calling for the Scottish government to redouble its focus on regulatory issues to ensure that this industry, which is so important to the Scottish economy, is both future-proofed and enabled to grow sustainably."

Some of the committee's key recommendations include;

Fish mortality

Powers to be given to the Fish Health Inspectorate (or another appropriate body) to limit or halt production at sites that record persistently high mortality rates. The Scottish government should work with industry and regulators to agree appropriate criteria and mortality thresholds for the use of these powers.

Scottish government to establish a research project focused on testing and improving the modelling of environmental conditions that are known to cause high mortality events on salmon farms. This should have the effect of providing early warning to industry and inform technological solutions and approaches to husbandry to mitigate high mortality events.

The publication of comprehensive, consistent and transparent mortality figures that include the number of fish at a farm, the freshwater and seawater mortality, per facility, with accurate numbers of dead salmon, wrasse and lumpsuckers per week and with cumulative mortality totals at the end of each production cycle.

Scottish government to publish an annual fish health report detailing the health and welfare status of all farmed finfish in Scotland.

Impact of salmon farms on the marine environment

Further research to address the significant gaps in knowledge, data, analysis and monitoring around the adverse risk of salmon farming on the marine environment, especially around discharges from farm pens and the use of medicines.

Scottish government to work with industry and academia to establish dedicated research pens. The industry should contribute to the cost of financing this infrastructure.

Scottish government to consider an expedited timetable for the introduction of a revised environmental quality standard for emamectin benzoate, rather than the planned four-year implementation period.

Farmed fish welfare

Scottish government to bring forward additional regulations and official guidance under the Animal Health and Welfare (Scotland) Act 2006 to set specific baseline standards for the welfare of farmed fish.

Scottish government to update the committee in relation to the ethics and welfare implications of the use of 'cleaner fish' to manage sea lice infestations.

Sea lice

Scottish government to introduce stricter conditions for 'no counts' (when salmon farms don't return a weekly sea lice count to the Fish Health Inspectorate) for the accepted reasons of stock that is subject to treatments or being held for harvest.

Data and transparency

Scottish government to prioritize upgrading and improving the "Scotland's Aquaculture" website to make data more accessible and user-friendly.

Wild salmon

Scottish government to publish a timetable for implementing the outstanding 42 recommendations of the Salmon Interactions Working Group report as a matter of urgency.

A memorandum of understanding between the Scottish Environment Protection Agency and other relevant bodies to ensure a coordinated approach to managing the impacts of farmed salmon on wild salmon.

An immediate end to the siting of farms in the close vicinity of known migratory routes for wild salmon.

Planning

Scottish government to address concerns about the slow progress in tackling issues with the planning and consenting process, especially regarding relocating existing farms. This was raised by the industry as one of the current pain points of trying to improve the Scottish sector.

Scottish government to ensure that communities share the benefits of salmon farms sited in their locality, through consultation with stakeholders and affected communities.

title: NGO files complaint against France, Portugal, Spain over alleged illegal bottom trawling
content:
Environmental NGO Bloom, in partnership with the Deep Sea Conservation and the Marine Conservation Institute, has filed a formal complaint with the EU Commission (EC) over widespread illegal fishing in protected marine areas.

A new study, published in the scientific journal Science Advances, revealed over 400 cases of fraud by French, Portuguese and Spanish vessels continuing to fish in areas that had been closed to protect vulnerable deep-sea ecosystems, the NGOs claim.

Despite regulations banning bottom trawling in waters deeper than 800 meters and the closure of 87 protected zones in 2022, Bloom alleged its satellite data analysis shows that industrial fishing fleets have ignored these rules.

According to the NGO, more than 3,500 hours of illegal fishing have been documented in areas meant to shield biodiversity-rich ecosystems that are home to corals, deepwater sharks, and sponges.

Bloom calls for "urgent action" from the EC to strengthen enforcement and close additional areas to safeguard marine life. The organization also urged France, Portugal, and Spain to stop "tacitly supporting destructive industrial fishing practices that continue to jeopardize fragile ocean ecosystems."

title: Canadian snow crab harvesters demand info from dockside monitoring agency
content:
A battle is brewing between the union representing fish and crab harvesters in the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador (NL) and a nonprofit organization providing dockside monitoring services to the fishing industry.

The Fish Food and Allied Workers (FFAW) has accused the Fish Harvester's Resource Center (FRC), which manages the harvester-funded dockside monitoring program in NL, of withholding financial information and preventing the FFAW from appointing new members to the board of directors.

"The FRC has not allowed the FFAW to reappoint new board members or hold a meeting to discuss the FRC's operations and financial situation," said new FFAW president Dwan Street in a press release on Monday (Jan. 13).

 "We've asked for a meeting and have been ignored, and we're concerned that this organization may no longer be operating in the best interests of fish harvesters. All we want is an open and honest conversation so that we can report back to our Inshore Council," said Street.

The Fish Harvesters Resource Centre organization has offices at the FFAW headquarters in St. John's, Newfoundland. Photo by Barb Dean-Simmons

FRC, established in 1993 as a non-profit, maintains a board of directors that includes representatives from both FFAW and the provincial government. It collects anywhere from CAD 0.02 per pound to CAD 0.05/lb from harvesters on their landings in order to pay for the services of the dockside monitors.

The monitors play a big role in the snow crab sector. In 2024, the NL snow crab fishery, the largest in the world, had a whopping quota of 57,568 metric tons.

The FRC and FFAW have a lot in common. Both organizations have offices in the FFAW building on Hamilton Avenue in the capital city of St. John's, NL. The FFAW is entitled to five of the 11 seats on the FRC's board of directors.

However, Street has concerns.

Last spring Greg Pretty, the previous union president, and a union representative on the FRC board requested information on its director appointment process as well as the by-laws of the organization, she noted.

"Specifically, they've asked us to ensure board seats are representative of the current industry and elected leadership. Despite repeated attempts to engage the FRC over the last year, executive director Velma Pike and chair Bill Broderick refuse to be transparent about their operations," Street said.

The FFAW wrote Pike and Broderick in December, notifying them of new appointments proposed by the union and requesting an urgent board meeting, said Street.

Recall that Broderick had indicated earlier this year that he was running for the role of president of the FFAW, as reported by Undercurrent News, but later withdrew his candidacy.

Pike notified the FFAW that the correspondence had been sent to their lawyer for response, and no meeting has been scheduled, Street added.

"This is not acceptable behavior to me or any person on the FFAW's executive board," she said. "We hope that public pressure will be the impetus needed to push Pike and Broderick to do the right thing and ensure that fish harvesters can continue to put their trust in the FRC. We need a meeting with the board – this cannot wait any longer." 

Broderick declined to offer comment when contacted by Undercurrent, saying the matter was being handled through the FRC's lawyer and the organization would issue a press release soon.

Meanwhile, a report on crab quality commissioned by the NL provincial government in 2024 has noted that the FRC does not have enforcement responsibility or a role in assessing crab quality. Some industry players considered this just another layer of oversight and another "clipboard" on the wharf, stated the September 2024 report by Brian Delaney of the firm Economic and Social Research Consulting.

title: Panel cements Washington state fish farming ban, further thwarts Cooke trout-growing effort
content:
The Washington Board of Natural Resources has voted, 4-0, to ban finfish aquaculture in the US state's waters, bringing what seems like a conclusion to a battle previously fought by Cooke Inc. and others to grow steelhead trout in net pens. 

The board spent several hours in Olympia, Washington, on Tuesday (Jan. 7) debating the resolution brought by outgoing commissioner of public lands Hilary Franz before making its decision. Two members of the six-person panel abstained.

The action makes good on one of Franz's final agenda moves before she hands over the reins to her successor, Dave Upthegrove, on Jan. 15. Franz, who held the commissioner post for nearly seven years, had aimed to halt future commercial finfish net pen aquaculture on state-managed aquatic lands, citing concerns over environmental degradation, biofouling, and broader ecological impacts, as outlined in her draft rule issued in October. 

Hail Mary pleas from both sides as Washington state board nears vote on fish farm ‘ban’

"This rule will make DNR's management of our state owned aquatic land similar to other states in the region," Franz said in a statement after the vote. "We are not leading, frankly, we are following. We are following other states that have already led, including Oregon, Alaska and California, which do not allow these types of commercial facilities. For me, I don't believe that cost is worth it. Avoidance is absolutely the best solution."

Jeanne Mcknight, executive director of the Northwest Aquaculture Alliance (NAA), a trade group that represents fish farmers in Oregon and Washington, was less joyful.

"Science lost today," she told Undercurrent News following the vote.

Cooke Inc, a Canadian seafood conglomerate with a large presence in the North America aquaculture arena, has been an outspoken opponent of the proposed ban on finfish net pen aquaculture in Washington state. It was the collapse of a Cooke salmon pen at Cypress Island and escape of 250,000 fish in 2017 that led to the state's passage of House Bill 2957 in 2018, mandating the cessation of non-native species farming by 2025.

Cooke responded by transitioning to farming native Pacific steelhead trout. However, Franz declined to renew Cooke's leases for steelhead farming in 2022. The Jamestown S'Klallam Tribe, Cooke's partner, contested this in court. Its permits remained pending, but Tuesday's decision -- which bans all finish farming in state waters -- now puts this project in limbo.

However, aquaculture industry representatives suggested to Undercurrent that the board's decision could potentially be challenged through alternative legal or legislative channels.

80% of commenters favored the ban

Tom Gorman, division manager at the Washington Department of Natural Resources (DNR), spent much of the morning explaining to the board why his agency moved to terminate remaining commercial finfish aquaculture leases on state lands following a 2017 salmon net pen collapse. He emphasized that the DNR's analysis found significant impacts from commercial finfish aquaculture that are difficult to mitigate.

The DNR received 561 public comments during the rulemaking process, with over 80% supporting the ban, he said. 

At Tuesday's hearing, supporters of the ban, including several tribes and environmental groups, argued that such a prohibition is necessary to protect wild salmon populations, uphold tribal treaty rights, and transition to more sustainable aquaculture methods.

Washington state official rushes to enforce fish farming ‘ban’ before leaving office

Amy Trainer, the Swinomish Tribe's environmental policy director, was among those who stressed that net pens pose a threat to salmon recovery efforts.

Several businesses, some tribal members and at least two aquaculture industry groups, NAA and the BC Salmon Farmers Association, argued that net pens can be operated responsibly and that the rule lacks sufficient transparency and scientific review. They raised concerns about the ban's economic impact, saying it would harm the local seafood industry and result in lost jobs. Industry representatives also criticized the rushed nature of the rulemaking process.

Drue Banta Winters, campaign manager for Stronger America Through Seafood (SATS), a pro-aquaculture lobbying group, sent a statement to Undercurrent following the vote.

"This decision in Washington State is out of step with the growing bipartisan momentum for open ocean aquaculture across the country and in the nation’s capital, as Americans and environmentalists recognize that aquaculture can be conducted without harming the environment, is beneficial for our communities, and is a sustainable source of protein farmed here at home," she said.

Winters noted how the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has published several scientific reports and publications analyzing the effects of netpen Atlantic salmon farming in the Pacific Northwest.

"They find no harm to Endangered Species Act (ESA)-listed salmonids from the operations of existing farms," she noted.

"Aquaculture is increasingly recognized by those on both sides of the aisle as a critical industry to boost our nation’s economy and ensure a steady supply of healthy, sustainable, American-raised protein," Winters said. "The US should be making every effort to expand aquaculture in the US, and today's decision in Washington state is a step in the wrong direction."

Two key components of final rule

DNR determined that no changes to the rule language were necessary, Gorman said. Following the decision, DNR must now file a CR-103 document, after which the rule will take effect within 31 days.

The final rule language has two key components:

First, DNR is proposing to add a new definition, which defines "commercial fin fish net pen aquaculture" as "a system of nets, cages or other containment systems in open water used to cultivate, feed and raise fin fish to marketable size for harvesting and selling, the same as a crop. Commercial finfish net pen aquaculture does not include operations and containment systems used to raise fin fish for open water release or used to raise fin fish solely for tribal, ceremonial, and subsistence uses."

Second, DNR is proposing to add a new section that states, "commercial fin fish net pen aquaculture shall not be authorized on state-owned aquatic lands."

title: Argentina enforces precautionary measures for hake, crab; Limits shrimp bycatch in new fishing plan
content:
In its final session of the year, Argentina's federal fisheries council (CFP, in its Spanish acronym) has approved a set of precautionary measures aimed at ensuring the long-term sustainability of the country's fisheries.

The new fishing plan, which sets maximum permissible catch limits for several key species in 2025, increases quotas for common hake and sets more cautious management for black hake and king crab. It also continued bycatch limits for shrimp in fresh fishing trawlers.

The CFP's decisions were heavily influenced by the latest reports from the country's fisheries research and development national institute, INIDEP, which has been monitoring fish stocks and conducting research to inform sustainable fishing practices.

Sharp drop in Argentina’s red shrimp, squid sales offsets hake export increase

As part of the 2025 fishing plan, the CFP has taken a precautionary approach to several declining fish stocks while ensuring the fishing sector's economic viability.

For common hake, Argentina's most commercially significant species, the CFP has agreed to increase the catch limit for the southern stock by 20,000 metric tons for the 2025 season, from 319,000t in 2024 to 339,000t.

This increase is intended to continue supporting the recovery of the reproductive biomass, a key indicator of the population's long-term health, according to the CPF. 

However, for the northern hake stock, which remains under stress, the total allowable catch (TAC) will remain more conservative, set at 30,850t, based on INIDEP's recommendation for a gradual recovery. 

"The northern stock's precarious condition requires a cautious approach, and the decision to maintain this reduced quota reflects the need to stabilize the reproductive biomass over time," said the CPF in a statement. 

In contrast, the management of back hake has raised concerns due to a significant decline in both its reproductive and total biomass. INIDEP's models suggest that fishing efforts concentrated in specific areas, such as the Burdwood Bank, may be exacerbating the decline.

As a result, the CFP has decided to set the TAC for black hake at 3,575t, a slight reduction from the previous year. Although this decision is intended to preserve the species and prevent further depletion, the CFP has also indicated that "more drastic measures may be necessary if the downward trend in biomass continues."

King crab management was another focal point of the meeting. While the fishing industry has called for higher quotas, INIDEP's latest findings suggest that current levels are sufficient to maintain the species' sustainability.

The increase in king crab catches over the past few years is attributed to improvements in fishing technology rather than any significant increase in biomass. Consequently, the CFP has maintained the TAC for king crab at 900t for the 2024-2025 season, with regional allocations reflecting the current stock conditions.

Early red shrimp catches in Argentina spark optimism, but oversupply, price competition threaten profits

"Any increase in catch limits could lead to overexploitation, a risk we are determined to avoid," the CPF explained.

It also addressed the issue of shrimp bycatch, which has been contentious among the fleet. Argentina's shipowners' association requested that the 20% bycatch tolerance for shrimp in fresh fish trawlers remain in place, citing the abundance of shrimp in areas overlapping with target species like hake and mackerel.

After careful consideration, the CFP decided to continue the 20% bycatch tolerance, which will remain in effect through April 2025. This decision is based on the argument that shrimp bycatch has benefited the fleet and helped sustain jobs in the onshore processing sector.

However, environmental concerns about the long-term impact of this bycatch policy remain, and the CFP has stressed that it will continue to monitor the situation closely.

The situation for southeast Pacific whiting remains unresolved, as a lack of sufficient data has made it impossible to assess the stock's status accurately. As a result, the TAC for this species will remain at 3,600t for 2025, the same level set for 2024. 

Finally, the CFP has expressed concerns about the squid fishing fleet, targeting illex squid.

While the fleet is in the process of obtaining certification for its sustainable practices, INIDEP has reported that observer coverage in 2024 was "inconsistent," particularly towards the end of the season.

title: Newfoundland salmon farmers criticized for abandoning plastic gear in ocean
content:
A traditional foe for Atlantic salmon farmers has accused the industry's producers in Newfoundand and Labrador (NL) of dumping significant amounts of plastic into the ocean, and says it has satellite images and recent field surveys to back up its charges.  

In a statement circulated on Wednesday (Dec. 18),  the Atlantic Salmon Federation (ASF) said satellite images taken over a 13-year period starting in 2011 reveal large-scale disposal of plastic at sea by salmon farming companies in the Canadian province. Debris include abandoned sea-cages, netting and ropes in two remote coves near the town of Gaultois on Newfoundland’s south coast — L'Anse a Flamme and The Locker.

According to the ASF, the coves are close to nine salmon farming sites leased to subsidiaries of Norwegian-backed Mowi Canada East and Canadian seafood giant Cooke Aquaculture.  

ASF alleged The Locker is particularly impacted, with satellite imagery showing as many as 25 discarded sea-cages in 2022. The group said its staff observed similar debris during a boat visit this past summer.

Some of the waste found by ASF dates back to 2011, with one rectangular salmon pen breaking apart and drifting by 2015, the organization alleged. It argues these practices violate provincial and federal laws, as well as salmon farm lease conditions, which carry potential fines of up to CAD 1 million ($693.3m).

ASF said it reported the alleged dumping to Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans and the NL Department of Fisheries, Forestry and Agriculture in August 2024. It said it is unaware of any follow-up enforcement actions.

ASF is a nonprofit with offices in both Canada (New Brunswick) and the US (Maine) that heavily represents recreational salmon farming interests. It has been sparring with Canada's salmon farmers for years.

On Monday (Dec. 16), the Newfoundland Aquaculture Industry Association sharply criticized ASF, accusing it of using substantial US funding to fuel campaigns that jeopardize the province's fishing and aquaculture industries while contributing little to Canadian salmon conservation. 

Canadian aquaculture group accuses US of fueling activism against Newfoundland marine sanctuary

ASF declined to comment in detail when reached by Undercurrent regarding the matter, describing some of the accusations as "very problematic" and alleging that certain claims contained "falsehoods."

"We’re weighing our response carefully," said spokesman Neville Crabbe. "In the meantime, we’re carrying on with our work, like we have for 75 years, focusing on actual issues, like large-scale dumping of aquaculture garbage in public waters."

Industry's cleanup commitments

Cooke Inc, one of the big salmon farmers operating in NL, told Undercurrent News this week that salmon producers in Canada are committed to preventing equipment from being released into the ocean.

“Within their 2024 Sustainability Report published earlier this year, all major salmon producers in Canada committed to ensuring no farming equipment is released from farm sites, and in case of accident, that there is prompt recovery of marine debris such as nets, tools, floats, pipes, etc,” said Joel Richardson, Cooke's vice president of public relations.

Richardson emphasized that companies have established procedures to manage waste responsibly and avoid environmental harm. He also pointed to ongoing efforts to address historical issues in NL.

“Aquaculture companies, including Cooke, in [NL] also have ongoing remediation plans within their operations, and that work will continue into 2025 for any coastal locations not yet completed,” he said.

Newfoundland and Labrador. Map from Victor Maschek / Shutterstock.

Mowi Canada East echoed the commitments. Gideon Pringle, its managing director, told Undercurrent that the company relies on a healthy ocean to operate.

“Mowi depends on a healthy ocean. Mowi focuses on avoiding any plastic litter ending up at sea because of our farming activities. We have well-established monitoring and control programs in place to identify and recover any missing equipment,” Pringle said.

Pringle noted that Mowi, along with other companies, conducts regular shoreline and coastal cleanups, targeting all man-made debris found in affected areas.

The NL aquaculture industry continues to deal with challenges tied to its history. Over the past 40 years, many salmon farming companies have faced financial difficulties or bankruptcy, leaving behind abandoned gear and equipment, said another source. Today, the industry has consolidated into a handful of major players who are tasked with addressing these legacy issues, he said. Cleanup and remediation efforts are ongoing.

title: Untitled
content:
The US is providing $12.5 million to Vietnam to better enable that country to beef up its maritime law enforcement and combat illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing.

The funding was announced by Marc Knapper, the US ambassador to Vietnam, during a meeting held earlier this month with Phung Duc Tien, agriculture and rural development minister at Vietnam's Department of Fisheries (DFRIES) surveillance training facility in Phu Quoc.

The funding comes from the US Department of State's Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs and will support three maritime law enforcement agencies in Vietnam: DFRIES, the Ministry of Public Security and Vietnam Customs.

The United States supports a free and open Indo-Pacific and a strong, prosperous, independent and resilient Vietnam, the US Embassy says in a statement.

"These new foreign assistance programs are just some of the many ways in which the United States and Vietnam are deepening cooperation on maritime law enforcement and maritime security capacity under the US-Vietnam Comprehensive Strategic Partnership and demonstrating how the two governments are working together to address shared regional and global challenges," the Embassy statement read.

Recall that the European Commission (EC) issued a "yellow card" warning to Vietnam in 2017, charging that the country was not doing enough to fight illegal fishing, as reported by Undercurrent News. It offered the possibility for Vietnam to take measures to rectify the situation within a reasonable timeframe. 

Since then, Vietnam has made significant efforts to gradually meet the requirements made by the EC, reported news agency Vietnam Plus in August 2024.

"The system for fisheries monitoring has been reorganized, with 28 coastal provinces now having fisheries control forces. A Supreme People's Court resolution criminalizing IUU-related offenses has taken effect," rural development minister Le Minh Hoan was quoted by Vietnam Plus.

title: Washington state man charged with illegal Dungy crab harvest
content:
The Dungeness crab season in the US state of Washington is closed until next month at the earliest, but that didn't stop one man from trying to illegally harvest 27 of the coveted crustaceans ahead of the holidays.

The Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife (WDFW) reported Thursday (Dec. 12), via social media, that enforcement officials "observed a subject crabbing from a local pier in the north sound." 

Upon further inspection, the officers discovered a man, who was not identified in the posting, as being in possession of 27 Dungeness crabs -- 22 of which were female and unlawful to possess. The remaining five crabs, while male, were undersized, with one in a "soft shell condition."

None of the catch was recorded, WDFW said . The man is being charged with criminal violations for 1st degree over limit, possession of female crab, possession of Dungeness crab that is undersized and soft shell, and failure to record. All the crabs were documented before being returned to the water.

Recall that earlier this month, Dungeness harvests in the US states of Washinton, Oregon and California -- representing between 10 million and 30m pounds of crab -- were delayed due to a number of factors, including concerns about whale entanglement and biotoxins that were found in certain areas. 

The inability to hit the water has resulted in tight supplies of Dungeness ahead of the holidays, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

title: New study claims benefits of large marine protected areas
content:
A new study published in Science claims to show that large-scale marine protected areas (MPAs) boost fish catch rates, even spilling over outside of the MPAs and particularly for migratory species like bigeye tuna, Maui Now reports.

Researchers, including John Lynham from the University of Hawaii at Manoa, analyzed public data funded by the National Science Foundation.

The team found that catch rates increased by 12-18% near MPAs, with the strongest benefits just outside MPA boundaries and in areas previously heavily fished. Bigeye tuna catch rates showed the largest gains, with positive impacts across all tuna species. Notably, MPAs like Mexico's Revillagigedo Islands and Hawaii's Papahanaumokuakea contributed significantly to these increases.

This research supports international conservation goals, such as protecting 30% of the ocean by 2030 and the UN's Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction Agreement.

"The economic benefits of conservation largely stay with the nations implementing MPAs," said co-author Juan Carlos Villasenor-Derbez of the University of Miami.

The study underscores the role of well-enforced MPAs in balancing ecological conservation with economic gains for global tuna fisheries, a $40 billion industry.

title: Alaska fisheries board tweaks rules for state pollock fishery on Prince William Sound
content:
Fisheries regulators in the US state of Alaska have mostly punted on proposals submitted by trawl critics to tighten rules of the state-managed pollock trawl fishery in Prince William Sound, as Undercurrent News reported.

Instead, at their meeting Friday (Dec. 13) in Cordova, Alaska, the Alaska Board of Fisheries removed regulations that had required vessels to transit into different fishing areas when they approached 60% of the guideline harvest level (GHL). 

The trawl industry said the requirement could inadvertently result in more bycatch as vessels had less discretion on where to target pollock. Some areas are also cleaner or have fewer non-targeted species than others.

Oceana campaign calls for US regulators to reform Alaska trawl sector

The state-managed fishery is dwarfed by the much larger federally managed fisheries in the Gulf of Alaska and Bering Sea. Still, it has come under criticism for intercepting salmon and other species as bycatch and damaging the seafloor with its wide trawl nets as it targets pollock.  

Trawl industry pleased with board

The appointed fisheries board took no action on all four of the proposals. They ranged from shutting down the fishery to setting hard caps on bycatch rather than tying them to harvest levels, which industry representatives had opposed.

"I think they all came away with a lot clearer understanding of how the pollock trawl fishery works in Prince William Sound," Julie Bonney of the Alaska Groundfish Data Bank, which represents shoreside processors and trawlers, told Undercurrent. "In the same token, I think the action that they did was really trying to get us to do a better job with bycatch." 

But members of the board -- who are appointed by the state governor and confirmed by lawmakers -- acknowledged there is increased scrutiny of the trawlers, especially in federal fisheries that have been the target of legal action and pressure campaigns for reform.

SalmonState, a pro-salmon fishing conservation group, said it had forwarded more than 800 comments in favor of reforms to the Board of Fisheries. 

"This is nothing like the Bering Sea," board member Mike Wood said, adding he thinks the state manages Prince William Sound effectively. "But people are [upset]. Like, they want to know something about the trawl fleet in Alaska."

With one exception, members took no action or replaced the language in the proposals that kept bycatch levels at 5% of the GHL of Alaska pollock set by fisheries managers. The proposal also required the retention of chinook salmon and counted fish by number, rather than by gross weight.

The Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) opposed the proposals and said bycatch is already managed effectively in the 15-vessel trawl fishery, which caught, on average, around 800 chinook salmon annually in recent years. 

Proposals would crack down on Alaska’s Prince William Sound pollock fishery

Data supplied by ADF&G says that between 2021 and 2023, the trawl fleet landed, on average, 6,017,225 pounds of pollock. Bycatch by weight averaged 71,826 lbs, most of that squid.

The Chenega IRA Council -- a federally recognized Alaska Native tribe -- had asked for bycatch limits to be replaced by a fixed cap that would shut down fishing if exceeded. That's how federal pollock fisheries are regulated, as happened in the Gulf of Alaska where the interception of "an unprecedented" number chinook salmon ended fishing early, as Undercurrent reported.

Chenega IRA council member Boyd Selanoff told Undercurrent there are concerns that as the GHL is raised, so are allowances for bycatch, irrespective of the health of other species like chinook salmon.

"There's no ceiling on that bycatch limit," he said. "That's the limit. When you get to that limit, you're done."

He also raised concerns about enforcement, saying there's little to stop an unscrupulous harvester from dumping bycatch overboard on its way back to Kodiak, where the shoreside processors are.

"I have trawl friends," Selanoff added. "I am not trying to shut them down. But if we are all in this -- to conserve, to protect, to get more data -- the only way to do that is to turn those cameras on you."

Fisheries observers in state waters?

Unlike the federally managed trawl fisheries, state waters don't have electronic monitoring or onboard observers. ADF&G commissioner Doug Vincent-Lang said he doesn't currently have funding to add any.

"Nor do I think it's a pressing enough issue to put observers on these vessels," he told the board. "But if it becomes necessary, I could do that under the regulatory authority you've given me."

Most of the vessels already have cameras installed to comply with federal requirements. Wood said that he has confidence the Prince William Sound trawl fishery is well-managed, but using the cameras could increase public confidence. 

"I think it would really behoove the trawl industry to voluntarily -- if you have that gear on board -- to turn it on and use it," he said. "Even though we can't require it, it would go a long way with the public."

Wood was the lone vote in favor of the failed proposal to mandate observers in the state-managed trawl fishery.

Bonney of the Alaska Groundfish Data Bank said it took five years to develop that program and it would be more complicated than simply switching on the cameras. But she said it could be done.

"We wouldn't have any objection about moving that forward to educate people and get all the pieces to work right so that you can actually monitor the fishery appropriately," she said.

Fisheries board member Curtis Chamberlain -- a practicing lawyer by trade -- recommended the trawl industry work with state regulators to craft a monitoring program, like the federal fisheries.

"I would strongly encourage that discussion in this fishery as well," Chamberlain said. "As a trial attorney, the negotiated outcome is far better than the one in other people's hands."

During testimony the day before, trawler Patrick "Paddy" O'Donnell said observers are useful for gathering data but didn't think the trawl fleet should be singled out. 

"If you're going to develop a program, then I think it should encompass everybody who fishes in Prince William Sound," O'Donnell said. 

SalmonState, the conservation group that led a public campaign in favor of the proposals, said while it had hoped the board would go further, the outcome was an important first step in a larger effort.

"No one even knew that there was a trawl fishery in Prince William Sound before this meeting," SalmonState operations director Ryan Astalos told Undercurrent. "And now they do."

title: Newfoundland fisheries minister stands by snow crab inspection protocols
content:
A new report on snow crab quality is proof that Newfoundland and Labrador's inspection protocol is working and regulators should "stay the course," asserts Gerry Byrne, the fisheries minister for the Canadian province.

The reputation of the quality of crustaceans coming out of the world's largest snow crab fishery has been shaken since provincial fisheries inspectors accused Quinlan Brothers, operator of the biggest snow crab factory in NL, of processing dead crab, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

However, the purpose of the just released 36-page report, authored by independent consultant Brian Delaney, was not to seek recommendations for significant changes, Byrne told Undercurrent News in an interview Wednesday (Dec. 11).

Rather, it was meant to refresh memories, to set the historical record straight on the province's regulations around quality control in the snow crab industry, he said.

"The whole point of the report was, really, just to create a baseline of historical and public policy reference. It wasn't meant to establish recommendations," he clarified.

The Delaney report came just a week before Quinlan Brothers was due to appear in a provincial court in Harbour Grace to enter a plea on charges that were laid under the province's Fish Inspection Act and regulations.

The company was forced to discard about 50,000 pounds of boxed crab in June, worth about CAD 250,000 ($176,971), as reported by Undercurrent. 

The charges against Quinlan Brothers have yet to be proven in court. The court process is expected to continue into the new year.

In August, Quinlan Brothers' owner Robin Quinlan invited media to tour its 22,700 square foot factory to show the protocols involved in processing snow crab.

FREE READ Quinlan Brothers holds media event to counter rotten crab publicity

"We have nothing to hide," Quinlan told reporters at that event. "We produce a premium product. We've done it for 50 years, and we're going to continue to do it."

Following the charges, Quinlan Brothers and the Association of Seafood Producers (ASP), the industry group that represents most of the seafood processing companies in the province, fired back at the province in a joint press conference, as reported by Undercurrent. 

Among their complaints was that the inspection protocols used by provincial regulators were not consistent with other quality controls, including the grading methods used by Independent Dockside Graders (IDG), a company certified by the province to grade crab and other seafood at docks around the province.

Jeff Loder, ASP's executive director, said the Quinlan incident was not the first time a processing company had encountered problems with the province's inspection process, too.

"We've had instances in the last two years where the crab was graded and deemed to be 100% good, with next to no critically weak crab, and then an inspector, a couple of hours later, says the crab is dead," Loder told Undercurrent in July.

Graders intimidated

While IDG is licensed by the province, it is a service paid for and directed solely by the processors, an outcome of collective bargaining between the ASP and the Fish Food and Allied Workers, the union that represents most of the province's fish harvesters, Delaney, a former assistant deputy minister of the NL fisheries department, noted in his report.

"IDG has no legal authority and only serves as a reporting function for the industry," the report stated.

IDG employees simply grade the crab at the dock to determine if it is lively, weak or dead and to assess it for barnacles to determine the price paid to the harvester, the document read.

Canadian snow crab clusters on display at Seafood Expo North America 2024. Photo by Barb Dean-Simmons

IDG employees use only visual inspection to assess the condition of the crab, while provincial inspectors use a crab life detector, a tool that uses electric shock to test reflexes to determine if a crab is alive, Delaney added.

If IDG determines that 20% of the load is critically weak or 4.0% is dead, the province's fisheries department must be notified.

"When this happens, provincial inspectors, if possible, inspect the load when it arrives at the food processing facility," the report explained.

US snow crab prices rise again as Canadian supply thins

In 2024, there were over 60 calls to the Department of Fisheries, Forestry and Agriculture due to those thresholds being reached, the Delaney report noted. It added that provincial inspectors, who were interviewed for the report, said warm weather and high water temperatures during the 2024 season impacted crab quality.

Dead crab was being processed and there was constant pressure to let the crab go through the processing lines, provincial inspectors reportedly told Delaney. Inspectors also suggested there was intimidation of graders who were pressured to underreport critically weak and dead crabs.

"Some processors worked under capacity this year while others suffered gluts. The lack of sharing amongst processors means crab quality was sometimes compromised," provincial inspectors also told Delaney.

"Criticism of government's grading processes by seafood producers may be misplaced given that it is generally only involved when a problem is identified. With over 9,000 landings and only hundreds of inspections, provincial inspectors are involved very little in the industry's affairs," the report concluded.

Meanwhile, there is an issue of inconsistency between crab grading protocols used by IDG and provincial inspectors, the Delay report noted, adding that industry and government cooperation on quality appears not to be as coordinated as it was in the past.

Byrne: Regulations offer assurance

Despite the headlines and the contentious public debate over the province's inspection protocols after Quinlan Brothers was forced by provincial inspectors to dump thousands of pounds of crab, Byrne said the market should feel assured that NL produces a high-quality product.

Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans reports that 56,126t of NL's 57,568t quota was landed during the 2024 season. The landings had a combined value of CAD 371.2m ($262.34).

Of the 56,699t of crab processed in NL in 2024, just 400,000 pounds -- or less than 1.0% -- were found to be of concern, Byrne offered.

Sweeping changes announced for world’s largest snow crab fishery

"So I would argue that crab quality is very, very high here," he said.

As for the publicity on the issue this past summer, Byrne said the ASP should be asked whether it is concerned that its decision to start a public debate on the matter may have diminished the reputation of its own members.

"What I do know is this: When consumers and buyers know that there are regulations in place, that the rule of law applies and is enforced, and we take action, that creates confidence in a product," the fisheries minister offered.

title: Bodies, debris from Alaska fishing vessel found week after sinking
content:
The bodies of two of the five crew members from the Wind Walker, a 50-foot fishing vessel that capsized near Point Couverdon, in the US state of Alaska on Dec. 1, have been found.

Three crew members remain missing.

Wildlife troopers from Juneau and Hoonah responded to a call on Monday (Dec. 9) about human remains on a beach in Spasski Bay, according to a dispatch from the Alaska Department of Public Safety, State Troopers. A team of responders were sent to the location, including representatives from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), law enforcement officers and members of the SEADOGS K9 search team. They found two bodies among washed up debris from the Wind Walker.

The remains were transported to Juneau where the State Medical Examiner's Office will perform an autopsy and identify the individuals. An additional search of the shoreline was conducted with dogs but no other human remains were found.

The US Coast Guard (USCG) was alerted to a capsized vessel southwest of Juneau early on the morning of Dec. 1, as reported by Undercurrent News. While USCG watchstanders were able to receive a mayday call, they lost contact with the crew of the Wind Walker in local conditions that consisted of heavy snow, 45-60 mile per hour winds and six-foot waves.

A nearby ferry vessel, the AMHS Hubbard, responded to an urgent marine information broadcast and was the first to arrive at the scene. Rescuers were only able to find seven cold-water immersion suits and two-strobe lights.

The Coast Guard suspended the search for the missing crew on Dec. 2 after a nearly 24-hour search spanning an area of the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Alaska that was about 108 square miles.

title: Untitled
content:
Thai Union Group has now responded to the suggestion that it owes $65 million to Red Lobster's new owners in relation to an unfulfilled promise to help pay off debt accrued by the massive seafood restaurant chain. No, it doesn't, the Thailand-based seafood giant argues.

Thai Union last week gave its answer to the complaint filed against it by Fortress Credit Corp., Red Lobster's new owners, in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York, in October. It has asked the federal court to dismiss the case without granting Fortress any relief. 

Recall that Thai Union exited its investment in Red Lobster months before the seafood restaurant chain filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on May 19, 2024, as reported by Undercurrent. RL Holdings, an entity created by funds managed by affiliates of Fortress, as well as co-investors TCW Private Credit and Blue Torch, completed the acquisition of the Red Lobster Chain, allowing the company to officially exit bankruptcy on Sept. 16, 2024.

However, in its complaint, Fortress maintained that Thai Union "guaranteed payments of the borrowers (Red Lobster) of up to $65 million upon the occurrence of certain events specified in the guaranty." Red Lobster's failure to pay back more than $89 million that it had in debt "triggered Thai Union's obligations under the guaranty," the complaint argued.

Fortress has asked the court to "enforce an unconditional, absolute and irrevocable guaranty made by Thai Union in connection with a financing agreement."

Thai Union posts record Q3 margins after Red Lobster exit

Thai Union argues in its response, however, that Fortress "does not have any basis to pursue relief." 

Thai Union acknowledges that "in the limited guaranty, it guaranteed, in certain circumstances, certain payments by the borrowers up to a specified amount ($65m) and for a specified time frame (prior to the termination date)." However, the company said its limited guaranty was not in effect "at any time relevant to the complaint." 

Red Lobster's Ultimate Endless Shrimp. Photo Courtesy of Red Lobster.

 

There's no shortage of bad blood between Red Lobster and Thai Union. Recall that the restaurant chain blamed its former parent company for many of its financial woes.

Jonathan Tibus, who was CEO of Red Lobster at the time of its bankruptcy, identified former CEO Paul Kenny and Thai Union as responsible for several costly decisions, as reported by Undercurrent. That included the Ultimate Endless Shrimp promotion, which allowed customers to pay $20 for an unlimited amount of shrimp. It helped increase foot traffic to the restaurant's locations by roughly 4% during the third quarter of 2023, but was also responsible for more than $11 million in operating losses.

Tibus also suggested that Thai Union took advantage of its position as both the entity that controlled Red Lobster and its biggest seafood supplier to buy more shrimp.

title: Overfishing has halved shark, ray populations since 1970
content:
Global populations of sharks, rays and chimeras have declined by more than half since 1970 due to overfishing, according to a recent study published in the journal Science.

The research, part of the Global Shark Trends Project, an international shark and ray conservation initiative, reported that the extinction risk for these species has grown by 19% over the past 50 years.

Researchers say this decline has profound implications for marine ecosystems. Large species, such as sawfish and rhino rays, are essential for healthy habitats from coastal areas to open waters. Their decreasing numbers disrupt marine food webs and the connections between different species. For instance, reef sharks help move nutrients from deeper waters to coral reefs, while rays oxygenate sediments, supporting marine life.

Reticulate whipray. Photo: California Academy of Sciences

The researchers used a new tool called the aquatic Red List Index (RLI) to track changes in extinction risks. This method provides a way to measure trends in ocean biodiversity, unlike previous methods that focused mainly on land species. Findings indicate that the decline started in rivers and coastal areas before spreading into the open ocean and deep sea. Larger species were the first to be targeted for overfishing because of their high value in global markets.

Sharks and rays have slow growth rates, mature late and reproduce infrequently, making them particularly vulnerable to overfishing. Moreover, the research found that threats like habitat destruction, climate change, and pollution mean that over one-third of these species now face extinction.

On a positive note, some regions, including Canada, the US, Australia, New Zealand and parts of Europe and Africa, have started to improve fisheries management. However, deepwater species often lack adequate protection, and enforcement of international agreements is variable.

The researchers recommend reducing fishing pressure, ending harmful subsidies, and strengthening global commitments to conservation. The aquatic RLI aims to guide efforts by identifying at-risk species and regions and tracking progress on biodiversity goals.
