title: US Pacific seafood processors oppose Alaska ballot initiative to guarantee paid sick leave
content:
Pacific Coast seafood processors are opposing an Alaska ballot measure they warn would drive up labor costs by requiring businesses in the US state provide paid sick leave to their employees.

Ballot Measure 1 -- another matter that could be decided along with the vote for US president on Nov. 5 -- would also raise the state's minimum wage, require medical leave and prohibit employers from holding mandatory meetings on political and religious affairs unrelated to the workplace.

The Pacific Seafood Processors Association (PSPA) says shoreside processors already pay more than the state's $11.73 per hour minimum wage, so they would not be affected by provisions to raise it to $15.00 by 2027.

But the group is troubled by a requirement for businesses with more than 15 employees to provide up to seven days of annual sick leave, which it believes would "negatively impact" their members and add at least $16.5 million to their annual labor costs.

"However, there will likely be additional unknown costs in order to comply with state enforcement, as well as managing the impacts to plant operations," new PSPA executive director Julie Decker wrote recently in posts to both LinkedIn and Facebook.

PSPA also maintains that temporary seafood workers are protected by industry standards.

"Seasonal workers are provided health insurance, transportation, food, and housing, but do not have the same level of benefits as full-time employees, which is common for most businesses across Alaska," the Seattle, Washington-based group said in a statement.

Seafood exempt from Canada’s new temporary foreign worker rules

The measure would give all seasonal and full-time workers the right to one hour of paid sick leave for every 30 hours worked. An employee would have to work 1,680 hours to be entitled to the maximum seven days of sick leave allowed per year.

Employers could also require documentation for paid leave exceeding three consecutive days.

The measure has largely been backed and funded by The Fairness Project, a pro-labor organization in Washington, D.C., which has contributed most of the $2.5m raised to support the ballot measure, campaign finance filings show.

The measure would also prohibit employers from holding mandatory meetings at work regarding political or religious affairs that are unrelated to the job. 

The Alaska Chamber spearheading opposition has said that would infringe on bosses' free speech. Several major firms, including Trident Seafoods, Copper River, UniSea, Alaska General and Westward Seafoods, are members of the group, which has been a major contributor to the nearly $85,000 raised in opposition, according to campaign finance reports.

PSPA said its members would not be affected by the provision against mandatory meetings. 

The initiative was polling favorably in May, with Alaskans reporting that they support its provisions by a 2-1 margin, according to Breakthrough Campaigns.

title: Washington state official rushes to enforce fish farming ‘ban’ before leaving office
content:
Hilary Franz, Washington state's commissioner of public lands, is in a race against time to enforce a ban on commercial finfish net pen aquaculture before her tenure ends on Jan. 15, 2025.

Franz issued a draft rule last week to permanently prohibit net pen farming on state-owned aquatic lands, fulfilling a court-mandated requirement to advance the ban. It seeks to halt future commercial finfish net pen aquaculture on state-managed aquatic lands, citing concerns over environmental degradation, biofouling and broader ecological impacts.

The proposal follows a ruling made Sunday (Oct. 20) by Thurston County Superior Court Judge Indu Thomas, in which she found that Franz's previous executive order lacked legal standing until a formal rulemaking process was completed.

The draft rule is open for public comment until Nov. 7, after which it will be submitted to the state's Board of Natural Resources for a vote on Dec. 3.

This expedited timeline has drawn criticism from stakeholders as Franz waited over a year before releasing the draft rule for public comment just last week, giving the public only three weeks to provide feedback.

Maria Smithson, a government and public affairs strategist affiliated with Salish Fish, a company owned by the Jamestown S'Klallam Tribe, accused Franz of "trying to hijack the process and silence people's voices" in order to "sneak this in as fast as she can" before her term ends in mid-January.

On her way out

Franz's push to finalize the ban comes as she prepares to step down from her role as public lands commissioner, a position that also puts her at the helm of the Department of Natural Resources (DNR). The position is currently being contested in an election to determine her successor. Franz has served two terms, from 2016 to 2024.

Her bid to represent Washington's 6th District in the US Congress ended last summer when she lost the Democratic nomination to Emily Randall.

"Hilary Franz lost the election because she is out of touch with voters on the Peninsula who know sustainably farming native fish is the best way to replace our lost and endangered wild fish stocks," said Smithson.

"Her activist agenda is pro-import, so bad for climate change, and unfair to Tribes who have nearly lost all access to salmon and steelhead. I think the voters chose the two best candidates for the November election -- both are concerned with the rural economy on the Peninsula and why locally grown and sourced seafood is so important in Washington's 6th Congressional District," she continued. 

How it came to this

The October 2023 order renewed attention to a debate that began several years ago, rooted in Washington's evolving approach to aquaculture management.

Franz's push for a permanent ban on finfish net pens stems from events that started with Washington's 2018 House Bill 2957, which mandated the cessation of fish farming involving non-native species, such as Atlantic salmon, by 2025.

HB 2957 was introduced after approximately 250,000 Atlantic salmon escaped from the Bainbridge Island farm of Canadian seafood conglomerate Cooke Aquaculture in August 2017, raising significant environmental concerns.

In response to the new rule, which took effect in March 2018, Cooke transitioned to farming native Pacific steelhead trout.

Despite Cooke's transition, the DNR, under Franz's leadership, declined to renew Cooke's leases for steelhead farming in November 2022, citing concerns about the state's best interests.

Shortly after, Franz issued her executive order banning all net pen finfish farming in Washington's state-owned waters. This order was contested in court by the Jamestown S'Klallam Tribe, a partner in Cooke's steelhead farming project, resulting in the Oct. 20 ruling in the tribe's favor.

'The eyes of the world are on us'

The Jamestown S'Klallam Tribe continues to push for the approval of its aquaculture lease, urging DNR to expedite the process. The tribe's efforts reflect the tension between those advocating for sustainable aquaculture and those raising environmental concerns about net pen operations. The commissioner of public lands, an elected role in Washington, plays a vital part in shaping such decisions.

Jeanne McKnight, executive director of the Northwest Aquaculture Alliance, has highlighted the global significance of the events unfolding in Washington state. She made it clear that this issue extends far beyond just the state's borders, stating that she constantly hears about it from leaders across the US and Canada.

"The eyes of the world are on us," McKnight told Undercurrent, referring to the attention the net pen ban has drawn from both the US and Canada.

She urged local and international stakeholders to participate in the public comment period, stating, "Let's have a vibrant, sustainable, innovative sector in this state -- and it doesn't all have to be net pens, but net pens attract other innovators."

Undercurrent reached out to Franz's office for comment but did not get a reply.

title: Untitled
content:
The sales price of frozen-onboard squid in Morocco has surged by over €1 per kilogram over the last month and a half, following the transition from the first to the second fishing season, according to industry sources.

"As of now, prices have reached €10.60 per kilogram for 1P (piece), €9.60/kg for 2P and €8.60/kg for 3P, FOB [free on board]," one source in the country told Undercurrent News earlier this week.

This rise in prices is primarily attributed to the scarcity of squid in various fishing grounds, which prompted processors and distributors in Italy and Spain to look quickly for other sources.

The graphs below show the trend in Moroccan squid prices imported into the EU on average until mid-September.

Upgrade to Pro to view
Falklands and Peru

The cancellation of the second fishing season in the Falkland Islands has also contributed to the sudden price hike, as loligo squid stocks from the first season in Europe have jumped in price, passing €6/kg, according to sources.

Spanish fleet faces €100m loss following Falkland Islands’ squid ban

Meanwhile, the giant squid shortage continues in Peru, causing prices to triple. The local fishing industry attributes the situation, which it defines as the worst crisis over the last 30 years, to illegal fishing by Asian vessels. 

Prices in Peru have surged past PEN 20 (approximately $5.40)/kg. "Stocks have nearly vanished, and rising prices are making it almost impossible for many consumers to purchase what is left," an executive within a Peruvian seafood exporting company told Undercurrent during Conxemar earlier this month.

The Peruvian government, however, has previously denied claims that the current scarcity of jumbo squid in Peruvian waters is due to illegal fishing by Chinese vessels. Instead, the ministry attributed the crisis to climate conditions, specifically the impact of the El Nino phenomenon, as Undercurrent also reported. 

Last week, several Peruvian congress members demanded answers from the production ministry regarding the entry of Chinese vessels into Peruvian ports. During a joint Defense and Production Commissions session, lawmakers criticized the ministry for its slow response in implementing a new framework to combat illegal fishing and enforce regulations that control foreign vessels' access to Peruvian ports.

The National Society of Artisanal Fishing (SONAPESCAL) reported that this meeting occurred amid protests from artisanal fishermen. It also highlighted complaints about Chinese vessels entering Peruvian ports without installing the required Satellite Tracking System, SISESAT. 

Moroccan cuttlefish, octopus

In addition to the squid price increase, the cuttlefish catch in Morocco has been low, with prices ranging between €5.50/kg and €6.00/kg FOB.

The octopus fishing season in Morocco ended last month, with final FOB prices in Agadir ranging between €14.9/kg for T1 and €9.2/kg for T8 FOB.

The graph below illustrates the recent rise in the average price of Moroccan frozen octopus imported into the EU until the end of September.

At the Conxemar seafood fair, processing companies indicated that octopus prices were rising due to strong demand. In the case of squid, prices have surged due to the limited supply available across different fishing zones, with processors rushing to find different origins and stocks trying to secure products for the coming months.

title: Bangladeshi shrimp exports shrink in ‘vicious cycle’
content:
Bangladesh's shrimp exports have fallen from around 55,000 metric tons in 2016 to just 25,000t in 2023, with the sector trapped in a "vicious cycle," according to the latest update from the Shrimp Insights blog, run by Willem van der Pijl.

The export-oriented shrimp industry suffers from a supply shortage and a lack of market access, he wrote. Around 17,500t of the 2023 total was black tiger shrimp, and the rest was a combination of farmed freshwater shrimp and wild-caught shrimp.

The EU accounts for 70% of the export volume, the UK 12%, and the US 6%. 

"Within these markets, Bangladesh sells mainly to the foodservice segment, which does generally not have very stringent quality and sustainability requirements but is extremely price-driven -- incentivizing buyers and suppliers to drive the price to the bottom, harming the perception of the quality and reliability of Bangladeshi shrimp in the international market."

That said, the chart above, from Undercurrent News' trade portal, shows that Bangladeshi shrimp was more expensive even than Vietnamese products when imported for much of the past seven years.

One reason for the Bangladeshi supply shortage is the growth of the domestic market, said Shrimp Insights. Official production numbers suggest that shrimp production in Bangladesh is relatively stable at around 135,000t, of which 70,000t is black tiger shrimp, 55,000t is freshwater prawn, and around 10,000t is wild-caught shrimp.

"Although these figures are most likely considerably inflated, these numbers confirm a considerable domestic shrimp market. According to industry sources, the domestic market may currently absorb around 50% of black tiger production. This would be around 35,000t, which was previously primarily exported."

That 35,000 t of harvested shrimp equals around 20,000-25,000t of finished product, meaning that with an export volume of just 17,500t, the domestic market's actual consumption of black tiger shrimp may be more than 50% and could even have reached 60-70%, the blog noted.

"Due to the lack of raw materials and low shrimp prices, processing plants go bankrupt, workers lose their jobs, and farmers aren't paid as much as possible for the shrimp they harvest. With a lack of long-term vision from most of Bangladesh's shrimp exporters, it's a vicious cycle that is hard to break."

Van der Pijl credited some companies, like Lenk Group, with efforts to improve the situation.

The company's owner, Heiko Lenk, said that, unlike most other shrimp producers, Bangladesh must still diversify its export markets.

"Today, more than 90% of its exports go to the EU. The primary EU market is price-oriented. Generally, buyers don't ask for quality, but price is eventually more critical even if they do. Instead of creating incentives to invest in the supply chain and processing plants to maintain the quality of the products, the focus on price incentivizes adding water to gain weight."

Without a strong vision from most of Bangladesh's exporters on how they want to build their market image abroad, heavy glazing (adding water around the shrimp) and soaking (absorbing water into the shrimp) have become standard practices, he said.

It is not unusual to get shrimp from Bangladesh with 40% glazing and 30% water added through soaking. These practices are not illegal, but to make things worse, buyers and sellers sometimes agree to apply a glazing and soaking tolerance (e.g., 2-5%) when they label the final product. If mislabeled, consumers eventually get less shrimp and more water than they should. Due to a lack of enforcement of EU labeling regulations, the mislabelling of shrimp from Bangladesh is widespread, according to Lenk, and may be as high as 80%.

title: Canadian province adopts more rules to curb illegal lobster trade
content:
Lobster buyers in Nova Scotia will have to provide the locations and details about all holding and handling facilities they own, lease or use, and will only be allowed to store or handle their lobsters at facilities listed on their buyer's license, under new rules adopted by the Canadian provincial government, reports the CBC. 

The new rules also apply to other fish and require the aligning of processor licenses with Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) requirements. Processors will also have to report the source location of fish and fish products entering the facility.

The new rules are among the measures the provincial government is taking to crack down on illegal fishing.

Recall that Nova Scotia has been lobbying Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) to do more to curb illegal lobster fishing, particularly in Lobster Fishing Areas (LFAs) 33 and 34  in the southwestern area of the province, as reported by Undercurrent News. 

As previously reported by Undercurrent, the province of Nova Scotia enhanced its enforcement activity earlier this year, increasing inspections at lobster pounds around the province, according to Nova Scotia fisheries minister Kent Smith.

In a letter sent to processing license holders earlier in October, Smith said the industry can expect more inspections at processing and handling facilities beginning in 2025. Conservation officers will also ask for records from facilities to increase auditing of processing records.

"It is our goal to actively scrutinize more records in greater detail and from more operations in Nova Scotia," he wrote.

That reporting will now include lobster purchases from other buyers, the location of sales, and monthly information from lobster buyers about the amount of dead loss. Buyers will also be required to record information on dead loss every day.

title: Barramundi seeks legal protections in Singapore as it begins ‘reconstruction’
content:
Singapore-based aquaculture business Barramundi Group has applied to the High Court of the Republic of Singapore for protection against winding-up orders and debt collections as it begins "reconstruction."

The "moratorium order" asks that: 

No resolution for the winding-up of the company shall be passed;
No receiver or manager shall be appointed over any property or undertaking of the company;
No execution, distress or other legal process against any property of the company shall be commenced, continued, or levied, except with the leave of the court and subject to such terms as the court imposes;
No enforcement of any security over any property of the company, or repossession of any goods held by the company under any chattels leasing agreement, hire-purchase agreement or retention of title agreement, shall be taken, except with the leave of the court and subject to such terms as the court imposes.

Barramundi said it requires the reliefs provided by the order to protect it from creditor enforcement action "while giving it breathing space to carry on negotiations for a restructuring and compromise of its debts with its creditors."

Barramundi Group shares placed in ‘recovery box’ as restructure begins

In support of the ongoing restructuring, Barramundi has obtained a bridging loan of SGD 400,000 (just under $306,000) from a shareholder. "The loan will aid the company with operational runway into the moratorium order and finalization of the restructuring plans."

It has applied for a six-month moratorium.

It previously said it was working with its financial advisers KordaMentha on a "comprehensive restructuring scheme." 

Barramundi Group sold its Australian farming subsidiary to Tassal Group in July 2023, then secured a BND 15 million ($11.2m) loan from an unnamed Bruneian financial institution in February this year to expand its operations in the country.

At the time, Barramundi Group said the loan would be used to develop its Brunei facilities, including the construction of a land-based broodstock and hatchery center and the deployment of sea cages at its Pelong Rocks site.

In response to news of the intended corporate restructure, Norway's Oslo Bors exchange, where Barramundi Group's shares are publicly traded, placed the firm's equity in its 'Recovery Box.'

The Recovery Box is a special compartment where the exchange places securities when the issuer faces circumstances that make their pricing particularly uncertain; the stock is then removed from the box once those circumstances are resolved.

title: Canadian-led high seas mission aims to combat IUU in North Pacific
content:
A Canadian-led multi-national enforcement operation to deter illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing in the North Pacific was announced Tuesday (Oct. 1) by Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO).

The mission, labeled Operation Pacific North Guard (Op.PNG), is the second Canadian-led high seas mission to detect and deter IUU fishing in international waters in that region.

Recall that during a 2023 mission, Canadian authorities reported they discovered more than 3,000 illegal shark fins, including from such threatened species as oceanic whitetip sharks, as reported by Undercurrent News.

Led by DFO officers and supported by personnel from the Canadian Coast Guard (CCG), this year's Op.PNG will include high seas patrols, air surveillance and satellite monitoring, DFO officials explained in a press release.

Officers of the US Coast Guard and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration will provide additional support.

For two months, fishery officers will patrol over 7,500 kilometers while onboard Canada's CCGS, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, a high endurance, multi-purpose vessel.

"The crew will conduct high seas boardings and inspection operations under international law to ensure compliance with regulations and to detect IUU fishing," the DFO said in a press release.

DFO enforcement officers will conduct sea and air patrols during a two-month-long Operation North Pacific mission. Image is screenshot from DFO video.

The Canadian fisheries officers will also collect environmental data and water samples to support Canada's understanding of the high seas environment, including the migration range of species of interest, such as Pacific salmon, and the levels of microplastics in the water, the DFO said.

Op.NPG is supported by funding from the Pacific Salmon Strategy Initiative, which aims to enhance conservation, protection, and enforcement efforts in high-risk areas for Canada's Pacific salmon stocks, the department added.

The 2024 OP.NPG also marks the first port call of a CCG vessel to Japan, DFO noted. Canada recently conducted aerial surveillance out of Hokkaido, Japan. Four DFO fisheries officers each completed three weeks of air patrols.

Canadian fishery officers have participated in Op.NPG since 2019. This year's operation involves 20 DFO enforcement officers.

Canada’s DFO details efforts to curb lobster poaching, while minister challenges province to act

"I have the greatest respect for the work of Canada's fishery officers, who protect fish stocks, carry out important scientific research, and safeguard global marine ecosystems. Canada and its fishery officers will always stand up for law-abiding harvesters, whose livelihoods are threatened by illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing," said DFO minister Diane Lebouthillier.

Lebouthillier and the DFO have recently been criticized by the lobster industry in Atlantic Canada over the issue of illegal fishing. Commercial lobster harvesters in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have been pressuring the minister to step up enforcement to stop out-of-season lobster fishing, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

Spot prices for Norwegian farmed salmon were flat in week 38 (Sept. 16-22) of 2024, according to the Sitagri Salmon Index (formerly the NASDAQ).

The index has prices for 3-6 kilogram salmon rising by just 0.6% week-on-week to NOK 72.47/kg per kilogram. In euro terms, it was up 1.4% at €6.15/kg.

Week 37 finally saw an end to six consecutive weeks of declines on the index, and with the flattening out, prices are up 1.3% over the past four weeks.

It's notable that the market is seeing a growing spread between large and smaller sizes, where all categories had been in lockstep just two months ago:

The Sitagri Salmon Index reflects a weekly spot price for fresh Atlantic superior salmon transported from Norway to Europe. It is calculated based on invoices for weekly spot sales to European customers reported by a panel of Norwegian salmon exporters.

The Fish Pool Price Status Report, meanwhile, presents the export volume of fresh, gutted salmon of all sizes, both head-on and head-off (not fillets or frozen export).

title: Canada’s salmon farm transition plan revives concerns over BC’s fit for land-based systems
content:
Canada's initiative to evolve British Columbia salmon farming into what some describe as  "Aquaculture 2.0" has reignited discussions about the province's readiness for large-scale, land-based operations and the practicality of a five-year transition period.

The Canadian government released its much anticipated draft plan for transitioning the BC salmon industry away from its reliance on net-pens on Friday (Sept. 20), missing the July 31 deadline it had established for itself by more than six weeks. 

The government's proposal to end open-net pen salmon farming in British Columbia by June 2029 aims to position BC as "a leader in sustainable aquaculture technology." However, the aquaculture industry is questioning the ambitiousness of the timeframe.

Criticism has also been directed at the plan's perceived political motivations and whether the foundation of the plan is based on scientific evidence. Environmental organizations have voiced support for phasing out open-net pen farms but are pushing for strict regulatory enforcement during the transition.

After much delay, Canada quietly releases BC salmon farm transition plan

"The framework is not supporting an achievable and realistic transition in our view," said Norwegian-owned Grieg Seafood in a statement shared with Undercurrent News on Monday (Sept. 23).

"The five-year period given to transition our operations to closed containment systems is unrealistic, and in the context of the rural, coastal and Indigenous communities that we work with, not responsible," Grieg said.

The company stressed that it supports a transition of the salmon farming industry in BC into new technologies and practices. However, "we are disappointed as there is no scientific basis to this decision and not enough time for the industry to consult on the challenges of this policy," Grieg said.

A senior policy leader in the industry, speaking anonymously, criticized the plan as politically driven and overly ambitious.

"This policy is a shambles ... any reasonable person knows this 'ban' is not necessary and not based in science — it's pure politics," the source said, adding that the plan was rushed and lacked scientific backing.

Dean Trethewey, managing director of Akvafuture Salmon, views the plan positively and said he appreciates the government's support for the sector's shift. However, he pointed out that while BC is an ideal location for floating closed systems, land-based farming presents significant challenges.

He highlighted the energy-intensive nature of land-based farming and pointed out that BC's hydropower infrastructure is still developing, which could pose significant challenges for scaling these systems effectively.

Similarly, Dallas Smith, a spokesperson for the Coalition of First Nations for Finfish Stewardship (CFNFS), raised concerns about the lack of infrastructure in remote communities to support land-based systems.

High-cost hurdles

Their concerns are well-founded based on a 2022 report commissioned by the Ministry of Agriculture and Food. The report, produced by Vancouver, BC-based microeconomist Edwin Blewett, highlighted substantial obstacles to land-based salmon farming in BC, including high initial costs, regulatory uncertainty and inadequate infrastructure.

The report estimated that replacing open-net pen farming with RAS would require a massive investment of approximately CAD 1.8 billion ($1.3bn). Even with this investment, the report concludes that it would take at least a decade to establish a fully functional RAS sector capable of producing at scale, casting doubt on the government's five-year transition timeline.

Economically, the report showed that while medium to large-scale RAS farms could potentially be viable — with internal rates of return (IRR) of 5.8% for medium farms and 8.7% for large farms — these figures are still considered too low to attract the necessary investment for large-scale land-based systems in BC. This adds skepticism about whether RAS can be seen as a practical, immediate replacement for open-net pen farming.

Photograph from Taste of BC Aquafarms Facebook page.

The CFNFS has noted initial satisfaction with the draft plan's inclusiveness of Rightsholder First Nations. However, the coalition emphasized the need for a thoughtful, careful transition that provides business certainty and economic participation rather than compensation. It also expressed disappointment with the unpredictable engagement process and committed to holding the government accountable for a responsible, realistic and achievable transition.

Cermaq Canada, one of BC's biggest salmon producers, acknowledged receiving the draft and appreciated the involvement of additional government ministries in the process. However, the company stressed the need for a thorough review of the plan in collaboration with First Nations partners.

"We strongly believe that our industry has a critical role to play in advancing economic reconciliation in British Columbia while supporting good jobs and a healthy coastal economy," Cermaq noted, highlighting its commitment to a sustainable future despite the challenges.

DFO gives way

Further consultations are expected before the plan is finalized in 2025. These will be led by Ryan Turnbull, the parliamentary secretary to the minister of innovation, science and industry, and supported by an interdepartmental task force, led by deputy minister Sony Perron.

The Industry Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED), not the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO), is leading the transition process.

ISED, a key federal department responsible for promoting innovation and economic development, is tasked with ensuring the transition aligns with broader goals of fostering sustainable economic growth and supporting technological advancements, particularly in sectors like aquaculture.

ISED will "act as a government of Canada secretariat. The task force will be coordinated by ISED. There are no changes to any departmental mandates," a spokesperson for ISD told Undercurrent.

title: Binniker to head NOAA law enforcement unit
content:
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric administration (NOAA) announced Friday (Sept. 20) that James Binniker has been named as the new director of its Office of Law Enforcement.

The office is responsible for enforcing more than 40 federal statutes, including those related to marine conservation and illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing, across more than 3 million nautical miles of open ocean, 95,000 miles of US coastline, as well as in 16 national marine sanctuaries and marine national monuments. It's also responsible for enforcing the laws that implement US treaties and international law.

Binniker, who was to assume his new role on Monday (Sept. 23), served as the acting director of the office from February until July 2024. He previously had been serving as the assistant director since 2022.  

In his earlier role, he led a team of foreign affairs specialists, investigative analysts and special agents. They developed policy and strategic plans to IUU fishing, foreign partner capacity building and support to field personnel conducting enforcement operations.

Prior to joining NOAA, Binniker served in the US Coast Guard (USCG) for 26 years in multiple capacities. His last assignment at USCG was as the chief of the fisheries enforcement division in the Office of Maritime Law Enforcement Policy.

"The breadth of ocean and coast NOAA's Office of Law Enforcement must cover and the number of laws they must enforce are immense; so it's crucial that leadership continue to set priorities and pursue those enthusiastically as we strive to fulfill our sustainability and stewardship missions," said Janet Coit, the assistant administrator for NOAA Fisheries. "With James' extensive enforcement background and incredible level of experience with marine issues nationally and internationally, he will hit the ground running — especially in our ongoing fight against illegal unregulated and unreported fishing globally."

title: Province still waiting for reply from Canada’s fisheries minister regarding illegal lobster fishing
content:
Though illegal, out-of-season lobster fishing continues off the south coast of Nova Scotia, Canadian fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier has still not returned calls from Kent Smith, the east coast province's fisheries minister, reports the SaltWire.

Recall that Smith wrote Lebouthillier on Aug. 22 asking her to beef up enforcement, particularly on the south shore of Nova Scotia, where poaching appears to be rampant, as reported by Undercurrent News. He wrote her again on Wednesday (Sept. 18), noting that she has yet to respond.

"Minister, your lack of communication and meaningful action is sending a strong message to our fishing industry that you do not care, that you are content with ongoing concerns regarding public safety going unanswered, that the future sustainability of our province's most valuable export is not important, and that the economic stability of thousands of Nova Scotians is of no consequence to you or your senior leadership," Smith said in his recent letter.

He asked the federal minister to engage the Canada Revenue Agency, Canada Border Services and other federal resources to help combat the problem.

Meanwhile, DFO enforcement officers were at the Digby ferry terminal on Wednesday, checking a truck known to transport lobster to Maine. The tip-off came from the United Fisheries Conservation Alliance, an organization that represents several commercial lobster fishing groups in the province, reported SaltWire.

Commercial fishermen watched as DFO officers stopped the driver, and inspected the truck at the terminal, and then allowed the truck to continue. 

The driver of the truck told SaltWire on Thursday (Sept. 19) that he was carrying haddock and bloodworms, but not lobster.

title: Peru squid shortage leads to calls for resignation of production minister
content:
The artisanal fishing sector in Piura, northern Peru, together with local authorities have urged the federal government to resolve the shortage of giant squid in national waters, and they're demanding the resignation of several key officials.

The regional government of Piura convened a meeting on Tuesday (Sept. 17) with critical artisanal fishing organizations from northern Peru to address an unprecedented food crisis caused by the absence of giant squid, a vital resource for the country's economy and food supply, according to industry sources.

Giant squid, called "pota" in Peru, is a cornerstone of the Peruvian diet. It provides affordable protein and generates $750 million annually in exports. According to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the species contributes to combat food insecurity in the country.

However, its recent disappearance from Peruvian waters has sent prices soaring, from PEN 3.00-4.00 ($0.80-$1.06) per kilogram to PEN 12.00-18.00 ($3.18-4.78)/kg, making it unaffordable for many local families.

This shortage has been going on for months, with some processors blaming climate change and others the activity of the Asian fleet in international waters, which they said also illegally crossed into Peruvian waters, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

Fishing industry leaders, such as Edwin Houghton, president of the Paita Fishing Vessel Owners Association (APAMARPA), attributed the crisis to unmonitored operations by Chinese fishing fleets.

"Peruvian authorities allow Chinese fleets to operate without oversight and use our ports. Can less fortunate families afford squid at PEN 18.00/kg?" Houghton questioned.

Piura's regional government and artisanal fishing unions are urging immediate central government action. They have called on president Dina Boluarte to declare a state of emergency for artisanal fishing across Peru.

Additionally, they reaffirmed their opposition to Chinese president Xi Jinping's participation in the upcoming APEC forum. They demanded the resignation of several ministers, including also production minister Sergio Gonzalez Guerrero, whom they accuse of failing to address the illegal fishing crisis.

Peru harvesters accuse China of undermining marine protection, declare Xi Jinping ‘persona non grata’

Elsa Vega, president of the National Society of Artisanal Fishing, also known as SONAPESCAL, highlighted that over 300 illegal Chinese vessels have entered Peruvian waters in recent years. Despite requests for these vessels to comply with the production ministry's satellite tracking requirements, enforcement has been lacking.

"We reject any further entry of Chinese fishing boats until minister Gonzalez enforces regulations properly," Vega declared.

The meeting concluded with a warning: The country's major ports will see widespread strikes if the minister does not take immediate action. Although Gonzalez previously announced measures to combat illegal fishing, according to the fishing representatives, no action has been taken.

"Minister Gonzalez has gone silent. If he cannot govern the production ministry, he should step down," said Houghton, echoing the growing frustration among fishing leaders.

title: Europeche praises EU plan to curb ‘overfishing’ by non-EU rivals
content:
A major European fishing industry group has welcomed new European Commission legislation to combat unsustainable fishing by non-EU countries in shared waters.

The EC proposal would strengthen existing regulations, allowing the EU to identify countries that permit overfishing of jointly-managed fish stocks and impose penalties like import bans. Europeche, representing EU fishers, said the plan marks progress toward "protecting oceans and ensuring the sustainability of both fish populations and European fleets."

Europeche managing director Daniel Voces said Norway's "unilateral and unlawful" overfishing of mackerel and cod as a key factor behind the amendment. For years, EU captains have faced unfair competition from some non-member states that disregard catch limits, he said.

"This is a much-needed response to the long-standing frustrations of the European fishing sector...The EU needs stronger, clearer tools to enforce responsible fishing practices and protect our industry."

The group now urges EU leaders to quickly enact the updated measures, aimed at addressing overfishing concerns and promoting the long-term health of jointly-managed stocks like cod, mackerel and herring.

title: Canada’s fisheries minister under fire in Parliament over cod, lobster decisions
content:
Canada's fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier gave as good as she got in a heated House of Commons exchange Monday (Sept. 16) over lobster and cod-related issues.

Conservative members went on the attack against Lebouthillier, the Liberal member who heads the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO), when Parliament resumed after a two-month summer break. 

In particular, Lebouthillier was put on defense over the issue of illegal lobster fishing in the Maritime provinces of New Brunswick (NB) and Nova Scotia (NS) and on her decision to resume a commercial fishery for Atlantic cod in the province of Newfoundland and Labrador (NL).

The opposition members didn't ask for any specific details regarding the level of enforcement by DFO officers in Maritimes lobster fishing areas, and Lebouthillier didn't offer any specifics in her responses. However, the debate saw some harsh accusations and testy exchanges.

"In my riding, there are no DFO enforcement officers on the Canada/US border. Poachers from Maine are illegally fishing for lobster in our waters. They are stealing Canada's natural resources," charged John Williamson, a Conservative member of Parliament representing the riding of Southwest NB.

John Williamson, a Conservative member of Parliament in Canada. Photo is screenshot from hearing aired by Canadian Parliamentary Channel.

His comments in the House of Commons came just two days after lobster harvesters staged a peaceful protest in the NB tourist town of Saint Andrews. The event was organized by the Fundy North Fishermen's Association, which called for Lebouthillier's resignation, as reported by Undercurrent News. 

The lobster fishermen want the minister to enforce the law and protect Canadian sovereignty, Williamson said.

"After nine years of the Liberals, taxes [are] up, costs [are] up, crime's up, and time's up for this atrocious Liberal fisheries minister," Williamson declared.

"She has failed to protect one of Atlantic Canada's most important industries, the lobster fishery. Will she do her job, or will the prime minister fire her?" Williamson shouted.

Canadian Parliament buildings in Ottawa, Ontario. Photograph by DD Images on Shutterstock.

Lebouthillier, a member representing the Gaspésie—Les Îles-de-la-Madeleine, in Quebec, who was appointed fishery minister in late July 2023, was just as feisty in her response.

"Our DFO officers do a very difficult job. They do it every day. But the opposition keeps saying there's no enforcement on our waters. That is completely false. Moreover, it is irresponsible. This work is ongoing," she fired back.

At one point, Greg Fergus, the Liberal member who serves as the speaker of the house, had to remind Williamson not to interrupt while Lebouthillier was speaking.

"If he can shout. I can shout," said Lebouthillier in the last 12 seconds allowed for her reply.

"We are deploying the necessary additional resources to protect our oceans and our resources," she concluded.

The attack on Lebouthillier over illegal lobster fishing continued with questioning from Rick Perkins, the Conservative member for the federal riding of South Shore-St. Margaret's, in NS, which includes the area of St. Mary's Bay, where poaching is reported to be significant.

"Poachers are attacking with shotguns and knives. Meanwhile, Liberal fisheries minister number six lives in denial, refusing to listen to the union while 20,000 pounds of lobster a day are poached through the Saulnierville wharf alone (and) Americans are fishing in Canadian waters," Perkins declared.

Rick Perkins, a Conservative member of the Canadian Parliament for the federal riding of South Shore-St. Margaret's in Nova Scotia. To his left is Clifford Small, the only Conservative member from Newfoundland and Labrador. Photo of screenshot from Canadian Parliamentary Channel.

"Will the prime minister listen to fishermen for a change and call an election so Conservatives can fix the fishery?" Perkins asked.

It's no secret in Canadian political circles that the Conservative party, led by Pierre Poilievre, would like to see the Liberal government fall, forcing an election this fall.

After forming a minority government in 2021, the Liberals signed a supply and confidence deal with the New Democratic Party (NDP) in 2022. The NDP agreed to support the government's budgets until June 2025. However, NDP party leader Jagmeet Singh announced on Sept. 4 that his party was terminating that deal.

Since then, Poilievre has said he would trigger a non-confidence vote as soon as possible, as reported by the CBC. 

That should mean more heated exchanges in Parliament and likely more questions for Lebouthillier.

Lebouthillier also challenged on cod

The third Conservative MP to challenge the fisheries minister on Monday was Clifford Small, who represents the NL riding of Coast of Bays-Central-Notre Dame, which encompasses fishing towns on that province's northeast coast.

He challenged Lebouthillier on cod.

Recall that, in June, the minister declared an end to the 32-year-long moratorium, allowing a commercial fishery for the Atlantic cod stock in fishing zones from 2J on the Labrador coast to 3L off the province's eastern shore.

"After nine years of the Liberals, taxes [are] up, costs [are] up, crime's up, and time's up," Small said, beginning with a mantra that appeared to be a theme leading Conservative questions on Monday.

"This government broke the promise to allocate the first 115,000 tons of northern cod to the inshore harvesters, and they caved to NAFO (Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization) pressure to allow foreign countries back in with 5.0% of the northern cod quota. So this minister, does she work for foreign countries, or does she work for Canadians?" Small asked.

Newfoundland harvesters’ suit seeks immediate halt to 2024 cod allocation

"Our government is aware of the cultural, historic and economic importance of northern cod to the people of Newfoundland and Labrador. That's why after 30 years of the closure, I announced new modern fishing which will lead to a significant windfall for Newfoundland and Labrador, all while leading to well-paying jobs," Lebouthillier declared, adding, "Our government is committed to sustainable, prosperous fishing that will support the generations of today and tomorrow.

You can see the full exchange between Lebothillier, Williamson, Perkins and Small on the Canadian Parliamentary Channel here beginning at 1:11:49.

title: EU dismisses appeal to access member states’ fishing audit reports
content:
The Court of Justice of the EU has ruled that key information on how EU member states implement bloc-wide fisheries rules can remain confidential, dismissing a lawsuit from environmental NGO ClientEarth.

ClientEarth had originally brought a transparency case against the European Commission, the EU's executive arm, for denying access to audit reports detailing illegal fishing enforcement failures by France and Denmark back in 2021.

EU issues ‘yellow card’ to Senegal over IUU

Such audit reports assess if countries properly enforce EU fishing laws and inform potential legal action for breaches. ClientEarth argued the information would allow for public oversight of the Common Fisheries Policy, but the court disagreed.

"We are very disappointed by this judgment," said ClientEarth senior lawyer Anne Friel, claiming it deprives people of basic rights and allows illegal fishing to go "hidden and unpunished." She said transparency is essential for civil society to participate in fisheries policy decisions.

The judgment comes soon after the new European Commission pledged greater ocean protections but dropped fishing discards cases against member states without explanation, Friel added. She urged the EU to deliver on promises to better implement environmental laws.

"The implementation of EU environmental laws is everyone's business -- and increasing transparency is crucial," Friel said.

title: Indian fishers press gov’t to ban pelagic trawling, curb juvenile fishing
content:
Fishermen in Kerala, India's southwestern coastal state, are urging the government to take decisive action against unsustainable fishing practices, calling for a ban on pelagic trawling and stricter enforcement of laws against juvenile fishing, reports The Hindu. 

In a direct appeal to Kerala's chief minister, the fishermen, represented by the Independent Fishermen's Union, claim that rampant illegal fishing in the northern districts is depleting fish stocks and harming their livelihoods.

They claim that undersized fish, which are vital to the ecosystem, are being caught in large numbers and sent to fish meal factories in a neighboring state in violation of rules that regulate the minimum legal size for a catch. The fishermen called for stronger enforcement, urging the government to appoint enough personnel to monitor fishing boats and ensure compliance with regulations.

The union also demanded a total ban on pelagic trawling, which it argues is harmful to the marine ecosystem. In addition to these demands, it requested two months of financial relief for fishermen who are struggling to make ends meet during the off-season.

title: Frustration grows among Aussie fishers as China’s live lobster ban goes on
content:
Australian rock lobster fishermen are growing increasingly frustrated and uncertain as China's government continues to enforce a ban on live rock lobsters, despite earlier promises of a resolution, reports ABC News. 

Aussie lobster co-op goes into retail while it awaits Chinese green light

The trade restrictions, which began in late 2020, were imposed by China's customs agency due to alleged excessive levels of heavy metals. This move was part of a broader trade dispute with the Australian government, and while China has since lifted most of its trade barriers -- including tariffs on barley and wine -- lobsters remain blocked.

It is also the fourth fishing season in a row without the lucrative live trade to China.

In June, Australian trade minister Don Farrell expressed confidence that the ban would be resolved "very quickly," but the issue persists.

On Sept. 12, a Chinese diplomat pledged to allow greater access to his country for Australian products, saying that more barriers for market access will be lifted -- but with no timeline on when, how, or whether that will finally include an end to the live lobster ban.

title: IATTC approves 50% quota increase in eastern Pacific bluefin tuna
content:
Japan's Fisheries Agency (JFA) announced on Monday (Sept. 9) that the Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission (IATTC) has agreed to a 50% increase in Eastern Pacific Ocean bluefin tuna quotas for 2025 and 2026.

The decision, which was made at the annual meeting, held in Panama City, Panama, Sept. 2-6, raises the overall Pacific bluefin tuna quota from the current 7,990 metric tons to 12,585t for 2025 and 2026.

By country, Mexico's catch limits will increase from the current 6,973t to 10,763t for 2025 and 2026, while the US quota will rise from 1,017t to 1,822t.

The decision aligns with the measures agreed upon at the joint working group of the IATTC and the Northern Committee of the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission (WCPFC).

Maersk StarFreeze containers look to ‘revolutionize’ tuna transport

The IATTC's conservation and management measures for bluefin tuna will now include a quota 1.5 times larger than current limits, similar to the measures agreed upon by the WCPFC for larger fish.

Following the WCPFC's decision to allocate an additional quota of 300t annually to South Korea, the same amount will be equally divided between Mexico and the US, each receiving an extra 150t.

This adjustment balances the allocation between the Eastern and Western Pacific management bodies, JFA said.

The measures agreed upon by the joint working group have been adopted in eastern Pacific waters, helping to mitigate one potential point of contention in the bluefin tuna quota discussions set for the WCPFC's annual meeting, which starts on Nov. 28.

IATTC approves two-year extension of tuna management measures

The IATTC annual meeting also focused on sharing and reviewing each country's bluefin tuna sustainability efforts. It was agreed to develop unified enforcement measures by 2026 and to explore the establishment of a catch documentation scheme by the same year.

Conservation measures for tropical tuna species, including bigeye and yellowfin, were extended for two years following the latest resource assessments, which found bigeye stocks to be neither overfished nor experiencing overfishing.

The extended fishing ban period introduced in 2022 has reduced fishing pressure on juvenile fish. The IATTC Secretariat's management project, which monitors the composition and age of catches during purse seine vessel landings, supported this assessment.

However, the stock assessment for yellowfin tuna was not completed in time for the annual meeting. As a result, immediate management changes are not required, but a review of the measures will be conducted if the status of yellowfin tuna stocks deteriorates. The current measures will be extended for two years until 2026.

Bigeye quota for longliners remains flat

For purse seine vessels, the fishing ban period remains 72 days for all vessels. However, vessels that caught 1,200t or more of bigeye in the previous year will face a ban extended to 82 days, those catching 1,500t or more to 85 days, and those catching 1,800t or more to 88 days.

The use of fish aggregating devices will continue to be limited to 340 units per vessel.

The bigeye quota for longline vessels remains unchanged at 32,372t. The breakdown for each nation includes 32,372t for Japan, 11,947t for Korea, 7,555t for Taiwan, 2,507t for China, and 750t for the US.

title: Vietnam tuna fishermen feel pinch as law restricts catch sizes
content:
Vietnamese tuna fishermen are facing severe economic challenges due to new regulations under a new decree that set strict size limits for tuna catches, Saigon Giai Phong News reported.

The decree mandates that tuna under 50 centimeters cannot be harvested, purchased, or exported, significantly reducing the value of local catches. Fishermen report that tuna prices have halved, leading to losses of up to VND 200 million ($8,100) per voyage. Businesses have also threatened to stop procuring tuna.

The Vietnam Tuna Association and the Vietnam Fisheries Society (VINAFIS) argue that the size restrictions are impractical, given that the majority of tuna caught in Vietnamese waters are below the regulated size. Meanwhile, local fisheries departments assert that these restrictions are too stringent, particularly as importing countries do not enforce such size requirements.

The regulations were implemented to combat overfishing and prevent the depletion of fish stocks. However, VINAFIS is calling for revisions as fishermen face potential bankruptcy. A meeting is planned to find a balance between sustainability and the livelihoods of Vietnam’s fishing communities.

The Vietnamese fishing sector anticipated this outcome. In August, during the Vietfish conference, fishing representative Bui Thanh Ninh explained that new size restrictions on landings, including for tuna, meant fishermen would be practically unable to catch skipjack during the key seasons of August and September.

Tuna has driven a 2024 hike in the sale of marine (non-aquaculture) products to the EU in the first seven months, according to data from the Vietnam Association of Seafood Exporters and Producers.

Overall marine product exports dipped year-on-year in 2023 to just under $360m. Some $176m of that was tuna.

title: Seafood New Zealand rejects claims of sector’s ‘greenwashing’
content:
Industry body Seafood New Zealand has contested the findings of a study about "greenwashing" in the country, explicitly rejecting the idea that local companies are engaging in the practice.

A study recently produced by the University of Auckland has raised concerns about the labeling practices of fish and seafood products sold in New Zealand supermarkets.

The research analyzed the labeling and claims on packaged fish and seafood products, such as canned tuna or other fish, vacuum-packed salmon, or frozen fish. It suggests that approximately 80% of the sustainability claims made by manufacturers are vague, raising suspicions of widespread greenwashing in the industry.

The study also raised concerns that the lack of clear labeling and traceability in the seafood sector leaves consumers unsure about the sustainability of their products. While acknowledging that some products, like those with Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certification, offer verifiable sustainability claims, the study pointed out that many products do not meet this standard.

The researchers also pointed to the challenge for small-scale fishers, who may find certification programs too costly to participate in. This leads to a reliance on less specific claims about sustainability.

In a statement, Seafood New Zealand argued that the study fails to distinguish between locally sourced and imported seafood, which creates confusion for consumers and makes it difficult for the industry to comment on specifics.

It emphasized the country's management system, which it said closely monitors fish stocks and ensures sustainability, and encouraged shoppers to trust the New Zealand provenance.

"What consumers need to know is that New Zealand fish is sustainable," it claimed. "We all operate under the strictly enforced and internationally recognized quota management system, which monitors our fish stocks and sets limits for what fishers can catch."

"If you are buying New Zealand brands or selecting New Zealand species from the fresh fish counter or a fishmonger, you can feel reassured that our fishers are closely monitored by independent government agencies, along with the health of the fish and the oceans."

Kiwi seafood isn't always labeled with any environmental claims at all because it is sold at the fresh fish counter or the fishmonger part of the supermarket, wrapped when sold, but with no specific packaging, it acknowledged.

"Adding detailed packaging to this type of fish adds significant expense at a time when we are trying to keep the price of fish down for consumers. We would encourage consumers to talk to their retailer -- ask where the fish has come from. If it's from a New Zealand source, you are in good hands."

title: US shrimpers demand tougher restrictions on Peru, Guatemala
content:
US wild catch shrimpers are raising concerns about imports from Peru and Guatemala, claiming these countries' fishing practices harm sea turtles and create unfair competition.

The Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA), a group that represents harvesters in the US Gulf of Mexico and Southeastern US, and the Port Arthur Area Shrimpers' Association (PAASA), a group that represents harvesters in Southeast Texas, have joined forces to call for stricter enforcement of sect. 609 of P.L. 101-162.

The law provides that wild-caught shrimp or products from wild-caught shrimp harvested with commercial fishing technology that may adversely affect protected sea turtles species may not be imported into the US. 

The SSA and the PAASA are pushing the US State Department to suspend Peru and Guatemala's certifications.

There have been gaps in sect. 609 enforcement, the two groups maintain. For instance, over the past 18 months, the US has imported over $6.8 million worth of wild-caught shrimp from countries lacking proper sect. 609 certifications, including Burma, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Venezuela. These imports potentially undermine American shrimpers, who must use turtle excluder devices (TEDs) to protect sea turtles.

Turtle excluder device. Photo: NOAA

The groups argue that Peru's shrimp industry continues harmful practices, and Guatemala lacks data and enforcement regarding sea turtle bycatch.

Not all bad news

On a positive note, the SSA recognizes recent improvements in enforcement. NOAA Fisheries' "operation shrimp cocktail" has successfully blocked non-compliant shrimp from China and Vietnam, and imports of Indian wild-caught shrimp have declined as a result of India's efforts to adopt TEDs.

Also, since changes to the Harmonized Tariff Schedule in July 2021, the US has imported over $27.4m worth of wild-caught shrimp from Panama, which has effectively implemented TED use, said the SSA. Guyana has also made strides, achieving a 100% pass rate in TED implementation last year and supporting over $16.7m in shrimp imports, it added.

As the 2025 certification process approaches, the SSA urges the State Department to ensure that only countries genuinely complying with sect. 609 are certified. Effective enforcement is crucial not only for fair competition but also for protecting migratory sea turtles from harmful fishing practices.

Support for stricter enforcement is growing in Congress. Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Mississippi Republican, has been instrumental in securing funds for NOAA Fisheries to enhance sect. 609 enforcement. Also, the Senate Appropriations Committee has expressed concern about inadequate enforcement, directing NOAA Fisheries to report on the program's implementation in its biennial report to Congress.

title: VASEP rejects claims of labor abuse in Vietnamese shrimp industry
content:
The Vietnam Association of Seafood Exporters and Producers (VASEP) has rejected claims made by a recent Sustainability Incubator report alleging labor abuses in the country's shrimp industry, Vov reported.

Low shrimp wholesale prices driving labor abuse in Vietnam, report finds

The report concluded that price pressures driven by international retailers and feed companies since 2020 have had a direct impact on increasing unpaid labor in Vietnam's shrimp sector, resulting in human rights violations, labor exploitation and an increasing vulnerability to forced labor.

In a statement, VASEP described the report as misleading, unfounded, and harmful to the industry's reputation.

VASEP emphasized that its member companies, responsible for 80-84% of Vietnam's seafood export value, adhere to both national and international standards concerning food safety, social responsibility, and environmental protection.

The association highlighted the industry's commitment to ethical practices, with over 200 processing factories certified by international organizations such as the Best Aquaculture Practices and the Aquaculture Stewardship Council.

It noted Vietnam’s significant efforts to improve labor conditions, stating that shrimp producers follow the 2012 Labor Code and Decree 45/2013, which enforce worker rights, health, and safety.

VASEP concluded that the report's findings are inaccurate and fail to reflect the industry's dedication to sustainability and social responsibility.

title: Peru harvesters accuse China of undermining marine protection, declare Xi Jinping ‘persona non grata’
content:
Peru's commercial fishing industry association, the National Society of Artisanal Fishing, also known as SONAPESCAL, has accused China of interfering with Peruvian regulations aimed at protecting the country's marine environment.

Over the past two years, more than 300 Chinese industrial fishing vessels have entered Peruvian ports without complying with a critical legal requirement, according to the association: the use of the Satellite Tracking System (SISESAT), which is mandated by a Peruvian decree approved in 2016.

This decree ensures that foreign fishing vessels entering Peruvian ports are monitored to prevent illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing, fulfilling Peru's international obligations under the Port State Measures Agreement, said SONAPESCAL president Elsa Vega.

Following a meeting, in May 2023, between the Chinese ambassador and then fisheries and aquaculture vice-minister Ursula Desilu Leon Chempen, Peru began exempting Chinese vessels from this tracking requirement, Vega said.

Peru faces $300m loss as Chinese fleets operate unchecked in national waters

According to SONAPESCAL, this exemption has facilitated the illegal entry of Chinese vessels into Peruvian waters, contributing to the severe decline of the giant squid population, a critical resource for local fishermen.

Despite production minister Sergio Gonzalez Guerrero's commitment to reinstate the SISESAT requirement by mid-August 2024, no action has been taken, leading to growing frustration among Peruvian fishermen.

The situation has escalated to the point where artisanal fishermen are threatening nationwide protests and have declared Chinese president Xi Jinping, expected to visit Peru in November for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, a "persona non grata."

They accuse China of being responsible for the collapse of its giant squid fishery in 2024, which has devastated the livelihoods of thousands of Peruvian fishermen.

SONAPESCAL has called on president Dina Boluarte to intervene and ensure that the tracking requirement is enforced to protect Peru's marine resources.

Earlier this year, Peruvian giant squid suppliers at the Global Seafood Expo in Barcelona told Undercurrent News that Peru had experienced a prolonged period, lasting approximately nine to 10 months, without substantial giant squid catches. 

According to a supplier, Chinese vessels in international waters were catching the available supply. This source highlighted that the Asian fleet has been unloading giant squid in China, potentially impacting Peru's supply.

Conversely, another source pointed to environmental conditions as a significant factor affecting the giant squid fishery in Peru. Last year, the El Nino phenomenon impacted oceanic temperatures, adversely affecting the availability of anchovy and giant squid stocks along Peru's coast. Several Peruvian sources at the expo said they could not provide market prices due to insufficient raw material availability.

title: Canadian province seeks federal help to kick organized crime out of largest lobster fishery
content:
Canada's largest lobster fishery, off the coast of the province of Nova Scotia, doesn't just have an issue with First Nation groups harvesting during closed seasons. It also has a problem with organized crime, says Nova Scotia fisheries minister Kent Smith.

Harvesters have been the victim of both arson and drive-by shootings in recent times, Smith told Undercurrent News in an interview. The situation is so dire, in fact, that Smith is pleading with the federal government to do more to police the fishery.

"I am hearing directly from fishers that have been threatened, that have had property damaged and that live in constant fear of repercussions for speaking out," he said in a letter sent to Canada's fisheries minister Diane Lebouthiller on Aug. 22.

Earlier this year, sources told Undercurrent there's a lucrative black market in the east coast CAD 2.0 billion ($1.5bn) lobster fishery, making it difficult for Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) managers, who depend on landings and sales records, to assess the health of the stock and determine fishing rules.

Illegal sales also mean lost tax revenue for the country, sources said.

Smith's letter specifically references problems with illegal lobster fishing in southwest Nova Scotia, an area that encompasses Lobster Fishing Areas (LFAs) 33 and 34, which together account for nearly a third of the 100,000 metric tons of lobster landed annually by Canada.

Map courtesy of Lobster Council of Canada.

The letter goes on to reference enforcement issues in other areas of the province related to other species.

Canada seizes major shipment of illegal elvers worth CAD 500k

"For example, the lack of action of your department on the management and enforcement of illegal harvesting of elvers shut down the whole fishery in Atlantic Canada this spring, impacting hundreds of people employed in rural communities and removing tens of millions of dollars from the Nova Scotia economy," Smith wrote.

Recall that, in March, Lebouthillier decided to shut down the elver fishery in Atlantic Canada, saying it was not possible to have a safe and sustainable fishery in 2024, as reported by Undercurrent.

First Nations fight for access

Smith does not reference Indigenous harvesters or the moderate livelihood fishery in his letter. However, the moderate livelihood fishery has been a long-standing point of contention ever since a 1999 Supreme Court of Canada ruling, also known as the Marshall Decision, affirmed First Nations' treaty rights to fish in pursuit of a moderate livelihood.

Following that decision, Canada spent nearly CAD 1.0  billion ($731.0m) buying commercial lobster licenses and transferring them to First Nations. Those licenses are subject to the same rules applied by DFO to other commercial fishers.

DFO also capped the quota for the moderate livelihood fishery at 45,000 pounds annually.

However, some First Nations, like the Sipekne'katik who fish in the area of St. Mary's Bay, Digby County, in LFA 34, have not signed on to the agreements and are contesting DFO's rules that govern the moderate livelihood lobster fishery.

The South Shore of Nova Scotia is a major lobster fishing area in Canada. Photo from Google Maps

The Sipekne'katik First Nation and the Canadian government are now engaged in mediation in an effort to find a resolution on the definition of a moderate livelihood fishery, as recently reported by Undercurrent. A Supreme Court judge has set a December deadline to reach agreement, or else the matter moves back to court.

Organized crime terrorizing communities

However, with the lobster season in southwest Nova Scotia set to open soon — harvesters hit the water the last week in November for a season that runs until the end of May — Smith said there's an urgency to ensure the safety of all participants by ensuring sufficient resources to combat illegal fishing.

"I believe you and your department are not taking this issue seriously, and our communities are paying the price," he wrote in his Aug. 22 letter.

"The inability of DFO to prevent even a portion of the illegal and out-of-season harvesting of lobster in this year over the past years has enabled and emboldened the growth of organized crime that is terrorizing the community," he continued.

FREE READ Canadian officers refuse to work in lobster fishery over safety concerns

Smith noted that, in January 2022, a federal/provincial steering committee was established to address illegal and unreported landings and cash sales in Atlantic Canada's lobster fisheries.

That committee met in April that year, Smith said, with representatives from the DFO, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP), Canada Border Services, Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and the provinces, and identified long-term and short-term actions to deal with the issue.

A sub-committee on policy "has seen significant progress and collaboration," Smith wrote.

But the operations sub-committee, which is chaired by DFO's conservation and protection division, only had its first meeting in June 2024, he said.

"This demonstrates to me that enforcement work is not a priority for DFO and that cooperation on operational enforcement on this issue is not happening," Smith wrote.

Lebouthiller has not provided a formal response to Smith's letter, but department officials offered a reply via e-mail in response to a query from Undercurrent.

Canada, First Nations move to mediation to settle lobster fishing dispute

"Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) is committed to working with Indigenous communities, the provinces, industry and other stakeholders to provide for a sustainable and orderly lobster fishery. As a reflection of this commitment, we allocate significant enforcement resources to monitoring compliance with the Fisheries Act and associated regulations in the lobster fishery," the department stated.

"All fishing activity is subject to compliance verification by fishery officers, who conduct patrols and inspections across all fisheries regulated by the department, by sea, land and air. Fishing activity occurring without a required license or not in compliance with the conditions of the license is subject to enforcement action," said DFO officials.

"As part of this work, fishery officers collaborate with other law enforcement agencies, including Nova Scotia’s provincial Conservation Officers, to address unauthorized fishing activities that cross mandates, such as the unauthorized purchase and sale of lobster harvested under a license to fish lobster for food, social and ceremonial purposes," the department added.

Lobster fishing boats in LFA 34, in south west Nova Scotia. Photo from Nova Scotia Lobster Crawl Facebook page

Over the weekend, fishery officers conducted aerial and at-sea patrols in Southwest Nova Scotia, DFO officials said, adding that the department will "continue to deploy enforcement resources strategically to deter and disrupt unauthorized harvest and sale of lobster."

Nova Scotia government ramping up inspections

Smith said his request for a meeting with Lebouthillier has been declined. However, he stressed the priority is enforcement, and DFO must ensure it has sufficient conservation officers in place before the season begins in southwest Nova Scotia.

"What's paramount here is getting the C and P (conservation and protection) officers back on the water. The illegal harvesting of lobsters is the responsibility of DFO, and without their officers on the water, it's free reign right now," he stated.

However, DFO is facing another challenge to cede to that request.

Recall that some DFO enforcement officers in Nova Scotia have refused to work, citing concerns for personal safety, as reported by Undercurrent.

Canada’s black market for lobster creates data gaps for fisheries managers

Meanwhile, the government of Nova Scotia has instructed officials in its Department of Natural Resources, which has jurisdiction over fish processing facilities, to ramp up inspections at local processing plants to make sure everyone knows that only lawfully harvested products are permitted, Smith said.

The province's justice minister, Barbara Adams, also noted in a letter to Lebouhillier last week that due to an increase in crime linked to illegal fishing. the province is providing funding to beef up policing in the municipal district of Clare, in Digby County, home of the Sipekne'katik First Nation.

The number of RCMP officers at the Clare location has been increased from seven to 14, and the detachment is now operational 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Adams said.

"All costs associated with those operational changes are borne by the province,"
Adams added, while also stressing the need for the federal government to ramp up its efforts as well.

"While we have increased provincial resources in response to the needs of the community, an increased and concerted effort from your department, as well as other federal government enforcement agencies at Canada Revenue Agency and the Canadian Food Inspection Agency are essential to effectively address the root of the problem," Adams wrote to Lebouthillier.

title: Canadian lobster harvesters file suit to stop First Nation fishery
content:
A group that represents commercial lobster harvesters has sued both the Sipekne'katik First Nation and the Canadian attorney general in an effort to stop what it alleges is illegal fishing in Nova Scotia's St. Marys Bay. 

The United Fisheries Conservation Alliance (UFCA) filed its notice of action on Friday (Aug. 23) in the Nova Scotia Supreme Court, also naming Sipekne'katik fishers and chief Michelle Glasgow as defendants, reports Saltwire, an Atlantic Canada news service.

The UFCA is asking the court to declare the First Nation's self-regulated lobster fishery in St Marys Bay illegal and demand regulation under the federal Fisheries Act.

It argues that the unregulated fishery, which the Sipekne'katik launched in 2020, has significantly depleted lobster stocks in the bay, forcing commercial fishermen out of the area and leading to the closure of a local processing plant.

The legal dispute centers on the definition of a "moderate livelihood," a concept introduced by the Supreme Court of Canada in the 1999 Marshall decisions. These decisions affirmed Mi'kmaq treaty rights to fish and hunt for sustenance — a right that the Sipekne'katik First Nation, as part of the Mi'kmaq, seeks to exercise.

While the federal government and Sipekne'katik had agreed to enter mediation on this issue, the UFCA opposes the move, accusing both parties of abandoning a transparent court process in favor of secret negotiations.

According to the report, tensions in St Marys Bay are escalating as First Nations fishers continue to pursue their fishery outside the commercial season, which begins in late November. Federal fisheries officers have recently refused to enforce regulations, citing threats to their safety and a lack of support from their superiors, the report continued.

Federal officials, including fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier and prime minister Justin Trudeau, are in Halifax, Nova Scotia, for a cabinet retreat, drawing further attention to the ongoing conflict, the news service noted.

title: Minister unclear on how she’ll prevent ‘powder keg’ threatening Canada’s biggest lobster fishery
content:
Canadian fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier won't commit to changing course to defuse a "powder keg" threatening to explode in southwest Nova Scotia before the country's largest lobster season kicks off there in late November, the local news service Saltwire reports.

Tensions have continued to erupt in the province over wide-scale unlicensed lobster fishing by First Nation groups taking place out-of-season since 2020, the article recounts. Commercial harvesters have reacted violently in a few instances.

But federal fisheries officers are refusing to make enforcement patrols after submitting Canadian labor code complaints, stating comments made by Lebouthillier that imply they are racist and lack the support needed from top-level Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) brass, according to the article. 

The news service reports that it asked Lebouthillier whether she had plans to defuse the situation during a Friday (Aug. 16) press conference at the Canadian Council of Fisheries and Aquaculture Ministers meetings, held in Prince Edward Island.

"We are working closely with the government of the province," she reportedly responded, speaking in French. "And we will continue. We will continue to work on these difficult areas. What is important for me is to ensure there is peace on the water. The work will continue."

Lebouthillier didn't offer any specifics on what she intends to do or whether those fishing and selling their catch without DFO-approved licenses would be charged and prosecuted under the Fisheries Act, according to the article.
