title: Maldives plans tuna longline fishery reopening with stricter sustainability rules
content:
The Maldives government has announced a new draft regulation for the tuna longline fishery, outlining its intention to reopen it under strict conditions. 

The draft, available for public comment on the country's ministry of fisheries, marine resources, and agriculture's website, includes provisions to ensure that the longline fishery aligns with international best practices and sustainability standards.

The draft regulation outlines stringent measures for the longline fishery, including mandatory vessel locating devices, electronic monitoring systems, and safety provisions for crew members.

Specific areas, such as within 100 miles of the Maldives' baseline and south of six degrees North latitude, are designated as off-limits to protect handline fishing areas and reduce potential conflicts. Bycatch management measures, including protocols for handling sharks and other non-target species, are also part of the regulation.

However, international scientists and conservation groups are raising alarms about the potential negative impacts of reopening longline fishing.

The Blue Marine Foundation stated that the new regulation could threaten the Maldives' shark sanctuary status and impact local fisheries and tourism. Longline fishing, which was banned in 2010 due to overfishing concerns, poses risks to marine biodiversity and the economic stability of local fishers, it said. 

The Maldives Ocean Alliance and the Yellowfin Tuna Fishermen's Union have also launched a petition urging the government and international community to reconsider. Concerns include the potential for increased bycatch of vulnerable species and the undermining of sustainable fishing practices that are integral to the nation's economy and marine health.

"Allowing longline fishing poses grave risks to local livelihoods and food security, as it could threaten crucial fish stocks. It would introduce competition that undermines the economic stability of local fishers whose livelihoods depend on sustainable fishing techniques like one-by-one," said Shaha Hashim, chairperson for the Maldives Resilient Reefs and member of the Maldives Ocean Alliance. 

"Further declines in yellowfin and bigeye tuna stocks could affect the livelihoods of traditional one-by-one fishers, who would face competition from groups capable of catching large quantities through longlines. The draft regulation allows for shark bycatch to be landed, a move that threatens the Maldives' status as a shark sanctuary. Sharks, which have seen a decline of over 70% in the past 50 years, are crucial to fisheries, tourism and ocean health," concluded Hashim.  

In response to these concerns, the draft regulation is being shared with stakeholders, including handline fishers, tuna processors, and enforcement agencies, for feedback.

title: Peru sets deadline for new regulations to combat illegal fishing by Chinese vessels
content:
Peru's Ministry of Production, known as Produce, is on the brink of releasing a pivotal new decree aimed at curbing illegal fishing practices, reports the Latin American Committee for the Sustainable Management of Giant Squid (Calamasur).

This development comes in response to mounting protests from artisanal fishing communities and a severe crisis affecting the squid fishing industry.

Recent demonstrations by local fishing groups have highlighted the problem of Chinese fishing vessels entering Peruvian ports without adhering to mandatory satellite tracking regulations. These protests have underscored the urgent need for effective measures to address the influx of unregulated foreign vessels.

A recent event organized by Calamasur in collaboration with Peru's Scientific University of the South delved into potential solutions to the problem. 

In June, Sergio Gonzalez, Peru's minister of production, announced plans to address the problem of unregulated fishing vessels. He said Produce would soon implement a regulation designed to rectify previous administrative oversights.

A draft regulatory framework was published on July 16, stipulating that, to enter Peruvian waters, all foreign squid fishing vessels must enable Peru's new control center satellite tracking system (SISESAT). Produce is expected to formalize these measures through a supreme decree to prevent illegal fishing by Thursday (Aug. 15).

Strong Argentine squid landings hit Chinese markets

Fishing groups have criticized the previous lack of enforcement of Supreme Decree No. 016-2020-PRODUCE, which mandates that squid fishing vessels use the SISESAT tracking device for at least six months before their arrival in Peru. This measure, enacted in 2020, was intended to prevent logistical support for vessels potentially involved in illegal fishing.

As many as 251 Chinese vessels have entered Peru since May 2023 due to the suspension of this decree, reported Alfonso Miranda, Calamasur's president. He emphasized that the entry of these vessels without the SISESAT equipment "not only violates national regulations but also breaches the Port State Measures Agreement, which Peru ratified in 2017."

Piero Rojas Vasquez, a fisheries law expert, provided insight into the proposed regulatory changes. He emphasized that the new draft requires "all squid fishing vessels, regardless of their purpose for entering Peruvian ports or shipyards, to be equipped with the SISESAT satellite tracking device."

He concluded: "Failure to comply will result in these vessels being denied clearance to leave Peru and resume their fishing activities at sea."

title: Conservation groups sue to force US trade enforcement related to marine mammal protections
content:
Three conservation and animal protection groups have filed a lawsuit against the US government seeking for them to start enforcing rules that block the import of seafood from countries where marine mammals are too often bycatch.

The 54-page complaint, filed Thursday (Aug. 8) in the US Court of International Trade by the Natural Resources Defence Council, Center for Biological Diversity and Animal Welfare Institute (AWI), names a long list of defendants, including: the US Department of Commerce; US commerce secretary Gina Raimondo; the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS); assistant NMFS administrator Janet Coit; the US Department of Treasury; treasury secretary Janet Yellen; the US Department of Homeland Security; and homeland security Alejandro Mayorkas. 

It seeks a court order directing the government to implement the Marine Mammal Protection Act's (MMPA's) mandate to ban seafood imports from countries whose fisheries kill too many marine mammals.

Congress enacted the MMPA in 1972, including provisions aimed at protecting marine mammals from bycatch and banning seafood imports from noncompliant fisheries, explains a press release from the group. But the NMFS did not adopt a rule to implement these provisions until 2016, they allege.

The MMPA "import rule," as it is known, requires foreign fisheries to provide evidence that their bycatch prevention measures meet US standards, the groups recount in their release. The rule initially included a five-year exemption period to give countries sufficient time to assess marine mammal stocks, estimate bycatch, and develop rules to reduce bycatch. After that time, NMFS was supposed to determine whether countries’ fisheries were meeting US standards and, if they were not, the US was supposed to ban imports from noncompliant fisheries.

However, in 2020, NMFS extended implementation of the rule by one year because of the COVID-19 pandemic. And since then, NMFS has delayed implementation twice more, and the ban on harmful fishery imports is now on hold until January 1, 2026, the groups advise.

"The US government has violated the MMPA for far too long, causing significant harm to marine mammals worldwide," Kate O’Connell, senior policy consultant for AWI's Marine Wildlife Program, is quoted as saying in a press release. "It is reprehensible that more than half a century after the MMPA was enacted, Americans are still buying seafood dinners with an invisible side of whale, dolphin, porpoise, or seal. Enough is enough."

About 70% to 85% of seafood consumed in the United States is imported from over 130 countries, including Canada, Indonesia, Ecuador and Mexico, the groups noted. The US is the world's largest seafood importer, with more than $21 billion worth of seafood products imported annually, accounting for more than 15% of the global value of all marine food products in trade.

Implementing the MMPA import provision now and requiring other countries to meet the same standards as US fishers would help level the playing field and provide a powerful incentive for countries around the globe to better protect marine mammals, the groups argue.

The groups are represented by Anderson & Kreiger LLP and by in-house attorneys at the CBD and NRDC.

title: US rejects Vietnam’s bid for ‘market economy’ recognition
content:
In a blow to a potential easing of regulation around seafood exports from Vietnam to the US, the latter's Department of Commerce has rejected Vietnam's bid to be designated as a "market economy," the Financial Times reported.

June sees Vietnamese vannamei shrimp exports hit two-year high

The news site described the decision as a blow to Vietnam, which is pushing to deepen trade ties with its most important export market. Vietnam aims to grow in clout as a manufacturing alternative to China.

The upgrade from Vietnam's current designation as a "non-market economy" would have further boosted exports and reduced punitive tariffs on products such as shrimp from the Southeast Asian country.

The US Southern Shrimp Alliance welcomed the decision, claiming that as a Communist country, Vietnam "continues to enforce laws that prohibit the private ownership of land."

"At the end of [this] proceeding, Commerce concluded that Vietnam continues to be a non-market economy for the purposes of the antidumping duty laws."

The alliance, joined by a large, diverse group of US industries, objected to Commerce's decision in 2023 to conduct a formal administrative proceeding, arguing that the "federal government was wasting time and limited resources in order to curry favor with another non-democratic government aspiring to be a client state of the Chinese Communist Party."

It made multiple submissions opposing Vietnam's request to be treated as a market economy.

On July 24, seven US Senators wrote to Commerce to express their concerns regarding the "damage that would be done to American industries by taking steps to appease the Communist Party of Vietnam," it said.

title: Newfoundland fisheries minister open to discuss crab inspections with industry but warns of potential fallout
content:
Gerry Byrne is open to discuss the approach being taken by inspections at snow crab processing plants in the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador (NL), but the industry should take heed.

Any changes could backfire, he warned.

"The market understands and appreciates that when they buy from [NL], quality is supreme," said the recently named minister of NL's Fisheries, Forestry and Agriculture (FFA) in an interview with Undercurrent News late on Thursday (Aug. 1).

"If we go ahead and amend our regulations to allow for crab, which may be somewhat of lower quality, then we potentially invite our competitors to differentiate themselves from us by saying that [NL] crab is potentially dead before it's processed. And that's not a place I want to be," he continued.

As previously reported by Undercurrent, the Association of Seafood Producers (ASP), the group that represents the majority of crab processors in the world's largest snow crab fishery, has taken issue with the protocols used by the province's fisheries inspection officers, calling them "outdated."

Gerry Byrne, Newfoundland and Labrador's minister of fisheries and land resources. Photo from Gerry Byrne's Facebook page.

The ASP publicly criticized the province's inspection system after Quinlan Brothers, owners of the largest crab processing facility in Canada, was forced to discard about 50,000 pounds of frozen crab legs.

The province confirmed last week that it charged Quinlan Brothers with four violations of the province's Fish Inspection Act and Fish Inspection Operations Regulations in relation to inspections made by officials from its fisheries department between May 30 and June 29, 2024.

The allegations have not yet been proven in court.

It wasn't the first time a processor encountered problems with the inspection process, ASP executive director Jeff Loder told Undercurrent in an earlier interview.

"We've had instances in the last two years where the crab was graded and deemed to be 100% good, with next to no critically weak crab, and then an inspector, a couple of hours later, says the crab is dead," he said.

Quinlan Brothers operates the largest snow crab processing factory in Canada, at Bay De Verde in the province of Newfoundland and Labrador. Photo from Quinlan Brothers website

Quinlan Brothers' side of the story

The announcement that charges were being filed was followed in haste on Thursday with a press conference in St. John's, called by Robin Quinlan, the owner of Quinlan Brothers, as reported by Undercurrent.

Quinlan offered his side of the story regarding the sequence of events that happened when provincial inspectors visited his plant on two occasions this year, once in May and again in June.

Like any other food processing facility that uses raw material -- whether it be crab, a dead fish or a dead chicken -- quality control systems are in place at the plant, and there are inspections by the federally-regulated Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) to ensure that what comes out at the end of the production line is safe to eat, Quinlan asserted. 

He said the FFA inspectors did what they normally do during their June visit, sampling small lots of crab in the holding area of the company's Bay de Verde factory.

"The FFA indicated to our plant personnel that what they had seen was not acceptable and they wanted the crab culled," Quinlan recounted.

The inspectors wanted the company to cull the crab right there, in the holding area, which would involve going through every box of thousands of pounds of crab and assessing each crab to determine whether it was alive or dead before sending it off for processing, he said.

However, tests conducted by Independent Dockside Graders (IDG), a company certified by the province to grade seafood prior to processing, had already determined that 99% of the crab was alive, said Quinlan.

He said the same scenario played out at Bay de Verde, in May, when IDG had determined a load of crab was 99% alive, but the FFA inspectors decided differently.

Quinlan said he was contacted by his senior production people during the June inspection. They reported a "significant difference" in the grading results between IDG and FFA.

"I talked to my most senior quality inspector, with over 40 years' experience in grading crab, and he indicated to me that he was happy with what he's seen," he said.

Robin Quinlan, far right, at press conference called by Quinlan Brothers on Aug. 1, 2024. Image is still from video.

There was actually a crab buyer at the Bay de Verde plant that day and they said they were satisfied with that crab and wanted to buy it, he added. 

"So now we have a problem because we have a request to cull crab and we feel that the results are not correct," Quinlan explained.

The company suggested to the FFA inspectors that the crab could be culled by trained workers on the processing lines, and the inspectors could even come into the plant to watch that process, Quinlan told reporters.

The FFA inspectors refused, he said.

"So, I had a choice to make, either leave the live crab in boxes to die, bring inexperienced people into the holding room and ask them to do something that they're not trained to do, or take the crab and put it on our production lines where experienced people could cull the crab," said Quinlan.

By culling the crab on the production lines the workers, as part of their usual workflow, could sort and grade crab as well, keeping the good crab for processing, Quinlan reasoned.

"And that was my decision," he said. "The crab was moved from the holding room to the production lines."

Those boxes of crab were marked and held separately in the company's cold storage space. The company expected that crab would be tested further to ensure it met food health and safety guidelines, Quinlan explained.

Instead, provincial officials seized those boxes of crab in July, took them to an industrial waste disposal site and buried them.

17 steps to ensure a quality product

There are 17 steps involved in crab processing at the company's Bay de Verde factory, Quinlan detailed at the press event.

Essentially, the crabs are cleaned to remove barnacles and leeches and given a high-pressure wash, then butchered, graded, sorted and packed.

"We cook it, we cool it, then we freeze it. The freezing stage is an opportunity to remove anything else that you feel is not suitable," he explained.

"If you go in the Bay de Verde plant, you'll see approximately 190 people and 65% of those people actually come in contact with every piece of crab," said Quinlan.

Every single crab that is butchered is cut into two sections and, before those sections are moved to the next stage of processing, they are physically picked up and examined, said Quinlan.

Workers at Quinlan Brothers processing plant in Bay De Verde. Photograph by Quinlan Brothers

"Our production people are trained to look at that piece and decide: Is the shell too dark? Are there leeches, barnacles, or discoloration? It's culled for tainted, wholesome or decomposed crab," he said. At this point, you have the opportunity to remove that crab from your pack to ensure you get the best quality crab."

That's no different than the processes used at any other seafood or food processing facility, Quinlan argued.

"You take a raw material, you use trained expertise, quality management programs, quality control systems, inspections by the [CFIA] to make sure what comes out of the end of that production line is what it should be," he said.

The company maintains high-quality standards and, since the rebuild of its Bay de Verde operation in 2017, following a fire in 2016, "Quinlan Brothers has packed and successfully sold 87 million pounds of the finished product in international markets," Quinlan said.

"We have not had one complaint or rejection for tainted or unwholesome or decomposed product," he said.

Byrne: Be careful what you ask for

Byrne told Undercurrent he is willing to have a discussion with the processors and the industry as a whole. However, he said he's not convinced that self-regulation by crab processors is the right answer.

A request of self regulation is how Byrne said he interpreted Robin Quinlan's comments during the Thursday morning press conference.

"Really, what the industry is calling for is self-regulation as opposed to inspected regulation," Byrne said. "If you think through the logistics, the flow of product and how it would be culled by the company itself. I mean, you can't have an inspector on the line in every plant, in every community in operation at every moment. So, really, what the industry is calling for is self-regulated inspections, self-initiated inspections of its own product. That's an interesting concept, which I think we need to have a public discussion on."

As previously reported by Undercurrent, Byrne was appointed provincial fisheries minister on July 19, replacing previous minister Elvis Loveless. It's the second time in the role for Byrne, who held the post from 2017 to 2020.

Newfoundland names new-old fisheries minister

On this latest industry controversy, Byrne remains a bit cloudy on what processors want.

"I got a recap of the press conference. I was left still not completely certain what exactly it was that the ASP was looking for. They really did not describe exactly what it was that they were looking for or what amendments or changes they were looking for," he told Undercurrent.

"But it appeared to me what was really on the table was whether or not dead crab and dead lobster, in the opinion of trained inspectors, should go to a cooker for additional processing," said Byrne.

"I am prepared to have that conversation," he continued. "But we all have to know the potential consequences," he said.

"If we go down this road, we may be subject to criticism. The marketplace may not necessarily react positively to this. As a result, the price that is acquired by our wholesalers and the price that our processors can give to our harvesters may be impacted," said Byrne.

"And I would never, ever, ever want it to be ever said by a processor that, well, because the government gave us a green light to put dead crab in the cooker, we are now getting a lower price from the marketplace, from our buyers, and so we now are passing that on to you, to the harvester as a result, Byrne added.

Byrne: Our enforcement works

Although there are federal protocols used by the CFIA to test finished product to determine that it's safe for human consumption, Byrne indicated having just that one test at the end of the processing stream is not necessarily the ultimate solution.

"That's not necessarily a human health and safety issue but it is potentially … a quality issue. And to pick that up at the end of the processing cycle may be somewhat more problematic," he offered.

"This province has taken a decision in the past that dead crab, or dead lobster, should not then be placed in a cooker and processed."

That's what this debate is currently about: taking morbid or dead crab and putting it into a cooker and then processing it, the minister declared.

Newfoundland processors dumped five times as much crab as in 2022 

As for the possible perceptions created and the potential ramifications for the province's snow crab sales as a result of the very public debate on this issue in the past couple of weeks, Byrne suggested the public discussion on the issue should offer assurances to the marketplace.

"What this narrative, what this situation does describe to the world is that our fish inspection system works," he said.

"When we find alleged violations of our Fish Inspection Act, we act on them. That's where the international marketplace should, and does, take great comfort in this jurisdiction, over places where the law is flouted and ignored," Byrne said.

"If you disagree with our law, you have a right to express your opinion. You have a right to challenge," Byrne said. "That's part of our democracy and our constitution. But while the law exists, you do not have the right to pick and choose which laws you will obey and which laws you will ignore. That's the message to the world, that Newfoundland and Labrador lives by the rule of law."

title: Illegal fishing shuts down Bristol Bay’s Egegik salmon harvests
content:
The Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADFG) has shut down commercial salmon fishing in the Egegik district of Alaska's Bristol Bay due to "numerous reports of illegal fishing activity in closed waters."  

The shutdown, announced in an ADFG emergency order, began a week ago, at 5 p.m. last Thursday (July 25), for harvesters using drift gillnet gear. The use of set gillnet gear was prohibited after 9 a.m. on Sunday (July 28). 

"We were receiving daily phone calls between Fish and Game and wildlife troopers, you know, multiple boats upwards of 50 at times fishing outside of the district," Aaron Tiernan, an ADFG biologist, reportedly told the Alaska radio station KDLG.

During the peak of the season, extra Alaska Wildlife Troopers flood Bristol Bay from around the state, but as fishing winds down, they start leaving to patrol other areas, he said.

"More and more reports come in. Because there's less enforcement going on overall, and we need to try to protect stocks that are going north and south or even into Egegik."

He added: "Efforts that have been made in the past have not changed activities. So I felt like it was time to try something new."

title: China’s distant water fishing fleet faces profit squeeze, environmental pressure
content:
China's distant-water fishing fleet, the world's largest, is grappling with declining profitability and increasing international scrutiny over its environmental and social impacts, according to a new report by financial think tank Planet Tracker.

The report, titled "Fishful Thinking: Solving China's distant-water challenges," found that the fleet's 1,446 vessels analyzed generated an average estimated gross margin of just 14%, with at least 45% of profits coming from government subsidies. 

FREE READ Global concern as India’s push for broader exemptions delays WTO fishing subsidy reform

"The Chinese distant-water fleet is overall in a mediocre financial situation," Planet Tracker states in the report, noting that the most profitable operations like tuna purse seining are state-owned, while fragmented, unprofitable ones such as squid jigging are privately owned.

The group claims that this low profitability is driving some companies towards illegal activities to boost revenue, particularly in the squid fleet off South America. It also suggests that climate change and the World Trade Organisation's Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies are likely to further erode profits in coming years.

Planet Tracker recommends China overhaul its "compliance subsidy" system to better reward transparency and sustainable practices. It proposes China issue a CNY 5.5 billion ($761.5 million) "blue sustainability-linked sovereign bond" to fund implementation of 100% observer coverage and traceability across its distant-water fleet.

"Changing the incentive system is not enough though. There should also be adequate legislation to make sure the spirit of this transition towards traceable and transparent seafood sourcing is respected -- and that legislation needs to be properly enforced," said Planet Tracker. 

World Trade Organization moves closer to final ratification of fisheries subsidies agreement

For investors and companies in the seafood supply chain, Planet Tracker warns of reputational and regulatory risks from association with unsustainable or illegal fishing practices. It notes that US companies have exited supply arrangements with suppliers involved in wrongdoing, including in late 2023 when Chinese processors were accused of forced labor by NGO Outlaw Ocean Project.

Planet Tracker also highlights the potential impact on African coastal states as climate change may drive Chinese vessels to increasingly fish in their waters. It suggests these countries form a coalition to negotiate higher access fees and stricter environmental standards.

"To avoid seeing their natural capital being depleted, African coastal states need to significantly raise their access fees and condition access to sustainability credentials. Forming a coalition could help achieve this," the report authors write.

"None of these solutions are easy to implement, and might sound like wishful thinking to some," Planet Tracker concludes. "But the status quo does not benefit anyone, certainly not the ocean. It needs to change."

title: Japan donates fisheries research vessels to Pacific island nations
content:
The Japanese government has decided to donate one fisheries research vessel each to the Pacific island nations, the Yomiuri Shimbun reports. The aim is to alleviate concerns about the discharge of treated water from the wrecked nuclear power plant.

The Pacific Island nations include the Marshall Islands, Micronesia, Papua New Guinea and Vanuatu.

Japanese prime minister Fumio Kishida will announce the project at the "Pacific Islands Summit (Pacific Islands Leaders Meeting)," held in Tokyo for three days and starting on Tuesday (July 16). Leaders from the Pacific island nations involved will be in attendance.

South Korea signs fisheries MOU with Kenya, Seychelles as it sees African potential

The aim is to support these four countries in independently conducting fisheries resource and marine environment surveys, thereby alleviating concerns regarding the discharge of treated water from Tokyo Electric Power Company's Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant into the ocean.

During the summit, a crucial agenda item will be gaining understanding and support for Japan's scientifically grounded claims while countering China's labeling of the treated water as "nuclear-contaminated water."

Additionally, Japan will provide a patrol boat to Nauru to assist in combating illegal fishing. Nauru's territorial waters and Exclusive Economic Zone are reportedly plagued by illegal fishing, drug trafficking and human trafficking. The provision of the patrol boat aims to strengthen maritime surveillance and law enforcement capabilities.

title: US Homeland Security adds seafood to forced labor priority list
content:
The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is strengthening its strategy to remove forced labor from American supply chains by adding seafood to the list of high-priority sectors for enforcement under the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA).

DHS, which chairs the Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force (FLETF), announced on Tuesday (July 9) that it was updating its strategy to prevent the importation of goods produced with forced labor in China to include seafood, as well as the aluminum and polyvinyl chloride (PVC) sectors.

These industries were identified due to the higher risk of forced labor of Uyghurs and other ethnic minorities from the Xinjiang region, the federal agency explained in a statement.

"Forced labor is a form of modern slavery, and the Department of Homeland Security is committed to eradicating it from our supply chains," said DHS secretary Alejandro N. Mayorkas.

US expands ban on Chinese seafood over forced labor concerns, includes Argentinian red shrimp

"Our department will continue to work closely with our partners in government and with stakeholders across industry and civil society to lead US efforts to end forced labor by enforcing customs laws, supporting economic fairness, and safeguarding the human rights of all," he promised.

Originally published in June 2022, the UFLPA strategy outlines a multi-pronged approach to combating forced labor in global supply chains. The update comes after DHS added three Chinese companies from the seafood, aluminum and footwear sector to the UFLPA entity list in June.

Recall that, in late 2023, a report compiled by the independent journalism outfit, The Outlaw Ocean Project, published in The New Yorker, found Chinese deep-sea fishing vessels and seafood plants employing workers from the Muslim Uyghur minority. They were forcibly displaced from their home province, Xinjiang, to produce value-added products which were then sold to significant customers in Europe and North America, the report found.

US commission urges Dep’t of State, Homeland Security to act on Chinese imports

Chinese seafood processor Shandong Meijia Group (also known as Rizhao Meijia Group was among the companies added to the list last month, as reported by Undercurrent News. The list now contains 68 companies from China whose goods are restricted from entering the US, said the DHS.

US representatives Raúl M. Grijalva, the ranking Democrat on Natural Resources Committee, and Jared Huffman, the ranking Democrat on the committee's oceans panel, were quick to applaud the action.

“As the world’s largest importer of seafood, the United States has a duty to hold the industry accountable for these unacceptable practices and keep tainted products off American families’ dinner tables," they said in a statement. "The [president Joe] Biden administration’s work to enforce a higher global standard for the seafood industry is commendable and we look forward to continuing to work with them to keep that momentum going.”

The Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA), a trade association that represents the harvesters and processors of wild-caught shrimp in the southeastern US, also applauded the latest update from the DHS.

Not all Chinese plants processing Argentinian shrimp on US ban list, large supplier WOFCO stresses

China's processing sector significantly impacts the US shrimp market, the SSA said in a press release, noting that a review of bill of landings data indicates that at least 12 million pounds of Argentine red shrimp processed in China was exported to the US in 2023. This shrimp was sold in restaurants and retail stores across the US without any indication that it may have been packed by Chinese seafood companies using Uyghur labor, SSA said.

"Seafood purchased by American consumers cannot become a vehicle for the Chinese Communist party's abuse of its own people. With today's announcement, US importers are made aware that processing seafood in China, while cheap, may come at a tremendous cost," said SSA executive director John Williams.

title: Canada, First Nations move to mediation to settle lobster fishing dispute
content:
A lawsuit to determine what constitutes a "moderate livelihood" lobster fishery in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia has been put on hold as the Canadian government and the Sipekne'katik First Nation have moved to mediation, reports SaltWire News.

A pretrial hearing was set to begin Friday (June 21) in preparation for a 2025 trial, but Canada's attorney general and the First Nation asked the court the day before to adjourn the entire process to allow them to enter into a "nation-to-nation" mediation.

The court, in allowing the mediation to proceed, gave both parties eight months — until mid-December — to reach an agreement through mediation or have the trial process begin again.

"The mediation methodology discussed by the parties centers on building long-term solutions to the historical issues that have divided our nations," said Kevin Brian Dorey, operations director for Sipekne'katik, in an affidavit to the court.

However, some commercial lobster fishers are not pleased with the turn of events.

"Here we see the federal government opting to exclude us yet again by opting to pursue a secret deal reached behind closed doors," said Colin Sproul, president of the United Fisheries Conservation Alliance. That group, representing a broad group of commercial fishermen, had won intervenor status in the lawsuit.

The moderate livelihood fishery has been a long-standing point of contention ever since a 1999 Supreme Court of Canada ruling, also known as the Marshall decision, affirmed First Nations' treaty rights to fish, hunt and gather in pursuit of a moderate livelihood under the terms of the Peace and Friendship Treaties of 1760 and 1761.

Since the Marshall decision, the federal government has spent nearly CAD 1.0 billion ($731 million) buying commercial lobster licenses and transferring them to First Nations.

Those licenses require First Nations to participate in fisheries during the same seasons and be subject to the same Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) regulations as commercial fishermen.

While some First Nations in Nova Scotia have signed on to annual moderate livelihood agreements with DFO, the Sipekne'katik, who fish in the St. Mary's Bay area of Nova Scotia, in Lobster fishing area 34, have not. Although the fishery is permitted, Sipekne'katik officials have previously rejected DFO's allowable limit of 45,000 pounds.

At a meeting in June, lobster fishers from Nova Scotia's southwest coast urged the DFO to increase enforcement to crack down on illegal fishing, as previously reported by Undercurrent News.

title: Vietnam tuna exports expected to grow by 20% between Jan-Jun
content:
Vietnamese tuna exports are projected to reach $456.8 million in the first half of 2024, marking a 20% year-on-year increase, according to the Vietnam Association of Seafood Exporters and Producers (VASEP), Vietnam Plus reported.

Following a decline in 2023, exports surged by 22% in the first five months of this year to $388 million.

Shipments of canned tuna products, bagged tuna, and frozen loin/fillet increased by 44%, 24%, and 7%, respectively, as reported by VASEP.

Exports of frozen whole tuna nearly tripled, according to the association.

Exports to most markets have risen, with shipments to the US and the EU -- the two largest markets -- growing by 30% and 37%, respectively, accounting for 37% and 22% of total exports.

Exports to Israel, Russia, and South Korea also increased significantly by 64%, 58%, and 66%, respectively.

Speaking at the association’s annual general conference on June 10, Cao Thị Kim Lan, director of the state-owned Binh Dinh Fisheries Joint Stock Company, also known as Bidifisco, noted that in 2023, Vietnam became the world’s fifth-largest exporter of tuna, up from eighth place a decade ago, trailing only Thailand, Ecuador, Spain, and China.

Lan highlighted a milestone achieved in 2022 when tuna exports surpassed $1 billion, expressing optimism that this year could match that record if "raw material shortages" are addressed.

She emphasized the potential of the tuna industry. "We have high-tech tuna processing factories, experienced and skilled laborers, and reputable products that are exported to nearly 100 markets," she noted.

Raw material shortage

Lan pointed out that over 50% of exports are processed from imported tuna, presenting a challenge due to difficulties in obtaining statements of catch at fishing ports.

These statements, issued by competent authorities, verify that raw materials are not sourced from illegal fishing activities.

She attributed the difficulties to issues related to safety conditions and illegal fishing waters.

Additionally, technical errors with the VNPT electronic monitoring system on some fishing vessels cause disconnections from the system for extended periods, from six hours to two or three days, complicating the verification process for buyers.

Lan urged competent agencies to enforce hygiene and food safety regulations for fishing vessels and ports. She also recommended that Vietnam's Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development amend regulations to allow for the immediate issuance of raw material certificates upon unloading at ports under staff supervision.

"In cases where fishing vessels lose connection due to telecom service providers’ faults, the ministry should provide guidance on issuing certificates to businesses," she added.

Buyers could not know these issues when they purchase the fish, she said.

Lan called for the establishment of "a digital input data system connecting fishing ports and the government, providing essential information for the government and ministries to issue appropriate directions and policies."

title: Canada’s black market for lobster creates data gaps for fisheries managers
content:
It's Canada's most lucrative fishery, with an annual export value of more than CAD 2.0 billion ($1.5bn). However, the nation's North American lobster fishery has a problem.

There's a lucrative black market, sources tell Undercurrent News, that's making it difficult for Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) managers who depend on landings and sales records to assess the health of the stocks and determine fishing rules.

It also fools the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), cheating the nation out of tax revenue.

Since last November, a Canadian parliamentary committee — the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Oceans-Pecheries Oceans (FOPO is the official acronym) — has been studying the issue of Illegal, unregulated and unreported (IUU) fishing in the country and has been told how cash transactions are leaving no paper trails.

Canada approves 25 exploratory lobster licenses in Quebec

Canada's fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier alluded to the problem in a notice to fish harvesters in May, at the beginning of the spring lobster fishery. 

"While the use of cash in the sale is not illegal, landings or revenues that are not reported/declared, and which often involve cash transactions, are illegal," she said in the May 7 notice, adding: "From my many visits to the field over the past few months, I know that this is an issue at the heart of the priorities of many stakeholders, both in the catching and processing sector."

Container loads for cash are the major concern

Cash sales are commonplace in the lobster industry throughout the Atlantic provinces.

Typically, harvesters offer their catch for cash to tourists and other locals, usually to fetch a better price per pound or to get their catch to local dinner tables when catches are high but export markets are weak. 

Lobsters pile up in Atlantic Canada

Often, it's not hard to find a lobster harvester offering up a good deal on the crustaceans to locals dying for their first taste of lobster in the spring on such special holidays in May like Mother's Day or Queen Victoria's birthday. There's nothing illegal about that, as long as harvesters keep a paper trail and report it as income.

Not all do.

However, those cash sales are not the main problem, Nat Richard, executive director of the Lobster Processors Association in New Brunswick, told Undercurrent.

"We're not talking about this issue in terms of tourists or locals buying lobster from the wharf," he said. 

The issue is container loads of lobster shipped out of Atlantic Canada with no record of how many lobsters and how much money.

"We're talking about industrial-sized purchases of lobster, paid in cash," said Richard, adding he's been hearing concerns about this for the 14 years he's been involved in the industry.

It's not just the absence of a money trail, but all that missing lobster data that concerns those who do play by the rules, he added.

"It is essential that we have access to real-time, reliable -- and I emphasize reliable data -- on lobster landings. That is absolutely essential to good management of our fishery," he said.

Nat Richard.

It's not that the lobster industry is riddled with bad players, Richard clarified.

"I don't want to suggest that this is a widespread problem," he said. "The vast majority of harvesters are law-abiding citizens (and) they don't look kindly on these kinds of practices."

However, those unreported container load shipments are a big enough risk and concern for the whole industry and "it needs to be taken with absolute seriousness," Richard said.

Lebouthillier's notice to harvesters in May was "encouraging," he said. "I tip my hat to minister Lebouthillier for doing what she did. It's a modest first step and acknowledgment of the problem."

Debate over dockside monitoring

While the industry consensus is that illegal catches and sales are a big problem, there are differences of opinion on how to tackle it. Dockside monitoring was one of the solutions offered to the FOPO committee by a former DFO senior manager.

"Illegal fishing is most often driven by a profit motive — to make money — and occurs in the commercial fishery in primarily two ways. The first is to cheat on quotas or enterprise allocations and land more fish than permitted by the license. This is prevalent in such high-value fisheries as crab and halibut," Morley Knight, a former DFO regional manager and assistant deputy minister, told a FOPO hearing in December 2023.

Morley Knight, former assistant deputy minister with Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans, testifying at a federal fisheries committee hearing in 2023. Photo: screenshot from Canadian Parliamentary channel

"The second common objective is to avoid taxation. This occurs in such high-value fisheries as lobster. While there is no quota to abide by, there is a significant incentive to not report all catch and to avoid being taxed on the income," explained Knight, who now works as a fisheries management consultant.

Lobster is the most lucrative fishery on Canada's east coast, but it doesn't have a program to monitor landings during the season, Knight noted, pointing out that almost all quota fisheries have a dockside monitoring program (DMP).

"Industry may resist, but an effective DMP would resolve most of the current problems in the lobster fishery," he offered.

Canadian lobster harvester challenges constitution, could change rules around Indigenous fishing rights

DFO "should also establish a catch certification program for all commercial fisheries," Knight added.

"More than a decade ago, DFO set up a catch certification office in Prince Edward Island to meet the European Union (EU) requirements for government certification that any product going into the EU was legally caught and recorded," he recounted. "A logical next step would be to implement this process for all exports and subsequently require it for all product coming from a fish buyer or processor, regardless of whether it's being exported or not."

Lobster processors in the Canadian province of New Brunswick don't have a formal position on DMP, but Richard said he believes it's one prescription that could help eliminate the problem.

"I think it would be a very powerful deterrent … but it would take time to build up that kind of capacity," he said.

Others,though, are leery of a DMP.

Logistically, it would be onerous, suggested Allan Clark, former regional director of enforcement with DFO Maritimes, in a brief to the FOPO in January.

"Your committee first needs to understand what mandatory dockside monitoring would look like for inshore lobsters," said Clark, offering the example of southwest Nova Scotia, the unrivaled regional capital of lobster fishing in Atlantic Canada.

Map courtesy of Lobster Council of Canada.

"The inshore lobster fishery of southwest Nova Scotia by itself consists of 1,653 licensed commercial lobster vessels landing at least one fishing trip daily over a six-month season," he said.

"That equates to 1,653 landings per day, spread out over possibly 405 different unloading locations in seven different counties. The scope and magnitude to meet each and every inshore lobster vessel at landing, to weigh out each vessel's daily catch, would be totally impractical, if not operationally impossible."

Clark concluded: "In my view and experience, that's an impossible task."

One alternative to dockside monitoring could be a mandatory, daily, at-sea log, requiring harvesters to record and report the total count and weight of lobsters caught before offloading their catch, he suggested.

To be effective, a reporting system should also have to apply to lobsters caught in the off-season, as well as during the DFO-sanctioned seasons, he added, noting history shows that many of those out-of-season lobsters are the ones being sold illegally and are unaccounted for.

"Lobster buyers and all other persons, including (First Nations) bands, should also be required to keep accurate records of all lobsters purchased, held or stored," Clark offered.

However, on the argument that the lobster fishery is too large to commandeer through DMP, Richard points to another large fishery where it has been a tool.

"We have 100% monitoring of our crab fishery, and that's not an insignificant fishery," he said.

Nova Scotia ups the ante while Canada collaborates

Meanwhile, change is already happening in one jurisdiction.

In Nova Scotia, the Canadian province that lands and exports the most lobster in the country, the government has taken a step to deter illegal sales. This spring, Nova Scotia's House of Assembly adopted legislation to raise the maximum fines for violations under the province's Fisheries and Coastal Resources law.

Anyone convicted of buying or processing illegally-caught seafood now risks fines of up to CAD 1.0 million. For subsequent offenses, the maximum increases to CAD 2.0m. Previously, the maximum fine was CAD 100,000.

Among the illegal activities that could result in a penalty are: buying or processing illegally caught seafood, and buying or processing fish without a license, a spokesperson for provincial fisheries minister Kent Smith told Undercurrent.

"Dumping Day" in Nova Scotia's Lobster Fishing Area 34 in December, 2023. Photograph by Brenda Tate.

"This change is a strong deterrent to illegal activity, and we trust the courts to put an appropriate fine in place," said the spokesperson, adding the province's fisheries department is working with the province's Department of Natural Resources and Renewables conservation officers to support the effort.

"And fisheries and aquaculture continues to make it clear to DFO that we expect them to do the same," added the spokesperson.

Meanwhile, the DFO is working with all Atlantic provinces through a steering committee focused on the illegal cash sales of lobsters.

That committee includes representatives from several federal departments and agencies, such as DFO, the CRA, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Canada Border Services Agency and the Canadian Food Inspection Agency, as well as provincial government departments in the region, said a spokesperson from minister Lebouthillier's office.

Canada's reputation at stake

The FOPO committee wrapped up hearings last month and is now working on its draft report. A final report, with recommendations, could come within weeks.

Meanwhile, the pressure to find solutions is coming not only from within the local industry, Richard noted, but from seafood peers worldwide.

Canada is currently chairing an international coalition of countries to combat IUU globally, Richard pointed out, referencing the appointment of Paul Lansbergen, president of the Fisheries Council of Canada, to the International Coalition of Fisheries. 

Testing of Canada’s Fisheries app in progress as DFO eyes e-logs

So there's the Canadian reputation to uphold, as well as being a credible voice on the IUU issue, Richard noted.

"From the point of view of our global reputation (and) the integrity of our data for the purpose of managing our fisheries, namely lobster in this case, (and) the risk in terms of market access, in terms of certification, it is absolutely essential that both levels of government come at this an intelligent, creative, and forceful manner," he said.

Canada is the world's largest producer of North American lobster, exporting 98,153 metric tons worth CAD 2 bn in 2022, as reported by Undercurrent.

"For a multi-billion dollar fishery, we can't afford to have these kinds of questions around our industry," Richard stressed.

title: Untitled
content:
The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has added another big Chinese seafood processor to the list of companies prohibited from exporting products to the US over issues of forced labor, simultaneously shutting the door on a major source of processed Argentina red shrimp. 

Shandong Meijia Group Co., Ltd. (also known as Rizhao Meijia Group) has been added to the "entity list" maintained under the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA), DHS' Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force (FLETF) announced Tuesday (June 11).

Two of the subsidiary members of the Shandong Meijia Group — Rizhao Meijia Aquatic Foodstuff Co. and Rizhao Meijia Keyuan Food Co. — are active exporters of Argentine red shrimp to customers in the US and Canada.

The DHS statement hints at an expansion of FLETF's plans to zero in more on seafood, footwear and aluminum products manufactured in China with the use of forced labor. 

 "We have shown again through today's enforcement actions that the United States is taking concrete steps to keep goods made with forced labor out of U.S. supply chains," said Robert Silvers, DHS' under secretary for policy and FLETF chair, in the statement.

"It is imperative for companies to conduct due diligence and know where their products are coming from," he said. "The [FLETF] will continue to designate entities that meet the UFLPA's criteria for inclusion on the Entity List, and US Customs and Border Protection will continue its vigilant enforcement at our ports."

Recall that, in 2023, a report compiled by the independent journalism outfit, The Outlaw Ocean Project, published in The New Yorker, found Chinese seafood plants using forced labor, workers from the Muslim Uyghur minority who were allegedly forcibly displaced from their home province, Xinjiang, to produce value-added products which were then sold to significant customers in Europe and North America.

Chinese-processed red shrimp 32% of amount

The Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA), the trade association that represents harvesters and processors of US domestic shrimp in the Gulf of Mexico and southeastern coast, was quick to celebrate the news with a press release issued on Tuesday.

Earlier this year, SSA petitioned the FLETF to add eight Chinese seafood processing plants, including the Shandong Meijia Group and its subsidiaries, Rizhao Jiayuan Food Co. and Rizhao Meijia Keyuan Food Co., to the UFLPA's entity list, as reported by Undercurrent News.

The US has been becoming more and more a fan of wild-caught Argentina red shrimp, importing as much as 31.5 million pounds of it in 2023, though the volume has been slipping since 2020 when the US imported 38.2m, based on a chart created by UCN's trade portal. 

Based on an SSA review of bills of lading and ship manifest data, as much as 12m lbs (32%) of that amount was processed in China, though the country of origin label still identifies Argentina, said attorney Nathan Ricard, a partner at Picard Kentz & Rowe, in Washington, D.C., who represents the SSA.

Since January 2023, over 265 containers of Argentinian shrimp were shipped to the US by Chinese exporters, SSA had advised in its earlier letter to DHS. The product competes for sales against the pink shrimp caught by US shrimpers in the Gulf of Mexico and the South Atlantic, SSA said.

"This wild-caught shrimp was sold as sushi in restaurants and in retail grocery stores across the United States without any indication that it may have been packed in Chinese seafood processing plants using Uyghur labor," the SSA said in its statement issued on Tuesday.

Ricard told Undercurrent that it's unclear why the Argentinian shrimp would travel all of the way to China for processing before being sent to the US. He added that product descriptions used in 2024 have become more vague and made the China-processed Argentinian shrimp harder to identify.

title: Canada investigates lobster trap vandalism in Nova Scotia
content:
Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans is investigating after lobster traps belonging to an Eskasoni fisherman appeared to be deliberately damaged last week near Louisbourg, in the province of Nova Scotia, the CBC reports. 

Charles Francis is one of the First Nations lobster fishermen authorized by DFO to participate in a moderate livelihood fishery. The Mi'maw treaty right was affirmed by Canada's Supreme Court in 1988.

The moderate livelihood authorization between DFO and Mi'kmaw harvesters allows designated First Nations community members to catch and sell lobster during the commercial season without increasing the number of traps licensed in lobster fishing areas (LFAs).

Francis usually deploys 178 lobster traps. However, when he went fishing Saturday (June 1), he discovered that about 70 of his traps had been hauled up and smashed, he said.

"We couldn't believe it. At first, we thought everything was all right in this area because nobody said anything to us and nobody paid attention to us," Francis is quoted as saying by CBC.

The DFO said it is investigating reports of tampering with lobster gear in both the moderate livelihood and commercial fisheries in eastern Nova Scotia lobster fishing areas, particularly in LFAs 26 and 27, which include eastern Cape Breton and Louisbourg.

DFO also authorizes moderate livelihood fisheries for four First Nations in southwest Nova Scotia. The department has said these fisheries do not affect the lobster stocks because the trap allocations come from those that have previously been removed or retired from the same LFAs. 

The Assembly of Nova Scotia Mi'kmaw Chiefs issued a statement calling on DFO and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to increase enforcement efforts.

Eskasoni Chief Leroy Denny said Mi'kmaw communities have been working for years to build governance and management over their treaty right to fish.

"Our harvesters should not have to deal with these continued acts of vandalism, racism and threats to their safety," he said.

"They have the right to be on these waters," said the chief.

title: Chile salmon industry breathes easier following commission rejection of indigenous claim to coastal territories
content:
The Chilean salmon industry can loosen up its shoulders a bit following a vote held Monday (June 3) by the commission for coastal border use in Chile's Aysen region to enforce a prior verdict against allocating over 600,000 hectares (2,316 square miles) of the nation's coastal territories to local Indigenous groups.

The vote, which blocked the transfer of 393,945 hectares to the Antunen Rain community, was broadcast and is available for replay on Facebook. The commission voted against, with 27 votes against, 3 in favor and one abstention, Aqua reported.

The salmon workers' union, known as Multisindicato de Trabajadores del Salmon, Pesca y Ramas Afines (MTSA), issued a statement in anticipation of the vote, expressing concern about the industry's situation and the livelihoods of thousands dependent on coastal resources, News ESEuro reported. 

The organization highlighted two pressing issues.

First was the ongoing deliberations within the Aysen Regional Development Committee (CRUB), where two indigenous communities persist in pursuing over 600,000 hectares.

"These efforts, backed by national and international NGOs, disregard the disproportionate nature of the request and the significant rejection it faced in the regional CRUB vote last February," stated representatives from the Multisindical.

Secondly, the forthcoming CRUB votes in the Los Lagos region, where five requests from the Coastal and Marine Protected Areas Management Entity (ECMPO) are under scrutiny, have sparked conflicts among neighbors, coastal inhabitants and those reliant on marine resources.

While expressing support for Law 20,249, commonly known as the "Lafkenche Law," which acknowledges Chile's indigenous peoples, the MTSA criticized its flawed implementation. They raised concerns about the undue burdens imposed on coastal residents and sectors traditionally tied to maritime activities.

title: FDA escalates Choice Canning shrimp refusals, issues import alert
content:
Choice Canning Company Unit II, a large Indian shrimp processor recently caught up in a big public controversy surrounding its business practices, has now been "red listed" by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). 

The company is identified on FDA Import Alert 16-129, issued May 20 and titled "Detention Without Physical Examination of Seafood Products Due to Nitrofurans." The document represents an escalation of earlier reports by the FDA that Choice was one of at least three Indian companies and one Chinese business for which it had stopped 15 shrimp import lines chiefly over adulteration-related concerns in early April, as reported by Undercurrent News. 

Choice had attempted to excuse itself from the matter by saying, in April, that the shrimp flagged by the FDA as coming from its factory was instead processed and shipped by another company, Alpha Marine, that was using a facility previously leased by Choice, as also reported by Undercurrent.

Choice Canning says FDA shrimp refusals were for another Indian packer

Choice has attracted significant US scrutiny in recent months after Joshua Farinella, a former general factory manager turned whistleblower, made allegations that it had been responsible for instances of labor abuse, antibiotic fraud and deliberately misleading auditors at its factory in Amalapuram, Andhra Pradesh, as has been reported by the independent journalism outfit Outlaw Oceans. Choice Canning has strongly denied these claims.

The recent FDA import alert places Choice alongside 12 other Indian shrimp processing companies facing scrutiny for their shipments to the US.

The red list identifies companies whose seafood products may contain unapproved drugs. If a company's products are on this list, the FDA can hold their shipments at the border without physically examining them. Shrimp products, followed by tilapia, have surfaced as the top seafood categories on the FDA's red list due to concerns regarding drug residues and other regulatory violations.

An overhead view of the Bapatla, India,shrimp processing factory in March 2024. Credit: Choice Canning

Having an entry line refused doesn't automatically mean a company is red listed, Nathan Rickard, a partner at the law firm Picard Kentz & Rowe LLP, clarified to Undercurrent in a recent interview. He said the federal agency retains the discretion to decide whether to escalate the matter.

Nitrofurans are a type of antibiotic used to help get rid of bacterial infections in both people and animals, as noted by the FDA, Rickard explained. The US agency treats nitrofurans separately from the general catch-all import alert for veterinary drug residues in seafood (Import Alert # 16-124).

"Having a dedicated import alert just for nitrofurans shows that the FDA has singled out this antibiotic as a unique concern, warranting its own focused regulations and enforcement approach separate from other drugs covered under the general catch-all alert," he told Undercurrent.

Choice Canning responds

Jacob Jose, vice president of sales & procurement at Choice Canning in New York, was adamant in his discussion with Undercurrent on Tuesday (May 28) that the most recent FDA action is not an additional news development. He asserted that being placed on an import alert is "automatic" following an FDA product refusal. 

However, the timing of FDA's import alert announcements versus its refusals seems to back up Rickard's explanation that these are separate actions. The federal agency publicly listed refusals of shrimp entry lines from three Indian exporters -- Choice Canning Company Unit II, Kader Exports Unit 5 and B-One Business House Pvt Ltd – in May for actions taken in April. 

Of these three, Kader Exports Unit 5 was placed under Import Alert 16-129 for nitrofurans in its shrimp on April 1, 2024 and Choice Canning was later added to to this same import alert on May 20. But B-One Business House Pvt Ltd, which had a shrimp entry line refused due to nitrofurans on April 2, is not yet listed on Import Alert 16-129.

The FDA's website details the process for red-listing firms or products on an import alert. Violation information and recommendations for placement on import alert are sent to the Division of Import Operations (DIO) and the Center for Food Safety and Applied Nutrition. Once this information is received, "DIO and possibly the Center will determine whether there is sufficient evidence to add the firm/product to an import alert," the agency said.

Photo from Choice Canning's LinkedIn page

Jose also asserted that being listed on the import alert has not impacted Choice Canning's business or reputation. It only affects the specific factory/address listed, and not Choice Canning as a whole, he said.

He said he has sent documents about the situation to all of his company's customers to help them understand that the matter was related to a factory Choice stopped using after September 2023. Choice canceled its FDA registration for the targeted plant on the date it found out about the import refusal, he said.

Since the import alert was specific to that factory address, Choice's name would remain associated with it even though the company no longer had any connection to or control over the factory going forward, he said.

If Choice were still using that plant, the company could file a petition with the FDA to have it removed from the import alert after having 5-10 shipments pass consecutively, Jose said. Choice will not pursue such a petition because it earlier canceled its FDA registration for the factory, he said.  

Why the 'green list' approach is better

The Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA), a group that represents the harvesters and processors of domestic, wild-caught shrimp, declared in May that the latest case involving Choice casts a spotlight on what it believes is a failed approach by the FDA to curb the importation of shrimp containing antibiotics.  

At the heart of the criticism is the FDA's heavy reliance on "red lists" of banned exporters rather than implementing more comprehensive "green lists."

Regarding the red list, Rickard noted the lack of transparency in the FDA's updates. He said the FDA updates the red list on an ad-hoc basis, with no regular schedule. The only way to know if a company has been removed from an import alert list is if it just disappears from that list, indicating it took the steps to demonstrate to the FDA that it has addressed veterinary drug residues in its seafood, he said.

"You don't know if an exporter is working to get off the import alert and not succeeding and you don't know if they're not trying, potentially making their shipments under a different name or through a different company. You only know if they're removed because then they just disappear from that import alert," said Rickard.

An FDA inspector in Los Angeles, California, one of about 400 FDA investigators across the country

The "green list," by contrast, identifies companies that have proactively demonstrated compliance with FDA regulations before their products reach US ports. The SSA has argued that if the FDA more commonly adopted the green list approach, such incidents could be minimized.

Green list shifts the burden of proof to suppliers by requiring them to demonstrate safety compliance for approval to export. This approach would place the responsibility on foreign suppliers and create strong incentives for eliminating problematic antibiotic use from their supply chains, explained Rickard.

However, the FDA has resisted calls to move towards great use of the green list for major shrimp supplying countries like India and Vietnam. The FDA's stance is rooted in its current regulatory framework, which allows for country or region-wide import alerts based on evidence of non-compliance.

Another concern noted about the FDA is its limited antibiotic screening of less than 0.1% of imported shrimp shipments. Seafood import opponents have requested increased testing at ports.

US shrimpers file request with CBP to ban Indian imports made with ‘forced labor’

In an email interview with Undercurrent, an FDA spokesperson cited the large import volumes that make comprehensive testing infeasible. The spokesperson said the agency has already ramped up its sampling of imported shrimp in recent years, concentrating on the biggest exporters. The FDA also uses advanced technology to better target and utilize its resources for these inspections.

The FDA currently has about 400 trained investigators across the country who handle inspections and activities related to import operations, the spokesperson said. These investigators may specialize in specific types of inspections or perform a variety of tasks based on their location and training.

Additionally, the FDA works closely with importers and brokers to determine the most convenient times and locations for sampling and examination.

title: NGOs threaten legal action over trawling in Mediterranean protected areas
content:
Environmental NGOs Bloom and ClientEarth said they are ready to launch legal action against the French government unless it enforces a Europe-wide ban on "destructive" fishing practices in marine protected areas (MPAs) in the Mediterranean.

Despite EU regulations prohibiting bottom trawling in MPAs, they claim France continues to allow these activities, undermining marine conservation efforts.

The NGOs want France to revise three decrees authorizing bottom trawling in certain French MPAs, which they say should be banned.

The 2006 EU regulation bans bottom trawling, pelagic trawling, purse seining, and dredging in MPAs with vulnerable habitats like seagrass meadows and coral reefs.

Given the "catastrophic state" of marine ecosystems in the Mediterranean, they said this regulation is vital. According to the two NGOs, 95% of MPAs are no more regulated than adjacent waters.

As France prepares to host the United Nations Conference on the Oceans in June 2025, Bloom and ClientEarth have demanded the revision of decrees permitting bottom trawling in French MPAs.

"The fact that France is allowing trawlers to fish in protected areas that should be closed to trawling is a scandal. The European legal framework is not being respected," said Nils Courcy, a legal expert at ClientEarth.

Swann Bommier of Bloom urged president Emmanuel Macron to align his actions with his environmental rhetoric.

According to the two organizations, a "win would set a precedent for protected areas all over the EU."

title: BC First Nation says new marine protected area is working to stop herring, geoduck harvests
content:
The Kitasoo Xai'xais First Nation of British Columbia reports that the marine protected area (MPA) it started two years ago -- the world's first initiated by an indigenous group -- is working to halt the commercial fishing of herring spawn and geoducks.

The Kitasu Bay MPA was created in June 2022 after more than three decades of persistent advocacy by the First Nation's leadership, both hereditary and elected, to Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) and the fishing industry, the tribe's stewardship office, the Kitasu-Xai'xais Stewardship Authority (KXSA), told Undercurrent News in a recent interview. 

Kitasu Bay, once a bustling hub for commercial fishing, has seen a transformation in commercial and recreational fisheries since the MPA's establishment, said Santana JL Edgar, KXSA's marine planning coordinator. The area is crucial for the herring spawn, an essential part of the local marine ecosystem. 

The MPA regulations now allow for spawn on kelp (SOK) fisheries. SOK is harvested, processed and packaged for Asian markets while allowing the herring to return and spawn again the following year.

Herring spawn. Photo: Pacific Herring Spawn Reporting Facebook page

Furthermore, the MPA has led to an agreement among geoduck fishers to cease harvesting in Kitasu Bay, recognizing the importance of preserving this marine area.

Edgar said the enforcement of the MPA by Kitasoo Xai'xais First Nation's "guardian watchmen" has been pivotal in eliminating unauthorized commercial fishing activities.

Regular patrols also protect against the illegal harvest of halibut, rockfish and coldwater shrimp. And, while the MPA allows for limited recreational fishing activities, such as shrimp and red sea urchin fishing, Edgar said these activities' impact on the bay's ecosystem remains minimal.

A coastal guardian watchman (left) upholds and enforces traditional and contemporary Indigenous laws and works with Parks Canada in ensuring resources are sustainably managed. Photo: Kitasoo Xai'xais/Moonfish Media

Industrial activities, like forestry and mining, are also banned in the MPA, as is the use of drones unless specifically allowed by the KXSA. Sewage may not be discharged into the waters.

During sensitive times like the herring season -- a springtime spectacle where female fish release eggs, which are then fertilized by males -- visitor access is limited, and hunting of wildlife is banned.

Specific zones have been set up where activities, like anchoring and land access, are controlled to maintain the area's ecological health. All visitors must follow these zones and get permission from KXSA for certain activities, promoting respect and responsibility towards nature, said Edgar.

Kitasu Bay, in April 2024, became one of only 30 MPAs to meet the standards necessary to be recognized as a "blue park" by the Marine Conservation Institute, a 25-year-old, Seattle, Washington-based organization.

Kitasu Bay MPA. Source: Kitasoo Xai'xais /Moonfish Media

With 517 band members, the Kitasoo Xai'xais First Nation -- located in Klemtu on BC's central coast, 500 kilometers north of Vancouver -- is one of 17 Indigenous groups in the province engaged in salmon farming. It embarked on salmon aquaculture in the 1980s, and its partnership with Mowi began in 1998.

title: Pew urges IOTC to reignite stalled tuna harvest control rule talks
content:
In anticipation of the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC) meeting next week, international NGO the Pew Charitable Trusts has emphasized the need for parties to adopt sustainability rules for skipjack tuna and swordfish fisheries, and to reignite stalled efforts to develop a harvest strategy for yellowfin tuna.

Yellowfin prices on the rise amid slow catches as IOTC meeting approaches

The IOTC is having its annual meeting on May 13-17 in Bangkok, Thailand. Some stakeholders already gathering this week in Thailand to discuss key agenda items, according to Pew.

Highlighting the NGO's priorities for the meeting, Glen Holmes, senior officer at Pew, wrote in an opinion piece that a key proposal at the forefront of discussions is the adoption of a management procedure (MP) for Indian Ocean swordfish, put forth by Australia, which aims to maintain the current healthy population of this species for years to come.

The implementation of such a procedure not only ensures the sustainability of swordfish but also sets a precedent for other regional fisheries management organizations (RFMOs) to follow suit with their non-tuna species, according to Holmes.

He noted that, despite the IOTC being responsible for overseeing a wide range of highly migratory species beyond just tuna, it hasn't worked much so far to improve the management of stocks such as swordfish, Spanish mackerel and billfishes.

"But that could change soon," he said. "The Indian Ocean swordfish population is healthy and the management procedure proposed by Australia would keep it that way for many years to come," he wrote. 

Glen Holmes, senior officer for international fisheries at the Pew Charitable Trusts Australia. He helps lead Pew’s international fisheries project, where he focuses on engagement in regional fisheries management organizations (RFMOs) across the Indo-Pacific, including three of the world’s five tuna RFMOs: the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission, the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission, and the Convention for the Conservation of Southern Bluefin Tuna.

Holmes pointed to the IOTC's adoption of the world's first MP for bigeye tuna in 2022 as evidence of the Commission's readiness to embrace innovative management strategies. The adoption of the swordfish MP would build upon this momentum and demonstrate a firm commitment to sustainable fisheries management, he said.

Nevertheless, Holmes highlighted persistent concerns regarding the management of skipjack and yellowfin tunas within the Indian Ocean. Despite previous efforts to implement harvest control rules (HCRs), member states have consistently exceeded catch limits, indicative of ineffective management. Proposals from the EU to expand HCRs into fully specified MPs for skipjack tuna are welcomed, but a comprehensive approach must also address "equitable" catch distribution to ensure the sustainability of skipjack fisheries, he said.

Moreover, urgent action is required for yellowfin tuna, which has been classified as overfished since 2015. Holmes stressed the need to end yearly negotiations on catch limits and swiftly implement measures to curtail overfishing, including developing and adopting a robust management procedure.

"Managers should end yearly negotiations of yellowfin catch limits, immediately reduce those limits to end overfishing and fast-track the development and adoption of a management procedure," Holmes said.

In addition to improved management procedures, Holmes advocated for enhanced vessel monitoring and inspection practices across IOTC's jurisdiction. While vessel monitoring systems (VMS) are mandated for many boats, inconsistent reporting and inadequate enforcement hinder effective monitoring and contribute to illegal fishing activities, according to Holmes. Pew called for a concerted effort to standardize VMS practices and expedite centralized reporting to bolster enforcement capabilities.

Furthermore, the introduction of a high seas boarding and inspection scheme, proposed by the EU, India, and Seychelles, aims to strengthen the monitoring and surveillance of fishing vessels within IOTC's convention area, according to Pew.
