title: Peru fishery sector began 2024 with sharp decline in anchovy landings
content:
Peru's fishing sector witnessed a significant downturn in landings during the first two months of the year, with a total of 346,400 metric tons, marking a 64.2% decrease year-on-year, based on data published by the country's ministry of production, known as Produce.

The decline can largely be attributed to reduced landings of anchovy aimed for indirect human consumption (IHC), which dropped by 41.4% y-o-y to 123,300t. Additionally, there was a notable reduction in landings aimed at direct human consumption (DHC), which fell by 40.9% to 223,000t. 

In terms of value, fish landings between January and February amounted to PEN 545.1 million ($144.7m), down 28.5% y-o-y. 

The drop is also attributable to the above-mentioned drop in landings for IHC, which recorded PEN 18.6m less, and in landings for DHC, which recorded PEN 73.3m less in the first two months of the year.

"Notably, February 2024 witnessed a complete absence of anchovy fishing in the north-central zone due to the enforcement of the summer reproductive ban," Produce explained in a report.

"Furthermore, in the southern zone, the beginning of the first fishing season of 2024 was withheld owing to a substantial presence of juveniles, underscoring the sector's commitment to sustainable fishing practices," it added. 

However, despite this rough start to the year, Jose Arista, the country's minister of economy and finance, recently reported a recovery in landings in April due to better weather conditions and the start of the first anchovy fishing season in the southern zone.

"Following improved conditions post-El Nino, the anchovy fishing season that commenced in mid-April is expected to be highly favorable. As of April 25, 530,000t of anchovy have been recorded, compared to a mere 6,000t for the entire April 2023," he remarked on Twitter.

 

Regarding fishing destined for DHC, out of the 223,000t landed, around 47.4% was allocated to the production of frozen products, 36.9% for fresh consumptions, 13% for canned production and 3.7% for cured products. 

Fishing landings intended for the production of frozen products recorded a volume of 105,700 between January and February, representing a significant decrease of 147,000t (down 58.2%) compared to the same month in the previous year. This sharp reduction was primarily attributed to the dwindling supply of squid, with its volume plummeting by some 79.7% y-o-y to 31,200t.

Furthermore, in the fishing industry for canned products, there was an intake of 28,900t, a volume lower by 23,700t (down 45%). This decline was predominantly influenced by the decreased intake of anchovy, mackerel, horse mackerel, abalone, and tuna.

Landings aimed at fresh consumption amounted to 82,300t in the first two months of the year, signifying a slight 1.5% increase y-o-y. 

According to Produce, this was mainly influenced "by an increase in landings of species such as bonito tuna, mahi mahi, mackerel and squid aimed for fresh consumption, offsetting a drop in supply of resources such as shrimp, horse mackerel or hake," it concluded.

title: Tri Marine attains MSC label for skipjack tuna in the Eastern Pacific
content:
Fishing firm Tri Marine has attained earlier this year the arine Stewardship Council (MSC) certification for skipjack tuna in the Eastern Pacific for its Spanish and Ecuadorian fleet.

Tri Marine said on World Tuna Day that securing the MSC certification for skipjack caught in the Eastern Pacific represented a "significant sustainability milestone" for its Spanish and Ecuadorian fleet, and subsidiaries Atunera Dularra and Conservas Isabel Ecuatoriana. This certification was obtained as part of AGAC's four oceans integral purse seine tropical tuna fishery. It applies to all skipjack caught within the Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission (IATTC).

The fleet has already obtained certification for skipjack, bigeye, and yellowfin in the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission area, as well as yellowfin in the IATTC, according to the firm.

Tri Marine expects to include bigeye in the certification scope by August, it said.

"Upon completion, all tuna caught by the fleet will be eligible for MSC certification, further solidifying Tri Marine's commitment to sustainable practices," it said.​

To achieve MSC certification for skipjack in the IATTC, the fleet initiated a fisheries improvement project in 2016 and then undertook an MSC pre-assessment in 2019. The fishery then moved into MSC full assessment in 2020. Yellowfin received full certification in 2021, followed by skipjack in 2024.​

Tri Marine said IATTC enforces some of the world's "most effective tuna management measures", including fleet capacity restrictions, a 72-day fisheries closure period, limits on bigeye catches, and fish aggregating device-management requirements.

The fleet, owned by Atunera Dularra and Conservas Isabel Ecuatoriana, consists of two Spanish and two Ecuadorian-flagged large-scale purse seiners operating in the Eastern and Central Pacific. Annually, they catch approximately 30,000 metric tons of tuna, with the volume processed by both Seafman and Conservas Isabel Ecuatoriana in Manta, Ecuador.

All four vessels maintain strict compliance with 100% observer coverage overlayed with voluntary electronic monitoring. The fleet employs 187 crew members and is owned by Bolton under Tri Marine's management.​

Meanwhile, industry association Ecuador's Tuna Conservation Group, also known as Tunacons, of which Tri Marine is a member, together with Nirsa, Eurofish, Marbelize, Grupo Jadran, and Servigrup, is organizing an event on World Tuna Day to underscore its commitment to sustainability. Tunacons represents the largest MSC-certified tuna fishery in the Eastern Pacific Ocean.

Tunacons achieved the MSC certification for its skipjack fishery last year, just over a year after obtaining the certification for its yellowfin catches.

Ecuador is the second largest tuna exporter globally. Its tuna industry plays a significant role in its economy through export revenue, contributing over $1.3 billion annually to the country's economic development.

The capture and processing of tuna also hold profound social importance, providing over 250,000 stable jobs in both industrial and artisanal fishing, according to Tunacons. This employment impacts more than a million people when considering families dependent on this industry.

title: Russian crab tycoon sentenced in absentia over contract killing
content:
A Russian regional court has sentenced a crab tycoon to 17 years imprisonment,  despite claims of the defendant's earlier death in London, the UK.

On April 26, the Primorsky Regional Court of Russia's Far Eastern Primorie region sentenced Oleg Kan, once known as the "crab king," in absentia for his connections to a contract killing.

Kan was sentenced in accordance with part three of article 33 and paragraph "H" of article 105 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation, state-backed news channel TASS reported. The court also ruled that the defendant would have to pay compensation for moral damage of RUB 3 million ($32,563) to each of the five claimants.

Kan was earlier charged with complicity in the contract killing of another crab businessman, Valery Phidenko, who was allegedly plotting in turn to murder Kan. In October 2010, Phidenko was shot three times and killed by a contract hitman near the "Three Heroes" restaurant in Vladivostok. These charges against Kan were filed in absentia because the defendant fled Russia on a private jet.

On April 26, 2024, Kan's defense team pledged to appeal the verdict. Konstantin Trapaidze, one of Kan's lawyers, told journalists in Vladivostok that anyone has the right to a fair trial, regardless of whether a person is alive or dead.

During court hearings last month, legal representatives of Kan requested that the court close the case as they claimed that the defendant had died in the UK in 2023.

In a ruling released on April 3, the Arbitration Court of Primorie region refused to accept information on Kan’s death as evidence as it was based on the death certificate issued in the UK; specifically, by Cromwell Hospital, London. The court determined that the certificate also "did not contain information that would allow it to be reliably established that it was Kan's body that was sent for cremation."

Earlier this month, a local commercial court ruled in favor of repossessing Kan’s assets.

On April 16, the Arbitration Court of Primorie region authorized bailiffs to repossess his crab assets. The public record indicated that Kan's former assets -- including Primorie Fishery Company, SevRybFlot, Moneron, Kuril Universal Complex, Aquamarin and Priboi-T -- were recorded as the property of the Federal Agency for State Property Management (also known as Rosimushchestvo).

Moneron and Kuril Universal Complex used to be Kan's top-performing crab assets. In 2023, Moneron reported RUB 2.3 billion in net profit, while Kuril Universal Complex's net profit was reported at RUB 2bn.

Earlier this year, Russian authorities started legal procedures to seize the sizable assets of Far Eastern Russia's crab businesses. On Jan. 23, the Prosecutor General's office filed a lawsuit requesting the annulment of crab quotas and seeking damages from companies as well as individuals, including Oleg Kan, totaling RUB 358.7bn, or almost $4bn.

Companies allegedly controlled by Kan had the right to catch more than 8,000 metric tons per year of crab quotas.

Russian law enforcement agencies accused Kan in August 2023 of complicity in the smuggling of 3,000t of crab out of the country between 2014 and 2019, so as to dodge the applicable export duties and taxes.

title: Russia commences seizure of almost $4bn in crab assets
content:
Russian authorities have begun the process of repossessing Far Eastern crab assets worth nearly $4 billion, including quotas amounting to nearly one-tenth of the country's total allowable catch.

On April 16, the Arbitration Court of Russia's Far Eastern Primorie region authorized bailiffs to repossess more crab assets following a court ruling earlier this month, after the Fifth Arbitration Court of Appeal turned down a series of appeals filed by defendants earlier in the month.

Death of Russian ‘crab king’ cited as defense in $4bn lawsuit

Previously, in 2024, Russian authorities began legal procedures to seize sizable Far Eastern assets of Russian crab businesses on the grounds that the companies holding them were ultimately foreign-owned.

On Jan. 23, the Prosecutor General's office filed a lawsuit requesting the annulment of crab quotas and seeking damages from companies as well as individuals -- including Russia's former "crab king," Oleg Kan, for whom lawyers have tried to argue death as a defense -- totaling RUB 358.7 billion ($3.8bn).

Another lawsuit sought to annul crab quotas owned by businessman Dmitry Dremlyuga and damages from these companies as well as individuals totaling RUB 17.4bn.

According to the lawsuit, companies controlled by Dremlyuga -- including Merlion, Fish Island, Crab Marin, Apella, Crab DMP, and Pacific Marin, were involved in illegal fishing by fraudulently creating a semblance of legitimate economic activities.

Another lawsuit has leveled similar claims against companies controlled by Kan, including Primorie Fishery Company, SevRybFlot, Moneron, Kuril Universal Complex, and Aquamarin.

The lawsuits have claimed that all these companies were under foreign control and, therefore, illegally acquired crab quotas.

Companies allegedly controlled by Kan had more than 8,000 metric tons per year of crab quotas, and Dremlyuga's entities had the right to catch some 1,000t per year.

Dremlyuga is a citizen of Ukraine, while Kan is, or was, a permanent resident of South Korea and not a Russian tax resident.

In two rulings released on Jan. 25, the Arbitration Court of Primorie ordered the freezing of crab quotas and assets of 45 local companies and businessmen, including Kan, Dremlyuga and Dmitry Pashov.

In 2021, Russian authorities seized sizable real estate assets controlled by Kan. In December 2023, Primorie regional courts ruled to seize real estate and other assets controlled by Dremlyuga worth RUB 4.3bn.

In August 2023, Russian law enforcement agencies accused Kan of complicity in smuggling 3,000t of crab out of the country between 2014 and 2019 so as to dodge the applicable export duties and taxes. Kan was earlier charged with complicity in the contract killing of another crab businessman, Valery Phidenko, in October 2010.

These charges against Kan were filed in absentia because the defendant fled Russia on a private jet.

In January, the Arbitration Court of Primorie region ruled to impose a total ban on all the defendants' business operations and the freezing of their assets. The court also ordered the seizure of assets of former Sakhalin regional lawmaker Pashov, who faced similar crab smuggling charges to Kan in June 2020. He was sentenced to four-and-a-half years in jail.

Before that, Pashov was known as the country's richest government employee, with assets worth RUB 6.2bn.

In a ruling released on April 3, the Arbitration Court of Primorie ruled in favor of the Prosecutor General's office and ordered the repossession of Kan's assets.

Russian gov’t moves to seize over $4bn in crab assets

Some representatives of the defendants claimed the judge had refused to allow petitions filed by the parties to separate the claims into separate proceedings and refused the defendants to exercise their right to judicial protection. They also argued that the court did not ensure equal treatment of all parties since it did not prevent insults that the representative of the plaintiff addressed to the representatives of the defendants.

The court turned down the defendants' arguments and determined that since 2014, Kan had "created a gang in the region, a number of individuals were involved in his criminal activities, including representatives of state authorities and law enforcement agencies who lobbied for his interests."

The court ruled that "in order to create the appearance of legality, the movement of goods across the customs border, Moneron, Kuril Universal Complex, and Primorie Fishery Company -- and offshore foreign companies controlled by Kan -- concluded fictitious contracts for the supply of live crab at a reduced price in US dollars. In fact, deliveries were made to China and Japan at a different cost, the amount of which, in some cases, is twice the value of the goods indicated in the customs declarations in the Russian Federation."

The court also ordered the Russian fishery agency Rosrybolovstvo to annul all the agreements with businesses controlled by Kan relating to the disputed crab quotas. 

During court hearings in March 2024, Oleg Kan's legal representatives requested the court close the case as they claimed that the defendant died in 2023. According to Russian public notary data, Kan died on Feb. 14, 2023, and the inheritance proceedings started in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk.

In a ruling released on April 3, the Arbitration Court of Primorie region refused to accept information on Kan's death as evidence since it was based on a death certificate issued in the UK -- specifically, by Cromwell Hospital in London -- and the deceased was identified solely by a verbal statement of a certain Ilya Umansky, who sent the body for cremation.

The court determined that the certificate also "did not contain information that would allow it to be reliably established that it was Kan's body that was sent for cremation."

The public record, released on April 12, indicated that Kan's former assets, including Primorie Fishery Company, SevRybFlot, Moneron, Kuril Universal Complex, Aquamarinand Priboi-T, were now recorded as the property of Russia's Federal Agency for State Property Management (also known as Rosimushchestvo).

Moneron and Kuril Universal Complex used to be Kan's top-performing crab assets. In 2023, Moneron reported a net profit of RUB 2.3 bn, while Kuril Universal Complex's net profit was reported at RUB 2bn.

title: EU salmon processors launch union, petition over Norway’s ‘production fish’ export rules
content:
European salmon processors have come together to form the EU Salmon Processors Union (ESP) and to lobby the European Commission (EC), firstly, over Norwegian "production fish" export rules.

ESP involves multiple processors from Poland, Denmark, Belgium, Spain, the Netherlands, and France -- which companies specifically have not been disclosed yet -- and it has launched a petition for "anyone who is negatively impacted by this export ban."

EU confirms it will raise ‘production fish’ issue with Norway after Danish complaint

"This is part of a lobby program in which we will address government at all levels; local, regional, national and of course at European level," a spokesperson for the organization said. "We request all EU salmon processors, big and small, to sign the petition."

"As salmon processors in Europe, we are facing a crucial challenge that affects us all, and it is high time we take collective action," said ESP upon its launch.

"Norway categorizes salmon as superior, ordinary, and production-grade salmon (also known as prod-fish). It allows superior and ordinary to be exported but prohibits the sale of prod-fish."

"Prod-fish must be processed domestically into fillets so that visual deformities can be removed and the quality image of Norwegian salmon is secured. The share of production fish, however, used to be less than 8% of the total harvested salmon volume in Norway, but in recent years this share rose to over 40% in some months, creating a disorderly and chaotic situation for both farmers and European processors."

"It is evident that we can no longer remain passive while this ban harms and threatens the very existence of our industry. This export ban favors a couple of domestic Norwegian salmon processors, while leaving thousands of EU salmon buyers with lacking availability and extreme prices for superior and ordinary salmon."

The EU Commission confirmed to Undercurrent in March that it was to open talks with Norway after finding the latter country's policy of processing all downgraded salmon in-country should be considered a "barrier to trade."

That came after a complaint by Denmark to the EU, Poul Melgaard Jensen of the Danish Seafood Association confirmed to Undercurrent.

The ESP's arguments to the EC include:

"Disinformation: The argument that Norwegian salmon would suffer reputational damage by allowing prod-fish into the open market is unfounded. Other salmon farming countries, such as the Faroe Islands, Scotland, and Ireland, have no or less stringent rules and still enjoy an excellent reputation, selling their salmon at premium prices compared to Norwegian salmon."

"Fraud: The current situation encourages fraud, with prod-fish being illegally exported. This creates an uneven playing field and undermines our industry's integrity. Both the authorities and the industry have completely lost grip on the situation, making it impossible to enforce law and order."

"Protectionism: The ban on the export of production-grade salmon results in unfair competition and amounts to illegal protection for Norwegian processors. This goes against the principles of free trade that the European market stands for."

"Price instability and market inefficiency: The ban causes extreme high pricing for superior and ordinary fish and extreme low pricing for prod-fish, none of which reflect the real market price. Returns for both Norwegian farmers and EU processors are negatively impacted by this."

"Vague regulation: Although the authorities strictly forbid the export of production fish, they have given a 10-year dispensation to one single salmon harvesting company. This company uses a vessel to harvest salmon in Norwegian waters and then sails to the EU, where its complete harvest (including prod-fish) may be bought by EU processors."

This, presumably, refers to Sekkingstad, for which the harvest vessel Norwegian Gannet harvests and guts all fish on board and lands to Hirtshals in Denmark.

The ESP wants the export ban on prod-fish to be lifted or at least to be given a dispensation for as long as the prod-fish share exceeds 8% of the total harvest volumes.

"We have established systems and procedures to correct any deviations and prevent damaged salmon from entering the market. Our options to correct and upgrade production-grade salmon into premium value-added products are limitless."

title: Philippines coast guard seizes two vessels for suspected IUU
content:
Two fishing vessels were seized by the Philippines Coast Guard (PCG) off Palawan for suspected illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing, leading to charges against 35 individuals, Phil Star reported.

The PCG's Eastern Palawan station operated against the vessels Spring Beauty and Lotus 02 last week at approximately 2.9 nautical miles southwest of Brgy Cocoro, Magsaysay, Palawan, it said on Facebook.

The vessels were swiftly intercepted and boarded after suspicions were raised about IUU fishing activities using purse seine gear within Magsaysay's municipal waters.

The maritime law enforcement team confirmed these suspicions upon inspection.

title: Massive Chinese shrimp farming greenhouse park at risk over illegal groundwater usage
content:
A shrimp farming greenhouse park in the Chinese province of Guangdong is facing significant pressure from the local government over environmental challenges from its alleged illegal groundwater extraction, Undercurrent News has learned.

As reported by Undercurrent, China's shrimp aquaculture industry is experiencing a renaissance driven by the widespread adoption of greenhouse raceway farming systems.

China’s shrimp farming rennaisance driven by humble greenhouse tech

However, the government of Yangjiang, in Guangdong, has said it will cut the power supply to an aquaculture zone consisting of 3,500 greenhouses on April 15 because of farmers' "illegal extraction of groundwater," which has resulted in the cracking of a nearby bridge, according to a government notice issued on April 8.

"The illegal extraction of groundwater by the Yangjiang Yanghai Aquaculture Farm has led to the tilting and cracking of the Hailing Island Bridge project. Further groundwater extraction could result in embankment collapse, bridge collapse, and pose significant safety hazards," the government said in a warning letter to the farmers.

The government's initial plan was to carry out the power cut on April 8. However, following the farmers' request, the action has been postponed for one week.

"The government has repeatedly informed you to cease your illegal activities, but to date, you have refused to comply. We now order you once again to dismantle the illegal groundwater extraction facilities. Failure to do so will result in enforcement measures and any resulting losses will be your responsibility," the government letter said.

It said the power would be cut to "eliminate the significant safety hazards caused by illegal groundwater extraction," but that power would be reinstated if and when the reason for the power outage was rectified.

The Yanghai farm, as stated by its executive Shen Xiaojie, has 3,500 shrimp greenhouses, construction of which began early in 2022 and where aquaculture began by the end of the same year.

In the southern provinces of China, there are a total of 30,000 to 40,000 greenhouses, with the Yanghai farm accounting for roughly one-tenth of this number.

"Currently, there are 85 farmers engaged in shrimp production on our site, with a considerable amount of shrimp yet to be harvested. It is estimated that [the power cut] will result in a loss of CNY 150 million ($21.2m)," Shen said in a public statement.

"We have submitted a report to the government explaining our situation. The 85 farmers have signed a commitment letter agreeing to close the water wells and dismantle the underground water extraction facilities as requested. We earnestly request the government to ensure normal electricity supply during the farming period," he added.

One farmer at the site told local publication Aquaculture Wealth that should the government cut power, the juveniles he had just stocked would die from lack of oxygen.

"I will be unable to repay my debts and unable to sustain my family's livelihood," he said.

Last year, the farmer spent over CNY 6m to purchase 200 greenhouses in Yanghai. Including equipment costs, the total expenditure amounted to over CNY 10m.

"In 2023, each of my greenhouses yielded around 1,000 kilograms of shrimp, very productive," he said. "One month ago, I stocked post-larvae in 80 greenhouses, with inputs including feed, seed, and animal care costing between CNY 400,000 and CNY 500,000. If the power is cut, all the shrimp will die within half an hour."

Aquaculture Wealth reported that most farmers rely on loans for funding, with shrimp farming income serving as their sole household income source. If the power supply is cut, each household will lose over CNY 1m.

China, US show promising signs for Vietnam shrimp exporters

"My greenhouses are expected to be ready for harvest on April 20, which is the earliest possible time," another farmer said. "After receiving the power outage notice on April 15, some merchants lowered prices, resulting in difficulties selling the recent batches."

Shen emphasized that greenhouse farming in the region is an important economic source for farmers and their families. The losses caused by the power cut would be unbearable for them, he claimed.

He referred to a legal opinion that said if a forced power outage leads to losses, the responsibility should lie with the power supply agency. According to China's laws on electricity, the power supply can only be cut off if users violate electricity usage regulations, and users must be notified before the power outage occurs.

The determination of whether there was a violation in the use of groundwater falls under the jurisdiction of the environmental protection department, and the power supply agency lacks the authority to intervene.

"If losses occur due to a forced power outage, farmers have the option to file a lawsuit and seek compensation from government departments or the power supply agency," said the lawyer behind the legal opinion.

"Shrimp farmers should keep their evidence, including production records, on-site photos, videos, etc."

Shen acknowledged that given the scale of Yanghai Farm, long-term use of groundwater is not a sustainable solution.

"We will encourage farmers to abandon the use of groundwater and transition to using seawater, a process that [we] began preparing for at the end of last year."

However, most farmers are more concerned about immediate issues, namely, what they will do once the power is cut. Even with diesel generators, they can only sustain limited aeration at high costs.

Fish First reported that on April 5, there were farmers who were forced to harvest their shrimp early at low prices because they wanted to minimize potential losses in the future.

The ex-farm price for size 80-100 counts per kilogram was CNY 32/kg. The shrimp were originally planned to be harvested during the Labor Day holiday on May 1 to fetch higher prices.

In addition to power cuts, greenhouse farmers in Southern China may also face further challenges from the government, Fish First said. Starting from May 1, Guangdong Province will implement the local mandatory standard "Water Discharge Standards for Aquaculture Effluents," which may also introduce new challenges to greenhouses, as they have long been a subject of controversy regarding discharge and pollution.

title: Untitled
content:
China's government said it has cracked down on more than 20,000 cases of illegal fishing in the Yangtze River over the past three years, giving a boost to the river's ecology, including the endangered finless porpoise population.

The announcement comes as China enforces a 10-year fishing ban on its longest river that took effect Jan. 1, 2021. The ban covers all tributaries, lakes and estuaries of the Yangtze. 

China's Ministry of Public Security said it has made enforcing the fishing ban a priority and claims it has resolved over 20,000 fishing-related criminal cases since 2021. A ministry spokesperson said the crackdown has "significantly curbed" large-scale illegal fishing in the river.

It is difficult to independently verify the claims because of China's tightly controlled media.

The ban has raised concerns about the livelihoods of some 300,000 fishermen who rely on the Yangtze. But China's agricultural minister Tang Renjian said that 231,000 unemployed fishermen have received government support and 154,000 have transitioned to new jobs.

Tang said surveillance equipment now covers the Yangtze's main streams, estuaries and lakes. The number of fishery law enforcement personnel has quadrupled. Reported illegal fishing fell 28% last year compared to 2021, Tang said.

The government said there are signs the ban is having ecological impacts. The Yangtze finless porpoise population increased to 1,249 last year, up 237 from 2017, Tang said. Some fish species are migrating farther upriver, reaching areas that have been closed off to fishing for years.

But Tang said restoration efforts must continue. "Many rare species haven't reached a sustainable state," he said.

In 2006, the Yangtze River dolphin was declared functionally extinct by the World Wildlife Fund for Nature, the first cetacean extinction due to human activity.

title: Death of Russian ‘crab king’ cited as defense in $4bn lawsuit
content:
As Russian authorities try to seize crab assets worth nearly $4 billion -- including catch quotas amounting to roughly a tenth of the country's total allowable catch (TAC) -- lawyers have claimed that one key defendant is no longer alive.

Russian crab asset seizure involves nearly 10,000t of quotas

During court hearings held earlier this week, legal representatives of Russia's former "crab king," Oleg Kan, requested the court to close the case. On March 19, lawyers claimed that Kan died last year; prosecutors described the announcement as unconfirmed, according to local media reports.

According to Russian public notary data, Oleg Kan died on Feb. 14, 2023, and the inheritance proceedings started in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk.

Media reports on March 21 said prosecutors had rejected claims of Kan's death, citing the lack of a Russian death certificate. Lawyers reportedly responded that the Russian authorities refused to accept the UK certificate, as Kan allegedly died in London, and had been buried in South Korea.

In January 2024, Russian authorities launched legal procedures to seize several sizable Far Eastern crab business assets. On Jan. 23, the Prosecutor General's office filed a lawsuit requesting the annulment of crab quotas and seeking damages from companies as well as individuals, including Kan, totaling RUB 358.7bn ($3.87bn), according to the court documents.

The lawsuit states companies controlled by Kan, including Primorie Fishery Company, SevRybFlot, Moneron, Kuril Universal Complex, and Aquamarin, were involved in illegal fishing by fraudulently creating a semblance of legitimate economic activities. The lawsuit claimed that all these companies were under foreign control and, therefore, illegally acquired crab quotas. Companies allegedly controlled by Kan had more than 8,000 metric tons per year of crab quotas, nearly one-tenth of Russia's overall crab TAC.

In two rulings released on Jan. 25, the Arbitration Court of Russia's Far Eastern Primorie branch ordered the freezing of crab quotas and assets belonging to 45 local companies and businessmen, including Kan. The court imposed a total ban on all the defendants' business operations and froze all their assets. A trial date was set for April 3.

In August 2023, Russian law enforcement agencies accused Kan of complicity in smuggling 3,000t of crab out of the country between 2014 and 2019 so as to dodge the applicable export duties and taxes.

Kan was earlier charged with complicity in the contract killing of another crab businessman, Valery Phidenko, in October 2010. These charges against Kan were filed in absentia after he fled Russia. In 2021, the authorities seized sizable real estate assets controlled by Kan.

In a separate 2024 lawsuit involving the criminal charges relating to the alleged contract killing, Kan's lawyers did not seek the closure of the case on the grounds of the defendant's death, according to the state-run TASS news agency.

On March 20, Kan's lawyer, Konstantin Tropaidze, reportedly insisted that Kan should be acquitted but declined to request that the court drop the charges and refused to comment on the defendant's alleged death.

title: Canada needs to put some elver rules in writing, harvesters tell Senate panel
content:
Licensed elver fish harvesters in the Canadian Maritimes say the federal government should set enforceable regulations to govern the moderate livelihood fishery by Indigenous groups.

Industry representatives told a Senate committee in Ottawa on Thursday (Feb. 29) that the failure to define or regulate moderate livelihood rights by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) is one reason for the uncontrolled harvest of baby eels on dozens of rivers in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, the CBC reports.

The elver fishery in the Maritimes was worth CAD 47 million ($35m) in 2022, with DFO-approved licenses held by eight commercial harvesters and some Mi'kmaw and Wolastoqey communities.

A Fisheries and Oceans map shows the number of licenced elver rivers in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Screenshot

However, other First Nations have been fishing elvers without DFO consent, claiming they don't need government approval.

Commercial dealer Mitchell Feigenbaum says the department must put its requirements in writing rather than relying on negotiations.

"Those efforts rarely bear fruit [and result in] the status quo [being left] in place," he told the senators. "First Nation individuals asserting their treaty rights go out and fish. If DFO tries to enforce the law, the courts and the prosecutors say, 'Well, there's no regulation that says they can't.' So DFO simply needs to make a regulation saying, 'Here's what the dos and don'ts are, and they need to apply it to all First Nations.'"

title: EU adopts updated tuna measures for Atlantic Ocean
content:
The EU Council has officially approved a regulation integrating specific fisheries management, conservation, and control measures within the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas convention area into EU law.

This adoption also entails revisions to the multiannual management plan for bluefin tuna in the eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean regions.

Belgian Flemish minister for fisheries, Hilde Crevits, highlighted the significance of these regulations in ensuring sustainable seas, food security, and industry profitability.

Critical updates include defining support vessels and fish aggregating devices, implementing capacity limitations and discard prohibitions for tropical tuna, and enhancing reporting requirements for bluefin tuna catches. Additionally, provisions for albacore fisheries, sea turtle, and shortfin mako shark conservation have been reinforced.

More specifically, in the case of tropical tuna, the EU Council has established capacity limitations and the prohibition of discards by purse seiners (except under certain circumstances). This means that by Jan. 31 of each year, EU countries will have to prepare annual fishing capacity management plans for tropical tuna; additionally, every three months, EU states will have to communicate to the EU Commission information on the number of tropical tunas -- by species -- caught by vessels carrying their flag.

In the case of bluefin tuna, the EU Commission established updated provisions on the carry-over of non-harvested live bluefin tuna from previous years’ catches. It also put in place recreational fisheries quota provisions and updated rules for the preparation of an annual monitoring, control and inspection plan as well as prohibition of the automatic carry-over of any unused quota.

Following the Council vote, the regulation proceeds to signing by both the EU Council and the European Parliament before publication in the EU Official Journal and enforcement within 20 days.

title: Tradex: Russian 2024 Pacific salmon forecast among lowest in decade
content:
Russia's forecast of its Pacific salmon harvest in 2024 is one of the lowest in a decade, British Columbia, Canada-based Tradex reports in its latest 3-Minute-Market-Insight. 

In a report made a week ago, scientists predicted the catch volume to be about 320,000 metric tons, 38% below the 512,000t predicted for 2023 and less than 1% below the 321,820t predicted for 2022. 

Russia has struggled to meet its forecasted catch volumes for the last two even-year cycles, underscoring a trend of not fully realizing the forecast, Tradex noted. In 2022, the actual harvest was 268,000t, 17% below the projection. 

"However, experts are optimistic about a turnaround, predicting a progressive increase in the Pacific salmon catch starting from 2024, in subsequent even-numbered years," the wholesaler reported.

Table shared by Tradex in February 2024.

Last year's actual catch was 608,604t, setting a record for the highest odd-year harvest and ranking second only to the exceptional haul of over 677,000 tonnes in 2018, Tradex noted.

Pink salmon, as usual, will make up the largest share of the catch in 2024. A total of 193,000t is projected to be caught, 60% below the 478,473t caught in 2023 and 35% more than the 143,445t caught in 2022.

"When compared with the expectations for the 2024 Alaska salmon season, it's noteworthy that Alaska’s pink salmon harvests in 11 years are typically lower than in odd years," Tradex noted. "This trend suggests potential supply constraints for the USA market, especially in light of the ban on Russian-origin salmon entering the US now being enforced."

The average for the past five even years for salmon seasons in Alaska computes to around 61 million pink salmon, or roughly 96,000t.

title: Russia’s VARPE calls US seafood prohibitions new ‘iron curtain’
content:
One Russian industry group has dismissed the delayed enforcement of the US ban on all imports of Russian seafood until June as insignificant, arguing that the measure undermines the global seafood market.

US extends deadline on Russian-origin imports amid global shipping delays 

Under a Feb. 20 amendment to the import ban from the US Department of the Treasury, US importers will now have until May 31 to bring in containers of Russian-origin salmon, cod, pollock and crab ordered before Dec. 22 rather than the original deadline of Feb. 21, as the Red Sea shipping crisis disrupts supply chains. 

On Feb. 21, the All-Russian Fishery Association (known under its Russian acronym VARPE) said the delayed enforcement would not change the adverse repercussions of the ban.

"Some delay in the establishment of the US 'iron curtain' against Russian fish products is procedural in nature and will not reduce the scale of the consequences for the American market," said VARPE head German Zverev. There are opponents of the "iron curtain" in the US, but so far, their voices have been ignored, he claimed.

The delay will entail no significant consequences for Russian exporters because the salmon fishing season is yet to start, Pacific cod fishing volumes are limited, and the direct supply of Russian pollock and crab to the US has already been discontinued, according to Zverev.

However, the architecture of the global fish market appears to be falling apart, and the major importers of fish products -- the US and the EU -- "will be the first to suffer from this," he claimed.

US president Joe Biden's Dec. 22 executive order closed the route for Russian fish via China and other third countries into the US, initially blocking imports of Russian pollock, salmon, cod and crab processed in third countries from Feb. 21, 2024, after Biden dropped direct imports in 2023 when Russia first invaded Ukraine.

Trident still using Russian pollock in Europe after toasting latest US ban

There have been rumors of an extension in the market for a while from Undercurrent News sources amid the ongoing Red Sea shipping crisis.

According to sources, East Coast US processors and suppliers were pushing for a complete extension, but what is in place only applies to orders made before Dec. 22. 

"So, not much of a change really, the East Coast guys didn't get their way," one whitefish sector source told Undercurrent. "It's just about allowing orders that have been delayed to get in."

title: US senator touts Russian seafood ban, ‘Freedom Fish’ in address to Alaska legislature
content:
US senator Dan Sullivan praised the expansion of the ban to better lock out the US import of Russian seafood and gave wild-caught pollock a new nickname during his address to a joint session of the Alaska State Legislature on Wednesday (Feb. 21).

"We worked on it relentlessly," the Alaska Republican said of his push for president Joe Biden's executive order (EO 14114), issued in late December, that closed a loophole that previously allowed for Russian-origin pollock, cod, salmon and crab products to enter the US market if they were processed in another country. 

US senator Lisa Murkowski, another Alaska Republican, had similarly praised the congressional delegation's pursuit of the expanded ban during her annual address to state lawmakers in the capitol of Juneau last week, as reported by Undercurrent News. 

State of Alaska fisheries tops Murkowski address to lawmakers

"Our fishing community is going through a really, really, really rough time, and a lot of this was driven by the Russians," Sullivan told both chambers of the legislature, adding that he expected the rule to "help firm up prices" in Alaska, where the market for seafood products across species has crashed.

The expanded ban has been celebrated in Alaska, but has received a mixed reception across the industry, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

Responding to a question from state representative Louise Stutes, a Kodiak Republican, Sullivan said US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) will lead enforcement of the ban, although importers will also be mandated to declare the source of their fish when it enters the country.

Sullivan said he’s been in touch with US processors that previously depended on Russian products about finding a new seafood source.

"You need to rely on 'Freedom Fish' from Alaska," he said of his conversations, suggesting a new nickname for the US' most harvested fish species.

Wild Alaska pollock on crushed ice. Image courtesy of Genuine Alaska Pollock Producers.

The expression hearkens back to February 2003 when a North Carolina restaurant changed the name of its French fries in response to France's opposition to the proposed invasion of Iraq. It gained more traction when Bob Ney, the Republican then chairing the Committee on House Administration renamed the menu item in three Congressional cafeterias.   

The day of Sullivan's speech also happened to be the date the ban was supposed to go into effect, however, the US Department of Treasury extended that deadline due to shipping disruptions in the Red Sea. Importers now have until the end of May for seafood products from Russia to enter the US if they were purchased before Dec. 22, as reported by Undercurrent.

US extends deadline on Russian-origin imports amid global shipping delays 

Sullivan spoke for more than an hour during his annual address, touching also on energy production, national defense and the state’s housing shortage. Only about 10 minutes of the presentation were dedicated to fisheries-related issues, including efforts to boost marine debris clean up, and what Sullivan called a "frivolous, manipulative lawsuit" brought by the environmental group Wild Fish Conservancy last year to shut down the king salmon troll fishery in the state’s Southeast region. 

Sullivan also touted his work boosting research on crashing numbers of king and chum salmon that have hit communities in the western part of the state. 

The senator spent time reiterating a similar call from Murkowski last week for the US Department of Agriculture to include seafood-specific provisions in the farm bill reauthorization.

Hundreds of seafood harvesters, processors and other industry groups have pushed to be included in the sweeping legislation, which is reauthorized every five years and encompasses everything from agricultural policy to food aid programs. The current farm bill expired in September and a new version has yet to be passed. 

"Stay tuned on that one," he said. "It’s going to be an epic battle."

title: Ecuadorian exporters face consumer backlash in China over sulfite shrimp
content:
Additional reporting by Louis Harkell.

Ecuadorian shrimp is again under the microscope in China after a Chinese blogger and "professional anti-counterfeiter" found shrimp sold on a popular e-commerce platform contained excessive preservatives. 

Blogger Wang Hai, well-known in China for his videos exposing counterfeiting, had samples tested of shrimp purchased in a December livestream sale on East Buy, one of China's largest online sellers of Ecuadorian shrimp. Results showed 0.155 grams per kilogram of sulfur dioxide -- surpassing China's 0.1g/kg limit for the preservative.

Popular Chinese live-streamer sued for selling farmed Ecuadorian shrimp as wild

The 50-year-old blogger sent testing samples shortly after purchase, receiving results last month that showed 55% more preservative than allowed under Chinese food standards.

East Buy has aggressively marketed Ecuadorian shrimp in China while fending off allegations last year that it misrepresented farmed product as premium wild-caught. The company claims monthly checks show its shrimp meets Chinese requirements.

Sales staff in the December session emphasized only shrimp, water and salt was used in processing -- with no mention of additives like sulfite, which prevents discoloration.

Wang speculated sodium metabisulfite -- a preservative widely used in shrimp -- was added and is demanding refunds for mislabeling. Sulphur dioxide is the residual chemical from the use of sodium metabisulfite and other sulfite preservatives.

A major Shanghai importer cautioned demand could temporarily sag amid increased inspections but said trade would likely rebound given global differences on shrimp standards. Under EU and US regulations, companies must label food products as containing sulphur dioxide above 10 milligrams per kilogram.

"This incident originated from the differing requirements of various countries regarding sulfite residue, and imported shrimp happened to the catalyst," the importer told Undercurrent News.

Lackluster farm-gate prices during Spring Festival flag China’s shrimp industry struggles

"Ecuadorian shrimp has been exported to China, the US, and Europe for a long period of time, adhering to international standards that differ from those of China. If strictly enforced, it would have a significant impact on international trade," he said.

"So, there is no need to be nervous. The eventual outcome is that after a period of strict inspections, things gradually calm down, as there is indeed nothing substantial to investigate, and industry practitioners are well aware of this," he said.

Top shrimp importer Quanlian Jicai warned orders have already declined since Wang's findings seemingly spooked consumer confidence. It projects overseas purchase orders will slide further amid retail uncertainty.

Regulators have yet to comment on the case as of Thursday (Feb. 22).

title: Alaska bill to expand electronic vessel monitoring draws backlash from harvesters
content:
A bill aimed at increasing electronic monitoring on fishing vessels is getting pushback in the US state of Alaska.

Public radio station KFSK, in Petersburg, reports the legislation, which was introduced by governor Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, would require electronic monitoring in state fisheries instead of having mandatory observers aboard fishing vessels.

Alaska Department of Fish and Game commissioner Doug Vincent-Lang told KFSK that the legislation is intended to boost fisheries enforcement and help out law enforcement.

But at a public hearing on the bill in the state capitol of Juneau last week, lawmakers overwhelming heard from harvesters who opposed the bill, according to the public radio station. A sticking point is that not all vessels are required to have observers on board, meaning the law would add some form of monitoring where it's not currently mandated. 

"I can’t stress enough that EM programs are very complicated. They are resource intensive and just as burdensome as observer programs, and should be given the same rigorous vetting, prior to considering a new program," said Charlotte Levy, the natural resources assistant director with the Aleutians East Borough, which is home to major processing plants owned by Trident and Peter Pan seafoods.

Fishermen and industry groups at the hearing also cited the costs that harvesters would ultimately be forced to shoulder to adhere to the program.

The bill is currently in the state's Senate Labor and Commerce Committee.

title: Rope that entangled dead right whale identified as likely Maine lobster gear
content:
North American lobster harvesters in the US state of Maine were dealt some very bad news on Wednesday (Feb. 14).

Based on preliminary observations, the rope that entangled a female, juvenile North Atlantic right whale, found dead on a beach in Martha's Vineyard, Massachusetts, late last month, had purple markings that match the gear used by Maine harvesters, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) announced in a statement on its website.

In its battle to avoid strict new requirements in order to better protect endangered right whales, including a ropeless gear mandate, the US lobster industry has previously been able to claim a near spotless record of zero entanglements since 2004 and zero mortalities ever. US senators and representatives from Maine used the record to help get a law passed in late 2022 that requires NOAA wait until at least 2028, to publish new rules.

Such arguments will now be more difficult to make.

Conservation groups were quick to take shots at policymakers and the lobster industry on Wednesday.

"Today the federal government re-confirmed that critically endangered North Atlantic right whales can and do get entangled in fishing gear from Maine," said Gibb Brogan, a campaign director at Oceana, in a press release. "The lobster fishery and the Maine delegation have repeatedly denied culpability for whale entanglements, and they can no longer stand on this fantasy. Maine needs to take responsibility for the harm it is causing to this critically endangered species and find a workable solution instead of denying facts and dragging its feet to make changes." 

Image of North Atlantic right whale #5120 after its body was found on a beach in late January 2024. Image courtesy of NOAA.

Some of the rope found entangling North Atlantic right whale #5120. Image courtesy of NOAA.

Patrick Keliher, commissioner of Maine's Department of Marine Resources (DMR), issued a statement on Wednesday as well, acknowledging NOAA's finding. He said he and other "key policy, science, and enforcement staff" went to Gloucester, Massachusetts, to inspect the gear found on the whale, review NOAA's findings and question them regarding any discrepancies. 

"Unfortunately, the gear is consistent with Maine trap/pot gear," Keliher said, adding: "This is very unfortunate – our goal is zero entanglements. Certainly, this is a rare event, in fact it is the first right whale entanglement with known Maine gear since 2004. It is also the first right whale mortality with known Maine gear that DMR is aware of since the establishment of the Take Reduction Plan."

Whale was previously seen struggling

The deceased whale is identified as #5120 in NOAA's right whale catalog, a female reported to have been born in 2021.

The whale was last observed gear-free in the Great South Channel on May 1, 2022, the commissioner recounted. It was next observed entangled in August 2022 by Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans off the coast of the province New Brunswick, in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Several sightings occurred in 2023, both in the US and Canada, where the whale was still entangled and seen in declining health.

Patrick Keliher. Photograph from Maine Department of Marine Resources.

A necropsy was completed on Feb. 1, 2024, in which the preliminary results confirmed a chronic entanglement with rope embedded in the tail. There is no sign of blunt force trauma indicative of a ship strike, Keliher said. 

He added that no buoy was collected with the rope, which might have helped identify the gear's owners and potentially help determine a precise location of entanglement. It also remains unclear if the gear was in state or federal waters, he said.

"With only two purple marks retrieved and portions of the surface system missing, Maine DMR analysis of the recovered gear could indicate different gear configuration scenarios, some of which suggest state waters and others which suggest federal waters," he said. "We are continuing to investigate to see if we can better answer this question."

The Maine lobster industry has invested millions of dollars to adopt gear marking, insert weak points and meet new trawling-up requirements, said Keliher.

"Entangling a whale is not something any fishermen wants see or hear about," he said.  "This news will undoubtedly also bring with it a fear and anxiousness around what could come next from NOAA.  It is important to point out that while terrible news, it doesn’t change the fact that Congress has stated in law that this fishery is in compliance with the Endangered Species Act and the Marine Mammal Protection Act until December 31, 2028."

title: California-based Ocean Group recalls salmon, tuna products over listeria concern
content:
Los Angeles-based Ocean Group has initiated a recall of its salmon and tuna products due to possible contamination with listeria monocytogenes, Food Poisoning Bulletin reports.

Because the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) posted the information about the recall on its enforcement page instead of its foodborne illness page, no information has been provided about illnesses, the news service explained.

The recall was initiated on Dec. 29, 2023 and reported by Food Poisoning Bulletin on Jan. 29. 

The recalled items, which were distributed to retailers in California, include products known as Salmon Bakka Frost Fillet, Salmon Bakkafrost Faroe Islands, Salmon Canada canned salmon, Tuna Hawaii, Tuna Bluefin Spain, Tuna Blue Fin, Fresh Tuna Bluefin Portion Mexico and Tuna Fresh Boston Bluefin Wild, among others. The expiration dates for the items ranged from Dec. 11 to Dec. 29.

Consumers are urged to discard the items even if they were frozen, as that doesn't eliminate the pathogen's risk.

title: Video of jet skier harassing menhaden seiners used to advance US state legislation
content:
A video of a man on a jet ski harassing two purse seining boats as they attempt to close their net on a pool of menhaden is being used to make the case for legislation in the US state of Virginia to better deter such behavior.

HB 928 and HB 1465, introduced in January as part of the 2024 Virginia legislative session, would increase the penalties for intentionally interfering with commercial fishing operations. The bills, introduced by delegates Hillary Pugh Kent and Robert S. Bloxom, Jr., both Republicans, would particularly aid Omega Protein, the Reedville, Virginia-based menhaden processing division of Canadian seafood giant Cooke, and also Ocean Harvesters, a US-owned company with a long-term supply contract to provide menhaden to Omega Protein.

A grainy image shot by a spotter plane is reported to be that of a jet skier harassing menhaden purse seining vessels.

HB 928, Kent's bill, was considered, amended and passed by the chamber's Courts of Justice - Criminal Subcommittee by a unanimous, bipartisan 8-0 vote on Friday (Feb. 2). It would increase penalties to those attached to a Class 1 misdemeanor, which would include confinement in jail for not more than 12 and a fine of not more than $2,500, either or both. Additionally, anyone convicted would be forced to forfeit their hunting and fishing licenses for one year for a first offense and for three years for a second offense.

The bill must now get approval from the full committee and, ultimately full House floor.

HB 1465, Bloxom's bill, also would threaten the penalties associated with a Class 1 misdemeanor to anyone who comes within 50 feet of a commercial fishing vessel without the consent of the owner or person in charge with the intent to coerce, intimidate or harass the captain or crew. The bill would make it a Class 6 felony to communicate to another person by any means any threat to kill or do bodily injury to a person or persons engaged in the activity of commercial fishing on Virginia waters.

HB 1465 would allow law-enforcement officers to seize motorboats, personal watercraft or vessels.

Groups report where commercial vessels are headed

To help make the case for HB 928 at Friday's hearing, Kent shared with the subcommittee a short 1.5-minute video captured by a spotter plane of an incident that took place on Sept. 23, 2023, in the Chesapeake Bay, roughly 1.5 miles east of Buckroe Beach off the town of Hampton, Virginia.

It shows a man on a jet ski aggressively riding up on two small purse seining boats, spraying the crew with his wake and even going into the middle of where they are attempting to deploy their net before exiting narrowly out of the circle. The boats were being deployed by the Rappahannock, a vessel owned by Ocean Harvesters, according to a press release published by the Menhaden Fisheries Coalition (MFC). 

Though no sound plays in the video, the man yelled obscenities at the crew, including, "how do you like this m*****f***ers," according to the coalition. 

Menhaden. Credit: NOAA photo library

"Menhaden fishing [requires] long days and short nights. The entire process can be dangerous, and there are a lot of moving parts," Rappahannock captain and hearing witness Lee Robbins told the subcommittee. "Everyone needs to be focused, and you've seen that video. It was hard to be focused with that going on. My crew was distracted and very fearful for their life that day. Someone could have been seriously hurt or killed. We've been receiving threats on social media regularly."

The jet ski incident was reported to the US Coast Guard and the Virginia Marine Resources Commission (VMRC) and investigated by the VMRC, according to the coalition.

When the investigator was unable to get a commitment from local prosecutors to take the case, it was prosecuted as a VMRC offense, the coalition said. The perpetrator, who is identified as Stuart D. Bennett, a Hampton, Virginia, resident, in Hampton General District Court documents, pled guilty in December to a class 3 misdemeanor for which he received a $500 fine. He later bragged about his actions on social media, showing no remorse, according to MFC.

Bennett could not be located by Undercurrent for comment before press time.

MFC said the incident was the third of this type that occurred during the late summer months of 2023. The coalition says such attacks are "being instigated and fueled by the rhetoric of participants in various sport fishing organizations." Such groups monitor and report where commercial boats are operating and where they are anchoring each evening, MFC said.

The press release includes a long list of social media threats that MFC says it has recorded, including:

"Where's an errant WWII German U-Boat when you really need one…? I've got a small boat and plenty of bottle rockets."
"You got whale war, it's time for menhaden war."
"Unfortunately, there's not much that can be done, at least non-violently."
"Sink them and blame it on Putin. Need to do like they do on Whale Wars."
"Where's the Sea Shepherd… Get the prop fouler out. It can't be that illegal to mess with them."
"I have several rifles with scopes and suppression. If someone is a better shot than me, you're welcome to borrow them to sever the net ropes."

"Dangerous incidents are growing in number and aggression and physical injury, and the lives of union-member, commercial fishermen are being increasingly threatened," the MFC said. "These hazardous confrontations have been conducted on jet skis and with recreational boats, endangering all involved. Current law provides for minor penalties, like small fines, which are an insufficient deterrent to individuals with the financial means to own and operate recreational watercraft."

In addition to Omega Protein, the MFC also counts as members: Daybrook Fisheries, in Louisiana; Westbank Fishing, in Louisiana; and Lund's Fisheries, in New Jersey.

Menhaden study proposal postponed again

While legislation to better protect commercial menhaden fishing vessels appears to be moving forward in Virginia, conservation groups' efforts to check the health of the menhaden population in the state's portion of the Chesapeake Bay remain stalled.

The Virginia House of Delegates Rules-Studies Subcommittee voted last week to delay, until the 2025 legislative session, consideration of funding for a study of menhaden numbers and the impact environmental and various types of fishing have on them, WFRX TV, a Fox network affiliate in Roanoke, Virginia, reports. The research project would take three years to conduct.

The vote marks the second year in a row the study proposal, which has bipartisan support and is backed by the Virginia Saltwater Sportfishing Association, has been delayed, according to the news service.

title: US domestic shrimp sector petitions to stop imports of Argentinian reds
content:
The Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA), a trade association that represents the harvesters and processors of US domestic shrimp in the Gulf of Mexico and southeastern coast,  has joined the call for action against seafood supply chains exploiting Uyghur labor.

But rather than focus on Chinese-origin farmed shrimp, the target of the SSA is Argentinian wild-caught red shrimp that's been processed in China before being exported to the US.

China exported more than 12 million pounds of Argentinian shrimp to the US in 2023, advises SSA in a six-page petition sent by John Williams, SSA's executive director, Monday (Jan. 29) to Robert Silvers, the under secretary for strategy, policy and plans at the US Department of Homeland Security and also chairman of the Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force.

The shrimp is caught in the Atlantic Ocean by Argentinian fishermen but processed in Shandong province in plants linked to forced labor practices, Williams advised in his letter, which was CCed to dozens of US lawmakers.

Since January 2023, more than 265 containers of Argentinian shrimp were shipped to the US by Chinese exporters, he said. The product is labeled as wild-caught and competes for sales against the pink shrimp caught by US harvesters in the Gulf of Mexico and South Atlantic Ocean. 

"Bills of lading information show that another 20 containers of shrimp from Ecuador, comprising roughly 800,000 lbs, was shipped to the United States by Chinese exporters over the last year," he added.

US lawmakers ask Biden administration to block seafood from two Chinese provinces

US import statistics don't show the shrimp coming from a Chinese processing plant but indicate it's from Argentina, he said. 

"In fact, according to official US import statistics, the United States imported less than 90,000 lbs of Chinese-origin frozen shrimp last year, while importing roughly 27m lbs of Argentinian-origin frozen shrimp," the letter continued. "As with our import statistics, American consumers are provided no indication as to whether the Argentinian shrimp being sold in grocery stores was shipped here from China."

It's unusual for SSA to take on a wild-caught shrimp product. The group is better known for railing against the import of farmed shrimp from India, Ecuador, Indonesia and Vietnam.

The Outlaw Ocean Project, an investigative journalism group founded by Pulitzer-prize-winning reporter Ian Urbina, published a two-part series in October that shed light on the use of forced Uyghur labor in Chinese seafood processing firms, as reported by Undercurrent News. The series, published in The New Yorker, has led to hearings on Capitol Hill, legislation and multiple calls for action by the president Joe Biden administration. 

US congressional panel’s report recommends expanding SIMP for Chinese seafood

The SSA, in its letter, has recommended adding eight Chinese seafood processing plants in Shandong to the Entity List under the Uyghur Forced Labor Protection Act (UFLPA). They include: Weihai Wendeng Xinghe Food Co., Yantai Longwin Food Co., Chishan Group Co., Shandong Meijia Group, Qingdao Tianyuan Aquatic Foodstuffs Co., and The Rongsense Group.

All were identified by the Outlaw Ocean Project and the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party for clear evidence of employing Uyghur labor in their factories, Williams said. 

SSA also is urging the task force to formally recognize seafood as a priority sector for UFLPA enforcement, aiming to extend safeguards to other seafood processing plants in China exploiting Uyghur labor. 

"Our shrimp industry is facing a huge number of challenges right now, and commercial fishing families across the southern coast are suffering," Williams said. "While our boats are tied up, seafood importers are scouring the globe to find the most vulnerable populations to make a buck off of. This is morally wrong, and it is against the law. We ask for nothing more than the enforcement of our laws," Williams said.

title: Major seafood buyers support US proposals to address IUU fishing in South Pacific
content:
The South Pacific Regional Fisheries Management Organization (SPRFMO) kicked off its annual meeting in Manta, Ecuador, with a strong show of support from over 30 major seafood companies and industry associations.

These entities, which include some of the largest US and EU processors, retailers and distributors, such as Costco Wholesale, Aldi and Grupo Profand, have rallied behind the cause of combating illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing and addressing human rights violations in the South Pacific.

Fishing industry raises alarm on unlicensed Chinese vessel’s entry into Peruvian waters

According to industry sources, even though the organization has previously adopted management measures focused on ensuring resource sustainability, until now, it has never implemented specific measures on labor rights.

Sources also pointed out that some long-distance fishing fleets operating near Peruvian waters and/or transshipping along the Humboldt Current employ fishermen of a different nationality, who, in some cases, are subjected to severely exploitative conditions, such as forced labor and human trafficking.

To urge the SPRFMO to take swift action, the companies submitted a letter to the heads of delegation of members and cooperating non-contracting parties (CNCPs) participating in the organization's annual meeting. It underscored the need for concrete measures and procedures to identify and combat IUU fishing activities in the convention area.

"We recognize the efforts of the SPRFMO in recent years to manage the jumbo flying squid stock, and are aware of the progress that the SPRFMO has made on ensuring the sustainability of this fishery," the letter reads. "Building on this progress, it is essential to increase efforts to curb IUU fishing in the convention area.

"We wish to see the commission accelerate the fight against the IUU fishing in the convention area by implementing appropriate procedures and measures to identify infringements and violations by vessels on the high seas," it continues.

The letter also noted that the organization had so far not included any fishing vessels on the IUU list.

The signaries to the letter also include Seattle Fish & Gourmet Provisions, SeaFarms, Quirch, Picard, Sysco France, Frinsa, High Liner Foods, GlobalPez, Fortune International, Denner, which is part of Grupo Migros, Cabomar, Congalsa, Conxemar, PanaPesca, Brianna Hughes, Wofco, Lund's Fisheries, Santa Monica Seafood, Grupo Conframar, Grupo Eroski, among others. 

The key requests made in the letter include labor guidelines, such as establishing a specialized working group and the implementation of the first Conservation and Management Measure (CMM) focused on guidelines for the safety and equitable treatment of crew members. These proposals were put forth by the US, Ecuador, Australia and New Zealand.

Photo: Vessel fishing in the South Pacific.

Additionally, the companies called for amendments to the jumbo-flying squid CMM to gradually increase onboard observer coverage to 20%, as Australia and New Zealand suggested.

The letter also emphasized the importance of discussing and considering five proposals to improve monitoring, control, and surveillance measures to combat IUU fishing in the jumbo-flying squid fishery.

The SPRFMO commission, comprising 17 state members, including nations like the United States, China, and the European Union, will deliberate on these proposals during the annual meeting, which runs from Jan. 29 to Feb. 2. If adopted, these actions are expected to enhance transparency and enforce stricter controls to prevent IUU fishing in one of the world's most critical squid stocks.

title: EU tuna purse seine fleet, scientists discuss potential for improved stock assessments
content:
The second meeting of fishing body Europeches tuna group on Jan. 23 brought together 23 experts from across Europe in Montpellier, France, to discuss the theme "Towards robust stock evaluations for better management."

During the initial panel, scientists highlighted their requirements for improving stock assessment processes, emphasizing the critical role of data availability. New methods, such as those based on buoy, sonar, and genotype, were discussed as potential tools to determine stock abundance.

Additionally, concerns were voiced by fishing industry representatives regarding potential misinterpretations of scientific advice due to the inherent uncertainties in stock assessments.

They cautioned against uneven management actions within regional fisheries management organizations (RFMOs), citing potential negative consequences for purse seine fishing fleets and the overall recovery of stocks. Strengthening compliance enforcement processes for RFMOs and flag states was also deemed crucial.

In a second panel, scientists spoke about the functioning and implications of multi-species management strategy evaluation for tropical tunas. This process focuses on the impact of fishing and management strategies on all tropical tuna stocks within each region, recognizing the fisheries' multi-species nature and the targeted stocks' interconnectedness.

"Through open dialogue and frank exchanges of perspectives, both scientists and purse-seine industry representatives have successfully achieved a deeper mutual understanding, marking the first step towards developing effective solutions," said Anne-France Mattlet, director of Europeche's tuna group.

title: Untitled
content:
The European tuna fleet is set to face an even more challenging predicament in 2024 as it grapples with mounting competition from Asian-backed firms in the Indian and Atlantic Oceans.

According to industry group Europeche, an already "uneven playing field" will become even tougher this year, compounding the difficulties faced by the European tuna fleet.

With rising operational costs due to higher fuel prices and inflation in other costs, and fierce competition from foreign fleets, European tuna fishing firms find themselves squeezed, Anne-France Mattlet -- director of Europeche's tuna group, told Undercurrent News.

The tough operating landscape has intensified, and the Spanish tuna fleet in the Atlantic area has shrunk from 22 to just 10 vessels in four years. Similarly, the French fleet has declined, losing three vessels this year alone, partly via Bolton Group-owned Via Ocean's decision to cease activities.

Bolton to end French tuna fleet’s operations amid ‘economic challenges’

Via Ocean, previously known as Armement Saupiquet and a subsidiary of the Bolton Group since 2019, decided to halt its fishing operations imminently due to financial challenges. Meanwhile, French fishing firm Sapmer has sold its three Mauritian-flagged tuna purse seiners and its assets there, citing high costs and limited quotas.

Europeche has declared the fight to supply European markets an "uneven playing field" on numerous occasions, and Mattlet said that remained a key part of the struggle in 2024.

European fleets adhere to strict regulations and are closely monitored with vessel monitoring systems and onboard observers; they also apply higher social, maritime and environmental standards, she claimed. Europeche has raised concerns about non-European vessels, and welcomed the EU Commission's progress on banning fish products with links to forced labor in early 2023.

Furthermore, Mattlet voiced concerns about the lack of available data on the compliance and scientific practices of non-EU fleets in the area managed by the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT), highlighting the urgent need for transparency and standardization across all fleets.

For example, without any clear list of non-EU purse seiners operating in the Atlantic, it is impossible to control compliance with the ban on fish aggregating devices (FADs), according to Europeche. The ICCAT ban on fishing with FADs began in January and lasts for three months.

Inconsistencies in compliance raise questions about the fairness of competition, Mattlet noted.

China, Indonesia, Thailand, and Vietnam account for just about 98% of the 35,000 metric tons of tuna loins shipped to the EU under the autonomous tariff quota (ATQ) system, according to Europeche's analysis. 

Mattlet said there was a contrast between the high standards upheld by European fisheries and the lower standards applied by those fleets whose produce eventually entered European markets duty-free. This system is deeply flawed and needs to be addressed urgently, she argued.

In September 2023 -- in relation to the ATQ regulations to be implemented from 2024 onwards -- the Basque Country's Izaskun Bilbao Barandica, a member of European Parliament for the Renew party, asked the EU if it believed the ATQ system for tuna allowed European shipowners to be competitive.

"How will it incorporate sustainability criteria into the ATQs to assure consumers of canned tuna that all canned tuna complies with European social and environmental standards, in line with the farm to fork strategy?" She further asked.

The European Commission replied that the ATQs' purpose "is to grant access to raw materials or semi-finished fisheries goods that are not available in the EU in sufficient quantities."

"They ensure the supply of fish to the EU processing industry, which would otherwise not be able to satisfy consumers’ demand. The ATQs apply erga omnes to all third countries and the EU importers who provide fish to the EU processing industry are free to choose the source of their supply."

Upgrade to Trade Portal to view

It also said it was aware of the sustainability concerns and that it intended to assess the ATQ regime in terms of the environmental sustainability of stocks but also in terms of social and economic sustainability "in order to consider future policy choices."

Europeche is keen to stress that the European Commission stays hot on those environmental, social and economic factors. Mattlet hopes such criteria will be included in upcoming regulations, suggesting this could see a decrease in ATQs for unsustainable products entering European markets.

Yellowfin overfishing

Addressing the issues in the Indian Ocean, where Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC) parties have been unable to stop yellowfin overfishing in the last few years due to the lack of agreement on quota reductions, Mattlet acknowledged the challenges posed by the decision of several coastal states to object to the yellowfin tuna management plan.

While some parties, including the EU, decreased their catches in line with the management plan, others decided not to apply it and dramatically increased their catches, disrupting the balance, she said. Mattlet stressed the need for a common, universally accepted approach to management in the Indian Ocean to mitigate these issues effectively.

She is cautiously optimistic that challenges can be overcome. She acknowledged the risks but emphasized that sustainable fishing was possible through good management by regional fisheries management organizations.

She called for increased transparency, better vessel monitoring, and collaboration among contracting parties to the IOTC and ICCAT to ensure the successful implementation of management plans and to adapt measures where needed.

The next meeting of the IOTC will take place in Bangkok, Thailand, during the week starting May 13, just one week before the Infofish tuna conference.

In a separate interview, Julio Moron Ayala, president of the Spanish fishing industry association Cepesca, also warned of the dire situation in the Atlantic Ocean's tuna fishing industry.

He cited various factors contributing to "this disaster," including ICCAT's three-month FAD fishing ban and the influx of Asian vessels under African flags, which undermined European operators, he said.

Moron also highlighted "unfair competition" in terms of operating costs and social costs between European and extra-European vessels, as well as lax regulation enforcement, especially regarding ICCAT FAD closure compliance.

Furthermore, economic conditions are worsening, leading many fishing companies to bankruptcy, he said. The increased fishing of smaller species, such as sardines, by extra-European fleets off the African coast is negatively impacting local populations and tuna availability, according to Moron. Although scientific reports indicate the recovery of certain tuna species in the Atlantic region, economic performance remains difficult.

The influx of tuna products from Asia under the ATQ system will keep European raw material prices low until March, he predicted. This will happen each year under the current ATQ system, which runs until 2026, he predicted. The graph below shows skipjack tuna prices for delivery in Bangkok, Thailand.
