title: Cepesca head calls for holistic approach to EU fisheries policy this year
content:
A comprehensive overhaul of the European fisheries policy is needed after the upcoming European elections, according to the Spanish fishing sector.

Julio Moron Ayala, recently named as president of the Spanish confederation of fisheries, also known as Cepesca, has emphasized the need for a policy that transcends the boundaries of environmental considerations and instead takes a holistic approach, factoring in food security, public health, and the well-being of European citizens.

With the upcoming European elections on the horizon, Moron told Undercurrent News he hopes to inspire a transformative shift in the European Commission's approach to agriculture and fisheries, placing "sustainable fish production and consumption at the forefront of the political agenda" as the battle against climate change rages on and global food security becomes increasingly precarious.

European fishing trade body Europeche has also called for a structural shift within the European Commission, specifically proposing the establishment of a dedicated EU fisheries commissioner for the term 2024-2029, separate from environmental affairs, with a strong focus on ensuring food security. 

The 2024 European Parliament election is scheduled to be held on June 6-9, 2024.

Moron did acknowledge the European Council's management of EU communal waters, noting that most fish populations are being managed responsibly. He commended the recent endorsement of the management approach by the European Court of Justice, which considers both socio-economic considerations and environmental sustainability. Moron stressed the importance of balancing these factors, acknowledging that fishing is a vital source of food for the population.

Moron also touched on the challenges facing the fishing industry in Spain and the EU, noting that Cepesca has been involved in disputed negotiations with Norway in the North Sea, the EU, and Iceland.

He emphasized the challenges local fisheries face in the Mediterranean, particularly issues related to engine power and increased downtime for Mediterranean fleets.

He also discussed the "dire situation" in the Atlantic Ocean's tuna fishing industry. He cited various factors contributing to "this disaster," including the three-month fishing ban and claimed an influx of Asian vessels under African flags that has undermined European operators.

Moron, who is also the director at the Spanish Organization of Associated Producers of Large-scale Tuna Freezer Vessels and the Association of Large-scale Tuna Freezer Vessels, claimed "unfair competition" regarding operating and social costs between European and extra-European vessels, as well as lax regulation enforcement, especially regarding the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas' fish aggregating device closure compliance. 

Economic conditions are worsening, leading many fishing companies to bankruptcy, he said, adding that increased fishing of smaller species, such as sardines, by extra-European fleets off the African coast is negatively impacting local populations and tuna availability.

Although scientific reports indicate the recovery of certain tuna species in the Atlantic region, economic performance remains difficult, he said.

Positive achievements

Despite these challenges, Moron pointed out several significant successes in EU fisheries management.

One notable achievement is the recovery of certain fish populations, such as albacore tuna, thanks to "spectacular management" efforts, as well as the success story of the bluefin tuna in the Mediterranean Sea, which has been effectively managed through quotas, he claimed.

The management of anchovy, sardine, hake, and crayfish in European waters is also headed in the right direction, he said, arguing that simplistic approaches, such as closing protected maritime zones or banning fishing entirely, are not the solution.

Instead, he advocated for a more challenging yet effective fisheries management approach, emphasizing that results have been demonstrated in many global fishing grounds.

One of the achievements Moron highlighted was the sustainability of tuna populations, with nearly 85% of consumed tuna worldwide coming from sustainable sources. He is optimistic this figure will continue to rise with the help of scientific assessments.

title: European fishing industry condemns French authority’s sudden Bay of Biscay closure
content:
The European Association of Fish Producer Organisations (EAPO) and Europeche expressed "deep concern and disapproval" over the unexpected decision by the French national authority to urgently close the Bay of Biscay to fishing activities. 

The abrupt enforcement, effective from Jan. 22 to Feb. 20, targets a broad range of vessels over eight meters, impacting over 500 EU fishing vessels and the entire sector dependent on these fisheries. 

The fishing ban, initially limited to French vessels, has been expanded to include all EU and third-country fishing boats, despite the rules outlined in the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP).

EAPO and Europeche have condemned the lack of prior consultation and the absence of compensation for affected vessels, calling it "a severe blow to European unity and the collaborative framework of the CFP."

"How can France unilaterally close its waters to all EU vessels with no prior consultation, a mere four days prior to the closure and without providing any compensation? France's rushed use of article 13 exposes the deficiencies within the CFP and deals a severe blow to European unity that is central to it," said EAPO president Esben Sverdrup-Jensen. 

The urgency claimed by France is met with skepticism by the European fishing industry, especially considering the ICES advice and the Commission's proposal for revising the joint recommendation for winter 2025. 

Europeche president, Javier Garat, also emphasized the importance of a thorough EU impact assessment and a full review of the decision to ensure compliance with the CFP and its safeguards.

"While our members remain dedicated to responsible and sustainable fishing, the precedent established by this decision undermines the trust our fishers place in the CFP," Garat said.

"It is challenging to advocate for consultation, cooperation, proportionality and a bottom-up approach when this decision contradicts those principles. A thorough EU impact assessment and a full review of these decisions is imperative to ensure compliance with the CFP and its safeguards. As guardian of the treaties, the Commission must step in to secure that EU rules are applied correctly," he concluded.

title: Chinese processors eye Europe ‘battlefield’ for whitefish, Pacific salmon
content:
Additional reporting by Louis Harkell.

Chinese seafood processors are shifting their focus to the European export market after the recently expanded US ban on imports of certain Russian whitefish products, according to Undercurrent News industry sources in the country.

The ban, announced in an executive order by US president Joe Biden on Dec. 22, blocks most imports of Russian salmon, cod, crab and pollock, even when processed in third countries like China. This has dealt a major blow to China's seafood export industry, which relies heavily on Russian raw materials.

"If they can't sell to the US, they will look for buyers in Europe," a seafood industry veteran of 20 years told Undercurrent last week. "The battlefield in Europe will be highly competitive."

The executive of a major Dalian processor agreed, noting that Chinese exporters targeting Europe also face the prospect of higher tariffs and stiffer competition from US firms.

China's seafood processing industry employs tens of thousands of workers, especially in Shandong and Liaoning provinces. Labor costs have been rising, eroding China's competitive advantage. "Our labor costs have been rising and are now higher than those in Vietnam and India," said the first source.

In the fall of last year, several Chinese processing factories were also identified as employing Uyghur workers from Xinjiang, which under US law precludes them from supplying that market. This and other pressures also weigh on client purchases.

"It is not feasible for such a large industry to undergo big changes, given a short transition period," the second executive said. "Many are unprepared; a lot of people depend on it for their livelihoods."

"It's hard to say how many opportunities lie ahead in the future," the first Dalian executive added.

Exports to Europe greater than US

According to Undercurrent's seafood trade portal, China exported 47,703 metric tons of frozen cod fillets to the EU and UK in 2022, or 46% of total cod fillet exports. Exports to the US topped 26,843t, or a 26% share.

In pollock, China's exports to the EU and UK hit 125,697t of frozen fillets, or 60% of the total. The US received a relatively tiny 11,087t, or 5%. 

Lastly, China exported 20,718t of Pacific salmon fillets to the EU and UK in 2022, or 29% of total exports. By comparison, the US was sent 27,810t of fillets in the category, a 39% share. 

Some see a chance to expand China's domestic whitefish market. At November's China Fisheries and Seafood Expo, the chair of Dalian Haiqing Food expressed optimism about growth in demand, especially if prices fall.

However, the sources said Chinese consumers need to be educated on the differences between wild-caught species like pollock and cod. "The market needs to be categorized, with cod targeting high-end demand and pollock the more affordable segment," one said.

"At the very least, processors will make every effort to adjust and review their operations to make a positive impression on the European market," the industry veteran said.

title: Editor’s choice: Loophole in ban on Russia lets most pollock imports into US; Ecuador’s shrimp industry ‘on edge’
content:
EMEA editor Neil Ramsden brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous fortnight. 

The implications of president Joe Biden's new executive order (EO) to keep more Russian seafood out of the US continued to be our most-read news last week; specifically, the revelation that the hole in the EO is big enough for a truck full of frozen Alaska pollock fillets that is. The order gave importers 60 days -- until Feb. 21 -- to get into compliance, but the devil is in the details of the documents instructing US border agents on how to enforce import bans. In the case of EO 14114, one memo instructs agents to limit the expanded ban to include only Russian-harvested cod, salmon, crab and pollock with certain harmonized tariff schedule codes. 

The US pollock industry is working now to close the loophole, and success is a certainty, Craig Morris, CEO of the Genuine Alaska Pollock Producers, told Undercurrent News.

Meanwhile, the gap between Russian and Norwegian headed and gutted Atlantic cod prices has widened to a chasm again after the EO, having closed to $100-$200 per metric ton before. With the order meaning US importers cannot bring product processed in third countries using Russian raw material after Feb. 21, prices for 1-2.5-kilogram H&G Norwegian Atlantic cod delivered to China have leaped to over $4,600/t from $4,100-$4,200/t in December.

The US will be short of some 90,000t of cod, live weight equivalent, following the newly expanded US ban on Russian fish to include products processed in third countries, according to a seafood analyst with the Norwegian Seafood Council. 

Undercurrent has created an infographic showing the current state of play when it comes to what seafood products are limited from entering the US.

Ecuador's shrimp sector faces growing challenges as heightened security risks overshadow its resilience and long-term prosperity, exploding this week in multiple incidents. "We ended 2023 with a total of 77 criminal incidents against the shrimp sector, resulting in 58 injuries and four fatalities, but we started 2024 even worse, with extremely high levels of insecurity across all regions of the country," a mid-sized Ecuadorian shrimp producer, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told Undercurrent last week. 

Trident Seafoods' Japanese operation has sold its majority stake in a salmon roe joint venture (JV) to its local partner, a move the US industry giant told Undercurrent is not connected to its ongoing domestic restructure. On Dec. 29, 2023, Trident Seafoods Japan sold off all its shares in Trident Niigata Foods to the wholesaler Niigata Reizo. Trident Niigata Foods is a fish roe producer, established in 2015 as a JV with 3,000 shares held by Trident Seafoods Japan and 1,500 shares from Niigata Reizo. 

Also last week, the International Finance Corporation, a key entity within the World Bank Group, approved a loan of up to $20 million for Omarsa, Ecuador's second-largest shrimp processor. The aim is to promote a competitive and sustainable shrimp sector focused on exports in Ecuador.

The sale process for at-sea pollock processing giant American Seafoods Group (ASG) is seemingly being delayed by the US government's failure to finalize a settlement reached by the two parties nearly six months ago. A complaint filed by Seattle, Washington-based pollock giant ASG subsidiaries Kloosterboer International Forwarding and Alaska Reefer Management in Alaska District Court on Jan. 4 argues the company is stuck in "corporate purgatory" over the US government's failure to finalize a settlement reached by the two parties nearly six months ago.

However, a federal judge in the US state of Alaska has granted one final extension to the US government to review the terms of its settlement with ASG, giving it until Feb. 5 to finalize its agreement with the at-sea pollock processing giant.

US representative Jared Huffman has stepped up his attack on Sysco, leading a group of lawmakers to press president Joe Biden to cancel all federal contracts with the world's largest broadliner unless it ends its relationships with all Chinese companies involved in forced labor and illegal unreported and unregulated fishing.

It's a common refrain heard among seafood wholesalers. If retailers would only pass along the dramatic drop in prices for shrimp they are getting from them, consumers would respond and buy more, improving the state of the market, they say. But it's more complicated than that, argues Angel Rubio, an analyst with the US-based pricing service Urner Barry.

And finally, Grimsby, UK-based processor and distributor Atlantic Fresh has sold out of its French import business, SAS Atlantic Fresh Europe. In its 2022 financial report, filed to the UK's Companies House at the end of 2023, it said that as of November 2023, it had "disposed of its entire shareholding" in the Boulogne-sur-Mer-based division.

title: Untitled
content:
Focus on Labour Exploitation (FLEX), in collaboration with the International Transport Workers Federation (ITF) and the Fair Food Programme, has launched an initiative aimed at combating worker exploitation in the UK fishing industry.

This project, known as the Worker-driven Social Responsibility (WSR) program, marks the first of its kind in Europe and is set to address the critical issue of labor abuse within the sector, according to the organizations, according to the groups.

The WSR program, after an intensive 12-month planning phase, is now officially launched as a two-year pilot initiative. Its primary objective is to establish worker-driven, market-enforced mechanisms and systems designed to enhance working conditions and tackle labor exploitation in the UK fishing industry.

Lucila Granada, CEO of FLEX, expressed her enthusiasm for the initiative.

"WSR truly is a ground-breaking model, and we are excited to be bringing it to the UK to help restructure the power imbalances that exist in the fishing industry between worker and employer, and in particular, safeguard and improve working conditions for migrant fishers who are a vital part of the UK’s fishing industry," she said.

The WSR model, with over a decade of proven success across various industries, addresses the power imbalances between workers and employers and between buyers and suppliers, which contribute to abuses within global supply chains.

Chris Williams, ITF fisheries expert, emphasized the importance of the pilot in providing greater protection and improved working conditions for migrant fishers and tackling the issues surrounding seafarer's transit visas.

The UK pilot program will commence in northeast Scotland.

title: EU fisheries’ control system receives digital revamp
content:
The EU has implemented a significant overhaul of its fisheries control system in early January, introducing new rules aimed at modernizing and strengthening the regulation of fishing activities within its waters and by EU vessels abroad.

The revamped regulations seek to combat overfishing, promote sustainability, and create a more streamlined and uniform control system, it said.

According to an EU press release, one of the primary objectives of these revised regulations is to use new technology to monitor fishing activities more effectively and improve catch traceability.

Key changes include better tracking of fishing vessels and mandatorty electronic reporting and catch recording. The EU hopes further digitalization will better enforce control rules seamlessly from when fish are caught to when they reach consumers.

Virginijus Sinkevicius, the EU commissioner for the environment, oceans, and fisheries, emphasized that this new control system is the product of five years of negotiations. It is designed to protect marine resources better and ensure the strict enforcement of fisheries control rules throughout the supply chain, he said.

Under the new regulations, fishing activities will be entirely digitalized, including geo-localization and electronic reporting for all fishing vessels, regardless of size. This includes catch recording and reporting in recreational fisheries and user-friendly mobile apps for fishers.

The new regulations also include new rules for remote electronic monitoring, including onboard cameras, for fishing vessels above 18 meters, especially those at high risk of non-compliance with the landing obligation.

Harmonized sanctions have also been introduced for serious breaches of the common fisheries policy.

The European Commission will continue working on the necessary regulations to ensure uniform implementation across the EU, it said.

title: Biden’s expansion of ban on Russia lets most pollock imports into US
content:
The hole in president Joe Biden's new executive order (EO) to keep more Russian seafood out of the US is big enough that you could drive a truck through it -- a truck full of frozen Alaska pollock fillets that is, Undercurrent News has discovered.

There was much rejoicing in the US state of Alaska on Dec. 22, 2023. That's the date Biden signed EO 14114, further expanding his nearly two-year-old ban on Russian seafood to include products that were processed in other countries, thereby changing their countries of origin. The order gave importers 60 days -- until Feb. 21 -- to get into compliance.

The Alaska pollock industry and others had complained that such an expansion was needed to stop a lot of Russian products that were still getting into the US. But they soon will be complaining again.

The devil is in the details of the documents produced by the Department of Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), which gives instructions to US border agents on how to enforce import bans. In the case of EO 14114, one memo -- also issued on Dec. 22 --instructs agents to limit the expanded ban to include only Russian-harvested cod, salmon, crab and pollock with certain harmonized tariff schedule (HTS) codes. 

Russians see Alaskan pollock ‘monopoly’ the only result of new US trade ban

The lists of HTS codes covered by the ban are long for cod, salmon and crab, each including 23-43 items. However, when it comes to pollock, OFAC included only three codes: 0304.53.0025, 1604.19.1000 and 1604.19.2500.

Those HTS codes account for about 11,039 metric tons of pollock or other related seafood worth $31.8 million that was imported into the US during the first 11 months of 2023, Undercurrent News found in a review of seafood trade data maintained by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. 

Left off the banned list were key categories such as frozen fillets (030475000) and frozen fillets in blocks bigger than 4.5 kilograms (0304751000). Combined, they accounted for a much larger combined 21,277t of fish worth $74.5m imported by the US in the first 11 months of 2023. 

The pollock products left off the banned list were sourced by the US from nine different countries, but China was the largest source by far, accounting for 19,365t worth $67.7m during the first 11 months of 2023. 

Expanded US ban on Russian seafood gives importers 60 days to receive product

Alaska pollock industry sources contacted by Undercurrent this week said they were unaware of the loophole but digging in for more details. One policy expert contacted by Undercurrent said he was hopeful that OFAC would address what he believed to have been a simple error in the implementation of the EO. He noted that the agency had the power to close the loophole without another action by the president.

The source noted the language in OFAC's memo, which says the order includes "any subsequent revisions to the list of HTSUS classifications." He said he expected such revisions to be forthcoming.

title: Canada training Ecuador, Peru on new tech to combat illegal fishing
content:
Canada is collaborating with Ecuador and Peru to combat illegal fishing by introducing and implementing its space-based Dark Vessel Detection (DVD) platform, Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) reports.

DFO said Thursday (Jan. 4) on its LinkedIn page that its officials and representatives from MDA, a space research and technology firm in Brampton, Ontario, went to Ecuador and Peru to provide training and support to officials from their national fisheries. 

The DVD platform uses satellite technology to locate and track vessels whose location-transmitting devices have been switched off. The platform provides real-time data and comprehensive monitoring capabilities, allowing authorities to effectively track and intercept illegal fishing vessels. With the technology, authorities expect to better enforce fishing regulations, detect unauthorized fishing activities, and hold violators accountable.

Both Ecuador and Peru are vulnerable to illegal fishing due to the presence of massive distant water fleets operating in the region, said the DFO. By implementing the DVD platform, both countries aim to protect their fish stocks and marine biodiversity from the harmful effects of illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing.

title: Scottish Greens demand talks over troubled salmon farming industry
content:
Amid escalating concerns over the state of Scotland's salmon farming industry, the Scottish Greens have urged the rural affairs secretary, Mairi Gougeon, to engage in discussion.

Rural affairs spokesperson Ariane Burgess highlighted mounting problems in the industry, citing increasing numbers of farmed fish deaths, diseases, and deteriorating conditions in Scotland's waters.

While the Scottish Greens had previously advocated for a moratorium on salmon farm expansions, they have opted to collaborate with the Scottish government and industry to foster improvements, they said.

Burgess wrote a letter emphasizing the situation's urgency, referencing "the Scottish Green parliamentary group's strong concern about the slow pace of reform of the fish farming industry."

"This is an important issue for our party members, constituents and environmental NGOs and is a growing concern for the public," she said.

"I trust that we can work together to deliver urgent, meaningful action required to address the environmental impacts of the industry and reduce fish-farmed deaths, disease and suffering."

Burgess also outlined specific areas of concern, such as removing exemptions for the aquaculture sector from the new National Planning Framework, implementing spatial plans to prevent site establishment in unsuitable areas, and enforcing the Scottish Environmental Protection Agency's regulations across fish farms.

Additionally, she highlighted the importance of minimizing harm to wild salmon, strategic planning to avert long-term damage, enforcement mechanisms for license breaches, and reducing chemical usage and waste in the industry.

"This program has been delayed, and, given the deterioration of welfare and environmental standards that this year's mortality rate, in particular, reflects, the commitments no longer appear to be adequate to the challenge at hand," she concluded.

title: Untitled
content:
While the Alaskan seafood sector has largely proclaimed the expanded measure on Russian seafood as a win, the Russian whitefish sector foresees little added impact, instead just noting the "monopoly" Alaskan producers will have in the US.

Alexey Buglak, head of Russia's Pollock Catchers Association, told Undercurrent News that Russian companies had not supplied significant volumes of pollock to the US domestic market for many years, "so the decision will not have a significant direct impact on the Russian pollock industry."

Of course, the US banned direct imports from Russia in March 2022 anyway.

"Alaskan pollock fishermen have been trying to squeeze Chinese pollock fillets out of the US domestic market for many years," he added. "These efforts intensified several years ago when, along with a decline in pollock consumption in the US, the share of Alaskan pollock fillets began to decline," he claimed.

China has supplied the US with some 20,000-25,000 metric tons of twice-frozen pollock fillets, mainly produced using fish of Russian origin, for the past several years, he said.

"I think that the redistribution of volumes at the market will happen quite quickly. The resulting gap in the US market will be filled by Alaskan pollock, and the vacated niche in foreign markets will be filled by second-frozen fillets from China or a Russian product."

"In my opinion, we can definitely say that American processors and consumers will lose more from this decision. The first will have to overpay for Alaskan fillets, which will be even more expensive -- extra growth in demand will lead to rocketing pricing. And for the second, consumers, this will automatically lead to an accelerated increase in retail prices for pollock products."

This largely tallies with comments made by Michael Kotok, president of US importer Arctic Fisheries, who claimed the Alaskan seafood sector had "duped the government by masquerading their monopolistic behavior as patriotism," in a thinly veiled jab at Trident Seafoods, which is having to look at selling four plants in Alaska.

"This Amendment further restricts Americans' access to seafood, including various species preferred by consumers. Russia 1 US 0," he claimed. "This Amendment raises prices of seafood to Americans. We raised our prices minutes after the announcement of the amendment. Similar species from other origins will rise in price as well. We weren't the only ones to raise prices, others followed. Russia 2 US 0."

Savely Karpukhin, deputy CEO of Russian Fishery Company, told Undercurrent his firm had not supplied any fillets to Trident's factory in Germany (formerly Pickenpack) for some time; "we have previously, but as far I know, they stopped buying Russian origin raw material at all."

"We know some Asian processors (not only Chinese) who have been supplying the US market with double-frozen pollock fillet products (not blocks, rather ready meals and other value-added products), but now they will obviously lose this part of the business."

US producers will be happy to see the closure of the "loophole" that allows Russian fish to enter the US via processing in third countries as "this is the final step to defend the US domestic market," Karpukhin presumed.

"Now US producers will have a pure monopoly on the domestic market, where the prices are more lucrative compared to the EU and other significant markets." 

The impact of the amendment should be good for US producers, assuming they manage to substitute more affordable Russian-origin products with US raw material and "keep this volume alive," he added, noting this was a significant "if."

"Otherwise, there will be just less consumption domestically in the US (if this volume just shrinks and the consumers move to other proteins) and, making things worse for Russian producers, they will make it even worse for themselves, since overall harvesting/ production volume is growing and the pressure on the market remains strong. Everybody now should be focused on growing the consumption volume, in any form, in all the markets instead of imposing new limitations. I hope they will succeed in their own domestic sales."

Silver Bay, Trident welcome the move

It's been less than a week since the president Joe Biden administration's announcement on Dec. 22 that Russian seafood processed in third countries would no longer be allowed in the US.

Still, industry groups and lawmakers in the US state of Alaska are already applauding the news, calling it a win for the state's seafood sector.

Silver Bay Seafoods and Trident both welcomed the expanded ban in statements, with Trident CEO Joe Bundrant calling the executive order an "enormous win" for the US. 

Trade groups that advocate for fishermen and processors, including the United Fishermen of Alaska and the Alaska Seafood Marketing Institute, also expressed their support, as did the Pacific Seafood Processors Association (PSPA).

Biden to expand ban on Russian seafood to include product processed in other countries

"We thank Senator [Dan] Sullivan and our Congressional Delegation for their leadership on this issue, which is vital to US fishermen and processors," said PSPA president Julie Decker.

Alaska's congressional delegation, made up of US senators Lisa Murkowski and Sullivan – both Republicans – and US representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat, have been some of the loudest critics in Washington DC of the loophole that allowed Russian seafood to enter the country after being processed in a third country, despite a ban imposed by the Biden administration in 2022.

Each was similarly quick to issue statements lauding the executive order, with Murkowski commending "the relentless and dogged advocacy of Senator Dan Sullivan and other Alaskans who have led on this charge to protect Alaska's fishing industry."

"In the midst of a truly difficult time for Alaska's fishermen, these are stabilizing steps that will help end Russia's evasion of sanctions and China's dumping of overharvested Russian fish onto American markets," Murkowski said. "That, in turn, will help seafood prices recover, restore balance and basic fairness to markets, and cut off a key source of funding for Putin's catastrophic war in Ukraine, all at the same time."

Sullivan similarly touted the ban as a win for the US and for Alaska's fishing industry at a press conference on Dec. 22.

Alaska sablefish harvesters urge restraint on catch for 2024 with market weak

"I think this is going to force some of the American importers to finally wake up that their business model relying on Chinese and Russian fish wasn't a good one," he said. "Alaskan fishermen will be able to supply these markets."

Sullivan said that US Customs and Border Patrol is currently working with the US Treasury Department to come up with enforcement rules and tracking methods that can be implemented as "expeditiously as possible." Meanwhile, according to language included in the executive order, companies have until Feb. 21 – 60 days from issuance – for seafood products to make it into the US from orders placed before the executive order was signed.

Just how the ban will play out on the market once Russian imports to the US ebb is unclear, though. The National Fisheries Institute, for its part, called the expanded ban an "unfortunate step" on Friday, as previously reported by Undercurrent, saying other measures like tariffs may have been as impactful without jeopardizing American processing jobs.

title: Expanded US ban on Russian seafood gives importers 60 days to receive product
content:
President Joe Biden's expansion of his ban on Russian seafood to include product processed in other countries went into effect instantly on Friday (Dec. 22). However, products ordered before the ban still have 60 days to make it into the US.

The White House announced Friday morning that Biden intended to sign a new executive order (EO) expanding on EO 14068 by prohibiting seafood of Russian origin that was processed in other countries, like China, as reported by Undercurrent News. The statement announcing the action has since been updated to say that Biden has signed the order, Undercurrent has confirmed.

Questions abound in the seafood industry about how the order will be enforced. But a memorandum issued by the US Department of Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) and found by Undercurrent answers one of the most common queries: How fast does the order go into effect?

Biden to expand ban on Russian seafood to include product processed in other countries

In General License No. 83, published Friday, OFAC director Bradley Smith clarifies: "(a) Except as provided in paragraph (b) of this general license, all transactions prohibited by the determination of Dec. 22, 2023, made pursuant to section 1(a)(i)(B) of Executive Order (EO) 14068, as amended by EO of Dec. 22, 2023 ('Prohibitions Related to Imports of Certain Categories of Fish, Seafood, and Preparations Thereof'), that are ordinarily incident and necessary to the importation into the United States of seafood derivative products, pursuant to written contracts or written agreements entered into prior to Dec. 22, 2023 are authorized through 12:01 a.m. eastern standard time, Feb. 21, 2024."

US president Joe Biden at a press event hastily called on March 11, 2022, to discuss further actions against Russia in relation to invasion of Ukraine.

NFI not a fan

Several seafood executives told Undercurrent Friday that they were stunned by Biden's expansion of his earlier EO, which was signed back on March 11, 2022, and put into effect on June 23, 2022, as a response to Russia's invasion of Ukraine. It dealt a painful blow to many US importers.

Previously, Russia was the US' eighth-largest source of seafood, accounting for imports of 48,867 metric tons worth $1.2 billion in 2021, a 34% increase in value over what it sent the US in 2020. Russian seafood exports to the US in 2021 included roughly 80 items, but the most valuable were frozen snow crab, 18,799t worth $509.2m, and frozen red king crab, 8,486t worth $419.7m.

However, the earlier ban left open a major loophole that the Russians have exploited, said critics of the policy change.

A considerable amount of seafood imported by the US -- including Alaska pollock, wild-caught salmon and cod -- is being harvested in Russia but is listed as coming from other countries where it's processed, including especially China. That allowed it to enter the US due to the rules around country-of-origin labeling.

Some in the seafood industry are celebrating Biden's action.

The Alaska Seafood Marketing Institute (ASMI) thanked the administration along with all three members of Alaska's delegation to Congress who worked to get the change, including US senators Lisa Murkowski and Dan Sullivan and representative Mary Peltola.

"This action will level the playing field and allows Alaska’s fishing industry to compete fairly in the U.S. market at a time when it is needed most," ASMI said.

Peltola was part of a large 38-member, bi-partisan group of US lawmakers to press Biden for an expansion of the Russian seafood ban. The US imported $300 million in salmon and pollock from China in 2022 -- some caught in the US and reprocessed in China, but a majority likely originating from Russia, according to an International Trade Commission report they quoted.

Russian caught pollock Credit: Gidrostroy

She also issued a statement.

"I cannot stress enough the importance of safeguarding our North Pacific Ocean and ensuring the economic well-being of Alaskan fishermen," she said. "We must not turn a blind eye to the alarming threat that unregulated foreign trawlers pose to our local fishermen and marine ecosystems. Today, we have achieved a major milestone in pro-fish policymaking, equipping us with the necessary tools to fiercely protect our interests and promote sustainable fishing practices."

Not everyone is a fan of the administration's action, however. The National Fisheries Institute (NFI), which represents a large number of US seafood importers, processors and wholesalers, issued a statement on Friday that suggested a better approach was available.

"The unintended consequences of this effort will very likely include layoffs right here at home," NFI said. "Let's be clear, American seafood processing jobs are now in jeopardy. It is an unfortunate step considering a proposal was made several months ago that would, consistent with EU and UK policies, have imposed a tariff on these products. Those tariffs would have then funded Ukrainian relief efforts, while keeping the raw material for American processing jobs flowing. An opportunity was missed to punish Russia, and support Ukraine at the same time without costing important US jobs."

Prepare for the flood

Recall that there were similar questions about how fast Biden's original ban on the import of Russian seafood should go into effect, as reported by Undercurrent.

OFAC, in its March 11 order, instructed US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to not accept containers of Russian seafood after "12:01 a.m. Eastern Daylight Time, March 25, 2022" -- just two weeks from the date of the EO. The administration then revised its instructions to give seafood importers more than three months.

Some were critical of the move later, as it resulted in a flood of Russian products into the US. In total, the US imported 23,141t of seafood worth $915.4m from Russia in the first six months of 2022, 10% more volume and 86% more value than the first six months of 2021, as reported by Undercurrent.  

Russians dismissive of ban expansion

Two Russian seafood industry groups disagreed Friday about the potential impact of the US' expansion of its ban.

They are unlikely to have any direct repercussions for the Russian seafood sector, said Alexander Fomin, executive director of the Russian Association of Processing and Trading Businesses of the Fishery Market. However, they may adversely affect Russian seafood exports to China, he told the Kommersant, a business daily newspaper.

Fomin doesn't believe the change will be a real blow to Russian exports of salmon, cod and pollock, but hopes that Russian crab products processed in China could start making their way more to the US have been dashed, he said. The expansion of the ban could lead to a decrease in the volume of crab exports to China and also a further decline in prices, he said.

Russia salmon fishing. Credit: TASS

Russia's seafood trade with China reached 1.1 million metric tons in the first 11 months of 2023, a 94% year-on-year increase. China spent nearly $2.3 billion, 31% more than the previous 11-month period. Russia's exports to China exceeded 1m metric tons, up 102%, and $2.0bn, up 38%.

Another industry group, the All-Russian Fishery Association (known under its Russian acronym VARPE), meanwhile, was more dismissive of the prohibitions. The new restrictions are "painful" for the US domestic seafood market amid a tight supply of crab and cod products, VARPE head German Zverev told journalists in Moscow on Friday. The prohibitions will affect US consumers and not Russian fishermen, he said.

title: Controversy surrounds PNG’s first MPAs co-managed by indigenous groups
content:
Papua New Guinea (PNG) had created two vast new marine protected areas (MPAs) surrounding the waters of Lovongai and Murat in New Ireland, the country's northeastern province, reports Mongabay. 

The MPAs -- first to be co-managed by indigenous communities and which triple the country's marine area under protection, despite comprising less than 1% of PNG's marine territory -- have also raised concerns. 

Chiefly, there are potential problems from foreign-led conservation in an area experiencing poverty, conflict and minimal government support. 

John Aini, a community leader from Lovongai, expressed doubt that MPAs were the best form of management for community fisheries, noting previous experiences when outside groups instituted top-down initiatives preventing communities from accessing the ecosystems they depend on.

The new MPAs, which prohibit the harvesting of certain endangered species and include rules to ensure sustainable fishing practices, are up for review every five years. Communities can request revisions for their area at any time.

However, they do not address concerns about commercial overfishing of sea cucumbers, as national laws override the local MPA laws, while securing sufficient funding for their enforcement is likely to be a challenge.

title: EU: No new regulation needed for unclear plant-based seafood labeling
content:
The EU's directorate general for maritime affairs and fisheries (DG MARE) has dismissed concerns raised by the Market Advisory Council (MAC) about unclear labeling of seafood substitutes, reiterating that existing regulations are clear enough and it is up to member states how they enforce them.

Australian food sector warns consumers ‘being tricked’ by plant-based packaging

The MAC originally provided advice to the European Commission on labeling of plant-based seafood products back in June 2021, and the commission concluded that existing regulations did not need to be modified later that same year.

Two years on, the MAC again wrote to the commission in May regarding new cases of unclear labeling practices, noting new plant-based products in the Netherlands, Spain and the Czech Republic -- among others -- that used names of seafood species, referred to the sea, or featured illustrations of wild seafood on the packaging.

However, DG MARE has once again ruled that existing EU regulations are sufficient.

"It is for member states to enforce the applicable EU rules, notably to ensure that EU consumers are not exposed to misleading food information," it said. "The assessment of whether or not a given term can mislead consumers has a linguistic and cultural dimension, and national authorities are best placed to carry out such an assessment in light of the existing provisions of the FIC [Food Information to Consumers] regulation."

Specifically, Article 7 of the FIC states that food information "shall not be misleading as to the characteristics of the food and, in particular, as to its nature, identity, properties and composition."

The same article also describes misleading as "suggesting, by means of the appearance, the description or pictorial representations, the presence of a particular food or an ingredient, while in reality a component naturally present or an ingredient normally used in that food has been substituted with a different component or ingredient."

However, DG MARE adds that similar examples highlighted by the MAC for plant-based seafood "can presumably be found for substitutes of other food categories."

"Given that the FIC regulation applies to all food products, it is up to member states in their enforcement responsibility to decide whether specific cases are not in line with the provisions of the FIC regulation," DG MARE concluded.

"The regulation provides a clear and sufficient framework for this assessment, and there is, therefore, no need for further specific measures in the case of seafood substitutes at this point."

title: Northwest US shellfish harvesting area closed due to toxin threat
content:
Thurston County, in the US state of Washington, announced the closure of several shellfish harvesting spots over the weekend due to the presence of biotoxins that produce diarrhetic shellfish poisoning.

The closure of harvesting areas for all species in Dana Passage, Pickering Passage and Peale Passage has been enforced, along with Budd Inlet, reported KIRO7. The Burfoot Park, Boston Harbor area, Hope Island and most of Harstine Island have been included in the closure area, too. The locations are near Olympia, the state's capital.

As noted in a news release from the Thurston County government, "biotoxins are produced by naturally occurring plankton which can become concentrated in shellfish. Biotoxins do not harm shellfish but can cause illness or death in humans and other mammals that consume them. Cooking does not destroy the toxin and does not make the shellfish safe to eat."

The symptoms of diarrhetic shellfish poisoning include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea.

title: Atlantic Red Crab, Sea Watch International spotlighted again over child labor allegations
content:
Two seafood processing plants in New Bedford, Massachusetts, are again in the spotlight over reports of federal investigations into alleged child labor practices.

The New Bedford Light reported Monday (Dec. 18) that the US Department of Labor (DOL) is investigating both Atlantic Red Crab and Sea Watch International as well as Workforce Unlimited and B.J.’s Service Company, staffing agencies that operate in New Bedford and Rhode Island, based on a DOL letter dated Nov. 16.

A DOL spokesperson reportedly confirmed Monday that it is investigating the seafood companies. 

"The Wage and Hour Division is wholly committed to the strategic enforcement of worker protections focused on the nation’s most vulnerable workers," the spokesperson said in a statement. "Combating illegal child labor and enforcing the rights of workers employed in industries that pay low wages and have a history of high rates of violations are among our highest priorities. This includes seafood processing.”

The news follows a report published by Frontline, a PBS-related investigative news journal, in September. The Frontline article spotlighted two Guatemalan teenagers who recently arrived in the US after swimming across the border from Mexico.

Atlantic Red Crab owner Jon Williams reportedly told Frontline that one of the teens his company employed was hired through a staffing agency and removed from the premises when the violation was discovered.

"It isn’t like I hired this person, but the staffing agency sent that person to my building," he said. "And yes, that person worked in my building. I can't deny that. But sometimes I have 150 people working in my building, and they all wear hairnets and face masks. So it’s pretty hard to tell an 18-year-old from a 16-year-old."

Similarly, The New Bedford Light reportedly interviewed former New Bedford seafood plant workers who were children when they started. That included one woman from Guatemala who said she worked for Maryland-based Sea Watch International when she was 15, sorting clams, crushing shells and extracting meat for packaging. 

The US is experiencing an unprecedented surge in child labor, The New Bedford Light noted. The number of children employed in violation of federal law has increased more than five-fold since a low point in 2015.

title: Canadian lawmakers call for raising of lobster poaching fine amidst disappointing catches
content:
Liberal provincial lawmakers are asking for lobster license rules to be enforced and heftier fines for illegal catches in Canada's largest lobster fishery, where landings are down to open the season, reports the radio station 101.5 The Hawk.

Landings are down as much as 75% offshore and 30% inshore off the southeastern and southwestern coasts of Nova Scotia -- Lobster Fishing Areas 33 and 34 -- marking the most significant decline in a quarter century, according to the radio station.

The experience has caused some Liberal lawmakers in the province to focus on poaching. They're calling for the Progressive Conservative Party, which took power in late 2021, to make good on promises that they would escalate fines for illegal fishing activities from CAD 100,000 ($73,655) to CAD 1 million. 

"The lobster fishery is the lifeblood of our economy and demands protection," opposition leader Zach Churchill is quoted as saying. "We’ve consistently urged the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) and the provincial government to bolster the presence of enforcement officers on the ground to thwart the unlawful poaching of lobster. The province must promptly elevate the fine for illegal catches from $100,000 to $1 million, and wrongdoers should also face the revocation of their licenses."

title: Canadian snow crab holds its own in Japan despite flood of cheaper Russian product
content:
Russian snow crab might be flooding the Japanese market at much lower prices as a result of bans blocking its import by the US and other countries, but the Canadian product is holding its own in the Land of the Rising Sun, crab market expert Les Hodges tells Undercurrent News.

Japan imported 3,408 metric tons of frozen Canadian snow crab during the first 10 months of 2023, 12% more in volume than the 3,054t it imported during the same period in 2022, he reports based on data from the Japanese customs service in his latest monthly newsletter for friends and colleagues.

Snow and king crab consultant Les Hodges.

It's been the year of the snow crab in Japan, which has imported an overall 14,622t of the frozen crustaceans from all countries during the first 10 months, 5% more than the 13,954t imported during the same period in 2022. 

"Japan seafood traders are reporting that sales are better than expected and the consumer is enjoying the lower prices," Hodges told Undercurrent.

Japanese consumers paid an average price of $14.08 per kilogram for snow crab from all countries, down 39% from the $23.17/kg paid during the first 10 months of 2022, according to the Japanese data Hodges shared with Undercurrent.

Of course, the reduced prices have dramatically lowered the overall value of Japan's frozen snow crab imports. The data shows they were worth just $205.8m overall during the first 10 months of the year, down 36% from the $323.2m spent during the same period in 2022.

The Japanese news service Asia Nikkei reported last week that frozen Russian snow crab was flooding Japan, causing a dramatic price drop. Russia accounted for 9,621t -- a 66% share of the country's snow crab market -- during the first 10 months of the year. It was an improvement of 5% over the first 10 months of 2022 when Russia sent Japan 9,130t.

As articulated by the Japanese news service and reported earlier by Undercurrent, the flood of Russian snow crab is due in large part to the import ban placed on all Russian seafood by US president Joe Biden in March 2022. The ban took effect in late June 2023, eliminating a market in the US that took 18,823t of frozen Russian snow crab worth $509.9m in 2021. 

Japan has raised tariffs on Russian seafood but has not issued a wholesale ban on the products like it has for Russian vodka and timber products, by contrast.

Adding Russian crab to the blacklist "would have a large impact on Japan's seafood processing industry," a representative of Japan's Fisheries Agency reportedly explained to Nikkei.

Russia made up 8.6% of Japanese seafood imports in 2021 in terms of value, but the country was the source of 56% of its crab imports, 46% of its sea urchin imports, and 56% of its cod roe imports, according to the news service. 

Snow crab legs with lemon slice and mayonnaise. Photograph by Y.A. Photo on Shutterstock.

Meanwhile, desperate to sell its snow crab in other markets, Russia's average wholesale price in Japan during the first 10 months of 2023 was just $12.94/kg, down 39% from the average $21.07/kg paid during the same period in 2022, according to Japan's custom service data.

That's 25% higher than the average wholesale price in Japan for frozen Canadian snow crab, which was $17.34/kg during the first 10 months of 2023, down 39% from the $28.35/kg paid during the same period in 2022.

So how is the more expensive Canadian product staying competitive?

Hodges said it's the taste. Russian crab is usually frozen in brine, making it salty, while Canadian snow crab is quick-cooked and frozen. The Japanese "prefer to add their own salt," Hodges said.

However, the price reduction has hurt Canada, where exporters have received just $59.1m in value from their exports of frozen snow crab to Japan during the first 10 months of 2022, 32% less than the $86.5m received during the same period in 2022. 

Russia, too, has seen a drop in the value of its frozen snow crab exports to Japan due to its reduced prices. It received $124.5m for its exports to Japan in the first 10 months of 2023, 35% less than the $192.3m received during the same period in 2022. 

After the holiday lights have been taken down

The biggest market for Canadian snow crab, of course, remains the United States. Hodges noted in his latest newsletter that the US ate up about 80% to 85% of the Canadian catch at the start of this year's crab fishing season, which began in early April in the southern Gulf of Saint Lawrence but was delayed until May 19 in Newfoundland and Labrador (NL) because of a dispute over dock prices, as previously reported by Undercurrent. 

The US' National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has yet to make its seafood trade data for October available, but Canada represented about 92% of the US' total snow crab imports during the first 10 months of the year, Hodges reported.

"The lower prices in 2023 resulted in a significant increase in retail and food service support over the summer and fall," he said. "Snow crab led the market in premium shellfish."

Snow crab clusters for sale on Aug. 15, 2023 at a Safeway in Silver Spring, Maryland. Photograph by Jason Huffman.

US snow crab imports have dropped from the summer levels over the past two months, "which was expected."

In October 2023, the US took in 887t of snow crab from all countries (mostly Canada), a 43% decrease from October 2022, he noted. In total over the first 10 months, the US has imported 52,435t of snow crab in 2023.

Canada broke its previous all-time 12-month record for snow crab exports to the US -- 46,295t set in 2009 -- back in August, as reported by Undercurrent, so its October number will only serve to build on its record. 

Flood of Canadian snow crab into US sets record with prices still flat

As noted by Hodges, snow crab sales have been assisted in the US by low prices. The average wholesale price range for frozen 5-8 ounce snow crab clusters from NL on Thursday (Dec. 7) was $5.30-$5.55 per pound, slightly reduced from the $5.45-$5.75/lb range reported on Dec. 5 and much reduced from the average range of $7.90-$8.15/lb reported on Dec. 6, 2022, according to Urner Barry. 

Among the reasons wholesale prices have dropped so much in the US is that a large amount of Canadian snow crab was purchased in 2022 when prices were at all-time highs. But much of it didn't make it to retail or foodservice during the year and was still available in inventory when the 2023 season opened with a massive combined quota in Canada of more than 100,000t thanks to an 8.5% increase, as reported by Undercurrent.

Now the question is how much of the 2023 Canadian snow crab will still be in inventory at the beginning of the 2024 season. Sales have been sluggish through the fall, said Hodges. Based on his data, his best estimate right now is that there are about 11,339t to 12,246t of Canadian snow crab that have still not been shipped to market. 

Canadian snow crab blizzard winds down in US

"I've had people tell me that sales have slowed, especially on five-eights (oz clusters)," he told Undercurrent.

Based on his experience, Hodges figures there will still be some crab in storage after the Christmas lights are taken down and the last of the New Year's Eve fireworks have fizzled out.

"As we move into the holidays, (snow crab) is expected to continue being promoted, although it is noted that many retailers have raised the price to the consumer over the last month," he said. "If my numbers are right there's a potential of approximately 5m pounds [2267t]  sold each month before the new season begins.

title: US Coast Guard reshuffles Oregon-based cutters amid worker shortage
content:
A shortfall in recruitment and retention is speeding up the US Coast Guard's plan to decommission cutters and relocate personnel in the US state of Oregon.

The Daily Astorian reports that the USCG will decommission or relocate two 1960s-era legacy cutters from the 17th Street Dock in the city of Astoria, Oregon, this spring. Personnel will also be transferred to appropriately staff the vessels.

"Like many other military services, the Coast Guard continues to experience recruiting and retention challenges," petty officer Steve Strohmaier told the newspaper in an email. "The service is short nearly 10% of our entire enlisted workforce; the shortage exceeds 10% in some mission-critical rates. This is one of the largest workforce shortages in the Coast Guard's 233-year history, and it is impacting our daily operations."

Although, the region won't be without a USCG presence -- two new legacy cutters will be transferred to the area early next year as part of a $30 million contract to expand facilities at nearby Tongue Point in Astoria. The new 154-foot cutters typically operate with 24 crewmembers, and participate in coastal security and fisheries law enforcement.

title: New Jersey lawmaker joins call for tighter scrutiny of Chinese seafood imports
content:
US House representative Frank Pallone has joined the call for more screening of seafood products imported from China in response to recent reports about the use of forced labor.

The New Jersey Democrat hosted a press conference Monday (Dec. 4) to bring attention to the letter he sent to US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) the same day, asking the agency to better ensure compliance with international and domestic trade, safety and labor standards.

"The [Peoples Republic of China's] flagrant disregard for international and domestic laws allows China to export seafood that is often sold at low prices to establish a market advantage and drive out American seafood producers," he wrote. "The unscrutinized import of these seafood products, which are not held to the same rigorous environmental and labor standards as American seafood, harms domestic fishing industries and coastal economies.

US lawmakers ask Costco for audits of China-sourced seafood

"The United States must live up to its role as a leader in defending free and fair-trade systems based on the rule of law," he said. "Your agency has a responsibility to ensure our food imports are of the highest quality and in compliance with all applicable trade, safety, and labor standards. Any failure to do so will pose a significant threat to public health and our economic security."

The US imports about $2 billion worth seafood annually from China.

As reported by Undercurrent, Capitol Hill has been stoked up to address the issue of forced labor in the Chinese seafood industry by a two-part investigative series reported by the Outlaw Ocean Project and published in The New Yorker on Oct. 9.

The articles provided haunting details about crew members being held captive, beaten and suffering from malnutrition aboard vessels in China's distant water fishing fleet. They also shared a thorough accounting of the Chinese program used to enlist and transport a large number of Uyghurs over 1,000 miles from Xinjiang, in the land-locked, northwestern part of China, to seafood processing plants in Shangdong, on the east coast.

Following a two-hour hearing by the Congressional-Executive Commission on China, which featured the investigative reporter Ian Urbina as one of four witnesses on Oct. 24, the commission's co-chairman -- representative Chris Smith, a New Jersey Republican, and senator Jeff Merkley, an Oregon Democrat -- wrote the Department of Homeland Security, CBP's parent agency. They requested the issuance of withhold release orders in relation to all seafood processing facilities in Shandong and Liaoning, China. Such orders direct CBP to detain a shipment of goods over concerns related to the suspected use of forced labor. 

Joint US Congress, White House panel schedule hearing to discuss report on use of forced labor in Chinese seafood

Pallone's letter to CBP doesn't go quite that far.

"I urge CBP to enhance screening for all imported seafood from China to discourage unfair trade practices, economic coercive measures, and other illegal activities," he said. "Without proper enforcement and stepped-up screening by CBP, seafood products tainted with the use of forced labor from Chinese boats and processing centers will continue entering the US. market. Not only is this a violation of international and US law, but it also causes significant harm to American consumers and our domestic seafood industry. I request CBP provide a briefing regarding the agency's efforts to monitor seafood imported from China and guarantee compliance with international and domestic trade, safety, and labor laws."

title: Untitled
content:
A recent illegal fishing case involving Korean vessels sounds an alarm bell about the potential inclusion of illegally caught fish in the global tuna supply chain, according to an NGO.

Last March, Thailand and South Korean authorities took action against a Korean fishing vessel suspected of involvement in illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing. Law enforcement in Bangkok, Thailand, intervened to prevent the South Korea-flagged Sun Flower 7 from offloading over 4,000 metric tons of tuna valued at approximately $7 million.

South Korea's Ministry of Fisheries later imposed a fine on the Sun Flower 7 for severe violations of the country's distant-water fishing regulations, the Environmental Justice Foundation reported.

The Thai and South Korean governments accused the vessel of retrieving fish-aggregating devices (FADs) within Kiribati's exclusive economic zone without authorization to fish in that area.

Accountability.Fish has released a new position paper urging the Western & Central Pacific Fisheries Commission (WCPFC) to take immediate steps to improve transparency and accountability in light of this case.

According to the NGO, it has brought to the forefront several unanswered questions about legal interpretations within the WCPFC's rulings. The situation is further complicated by the absence of independent observers aboard the reefer vessels that support the purse seiner fleet, according to Accountability.Fish.

The NGO's position paper, coinciding with the commencement of the WCPFC's general meeting in Rarotonga, Cook Islands, highlights the need for enhanced oversight of FADs in the region and advocates for the complete opening of the compliance process to independent observers.

Ryan Orgera, Global Director of Accountability.Fish, stressed the significance of this issue.

"The lack of openness in the current process presents major risks to the world's tuna markets and marine ecology. Large tuna traders and retailers are concerned that tuna certified as sustainable by the Marine Stewardship Council [MSC] could potentially need to be withdrawn from the market if it is later determined to be an illegal catch. Yet, the current process offers no reliable means to verify this," he said.

One of the central concerns raised by Accountability.Fish is the lack of transparency and openness in the WCPFC's compliance procedures.

However, veteran fisheries advisor Francisco Blaha criticized the call for more transparency at the upcoming WCPFC meeting, which he will attend, on his blog.

"There is a lot of cheap talk about the 'secrecy' of the WCPFC... I think it is quite the opposite [...]. All the documents are available online," he wrote on his blog ahead of the meeting.

"Only a couple of compliance reporting meetings are closed to observers (NGOs and multilateral organizations)…these are the sessions where countries present their compliance status. Things are discussed between countries [...]. We have had bad experiences with NGOs running their agenda at the expense of the smallest members, so I understand the reluctance in this area," he wrote.

He said there was "a lot of pressure on the decision-making, and some NGOs use their online presence to represent their interest as opinion holders, which sometimes does not reflect the direct needs of the Pacific Islands, the real stakeholders in the fishery."

Blaha also said that the issues of harvest strategies are "piling up again this year under the banner of keeping the stocks green [see graph below]."

"Yet it is evident that the interest of those behind this campaign is to maintain the blue [MSC logo], and you all know I have a VERY dim view of the private certifications business and their neo-colonial ways," he noted.

The latest tuna stocks and catch status by each regional fisheries management organization. Source: Francisco Blaha on X.

title: Japan to enforce stricter regulations on Pacific bluefin tuna fishing
content:
Japan is ramping up its management of Pacific bluefin tuna catches to curb illegal fishing activities, reports The Japan Times. 

The country's fisheries agency is preparing to enforce stricter reporting requirements on catches of Pacific bluefin tuna to crack down on unreported hauls.

Under the proposed plan, fishery operators must report the total weight of Pacific bluefin tuna caught and the number of individual tunas captured. The aim is to enhance transparency within the fishing industry and prevent illegal catches.

The agency aims to pass legislation to enforce these changes by the following year and is contemplating penalties for non-compliant operators.

This initiative was triggered by the discovery in 2021 that some catches of the renowned Oma-branded bluefin tuna from the Aomori prefecture had gone unreported, raising concerns about the authenticity and legality of the catches.

In addition to reporting catch details to local governments, fishery operators must now furnish buyers with comprehensive information about each bluefin tuna weighing 30 kilograms or more. This data will include specifics such as the fishing vessel's name, fish weight, and the date of unloading at a port.

To streamline this process, the agency plans to introduce transaction slips, QR codes, and other methods for transmitting crucial information to buyers. The agency is allocating JPY 54 million ($362,132) to implement port-monitoring equipment better.

Discussions are also underway regarding establishing a new inspection post dedicated to overseeing unloading operations, potentially coming into effect in the fiscal year 2024.

title: Untitled
content:
A report into the 2021 capsizing of a crab fishing boat in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia suggests Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) officials consider the risks to the safety of harvesters when deciding dates and times for season openings.

The recommendation was one of three contained in a Transportation Safety Board Canada (TSB) report into the sequence of events that led to the capsizing of the 13.61-meter (40-foot) crab fishing boat, Tyhawk, and the death of two crew members, including the captain.

The report was made public this week during a press conference at Dartmouth, Nova Scotia.

DFO moved the opening date for the 2021 snow crab season in the Gulf of Saint Lawrence forward by almost three weeks from previous years, starting at one minute past midnight on April 3, the report noted.

"This resulted in an increased likelihood of colder water, ice and freezing rain," the TSB said, adding that opening the fishery at midnight also increased the risk of fatigue among crew members.

However, because the season-opening decision had "been made routinely" for the last several years, it was not seen as a new situation, and the hazards were not seen as additional risks, TSB said.

Beginning in 2018, DFO began implementing fisheries management measures to protect the North Atlantic right whale. The suggestion of an earlier start to the Gulf crab fishing season to avoid conflict with right whale migration also came from the fishing industry.

Canada shuts down part of PEI lobster fishery over whale sighting

Still, the TSB recommended that DFO ensure its policies include "comprehensive identification of hazards and assessment of associated risks to fish harvesters when fisheries resource management decisions are being made." The board also said independent safety expertise should be included in the process.

Stability issues

The investigation also determined the stability of the Tyhawk had been compromised, in part by the addition of a removable deck used for snow crab fishing. This removable deck had not been evaluated for its impact on the vessel's stability, the TSB noted.

Under current Canadian regulations, stability assessments are required when a vessel has undergone major modifications. However, the definition of a "major modification" is open to interpretation, the federal agency said.

While the lead agency, Transport Canada (TC), does provide some guidance to help fishing masters identify major modifications, the guidance requires knowledge of stability to interpret it correctly. Compliance with the guidance is also voluntary, the TSB noted.

"Without a clear definition of what a major modification entails, masters and TC may not identify the impact of a major modification on vessel stability. As a result, there is a risk that vessels will operate without adequate stability for their intended operations," the TSB report noted.

Canada warns lobster vessel captains of plans to enforce safety rules

Furthermore, said the TSB, TC does not require vessel owners to seek pre-approval of planned modifications, to help determine whether those modifications could negatively affect stability.

The Tyhawk, it seems, slipped through those regulatory cracks.

TC had issued a deficiency notice for the boat in 2013 because of its removable deck and advised its owner that a stability assessment was required, TSB pointed out.

"The master completed a stability questionnaire in May 2015 and identified the existence of a removable deck, but he did not recognize the deck as a modification that would require a stability assessment."

The full stability assessment was not completed, and subsequent inspection documentation by TC did not reference the removable deck.

For greater clarity around stability, the TSB recommended the adoption of new criteria to define major modifications to small fishing vessels.

The board also recommended that TC "require that planned modifications to small fishing vessels and other small commercial vessels be assessed by a competent person, that all records of modifications to these vessels be maintained, and that the records be made available to the department."

The last voyage

The TSB report describes, in detail, the chain of events that led to the Tyhawk tragedy.

The vessel was built in 2021 to fish for lobster with a Northumberland-Straight-style design. A removable aluminum deck and a boom were added to allow more space to stow crab traps and live catch.

There was still ice around Richibucto Harbour, New Brunswick, at 4:35 a.m. on April 2, 2021, when the Tyhawk left port to harvest snow crab in crab fishing area 12. DFO had assessed weather conditions and notified harvesters the day before that the crab fishing season would open at 12:01 a.m. on April 3.

Craig Sock, the master of the Tyhawk, had four crew members and added another four in Cheticamp.

Snow crab being harvested in the Southern Gulf of Saint Lawrence. Photograph from Facebook page of Associations Des Crabiers Acadiens.

The following day, April 3, the Tyhawk made the two-hour trip from Cheticamp to the fishing grounds, about 20 nautical miles from shore.

On the first voyage, with the captain and all eight crew on board, they set 75 crab traps.

"During this voyage, ice was accumulating on the vessel," the TSB report noted.

Later that day, the master and four crew members made a second voyage, setting 50 more crab traps. However, on the second trip, the weather worsened, and the Tyhawk was forced to battle winds of 20 to 25 knots along with 1-2m waves.

"Waves were hitting the starboard side, and rain and freezing rain were falling."

The master and three crew members were resting below deck, and another crew member was on watch at the time of the incident. A second crew member had noticed water accumulating in the bilge when he entered the wheelhouse, and bilge pumps were started.

Meanwhile, another crew member went under the removable deck to get some of the gear and noticed water on the main deck, underneath the removable deck.

By now, the weather had worsened, and the boat's movements were "more severe."

"Following a significant heel to starboard, the vessel’s main deck submerged," the report noted. The vessel's center of balance became compromised.

The crew, now in peril, could not retrieve the lifejackets and immersion suits stowed in the accommodation space. The life raft had slid under the removable deck and could not be launched.

The boat's master used his cell phone to text a distress message to the master of the Northumberland Spray, who was fishing approximately six nautical miles away. 

Shortly afterward, the Tyhawk capsized, said the report, noting that everything happened in just a few minutes. At 5:42 p.m., the crew was in the water, clinging to the hull, just seven minutes after it had started the bilge bumps. One of the crew members managed to call 911.

Meanwhile, the boat's emergency position-indicating radio beacon had floated free and the distress signal was received by the Joint Rescue Coordination Center in Halifax.

Rough seas. Credit: Oskar Porkka/Shutterstock.com

As the crew hung on for their lives, the Tyhawk continued to sink lower in the water and wave action repeatedly swept Sock and another crew member into the ocean.

A nearby fishing vessel, Northumberland Spray, arrived to rescue the crew. By then, however, Sock could not be found.

When the Northumberland Spray got back to Cheticamp, a second crew member was also pronounced dead.

A search continued for Sock through the night and all the next day. By April 4, however, he was declared missing at sea.

Watch list

The tale of the Tyhawk is an all-too-familiar story in Canada's fishing industry. From 1992 to 2010, the TSB made 42 recommendations to improve fishing vessel safety.

In 2012, the board released a wide-ranging report on the causes of fatal fishing vessel accidents, highlighting systemic factors, including vessel modifications and their impact on stability, lack of or failure to use personal flotation devices, unsafe work practices, and inadequate regulatory oversight.

Statistics from Canada's Transportation Safety Board show loss of life is an annual occurrence in the nation's commercial fishing industry.

From 2010 to 2021, the TSB conducted 37 commercial fishing–related investigations where recurring unsafe conditions were identified.

"During this same period, 128 fatalities resulted from 87 fishing accidents," the TSB noted in its watchlist report. "The two most common reasons for fatalities were falling overboard and problems with vessel stability."

While some fish harvester associations in Atlantic Canada have been working to improve safety in the industry, and some provincial workers' compensation boards have increased education and enforcement, the TSB said new issues are cropping up, including the use of drugs and alcohol on fishing boats.

With an average of 11 fish harvesters losing their lives on the ocean each year in Canada, the TSB said the issue of commercial fishing safety will remain on its watchlist "until there are sufficient indications that a sound safety culture has taken root throughout the industry.

At the press conference in Dartmouth, TSB chair Kathy Fox said, "Over the past 30 years, the TSB has been sounding the alarm over the numerous safety deficiencies that continue to put at risk the lives of Canadian fish harvesters. Too many fish harvesters still don't make it home from what could have been a preventable accident."

title: Canada warns lobster vessel captains of plans to enforce safety rules
content:
Transport Canada has warned Nova Scotia fishing fleets less than a week before they are expected to open the nation's biggest lobster season they won't be able to sail unless they have written safety procedures and can show proof that their crew members are familiar with those plans.

The federal agency said it will also be looking for records of safety drills conducted on board the vessels, CBC News reports. 

Failure to demonstrate compliance could result in a deficiency notice or detention of the vessel, Transport Canada spokesperson Sau Sau Liu has advised.

The increased scrutiny comes three years after the loss of the scallop dragger Chief William Saulis and its six crew members in 2020. Lack of safety procedures was cited in a March 2023 Transportation Safety Board report on its investigation of the William Saulis tragedy.

Nearly $160k raised for families of lost Canadian scallop vessel crew

In addition to the Transport Canada measures, Nova Scotia's Department of Labour, Skills and Immigration is seeking proof of annual inspections of hoists on board fishing vessels. Hoist regulations have existed for years but have never been exercised for lobster vessels, the agency said.
