title: Caribbean island establishes world’s first sperm whale reserve
content:
Dominica, an island country in the Caribbean, has expressed its commitment to develop a new 490 square mile sperm whale reserve off its western coast.

Experts involved in the planning and implementing the reserve argue that protecting this vast marine area will yield benefits locally and globally.

Sperm whales, averaging 52 feet in length, are the largest-toothed predators on our planet and are known for their exceptional intelligence and unique social structures. While they are found in various waters worldwide, Dominica is one of the few places where these remarkable animals can be consistently observed year-round.

The island's west coast serves as crucial feeding and nursing grounds for the resident sperm whale population.

Dominica prime minister Roosevelt Skerrit emphasized the significance of these creatures to the nation in a statement.

"The 200 sperm whales that call our sea home are prized citizens of Dominica," he said. "We want to ensure these majestic and brilliant animals are safe from harm and continue keeping our waters and our climate healthy. Dominica is honored to establish the first sperm whale reserve on our planet."

Once the reserve is officially established, a designated senior whale officer and observers on tourism and research vessels will enforce enhanced whale tourism regulations. Sustainable artisanal fishing practices, designed not to interfere with sperm whales' behavior or food sources, will also be permitted.

The reserve will cover less than three percent of Dominica's waters. Implementing designated ship corridors has been shown to reduce the risk of ship strikes and noise pollution in critical feeding and nursing areas, benefiting both the whales and fishermen.

title: Pacific islands approve management options for tuna fishery
content:
Members of the Pacific Islands Forum Fisheries Agency (FFA) have agreed on management options for the multi-million dollar tuna fishery in the Western Central Pacific.

Manu Tupou-Roosen, the FFA's director general, emphasized that cooperation among FFA members was essential for safeguarding the long-term prosperity of the region's fisheries resources, benefiting Pacific communities and economies.

The FFA members addressed several key priorities during these meetings, including climate change. It said members recognized the urgent need to address the impact of climate change in the Pacific region, which poses a significant threat to the livelihoods, security, and well-being of its people.

They called for the development of resilient tuna harvest strategies and urged more robust recognition of climate change within the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission (WCPFC)'s work.

Additionally, FFA members supported a precautionary approach in reviewing the tropical tuna measure to balance the interests of fishing and coastal state members. Proposed measures included restrictions on purse seine fishing in international waters and addressing the impact of other commercial fisheries in areas like Indonesia.

Thirdly, they discussed South Pacific albacore, looking to revise the interim target reference point for the species to aid in developing the management procedure. This reference point is crucial for guiding the fishery's objectives and ensuring resource sustainability.

FFA members also expressed concerns about the Compliance Monitoring Scheme operation and emphasized the need to address imbalances between purse seine and longline obligations. They stressed cooperation and prioritized addressing audit points to enhance compliance.

The members prioritized the review of the transshipment measure, focusing on bringing transshipment to the port, improving monitoring, and enhancing cooperation among relevant authorities to understand better fish catch quantities.

Finally, FFA members emphasized the importance of crew labor standards and supported the development of binding conservation and management measures for labor standards. The focus is on effective implementation, monitoring, and enforcement to ensure fair labor practices in the industry.

These positions will serve as the basis for FFA's engagement at the annual session of the WCPFC in Rarotonga, Cook Islands, scheduled for Dec. 4-8, 2023.

title: Tribe moves quickly in wake of Washington state judge’s ruling, urges prompt approval of steelhead farm
content:
A Native American group has wasted little time in responding to a US state of Washington judge's ruling to nullify the blocking of its planned steelhead trout farm.

The Jamestown S'Klallam Tribe has asked public lands commissioner Hilary Franz and the state's Department of Natural Resources (DNR) to please expedite the approval of the aquaculture lease application it submitted for Port Angeles Harbor in 2021.

The effort follows the Oct. 20 ruling by Thurston County Superior Court judge Indu Thomas' summary judgment, determining that a ban put in place by Franz and DNR is now just an internal policy directive for initiating rulemaking rather than a legally enforceable measure, as Undercurrent News reported.  

In an email to Undercurrent on Thursday (Nov. 9), W. Ron Allen, the tribe's CEO and chairman, expressed frustration with Franz's actions, stating that they are preventing the tribe from producing the traditional food its citizens depend on and calling it a violation of the tribe's treaty rights. His group had earlier filed the lawsuit against Franz that Thomas was ruling on, alleging that her actions exceeded her authority and violated the Washington state constitution.

Allen has criticized the commissioner for not respecting the tribe's treaty rights and further criticized her claims that fish farming harms wild fish and natural habitats, citing peer-reviewed scientific research that he said debunks the claims. He questioned Franz's promotion of land-based salmon farming, pointing out the large carbon footprint and water needs associated with these systems.

Undercurrent has contacted DNR for comment but has yet to hear back.

title: Ex-Peru gov’t minister files lawsuit against incumbent over alleged illegal fishing
content:
A former government minister has filed an official complaint with Peruvian prosecutors alleging that political leaders have failed to prevent fishing fleets from China and other countries from illegally harvesting Peruvian stocks.

Rafael Rey Rey in 2010. Photo: Wikipedia.

From 2006 to 2008, Rafael Rey Rey headed Peru's production ministry (Produce), which regulates the country's fishing and aquaculture industries.

Now a board member of the Banco Central de Reserva del Peru, the country's central bank, Rey filed a complaint on Oct. 26 with Lima-based prosecutors.

In the complaint, Rey alleges that Raul Perez Reyes Espejo, a former Produce minister who now serves as Peru's transportation and communications minister; Ana Maria Choquehuanca de Villanueva, the current head of Produce; and Ursula Desilu Leon Chempen, the government's current fishing and aquaculture vice-minister, violated laws designed to safeguard the country's natural resources.

Rey's complaint, seen by Undercurrent News, alleges that the named officials failed to fulfill their constitutional duties and enabled illegal fishing to take place and that this caused the depletion of Peru's aquatic resources.

Rey's complaint.

These actions are believed to have been carried out for the potential benefit of foreign nations and warrant investigation and possible legal consequences, Rey claimed.

The allegations are serious ones in Peru, which is both the world's largest anchovy harvester and the number one producer of fishmeal and fish oil, two critical components of aquafeed. 

Choquehuanca was appointed as Produce minister on Sept. 6, replacing Reyes. She took over months after Produce canceled the country's first commercial anchovy harvesting season of 2023 due to estimates of elevated numbers of juvenile anchovies in the biomass.

The Peruvian government has stepped up measures to fight illegal fishing in recent years, including the 2020 implementation of a satellite-based monitoring system to track foreign vessels entering its ports in real-time. The information is publicly available with the support of the non-profit Global Fishing Watch.

This measure is intended to ensure foreign and domestic vessels comply with Peruvian fishing regulations.

Specifically, it tracks vessels active near the edges of the country's exclusive economic zone, a historical hotspot for illegal activity.

According to Rey's complaint, since 2020, some vessels from China -- seen as habitual offenders of illegal fishing -- have reportedly avoided Peruvian ports to remain off the radar. Between June and mid-August 2023, over 50 foreign fishing vessels arrived at Peruvian ports without the mandatory satellite control equipment, Rey noted.

The vessels cited reasons for the missing equipment, such as certificate renewals and crew changes, the complaint alleges.

Additionally, Rey claimed that some Chinese-flagged fishing vessels spent extended periods at a Peruvian shipyard in Callao. Calling at ports in this way, ostensibly for reasons like crew changes, certificate renewals, maintenance, and repairs, does not fall under Peruvian laws, according to Rey.

This suggests a failure by Peruvian officials to enforce these rules, the complaint reads.

Rey further claimed that the Peruvian production ministry's lack of oversight in these cases has allowed foreign distant-water vessels to evade legal requirements in violation of the law. The complaint added that on May 24, China's ambassador to Peru and other embassy officials visited Peru's vice-ministry of fishing and aquaculture.

"Coincidentally, after this visit, there was a significant increase in the irregular arrivals of Chinese-flagged vessels," Rey claimed in the complaint.

Despite verbal and written protests from individuals, business groups, and artisanal fishermen, the ministry failed to take action.

A Peruvian fishing sector source, who asked to remain unnamed, told Undercurrent that Rey's complaint calls for a thorough investigation of Reyes, Choquehuanca and Leon, who could face criminal or civil penalties including removal from office or imprisonment.

Lima's attorney general is expected to investigate Rey's complaint. If it is found viable, the officials could be called before Peru's Congress, which could further refer them to the Supreme Court of Justice, the source told Undercurrent.

Representatives of the Produce ministry did not reply to a request for comment from Undercurrent. Reyes, Choquehuanca and Leon also did not reply to a request for comment, and the Chinese embassy in Peru did not respond in time for publication.

Illegal fishing is a global business estimated at $10 billion in annual sales. According to an investigation by the Outlaw Project published in The New Yorker last month, the Chinese fleet's annual catch totals over five billion pounds (2.2bn metric tons) of seafood through long-distance fishing, with the majority being squid.

Last month, under Choquehuanca's watch, Produce officially opened Peru's second anchovy fishing season.

However, the outcome of the season remains uncertain since some harvesters went on strike at the end of last month. Between Oct. 21 and Nov. 4, Peru's anchovy landings totaled 401,500t, nearly 24% of the quota set for the season, which makes it seem possible that the sector could achieve the full quota, according to sources.

Giant squid harvesting is one of Peru's most profitable fishing sectors for direct human consumption. It supports over 2,500 artisanal vessels and generated some $850 million in exports in 2019, according to official statistics.

title: Process delays see Arctic Fish farming license expire amid sea lice issues
content:
A license to farm salmon at sea in Iceland's Westfjords belonging to Arctic Sea Farm -- part of Arctic Fish -- has expired, but authorities will not be removing the company's activities from the water, reports RUV.

"We consider that to be an administrative challenge where different institutions, impacting each other, are involved to finalize their work for a renewed license in this specific area," CEO Stein Ove Tveiten told Undercurrent News.

Iceland to embrace stricter aquaculture policies following escapes

"Arctic Fish has addressed the matter and made the relevant applications and documentations within the timeframe as requested and required. We expect this matter to be resolved in the near future."

Information available on aquaculture database AquaFacts shows the two sites -- Hvanndalur and Kvigindisdalur -- each have a maximum capacity of 7,800 metric tons. Their 10-year licenses expired on Aug. 27, 2023.  

RUV reports the company -- which is majority owned by Mowi -- submitted the relevant renewals for Patreksfjordur and Talknafjordur in December 2022, yet due to delays, the license expired two months ago.

Anti-aquaculture groups have called on the food agency Matvaelastofnun to enforce the law and halt farming activities. 

Matvaelastofnun is waiting for Vegagerdarinnar, the road administration office, to submit its assessment of the effects of the farm sites on shipping routes. Matvaelastofnun does not have the authority to issue a temporary license in the meantime.

RUV notes the state could become liable for damages if the aquaculture activity was halted because it has taken so long to process the case.

Meanwhile, Ove Tveiten also confirmed to Undercurrent the company has had problems with sea lice in recent months.

On Oct. 26, RUV reported that some 1,000t of salmon had to be harvested early in Talknafjordur by Arctic Fish and Arnarlax, with estimated losses for the two firms running into the billions of Iceland kronur.

"Regarding lice, we have had a higher lice pressure than earlier years," said the Arctic Fish CEO. "We are working closely with the relevant authorities to secure the situation. Increased sea lice pressure in the area has unfortunately made it necessary to take out some fish from a site."

"Arctic Fish are dedicated to the care and well-being of our fish, and we are taking the necessary measures to secure the situation," he added.

Berglind Helga Bergsdottir, specialist veterinarian at Matvaelastofnun, confirmed the news, but said the agency did not order the disposal.

"The companies and their veterinarians anticipated that the salmon would not survive the winter with the injuries they have," she said, adding that sea lice have spread around the fjord's pens in October at a speed that has not been seen before.

title: Scientists say climate-caused starvation killed Bering Sea snow crabs
content:
Mike Litzow, the director of the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Association (NOAA) lab, in Kodiak, Alaska, believes the study published recently in the journal Science is "the best analysis so far" to explain what happened to the snow crab population in the Bering Sea.

More than 10 billion snow crabs died of starvation between 2018 and 2022, as the animals squeezed into a smaller habitat area with less food sources due to warming waters caused by a marine heat wave that occurred over the same time.

Climate-caused starvation was one hypothesis put forward by scientists when the population crashed, resulting in the first-ever closure of the Bering Sea snow crab fishery last year. 

Trawl survey results this summer showed further population declines for snow crabs in the Bering Sea, leading to the second year in a row that fishery will remain closed. Researchers said there's also no indication the crabs migrated to other areas, like the northern Bering Sea or to Russia. 

"It's clearly a mortality event," Litzow, one of the study's authors, told Undercurrent News, in an interview last week "We could have had a really different answer – cod predation could have popped out, or disease could have popped out as the cause. But it really did lead us back to that initial idea of temperature, which has been a leading hypothesis all along."

At face value, however, snow crabs have surprising resilience to warmer temperatures. 

NOAA's lab in Kodiak, Alaska (Kirsten Dobroth)

Using the NOAA facility in Kodiak, which is outfitted with saltwater tanks that hold crabs at various temperature and pH levels, Litzow said scientists were able to conduct experiments that have shown that, with no other stressors, snow crabs can survive in temperatures as high as 23 degrees Celsius (73 degrees Fahrenheit). 

Other variables outweigh those findings, though. 

Crabs' metabolic needs go up when the water is warm because, simply put, they need to eat more. Sea ice accumulates in the winter and melts in the summer, feeding a layer near the ocean floor with near-freezing, nutrient-rich water called the cold pool, which is critical habitat for snow crabs.

A marine heatwave between 2018 and 2019 depleted the usual layer of ice that covers the Bering Sea in the winter months, pushing a large number of crabs into a vastly smaller cold pool than they typically need to thrive.

"They were in a really small area in 2018 and 2019," Litzow said of the snow crabs. "They were smaller, and lighter for any given size … their condition was really poor in 2019. We know from the lab that they have higher metabolic needs when it's really warm, and so that was the trail of breadcrumbs."

'Canaries of the Arctic'

A flourishing cohort of young snow crabs was observed in the Bering Sea in 2018 – just before the population crashed. Some researchers, including Litzow, have called the species "canaries of the Arctic," as changing ocean conditions may similarly disrupt predictability and reliability across other fisheries in Alaska. 

Pollock and Pacific cod, for instance, have been observed further north in the Bering Sea, particularly during marine heatwave events.

Climate change's potential for disrupting fisheries in Alaska has gotten more attention at the management level, too. 

Alaska out of snow crab game at least four years, ADF&G report suggests

At the North Pacific Fishery Management Council (NPFMC) meeting in Anchorage, Alaska, earlier this month, NOAA administrators spent time breaking down how the agency intends to use $3.3 billion in federal funding allocated through the Inflation Reduction Act, which was signed into law by president Joe Biden last year.

Nearly $350 million of that money is earmarked to support "Climate Ready Fisheries."

Some of the money within that funding bucket will go towards supporting individual species. For instance, $42m from the Climate Ready Fisheries fund is intended to boost initiatives and programs for Pacific salmon. Another $20m will address the impacts of climate change on red snapper, as previously reported by Undercurrent.

And $20m will go toward the US's eight regional fishery management councils – including the NPFMC. 

The money will "support the councils' development and advancement of climate-related fisheries management and implementation efforts," according to NOAA. Each council will receive about $375,000 right off the bat. Then, councils will have an opportunity to compete for $17m in additional funding for projects supporting work related to climate change.

The NPFMC recommended using the initial funding amount to hire a climate-ready fishery analyst as soon as possible at its October meeting, "with the primary tasks being to be the lead staff person on climate resilience related activities (meetings, reports, workshops) and documents (proposals, discussion papers, NEPA analyses)." 

The NPFMC also outlined a four-year timeline for incorporating more "climate-informed fishery management" into its overall approach.

Gaps in management and research

The Science study published earlier this month notes that the "results do not support a strong connection between variability in snow crab mortality and indices of trawling," among other things, and that trawling activity in the Bering Sea has remained relatively consistent for two decades.

However, trawling's effects on the snow crab population have been the subject of increased scrutiny from the public in Alaska and other industry and environmental groups.

Litzow told Undercurrent that the NOAA lab in Kodiak has started looking at how fishing gear might impact snow crabs as the stock attempts to rebuild – particularly when the crabs are in vulnerable larval and molt stages.

The NPFMC has also established a working group to study unobserved mortality across crab species in the Bering Sea – the group met for the first time this month. 

Unobserved mortality refers to crabs killed by fishing gear that remain on the ocean floor and don't end up being counted on board fishing vessels by observers. Disagreement and concern over the lack of information around unobserved mortality came up at a Trawl Performance Standard Workshop hosted by the council and NOAA's Office of Law Enforcement during the NPFMC meeting earlier this month.

Litzow said those numbers are hard to track, and the working group is a good step in gathering more comprehensive data. 

US to boost funding for coastal habitat restoration, climate resiliency projects nationwide

Other groups, like Alaska Bering Sea Crabbers (ABSC) – a trade organization that represents the fleet – argued at the October NPFMC meeting that the council hasn't gone far enough to prioritize conservation in its management strategies. ABSC also argued that climate change is an unpredictable variable, and fisheries policies should be quicker and more flexible in times of crisis.

Still, the research released this month identifies one piece of the puzzle about why so many snow crabs disappeared from the Bering Sea. A burgeoning cohort of immature crabs has also been observed by scientists over the last two years – Litzow said water temperatures have stayed cool over that same period. 

Despite the unknowns, it could be a bright spot for the fishery in the years to come.

title: Sea shepherd, Italian authorities collaborate to reduce illegal fishing
content:
Illegal longline fishing in the Tyrrhenian Sea off the coast of Calabria, Itlay, has seen a significant decline of 70% this summer, thanks to the efforts of the international marine conservation organization Sea Shepherd and Italy's financial law enforcement agency, the Guardia di Finanza, according to the NGO.

This positive development comes as a result of Operation SISO 6, a collaborative campaign that spanned the summer months, Sea Shepherd said in a press release.

Throughout the summer, Sea Shepherd's crew aboard the vessel Sea Eagle worked in close cooperation with Italian authorities to patrol the Tyrrhenian Sea.

Joint operations led to the removal of 30 kilometers of mainlines and the confiscation of 2,000 hooks, all of which posed significant threats to marine life in the area, the NGO said.

title: US domestic shrimp sector seeks tariffs against India, Ecuador, Indonesia, Vietnam
content:
The American Shrimp Processors Association (ASPA), a trade association that represents both harvesters and processors of US domestically caught and farmed shrimp, announced Wednesday (Oct. 25) that it has filed petitions seeking anti-dumping duties on imported frozen shrimp from Ecuador and Indonesia.

ASPA is also seeking countervailing duties against imported shrimp from Ecuador, India, Indonesia and Vietnam.

"We are truly proud to file these cases on behalf of shrimp boats and shrimp processors," said Trey Pearson, ASPA's president and general manager of JBS Packing, a supplier of US wild-caught seafood based in Port Arthur, Texas, in a press release. "The overwhelming outpouring of support from the entire shrimp industry demonstrates how important trade relief is to everyone."

Louisiana governor passes along disaster request on behalf of shrimpers hurt by low-cost imports

The petitions were filed at both the US Department of Commerce and International Trade Commission, which is expected to announce whether it will initiate investigations by Nov. 15. The ITC is expected to vote on whether there is a reasonable indication of injury to the domestic industry on Dec. 8.

If both determinations are affirmed, full investigations at the two agencies will last into the fall of 2024, ASPA said.

Pearson said the group's petitions include nearly 800 shrimp harvesters representing over half of all domestic landings. ASPA reports that its members account for more than 85% of domestic shrimp processing.

Frustrations have been boiling over for the US domestic shrimp industry in recent times as the ever-increasing amount of imports have contributed to a glut of inventory and the disintegrating prices of both imports and domestically landed shrimp, as has been reported by Undercurrent News.

In late August, the Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA), which represents harvesters in the US Gulf of Mexico and also the US southeastern coast, sent a letter to the governors of North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana and Texas, asking them to seek disaster relief. 

US senator Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana Republican, has introduced two bills intended to better level the playing field for US-harvested and -farmed shrimp and rice by making life more difficult for importers of the same products from India, as reported by Undercurrent. It would slap shrimp imported from India with an escalating set of tariffs, with higher new rates phasing in for three consecutive years, starting in January 2024.

Credit: Jahidul-hasan / Shutterstock

'Dozens of government subsidy programs'

Shrimp imports from India, Ecuador, Indonesia and Vietnam increased by more than 200 million pounds from 2020 to 2022, taking market share from an already vulnerable domestic industry, ASPA said. They were valued at more than $6.6 billion in 2022, accounting for more than 90% of all imported frozen warmwater shrimp that year.

"Imports also deeply undersold domestic shrimp, driving down prices to historically low levels in 2023 for both fishermen and processors," ASPA said. "As a result, the domestic industry's profit margin has all but disappeared, threatening the future viability of an industry that is critical to the Gulf region's economy and cultural heritage."

ASPA said it has documented "dozens of government subsidy programs" benefitting shrimp farmers and processors in Ecuador, India, Indonesia and Vietnam, including subsidized loans, tax concessions, grants, export credits, and the provision of land, water and other inputs.

The group estimates dumping margins for Ecuador ranging as high as 111% while dumping margins for Indonesia range as high as 37%.

US shrimp imports see second straight month of year-on-year volume gains

If successful, antidumping and countervailing duty orders could result in tariffs that offset the dumping and subsidies undertaken by foreign companies and foreign governments, the group said. 

ASPA is represented in its trade petitions by attorneys Elizabeth Drake, a partner at Schagrin Associates, in Washington, DC, and Eddy Hayes, a partner at Leake & Andersson, in New Orleans, Lousiana.

"These petitions are necessary due to continued unfair trade practices causing significant market distortions and price depression in the United States," the two attorneys are quoted as saying. "... This should bring a measure of market correction and badly needed relief to the entire domestic shrimp industry."

Shrimp import numbers climbing again

As Undercurrent recently reported, the US imported 73,617 metric tons of shrimp in August 2023, 3% more than the 71,666t imported in August 2022, according to the latest update of seafood trade data by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). That marks a second consecutive month of year-on-year volume increases after 13 consecutive months of y-o-y decreases. Nine of the 20 largest source countries saw volume improvements.

However, shrimp prices are still down. The average price paid across all source countries was $8.14 per kilogram, 12% below the average price of $9.28/kg paid in August 2022. As a result, the overall value of shrimp imported by the US was just $599.6m, down 10% from the $664.8m of import value in August 2022.

title: US lawmakers ask Biden administration to block seafood from two Chinese provinces
content:
The two US lawmakers who led a hearing this week to discuss an investigative report about the use of forced Uyghur labor in the Chinese seafood industry are now asking the president Joe Biden administration to halt imports from seafood-processing facilities in two Chinese provinces. 

In a letter sent Tuesday (Oct. 24) to US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) secretary Alejandro Mayorkas, representative Chris Smith, a New Jersey Republican, and senator Jeff Merkley, an Oregon Democrat, request the issuances of withhold release orders (WROs) in relation to all seafood processing facilities in Shandong and Liaoning. Such orders direct DHS's Customs and Border Protection to detain a shipment of goods over concerns related to the suspected use of forced labor.  

Journalist behind forced labor report to Congress, White House staff: MSC not enough; expand SIMP

Earlier in the day, Smith and Merkley chaired a nearly two-hour hearing by the Congressional-Executive Commission on China to review a two-part reporting series by the Outlaw Ocean Project (OOP) that was published Oct. 9 in The New Yorker. As reported by Undercurrent News, the hearing featured four witnesses, including Ian Urbina, the former 17-year New York Times journalist who wrote the articles as the founder and director of the OOP. 

The articles provided haunting details about crew members being held captive, beaten and suffering from malnutrition aboard vessels in China's distant water fishing fleet. They also shared a thorough accounting of the Chinese program used to enlist and transport a large number of Uyghurs over 1,000 miles from Xinjiang, in the land-locked, northwestern part of China, to seafood processing plants in Shangdong, on the east coast.

Additionally, during the hearing, the commission heard from Greg Scarlatoiu, executive director of the Committee for Human Rights in North Korea, regarding the use of North Korean workers in plants in Liaoning.

"The evidence presented by the Outlaw Ocean Project and detailed in the New Yorker and other publications globally is compelling and well-documented," the two lawmakers wrote in their letter to Mayorkas.

"Major wholesalers, restaurants, grocery chains, food service companies and the US government all import large amounts of seafood from the processing plants in Shandong and Liaoning. From the fish sticks served at school lunches to the fish sandwiches and calamari sold at major restaurants and grocery chains, the plates of American consumers are filled with products likely tainted with forced labor. At the very least, we should all agree that American veterans, school children and men and women in uniform should not be unwitting accomplices to egregious human rights abuses."

US lawmakers push Customs to better enforce anti-Uyghur forced labor law

Smith and Merkley called for the Biden administration to add seafood businesses involved in using Uyghur forced labor to a ban list created under the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA), a law passed in late 2021. 

The request follows another letter sent Oct. 20 by US representatives Raul Grijalva and Jared Huffman to CBP commissioner Troy Miller, asking him to better enforce UFLPA against Chinese seafood coming into the US from processing plants caught using forced Uyghur labor, as reported by Undercurrent.

At least one member of the Biden administration can be expected to support the kind of tough steps advocated by lawmakers. Thea Lee, deputy undersecretary for international affairs at the Labor Department and a member of the commission, said at the hearing that "further urgent action is needed."

title: Global seafood giants assert ‘proactive steps’ against IUU fishing, modern slavery
content:
The Seafood Business for Ocean Stewardship initiative, or SeaBOS, has released its first-ever impact report with insights into how member firms deal with several sector challenges, including illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing and modern slavery.

‘We had expected to have come further’: World’s largest seafood firms disappointed by supply chain reports

According to the report, in a stark reality check for the global seafood industry, these two issues persist as deeply rooted challenges, "undermining human rights, food security, and the sustainability of seafood production."

"As industry leaders, we aim to eradicate these detrimental practices and foster ethical operations, for our sake and that of future generations," it also reads.

To do that, the report announces members have co-developed a tool kit including policy documents, audit protocols and advanced traceability mechanisms, and has "engaged in external reporting for accountability and transparency and with governments, civil society, and other stakeholders to influence policy changes."

The initiative consists of nine of the largest seafood companies globally -- Cargill, Cermaq Group, Charoen Pokphand Foods (CPF), Dongwon Industries, Kyokuyo, Maruha Nichiro, Nippon Suisan Kaisha (or Nissui) and Thai Union Group.

"Our actions, while fostering new industry norms, have also highlighted the need for more effective public policies and legislation," it adds. "Separately, we have written to the World Trade Organisation to recommend the removal of harmful subsidies from seafood production."

Thai Union, for example, claims it has launched audit programs and a vessel improvement program and code of conduct (VCoC) to ensure 100% on-the-water monitoring by 2025.

Companies like Skretting -- Nutreco's aquaculture feed arm -- Nissui, Maruha Nichiro and Kyokuyo are leveraging tools such as EcoVadis, the SeaBOS toolkit, and supplier surveys to monitor risks.

Cargill, for its part, has focused on risk assessments in Norway and Scotland, while Cermaq enforced strict codes against forced labor and CPF ensured the integrity of its fishmeal sources, all three claimed.

Dongwon claimed it complied with Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) standards and underwent joint inspections with Korean regulatory bodies, "ensuring adherence to labor laws and regulations."

"Cumulatively, SeaBOS members are proud to be supporting a more transparent and humane seafood industry," the document also reads. 

Is that enough, though?

These global leaders in the seafood industry acknowledged the persistent challenges of modern slavery and IUU fishing within their ranks.

The International Labour Organization, in collaboration with the Walk Free Foundation and the International Organization for Migration, claimed that a staggering 128,000 fishers are still entangled in forced labor conditions aboard fishing vessels.

"The economic toll is immense, especially in hotspots like West Africa, where annual losses due to IUU fishing reach an estimated $9.4 billion, wreaking havoc on coastal nations," the report adds.

"Despite two decades of extensive efforts by national, regional, and international institutions, these deeply ingrained issues continue to plague the seafood industry, affecting the lives of thousands of fishers worldwide," the report also reads.

Thus, these efforts, while significant, are deemed insufficient. In the words of Therese Log Bergjord, CEO of Skretting, "there is no question."

"As industry leaders, we are responsible for making a positive impact. We cannot do it alone, and we do not. As an industry, we must seek inputs based on science and then, and this is the critical step, we must act," she concluded. 

SeaBOS told Undercurrent News of its disappointment over recent reports linking major firms to accusations of forced labor in China.

An investigation by the Outlaw Ocean Project, published in The New Yorker, claims to have linked numerous suppliers and retailers in Europe and the US to factories in Shandong province accused of using forced Uyghur labor transferred from Xinjiang. Eleven of the plants carried the MSC chain-of-custody certificate.

Then, on Oct. 17, the World Benchmarking Alliance (WBA) unveiled a report assessing 30 of the most influential global seafood companies, finding "a concerning lack of transparency around progress towards their sustainability commitments."

"The seafood sector can, and must, do better. It is problematic and disappointing that a) the investigation includes information about SeaBOS members and b) that our members do not score better in the WBA index in this edition. We have worked hard on, e.g., addressing the risk of IUU fishing and labor abuse, improving traceability and transparency, in collaboration with science since 2017," Martin Exel, managing director of SeaBOS, told Undercurrent.

"All SeaBOS members have engaged with the SSI [Seafood Stewardship Index] since 2018. We had expected to have come further than this, but clearly, much more work remains," he added.

title: Journalist behind forced labor report to Congress, White House staff: MSC not enough; expand SIMP
content:
It's no longer enough to have your fish or shellfish certified as having been sourced sustainably by the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC), asserted Ian Urbina to a panel of US lawmakers and White House staff on Tuesday (Oct. 24).

Seafood should also be confirmed as having been sourced under humane conditions, said the journalist, who caused a stir earlier this month by publishing a two-part series that shone a spotlight on the use of forced Uyghur labor in the Chinese seafood sector. 

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) should also expand the Seafood Import Monitoring Program (SIMP), he suggested, supporting an idea mostly opposed by the US seafood industry. 

"I think the infrastructure that exists for the private sector to monitor and trace its supply chain also has to evolve a lot and hopefully this will be a poke in that direction in that they can no longer, I think, simply put forward that they're MSC-certified or that they've been accredited as a good steward by a private entity and therefore they're showing part of the ocean conservation team," said Urbina, the founder and director of the Outlaw Ocean Project (OOP).

Urbina, a former 17-year reporter for the New York Times and the winner of a Pulitzer Prize, was one of four witnesses to appear before the Congressional-Executive Commission on China (CECC) during a nearly two-hour hearing focused on the OOP's two-part series, which was published in The New Yorker on Oct. 9. The panel is made up of nine US senators, nine US representatives and five senior administration officials appointed by the president.   

US lawmakers push Customs to better enforce anti-Uyghur forced labor law

The series provided haunting details about crew members being held captive, beaten and suffering from malnutrition aboard vessels in China's distant water fishing fleet, as well as a thorough accounting of the Chinese program used to enlist and transport a large number of Uyghurs over 1,000 miles from Xinjiang, in the land-locked, northwestern part of China, to seafood processing plants in Shangdong, on the east coast.

The report made a big splash in the seafood industry.

Several major US retail chains, including Albertsons Companies and Shaw's, and German retailers Aldi and Lidl, have ended their relationships with Chinese processing companies in advance and following the publication of the report.

Albertsons has dropped two products from High Liner Foods involving flounder and yellowfin sole after it was revealed in the report that one of Canada's largest seafood companies was buying from Yantai Sanko Fisheries, a Chinese processor accused of taking on Uyghur workers under the Chinese government's labor transfer program. The United Nations and human rights organizations consider this to be forced labor. 

Urbina told the congressional-administrative panel on Tuesday how the OOP team spent four years working on their project, describing how they decided to focus on the Chinese squid fleet. He said his team was successful at getting on vessels but, when that didn't work, they threw plastic bottles onto the backs of the vessels as they were steaming ahead. Crew members responded by throwing the bottles back with notes inside.

A still from a video contained in the Ocean Outlaw Project series shows plastic bottles being thrown on to the back of a Chinese fishing vessel.

Uyghurs were confirmed as working at certain seafood processing plants with the help of both social media posts by the workers and also memorandums published by companies thanking the Chinese government for their help in providing employees, he said.

US pollock sector calls for big changes in wake of report on Chinese forced labor

The investigative reporter described the difficulty that exists in determining the source of seafood and whether labor abuses are occurring, noting the "many handoffs" that occur for seafood in trade.  

"What certification regimes that have emerged in the private sector, whether they focus on environmental or labor concerns, do a very poor job even at identifying and countering such crimes in these supply chains," he told panel members.

Urbina said his team focused on China, in part, because it is the "undisputed superpower of seafood" as its distant water fishing fleet is vastly larger than any other country's and because it also serves as a processing hub for much US-sourced seafood.

"China matters and was the focus of our investigation, not just because it is the global linchpin of seafood production, but also because China is the most opaque of settings, the most prone to illegal fishing practices and, come to find out, the most dependent on forced labor when it comes to seafood," he said.

Urbina said his team found a "widespread pattern" of abuses on Chinese vessels and in processing facilities. He said the OOP investigation determined that half of the Chinese fleet, 357 of 751 vessels studied, were "tied to human rights or environmental violations on land." He described the problem with forced labor as being "deep and consistent," noting how China helped its seafood industry during the pandemic by "moving thousands of workers across the country from Xinjiang."

Eleven Chinese plants linked to forced labor were MSC-certified

Since 2018, he said, "More than a thousand workers from Xinjiang have been forcibly relocated to at least 10 seafood processing plants in Shandong that supply dozens of major US seafood brands, as well as brands in at least 20 other countries."

Since 2018, MSC certification requires fisheries and at-sea supply chain businesses to publicly report on their labor practices, declaring they do not include forced labor. MSC-certified supply chain businesses that undertake processing, packing and manual off-load must, therefore, undergo a yearly, independent third-party labor audit or submit a self-assessment report to MSC and allow MSC to commission an independent audit.

However, OOP reported finding 11 plants accused of using forced Uyghur labor transferred from the Xinjiang region with MSC chain-of-custody certifications, as reported by Undercurrent.

Urbina was joined at the witness table on Tuesday by Robert Stumberg, a law professor at Georgetown University; Greg Scarlatoiu, executive director of the Committee for Human Rights in North Korea; and Sally Yozell, director of the environmental security program at the Stimson Center. Among those present on the panel were its co-chairs, representative Christopher Smith, a New Jersey Republican, and senator Jeff Merkley, an Oregon Democrat, as well as Thea Lee, undersecretary at the US Department of Labor.  

US retail giant drops High Liner products linked to Chinese supplier allegedly using forced Uyghur labor

Stumberg and Yozell both called for the expansion of SIMP in their testimony, with Yozell mentioning the prospective future inclusion of pollock, cod and haddock, in particular. Urbina said he agreed with the sentiment.

"Bob and Sally have both said SIMP is a flawed tool but the one that's probably the most developed on the table," Urbina said. "Building on SIMP, expanding it, redefining it, getting more agencies involved in it, is at least what I hear from experts is probably the best step for trying to get the supply chain of this product more under control."

Urbina pointed to SIMP again when discussing the problem of federal agencies not communicating with each other enough, too.

"So you even look at things like trafficking getting introduced as an element within SIMP," he said. "The bigger issue is that the agency that oversees SIMP isn't built to be looking at trafficking issues and labor issues. [The Burea of International Labor Affairs, or ILAB] is and even State is, but the whole program resides under an agency that's a bunch of folks that are really, really strong on fishery issues and marine issues, but not labor issues. But everyone is defensive about their jurisdiction and therefore there's language in the rule but not real actual implementation of it."

title: Untitled
content:
The international conservation group Oceana has responded to the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium's latest report on the endangered North Atlantic right whale population by calling for the US and Canada to reduce ship strikes by better enforcing boat speeds.

The consortium, in its report released Monday (Oct. 23), in conjunction with a meeting in Halifax, Nova Scotia, estimated the current population of right whales was at about 364 in 2022, up from 340 the year before, as reported by Undercurrent News. It noted that analysis by the New England Aquarium has detected 32 "human-caused injuries" in 2023, including six fishing gear entanglements with attached gear, 24 entanglement injuries with no attached gear, and two vessel strikes.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) and Transport Canada (TC)  must increase protections to save the whales from extinction, Oceana US said in response.

Right whales are slow-moving animals, with a top swimming speed of around 6 miles per hour, the group said. They usually swim near the surface and, without a dorsal fin and with their dark color, they're not easy to spot.

"NOAA’s job is to prevent the extinction of critically endangered animals like North Atlantic right whales, yet this species is still not on a path to recovery and desperately needs stronger safeguards from ship strikes and fishing gear entanglements," said Gib Brogan, Oceana's campaign director in the US.

Right whale calf found dead off North Carolina coast, used to make case for emergency rule changes

The US chapter of Oceana released its own report in advance of the consortium publishing its latest population estimates, showing that most boats are speeding through slow zones designed to protect the critically endangered North Atlantic right whales.

In the US there are mandatory slow zones -- seasonal management areas (SMAs) -- where boats over 65 feet have to slow down to 10 knots, as well as voluntary slow zones, dynamic management areas (DMAs) where the speed rules are triggered by whale sightings, Oceana US explained.

The group said it analyzed vessel speeds in both SMAs and DMAs/Slow Zones to investigate if there have been improvements in compliance levels to protect these whales since the 2021 report. From November 1, 2020, to July 31, 2022, the analysis showed that once again, high percentages of vessels were speeding through both voluntary and mandatory management areas all along the Atlantic Coast, Oceana contends.

Canada spends another $3.4m to help snow crab, lobster harvesters go ropeless

But Oceana didn't leave commercial lobster and crab harvesters off the hook.

"Transitioning to ropeless fishing gear is the best way to reduce the risk of entanglement and demonstrate the strong government action required under the US Marine Mammal Protection Act in order to protect access for Canadian commercial fisheries to the lucrative US market," said Kim Elmslie, campaign director at Oceana Canada.

According to Oceana, about one-quarter of the right whales become entangled in fishing gear in the US and Canada each year, and "about 85% have been entangled at least once. Ropes have been seen wrapped around whales' mouths, fins, tails and bodies, which slow them down; make it difficult to swim, reproduce, and feed; and can cause death, the group argues. 

As previously reported by Undercurrent, both the American and Canadian governments have funded programs to develop and introduce ropeless gear.

title: Daily recap: US state net-pen ban not legally binding; Tuna catches rise, pressuring prices
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Friday, Oct. 20:

Washington state net-pen ban not legally binding, judge rules

The decision by public lands commissioner Hilary Franz to ban commercial net pen aquaculture on state-owned aquatic lands in the US state of Washington has no legal weight, a state judge has ruled.

US lawmakers push Customs to better enforce anti-Uyghur forced labor law

US representatives Raul Grijalva and Jared Huffman are pushing Customs and Border Protection -- the federal agency that has the power to stop imports -- to better enforce a new law and prevent Chinese seafood coming into the US from processing plants caught using forced Uyghur labor.

Tuna catches in the Eastern Pacific rise, pressuring prices

While tuna catches in the Eastern Pacific have substantially improved in recent months, market dynamics, especially slower demand in Europe, have posed challenges for processors.

Norway-Russian science advises tripling Barents Sea capelin quota for 2024

Norwegian and Russian marine scientists have recommended more than tripling the Barents Sea capelin quota from 62,000 metric tons in 2023 to 196,000t in 2024.

Norway salmon prices finally halt their lift, but Chilean, Scottish rise

Spot prices for farmed Norwegian salmon look to finally be correcting down in week 43 of 2023, commencing Oct. 23, though the extent of that correction is disputed. Meanwhile, Chilean prices are lifting, and Scottish have been pushed up by Storm Babet, sources told Undercurrent News.

Scottish shellfish firm rescues 3,000t crab factory from administration

UK crab, lobster and fresh seafood supplier Orkney Fishermen's Society (OFS) has successfully been sold out of administration to Orkney Crab, a subsidiary of Scotland's PDK Shellfish.

title: US lawmakers push Customs to better enforce anti-Uyghur forced labor law
content:
US representatives Raul Grijalva and Jared Huffman are pushing Customs and Border Protection (CBP) -- the federal agency that has the power to stop imports -- to better enforce a new law and prevent Chinese seafood coming into the US from processing plants caught using forced Uyghur labor.

In just the latest move responding to the Outlaw Ocean Project two-part series, published in the New Yorker on Oct. 9, Grijalva of Arizona and Huffman of California, both members of the House Natural Resources Committee, sent a two-page letter to CBP commissioner Troy Miller on Friday (Oct. 20). They urge him "to use the full authority granted under the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA) [of 2021] and sect. 307 of the Tariff Act of 1930."  

Report: Chinese plants using forced Uyghur labor supplying major European, US retailers

Under the UFLPA, which was passed in Dec. 2021 and went into effect in June 2022, it is illegal to import any goods, wares, articles, or merchandise mined, produced, or manufactured in the Xinjiang Uygher autonomous region of China, and under the Tariff Act, it is illegal to import into the US any goods derived, wholly or in part, from forced labor, remind the two lawmakers.

The second of two articles written by Outlaw Ocean founder Ian Urbina, a former Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist, claims to provide evidence of a Chinese program that has enlisted and transported a large number of Uyghurs from Xinjiang, in the land-locked, northwestern part of China, over 1,000 miles to seafood processing plants in Shangdong, on the eastern coast.

The articles have generated so much attention that a joint panel of Congress and White House officials has called a special hearing to learn more about the report, as reported earlier by Undercurrent News.

"According to one article, since 2018, the Chinese government forcefully transferred at least 1,000 Uyghurs and other Muslim minorities from Xinjiang to work in 10 large seafood companies in Shangdong. Five of the companies have exported over 47,000 metric tons of seafood to the United States since then, including 17% of all squid imported into the United States," the Grijalva and Huffman letter states. 

They say they are also "deeply concerned with evidence suggesting North Korean labor use in seafood plants in Northeastern China." Three Chinese plants using North Korean workers have reportedly supplied seafood to more than a dozen US seafood importers in the US. 

Chinese officials have rejected the claims, claiming they are "completely fabricated," as reported by Undercurrent.

Joint US Congress, White House panel schedule hearing to discuss report on use of forced labor in Chinese seafood

The two Democrats previously headed the House Natural Resources Committee and its oceans subcommittee, respectively, but now are ranking members of the same panels as a result of Republicans seizing the majority in the House.

They've asked Miller to, by no later than Nov. 15, provide Congress with a document describing the actions taken by CBP and its Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force to prevent the import of seafood linked to forced labor. They also want the agency to present a document describing any efforts to "develop and refine a strategy for targeting sectors, like seafood, that are likely to violate UFLPA or [the Countering America's Adversaries Through Sanctions Act]."

Additionally, on Friday, Grijalva and Huffman wrote a four-page letter to Gina Raimondo and Richard Spinrad, the commerce secretary and the under-secretary for oceans and atmosphere, respectively, asking them to address a long list of questions focused on the requested expansion of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Seafood Import Monitoring Program (SIMP).

"Expanding [SIMP] to all imported seafood -- and ensuring the program is functional, well-implemented enforced -- is key to closing US markets to seafood derived from [illegal, unreported and unregulated] fishing and abusive labor practices," they wrote.

title: Daily recap: Blue Harvest bankruptcy trustee seeks speedy auction; Black tiger output to hit 600,000t
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Tuesday, Oct. 17:

Blue Harvest bankruptcy trustee seeks speedy auction of vessels, permits

The new owners of Blue Harvest Fisheries' remaining commercial vessels and its federal and state fishing permits could be determined in as little as two weeks if the trustee in the failed US company's Chapter 7 bankruptcy case has his way.

Black tiger shrimp output forecasted to hit 600,000t by 2024

The production of Penaeus monodon shrimp, more commonly known as black tiger, is set to increase this year and next, Rabobank analyst Gorjan Nikolik predicts. Nikolik, who presented the shrimp forecast at the Global Seafood Alliance Responsible Seafood Summit in Saint John, New Brunswick, Canada, earlier this month, predicted 600,000 metric tons of black tiger production by 2024, a 7% increase year-on-year.

US pollock sector calls for big changes in wake of report on Chinese forced labor

The US' wild Alaska pollock industry has responded to the Outlaw Ocean Project report published by The New Yorker by proposing several new requirements and stiffer enforcement of trade-related policies across the US and EU. The Genuine Alaska Pollock Producers (GAPP), the group that acts as a marketing agency for US pollock producers, in a blog post published Monday, said its members were "horrified" by the report. 

Chile secures coho salmon export agreement with China

In the midst of the state visit of Chilean president Gabriel Boric to China, the two countries have signed a protocol agreement to allow fresh Chilean coho salmon exports to the Asian giant. Sady Delgado, AquaChile's general manager, who is also in China at this time, expressed enthusiasm for the agreement. 

Turkey's largest bass, bream farmer diversifies markets amid European slowdown risk

In the face of economic challenges in Europe affecting the consumption of seafood, Turkey's largest seabass and seabream farmer, Kilic Deniz, is adapting its strategy by expanding into new international markets. Sinan Kiziltan, Kilic's vice president, spoke to Undercurrent News about the company's efforts to navigate changing market conditions.

title: US pollock sector calls for big changes in wake of report on Chinese forced labor
content:
The US' wild Alaska pollock industry has responded to the Outlaw Ocean Project report published by The New Yorker by proposing several new requirements and stiffer enforcement of trade-related policies across the US and European Union. 

The Genuine Alaska Pollock Producers (GAPP), the group that acts as a marketing agency for US pollock producers, in a blog post published Monday (Oct. 16), said its members were "horrified" by the report. GAAP earlier fought to make sure that only its products could be called "Alaska pollock" and now hopes to secure the same kinds of protections in Europe.  

"For three years, GAAP has been tirelessly advocating for the name protection of wild Alaska pollock in Europe, so that consumers there can enjoy the same transparency consumers in the US are now accustomed to," wrote GAAP CEO Craig Morris. "Current laws and practices in Europe do not make clear the origin of fish and, in some cases, lead to misleading labeling. Nevertheless, GAPP will continue efforts to advocate for proper labeling for wild Alaska pollock with European regulators.

Report: Chinese plants using forced Uyghur labor supplying major European, US retailers

"Of equal importance, GAPP will also continue work with key customers in Europe to work towards wholly transparent on-pack labeling, ensuring consumers can make truly informed buying decisions," he said.

As reported by Undercurrent News, the two-part series published Monday by the group Outlaw Ocean Project has stirred a considerable amount of reaction from the US seafood industry. One article provided haunting details article about crew members being held captive, beaten and suffering from malnutrition aboard vessels in China's distant water fishing fleet.

A second article provided a thorough account of the Chinese program used to enlist and transport a large number of Uyghurs from Xinjiang, in the land-locked, northwestern part of China, over 1,000 miles to seafood processing plants in Shangdong, on the eastern coast. 

The Congressional-Executive Commission on China (CECC), a joint panel made up of US senators, representatives and administration staff, announced Thursday (Oct. 12) that it would hold a hearing on Oct. 24 to focus on the report, as reported by Undercurrent.

On Thursday (Oct. 12), Stephanie Madsen, executive director of the At-sea Processors Association (APA), the trade association that represents Alaska's catchers and processors of pollock, also made known her feelings about the recent Outlaw Ocean Project report in a blog post on Medium.

"No one who has read The New Yorker’s gut-wrenching new reporting on human rights abuses in the Chinese seafood sector can think that the status quo is acceptable," she wrote.

Joint US Congress, White House panel schedule hearing to discuss report on use of forced labor in Chinese seafood

"These human rights abuses should be intolerable for all of us," she said. "Equally intolerable is a system that allows seafood products harvested and processed under these conditions to enter global commerce."

APA is calling for the adoption of a more uniform and robust system of import controls by seafood-importing nations, Madsen advised. She noted how the European Union, in 2010, implemented a new Illegal, Unregulated and Unreported (IUU) Regulation, which requires a catch certificate to accompany all seafood imports. The system also empowers regulators to ban seafood imports from flag states that do not cooperate in efforts to counter IUU activity.

"It is past time for US authorities to follow Europe’s lead and require a flag state catch certificate to accompany all seafood imports," she wrote. "Linking this system to [the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's] biennial IUU report will give US authorities far greater leverage to secure improvements in counter-IUU measures by our trading partners. If this innovation is coupled with closer US-EU cooperation on seafood supply chain reforms and counter-IUU measures, there is an opportunity to force necessary changes in seafood supply chains covering a significant portion of global seafood consumption.

"Other major seafood importing nations, such as Japan, could hopefully be encouraged to follow suit," she added.

Lund’s, Trident, NFI respond to report spotlighting forced labor in China

A second step that Madsen has proposed is for US authorities to ensure that the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act is being fully enforced for seafood.

"If investigative journalists have been able to identify the use of Uyghur laborers at specific seafood processing plants in China, US Customs and Border Protection authorities should be able to do so as well," she wrote. "It is already illegal for any such product to enter the United States market. We need comprehensive implementation of this landmark law with respect to seafood imports immediately."

title: Untitled
content:
A Canada-led joint operation in the North Pacific this year reports to have discovered more than 3,000 illegal shark fins, including threatened species such as oceanic whitetip sharks.

According to a press release from Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO), officials from the Canadian Coast Guard (CCG), US Coast Guard (USCG) and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) also documented incidents of marine pollution and other violations.

Outlaw Ocean reveals ‘crimes at sea’ aboard Chinese fishing vessels

"Operation North Pacific Guard" is an annual, multi-national effort to coordinate fisheries enforcement to detect and deter illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing in the North Pacific.

DFO officers have taken part in the operation on USCG vessels since 2019, but this was the first time the operation was led by Canada. For two months, officers and support personnel patrolled more than 12,000 nautical miles on the chartered vessel, the Atlantic Condor, the equivalent of traveling halfway around the world.

"The goal of the mission was to find illegal high seas driftnets, illegal fishing activity, and inspect fishing vessels under international law to ensure compliance with fisheries regulations," DFO said in the press release.

According to the department, boarding teams interacted with more than 400 crew members from different nations onboard their vessels.

Canadian fishery officers, along with the US Coast Guard, located illegally possessed shark fins during a joint two-month operation in the North Pacific in 2023.

Canada also conducted air surveillance (based out of Japan) in support of Operation North Pacific Guard, with Canadian fishery officers flying 31 patrols.

Information from the air patrol was shared with enforcement partners in Japan and the US.

Canada is now working with the appropriate flag nations to support further investigations and sanctions on offending vessels, including providing evidence for 58 violations detected during these patrols.

During the mission, officers also collected environmental data and water samples to improve Canada's understanding of the high seas environment, including the migration range of species of interest, such as Pacific salmon.

This patrol was supported by funding from the Pacific Salmon Strategy Initiative, which aims to enhance conservation, protection, and enforcement efforts in high-risk areas for Canada's Pacific salmon stocks.

title: Joint US Congress, White House panel schedule hearing to discuss report on use of forced labor in Chinese seafood
content:
The special report that shone a spotlight on the Chinese seafood industry's use of forced labor, including Uyghurs, has gained the attention of both the US Congress and the White House.

Some European, US seafood buyers dropped Chinese processors accused of forced labor this summer

The Congressional-Executive Commission on China (CECC) announced Thursday (Oct. 12) that it would be holding a hearing in less than two weeks -- on Oct. 24 -- to "continue the CECC's efforts to ensure that [Chinese] goods and products made with forced labor do not enter US markets."

The panel, created by legislation in October 2000, is made up of nine US senators, nine US representatives and five senior administration officials appointed by the president. Co-chaired by representative Christopher Smith, a New Jersey Republican, and senator Jeff Merkley, an Oregon Democrat, its job is to monitor human rights and the development of the rule of law in China.

Other members of the commission include Alaska senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican, who already has introduced legislation aimed at blocking Russian seafood from entering the US after it was processed in China.  

"US imports of seafood caught or processed with forced labor may be prohibited under the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act [UFLPA], the Countering America's Adversaries Through Sanctions Act and other laws," reads a preview of the hearing, which is scheduled to begin at 10 a.m. EST. 

"Nevertheless, the US government, major grocery chains and restaurants continue to purchase seafood caught and processed using forced labor in China. This hearing will continue the CECC's efforts to ensure that PRC goods and products made with forced labor do not enter US markets. Witnesses will provide testimony about the human rights abuses on board China's IUU [illegal, unregulated and unreported] fishing fleet, the seafood supply chains tainted by forced labor in China, and the exposure of the US government and American consumers to these supply chains. Witnesses will also provide recommendations for US action."

The Outlaw Ocean Project series, which was published in conjunction with The New Yorker on Oct. 9, provided haunting details about crew members being held captive, beaten and suffering from malnutrition aboard vessels in China's distant water fishing fleet as well as a thorough accounting of the Chinese program used to enlist and transport a large number of Uyghurs from Xinjiang, in the land-locked, northwestern part of China, over 1,000 miles to seafood processing plants in Shangdong, on the eastern coast. 

Several major US retail chains, including Albertsons Companies and Shaw's, and German retailers Aldi and Lidl, have ended their relationships with Chinese processing companies in advance and following the publication of the report.

Albertsons has dropped two products from High Liner Foods involving flounder and yellowfin sole after it was revealed in the report that one of Canada's largest seafood companies was buying from Yantai Sanko Fisheries, a Chinese processor accused of taking on Uyghur workers under the Chinese government's labor transfer program. The United Nations and human rights organizations consider this to be forced labor. 

High Liner has dropped Yantai Sanko as a supplier, Jennifer Bell, vice president of corporate communications, told Undercurrent on Wednesday, Oct. 11.

Still from video uploaded to a Chinese government Douyin account in 2023 depicting a labor transfer organized by the Kashgar authorities. Source: The Outlaw Ocean Project.

Ian Urbina, the author of the story, is one of three witnesses expected to testify at the hearing. He is the director and founder of the Outlaw Ocean Project, a former 17-year reporter for the New York Times and the winner of a Pulitzer Prize.

The commission also expects to hear from Robert Stumberg, a law professor at Georgetown University, and Greg Scarlatoiu, executive director of the Committee for Human Rights in North Korea. It advises that other witnesses may be called.

Stumberg can be expected to call for stricter enforcement of existing laws. Passed in 2021, the UFLPA declared that all goods produced "wholly or in part" by workers in Xinjiang or by ethnic minorities from the region should be presumed to have involved state-imposed forced labor and are therefore banned from entering the US. 

That law is "distinctly powerful," he is quoted in the article as saying. 

Rather than primarily relying on advocates or journalists having to prove the existence of forced labor tied to a certain product, the law mandates that suppliers and importers prove that they have no connection to Uyghur labor, the article reports him as saying. The US government has already investigated the working conditions in a variety of other industries, including those for solar panels, auto parts, computer chips, palm oil, sugar and tomatoes.

"Seafood should be next," he said.

title: US bills would raise tariffs on Indian shrimp, create trade enforcement task force
content:
US senator Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana Republican, has introduced two bills intended to better level the playing field for US-harvested and -farmed shrimp and rice by making life more difficult for importers of the same products from India.

"When you eat seafood gumbo, you expect the shrimp and rice to be grown in Louisiana with our health standards," Cassidy said in a press release. "Americans' health should not be harmed because some countries have chosen not to play by the rules. Bringing China and India into compliance will level the playing field for Louisiana shrimpers and the food they produce."

The India Shrimp Tariff Act, S. 2979, would slap shrimp imported from India with an escalating set of tariffs, with higher new rates phasing in for three consecutive years, starting in January 2024. The fees would be intended to match the subsidies received by the Indian shrimp farming industry, explained the press release.

India is the world's top shrimp exporter, accounting for roughly 40% of US shrimp imports, "largely due to massive state subsidies," Cassidy's office noted.

S. 2979 has no co-sponsors, but it's supported by the Louisiana Shrimp Association, the Louisiana Shrimp Task Force, the American Shrimp Processors Association and the Southern Shrimp Alliance (SSA).

"Forty percent of imported shrimp in this market comes from India," said SSA executive director John Williams. "India isn't the dominant supplier because it is better at farming shrimp than the rest of the world. Rampant use of banned antibiotics in their aquaculture, tolerance for forced labor practices in their peeling sheds, and substantial export subsidies awarded by the Indian government are killing this market."

Cassidy's other bill, the Ag Disputes Act, S. 2992, would create a special task force to enforce agricultural trade disputes. It would consist of employees from the US Department of Agriculture's (USDA's) Foreign Agricultural Service, the US Trade Representative (USTR) and other federal agencies as determined by USDA and USTR.

The press release noted that India has repeatedly raised its minimum price support for rice and now owns 40% of the world's market share. India is also the world's largest producer of pulses and second largest producer of wheat, peanuts and cotton.

S. 2992 is co-sponsored by five other Republican senators, including Iowa's Joni Ernst, Arkansas' John Boozman, Alabama's Tommy Tuberville, Mississippi's Cindy Hyde-Smith, and Roger Wicker. The USA Rice International Trade Policy Committee also supports the bill. 

"A [World Trade Organization] case against India's rice subsidies is long overdue and long-term policy changes in India would help to make rice farmers from the US and other origins that play by the rules more competitive on the world market," said Bobby Hanks, CEO of Supreme Rice and chair of the rice policy committee.

Both bills were introduced on Sept. 28 in the Senate Finance Committee.

title: Federal jury convicts US flounder fisherman in overfishing scam
content:
A US trawler fisherman from Long Island, New York, was found guilty of federal criminal conspiracy, mail fraud and obstruction of justice in a New York court this week.

Christopher Winkler of Montauk, New York, was convicted by a federal jury for crimes associated with his captainship of the trawler New Age from 2014 to 2017.

Evidence presented in court showed that on at least 200 fishing trips, Winkler targeted summer flounder (fluke) and black sea bass and harvested those fish over quotas and state trip limits.

He also falsified fishing vessel trip reports (FVTRs) for those trips. His co-conspirators falsified corresponding dealer reports. Both sets of false documents were used to cover up fish that Winkler took over quotas.

"Fluke and black sea bass play a vital part in our marine ecosystem and quotas are designed to prevent overfishing and stabilize populations for the public good," said assistant attorney general Todd Kim of the Justice Department's environment and natural resources division in a press release. "We will continue to seek justice against those who flout laws that protect fisheries and the fishing industry."

This photo of the fishing vessel New Age, taken from surveillance footage, was one of the pieces of evidence presented in the case against Christopher Winkler, heard in the Eastern District of New York. Submitted photo

Fishing quotas for fluke and black sea bass were designed by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the New York Department of Environmental Conservation to ensure a long-term, sustainable population of the fish. As part of the fisheries management plan, NOAA requires fishing captains like Winkler to accurately complete an FVTR at the end of each fishing trip.

Winkler was required to declare his catch – which included fish species and weights – to NOAA and the State of New York. To cover up his illicit harvest and landings, Winkler falsified approximately 200 FVTRs that he then mailed to NOAA.

Similarly, a fish dealer – which is the first company that buys fish directly from a fishing vessel –must specify what it purchases on a federal form known as a dealer report. NOAA uses this information to set policies designed to provide for biologically and economically viable fish stocks.

Winkler sold illegal fish to three fish dealers. Because a mismatch between FVTRs and dealer reports would have alerted fisheries statisticians and enforcement personnel, Winkler's co-conspirators falsified dealer reports to cover up that fish were taken in excess of quotas.

The entire scam netted an overharvest of approximately 200,000 pounds of fluke and black sea bass, valued conservatively at least at $750,000 (wholesale).

"While most US fishermen follow the law, some still feel that they are above it," said Michael Henry, acting assistant director of the Northeast division of NOAA's office of law enforcement. "It is our job to protect honest fishermen and good actors, and this verdict should serve as a reminder that those who break the rules will be held accountable."

NOAA's office of law enforcement investigated the case as part of Operation One-Way Chandelier.

In a related case, Bryan Gosman and Asa Gosman of Bob Gosman Co. -- a Montauk-based fish dealer -- previously pleaded guilty to a charge of criminally conspiring with Winkler in November 2021.

They testified at the trial against Winkler, where it was revealed that Gosman had served as a lookout for Winkler on at least 16 occasions during the conspiracy, often communicating by text before the defendant arrived at the dock.

All three defendants will be back in court at a later date for sentencing.
