title: EPA: American Seafoods ‘stood apart’ on Pacific Northwest clean water act violations
content:
American Seafoods Group (ASG) vessels "stood apart" from the other Oregon and Washington offshore fish processors in the number and severity of violations of the US Clean Water Act, according to a press release from the country's Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) on a fine of close to $1 million for the company. 

ASG, which agreed to settle what it called a "paperwork issue" over the Clean Water Act violations back in August, "cited the companies for hundreds of violations", including discharging waste in the protected Heceta/Stonewall Banks complex along the Oregon coast, failure to monitor its discharges and missing or inaccurate information in required annual reports, it said. 

Investigation underway into death of American Seafoods crew member from suspected ammonia exposure

"EPA evaluated the compliance of the Oregon and Washington seafood processing industry and found that American Seafoods Company and the owners of its vessels stood apart from the other Oregon and Washington offshore fish processors in the number and severity of violations. The vessels are the American Dynasty, American Triumph, Northern Eagle, Northern Jaeger and Ocean Rover," it said in a statement published on Sept. 28. 

Discharge of seafood processing waste in prohibited areas and within the 100-meter depth contour of Washington and Oregon exacerbates already existing low-oxygen conditions, which negatively impact most fishes, crabs and other marine life, said the EPA. 

The agency requires ASG's subsidiaries to conduct "corporate-wide, systemic improvements to ensure compliance with its permits" and also requires the companies to pay $999,000 in penalties, which Undercurrent News previously reported. 

American Seafoods agrees to settle ‘paperwork issue’ over discharge permits for $999k

"In amassing hundreds of violations from illegal discharges to sloppy and even non-existent record-keeping, American Seafoods Company demonstrated a clear disregard for the fragile and valuable resources that sustain its business," said Ed Kowalski, director of EPA's enforcement and compliance assurance division in Seattle, Washington, where ASG is based. 

"When issuing a permit, EPA confers to the permit holder the responsibility to protect our nation's resources. We expect the company-wide, systematic overhaul of its operations will re-focus American Seafoods Company on the true value of its permit, the importance of tracking compliance with the permit, and the resources that permit entrusts it with protecting." 

ASG, which controlling shareholder Bregal Partners is seeking to divest, referred Undercurrent to its previous statement from August.

Later in the month, it emerged an investigation from US government agencies is underway into the death of a crew member aboard a Bering Sea factory trawler owned by ASG. The crew member on ASG catcher processor Northern Eagle died from suspected ammonia exposure, public radio station KUCB, which is based in Unalaska, Alaska, first reported.

US pollock sector dodges $400m bullet as American Seafoods settles Bayside railway litigation

The Coast Guard, Alaska State Troopers, and the federal National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's law enforcement unit are investigating the incident. 

in July, ASG reached a "global settlement" of just under $10m with the US government over its use of the 100-foot Bayside Canadian Railway to meet an obscure Jones Act exception known as the "third proviso." 

The settlement from ASG's logistics subsidiaries Kloosterboer International Forwarding and Alaska Reefer Management will withdraw claims against all the other industry companies who had also been issued penalties for using the "Bayside program" to transport pollock and other seafood from Alaska to the US East Coast.

title: FDA warns Indonesian tuna processor over ‘serious violations’
content:
The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has issued a warning to Winson Prima Sejahtera, an Indonesian tuna processor, for serious violations of the hazard analysis and critical control point (HACCP) regulation.

The FDA identified several significant deviations in the company's operation after an assessment conducted from April 2-9, 2023, it said in a letter you can read in full by clicking here. 

These include the failure to conduct a hazard analysis for the yellowfin tuna it produces, not listing the food safety hazard of pathogen growth, including salmonella, and not implementing the monitoring procedures and frequency listed in the HACCP plan.

The FDA has given Winson Prima Sejahtera 15 working days to respond to the warning, outlining the specific steps it is taking to correct these deviations. If the company fails to respond or if the response is found inadequate, the FDA may take further action, including refusing admission of the company's products.

Winson Prima Sejahtera is a member of the International Pole & Line Federation, according to the latter's website. The company lists Canada and the US as the main markets. Albert Winson, listed as the company's point of contact, was not immediately available for comment.

title: Editor’s choice: US processors investigated over child labor claims; Potential Alaska red king crab opening
content:
EMEA editor Neil Ramsden brings you a roundup of the main stories from the previous week. 

By far our most-read story last week was the news that seafood processing plants in New Bedford, Massachusetts, are once again at the center of an immigrant labor scandal, this time the focus also being on the alleged use of underaged workers. Frontline, a PBS-related investigative news journal, reports that the US Department of Labor is investigating New Bedford plants owned by both the Atlantic Red Crab Company and Sea Watch International, a Maryland-based clam processor.

Meanwhile, signs are pointing in the direction of an opening for the US state of Alaska's Bristol Bay red king crab fishery this fall. Members of the North Pacific Fishery Management Council's crab plan team indicated the Bering Sea stock is above the minimum regulatory threshold needed to open the commercial fishery at a meeting in Seattle, Washington. An official decision and total allowable catch won't be announced by Alaska's Department of Fish and Game until October.

Staying in the US, Blue Harvest Fisheries' filing for bankruptcy protection has taken yet another sizable 6,000 metric ton (12%) bite out of the already diminished quota remaining in the New England groundfish fishery. Because the ownership of the New Bedford, Massachusetts-based company's five remaining commercial fishing vessels is now in question, they aren't able to harvest any of the quota for which permits are attached.

US pollock and hake harvesting firm Arctic Storm Management Group held a christening ceremony for its new "first of a kind" pollock factory trawler, Arctic Fjord, last week. Arctic Storm held the christening event in its home port of Seattle, Washington, which was attended by many executives in the sector but was not open to the media. You can see photos of the event shared with Undercurrent here.

The increase in Ecuador's farmed shrimp production will offset deep forecasted drops from India, Vietnam and Indonesia, meaning global exports could be stable or even up in 2023. Gabriel Luna, an industry analyst and the owner of the consultancy GLuna Shrimp, told the audience at the recent Global Shrimp Forum in Utrecht, the Netherlands, that Ecuador could increase production by around 15% in 2023, taking its total to close to 1.5 million metric tons.

Investor Summa Equity has selected Norway's DNB Markets to run a sale process for the European €400-million-plus-turnover salmon processor Milarex, which plans to build a large processing plant in the US, now its primary market, sources told Undercurrent. Talk of the sale process for Milarex, which is headquartered in Norway and operates a large salmon smoking and processing plant in Poland, had been circulating for several days last week.

Prices for all grades of surimi have collapsed as new Russian and incumbent US pollock suppliers battle for sales in a market that has shrunk due to inflation hitting demand, multiple well-placed sources in the sector told Undercurrent. Several players in the surimi sector described the situation as a "perfect storm," where the market has "completely collapsed" due to weak demand and high stocks meeting additional supply out of Russia and strong US production, as one Russian source who spoke under an agreement of anonymity put it. The Russian supplier and a European buyer both said the situation is "tragic."

Indian shrimp is the "biggest headache" of all food imports to the EU for a large European importer that trades in everything from canned fruit to bottled tomato ketchup, according to an executive with the firm. The comments by Claus Norup, head of frozen seafood for German company I Schroeder KG, highlight the continued difficulties importers face dealing with inconsistent regulations and enforcement across EU member states. 

Meanwhile, Russian authorities have introduced new export tariffs applicable to a number of products, including seafood. The new levies -- of up to 7% of the products' customs value -- take effect next month and will remain effective until the end of 2024. Despite Russia's official pledges of "de-dollarization," the new tariffs are pegged to the ruble-US dollar exchange rate.

Finally, large US industry players Trident Seafoods and Pacific Seafood Group and a group of associations joined calls to push for support in this year's farm bill reauthorization. The clock is ticking on whether legislation aimed at boosting the US's seafood industry will be included in this year's farm bill reauthorization. The current farm bill, which encompasses a sweeping umbrella of agricultural and nutritional policy in the US, expires at the end of the month.

title: Calamasur claims Chinese squid vessels back in Peruvian waters are flouting satellite tracking rules
content:
The Peruvian fishing sector claims the Chinese fleet has resumed entering its national waters in recent months without complying with the mandated satellite tracking device installation.

In 2022, China outpaced Peru in giant squid landings, harvesting 504,000 metric tons of the resource, while Peru landed 457,000t, according to data from the committee for the sustainable management of the Southern Pacific jumbo flying squid, also known as Calamasur. 

Alfonso Miranda, president of the industry association Calamasur, has raised concerns about the recent resurgence of Chinese fishing fleet activities in Peruvian waters, with over 70 vessels now plying their trade. 

In an interview with Undercurrent News last week, Miranda highlighted that the Peruvian government had previously taken steps to address this issue. In 2020, Peru issued Supreme Decree 016-2020, which mandated the installation of satellite tracking devices on fishing vessels to enter its waters.

According to Miranda, the 2020 decree aimed to better monitor these squid fishing vessels due to the fact that they were severely questioned for illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing and human rights abuses on board. Following the decree's approval, only a small group of these vessels have continued to enter Peruvian ports between 2021 and 2022, citing force majeure reasons to justify their entry.

Alfonso Miranda at the Anfaco tuna conference on Sept. 14 in Vigo, Spain.

According to Miranda, the majority of the Chinese fleet operating in international waters outside of the Peruvian exclusive economic zone, instead of utilizing Peru's satellite tracking system, opted to travel back to China, a journey spanning 17,000 kilometers, for a cost of approximately $1.5 million and taking 90 days for a round trip. "This decision was made despite the much cheaper alternative of paying just $200 per month for the install of a tracking device," Miranda noted. 

The Peruvian executive pointed out that, more recently, things have changed. Between July and August of this year alone, they made more than 75 arrivals in Peru without using satellite positioning and claiming to enter a Peruvian port to disembark crew, despite this being prohibited under the decree's regulations.

An official list produced by the Peruvian production ministry and seen by Undercurrent showed that 56 Chinese vessels entered Peruvian ports between June 1 and Aug. 18.

Fishing industry raises alarm on unlicensed Chinese vessel’s entry into Peruvian waters

The executive expressed his concern: "Evidently, this lack of transparency indicates that those who avoid satellite tracking are hiding something significant. However, they decided to exert political pressure on Peru because it was so costly. They first exploited a loophole related to 'forced arrivals,' creating the impression of forced arrivals when it wasn't necessarily the case."

Furthermore, the president of Calamasur disclosed a significant development that had gone largely unnoticed by the public. He stated that the Chinese ambassador to Peru, accompanied by high-ranking officials, made an unannounced visit to the Ministry of Production last May. "It appears that this visit aimed to pressure the government into repealing the decree," he said.

Despite the pressure exerted by Chinese authorities, the Peruvian government did not repeal the decree due to strong opposition from artisanal fishermen. Instead, they pledged to strengthen its enforcement. However, in practice, it appears that the decree has been effectively revoked by Peruvian authorities, Miranda noted. "Over 70 foreign vessels have entered Peruvian waters since the ambassador's visit, citing various reasons for their presence, such as crew changes and document renewals. Some have even ventured into prohibited national shipyards," Miranda told Undercurrent last week.

Miranda stressed the importance of satellite tracking devices, stating, "The requirement for satellite tracking should be strictly enforced, as it also relates to vessel assistance activities such as crew changes and document alterations.

Without these devices, we are reverting to the previous state, where these vessels will continue to fish illegally in our maritime domain, despite the government's reluctance to admit it."

This controversy raises concerns about Peru's response to international pressure and its potential consequences. Miranda argued, "Peru may have succumbed to international pressure, jeopardizing the primary resource of artisanal fishing and the fishing industry, which provides significant employment in the country."

The timing of these events coincides with a change in leadership within Peru's production ministry, adding further complexity to the situation. Ana Maria Choquehuanca has recently taken office as Peru's new minister of production, replacing Raul Perez Reyes, in a ceremony presided over by Peruvian president Dina Boluarte.

The question remains whether Peru will uphold its commitment to maritime sovereignty and the protection of its vital fishing resources or continue to grapple with external pressure that could undermine its fishing industry.

title: Daily recap: Russian supply not at root of surimi market collapse; EU shrimp import rules a headache
content:
Here's a recap of the top daily seafood stories from Thursday, Sept. 21:

New Russian supply not main cause of 'complete collapse' in surimi market

Prices for all grades of surimi have collapsed as new Russian and incumbent US pollock suppliers battle for sales in a market that has shrunk due to inflation hitting demand, multiple well-placed sources in the sector told Undercurrent News. Several players in the surimi sector described the situation as a "perfect storm," where the market has "completely collapsed" due to weak demand and high stocks meeting additional supply out of Russia and strong US production, as one Russian source who spoke under an agreement of anonymity put it. 

Shrimp import rules the 'biggest headache' for European food imports

Indian shrimp is the "biggest headache" of all food imports to the EU for a large European importer that trades in everything from canned fruit to bottled tomato ketchup. The comments by Claus Norup, head of frozen seafood for German company I Schroeder KG, highlight the continued difficulties importers face dealing with inconsistent regulations and enforcement across EU member states. 

VASEP forecasts notable drop in Vietnam's tuna exports to $850m in 2023

The Vietnam Association of Seafood Exporters and Producers (VASEP) forecasts tuna exports to drop to $850 million in 2023, with canned products amounting to $250m, explained Le Hang, the association's communication director. 

Low demand for imported shrimp in China persists ahead of National Day

China's demand for imported shrimp remains lackluster leading up to the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holiday despite the long break from Sept. 29 to Oct. 6, according to Undercurrent's industry sources.

Atunlo exec claims lack of controls on frozen tuna at some EU border points

Jose Pernas, general manager at vertically integrated tuna firm Atunlo, used his presentation at the recent XI ANFACO World Tuna Conference to raise a red flag over a lack of control at certain European borders when it comes to the import of frozen yellowfin tuna.

Trade insights: China records first monthly drop in shrimp imports in 2023

China's appetite for imported frozen shrimp shrank in August for the first time in 2023 but remains strong so far this year. China's imports of frozen shrimp fell 12% by volume last month compared to August 2022, according to data released on Sept. 20 by China's General Administration of Customs.

title: Untitled
content:
UTRECHT, Netherlands -- Indian shrimp is the "biggest headache" of all food imports to the EU for a large European importer that trades in everything from canned fruit to bottled tomato ketchup, according to an executive with the firm.

The comments by Claus Norup, head of frozen seafood for German company I Schroeder KG, highlight the continued difficulties importers face dealing with inconsistent regulations and enforcement across EU member states. 

Seafood regulations panel at the Global Shrimp Forum in Utrecht. Credit: Louis Harkell / Undercurrent News

Speaking during wide-ranging discussions on shrimp import challenges at the recent Global Shrimp Forum (GSF) in Utrecht, Netherlands, Norup singled out Indian shrimp as the top compliance challenge among thousands of containers of food the company imports annually.

This follows changes in EU rules requiring half of all consignments of Indian shrimp to be checked by border inspection due to concerns about antibiotics use in Indian aquaculture.

Norup said this could lead to delays of two to five weeks at Hamburg port on arrival for testing.

"We don't have any other product in our company that causes so much trouble; we do canned fruit, frozen ketchup, and shrimp from India is the biggest headache for our company. That really is the case," he said.

To ease the "headache" of Indian shrimp imports, the company negotiated an agreement in Hamburg port where veterinary authorities test fewer containers from trusted suppliers. It now only imports Indian shrimp into a certain region in the port of Hamburg.

Norup negotiated the arrangement after meetings with the north German city's justice department, responsible for the port's veterinary offices. "We told them, if it takes more than seven days to get containers checked, we'll send you the invoice. So, we started to send invoices. After we sent a number of invoices, we got a meeting," said the executive.

"It didn't make sense for them to be testing so much and for it to be taking so long," Norup explained. "We are testing products ourselves, in India they are testing also."

He lamented this workaround limits logistics flexibility.

"The port isn't big enough [for all our imports]. So we use different ports for other products; but there we use the same system as everybody else. This system just didn't work for us with shrimp." 

EU rules on composite products causing ‘difficulties’ for seafood importers, concedes official

Norup criticized inconsistent enforcement for products. Due to strict inspections by Hamburg authorities for shrimp from Vietnam, his company decided to avoid sourcing from the Southeast Asian country. Another time, it lost €70,000 ($74,830) on a container of shrimp from Ecuador.

"That is the situation we see today where we're expending a lot of effort and a lot of work to get [imports] going smoothly," he said. "Not all companies can do this."

The importer's struggles highlight ongoing tensions between European regulators and industry that ran throughout the breakout panel discussion at GSF.

Guus Pastoor, chairman of the European Fish Processors and Importers Association, kicked off discussions by noting the increasing complexity of regulations governing seafood imports.

"It's taking more and more time. And for you as a business, we can see it's taking more and more effort to stay up-to-date," Pastoor said.

His concerns were echoed by Norup and other importers, who voiced frustrations to EU officials over what they see as unnecessary trade barriers. 

NFI exec warns new 2026 seafood traceability plan has flown ‘below radar’

Sylvie Coulon of the EU Directorate-General for Health and Consumer Protection acknowledged member states are responsible for enforcement, leading to inconsistencies. She indicated the EU has tools to identify risk issues but said ultimate authority rests with member states.

"We have tried for many years to harmonize the regulation at the borders," she said. "But the responsibility at the moment falls onto member states."

In response to Norup's struggles, Coulon said companies could inform her office of unreasonable actions by authorities in specific countries. However, she admitted the Commission has limited power to influence enforcement by national agencies.

"We have tools to check and to monitor, and from time to time, to identify risk issues. But it is up to the member state to implement the regulation," she said.

Vibrio alerts for Ecuadorian shrimp

Tensions over testing standards also surfaced during discussions about European authorities' vibrio bacteria inspections on Ecuadorian shrimp. An audience member noted some countries are not only blocking but destroying shipments due to vibrio, without allowing re-export.

The audience member questioned the legal basis for this approach, given no EU standard exists for vibrio in raw shrimp. Coulon responded that the issue was also raised by others outside the panel meeting.

She said Rapid Alert System (RAPEX) notifications related to vibrio on Ecuadorian shrimp originate from member state agencies. She said this means it's important to engage national authorities in cases where RAPEX alerts seem unwarranted.

Another audience member raised concerns that increased border inspections under the EU's food fraud network could target labeling and net weight compliance. Coulon explained that this was part of a trend towards increasing strictness of import regulations.

Pastoor summed up the central dilemma:

"It's a trade-off between food safety and food waste. We can see containers of food destroyed because of administrative reasons, not because of food safety. That's a topic we need to address."

title: Biden right whale commitment includes $17.9m for ropeless lobster gear
content:
The president Joe Biden administration  on Monday (Sept. 18) announced that it would use $82 million in funding from the Inflation Reduction Act to help in the conservation and recovery of endangered North Atlantic right whales. The investment includes about $17.9m to support furthering on-demand ropeless fishing gear technology.

The issue is of consequence to US harvesters of North American lobster, who are being encouraged against their wishes to use ropeless gear and threatened with losing their ability to fish.

National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) said it will invest in four major areas over the next three years, including monitoring and computer modeling of whale distribution, vessel strike risk reduction, on-demand fishing gear and enforcement efforts. NOAA also anticipates using the funding as follows:

About $35.8m for monitoring and modeling, including approximately $17.2m for passive acoustic monitoring along the US East Coast;
$3.5m for a satellite tagging monitoring program, in addition to $5.6m for high-resolution satellite artificial intelligence;
$5.2m for modeling advancements;
About $20.1m to be spent on vessel strike risk reduction efforts, including approximately $16.7m dedicated to whale detection and avoidance technology development; and
About $5 million to be invested in enforcement efforts, supporting new equipment, technologies and operations.

North Atlantic right whales are approaching extinction with fewer than 350 individuals remaining, including fewer than 70 reproductively active females, NOAA noted in its statement.

"During the past decade, right whales have changed their distribution patterns, spending more time in areas with fewer protections from vessel strikes and entanglements," said Janet Coit, assistant administrator for NOAA Fisheries. "The species has experienced a severe population decline that has underscored the urgency to take new and innovative actions for their recovery. This funding allows us to invest in technologies to reduce the risk of vessel strikes, increase the use of on-demand fishing gear and improve enforcement of existing federal regulations."

title: NGOs hope Dutch authority’s court appearance could set EU precedent
content:
Sept. 20 will see the first public hearing in a fisheries control lawsuit against the Dutch Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA), brought by NGOs ClientEarth and Low Impact Fishers of Europe (LIFE).

In June 2021, ClientEarth and LIFE launched an administrative request to the NVWA to enforce EU fisheries control laws and properly check the hundreds of thousands of metric tons of fish landing in its ports each year, they said.

"But the Dutch authorities replied negatively, prompting the two organizations to go to court in January 2023. The legal action is the first of its kind to challenge breaches to EU fisheries control rules by an EU member state and could set a precedent at the EU level."

The case takes issue with the fact that NVWA -- which is the responsible authority for implementing and enforcing fisheries laws -- is "routinely failing to check how much fish is actually being brought on shore by industrial fishing vessels, potentially letting thousands of tons of fish per year illegally enter the EU market, while putting some species at serious risk of overfishing and threatening the livelihoods of small-scale fishers who also target the same stocks," the NGOs claimed.

This is backed by several reports, including by the NVWA itself, which revealed in 2022 that fraud was rampant in the Dutch fishing industry.

"The Dutch authorities never provided us with concrete evidence that they were taking appropriate measures to prevent fish fraud and overfishing, so we took them to court," said ClientEarth lawyer Nils Courcy.

"We are looking forward to hearing the NVWA's arguments for not enforcing the law and whether they have taken any further measures to ensure that the millions of kilos of fish landed in Dutch ports every year are caught legally and are fully traceable."

"As the gateway for a large portion of EU fish to enter the market, the Netherlands has a crucial guardian role to play in preventing fish fraud and overfishing. We hope this judgment will help set a precedent and improve fisheries control activities in the Netherlands as well as in other member states. Without this, there can be no such thing as sustainable fisheries."

Illegal fishing and fish fraud undermine sustainability and put fisheries at risk, added LIFE's Brian O'Riordan. Small-scale fishers are particularly impacted by such activities that both deplete the resources on which they depend, and also depress market prices, he added.

"It is therefore vital that the Netherlands and other EU member states have a properly functioning control system in place to prevent illegal fishing and fraudulent practices. This is currently not the case."

A judgment on this case is expected soon. Meanwhile, an EU infringement procedure against the Netherlands for breaches of the fisheries control regulation is still ongoing, the NGOs concluded.

title: US state of Maine rescinds two leases needed by Nordic Aquafarms
content:
Nordic Aquafarms (NAF) has suffered what appears to be a major setback in its five-year, $500 million effort to build a 12,000 metric ton per year Atlantic salmon recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) in the US city of Belfast, Maine.

The Maine Bureau of Parks and Lands (BPL) has rescinded two leases needed by the company to lay pipes for its proposed land-based farm, the Bangor Daily News reports.

The decision comes after the Maine Supreme Judicial Court, in February, ruled that project opponents Jeffrey Maybee and Judith Grace own the intertidal flats and a conservation easement on the property is enforceable. Since the ownership case was decided after the leases were granted, the court remanded the case to state regulatory agencies, the news service explained.

Andy Stevenson, a spokesman for opponent Friends of Harriet L. Hartley Conservation Area, said Maine's Board of Environmental Protection must now re-examine the permits that it issued NAF in 2020.

NAF spokesperson Jacki Cassida told the news service that the Norwegian company is likely to reapply for the leases from BPL when the legal issues are resolved, and "the pause on our project and patient stance remains unchanged as legal proceedings continue."

title: Untitled
content:
The US and the Republic of Palau have signed a bilateral law enforcement agreement allowing the US Coast Guard to enforce regulations at sea in Palau's exclusive economic zone (EEZ) on behalf of Palau, in the absence of a Palauan officer, reports MSN.

Signed on the sidelines of the fifth annual Joint Heads of Pacific Security meeting, held Aug. 23-24 in Palau, the agreement has been termed a "regional milestone" by both countries and one that will "strengthen maritime security in the South Pacific."

The agreement comes at a time when China is trying to increase its footprint in the Pacific Island countries (PICs), which includes Palau. According to information shared by China's foreign affairs ministry, he has so far established diplomatic relations with 10 PICs.

The Pacific Islands are geostrategically significant, particularly owing to their importance for maintaining critical logistical supply lines and projection of military force, according to a 2020 analysis by The Brookings Institution, a nonprofit public policy organization.

Following the agreement with the US, Palau's president, Surangel S. Whipps Jr., was quoted as saying in a statement issued by the US Coast Guard that it helps Palau "monitor our exclusive economic zone, protect against illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing, and deter uninvited vessels from conducting questionable maneuvers within our waters."

title: Canadian lawmakers beg new fisheries minister to enforce Nova Scotia lobster season dates
content:
Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) has agreed to send "additional assets" to St. Mary's Bay, in Nova Scotia, following reports of illegal lobster poaching there, a Canadian lawmaker has reported.

Chris d'Entremont, a member of Parliament (MP) representing the western part of the province, and Rick Perkins, an MP representing the area of South Shore-St. Margarets, Nova Scotia, on Aug. 21, sent a strongly worded letter to new fisheries minister Diane Lebouthillier to complain about off-season lobster fishing in a vital part of Lobster Fishing Area (LFA) 34.

Both are members of Canada's minority Conservative Party, while Lebouthillier is a Liberal from the province of New Brunswick.

"Our communities are gravely concerned about the escalating levels of illegal lobster fishing taking place within this vital breeding area," they said. "We are jointly calling upon you to set a new standard within the department and enforce the law with the utmost urgency. It is crucial that we avoid repeating the inaction of your predecessors, Bernadette Jordan and Joyce Murray, who failed to address the pressing issue of criminal poaching activities."

Chris d'Entremont, Canada's deputy speaker of the House of Commons. Credit: Bernard Thibodeau, House of Commons Photo Services.

d'Entrement, who is deputy speaker of the House of Commons, posted an update on the situation on Aug. 23.

"Following the joint letter sent to minister Diane Lebouthillier's office on Monday by MP Rick Perkins and I regarding the illegal lobster poaching in St. Mary's Bay, my office has received some updates from [DFO] this morning," he wrote. "They have ensured us that additional assets will be deployed in the coming days to enforce the law and immediately halt lobster poaching activities. We shall see."

He promised that his office will be "closely monitoring this situation and will continue to hold the minister and her department to account until it is fully resolved."

DFO said in a Facebook post made Sunday (Aug. 27) that its officers had seized 321 lobster traps in Southwest Nova Scotia since July 17 for non-compliance with regulations. The lobsters were released back into the ocean.

"Enforcement activity is not always visible. Fishery officers use a range of monitoring and compliance tactics on and off the water. Anyone fishing without authorization is subject to enforcement action," DFO said in its post.

The scene of prior conflict

Canada is the world's leading producer of North American lobster (Homarus americanus), and LFA 34 is Canada's largest lobster fishery, accounting for 20,594 metric tons landed in 2021. The LFA 33 and 34 seasons begin every year on the last Monday in November and ends on May 31 of the following year. 

St. Marys Bay, near Digby, was the scene of confrontation in September 2020 when the Sipekne'katik First Nation started a self-regulated "moderate livelihood" lobster fishery that ran outside the commercial season, leading to confrontations on the water with licensed harvesters. There were riots at two lobster pounds, one of which was later burned down in a deliberately set fire.

A Canadian lobster. Photograph courtesy of Tangier Lobster, in Nova Scotia.

The Supreme Court of Canada ruled that the Mi'kmaq group has a right to earn a moderate livelihood from fishing, but the government also has the right to regulate that fishery for conservation and other purposes. And DFO has said that harvesting for moderate livelihood purposes is not permitted outside of the commercial seasons.

DFO said a small-scale food, social and ceremonial (FSC) fishery is allowed in St. Marys Bay within the LFA 34 season dates, but the Sipekne'katik have rejected their 2023 FSC limit of 45,000 pounds, according to CBC. In a May letter to DFO, the band said the FSC limit was made without adequate consultation and is an infringement of their rights. When DFO started seizing unauthorized traps in July, the band sued.

"There is no factual evidence that lobster are threatened or a species at risk, therefore there can be no justifiable infringement for conservation purposes," the suit claims.

This year the Sipekne'katik's council authorized 175 traps per vessel to pursue a moderate livelihood fishery and 25 traps per vessel for the ceremonial fishery, according to documents filed as part of the suit.

A map of Canada's lobster fishing areas as produced by the Cape Breton Fish Harvesters Association.

'The brazen presence of these illegal boats...'

The Canadian lawmakers and others upset about the lobster poaching have yet to identify First Nation groups as the culprits on this occasion.

"The opportunity now lies before you to send a resounding message to both the fishing industry and criminals involved in this illegal activity," d'Entremont and Perkins wrote in their letter to Lebouthillier. "This is not a mere food and ceremonial fishery; rather, it is an unlawful, out-of-season commercial endeavor that poses a significant threat to the stability of lobster stocks and the wellbeing of our communities. The brazen presence of these illegal boats dropping pots in the very nursery of these marine creatures is cause for serious alarm." 

They continued: "The stock must be safeguarded against criminal activities and poaching, especially given the unprecedented yield per pot during this season," the lawmakers said in their Aug. 21 letter. "With as much as 100 pounds of lobster per pot being pulled from the warm waters daily, the delicate reproduction cycle of these creatures faces an imminent threat. What we are witnessing is a full-scale summer season of poaching with license plates from New Brunswick, Quebec and the New England states readily visible along the wharf," they wrote.

Colin Sproul, president of the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance, dismissed the reports of DFO enhancing its enforcement efforts as "patently untrue," Global News reported. He called the current situation in St. Mary's Bay "outrageous," saying an "industrial level" commercial fishery is still taking place in the bay.

"As sad as it is to say, we're fast approaching the situation of 2020 in advance of the fishery crisis. There's uncontrolled industrial-scale fishing in St. Marys Bay and in adjacent waters with little to no enforcement effort," Sproul reportedly told the CBC.

title: Investigation underway into death of American Seafoods crew member from suspected ammonia exposure
content:
An investigation from US government agencies is underway into the death of a crew member aboard a Bering Sea factory trawler owned by American Seafoods Group (ASG). 

Last week, a crew member on ASG catcher processor Northern Eagle died from suspected ammonia exposure, public radio station KUCB, which is based in Unalaska, Alaska, first reported.

American Seafoods agrees to settle ‘paperwork issue’ over discharge permits for $999k

The Coast Guard, Alaska State Troopers, and the federal National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's law enforcement unit are investigating the incident. 

Coast Guard officer John Hightower told Undercurrent News he did not have a timeline for the investigation and said no one else was permanently affected by the exposure.

"The vessel has since been cleared as safe to sail and has resumed normal operations for the time being," he said.

According to Hightower, Coast Guard watchstanders received a satellite call from the vessel around 4 a.m. on Friday, Aug. 18, that a crew member had been found unresponsive in a space filled with dangerous levels of ammonia. 

Northern Eagle was already en route to Dutch Harbor at the time of the call; it arrived in port early Saturday morning.

US pollock sector dodges $400m bullet as American Seafoods settles Bayside railway litigation

"The single affected crew member was treated by Unalaska Fire Department EMS personnel who pronounced him deceased later that morning," Hightower told Undercurrent via email.

Northern Eagle is the longest catcher-processor in ASG's fleet, according to the company's website, at 341 feet. The vessel fishes for Alaskan pollock, Pacific hake and yellowfin sole. The company's website said Northern Eagle was rebuilt in 2012 and outfitted with new, ammonia-based freezing equipment to reduce the vessel's carbon footprint.

ASG has six catcher-processors and one mothership, which it recently acquired from Phoenix Processor Limited Partnership.

A spokesperson for ASG said via email Tuesday that the company was "shocked and saddened at this loss," and was providing grief counseling to crew members and cooperating with local authorities during the investigation.

ASG -- which is currently for sale -- has also just agreed to settle a dispute it terms a "paperwork issue" with the US government's Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) for a total of $999,000, the company previously told Undercurrent.

American Seafoods inks deal for processor vessel from Phoenix

According to the EPA, the company had "discharged" into a prohibited zone and failed to submit quarterly processing photographs, in addition to other allegations over record keeping.

"This dispute with the EPA is a paperwork issue related to reporting, filing, and interpretation of data in a new NPDES [National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System] permit covering Washington and Oregon," a company spokesperson told Undercurrent.

ASG "looks forward to putting this misunderstanding behind them," he said.

title: Ocean Harvesters issues fiery response to criticism of US menhaden fleet’s wastewater handling
content:
Ocean Harvesters, the US state of Virginia company that commercially harvests Atlantic menhaden (Brevoortia tyrannus) for Cooke's Omega Protein, is firing back at an effort by recreational fishers, boat sellers and conservation groups to seek stricter enforcement of wastewater discharge regulations against their vessels. 

"The fact that this is the second petition from the same groups aimed at shutting down a 145-year-old historic fishery, illustrates that they are throwing every issue they can think of against the proverbial wall to see what might stick," reads a statement sent to Undercurrent News by Ocean Harvesters, which is also minority owned by affiliates of Canada's Cooke, as foreign entities cannot own more than 25% of US fishing vessels or permits.

"To compare seawater released from our fishing operations to sewage outflow is factually incorrect," the company continued. "It is increasingly obvious that this collection of special interest groups will stoop to any level to support the recreational desires of the affluent over blue-collar families. It seems they will stop at nothing until they destroy the well-paying union jobs with medical benefits, that provide a quality of life for rural, minority blue-collar workers."

Atlantic menhaden.

The Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership, Virginia Saltwater Sportfishing Association, Coastal Conservation Association, American Sportfishing Association and Marine Retailers Association of the Americas are among the groups that announced Wednesday (Aug. 16) that they have endorsed a petition that asks Virginia to better enforce or change regulations that they say prohibit commercial menhaden fishing vessels from dumping contaminated water into the US' Chesapeake Bay, as reported by Undercurrent.

The petition, put forth by Andy Cortez, a long-time Virginia conservationist, in July, argues that the vacuum pump water they release contains waste discharges that are not permitted under state water quality code. It calls on the State Water Control Board (SWCB), a division of Virginia's Department of Environmental Quality, to regulate the contaminated wastewater as a point source pollutant, similar to a sewage or factory outflow.

Cortez said the discharged water contains levels of nitrogen, phosphorous, suspended solid waste and organic matter that are not in compliance with at least three state water quality codes. His petition also requested that SWCB either amend existing Virginia Pollutant Discharge Elimination System permit regulations or develop a new regulation.

The petition is reported by the Hodges Partnership, a public relations firm, to be the second within a month that raises concerns about the "harmful impacts" of the industrial menhaden fishery within Virginia waters. An earlier petition urged the state's fishery regulators to limit allowable fishing zones of the industrial menhaden fleet based on the depth of their 1,400-foot-long, 500-pound purse seine nets that "often extend deeper than the Chesapeake Bay waters they fish, resulting in fish spills, the unintended mortality of game fish, and damage to the seabed," according to the firm.

Ocean Harvesters catching menhaden in the Chesapeake Bay. Picture is still from company video.

Both petitions would seem to directly hit Ocean Harvesters and Omega Protein.  

"We consider it unfortunate that some groups believe the leisure activities of their members or customers take precedence over working families who have derived their livelihood from these waters since the 1800s," Ocean Harvesters said in its response, adding:
 
"The bay is our workplace. It is their playground. But unlike these groups, we believe the bay should be shared. We strongly support, and enjoy ourselves, the recreational activities which have taken place on Chesapeake Bay waters for over a century. 

The company stressed that it strongly defends the integrity of its fishing operations and is in full compliance with all applicable laws, regulations and environmental mandates.

"Regulators at the state and federal level regularly review our operations," Ocean Harvesters said.

title: Lund’s, Silver Bay, Del Mar achieve MSC status for largest US squid fishery
content:
Lund's Fisheries, Silver Bay Seafoods and Del Mar Seafoods have been successful in achieving Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certification for the California market squid purse and drum seine fishery, the largest by tonnage in the US.

The independent third-party auditor SCS Global Services took 15 months to review the health and practices of the fishery, according to a statement released Wednesday (Aug. 16) by Cape May, New Jersey-based Lund's. It's the second California squid fishery to be certified in the past few weeks after an alliance of six squid processors announced their MSC certification on July 31.

First group of Cali squid catchers gets MSC approval, second likely coming soon 

The certification has been expected since at least November 2022, when SCS Global published its draft report, advising that the fishery has many strengths, including "documented adaptable management strategies, monitoring, and enforcement" and "very little bycatch," as reported earlier by Undercurrent News. The public was given 60 days to comment.

The fishery, which is comprised of 76 licensed vessels, is managed by the National Marine Fisheries Service, the Pacific Fishery Management Council and the California Department of Fish and Wildlife. It operates within three nautical miles in California state waters, primarily between Monterey and the southern California bight.

Though the total allowable catch is set every year at 118,000 metric tons, the fishery seldom gets close to that number. In 2022, 64,052t worth $84.4 million were landed, an increase of 42% in volume and value over 2021, according to data maintained by the Pacific Fisheries Information Network.

$400m Peruvian group snaps up US squid supplier

California's commercial market squid fishery season runs from April 1 through March 31 of the following year, though landings are strongest during the late fall and early winter, according to the assessment report. 

Lund's president Wayne Reichle underscored the significance of the collaborative efforts in a statement.

"Aligning with two esteemed California squid producers, alongside SCS and MSC, reaffirms our commitment to the enduring viability of the California market squid fishery," he said. "The MSC certification distinguishes us as the sole US seafood producer engaged in harvesting, processing and distributing all three MSC-certified domestic squid species."

Silver Bay president and CEO Cora Campbell noted how her company participates in many MSC-certified fisheries in Alaska.

California market squid purse seine fishery nears MSC certification as global supply dips

"Expanding our relationship to encompass the California market squid fishery is a natural next step to offering our customers across the globe access to a full suite of certified products," she said.

A backdrop of rising prices, sinking harvests

The MSC news comes amidst a backdrop of rising prices and low harvests for other species. Demand for other squid species has been keeping general prices elevated, particularly in light of low Chinese catches of Japanese flying squid (Todarodes pacificus) and Argentine shortfin squid (Illex argentinus).

California market squid (Doryteuthis opalescens, formerly classified as Loligo opalescens) is a favorite for many calamari-lovers due to its mild and slightly sweet flavor.

title: Recreational harvesters back petition for better regulating US commercial menhaden fleet’s water discharges
content:
A coalition of recreational fishing and boating groups have endorsed a petition that asks the US state of Virginia to better enforce or change regulations that they say prohibit commercial menhaden fishing vessels from dumping contaminated water into the Chesapeake Bay. 

The petition, put forth by Andy Cortez, a long-time Virginia conservationist, in July, argues that the vacuum pump water released in Virginia waters contains waste discharges that are not permitted under state water quality code, explains a statement issued by The Hodges Partnership, a Richmond, Virginia-based public relations firm.

Ocean Harvesters christens new Atlantic menhaden vessels

It calls on the State Water Control Board (SWCB), a division of Virginia's Department of Environmental Quality, to regulate the contaminated wastewater as a point source pollutant, similar to a sewage or factory outflow, a press release issued on Wednesday (Aug. 16) explained.

Cortez said the discharged water contains levels of nitrogen, phosphorous, suspended solid waste and organic matter that are not in compliance with at least three state water quality codes. His petition also requested that SWCB either amend existing Virginia Pollutant Discharge Elimination System permit regulations or develop a new regulation.

"The discharge from these commercial fishing boats is producing a point source pollutant that exceeds what is acceptable under state law," Cortez said. "These vessels are demonstrating a blatant disregard for the health of Virginia's waterways, and it's time that they be regulated in ways that help protect some of our most valuable and vulnerable resources."   

Among the conservation groups endorsing the petition are the Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership, Virginia Saltwater Sportfishing Association, Coastal Conservation Association, American Sportfishing Association, and Marine Retailers Association of the Americas. 

The petition would seem to directly hit Ocean Harvesters, the big Virginia-based commercial harvester of menhaden that supplies Omega Protein, a division of Canadian seafood giant Cooke. Ocean Harvesters is also minority owned by Cooke affiliates, as foreign entities cannot own more 25% of US fishing vessels or permits. 

Ocean Harvesters to start menhaden season with two newly converted steamers

A spokesperson for Ocean Harvesters was working to provide a response at press time.

The petition is reported by the Hodges Partnership to be the second within a month that raises concerns about the "harmful impacts" of the industrial menhaden fishery within Virginia waters. An earlier petition urged the state's fishery regulators to limit allowable fishing zones of the industrial menhaden fleet based on the depth of their 1,400-foot-long, 500-pound purse seine nets that "often extend deeper than the Chesapeake Bay waters they fish, resulting in fish spills, the unintended mortality of game fish, and damage to the seabed," according to the firm.

"Omega Protein has violated water quality laws before, so unfortunately, it isn't surprising they're under scrutiny again for polluting Chesapeake Bay," said Dinkus Deane, president of the Virginia Anglers Club, reported to be one of the Commonwealth's oldest fishing clubs. "Good neighbors don't dump their waste in their neighborhood and put local folks' health, livelihoods, and marine life at risk. Virginia's Department of Environmental Quality is obligated to regulate the contaminated wastewater, and if Omega is truly a good neighbor as they claim, they'd do the right thing and stop this practice immediately until a remedy is found."

title: Whaling commission issues extinction alert for Mexico’s vaquita porpoise
content:
The International Whaling Commission (IWC) has issued an extinction alert for the critically endangered vaquita porpoise, marking its first-ever extinction warning, reports Reuters. 

The vaquita, the world's smallest porpoise native to Mexico's Gulf of California, has seen its population decline to less than a dozen due to illegal gill net fishing for the totoaba fish, highly valued in Asia.

The IWC's scientific committee reported an alarming 83% drop in the population between 2015 and 2018, with only nine or ten individuals remaining.

However, it believes that complete enforcement of the ban on gill netting in the vaquita's core habitat could give the species "a chance of recovery." 

"The extinction of the vaquita is inevitable unless 100% of gillnets are substituted immediately with alternative fishing gears that protect the vaquita and the livelihoods of fishers," it said. 

Earlier this year, the US interior secretary declared that Mexico had failed to halt the illegal wildlife trade threatening the vaquita. However, the US government ruled out a trade embargo in July.

title: Oregon panel votes to extend Dungy crab trap restrictions indefinitely
content:
The Oregon Fish and Wildlife Commission voted late on Friday (Aug. 4) to extend limits on crab traps and the depths at which they can be placed in the months when humpback whales are more likely to swim in the coastal waters, the Associated Press reports. 

The measures, which were put in place in the US state in 2020 and are supposed to end after this season, have no sunset date.

Humpbacks, which migrate off Oregon's coast, and other whales can get caught in the vertical ropes connected to the heavy traps and drag them around for months, leaving the mammals injured, starved, or so exhausted that they can drown, conservationists have argued.

In the last decade, nine humpbacks were entangled in Oregon Dungeness crab gear, including two tied to the state in 2022, according to data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

But crabbers fear the extension of the regulations will harm the industry. The move comes during an already turbulent period for Oregon's Dungeness crab fishery, as it also contends with warming oceans, smaller crabs and shortened or canceled seasons due to high levels of domoic acid, a naturally occurring neurotoxin caused by algae blooms that make the crabs inedible, The Washington Post advised in an article published Friday.

The sector is the backbone of the Pacific Northwest's commercial fishing industry. In 2021-2022, Oregon crabbers landed more than 17 million pounds and delivered a record $91 million worth of crabs due to high market prices.

The returning Oregon pot limits are enforced at the start of the season, in December, and tightened by 20%, with an added 240-foot (73-meter) depth limit, from May 1 through the end of the season, when humpbacks are most common along the Oregon coast.

Crabbers say the depth restrictions already have impacted their ability to turn a profit. One harvester told the Post that the state's Dungeness fleet switched to halibut fishing alone after May 1, when crab pots couldn't sink deeper than 240 feet, which he said cost him "a significant amount of money."

But Francine Kershaw, a senior marine scientist at the Natural Resources Defense Council, has argued that restrictions need to be further tightened. The number of traps in the water should be reduced by 40%, trap depths should be restricted to 168 feet (51 meters), and those rules should start earlier, on April 15, to align with peak exposure to whales, she said.

title: World Bank approves new funding to fight against IUU fishing in Pacific
content:
The World Bank's board of directors has approved $9 million in funding for a program aimed at enhancing regional collaboration to combat illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing in the Pacific Ocean.

The funding will support the Pacific Islands Forum Fisheries Agency (FFA) in its efforts to strengthen monitoring and reporting tools, improve surveillance and enforcement across maritime borders, and harmonize regional policies.

The countries receiving support through this project include the Federated States of Micronesia, Fiji, Kiribati, Marshall Islands, Nauru, Palau, Papua New Guinea, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu.

"Fisheries are vital to the economies of Pacific countries, and in six FFA member countries are the source of more than 40% of government revenue," said FFA's director general Manu Tupou-Roosen. 

The Pacific region is home to 60% of the world's tuna catch, he added.

"Yet while the four major tuna stocks in the Western and Central Pacific Ocean are healthy and not overfished, there is no room for complacency as the overall mass of most tuna stocks is declining, and IUU fishing is estimated to amount to a value of $333.49 million annually or around 6.5% of total fish catch in the area," said Stephen Ndegwa, the World Bank's country director.

title: Tri Marine installs electronic monitoring on distant-water tuna longliners
content:
US-based Tri Marine International, the tuna supply division of Italy's Bolton Group International, announced it has successfully installed new electronic monitoring capabilities onboard distant-water tuna longline vessels.

The move, which was accomplished in partnership with Lexington, Kentucky-based Flywire, represents the second phase of a planned multi-year collaboration and was conducted by a team of colleagues from the US, Taiwan and Trinidad, the company said in a statement. 

The statement doesn't clarify how many vessels have had EM devices mounted on them.

Tri Marine reported to be a leader in EM since facilitating the first EM-related pilot project on distant water tuna longliners in the Western and Central Pacific in 2014, in partnership with the Secretariate of the Pacific Community, Solomon Islands Ministry of Fisheries and Marine Resources, The Nature Conservancy and the vessel owner.

The company said it continues to advance innovative solutions in an ongoing effort to develop EM beyond an enforcement-only transparency tool.

Tri Marine said its ultimate goal in partnering with FlyWire is to establish an EM program that generates needed scientific contributions while also creating a higher-value proposition for suppliers and customers. It said its two-year collaboration with the technology company has resulted in reducing the cost of EM hardware by 80%.

The company said it also intends to increase the observer coverage rate related to its recently certified Atlantic albacore longline fishery.

"It is amazing to see what's possible with a different approach to EM. Because our team is focused on fishermen, we are succeeding in driving down costs, increasing value and managing data risk," said Christa M. Svensson, Tri Marine's global sustainability program manager.

The Milan, Italy-based Bolton Group formally took control of the core tuna business of Tri Marine in July 2019, leading to the creation of a new business unit, as reported by Undercurrent News. The two firms were expected to create an integrated tuna business with turnover of over $2.5 billion.

title: Canada to begin patrolling Indo-Pacific to protect salmon this fall
content:
Canada's Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) will begin its first high-seas mission to combat illegal, unregulated and unreported (IUU) fishing this fall in the North Pacific. 

The country blames IUU fishing in the Indo-Pacific for falling Pacific salmon populations. This fall, Canadian fishery officers -- in conjunction with the Canadian and US coast guards -- will begin patrolling the region, conducting boardings and inspection operations, and harvesting scientific data. The overall mission has been dubbed Operation North Pacific Guard.

DFO has contracted with Atlantic Towing for a vessel for the operation. Funding was sourced through the federal agency's Pacific Salmon Strategy Initiative, which will provide CAD 46 million ($34.86m) over the next five years.

"Pacific salmon is vital to the food security, cultures, and economies of numerous First Nations, as well as the livelihoods of thousands of workers in rural and coastal communities in British Columbia and Yukon," said Canadian fisheries minister Joyce Murray.

"As fish are not bound by borders, we must take decisive action to safeguard these species. This high seas enforcement operation will assist in the rebuilding efforts we are undertaking domestically. I wish the fishery officers, Coast Guard personnel, and crew a safe and successful journey and thank them for their efforts in curbing illegal fishing activities."

title: Peru fish landings down 89% with anchovy catches for fishmeal, oil almost nonexistent
content:
Peru saw its wild-caught seafood landings fall year-on-year to 132,200 metric tons worth PEN 185.2 million ($51.9m) in May, down by 89% in volume and 71% in value, based on data published by the country's ministry of production, known as Produce.

According to the ministry, this was driven by a 99.3% drop in landings of raw material destined for indirect human consumption (IHC), fishmeal and fish oil, which has raised concerns among industry stakeholders.

"The month of May witnessed a significant decrease in anchovy landings in the southern ports of Pacocha and Ilo, primarily due to the dispersion of the resource, making extraction challenging," said Produce.

"Furthermore, during the same month, no anchovy landings were reported in the north-central zone. This was a direct result of the ongoing summer reproductive ban, which aims to protect the species during their breeding season. The ban, enforced to ensure the sustainability of the anchovy population, has led to a halt in fishing activities in the region," it added.

Moreover, it is important to note that May 2022 marked the beginning of the first anchovy fishing season last year, establishing a high baseline for comparison, commonly referred to as "the baseline effect," according to Produce.

"This baseline effect is crucial in understanding the year-on-year changes in landings and provides valuable insights into the overall health of the anchovy fishery," it pointed out.

Landings for IHC fell to 7,600t worth PEN 3.3m in May 2023 compared to 1.07m metric tons worth PEN 456.1m the year before, as the second chart below -- available on Undercurrent News' supply page -- shows.

"Following the contrary trend, landings resulting from catches intended for direct human consumption (DHC) rose by 37.3%, mainly influenced by higher catches of fish and seafood destined for frozen and cured seafood production," said Produce. 

Thus, fishery landings for the value-adding of frozen products amounted to 79,700t worth PEN 68m, up by 92.2% but down 11.4%, respectively, y-o-y.

"This was mainly influenced by higher catches of squid, whose volume increased by 175.9%, going from 26,900t in May 2022 to 74,300t in May 2023," Produce also stated. "Additionally, catches of bonito tuna also rose by 90.6%."

Conversely, catches of shrimp, bigeye tuna, fan shells, anchovy and hake destined for frozen seafood production fell by 37.3%, 47.7%, 77.8%, 83.7% and 92.1%, data published by the ministry also shows. 

Fishing for canneries, however, amounted to 4,600t, a figure coincidentally 4,600t lower than during the same period a year before, mainly due to a decrease in mackerel landings (down 85.6%), horse mackerel (down 60.5%), tuna (down 86.3%) and anchovy (down 89.2%) for this purpose. 

This, however, was partly offset by a notable increase in catches of bonito tuna (up 628.8%).

Landings for the manufacture of fresh products amounted to 29,400t, a slight decrease of 3.7% y-o-y due to the domestic market taking less horse mackerel, which fell by 64.2% from 5,800t to 2,100t; mackerel (down 70.5%); hake (down 83.3%), Peruvian silverside (down 58.9%) and squid (down 82%).

"In contrast, landings of bonito tuna, giant squid, lisa, shrimp and mahi mahi increased during this period by 49.9%, 19.1%, 27.6%, 166.2% and 280.2%, respectively," Produce said. 

Regarding landings for the manufacture of cured products, they amounted to 5,100t worth PEN 3.7m, up by % in volume but down 15.8% in value year-on-year. 

In May, 64% of the total landings for DHC were allocated to the manufacturing of frozen fish products, followed by the manufacturing of fresh (28.3%), cured (4.1%) and canned (3.7%) products.

title: California market squid purse seine fishery nears MSC certification as global supply dips
content:
The purse seine fishery for California market squid caught off the West Coast of the US is moving steadily toward certification by the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) against a backdrop of rising prices and low harvests for other species. 

The certification of the California market squid (Doryteuthis opalescens, formerly classified as Loligo opalescens) purse seine fishery is in its final stages and will likely be complete by the end of July, according to a final assessment report and recommendation published July 7 by MSC. Certification proceedings for the fishery began in October 2022 when auditing company MRAG Americas was contracted by the Cal Marine Fish Company, a subsidiary of Inter Oceanic Holdings, a fish and bait company based in Bellevue, Washington. 

"The MRAG Americas assessment team has determined that the fishery meets the requirements for a well-managed and sustainable fishery," according to the recommendation. "Please note this decision is a determination and not the final certification result." Objections to the planned certification are due by July 28.

The state of California, where the largest number of market squid are landed, recorded a 51,120.8 metric ton total harvest worth $67.3m at the dock in the 2022-2023 season, the most recent year for which data is available from the California Department of Fish and Wildlife. 

The state's commercial market squid fishery season runs from April 1 through March 31 of the following year, though landings are strongest during the late fall and early winter, according to the assessment report. 

There is another concurrent certification for another group of market squid players that contracted with auditor SCS Global Services. That certification is expected in early August. Harmonization meetings between SCS and MRAG took place in January. 

20,000 leagues under TAC

Had the already fabulously wealthy Captain Nemo in Jules Verne's 1872 novel "20,000 Leagues Under the Sea" kept the giant squid that attacked his submarine on ice till 2023, he might have become quite a bit wealthier. 

Asian demand for other squid species is keeping general prices elevated, particularly in light of low Chinese catches of Japanese flying squid (Todarodes pacificus) and Argentine shortfin squid (Illex argentinus). US exports of all squid and cuttlefish to China totaled 2,051t in April, the last month for which data was available from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Total exports in April, a relatively low month, were 3,704t. 

US squid and cuttlefish exports to China, from UCN Trade Portal.

More stringent Chinese enforcement of UN sanctions on North Korea is chiefly to blame for an estimated 2023 flying squid catch of around 50,000t, or half of the usual volume, for possibly the third year running. According to the Food and Agriculture Organisation of the United Nations, the global catch of Japanese flying squid fell below 100,000t for only the second time in 2021. Market sources previously told Undercurrent News that 2022's catch was also around 50,000t. 

"In the past several years, people are willing to say, 'Okay, the catch this year will probably be better.' But in reality, every year the catch is not that great," Landy Chow, marketing manager for frozen seafood distributor Siam Canadian, previously told Undercurrent.

Meanwhile, the January-April Illex squid season was a "disaster," according to at least one harvester. Squid harvesting was halted in May for 21 days due to reported small sizes, but it is unclear how long the second season will last - possibly through the end of July. 

Argentinian Illex prices recently reached $3,800 per metric ton, a sharp increase compared to $3,200-3,400/t in early April, which was already well above previous price levels. Nevertheless, the overall catch volumes remain significantly lower than in previous years.

"The January-April campaign for Illex squid was a disaster, and now it is picking up again," said an executive with a fishing company, who preferred to remain unnamed. "Prices are firm at $3,800/t CFR on average for all destinations and are not expected to go down as there is a lot of demand, mainly in Asia."

title: World’s largest fishing country tests catch quotas as alternative to annual ban
content:
China, the world's largest fishing nation, is exploring new approaches to fisheries management that could consign its controversial annual fishing ban to the scrapheap.

Each year during the summer, China bans fishing for three- to four-and-a-half months. The ban spans the East China Sea, Yellow Sea, and South China Sea, as well as inland freshwater lakes and rivers.

China’s Guolian obtains world’s first ASC certification for crayfish

The fishing halt -- covering most of China's 14,000-kilometer coastline -- is the Chinese government's primary tool to restrict fishermen from plundering the country's territorial waters.

However, the ban, which usually begins on May 1 and ends in August or September, is considered as controversial as it is cumbersome; anecdotal reports suggest the moratorium has failed to prevent declines in some fish stocks, while the lack of landings for several months causes supply shortages for local processors. 

In the report -- by the US-based Natural Resources Defense Council, Environmental Defense Fund and China's Qingdao Marine Conservation Society -- researchers found China has been exploring "a variety" of fisheries management approaches that could potentially work as an alternative.

Since 2017, the focus has been on total allowable catches (TACs) -- whereby volume catch limits are based on scientific assessment and analysis -- which have been trialed in 11 Chinese provinces, it said.

"China has always attached great importance to the conservation and sustainable use of marine fishery resources," Tang Yi, dean and professor from the College of Marine Culture and Law, Shanghai Ocean University, wrote in the report.

"However, the use and management of fishery resources in China remain basic and inefficient, while fishing capacity still exceeds the carrying capacity of fishery resources," he said.

Source: Progress of China's TAC System report.

A shift towards TACs in China

A shift towards TACs would represent a marked change in the world's largest fishing nation, which according to official figures, landed 13.1 million metric tons of fish from marine and freshwater sources in 2021.

Since the country's opening up and economic reforms, the country's growth and development have often been prioritized at the expense of environmental protection. According to industry observers, as a result, today, most of China's domestic fishing grounds are exploited beyond their maximum sustainable limit.

In 2017, in a bid to strengthen scientific fisheries management, the country launched its first trials of total allowable catch (TAC) systems in the coastal provinces of Zhejiang, Shandong and Fujian, among China's central fishing provinces, according to the green groups' report.

By late 2020, most coastal provinces had initiated at least one TAC pilot program, mainly for single species like crabs, jellyfish and shrimp -- species with a short life span -- across a limited geographic distribution and a small number of fishing vessels.

In Zhejiang province, pilots targeted gazami crab and juvenile anchovy fisheries, while Fujian province tested TAC management for a mix of four swimming crab species.

For the juvenile anchovy fishery -- which used purse seine -- scientists set a TAC within a 10% margin of the three-year annual average catches, so 4,000t. For gazami crab, the quota was based on six years' historical catch, at 3,200t.

The report said that tools tested include fishing logbooks, electronic monitoring, onboard observers, and requirements to land catches at designated ports for inspection. 

Source: Progress of China's TAC System report.

"The pilots experimented with new catch monitoring and enforcement systems," said Li Wei, oceans program director at the Natural Resources Defense Council in Beijing. "All pilots underwent substantial discussion and examination regarding the fishery selection, implementation plan, and regulatory measures."

Source: Progress of China's TAC System report.

Emma Yu, Emma Yu, an executive at Zhoushan City Shuangying Aquatic Products, told Undercurrent News that she'd welcome a quota system.

Her company processes Pacific chub mackerel caught in the East China Sea into butterfly fillets, which it exports primarily to Poland and other Eastern European countries.

"A quota system would provide more stability in our supply chain and operations," she told Undercurrent at the recent Seafood Expo Global in Barcelona. "With the fishing moratorium, we experience wide fluctuations in raw material availability and pricing."

She noted that during the summer, when there's no supply due to the moratorium, the company must rely on frozen fish stored in warehouses to meet production targets.

"Quotas would enable us to better plan our procurement and production schedules," Yu said. "With individual quotas, each fishing vessel owner would also be accountable for staying within their limit. There would be an incentive to be more responsible."

Challenges with implementation

While Li called the pilots "successful," others said major obstacles remain before China can fully adopt science-based TAC systems.

Challenges include a lack of stock survey data, poor coordination among government agencies, inadequate monitoring and enforcement, and technical difficulties with reporting tools like electronic logbooks, the report found. In the pilots, TAC limits were based mainly on recent catch history, not scientific stock assessments, the green groups' report said. 

Source: Progress of China's TAC System report.

Chinese project science directors also routinely could not evaluate the accuracy of pen and paper entries, it said, although fishermen were not suspected of misreporting intentionally. Meanwhile, with quotas set relatively high, the TAC faced fewer challenges of self-policing.

"For uptake of a TAC must be monitored on a scale appropriate to its effective implementation," the report noted. 

Moreover, transshipment -- described as prevalent in China given the country's "economic conditions" -- could introduce loopholes that enable the landing of illegally caught fish.

Source: Progress of China's TAC System report.

Songlin Wang, an expert on fisheries management at the Yellow Sea Fisheries Research Institute, said he does not foresee TAC systems becoming a major tool shortly.

"But I fully support continuous trying and testing," Wang told Undercurrent. He added that TAC may be feasible in some areas and for some species "over the next few years" as fishing capacity declines in coastal waters.

Since Pacific chub mackerel's migratory pathway covers several provinces, this would require a science-based regional effort, he noted. "The major Pacific chub mackerel straddles between two of China's fisheries management units: the Yellow Sea and the East China Sea," he said.

Wang said two more significant priorities should be protecting critical habitats and reducing the mortality of juvenile fish before moving to quota-based management.

The report underscores the complexity of implementing TAC systems in China, where small-scale fishermen dominate coastal fishing grounds often shared by multiple gear types and species.

Tang said with this in mind swift adoption of TACs in China was unlikely on the cards. "The gap between what we have and want still remains large," he said.
