title: Prolonged West Coast Canadian dock worker strike threatens seafood supply chain, exports
content:
On the 13th day of the dock workers' strike at the ports of Vancouver and Prince Rupert, a resolution still appears far away, bringing attention to potential disruptions in the seafood supply chain.

While fresh or chilled farmed salmon exports from British Columbia to the US remain unaffected because these are trucked, there are growing concerns about the impact on frozen exports and the delivery of raw materials for feed.

Salmon feed inventory. Photo: Liza Mayer

Industry players told Undercurrent News that they are concerned about potential delays and congestion in the supply chain, highlighting the significance of the Port of Vancouver in the movement of seafood in and out of British Columbia. In 2022, the Port of Vancouver handled imports and exports of 208,933 metric tons of fish and other seafood.

"While we can't speculate on what the specific impacts may be (on the seafood trade), CAD 1 ($0.76) of every CAD 3 of Canada's trade in goods outside of North America moves through the Port of Vancouver so any disruption to port operations has a significant impact globally and on Canadians who rely on the businesses that import and export goods through the port for employment and for reliable access to the products that support each of us every day," the Port of Vancouver said in a statement to Undercurrent.   

Why dock workers are on strike

The International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) strike centers around fair wage increases and improved working conditions. However, shipping companies and terminal employers have been reluctant to meet the workers' demands, accusing them of being resistant to change and motivated by greed. These companies argue that legislation is necessary to enforce a return to work to safeguard the national economy.

However, a recent study by economist Jim Stanford -- cited by ILWU -- challenges that narrative. The study reveals that shipping companies and terminal operators have contributed to disruptions in Canada's economy and exacerbated inflation. It highlights that the six largest global shipping lines, all members of the BC Maritime Employers Association, control a staggering 70% of world shipping, giving them significant control over prices and practices.

Financial data from five of these companies show profits exceeding $100 billion in 2022, representing a remarkable 1,500% increase since 2019. In stark contrast, the study said that longshore base wages in British Columbia saw less than a 10% increase during the same period.

The shipping industry's soaring profitability has played a substantial role in global inflation, said the ILWU. Container shipping costs surged as the global economy reopened, and although container charges have moderated, overall shipping costs, including terminal fees, remain high. The Centre for Work report, cited by the ILWU, further supports the notion that labor is not the cause of rising costs and inflation but rather the "greed" of shippers and terminal operators who have exploited economic and health emergencies to maximize their profits.

In a statement on Monday (July 10), Rob Ashton, president of ILWU Canada, criticized the government for failing to intervene and impose fair contract terms on shipping companies. Ashton argues that it is hypocritical for the government to consider forcing longshore workers back to work while ignoring the exploitative practices of shipping companies and terminal operators. Terminal operators have taken advantage of the pandemic disruption to increase charges, further burdening the industry with higher costs, he said.

Despite having wages comparable to other skilled industrial jobs, longshore workers face unpredictable working schedules and periods of unemployment and must wait several years to qualify for benefits. In recent years, their wages have failed to keep up with British Columbia's high cost of living, resulting in a 2.5% decline in the real purchasing power of longshore salaries since 2017. Furthermore, their wage growth must catch up to the Canadian economy, said the union.

Undercurrent spoke to the Port of Vancouver Authority, the Canadian Aquaculture Industry Alliance, and Mowi and other members of the BC Salmon Farmers Association for this report.

title: OSHA formalizes alliance with New England immigrant group to protect seafood workers
content:
The US Department of Labor's Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) in the states of Massachusetts and Rhode Island have formalized an alliance with New England immigrant advocate group Centro Comunitario de Trabajadores, according to a statement issued by OSHA. 

The OSHA offices in Braintree, Massachusetts, and Providence, Rhode Island, signed the agreement on June 29 "to address workplace safety and health hazards the center's immigrant and low-wage workers in southern New England face" -- many in the seafood processing sector, according to the statement. 

In early June, OSHA sent a searing 14-page memo instructing officials to begin conducting "programmed inspections, emphasis programs and compliance assistance and training" at New England seafood processing operations and related merchant wholesaler operations, as Undercurrent News reported.

According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, seafood processors experience an injury and illness rate of 6.8 per 100 full-time equivalent employees, which is 2.5 times higher than the national average of 2.7. Incidents cataloged by the OSHA memo include a January 2019 incident in New Bedford when a processor was strangled when his jacket sleeve got caught in a rotating shaft, as well as a November 2019 incident when a cleaning company owner was killed in Braintree when he was trapped in a spiral freezer at an unnamed seafood processing company's plant after the hot water and steam cleaning cycle began. 

"The Centro Comunitario de Trabajadores' alliance with OSHA will help us reduce the number of workers injured on the job in the New Bedford area, including the many employed in the seafood processing industry," said Centro Comunitario de Trabajadores executive director Adrian Ventura. "The center looks forward to working with other area organizations to better inform our region's immigrant and low-wage workers and their employers about the importance of workplace safety and health."
